Cambodia’s real gross domestic product (GDP) growth was estimated at 4.8% in 2025 and 2026 projections are at 4.3%. The government’s rebasing of GDP made it 30% larger on average across years, so comparison and targets using old GDP figures need to be revisited. The Thai-Cambodia border conflict, rising trade restrictions and downturn in the real estate sector continues to threaten macroeconomic stability. The rights and inclusion of children, youth, adults, and older persons with disabilities were reaffirmed with the finalization of the third phase of the National Disability Strategic Plan (NSDP3) and an analysis of the national budget conducted in 2025 revealed a positive trend in government spending on disability–specific programming with allocations having doubled between 2020 and 2024. An independent assessment commissioned by the Ministry of Social Affairs, Veterans and Youth Rehabilitation (MoSVY) and funded by UNICEF, recommended maintaining the suspension of inter-country adoptions of children until robust safeguards and oversight mechanisms are in place and prioritize strengthening domestic adoption in line with international standards. The assessment found that while the legislative framework has improved, gaps remain in the enforcement and operationalization of laws and policies, particularly in relation to minimum standards for alternative care and adoption procedures.
Progress toward Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 continued, with participation in organized learning a year before primary school rising to 71.4% (71.9% boys, 70.9% girls) and completion rates improving across all levels —101.5% at primary, 60.3% lower secondary, and 38.5% upper secondary. Grade 5 proficiency increased from 27% to 39% in reading and 39% to 62% in math between 2019 and 2024). With UNICEF’s technical and financial support, teacher quality advanced through Early Grade Mathematics training as part of the Early Grade Learning (EGL) expansion. Equity for indigenous children was strengthened through UNICEF’s support in developing and launching the Multi-lingual Education Action Plan 2024-2028. Government leadership led to the establishment of Early Childhood Development (ECD) technical working groups in four provinces, along with the development of provincial ECD action plans, while UNICEF-supported Social and Behavior Change (SBC) initiatives engaged over 2 million people nationwide, helping boost community participation in early childhood development and education activities. 
Administrative data and evidence generated by UNICEF highlighted advances in legal and policy frameworks, alongside persistent protection gaps affecting children in conflict with the law, children without parental care, migrants, and those exposed to violence and abuse. The Juvenile Justice Law Assessment confirmed limited use of diversion and non-custodial measures, with diversion remaining at six per cent in 2025, reflecting continued reliance on detention and uneven access to legal aid and case management. The 2025 inspection of residential care facilities documented a 70 per cent reduction in the number of children living in institutions compared to 2015, although the decline has been slower for children with disabilities and for girls (53 per cent of children still living in institutions are girls). Physical violence against children remains widespread and largely tolerated, with reporting remaining low in line with previous years. Progress toward full prohibition of corporal punishment in all settings and online grooming through a new Child Protection Law continues to be constrained by bureaucratic processes.  
In 2025, the Ministry of Health launched the Health Strategic Plan 2025–2034, which positions health as a core pillar of human capital development under the Pentagonal Strategy and prioritizes progress toward Universal Health Coverage by 2035. The rotavirus vaccine was introduced this year, and the measles outbreak response reached 1,008,039 children (with 524,180 girls). Targeted efforts to reduce newborn mortality rate (NMR) continued with the introduction of a decentralized newborn care model, combining a blended clinical coaching model, enabling 8,251 sick newborns to receive intensive care closer to home. The neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at the National Maternal and Child Health Center (NMCHC) was strengthened with essential equipment and orientation and 149 health facilities across five vulnerable provinces were equipped with fetal dopplers and resuscitators, contributing to improved quality of maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) services.        
The government continued to implement key social protection measures in 2025, particularly family package social assistance programmes and other programmes for poor and at-risk households which benefited 90% of all ID Poor households (47% female headed households and 51% of Family Package cash recipients are female, 56,530 - out of which 29,326 are female - are persons with disabilities registered in the family package). The impact of the border conflict with Thailand led to influx of nearly one million returning migrants from Thailand and nearly half million internally displaced persons and with limited fiscal space and uncertainties of border conflicts, it is quite challenging for government to implement timely shock responsive social protection programmes. Similarly, with limited fiscal space, the government budget allocation for social sectors (education, health, social protection) continues to fall short of international benchmarks and could undermine Cambodia’s progress toward reaching Cambodian Sustainable Development Goals (CSDGs) and key targets in Pentagonal Strategy Phase 1. 
Cambodia’s WASH sector has evolved as reflected in 2025 WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Report with significant improvements in sanitation coverage—in 2025, 52% of the population have access to safely managed sanitation as compared to 36% in 2024, but there has been limited progress in access to safely managed water with 30% having access now as compared to 29% in 2024. Remaining gaps—most acute in rural and climate-vulnerable areas—have driven a strategic shift from access alone to climate-resilient services and solutions. Cambodia’s national climate framework centers children and social services in climate action. With sustained UNICEF advocacy, technical and financial support to the Ministry of Environment (MoE) climate-smart social sectors have been fully integrated into the Cambodia Climate Change Strategic Plan 2024–2033 (CCCSP/NAP) and nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) positioning the country as a global leader in child-sensitive, multisectoral climate adaptation. Cambodia’s climate agenda now prioritizes climate-smart social sectors, embedding climate risk into WASH, health, education, child and social protection planning, standards and financing. This positions essential services as frontline climate adaptation systems that protect children’s rights amid escalating climate risks.

In 2025, Cambodia’s education sector advanced significantly with UNICEF’s support for policy development, system strengthening, and inclusive programming. A major milestone was the launch of the Multilingual Education Action Plan 2024–2028, developed with strong indigenous community participation to promote linguistic diversity and inclusion. This was complemented by the review of the Gender Mainstreaming Strategic Plan, providing a robust evidence base for gender-responsive planning. The findings informed decision-making by guiding MoEYS and UNICEF to strengthen gender-responsive planning, integrate gender priorities into subnational action plans, and tailor capacity-building efforts—such as leadership development and positive discipline training—to better address school-related gender-based violence and advance gender-transformative outcomes. At the subnational level, UNICEF strengthened early childhood care and development (ECCD) governance by finalizing the Provincial Action Plan in Preah Vihear, conducting a situation analysis in Siem Reap, and training 85 provincial working group members in planning and results-based management. A new early childhood education costing tool was introduced to enable provinces to conduct evidence-based planning and strengthen budget advocacy by identifying resource needs and assessing the affordability of achieving universal five-year-old enrollment by 2030. Systemic improvements in teaching and learning were equally significant. UNICEF supported the rollout of an Early Grade Learning training package for Grades 1–3, benefiting over 9,500 teachers in six provinces, and Early Grade Mathematics training for 686 Grade 2 teachers. These large-scale capacity-building efforts directly contributed to improved learning outcomes, as reflected in the significant rise in Grade 5 reading and mathematics proficiency measured by the 2024 Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM). Teacher education reform progressed with the BA+1 progra
m in Mathematics and Physics and training for 696 teacher educators on the new Teacher Education Curriculum Framework and Professional Standards, helping align pre-service and in-service training with national competency standards and ensuring more consistent, higher-quality instruction nationwide. To equip adolescents with 21st-century skills, UNICEF expanded Local Life Skills Education and Volunteer for My Community programs nationwide, integrating them into pre-service teacher education curricula. To promote safe and protective learning environments, 2,821 school directors and teachers were trained on positive discipline and child protection, with a focus on preventing school-related gender-based violence. Quality early childhood education was strengthened through training 313 preschool teachers and distributing learning materials to 3,290 community preschools, including those in conflict-affected areas. Nurturing Care Parenting sessions reached 19,000 parents across 240 villages. A nationwide social and behavior change campaign engaged 3.5 million people and two million online users with gender-transformative messages challenging harmful norms and promoting positive role models. Collectively, these achievements strengthened education systems, improved teaching quality, and advanced equity and resilience, ensuring better learning opportunities for all children in Cambodia.
Guided by the 2022 UN CRC Concluding Observations and Cambodia’s SDG 16 and 5 targets, the child protection program made significant progress in strengthening national and subnational child protection systems. Using advocacy and technical leadership as key strategies, UNICEF linked evidence generation—largely supported by core resources—to legal reform, programme prioritization, and institutional capacity development across justice, alternative care, migration, climate resilience, and public finance for child protection. Particularly, UNICEF’s advocacy and technical guidance contributed to complete the interministerial revisions of  the child protection law retaining the provision on full prohibition of child marriage with no exceptions for girls aged 16 years as in the current legislation; and to developing subnational guidelines for child protection budgeting and to the appointment of two district-level social agents per district, accelerating diversion of children in conflict with the law. A study on children affected by cross-border migration between Cambodia and Thailand supported by the European Union through UNICEF, identified protection risks facing children in the context of migration, and informed the development of a bilateral MOU that spells out the roles and responsibilities of the two countries in the repatriation and reintegration process. UNICEF child protection team high-level advocacy efforts with Government, UN agencies and development partners, combined with technical advice to line ministries, resulted in the integration of child protection interventions into Cambodia’s Third Nationally Determined Contribution, including targets related to adaptation and strengthening the social service workforce for climate-responsive case management. This made Cambodia the first country ever to include child protection in its NDC. Further, UNICEF’s technical leadership facilitated excellent cross-sectoral collaboration, bringing the child protection, environme
nt, and disaster risk management sectors together for a three-day orientation on the role of the social service workforce in climate adaptation, strengthening system-wide coordination and resilience. Social Service Workforce professionalization advanced through the development of accreditation and licensing frameworks under a government directive (Prakas). In parallel, UNICEF provided ongoing technical oversight to social workers on the ground, enabling them to deliver quality case management and referral services to over 3,300 children at risk of abuse, neglect and physical and emotional violence. Additionally, district level social workers trained with UNICEF’s technical and financial support were able to provide Psychosocial First Aid to 3,289 children displaced by the Cambodia–Thailand border conflict, underscoring the critical role of the workforce in responding to emergencies. Complementing system-level work, three SBC flagship initiatives, namely the Positive Parenting program, Cambodia Protect, and the Pagoda Program involving Buddhist monks, reached collectively more than 30,000 people to challenge entrenched cultural norms that perpetuate violence against children, unnecessary family separation, and child marriage. By actively engaging families, youth, religious leaders, and local actors, these initiatives strengthened protective attitudes and practices, enhanced caregiver knowledge, and promoted gender-equitable norms directly contributing to safer environments for children and more resilient, informed communities.
UNICEF strengthened the enabling environment for maternal, child, and adolescent health and nutrition by supporting the Government to deliver key policy and systems milestones including the Fast Track Roadmap for Nutrition and the National Strategy for Food Security and Nutrition. UNICEF strengthened the national evidence base by completing a multisectoral Child and Adolescent Mental Health service mapping, overweight and obesity landscape analysis, and supporting the inclusion of children’s environmental health indicators in the 2024 Inter-censal Population Survey. The transition to DHIS2 was piloted in 260 health facilities across six provinces, preparing for national scale-up, and setting the foundation for more reliable data for decision-making and public health surveillance at all levels of the health system. Nutrition and vaccine supply chain and health care waste management assessments informed reforms, guidelines, and national strategies. Wasting treatment expanded to 756 health facilities and integrated nutrition/health messaging on social protection platforms reached 166,896 cash transfer recipients (85,807 pregnant women and 81,089 children under two of which 37,799 girls). UNICEF advocacy resulted in doubling government financing for Ready to Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) for 2026 and a 5% annual increase through 2030.. This marks a critical transition toward domestic financing and long-term sustainability for treatment of wasting. An additional decentralized newborn care model was established, enabling 8,251 sick newborns to receive intensive care closer to home including an integrated WASH, healthcare waste management, and solarization approach. Such climate-resilient measures were introduced in 50 health facilities, benefiting an estimated 280,000 children under 5. Immunization outcomes improved, with 12 of 17 zero-dose districts reaching at least 80% Penta-1 coverage, national coverage reaching 93% for DPT3 and 100% for MR-1, the measles outbreak respo
nse reaching 1,008,039 children, and the rotavirus vaccine successfully introduced. UNICEF deployed mobile health and nutrition teams to 26 displacement sites across three provinces in December 2025, providing critical services, including screening/treating 1,163 children for malnutrition, more than 20% of whom were acutely malnourished. UNICEF strengthened sub-national capacity to address barriers to care. Integrated SBC and community engagement approaches directly linked 790,981 people to essential services, including immunization, nutrition, and maternal care. Parenting and nurturing care participation increased by 47% to 52,625 caregivers, adolescent engagement reached 120,000 young people, and 1,460 frontline workers were trained in interpersonal communication. Child injury prevention advanced with a Safe School Zone guideline, survival swimming program, and nationwide road safety and drowning prevention campaigns reaching millions online. Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) efforts also supported measles outbreak response among affected communities and displaced populations, reaching 15,405 people (9,842 female) in 26 displacement sites.
In 2025, three major milestones were achieved in advancing social protection, nearly 490,623 children (female: 250,356) benefited from monthly cash transfers under Family Package Social Assistance, including 79,336 aged 0–2 years, 313,770 in primary school, 72,547 in lower secondary, and 24,970 in upper secondary, alongside 1,377 students with disabilities. The programme also supported 46,123 persons with disabilities and 5,753 people living with HIV/AIDS, while children in ID Poor and at-risk households continued accessing health equity funds. Second, UNICEF supported the rollout of a national social protection registration portal, enabling integrated registration and interoperability across Family Package, Disability Identification, and ID Poor systems—setting a new standard for coordinated, data-driven service delivery. The integrated portal reduces duplication, streamlines beneficiary identification, and accelerates access to entitlements. Third, the innovative Gender-Responsive Social Protection capacity-building initiative was successfully implemented nationwide, and the shock-responsive Family Package operational manual was finalized, pending government adoption. At sub-national level, the government adopted inter-ministerial circular 007 and treasury guideline 7221 to streamline social service, sanitation, and environment budgeting, enhancing equity and efficiency. Citizen participation and transparency improved through the launch of the Commune/Sangkat Budget Monitoring System and Cambodia conducted its first disability-inclusive budget and Official Development Assistance (ODA) review, adopting a monitoring tool for the National Disability Strategic Plan 2024–2028 and integrating a Disability Inclusion (DI) marker into the ODA database, following endorsement of the Amman-Berlin Global Declaration.
In 2025, UNICEF supported the government’s Decentralization and Deconcentration (D&D) reform and advanced system strengthening in three target provinces. Efforts focused on institutional capacity building, improving planning, budgeting, and monitoring, and promoting child-centric governance. Key achievements include the rollout of Rights and Results-Based Management (RRBM) training, with materials developed and 40 national-level professionals trained, creating a pool of experts. Training was extended to 90 professionals and 30 senior leaders in three provinces, with the National School of Local Administration identified as the lead partner for sustainability. UNICEF provided technical support for sub-national planning, including the formulation of investment programs for 2026–2028 to promote evidence-based, results-oriented, and child-rights focused plans. Work is ongoing to develop Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) action plans in two provinces and provincial monitoring dashboards to strengthen accountability. Youth engagement was deepened through structured youth–district governor dialogues, amplifying adolescent voices in local decision-making. A review of Subnational Administration (SNA) investment programs is underway to inform 2026 actions and advocacy, ensuring investments increasingly reflect the rights and needs of children and adolescents.
For the first time, Cambodia’s national climate framework places children and social services at the centre of climate action, positioning the country as a global frontrunner in child-sensitive climate action. Through sustained UNICEF support to the Ministry of Environment, climate-smart social sectors were fully integrated into the Cambodia Climate Change Strategic Plan 2024–2033 and NDC 3.0 and positions Cambodia as a global leader in child-sensitive, multisectoral adaptation. Youth engagement underpinned this shift, with 111 young people co-developing the sub-national Children’s Climate Risk Index (CCRI) and 175 supporting NDC 3.0 through Local Conference of Youth (LCOY) 2025. Using the CCRI, 401 sub-national officials and community members in seven high-risk provinces strengthened understanding of child-specific climate risks. As a result, 20 of the highest-risk communes developed risk-informed, child-centered climate action plans embedded in three-year rolling investment plans. WASH results demonstrate how targeted investments in data, standards and financing translate into measurable gains for children. To address fragmented evidence on service quality, UNICEF led the national consultation and launched the updated Joint Monitoring Plan (JMP) country file, strengthening SDG 6 monitoring. A structural shift from access to safety followed, with water-quality testing integrated for the first time into the Cambodia Socio-Economic Survey. A major WASH financing gap in health care facilities (HCF) was addressed through a costed national WASH-in-HCF roadmap (2025–2030) and climate-resilient design standards, enabling prioritized investment. Capacity was strengthened through Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) in 15 facilities across four provinces, while menstrual health and hygiene modules were rolled out in 26 schools. UNICEF also advanced climate-resilient WASH financing and market-shaping efforts, strengthening the mobilization of 
private capital for climate-resilient water systems. Performance assessments of private water operators informed regulatory reform, while investment readiness support and impact-investor engagement aim at catalyzing concessional lending. This directly influenced the approval of the Water Infrastructures and Smart Energy (WISE) United Nations Joint Programme—Cambodia’s first blended-finance facility for climate-resilient water and renewable energy—mobilizing private capital for solar-powered water systems. Direct results include 58,074 people gaining climate-resilient, safely managed water services, and 28,954 gaining safely managed sanitation. Climate-smart investments—solarization of 49 health facilities, decentralized wastewater treatment, and solar systems in schools—reduced service disruptions during climate shocks. Emergency WASH support also reached conflict-affected communities, with recovery expanding to 30,000 people.
UNICEF continued to lead the United Nations in Cambodia Task Team for Protection of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (UNCT PSEA Task Team) and provided technical guidance for the rollout of the Interagency PSEA SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) to government partners. Ninety-five percent of government ministries working with UN agencies, including all institutions partnering with UNICEF, were reached through two orientation sessions, which resulted in the development of action plans to prevent and respond to SEA across UN-funded programs and fostered a common understanding among government of the PSEA zero-tolerance policy, while ensuring alignment with national legislations and code of conducts. Due to the cross-border conflict in the second part of the year, the Country Office (CO) intensified awareness raising efforts on SEA safe reporting channels, reaching more than 67,000 people across the country.
UNICEF reinforced its position as a leading voice for children and youth in Cambodia through integrated online and offline communication and public advocacy strategies. Leveraging a digital-first approach and robust media engagement, the CO secured over 300 UNICEF mentions across more than 20 major national and international outlets. In 2025, the CO launched four new high-impact campaigns and sustained five ongoing public communication initiatives, influencing parents to adopt positive practices for their children and influencing policymakers and the private sector to invest in child-centered, climate-resilient essential services. These efforts were supported by compelling multimedia storytelling, which positioned UNICEF Cambodia’s website as a leading platform on child rights with over 190,000 unique visitors in 2025. Digital engagement reached unprecedented levels, with social media overall reach exceeding 22.8 million, and the follower base growing by 19% to 688,800. Through multi-channel storytelling, and strategic alliances, UNICEF Cambodia delivered impactful child rights content, forging new partnerships with celebrities, content creators, youth networks, media, and the public-private sector. Strategic events, including World Children’s Day in Preah Vihear, mobilized over 15,000 participants and highlighted UNICEF’s ability to meaningfully engage youth on child rights in hard-to-reach areas. During the Cambodia–Thailand border crisis, the CO implemented a rapid emergency communication strategy to counter misinformation and build public trust. The CO pioneered local fundraising through an Urgent Appeal campaign, raising over $15,000 from individuals, $100,000 from private sector donors, and $1 million via public partnerships. CO advanced on Child Right Business efforts with Chambers of Commerce, including formalizing the partnership with the European Chamber of Commerce to promote responsible business practices, advocate for child rights and child lens investm
ent and jointly promote campaigns.
UNICEF advanced Government implementation of the National Action Plan for Early Childhood Care Development (NAP-ECCD) 2022–2026, building on last year’s mid-term review by supporting the finalization of Operational Guidelines for province-specific ECCD plans, known as Provincial Action Plans (PAPs), to accelerate implementation across 25 provinces. Governance and planning capacity were strengthened through training of 85 Provincial Women and Children Consultative Committee (PWCCC) members and ECCD Working Groups (22 women) on PAP-ECCD development and Results-Based Management (RBM), ensuring alignment with child rights principles. Evidence-based ECD planning was strengthened by integrating the ECD Index 2030 and Child Functioning Modules into the upcoming 2026 Cambodia Demographic and Health Survey (CDHS). These modules, absent in the previous round, will enable comprehensive measurement of cognitive, socio-emotional, and language development, improve monitoring of child related SDGs, and guide targeted investments for inclusive ECD services and inform development of the next NAP-ECCD (2027-2030). Financing capacity for ECD improved through the introduction of an Early Childhood Education (ECE) costing tool and a provincial simulation model, enabling provinces to assess affordability and advocate for universal five-year-old enrollment by 2030. Efforts towards institutionalization and sustainable financing of village health support groups (VHSGs) continued through the ongoing development of Operational Guidelines for Community Participation in Health. These guidelines, expected to be finalized in 2026, will include costing frameworks to enable Government to assess affordability and advocate for integration into national and subnational plans and budgets.
Integrated SBC interventions directly engaged 1,585,940 vulnerable children and families (61% female) in reflective dialogue to shift harmful norms—such as low parental engagement in early learning and tolerance of harsh discipline—while improving access to essential services. These efforts contributed to stronger caregiver engagement and increased uptake of ECD and parenting services. In addition, a new ECD multimedia campaign launched in October 2025 reached over 5 million people nationwide, further reinforcing positive caregiving practices and demand for early childhood development services. Partners, including six government ministries and five Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), are increasingly adopting advanced ECD and SBC approaches. These include nurturing care parenting based on the Nurturing Care Framework, and Minimum Quality Standards for Community Engagement, complemented by innovative SBC tools such as Human-Centered Design, interpersonal communication skills, feedback mechanisms, and behavioural nudges to promote behaviour change. Capacity-building initiatives strengthened SBC skills for 135 government officials across sectors (61 women) and 34 CSO staff (12 women), while 1,952 ECD frontline workers (55% females) acquired interpersonal communication skills to deliver inclusive ECD services. Integrated parenting sessions reached 52,625 parents and caregivers (35% men), and the Parenting Chatbot engaged 8,191 caregivers, including 45% men, fostering greater participation and demand for ECD and positive parenting services.
UNICEF Cambodia advanced gender-transformative outcomes by translating evidence into action across sectors. Girls’ leadership and visibility were elevated through digital and Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) initiatives, most notably with adolescent girls-led teams winning four out of seven categories at UNICEF’s global Game Jam demonstrating girls’ innovation potential on an international stage. Girls’ meaningful participation was also strengthened in sensitive and high-impact areas such as child marriage prevention, where adolescent girls influenced programme design and evidence generation. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened gender responsiveness within the social protection system by building the capacity of 142 national and sub-national policymakers and service providers (28 female) through gender-responsive social protection training. Together, these efforts contributed to shifting gender norms, creating visible role models for girls, and fostering more inclusive systems that expand girls’ agency, resilience, and opportunities.
UNICEF has steadily increased the meaningful participation of adolescents in all aspects of programming in Cambodia and a total of 242,334 adolescents, 54% of them girls, including those with disability and ethnic minority, participated in or led UNICEF-supported programmes.  Programme results include 411,287 scholarships for grades 1–12 (52% girls), helping poor children stay in school; over 90,000 nine-year-old girls receiving HPV vaccinations; and strengthened child-marriage prevention efforts led by 298 adolescents and youth (241 female), including AYRG members, addressing harmful gender and social norms. Young people influenced commune planning and budgeting, contributed to national climate policy including Cambodia’s NDC 3.0, and engaged in structured social innovation platforms such as Generation Future. Together, these results reflect a scalable, integrated model that institutionalizes youth participation within public systems while strengthening the pipeline from skills development to civic leadership.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, key capacity development initiatives, including the Teacher Qualification Upgrade program and new Continuous Professional Development (CPD) courses, were delayed due to extensive assessments and prioritization of training needs. Border conflict with Thailand further disrupted ECCD action plans and Nurturing Care Parenting sessions. Policy dialogues provided critical lessons: the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) Compact Mid-Term Review reaffirmed UNICEF’s leadership in aligning partner support with MoEYS reforms and mobilizing resources. At the subnational level, budget advocacy proved most effective when paired with capacity-building and evidence-based planning using tools like the ECE costing model, which enabled provinces to quantify resource gaps and strengthen evidence-based budget requests for the ECE sub-sectors. Looking ahead, UNICEF will accelerate teacher education reforms including strengthening gender equality in teacher training, expand inclusive education, and strengthen ECCD governance to build a resilient, equitable education system. UNICEF will continue engagement with the GPE to support MoEYS in advancing key education reforms and programmes. In parallel, in its role as Coordinating Agency, UNICEF will lead the application process for the upcoming GPE funding round (GPE 2030), in close collaboration with MoEYS and key development partners and also explore opportunities to strengthen private sector engagement in GPE initiatives to maximize the financial and programmatic impact on educational outcomes.
The child protection program faced several constraints that affected results in some areas. Notably, the suspension of USAID funding required careful re-prioritization and strategic use of core resources to advance key priorities. Ongoing public administration reforms offered opportunities to strengthen institutional capacity but also caused delays in decision-making, affecting processes such as the finalization of the Child Protection Law and the appointment of additional provincial social workers. Blurred mandates among institutions slowed coordination, particularly on the violence against children (VAC) and GBV agenda and led to inconsistent response and accountability pathways. Also, the cross-border conflicts since July diverted resources and efforts from regular programming. Moving forward, UNICEF will use these lessons to refine contingency strategies, and strengthen partnerships, particularly with the private sector, to sustain impact for every child.
Malnutrition prevention and identification are lagging due to limited provision of growth monitoring and causes such as maternal nutrition not being addressed systematically. Data quality gaps and the complexity of multisectoral coordination persist, particularly for emerging priorities, such as mental health. The suspension of funds such as those from the U.S. government created gaps the health sector, while the border crisis disrupted implementation and exacerbated inequalities. Priorities for the coming year include advancing decentralized newborn care, childhood NCDIs and disability in PHC, evidence-generation on children’s environmental health, and the nutrition–climate nexus. UNICEF will continue focusing on strengthening supply chains, information systems, and workforce capacity to improve equitable health outcomes.
The WASH programme demonstrated adaptive and agile management in advancing climate resilient results, despite limited and increasingly constrained resources. What worked was a strong focus on systems strengthening—data, standards and financing—allowing scarce resources to catalyze scale (including leveraging private sector) and better targeting the most marginalized children. Evidence-based planning enabled course correction and sub-national prioritization. Key challenges remain persistent service-quality gaps, fragmented financing, and funding constraints that limit direct service delivery. Building on these lessons, the office will further sharpen climate-smart social sector strategies, leverage partnerships and innovative financing, and use its convening role to maximize impact beyond UNICEF resources, ensuring children furthest behind are reached first. 
Social protection remains a priority in the pentagonal strategy phase 1 (PS1) and gradual progress and expansion is being made toward achieving targets; however,  current transfer values are insufficient to offset rising cost-of-living pressure and recurrent emergencies. With limited fiscal space, the government prioritizes public expenditure on targeted and priority programmes set in the PS1 and those critical for reforms. At sub-national level, the fiscal space continues to exist though not sufficient to meet the increasing demand; thus, there is a need to look at efficiency and shape the direction of sub-national budget toward national priorities. Significant capacity gaps in result-based planning and budgeting continue to exist signaling the need to increase investment in RRBM capacity building. 
The surge of online misinformation during the border conflict with Thailand significantly heightened reputational risks for UNICEF. With funding in decline, maintaining communication capacities will be critical to safeguard the CO’s ability to implement effective emergency communication strategies in volatile contexts, while also meeting the growing demand for local fundraising through targeted online and offline marketing campaigns. 
In 2026, UNICEF Cambodia will deepen private sector engagement across health, nutrition, education, WASH, child protection, social policy and climate action. Through youth empowerment putting adolescent girls in the center, digital transformation, innovative finance, and the promotion of child rights and gender equality and responsible business practices, UNICEF Cambodia will scale cross-sectoral solutions delivering equitable and sustainable results for children and young people nationwide. UNICEF and the Ministry of Environment will collaborate to develop Cambodia’s first proposal to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage under the Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM). The partnership will combine UNICEF’s technical expertise in child-centred, climate-resilient social services with the Ministry’s leadership on national loss and damage priorities and international climate finance.
In 2026, UNICEF jointly with the Royal Government of Cambodia (RGC) will finalize two ongoing initiatives to respond to the 2022 concluding observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC). First, completion of a Child Rights Budget Analysis to generate evidence and provide actionable recommendations for strengthening the adequacy, equity, and efficiency of public spending to achieve better outcomes for every child. The country is in the process of implementing its Pentagonal Strategy Phase 1 2023-2028, new five-year National Strategic Development Plan (NSDP) 2024-2028 and Neary Rattanak (gender equality and women’s empowerment) VI Strategic Plan (2024-2028). This period at mid-term presents a window of opportunity to ensure that children are placed at the heart of the country's development and fiscal agenda. The 2022 Concluding Observations from the CRC specifically recommended that the RGC increases resource allocations for children, leveraging public financial management (PFM) reforms to track spending and assess the distributional impacts of investment. Second, finalization of the assessment on Cambodia’s readiness to ratify Optional Protocol on Communications Procedure (OPIC) is expected to contribute to the Government’s commitment in this area and will inform the development of a Road Map toward ratification, to be jointly developed with national stakeholders and young people. Building on the consultations conducted through the Review, UNICEF will support the strengthening of young people’s capacity to advocate for ratification, including through the co-creation of age-appropriate and gender-responsive communication materials and a targeted advocacy plan on both the CRC Concluding Observations and OPIC.

China has the world’s second-largest child population, with an estimated child population of 298 million, accounting for 21.1% of the total population in 2020.[1] The country is experiencing a profound demographic transition that has significant impacts on children and their families. The number of births has been continuously decreasing since 2016, with only 7.92 million born in 2025. The population is also ageing quickly, with 23% of the population aged 60 years and older in 2025. In 2025, the Government of China (GoC) introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy programme, offering 3,600 yuan per year for each child under the age of three, as part of broader efforts to support families. 

China is confronted with the realities of ensuring balanced development, especially in western and central regions. The regional disparities pose an obstacle to ensuring adequate public expenditure for children. China eliminated absolute rural poverty in 2020, but efforts are needed to strengthen the social protection system. In 2025, the GoC issued the Opinions on Further Strengthening Welfare Protection for Children in Difficult Situations, which aims to enhance welfare protection for children through scientific classification and precise identification of needs and strengthening support systems.

Rapid urbanization in China, accompanied by massive internal migration, has resulted in approximately half the child population impacted by migration. Many migrant children have inadequate access to quality services, while children left behind primarily in the care of grandparents face multiple vulnerabilities. Recent reforms to the hukou system seek to address access issues.

Challenges remain in providing accessible, affordable, quality healthcare services in remote areas and among vulnerable groups. This is particularly so at the community level, where health facilities need to improve management of high-risk pregnancies and the quality of maternal health and nutrition services. 

Gaps remain in service provision for the care of children under 6. Responsive caregiving, one of the most fundamental elements for optimal early childhood development (ECD), requires further expansion. 

Maternal mental health problems are receiving increased attention with data indicating 16.3% of mothers experience symptoms of depression and anxiety during the perinatal period,[2] whilst lack of awareness contributes to low levels of access to mental healthcare. 

China still has challenges with overweight children and maternal anaemia. The rate of overweight (including obesity) in school-aged children (aged 6–17 years) has increased sharply, to 19% in 2017.[3] Micronutrient deficiencies, particularly anaemia, persist and are more prevalent among young children under the age of 2 years and pregnant and breastfeeding women,[4] especially in the western rural areas and among ethnic minority groups.

To achieve universal provision of high-quality preschool education, more effort is needed to enhance the capacity of teachers and bridge urban-rural and regional gaps. In 2025, the Preschool Education Law came into effect, which aims to strengthen ECD’s sustainable development. The Opinions on Gradually Implementing Free Preschool Education sets out framework for gradually making preschool free nationwide and mandated that childcare and education fees for the final year of preschool in public kindergartens waived nationwide starting from the autumn semester of 2025. 

Particularly in rural areas, some adolescents and youth in technical and vocational education and training schools are not acquiring sufficient transferable skills. Adolescents in rural areas are lagging behind their urban peers, with an attendance rate of only 58.2% for 19-year-old adolescents living in rural areas.[5] In 2025, the GoC released the Action Plan for Revitalizing County-Level General Upper Secondary Education to promote high-quality, more equitable development of senior high school education in county areas.

Not all children are learning in protective school environments; children attending rural and boarding schools are often at risk. Cases of violence underscore the need for stricter oversight and accountability at schools and better linkages with child protection services. The availability of mental health resources is uneven, particularly in rural or underfunded schools. In 2025, the GoC issued the Ten Measures to Further Strengthen Mental Health Work for Primary and Secondary Students to reduce psychological pressure and improve mental resilience among students. 

Lack of nationally representative data on violence against children, including online violence, hinders policy development. Eliminating violence against children remains an important priority. Crimes against children have been rising, and children face increased exposure to online risks and potential harms. 

The number of children in alternative care has decreased significantly over the past decade, yet 144,000 orphaned children remain in alternative care, including 38,000 in residential facilities and 105,000 in kinship and foster care.[6] A large proportion of abandoned children living in residential care (i.e. child welfare institutions) have severe disabilities or serious illnesses.[7] Support to vulnerable families need to be further strengthened to prevent family separation.

China is consolidating a preventive and responsive child protection system at the national and subnational level. Safe mechanisms for reporting violence against children, supporting child victims of violence and referring cases to specialized services and the child justice system require further strengthening in terms of making these services more child-friendly and reducing geographical disparities in access. In 2025, the GoC issued Opinions on Strictly Punishing and Preventing Sexual Crimes Against Minors According to Law, which aims at enhancing both punishment and prevention of sexual violence and other related crimes against minors. 

China places a high priority on addressing climate related threats, particularly environmental threat adaptation for vulnerable groups such as children, such as the recurrent floods in the Yangtze basin, and strives to strengthen health outcomes and interventions for children faced with climate change challenges. 

Disparities between girls and boys in child development have decreased due to evolving policies, legislation, family structure and social values. While overt discrimination against girls and women in accessing public resources and opportunities has diminished, biases within families and communities still impact the potential of both girls and boys.

Significant gaps exist in data for monitoring the country’s progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.  By 2025, global databases contained internationally comparable data for China for only 26 (or 59%) of 44 child-related indicators applicable to China context.[8] 

China’s new Country Programme Document (CPD) for 2026-2030 has been approved by the UNICEF Executive Board in September 2025. Recognizing the status of China as an upper-middle-income country and given its transition towards high-income status, the new country programme, starting in January 2026, was designed with a gradual exit strategy.

Overall Programme Engagement in 2025 
2025 marks the final year of the GoC-UNICEF Country Programme for 2021-2025 with continued partnerships for realizing the rights of vulnerable girls and boys with 31 implementing partners across 31 provinces/autonomous regions/municipalities implemented through pilot programmes which served to illustrate programming that go to scale and areas for policy change. Together with our partners, with nationwide coverage, UNICEF helped strengthen services for children, generated evidence and supported policy reforms across health, education, child protection, social policy, building on and forging new partnerships including engaging in South-South and Triangular Cooperation (SSTC) to advance shared development priorities. Programmes increasingly emphasized equality focusing on Western and Central regions, inclusion and climate-resilient services with tested models at provincial level that informed national frameworks. These efforts contributed to responsive child related services and improved outcomes for children, while laying the foundation for the 2026-2030 country programme.

Child Health and Development
UNICEF advances child development by strengthening health systems, scaling nutrition interventions, and building capacity nationwide to ensure equitable, quality care and healthier futures for children and families. 

UNICEF supported the establishment of 161 provincial and county-level Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) centres of excellence. More than 900,000 health professionals have enhanced capacity to practice EENC after studying the online course from 2023 to 2025. UNICEF provided technical inputs to the multi-sectoral fertility-friendly health facilities initiative. Over 700 maternal nutrition counselling trainers, including 420 from 6 western and central provinces, were certified to provide comprehensive periconceptional nutrition counseling and interventions. The UNICEF-supported EENC national guidelines were released for nationwide application China.

The adolescent mental health programme organized 1,377 training sessions for 2,019 facilitators and 3,730 adolescent peer supporters (including 1,704 girls). The mental health service package reached 94,333 students across 10 provinces, including 27,540 from 4 central and western provinces. On the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B (EMTCT), UNICEF supported 9 provincial EMTCT validations and the training for 40 community-based organizations. The school-based road safety education package reached 99,225 students from 97 schools in 3 western provinces, where a UNICEF-supported road risk assessment mechanism involving education, health, and traffic authorities was established. 

The Early Childhood Development (ECD) scale-up efforts supported 8.88 million services in person-times[1] that benefited 1.08 million children aged 0-3 in 192 counties of 30 provinces. Over 24,000 community workers from 1,958 township health centers and 17,773 village clinics are now able to deliver quality ECD services and encourage father engagement in caregiving. UNICEF also directly supported capacity-building of frontline health workers in 6 western and central provinces to support children at risk of developmental delay. Assessment results reported in 2025 showed that the UNICEF-supported Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) Counselling programme increased caregivers’ access to services from 15% to 78% between 2021 and 2024. 

UNICEF supported the Nutrient Profiling (NP) Model application through schools and restaurants. More than 26,500 students benefited from the school-based traffic-light food labelling pilot project in Zhejiang, which informed the development of national guidelines on in-school food retailing. UNICEF provided technical advice to China National Center for Food Safety Risk Assessment in piloting child-friendly menu labelling that was scaled to over 1,700 stores in 13 provinces. Over 710,000 students (340,000 girls) attained knowledge on ‘know-how to eat healthily’ after attending the nutrition classes, while the healthy diet online knowledge hub was launched for children and caregivers. By December, 119 companies were certified as Family Friendly Workplace after adopting UNICEF-supported policies, which have benefited more than 1.21 million employees.

The UNICEF-supported Children’s Environmental Health (CEH) portal, China’s first CEH data and advocacy knowledge hub, was launched. UNICEF and Ministry of Environment and Ecology (MEE) jointly developed CEH guidelines. The climate change education tools co-developed with UNICEF were piloted with 42,225 students (20,186 girls) across 16 schools from 11 provinces. Furthermore, UNICEF and MEE signed an MOU to advance child-focused climate action, youth engagement, and South-South cooperation. The MOU was signed during COP30 in Brazil, where MEE endorsed the global declaration on children, youth and climate action.

Through high-level advocacy UNICEF obtained Chinese government’s commitment to support UNICEF’s ongoing SSTC initiatives on child health, including strengthening of emergency preparedness capacity of Africa CDC, and establishment of maternal and child health medical centers in Ethiopia, Nigeria and Mozambique.
 
Education
UNICEF drives inclusive, quality education by scaling early learning, strengthening teacher capacity, and promoting life skills, digital literacy, and gender-responsive STEM to empower children and adolescents nationwide.

The community-based family support and responsive care model for children aged 0–6 has been scaled up to 613 villages/communities, with 85% of ECD centers now funded by local governments and UNICEF providing technical assistance. This approach has reached 269,000 caregivers and 258,000 children (approximately 50% are girls) across 18 provinces with sustainable funding from local governments. 

Through an online scenario-based assessment system developed by UNICEF and the Open University, 30,000 pre-school teachers in 23 counties had their competencies assessed. Targeted training was delivered by county-level institutions whose capacities were strengthened. The assessment tool will be rolled out to other provinces and scaled nationally in the coming two years by UNICEF and MoE. 

UNICEF facilitated the expansion of inclusive preschool education from 37 to 930 kindergartens in 2025 to test a scalable inclusive education model, directly benefiting 18,500 teachers (90 percent female) and 130,000 girls and boys.  At the national level, China’s first-ever online teachers training courses on inclusive education were launched on Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) and teacher training platforms, attracting over 1 million views in the first month. In basic education, the inclusive education model now operates in 1,000+ schools, reaching 80,000 teachers and principals and 1 million students (50 percent girls) including 10,000 students with special educational needs. These results informed the review of Inclusive Education policies in Henan, Sichuan, and Shandong, helping to identify gaps and integrate evidence into provincial plans to scale best practices and guide national inclusive education implementation. 

Guided by the Life Skills, Social and Emotional Competency, and Digital Education Competency frameworks, 1.04 million children and adolescents strengthened their transferable, digital and green skills through various intervention projects. The life skills project expanded to 139 vocational schools in 20 provinces, with 10 curriculum sets featured on the National Smart Vocational Education Platform. The social and emotional learning replicated its whole-school approach in 485 schools across 8 provinces, supported by a large-scale survey of 800,000 students (50 percent girls) and 60,000 teachers (70 percent female).  The survey was on students’ social and emotional competency and skills and contributed to the establishment of the country’s largest database to strengthen evidence base, inform policy and guide programmatic interventions for scaling up social and emotional learning.  

UNICEF supported delivery of two gender-responsive STEM Project Based Learning (PBL) packages, strengthening the skills of 10,000 students, with an equal number of girls, across 568 pilot rural schools. The STEM4Girls Camps demonstrated success in advancing girls’ confidence in STEM and inspiring their career aspirations. Through the GenU green entrepreneurship initiative, mobilized 3,000 youth (51 percent girls) and accelerated the growth of 50 green startups. With UNICEF support, the Guidelines for Child Protection in Schools were finalized, including self-assessment indicators and case studies, based on international comparative research and piloted in 72 schools. Eleven research projects on teacher trainer competencies were completed, and Quality Monitoring Indicator Systems for High School and Preschool are progressing, which are planned to be replicated across the system.  

Under the SSTC strategy, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education and the National Center for Education Technology in hosting a study tour for officials from 15 countries, including 10 African nations. Additionally, the Global Gateways dashboard, developed with UNICEF support, will be launched jointly with UNESCO next year.
 
Child Protection
UNICEF has worked closely with national partners to strengthen China’s child protection system through legislative reform, evidence generation, integrated service models, and workforce development. These efforts aim to create a more responsive and inclusive system that safeguards the rights and well-being of all children, particularly the most vulnerable.

Legal reform has been a cornerstone of this work. UNICEF supported the National People’s Congress on studies that informed proposed changes to the Criminal Code on child online abuse and trafficking, contributed legislative input on regulating digital platforms, and offered recommendations to strengthen the criminal justice system. A landmark international seminar on criminal procedural law brought together over 150 experts from multiple countries, fostering cross-sectoral exchanges and generating insights that will guide future reforms.  UNICEF partnered with the tech industry to develop case studies on online safety, promoting learning on safety-by-design practices, and piloted a civil society-led Child Online Protection Hotline to respond to emerging risks.

To build child-friendly justice UNICEF helped the Ministry of Public Security operationalize “one-stop” service centers for child victims of sexual abuse in six pilot sites, training 60 police officers on dealing with these cases and protect child rights. Through civil society, a network of 51 pro bono juvenile lawyers was mobilized to expand specialized legal aid for children. UNICEF also documented innovative models developed by local prosecutors on community-based support for juvenile offenders and assistance for victims, providing practical insights to inform provincial and national policy guidance.

At the service delivery level, UNICEF advanced the second phase of the Integrated Child Protection Model with the Ministry of Civil Affairs, consolidating county-level systems in 16 counties across six provinces and reaching 156,412 vulnerable children (72,866 girls and 83,546 boys). Primero, a digital case management system, became operational in 16 counties and made referral and service delivery more efficient. Planning for the next phase is underway, with a focus on expanding to western and central areas and connecting services across levels to ensure comprehensive protection and a continuum of service. Care reform remained key in advocacy and capacity building, aiming for stronger gatekeeping measures to prevent unnecessary family separation and ensure family-based care. Positive parenting programs scaled up in 22 counties across nine provinces benefited 200,000 caregivers through school outreach, reducing violent discipline as seen in the study on effectiveness of parenting programmes completed in 2025. Collaboration with the tech industry amplified this impact, reaching over one million caregivers online.

Through multi-sectoral workshops and consultations, UNICEF and the China Disabled Persons’ Federation promoted disability inclusion and children’s rights in implementing the Law on the Construction of Barrier-free Environments, leveraging judicial mechanisms to reinforce legal protections and child-friendly spaces.

UNICEF also invested in building a skilled workforce. Standards for school social work, competency frameworks, and social investigation protocols were supported. Training reached: 80 justice social workers and 20 police officers trained on child rights and psychosocial support; 124 frontline workers trained in case management with 4,696 online participants; 40 senior social workers enhanced supervision skills and implemented a sustainable mechanism for follow-up in 8 provinces; and 947 child directors and civil affairs officials equipped to cascade knowledge regionally. The online training platforms for social workers continued operating, reaching a total of 246,847 (56,670 in 2025) professionals and paraprofessionals by the end of 2025.Together, these initiatives tell a story of progress, of laws informed by evidence, services integrated and scaled, justice made child-friendly, and families empowered, laying the foundation for a stronger, more inclusive child protection system in China.

Through SSTC exchanges, child protection global practices enriched national counterparts’ understanding in areas such as integrated child protection models, digital case management and child friendly justice systems. This included study tours to Italy and Croatia to expose partners to international standards and best practices.

Social Policy
UNICEF contributed to strengthened national capacity to reduce multidimensional child poverty, expand inclusive social protection, improve equitable access to essential services, and advance child- and family-responsive public finance, governance and care systems. UNICEF’s strategy focused on generating high-quality evidence, strengthening institutional frameworks, and translating analysis into policy and system-level change.

UNICEF enhanced the national evidence base on child poverty by initiating collaboration with the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey covering over 5,000 children. Through technical advice on child-sensitive indicators and analytical use of CFPS data, UNICEF is updating China’s Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) to identify trends, inequities, and systemic bottlenecks affecting children’s wellbeing. High-level policy dialogues convened with national stakeholders supported the use of this evidence to inform poverty reduction strategies and policy refinement. In parallel, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Civil Affairs (MCA) to assess the feasibility of applying artificial intelligence in social assistance systems, laying the groundwork for piloting and potential national scale-up to improve targeting, efficiency, and access for vulnerable populations.

UNICEF supported national and local partners to strengthen an integrated social protection system responsive to children’s multidimensional risks. The UNICEF–MCA Cash Plus initiative was expanded to ten additional pilot areas, reaching over 2,000 low-income children with combined cash and service support, and generating operational evidence for service-oriented social assistance reform. UNICEF provided analytical input and policy advice to MCA and key institutions, including National Healthcare Security Administration (NHSA), National Health Commission (NHC), and National People’s Congress (NPC), contributing to deliberations on the Social Assistance System Law, healthcare security reforms, and effective implementation of the nationwide childcare subsidy policy. Strategic collaboration with the China Association for Social Security (CAOSS), a social protection leading think tank was further institutionalized through efforts in joint research, a biennial social assistance forum and policy dialogue. This partnership informed legislation reform, financing models for children, and implementation of child-sensitive social protection policies. Joint work with the ILO mapped social protection programmes against life-cycle risks, identifying coverage gaps and informing technical dialogue on contributory, non-contributory, and shock-responsive schemes.

UNICEF supported national and subnational governments to expand inclusive urban and public service delivery. The Child-Friendly Cities (CFC) initiative was scaled to 116 cities, covering one-third of all cities and potentially benefiting 110 million children. Systematic policy reviews, technical guides, and joint assessments strengthened the CFC framework targeting government bodies such as NHC, National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), Ministry of Finance (MOF), for nationwide scaling. Participatory advocacy also engaged 2,000 children across 40 cities, strengthening child participation in local governance. UNICEF provided technical assistance to the development of the 15th Five Year Plan, including on Basic Public Services, prioritizing migrant children and other underserved groups. UNICEF advanced care economy research and commenced national engagement in the Environmental Social Governance (ESG) space through systematic analysis and dialogue where UNICEF engaged with national and local government authorities, regulators (stock exchange), investors, industry associations, think tanks and other international organizations, positioning childcare and care services as investable social infrastructure that delivers child outcomes, gender equality, and sustainable growth.

In partnership with the MOF, UNICEF supported evidence-based fiscal policy development for childcare, health, employment, and family support. Joint reviews of childcare financing informed the introduction of new national childcare subsidies in 2025, backed by RMB 90 billion annually. UNICEF also supported cost-effectiveness analysis in primary healthcare, international expenditure benchmarking, and research on high-quality and full employment contributing to the 15th Five-Year Employment Plan. Through OECD exchanges and a new partnership with the State Tax Administration, UNICEF advanced family-friendly fiscal and tax policies. Joint advocacy with UN partners strengthened the evidence base for integrated care systems as a driver to support government economic policy.
 
Partnership and Engagement
Public Partnerships Section
In support of South-South and Triangular Cooperation and resource mobilization, UNICEF significantly strengthened its partnerships with key Chinese government entities such as Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), China International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA) and national think tanks such as Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation (CAITEC) and with Member States—particularly those on the Executive Board—and China-based Multilateral Development Banks and policy banks. Engagements at major inter-governmental cooperation platforms, including Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), Boao Forum, China International Import Expo (CIIE), and the Canton Fair, were enhanced. 

By year end, UNICEF mobilized over USD 20 million from public partners. This included USD 1.55 million in Regular Resources, USD 0.7 million in triangular cooperation funds; USD 16.3 million from CIDCA for projects in Zimbabwe, Sierra Leone, Myanmar, Malawi, Djibouti, and Gaza; USD 1.5 million from China EXIM Bank for Bangladesh; and USD 40,000 from the Chinese Embassy in Burundi. 

Multi-year MOUs were signed with China EXIM Bank to expand the partnership on social impact projects including in Asia and Africa, especially on climate resilient WASH, and with the Alliance of Chinese Business in Africa for Social Responsibility (ACBASR) on corporate social responsibility, renewable energy for social sectors and bridging the digital divide. A Letter of Intent was formalized with the Red Cross Society for emergency supplies. 

UNICEF advanced pilot cooperation in Kenya under the Africa Solar Belt Initiative with MEE and launched the Lancang-Mekong Water for Children Initiative involving establishing a funding facility of USD 10million to accelerate the SDGs related to climate and WASH, aligned to the UNICEF Africa Strategy and UNICEF’s regional level MoU with ASEAN. 

Additionally, UNICEF co-hosted a Sub-forum on Debt-for-Development during the Sixth Forum on China International Development, with CAITEC. This event convened representatives from government, academia, and key partners such as UNDP, WFP, RCO, AIIB, and ADB.

UNICEF also finalized internal strategies in support of UNICEF’s Africa Strategy and South-South and Triangular Cooperation.
 
Communication
UNICEF’s ‘Step up for Climate’ campaign engaged over 88,000 children and youth to take climate action. Government partners, media, digital platforms, celebrities and companies supported the campaign. For World Children’s Day, innovations with digital platforms, online influencers and advertising boosted social media impressions to 410 million (more than double 2024). Of the 48 cities participating in light ups, 43 did creative light-ups, substantially increasing the proportion to 90%. 

International communication was strengthened with storytelling about China-funded projects and the delivery of supplies to six countries. A second international social media channel was launched on LinkedIn. The new Country Programme process was supported through overarching narrative, messaging, and storytelling.

Domestically, multimedia stories were produced covering UNICEF’s response to the Xizang earthquake and programmes including green skills, cash plus and child protection.

Media partnerships were strengthened through an MOU with online newspaper The Paper. There were around 29,000 media mentions of UNICEF in 2025, including interviews and op-eds.

UNICEF followers on Chinese social media grew from 6.76 million to 7.45 million. Digital channels supported organic fundraising through the I Am campaign and coverage of UNICEF’s response to global emergencies such as Gaza.
 
Partnerships & Innovation
UNICEF continued its success in mobilizing resources through its circle of friends, digital outreach and increased partnerships with business and High Net Worth Individuals (HNWIs).  UNICEF advocated for child rights in government policies and influenced business practice in line with UNICEF’s priorities in gender and family friendly policy, working closely with programmes on connecting with relevant stakeholders.
 
Over 600,000 friends of UNICEF continued to support programmes  through individual giving, ensuring stable revenue. Retention and refreshed acquisition were prioritized by engaging inspired-gift buyers and converting them to donors, supported by strengthened loyalty journeys. The new China Giving Platform (CGP) fundraising system launched in May improved performance, enhanced database security, and increased revenue through instant-deduction registration. 
 
UNICEF focused its HNWI strategy on broadening support beyond financial donations. This approach included engaging in advocacy with influential decision-makers, leveraging the networks of HNWI to expand UNICEF’s community of supporters including for UNICEF events like World Children’s Day and encouraging support for UNICEF’s programs both within China and internationally through International Council membership.  

High Value Income Channels delivered solid results throughout the year focusing on renewing existing partnerships such as CHERY Automotive and activating China based companies for programmes globally, thus expanding the delivery of funding to more countries around the world for example ‘Transsion’. 

Collaboration with China Africa Business Council (CABC) for identifying partners for programmes in Africa commenced with the signing of a MOU.

[1] ECD services include three pillars: parenting risk factors screening and counselling, care group activities, and home visits.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Child Health and Development
Challenges: China is on track to achieving the SDGs for children by 2030 with majority of Survive and Thrive indicators having met the targets. Health and nutrition programme outcomes will undergo a two-year transition period before phasing out by December 2027. In response, the office adopts a mixed strategy of complete handover to government and transitions to social policy and child protection programmes to avoid interruption of UNICEF efforts.

Lessons learned: In 2025, CHD leveraged high-level events and conferences - such as Boao Global Health Forum, World Health Forum by Tsinghua University, China-ASEAN Expo, and Medical AI Conference - to augment health and nutrition advocacy and visibility of UNICEF programmes. For the first time, UNICEF attended the Forum on the Development of Xizang, laying the foundation for expanded UNICEF engagements on health and climate in Xizang.

Future outlook: The health and nutrition programmes will prioritize vulnerable groups and resource-stricken areas, as well as policy advocacy, sustainable financing, evidence generation, and health systems strengthening (HSS) through primary health care (PHC) and community health platforms. Our working areas will focus on ECD for children with disabilities, non-communicable diseases (overweight, obesity, maternal mental health), and application of nutrients profiling model to create healthy food environment, promotion of healthy diet, and climate-resilient health system.
 
Education
Challenges: Inclusive education currently falls under Special Education, which primarily focuses on children with physical impairment. More systematic policy advocacy and institutional capacity development efforts are needed to ensure an integrated approach to inclusive education that benefits all children, including those with disabilities. 

Lessons learned: As the Education Program transitions, more forward-looking and innovative approaches are required to ensure sustainability. This includes public-private partnerships to mobilize funding, especially at the local level of government and establishing cross-sectoral collaboration mechanisms not only among government agencies but also with the private sector, civil society, communities, and families. 

Provincial education departments play a critical role in scaling up through a whole-province approach, generating evidence and experience for elevating tested models to national policy and programs. Strengthening their institutional capacity is therefore essential during the transition phase. 

Future outlook: Ensure smooth project handover to government counterparts and within the country office, document successful models to advance SSTC in vocational education, digital learning and teacher training, and leverage evidence to help MOE strengthen governance by integrating inclusive education into EMIS, life skills into TVET, and quality indicators into education supervision.
 
Child Protection
Challenges: Advancing the VAC and the disability agenda remains challenging due to public sensitivities, and complex policy and legislative processes requiring sustained advocacy and long-term engagement. Service delivery coordination and workforce engagement, especially in remote areas, face further hurdles from regional disparities, limited resources and fragmented departments.

Lessons Learned: When advocating for sensitive child protection issues, diversifying advocacy channels is essential including leveraging influential champions, providing academic briefs and pitching positive lessons, with China’s success stories in general offering strong entry points. Provincial innovations can also serve as catalysts for influencing national policy, as seen in the justice sector.

Future Outlook: Focus on scaling up by leveraging existing systems and digital platforms for initiatives including capacity building and positive parenting, while strengthening upstream work through entry points such as public financing and promoting triangular collaboration. Successful provincial and local experiences should also inform national reforms in safeguarding children.
 
Social Policy
Challenges: Data availability and interoperability across administrative systems remain uneven, limiting the timely use of child-sensitive evidence at subnational level. Fragmentation across social protection, health, education, and care systems constraints coverage for vulnerable groups, particularly migrant children. Local-level capacity gaps slowed scaling of integrated models such as Cash Plus and Child-Friendly Cities, while fiscal pressures and competing priorities affected the pace of child-focused investment. Emerging areas, including AI-enabled social assistance and ESG-linked care financing, required extensive feasibility assessment and risk management, extending implementation timelines. Gaps also persist in designing care systems that engage both parents, with limited attention to fathers’ caregiving roles.
 
Lessons learned: These challenges reinforced key lessons. Evidence is most influential when embedded early in policy and planning processes, as demonstrated through engagement in the 15th Five-Year Plan and legislative reforms. Integrated, life-cycle approaches that combine income support, services, and care deliver stronger and more sustainable outcomes for children. National frameworks require sustained subnational accompaniment to ensure implementation quality, while child participation strengthens policy relevance and accountability. Framing child and care investments as drivers of economic resilience and “common prosperity” enhanced policy traction.

Future outlook: Looking ahead, UNICEF will focus on scaling proven models, deepening system integration, strengthening subnational capacity, and advancing AI, care economy, and ESG engagement to embed child equity at the heart of China’s high-quality development. A particular focus will be placed on building inclusive care systems that actively support fathers’ participation in nurturing care, ensuring more equitable and sustainable outcomes for children.
 
Partnership and Engagement
Challenges: Navigating changes in the environment for resource mobilization has proven challenging as new partnerships require considerable time and technical support to develop necessitating a repositioning of internal capacity, stronger engagement across teams and an integrated approach to managing partnerships. Fundraising modalities agreed under the new CPD which will require readjustment. A partnership with a local foundation to publicly fundraise is being negotiated, and progress is slowly being made under a new resource mobilization strategy. 

Lessons learned: Strategic engagement and advocacy have enabled China CO to seize opportunities with CIDCA and Chinese financial institutions including Exim and Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) to embed child rights in inclusive investments. Building on existing multilateral platforms and initiatives such as the Forum for China Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), and China-ASEAN provides opportunities to leverage commitments and investments in favor of child rights and exponentially expands partnership opportunities. 

Future outlook:  Continued engagement with Chinese financial institutions and MDB’s will be explored to leverage resources for child rights. Expanding resource mobilization strategies through strengthened digital engagement and innovative financing are prioritized to strengthen flexible resources and sustainability of resource mobilization across the country programme.  Further integration across communications, public and private partnerships will be strengthened for expanded partnerships for China and from China. 

Programme and Operational Effectiveness
Challenges: Geopolitical tensions made the CPD approval uniquely challenging, with China the only case requiring an Executive Board vote.
