Securing endorsement required intensive coordination and advocacy during the year by UNICEF (Country Office, Regional Office, HQ) and the Government of China to emphasize and bring the focus back on the child.

Lessons learned: Access to child-related data is often limited due to data gaps, unpublished information or sensitivity. Evaluations, especially at subnational level, require multiple clearances and extensive consultations with line ministries, adding time. UNICEF continued to advocate and build partnerships with government partners and affiliated institutions to strengthen ownership and understanding of results for children.

Future outlook: Looking ahead, UNICEF will focus on addressing the last mile on SDGs for children. As China ascends to a high-income country context status, focus will be on upstream programming, influencing policy and strengthening child-rights monitoring. A shift towards a partnerships office will encourage further leveraging of resources for children, engaging in South-South and Triangular cooperation including advocating for the rights of children.

The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is a low-income country with a population of 26.4 million people, including 1.7 million children under five. Following periods of economic contraction during the COVID-19 pandemic, the economy has gradually experienced modest growth. 
  
This has been made possible by the DPRK government’s gradual and selective reopening of its borders in 2024. As a result, UNICEF DPRK managed to transport a significant quantity of vaccines, medicines, and equipment into the country and resume essential services for children and women. 
  
Due to the reopening of the borders, some diplomatic missions have returned to Pyongyang, and selected DPRK officials have resumed overseas travel. However, the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) and its international staff have not been permitted to return or conduct exploratory missions. Consequently, UN international staff remain stationed outside the country, working remotely with no clear timeline for their return. This continued absence significantly hampers the programmatic activities of the UN.
  
As in previous years, data availability on children and women remains limited in 2025. The 2017 DPRK Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey Findings Report continues to serve as a key source of information. UNICEF operates a remote monitoring system in close collaboration with the  Ministry of Public Health (MOPH) and the Ministry of Urban Management (MOUM), which has been instrumental in assessing service quality at health facilities, tracking the distribution and utilization of UNICEF-procured supplies, and identifying areas for improvement. Data from these remote monitoring visits is triangulated with information collected by the Child Data Monitoring Unit of the Central Bureau of Statistics, with UNICEF  support, to gauge overall coverage of key interventions and the planned results of the annual work plans. 
  
Despite prevailing data gaps, available systems clearly demonstrate challenges faced in providing basic social services. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, immunization coverage in the DPRK exceeded 96 percent for all routine vaccines. However, vaccines could not be delivered to the DPRK in 2020 due to border closures, resulting in vaccine stockouts by late 2021 and the cessation of vaccination activities in 2022. 
  
In 2023, UNICEF resumed the delivery of limited quantities of vaccines to the DPRK, but overall vaccine coverage levels remained low. None of the children received their routine vaccines in 2023. However, since 2024, UNICEF has successfully organised 11 chartered flights to deliver vaccines that had been in the pipeline since  2021. More than 10.4 million doses of vaccines were delivered to the DPRK. The MoPH organised rounds of national multi-antigen catch-up campaigns in 2024 and 2025, resulting in full vaccination coverage of over 99 per cent of all children who had missed their routine vaccinations since 2022. 2025 has been an important year for the DPRK in bringing immunisation coverage back to the level prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.
  
In the area of nutrition, the DPRK made substantial progress between 2000 and 2017 in reducing stunting and wasting among children under five years of age, which in 2017 affected 19.1 per cent (stunting) and 2.5 per cent (wasting) of children. However, in 2025, about 50 per cent of the targeted severe acute malnutrition (SAM) cases were identified and managed, an increase of 10 per cent compared to 2024. 

Agricultural outputs are an important underlying determinant of child nutritional status. Supported by overall favourable meteorological conditions, the country reportedly recorded improved harvests in 2023 and 2024. It is unclear, however, how this has affected the prevalence of undernourishment (defined as the percentage of the population whose habitual food consumption is insufficient to provide the dietary energy levels required to maintain a normal, active, and healthy life), estimated to be 45.5 per cent from 2020 to 2022 according to the latest available estimates. The lack of recent data and information thus limits assessments of food security and nutrition in the DPRK.
  
Access to safe water and sanitation continues to pose serious challenges. The 2017 survey indicated that while 93.7 percent of the population used improved drinking water sources, only 66.4 percent had access to safely managed water that meets standards of availability, accessibility, and safety. Regional disparities in access to safe water and adequate sanitation services among the different provinces persist. Additionally, 15.3 percent of the population lacks basic sanitation  facilities. As a result, one in three households still relies on contaminated water, and 3 in 20 people live in unhealthy environments due to unsafe waste  disposal and inadequate sanitation.
  
In summary, UNICEF continued supporting women and children throughout the year through international staff based in Bangkok and government-seconded national staff in Pyongyang. 
  
Although the DPRK Government has not authorized technical missions or the return of international staff, the planned in-country mission in November with GAVI and implementing partners UNICEF and WHO has been postponed to early 2026. Nevertheless, senior MOPH officials and UNICEF DPRK staff attended the international vaccine procurement forum in Cairo, Egypt, from 10–13 November, where stakeholders shared ongoing efforts to secure vaccines.

A) Major contributions and drivers of results:

In 2025, UNICEF continued to provide life-saving interventions across the Health, Nutrition, and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) sectors to women and children in the DPRK. The UNICEF DPRK’s capacity to transport essential supplies also improved compared to previous years. By November 2025, UNICEF had successfully delivered supplies worth $10.8 million to the DPRK during the year, including $8.4 million for health programmes, $1.9 million for nutrition programmes, and $0.5 million for WASH programmes.
  
1. Health:
  
a. Vaccination 
  
UNICEF arranged  six chartered flights to transport 3.3 million doses of vaccines, including: 300,000 doses of Hep B, 1,505,000 doses of MR, 2,964,400 doses of Pentavalent, and 832,965 doses of IPV vaccines to DPRK in 2025. The MoPH organized two rounds of national multiantigen catch-up campaigns, in February and June, and used some vaccines to restore routine immunization. 
  
UNICEF also supported the campaigns by facilitating the transfer of vaccines from the Central Warehouse to provincial and county warehouses, procurement and installation of cold chain equipment, microplanning, execution of the plans, field  monitoring, and capacity building of household doctors overseeing the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI). This increased availability of essential vaccines marks a significant milestone towards safeguarding children’s health and survival in the country, with additional benefits for health security in neighbouring countries. 
  
A substantial number of children who had  missed their routine vaccinations since 2023 were finally vaccinated against various antigens. This initiative and the routine immunization programme facilitated the complete vaccination of 278,121 children with BCG, 979,880 with Pentavalent, 762,803 with measles-rubella (MR), 533,162 with inactivated poliovirus (IPV), 275,205 with Hep B, and 276,378 pregnant women with  tetanus-diphtheria (Td). 
  
At the end of 2025, 99 per cent of the 2022-2025 birth cohorts who had missed their full routine vaccination dose were fully immunised. The DPRK has successfully restored vaccination coverage to pre-COVID pandemic levels. This was possible through continuous efforts by Gavi and UNICEF to make the vaccine available in the country despite the challenges. 
  
UNICEF contracted an international Biomedical Engineer to support the MoPH remotely in developing standard operating procedures and training manuals for preventive and curative maintenance of cold chain and waste management equipment. The draft documents have been shared with the MoPH for review and comments. Finalization of the documents is expected by the first quarter of 2026. 
  
UNICEF also contracted Contigo Tor to assist the MoPH with waste management assessment in 136 health facilities, including hospitals, clinics, and polyclinics. The agency drafted and refined the questionnaire with UNICEF, MoPH, the Ministry of Land and Environment Protection, the MOUM, and the technical team from the Population Centre. After pretesting at three facilities and revising, nine teams of three members each conducted data collection, which has been shared with the agency. The report is expected by the first quarter of 2026.
  
WHO and UNICEF will publish updated estimates of national immunisation coverage – including for the year 2025 – in July 2026. These updated estimates are expected to show significant improvements in coverage of key antigens and, therefore, reverse the declines observed during the COVID-19-related closure of the country.  
  
b. Maternal and newborn care 
  
The total number of institutional deliveries reported for 2025 was 270,748 (94.6%), an increase of 0.6 per cent compared with 2024, which was 276,077 (94%). The national caesarean section rate decreased by 0.26 per cent (11.8%) in 2025, compared with 12.04 per cent in 2024. The national caesarean section rate remains within the globally recommended rate, indicating that obstetric complications are being well managed and caesarean sections are not over-medicalized.
  
In  2025, following the recommendations of a 2023 needs assessment carried out  across 250 hospitals, UNICEF continued supporting efforts to strengthen the  delivery of quality Basic and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn  Care (BEmONC) and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEmONC)  services. To improve the availability of essential equipment, instruments, and medicines, UNICEF shipped a substantial supply of items to the DPRK, including critical components such as caesarean sets, delivery sets, cervical tear suture sets, sterilisation tools, and essential medicines. 
  
To  ensure appropriate use of these supplies, in 2025, UNICEF also supported updating the National  Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care guidelines and training manual. UNICEF supported the training of master trainers for five batches on the updated EmONC guidelines, and 140 trainers from 74 counties participated. The trained obstetricians will build the capacity of maternal and newborn service  providers in their respective counties as per the plan. The training will continue in 2026 for the service providers from the remaining counties. As a result, more than 78,000 pregnant and postpartum women and their newborns are expected to benefit from the improved care enabled by these supplies.
  
c. Child health care
  
The MoPH reported that in 2025, nationwide, around 483,936 children with diarrhoea received medical attention, but only 44 per cent (213,865) received oral rehydration salt (ORS) and zinc. However, this is an improvement of over 12 per cent compared to 2024. In 2025, a total of 33,199 children with pneumonia received care, and only 36 per cent received antibiotics, which is about 60 per cent less than in 2024. The reason may be that the MoPH data did not reflect the number of children receiving antibiotics in the first and second quarters of 2025. 
  
UNICEF supported capacity-building training for newly appointed 144 paediatricians in 72 counties and Ri hospitals who are effectively implementing the updated integrated management of newborn and childhood illnesses (IMNCI) guidelines. In addition to this guideline work, UNICEF also procured and delivered a large quantity of essential medicines, including antibiotics, antipyretics, oral rehydration salts (ORS), ORS and zinc kits, and zinc tablets. These essential drugs and commodities were distributed to more than 1,850 health facilities across 50 UNICEF focus counties and are sufficient to benefit over 5 million people, including more than 600,000 children under five.
  
2. Nutrition:
  
In 2025, UNICEF DPRK achieved significant progress in the treatment and prevention of wasting, a life-threatening form of acute malnutrition, and in addressing micronutrient deficiencies. These improvements were made possible through the timely provision of therapeutic and supplementary foods as well as essential micronutrient supplements.
  
a) Treatment of wasting
  
Nearly 34,798 children with wasting (40  per cent of the expected annual target for 2025) were identified and treated at 189 Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) sites. Due to resource constraints, only 17,595 children with severe wasting (49 per cent of the target) were identified and received treatment. This is 20 less than 2024. A total of 15,573 children with moderate wasting and concurrent illnesses (33.1 per cent of the target) were identified and treated following the MAM protocols, which has increased by 3.3 per cent from 2024. 
  
MoPH  has established an additional 20 CMAM treatment centres across 20 counties, increasing the total to 209. UNICEF supported two batches of capacity-building training for 40 service providers from these new sites to ensure quality of care.  

b) Micronutrient supplementation 
  
In 2025, alongside improvements in the treatment of wasting, UNICEF supported the MoPH  to organise nationwide biannual Child Health Day events, delivering key nutrition and health interventions. Nearly 1.34 million children aged 6–59 months received lifesaving, high-dose vitamin A supplements, accounting for 99 per cent of the annual target.
  
In addition, some  23,900 children aged 6–23 months were provided with micronutrient powders to  enrich their home foods with essential vitamins and minerals. Furthermore, approximately 128,900 pregnant women (43 per cent of the 300,000 target) received  multiple micronutrient supplements.
  
3. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH):
  
In 2025, UNICEF successfully supported the completion of two water supply projects, which helped to cover 5 schools and 4 health facilities in the project catchment areas. These projects provided access to safe water for over 23,000 people in two counties in two  provinces namely South Pyongan and Kangwon. In addition, two water supply projects in Tokchon and Kwaksan Counties are on-going and expected to be completed  in 2026. UNICEF collaborated with the MoUM to develop new gravity-fed piped  water systems, and in some cases, to repair and rehabilitate existing water systems to restore their functionality and ensure access to safe water, contributing to the prevention of water-borne diseases. 
  
In close collaboration with UNICEF, the MoUM successfully delivered WASH supplies, including 300 water filters, 3,000 sets of hygiene kits, and 200 rolls of tarpaulin. These supplies were  distributed across 19 counties in seven provinces, benefiting some 12,000 people in need. This initiative aimed to promote safe hygiene practices and handwashing as part of a preventive cross-sectoral intervention alongside health and nutrition programmes in seven provinces. Additionally, UNICEF supported the MOUM to provide training to 66 provincial officials on water quality monitoring and surveillance. 
  
With these three interventions – namely, completion of water supply projects,  distribution of WASH pre-positioning supplies, and the promotion of integrating safe hygiene practices with the Child Health Days – the WASH programme has reached more than 35,000 people.
  
Thanks to generous contributions from the people of China and humaneterian thematic fund, UNICEF DPRK is procuring additional  critical supplies worth US$150,000 to support the country’s most vulnerable children, including essential Health, Nutrition, and WASH supplies. To date, UNICEF DPRK has received 3,400 cartons of handwashing soap and 1,000 units of 20-liter water containers that will enable us to support approximately 22,200 people during an emergency. The remaining Health and Nutrition supplies will  be delivered soon. In addition, UNICEF continues to stockpile vital WASH supplies within the country to ensure readiness for future emergency responses.
  
4. Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation
  
In the  absence of international professionals in-country, the remote monitoring of the programme started in December 2021. In 2025, UNICEF continued its efforts to implement remote programme monitoring of the Health, Nutrition, and WASH programs. On a quarterly basis, teams from Government ministries and UNICEF national seconded staff visited villages and neighborhood facilities across multiple provinces. Key information was obtained from these visits, including noting good practices, stocks of supplies of medicines, drugs, vaccines, and medical  consumables, and WASH equipment at the facility level. They also helped highlight the knowledge and capacity gaps among service providers. For example, the  MOUM engineers have been able to conduct monitoring visits to all water supply projects using an agreed checklist and template and provide technical on-site training to People’s Committees to complete the construction of the projects. 
  
UNICEF  supported the Child Data Management Unit within the Central Bureau of Statistics in the collection and processing of data, resulting in an expansion of information received through quarterly data sets. This practice enables  better triangulation of data between county-level distribution plans and the number of children receiving UNICEF services, supporting improved programme assurance in the absence of international staff field visits and enabling  monitoring of how resource allocations and programmes are impacting key child rights indicators. 
  
Based on these results, a Power BI dashboard was launched, including information on population, births, children under 5, children above 5, adolescents, and population per age band, disaggregated by year and province. It also includes data on fund analysis, immunization, MCH, and nutrition. The Power BI dashboard is expected to be updated regularly as monitoring data becomes available. However, its potential to generate evidence-based programme decisions is limited by the lack of disaggregated data in gender and other areas, and the challenge of getting timely data.
  
The  primary limitation of the remote monitoring modality is that international staff were unable to directly verify programme implementation and field conditions, which reduced opportunities for in-person validation and real-time assurance. To mitigate this, UNICEF relied on structured visits by national counterparts using standardized checklists to collect field-level evidence. Monitoring teams were required to include clear, time-stamped photos in  reports to strengthen documentation and verification. In addition, the CO has been trying to regularly feed monitoring data into Power BI dashboards, allowing for trend analysis, triangulation of information, and early identification of gaps. These measures helped maintain data quality and a credible level of programme assurance under current access constraints.
  
In 2025, the DPRK team continued to make substantial progress in implementing the Management Response to the Country Programme Evaluation. The country team has completed all activities that can be done (77% of the planned activities), while the international team remains outside the country. Once the team returns, the remaining three recommendations, which focus on the next country programme, will be implemented.

B) Partnerships  
        
Despite the continued remote working modality of international staff from Bangkok, partnerships remained important for UNICEF’s work to drive results for children.
  
Through its team of national staff in Pyongyang, and remote support from its Bangkok-based staff, UNICEF maintained productive working relations with the Government of DPRK that were guided by signed annual work plans. In 2025, the Country Programme was extended with the approval of the UNICEF Executive Board for a further 12 months, until 31 December 2026.
  
UNICEF supported the MOPH in immunization and other health programmes, as well as in  key nutrition responses. UNICEF also supported the MOUM on WASH responses and the Central Bureau of Statistics in monitoring and collecting data on the status of children, to the extent possible, and on the implementation of the  Country Programme. 
  
UNICEF was an active member of the UN Country Team (UNCT), providing input to regular  UNCT meetings and initiatives led by the Resident Coordinator’s office. Among the different UN partners, UNICEF worked closely with the WHO to ensure alignment of approaches in the fields of immunization. 
  
Among  UNICEF’s resource partners, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, provided crucial resource support for health system strengthening, ensuring the availability of supplies, human resources, and an enabling environment. Gavi funds made it possible to ensure the availability of vaccines and their delivery to the DPRK, procurement of cold-chain equipment, nutrition  therapeutic supplies, and interventions to improve WASH facilities in health facilities. Throughout the year, UNICEF greatly appreciated Gavi’s unwavering support for the DPRK immunization programme despite the challenging operating environment. In addition, UNICEF DPRK gratefully acknowledges the support of all donors, including Natcom/Switzerland and those providing thematic and humanitarian funding, whose contributions have been vital in sustaining essential services for children and women in the DPRK.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges, Lessons Learned, and Future Outlook

The major challenge of the country programme is the uncertainty of international staff returning to the country. This continued absence limits UNICEF’s ability to raise funds and implement and monitor programmes. UNICEF has therefore frozen the recruitment of vacant positions and prioritized continuity of critical programmatic activities focusing on lifesaving and humanitarian interventions. The office was operating with minimal international professionals on board. 2025 was a challenging year for the DPRK team, especially with the Future Focused Initiative (FFI) process, and overall dwindling of development assistance. However, the team remained focused and worked tirelessly to deliver results for the children and women of the DPRK.   
 
The continued hybrid approach to programme management, with international staff based in Bangkok, Thailand, and the seconded national team in Pyongyang, requires careful coordination and planning to ensure both programme and financial assurance controls are in place and implemented effectively. The approach showed that significant results for women and children can still be achieved through this approach. 

With the continued absence of international staff from the country, the Country Office’s remote monitoring systems remained highly relevant. The systems were based on a combination of field visits by national staff and consultants from the MOPH and the MOUM, using a monitoring checklist and sharing of trip reports with international staff outside the country for review and feedback. Despite prevailing limitations, including delayed submission of monitoring reports, the system helped assess the quality of care, the competency of service providers, project completion rates, and the overall availability and utilization of supplies and commodities.

Despite the reopening of selective diplomatic missions and limited tourism for friendly nations in 2025, there is still no definitive information regarding the potential return of international UN staff to the country. Moreover, the geopolitical environment has grown increasingly complex. In response, UNICEF plans to maintain a hybrid operational approach, with international staff based in Bangkok and national staff operating from Pyongyang. However, UNICEF remains prepared to facilitate the immediate return of its international staff should the necessary approvals be granted.

Obtaining the UN sanctions committee’s approval for life-saving supplies has become increasingly challenging. These delays will inevitably slow down programme implementation and negatively impact child survival outcomes.

The East Asia and Pacific (EAP) region is home to 490 million children across the 28 countries where UNICEF implements programmes. 2025 continued to be shaped by profound geopolitical shifts, persistent socio-economic pressures, intensifying climate-related disasters, and humanitarian emergencies. These dynamics had significant implications for child rights, continuing to widen disparities that leave millions of children without equitable access to essential services, affecting progress toward the 2022–2025 UNICEF Strategic Plan outcomes and the region’s ability to meet the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Despite the challenges, UNICEF remained focused on supporting governments to sustain investments in children, strengthen system resilience, and uphold the commitment to leave no child behind.

Demographic and Population Trends
The region’s demographic landscape is undergoing rapid, uneven change with far-reaching consequences for child rights. In East and Northeast Asia, fertility rates have fallen well below replacement level, leading to natural population decline and rapidly aging societies. As populations age, there are fewer working-age people supporting a growing number of older people. This is putting heightened pressure on public finances and reducing budgets for essential child-focused services, including early childhood development, primary health care, nutrition, protection, and education. 

Conversely, several Southeast Asian and Pacific countries (except for Malaysia and Thailand) maintain youthful and expanding populations. These large youth cohorts offer potential economic dividends but also face widespread informal employment, persistent youth unemployment, and exposure to climate-related shocks. These factors undermine young people’s transition into stable livelihoods and increase vulnerability among adolescents, particularly girls, migrant children, displaced populations, and those in urban poor communities.

Migration continues to reshape population dynamics, with significant internal and cross-border mobility influencing family structures and care arrangements. Families affected by migration, undocumented migrants, and unregistered children experience barriers to accessing education, health, social protection, and civil registration systems. In addition, these population movements lead to rapid urbanization and result in overstretched social services, highly affecting urban poor children. The resulting inequalities underscore the need for policies that respond to changing population trends and that prioritize early childhood investment, adolescent programming, and strengthened social sector systems for all children. 

Political and Socioeconomic Landscape 
The region’s political environment in 2025 was characterised by contested governance and widening inequality. Geopolitical tensions, including territorial disputes in the South China Sea and renewed border frictions between Thailand and Cambodia, increased regional uncertainty. Gen Z-led protests in several countries reflected growing frustration linked to inequality, corruption, and limited economic mobility. Shrinking civic space and challenges to international law further constrained pathways for child-centered policy dialogue. 

Myanmar’s prolonged conflict continued, leading to severe humanitarian consequences, with large-scale displacement, restricted access, and significant disruptions to education, health, nutrition, and protection services. These conditions deepened vulnerabilities among children and placed sustained demands on humanitarian coordination. 

Economic performance remained uneven across the region. While some high-income economies demonstrated moderate recovery driven by exports and investment in technology, others faced persistent inflation, slowing growth, elevated debt, and reduced fiscal space for social sectors such as health, education, and social protection. Household purchasing power declined across many lower- and middle-income countries, affecting food security, access to health care, school attendance, and uptake of social services. External factors, including shifts in global trade regimes, tariffs, and supply chain disruptions, particularly impacted migrant workers and informal laborers, whose children are often among the least protected.

For UNICEF, these dynamics translated into heightened operational risks, increased delivery costs, and more complex access environments, reinforcing the need for flexible financing, risk-informed approaches, and stronger subnational partnerships to sustain service delivery at scale. 

Sustainable Development Goal Trends 
Progress toward the SDGs remains insufficient, with several child-related indicators stagnating or regressing. More than 312,000 children under five died in 2025, including 153,000 newborns. Immunization coverage stagnated, leaving 1.8 million infants without any DTP dose. Malnutrition persisted with 14.9 million children stunted and 4 million wasted, while childhood overweight increased to 8.3 million children—one quarter of global cases. Learning poverty (the inability to read and understand a simple text by age 10) remains high, with 34 percent of 10-year-olds unable to read and understand a simple text. 

In a region where most countries are considered middle-income, child marriage persists, with one in 11 women married before age 18. While access to basic drinking water and sanitation remains limited for millions, over one-third of children live in households that cannot afford basic necessities. Public expenditure on health, education, and social protection remains inadequate, and data gaps impede effective policies aiming to target the most vulnerable children.

Climate Change and Disasters 
The EAP region continued to face an intense series of climate- and conflict-related emergencies in 2025. Severe storms, floods, landslides, heatwaves, droughts, and earthquakes affected Indonesia, Lao PDR, Myanmar, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, China, Timor-Leste, and Viet Nam. These emergencies damaged infrastructure, disrupted health, WASH, and education systems, and displaced large numbers of families within and outside their countries. Children lost access to classrooms, safe water, immunization services, and nutrition support, while repeated shocks eroded household resilience. In the Philippines, successive typhoons and earthquakes caused widespread damage, undermining already fragile systems.

Across the region, concurrent outbreaks of measles, polio, dengue, and acute watery diarrhea overstretched public health systems. In conflict-affected Myanmar, overlapping crises, including the devastating earthquake in March, compounded hardship and significantly impeded humanitarian access. Border tensions between Cambodia and Thailand triggered population movements and service disruptions.

These converging risks intensified inequities and reinforced the need for child-centered climate adaptation, anticipatory action, resilient systems, and expanded regional emergency preparedness.

Technology, Digital Transformation and Social Media 
Digital transformation advanced significantly across the region, with governments investing in digital public infrastructure, connectivity, and data-driven systems. 

Digital progress remains uneven, with persistent divides in access, digital literacy, affordability, and connectivity continuing to exclude rural communities, indigenous groups, migrant families, children with disabilities, and those in fragile settings. The rapid expansion of AI in public systems offered opportunities yet intensified risks related to online safety, privacy, disinformation, algorithmic bias, and data protection. Countries adopted varied regulatory approaches, from comprehensive cross-sector frameworks to narrower, sector-specific guidance, resulting in inconsistent protection standards. 

As digital transformation accelerates in the region, government will require upstream technical support for programming to enhance AI governance and embed ethics and safeguarding standards to ensure inclusive, accountable, and equitable digital ecosystems.

In 2025, UNICEF East Asia and the Pacific Regional Office (EAPRO) enabled 14 Country Offices to accelerate progress across the 2022–2025 Strategic Plan outcomes, advancing national and regional priorities and driving results at scale for children amid a complex operating environment. The region faced intensifying climate and conflict-related crises, uneven economic recovery, demographic transitions, digital acceleration, and constrained fiscal space. These pressures reinforced systemic inequities and threatened progress in child survival, learning, protection, and social inclusion. Against this backdrop, EAPRO provided strategic guidance, technical leadership, evidence-driven policy support, capacity strengthening, and resource mobilization to help governments maintain and expand essential social services for the most vulnerable children. Regular Resources remained a critical enabler, allowing UNICEF to respond flexibly, sustain core technical capacities, leverage partnerships, and provide high-quality support across all programme areas.
 
Health and Nutrition: Despite serious challenges, including a resurgence of measles, vaccine-derived polio, and diphtheria, and a rise in zero-dose children and HIV cases, UNICEF supported countries in protecting children’s health and improving child survival outcomes. EAPRO worked with governments in Cambodia, Indonesia, Philippines and Viet Nam to identify and address barriers to domestic health financing and with Lao PDR, Papua New Guinea, Philippines to strengthen the adequacy, timeliness, and sustainability of budgeting for vaccine procurement.  Countries benefited from targeted technical support, regional webinars, and exchanges on Primary Health Care expansion, which built capacity for system resilience and universal coverage. The “Healthy Environment for Healthy Children” agenda expanded, with lead contamination assessments in Cambodia and Viet Nam driving policy dialogue and action. UNICEF’s leadership was pivotal in sustaining momentum for immunization and Primary Health Care, even as official development assistance (ODA) declined and government spending reduced. 

UNICEF positioned nutrition as a core human capital and resilience priority, integrating it into ASEAN’s Strategic Plan (2026–2030) and Vision 2045. EAPRO supported countries to strengthen food environment policies, including technical assistance on school nutrition, nutrient profile models, front-of-pack labeling, and marketing restrictions. Regional initiatives advanced policy action on overweight, obesity, and school-age nutrition and harmonized data and indicator standards. The Nutrition Environment Assessment Toolkit for Schools was scaled, supporting national guidelines and monitoring frameworks. Countries aligned wasting and emergency nutrition responses with WHO recommendations and improved preparedness through updated toolkits and simulation exercises. Over US$ 45 million was mobilized through the Child Nutrition Fund, supporting climate-smart programming and expanded use of nutrition data for decision-making. Evidence generation was advanced through participatory research, retail food environment analysis, and the launch of a regional report on childhood overweight.

Education and Early Childhood Development: UNICEF’s multi-pronged strategy that involves technical assistance, partnerships, advocacy, and public goods, enabled 13 countries to enhance early childhood education, foundational learning, inclusive and gender-transformative education, and climate-resilient and digital learning. Seven countries received regional fundraising support for climate-resilient education, and all 13 targeted countries integrated climate resilience into planning. Digital transformation advanced through investment cases and analyses of educational technology, supporting digital learning in 18 countries. Disability-inclusive education progressed via technical support, policy reviews, and regional workshops. National commitments to safe, gender-transformative learning environments were strengthened, and learning assessment systems improved through the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) programme and targeted workshops. EAPRO’s expertise and guidance generated public goods that strengthened evidence-informed policymaking and advocacy, including regional action plans, research partnerships, and the first regional study linking climate shocks to learning outcomes. Digital learning resources and capacity-building courses were expanded, and evidence-based policymaking was reinforced through the SEA-PLM 2024 Regional Report, the first post-COVID regional evidence on learning outcomes at the end of primary education. Regional progress on multilingual and gender-equal education was supported by new tools, forums, and partnerships. Early Childhood Development (ECD) coordination and partnerships were strengthened, notably through the Nurturing Early Starts Together (NEST) partnership. Evidence on digital early learning and early childhood education quality was advanced, and capacity of country offices for ECD system strengthening improved. Parenting support was expanded via a regional hub, and preparedness for nurturing care during emergencies was enhanced with new resources and toolkits. UNICEF’s leadership was reinforced through high-level forums and global engagement.
 
Child Protection: UNICEF’s regional leadership drove significant progress on ending violence against children (VAC), including online, as evidenced by implementation reviews of key ASEAN frameworks. Three new national plans on VAC—Cambodia, and on child online protection—Philippines, Indonesia, were adopted. Sustained advocacy resulted in the first regional framework on addressing intersections between ending violence against children and women, to be adopted by ASEAN in 2026. Lao PDR became the seventh EAP country and sixth ASEAN member state to recognise social work as a profession. To create fiscal space, Child Protection and Social Policy collaborated on Public Finance Management for Child Protection Systems Strengthening & Social Service Workforce Strengthening, covering eight countries. Eleven countries in Asia and the Pacific now have Primero/Child Protection Information Management Systems, strengthening case management and administrative data. EAPRO’s flagship work on climate-resilient child protection and social service workforce included rolling out a technical and advocacy package, supporting nine country offices to integrate child protection into country climate programmes, and piloting the Disaster and Climate Resilience for Child Protection Modular training package in Cambodia. ASEAN Social Workday launched the Regional Guidance on the Role of Social Workers in Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Resilience, alongside a Pocket Guide for social workers. The first climate marker developed for Primero was introduced in Timor-Leste to generate evidence on intersections between climate impacts and child protection. Innovative work in the EAP region directly led to US$ 3 million being secured for the global scale-up of legal empowerment for climate justice. Critical research and tools to strengthen Mental Health and Psychological Support were finalised, including a Guidance Note on Perinatal Mental Health in primary health care, research and guidance on adolescent suicide, and the Caring for Caregivers of Adolescents Toolkit.
 
WASH and Climate: EAPRO provided comprehensive support to all 14 country offices to strengthen capacity and commitment to ensuring that children and adolescents have access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services and live in safe, sustainable environments. Technical advisory services, oversight, evidence generation, capacity building, regional convening, and resource mobilization contributed to climate-resilient WASH programming, emergency preparedness and response, and strengthened regional knowledge products. All 14 country offices received technical support and capacity-building on climate-resilient WASH, including assistance with multi-country initiatives, proposal development, and resource mobilization. UNICEF’s sector leadership was reinforced through regional coordination platforms and partnerships with institutions such as the University of Technology Sydney and Swedish Environmental Research Institute and Stockholm International Water Institute, focusing on community resilience to climate change, WASH systems strengthening, and circular economy approaches. EAPRO led studies, guidance, and webinars on climate-resilient WASH financing and sanitation-related emissions. 

EAPRO managed the DFAT Australia funded ‘Improving climate resilient WASH in East Asia and Pacific countries’ partnership which advanced WASH climate rationale development, improved WASH data availability, promoted climate resilient WASH solutions, strengthened the integration of climate resilient WASH in national policies, and expanded evidence generation and learning across six focus countries (Cambodia, Indonesia, Timor -Leste, Kiribati, Solomon Islands, and Papua New Guinea). 

EAPRO also managed the Republic of Korea funded WASH in health care facilities programming, which strengthened national WASH in healthcare facility data and planning systems, and improved WASH services in over 50 healthcare facilities in Cambodia, Indonesia, Fiji, and Papua New Guinea. 

EAPRO supported 14 Country Offices through the Climate Programme Preparation process, including in-country missions and remote technical consultations. Regional climate programming guidance was reinforced through technical briefs and the completion of Country Climate Risk Assessments and Children’s Climate Risk Index analyses, strengthening the evidence base for climate-responsive programme design and alignment with national policies. EAPRO further provided technical leadership on renewable energy solutions through the Solar Hub and supported coordinated donor engagement, reporting, and monitoring for the KOICA-funded Climate Action for the Last Mile Programme and regional climate initiatives. 
 
Social Policy: In 2025, UNICEF advanced children’s rights by strengthening the evidence base, tools, and policy dialogue that informed government decisions toward more efficient and equitable financing of social sectors and gender and shock responsive social protection systems. Social policy engagement focused on strengthening national systems, particularly public finance, social protection, and local governance, while also supporting programme expansion to reach the most vulnerable children, including during shocks. Support was aligned with national reform processes and delivered through analytical work, capacity building, and sustained policy dialogue, helping governments translate policy commitments into improved outcomes for children. 

Public Finance for Children remains a core entry point for strengthening national systems. Through the EU–UNICEF Regional Public Finance Facility, UNICEF supported governments to strengthen social sector budgeting and financing reforms. The second South–South Knowledge Exchange in Colombo brought together policymakers from South and Southeast Asia to discuss how public finance reforms can help sustain investment in education, child protection, health, and nutrition. The Regional Social Sector Budgets Tracker was finalized as a practical tool to support evidence-based budget discussions and allow countries to compare spending across the region. Collaboration between child protection and education strengthened the alignment between financing discussions and service delivery priorities. 

UNICEF supported the strengthening and expansion of social protection programmes to reduce child poverty and vulnerability. Efforts focused on programme approaches that are more inclusive, gender-responsive, and better able to respond to crises, while improving coverage, benefits, delivery systems, and institutional coordination. The DFAT Australia-supported Gender-Responsive Social Protection programme helped ensure that gender, disability and care needs were reflected in reform processes, contributing to more accessible and sustainable systems. UNICEF also strengthened social protection and humanitarian cash preparedness, including through engagement with ASEAN, reinforcing national systems as primary platforms for timely and scalable responses to shocks.

Child Rights, Disability, and Participation: UNICEF advanced child rights across East Asia and the Pacific through strategic capacity building, knowledge sharing, and high-level advocacy. A comprehensive training series strengthened justice systems and child protection frameworks, equipping stakeholders with practical tools to implement child-friendly justice, emphasizing legal empowerment, digital safety, and cross-sector collaboration to align with the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). UNICEF developed and disseminated compendiums for all countries, consolidating best practices, legislative updates, and programmatic innovations for evidence-based planning and harmonized interventions. The CRC Committee’s visit to Viet Nam, coinciding with the nation’s 50-year celebration of progress since ratifying the CRC, highlighted achievements in legal reforms, social protection, and inclusive education, and fostered dialogue on emerging challenges such as digital transformation and mental health. 

UNICEF co-hosted the Asia Disability Summit, highlighted key priorities for children with disabilities at the Structural Reforms and Disability Policy Dialogue workshop, and co-hosted consultations on the new ASEAN Disability Rights Framework. Disability was integrated into ASEAN policy dialogues on climate resilience, disaster management, and adaptive social protection. Over 600 stakeholders were trained on disability inclusion, and the first pilot of disability inclusion in the subnational children's climate risk index in Cambodia was supported. The regional office developed 15 knowledge resources and reports, including on disability screening, inclusive humanitarian action, and Gender Based Violence and Disability, and rolled out the Asia-Pacific disability data report. To address shrinking civic spaces, UNICEF supported the implementation of the Youth-Led Action initiative, reaching almost 23,000 girls and youth, and enabling country offices to work with young people as equal partners in flagship initiatives. The 3rd Young People Action Team cohort included 49 members from 13 countries, collaborating in 45 regional initiatives. The Green Upshift initiative focused on girls and rural youth, and the Youth Empowerment Climate Action Platform advanced girl-led climate action and youth capacity building.

Development Effectiveness: In 2025, EAPRO strengthened programme quality, evidence use, and delivery across the region, supporting 14 Country Offices in alignment with the UNICEF Strategic Plan and national United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF); and converting that alignment into tangible, measurable results for children. Four new Country Programme Documents (China, Indonesia, Malaysia, Timor-Leste) and two Mid-Term Reviews (Lao PDR, Thailand) were completed with explicit equity and risk lenses, producing results-oriented designs focusing on the most marginalized children. 

Twenty-three (23) evaluations were completed and two Country Programme Evaluations were initiated. Two regional evaluations on adolescent girls and child protection systems addressed cross-country knowledge gaps while national evaluation capacity was strengthened in Cambodia, China, Mongolia and Thailand. To raise efficiency, an AI-enabled evaluation tool was piloted to accelerate desk reviews and synthesis, reducing staff workload and turning evidence around faster for programme decisions. Collectively, these efforts strengthened the use of evidence for better programme design and programme adaptation.

Targeted technical assistance ensured that strategic planning processes systematically integrated gender and adolescent priorities, with concrete results: national action plans were adopted in Cambodia and the Philippines, and subnational training in Lao PDR reached nearly 300 officials and partners on gender and disability responsive programming. Across sectors, EAPRO supported advanced gender-responsive social protection, adolescent health and nutrition, and efforts to end child marriage, helping Country Offices translate commitments into financed, monitorable actions. 

UNICEF supported more than 650 digital initiatives across 14 country offices, strengthening digital learning, health information systems, and social protection delivery. Expanding mobile platforms and emerging applications of AI created new opportunities to close service gaps, increase efficiency, and reach children in remote areas. With 134 active digital initiatives in 2025, country offices increasingly used technology to deliver faster, more responsive programming. AI-assisted air-quality analytics, and predictive vaccine-logistics tools enabled teams to anticipate supply risks, target pollution-related child-health interventions, and sustain last-mile service continuity. EAPRO’s governance and compliance support ensured that this growth was matched by safer, better-governed digital systems across all country offices. Strategic communications further amplified impact, with regional media engagement reaching an estimated 1.5 billion people and strengthening advocacy for child rights and urgent child-focused policy issues.

Planning, monitoring, assurance and safeguarding capacities were strengthened: Over 1,100 staff completed training on core planning, monitoring, reporting and knowledge management tools and processes, which improved the quality of country programme development and implementation. High levels of financial assurance were maintained across the region with 94 percent of programmatic visits and 93 percent of required spot checks completed. In addition, 96 percent of active civil-society partners met Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) standards, upholding a strong partner safeguarding and fiduciary integrity. 
 
EAPRO sustained timely humanitarian and disaster risk reduction support to multiple responses across the region. The regional office coordinated the Myanmar Level 2 response and disbursed US$ 348,000 from the Regional Rapid Response Fund to speed up country operations, while targeted technical missions and remote support strengthened emergency coordination and the integration of Accountability to Affected Populations across response plans. Lessons from After Action Reviews were incorporated into preparedness tools and leadership coaching, building a learning loop between crisis response and future readiness. 

To underpin development effectiveness with sustainable financing and policy leverage, the Regional Office strengthened pipeline management, donor engagement and regional coordination. The team convened regional donor briefings and bilateral engagements, produced ODA trend analyses to guide decisions, and promoted consistent use of the UNISON system to ensure alignment of country and regional views of the partnership pipeline. At the intergovernmental level, the team coordinated the 2025 ASEAN–UNICEF Joint Work Plan review and identified new collaboration tracks (health, social protection, disaster management, and digital transformation), positioning UNICEF to translate advocacy into region-wide standards and country action.

EAPRO advanced an innovative-finance pipeline, including the first policy-bank Memorandum of Understanding with the Export-Import Bank of China (China EXIM) to unlock concessional financing for child-focused investments, piloted at US$ 3 million in WASH and now being scaled to Cambodia and Bangladesh. EAPRO also restructured Cambodia’s US$ 11 million SDG Fund programme into a standalone modality with UNCDF, achieving a US$ 2 million SDG fund approval under Water, Innovative, Sustainability and Equality; and institutionalized skills through a regional training module made available on the AGORA platform. Renewed collaboration with Asian Development Bank and formalized opportunities with Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and New Development Bank created the conditions for larger, blended, and country-led financing aligned to child outcomes. These shifts reinforced value for money and sustainability—core tests of development effectiveness.

Private Sector Fundraising: Country offices with established fundraising operations, projected US$ 183 million by year-end, surpassing the 2025 target. The Market Development Team (MDT) worked with Fundraising Chiefs, Private Sector Fundraising and Partnerships teams, Representatives, and Deputy Representatives to ensure smooth fundraising operations that enabled revenue growth. The team led private sector plan development and review, secured US$ 4.5 million in investment funds, and provided guidance on policy, risk mitigation, legal, and Payment Card Industry compliance. Individual Giving remained the core private sector revenue stream, forecast to deliver US$147 million and acquire over 500,000 new pledge donors. The high-value partnership team, through support to country offices and direct management in Singapore, secured US$ 36 million. Major partnerships included Temasek Foundation (US$ 2.5 million), a new US$ 1 million International Council member in China, a US$ 5 million education partnership in Indonesia, and a US$ 4 million nutrition partnership in Indonesia with Tanoto Foundation and Gates Foundation. The team supported the expansion of the Chery Phase II global partnership (US$ 6 million) and the development of a multi-country climate and health partnership with the Prudence Foundation (US$2.6 million). A total of 680 due diligence cases were completed for Asia, with turnaround time reduced from nine to seven working days. Programme Coordination advanced strategic content, capacity building, and system enhancements, developing 37 investment cases and bespoke proposals, securing US$ 2.2 million from UNICEF National Committees, and supporting fundraising initiatives in EAP country offices.
 
Management: Throughout 2025, the Regional Management Team strengthened strategic dialogue. Under the organization-wide Future Focus Initiative, EAPRO and ROSA were consolidated into the newly established Asia Pacific Regional Office (APRO)., For this consolidation, the regional team developed and submitted a high-quality regional office management plan and programme budget review while keeping staff engaged and informed through various forums. 

The Regional Operations team advanced operational excellence, providing support to all 14 Country Offices through accelerated budget reviews, enhanced budget planning capacities, strengthened supply systems, and improved risk and performance oversight. The Regional People and Culture team delivered a comprehensive Staff Support strategy, with nearly 100 online and in-person webinars, briefings, advisory and counselling sessions for around 6,200 participants. The team advised 12 Country Offices on the Staff Support plan implementation, enhancing recruitment, capacity development, and performance management while promoting an ethical and value-based workplace culture across all offices. 

Country offices made progress on digital transformation, completing compliance reviews, improving ICT standards alignment, and establishing governance mechanisms. All 14 offices underwent a comprehensive cybersecurity resilience assessment. 

The Security team strengthened security culture across EAPR, enabling programmes to operate at an acceptable level of security risk despite deteriorating security situations in Myanmar and other contexts.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2025 was marked by change and increasing uncertainty for UNICEF and the wider development sector. UNICEF's Future Focus Initiative led to significant organizational restructuring, highly impacting EAPRO. In addition to the consolidation of programme technical capacity under newly established Centers of Excellence and the related transition of knowledge and funding, EAPRO was consolidated with the Regional Office of South Asia into a new Asia and Pacific Regional Office (APRO). This process required the whole team to be flexible and adjust priorities and plans accordingly. The joint APRO PBR submission was developed under a tight timeframe and resulted in the abolishment of all positions in EAPRO. This process significantly impacted staff morale, diverted focus away from planned results, and required adjustment of plans at various times. The office applied an empathic and transparent change and people management process to ensure delivery of results and adequate support to the country offices. 

The increasingly constrained funding landscape, marked by declining ODA and reduced donor flexibility, required deliberate prioritization and strengthened relationship management to ensure that limited resources were channeled toward programmes with the greatest impact for children. As engagements with partners expanded across HQ, regional, and country levels, the need for coherent coordination became more evident to avoid fragmented outreach and missed opportunities to position UNICEF effectively.

Institutional readiness to engage with international financial institutions (IFIs), innovative finance instruments, and regional platforms varied across country offices. Inconsistent use of UNISON limited the regional visibility of pipelines, affecting the ability to plan strategically. IFI partnerships, in particular, required longer timelines, strong technical inputs, and sustained coordination across all levels of the organization. Consistent application of UNISON and early public-partnership engagement accelerated decision-making, established unified positions, and allowed for evidence-based dialogue with partners. Innovative finance initiatives further demonstrated UNICEF’s capacity to leverage non-traditional resources when supported by solid technical design.

Humanitarian action presented additional challenges. Resource constraints and ongoing internal restructuring contributed to turnover and reduced readiness across several offices. Subnational preparedness work was affected, and the reduced availability of HQ support placed greater pressure on regional teams to maintain technical guidance. Blended learning approaches, After-Action Reviews, and Frontier Data Lab analysis helped strengthen leadership competencies and improve data-driven preparedness and response, underscoring the importance of systematic integration of gender, disability inclusion, and Accountability to Affected Populations across all humanitarian actions.

Capacity gaps in gender analysis and mainstreaming continued to challenge the Regional Office. Organizational transitions affected participation in regional gender coordination, which risked reducing UNICEF’s influence in advancing gender equality across the region. The year reaffirmed the value of a dedicated senior gender technical advisor at the regional level to provide strategic direction, sustain accountability, and drive integration across sectors. Strong partnerships, including with governments such as Australia and China, showed how coordinated regional efforts can improve results at the country level and strengthen UNICEF’s global role in advancing gender equality.

Limited resources and competing priorities affected both the scale of evaluations and their methodological rigor. Variability in theories of change, results frameworks, and available data continued to make evaluations difficult across offices. However, evaluations that were integrated early in programme design and that involved users throughout the process produced more relevant insights and had greater influence on decision-making. Multi-country approaches improved coherence and efficiency, while the engagement of young people enriched findings and reinforced the credibility of results. Continued emphasis on quality assurance, attention to cross-cutting issues, and providing clear expectations contributed to a shift from compliance-driven to learning-oriented evaluation practices.

Overall, 2025 underscored the importance of strategic coherence, evidence-based planning, and sustained technical leadership. When these elements aligned, UNICEF EAPRO was better positioned to navigate structural constraints, maintain influence with partners, and advance tangible results for children across the East Asia and Pacific region.

Looking ahead, EAPRO will focus on fewer, higher-impact public partners and IFIs where multi-year, flexible financing and policy influence are realistic. Regional analysis will guide engagement, moving away from ad hoc opportunities. Innovative finance skills will be embedded through regional AGORA training modules and hands-on support to country offices and will be incorporated into strategic planning. UNISON will be used consistently as a management tool, not just for reporting. 

Targeted entry points at ASEAN and UN Regional Collaboration Platforms (RCP) will be identified to create impact more strategically. With ASEAN, the approach will focus on long-term policy influence rather than an event-based partnership. RCP and UN regional mechanisms will be leveraged to shape agendas more effectively. Planning for scale from the start will be prioritized in areas of innovative finance and IFI engagement.

To accelerate progress on safeguarding and PSEA, EAPRO will advance innovation through comprehensive suites of documents: government engagement resources, including strategic recommendations and guidance notes to embed PSEA within national systems, fostering sustainable, system-wide accountability; and PSEA preparedness and response guidance, enabling country offices to rapidly scale up PSEA measures during acute, time-bound emergencies, particularly in development contexts.

Humanitarian action will be strengthened by building on lessons from AARs and blended learning approaches. The Regional Office will continue to provide remote coaching, streamlined guidance, and accessible learning opportunities, while expanding partnerships with technical agencies such as UNITAR and UNOSAT. These partnerships will help to offset resource constraints and support subnational climate and disaster risk assessments.

Evaluation quality, innovation, and use of evidence will be strengthened by integrating crosscutting issues, investing in capacity-building for governments, and expanding the use of innovative methods, including ethical AI-enabled tools. Building evaluation capacity for governments and partners will remain central, ensuring nationally owned, sustainable evidence systems that generate credible insights to guide policies and budgets for children.

Through these efforts, the Regional Office will apply lessons learned to strengthen programme agility, deepen partnerships, and advance scalable, equitable results for children across the region. The office will continue to deliver on country programme oversight, advocacy and communication, humanitarian coordination, and operational support and explore new opportunities for collaboration, ensuring UNICEF remains adaptive, resilient, and impactful in advancing children’s rights in the region. Collaboration with the Centers of Excellence will be strengthened to ensure streamlined support to country offices. The Regional Office will further work on the transition to the APRO starting on July 1, ensuring a smooth transition process with a continued focus to help Country Offices achieve results for children.

With a child population of 1.1 million (39 per cent of the total population) [1], the 14 Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) [2] covered by UNICEF Pacific have small, culturally diverse populations, high environmental vulnerability, and limited income sources. 


  


The accelerating impacts of climate change increasingly shape the lives of children, particularly those in remote and outer islands, heightening vulnerabilities, disrupting essential services,  and placing added strain on national systems and community resilience. 


  


Natural disasters in the Pacific are a frequent occurrence. Following the 7.3 earthquake that struck Vanuatu in  December 2024, UNICEF worked with government and civil society partners to  reach over 30,000 people with health, nutrition, water and sanitation, and  protection services, while social mobilization efforts reached more than  100,000 people. 


  


In Fiji, cyclone threats prompted the Government to roll out the “Get Ready, Disasters Happen” campaign. The  increasing frequency and overlap of natural and climate-related disasters  continue to stretch response capacities and highlight the need for scalable,  shock-responsive systems that can safeguard children before, during, and  after crises.


   


Across the Pacific, social infrastructure remains highly vulnerable to climate and disaster risks, resulting in  frequent disruptions to essential services. Although some climate- and  disaster-resilient building standards exist, many facilities still fall  short, leaving schools and health centres exposed. Schools, often used as  evacuation centres, created repeated interruptions to learning. Many  facilities also lack access to reliable, clean energy and depend on costly  and intermittent fossil fuels. Pacific governments and partners have  reaffirmed their commitment to investing in more resilient social  infrastructure, recognizing its essential role in protecting child well-being  and strengthening community resilience.


    


Current Status of Child Rights and Challenges:  


Health and Nutrition


Numerous public health emergencies tested Pacific countries in 2025.  Between January and June 2025, Fiji reported 1,226 new HIV cases which is more  than 77 per cent of the 2024 total, representing the highest increase ever recorded and positioning the country among the fastest-growing HIV epidemics  globally[3].  In response, the Government prioritized expanded testing, treatment, and  harm-reduction services. 


  


Dengue outbreaks affected Tonga, Tuvalu,  Kiribati, Nauru, the Cook Islands, Samoa, and Fiji where as high as 5,600 and  10,000 cases were reported for Samoa and Fiji respectively [4].  


  


Measles preparedness was strengthened in  Samoa, Kiribati, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and Fiji, and pertussis outbreaks  in Samoa and Vanuatu triggered targeted vaccination campaigns.  Climate-related shocks increasingly intersect with health emergencies by disrupting routine services and heightening exposure to vector- and water-borne  diseases.


   


Several PICs are nearing key child health SDG  targets, but large disparities persist. Kiribati  has high under-five and neonatal mortality rates at 55 and 22 per 1,000 live  births respectively, while Fiji has seen a gradual increase from 7 to 15 per  1,000 live births for neonatal mortality rate since 2013[5].  Childhood obesity continues to rise across Pacific Islands among the highest in the world, driven by unhealthy food environments  and reliance on high-calorie imported foods. This trend fuels a severe Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) crisis responsible for 65 to 80 per cent of deaths[6].  Climate change further exacerbates nutrition and health vulnerabilities by  disrupting local food production and access to affordable nutritious foods.


   


Despite challenges, public health responses have also created opportunities for new approaches. Persistent vaccine  hesitancy, particularly regarding Human Papillomavirus (HPV)  vaccine and routine immunization, has encouraged more  community-driven approaches, including the use of faith leaders, trusted  community members and vaccine ambassadors.


  


Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)


According to the 2025 Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) update, in the 14 PICTs, about 361,000  people do not have access to safe drinking water, while more than 900,000  lack adequate basic sanitation services.[7] Climate-related pressures, including changing rainfall patterns,  saltwater intrusion, droughts, and flooding, continue to disrupt water  availability, degrade water quality, and damage WASH infrastructure,  disproportionately affecting children in remote and outer islands.


  


Stronger monitoring is  the basis of informed decisions.  Enhancements  to WASH monitoring systems in 2024 began generating results in 2025. In  Vanuatu and Solomon Islands, partnerships with the University of Technology  Sydney and the British Geological Survey produced a groundwater atlas and  hydrogeological mapping roadmap, enabling governments to design climate-resilient  water schemes, prevent saline intrusion, and safeguard limited water  resources. Integration of WASH in Schools (WinS) indicators into Education Management  Information Systems (EMIS) in Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Kiribati, Fiji,  and FSM created a feedback loop between education and WASH sectors. As a  result, nationwide WinS data are now available for Solomon Islands, and nationwide WASH-in-health-care-facility data are available for Fiji. 


   


Pacific governments have made progress in strengthening WASH data and investing in climate-resilient infrastructure,  including initiatives to improve water security for household, school, and  healthcare facilities. However, gaps in sanitation remain significant, with open  defecation (ODF) persistent in some communities, contributing to communicable  diseases, malnutrition risks, and threats to dignity and protection particularly  for women and girls.


  


Learning and Skilling


In 2025, Pacific governments continued advancing equitable, inclusive,  and climate-resilient education and early childhood development (ECD)  systems. Nevertheless, learning outcomes remain an area of concern. The 2025 Pacific  Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (PILNA) results, expected in 2026,  are anticipated to mirror the 2021 pattern of low and declining reading  proficiency across several countries, with girls performing better than boys.  Overall, based on the most recent available  data from PILNA 2021, only 67 per cent of Grade 4 students (8–9 years old) met  minimum numeracy proficiency, and just 43 per cent met minimum reading proficiency.  Among Grade 6 students (11–12 years old), 72 per cent met the minimum numeracy  standard, while 53 per cent achieved minimum reading proficiency. Learning  outcomes vary substantially across countries in the region[8].  Early learning participation before primary school is generally high  but lags in Samoa and Solomon Islands, and secondary completion rates fall  below 50 per cent in some areas[9].  Climate-related disruptions including damaged infrastructure, inaccessible roads, displacement, and prolonged school closures continue to undermine  learning continuity and widen inequities for the most vulnerable children.


  


Protection


Violence against children (VAC) remains pervasive across PICT. Oceania  has the world’s highest estimated childhood sexual abuse rate at 34 per cent[10],  with several countries reporting violent discipline in more than 80 per cent of  households[11].  Gender-based and family violence, often under-reported, intersects with VAC and  is reinforced by harmful social and gender norms. Emerging drivers include family separation linked to labour mobility, rapid digital penetration  exposing children to online harm, and climate-induced displacement and  livelihood disruption, which elevate psychosocial stress and exposure to  violence. 


  


Services remain fragmented and under-resourced, underscoring the need for integrated and inclusive child  protection systems across homes, schools, community, health, and justice  sectors.


  


Social Policy and Social Protection


Child-sensitive social protection coverage remains limited across most  Pacific countries with only five out of the 14 PICTs showing marked  improvements from 2022. These include the Cook Islands (80 per cent to 100  per cent), Fiji (three per cent to 11 per cent), FSM (zero per cent to seven  per cent), Kiribati (zero per cent to 1.3 per cent), and Nauru (zero per cent  to 66 per cent). Other PICTs lack adequate child-focused programmes or the  data required to assess their reach, restricting coverage of children under  national social protection systems. These gaps intensify multidimensional child poverty, restricting access to essential services across health,  education, WASH, child protection, and ECD. 


    


Limited finance, compounded by economic, climate, and social shocks, continue to challenge government responses.


  


Gender inequality continues to undermine  women’s economic security and children’s wellbeing across the Pacific. Women  remain over-represented in informal employment and carry a disproportionate  burden of unpaid care and domestic work, limiting labour force participation  and access to social protection. These constraints heighten risks of  household poverty and food insecurity and reduce investments in children’s  health, nutrition, early learning and education, with particularly adverse impacts on girls. Strengthening gender-responsive and child-sensitive social  protection remains critical to improving outcomes for women and children in  the region.


    


UNICEF Pacific remains committed to supporting  increased investment in effective, equitable, and accountable social  protection systems. Priority areas include boosting immunization, responding  to the HIV emergency, tackling NCDs through healthier diets, improving learning outcomes, and strengthening child protection systems. UNICEF is also  intensifying investments in climate-resilient infrastructure, water security,  climate-smart WASH systems, and community resilience, including work with  young people on climate-related relocations.

2025 marked a pivotal moment for UNICEF Pacific, as it reached the midway point of its 2023–2027 multi-country programme amid significant global changes. 


  


The UNICEF programme focuses on ensuring  access to quality health and nutrition services and to safe, equitable, and  affordable water, sanitation, and hygiene. It also aims to strengthen  learning outcomes and building the skills and resilience children need for  their future. In parallel, the programme is prioritizing investments in  integrated child protection services to prevent and respond to violence,  abuse, and exploitation, all within a climate-smart, shock-responsive,  child-sensitive social protection system. Outlined below are the highlights  of progress achieved through the year. 


  


Improving and Sustaining Health and Nutrition Services   


  


Across the Pacific, efforts to strengthen  health and nutrition services delivered tangible gains for children and  families while laying foundations for long-term resilience. Immunization  coverage improved in several PICTs[1], through intensified outreach, supplementary activities, and  catch-up campaigns aimed at avoiding  preventable diseases amongst children. 


   


Tonga raised HPV  coverage to 60 per cent (target 80 per cent) among girls aged 10–14 years,  while Samoa maintained 74 per cent coverage (target 100 per cent) for the  second dose of MMR. Kiribati’s Measles–Rubella campaign reached 92 per cent (target  100 per cent) of children aged 1–8 years and boosted coverage across all  antigens through expanded outreach. In the Solomon Islands, the HPV “Big  Catch-Up” campaign vaccinated 24,351 girls aged 9–14 years, achieving 79 per  cent of the target. Countries also introduced new vaccines and transitioned  to improved schedules. Fiji, Cook Islands, Samoa, and Tokelau adopted the  Hexavalent vaccine, with plans for Nauru, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Kiribati in  early 2026. Guided by Effective Vaccine Management Plans (EVMP), 158  facilities received major cold chain upgrades, expanding national and  subnational storage capacity.


  


In response to Fiji’s HIV crisis, UNICEF  supported the development of a national plan to eliminate mother-to-child  transmission (EMTCT). The “One Stop Model” clinic pilot was launched at the  national referral hospital, and capacity for point-of-care testing was  strengthened at the primary health care level. HIV prevention efforts also  included media engagement and life skills education for young people.


  


Nutrition advocacy gained momentum  through youth leadership and high-level policy dialogue. Fiji and Tonga  launched the youth-led Fix My Food (FMF) initiative, shifting the  conversation from expert-driven to youth-led and community-owned. A female  adolescent FMF advocate amplified Pacific voices globally during the 2025 UN  General Assembly, underscoring youth participation as a driver of policy  change. This visibility resonated at the Pacific Regional ECD forum, where  commitments moved beyond broad declarations to concrete actions: promoting  early stimulation and adequate nutrition during the First 1,000 days and  protecting traditional food systems by regulating the marketing of processed  foods.


  


Policy advances began translating into  practical tools and data that influence consumer and government behaviour. In  Fiji, a Legal and Institutional Landscape Analysis laid the groundwork for  front-of-pack nutrition labelling and marketing restrictions on unhealthy  foods targeting children.
