Dietary intake assessments and food systems mapping  progressed in Micronesia, Cook Islands, and Niue, addressing critical data  gaps and informing context-specific dietary guidelines. In the Solomon  Islands, a pilot for locally sourced school meals improved student diets and  reinforced food sovereignty—an essential step in small island contexts  dominated by imported processed foods.


  


These achievements highlight UNICEF’s  comparative advantage of bridging policy and practice, elevating youth  voices, and helping government re-purpose COVID-19 response capacities for  routine systems. Outreach, risk communication, and community partnerships  originally built for pandemic response now support immunization catch-ups,  HIV integration, and dengue preparedness—transforming emergency measures into  durable and long-term public health assets.


    


Expanding Access to Quality Education


  


In 2025, Pacific  education systems advanced a coherent reform agenda spanning early childhood  education (ECE), primary learning, system strengthening, and multi-sectoral  ECD. These efforts laid the policy and institutional foundations for more  equitable, inclusive, and climate-resilient education in the years ahead.


    


To build strong  early learning foundations, countries improved ECE curricula, teaching and  quality assurance. Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) finalized its first National ECE  Curriculum Framework and Teacher’s Guide, embedding literacy, numeracy,  socio-emotional development, and indigenous knowledge. Kiribati trained 98  per cent of ECE teachers and prepared a workforce strategy for continuous  professional development. Solomon Islands advanced a new ECE framework for  3–4 year-olds integrating climate, gender, and inclusion, while Vanuatu  rolled out in-service training on inclusive pedagogy, Disaster Risk Reduction  (DRR) education, and psychosocial support. Across Kiribati, Tuvalu, Tonga,  and Vanuatu, locally authored Pacific-language storybooks, Tonga’s updated Heilala Quality Standards, and  Vanuatu’s home-reading initiative linked to parenting support signalled a  shift toward coherent ECE systems that better support school readiness.


  


At the primary education level, Pacific  countries deepened work on teaching quality, inclusion, and resilience.  Investments in teacher retention and career pathways, critical for a  workforce largely female, were central to reforms. Five Ministries of Education  moved from design to early implementation of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) System Transformation Grants - Fiji’s  Yavutu Programme will strengthen foundational skills and transitions; FSM’s  Wayfinding Programme embeds traditional knowledge and identity; Solomon  Islands completed a baseline to guide teacher development and digital  resourcing; while Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI)  and Tuvalu advanced initiatives on digital infrastructure and teacher  qualification upgrades.


  


Inclusive and  quality education moved further into practice. Solomon Islands piloted an  innovative digital monitoring tool to monitor implementation of inclusive  education in 74 schools, training 350 leaders and teachers; Tonga began  developing its first Inclusive Education Manual; and Vanuatu piloted  leadership training on its new policy. Fiji integrated wellbeing, digital  safety, and child protection into leadership training for 900 school heads  and launched multi-sectoral dialogue on drug and HIV risks, while Vanuatu  tested school-management and grant-mechanism training to strengthen  accountability. At the regional level, the 2025 Inclusive Education Paiaudaud convened Pacific governments  and partners to share progress, challenges, and practical approaches to  advancing inclusive education systems across the region.


  


With UNICEF’s support, education sector planning  also progressed. Tuvalu endorsed TESP[2] IV;  Samoa completed a sector review and new plans; Fiji advanced an Education  Sector Analysis and Act review; FSM and RMI finalised plans for 2025–2029.  Kiribati strengthened data capacity, and Solomon Islands completed the first Education  Information  and Communication Technology (ICT) Master Plan. These plans combine  literacy and numeracy priorities with identity, wellbeing, and climate  resilience.


  


Regional advances were made in ECD  programmes through investments in policy, coordination, and parenting  support. Across PICTs, ECD policies expanded from two countries in 2022 to 10  in 2025[3]. Parenting initiatives in FSM, Samoa, Vanuatu, and Kiribati  strengthened nurturing care, while advocacy at the Regional ECD Forum secured  ECD as a standing agenda item at the Pacific Leaders’ Forum, anchoring it in  high-level accountability.




With UNICEF’s  support, discussions at the Pacific Women Leaders Meeting elevated the role  of fathers and male caregivers and highlighted the disproportionate  caregiving burden placed on mothers and women. This helped catalyse  commitment to invest in gender-responsive parenting programmes that address gender  norms and barriers. Parenting and community initiatives  supported by UNICEF in FSM, Samoa, Vanuatu, and Kiribati strengthened  nurturing-care practices, expanding community-level awareness by engaging with  local ECD champions. Advocacy from the UNICEF- supported Regional ECD Forum  held in Samoa culminated in Pacific Leaders endorsing ECD as a standing  agenda item at the annual Pacific Leaders’ Forum, anchoring ECD in high-level  political accountability.


  


Strengthening Climate Resilient WASH Services Across  the Pacific


  


In 2025, the WASH  programme strengthened its role as a foundation for climate resilience and  child wellbeing in the Pacific. It advanced governance, planning, financing,  capacity building, and service delivery with children’s rights at the center.  UNICEF supported national and local coordination, helping countries update  policies, standards, and regulations. 


  


In Kiribati, work  with the Ministry of Infrastructure and Sustainable Energy (MISE) improved  sector coordination through the National Water and Sanitation Committee.  Vanuatu launched its WinS policy and standards, ensuring child-friendly  services and hygiene practices. UNICEF also supported Vanuatu’s National  Adaptation Plan (NAP) revision to embed water security and sanitation  resilience in climate strategies. In Solomon Islands, the WinS policy and  costed plan reached final endorsement, turning policy intent into actionable  plans.


   


In Fiji, UNICEF partnered with the  Department of Water and Sewerage (DWS) to validate a costed rural water and  sanitation master plan with climate-proofing measures, aiming for universal,  climate-resilient WASH services by 2030[4] . In Solomon  Islands, UNICEF supported two costed Provincial ODF plans, creating roadmaps  to eliminate open defecation and achieve universal sanitation. These plans  are tools for accountability, ensuring vulnerable communities, girls,  children with disabilities, and families on remote islands are prioritized and  reached first.


  


Enhancements to WASH monitoring systems  in 2024 began paying off in 2025. In Vanuatu and Solomon Islands,  partnerships with the UTS and British Geological Survey produced a  groundwater atlas and hydrogeological mapping roadmap. These tools help  governments design climate-resilient water schemes, reduce saline intrusion,  and protect resources. Integration of WinS indicators into Education  Management Information Systems (EMIS) systems in Vanuatu, Solomon Islands,  Kiribati, Fiji, and FSM created a feedback loop between education and WASH  sectors. Nationwide WinS data are now available for Solomon Islands, and WASH  in health care facilities data for Fiji.


  


Capacity building shifted from ad hoc  workshops to institutionalised training that leaves lasting skills in  communities. In Vanuatu, UNICEF (working with Department of Water Resources  and the Vanuatu Skills Partnership) developed and accredited a three-month  Level II Plumbing Certificate, producing 45 trained WASH technicians,  including women and persons with disabilities. In Fiji, UNICEF collaborated  with the Fiji National University to create a formal plumbing module,  training 25 plumbers and advancing the institutionalisation of the programme.  These investments move the sector from “build and leave” to “build, train,  and sustain,” ensuring communities retain qualified local technicians long  after project completion.


 


Direct service delivery generated lasting  improvements for families, schools and clinics. In 2025, 40 villages achieved  ODF status and more than 4,055 people gained access to basic sanitation.  Seventeen communities, home to 2,281 people (1,118 women and 1,163 men), were  provided with climate-resilient water supply services. Climate-resilient WASH  infrastructure was strengthened in 92 schools and 51 health facilities,  directly or indirectly benefiting more than 120,000 people, including 23,333  children, across six PICs. Beyond the numbers, these gains translate into  girls staying in school because safe, private toilets are available; health  workers able to maintain infection-prevention measures; and families whose  water systems withstand the next storm.


   


Protection and Prevention VAC


  


The Pacific registered significant progress in 2025  toward stronger protective environments for children, with legal reforms,  policy development, and service innovations unfolding in parallel at national  and regional levels. Fiji, Tonga, Samoa, Kiribati, Vanuatu, and Solomon  Islands advanced key legislation and policies for child justice and  protection, including new acts and frameworks that clarify roles, strengthen  oversight, and improve coordination. These reforms matter because they move  child protection from discretionary responses to rights-based systems with  standards, budgets, and clear lines of accountability. UNICEF’s role as a  trusted technical partner and advocate was evident in drafting support,  costing, and capacity building that helped governments move from intention to  implementation. 


  


Regional initiatives created shared platforms for  quality and scale. Collaboration with the University of the South Pacific (USP)  advanced child protection curriculum development, embedding contemporary  practice into pre-service and in-service training. Multisectoral mental  health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) integration ensured that schools,  health facilities, and community services can offer early support to children  and adolescents facing all forms of family violence, loss, or trauma crucial  in a region where climate shocks and mobility disrupt social networks. Promotion  of diversion programmes for children in conflict with the law connected  vulnerable adolescents to rehabilitative services, offering them the chance  to mature into productive members of society rather future offenders of more  serious offences. Standards for school counselling were established, and  national capacities were strengthened through safeguarding training for  church enablers, recognizing the vital role that faith communities play in  social support and child development. 


  


Digital platforms were developed to provide safe,  culturally responsive information for adolescent boys and girls, meeting them  where they are and extending services beyond traditional entry points. These  platforms offer constructive alternatives to the harmful social and gender  norms that young people often encounter online, empowering girls while  fostering positive masculinity and allyship among boys. Efforts to address  child marriage and adolescent pregnancy moved forward, accompanied by youth  leadership through advocacy programmes that position adolescents not just as  beneficiaries but as co-creators of solutions. The Young Pasifika Wayfinders advisory  group, launched in May 2025 and composed of adolescent boys from 11 Pacific  Island countries, informs UNICEF programming and leads advocacy on gender  equality and adolescent well-being.


  


Evidence and accountability mechanisms gained  traction. Government endorsements of child protection oversight bodies signal  a readiness to monitor, learn, and improve service quality over time. UNICEF  supported the generation and application of data linking budget processes,  service coverage, and outcomes to inform course correction. The most important  progress may be strategic rather than operational: two years into the  multi-country programme, UNICEF is increasingly recognised as a key child  protection agency in the Pacific. 


  


The COVID19 era left deep lessons that are now  institutionalised. The pivot to remote and hybrid modalities during the  pandemic catalysed digital safeguarding approaches and multisector referral  pathways that persist today. Investments in frontline worker training and  case management systems during COVID19 are now the backbone of a more  responsive protection system. For children, the likely impact is safer homes  and schools, earlier detection and response to harm, and better mental health  support, all of which increase the chances of staying in school, forming  healthy relationships, and realizing their potential.


 


Improving Evidence on Child Rights and Promoting Social  Protection for Children


  


In 2025, the Pacific strengthened its evidence base,  policy dialogue, and financing for children, with UNICEF Pacific playing a  catalytic role across the cycle from data generation to budget influence and  programme design. Two landmark studies, the Fiji and Samoa Multidimensional  Child Poverty Reports, provided governments with comprehensive,  equity-focused diagnostics. By moving beyond income to capture deprivations  in health, education, WASH, housing, and protection, the reports offered government  planners clear maps of where children are being left behind and are already  informing FY2025/2026 budget submissions and sector plans, making them  grounded and evidence backed. 




Complementing these studies, UNICEF produced updated  Children’s Country Factsheets 2025, consolidating demographic, social, and  economic data for all 14 PICTs. Samoa received a full suite of sectoral  budget briefs, while Fiji and Vanuatu received budget snapshots highlighting  changes in child-focused allocations. This suite of products does more than  “inform”, it shifts incentives by making child focused spending visible to  political leaders and the public.  


  


Regional policy dialogue advanced as well. In  partnership with the Government of Fiji (Ministry of Women, Children, and  Social Protection) and with technical support from UNICEF’s East Asia and  Pacific Regional Office, UNICEF convened a Gender Responsive Social  Protection (GRSP) workshop in Suva. Combining technical training and  high-level consultation, the workshop deepened regional commitment to  child-sensitive, gender and shock-responsive social protection placing the  Pacific on the front foot to design programmes that can flex during cyclones,  price shocks, or disease outbreaks. 


 


Major analytical work on the Cost of Inaction in ECD  in Samoa and Fiji moved from inception to validation in 2025. By quantifying  the economic losses associated with under-investment in early years services,  these studies make a compelling case to finance ministers to invest now or  pay more later in remedial education, health costs, and lost productivity.  Final reports will be launched in early 2026, but the policy discourse is  already changing, with ECD framed as infrastructure for human development  rather than a discretionary social programme.


  


UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy reached regional  decision makers. A paper on the Cost of VAC in the Pacific, based on earlier  economic analysis, was presented to the Pacific Islands Forum for Economic  Ministers Meeting (FEMM) in July 2025. By reframing violence prevention as  both a human rights imperative and an economic priority, UNICEF advocated  with Pacific leaders to view child protection as core to national development  and growth. Nationally, evidence translated into budget wins. 


    


In Fiji, UNICEF supported costing of the Child Care  and Protection Act and the Child Justice Act. Subsequently, there was a 24  per cent increase in budget allocation for child protection in the 2025/2026  National Budget, particularly for the Department of Children. Broader  advocacy contributed to a 120 per cent increase for school WASH facilities  and a 45 per cent increase in ECCE. 


  


Progress in inclusion and disability  rights continued. In partnership with the Pacific Disability Forum (PDF),  UNICEF completed CRPD trainings and disability situation analyses in 10 PICTs[5],  strengthening national capacities for disability-inclusive planning. A new  initiative with the USP will support young Pacific researchers to lead  child-related studies, building a pipeline of local evidence and  Pacific-owned solutions.


  


Safeguarding Children Amidst Overlapping Emergencies  in the Pacific


  


In 2025, UNICEF reinforced its role as a cornerstone  of humanitarian action and resilience-building in the Pacific, responding to  16 emergencies across nine countries. Events ranging from a 7.3-magnitude  earthquake in Vanuatu to outbreaks, cyclones, and flooding further strained  systems already challenged by climate change and geographic isolation.  UNICEF’s approach combined life-saving assistance with system strengthening  to ensure children’s rights remained central to recovery and preparedness.


  


Following the December 2024 earthquake in Vanuatu,  UNICEF restored primary health services and deployed integrated outreach.  More than 1,000 infants were vaccinated, and 1,382 caregivers received  feeding counselling. In Kiribati, a typhoid outbreak prompted a campaign  reaching 30,948 children, while in Samoa, 1,200 pregnant women and newborns  were vaccinated against pertussis. Emergency nutrition screening reached  2,617 children and ensured treatment for 21 severe malnutrition cases.


  


UNICEF expanded MHPSS, providing services to 2,100  children and caregivers in Vanuatu and delivering mental health messaging to  over 227,000 people. Peer-support and sport-for-development initiatives  engaged 5,600 children in Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, shifting MHPSS from a  reactive service to a resilience approach.




Education continuity was restored quickly. In  Vanuatu, UNICEF established 55 Temporary Learning Spaces (TLS) for 12,000  children. In Samoa, digital and TV-based platforms supported learning during  dengue-related closures. In Solomon Islands, 13 schools piloted  disaster-risk-reduction and climate-resilience training.




As WASH cluster co-lead, UNICEF restored water  services for 12,037 people in Vanuatu, distributed hygiene kits to 13,200  individuals, and upgraded WASH facilities in 22 schools and 13 health  centres, with prepositioned supplies ensuring readiness across the region.


  


Enhancing Climate Action for and with Children in the  Pacific Islands 


  


In 2025, UNICEF Pacific advanced climate action for  and with children, achieving significant progress in strengthening climate  resilience across key sectors. Strategic advocacy and technical support  helped ensure child-centred priorities were explicitly included in NDCs 3.0  for Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and the RMI, while technical assistance  supported the development of child-sensitive National Adaptation Plans to be  finalised in 2026. These advancements improved alignment between climate  finance and children’s needs, laying the foundation for longer-term gains in  social services. Complementing policy work, UNICEF supported governments in  evidence-based planning through subnational Children’s Climate Risk Index and  Disaster Risk Models in Fiji, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu—providing  actionable data to target adaptation investments toward the most at-risk  children.


  


UNICEF translated climate policy gains into concrete  results across the Pacific. Upgrades to 137 health facilities, 118 schools,  and 30,000 households strengthened climate and disaster resilience, while  solarization improved reliable energy access for essential services.  Education outcomes benefited from resilient school infrastructure, expanded  connectivity, teacher training, and climate-focused learning. WASH systems  were strengthened through technical guidance, monitoring, and community  engagement. UNICEF also advanced shock-responsive social protection, preparedness for climate-related relocations, and psychosocial support for  children affected by displacement.


   


[1] According to administrative data from Ministries of Health in Pacific Islands.
[2] Tuvalu Education Sector Plan 
[3] Costed implementation plans and functioning multi-sectoral coordination mechanisms are now in place in multiple countries, and RMI, Tuvalu and Tokelau have embedded climate resilience within their ECD frameworks, positioning ECD within climate-finance and adaptation agendas
[4] The plan details strategies, costs, and institutional arrangements across all four regions including rural, remote, hard-to-reach islands so that governments and partners can prioritize investments and sequence delivery.
[5] Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Republic of Palau, Republic of Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, the office conducted a Mid-Programme Reflection (MPR) to assess the programme business model and sharpen priorities amid funding and implementation constraints. Key lessons underscored the need to move beyond a predominantly policy-heavy approach towards stronger delivery of quality services, expanded partnerships with civil society and FBOs and more integrated programming particularly across Child Protection, GBV, Health and Education. These insights informed strategic shifts towards fewer, higher-impact interventions, strengthened service delivery and accountability, and improved positioning for the remainder of the programme cycle and transition to the next multi-country programme.


    


Another  lesson from 2025 was the importance of adaptive and flexible  multiple-scenario planning to navigate the impact of geopolitics, governance  shifts, and resource constraints. For instance, elections, fiscal tightening,  and structural health sector changes such as Nauru’s move to a stewardship  model highlighted the importance of clear roles and coordination frameworks.  Funding volatility in the North Pacific reinforced the need for diversified  financing and multi-year instruments to sustain essential services.  Persistent data gaps underscored the value of investing in digital systems  and interoperable platforms to enable evidence-based decision-making.


    


Human  resource challenges remain a critical bottleneck. High turnover and limited  capacity showed that one-off trainings are insufficient. Government  workforces required to institutionalize learning through Continuous  Professional Development (CPD) modules, complemented by practical job aids  and digital tools that endure beyond external support. This ensured longer term  capacity development to overcome high staff turnover and knowledge loss.  Cross-sector engagement bringing in education, NGOs, and community actors, proved  essential for resilience and sustainability.


   


Emergency  preparedness emerged as a powerful lever for service delivery. Vanuatu’s  post-earthquake outreach and pertussis outbreak response demonstrated how  surge operations can accelerate coverage and build community confidence.  However, these experiences taught us that emergency-driven scale-up must be  balanced with routine service continuity to avoid long-term disruptions.  Integrating emergency investments into primary health care systems is a  critical innovation for resilience.


  


Governance  reforms in Kiribati, through the establishment of Island Health Management  Teams, illustrated progress in local accountability and community engagement.  Yet, lessons from 2024 and 2025 show that structures alone are not enough operationalization  requires evidence-based planning, monitoring, and budgeting tools. Similarly,  Vanuatu’s Village Health Workers Programme highlighted that community  ownership can drive availability and accountability, but sustainability  depends on strong oversight, transparent financing, and integration with  national systems.


  


In  WASH, climate-resilient infrastructure faced high costs due to market and  logistics constraints. Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) with suppliers and  engineering firms proved to be instrumental towards ensuring reliable access  to materials and technical expertise. Investment in accessible and climate resilient  WASH services in deprived communities, schools and health facilities continue  to improve dignity, safety and health of women and children. Partnerships  with colleges in Micronesia, Palau, and RMI and training of plumbers in  partnership with Fiji National university to build local technical capacity  represent another forward-looking approach to address workforce shortages and  strengthen maintenance systems.


  


Education  reforms advanced despite fiscal tightening and disaster-related disruptions.  Lessons emphasize the need for predictable financing for core system  functions and embedding resilience across teacher development, school  planning, and infrastructure. Digital coaching tools piloted in FSM and  Solomon Islands demonstrated how technology can improve instructional  practice and accountability, but scaling requires reliable connectivity and  integration into national monitoring systems. Lessons from ECE/ECD programming  further highlight that early investments in quality pre-primary services,  inclusive pedagogy, and school readiness, particularly for boys, children  with disabilities, and those in remote communities, are critical to  addressing persistent learning gaps and preventing inequities from  compounding over time.


   


Social  and Behaviour Change programming showcased innovation through culturally  tailored strategies and digital solutions. Engaging traditional leaders,  youth advocates, and using Human-Centred Design approaches in Cook Islands  and Tuvalu fostered local ownership. Digital platforms like Bebbo and Bula  Baby apps, combined with offline booklets and real-time feedback mechanisms,  bridged geographic gaps and strengthened accountability. Social listening  systems and SMS reminders provided actionable insights to counter  misinformation, while creative formats like radio dramas reached wide  audiences and adapted content based on community feedback.


  


Climate  action efforts reinforced that early and sustained government engagement is  critical to integrate child priorities into adaptation plans and unlock  climate finance. Co-designed data tools helped translate climate risk into  investment decisions, while partnerships with organizations like GGGI linked  social services to climate adaptation strategies. These innovations point to  the need for multisector collaboration and long-term investment in youth  leadership to build resilience.


  


Child  protection programming highlighted systemic gaps in workforce capacity and  funding. Lessons learned include the importance of integrating child  protection with gender-based violence prevention and leveraging digital  platforms like Lahaa to reach adolescent girls with multi-sectoral content.  Developing minimum standards and strengthening linkages between formal and  customary systems are key innovations for extending protection to remote  communities.


   


Social  policy initiatives demonstrated the transformative power of evidence-based  advocacy. Country factsheets, multidimensional poverty reports, and economic  analyses such as the Cost of Inaction in ECD informed policy reforms and  budget allocations, including significant increases for child-focused  services in Fiji. Platforms for youth participation and partnerships with  civil society amplified children’s voices in national dialogues, reinforcing  that inclusive policymaking is both a lesson and an innovation for  sustainability.


  


UNICEF  Social Policy supported Fiji to advance gender-responsive social protection  through advocacy, evidence generation, capacity building and policy dialogue.  With support from EAPRO, we strengthened Fiji’s engagement on gender  responsive social protection through regional and in country capacity building  and policy dialogue workshops held in Bangkok, Thailand and Suva, Fiji and a  recently completed Fiji case study on women’s economic empowerment and unpaid  care.  The Fiji capacity building and  policy dialogue highlight the importance of linking evidence-based capacity  building with policy engagement and maintaining ongoing presence when Pacific  governments seek to expand social protection for children and marginalized  groups. UNICEF also assisted in submitting a Cabinet Paper for a Universal  Child Benefit scheme, expected in 2026–2027, and is supporting Samoa on a  similar initiative that is expected to support more gender responsive social  protection in the region. Through our advocacy, UNICEF was included as a key  partner to support implementation of social protection related initiatives in  the Fiji Women’s Economic Empowerment National Action Plan 2025-2030.




Looking  ahead, the overarching lesson is clear: resilience in Pacific programming  depends on embedding systems thinking, leveraging technology, and fostering  partnerships that bridge sectors and geographies. Innovations such as CPD  institutionalization, LTAs for WASH, digital SBC tools, and climate-finance  linkages are not just responses to challenges, they are pathways to  sustainable impact. By consolidating these approaches and scaling what works,  UNICEF and partners can ensure that every child in the Pacific survives,  thrives, and reaches their full potential.

As the world’s fourth most populous country, Indonesia’s population reached an estimated 284 million in 2025, with children aged 0 to 17 years accounting for approximately 28 per cent, or 80 million. 
Indonesia is undergoing a period of significant transformation under the National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN) 2025–2045. The year 2025 marked the first year of implementation of the Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN) 2025–2029, with the Government demonstrating strong political commitment to the Asta Cita framework that underpins the vision of Golden Indonesia 2045. This vision aims to position Indonesia among the world’s top five economies by 2045 and places strong emphasis on human capital development, inclusive social development, governance reform and sustainable economic growth. The RPJMN prioritizes social sector reforms with direct implications for children’s rights, including commitments to universal healthcare coverage, improved education quality, reduction of malnutrition and adaptive social protection systems to reduce poverty. National targets for 2029 include increasing birth registration among children under 4 years, reducing child marriage, and lowering the prevalence of female genital mutilation (FGM), with implementation pathways embedded within the RPJMN framework. UNICEF and the Government of Indonesia adopted a new Country Programme Document (2026-2030) aligning child-focused outcomes with UNICEF global strategic plan, the Government’s Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN) and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).  
The national economy continued to recover from the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, having regained upper-middle-income status in 2023, with IMF’s GDP estimation of USD1.44 trillion in 2025. Economic growth remained positive in 2025, reaching 5.04 per cent in Q3 of 2025, while inflation remained relatively low at 2.92 per cent in December 2025. Despite these macroeconomic gains, Indonesia’s fiscal space remains constrained. Public expenditure in 2025 stood at 14.5 per cent of GDP, one of the lowest levels among the upper middle-income countries.
While Indonesia continued to make progress in reducing monetary child poverty, from 11.4 per cent in 2024 to an estimated 11.0 per cent in 2025, multidimensional child deprivations remain a concern. In 2023, more than 37 per cent of children were deprived in at least two basic dimensions of child rights, including education, health, nutrition, protection, housing, and access to clean water and sanitation. These findings underscore persistent structural inequalities that extend beyond income poverty and point to the need for coordinated, multisectoral policy responses, including strengthened social protection systems.
Indonesia made progress in reducing stunting among under-5 children, with a rate of 31 per cent in 2018 and 19.8 per cent in 2024 (20.8 per cent boys and 18.6 per cent girls). There is a need to further accelerate these efforts and to address other forms of malnutrition such as wasting (7.4 per cent), overweight (3.4 per cent) and anemia (23.6 per cent). Overweight and obesity are increasing among school-aged children and adolescents, while maternal nutrition challenges persist, with 27.7 per cent of pregnant women anemic and 16.9 per cent experiencing chronic energy deficiency. The Government established the National Nutrition Agency in August 2024, revised the national stunting strategy, and launched the President’s Free Nutritious Meals Programme as part of broader efforts to address malnutrition across the life course.
Progress in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) is mixed. The proportion of households practicing open defecation declined from 3.2 per cent in 2024 to 2.35 per cent in 2025, however access to safely managed sanitation remained low at 10 per cent nationally and below 2 per cent in some provinces in the eastern parts of the country. These low rates are largely due to poor septic tanks and limited desludging services. Access to safely managed drinking water increased to 20.45 per cent in 2023, yet water quality concerns persist, with high levels of E. coli contamination reported in boreholes (47.1 per cent) and piped water systems (33.2 per cent). These challenges highlight ongoing gaps in service quality, infrastructure management, and regulatory oversight.
Indonesia remains highly vulnerable to climate change, environmental degradation and geophysical hazards. In 2025, more than 3,000 disaster events affected over 10.5 million people and about 3.17 million children. Indonesia ranked 46th out of 163 countries on the Children’s Climate Risk Index, reflecting significant exposure to climate-related shocks.  In November severe flooding in Aceh, North Sumatra, and West Sumatra provinces affected 3,5 million people and displaced over one million. UNICEF estimates that one-third of the people affected are children. The government declared a provincial emergency. Emergency relief efforts have been led by the national and local governments of three provinces, with the support of the National Disaster Management Agency, the army, search and rescue teams, line ministries and humanitarian partners. As requested, UNICEF is providing technical assistance to the key line ministries and the local authorities for their emergency response efforts.
Indonesia has made significant progress in reducing under 5 mortality, with a rate of 32 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2017 and 21 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022. While almost all births are attended by skilled health personnel, the maternal mortality ratio remains at 189 deaths per 100,000 live births, with wide disparities between regions. While full immunization coverage against vaccine preventable diseases remains high (87.3 per cent in 2024), over 660,000 children aged one year and younger were categorized as zero dose as they had never received any vaccine.
In 2024, 13.6 per cent of children aged 3 to 4 years (14.2 per cent girls, 13.0 per cent boys); and 60.5 per cent of children aged 5 to 6 (60.9 per cent girls, 60.1 per cent boys) were enrolled in pre-primary education. Furthermore, 63.8 per cent of children (63.8 per cent girls, 63.9 per cent boys) have attended Early Childhood Education. A major step has been taken to enhance early learning and development through the introduction of one year of universal pre-primary education within basic education. Indonesia has achieved near universal participation in primary education with a net enrolment rate (NER) of 99 per cent. The gross enrolment rate (GER) in junior secondary education is 92.2 per cent, compared with a NER of 81.7 per cent; while the GER for senior secondary education is 87.3 per cent, compared to a NER of 64.3 per cent. Analysis of National Assessment data reveals girls across all education levels are leading boys in achieving minimum proficiencies in literacy and numeracy.
Several instruments to reinforce national commitments to prevent and respond to violence, exploitation, and harmful practices were finalized in 2025. The Government has adopted a comprehensive national road map for online child protection. The President signed a government regulation on children’s access to the internet as well as one on prevention of crimes of sexual violence and the mitigation, protection and recovery of victims. Between 2024 and 2025, about 2.8 million instances of harmful online content were blocked. The rate of child marriage has decreased from 10.4 per cent in 2020 to 5.9 per cent in 2024. Nonetheless, challenges remain. In 2024, one third of children (7.6 million) aged 13–17 years reported having experienced one or more forms of violence in the previous 12 months. The 2024 National Women’s Life Experience Survey revealed that 46.3 per cent of women aged 15–49 years have been subjected to female genital mutilation/cutting despite the Government’s regulation that emphasizes the eradication of the practice. 
In the social policy domain, the Multidimensional Deprivations Analysis supported by UNICEF was used by the Ministry of Finance in the policy engagement with the National Assembly on budgetary allocations in Indonesia. In addition, UNICEF engaged the Ministry of Home Affairs (MoHA) and Ministry of Finance (MoF) on sub-national budgeting information system using the findings of AI-based child budget tagging. As a result, both MoHA and MoF agree in principle to use these findings to update the guidelines on local government budget preparation for 2027 and beyond. The Government also advanced the integration of major social assistance schemes under a unified social welfare card and a consolidated registration system. However, children with disabilities still face challenges in accessing social benefits as they are still underrepresented in data systems and social protection policy design in Indonesia.
Following a dialogue between the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child (the Committee) and the Government of Indonesia (GOI) to examine the implementation of the United Nations Convention of the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) for the 2014–2024 period in May 2025, the Committee adopted its Concluding Observations (CRC CO) for the GOI in June 2025.  The GOI advanced implementation of the CRC Concluding Observations by developing ministry-specific action points, led by MoWECP and Bappenas, while the Ministry of Foreign Affairs engaged child-focused civil society organizations to support inclusive follow-up.

In 2025, UNICEF Indonesia focused on a strategically selected set of results that demonstrate progress against national priorities and the UNICEF Strategic Plan, while reinforcing accountability and positioning UNICEF as a trusted partner for children. These achievements reflect UNICEF’s contribution to evidence generation, systems strengthening, policy reform, service delivery and capacity development, aligned with the UNSDCF and the Government of Indonesia’s RPJMN 2025–2029 and Asta Cita priorities. 
UNICEF had a key technical role in the Government’s flagship Free Nutritious Meals Programme, which started in January. Implementation was strengthened through the implementation of the Centre of Excellence in close collaboration with the Ministry of National Development Planning, the National Nutrition Agency and IPB University to support capacity development, evidence generation, nutrition education and shaping policies and guidelines for the programme. By end of 2025, the programme reached over 55 million children and women against a target of 82 million beneficiaries. While the target was not fully achieved, progress made within the first year of implementation represents an important milestone and demonstrates the Government’s commitment to addressing nutrition challenges nationwide. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health (MOH) to conduct a comprehensive review of the national nutrition programme, assessing progress, bottlenecks and implementation challenges across the lifecycle. This analysis generated evidence to inform national strategic priorities, guide investment decisions, and strengthen the delivery of essential nutrition services. The review also provided a critical evidence base to inform UNICEF nutrition programming under the 2026–2030 Country Programme.
Provincial capacity for young child nutrition was strengthened through a combination of online and in-person Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) training modalities. More than 3,000 health workers participated in these capacity-building initiatives, improving the quality and consistency of counselling and service delivery. UNICEF also provided technical support to strengthen nutrition data systems, including support to the national nutrition survey, through questionnaire development and data analysis, and improvements to nutrition surveillance systems covering wasting, food supplementation and growth monitoring.
UNICEF contributed to strengthened nutrition governance by successfully advocating for revision of the national guidelines on the management of acute malnutrition. As a result, a policy review was carried out and led to the release of the national guidelines aligned with global recommendations and the allocation of over USD 500,000 for the procurement of RUTF. The Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) services were provided in 176 districts in 2025 against an overall target of 161 districts. Ongoing effort from the government have the potential to expand to all remaining districts by 2030. During the year, nearly 5.7 million children were screened for wasting, and 34,806 children with severe wasting received treatment. UNICEF supported the Government in updating national IMAM guidelines, finalising technical guidance on the local production of therapeutic foods, and establishing six IMAM Centres of Excellence to strengthen service quality, learning and scale-up.
Adolescent nutrition programming was strengthened across all 350 targeted districts through capacity development, monitoring, and youth engagement. As a result, 13.4 million adolescent girls received iron and folic acid supplementation.  
With regards to maternal nutrition, UNICEF’s high-level advocacy contributed to the finalisation of the national scale-up plan and the official launch of the strategic shift from iron folic acid supplementation (IFA) to multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS). As a result, the maternal nutrition outcomes were enhanced through Mother Support Groups for nutrition education and counselling as well as the national roll-out of the MMS, reaching 581,465 pregnant women in 15 priority provinces against a target of 1.3 million. Delays in implementation were partly due to the timing of MMS availability. The Ministry of Health has been leading the finalisation of a roadmap to scale up the programme and invest USD 1.6 billion to improve maternal nutrition and address child wasting nationwide over a period of five years.
To address the growing challenge of overweight and obesity, UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministries of Health and Education,  produced 20 new knowledge products in 2025, bringing the total to 80. These were disseminated through policy dialogues and communication campaigns, reaching 858 decision-makers and more than 203,000 community members, including children, adolescents and caregivers. In partnership with the Government, UNICEF supported the scale-up of school- and community-based obesity prevention initiatives to 18 additional districts, expanding coverage to 30 districts, and reaching 26,627 children, nearly half of whom were girls.
UNICEF also supported the development of evidence-based products to inform national nutrition policies on preparedness and response to natural and human-made hazards. Emergency Preparedness Plans were strengthened in eight selected provinces to safeguard essential nutrition services during emergencies, including during the recent flood emergency in Aceh, North Sumatra, and West Sumatra.
UNICEF continued to support the Government in eliminating open defecation, expanding safely managed WASH services, and strengthening climate resilience. National progress included a reduction in open defecation to 2.35 per cent of households and an increase in access to safely managed drinking water from 11.8 per cent in 2020 to 20.45 per cent in 2023. UNICEF’s contribution focused on addressing systemic bottlenecks in governance, data, financing, and climate integration. 
Through high-level advocacy and technical leadership, UNICEF’s support enabled 18 of 37 government priority districts to achieve Open Defecation Free (ODF) status, improving sanitation conditions for approximately 12 million people. UNICEF also supported the expansion of safely managed sanitation through targeted provincial engagement and evidence generation, including the development of actionable roadmaps in Aceh and West Nusa Tenggara. Strengthened local capacity, digital desludging systems and diversified financing pathways enabled greater access to improved services, particularly for low-income households.
UNICEF supported the evaluation of the national sanitation programme (PPSP), which reaffirmed its significant contributions, including the development of Strategic Sanitation Plans in 486 of 514 districts and reductions in open defecation, with basic sanitation access exceeding 85 per cent. The evaluation identified implementation gaps that limit the transition to safely managed, inclusive and climate-resilient services and recommended strengthened institutional ownership, regulatory compliance, private sector engagement and equity-focused approaches.
Policy advocacy was further advanced through the development of policy briefs linking WASH priorities to the Quick Wins Programmes of the Government, including the Free Nutritious Meals and School Renovation programmes. To support government scale-up of climate-resilient and inclusive WASH services in schools and health facilities, UNICEF demonstrated these models in 43 schools and 46 health-care facilities, benefiting over 12,000 students and 2.2 million people. UNICEF integrated menstrual health and hygiene into school WASH programmes,  and through the Oky app, 7,486 girls and 1,021 boys were reached (478,300 users nationally), with 85 per cent reporting increased knowledge. 
Systemic reforms to improve water quality advanced through the integration of fragmented data systems, updates to national strategies, and the expansion of Water Safety Plans. Digital platforms, including the Surabaya water quality system and the East Nusa Tenggara WASH dashboard, strengthened real-time monitoring and risk-informed planning. The national WASH climate resilience framework and PERIKSA, an assessment tool to help evaluate the extent of climate resilience of facilities and systems, are being further scaled up, with a web-based version now nearing completion. A compendium of greener sanitation technologies will inform sustainable infrastructure choices and contribute to national adaptation and carbon reduction goals.
Emergency preparedness was strengthened through the development of child-sensitive, climate-resilient contingency plans in seven provinces and the adoption of a new five-year WASH Cluster plan. During the Lewotobi volcanic eruption and floods in Sumatra, UNICEF supported government coordination and response effectiveness.
During the reporting period, UNICEF contributed to Indonesia’s health transformation agenda, building on momentum achieved in previous years. Support focused on maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health, health system strengthening, and emergency preparedness. UNICEF supported the expansion of the Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) system to include a new module on under-five deaths,  resulting in an updated 2025 MPDSR guideline. To support scale up of MPDSR, implementation guidelines for hospitals were also developed. UNICEF trained eight military facilities using these new guidelines, and through this training of trainers,  will reach 120 more military hospitals. Additionally, in 20 hospitals across Aceh, Java, Kalimantan, Maluku and Papua, already implementing MPDSR, improvements in quality of care, including on clinical governance,  were initiated.
UNICEF further contributed to strengthening the universal child health screening programme (CKG), benefiting over 11.9 million children through improved care pathways, supply forecasting and workforce planning.
Immunisation remained a core area of support. Following the introduction of four new vaccines in 2024, HPV vaccination sustained high coverage, reaching 95 per cent in 2023 and 89 per cent in 2024, with a transition to a single-dose schedule in 2025. To address HPV vaccine hesitancy, interpersonal communication approaches were applied, in collaboration with MOH and partners, and reached over 43,000 children and caregivers, resulting in improved vaccine understanding, while a digital campaign reached over 10 million. UNICEF launched a digital immunisation training module on the Plataran Sehat platform, reaching 60,000 health workers and strengthening cold chain management nationwide. Malaria elimination efforts advanced, with 18 UNICEF-supported districts achieving elimination status, contributing to a total of 412 malaria-free districts nationwide (80 per cent).
Adolescent health interventions were scaled through digital platforms and school-based initiatives in five provinces (Aceh, West Java, Central Java, East Java, and South Sulawesi). More than 35,000 adolescents engaged through FunDoo and U-Report, while the Youth Health Check initiative screened 7.2 million students for health risks. UNICEF strengthened girls’ agency through an adolescent-led scorecard engaging 2,905 adolescents (70 per cent girls), revealing persistent gender and disability-based barriers and distinct service needs that require gender-responsive health services. UNICEF supported the Government in the revision of Government Regulation No. 28/2024 on smoking prevention, which raised the legal age for tobacco use from 19 to 21 years, strengthened regulatory measures on nicotine content, and expanded smoke-free zones by increasing minimum distances between tobacco retailers and schools. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Transportation in developing a policy brief on “Road Safety Strategy for Children and Adolescents in Indonesia”, which contributed to the revision and updating of the “Indonesian National Road Safety Plan 2021-2040”, which explicitly prioritises child and youth road safety.
The development of national emergency preparedness guidelines, the Health Emergency Operations Centre manual, mass gathering protocols, and the National Action Plan for Health Security (2025–2029) contributed to the strengthening of the health system's resilience. Successful piloting of these guidelines in West Nusa Tenggara informed replication in other districts, and supported the national scale-up strategy, enhancing readiness for health emergencies and climate-related risks.
In support of the Government’s priority to implement 13 years of compulsory education, UNICEF provided technical input into the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education’s overarching ‘grand’ design for this reform, which is intended as a blueprint to ensure access of every child to inclusive and quality pre-primary, primary and secondary education. Key areas of UNICEF’s input included revision of the National Education Law; addressing inequalities between civil servant and contract teachers in their entitlements and the important of recognition of prior learning for ECE teacher qualification upgrading; shared results from key research, showing the impact of best practice approaches in early childhood education (play-based methodologies and parental engagement) quality early grade learning (structured pedagogy); and discussed strategic steps to optimizing the use of ‘one roof schools’ (SATU-ATAP) to improving access to ECE.
National assessment data from 2023-2024 indicated that approximately two-thirds of primary, junior secondary, and senior secondary students achieved minimum proficiency levels in literacy and numeracy. Students in the eastern region of the country are lagging significantly behind students in other regions in achieving minimum proficiency levels in literacy and numeracy. UNICEF’s education programming focused on strengthening local education ecosystems, particularly in easter regions, through targeted support at national and subnational levels.
In early childhood education (ECE), UNICEF worked with 10 local governments in East Nusa Tenggara and Papua to improve service quality and access and draw lessons for expansion. These efforts benefited 3,335 disadvantaged children (51 per cent girls), 272 teachers and principals (90 per cent female), and 2,115 parents and caregivers (74 per cent female). With UNICEF’s advocacy support, local governments allocated more than USD 930,000 in 2025 to expand ECE services. Cumulatively, ECE scale-up reached 34 districts during 2021–2025 programme cycle, starting from a baseline of just two districts. 
For early grade learning (EGL), UNICEF extended programming to six provinces in East Nusa Tenggara and Papua. In 2025, approximately 27,000 primary school children, 511 teachers, and 129 schools benefited. Cumulatively, EGL scale-up reached 38 of 40 targeted districts during 2021–2025, supporting 58,000 children (49 per cent girls). Local governments allocated IDR 50.7 billion (USD 3 million) to expand EGL initiatives, benefiting 390 schools, 3,000 teachers and 100,000 community stakeholders. A planning and budgeting guideline was developed and disseminated to facilitate national scale-up.
UNICEF also supported national and subnational efforts to address out-of-school children (OOSC). In 2025, UNICEF’s technical support enabled expansion to three additional districts, preventing 61,000 (40 per cent girls) children from dropping out and supporting 33,500 (45 per cent girls) children to return to learning. Cumulatively, 59 districts implemented OOSC programmes during 2021–2025, preventing dropout among approximately 237,000 (49 per cent girls) children and supporting 104,900 (40 per cent girls) children to return to learning. Local governments mobilized more than USD 3.5 million to support these efforts.
For adolescent skills development, UNICEF continued to scale up the programme, reaching 8,148 adolescents (60 per cent girls) across 174 schools in 33 districts in two provinces, supporting the development of 21st-century, digital and entrepreneurial skills. Adolescents, particularly girls, were empowered through this programme to develop more than 500 digital and non-digital adolescent-led solutions to address pressing community challenges in their schools and communities. The results achieved from 2021 to 2025 led to programme scale-up, with more than 31,000 (61 per cent girls) disadvantaged adolescents reached, in 38 districts across three provinces. UNICEF is using the results from this investment to enhance the availability of quality adolescent skills development content available to all senior secondary teachers and students on the national digital learning platform; and, at the sub-national level, working with local governments to establish and prioritise regulatory and financing systems that can be leveraged to scale-up the programme from local government resources. 
The Government of Indonesia registered progress in relation to policies addressing child marriage and Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). In partnership with the Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and Child Protection (MoWECP), UNICEF supported the national rollout of Child Marriage and FGM Prevention Guidelines for Family Learning Centres (PUSPAGA) and a study on unregistered (siri) marriages linked to child marriage. The Ministry of Population and Family Development also issued early detection and referral guidelines that integrate FGM prevention across 90,000 Early Childhood Development Centres and 4,000 childcare centres under the TAMASYA programme.
Violence prevention efforts were expanded through positive discipline training in 200 selected schools, reaching 542 school personnel. Positive discipline and bullying prevention were institutionalised through the issuance of the Minister of Primary and Secondary Education decree on safe and comfortable school culture (Decree No. 6/2026). Nationwide initiatives to enhance mental health literacy reached 166,760 adolescents (95,012 girls and 71,748 boys) and 16,066 caregivers (8,533 females and 7,533 males). More than 611,000 children were mobilised as Agents of Change, contributing to a presidential call to end child marriage and FGM/C. Adolescents further amplified messages on mental health, harmful practices and online safety through U-Report chatbots, social media campaigns and partnerships with youth-led groups. Life Skills Education (LSE) sessions were delivered to National Children’s Forum members across all 38 provinces, integrating knowledge on FGM/C prevention and strengthening decision-making skills. Under the BERANI II programme, LSE sessions in East Java, West Nusa Tenggara and South Sulawesi reached 19,383 children and contributed to a 70 per cent reduction in child marriage dispensation applications in targeted districts.
Service delivery capacity also improved significantly. Integrated protection services have been established in 358 of 514 districts/cities and 34 of 38 provinces, supported by special allocation funds for operational and infrastructure needs. UNICEF sustained its contribution through policy advocacy and systematic capacity building, including the establishment of a national pool of master trainers. These trainers led cascading and regular training programmes across provinces and districts, strengthening the functionality, consistency, and quality of service delivery nationwide. In parallel to strengthening the services, MoWECP launched SIMFONI PPA V.3 (powered by Primero), an upgraded case management and coordination system in handling any case of violence against children and women comprehensively. UNICEF supported the development of Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) training modules and accountability tools for service providers, benefiting approximately 2,135,594 people (1,072,165 male and 1,063,429 female). 
The Ministry of Social Affairs introduced costing models and workforce ratios to enhance service quality and efficiency, to which UNICEF supported processes on costing, workforce ratio models, and standardised definitions, resulting in an agreed national definition and the establishment of a working group to develop and introduce workforce planning models in Indonesia. Over 300 villages established community-level child protection mechanisms, with UNICEF’s contribution towards building the capacity of village leaders and community actors, advocating for child protection regulations and financing through village funds, and developing national guidelines and a compendium of good practices on community-level child protection mechanisms.
Through UNICEF support, an integrated model linking health facilities with civil registration offices resulted in increased birth registration for newborns. This is now replicated across remote districts of Papua and Southwest Papua under newly issued local regulations. Emergency preparedness was reinforced through the development of Child Protection in Emergencies (CPiE) Coordination Guidelines and CPiE training in six provinces, ensuring stronger readiness to protect children during emergencies.
UNICEF contributed to strengthening child-responsive planning and budgeting at national and subnational levels. Nationally, UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy, through sectoral budget briefs, analyses of multidimensional child deprivations, fiscal policy reviews and budget credibility assessments, helped the Ministry of Finance to integrate stronger child-focused priorities into primary policy documents, including the Macroeconomic Framework and Key Fiscal Policies (KEM-PPKF) 2026 and the RPJMN 2025–2029. The jointly developed Multidimensional Deprivation Index informed fiscal planning and contributed to the formulation of new child-rights budgeting indicators hosted by MoWECP and the National Development Planning Agency (Bappenas).
At the subnational level, the most transformative progress was UNICEF’s contribution to the development of AI-based child budget tagging, which has now been adopted by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MoHA) and the Ministry of Finance (MoF). In August 2025, the tagging results were embedded within the Local Government Information System (SIPD), MoHA’s subnational planning and budgeting platform used by all local governments, enabling more consistent identification and prioritisation of child-related investments throughout the planning and budgeting process. The tagging results were also integrated into a child-related spending dashboard, incorporated into MoF information systems in January 2025, enabling real-time analysis of allocations, disbursements, and spending patterns. This has already informed immunisation and nutrition financing reviews across 11 provinces, revealing gaps in adequacy and opportunities for better resource alignment.
Further governance improvements included institutionalising the Management Information System for child participation and continued progress under the Child Friendly Cities Initiative. 
UNICEF also advanced innovative financing. In Aceh, USD 29.43 million in Islamic Social Funds supported child- and family-focused programmes, directly benefiting more than 153,000 people, including 18,432 children in 2021-24. In East Java, the Integrated Subnational Financing Framework (ISFF) was developed and incorporated into the 2025–2029 development plan, opening avenues for municipal bonds and other financing instruments. To scale ISFF nationally, Indonesia would need to institutionalise it in national planning guidance and standardise it as a replicable toolkit. To promote public engagement, UNICEF continued its support of the Ministry of Finance’s fiscal literacy initiatives, including the Budget Olympics, which have engaged over 60,000 students since 2022.
UNICEF also contributed to the strengthening of Indonesia’s social protection system to reduce child poverty through evidence generation, advocacy and system improvements. A significant achievement was integrating the Social Protection Information Management System into the National Socioeconomic Single Data (DTSEN) in accordance with Presidential Regulation No. 4/2025, establishing DTSEN as the primary platform for welfare data and emergency targeting. UNICEF and Bappenas also initiated a Scalability Framework to reinforce emergency social protection actions. The Government committed to integrating PKH cash transfers, Sembako, PIP scholarships, KIS health insurance subsidies, and electricity subsidies into a single Social Welfare Card, improving targeting and adjusting benefits based on local living costs. UNICEF strengthened the evidence base through gendered political economy analysis on unpaid care work, while EAPRO-supported capacity-building culminated in Indonesia’s first gender and social protection policy dialogue, signalling growing government ownership of inclusive social protection reform.
Child-focused reforms advanced through prioritising disability actions in the 2025–2029 National Action Plan and initiating a study using INDOMOD to estimate the cost of caring for a child with a disability. UNICEF also strengthened policymaker engagement and trained over 180 officials on gender, climate and disaster-responsive social protection.
UNICEF supported the scale-up of the child-centred disaster management planning by integrating the Child-Centred Contingency Planning Guidelines and training module in the National Disaster Management Authority’s training programme and by providing capacity development for over 292 government and other partners in South Sulawesi, Papua, East Nusa Tenggara and West Nusa Tenggara. A total of 94 implementing partners’ representatives were sensitised on the Accountability to the Affected Population framework and tools.
UNICEF continued climate and environment action through policy advocacy, guidelines and tools development, and children and youth empowerment for CEED actions. Specifically, UNICEF advocated for and supported 69 children and youth to contribute to the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (NAP) led by the Ministry of Environment. The recommendations from the Children & Youth (C&Y) consultation were integrated into the NAP. The C&Y NAP pre-consultation gathered inputs from 6,549 adolescents and youth. UNICEF supported youth-led climate and environment action through initiating the Green Rising movement in Indonesia. The six youth teams received seed funding for climate and environment action,  which resulted in 4,230 trees planted, 3,904 adolescents and youth engaged in action, and 3,240 kg of waste collected. A total of 11,671 youth participated in the digital Climate ActBot campaign, as part of this initial Green Rising initiative.
UNICEF Indonesia utilised strategic communications and public advocacy approaches to promote child rights and support programmatic efforts, achieving an estimated 435.9 million digital reach across all UNICEF Indonesia social media accounts and 26.5 million social media engagements. Media coverage,  which mentions UNICEF,  doubled to 6,800 articles and reports, compared with 2024. With 2.8 million social media followers, 1.6 million website visitors, and strengthened influencer partnerships, including the launch of the UNICEF Champion initiative, audiences were engaged on issues including nutrition, online safety, health, mental health, and climate action. On World Children’s Day, the My Day, My Rights campaign highlighted the voices of children and engaged Ministers of Bappenas, MOH, MoWECP and Foreign Affairs, along with other key officials and the UN Resident Coordinator. The campaign reached 26.5 million users through UNICEF channels, with an additional 10 million reached via celebrity partners. In collaboration with the Ministry of Religious Affairs, UNICEF developed an online course on Islam and Child Rights, to be integrated into the Ministry’s learning platform to promote child rights through religious leaders’ engagement.
UNICEF’s efforts reached over 110,000 adolescent girls, strengthening their skills, enabling them to refuse child marriage, and driving government reforms in three provinces. UNICEF supported Indonesia’s first socio-economic model to guide investments in girls’ education, protection and future economic contribution. The Statistical Adolescent Profile set a regional precedent for data-driven policymaking on adolescents. Through advocacy, adolescents’ participation rights are included in the 2025–2029 National Development Plan and subnational decision-making through new regulations and monitoring systems. UNICEF also made children with disabilities visible across sectors, leading to national commitments such as integrating the Child Functioning Module into the 2025 Family Data Survey.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The dynamic nutrition landscape required UNICEF to remain agile and responsive to evolving national priorities. In 2025, UNICEF proactively engaged line ministries and the newly established National Nutrition Agency to develop technical guidance for the management of the Free Nutritious Meal Programme, reinforcing UNICEF’s position as a key government partner for programme rollout. The target for the flagship nutritious meals programme increased mid-year. UNICEF supported the Government in reviewing and address the periodic challenges in implementation. In addition, UNICEF advocated for a more multi-sectoral approach to the programme, which was progressively adopted. 
In parallel, UNICEF responded to the MOH’s request for technical assistance to conduct a comprehensive review of the national nutrition programme. This evidence-generation effort informed the identification of priority gaps and opportunities and contributed to shaping national strategic directions. These experiences underscored the importance of flexibility, timely technical support and strong institutional partnerships in navigating policy transitions while sustaining progress across the nutrition continuum.
Persistent structural barriers continued to constrain equitable WASH progress. Limited subnational financing and insufficient mechanisms to support low-income households restricted access to safely managed sanitation. Variations in the understanding and application of climate-resilient sanitation approaches hindered consistent integration across regions. In schools and health facilities, sanitation remained a low operational priority despite national programmes, reflecting uneven commitment, data use and climate-informed planning. Varied technical capacity further resulted in inconsistent water quality monitoring and risk-based management, while emergency coordination mechanisms required significant strengthening. Key lessons from 2025 demonstrate that sustainable scale-up depends on strong systems. Early integration of climate resilience and GEDSI principles improved uptake, while unified digital tools strengthened accountability. Platforms such as the NAP process and WASH FIT expansion showed how sustained advocacy can drive government ownership. Moving forward, UNICEF will leverage momentum around Asta Cita priorities and the climate agenda to strengthen regulatory frameworks, financing mechanisms, emergency coordination and inclusive service delivery. Implementing sanitation evaluation recommendations remains essential for accelerating safely managed sanitation.
Despite continued progress, several challenges persisted in Indonesia’s health sector, including geographic disparities in service delivery, limited digital connectivity in remote areas, and systemic underinvestment. Health expenditure remained modest, accounting for only 5–6 per cent of the 2025 State Budget (i.e., IDR218.5 trillion), below global benchmarks (15 per cent) for universal health coverage. Immunization efforts continued to face vaccine hesitancy and supply chain constraints, while malaria elimination and adolescent health programmes required sustained resourcing and context-specific adaptation. Key lessons from 2025 emphasize the value of high-level policy advocacy, the use of digital solutions to strengthen immunization and health information systems, and sustained engagement with provincial governments to mobilize local resources. Flexible programming and rapid adaptation to evolving national initiatives, including the Free Nutritious Meals Programme, proved critical. Looking ahead, UNICEF will prioritize inclusive digital transformation, decentralized planning, and innovative financing to address equity gaps and strengthen community-linked quality services.
While the adoption of a 13-year compulsory education framework represents a positive policy shift, significant efforts are still required to operationalise this commitment, particularly to universalise one year of pre-primary education. A key lesson from 2025, which also marks the final year of the current country programme, was the effectiveness of a systematic approach that balances national-level evidence generation and policy engagement with sustained subnational support to strengthen local education ecosystems. This approach enabled national influence while expanding the quality and reach of services for disadvantaged children. Looking ahead, substantial opportunities exist to leverage large-scale national education transformation initiatives to improve learning outcomes across sub-sectors. This includes advancing digital teaching and learning reforms, underpinned by the promotion of gender-responsive and disability-inclusive policies and practices, to ensure equitable access and improved learning quality.
While quantitative targets for integrated protection services for women and children (UPTD PPA) were achieved, evaluation findings highlighted inconsistent compliance with national standards, underscoring the need to strengthen service quality and systematic oversight. Budget reductions affecting both the Government and UNICEF, alongside broader global financial constraints, limited the capacity to address emerging risks. Looking ahead, several opportunities offer a strong foundation for advancing child protection outcomes. These include the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child Concluding Observations, and ASEAN Regional Plans of Action on eliminating child marriage and FGM, ending violence against children, and preventing online sexual exploitation and abuse. Nationally, new regulations on online child protection and derivative regulations under the Sexual Violence Crime Law provide important advocacy entry points. Evidence from the UPTD PPA evaluation, workforce costing studies, and learnings from community-based systems will continue to inform system strengthening and national scale-up.
The success of subnational child budget tagging innovation was driven not by artificial intelligence alone, but by its transformation into a practical governance tool that enhances consistency, transparency and evidence-based decision-making across public finance systems. Embedding tagging results directly into platforms routinely used by local governments ensured that child-focused classifications became automatic rather than discretionary. This institutionalisation strengthened accountability and enabled more systematic prioritisation of investments for children. The experience underscored the importance of aligning technical solutions with strong national ownership, collective leadership, effective coordination, and long-term system strengthening. Moving forward, sustaining these gains will require continued capacity development, policy reinforcement, and integration of child-responsive budgeting practices within broader public financial management reforms.
Public resource allocation and expenditure efficiency remain important considerations for advancing service delivery outcomes. Indonesia’s decentralised governance framework assigns substantial responsibility for social service delivery to subnational governments, including provinces, districts and villages. These responsibilities are exercised within the context of differing institutional, technical and fiscal capacities across regions, which influences the extent to which evidence-based programmes can be systematically prioritised and implemented. In 2025, these dynamics were further shaped by the introduction of Intergovernmental Transfer (TKD) efficiency measures under Presidential Instruction No. 1/2025, intended to enhance the alignment of public expenditure with national priorities. The resulting 5.5 per cent reallocation of transfers had a greater effect on regions with higher dependence on central government funding. 
Budget reductions at the national level constrained subnational capacity to develop and review contingency plans; at the same time, prior investments made by UNICEF in sectoral emergency preparedness bring value. Several guidelines and tools previously supported by UNICEF were used during the flood emergency response that was led by the government. Continuation of selected refresher orientations or updating of tools and protocols based on lessons from the response will be part of UNICEF’s regular support in the future.  The overall budget efficiency measures at the national level constrained subnational capacity to develop and review contingency plans. Progress was made in climate policy advocacy through meaningful child and youth participation, ensuring child-sensitive climate, environmental and disaster risk analysis across sectors requires sustained, coordinated action. UNICEF will continue leveraging its convening role to promote cross-sectoral leadership, strengthen climate-smart social services, support child-centred contingency planning, and expand partnerships that sustain visibility and systemic change.
The ability to adapt in multiple ways is key. A growing interest in ‘impactful journalism’ has created opportunities to engage audiences through long-form television programming, podcasts and digital platforms such as YouTube, offering new avenues to elevate child rights issues and public awareness.

In 2025, children in the Lao People’s Democratic Republic (Lao PDR) continued to experience intersecting economic, social and environmental pressures, even as the country advanced key political and policy reforms in preparation for graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026. Macroeconomic conditions improved compared to earlier acute crises, supported by a more stable exchange rate, easing inflation and modest growth. However, progress remained fragile and uneven, with the most disadvantaged children facing persistent risks to their survival, learning, development and protection.
Lao PDR ranks 121st out of 167 countries on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Index, with a score of around 62.5, indicating that significant challenges remain in achieving the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Moderate progress has been observed in No Poverty (SDG 1), Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6), Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 8), and Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9). However, progress has stagnated in Quality Education (SDG 4), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10), and Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12), while Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3) and Zero Hunger (SDG 2) continue to face major challenges. Sustainable Cities and Communities (SDG 11) and Climate Action (SDG 13) show declining trends, reflecting the growing impact of urbanization and climate-related hazards on children.
