At the policy level, 2025 marked a decisive transition. The formulation of the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (NSEDP, 2026-2030) and the restructuring of the government signaled renewed commitment to macroeconomic stability, climate resilience and human development, aligned with the 2030 Agenda. Progress in strengthening the child protection and social service workforce—particularly through the promulgation of the Law on Social Work and implementation of the National Plan of Action (NPA) for Child Protection System Strengthening—demonstrated increased national ownership of child protection reforms. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) review of the state party report submitted in 2024 remained pending by CRC Committee, listed under future sessions. 
Macroeconomic pressures continued to constrain public investment in social services, with direct implications for children. Government spending on social protection remained low at an estimated 2–4 per cent of the 2025 state budget, reflecting persistent gaps in coverage and financing (Ministry of Finance, 2025). Fiscal consolidation has been achieved largely at the expense of essential services: combined public expenditure on education and health declined from 4.9 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2013 to 2.3 per cent in 2024, with health spending stagnating at around 1 per cent and education expenditure more than halving since 2019 (ADB, 2025).  These reductions in public spending have in turn weakened the availability and quality of essential services for children, contributing to fewer learning resources in schools, reduced access to basic health services, and widening disparities affecting the most vulnerable households.
These constraints were compounded by a sharp decline in Official Development Assistance (ODA). Lao PDR is among the most affected countries in the region by ODA withdrawals, with funding projected to fall by 17.4 per cent in 2025 and a further 10 per cent in 2026. As a result, an estimated USD 25 million in UN funding for 2025 has been cut or is at risk, placing critical health, nutrition and education programmes under strain as the country approaches LDC graduation.
Economic growth in 2025 was projected at around 4.2 per cent, driven by recovery in tourism and transport alongside expansion in energy, mining and manufacturing (World Bank, 2025). With two-thirds of the population living in rural areas and nearly half engaged in low-productivity agriculture, growth remained capital-intensive and generated limited employment. Although food insecurity declined to 6 per cent by mid-2025 as prices stabilized, nearly half of households continued to rely on coping strategies, indicating persistent structural vulnerabilities. Poverty—projected to affect around one-third of the population — continued to constrain household investments in children’s nutrition, education and healthcare, sustaining risks of child mortality, undernutrition and school dropouts.
Demographic trends reinforced both risks and opportunities. With an estimated population of 7.6 million and more than one-third under the age of 18, Lao PDR has a young population with long-term development potential if adequately supported. However, according to Lao Social Indicator Survey III 2023 (LSIS III), adolescent birth rates remained high - 89 per 1,000 adolescent girls aged 15–19, rising to 146 per 1,000 among poorer households and 197 per 1,000 among Hmong-Mien, reinforcing cycles of poverty and limiting girls’ opportunities. The country has the highest rate of child marriage in the region, despite its prohibition by law – 30.5% of young women were married before age 18, and 6.1% before age 15, with significant variations across ethnic groups.Together, these trends are underpinned by harmful gender norms that normalize early marriage and childbearing, with implications on adolescents’, especially adolescent mothers’, access to health and nutrition knowledge and services, and perpetuating negative intergenerational outcomes for their children. Undernutrition persists, with wasting - the most immediate and life-threatening form of malnutrition in children - worsening and almost doubling in the last decade, from 5.9 per cent in 2011 to 10.7 per cent in 2023, with no improvement in 2025 as per the nutrition surveillance data. In addition, 36.2 per cent of children under five stunted in 2025, placing Lao PDR at risk of missing global reduction targets (National Nutrition Surveillance). In addition, only 65 per cent of children under five are registered at birth, the lowest rate in the region, limiting children’s access to essential services and social protection (LSIS III).
Education outcomes remain weak, particularly for children from poor, rural and disadvantaged backgrounds including ethnolinguistic groups. Participation in early learning is low, with 64.4 per cent of children aged 3–5 enrolled in pre-primary education in 2024/25 (Lao Education and Sports Management Information System (LESMIS)) and 66.6 per cent participating in organised learning one year before primary school (LSIS III)—well below the SDG target of 90 per cent. Out-of-school rates have increased across all levels, driven by poverty, child labour, early marriage and limited perceived returns to education. Currently, 58% of adolescents of upper secondary school age are not attending any levels of education. While overall out-of-school rates between girls and boys are not significantly different, the causes and consequences of school dropout carry gender-specific risks such as child marriage and adolescent pregnancy, which often result in girls’ permanent exclusion from education.Learning outcomes are critically weak: Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics 2024 (SEA-PLM) shows that nearly half of Grade 5 students remain at ‘very low’ reading and mathematics proficiency levels, whilst few reached the minimum proficiency levels (11 percent reading; 32 percent mathematics).  On average, girls showed greater average performance than boys in reading and mathematics  especially at the primary education age, and this difference between boys and girls has widened between 2019 and 2024 for Lao PDR. Teacher shortages, low teaching quality and weak learning environments—over one-third of primary classes are multigrade and 91 per cent of children report not being able to attend class due to teacher absence (LSIS III)—further undermine education as a pathway out of poverty.
Labour market dynamics and limited opportunities for adolescent development further heightened children’s vulnerability. High levels of child labour (23.1 per cent; LSIS III), child marriage (30.5 per cent; LSIS III), upper-secondary school dropout (13.5 per cent; LESMIS, 2025) and out-of-school adolescents at upper secondary level (58 per cent; LSIS III), underscore the strong link between economic insecurity and child rights deprivations. Employment growth remained concentrated in informal self-employment, while outward migration—particularly among young workers—accelerated due to low wages and limited decent work opportunities. Although nominal incomes rose in 2025, they did not keep pace with cumulative inflation, reinforcing inequality and reliance on negative coping strategies, also for adolescents.
Up to one million children in Laos are highly exposed to riverine flood risk and up to two million to cyclones, heatwaves, and air pollution, disproportionately impacting poor and rural populations (UNICEF EAPRO, 2023). These risks contribute to high disease burdens, with 5 per cent of under-five deaths linked to diarrhoeal disease, 18 per cent to air pollution, and 24 per cent of disability-adjusted life years attributable to preventable environmental risks (IHME, University of Washington, 2023). In addition, at least one-third of children lack access to safe water and sanitation, while climate-related shocks repeatedly damage transport networks, schools, health facilities and water systems. Together, these challenges underscore the urgency of investing in climate-resilient infrastructure, and disaster-risk-informed service delivery to ensure equitable access to essential services for children.

In 2025, UNICEF Lao PDR achieved significant and scalable results for children by combining high-level policy advocacy with systems strengthening, community engagement, and innovation. Despite fiscal constraints and climate vulnerabilities, UNICEF’s work remained strategically aligned with national priorities under the 10th NSEDP and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).
This section highlights key strategic results where UNICEF’s partnerships, technical leadership, and resources were instrumental in driving systemic change and improving the situation of children described in the previous chapter.
Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives
UNICEF contributed to the Government of Lao PDR’s efforts to reduce child mortality and malnutrition by strengthening primary healthcare, immunization, and nutrition systems. The results reflect evidence-based policy adoption, digital transformation, resilient supply and cold chain systems, and integrated service delivery. This work aligns with SDG 3, the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, and the UNICEF Strategic Plan change strategies on systems strengthening, community engagement, risk-informed programming, and innovation.
A major outcome was the government’s adoption of the National Immunization Strategy (NIS) 2025–2030, providing a costed, government-owned roadmap to close immunity gaps and improve equitable coverage. Following an analysis of gender-related barriers to immunization, UNICEF supported the development of a Gender Roadmap and the establishment of a National Working Group on Gender in Immunization to address coverage gaps. Operationally, UNICEF supported outbreak preparedness and response when measles and vaccine-derived poliovirus exposed persistent vulnerabilities. In partnership with WHO, UNICEF helped vaccinate 35,960 children across ten severely affected provinces and mobilized 1.6 million polio vaccine doses for 2026 campaigns to mitigate immunity gaps amid fiscal constraints. 

At the same time, UNICEF supported a nationwide digital transformation of immunization through the Electronic Immunization Registry (EIR), enabling real-time, disaggregated data use across 18 provinces and 148 districts. By November 2025, 88.7 per cent of newborns were registered and Penta1 coverage reached 92.79 per cent, signaling better micro-planning, follow-up, and equity in last-mile service delivery. Cold chain resilience improved markedly: equipment malfunction rates fell from 6 per cent to 1.18 per cent across 1,338 health facilities, supported by climate-resilient solar solutions and vehicles for last-mile delivery. These results were made possible by UNICEF’s contribution to the NIS pillars on vaccine supply and cold chain logistics, and demand generation, coordinated through national consultations and the Interagency Coordination Committee, as well as sustained technical assistance and system investments enabled through Regular Resources.

Nutrition outcomes improved through an integrated approach that combined service delivery, social behaviour change (SBC), and strengthened policy frameworks. In 2025, children aged 6–23 months consumed more diverse diets, with 66 per cent achieving minimum dietary diversity during the lean season compared to 35 percent in 2024, surpassing the Country Programme target of 55 per cent. This progress was supported by UNICEF-led promotion of better practices, and a broader reduction in household food insecurity (6%, the lowest since 2022). Major contributions included building national and subnational capacity to design, plan, and implement SBC interventions, and updating the National Mother, Infant and Young Child Nutrition Counseling Package, enabling frontline workers to provide higher-quality, context-adapted counselling. 
Exclusive breastfeeding reached 57 per cent —just shy of the 60 per cent target - supported by the efforts of 87 Breastfeeding Advisors stationed across all 18 provinces, who are trained on a 3-months programme that the Ministry of Health (MoH) run in collaboration with UNICEF,. Protecting breastfeeding environments remains a critical priority for MoH, with UNICEF’s support. As part of this collaboration, an innovative AI-based tool was deployed to detect violations of the Decree on the Control of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes in online marketing, enhancing sustainability and enforcement. Policy advocacy catalyzed a shift from iron-folic acid to multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant women, now integrated into national strategies—laying the groundwork for future reductions in anemia, with impact expected post-2025. Under the government’s leadership, curative nutrition services scaled effectively: Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) sites grew from 205 to 392 and Family Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) approaches were introduced to expand early detection and referral of cases of severe acute malnutrition. 
Another key milestone was the launch of the development of the 10-year National Nutrition Strategy (2026–2035) and the NPA on Nutrition (2026–2031). These plans, grounded in a systems-based approach and aligned with the 10th NSEDP, will guide the country’s nutrition priorities for the coming decade. UNICEF plays a convening role – supporting the Government of Lao PDR throughout this critical process.
The delivery of nutrition interventions through the education system was also strengthened. Working with the Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES), Operational Guidelines for Nutrition Interventions in Secondary Schools were drafted to assist Lao PDR meet its ASEAN commitments on implementing the School Nutrition Package’s Minimum Standards. These guidelines establish a solid foundation for consistent, high-quality nutrition programming across schools nationwide. Complementing this effort, UNICEF provided technical support to the MOH to advance regulations on the sale and promotion of food in schools. This initiative, led jointly by the MoH and MoES, addresses food safety and the broader school food environment—marking a critical step toward creating healthier settings for children.
In parallel, UNICEF strengthened Government’s capacity for emergency preparedness, through the updated Interagency Contingency Plan (IACP), and the review of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for nutrition in emergencies, reinforcing systems that safeguard children’s nutrition during crises.
Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns
Facing a protracted learning crisis, UNICEF’s 2025 education strategy focused on strengthening the enabling environment, improving foundational skills, and leveraging digital innovation to reach and empower the most disadvantaged learners. These efforts align with SDG 4, the UNSDCF, and the UNICEF Strategic Plan change strategies on systems strengthening, equity, and innovation.
A major achievement was UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy and technical leadership as co-chair of the Early Childhood Education (ECE) and General Education working group, which supported and influenced the development of the 10th Education and Sports Sector Development Plan (2026–2030). This plan now reflects equity-focused and cost-effective priorities. Based on positive impact evidence, key UNICEF-supported interventions—such as parenting and community-based school readiness programmes, formative assessment, and Fundamental Quality Standards (FQS)—were institutionalized as core strategies. This institutionalization is expected to benefit 3,389 pre-primary and ECE centres and 8,635 primary schools nationwide, strengthening school readiness and improving foundational learning for children. Thanks to the specific equity-focus those UNICEF-supported interventions carry, children, communities and schools in remote and most disadvantaged, including non-Lao speaking, have benefited most. 
UNICEF also strengthened the MoES’s capacity to generate and use SEA-PLM 2024 primary learning assessment data, which revealed persistent learning poverty with clear disparities, with only 11 per cent of students meeting minimum proficiency in reading and 32 per cent in mathematics. This evidence is informing revisions in assessment policy, curriculum, and teacher development, contributing to improved, inclusive teaching and learning practices for better and more equitable learning outcomes.
In early childhood education, UNICEF supported nationwide dissemination and implementation of the ECE Decree endorsed by the Prime Minister, and accelerated the rollout of Fundamental Quality Standards (FQS). Through school self-assessments and development planning, all ECE settings—urban, rural, public, and community-based—now operate under a specified, standardized framework that has advanced quality ECE services, directly benefiting young children with improved school readiness.
At the primary level, UNICEF expanded innovation to tackle learning poverty. The Eduten platform, an AI-enabled adaptive learning tool, provided personalized mathematics exercises to approximately 1,400 Grade 3–4 students in target schools. UNICEF also built the capacity of 105 teachers to use data-driven learning analytics, showcasing how digital transformation can adapt instruction to individual learning needs including especially slow learners.
For adolescents often left behind, the UPSHIFT programme was a highlight of skills development and youth engagement. Over 160 adolescents (70% girls) participated in social innovation bootcamps across three provinces, with nine teams receiving micro-grants and mentoring to implement community-driven projects on climate resilience and waste management. This initiative strengthened 21st-century skills, digital literacy, and problem-solving agency in adolescents. Furthermore, the Khang Panya Lao digital learning platform saw nearly 160,000 nationwide users, expanding access to curriculum-aligned content and promoting inclusive learning opportunities.
Goal Area 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation
UNICEF achieved a critical milestone in child protection by strengthening the legal and workforce foundations of the national protection system and scaling preventive services. These results align with SDG 16, the UNSDCF, and the UNICEF Strategic Plan change strategies on systems strengthening, evidence-based advocacy, and community engagement.
The most significant achievement was the promulgation of the Law on Social Work, developed with extensive technical and financial support from UNICEF. This Law legally defines the social work profession, establishes certification criteria, and creates a Council of Social Work Professions—providing the long-awaited statutory foundation for professionalizing the social service workforce. UNICEF immediately began supporting the operationalization of the Law on Social Work by partnering with the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, and National University of Laos to develop a standardized training package for para-social workers, ensuring the workforce is equipped to deliver quality protection services.
UNICEF also supported the Government in reviewing and drafting the next NPA on the Elimination of Violence against Children (NPA on EVAC) 2026–2030. Through inclusive consultations, including dedicated youth sessions, the plan addresses urgent priorities such as child marriage and online safety. Given the importance of addressing GBV and Violence against Women (VAW), UNICEF is also supporting the government to address the inter-section between VAC and VAW in the next NPA. This participatory and evidence-based process strengthens national ownership and ensures relevance to emerging protection risks that children face. Inclusion of child marriage as an emerging child protection issue to be prioritized in the next phase of NPA is supported by the DFAT funded Towards Universal Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights in the Indo-Pacific (TUSIP): Ending Child, Early and Forced Marriage (CEFM) in Southeast Asia. Elevation of child marriage – one of the highest rates in ASEAN – in the National Plan is expected to help the government and stakeholders address child marriage in multi-sectoral and holistic manners. 
UNICEF supported the provision of justice and social services for 1,656 child survivors of violence and updated the counseling manual for Lao Women’s Union counselors, improving service quality and survivor support. In addition, preventive services expanded significantly through the Love and Care for Every Child programme, a large-scale social and behavior change initiative promoting positive parenting. In 2025, the programme reached 452 villages across 14 districts, supported by 2,039 trained facilitators, and delivered essential messages to 69,644 individuals, including pregnant mothers and families with young children. This work is building protective family environments from the ground up.
These achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s role as a trusted systems partner, driving legal reform, workforce professionalization, and community-based continuum of child protection services. They reflect a strategic focus on systemic change and equity, ensuring that children are better protected from violence and harmful practices, in particular child marriage.
Goal Area 4: Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment
In 2025, UNICEF supported Lao PDR’s progress toward national sanitation targets and advanced climate-resilient, inclusive WASH systems. Basic sanitation coverage reached 89 per cent, keeping the country on track for its Open Defecation Free (ODF) target by 2030. UNICEF’s equity-focused and risk-informed approach, using climate and equity data, ensured that last-mile households—the poorest and most vulnerable—were prioritized in resource allocation, thereby reducing disparities in access.
Beyond sanitation, UNICEF strengthened systems for sustainable water security by supporting the Government to develop national guidelines for climate-resilient water safety planning and conducting life-cycle costing analyses for community-managed systems. Replicable models for metered water supply schemes and flood-resilient WASH designs were piloted in communities, schools and health facilities. 
Data collection in Houaphanh Province focusing on women’s time-use change in WASH tasks confirmed that improved household water access reduced women’s time burden, improved menstrual health and hygiene, and enabled girls to dedicate more time to education and play, reinforcing transformational programming to advance gender equality Gender capacity within the sector was also strengthened at scale, including through the rollout of the first WASH Guidelines on Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI). This was accompanied by GEDSI minimum standards requirements in project implementation and relevant training with government partners.
UNICEF also advanced climate mainstreaming across social service sectors, guided by the UNICEF Lao PDR Climate Strategy (2024–2026). Key achievements included piloting green school concepts, developing early warning systems for air pollution, and engaging youth in climate action initiatives. As contribution to the Early Warning for All roadmap for Lao PDR, UNICEF established air quality monitoring systems in all 148 Districts of Lao PDR with support from UNICEF’s Office of Innovation to utilize machine learning to provide real time information on air pollution through schools and health centers. These efforts strengthened systemic resilience and equipped children and adolescents with green and transferable skills, aligning with SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and SDG 13 (Climate) as well as the UNICEF Strategic Plan.
Goal Area 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life
UNICEF advanced child-sensitive social policy by generating evidence and piloting inclusive social protection model for children with disabilities and support them with cash assistance, assistive technologies and their families with livelihood skills development to reduce vulnerabilities linked to poverty and exclusion. UNICEF piloted a child disability grant in Xiengkhouang Province, reaching 496 children with monthly cash transfers and assistive devices. Evaluation results showed improved household economic stability and children’s mobility. Lessons from this pilot informed the Government’s roadmap for a Disability Management Information System (DMIS), marking progress toward integrating inclusive social protection into national systems.
Through technical and financial leadership, UNICEF supported completion and dissemination of LSIS III, setting SDG baselines and informing the 10th NSEDP. Evidence from LSIS III and a UNICEF-partnered study with Lao Academy of Social and Economic Sciences (LASES)—showed that eliminating child marriage could yield an annual economic return of USD 41 million—catalyzed high-level dialogue with ministries and the National Assembly, influencing policy discussions on prevention of child marriage.

Cross-Cutting Enablers and Conclusion
Underpinning these sectoral results were UNICEF’s core organisational strategies. Strategic partnerships with government, UN agencies (notably WHO, UNFPA, IOM, and WFP), the World Bank, and a diversifying donor pool were fundamental. Innovation and digital transformation, from the EIR and AI monitoring tools to digital learning platforms, provided new pathways to scale and equity. Equity-focused programming, underpinned by a transformative approach to gender equality, ensured these gains reached girls, children with disabilities, and ethnic communities while tackling harmful gender norms, roles, and relations.
Crucially, Regular Resources (UNICEF’s core funding) provided the indispensable flexibility to seed innovations like the disability grant pilot, respond to outbreaks, invest in foundational data systems like the Equity Analysis, and maintain strategic advocacy. This core support allowed UNICEF to maitain its role as a strategic, agile, and principled partner for children in Lao PDR during a critical year of transition.
In summary, UNICEF’s 2025 contributions were strategically targeted at strengthening national systems, closing equity gaps, and integrating resilience into services for children. By aligning with national priorities and leveraging UNICEF’s global expertise, the Country Office helped lay a stronger foundation for sustainable progress toward the SDGs, ensuring that the path to LDC graduation is also a path of expanded opportunity for every child.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF Lao PDR's programme implementation demonstrated the resilience of adaptive management practices while facing persistent structural barriers that constrain progress toward equity-focused results for the most marginalized children. 
Critical Challenges Constraining Progress
Financing Volatility and Sustainability: The shifting donor landscape, most notably mid-year reductions in funding and partner reprogramming, has created significant vulnerabilities in programme sustainability. In health, donor flux disrupted planned Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and Primary Health Care (PHC) interventions and increased reliance on UNICEF bridging support. In nutrition, misaligned timelines between implementation and technical assistance budgets hindered planned partnerships. These financing disruptions underscore a critical gap: while the underlying theories of change remain sound, sustainability assumptions must be grounded in diversified financing mechanisms and demonstrable government ownership—not contingent on external partner stability. Additionally, Lao PDR's fiscal constraints—with less than 4% of GDP allocated to health, education, and social protection combined—create a structural constraint that extends beyond UNICEF's programming scope and demands advocacy for national-level budget prioritization.
Human Resource Constraints at Community Level: Across health, nutrition, child protection, and education, human resource constraints have emerged as a fundamental bottleneck. For example, the lack of harmonized incentives for Village Health Volunteers, insufficient post-training supervision in nutrition and parenting programmes, limited capacity and awareness around gender-responsive and age-appropriate care, and the struggle of community-based village facilitators for school readiness programme to balance economic survival with programme commitments have all constrained quality of service delivery and staff retention, and may inadvertently reinforce discriminatory norms. These challenges reveal that community-level actors—despite their centrality to PHC, immunization, nutrition, education and child protection outcomes—remain insufficiently resourced and supported. 
Data Systems and Information Management: One of the recurrent challenges across health, nutrition, and WASH programming has been the fragmentation of data systems and inconsistencies in core metrics. In health, discrepancies between District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2) administrative coverage, WHO-UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC), and LSIS III findings—reaching 15–20 percentage points for key antigens—have undermined immunization planning and the identification of zero-dose children in mobile, border, and ethnic communities. Similarly, weak data management in nutrition has hindered IMAM implementation and delayed evidence-based decision-making, while WASH programming has struggled with limited accountability mechanisms for monitoring service sustainability in institutions. These gaps reveal a systemic need for stronger data governance, interoperability across platforms (e.g. DHIS2, LESMIS), and routine quality assurance processes that enable targeting of the most vulnerable populations. Weaknesses in the data system also includes gaps in gender data, including limited sex- and age-disaggregated administrative data, outdated or missing data on gender-based violence and gender norms, and absent intersectional data on disability.
Lessons Learned: What Worked
Innovation and Digital Enablers: The EIR and associated dashboards have demonstrated tangible value in improving data visibility and supporting district-level decision-making, validating the innovation pathway within the health theory of change. The Climate-Resilient Water Safety Planning guidelines, developed and ready for piloting, similarly offer promise as a structured technical assistance package to address rural WASH deprivations. Machine learning applications for air quality monitoring and analysis of children’s vulnerabilities and risk allow for informed programming with the Government of Lao PDR for key social sectors. These innovations show that targeted investments in digital tools—when coupled with capacity building and appropriate infrastructure and services—can enhance programme effectiveness and enable more rapid scale-up.
Integrated, Multi-Sectoral Service Delivery and Community-Led Approaches: A key lesson from programming is the power of integration, for example in the child protection and education sectors. The back-to-school campaign's shift toward strengthened interpersonal communication and empowerment through integration into the parenting programme increased reach and relevance. Similarly, parenting interventions integrated into school orientation sessions and immunization services maximized efficiency and demonstrated that single-touchpoint, sectoral approaches miss opportunities for compound impact. In WASH, the successful collaboration between Nam Saat and Nam Papa in Luang Namtha to improve safely managed services for community clusters illustrates how strategic partnership can overcome institutional silos. The child protection programme's evidence that peer-to-peer approaches have more meaningful impact than adult-led one-way communication—particularly for sensitizing adolescents to issues such as child marriage—points to a powerful lever for engagement. 
Government Commitment to Systems Strengthening: Despite fiscal constraints, Lao PDR has demonstrated meaningful commitment to foundational systems work: finalization of the sustainability plan of the National Information Platforms for Nutrition (NIPN), development of a Disability Management Information System roadmap, efforts to update the National Plan of Action for Child Protection Systems, and progress on a cohesive Digital Education costed Action Plan. These initiatives signal that government counterparts recognize the imperative of systems change and are willing to invest politically in this agenda.

Future Outlook
Building on these lessons, and the recommendations provided in the Country Programme Evaluation conducted in 2025, UNICEF Lao PDR will implement the following strategic adjustments in 2026, ensuring a smooth transition towards the new Country Programme.
Advance Multi-sectoral Priorities through Integrated Delivery: The situation of child rights in the country, plus the lessons learned from the past and current Country Programmes, call for enhanced multi-sectoral programming structured around 4 priorities: the first 1,000 days, learning and skills, adolescent development and climate and environmental impacts on children. The first 1,000 days of life remains central to breaking intergenerational cycles of poverty, as persistent malnutrition, gaps in maternal and child health services, low coverage of birth registration and inadequate parenting practices continue to undermine early childhood development. The learning and skills priority is crucial to address learning poverty, declining participation in early childhood education and high dropout rates that threaten children’s ability to acquire foundational and transferable skills. Adolescent development requires sustained attention, given persistently high rates of child marriage, adolescent pregnancy, child labour and limited opportunities for safe transitions from school to work. Lastly, climate and environmental impacts on children increasingly shape all dimensions of child well-being, amplifying inequalities and requiring integrated, climate-resilient approaches across social sectors.
Focus on accelerators: To rapidly deliver results at scale, UNICEF will invest in four accelerators, listed in the paragraphs below, selected for their proven potential to generate a multiplier effect across sectors and contexts.
Invest in Adolescent Girls: UNICEF will anchor child marriage prevention and response as the cross-cutting pillar of this accelerator, which will be delivered through a multisectoral approach that strengthens girls' agency and empowerment, prioritizing girls’ school dropout prevention, re-entry and retention in education for pregnant girls and adolescent mothers, targeted maternal health and nutrition services for adolescent mothers, employability and advocacy skills, and social norms change through engagement of families and men.
Enhance inclusion of children with disability: Our efforts will also focus on generating and facilitating access to key data and evidence on children with disabilities—such as the cost of disability, financing needs, and basic support packages—so that policymakers can use this information for planning and budgetary decisions. We will support the development and rollout of a national Disability Management Information System to identify and assist children with disabilities and their families. Additionally, we will work to ensure interoperability and linkages among various management information systems (e.g., Social Registry, DHIS, Immunization Registry, Vital Statistics) to facilitate early identification and early intervention opportunities, as well as improved sectoral planning. We also aim to increase awareness of the needs and necessary support for children with disabilities and their families during emergencies. Collectively, these interventions will pave the way for more comprehensive disability-inclusive programming, ensuring that children with disabilities are not left behind.
Support Workforce for the Last Mile: UNICEF will support the professionalization of frontline workers - critical to all sectors. This includes finalizing a harmonized incentive structure for community volunteers (e.g., Village Health Volunteers) and operationalizing the new Law on Social Work to build a skilled social service  workforce for child protection and inclusion.
Catalyze Responsible Innovation: Digital transformation (e.g. Khang Panya Lao, AI tools) will be paired with investments in digital literacy and infrastructure to ensure equitable access. Youth engagement initiatives like Project Sinxay will be scaled, positioning young people as agents of change, while ensuring they are equally equipped with knowledge and skills to stay safe online.
Strengthen Foundational Enablers for All Sectors: Underpinning our thematic work, a major push will focus on core systemic bottlenecks that will impact all domains of child rights. 
On Data for Equity & Accountability, UNICEF will accelerate the scale-up and interoperability of digital systems (e.g. Child Protection Information Management System, EIR, education data), advocate for robust data governance, and build sub-national capacity to use data for targeted actions, ensuring all programmes can effectively reach the most marginalized. 
On Financing for Sustainability, advocacy will be intensified on protecting and increasing child-focused public expenditure. UNICEF will explore innovative financing and support public financial management to secure sustainable domestic resources for education, health, social protection, and child protection systems. 
On Strategic Collaborations, UNICEF will diversify partnerships with civil society, academia, and the private sector to leverage technical expertise and local networks, while strengthening alliances with ASEAN and development partners for policy influence.

This forward-looking, integrated approach reflects UNICEF's commitment to Adaptive Management. By anchoring our sectoral work in these multi-sectoral priorities, accelerators and enablers, UNICEF will make a shift from addressing symptoms to fortifying the core systems that uphold children's rights. This will ensure that our partnerships remain relevant and impactful, driving equitable outcomes for every child in Lao PDR as the country enters a new phase of development.

Malaysia is currently navigating a pivotal transition toward high-income status, projected for achievement between 2028 and 2030.[i] In 2025, the unity government maintained macroeconomic stability, advanced key digital safety legislation, and laid the groundwork for education reforms, contributing to a growth rate of 5.1 per cent in 2024.[ii] This economic progress, however, occurs as Malaysia enters the later stages of its demographic transition, characterized by rapid urbanization and declining fertility. This juncture presents a critical opportunity to ensure that the benefits of growth are shared equitably across the population.
 
Malaysia is home to approximately 9 million children under 18, including 2.3 million under five.[iii] According to Children Statistics Malaysia 2025, progress in child well-being between 2022 and 2024 was mixed. Child survival improved modestly, but participation in education declined at the upper secondary level, and learning outcomes remain a concern. Early childhood care expanded unevenly, with a decline in registered childcare centres in several states. 
 
Poverty has declined significantly, with absolute poverty standing at 5.1 per cent in 2024 and hardcore poverty largely eradicated nationwide except in Sabah.[iv] Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence at 17.7 per cent.[v] Furthermore, some groups – particularly stateless, undocumented, and refugee children – are excluded from official poverty statistics, masking the full extent of deprivation.
 
These risks are compounded by environmental pressures and climate shocks, such as flooding and pollution, while children remain underrepresented in climate-related decision-making.[vi] 
While income inequality has declined slightly, with the Gini coefficient falling from 0.404 in 2022 to 0.390 in 2024, it remains higher than regional peers.[vii] Nevertheless, inequality remains an issue in Malaysia and ranks higher compared to regional peers such as Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam. Without stronger measures to promote economic mobility, an estimated six in ten Malaysians could still fall below the high-income threshold even after the national milestone is reached.[viii] 
 
As of end-October 2025, Malaysia hosted 64,801 registered refugee and asylum-seeking children.[ix] Children affected by migration – including undocumented, stateless and refugee children – face restricted access to education, health and child protection services, increasing their exposure to exploitation and abuse.
 
While Malaysia has made important progress in child protection, significant gaps persist despite its trajectory towards high-income status. Key indicators have deteriorated, including a 15 per cent increase in reported sexual crimes against children between 2022 and 2023 and a 12.7 per cent rise in children needing care and protection in 2024. [x] Although social protection coverage has expanded, gaps in adequacy and reach remain, leaving many children without assistance and vulnerable to persistent deprivation. Children continue to face serious protection risks, including widespread violent discipline (affecting 67 per cent – among the highest rates in the region), online sexual exploitation, bullying, institutionalization, and a low minimum age of criminal responsibility. An estimated 14.1 per cent of women and 11.6 per cent of men report having experienced sexual violence during childhood.[xi] Social services remain under-professionalized, institutional care is still prevalent, the minimum age of criminal responsibility remains at 10 years, and child marriage persists despite existing policy commitments. 
 
Malaysia continues to face a triple burden of malnutrition. Latest data (2022) show that 21.2 per cent of children under five are stunted, 46.5 per cent of children aged 6–59 months are anaemic, and 5.6 per cent are overweight.[xii] 
 
Significant education reforms advanced in 2025. The Education (Amendment) Act 2025 made secondary education compulsory, marking a major milestone. Progress was also made toward introducing mandatory preschool for five-year-olds under the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan, an important step given that around 42 per cent of 11-year-olds cannot read a simple text.[xiii]
 
Adolescents face growing mental health challenges, skills gaps and risks such as child marriage and limited civic participation. In 2022, one in four adolescents reported symptoms of depression.[xiv] 
 
Overall, policy reforms in 2025 have improved the enabling environment for achieving UNICEF Strategic Plan outcomes, particularly in learning and child protection. However, fiscal pressures that limit the expansion of social expenditure, implementation capacity gaps and persistent exclusion underscore the need for continued systems strengthening, advocacy for targeted financing for children and improved disaggregated data to deliver results at scale for the most vulnerable children.

In 2025, UNICEF Malaysia finalized its new Country Programme Document (CPD 2026–2030) and navigated a shifting economic landscape to advance child rights through a dual focus on national systems strengthening and regional leadership. By leveraging Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship and the upcoming Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) review, the office accelerated long-standing policy reforms and pioneered innovative models. It also turned child and youth voices and data into policy traction across social protection, education, child protection, nutrition, climate action, and adolescent wellbeing.
 
Building evidence on the situation of children
 
UNICEF shifted its evidence-generation strategy from localized case studies to comprehensive national data analysis to support decision making at the highest level.
 
The 2025 Child Poverty Study utilized 2022 Household Income and Expenditure Survey data to estimate a 10 per cent poverty rate among households with children. This evidence was critical in shaping the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan and strengthening advocacy for family-friendly social protection policies. 
 
Social sector and education budget briefs provided analysis of child-sensitive expenditures in the 2025 budget, informing parliamentary discussions and preparations for Malaysia’s CRC engagement in early 2026. In eastern Malaysia, the finalized Child Wellbeing Indices for Sabah and Sarawak will guide state-level child rights engagement.
 
The Wasted Potential study calculated the economic trajectory of 290,437 children born in Malaysia without citizenship. It estimated that excluding these children from education could result in forgone earnings amounting to between 4.00 and 9.49 per cent of GDP in 2025, providing a powerful fiscal argument for inclusive education. UNICEF also contributed to the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) report, revealing gaps and trends in learning quality and informing the Ministry of Education’s new Malaysia Education Blueprint.
 
UNICEF supported the evaluation of the National Plan of Action for Nutrition (NPANM III), informing the revised action plan and nutrition policy with an emphasis on cross-sectoral accountability, governance, and data systems. An assessment of Growth Monitoring and Promotion was initiated, with implementation research in Pahang and Sabah identifying gaps in data use, service quality, and follow-up.
 
UNICEF also mapped childcare services (TASKA) to strengthen the evidence base for family-friendly policies and is establishing partnerships with MWFCD, the Ministry of Human Resources, and the State of Selangor to support a Care Strategic Framework and Action Plan, breastfeeding-friendly workplaces, and community-based childcare models.
 
Finally, UNICEF partnered with UNDP to support the Legal Affairs Division of the Prime Minister’s Department (BHEUU) in integrating children’s rights across all chapters of the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights (NAPBHR). Launched in 2025, the plan is the first one informed by direct consultations with children and youth. The plan aims to identify and address emerging risks for children, including those linked to the digital economy.
 
Strengthening policy frameworks and advocating for children and families
 
UNICEF transitioned evidence into action by embedding children's needs into the highest levels of national and regional policy.
 
At the regional level, UNICEF leveraged Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship to advance child rights through strategic planning, advocacy and partnerships, with a strong emphasis on youth participation. UNICEF facilitated platforms that enabled young people to engage directly with policymakers, ensuring that youth-informed priorities were embedded in ASEAN workplans on reducing out-of-school children, ending violence against children, protecting the rights of children affected by migration, strengthening online safety, and promoting child and youth mental health, particularly for children with disabilities.
 
At the national level, UNICEF provided thought leadership and technical inputs aligned with Malaysia’s transition toward high-income status. UNICEF’s vision of an equitable, high-quality education system that equips young people with globally relevant skills informed the Malaysia Education Blueprint 2026–2035 and the work of the Educational Safety Reform Committee. UNICEF also supported the development of policy instruments on digital safety, including subsidiary regulations under the Online Safety Act 2025, revisions to the Content Code under the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission, and inputs into a Draft National AI Plan of Action. 
 
UNICEF supported seven city and municipal councils in Sarawak to finalize Child-Friendly Cities Initiative (CFCI) action plans, developed collaboratively with newly established children’s councils and backed by three-year implementation budgets. In addition, Kuala Lumpur, Penang Island, and Kota Kinabalu formally committed to join the CFCI, while Petaling Jaya continued successful implementation of its second action plan cycle.
 
UNICEF elevated children as central actors in the climate agenda. The ASEAN Children and Youth Climate Summit, supported by UNICEF, resulted in the Langkawi Declaration, which called for climate-resilient education and inclusive finance. This document marked the first formal recognition of youth policy advice by ASEAN environment ministers and the COP30 President. Locally, UNICEF provided technical inputs to Malaysia’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) and National Adaptation Plan (MyNAP). To ensure these plans were data-driven, UNICEF developed a children’s climate risk index to identify vulnerable districts and gathered insights from 361 young people across six states to directly inform the NDC 3.0 submitted in October 2025.
 
Collaboration with the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development (MWFCD) ensured that lived experiences of children with disabilities, indigenous youth, and those affected by migration are reflected in the Regional Plan of Action on Ending Violence Against Children as well as the Ha Noi Declaration on Social Work. UNICEF also addressed emerging threats by supporting digital safety regulations under the Online Safety Act 2025 and providing inputs for a National AI Plan of Action. To address high rates of children in institutionalized care, UNICEF convened the first International Conference on Alternative Care held in Southeast Asia, placing the experiences of care leavers at the heart of policy discussions.
 
At the national level, UNICEF’s technical contributions strengthened the enabling environment for justice. The revised Special Guidelines for Handling Child Sexual Abuse Cases, launched in October, now incorporate the needs of marginalized children and reduce invasive examinations for survivors. 
 
Furthermore, UNICEF’s advocacy for integrated school safety informed parliamentary deliberations on the Anti-Bullying Bill and the development of a new School Child Protection Policy. UNICEF advocacy consistently emphasized integrated approaches that combine prevention, response, and mental health support – both within and beyond school settings – to promote safer and more inclusive learning environments. 
 
UNICEF also supported the Ministries of Health and Domestic Trade and Cost of Living in convening government agencies, major retailers, and industry associations to improve the availability, pricing, placement, and promotion of healthy foods – laying the groundwork for implementing the forthcoming Healthy Retail Food Environment Guidelines and addressing rising childhood overweight.
 
Modelling innovation to advance the rights of children
 
In 2025, UNICEF Malaysia utilized innovation and technology to bridge service gaps, demonstrate scalable models for social protection, education and climate resilience.
 
Building on the Living on the Edge study, UNICEF designed the ASUH-KL "Cash-Plus" programme to address urban poverty and stunting in low-cost housing. In partnership with Kuala Lumpur City Hall, the Ministries of Finance and Health, and the University of Malaya, the initiative combines monthly cash transfers with nutrition-sensitive behaviour change interventions, supported by a digital management information system for enrolment and monitoring. By December 2025, more than 650 children and pregnant women had been enrolled, with baseline data confirming high levels of monetary and food insecurity to inform impact assessment and advocacy for scale-up.
 
UNICEF also strengthened national disaster preparedness by supporting the Ministry of Education to roll out teacher guides and student modules nationwide, benefiting over 45,000 students in high-risk areas. Youth leadership was further fostered through the Youth Climate Adaptation Lab, where 40 young people developed strategies for community resilience under Malaysia's National Adaptation Plan. Additionally, the Youth Environment Living Labs (YELL) supported eight youth-led projects on water and food security, providing training to 3,000 young people and securing conservation internships for groups including the Orang Asli.
 
A landmark innovation in 2025 was the pilot of an AI-enabled early warning system to prevent school dropouts. Reaching 5 million students across six zones, the system successfully returned 9,077 children (3,287 girls and 5,790 boys) to the classroom. Recognized as a regional best practice, it has been integrated into the national Anak Kita learning recovery programme. Furthermore, Complementary learning initiatives reached over 850,000 children and teachers through the Learning Pioneers programme and Future Skills for All via DELIMa, now implemented in all 185 secondary schools in Sarawak. Inclusive components ensured participation of children with disabilities, including students in schools for the deaf.
 
In Penang, UNICEF expanded a refugee-inclusive child protection model providing joint case management for all children regardless of status, reaching 135 at-risk children and training 240 caregivers in 2025. To improve mental well-being of young people, the WHO-UNICEF Helping Adolescents Thrive (HAT) module was rolled-out across 27 teacher training institutes, equipping 5,000 trainee teachers with essential support skills. Finally, UNICEF identified a scalable pathway for positive parenting by leveraging the KEMAS preschool system – in partnership with the Ministry of Rural Development – by training 75 master trainers, the programme is positioned to reach 300,000 children by 2027.
 
Key enablers and fundraising
 
In 2025, UNICEF delivered an integrated portfolio of advocacy, media engagement, narrative-shaping, stakeholder mobilization, and evidence-driven communication, positioning the organization as a key partner shaping Malaysia’s policy environment. Social media engagement rose by nearly one million to 2.4 million, reinforcing UNICEF’s central role in child rights discourse. The World Children’s Day celebration highlighted child rights by illuminating the Merdeka 118 skyscraper in blue, linked to the Janji Kita (Our Promise) digital campaign on CRC reporting, child-friendly cities, digital safety, and child poverty. 
 
Throughout the year, UNICEF intensified efforts to raise awareness of child rights and support the Government in their reporting process to the CRC. Engagement with government ahead of Malaysia’s 2026 CRC Dialogue was complemented by advocacy in public forums with technical experts, strategic media interviews, and collaboration with influencers and young people to voice their perspectives. High-level advocacy events brought together parliamentarians and key opinion leaders, ensuring child rights remained central to national conversations and strengthening ownership among lead ministries, particularly the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development. A Technical Working Group was established to discuss the lifting of CRC Reservations, with substantive work expected in 2026 following the Concluding Observations and Recommendations from the 100th Session in January 2026.
 
Public advocacy and media relations around the ASEAN ICT Forum on Child Online Protection, drove public discourse and awareness for child online participation and safety. Youth-led advocacy, media campaigns and outreach to key opinion leaders during the ASEAN Children and Youth Climate Summit highlighted the importance of child and youth participation in decision making, culminating in the formal presentation of the Langkawi Declaration to ASEAN environment ministers and the COP30 president. In Sabah, the Tuai Cerita programme raised awareness of child labour risks in the oil palm sector through community-driven storytelling and local narratives by key opinion leaders.
 
Media partnerships expanded significantly through targeted engagement with leading media outlets, including The Star, Bernama, Astro Awani, Sarawak Tribune and TV Sarawak. These engagements resulted in exclusive coverage of UNICEF events and strengthened media understanding of UNICEF Malaysia’s programmes and impact. In total, more than 2,000 media articles cited UNICEF insights and spokespeople on child rights issues, amplifying the organization’s voice and influence in national discourse. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF Malaysia also strengthened inter-agency collaboration through close partnerships with WHO, UNDP, ILO and UNFPA, while playing a leading role within UN Country Team structures to support a smooth transition to the 2026–2030 programme cycle. With WHO, UNICEF advanced adolescent mental health systems, introducing Malaysia’s first Youth Mental Health Index and institutionalizing the Helping Adolescents Thrive initiative within national teacher training. With UNDP, UNICEF co-led the Youth Environment Living Labs, empowering thousands of young people to deliver youth-led climate solutions and amplify youth voices nationally, regionally and globally. Collaboration with ILO focused on addressing child labour in the palm oil sector through research, policy engagement and advocacy, while partnership with UNFPA strengthened evidence and policy dialogue on urban child poverty and social protection, including the launch of the ASUH-KL cash-plus programme. UNICEF further provided system-wide leadership by chairing the People Results Working Group, leading two subgroups (social protection and disability inclusion), co-chairing UNCT working groups, and supporting Common Premises reporting.
UNICEF also strengthened disability inclusion by building government and regional capacity, amplifying the voices of youth with disabilities, advancing inclusive care systems, and strengthening evidence and coordination. This included national officials’ learning on gender- and child-sensitive care systems, contributing to ASEAN-level disability and care policy frameworks, training youth with disabilities as Disability Equality Trainers, and leading inter-agency action as chair of the UNCT Disability Inclusion Subgroup.  UNICEF finalized the impact evaluation of early intervention centres for children with developmental delays in Sarawak to inform future scale-up and advanced disability-inclusive data systems through advocacy for improved national surveys and strengthened government capacity on disability data.
Aligned with the corporate Future Focus Initiative, UNICEF reviewed its operational framework in Malaysia, including optimizing its Putrajaya and Kuala Lumpur offices. The consolidation plan, to be implemented in 2026, is expected to generate savings and create a more collaborative workspace.
 
The office enhanced efficiency and innovation by implementing the Procurement Case Manager to streamline service contracting, finalizing its first Technology for Development (T4D) Strategy to strengthen digital impact and inclusion, and introducing Copilot Pro, a secure AI tool for productivity and context-aware decision-making.
 
As a hybrid programme and fundraising office fully funded by Malaysian individuals and the private sector, UNICEF Malaysia raised RM94.4 million (US$21 million) in 2025, slightly below 2024 figures. In response to a challenging global funding environment, the office launched resilience-focused fundraising products (BencanaReady), improved donor quality, enhanced business intelligence automation, and established strategic partnerships with Bursa Malaysia and UMobile on climate readiness and sustainability.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF effectively leveraged platforms to advance child rights in Malaysia. Through strategic planning, advocacy, coordinated communication, and partnerships with government departments, UNICEF used Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship to amplify child and youth voices, promoting child-focused climate action, youth mental health (including children with disabilities), and digital safety in national and regional commitments.
 
Despite progress, some indicators – such as stunting and adolescent mental health – remained resistant to change, highlighting the need for targeted, life-cycle interventions supported by robust, shock-responsive systems.
 
UNICEF will launch its Country Programme 2026–2030, continuing its focus on child rights while aligning with the global Strategic Plan 2026–2029. This approach reflects Malaysia’s transition toward high-income status and prioritizes reducing inequalities, measuring and mitigating child poverty, supporting early childhood development, and fostering adolescent participation in policymaking. Strengthening child protection systems and building resilience to climate and environmental risks will also remain central.
 
Progress for vulnerable populations – including children affected by migration, indigenous children, and children with disabilities – remains constrained by legal barriers, social norms, and limited disaggregated data. Monitoring complex metrics such as child poverty and violence against children will continue to be a priority.
 
Two pathways proved crucial for influencing policy and delivering results in 2025. First, collaboration on government-led initiatives enabled quick, scalable wins, such as integrating HAT mental health modules into pre-service teacher training. Second, localized evidence generation – including evaluations of the National Plan of Action for Nutrition, child poverty studies, and a prototype children’s climate and disaster risk index – helped shape key national agendas like the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan and MyNAP.
 
Integrated approaches combining policy advocacy, capacity strengthening, service delivery, and social norm interventions proved more effective than isolated efforts. Partnerships with civil society organizations such as MASW, NECIC, HOST International, MILAD, and MPMS were critical for reaching marginalized groups and embedding inclusive practices. Child and youth participation influenced policy, including parliamentary commitments and ASEAN resolutions, emphasizing the need for institutionalized mechanisms to amplify their voices.
 
UNICEF also demonstrated that structured engagement with the private sector can drive policy change, mobilize resources, and strengthen accountability. Business partnerships contributed to the adoption of Malaysia’s National Action Plan for Business and Human Rights, expanded commitments to child-sensitive business practices, improved food and environmental standards, addressed child labour risks and advanced child online protection. Through advocacy, partnerships and campaigns, private sector collaboration amplified public awareness, supported programme delivery and innovation, and complemented government action – highlighting that sustained progress for children requires responsible business engagement alongside government, civil society, children, youth and communities.
Despite UNICEF Malaysia’s distinctive fundraising model, global funding trends affected income stability, with donor attrition outpacing acquisition. Key lessons include the need for strategic investment in sustainable donors – such as credit card donors over 30 – and in modernized digital infrastructure.
 
Looking Ahead
 
UNICEF Malaysia’s 2026–2030 work, guided by lessons from 2025, will continue to push for systemic reforms and policy-level engagement with elements of life-cycle programming. It aligns with national priorities, including the Malaysia Madani Economy Framework and the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan. The upcoming CRC recommendations will offer opportunities to strengthen partnerships and government support for child rights.
 
Key priorities include supporting national policy frameworks and services amid more limited resources and climate vulnerabilities. Strengthening child-focused climate resilience and disaster reduction, as highlighted in the 2025 Langkawi Declaration, will be central.
UNICEF will enhance cross-sectoral cooperation to ensure equitable access to quality foundational learning, particularly at the preschool level, building on contributions to STEM and digital transformation agendas. Early childhood development, nutrition, responsive caregiving, and family-friendly policies will remain a focus.
 
A new Technology for Development (T4D) strategy will scale innovative solutions to support operational excellence and development outcomes. For instance, UNICEF will assist the government in localizing an AI-powered platform to monitor breaches of the Breast-Milk Substitutes Marketing Code across digital media.
 
Inclusive and professionalized child protection systems will continue to be strengthened through capacity-building for frontline workers, justice professionals and families; improved reporting mechanisms; advanced Alternative Care reforms; enhanced safeguards for children both online and offline. In parallel, UNICEF will strengthen its digital fundraising infrastructure and ensure compliance with Payment Card Industry standards to support operational efficiency and long-term income stability.
 
Young people played a central role in 2025, advocating on child rights, mental health, climate change and digital rights, contributing to regional commitments and parliamentary recognition. Their engagement through platforms such as CFCI underscores the importance of institutionalizing youth participation in policymaking. As Malaysia moves toward high-income status, child and youth leaders – supported by UNICEF – will continue to shape the issues that matter most to them.

In 2024, Mongolia transitioned to UMIC status, following strong post-pandemic recovery driven largely by a surge in coal exports. By late 2024, GDP reached USD 23.4 billion, and per capita income exceeded USD 7,000, marking Mongolia’s transition to upper-middle-income status. However, by 2025, the economic landscape began to show signs of slowing down, as the country faced fiscal pressures and widening regional disparities. 
Real GDP growth reached 5.9 per cent year-on-year by the third quarter of 2025, bolstered by an agricultural recovery, increased copper production, and manufacturing expansion. However, the deceleration in coal mining, particularly as prices dropped, negatively impacted the transport, trade, and service sectors, resulting in a 12 per cent drop in Mongolia's foreign trade surplus by November 2025. Mongolia's continued heavy reliance on a single export market—China, which absorbs about 90 per cent of Mongolia's exports, remains a critical vulnerability amid fluctuating commodity prices. 
Inflation averaged 6.8 per cent in 2024 and peaked at 9.6 per cent in February 2025. Inflation fluctuated between 8 and 9 per cent, remaining well above the central bank's target range. Although foreign exchange reserves increased to USD 6.0 billion by December, the Mongolian tugrug depreciated by around 5 per cent in 2025, further eroding household purchasing power and raising the cost of essential goods, making life more difficult for the most vulnerable populations.
Fiscal pressures on the government continued to mount. By the end of the first ten months of 2025, government revenues totaled USD 23.3 billion, while expenditures reached USD 24.9 billion, resulting in a fiscal deficit of USD 1.6 billion. External debt rose to USD 39.6 billion, with 96 per cent of the general government debt denominated in foreign currency. This heightened the country's vulnerability to exchange-rate volatility. In response, the government introduced expenditure controls, including civil service downsizing and delays in capital investments. These measures, however, had limited impact on easing fiscal stress and constrained public service delivery, particularly at the subnational level.
Despite fiscal tightening, social sector financing remained policy priority. Nominal budget allocations for education, health, and social protection increased in 2025, largely reflecting wage adjustments for civil servants rather than expanded programmatic investments. Widespread strikes by teachers and health workers in October–November 2025 led to agreements with trade unions on phased salary increases for 2025–2026 fiscal year. Nonetheless, the constrained fiscal environment delayed new initiatives and limited the expansion of services for underserved populations. Local governments were hit particularly hard, with provincial budget cuts averaging 15 per cent, leading to reduced capacity to deliver essential services.
Following the June 2025 Parliamentary session, Zandanshatar Gombojav was appointed as Prime Minister of Mongolia, leading a new coalition Government formed by the ruling Mongolian People’s Party and partner parties. Political instability persisted through late 2025, the ruling party new leader appointed, Uchral Nyam-Osor, elected as the new Speaker of the  parliament, reflecting ongoing shifts in restructural changes and broader governance changes continuing.
By late 2025, the economic and fiscal pressures had significantly eroded household resilience, particularly among low-income families. The government initiated bold policy shifts, notably in the energy sector, to reduce systemic losses. As an initial step, electricity flat tariffs were increased in November 2024 under a new three-tier system based on consumption, raising average household electricity costs. While these reforms aim to strengthen energy security and  sustainability. The rising costs of electrcity, food, fuel and healthcare disproportionately affected vulnerable households, while service providers, such as schools and health facilities, faced rising operational costs within constrained budgets. 
The economic challenges faced by Mongolia intersected with longstanding vulnerabilities that children face. Approximately two-thirds of children in Mongolia experience multidimensional deprivation, which is more pronounced in rural and remote areas. These children are more likely to suffer from malnutrition[1], lack of access to basic health services, and poor educational outcomes. Rural children are also at higher risk for maternal and child mortality, as well as inadequate access to prenatal and postnatal care. 
While multidimensional deprivation affects both boys and girls in Mongolia, evidence suggests distinct gender patterns, particularly in education, where boys are more likely to drop out before completing secondary school—especially in rural areas—while girls are over-represented in upper secondary and tertiary education. Health and nutrition challenges affect both sexes, but adolescent girls face additional risks related to early pregnancy, unpaid care burdens, and limited access to adolescent-responsive health services, underscoring the need for gender-responsive approaches despite limited sex-disaggregated data. Education continues to be one of the most unequal sectors in Mongolia,The child protection landscape in Mongolia remains a significant area of concern. While legal frameworks for child protection improved substantially, implementation is uneven especially rural ones, continue to suffer from a lack of trained social workers and child protection personnel. Domestic violence remains a pervasive issue, with increasing reports of abuse against children, both in families and within institutions. Online exploitation and abuse of children have emerged as significant threats. According to the 2017 study on gender-based violence, 10.7 per cent of women reported experiencing sexual violence before the age of 15, with perpetrators most often identified as family members, underscoring the risks children face even within protective environments. More recent data show that as of 2024, 675 victims of violence were registered, including 643 women and 463 children aged 0–17. However, the lack of sex-disaggregated data for children limits analysis of gender-specific risks and response needs (NSO). 
Environmental risks also present a threat to child well-being. An estimated 24 per cent of females and 27 per cent of males live in areas of high environmental risk, and over 80,000 children were affected by the severe dzud in winter 2022–2023, although sex-disaggregated data for children are not available. Seasonal air pollution, especially in Ulaanbaatar, continues to pose significant health risks to all, specifically amongst children. In 2025, the government introduced green and yellow zones in the capital, restricting polluting activities and vehicles in designated areas. The Cabinet also approved comprehensive air pollution regulations, including tax incentives for investments in clean energy, energy-efficient housing and green urban development. Parliamentary Resolution-57 (June 2025) further enabled access to green financing for households and businesses, supporting Mongolia’s transition toward low-carbon development. These measures have increased opportunities for private sector engagement in climate mitigation, including cleaner heating solutions shifting from raw coals, housing insulation and renewable energy. 
In 2025, Mongolia faced multiple overlapping shocks affecting children and vulnerable populations. A major measles outbreak recorded 13,777 cases, primarily among children, following prolonged declines in routine immunization coverage. Catch-up vaccination reached over 151,000 children. Climate-related hazards intensified, with dzud risks affecting 30 per cent of the country in the reporting year, exposing an estimated 30,000 children, while wildfires increased by 56 per cent, damaging pastureland and rural livelihoods across 12 provinces. 
Recent amendments to the Corporate Income Tax Law allow businesses to deduct up to 1 per cent of taxable income for eligible corporate social responsibility expenditures, including environmental protection, education, health, disaster relief and social services which is a major resource mobilization effort on increasing social sector investments. 
Mongolia’s 2025 context is defined by economic deceleration, fiscal tightening, political transition and growing environmental shocks. These challenges have constrained the quality and expansion of essential services in health, education, child protection, and WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene), particularly in rural areas, and are compounded by persistent gender norms and customary practices that limit women’s ownership and control of high-value assets, including land and dwellings, restricting their economic decision-making[2]. At the same time, emerging policy reforms including sustainable finance, energy transition, air pollution control, and corporate tax incentives—create opportunities for innovative partnerships.
