In 2025, UNICEF Mongolia delivered measurable national-scale breakthroughs for children by embedding child rights into law, budgets, digital systems, climate policy and service delivery. A total of 720,000 children were brought into a new digital school health card system, strengthening access to quality primary health care through improved health monitoring, continuity of care, and early detection of health needs. National HPV vaccination coverage doubled, expanding children’s and adolescents’ access to essential, life-saving preventive health services and reducing future health risks. Over one million children gained access to improved school nutrition services through increased budget allocations, ensuring that more children have access to nutritious diets that support healthy growth, learning, and overall well-being. At the same time, 375 rural children (218 girls) are now accessing education locally through newly built bagh schools, which apply the green school concept and promote environmentally sustainable practices. This represents a pilot initiative jointly implemented with the Government and supported by the private sector to test an integrated, climate-resilient rural school model for future scale-up. These schools provide safe and protective learning environments that incorporate child-friendly and protection-sensitive standards. They also holistically integrate nutrition and WASH services, ensuring that children learn in healthy, clean, and supportive settings. Together, these improvements directly contribute enabling every child, especially those in remote areas, to learn and acquire the skills they need for the future in sustainable, inclusive, and protective education environments.     
In the area of child protection, 50,000 children were identified as at risk, and 15,675 children were protected through a strengthened child protection system, ensuring timely detection, referral, and response to cases of violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect, and harmful practices. In addition, for effective enforcement of the child protection law, an important national standard for response and rehabilitation services for survivors of sexual abuse was developed and shared with 38 social work and medical science faculties for inclusion into the academic curriculum and for practical application. These system-wide improvements directly help ensure that every child and adolescent is protected through a more coordinated, accountable, and effective safeguarding mechanism.
37,490 people, including 15,700 children, gained access to solar-powered safe water and sanitation services, strengthening the availability of safe and equitable WASH services while promoting climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable solutions. By integrating renewable energy into water systems, this intervention directly advances Goal Area 4, ensuring that every child, especially in vulnerable communities, can live, grow, and learn in a healthier, safer, and more sustainable environment.
These results reflect a shift from project-based delivery to systemic, financed and institutionalised national solutions across health, education, protection, nutrition and climate resilience.
Health, Nutrition and Development: In 2025, UNICEF Mongolia focused on strengthening the foundations of child health and development systems, rather than simply expanding service coverage. The year marked a shift toward prevention, data integration and institutionalised  national commitments with a strong lens applied across adolescent health, nutrition and early childhood development. These efforts help close persistent gender gaps in access, continuity of care, and caregiving responsibilities, particularly for adolescent girls, pregnant women and young mothers.
A major system breakthrough was achieved through the Digital Student Health Card (SHC), which now links school health records to the national health and education information systems. By making adolescent health needs visible and trackable, the SHC addressed long-standing gender-blind spots—especially for the adolescent girls, whose needs often remain underreported due to stigma, limited school-based services and fragmented referral pathways.
In 2025, the SHC reached more than 720,000 children, enabling schools, parents and health providers to track immunisation status, screening results and follow-up needs in real time. This removed a long-standing barrier that had prevented continuity of care for adolescents, particularly girls transitioning into puberty, when health risks increase but service utilization often declines. UNICEF also supported the drafting of the Law on Child Health and Safety in School Settings, ensuring the digital school health system and school-based services —including those addressing sexual and reproductive health— are anchored in national legislation.
This digital shift directly  contributed to a major increase in HPV vaccination coverage, which rose from  25 per cent in 2024 to 53 per cent nationally in 2025, despite outbreaks and vaccine  hesitancy. By advocating for HPV vaccine uptake by both boys and girls, UNICEF advanced gender-equitable prevention within the national immunization programme. UNICEF combined digital visibility through SHC, cold-chain strengthening, updated service guidelines, and nationwide risk-communication. In priority provinces supported by UNICEF’s SBC programme, coverage exceeded 80 per cent, demonstrating that system readiness and behaviour change together produced national impact.
UNICEF strengthened early detection and survival for newborns by equipping all maternity hospitals with  pulse oximetry screening and installing tandem mass spectrometry at the  National Center for Maternal and Child Health. Before 2025, congenital heart  and metabolic disorders were detected only after severe complications,  disproportionately affecting infants born to young mothers or those with nutritional  vulnerabilities. With UNICEF-led training and HMIS integration, every newborn  born in a facility—covering almost the entire birth cohort—now benefits from  early screening and referral, reducing preventable stress and care burdens on  mothers, shifting Mongolia toward preventive neonatal care rather than crisis treatment.
On nutrition, a major policy shift was achieved when maternal and child nutrition was embedded into the  National Plan of Action on Maternal, Child and Reproductive Health (2025–2028). For the first time, Mongolia now has a nationally defined minimum nutrition service package for pregnant women and adolescent girls, with clear indicators and targets, replacing project-based nutrition with a state-governed, budget-anchored framework. This reframed women’s and girls’  nutrition as a public responsibility rather than a private household burden.
Also, nutrition services were scaled and sustained. UNICEF translated policy into delivery by strengthening  national systems. In 2025, a national maternal nutrition training package was  rolled out, strengthening the capacity of a predominantly female frontline  health workforce to deliver gender-responsive care. 54,990 bottles of  Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS) were procured and distributed, reaching 64.5 per cent of pregnant women nationwide. All maternity hospitals,  covering about 98 per cent of newborns, implemented the Ten Steps for Successful  Breastfeeding, protecting women’s rights to have skilled breastfeeding  support. In addition, an AI-enabled system began monitoring compliance with the breast-milk Substitutes Code. These reforms ensure that nutrition services are no longer donor-dependent, but embedded in national protocols, budgets and regulatory systems, reducing inequities that have historically affected adolescent girls, low-income mothers and women in rural areas.
Additionally, school meals, milk and micronutrients were protected. UNICEF also helped secure a 62 per cent increase in the national school meal budget, improving nutrition protection for over one million children. This investment particularly benefits girls from low-income households by reducing gendered food insecurity and supporting school attendance and learning. This included school milk and fortified foods, supported by UNICEF’s budget forecasting tool, which shields food quality from inflation and makes school nutrition financially resilient. 
In Early Childhood Development, UNICEF supported the updating of the national ECD curricula, integrating nurturing care and gender equality principles, and the integration of nurturing care into university pre-service training, strengthening and professionalizing a predominantly female ECD workforce. Community ECD centres in underserved areas were also expanded.    
These reforms strengthened both service quality and the national ECD workforce, ensuring that more children enter school healthier, better stimulated and developmentally ready. By supporting gender-responsive parenting and actively engaging fathers and male caregivers, UNICEF addressed the “care gap” by reframing nurturing care  as a shared responsibility rather than a gendered burden. Together, these actions improved survival, nutrition and developmental outcomes for hundreds of thousands of children, while advancing Mongolia’s preventive, data-enabled, gender responsive and nutrition-sensitive child health system. By promoting gender-responsive parenting, UNICEF addressed the "care gap" by actively engaging fathers and male caregivers, making nurturing care a shared responsibility rather than a gendered burden, and fostering more equitable home environments and improved developmental outcomes for children.
Education: In 2025, UNICEF Mongolia strengthened the education system’s ability to reach remote, mobile and marginalized children, while modernizing national  education delivery for the digital age. Nomadic children were reached through  Teacher with a Tablet. The Teacher with a Tablet model closed a persistent  equity gap in access to early childhood education, continuity of learning, and exposure to age-appropriate foundational learning opportunities for herder children aged 2–5. As a result of the Teacher with a Tablet initiative, one in three targeted children gained access to home-based early childhood education services. Girls accounted for 51 percent of children participating, reflecting equitable reach across genders. These results were  achieved through the training of 560 teachers (of whom 557 were female), who  were equipped to effectively deliver and manage home-based early childhood education services in remote rural communities.
In 2025, 5,454 nomadic  children accessed structured early learning through visiting teachers using  tablet-based content adapted to mobile livelihoods — delivering school  readiness without separating children from their families. This demonstrated  a scalable national solution for Mongolia’s pastoral context.
In 2025, UNICEF provided  technical assistance to the government for the rollout of the new national  preschool curriculum, which was implemented nationwide. The curriculum embeds inclusion, climate resilience and holistic child development, aligning preschool  education with Mongolia’s national reform agenda and UNICEF-supported teacher  training and ECD standards.
Through the One Bagh, One School initiative, five new solar-powered bagh schools were built in 2025, giving 375 rural children access to education close to home, instead of long-distance dormitory placement. Each school is equipped with WASH, digital learning and energy-efficient heating. This was achieved by mobilising  private-sector co-financing through tax-incentivised corporate giving,  creating a new domestic financing model for rural public schools.
The Bagh School model is now emerging as a national policy instrument. By proving that small, multi-grade, solar-powered schools can deliver the full national curriculum at lower cost, UNICEF created a model that reduces family separation, fiscal pressure and  rural depopulation—and has already attracted government and private-sector replication interest.
In 2025, UNICEF advanced digital education in  Mongolia by digitising Grades 1–3 curricula in Mongolian and minority  languages. More than 22,000 children accessed online learning platforms, strengthening their digital literacy, foundational skills, and  ability to learn independently. An additional 2,000 children in low-connectivity areas benefited from offline audio learning.
UNICEF also supported broader digital transformation efforts, including AI teacher certification, Girls Code, and national dialogues on preparing children for a digital economy.  Through its bootcamps, Girls Code continued to equip rural girls with  practical STEM, digital, English, and introductory AI skills, opening  pathways to future ICT education and careers.
Together, these initiatives enhanced equity,  resilience, and future-readiness across Mongolia’s education system.
Child Protection: UNICEF helped Mongolia move toward a more professional, better financed and  more accountable child protection system, with strengthened capacity to  prevent and respond to gender-based violence (GBV) against children,  particularly girls. Two national service standards (on sexual abuse response  and psychological services) were approved and disseminated, anchoring quality  care and survivor-centred care in professional training and service delivery.
Between 2020 and 2025, the child protection state budget increased from 8.0 billion MNT to 20.6 billion  MNT, enabling significant system strengthening. Increased and sustained  public financing supported earlier identification and response to child  protection and GBV risk, with 50,000 children identified as at risk, and  15,675 children receiving services, including case management, referral, and  follow-up support to address violence, exploitation, sexual abuse, neglect,  and harmful practices. The expanded budget strengthened workforce, improved  service coverage, and enhanced safeguarding for children exposed to GBV and  other protection risks. 
The Law on Social Work was  submitted to Parliament, professionalising the workforce, while PRIMERO is  being deployed to link case management with financing, ensuring continuity,  accountability and sustainability. To address digital risks, UNICEF trained teachers  and social workers and reached 9,698 children, 1,036 teachers and 4,954  parents, while a national youth hackathon generated nearly 500,000 views, strengthening prevention and peer-led advocacy. 
UNICEF promoted the culture of zero tolerance for  SEA through tailored awareness and capacity-building tools in Mongolian for  partners including targeted videos and a self-paced e-learning course. Forty  government child protection staff were trained as trainers and PSEA  assessments of three national NGOs, informed  follow-up capacity-building and action plans to strengthen compliance.
Together, these reforms aim to transform child protection from crisis response into a preventive, professional national system.
WASH and Climate Change: In 2025, UNICEF Mongolia integrated climate resilience, green financing and  child-centred infrastructure into national development pathways. 
NDC3.0 was approved in 2025, embedding children’s rights in Mongolia’s national climate commitments. Through the Solar WASH programme, UNICEF delivered safe water and sanitation to 37,490 people, including 15,700 children, in schools, kindergartens and health facilities. With 30–50 per cent local government co-financing, operating costs were  reduced and local ownership ensured.
At system level, UNICEF led the first nationwide costed assessment of WASH in schools and kindergartens, identifying MNT 32.1 billion in investment needs and embedding them into state and local budget planning — such evidence supports the integration of WASH into education sector planning and financing, rather than treating it as ad-hoc projects.
On climate action, UNICEF designed and advocated the child-responsive elements of NDC3.0, ensuring  commitments on education sector adaptation, social protection, clean energy  and youth participation. UNICEF mobilised over USD 800,000 in domestic  co-financing, delivered low-carbon heating, insulation and solar systems, and  engaged 5,474 children and adolescents in climate action. These investments  reduced air pollution, strengthened climate resilience and directly improved  children’s learning, health and home environments. 
UNICEF’s Cooking, Heating and  Insulation Package (CHIP) advanced gender-transformative climate action by  addressing barriers that disproportionately affect women, while benefiting  entire households. By combining affordable energy-efficient solutions, inclusive  green financing, and targeted training, CHIP reduced health and workload  burdens for women—particularly pregnant women and women-headed  households—while improving living conditions for children and families and  expanding women’s participation in the clean energy value chain, where women  accounted for 60 per cent of the workforce. 
Social Inclusion and  Evidence: In 2025, UNICEF supported the strengthening of legally grounded, evidence-informed and equity-oriented approaches within  Mongolia’s social protection and public finance systems.
On child-sensitive laws and  inclusive reform, Mongolia entered a pivotal reform phase with the revision  of the Social Welfare Law and the initiation of a new Family Support Law. UNICEF played a central technical and advocacy role to ensure both laws embed  child rights, gender equality, disability inclusion and lifecycle vulnerabilities—issues previously weakly reflected in law.
A national Gender-Responsive Social Protection training, convened by UNICEF, engaged 64 senior  decision-makers, including Members of Parliament and ministry leaders,  directly strengthening the quality of legal drafting and reform processes.
In social protection, UNICEF addressed fragmented evidence by enabling integration of social protection  data with health, education and child protection systems, allowing  policymakers to identify families facing overlapping vulnerabilities such as poverty, disability, caregiving burden and violence exposure. This shifted Mongolia’s reform process from sector-specific to equity-based policy design.
To support the new Family Support Law, UNICEF initiated the first national Cost of Raising a Child  study, which will determine whether benefits are adequate, equitable and fiscally sustainable, anchoring future budgets in real household needs.
In 2025, despite fiscal tightening, UNICEF helped  safeguard and expand public finance for children in Mongolia. A total of USD 37.9 million was secured to sustain school and dormitory meal programmes,  ensuring continued access to nutritious meals for students nationwide.  Funding for child protection increased by 47 per cent, enabling stronger services for vulnerable children. In addition, the introduction of child budget tagging improved transparency and oversight of child-related spending across sectors, supporting more accountable and targeted investment in children’s well-being.
These reforms protected services for nearly 380,000 children, ensuring that inflation and budget cuts did not erode investments in their survival, learning and protection.
On Adolescent Development and Participation, in 2025, UNICEF strengthened Mongolia’s  national systems for adolescent development, participation, and mental health  by securing a 4.8 billion MNT government investment dedicated to improving school safety and mental health services.  This shift enabled the move from donor dependent youth activities toward structured, skills-based and youth-led innovation embedded in national priorities. 
In 2025, more than 14,800 adolescents (57 per cent girls) gained advocacy, life, and leadership skills, empowering them to identify local challenges, design solutions, and positively influence peers, communities, and institutions. Through UPSHIFT-powered innovation and digital advocacy programmes, the Energy Shift Leaders 2025 initiative—under the global Green Rising platform—supported 96 adolescents (56 girls) as peer trainers on renewable energy. Targeted  measures ensured girls’ meaningful participation, enabling them to develop green skills and contribute to a just energy transition. These young leaders promoted knowledge sharing and sustainable practices in schools, advanced greener learning environments, and strengthened youth climate leadership in their provinces
For evaluation and MICS+, UNICEF significantly strengthened the national evidence ecosystem through both evaluation and the next generation of MICS Plus. In 2025, UNICEF supported high-quality, utilization-focused evaluations that informed policy decisions in child protection, nutrition and education, ensuring that lessons were translated into reforms rather than remaining as reports. The MICS Plus platform was expanded beyond household data to integrate administrative records, climate exposure and service coverage, allowing Government to analyze who is being left behind and why. This marked a shift from periodic data collection to a more continuous, policy-relevant evidence system. By strengthening national ownership of data, UNICEF ensured that evidence increasingly drives budget decisions, targeting of social protection, and prioritization of reforms under the UNSDCF.
On planning and monitoring, UNICEF further strengthened results-based planning and monitoring as a joint  accountability platform with Government. Programme planning was increasingly aligned with national strategies, medium-term expenditure frameworks and  UNSDCF outcomes, enabling child-focused results to be embedded within  national development processes. Digital dashboards, outcome-level tracking  and disaggregated data improved the ability of sector ministries to monitor  progress and identify bottlenecks. Importantly, monitoring was used not only  for reporting but for management action, enabling course correction and  prioritization across sectors. This strengthened the credibility of UNICEF as  a partner that supports delivery of results, not only project implementation.
On Social and Behaviour Change & PSEA, UNICEF advanced Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) to  support vaccine confidence, climate action and parenting practices through  nationally coordinated communication strategies. At the same time, Protection  from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) was reinforced through partner  compliance, training and reporting mechanisms, ensuring that UNICEF-supported  programmes remain safe and accountable for all communities.
On humanitarian action, in 2025 UNICEF supported Mongolia to shift from ad-hoc emergency response to a  more anticipatory, system-linked model. Using early warning and risk  analysis, UNICEF pre-positioned supplies and triggered early action for dzud, extreme cold and urban shocks, reducing disruption to essential services for  children. UNICEF delivered cash, nutrition, WASH and child protection support  through government disaster and social protection systems, ensuring that  emergency assistance strengthened national safety nets and child resilience  rather than creating parallel mechanisms.
Private Sector Partnerships: Private sector engagement became a major strategic driver of UNICEF Mongolia’s results in 2025. Moving beyond corporate social  responsibility, UNICEF positioned the private sector as a co-investor in  national systems for children. Through innovative partnerships with mining  companies, banks, telecommunications firms and SMEs, UNICEF mobilized  domestic financing for education, WASH, digital learning, climate resilience  and social services.
Flagship initiatives such as One Bagh, One School, SolarWASH and digital education platforms demonstrated  how private capital, technology and logistics can be aligned with public policy objectives. Companies provided co-financing, renewable energy solutions,  connectivity and operational expertise, reducing costs for Government while  expanding service reach. Importantly, UNICEF ensured that all private sector  engagement was aligned with child rights, national priorities and public  ownership, avoiding parallel systems or reputational risk.
UNICEF also strengthened the  enabling environment for private sector engagement by developing partnership  frameworks, due diligence systems and impact tracking, allowing Mongolia to  move toward more predictable, transparent and scalable domestic resource  mobilization for children. These partnerships directly support the UNSDCF’s focus on inclusive growth, innovation and sustainable financing, while reducing dependence on external aid. Through these efforts, UNICEF helped  position Mongolia’s private sector not as a peripheral donor, but as a core  actor in national child-centred development.
The partnerships were governed  by child-rights standards, national priorities and public ownership,  strengthening government systems rather than creating parallel ones. With improved due diligence, partnership frameworks and impact tracking, UNICEF enabled more predictable, transparent and scalable domestic resource mobilization, reducing reliance on external aid and advancing the UNSDCF  agenda on inclusive growth and sustainable financing.
In 2025, UNICEF Mongolia strengthened digital and strategic communication as a core delivery and accountability tool, not only as visibility. UNICEF expanded the use of  digital platforms, social media and data-driven content to promote vaccine  confidence, climate action, parenting practices, adolescent participation and  child rights. Targeted campaigns reached millions of users, including  hard-to-reach youth and parents, while real-time engagement allowed UNICEF to  counter misinformation and adapt messages quickly during outbreaks and  climate events. By integrating digital communication into programme delivery,  UNICEF enhanced both demand for services and public trust in national  systems, supporting the UNSDCF’s focus on inclusive, informed and participatory  development.
UNICEF reinforced strategic  external relations to support Mongolia’s child-centred development  agenda. Through proactive engagement with Parliament, line ministries, embassies, UN agencies and development partners, UNICEF positioned children’s rights, climate resilience and equity as cross-cutting national priorities. High-level advocacy, evidence-based briefs and coordinated UN messaging  helped align partner support with UNSDCF outcomes and national reforms, while strengthening Mongolia’s profile as a country committed to investing in its  human capital.
In the areas of Operations, UNICEF Mongolia strengthened operational effectiveness to ensure timely, accountable and high-quality delivery of results for children. Governance  systems were reinforced through structured oversight, taskforces and regular management forums that aligned operations with programme priorities and  UNSDCF outcomes. The Country Management Team and other senior-level  coordination mechanisms facilitated decision-making on resource allocation,  risk mitigation and operational adjustments, enabling the office to remain  agile amid changing social, economic and environmental contexts.
Financial management and  administrative systems were strengthened through risk-based HACT  assurance, enhanced monitoring, and timely cash transfers, with 93 per cent  of disbursements processed on time. UNICEF expanded the use of digital tools,  including eZPlan and updated spot check templates, to improve transparency,  streamline reporting and ensure value-for-money across all implementing  partners. Training and guidance on financial compliance, anti-fraud measures,  and programmatic risk management further reinforced accountability and  institutional capacity.
Human resources management  focused on building a high-performing, motivated workforce aligned with  strategic priorities. Recruitment processes were streamlined, performance  management systems were enhanced, and staff development and recognition  exercises ensured the identification and retention of high-potential staff.  Targeted training on financial, operational and safeguarding requirements  strengthened both technical and leadership capacity.
Sustainability and  environmental responsibility were advanced through reduced international  travel, energy-efficient office operations, and strengthened internal  controls. These operational improvements allowed UNICEF Mongolia to support  programmes without delays, optimize resource use, and maintain high standards  of accountability, reinforcing its role as a reliable partner to Government,  UN agencies and civil society. Collectively, these achievements ensured that  operational effectiveness is not an internal exercise but a strategic enabler  for achieving results for children, underpinning Mongolia’s broader UNSDCF  commitments to inclusive, efficient and results-driven governance.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
1. Fragmented Systems and Uneven Service Quality Across Sectors
Despite substantial efforts to strengthen systems, Mongolia continues to face significant challenges related to the fragmentation of services and uneven quality across sectors. Key obstacles include gaps in interoperability at the implementation level and weak accountability at the policy level. These barriers hinder the effective integration of services across education, health, child protection, and social welfare systems. The lack of standardized procedures and systems further complicates efforts to address the diverse needs of Mongolia’s rural, urban, and nomadic herder populations. As Mongolia transitions to upper-middle-income country (UMIC) status, geopolitical shifts and governance risks compound these challenges, shifting policy priorities and exacerbating service delivery inequities. Equity in service quality remains a critical gap that must be addressed with a more inclusive and context-sensitive approach to service design and implementation.
2. Financing Bottlenecks and Fiscal Pressures
Despite notable gains in financing for critical sectors such as child protection and school meals, Mongolia’s fiscal pressures remain a major challenge. Tightening fiscal space, inflationary pressures, and the country’s growing reliance on external financing have made it difficult to sustain investments in social services. The fiscal shift that comes with Mongolia’s UMIC transition is further complicated by governance challenges and incomplete fiscal discipline. Previously fragmented funding for child protection and outdated school meal methodologies exacerbated issues related to adequacy and equity. These challenges highlight the need for evidence-based costing, improved budget protection, and strengthened fiscal discipline to safeguard social sector investments and prevent deprioritization of critical services.
3. Workforce Capacity and Coordination Limitations
Mongolia faces long-standing gaps in workforce capacity across sectors, particularly in the areas of child protection, early childhood development (ECD), and social protection. Weak governance structures and politically influenced human resource policies have hampered efforts to build a responsive, agile workforce. Coordination across sectors remains poorly defined, and there is a lack of systematic monitoring and accountability mechanisms. These issues are especially pronounced in cross-sectoral domains, including child protection, WASH, and climate action. As a result, scaling programs that integrate services across sectors has been difficult, and sustainability remains a challenge.
4. Persistent Digital Divide and Weak Data Governance
While Mongolia has made strides in digitizing curricula and offering offline learning solutions, gaps in digital connectivity and uneven data governance continue to limit equitable access to education and other essential services. The digital divide, particularly between urban and rural areas, hinders children’s ability to access quality education, and weak data governance practices—including issues related to interoperability, privacy, and AI readiness—prevent the full utilization of data for improving service delivery. As Mongolia moves towards scaling digital solutions, there is a need for a more comprehensive strategy to address connectivity gaps, ensure data privacy, and support sustainable digitalization across all sectors.
Lessons Learned
1. Private Sector Engagement as a Structural Lever
A key lesson learned in 2025 was the value of private sector engagement as a critical lever for sustainable financing. Through eight memoranda of understanding (MOUs), tax incentive advocacy, and digital fundraising initiatives with platforms such as Hipay, Shoppy, and Qpay, the office was able to diversify its resource base. These efforts resulted in recurring revenue that financed initiatives such as safe water campaigns and bagh school programs. This approach demonstrated how strategic communication, coupled with incentives, can convert corporate interest into lasting impacts for children.
2. Integrated Evidence and Real-Time Data for Rapid Decision-Making
The use of integrated evidence and real-time data has proven to accelerate decision-making and inform policy dialogues. Tools like the MICS Plus and subnational SITANs (Situational Analyses) supported rapid responses to key issues such as fertility rates and the need for monitoring and evaluation reforms. By incorporating real-time data into integrated dashboards, UNICEF was able to shift budget planning from incremental to analytical, particularly for school meals and child protection programs. These systems boosted resilience to economic shocks and allowed for more targeted interventions in vulnerable communities.
3. Proximity Models and Multigrade Teaching to Reduce Inequities
In response to challenges in rural education access, the implementation of proximity models such as “One Bagh, One School” brought education closer to children in remote areas, reducing the reliance on long-distance travel and dormitories. Multigrade teaching, combined with energy-efficient facilities and digital content, proved to be scalable solutions for remote areas. This approach not only improved education access and attendance but also maintained educational quality and inclusivity, contextualizing global standards to meet Mongolia’s specific realities.
4. Cross-Sector Climate Action Yields Child-Centered Gains
Integrating climate action into social service delivery has provided multiple benefits for children. For instance, efforts to align climate priorities with Mongolia’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 and pilot projects for upgrading CHIP (Climate Smart Health Infrastructure) facilities led to improvements in health and reduced energy costs. These actions also demonstrated how integrating climate mitigation and adaptation strategies into social programs can yield long-term child-centered gains, reducing vulnerability and enhancing resilience against environmental shocks.
5. Scaling from Pilots to National Coverage
The successful expansion from 3 aimags (provinces) to all 21 aimags demonstrates that early piloting combined with strong government ownership and system integration is critical for sustainable scale-up. Key factors that enabled this scale-up transition included strong policy anchoring that embedded new models—such as digital health, One Bagh One School, and climatesmart WASH—into national strategies and laws, ensuring institutionalization rather than temporary projects. Crosssector collaboration across health, education, social protection, and WASH created integrated delivery platforms that improved both equity and efficiency. Government leadership at national and aimag levels strengthened planning, budgeting, and monitoring systems, making services more sustainable and reducing reliance on donordriven initiatives. Innovation and adaptability, including the introduction of digital and climatesmart solutions, enabled services to reach remote and nomadic populations, helping to reduce disparities and ensure no one is left behind. Finally, the shift from UNICEF acting as a service provider to serving as a national systems partner facilitated coinvestment and laid the foundation for longterm, scalable impact.
