6. Gender-related disparities continue to affect children and caregivers across Mongolia, despite progress in mainstreaming gender considerations in national reforms. Service systems across health, education, child protection and social protection remain largely gender-blind, resulting in uneven outcomes for girls, boys and women caregivers. Boys in rural and herder communities continue to face higher risks of school dropout due to labor demands, while adolescent girls experience disproportionate exposure to online risks, violence and harmful norms that are not yet fully addressed in existing child protection protocols. Women, particularly in rural households, continue to shoulder the majority of unpaid caregiving work, limiting their access to services, training and livelihood opportunities. These challenges are compounded by weak gender-disaggregated data within administrative systems, reducing the ability of policymakers to detect gendered vulnerabilities or to measure outcomes meaningfully.
Future Outlook
1. Strengthen Systems and Ensure Interoperability
Going forward, the focus will be on consolidating system strengthening efforts to enhance interoperability and accountability. Key priorities include the full implementation of  integrated case management systems such as PRIMERO and the development of cross-sector coordination platforms. These platforms, along with public scorecards, will promote mutual accountability across child protection, health, education, and social protection sectors, ensuring that resources are used effectively and that service delivery is equitable.
2. Scale Service Models in Remote Areas
To address the geographic disparities in service delivery, expanding proximity models like bagh schools and Teacher-with-Tablet home-based ECE will be essential. Scaling these models will require investment in resilient infrastructure, including solar-powered schools and safe WASH facilities. Offline content solutions and digital connectivity improvements will continue to play a critical role in bridging the digital divide and building a more equitable education system, especially in rural areas.
3. Institutionalize Analytical Budgeting for Child Services
Institutionalizing analytical budgeting, including child budget tagging, will be a priority to ensure that investments in child services are protected, especially during times of fiscal uncertainty. Routine costing for school meals, child protection services, and other essential services will be integrated into public financial management (PFM) cycles and mid-year reviews, facilitating better equity tracking at the provincial level.
4. Expand Climate-Smart Social Services
Mongolia must continue to integrate climate-smart solutions into social service delivery, with a focus on green loans, community solar financing, and low-carbon heating transitions. These efforts will not only reduce energy costs but also provide children with healthier, more sustainable environments in which to grow and learn. These efforts should be guided by a gender lens, addressing barriers that limit women’s access to clean energy, finance, and skills, to ensure climate-smart social services are inclusive, effective, and benefit vulnerable households.
5. Strengthen Humanitarian Preparedness
Enhancing preparedness systems, including pre-positioning supplies, training responders, and refining vulnerability analyses, will be crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of emergency responses. Embedding child protection in emergency protocols and expanding responder training nationwide will help ensure that Mongolia is better equipped to respond to future shocks without sacrificing the well-being of children.
6. Institutionalizing gender equality for an inclusive transition
Looking ahead, Mongolia’s progress will depend on more intentional integration of gender-responsive approaches across national systems. Priorities include strengthening gender-sensitive data systems, embedding gender-responsive budgeting in health, education, social protection and child protection, and expanding adolescent services that address the different risks faced by girls and boys, including mental health and digital safety. Continued efforts are needed to improve prevention and response to gender-based violence, particularly in rural areas where service availability remains limited. Promoting women’s leadership and ensuring that climate-resilient and green development initiatives benefit women and girls will also be essential as Mongolia advances its low-carbon transition. By institutionalizing these approaches within policies, financing systems and service delivery models, Mongolia can ensure that its transition to UMIC status results in equitable outcomes for all children, adolescents and caregivers.

In 2025, children in Myanmar continued to be profoundly affected by a complex and protracted crisis, with escalating conflict and disasters placing severe pressure on their safety, wellbeing and access to essential services. Nearly five years into the conflict, violence has intensified, disasters have multiplied, including a major 7.7. magnitude earthquake - and essential services are under immense strain amid a deepening economic decline and disappearing safety nets, placing an increasing number of children at heightened risk. As the year draws to a close, access to safe and protective spaces for children continued to shrink in many affected areas, more than one-third of all children in the country (i.e. 6.9 million children), remain in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.


Children account for one in three of the over 3.6 million people displaced across Myanmar, uprooted from their homes, schools and communities by conflict and insecurity. Their lives are increasingly marked by fear and instability, as airstrikes, clashes and the widespread use of landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW) turn homes, playgrounds and paths to school into danger zones. In the first half of 2025 alone, 357 civilian casualties from landmines and ERW were recorded — 27 per cent were children — continuing Myanmar’s tragic ranking as the world’s most landmine-affected country.


The March earthquake compounded an already dire crisis in a part of the country already affected by conflict, displacement and other natural disasters. Many children who had already endured years of conflict and displacement faced another wave of loss, trauma and fear as homes, schools and health facilities collapsed around them. More than 3,600 people were killed and over 5,000 injured. For children, the destruction meant not only the loss of shelter, learning and health facilities, but deep emotional scars and growing uncertainty about the future.


Access to health care, safe water and education remains critically limited. Nearly one million children continue to miss out on basic immunizations, while 4.7 million are not accessing an education, exposing them to heightened risks of early marriage, violence against children, gender-based violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, and recruitment by armed actors. Malnutrition, unsafe sanitation and eroding social safety nets are pushing families deeper into poverty, with more than half of all children now living below the poverty line. Rising food prices and shrinking incomes affected the quality of children’s diets, with many children aged 6-23 months unable to access adequately diverse and nutritious diets. 


In some of the most intensely affected and hardest-to-reach areas — including Rakhine, Shan and Sagaing — fighting, insecurity and access restrictions continue to impede humanitarian operations, even as needs escalate. Access remained a major challenge.


With elections starting in December 2025, the political and operational environment remains volatile in the immediate term, with implications for access and programme delivery.


Despite these immense challenges, UNICEF — with the critical support of partners — continued to stay and deliver under difficult and often high-risk conditions throughout 2025. In the immediate aftermath of the earthquake, this support enabled rapid, lifesaving assistance for children and families, including emergency health care, safe water, nutrition services, protection support and temporary learning spaces. At the same time, sustained investments helped reinforce local systems and community capacities, laying the groundwork for recovery and longer-term resilience in areas already strained by years of conflict and disruption.


Through strong local partnerships, UNICEF remained alongside children most in need — delivering life-saving support at scale in frontline areas and as close as possible to affected communities, reaching children when and where it mattered most, protecting young lives and supporting recovery, resilience and well-being amid ongoing crisis.


Yet the scale of the crisis continues to outpace available resources. In 2025, UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was only about 20 per cent funded, despite growing needs driven by the ongoing conflict, devastating earthquake, deepening poverty, economic decline and the erosion of essential services and social safety nets.


Without urgent and sustained support, millions of children face mounting trauma, deprivation and loss — placing their survival, learning and future at grave risk. Every day without action pushes more children beyond the reach of help, and further away from the safe, dignified and hopeful future they deserve.

Despite the immense challenges, UNICEF has adapted its operations to ensure continuity of critical services for children while promoting durable, community-based systems through partnerships with local organizations and the private sector.


Throughout 2025, the Transitional Cooperation Framework (TCF) continued to guide planning and engagement, strengthening the humanitarian–development–peace nexus and emphasizing decentralized approaches for greater impact. In 2025, Donors and partners increasingly recognized the need for multi-faceted strategies that sustain local systems like health and education while strengthening resilience and community structures.


UNICEF enhanced integrated delivery through its five field offices and a national network of partners.  This close coordination between national partners, field offices and technical sections remained critical to delivering principled, needs-based assistance in Myanmar’s volatile and dynamic environment.


In the area of health and nutrition, UNICEF implemented extensive, multi-sectoral interventions to address the compounded impact of protracted conflict and the Mar-2025 earthquake that severely damaged health infrastructure.


UNICEF delivered essential health services to over 617,000 people (65 per cent women and girls) in targeted areas, including primary health care, maternal and child health care. Nutrition interventions reached more than 3.2 million children under five with vitamin A supplementation, treatment for severe acute malnutrition using therapeutic food, and preventive nutrition services for children and pregnant women at risk of malnutrition. Over 577,000 children were vaccinated against measles. 


Essential medicines were provided to treat leading causes of death among children under five, including amoxicillin, oral rehydration salts, and zinc tablets. UNICEF also supplied safe-delivery health kits—such as clean delivery and community newborn kits—and delivered essential nutrition services, including screening, treatment of severe acute malnutrition, IYCF counselling, and micronutrient supplementation.


Following the Mar-2025 earthquake, UNICEF delivered more than 80 metric tons of emergency supplies, including medical kits, tents, hygiene kits, and water purification tablets, to help restore essential services and support affected communities. 


The education programme prioritized foundational learning for children affected by conflict, displacement and exclusion. Focusing on early learning, non-formal education and emergency education, UNICEF reached over one million children and adolescents, advancing sectoral priorities and global commitments on learning, equity, and inclusion.


Early learning supported school readiness, expanding access to developmentally appropriate, play-based learning alongside parenting and caregiving initiatives. Investments in early childhood workforce capacity enhanced educator skills, strengthened service quality, and supported future scale-up.     


Flexible learning pathways expanded for crisis-affected learners impacted by conflict and the earthquake. Education in emergencies was delivered through camp-based and temporary learning spaces, community and monastic schools, supported by learning materials, trained educators, psychosocial support and strengthened community-based education management.


Non-formal education programmes re-engaged out-of-school children and adolescents, including with life skills, supporting progression toward foundational competencies. Equity and inclusion were embedded across programming through targeted support for children with disabilities, reinforced child safeguarding, and sustained community engagement.


UNICEF’s WASH response prioritized scaling up lifesaving WASH services, supporting earthquake-affected population in recovery, reconstruction of damaged WASH infrastructure and gradually transitioning to sustainable service delivery. Resilient WASH services are being scaled up for communities, learning centers and health facilities, while maintaining the lifesaving response to meet humanitarian needs. 


Priorities included lifesaving WASH response for conflict-affected populations (distribution of critical WASH supplies, emergency water supply, emergency latrines, and hygiene promotion); implementing durable WASH solutions; and community resilience-building (climate-resilient water supply and sanitation services, improved WASH services in schools, community empowerment, and SBCC in communities and institutions).


Major WASH results in 2025 include more than 950,000 people reached with critical WASH supplies, more than 143,000 people accessing appropriate sanitation services, and over 1.20 million people accessing a sufficient quantity and quality of water for drinking and domestic needs.  A total of 110 schools and 34 healthcare facilities were supported with basic WASH services, while 260 schools received WASH supplies. Nearly 38,000 children in learning spaces now use safe and appropriate WASH facilities and services. Moreover, with a focus on menstrual hygiene management, UNICEF supported 8,404 women and adolescent girls through the provision of appropriate menstrual materials and related services. MHM awareness campaigns, including activities marking Menstrual Hygiene Day, helped reduce stigma, improve knowledge, and promote dignity and school attendance for girls. Nearly 40,000 people now live in water safe communities and over 14,000 people gained access to basic WASH services.


In the area of child protection, UNICEF and partners reached over 1.34 million children, adolescents, and caregivers with critical child protection services. These included mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), explosive ordnance risk education (EORE), gender-based violence (GBV) risk mitigation, case management, and safe channels to report sexual exploitation and abuse. This represents more than double the original target, demonstrating UNICEF’s agility and leadership in a rapidly deteriorating context.


UNICEF continued leading child protection coordination, ensuring service continuity across conflict-affected areas. Key achievements included strengthening the social service workforce and supporting community-based protection mechanisms, enabling local actors to lead MHPSS, case management and GBV risk-mitigation. These efforts helped stabilize the fragmented system and improve support for vulnerable children.


UNICEF played a central role in safeguarding children from grave violations: 410,296 people received life-saving EORE, mitigating the escalating threat of landmines and explosive remnants of war; 143 survivors of explosive weapons—many of them children—received medical care, psychosocial support, rehabilitation, and assistive devices; 92 per cent of children formerly associated with armed forces and groups received comprehensive reintegration support, including family tracing, counselling, and education or vocational pathways.


Localization remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s child protection strategy. Through direct partnerships with local NGOs, CBOs, and faith-based organizations, UNICEF ensured service continuity in areas inaccessible to international actors. Local procurement of supplies further strengthened community resilience and reduced operational delays.


UNICEF's social policy programme in 2025 significantly expanded the reach and quality of humanitarian assistance and disability-inclusive services for the most vulnerable children and families.


A total of 141,320 people were supported with social protection and humanitarian assistance, comprising pregnant women and young children through the Maternal and Child Cash Transfers (MCCT) programme, and children enrolled in the Child Disability Benefits scheme. At least 87 per cent of MCCT beneficiaries were reached with social and behaviour change communication.


Major progress was achieved in disability-inclusive programming. Some 61,660 people are registered in the Disability Management Information System (DMIS), representing nearly a 30 per cent increase from the previous year and enabling access to disability benefits and specialist support. In partnership with local organisations of persons with disabilities and NGOs, 23,025 people with disabilities received assistive devices and specialised services. 


In 2025, UNICEF Myanmar strengthened Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) and Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) to improve programme effectiveness, community participation, and equitable access to essential services for children and caregivers affected by the crisis.


Through social media and community engagement, UNICEF provided accurate, timely, and actionable information across all sectors, reaching 3.9 million people. SBC mobilized partner support for earthquake response, integrating community concerns into needs assessments and informing programme priorities. Lifesaving supplies were delivered with community engagement, and psychosocial support messages were disseminated via mass media.


Communication strategies were tailored for diverse groups, including ethnic-language communities, “media dark” areas, and displaced populations, through partnerships with local and ethnic service providers. Community engagement reached 445,676 people in hard-to-reach areas, surpassing the 250,000 target.


To strengthen evidence generation, two studies examined behavioral drivers—gender roles in immunization and community views on acute watery diarrhea—providing insights for stakeholders. Social listening interventions addressed rumors and misinformation during disease outbreaks.


Capacity building was central to SBC/AAP efforts. UNICEF trained 1,342 individuals from partner organizations and frontline workers on interpersonal communication, risk communication, and AAP principles, ensuring harmonized messaging in high-risk areas.


Community feedback mechanisms expanded across humanitarian response areas, reaching 264,794 people, while 157,209 provided feedback via partners and call centers. This helped identify emerging needs, counter misinformation, and address concerns on service quality, safety, and equitable access.


In the area of protection from sexual abuse and exploitation (PSEA), in 2025, UNICEF Myanmar continued implementing the PSEA Action Plan with tailored capacity-building efforts that enabled all medium- and high-risk IPs to scale up and comply with PSEA standards. PSEA capacity-building initiatives involved 62 IPs (295 participants).


UNICEF staff (161) across five offices received PSEA(H) refresher training, emphasizing internal reporting mechanisms and promoting changes in social attitudes and normative behaviours. PSEA messages reached 767,960  people in communities and IDP camps through posters and digital channels (Viber), raising awareness of zero tolerance and UNICEF co-chaired the PSEA Network in 2024–2025, providing leadership and funding to implement the Network Workplan endorsed by the HCT/UNCT. The Network developed a Joint SEA Risk Assessment and Mitigation Plan, validated by 32 organizations, and trained 16 civil-society investigators. Five sub-national PSEA Networks were reactivated with new Action Plans, while reporting mechanisms were strengthened and field missions and trainings conducted, including during the earthquake response, to reinforce coordination and safe reporting.


Cluster coordination 


UNICEF continued its leadership role as Cluster Lead Agency for Nutrition, WASH, Child Protection Area of Responsibility (AoR), and Mine Action AoR, while co-leading the Education Cluster with Save the Children. 


To address heightened humanitarian needs with scarce resources, the UNICEF led cluster/AoRs used an access lens to map service gaps and address bottlenecks.  Localization remained a key priority, and it will be increasingly important in 2026 in the context of the humanitarian reset and establishment of sub-national Area Based Coordination structures. 


The Nutrition Cluster delivered critical interventions for severe and moderate acute alnutrition, alongside preventive measures such as Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) counselling, supplementary feeding, and micronutrient supplementation.  Capacity-building to partner staff was provided on cluster coordination, information management, IMAM, and IYCF. 


The Education Cluster continued capacity building initiatives in areas like Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL), Mine Risk Education, MHPSS, PSEA, Inclusive education and EiE Fundamentals. 184 partner staff benefitted from these trainings. Compared to previous years, the Education Cluster increased the number of beneficiaries reached in the hardest to reach locations in 2025-nearly 63 per cent of beneficiaries were reached in locations that are highest in access and sector needs severity. 


The WASH Cluster coordinated over 70 partners to restore water systems, expand safe sanitation, and deliver hygiene promotion in high-risk areas. Scale up of Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) and cholera preparedness, severity mapping in collaboration with the Health Cluster, and earthquake-resilient WASH designs were other priorities. More than 200 frontline staff were trained on WASH in emergencies.


The Child Protection AoR enhanced quality of child protection services through online and in-person training. Monitoring and reporting was scaled up post-earthquake, and guidance for CP programming in response was developed. Over 120 partner staff were trained on child-friendly spaces.


The Mine Action AoR scaled up Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) and victim assistance, including EORE messages for non-mine action experts during response to natural disasters. Online and in-person trainings supported mainstreaming mine action across clusters. Digital EORE campaigns were deployed through community networks and local media to overcome access challenges.


In the area of operations, the country office ensured access to affected populations, particularly after the March 2025 earthquake. Logistics opportunities were tapped quickly, enabling UNICEF to successfully provide support. 


Through training, innovation, and modernization, digital systems remained a secure and dependable backbone for UNICEF’s work. The Digital Impact team strengthened UNICEF Myanmar’s digital backbone by modernizing platforms, securing data, and expanding automation despite severe connectivity and operational constraints. Infrastructure upgrades, stronger continuity systems, and smarter digital tools enabled more resilient, efficient, and secure delivery of results nationwide.  


A strong focus on security enabled programme delivery and safeguarded personnel across Myanmar. As an active member of the inter-agency Security Cell, UNICEF consistently advocated its operational priorities, ensuring that Security Risk Management (SRM) documents were adapted to support programme access and continuity in high-risk areas. UNICEF also chaired and co-chaired four Security Cell Working Groups, fostering inter-agency coordination and strategic alignment.


Staff security and safety continued to be a priority, with training (SSAFE and IFAK) conducted in all offices. Safe and Secure Approaches in Field Environments (SSAFE) and Individual First Aid Kit (IFAK) first aid responder trainings equipped UNICEF personnel with the skill, knowledge and tools to operate in high-risk and very-high risk environments. Both trainings are recommended SRM measures and enable UNICEF programmes to operate at an acceptable level of risk across the country The office also provided Women Security Awareness Training (WSAT).


UNICEF successfully facilitated and led the first inter-agency convoys to earthquake-affected areas in Mandalay and Nay Pyi Taw, ensuring timely access for humanitarian actors and critical supplies. Additionally, the office undertook extensive preparedness initiatives in anticipation of the December 2025 elections, working closely with all field offices and ASMTs to strengthen contingency planning and risk mitigation strategies. 


In 2025, in the area of advocacy and communications, UNICEF Myanmar remained a leading voice for children through public advocacy and communications advancing evidence-based advocacy on urgent child rights concerns, championing expanded access to life-saving vaccinations, and using strong, sustained communications to spotlight the needs of the most vulnerable. UNICEF also strengthened the capacity of local partners to generate credible visibility and mobilize support in hard-to-reach areas, amplifying community perspectives where access is limited.


Digital engagement grew significantly in 2025, driven by timely humanitarian updates and compelling storytelling. UNICEF Myanmar’s social media content reached 16.8 million people—an increase from the previous year—and its X platform expanded to 7,231 followers while keeping a strong 7.02 per cent engagement rate. More than 70,000 users visited the UNICEF Myanmar website, reflecting continued public interest in the situation of children and UNICEF’s response.


UNICEF Myanmar’s Facebook community expanded to 1.06 million followers, with 27,000 new followers added in 2025, and an average post engagement rate of 4.95 per cent, far exceeding the 1.8 per cent industry benchmark. YouTube also saw exceptional growth, gaining 5,600 new subscribers and reaching 9,200 total subscribers as video storytelling became a central engagement tool. Across platforms, users shared UNICEF content 27,401 times—a more than tenfold increase over last year—demonstrating the critical role of digital engagement in mobilising global support for the most vulnerable children in Myanmar. In 2025, UNICEF Myanmar used digital platforms to champion the rights and safety of children through 30 impactful campaigns. UNICEF’s response to Myanmar earthquake drove massive engagement, highlighting the urgent needs for protection, clean water and shelter.


In 2025, UNICEF strengthened the communication skills of more than 150 frontline partners across education, WASH, nutrition, child protection, health and broader humanitarian response, many of whom work in the hardest-hit conflict-affected and earthquake-impacted areas. Through targeted training in communications, ethical photography, video documentation and human-interest storytelling, partners gained the capacity to safely capture and convey the realities facing children and their families. 


As Myanmar’s crisis evolves, young people remain among the most affected, facing barriers to safe information and participation. In 2025, UNICEF strengthened youth engagement through U-Report, equipping adolescents with the knowledge, platforms and skills to express their views and drive positive change for children


U-Report Myanmar maintained one of Southeast Asia’s highest poll response rates at 96 per cent despite connectivity challenges, while expanding co-creation with youth to shape content and lead community discussions. Its digital presence grew steadily, reaching over 138,000 Facebook followers and 12,000 YouTube subscribers, driven by youth-led content on mental health, child rights and life skills.”


UNICEF also continued to invest in youth capacity-building. 350 youth volunteers from diverse regions—including hard-to-reach areas—were trained in areas including MHPSS, PSEA, digital content creation, ethical storytelling, debate skills, EORE, CRC, facilitation skills and mobile videography. These young leaders increasingly serve as UNICEF’s advocacy allies, supporting community-level awareness raising and amplifying child rights issues across digital and offline spaces.


In 2025, Myanmar’s youth voices also gained ASEAN visibility. Five young people were selected to participate in ASEAN Youth Forum on Climate Change and contributed in the development of ASEAN Youth Declaration, contributing perspectives from Myanmar to regional and international dialogue. 


Despite a constrained environment, UNICEF advanced programme advocacy by coordinating a joint immunization initiative with UN agencies, embassies and partners, aiming to strengthen collective action and address the widening immunization gap affecting children and pregnant women in Myanmar. 


In the area of resource mobilization, UNICEF Myanmar expanded and diversified its donor base in 2025, with notable progress in bringing on board International Financial Institutions (IFIs). Both the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) initiated multi-year grants with larger funding envelopes, signifying increased confidence to re-invest in Myanmar’s social services.


Emerging and new donors also played an increasingly important role, including the Republic of Korea, KOICA, CIDCA, and the UK FCDO. Importantly, all of these donors, identified as priority targets last year, have now become active contributors in 2025.


A range of support modalities were mobilized, including the first chartered supplies to arrive in Myanmar after the earthquake (supported by ECHO) - paving the way for other chartered flights, and China’s PSFR-supported supplies, which were vital during the emergency response.


A significant milestone this year was the strong support from UNICEF National Committees and PSFR offices, which together contributed US$16.5 million primarily for humanitarian assistance, including support for the recent earthquake.


Donors also demonstrated increasing interest in longer-term recovery needs, including Japan’s grant to support earthquake recovery, the new CIDCA grant approved for post-earthquake efforts, and growing interest from other partners such as in the current discussions KOICA’s joint HDP nexus project with UNDP and WFP. 


Throughout 2025, UNICEF continued regular donor briefings, bilateral meetings, and field visits with key donor partners. Project field visits, including with high-level delegations, were conducted with Japan, Korea, and ECHO, helping to strengthen transparency and partnership collaboration.


As part of private sector engagement, UNICEF, in partnership with Rakuten Viber, continued to reach communities across Myanmar with lifesaving messages through the Knowledge Talk Viber channel. The one-year extension of this partnership will further enhance outreach and support for both humanitarian and development activities.


Looking ahead, UNICEF aims to retain and deepen engagement with partners and donors, with a focus on leveraging larger and multi-year funding to enable investment in resilience-building of communities and scale up of activities.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF faced a series of compounding external challenges that demanded agile and innovative responses to sustain effective service delivery for children across Myanmar. The year was marked by intensifying armed conflict, which continued to restrict humanitarian access, and a devastating 7.7 magnitude earthquake in March, centered in Sagaing, that caused widespread destruction, loss of life, and severe disruption to infrastructure and services. The earthquake further exacerbated existing vulnerabilities, triggering large-scale displacement and increasing the demand for emergency assistance. Despite initial hopes for a humanitarian ceasefire following the earthquake, hostilities escalated sharply, with April recording the highest number of airstrikes since 2021. 


The challenges of working in areas where limited partners were operating - until new partners were brought on board -  along with prolonged and expanding internet and communication blackouts—both due to earthquake-related infrastructure damage and ongoing restrictions—significantly hampered coordination, information flow, and remote support for field operations. Civil society organization registration requirements and conscription laws continued to impact the availability of partner staff and community volunteers, leading to withdrawals from key project areas. 


Security risks for UNICEF and partner personnel remained high, at times limiting the ability or delaying the conduct of programming and monitoring visits.


Operationally, the organization grappled with rising commodity prices, persistent inflation, and cash withdrawal constraints, all of which complicated financial transactions and procurement. Movement restrictions on supplies—particularly in Rakhine (since November 2023) and Kachin (since March 2024)—further strained contingency stock levels and reduced the capacity to respond swiftly to emerging needs. 


To enable the movement of personnel in such a highly volatile and fluid environment requires a high degree of agility and flexibility, with UNICEF taking advantage of short windows of opportunity when fighting temporarily ceased and access was possible. However, in the absence of hardening measures, the UN is largely reliant on preventative security measures such as training, liaison and information collection, analysis, advice, and coordination, security assessment missions and participation of security staff on programme missions.


Programmes in 2025 continued to face access and security constraints due to ongoing conflict, displacement, and climate shocks, including floods, earthquakes, and droughts. In some areas, limited infrastructure, weak local capacity, and uncertainty around governance and land use made it difficult to shift quickly from emergency services to durable solutions. Funding gaps and delays also affected the scale and speed of early recovery efforts.


Protracted crisis coupled with recurrent natural disasters (floods, cyclones and earthquake) demonstrated the need to further prioritise community resilience, build climate and disaster resilient WASH services infrastructure, while continuing to meet the WASH needs of displaced populations. The earthquake demonstrated the need to build climate and disaster resilient WASH infrastructure to ensure continued service delivery.  Durable water systems, climate-resilient sanitation, and renewable energy solutions reduced repeated emergency costs and strengthened community ownership. Strong community engagement, local partnerships, and hygiene behaviour change were key to sustaining results and supporting healthier living environments.


Going forward, WASH will focus on linking humanitarian response to longer-term recovery. Priority will be given to climate-resilient water supply, improved sanitation, sustained hygiene promotion, and renewable energy systems, while promoting peacebuilding and social cohesion through inclusive, community-managed WASH services that support stability and recovery for children and families.


In education, ASER-based learning assessments conducted in 2025 revealed persistent gaps in literacy and numeracy, with fewer than half of assessed children meeting Grade 2 standards, underscoring the need to sustain and strengthen foundational learning interventions. 


Greater focus will also be placed on adolescents and the most marginalized by expanding pathways that link foundational learning to skills development - including upskilling, life, digital and green skills - and by leveraging digital solutions such as the Learning Passport to enhance access, inclusion, and future opportunities.


On health and nutrition, delivering health and nutrition programmes across the country continued to be a challenge. UNICEF received substantial and more flexible support from major donors to enable greater reach in hard-to-reach and conflict-affected areas. In 2026, UNICEF will focus on strengthening partnerships amongst all service providers to advance universal health coverage and prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis. 


In the area of child protection, shifting from direct implementation to community-led and localized delivery when access was restricted, expanding digital outreach for MHPSS and EORE, and reprioritizing geographic focus based on real-time conflict dynamics, were critical to our success. Also key was leveraging multisectoral entry points to extend child protection services through joint interventions with education, health, and WASH programmes. Together, these adaptive measures enabled UNICEF to sustain a high-impact child protection response despite unprecedented operational constraints.


In 2026, UNICEF Myanmar will strengthen community-led case management, MHPSS, and EORE networks; integrate child protection more fully across Education, Health, Nutrition, WASH, and Social Protection platforms; and develop remote and mobile service modalities to overcome access constraints. 


In the area of social policy, valuable lessons emerged for future scale-up. Several innovations proved highly effective - an integrated accountability platform consolidating community feedback, payment verification, and referrals through a dedicated call centre. Investments in routine systems such as the DMIS proved essential for shock-responsive programming, enabling rapid earthquake and flood response and demonstrating how development investments build emergency capacity. An ongoing MCCT evaluation with the World Bank and a completed impact assessment of Child Disability Benefits are systematically generating evidence on what works.


Cross-programme mainstreaming of disability inclusion is advancing through targeted interventions, though broader integration across sectors remains a work in progress and will be a priority for 2026. 


Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF will continue to advance inter-agency strategy and coordination while consolidating new financing partnerships with the World Bank and Asian Development Bank for sustained coverage. Priorities include further scaling up MCCT and Child Disability Benefits, while strengthening linkages to health services and social and behaviour change communication. Moreover, strategies for reducing gender gaps in access to essential services and resources and women’s access to GBV related health services will be strengthened.  UNICEF will continue to expand disability screening and DMIS registration, scale community support services and assistive technology provision, and strengthen coordination and evidence generation to inform programming.

Papua New Guinea (PNG) has one of the fastest-growing populations in the Pacific. The population is young (around 60 per cent under 25), predominantly rural (about 80 per cent), and still expanding rapidly. The official 2024 census puts the population at 10.185 million (approximately 5.3 million female and 4.8 million male), representing a 40 per cent increase since 2011[1]. 

Real GDP growth is projected to rise to about 4.5 per cent in 2025 (from 3.8 per cent in 2024), supported by stronger resource-sector production and improved agriculture, though the economy remains vulnerable to commodity-price shocks[2]. The 2026 National Budget sets total expenditure at K30.913 billion, about K2,882 per person highlighting fiscal constraints despite record headline totals[3]. Social sector allocations increased but remain below common benchmarks: education rose to K4.935 billion (+11.3 per cent), about 3.4 per cent of GDP (below the 4–6 per cent benchmark), and health rose to K3.204 billion (+15.8 per cent), about 2.2 per cent of GDP (below the commonly used 5 per cent benchmark) [4][5]. Per-capita spending remains modest, roughly K430 for education and K268 for health and rapid population growth further dilutes gains, leaving large infrastructure and workforce gaps, especially in rural and remote areas[6].

Service delivery is further constrained by weak subnational public financial management and logistics. Delays in fund releases and liquidation reduce outreach and supervision, while stock-outs persist due to limited forecasting and distribution planning. These system constraints mean that budget increases do not automatically translate into reliable service coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach districts and conflict-affected provinces alike.

Despite pockets of progress for girls and women particularly through stronger policy frameworks and localized service improvements, these gains have been uneven. Benefits have largely accrued to women in urban and better-served districts, while rural women, children, adolescents, and those in conflict-affected areas remain largely excluded. As a result, Papua New Guinea continues to rank among the weakest globally on gender equality, with progress constrained by persistent gaps in health outcomes, voice and agency, and access to economic and social opportunities.  In the UNDP Gender Inequality Index (GII), PNG is ranked 156th of 193 countries (GII 0.584), performing worse than the global average (0.455) and the East Asia and the Pacific regional level (0.315)[7]. Political representation is a stark example: women hold just 2.7 percent of seats in the National Parliament (3 of 111 members). Reproductive health indicators also point to inequality, with maternal mortality (192 per 100,000 live births) and adolescent birth rates (54.1 per 1,000 girls aged 15–19) remaining high. If these gaps persist, existing inequalities in health outcomes, education completion, and economic participation will widen, reinforcing intergenerational cycles of disadvantage and limiting national productivity gains.
 
Progress in maternal and newborn health remains slow. In 2025, only 27 per cent of pregnant women completed four antenatal care (ANC) visits, about 31 per cent of births occurred in health facilities, and early postnatal care within two days reached around 55 per cent. These levels indicate persistent barriers to completing the continuum of care from pregnancy through delivery and immediate postnatal support.

PNG’s HIV epidemic is escalating. The Government declared a National HIV Crisis on 26 June 2025 following evidence of rapidly rising transmission, including an estimated 11,000 new infections in 2024 (about 30 per day). Mother-to-child transmission is alarmingly high at 36 per cent, linked to low ART coverage (28 per cent), late ANC contact and weak integration of HIV services (only 47 per cent of ANC attendees tested). Strengthening integrated ANC, testing and treatment services is essential to protect women, newborns, children and adolescents.

Child morbidity remains concerning. Pneumonia case fatality among under-fives admitted to facilities was 1.9 per cent in 2024—nearly double the national target—while diarrhoeal incidence rose to 146 per 1,000 under-fives (SPAR 2024, NDoH).

Routine immunization coverage improved slightly but remains fragile. By late 2025, Pentavalent-3 coverage reached about 50 per cent, while measles first-dose coverage remained below 50 per cent. These vulnerabilities were underscored by the polio outbreak, with 60 detections confirmed by November (including five human cases and 55 positive environmental samples). Low routine coverage especially in conflict-affected and hard-to-reach areas continues to heighten outbreak risk.

Malnutrition remains severe and undermines survival, learning and long-term productivity. Approximately 48 per cent of children under five are stunted, more than double the average among regional peers (22 per cent). Wasting affects 16 per cent and 27 per cent are underweight (Household Income and Expenditure Survey 2009/2010). Micronutrient deficiencies are widespread: 49 per cent of children under five have anaemia and about 26 per cent have Vitamin A deficiency. Suboptimal childcare and feeding practices remain key drivers, alongside poverty, food insecurity and poor WASH.

Education outcomes remain below global standards despite free education policies. Only 12 per cent of girls and 16 per cent of boys complete Year 12, with high dropout among girls transitioning from primary to secondary school. PNG participates in the Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (PILNA) every three years, but lacks national learning assessments to routinely track learning outcomes. A skills mismatch persists, contributing to graduate unemployment and reliance on foreign workers.
 
The governance framework includes a reformed structure and curriculum, a national education plan, tuition fee subsidies and a special education policy, but implementation is constrained by financing and uneven capacity across provinces. Early childhood education is expanding (mandatory preschool and optional kindergarten), yet limited investment in teacher training, learning resources and quality assurance constrains quality and scale. Long distances to schools, safety concerns and social norms further discourage regular attendance and early enrolment in many communities.
 
Access to WASH services remains critically inadequate. According to JMP (2024), only 53.3 per cent of the population has at least basic water services and just 23.6 per cent has at least basic sanitation; over 80 per cent lack safely managed sanitation. Nearly half of households depend on unimproved water sources, increasing vulnerability to cholera and typhoid. Schools and health facilities face similar shortfalls; only 46 per cent of schools have basic WASH services, undermining health outcomes and school retention, particularly for adolescent girls.
 
Although PNG has a National WASH Policy (2015–2030) and climate adaptation frameworks, most prominent being its National Adaptation Plan (2023-2027), implementation is constrained by financing gaps and limited capacity. Without urgent investment in climate-resilient WASH systems, governance reforms, and disaster preparedness, PNG risks reversing progress toward the SDGs and deepening inequities for its most vulnerable populations including children. 

PNG faces compounding humanitarian risks from climate shocks and insecurity, with limited capacity to absorb and recover from recurring crises. The country is among the least climate-resilient globally, ranked 167th of 187 on the ND-GAIN index and was 54th on the 2024 Fragile States Index, signaling high exposure and fragility. Recurrent floods, landslides, cyclones and drought often compounded by tribal violence and election-related unrest continue to drive displacement and disrupt essential services.
