The current Country Programme cycle (2024–2028) is in the second year of implementation, anchored around three overarching priorities: (i) improving the quality and accessibility of basic social services to build public confidence and encourage their use; (ii) strengthening resilience and reducing risks to children, families and services in the face of disasters and crises; and (iii) reducing violence, abuse and exploitation of children and women. In this second year, UNICEF Papua New Guinea delivered strong results across these priorities, while generating lessons to further strengthen delivery in subsequent years.
 
Strengthening quality social services and fostering demand generation
 
UNICEF supported the Government of Papua New Guinea and partners to improve the quality, reach and uptake of essential services: maternal and newborn health, HIV, nutrition, immunization, early childhood education (ECE), WASH in schools and health facilities, and birth registration, while strengthening community demand through targeted social and behaviour change communication (SBCC).
 
In maternal and newborn health, UNICEF collaborated with partners to revise the Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmONC) framework, incorporating 14 updated signal functions, and piloted the revised approach in four provinces. Seventy-nine health workers were trained, and the intervention is expected to benefit more than 15,000 mothers annually. UNICEF also expanded clinical mentoring to four additional provinces. Newborn services were strengthened by complementing the 2024 upgrade of neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in 10 provinces with broader newborn care improvements across 14 provinces, expected to enhance care for over 25,000 newborns.
 
Nationally, 90,900 mothers (31.5 per cent) delivered in health facilities and 73,485 pregnant women (25.5 per cent) completed four antenatal care visits. HIV and syphilis testing reached 55.5 per cent (77,519 of 139,648). UNICEF’s technical support to BEmONC implementation and capacity strengthening including training of more than 550 health workers contributed to improving emergency obstetric and newborn care across the 14 provinces.
 
With HIV prevalence projected to reach 1.5 per cent and HIV declared a public health emergency in 2025, UNICEF supported the National Department of Health (NDoH) to develop the Ministerial HIV Response Plan and strengthen coordination through HIV and prevention of parent-to-child transmission (PPTCT) Technical Working Groups. UNICEF supported the launch of the Triple Elimination Strategy on 1 December 2025 (World AIDS Day). UNICEF procured and distributed 2,100 Bioline Dual Test Kits, enabling testing for an estimated 52,500 women, and facilitated procurement of antiretroviral medicines and other supplies, bringing total health supply investments to over US$ 1.9 million. Interventions to strengthen the uptake of HIV services among pregnant women remain prioritized to contribute to ensuring that zero babies are born with HIV by 2030.
 
In nutrition, UNICEF supported the Government to launch its first nutrition-sensitive social protection project, reaching over 10,000 mothers and children under two with nutrition grants. More than 80 per cent of households used the grants to purchase food. UNICEF enhanced the effectiveness of cash support through SBCC and integrated services (including backyard gardening) and improved access to immunization and antenatal care, resulting in over 80 per cent of targeted mothers (80,344) adopting improved child feeding practices.
 
To strengthen treatment for children with wasting, UNICEF partnered with the Government to roll out the new Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) guidelines, training over 100 health workers from Morobe, Central and Madang. The Community Nutrition Approach further strengthened early detection, referral, treatment and follow-up at household level. UNICEF also introduced the Community Nutrition Actions (CNA) model, delivering essential nutrition services through Village Health Assistants (VHAs) conducting household visits, an approach effective for rural populations who comprise over 80 per cent of PNG’s population. Due to its success, the Government adopted the CNA model as the foundation for its US$90 million Child Nutrition and Social Protection (CNSP) project, currently implemented in two provinces and expanding to four by year-end.
 
UNICEF’s sustained advocacy contributed to increased Government financing for nutrition: in 2025, US$479,000 was allocated for nutrition supplies (the second highest level since 2019), and the Government committed to releasing US$2.4 million to conduct a National Nutrition Survey. To strengthen sustainability and standards, UNICEF is supporting the revision of the School Health Policy to align with international norms.
 
For immunization, UNICEF strengthened both supply- and demand-side interventions. On the supply side, UNICEF strengthened supply chain governance through revised standard operating procedures (SOPs), job aids and regular vaccine situation analyses at national and provincial levels, keeping the EPI National Logistics Working Group functional and supporting coordinated action to prevent stockouts and maintain uninterrupted vaccine availability. On the demand side, UNICEF supported Advocacy, Communication and Social Mobilization (ACSM) activities for MNTE, polio and integrated immunization campaigns, addressing misinformation, low risk perception and gender-related barriers. UNICEF also applied Human-Centred Design in three provinces, training 24 Village Health Assistants to conduct household visits, distribute IEC materials and identify zero-dose children. As a result, UNICEF reached 895 caregivers in hard-to-reach areas.
 
UNICEF advanced ECE as a national priority through advocacy and system strengthening. ECE gained prominence through the Special Parliamentary Committee for Children and Youth and its integration into the World Bank-supported Learning Enhancement and Access Project (LEAP). UNICEF supported development of ECE Implementation Guidelines and influenced plans to scale UNICEF-supported ECE models to 127 schools across all 22 provinces. Sustained advocacy also contributed to a landmark National Executive Council decision to fund ECE teacher salaries, strengthening sustainability.
 
Through the Convergence Programme, UNICEF supported six holistic ECE model schools with church networks, integrating WASH improvements, teacher development and community engagement. Partners enrolled 3,890 children (including two children with disabilities), distributed 6,710 storybooks, and trained 109 teachers and 67 Board of Management members on ECE standards. Two model schools were recommended for registration, with 13 additional schools pending assessment in 2026.
 
Beyond ECE, UNICEF supported the PNG Partnership Compact, aligning 17 agencies to advance the 1-6-6 school restructuring and rollout of the Standard-Based Curriculum. As Grant Agent for the Global Partnership for Education, UNICEF will manage US$12.18 million to strengthen teacher quality, curriculum implementation and gender-responsive planning. UNICEF also secured AUD 33 million from DFAT for the Smarter Safer Schools (3S) Programme, targeting 600 schools with climate-resilient WASH, violence prevention and health services. These interventions are aimed to contribute to improved learning outcomes, teacher performance, student wellbeing and system efficiency.

In WASH, UNICEF improved learning and care environments and strengthened daily hygiene practices. Nine schools now have reliable water supply and improved handwashing and gender-segregated sanitation facilities. Seventeen schools received WASH training, 14 established hygiene clubs, and 114 student hygiene promoters reached approximately 5,000 peers (2,640 boys and 2,400 girls). UNICEF also addressed menstrual health needs for 8,432 girls and women, reducing barriers to school attendance and participation. Seven health care facilities gained reliable access to improved water sources, and four facilities upgraded handwashing and gender-segregated sanitation facilities, strengthening infection prevention and control and improving patient safety and dignity. Overall, around 35,000 people (18,884 men; 16,816 women) have been benefiting from these WASH improvements.
 
UNICEF strengthened birth registration by supporting registration of 36,308 children and issuing 4,136 birth certificates for children under five. UNICEF integrated registration into services in five hospitals, trained 57 health and Civil Registry staff, and provided critical inputs including 20,000 birth certificate forms, equipment and furniture. Mobile campaigns aligned with MNTE and polio outreach increased access in NCDC, Madang, Morobe and Rigo District. UNICEF also expanded school-based registration in two NCDC schools and leveraged private sector partnerships to take services closer to families through outreach at CPL shopping centres and marketplaces. As a result, more children especially those previously unreached gained legal identity, reducing barriers to essential services and strengthening the foundation for equitable access to health, education and protection interventions.
 
Building resilience and reducing risks to children and families
 
UNICEF strengthened resilience for children and families in Morobe and Central provinces through an integrated, climate-smart approach supported by KOICA, strengthening local systems, community preparedness and government planning across education, WASH, child protection and health.

In education, UNICEF built capacity in Disaster Risk Management (DRM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), working with the Guidance and Counselling (G&C) Division of the National Department of Education and leveraging UNICEF-developed knowledge products. Building on conflict and climate vulnerability assessments across 40 communities (including 20 schools) in Huon-Gulf and Bulolo districts, UNICEF trained 131 teachers (47 female), including 10 Provincial Department of Education officials, and supported endorsement of 13 School Learning Improvement Plans integrating resilience actions. These efforts strengthened school preparedness and positioned UNICEF as a driver of inclusive, climate-smart education in PNG.

In WASH, UNICEF advanced climate-resilient infrastructure and planning. Solar-powered borehole systems were designed and progressed to provide reliable, low-emission water supply for more than 11,300 people in Central Province. Hydrogeological assessments guided sustainable groundwater use, and designs incorporated measures to mitigate flooding and high-water table risks. UNICEF embedded climate rationale through participatory Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessments (CRVA) and hazard mapping, enabling 18 communities in Morobe and Central provinces to develop locally grounded, climate-resilient action plans identifying hazards, vulnerable groups and priority adaptation measures. Partnerships with the Climate Change and Development Authority and provincial administrations strengthened access to climate finance and integrated child-focused indicators into national adaptation efforts.

UNICEF reinforced community systems to prevent, manage and recover from shocks. Across Morobe and Central, 959 stakeholders (502 male; 457 female) were trained in climate resilience, disaster preparedness and WASH governance. In parallel, 956 people from 29 communities were trained in conflict analysis and climate risk assessment, resulting in 15 conflict-sensitive peacebuilding plans and 29 climate resilience plans. These community outputs informed two district WASH plans and the Morobe Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction Plan, strengthening coherence between community priorities and government planning. UNICEF also built the capacity of 25 humanitarian stakeholders (24 males; 1 female) in disaster risk analysis and emergency response as part of the DRR plan development process.

In health, UNICEF supported solarization of nine vaccine stores and 11 health facilities, reducing outages and safeguarding vaccine potency, especially in remote settings. UNICEF installed clean-air incinerators that comply with international emissions standards in three major provincial hospitals, replacing unsafe open burning and dumping practices; expansion to three additional provinces in 2026 will extend coverage to an estimated 25 per cent of major hospitals.

UNICEF also supported prevention-focused initiatives for child safety and wellbeing. The PNG Teen Entrepreneur Programme reached 2,080 students in seven pilot schools in Western Highlands Province, while the Safe Journey to School initiative promoted road safety among around 28,800 students and strengthened pre-service teacher education on positive behaviour and violence prevention.

Finally, UNICEF strengthened vaccine security and national ownership by leading forecasting, costing and planning for 2026, informing the Government’s decision to allocate K26 million for vaccine procurement (a 73 per cent increase over 2025). UNICEF supported cold chain expansion and reliability: new equipment was installed in 193 health facilities (including 93 health posts) and capacity was extended to 173 facilities. As a result, 97 per cent of facilities have functional cold chain equipment, and all registered facilities are fully equipped, bringing vaccines closer to communities and reducing service delays. These interventions reduced service disruptions during climate shocks and emergencies, directly lowering the risk of vaccine spoilage and interruptions for remote populations.
 
Reducing violence, abuse and exploitation of children and women
 
UNICEF advanced the Ending Violence Against Children (EVAC) agenda through policy engagement, systems strengthening, workforce development and frontline support—driven by stronger national leadership, improved service standards and expanded capacity of Government and community actors.

A major milestone was the establishment of PNG’s first Special Parliamentary Committee on Child and Youth Wellbeing in May 2025, following the visit of the UN Secretary-General’s Special Representative on Violence Against Children. The Committee convened its inaugural sitting in October 2025, creating a platform for parliamentary oversight and accountability on child protection and child rights reforms. As the 33rd EVAC Pathfinding Country, PNG developed a national EVAC Roadmap with UNICEF technical support, setting out multisectoral commitments aligned with international pledges and national priorities. In parallel, UNICEF together with OHCHR, DJAG/Juvenile Justice Services, the Human Rights Secretariat and Save the Children supported PNG’s contribution to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child’s draft General Comment 27 on access to justice and effective remedies, including two rounds of child consultations in November 2024 and June 2025.

At systems level, UNICEF supported development and institutionalization of key national frameworks. National Child Protection Case Management SOPs were finalized through a participatory process involving 27 stakeholders and eight National Task Force meetings; validation was completed and the national launch was scheduled for November 2025. UNICEF also supported development of the Child Protection Minimum Service Package (MSP) and its integration into both the National Capital District and the Juvenile Justice Service model, helping harmonize justice, legal, psychosocial support and referral pathways. The MSP process engaged 41 stakeholders and included consultations with 23 boys in detention at Bomana Correctional Services, who highlighted priorities such as access to education and legal assistance. UNICEF also supported development of a Parenting for Child Development (P4CD) institutionalization framework with the National Office for Children and Family Services (NCFS), aimed at integrating P4CD into Government initiatives and establishing more sustainable financing mechanisms.

On prevention, UNICEF and partners expanded evidence-informed parenting and psychosocial support. A total of 275 P4CD facilitators were trained in collaboration with faith-based organizations and delivered six-week sessions to 3,722 parents and caregivers, benefiting 3,846 children. Monitoring and focus group discussions indicated improved parenting practices, including reduced harsh discipline and stronger responsive caregiving. Gender-transformative parenting modules were developed and will be rolled out in 2026 to strengthen efforts to address the root causes of violence against women and children. Preparedness for child protection in emergencies was strengthened through training of 26 community facilitators, alongside distribution of 300 Child Friendly Spaces toolkit packages and 282 dignity kits.
Investments in the social service workforce reached 507 professionals. In Madang, 92 participants completed an intensive five-week child protection systems training, while 30 workers in Morobe received similar capacity building. UNICEF supported the launch of a Certificate II in Government Social Services pilot, with 22 professionals enrolled through a partnership with the Somare Institute of Leadership and Governance. Additional capacity building included 252 community leaders and child protection officers trained on P4CD coordination, 33 Village Court Officials trained on information management systems and climate-resilient child protection approaches, and 26 facilitators completing practical training on Child Friendly Spaces implementation in NCD and Morobe.
 
Emergency and Humanitarian response
 
UNICEF sustained lifesaving support to crisis-affected communities and strengthened preparedness and coordination despite insecurity, access constraints and partner disruptions.
 
In the Autonomous Region of Bougainville, UNICEF supported a coordinated drought response reaching 10,948 people (5,255 females; 5,693 males) with essential WASH, health and nutrition supplies, including hygiene kits for 100 households, a complete midwifery kit expected to support 50 safe deliveries, and nutrition commodities (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food, Micronutrient Powder and MUAC tapes) to enable the treatment of severe and moderate acute malnutrition.
 
UNICEF completed WASH support for communities affected by the May 2024 landslide in Mulitaka, overcoming delays driven by tribal conflict and insecurity in late 2024. When materials were stolen and an implementing partner withdrew, UNICEF adapted by engaging private companies and working with Government counterparts to complete and hand over WASH facilities at Mulitaka Primary School and the Health Center. These efforts restored access to safe water and sanitation for internally displaced people and surrounding communities, while helping maintain continuity of education and essential health services.
 
Following detection of poliovirus type 2 in Lae and confirmation in Port Moresby, the Government of PNG together with WHO and UNICEF declared a polio outbreak on 15 May 2025. UNICEF led vaccine logistics, social mobilization and integrated service delivery, complementing WHO’s surveillance and technical leadership. Two rounds of nOPV2 were conducted across 17 mainland provinces and fractional IPV was delivered in all 22 provinces, targeting 2.98 million children under 10. Coverage reached 82.4 per cent in round one and 83.2 per cent in round two for nOPV2, and 80 per cent nationwide for fractional IPV. Integrated services were delivered alongside vaccination: 828,345 children under five received vitamin A supplementation and 767,541 received albendazole deworming tablets. In parallel, the Maternal and Neonatal Tetanus Elimination (MNTE) campaign reached 393,117 women of reproductive age with tetanus vaccination, supporting progress toward eliminating maternal and newborn tetanus.
 
Although no large-scale education emergency occurred in 2025, UNICEF continued to lead the Education Cluster, ensuring timely information flow and coordination, disseminating Disaster Management Team (DMT) updates, representing the sector in the Inter-Agency Coordination Group (IACG), and coordinating feedback on contingency planning. For localized incidents, UNICEF collected real-time information through District Education Advisors and triangulated updates through church networks, enabling evidence-based inputs to DMT decision-making.
 
To enhance operational efficiency, UNICEF established three Long-Term Agreements with suppliers in Port Moresby, Lae and Mt. Hagen and secured free warehouse space for pre-positioned supplies through a Contingency Programme Document with the Catholic Archdiocese of Mt. Hagen. UNICEF also co-facilitated Emergency Preparedness, Response and Partnership training for 36 participants (15 females; 21 males), improving disaster reporting, supporting development of a draft Provincial Response Plan for Enga, and registering three CSOs on the United Nations Partner Portal (UNPP) as potential first responders.
 
 Key enablers for results:
 
Results were enabled by strong community engagement, strategic partnerships, evidence-based advocacy and effective resource mobilization. UNICEF worked through ward committees, community influencers and health authorities to strengthen demand promotion for immunization and essential health services, child protection services, education and WASH, supporting community ownership and more sustainable behaviour change. Evidence-based advocacy helped elevate children’s rights on the political agenda, including Parliament’s establishment of PNG’s first Special Parliamentary Committee on Children and Youth and its rapid initiation of a national inquiry.

Private sector engagement expanded opportunities to boost immunization outreach, expand birth registration and strengthen water supply initiatives. A new memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the PNG Council of Churches strengthened community influence through faith networks, supporting dissemination of positive parenting and child wellbeing messages. Sustained resource mobilization underpinned by strong programme delivery and donor confidence enabled implementation at scale, with the office mobilizing USD 23,637,375, achieving 131 per cent of its annual ORR ceiling.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
 
In 2025, UNICEF PNG’s programmes operated in a context of structural fragility, geography, and shocks. Across health and nutrition, education, child protection, WASH/climate, and emergencies, progress was slowed by common systems and operational constraints.
 
Health and nutrition. Health and nutrition services faced severe workforce shortages and weak subnational management. High vacancy rates and limited capacity reduced the coverage and quality of services for mothers, newborns, children and adolescents, including outreach and mobile delivery. Public financial management weaknesses compounded these constraints: delayed fund flows and liquidation especially at subnational level, often released operational resources too late or at insufficient levels for supervision, routine monitoring and outreach.
 
Stock-outs of medicines, vaccines and nutrition supplies reflected weak forecasting, distribution planning and limited real-time data for resupply. While polio-response distribution reforms reduced provincial-level stock-outs, an estimated 20–30 per cent of facilities still experienced vaccine shortages. Transport shortages, fuel constraints and insecurity continued to restrict last-mile delivery and raise costs.
Nutrition programming was further affected by evidence gaps. The last national nutrition survey was conducted 15 years ago, and routine information systems include limited nutrition indicators, constraining prioritization, targeting and course correction. UNICEF will continue supporting Government readiness for a new National Nutrition Survey to strengthen decision-making and accountability.
 
In education, fragmented governance and weak coordination between national and provincial levels slowed implementation of key reforms, including the 1-6-6 restructuring and expansion of early childhood education (ECE). Budget limitations and weak consultation mechanisms with Treasury and subnational stakeholders reduced the realism of costing and planning for the National Education Plan. Persistent infrastructure deficits particularly WASH and climate resilience undermined learning environments, while teacher shortages and limited training constrained foundational learning quality.
 
High turnover of trained facilitators especially in remote provinces disrupted Child protection and birth registration services, and referral pathway information varied across wards and provinces, creating confusion and protection risks. Birth registration lagged due to logistical barriers, paper-based processes, slow record transmission, system outages, and certificate-printing backlogs; in some cases, internal administrative delays slowed procurement, recruitment and implementation. Chronic underfunding across child protection continued to limit scale and sustainability.
 
WASH progress was constrained by policy and institutional gaps. The absence of an implementation plan for the National WASH Policy (2015–2030) and delayed operationalization of the National WASH Authority (NWASHA) left roles unclear and services fragmented, particularly in rural areas. Government funding remained low, and although platforms like mWater exist, real-time data was not consistently used for decision-making. Frequent landslides, floods and drought disrupted continuity, while insecurity in the Highlands increased delivery risks and costs.
 
Lessons learned
 
Integrated service delivery during the polio response worked well, enabling catch-up immunization alongside nutrition interventions. This confirmed that high-intensity campaigns can serve as effective platforms for multiple child outcomes when coordination, supplies and supervision are aligned.
 
Subnational technical assistance proved high impact. Focused provincial and district support strengthened microplanning, routine monitoring, and problem-solving where implementation happens.
 
The CNA model showed potential beyond nutrition, improving immunization and institutional deliveries in the two districts where it operates and offering a practical pathway for convergence across sectors.
 
Evidence-based advocacy was essential to unlocking reforms. UNICEF engagement elevated ECE as a national priority, supporting decisions to fund teacher salaries and secure inclusion in major financing streams such as LEAP and GPE grants. The Convergence Programme showed how community and faith-based networks can mobilize support for ECE infrastructure and strengthen parental involvement, while the Teen Entrepreneur Programme highlighted the role of life skills and community engagement. Pilot reviews underscored that scale-up requires clearer roles, stronger monitoring, and government-led ownership.
 
For WASH, experience reinforced that sustainable models must be climate-resilient, conflict-sensitive and grounded in inclusive community engagement. Co-creation with communities—especially youth and women—improves ownership and functionality, while low-cost technologies (e.g., gravity-fed systems and rainwater harvesting) and representative WASH committees support sustainability and accountability.
The establishment of a UNICEF field presence in Mt. Hagen strengthened sustained engagement with provincial authorities and improved readiness for localized emergencies. Proximity, combined with pre-positioned supplies and LTAs, enables faster support to Provincial Disaster Coordinators, and partnerships with trained local CSOs can strengthen first-responder capacity using local knowledge and community presence.
 
Future outlook 
 
In 2026, UNICEF will accelerate results by expanding integrated delivery models and strengthening subnational execution. UNICEF will extend the geographic reach and service package of the CNA model and scale up the School-based Nutrition Intervention Acceleration (SNiA) approach to reach more school-aged children and adolescents with combined health, nutrition, protection and education services. Advocacy will prioritize faster recruitment of health workers, timely financing for commodities, and adequate operational funding for outreach, supervision and routine monitoring, alongside stronger district-level accountability and data use.
 
In education, UNICEF will focus on institutionalizing ECE and foundational learning, strengthening teacher capacity, and embedding gender-responsive and inclusive practice. The Smarter Safer Schools (3S) programme will scale climate-resilient WASH and violence prevention across 600 schools, while GPE support will strengthen teacher workforce development and curriculum implementation with a focus on learning outcomes. Additional priorities include strengthening education data systems, expanding remote learning options, and advancing shock-responsive education to manage climate and disaster risks.
 
For child protection, UNICEF will support provincial rollout of validated CPCM SOPs, scale accredited certificate programmes through SILAG, and operationalize the EVAC Roadmap. The Minimum Service Package for Child Protection will expand, with stronger links to justice, health and education platforms. Birth registration will focus on clearing backlogs, ensuring services in hospitals, enabling on-the-spot registration and certification (including digital signatures), and strengthening coordination through the CRVS Committee, alongside evidence-informed advocacy to increase subnational allocations for child protection services and workforce strengthening.
 
In WASH, UNICEF will advocate for the operationalization and resourcing of NWASHA and a clear implementation roadmap for the National WASH Policy. Expansion of mWater will strengthen real-time monitoring and evidence-based planning, while climate-resilient WASH will scale through community ownership, context-specific design and stronger sector coordination. UNICEF will deepen collaboration with DNPM, NDoH, NDoE and CCDA and explore innovative financing to close resource gaps.
Across sectors, UNICEF will deliver faster by integrating platforms, strengthening systems, and protecting service continuity during shocks.

The Philippine economy continued its expansion in 2025, though growth slowed to an average of 5 percent in the first three quarters.[1] Despite this, the World Bank projects ongoing growth in 2026-2027, and a steady decline in poverty, with rates expected to fall to 12.5 per cent in 2027 from the latest figures of 15.5 per cent in 2023.
 
The 2025 mid-term review of the Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 builds on achievements so far and sets priorities to boost productivity across economic sectors, accelerate innovation and human capital development, and advance infrastructure. The review reinforced commitment to inclusive social protection programmes that are responsive to new vulnerabilities, including those affecting children. It emphasized expanding healthcare access and reforms, including broader PhilHealth coverage, improved social determinants of health and a focus on mental health. In education, it highlighted improving quality, inclusion and resilience across basic education and lifelong learning, particularly through digital learning and stronger teacher support. Integrated climate adaptation across sectors and strong disaster risk reduction remain priorities.
 
Calls for government transparency, especially around infrastructure spending, increased amid corruption allegations. This prompted a policy shift to building trust and accountability in public investments, providing an opportunity to leverage UNICEF engagement in public finance management for children as evidence and tools for policy reform.
 
Amid these reforms, children continue to experience poverty and multidimensional deprivations. According to the Philippine Statistical Authority, 23.4 per cent of children – about 9.29 million children – live in poverty.[2] Regional disparities are pronounced, with child poverty rates in 10 out of the 18 regions exceeding the national average. Child poverty in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) dropped from 42.4 per cent in 2021 to 40.1 per cent in 2023, though regions like Negros Islands and the Zamboanga Peninsula saw increases. 
 
New research from UNICEF explores the effects of climate change and social norms on children’s development and well-being in the Philippines. The latest Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, launched by UNICEF in November 2025, highlights that over 97 per cent of children are exposed to three or more climate-related shocks—some of the world’s highest risks from climate change. A study on child, early and forced marriage and unions[3] provides insights into the different factors that drive CEFMU.  
 
On a positive note, in March 2025, the Deputy Permanent Representative of the Philippines to the United Nations formally requested the country’s removal from the annexes of the Secretary-General’s Annual Report on Children and Armed Conflict, based on fewer reported and verified grave child rights violation cases in recent years. The Secretary-General’s June 2025 report acknowledged substantial reductions in violations and improvements in prevention measures, facilitating the Philippines’ removal in the next reporting cycle.
 
The Philippines continues to grapple with a learning crisis. The SEA-PLM 2024 Regional Report underscores deep inequities in education: disparities persist between high and low performers, girls and boys, rich and poor households, and children who speak the test language at home versus those who do not. While progress has been made – with high-performing learners in Mathematics increasing from 17 per cent in 2019 to 26 per cent in 2024, and in Reading from 10 per cent to 14 per cent – these gains were uneven, highlighting the urgent need for targeted interventions. [4] According to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM2), learners in some regions lost up to a months’ worth of school days because of climate-related disruptions in school year 2024–2025. 
 
To accelerate education reforms, the Department of Education (DepEd) launched a Quality Basic Education Development Plan 2025–2035 emphasizing digitization, decentralization and public-private partnerships. Its success hinges on legislative reforms from EDCOM2 and effective policy implementation. The Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) System Act was signed in May 2025, mandating local government units (LGUs) to provide comprehensive services for children under five.
 
Sixty-one percent of the children in the Philippines were fully immunized by the end of 2024, according to the Department of Health’s (DOH) Field Health Services Information System. As of November 2025, the country reported 4,743 measles-rubella cases, a 36 per cent increase from the same period in 2024, making the country prone to an outbreak. In response, DOH, with support from UNICEF, the World Health Organization and other partners, is planning a measles-rubella Special Immunization Activity that will launch in January 2026. With a view to increasing coverage more broadly, the government adopted a costed National Immunization Strategy 2026-2030, which establishes a blueprint for improved immunization outcomes. It also pursued a project, backed by the World Bank, to improve the resilience of health facilities to the effects of climate change and better prepare them to respond to emergencies. 
 
Child stunting declined from 26.7 per cent in 2019 to 23.6 per cent in 2023, placing the country on track toward SDG targets. However, wasting remained at 5.6 per cent, while overweight and obesity are rising at alarming rates, affecting 12.9 per cent of children aged 5–10 years and 12.5 per cent of adolescents aged 10–19 years. The National Nutrition Survey 2023 highlighted declining infant and young child feeding practices, with early initiation of breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding falling to 61.2 per cent and 50.4 per cent, respectively, and only 13.9 per cent of children meeting the minimum acceptable diet.  
 
In BARMM, while indicators remain among the worst in the country, basic literacy rate[5] improved to 78 per cent in 2024 (73.2 per cent in 2019) among children aged 5-9; 95.9 per cent (from 94.1 per cent) among 15–19-year-olds; and 96.1 per cent (from 91.3 per cent) among 20–24-year-olds.  Fully immunized child coverage rose to 59 per cent in 2025, with 23 municipalities achieving at least 70 per cent PENTA3 vaccination coverage. Eighty-three barangays (villages) have Zero Open Defecation status (3.3 per cent of all barangays in BARMM) as of end-2025. The regional under-five mortality rate reached 7.36 per cent in 2024, driven by systemic and contextual challenges, including shifting disease patterns and climate change. 
 
The Bangsamoro authorities, with UNICEF technical support, launched a four-year plan to strengthen social safety nets and expand essential services for vulnerable groups, including children. They also introduced a disaster response framework, with an emphasis on the safety and well-being of children and their families. BARMM’s first Parliamentary elections, initially scheduled in October 2025, were postponed. Development challenges and inequities, exacerbated by years of conflict and underfunding, persisted.
 
During the first half of 2025, the Philippines was still recovering from six tropical cyclones that struck in late 2024. New large-scale emergencies unfolded later in the year, including powerful earthquakes in Davao Oriental and Cebu provinces in October, and Typhoon Tino in the Visayas in early November. Super Typhoon Uwan – the strongest in 2025 – devasted provinces in Luzon soon after, affecting more than 7.9 million people. Recurrent shocks, such as in the Catanduanes province, compounded vulnerabilities and slowed recovery. The Government of the Philippines mobilized national and local systems in response, though gaps in assistance persisted, especially in remote and isolated areas. 
 
To complement this summary, a complete and regularly updated picture of the situation of children in the Philippines—including key data, analyses, and sector-specific insights—is available through the Situation of Children digital platform at www.situationofchildren.org/ph.

In the second year of its 9th Country Programme for Children, UNICEF Philippines achieved progress across its five strategic shifts: public finance for children, climate action, social and behavioural change initiatives, systems strengthening, and support for BARMM. 
 
In BARMM, UNICEF reinforced the transitional government’s post-conflict recovery efforts through a three-year programme that improved community resilience and service delivery in 44 conflict-affected municipalities. The programme, which closed in August 2025, was supported by the European Union under the Peace and Development in BARMM framework. It contributed to increases in access to early learning, primary education, immunization, antenatal/postnatal care and Zero Open Defecation certifications. It also delivered “peace dividends” by extending essential services and reinforcing government legitimacy, helping to build trust in BARMM’s transitional institutions. 
 
As a last-mile responder, UNICEF addressed critical gaps in underserved or isolated communities affected by emergencies in 2024 and 2025. It prioritized a cash-first approach, which enabled typhoon-affected families in Catanduanes to address their needs flexibly. It complemented this with material and technical assistance in other disaster-affected areas. UNICEF also strengthened coordination, information management and local emergency preparedness through strategic guidance to national and local partners, especially as co-lead of the WASH, child protection and nutrition clusters. 
 
HEALTH AND NUTRITION
 
UNICEF’s technical support and partnership with the Department of Health (DOH) resulted in the costed National Immunization Strategy for 2026-2030 and the launch of DigiVacc. The latter is a set of digital applications, developed with funding from the Government of Japan, that empowers healthcare workers and families to track and record and immunization services and information more efficiently. These innovations are designed to improve tracking and early detection of zero-dose children and accelerate the achievement of improved immunization outcomes.
By directly supporting service delivery and social and behavioural change in 58 provinces and 396 LGUs, UNICEF contributed to the immunization of 802,053 children and provision of 500,000 people with key health messages. Outreach missions and technical assistance jointly implemented by UNICEF, the United Nations Population Fund and the World Health Organization Philippines, through a project funded by the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), expanded adolescent-friendly primary health services to remote areas, with 3,050 adolescents (1,144 boys; 1,906 girls) in Samar and Southern Leyte receiving care and information that could help reduce longer-term health risks. 
A milestone in standardizing care, aimed at improving detection and referral and contributing to reduced mortality, was achieved through the approval of the Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Acute Malnutrition among Children aged 0–5 years, which were developed with UNICEF support. In October 2024, UNICEF’s technical support led to the approval of the PhilHealth Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) Outpatient Therapeutic Care (OTC) Benefit Package. In 2025, 100 primary health care facilities were accredited to deliver SAM services for an estimated 17,285 children. Healthcare officials and workers at these facilities learned more about the package during sessions supported by UNICEF. 
Through UNICEF’s strategic technical assistance to the DOH and the World Bank, the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project (PMNP) strengthened coordinated nutrition and social and behavioral change (SBC) interventions in 275 municipalities. It trained 20,615 frontline nutrition workers and enabled 706 local government staff to craft and implement SBC plans in all PMNP municipalities. These resulted in improved service delivery for 704,284 children aged 0–5 and 36,879 pregnant women. The PMNP’s midline evaluation, conducted by UNICEF, confirmed its scalability and informed the design of the PMNP 2.0 initiative, supported by an additional US$500 million World Bank loan and set to commence in January 2027. 
UNICEF’s generated evidence and advocacy efforts facilitated the inclusion of Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS) in the National Essential Medicines list, enabling the government to plan, budget and procure MMS using domestic resources. To facilitate the transition to MMS, UNICEF through the Child Nutrition Fund donated 90 million tablets, enough for some 500,000 women. UNICEF also supported the costing of the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition 2023–2026 (pregnancy to age 5), informing legislative advocacy and the 2026 national budget allocations for the DOH, National Nutrition Council and Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD). 
Efforts to promote healthy food environments resulted in the filing of three bills regulating unhealthy food marketing, including the establishment of front-of-pack nutrition labelling, in the 20th Congress of the Philippines. Local ordinances on unhealthy food marketing were enacted in Pasig, Valenzuela and San Pedro cities
As nutrition cluster co-lead, UNICEF facilitated service continuity of nutrition services following multiple typhoons and earthquakes. This enabled 24,534 children (12,647 boys and 11,887 girls) and 3,538 pregnant women to receive lifesaving nutrition interventions and commodities. UNICEF also supported service continuity in health facilities by donating emergency health kits, power generators and other material assistance. 
In BARMM, UNICEF’s support for the Reaching Every Purok strategy and programme management contributed to increased immunization coverage and improved nutrition outcomes. Over 6,600 health and nutrition workers and local leaders strengthened their skills in immunization, cold-chain management, adolescent health, nutrition and governance through training and coaching. To increase sustainability, UNICEF provided technical support for the establishment of the Bangsamoro Nutrition Commission, development of the BARMM Health Master Plan, and operationalization of local Nutrition Action Plans. 
LEARNING AND SKILLS
In partnership with EDCOM2, the ECCD Council and the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), UNICEF strengthened ECCD governance and financing – essential to better early childhood outcomes – through strategic policy engagement and expert advice. This helped secure the ECCD’s reintegration into the 2026 Program Convergence Budget and an additional US$17 million allocation from the national budget for new child development centres in low-income LGUs. 
Legislative advocacy resulted in the enactment of the ECCD System Act, while tools like the ECCD LGU Capacity Assessment Tool and ECCD-Early Childhood Education (ECE) Calculator empowered local governments to plan investments more efficiently. The validation of the revised Philippine Early Learning Development Standards and national training regulations for child development workers, meanwhile, is improving service quality. The ECCD-ECE LINK modelling initiative promoted scalable, inclusive practices, while enhanced child mapping supported referrals of children with disabilities to the services they required. 
UNICEF policy advocacy and technical assistance to DepEd contributed to better incentives for teachers in hardship areas, with 41,067 teachers and 5,624 schools receiving allowances without additional costs to the government. Additional funding was unlocked for previously overlooked areas (e.g. ECE, Alternative Learning System or ALS) in all 47,000 public schools following UNICEF advocacy that led to the 2025 SEF Joint Guidelines. Technical assistance from UNICEF facilitated better access to inclusive education for 2.4 million children annually through the Special Needs Education roadmap. Teaching guides and frameworks, developed with UNICEF expert advice, for the new kindergarten to Grade 3 curriculum are helping teachers improve learning for some 2 million leaners per grade.  The Social and Emotional Learning assessment, designed by UNICEF, was integrated into the National Achievement Test, institutionalizing holistic assessments for around 6 million learners in Grades 5-7. 
Flexible learning options were expanded through ALS Life Skills micro-certificates, which benefited 2,900 learners, and the ICT4ALS project, which digitized modules for 8,000 learners. Over 4,700 young people, meanwhile, earned micro-credentials that can help them pursue employment or other income-earning opportunities.
UNICEF also contributed to building safer and more resilient learning environments through a guidebook, developed with DepEd, on school safety and inclusivity. In disaster-affected areas, UNICEF helped ensure learning continuity for 16,349 children (8,108 female, 8,241 male) by providing learning and teaching resources that supplemented the government’s response. It helped the expanded Education Cluster finalize its terms of reference and develop a three-year strategic plan designed to improve the education sector’s emergency preparedness and response. 
In BARMM, UNICEF strengthened education outcomes by helping establish of the Bangsamoro ECCD Technical Working Group and supporting the implementation of the Bangsamoro Education Reform and Development Plan 2035 at division and school level, which improved education governance. Capacity-building efforts and infrastructure upgrades provided more than 58,000 children and youth (43 per cent male, 57 per cent female) with safer and more conducive learning environments. These system-strengthening efforts were supported by resources from the European Union, KOICA and BDO Foundation. 
CHILD PROTECTION
The Revised National Protocol on Case Management of Child Victims of Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation, and Discrimination (CANE+D), spearheaded by the Department of Justice (DOJ)-led Committee for the Special Protection of Children, was finalized, marking a major milestone toward a more coordinated, accountable and child-centred protection system. UNICEF supported this process through consultations, technical working sessions and the DOJ Visioning Workshop that harmonized procedures across the justice, social welfare, health and law enforcement sectors. This reform strengthens national accountability mechanisms and supports CRC recommendations on child-sensitive justice and access to protection services. UNICEF also supported the development of the MAKABATA Implementing Guidelines under Executive Order No. 79, reinforcing a “no wrong door” approach and clarifying roles across national and local actors. The CANE+D Protocol and MAKABATA Guidelines are expected to improve service quality, continuity and referral, particularly for children in vulnerable and high-risk situations. 
Further addressing systems fragmentation, UNICEF co-designed the country’s first scalable Child Protection Systems Model with the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and four model LGUs, creating a Theory of Change framework and securing a memorandum of agreement and budget allocation for implementation in 2026. 
UNICEF facilitated progress in monitoring and reporting grave child rights violations through the 19-year process that culminated in the Government’s request for removal from the annexes of the Secretary-General’s annual report. UNICEF supported this request, in liaison with the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict (SRSG-CAAC), particularly to ensure that the government remained committed to continuing prevention, monitoring, reporting and response.
 
Key roadmaps to address emerging and persistent protection risks were launched with UNICEF expert guidance. The National Coordination Center against Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (OSAEC) and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials (CSAEM) finalized its first multi-year strategic plan and developed a costed implementation framework, while the Inter-Agency Committee on Ending Child Marriage launched the National Plan of Action to End Child, Early and Forced Marriages and Unions. UNICEF’s guidance ensured that both plans apply a systems-based and equity-focused approach that prioritizes prevention, coordination and sustainable financing. 
With the DSWD Academy and the University of the Philippines, UNICEF designed and tested the Executive Course on Child Protection for local chief executives and multi-disciplinary teams, which seeks to increase understanding for the need for child protection systems and catalyse greater prioritization and budget allocation. The course is included in DSWD Academy’s 2026 offers and integrated into DSWD plans in coordination with the DILG. DSWD is also partnering with the Union of Local Authorities of the Philippines and various leagues of local chief executives for nationwide scale up. This embeds child protection into the national governance framework, making the course a permanent pillar for local executive development and accountability. 
 
On prevention, UNICEF and civil society partners successfully concluded the SaferKidPH’s initiative, a programme funded by the Government of Australia that institutionalized OSAEC prevention through key laws and policies, such as the Anti-OSAEC and CSAEM Act (Republic Act 11930), and influenced parents and children to adopt safer behaviours online through social media campaigns and information sessions in schools and communities. SaferKidsPH engaged children and youth as active participants and collaborated with the private sector to establish their own child protection initiatives.
In view of increased protection risks after large-scale emergencies, UNICEF supported the provision of psychosocial support services to 1,983 children through trained government social workers. More than 929,000 people, including 370,061 children (180,923 girls, 189,138 boys), also learnt more about abuse prevention, reporting mechanisms and services available to them. 
In BARMM, UNICEF strengthened systems through expanded birth registration, evidence-based advocacy to end child marriage, and capacity-building support for 45 multidisciplinary teams and women and 22 children protection units. Communities became more aware of referral pathways for child protection concerns and gender-based violence through UNICEF campaigns. 
CHILD-SENSITIVE PUBLIC POLICY
In a global first, UNICEF led the integration of Child-Responsive Public Finance Management (ChPFM) into the 2024 Public Expenditure and Financial Accountability (PEFA) assessment, which guides the implementation of the government’s PFM Reform Roadmap. The ChPFM seeks to ensure that public finance systems and budgetary processes systematically include investments in key social services and ensure that these are well-funded to efficiently support children’s development. 
Through the European Union-UNICEF Public Finance Facility, UNICEF advanced evidence generation – notably on the linkages of child poverty and regional budget allocation and ongoing review of the Programme Convergence Budgets for ECCD – to inform the government’s priority budget reform. The Joint Memorandum Circular to support LGUs in using the Child Budgeting and Expenditure Tracking Tool (CBETT) is another milestone in strengthening subnational capacity to plan, budget and track resources for children in a more transparent and accountable manner. UNICEF played a catalytic role by providing technical foundations, policy guidance and inter-agency coordination. It also championed child participation in government budgeting processes through the Open Government Partnership. 
UNICEF ensured that children and families were prioritized in social policy reforms and development plans. It helped shape the government’s Integrated Social Protection Framework and an Adaptive Shock-Responsive Action Plan, which facilitate transformative service delivery to address more frequent and intense shocks. Disability-inclusive social protection was advanced through Project CHERISH (Aruga), whose model was designed and launched with UNICEF support. In addition to providing 400 children with disabilities with allowances to access social services, the project produced a module on home care for children with disabilities and a referral pathway for community-based services in four pilot LGUs. The government committed to reaching more children with disabilities by scaling the project to 10 LGU in 2026. To preserve the relevance of the country’s flagship social protection program (Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program or 4Ps), UNICEF helped DSWD reflect current vulnerabilities in the programme’s theory of change and results framework. UNICEF continues to build evidence on gender responsive social protection through policy dialogues and a study aimed at addressing some of the drivers of adolescent pregnancy and child marriage using social protection in support of the National Action Plan on CEFMU. Capitalizing on its convenor role, UNICEF organized an Indigenous Peoples’ summit that facilitated policy discussions on the inequities faced by indigenous children, resulting in government and private sector commitments to address child poverty among indigenous communities.  UNICEF also facilitated a meeting of 191 regional directors from various government agencies to support the integrated delivery of social services for 4Ps households and help them sustain self-sufficiency. 
UNICEF’s partnership with the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and the Securities Exchange Commission laid strong foundations for the protection of child rights in workplaces, social protection systems and business practices. This led to the development of a child rights’ baseline that the country’s 86 publicly listed companies can use when preparing their sustainability reports. UNICEF, with other United Nations agencies and the World Bank, also supported the development of the Global Accelerator Roadmap for social protection and decent jobs in the transportation and construction sectors, to strengthen the Trabaho Para sa Bayan Act that seeks to address unemployment. Through DOLE’s Family Welfare Programme, UNICEF championed family-friendly policies by providing capacity-building support and helping convene a nationwide Community of Practice. 
Cash grants from UNICEF, provided through government social protection systems, enabled 7,873 households in Cantanduanes and Cagayan to flexibly addressed their needs following the super typhoons in 2024 and 2025. Families used the cash for food, medicine and education and confirmed their preference for cash assistance. These efforts contributed to building evidence on the benefits of delivering aid through social protection systems.
In BARMM, the launch of the Bangsamoro Social Protection Plan 2024–2028 was facilitated by UNICEF through technical assistance and policy advocacy, with support from the Australian government. UNICEF’s expert advice also contributed to the expansion of the region’s Beneficiary Data Management System, which now covers 74,674 households, and strengthening of the FAST digital payment system for more secure cash transfers. UNICEF advanced public finance for children by establishing a technical working group and testing the CBETT tool in two LGUs. With UNICEF coaching and training, 83 LGUs increased their knowledge on child-focused governance, had better pass rates in the Child-Friendly Local Governance Audit (CFLGA), and reinforced child-responsive planning. 
 
CLIMATE, ENVIRONMENT AND RESILIENCE
With the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Climate Change Commission (CCC), UNICEF launched the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, including the Philippines Children’s Climate Risk Index that identifies provinces with the highest hazard exposure and child vulnerability. The report provides the government and development partners with recommendations for priority investments for children that are aligned with the National Adaptation Plan. 
 
Perspectives of children and young people were considered in the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and Just Transition Framework, based on position papers and sectoral inputs shared with CCC, DENR and other partners. These inputs were formulated during national children and youth consultations convened by UNICEF in support of the government’s preparations for its NDC submission. UNICEF’s bilateral engagements with DepEd, DSWD, DOH, DENR, DOLE and other national government agencies facilitated the inclusion of social services in agency-level climate commitments. 
 
UNICEF strengthened climate resilient WASH governance by helping the Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) develop a Cooperation Framework for Water Supply and Sanitation in Local Governance, addressing long-standing fragmentation and clarifying roles across national agencies, provinces and LGUs. The framework promotes a province-led, inclusive, evidence-informed approach to planning, financing and capacity development, with climate resilience embedded throughout. To reinforce accountability, UNICEF helped institutionalize a monitoring framework to ensure that public investments are assessed on climate-resilient WASH outcomes rather than physical completion. 
 
With support from the Government of New Zealand, UNICEF enabled LGUs in Caraga Region to model climate-resilient WASH service delivery complemented by stronger WASH governance. More than 7,200 people gained access to basic sanitation and over 8,800 people to climate-resilient basic water services. Around 20,000 people also gained access to water and sanitation services indirectly through systems-strengthening efforts, including training and budget allocation advocacy. Ten LGUs increased their annual WASH spending from multiple sources, and 16 adopted risk-informed WASH sector plans with climate and disaster risk management components, demonstrating models for scale up. 
 
Meaningful youth participation was institutionalized through the UNICEF’s collaboration with the National Youth Commission, which resulted in an interagency mechanism for children’s and youth engagement in climate action and disaster resilience. The mechanism is embedded within the Philippine Youth Development Plan, ensuring a permanent, government-owned platform for youth priorities in policy and programming. The Kabataang Resilient Network grew beyond 100 youth leaders and 30 organisations, while the Sangguniang Kabataan climate action and disaster resilience training module moved youth from awareness to localised action. 
 
In response to emergencies, including the effects of typhoons in 2024, and with support from the UK Government and other donors, UNICEF delivered life-saving WASH assistance that enabled over 89,000 people (47,000 males; 42,000 females) to access safe water and more than 9,700 people to have safe and appropriate sanitation facilities. Over 46,800 (23,600 males; 23, 200 females) people received hygiene and water kits, supporting their recovery. 
 
In BARMM, UNICEF improved the water and sanitation situation for vulnerable children through systems strengthening and support for service delivery. Some 50,320 (24,650 males; 25,670 females) more people were living in 40 communities that gained Zero-Open-Defecation certifications in 2025, while 48,448 (23 740 males; 24,708 females) gained access to basic water services. Over 25,000 children had safer and more dignified learning and care environments following UNICEF-supported upgrades in learning facilities. Demonstrating institutionalized improvements, 46 LGUs reinforced their DRRM plans while 96 LGUs strengthened their capacities to anticipate, prepare for and respond to disasters in a child-focused manner. 
 
UNICEF Philippines deepened its partnerships with corporate, philanthropic and individual donors, raising PHP 431.9million. Cebu Pacific sustained their in-flight fundraising programme, and SM Prime, SM Supermalls and BDO Foundation also continued their vital support. LIXIL and Hocheng (HCG) Philippines Corporation provided in-kind contributions that helped improve water and sanitation in typhoon-affected schools and underserved communities. Philanthropic contributions from  The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints specifically supported education and WASH and Temasek Foundation’s funds contributed to the emergency response. Individual donors contributed essential unrestricted funds that enabled rapid and flexible responses to children’s needs. These included donations made through digital platforms and e-commerce partners and face-to-face venues in SM malls and IKEA. UNICEF’s collaboration with Ang Ilustrador ng Kabataan on a merchandise collection engaged existing and new supporters in meaningful, creative ways.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Fragmentation of systems and policies, leadership transitions at national and subnational levels, successive emergencies, and resource constraints persisted across different sectors. UNICEF relied on its technical expertise and adaptive management to mitigate the impact on its programmes. An internal audit of UNICEF Philippines and three evaluations provided insights and lessons for future programming. 
 
The audit recognized that the country office operates in a complex, risk-prone environment and deals with significant cash transfers and partnerships. It found that governance, risk management, and controls were overall adequate and recognized several of the office’s workstreams as best practices, particularly its engagement in innovative financing models and its system-integrated modelling for scale. Other strengths recognized were the office’s strong field presence and adaptive team culture. Areas for improvement included risk/fraud management, business continuity planning, programme and partnership oversight, cash transfer assurance, travel, and vendor management. 
 
The PMNP’s substantial progress in strengthening nutrition governance, service delivery and financing at the municipal level was confirmed in the midline evaluation conducted by UNICEF. Key achievements include the institutionalization of Municipal Nutrition Action Plans, improved alignment of local budgets with nutrition priorities, and the distribution of performance-based grants that incentivized compliance and supported service delivery. Training initiatives enhanced health workers’ skills in diagnosing malnutrition and delivering culturally appropriate interventions, while the multisectoral approach—integrating health, WASH, early childhood care, and social and behaviour change—was recognized as essential for addressing complex nutrition challenges. Challenges identified included manual and fragmented data systems, regional disparities in resources and staffing, and ongoing risks to sustainability due to budget constraints and reliance on external funding.
 
The midline evaluation noted that LGUs with stronger leadership, integrated planning, and routine use of data achieved faster improvements, while fragmented coordination and workforce turnover slowed results in more marginalized areas. UNICEF adapted by intensifying coaching, simplifying tools and strengthening real-time monitoring and learning. In 2026, UNICEF will focus on accelerating progress in lagging LGUs—through integrated service delivery, strengthened local governance, and sharper use of evidence—to translate national reforms into equitable, measurable gains for the most vulnerable children.
 
An evaluation of the CFLGA found that the audit provided a structured framework for monitoring, alignment, and coordination among LGUs and national agencies. It noted that the audit enables planning based on nationally recognized indicators and facilitates collaboration. However, gaps such as the lack of data-sharing protocols and unclear institutional mandates limit its potential for harmonizing efforts and integrating evidence-based decision-making. While there has been progress, especially in lower-income LGUs, disparities persist across sectors and regions. The protection sector is a strong point but governance lags. The audit’s focus on standardized indicators ensures accountability but can be rigid, sometimes failing to account for local context or outcomes. The absence of disaggregated, equity-sensitive indicators makes it difficult to assess and address the needs of vulnerable groups. The evaluation highlighted the following:

 
Government-led     initiatives, though challenging, are most sustainable: Working within     government structures and resources may be difficult, but it offers the     best chance for sustained results for children. 
UNICEF’s role is most     effective as a targeted supporter: Filling capacity gaps and providing     targeted assistance, rather than leading with substantial resources, is     more efficient and sustainable. 
Inclusive governance     requires more than frameworks: While the CFLGA embeds indicators for     vulnerable children, implementation is uneven. Without ongoing systems     strengthening, incentives and meaningful child participation, the audit     risks being symbolic rather than transformative. 
Data systems and feedback     loops are critical: Better data collection, validation, and feedback     mechanisms are necessary. Disaggregated data and timely dissemination of     results are essential for targeted interventions and continuous     improvement.
 
The evaluation of the EU-funded programme implemented by UNICEF in BARMM, meanwhile, confirmed that a systems-based, participatory, and data-driven approach—grounded in local realities and supported by strong partnerships—can deliver sustainable, inclusive, and peace-building results even in fragile, post-conflict settings. The evaluation found that:
·       Embedding reforms in local government systems (e.g., disaster risk reduction, child protection, youth participation) led to sustainable improvements. Gains are more likely to endure beyond the programme’s lifecycle when practices are institutionalized through ordinances, plans, and budget allocations.
·       The programme’s cross-sectoral design enabled bundled services and more cohesive delivery. This approach addressed multiple, overlapping vulnerabilities and reinforced local ownership and accountability.
·       Active participation of community members, youth, and frontline service providers fostered trust, improved service uptake and ensured that interventions were contextually relevant. Community voices were central to the evaluation and programme design. The programme’s support for youth-led initiatives and integration of ALS provided at-risk youth with alternatives to violence and contributed to social cohesion and peacebuilding.
·       The use of data-driven tools (e.g., Situation of Children dashboard, CFLGA) improved planning, budgeting and monitoring at the local level. This led to more targeted and effective interventions.
·       Regular coordination meetings, joint planning, and shared tools across provincial and regional levels reduced duplication, improved efficiency, and helped institutionalize best practices.
 
While progress has been notable, the evaluation identified areas where continued support can enhance results. Persistent inequities in access and varying capacities across LGUs occasionally affected consistency in service delivery, while limited digital infrastructure posed challenges for data management, reporting, and integration of digital monitoring tools. Some ongoing regional challenges, such as political turnover and shifts in local leadership, affected continuity, particularly in rural areas. Staff transitions, within government partners, were also noted throughout the programme cycle, which may impact institutional memory. Procurement processes and a rapidly evolving global funding environment occasionally limited financial flexibility, affecting the timing and cost-efficiency of interventions. 
 
Additional areas for strengthening include cold-chain management and stock monitoring for health commodities, embedding disability-inclusive data and accessibility, and consolidating safe child protection pathways and youth engagement mechanisms. Addressing these opportunities will be important to sustain UNICEF’s achievements and further institutionalize child-responsive governance across BARMM.
 
UNICEF will use these learnings to continue leveraging evidence, partnerships and innovation for lasting results for children in the Philippines. In 2026, it will prioritize demonstrating innovative models, co-creating these with government and development partners to ensure relevance and potential for scale up. This will include a review of its modelling approach. Initiatives to ensure that public finance and budgetary processes, at the national and subnational level, consider the needs of children and invest in social services for them will be scaled up. The midterm of the 9th Country Programme for Children will be an opportunity to assess progress on the key shifts and make the necessary adjustments.

In 2025, Thailand operated within a dynamic political, economic and environmental landscape while continuing to advance national development priorities and uphold the delivery of essential public services. The year presented a combination of challenges and opportunities, as political transition, global economic headwinds, threats to multilateralism and climate-related shocks intersected with important policy reforms and national responses in key social sectors.
Following the Constitutional Court’s removal of Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra, the Government undertook a managed transition to maintain continuity in public administration and services delivery amid renewed political uncertainty, as shifting government configurations and inter-party negotiations set the stage for a constitutional referendum and general election scheduled for early 2026, underscoring ongoing challenges in governance and political continuity needed for reforms. 

Thailand’s economy remained broadly stable amid global uncertainties, with GDP growth estimated at around 2.2%, albeit at a pace below historical averages and some regional peers. While slower growth constrained fiscal space, macroeconomic stability was preserved, and the Government implemented targeted stimulus and relief measures to support households and maintain consumption, helping to mitigate economic stress for families. 
At the same time, public spending pressures increased due to demographic change, disaster response, and global uncertainties. While budget allocations to social sectors declined as a share of total expenditure compared to previous years, the Government maintained core investments in education, health and social protection. Ongoing policy dialogue throughout 2025 helped sustain attention to the importance of human capital investment as a driver of inclusive growth.

In mid and end 2025, rising tensions along the Thai Cambodian border escalated into armed conflict, creating localized humanitarian needs and temporarily disrupting services in affected areas. As a result, 437,000 people including 86,000 children were displaced into evacuation shelters while thousands of schools and hospitals were temporarily closed, generating protection, education and psycho-social needs for affected children and adolescents. The Government led a coordinated response, prioritizing civilian protection, evacuation, and the restoration of essential services. By the end of the year, diplomatic engagement resulted in a ceasefire, underscoring Thailand’s commitment to peaceful resolution and regional stability.
Climate-related hazards also emerged as a defining feature of 2025. Severe flooding during the monsoon season affected both northern and southern Thailand, impacting livelihoods, infrastructure and public services. Particularly severe flooding in the Southern Border Provinces affected over 3 million people, including 520,000 children, devastated livelihoods, disrupted education for more than 148,000 students, and caused over THB 1 billion in damage to public health service facilities, exacerbating socio-economic vulnerabilities in a region where poverty rates are five times the national average. These events also reinforced national recognition of climate change as a structural risk. In terms of cost of damages from climate related hazards as a share of GDP, only Myanmar has a higher percentage of countries in ASEAN. The scale of flooding strengthened momentum for integrating climate resilience, disaster risk reduction, and preparedness into national planning and sectoral strategies, including education, infrastructure and social protection. 

The intensification of humanitarian emergencies not just in Thailand, but around the world, coincides with a shift in the global development and humanitarian financing landscape linked to a weakening of multi-lateral institutions including significant funding cuts for UN agencies and CSOs in the face of global economic and geo-political uncertainty and proliferation of conflicts. In Thailand, the reduction of foreign aid contributions to humanitarian response efforts had a significant impact on provision of assistance for both recent and longstanding displaced children and families along the Thai-Myanmar border and the ability of UN agencies, INGOs, and CBOs to deliver, leading to a decrease in to the provision of essential services to vulnerable children and their families.

These trends, combined with the demographic decline and entrenched socio-economic disparities, disproportionately affect children and vulnerable households, reinforcing the need for inclusive, child-sensitive economic and social policies. A child-centered focus and equitable human capital development is essential for Thailand to leverage the full of potential of children for economic transformation. 

Despite these overarching challenges, 2025 also marked a year of momentous progress in strengthening Thailand’s legal and policy protection framework for children. Thailand achieved a historic milestone in safeguarding children’s rights by becoming the second ASEAN nation and 68th globally to prohibit corporal punishment in all settings. This reform addressed the social normalization of violence and strengthened legal safeguards for millions of children.
The enactment of the Marriage Equality Act in January 2025 marked a historic milestone, reinforcing Thailand’s regional leadership on inclusion and non-discrimination. Importantly, the amended Civil and Commercial Code also raised the legal age of marriage to 18 years, aligning national legislation with international standards and strengthening protections for adolescents. Together, these reforms reflected the Government’s continued commitment to inclusion, social cohesion, and the protection of vulnerable populations.

Overall, 2025 highlighted both Thailand’s exposure to external and internal shocks and its capacity to manage them. Children were among those most affected by service disruptions and household-level stress during periods of flooding and conflict-related displacement. At the same time, strengthened legal protections, sustained service delivery, and government-led responses helped mitigate longer-term impacts. These dynamics reinforced the importance of continued investment in children as a foundation for Thailand’s future economic resilience, social cohesion and sustainable development.

Within this context, UNICEF worked in close partnership with the Royal Thai Government, aligning its technical assistance and support with nationally defined priorities. UNICEF’s contributions focused on complementing government leadership, strengthening systems, and supporting evidence-based approaches to ensure that progress achieved in 2025 translates into lasting gains for children and families across the country.

In 2025, UNICEF played a catalytic role in advancing children’s rights in Thailand amid a year marked by political transition, environmental shocks, and accelerating social and technological change. Through strategic partnerships with government, civil society, academia, and the private sector, UNICEF combined evidence generation, policy influence, and system-level support to address persistent child rights deprivations. 

Supporting children and their families in the critical early years

Despite huge progress made in recent decades, critical obstacles to child development remain with 23% of children under 5 (780,000) not developmentally on track. These rates, particularly among children from low-income households, reflect inadequate social assistance and limited access to quality childcare and parental support.
