These early disadvantages set the stage for long-term inequality.

UNICEF is working in close collaboration with the Department of Health (DoH) on improving knowledge of parents by supporting Parent Schools (PS) programme delivered through public hospitals. In 2025, across six provinces, 23 hospitals implemented the enhanced PS model following capacity building and provision of standardized communication materials with health workers strengthening their capacity to deliver structured parenting guidance on nurturing care, engaging 23,513 parents and caregivers while an additional 30,553 parents and caregivers were reached through online live parenting sessions. Early results of this pilot indicate improved readiness within public health facilities to deliver family-facing services at scale with learnings and tools from this model to be disseminated all hospitals in 2026[AD1] .
Embedding nurturing care and nutrition guidance within national platforms remains a key priority. During the year, updated Food-Based Dietary Guidelines were incorporated into the revised Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Book distributed nationally to all pregnant women and newborns - over 500,000 copies annually - strengthening consistency and reach of early development messaging delivered by health workers. 

UNICEF supported the Bureau of Nutrition to improve nutrition quality in ECD settings through development and testing of a standardized menu and recipe resources for ECD teachers and cooks to be shared with all ECD centers in the coming year.  In parallel, UNICEF supported enhancements to the Thai School Lunch system, used by more than 30,000 schools and ECD centres, including a monitoring dashboard to understand the quality of the meals according to the updated dietary recommendations, and strengthening accountability for nutrition provision.
The promotion of family friendly policies remains an essential strategy to increase workforce participation, reduce inequality, support child development, and foster long-term social and economic sustainability. Advocacy for childcare expansion was advanced through a national childcare supply-and-demand study and investment case to inform policy dialogue on public childcare provision. The nationally represented survey found that nearly 40% of households with children under 18 months and about 50% with children aged 18–24 months expressed a desire for formal external care options. The study also estimated the cost of inaction, as well as the high return for investment where Thailand would gain TH 2.35 to THB 7.36 THB in productivity for every 1 THB invested. 

In parallel, a feasibility study on expanding paid parental leave to informal workers was initiated with the National Economic and Social Development Council and a multi-stakeholder network including a broad range of Government agencies, businesses and employee associations, whose findings will inform further policy options. 

Combatting an obesity epidemic…...

Trends in overweight obesity are increasing at an alarming rate with 13% of children currently overweight, a figure set to rise to over 60% in 2035. UNICEF supported national efforts to protect children from exposure to unhealthy food marketing, by advancing the Draft Act to Control Marketing of Unhealthy Food and Drinks to Children.  A joint three-year advocacy strategy for the Draft Act was co-developed by the Department of Health and UNICEF through multi-stakeholder consultations, strengthening civil society coordination and positioning the Thai NCD Alliance to serve as the national coordination lead from 2026. Regulatory readiness was further enhanced through technical assistance in developing a nutrient profiling model. The model establishes a robust evidence base to inform marketing restrictions and provides a phased pathway for regulatory implementation and enforcement.

In parallel, UNICEF engaged the private sector to promote healthy food environments for children and adolescents, complementing national regulatory efforts. Technical assistance was provided to BJC, one of Thailand’s largest consumer goods and retail companies, to support the implementation of its Healthy Checkout Lane (HCL) initiative. 

In Thailand’s Southern Border Provinces (SBP), UNICEF, in partnership with Kenan Foundation Asia, strengthened community engagement and participatory approaches with adolescents to promote healthier lifestyles. More than 2,077 adolescents across six District Learning Encouragement Centers (DLECs) co-designed local activities with their teachers on nutrition, physical activity, and mental well-being, generating locally relevant solutions. These included three social media campaigns promoting healthy lifestyles, including nutrition, physical activity, and mental health reaching 50,875 adolescents across the SBP.

The cornerstone of development is children’s education......

While access to primary and lower-secondary education is nearly universal, the quality of learning remains a major concern. Less than 60% of students attending grades 2 and 3 possess age-appropriate foundational literacy and numeracy skills, especially those from disadvantaged backgrounds. Moreover, academic skills, as measured by the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), are below the standards of developed countries in all subjects. Resource constraints, teacher shortages, and unsafe or unsupportive school environments further exacerbate these challenges.

During the year, UNICEF strengthened teaching and learning in basic education by accelerating foundational literacy and expanding equitable STEM and digitally supported instruction. Foundational reading served as the primary entry point for improving learning outcomes. Through the A Book a Week campaign, 109,190 learners (51% girls) across 229 schools participated, supported by teachers using national assessment data and AI-enabled tools to tailor instruction. Live professional learning reached 62,000 teachers, complemented by mobile libraries reaching 13,659 children and distribution of 5,000 grade-appropriate books benefiting over 10,000 learners. These combined efforts contributed to the launch of a new Grades 1–3 literacy-focused curriculum, piloted in 4,400 schools in 2025, reinforcing early reading as a national priority.

Strengthening the capacity of teachers is essential to improving foundational learning outcomes. Through the ONE TEACHER Thailand (OTT) peer-learning network, 200 core teachers (80% women) delivered micro-learning modules on digital learning tools and child online protection reaching over 200,000 educators nationwide. OTT has emerged as a key platform for diffusing effective practices, including AI-supported reading instruction, with early findings indicating improved digital and classroom practices. System readiness for sustained impact was strengthened through development of a draft Digital Competencies Framework for Teachers, aligned with national ICT priorities and UNESCO standards, positioning teacher training as a central lever for improving foundational learning and equitable STEM education.

Thai students rank among the lowest globally in their sense of safety in school common areas—such as corridors, cafeterias, and toilets—raising concerns about school climate and student protection and impacts on learning outcomes. Most schools lack trained professionals, and designated teachers often juggle multiple roles without adequate preparation. Only 50% of adolescents report receiving any instruction on stress management, leaving nearly 2 million students aged 13–17 without structured socio-emotional learning. UNICEF is therefore advancing the Safe to Learn framework with the Office of the Basic Education Commission, positioning school safety, student well-being, mental health and violence prevention as core system responsibilities. The Safe to Learn benchmarking exercise, completed in late 2024 and reviewed and disseminated in 2025, identified priorities to strengthen teacher capacity in positive discipline and classroom management, integrate social and gender norms into national guidance, and promote whole-school approaches to preventing violence. While the process strengthened technical foundations and policy dialogue, progress toward operationalization was constrained by leadership changes and shifting government ownership and will remain a priority in 2026. 
In a year marked by the intensification of flooding and extreme weather events underscoring the criticality of climate change adaptation and resilience, UNICEF advanced child-sensitive climate policies by integrating climate-smart education and youth participation into Thailand’s revised 2025 National Climate Master Plan (2015–2050) and the Draft Action for Climate Empowerment Plan. This was underpinned by several evidence-generation activities supporting policy advocacy, such as a national school survey on climate impacts and support needs, climate-resilient infrastructure studies, and an education-sector climate risk analysis. 
In partnership with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF scaled climate-smart education nationwide, trained over 518 teachers, and engaged learners and teachers from 6,000 schools strengthening leadership capacities and increasing climate-smart initiatives. 

Enshrining children’s rights in legal frameworks and policies…...

Building on the momentum of recent breakthroughs in Child Protection legislation, including banning of corporal punishment in all settings and last year’s withdrawal on the reservation of article 22 of the Convention of Child Rights, UNICEF continues to position critical legislation for future adoption through sustained advocacy. Progress was made on the draft bill to criminalize Online Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse and the revised Child Protection Act which both received cabinet approval, though a full adoption was delayed by the dissolution of Parliament. 

Rapid developments in the field of Artificial Intelligence will have profound implications on the lives of children and UNICEF is closely monitoring both foreseen and unforeseen impacts. A new partnership established with the Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA) provided an important avenue to integrate online safety and child protection concerns into the rapidly evolving digital and AI governance frameworks including draft AI legislation. The partnership also extends support around digital well-being guidelines for children and parents, ensuring the integration of online safety protocols and #CautionFirst media into national standards but also highlighting the risks of social media and screen time on socio-emotional development, mental health and educational outcomes. 

Protecting children in residential care……

More than 135,000 children in Thailand, many of them undocumented, live in various types of residential care, mostly unmonitored institutions which place children at elevated risk of abuse. 

UNICEF supported and advocated for the regulation of private residential care facilities. Through high-level advocacy with the Ministry of Social Development and Human Security (MSDHS), UNICEF supported the development of registration guidelines to initiate a pilot in four provinces that host over 60% of Thailand’s private facilities. This initiative directly addresses the risk of unregulated institutionalization, ensuring private care providers align with national standards.

In 2025, UNICEF also engaged religious leaders to promote child safety, well-being, and protection.  A series of training sessions was conducted with Buddhist and Islamic faith leaders on child safeguarding and child protection, aimed at shifting toward child-centered approaches. Participants reported reduced use of violent discipline and lower dropout rates, directly addressing the prevalence of corporal punishment. 

Through partnerships with Legal Status Network Foundation (LNSF), ILO, UN Women, UNODC, IOM and UNHCHR, UNICEF supported 33,460 undocumented and stateless children (52% boys, 48% girls) in navigating legal identity applications up from 9,417 in 2024. This massive scale-up resulted in 2,987 children successfully obtaining registered status, permanent residency, or Thai nationality, granting them access to essential rights.   

The fight against child poverty……

Child poverty remains persistently higher than the overall poverty rate with 7.9% of children living in poverty compared with 4.9% of the general population indicating that national gains have not fully translated into better outcomes for all children. 

Thailand’s Child Multidimensional Poverty Index reveals that 22% of children live in poverty when considering multiple dimensions such as education, health, and living standards. The implication is that these children are at increased risk of all forms of child rights deprivations, from early development delays, nutritional deficiencies, educational outcomes to future employability. Social protection schemes such as the Child Support Grant are decisive to evening out inequalities and providing support for children living in poverty.
 
In 2025, UNICEF continued to support the strengthening of national efforts to expand the Child Support Grant (CSG) under the leadership of MSDHS on submitting a proposal to the Secretariat of the Cabinet to expand the Child Support Grant (CSG) to cover all children under six years old and pregnant women. Although the proposal was returned for further clarification and delayed due to changes in government, it established a concrete policy option for universal child benefits for future advocacy.

The Child Support Grant is one of many social insurance schemes aimed at reducing poverty and providing relief for low-income families, yet a key challenge is that many eligible families are not covered by applicable schemes, while data remains fragmented across different agencies making monitoring and identification of those in need difficult. 

To promote integration across social protection schemes, UNICEF partnered with MSDHS and invested in developing the next phase of a de facto “single registry” of vulnerable households in Thailand (MSO Logbook). With UNICEF’s support, the platform is being positioned as an integrated social registry, with plans to incorporate the disability grant and other social transfer programmes under the Ministry. This integrated social registry will ultimately enable more accurate identification of vulnerable households, reduce duplication and exclusion across programmes, and improve coordination and efficiency in delivering social protection benefits to those most in need. 

Leveraging resources for children in Thailand…...

UNICEF, in partnership with NESDC and Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI) and the European Union, commissioned and launched the report “Human Capital Development in Thailand: An Examination of Gaps, Bottlenecks, and Policy Options” in July 2025. The launch convened high-level representatives from government, academia, civil society, and the private sector, including the Advisor to the Prime Minister and the Deputy Minister of Education, and featured a panel discussion to elevate human capital in demographic and economic policy debates. 
The evidence was used to advocate for increased and better-targeted public spending on children, including through a roundtable with Members of Parliament and Senators co-hosted with the Parliamentary Budget Office. Building on earlier engagement with the Budget Bureau, sustained advocacy throughout 2025 contributed to increased allocations for health and education, and child protection (including notable gains for the 15-year Free Education Programme¿, skills development initiatives¿ and the Kinship Grant)¿ in the 2026 Budget Bill, reversing the trend of gradual decrease in allocations to social sectors.

In a similar vein, the report “Sustainable Financing of the Social Sectors in Thailand: Fiscal Space Analysis and Revenue Reforms” including recommendations on fiscal space and revenue reform options was shared with the Ministry of Finance. In December, the Ministry presented a package of economic and fiscal policies to the National Committee on Economic Policy, including a Personal Income Tax proposal aligned with UNICEF’s recommendations. The proposal introduces differentiated tax credits to ensure incentives benefit middle- and low-income groups highlighting UNICEF’s critical role in advocating for and leveraging resources for children using evidence-based research. 

Complementing this work and looking into the future, UNICEF advanced a strategic foresight initiative with NESDC to strengthen forward-looking policymaking for children and young people. Applying foresight methodologies, the exercise explored emerging trends, future scenarios, and strategic responses for the medium to long term which will inform the 14th National Economic and Social Development Plan (NESDP 2028–2032) and UNICEF’s next Country Programme (2027–2031). With UNICEF’s support, NESDC is also working to integrate young people’s perspectives into national survey instruments for the next NESDP. 

Empowering youth in Thailand with participation and skills……

UNICEF supported the Children and Youth Council of Thailand (CYCT) to develop their 10-Year Strategy, Powered by Youth, Driven by Vision, through participatory foresight processes. UNICEF’s technical assistance also enabled a nationwide youth survey to support the operationalization of the strategy at provincial level, capturing the priorities, aspirations, and contextual realities of 21,090 children and young people. These findings informed the development of a two-year CYCT action plan with clear indicators to track progress against the 10-year strategy. As a key validation and decision-making step, the UNICEF-supported CYCT National Assembly convened 130 youth representatives from across the country to review, refine, and finalise the action plan, strengthening youth influence within national and subnational governance processes. 

Over 13% of young people in Thailand aged 15–24 years are not in education, employment or training (NEET). Young women with care responsibilities, persons with disabilities, and ethnic minorities are at special risk with limited access to education and training and unemployment opportunities. NEET youth are disproportionately affected by mental health issues and many resort to harmful practices as coping strategies. To provide alternative opportunities UNICEF has developed a pilot of integrated services for NEET youth under implementation in five provinces, using intersectoral taskforces to deliver coordinated, youth-centered support linking education, health, skills development, and employment. The approach strengthened local referral systems and enabled timely pathways back into education, training, or work. In the Southern Border Provinces, 1,835 youth participated, with 77% successfully reintegrated. 
Recognizing the critical role of frontline service providers UNICEF strengthened the professionalization of youth work in Thailand by building the capacities of 481 service providers, including 124 certified Master Trainers, in partnership with the Thailand Professional Qualification Institute. Based on national Youth Work Standards, the training integrated inclusive and gender-responsive approaches and equipped practitioners—primarily youth mentors and case managers under the NEET pilot and Thailand Zero Dropout (TZD) programme—to support vulnerable youth.

These youth work initiatives have generated strong government ownership, leading to its integration into the TZD programme. Under TZD, the Government has committed to deploying at least one trained youth worker in every tambon (sub-district) through the “One Tambon, One Youth Worker” model to identify, reach, and support out-of-school and at-risk young people. Given the national scale of TZD, this partnership has significant potential to expand Thailand’s youth service workforce, embed youth work within local governance systems, and institutionalize equitable youth support services nationwide. 

Supporting Children Through Crisis and Displacement

Under the leadership of the Government, a strong response was mobilized to address immediate humanitarian needs following armed conflict along the border and severe flooding in northern and southern Thailand. Working hand in hand with partners on the ground, UNICEF identified child-specific needs and complemented the overall response through child-focused protection, education and psychosocial support. This included the provision of recreational and educational materials to 18,000 flood-affected children and 30,000 children temporarily displaced by conflict. In addition, more than 100 child-friendly spaces were established in evacuation centres, reaching nearly 10,000 children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Working in an upper-middle-income country, UNICEF needs to continue to generate robust evidence and high-quality data to make this investment case. However, while evidence can shape choices and clarify trade-offs, prioritizing investments in equitable human capital development remains a political decision—one that depends on sustained political will. This remains a challenge in Thailand’s frequent reshuffling of cabinets and will require strategic and persistent political lobbying with key decision makers. Alongside this, UNICEF must help stimulate and sustain public demand for child-centered priorities, ensuring that evidence is translated into compelling narratives that resonate with voters, influencers, and decision-makers alike, and that children remain visible in national public debates requiring a multi-year advocacy strategy that focuses on a few key issues over time. When strategically linked to advocacy efforts, child rights monitoring becomes a powerful tool for driving systemic change and by aligning monitoring, accountability, and advocacy strategies, UNICEF can more effectively shape public discourse, support reforms, and promote sustained action to protect and advance the rights of every child. 

The relationship between UNICEF and the private sector is increasingly moving beyond traditional fundraising toward more deliberate, solution-oriented partnerships. Many companies now view engagement with UNICEF not only as a financial contribution, but as an opportunity to co-develop responses to complex challenges affecting children. In this context, there is an opportunity for UNICEF to engage more strategically with private sector partners as part of broader, multi-stakeholder approaches to policy dialogue and systems change. Private sector actors often bring complementary perspectives, networks, and convening power that can help reinforce shared priorities with government counterparts. Thoughtfully structured strategic alliances can therefore enhance coherence across advocacy, policy engagement, and implementation efforts.

Three evaluations, ECD, Education, Child Protection, were conducted timely to feed into the design of the next Country Programme. Some of the key findings of these evaluations point to the need for UNICEF to continue and reinforce its system-strengthening approach to address structural constraints that limited the depth and sustainability of results. 
UNICEF must continue to adapt its programming to respond to emerging and interconnected risks facing children, particularly those driven by climate change and rapid technological transformation. This year’s environmental shocks underscored the growing exposure of children to climate-related hazards, reinforcing the need to strengthen disaster risk reduction, climate resilience, and shock-responsive social protection systems that can anticipate, absorb, and respond to crises. 

The digital revolution is reshaping childhood in profound ways, with rising concerns around mental health linked to social media use, excessive screen time, and online harms. UNICEF must therefore expand its focus on understanding, monitoring, and responding to the implications of digital transformation on children’s mental health, development, and social relationships, while supporting policies and systems that promote safe, healthy, and inclusive digital environments. Together, these shifts call for more adaptive, forward-looking programming that protects children not only from today’s shocks, but from the evolving risks shaping their futures and will remain a priority for 2026 and the new Country Programme. 

Thailand’s aspiration to become a high-income country by 2038, its strategic geopolitical position within ASEAN, and its ambition to join the OECD present opportunities to advance reforms and invest in children. Thailand’s commitment to human capital development, aimed at boosting workforce productivity and addressing the challenges of an ageing society, positions UNICEF to advocate strongly for greater investment in children.  

While challenges persist, Thailand’s established technocratic governance system provides a strong foundation for policy implementation. The country’s financial and human resources, coupled with its track record of fiscal discipline, position it well to prioritize long-term investments in child welfare. Therefore, UNICEF’s success hinges upon leveraging resources and generating and operationalizing political will that employs a long-term horizon view.

These deliberations have been part and parcel of the development process of the new UNICEF Country Programme (2027-2031). UNICEF will continue to sharpen its business model tailored to Thailand’s upper middle-income. This model will focus on upstream policy work and system strengthening, leveraging domestic resources, and mobilizing highly specialized technical expertise. Advocacy efforts will include building coalitions with civil society and private sector partners and influencing political priorities.

In 2025, Timor-Leste witnessed differentiated progress on child rights: while there were strong health gains, including malaria elimination (WHO, July 2025), and advancing education and protection reforms, nutrition gaps, learning regression, and inequities persisted. Therefore, the focus in the country remained on strengthening systems, which is aligned to UNICEF’s 2022–2025 Strategic Plan, especially around survival, learning, protection, WASH, and social protection. 
To substantiate recent progress, UNICEF played a leading role in supporting the rollout of the Demographic and Health Survey, a comprehensive national survey on child health and nutrition, with results expected in 2026. Significant milestones were also achieved in the education sector, including the completion of the first-ever Joint Education Sector Review and the development of the draft Education Sector Plan 2026–2030 and the Teacher Competency Framework.
Child protection gained strong political visibility in Timor-Leste, with increased national commitment to ending violence against children. Building on ten national Ending Violence Against Children (EVAC) commitments, the country joined the Global Pathfinding Alliance. The Government also initiated planning for the rollout of a social protection programme targeting children in their first 1,000 days, allocating a pilot budget and scheduling implementation to begin in 2026.
In addition, the Government introduced Resolution No. 6/2025, outlining a roadmap for administrative decentralisation and the establishment of local government bodies between 2025 and 2028. This demonstrates strong commitment to strengthening local governance and presents opportunities for UNICEF to promote child-friendly local governance.
 
With support from UN agencies, the Government conducted month-long consultations on its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and actively engaged in Climate COP30. In July 2025, UNICEF supported the development of the “Climate Rationale for WASH in Timor-Leste” through sector-wide stakeholder consultations. The document is scheduled for finalization and launch in 2026, strengthening evidence-based climate-resilient WASH planning and investment.
 
Positioned strongly to provide policy and programme advice and to leverage public and private financing at scale, UNICEF’s new Country Programme Document (2026–2030) (approved in September 2025) will focus on strengthening basic social service delivery systems and improving access to essential supplies. 
 
The programme will focus on addressing persistent equity challenges and gender disparities across sectors such as nutrition, education, employability, and access to essential services, which disproportionately affect young people and people with disabilities. In addition, UNICEF will continue to prioritize equitable access to essential supplies. For instance, in 2025, a global shortage of vitamin A capsules, combined with shipping challenges to Timor-Leste, adversely affected the implementation of the vitamin A supplementation programme. Consequently, only 18% of children aged 6–59 months received the recommended two doses of vitamin A. Moving forward, UNICEF’s continued focus will be on strengthening systems to ensure timely delivery of essential services. 
 
Regarding the political landscape, the country experienced strengthened regional integration and economic stability through diversification and international partnerships. In October, the country achieved a diplomatic milestone by becoming a full member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The membership is expected to significantly enhance regional cooperation, and support national development priorities including social and economic inclusion. The nation also commemorated the 50th anniversary of the Unilateral Proclamation of Independence in November, reinforcing political stability and social cohesion.
Timor-Leste enhanced its international profile by hosting several diplomatic events. In April, the country convened the 6th Ministerial Meeting of the G7+ (made up of conflict-affected countries), resulting in the Dili Resolution on debt relief and increased climate financing. In May, Dili hosted the Pacific Regional Seminar of the UN Special Committee on Decolonization, focusing on self-determination for non-self-governing territories. 
On the economic front, Timor-Leste's financial stability depends on the Petroleum Fund, which stood at US$18.95 billion in the third quarter of 2025. High annual withdrawals from the Fund to support the national budget has been a norm. In November, the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources and Woodside Energy signed an agreement to develop the Greater Sunrise gas fields, with production expected between 2032 and 2035. The 2026 General State Budget of approximately US$2.29 billion prioritizes infrastructure (nearly US$436 million) and energy investments and authorizes issuing new public debts of up to US$850 million, signaling a shift towards external financing to support major development projects. The economic growth, at 4.1 per cent in 2024 and 3.9 per cent in 2025, has been largely driven by high government spending and is not considered self-sustaining due to structural constraints, according to the World Bank and IMF.  
A significant development was the abrupt termination of USAID’s programs and the closure of the agency's operations in the country, as part of a global policy shift by the U.S. government. This led to the midstream cancellation of several major projects across critical social sectors, creating a substantial funding gap for local and international organizations, including UNICEF.
In late 2025, student-led protests prompted cancellation of the government plans for lifetime pensions and vehicles benefits for elected representatives. The unrest was resolved without major escalations. In October 2025, a United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) report warned that transnational criminal syndicates were using shell companies in the Oecusse (RAEOA) region to support illegal gambling and cyber-scam operations. In response, the Government revoked online gambling licenses and suspended new applications.
 
The year 2025 also marked finalization of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), which the Government approved formally in December. Out of the 17 Goals, progress is visible in nine, with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) showing the most significant progress. SDG 1 (No Poverty) is also likely to be achieved by 2030 if current trends continue. Conversely, SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) are regressing. Of 93 assessed SDG targets, only 16% are on track, 56% need faster progress, and 28% are moving away from baseline. Data gaps for SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water) hinder effective monitoring and response

Health
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened health systems by supporting national strategies, improving maternal and childcare, expanding immunization, digitalizing health data, and promoting climate-friendly innovations to ensure resilient, equitable healthcare. This was done by supporting the development of the costed Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) Strategy 2025–2030 and the costed National Immunization Strategy (NIS) 2026–2030 for the Ministry of Health (MOH)
UNICEF expanded investments in green technology and climate-friendly medical equipment for medical waste management in five referral hospitals and one national hospital. These upgrades improve disposal efficiency, reduce cross-infection and lower occupational risks. In addition, an oxygen plant at Baucau Referral Hospital, due in January 2026, will strengthen subnational capacity to manage newborn care and oxygen supply to other health facilities.
In 2025, 8,784 live births were attended by skilled health workers in community health centers, and 37,161 measles vaccine doses were administered to children through the national routine immunization programme.
UNICEF strengthened the health system performance through the digitalization of health data, equipping 14 municipalities and 73 community health centers with 98 tablets and routers to enable real-time immunization data recording and reporting into the national database. In parallel, 259 health workers (138 males, 121 females) were trained in health data management. Service quality was further enhanced through the provision of tools and training on safe and clean delivery (39 participants/reaching 95% of all), early newborn care (89 health workers/94.7%), antenatal and postnatal care (94 health workers/100%), and maternal and perinatal death review (37 participants/100%).
UNICEF continued procurement of all routine vaccines on behalf of the MOH and developed the annual costed vaccine forecast for 2026, incorporating donor co-financing requirements. UNICEF, in coordination with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, ensured an uninterrupted supply of COVID-19 vaccines to Timor-Leste, including the delivery, storage and distribution of the final batch of free vaccines in 2025 to meet local demands. 
Community engagement and social behaviour change played an integral role in strengthening access to services. Trainings and support provided to the Mother Support Groups (MSGs) across all municipalities helped increase awareness levels on essential newborn care, Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR), rights of people with disabilities, early detection of growth and development delays, immunization, nutrition, referral, and reporting, making the model sustainable. 
UNICEF also ensured media coverage and visibility of all key health activities, results, and achievements through social media and engagement with local media outlets. The confirmation of Pandemic Fund support for the next three years and Gavi funding for the next five years further demonstrates UNICEF’s leadership, advocacy, and commitment to building resilient local health systems in Timor-Leste.
Nutrition 
UNICEF, in collaboration with the MOH, Government of Timor-Leste, made significant progress in expanding nationwide coverage of child nutrition services. The services reached 729 (314 female, 416 male) children suffering from Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), with a 79.6% cure rate. In addition, 64,383 (32,714 male, 31,669 female) children aged 6-59 months received Vitamin A supplementation, and 133,325 children aged 12-59 months were given deworming tablets. In parallel, UNICEF supported the distribution of multiple micronutrient powders (MNP) to 36% (21,936 out of a target of 60,349) of children aged 6-23 months across all 14 municipalities.
Financial support from Children's Investment Fund Foundation, China, the European Union and Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) enabled support to the MOH at all levels to strengthen the Primary Health Care (PHC) network's capacity. UNICEF also facilitated modeling of revitalization, growth monitoring, and promotion in one municipality as a learning site for future progressive scale-up in other municipalities.
In 2025, the University of Sydney, in partnership with UNICEF, conducted formative research to identify the drivers, determinants, and opportunities for improving the diets of children aged 6-23 months. Building on the findings, UNICEF engaged with the Interministerial Task Force on Social Affairs and the National Food and Nutrition Security Council of Timor-Leste (CONSSAN-TL), to advocate for policies (under adoption) aimed at improving access to affordable, convenient, nutrient-rich foods and to integrating nutrition objectives into social protection and feeding practices.
UNICEF worked alongside the Stunting Unit (UNMICS) to disseminate the multisectoral national nutrition action plan (PANKOS) to combat stunting in the municipalities of Bobonaro, Covalima, and Ermera. The socialization served as an advocacy to raise the attention of the Municipal Presidents to their roles in stunting reduction and the importance of resource allocation at the municipal level. In addition, a multisectoral dashboard was developed to visualize and track PANKOS results and resource allocation. The dashboard will be linked to the municipality dashboard to ensure the visibility of nutrition indicators and facilitate planning and budgeting processes for Municipalities.
UNICEF continued to support the digitalization of nutrition data, linking it to the District Health Information Software (DHIS2). Data visualization, implemented in all 13 municipalities, enables access to nutrition coverage data, improving decision-making and planning (supplies and coverage monitoring) by the National Directorate of Nutrition.
UNICEF reached 29,998 girls aged 12-16 with micronutrient supplementation out of a target of 77,770. Furthermore, together with local NGOs like Alola Foundation, HIM, and TimorAid, UNICEF provided mentorship to over 6,000 members of MSGs to deliver nutrition interventions at the community level empowering families and adolescent girls with nutrition knowledge. Using the Kobo Platform, UNICEF also supported MSG, which collected approximately 150,000 households’ data on nutrition, MNCH, and WASH, supporting MoH efforts to monitor and increase coverage and availability of supplies. 
 
WASH
UNICEF advances climate-resilient WASH services by supporting policy development, scaling nature-based water solutions, improving sanitation, and rehabilitating health facility infrastructure to ensure safe water and hygiene for communities nationwide. UNICEF supported the National Regulatory Directorate of Water and Sanitation (DNRAS, Ministry of Public Works) and the Vector Control and Environmental Health Department (MOH) for policy development. The key achievement has been the development of the “Climate Rationale for WASH Services,” which outlines strategic priorities for enhancing resilience in WASH services affected by climate change. The document is under finalisation, along with the “Climate and WASH funding evaluation study”.
In sanitation, the MOH initiated the development of a Sanitation and Hygiene Roadmap to advance climate-resilient, safely managed sanitation for all. The roadmap provides an integrated framework to coordinate investments, strengthen governance, and mobilise resources to eliminate open defecation, sustain behaviour change, and expand safely managed sanitation services. By end - 2025, key stakeholder meetings were held to define its objective, with further consultations planned through 2026 to finalize the roadmap. UNICEF continued to support Open Defecation Free (ODF) declaration and verification processes, and as of December 2025, Manatuto is ready for a municipality-wide declaration. 
To accelerate the uptake of Nature-based Solutions (NbS), UNICEF supported DNRAS in developing and standardising a community-based water catchment management approach. Tools such as the Training of Trainers manual, community orientation booklet, Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) checklist, and site selection guidelines have been developed for validation in early 2026. UNICEF also continued to scale up community-based water catchment management. In 2025, NbS was implemented in four municipalities (Ainaro, Viqueque, Aileu and Dili), supporting 105 sub-villages. Implementation was carried out by 151 trained local practitioners (43 female, 108 male) as community facilitators. In total, 1,172 community members (444 female, 728 male) participated in community construction work after learning about water conservation and catchment management. Together, the communities constructed 1,277 nature-based infrastructure systems, including 182 retention ponds, 476 terraces, and 619 natural check dams. These structures are estimated to capture and conserve at least 124,143 cubic meters of rainwater during a single rainfall event, significantly increasing local water availability for households, agriculture, and community services.
Until 2024, UNICEF invested heavily in the construction and rehabilitation of WASH in Health Facilities across the country as part of the COVID-19 response. In 2025, UNICEF handed over 10 facilities in Oecussi and Lautem to the Government of Timor-Leste.  Following changes in external funding arrangements, particularly from USAID in early 2025, some construction and rehabilitation activities experienced delays. However, UNICEF, with its Regular Resources, resumed work at 7 Community Health Centres in Liquica and Manufahi, and at 16 health posts in Dili, Baucau, Covalima and Manatuto, which will be completed in 2026.
Education
UNICEF strengthened education systems by coordinating sector planning, promoting digital learning, advancing inclusive and climate-smart education, and expanding early childhood programs to ensure equitable, quality learning for all children. It continues to play a leading role in sector coordination through the Açao Conjunta para Educaçao Timor-Leste (ACETL) and the Local Education Group (LEG), co-chairing with the Ministry of Education (MoE). The LEG brings together bilateral and multilateral partners and civil society organizations to strengthen collaboration in education. Key achievements include the country’s first-ever Joint Education Sector Review and the drafting of the Education Sector Plan 2026-2030 and the Teacher Competency Framework, aligned with the Southeast Asia Teacher Competency Framework to improve teacher quality and learning outcomes. 
UNICEF advocated for greater use and access to digital solutions in classrooms, in order to improve learning outcomes access and ensure equity. As a result, the National Teacher Training Institute (INFORDEPE) has integrated technology and blended learning as a key strategy in its new five-year strategic plan. The pilot to digitize school inspection was launched in four municipalities, and lessons are being documented for scale-up. In 2025, 360 teachers (planned: 250) were trained (202 male, 158 female) in ICT and the digital platform, Learning Passport, benefiting 2,239 children (980 male, 1259 female). 
Data and evidence-generation efforts continued, including the launch of an ongoing study on out-of-school children, baseline assessments of teachers' and children's knowledge, attitudes, and practices on ICT usage, and dissemination of findings from the School Readiness programme study to inform evidence-based policy and programming. 
Climate resilience was prioritized through the first national workshop on ‘Climate-Smart Education’ that brought together the MoE departments, Instituto Nacional de Formação de Docentes e Profissionais da Educação (INFORDEPE), and partners to develop a framework integrating climate adaptation into EMIS. The framework proposes to use climate markers for schools and curricula, and to integrate technology, children’s leadership, and 21st-century skills into school practices. This was followed by practical action: 2,210 students (1,143 male, 1,067 female) and 106 teachers (58 male, 48 female) from 16 schools in Aileu participated in climate education and implemented greening activities, including rainwater harvesting. 
Inclusive Education remains a priority, with UNICEF supporting MoE to initiate national and sub-national training of teacher mentors on the use of the Child Functioning Screening Tool and Universal Design for Learning to strengthen inclusive pedagogy across schools. A milestone was the launch of national capacity building for school leaders and teachers on Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (PSEAH) led by MoE in collaboration with the Government of Australia, following a comprehensive review of t existing code of conduct, laws, and regulations. 
Most children in Timor-Leste lack access to Early Childhood Education (ECE). UNICEF collaborated with MoE and supported 5,707 children (2,752 female, 2,955 male) through 87 community-based preschools and school-readiness programs and trained 148 facilitators in child-centred pedagogy and inclusive education. A multimedia-based parenting program promoted early learning for children aged 0–8 years.
Child Protection
In 2025, Timor-Leste reached significant milestones to strengthen the Child Protection (CP) system. Building on its pledge at the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children (EVAC) held in Bogota in November 2024, the Government advanced commitments to end violence against children. EVAC was elevated to the highest political level with Timor-Leste’s induction into the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children, in the presence of the UN SRSG on EVAC, opening an opportunity to strengthen CP and social welfare systems for prevention and response.
The Child Protection System Strengthening Framework was endorsed, and work began on a costed national EVAC plan aligned with the ASEAN Plan of Action to eliminate EVAC. UNICEF supported a training programme for 87 justice professionals on CP law, and the long-pending Juvenile Justice Law, first drafted in 2010, resumed development. The updated law introduces diversion and child-sensitive procedures, better aligning the justice system with international standards.
Legislative reforms advanced with the development of an adoption law (draft) and a decree-law on foster and kinship care (draft), laying the groundwork for family-based care and care reform, both expected to be finalized in 2026. UNICEF leveraged Regular Resources and global thematic funds to sustain high-level advocacy and programming, recruit technical expertise, and support Government consultations, including a study tour to Indonesia on adoption, inter-country adoption, and alternative care - all contributions that informed drafting of laws. 
Capacity building of the social service workforce continued: 768 workers (49% female) were trained, enabling preventive and response services that reached 2,890 children (63% female). An accredited Certificate III course in community services for the first cohort of 43 trainees (including CP Officers, GBV focal points, and administration post-level workers) was launched, marking a milestone in strengthening knowledge, skills, and standards to deliver inclusive, quality services.
A validated landscape analysis classified Timor-Leste at an initial maturity stage and reported a 390% increase in child sexual abuse material reports between 2019 and 2023, underscoring urgent gaps in policy, institutions, and programmes, and to be used in advocacy. An ICT Forum on Child Online Protection identified priorities aligned with ASEAN guidelines on comprehensive legislation against online sexual exploitation and abuse, and UNICEF engaged with the Ministry of Justice to integrate child online protection in the draft Cybercrime Law. 
Community-level action tackled harmful social norms through information sessions, home visits, and dialogues. UNICEF trained 259 Child Protection Network members (50% female) and engaged 133 youths, parents, and leaders (59% female). Through the Girl Empowerment Programme, implemented with Pradet (a national NGO), 96 adolescent girls gained knowledge, confidence, and resilience, and were linked to protection services.
With regional support, a climate marker was integrated into the Primero case management system to track climate-related protection risks, identify hotspots, inform policy and investment, and elevate CP within the climate agenda. With HQ support, the Child Functioning Module was also integrated into Primero to guide disability-inclusive case planning and to strengthen monitoring and reporting of children facing difficulties across different domains. UNICEF initiated a climate-resilient programme to support parents and caregivers facing climate-induced risks, reaching 152 vulnerable families.
Social Policy and Evidence Generation
UNICEF continued to influence the 2026 budget with a focus on children through targeted advocacy, supporting children, climate, and nutrition markers, and helping decision-makers link funding to children’s well-being, climate resilience, and improved nutrition. Beyond PFM advocacy with the Ministry of Finance, UNICEF trained 348 young people in budget literacy, 50% of them being women, enabling more informed participation in national priority-setting.  
UNICEF also supported registration of 34,369 children under Bolsa Da Mae, including 42 children with disabilities, with a focus on shock responsiveness. In consultation with key stakeholders, UNICEF developed and shared a policy advocacy document to strengthen social protection programs, against climate-related shocks and future risks. 
In 2024, UNICEF launched an independent evaluation of its Country Programme for 2021–2025, with the final report released in 2025. Findings informed the new CPD 2026-2030. UNICEF also strengthened child rights and inclusion by embedding disability data in the 2025 DHS, helping guide inclusive government planning. 
Adolescent and Youth Empowerment
UNICEF, together with the Ministry of Youth, Sports, Arts and Culture and local NGOs, empowered young people across Timor-Leste by expanding opportunities for community participation and leadership. This included registering 13 youth-led civil society organizations with 130 young people, 35% of whom were women, strengthening their formal recognition, and role in decision-making. UNICEF also trained 177 adolescents (87 male, 90 female)in leadership and life skills, enabling them to take initiative and contribute more confidently. In addition, UNICEF and partners supported 17 youth innovations, with five groups receiving seed funding, three of them being women-led. Civic education was further strengthened for 142 Youth Parliament members, with 50% women and two members with disabilities, deepening their understanding of public institutions, rights and responsibilities.
UNICEF advanced disability inclusion through partnerships with the Asosiasaun Defisiénsia Timor-Leste (ADTL), Ministry of Social Solidarity and Inclusion (MSSI) and youth-led civil society. It supported accessible infrastructure in three youth centres, promoted community-based services and disseminated the Operational Guidance on the Rights to Participation of Adolescents and Youth with Disabilities in four municipalities. Life-skills based education (LSBE) training reached 588 participants. Together with UN Women and the UN Human Rights Office, UNICEF supported MSSI’s Initial Report and consultations on the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) and with ADTL, supported entrepreneurship initiatives for young people with disabilities.
Climate Change 
UNICEF initiated implementation of Timor-Leste’s Climate-Smart Social Services and Infrastructure (C3SI) initiative, funded by KOICA, to strengthen resilience across social sectors. Under this, UNICEF is solarizing critical social service facilities, including schools, health facilities, and community centres and upgrading climate-resilient WASH systems in two priority locations: Hera (Dili Municipality) and Vila (Atauro Island). Building on this model, UNICEF held a national multi-sector consultation to expand climate investment opportunities, particularly through significant international climate funds, such as the Green Climate Fund (GCF). In addition, UNICEF supported the Government in developing an integrated child-centric upcoming NDC 3.0 revision, ensuring that the sectoral priorities explicitly address the needs and vulnerabilities of children across key social services. 
Communication and Advocacy
National-level advocacy delivered policy gains and visibility for child rights through a coordinated, country–wide effort that engaged 28 senior policymakers and partners. This led to the Council of Ministers' Resolution No. 50/2024, declaring 1 June as National Children’s Day. Investments in child rights were promoted through high-level partner events and strategic field visits, including delegations from Wiggles and McCuskers in Australia, KOICA, Vinci Energies and UNICEF China. Impact was reinforced through extensive media and digital outreach (122 media articles, reaching 1.7 million people). Child participation was scaled up and institutionalized, with 2,833 children and young people, with approximately 50% females, engaging in advocacy and communications.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF in Timor-Leste has continued to prioritize system strengthening, aligned with UNICEF’s 2022–2025 Strategic Plan, especially around survival, learning, protection, WASH, and social protection. However, political, social and economic instability has constrained progress. The health system faced significant operational challenges due to high staff turnover at national and municipal levels, and insufficient recurrent budget allocations, limiting coverage of essential costs. These constraints have led to shortages of basic medicines and delays in technical initiatives. In response, the current strategy emphasizes strengthened multi-sectoral collaboration to optimize resources and reduce duplication. A key lesson learned is the need to decentralize financial flows, including exploring direct disbursements to Municipal Health Authorities, to strengthen outreach services and support localized training. 
In the nutrition sector, persistent supply stockouts, particularly vitamin A capsules, left a significant number of children without supplementation, increasing their vulnerability. To address this, UNICEF will implement a joint systems transformation project including a financing platform to improve access to affordable, convenient, nutrient-rich foods for children aged 6-23 months. Community and social behaviour change outreach initiatives revealed notable disparities among children’s caregivers, indicating to the need for stronger targeting and engagement of men in future nutrition, health, and WASH awareness programs.
Access to sanitation and clean water remained a challenge, as structural changes within the National Directorate of Water and Sanitation Service in 2025 led to staff transitions and temporary gaps in institutional knowledge and technical capacity, affecting programme delivery. UNICEF is supporting efforts to strengthen systems and rebuild capacity.
Key challenges in the education sector included a state budget below the international benchmark, limited access to quality Early Childhood Education, and the need for a climate-smart and resilient system. Gaps in reliable data persist, and the country’s withdrawal from the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics initiative signaling the need for renewed advocacy for a national standardized learning assessment. At the same time, increased use of digital solutions to complement classroom learning, strengthen climate resilience and inclusion, improve school inspections, and prepare for digital Education Management Information Systems offers a strategic entry point for the new Country Programme and resource mobilization. Leveraging the Global Partnership for Education’s innovative financing, including the Multiplier Grant, and the new operating model offer opportunities for strategic partnerships with the private sector and foundations.
For Child Protection, key challenges in 2025 stemmed primarily from shifting government priorities affecting the implementation of the Law on the Protection of Children and Youth in Danger and the establishment of the National Institute for Social Inclusion (NISI) for training the social service workforce. Several provisions of Law No. 6/2023 remain unclear, and the absence of secondary regulations has hindered effective operationalization, despite the law’s strong legal foundation. UNICEF will continue supporting the Government in drafting and adopting these instruments to ensureconsistent implementation. 
Differing perspectives on institutionalizing the social service workforce programme, limited numbers of certified trainers, and high staff turnover, particularly in finance, further constrained progress and delayed fund transfers under new financial procedures. In response, UNICEF and government partners will develop a social service workforce strategy in early 2026 and undertake a comprehensive analysis of implementation challenges to inform planning. 
The abrupt end of USAID support affected child protection-related emergency preparedness activities. A key lesson learned was the importance of joint planning and early government ownership of innovative approaches, which proved critical for advancing child online protection and for Timor-Leste’s successful entry into the Pathfinding Alliance.
Social protection has received strong political commitment, yet it faces structural imbalances due to a disproportionate allocation of resources to veterans' pensions at the expense of broader poverty-reduction programs, particularly for children.  Critical gaps remain in addressing child malnutrition and stunting, as well as in funding for programmes like the Bolsa da Mãe, a conditional cash transfer programme for schoolchildren, which fluctuates or remains insufficient. Fragmented delivery mechanisms and the absence of a unified digital ID system further challenge the system. While UNICEF has supported the government in registering children under the Bolsa Da Mae, the areas of social protection focused on disability and climate change require further innovation and more substantial commitments. Looking ahead, the focus will be on implementing a comprehensive decentralization strategy aimed at strengthening local governance to empower municipal authorities responsible for planning, budgeting, and implementation, ensuring greater accountability and equity across all municipalities.
While there is strong political buy-in and high visibility for equity issues and child rights, a key challenge remains in translating national-level commitments into sustained, well-resourced implementation at municipal and community levels, particularly in remote areas with limited capacity and media access, and gender-responsive service delivery. Experience has shown that pairing evidence-based advocacy with high-level champions and child- and girl-led platforms is critical to achieving concrete policy results and ensuring credibility and sustainability. Future external advocacy will focus on institutionalizing commitments within sector plans and budgets, and scaling inclusive, digital, and adolescent-led advocacy through strategic partnerships to ensure continued momentum and reach to the most vulnerable children. 
Going forward, under the new country programme 2026-30, UNICEF will continue its close collaboration with the Government of Timor-Leste and line Ministries, civil society, UN sister agencies and other development partners, including evidence-based advocacy for increased government budget allocation and expenditure in the critical social sectors affecting children. There will be an emphasis on addressing gaps in gender-based violence, PSEA risks, barriers faced by adolescent girls, and unequal access to safe and inclusive education, especially for children with disabilities and those in hard-to-reach communities. Further, UNICEF will continue strengthening strategic partnerships with the governments of Australia, New Zealand, Korea, Japan, China, and the Great Britain, and with EU, KOICA, FCDO, UNICEF in Australia, Japan and  New Zealand; the global funds such as GPE, GAVI, the Pandemic Fund, Child Nutrition Fund, Climate Change Fund, and increasingly with private sector donors, foundations, philanthropists and individuals giving.

Shifts in national context affecting outcomes for  children
  
In 2025, Viet Nam achieved robust 8.02 per cent GDP growth – among the world’s highest, driven by a 16 per cent year-on-year jump in exports, set against inflation at 3.5 per cent and a continued reliance on public investment. This was achieved despite increased global trade tensions, continued declines in official development assistance (ODA) and reduced access to concessional financing. Viet Nam outlined its vision for ‘a new era of national rise' towards high-income status by 2045, through double digit growth based on human capital development, digital and green transformation and institutional modernization.
  
To accelerate this process, Viet Nam undertook sweeping governance and administrative reforms, resulting in the consolidation of ministries, merger of provinces, removal of the district administrative level and a significant reduction in the civil service. While intended to optimize efficiency, the scale and pace of reforms created new challenges for service continuity and coordination, particularly in rural and remote areas. A set of Party resolutions was adopted to accelerate digital transformation and strengthen human capital development through important investments in education and health. 

Viet Nam marked several key moments in 2025, 80 years of independence and 50 years since reunification, demonstrating its continued socio-economic transformation and enduring commitment to peace, stability and development. As a staunch supporter of multilateralism, Viet Nam also celebrated the 80th anniversary of the United Nations and 50 years of UNICEF’s continued presence in country – milestones that presented an opportunity to take stock on progress achieved, continued challenges and the road ahead to build a more inclusive, equitable, and resilient future for all children.
  
Where children stand today
  
While children in Viet Nam continued to benefit from strong national gains in health, education and poverty reduction in 2025, persistent inequities and newly emerging risks translated into uneven outcomes. Multiple and overlapping deprivations mean children continue to be left behind, especially those with disabilities, in rural areas, and those learning in a non-native language, encountering barriers to learning and reaching their full potential. Harmful social norms persist, especially related to gender, mental health and violence. Climate shocks, reform challenges and shrinking ODA tested the resilience of Viet Nam’s social systems, impacting children in remote, disaster-prone and marginalized communities.
  
Survival, nutrition, and healthy development
  
Child survival and health outcomes continued to improve in 2025, with a post-pandemic rebound in routine immunizations. Persistent gaps remain with maternal mortality at 100–150 per 100,000 live births in mountainous and ethnic regions, while neonatal mortality in remote provinces is  13.3 per 1,000 live births.  While stunting remains a challenge, at 18 per cent nationally and 27–30 per cent among ethnic children, in contrast almost one-in-five children aged 5–19 years is overweight – representing one of the fastest increases in overweight and obesity rates in Southeast Asia at 38 per cent. Gaps in neonatal and postnatal care persisted in remote provinces. Ministry of Health data show national postnatal care within the first week exceeded 70 per cent in 2024, but remained lowest in the Northern Midlands and Central Highlands (64 per cent). Recent data revealed that one-in-five adolescents aged 10–17 years experiences mental health problems, most commonly anxiety mainly due to family-related stressors. Low societal awareness, with limited access to support services, leaves many without help. 
  
Learning and skills
  
Learning outcomes in Viet Nam remain strong, with national reforms advancing more inclusive, competency-based and digital-ready education. This progress is reflected in regional assessments, with Viet Nam leading ASEAN in Grade 5 reading (66 per cent) and mathematics (88 per cent), with the highest share of students reaching minimum proficiency despite a slight decline from 2019, according to 2024 Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEAPLM). However, persistent gaps in access and learning remain for ethnic community and rural area children, with 20 per cent of Mekong Delta children out of school versus 10 per cent in urban settings, more than half of children with disabilities out of school at upper secondary school and children’s learning constrained by climate shocks or limited connectivity. According to the National Statistics Office, one-in-10 young people aged 15–24 were not in employment,  education or training in 2025, with a higher share among adolescent girls. Youth unemployment remains high at 7.93 per cent, with only 20 per cent of young people accessing vocational training, leaving many unprepared for rapidly evolving labour-market demands. 
  
Protection from violence, abuse and neglect 
  
Viet Nam continues to face acute challenges, with violent discipline commonplace for children (72.4 per cent in 2021), 40 per cent feeling unsafe and more than 70 per cent having had unwanted experiences while online[i]. In response, efforts to protect children from violence and harm advanced in 2025, with growing national attention to child online safety, as evidenced by Hanoi’s hosting of  the UN Convention against Cybercrime in 2025, along with nationwide campaigns on online protection targeting children and young people, in a step towards strengthening protection from online sexual abuse, grooming, and technology-facilitated  violence. This reflects an increased focus towards addressing rapidly changing technologies that demand adaptive responses focused on safety by design, strong partnerships and accountability of the corporate sector. Access to protection services and mental health and psychosocial support remains uneven, particularly for children in remote, disaster-affected and ethnic communities.  
  
Climate, disaster and environmental risks, safety-managed water and sanitation
  
As part of a climate crisis-driven trend of increasingly severe storm seasons, 14 major events caused extensive flooding across northern and central provinces of Viet Nam, leaving more than 1.5 million vulnerable children at heightened risk. Economic losses hit US$4.2 billion, with large-scale destruction of homes, schools, health facilities, and critical infrastructure. Flooding repeatedly disrupted water supplies, contaminated sanitation systems, interrupted schooling for more than 2.5 million students and strained essential services. Storms and flooding seriously impacted families and children in exposed mountainous areas, where 50–70 per cent of the population lack access to tap water and hygienic sanitation facilities. Viet Nam advanced its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 for 2026–2035, underpinned by a stronger emphasis on climate resilient health and other systems, co-benefits between mitigation and adaptation, and addressing damage. Towards these goals, UNICEF-supported consultations with children and adolescents helped integrate child-sensitive climate actions into the NDC 3.0 Framework. Government and UN partners also launched a Youth Participation Roadmap within NDC 3.0 to ensure youth voices shaped national decisions leading up to COP30 and beyond. 
  
Poverty, social protection and basic living conditions
  
Despite robust national economic growth, multidimensional poverty and deprivations are a reality for many children, particularly among ethnic communities and those living in remote and disaster-prone areas. A decline in national multi-dimensional poverty to 4.1 per cent contrasts with child multidimensional poverty lagging at 8.4 per cent, compounded by a more than three-fold higher rate (33 per cent) among ethnic children. In 2025, ongoing governance reforms, dynamic financing conditions and uneven access to basic services continued to limit the reach of social protection and other child-focused support systems that reinforce disparities despite overall national development gains.
  
What this means for UNICEF and results at scale
  
In this evolving context, UNICEF’s work in 2025 increasingly focused on supporting systems that can deliver results for children at scale. As governance reforms, recurring climate emergencies, and declining financing reshaped the operating environment, UNICEF prioritized policy engagement, systems strengthening and evidence generation to sustain gains made in recent years, while addressing persistent inequalities. The 2025 context reinforced the need for UNICEF to work across sectors and with government and partners to protect progress for children, strengthen national capacity and ensure that reforms and investments translate into tangible results for those currently or most-at-risk of being left behind.

In 2025, UNICEF supported the government and partners to deliver targeted results for the most vulnerable children, headlined by improved maternal and newborn care in ethnic communities, increased immunization rates among underserved children and key contributions to landmark nutrition legislation, such as a sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax, new national school meal guidelines and more inclusive, digitally-enabled education and early childhood reforms. Notably, UNICEF-supported climate-resilient and emergency WASH services reached vulnerable communities in need. Progress was also made in strengthening child protection laws, services and child-friendly justice, with all results underpinned by gender equality, disability inclusion, digital transformation, climate and disaster risk resilience approaches.

Health, nutrition, water and sanitation

Key gains were realized in maternal, newborn and child health by strengthening national policies and health systems to deliver critical nutrition services to climate disaster-hit communities. In close collaboration with the Ministry of Health, WHO and other partners, UNICEF contributed to key frameworks, including Resolution No.72 on Health, the amended Law on Disease Prevention, and the National Target Programme on Health, to advocate for a strong focus on primary health care, child nutrition and immunization. UNICEF support of the updated national newborn care guidelines realized training for 1,178 health workers and the provision of essential equipment and vaccines that reached 923,950 women and 753,544 newborns in vulnerable areas to ensure the underserved can access quality care. UNICEF helped to develop models for community-based services, including capacity building in ethnic community-dominated vulnerable areas in Dien Bien and Gia Lai provinces for scaling-up and replication in other provinces. 
Immunization services were strengthened through a three-year action plan, including vaccine procurement of nearly two million doses of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and inactivated polio vaccine, outreach sessions and social behaviour change campaigns on routine and rota vaccinations and to counter measles outbreaks, reaching an estimated six million people. In disaster-hit provinces, UNICEF supported the restoration of disrupted routine immunization and newborn care services, benefiting 35,811 people, including pregnant women and young children. Digital health transformation was advanced through support to the e-Maternal and Child Health system, optimizing interoperability and data quality to inform service delivery and monitoring.
With UNICEF’s sustained advocacy and support, the Ministry of Health reaffirmed its commitment to children’s environmental health by joining the global Partnership for a Lead-Free Future and finalizing a legal review on lead exposure, disseminated a national assessment of environmental pollution impacts on child health, trained healthcare workers on mitigating air pollution impacts on maternal and children’s health and conducted a survey on air pollution and public awareness campaign that reached more than two million people through social media channels. More than 600 children and other participants engaged in interactive activities at an exhibition featuring children’s stories and photos on air pollution.

On nutrition, impactful UNICEF advocacy contributed to a new excise tax law on sugar-sweetened beverages adopted in June 2025, and national School Meal Nutrition Guidelines issued in December 2025. Enhanced systems readiness through a revised national nutrition surveillance approach using a sentinel model and real-time dashboard  realized key delivery results, including nutrition education for 9,132 students, iron-folic acid supplementation for 5,907 adolescent girls, obesity-prevention pilots reaching 9,678 students in Danang, and counselling support for children and caregivers. In emergencies, as a sector lead in this area, UNICEF supported the screening of 47,527 children under-five, treatment of 1,480 children with severe acute malnutrition and 7,037 with moderate acute malnutrition, and infant and young child feeding counselling for 3,643 caregivers, helping protect child nutrition and development during disruptions.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) systems were strengthened and climate adaptation was advanced through UNICEF’s installation of solar and wind energy systems in 15 rural water schemes, serving 69,817 people and extending pipelines to reach around 9,000 previously unserved people, while rainwater harvesting systems were expanded to 50 schools and 10 household clusters in Dien Bien province. At the policy level, UNICEF supported the drafting of two national circulars on unit costs for rural water investment and operation and maintenance, strengthening the sustainability and scalability of rural water services. UNICEF co-led the WASH Emergency Sector Group to co-ordinate the response strategy and plans among partners to ensure climate-resilient and emergency WASH interventions protect children’s health, dignity and safety in high-risk and disaster-affected areas. Climate-resilient and emergency WASH services reached more than 200,000 people, including more than 107,200 children, and improved conditions in 224 schools and 64 health facilities, helping maintain access to essential services during repeated typhoons and floods. Emergency recovery efforts restored five water schemes and 18 facilities, while WASH supplies and cash assistance supported 59,000 people across multiple emergency responses.

Learning and skills

As a key highlight, UNICEF worked to operationalize national competency frameworks on digital learning and AI, which reached 1.3 million educators. Education reforms were advanced through universal access to early childhood education (ECE) for children aged 3–6, quality ECE programmes for urban and industrial zones and a child-centred ECE curriculum to be piloted in 20 provinces. UNICEF co-hosted the AI Nation Forum to promote responsible and child-centred digital transformation in education, together with key partners advocating for the safe, inclusive and ethical use of AI in learning. 

Through UNICEF’s Skills4Girls and Equal and Empowered Girls’ Education programmes, key steps towards gender equality in education were taken through strengthening girls’ foundational, digital and transferable skills, gender-responsive teaching, supportive school environments and tackling harmful gender norms that constrain adolescent girls’ participation, leadership and well-being.

Viet Nam’s participation in SEAPLM assessments and Data Must Speak analytics was supported with UNICEF-backed, evidence-informed planning and assessments, improving the availability and use of learning data to identify disparities and guide system-level responses. These efforts will contribute to improving the capacity of the education system to address gaps affecting children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

As the co-lead of the Education Sector Group in Viet Nam, with the Ministry of Education and Training, UNICEF championed progress towards more inclusive, resilient and future-ready learning by strengthening education systems and advancing national reforms, while efforts to protect learning continuity and well-being during repeated climate-related emergencies were coordinated as co-lead of the Education in Emergencies Sector Group. UNICEF supported joint assessments and response planning, delivered education supplies to more than 42,000 students, and trained 8,550 educators on climate-smart education and mental health and psychosocial support approaches. Cash assistance for the Typhoon Yagi response reached 1,660 households, supporting 8,028 people to mitigate the impact of shocks on schooling. 

Protection from violence, exploitation and abuse

With the overarching goal of ensuring children realize their rights to protection from violence, exploitation and harm, including in digital environments, UNICEF supported strengthened legal frameworks, services, systems and influenced the development of new national child protection priorities to 2030. Access to child protection and mental health and psychosocial support services was expanded through strengthened education and community-based systems. The issuance of Circular No. 18/2025 formalized school social work and counselling services, supporting system-level integration of psycho-social support within schools. UNICEF-delivered training for 327 school counsellors and managers and equipment for 105 counselling rooms enabled 35,575 students (49 per cent girls) to access psychosocial support services.
