Child protection units addressed increasingly complex cases, providing case management support to 104 children affected by abuse, while hospital-based child protection units managed 88 cases, including 29 cases of sexual abuse, with strengthened multi-sectoral coordination. As part of the landmark UN Convention against Cybercrime in Hanoi, UNICEF convened partners for a pre-event focused on technology-facilitated gender-based violence and child sexual exploitation, highlighting good practices to strengthen child-centred and gender-responsive online safety approaches. These efforts reinforced national attention to online child protection and the need for stronger, coordinated responses across sectors.

To realize child-sensitive justice, UNICEF delivered training for 1,283 justice specialists, helped expand the introduction of child-friendly investigation rooms and finalized a national child justice data report to inform child-focused sectoral development. To support children during emergency responses, UNICEF reached 486,000 people, in ethnic and Vietnamese languages, with messages on protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and gender-based violence, distributed child protection in emergencies kits and provided psychosocial support to more than 33,000 children and caregivers, as well as trained 467 frontline staff to strengthen preparedness and responses. 

Child-centred disaster risk reduction (DRR) and climate action

To advance child centred DRR and climate action – especially resilience - UNICEF played impactful roles in strengthening policy frameworks, building local capacities, and amplifying children’s voices in national climate action. Based on UNICEF technical expertise, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment proposed amendments to the Law on Disaster Prevention and Control aligned with children’s needs and contributing to a more child-sensitive DRR policy framework. At subnational level, UNICEF enhanced preparedness, by training 180 officials in high-risk northern mountainous provinces on risk-informed planning and child-focused emergency response.

More than 13,000 children and adolescents nationwide were engaged through UNICEF skills building, leadership initiatives and community based climate resilience activities, including the Safe, Green and Clean Communities Initiative. The voices of young climate advocates were amplified in a new UNICEF-supported youth led journalism initiative that empowered 250 young people to shape the public discourse and environmental decision making, with plans underway for national scaling up. Public engagement was driven by the “Clear Air – Colourful Lives” pollution campaign, which reached 1.7 million people online and activated hundreds of adolescents as evidence based advocates for cleaner air.

A UNICEF footprint is visible in Viet Nam’s NDC 3.0, with technical inputs to ensure that child health, climate resilience and loss and damage considerations are integrated into the country’s climate agenda. Together, these efforts strengthened DRR governance, expanded climate resilient community action, and advanced the role of children and youth as essential stakeholders in Viet Nam’s climate commitments.

Social protection, including poverty reduction

Tangible gains towards robust social protection and improved basic living conditions for children, particularly those impacted by poverty and shocks, were achieved with UNICEF-supported, evidence-based policy dialogues. As a key highlight, in partnership with UNICEF, the Ho Chi Minh National Academy of Politics – the Communist Party training academy think-tank, produced a landmark report ‘50 Years of Progress for Children in Viet Nam: Opportunities and Investments for Future Generations’, with forward-looking recommendations on child rights, including to align the legal definition of a child in line with international standards and to introduce universal child benefits to reduce child poverty. Framed as a resolution for the Party and government to consider, the report proposes legislative and regulatory actions, a financing roadmap, and a monitoring framework. UNICEF also supported advocacy for family-friendly workplace policies, including collaboration with the Viet Nam General Confederation of Labour and private sector partners, and expanded integrated early childhood development parenting programmes.

In collaboration with the National Institute of Nutrition and Ministry of Health, UNICEF designed a Nutrition Cash Plus Initiative in Gia Lai province – a ethnic community-dominated region with high rates of child malnutrition – delivering combined cash and nutrition support to 245 children and pregnant women, with monitoring systems tracking results. Initial endline assessment findings underlined strong improvements—severe stunting fell by 5.5 percentage points, moderate stunting by 3.4 points, children’s dietary diversity improved by 12 per cent, and women’s nutrition knowledge increased by 65 per cent. These results provide a solid evidence base to support the initiative’s scaling-up through the new integrated National Targeted Programme, which will focus on vulnerable communities in rural and remote areas.  

To provide vulnerable families with a safety net during emergencies, multi-purpose cash assistance and integrated services were delivered. Humanitarian cash assistance reached 4,778 households, supporting 25,524 people to meet essential needs related to food, shelter, health, education and livelihoods. High satisfaction rates were reported by beneficiaries, with additional assistance for 1,300 households planned for early 2026, strengthening the continuity of support for vulnerable families.

Adolescent/youth engagement and empowerment 

Adolescent and youth engagement and empowerment was significantly advanced in 2025 with UNICEF fostering meaningful adolescent participation and leadership across multiple platforms. Through the UPSHIFT Programme implemented together with AIESEC – the world’s largest youth-led non-profit organization - UNICEF strengthened entrepreneurship and social innovation skills for more than 100 young women — 40 per cent from disadvantaged backgrounds — while reaching more than half a million youth digitally. The second cohort of the Youth-led Action Initiative equipped 19 new Youth Advocacy Champions to cascade advocacy skills to more than 1,500 adolescents, with expansion planned for 2026, including for youth with disabilities. Youth climate action voices were amplified through strategic engagement with the Youth Climate Action Network, mobilizing more than 1,700 young people during Climate Action Week and supporting youth delegates to represent Viet Nam at COP30 in Brazil. Internally, UNICEF embedded youth perspectives in strategic planning, engaging more than 1,000 young people in developing the next Country Programme and ensuring active youth representation in key consultations and milestone events throughout the year. Youth engagement platforms, such as U-Report, reached nearly 23,000 young people, supported youth-led participation and public dialogues. 
 
Emergency responses

Impactful roles were played in emergency responses to repeated typhoons and floods across Viet Nam in 2025, with UNICEF rapidly scaling-up life-saving assistance and early recovery support thanks to generous contributions of partners. Responding to a government request for assistance, critical multi-sectoral interventions were delivered for affected children and families to restore access to WASH, health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection services, with hard hit north and central region provinces prioritized. Working closely with the Viet Nam Disaster and Dyke Management Authority, under the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, UNICEF significantly contributed to rapid post disaster assessments and the ‘UN Viet Nam Joint Response Plan for Multiple Typhoons and Floods 2025’ and its subsequent addendum, which broadened responses to additional central and southern provinces. As a co-lead of the national coordination mechanisms for WASH, nutrition, education and child protection under the Disaster Risk Reduction Partnership, UNICEF ensured harmonized action across sectors and partners. With a revised funding need of US$15.1 million to deliver its expanded multisectoral plan, UNICEF mobilized significant support from European Commission Humanitarian Aid Office (ECHO), Ireland, Japan, New Zealand, United Kingdom as well as UNICEF National Committees in Germany and Republic of Korea and private sector partners. Since the early onset of the disaster season, UNICEF led preparations, deployed staff, pre-positioned essential supplies, and worked closely with national and subnational partners to deliver life-saving assistance as well as supporting recovery and community resilience, fully aligned with its Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action and government priorities.

Contributing Factors

Partnership, fundraising, communication, and advocacy

UNICEF successfully mobilized and leveraged resources and influence for children through a diverse range of public and private sector partnerships as well as targeted advocacy and communications activities. Shared-value private sector partnerships were expanded through local and global corporate partners – including to measure air pollution, increase access to education, maternal and child health and improve WASH outcomes. New innovative formats and platforms were tested to mobilize and leverage support from major donors and individuals. 

Strategic resource and advocacy partnerships with key public sector partners were solidified – including with Australia, the European Union, Ireland, Japan, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and several UNICEF National Committees – to support programmes in disaster preparedness, child justice, violence against children, climate resilience and the large-scale emergency response to various typhoons and floods in 2025. 

UNICEF convened partners, including UN agencies, development partners, civil society, academia and national authorities on various priority topics for children’s rights, including AI and education, child online safety, protection and environmental protection. To ensure coordination in key sectors, UNICEF co-led and contributed to various development and emergency partners sector groups – WASH, education, nutrition, child protection and health – as well as the Ethnic Minorities Working Group, under the Development Partners Group. As part of the UN Country Team, UNICEF co-chaired the Programme Management Team and one of the results groups. Engagement in multiple joint UN programmes allowed UNICEF to contribute to integrated outcomes in results areas. 

Communication and advocacy efforts focused public attention on key child rights issues. The 50th anniversary of UNICEF in Viet Nam and the 35th anniversary of the country’s ratification of the CRC served as a platform for high-level engagement, reaching millions of people and increasing public recognition of UNICEF’s role. Strategic use of digital platforms and media partnerships expanded reach to 83.4 million people, with increased social media engagement amplifying UNICEF programme messages. UNICEF strengthened collaboration with national and provincial media, particularly Viet Nam Television. High-level partner visits, joint campaigns and coordinated advocacy reinforced shared priorities. Together, these efforts provided resources, support and influence in a financially constrained, complex and fluid environment and helped to sustain momentum for delivery of results for children.

Cross-cutting priorities

Cross-cutting commitments to gender equality, disability inclusion, digital transformation and climate resilience strengthened results across sectors. Gender-responsive approaches expanded girls’ participation in education, nutrition and psychosocial support, while disability-inclusive design improved access to learning, counselling and protection services. Investments in digital systems and responsible AI – encompassing health, education, data and cash platforms – supported more efficient, inclusive and evidence-based delivery. Climate resilience and DRR were integrated across WASH, education, social and child protection and youth engagement, strengthening preparedness and participation in areas most exposed to shocks.

Together, these results demonstrate how UNICEF Viet Nam combined policy influence, systems strengthening and emergency response in 2025 to protect hard-won gains, address persistent inequities and advance national priorities for children in an increasingly complex and shock-prone context.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
What worked well in 2025

UNICEF contributed to several system-level reforms that will strengthen inclusive, child-focused human capital development, including increases in supply and demand for previously declining routine immunizations, the landmark sugar-sweetened beverage excise tax and school meal guidelines, policies to improve rural water services, universal access to ECE and a new child-centred curriculum. Child-friendly interview rooms were scaled-up and school counselling services institutionalized. UNICEF supported child-sensitive DRR legal and policy frameworks and influenced Viet Nam’s NDC 3.0 to reflect children’s needs. 

Strategic alliances were strengthened, including with the National Assembly and the Ho Chi Minh Political Academy, to anchor children’s rights in the new Socio-Economic Development Plan. UNICEF’s 50-year anniversary in Viet Nam coincided with the 35th anniversary of Viet Nam’s ratification of the CRC to create a strategic platform to advance child rights. A series of high-level events with senior government and UNICEF leaders and the Chair and Vice-Chair of the United Nations CRC Committee underscored achievements, gaps and emerging challenges and opportunities which will define UNICEF’s future programming.

UNICEF’s integrated multi-sector emergency response enabled more rapid and equitable support during a prolonged typhoon season. Investments in data, monitoring and knowledge management as well as youth participation and accountability to affected populations, including in emergencies, shifted the focus from activity tracking to more real-time monitoring and feedback-loops to improve programming. Internal humanitarian performance monitoring improved coherence and targeting.

Despite a constrained financial environment, UNICEF strengthened the quality of partnerships and visibility of results. Shared value public and private sector partnerships were expanded, new philanthropic platforms were launched, and high-impact communications sustained strong public engagement to strengthen UNICEF’s position as a trusted partner for children in Viet Nam.

Constraints and areas for acceleration and/or improvement

In 2025, several constraints limited the pace and flexibility of programme delivery. 
-       Unprecedented governance and administrative reforms in 2025 led to delays in programme implementation due to changes and reductions in personnel, ministerial portfolios, administrative boundaries and procedures. 
-       Income generation remained below expectations due to sharp declines in ODA (affecting RR and OR), prolonged negotiations with partners and staffing constraints reduced financial flexibility despite improvements in longer-term partnerships. 
-       Lengthy government procedures and delays in ODA implementation as well as reimbursement of value-added tax slowed programme implementation. 
-       Access to government data remains limited, constraining UNICEF’s programme activities. The need for robust data and evidence, especially on public finance for children, remain key governance issues.
 
How the office managed adaptively and with agility

UNICEF took a series of mitigation actions to ensure timely programme implementation, despite large-scale governance and administrative reforms, including increased coordination and communication with partners, direct implementation and reprogramming. In a constrained and uncertain funding environment, UNICEF applied scenario planning and affordability analyses, enabling timely adjustments during the year and helping position the office for the next Country Programme (2027–2031). Despite the dearth of data, UNICEF advanced its work on public finance for children at subnational level and supported the National Statistics Office to build a Sustainable Development Goals data platform to ensure child-focused data is visible and actionable for decision-makers.

In response to rapidly evolving humanitarian needs, UNICEF pre-positioned essential supplies, focused on implementation through ministries and provinces with existing cooperation agreements and rapidly scaled cash assistance, to build on lessons learned from the Typhoon Yagi response in 2024. Real-time monitoring tools, behavioural insights and nutrition surveillance supported data-driven course corrections when access and service delivery were disrupted, informing adjustments, outreach and targeting. Flexible procurement arrangements, including pre-emergency procurement and use of local long-term agreements, enabled faster and more accountable delivery of critical supplies. Structured internal learning processes, including the Yagi After-Action Review and the Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) conducted in 2025, strengthened attention to equity and outcome-level monitoring, with insights feeding directly into 2026 planning and future programming.

Lessons learned for achieving and accelerating results at scale—especially for the most marginalized

Based on these experiences and CPE recommendations, UNICEF will focus on the following opportunities in 2026 and the next Country Programme (2027–2031):
    
-       Adapt to upper-middle-income transition by focusing on closing equity gaps and emerging challenges (mental health, digital transformation, climate change) in alignment with the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029 and SDGs.
-       Review UNICEF’s sub-national engagement and footprint by focusing on equity, relevance, scalability and entry points to embedding climate resilience, and support local governance at the same time as enhancing model design and sustainable national scaling.
-       Strengthen partnerships, advocacy and communication by building institutional capacity, maximizing synergies and ensuring solid measurement of results.
-       Increased focus on public finance management, leveraging and financing from national budgets, public and private sector partners, and international financial institutions.
-       Enhance gender-transformative, climate-sensitive, and disability-inclusive programming and address harmful social norms through more effective social and behaviour change approaches, including by engaging with children, youth and parents.
-       Nurture and strengthen UN system coherence and efficiency, with UNICEF’s engagement in leading and contributing to joint initiatives and programmes with a focus on child rights, in particular shaping UN engagement in human capital development, national digital transformation, governance reform, DRR and climate change adaptation, amongst others.

Critical challenges and gaps requiring innovative approaches

UNICEF Viet Nam’s experiences and lessons learned in 2025 highlighted the importance of adaptive, innovative and risk-informed programmes to deliver results for children, in particular in a context of rapid socio-economic development, large-scale government reform, accelerated climate risks and new threats to child rights. These programmatic shifts are necessary for UNICEF to stay relevant and achieve results at scale in a rapidly changing country context, respond effectively to new challenges (AI, an ageing society and limited civic space) and build inclusive, shock-responsive and climate-resilient systems, ensure stronger use of data and technology and benefit from diverse shared-value partnerships. These lessons learned are shaping programme adjustments in 2026 and informing the next Country Programme (2027–2031).

Shrinking ODA and complex administrative procedures in Viet Nam continue to constrain the pace and scale of delivery, pointing to the need for new approaches to domestic resource mobilization, blended financing and public-private partnerships at scale. Persisting inequities require a sharper focus on rural and remote regions, but also on marginalized urban areas. Persistent access and inclusion gaps highlight the importance of co-designing solutions with marginalized communities, including children themselves. Stronger use of real-time data and innovative models are needed to extend specialist support to frontline providers. Climate-related disruptions and large-scale disasters have become the ‘new normal’ and will require accelerated investments in preparedness and response, climate mitigation and adaption to ensure continuity of services and community resilience. Emerging risks and opportunities linked to digital transformation and mental health require closer cross-sectoral collaboration with the technology sector, alongside stronger safeguards, clearer accountability and expanded prevention and response systems, as well as meaningful children’s and youth participation.

Forward-looking

Looking ahead, UNICEF Viet Nam will focus on programme strategy adjustments in 2026 that will set the scene and support transition to the next Country Programme (2027–2031) and help address persistent inequities, institutionalize climate-resilient and shock-responsive systems as well as strengthen governance and public finance for children. A strong focus on cross-sectoral cooperation will provide integrated response and accelerators such as digital transformation will ensure relevance in line with the country’s ambitions. Effective shared-value partnerships, evidence-based advocacy and adaptive communications are needed to secure resources and influence. Expanded child participation and parenting support as well as effective social and behaviour change will also be a key priority. New collaboration opportunities with government, private sector, academia, technology partners and community organizations, as well as with development partners and International Financial Institutions, will be necessary to achieve impact at scale.

In 2025, Albania advanced its European Union (EU) accession process by opening all six negotiation clusters: (1) Fundamentals (rule of law, judiciary, public administration, economic criteria); (2) Internal Market; (3) Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth; (4) Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity; (5) Resources, Agriculture and Cohesion; and (6) External Relations. UNICEF engaged primarily in Cluster 1—focusing on rule of law, governance, and fundamental rights—and Cluster 3, with emphasis on education, skills, social protection, and human capital development. As a result, child rights, social inclusion, and equitable access to quality services became more visible in EU-related policy dialogue. While economic growth and institutional reform remained core priorities, advocacy by national institutions and partners, including UNICEF, reinforced recognition of human capital investment as essential for sustainable development and EU readiness.

Albania ranked 45th out of 167 countries in the 2025 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Index, reflecting steady improvements since 2015, particularly in governance and institutional reform. Addressing child poverty and inequality remained a central concern, underscoring the need for integrated approaches across health, education, social protection, and child protection systems.

Parliamentary elections were held on 11 May 2025. While institutional continuity was maintained, political polarization at times slowed key appointments and delayed reforms in oversight and accountability institutions. This underscored the need for sustained, non-partisan engagement to protect and advance children’s rights beyond electoral cycles.
Albania scored 42 out of 100 on Transparency International’s 2024 Corruption Perceptions Index, up from 37 in 2023, reflecting recent progress in anti-corruption enforcement. However, Albania continued to rank 80th out of 180 countries, indicating that corruption remains a significant structural challenge. 

Macroeconomic conditions remained favorable in 2025, with Albania among the faster-growing economies in Europe, supported by tourism, energy, and construction. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth reached approximately 3.5 per cent, inflation remained below 3 per cent, and public debt continued its downward trajectory, contributing to improved labour market outcomes and declining poverty. However, convergence with European Union standards remained uneven. GDP per capita continued to lag EU averages, while persistent disparities in income, employment, and access to quality services—particularly for children in rural areas, larger households, and marginalized communities—risked undermining human capital development and inclusive growth. In this context, the 2025 International Conference on the European Child Guarantee, hosted in Tirana and organized by UNICEF, reinforced national efforts to advance EU-aligned, integrated, and cross-sectoral policies to reduce child poverty and strengthen social inclusion.

As an elected member of the Human Rights Council for 2024–2026, Albania continued to uphold its international human rights obligations, taking concrete steps to improve juvenile justice, protect children with disabilities, promote gender equality, and enhance youth participation. Key legislative reforms were adopted to strengthen the rights of children and young people, consolidating the legal framework in areas including alternative family care, youth participation and volunteerism, and gender equality. The Law on Alternative Family Care advances Albania’s transition from institutional to family- and community-based care, strengthening child protection outcomes while aligning national practice with the 2023 Convention on the Rights of the Child concluding observations and key EU child-rights and social inclusion benchmarks. The revised Youth Law strengthens young people’s role in society by expanding opportunities for education, skills development, employment, and meaningful participation in decision-making, contributing to human capital development and inclusive governance. Complementing this, the legal framework on volunteerism promotes safe, structured civic engagement, particularly for adolescents and youth, fostering active citizenship and social cohesion. The new Gender Equality Law introduces innovative measures to advance gender equity, including strengthened anti-discrimination protections, mandatory gender quotas in public institutions, and formal recognition of unpaid care work as a key component of economic and social policy.  

The National Statistics Institute’s thematic analysis of the 2023 Population and Housing Census data confirms an accelerated population decline driven by emigration and low fertility, alongside widening territorial disparities affecting access to essential services. Emigration increasingly involves skilled and well-educated professionals, placing additional strain on human capital formation and service delivery, particularly in smaller municipalities. 

According to the EU Progress Report for Albania 2025, challenges in the education sector remained pronounced. Despite improvements in educational attainment, learning outcomes and digital competencies continued to lag EU benchmarks. Structural constraints, including low public expenditure, teacher shortages in remote areas, and uneven access to quality services, contributed to persistent inequities. Youth unemployment and high rates of young people not in employment, education, or training remained a concern (Labour Force Survey, 2024), particularly for girls and young women facing barriers related to unpaid care responsibilities and informal employment. These dynamics placed increased emphasis on strengthening pathways from education to employment, skills development, and mental health and psychosocial support for adolescents and youth.

Institutional capacity to protect children and young people remained limited, while violence against children, including online bullying, continued to pose significant protection concerns (EU Progress Report for Albania, 2025). Sustained public attention to school-based and online violence increased pressure to ensure safer learning environments and strengthen prevention-focused responses. Progress was made in developing the National Action Plan for the Prevention of Violence and Safer Schools; however, consistent implementation, enforcement, and effective intersectoral coordination remained critical challenges, requiring sustained political commitment and strengthened institutional capacity.

Albania made progress in managing migration and protecting people on the move through a more structured and protective migration system. However, further support and attention are needed for unaccompanied and separated children.

Despite relatively low greenhouse gas emissions, Albania remained highly vulnerable to climate change, facing increasing risks from floods, wildfires, and extreme weather events. The Government finalized the Second National Adaptation Plan (2026–2036), strengthening commitments to climate resilience, while the impacts of climate change and environmental degradation on children’s health, education, and protection gained prominence in national policy debates aligned with EU and global agendas.

In the final year of the country programme, UNICEF will reinforce resilient systems that protect every child’s rights, safety, and well-being, spanning prevention, response, and emergency preparedness, while generating evidence and lessons to inform the 2027–2031 programme cycle.

Every child survives and thrives 

Building Albania’s human capital begins with early investments in health, nutrition, responsive caregiving, and supportive parenting. The Universal Progressive Home Visiting (UPHV) Programme, implemented by the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare with UNICEF support, continued to play a critical role in ensuring children have the strongest possible start in life. In 2025, primary health care teams conducted 18,158 home visits, reaching 5,482 children under five, including 2,746 girls—across seven out of 12 regions. These visits enabled the early identification of 597 children at risk, who were promptly connected to support services, preventing potential development, health, or protection challenges later in life.
 
To strengthen national ownership and ensure long-term sustainability, Albania’s national institutions, in close partnership with UNICEF, jointly conducted a maturity assessment of the UPHV model. The collaborative assessment produced actionable recommendations, including the development of a national UPHV policy and regulatory framework, dedicated financing to ensure service continuity, and reinforced governance through cross-sectoral coordination. These measures position Albania to scale the programme nationwide and fully integrate it into the core structure of the primary health and social welfare system.
 
Capacity development remained central to improving service quality for young children. Health professionals across seven regions received training in newborn care, monitoring growth and development of children under five, supporting parenting skills, and early identification and referral of postpartum depression. These competencies are essential for improving caregiver behaviors, reducing preventable newborn complications, and supporting early childhood development—critical foundations for future learning and productivity.
 
UNICEF undertook a nationwide campaign, “Vaccinate with Trust,” airing 160 spots across major media outlets, to strengthen public confidence in vaccination. In close collaboration with WHO, in one district of Albania, UNICEF facilitated dialogue on immunization progress and challenges, identifying concrete intersectoral actions to boost childhood vaccination. These efforts led to the development of a local intersectoral action plan designed to increase coverage and strengthen community engagement, providing a model for other districts to develop similar plans and accelerate national immunization efforts.
 
The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the Neonatology Service, with UNICEF support, advanced neonatal care through the development of national protocols, capacity building for health professionals, strengthened connections with primary health care to ensure proper follow-up for at-risk newborns, and provision of essential hospital equipment. In addition, UNICEF supported eight maternity units with neonatal equipment provided by the Credins Foundation, including ten incubators, two mobile ventilators, and one continuous positive airway pressure machine. This upgrade, combined with revised national protocols and training for health professionals from all maternity hospitals in the country on national neonatal care standards, is contributing to the reduction of preventable newborn illnesses and deaths, laying the foundation for a healthier and more resilient future workforce.
 
Support for parents and caregivers was expanded through the Bebbo parenting app, which reached 28,113 new users and engaged 7,478 returning users in 2025. The app provides caregivers with practical, evidence-based tools to promote children’s cognitive, emotional, and physical development from birth through school age, further strengthening the family environment.
 
Early detection and intervention for developmental challenges were strengthened through a new training framework on identifying autism spectrum disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and other developmental delays. This initiative enhanced the skills of more than a hundred health professionals across the entire country. Developed by the National Center for Child Development with UNICEF support and accredited by the National Agency for Quality Assurance in Health Institutions, the program helps ensure that children with developmental differences are identified earlier and connected to appropriate support, reducing long-term learning barriers and improving their potential to thrive.
 
Every child learns 

In 2025, Albania made strong progress in early childhood and education, reaching thousands of children and youth with improved learning opportunities, inclusive education, and digital skills, while advancing youth employability. Key results include expanded Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) coverage, the adoption of a new pre-university curriculum, strengthened inclusive education systems, innovative digital learning initiatives, and the implementation of the Youth Guarantee for thousands of NEET youth.
 
Investments in ECEC for children aged 0–3 focused on improving quality through alignment with national standards, updated curricula, workforce development, enhanced parenting and home-based support, and robust quality assurance mechanisms in line with the EU ECEC Quality Framework.
 
To protect developmental gains during crises, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education in developing a national model for ECEC in Emergencies, ensuring system preparedness and continuity of essential ECD services. Building on successful implementation of the Reggio Emilia approach in five municipalities, UNICEF also helped scale effective ECD practices through public–private partnerships, including collaboration with Comodita Home.
 
Strengthening fiscal and strategic planning, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education in producing an ECEC Costing Study for the ECEC Roadmap for ages 0–6. The study provides a foundation for achieving 25% national coverage for children 0–3 while establishing sustainable, European-standard service delivery systems. High-level policy dialogues with the World Bank and the French Development Agency reinforced shared commitments to quality, equity, and sustainable financing of early childhood services.
 
UNICEF also supported the Mid-Term Review of the National Education Strategy 2021–2026, updating objectives to address emerging priorities such as artificial intelligence, enhanced institutional coordination, and strengthened accountability. The review highlighted weaknesses in financial planning and reporting, emphasizing the need for improved expenditure management to maximize education investments.

As part of broader youth employability reforms, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation, the Ministry of Education, and UNDP to conduct a permeability study under the Youth Guarantee. This analysis supports smoother transitions between general education and vocational education and training (VET), enabling learners to pursue pathways aligned with labor market needs.
 
A major system milestone was the 2025 approval of a new curriculum framework for the entire pre-university system, together with detailed curriculum programs for three grades. Supported by UNICEF, this reform involved extensive technical expertise and consultation, resulting in a more inclusive, competency-based, and future-focused curriculum aligned with EU frameworks and global standards. The Ministry of Education also institutionalized Career Orientation Coordinators, establishing a national structure to enhance student career planning and strengthen linkages between general education and VET.
 
To advance inclusive education, UNICEF helped the Ministry of Education develop a National Comprehensive Compendium guiding the transformation of special schools into resource centers. The compendium clarifies governance, standards, legal frameworks, and staff roles, supporting a coherent systemwide approach for children with diverse learning needs. Training reached teachers, school directors, and support staff in eight (all) special schools and assistant teachers in mainstream schools, improving school-level capacity to support inclusion.
 
UNICEF contributed to creating safe learning environments by supporting the National Action Plan for the Prevention of Violence and Safer Schools. In collaboration with the Agency for Quality Assurance in Pre-University Education, UNICEF helped develop two foundational resources: Principles of Professional Ethics for School Psychosocial Services and Security Officers, and Standardized Protocols and Procedures for School Safety for Psychosocial Staff. These tools strengthen prevention and response to violence, including cyberviolence, and promote ethical and safe digital behavior—conditions essential for student well-being, retention, and learning.
 
Efforts to prevent school dropouts and early school leaving intensified in 2025. The After School Programme, designed, costed and piloted by the Ministry of Education with UNICEF support, reached 600 students with structured learning, socio-emotional support, sports, arts, and language activities. For the first time in public schools, the programme introduced a meal component, reducing barriers for vulnerable children and supporting working parents. UNICEF also advocated scholarships for youth at risk of leaving school, strengthening protective measures under the Youth Guarantee.
 
The Early Warning System and Social Emotional Learning initiatives were integrated into the VET system, reaching students and teachers across 12 schools. These measures improve the system’s ability to identify at-risk learners early and provide timely support that enhances retention, learning, and employment transitions.
 
The Digital Education Action Plan, advanced by the Ministry of Education with UNICEF’s support, bridged policy reforms with classroom innovation. UNICEF provided technical inputs on data protection, alignment with the EU Digital Education Action Plan, emerging EU guidance on artificial intelligence, and the evolving role of teachers in AI-enabled learning.
 
Innovation in education was demonstrated through the launch of the GIGA Initiative to monitor school connectivity nationwide. Partnering with International Telecommunication Union and the Ministry of Education, UNICEF helped identify connectivity gaps and inform policy decisions and investments to advance equitable access to digital learning. By the end of 2025, 697 schools were mapped, with full mapping of public schools planned for 2026.
 
To boost youth innovation and future skills, UNICEF supported the AI Hustle Hub, which delivered an AI literacy course developed with Harvard University lecturers, organized three national bootcamps on social impact, equipped young people with skills to design AI-based solutions, and reached 2,000 youth through supported youth-led innovations. These initiatives directly enhance digital, entrepreneurial, and socio-emotional skills that today’s economy demands.
 
In 2025, the Government advanced Albania’s youth-focused human capital agenda through strong commitment to the Youth Guarantee. UNICEF helped leverage the framework to ensure coordinated action across the system, integrating measures to address multiple barriers to education participation. An inclusive consultation process resulted in an evidence-based National Youth Guarantee Action Plan (2026–2028), and 2,207 NEET youth in Tirana, Shkodra, and Vlora entered the employment scheme. 
 
UNICEF also supported revisions to the Law on Youth and Law on Volunteerism, strengthening frameworks to expand opportunities, recognize volunteerism, and improving youth participation. Through U Report, 3,723 young people contributed to national dialogues on mental health, social inclusion, and career pathways.
 
Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation

In 2025, UNICEF strengthened Albania’s child protection system, supporting reforms and services that ensure children grow up safe, nurtured, and able to reach their full potential.
Through regional peer learning, UNICEF enhanced Albania’s child protection capacity by facilitating access to international best practices on diversion, violence prevention, and cross-border protection of unaccompanied and separated children (UASC). At the local level, a needs assessment across 14 municipalities identified critical gaps in specialized services, informing the establishment of new services, including Albania’s first trauma-informed care center, which provided direct support to children and built professional capacity in trauma-informed approaches.
 
To promote justice for children, UNICEF supported the Juvenile Criminality Prevention Centre in delivering educational sessions for adolescents, empowering them with knowledge of their rights and the justice process. By strengthening legal literacy and participation, these initiatives reduce vulnerability to harm and foster positive youth development.
 
UNICEF played a catalytic role in advancing Albania’s deinstitutionalization reform, led by the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the State Social Service, by reinforcing legal, policy, and service delivery frameworks for family-based care. The adoption of the Law on Family-Based Alternative Care marked a major milestone, establishing a clear framework for transitioning children from institutional settings to safe, nurturing family environments. UNICEF also supported the development of the National Plan for the Transformation of Residential Child Care, guiding government action toward sustainable alternatives. Local pilot initiatives demonstrated models of strengthened family-based services that enhance children’s developmental outcomes and provide evidence for scale-up.
 
To safeguard UASC, UNICEF provided technical support to the State Agency on Child Rights and Protection to revise national procedures on return, referral, and protection, addressing gaps in guardianship, temporary care, coordination, and durable solutions. UNICEF also contributed to a review of guardianship models to strengthen legal representation and ensure responsive care for children without parental support.
 
At the municipal level, UNICEF—working with IOM and UNHCR—focused on improving local protection responses for UASC. Targeted trainings helped authorities clarify roles, enhance cross-sector coordination, and strengthen capacity to identify and refer children on the move. These measures ensure that children at risk are quickly connected to protection services, safeguarding their safety, well-being, and developmental trajectories.

Every child lives in a safe and clean environment 

In 2025, UNICEF supported Albania in strengthening children’s resilience to climate and environmental risks. Through the UNICEF–Swedish Environmental Protection Agency partnership under the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans, UNICEF contributed to the country’s first Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and supported the Child Environmental Health Assessment, the latter led by the Institute of Public Health, enhancing evidence on exposure to pollution, lead, and other environmental hazards. Frontline capacity was expanded with 149 home visitors trained to identify and mitigate household environmental risks. Over 500 young people led air quality initiatives, reaching 5,500 peers, while climate education and green skills were integrated into national curriculum reforms, equipping students with the knowledge and competencies needed for a sustainable and environmentally resilient future.
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life 

In 2025, UNICEF supported major system-strengthening reforms that contributed to Albania’s advancement on EU accession priorities, notably under Chapters 19 on Social Policy and Employment and 23 on Fundamental Rights.
 
Albania strengthened its leadership on the EU Child Guarantee through high-level advocacy, international knowledge exchange, and peer learning, positioning the country as a regional frontrunner among EU accession states and the first to make rapid progress toward drafting a National Child Guarantee Plan of Action.
 
UNICEF Albania played a pivotal role in strengthening national accountability for children by providing technical support to publication of the Monitoring Report of the National Agenda for Children’s Rights 2021–2026. UNICEF’s support focused on strengthening the monitoring methodology, enhancing the quality and coherence of cross-sectoral reporting, integrating child-focused indicators and budget analysis, and ensuring that children’s perspectives were systematically captured through structured consultations.
 
UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to complete the functional review of the State Social Services; a similar exercise advanced for the State Agency for Child Rights and Protection. These reforms strengthen governance, clarify institutional mandates, and improve the human and technical capacities required for EU accession. Complementing this, UNICEF partnered with the University of Tirana to update social work curricula, ensuring the next generation of professionals is equipped with modern, competency-based skills to support vulnerable children and families.
 
UNICEF strengthened Albania’s social sector to better protect children in times of crisis. Frontline professionals across multiple municipalities were trained in shock-responsive social protection, enhancing local systems’ capacity to mitigate the impact of shocks on children’s well-being. Additional targeted online mentoring reinforced accountable, adaptive, and sustainable municipal social care services that safeguard children today and build resilience for the future.
 
To bring services closer to communities, UNICEF supported the establishment of Needs Assessment and Referral Units across several municipalities, now serving as the first point of contact for children and families in need. To enhance case management and coordination, staff were trained on the National Electronic Registry of Social Services, enabling more effective identification, tracking, and referral of cases—strengthening the responsiveness and quality of protection and social services at the local level.
 
Building on a formal United Nations–World Bank partnership, with UNICEF in a leadership role under the M-GA joint initiative, Albania advanced reforms to strengthen the inclusiveness of its social protection system for children with disabilities. With UNICEF’s technical assistance, the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare launched the national biopsychosocial assessment, introducing a holistic and rights-based approach to determining children’s needs. Around 280 professionals participated in regional forums on child-friendly assessment methods. These efforts contributed to new child-friendly guidance for assessing children with disabilities, aligned with training for Multidisciplinary Commissions, ensuring children receive fair, comprehensive assessments and improved access to appropriate support.
 
Progress under the SDG Accelerator Programme (LEAP) also deepened. A high-level partners’ meeting engaged national stakeholders, generating stronger political and financial commitment to scaling reforms, including advancing the universal child benefit, expanding the Universal Home Visiting Programme, and enhancing coordinated services for vulnerable families. These efforts directly strengthen children’s wellbeing, reduce long-term vulnerability, and build the foundations of Albania’s future human capital.
 
In 2025, UNICEF wrapped up support to at-risk Afghan families by ensuring children’s continued learning, health, and protection. Early learning and non-formal education reached over 250 children, while 820 children and adolescents accessed essential health and nutrition services and 918 received hygiene items to prevent infectious disease. UNICEF also provided mental health and psychosocial support to 4,200 Afghans, including 2,310 children, and supported 980 women and girls with protection and GBV services. Frontline workers were trained on PSEA, ensuring a safer, more protective humanitarian response for all children.
 
UNICEF strengthened Albania’s evidence systems by supporting INSTAT to publish the Census 2023 Thematic Report on Children and Youth, transforming census findings into the country’s most comprehensive, disaggregated data source on the young population. UNICEF also provided technical assistance for preparations for the 2026 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), led by INSTAT in collaboration with relevant ministries. Support included adapting survey tools to the national context, selecting priority indicators, testing questionnaires, completing household listings, and preparing digital data collection systems. These efforts ensure Albania has high-quality, actionable data to inform and strengthen monitoring frameworks for the Child and Youth Guarantee.
 
In 2025, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to initiate the establishment of Local Social Funds in several municipalities, developing step-by-step guidelines and facilitating consultations to strengthen local financing for child and family-focused services. Gjirokastër became the first municipality to operationalize its Social Fund, with the remaining municipalities set to follow in 2026.
 
To reinforce evidence-based and equitable financing for children, UNICEF and the Ministry of Finance and Economy initiated Albania’s first child-focused public expenditure analysis, assessing how national budgets align with children’s rights and SDG commitments. This work positions Albania as a regional leader in child-responsive public finance and will continue in 2026 with an updated child tagging exercise to further advocate for increased and better-targeted public investments in children—critical for strengthening the country’s long-term human capital.
 
UNICEF convened private sector and key partners to advocate reforms to the sponsorship law, prompting the State Minister for Anti-Corruption and Public Administration to advance the process, potentially including wide stakeholder consultation for law amendments in 2026. These reforms are expected to mobilize greater private sector resources for the social sector, enabling expanded investment in children’s services, programmes, and well-being across Albania.

According to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index, children born in Albania today are projected to reach only 63 per cent of their potential productivity, below the regional average of 69 per cent. Human capital development has become increasingly central to Albania’s EU accession pathway, where reform readiness is assessed through investments in people, skills, and inclusive systems. In this context, UNICEF has prioritized human capital as a strategic pathway to safeguarding the rights of children and young people, expanding their opportunities, and ensuring their equitable participation in Albania’s social and economic life.
 
Building on its mandate, UNICEF co-leads the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) Outcome on Human Capital Development and has been requested by UN agencies, the European Union, and the World Bank to convene a joint thought process on this agenda. Leveraging its comparative advantage, UNICEF applies a life cycle and equity-focused approach that links child well-being, education, social protection, and youth transitions with long-term economic and demographic outcomes. In its role as convener, evidence broker, and neutral facilitator, UNICEF has brought together government institutions, EU partners, the World Bank, UN agencies, academia, civil society, and the private sector to align sectoral policies and mobilize collective action around shared human capital development objectives.

With UNICEF playing a leading role, a key milestone in this process was the development of a joint Strategic Paper on Human Capital Development, in collaboration with the European Union, the World Bank, and UN entities. The paper establishes a shared definition and framework for building, protecting, and utilizing human capital across the life course, spanning early childhood development, inclusive education, youth employability, the care economy, and active ageing. It provides a common reference point for aligning policy interventions and investments with long-term social and economic objectives.
 
Building on this analytical foundation, UNICEF, on behalf of the UN in Albania, the World Bank, and the EU, convened the high-level national conference “Academia as the Catalyst for Human Capital Development” with the College of Europe – Tirana Campus. Leading the event, UNICEF created a platform for evidence-based dialogue on human capital development. The conference showcased European social inclusion models, including the Child Guarantee and Youth Guarantee, highlighting opportunities to adapt and pilot these tools within Albania’s systems in line with fiscal realities and EU accession benchmarks. It also strengthened partnerships with academic and think-tank institutions, leveraging their expertise to inform child-focused, human capital–centered policies and strategies.
 
Through its convening and advocacy role, UNICEF has elevated the European Child Guarantee as a strategic tool to address intergenerational poverty and unequal access to essential services. By linking early childhood development, inclusive education, health, nutrition, and social protection, the Guarantee offers a coordinated, child-focused framework that prioritizes the most vulnerable children. Similarly, discussions on the Youth Guarantee underscored its critical role in supporting school-to-work transitions, preventing long-term youth exclusion, and improving employability through timely access to education, training, apprenticeships, or employment—particularly for young people not in education, employment, or training (NEETs). These exchanges further strengthened the policy case for piloting and scaling inclusive, EU-aligned approaches within Albania’s broader human capital reform agenda, while keeping child rights and equity principles at the core of UNICEF’s mandate.
 
UNICEF strategically expanded and activated its Business Advisory Board to position the private sector as a partner in protecting and promoting children’s rights and well-being. Through joint advocacy, public awareness campaigns, service delivery, and targeted investments in health, early childhood education, and child protection, UNICEF mobilized business leadership to support children across the life course. This initiative opened new avenues for sustainable collaboration and strengthened alignment between private sector engagement and national priorities for child development.
 
The reconstitution of the Friends of Children parliamentary caucus following the elections represents another significant achievement. The caucus ensures that children’s rights remain a high-level legislative priority and strengthens the link between evidence-based advocacy and political action. Through parliamentary engagement, UNICEF has helped integrate child-focused approaches into broader legislative and policy frameworks, reinforcing the role of governance in promoting equitable outcomes for all children.

Through its convening power, UNICEF has shown how evidence, policy expertise, and inclusive dialogue can turn human capital discourse into actionable reform. Key elements of UNICEF’s added value include:
• Translating global and European frameworks—the Human Capital Index, life-course approach, Child Guarantee, and Youth Guarantee—into actionable national policy dialogue led by the government.
• Bridging research, EU policy instruments, and reform implementation to ensure decisions are grounded in evidence and best practices.
• Anchoring human capital investments in child and youth outcomes, reinforcing their central role in economic resilience, social cohesion, and demographic sustainability.

The Albanian experience demonstrates that strategic convening, grounded in evidence and proven policy models, enables governments to implement reforms that are coherent, equitable, and sustainable. UNICEF’s leadership has strengthened national ownership of human capital strategies while ensuring alignment with child rights and equity principles.
 
By integrating EU social inclusion frameworks into national reform pathways, UNICEF has enhanced policy coherence and maintained a long-term focus on outcomes for children and young people. The approach leverages domestic financing commitments, such as scaling up the Youth Guarantee, to sustain and expand reforms. UNICEF’s ongoing engagement will focus on consolidating these gains, supporting government-led dialogue, piloting and scaling solutions, and guiding investments in resilient systems that safeguard every child’s rights, safety, and well-being.
 
UNICEF will continue supporting the Government of Albania and partners in high-level policy dialogue, and in modelling and scaling up solutions such as the European Child Guarantee and Youth Guarantee, to strengthen resilient systems that safeguard every child’s rights, safety, and well-being. This work will guide the final year of the UNICEF Country Programme of Cooperation and lay a strategic foundation for the next programme cycle (2027–2031) and the UNSDCF, ensuring that child-focused investments are sustainable, coordinated, and aligned with Albania’s EU accession benchmarks and international obligations, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the SDGs.

In 2025, Armenia navigated a complex transition from emergency humanitarian response to long-term integration, set against a backdrop of shifting geopolitical dynamics. While the security situation stabilized relative to previous years, the environment remained fragile. A defining development of the year was the advancement of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a US-backed connectivity framework intended to reshape regional transit, signed by parties in the second half of the year.[1] While the peace process with Azerbaijan continued with intermittent negotiations, the peace treaty  has not been finalized and signed by year-end.[2] Within this context, Government priorities increasingly shifted from emergency humanitarian response to the long-term integration of the displaced population and systemic social reforms.
The efforts towards integration of refugees were anchored in the Framework for the Stabilization of the Livelihoods of Refugees and Host Communities, developed under Government leadership with support from UN agencies.[3] It serves both as a strategic policy framework for livelihoods and economic opportunities for refugees and as a mechanism for ensuring a coordinated, cross-sectoral approach to their integration. During the year, measures were implemented or extended to support housing access, income security, and economic inclusion for refugee households. These included partial compensation of rental housing costs for eligible families, the extension of cash support and emergency social assistance programmes until December 2026, and the introduction of self-employment support combining training, mentoring, and start-up grants.[4]
Armenia’s economy continued to expand in 2025, with real GDP growth estimated at around 5.2 per cent, reflecting normalization following exceptionally high growth rates observed in earlier years. Growth was driven mainly by private consumption and solid performance in construction, information technology, and financial services.[5][6] Economic growth was accompanied by renewed inflationary pressures, particularly affecting the cost of essential goods and services. Consumer price inflation increased compared to the previous year, driven mainly by rising food prices and service tariffs, according to official statistics.[7] These price dynamics disproportionately affected low-income and vulnerable households, which allocate a larger share of their expenditure to basic consumption. 
Economic growth and sustained consumption in recent years have contributed to a continued reduction in income-based poverty in Armenia. According to international poverty measures, the share of the population living below the lowest poverty threshold ($3.0) has declined to very low levels (0.8%), while poverty rates measured against higher international thresholds have also decreased compared to previous years (i.e. for the upper middle-income class poverty line ($8.3) the rate dropped to 47.4% in 2024 compared to 57.0% in 2021). National poverty estimates for 2024 indicate that just over one in five people lived below the national poverty line (21.7%), with extreme poverty remaining very low (0.6%); however, these figures are not directly comparable with earlier years due to methodological updates following the 2022 Census. Child poverty remained higher than the national average, affecting more than one in four children (28%), underscoring that economic gains have not benefited all population groups equally. [8]
A major milestone for children in Armenia was achieved in 2025 with the adoption of a new Child Rights legislative framework, modernizing the country’s child rights and child protection system.[9] The reform strengthened the legal and institutional foundations for protecting children’s rights and enhanced the State’s capacity to meet its obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It clarified institutional mandates, reinforced prevention and early intervention approaches, strengthened coordination across sectors, and enhanced safeguards for children in vulnerable situations. The new framework also provides a stronger basis for addressing priority areas highlighted in the CRC Concluding Observations, including violence prevention, alternative care, child participation, and access to child-friendly services. As such, it represents an important enabling condition for sustained, system-level improvements affecting children across sectors.
Public expenditure trends in 2025 reflected both progress and remaining structural constraints in financing social sectors relevant to children. Expenditures of the consolidated budget of the Republic of Armenia as a share of GDP remained broadly unchanged for health at around 1.5%, while increasing for education to 2.8%, compared to 2.4% in the previous year, and for social security to 8.4%, compared to 7.5% previously. These shifts indicate a gradual re-prioritization toward social sectors within the budget. At the same time, spending levels for health and education remained below regional averages, underscoring continued challenges in ensuring adequate, efficient, and equitable financing for services essential to children’s rights and well-being. Strengthening public finance for children, including through improved targeting, execution, and efficiency of spending, remained a key policy priority.[10]
In the health sector, a significant policy development occurred in December 2025 with the adoption of the Law on Universal Health Insurance, enabling its introduction from January 2026. The law provides for a phased rollout, with the first phase prioritizing children under 18, mothers of children under two, persons with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups, with insurance packages fully subsidized by the state.[11] The reform addresses a critical inequity in Armenia’s healthcare system, which has historically been dominated by high Out-of-Pocket (OOP) expenditure. In 2021, OOP payments accounted for 78.7% of health spending—significantly higher than the WHO European Region average of 26.6%.[12]
Education coverage in Armenia remained high in 2025, with near-universal participation in compulsory schooling. Under the Government’s “300 schools, 500 kindergartens” programme, more than 100 schools and around 280 kindergartens and preschool facilities had been completed by the end of the year. Public financing for the operation and maintenance of schools increased. Teacher workforce reforms advanced, with around 31% of teachers having completed voluntary certification by the end of 2025. More than 4,000 new teachers entered the school system during 2024–2025, with the majority under the age of 45. Armenia conducted the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) for the first time in 2025, following accession to the programme in 2023, with the results expected in 2026. Early childhood education increased in 2025, rising to 39.1% nationally, compared to 36.2% in the previous year, but overall participation remained limited. The urban–rural enrolment divide continued, with enrolment levels almost twice as high in urban areas (48.3%) as in rural areas (27.3%), despite some improvement.[13] During the year, the Government piloted nursery services for children under two years of age and continued the establishment of early childhood age groups within the preschool system. Inclusion improved, with more than 1,700 children with special education needs enrolled in kindergartens nationwide, with full state financing.. [14]
In 2025, the Government advanced key reforms in the social protection sector aimed at ensuring continuity of support for families with children and strengthening the effectiveness of benefit delivery. These reforms confirmed the continuation of monthly support for families with a third and each subsequent child born on or after 1 January 2026, covering children up to six years of age, and harmonized the amount of the lump-sum birth allowance. The changes also established the legal basis for the transition to non-cash payment of pensions and regular social benefits. In parallel, Armenia piloted a new family vulnerability assessment system in Syunik and Kotayk regions from March 2025, marking a shift from a proxy means test toward a hybrid assessment model. Under the new system, families assessed as extremely vulnerable are entitled to a guaranteed minimum income linked to the cost of a food basket and have access to services and activation programmes, with the pilot informing plans for nationwide rollout from July 2026.[15][16]
In 2025, Armenia continued efforts to reduce reliance on institutional care and expand family-based alternatives for children without parental care. According to data presented by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, approximately 500 children were living in residential care institutions during the year, almost half of them in private residential institutions. This figure does not include children placed in special schools or adults over 18 residing in residential care facilities.  In parallel, progress continued in the development of alternative care, with 201 children placed in foster care across more than 100 foster families in 2025, reflecting sustained efforts to expand family-based care options.[17] Around 460 children were enrolled in special schools as of the beginning of 2026.[18] Traditionally, a significant proportion of children placed in institutions in Armenia have been children with disabilities; however, disaggregated data are not available for the children referred to in this report. The reform process aimed at transforming special schools into resource centres to support inclusive education continued during the year; however, implementation progressed more gradually than initially anticipated, highlighting the need for sustained efforts to complete the transition.
Armenia also advanced several other policy developments relevant to children and adolescents. In 2025, the country adopted its first Youth Policy Law, which defines youth as persons aged 13–35 and therefore explicitly includes adolescents. The law establishes a formal framework for youth participation and youth-focused policy development and strengthens legal guarantees related to participation, including the right of adolescents to be heard in matters affecting them. Government also approved a new Gender Equality Strategy and Action Plan, reinforcing commitments to gender equality, non-discrimination, and the prevention of gender-based violence, with implications for the protection and empowerment of girls and adolescents. Legal reforms related to climate and DRR policy were also advanced through adoption of the updated Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement and the Law on Disaster Risk Management and Population Protection, strengthening risk-informed climate action, disaster preparedness and response, and more coordinated, people-centred governance that explicitly considers the rights, needs, and vulnerabilities of children. Notably, recommendations from the Climate Change Youth Advisory Board supported by UNICEF were reflected in the draft climate legislation. As officially communicated, the principles of intergenerational justice and the best interests of the child were incorporated into the draft law, strengthening the child-centred approach to climate policy development and implementation.
