2025 was the last year of the 2021-2025 Armenia-UNICEF Country Programme and of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and a year that saw persisting residual humanitarian needs among the refugee population as well as a sudden and unexpected reduction of overseas development assistance (ODA) to the country together with the withdrawal of international actors that used to play key roles in support of the ongoing reform processes in Armenia. Nevertheless, UNICEF Armenia was able to maximize efficient use of available resources and ensure uninterrupted essential services to children as part of the ongoing emergency response and to maintain a similar level of programme delivery in support of the development agenda as in previous years. Progress towards the outcomes identified in the 2021-2025 Country Programme Document (CPD), the UNSDCF and related Sustainable Development Goals accelerated through key advancements in the ongoing reform processes. In parallel, UNICEF Armenia continued to contribute to national efforts to address the evolving needs of a total of 46,000 ethnic Armenian refugee children and their families displaced between 2020 and 2023, combining humanitarian response strategies and system strengthening approaches.  
As evidenced in the 2025 Country Programme Evaluation, “UNICEF [Armenia] has demonstrated a clear track record of systematically applying programming across the humanitarian-development nexus and generating positive outcomes that reinforce both humanitarian and development goals”. Investments made as part of the development agenda in strengthening shock-responsiveness of national systems prior to the emergency continued to pay off by ensuring results at scale for the emergency response. UNICEF’s constant dialogue with relevant Ministries and Government agencies and its convening role in enabling dialogue with and within civil society actors allowed timely adjustments to response modalities as needs of refugee and host community children evolved. This constructive dialogue also allowed identification of lessons learnt and areas of improvement in operating frameworks for service delivery, which are being considered in the operationalization of recent legislative reforms in relevant sectors.  
Good progress was made towards country programme outcomes since the beginning of the cycle. Enrolment of children under 5 years of age in preschools increased to 39% in the last academic year compared to 32% in 2021-2022, as a result of continued efforts, also supported by UNICEF, to invest in and prioritize early childhood education. Continued partnership and investment in inclusive education led to a fivefold increase in the number of children with special educational needs receiving pedagogical-psychological support services in mainstream schools and preschools.  The number of children in residential institutions nearly halved, despite the existence of contributing factors to placement into residential care, including the 2023 refugee inflow and the socio-economic effects of COVID-19 in earlier years. The number of placements into foster care more than doubled, as a result of continuous partnership with the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MLSA) and other actors to advance alternative care. Child poverty was reduced mainly due to economic growth and the effects of the rollout of universal childcare benefits for all parents until the age of 2 started in 2023 with UNICEF’s support. Despite intensifying anti-vaccination messaging in society, immunization coverage was sustained at over 90% for all antigens, due to continued joint efforts in strengthening immunization services and communication strategies. As a result of expanded education and skills building on climate change, the share of adolescents who feel well-informed about climate mitigation actions doubled.
 
Most of these outcome-level results can be at least partially attributed to UNICEF Armenia’s support, building on its longstanding engagement and reputation as a reliable and knowledgeable partner for national stakeholders. In 2025, UNICEF Armenia continued positioning itself as a partner of choice and effective convener in key social sectors related to children and youth, and actively contributed to advancing the ongoing comprehensive national social reform agenda, a unique opportunity to address key systemic bottlenecks hindering the realization of child rights. Good progress was made in 2025 on several legislative and regulatory frameworks. The first ever Law on Youth Policy was adopted, setting the legal foundations of the state youth policy, which defines measures to strengthen the quality of youth services, prioritizes the professionalization of youth work, regulates the network of youth aggregation points across the country, and enables local youth policies at community level. The legal package including the new Law on Child Rights and Child Protection System and the amendments to the Family Code and other legislative acts was adopted, introducing provisions that transform Armenia’s child rights architecture and child protection system, moving to a more child-centered approach to child rights’ protection in line with the 2024 recommendations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC). It establishes a unified child rights and child protection system grounded in prevention, early identification, and inter-agency accountability; it defines roles and responsibilities of child protection actors   and how the best interests of the child are to be considered in legal and administrative proceedings. It also clarifies what constitutes violence against children and prohibits corporal punishment in all settings. The Law on Disaster Risk Management and Population Protection and the Nationally Determined Contributions 2026–2035 on climate change were adopted, intr
oducing concepts of child rights and intergenerational equity and recognizing children as a climate-vulnerable group. They strengthen child-focused adaptation, preparedness, response and recovery measures, institutionalize youth participation in climate governance, recognize education and skills as investment in climate action and promote shock-responsive social protection for children and families affected by climate shocks. These provisions will be complemented by the Law on Climate, which is awaiting Parliament’s approval in early 2026. Amendments to the Criminal and Criminal Procedure Codes prepared based on lessons learnt from the recently piloted Barnahus model (multi-disciplinary, inter-agency response for child victims and witnesses of violence) await approval in 2026. UNICEF efforts also aimed at ensuring that new provisions introduced through all these reform processes are responsive to gender considerations and to the needs of children with disabilities.
 
Substantial progress was made towards operationalizing policies and legislative provisions and strengthening systems at central and local levels to ensure upgraded, more integrated, and inclusive services for children and families. Following adoption of the new Law on Social Assistance in 2024, UNICEF continued supporting MLSA in the development of secondary legislation pieces, with 12 out of 50  approved, primarily relating to the vulnerability assessment system, community social projects, case management guidelines and home visiting, rapid needs assessment, social assistance management information system and care provision. The new vulnerability assessment system is being piloted in two regions and links cash benefits to services and activation programmes. In line with the provisions of the recently adopted legislative package on the child protection system, UNICEF continued its technical support on the deinstitutionalization reform and a total of three residential institutions of different types were either closed or transformed into resource centers. In parallel, efforts to strengthen the foster care system in line with international best practices continued, including an awareness raising campaign and a training programme that led to an expansion of the pool of trained foster families, including for emergency foster care.  In partnership with MLSA, new services aligned with the disability assessment model were introduced, including personal assistance solutions, voucher-based services, and tailored service packages for children with disabilities and their families. Accessibility of assistive technologies (AT) was expanded with the inclusion of Eye-Gaze systems and augmentative and alternative communication in MLSA’s approved AT list, following a UNICEF-supported pilot.  Recognizing teachers and school managers as the linchpin of the ongoing education reform, UNICEF contributed to modernizing the professional development system, with new learning modules across 
11 domains developed for teacher proficiency testing as part of the state certification programme. In parallel, policy recommendations for amendments to the appointment process for principals were approved by the Government. In the framework of the ongoing primary health care (PHC) and universal health insurance (UHI) reforms, UNICEF adapted and tested the WHO PHC Pocketbook for children and adolescents, which will be introduced in the PHC system as mandatory standards within the UHI.  Through the collaboration between UNICEF and the Ministry of Health (MOH)’s technical expert group on child nutrition, new protocols on parental counselling on child nutrition, including on breast-feeding and complementary feeding, in maternities and PHC facilities were developed.  Following the adoption of the Law on Youth Policy, UNICEF supported professionalization of the youth work sector, through a comprehensive needs assessment and the development of job descriptions for youth workers, as well as operational frameworks for youth environments. UNICEF also contributed to expanding and strengthening the network of youth aggregation points across the country, by demonstrating minimum quality standards in one new pilot facility in the form of co-creation lab. In partnership with the Ministry of High-Tech Industry (MoHTI), UNICEF developed a Roadmap on Child Online Safety, which was informed by the findings of the Disrupting Harm Study for Armenia and sets the foundations for systemic work in this field. UNICEF supported the launch of CyberChat, a new service for children and caregivers that provides support on cyberbullying, online exploitation and abuse and other threats. 
UNICEF continued to engage in evidence-based policy dialogue on public finance for children linked to the mentioned reform processes, proposing solutions on key investments and efficiency gains in public spending. Financial projections for the vulnerability assessment system reform were conducted for the 2026-2028 Medium-term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) of the Government to inform expansion and rollout of the reform. Findings from the UNICEF-supported costing of the new minimum care standards with a life cycle approach (including for people with disabilities and children) and the costing of the new foster care system (including for emergency situations) are informing policy discussions and budgetary decisions to be brought forward for approval in 2026. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education Science Culture and Sports (MoESCS) in strengthening public finance management by aligning MTEF and annual budget allocations with the strategic objectives of the Education Development State Programme 2030. Findings from the cost-benefit analysis of integrated preschool education services and from the study on extra costs of disability borne by households with children with disabilities informed discussions that are expected to influence improvements in budget allocations in 2026. At the local level, UNICEF supported risk-informed planning and preparedness through the completion of Climate Risk Assessments in 185 settlements across 9 consolidated communities. These assessments strengthened local understanding of climate and disaster risks, vulnerabilities, and priority adaptation measures, and laid the groundwork for integration into community development plans and budgets. Public finance management experts analyzed community budgets to identify fiscal space, absorption capacity, and potential financing for climate adaptation, with findings integrated into climate risk assessment reports and discussed through community consultations.
Technical assistance on data and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems was another cornerstone of UNICEF’s approach to support the enhancement of systems along the reform processes. The Government officially agreed to conduct the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), thereby facilitating the production of key indicators on the situation of children, many of which are outdated or will be made available for the first time. In collaboration with MoESCS, UNICEF contributed to strengthening M&E frameworks, ensuring that child-related investments in education can be tracked and assessed for results. For the first time, Armenia participated in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), which will provide the first internationally benchmarked data on student learning outcomes, serving as a vital tool for future evidence-based policymaking. Collaboration with the National Institute of Health and the National Center for Disease Control resulted in a set of indicators being identified to monitor hygiene and infection prevention and control at PHC level through an e-based data recording and reporting system to be integrated into MOH’s e-Health system. Discussions are ongoing for the establishment of a new national digital child protection and case management system, which will enable institutions to register cases, follow children across services, monitor outcomes and generate reliable, disaggregated data for improved service delivery and policy-making. UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Finance in developing its new evaluation function.
 
Recognizing social norms and parental practices as one of the key elements for improving child wellbeing in different aspects, UNICEF worked in different complementary directions. Having reached its fourth season, the “Parents’ Meeting” TV programme aired in collaboration with Public TV of Armenia became an important nationwide platform for raising awareness on a variety of topics, including pregnancy, C-section, obesity, childhood fears and stress management, bullying, online safety, importance of play, and positive approaches to discipline. Gender stereotypes in parenting were also tackled with focus on girls’ and boys’ puberty, and importance of fathers’ role in parenting and during pregnancy. 95 reels/video assets were produced and disseminated through UNICEF Armenia’s digital channels, reaching 2,623,116 accounts, generating 3,157,470 views, and engaging 83,193 accounts on Facebook alone. Outreach to parents was complemented with targeted initiatives at community level, which were also informed by findings from social listening on information gaps and areas of interest for caregivers. New subjects on school-aged children healthy nutrition and mental wellbeing were introduced in the parenting education system at PHC level, reaching more than 13,000 parents and adolescents. A Training of Trainers program on parental education focused on nurturing care, child development, and early learning reached 37 MoESCS-approved preschool educator-mentors who will support preschools within their catchment areas and are expected to cover 47% of preschools nationwide. UNICEF and partners reached 1,259 parents through online positive parenting programmes on parenting in digital age.
 
Direct service delivery through implementing partners allowed UNICEF to cover residual needs of refugee and host community children and to ensure continuity of essential services until they can be fully absorbed by state systems. 1,306 refugee and host community households with 5,527 members, including 2,261 children (1,157 girls, 1,104 boys, including 69 children with disabilities) were reached through e-card assistance, covering different needs. 59% of households reported that this support helped significantly, and 38% reported it mostly helped improve their situation. 7,403 children aged 2-5 (48% girls, 5% refugees, 3% with special needs) benefited from services at 37 preschools with trained staff on child-centered education, inclusive pedagogy, positive parenting, psycho-social support and trauma-informed practice. 13 facilities were refurbished and equipped to expand access for refugee and host community children. 6,000 children received remedial education combined with mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) in school, and essential learning materials. Family needs assessments and child protection case management facilitated access to services for 1,231 refugee families, with guidance and support provided on education, health, employment, housing, and relocation. 6,914 children and 4,623 caregivers received MHPSS services. 80 refugee and host-community children with hearing impairments were assessed and provided with hearing aids and earbuds. 4,462 children participated in community-based child-friendly spaces and child protection and support hubs, with two additional child-friendly spaces established. Age-specific solutions were tested with 45 refugee and host community young people to provide them with means to gain insights into their emotions and process traumatic experiences in a safe and supportive environment through storytelling camps. UNICEF also continued to consider lessons learnt from the emergency response and integrate them in preparedness
 actions. In partnership with MLSA, UNICEF contributed to strengthening the shock-responsiveness of the social protection system, through a capacity development programme for Unified Social Services (USS) social workers. 105 social workers from all 49 USS territorial centres were coached and supported to identify, assess and prioritize the needs of vulnerable refugee and host community families. As peace talks showed some progress and created a momentum to advance in this agenda, UNICEF actively engaged in the development of an inter-agency framework with a focus on defining specific approaches for children, including safeguarding measures.
 
UNICEF continued to accelerate advocacy and technical support to promote the MHPSS agenda for children in the country. Emergency response situations over the past five years contributed to greater awareness of the importance of seeking help and of scaling-up delivery and diversifying services using different channels. UNICEF engaged in MHPSS through a combination of humanitarian and development programming with a comprehensive system strengthening approach in healthcare, community-based social services and communities at large, and schools. This year, mental health services for children were mapped in two more regions to enable capacity building and referrals in almost the entire country. Over 300 PHC providers were trained on psychoeducation and wellbeing promotion as well as early identification of mental health issues and management of cases, including referral.  New guidelines on “Early Identification of Child and Adolescent Psychosocial Problems at PHC level” were developed and approved by the scientific board of the Pedagogical University for integration into the curriculum. In the education sector, over 300 teachers and school staff were trained in social-emotional learning and the MHPSS in Education Framework, while new assessment tools and operational guidelines for provision of MHPSS in schools were developed. A recently established peer support volunteer (PSV) programme for MHPSS reached over 23,000 children and caregivers through a network of 878 adult and 2,050 adolescent PSVs trained on psychological first aid, self-support and mental well-being, and equipped with referral pathways to be able to guide parents or adolescents to reach specialized support services. In line with the humanitarian-development nexus approach, this service was designed to support mental well-being in underserved communities also beyond the emergency phase.  
 
While child and youth participation initiatives are expanding in the country with varying levels of understanding of this right, UNICEF aimed at demonstrating minimum standards and promote adequate mechanisms. To this end, UNICEF continued to support and capacitate a selected range of participation mechanisms, this year prioritizing climate change as an area of engagement. In partnership with the Ministry of Environment, UNICEF officially launched the Climate Change Youth Advisory Board establishing a structured platform for youth to contribute to national dialogue, policymaking and community and peer engagement around the climate agenda. Given the linkages between the climate change and biodiversity agendas, in preparation for Armenia’s role as host of 17th Community of Practice (COP) on Biodiversity, the Youth Board agreed with the Minister of Environment and UNICEF on their role in enabling youth engagement for this event. To amplify children's and youth voices within the global climate action agenda, UNICEF Armenia supported youth delegation members at COP 27 and 28 who then led and organized the gathering of over 100 young people to discuss national priorities ahead of COP30 and formulate youth-led recommendations that were included in Armenia’s National Youth Statement.  
 
As of December 2025, the Country Programme concluded with a total expenditure of USD37.3 million, including development and humanitarian funding. In 2025, financial expenditure was USD8.6 million, an overall 60% increase compared to the beginning of the Country Programme, and a 16% decrease compared to 2024, due to the reduction of humanitarian funding and the effects of ODA reduction mentioned above. UNICEF Global Humanitarian Thematic funds and UNICEF core resources were instrumental to maximize the humanitarian response to urgent and residual needs of affected children as well as to sustain critical technical assistance to advance the child rights agenda. This year, UNICEF Armenia also continued to expand and diversify the range of partners by increasing engagement with diaspora organizations. Effective implementation of the programme, including the emergency response, was possible thanks to the coordinated efforts of the programmes, operations, communications and monitoring and evaluation teams based in the Yerevan Country Office and the Goris Field Office.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2025 was the last year of the country programme and, as part of the preparation of the new CPD and UNSDCF, UNICEF Armenia reflected on the lessons learnt across the entire period. Insights for this reflection often draw on the findings of the independent Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) and other studies. The following lessons learnt informed decisions for the new Country Programme from the point of view of the programme direction and priorities, mix of strategies and operational choices:
-        The CPE underscored the organization’s pivotal role in advancing child rights in a rapidly evolving national and regional context. Despite a challenging environment, including economic fluctuations, the COVID-19 pandemic, and continuing socio-political tension and conflicts in the region, UNICEF Armenia demonstrated significant adaptability and commitment to addressing the needs of vulnerable children and adolescents in both emergency and non-emergency situations. That has been made possible through clear prioritization and coordination within the office. In addition, the CPE found that UNICEF Armenia’s advance planning and investment in emergency preparedness contributed significantly to the emergency response’s efficacy. According to the findings, this flexibility has allowed partners to pivot more easily from one crisis to the next.  Based on these observations, the Country Office concludes that it relied on a useful mix of resources and an internal operational framework that are sufficiently effective and efficient in identifying needs, anticipating risks and reacting adequately and in a timely way.
-        The CPE also highlighted that the comparative advantage of UNICEF Armenia is in long-standing advocacy and policy engagement through holistic approaches that contribute to reform processes with critical institutional knowledge, localization of international best practices and innovation. The CPE also found that the County Office's successful implementation of system strengthening, advocacy and communication, and data generation demonstrate its comparative advantages. Considering the fact that the country is undergoing a comprehensive set of social reforms, which represents a pivotal moment to address key systemic bottlenecks to the advancement of the child rights agenda at scale, the CPE findings confirm that UNICEF Armenia should continue nurturing this identified comparative advantage to support Armenia’s child rights agenda in this process by ensuring alignment with international standards and good practices.
-        The CPE concluded that the success of a number of UNICEF Armenia’s interventions lied in their alignment with national priorities and their capacity to be upscaled, thus underscoring the importance of continuing this approach that puts national ownership at the center in the new Country Programme.  
-        Based on the findings of the 2024 positioning exercise conducted by the UNICEF Europe and Centra Asia Regional Office, UNICEF Armenia is the partner of choice in the delivery of results for children, operating within a wide-ranging network of stakeholders and actors at both the national and local levels. The CPE also observed that, in addition to cultivating strong relationships with government entities, UNICEF Armenia has also engaged successfully with a wide range of civil society stakeholders. Engagement with diverse stakeholders has not only allowed UNICEF to build trust with and through local partners, but it has enabled it to expand its programmatic reach. These findings have led to the conclusion that partnership diversification and leveraging should continue in a systematic manner and new modalities to further strengthen UNICEF’s convening role should be explored. 
The Gender Programme Review conducted in 2024 as well as the CPE highlighted that gender discrimination remains comparatively unaddressed in the country and therefore recommended to better streamline UNICEF Armenia’s programming on gender, with more targeted and intentional prioritization of key needs. This finding was taken into consideration in the design of the new Country Programme, by mainstreaming gender considerations across all outcomes and including programmatic strategies that address social norms and behaviors, and data gaps.

Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF in partnership with the Government of Belarus (GOB) developed a new Country Programme for 2026-2030 (CP). The CP is aligned with UNICEF Strategic Plan for 2026-2029; national priorities of Belarus; the Convention on the Rights of the Child; and the 2026-2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

In 2025, the GOB developed new national programmes, including the National Strategy of Sustainable Development till 2040 and the Programme of Socio-Economic Development of Belarus for 2026-2030. This Programme sets forth the following priorities: (1) demographic security; (2) human capital development; (3) comfortable living environment; (4) technological progress and digital transformation; (5) regional development; (6) defense capacity; (7) tourism.
UNICEF’s CP 2026-2030 will contribute specifically to demographic security, human capital development and digital transformation. To do so, UNICEF will support national efforts in early childhood development, adolescents’ health, including mental health, and family-friendly policies; enhancing access to inclusive education, promoting digital learning, and strengthening life skills; enhancing child protection, including online, and promoting a supportive family environment. The CP aims to advance the equity and inclusion agenda, and address disparities in services for vulnerable children and families at the regional level.
In 2025, Belarus was ranked 32nd out of 167 countries in the Sustainable Development Report with a score of 78.47[1] and 65th among 193 countries in the Human Development Report with an Human Development Index of 0.824.[2] The Social Progress Index recorded a score of 70.3, rating Belarus 66th out of 170 countries.[3] The Gender Development Index of 1.009 places the country in Group 1, showing gender parity in health, education, and income. With a Gender Inequality Index of 0.080, Belarus ranks 27th out of 172 countries.[4]

On January 1, 2025, the population was 9,132,629[5], continuing a gradual decline, while the child population was 1,764,309[6] also marking a sustained decrease. The annual number of births decreased by half in the past eight years.[7] The fertility rate remains low at 1.08 births per woman[8], prompting the GOB to advance measures to support families with children.
Economic performance weakened compared to 2024. In 2025, GDP growth slowed to 1.3%[9] compared to 4% in 2024[10]. The annual inflation rose to 6.8%[11] compared to 5.2%[12] in 2024. In January-September 2025, the national poverty rate was 3.4%.[13] While official data on child poverty is no longer available, trends from previous years indicate that child poverty is likely higher than the overall poverty rate.

Belarus maintains a robust social protection system, with near-universal coverage for children aged 0-3 years. In 2024, there were 40,578 children with disabilities.[14] Belarus continues to advance the rights and social protection of these children. Amendments to welfare legislation, effective January 2025, introduced additional benefits for families caring for children with severe disabilities, and improved access to sick leave and medical services for families with multiple children with disabilities.

In 2023, 30% of children in need of special education lacked access to inclusive education in preschool and general secondary educational establishments.[15] In 2024-2025, the Ministry of Education with UNICEF support piloted an Inclusion Index to assess progress in inclusive education and culture among key educational stakeholders. The Index identified positive trends while highlighting differences between educational establishments.

Belarus maintained progress on health-related SDGs. By 2025, there were 58 Early Childhood Intervention centers across the country providing services to children with developmental delays and disabilities. The Ministry of Health continued to support a network of 58 Youth-Friendly Health Centers, which provide health services and counseling. In 2025, Belarus launched free papillomavirus vaccination for 11-year-old girls, adding it to the national vaccination calendar.

Belarus prioritizes practical steps to strengthen the child protection system under the National Action Plan to improve the situation of children and protect their rights. In 2025, Belarus adopted a Law “On Amendments to Laws on Ensuring the Rights of the Child”. The law updates several foundational statutes, including the Law “On the Rights of the Child”, the Marriage and Family Code, and legislation on social protection of orphans.[16]

Belarus is committed to preventing and responding to violence against children, including sexual violence and abuse, and protecting child victims. While there is a lack of public statistics on violence against children, the topic remains high on the public agenda. Overall, the number of children victims of different crimes decreased from 3,050 in 2023 to 2,251 in 2024.[17] Despite progress made in reducing the number of children in residential care institutions, in 2024 4,843 children remained in residential facilities, 263 children - in correctional settings.

By the end of 2025, 43,400 Ukrainian refugees were registered in Belarus, with children accounting for 37%. According to the UN, many families experience difficulties with registration and documentation, enrolling children in schools and kindergartens. Refugees lack clear guidance on their rights and available services while humanitarian actors observe gaps in coordination between service providers. The GOB, in cooperation with UN agencies, works towards addressing these issues. UNICEF supports these efforts with special focus on access of the most vulnerable children to essential services and child protection.[18] [19]

Belarus sustained progress on gender equality through the implementation of the National Action Plan for Gender Equality (2021–2025). In 2025, the Government scaled up the mechanism for gender expertise in drafting laws, reinforcing its commitment to mainstreaming gender considerations in policymaking.

The country registered 49 orange-level weather warnings over June-July 2025, among the highest numbers recorded in recent years[20], and current national sustainability programmes lack child-focused provisions. While the overall risk of climate change effects on children is assessed as moderate, there is a need to mitigate climate and environmental risks to ensure a sustainable future for children and youth.

Goal 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives
Nurturing Parenting Environments:
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened and expanded its flagship parenting application, Bebbo — the only comprehensive early childhood development mobile platform available in Belarus. The app provided more than 30,000 parents and caregivers, including families of vulnerable children, with accessible, evidence-based information and practical guidance on early childhood development. Over the year, users improved their parenting knowledge and skills through more than 30 newly added articles on inclusive nutrition and feeding for children with disabilities, nurturing care for premature babies, psychological support for parents, and maternal care, hygiene, and nutrition during pregnancy.

In addition, 91 parents of young children, including children with disabilities, enhanced their skills in child development, care and positive parenting through 11 trainings and workshops, as well as 24 individual and group counselling sessions. These interventions helped parents prevent burnout and strengthened their overall psychological well-being.
 
Strengthening Systems for Inclusive Early Childhood Development:
In 2025, UNICEF contributed to increase the availability, quality and financial sustainability of services for young children with developmental risks, including delays and disabilities, and their families, through enhanced Early Childhood Interventions (ECI) services and the establishment of seven developmental follow-up (catamnestic observation) centers for families with premature babies. Additional online support to these families was provided via seven regional chats (504 participants) and the ‘Small Heroes’ Telegram channel, which shared information, counselling, and success stories with 536 subscribers.

The assessment of the ECI system accessibility and sustainability was finalized. It covered 47 ECI centers for children with developmental risks, including delays and disabilities, under three years old. A costed model for sustainably financing ECI services was developed, outlining the service classification, methods for allocating direct and indirect costs, and procedures for consolidating expenditure data, together with funding recommendations for regions. This informed an updated regulatory framework adopted by the MoH in October, which now includes revised ECI standards, enhanced quality-assessment procedures, and recommendations on sufficient financing.

UNICEF partnered with the MoH to develop a Premature Babies Register, integrated into the Centralized Health Information System, enabling the health system to collect and analyze data and supporting informed decision-making to strengthen the quality of services for small and sick babies.
 
Inclusive Nutrition for babies and young children
UNICEF continued to support national efforts to ensure that vulnerable newborn and young children benefit from adequate nutrition. With UNICEF support, the MoH updated Clinical Protocols on Feeding, accompanied by methodological recommendations on young child development, health monitoring, breastfeeding and inclusive nutrition. The protocols and recommendations were disseminated among neonatologists, pediatricians, and intensive care specialists.

With UNICEF support, an Inclusive Nutrition and Feeding Resource Center was established in Minsk. In 2025, parents of 131 children with developmental delays and disabilities received counseling on inclusive nutrition and feeding. The center also strengthens specialists’ capacities: 300 professionals have been trained on care and services to premature babies and children with disability, nutrition and feeding, notably through exposure to international best practices of the Institute of Early Intervention of Saint Petersburg (Russian Federation).
The results, lessons learned, and best practices from UNICEF–MoH cooperation in early childhood development were presented at the International Conference “The First 1,000 Days of Health: A Successful Start and a Foundation for the Future” in November 2025. The conference gathered 600 participants (200 in-person and 400 online) from Belarus, Russia, Turkey, and Tajikistan.
 
Advancing Adolescents’ Health and Well-Being:
UNICEF focused on institutionalizing psychological wellbeing within the education system and strengthening access to adolescent-friendly psychosocial support, both offline and online. UNICEF contributed through the integration of specific elective courses into the national curriculum, national capacity development, and enhancing digital service delivery.

As a system-level intervention, a matrix of homeroom sessions on psychological well-being for grades 4–11 was developed, integrated into the Ministry of Education (MoE)’s internal regulations, and published on national education portals. It institutionalized psychological well-being as a mandatory component of school and vocational education. Over 2,600 schools and 160 vocational institutions conducted nine sessions, reaching more than one million students.
To deepen learning and skills development beyond universal homeroom sessions, UNICEF and partners introduced elective course “My Psychological Well-being and Peer Support in Crisis Situations” for grades 5–7, building on an existing course for grades 8–11. The programme strengthens adolescents’ emotional self-regulation and peer-support skills while training teachers to foster a supportive classroom environment. Twelve schools have initiated pilots, benefiting approximately 840 students with an additional 50 schools preparing for piloting it for 3,500 students, creating a pathway for gradual scale-up.

To support sustainable implementation, a dedicated in-service training curriculum was integrated into the network of Regional Institutes of Education Development. Through six regional seminars (350+ participants) and regional consultations (over 500 participants), institutes’ trainers and multidisciplinary school specialists (teachers, psychologists and social pedagogues) enhanced their capacities to maintain psychologically safe learning environments in schools. In parallel, a supervision system for school psychologists and social pedagogues was established, through six online group (450+ participants) and 247 individual sessions.

To ensure consistency and long-term access to materials on psychological well-being, a digital repository was established. It includes an updated resource page hosted by Belarusian State Pedagogical University, a Telegram channel, expanded from 157 to 784 subscribers, with average post reach of 1,000–6,000 views, and publications on national portals. Altogether, these channels support nationwide dissemination and ongoing professional learning of more than 10,000 psychologists and social pedagogues.

Complementing school-based interventions, UNICEF prioritized access to confidential, high-quality online psychological support for adolescents in crisis through the talk2ok.by - the national platform offering free professional counselling for young people. In 2025, 684 adolescents received support through the platform, with more than 5,500 visitors. The number of active qualified psychologists increased from 35 to 84, exceeding the original target of 70, supported by onboarding (50+ individual consultations) and professional development. Over 73% of psychologists on the platform are now equipped with knowledge in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing.
 
Goal 2: Every Child Learns and Acquires Skills
Accessing Quality & Inclusive Learning Opportunities:
UNICEF advanced its collaboration with the Ministry of Education to strengthen the national inclusive education system. In 2025, a three-year project supported by the Russian Federation was completed, targeting multiple dimensions of the system: development of methodological and training materials, capacity-building of teachers and specialists, enhanced monitoring of progress, and promotion of positive social norms towards CWD. The initiative also improved accessibility in 118 pilot schools and pre-schools by providing over USD 700,000 in inclusive and assistive equipment, expanding participation opportunities for children with special educational needs. With UNICEF’s support, national partners developed new Methodological Recommendations for Multidisciplinary Assessment Commissions, introducing a shift to strength-based, child-centred assessments and greater parental involvement. National and international experts reviewed results at the final roundtable and identified priorities for further strengthening inclusive practices.

The project advanced enabling environment for inclusive education by shifting social norms, eliminating stigma toward CWD, and improving the overall environment for their learning and participation. Through the “Just Kids at School” campaign, more than 1.82 million people were reached via media, complemented by over 409,000 social-media engagements and over 208,000 views on project platforms. Storytelling and media content emphasized dignity and everyday school experiences. Parents, educators and psychologists strengthened their skills through guidance materials and public events, including a national forum reaching 1,300 participants. Journalist training improved the accuracy and ethics of disability-related media coverage.

UNICEF strengthened national capacity to track inclusive education progress and inform evidence-based policy making. A multidimensional Inclusion Index was developed and piloted in over 1,100 schools and pre-schools, providing system-level metrics to monitor progress. A complementary survey captured parents’ and teachers’ knowledge and attitudes. A project evaluation and targeted research identified remaining barriers and opportunities, generating actionable evidence to guide future decisions and programming.
 
Advancing Skills, Participation & Engagement:
UNICEF fostered the integration of socio-emotional skills (SES) development in vocational education, by informing students about available resources and tips to improve emotional self-control, constructive communication, and relationships. With strong SES, adolescents can better adapt to new life circumstances, stay safe, and interact appropriately with others. Guidelines for pedagogues “Development of Social-Emotional Skills among College Students” were developed, tested in three colleges and are available online. The developed resources were introduced in the Technical and vocational education and training system, which enhanced social-pedagogical support to first-year students living in dormitories, and orphans.

UNICEF continued to empower adolescents and youth, fostering youth engagement for the SDGs, adolescent participation in local governance, and their creative engagement around social projects to enhance the life of the most vulnerable children, through UPSHIFT scale-up.
Under the project on Localizing SDGs, the “SDG Movement” festival offered a vibrant space for young people to dialogue on SDGs, reaching over 1.9 million views online, while the “Sustainable Summer” reached more than 600 children in camps across five regions, using creative games and quizzes to connect global goals with everyday life.

Under the Child and Adolescent-Friendly Cities platform, with UNICEF support, 36 cities implemented child-friendly policies, with two new cities joining and five reaffirming their honorary status. Six strategic sessions and the National Forum “Designing the Future Together” convened over 150 stakeholders, including adolescents, municipal leaders, and experts, to exchange experience and share best practices. Youth-led governance was expanded through 47 child and youth councils supported by interactive trainings and mentorship, and over 200 adolescents developed social projects aligned with SDGs. The UPSHIFT methodology was scaled nationwide, equipping 138 pedagogues and over 600 children with entrepreneurial and project design skills. These efforts were amplified through the platform detivgorode.by, publishing over 75 updates to promote youth voices.
 
Goal 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation
System Strengthening for Family-based Care:
UNICEF advanced reform of deinstitutionalization and prevention of institutionalization in Vitebsk region by strengthening family-based care, enhancing capacities of frontline professionals, piloting innovative community-based services for vulnerable children and families. A Regional Roadmap was developed which describes piloted innovations recommended by the Vitebsk regional Commission on Affairs of Minors for implementation in all districts of the region.

As a result of a two-year project, 360 children were transitioned from residential care into safe and nurturing family environments. This result was enabled by needs assessments, individualized case management, and improved intersectoral coordination across education, health, and social protection.

To reinforce a multi-sectoral response system in the Vitebsk region, 255 specialists from education, health, and social protection were trained on mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS)-informed case management and effective communication with families in crisis, which improved families’ engagement with social services. Intersectoral teams worked together in ten pilot districts, receiving regular supervision, which strengthened their capacity to jointly assess risks, plan tailored support, and prevent family-child separation as well as facilitate reunification and placement to alternative family-based care.

The project expanded inclusive services for children with disabilities through the introduction of home-based respite care to reduce parental burnout, and deployment of a mobile resource room. Specialized equipment and staff training enabled provision of developmental and rehabilitation support to 124 families.

Building System Responses for Prevention of Violence:
UNICEF supported national efforts to improve protection of children from violence, including sexual violence, by conducting a comprehensive analysis of relevant national legislation to identify gaps in prevention, reporting, and access to justice. Capacities to prevent and respond to violence were strengthened through specialized training on sexual violence and trauma-informed approaches (105 frontline workers and MHPSS professionals), which further expanded access to quality crisis services for child survivors.

To enhance digital safety and access to timely support, UNICEF expanded outreach of the national child protection resource Kidspomogut.by, focused on cyber violence prevention and response. In 2025, the platform attracted over 160,000 new users, significantly increasing children’s and caregivers’ access to reliable information, psychosocial support services, and guidance on how to stay safe online and seek help when exposed to harmful digital behavior.

UNICEF successfully finalized the 5-year experimental programme “Safe and Enabling Environment in School”, focusing on testing bullying prevention mechanisms in school settings. The programme covered 43 schools with a student population of 25,000 and resulted in the development of a methodology and normative framework for integrating the bullying-prevention model into every school. The MoE recommended education professionals to use the developed materials and expressed commitment for further scale-up the programme, which could extend the reach of the programme to all school-age children.

Protection children on the move:
In areas hosting Ukrainian refugees, UNICEF and partners strengthened local multidisciplinary teams to support refugee families with children. Social workers, psychologists, and education specialists were equipped to conduct best interests’ assessments, provide case management, and deliver MHPSS services, contributing to the prevention of unnecessary family separation, safe reunification, and reduced reliance on residential care.

To ensure quality and continuity, UNICEF supported staff well-being and scaled up community-based MHPSS and child protection capacities. A total of 481 frontline workers were trained on child rights and burnout prevention, while 43 specialists received group and individual supervision, reducing secondary trauma and burnout. More than 8,700 children, caregivers, and service providers accessed MHPSS information and resources, strengthening community resilience and help-seeking behavior.

UNICEF expanded access to inclusive MHPSS and individual case management for conflict-affected Ukrainian children and caregivers. Overall, 2,968 individuals received MHPSS services, while 587 children at heightened protection risk and 671 caregivers benefited from targeted case management and gender-based violence risk mitigation, improving family safety and protective practices.

Enhancing Restorative Practices:
To promote restorative practices under the “Justice for children” agenda, UNICEF completed a mapping of services available to child survivors of sexualized violence, assessing referral practices, capacity of specialists, and availability of safe, child-friendly support. The results will inform national policy-level dialogue and guide the development of integrated referral pathways to ensure timely, survivor-centered assistance for every affected child. The mapping is also a baseline for the 2026-2027 intersectoral project “Strengthening national capacity of Belarus in preventing violence against children” funded by the India-UN Development Partnership Fund.
 
Goal 4: Every Child lives in a Safe and Sustainable Climate & Environment
Adolescent Voices for Climate Change:
UNICEF continued to promote Adolescents and Young People Activism within the Climate Change Agenda. The “Sustainable University” under the project on localizing SDGs brought together 300 students from eleven universities for lectures, workshops, and roundtables on climate action and ecological responsibility. Over 120 adolescents took part in the Plogging Races, online and offline trainings to develop their eco-friendly and responsible consumption behavior.
The National Forum “Green Professions: Path to a Sustainable Future” was held within the “Clean and Sustainable Environment for Every Child” project with participation of 86 adolescents, pedagogues, university experts, and representatives of private companies. It introduced youth to green careers through exhibitions, expert dialogues, workshops, and visits to businesses, inspiring them to pursue sustainability-focused professions.

Goal 5: Every Child has Access to Inclusive Social Protection & Lives Free from Poverty
Access to Inclusive Social Protection:
UNICEF continued to strengthen the capacity of the social protection system in working with vulnerable families with children. In Brest and Gomel regions, UNICEF supported the establishment of two Resource Centers on family care by the local authorities. Equipped with curriculum development and educational material, the Resource Centers function as platforms for the repository and sharing of expertise and knowledge. To strengthen sustainably supervision and peer support, 30 master trainers and 300 social workers were trained on case-management, interaction with vulnerable families and prevention of domestic violence. This pool of newly trained professionals will continue to disseminate best practices within and across regions, enhancing the relevance and quality of social services to the most vulnerable children and their families.

Accountability and Data for Children
Accountability to affected populations was strengthened through integrated feedback mechanisms across refugee and migrant services, reaching 1,732 people in 2025. Feedback informed improved communication and transparency, while 3,456 children and caregivers received information on Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) and reporting mechanisms.
To advance child rights monitoring, UNICEF supported the National Statistical Committee to enhance the availability and quality of data on children. Under the project on localizing SDGs, new guidance and tools for microdata dissemination were developed and the national information and analytical system improved.
 
Partnerships
UNICEF advanced its partnership agenda by harnessing traditional alliances, expanding corporate engagement, and exploring new funding opportunities to deliver results for children amid continuous geopolitical uncertainties. Guided by a resource mobilization strategy, the CO maintained strong ties with traditional donors like Russia while securing new streams of support, including a USD 1 million contribution from the India-UN Development Partnership Fund to prevent violence against children. Donor meetings and sustained engagement reinforced relationships with Canada, Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, Sweden, Italy etc. Opportunities are being pursued with China, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Türkiye positioning UNICEF as a trusted partner for both traditional and emerging donors.

Private sector engagement focused on embedding child rights into business practices and leveraging Belarus’ growing Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) agenda. UNICEF organized the 1st Child Rights in Business Conference and launched UNICADEMY – Corporate Social Responsibility Academy for Business, promoting the adoption of safer products, ethical marketing, and family-friendly policies. Corporate fundraising increased with contributions reaching over USD 133,300 supported by Belarus’s first CRM campaign with 21vek.by, a new three-year partnership with Priorbank, and extended collaboration with BelVEB Bank. Creative engagement formats, such as the Team of UNICEF Friends’ engagement at Minsk Half Marathon, united businesses, diplomats, and partners to support CWD.

Strategic communication and digital engagement continued to support results for children and resource mobilization. UNICEF expanded its digital community to 60,000 followers across social media and messaging platforms (30% more than 2024), strengthening visibility and sustained engagement. Digital fundraising was also improved, with monthly individual contributions rising from USD 4,000 to USD 5,500 by year-end (a 37.5% increase), driven by coordinated digital advertising with UNICEF regional Private Sector Fundraising (PSFR) Cluster. Overall, gross income generated by in-country PSFR from all channels reached over USD 218,000, marking a significant step forward in resource mobilization efforts.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
A key challenge for UNICEF throughout the year was to support effective intersectoral coordination, which remains critical for advancing integrated approaches to child rights and child-focused policy and quality services. Despite some progress, aligning priorities and actions across sectors and among national partners in health, education, social and child protection and emergency response, has proven complex and time intensive. These efforts underscore the need for strengthened coordination mechanisms and agile and supportive internal systems to deliver results in a rapidly evolving context.

During the first half of 2025, the CO finalized the CP development. It constituted additional workload for staff and required strategic prioritization and proper planning of time and resources allocation. Some programme-related activities were moved to the second part of the year, in agreement with national counterparts. Regular assurance quality processes, including programmatic visits, and monthly oversight of progress through Programme Management meetings helped ensure quality results under tight timelines. As a result, the CPD was developed in a timely manner, key programmatic interventions planned were implemented and the budget fully utilized. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs facilitated the CP finalization, coordinating key national ministries’ contributions and the Belarus’ Permanent Representative to the United Nations presented the CP to the UNICEF Executive Board in September 2025.

Internally, UNICEF faced significant organizational shifts linked to the UN80 reform and global UNICEF workforce optimization and rightsizing, which resulted in staff mobility. The CO engaged in a participatory change management process, to develop a fit-for-purpose structure to deliver its 2026-2030 CP with reduced funding, while providing support to affected staff.

Interventions in inclusive education revealed gaps in the teaching potential of the faculties of colleges, universities, and Educational Development Institutes, responsible for training a new generation of teachers and re-training practicing teachers at regional level. This hampered the implementation of the new educational programmes on inclusive education developed by the government with UNICEF support and put at risk the provision of quality inclusive education in pre-schools and schools nation-wide. To address this bottleneck, additional Training of Trainers TOT) on inclusive education for teachers of 19 pedagogical colleges in the technical and vocational education and training system. Looking forward, UNICEF and its partners would need to consider how to reduce these disparities in teachers’ capacities between Minsk and the regions and extend the TOT component.

Another lesson learned is that inclusive education in pre-school and school settings requires additional efforts to mobilize stakeholders of the educational process (administration, teachers, students, parents) through the application of the “whole-of-school approach”.

Evidence from mental health programming and online counseling demonstrates that supervision, peer support, and real-time consultations are decisive for service quality, staff wellbeing, and beneficiaries’ trust. Where supervision was embedded, higher retention of psychologists and more consistent service delivery were observed. This highlights the need to institutionalize supervision as a core component of national professional development systems across education, health, and social protection.

Despite significant achievements in private sector engagement and corporate fundraising, challenges remain. Direct contributions from businesses are still limited, as corporates prefer highly visible projects – such as purchasing assistive equipment or funding renovations - over flexible funding that could address systematic need. The unstable geopolitical and economic context restricted traditional donors’ support; building donor relationship resulting in funding remained slow. Moving forward, UNICEF will focus on advocacy for unrestricted funding, innovative engagement models and adaptive strategies to sustain and grow partnerships that deliver results for children. UNICEF will continue to position itself as a trusted partner across both public and private sectors.

In 2025, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), an upper-middle-income country, demonstrated continued commitment to advancing child-related reforms and system strengthening, despite a complex operating environment marked by structural constraints, political fragmentation and recurring shocks. These dynamics affected approximately half a million children country-wide and shaped the conditions under which results for children were pursued, particularly for those most at risk of exclusion, focusing on system strengthening and targeted approaches to reach the most marginalized children.
Socio-economic conditions remained challenging. According to the most recent Household Budget Survey (HBS) data, around one in five children lives in households at risk of poverty or social exclusion, with higher risks observed among children in rural areas, larger households, and families facing unemployment or informal work. These disparities are compounded by territorial inequalities and fragmented governance arrangements, which continue to affect the coherence and effectiveness of service delivery across cantons and municipalities.
Progress toward SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) continued to be affected by persistent gaps in routine immunization coverage.  Measles and pertussis outbreaks began in late 2023 and continued through 2024–2025, mainly affecting unvaccinated children. Around 9,300 measles cases were reported countrywide, with the highest incidence in low-coverage areas: Sarajevo and Zenica-Doboj cantons (FBiH) and Bijeljina (RS). This situation highlighted ongoing vulnerabilities in immunization uptake and the continued need to strengthen routine immunization systems and public confidence in vaccines to ensure that all children can benefit from essential preventive health services.
Mental health remained a growing concern for children and adolescents in BiH in 2025. Analysis of over a decade of data from Plavi telefon, the country’s only child helpline, shows that mental health-related concerns consistently represent the most frequent reason children and young people seek support, accounting for more than a quarter of all recorded topics. Data also indicates gendered patterns in both vulnerability and help-seeking, with adolescent girls, more frequently reporting emotional distress, anxiety, depressive symptoms and suicidal thoughts, while boys are less likely to seek support despite significant psychosocial risks. These often intertwined with family conflict, peer violence and feelings of isolation. The high and sustained demand for counselling points to unmet needs and limited availability of accessible, child and adolescent-friendly mental health services. These patterns reinforced the need for upstream prevention, early identification and integrated, community-based responses capable of reaching children at scale. They also highlight the need for gender-responsive approaches that address stigma, social norms and barriers to help-seeking, and ensure gender-sensitive access to professional mental health care and psychosocial support. 
BiH remains a transit country for refugees and migrants, with children forming a significant share of those on the move. In 2025, 3,946 children (385 girls and 3,561 boys) were recorded in temporary reception centres (TRCs), most of them unaccompanied or separated (3,116 or 79%). A sharp increase in unaccompanied and separated children (52 per cent increase from second to third quarter of 2025) intensified pressure on child protection services, while the ongoing transition from internationally supported to government-led response exposed institutional capacity gaps, highlighting the need for sustainable, government-owned child protection systems.
In 2025, child-related data and evidence gained increased prominence within policy and institutional discussions in BiH. While administrative data systems remained fragmented, with uneven disaggregation and limited interoperability across governance levels, stakeholders demonstrated growing motivation to strengthen the availability, quality, and use of child-focused data. In parallel, renewed political will emerged to re-establish a state-level, actionable and measurable policy framework for children, marking the first such comprehensive document since the expiration of the previous Action Plan for Children in 2019. Together, these developments point to a more enabling environment for strengthening accountability, evidence-informed decision-making and coordinated action on children’s rights.
Gender inequalities remain a cross-cutting driver of child vulnerability in BiH, shaping unequal exposure to violence, mental health risks, health outcomes and access to essential services, educational outcomes and economic opportunities. Harmful gender norms and stereotypes continue to affect girls and boys differently, contributing to gender-based violence, child marriage, limited participation of girls in skills development and economic pathways, and heightened risk-taking and disengagement among adolescent boys. 
At the same time, the European Union (EU) accession process remains a central driver of structural reforms in BiH, reinforced by the submission of BiH’s reform agenda to the European Commission. Additionally, BiH expressed interest in the European Child Guarantee (ECG). The alignment of social inclusion, child protection, health, education and justice systems with EU acquis created strong reform incentives, while also exposing longstanding governance and capacity gaps. Translating accession commitments into tangible improvements for children presents both an opportunity and a challenge, requiring sustained political commitment, coordination and public investment.

Every child survives and thrives 
In 2025, with EU support, UNICEF worked with government institutions and civil society organizations (CSOs) to strengthen more equitable and resilient health systems for children in BiH. System-wide, equity- and gender-responsive improvements in immunization, early childhood development (ECD), nutrition, mental health and healthy environments expanded access to quality services and reduced disparities, particularly for vulnerable groups. These results were driven by sustained policy dialogue, strengthened institutional capacities, improved data use, and community-based social and behavior change approaches that addressed gender-related barriers to access and care.
In partnership with Ministries of Health (MoHs), Public Health Institutes (PHIs) and professional associations, UNICEF strengthened immunization systems and enhanced service quality and safety across entities and Brcko District (BD). Entity immunization strategies were finalized, alongside continued advocacy for their adoption and integration into planning frameworks, additional Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) standard operating procedures were introduced, cold-chain infrastructure modernized, and  health workers trained on immunization protocols, risk communication, and emergency response. Targeted outreach through partnerships with Cantonal PHIs Tuzla and Zenica-Doboj, CSOs and local actors, resulted in catch-up immunization for 637 children (328 girls, 309 boys) from 1,084 Roma families visited. The Electronic Immunization System in Republika Srpska (RS) advanced toward full operationalization, strengthening data quality, service planning, and follow-up of missed children. In Sarajevo Canton, coordinated action by UNICEF, UNFPA and the Cantonal PHI  to support strengthened outreach and improved availability of services led to a significant increase in HPV vaccine uptake, reaching 1,589 adolescents (including 470 boys) with first doses in three months. This represented a sevenfold increase compared to average uptake in the first three quarters. 
UNICEF supported the strengthening of ECD services across both entities, contributing to early detection and support to children with disabilities or developmental delays. In the Federation BiH (FBiH), building on a new regulatory framework and designation of the PHI as training hub, UNICEF supported design and delivery of ECD training for professionals. In RS, four new ECD centers expanded service access for over 18,000 children through an inclusive, gender-responsive (through targeted interventions to father parents and caregivers) and multisectoral model, complemented by health worker capacity building.  
With UNICEF technical support, preschool nutrition services improved in quality and reach for over 50,000 children nationwide, through accreditation of 69 preschool institutions across BiH as “Nutrition-Friendly” and the development of a regulatory framework for preschool nutrition services in RS. Complementary health worker training, breastfeeding campaigns and community outreach via Mother-Baby Corners (MBCs) improved breastfeeding and infant and young child feeding practices, including among refugee and migrant families, while addressing gendered caregiving roles and promoting fathers’ engagement. A national KAP study generated evidence to align public messaging with global nutrition recommendations, identifying a gap between knowledge and practices, with many children unable to identify basic nutrition principles and unhealthy food choices prevailing, while parents overestimated their nutrition knowledge despite limited understanding of key food groups.
As part of its broader mental health programming, UNICEF supported school-based mental health promotion and violence prevention in Una Sana Canton, through the MindMatters programme, implemented with the Ministries of Education (MoEs) and Health and CSO Genesis Project. The initiative reached 2,674 students (1360 girls, 1314 boys) from 68 schools, 1,475 teachers (1350 female, 185 male) and 2,022 parents (1620 female, 402 male), improving emotional literacy, reducing stigma, and strengthening school collaboration. The programme also supported the institutionalization of psychosocial support and crisis response through bylaws, while addressing gender patterns of mental health risks and help-seeking. These results demonstrate a replicable partnership model for school-based mental health promotion, working with government institutions as well as CSOs. 
In partnership with PHIs, UNICEF advanced healthier preschool environments by supporting indoor air quality monitoring in 15 kindergartens across six regions in RS and three cantons in FBiH. Capacity building of over 200 preschool staff and parents strengthened daily practices to keep indoor air clean and safe for children. Evidence generated through this work informed policy dialogue to strengthen the existing rulebook on indoor air quality monitoring for preschool and school settings in RS and to initiate the development of a regulatory framework in the FBiH.
 
Every child learns 
UNICEF delivered significant results to advance equitable, inclusive and future-ready education in BiH, by strengthening education governance, expanding access, improving teaching quality, and amplifying the voice of children and adolescents in education policy and practice.
UNICEF’s system-strengthening and convening role accelerated digital transformation in education through the Giga initiative. The Advisory Board, bringing together the Ministry of Communications and Transport (MoCT), the Ministry of Civil Affairs (MoCA), the Communications Regulatory Agency (CRA), and observers from ITU, UNESCO and the EU Delegation, endorsed priority actions to expand school connectivity—particularly for marginalized communities— reinforcing country-owned, multisectoral, evidence-based reforms aligned with global digital education initiatives. 
Together with UNESCO, UNICEF supported 11 education authorities to finalize their draft 10-year education programmes, covering Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) through higher education. The support strengthened education governance by improving the measurability and feasibility of proposed reforms through the development of SMART indicators and costed measures, while ongoing public consultations continued to build ownership and consensus and are expected to carry into next year. 
UNICEF assessed the impact of the IT girls programme and found that participation in IT Girls clubs is associated with higher interest and ambition in STEM education and careers, stronger digital and programming skills, and increased confidence among girls, addressing gender-based barriers in STEM. The assessment showed particularly strong effects among girls with initially low interest in STEM, while teachers reported improved engagement, creativity, teamwork and leadership, alongside positive shifts in gender norms and reduced gender stereotypes and digital skills gaps. 
UNICEF laid the groundwork for advancing public–private partnerships (PPPs) in ECEC by mapping existing PPP practices and developing a context-specific PPP model for BiH, drawing on international good practices and local capacities. In partnering with its Business Advisory Council (BAC), UNICEF generated evidence, positioning ECEC as productivity-enhancing investment for businesses.  To address structural barriers and improve effective use of public resources in ECEC, UNICEF, with EU support, supported infrastructure expansion, and upgrading. The total of 9 preschools were reconstructed or upgraded in 2025, improving the quality and safety of learning environments for over 3,300 children. Local co-financing for sustainable operations was secured in three locations, namely Lukavac, Ljubuski and Ljubinje, where city and cantonal authorities assumed responsibility for operational costs, including the establishment of four new preschool groups. 
UNICEF strengthened teaching quality by empowering teachers to integrate “Tinkering with e-waste” into the IT Girls methodology and by advancing the integration of the EU GreenComp framework into preschool and primary curricula in Canton Sarajevo. Learning outcomes improved for more than 4,400 children (42% girls), through gender-responsive approaches, including children on the move, through UNICEF’s support to the Akelius digital language-learning programme. Schools reported significant gains in language skills, confidence and classroom well-being, alongside strengthened digital and pedagogical practices among teachers.
UNICEF strengthened adolescent participation, digital skills and civic engagement through youth-led action, inter-ethnic collaboration and digital platforms. Over 3,000 adolescents and young people shared their perspectives and actively participated in empowerment and skilling opportunities, including via U-Report, through IT Girls programme, UPSHIFT, Dialogue for the future (Community of volunteers and Community of schools) and the Network of Student Councils, among others. 

Every child is protected 
In 2025, BiH made measurable progress in strengthening child protection systems and reducing children’s exposure to institutionalization, with a clear shift toward family and community-based alternatives. 
With UNICEF technical support and policy advocacy, the endorsement process of the Road Map for Deinstitutionalization of Children in BiH and entity level social and child protection strategies, laid the foundation for expanded family support services, strengthened gatekeeping, and foster care prioritization. Furthermore, UNICEF-supported partnerships with ministries and professional associations, namely associations of social workers, psychologists and supervisors, resulted in a strengthened social service workforce (SSW), including through the adoption of foster care training curricula, targeted capacity building of CSW professionals, and institutionalization of professional supervision through university programmes, thereby improving quality, sustainability and retention of SSW.
UNICEF contributed to a more coherent, government-led and child-centered migration and child protection response. With other UN agencies, UNICEF supported government authorities prepare a child-centered transition plan, strengthening ownership and the humanitarian-development nexus and enhancing safeguarding standards, workforce capacities and gender-responsive risk identification. In partnership with World Vision, over 3,900 children on the move (90 per cent boys, most unaccompanied and separated) benefited from improved access to quality services, including 24/7 support, legal guardianship, case management, mental health and MHPSS. Access to critical services has contributed to a safe environment, risk prevention, timely assessment of the best interests of children, and a holistic response to their needs. Services were gender-responsive and age-sensitive, tailored to respond to distinct gendered risk profiles, with boys predominantly exposed to mobility-related protection risks, while girls face heightened risks of GBV and exploitation. 
At the same time, UNICEF advanced violence prevention and response, gender equality and child justice reforms. At the strategic level, BiH representatives developed and presented a pledge to end violence against children at the regional ministerial conference on Ending Violence Against Children, thereby reinforcing high-level political commitment, reaffirming alignment with the CRC and SDGs and positioning the country within a shared European agenda on violence prevention. To address persistent weaknesses in routine administrative data underpinning violence prevention and response, UNICEF initiated the Administrative Data Maturity Model (ADAMM) methodology in the child protection sector, supporting practitioners to identify gaps and inconsistencies in definitions, tools, and data flows, and establishing an early concrete entry point for longer-term system reform, requiring sustained investment, standardized practices and clear institutional leadership. Additionally, through the new joint UN Gender Equality Accelerator Programme, UNICEF supported evidence-based, gender-responsive and child-sensitive policy dialogue, that resulted in a stakeholder-driven roadmap outlining priority actions for UN support, including strengthened GBV data systems. The roadmap integrates gender-transformative and child protection principles, including  GBV prevention and response, improved referral pathways and access to child-friendly justice.
At the service level, UNICEF strengthened protection to prevent and respond to violence against children (VAC), ensuring gender-responsive MHPSS access for over 10,000 beneficiaries including children, adolescents and survivors. Online support was provided via the Blue Phone helpline in collaboration with Bosnian-Herzegovinian Association for Integrative Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy BHIDAPA and mental health professionals. In 2025, Blue Phone recorded 3,350 calls, including 809 calls from adolescent girls, underscoring gender-specific help-seeking patterns and vulnerabilities, and 1,948 online counselling cases, including 771 from adolescent girls, reflecting gendered vulnerabilities.
