The most common reasons for seeking help were related to mental health, abuse and violence, peer relationships, and family relationships. 59 cases of suspected violence involving 77 individuals, including 35 adolescent girls, were referred to competent authorities. Complementary digital outreach reached 378,000 people, expanding awareness of available MHPSS support, parenting, and violence prevention services. Furthermore, a UNICEF-supported study of long-term Blue Phone service data (2013–2025) generated a wealth of data which is being used to raise public awareness, inform gender- and age-responsive policy dialogue and support advocacy on service capacity, sustainability and improved accessibility of protection and MHPSS services for children. 
In partnership with entity ministries of justice (MoJs), UNICEF strengthened institutional capacity and coordination through UNICEFs Justice for Children Forum. Thirty-five prosecutors improved their capacity to prosecute sexual and domestic violence cases involving children, and child justice priorities were successfully included in EU IPA 2024 funding secured from 2026. UNICEF provided technical support to the FBiH MoJ to draft a new Family Law, embedding best practices from the region, strengthening child participation in proceedings, best interest determination mechanisms, adoption procedures and alimony mechanisms.
 
Every child has a fair chance in life 
In 2025, measurable system-level results in social protection demonstrated UNICEF’s strategic contributions to advancing equity, resilience and child-focused reforms in BiH. 
Child benefit reforms progressed through UNICEF-supported system strengthening and sustained policy dialogue with ministries. In the FBiH, in partnership with the Ministry of Labor and Social Policy (MoLSP) and partners, UNICEF supported expansion of child cash benefits increasing coverage and adequacy, strengthening income security for families with children and reinforcing social protection as a core investment in reducing child poverty and strengthening human capital, contributing to gendered poverty risks faced by women-led households. In RS, UNICEF supported the initiation of legislative revisions to enhance equity in child benefits. 
Disability inclusion advanced through institutional reform and scaled service delivery. In the FBiH, UNICEF’s long term partnership with cantonal authorities resulted in the institutionalization and full operationalization of the ICF-based child disability assessment and referral model in an additional canton. RS completed the piloting phase and prepared to advance this reform through system-wide adoption of functional assessment principles. As a result, approximately 700 children with disabilities and their families across three Cantons in FBiH and one region in RS benefited from improved assessment, referral and access to services. 
UNICEF played a catalytic role in embedding shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) into BiH’s policy and financing frameworks, contributing to the adoption of the country’s first locally funded emergency cash assistance scheme and the integration of SRSP as a core element of entity-level disaster risk reduction strategies and risk-assessment methodologies. Through technical leadership in child-sensitive and gender-responsive disaster risk analysis, UNICEF strengthened social-sector capacities to anticipate, plan for, and respond to shocks, while advancing climate-informed and inclusive social protection through the Green Transition & Jobs / Social Protection Accelerator in partnership with the World Bank, moving BiH closer to pathfinder status. In the City of Bihac, UNICEF supported the establishment and institutionalization of the first locally financed shock-responsive cash scheme, enabling rapid crisis activation through a regular municipal budget allocation. Building on this public financing mechanism, UNICEF further catalyzed an innovative expansion of SRSP through the Accelerator by launching the country’s first PPP for climate risk protection, bringing together social welfare services, municipal authorities, finance departments, the Mayor’s office, and private insurance providers to co-finance and subsidize climate risk insurance for vulnerable families. 
At the local level, UNICEF-supported SDG localization delivered tangible results through 14 Leave No One Behind projects implemented in nine local governments and five cantons, totaling BAM 2.16 million ($US 1.3 million), including 34 per cent co-financing from local and cantonal budgets, demonstrating strong domestic ownership. The interventions strengthened local governance and service delivery by operationalizing permanent multisectoral coordination mechanisms in seven locations and applying the Social Protection and Inclusion (SPI) model across eight local self-government units. As a result, new and improved inclusive services were introduced, directly benefiting 43,772 people—nearly half women—including 5,644 children—while targeted support reached 1,854 children and youth and 779 parents, and increased professional capacities of over 380 professional service providers, contributing to more coordinated, inclusive and sustainable local social protection systems.
 
Child rights monitoring and evidence-based advocacy 
UNICEF contributed to incremental yet meaningful improvements in BiH’s capacity to track, monitor, and report on children’s rights, including the integration of gender equality and non-discrimination principles, by addressing key bottlenecks in evidence generation, coordination, and data systems. 
A major achievement was integration of CRC priorities into the Action Plan for Children (APC) 2026–2030, which will serve as a central results framework for tracking progress across sectors. With UNICEF’s technical support, APC indicators were aligned with CRC domains, the SDGs, and UNICEF theories of change, strengthening coherence and measurability. In the FBiH, UNICEF also supported alignment between APC indicators and sectoral strategies, clarifying reporting responsibilities and laying the groundwork for consistent entity-level tracking. While full institutionalization of monitoring practices remains pending, this work strengthened system coherence. In parallel, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Human Rights and Refugees, in partnership with OHCHR, to establish the foundations of the EU-supported National Recommendations Tracking Database (NRTD). UNICEF strengthened the evidence base for CRC monitoring through the Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents (SitAn), which consolidated quantitative and qualitative data into a single comprehensive reference, providing updated sex-disaggregated baselines across key child sectors and informing policy dialogue, planning, and advocacy.
UNICEF supported the development and piloting of a Child Rights Education programme in Canton Sarajevo, integrated into the Grades 4–6 curricula, enabling children to formally learn for the first time about the Convention on the Rights of the Child, its core principles, and corresponding rights and obligations, including gender equality. In the first phase, 68 teachers implemented workshops benefiting 1,263 students. Following evaluation, the programme is planned for expansion to additional schools.
UNICEF strengthened its positioning and accountability with stakeholders by expanding sustainable financing through innovative partnerships (such as insurance companies), deepening private sector engagement and amplifying child rights advocacy. The BAC revival marked a key achievement, re-establishing it as a strategic platform for structured, high-level private sector engagement and advocacy on children’s rights, including gender equality and protection from violence, and laid foundation for longer-term corporate partnerships. UNICEF conducted a survey among 533 (357 female, 176 male) employees across 4 companies, members of the BAC, assessing the importance of preschool education for workplace productivity and to create recommendations for strengthening PPPs. The survey has also provided key insights and clear guidelines for future joint advocacy efforts around ECEC. Overall, the companies have shown strong interest in family-friendly policies and modeling the practices. 
A landmark result in sustainability and resource mobilization was the launch of UNICEF’s individual giving operation which exceeded year-end targets. The initiative reached over 1.5 million people, mobilized more than US$ 15,000, and established a base of 534 individual donors from the local population, contributing to a more diversified and resilient funding base. World Children’s Day 2025 served as a key advocacy event, mobilizing partners in a week-long campaign under the theme “Growing Together: From Voices to Action”. Through interconnected events across communities, academia and government institutions, children and young people were engaged as co-creators, moderators and advocates, contributing to a Youth Declaration articulating priorities for the next decade. The campaign increased public visibility of child rights, strengthened collaboration among municipalities, academia and authorities, and reinforced evidence-informed dialogue. Culminating in a high-level event on 20 November, World Children’s Day contributed to renewed political and public commitment to the CRC and positioned children’s rights at the centre of BiH policy and reform agenda.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
BiH made measurable progress in strengthening systems for children, yet persistent structural gaps, capacity constraints and fragmented financing continued to limit the pace and scale of results. Across sectors, UNICEF demonstrated adaptive and agile management, adjusting strategies in real time based on evidence, emerging risks and feedback from institutions and communities, particularly in response to outbreaks, shocks and service delivery bottlenecks affecting the most vulnerable children. 
System fragmentation remains a core constraint to achieving and sustaining results for children. This was most evident during the measles and pertussis outbreaks, which disproportionately affected cantons with the highest concentrations of zero-dose and under-immunized children, including Sarajevo, West Herzegovina, Zenica-Doboj, Tuzla and Una-Sana. While health sector gaps such as low coverage and uneven facility readiness were critical, response efforts were further constrained by weak linkages with education, social protection and communication systems, limiting timely outreach to families and vulnerable groups. Where UNICEF convened health authorities, education actors, social services, media partners and UN agencies, coordination improved, confirming that outbreak resilience depends on functional multisectoral collaboration rather than sector-specific and time-bound crisis response or campaign. Going forward, UNICEF will support institutionalizing multisectoral preparedness, including strengthening interoperable data systems, coordinated outreach mechanisms, partnerships between public institutions and civil society/community-based organizations as well as strengthening structured crisis communication by health authorities.
Across sectors, capacity and workforce shortages emerged as the most binding constraint to translating policy intent into services. In mental health, the limited availability of child and adolescent specialists, alongside outdated diagnostic tools and training curricula, constrained early and appropriate responses as needs emerged at increasingly younger ages. In child protection and social services, workforce gaps, particularly for disability assessment and family support, were identified as the primary obstacle to implementing reforms, even where legal frameworks were in place. These challenges highlighted a shared lesson: legislation and technical models cannot deliver impact without sustained investment in human capital. UNICEF’s experience confirmed the need for long-term, institutionalized training pathways, coordinated advocacy and evidence generation to ensure that workforce development is treated as a system priority rather than a project-based add-on.
Financing constraints and weak financial planning/budgeting capacity further limited the scale and sustainability of reforms. Development of 10-year education quality programmes revealed significant gaps in financial forecasting and developmental budgeting among education authorities, requiring UNICEF to provide tailored technical support. In early childhood education and care, advocacy confirmed that while evidence on returns on investment is essential, decision-makers also require practical financing pathways, particularly given the estimated ECEC financing gap of USD 714 million, equivalent to 0.52 per cent of GDP annually. At the same time, progress towards universal coverage of child benefits demonstrated that reform is possible even in constrained environments: in the Federation of BiH, benefit levels increased by 60 per cent, reaching nearly 11,000 additional children. The key lesson is that financing determines whether reforms remain aspirational or reach scale, reinforcing the need for UNICEF support to financial planning and child-responsive public finance reforms.
Efforts to advance digital transformation revealed both strong potential and persistent structural barriers. Digital initiatives in education demonstrated opportunities to improve equity and quality, but also exposed gaps in connectivity, infrastructure maintenance and institutional capacity. Similar challenges were evident across health, child protection and social protection, where fragmented administrative data systems and limited interoperability constrained planning, monitoring and coordination. Early initiatives such as the ADAMM and the NRTD confirmed that incremental improvements are possible, but also underscored that digital tools alone do not address inequities without governance, capacity and sustained investment. UNICEF will therefore prioritize long-term strengthening of routine administrative data systems, standardized monitoring practices and cross-sector interoperability.
Progress in policy and legislative reform highlighted both opportunity and fragility. Advances in drafting key social protection and social service laws—including the Law on Social Services, the Law on the Establishment of the Family Fund and the Law on the Social Service Workforce—demonstrated technical readiness, yet political impasses prevented adoption by year-end. In ECD and nutrition, reforms advanced but uneven implementation underscored the risks of limited institutionalization and unclear regulatory frameworks. The lesson from 2025 is that policy progress without sustained ownership and follow-through remains vulnerable, requiring continued engagement beyond drafting stages. UNICEF will therefore continue to focus on supporting implementation pathways, regulatory clarity and sustained institutional engagement to ensure reforms translate into improved services for the most vulnerable children and their families.
Finally, the transition toward a government-led migration and child protection response illustrated challenges of complex governance structures leading to delayed decision-making, unclear mandates and limited human capacity. UNICEF technical support contributed to planning solutions to address these bottlenecks, resulting in inclusion of migrant and refugee children. It also ensured a child rights-based approach was integrated, laying foundations for operationalizing solutions and budgeting services to ensure long-term sustainability and strengthening of the system for refugee/migrant children and families and the local population.
Through sustained engagement with authorities across security, migration and social welfare sectors, and coordination with EUD, IOM and UNHCR, UNICEF supported development of a formal child-centred transition action plan, expected to be adopted in early 2026. A key lesson is that continuity of services for children must remain non-negotiable during systemic transitions of donor-supported services to government.
The CO identified gaps in sex-disaggregated data and systematic use of gender analysis across sectors, limiting identification of gendered risks and outcomes. In response, UNICEF strengthened requirements for sex-disaggregated reporting and advanced cross-sectoral gender mainstreaming, in line with GEM-2/3 commitments, while highlighting the need for sustained investment in data, financing and partnerships to scale gender-responsive services.
Across all areas, 2025 reaffirmed UNICEF’s role as a convener—bringing together sectors, institutions and partners to strengthen coherence, and protect the most vulnerable children—while highlighting that sustained investment, coordination and leadership are essential to convert progress into durable, system-wide change. In response to these lessons, UNICEF introduced three leadership areas to sharpen strategic focus, strengthen cross sectoral coordination and reinforce its convening and influencing role, ensuring that evidence, partnerships and advocacy are more systematically aligned to drive integrated solutions and accelerate results for children

Bulgaria has a resident population of over 6,445,400, out of which 1.1 million are children (17 percent, NSI, 2024). The country’s population continued to decrease due to a combination of low birth rates, an aging population, and net emigration. As of 2024, more than 77.1 per cent of the population lived in urban areas. With a Human Development Index of 0.795 (2021), Bulgaria is in the high human development category, ranking 68 out of 191 countries. The gender development index is 0.995 (2021), which places Bulgaria in the group of countries with high equality in HDI achievements between women and men. With 58.1 points out of 100, Bulgaria continues to hold the 17th place in the EU on the Gender Equality Index.
  
At global level, Bulgaria continued be a strong voice for child rights as a co-chair of the ‘Group of Friends of Children and the SDGs’, member of UNICEF Executive Board (2023-2025) and second term member of the UN Human Rights Council (2024-2026). The promotion and protection of child rights remained a cross-cutting priority in Bulgaria’s Official Development Assistance, which continued to support bilateral initiatives for children in the Western Balkans and Eastern Partnership, as well as humanitarian responses in Afghanistan, Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Ukraine through multilateral channels, including UNICEF.

Bulgaria’s ODA is an integral part of its foreign policy, implemented in synergy with EU priorities. The ODA programme prioritizes regions of strategic importance - the Western Balkans, Eastern Partnership countries, the Middle East and North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Asia. Sectorally, Bulgaria concentrates its support on quality education and healthcare, good governance and civil society development, and economic growth, with protection of child rights serving as a cross-cutting priority. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs provides regular annual contributions to UNICEF’s core resources and has supported UNICEF programmes in Armenia and Georgia, as well as humanitarian responses in Afghanistan, Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Ukraine. In 2025, Bulgaria registered a four-fold increase in its core contributions - now accounting for nearly 30% of its total ODA to UNICEF.
  
Political Situation   
Bulgaria has been a member of the European Union since 2007 and was classified as a high-income country by the World Bank for Fiscal Year 2025. The country fully joined the Schengen Area on 1 January 2025 and entered the Eurozone by adopting the euro on 1 January 2026. Bulgaria is also an OECD candidate country, with accession expected in 2027.
  
In 2025, Bulgaria continued to experience significant political instability, characterized by a fragmented party system, low public trust, and large anti-government protests at the end of the year. Although the regular government of Prime Minister Rossen Zhelyazkov initially restored some predictability, it resigned in December 2025, reflecting the ongoing fragility of the political environment.
  
Against this backdrop of prolonged political instability and constrained policy continuity, UNICEF remained a trusted partner and reliable adviser to government institutions, providing consistent technical support across key child-related policy areas. Despite the frequent changes in national leadership, UNICEF continued to engage effectively with line ministries holding child-rights portfolios, ensuring that essential reforms and programmes remained on track. At the same time, UNICEF expanded its technical assistance to municipalities, many of which were less directly affected by the national-level political uncertainty.
  
Economy and Social Vulnerabilities    
In 2024, Bulgaria reached 66% of the EU average GDP per capita (PPP), showing steady but modest convergence. Growth continued in 2025 with GDP up 4.6% to USD 112.68 billion. Unemployment fell to 3.4%, but youth unemployment stayed at 8.7%, with a widening gender gap in school-to-work transitions. The NEET rate remained at 11%, and structural barriers persisted, especially for vulnerable groups. High inactivity among Roma and persons with disabilities, skills shortages, and low digital skills—only 35.5% with basic digital competencies—continued to limit inclusive growth.

In 2025, Bulgaria remained among EU countries facing major risks to social convergence, with high income inequality (Gini 38.4, 2024), deep regional divides, and persistent poverty. Child poverty was especially acute: 35.1% of children were at risk of poverty or social exclusion, the highest rate in the EU. While severe deprivation declined slightly, many families still faced financial insecurity and limited access to essential services, underscoring the need for child-sensitive social protection and more integrated support.

Refugee Response
In 2025, Bulgaria continued to feel the impact of the war in Ukraine and regional instability, remaining both a host and major transit country. By year’s end, about 80,000 Ukrainians lived in Bulgaria under temporary protection, while over 2.3 million had transited the country since the conflict began and 223,000+ had received temporary protection. Bulgaria also received asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and North Africa, though new registrations dropped sharply. This decline was tied to Bulgaria’s full Schengen accession on 1 January 2025, which enabled easier onward movement. While this reduced pressure on national systems, it increased unreported entries and departures, heightening risks for unaccompanied children travelling without safeguards.

Humanitarian needs persisted for both Ukrainian refugees and other asylum seekers. Rising onward movement made reception capacity unpredictable and service gaps continued. Unaccompanied and separated children faced significant difficulties accessing education, healthcare, alternative care and child-sensitive procedures. Some were still detained despite legal prohibitions, and reception conditions remained below standards, with heavy reliance on the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) and EUAA. Bulgaria was included in both the Regional Refugee Response Plan for Ukraine and the UNICEF Regional Humanitarian Appeal for Children.

Child Rights and Climate
The complex political context in 2025 prompted  renewed efforts to strengthen child-rights advocacy. National dialogue on  children’s issues expanded through deeper engagement with academia, civil  society and young people. Following the 2024 Concluding Observations of the  Committee on the Rights of the Child, the Government—after consultations  across relevant institutions, including the Ministry of Environment and Water  - developed a comprehensive Action Plan to monitor progress and implement the  CRC recommendations.
  
Bulgaria also presented its second Voluntary National Review on the SDGs and underwent its regular Universal Periodic Review, both underscoring the situation of children and the need to reinforce child-rights safeguards.

Every child is protected from violence and have access to services in early years 
In 2025, UNICEF continued to support the government institutions in enhancing the legal and policy framework, governance, and coordination in Early Childhood Development (ECD), Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC), and Child Protection (CP) systems. This support contributed to several key policies, programmes, and action plans.

In 2025, UNICEF’s support contributed to a measurable shift toward a more coherent and effective national ECD system in Bulgaria. Improved intersectoral coordination, stronger policy alignment, and expanded professional capacity across health, education and social services enhanced access to quality support for young children and their families. The scale-up of early childhood intervention (ECI) services, reform of home-visiting models, and the launch of national learning platforms for parents and professionals helped advance a more equitable, prevention-oriented and family-centred approach. Together, these efforts laid a sustainable foundation for earlier identification of developmental risks, higher-quality services and better outcomes for all children - particularly those in vulnerable situations.
The joint project with the Ministry of Education and Science, funded by SG Reform, is accelerating reforms in quality education and informing the draft Ordinance on Managing the Quality of Pre-school and School Education. An “as-is” analysis of governance and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems related to quality in early childhood education and care (ECEC), along with a review of good practices from other EU Member States, was completed. Building on this groundwork, a concept and a framework for monitoring and evaluating ECEC quality were developed, and piloting of the new tools has begun, with completion expected in 2026. This initiative is helping to advance a more coherent, evidence-based approach to improving education quality nationwide.

To advance childcare reform, UNICEF, together with International Social Service–Bulgaria and Veliko Tarnovo Municipality, co-organized the National Residential Care Conference in November 2025, held under the patronage of the Minister of Labour and Social Policy. Bringing together over 200 participants, the conference reviewed progress, identified remaining challenges, and set out a renewed vision for public and residential care, including support for care leavers. Its report will be submitted to the National Council for Child Protection, the National Council on Social Inclusion, and the Social Policy Committee of Parliament.

UNICEF also supported amendments to the Ordinance on the Quality of Social Services, finalized in November, which clarify staffing requirements and will guide MLSP in developing new financial standards under the Social Services Act.

In 2025, UNICEF initiated validation of a new training programme on interpersonal communication and community engagement for social workers, developed with Columbia University’s School of Social Work and the Global Health Research Center of Central Asia. The programme is being piloted in Sofia, Plovdiv and Kazanlak, involving 90 professionals across different sectors.

In 2025, UNICEF Bulgaria strengthened systemic responses to violence against children through policy reform, capacity building and the expansion of integrated services. The office contributed to the development of two national action plans - on violence prevention and on child marriage - and enhanced the State Agency for Child Protection’s capacity to manage the National Child Helpline. The multidisciplinary “Zona ZaKrila” model was scaled up to eight additional regions, providing integrated support to 442 girls, 333 boys, and 660 parents.

UNICEF also advanced national efforts to prevent and respond to online child sexual abuse. The Safer Internet Centre processed 3.6 million reports of illegal content, referred 188,954 cases to the Cybercrime Directorate, and provided direct assistance to 56 children and 64 parents. A national self-assessment of online safety policies was launched to strengthen systemic prevention. To address gender stereotypes and prevent domestic violence, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Education to pilot a school-based programme on gender equality and healthy relationships for 8th–9th graders in five schools.

UNICEF also strengthened child-friendly justice through evidence generation, advocacy and targeted capacity building. A national study on children with offending behaviour and those in conflict with the law was completed, providing a critical evidence base to inform upcoming legislative and policy reforms and improvements to programmes and services. Through civil society partnerships, UNICEF supported 90 legal aid cases and 12 strategic litigations, while contributing to policy dialogue on shared parenting and amendments to the Family Code. Capacity-building efforts included training 63 lawyers on child-friendly justice and domestic and gender-based violence, and 108 law enforcement officers on child rights - laying the foundation for institutionalized training for judges and prosecutors in 2026.

UNICEF’s response for refugee and migrant children in 2025 combined direct support with systems strengthening. Across six locations, 8,102 children and 5,626 caregivers received child protection and MHPSS support, while over 3,500 additional children were reached with integrated protection and education services through partnerships with the municipalities of Ruse, Stara Zagora and Burgas. UNICEF identified 280 unaccompanied and separated children (UASCs) in detention, secured their release, and ensured alternative care for more than 100 of them. The Safe Zone in Harmanli - established with UNICEF support and hosting 1,113 UASCs - was formally handed over to IOM. UNICEF advanced inclusive service delivery by piloting Laaha for Ukrainian women and girls and supported legal aid through 19 strategic litigation cases, securing 15 successful rulings on family reunification and access to family benefits.

Bulgaria’s 2025 entry into the Schengen Area reshaped migration dynamics, facilitating onward movement and heightening risks for children on the move - especially UASC. UNICEF engaged with government and EU institutions through high-level EU Pact discussions, national Schengen dialogues, and coordination with FRA, EUAA and Frontex Fundamental Rights Officers to reinforce safeguards at borders and reception centres. UNICEF supported key policy and legislative processes to align Bulgaria with the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, including procedural guarantees for children and proposals for guardianship reform. Capacity-building efforts expanded, with 63 lawyers, 12 UASC representatives, and 38 child protection and social service professionals trained, alongside the launch of a new four-year AMIF partnership with SAR to strengthen alternative care, case management and foster-care outreach for UASCs.

Despite these advancements, persistent gaps in reception conditions, overstretched institutional capacities and limited coordination continued to undermine the quality and consistency of protection for children on the move. Addressing these systemic challenges remains central to UNICEF’s ongoing humanitarian engagement in Bulgaria.

Based on the newly developed guidance on PSEA, child safeguarding and GBV risk mitigation, UNICEF rolled out training for 21 staff from 15 new implementing partners, delivered an additional workshop for 9 participants, and trained 10 staff of the National Child Helpline 116 111. In total, 40 partner staff strengthened their capacity on PSEA reporting requirements and safeguarding procedures.

Every Child Learns and Participates
In 2025, UNICEF Bulgaria strengthened the national education system through sustained advocacy, technical expertise, and strong partnerships, expanding access to inclusive, safe, and high quality learning opportunities for vulnerable children and adolescents. Across programmes focusing on skills development, digital literacy, inclusive education, violence prevention, and emergency support, UNICEF directly benefited 11,262 boys and 11,055 girls, while 1,631 professionals and parents enhanced their knowledge and skills in violence prevention, social emotional learning, youth engagement, civic participation, mentoring, and parental support for children with disabilities.

Progress in inclusive education advanced through sustained system level work and direct support to educators and families. The “Voice for Every Child” initiative convened over 120 specialists to exchange effective practices in augmentative and alternative communication and to identify regulatory and methodological needs for sustainable integration of AAC approaches advancing inclusion of children with disabilities. Professional learning communities established under the initiative were institutionalized within regional education processes, helping ensure continuity and peer support. UNICEF further initiated a situational analysis of inclusive education policies to guide future reforms. Support to Centres for Special Educational Support combined systemic assessments with tailored family focused services, delivering assistance to 267 children with disabilities, 57 specialists, and 266 parents through capacity building and the Workshops for Parents+ programme.

UNICEF strengthened quality education by supporting national modernization efforts. Collaboration with the National Education Inspectorate resulted in the development and piloting of an innovative inspection model that links external inspection with internal school self evaluation, supported by new tools and procedures grounded in international evidence. Literacy development remained a priority: the Future 2.0 Literacy Forum mobilized national experts to address declining reading performance, while a complementary initiative expanded early reading opportunities through children’s literature, reading corners, clubs, and professional learning communities, promoting inclusive approaches and accessible materials for diverse learners.

UNICEF advanced violence prevention and student well being by strengthening safe and positive learning environments. Through the Steps Together programme, mentors across 28 Regional Inclusive Education Centres supported 42 schools and four kindergartens, reaching 4,382 boys and 4,052 girls with practices that integrate anti bullying protocols, disability aware peer support and accessible reporting channels. Expanded work on online safety and digital literacy informed significant public investment, contributing to an annual allocation of €327,231 and an EU co-financed call of €17.8 million for broadening national reach. UNICEF also supported digital well being policy development through the Erasmus+ TechWell project, promoting safer and more accessible digital environments for all learners.

In 2025, UNICEF worked with national and local partners to advance youth-focused interventions and expand access to skills development and civic engagement opportunities, with a strong emphasis on adolescent girls and boys from vulnerable and disadvantaged communities. UNICEF and its partners directly engaged 830 adolescents in non-formal learning, civic engagement activities, environmental initiatives, and volunteering, while strengthening school-based and local mechanisms for child and youth participation. Young people played a key role in adapting UNICEF’s Youth Advocacy Guide to the Bulgarian context, ensuring it reflects local realities and promotes meaningful youth engagement.

Through UNICEF’s programme UPSHIFT 1,072 adolescents aged 14–19 developed essential life skills and entrepreneurial mindsets while designing solutions to address pressing community challenges. Youth-led initiatives under the programme reached over 52,000 individuals through offline and digital activities, fostering broad community support for adolescent-driven solutions. Additionally, 136 professionals, including youth workers, educators, and mediators, enhanced their capacities through targeted training and activities to advance meaningful youth engagement and participation.

UNICEF supported the Ministry of Youth and Sports in conducting a mid-term review of the National Youth Strategy 2021–2030. The final report, including recommendations to strengthen national youth policies, programmes, and the monitoring and evaluation framework, will be released in 2026. Furthermore, UNICEF facilitated the participation of representatives from the Youth Policy Directorate in a JPAL international  capacity-building workshops on evidence-based policymaking, monitoring, and impact evaluation.

In 2025, over 6,917 children with temporary protection were enrolled in the Bulgarian education system across hundreds of kindergartens and schools. However, data from the Ministry of Education and Science shows that only 1,087 children received additional Bulgarian language instruction - just 15% of those enrolled. Given the importance of language acquisition for successful integration, UNICEF continued to prioritize Bulgarian language learning and catch-up support. UNICEF-supported programmes reached 10,518 children with formal and non-formal learning opportunities and 5,722 children received learning materials.

Throughout the reporting period, summer preparatory programmes were implemented in Sofia, Stara Zagora, Burgas and Varna, offering enrolment support, intensive language learning, subject preparation, recreational activities, and MHPSS services ahead of the 2025/2026 school year.
State-funded transportation for children under temporary protection continued in Burgas, Varna, and Dobrich. UNICEF also advocated for expanded access to Bulgarian language education in the proposed amendments to the Law on Pre-school and School Education. The amendments include new forms of language support, such as a preparatory class.

Every child’s right is protected and has access to social protection and services

Throughout the year, sustained engagement with national authorities highlighted children’s heightened vulnerability to climate change. In 2025, UNICEF strengthened national child rights monitoring by supporting government institutions, civil society, academia, and independent oversight bodies. NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

Strategic Partnerships as Catalysts for Systemic Change in a High Income Context
UNICEF’s long-standing cooperation with government institutions and the European Commission has established it as a reliable and strategic partner in Bulgaria. The Country Programme Evaluation, commissioned by ECARO and conducted in 2025, highlighted UNICEF’s hybrid approach as a core strength, combining high-level policy engagement with targeted pilots and models. These locally implemented initiatives generate practical evidence that reinforces the credibility of UNICEF’s policy recommendations and supports a more constructive, evidence-based dialogue with decision-makers.

Through initiatives such as child advocacy centres, the EU Child Guarantee, Steps Together, and Home Visiting Nurses, UNICEF has reinforced its role as a knowledgeable resource on child rights and an effective convener across sectors. Despite periods of political instability and frequent changes in government, UNICEF contributed to continuity in national programmes and helped keep key reforms moving forward.

Building on this experience, UNICEF will continue to strengthen its strategic positioning within Bulgaria’s high-income context. As the country prepares to absorb substantial EU and donor investments, UNICEF will deepen its role as a trusted technical partner in the design, rollout, and evaluation of large-scale programmes that benefit children and families.

Over 2025–2029, UNICEF will operationalize the four-year AMIF-supported initiative with SAR, municipalities, and IOM to enhance national capacity for alternative care and foster family recruitment for unaccompanied refugee children. Parallel to this, UNICEF will advance the two support measures under the Bulgarian–Swiss Programme on Migration—totalling USD 8.27 million—while preparing for programme launch following parliamentary ratification in 2026.

Through the Swiss–Bulgarian Cooperation Programme, UNICEF will continue its collaboration with the Ministry of Health to strengthen national systems for health promotion and noncommunicable disease prevention among children and adolescents. Concurrently, ongoing negotiations under the EEA Grants will aim to secure EUR 3 million for a comprehensive national initiative that expands adolescents’ and young people’s access to learning, skills development, and civic engagement—scaling up models such as UPSHIFT and integrating digital, green, and AI-related competencies.

Municipal capacities at the core of expanding child Services and innovations
Strengthening municipal capacities is fundamental for scaling child-focused services and achieving sustainable impact at the local level. UNICEF’s deepening collaboration with municipalities has focused on building their ability to design, deliver and expand high-quality services for the most vulnerable children. Through targeted technical assistance, joint modelling of innovative approaches and support for evidence-informed decision-making, municipal partners have taken the lead in expanding early childhood intervention (ECI) services, advancing the Barnahus/Zona ZaKrila model, and piloting the new Zona ZaKrila+ service.

Enhanced local capacities also enabled the rollout of UPSHIFT+ and the launch of efforts to establish alternative care services for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) in four municipalities. UNICEF further initiated new partnerships with three municipalities to strengthen their planning and governance capacities through the participatory development and implementation of Local Action Plans for the European Child Guarantee, including structured engagement with local businesses as key stakeholders.

Need for a Shared Framework to Operationalize Integrated Support
Piloting of integrated services in Bulgaria—including Child Advocacy Centres, early childhood intervention (ECI) services, and other cross-sectoral measures—has demonstrated significant potential to improve outcomes for children and families. However, these experiences revealed that the lack of a shared terminology and a coherent operational framework for integrated support substantially constrains the effectiveness, scalability, and sustainability of such initiatives.

While the Social Services Act introduces important concepts such as an integrated approach, coordinated service provision, and cross-sectoral services, it does not clarify how these principles should work in practice. The absence of unified procedures, governance arrangements, and financing mechanisms leaves municipalities and service providers without the practical tools needed to ensure consistent application and coordination across sectors.

UNICEF review of EU and national practices, identified promising models of integrated support and highlighted valuable lessons for Bulgaria. At the same time, the analysis underscored a persistent gap: good practices are not yet translated into an actionable, context-appropriate framework that can guide policy, planning, and implementation at scale. Developing such a shared framework—grounded in evidence, aligned with legislation, and feasible for local authorities—is essential for advancing integrated services that deliver sustained impact for children and families.

Engaging Adolescents as Co-Creators Strengthens the Impact of Youth Programmes
Experience in 2025 showed that meaningful youth engagement is most effective when adolescents are not only participants but active co-creators of programmes and tools. Involving young people - especially those from vulnerable communities- in shaping initiatives such as the Youth Advocacy Guide ensured greater relevance, ownership, and impact. Equally, structured opportunities like UPSHIFT or Steps Together demonstrated that when adolescents are empowered to design solutions to real school or community challenges, they build essential life skills while generating wider social benefits. Strengthening the capacities of educators and youth workers further amplified these outcomes, creating supportive environments that sustain meaningful participation. Overall, investing in youth-led processes proved critical for fostering empowerment, civic engagement, and long-term community change.

Strategic, multi-channel advocacy and communication drive visibility, influence, and programmatic gains
The experience in 2025 demonstrated that a strategic, data-driven, and partnership-based approach to advocacy and communication can significantly amplify UNICEF’s influence, visibility, and ability to mobilize support for child rights. By combining strong media partnerships, integrated campaigns, and high-profile events with coordinated engagement across government, the diplomatic community, private sector, and National Committees, UNICEF Bulgaria strengthened its public positioning and translated communication reach into tangible programmatic results. A key learning is that high-quality storytelling, credible evidence, and cross-sector alliances substantially enhance public trust and positive institutional perception.

Family Separation Risks Arising from Restrictive Housing Rules for Ukrainian Refugees
A key challenge in the Ukraine refugee response in 2025 was the narrow eligibility criteria for state supported accommodation. These restrictive rules often led to family separations, as only certain household members were deemed “vulnerable” while others were not. The issue was particularly pronounced for children and persons with disabilities who lacked Bulgarian issued documentation to verify their disability status. As a result, many families were left without stable access to support and were forced into fragmented or insecure housing arrangements.

However, according to the National Security and Intelligence Agency’s 2025 annual report, radicalization and extremism poses a major threat to stability, while extremist ideas are most often promoted among young people and minors. [4]
The at-risk-of-poverty and the persistent at-risk-of-poverty rates for children (0–17 years) both grew: from 16.1 per cent in 2023 to 18.3 per cent in 2024 (higher for girls), and from 15.6 per cent in 2023 to 17.7 per cent in 2024 respectively. However, severe material and social deprivation rate for children showed a decreasing trend from 1.8 per cent in 2023 to 1.2 per cent in 2024 (below EU average). [5] These three indicators of relative poverty signal raising inequalities in society, despite the overall positive impact of GDP growth. The Government’s commitment to addressing child poverty and inequities continues through the implementation of the European Child Guarantee National Action Plan. 
Roma children remain among the most vulnerable to rising inequalities, facing persistent poverty, segregation, insufficient educational inclusion, and lack of community services. Elementary school dropout numbers among Roma pupils continue to rise, and transition rates from elementary to secondary school remain very low, far below the national average, at 14% in 2024. [6] In certain parts of Croatia there are still fully ethnically segregated classes. 
The Not-In-Education, Employment or Training (NEET) rate for adolescents (15-19) continues to drop, from 8.5 per cent in 2022 to 5.8 per cent in 2024, still higher for boys (6.3 per cent) than girls (5.2 per cent). [7] 
Croatia continued to invest in early childhood education (ECE) enrolment. The most recent enrolment rate for children aged 4 - 7 is 89 per cent, with a national objective set at 97 per cent by 2030. [8] In addition to the Governments’ financial support for kindergartens channeled to municipalities, sub-national authorities continue to invest in ECEC infrastructure, mainly through EU funding.
Since the beginning of the conflict in Ukraine, 32,455 Ukrainian citizens requested temporary protection. However, due to unreliable data on entries and departures (especially since Croatia joined the Schengen Area), it is difficult to determine how many of these persons still reside in Croatia. By September 30, over 20,532 international protection applicants (IPA) were accommodated in reception centres, with 29% women and 37% children (out of which 32% girls). Most IPAs (>75%) came from Syria, Turkey, Russia, and Afghanistan. Despite seeking asylum in Croatia, most IPAs remain very briefly before moving on to western Europe. Although IPA numbers halved from 2023 (43,099), the number of identified unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) rose significantly to 1,980 (3 per cent girls) compared to 2023 (1,516). There has been a steady increase in Ukrainian refugees benefiting from temporary protection since 2023, totalling 28,070 individuals - 64% women and girls, and 30% children.
Since 2020, the number of reported crimes perpetrated by children is rising, with an annual growth rate of over 19 per cent in 2024. This poses a significant burden for the juvenile justice system and underscores the importance of enhanced prevention and rehabilitation measures.  [9]
The number of children in detention and transition reception centres also increased from 179 (2023) to 253 (Q3 2024), with 41 per cent of girls and 41 per cent of children under the age of 7.[10] The number of unaccompanied minors who applied for international protection continues to rise, with peak 1,980 cases recorded in 2024. [11] 
The Government continued to strengthen the child protection system resulting in an increased number of children living with their biological families who are supported by child protection specialists and case managers, from 8,622 (2022) to 12,852 (2023). EU funds improved access to family- and community-based services and introduced new support mechanisms for at-risk families. However, challenges remain in preventing child-family separation, gatekeeping and deinstitutionalization.
 The proportion of children in family-based care decreased from 59 per cent in 2022 to 53,3 per cent in 2024, while the number of children in residential care increased from 203 in 2022 to 256 in 2024, following several tragic incidents since 2021 involving the deaths of several children returned to, or insufficiently protected from unsafe family environments. [12]
According to the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE), Croatia scores 57.1 points in the Gender Equality Index 2025, which places it as 21st among the EU member states, and significantly below the EU score (63.4). Croatia scores particularly low in the category of women in positions of power (21.8). [13]
