During 2025, UNICEF Croatia—working in close collaboration with the Government of the Republic of Croatia, civil society, private sector and academia—has delivered comprehensive results across the Country Programme Document’s areas by convening key stakeholders, forging innovative partnerships, and scaling effective interventions. 
In 2025, UNICEF’s strategic partnership with the Government of Croatia delivered high-impact results, accelerating progress on Early Childhood Development priorities outlined in the Child Guarantee National Action Plan. The approach focused on policy reforms, institutionalizing professional capacity, and fostering knowledge exchange, leveraging UNICEF’s role as a trusted technical partner and convener. This ensured sustainable improvements in integrated Early Childhood Interventions (ECI), equitable Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC), and nutrition, while addressing systemic issues like stigma, discrimination and gender disparities. These efforts improved development outcomes for over 16,803 at-risk young children, supported 1,676 caregivers, enhanced the skills of 1,744 professionals and decision-makers, and reached more than 122,132 parents, including migrant families, through online platforms.
A key policy milestone was the final draft of the National Early Childhood Intervention Strategic and Action Plan (2026–2030). Through technical assistance and a consultative process involving over 300 stakeholders, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health (MoH) toward this foundational framework to scale up quality ECI services. This policy marks a shift from fragmented services to a cohesive, cross-sectoral ‘one family, one plan’ approach. If approved in 2026, the Plan is expected to benefit more than 25,000 children who may be at risk of developmental delays and disabilities, representing about 10.5% of all children between the ages of 0 and 5. Additionally, with the financial support from the Swiss Confederation, UNICEF supported the strengthening of the screening protocols for asylum seekers, along with tools and know-how for early identification of vulnerable migrant children and caregivers. 
At the same time, UNICEF reinforced the foundational capacity for the new National ECI system by training 222 ECD professionals in evidence-based, gender- and culture-sensitive early detection and intervention. These efforts have already enhanced specialized support for 1,124 young children and 1,923 caregivers, and ensured a skilled, inclusive workforce is ready to implement the national policy framework. Additionally, with the financial support from the Swiss Confederation, UNICEF supported the strengthening of the screening protocols for asylum seekers, along with tools and know-how for early identification of vulnerable migrant children and caregivers. 
Furthermore, UNICEF secured national accreditation and permanent deployment of a standardized online professional development course ECEC educations and 90 ECEC educators working with refugee and migrant children have already taken the course. This institutionalizes intercultural competency and improves learning environments for an estimated 1,800 young children.
In parallel, UNICEF partnered with the Croatian Employers’ Association (HUP) and the Ministry of Demography and Immigration (MDI) to institutionalize the Family-Friendly Business Practices framework, elevating family support from voluntary initiatives to a scalable national model.  In 2025, two large workshops for parents of young children and (separately, through the CSR Academy) for adolescents, brought together more than 70 companies reaching  450 parents of 718 children. 
 The “Communication for Every Child” initiative has greatly expanded access to assistive technology by scaling the open-source AAC application, CBoard, to reach 10,159 users with complex communication needs. In partnership with MoH and two clinical hospitals, UNICEF is launching a scalable e-learning program to address critical skill gaps in AAC use within hospital settings. So far, this effort has strengthened the capacity of 244 healthcare professionals. 
UNICEF partnered with the Croatian Institute of Public Health (CIPH) to advance implementation of the Obesity Prevention Action Plan, embed preventive measures into the  health care system, and align legal compliance on marketing breastmilk substitutes with EU standards. UNICEF and CIPH developed an accredited and sustainable capacity strengthening ecosystem on nutrition and obesity, reaching 1,567 ECD professionals across the education, health and social welfare sectors. A national educational programme was launched to address the skills gaps of 130 primary healthcare physicians in preventing childhood obesity, to provide guidance to parents on healthy nutritional habits. Furthermore, guidelines and training for school cooks to improve the quality of school nutrition nationwide were developed. Lastly, UNICEF generated evidence through a research on unhealthy food marketing around schools, the findings of which will inform future policy reforms.
The comprehensive online Parenting Hub maintained strong engagement, reaching over 106,000 parents and caregivers with expert, gender-equitable guidance and promoting responsive caregiving. In parallel, through the “Parenting in Croatia” platform, UNICEF connected with 16,038 unique users. By offering culturally sensitive, gender-transformative content—from health to legal advice—the platform has become a lifeline for migrant and refugee families. This digital intervention closes information gaps, empowering vulnerable populations to navigate complex systems, claim their rights, and access essential services.
The programme “Growing up Together”, developed in partnership with the Ministry of Labour, Pension System, Family and Social Policy (MLPFSP), provided structured support to over 550 families in difficult circumstances through workshops for parents of children aged 3-6 in 2025, and has been formally integrated into a wide range of national statutory services, including those provided in kindergartens, Family Centre, private sector,  ensuring future sustainability and scale. 
To support the government’s efforts to strengthen an inclusive education system, UNICEF collaborated with the University of Zagreb, the Education and Teacher Training Agency, and the Croatian Academic and Research Network to develop, pilot, test, and establish 20 online modules for in-service professional development on inclusive and intercultural pedagogies. This partnership also produced a free online course aimed at continuous professional development for teachers, headteachers, and professional associates working with refugee and migrant students in secondary education across the country. Based on a 2024 needs assessment involving educators and students, the 10-module programme is now available nationwide. 
In partnership with central and local authorities, as well as through community engagement and collaboration with implementing CSO partners, UNICEF has reached 27 per cent of adolescents in Croatia—over 100,000 young people (out of an estimated 368,000, according to the Croatian Statistics Office) across all the interventions tackling mental health, skills building, education, and participation. Of these, more than 51,000 adolescents and youth participated in initiatives promoting meaningful participation and civic engagement, financially supported and politically endorsed by local public authorities. UNICEF supported programs to address mental health for over 36,000 primary and secondary school students, reached 9,600 students in peer violence prevention, and additional 3,000 students through other targeted interventions. Additionally, over 7,000 teachers enhanced their pedagogical practices to build student skills grounded in equity, inclusion, and gender-transformative principles.
UNICEF  prioritized the empowerment of adolescent girls and the promotion of gender equality as key drivers of broader social transformation.  In 2025, thanks to successful leveraging of investment from local authorities, UNICEF has expanded the UPSHIFT programme to all 48 schools founded by Varazdin County, which promoted gender-responsive solutions to persistent barriers faced by girls in education, employment, and leadership, and improve students’  life skills, entrepreneurship, problem-solving and resilience. Advocacy efforts in 2025 with local authorities in  Istria, Medjimurje and Sisak-Moslavina counties to implement and locally invest in UPSHIFT are expected to lead to its expansion in those counties. 
As schools struggle to incorporate the growing need to support students’ mental health and wellbeing, UNICEF has expanded the Schools of Support programme to schools in five counties (Sisak-Moslavina, Varazdin, Medjimurje, Koprivnica-Krizevci and Bjelovar-Podravina) to reach over 36,000 students. Since 2021, the programme developed a network of 92 schools across the five counties so schools can provide peer-support to one another and to new schools under the guidance and quality assurance of UNICEF’s implementing partner. The programme targets school leadership and teachers separately, to improve leadership capacity and enhance teachers’ pedagogic competences relating to mental health, resilience and wellbeing. To ensure a sustainable expansion of the Schools of Support initiative, UNICEF intensified advocacy efforts with national and local authorities to ensure its inclusion in their plans and budgets.
Between 2024 and 2025, UNICEF updated its violence prevention program, “For a Safe and Enabling School Environment,” and launched a pilot initiative in partnership with the City of Zagreb, co-financing under its 2024–2026 Action Plan for the Prevention of Peer Violence Among Children. The initiative applied gender-responsive strategies to reflect the distinct ways boys and girls experience and perpetrate violence, while strengthening teachers’ relational competencies and promoting socio-emotional learning among students. To date, 26 schools have joined the program, and teacher resources have been developed and tested to support implementation. Reaching over 9,600 students and 1,105 teachers and other school professionals, the programme lays the groundwork for systemic change; its effectiveness is jointly monitored and evaluated by UNICEF and the City of Zagreb to ensure future scale-up and sustainability.
As part of efforts to systematically promote meaningful participation of young people in education, UNICEF supported the development of national policy guidelines for student councils in Croatia, applicable across primary and secondary education. The guidelines were developed through an analysis of the existing institutional and legal framework governing student councils and the identification of policy recommendations to strengthen their effectiveness, representativeness and influence in school decision-making processes.
A major nationwide achievement was the implementation of Media Literacy Days, delivered in partnership with the Agency for Electronic Media, the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Science, Education and Youth (MoSEY). The initiative engaged more than 37,000 adolescents and young people through over 730 events and more than 2,100 activities held across 191 cities and towns throughout Croatia. Nearly 400 primary and secondary schools participated, creating wide geographic and socio-economic reach. The activities this year focused on artificial intelligence, misinformation and digital risks. 
Amid persistent migration challenges, UNICEF prioritized strengthening child protection systems and supporting the integration of vulnerable children, including displaced persons from Ukraine and unaccompanied minors. Thanks to the Swiss Confederation’s contribution, UNICEF partnered with national authorities, Ombudsman Offices and 22 implementing organizations to provide timely, coordinated assistance. More than 7,000 children accessed protection, mental health and psychosocial services, while 858 unaccompanied children received individualized care, including guardianship and inclusive family and community-based support. Mental health and psychosocial services reached an additional 2,286 children and families, including through a newly developed multilingual counselling chat service. Specialized training strengthened the capacities of nearly 1,200 professionals across social welfare, education, health and asylum systems to identify and respond to risks such as gender-based violence and trafficking. UNICEF also generated evidence on benefit adequacy and service access for migrant children and families, informing recommendations for improved social protection.
Between 2023 and 2025, nearly 2,000 UASC were identified and protected in alternative care. Generated evidence on UASC experiences guided the development of specialized short-term interventions and expansion of family- and community-based services. UNICEF supported guardianship reforms, improved access to foster care for UASC, and co-created guidelines for organized living arrangements (small-scale residential care). Intercultural mediators were introduced in reception and care settings to strengthen inclusion and service quality. 
Supporting Croatia’s national deinstitutionalization agenda remained a core priority. In partnership with the MLPSFSP, UNICEF focused on improving the quality of care by scaling up specialized interventions for girls and boys. Foster care capacities were strengthened through training for nine foster care team members across three counties in licensing, monitoring and supporting foster families, enabling better responses to the needs of 73 foster carers and 70 children, with materials made permanently available for national use. Nearly 90 education and health professionals in Split Dalmatia and Zadar Counties were also trained to meet the specific needs of children in alternative care. Awareness raising activities expanded the pool of potential foster carers, with new license applications indicating growing public interest. 
In partnership with MLPSFSP and the Faculty of Education and Rehabilitation Sciences at the University of Zagreb, UNICEF launched the two-year Programme CARE, aimed at enhancing accessibility and quality of family- and community-based services for children at risk of separation or already in alternative care. Within this framework, assessments of county social plans have been conducted to improve methodology of county service planning, initiating policy dialogues at the highest levels of government and plans for pilots in three counties expected in 2026. The CARE programme also supported the scale-up of specialized interventions for adolescents with complex needs by strengthening the capacities of 97 professionals from the social welfare and justice systems across 15 counties. These efforts directly benefited 147 adolescents (83 girls and 64 boys), ensuring access to these interventions for more than 1,700 adolescents in alternative care. UNICEF also worked to engage both women and men as foster carers to ensure diverse role models, strengthened the participation of young people in alternative care through the Youth Advisory Board, and advocated for establishing a National Youth Advisory Council within the National Plan for Children’s Rights.
In 2025, UNICEF conducted a study on parental knowledge, attitudes, practices, and socio-cultural and gender norms related to violence against children within families. Findings showed that one in two children in Croatia is exposed to violent child-rearing practices, and about 25% of parents continue to accept corporal punishment despite its legal ban since 1998. The study also identified gendered patterns—fathers and parents with lower education were more likely to view violent discipline as effective. These insights informed the development of an Advocacy Strategy, a Social and Behavioural Change Strategy, and a new parenting support programme for parents of adolescents, promoting non-violent, gender-equitable caregiving. To support violence prevention and positive parenting, a digital resource package was launched on the Parenting web hub, reaching 1.3 million views on social media. The study positioned UNICEF as a key partner to the Government and stakeholders to scale evidence-based interventions that challenge harmful norms, empower caregivers, and create environments where every child can thrive free from violence.
UNICEF Croatia strengthened corporate accountability for children’s rights by securing the adoption of the Code for the Protection and Promotion of Children’s Rights in the Digital Environment by the country’s three largest telecom companies, advancing national and global priorities on child online safety. This achievement, enabled by UNICEF’s convening power and long-standing partnerships, reflects strategic engagement through the Advisory Board on Children’s Rights and CSR and outreach to over 1,500 companies on ESG integration and family-friendly policies through participation in 13 national business conferences. Advancing these gender-responsive business practices positioned UNICEF as a leader in embedding children’s rights into sustainability frameworks. 
Through strategic communication, in 2025 the CO effectively positioned critical issues affecting children, youth and families on the public agenda, achieving record-high media engagement with 3,045 media reports (20% growth) and a 46% increase on national TV, supported by an extensive multimedia portfolio. In cooperation with partners, communication activities contributed to the engagement of 96,432 people, including 89,973 children, adolescents and youth, to participate in advocacy, communication, skills development, learning about child rights and civic engagement activities.   
UNICEF continued to leverage resources for child-focused programmes beyond the national borders, through the strategic cooperation with the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs, signing its first multi-annual Official Development Assistance (ODA) agreement for the period 2025–2027 for Moldova and initiating five new ODA-supported projects in Kenya, Moldova, Gaza, Jordan and Lebanon, totaling €1.9 million. The new partnership with the European Parliament and the engagement with Croatian MEPs further strengthened UNICEF’s role in promoting child rights and social inclusion regionally and globally.
UNICEF supported leveraging EU technical and financial instruments for effective implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG), which aims to improve availability, quality and access to essential services for children at risk of poverty and social exclusion. Building on the successful ECG testing phase, UNICEF continued partnering with the Government of Croatia and the European Commission (EC) through the implementation of the EC’s Technical Support Instrument (TSI)-funded programme to improve planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the Child Guarantee National Action Plan (NAP). Through the European Child Guarantee Learning Lab (ECG Hub) co-hosted by Croatia, UNICEF Croatia also supported implementation of the ECG-NAP and shared expertise with EU pre-accession countries, providing access to knowledge, data and best practices to improve planning and resource mobilization. A multi-country study visit brought delegations from Serbia, North Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, enabling structured exchanges with Croatian institutions across critical areas such as early education, healthcare, housing and nutrition. The hub also supported governments’ budget alignment with child-focused priorities and leveraged EU and domestic funding. These efforts lay the foundation for systemic reforms benefiting the most marginalized children across Europe.
To ensure greater transparency, monitoring and quality of public investments in children, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Demography and Immigration to improve child-responsive budgeting. UNICEF shared international models and technical expertise, leading to a renewed commitment to improve the 2018 child budget guidelines, develop a digital data system, and strengthen coordination and staff capacity. Discussions with the Ministry of Finance began to explore integrating child focused budgeting into broader fiscal planning, laying the foundation for more responsive public finance systems for children, while UNICEF’s new membership in the national Forum for Sustainable Financing represents a strategic opportunity to explore innovative financing mechanism.
A successful resource mobilisation strategy of the CO resulted in USD 5.5 million raised in 2025 from the private sector in Croatia, representing a 7.2 per cent increase in fundraising receipts (in local currency, EUR) compared to 2024. More than 89,000 individuals contributed financially and engaged with UNICEF's mission (some 2.3 per cent of the total adult population). Data protection and process security remained at the highest standard, which was formally recognized this year through certified Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards.
A record 25,000 business entities were engaged in promoting UNICEF’s efforts for children and advocating for children’s rights within the business community, resulting in donations from 2,050 Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) for UNICEF programmes. Furthermore in 2025, UNICEF launched a partnership with a leading ticketing platform that now enables voluntary donations alongside event ticket purchases. 
The “Schools for Africa” (SFA) programme, a cross-cutting initiative combining education on child rights with fundraising, was implemented for the 16th consecutive year, engaging children, along with their families and communities, and raising 75,000 EUR. In the 2024/2025 academic year, over 36.000 children in 200 pre-schools, primary and secondary schools across Croatia participated, demonstrating solidarity with their peers in both Ethiopia and DR Congo.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Declining aid contributions from traditional donors and partners to global development and humanitarian programmes have posed significant challenges for UNICEF, prompting a global organisational reform. In Croatia, cost-efficiency and prioritisation measures have been introduced, and change management processes started to ensure a future-ready   UNICEF presence attuned to the current child rights priorities in the country as well as to its potential to leverage acquired knowledge, partnerships and resources to benefit children beyond its borders. 
Resource mobilization opportunities in the country remain strong. Fundraising efforts allowed the CO to fully fund its programme, while also contributing to global programmes (i.e., emergency humanitarian response and Regional Thematic Funds). National funds and EU funds to national and local authorities, particularly the Recovery and Resilience Facility, provide sustainable financing avenues for scaling up family-based care, child rights monitoring, and inclusive services. The private sector engagement model, already yielding promising results, can be further expanded, with corporate partners investing in child-sensitive ESG practices and workplace policies. Individual Giving support continues to provide stable income for both national programming and international work. Moreover, UNICEF’s advocacy for embedding child-focused budgeting within national fiscal frameworks offers the most sustainable financing pathway: state budget allocations.
Despite efforts, access to ECI services remains a challenge, with only one in eight children receiving support. While strategic and action planning is underway, integrating health, social welfare, and education services will require sustained, multi-year commitments even after government endorsement. A key contribution to success has been UNICEF’s inclusive approach, engaging over 200 stakeholders—professionals, parents, civil society, and regional authorities—to build a strong collaborative foundation and secure government approval of the plan. With clear government commitment, the focus now shifts to operational integration and nationwide scaling. As a trusted partner to the MoH, UNICEF is mobilizing national and private funding while advocating for EU resources to ensure a sustainable financial model for service expansion and a robust, locally supported ECI system.
Building on its work in ECEC financing, UNICEF has proven a trusted partner to MoSEY in expanding nationwide kindergarten access. Beyond costing and financing, UNICEF has intensified consultations with the MoSEY to provide technical support for rolling out the new full-day pre-school curriculum—700 mandatory hours (4 hours daily) compared to the current 250—aimed at improving transitions from kindergarten to primary school. While increased public spending on kindergartens is commendable and follows two years of UNICEF advocacy, further measures, such as income-adjusted school fees, or reduced hidden costs, are needed to ensure ECEC is fully accessible and affordable for disadvantaged families. 
Despite Croatia’s legal ban on corporal punishment, harmful norms around violent discipline persist, with fathers more likely to justify and use such methods and boys disproportionately affected. These findings from UNICEF’s KAP study highlight that knowledge alone cannot shift deeply rooted attitudes—large-scale behavioural change requires sustained, gender-transformative approaches and multi-sectoral partnerships. Moving forward, UNICEF will strengthen its Social and Behavioural Change Strategy, prioritize interventions that challenge harmful gender norms, and forge new collaborations, convening government, academia, and civil society to accelerate progress toward a violence-free childhood.
Significant progress has been made in developing and standardizing community-based services that prevent family separation and reduce reliance on residential care. These achievements demonstrate UNICEF Croatia’s strong potential to deliver large-scale results within the current Country Programme, catalytically embedding solutions into national systems, supported by robust evidence and aligned with national and EU frameworks such as the Child Guarantee and other strategic initiatives. However, the rising number of children in residential care—currently 286 per 100,000 children—remains a major challenge. This increase reflects geographical disparities in service availability, including insufficient family-based care, limited community support for at-risk families, weak gatekeeping mechanisms, and gaps in case management practices.
The adoption of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum in 2024 presents both opportunities and challenges. While the Pact aims to improve migration management, its limited focus on children’s rights risks undermining progress toward child-centered asylum systems. Croatia’s national action plan goal includes expanding reception capacity for unaccompanied and separated children, supported by substantial EU funding (e.g. AMIF). This creates a window for UNICEF to advocate for child-rights-based reception standards, child-friendly asylum procedures, and investment in alternative care. 
Partnerships with both public and private sectors in the areas of child-sensitive workplace practices, adolescent wellbeing and ESG integration continue to yield results, relying on UNICEF’s comparative advantage as the convener with technical expertise and credibility across sectors. The programmes initially tailored to individual companies have evolved into a national model, co-developed with the Croatian Employers’ Association (HUP) and MDI, ensuring scalability and long-term sustainability through national partners’ commitment. 
The 2025 Evaluation of Croatia’s Child Rights Monitoring (CRM) System acknowledged notable progress achieved through current strategies, while further efforts are needed to create an environment where child rights are fully realized. Strengthening nationwide awareness and the role of CRM will require continued capacity development at all levels and the promotion of innovative, participatory approaches—areas that UNICEF will prioritize throughout the remainder of the Country Programme. The establishment of the Children’s Evaluation Reference Group, which enabled adolescents to contribute as co-creators, offers a valuable model for future government-led monitoring and evaluation.
The 2025 Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) recognizes that the “value added by UNICEF in Croatia is characterised by its capacity to leverage its unique position as a UN agency to drive systemic change, particularly through technical expertise, evidence-based policy advocacy, and its powerful convening role”. Similarly, it highlights that “Government counterparts recognise UNICEF as a partner that supports EU policy implementation, strengthens national systems for children, and enables Croatia to translate domestic expertise into credible international cooperation”. Furthermore, the CPE found that the Government “views UNICEF as a key technical partner for domestic reform and a strategic vehicle for its international cooperation and ODA ambitions”. Looking ahead, UNICEF will continue engaging catalytically and building on these strengths to ensure sustained national investments in children, promote equitable and inclusive systems, and contribute to the generation and sharing of knowledge and best practices globally.

In 2025, 72 million children across Europe and Central Asia region (ECAR) continued to face a rapidly evolving and increasingly complex environment shaped by overlapping geopolitical, demographic, economic and technological transitions.  
While indicators of child well-being compare relatively well in ECAR against global averages, progress is increasingly uneven and stagnating or reversing in some areas. A convergence of conflict, demographic shifts, climate change, fiscal pressures and rapid digital transformation not only amplifies inequalities but also tests the resilience of national systems that children – particularly the most vulnerable - depend on.

Economic pressures, poverty and demographic shifts
The region comprises four high-income countries (Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, and Romania), 14 upper-middle-income countries, and three lower-middle-income economies (Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan). Macroeconomic conditions across these countries remain fragile. Growth prospects are modest, with GDP growth for 2025 projected at around 1 per cent in European Union (EU), 3.2 per cent in South-Eastern Europe, and 2.5 per cent in Central Asian countries and Georgia.[1] One out of every four child - totaling 17.5 million children - are living in poverty. 
Demographic trends continue to diverge sharply across the region. Most countries in Europe face declining fertility and ageing populations, while Central Asia maintains a youthful and growing population. This generates both risks and opportunities: ageing societies may deprioritize child-focused investments, while youthful societies must expand services to harness their demographic dividend. Households face rising costs for food, energy and housing, increasing the risk of child poverty and social exclusion, particularly among already vulnerable groups.
Fiscal constraints increasingly shape government choices, with growing risks that investments in child-focused health, education and social protection are sidelined in favour of short-term economic or security spending.

War, displacement and migration
The war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, continues to affect 1.5 million children in frontline areas and a third of Ukraine’s children remain displaced. Over 3.8 million[2] people are internally displaced and 5.1 million[3] have sought shelter across Europe. The war and broader geopolitical instability continue to shape the regional context. Conflict and displacement are key drivers of vulnerability, disrupting access to essential services and undermining protection for children.
At the same time, migration flows continue to put pressure on national systems. Beyond Ukraine, displacement shapes wider migration patterns in the region. Mixed migration flows have strained services along the Mediterranean and Balkan routes, with over 436,000 refugees and migrants arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, Italy and Serbia in 2025. Armenia hosts over 142,000 refugees, including at least 36,000 children, while Türkiye shelters more than 2.4 million Syrian refugees.[4]
As a result of these dynamics, an increasing number of countries in the region are simultaneously countries of origin, transit and destination, with national systems that face sustained pressure to respond in inclusive and child sensitive ways. Children on the move, including unaccompanied minors, face heightened risks of exploitation, limited access to services and insecure legal status. These challenges are compounded by increasing political polarization and restrictive migration policies.  

Health and nutrition
The region continues to record relatively strong health outcomes, with under-five mortality at 10.5 per 1,000 live births, well below the global average of 37. 
While ECAR countries have achieved over 90 per cent coverage for at least one childhood vaccine, immunization coverage has been backsliding. Nearly 34,000 measles cases were reported in ECA in 2025, driven by vaccine hesitancy, weakened health systems and declining measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) immunization coverage.
Health systems are overstretched as a result of underinvestment in primary health care, persistent workforce shortages and widening inequalities in access. While public spending on health averages around 13 per cent of total government expenditure[5], high out-of-pocket payments in several countries signal the barriers to equitable access, particularly for low-income and marginalized families.
Data gaps remain a critical constraint: in many contexts, health data are insufficiently disaggregated, limiting the ability to identify or address inequities.
Education, learning and skills
While access to education remains near universal in most countries, the region faces persistent challenges in learning outcomes, inclusion and skills development. Structural inequalities continue to affect children with disabilities, Roma children and those in rural or migrant communities.
Across the region, a large proportion of students continue to lack foundational skills, including reading and mathematics – a reflection of systemic challenges in education quality. By the end of lower secondary, only about two-thirds of students, on average, reach the minimum proficiency.[6]
At the same time, digital divides between countries, and between urban and rural areas, are widening disparities in access to learning opportunities and future employment prospects. 
Of the estimated 5.2 million children with disabilities in the region,[7]only 1 million are enrolled in education.

Adolescent well-being and mental health
Adolescents face increasing pressures linked to economic uncertainty, digital transformation and social change. Mental health challenges are rising, with many adolescents reporting poor well-being, anxiety and sleep difficulties. Gaps in adolescent-responsive services and the insufficient integration of mental health into primary systems continue to limit effective responses.
The region faces persistent challenges in youth transition to employment. Around 12 per cent of youth (2.2 million aged 15–19 years) are not in education or employment (NEET).[8] Skills gaps and insufficient preparedness for evolving labour markets leave many young people at risk of exclusion.
These trends underscore the limitations of fragmented, service by service responses and highlight the need for integrated adolescent responsive systems across health, education and social protection.

Violence, protection risks and alternative care
Violence against children remains widespread, particularly in domestic settings, with children from minority groups, migrant families and conflict affected areas facing heightened exposure to violence, exploitation- and harmful practices. Nearly 1 in 3 children experience physical punishment at home by caregivers.[9] In 19 member states of the EU, up to 14 per cent of women reported having experienced sexual violence during childhood.[10]
Although progress on deinstitutionalization continues, children remain overrepresented in residential care, particularly those with disabilities. Approximately 130,000 children in ECAR currently reside in residential care facilities.[11]
Protection systems remain uneven in quality and coverage, with persistent gaps in prevention, early intervention and child-friendly justice mechanisms.

Social protection and public finance constraints
Fiscal tightening and shifting policy priorities are placing increasing pressure on social protection systems. Across the region, limited fiscal space, rising debt burdens and competing spending priorities (including defence and climate financing) constrain investments in children. 
Meanwhile, data on child-focused spending remain limited, and child-related allocations represent only a small share of overall social protection spending, indicating persistent gaps in targeting and prioritization. This limits governments’ strategic mobilization of social protection to prevent child poverty and respond effectively to shocks, rather than only mitigating their impact. On average, 40 per cent of children in ECAR are covered by at least one cash benefit, compared to 90 per cent in EU countries. 

Climate and environmental pressures
Climate change, air pollution, and environmental degradation are increasingly threatening children’s health and well-being in the region. More frequent heatwaves, floods, and droughts are disrupting services and livelihoods, while systems remain ill-equipped to absorb repeated shocks. Impacts are intensifying, with floods and landslides affecting Eastern Europe and the Western Balkans, and worsening water scarcity in Central Asia.
