In 2025, the Europe and Central Asia Regional Office (ECARO) delivered significant results for children across a complex regional landscape and a major organizational transition. Building on the strategic realignments initiated during the 2023 Mid-Term Review and consolidated in 2024, ECARO strengthened its role as a regional convener, technical authority and a trusted partner, supporting country offices to achieve durable, large-scale outcomes for children.
Across sectors, UNICEF’s regional contribution in 2025 continued to be characterized by three interlinked approaches: from pilots to institutionalized reforms, from fragmented interventions to integrated systems, and from programme delivery to policy, financing and accountability at scale. These were enabled through close partnerships with governments, the EU and other multilateral institutions, UN agencies, international financial institutions (IFIs), academia and civil society, as well as through sustained technical support to country offices.

Thriving: Advancing Child and Adolescent Health, Nutrition and Early Childhood Development
In 2025, ECARO strengthened UNICEF’s leadership in child and adolescent health across Europe and Central Asia, elevating children’s health and well-being as a central policy priority amid demographic decline, rising noncommunicable diseases, and persistent underinvestment in preventive, child-focused primary health care and early intervention services.
One regional milestone was the development and endorsement of the joint WHO–UNICEF Regional Child and Adolescent Health and Well-being Strategy,approved by all Member States. This strategy reestablished a shared regional vision for child and adolescent health, integrating maternal, newborn and adolescent health, nutrition, mental health, immunization and primary health care within a life course approach. UNICEF’s contribution was pivotal in shaping the evidence base, mobilizing political commitment, and ensuring alignment with broader EU and national policy frameworks.
Through sustained engagement with the European Commission, UNICEF strengthened its position as a trusted technical partner informing EU and national child health policies. Institutional cooperation agreements and policy dialogues supported Member States on early childhood development, immunization, mental health and nutrition, translating regional evidence into concrete policy action.
At the country level, ECARO’s technical leadership supported systemic reforms in primary health care and home visiting. 13 countries redesigned home-visiting systems, shifting from fragmented, project-based models to institutionalized, evidence-informed services embedded within national health systems. Across 11 countries with eligible population (pregnant women and young children) of over 8.6 million, more than 27 million visits were delivered. These are critical in enabling early identification of developmental risks and linkages to services at the national level. Maturity model assessments, conducted with WHO, enabled governments to identify bottlenecks and prioritize investments. These reforms strengthened developmental monitoring, parental counselling and the early identification of risks, particularly for the most vulnerable children.

In maternal and newborn health, UNICEF’s regional support contributed to measurable improvements in the quality of care, particularly in Central Asia. Countries adopted lifesaving innovations, strengthened neonatal intensive care services, and institutionalized perinatal quality improvement mechanisms. At the regional level, UNICEF’s contribution extended beyond technical assistance to strategic policy dialogue with governments and partners, the development of regional workforce development approaches, and support to countries on financing and investment strategies, enabling national reforms to shift sustainably from pilots to scale. Such examples include the strengthening of neonatal intensive care and perinatal quality improvement systems in Central Asia, where countries scaled lifesaving interventions through routine health services. In Tajikistan, referral-level facilities upgraded neonatal care with standardized equipment, infection prevention protocols and workforce training, benefiting thousands of premature and critically ill newborns as part of nationally embedded systems. In Moldova and Georgia, perinatal and early childhood care quality was institutionalized through national clinical guidelines, mortality audits, and the integration of child development monitoring into primary health care reforms.
 
Immunization remained a critical priority as the region continued to experience recurrent measles outbreaks during the year, including in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kazakhstan and Romania, underscoring persistent system vulnerabilities. UNICEF supported governments to address widening equity gaps in immunization coverage, particularly affecting Roma communities in countries such as Moldova and Romania, children in labour-migration contexts in Kyrgyzstan, and conflict-affected populations in Ukraine. Across the affected countries, UNICEF-supported immunization responses and system-strengthening efforts helped to ensure that 3.2 million children were reached with routine and catch-up vaccination services, particularly in outbreak-affected and marginalized communities. UNICEF supported governments to strengthen immunization systems through financing analysis, subnational equity assessments, demand generation and digital transformation. Regional cost-of-inaction analyses reinforced advocacy with ministries of finance, while targeted support reached zero dose and marginalized children, including Roma communities and children affected by conflict and migration. These efforts demonstrated both the public health and economic returns of sustained immunization investment.
In nutrition, UNICEF advanced a food systems approach, addressing the region’s dual burden of malnutrition. Regional advocacy and technical assistance supported legislative and policy reforms to protect breastfeeding, improve school food environments and reduce childhood overweight and obesity. Engagement with EU institutions and national governments positioned UNICEF as a key partner in prevention-oriented, multisectoral nutrition policy leadership.

Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) emerged as a defining area of UNICEF’s regional contribution in 2025. UNICEF supported governments in countries including Albania, Greece, Kazakhstan, North Macedonia, Poland and Serbia to integrate MHPSS into health, education and social protection systems, moving beyond stigma reduction toward institutionalized, multisectoral services. The uSupport digital mental health platform was successfully piloted in Kazakhstan and Poland, with preparations for scale-up currently underway, alongside policy reforms that have embedded mental health within national strategies, including those targeting adolescents and youth. The platform has also been further adapted for Romania and Armenia. These initiatives demonstrated how digital innovation, when anchored in national systems, can extend reach while strengthening service quality.

Learning: Tackling the learning crisis through system reform and innovation
In 2025, ECARO intensified its response to the region’s learning crisis, supporting governments to move from access-focused education reforms toward learning quality, inclusion and skills for the future. UNICEF’s regional contribution was anchored in evidence generation, policy dialogue and sustained technical assistance, particularly in EU accession and candidate countries.
Key achievement was strengthening of learning assessment and data systems. Regional frameworks and country-specific support enabled governments to translate PISA and national assessment results into actionable policy reforms. In Central Asia and Eastern Partnership countries (Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine), UNICEF supported reforms of education management information systems, strengthening data quality, interoperability and use for planning and accountability.
Countries across the region, with UNICEF’s support, expanded access for children with disabilities, Roma children, refugees and other marginalized groups by reforming legislation, financing mechanisms and teacher training systems. UNICEF’s technical guidance, including the ECARO-led Compendium of Case Studies on Inclusive Education, as well as regional communities of practice on inclusive and digital education, facilitated peer learning and accelerated reform momentum, particularly in Central Asia and the Western Balkans.
UNICEF supported governments in countries including Kazakhstan, Moldova, Poland, Ukraine and Uzbekistan to scale up digital learning solutions, while strengthening data protection, system governance and equity safeguards. The first regional mapping of artificial intelligence in education positioned UNICEF as a thought leader in the responsible navigation of emerging technologies. Methodologies developed at regional level were subsequently sought by global teams, underscoring the value of ECARO’s innovation and evidence-generation work. 
Climate change education became increasingly embedded within national curricula and teacher training, supported by UNICEF’s regional programme guidance, which strengthened the link between education, climate resilience and disaster risk reduction, particularly in Central Asia and the Western Balkans, where governments committed to integrating climate adaptation into education planning.
Refugee education and pathways to learning and skills remained a core regional focus. UNICEF supported host governments in countries including Czech Republic, Hungary, Italy, Moldova, Poland, Romania and Slovakia to institutionalize responses for refugee and migrant children, shifting from parallel humanitarian arrangements to integration within national education systems. In major refugee-hosting countries, over 330,000 refugee and migrant children accessed education services (both formal and non-formal), including over 220,000 children supported in Poland alone, alongside large-scale integration efforts in Czech Republic, Italy, Romania and Slovakia. Partnerships with European Commission services and the European Training Foundation strengthened skills development, career guidance and learning-to-earning pathways for adolescents affected by displacement.

Protecting: Strengthening child protection systems and preventing and respond to violence
In 2025, ECARO consolidated UNICEF’s leadership in child protection by supporting governments to increasingly shift the focus from reactive responses to preventive, system-wide approaches. Prevention of violence against children emerged as a high-level political priority across the region, reinforced by global and regional commitments.
One landmark achievement was the Regional Ministerial Conference on Violence against Children, which took place in Bucharest, Romania in October 2025, bringing together governments from across Europe and Central Asia, including EU Member States. The conference translated global commitments into concrete regional and national actions, elevating violence prevention on political agendas. UNICEF’s role as convener, technical authority and evidence provider was central to this process.
Governments continued to advance deinstitutionalization and care reform, including in high-income and EU Member States. UNICEF supported legislative reforms, national strategies and financing models that prioritize family-based care and preventive family support services. Analysis of alternative care data over the last decade from the region’s national statistical offices shows a decline in the use of residential care in countries with available data, and greater use of family-based care – although not in all countries and not for all children. The percentage of children in alternative care who are in family-based care in 18 countries ranges from 40 to 92 per cent with an average of almost 70 per cent.
The expansion and professionalization of the social service workforce was a notable regional trend in 2025. UNICEF supported governments in countries including Kazakhstan, North Macedonia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to cost, plan and institutionalize child protection social service workforce reforms, strengthening frontline capacity to prevent family separation and respond to violence against children.
UNICEF also advanced digital transformation in child protection, supporting countries in the preparation for the launch and rollout of digital child protection information management systems and data platforms. These investments strengthened evidence-based policymaking, planning, programming and accountability, including in humanitarian situations.
In the context of the war in Ukraine, ECARO provided coordinated, multi-country support to strengthen national child protection systems responding to refugee flows. UNICEF supported quality GBV and mental health services, cross-border coordination and safe return processes for children evacuated from institutional care. These efforts demonstrated UNICEF’s ability to operate effectively across the humanitarian-development nexus.

Including: Reducing child poverty and strengthening social protection and public finance
In 2025, ECARO deepened its leadership on child -focused social protection and public finance, responding to worrying trends of fiscal tightening and backsliding on child benefits across the region. UNICEF supported governments to protect and prioritize investments in children, particularly in crisis-prone and climate-affected contexts.
UNICEF supported countries including Albania, Armenia, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo*, Moldova, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan to integrate cash transfers into emergency preparedness and response systems, strengthening child-focused, shock-responsive social protection. As a result, UNICEF directly supported the provision of cash transfers to 104,000 households in four countries in the region operating through government-led systems or delivering directly. In addition, thousands more children received cash or benefit support during shocks and emergencies through national or government-led systems with UNICEF’s technical assistance. Technical assistance, partnerships and capacity building enabled governments to deliver timely, child-focused support during shocks, while strengthening preparedness for future crises.
Public finance for children remained a strategic regional priority. UNICEF supported ministries of finance in Greece, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia, Tajikistan and Ukraine to strengthen child-responsive budgeting and spending quality. Policy dialogue was informed by regional analyses on financing gaps in early childhood education and care, as well as country-specific public finance strategies, including UNICEF’s support to the development of Ukraine’s office-wide Public Finance for Children and Youth Strategy.
Disability-inclusive social protection advanced through UNICEF’s partnership with the World Bank, supporting governments to reform assessment systems, benefits and services. These efforts reinforced UNICEF’s leadership on inclusive policy design and implementation.
Family-friendly policies and care systems gained renewed prominence in 2025. At regional level, UNICEF’s advocacy and evidence work positioned care and childcare as economic and social priorities, aligning with EU and national agendas on demographic change, employment and human capital development.

Connecting and participating: Adolescents, youth and digital innovation
UNICEF’s regional work on adolescent development and participation expanded in 2025, responding to rising mental health challenges, skills gaps and social exclusion. UNICEF supported governments in countries including Armenia, Cyprus, Kazakhstan, Romania and Poland to institutionalize youth participation in policy processes, strengthening learning-to-earning pathways and adolescent mental health responses.
Youth engagement was increasingly embedded within national strategies, including the Cyprus National Mental Health Strategy and National Youth Strategy, with dedicated mechanisms and budget lines supporting sustained participation. UNICEF’s regional support facilitated cross-country learning and positioned young people as partners in policy design, not just beneficiaries.

Child Rights Monitoring
In 2025, ECARO consolidated UNICEF’s regional leadership in child rights monitoring, safeguarding core regional public goods during a period of organizational transition. UNICEF sustained its influence within intergovernmental statistical processes, including the Conference of European Statisticians, ensuring regional discussions on poverty, disability, violence against children and mental health were informed by child-focused perspectives.
Key regional assets were strengthened, including the launch of the regional SDG progress dashboard, the finalization of the Transforming Monitoring for Enhanced Equity (TRANSMONEE) violence against children data series, and completion of the updated regional situation analysis, which introduced foresight elements and a stronger focus on CRC implementation. UNICEF also provided technical support to twelve countries to plan and implement Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, financing as well as reinforcing data availability and its use for national policy and advocacy.

Gender equality, climate action and humanitarian leadership
All country offices in ECAR surpassed the 70 per cent benchmark under the Gender Action Plan (GAP). This marks the second consecutive year that ECARO has achieved this result across all country offices, making it the only region to do so. UNICEF continued to support gender-transformative programming, particularly for adolescent girls, through education, skills development, social protection and humanitarian action.
UNICEF supported governments in countries such as Kazakhstan, Moldova, Türkiye and Ukraine to integrate child-sensitive priorities into national climate policies, including Nationally Determined Contributions. In Central Asia, UNICEF’s regional climate business model initiative enabled all five governments to incorporate costed, child-focused investments into NDC 3.0 submissions, positioning children at the centre of climate adaptation and resilience planning.
In 2025, the Regional Office provided strategic humanitarian leadership across Europe and Central Asia, supporting country offices to respond to protracted displacement, mixed migration movements and recurrent shocks while strengthening preparedness and national systems. As mixed migration pressures continued — with nearly 180,000 refugees and migrants arriving along the Mediterranean and Balkan routes during the year — UNICEF leveraged flexible humanitarian thematic funding and coordinated regional technical support to increasingly bridge humanitarian response with system strengthening, notably through shock-responsive social protection, child-centred migration responses and anticipatory action. This approach enabled life-saving assistance to be delivered at scale while reinforcing national and local capacity to protect children in the face of ongoing and emerging crises.
 
Communication and advocacy
In 2025, ECARO strengthened its regional communication and advocacy function to amplify policy influence, support country offices, and position children’s rights prominently within regional policy debates. Building on strong collaboration with programme sections, communications and advocacy efforts translated technical evidence and policy reforms into accessible narratives for decision-makers, partners and the wider public. Regional communication campaigns and content supported flagship programme priorities including child health, violence against children, climate action and inclusion, while providing adaptable tools for country-level use, contributing to influencing decision makers. High-visibility advocacy moments, including regional exhibitions and coordinated digital campaigns, reinforced UNICEF’s role as a trusted voice for children in Europe and Central Asia and supported country offices in engaging governments, donors and the public around shared priorities.

Partnerships and resource mobilization
Partnerships remained a critical enabler of results in 2025, with ECARO playing a central role in strategic positioning, oversight, alliance building and resource mobilization across the region. The Regional Office supported country offices to deepen engagement with EU institutions, international financial institutions and private sector partners, aligning programme priorities with evolving donor and policy agendas. Despite a tightening fiscal environment and constraints on public funding, UNICEF maintained strong positioning with the EU and expanded collaboration with IFIs, while supporting country offices to navigate complex legal and operational requirements. The overall donor funding pipeline (public and private sector) increased from US$ 422 million in Q4 2024 to US$ 536 million by the end of 2025, representing 27% growth. Private sector fundraising in the region continued to perform strongly, exceeding annual targets (gross Income from Private Sector reached a record US$ 18.2 million, well ahead of the US$ 16.0 million PSP Target) and demonstrating the growing contribution of digital fundraising, major donors and high-value partnerships, with a particular mention for ECA Cluster, which exceeded US$ 3 million (from US$ 1.4 million PSP Target) income mark and became the 3rd largest business unit in the region. At regional level, ECARO provided quality assurance, strategic guidance and coordination, ensuring coherence between programme priorities, partnerships and reporting (100% compliance – timely submission of 307 reports on-time complete reporting was achieved again), and safeguarding UNICEF’s credibility with donors and partners during a period of organizational transition.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Despite significant achievements in 2025, UNICEF’s work across Europe and Central Asia faced persistent and emerging challenges that will shape priorities in the coming period[AS1] .
Shrinking fiscal space and competing political priorities remain the most significant constraints. Across income levels, governments face pressure to reduce social spending, with children’s issues increasingly framed as secondary to short-term economic concerns. This underscores the importance of UNICEF’s continued focus on public finance, investment cases and whole-of-government engagement.
System complexity and fragmentation continue to slow reform implementation. While policy commitments are often strong, their translation into coordinated action across sectors, levels of government and institutions remain a challenge. UNICEF’s experience in 2025 reaffirmed that sustained technical assistance, not one off support, is essential to institutionalize reforms.
Capacity gaps, both within governments and UNICEF structures, pose risks to sustainability. As organizational transitions unfold, it is essential to maintain critical technical expertise, cross-sectoral integration and institutional memory. Communities of practice, peer learning and knowledge management systems emerged as effective mitigation strategies.
Equity gaps are widening, particularly for children affected by poverty, disability, migration and conflict. While system reforms are advancing, targeted approaches remain necessary to ensure that the most marginalized children benefit from progress.
Climate risks and humanitarian pressures are intensifying faster than systems are adapting. UNICEF’s work demonstrated the value of integrating climate resilience and preparedness into core social systems but also highlighted the need for faster scale up and stronger financing mechanisms.

As ECARO navigated significant change following Future Focus Initiative decisions, including the consolidation of ECA and MENA regional offices, it continued to strategically position UNICEF in line with the new Strategic Plan. Despite this transition, ECARO focused on regional opportunities, leveraging co-financing through the Childcare and Early Learning Financing Facility, advancing the European Child Guarantee, and unlocking substantial climate finance to support millions of children.

Key takeaways

Durable results require policy, financing and     implementation alignment, not parallel programme delivery. 
UNICEF’s comparative advantage lies in convening, evidence and systems leadership, particularly in high and middle-income contexts. 
Digital innovation delivers impact only when embedded within national systems and governance frameworks. 
Youth and community participation strengthens policy relevance and sustainability when institutionalized, not tokenistic.

Outlook
Looking ahead, UNICEF ECARO will prioritize:

Protecting and expanding investments in children through public finance and policy advocacy. 
Sustaining system reforms in health, education, protection and social protection during organizational transition. 
Deepening climate-responsive and shock-responsive systems for children. 
Strengthening regional public goods – data, evidence, guidance and partnerships – that support country offices at scale. 
Ensuring continuity, integration and quality of technical assistance through the new Centres of Excellence.
In an increasingly constrained and complex regional environment, UNICEF’s role as a trusted partner for governments and institutions remains critical to safeguarding children’s rights and futures across Europe and Central Asia.

Contextual Update
  
In 2025, Georgia experienced significant political and socioeconomic developments with direct implications for children. Following parliamentary elections in late 2024, European Union (EU) accession talks were suspended, while political volatility and global tensions created a climate of uncertainty. In April, Parliament adopted the Foreign Agents’ Registration Act and amended the Grants Law, imposing strict requirements on organizations receiving foreign funds and constraining cooperation with civil society organizations (CSO)—traditional partners in child protection and education. In November, Parliament passed the Law on Rehabilitation and Support of Juveniles under 14, granting justice agencies leading roles and creating a closed institution under the Ministry of Justice.
   
Situation of children in Georgia
  
Georgia has made progress in advancing children’s rights, yet structural inequities, demographic shifts, and emerging risks continue to shape the lives of children and adolescents. As of 1 January 2025, there are 842,465 children (under 18), of whom 52% boys and 48% girls, representing 22.7% of the total population, underscoring both the importance and the vulnerability of the child and youth cohort in the context of declining fertility and emigration. The total fertility rate stands at 1.7, below replacement level. Age-specific fertility rate under 18 at 6.2 births per 1,000 girls, indicate early childbearing, while reduced compared to previous decades, remains a concern.
  
Absolute child poverty has declined substantially over the past decade, reaching 12.1% in 2024, down from 29.9% in 2013. However, 37.8% of children experience material and social deprivation, with rural children (47.1%) and children with disabilities (70.8%) disproportionately impacted. Despite expanded social protection programmes, including cash transfers reaching 32.1% of children under 16, coverage among boys accounts for 48%, indicating no significant difference in access by sex, many families continue to face material and social deprivation. 
  
High out-of-pocket health expenditures (51% of total health spending) and limited access to childcare services for children under two continue to put pressure on household budgets, particularly for families with multiple children, children with disabilities, or those living in remote areas and restrict women’s labour force participation.
  
Georgia has achieved notable improvements in health, with maternal mortality declining from 71.8 per 100,000 live births in 2021 to 25.3 in 2024, and neonatal, infant and under-five mortality have also declined, reaching 5.9, 8.2 and 9.5 per 1,000 live births respectively. As for sex disagragation, neonatal mortality in Georgia was 8.3 per 1,000 for boys and 6.4 per 1,000 for girls, while under-five mortality was 9.3 per 1,000 for boys and 7.8 per 1,000 for girls — demonstrating higher early-life mortality among boys. However, these rates remain nearly double those of European countries. Immunization coverage continues to decline, with Georgia having one of the lowest coverage rates of three doses of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine in the Europe and Central Asia region. Exclusive breastfeeding rate remains low at 20%.
  
Mental health concerns are rising. Among university students, 37% of females and 28% of males reported suicidal thoughts, and 7% attempted suicide in the past year. Underscoring the urgent need for accessible, youth-friendly mental health and psychosocial support services.
  
While primary school attendance is nearly universal (98%), disparities widen at the secondary level. The out-of-school rate for upper-secondary-age children remains high at 11% (14% for boys; 8% for girls), rising to 33% among Azerbaijani youth (28% boys; 39% girls), indicating gendered barriers to continued schooling.
  
Learning outcomes remain a concern. In Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022, over two-thirds of 15-year-olds performed below proficiency in reading, mathematics, and science. Participation in early childhood education and care (ECEC) has declined to 72.3%, with children in rural areas and from ethnic minority communities facing significantly higher barriers to access and remaining disproportionately excluded from services. Public ECEC services for children under two are non-existent, limiting early developmental support and reinforcing gender inequalities in unpaid care work.
  
The number of children with special educational needs enrolled in mainstream schools has increased dramatically—from 160 in 2009 to 14,535 in 2024—reflecting progress in inclusive education. However, systemic challenges persist, including insufficient human resources, limited professional development, and inadequate early childhood inclusion. 
  
According to the latest national data, 5.8% of children aged 2–17 years have functional difficulty in at least one domain (2.5% among children aged 2–4, and 6.5% among those aged 5–17), pointing to a substantial group with additional support needs.
  
Data on young people aged 15–29 highlight significant challenges during the transition from adolescence to adulthood. A considerable share of youth (24.1%) remains not in employment, education, or training (NEET), with young women disproportionately represented due to gender related barriers such as unpaid care responsibilities, limited access to childcare, and lower labour market participation. Despite improvements in educational attainment, many young people continue to face difficulties entering the labour market, reflecting gaps in career guidance, skills development, and alignment between education and employment opportunities.
  
Violent discipline remains a concern despite notable progress: the prevalence of violent discipline has fallen steeply since 2018 (68.8%), yet around one-third (32.5%) of children still experience some form of violent punishment at home. The burden of violence is higher for children with disabilities (44.3%) and boys (around 41%), compared to girls (approximately 34%). Reporting of child abuse cases has increased, with 2,083 cases registered in 2024, including physical abuse (475 cases) and sexual abuse (193 cases) reflecting both heightened awareness and persistent risks.
  
Georgia has closed all large-scale residential institutions, reducing the number of children in residential care to 289 in 2024, but challenges remain in expanding family-based care for older children and children with disabilities. Juvenile justice reforms have reduced child imprisonment to 141 cases over 90% involving boys in 2024, with a high diversion rate of 59%, yet gaps persist in child-friendly justice mechanisms and specialized services for victims and witnesses.
  
Child marriage, while declining, remains a persistent harmful practice: 6.9% of women aged 20–24 report having been married or in union before age 18, with significantly higher rates among some ethnic and rural communities. These patterns interact with gender norms, early school leaving, and limited economic opportunities, especially for girls in marginalized settings.
  
Environmental health risks continue to disproportionately affect children. Although childhood lead exposure has declined significantly in two regions, from over 60% in 2018 to 20% in 2023, lead contamination remains a national concern. Air pollution affects almost all children, and 24.9% of households rely on E. coli-contaminated drinking water. 
  
Climate change and environmental degradation exacerbate existing inequalities, particularly for rural communities. Strengthening climate-resilient Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems, environmental surveillance, and child-sensitive disaster preparedness remains a critical priority.

In 2025, UNICEF Georgia delivered measurable progress for children while reinforcing national reform agendas and UNICEF’s role as a trusted partner in complex and politically sensitive contexts. Despite political volatility and limited civic space, UNICEF sustained momentum by prioritizing system strengthening, evidence generation, and cross-sectoral coordination. UNICEF’s comparative advantage - combining technical expertise, convening power, child participation, and operational presence - enabled sustained progress across key sectors. Core resources played a catalytic role in sustaining reform dialogue, piloting innovations, and leveraging partnerships amid constrained donor funding.
 
Cross-sectoral results
UNICEF strengthened cooperation with the Administration of the Government of Georgia and the Interagency Commission on CRC implementation, contributing to coordinated national child rights efforts. During the Commission meeting, UNICEF presented 2026–2030 programme priorities, and partners agreed to institutionalize annual review meetings to track joint workplans and align strategic priorities.
UNICEF Georgia initiated groundwork for introducing Child Rights Impact Assessment (CRIA) as a strategic tool for child rights-based law and policy-making. Efforts focused on internal capacity building, expert consultations, and analysis of municipal decision-making processes, setting the stage for systematic application in the coming years.
To strengthen engagement beyond the public sector, UNICEF expanded collaboration with the private sector to advance children’s rights nationwide. The Child Rights and Business Principles were translated into Georgian, and dialogues with companies centered on youth skills development, positive parenting, and child-sensitive business practices. UNICEF launched a private sector mapping exercise to identify high-potential sectors aligned with the new Country Programme. Findings will inform the Private Sector Engagement Strategy in early 2026, alongside a revised concept and Terms of Reference for the Business Advisory Council.
Communication and advocacy remained central to UNICEF’s mandate. Despite a limited media space, UNICEF reached over 600,000 people with child-centered messages through media, digital platforms, and offline activities. Campaigns highlighted education, health, disability inclusion, and media literacy, while amplifying children’s voices through inclusive storytelling. An advocacy strategy on Violence Against Children was initiated, alongside targeted campaigns on positive parenting, youth skills, child rights in academia, lead surveillance, and child-friendly justice.
Data and evidence remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s work. In partnership with the National Statistics Office of Georgia (GeoStat), UNICEF supported the update of the Transformative Monitoring for Enhanced Equity (TransMonEE) database and enhanced GeoStat’s web portal for child and youth statistics. Several new indicators were added, enriching the portal as a centralized resource for disaggregated data on children and youth by sex, organized across different age groups. UNICEF also supported the routine collection and measurement of Georgia’s first Child Wellbeing Indicators Scorecard, consolidating approximately 65 indicators, including those from the Child-Related SDGs and the Child Rights Monitoring Framework.
Capacity-building efforts extended to academia and schools. UNICEF supported GeoStat in strengthening the knowledge of Child Rights Center representatives and academic staff through targeted session on the national statistical system, child-related data production, and practical applications of the child and youth statistics portal for research, teaching and monitoring national development goals. These activities enabled lecturers and researchers to deepen their understanding of age-disaggregated data, survey methodologies, and the integration of child-related statistics into academic curricula and research, fostering a stronger culture of data literacy within higher education institutions.
In parallel, UNICEF supported GeoStat in promoting data literacy among schoolchildren through the Statistics for Kids and Teenagers portal. Children explored interactive tools, quizzes, and visualizations that linked data to everyday life and child rights frameworks, strengthening critical thinking, numeracy, and evidence-based decision-making skills. The session also promoted children’s rights by linking statistical learning with key national and international child-rights frameworks.
UNICEF initiated advocacy with the Administration of the Government of Georgia to implement a Child Welfare Survey, expected to cover key domains such as material and social deprivation, social protection, health, education, child discipline, and other dimensions of child well-being.
The Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) was implemented by UNICEF, assessing the Programme of Cooperation’s contribution to national development results, UNICEF’s role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through the UNSDCF, and UNICEF’s strategic positioning in relation to its child rights mandate. Findings informed the design of the new country programme for 2026–2030. UNICEF also contributed to the Evaluation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), providing insights that guided the development of the new UNSDCF for 2026–2030.
 
Every child survives and thrives
UNICEF continued to provide technical assistance to eliminate mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, childbirth. By prioritizing the implementation of WHO recommendations from the 2024 comprehensive assessment. While working on EMTCT, UNICEF is addressing gendered health risks linked to women’s reproductive role and unequal access to care. Significant progress was achieved in syphilis EMTCT: public health personnel were fully trained on updated epidemiological surveillance guidelines; investigation forms were revised; and the Birth Registry was enhanced to capture syphilitic stillbirths and treatment adequacy. Reporting from private providers improved through mapping and tailored surveillance models. UNICEF played a pivotal role in securing national agreement on introducing benzathine penicillin G for syphilis prophylaxis in antenatal care and initiated discussions with its Supply Division to ensure procurement.
UNICEF concluded an EU-funded project that delivered transformative intervention in Georgia’s primary health care (PHC) system by integrating child development monitoring for children aged 0–6 years, including through innovative remote modalities. The project operationalized services in 50 rural PHC clinics, e and institutionalized reforms through the approval of two national guidelines on child health, development monitoring, and referral pathways. These guidelines standardized healthy child visits and teleconsultations while establishing formal linkages between health and social services for children at risk of developmental delays. A dedicated Continuous Medical Education course further strengthened PHC capacity. By actively engaging fathers alongside mothers, UNICEF helps to rebalance caregiving roles that are otherwise structured by gendered norms assigning the primary responsibility for childcare to women.
A major milestone was the development of Georgia’s first national electronic child development monitoring system, fully aligned with national guidelines and equipped with embedded screening tools (Ages & Stages Questionnaires (ASQ-3), Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT), EPDS), growth charts, and analytics. It is worth mentioning that the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is designed primarily to detect postpartum depression and it embeds a gender-responsive understanding of maternal mental health as a key determinant of child wellbeing. The system supports telemedicine and performance-based quality monitoring, recording over 14,000 healthy child visits and screening 2,443 children, enabling timely referrals, largely through remote modalities. Sustainability is ensured through integration into upcoming PHC reforms, with scale-up planned in six urban PHC centres.
UNICEF has played a key convening role in advancing Georgia’s national agenda on child and adolescent mental health. Drawing on internationally recognized leadership from Australia’s youth mental health reform experience, UNICEF mobilized global technical expertise alongside national stakeholders to support the Government in strengthening the evidence base, shaping policy dialogue, and translating best practices into context-appropriate strategic directions. Through a coordinated process that brought together international expertise and a multidisciplinary group of Georgian professionals from the health, social protection, education, and justice sectors, UNICEF facilitated a structured and inclusive policy platform. This enabled the effective alignment of global standards with national priorities and implementation realities. While the reform process remains ongoing, UNICEF has established a clear niche in youth mental health by introducing innovative service models and approaches to addressing workforce gaps, laying the groundwork for tangible system-level results in early 2026.
UNICEF successfully piloted behaviourally informed solutions to reduce zero-dose and under-immunization in Rustavi, Gori, and Marneuli, achieving measurable improvements at system, provider, and community levels. Immunization Standard operating procedures (SOP) were standardized in 63 PHC facilities, with 299 staff trained and 1,100 job aids distributed. Digital enhancements—including an updated immunization module, SMS reminders, dashboards, and automated reporting—were fully operationalized. Provider capacity was strengthened through training and supervision reaching around 200 clinicians, while interpersonal communication (IPC) CME courses increased participant knowledge from 65% to 94%. Caregiver engagement included behaviourally informed videos (one exceeding 646,000 views), expert-led parent sessions reaching about 300 caregivers, and an active mechanism addressing immunization misinformation.
To strengthen immunization efforts in Abkhazia region, a UNICEF-led team of international immunization specialists supported the development and planning of catch-up interventions targeting zero-dose and under-immunized children, to be initiated in 2026. A needs assessment identified critical gaps across all districts and informed targeted, behaviorally informed responses in coordination with local health workers. UNICEF also supported the development of training plans, protocols, job aids, and supportive supervision checklists. In parallel, an assessment of WASH infrastructure and healthcare waste management needs was conducted across all districts as a first step toward addressing facility-level gaps.
UNICEF strengthened the capacity of professionals working with Ukrainian children by engaging 51 specialists from government and non-governmental organizations to deliver quality mental health and psychosocial support services, ensuring continuity of care for displaced children and families.
Building on the successful pilot and national rollout of the in-service IPC/IPCI programme, UNICEF supported Tbilisi State Medical University in initiating integration of the curriculum into its six-year undergraduate medical programme. In collaboration with academia and EURACT, IPC/IPCI materials were reviewed, updated, and adapted for pre-service education. From 2026, approximately 1,000 medical students annually will receive structured IPC/IPCI training as part of their undergraduate studies, embedding infection prevention and control into future health workforce development.
 
Every child learns
UNICEF initiated the development of a Professional Development Programme for ECEC BA academic staff to enhance the quality of pre-service teacher education. Developed in partnership with seven state universities, the programme aims to strengthen universities’ capacity to deliver high-quality ECEC education. In parallel, UNICEF initiated the development of an eight-month Master-Class Programme for future ECEC teachers, bridging theory and practice and equipping senior BA students with applied skills for classroom work.
In partnership with the Ministry of Education, Science and Youth of Georgia (MoESY), UNICEF strengthened early bilingual education for ethnic and linguistic minority children. Responding to gaps in collaboration between bilingual and native-language teachers and the lack of child-centred resources, UNICEF supported the development of a practical guideline/thematic programme for ECEC teachers. Workshops for teachers in minority-dense regions improved understanding of holistic child development and bilingual approaches, benefiting both girls and boys, as well as educators, while supporting mothers’ engagement in early education through more inclusive and culturally responsive services.
UNICEF supported MoESY and the Mandaturi Office in strengthening inclusive education services through capacity building and development of system-level protocols. Training and consultations reached multidisciplinary specialists nationwide. As a result, two key protocols on psycho-educational assessment and consultancy services for children with special needs and disabilities were adopted and applied in practice by Mandaturi Office, strengthening service quality and consistency.
Together with the Communications Commission and the Ministry of Education and Science of Georgia (MoESY), UNICEF advanced the integration of media literacy into formal education. Media literacy was introduced into the tenth-grade national curriculum as an optional subject starting in September 2023. National standards and manuals were developed, and the National Teacher Training Centre conducted trainings to institutionalize teacher capacity-building within the education system. National conferences, panel discussions, and teacher trainings enhanced educators’ capacity and supported peer learning. As a result, media literacy is now fully integrated into 227 schools, and approximately 2,500 teachers have been trained to deliver media literacy education effectively.
UNICEF expanded skills development opportunities for adolescents through workshops on participation, skills, and media literacy, and by piloting the UPSHIFT Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship programme in four regions. 50 adolescents- with equal participation of girls and boys -developed innovative group projects addressing social issues, while selected adults were trained to support future programme expansion. UNICEF also finalized a qualitative study on youth skills and competencies, engaging government, academia, the private sector, and young people in dialogue on pathways to equip youth with relevant skills.
With support from the French Government, UNICEF partnered with three state universities to develop Georgia’s first multidisciplinary MA programme in Child Rights, drawing on international academic expertise. The programme has been approved by university academic councils and submitted for accreditation, expected in early 2026. In parallel, UNICEF supported the integration of Child Rights into the National Learning Fields Classifier, ensuring the long-term institutionalization of child rights education within the national academic framework.
Beyond the MA programme, UNICEF strengthened child rights education and research through the establishment of two additional Child Rights Centers and reinforcement of the Child Rights Academic Network of Georgia via strategic partnerships with Horizon Europe, Erasmus+, and the Shota Rustaveli National Science Foundation Foundation. UNICEF contributed to national academic benchmarks in collaboration with the National Center for Educational Quality Enhancement and advanced capacity-building initiatives focused on partnerships, research, and resource mobilization. Additionally, UNICEF initiated dialogue on emerging issues such as the use of AI in teaching and learning, laying the foundation for innovative collaborations with national and international education and research actors.
 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
UNICEF ensured high-level engagement by facilitating ministerial participation in the Regional Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. Georgia announced key pledges, including the expansion of Barnahus services, strengthened multidisciplinary responses, improved early identification and case management, and increased access to evidence-based rehabilitation. Follow-up actions included the establishment of an inter-agency working group under the CRC Implementation Commission to enhance coordination and expand geographic coverage.
In close collaboration with the UNICEF regional Child Protection team and the Human Rights Department of the Government Administration, UNICEF presented findings from a regional study on multidisciplinary and inter-agency services for child victims of violence. The workshop generated actionable recommendations to strengthen and expand Barnahus services in Georgia.
UNICEF initiated a comprehensive review of child–family separation prevention and reintegration processes and launched a national mapping of the social service workforce using the Global Social Service Workforce Alliance tool. Establishing a shared national definition will guide a coordinated, multisectoral workforce strategy.
To expand access to trauma recovery, UNICEF partnered with King’s College London to introduce Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (TF-CBT) training in Georgia, engaging 19 highly qualified professionals. This initiative is unprecedented, introducing the first evidence-based approach for supporting child victims of violence and children with traumatic experience and establishing systematic linkages between the professional community and relevant systems. To ensure sustainability and continuation of these efforts UNICEF signed an MoU with the Georgian Association of Cognitive Behaviour Therapy. In addition, UNICEF supported capacity building of the State Care Agency through Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) training of the psychologists.
UNICEF and its local partner successfully re-established psychological services for children in Abkhazia region. A core team of psychologists became operational, supported by international training and supervision. As a result, 31 children received psychological support between July and October 2025.
UNICEF advanced justice for children through evidence generation and stakeholder engagement. UNICEF conducted an analysis of national and international standards and convened over 50 stakeholders—including justice and welfare institutions, academia, civil society, and 50 children—to discuss introducing a child-specialized judge within the Georgian judicial system. UNICEF’s facilitation contributed to a consolidated concept now awaiting institutional-level discussion.
To promote meaningful participation in juvenile justice proceedings and fulfill the requirement of the Juvenile Justice Code on specialization of professionals working with children in the justice system, UNICEF supported specialization training for 25 State Care Agency professionals serving as procedural representatives. UNICEF also initiated cooperation with the Legal Aid Service to improve accessibility, quality, and child sensitivity of legal aid. Key achievements included recruitment of a specialized child lawyer, establishment of a child-friendly consultation space, development of information materials and a mobile application, and planning of trauma-informed training for lawyers.
Under the Family-Friendly Policy initiative, UNICEF strengthened private sector parenting capacity by developing and delivering a targeted programme for UN Global Compact Network Georgia. The initiative trained 22 parents and established a sustainable online learning module to expand access nationwide, promoting more equitable sharing of caregiving responsibilities between mothers and fathers and contributing to violence prevention within families.
In partnership with the Public Defender, UNICEF engaged 60 children—including children with disabilities, those in alternative care, and children from ethnic minorities—in interactive workshops on child rights, participation, and access to justice, strengthening awareness and confidence in seeking remedies. In addition, through partnership with the BookShelf project, more than 300 children in Batumi and Kutaisi participated in literature-based activities linking child rights to familiar published works, fostering rights awareness and literacy.
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
UNICEF finalized the second round of the national lead surveillance system and launched the third round, covering six regions of Georgia. Surveillance confirmed a declining trend in blood lead levels (BLLs) in the surveyed regions, with prevalence at approximately 20 per cent. Beyond monitoring prevalence and trends, the surveillance aims to identify sources of lead exposure. Investigations excluded water and salt as potential sources; however, continued nationwide surveillance and source investigation remain critical to eliminating lead exposure and safeguarding children’s health.
UNICEF finalized the project on indoor air pollution in kindergartens, generating critical evidence to inform policy and practice. Based on the analyzed data, a Continuous Medical Education (CME) programme titled “Indoor Air Pollution and Its Impact on Children’s Health” was developed and accredited for doctors specializing in pediatrics, family medicine, pulmonology, allergology/immunology, and infectious diseases. This evidence base will support further analysis and policy planning to protect children from harmful environmental risks.
UNICEF contributed to Georgia’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), ensuring integration of health, adaptation, and education components. The recommendations recognize the gendered impacts of climate change on children and caregivers, particularly girls’ increased exposure to environmental stressors and women’s roles in household water, energy, and care management. In addition, awareness-raising workshops on WASH, climate, and energy reached more than 500 adolescents, strengthening their understanding of environmental sustainability and resilience.
Environmental health and WASH remained key priorities. The Children’s Environmental Health e-course was translated, adapted, and accredited as an elective course by Tbilisi State University. In parallel, a Children’s Environmental Health assessment was conducted, with the final report expected in 2026. Using the climate-resilient electronic WASH monitoring tool developed with UNICEF support, a nationwide IPC/WASH assessment in medical facilities was launched by the National Center for Disease Control and Public Health (NCDC), covering 47 hospitals with over 100 beds, 284 PHC clinics, and 176 rural doctors’ offices. An electronic WASH monitoring tool for preschools was also developed and is planned for piloting in 2026 supporting gender-sensitive facility planning and accountability.
UNICEF improved water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure and conducted WASH promotion and training in 16 schools in Abkhazia region. As a result, access to essential WASH facilities improved for 1,872 children (963 girls and 909 boys). Gender-responsive WASH improvements—including safe, private sanitation facilities—are critical for girls’ dignity, attendance, and participation in school. Schools renovated between 2021 and 2024 received additional support for sustainable operation and maintenance of WASH facilities, creating cleaner, safer learning environments and promoting healthier practices. UNICEF also provided laboratory equipment—including microscopes, sterilizers, and autoclaves—to sanitary-epidemiological services in three districts.
In response to a water shortage emergency in Eastern Abkhazia in October 2025, UNICEF strengthened preparedness for future emergencies by installing water tanks, pumps, and pipelines in the Central District Hospital, three kindergartens, and four schools, including drilling a borehole at School No. 2. Reliable access to water during emergencies reduces caregiving burdens—disproportionately borne by women—and safeguards the health, hygiene, and dignity of girls and boys. As a result, 1,700 schoolchildren, 240 kindergarten children, and more than 100 hospital staff will have access to water and sanitation facilities during future emergencies.
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life
Georgia established its first child-centered framework for individualized social protection packages for children with disabilities, addressing intersecting inequalities related to disability, gender, and poverty. Developed through real-life assessments and consultations with organizations of persons with disabilities, the framework consolidates services such as assistive devices, education, rehabilitation, transportation, and home adaptation. A functionality-based conceptual framework and operational guide link bio-psycho-social assessments with tailored support, referral pathways, and case management across sectors. Progress was reinforced through EU-funded pilots and technical review by the national disability commission.
Georgia advanced systemic reforms with the development of its first Social Protection Strategic Note for Children and a child-rights-based budgeting methodology. These instruments establish a clear framework for integrating child priorities into national planning and resource allocation. Progress was sustained through consistent advocacy and collaboration with experts and academia, laying the foundation for coherent, rights based social protection systems.
UNICEF strengthened municipal systems to advance child-focused governance and service delivery, addressing territorial and gender disparities in access to services. Workforce capacity was assessed across 15 municipalities, generating actionable insights to guide targeted upskilling and supervision. Child-focused budgeting and emergency preparedness progressed through the development of a new methodology, an electronic budget assessment tool, and training materials piloted in five municipalities. Shock-responsive social protection readiness was assessed in Lanchkhuti and Zugdidi, while service equity improved through a new service-mapping methodology and the design of a minimum social service package. Regional peer-learning events reinforced momentum for scale-up.
In Abkhazia region, UNICEF resumed support for basic social services for children and families in difficult life situations. Operational and methodological support was provided to 25 district-based social workers. Between August and November 2025, case management and referrals were delivered to 125 vulnerable families, addressing protection risks, access to services, and alternative care. A social worker retreat in November strengthened coordination and identified priorities for 2026.
At the community level, UNICEF, in partnership with World Vision, supported para-social workers across 80 communities, resulting in referrals of 62 families (176 children). UNICEF also resumed the Ultra-Poverty Graduation Programme, supporting 30 vulnerable households with skills training, business assets, and technical assistance.

Overall, in 2025, UNICEF Georgia demonstrated its ability to deliver impact under constrained conditions while laying foundations for long-term change. By advancing gender-responsive social protection, strengthening equitable local systems, and addressing structural drivers of inequality, UNICEF acted as a convener and catalyst—uniting government, academia, civil society, partners, and children around evidence-based solutions, safeguarding reform gains, and remaining well positioned to advance child rights and gender equality in 2026.
