Challenges and Lessons learned
Implementation Context and Adaptive Response
The reporting period unfolded in a highly dynamic and politically sensitive environment, which significantly affected programme delivery. A rapidly evolving political landscape, coupled with reduced engagement from several international donors, resulted in lower-than-anticipated funding and necessitated the postponement or scaling down of planned interventions. Political volatility further constrained civic and media space, limiting opportunities for advocacy, communication, and public engagement.
In April, Parliament adopted the Foreign Agents’ Registration Act, requiring individuals and organizations receiving foreign funding to register. Subsequent amendments to the Grants Law introduced additional obligations for CSOs and donors to seek government approval for all foreign-funded grants. These legislative changes severely restricted collaboration with CSOs— traditional partners with strong technical expertise and outreach capacity. Frequent changes in government counterparts disrupted continuity and technical dialogue, while new restrictions under the EU grant further limited engagement with state institutions.
This shifting context required continuous reprioritization and adaptive planning. UNICEF adjusted its operational approach by increasing reliance on individual consultants and prioritizing direct engagement with rights-holders. Innovative methods were introduced to reach children and young people, with a focus on strengthening participation, empowerment, and pathways to skills and employment despite institutional constraints.
 
Child Justice and Rights Advocacy
The justice component was among the most affected areas due to limited cooperation with law enforcement agencies hindering efforts to advance child-friendly approaches at the systems level. Despite these challenges, UNICEF intensified efforts to empower children as rights-holders and raise awareness on access to justice. Activities focused on building the capacity of legal aid providers to deliver child-friendly services and exploring stronger collaboration with the Public Defender to reinforce child rights monitoring.
In November 2025, Parliament adopted the Law on Rehabilitation and Support of Juveniles under 14, granting justice agencies leading roles and creating a closed institution under the Ministry of Justice. UNICEF raised serious concerns, citing conflicts with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and national law, and urged revisions to ensure children remain under social welfare protection and never placed in closed facilities. The reform poses heightened risks for boys—who are more likely to be subjected to custodial measures. This development undermines Georgia’s progress in justice reform and represents a setback for child rights. UNICEF will continue advocating against child incarceration and for child-centered services within the welfare system.
 
Education and Skills Development
The challenging context also affected the education sector, leaving schools increasingly isolated from external opportunities and development-supported initiatives. In response, UNICEF prioritized partnerships with academia and direct engagement with children, teachers, and students to advance education and skills development programmes. In late November, the Government announced a new Education Reform agenda, introducing the National Concept for the Reform of the Higher Education System and the National Concept for General Education Reform. UNICEF was not consulted during the development of these concepts, which largely consist of broad statements and proposed initiatives. Additionally, in 2025, the activities under the school nutrition agenda were paused due to change of context and priorities in the country.
Strengthening data literacy remained a key priority, requiring tailored strategies for diverse audiences. University staff benefited most from methodological depth and integration into academic practice, while schoolchildren engaged better with interactive, gamified tools that make data relevant to their daily lives. Close collaboration between UNICEF and GeoStat demonstrated that combining statistical learning with child rights education significantly enhances participants’ ability to interpret data critically and apply evidence-based thinking in both academic and real-life contexts.
 
Operational Innovations and Risk Mitigation
Several innovative approaches were introduced to ensure operational continuity and efficiency. Establishing a remote authorization system in a geographically restricted and politically sensitive field office proved critical for maintaining uninterrupted operations, mitigating risks associated with limited mobility, and enhancing responsiveness.
The creation of the Programme Support Hub for the new Country Programme emerged as an effective strategy to optimize resources, resulting in significant cost-efficiency in staffing. Additionally, the development of the “Office Anywhere” concept strengthened emergency preparedness by enabling the Country Office to rapidly establish a fully functional office in any location. Successfully tested during emergency and Business Continuity Plan (BCP) simulations, the model relies on portable equipment—including Starlink satellite internet, Meraki network devices, mobile power sources, and spare laptops—all transportable in a single vehicle.
 
Future Outlook
The new 2026–2030 Country Programme Document introduces the seventh Country Programme since UNICEF established its presence in Georgia in 1993. The Country Programme Document (CPD) aligns with the 2026–2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and builds on lessons learned and achievements from previous programmes. Multidimensional child deprivation and poverty, and violence against children, are identified as flagship priorities. The accompanying Country Programme Management Plan outlines the human resources and governance mechanisms for optimal delivery of results, in line with UNICEF’s global Future Focus Initiative and the UN@80 reform agenda.
Building on strengthened cooperation with the Administration of the Government of Georgia and the Interagency Commission on CRC implementation, UNICEF will continue to advance coordinated national efforts for child rights. The institutionalization of annual review meetings agreed during the Commission session provides an important platform to align strategic priorities, track CPD outcomes and monitor joint workplans. At the same time, lessons from 2025 underscore the need for adaptive strategies in politically sensitive contexts, legislative restrictions on civil society engagement, and reduced donor presence. UNICEF will maintain its focus on resilience and innovation—leveraging partnerships, empowering rights-holders, and advocating for child-centered policies in justice, education, and social protection—while ensuring operational continuity through agile systems and preparedness measures. These approaches will be critical to safeguarding progress and driving results for children amid ongoing uncertainty.

There are 1,735,061 children in  Greece (51.5%  boys and 48.5% girls), accounting for 16.6 per cent of the  total  population, according to the Hellenic Statistical Agency (ELSTAT)  report  produced with the support of UNICEF in 2024. This indicates a  decrease of 5.3  per cent in the child population in the country  compared to the previous  census. The majority live with both their  parents under the same roof  (83.9%), 13 per cent live with one of their  parents, while 3,1 per cent do not  live with their parents.
  
  
  
Although a high-income country  and Member  State of the European Union (EU), Greece falls short in realizing   several aspects of children’s rights.  The  share of children at  risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2024 stood at 27.9%  (ELSTAT) ,  slightly  lower than 28.1 % in 2023. While the Government has  recognized  deinstitutionalization as a priority, achieving the  ambitious goal of zero  children in institutions by 2030 necessitates  the comprehensive reform of the  child protection system. This particularly  relates to the 2,846 children in  residential care, including 1,130  children in institutions under the  supervision of the Ministry of  Social Cohesion and Family (MoSCFA, October  2025) and 1,716  unaccompanied children in shelters under the Ministry of  Migration and  Asylum (MoMA, November 2025).
  
  
  
Children’s well being and health remains an issue  of concern. Greece’s National Action Plan  for Mental Health 2021–2030  emphasizes quality and safety of care,  proposing new guidelines and  data systems. WHO’s rapid  assessment of the quality of mental health care  in Greece revealed  challenges in data collection and highlighted the  importance of perception of  pediatricians, children and families among  the priorities areas for  monitoring the quality of mental health care.  There are no national protocols  for follow-up care, while long waiting  list times are reported for  psychiatric assessments for children and  young people with regional  disparities particularly for children and  adolescent mental health services. Regarding child and adolescent mental  health services,  there are no national procedures for transitioning  between services,  especially from child to adult mental health  services.
  
  
  
Greece’s education system  presents mixed  performance. The country has one of the lowest early school leaving rates in  the EU (3% compared to the EU average of 9.3%) (EU Commission, 2024). Data on  children with disabilities is limited, hindering  effective policy  responses. Refugee and migrant children,  despite having legal rights to  compulsory schooling, face structural and  logistical barriers - from  delayed reception classes to limited inclusion  supports - restricting  full access and sustained attendance compared with  native peers. Greece  has also low rates in all  three pillars of the European Skills’ Index  (ESI), ranking 28th  out of 31 countries in Skills Development, 27th in  Skills  Activation and 30th in Skills Matching (Cedefop).  This  reveals a mismatch between formal education and the skills required for   youth to access the labour market, with almost half of Greece  businesses  (47%) indicating that this gap hinders their growth  (CEDEFOP). In this  regard, the Future of Jobs Report 2025 (World  Economic  Forum) emphasizes that vocational education and training (VET)  is  critical for aligning education with labour market needs, supporting   school-to-work transitions, and equipping youth with practical and  green  skills. Furthermore, the Report reveals that among the core  skills demanded  by the labor market in Greece are empathy and active  listening, resilience,  flexibility and agility, analytical and creative  thinking. While in 2024,  Greece’s unemployment rate for youth 15-24  years old fell to 24.7%, down from  26.6% in 2023 (ILO  Data), this  remains far above the EU average of 14.3%, making Greece one  of the  countries with the highest youth unemployment in Europe (Eurostat).  In  addition, Greece ranks among the top four countries in the EU with the   highest percentage (14.2%) of young people aged 15-29 neither in  Employment,  nor in Education and Training (NEET 2024). This is  significantly high even  among youth with tert
iary education, at 16,8%  (Eurostat). 
  
Greece’s overall gender equality situation remains  a key structural challenge. Greece scored 57 out of 100 in the Gender  Equality Index for 2025, ranking 22nd  in the EU  for  2025  and below the EU index of 63.4 (EIGE). There is limited availability of  sex-disaggregated data, yet the available information and gender analysis  conducted indicate that girls and boys experience poverty, mental health  challenges, educational exclusion and transitions to employment differently,  influenced by gender norms, caregiving expectations and unequal access to  services. Adolescent girls face heightened risks related to mental health,  stigma and bodily autonomy, while boys are more exposed to early school  disengagement, behavioural stigma and harmful norms around masculinity that  affect help-seeking and wellbeing.   
  
Refugee and migrant issues  remained high in  the political agenda. ¿ total of 42,900 refugees and  migrants reached  Greece as of November 2025, mainly by sea, with the  majority arriving  in Crete (16,773), followed by Samos and Lesvos (MoMA,  November 2025).  Children account for 20.5 per cent and women 12.3 per cent of  arrivals  by sea (UNHCR, January 2026). Among total arrivals, 6,351 refugees  and  migrants have arrived in Greece by the land border (MoMA, November 2025).

By mobilizing the allocation of  domestic resources based on evidence-based planning and policies, UNICEF  focused on system strengthening and safeguarding children’s rights. Moreover,  UNICEF aimed to address specific structural deficiencies in the country’s  governance and public administration system, including coordination issues  at various governance levels, with the aim to drive the child  rights agenda and deliver results at scale for children. UNICEF strived to integrate gender-responsive and in several cases gender-transformative approaches, based on conducted gender analysis, addressing harmful social norms, unequal caregiving roles and gender-specific barriers affecting girls, boys and caregivers through system strengthening, service delivery and partnerships.
 
UNICEF continued working with the Ministry of  Health on the two main priorities for children’s health and well-being:  childhood obesity and mental health. To support and promote the State’s  efforts to prevent and combat childhood obesity, UNICEF provided technical  support to the Ministry of Health in implementing the National Action against  Childhood Obesity in Greece - a pioneering, multisectoral initiative that  promoted healthier lives for children and adolescents, while building  national capacity to address one of the country’s pressing public health  challenges. Progress was made in strengthening the capacity of the Ministry  of Health toward establishing a coherent national framework that promotes  healthy diets and physical activity. A comprehensive review of the national  legislative and institutional framework on nutrition and child health was  completed, identifying key gaps and priorities for improvement, while laying  the ground for a roadmap for future reforms, with long-term benefits and  impact for children’s health. In the European Centre to Address Child Obesity  – established with UNICEF support – the first tele-counselling sessions  started with 858 children (452 girls, 406 boys) having completed sessions by December 2025. Social  behavioural change was at the core of UNICEF’s interventions by mobilizing  schools, universities, provincial, municipal, authorities and communities to  adopt a healthier lifestyle. For this, UNICEF designed tailor-made,  age-appropriate aimed at strengthening children’s knowledge, attitudes, and  behaviours related to healthy nutrition and physical activity. The toolboxes  are evidence-based, available online, and include a comprehensive set of  educational, experiential, and interactive materials for teachers, parents,  and students aged 4–17. Implemented primarily through schools and reinforced by countrywide teacher training and complementary community-based activities,  these interventions helped promote heal
thier school environments and more consistent health messaging across schools, families, and communities, indirectly benefiting 93,858 children (est. 47,053 girls, 46,805 boys) in 2025; 18,857 children (10,509 boys, 8,348 girls) participated  in events to promote physical activities and 3,037 children (2,469 boys, 568 girls) benefitted from the provision of free placements in sports academies. School-based activities proved more effective in ensuring girls’ participation, while efforts to mobilise families and children directly were less successful, reflecting findings from the gender analysis on persistently lower participation of girls in organised team sports despite targeted efforts. Complementing these prevention  efforts, UNICEF leveraged the Sports for Development (S4D) approach, through  the training of sports teachers, strengthening the gender responsiveness of sport environments by addressing gender stereotypes, unequal participation, and harmful norms related to masculinity and promoting the integration of team sports into school and community settings as a tool for fostering cooperation,  self-discipline, inclusion, and healthy routines. In 2025, Finally, UNICEF  continued mobilizing schools, communities and young people to promote healthy  and sustainable eating habits, reduce food waste and strengthen civic  engagement. In 2025, over 70,400 adolescents (35,787 boys, 34,613 girls) participated in such activities.

As part of State  efforts to promote family and child health, UNICEF operationalized the  relevant partnership with the Ministry of Health, following a comprehensive gender analysis, in order to a) support  pediatricians in identifying developmental and behavioral disorders among  children as well as anxiety and depression among parents, while addressing gender-related gaps in early identification and referral; b) raise awareness  on menstrual health and hygiene among girls and boys aged 10-15 years old and;  c) address non-suicidal self-injury amongst youth (17-24 years old). The interventions of the programme between UNICEF and the Ministry of Health overall address gender-specific health risks and barriers, including adolescent girls’ mental health vulnerabilities, stigma around help-seeking and unequal caregiving burdens that disproportionately affect women, while promoting more equitable access to services for girls and boys. Focusing  on pediatricians across the country, UNICEF,  in partnership with the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens  (NKUA), supported the delivery of sensitization sessions on screening tools  and initiated the development of a national platform to include tools and  referrals to mental health services. To complement the services to which  pediatricians will be able to refer parents, UNICEF, in collaboration with  five local NGOs, partnered with Triple P International to pilot the first  positive parenting programme at national scale promoting shared caregiving responsibilities and challenging gender-stereotypical parenting norms, with targeted outreach to increase fathers’ engagement. By December 2025, 128 frontline professionals had been trained and started delivering positive  parenting sessions to approximately 1,500 parents (78% women, 22% men reflecting persistent gendered caregiving roles) and indirectly benefitting  almost 2,000 children. To promote adolescent health, UNICEF established a curriculum,  developed relevant training materials and delivered sessions on menstrual  health and hygiene to 61,004 children (49.5% girls, 50.5% boys based on available data) across 475 schools, in partnership with  two local NGOs. The training methodology approached menstruation as a matter of health, dignity and bodily autonomy, taking into consideration stigma reduction and gender equality, and engaged boys alongside girls to challenge harmful social norms and taboos. A study regarding policies on the promotion of menstrual  health and hygiene was initiated to further inform programming. Finally, UNICEF,  in partnership with NKUA, established and inaugurated the operation of a  Model Centre on Non-Suicidal Self Injury, which has delivered capacity building activities on identification and referral to 1,078 frontline health professionals (987 female, 91 male) and started the assessment of 44 patients (36 female, 8 male). The pattern also reinforces the importance of gender-responsive identification, referral and care pathways that promote equitable access for all.
  
UNICEF  played a critical role in advancing inclusive, equitable, and quality  education in the country. In the realm of  digital education, UNICEF, through the Akelius digital language learning  programme directly supported 433 educators, indirectly reaching 8,129 students (4,563 boys, 3,565 girls); sustained focus on equitable participation in digital learning initiatives, especially for girls living in marginalized environments is crucial. The programme enhanced digital infrastructure and internet  connectivity in participating schools, upgraded technical equipment, and  built teachers’ capacity in blended learning approaches, combining app-based  digital content with analogue teaching materials. In 2025, the  Akelius programme was used for the first time beyond refugee and  migrant learners, extending to host community students  to promote second-language learning, including English,  French, and German, fostering multilingualism and intercultural  learning. In alignment with national education reforms, the  programme was also introduced in pre-primary education to  support early English language learning, now a compulsory  subject in the national curriculum, ensuring the development of  foundational language skills from an early age. The programme further  expanded to Roma schools and pre-schools, supporting Greek  language acquisition for Roma children while simultaneously  strengthening digital literacy and educational inclusion,  contributing to reduced learning gaps and more equitable access to quality  education. In addition, to support MOERAS’ effort to fight school bullying –  an expressed priority of the Government – UNICEF piloted the Safe Schools Alliance  programme to promote bullying prevention and strengthen student mental  resilience in collaboration with regional authorities and Piraeus Bank. By  December 2025, this collaboration had delivered training to more than 377  additional educators, with an expected indirect reach of approximately 8,500 students in 2026. The programme includes 10-hour training focused on  recognizing signs of bullying and implementing curriculum-aligned,  interactive classroom sessions with their students and is supported by tailored resources. 

Efforts to improve the education system went hand in hand with strengthening skilling. UNICEF launched a joint programme  with the Public Employment Service (DYPA), aiming to equip young people in apprenticeship  schools countrywide with 21st century skills and green skills, in  line with modern labor market requirements, EU and national frameworks for  the empowerment of youth. To this end, 428 young people aged 15–24 (291 male and 147 female) were reached through  in-person skills-building workshops. Meanwhile, UNICEF prepared and mentored adolescents  and youth to participate meaningfully in high-level fora and raise issues of  their concern to policy-makers. Notably, 5,021 U-reporters have participated  in various polls since the launch of the polling platform, while two members  of UNICEF’s Child and Youth Advisory Board were mentored to present their key takeaways from  COP29 to the Climate Committee of the Hellenic Parliament,  advocating for stronger youth engagement in national climate policy and  urging the Greek Government to endorse the UNICEF Declaration on Children,  Youth and Climate Action. 
  
UNICEF strived to strengthen the child protection system, both top  down and bottom up by enhancing coordination, standardisation and frontline  capacity. At national level, UNICEF supported improved cooperation between  public prosecutors and municipal social services through the development of a  Protocol of Procedures for the Protection of Children at Risk, clarifying  roles, procedures and timelines for handling cases involving children at  risk. The protocol was accompanied by capacity building workshops, delivered  with the active participation of the Hellenic Association of Social Workers  (SKLE) and the participation of 788 professionals across Greece. In parallel,  a unified case recording system for child protection investigations handled  by prosecutors was developed by UNICEF for the Ministry of Justice to review  and adopt. The recording system aims to enhance data quality and consistency  across all prosecuting authorities, improve monitoring and evidence-based  decision making, while providing a foundation for system improvement, supporting  the integration of child-specific indicators into the national judicial data  collection system. Together, these reforms contributed to more gender-responsive child protection and justice services, including improved prevention of and response to gender-based and sexual violence, by recognizing how harmful gender norms shape exposure to risk, reporting patterns and access to protection for girls and boys.
 
At local level, UNICEF continued working with the Municipality of  Athens – the largest in the country, hosting approximately 93,000 children – for  the development of a child protection social service model focused on  child-centred risk assessment, case management and systematic data  collection. UNICEF provided technical support to establish the operational  framework for managing child protection cases and offered ongoing guidance to  social workers in their daily practice. The interventions also involved strengthening  the networks of community-based services to enable rapid and informed  responses to cases of child abuse. To support prevention and community  awareness, UNICEF collaborated with NKUA and its established Child Rights Centre  to carry out awareness-raising activities aimed at building an informed  community – primarily students and educators – on children’s rights and the consequences  of violence against children. In 2025, 56 child rights workshops were  delivered reaching 1,070 children, 230 students and 433 teachers.
  
UNICEF – with the support of the European Commission via the Technical  Support Instrument – worked with the Ministry of Social Cohesion and Family  Affairs (MoSCFA), as well as the National Center of Social Solidarity (EKKA),  appointed as National Coordinator (NC) of the European Child Guarantee (ECG) , with a view to establishing a sustainable system for monitoring the  situation of children in need, governed by a robust mechanism with clear  roles and accountabilities, as well as to take targeted action to address  childhood obesity and promote healthy nutrition of children in need with attention to the gendered dimensions of poverty, caregiving and social exclusion. Through  the technical support provided, both the Ministry and EKKA were equipped with  tools and processes to efficiently implement  the National Action Plan on the European  Child Guarantee, design evidence-based policies, and take targeted action on  fighting obesity as well as promote healthy nutrition among groups of  children in need.
  
Towards a more child-friendly justice system in Greece, UNICEF trained  for the second year – in collaboration with the Law School of the National and  Kapodistrian University of Athens – 23 legal professionals on child friendly  legal aid. Additionally, UNICEF contributed to the development of the  National Strategy for the Prevention of Violence and Delinquency of minors  through consultations with the Committee and the provision of policy  recommendations on  domestic violence, online violence, child friendly justice, and child  protection. UNICEF’s expertise on child friendly justice was  also showcased at the 13th International Seminar of the European  Forum for Restorative Justice on 16 May 2025 and the World Congress for  Justice with Children on 11 June 2025. 
  
To support the child  protection system for refugee and migrant children, UNICEF strengthened the  capacity of the Ministry of Migration and Asylum providing expert advice and  support. At the General Secretariat for Vulnerable Populations and  Institutional Protection, UNICEF’s expert provided technical support for the  implementation and monitoring of the national guardianship scheme for all  unaccompanied children. In March 2025, the findings of the first  participatory assessment of the guardianship implementation scheme were presented,  including strategies to retain and train guardians. Building  on these findings, and in response to emerging trends in the population of  unaccompanied children (with 53% of all unaccompanied children in Greece being Egyptian), UNICEF conducted a rapid assessment to capture the profile,  motivations, needs as well as recommendations to the authorities for their  protection and integration. In addition, through an expert seconded at the  Reception and Identification Service (RIS), UNICEF supported the development  of a training package to help staff working in refugee sites incorporate  harmonized child protection standards in their everyday work. UNICEF’s expert  trained 62 professionals who, in turn, trained 430 staff. To improve  learning outcomes and the wellbeing for migrant and refugee children, UNICEF  trained 410 educators through the Teach4Integration  initiative,  an intensive 400-hour synchronous and asynchronous professional  development programme, implemented in partnership with the Aristotle  University of Thessaloniki and the NKUA. The  programme strengthens teachers’ capacity to create safe, inclusive, and  supportive learning environments, addressing language barriers, psychosocial  needs, and risks of exclusion. UNICEF employed  digital solutions to improve the education prospects of 555 refugee and  migrant children, in coordination with the Ministry of Education, Religious  Affairs and Sports through the Akeli
us Digital Language Course. Complementing this effort, more than 1,160 educators registered in the UNICEF’s Teach for Inclusion 30-hour  asynchronous training, which equips teachers with practical tools  and inclusive pedagogical strategies to respond effectively to diverse  classrooms, including those enrolling newly arrived migrant and refugee  children.

By the end of 2025, 12 Child  Rights Centres had been established in collaboration with academia with the  vision to establish Centres in all 23 public universities of the 13  administrative regions of Greece. The Child Rights Centres model builds  upon the “whole-of-society’’ approach and has three key interlinked  functions: a) promoting child rights with a focus on schools,  Municipalities and community leaders; b) generating evidence-based  knowledge on children; and c) incorporating child rights into university  curricula. On 6 and 7 June 2025, UNICEF and the University of Patras  co-hosted an International Conference on the Role of Academia in promoting  child rights; a novel theme which attracted 144 speakers from 17 countries,  representing 37 universities and 12 research institutes and policy-making  bodies. The conference culminated to the creation of an English-language  European Master’s program on child rights, which will be offered within 2026  in partnership with UNICEF and the Child Rights Centers of the University of  Patras and the University of Peloponnese. The first Network Meeting of the  Child Rights Centres in Greece was attended by the Coordinators of 11  established Centres from across the country reaffirming their collective  commitment and highlighting the critical role of promoting, researching, and  teaching child rights as essential pillars for advancing the rights and  well-being of every child. Inspired by the successful experience of Greece,  Cameroon and Gambia COs initiated with the academic partners the  establishment of Child Rights Centres, and Cameroon replicated in November a  second international conference on the role of academia in promoting and  protecting child rights in Yaounde, during which an African academic network  for child rights was launched. 

UNICEF translated evidence, community-level action, and policy  advocacy into tangible results for children affected by climate and  environmental risks. This was achieved through school- and community-based interventions that strengthened children’s resilience to climate and environmental shocks capacity-building for educators, municipal staff, and health and social professionals on practical disaster readiness, psychosocial support guidance, direct engagement with families in high-risk and underserved areas to support household preparedness and protective practices . UNICEF-supported  interventions reached more than 2,500 children (713 girls, 696 boys) as well as caregivers, educators, health  and social professionals across high-risk and underserved areas. This demonstrated the effectiveness of decentralized,  community-based implementation models, particularly in Roma communities and disaster-prone municipalities. In parallel, UNICEF Greece piloted child-responsive disaster preparedness across multiple municipalities,  strengthening local capacities through in-person and online trainings,  tools, and child-friendly materials, while generating  nationally relevant insights informed directly by children and youth. Targeted interventions were combined with youth engagement at the Hellenic Parliament, UNICEF recommendations to the Presidency of the Government in the formulation of the European Social Climate  Plan and Fund; and advocacy efforts for child-sensitive EU and national NDCs.

In 2025, UNICEF worked with public and private partners to mobilize support for children. Public sector funding derived mainly from partnerships with the Greek Ministry of Health and the European Commission’s SG REFORM. While sizeable and predictable, public sector funding is tightly earmarked leaving little flexibility in programme implementation; as such, efforts to diversify resources continued. 

Significant progress was made in galvanizing stronger corporate partnerships and advocacy initiatives with the private sector reaching broader audiences and reinforcing its profile among corporate and high-value stakeholders. UNICEF renewed through 2026  its impactful collaboration with Piraeus Bank on combating school bullying and negotiated the renewal of its partnership with Lidl Hellas for 2026 proposing to expand it to new programmatic activities that will pave the way for scale-up and capacity building of professionals and young people on child protection country-wide. High-profile visibility opportunities were organized to promote and honour the long-standing partnerships with both donors. UNICEF substantially expanded its corporate pipeline, primarily targeting customer engagement opportunities with the retail and tourism sectors. New digital assets and offerings were also developed to attract high-value audiences and explore new fundraising opportunities. UNICEF also pioneered work on the intersection between business and child rights, conducting the first national assessment on the integration of child rights into corporate policies and practices. The main findings were presented at a landmark business event co-organized with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Hellas in December 2025 – the lead platform in Greece bringing together corporate actors for social causes. The event brought together more than 100 stakeholders from business, academia, and institutions in panels featuring youth and business leaders committed to advancing child rights in corporate strategies and aiming at further reinforcing engagements with businesses for fundraising purposes in 2026. UNICEF’s work was also showcased in high-level business-related forums, such as the Delphi Economic Forum, Athens ESG Forum, CSR in Action, CSR School, and business executive trainings. 

To promote greater financing for children, UNICEF, in coordination with Greece’s Ministry of Economy and Finance, hosted an expert workshop on the present and the future of child budgeting to exchange good practices and experiences on the various approaches in child budgeting from high income countries in Europe (Iceland, Spain and Scotland). 

As there is no United Nations Country Team in Greece, coordination takes place through interagency national and  local working groups, including with Heads of Agencies. To foster coherence in action among the largest UN agencies, regular Programme Management Team meetings were held with the participation of UNHCR, IOM, and the ad hoc inclusion of WHO, to facilitate  exchange of information, good practices and advocacy amongst senior management. In parallel, within the framework of  the refugee and migrant response, UNICEF co-chaired the PSEA working group and participated in the Child Protection and GBV sub-working groups.

Greece has the opportunity to capitalize on the achievements of the Child Guarantee and the availability of European funds to move forward with the scale up hand in hand with the – much necessary – reform of the child protection system. As such, achieving the ambitious goal of zero children in institutions by 2030 necessitates redoubled efforts at national and municipal level. To address this, UNICEF sustained its advocacy towards the line Ministry, including for the mobilization of available resources through ESF+, while simultaneously working with Municipalities to build bottom-up a more resilient child protection system. In line with its transition plan, the ACE programme was handed over to the Greek authorities in June 2024. Despite the political commitment for the provision of educational opportunities for refugee and migrant children, language and homework support remain limited. UNICEF has and remains committed to sustaining a strategic, high-level collaboration with MoERAS to assume an advisory role on inclusive education. With the end of the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility in June 2026, efforts by UNICEF will concentrate on the smooth and sustainable completion of the two large-scale programmes implemented jointly with the Ministry of Health. Efforts will continue to address patterns of caregiving, poverty and service access that shape children’s exclusion and risks in different ways for girls and boys.
UNICEF currently delivers its work through 80 personnel (58 female, 22 male), including through secondments to key line Ministries to strengthen their capacity. To carry forward its priorities, UNICEF will adopt a lean, agile business model that concentrates on the need to increase the capacity of the State to deliver results for children, reconnecting its resources to system over service delivery. Operational efficiency will be at the core of the endeavour, with sustainability prioritized in line with an enhanced focus on system strengthening. This will be realized through optimized resource allocation, flexible contract modalities, robust resource oversight and risk management, cost-efficiency, and strategic partnerships.
Moving forward, 2026 will mark a year of adjustment for UNICEF in Greece in view of global funding cuts affecting the entirety of the organization. This transition may mobilize greater synergies with other EU, high-income countries which will focus on partnership building, strategic positioning, and catalytic programming to generate at-scale results for children. The need for this greater focus was also reflected in the preliminary multi-country programme evaluation as the viable path forward. Presence in Greece will continue in line with the concept and parameters of the planned multi-country office for four high income countries in the EU. Through high-level policy advice, advocacy, evidence and knowledge generation, innovation, and selective timebound technical assistance, UNICEF will focus on a few unfinished reforms, such as child poverty, taking into consideration gendered inequalities that affect children’s well-being. These targeted efforts will enable transformative change and help unlock credible partnerships for children locally and around the world.

In 2025, Kazakhstan advanced an ambitious wave of legislative and regulatory reforms aimed at strengthening child well-being and accelerating the realization of children’s rights. The measures covered healthcare, education, family policy, social protection, violence prevention, and digital safety, reflecting a shift from fragmented interventions toward an integrated, preventive, and rights-based system.

Kazakhstan also reaffirmed its commitment to the UN 2030 Agenda, moving from broad alignment to deeper integration of the SDGs into national planning. A major milestone was the presentation of the Third Voluntary National Review, based on MICS 2024 findings, at the UN High-Level Political Forum. The opening of the UN Regional SDG Centre for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty further positioned Kazakhstan as a regional hub for advancing sustainable development and strengthening cross-border cooperation. Kazakhstan continues to make steady progress on gender equality, ranking 50th out of 172 countries in the Gender Inequality Index with a low inequality score of 0.182, reflecting strong outcomes in health, empowerment, and economic participation.
Government investments in human capital, coupled with structured institutional reforms, continued to demonstrate a strong commitment to enhancing accountability, improving service delivery, and advancing child-centred policies at both national and subnational levels.

Kazakhstan’s demographic profile provides a unique opportunity for long-term development gains. Nearly half of the population is under the age of 30, and over the next two decades this cohort will form the country’s largest labour force to date. With the right policies, this demographic shift can generate a significant demographic dividend through higher productivity, rising household incomes, and sustained economic growth.

Economic growth remained robust in 2025, driven by the oil sector and strong domestic demand. GDP expanded by approximately 6.3 percent in the first nine months of the year, outperforming international forecasts. Investment growth (16.1 percent) also supported the positive trajectory. However, inflation persisted as a major challenge, fluctuating between 10 and 13 percent according to IMF estimates. Expansionary fiscal policy -including substantial National Fund transfers and a non-oil fiscal deficit exceeding 8 percent of GDP - continued to exert upward pressure on prices. To strengthen fiscal sustainability, the Government adopted a new Budget Code and Tax Code in 2025, aiming to gradually reduce dependence on the National Fund and reinforce long-term discipline.

Despite overall progress, regional disparities remain pronounced. Regions with the lowest per capita income also experience the most significant child deprivations, as confirmed by MICS 2024. Place of residence and income level are the strongest predictors of disadvantage. Children from the bottom 40 percent of the income distribution particularly those in rural areas, face persistent challenges in education, access to safe drinking water, and financial inclusion. Digital access has improved nationwide, and gaps have narrowed, but urban low-income families continue to lag in mobile phone and internet access. Moreover, urban poor children show higher rates of acute malnutrition (wasting) compared to other groups. Wasting (4.5%) and underweight (2.4%) are less prevalent nationally yet remain concentrated among boys and children from disadvantaged households, with rural residence.

A positive trend is the reduction of overweight prevalence (7.5%) among children under five, however boys from richer households are more at risk, highlighting the importance of addressing gender and socioeconomic patterns in early childhood nutrition.

The largest inequality is observed in early childhood education and organized learning. Participation in early childhood education ranges from 55 % among children from poorer households with lowly educated mothers to 77 % among children from richer households with highly educated mothers. Similarly, participation in organized learning is lowest among children from poorer households and highest among girls from richer households with highly educated mothers, highlighting persistent socio-economic gradients early in life.

Poverty declined slightly in 2025, with 5.3 percent of the population living below the subsistence minimum, compared to 5.6 percent in 2024. Although the situation has improved, levels have not returned to 2022 figures. Children remain disproportionately affected: 7.2 percent lived below the poverty line in 2025, compared to 9.1 percent in 2022. Rural children are particularly vulnerable, with poverty rates at 10 percent, significantly higher than the 6.4 percent reported among urban children. In 2023, children accounted for 40 percent of the poor population, up from 27 percent in 2006. Climate shocks further compound vulnerabilities, especially for rural and low-income families. While Kazakhstan faces climate risks to a lesser extent than its neighbors, its adaptive capacity remains limited, increasing exposure to shocks.
Kazakhstan continued consolidating its reputation as a regional digital leader in 2025. Major investments in digital transformation supported more accessible, transparent, and efficient social protection services. UNICEF assisted the Government - particularly the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection - in transitioning from a categorical to a needs-based social assistance model, enabled by the Digital Family Card information system and a new scoring-based eligibility approach. During the year, Kazakhstan also adopted Central Asia’s first Law on Artificial Intelligence, launched a National AI Development Plan, and established a dedicated ministry for digital development and AI.

Following recommendations from the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which emphasized Kazakhstan’s continued reliance on a medical model of disability and gaps in anti-discrimination legislation, the Government adopted the Concept of Inclusive Policy for 2025–2030. UNICEF provided technical support in preparing a draft law to amend national legislation on disability rights, ensuring alignment with international standards and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

A particularly significant development in 2025 was the advancement of evidence-based social policy. The Bureau of National Statistics, with UNICEF’s support, finalized a multidimensional poverty measurement methodology. It was endorsed in January 2026 and will enable more precise targeting of social programmes, address structural inequalities, and operationalize the principle of “leaving no one behind” across national policies.

The number of children in residential care increased from 11,281 in 2023 to 13,532 in 2024, largely due to improved data accuracy following revisions to the national database on children in alternative care. Legislative amendments introduced in 2025 strengthened safeguards for children without parental care by prioritizing family-based care, formalizing a professional mentoring system, and raising qualification and accountability standards for professionals working with vulnerable children. Measures to prevent violence, including bullying and abuse were reinforced through stronger legal responsibilities, enhanced oversight mechanisms, and coordinated prevention programmes.

Every Child Thrives
 
Health
 
Infant mortality continued to decline from 7.67 in 2023 to 6.80 in 2024, marking a notable improvement in early childhood survival. In 2025, UNICEF provided extensive support to the Government of Kazakhstan to strengthen health services, particularly in early childhood development (ECD), patronage models, immunization, and adolescent mental health.
 
UNICEF supported the integration of early childhood development and early intervention services into the pediatric care standard at the primary health-care level, including the establishment and regulation of Development and Early Intervention Centers within polyclinics. The Guide for Monitoring Child Development (GMCD) was adapted to Kazakhstan’s context, and 16 national master trainers were prepared to lead capacity-building efforts.
 
To further strengthen the Universal Progressive Model of Patronage (UPMP), UNICEF offered technical expertise to integrate gender responsive approaches into pediatric PHC standards, updated training modules, and conducted a national assessment of the model’s goals, functions, outcomes, and resources. Training sessions were delivered for trainers and specialists to support nationwide scale-up. As the result, the proportion of health providers delivering home-visiting services with adequate skills in gender-sensitive caregiving, early stimulation and responsive parenting increased from 10% (2019) to 80% (2025).
UNICEF also strengthened the national immunization system by adapting a training module on interpersonal communication for vaccination. A master-training programme helped equip more than 200 trainers with skills to work effectively with parents and support increased uptake of child immunization.
UNICEF’s partnership with the Government of Kazakhstan on procurement services remains a critical mechanism for ensuring timely and equitable access to safe, affordable, and quality-assured medicines and health supplies. In 2025, UNICEF supported the procurement of four types of vaccines, antiretroviral medicines (ARVs), and OraQuick HIV self-tests, with a total value of USD 5.6 million, ensuring quality assurance, cost efficiency, and full transparency in line with international procurement standards. 

Under the Global Health Security agenda, youth engagement expanded significantly with the establishment of six UNICEF Youth Community Hubs in Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Aktau, Semey, and Kokshetau. Through the “Sau Bol” programme, more than 2,000 new volunteers were mobilized, and 4,476 completed online training to strengthen community-level preparedness for public health emergencies.
 
Nutrition
 
UNICEF continued supporting national efforts to address overweight, obesity, and micronutrient deficiencies among children, with a strong focus on improving the quality of school meals for 1.7 million primary school children. The Ministries of Health and Education officially adopted the national nutrition standard for educational institutions, developed with the Kazakh Academy of Nutrition and UNICEF.
 
The standard defines clear procedures for procurement, food preparation, community engagement, and nutrition education; establishes rules to limit sugar, salt, and saturated fats; and restricts the sale of unhealthy foods and beverages in schools. It also specifies required quantities and frequency of diverse food groups - meat, fish, dairy, fruits, vegetables, legumes, and grains to ensure adequate nutrition.
 
To ensure school menus meet national nutrient standards, UNICEF developed an online application that allows parents and schools to assess macro- and micronutrient composition of meals. With UNICEF support, the National Center for Public Health and the National Center for Healthy Nutrition trained 2,000 health workers, local departments, school meal providers, and school administrators on the new standards and use of the web application.
 
UNICEF also supported the development of recommended menus for schools and kindergartens and the launch of a dedicated national website on school nutrition, serving as a comprehensive resource for families, educators, and food providers.
 
Mental Health
 
According to national data, 16.6% of adolescents show poor mental well-being or signs of possible depression. Nearly half do not seek MHPSS services due to parental consent requirements. Self-harm remains the leading cause of death among adolescents and youth (10–24), with suicide rates increasing sharply with age and higher incidence in rural areas.
 
Promoting the mental health and well-being of children, and reducing high suicide rates, remains a national priority.
 
In April 2025, the Government initiated the development of the National Programme Children of Kazakhstan, and UNICEF provided technical recommendations to strengthen mental health policy, legislation, and intersectoral systems. Support focused on improving service accessibility, coverage, quality, and cross-sector collaboration.
 
In August 2025, the Orken Institute, with UNICEF support, began developing a national Comprehensive Plan for preventing bullying, suicide, and violence in secondary schools. Psychological support services were strengthened through a standardized trauma-informed training programme. UNICEF trained 51 national trainers, at least one per region who subsequently trained 204 professionals, including school psychologists and parenting specialists.
 
UNICEF supported mainstreaming MHPSS across government systems by helping establish a unified psychological services system within the education sector. Standards and guidelines for MHPSS in youth health centres were piloted and scaled, and an accreditation system was introduced to ensure quality.
 
Every Child Learns
 
In 2025, UNICEF’s evidence-informed advocacy supported the Ministry of Education in reviewing early childhood education and care (ECEC) financing and the national assistive technologies ecosystem to improve access, equity, inclusion, and quality. The ECEC and education agenda was delivered with the high-level engagement from the government, especially Ministers of education, health and social protection but also with technical dialogue with the UNICEF regional advisors and specialists on ECD, ECI, Education, Disability and Digital Learning, Financing.   
 
Despite high official enrolment figures, MICS 2024 shows only 68.7% of children aged 3–5 accessing preschool, revealing significant methodological discrepancies and highlighting the need for harmonised indicators aligned with international standards. Children in rural areas, low-income families, and children with disabilities remain the least likely to access quality, affordable preschool education. Only 1.4% of children with disabilities were enrolled in kindergartens in 2024, despite a 10% disability prevalence.
 
UNICEF recommended adopting an equity-sensitive per-capita funding formula, extending inclusion incentives to private kindergartens, and strengthening quality assurance mechanisms.
 
With UNICEF support, the Government developed the first ever joint Satty Bastau Comprehensive Plan on ECD and Early Intervention (2025–2027).This landmark plan represents the first coordinated action among the ministries of health, education, and social welfare to ensure the best start in life for every child. It establishes a unified framework to deliver high-quality early childhood development and early intervention services, especially for children with developmental needs and disabilities.
 
UNICEF also continued to technically support the Government service provision strengthening, more than 4,600 frontline workers and 1,000 parents accessed online training, and over 166,700 parents received information on developmental milestones through UNICEF’s platforms. The national conference in October 2025 culminated in the Astana Call to Action on the Best Start for Every Child, reaffirming national commitments.
 
UNICEF strengthened inclusive education through evidence-based reforms on early identification, intervention, and equity-sensitive financing. Through the Assistive Technologies Ecosystem Assessment, UNICEF recommended standardized terminology, unified data systems, and stronger parental engagement. UNICEF equipped 1,300 children with disabilities with assistive technologies and reached over 16,000 indirectly. Two national online training courses and a handbook for 5,100 computer science teachers were integrated into the Orleu platform.
 
UNICEF also advanced innovation through Digital Public Goods and inclusive game design modules co-created with girls, now available on the Learning Passport platform.
 
Skills
 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened national education systems to support future-ready skills. Technical assistance helped integrate social-emotional learning modules (ages 10–13) and mental health awareness programmes (ages 14–17) into the draft National Comprehensive Plan. Overall in 2025, 42 000 adolescents participated in UNICEF supported skills initiatives, of whom 50.7% were girls enchancing their STEM, civic engagement and employability skills.
Through Skills4Girls partnerships with KBTU, accessibility modules were added to the national game development course, enabling girls in STEM to co-create inclusive games that reflect diversity, ethics, and emerging global trends.
 With UNICEF’s support, Youth-led climate change education initiatives reached 60 schools, engaging 25,682 students, including 13,810 girls in research and project-based learning on climate mitigation and adaptation.
The UN Youth Advisory Council (50% female) continued shaping UN and Government policy dialogue. Council members participated in national youth events and initiated a U-Report survey to gather youth perspectives for future advocacy.
 
Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation
 
In 2025, UNICEF supported Kazakhstan in advancing child protection system reforms and elevating high-level advocacy and policy dialogue on VAC, mental wellbeing and early childhood development, through policy development, institutional capacity strengthening, and enhanced service delivery. The State counsellor, Child Rights Commissioner and the Senate played an important role in advancing UNICEF’s advocacy, strengthening national commitments to children’s rights, and accelerating child-centred reforms, including through the development of the National Programme Children of Kazakhstan (2026–2030). 

UNICEF contributed to the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan on Protection of Children from Violence, Suicide Prevention, and Ensuring Children’s Rights and Wellbeing (2023–2025) and to the development of the upcoming National Programme Children of Kazakhstan (2026–2030). UNICEF also supported the design of a national programme on suicide and violence prevention with strong emphasis on school-based interventions.
 
A national child protection system maturity assessment conducted with line ministries examined legislation, governance, service delivery, workforce capacity, coordination, child participation, and data systems. Findings informed the development of the Minimum Package of Child Protection Services and supported the establishment of Child Rights Protection Departments under local Akimats.
 
UNICEF supported the development of standards regulating child-friendly support rooms for child victims of violence—ensuring coordinated, child-sensitive, multi-sectoral assistance “under one roof”.
 
Thirty-one regional focal points were trained and cascaded training to specialists from Family Support Centers and mobile teams. More than 1,500 professionals were trained nationally, and specialists provided social, psychological, and legal support to approximately 20,000 families, with 15,400 families under regular monitoring.
 
UNICEF strengthened psychological support through standardized trauma-informed training for 51 national trainers and 204 frontline professionals.
 
In online child sexual exploitation and abuse, UNICEF supported coordination with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and contributed to competency assessments for cyber police units and police academies in 10 regions.
MICS 2024 shows violent discipline decreased from 52.7% in 2015 to 38% in 2025, a 28% reduction at national level. Though boys from poorer households and children of less-educated mothers consistently form the furthest-behind groups, particularly in urban areas. In contrast, girls from richer households living in urban areas are the least exposed to violent discipline. These patterns highlight the role of gender norms, household wealth, and parental education in shaping children’s exposure to violence.
UNICEF supported integrating a violence and bullying module into the National Education Database and piloted a monitoring framework for children returning from conflict zones.
Overall, 2025 saw significant progress in child protection reforms, strengthened legislation, and deeper recognition of child protection as an integrated, multi-sectoral system, and reached 1.4 million people through campaigns on violence prevention, positive parenting, and online safety.

Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment
 
In 2025, UNICEF accelerated child-sensitive climate action in Kazakhstan by positioning child rights and climate resilience at the centre of national climate policy and investment frameworks. 

Through evidence-based advocacy, targeted technical assistance, and youth engagement UNICEF supported the transition from policy commitments to institutionalized, child-responsive climate governance. As a result, Kazakhstan adopted a USD 1.2 billion investment envelope to upgrade 2,000 social facilities for children reaching 1,500 million children. This includes $239.1 million from the state budget and $982.6 million from other investors, with strong focus on climate-resilient education, green skills, and youth-led climate action.

A key milestone was the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources’ commitment to integrate child rights and child-specific vulnerabilities into Kazakhstan’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) marking a shift toward a child-sensitive NDC that recognizes children as both a high-risk group and agents of climate adaptation and mitigation. This was reinforced by endorsement of the Concept for Ecological Culture Development (2024–2029), embedding climate awareness, environmental stewardship, and intergenerational responsibility into public policy. 

At the global level, Kazakhstan joined 65 countries in signing the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action, signaling alignment with international child-centred climate agenda and strengthening access to climate finance partnerships and inclusive governance platforms. 
To operationalize these commitments, UNICEF, together with the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Regional Center on Emergencies and DRR, and the Bureau of National Statistics, developed Kazakhstan’s first Children’s Climate Risk Index (CCRI) model using UNICEF’s CCRI Disaster Risk Management methodology. Subnational data collection established a national baseline on children’s exposure, vulnerability, and adaptive capacity, supporting risk-informed planning, intersectoral coordination, and digital integration.
 
Critically for sustainability, the Government agreed to institutionalize CCRI DRM within national statistical systems and local planning processes, enabling predictable financing, scalability, and long-term evidence-based decision-making. Capacity-building in GIS, climate risk analysis, and modelling strengthened national ownership. 

Complementary interventions strengthened climate-resilient health systems, including regulatory reforms for air quality monitoring in schools and integration of environmental health into pediatric care, directly reducing climate-related health risks for children.

Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life

In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Kazakhstan in advancing inclusive, child-sensitive, and rights-based social protection reforms during a period of economic and institutional transition. Despite strong GDP growth driven by oil production and investment expansion, persistent inflation, fiscal vulnerabilities, and geopolitical risks continued to disproportionately affect low-income households and families with children, especially those with disabilities. UNICEF’s support focused on strengthening effectiveness, equity, and child rights integration within social protection systems and services to address multidimensional child poverty.
 
A major milestone was the completion of an innovative multidimensional poverty measurement methodology by the Bureau of National Statistics in partnership with UNICEF. Moving beyond income measures, the new approach captures child deprivations across education, health, and living standards. The methodology has been formally adopted in early 2026. Once institutionalized, it will allow more precise identification of children and families in difficult life situations, including those experiencing overlapping vulnerabilities.
 
UNICEF also supported the Government’s transition from a categorical to a needs-based social assistance model, led by the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection. The reform is anchored in the Digital Family Card integrated information system and a new scoring-based eligibility methodology piloted in Shymkent and Karaganda. UNICEF provided technical assistance to assess the scoring logic, conduct simulation analysis using household survey data, benchmark international practices, and deliver recommendations to enhance equity, transparency, and inclusion before national scale-up.
 
Another significant achievement was the Government’s adoption of the Concept of Inclusive Policy for 2025–2030, following the Concluding Observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Concept formally recognizes structural discrimination and introduces non-discrimination and reasonable accommodation as guiding principles. It also commits Kazakhstan to transitioning from a medical to a social and human rights–based model of disability. UNICEF continues providing technical support to draft legislation amending national laws on disability rights, ensuring alignment with international standards and the UN CRPD.
 
To inform fiscal and policy dialogue during broader governance reforms, including the adoption of new Budget and Tax Codes, UNICEF launched a study on fossil fuel subsidies to identify opportunities for redirecting fiscal resources toward targeted, child-sensitive social protection. UNICEF advocated for shifting from broad, untargeted subsidies to compensatory mechanisms that protect vulnerable families while maintaining fiscal stability. Findings will be presented in early 2026.
 
These results reflect strong national commitment to equity and inclusion, with UNICEF providing technical expertise to ensure children’s rights remain central to social protection modernization.
 
Cross-Cutting
Evidence Generation, Knowledge Management, and Evaluation
 
In 2025, Kazakhstan, with UNICEF’s technical support successfully completed and presented the results of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2024. Findings were shared with the Presidential Administration,Office of Prime-Minister,Parliament, and all 20 regional governments. Using MICS data and administrative sources, region-specific socio-economic profiles were developed to identify child rights deprivations and key achievements. Twenty regional consultations were jointly organized with the Bureau of National Statistics, strengthening evidence-based planning and local accountability. These results, together with the Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents, informed the draft flagship programme Children of Kazakhstan, marking a significant shift toward integrated, child-focused policy planning.

UNICEF supported the Government in shaping the landmark state programme “Children of Kazakhstan” through targeted technical assistance and policy advice, strengthening compliance with international standards and ensuring that children’s wellbeing as a core driver of inclusive and sustainable economic growth. 
 
UNICEF, in partnership with the Ministry of Education and other line ministries, facilitated national consultations to validate the Generation 2050 analytical report for Kazakhstan. The country co-hosted the regional launch of Generation 2050 – Central Asia at the SDG Hub, resulting in a joint commitment from Central Asian governments to develop a regional roadmap for investments in quality education, child protection systems, NEET reduction, and social protection transformation.
 
UNICEF supported youth consultations led by the Ministry of National Economy through U-Report during the preparation of Kazakhstan’s Third Voluntary National Review (VNR 2025). Responses from young people across all 20 regions were integrated into a dedicated youth chapter of the VNR. UNICEF also collaborated with the Bureau of National Statistics to prepare and present the statistical annex, strengthening national SDG monitoring systems.
 
UNICEF contributed substantial inputs to the UPR, CEDAW, and CESCR processes, with 20 percent of UPR concluding observations reflecting UNICEF’s recommendations, accelerating progress on core child rights priorities. UNICEF also played an active role in developing the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2026–2030, contributing to the Common Country Assessment, UNSDCF evaluation, and multilateral consultations with Government and civil society.
 
The Bureau of National Statistics continued to lead the national working group on child data, with UNICEF support prioritizing the testing of a minimum set of indicators on violence against children, alternative care, and children with disabilities, aligning the Child Rights Monitoring framework with national monitoring systems, preparing the annual Statistical Yearbook on Children and TransMonEE reporting. 
 
Kazakhstan actively contributed to the Steering Group on Statistics on Children led by UNICEF and UNECE, reinforcing its commitment to advancing methodological standards and sharing best practices across the region.

UNICEF, together with the Ministry of Digital Development and AI and the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, finalized a practical case study on the use of causal machine learning to evaluate and optimize social welfare policies. Using large-scale administrative and socio-economic data, the study estimated heterogeneous treatment effects of cash transfer programmes on household and child outcomes, including financial vulnerability, debt accumulation, and proxy indicators of social stability. Results revealed substantial variations in policy impacts across population groups, demonstrating that uniform programme design risks inefficient spending and missed opportunities for targeted support.

Communication and Advocacy
 
In 2025, UNICEF Kazakhstan significantly expanded youth engagement, communication, and public advocacy, positioning young people as active partners in advancing child rights and sustainable development. These efforts aligned with national political reforms that prioritize civic participation, digital governance, and inclusive policymaking. 
 
UNICEF launched a nationwide Youth Engagement Programme, marking a major shift toward structured, large-scale youth volunteerism. By year-end, nearly 10,000 young people were mobilized, with 4,476 actively engaged across all regions. Six UNICEF Youth Hubs were established in Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Aktau, Kokshetau, and Semey—each led by dedicated regional coordinators. The hubs serve as platforms for structured participation, peer learning, and community outreach, particularly on public health preparedness.
 
Across the hubs, 4,476 volunteers completed online training and contributed to community initiatives. Their efforts included planting 20,000 trees, collecting 500 tons of waste, and delivering awareness sessions on child rights and protection that reached one million people. More than 75 youth engagement activities were delivered across environmental action, advocacy, training, and institutional dialogue, providing safe, interactive spaces for young people to build skills, engage communities, and discuss protective behaviours, and child rights. A national UNICEF Youth Forum in Almaty convened leading youth volunteers to showcase 13 competitively selected projects on environment, mental health and community safety, connect with government, business and civil society leaders, and strengthen youth leadership nationwide. 
 A new pro-bono partnership has been established with Documentolog, leading Kazakh IT-company, for pro-bono development of UNICEF national volunteer digital platform.  
Institutional partnerships were strengthened through formal cooperation with the largest regional universities and local Departments for Youth Policy, reflecting strong government support for youth empowerment under the updated State Youth Policy Concept. U-Report Kazakhstan expanded significantly, reaching 13,605 registered U-Reporters, a 155% increase from 2024 and establishing itself as a national tool for youth feedback in policymaking. 
 
Influencer engagement remained an important component of UNICEF’s outreach. In 2025, 66 digital influencers supported UNICEF campaigns on online safety, positive parenting, early childhood development, ending violence against children, healthy behaviours, and mental health and wellbeing. UNICEF’s digital platforms continued steady growth. In 2025, total UNICEF social media followers reached 133,509, reflecting a 15 percent increase compared to 2024. 
 
Finally, UNICEF, the Ministry of Education, and the Constitutional Court co-organized a nationwide children's drawing contest to mark the 30th anniversary of the Constitution. The contest engaged 169 schoolchildren, and 30 winning artworks were published in a trilingual art book officially presented to the Presidential Administration, symbolizing Kazakhstan’s continued commitment to meaningful child participation in civic life.
