In 2025, UNICEF significantly strengthened its credibility and impact through strategic private-sector engagement, tripling resource mobilization for children’s rights. Building on the success of Kazakhstan’s first UNICEF Charity Gala, the second edition - Dreams Without Borders - demonstrated how sustained partnerships and innovative approaches dramatically amplify results. Through powerful storytelling, influencer engagement, and citywide branding, UNICEF not only raised USD 547,000 - three times the previous year’s figure - but also elevated national awareness of adolescent mental well-being. The event showcased the strong commitment of Kazakhstan’s business community to creating a better future for children.

The Gala highlighted the transformative power of cross-sector collaboration. Businesses, philanthropists, and artists contributed significant financial and in-kind support, including pro bono performances and media coverage valued at USD 379,000. Combining advocacy with cultural engagement, the event reached 11.3 million people, reinforcing the importance of visibility and credibility in driving social change. Resources mobilized will support capacity building for more than 50,000 frontline specialists and enhance mental health and well-being services for 140,000 adolescents nationwide - demonstrating that creative partnerships can deliver both awareness and tangible results.

The Gala strengthened UNICEF’s tradition of partnership with Kazakhstan’s private sector, grounded in the country’s strong culture of philanthropy. UNICEF also deepened its engagement with high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs), applying a more targeted and personalized approach to cultivate long-term relationships. Through tailored outreach, curated events, and strengthened value propositions, UNICEF broadened its pipeline of major donors and increased interest among Kazakhstan’s most influential philanthropists.

In 2024, after an eight-year break, Kazakhstan successfully completed the largest data collection operation in the Europe and Central Asia region - the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) - with strong support from UNICEF, UNFPA, and the Asian Development Bank. Covering 24,000 households with a 96.4% response rate, the survey generated high-quality data, including GPS-verified information, across five comprehensive questionnaires. The survey produced high-quality, nationally representative data on women, girls, adolescents, and households—providing a stronger baseline for analysing gender disparities in health, nutrition, education, protection, and adolescent well-being. MICS 2024 was incorporated into the National Statistical Annual Plan and endorsed by child-related ministries, marking a milestone in evidence-based policy planning. Notably, the Government covered 50% of the survey costs demonstrating growing institutional ownership and commitment to strengthening gender-sensitive data systems. UNICEF mobilized internal and additional resources and in-kind contribution from the Bureau of National Statistics, ADB and UNFPA. 
Implementation took place amid geopolitical and socio-economic challenges - including spillover effects from the war in Ukraine, sanctions on the Russian Federation, rising prices, and severe flooding across 10 regions in 2024. Through coordinated efforts, UNICEF and the Government ensured public trust, legitimacy, and visibility of the survey. Joint press briefings in Kazakh and Russian were conducted nationwide, supported by promotional videos, social media campaigns, and standardized call-center scripts. Police departments and local authorities validated the survey’s legitimacy, while flexible scheduling and repeated household visits maximized coverage. The use of CAPI (tablet-based) data collection significantly reduced paper use, fuel consumption, and carbon emissions supporting Kazakhstan’s green development agenda.
Kazakhstan’s advanced digital infrastructure enabled efficient verification of vaccination records and supported an innovative mental health module for youth aged 15–24. With technical support from UNICEF HQ and the Ministry of Healthcare, the module was culturally adapted, piloted, and linked to a referral mechanism. A total of 147 enumerators received specialized training and worked with 40 psychologists across 20 regions. Due to the sensitive nature of mental health and prevailing stigma, participation was limited, affecting representativeness. Although results were not published, this pioneering effort marked an important step toward integrating psychosocial well-being into national surveys and highlighted the need for continued awareness and destigmatization.
In 2025, UNICEF collaborated closely with the Senate, Presidential Administration and the Bureau of National Statistics to present the final MICS report, setting the stage for evidence-based national policy dialogue. With support from the Presidential Administration, UNICEF and BNS developed and disseminated 20 detailed socio-economic portfolios to Akimats, equipping local governments with actionable insights for subnational planning and human capital development. Bilateral consultations were held across all 20 regions, reinforcing the role of data in shaping governance priorities and reducing regional disparities.

Critically, MICS results became a cornerstone for the design of the national programme Children of Kazakhstan 2026–2030 and influenced multiple sectoral strategies and policy documents at both national and regional levels. The survey has strengthened evidence-based decision-making and firmly embedded data-driven governance within Kazakhstan’s long-term development agenda.
The findings of the Country Programme Evaluation (CPE), conducted across two programme cycles, significantly shaped the planning and design of the UNICEF Country Programme Document (CPD) for 2026–2030. Developed jointly with the Government of Kazakhstan, the CPD reflects lessons learned particularly on UNICEF’s strong strategic positioning in the country. The CPE highlighted that UNICEF’s sustained advocacy for children’s rights and the systematic use of data-driven approaches enhanced its credibility and influence. It also underscored the critical importance of adapting strategies to local contexts and strengthening multisectoral partnerships, which were essential for achieving sustainable, measurable results for children. These insights directly informed the prioritization, strategic choices, and forward-looking orientation of the new CPD.
In parallel, innovative analytical work undertaken by the Ministry of Digital Development and AI and the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection resulted in a pioneering case study on the application of causal machine learning to evaluate and optimize social welfare policies. By utilising large-scale administrative and socio-economic datasets, the study produced nuanced estimates of heterogeneous treatment effects for key cash transfer programmes. This enabled an assessment of differentiated impacts on household and child well-being—including financial vulnerability, debt accumulation, and indicators of social stability, revealing substantial variations across population groups. The findings demonstrated that uniform programme design may lead to inefficient spending and missed opportunities to better support the most vulnerable families.
Looking ahead, this work lays a robust foundation for institutionalizing data-driven policy design and expanding the use of AI-enabled tools within Kazakhstan’s social protection system. The study clearly illustrates how causal machine learning can strengthen evidence-based policymaking by improving targeting accuracy, enhancing cost-effectiveness, and minimizing unintended adverse effects. The insights generated are already contributing to ongoing government reforms and align closely with the vision and strategic priorities of the CPD 2026–2030.

In 2025, children in Kosovo[1] navigated a year defined  by stalled reforms and persistent gaps in essential services, further  compounded by prolonged political instability. With a population of 1.6  million, Kosovo is home to over 423,000 children under the age of 18, making  up 26% of the total population.[1] Despite the average age increase by five  years over the past decade, reaching 35, Kosovo continues to have the  youngest population in Europe. This demographic advantage, however, is not  yet translating into strong human capital outcomes. Limited investment in  education and healthcare continues to constrain opportunities for children and  youth—with a child born today in Kosovo estimated to reach only 57% of  her/his full potential.[2] 


  


Kosovo is classified as an upper-middle-income  economy, but it remains close to the lower threshold of this category.[3] Despite  experiencing robust growth in recent years, its GNI per capita $6,020 is only  slightly above the minimum for upper-middle-income status ($4,516)[4] and  remains well below that of other Western Balkan countries.[5] Moreover,  economic growth has not translated into a significant reduction in  unemployment or improved living standards. About 18% of the population lives  below the poverty line with poverty rates even higher among children, 23%  living in poverty and 7% in extreme poverty.[6] Labor force participation is  low at 40.7%, and especially limited among women, at just 24%. Youth face  significant challenges, with 33% of those aged 15–24 not in employment,  education, or training (NEET), significantly above the Western Balkan  average.[7] 


  


These socioeconomic challenges have been compounded  by a period of political instability. In 2025, Kosovo’s political landscape was  shaped by a prolonged institutional deadlock and repeated electoral cycles.  Parliamentary elections in February were followed by a post-election gridlock.  This stalemate hindered budget adoption, delayed critical reforms, and access  to international funding. Local elections were held in October, followed by  runoff elections in November in 21 out of 38 municipalities. Finally, snap elections  were held in December, paving the way for the formation of a stable  government in early 2026. 


  


At the same time, regional dynamics and relations  with the European Union (EU) have influenced Kosovo’s reform trajectory. The  EU-facilitated dialogue between Kosovo and Serbia continued, but domestic  political preoccupations on both sides stalled implementation of the 2023  Agreement and its annex, slowing progress toward normalization of  relations.[9] The punitive measures by EU began to be gradually lifted in May  2025, starting with the unfreezing of selected funding mechanisms, and  culminating in the announcement of their full lifting in January 2026. While  Kosovo began implementing the Reform Agenda under the EU Reform and Growth  Facility adopted in October 2024, political deadlock has delayed the  ratification of the associated Facility and Loan Agreements, with limited  overall progress on implementation of the reforms.[10] Despite these  challenges, Kosovo remains one of the most pro-European societies with 91% of  citizens reporting favorable views of the EU overall and 92% supporting Kosovo’s  accession to the EU. Additionally, Kosovo demonstrated clear commitment to  addressing child poverty and social exclusion, notably by advancing the  implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG).[11] 


  


Kosovo institutions continued making notable  progress in upholding and realizing the rights of children and adolescents,  driven by legislative advances in health, early childhood education, child  and social protection. 


  


In health, public spending stands at 4.15%  of GDP, with heavy reliance on out-of-pocket payments – accounting for 38% of  healthcare costs. [12] Child mortality rates continue to be among the highest  in the region, with under-five mortality rates particularly high among  marginalized groups, 27 per 1,000 live births in Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian  communities compared to 16 per 1,000 among general population.[13]  Immunization coverage has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels, with DTP3 at  80% in 2024 and only 37.5% among Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian children.


  


In early childhood education (ECE), access  remains inequitable. Access to ECE was expanded through the increased  enrollment of children aged 3-5 by 6.6%.[14] Yet inclusion of most marginalized  children remains challenging. Despite increased investments, which have  reached 9% of the overall education sector budget, inefficiencies in budget  utilization and inadequate resource allocation for quality aspects undermine  progress. 


  


Public spending on education accounts for  3.9% of GDP.[15] Kosovo ranked almost at the bottom in PISA education  assessment, reflecting gaps in educational quality.[16] Additionally, digital  literacy studies (ICILS), continued to indicate low levels of foundational  and digital skills among students, with only a small share reaching minimum  proficiency levels.


  


The year marked a conducive environment for  advancing youth participation and empowerment. Kosovo’s Nationally  Determined Contribution (NDC) and the new Climate Change Adaptation Strategy  included recommendations derived from youth consultations. 


  


Child protection challenges remain a critical concern in Kosovo, as  children in vulnerable situations continue to face violence, exploitation,  and harmful practices across home, school, community, and online settings.  Violence remains significantly underreported due to stigma, fear, and  persistent social norms governing gender roles and relations, limiting timely  access to protection and support services. In 2024, the Institute of Forensic  Medicine recorded 95 forensic examinations related to sexual violence,  including 57 cases involving children under the age of 16, underscoring the  scale and severity of these risks.


  


Despite increased budget allocations in recent  years, particularly for child allowances, resources remain limited, with only  1.6% of the total social protection budget allocated to social  services. 


  


Climate change and environmental degradation, including air  pollution, continue to have severe impacts, particularly on vulnerable  children and young people. Kosovo’s air quality ranks amongst the most  polluted in Europe, with daily PM2.5 levels reaching up to more than 25 times  the WHO’s safe limit for children.[18] 


  


Municipal administrations play a critical role in  implementing children’s rights but face challenges due to limited  funding and capacities that hinder adequate planning, implementation,  monitoring, and evaluation of programmes for children. With just five years  remaining, Kosovo is unlikely to fully achieve the 2030 targets as systematic  challenges threaten progress towards key SDG goals.

The final year of the UNICEF Kosovo Programme 2021–2025 focused on accelerating results for children while laying the foundation for the next programme cycle. Through evidence-based advocacy, strategic partnerships, and innovative approaches, UNICEF addressed systemic gaps to advance children’s rights and well-being. Key efforts included strengthening policy frameworks, promoting gender-transformative programming, improving service delivery across health, education, child and social protection, driving equitable digital transformation through frontier technologies and quality data, fostering climate-resilient social systems, and amplifying child and youth participation to ensure their voices shape decisions. These actions contributed to Kosovo’s progress toward the SDGs,  EU accession priorities, and Kosovo’s Development Strategy 2030.

 

Young children and their parents  


Over the five-year programme cycle, UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support to the Ministry of Education, Science, Technology, and Innovation (MESTI) contributed to the establishment of a reform-oriented legal framework through the adoption of the Law on Early Childhood Education, enabling universal access to pre-primary education, the diversification of ECE services, and a systematic increase in public investment in the sector. UNICEF’s interventions in 2025 strengthened health and early childhood development systems, advancing Kosovo’s priorities and contributing to SDG3, SDG4, SDG5, and SDG10. Efforts focused on improving equitable access and quality services while embedding gender-responsive and transformative approaches, laying the foundation for sustainable change and ensuring all children have the opportunity to thrive.

  

In health, a major achievement was government’s approval of Kosovo’s first Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) Strategy, developed with UNICEF’s support, and accompanied by a €1.8 million allocation to establish multidisciplinary ECI teams in Primary Health Care (PHC). UNICEF supported piloting of a family-centered ECI model in five municipalities, based on a comprehensive care framework, with early evidence showing strong family satisfaction and active family engagement. This groundwork sets the stage for scaling up the model Kosovo wide through its integration into the PHC system.

  

The Home Visiting programme training curriculum was revised and further aligned with the newly emerging international evidence on early childhood development (ECD), breastfeeding, maternal and mental health as well as family-centered care. The capacities of 540 healthcare professionals (12%) were strengthened on the implementation of the new curriculum. In 2025, the Home Visiting programme reached 13,483 children, including 1,680 children from Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian communities, through UNICEF’s technical assistance, building on its significant expansion and scale up Kosovo wide during this program cycle. In 19% of all home visits, fathers actively participated and were engaged in child development, challenging gender norms around parental roles.

   

The Ministry of Health (MoH) approved the Guidelines for Monitoring Development of Children (GMDC), developed with UNICEF’s technical support, and integrated them into PHC, establishing developmental monitoring as a standardized practice. Capacities of 500 health care providers were strengthened on applying GMCD, enabling comprehensive assessments for 3,814 children. UNICEF supported the scale-up of the Group Care for Parenting programme across 16 municipalities, covering 42% of all municipalities, through resource room activation, facilitator training, and monitoring. The expansion reflects growing government ownership, with structured parenting support now integrated into routine PHC services.

 

Significant progress was made in routine immunization, with 19,986 children (50% girls) aged 12 vaccinated against Human Papillomavirus (HPV), with vaccines expanded to boys. HPV vaccine administration contributed to advancing UNICEF’s gender-transformative programming in line with the Gender Action Plan. To address increasing vaccine hesitancy and the ongoing measles outbreak, UNICEF supported the National Institute of Public Health in developing the Measles Outbreak Control and Response Action Plan, establishing targeted strategies to increase Measles-Containing Vaccine (MCV) uptake. In 2025, UNICEF supported the MoH with the procurement of 10 routine immunization vaccines through UNICEF Supply Division, delivering 192,400 doses to around 100,000 children, with a total value of over US$1.3 million. 



In ECE, UNICEF supported MESTI to advance reforms. A landmark achievement was the endorsement of Kosovo’s first gender-responsive ECE curriculum for children aged 0–6, the most comprehensive reform of early education in decades. Developed and piloted over two years, the new curriculum demonstrated positive shift in pedagogical approaches, with educators recognizing children as active, capable learners, fostering inclusion and a stimulating environment, with parents as core partners. The training of trainers marked the initiation of curriculum rollout reinforced with on-the-job mentoring to ensure quality implementation. This was complemented by the operationalization of the Law on Early Childhood Education through the development of key by-laws, which included (a) revision of by-laws regulating process quality, enrollment mechanisms, and diversified service provision, and (b) drafting of a new by-law on ECD coordination, setting the foundation for integrated services across sectors.


 


UNICEF’s continued advocacy and evidence generation contributed to sustained growth in public financing and ECE enrolment. UNICEF commissioned a feasibility assessment on Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) to support equitable expansion of ECE access. Assessment findings generated policy dialogue with public and private stakeholders on innovative financing and led to a commitment to integrate its recommendations into the upcoming Kosovo Education Strategic Plan. 




Inclusion of children, especially the most vulnerable, in ECE services, remained a key priority. In 2025, 1,687 children aged 0-5 benefited from UNICEF supported programmes through community based ECE models in rural areas, first fully inclusive, universally designed preschool playground, and equipment of 14 (21%) public ECE institutions with assistive technology. Delivery of quality ECE services was further strengthened through enhanced capacities of 243 education professionals on inclusive approaches and coordination among education and early intervention services, laying the foundation for a Kosovo-wide scale-up.




UNICEF partnered with families, service providers, and municipalities to boost community awareness and parental engagement in early development and learning. In 2025, 820 caregivers attended positive parenting and early literacy workshops, while 23,900 parents (18% men) accessed nurturing care and wellbeing resources via the Foleja app.


 


Additionally, UNICEF’s strategic engagement with the private sector continued to deliver strong results, particularly in early childhood education. For the first time, a cause-related marketing partnership was signed with private sector to activate a campaign in Kosovo and Albania promoting the importance of investing in early years.



Skills development and empowerment of adolescents and young people 


Over the five-year programme cycle, UNICEF’s support to MESTI centered on expanding opportunities for innovative learning, resulting in rollout of interactive courses through shkollat.org, reaching over 220,000 students (75% of the student population). Youth legislative framework was advanced through development of the Law on Youth and Youth Strategy, including the institutionalization of Kosovo Generation Unlimited (K-GenU). In parallel, UNICEF strategically positioned the green agenda with adolescents and youth at the center, reinforcing their role as key agents of sustainable development. 


In 2025, UNICEF focused on advancing inclusive and equitable learning opportunities for children and young people, while leveraging strategic partnerships with traditional and non-traditional partners to advance adolescents participation. Major milestones were achieved in national climate policy development and green agenda through the formalization of partnership with European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Through system strengthening, strategic partnerships, and innovation, UNICEF supported the education reform for delivery of quality education and skills development, including transferable, digital and green skills, aligned with the needs of children and youth, particularly the most vulnerable and Kosovo’s development priorities.
  

In education, UNICEF in partnership with MESTI continued to support digital reform aligned with educational standards focusing on digital transformation and teacher professionalization in 2025. Through UNICEF’s technical assistance, the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) department was established, clarifying its mandate, the capacity needs and prioritization of actions for advancing the digital reform process. In addition, a Digital Roadmap for Pre-University Education was developed, providing diagnostics for digital skills, teacher readiness, curriculum alignment, governance arrangements, and system enablers to guide policy dialogue and planning. Additionally, sub-legal acts and guidelines for digital learning materials developed with UNICEF support contributed to regulating and standardizing a framework for digital content production and use. Through the partnership with MESTI and academia, evidence-based policymaking was strengthened by developing a teacher professional development needs assessment led by the Faculty of Education and creating a question pool for the Advanced Teaching License Examination, aligning teacher professionalization with contemporary pedagogical standards. 



Harmonization and re-accreditation of UNICEF-developed skills-building programmes (UPSHIFT, PODIUM, PONDER, and Green Skills) within the upper-secondary curriculum ensured sustainable scale-up. These programmes were also embedded in the Faculty of Education curriculum, for equipping pre-service teachers with competencies and practical experience needed to deliver skills-based learning.

  

Social cohesion programming was advanced in partnership with Peace Building Fund (PBF) and through joint action with International Organisation for Migration. Mediation clubs successfully resolved conflicts in schools while fostering more inclusive learning environments, evidenced by the endline study showing a 65% increase in students’ knowledge of civic engagement and conflict resolution. Over 22,000 students in 11 municipalities benefitted in 2024 – 2025. The social cohesion programme also incorporated a strong gender lens, contributing  significantly to positive shifts in attitudes toward gender equality.

 

In 2025, a major milestone in advancing adolescents’ and youth participation in the green transition was achieved through UNICEF’s Green Rising initiative and the partnership with the EBRD leveraging EUR 80 million investments for energy efficiency as well as the Kosovo Energy Efficiency Fund (KEEF). This collaboration focuses on engagement of adolescents and youth in energy efficiency initiatives and mobilizing them to protect their communities from the climate crisis, as well as strategic collaboration on knowledge generation.

  

Inclusive climate governance was further strengthened through meaningful adolescent and youth participation in national climate policy development. In partnership with the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure and through engagement of academia, UNICEF supported youth consultation process for the development of Kosovo’s voluntary NDC and the new Climate Change Adaptation Strategy. Youth recommendations informed actions related to climate education, disaster preparedness, environmental health, climate-responsive social services, and institutionalized youth engagement mechanisms.

  

UNICEF expanded partnerships through engaging in a strategic dialogue with the Ministry of Industry, Entrepreneurship and Trade (MIET) to strengthen and promote innovation for all children and adolescents as well as support youth in developing entrepreneurship skills. A two-day workshop with MIET and UNICEF, including UNICEF Office of Innovation in Stockholm, culminated with clear identification of entry points for partnership to strengthen innovation and create pathways for young people’s entrepreneurial success.

 

During the year, more than 32,000 adolescents and young people (55% girls) were reached through UNICEF-supported skills-building initiatives. Of these, 22,000 directly benefited from skills-building programmes delivered across formal and non-formal education programmes, including the K-GenU. In addition, over 10,000 adolescents and youth were reached through targeted outreach and informed about opportunities to participate in skills-building programmes and the K-GenU initiative via schools, youth centers, NGO networks, and other community-based channels.

  

K-GenU initiative continued to expand in partnership with the Ministry of Finance, Labour and Transfers (MFLT), increasing internship-hosting entities to 1,100, enabling paid internship opportunities for 613 young people (55% young women) and registration of a total 14,227 young people (66% young women) on the K-GenU platform. 

 
Social inclusion and child rights monitoring

In child and social protection, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to develop two Administrative Instructions (AIs) for operationalization of the Law on Social and Family Services. The AIs outlined the organization, responsibilities, and staffing of the Centers for Social Welfare, ensuring better structure and efficiency in serving vulnerable populations as well as procedures and principles for implementing public-private partnerships in social services, promoting more sustainable and inclusive service delivery.


  


In 2025, UNICEF consolidated progress and strengthened sustainability in child protection sector including through evidence generation, particularly on diversion measures and violence prevention to inform policy dialogue, guide reforms, and adapt interventions to emerging child protection risks. The assessment of the EU-UNICEF partnership “Protecting Vulnerable Children in Kosovo” confirmed that the programme laid critical groundwork for systemic reform, including the development and revision of key legal and regulatory tools such as the draft Law on Disability and operational standards for child-sensitive justice. In 2025, significant achievements were made, particularly in professional development, inclusive education, and community-based rehabilitation. Capacities of over 342 professionals, including educators, social workers, health staff, and police and probation officers were strengthened, significantly enhancing their ability to identify, refer, and support vulnerable children.


  


UNICEF in partnership with MoJ, Kosovo Justice Academy (KJA) and Kosovo Police strengthened child-friendly justice in Kosovo by operationalizing the “Police Warning” diversion measure and institutionalizing a new Justice for Children Training Curriculum within the KJA, alongside infrastructure upgrades to rehabilitation services, including an outdoor gym at the Educational Correctional Centre in Lipjan. Standard Operating Procedures and standardized tools were adopted by the Kosovo Police, while trainings reached 69 professionals (30% women). The Kosovo Academy of Justice integrated five curriculum modules into its 2025 annual programme, strengthening the capacities of 116 professionals (44% women) across justice institutions.


 


Children and caregivers from vulnerable groups were supported with essential services. 1,243 children with disabilities (43% girls) and 1,127 caregivers (78% mothers) benefited from community-based mental health and psychosocial support. Additionally, 274 children in street situations (46% girls) and 199 caregivers (78% mothers) accessed day-care and family-strengthening services in Prishtina and Prizren municipalities. In addition, 516,856 people were reached through digital campaign against cyberbullying. 




UNICEF jointly with EULEX and the EU Office in Kosovo convened key stakeholders on a high-level dialogue culminating with a call to action for protection of children against sexual violence, exploration and abuse. Advocacy around continued engagement and action plan development constitutes the next step bringing all partners together in fight of sexual violence against children.  




In 2025, UNICEF supported government’s commitment to introducing the ECG to reduce child poverty and social exclusion by ensuring vulnerable children access essential services, including health, education, housing, and nutrition. The introduction of the ECG and the Government’s commitment to implement it in 2026 is a key step in aligning Kosovo’s child protection and social inclusion efforts with EU standards. 




The shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) system was strengthened to help Kosovo respond to crises like natural disasters and emergencies. UNICEF’s SRSP Readiness Assessment identified opportunities to improve cash-based social transfers, with recommendations to scale up, expand coverage, adjust eligibility, and increase benefits during crises. A Guideline on SRSP was developed, outlining the legal framework and operational procedures, including the creation of new tools like pre-arranged financing mechanisms, a contingency fund for quick resource deployment, and clear activation triggers for emergency assistance.


 


Another significant achievement in advancing disability rights was the progress on drafting the Law on the Evaluation, Status Recognition, Benefits, and Services for Persons with Disabilities, supported by the development of disability assessment models aligned with international standards. Together with a comprehensive Situation Analysis on the rights of persons with disabilities, this laid the foundation for a more inclusive social protection system, ensuring equitable access to services for children and adults with disabilities. 




The child rights agenda in was strengthened through strategic public investments in evidence generation and by placing children at the center of national planning. In partnership with the Office of the Prime Minister, around half a million USD in public funding was mobilized to implement the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), covering both the general population and Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian communities. Led by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics (KAS) with technical support from UNICEF, the data collection was successfully completed in compliance with international standards, generating robust evidence to inform policy and programming and filling critical data gaps in outcomes for children and targeted groups based on gender, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and others. 




To further drive investments in children and human capital development, the Child Rights Strategy (2026–2032) and Action Plan (2026–2028) were developed based on the assessment of the previous Child Rights Strategy and through a participatory process, involving extensive consultations with children, relevant institutions, civil society, and other partners. The strategy will provide a clear roadmap for advancing the child rights agenda through a gender sensitive approach, prioritizing the ECG and addressing emerging issues affecting children through a cross-sectoral and a whole-of-government approach. Additionally, through UNICEF technical expertise, the mid-term review of the National Development Strategy 2030 for Human Capital Pillar was initiated which will assess progress, identify gaps, and adapt strategies to evolving national priorities, including alignment with the EU Reform Agenda and other priorities. This review ensures that investments in children and human capital remain responsive, result-driven, and aligned with Kosovo’s broader development objectives.


  


Accountability for child rights and evidence-based policymaking in Kosovo was strengthened through  capacity building and identification of impact evaluation practices for integration into government planning and programming. Through the regional partnership with Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL), key stakeholders including the Office of Prime Minister/Office of Strategic Planning, Office of Deputy Prime Minister and the MFLT enhanced their capacities to design, conduct and apply impact evaluation to advance evidence-based decision making and improve allocation of public resources for children and human capital development. In 2025, UNICEF initiated dialogue with the Kosovo government to advance Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence–based approaches for integration into government planning to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of programmes and public investments. Under the leadership of the Office of Prime Minister, the Strategic Planning Office and Information and Technology Unit and in partnership with the University of Saint Gallen, UNICEF supported the convening and capacity building of representatives from key ministries and relevant institutions on the integration of causal machine learning into government planning and programming. 




UNICEF strengthened the partnership with the academia through the signed Memorandum of Understanding with University of Prishtina expanding collaboration across different faculties, increasingly contributing to the generation of robust evidence through the mobilization of academic expertise. Building on this partnership, UNICEF convened stakeholders around the mental health agenda by initiating a mapping of Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services in Kosovo. This effort was complemented by the facilitation of high-level dialogue between academia, the Office of the President, and the Office of the Prime Minister, laying the foundation for advancing a comprehensive vision of improving mental health in line with UNICE's Global MHPSS Multisectoral Operational Framework. On the occasion of the World Mental Health Day, UNICEF supported the University of Prishtina in organizing the International Conference on Psychological Wellbeing – Research and Interventions, which served as a dialogue platform between academia and policymakers on integrated, cross-sectoral approaches to addressing mental health challenges in Kosovo. 




UNICEF continued to support strengthening of administrative data collection and reporting, namely through technical assistance with reporting on child protection and child mortality data and estimates at regional and global level, as well as compiling relevant data for Kosovo’s Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) application. Thought leadership, through strengthening internal learning and accountability continued to be at the center of UNICEF’s priorities. In 2025, UNICEF commissioned two external full-fledged evaluations covering (a) Investing in Early Years implemented in partnership with the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, and (b) Youth Empowered Through Inclusive Schools and Societies implemented in partnership with the PBF, as well as the assessment of the programme “Protecting Vulnerable Children in Kosovo” implemented in partnership with the EU. The evidence, lessons learned, and recommendations will inform future strategies of UNICEF and partners to further advance child rights in Kosovo. 


 


Through set-aside funding from headquarters, catalytic action was taken, including advancing MICS field work, technical assistance to developing the Kosovo government’s Child Rights Strategy, introducing machine learning and building the capacity of government on impact evaluation, undertaking a feasibility study of using PPP to advance ECE, development of municipal profiles to inform UNICEF's engagement in the context of the new Kosovo Programme 2026-2030 and advancing the expansion of K-GenU outreach to ensure equitable access to internship opportunities.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2025 marked the final year of the UNICEF Kosovo Programme 2021–2025 and UNICEF’s 30th anniversary in Kosovo. Coinciding with UNICEF’s global Future Focus Initiative, this year provided an opportunity for deep reflection on challenges, lessons learned, and strategic planning. The newly approved Kosovo Programme 2026–2030 charts a clear path forward, introducing an innovative business model to deliver impactful results for children. Developed through robust evidence and broad consultations with children, youth, Kosovo institutions and other stakeholders, it aligns with the UNICEF Strategic Plan and prioritizes accelerating progress toward the SDGs. Complementary to these efforts, UNICEF contributed to advance one UN programming approach through the development of UN Strategic Plan 2026-2030 for Kosovo that prioritizes human capital development. 


  


Kosovo’s programming environment is complex, characterized by a combination of challenges to the achievement of programme results as well as a number of opportunities for advancing children’s rights. Key challenges include limited fiscal space and budgeting for children, lack of institutional capacity, and political instability, alongside fiduciary and external concerns and social and economic issues exacerbated by significant funding cuts for development assistance. Opportunities include Kosovo's continued commitment to EU accession, evidenced by ongoing reforms in rule of law, governance, public administration, public financial management, green and digital transitions, human capital, and alignment with EU standards. Additionally, Kosovo’s youthful population offers a potential demographic dividend which provides a great opportunity for return in human development investments. 




Key lessons learned from the evaluations and assessments covering health, ECE, education, youth and child protection programmes in 2025 highlighted collaboration with municipalities as critical for a system-driven approach to sustainable service delivery, while partnerships with civil society  enabled outreach to marginalized populations through contextual familiarity and community trust and gender-transformative approaches. Involving decision-makers and introducing promising practices as well as witnessing successful models, significantly deepened policy commitment and facilitated informed dialogue. In 2025, cross-border collaboration has been strengthened with Kosovo hosting a delegation from Tajikistan to learn from Kosovo’s experience on effective HPV vaccine rollout as well as a delegation from Albania to learn on the MICS implementation, demonstrating broader regional influence, learning exchange and programme replicability. UNICEF Kosovo hosted board members from UNICEF National Committees representing eight countries, showcasing its convening power and on-the-ground programming that reaches the most vulnerable children.  




Budget execution at both central and municipal levels continued to pose challenges, with procurement delays, low spending rates, and administrative bottlenecks slowing the timely use of allocated resources. In this context, strengthened financial planning, procurement guidance, and continuous oversight are essential to translating resources into tangible services. UNICEF will continue working closely with authorities to improve budget execution, streamline operational processes, and ensure that available funds are fully and effectively utilized. Lack of data remained a critical systemic bottleneck affecting evidence-based planning and policy making across all sectors at both central and local level. UNICEF will continue advocacy efforts and technical assistance to strengthen administrative data through harmonization, data exchange and digitalization to increase efficiency and reduce administrative burden. 


 


In response to tightening public fiscal space and competing priorities, UNICEF intensified advocacy with Kosovo institutions at central and local level for secured and increased investments in data and evaluations for accountability, ensuring public resources are allocated based on evidence, impact, and where societal returns on investments are greatest. Through targeted dialogue and capacity building on innovative practices such as impact evaluation and causal machine learning, key government partners were convened and committed to integrating these approaches into strategic planning and programming for investments based on evidence. 


 


In 2025, leveraging strategic partnerships remained central to UNICEF’s priorities. Expanding collaboration with non-traditional partners, including the private sector, International Financial Institutions (IFI), business associations, academia, and other stakeholders, proved critical for advancing child rights in Kosovo. A comprehensive IFI mapping identified entry points for engagement to support Kosovo’s development priorities and SDG commitments. Notably, the partnership between UNICEF and EBRD unlocked significant opportunities for youth engagement, leveraging EUR 80 million for energy efficiency initiatives while collaboration with private-sector partner extended support to ECD beyond Kosovo into Albania. Building on the dialogue initiated this year, UNICEF will continue to strengthen strategic partnerships by expanding collaboration with academia and additional ministries covering local administration, entrepreneurship and trade.   




Introduction of public-private partnerships (PPP) in ECE centers presented important opportunities to expand children’s access to early learning, with strong impact on women’s economic empowerment. However, delays in approving ECE by-laws, inconsistent technical capacities across municipalities, limited data on private providers, and regulatory challenges in human resources’ recruitment constrained planning, implementation and the operationalization of new kindergartens. The PPP feasibility assessment underscored the need for a more integrated and coordinated approach to ECE centers governance and highlighted gaps in collaboration across municipalities and line ministries, while indicating continued affordability challenges for parents. This is further hindered by systemic barriers in budget planning, including the need to revise the education grant formula and strengthen operational support mechanisms to ensure sustainable financing. Collectively, these lessons provide a clear pathway for UNICEF to support a coordinated policy and financing reforms, essential for advancing Kosovo’s early childhood education and care agenda and consolidating progress for young children. 




Community engagement challenges, including a rise in vaccine hesitancy during the measles outbreak, demonstrated gaps in risk communication and public trust. The experience highlighted that proactive communication strategies, social media monitoring, and frontline staff support are critical to maintaining caregiver confidence and service uptake. UNICEF plans to conduct a cost of inaction analysis in 2026 to advocate with decision-makers on the need for a comprehensive approach and increased budget allocations to protect children from vaccine-preventable diareses.


  


Future outlook: With only six years left to achieve the SDGs, UNICEF remains pivotal in supporting Kosovo’s efforts to meet its commitments and advance its development priorities. As the new programme cycle begins in 2026, UNICEF will leverage its innovative business model to deliver impactful results for children and youth, strengthen gender transformative programming, guided by the UNICEF Strategic Plan. This approach will prioritize focus and scale to accelerate progress toward the SDGs, utilizing core resources and leveraging investments to drive systemic change and ensure the inclusion of the most vulnerable children, adolescents, and their families.  




In this rapidly changing environment, UNICEF’s strategy will focus on prioritizing, emboldening, and sharpening strategies that will bring results at scale for children, while expanding advocacy, mobilizing partners, including within the UN system, and leveraging public and private resources for financing to support the priorities of Kosovo’s institutions. Building on successes and lessons learned, programmatic shifts will include: (a) Focus: shifting from a broad menu of results to fewer high-level impact targets, with focused commitment to their achievement; (b) Scale and impact: shifting from an emphasis on delivering programmes to delivering outcome-level changes reaching all children, including most vulnerable groups; (c) Differentiation guided by equity: shifting from relative homogeneity of programmes to intentional sharpening of programmes based on evidence and strategies to reach children left behind; (d) Partnerships and leveraging: shifting the emphasis from narrow programme delivery to unlocking a collective contribution of actions and resources to generate transformative, sustainable change for children, e) Optimize resources: shifting in the approach and the business model to ensure higher return on investments and effectiveness of results for all children and focusing on most vulnerable groups. 


 


UNICEF will continue to be a trusted knowledge broker and thought leader on children’s rights and wellbeing, with a strong focus on generating robust, high-quality evidence and advancing innovative approaches to inform investments and financing in human capital development.

In 2025, despite the ongoing refugee response, Moldova’s greater political and macroeconomic stability created space for reform, but children’s outcomes still reflect deep, structural inequities. Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and national child rights commitments remains uneven, with the most significant gaps affecting children in poverty, those in rural and Roma communities, children with disabilities, refugee children and adolescents at risk of exclusion. Within the development-humanitarian-peace nexus, UNICEF continued to support refugee families and host communities to promote access to basic services, including health, education, child protection, WASH, and social protection, benefiting over 80,000 refugees, whilst proactively strengthening Government systems to sustain these services.

Since the start of the war in Ukraine, over 1.8 million refugees have fled to (or transited through) the Republic of Moldova from Ukraine. At the beginning of 2026, approximately 150,000 refugees (about 47 per cent of them children) remained in the country, representing nearly 6 per cent of Moldova's total population. Most of the refugees from Ukraine reside in private accommodation within host communities, including 42 per cent in the country’s capital, Chisinau.  The Government extended Temporary Protection (TP) for Ukrainian refugees in Moldova until March 2027. Registration for TP has steadily increased, and more than 86,000 refugees have been granted TP status to date, including approximately 20,000 children. [1] 

Although arrivals have declined and the country's refugee population remains relatively stable, Ukrainian refugees in Moldova are typically the most vulnerable among the populations in the countries of the refugee response. While acute humanitarian support is no longer needed, our work has focused on strengthening the system across the country - and where Ukrainians are most known to reside - to ensure that the system can reach and serve them as well across education, health and protection. This has also meant a more concerted investment in the public service system.

In health and nutrition, core survival indicators indicate both improvement and the need for further action. Under-five and infant mortality remain well above EU averages, signalling persistent gaps in maternal and child health care. Malnutrition continues to affect young children: stunting and wasting are present, exclusive breastfeeding remains below optimal levels, and one in four infants does not receive a minimally adequate diet. These patterns are closely linked to household poverty, rural disadvantages and limited access to diverse, nutritious food.

Immunization is a central concern. Coverage for DTP3 has fallen below 87 per cent and MMR1 to around 84 per cent, with some districts registering much lower levels.[2] Misinformation, low perceived risk of vaccine-preventable diseases and distrust in institutions drive hesitancy, particularly in marginalised communities. Recent measles and pertussis outbreaks highlight the health and financial costs of these gaps and threaten progress toward SDG 3. Without a sustained recovery in coverage, avoidable illness, deaths and system costs will continue to rise.

Early detection and intervention in disabilities and developmental delays offer a clear opportunity to prevent longer-term exclusion, yet access remains limited. A national roadmap is in place, and UNICEF has supported the expansion of Early Intervention Centres, but coverage remains low, and implementation is slow. Rural areas, where services and specialists are scarce, are most affected. Many children, especially those from vulnerable families, miss critical developmental windows, which have lasting effects on health, learning and social participation.

Education reform is advancing, but fragmentation and under-resourcing constrain impact. Demographic decline, underfunding and infrastructure deficits drive differences in access and quality between urban and rural areas and across social groups. Children from low-income households, Roma communities, children with disabilities and refugees experience the most significant barriers. In Roma-concentrated localities, preschool enrolment averages 39 per cent and school enrolment 43 per cent, with some communities recording as little as 6 per cent participation[3]. Persistent poverty, discrimination, parental illiteracy, migration and restrictive norms contribute to high dropout and low attainment, directly challenging Moldova’s commitments to inclusive, quality education and reduced inequalities.

Inclusive education policies have strengthened the formal framework, but implementation remains limited. Teacher training is fragmented, school infrastructure is often not accessible, and assistive technologies are limited. Surveys show that only about 40 per cent of parents and 60 per cent of teachers support inclusion of children with disabilities in mainstream schools. Many children with complex disabilities remain in segregated settings: around 600 attend special schools, while an estimated 200–300 receive low-quality home-based instruction or are not in school at all.[4]. Digitalisation has created new opportunities in some schools, but many still lack safe buildings, reliable electricity, and adequate WASH facilities. At the same time, adolescents face increased digital risks, including cyberbullying, with few systemic prevention or response mechanisms.

Violence against children and women remains widespread and normalised in many settings. Survey data indicate that two in five children, and a similar share of women and girls, have experienced violence or abuse. Harmful norms continue to underpin this reality: more than half of women view domestic violence as a private matter, well above the EU average, and one in four girls aged 15–19 reports violence in intimate relationships. Technology-facilitated abuse is rising, with 12 per cent of children aged 12–16 reporting indecent online proposals.[5] Displacement and insecurity associated with the refugee situation have heightened risks for Ukrainian women and children. 

The General Prosecutors' Office confirms these concerning trends on sexual violence and domestic abuse. Cases of intrafamilial child sexual abuse increased to 132, most of them involving girls. Although the overall number of children in conflict with the law fell to 493 in 2024 (a 44 per cent decrease from 2022), the share sentenced to imprisonment rose, driven by high reoffending during probation.[6]. This indicates limited investment in diversion, restorative justice, and reintegration, and undermines progress toward SDG 16.2.
The Ministry of Labour and Social Protection (MLSP) continues to make significant progress in strengthening its child protection system and in aligning it with the EU social acquis. However, the system remains under strain. Over 18,000 children remain at risk because of neglect, poverty and parental migration. Institutionalisation has decreased, but reliance on residential care is still pronounced for children with disabilities, who are overrepresented in institutions.[7] In some regions where state systems are weak or absent, services remain heavily dependent on external support.

In 2025, the Republic of Moldova consolidated its position on gender equality, ranking 7th globally in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report and closing 81.3 per cent of its overall gender gap, with particularly strong results in political empowerment. The European Commission’s 2025 Enlargement Report acknowledges Moldova’s steady reform efforts in governance, fundamental rights, and alignment with EU norms, while also highlighting the need to further strengthen implementation capacity and ensure sustainable funding for gender equality and anti-discrimination measures. 

Roma children face overlapping disadvantages in health, education, housing and access to services, compounded by discrimination and insufficiently funded inclusion strategies. Rural schools continue to struggle with poor WASH standards, which affect attendance, health and learning. Adolescents are at high risk of social and economic exclusion: 25.4 per cent are not in education, employment, or training (SDG 8.6.1), far above EU averages, with persistent gaps by gender and area of residence.[8] Implementation of youth policies is slower than envisaged, and the most marginalised adolescents remain underrepresented in decision-making and programme design.
Public spending on social sectors has grown in nominal terms but declined as a share of GDP, reflecting tight fiscal space and competing national priorities. Although inflation eased in 2024, child poverty rose to 33.6 per cent.[9] Children in rural areas are most affected, with almost half living in monetary poverty, which directly challenges the national and global pledge to leave no child behind. Overall, social protection coverage for children remains around one-third. While childbirth and childcare benefits and disability allowances reach many families, the main poverty-targeted programme has contracted, and benefit levels for children with disabilities remain below the subsistence minimum, limiting impact on poverty and exclusion.
Taken together, these trends indicate that Moldova’s current pace of progress is insufficient to realise universal children's rights. Mortality, malnutrition, learning exclusion, violence and poverty remain concentrated among the same groups of children, increasing the risk that they will fall further behind as the country advances. Closing this gap will require sustained, system-focused investment in health, education, protection, social protection and behaviour change, with explicit prioritisation of the children who are currently the least reached.
