In 2025, UNICEF contributed to measurable shifts in how Moldova’s systems support children’s health, early development, learning, protection and participation. The country’s political environment was relatively stable and EU-oriented, but child poverty, rural–urban gaps, discrimination and weak services continued to constrain outcomes. UNICEF’s work focused on changing how national systems function, rather than running standalone projects, with particular attention to children with disabilities, Roma children, refugee children, children in rural areas and adolescents at risk of exclusion.

Adolescent Development and Participation
UNICEF expanded adolescents' access to skills and participation opportunities. Through STEAM on Wheels and GirlsGoIT, about 10,800 adolescents and youth (54 per cent female) gained digital literacy, coding and problem-solving skills; this group included 648 refugees and 432 young people with special educational needs (SEN) and/or disabilities. Pupil participation structures were strengthened by working with representatives from all districts and municipalities. 

Thirty-five council representatives and 35 regional coordinators participated in training on student voice, collaborative governance, and cross-school problem-solving. The training also served as a consultation to map support needs and to inform future capacity-building for youth governance.

Career readiness was supported by training 35 teachers, youth workers, and NGO staff to serve as career orientation trainers, who subsequently delivered guidance activities for adolescents. Together with the Ministry of Education and Research (MER), UNICEF scaled up UPSHIFT, engaging 290 adolescent teams (around 1,160 participants) in a 10-week innovation and social entrepreneurship cycle. Seventy-five teams received seed funding to implement projects that reached at least 17,000 peers on themes including environmental action, peer support, healthy lifestyles, youth engagement, online safety, and careers.

Child Protection
UNICEF continued to support the MLSP in implementing the Social Assistance Reform RESTART and in building the social workforce. In 2025, 47,535 refugees and vulnerable children received child protection services with UNICEF support. Following the integration of 150 new staff, the number of state-funded child protection specialists rose to 215. More than 5,000 social workers and other frontline staff from multidisciplinary teams received training and mentoring on case management and the Caring for Child Survivors of Sexual Abuse guidelines.

The number of children in institutions decreased from 676 to 460. Family support services for 4,761 children helped prevent separation. Ninety specialists and caregivers from alternative care services received training on GBV risk mitigation, with a specific focus on adolescent girls’ needs and risks.

UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) and the MLSP in transposing EU child-related directives and in implementing the European Child Guarantee. Under the refugee response, 25,505 children and caregivers received Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) support, including on the left bank of the Nistru River. GBV prevention, risk mitigation, and response activities reached 73,900 women, girls, and boys, and more than 10,000 women and girls have used the Laaha platform since its launch in Ukrainian-language in 2024. Partnerships with private companies, including beauty salons and cinemas, helped to publicise such services.

Violence prevention remained a priority. In line with Moldova’s pledges at the 2024 Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children, UNICEF supported research on the intersections between violence against children and violence against women and a review of parenting programmes to incorporate domestic violence prevention and gender equality. Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) approaches were used to address harmful social and gender norms.

Access to justice for children who are victims or witnesses of violence improved through the construction of a second Barnahus in the south. Across the two centres, 592 children received support, and 328 justice professionals were trained. UNICEF also conducted a study on rehabilitation and re-education programmes for children in detention, including mothers with children under three in penitentiaries, to inform advocacy on restorative justice and alternatives to incarceration.

UNICEF continued its efforts to renew its Memorandum of Understanding and related work plan with the Municipality of Chisinau to improve existing services for vulnerable children and their families, including refugee families, and to strengthen child and social protection services. Since the beginning of the crisis, the implementation of this plan has strengthened child protection systems in Moldova’s largest municipality, which hosts over 40 per cent of the country's refugees. In collaboration with the National Congress of Ukrainians, a national campaign promoting child protection and GBV services was launched and reached around 350,000 people among Ukrainian social media channels, including Ukrainian refugees and members of local communities. 

Approximately 87,411 persons (including 64 per cent girls and women) were provided with access to safe and accessible channels to report sexual exploitation and abuse committed by humanitarian actors. The caseload of unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) decreased within a stable operational context. The referral process from the Border Police to the Guardianship Authority has not been as systematic as it once was (306 cases registered in 2024 and 5 in 2025), which may also be contributing to the low numbers. It remains important to continue monitoring the 470 open cases of separated children registered since 2022 (using Primero/CPIMS+ database). In 2025, 90 UASC were repatriated to Ukraine through Moldova.  

Child Rights Monitoring
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened child rights governance in Moldova by reinforcing independent oversight, expanding the national evidence base, and supporting meaningful child participation. Support to the Child Rights Ombudsperson improved monitoring, analysis, and public reporting, with the Annual Report on Children’s Rights informing parliamentary debate and high-level policy dialogue. Thematic analyses on children’s rights in families affected by parental mental health disorders and the impact of social assistance reform generated credible, rights-based evidence to inform future national reforms. UNICEF’s support for treaty-body engagement reinforced compliance with international obligations. The National Child Rights Forum enabled children, including those in vulnerable situations, to present evidence and recommendations directly to decision-makers.

National data and monitoring systems were strengthened through collaboration between UNICEF and the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), including enhancements to disaggregated child data, improvements in child poverty measurement, and alignment of national surveys with EU and international standards. UNICEF supported the NBS in implementing the National Action Plan for the Accession of the Republic of Moldova to the European Union, specifically Chapter 18 on Statistics, notably, the statistical survey Children's Activities as an ad hoc module to the Labour Force Survey (SDG 8.7.1) and European Health Interview Survey (EHIS), including the Child Module. These efforts aim to provide data to inform the reference framework of indicators for monitoring the SDGs in the EU context.  
 
Education
In general education, UNICEF worked with MER and other partners to reduce inequities, support digital transformation and advance curriculum and governance reforms. Assistive technologies were provided to 230 children with sensory impairments, and Resource Centres in 95 schools supported more than 2,200 children with intellectual disabilities. For the first time, psychopedagogical assistance was delivered through mobile teams, extending services to children in remote areas. A total of 2,018 school managers and teachers were trained on “whole school” approaches to student well-being. Competency standards were developed for SEN teachers, psychopedagogues and educational psychologists.

To promote Roma inclusion, UNICEF piloted educational mediators in three regions. In parallel, 4,665 refugee children and adolescents were enrolled in formal and non-formal education, supported by a standardised Romanian language programme and by frameworks for accelerated learning and preparatory classes. In August 2025, the Government announced financial support (1,000 MDL) for every child attending school in grades 1-9; Ukrainian refugees enrolled in Moldovan schools also benefited from this allowance. In parallel, UNICEF, through its partner organisations, developed and disseminated clarifications on enrolment procedures, with a focus on helping refugee families understand the process and access financial support.

EduTech Labs launched a new intervention round in September 2025.  To date, 32 out of 36 planned Labs are fully operational, representing 89 per cent activation for the 2025/26 school year. These Labs support 620 unique beneficiaries: 165 children enrolled in online learning, 130 attending catch-up classes, 101 participating in Romanian language classes, and 23 children benefiting from MHPSS sessions.

Digital transformation activities included the launch of the DigiProf Programme, with 4,100 teachers already trained in digital literacy and 74 certified, working towards a target of 10,000. The Digital Accelerator was piloted in 12 model schools. ICT packages were delivered to 140 schools, MozaWeb licenses supported 700 interactive panels, and 1,463 teachers were trained to use digital tools. Digitisation of 10 textbooks began, using interactive content aligned with international standards and Universal Design for Learning. EMIS functionality was upgraded, including specifications for a digital tracking tool to support real-time monitoring and predictive analysis. Moldova joined the GIGA initiative, which connects data ingestion and monitoring systems across 90 schools.

UNICEF supported curriculum reform by developing a management framework, a national reference framework, and methodologies for evaluating and designing learning programmes. An assessment of the existing curriculum was completed, and 200 experts received 84 hours of training on the new framework and cross-cutting theme integration. UNICEF also supported the mentoring system by backing the National Institute for Education and Leadership: 1,036 national and institutional mentors were certified, competency standards for mentors were adopted, and the first group of 50 mentors was trained on their applications. Advocacy and research underpinned this work, including an Inclusive Education Gap Analysis, policy support for the implementation of the “Education 2030” programme, and a roadmap to include refugee children. During Education Week and related events, approximately 4,000 stakeholders participated in 20 advocacy activities.

UNICEF also contributed to the Evaluation of the implementation of the National Strategy “Education 2030” (2023-2025), ensuring relevant recommendations informed the new Programme 2026–2030 developed with the CO's support.[1]

Early Childhood Development
In early childhood education and development, UNICEF helped expand access to services for children with developmental delays, disabilities, special educational needs, from ethnic minorities and from refugee families. Resource Centres were established in 185 preschools, in accordance with regulations and methodologies developed with UNICEF support. These centres served 29,789 children, including 430 refugee children and 804 children with SEN and/or disabilities.

Provider skills were strengthened to improve holistic development. More than 2,000 family doctors, educators, and social workers were trained in the Global Monitoring of Child Development (GMCD), benefiting more than 10,000 children. Approximately 150 specialists from the health, education, and social protection sectors received training in transdisciplinary, family-centred Early Childhood Intervention (ECI), reaching approximately 1,550 children with developmental delays. More than 2,772 educators enhanced their competencies in social-emotional learning, playful learning, interactive pedagogy, and inclusive practices, with an estimated impact on 110,000 children.

UNICEF backed the national “Read Me 100 Stories” and Social Emotional Learning (SEL) Level 3 programmes, distributing 84,400 books to 1,200 kindergartens and training educators in interactive reading and SEL. Work on parenting included contributions to developing a national Parenting Ecosystem concept, the contextualisation and launch of the LearnECD digital platform, and the delivery of positive parenting sessions with local authorities and private-sector partners. Digital tools such as the Bebbo app and SEL home kits complemented in-person efforts, and Resource Centres served as entry points for collaboration with families.

For preschool financing, UNICEF designed and tested a per-capita funding formula across four regions. The Government approved it for nationwide rollout from 2026. The formula allocates funds according to the characteristics and needs of enrolled children, including those with SEN and disabilities. UNICEF also worked with private partners to explore business models to expand childcare for children under three.

Health
UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Health (MoH) to strengthen care from pregnancy through adolescence. Perinatal services improved following the training of 320 doctors and nurses to manage ill, premature, and low-birth-weight newborns. The updated Perinatal and Pregnant Women’s Cards and a new mortality audit methodology, formally approved by the MoH, provided a clearer basis for accountability and continuous quality review.

For young children, monitoring systems became more sensitive to developmental risks. National growth standards were revised, and more than 1,500 nurses and family doctors were trained to use the GMCD tool in clinics and during home visits. This enabled earlier identification and referral of children falling behind.

UNICEF supported the development of the new National AIDS Programme 2026–2030, which now includes the goal of “triple elimination” of HIV, congenital syphilis and hepatitis B. 
On nutrition, UNICEF backed a national Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) study, an SBC plan for 2026–2028, and a feasibility assessment for the country’s first human milk bank. Regulations were updated to align with global standards, 1,271 caregivers increased their knowledge of IYCF, and 10 breastfeeding corners were established to improve access to counselling and support.

Health promotion in schools was reinforced through training for 1,358 school and preschool health workers on immunization and nutrition. Early Childhood Intervention services expanded with the opening of two new centres in Cimi¿lia and Chi¿inau. Across five UNICEF-supported centres, 1,691 children and 1,276 caregivers received support, while rural ECD offices reached a further 1,267 children with developmental delays.

To protect children from vaccine-preventable diseases, UNICEF helped institutionalise SBC within the National Immunization Programme through the 2027 Immunization Plan. The plan, aligned with EU integration priorities, focuses on behavioural and trust-related barriers, as well as on service delivery. Forty-eight communication specialists and 35 managers were trained in applying behavioural science, infodemic management, and a social listening system, which produced 10 analytical reports that informed communication responses. Research with Roma communities informed targeted approaches to close immunization gaps—community outreach combined digital and in-person engagement. More than 76,000 people were reached online, and about 11,000 parents participated in interactive sessions. UNICEF also trained journalists, produced documentaries, and convened 500 experts for policy dialogues on vaccination.

Adolescent health support grew through partnerships with the MoH and Youth Clinics. The 24/7 Youth Health Help Line provided mental health and psychosocial support to about 13,000 adolescents. Mobile youth-friendly services operated in underserved areas, offering mental health, sexual and reproductive health and counselling. Clinics in Chi¿inau, Cimi¿lia, Edine¿, and Orhei served around 5,400 children, including refugees. Some 30,000 adolescents took part in sessions on HIV prevention, healthy lifestyles, gender-based violence (GBV) and online safety. Capacity was reinforced through training for 56 youth-friendly health service specialists and 400 professionals in child protection, GBV, and case management, and for 200 district-level staff in intersectoral mental health collaboration. UNICEF also supported a new school nutrition order, assessments of nutrition policies and marketing practices, and the integration of immunization and nutrition topics into school curricula.

In Moldova, the inclusion of refugee children and caregivers in healthcare is hindered by significant financial constraints. Since the beginning of the crisis, UNICEF partnered with various organisations to cover the healthcare costs of refugee children with TP, reaching approximately 22,000 children nationwide.  In addition, 56 refugee children (18 girls and 38 boys) and 17 pregnant refugee women without TP were covered with specialised and hospital care in the Institute of Mother and Child. Additionally, 1,317 refugee children were vaccinated under the National Immunization Programme, and 12,893 children and adolescents (57 per cent girls) received MHPSS counselling and referrals via the Youth Health Help Line. Lastly, 5,253 adolescents and young people from refugee and vulnerable host communities (3,439 girls, 1,814 boys) received primary care from mobile youth-friendly health clinics, and 30,832 youths gained health knowledge and skills through clinic counselling sessions.  

Social Policy 
In social policy and social protection, UNICEF’s work focused on consolidating the RESTART reform and improving access to and the quality of services for families and children. Technical assistance to the MLSP supported 10 local action plans to address limited service availability, human resource gaps, and budgetary constraints. As a result, the number of people benefitting from social services rose from 62,475 in 2024 to 82,753 in 2025, with most new beneficiaries being families with children. Legislative measures were adopted to strengthen community-based assistance and more inclusive services.

A significant shift in coverage occurred in September 2025, with legal amendments that extended state-funded child benefits to refugee children from Ukraine. Children aged 0–2, children with disabilities aged 0–17 and children born in Moldova in refugee families became eligible for childcare transfers, disability benefits and birth grants. UNICEF supported this change by providing technical assistance to estimate the potential caseload of refugee children eligible for national social protection programmes and to assess the fiscal impact on government budgets. The support also included evidence-based advocacy and policy dialogue with the MLSP to promote government ownership and the full operationalisation and domestic financing of the inclusion of refugee children in national social protection programmes. The Government also approved a revised funding methodology for early childhood education, effective from 2026. The formula allocates resources based on kindergarten needs, including measures to support access for children with SEN and disabilities. UNICEF led the technical design. In addition, a costed roadmap for integrating about 25,000 refugee children into national schools was developed with UNICEF support, clarifying financing needs and sequencing.

The Government also approved a revised funding methodology for early childhood education, effective from 2026. The formula allocates resources based on kindergarten needs, including measures to support access for children with SEN and disabilities. UNICEF led the technical design. In addition, a costed roadmap for integrating about 25,000 refugee children into national schools was developed with UNICEF support, clarifying financing needs and sequencing.

WASH
School WASH was improved through interventions in 31 schools, benefitting 7,680 students and about 1,100 staff. School leaders received training in operation and maintenance to support the sustained use of the upgraded facilities.

UNICEF and partners delivered emergency WASH services to ensure equitable access to water and sanitation for refugees. In 2025, safe and appropriate sanitation facilities were provided at the major border crossing point in Palanca for 2,568 individuals, including 916 children. Water, sanitation, and essential hygiene supplies for cleaning and disinfecting common spaces (bathrooms, cafeterias, hallways) were provided in 17 refugee accommodation centres, thereby contributing to a healthy environment for all Ukrainian refugees housed there, reaching 4,024 refugees (including 1,416 children).

More than 65,400 people, including students, teachers, and caregivers, participated in youth-led CEED initiatives and campaigns. These activities included sustainable paper recycling, with a focus on its links to climate and environmental issues; the restoration of water wells and springs; energy audits and energy-efficiency measures; and the expansion of green spaces through tree-planting and gardening initiatives. The initiatives were implemented in schools as part of non-formal, extra-curricular education.

Gender
In 2025, UNICEF advanced gender equality and social norm transformation through coordinated national efforts. The Government approved its first Social and Behaviour Change Strategy and Action Plan with UNICEF support, and a joint review with UNFPA helped integrate gender-transformative approaches and indicators into the national parenting programme ecosystem. Moldova also conducted its first study on intersections between violence against women and children, identifying shared drivers, effective integrated interventions, and alignment gaps with international standards.

Significant policy and legal reforms strengthened gender-based violence prevention and response. Parliament expanded parental leave rights for fathers, while joint UN advocacy led to the establishment of a national Father’s Day. Amendments to national legislation introduced criminal liability for stalking and extended protection orders, further aligning national frameworks with international norms. UNICEF and the GBV Agency also initiated an assessment of justice-sector specialisation and the development of a specialised training curriculum for professionals handling Violence Against Women, Domestic Violence and Violence Against Children cases. 

In education, the School Barometer survey (2025) indicates that 85 per cent of students perceive equal opportunities for girls and boys, although gender stereotypes persist. UNICEF and UNDP-supported revisions of curricula and teaching materials, alongside UNICEF-supported initiatives such as GirlsGoIT and STEAM on Wheels, aim to challenge stereotypes and increase girls’ participation in STEAM fields. 

In 2025, the Parliament extended paternity leave for fathers of twins, multiple births, or adopted children, and, following joint advocacy by UNICEF, UN Women, and UNFPA, established a national Father’s Day on 29 June. UNICEF and UNFPA also conducted a National Review of Gender-Transformative Parenting and integrated gender equality across parenting programmes. 
On the legal front, 2025 saw major reforms strengthening protection against gender-based violence, including harassment, stalking, femicide, and digital violence. 

Amendments aligned national law with the Istanbul Convention and Council of Europe Group of Experts on Action against Violence against Women and Domestic Violence (GREVIO) recommendations, introduced criminal liability for stalking, extended protection orders from three to six months, explicitly criminalised femicide, and imposed penalties for forced marriage of up to 12 years when the victim is a minor.

Inclusion
On disability inclusion, UNICEF continued to support shifts from a medical to a rights-based model, though assessment practices remained primarily medical. Early intervention capacity expanded with the addition of two new ECI centres, bringing the total to 15. In the 2024/25 school year, 2,145 children with disabilities were enrolled in mainstream schools and 523 in schools for children with intellectual or physical disabilities.[2] Thirty-one schools were equipped with indoor WASH facilities compliant with UNDIS procurement standards. Assistive technologies were procured, minimum school accessibility standards and competency frameworks for specialised staff were developed, and training for educators and parents continued. UNICEF and the MLSP generated new evidence on the extra costs of disability, revealing that families with children with disabilities earn up to 20 per cent less per adult and rely more on pensions and benefits, increasing vulnerability to shocks. Awareness efforts included an annual Inclusive Education Conference and the “Learning Together” campaign, which used social theatre and activities in 60 schools to address stigma and exclusion.

For Roma children, UNICEF piloted an educational mediator model in Edine¿, Otaci, and Soroca. Mediators supported families with documentation and school enrolment, and facilitated coordination between psychopedagogical services, social workers, and health providers. Institutional anchoring was strengthened through agreements with district councils and the national psychopedagogical centre, revisions of local regulations, and targeted training for mediators. Support groups for Roma parents and information sessions for teachers and local authorities were designed to reduce stigma and improve collaboration. The pilot also informed national discussions on formally recognising the mediator role within qualification and occupational frameworks, as well as the design of the next Roma support programme.

Social Behaviour Change
SBC approaches were used systematically across sectors. In addition to the work in child protection, SBC work in health included developing the National Immunization SBC plan, interpersonal communication training and institutionalising both within the health sector. In education, the “Learning Together” campaign engaged thousands of children and adults in inclusive education activities, including 62 social theatre performances. Behaviourally informed communication supported the enrolment of Ukrainian children, reaching about 32,000 parents and children offline and 350,000 people online, alongside programmatic work that increased refugee enrolment in Moldovan schools from 1,800 in 2024 to more than 3,600 in 2025. 

For the first time, UNICEF supported the development and approval of a Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) strategy for the Government, aimed at addressing social norms.

Partnerships and Private Sector
Partnerships with the private sector expanded. Corporate fundraising, mainly from telecom and banking, increased by about 70 per cent, helping to fund programmes in education, health, and child protection. Members of a Business Advisory Board advocated for early childhood development, including crèche services that meet EU standards. Proposals, including tax incentives for ECD investment, were reflected in the Foreign Investors Association’s annual White Book. UNICEF also began collaborating with Viorica Cosmetics to raise awareness of violence against women and children, and with Happy Cinema, which screened a video on the Laaha platform. Parenting sessions in private companies introduced family-friendly workplace concepts. The private sector participated in national campaigns aligned with the principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child; four social media influencers joined the campaigns at no cost. A media partnership with TVR Moldova continued, with free airtime for spots on inclusive education and Bebbo.

Overall, in 2025, UNICEF Moldova deepened its role as a systems partner. Rather than focusing on fragmented interventions, the office concentrated on policy reform, financing mechanisms, service standards, workforce capacity and SBC through a gender lens.  This approach aimed to make gains for children more durable and to align national systems more closely with CRC obligations, EU commitments and the SDG principle of leaving no child behind.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF marked 30 years of supporting child rights in Moldova. The year delivered significant results while highlighting structural challenges that will guide the next programme phase following the Extended Programme Review. Across health, education, child protection, social protection, and SBC, experience confirmed that sustainable system change requires long-term investment in equity, local capacity, and norms, not only in policies or projects.

In health, progress in maternal, child, and adolescent care was tempered by behavioural and trust barriers. Immunization uptake remained uneven, particularly in Roma communities and some religious groups, where misinformation persisted despite available services. Rural human resource shortages constrained the delivery of ECI and mobile youth-friendly health services. Data gaps and weak monitoring systems slowed corrective action. At the same time, administrative and financial delays, such as in establishing Moldova’s first human milk bank, showed that innovation depends on both technical readiness and governance capacity. Equity gaps persisted for refugees and rural families, and cross-sector coordination for mental health and nutrition remained complex.

It was clear that behavioural science is central to health outcomes and addressing these challenges. Institutionalising SBC within theNational Immunization Programme shifted efforts from ad hoc campaigns to system-wide approaches that address demand, trust, and norms. Social listening, community dialogue, and media engagement improved health literacy and allowed rapid response to misinformation. Integrating health content into education promoted early adoption of healthy behaviours. Continuous capacity building for health workers in behavioural science and infodemic management strengthened resilience. Tailored solutions, such as mobile youth clinics and Roma-targeted interventions, highlighted the need for context-adapted service models to close equity gaps.

In early learning, education, WASH, and adolescent development, access is relatively high, but quality and equity gaps remain. School readiness, especially in literacy and numeracy, varies by income, location, and minority status. UNICEF is supporting a national assessment of school readiness to guide targeted interventions. Inclusive education remains underfunded, with teachers needing ongoing support to meet diverse learning needs. Negative attitudes toward children with disabilities persist, and refugee enrolment is limited by language and specialised support gaps. Implementation of the Roadmap on Refugee Inclusion is expected to improve access but will require sustained political and financial commitment.

Children’s participation in school governance is limited, particularly for vulnerable groups. In 2025, pilots with pupil councils demonstrated that adolescents can influence school life when given space, skills, and adult support. Unequal access to digital skills programmes, especially for girls and remote communities, was addressed through initiatives such as STEAM on Wheels and GirlsGoIT, which bring learning directly to communities. Environmental and green education remain fragmented, underscoring the need for a coherent national approach.

Child protection reform advanced, but major structural weaknesses remain. Despite progress under RESTART and alignment with the EU acquis, services remain underfunded and heavily reliant on donor support, including UNICEF. High child poverty, staff turnover, and low investment continue to undermine service quality. The approved basic social services package for alternative care and family support is not being financed, putting gains in refugee inclusion and deinstitutionalisation at risk. In social policy and public finance, macro-level stability improved, yet rising child poverty—especially in rural areas—revealed persistent gaps in social protection. The impact of RESTART remains uneven due to differences in workforce capacity, planning, and local implementation. Experience shows that reforms achieve results only where local action plans, capacity-building, and complementary investments are in place. UNICEF will continue supporting child poverty reduction through evidence-informed policy dialogue and strengthened local planning, budgeting, and workforce capacity.

Legal reforms following ratification of the Istanbul Convention strengthened frameworks against violence toward women and girls, but prevention remains limited. Few interventions address root causes such as gender inequality and patriarchal norms. Justice for children is underfunded, with inadequate investment in restorative justice and alternatives to detention. These realities underscore the importance of sustained financial and technical support for the MLSP and the MoJ, and alignment with EU standards provides a platform to advocate for predictable domestic financing. Partnerships with civil society remain critical to reach the most vulnerable children and caregivers, particularly refugees.

On the left bank of the Nistru River, despite limited institutional capacity, UNICEF remains the primary provider of child protection services. 
Research on disability inclusion indicates that coverage alone is insufficient when benefits fall below subsistence levels. Complex eligibility procedures and a medical model exclude some children with functional limitations. A rights-based, functional approach is essential. Early Intervention Centres improved access and outcomes, demonstrating the value of cross-sector collaboration and parental engagement. Inclusion requires long-term investment in infrastructure, human resources, and behaviour change.

Partnerships with the private sector reinforced resource mobilisation and innovation. Long-term collaborations, such as with the Orange Foundation, encouraged sustained corporate commitment. Public–private partnerships, in which local authorities co-financed infrastructure and the private sector invested in services, demonstrated a viable value proposition, with UNICEF providing technical expertise. Supporting companies in integrating child rights into corporate responsibility policies strengthens accountability and strategic partnerships.
The work on SBC highlighted that behavioural drivers, harmful norms, and low trust are significant constraints. Vaccine hesitancy, equity gaps, and entrenched beliefs about disability and gender limited access to health, education, and child protection outcomes. 

Institutionalizing SBC in public systems through evidence generation, social listening, participatory dialogue, and media engagement can shift knowledge, attitudes, and confidence when implemented consistently and at scale.

The Roma education mediator pilot illustrated the potential of targeted interventions while underscoring the need for systemic follow-up. Mediators improved enrolment and retention, but socio-cultural norms, migration, financial barriers, and local budget constraints limited results, especially for Roma girls. Scaling the model, embedding it in regulations, and linking it with health and social services are planned next steps, underpinned by evidence to advocate for sustainable public financing.

Together, these experiences point to the need to deepen system-level engagement, prioritise equity, strengthen local capacities, and integrate behavioural science across sectors. Addressing financing, capacity, norms, and accountability together is essential to close the gap between commitments and outcomes for every child.

I.                    Political and socio-economic developments
Local elections consolidated the government coalition and the ruling party. The governing coalition led by VMRO-DPMNE - a conservative, centre-right party- secured the majority of mayoral mandates nationwide (60/80), including in the capital Skopje, thereby extending its governance from the national to the municipal level. The results reinforced their mandate following the 2024 parliamentary elections and highlighted the continued fragmentation and weakened electoral performance of the opposition, amid record-low turnout.
 
Modest economic growth continued to constrain fiscal space in 2025. The country recorded economic growth of around 2.5-3 per cent, with inflation easing compared to previous years; however weak external demand and persistently high living costs limited real income gains for households. While rising wages and public investment supported consumption, poverty reduction slowed and socioeconomic disparities persisted, disproportionately affecting children and families in low-income and marginalised communities. North Macedonia’s labour market continued to face challenges with low employment and participation rates, where women and youth are disproportionately affected. Public spending on education, health, and social protection remained below EU averages, constraining the system’s capacity to adequately respond to children’s needs. 
 
Demographic shifts. The government prioritized its demographic resilience strategy, as the population continued to contract (0.5% reduction per year, 2% per year for children) and rapidly age. The demographic transition is driven by a low fertility rate of just 1,48 per woman and out-migration. This trend can be seen clearly through primary school enrolment, with a drop of 3.3% in the number of students entering primary between the 2023/2024 and 2024/2025 school years and a drop of 12% when comparing 2024/2025 to 2020/2021.  
 
Limited progress in EU accession negotiations, while EU Growth Plan advances.  The EU 2025 Accession Report assessed the country as maintaining a moderate level of preparedness, noting strong alignment with EU foreign policy but limited progress in rule of law, anticorruption, and constitutional reform, which continued to constrain advances in accession negotiations. In early 2025, North Macedonia entered the implementation phase of the EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans, under which the country is eligible to receive up to €750 million, conditional on delivery of a national Reform Agenda focused on governance reforms, competitiveness, digitalisation and the green transition, and supporting gradual integration to the EU Single Market. Following the fulfilment of initial reform conditions, Growth Plan disbursements reached €23.8 million by the end of 2025.
 
Kochani fire tragedy triggers national outcry. In March 2025 a fire at a popular nightclub in the eastern town of Kochani resulted in the deaths of 63 young people and injuries to more than 190, marking the deadliest fire in North Macedonia’s history. The fire, caused by indoor pyrotechnics in an overcrowded, unlicensed venue that lacked basic fire-safety measures, prompted nationwide mourning and widespread public outcry. It sparked demonstrations calling for accountability, criminal investigations and arrests of responsible officials, and emergency safety inspections of cafes, restaurants and entertainment venues. The tragedy also highlighted the need for mental health and psychosocial support for affected youth, families and communities and strengthened protection systems.
 
Advances made in resolving statelessness. North Macedonia became the first country in the region to resolve all known cases of statelessness resulting from the dissolution of SFR Yugoslavia. Through sustained efforts led by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Parliament, the last 317 individuals who had lived in legal limbo since the country’s independence were granted citizenship in 2025. To sustain this achievement, birth registration is essential to achieve full inclusion of Roma and other marginalized groups.
 
II.                 Updates on the situation of children 
Child poverty persistently high. The State Statistical Office published poverty data for three consecutive years in 2025, effectively addressing the earlier delays in reporting.  Despite minor decreases over the period 2022-2024, data shows that 29,5% of children live below the national poverty line and continue to be the most vulnerable group in society. Additionally, the child poverty rate increased to 54,8% for household with three or more dependent children and to 45,8% of single parents. [1] 
Fluctuating health indicators. The neonatal mortality rate continued its downward trend, dropping from 1.8 per 1,000 live births in 2023 to 1.2 in 2024, [2] while the under-five mortality rate increased from 2.4 per 1,000 live births in 2023 to 3.0 per 1,000 in 2024. [3] Vaccination rates remain below 95% and HPV vaccine coverage declined from 56% in 2023 to 50% in 2024. [4]. 
The learning crisis. As part of education reform aimed at improving learning outcomes, evidence generated in 2025 found major imbalances in the allocation of human resources for primary education across the country. While some regions experience a surplus of teachers, others face acute shortages, resulting in overcrowded classrooms and limited teacher attention for students, conditions that undermine the quality of teaching and learning.  At the national level, the system recorded a surplus of 2,236 teachers.
Violence against children a persistent concern. The Ministry of Interior recorded 1442 child victims of crime, 823 boys and 619 girls, however this is considered to be only the tip of the iceberg given low levels of reporting. 
Child Care reforms continue. In 2025, no children were cared for in large-scale residential institutions. A total of 621 children (295 girls and 326 boys) live in family-based care, including 137 children with disabilities (61 girls and 76 boys). Since the start of the social protection reform in 2020, the number of children in family-based care has increased by 42%, and by 191% for children with disabilities. The reduction in the number of children living in small group homes however has been slow—only 9% over five years—while the number of children with disabilities in such homes has increased by 35%. [5]. 
Significant impact of air pollution on children. WHO’s 2025 environmental health scorecard showed children in North Macedonia continue to face high exposure to PM2.5, five times higher than WHO air-quality guidelines.
