Child rights, poverty reduction and social inclusion
The National Action Plan on Child Rights 2025–2029 was adopted in August 2025, following a multi-year, multi-stakeholder development process involving line ministries, independent institutions, civil society and children themselves. The plan was developed with EU and UNICEF support; UNICEF contributed to evidence generation, policy development, indicator setting, fiscal analysis, and child participation mechanisms. Key government commitments include reducing child poverty and social exclusion – including a 15% increase in child benefits; expanding early childhood development services; strengthening protection from violence and neglect; improving inclusion in education and health services; and increasing children’s participation in decision making. The Plan also prioritizes design and implementation of the European Child Guarantee, placing children at the centre of the EU integration agenda. From an operational perspective, the Plan envisages the re-establishment of a permanent National Committee to ensure inter-ministerial coordination and accountability, responding to a key 2022 recommendation of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child and advancing an important EU accession criteria set out in the country’s Rule of Law Roadmap. 
Implementation of some of the National Action Plan’s policy measures has already begun. For example the Ministry of Social Policy, Demographics and Youth and UNICEF presented the results of an analysis and policy recommendations for a comprehensive package of services to be considered with the introduction of the European Child Guarantee. The government has appointed a National Child Guarantee Coordinator and initiated the creation of an interministerial work group to develop a National Action Plan for Implementation of the Child Guarantee 2026-2030.
Building on its systematic advocacy on child poverty, UNICEF supported an analysis and micro-simulation of cash benefits relevant for children at the request of the Ministry of Social Policy, Demographics and Youth. Preliminary results identified limitations of the system established through the 2019 social protection reform, particularly related to the adequacy and coverage of current benefits, which have not kept pace with the cost of living and are capped for two children. Other bottlenecks include disincentives to labour market entry, as families suddenly lose child benefits when a member is employed in the formal sector; and missed opportunities for human capital development, with pre-school excluded from the education grant. Policy recommendations were discussed with key stakeholders at technical level, based on results of the micro-simulation analysis on child poverty and fiscal implications. Two reform pathways were proposed: a universal child allowance with targeted top-ups, and an enhanced means-tested system, for discussion at a high-level policy advocacy event in 2026.
Important amendments to the Law on Disability Assessment integrate functional assessments of children and youth into the universal assessment system ensuring child-specific standards designed to capture developmental aspects of functioning in children and adolescents, including growth, learning, and evolving capacities. The revised law retains the existing institutional set-up and trained workforce for assessments of children and youth, a separate rulebook for child-specific provisions, the electronic register for children, parental participation, and ensures assessments are free of charge, all results achieved with UNICEF advocacy and technical support over the past decade. 
The State Statistical Office initiated planning for the 2027 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey, expected to inform over 150 indicators on the situation of children and women, with rich disaggregation to inform policy analysis and evidence-based decision making as well as status against the National Development Strategy and Sustainable Development Goals targets ahead of 2030. With UNICEF support, SSO conduced a Data Gap Assessment to determine which modules would add most value to the country’s data landscape. The assessment reviewed 49 potential modules across four dimensions of policy relevance, data recency, gaps in disaggregation for vulnerable groups, and effort required for implementation. It presented three evidence-based options for the scope of the survey, for decision by the State Statistical Office in consultation with the National Steering Committee. 
New partnerships to combat discrimination against vulnerable children were formed with the Commission for the Prevention and Protection Against Discrimination and the Macedonian Football Federation. Kicked off on World Children’s Day 2025, the joint campaign focuses on ending discrimination against Roma children and children with disabilities.
Education reforms
Primary and Secondary Education Law amendments expanded inclusive education by ensuring children in correctional facilities have access to primary and secondary education, and broadening affirmative measures for children with disabilities, including fee exemptions, transport and educational support services, and school level adaptations for diverse learners. The changes build on the Law on Primary Education (2019, 2024) and the National Concept for Inclusive Education (2020) developed with UNICEF support. It is yet to be seen if the amendments to the Law on Primary Education in late 2024 that allow parents to enrol children with disabilities in Resource Centres instead of mainstream schools will have a backsliding effect on inclusion. Enrolment in these centres has seen a positive trend, decreasing from 610 children in the 2022/23 school year to 535 in 2023/24 and 460 in 2024/25. UNICEF is supporting implementation of the Law on Primary Education with analysis for the establishment of Support Centres at municipal level, mandated to support learning of students with disabilities in mainstream schools, particularly those who follow a modified programme.
In August 2025, following several years of UNICEF evidence-based policy advocacy, partnership convening, and technical assistance, the Government adopted new funding formulas for primary and secondary education, marking a milestone in strengthening equitable, efficient, and quality education and advancing school optimization. The reform introduces transparent, standardized per student costing, updated to reflect real needs; additional allocations for inclusive education, including support for children with learning difficulties and disabilities, minority-language instruction and poverty-related disadvantages; and adjustment criteria enabling municipalities to better align funding, teacher allocation and resources with actual enrolment. The formulas will also introduce performance-based incentives for school improvement, and support investments in labor-market relevant vocational profiles. Adoption of the new funding formulas – an indicator under the national Reform Agenda - helped unlock €15.9 million under the EU Growth Plan and led to a 7% increase in education funding for 2026 (approximately $31 million). UNICEF supported implementation measures, including primary school optimisation plans in 32 municipalities (40%) and ongoing capacity-building of municipal officials to operationalise the new funding system.
As part of the education quality and financing reform package, the Ministry of Education and Science also adopted new Standards and Norms for School Facilities, Equipment, and Teaching Aids in Primary Schools, developed with UNICEF support. These standards set requirements for energy-efficient and safe infrastructure, adequate school facilities, modern teaching and learning materials, including assistive technologies, and the conditions necessary to support equitable and quality learning environments.
Green skills and climate action
Mainstreaming of environmental and climate change education in the education system further advanced in 2025. Building on progress from previous years, UNICEF technical support assisted the Ministry of Education and Science to adopt and roll out 14 new mandatory vocational curricula integrating green and digital skills, reaching an additional 7,000 students in the 2025/2026 school year. The Ministry prioritised environmental education for teacher professional development, training 6,000 secondary school teachers, and engaged 36,000 children from primary and secondary schools in outdoor environmental learning activities using teaching and learning materials developed with UNICEF support. The lessons learned through implementing the UPSHIFT programme on youth-led innovation on environmental challenges informed support to the Ministry to institutionalise the approach as an extracurricular activity -- strengthening its scalability, sustainability and system-wide impact. In parallel, all venues of the Experiential Learning Network – comprised of eleven public scientific institutions and established with UNICEF support - were included in the Ministry’s list of approved sites for school field trips and excursions which will facilitate the long-term sustainability of the Network. 
The Ministry also adopted child-focused Air Quality recommendations for schools, developed through a multisectoral process involving national and international experts in health, environment and education. Aligned with European air quality standards, the recommendations provide real-time tiered guidance on adjusting outdoor activities and ventilation during pollution episodes, while complementary measures promote improved indoor air quality, strengthening schools’ capacity to protect children’s health and ensure safer learning environments during periods of high air pollution. In partnership with GIZ, UNICEF also submitted a concept note to the National Delegated Authority for the Green Climate Fund Readiness Programme to strengthen national climate-financing capacities focused on schools and preschools.
Adolescent girls and young women leaders organized the country’s first Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), positioning girls at the forefront of national climate action. The event convened adolescents and young people from across the country to assess local environmental challenges and inform national priorities ahead of COP30 (November 2025). The conference led to the development of a National Youth Statement centred on climate justice and intersectionality and incorporated in the Global Youth Statement presented in Belem, Brazil. By linking environmental degradation with structural inequalities and human rights concerns, the process amplified youth voices in global climate dialogue and strengthened girls’ leadership and agency in shaping national and international climate narratives.
Emergency response following the Kochani fire
Following the tragic event in Kochani, continuity of learning and psychosocial support for students was rapidly restored. UNICEF immediately supported the Ministry of Education and Science in organizing a sensitive, safe, and structured return to teaching and learning under conditions of collective grief, including through the development of a national protocol to guide school operations. Leveraging its partnership with the national network of school psychologists and existing materials, UNICEF enabled timely psychosocial support for students countrywide and collaborated with the Chamber of Psychologists to strengthen the capacities of over 100 school psychologists to provide immediate support to affected students and their families.
Nurturing care and early childhood development
Following years of UNICEF evidence-based advocacy, the Ministers of Health, Education and Social Policy signed a Memorandum of Cooperation (MOU) in May 2025 to establish Early Childhood Intervention services. The MOU defines clear roles and responsibilities across the three sectors, enabling a coordinated, multisectoral approach to supporting young children and their families. A pilot service in Skopje, informed by international best practices, has been launched and is generating evidence to inform future scale-up. The pilot actively engages both mothers and fathers, with girls representing 40% of the beneficiaries. In parallel, the ministry is preparing to introduce universal developmental monitoring, informed by a survey showing strong family physician support for early intervention (79%) but limited preparedness (35%) due to absence of standardized tools or skills. To address this gap, fourteen age-specific developmental monitoring tools were developed and tested with 1,400 children in preparation for national roll-out. Together, these efforts lay the foundation for scaling-up early identification of developmental delays and disabilities and ensuring timely referral to multisectoral services so that every child receives the support they require to thrive.
Following up on capacity strengthening efforts over recent years, UNICEF supported a maturity assessment of home visiting services to evaluate strengths, gaps and opportunities for improvement. Key findings highlight the need for evidence-based practices, targeted staff training and standardized protocols to ensure equitable quality care. Key gaps include the lack of standardised tools to identify at-risk families and guide additional visits, as well as limited resources and weak evaluation systems for community outreach. Additionally, under the leadership of the Government Head Nurse, sectoral working groups developed draft regulations, legislation, and educational standards to advance the professionalization of nurses and midwives, which are now under ministerial review.
Cross-sectoral efforts led by the health sector continued to address the growing burden on non-communicable diseases among children. The intersectoral committee on child and adolescent mental health, established last year to implement the National Action Plan, developed standard operating procedures across health, education, and social policy sectors, and 20% more family doctors strengthened their mental health and psychosocial support skills, potentially benefiting up to 75,000 children aged 0–17.  A nationwide assessment of school nutrition environments generated actionable recommendations to strengthen the country policies and practices.
The national digital parenting application (Bebbo) reached more than 25,000 users - mothers (68%), fathers (8%) and caregivers (24%), representing a 25% increase compared to 2024, supported by a UNICEF-led parenting campaign. In 2025 the content was enhanced with the addition of a new pregnancy module, designed to respond to the distinct needs of mothers and fathers, promote shared parental responsibilities and encourage more equitable gender roles. While engagement of fathers remains limited, it has been identified as a priority area. In 2026, the roll-out of the playful learning programme through all home visiting nurses will place specific emphasis on engaging fathers, promoting inclusivity and challenging traditional gender roles in early childhood development.
Social Service and Justice Workforce Capacities
Addressing a key recommendation of the evaluation of the deinstitutionalisation and childcare reform, UNICEF supported a comprehensive mapping and analysis of the social service workforce. The analysis examined workforce capacity, accountabilities, geographic distribution, caseload and professional development countrywide, with gender perspectives integrated throughout the research process. Preliminary findings show that centres for social work - despite their central role linking national social policy with community-level implementation- face significant organizational, capacity, and support challenges. These constraints limit their agility to respond effectively to complex cases, particularly those involving gender-based violence. As part of this process, the government has established a technical committee comprising relevant national and international stakeholders to lead the re-organization of centres for social work and develop a costed National Action Plan addressing findings from the analysis.
Thanks to sustained UNICEF advocacy efforts over the past five years, changes in the Law on Primary Education eliminated barriers to education for children residing in correctional facilities. Primary education is now provided onsite, while older children are now enabled to attend high school outside of these institutions without incurring costs. 
Implementation of the Justice for Children (J4C) law advanced through the development of draft operational by-laws and infographics to guide professionals. A nationwide assessment involving courts, lawyers, Centres for Social Work, municipalities and civil society identified gaps in legal aid and restorative justice services and opportunities to strengthen child-focused justice. The Academy for Judges and Prosecutors approved a UNICEF-supported Justice for Children Training Programme for inclusion in continuous professional development which will ensure its sustainability as part of the core programme of in-service training. Additionally, wellbeing and safeguarding measures for children at-risk in small group homes were strengthened with the adoption of a manual and capacity building to support children’s well-being and mental health, and policies on child safeguarding and protection from sexual exploitation and abuse.
UNICEF in partnership with its private sector partner Telekom Foundation developed a peer-to-peer programme for safer digital environments, equipping 50 adolescents from across the country with coping strategies, resilience, and communication skills, and enabling them to act as advocates in their communities. Working in partnership with the Scouts Association and experts, adolescents created a gender-responsive toolkit for the prevention and protection against online bullying which addresses both girls’ and boys’ specific vulnerabilities and experiences in digital spaces. The co-created campaign #NetwithoutHate challenges harmful norms, opens dialogue on respect, empathy, consent, mental health and emotional expression and already reached over 3 million engagements. 
A private sector mapping analysis, focused on social responsibility priorities and their alignment with priorities for children, identified concrete opportunities for new partnerships with larger companies to advance adolescent skills development, climate action and early childhood development. Building on these findings, UNICEF will proactively engage interested partners to co-create and implement initiatives that deliver results for children.
Preparations for the new programming cycle and management 
The UNICEF 2026-2030 Country Programme was developed in close collaboration with a wide range of stakeholders including government, civil society, academia, development partners and young people. Grounded in the Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents 2024, it defines child-centred results contributing to the UN Stainable Development Cooperation Framework and the National Development Strategy 2024-2044. The overarching vision of the Country Programme 2026-2030 is to drive systemic change at scale for children and adolescents, with an intentional focus on ensuring that policies, budgets, services and measures benefit the most vulnerable children in the country. Building on the findings of the Country programme evaluation and aligned the new directions of the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026-2029, the programme is focused on prioritized areas and aimed at achieving scale and maximizing scale within the context of an upper-middle-income EU accession country. 
 
The programme focuses on two components: 1. Protection and nurturing care addresses the high rates of child poverty, violence against children and children not adequately reached by health system and contributes to strengthening the child and social protection system and enabling nurturing care. 2. Foundational learning and skills respond to the learning crisis and contributes to strengthening and optimizing the education system – from pre-school through secondary and fostering green skills and climate action. Cutting across these two components is a focus on reaching at scale most vulnerable children particularly those living in poverty, Roma children and children with disabilities and a focus on environment and climate change. Across these areas, UNICEF prioritized the provision of technical expertise and leveraging evidence, financing and partnerships as its main strategies to influence child-related policies and investments. 
 
In parallel with the development of the new programme, the Office prepared its Country Programme Management Plan 2026-2030 through a comprehensive office-wide process. The Plan identifies the financial, human resources and management priorities required to deliver the new programme results within a complex global context and UN reform process. It places strong emphasis on efficiency, affordability and a fit-for purpose country presence. Building on lessons learned from the previous country cycle, the Plan prioritizes: i) continuity in strategic partnerships; ii) maintaining strong technical expertise, iii) and implementing efficiency measures to reduce operating costs. Key efficiency gains already achieved in 2025 include reductions in rent through office space optimization and lowered electricity costs thanks to the installation of an energy-efficient cooling system.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Leveraging evidence and convening partnerships for public sector reforms
The approval of new education funding formulas and the ongoing implementation of the school network optimization demonstrate that systemic, large-scale reform is possible even under tight fiscal and political constraints, when change is grounded in high-quality data, communicated through clear, accessible evidence, and supported by broad, inclusive coalitions. UNICEF evidence-based policy advocacy led by high calibre national staff; sustained engagement with political leaders across parties and mandates, together with structured consultations that gave municipalities, educators, parents and students a voice, helped build ownership, reduce resistance and tailor solutions to local realities. Framing these reforms within wider public finance and EU integration agendas, and aligning them with development partner support, proved critical to maintaining momentum and creating incentives for change. Going forward, evidence-driven policy action, cross-sector partnerships and local engagement will remain essential to translating ambitious policy reforms into sustainable improvements in equity, efficiency and learning outcomes for children.
Building on existing networks and local capacities for a swift emergency response 
Following the tragic fire and mass casualties in Kochani, the country went into emergency mode – immediately seeking support from its partners. While the EU and neighboring countries rapidly responded with expert support for emergency medical care and evacuation, UNICEF offered immediate assistance to the Ministry of Education and Science in organizing a sensitive, safe, and structured return to learning during a period of collective grief. Thanks to its longstanding partnership with the national network of school psychologists and the Chamber of Psychologists and already existing materials on mental health, UNICEF enabled the rapid deployment of psychosocial support for affected students and their families, as well as students nationwide. Leveraging existing networks, local actors, and previous capacity-building investments allowed UNICEF to provide a swift, coordinated, and effective emergency response complementary to government and the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. Going forward, UNICEF will prioritize further strengthening capacities for emergency preparedness and response, with a focus on areas where it can add value by complementing government systems and EU support mechanisms.
Hands-on approaches strengthen evidence-driven policy making
The Ministry of Social Policy, Demographics and Youth developed an initial design for a randomised control trial (RCT) to assess the impact of cash benefits on children’s wellbeing, as a result of a joint JPAL-UNICEF capacity building initiative. With a hands-on approach, government officials strengthened skills in developing theories of change, designing experimental protocols, interpreting technical evidence and using global evaluation resources. Building on this progress UNICEF will support finalization of the design and implementation of the evaluation in 2026-2027.
UN partnerships accelerate reforms across sectors
Although the country has made progress toward achieving SDG target 16.9—ensuring legal identity for all—children from disadvantaged backgrounds, including Roma children, remain disproportionately at risk of being unregistered due to administrative barriers and related costs. To address this gap, UNICEF and UNHCR jointly advocated with key Ministers to revive and scale up the Welcome Baby initiative, which enables hospitals to issue birth certificates within 48 hours of childbirth at no cost to families. This initiative, previously piloted, was discontinued during the COVID-19 pandemic. Thanks to joint advocacy efforts, the government assigned the Ministry of Digital Transformation to lead an inter-ministerial working group bringing together all key stakeholders, requesting a fully digitalized system for newborn registration and electronic issuance of birth certificates, removing the need for parents to visit the Registry Office and ensuring that every child receives a legal identity from birth. Going forward, UNICEF and its UN partners will focus on addressing legal and administrative barriers that could hinder issuance of birth certificates under this new initiative, ensuring every child is issued a birth certificate free of charge.
Under the leadership of the UN Resident Coordinator, the UN has initiated a dialogue with the Prime Minister and his senior advisors to establish a Women’s Equality Accelerator—a pooled thematic fund dedicated to advancing women’s empowerment and gender equality in North Macedonia by leveraging government leadership and UN technical expertise. As part of this initiative ILO, UNFPA, UN Women and UNICEF have developed a joint programme to address the persistently low female labour participation and employment in the country - among the lowest in the Western Balkan region with the widest gaps compared to EU averages. UNICEF’s focus under the proposed joint programme will be to provide technical expertise, evidence-based advocacy and leverage partnerships to strengthen government investment in expanding the availability of early childhood development and care services. Overcoming this key structural barrier will be a critical accelerator to women’s economic participation, inclusive growth and human capital development. Going forward, leveraging government leadership and national financing to advance these priorities is expected to become a central pathway for mobilising the UN’s collective expertise, accelerating progress toward national development goals and upholding the commitment to leave no one behind.

Poland is a European Union Member State situated in Central Eastern Europe, bordering Ukraine as well as six other countries including Belarus and the Russian Federation and has remained a key frontline country of arrival for refugees fleeing the war in Ukraine. Given the continued uncertainty of the conflict and its prolonged nature, throughout 2025, Poland continued playing a vital role in hosting displaced populations. As of December 2025, 967,605 individuals remained registered under temporary protection (PESEL UKR), including approximately 38  per cent children, 59 per cent women and girls, and 7 per cent elderly  persons.
  
Major legislative changes  impacting Ukrainian refugees 
Nearly four years into the full-scale war, national legislation increasingly shifted from exceptional assistance. Major development was the drafting of the Act on the phasing out from  the Act on Assistance to Citizens of Ukraine in the Context of the Armed Conflict on the territory of that state (“the Phasing Out Act”) by the Polish  government, aiming to align the legal status of Ukrainian nationals with that of other third-country nationals benefiting from [1]  protection. While intended to support a transition toward  more sustainable arrangements, the reform also reduced certain forms of assistance previously available to refugees from Ukraine, particularly in areas such as collective accommodation. The draft legislation is in the process of consultations.
  
In parallel, Poland extended temporary protection  until 4 March 2026, maintaining access to healthcare for children but  introducing changes to the scope of services available to adults. Access to  family benefits — including 800+, (the  monthly child allowance of PLN 800 about EUR 186), programs “Dobry  Start” and “Active Parent” — became conditional on employment or insurance  coverage, school enrolment and income thresholds, with additional  verification mechanisms allowing suspension of payments where eligibility is  questioned. Safeguards allow unemployed families to temporarily retain  benefits for three to six months; however, the new rules have increased  vulnerability among households facing labour-market or administrative  barriers.
  
Moreover, the Government  announced the introduction of a three-year residence permit (CUKR), intended to replace the PESEL UKR status and align refugees with the general temporary  protection framework under migration law. Applications would be processed  exclusively through an online system (MOS portal). While the reform aims to  provide stability, digital-only procedures create barriers for families  lacking internet access, language proficiency or administrative capacity, potentially affecting children’s access to services linked to legal status.
  
Current status of Ukrainian  refugees and children rights in the country
Almost 200,000 children and  adolescents from Ukraine stayed enrolled in Polish schools and preschools in  2025. The mandatory school attendance policy introduced the previous year  increased support needs for students, families and the education system,  including shortages of qualified teachers, limited availability of Polish-as-a-second-language support, and gaps in mental health and social integration services. Adolescents and children who had experienced prolonged  learning interruptions required tailored support to ensure retention in the  education system and access to skills development and career guidance. At the  same time, labour-market trends affected education participation: a UNHCR–Deloitte analysis found that almost 25 per cent of Ukrainian youth aged  15–19 were already participating in the workforce, compared to 4 per cent of their Polish peers, increasing the risk of early school leaving and informal  employment. The analysis also showed that Polish language proficiency was  associated with a 16 per cent increase in median net wages, highlighting the importance of sustained language learning and skills development for adolescents’ long-term inclusion and transition to work.
  
Child protection monitoring highlighted the persistent  risks faced by refugee children and adolescents. Since 2022, more than 49,000 unaccompanied Ukrainian children were appointed a temporary guardian in Poland[2]. This represents more than 5% of all children from Ukraine who entered Poland. As of July 2025, more than 22,000 unaccompanied children with temporary  guardians remained under the supervision of local social welfare structures (data from the Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy). These children are at increased risk of violence and exploitation as the safeguards established by the special legislation, may be discontinued. 
  
Around 600 children evacuated from Ukrainian residential care institutions remain in  Poland along with around 200 children from Ukrainian foster care. The protection of children from Ukrainian institutional is likely to be continued according to the special legislation draft. The Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy has leveraged significant EU funds to ensure the long-term  protection and supervision of children from institutional care. However,  Ukrainian foster parents and children evacuated with them, have not been  included in the proposed legislation and their support maybe up to local  authorities and NGOs. 
  
Collective accommodation  centres remain a critical element of Poland’s refugee response. Legislative  changes under the Phasing-Out Act will progressively narrow eligibility,  limiting support to 60 days from first entry and no longer than 12 months  from activation of temporary protection, after which assistance is restricted  to specific vulnerable groups. As of end of 2025, slightly fewer than 14,000  people were residing in 398 state-funded shelters (32 per cent were retirees,  12 per cent persons with disabilities, 3 per cent caregivers of persons with  disabilities, 3 per cent single parents with at least three children, 1 per  cent temporary guardians, 3 per cent children not receiving the 800+ benefit,  and 1 per cent pregnant women or carers of infants under 12 months), with  approximately half expected to remain eligible after 1 July 2026. These  changes are likely to result in shelters increasingly accommodating mainly  persons with disabilities, retirees, and children in institutional care,  while increasing risks of homelessness and social exclusion among single  parents, predominantly mothers with children, and contributing to heightened  stress and uncertainty among children and caregivers[3].
  
The access to most family benefits previously available to refugees from Ukraine  — including caregiver allowances, family allowances, parental benefits, and  nursing allowances will depend on fulfilling the „labour activity” condition.  The latest legal amendments restrict social assistance (based on the Act  on social assistance) for holders of UKR status exclusively to: shelter,  meals, essential clothing, targeted cash assistance.  This represents a dramatic reduction in the support spectrum, disregarding  families with many children, students, children and persons with  disabilities, foster families, or households with chronic vulnerabilities not  captured under the narrow definition.
  
Migration governance  developments also shaped the broader child protection environment. In March  2025, the Government temporarily suspended the right to apply for  international protection at the Belarus border, while maintaining exemptions  for vulnerable groups including unaccompanied children and individuals facing  serious harm. Between March and December 2025, more than 420 applications  were rejected while over 70 vulnerable individuals were admitted to the  procedure, generating concerns among civil society and highlighted the  importance of safeguarding child-sensitive procedures within broader  migration management policies.
  
In November 2025, the  parliament adopted legal amendments which introduced a possibility to order detention of children for migration reasons also in cases of unaccompanied children  above 15 years who have applied for international protection. 
  
The humanitarian financing  environment also evolved significantly during 2025. A temporary global stop-work order affecting humanitarian funding required reprioritization of  programmes to ensure continuity of critical services for the most vulnerable children, particularly unaccompanied and separated children. Although funding  was reinstated later in the year, the interruption affected programme  implementation during the first quarter and demonstrated increasing volatility in humanitarian financing. Concurrently, the closure of certain  humanitarian field structures and adjustments in inter-agency coordination  accelerated the transition toward government ownership and localized service  provision.
  
In summary, Poland’s operating environment continued  evolving from emergency response toward sustainable inclusion within national  structures. While policy normalization supports long-term stability, it also  risks widening inequalities if vulnerable groups, such as adolescents, children with disabilities, unaccompanied children or Roma community who face  barriers to accessing systems designed for the general population. The context therefore required continued focus on strengthening public institutions, supporting social cohesion and ensuring equitable access to  services for the most vulnerable children.

[1] Under the general institutional framework implementing the Temporary Protection Directive (2001/55/EC), as transposed into national law by the Act on Granting Protection to Foreigners on the Territory of the Republic of Poland.
[2] Data from Ministry of Justice.
[3] After 60 days, assistance is limited to persons with disability certificates or their carers not receiving caregiver allowance; persons of retirement age without a Polish pension, employment, or adult descendants in Poland; pregnant women or carers of children up to 12 months; persons from foreign institutional foster care; and individuals discharged from hospitalization financed by National Health Fund NFZ after at least seven days. Persons residing in shelters as of 4 March 2026 remain subject to previous rules until end-June 2026, while those accommodated from 5 March 2026 onward fall under the new provisions. Frequent legislative changes and information gaps have increased stress and uncertainty, negatively affecting well-being and resilience, while the requirement to leave shelters raises risks of return to Ukraine or further displacement within Poland. In addition, some shelters continue to operate privately without state funding, with no adequate mechanisms to monitor their number, residents, or situation.

In 2025, Poland remained the second largest refugee-hosting country in Europe. As the response evolved from emergency support toward longer-term inclusion, UNICEF Refugee Response Office (RRO) Poland increasingly focused on strengthening national systems alongside addressing remaining humanitarian needs. Working with central and local government institutions, civil society organizations and academia, UNICEF supported community engagement and reinforced education, mental health and child protection services to enable sustainable inclusion of refugee children and families. The office also started documenting and promoting innovative solutions developed during the response and worked with partners to adopt and integrate them into mainstream public services. By prioritizing equity, sustainability and capacity-building, the response shifted from direct service delivery to institutional strengthening, helping Polish systems become more resilient and better equipped to support vulnerable children both now and in the future recovery of Ukraine. 
  
Child Protection
In 2025, UNICEF supported the national child protection system at both central and local levels, enabling a more effective response to the needs of refugee children. 
  
Alternative care
In 2025, UNICEF continued to strengthen the alternative care system to ensure that unaccompanied and separated children in need of care are provided with quality family-based care and tailored services.
  
At the beginning of 2025, nearly 800 children evacuated from Ukrainian institutions in 2022 remained in facilities across Poland, with three locations hosting up to 100 children each. Although numbers gradually declined due to returns, placements in Ukrainian foster families, resumed adoption procedures, and aging out, UNICEF continued prioritising support and advocacy for this highly vulnerable group.
  
During the year, the relocation of the remaining groups from Hotel Ossa—initially hosting around 500 children—was completed. By December 2025, 213 children were living in small group homes (154 in 16 homes in Lódz; 59 in 6 homes in Powiat Wroclawski), while children relocated earlier from other facilities continued to reside in small group homes in Powiat Slupski and Lódz. All children received integrated support services, including psychological assistance, regular and specialist medical care, psychophysical assessments, and school enrolment.
  
A gender-based violence risk-mitigation framework was maintained throughout the year, combining age-appropriate psychoeducation on bodily autonomy, consent, and safety with mandatory PSEA training for all staff. Care leavers transitioning to independence benefited from life-skills workshops, supported training apartments, and vocational guidance to facilitate access to the  labour market.
  
Children remaining in large-group or remote locations—including Moryn, Koscierzyna,  Garczyn, and Hotel Poseidon—received ongoing psychological support, integrational activities, case management, and referrals to specialist services. UNICEF also ensured life-saving assistance for children and young adults with severe disabilities in a care facility in Torun through access to critical medical care, mental-health services, and crisis intervention.  Caregivers and children participated in online workshops on violence prevention and digital safety, addressing grooming, cyberbullying, and sexting.
  
In parallel, UNICEF strengthened the national alternative care system to expand access to quality family-based care. A therapy room in the Gdynia Family Foster Care Department was renovated to enhance specialised support for foster families. The “Light House” centre in Biala Podlaska continued to provide trauma-informed therapeutic and rehabilitation services to evacuated Ukrainian foster families, benefiting 554 children and caregivers. A second  centre replicating the model was established in Lódz.
  
Foster-family recruitment and support efforts continued in Lódz, with outreach to the Ukrainian community and the completion of training by 18 candidates. Gdynia launched the “Heart Test” campaign—originally developed in Lódz with UNICEF support—to promote foster parenting for both Polish and Ukrainian children, accompanied by a new website, local outreach, and strengthened inter-municipal cooperation.
  
In Katowice, support for family-based care for Ukrainian children was expanded through training for prospective foster parents (three families completing the HOPE programme), rental subsidies and material support for three foster families, and strengthened coordination through three dedicated foster-care coordinators. In total, 11 children benefited from this package of support.

Social Inclusion of Most Vulnerable Refugee Children and Families   
UNICEF worked with national and local partners to strengthen social services for the most vulnerable refugee children and families, supporting social inclusion and providing MHPSS through Spilno Hubs, municipal programmes, support for evacuated children, and interventions in collective accommodation centres. Over 27,000 refugee children received individual case management, while 139,924 vulnerable host-community members were reached indirectly through capacity-building activities.
  
Six Spilno Hubs in Lublin, Katowice, Bialystok, Lódz, Kraków and Gdynia delivered integrated education, child protection, health and MHPSS services to 16,259 children and 7,016 caregivers, complemented by legal counselling, Polish language courses and labour-market integration support. UNICEF also documented and developed a comprehensive business model and roadmap for Spilno Hubs, defining services, governance and financing arrangements to ensure sustainability, scalability, and alignment with local social inclusion policies.
  
In partnership with the Ministry of  Family, Labour and Social Policy, UNICEF delivered a national  capacity-building programme for 39 Foreigner Integration Centres, enhancing  the skills of 163 managers and frontline staff in violence prevention, GBV,  and child safeguarding to improve child-sensitive service provision.
  
UNICEF supported vulnerable refugees in 35 collective accommodation centres across five regions, including Roma families, through case management, MHPSS, and violence-prevention services reaching over 2,000 people. The programme strengthened links to local education, health, social assistance and labour-market systems to promote independence and stable living conditions. In cooperation with the Polish Migration Forum, UNICEF also supported 325 psychological and psychiatric consultations, 291 legal consultations, and strengthened the capacities of 144 professionals and caregivers.
  
To improve support for the large group of children under temporary guardianship, UNICEF assisted municipalities with the highest caseloads. As of July 2025, 22,256 temporary guardians were supervising 23,870 children in Poland. UNICEF facilitated inter-ministerial and inter-municipal dialogue on good practices and challenges and supported a capacity-building programme for 97 social welfare professionals working with 1,067 Ukrainian children. Ten tailored online trainings strengthened skills in culturally sensitive communication, violence prevention, NVC, understanding Ukrainian child-rearing norms, and effective case management.
  
UNICEF also partnered with the Family Assistants Association and the Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy to enhance the national network of family assistants, preventing family separation and child protection risks among vulnerable and refugee families.  The opening conference brought together 167 participants, followed by targeted online workshops and distribution of educational materials that reached 2,787 family assistants.
  
Additional workforce strengthening took  place in Poznan, where 208 professionals—including social workers,  coordinators and family assistants—received training on crisis intervention,  intercultural communication, working with socially excluded groups, and  solution-focused approaches to improve support for refugees.
  
Local child protection systems were reinforced through partnerships with Kraków and Warsaw, supporting community-based youth centres offering integration, recreational and educational activities, psychological and therapeutic services, and counselling for parents. More than 7,000 Ukrainian refugees benefited from these interventions.
  
UNICEF continued targeted support for children with disabilities. In Kraków, the Education and Rehabilitation Centre supported around 40 children with intellectual and multiple disabilities through specialised rehabilitation, therapy, educational support, and integration services. UNICEF also expanded assistance to vulnerable Roma communities through partnerships with Foundation Towards Dialogue and the Central Roma Council, providing MHPSS to 1,167 caregivers and children and strengthening the capacity of 180 social welfare professionals, police officers and accommodation-centre staff to better support Roma families.

Access to justice and prevention of violence against children  
Between January and December 2025, UNICEF and its partners provided GBV risk-mitigation, prevention, and response services to 119,610 refugees and vulnerable host-community members, including 68,174 girls and women. In partnership with the Ministry of Justice and a multidisciplinary group of experts, UNICEF developed a model for multi-agency cooperation to strengthen identification of child-protection risks and improve responses to violence against children.
  
In cooperation with Ministry of Justice, a total of 3,214 justice professionals were trained in child protection and migration procedures, contributing to the largest child-friendly-justice training initiative implemented in Poland to date.  Selected short courses were uploaded to the judges’ and prosecutors’ educational platform, and full training modules will be digitalized in 2026 to ensure long-term sustainability. Together with UNHCR and IOM, UNICEF supported capacity-building for approximately 20 judges involved in migration-detention cases, focusing on alternatives to detention and the protection of children on the move.
  
In cooperation with the Police Headquarters, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of 50 regional coordinators responsible for domestic-violence response and juvenile cases, improving skills in identifying and responding to child abuse, including among refugee and migrant children. In November 2025, UNICEF co-organized the national conference Access to Justice for Refugee and Migrant Children with the Ministry of Justice and the National School of Judiciary and Public Prosecution, bringing together over 150 participants from government institutions, civil society, and international organizations.
  
UNICEF supported the Institute of Forensic Research in developing new methodologies for interviewing children and guidelines for expert witnesses, which were distributed in 3,700 copies. A pilot child-friendly legal-aid training for 19 lawyers was conducted, accompanied by adaptation of the UNICEF ECARO training module to the Polish context and supported by both national bar associations.  UNICEF also engaged in advocacy to strengthen children’s access to legal aid.
  
In partnership with the Avalon Foundation, UNICEF organized sexual-education workshops for 282 evacuated children and adolescents from Ukrainian residential care facilities, particularly those with disabilities. Additional training sessions for 114 caregivers and staff and 116 social-welfare professionals enhanced their capacity to support children’s healthy psychosexual development.
  
Education
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened inclusive education systems in Poland by advancing evidence-based policy reforms and delivery capacity - training 56,376 teachers and caregivers across 1,502 schools, piloting school well-being and anti-bullying models reaching over 180,000 Ukrainian refugee children, and supporting municipalities and digital platforms to expand inclusive, psychosocial and language support at scale. In parallel, UNICEF advanced the institutionalization of inclusive early childhood education by strengthening national early childhood education and care policy frameworks, piloting inclusive service models and reinforcing municipal delivery systems - supporting 38 institutions, building educator and parent capacities, deploying intercultural support, and reaching over 15,000 refugee and host-community children. UNICEF also strengthened adolescent skills development and school-to-work transitions by embedding career guidance, skills pathways and youth engagement within national and municipal systems, reaching over 25,000 Ukrainian adolescents and positioning education, employability and youth participation as core pillars of inclusive recovery and human capital investment.

Inclusive education within national systems  
A cornerstone of UNICEF’s systems support was the Accessible School for All programme (a national initiative implemented with the Ministry of National Education and the Educational Research Institute) aimed at strengthening inclusive education and school well-being, including for refugee learners and children with diverse educational and psychosocial needs. In 2025, the programme  supported 2,346 teachers from 867 educational institutions to strengthen their ability to respond to academic, social, and emotional needs through evidence-based approaches. It also piloted the “I’m Well” programme in 52 primary schools, testing lesson scenarios with 1,360 children and adolescents, to strengthen peer relations, empathy and classroom inclusion. The programme also generated system-level resources, including a catalogue of educational and specialist practices and research on school well-being in diverse classrooms, and culminated in a national conference sharing lessons learned and policy recommendations.
  
UNICEF further supported the  piloting of the Anti-Bullying  in Schools programme (a  whole-school approach in partnership with the Ministry of Education and the  national Teacher Training Centre), which trained 20 national experts and supported implementation in 20 schools,  reaching 7,128 children (including 285 Ukrainian students)  and 733 teachers.  This helped embed practical anti-violence routines into daily school life and  strengthened school-level responses to peer violence.
  
Alongside national reforms,  municipalities delivered direct education services ensuring participation in  learning. Across major cities, nearly 11,000  children participated  in catch-up learning and language classes supporting curriculum alignment and  exam readiness. In Warsaw alone, 2,631  students joined  bilingual and intensive Polish language programmes, while the Warsaw Edu Hub  provided learning and supervision services for 6,486 children and youth.  Municipal initiatives supported specialized needs. In Gdynia, special  education assessments reached 498  children, while inclusive education policy development engaged local  stakeholders and will cover over 42,000  students once adopted.  Intercultural assistants supported integration and communication in schools,  including 450  adolescents in Wroclaw through catch-up  classes and Roma inclusion support in accommodation centres. These measures  ensured that refugee students participated within the public education system  rather than parallel structures, strengthening local institutional  preparedness and resilience.
  Early childhood education and care  
UNICEF advanced inclusive ECD  through policy engagement, municipal cooperation and capacity-building. By  supporting 38 early  childhood institutions, training 358  educators, engaging 329  parents, deploying 19  intercultural assistants to  support 149 children (including children with  disabilities), and distributing nearly 1,000  early childhood development kits benefiting over 15,000 children,  UNICEF strengthened both service quality and inclusion in early learning  environments. The Inclusive Early Childhood Education and Care project,  launched in July 2025 with the Comenius Foundation and the Ministry of  Family, Labour and Social Services, piloted a child development monitoring  tool in 14 institutions across four regions. Developed through evidence  review and expert consultations and refined using feedback from 154 surveys  and caregiver focus groups, the model is expected to improve access to early  support for young children and reinforce inclusive early childhood services  nationwide in the following year.

Digital learning and language acquisition  
Language acquisition remained central to education integration and learning outcomes. UNICEF expanded structured language learning support through the Akelius programme (a blended digital language-learning approach), training 632 teachers and educators across Poland. These educators reached 6,598 refugee students, supporting Polish language learning, essential for participation in education and social life.
  
Digital tools further strengthened learning continuity and teacher capacity. Through the Learning Passport platform (a digital learning and training platform), UNICEF supported 1,590 teachers using digital resources and reached 24,926 refugee children with mental health and psychosocial support content and cross-cultural communication support delivered through trained educators.  Complementing this, UNICEF expanded access to an AI-powered bilingual Dictionary of the Language of School Education, supporting Ukrainian children, caregivers and teachers to navigate specialised terminology used in Polish schools; the resource reached 3,700 unique users, strengthening classroom participation and parent–school communication.
  
To support learning continuity  and bridge curriculum gaps, UNICEF partnered with the Katalyst Education  Foundation to develop scalable digital learning solutions. Pi-Station Ukraine produced 300 free video lessons aligned with the Ukrainian national  curriculum and accessible in perpetuity. In 2025, these lessons supported 26,200 Ukrainian students in  Poland and also reached 14,014  teachers and 2,491 caregivers,  reinforcing structured learning support within households and schools.
  
To complement educational interventions with psychological support, the uSupport platform, provided accessible psychological assistance to adolescents navigating displacement-related stress and their local peers. Thirteen psychologists from Ukraine and Poland were trained to deliver online consultations in line with safeguarding standards, and the platform recorded 136,995 page views, with over 5,000 clicks on advertisements promoting free consultations.  Overall, in 2025, uSupport project team laid the groundwork for the next phase of implementation, which is scheduled to be finalized in October 2026.  As part of this phase, approx. 400 psychoeducational sessions will be delivered.

Adolescent pathways and skills development  
UNICEF addressed the heightened risk of adolescent disengagement from education by combining retention-focused initiatives with structured skills-building and pathways support. In partnership with the Ministry of National Education and sector partners, UNICEF implemented the Back to Learning campaign to reduce early dropout among Ukrainian adolescents. Co-designed by 16 Ukrainian adolescents with the University of Silesia, the campaign strengthened peer-led engagement in education and generated 52,000 online interactions among secondary-school students aged 15–18. UNICEF also supported evidence generation through a mixed-methods study on adolescents’ educational pathways, including participatory workshops across eight locations with over 300 adolescents participating.
  
In parallel, more than 25,000 children and adolescents benefited from skills-building activities. UNICEF implemented UPSHIFT (a youth innovation and life-skills  programme) in formal and non-formal education, with more than 1,200 young people directly benefiting from training and project-based learning. Through partnership with the Pro Futuro Foundation, 5,760 Ukrainian youth accessed non-formal education interventions, including offline and online activities supporting skills development and future orientation, including for out-of-school and at-risk youth.

Community engagement, accountability and social and  behavioural change  
As access to services increasingly depended on trust and understanding, UNICEF strengthened community engagement and behavioural approaches to improve service uptake among refugee families and host communities.
  
Cooperation with the Institute of Mother and Child Foundation strengthened preventive health engagement.  More than 500 psychologists and psychotherapists were trained on barriers to mental health service access and over 700 healthcare professionals on vaccination barriers, while outreach activities reached approximately 50,000 members of the Ukrainian community. A cross-sectoral workshop with 14 government representatives was conducted to better understand the need for coordination of mental health services in the country, and a memorandum of understanding with the National Health Fund advanced system collaboration, including training of trainers on violence against children for 18 healthcare professionals.
  
Another important result is the establishment of Poland's first behavioural team in public health (BOND), led by the Chief Sanitary Inspectorate. The overall goal of the Team is to integrate the science of human behaviour with the design of health policies, including prevention. The team was equipped with tools that help better understand people’s everyday choices and design policies that are more closely aligned with actual needs. The institutions comprising the team have signed a letter of intent for further multi-year collaboration. 
  
UNICEF reinforced trusted communication and participation. Spilno digital platforms reached about 400,000 users, generated 175,000 interactions, and attracted over 210,000 new website users, while social media communities grew to 43,000 followers, enabling continuous dialogue and feedback. A child-friendly feedback mechanism was co-designed with children and piloted, and more than 120 social workers were trained on safe outreach to adolescents.
  
Finally, communication, advocacy and operational stabilization underpinned the achievement and sustainability of programme results. Evidence-based communication and strategic media engagement strengthened public trust and informed national discussions on the rights and inclusion of refugee children, supporting policy uptake aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals on quality education, reduced inequalities and child protection. Partnerships with government, civil society and donors reinforced ownership of solutions and visibility of results, facilitating their integration into public systems. At the same time, following structural adjustments and a management transition, the office stabilized operations and strengthened its human resources framework to ensure continuity of programmes and prepare a responsible transition toward nationally sustained services.
  
Conclusion  
UNICEF’s 2025  initiatives in Poland demonstrated the impact of working at the humanitarian-development nexus to address complex and persistent humanitarian challenges while strengthening capacity  and systems’ resilience. By integrating refugee needs into national systems –  from health care and education to child protection – UNICEF ensured that over 200,000 Ukrainian children and adults accessed vital services and benefitted from improved  national and local capacity. Partnerships with government bodies,  NGOs, and international agencies laid the groundwork for sustainable  progress, aligning with Poland’s commitment to the SDGs.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
