Operating under uncertainty and funding constraints  
In March 2025, global stop-work order required immediate reprioritization of activities across the refugee response interventions in Poland. Planned interventions had to be paused,  reprogrammed, or redesigned within a short timeframe, causing implementation  delays and requiring renegotiation with partners and service providers. This transition required rapid adaptation of implementation modalities, revision of partnership arrangements and strengthened coordination with central  ministries.
  
While disruptive, this moment accelerated a strategic shift already underway — moving from humanitarian service delivery toward strengthening systems resilience and developing nationally owned solutions. Municipal partners increasingly assumed operational responsibility for services previously supported through humanitarian funding, particularly in education, child protection and psychosocial support. 
  
The experience demonstrated the importance of flexible programme design and diversified implementation partnerships. Programmes embedded within public systems proved more resilient to funding fluctuations than stand-alone humanitarian structures. As a result, UNICEF further prioritized integration into national and local service delivery frameworks as a risk-mitigation strategy as well as a sustainability approach.

Evidence and innovation for sustainability  
In April 2025, UNICEF convened over 50 representatives from relevant ministries, municipalities and national institutions to review joint achievements in support of refugee children and adolescents and identify priorities for longer-term collaboration on refugee integration and social inclusion. The consultations also helped identify opportunities for strengthening sustainable service delivery models within national and local systems.
  
Building on these discussions, UNICEF initiated a collaboration with PwC Polska to analyse  seven service models and programmes developed with municipalities and national partners since 2022 and transform them in generic service and business models. Those are: Accessible for School, Growing Up Together, Blue Sneakers Initative, Lighthouse centre, Spilno centers, Education and Rehabilitation Centre for Children with Disabilities and Sun Centers. The study examines operational design, cost structures, scalability and integration pathways into national and local systems. The objective is to enhance sustainability of service models and programmes developed with UNICEF support and ensure their long-term integration in national and local systems Technical consultations convened national ministries, municipalities and partners to identify integration pathways and define roadmaps for long-term sustainability.
  
Future Outlook
2026 will be final year of UNICEF’s refugee response in Poland. The priority will be to ensure a responsible and orderly closure by completing partnerships, transferring key services to local and national stakeholders, and supporting long-term sustainability and system resilience.
  
UNICEF will continue to strengthen the capacities of public authorities and civil society organizations to institutionalize the most effective service models developed during the response, ensuring their integration into national and municipal systems. The focus will shift from direct service delivery to stewardship—supporting Poland in maintaining innovations, enhancing preparedness for future crises, and preserving the capacities built across sectors to protect and include vulnerable children beyond the humanitarian phase.

In 2025, Uzbekistan consolidated strong socio-economic progress, delivering measurable gains for children and families while advancing systemic reforms aligned with child rights and the Sustainable Development Goals. 


Poverty reduction accelerated significantly. At the beginning of 2025, the national poverty rate declined to 8.9 per cent, down from 11 per cent in 2023 and 17 per cent in 2022, with projections indicating a further decrease to around 6 per cent by year’s end. The Government reaffirmed its ambition to reduce poverty to 4.5 per cent by 2026. Sustained economic growth (approximately 6 per cent GDP growth) and rising disposable incomes were the main drivers, complemented by targeted social protection interventions. 


The “Kambag¿allikdan farovonlik sari” (“From Poverty to Prosperity”) programme continued to expand, prioritizing access for low-income households to integrated social services and limited cash support. Its budget is expected to increase from UZS 16.0 trillion to 17.3 trillion. At the same time, fiscal space for child-specific cash benefits contracted, with planned allocations declining to UZS 7.4 trillion, compared to UZS 10.33 trillion in 2024, reflecting tighter targeting within a constrained fiscal framework. 


Despite these pressures, Uzbekistan sustained strong public investment in child-sensitive social sectors. Approximately half of total public expenditure in 2025 was directed to education, health, and social protection. Education spending rose to UZS 84.3 trillion, up from UZS 70.1 trillion in 2023, while health spending increased to UZS 41.3 trillion, compared to UZS 34.4 trillion previously. Social protection spending reached UZS 92.2 trillion, driven mainly by pensions. These allocations underscore continued prioritization of human capital development, even as child-related transfers were more tightly targeted. In 2025, the Government adopted a resolution to conduct a national census, strengthening the evidence base for equitable social policy and child-focused planning. 


Gender equality and women’s participation in public life continued to advance. Uzbekistan improved its standing in the Global Gender Gap Report 2025, ranking 110th of 148 countries with an overall score of 0.678, reflecting near parity in education and health and sustained gains in political empowerment. The 40 per cent gender quota introduced in the 2024 elections resulted in continued high representation of women in legislative and executive bodies in 2025, strengthening women’s influence on policies and budgets affecting children and families. 


High-level international engagement reinforced national commitment to child-focused reforms and human centered inclusive development. At the World Social Summit in Doha, Uzbekistan was commended for its significant poverty reduction and for advocating for the establishment of the Global Social Justice Fund and the Global Initiative for Social Responsibility. Uzbekistan’s continued progress toward WTO accession reflects structural economic reforms with potential to promote inclusive growth, fiscal sustainability, and improved outcomes for children and vulnerable families. The first visit of the UNICEF Executive Director to Uzbekistan provided a strategic platform for policy dialogue and reaffirmed government ownership of key reforms in child protection, health, education and social protection at the highest level.  


In 2025, Uzbekistan confirmed its commitment to ending violence against children through the enactment of the Law on the Protection of Children from All Forms of Violence, approval of inter-sectoral procedures to strengthen identification, referral and response, and adoption of a multi-sectoral strategy and action plan (2025–2030). Uzbekistan further reinforced its leadership by joining the Pathfinding Global Alliance on Ending Violence Against Children and announcing a national pledge under the Bogotá Call to Action.  


Climate action emerged as a defining area of progress. Uzbekistan adopted Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 (2025–2035), formally integrating children and youth priorities into national climate commitments for the first time. The framework includes costed measures across education, WASH, health and disaster risk reduction, positioning Uzbekistan as a regional leader in child-centred climate policy.  


Health outcomes for children continued to improve, though preventable risks persist. The under-five mortality rate declined to 13.3 deaths per 1,000 live births, while neonatal mortality fell to 7.6 deaths per 1,000 live births, with neonatal deaths accounting for approximately 57 per cent of under-five mortality. By 2025, all 231 perinatal centres nationwide were equipped with essential newborn care devices, strengthening readiness to manage prematurity, infections and birth asphyxia. Standardized clinical practices and trained personnel increased the likelihood of timely, life-saving care, particularly in high-risk referral facilities. 


Preventive and early childhood services expanded through the institutionalization of the Universal Progressive Home Visiting model, enabling standardized home visits, risk screening and referrals for pregnant women and children aged 0–5. The National Programme to Support Breastfeeding established national targets, reinforced the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative and aligned legislation with international standards, creating conditions to increase exclusive breastfeeding from the current level of 25 per cent. 


In the WASH sector, implementation of the Clean Hands State Programme improved health and learning environments. Investments in school water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure benefited more than 70,000 children in 131 schools, reducing exposure to infectious diseases and supporting school attendance, particularly for girls. 


Education reforms delivered system-wide results. UNICEF supported curriculum and assessment reforms benefiting 6.5 million students, integrating competency-based learning, climate education, social and emotional learning and digital skills. In early childhood education, revision of the Ilk Qadam curriculum introduced a child-centred approach for 2.4 million children. Teacher professional development reforms updated standards, and the establishment of 11 Regional Training Centres laid the foundation for in-service training of 170,000 educators over five years. Inclusive education was strengthened through a new national strategy and pilot models in 50 schools, enabling improved access for 3,483 children with disabilities. Beyond formal schooling, 12,500 adolescents and youth were empowered through non-formal education initiatives focused on climate action, green skills, and STEM. 


Finally, 2025 marked a strategic transition with the adoption of the UNICEF Country Programme for 2026–2030, providing a strong foundation to sustain and deepen progress for children. Together, these outcomes demonstrate Uzbekistan’s continued commitment to child rights and UNICEF’s catalytic role in supporting inclusive, resilient and sustainable development for every child.

Goal area 1. Every Child Survives and Thrives 


In 2025, UNICEF supported system-wide health reforms that delivered measurable improvements in coverage, quality and equity for children and adolescents. Under the Vision 2030 Programme, UNICEF enabled 100 per cent coverage of essential newborn care equipment across all 231 perinatal centres, up from 50 per cent, significantly strengthening national readiness to manage complications during childbirth and the neonatal period. These improvements benefit all newborns delivered in public facilities nationwide. 


UNICEF institutionalized Perinatal Death Audits in 100 per cent of perinatal centres, strengthening accountability for quality of care and enabling routine identification of avoidable factors contributing to maternal and newborn deaths. UNICEF further strengthened decision-making by supporting national electronic perinatal reporting systems and digital health integration, improving availability of real-time data on newborn outcomes. 




Preventive services expanded through UNICEF’s support to institutionalise the Universal Progressive Home Visiting model. Standardized home visits and risk screening enabled earlier identification of developmental risks, resulting in 11 per cent of children aged 0–5 with identified developmental delays accessing early intervention services. 


In nutrition, UNICEF’s technical leadership contributed to the Cabinet’s endorsement of the National Programme to Support Breastfeeding, establishing the policy and service delivery conditions needed to increase exclusive breastfeeding rates from the current 25 per cent. UNICEF also supported service delivery improvements that reached 926,422 newborns with breastfeeding counselling through routine neonatal care and ensured 489,865 children received vitamin A supplementation in the most at-risk regions. 


In immunisation, UNICEF-supported systems and supply-chain strengthening contributed to reaching 3.5 million children through the National Immunisation Programme and sustaining 96 per cent coverage for two doses of measles, mumps and rubella, protecting approximately 2 million children from outbreaks. 




Goal area 2. Every Child Learns 


In 2025, with UNICEF support, significant results were achieved across system strengthening, digital transformation, quality and inclusive education, early childhood education, and youth skills development, contributing to long-term education sector reform. Interventions impacted all students including expanded quality preschool for 2.4 million children and strengthened inclusive education for 3,483 children with disabilities. 


As coordinating agency of the education sector, UNICEF enhanced coordination and participation in the Local Education Group, including private sector actors and organizations of young people with disabilities. Reviews of development partners’ workplans against the Partnership Compact for Education Reform 2023–2026 improved alignment with national priorities and reinforced government leadership. In 2025, this resulted in the signing of the first Smart Education agreement (USD 220 million), the largest education investment in the country, between the Islamic Development Bank, the Islamic Solidarity Fund for Development, the Global Partnership for Education, and the Government of Uzbekistan. Within this framework, UNICEF launched its technical assistance with two agreements totaling USD 19.2 million to support quality and inclusive education reforms. 


Digital transformation was supported through implementation of the Vision 2030 Project (USD 16.2 million). UNICEF co-developed the Education Technology Integration Framework with the Ministry of Pre-school and School Education, supported nationwide digital readiness assessments, and facilitated the endorsement of standards for assistive technology and digital solutions. These efforts laid the foundation for Uzbekistan’s first National Artificial Intelligence Framework in Education being currently developed jointly with the World Bank.  


UNICEF facilitated Microsoft Shape the Future agreement securing Windows 11 Education at reduced costs, generating savings of USD 115 per device, with a perpetual license covering all education procured devices until 2027. Connectivity partnerships were further strengthened through Giga, including the launch of a tripartite agreement to develop public digital goods assessing real-time AI readiness of schools.  


Quality education improved through curriculum and assessment reforms, expected to benefit all 6.5 million students. In 2025, UNICEF supported the establishment of a legal framework clarifying curriculum development roles and quality assurance and strengthened national capacity through training of 121 curriculum authors. With FCDO support, a comprehensive review of the national learning assessment system informed the drafting of a Learning Assessment Framework and roadmap. Partnerships with Cambridge Assessment and Press supported the transition toward competency-based education aligned with international standards. 


AI enabled digital learning solutions reached over 9,300 students through Eduten, an AI-powered mathematics platform aligned with the national curriculum and available in Uzbek, Russian, and Karakalpak. 


Inclusive education advanced through policy, infrastructure, and practice reforms. UNICEF co-developed the National Inclusive School Framework in 2025. Inclusive infrastructure standards were applied in 160 schools, including 50 UNICEF-supported model schools with inclusive School Improvement Plans. Overall, 51,641 students, including 517 children with disabilities, benefited from improved learning environments. 


In early childhood education, UNICEF supported revision of the Ilk Qadam curriculum, benefiting all 2.4 million preschool children. Ten regional training centres were established, supported by a certified network of 26 trainers, improving professional development for 5,497 preschool teachers. A landmark partnership with the Ministry of Pre-school and School Education and Fondazione Reggio Children initiated the establishment of Central Asia’s first Research and Innovation Center in Early Learning. 


Youth skills and participation initiatives reached 12,500 adolescents and youth (6,438 girls and 6,057 boys) through climate action, inclusion, and STEM programmes, strengthening pathways to further learning and employment. 




Goal area 3. Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation 


2025, with UNICEF support, Uzbekistan accelerated comprehensive child protection reforms, strengthening prevention, response, and care systems across social services and justice sectors. Progress was driven by landmark legal, policy, and institutional changes, combined with large-scale capacity building, contributing to improved protection of children from violence, reduced reliance on institutional care, and more child-friendly justice responses. 


A major milestone was the enactment of the Law on the Protection of Children from All Forms of Violence, establishing a unified legal and institutional framework for coordinated prevention and response across social protection, justice, education, and health sectors. Implementation was reinforced through approval of inter-agency standard operating procedures for the identification, assessment, referral, and reporting of violence against children, strengthening consistency of frontline practice. To accelerate operationalization, the National Agency for Social Protection recruited an additional 160 child protection professionals at regional and district levels. Political commitment was further reinforced through Uzbekistan’s accession to the Pathfinding Global Alliance on Ending Violence Against Children and a national pledge under the Bogotá Call to Action, alongside adoption of a multi-sectoral strategy and action plan to end violence against children (2025–2030). 


In parallel, UNICEF supported the Government to advance deinstitutionalization and family-based care. Implementation of reforms informed by the De-institutionalization Strategy developed with UNICEF support in 2022 led to a decline in the rate of children in institutions from 255 per 100,000 children in 2021 to 172 in 2024, with an approximate 5,000 children from specialized boarding schools for children with disabilities reintegrated into their families and community-based care in 2024 and 2025. Reforms strengthened prevention and gatekeeping, expanded family- and community-based care options, improved foster care readiness, and supported reintegration planning for adolescents transitioning out of residential care. 


UNICEF also strengthened the social service workforce to deliver integrated, trauma-informed, and gender-sensitive services. Through blended learning, supervision, and practice tools, 9,551 social service professionals enhanced capacities in integrated case management, early risk identification, prevention of unnecessary separation, and response to violence, abuse, neglect, and exploitation. 


In the justice sector, major legislative amendments further strengthened safeguards, including expungement of criminal records for offences committed under age 18 (with limited exceptions) and a reduction of the minimum term of deprivation or restriction of liberty from six months to one month – reinforcing proportionality, rehabilitation, and the best interests of the child. UNICEF undertook sustained, high-level advocacy to promote diversion and alternatives to deprivation of liberty for children in conflict with the law. These efforts generated commitment at the highest level, including a presidential mandate to review legislation, and led to the establishment by the Senate of the Oliy Majlis of an Inter-Agency Working Group to align national legislation with international child justice standards. In parallel, over 14,700 justice and allied professionals strengthened competencies across legal aid, law enforcement, prosecution, adjudication, social protection, and education.  




Goal area 4. Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment 


In 2025, UNICEF Uzbekistan contributed to improved environmental safety and resilience for children by strengthening national policy frameworks, generating large-scale risk evidence, reinforcing preparedness institutions, and building capacities that support longer-term climate and disaster risk reduction outcomes. The emphasis was on enabling Government systems to identify, prioritise, and address environmental and climate risks affecting children. 


At policy level, UNICEF provided technical support to the Government in the development and national adoption of Uzbekistan’s NDC 3.0 (2025–2035), ensuring the formal integration of children and youth priorities within the country’s climate commitments. A dedicated Children and Youth chapter was embedded in the NDC, supported by costed mitigation and adaptation investment areas relevant to education, WASH, health, and disaster risk reduction. This result institutionalised child-centred climate considerations within a nationally owned framework and strengthened alignment between environmental protection objectives, sectoral planning, and climate-finance readiness. 


To support evidence-based decision-making, UNICEF led the implementation of a Comprehensive School Safety Assessment (CSSA) covering more than 1,100 schools, representing approximately 10 per cent of the national school stock. The assessment generated standardized data on structural and non-structural safety, environmental hazards, and preparedness capacities at school level. The scale and methodology of the CSSA enabled aggregation and analysis across administrative levels, providing Government counterparts with a usable evidence base to inform prioritisation of safer school infrastructure, preparedness measures, and climate-resilient education investments. This output addressed a critical gap in nationally comparable data on risks affecting children in learning environments. 


Preparedness and response capacities were further strengthened through UNICEF’s support to the establishment of sub-national Public Health Emergency Operations Centres (PHEOCs) in Termez and Nukus. UNICEF’s contribution focused on institutional set-up, alignment with the Incident Management System, development of standard operating procedures, and capacity building of designated staff. These PHEOCs enhance coordination and information management for public health emergencies and climate-related shocks in high-risk regions, contributing to reduced response time and more coherent decision-making during crises that pose environmental and health risks to children. 


Complementing system and infrastructure strengthening, UNICEF delivered COP-focused climate capacity building for youth and eco-volunteers, benefiting an estimated 1,000  young people through peer-to-peer outreach, community activities, and advocacy initiatives. This initiative aimed to strengthen climate literacy, understanding of international climate processes, and linkages between global climate commitments and national policy priorities, including NDC implementation. The result contributed to the development of informed youth constituencies capable of engaging in climate dialogue, advocacy, and accountability related to environmental protection and resilience. 


In 2025, UNICEF contributed to measurable improvements in children’s access to safe, functional WASH services by supporting policy reform, domestic financing, and system strengthening. UNICEF’s technical assistance enabled Government adoption of the Clean Hands State Programme, which mobilised 780 billion UZS (approximately USD 60–85 million) in public funding to improve WASH infrastructure and services for 70,194 children in 131 schools. These investments directly address gaps in basic water and hygiene services that increase children’s exposure to infectious diseases and contribute to absenteeism, particularly among girls. 


UNICEF’s upstream support helped translate policy commitments into results at a scale. By advising on standards, costing and implementation models, UNICEF supported a shift towards nationally led, climate-resilient WASH service delivery aligned with SDG 6 and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. At community level, UNICEF-supported water supply improvements enabled 200,000 people, including 5,000 children, to gain access to safe drinking water in Karakalpakstan, reducing reliance on unsafe sources. 


UNICEF also strengthened WASH systems in health care facilities, improving services for 249,700 people across 35 facilities in four districts. Training of 300 health workers on WASH and infection prevention improved compliance with hygiene standards and reduced health-care-associated infection risks. Introduction of WASH Facility Improvement Tool assessments at national level established the foundation for routine monitoring and quality improvement, positioning the Government to track progress against WASH service indicators over time. 


Overall, UNICEF’s 2025 contribution focused on enabling conditions for improved environmental safety for children: national policies that explicitly recognize children, evidence that identifies and prioritises risks, institutions that can manage emergencies, and capacities that support sustained engagement on climate and environmental issues. While many outcomes will materialise over subsequent cycles, these results establish the foundations for more effective, child-centred environmental and climate action. 




Goal area 5. Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life 


UNICEF’s support delivered strategically significant results that strengthened accountability systems and advanced national and regional priorities. The first International Forum of Central Asian Commissioners for Children’s Rights resulted in a Declaration and sustainable platform aligned with global networks, reinforcing prevention of violence, online safety, and access to justice. Capacity development for law enforcement, judiciary, and social sectors—through a CRC-based online course—embedded child rights standards into national systems, supporting durable institutional change. Parliamentary engagement and civil society capacity building enhanced monitoring of Treaty Bodies’ recommendations, legislative oversight, and child-sensitive budgeting, directly strengthening accountability to international commitments.  


UNICEF supported the National Agency for Social Protection in improving its strategic and operational efficiency, increasing internal transparency and accountability through establishing institutional capacity to implement results-based management and programme-based budgeting. Strengthening institutional capacity to provide social support services has been enhanced not only at the central levels, but also at sub-national levels, too. In 2025, UNICEF sustained strategic partnership with the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, enabling continued financing of the UNICEF-led joint programme with UNDP that advanced inclusive youth participation and child-friendly local governance systems in Uzbekistan. UNICEF strengthened institutional capacity of 120 officials in 12 pilot districts, enabling improved use of local data, advancement of child-rights budgeting, and stronger coordination to deliver more responsive and inclusive local support services for children and young people.  


The actuarial study on the maternity benefits reform options, which was prepared by UNICEF, played important role in finalizing the national Law on the State Social Insurance, which was adopted in October 2025, and launching the national maternity benefits within the national social insurance system from 1 January 2026.     


UNICEF conducted a joint study with the Centre of Economic Research and Reforms in examining child poverty in Uzbekistan. Monetary and multidimensional child poverty levels for 2024 were estimated as 11.4% and 21.4%, respectively. Social protection programmes were found to play an important role in containing the child poverty. Estimates indicate that in the absence of the social protection programmes, child poverty in Uzbekistan would be as high as 18.8%, instead of actual 11.4%.   




Gender Equality and Social Inclusion 


In 2025, Uzbekistan consolidated reforms advancing gender equality and non-discrimination, building on the 2023 Constitution and the National Strategy on Achieving Gender Equality to 2030. Legislative and policy frameworks increasingly reflected gender-responsive and child-sensitive approaches, strengthening protections and expanding opportunities for women and girls across sectors. 


Following adoption of the Law on the Protection of Children from All Forms of Violence, efforts in 2025 focused on strengthening implementation and coordination across social services, education, health and justice systems, enabling more integrated prevention and response to intersecting risks of violence against women and children. 


Gender parity in education was sustained, with women representing 52 per cent of bachelor’s and 62 per cent of master’s enrolments. UNICEF prioritized girls’ retention, skills development and transition to decent work, including in STEM and green pathways, while expanding adolescent girls’ leadership and participation through youth, civic and climate platforms, with targeted support for girls with disabilities and from low-income households. 


UNICEF advanced gender equality by removing structural barriers to adolescent girls’ and young women’s access to health, HIV, mental health, SRHR and WASH services. Gender-responsive reforms strengthened integrated, confidential care and multisectoral referrals, building the capacity of 2,000 primary health care workers. Adolescent-friendly digital and peer-led models expanded girls’ agency, with eight Adolescent Health Clubs where 160 peer educators reached 1,005 girls. 


In WASH, UNICEF supported gender-responsive WASH in Schools standards embedding menstrual health into policy and practice. Improved, safe and accessible WASH services reached 70,194 children in 131 schools, enabling adolescent girls to manage menstruation with dignity, reduce absenteeism and participate fully in education, demonstrating an integrated, systems-focused approach across health and WASH. 


In 2025, UNICEF strengthened disability inclusion across social protection, education and skills development by translating evidence into scalable, system-level solutions that advance equity for children and young people with disabilities. 


Under the UN Joint Programme on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, UNICEF finalized a national study on the goods and services required for the inclusion of children with disabilities. The study provided a robust evidence base to inform disability-inclusive social protection, shifting policy dialogue from fragmented assistance towards standardized, rights-based support. Building on this evidence, UNICEF advanced the development of optimized Social Support Packages designed to improve adequacy, efficiency and sustainability of public financing while reducing regional disparities. 


Institutional capacity was strengthened through targeted technical assistance. Government officials and national experts enhanced their capacity to design and cost Social Support Packages, strengthening readiness for policy uptake and scale-up. Participatory consultations with 52 parents of children with disabilities in Tashkent and Navoi ensured that proposed packages reflect lived experience and prioritize essential goods and services. 


In education and skills development, UNICEF strengthened inclusive learning and pathways to independence. 147 teachers from inclusive Zamin schools across five regions enhanced their capacity to create accessible and supportive learning environments. In partnership with Quyoshli Olam, UNICEF delivered hands-on vocational masterclasses in ceramics, soap-making and handicrafts, reaching over 200 students from specialized schools. In addition, 22 adolescents and youth with intellectual disabilities completed structured skills training through Tabassum workshops, strengthening functional skills, confidence, and social participation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges 




In 2025, UNICEF-supported programmes demonstrated that sustained policy reform, domestic financing, and systems strengthening can deliver results at scale. At the same time, persistent and measurable challenges continue to constrain equitable progress for the most marginalized children, particularly those living in rural, climate-stressed and high-density areas. 


Despite continued reductions in child mortality, preventable risks remain concentrated in the neonatal period. Neonatal deaths account for 57 per cent of under-five mortality, with neonatal and under-five mortality rates at 7.6 and 13.3 deaths per 1,000 live births, respectively. Annual birth volumes exceeding 1 million births continue to strain service delivery across the health system. While investments have improved facility readiness, quality gaps at primary and referral levels limit early detection, prevention and continuity of care. Nutrition outcomes remain fragile, with exclusive breastfeeding at 25 per cent, reflecting persistent gaps in counselling, social norms, workplace protections and enabling environments for mothers. 


In WASH, national averages mask deep inequalities. As of 2023, 70 per cent of schoolchildren had access to basic drinking water, 80 per cent to basic sanitation and 90 per cent to basic handwashing facilities. However, 15 per cent—approximately 1.4 million children—attend schools with no water and no toilets. Rural–urban disparities are pronounced: basic drinking water coverage stands at 50 per cent in rural schools, compared to 80 per cent in urban schools, while basic sanitation coverage is 62 per cent versus 86 per cent, respectively. In climate-vulnerable regions ageing infrastructure, intermittent supply and high groundwater salinity further undermine reliability and health outcomes. 


Education remains central to Uzbekistan’s human capital agenda. While near-universal access to basic education has been achieved, quality and inclusiveness continue to present challenges across all levels. Early childhood education has expanded rapidly, with preschool enrolment rising from under 30 per cent in 2017 to approximately 78 per cent in 2025, reaching more than 2.4 million children aged 3–6. Remaining gaps include strengthening teacher qualifications and reaching the last quarter of children, particularly those in remote, low-income and marginalized communities. 


In primary and secondary education, demographic growth has intensified pressure on infrastructure and staffing. Government investments have expanded capacity, creating approximately 800,000 new student places through school construction. However, ensuring that new and existing schools are inclusive, digitally enabled and equipped with climate-resilient WASH facilities remains uneven. In social protection, reforms remain predominantly focused on poverty reduction. This narrows the preventive and transformative potential of the sector, constrains integration between benefits and services, and limits responses to psychosocial support, mental health needs and disability inclusion. As a result, multidimensional vulnerabilities affecting children risk remaining insufficiently addressed within mainstream reforms. 


Climate governance presents additional systemic challenges. Climate change is still widely perceived as the responsibility of specialized environmental institutions, limiting whole-of-government coordination. This has constrained development of integrated response mechanisms, including shock-responsive social protection, which remains underdeveloped despite increasing climate-related risks to children and families. 




Lessons Learned 


Education reforms highlight key lessons for large-scale system change. Rapid expansion of early childhood education confirmed that access, quality and professional development must advance in parallel. Strong coordination and systems strengthening are essential to prevent fragmentation and ensure efficient use of resources, including through structured private sector engagement. Capacity gaps at school level underscored the importance of investing in leadership and quality assurance, while contextualizing international expertise within national institutions. Digital transformation and inclusive education require phased, evidence-based approaches that account for uneven readiness, connectivity and teacher support. Results were strongest where schools and communities co-designed solutions, translating national policy and global best practices into classroom-level change. 

In 2025, UNICEF completed evaluation of child protection programme, and systematically applied the lessons learned to strengthen the design, prioritization, and results framework of the 2026–2030 Country Programme Document.  

The work of UNICEF in Uzbekistan, a lower-middle-income country, demonstrates how a predictable and modest investment of regular resources (USD 2.18 million) mobilized more than USD 24.9 million in additional resources for UNICEF’s country programme in 2025 and leveraged USD 4.78 million nationwide for child-rights programmes.  


Looking ahead, lessons point to the need for sustained systems strengthening. UNICEF will prioritize four areas: strengthening health and WASH systems through policy and financing support; reinforcing a primary health care approach to advance universal health coverage; expanding schools as platforms for integrated health, nutrition and WASH interventions; and strengthening community systems to reduce stigma, harmful norms and delays in health-seeking behaviour. 




Future Outlook 


In 2025, UNICEF-supported child protection reforms demonstrated that sustained advocacy, strategic timing and strong institutional leadership can accelerate change at scale. High-level engagement, including the visits of the UNICEF Executive Director and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, helped galvanize multi-sectoral commitment. The National Agency for Social Protection emerged as a key institutional champion, strengthening coordination across social protection, justice, education and health sectors. The principal challenge now is implementation quality. Results will depend on strengthening frontline capacity and supervision in the police and social service workforce, ensuring consistent child-sensitive responses, and scaling prevention through family support and schools, with a focus on equitable subnational service delivery for the most marginalized children. 


UNICEF’s next phase will focus on scaling quality and inclusive education reforms so innovations reach every classroom, while positioning Uzbekistan as a contributor to education innovation. Digital transformation will advance through partnerships, including Giga, and collaboration with international financial institutions and the private sector. In early childhood education, the Research and Innovation Center established with Fondazione Reggio Children will support pedagogical innovation and South–South cooperation in Central Asia. 


In addressing behavioural challenges, UNICEF will shift from introducing Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) approaches to embedding them systematically within national frameworks, enabling evidence-based integration that strengthens community engagement, drives sustained behaviour change, and supports long-term development outcomes. 


In 2026, UNICEF will strengthen strategic engagement with the emerging private sector to mobilize innovation, financing, responsible business practices and family friendly policies that advance child rights and contribute to sustainable, inclusive outcomes for children.

In 2025, Kyrgyzstan experienced strong economic performance alongside major administrative-territorial reforms, adjustments in the political calendar and the continued implementation of national development policies, developments that together shaped the environment for further advancing children’s rights. 
Economic growth remained robust throughout the year, with gross domestic product expanding by around 10 per cent during the first nine months of 2025, driven primarily by industry, construction and trade. This momentum created increased fiscal space and supported public investment, including in social sectors. At the same time, the structure of the economy continues to expose households to external shocks, including fluctuations in global markets and reliance on remittances. Inflationary pressures remained a concern for low-income families, with implications for child poverty, nutrition and access to essential services. While macroeconomic conditions were favourable compared to some earlier years, translating growth into equitable and durable improvements in children’s lives remains a central policy challenge.
A notable development in 2025 was the improvement in regional stability. In March, the Presidents of the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan signed a historic agreement on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border, reopening border crossings and restoring transport links that had been closed following years of tension. Also, Kyrgyzstan joined Tajikistan and Uzbekistan in signing an agreement defining the tripoint junction of the three countries’ borders, accompanied by a declaration of friendship. These steps marked a significant reduction in geopolitical risk in the Fergana Valley and contributed to a more stable environment for border communities, where children had previously been disproportionately affected by insecurity, disrupted services and displacement.
At the national level, the Government continued implementing its administrative and territorial reform, consolidating local government units to improve efficiency, service delivery and budget planning. By 2025, the number of aiyl aimaks (rural local government units) had been reduced from 452 to 235, accompanied by cost savings and expanded responsibilities at local level. While still in transition, the reform has the potential to improve access to health, education and social services for children if accompanied by adequate financing, capacity building and accountability mechanisms at subnational level.
The political landscape also evolved during the year. In September 2025, the Jogorku Kenesh (Parliament) voted to dissolve itself, leading to early parliamentary elections held on 30 November. 
The broader civic space context continued to change. Legislative developments adopted in 2024 and 2025 introduced new requirements for civil society organizations receiving foreign funding and for media outlets, including mandatory registration provisions. The authorities introduced these measures with the stated objective of enhancing transparency and regulation; however, they raised concerns among national and international stakeholders regarding the operating environment for civil society and independent media.
UNICEF adapted its partnerships accordingly, strengthening due diligence, risk management and safeguarding while maintaining principled engagement with Government and non-state partners in line with its mandate and the UN system’s commitments.
In 2025, the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) Action Plan, developed by the Child Rights Commissioner with participation from all relevant ministries and organizations, was approved by the Cabinet of Ministers, positioning child rights as a national priority.  The new National Development Programme 2030, informed by UNICEF’s 2024 spending analysis requested by the President’s Administration, was also approved and it includes key priorities on reducing child poverty, violence against children and women, promoting family-based care, and ensuring better access to education and health for the most vulnerable. 
Climate action gained renewed prominence in 2025 with the submission of Kyrgyzstan’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, aligned with the National Development Programme 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals, and recognizing children and young people as central to the country’s climate future. This policy context created a strategic window for UNICEF supported regional climate initiatives, to strengthen the availability of child-sensitive evidence and to support investment planning and implementation readiness across sectors. The updated climate framework emphasizes adaptation, resilience and inclusive development, reflecting high exposure to climate related risks such as water scarcity, glacial melt and increasingly frequent extreme weather events. 
Progress in child outcomes continued but remained uneven. Under-five mortality has declined steadily, reaching 16.5 deaths per 1,000 live births according to the latest Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 2023), and skilled birth attendance is nearly universal. However, neonatal mortality continues to account for 67% of infant deaths, pointing to ongoing gaps in quality of care during pregnancy, birth and the early postnatal period. 
Recurrent measles outbreaks since 2023 further continue to highlighted systemic weaknesses in immunization coverage and the critical role of trust and demand for services.
In 2025, Kyrgyzstan advanced major education reforms under the Altyn Kazyk transformation, including the nationwide introduction of the 12-year schooling system and the launch of updated State Education Standards, creating significant momentum for systemic change. Progress also continued in expanding early childhood education, strengthening STEM opportunities for girls, and promoting inclusive learning pathways for all children—efforts supported by UNICEF in close partnership with the government and national stakeholders. Despite these gains, learning outcomes remain below desired levels, particularly for children from rural areas, low-income households, and those with disabilities.
The National Gender Equality Strategy until 2030 is under implementation to safeguard the rights of women and girls and improve access to essential services. However, persistent social norms continue to limit women’s participation in public, political and economic life. Conservative religious and traditional expectations often discourage women from pursuing leadership roles, reinforcing domestic responsibilities. As a result, women face structural economic exclusion despite legal protections. Occupational segregation concentrates women in lower-paid sectors, contributing to a gender pay gap of approximately 25 per cent in men’s favour. Unpaid care responsibilities, limited access to affordable childcare services and unpaid paternity leave further constrain women’s employment, particularly among those aged 25–34, while high rates of informal employment and gender-based violence continue to undermine women’s economic security, safety and access to services.
Throughout 2025, these contextual factors shaped UNICEF’s strategic focus on strengthening systems, supporting equity-oriented reforms and working through national and local institutions to deliver results at scale for all children.

In 2025, Kyrgyzstan advanced a reform agenda that put systems, standards and evidence at the centre of change for children.  UNICEF’s contribution focused on translating policy ambition into practical improvements that families could see and feel—in health clinics,classrooms,  social service offices and climate policy dialogues—so that progress would be equitable, durable and nationally owned. The 2025 results illustrate how sustained partnerships with Government and stakeholders can deliver scale, even in a context of rapid institutional change and pressure on household incomes.  
Following  sustained UNICEF advocacy and technical support, child poverty reduction was  firmly embedded as a national priority in 2025.  The newly adopted National Development Programme 2030 (NDP) now includes  measurable targets to reduce child poverty from 33.1 to 25 per cent and to  expand coverage of benefits for children from poor families to 30 per cent,  expanded early childhood education, and strengthening primary health care.  Building on this policy shift, the Government announced plans to introduce a  new child benefit for children aged 0–3 starting in 2026, marking a  major breakthrough in strengthening social protection coverage for children  during the most critical period of their development. The initiative was  highlighted by the Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers of the Kyrgyz  Republic during national consultations on 25 November 2025, following the  Doha Forum at the Second World Summit for Social Development. This milestone  represents a flagship result of UNICEF’s long-term efforts to support evidence-based  policymaking, reduce child poverty and advance equitable investments in young  children and families.
  
Every  child survives and thrives
  
Immunization  efforts supported by UNICEF delivered significant results in 2025, helping to  curb one of the largest measles outbreaks in recent years. While the outbreak persisted into early 2025, with 1,961 cases  reported in January, sustained outbreak response initiated in 2024 and the  nationwide Big Catch-up Campaign led to a dramatic decline,  reducing cases to just one by December. In 2025 alone, the campaign  reached 564,562 children, identifying and vaccinating zero dose and under  vaccinated children, including those from migrant families and other  vulnerable groups. UNICEF supported mobile immunization sessions  ensured equitable access for 19,457 children living in remote  settlements, addressing geographic and socioeconomic barriers to services. To  strengthen service quality at the frontline, UNICEF supported the development  of practical job aids grounded in behavioural science, enabling  medical workers to implement updated immunization guidance more effectively.
Based on 2024  Assessment of Gender Barriers to Immunization in the Kyrgyz Republic, sex-disaggregated  data in immunization reporting will be introduced as a priority target in 2026.  
Recognizing  that vaccine recovery requires both service delivery and public trust, UNICEF  intensified social and behaviour change efforts to address vaccine  hesitancy amid persistent antivaccination narratives. Nationwide media  campaigns enabled three million people to access accurate immunization  information, while 500,000 parents were engaged through community  networks using gender transformative approaches that encourage joint decision-making.  Guided by social listening and behavioural insights, targeted initiatives  reached thousands of hesitant fathers and 20,000 young mothers  in maternity wards. To institutionalize these gains, interpersonal  communication modules were integrated into preservice and in-service  training for medical workers, strengthening systemwide capacity for high-quality  counselling. Behavioural insights from 2025 will guide further tailored  solutions in 2026, including for children affected by migration. 
A  subnational success story in IssykKul demonstrated the impact of  integrated investments and strong local leadership. With Gavi financing and  UNICEF support—expanding cold chain capacity, refrigerated transport and  remote temperature monitoring—the region maintained the lowest measles  incidence in the country and zero measles related deaths in 2025,  despite seasonal mobility and high tourist flows. Effective stock management,  rapid outbreak response, community engagement and contact tracing showed how  a resilient district level “immune system” can hold during national  surges. The evaluation of immunization programming covering 2018-2023 informed  the development of the National Programme for Immunization 2025-2023 and GAVI  6.0 planning. 
UNICEF  also generated critical economic evidence through a cost benefit  analysis of nutrition interventions and a national review of childhood  overweight and obesity, helping the Ministry of Health assess the economic  case for fiscal measures such as sugar sweetened beverage taxation.  These findings informed the draft Plan on Prevention of Micronutrient  Deficiencies (2026–2030) and address gendered nutrition gaps affecting  children, adolescent girls and women. Complementary work aims to combine  prevention at scale with supportive information environments and healthier  food systems. 
One  of the most significant achievements of 2025 was the national adoption and  rollout of the WHO/UNICEF Pocket Book of Primary Health Care for Children and  Adolescents. For the first time, frontline health workers nationwide  received a standardized, rights-based guide on preventive care, common  childhood conditions, referrals and adolescent health. As a national  standard, it improves consistent, timely, and gender-responsive care for 2.5  million children and adolescents. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health  and WHO through development and implementation, ensuring alignment with child  rights principles and integration into training and supervision systems. 
Digital  health continued to unlock access for families in hard-to-reach districts. Building on earlier pilot, the telemedicine platform  extended its reach from four to ten 10 hard-to-reach areas, benefiting rural  children who would otherwise face long journeys and high costs to access  specialist care. The Ministry decided to register the telemedicine platform  in the National Register of Digital Products which strengthens its  sustainability. Within the UN Joint SDG Fund programme on digital health  transformation—implemented by UNICEF, WHO, UNDP and UNFPA—the country  approved governance and implementation tools to ensure scalability, national  ownership and sustainability. UNICEF’s support focused on strengthening the use  of digital solutions for child and maternal health and ensuring that telemedicine  services are formally integrated into national digital health systems and  aligned with long-term sector digitalization priorities.
  
Every  child learns
  
Education  reform reached a turning point in 2025. The updated State Education  Standards, developed and launched in May with UNICEF support, established  a coherent national curriculum framework from pre-primary to secondary  education—embedding competency based learning and crosscutting  priorities such as gender equality, disability inclusion, climate  resilience and school safety. UNICEF provided sustained technical support  to the Ministry of Education and the Kyrgyz Academy for Education, helping  align the standards with international evidence and child rights principles,  and convening stakeholder consultations to ensure system actors—from  policymakers to teachers and parents—could shape and own the change. The country also initiated implementation of a 12-year schooling system,  aimed at better preparation for tertiary education and the labour market, and  at improved comparability with global standards.  
UNICEF  complemented policy work with investments in early childhood education and  equity. With national counterparts, UNICEF supported the development of  new preschool standards, improved governance, quality assurance and financing  modalities—such as voucher-based approaches and homebased models—to  expand access where the supply of places is most constrained. This has  focused on ensuring that that preschool experiences are safe, stimulating and  developmentally rich - not just expanding coverage – especially for  children in low-income households and remote communities, and for those with  disabilities who require adapted environments and trained staff. Based on  state statistical data, the access to ECE for children of age 1-6 increased  from 28.3% (m:50.7%, f: 49.3%) to 32.3% (m: 51.0%, f: 49%) in 2024. Preliminary data indicates the ECE access increased to 50% of children in 2025.  
In the classroom, UNICEF prioritized teacher support and student wellbeing.  Following behavioural insights work on mental health, a new course on psychological  wellbeing and peer support in crises was integrated into teacher preparation—building practical skills that help educators support learners in  times of stress and prevent small challenges from becoming barriers to  learning. In parallel, with support from a UK-funded regional programme, Grade  4 English language teachers were trained to deliver updated curricula,  and new textbooks were printed for nationwide distribution in the 2025–26  academic year—one of several examples of targeted instructional support  designed to raise foundational literacy in a foreign language at  scale.  
UNICEF  continued to model inclusive education and early identification.  Building on pilots with local health, education and social services,  professionals were trained to recognize developmental delays early and connect  families to services—with 81 young children reached in the 1st  year (m:59%; f:41%) - an approach that reduces stigma, accelerates support  and can be replicated at oblast level. Education standards developed with  UNICEF technical support embedded competency based learning and crosscutting  priorities including disability and inclusive learning from the start  of education.  
Further  strengthening system coherence, the state programme on Climate Change  Education, led by the Ministry of Education with UNICEF’s technical  support, was formulated to establish a unified and forward-looking vision for  climate education across all levels of the education. 
Through STEM4Girls,  implemented with the Ministry of Education and private sector partners,  Kyrgyzstan consolidated five years of progress: by March 2025, STEM4Girls  programme reached ~50,000 girls, significantly shifting aspirations and  stereotypes and celebrated girls’ achievements in science and innovation. Thousands  of adolescents engaged in hands-on STEM learning, mentorship and community  projects that connected their skills to real problems, such as water quality,  waste management and energy efficiency. Different events, storytelling and  partnerships helped shift perceptions of what girls can and should study, a  cultural change that is essential for closing gender gaps in the  future workforce. In October, renewed private sector support signalled continued  momentum and national recognition of the initiative’s impact on girls’  confidence, skills and aspirations. 
UNICEF  strengthened adolescent health literacy on stigmatized topics,  particularly menstrual health, through digital tools and youth led outreach  that normalized conversations, increased knowledge, and encouraged more  supportive attitudes among families and peers. The OKY Period Tracker,  cocreated by UNICEF with and for girls, is now used by over 18,000 girls  in Kyrgyzstan, helping them understand and manage menstruation, access  accurate information, and challenge harmful norms. These efforts contribute  to improved wellbeing, school participation and gender equality, and play a  critical role in promoting dignity, inclusion and regular  attendance—complementing broader education reforms to ensure every adolescent  is safe, informed and able to continue learning.
  
Every  child is protected from violence and exploitation
  
A  landmark system gain in 2025 was the Government’s decision to  create 550 child protection social worker positions, dedicated to  supporting children and families in difficult life situations. The  expansion—formalized by presidential decree in January—tripled the size of  the dedicated workforce and improved coverage ratios from roughly one  social worker per 10,000 children to around one per 4,000,  signalling a shift to a nationally owned, preventive and family centred  system. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Labour, Social Welfare and  Migration and academic partners to clarify roles, develop competency-based  training, and roll out practical modules on casework, professional  ethics, positive parenting, gender sensitive practice and selfcare. The new  cadre is helping to prevent violence, reduce reliance on  institutional care and strengthen family support at community  level. This initiative builds on earlier efforts to support children  returning from conflict zones and now extends to all children in vulnerable  situations. 
UNICEF supported national justice legislative reforms  that ensured application of diversion measures, contributing to an increase  of use of diversion from 528 cases in 2024 to 637 cases for nine months of 2025 and helping more children receive community-based  support instead of detention. 
Policy  coherence advanced in parallel. The Action Plan (2025–2028) to implement  the Convention on the Rights of the Child—coordinated by the Office of  the Child Rights Commissioner—was presented with UNICEF support, providing a  platform to align sectoral reforms, monitoring and budgets with CRC  concluding observations. The visit of CRC Committee members to Kyrgyzstan in  April 2025 reinforced accountability and created opportunities for practical  exchange with ministries, parliamentarians and civil society, keeping the  focus on ending violence, expanding family-based care and  ensuring equal access to services for the most vulnerable children.   
Kyrgyzstan also  contributed to regional leadership on one of the most complex child  protection challenges of our time: the reintegration of children  repatriated from conflict zones. In 2025, the Government, with the  European Union and UNICEF, hosted a regional convening in Bishkek to  consolidate lessons on child centred reintegration, psychosocial support,  education access, family services and social inclusion—helping to strengthen  national systems and cross border collaboration so that children can rapidly  reintegrate. Trained social  service workers supported the reintegration of 547 repatriated children (199 girls, 199 boys) and mothers (149).
  
Every  child lives in a safe and clean environment
  
The  climate agenda for children was significantly advanced in 2025 with concerted  efforts as part of the Central Asia Climate Business Model Initiative (BMI). In  October, Kyrgyzstan presented its updated Nationally Determined  Contribution (NDC) 3.0, aligning climate ambition with the National  Development Programme 2030 and the SDGs. UNICEF worked closely  with Government and UN partners to ensure that children’s vulnerabilities  and priorities were visible in the national dialogue and that adaptation  and mitigation measures consider the services children rely on—health  facilities, schools, social protection systems and safe water. The NDC 3.0  includes costed child-specific targets and is expected to  benefit 2.3 million children through improved health, education,  and social protection outcomes, including targets such as modernizing at  least 1,400 social infrastructure facilities (schools, hospitals, etc.)  reaching around 1.8 million children and young people by 2030. Similarly, education  remained a critical lever for building resilience to climate change. Jointly  with the World Bank, UNICEF supported the government with risk-informed  programming through presenting the CCRI-DRM/INFORM subnational model, with  adoption planned in 2026.  
Education also remained a key entry point for  climate resilience. Under the BMI, climate competencies were integrated  into the State Education Standards, making climate change education part  of the national curriculum rather than an isolated topic. UNICEF supported  the Ministry of Education to operationalize these commitments by developing  teacher guidance and learning materials for Grades 1–6 and supporting school  level implementation. Thousands of teachers are now applying the updated  standards, helping build children’s environmental knowledge, problem-solving skills  and resilience while promoting safer, more energy efficient schools. 
UNICEF also supported the development of a new  model for energy efficient, climate resilient education infrastructure,  to be piloted in 2026. The model aims to create safer, healthier learning  environments in preschools and schools and to inform future national  infrastructure standards. UNICEF’s work is already helping influence  planned investments by international financial institutions and bilateral  partners, with initial discussions underway with the Islamic Development  Bank and others on opportunities for scaleup.
Young  people helped connect national climate commitments to community realities  through the Youth Climate Caravan 2025. Adolescents from all seven regions  built climate literacy, discussed local risks and proposed practical  solutions, culminating in youth recommendations submitted for NDC 3.0.  UNICEF, together with UN and national partners, provided technical and  logistical support in coordination with relevant ministries, ensuring  meaningful youth engagement in climate decision-making.
  
Every  child has an equitable chance in life
  
In 2025, the  Kyrgyz Republic accelerated social protection and child protection reforms  under the newly approved National Development Programme 2030, which was  informed by UNICEF’s 2024 public expenditure analysis. The NDP 2030 sets  clear national priorities for reducing child poverty, preventing violence  against children and women, promoting family-based care, and ensuring  equitable access to education and health services for the most vulnerable.
The Government  advanced plans for the introduction of a universal child benefit for  children aged 0–3, reflecting UNICEF’s longstanding evidence-based  advocacy for expanding inclusive and child sensitive cash benefits and  closing persistent coverage gaps for the youngest children. This reform is  expected to contribute significantly to reducing multidimensional child  poverty—which continues to affect one in two children nationwide—and to  strengthening the national social protection floor in alignment with global  best practice. 
Analysis  of applications by families to child-focused cash assistance show that the  number of female caregivers is almost 200% more than male caregivers  suggesting that female caregivers in extremely poor households are more  cognizant of the impact of child-focused cash assistance to support their  children’s needs.
UNICEF advanced  public finance for children by supporting national counterparts to  strengthen budgeting processes, evidence-based planning, and the efficiency  of social spending. This contributed to better alignment between national  financing priorities and the needs of children and supported the delivery of  more equitable social protection measures envisioned in the NDP 2030. UNICEF  also expanded efforts to generate new data on human capital, providing  evidence to guide long-term investments in children. This included  contributing to regional analysis—most notably the Generation 2025  report for Central Asia—which underscores the critical importance of early  childhood development, learning outcomes, and social protection coverage for  accelerating human capital formation across the region.
UNICEF  continued strengthening inclusive services to ensure children with  disabilities can access early identification, early intervention and  inclusive education. Local multidisciplinary teams improved referral  pathways, reduced delays in support, and increased the confidence of teachers  and health workers in family-centred approaches—helping reduce stigma and  boost demand for services. A key milestone was the early intervention  pilot in Suzak, where 81 young children with developmental delays  were identified early and linked to services, and 39 specialists  enhanced their skills in early identification and referral. More than 800 parents  formed self-help groups, providing peer support and strengthening community- level  advocacy for inclusion. Combined with UNICEF’s policy and capacity-building  support at national and local levels, these efforts helped embed inclusive  practices so that more children receive timely, appropriate support.
  
Looking  across the year
  
Across sectors,  a consistent lesson emerged: reaching more children makes a difference  only when services are high-quality and inclusive. Standardized clinical  guidance strengthened frontline health care nationwide, while telemedicine  helped reduce gaps in access for children and families in remote areas.  Education reform embedded inclusion, safety and climate resilience into what  children are expected to learn, and the transition to a 12-year system  expanded pathways to further education and work. Expanding the child  protection workforce strengthened prevention and family support at community  level. Climate action also benefited from the meaningful participation of  children and young people, ensuring that decisions shaping the country’s  response reflect and support their needs, perspectives and future wellbeing.
Two  crosscutting factors underpinned UNICEF-supported results in 2025. First,  evidence and data guided action, such as the prioritization of social  sectors with very specific targets related to child poverty reduction and  primary healthcare coverage, as well as clinical standards and immunization planning  to formative research shaping social and behaviour change. The latter also  enabled UNICEF and partners to identify bottlenecks early, design people centred  solutions and adapt quickly. Second, strategic communication  strengthened trust, with UNICEF investing in two-way engagement to  address vaccine hesitancy and support understanding of education reforms by  amplifying the voices of parents, educators and young people.

UNICEF’s  role across these achievements was consistent: convene partners, bring  credible evidence, strengthen national systems and amplify children’s voices. This approach helped transform policy ambition into practical,  measurable improvements in children’s lives—especially for those furthest  from services. The task ahead is to maintain momentum, safeguard  quality and ensure that the benefits of reform are felt equally by  every child and family, in every community.
