UNICEF’s programme experience in 2025 confirmed that sustained progress for children in Kyrgyzstan depends not only on individual interventions, but on the coherence, quality and resilience of national systems. While important achievements were realized during the year, several challenges and lessons emerged that will inform strategic adjustments and partnerships moving forward.
A core lesson from across sectors is that ambitious reforms require strong alignment between policy decisions and implementation capacity. Major initiatives launched in 2025—such as the updated State Education Standards, the transition framework toward 12year schooling and the expansion of the child protection workforce—demonstrate high-level political commitment. However, translating these reforms into improved day-to-day experiences for children depends on sustained investment in human resources, supervision, quality assurance and local level coordination. UNICEF’s engagement highlighted the importance of supporting not only normative frameworks, but also the practical conditions that enable frontline workers, teachers and social workers to deliver results.
In the health and nutrition sector, the measles outbreak underscored the continuing vulnerability of immunization systems to service disruptions and declining trust. Although the emergency response and catchup vaccination efforts reached large numbers of children, the persistence of transmission during 2025 demonstrated that restoring coverage requires a simultaneous focus on supply, service delivery quality and demand. Evidence from the year reinforced the value of behavioural insights, community engagement and partnerships with trusted local leaders as essential complements to technical solutions. Looking ahead, reductions in external financing for immunization heighten the importance of efficient public financing, integrated primary health care and nationally led coordination mechanisms.
The expansion of the child protection social service workforce represented a major systemic gain, yet also revealed new challenges related to quality, retention and supervision. The rapid scaleup of personnel requires continued attention to professional development, case management standards and wellbeing of social workers, particularly those operating in high stress environments. UNICEF’s support confirmed that workforce expansion must be accompanied by institutional strengthening to ensure that increased coverage translates into effective prevention and response to violence, neglect and family separation. 
Operating in a complex and evolving context also reinforced the importance of principled, risk informed programming. Changes in the regulatory environment affecting civil society and media, combined with political transitions and a dynamic socioeconomic landscape, require UNICEF to continuously assess risks to partners, communities and programme delivery. In 2025, adaptive management, strengthened safeguarding measures and close coordination within the UN system proved essential to sustaining results and maintaining trust with Government counterparts. 
Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF will continue to focus on a limited number of strategic priorities that build on the gains and lessons of 2025. These include supporting the child sensitive implementation of Kyrgyzstan’s NDC 3.0, with particular emphasis on resilience of health, education and social protection systems; consolidating improvements in primary health care quality through national rollout of standard clinical guidance and digital innovations; translating education reform into sustainable, system-wide practices by strengthening teaching quality, inclusive practices and learning assessment systems; and deepening child protection system strengthening, with a focus on prevention, family-based care and professional supervision. Experience from regional climate coordination mechanisms, including the Climate Business Model Initiative, highlighted the potential of pooled technical assistance models to enhance efficiency, consistency and learning across countries, particularly for specialized climate expertise.
Across all areas, UNICEF will elevate its focus on focus, scale and impact, and equity in advancing results for children. working with Government, civil society and development partners to ensure that reforms translate into tangible, lasting improvements in the lives of children and their families—and that no child is left behind.
UNICEF will support the Government in translating this agenda into practical investments in early childhood development, learning outcomes, adolescent skills, health, nutrition and protection systems, ensuring that children and young people are equipped to become a healthy, educated and productive workforce. Together, UNICEF and national counterparts will assess demographic trends, climate risks and socioeconomic shifts to define a strategic programme that strengthens systems, reduces inequalities and supports sustained human capital formation from birth through adolescence—so that today’s children can drive inclusive growth and prosperity in the decades to come.
In 2026, UNICEF and the Government of the Kyrgyz Republic will also jointly embark on the development of a new five-year Programme of Cooperation for 2028–2032, with a strong and explicit focus on human capital development. Building on the results, evidence and partnerships of the current programme cycle, the forthcoming Country Programme Document will be developed through an inclusive, forward-looking process aligned with national development priorities, the Sustainable Development Goals and the country’s commitment to maximizing its second demographic dividend.

Montenegro is an upper-middle-income country in the Western Balkans with a developed legal and institutional framework and is an EU frontrunner candidate country. Montenegro’s population of 623,633[1] is declining rapidly. The 2023 Census data, published on 15 October 2024, point to two concerning demographic trends. The first is population ageing, particularly pronounced in the northern and central regions, accompanied by a decline in the share of children in the total population—from 23.4 per cent in 2011 to 21.7 per cent in 2023. The second trend is the continued depopulation of the northern region alongside accelerated urbanization, especially in Podgorica and the coastal area. Of the total number of children aged 0–17 (134,420), 1.13% (a total of 1,527) have at least one difficulty/limitation in performing their daily activities. However, these numbers seem underestimated, having in mind the global average of children with disabilities(5-10%). As for the Roma population, according to self-identification in the Census, there are 2,757 Roma children (1,355 girls and 1,402 boys) and 812 Egyptian children (399 girls and 413 boys). 
The latest iteration of the SDG rankings had Montenegro ranked 55th out of 193 countries.[2]  With the Human Development Index value of 0.862, Montenegro ranks 48th out of 193 countries and territories.[3] The 2023 Gender Equality Index stood at 59.3, below the EU average of 68.6.
Following its consolidation in 2024, the current Government majority, made up of a diverse coalition of parties, was relatively stable despite occasional political tensions, especially in the run-up to frequent local elections. A major security challenge for the Government was the 1 January 2025 mass shooting in Cetinje, which claimed 13 people’s lives including two children. 
Montenegro has achieved substantive overall socio-economic progress over the past year, as reflected in the latest European Commission Report.[4] As for the rights of the child, the legislative and institutional framework is largely aligned with the EU Acquis and relevant international standards. However, equity issues for children are stark: Roma children, children with disabilities, and those living in poverty often face limited access to quality education, healthcare, and safe living conditions, deepening social exclusion and hindering their opportunities to thrive. Challenges remain in terms of: (i) poor accountability (limited public availability of data and follow up actions to Child Rights Committee recommendations); (ii) inappropriate and insufficient capacity; (iii) a lack of  sufficient funding for child rights institutions; (iv) a lack of quality assurance for existing laws, strategies and action plans; and (v) insufficient cross-sectoral cooperation. 
Montenegro’s growth is stabilizing after a strong post-pandemic rebound, with GDP expanding by 3.2 percent in 2024 and projected to grow by 3.3 percent in 2025. The small, open, and Euro-based economy remains highly vulnerable to external shocks, with heavy reliance on tourism adding to this exposure. Inflation has been stronger than expected (estimate 4-5%), while fiscal space remains constrained and public debt stable at around 60 percent of GDP.[5]

Goal area 1 - Survive and Thrive:   

Montenegro has made significant progress in reducing child mortality, with rates among the lowest in Europe. According to the latest UNICEF data (as of 2023), the under-five mortality rate (U5MR) stands at 3 deaths per 1,000 live births, the infant mortality rate (IMR) at 2 per 1,000, and the neonatal mortality rate (NMR) at 1 per 1,000. These figures reflect a steady decline over the past two decades, driven by improved healthcare access, mainly on tertiary level. At the same time, several challenges remain and preventable causes persist on lower organizational levels – namely primary level of health care, where UNICEF assessed quality of service/human capacities and certain, mainly preventive service utilization (e.g. immunizations) as key issues. The low immunization coverage rates are still a cause of serious concerns, as the timely national coverage rate achieved with the first dose of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR1) vaccine during 2025 remains at 32.3% for the last cohort of eligible children born in 2023( National immunization e-registry IPH website: Microsoft Power BI) placing Montenegro among the 10 countries with the lowest MMR1 coverages globally. At the same time, local coverages with the same vaccine in almost half of municipalities (10 out of 25) remain even below the national average.
Montenegro has high skilled birth attendance rate (99%), h however quality of care remains an issue according to an assessment from 2023.  The report pointed to the lack of up-to-date protocols, inadequate preparedness for obstetrical and neonatal emergencies, over medicalisation of care, inadequate data management and insufficient attention to respecting mother’s and newborn rights. 
Conservative estimates of the Situation Analysis of Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) in Montenegro show that, between 10% (3,700) and 15% (5,550) of children from 0 to 6 years require ECI services annually, among which only every third to second child (from 31% to 46%) has been identified and served.
A comprehensive analysis of the available human resources in the primary healthcare system, shows significant regional inequalities in the health workforce for maternal and child health (MCH), affecting the accessibility, availability and quality of services, especially in underserved areas.  The number of curative home visiting nurses is five times greater than that of preventive home visiting nurses, despite standards envisioning the opposite ratio. Many paediatricians are at their patient registration quota limits, resulting in adult doctors treating more children, which leads to a suboptimal quality of care at the primary level. An ageing workforce compounds the issue, with 11% of the 81 paediatricians at the primary healthcare level already over the retirement age. According to the said Analysis of human resources, the number of paediatricians will decline by 25% by 2028. The 2022 Montenegro Nutrition Survey (MONS) showed that more than 25% of non-pregnant women are anaemic, denoting a “moderate” public health problem, according to the WHO criteria. Nearly 60% of non-pregnant women are iron-deficient. The combined vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency affect 43 per cent of all women, with the highest prevalence found in breastfeeding women (58%). Anaemia is found in 13% of children aged 6–59 months, while more than 40% of children are iron-deficient.   
The latest findings from the European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs (ESPAD), flagged growing concerns among youth (15-16) in Montenegro over mental health needs (38% reported “not good” status in last two weeks), increasing e-cigarette use, the non-medical use of pharmaceutical drugs, and a sharp uptick in online gaming and gambling . The prevalence of early cannabis use (3%) and current cannabis use (4.9%) among Montenegrin youth aged 15–16 is slightly higher than the EU average (2.51% and 4.97%, respectively), with boys consistently reporting higher usage than girls. Notably, lifetime use of illicit drugs other than cannabis is significantly higher in Montenegro (7.55%) compared to the EU average (5.03%), as is the use of tranquillisers or sedatives without a prescription (10.53% vs. 8.44%). Gambling is more prevalent in Montenegro (28.06%) than in the EU (23.32%), particularly among boys (40.12%).

As per Ministry of Finance Macroeconomic and fiscal guidelines 2025-2028,  public spending on health in 2025 was estimated at 6% of GDP while projections for 2026, 2027 and 2028 have a decreasing trend accounting for 5,83%, 5,69% and 5,55% of GDP respectively. Internationally comparable national health accounts data highlight the historical and persistent reliance of Montenegro’s health system on out-of-pocket payments. In 2022 such payments accounted for 37% of current spending on health (EU average 19%). Data from national household budget surveys show that 79% of households incurred out-of-pocket payments in 2021. The average annual amount spent out of pocket per person doubled in real terms between 2006 and 2021. Richer households spend much more on average than poorer households, but out-of-pocket spending has grown more rapidly in poorer households. Out-of-pocket payments accounted for 4.8% of household budgets on average in 2021, up from 3.3% in 2006. Out-of-pocket payments are mainly driven by outpatient medicines in all consumption quintiles but to a much higher degree in poorer quintiles.  Spending on other types of care tends to fall with household income and this was particularly the case in 2021.(Can people afford to pay for health care? New evidence on financial protection in Montenegro)

Goal area 2 - Learn:   
    
The education system currently serves more than 122,000 children across pre-primary, primary and secondary levels. Enrollment in early childhood education (ECE) increased by 3 per cent compared to the previous school year, reaching 26,786 children (14,010 boys and 12,776 girls). Notably, enrollment of Roma and Egyptian children in ECE rose by 14.43 per cent, with 333 children enrolled, while enrollment of children with disabilities declined by 3 per cent, underscoring persistent inclusion gaps. In primary education, the number of children with disabilities enrolled increased by 7 per cent compared to 2024 , whereas enrollment of Roma children decreased by 1 per cent in primary and by 8 per cent in secondary education. 
Education financing has expanded significantly, with a strong investment cycle through the EU Growth Plan focused on digitalisation, including the establishment of more than 100 EdTech laboratories, particularly in northern municipalities. Over €145 million in grants and loans is planned for investment over the next two years, largely targeting school infrastructure modernisation and digital learning environments, with expected long-term gains in equity and learning outcomes. 
However, learning achievement remains a concern: TIMSS 2023 results, while improved since 2019, remain below the international average, with 16 per cent of pupils not reaching basic proficiency in mathematics and 20 per cent in science, while PISA 2022 shows 60 per cent of students below basic proficiency in mathematics and 53 per cent in reading. Long-term disparities continue to hinder equitable access and outcomes, particularly for vulnerable groups, as PISA 2022 reveals a wide performance gap between advantaged and disadvantaged students—equivalent to more than three years of schooling—reflecting inequalities in learning outcomes, school engagement and educational aspirations. Encouragingly, TIMSS Longitudinal digital assessments conducted in 141 primary schools with approximately 4,300 Grade 5 students, are showing substantial gains, with average scores increasing by 17 points in mathematics and 18 points in science compared to 2023, and by 41 and 26 points respectively compared to 2019, indicating positive momentum despite ongoing challenges.

Goal area 3 - Protection from Violence and Exploitation:  
     
Child protection reforms have yielded notable progress, in spite of persistent risks for children. Sustained deinstitutionalization efforts have resulted in the lowest number of children ever placed in residential care, with a 22 per cent decrease compared to 2024, a 44.7 per cent reduction since 2020 and a 74.8 per cent decline since 2010; notably, no children under the age of three remain in residential care. The proportion of children with disabilities in residential care has also fallen significantly, from 47 per cent in 2024 to 33 per cent, while family-based care has expanded, with foster care placements increasing by 12 per cent since 2020 and non-kinship foster care rising by 45 per cent. 
In 2025, the child protection system reached 2,420 children who had experienced violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect, reflecting both the scale of protection needs and the system’s outreach capacity. At the same time, serious protection concerns persist. All 14 reported cases of sexual violence against children in 2024 involved girls, underscoring their heightened vulnerability. Successive EU Reports have highlighted gender-based violence and violence against children as areas of concern, pointing to weak institutional responses and limited service availability. Montenegro has yet to implement UN recommendations to raise the minimum age of marriage, and arranged child marriages in Roma communities remain prevalent, affecting 32.5 per cent of girls and 15.8 per cent of boys aged 15–19. Peer violence is also widespread, with 43 per cent of students witnessing violence at school, 17 per cent reporting victimization and 6.7 per cent admitting violent behavior during the 2022/2023 school year. Increased reliance on digital technologies further exposes children to online risks, highlighting gaps in digital child protection. 
The juvenile justice situation in Montenegro highlights ongoing challenges in addressing youth involvement in crime, particularly in relation to serious offences.[6] In the juvenile justice system, 267 juvenile offenders were reported in 2024, with serious offences remaining a concern, as crimes against life and body accounted for 21.5 per cent of all reported juvenile crimes, indicating the need for strengthened prevention, diversion and rehabilitation measures.  The lack of specialization of judges in family law related cases, where children’s rights are decided, including custody, divorce cases, determination and elimination of parental rights remain a matter of concern. 

Goal area 4- Safe and clean environment:   
    
Children in Montenegro face significant and compounding climate; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) as well as disaster risk challenges that disproportionately affect their health, safety and development. According to UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index, 99 per cent of children are exposed to air pollution, a critical concern given children’s heightened vulnerability, with documented impacts including low birth weight, asthma, respiratory infections, allergies and increased risk of chronic diseases later in life. Air pollution poses a particularly severe risk in urban areas, with European Environment Agency data indicating that Montenegro has one of the highest premature mortality rates in Europe linked to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), at 174 deaths per 100,000 people—more than three times the EU average. 
WASH conditions further exacerbate inequities, especially in schools and vulnerable communities. UNICEF-supported assessments show that while 81.8 per cent of schools meet WHO basic water service standards, only 52.3 per cent provide even limited hygiene services, and menstrual hygiene management remains largely unaddressed. Conditions are more acute in Roma and Egyptian settlements, where nearly 16 per cent of households rely on defective water supplies, almost half of settlements lack waste disposal containers, and some areas report the absence of sanitation infrastructure and instances of open defecation. WASH challenges also affect healthcare facilities, where 25 per cent of assessed institutions were classified as high or critical risk in medical waste management. 
Disaster risk reduction capacities remain limited, with fewer than 10 per cent of state educational institutions having earthquake protection and rescue plans in place. Overall, climate change adaptation and DRR policies require stronger child-sensitive approaches, with greater prioritization of vulnerable groups. 

 Goal area 5- Equitable Chance in Life:   
     
Social policy reforms in Montenegro have expanded coverage of social benefits and services, however child poverty and inequalities remain persistent challenges. Administrative data indicate that 131,176 children—around 97 per cent of all children—receive the universal child allowance (UCA), with total allocations reaching approximately €50 million, ten times higher than a decade ago. 
According to the MONSTAT 2024 Survey on Income and Living Conditions, children remain the most vulnerable group to poverty in Montenegro, with 25.6% living at risk of poverty. Additionally, 22.1% of young people aged 18 to 24 face the same risk. Particularly concerning is that 34.6% of children aged 0–17 are at risk of poverty or social exclusion. This includes children who are not only in poverty but also experience severe material and social deprivation and/or live in households with very low work intensity, highlighting the multiple and overlapping disadvantages children in Montenegro continue to face. Gini coefficient, as an indicator of income inequality in 2023 was 29.4, according to EU-SILC, and the population living in the Northern region was at a much higher risk of poverty (34.2%) in comparison to the population in the Southern region (11.6%), which demonstrates that additional packages of the social and child protection should be devised and targeted at the population from the northern, rural and remote areas. Children with disabilities and Roma children continue to face significant barriers and inequalities in their access to basic services, such as health care and nutrition, education and housing.  According to the Multidimensional Child Poverty in Montenegro Analysis (2021), 96% of Roma children experience deprivations in at least one domain of their wellbeing, and 65% of children under two years of age experience simultaneous deprivations for nutrition, ECD and housing. The same analysis points to the fact that the stigma regarding poverty is often compounded with the stigma regarding disability or ethnic affiliation (e.g. Roma), and that parents of children with disabilities often rely only on themselves to cope with problems.  Survey on Income and Living Conditions (SILC)  data showed that at-risk-of-poverty rate for children declined from 28.4% in 2022 to 25.6% in 2024. The risk of poverty for children under 18 in Montenegro (25.6%) is notably higher than the EU average of 19.3%, while youth aged 18 to 24 also face slightly higher poverty risk (22.1% compared to the EU average of 21.4%). Most strikingly, the share of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in Montenegro (34.6%) exceeds the EU average of 24.2% by more than ten percentage points. These figures illustrate the urgent need for targeted social and economic policies to reduce child poverty and exclusion in line with EU standards and commitments under the European Child Guarantee.

Youth unemployment is a major structural challenge, standing at 25.9% for the population aged 15–24 as per the latest World Bank /ILO data.  Share of youth aged 15-24 not in employment, education or training (NEET) stands at 20% as per 2024 ILO data nearly double the EU average of 11%.. It is concerning to note that youth in Montenegro face significantly higher levels of vulnerability in the labour market compared to their European peers.  Similarly, youth unemployment in Montenegro is 25.9%, markedly higher than the EU average of 15.9%. These gaps point to systemic challenges in supporting young people’s transition from education to employment and underline the urgent need for targeted interventions to improve access to quality education, skills development, and inclusive labour market opportunities for all youth in Montenegro.

GA 1 - Survive and Thrive:    
 In 2025, UNICEF achieved transformative results in health and early childhood development (ECD) by strengthening multisectoral systems, expanding equitable services, and promoting evidence-based policies, directly contributing to national priorities, Sustainable Development Goals, and Montenegro’s commitments under human rights frameworks, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child. UNICEF supported the Government in implementing the second Action Plan under the Early Childhood Development Strategy 2023–2027, providing technical guidance and participating in the multi-sectoral National Coordination Body. Capacity-building of ECD professionals, development of professional guidelines, and scaling up of services were prioritized, ensuring that quality early childhood services reached more children and families across the country.
Significant policy and system-level results included technical assistance for the adoption of the National Plan of Measures for Immunization 2026–2028, supported by ACT-A investments from the Republic of Korea, and contributions to the new Healthcare Law, which included key provisions on early intervention and breastfeeding. UNICEF also strengthened the national immunization registry in collaboration with the Institute of Public Health. To improve home-based care, an assessment of home visiting services using the maturity model approach was conducted and presented at the national conference “The Best Start in Life for Every Child in Montenegro”, nd a new integrated model of home visiting by patronage nurses was developed and shared with decision makers. Towards the end of the year, UNICEF initiated a survey on breastfeeding and vaccine promotion practices among maternity ward and community healthcare workers, aimed at integrating counselling practices more effectively.
UNICEF expanded access to parenting support through multiple modalities, including online, group-based, and home visiting programmes. The Bebbo mobile app was promoted by UNICEF and the Institute for Public Health, reaching nearly 1,700 downloads in 2025 and a cumulative total of 16,000 downloads since launch. The Caring Families programme was expanded reaching a total of 17 municipalities, with 316 caregivers participating, including 14% fathers. The programme was adapted for parents of children with developmental delays and disabilities, reaching 62 caregivers, ensuring equitable support for families with additional needs.
To increase coverage with the first dose of measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, UNICEF supported a nationwide call centre initiative, resulting in 800 additional children receiving the vaccine. Partnerships with the Students’ Council of the Medical Faculty of the University of Montenegro provided keynote presentations on immunization and breastfeeding and trained over 20 senior medical students in interpersonal communication for immunization (IPC/I), promoting sustainable health promotion practices.
Family-centred early intervention, introduced in 2023, expanded in 2025 with oversight from the Ministries of Health, Education, and Social Welfare, and UNICEF support. Services were delivered in Bijelo Polje, Berane, and partially in Podgorica, with training initiated in Cetinje, Tivat, and Bar, reaching 525 children (66% boys) through child development monitoring and early intervention. An Operational Plan for scaling up family-centred early intervention was drafted with UNICEF technical assistance and ACT-A support.
UNICEF strengthened maternal and neonatal health through training on essential care during labour and birth and preeclampsia/eclampsia management, reaching over 80 health workers in all public maternity facilities. Four neonatal clinical guidelines were finalized with UNICEF support, including one on preeclampsia/eclampsia.
UNICEF promoted health-seeking behaviours and ECD awareness through digital media campaigns, including promotion of the Bebbo app, Caring Families (Parenting for Lifelong Health) programme, preschool enrolment, breastfeeding, and immunization. International observances, such as World Breastfeeding Week and World Prematurity Day, were commemorated to increase public engagement. Montenegro’s adaptation of the Caring Families programme for Roma communities and parents of children with disabilities was shared at national and international conferences. Additionally, UNICEF supported NGO Parents in operating a parental helpline and trained staff on immunizations and interpersonal communication.
 
GA 2 - Learn:    
    
In 2025, UNICEF achieved transformative results in education, by supporting systemic reforms that advanced national priorities, strengthened equity, and fostered sustainable, child-centered learning environments. A key strategic achievement was the development and Government adoption of the Education Reform Strategy 2025–2035, co-created with UNICEF and EU support, which sets a comprehensive pathway for enabling children to acquire 21st-century skills while strengthening quality, inclusiveness, resilience, governance, and school infrastructure across all education levels. To ensure long-term sustainability, UNICEF facilitated the development of a Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (2025–2027) and Action Plan (2025–2026). In order to strengthen system governance, UNICEF also conducted a functional review of the Ministry of Education, Innovation and Science (MoESI), and assessments of the teacher professional development, and teaching assistants for children with disabilities. Following the functional review of the MoESI, a new directorate for strategic management is currently being established. Furthermore, the development of a new National Curriculum Framework was initiated, as a key policy document enabling effective integration and delivery of quality and inclusive teaching practices and skills development programs. The establishment of a human resources database within EMIS further enhanced the capacity for long-term planning and monitoring of education workforce needs. Gender-sensitive analysis of textbooks and capacity building for school psychologists, strengthened the protection and well-being of children, directly supporting Montenegro’s obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child and recommendations from the CRC Committee.
UNICEF’s interventions reached over 80,000 children and adolescents through integrated, large-scale programmes that prioritized equity and inclusion. Targeted support ensured that all Roma children in early grades (782) and preschools (333) accessed quality learning, accompanied by capacity building for teachers and the development of the picture dictionary “Let’s Learn the Romani Language Together” to promote linguistic and cultural inclusion. Inclusive education was further advanced through individualized support, assistive technologies, and inclusive learning environments for all children with disabilities in preschools (204) and primary schools (351). Through Peacebuilding Fund support, Social and Emotional Learning programmes expanded to 64 per cent of primary and secondary schools, reaching over 46,300 students. In parallel, through the Montenegro Acceleration Fund, digital skills integration was enhanced through STEAM workshops, summer camps, and teacher training for over 300 educators. In 2025, over 21,623 children accessed the UNICEF-supported Digital School platform based on the Learning Passport prototype, reflecting innovative scaling through establishment of EdTech Hubs in schools for developing a comprehensive set of skills through regular and extra-curricular, as well as non-formal education, as well as provision of quality digital content for students, teachers, and parents.
Enrolment data highlights both progress and remaining equity gaps: early childhood education increased by 3 per cent to 26,786 children, while enrolment of Roma and Egyptian children rose by 14.4 per cent. Children with disabilities experienced a slight decline in preschool enrolment (3 per cent), underscoring the continued need for targeted inclusion measures. UNICEF supported over 60 preschool professionals and 12 preschools in 11 municipalities to strengthen outreach and inclusive practices, promoting local ownership and sustainable improvements.
In summary, in cooperation with international partners and national institutions and organizations, UNICEF played a key role in establishing a strong policy environment and supporting large-scale and sustained programmatic interventions for long-terms reforms in education. 

GA 3 - Protection from Violence and Exploitation:  
In 2025, UNICEF Montenegro achieved transformative results in child protection, advancing systemic reforms, equity, and sustainable services, while supporting the Government to fulfill obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child and recommendations from the CRC Committee. UNICEF strategically supported the acceleration of deinstitutionalization through high-level advocacy and technical assistance for the implementation of the Strategic Framework adopted in late 2024. A key milestone was the finalization of the draft Law on Social and Child Protection, currently pending adoption, which introduces preventive services to preserve families, provides intensive support to children at risk of separation, expands family- and community-based care, and establishes the Centre for Foster Care. The Law also clarifies mandates between the Centre for Foster Care and Centres for Social Work and strengthens gatekeeping by prohibiting placement of children under seven in large-scale residential institutions. These  efforts contributed to the lowest-ever number of children in residential care, with a 22% decrease compared to 2024, 44.7% since 2020, and 74.8% since 2010. Importantly, there are no children under three in residential care, and the share of children with disabilities in residential care fell from 47% in 2024 to 33%. At the same time, the number of children in foster care increased by 12% since 2020, with non-kinship foster care rising by 45% over the same period.
To ensure the sustainability of family- and community-based care, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Welfare and Family and Child Development (MSWFCD) in building professional capacities for foster care. A Reference Group for foster care development was established, and close to 100 professionals received training on urgent and specialized foster care. Four training programs were accredited by the Institute for Social and Child Protection (ISCP), guaranteeing integration into the national professional development system and long-term sustainability. UNICEF also promoted a public-private partnership between the Ministry and a diaspora-led company, Piece of Cake, to support the start-up phase of the foster care services.  
UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support also advanced the establishment of the Barnahus model by 2027. A cross-sectoral working group led by the MSWFCD has nearly finalized national Standards and a Roadmap for the MDIA–Barnahus, pending government validation. Recognized as a public legal entity in the draft Law on Social and Child Protection, the Barnahus model defines accountabilities, funding modalities, staffing, and resources, marking a major milestone in advancing Montenegro’s response to violence against children.  On violence prevention more broadly, UNICEF strengthened systemic capacity by training over 100 cross-sectoral professionals on gender-based violence, violence against children, and intersectoral cooperation. Furthermore, in partnership with the Judicial Training Centre, more than 100 justice and social work professionals improved competencies in child-friendly standards for children in conflict with the law and for child victims and witnesses, reinforcing consistent application of the best interests of the child in family law proceedings, including parental rights cases.
UNICEF also addressed equity gaps and harmful practices affecting Roma and Egyptian children, including child marriage. Peer education programs reached 60 girls and boys aged 10-19 , strengthening knowledge and skills on child rights, the consequences of child marriage, gender equality, and healthy lifestyles. Primary school students at risk of arranged marriage or school dropout participated in six thematic workshops for emotional and social support, while high school students were trained as peer educators to promote gender equality and non-violence. Additionally, 50 parents increased awareness of the risks of child marriage and the importance of continued education for their children, contributing to supportive environments for Roma and Egyptian children. 
To address peer violence, UNICEF supported the CSO Association of Mediators to pilot school mediation in six elementary schools, training 36 school representatives and 120 children as peer mediators, equipping them with skills to resolve conflicts constructively and foster empathy. In parallel, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation to tackle sexual harassment in schools. A working group, supported by two CSOs, developed the first national Protocol on Sexual Harassment in Schools, establishing clear procedures for safe and respectful student-teacher interactions, with implementation planned for 2026 through targeted training.
UNICEF advanced disability-inclusive programming and budgeting by strengthening ministries’ capacity for Convention of Rights with People with Disability-compliant budgeting. Twenty-two participants from the Ministries of Finance, Social Welfare, Education, Health, Human and Minority Rights, and the General Secretariat learned about leveraging domestic financing mechanisms to ensure sustainable implementation.
Finally, UNICEF contributed to global and national efforts to combat online child sexual exploitation through the Disrupting Harm research initiative, in collaboration with UNICEF Innocenti, INTERPOL, and ECPAT International. A national validation workshop in December 2025 reviewed draft findings and recommendations, ensuring local perspectives inform the final report to be published in early 2026.
GA 4 - Safe and clean environment:   
In 2025, UNICEF completed the national WASH bottleneck assessment through the implementation of the Bottleneck Analysis Tool (BAT) that involved a systematic identification of all factors preventing the attainment of sector objectives. To accelerate progress in coverage and use of water, sanitation and hygiene services, particularly by poor and vulnerable, specific  bottlenecks have been identified through the analysis and systemic dialogue between sector decision-makers and stakeholders. The dialogue has been facilitated through a series of meetings, online and in person, as well as through the WASH BAT National workshop that gathered more than 50 stakeholders from all municipalities, local waterwork companies, health and educational institutions, key line ministries and local communities. A costed and prioritised National WASH improvement Action Plan has been developed that will be used by the Government, UNICEF and key sector partners, to establish multi-stakeholder coordination mechanism (e.g., a national WASH steering committee) and to operationalize actions implementation. At the same time UNICEF will use the plan to advocate for increased domestic budget allocations for WASH in national planning and budgeting processes, while leveraging additional resources from development partners, private sector contributions, and innovative financing mechanisms. 
 
The Country Office has supported two primary health care center s and 6 teams of the Ministry of Health and State Sanitary inspectorate in further strengthening WASH resilience and emergency preparedness through procurement of water testing equipment that is to be used for better water quality control – turbidity, free and total chlorine concentrations, microbiological and chemical parameters, both in developmental and emergency settings.
 Through the partnership with the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency (SwEPA), and supported by the Swedish International Development Agency (SIDA), UNICEF Montenegro developed adolescent and youth-friendly learning materials on Air Quality and Climate Change. UNICEF also supported the Montenegrin Ministry of Ecology and Environmental Protection Agency in the development of the Air Quality web portal and mobile app, by organizing focus groups and providing feedback from adolescents and youth. In 2025, more than 2,500 adolescents were reached with awareness on Air Quality and climate change, as well as played an active role in designing and implementing community initiatives on Air Quality.
 
Through the sub regional programme on air quality, UNICEF also advocated for the development of child-friendly NDCs, and supported the implementation of the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans. 
UNICEF delivered significant results in strengthening child-centred disaster risk reduction across the education and emergency preparedness sectors. In partnership with the Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation, UNICEF enhanced the education system’s capacity to prevent and respond to disasters through the development of national guidelines for preventive disaster risk reduction planning and a comprehensive assessment of rescue and protection equipment in all educational institutions. System-wide capacity was further strengthened through accredited disaster risk reduction education seminars, reaching 107 teachers, professional associates and education staff, as well as 109 school directors, covering 52% of all schools nationwide. At the regional level, UNICEF supported the Regional Office Emergency Section and the DPPI SEE Secretariat in convening a regional consultation with South-East European member states on child-sensitive risk assessment and emergency needs analysis. The consultation strengthened knowledge and practical application of child-sensitive risk analysis, promoted peer learning, and enhanced coordination between disaster management authorities and child-focused institutions, contributing to more inclusive and effective preparedness, response and recovery planning across the region.
 
GA 5 – Equitable Chance in Life:   
In 2025, UNICEF continued to play a central role in supporting the Government in the ongoing reform of the social and child protection (SCP) system. UNICEF successfully ensured that the proposed reforms incorporated objectives fully aligned with the national strategic framework whose development it had previously supported. In this context, UNICEF provided expert and technical assistance to the Ministry of Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography (MSWFCD) to advance the legislative framework for social and child protection. The draft Law on Social and Child Protection, developed under the leadership of the MSWFCD, is currently pending adoption. As a result of UNICEF’s continued policy engagement and evidence-based advocacy, the reform’s core elements include the enhancement of family support allowance and universal child allowance. These measures are designed to ensure more adequate benefit levels while strengthening targeting mechanisms to more effectively reach children with disabilities and children living in households facing socioeconomic vulnerabilities. In addition, UNICEF ensured establishing legislative foundations for shock-responsive SCP, strengthening the system’s capacity to respond to crises. 
The reform process is closely aligned with Montenegro’s commitments under EU integration framework, particularly the priorities outlined in the European Commission’s Montenegro Report (2025) and national Reform Agenda. In this context, UNICEF positioned itself as a key partner in operationalizing the European Child Guarantee (ECG) in Montenegro. UNICEF supported the appointed National Coordinator for ECG, by facilitating exchanges with EU countries experienced in implementing the initiative, enabling Montenegro to draw upon lessons learnt. UNICEF is also providing technical support in developing the Deep Dive Analysis that will inform ECG National Action Plan (NAP), currently in preparation. Through its role in NAP Working Group, UNICEF has contributed recommendations for the scope and content of NAP and has undertaken to develop guidelines to ensure meaningful child participation throughout the process.
At local level, UNICEF continued strong cooperation with municipalities under the Memorandum of Cooperation with the Union of Municipalities of Montenegro. The key achievement under this partnership was the implementation of a pilot support program for nine (9) young people transitioning from alternative care upon leaving the Children’s Home “Mladost” in Bijela. This support programme provided individualized assistance to support their integration into community life, including access to housing, development of daily living skills, employment support, and psychosocial and mentoring services. 
To reduce regional disparities in access to SCP services, UNICEF supported MSWFCD in provision of support to four northern municipalities to establish a minimum of three community-based social services. UNICEF supported the municipalities to conduct needs assessments and design services based on identified priorities, ensuring that the rights and well-being of children with disabilities and their families are strengthened at the local level, in line with Montenegro Reform Agenda and Growth Plan, as well as national SCP reform priorities.
In parallel, UNICEF continued advocacy to raise awareness of the harmful effects of multidimensional child poverty and social exclusion, with particular attention to Roma children and children with disabilities. This advocacy aimed to reinforce social inclusion and support improved social policies.
 
Child rights monitoring    

In 2025, UNICEF Montenegro advanced transformative results in child rights monitoring, data systems, partnerships, and participation, strengthening the national framework for evidence-based planning, policy reform, and accountability for children. Through continuous advocacy and technical assistance, UNICEF helped elevate child rights on the political agenda, progressively reinforcing national coordination and monitoring mechanisms across key duty bearers, including the Government, Parliament, Ombudsperson’s Office, judiciary, civil society, and local communities, in alignment with Montenegro’s commitments under the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and EU accession requirements.
Key achievements include the expansion of the mandate of the Council on the Rights of the Child to cover all areas of the CRC, with an Annual Working Plan for 2025 that emphasized cross-sectoral cooperation, strengthened monitoring, accountability for results, and acceleration of reforms in health, education, and social protection, including the Child Guarantee and child rights budgeting. The Council systematically addressed equity-focused priorities such as Roma children and families, children with disabilities, those exposed to violence and peer violence, and immunization, while ensuring meaningful child participation in its processes. The CO supported the Ministry of Social Welfare in developing and submitting to the General Secretariat the report on the implementation of the previous national Child Rights strategy, following a Child Rights Council–led external evaluation, as a basis for preparing the next overarching Child Rights strategic framework in line with the CRC Committee’s Concluding Observations to Montenegro.
UNICEF supported evidence generation and strengthened data systems. The Statistical Office of Montenegro (MONSTAT), with UNICEF support, launched the seventh round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7), covering a nationally representative sample of 6,720 households, with additional targeted surveys among Roma and Egyptian communities. This initiative, co-financed by the Government (EUR 300,000) and UNICEF (USD 700,000 from core resources), fills critical data gaps across health, education, child development, social protection, water and sanitation, and housing, supporting evidence-based policymaking, CRC reporting, and SDG monitoring. UNICEF also strengthened capacities of central and local institutions for the generation and utilization of sectoral data, including social protection (SWIS) and education (EMIS) systems, and fostered inter-sectoral data coordination between the Ministries of Interior, Social Welfare, and Justice, although gaps remain in creating a consolidated, interoperable child rights database. CO also supported the design of future capacity-building initiatives, including inter-sectoral training and an analysis of administrative data systems to improve coverage, functionality, and disaggregation of child rights data. The number of child-related indicators monitored under the national SDG framework is projected to reach 43 by 2030, reflecting progress in systematic tracking of child rights outcomes.
To enhance accountability and oversight, UNICEF supported the Parliament and the Ombudsperson in expanding their roles in child rights monitoring. Parliamentary committees integrated child rights into annual work plans and organized sessions on Early Childhood Development, Social and Child Protection System Reform, Deinstitutionalization, and violence against children. The Ombudsperson strengthened its capacities in monitoring child rights violations, including violence against children, education, juvenile justice, and protection from hate speech, and established a multi-stakeholder platform for independent monitoring of UN CRPD compliance in collaboration with ten disability rights organizations. UNICEF also provided technical assistance to define the mandate of the Deputy Ombudsperson for Children in the Draft Law on Ombudsperson.
UNICEF promoted strategic partnerships and sustainable financing to leverage domestic resources and secure long-term results. In the context of shrinking donor funding, CO Montenegro mobilized around  half a million USD from the private sector for 2026–2027, including contributions from high-net-worth diaspora individuals, to support the establishment of the first Foster Care Center and pilot services preventing family separation. In addition, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education, Science, and Innovation in financing the implementation of the Education Reform Strategy 2025–2035 through the Mid-Term Expenditure Framework, with technical guidance from the EU Delegation and GOPA consultancy. A study visit to Estonia, involving key representatives from the Ministries of Finance, Social Welfare, and Education, provided lessons on linking strategic planning to budget allocations, which were shared with GOPA and OECD SIGMA to support national public financial management reforms.
Collectively, these initiatives strengthened the national child rights monitoring system, enhanced evidence-based policymaking, ensured meaningful child and adolescent participation, and leveraged sustainable domestic financing and partnerships. 

Adolescents and young people 
  
 In 2025, UNICEF advanced transformative outcomes in adolescent development and participation by promoting multi-sectoral policies, skills enhancement, and civic engagement, aligned with the UNICEF Country Programme 2023–2027 and Montenegro’s EU accession priorities. These efforts contributed to Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 8 (Decent Work), and 16 (Peaceful and Inclusive Societies), strengthening adolescents’ resilience, employability, and inclusion.
A central pillar of UNICEF’s work was the implementation and scaling of innovative non-formal learning programmes that equip adolescents with socio-emotional, leadership, and life skills not fully addressed in formal education. Through the Air Quality programme and the joint UN programme supported by the Peacebuilding Fund (PBF), over 7,000 adolescents developed competencies in child and adolescent participation, conflict mediation, communication, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, project management, financial literacy, and time management. These initiatives also facilitated adolescent-led community projects, fostering civic engagement and active citizenship.
UNICEF further strengthened school-to-work transition through the Prilike programme, which reached nearly 2,000 adolescents across twelve schools in all three regions of Montenegro. Activities included career meetups, company matching, placements, and group or individual workshops, providing practical exposure and skills for future employment. This multi-stakeholder initiative, aligned with the Education Reform Strategy and the Career Guidance system revision, institutionalizes school-to-work support and builds a sustainable knowledge base through private sector and civil society partnerships, serving as a precursor to the EU Youth Guarantee scheme.
Environmental awareness and community engagement were advanced through the Air Quality programme in the Western Balkans, in which over 2,500 adolescents actively learned about air quality and climate change and designed and implemented local community initiatives. Similarly, UNICEF promoted social cohesion through the PBF-supported joint UN programme, including the development of child parliaments linked to local parliaments, peer learning workshops, and community projects. These activities reached 3,379 children and adolescents, of whom 57.4% were girls, enhancing participatory skills and promoting inclusive civic engagement.
In response to the mass casualty event in Cetinje, UNICEF provided targeted psychosocial services over eight months, supporting nearly 1,000 beneficiaries, which represents more than 50% of the 6–18 population in the affected area, demonstrating UNICEF’s capacity for rapid, large-scale, and equity-focused response.
Advocacy remained a critical component of UNICEF’s adolescent strategy. During World Children’s Day 2025, UNICEF highlighted persistent gaps, including that 75% of adolescents do not meet WHO physical activity guidelines and the very low participation of children and adolescents with disabilities in school sports. Inclusive sporting events were organized in partnership with Special Olympics and Paralympics, building on joint initiatives with the Ministry of Sports and Youth, including the Strategy for Sports, to ensure equity, participation, and social inclusion in extracurricular activities.
Collectively, these strategic actions demonstrate UNICEF’s integrated approach, combining innovative non-formal learning, civic engagement, environmental action, psychosocial support, and advocacy to strengthen adolescents’ life skills, employability, and resilience. By reaching over 7,000 adolescents through life skills programmes, 3,379 through social cohesion initiatives, and nearly 2,000 through school-to-work activities, UNICEF ensured large-scale, equitable, and sustainable impact. These interventions leveraged national partnerships, private sector collaboration, and multi-stakeholder engagement, creating the foundation for lasting, transformative outcomes in adolescent development and participation in Montenegro.

Gender equality    

During the reporting period, the Country Office demonstrated strong alignment of its gender programme with the priorities of UNICEF’s Gender Action Plan (GAP) 2022–2025, advancing gender equality across education, health, child protection and social norms change. The CO’s work addressed key GAP pillars, including adolescent girls’ empowerment, gender-responsive services, and the transformation of harmful gender norms and discriminatory practices.
In education, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation to address gender-based sexual harassment in schools. In collaboration with two civil society organizations, a multi-stakeholder working group developed the country’s first Protocol on Sexual Harassment in Schools, establishing clear standards of conduct and response procedures between students and teachers. This represents a significant step toward safer, gender-responsive learning environments. Gender equality was also systematically embedded in the flagship Education Reform Strategy, with gender-disaggregated indicators, a dedicated section on gender equality, and curriculum and textbook analyses informing concrete policy measures.
Adolescent empowerment was a core focus, particularly for marginalized groups. UNICEF supported non-formal education programmes for Roma and Egyptian adolescents, with a strong emphasis on girls’ empowerment, life skills development, and tackling discrimination. These initiatives strengthened girls’ voice, agency and decision-making, contributing to efforts to prevent child marriage, promote continued education, and improve long-term life outcomes, while also engaging boys to challenge harmful gender norms.
In child protection, UNICEF supported the establishment of the Barnahus model, ensuring that entry points for gender-responsive service delivery are integrated into the planned multidisciplinary response for child victims and witnesses of violence, including sexual violence. This approach aligns with GAP priorities on survivor-centred, gender-sensitive services.
In health, the assessment of maternal and neonatal services completed and launched in 2024 informed targeted capacity-building in 2025, strengthening the quality and responsiveness of maternal health services. Additionally, UNICEF continued to promote gender-transformative caregiving through the Caring Families programme, with a deliberate focus on recruiting and engaging fathers to challenge traditional gender roles and promote shared caregiving responsibilities.
Despite these advances, gender gaps persist, particularly in girls’ access to digital learning opportunities. Girls, especially Roma girls and girls with disabilities, remain underrepresented in digital and technology-enabled learning, notably in rural and underdeveloped areas. Building on existing EdTech infrastructure, the CO is positioning future programming to expand girls’ including Roma girls and girls with disabilities access to 21st-century skills, strengthen confidence and leadership, and foster more gender-equitable digital learning environments, in line with the GAP and UNICEF’s broader commitment to leaving no one behind.
Overall, the CO’s gender programming reflects strong strategic alignment with GAP 2022–2025 priorities, combining policy reform, service delivery, and social norms change, while identifying clear areas for continued focus and scale-up.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Over the past three years of implementing the Country Programme 2023–2027, UNICEF Montenegro has made significant strides in advancing child rights, equity, and inclusion across multiple sectors, yet the country continues to face a complex set of challenges that require strategic reflection and programmatic adjustments for the remaining period of 2026–2027. The UNICEF global Future Focus Initiative and the UN80 reform rationalization exercises have prompted a reassessment of priorities in the context of more limited resources, compelling the Country Office to focus on interventions with the highest potential for transformative, sustainable impact. A comprehensive programme review conducted in the fourth quarter of 2025 highlighted both areas of significant progress and persistent gaps, offering a foundation for refining strategies to ensure that future efforts are aligned with national priorities, Montenegro’s EU accession agenda, and the forthcoming UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029.
One of the most persistent challenges has been the disconnect between policy and practice. Across sectors, legislative and policy frameworks often outpace institutional capacity, resulting in reforms that are robust on paper but inconsistently implemented in practice. While Montenegro has adopted several progressive strategies, including the Education Reform Strategy 2025–2035, the Social and Child Protection Strategy, Deinstitutionalization Strategy, Violence Against Children Strategy, and the Early Childhood Development Strategy 2023–2027 - gaps in operationalization and in systematically resourcing strategies and policy targets the Country Office increasingly invested in costed action plans and results-based budgeting  capacity building), have limited the realization of intended outcomes.  Addressing these structural and operational gaps is critical to ensuring that Montenegro’s ongoing EU accession reforms translate into tangible improvements in living standards, social equity, and sustainable development outcomes.
In 2025, UNICEF Montenegro recognized the need to prioritize interventions that reach the most vulnerable children and that are demonstrably sustainable and scalable. A key example is the operationalization of the European Child Guarantee framework, which provides a strategic lens for reaching children at heightened risk of exclusion. UNICEF aims to build on proven models such as the contemporary transdisciplinary, family-centered early intervention, ensuring that these services are embedded at the local level and reinforced by adequate budget allocations. Lessons learned over the Country Programme implementation period indicate that effective local partnerships, particularly with municipal authorities, are crucial for sustainability. Engagement with local self-governments in planning and budgeting processes not only ensures that services are responsive to community needs but also strengthens the likelihood of sustainable financing. For instance, collaboration with the Podgorica municipality, which holds the largest municipal budget and has ambitious goals as the European Youth Capital, could demonstrate how strategic local partnerships can significantly enhance the reach and impact of social services, offering a replicable model for other municipalities.
Deinstitutionalization and combating violence remain strategic priorities and essential benchmarks for EU Chapter 23 closure. UNICEF Montenegro has supported the Ministry of Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography in advancing the SCP, DI and VAC strategies, particularly by promoting family- and community-based care, strengthening foster care systems, and reducing the number of children in residential institutions. While progress has been substantial, including historically low numbers of children in residential care, the challenge remains in consolidating gains, ensuring adequate funding, and scaling professional capacity development for social service providers. Lessons learned highlight that sustained advocacy, continuous technical assistance, and close monitoring of implementation processes are necessary to maintain momentum and achieve fully operational deinstitutionalization systems that are resilient to policy shifts or funding fluctuations.
In the education sector, UNICEF and partners helped Montenegro lay strong foundations for long-term education reform by adopting the Education Reform Strategy (2025-2035), and also advancing inclusive policies, modern curricula, stronger systems, and equitable programs that improved access, skills development, and learning outcomes for children, especially the most vulnerable. This process has demonstrated that policy adoption alone is insufficient without parallel investment in evidence generation, public finance interventions, close partnership with EU and IFIs capacity building efforts, and cross-sectoral coordination.
Key data initiatives such as the seventh round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) and the Disrupting Harm research on online child sexual exploitation, scheduled for publication in early 2026, represent critical tools for advocacy and policy dialogue. The office has learned that systematic and timely evidence generation is vital to demonstrating the need for reform and for mobilizing resources, particularly by quantifying financial implications of interventions such as the European Child Guarantee and child allowance schemes. Evidence-based advocacy has proven effective in influencing decision-makers when paired with clear financial and operational analyses, highlighting the need for strengthened data-to-policy linkages in the next CPD period.
A recurrent lesson has been the importance of budget advocacy and fiscal planning. Despite strategic priorities being funded under various ministries, allocations often remain insufficient, fragmented, or invisible as separate budget lines, reducing transparency and limiting accountability. UNICEF Montenegro has emphasized the need to engage the Ministry of Finance and other relevant line ministries directly in funding discussions, using clear accountability papers and articulated asks to secure commitment for reform implementation. The office has also leveraged study visits, such as the 2025 delegation to Estonia, to enhance understanding of linking strategic planning with budget allocations, lessons that have been shared with the EU Delegation and SIGMA (OECD) to support public financial management reforms. These experiences underscore that ensuring visible, well-planned, and sufficient funding is a prerequisite for transforming policy into practice.
From an implementation strategy perspective, several approaches have proven particularly effective. Multi-sectoral collaboration, integration of services, and leveraging both domestic and international partnerships have accelerated results across health, education, social protection, and child protection. For example, partnerships with local governments, the Ministry of Finance, civil society, and private sector actors, including high-net-worth individuals from diaspora and VOLI, the largest retail chain, have mobilized critical resources for interventions such as foster care, prevention of family-child separation, and community-based social services. Similarly, integrated programming across sectors, combining education, health, and social protection has amplified impact, particularly for the most vulnerable groups, such as Roma children, children with disabilities, and children at risk of violence or neglect.
However, not all strategies have yielded consistent outcomes. Implementation inconsistencies, delays in institutionalizing policies, and limited capacity at municipal and service-provider levels have constrained impact. These lessons indicate that future adjustments should focus on strengthening operational capacity, improving monitoring systems, ensuring sufficient and predictable financing, and enhancing evidence-based advocacy. Engaging new partners, particularly at the municipal level and in the private sector, offers an opportunity to extend the reach and sustainability of results, while continued alignment with the EU agenda, national priorities, and the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029 ensures relevance and strategic coherence.
Looking forward, UNICEF Montenegro envisions a focused, evidence-driven, and equity-oriented programmatic approach for 2026–2027. Emerging priorities include fully operationalizing the European Child Guarantee, sustaining social services at the local level, scaling evidence-based early interventions, and consolidating gains in deinstitutionalization and child protection. The office will continue to prioritize large-scale, high-impact interventions that strengthen systems, leverage partnerships, and promote meaningful child participation. Strengthening financial and institutional sustainability through improved budget advocacy, engagement with the Ministry of Finance, and strategic municipal partnerships will be central to ensuring that legislative and policy frameworks translate into tangible outcomes for children. Emphasis on evidence generation and its systematic use in advocacy will remain a core strategy, ensuring that policymakers understand both the social and financial implications of proposed reforms, thereby accelerating the implementation of policies and programmes that reduce inequities and strengthen protection for all children.
In summary, the combination of lessons learned, evidence generation, strategic partnerships, and targeted advocacy provides UNICEF Montenegro with a clear pathway to maximize impact during the remaining country programme period. By addressing institutional capacity gaps, strengthening budget planning and visibility, sustaining proven models of early intervention and social services, and leveraging EU accession reforms and national policy momentum, UNICEF Montenegro aims to ensure that children’s rights, equity, and protection remain central to Montenegro’s development trajectory, achieving transformative outcomes and laying the foundation for a resilient and inclusive future for children.

Romania’s political landscape in 2025 was volatile,  with a new Parliament, new President, and change of Government. Long-term engagement with a wide range of national stakeholders enabled UNICEF to partner with both the Parliament and the Government to ensure children are prioritized and engaged in policy-making. 
  
While child rights continued to be a critical priority, challenges persisted. From 2023 to 2024 the rate of children at risk of poverty or social exclusion decreased by 5.2-percentage points, yet one out of three children (33.8%) remained at-risk of poverty or social  exclusion. 
  
Romania  maintained its high-income (HIC) status for the third consecutive year yet had the highest budget deficit among the EU member states, reaching 9.3% of national GDP in 2024, far above the 2030 EU target of 3.9% of GDP. To respond to the high deficit and pressures from the European Union, the Government implemented significant fiscal consolidation measures in 2025, such as reducing national spending and raising taxes, that decreased the budget deficit to approximately 8.6% of GDP. At the same time, Romania’s GDP growth remains low (+0.7% in 2025). Fiscal consolidation has also dampened private and public consumption which is further affected by persistent high inflation (9,7% in 2025). Experiences from the previous financial crisis underscore the importance of protecting social spending during fiscal austerity periods, as children’s and families' needs for public services increase with funding drops.
  
At  the same time, these measures impacted the education sector through major structural and financial  adjustments, as 8.1% of schools and institutions were reorganized as satellite units with increased class size limits. Teachers’ workloads also grew with the didactical norm increased from 18 to 20 hours per week, and principals and general school inspectors were required to have more teaching hours. These conditions place additional stress on an already weak system. In addition, student benefits and social programmes were affected, with  scholarship schemes substantially narrowed, reducing access to merit and  social support including scholarships for children from single-parent  families. State-funded school meals programmes were suspended, while private education subsidies were reduced and stricter thresholds introduced for maintaining legal entity status.
  
At  the beginning of 2025, the Ministry of Labour, Family, Youth and Social  Solidarity (MLFYSS), together with the National Authority for Protection of Child Rights and Adoption (NAPCRA), launched the national scale-up of the  integrated community services (ICS), targeting approximately 2,000 rural  municipalities. The ICS model, components previously tested under UNICEF supported  minimum package of services, strives to ensure that every child and every  family in need can access a minimum set of integrated health, education and  social protection services in their communities. The initiative is financed by €650 million in EU funding under the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+), representing one of the largest child-focused social investments in the country’s history. 
  
The  country’s medium-term growth will be driven by its ability to absorb EU funds. Romania is eligible to receive up to €77 billion in  funding by 2030. The Government is implementing the European Child Guarantee,  an EU structural instrument, focusing on improving access to basic services  particularly for the most vulnerable. However, there have been  significant implementation delays of the social cohesion component of the EU Multiannual Financial Framework which could generate a missed opportunity for children if not accelerated.  
  
Important  steps to advance children’s well-being are being taken, yet evidence from recent studies highlight emerging child rights issues. Specifically, children need greater knowledge and skills to advance their mental health and well-being, building resilience and advancing healthy behaviors. Findings from a 2022  literature review conducted by UNICEF[1] together with a lower-secondary education survey[2] revealed that many adolescents have poor mental health with up to 25% showing self-harm tendencies, and 23% at-risk of emotional disorders. The 2024 ‘European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs’ report underscored a significant portion of adolescents practicing risky behaviors in Romania; 37% reported smoking and 34% had least one episode of heavy drinking. Meanwhile, Romanian children show low levels of skills, with 1 in 2 children not achieving basic competency in reading, mathematics and science[3] and 3 in 4 children being low achievers in digital skills[4]. Children’s well-being is also threatened by growing violence, especially in the online space. Preliminary findings from a  2025 prevalence study by UNICEF and NAPCRA revealed that 29% of children have experienced violence, with 15.8% affected in the past year. Children with disabilities were especially vulnerable, with 46.2% reporting lifetime exposure and 30.8% affected in the past year, underscoring the need to protect vulnerable groups. 
  
The ongoing Ukraine war increases children’s risk of vulnerability, with Romania positioned as a hub country with over 9.8  million border crossings since 2022. A total of 199,538 individuals from Ukraine have obtained temporary protection permits in Romania, including 52,371  children (27% of the total). The 2025 Socio-Economic Insight Survey revealed high vulnerability of the Ukrainian population residing in Romania, where 55% surveyed households included children. Additionally, 10,951 unaccompanied and separated children arrived in Romania since 2022, requiring access to specialized services to ensure their protection and facilitate family  reunification. Continued uncertainty requires integrated strategies in Romania’s national preparedness and resilience plans, combining emergency preparedness,  social cohesion, and system strengthening to support refugee children’s integration into Romanian communities. 
  
In  2025, the Romanian Government received Concluding Observations on the combined six and seventh periodic reports to the Committee on the Rights of  the Child. While the Committee praised the Government’s progress achieved in various child rights areas and legislative and policy measures taken to  support children, it also highlighted concerns, calling for urgent measures to address the following areas: abuse, neglect, sexual abuse and exploitation; children deprived of a family environment; children with disabilities; health and health services; standard of living and  asylum-seeking, refugee and migrant children.
