In 2025, UNICEF reinforced its position as a strategic partner to the Government and Parliament in Romania, leveraging the EU Child Guarantee to promote multi-sectoral collaboration and improve access to essential services to break the cycle of poverty for children. Over 2025, UNICEF’s role grew as a technical assistance partner to the Government on key child rights; a collaboration reflected by five projects supported through the European Commission’s technical support instruments (TSIs) and a Ministry of Health (MoH) project implemented under the Government’s Swiss Cooperation Programme. This year, UNICEF Romania mobilized over US$ 8.47 million, including US$ 4.1 million from private fundraising and US$ 4.37 million from the Government of Romania, and managed to leverage over US$ 690 million for scale-up of initiatives for children.
  
UNICEF partnered with the Parliament to increase policymakers’ capacities to prioritize child rights and child participation, leveraging Romania’s declaration of 2025 as the National Year of the Child. The Romanian Senate continued to champion children’s engagement in policy dialogue. With UNICEF support, the National Authority on Child Rights Protection and Adoption  (NAPCRA) finalized the secondary legislation for the amendments to the Child Protection law that require national and local authorities to consult children on policies affecting their lives.
  
Goal 1: Every Child  Survives and Thrives
  
Strengthening  Primary Healthcare System & Immunization 
  
Throughout the year, UNICEF supported primary health professional networks and local public health authorities which serve as gateways to improve child and adolescent health and well-being. UNICEF provided technical expertise to the Ministry of Health in development of the 2026-2030 National Reproductive Health Strategy Plan, covering a wide range of areas across all levels of care and bringing together actors from education and social protection sectors to implement joint measures. 
  
UNICEF continued to serve as a regional knowledge broker, sharing best practices among neighboring countries such as Serbia, Montenegro and Kazakhstan on immunization, medical emergency response, and management of child mass casualty situations. UNICEF also generated evidence on infant mortality and recommendations on methods to integrate public health and primary health interventions leading to improved child and adolescent health outcomes. UNICEF supported the MOH’s scaling up of 200 Integrated Community Centres (ICCs), previously modelled with UNICEF support, by establishing standard operating procedures.
  
UNICEF complemented government efforts to raise awareness about the benefits of child immunization, driving demand for vaccines and vaccination services at the community level. An online communication campaign reached nearly 235,000 women from eleven counties with the lowest vaccination rates, providing young mothers with facts about the benefits of immunization and debunking myths found on online social platforms. 
  
Ukrainian families still faced barriers in accessing primary healthcare, as many doctors treated them informally to avoid administrative burdens. In 2025, UNICEF advocated for simplification of registration processes and continued health information campaigns on prevention, vaccination, nutrition, and perinatal care reaching 1,500 Ukrainian children and caregivers through the ‘Mother and Baby space’ at the Ukrainian Refugee Center in Bucharest at RomExpo. 
  
Enhancing Mental Health and Psycho-Social Support (MHPSS) Systems for Children and Adolescents
  
In 2025, UNICEF advanced systemic improvements in adolescent mental health in Romania through policy advocacy, capacity building, and innovation, providing user-friendly resources for professionals working with children. At the same time, UNICEF broadened public discourse among young people to reduce stigma. The national health system was strengthened through an e-learning programme delivered in partnership with Romania Angel Appeal (RAA), enabling health professionals to identify and address adolescents’ mental health needs. Under the Bucharest  MHPSS model, UNICEF convened an intersectoral network of stakeholders, training 430 professionals on managing adolescent mental health cases and conducting informal psycho-social interventions, reaching more than 5,000 children.
  
In partnership with the Centre for Mental Health and the RAA, UNICEF reviewed primary and secondary MHPSS legislation to inform Romania’s mental health policy reform and advocate for measures that facilitate children’s timely access to services. The Romanian Parliament has expressed openness to joint efforts that ensure adolescents receive timely mental health support in schools and beyond.
  
With frontline professionals and young people, UNICEF co-designed innovative solutions for mental health and well-being. A screening tool, developed in collaboration with the Institute of Trauma Study and Treatment, supported over 4,000 children aged 10–19 to understand their mental health needs and encouraged conversations with caregivers. In partnership with Spotify, UNICEF produced locally adapted episodes of the On My Mind podcast. The digital platform “U-Support”  was also piloted in Romania, enhancing access to self-help resources for over 3,400 adolescents; resources that include psycho-education materials, an early warning system, and a referral mechanism. Furthermore, the Office supported UNICEF’s global supply division in designing the MindMe kit and piloting it in flood-affected areas of Gala¿i where it supported over 170 children. This kit will be made accessible globally as a resource to build children’s  resilience in emergencies, engaging them in activities that prevent and manage anxiety and depression while promoting positive mental health.
  
Strategic media partnerships with the Centre for Independent Journalism and Romanian universities promoted responsible reporting and stigma reduction. As a result of workshops held in  November 2025, representatives from five major universities—Bucharest, Cluj, Sibiu, Gala¿i, and Craiova—committed to integrating mental health topics into the curricula of Journalism, Communication, and Letters faculties. Additionally, over forty journalists from national and local media enhanced their understanding of solution-oriented journalism and responsible reporting; exposure to multiple case studies demonstrated how  performative media language can influence social mental health trends.
  
Goal 2: Every Child Learns and Acquires Skills 
  
Advancing Policy Frameworks
  
In 2025, UNICEF played a catalytic role in driving  system-level reform in Romania’s education sector, generating measurable  policy impact, institutional change, and strengthening national capacities.  Completion of the TSI Project on School Desegregation resulted in the Ministry of Education (MoE) adopting Order 7701/2024, establishing the first legally binding national monitoring methodology on school segregation. This milestone institutionalized a systemic mechanism for monitoring, preventing and responding to segregation, and in turn enabling the Government to identify proactively inequities. Building on this foundation, the National  Strategy for School Desegregation and accompanying Action Plan established a long-term framework for sustained reform and scaling of inclusive practices.
  
In its convening role, UNICEF supported key MoE structures, such as the National Curriculum Commission, the National Council for Financing Pre-University Education and the National Commission for School Desegregation, to shape evidence-based policies on curriculum, equity, and  resource allocation. These strategic partnerships fostered alliances aimed at aligning national educational frameworks more closely with EU standards.
  
Strengthening System Responses
  
Fragmented monitoring systems continued to hinder evidence-based decision-making in Romania’s  education reforms. To overcome these systemic barriers and fill data gaps, UNICEF supported evidence generation through assessments of the cost of  complementary early childhood education and care (ECEC) services, evaluations of inclusion practices for children with disabilities, studies on digital and science literacy, and research on appreciative parenting programmes. This knowledge generation will strengthen normative and budgetary reforms that expand access  to quality inclusive ECEC and education, reduce segregation, particularly for Roma children, and promote inclusive teaching for children with disabilities.
  
In 2025, UNICEF also generated evidence to support the integration of social-emotional learning (SEL) in classrooms, including the first national analysis of students’ well-being and mental health, research on EU best practices, and the development of practical teaching tools to  embed SEL in classrooms. Piloting is currently underway in 20 schools across the country to prepare for national scale-up. At the regional level, UNICEF  Romania facilitated knowledge sharing on SEL and desegregation issues through the co-hosted TSI–TAIEX workshop, positioning Romania as an active contributor to the EU education reforms dialogue.
  
By generating high-quality  evidence, institutionalizing pilot models into national frameworks, and building the capacities of teachers, school authorities, and local institutions, UNICEF ensured that reforms moved beyond project-level interventions toward sustained, at-scale practices. Strategic partnerships were central to achieving system-level results and strengthening UNICEF’s positioning as a trusted technical partner to the Romanian Government and a convener of key stakeholders and instruments that enhance Romania’s capacity to  deliver equitable and inclusive educational reforms. 
  
Integrating Ukrainian Children into the National Education System
  
In 2025, UNICEF continued to address systemic gaps in the enrollment procedures, refugees’ need for language support, and access to ECEC. Over 23,000 children were enrolled in the national education system as an audient or student. In partnership with  Step-by-Step, HoltIS and JRS, UNICEF supported over 16 Play, Learning & Parenting Hubs, benefiting over 4,800 young children gained access to ECEC and complementary learning, and parenting education activities reaching over 2,700 caregivers and benefiting over 3,700 children.
  
Goal 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence, Abuse and Exploitation
  
With the Ministry of Labor, Family, Youth and Social Solidarity (MLFYSS), the National Authority for Protection of Child  Rights and Adoption (NAPCRA), and other key counterparts, UNICEF catalyzed  results, addressing key protection issues for children living in poverty, in  the childcare system, facing abuse, neglect, and exploitation, and affected  by the war in Ukraine. UNICEF also partnered with colleagues to position Romania as a champion at the regional level in fighting violence against children. 
  
Strengthening the Social Services Workforce
  
Together with the National College of Social  Workers (CNASR), UNICEF strengthened Romania’s social services workforce, serving as a critical enabler for reducing equity gaps and implementing social assistance reforms following the 2024 normative framework  developments. To boost motivation and expand coverage in rural and remote areas, UNICEF and CNASR designed and piloted an incentive package in 20 counties, reaching 450 social workers and 190 local authority representatives. These incentive packages combined financial measures such as rural bonuses, relocation grants, or housing subsidies with non-financial measures such as mentorships or mandatory training programmes. Job fairs attracted 185 participants, supporting recruitment efforts. Curriculum development was finalized in June, laying the foundation for improved  professional standards. While challenges remain, progress is on track, positioning the workforce to better serve vulnerable communities and deliver on reform objectives.
  
Enhancing Child Rights and Child Protection System
  
UNICEF continued to provide technical assistance to  advance child protection reforms with a strong focus on children with  disabilities (CWD). New childcare modalities were tested to ensure quality family-type care for children with severe disabilities, who comprise 30% of  those still living in residential care. Technical assistance was also provided to local administrations in the design of six project proposals planning to leverage €7.5 million through EU structural funds to advance rehabilitation and family support services for children with disabilities. 
  
UNICEF continued to ensure safeguards for vulnerable refugee children, partnering with national and local authorities in the development of Romania’s first national guide on  best interest assessment of unaccompanied children, as well as a local governance model for child refugees’ social integration. UNICEF advanced anti-trafficking efforts through the development of normative frameworks focused on identification, referral, and intervention. These efforts were complemented by capacity-building activities for the national childcare system and awareness initiatives aimed at adolescents, including an educational board designed to help them  recognize signs of trafficking.
  
Addressing Violence against Children
  
Although Romania’s child protection legislation aligns with international standards, violence against children (VAC) remains widespread. Experts highlight fragmented legislation, lack of integrated services, and absence of unified data systems as barriers to effective protection. Through a TSI project on VAC with NAPCRA, UNICEF is working to close these gaps by promoting evidence-based, child-centered reforms. A landmark prevalence study conducted by UNICEF and NAPCRA revealed that nearly one in three children (28.9%) report exposure to violence, with 15.8% of cases occurring within the past year. The study provides extensive data on the types of violence disaggregated by age, gender, and family setting. This research complemented by a legislative assessment and mapping of existing services, together form the basis for an evidence-driven national roadmap to address VAC; guide capacity-building for professionals, caregivers, and children; and close critical gaps in legislation, service integration, and  unified data systems. 
  
In October 2025, Romania hosted the Regional Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Europe and Central Asia convening over 200 participants from more than 30  countries. Governments pledged legislative reforms, integrated child protection systems, and digital safety measures, while children’s voices shaped solutions on cyberbullying, mental health, and safe reporting, reinforcing that protection must be real, accessible, and  trusted.  
  
Goal 4: Every Child lives in a Safe and Sustainable Climate & Environment
  
UNICEF advanced children’s and adolescents’ leadership in Romania’s climate agenda by partnering with the Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests, the Ministry of Education,  and the Chamber of Deputies’ Environment Committee to promote inclusive, participatory policy dialogue. In 2025, together with its partners, UNICEF facilitated structured engagements between children and decision-makers, including the Local Conference of Youth, local youth dialogues, national consultations, and meetings with the Environment Committee. Romanian children further expanded their climate knowledge and advocacy skills through capacity-building sessions delivered by UNICEF HQ experts. Children became advocates and role models for peers engaged in initiatives such as the Romanian Commercial Bank’s Zbor/Fly programme and The Youth Platform for Sustainability, inspiring broader youth participation in climate action. 
  
Children also served as keynote speakers at the International Climate Change Summit in Bucharest, the largest Eastern European event on climate innovation and sustainability with more than 1,000 participants, amplifying their voices in national and global climate  processes. The Romanian children and youth advocacy messages and climate action initiatives also were shared for the third year in a row at the 2025 UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Brazil.  
  
The Office reinforced its commitment to a child-focused climate agenda, developing the first-ever Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in Romania. In partnership with the Italian National Committee for UNICEF, children from Romania and four other countries participated in an international climate hackathon, developing concrete solutions to make Bucharest a greener and child-friendly city. Climate education was integrated into Romania’s school system by institutionalizing the Green Week programme across all pre-university schools, embedding  environmental awareness and sustainability into classrooms nationwide.  
  
UNICEF has also strengthened the Government’s capacity to communicate with and engage children and adolescents in emergency preparedness. Under the regional’s office initiative, the country office in collaboration with the Government conducted  a foresight exercise assessing the “child-friendliness” of the emergency system in the efforts to strengthen the national system’s disaster risk reduction  responses. These efforts resulted in a set of recommendations and an action plan for key stakeholders. Significant regional interest in this preparedness approach has been expressed, with the Government sharing lessons from the foresight exercise with other EU member states in several forums and the EU Delegation communicating interest in adapting the methodology.  In collaboration with the Department of Emergency Situations (DSU), UNICEF also developed a series of animations to teach children how to respond to emergency situations, reaching children nationwide through schools, social media and DSU’s mobile application.
  
Goal 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life    
  
Leveraging Resources to Reduce Child Poverty - EU Child Guarantee
  
As part of a newly awarded TSI project, UNICEF is supporting Romania to strengthen the effectiveness of child rights policies with focus on advancing the European Child Guarantee  framework. The project reinforces Romania’s National Action Plan for  Implementing the Child Guarantee (CG-NAP) by improving monitoring and  evaluation systems, enhancing budget planning and accountability, and  embedding meaningful child participation in decision-making. These efforts will  ensure that Romania’s Child Guarantee commitments translate into tangible  results for children, including reducing the risk of poverty or social exclusion for 500,000 children. Romania’s progress is setting an important precedent for the region, demonstrating how strong policy frameworks can be operationalized to deliver real impact.
  
In 2025, the CO participated in a regional business model to advance knowledge sharing and strategies for implementing the European Child Guarantee (ECG) across EU member states and  candidate countries. A key milestone was the establishment of ECG Hubs in Croatia and Romania, serving as platforms for peer learning and technical exchange across five EU member states and nine candidate countries.
  
Romania leads the documentation process for knowledge management interventions, systematically  capturing and disseminating promising and emerging practices from EU countries in priority areas, such as evidence-based development of ECG  National Action Plans, monitoring and evaluation frameworks, budget  allocation and expenditure tracking, effective implementation at local level of key interventions under the CG-NAP (‘localization’), child participation,  integrated community-based services and ECEC.  This approach strengthens policy coherence,  supports scaling of effective models, and positions Romania as a regional leader in advancing inclusive, evidence-based reforms and governance for children.
  
Advocating for Child Rights and Children’s Voices High on the Agenda
  
Through strategic partnerships with the Government, Parliament, and the President’s Office, UNICEF advanced advocacy and policy dialogue collaboratively with children and adolescents, contributing to systemic changes in how children’s voices influence governance and policymaking. As in previous years, children were speakers at international conferences and high-level events at the Government and the Parliament, amplifying children’s voices in over 80 engagements at local, national and international levels. 
  
Through amendments to the Child Protection Law 272/2004, Romania became the first country in Europe to institutionalize at both national and local levels consultations with children in decision-making processes. In 2025, UNICEF supported NAPCRA in operationalizing these  amendments with development of three official operational guidelines that provide a unified, practical framework for all public authorities. As part of the Office’s new TSI project, UNICEF is also strengthening social norms and professionals’ capacities to promote meaningful child participation. 
  
UNICEF enhanced other national platforms for participation, including the UNICEF-supported Children’s Board, 7 local Children’s Councils, and the National Students’ Council, equipping over 230,000 children and young people nationwide with skills and capacities to develop advocacy messages, express their views, and engage. UNICEF continued to strengthen awareness and engagement on gender equality via child and youth co-created advocacy initiatives and social media channels, highlighting key messages from community level to high-level forums like the Commission on the Status of Women Conference and UNICEF’s Global Girls Advisory Board. UNICEF also partnered with the National Agency for Equal Opportunities between Women and Men to promote  gender equality and fight domestic violence and all forms of discrimination.
  

Advancing Social Policy and Fiscal Space for Inclusive Systems   
  
Romania’s social protection system continued to face pressures in 2025, with social benefits levels capped at 2024 level, including state allowance for children and other social benefits dedicated for children. Navigating these challenges, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Finance to develop a national methodology for public spending reviews: a tool designed to support the Ministry of Finance to monitor child-related expenditures across all sectors and recommend measures to improve public spending efficiency while safeguarding investments in social  protection for children and families.
  
In  2025, UNICEF followed a system-strengthening approach to address Ukrainian refugees’ needs, built around shock-responsive social protection, integration of refugees into the national social protection system, and capacity development at the municipal level to support long-term inclusion of refugees and migrants in Romanian service delivery systems. Through the continuation of a TSI with 2 municipalities in Romania and including 2 other countries (Poland and Slovakia), UNICEF strengthened local administrations’ capacities to enhance refugee and migrant children’s and caregivers’ access to quality and inclusive services, contributing to long-term integration strategies for the above-mentioned vulnerable groups. During the first nine months of 2025, the Government invested around $4.7 million to enroll Ukrainian refugees in 11 social benefit programmes. In the second half of 2025, UNICEF and MLFYSS commissioned a review of refugee enrollment in the national social protection system, identifying bottlenecks, and providing recommendations to streamline the process. As a result of UNICEF’s support, more than 5,400  Ukrainian children accessed the universal child allowance, 461 low-income families received poverty-targeted benefits, and 267 persons with disabilities obtained disability support. 
  
To build a national shock-responsive social  protection, UNICEF provided technical assistance with the Prime-Minister team and MLFYSS to develop policy recommendations for amending the national social protection system’s legal, financial, and operational frameworks, allowing for vertical and horizontal expansion of social benefits during emergency situations.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The Office had multiple lessons over 2025 including participation in UNICEF’s Business Model Initiative, testing approaches and enhancing evidence generation to inform strategic shifts in the Office’s high-income country (HIC) agenda. Key learning from this process underscored the importance for the Office to accelerate leveraging roles that advance results at-scale for children.
·       Strengthening governance systems & policy frameworks
In Romania’s high-income context, UNICEF’s added value is accompanying government reform processes through policy dialogue and targeted, government-funded timebound technical assistance to ensure children’s rights remain central to political commitments, policies, budgets, and institutional frameworks. System strengthening initiatives, such as child-focused budget reviews or monitoring tools for national strategies, build capacity to achieve policy visions for children. Targeted expertise can accelerate reform processes, addressing emerging child rights issues such as children’s post-COVID mental health challenges, growing online violence against children, or harms posed by climate change.
UNICEF’s convening role is increasingly critical, connecting stakeholders, policies, data, and service delivery across sectors and governance levels. The Office builds connected systems horizontally and vertically; for example, UNICEF partners with national authorities to develop data systems that align actions, while ensuring through development of monitoring tools at local levels that national frameworks translate into coherent local action. This vertical and horizontal coordination creates a continuous feedback loop between policy and practice, ensuring that evidence from communities informs national decisions, and that national reforms empower local actors. 
·       Leveraging data & information systems
As custodian of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, UNICEF is uniquely positioned to strengthen Romania’s expertise through multi-country platforms that elevate child rights. By facilitating high-level dialogue on obligations, these platforms can drive scalable system innovations within Romania and across neighboring countries, pooling knowledge and experience to produce cutting-edge learning tools and knowledge products.
Partnering with the Government, UNICEF has already promoted knowledge exchange between Romania, EU member states, and pre-accession countries. For example, the Romania and Croatia Office and Europe and Central Asia Regional Office established in 2025 a regional knowledge hub on implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG) Framework. This hub advances cross-regional learning and expertise that has enabled Romania to strengthen the political dialogue and strategic policy space among EU and pre-accession countries. In 2025, Romania transferred good practices across neighboring countries (e.g., Albania, North Macedonia, and Moldova) on issues such as establishment of results-based national action plans, implementation of monitoring tools for countries’ ECG action plans, or integration of meaningful child participation. Likewise, Romania’s lessons from the Ukrainian refugee response create the momentum for learning exchange on child-centred emergency preparedness of national systems, establishing shock-responsive social protection or child-centred emergency communication.
Advancing regional learning fosters innovation and fresh perspectives for both host and visiting countries. These collaborative platforms can evolve into change-making engines, mobilizing greater investments for children and enabling replication of innovative approaches globally. Romanian pioneering of ‘expert hubs’ in areas like ECG implementation and emergency preparedness, offer tailored support to candidate countries and curate cross-country collaboration that can translate into regional and/or global experience exchanges.
·       Advancing partnerships and resources for children
These Office shifts require strengthening strategic advocacy and sustained engagement with the Government, Parliament, EU institutions, national authorities, CSOs, and the private sector to shape agendas and secure commitments for children. Actions must also extend to local levels to guarantee systemic change reaches rural communities where vulnerabilities are greatest.
The Office’s partnerships have evolved with a focus on strategic cooperation rather than development aid. In these partnerships, the Office has accompanied the Government’s reform agendas through policy dialogue and targeted technical assistance to ensure children’s rights remain at the heart of political commitments, policies, budgets and institutional framework.  In 2025, the Office’s partnership technical expertise with the Government was demonstrated by five government projects supported through the European Commission’s technical support instruments (TSIs) and a Ministry of Health (MoH) project implemented under the Government’s Swiss Cooperation Programme. UNICEF’s technical support focuses on generating high-quality evidence, institutionalizing pilot models into national frameworks, and building the capacities of professionals, authorities, and local institutions, which in turn ensures that reforms move beyond project-level interventions toward sustained, at-scale practices. Strategic partnerships were central to strengthening UNICEF’s positioning as a trusted technical partner for the Government and convener of key stakeholders that enhances Romania’s capacity to deliver equitable and inclusive reforms. 
The Office also will broaden collaboration with IFIs and the private sector to unlock strong partnerships and innovative financing, moving beyond funding to joint efforts that amplify expertise, voice, and influence, which in turn accelerate results and close equity gaps. Building on achievements in business engagement and policy influence, this shift will leverage multi-sectoral partnerships for greater impact.
Amid limited fiscal space globally and in Romania, the Office will work with the Government to identify efficiencies that sustain positive outcomes for children, such as child-sensitive public expenditure analysis and platforms for financial data transparency to optimize existing resources.
Looking ahead, insights from the 2025 business model initiative will refine strategies, strengthen partnerships, and maintain agility in advancing child rights. The Office’s fine-tuning of working on an HIC agenda will position the Office as a model for partnership building, strategic advocacy, and catalytic programming through high-level policy advice, evidence generation, innovation, and targeted technical assistance.

In 2025, Serbia’s economic growth has slowed due to heightened domestic and external uncertainties. Growth is projected at around 2 per cent in 2025, with a recovery expected in 2026 and 2027. Long-term macroeconomic policies and strong financial buffers are helping the country manage this challenging environment. Public debt has fallen to below 50 per cent of GDP, and Serbia secured its first investment-grade sovereign credit rating in 2024. 
Serbia currently faces significant fiscal risk, particularly around energy-sector state-owned enterprises. Naftna Industrija Srbije (NIS), Serbia’s dominant oil and gas company that contributes up to 7 per cent of GDP, is majority-owned by Russia’s Gazprom Neft, and United States sanctions targeting Gazprom Neft have created legal, financial and operational risks for the company. This may disrupt fuel supply chains, increase energy costs and affect growth. 
Serbia’s close integration into European value chains has supported higher foreign direct investment, job creation and economic growth compared to other Western Balkan countries. However, when measured against newer European Union (EU) member states, Serbia’s performance is less favourable, particularly in terms of labour productivity and the quality of public services and institutions. Public financial management systems have steadily improved, but the mid-term budgetary framework plays a limited role, while shortcomings in public investment management, including around the organization of the EXPO exhibition in 2027, raise concerns about procurement practices and accountability. 
While Serbia has achieved high levels of basic service coverage, it is among Europe’s least equal countries in terms of income. In 2024, 13.6 per cent of the population experienced severe material and social deprivation. The at-risk-of-poverty rate for children was 19.5 per cent in 2023. Poverty is on the decline, but overall spending on core poverty-targeted programmes remains modest, while increased spending on birth grants, a non-targeted pro-natality measure, has been absorbing an increasing share of the social assistance envelope. The remaining poor are increasingly concentrated among pensioners, the long-term unemployed or those completely out of the labour force, including families with children. Targeted policies and cash assistance will remain a prerequisite for further progress. 
To address the cost-of-living crisis, the Government imposed margin and price controls on distributors and retailers of food and household essentials, covering one third of the consumption basket or 80 per cent of retail turnover. These controls, in place for six months starting 1 September 2025, resulted in a temporary easing of inflation and limitation on the perceived excess profitability of external retail chains. This provided short-term relief, as households in Serbia spend a large proportion of their income on food – 36.6 per cent compared to 17 per cent of those in the EU. The impact of these measures could be sustained with longer-term strategies and targeted policies to protect families in need. 
Throughout 2025, the social and political context of Serbia was marked by year-long demonstrations that began after the tragic death of 15 people on 1 November 2024, caused by the collapse of a concrete canopy in the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station. The incident, blamed on corruption leading to substandard renovation work on the railway station, sparked widespread dissatisfaction with current political structures. The initial protest escalated into a nationwide student movement demanding an end to corruptive practices, greater transparency, and identification and prosecution of those responsible for the incident. Students became the leading force in demanding government accountability and systemic reform. Throughout the year, Serbia saw a surge in civil disobedience, with student-led protests and traffic blockades occurring in Belgrade and other cities and increased frequency of arrests of protesters. In January 2025 the Prime Minister announced his resignation, and the Government underwent a reshuffle. Tensions however remained high, with several large-scale demonstrations organized by both political factions and high political polarization and breakdown of social fabric in the country. 
Media and civil society organization (CSO) reports addressed police violence against youth and minors on several occasions. Backsliding in the enabling environment for civil society as well as journalists, media professionals and outlets has also been noted by several human rights monitoring mechanisms. Several child rights were at stake: freedom of expression, and the right of association and peaceful assembly, but also right to education, with many schools deciding to support the student movement through blockades or suspension of classes. 
The Serbian Government has continued to declare EU membership its strategic goal, but the European Commission’s Enlargement Report remained critical towards Serbia, noting a slowdown in reforms, especially in the area of judiciary and fundamental rights, a backsliding on freedom of expression and an anti-EU narrative used in Serbian media outlets and by high-level political office holders. Serbia has actively engaged in and started to deliver on the implementation of the new Growth Plan for the Western Balkans, approved in 2024, which offers Serbia an opportunity for reforms and potential funding of up to EUR 1.7 billion under the European Commission’s Reform and Growth Facility. The Reform Agenda adopted by Serbia under the Reform and Growth Facility covers reforms in the areas of: (i) business environment and private sector development; (ii) green and digital transition; (iii) human capital; (iv) fundamental rights and the rule of law. At a global level, Serbia continues to balance between major world powers – United States, Russia and China – complicating its EU path and introducing diverse geopolitical scenarios. 
Serbia continued to progress in e-governance. As assessed by the World Bank, at the end of 2025, Serbia ranked second in Europe and sixth globally for the digital transformation of public administration. An increase of ICT exports continued, likely to amount to around EUR 4.5 billion at year end, with further potential for growth. 
Policy development and coordination are regulated but not systematically enforced. Serbia has not yet adopted a Country Development Plan as a key national strategic document. The public consultation process remains insufficient, and Serbia still lacks a roadmap for developing child-focused budgeting and an action plan for children. 
In the past Country Programme cycle, Serbia made positive progress towards the child-related targets of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including the reduction of maternal, under-5 and neonatal mortality, stunting and wasting, as well as access to early childhood development (ECD) services and preschool education. The country achieved high levels of basic service coverage by actively pursuing national reforms including health care, ECD, preschool, inclusive education, childcare reform, deinstitutionalization and access to mental health services. All these achievements were supported by UNICEF’s technical assistance, policy advice and capacity-building. However, disparities and high levels of inequities persist, by rural–urban status, wealth quintile, ethnicity and disability. These inequities disproportionately affect children in rural and marginalized areas, including those from ethnic minorities, Roma children, children with disabilities, and those impacted by migration.

In this fifth and final year of implementation of the Country Programme 2021–2025, the Serbia Country Office focused on closing important projects related to national reforms and sustaining the impact of system-level changes, in the areas of child and maternal health, Early Childhood Development (ECD), inclusive education, preschool education, digital education, child protection reform, youth policy and public finance for children. The country office undertook consultations with the Government and all partners for the planning and design of its Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026–2030. 
USING THE POWER OF EVIDENCE TO DRIVE CHANGE FOR CHILDREN (CHILD RIGHTS MONITORING)  
In early 2025, UNICEF published and disseminated its Situation Analysis (SitAn), which provides the Government and other duty bearers with an independent analysis of the situation of children in Serbia to deepen stakeholders’ understanding and evidence base of children’s needs, potential and capacity, and guide stakeholders’ policy advocacy and partnership responses. 
The seventh round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 7) was initiated and implemented in partnership with the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia. Funding of over US$1 million was secured by UNICEF, UNFPA and the Government of Serbia. As in previous rounds, one survey is conducted for the general population and one for Roma settlements, providing a unique overview of the developmental landscape for many marginalized groups. Following careful consideration with relevant government line ministries and stakeholders, several areas of enquiry were expanded or introduced: reliance on clean fuels, mental health, food insecurity experience, water quality testing and others. 
UNICEF participated in the global evaluation on Early Childhood Development (ECD), which produced a case study report for Serbia that will be presented to stakeholders in early 2026. It is anticipated that the findings and recommendation will reinvigorate discussions about governmental cross-sectoral collaboration on ECD.  
Through its partnership with the Child Rights Centre, UNICEF continued to support the monitoring of indicators on the implementation of Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) recommendations, and the CSOs produced an alternative report that was presented to the UN Child Rights Committee of the State Party. An online monitoring platform is publicly available, and a child-friendly report enabled the participation of children in monitoring the status of recommendations. UNICEF continued to support CSOs and independent institutions actively advocating for child rights across different sectors, supporting both their public reporting as well as engagement in formal advisory mechanisms and UN human rights mechanisms. CSO members of the Network of Organizations for Children (MODS) effectively organized and participated in public policy consultations on the EU Child Guarantee. 
PROGRAMMING AT-SCALE RESULTS FOR CHILDREN 
Goal area 1 – Health & Early Childhood Development 
UNICEF advocacy significantly advanced the recognition of family-friendly care as a core component of quality maternal, neonatal and child health (MNCH) services, contributing to Ministry of Health (MoH) investments. A study visit to the WHO Collaborating Centre for MNCH in Trieste catalysed MoH endorsement of UNICEF’s concept to leverage ongoing infrastructure investments to model a child- and family-friendly children’s hospital. UNICEF supported regulatory amendments, neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) equipment investments, and capacity-building to operationalize neonatal care guidelines, including international training for neonatologists and nurses from eight NICUs. UNICEF advocacy and technical assistance to maternity wards and NICUs contributed to continued reductions in neonatal mortality, which declined nationally from 3.78 (2020) to 2.89 (2024), and in Niš from 7.26 to 4.3 per 1,000 live births. Persistent maternal mortality fluctuations and regional disparities highlighted the need for continued system strengthening. UNICEF, in partnership with MoH, supported the development of new antenatal care guidance, presented to more than 800 gynaecologists and 50 primary health care (PHC) facilities. An Institute of Public Health (IPH) assessment of antenatal care capacities is informing MoH investments, while a digital pregnancy e-health record is being piloted for national scale-up in 2026. Approximately 58,000 women were reached through a podcast, focus groups and workshops, promoting the campaign ‘You and Me from the Start – Tracking the pregnancy journey together’. Furthermore, social and behaviour change (SBC)-informed tools to increase vaccination coverage are being implemented nationwide. In Novi Pazar, the area most affected by measles, their use already contributed to a 25 per cent increase in MMR1 coverage. 
With UNICEF support, Serbia has successfully integrated responsive and playful caregiving, early stimulation, parental mental health and well-being, and violence prevention into routine PHC services: home-visiting nurse services, paediatric care, and developmental counselling services. By end 2025, comprehensive capacity-building reached more than 60 per cent of all nurses across the country and competent support was provided to 111,000 caregivers, supported by national policy, guidelines and standardized tools, with reinforced emphasis on gender-responsive and non-violent parenting, caregiver mental health and well-being, and outreach to rural and Roma families. Findings of the costing exercise of home-visiting services conducted in 2025 is expected to improve service efficiency and targeting. The skills of paediatricians and health professionals have been strengthened to ensure early identification of developmental risks and timely referral, through both in-service training and the integration of parenting, child development and nurturing care principles into pre-service curricula at medical faculties and medical schools for nurses. Through a stronger integration within PHC services and preschools, the Bebbo parenting app, which surpassed 136,000 downloads in Serbia.. 
Significant progress was achieved in scaling up the intersectoral family-centred early childhood intervention (FECI) model, coordinated by developmental counselling services in PHC centres (together with preschool and social welfare institutions), and now reaching approximately 80 per cent of districts nationwide. The model promotes coordinated, multidisciplinary support for children with developmental risks or disabilities and their caregivers. Services reached close to 9,000 children and caregivers, including those from small rural municipalities historically lacking access to specialized support. Work also began on inter-municipal service delivery models, enabling small and resource-constrained municipalities to benefit from the expertise of larger centres. Amendments to by-laws ensured full legislative recognition of all FECI service components within the PHC system, enabling uniform implementation nationwide. 
The upcoming establishment of the Institute for Early Childhood Development and Inclusion will mark an essential step in consolidating Serbia’s national early childhood intervention (ECI) architecture. UNICEF provided technical support in designing training for institute personnel, laying the groundwork for a national professional development system for ECI. 
Parenting and ECD interventions have been integrated into local government budgets and action plans in a growing number of municipalities. With UNICEF technical assistance, local governments have been supported to mobilize and allocate domestic resources, including through national grant schemes administered by the Ministry of Family Care and Demography for parenting support. UNICEF supported over 50 local self-governments (LSGs) – i.e., close to one third of LSGs across Serbia – to strengthen cross-sectoral policy, strategic and financial planning for Early ECD, parenting support and ECI. This resulted in the mobilization of approximately EUR 500,000, financed exclusively in 2025 from local government resources, and over EUR 4 million from national grants channelled to 34 municipalities. This demonstrates the feasibility of sustainable, decentralized financing models and aligns directly with the Global Call to Action on increased public investment, decentralized financing, and long-term budgetary commitment. 
Goal area 2 – Education 
Over the five-year period, Serbia achieved transformative progress in early childhood education (ECE), continued to expand ECE coverage from 52% in 2015 to 68% in 2024, and to increase quality and equity. Under the leadership of the Ministry of Education (MoE), in partnership with World Bank, and with UNICEF technical assistance, the new preschool curriculum “Years of Ascent” was rolled out nationwide, marking a systemic shift towards play based, child-led learning. Close to 22,400 educators (95% of all pre-school teachers) in public and private ECE institutions were empowered through a comprehensive capacity building program to apply a new, high-quality, inclusive pedagogy, benefiting more than 235,000 children. To promote inclusion and reduce gaps in preschool attendance, UNICEF supported Inclusive Teams in all 162 preschool institutions to plan policies and support vulnerable children and families. Additionally, over 3,300 primary school staff, including psychologists, pedagogues, teachers, and principals, were trained to ease preschool-to-primary transitions, reducing stress and improving pedagogical alignment. UNICEF also developed the first analysis on public–private partnerships in ECE and strengthened the capacities of municipalities to implement quality and equitable mechanisms for such partnerships, which have contributed to increase in ECE coverage in recent years. 
UNICEF’s technical assistance played a pivotal role in strengthening the institutional, legal and policy framework for inclusive education (IE), throughout the four-year national reform, led by MoE with UNICEF technical assistance and EU financial support. The four-year IE reform resulted in a substantial decrease in enrolment in special schools (from close to 7,500 in 2014 to less than 4,700 in 2024), and the tripling of individual education plans supporting children with special needs in regular schools (from 7,000 in 2013 to more than 20,000 children in 2024). With EU support and UNICEF technical assistance, MoE established 12 resource centres (RCs), an innovative mechanism aimed at supporting regular schools with applying inclusive practices and using assistive technologies (AT). The resource centres supported 975 schools attended by close to 7,000 students with disabilities (467 schools, 2,800 teachers, and 2,821 children with disabilities in 2025). UNICEF also supported model schools for inclusive education, and their cooperation with other schools. In 2025, UNICEF continued to partner with MoE on strengthening RC capacities to provide AT, and piloted social robotics in education.  In cooperation with MoE and national institutions, new capacity-building programs on IE and learning support were developed, strengthening competencies of over 9,000 professionals, and benefiting close to 125,300 students.  
To address learning crisis and improve quality of education, in partnership with the Institute for the Evaluation of Education Quality, UNICEF modeled and piloted a school improvement program, expected to benefit 186 schools and 93.000 students with low performance.  
Digital transformation accelerated in recent years, especially through internet connectivity, laying the foundation for data-driven policies and modern learning practices, fostered through digital education. Since 2019, UNICEF has supported the launch of the National Educational Platform (NEP) as the central hub for online teacher training and digital resources, complemented by the Learning Passport, which provides structured access to quality learning materials widely used by preschool and school staff (totalling 327,000 active users in 2025) and which hosts virtual learning communities for preschool professionals. In this five-year period, trainings were conducted through the NEP, improving the competencies of close to 423,000 teachers. Digital mentors supported half of all schools in Serbia. To strengthen digital competencies of both students and teachers, Serbia invested in infrastructure, connectivity, teacher training and a new Digital Competency Framework, with UNICEF support. To enhance digital safety, UNICEF developed resources such as the ‘Digital Compass for Parents’ to help parents guide children’s safe and responsible online engagement, focusing on digital literacy, protection from online risks, and positive participation in the digital world. In 2025, EdTech libraries and school were equipped with devices and connectivity, and supported through STEM sets, mini-grants, guides and teacher training, and will inform further reforms financed by World Bank and EU.  
Goal area 3 – Child Protection 
In 2025, Serbia made significant strides towards ensuring that girls and boys vulnerable to violence, abuse and exploitation are better protected through strengthened institutional and legislative frameworks. UNICEF contributed to expanding family-based care and parenting support, advancing reforms to prevent violence and child marriage, and reinforcing justice systems to uphold the best interests of the child. 
With UNICEF support, Serbia made significant progress in strengthening family-based care options for children in need of alternative care. The quality of foster care was improved through comprehensive capacity-building for professionals and foster families, thus enhancing skills in standard and specialized care. UNICEF continued to support local foster care campaigns, which resulted in an increasing number of foster families. Serbia invested in improving the quality and availability of local social services, including home help service, day-care services, family counselling, and early childhood interventions especially for families of children with disabilities, through strengthening capacities of professionals to deliver evidence-based parenting programs. These programs integrate structured, family-centered support for children with developmental disabilities. Services now provide more consistent, structured engagement with parents, demonstrating measurable improvements in service quality and reducing risks of unnecessary family separation. UNICEF supported Ministry of Labour, Employment, Veterans and Social Affairs (MoLEVSA) in developing the new Social Protection Strategy. 
With UNICEF support, Serbia strengthened its child protection system, with specific attention to addressing child marriage, violent disciplining, and sexual exploitation and abuse. UNICEF’s advocacy helped secure high-level government commitment to develop a new national strategic framework for ending violence against children (VAC), leading to the Minister’s endorsement and Serbia’s formal pledge to end VAC at a regional conference in Romania. This commitment has already driven measurable progress towards legislative reform. In collaboration with UNICEF, the Government initiated procedural steps to amend the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence and the Criminal Code, which, once adopted, will strengthen legal safeguards for children. The Government announced Family Law amendments for 2026 that will introduce a ban on corporal punishment and child marriage. UNICEF support to the National Coalition for Ending Child Marriage also contributed to advance legal reforms. Efforts are underway to mainstream VAC prevention programmes across health, education and social welfare systems, including programmes focused on strengthening parenting skills for non-violent child discipline.  
Cooperation with the Ministry of Justice resulted in the signing of the three-year EU-funded project ‘Promoting Children’s Access to Justice’ aimed at strengthening the child justice system by reinforcing institutional capacities and ensuring the sustained implementation of an improved legal and policy framework for children in conflict with the law, child victims/witnesses, and free legal aid provision. In addition, UNICEF contributed to the new Juvenile Justice Law and amendment to the Law on Protection from Domestic Violence, and supported capacity-building of judges, prosecutors, lawyers, and representatives of centres for social work in the protection of children in criminal proceedings, child participation, the best interests of the child, and child-sensitive communication. 
UNICEF supported  Serbian Commissariat for Refugees and Migration (SCRM) and MoLEVSA to strengthen national systems for the protection of refugee and migrant children, through the promotion of child-sensitive data protection standards, the revision of  the Standard Operating Procedures for the Protection of Refugee and Migrant Children,  the development of training curricula on gender-based violence and child protection in emergencies, and the support to  the SCRM Migration Training Center, and to the delivery of comprehensive child protection, gender-based violence prevention and response, and Mental Health services. 
 
Goal area 4 –Young People 
UNICEF successfully provided technical assistance to the Government and civil society to implement the Youth Strategy, enhancing youth participation, civic engagement, and access to quality non-formal education through youth centres, clubs, and digital learning and career guidance tools. 
In partnership with the MoH, MoE, MoLEVSA, Ministry of Tourism and Youth (MoTY), and other ministries, UNICEF continued to promote and support the availability and accessibility of quality mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services nationwide. In the aftermath of the Third International Conference on Mental Health, co-organized by UNICEF and the MoH, six ministries renewed their commitment to the inter-ministerial Memorandum of Understanding and its Action Plan on Mental Health, mobilizing national resources to improve service quality, accessibility and intersectoral coordination around mental health for children and adolescents in Serbia. In 2025, UNICEF focused its support on capacity-building of front-line professionals from the health, education, child welfare and youth sectors, embedding referral pathways in health, education, social welfare and youth systems through the implementation of the Youth Minimum Service Package in 10 per cent of the municipalities across the country, and contributing to the revision of the legal framework, including the Amendments to the Law on the Protection of Persons with Mental Disorders. The nationally recognized SveJeOK platform reached more than 140,000 users (up 47 per cent from 98,000 in 2024), following a nationwide campaign that reached more than 1 million people with messages on self-care, family and peer support. 
To address not in education, employment or training (NEET) rates and improve transitions from education to employment, UNICEF developed regulatory standards for career guidance and counselling services in partnership with the Office for Dual Education. Full implementation is expected through the Youth Guarantee, promoting equitable, inclusive lifelong learning and recognition of non-formal, informal and prior learning. The UPSHIFT programme directly supported 1,000 youth with seed funding to address issues of poverty, gender inequity and social disengagement and reached an additional 10,000 across 40 municipalities. Gender-focused initiatives, including Girls’ Skills in ICT, addressed systemic barriers limiting girls’ participation in the tech sector, providing non-formal education, mentorship and evidence-informed advocacy.  
UNICEF empowered youth across Serbia to influence local policies, volunteer and engage in civic action. Through youth centres, U-Report and consultations, adolescents – including those most at risk – shaped services and decisions while supporting local governments to integrate youth voices into policymaking. The most significant achievement in 2025 was the scale-up of the Local Volunteering Service model developed by UNICEF and integrated to the national youth system through the Ministry of Tourism and Youth’s investment of US$500,000 to support nationwide expansion, marking a shift from project-based support to sustainable public financing. Digital participation through U-Report, now gathering 25,000 adolescents and young people, transformed youth engagement from isolated consultations into structured, evidence-informed processes. During the 2021–2025 CPD period, U-Report was used in youth consultation processes in close to 15 per cent of municipalities in Serbia. UNICEF Youth Advisory Board members were supported to enhance their skills in advocacy, communication, teamwork and leadership through structured engagement and the National Assembly, and contributed to policymaking on digital violence, mental health, inclusive education and violence prevention. 
Goal Area 5 - Social Policy  
Over the five-year period of the CPD (2021–2025), UNICEF has prioritized better evidence, stronger institutions and child-sensitive budget tools as key pathways to change towards more equitable, efficient, transparent and child-focused public finance and accountability systems. In 2025, UNICEF made significant progress to ensure child-focused national and local budgeting, and three mutually reinforcing achievements significantly advanced this agenda. 
First, UNICEF, together with partners, equipped the National Assembly with a dedicated child-rights public finance tool and related capacity-building, through the development and publication of the manual Budgeting Focused on Children’s Rights, prepared for Members of Parliament (MPs) as a practical guide to child-responsive budgeting, programme budgeting and parliamentary oversight of public funds for children. The manual explains how MPs can track allocations for children across programmes, use performance information and link budget scrutiny to Serbia’s Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and SDG obligations. In 2025, UNICEF facilitated the first training cycle using the manual, bringing together MPs and Assembly staff from key committees (finance, social policy, child rights) to apply the tool to the 2025 budget and Final Account discussions, thus strengthening the National Assembly’s role in child-rights monitoring and budget oversight. 
Second, UNICEF completed a public finance management (PFM) assessment under the UN SDG Fund for localization of SDGs, focusing on green, child-relevant public finance. The analytical report Public Finance Analysis: Sustainable Public Finance for Green Energy and Efficiency examined how local PFM systems, transfers and budget classifications support or constrain investments in energy efficiency and energy-poverty mitigation across 10 municipalities, with a strong emphasis on implications for vulnerable households and children. The assessment proposed child-sensitive, SDG-linked reforms at both central and local levels and will inform dialogue with the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Mining and Energy, and the Standing Conference of Towns and Municipalities (SCTM) on how future national and municipal budgets can better combine climate and child-sensitive objectives. 
Third, UNICEF helped position child poverty and human-capital financing at the centre of macro-fiscal debate through high-level advocacy and coalition-building. Together with the EU Delegation and the World Bank, UNICEF co-convened the high-level event ‘From Economic Growth to Shared Prosperity: Tackling Multidimensional Poverty in Serbia’ to mark the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty. A panel session on Financing Human Capital brought together the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Labour, Employment, Veteran and Social Affairs (MoLEVSA), EU, World Bank and UN agencies, with UNICEF Serbia presenting evidence on child poverty, social spending and the returns on investing in children. The event strengthened a cross-government and development-partner coalition around child-sensitive macro-fiscal policies and created a platform for follow-up work on social protection adequacy, energy poverty and SDG-relevant budget reforms. 
Progress has also been made in securing interest of the Government of Serbia in the EU Child Guarantee. Selected representatives were supported to participate in annual networking events organized by the European Commission, and in a study visit to Croatia. Further steps by the Government of Serbia are expected in 2026. 
In 2025, UNICEF made a breakthrough in supporting Serbia’s efforts to modernize public services and make them more user-centred, accessible and inclusive. Through the Joint UN Programme on citizen-centred service design, funded by the SDG Fund, and with participation of UNDP, FAO and national counterparts, UNICEF is supporting the Government in transitioning from institution-centric to people-centric models of service delivery across the social welfare system, through the development of an AI-powered assistant/chatbot for MoLEVSA and the Ministry of Family Welfare and Demography, working closely with the Office for IT and eGovernment, to be launched in early 2026. 
Climate & Environment 
UNICEF continued its comprehensive advocacy for integrating children’s needs and rights into national policies addressing environmental protection, climate change, pollution and energy transition. Through strategic engagement with policymakers, participation in key public events, active involvement in public consultations (such as the Air Quality Law, Energy Just Transition Action Plan, NDC 3.0, and the Program for Industrial Safety), as well as collaboration with the media, UNICEF provided crucial technical input to raise awareness about the disproportionate impact of climate change, pollution and energy transitions on children. 
In 2025, UNICEF initiated a dialogue on children’s environmental health, bringing together key sectors and institutions for the first time in Serbia to address the challenges related to the impact of the environment on children’s health. UNICEF supported the health system by assisting paediatricians through the development of accredited training, creation of a manual, and adaptation of the WHO-UNICEF online educational course on children’s environmental health. 
UNICEF also addressed child poverty through energy efficiency initiatives by providing small energy measures to 100 households and raising awareness about rational energy consumption. UNICEF established valuable collaboration with the Ministry of Energy and Mining, opening new avenues for deeper cooperation and enabling further technical support on the specific vulnerabilities of children to the impacts of energy-related pollution and the energy transition. UNICEF has significantly advanced the integration of child-sensitive WASH priorities into climate action through evidence-based advocacy, capacity-building and demonstration initiatives. At the local level, UNICEF strengthened governance systems by equipping LSGs with a Practical Guide, expert mentoring, and multi-stakeholder and youth-driven consultations, resulting in concrete climate-resilient WASH measures embedded in 2026 local budgets and expected to benefit over 30,000 children. 
Innovation  
UNICEF Serbia has a long history of using innovation for results at scale and systemic changes: (i) Integrated into the National Education Platform, the Learning Passport is an open-source portal for educators, accessible online and through mobile devices (Apple and Google apps), is state owned and entirely financed and managed by the Ministry of Education. (ii) Bebbo, the parenting app, was created in Serbia as ‘Halo Beba’ and is now recognized as a digital public common good, reaching 1 million parents in 14 countries. (iii) U-Report gathers the voices and opinion of 25,000 young people in Serbia and is strategically used to influence national and local policies. (iv) SveJeOk.rs is a major MHPSS platform used by more than 50,000 young people in Serbia. (v) Providing 24/7 psychological counselling of children and young people, NADEL, is now being integrated into national systems. UNICEF Serbia, as part of the COMPASS cohort, adopted its own Innovation Strategy, to anchor innovation in its programmes, systems, governance bodies and strategic plans for the next CPD 2026–2030. 
ADVOCACY AND PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT 
In 2025, UNICEF’s communication and advocacy work played an important role in advancing the priorities of the CPD 2021–2025. Through clear, evidence-based and child-centred messaging, UNICEF strengthened public understanding of child rights, generated stronger demand for services, supported programme efforts to address the structural barriers affecting children and youth, and contributed to fundraising efforts. 
In 2025, communication and advocacy supported all CPD 2021–2025 priorities – ECD, inclusive education, adolescent well-being, social inclusion and fundraising efforts – while laying the groundwork for our advocacy in support of the priorities of the next CPD. Through sustained engagement, evidence-driven messaging and a consistent presence across media, UNICEF helped shift attitudes, strengthen demand for services, and reinforce national commitments to child rights. 
The campaign ‘You’re Not Bad, You’re Just Feeling Bad’, aimed at advancing mental health and psychological well-being, reached more than one million people, and helped reframe mental health challenges in ways that resonated with adolescents and families, contributing to a more accepting environment for help-seeking and early support. A dedicated digital campaign promoting the Bebbo parenting app resulted in more than 21,000 new downloads, expanding parents’ access to ECD guidance. 
Communication and advocacy contributed to advancing results across UN joint programmes – SDC PRO, SIDA EVEC, MPTF, and Green Futures, Brighter Beginnings – by showcasing community-level achievements, promoting inclusive practices and elevating local services. Public dissemination marking the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty achieved wide traction, raising awareness among decision makers and the public about the scale and complexity of multidimensional poverty in Serbia. 
In the context of the social turmoil and protests, UNICEF monitored the impact of the situation on child rights, fulfilling its mandate and maintaining a neutral, impartial and independent position towards all involved parties. Support was extended across the full spectrum of child rights – including the right to education and its continuity, freedom of expression, and the right of association and peaceful assembly – with a continued call for all stakeholders to prioritize the well-being of children and families. UNICEF continues to closely monitor the situation, highlight key child rights violations and advance on their promotion and fulfilment, through targeted advocacy with the Government. 
Evidence generation and communication also advanced national dialogue. UNICEF’s convening power and advocacy based on evidence, analysis and insights continued to be recognized by partners, with several parliamentary political caucuses engaging with UNICEF on public finance. UNICEF supported the public launch of the new MICS data collection cycle, highlighting its importance for understanding the situation of children and monitoring inequalities. Clear messaging helped policymakers, professionals and families understand why MICS matters and set the foundation for informed uptake once results are released. 
Partnerships with media remained essential in an increasingly fragmented information environment. In 2025, UNICEF secured 1,819 media mentions across national and local outlets, ensuring steady visibility for child rights issues. Continued engagement with public broadcasters supported more responsible, child-sensitive reporting.
