UNICEF maintained high-level quality cooperation with UN sister agencies, co-chairing the interagency-level Result Working Group 2 (UN RG2) and Monitoring and Evaluation Group and fostering a fruitful Policy Dialogue on Human Capital and Multi-Dimensional Poverty between the UN RG2 and EU Delegation. 
In 2025, UNICEF, as the co-chair of the UN RG 2, played a pivotal role in initiating a policy dialogue and helped position child poverty and human-capital financing at the centre of macro-fiscal debate through high-level advocacy and coalition-building. Together with the EU Delegation and the World Bank, UNICEF co-convened the high-level event ‘From Economic Growth to Shared Prosperity: Tackling Multidimensional Poverty in Serbia’ to mark the International Day for the Eradication of Poverty. Most notably, a panel session on Financing Human Capital brought together the Ministry of Finance, MoLEVSA, EU, World Bank and UN agencies, with UNICEF Serbia presenting evidence on child poverty, social spending and the returns on investing in children. The event strengthened a cross-government and development-partner coalition around child-sensitive macro-fiscal policies and created a platform for follow-up work on social protection adequacy, energy poverty and SDG-relevant budget reforms. 
UNICEF’s cooperation with the EU continued in IE and digital education and expanded to joint advocacy for securing interest of the Government of Serbia in the EU Child Guarantee. Selected representatives were supported to participate in annual networking events organized by the European Commission, and in a study visit to Croatia, where UNICEF and the Government of Croatia presented their work on implementation of the EU Child Guarantee. Further steps by the Government of Serbia are expected in 2026. 
Partnership with the World Bank remained instrumental to support the reform process of the early childhood education and care (ECEC) subsystem in all five areas of system strengthening: policy, regulation and planning, financing, workforce development, data and quality assurance, and partnerships. Following the approval of a WB loan for the implementation of the Inclusive Primary School Project, discussions were initiated with MoE and WB on potential collaboration and partnership.  Dialogue and collaboration were successfully strengthened with the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB) around child and maternal health. 
In partnership with UNDP, FAO and the Office for IT and e-Government, UNICEF continued to implement the three-year Joint UN Programme funded by the SDG Fund to provide a use-case for citizen-centred services in the social protection sector. The Joint Programme, called ‘Clicking Together with Citizens’, is designed to assist the Government in achieving its strategic goal of enhancing public services for all, with a focus on the most vulnerable, and to fast-track the achievement of SDGs by transitioning from an institution-centric to a people-centric approach in public service design. UNICEF is supporting the Government in transitioning from institution-centric to people-centric models of service delivery across the social welfare system, as well as the development and responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) as outlined in the national AI Strategy. In practice, UNICEF is supporting the development of an AI-powered assistant/chatbot for MoLEVSA and the Ministry of Family Welfare and Demography, working closely with the Office for IT and eGovernment, to be launched in early 2026. 
With Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation support, four agencies (UNICEF, UNOPS, UNFPA, UNEP) successfully implemented the joint four-year project ‘PRO – Local Governance for People and Nature’, advancing the capacities of local governments to develop local social protection policies and services to improve the well-being of vulnerable groups. 
With Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency support, UNICEF, together with UNDP, UN Women and UNFPA, continued to implement a three-year project ‘Empowering Change, Ending Violence’ in close coordination with the Government’s coordination body for gender equality. The project will foster non-violent and gender-responsive positive parenting, advocacy for the elimination of child marriage, and support leadership of young Roma women and girls. 
UNICEF continued to nurture its partnerships with data and evidence institutions, including the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia as major partner for the implementation of the MICS 7, the Republic Institute for Social Protection, think tanks, CSOs and academia. 
In public finance, key partners included International Monetary Fund, Fiscal Council, Serbia’s National Assembly, the Center of Excellence in Finance, and the Belgrade Fund for Political Excellence. 
The Standing Conference of Towns and Municipalities (SCTM) remained a major partner for UNICEF’s engagement with LSGs around the provision of local services for the most vulnerable children. 
UNICEF continued to support CSOs and independent institutions actively advocating for child rights across different sectors.

In 2025, Tajikistan consolidated political stability and advanced a reform-oriented development agenda. The year was characterized by significant political, economic, environmental, and social developments.
At the political level, parliamentary and local elections were conducted, reinforcing institutional continuity. A historic resolution of long-standing border issues with the Kyrgyz Republic, alongside trilateral agreements with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, marked a critical milestone for regional peace and cooperation. However, the year also saw an uptick in the frequency and intensity of security incidents on the southern border with Afghanistan, creating localized instability and complicating humanitarian access and service delivery in affected areas.
Tajikistan strengthened its international standing in 2025 through leadership on global public goods, particularly climate action and digital transformation. The country hosted the first High-Level International Conference on Glaciers’ Preservation, attended by heads of state, senior UN leadership, including the UNICEF Executive Director and Regional Director, and international experts. These efforts, alongside the advancement of key UN resolutions on glacier and cryosphere preservation, artificial intelligence for sustainable development in Central Asia, and others, underscore Tajikistan’s growing role in shaping international agendas relevant to child rights.
Economically, Tajikistan maintained robust growth, with gross domestic product reaching 173 billion somoni (approx. US$ 15.8 billion) in 2025 and real growth estimated at 8.4 per cent. Over the past decade, sustained economic expansion has contributed to rising incomes, declining poverty, and improvements in life expectancy. However, the country’s high population growth rate continues to exert pressure on public services and infrastructure. Children and youth represent a large and growing share of the population, underscoring the centrality of sustained investments in human capital to unlock the demographic dividend, as highlighted in Generation 2050 analysis, to ensure that demographic trends translate into inclusive and equitable development outcomes. The economy remains heavily reliant on external remittances, which constitute over 40 per cent of GDP. Recent tightening of migration policies in key destination countries has introduced new uncertainties, potentially affecting the volume of remittances and the stability of household incomes for many families heightening the risk for children left behind.
The adoption of the Medium-Term Development Programme for 2026–2030, as the final phase of the National Development Strategy to 2030, sets ambitious targets for economic growth, poverty reduction, and middle-class expansion. However, financing this ambitious plan presents a significant challenge in the context of declining ODA, the risk of substantial public investment in projects like in Roghun Hydropower Plant (HPP) crowding out funding for the social sectors, which are critical for human capital accumulation. The Programme prioritizes digital transformation, rapid industrialization, green and circular economic models, innovation, and human capital development. These priorities closely align with UNICEF’s strategic focus on strengthening social systems, promoting equity, and preparing children and adolescents with the skills required for a rapidly changing economy. Digitalization and artificial intelligence featured prominently in the national policy agenda in 2025.
Energy security and climate change remain defining contextual factors. Tajikistan continued major investments in hydropower infrastructure, including progress on the Roghun HPP, alongside new commitments to large-scale solar energy development. At the same time, climate variability manifested through heat stress, altered precipitation patterns, and glacier retreat continues to pose risks to water availability, agriculture, energy supply, and household livelihoods. According to UNICEF’s Situation Analysis (SitAn), approximately 1.6 million children are at high climate risk and climate-related shocks cost the economy an estimated 0.4 - 1.3 per cent of GDP annually. The designation of 2025 as the International Year of Glacier Preservation and 2025–2034 as the Decade of Cryospheric Sciences underscores the growing urgency of climate action in a country, where environmental risks disproportionately affect children, particularly those in rural and remote areas.
Public finance trends in 2025 indicate expanding fiscal capacity, with state budget revenues reaching 50 billion somoni (approx. US$ 5 billion). The Government emphasized the need to enhance the efficiency and results orientation of public expenditure, expand green finance instruments, and strengthen capital markets. These shifts create important opportunities to advance child-sensitive and climate-responsive public finance; however, ensuring that macroeconomic gains translate into equitable outcomes for the most marginalized children remains an ongoing challenge.
Social sectors continued to receive strong policy attention. However, while social spending accounted for around 46 per cent of total 2025 state budget expenditures, the share of social spending as a percentage of GDP declined from 13.8 per cent to 12.6 per cent between 2019 and 2023 (SitAn). The overall quality of spending in the social sector leaves room for improvement to maximize impact on child outcomes. Education and science were reaffirmed as long-term national priorities, with education expenditure projected to increase substantially in the coming years. Demographic projections suggest significant growth in student populations over the next decades, necessitating sustained investments in teacher workforce development, school infrastructure, and system reforms. Yet quality gaps persist, only 16 per cent of schools have internet access, highlighting uneven progress (SitAn). Ensuring equitable access to quality learning, particularly for girls, rural children, children with disabilities, and those affected by poverty remains central to achieving SDG 4.
Health sector investments expanded over the past decade, supported by increased budget allocations and ongoing reforms aimed at improving financing efficiency and digitalization. However, health sector spending as a percentage of GDP remains low, and out-of-pocket expenditure in the sector is high, standing at just 2.5 per cent of GDP and account for a high 62 – 71 per cent of total health spending, underscoring persistent challenges in financial protection. Concurrently, social protection and employment policies emphasized job creation, wage adjustments, pension indexation, and targeted support for vulnerable groups.
In December 2025, the MOHSP announced major state-led programmes to support children with disabilities, including the introduction of intersectoral case management to coordinate social, medical, educational and legal services, as well as investments in modern rehabilitation technology and assistive devices to improve access to prosthetics and orthotics.
On child poverty, the Government officially released updated child monetary poverty data in mid-December 2025, the first since 2016, showing a decline from 27.2 per cent in 2021 to 20.4 per cent in 2023. However, multidimensional child poverty remains high at 36 per cent, with significant regional disparities, particularly in Khatlon and Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Oblast (GBAO) (SitAn). Given the recent timing of the data release, its integration into policy dialogue and planning is still nascent.
Youth and gender equality were highlighted as integral to national development. The Government reiterated its commitment to youth participation as a driver of social and economic progress and to advancing the role of women and girls across all sectors. However, persistent gender norms continue to constrain adolescent girls’ well-being. According to SitAn, 7.3 per cent of girls aged 15-19 have already been pregnant, and 48 per cent of women justify domestic violence under certain circumstances, underscoring the deep-rooted social norms that impede gender equality and child rights. Specific challenges for adolescent girls and young women include the risk of early marriage, disproportionate care burdens, barriers in STEM education and high NEET rates.
Overall, Tajikistan enters the final phase of its National Development Strategy with a strong foundation of political stability, ambitious reform priorities, and increasing international engagement. At the same time, demographic pressures, climate risks, digital divides, and equity gaps pose significant challenges to the realization of children’s rights. These contextual dynamics frame UNICEF Tajikistan’s operating environment in 2025 and reinforce the importance of integrated, equity-focused, and systems-level approaches to ensure that no child is left behind.

In 2025, UNICEF Tajikistan translated policy commitments into measurable outcomes for children, aligning reforms with service delivery at scale and embedding digital tools and climate resilience into national systems. Through strong partnerships with Government, UN agencies, international financial institutions, donors and the private sector, UNICEF’s support improved coverage, quality and equity across health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection and social policy - anchored in UNSDCF and the SDGs.

Health, Nutrition and WASH: Survival, Quality and Equity at scale
UNICEF’s support in 2025 focused on strengthening the resilience, quality, and equity of Tajikistan’s health system, with particular attention to newborn survival, immunization, infection prevention and control, and primary health care. These efforts contributed to improved continuity of care for women, newborns, children, and adolescents nationwide.
A landmark achievement was the introduction of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine into the national immunization schedule, a breakthrough for adolescent girls’ health and cervical cancer prevention. Within seven weeks of the October launch, more than 516,921 girls aged 10-14 years - over 95 per cent of the target population - were vaccinated. UNICEF led procurement, cold chain readiness, risk communication and community engagement, achieving high acceptance through religious leaders, community health teams, journalists, and digital social listening mechanisms. Campaigns reached over 4.4 million people, reinforcing public confidence and driving uptake.
A measles outbreak was contained through an integrated response that restored confidence in immunization and strengthened routine services. Over 685,000 children under five were vaccinated with coverage exceeding 98 per cent. Investments in cold chain resilience, WHO-prequalified equipment and national maintenance plans, reduced stock loss and improved continuity of vaccine services nationwide.
Newborn and child survival advanced through targeted improvements in referral-level services and workforce skills. Seventy-five facilities were equipped with Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machines, oxygen concentrators and incubators reducing preventable complications for more than 2,837 premature and critically ill newborns. Clinical training cascades strengthened neonatologists, pediatricians and nurses, while a nationwide focus on infection prevention and control raised compliance with standards in over 150 primary health care facilities and 36 hospitals, lowering the risk of health care associated infections.
Nutrition systems moved from fragmented interventions to standardized, accountable care pathways. The updated national guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of acute malnutrition institutionalized outpatient management as standard practice, added care of infants under six months at risk and integrated malnutrition indicators into routine health information closing critical data gaps. Service scale remained substantial: over one million children of 6-59 months accessed micronutrient supplementation, and nearly 200,000 pregnant and lactating women received counselling on breastfeeding and infant feeding, supporting healthy growth in the first 1,000 days. Responding to rising adolescent nutrition risks, provisions in the draft Education Code began to reshape school food environments and integrate nutrition education and physical activity. With WFP and WHO, UNICEF completed the country’s first nutrition supply-chain maturity assessment, produced a costed roadmap and initiated an electronic logistics management information system that will reduce stockouts and losses of life saving therapeutic foods.
Early Childhood Development (ECD) continued its shift from pilots to systems. Launch of a new Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) unit within primary health care provided a scalable service model for young children with development delays and disabilities. A national ECI situational analysis quantified service gaps and informed the forthcoming multisectoral ECD Strategy, ensuring investments are evidence-led and interlinked across health, education and social services. Parenting support reached millions of caregivers through digital and mass media, including Bebbo app, improving responsive caregiving and early simulation at scale.
WASH gains amplified health and dignity while reducing infection risk. National adoption of the Water and Sanitation Programme (2025–2029) and the Climate-Adaptive WASH in schools plan to 2030 aligned sector targets with global standards and created an operational pathway to equitable access.
Under the EU-funded Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) initiative, WASH and health care waste management systems were rehabilitated in 17 secondary-level hospitals and 750 primary health care facilities, improving hygiene, safety, and accessibility for nearly one million people, including women, children, and persons with disabilities, and strengthened national capacity to prevent healthcare-associated infections. In schools, the “Three Star Approach” to WASH improved hygiene behaviours and operations in 50 schools, directly benefiting over 58,000 children and more than 2,700 teachers contributing to better attendance and learning conditions.

Learning and Skills: From Commitment to Classroom Change
Education reform progressed from fragmented projects to a coherent, competency-based system that links policy, planning, teaching, assessment and accountability. The competency-based education roadmap and its monitoring framework were used and endorsed through the Partnership Compact Mid-Term Review and the Joint Sector Review, aligning partners behind shared reform direction. With UNESCO-Internal Institute for Educational Planning (IIEP), an education costing simulation model was adapted and operationalized to test reform options within realistic fiscal space, allowing decision-makers to sequence and prioritize. A new Coordination and Analytical Unit began strengthening sector coordination and Education Management Information System (EMIS) modernization improved gender- and disability-responsive data, enabling equity-focused planning at national and sub-national levels.
Policy change was intentionally converted into measurable shifts in classroom practice. An endorsed State Standard for general education defined key and subject-specific competencies and guided curriculum, assessment, and teacher development reforms. In 2025, UNICEF supported the introduction and piloting of competency-based curricula and textbooks in mathematics and Tajik language for Grade 6 in 30 pilot schools moving pedagogy away from rote learning. The School of Authors and targeted professional capacity development created a cadre of national multipliers, while early steps on competency-based classroom assessment prepared the system to align teaching, learning and evaluation.
Inclusivity and safety were advanced as core system expectations. Building on the National Concept on Inclusive Education, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education and Science to draft a strategy and actionable plan to include children with disabilities in mainstream schools, shifting the default from separation to inclusion. School leaders across the country used the Comprehensive School Safety Framework to update safety plans, run drills, and integrate preparedness into school improvement processes, reducing learning disruptions during shocks. Findings from national diagnostic on climate change education informed policy dialogue and set the stage for curriculum updates. Provisions supported in the draft Education Code address school nutrition and healthier learning environments, tackling barriers to adolescent well-being.
Digital transformation advanced through a strong focus on governance and safe learning spaces, rather than devices alone. Modernization of the Education Management Information System integrated gender- and disability-responsive indicators and strengthened the capacity of 400 EMIS focal points, with dashboards now informing data-driven planning for marginalized learners. In parallel, under Giga, data-sharing agreements between education and communications authorities enabled investment in school connectivity, while UNICEF’s analytical work on education technology and artificial intelligence supported the establishment of principles for responsible, child-centered AI that enhance learning without widening digital divides.
Adolescents were positioned as co-creators of climate solutions and civic actors. The country’s national climate education toolkit was developed and officially recognized for use in schools and centres for additional education. One hundred Eco Clubs in schools and universities trained nearly 2,000 adolescent climate champions, who then reached an estimated 12,000 peers through outreach, projects and local advocacy.
Adolescents shaped district development plans, issued Tajikistan’s first-ever national youth climate statement, and represented the country at global forums, including COP30 in Brazil – strengthening youth voice in policy processes.
Pathways from learning to employment were institutionalized and scaled with gender lens. A national, gender-responsive career guidance system now spans primary and secondary education, reinforced by an AI-enabled career platform, that helps adolescents map interests to opportunities and build digital portfolios.
Adolescent Innovation Labs (AILs) and Impact Sourcing Hubs (ISHs) reached more than 22,000 adolescents and young people with social, financial, entrepreneurial, digital and green skills, while ISHs connected vulnerable youth to remote work, improving income prospects where local labour markets are thin. With major externally funded programmes concluding, UNICEF prioritized institutionalization, handover to Government systems and public-private partnerships increasing sustainability and reach.

Child Protection: Coherence, Digital Accountability and Family-Based care
Child protection made a decisive move from piecemeal changes to a single national framework. The Government developed the State Programme for the Protection of the Rights of the Child (2026–2030), a comprehensive implementation-ready plan that consolidates legislation, services, workforce development, coordination, and monitoring into one coherent system.
UNICEF played a catalytic role in shaping the Programme’s structure and evidence base, and ensured alignment with international child rights standards, so that the next phase is scalable and monitorable.
Digitalization underpinned faster, more consistent protection responses. Rollout of Primero Child Protection Information Management System (CPIMS+), secured high-level government commitment for integration into the national digitalization framework, enabling real-time case data, stronger referrals and system-level analytics once fully operational. Alongside technology, UNICEF invested in people and standards: over 200 social workers and community leaders were trained in standardized case management, referral pathways, inter-agency coordination and foundational reforms on professional standards, ethics, supervision, quality assurance and costing advanced, professionalizing the workforce and improving service consistency.
Results for children included preventing unnecessary separation and expanding family-based alternatives. Through new national guidelines and UNICEF supported Family and Child Support Centres, 500 children under the age of four avoided placement in residential care. A further 128 children were referred to non-residential day care services, and 133 children received psychosocial support and counselling, evidence that prevention and community-based support are taking hold as first resort.
In justice, a draft Supreme Court decree promoting alternatives to detention was approved by the Plenum, embedding restorative approaches. Diversion programming for children in conflict with the law progressed and new inter-agency SOPs will operationalize the legal ban on corporal punishment by standardizing identification, referral and response to violence. Research on child sexual abuse and child marriage strengthened political attention and drove legal and procedural alignment with child-sensitive justice norms.
When shocks hit, preparedness translated into faster, more inclusive protection. After the earthquake in Tojikobod district, rapid assessments and psychosocial support reached 468 affected children. Integration of child protection and disability inclusion into national contingency planning and training for 80 Border Troops officers improved front-line protection for unaccompanied and separated children, including those on the move.

Social Policy and Child Rights Monitoring: Evidence to Budget, Budget to Outcomes
UNICEF helped to re-establish child-poverty evidence as a routine public good, supporting Government to release official child monetary poverty data, the first since 2016, using revised methodology. This reset in the evidence base improved the quality of policy dialogue and anchored discussions on who is being left behind in current, nationally owned data. Complementary analyses across nutrition, education, early childhood development, and climate risks began to reshape programme choices and investment priorities.
At national and sub-national levels, UNICEF strengthened the link between evidence and public finance. Technical assistance on child responsive budgeting and SDGs localization helped central and local authorities analyze expenditure trends, identify gaps and align plans and budgets with child focused priorities, improving the match between resources and needs in underserved districts.
Work on shock-responsive social protection, readiness improved preregistration systems, targeting approaches, and digital payment preparedness, enabling faster, more predictable scale-ups of cash-based support for children and families during climate and economic shocks. Analytical support informed Government deliberations child-sensitive benefit expansion, including considerations of Universal Child Benefits, positioning social protection as a core instrument for resilience.
Child rights monitoring capacity was institutionalized rather than episodic. Government institutions clarified roles and coordination for tracking and following up CRC recommendations, moved beyond ad-hoc reporting and improved the use of child related data for accountability. At local level, child- and youth-led monitoring mechanisms embedded adolescent voice in planning and reporting, ensuring that children’s perspectives influence resource allocation and service improvements.

Cross-cutting Enablers: Partnerships, Digital Transformation, Climate Leadership and Operational Excellence
UNICEF’s ability to deliver systemic results in 2025 rested on strategic partnerships that aligned policy, financing and innovation behind national priorities. Programme coordination drove coherence and accountability across planning, delivery, and advocacy. The PME unit’s prioritization workshops and evolving Theory of Change provided a shared results framework, while a new Data Warehouse connected programme, administrative, and climate evidence today decision making - reducing fragmentation and enabling equity focused targeting.
Oversight mechanisms were standardised and strengthened. Joint monitoring compensated for field office closures; the Field Monitoring Module captured 55 visits with actionable follow-ups, and 44 HACT PVs were completed on time - anchoring risk management and improving implementation quality. Third party verification across 1,500+ PHCs, 24 schools, 46 AILs, 5 ISHs confirmed delivery/functionality of EU funded equipment, with dashboards enabling swift corrective actions. Programme coordination also ensured donor reporting discipline: from June, PME quality assured 19 reports (13 via FIORI), sustaining timeliness and consistency.
UNICEF orchestrated advocacy and partnerships to unlock systemic change. External communications reached 4.4 million+ people, achieved 33.4per cent national brand recognition, and grew social audiences by around 25 per cent, while donor advocacy and technical events connected evidence to policy dialogue. In health and nutrition, collaboration with WHO, WFP, and the EU ensured rapid vaccine readiness, IPC/WASH upgrades, and supplychain modernization. In education, UNESCOIIEP and Giga enabled coherent reform planning and digital connectivity governance. In child protection, close engagement with line ministries and the judiciary secured adoption pathways for the State Programme and accelerated Primero CPIMS+ integration. Partnerships with IsDB, FCDO, the Russian Federation, and others leveraged financing and technical expertise to scale proven models, while private sector alliances with Tcell, Alif Bank, and the AI Council expanded adolescent skilling, AIenabled career guidance, and digital parenting outreach (including Bebbo, which saw +20 per cent downloads).
Coordination accelerated SBC and gender actions across sectors. The Three Star WASH rollout mobilised 2,705 teachers, reached 58,609 children and around 63,000 caregivers, improved school performance (avg 1.0 to 1.8) and facilities (running water stations 35 to 88, MHM bins 53 to 65). Health demand generation strengthened through training of 27 Healthy Lifestyle Center staff (knowledge 59 per cent to 83 per cent; HCD 74–87 per cent), and distributed capacity (>4,000 teachers, 3,000 health workers, 280 CHTs) supported precision outreach across 14 zero-dose districts - with administrative coverage reports indicating high HPV/Big Catchup/MR uptake in targeted areas.
Child-centred DRR/climate coordination connected youth, policy, and investment. UNICEF facilitated youth platforms (Children & Youth Forum; first LCOY; youth delegate to COP30), initiated regional collaboration with the ECO Secretariat, and institutionalised inclusive preparedness (training 1,100+ teachers/caregivers; adapted drills for around 1,600 children with disabilities). Coordination linked education resilience and finance (BMI audits; GCF concept for 69 school retrofits), advanced climate education (50 Eco Clubs, national workshop/roadmap), and strengthened risk evidence (enhanced CCRI analytics). The office also coordinated multisector earthquake response, reaching 13,004 people, maintaining learning for 10,630 children, and providing hygiene/dignity kits (416) and psychosocial support (294).
In addition, UNICEF strengthened child-responsive Early Warning Systems (EWS) and Anticipatory Action by linking risk monitoring and forecasting to early action protocols (currently under development) and by pre-positioning essential emergency supplies with CoES to enable rapid support to children and families. The office reinforced national emergency preparedness and response coordination through joint planning, simulations, and operational readiness measures with government authorities and partners, including the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and the Red Crescent Society of Tajikistan. Efforts also advanced shock-responsive and humanitarian cash transfer mechanisms (HTC/SRSP) to deliver timely, child-focused assistance during crises, ensuring faster and more predictable support while strengthening national systems and local capacity.
UNICEF Tajikistan advanced child-sensitive climate resilience through a coherent package of evidence, policy engagement, pilot investments, and financing readiness. The publicly available CCRI/DRM analysis strengthened national risk evidence and informed cross-sector planning and prioritization for children. Under the regional Climate Business Model Initiative (BMI), UNICEF conducted energy audits and school safety assessments in two pilot schools in Varzob and Rudaki, identifying cost-effective energy efficiency and climate-resilient retrofit measures to improve learning environments and reduce climate-related risks. The results are informing a pipeline for scale-up through the Green Climate Fund (GCF) proposal and broader climate-resilient school infrastructure investments. Climate education and youth engagement were further strengthened through Eco-Clubs in 50 schools and the introduction of the Climate Activist Toolkit, with ongoing digitalization to expand access. At the policy level, UNICEF supported integration of child-responsive measures into NDC 3.0 through gap analysis, narrative inputs, and sector costing (estimated investment needs of USD 1.9 million), contributing to stronger national climate planning, partnerships with the National Designated Authority, and financing readiness for implementation.
 
Operations underpinned coordination effectiveness - building financial/grant management capacity; aligning cash forecasts and payments to programme timelines; overseeing construction and rehabilitation works; supporting PBR decisions; and managing assets and staffing/wellbeing - so that programmes had the systems and resources to deliver on time and to standard.
Operational Excellence
In 2025, UNICEF Tajikistan sustained high levels of operational effectiveness in a context of financial constraints, reduced donor funding, and organizational transformation. Through strong governance, prudent financial and risk management, operational innovation, and a people-centred approach to change management, UNICEF ensured uninterrupted programme delivery and safeguarded accountability for results for children.
Strengthening Governance, Risk Management, and Business Continuity
A key achievement in 2025 was the reinforcement of risk-informed governance and internal control systems during a period of fiscal uncertainty. The Operations team provided strategic advice to key governance bodies, including the Country Management Team, Contract Review Committee, Partnership Review Committee, Property Survey Board, and Joint Consultative Committee, strengthening oversight, compliance, and transparency in decision-making.
The development and implementation of a risk-informed Annual Management Plan enabled the office to proactively prioritize quality assurance, partnerships, financial sustainability, and staff wellbeing. Progress against management priorities was reviewed systematically, contributing to timely corrective actions and organizational stability. In addition, the conduct of a Business Continuity Plan simulation exercise strengthened preparedness for emergencies and informed concrete actions to ensure continuity of critical operations.
Ensuring Financial Integrity and Value for Money
Despite funding constraints, UNICEF Tajikistan maintained sound financial stewardship and donor compliance, ensuring that resources were used efficiently and transparently in support of programme delivery. The office achieved 100 per cent utilization of its allocated resources (US$ 24.7 million), while meeting all key performance indicators for donor financial reporting, including the timely submission of 38 donor reports and successful completion of EU expenditure verification with no major findings.
Robust treasury management, accurate cash forecasting, and timely vendor and partner payments ensured continuity of services and sustained partner confidence. The office strengthened HACT assurance through audits, spot checks, and micro-assessments, mitigating fiduciary risks and reinforcing accountability across implementing partners. Cost-efficiency measures - including reduced security costs, optimized travel arrangements, and shared UN services - generated savings while maintaining service quality.
Delivering Reliable Supply and Logistics Systems
Operational effectiveness was further demonstrated through strong supply chain and logistics performance, critical to delivering life-saving services for children. UNICEF managed a procurement portfolio of approximately US$ 15.9 million, including vaccines, medical equipment, nutrition supplies, and construction works, ensuring timely delivery and quality assurance.
Beyond procurement, UNICEF strengthened national systems through the introduction of traceability and verification tools, improved forecasting and supply planning, and progress toward digital logistics systems. These investments enhanced transparency, reduced stock risks, and contributed to the sustainability of health and nutrition programmes.
Managing Organizational Transformation and Workforce Resilience
A major operational achievement in 2025 was the successful management of organizational restructuring under the Programme Budget Review (PBR). UNICEF designed and implemented an optimized, affordable staffing structure aligned with realistic funding projections while maintaining technical capacity. The change process was managed transparently and inclusively, with strong engagement of staff, the Staff Association, and regional support structures.
Innovative operational solutions were introduced, including the establishment of a Programme Support Hub - the first of its kind in the region - to centralize and standardize programme transactional support. This innovation is expected to improve efficiency, service quality, and compliance, supporting programme teams to focus on results for children.
Advancing UN System Efficiency and Sustainable Operations
UNICEF continued to lead the UN Efficiency Agenda through its role in managing common premises and services for multiple UN agencies. Cost reductions expanded shared services, accessibility improvements, and environmentally sustainable practices strengthened operational efficiency while reinforcing a unified UN presence in Tajikistan.
Environmental sustainability was further advanced through green building upgrades, renewable energy solutions, waste recycling initiatives, and tree planting in schools, aligning UNICEF operations with the Global Sustainability and Climate Action Plan and reinforcing UNICEF’s leadership on climate-responsible operations.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Key Challenges
Policy-implementation gaps persist across sectors. Despite strong policy frameworks, such as the State Programme on Child Rights (2026-2030), competency-based education standards, climate-adapted WASH plans, and inclusive education guidelines, operationalization is hindered by limited financing, weak inter-ministerial coordination and insufficient subnational capacity.
Health and nutrition systems remain fragile. Chronic shortages of skilled health workers, especially in rural areas, high staff turnover and dependence on imported therapeutic foods limit the resilience and scale of services for newborns, malnourished children and adolescents.
Climate change is actively undermining child outcomes. With 1.6 million children in high climate-risk zones (SitAn), extreme weather increasingly damages WASH infrastructure, disrupt schools and strains health facilities. National climate leadership has yet to translate into localized budgeted adaptation in social sectors.
Business Model Initiative. Experience from regional climate coordination mechanisms, including the Climate Business Model Initiative (BMI), has highlighted the potential of pooled technical assistance models to enhance efficiency, consistency, and cross-country learning, particularly for specialized climate expertise.The BMI’s unique approach has enabled the integration of NDC revision processes, school-proofing activities, and a strong focus on resource mobilization to support the implementation of relevant regional initiatives.
Harmful gender norms constrain adolescent well-being. SitAn data shows 7.3 per cent of girls aged 15-19 have already been pregnant and 48 per cent of women justify domestic violence under certain circumstances, highlighting deep-rooted barriers to girls’ health, safety and agency.
Digital transformation risks deepening inequities. While digital tools (Primero CPIMS +, EMIS, HMIS, nutrition logistics) improve data use, only 16 per cent of schools have internet access and rural facilities often lack reliable power, threatening to widen gaps for girls, children with disabilities and remote communities.
Child protection remains fragmented. Despite the State Programmes’s adoption, services are siloed across health, education, justice and social sectors, delaying coordinated support for children with intersecting vulnerabilities (e.g. disability, poverty, violence).
Fiscal constraints threaten sustainability. Although social spending accounts for 46 per cent of the 2025 budget, its share of GDP declined from 13.8 per cent to 12.6 per cent (2019-2023). New reforms (e.g. career guidance, ECI, adolescent skills) risk stalling without predictable domestic financing for recurrent costs.
Shock-responsive social protection lacks scalability. Tajikistan lacks a pre-registered, interoperable social registry and digital payment infrastructure (though the quasi-state “Amonatbank” claims that their bank cards is the most used by population for pensions, government salaries and social benefits) to rapidly scale cash support during climate or economic shocks, despite high vulnerability and remittance dependence (>40 per cent of GDP).

Key Lessons Learned
Policy reform delivers results only when matched with implementation enablers. The HPV vaccine rollout succeeded because it bundled procurement, cold chain upgrades, community engagement and real time monitoring. In contrast, nutrition and ECI services saw slower uptake where training, supervision or supply systems lagged.
Community trust is essential for service uptake. Engaging religious leaders, youth champions, community health workers, and local media was decisive for overcoming vaccine hesitancy and promoting responsive parenting. Top-down communication alone is insufficient.
Systems integration drives efficiency and equity. Linking WASH and infection prevention in health facilities, embedding nutrition into routine health data, and connecting career guidance to labor markets amplified reach and reduced duplication.
Youth agency is a force multiplier. Adolescent climate champions and Eco Clubs not only improved local action, but also strengthened national advocacy, evidenced by Tajikistan’s first youth climate statement and representation at COP30.
Digital tools accelerate accountability, but only with governance. Primero CPIMS+, EMIS, HMIS and nutrition logistics systems improved data use, but their sustainability depends on data protection protocols, institutional ownership, and capacity building.
Prevention is more effective and cost-efficient than remediation. Family support centres prevented 500 children under four from entering residential care, demonstrating that early, community-based support delivers better outcomes than institutional responses.
Private sector partnerships enhance sustainability, but require clear handover plans. Collaborations with Tcell, Alif Bank, and the AI Council expanded digital parenting (e.g. Bebbo app), remote work, and AI career tools, but risk collapse without integration into public systems.
Using evaluation findings to inform operational decisions strengthens results. The Immunization Evaluation demonstrated that explicitly translating evaluation findings on data quality gaps and zero-dose identification into operational decisions strengthens results; this evidence informed adjustments in UNICEF programming and government engagement, including revisions to home-visiting tools, improvements in vaccine forecasting and logistics, and closer integration of these actions into national immunization planning and budgeting processes.

Future Outlook
Operationalize the State Programme for Child Rights (2026–2030) by supporting its financing, defining institutional roles, rolling out Primero CPIMS+ nationwide, and expanding the trained social service workforce to ensure coherent, scalable protection.
Anchor education reform in classrooms by expanding competency-based curricula to additional grades, aligning teaching with assessment, institutionalizing the Coordination and Analytical Unit, and embedding EMIS data into equity-focused planning.
Strengthen climate resilience in social sectors by supporting the implementation of climate-adapted WASH standards in schools and health facilities, integrating disaster risk reduction into school safety plans, and scaling the national climate education toolkit through Eco Clubs and teacher training.
Institutionalize adolescent skills and employability pathways by integrating Adolescent Innovation Labs (AILs) and Impact Sourcing Hubs (ISHs) into national education and employment frameworks, deepening private sector partnerships, and prioritizing inclusion of young women and marginalized youth.
Advance shock-responsive social protection by supporting the development of a pre-registered social registry, interoperable digital payments, and evidence-based policy dialogue on universal child benefits, ensuring faster, fairer support during crises.
Make child poverty analysis routine by supporting the regular production and use of child monetary and multidimensional poverty data in national and subnational planning and budgeting cycles.
Embed child participation and rights monitoring in governance by institutionalizing youth-led mechanisms in local development planning and integrating CRC follow-up into routine government accountability systems.

Three key developments influenced UNICEF’s work on supporting the realization of children’s rights in Türkiye in 2025. The change of regime in Syria triggered the voluntary return of Syrian refugees from Türkiye to Syria. While 578,000 Syrians having voluntarily returned[1] to date; Türkiye continues to host a sizeable number (2.36 million) of Syrians under temporary protection— 48%[2] (1,118,119) of whom are children. 
Two years after the earthquakes, recovery efforts continue, as do unmet needs of those affected. As of February 2025, more than 649,000[3] people remained in container sites, with prolonged displacement and service disruptions disproportionately affecting vulnerable children and families, including refugees in south-east Türkiye. In informal temporary settlements, inadequate shelter, heightened risks of violence, abuse, and exploitation, and limited access to water, sanitation, and hygiene services remain challenges.
Difficult socioeconomic conditions triggered by high inflation (annual rate of 31% for 2025[4]) compounded the vulnerabilities of many children and their families. Child poverty modestly declined from 32% in 2024 (31% for boys, 33% for girls) to 31% (30% for boys, 32% for girls) in 2025[5]. In absolute terms, this still means that 6.7 million children are living in poverty in 2025[6]. The risk of poverty or social exclusion remains considerably higher for children, at 37% in 2025, compared with 28% for the overall population[7].
Public social spending, accounted for 12% of GDP, remaining below the OECD average of 21%[8]. Unemployment rates showed improvement, with the overall rate declining to 8.5% by the end of third quarter of 2025[9], from 8.7% in 2024 and 9.4% in 2023[10]. Youth unemployment (ages 15–24) stands at 15%, with 12% among young men and 22% among young women[11] , highlighting a notable gender gap in the labour market.
In terms of demographic changes, Türkiye’s child population has been slowly declining, reaching 21.8 million in 2025. Yet, children still account for 26% of the total population, underscoring the need to expand investments in child centered policies and programmes.
Education enrolment declined across most levels in the 2024/25 school year. Net pre-school enrollment for children aged 3–5 fell to 49%, down from 52% in the previous year. Lower and upper secondary enrollment also decreased, to 89% and 83% respectively, while primary school enrollment increased slightly to 95%[12] . A total of 17% of 15–19-year-olds were neither in employment, education, nor training (NEET), including 14% of boys and 21% of girls[13], highlighting challenges in the learning to earning transition. These trends make UNICEF’s work in education and adolescent development and participation even more vital, as declining enrolment, rising NEET rates, and a large child population highlight the need to ensure that every child can access quality learning and build the skills needed to transition successfully from school to work. 
Türkiye has 10.1 million children aged 0-8,[14] representing the early childhood development period. While this stage is widely recognized as foundational for long-term development, national systems for early identification of developmental delays and early intervention are still evolving. According to latest available statistics[15],  71% of children (of age 4 and below) achieved the minimum number of milestones expected for their age[16]. Cross-sectoral coordination, data availability, service standards, and institutional capacity remain areas for further development, and dedicated state funding for nurturing care has yet to be established. 
Child protection remains a critical priority in Türkiye. Building on its strong international reputation for institutional care reform, the country has expanded foster care, reaching 10,430 children[17], while residential care placements rose to 15,135, the highest level since 2011[18]. At the same time, violence against children and girls continues to require sustained attention. More than half of all children (54%)[19] are exposed to violent forms of discipline, and bullying disproportionately affects children with functional difficulties (27%)[20]. Among girls and young women aged 15–24, exposure to violence remains significant, with 25% reporting psychological violence, 13% digital violence, and 10% physical violence[21]. Although the number of officially registered marriages among 16–17-year-olds continues to decline, the markedly higher incidence among girls (9,354 compared to 617 boys) highlights persistent gender disparities[22]. 
Children’s contact with the justice system continues to rise, underscoring the critical need for strengthened child-friendly justice and diversion mechanisms. In 2024, the number of children brought into contact with security units increased by 10%, reaching 612,651 cases, nearly half of which (46%) involved children as victims[23]. The number of children taken to court for alleged offences also grew by 12%, from 78,173 in 2023[24] to 87,793[25] in 2024. As of December 2025, 4,666 children aged 12–18 were held in detention[26]. These trends highlight the importance of UNICEF’s efforts to expand preventive services, promote diversion from judicial proceedings, and strengthen child-sensitive procedures that protect children’s rights and wellbeing. The overall situation underscores the ongoing need for robust investments in child protection systems, services, and prevention.

In 2025, UNICEF Türkiye supported strengthening child-focused systems, services and policies to serve vulnerable children, women and families. Interventions in early childhood development, education, child protection, adolescent development and participation were scaled through partnerships with government, civil society, and the private sector, embedding sustainability, equity, and resilience across national and local systems.
To ensure every child survives and thrives, UNICEF focused on strengthening early childhood health and development outcomes by embedding early identification, early intervention and nurturing care within national systems. Support to both centre and home-based ECD models enabled early support for children at risk, improved caregiving practices and more coordinated, inclusive service delivery. Through advocacy and technical assistance with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF supported national agreement on a context-appropriate early identification algorithm and the development of a costed action plan with indicators and targets. Early intervention was embedded within existing social and education service platforms through coordinated leadership by the Ministry of Family and Social Services and the Ministry of National Education, shifting service delivery from fragmented referrals to more coherent, cross-sectoral provision. This enabled the expansion of Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) services in Ankara, Bursa, Mersin, Kahramanmaras and Hatay, with scale-up underway in an additional three provinces.  
Revisions to the national immunization policy were supported and partnership with the Health Institute of Türkiye forged to address behavioral barriers and improve the quality of immunization counselling. The capacities of 4,037 professionals across health, social services and outreach programmes at national and municipal levels were enhanced to improve the quality of counselling and responsiveness of ECD services.
Caregiving practices, including involved fatherhood and early care-seeking behaviors were improved through integrated ECD counselling and parenting support that reached 91,119 children and caregivers (92.5% women, 57% refugees). Parenting support was institutionalized through the launch of the National Parenting Support Programme in government Healthy Living Centres, complemented by a national campaign that reached 306,000 people and digital outreach through the UNICEF-supported Merhaba Bebek app.
In partnership with the Ministry of Health, earthquake recovery efforts supported the restoration and resilience of essential health, nutrition and early childhood development services for vulnerable children and families. UNICEF completed the handover of eight prefabricated containers, previously used as Mother–Baby Corners as part of the earthquake response, to the Ministry of Health to support 160,000 beneficiaries with routine maternal and child health services. In Gaziantep and Hatay, UNICEF supported the resumption of the Neonatal Resuscitation Programme by delivering eight sets of training equipment to Provincial Health Directorates, enabling the restoration of health worker training.
Community-based ECD support and Infant and Young Child Feeding services reached 69,214 parents, including 2,219 counselling sessions at border points for families voluntarily returning to Syria. Preventive care and immunization systems were strengthened through support to revised national guidelines disseminated to over 30,000 health professionals, delivery of 38,000 vaccine doses, and immunization counselling for 11,357 parents, alongside newborn support for 3,000 infants through baby boxes. Sustainability and preparedness were further reinforced by capacitating national breastfeeding evaluators, engaging 230 public health specialists on vaccine confidence, and implementing targeted behavioral interventions to reduce vaccine hesitancy. National preparedness was strengthened through updated emergency nutrition guidance and strengthened coordination within the disaster response framework.
Access to quality Early Childhood Education (ECE) improved for vulnerable children as municipal and civil society partner systems were strengthened to address declining participation among children aged 3–5. With UNICEF’s support, eight municipalities expanded home- and community-based ECE, reaching 7,420 children (49% girls), including 3,134 refugees, and extending early learning beyond formal settings. This change was reinforced by improving the quality of services and caregiving practices and stimulating demand for early learning. The capacities of 554 teachers were enhanced to be able to implement curriculum, play-based learning and strategies for inclusive ECE. And UNICEF-supported parental engagement initiatives reached 12,083 parents and caregivers, which strengthened positive parenting, early stimulation and demand for inclusive early learning services.
In earthquake-affected provinces, UNICEF partnered with Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and municipalities to restore and expand early learning opportunities. Home- and community-based ECE reached 4,963 children (50% girls), with 1,221 parents engaged in parenting sessions. 
Improvements in the quality and inclusiveness of education at primary and lower secondary levels were made possible by strengthening teaching practices and policies in partnership with the Ministry of National Education (MoNE). UNICEF’s technical support to enhanced learning content and teacher capacity, including the training of 43,590 teachers on Social and Emotional Learning and bullying prevention, benefitted nearly 1 million students (49% girls). Other notable developments supported by UNICEF include the finalization of the K–12 Special Education Strategy and development of disability screening tools, and strengthened identification, retention and support for children with disabilities.
To address the issue of approximately 250,000 Syrian refugee children who are out of school, UNICEF and its partners strengthened national capacities by providing technical and financial support to 2,350 education support workers who provided targeted support to Syrian children access formal education. Joint research with the Ministry of National Education across 17 provinces informed evidence-based interventions to address absenteeism. Continuity of learning for refugees improved with 16,508 children and adolescents enrolled in formal education, while 1,784 Syrian parents and caregivers received tailored guidance on Syria’s education system and documentation requirements for voluntary return, marking progress toward integrated, responsive support systems.
The education system’s resilience was further reinforced through disaster risk reduction, climate education, and digital transformation interventions, guided by a nationwide SWOT analysis across 81 provinces that identified gaps and opportunities. Capacity-building of 19,920 teachers on climate and disaster-risk education benefitted 583,904 students, while 950,000 teachers gained accredited digital competencies through the national ÖBA platform.
In collaboration with MoNE and the Ministry of Family and Social Services (MoFSS), a system-wide approach strengthened identification, monitoring, and response to absenteeism and dropout among vulnerable adolescents, including refugees. The Inter-Institutional Schooling Monitoring Framework was piloted in 15 provinces and 75 schools, creating a scalable referral pathway to social services. 
UNICEF strengthened secondary and vocational education to improve inclusion, retention, and employability for vulnerable adolescents, including refugees and students with disabilities. In partnership with MoNE, Ministry of Youth and Sports Development, municipalities and CSOs, 374,374 adolescents received language, academic, and outreach support. Over 270 vocational teachers were trained in special education, benefiting 26,000 students (36% girls) and 5,000 teachers. Teaching programmes for adolescents with severe intellectual disabilities and autism were revised, and an inclusive work-based learning model promoted safe transitions to employment. An innovative partnership model between MoNE and the private sector strengthened safety, inclusivity, and employability in Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), with 120 students completing internships and master trainers enhancing professional development. This has laid the foundation for similar partnerships with the private sector to amplify results. 
Green skills are increasingly critical for preparing young people to thrive in a future shaped by climate change, technological shifts, and new labour-market demands. In recognition of this, UNICEF supported the development of 150 curriculum-linked activities that stand to benefit two million 9th- and 10th-grade students with essential green and digital competencies and learning recovery mechanisms.
To tap into the potential of Türkiye’s young population, UNICEF’s adolescent development and participation programme worked with its partners to amplify children’s voices in policy-making, foster youth engagement and create skills development opportunities outside of the formal education system. UNICEF and MoFSS strengthened adolescent participation and empowerment through Provincial Child Rights Committees reaching 31,545 adolescents (17,413 girls), while partnerships with Gaziantep, Kilis, and Sanliurfa municipalities advanced youth engagement via child and youth councils. Leveraging the expansive coverage of MoYS youth centers, 315,597 young people (164,456 girls) participated in civic engagement and empowerment programmes. Working with the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change, UNICEF helped advance youth participation in climate action through the Youth Climate Envoys Platform, which represents all universities in Türkiye and contributed significantly to shaping Türkiye’s child and youth sensitive NDC 3.0. Youth Climate Envoys organized 2025 Local Conference of Youth (LCOY) in Türkiye, based on the successful implementation of 2024 LCOY and youths sensitive NDC 3.0.
In earthquake-affected provinces, partnerships with government, municipalities, CSOs, and the private sector enabled over 99,000 adolescents and youth (50% girls) to access safe spaces, skills development, and participation opportunities. MoYS youth centres reached 91,371 young people, while Youth-Friendly Spaces and MakerUp STEM programmes in Hatay engaged 4,050 adolescents in digital and 21st-century skills. 
To ensure children are protected from violence, abuse and neglect, UNICEF worked with multiple Ministries, municipalities and CSOs to strengthen child protection and gender-based violence prevention and response systems, advancing policy, service delivery and community engagement.  Community-based services reached 110,806 individuals, including 83,159 children (54% girls); nearly half were identified through case management, with 27,457 referred to specialized services. A total of 52,147 individuals received mental health and psychosocial support. 
UNICEF supported coordinated actions between MoFSS and MoNE to improve early identification, referral, and follow-up of children at risk, and a unified national counselling framework, ensuring consistent, child-centred case management. Collaboration with MoFSS, MoNE, the Presidency of Migration Management (PMM), and CSOs contributed to improved detection, screening, and referral of vulnerable children, including at border points and earthquake-affected provinces.
With UNICEF’s technical expertise, funding, and policy guidance, temporary foster care expanded to 30 provinces, with 14 provinces actively placing children – paving the way for family-based care alternatives. 
UNICEF advanced gender equality and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) prevention and response systems by integrating child survivor-centred services into national structures and improving referral pathways through coordinated training of government and frontline workers. In partnership with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF supported Child Monitoring Centres and trained 106 service providers to deliver child sensitives GBV services, while in MoFSS women’s shelters, 293 staff received training that improved trauma informed care competencies by 10%. Multisectoral coordination was further reinforced by building the capacities of 632 CSO and municipal workers across justice, health, education, and social services. At the community level, 9,069 caregivers participated in gender transformative parenting programmes, GBV and child marriage prevention and response services reached 13,639 individuals, 80% of whom were women and girls. UNICEF also expanded safe digital support through platforms like Laaha, providing girls with protective information on wellbeing, menstrual health and GBV, and Benim Sesim (UNICARE), where feedback mechanisms expanded survivor support and accountability. 
Strengthening child-friendly justice was another area of focus, with UNICEF supporting the Ministry of Justice advance child justice reform by embedding diversion and restorative justice as alternatives to detention for children in conflict with the law. UNICEF-supported advocacy halted a proposed amendment introducing harsher penalties for children. Legal aid reached 2,495 children, including 1,005 (231 refugees) through the Legal Empowerment, Aid and Protection Programme in earthquake-affected areas. 
In the 11 earthquake-affected provinces, UNICEF adapted and expanded community-based Child Protection (CP) and GBV services. This included the scale-up of mobile outreach services and continued operation of Birlikte Hubs, which delivered integrated CP/GBV and early childhood education services. Notably, UNICEF facilitated the transfer of nine Birlikte Hubs from CSOs to Ministry of Health, MoFSS and municipalities, thereby ensuring sustained access to protection and ECD services for vulnerable children and families.
To ensure every child has access to safe and equitable WASH services UNICEF strengthened municipal WASH systems in earthquake-affected provinces. Over 2 million people benefited from infrastructure recovery, digital upgrades, and institutional capacity building. In Adiyaman, a GIS-based asset management system improved network mapping and decision making for 300,000 residents; in Gaziantep, AI-supported water network management reduced losses and optimized water distribution to 250,000 people, while in Hatay - damaged water and sewage systems were restored. Additionally, 70,750 hygiene kits and protection messaging reached 347,882 people, and 85,778 used feedback channels to inform service adjustments and reinforce accountability. These actions strengthened technical capacity, digital monitoring, and emergency preparedness, embedding the systemic shift toward efficient, climate-resilient WASH services.
UNICEF contributed to strengthening Türkiye’s social protection system by collaborating with MoFSS in making it more child-sensitive and shock-responsive. This included building the capacities of over 400 government staff to identify gaps; refine targeting and enrollment mechanisms; and through a cash-preparedness and readiness exercise – improve understanding and metrics of shock-responsive social protection, creating a technical foundation and policy commitment for better preparedness and future emergency cash responses. 
Local governance was strengthened by embedding child-focused priorities into subnational planning and financing, promoting evidence-based, coordinated municipal action. In Ankara, Izmir, and Gaziantep, 195 municipal and CSO staff enhanced their capacity to analyse child wellbeing data—and translate this into cross-sectoral responses. Child-responsive financing was reinforced through the institutionalized child budget monitoring dashboard, rolled out to 50 municipalities, and the introduction of a child tag in the International Cooperation Monitoring System, enabling systematic tracking of investments for children.
National capacity for child-related data systems was strengthened in partnership with the Presidency of Strategy and Budget, TurkStat, and line ministries. UNICEF supported the first ever Data Landscape Analysis for Child-Related Data, resulting in an actionable roadmap to address data gaps and improve governance. Technical support and advocacy with Turkstat resulted in the inclusion of a module on cyberbullying in a national survey, and this will generate Türkiye’s first nationally representative digital violence data in 2026. UNICEF also supported TDHS 2024 (results in 2026) and initiated a national bullying survey with MoFSS to inform prevention strategies. These actions reinforce sustainable, integrated systems and evidence-based policy for vulnerable children. The work on data and evidence was reinforced with learning from evaluations, with three evaluations completed; one on the Syrian Support Workers and how they have been able to support Syrian refugee children access services; one  on Support for School Enrolment for out of school vulnerable children and a baseline for a randomized control trial (RCT) impact evaluation on the elimination of child marriage. Learnings and recommendations have helped inform programme design.
As custodian of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, UNICEF strengthened child rights monitoring and accountability by reinforcing independent oversight and civil society engagement. The Ombudsman Institution was supported to revise and endorse a Child Rights Strategy and child friendly decision writing procedures, while the Human Rights and Equality Institution enhanced systematic monitoring through a dedicated expert group. UNICEF expanded civic space by building the capacity of 437 stakeholders—including 122 CSOs and 315 media professionals—which enabled the first CSO child rights submission to the Universal Periodic Review. High-level advocacy, including the first country visit of the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children, prompted the Government of Türkiye to strengthen accountability by committing as a Pathfinding country. This commitment is translating into concrete actions to address violence against children, including online violence. 
UNICEF amplified public engagement and advocacy for children’s rights, achieving nationwide visibility. Over 120 million people were reached digitally and 60,000 media mentions sustained high visibility on child rights, driving policy dialogue, social mobilization, and fundraising. Strategic advocacy and donor visibility were strengthened through targeted multimedia content, National Ambassador engagement, coordinated campaigns, and partnerships with government, civil society, and the private sector.
In a year that was marked by substantial global funding cuts to the UN system, a transition from emergency response to longer term recovery and resilience; and in preparation for the start of the 2026-2030 UNICEF programme cycle; the office recalibrated the size and skills composition of its human resources. This was driven as much by affordability as it was on the need to realign the skills set of staff to deliver results for children. With increased nationalization and a leaner structure better suited to deliver impact at scale - UNICEF Turkiye maintained staff engagement through a Staff Wellbeing and Support Strategy, supported career development initiatives, and fostered an inclusive work environment. Operational continuity was sustained through the relocation of the Gaziantep Field Office to WFP managed premises, optimizing resources in a changing global and national context.
UNICEF used its convening role to expand and strengthen partnerships around delivering results for children. Existing partnerships were nurtured, and new relationships forged with public and private sector donors to expand and diversify UNICEF’s donor base.  In 2025, a total of approximately US$ 83 million was mobilized from public and private donors. UNICEF’s Business Advisory Board (BAB) served as a strategic platform for private sector engagement; private sector partners contributed approximately US$6 million in financial and in-kind contributions and driving advocacy and innovation for children and young people. Through the BAB, leading businesses advanced child rights principles and strengthened partnerships for sustainable impact. By the end of 2025, the total amount raised against the Syrian refugee response under Humanitarian Action for Children appeal reached US$ 35.4 million with an additional US$ 9.4 million that was carried forward from 2024 funds, leaving the funding gap at 48%.  UNICEF advanced resource mobilization by initiating strategic dialogues with new partners, including international financial institutions like the Asian Development Bank, Islamic Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, to explore financing opportunities for children.
Strategic partnerships with key government institutions—including PSB, MoNE, MoFSS, MoYS, MoH, Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, Ministry of Labour and Social Services, Ministry of Justice, the Justice Academy, Ombudsman, Union of Municipalities, PMM, water authorities, Union of Bar Associations, TESK, and TurkStat—enabled UNICEF to strengthen national systems, coordinate cross-sectoral responses, and deliver results at scale for children. This was complemented by partnerships with 44 implementing partners by way of civil society organisations and academia. 
Programme, financial and operational oversight was ensured through programme visits, spot checks and audits; and all internal audit recommendations were addressed and closed on time. Supply and Logistics strengthened programme delivery and emergency readiness through improved supply chain performance, digitization, and sustainability, including enhanced commodity visibility, solar solutions, eco-friendly construction, and expanded partnerships.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The closure of most temporary accommodation centers and container cities, the evolving situation in Syria, combined with the intention of many Syrian refugee families to return to Syria, and rise in irregular migration meant that UNICEF had to adapt its interventions and core preparedness measures to meet evolving needs and enhance readiness. These pressures were compounded by declining and highly earmarked funding and limited capacity of statutory service providers at sub-national levels, leaving vulnerable children and families in Türkiye in a precarious situation.
The closure of temporary accommodation centres for Syrians under Temporary Protection and container cities for earthquake-affected populations created a highly fluid operating environment. Differences in coordination mechanisms, limited advance planning and timely transfer of services and case follow-up, including continuity of school enrolment for children relocating to new provinces. Short evacuation periods further constrained access to protection and services. UNICEF and partners adapted by strengthening real-time tracking of site closures, coordinating the relocation of UNICEF-supported services, and following up with school-age children to support enrolment in receiving provinces. To ensure continuity of critical and life-saving support, centre-based ECD services were transformed into mobile modalities, with qualified teams conducting outreach and home visits to families in need. This enabled vulnerable families to continue accessing essential ECD support despite relocation. Additionally, transportation support for mobile teams helped reach families with children with disabilities and those living in remote areas, ensuring equitable access to services.
Fluidity was further amplified following the change in regime in Syria and the start of a new phase in Türkiye’s migration management with the initiation of voluntary returns. While the Government managed the process, return trends fluctuated due to seasonal factors, school calendars, conditions in Syria, and economic pressures, limiting predictability and planning. UNICEF demonstrated flexibility in both programming and funding to respond effectively to evolving mobility patterns and protection needs. 
To support the safe, voluntary, and dignified returns, UNICEF worked with government and CSOs, in close coordination with UNHCR and other agencies, to support families’ urgent needs, including improving conditions at border crossing points, providing counselling and breastfeeding spaces, and distributing hygiene and psychosocial support materials for children and families on the move. UNICEF’s rapid establishment of a Mother Baby Corner at the Cilvegözü border crossing demonstrated the importance of context-specific ECD service delivery in high-flow settings. Continued engagement with government counterparts enabled the expansion of health, nutrition, and ECD counselling services to additional border crossings.
Referral pathways for unaccompanied and separated children were improved by UNICEF’s support to the roll out of an advanced case management framework between PMM and MoFSS. UNICEF also supported the roll out Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE), and the dissemination of family information packages in communities and border crossing points to ensure that families choosing to return, did so with the right information and tools to navigate this change. To support children successfully transition from the Turkish education system to the Syrian education system, expanding access to Arabic language courses was supported. Recognizing the importance of intergovernmental coordination to facilitate smooth education transition, the Turkish Ministry of National Education’s participation in two sub-regional inter-ministerial coordination conferences was supported by UNICEF with the Syrian Ministry of Education and other countries hosting Syrian refugees. The importance of greater coordination at the subregional level between governments as well as with international partners was a key lesson. 
The importance, and potential, of forging innovative partnerships to catalyze resources for children was another key lesson. UNICEF piloted an innovative partnership model that brought together a leading private sector company, an International Financial Institution (IFI) and the government around child- and youth-centered outcomes.
