UNICEF convened and connected the government, private sector and IFI, so that corporate commitments translated into tangible “learning-to-earning” results: funding for technical and vocational education and training, supervised on-the-job training for students, enhanced capacities of teachers and improved workplace-learning quality. This demonstrated clear success in aligning funding, policy, and corporate assets around children’s and young people’s prospects, establishing a replicable model UNICEF intends to scale with additional companies and IFI engagements.
To ensure that communities, particularly children and caregivers, could consistently access safe, responsive, and inclusive feedback mechanisms to express needs, raise concerns, and influence services, UNICEF invested efforts in institutionalising Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) as a core function across its programmes.  Child-centred accountability was advanced by co-creating and testing three age-appropriate feedback pathways for children aged 4–17. Developed through participatory sessions involving children, caregivers, and partner staff, these pathways ensured feedback mechanisms were developmentally appropriate and meaningful. Overall, 85,778 individuals (44 % Syrian) accessed feedback and complaint mechanisms, including more than 4,000 community members providing input on municipal services. This engagement was used to adjust to interventions to adequately respond to the feedback, and in doing so - strengthened transparency and responsiveness across sectors. Parallel capacity-building with municipalities and partners deepened institutional understanding of AAP, supporting integration into routine service delivery. Collectively, these achievements position UNICEF as a leader in inclusive and participatory accountability systems. 
UNICEF will build on these lessons to remain agile in a dynamic programming context, scaling innovative partnerships, strengthening intergovernmental coordination, and embedding child-centered accountability. Future efforts will focus on flexible programming and expanded outreach to ensure every child has access to safe, inclusive, and quality services.

During the reporting period, the Government of Turkmenistan maintained a strong emphasis on stability and neutrality, pursuing long-term development priorities, supported by sustained revenue from the hydrocarbon sector, which accounted for the vast majority of exports. While official statistics report robust growth of 6.3 per cent in 2025, international financial institutions projected more moderate increase, with the IMF estimating 2.3 per cent growth. The UN resolution declaring the International Year of Peace and Trust, adopted at Turkmenistan’s initiative, coincided with the 30th Anniversary of Turkmenistan’s Permanent Neutrality, bringing together numerous heads of state and reinforcing the importance of multilateralism, encouraging deeper diplomatic engagement and collective action for global stability and regional peace. 

In 2025, 76 per cent of the state budget was allocated to social needs, with education receiving 37 per cent of social expenditures, healthcare 13 per cent, and social protection 37 per cent. Public expenditure represents less than 10% of the country's GDP with the target set to be at least 15% of GDP on social spending by 2030. The discontinuation in 2025 of the long-standing practice of annual 10 per cent raises in public sector wages and social benefits is expected to increase economic vulnerability among low-income and at-risk population groups. In response, discussions are ongoing to strengthen household well-being monitoring, introduce national poverty measurement and review the effectiveness of social safety net programmes. 
 
The public release in 2025 of the  Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) key results marked a significant milestone, providing data to monitor 29 SDG indicators alongside national development targets and sectoral strategies. This directly supports the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025, which emphasizes robust data systems, evidence generation, and results monitoring. MICS data highlights areas where progress has been made, for example in maternal mortality, as well as areas where further focus is required, for example pre-primary education, and child health. High disparities remain between urban and rural areas.  

For the first time, the MICS included a module on violence against women, revealing an intimate partner violence prevalence rate of 9.6 per cent, compared to 12 per cent reported in the 2022 Survey on Health and the Status of Women in the Family. The prevalence of psychological, physical, or sexual violence in the past 12 months is notably higher in urban areas (15.1 per cent) than in rural areas (4.5 per cent). Collectively, the findings underscore the need for targeted, context-specific prevention and response strategies.  

Gender norms continue to play an important role in shaping childrearing practices, family responsibilities, and access to opportunities for women and girls. Childcare and domestic responsibilities are largely borne by women, influencing early childhood care arrangements, parental engagement, and the distribution of time and resources and need to be sufficiently analysed in national child-focused research and programming. 
 
Implementation of the 2023–2028 National Action Plan for the Realization of Children’s Rights (NAPC) continued through a national inter-agency coordination mechanism. To ensure systematic follow-up to the 2024 CRC Concluding Observations, a dedicated Roadmap has been initiated for implementation and monitoring of priority actions, including the prevention of and response to violence against children. A major milestone was the Government’s designation of the Prosecutor General’s Office as the coordinating body for the development of a National Programme on Child Protection and Justice for Children, addressing a key CRC recommendation to strengthen inter-agency cooperation.
 
Education sector reforms continued in 2025, including the rollout of 12 years of compulsory education, curriculum modernization, and sustained investment in school infrastructure, in line with SDG 4. These reforms reflect national progress toward UNICEF Strategic Plan goal that “every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future” through modernized curricula, equitable access to quality education, and strengthened learning environments. Participation in early childhood education has increased in recent years; however, access to organized learning one year before primary school remains limited, with only 44 per cent of children enrolled. In 2025, Turkmenistan reported 4,044 children living in residential care, of whom 3,298 with disabilities, highlighting the urgency of accelerating deinstitutionalization and inclusive education reforms. The Ministry of Education continued implementation of inclusive education in selected model schools and kindergartens. 

Women dominate education (70%) and health and social services (73%), sectors vital to child well-being, yet little analysis examines how working conditions and disparities affect service quality. Women face greater economic vulnerability due to caregiving roles and higher rates of informal work (29.5% vs. 18% for men), affecting about 530,000 workers. Risks are especially acute in agriculture, where women make up 48% of over one million workers, but fewer than 50,000 are formally employed. 

In 2025, Turkmenistan hosted several high-level international events, including the Third UN Conference on Landlocked Developing Countries (LLDC3). These platforms strengthened the country’s global engagement and reaffirmed its commitment to multilateral cooperation, sustainable development, and peaceful dialogue. Importantly, the outcomes of the conferences provided renewed momentum for advancing the Sustainable Development Goals, including child-related priorities such as equitable access to education, health, social protection, and climate resilience. 
 
During the reporting period, Turkmenistan’s context was shaped by regional instability. Amid the 2025 crisis in Iran, Turkmenistan facilitated the safe transit of thousands of foreign nationals evacuating from Iran, demonstrating strong neutrality and regional cooperation. As a humanitarian partner, UNICEF ensured readiness and preparedness to support if needs arise.  

Turkmenistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, with 80% desert territory and a medium-high Children’s Climate Risk Index ranking. Rising temperatures, heatwaves, and droughts are straining water and food security and increasing health risks, particularly for women, girls, and children in rural areas. Regional pressures—including upstream infrastructure projects and declining reservoirs—are heightening hydrological instability. The reporting period also offered an opportunity to support updated national climate commitments (NDC 3.0) with child-sensitive, costed measures. 

The 2026–2030 Country Programme Document (CPD), approved in September 2025, marks UNICEF’s seventh programme in Turkmenistan and aligns with the 2026–2030 UNSDCF. Building on past lessons, it prioritizes early childhood development, disability inclusion and care, and climate action with youth engagement. The CPD aligns with UNICEF’s new Strategic Plan and UN@80 agenda.

In 2025, UNICEF Turkmenistan focused on system-level results aligned with national priorities, the NAPC, the UNSDCF, the UNICEF Strategic Plan, and the SDGs. Progress centred on evidence-based policy dialogue, sustainable financing, and scalable models in health, inclusive education, ECD, child protection, and social services, with a strong equity focus. Social and behaviour change efforts promoted positive parenting and supportive community norms to strengthen ECD and child well-being. 

Every Child Counts: Data and Accountability for Results 

A central enabler across sectors in 2025 was strengthened data and evidence. Government leswWith UNICEF support, Turkmenistan launched MICS and produced the first-ever child-focused thematic report from the 2022 Population and Housing Census, closing major evidence gaps and restoring routine, disaggregated child data by sex, age, location, and disability. The Census 2022: Situation of Children in Turkmenistan confirms that children make up 34.9% of the population, while MICS highlights disparities in early learning, child health, and the continued use of violent discipline—evidence now guiding policy dialogue and 2026 budget priorities.

For the first time since 1995, actionable census disaggregation enables targeted planning in ECE, child protection, disability inclusion, and child and adolescent health, supporting monitoring of CRC, CEDAW, and SDG commitments. UNICEF ensured methodological quality and translated findings into policy options, linking evidence to decision points such as UNSDCF reviews, sector planning, and the budget cycle. The data is now informing gender-responsive and geographically targeted interventions, including scaling pre-primary education, strengthening social services, expanding primary health care, and adapting inclusive education models.

UNICEF provided methodological assurance, analysis and translation of findings for MICS into policy options with sector ministries. The office linked evidence to decision points (UNSDCF reviews, sector planning, and the 2026 budget cycle), ensuring data is used, not merely generated. The UNICEF regular resources (RR) supported the data analysis, communications and convening required to socialize findings across ministries. The new evidence surfaces gendered patterns in early marriage/childbearing, continued investments required for child health and geographic disparities in ECE participation. 

Independent Oversight for Children’s Rights - Ombudsperson and CRC Follow-Up  

In 2025, UNICEF helped translate evidence into governance. With support to the Ombudsperson’s Office and the Interagency Commission’s Working Group, follow-up to the CRC Concluding Observations moved from principle to practice. A dedicated unit on women’s and children’s rights began building standard procedures for receiving and addressing children’s complaints; and a Roadmap anchored to the NAPC coordinated ministerial responsibilities and timeline so the CRC becomes a practical management tool for ministries and not just an international commitment.  

UNICEF facilitated the partnership with Türkiye with targeted technical support, to support procedures that are practical for frontline staff, not only policy actors. By pairing accessible complaints and redress mechanisms with whole-of-government coordination, UNICEF is strengthening accountability to the CRC, closing institutional gaps, and improving protection outcomes for children across social services, education, justice, and health.

By equipping the Ombudsperson’s Office with confidential, child-friendly complaints protocols and aligning ministries around a CRC Roadmap anchored in the NAPC, Turkmenistan is reducing institutional gaps, clarifying roles, and creating a closed feedback loop where violations can be reported, referred, remedied and prevented through policy change. This aims to strengthens accountability to the CRC and improves day-to-day protection outcomes for children across social services, education, justice, and health.  

Child rights in climate/DRR and NDC 3.0. Embedding children’s rights in climate and DRR policy is critical to avoid widening inequities. UNICEF supported line ministries to integrate child- and youth-focused proposals into NDC 3.0, ensuring national climate plans address child-specific risks and link education, health, and social protection systems to climate resilience. Building on Green School and DRR initiatives, this work moved child rights from pilot programmes into binding policy frameworks with multi-year financing horizons. In partnership with key ministries and UNDP, UNICEF supported the drafting and submission of proposals on school safety and early warning, climate-resilient WASH and health services, risk-informed social protection, and youth participation, with RR enabling cross-sector technical coordination and policy engagement. 

Every Child Survives and Thrives: Primary Health Care, Immunization and Nutrition 
In 2025, UNICEF continued to prioritize system-level efforts to reduce preventable maternal, newborn, and child deaths in Turkmenistan by scaling up essential health and nutrition services, sustaining high immunization coverage, and strengthening ECD systems. UNICEF supported the Government through policy development, capacity building, evidence generation, and service delivery strengthening to improve health outcomes for children nationwide. 

Sustainable immunization with high coverage In 2025, Turkmenistan achieved a major child survival milestone: sustainable, multi-year domestic financing for routine immunization and an updated national schedule—aligned with WHO guidance—introducing IPV and hexavalent vaccines, maintaining 95% coverage. UNICEF supported policy dialogue on fiscal sustainability, procurement, and Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) to strengthen cold chain and logistics, alongside interpersonal communication to address vaccine hesitancy, with RR enabling flexible, continuous support to scale delivery and ensure programme resilience.

Quality childcare through IMCI and newborn care. At the primary health care level, the National Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) scaleup standardized case management for the leading causes of under-five mortality. Training cascades reached approximately 1,700 primary healthcare workers, while complementary investments upgraded neonatal emergency care - from resuscitation and bCPAP competencies to preventive maintenance of oxygen systems in Mother and Child Health hospitals. UNICEF’s role was to institutionalize quality, embedding IMCI into PHC routines, and aligning newborn care skills with practical supervision. RR funding allowed the Country Office to consolidate learning across velayats and keep mentorship going after the initial trainings - turning episodic workshops into a durable improvement in clinical practice. 

Nutrition systems and infant feeding. Nutrition systems have advanced with UNICEF supporting a renewed MoU on national flour fortification and submitting a revised draft Law on Promoting and Supporting Breastfeeding aligned with the International Code. The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative certified four primary facilities and trained 144 providers, reinforcing optimal feeding practices from birth. UNICEF’s efforts spanned legislative drafting, producer engagement, and workforce development, strengthening caregiver support, respectful maternity care, and adherence to the International Code. These interventions addressed gender-related barriers to optimal feeding, including social norms, women’s decision-making autonomy, and postpartum support access. While focused on early childhood and maternal health, future programming will link with adolescent health to support nutrition, mental health, and health-seeking behaviors. RR funding enabled legislative and workforce initiatives, advancing nutrition systems and infant feeding.

Data and Assessments – Strengthened National Evidence Systems. UNICEF strengthened national systems for evidence-informed decision-making in child health and nutrition. Key system-level assessments were completed, including a comprehensive review of primary healthcare services using the Universal Progressive Home Visiting maturity model, a National School Nutrition Environment Assessment (NEAT-s), and an assessment of breastfeeding practices. Together, these assessments generated a consolidated national evidence base to inform policy reform, service quality improvements, and resource allocation. Findings and evidence-based recommendations will be disseminated in early 2026 to support policy dialogue and programme design. 

Early Childhood Development – Systems, Services, and Capacity Strengthened. Under the National Early Childhood Development Strategy (2020–2025), UNICEF helped strengthen national ECD systems, including drafting the new 2026–2030 Strategy and Action Plan, providing a multi-sectoral framework across health, education, social protection, and finance. Consultations with 40 specialists aligned priorities with international standards and built consensus on implementation.

In 2025, 38,241 children accessed ECD services through demonstration primary healthcare facilities. Of these, 4,358 were identified with developmental delays, 4,120 received early intervention, and 725 showed improved outcomes, demonstrating effective referral and follow-up mechanisms. Services reached boys and girls equally, with the GMCD scale-up supporting timely detection even in contexts influenced by gender norms.

Capacity for quality ECD services improved through GMCD expansion to 12 additional Houses of Health and training for 297 health workers, while 10 national ECD specialists strengthened skills via online training. National and international consultations and training initiatives funded by RR further reinforced institutional competencies.

Enabling environment and demand generation: Routine healthcare platforms were leveraged to strengthen caregiver knowledge and demand for ECD services. A caregiver manual in Turkmen and Russian was developed to support monitoring of child development (0–5 years), promote responsive caregiving, and encourage timely care-seeking. Consultations showed high trust in institutional services among parents (72 per cent), alongside moderate confidence in identifying developmental delays (53 per cent), highlighting progress in service credibility while underscoring the need for continued caregiver empowerment. 

Every Child is Protected from Violence and Socially Included - System Reform, Services and Justice for Children 
In child protection and social inclusion, 2025 marked a turning point. The Government designated the Prosecutor General’s Office to coordinate the forthcoming National Programme on Child Protection and Justice for Children - a decisive step toward a coherent system with clear inter ministerial accountability. UNICEF paired neutral facilitation with evidence on the drivers of family separation, supporting a draft Concept on Alternative Care that prioritizes family-based solutions and sets the pathway for gatekeeping, case review, and integrated service packages. Peer learning (e.g., cross-learning with Moldova) helped contextualize feasible models for Turkmenistan, while RR financed the timely technical inputs and convening that moved the process forward. With limited donor funding in Turkmenistan, RR funds were pivotal to finance the institutionalization study on drivers of child institutionalization and sustain hands-on capacity building on international standards. 

Alternative Care of Children. To reduce family separation and improve care for children without parental care, UNICEF supported evidence generation and policy development aligned with the 2009 Guidelines for the Alternative Care of Children. Studies on drivers of institutionalization, including for children with disabilities, informed planning with social and education ministries. UNICEF helped draft a Concept on Alternative Care emphasizing family-based care and launched a “Strong Family” roadmap with priority reforms such as gatekeeping, case reviews, and integrated services. Preparatory work for foster care pilots in 2026 included procedures, training, and coordination planning. By 2024, 4,044 children lived in residential care—82% with disabilities and 38% girls—highlighting the need for gender- and disability-responsive alternatives. Regional learning, including a study visit to Moldova, informed feasible models for prevention, family support, and alternative care.

Justice for Children. UNICEF supported partners with practical improvements across investigation and court stages. The diversion and restorative justice pilot in Ashgabat continued to show promising results, with strengthened risk and needs assessment, improved case planning, and increased interest from the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MoIA) and partners in expanding non-custodial approaches. In 2025, the pilot supported 6 diversion cases, including 2 girls, demonstrating early application of child-sensitive approaches in practice. Building on a training-of-trainers package for child-friendly investigations, UNICEF advocated for institutionalization of the modules within the MoIA training system and supported dialogue on adapting materials to the national context. Progress was also made in court procedures, including technical support for child-friendly rooms, advancement of family judges, and exploration of additional safeguards such as court-based psychological support.  

Community-based social services scaled within existing ceilings. In 2025, UNICEF supported Turkmenistan to strengthen social and child protection by scaling community-based social services and integrating them more closely with the social protection system. Building on the Law on Social Services, over USD 4 million in state funds has been allocated since 2022, enabling more than 7,000 vulnerable families to access family-centred support, including over 2,000 in 2025(of which 30 per cent children, 60 per cent women, and 33 per cent people and children with disabilities). Workforce strengthening benefited frontline providers—predominantly women—through improved training, supervision, and case management tools.

Community-based services also informed policy dialogue on child-responsive budgeting and efficiency with the Ministry of Labor and Social protection of Population (MoLSP) and the Ministry of Finance and Economy. While budgets remained flat in 2025, advocacy led to the creation of 10 additional state-funded social worker posts, expanding coverage from 18 to 35 districts within existing ceilings. UNICEF further supported strengthening of the social service workforce through in-service training, improved standards and tools, and pre-service education, supporting a bachelor’s programme in social work at two universities with 100 students enrolled. A blended certification programme completed by 65 practitioners and policymakers further strengthened case management and referral pathways, with UNICEF regular resources enabling these results and supporting scale-up efforts.

Shock responsive social protection. UNICEF also advanced shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) to reduce crisis-related vulnerabilities affecting children. SRSP training and a national simulation exercise in April 2025 improved multisector coordination among ministries, financial institutions, local authorities, and the National Red Crescent Society. The revised draft National Action Plan on Strengthening Social Protection System Preparedness for Shocks outlined clearer mechanisms for cash delivery, coordination, communication, and accountability during emergencies. 

Strengthening Social Protection Systems. From April to October 2025, the Inter-Agency Social Protection Assessment (CODI) was conducted, with preliminary findings discussed during a four-day national dialogue in November. The final CODI report, together with Turkmenistan’s contribution to the Generation 2050 Regional Report, will guide evidence-based prioritization and advocacy for financing child-focused social protection reforms in 2026. 

Every Child Learns: Inclusive Education, Early Learning, Climate and Safety 
In 2025, UNICEF supported the strengthening of institutional capacity across the education sector to deliver inclusive early learning and pre-primary preparation, promote gender-responsive and climate change education, and improve learning environments at home and in schools. A comprehensive approach to disability inclusion enhanced the readiness of national partners to implement inclusive education nationwide. 

Inclusive education (IE): an operational model ready to scale.Through sustained technical support with the Ministry of Education and multi-sectoral social sector partners, UNICEF helped operationalize the national inclusive education (IE) model. Piloted in four mainstream facilities, the model delivers inclusive teaching, multidisciplinary support, assistive technologies, and improved accessibility, with the aim to expand IE to 13 additional kindergartens and 13 secondary schools in 2026.

In 2025, Individual Education Plans (IEPs) were institutionalized as a standard tool in mainstream education, strengthening individualized support and parental engagement, including parents’ involvement where professional support is limited. Facility assessments informed a standardized accessibility methodology and planned infrastructure upgrades for 2026. Targeted support on autism spectrum disorders resulted in a draft inter-ministerial action plan for adoption in 2026. UNICEF advocacy also advanced gender-responsive education, embedding gender-oriented materials into in-service teacher training and secondary school practice.

Pre-Primary Preparation (PPP): unlocking access for five-year-olds. Addressing early learning gaps, UNICEF advocacy supported secure government funding to pilot a one-year, half-day Pre-Primary Preparation (PPP) programme, responding to the exclusion of 56 per cent of five-year-olds from pre-primary education (SDG 4.2.2). 65 new pre-primary classes will be opened in 55 mainstream schools in September 2026. This school-based model overcomes kindergarten infrastructure limitations and provides a scalable, equitable approach to early learning, particularly benefiting children in underserved regions and low-income households. 

To strengthen learning environments at home and improve school readiness, UNICEF supported the MoE to pilot a Parenting Support Programme (PSP). A structured PSP curriculum - including a teacher’s manual and a parent toolkit - was developed and translated into Turkmen. The programme promotes positive discipline and enriched home learning environments, addressing the gap between parental attitudes and practices (only 4.7 per cent of caregivers believe physical punishment is necessary, yet 42 per cent of children experience it; MICS 2024). In total, 144 kindergarten teachers were trained, creating a national cadre to support scale-up. The programme is anchored within the National Action Plan for Children (2023–2028) and the National ECD Strategy, providing a sustainable platform for nationwide family engagement. 

Green, safe and climate-resilient schools. In 2025, UNICEF advanced child-centred climate action in Turkmenistan through an integrated regional approach linking climate policy, climate-resilient education, DRR, and youth engagement. A climate change adaptation (CCA) and disaster risk reduction (DRR) preschool programme was launched and disseminated nationwide (including preschool administrators, methodologists, regional education departments, and higher education institutions ), while development of a higher education curriculum is ongoing. UNICEF also received funding for disability-inclusive DRR, documented in a global case study.

The Green School Programme, endorsed in March 2025, piloted 20 schools with the appointment of a national coordinator, conducted energy audits, published materials, and supported Environmental Committees in awareness campaigns and efficiency improvements.

Together with the MoE and National Red Crescent Society of Turkmenistan (NRCST), UNICEF trained over 3,500 students, educators, and volunteers in emergency preparedness and DRR, highlighting gender gaps among teachers and promoting safety, climate adaptation, and psychosocial support in model schools. Additional small-scale initiatives - such as early warning systems, classroom greening, waste management improvements, and lighting assessments - enhanced the safety, functionality, and psychosocial well-being of learning environments in targeted model schools. 

Every child participates In 2025, UNICEF Turkmenistan strengthened child and youth participation in programme and policy development, using strategic advocacy and social behaviour change (SBC) approaches. Consultations, workshops, and interactive initiatives engaged young people on their rights under the CRC, social inclusion, health, and climate action. Partnerships with government, civil society, and media amplified youth voices and translated their perspectives into policy dialogue and community-level action.

Cultural and public platforms advanced child rights advocacy. On the International Day for Protection of the Child, 300 children in Ashgabat performed the traditional Kushtdepdi dance, supported by the Ministries of Culture and Education, the Ombudsperson’s Office, and media partners. Complementary CRC awareness sessions extended outreach to schoolchildren, demonstrating how creative partnerships can deliver rights-based messages broadly.

Youth leadership in climate action was strengthened through the Youth Climate Summer School, launched on World Environment Day. The three-month initiative strengthened young people’s communication and advocacy skills on climate change through expert-led sessions, site visits, and engagement with national and international partners. Thirty-

World Children’s Day 2025 served as a high-visibility platform to promote inclusion under the theme “Neutrality and Humanism: Comprehensive Support for an Inclusive Future.” Jointly organized with national partners, the event mobilized families, service providers, and institutions around inclusive services, particularly for children with disabilities, strengthening cross-sectoral collaboration.  participants developed advocacy projects and produced a National Youth Statement for LCOY 2025, reinforcing their role as climate advocates.

To broaden social engagement, UNICEF launched a national edutainment series on climate change, education, parenting, social inclusion, and early childhood development, complemented by print materials and participatory feedback tools. Collectively, these initiatives enhanced public awareness, promoted positive behaviours, and reinforced strategic partnerships with media, educators, and families.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF used adaptive programming in Turkmenistan to refine strategies, strengthen systems, and expand services for children. Data from MICS and national assessments highlighted gaps in equity, coverage, and sustainability, guiding adjustments for the 2026–2030 Country Programme. Despite incorporating previous evaluation recommendations, challenges in national capacity for strategic planning and results-based management remain, underscoring the need for continued targeted support.
 
Strategic Partnerships with Government for Public Finance for Children. A key learning in 2025 was strategic engagement with government on public finance for children. Ongoing consultations enabled UNICEF and the Government to explore co-financing for the upcoming Country Programme, reflecting greater engagement on child-responsive planning, budgeting, and spending. The Country Office strengthened upstream dialogue, aligning discussions with national planning and budget cycles. Moving forward, UNICEF will institutionalize structured co-financing dialogue, using evidence-based advocacy on budget efficiency, equity, and impact. Insights from the Generation 2050 Regional Report will guide investments in early childhood, health, and community-based social services, maximizing the impact of state budgets for children.

Disability Inclusion and Multi-Sectoral Partnership. Experience in advancing disability inclusion and inclusive education highlighted the importance of system integration and scale. Piloting the national inclusive education model showed that meaningful outcomes for children with disabilities require coordinated, multidisciplinary action across education, health, and social protection. Collaboration among schools, health professionals, and social workers enabled individualized learning and participation support in pilot mainstream schools and kindergartens in Ashgabat. Capacity development at the Health Rehabilitation Center strengthened multidisciplinary services, addressed specialist shortages, and offered a replicable model for national scale-up.

Implementation also revealed gaps: insufficient specialized personnel, limited accessible infrastructure, and lack of assistive technologies. Strong parental engagement was crucial, particularly when parents supported classrooms, but sustainable staffing solutions remain needed. Underrepresentation of children with autism highlighted gaps in early identification, specialized services, and outreach. Lessons emphasized the value of multidisciplinary teams, jointly developed Individualized Education and Intervention Plans, ongoing capacity development, and meaningful parent involvement.

These insights informed policy shifts and discussions toward a functional, socio-psychological approach to disability assessment, supporting inclusive education and the transformation of rehabilitation facilities into inclusive resource centers. From 2026, the model will aim to expand to 13 kindergartens and 13 schools nationwide, supported by the National Concept on Inclusive Education, the National ECD Strategy (2026–2030), and an inter-ministerial ASD action plan.

Equity Programming. Evidence from MICS and other national data sources played a critical role in informing adaptive management. While national averages suggest progress across several child wellbeing indicators, disaggregated data reveal persistent inequities by geography, socio-economic status, disability, and caregiver education. MICS findings highlighted gaps in early stimulation, nutrition practices, and caregiver confidence in identifying developmental delays, reinforcing the need to strengthen demand-side interventions alongside service expansion. Census 2022 data indicate that boys make up 52% of children and girls 48%, a distribution consistent across rural and urban areas. This demographic information will guide UNICEF in ensuring gender-responsive planning and equitable access to services. Data limitations - particularly related to disability disaggregation and functional difficulties - constrained more precise targeting of the most vulnerable children. In response, UNICEF will prioritize equity-focused programming as we support dissemination of results, strengthen the use of disaggregated data for planning and monitoring, and support integration of child-sensitive indicators into routine administrative and sectoral information systems. 

Protecting Children through Climate Action, Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Preparedness. In 2025, UNICEF’s experience showed that integrating climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction (DRR) into core social sectors—education, health, WASH, social protection, and youth engagement—is more effective than stand-alone interventions. Regional coordination, demonstrated that pooled expertise and shared technical assistance accelerate implementation, improve efficiency, and strengthen sectoral coherence. The Green School Programme provided a practical entry point for mainstreaming climate education and promoting safe, climate-resilient learning environments. Gender considerations ensured equal benefits for boys and girls, including access to WASH facilities and safe learning spaces. However, national ownership and sustainable financing remain critical, and the ambition is  for increased domestic investment to expand the programme to 500 schools by 2030.

Experience also demonstrated the importance of embedding child- and youth-sensitive priorities within national climate commitments. UNICEF will therefore advocate for stronger integration of child-sensitive considerations into Turkmenistan’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), expected in early 2026, to strengthen access to domestic and international climate finance. 

From 2026–2030, UNICEF will strengthen child-sensitive emergency preparedness and response, integrating gendered risks into disaster risk management and climate resilience frameworks. Schools will be equipped to manage differentiated risks in emergencies, including safety, protection, first aid, and evacuation, supported by shock-responsive social protection, health, nutrition, and education in emergencies. UNICEF will work with National partners for a National Child-Centered DRR Strategy and support Turkmenistan’s participation in regional climate education and policy platforms to share knowledge, align priorities, and access innovative financing. 

By 2030, lessons from 2025 will guide systematic integration of equity, resilience, and child- and gender-sensitive approaches across sectoral policies. Emphasis will be placed on financing climate-resilient social services, strengthening inclusive systems, and improving data-driven decision-making to reduce children’s vulnerability, reach the most marginalized, and ensure sustainable, equitable results.

In 2025, the situation of children and young people in Ukraine continued to be shaped by protracted war, deepening humanitarian needs and related response as well as an ambitious reform and recovery agenda. The security situation remained volatile and unpredictable, including intensified missile and drone attacks affecting urban areas, civilian infrastructure and essential services; the fluid and unpredictable political environment was marked by increased diplomatic activity and ongoing governance reforms. The operating environment in 2025 was also shaped by geopolitical dynamics, including shifting global priorities and declining international aid which has influenced the scope, scale and nature of international support. These dynamics created opportunities and constraints for advancing the rights of children and young people, with implications for the ability of national and subnational systems to deliver results for children and young people at scale; thus, reinforcing the need to demonstrate impact, sustainability, and alignment with recovery and development goals as well as EU accession objectives. 

Socio-economic pressures intensified, with declining household coping capacities and a constrained fiscal space for social services. These pressures disproportionately affected the most vulnerable children, including young people, particularly those in frontline areas, IDPs, and vulnerable children and young people including those from marginalized groups, affecting progress across multiple SDGs, including poverty reduction, health, education, and protection. 
Children, young people, and their families continue to face significant barriers to education. As of October 2025, 1,786 general secondary education institutions have been damaged and 222 destroyed, while 1,353 early childhood education institutions have been damaged and 132 destroyed (MoES / RDNA5). Despite mitigation efforts, access remains uneven: around 3.6 million children are enrolled in general secondary education, including approximately 280,000 internally displaced students. Learning modalities reflect ongoing security constraints (though a significant improvement compared to previous years). As of October 2025, 71.5 per cent of students attend school face to face, while 18.9 per cent follow blended modalities and 9.6 per cent rely exclusively on remote learning, particularly in frontline areas (MoES). PISA 2022 results show learning losses equivalent to nearly two years of schooling since 2018, with pronounced gender, socio-economic, and rural–urban disparities. Preschool enrolment declined to an estimated 51 per cent in 2025, leaving around 320,000 young children without access to ECE (MoES/RDNA5).

Since the beginning of the war until end 2025, there were 2316 attacks on healthcare facilities recorded according to WHO.[1] In 2025, Ukraine recorded 162,748 live births, according to Ministry of Health (NHSU data), the lowest number of births ever recorded in the country, underscoring deepening demographic crisis. Preventive health services remain uneven: DTP3 coverage declined to 75.3 per cent in 2025, while MMR2 coverage increased to 93.7 per cent (Public Health Centre of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine). The war has also severely affected children’s and young people’s mental health, with around half of caregivers reporting signs of traumatic stress in their children, alongside rising anxiety, depression, and PTSD among adolescents and young people (RDNA5).

Access to safe water and sanitation remains critically constrained. According to the 2025 National Report on Water and Wastewater, only 67.7 per cent of the population has access to centralized water supply and 52.7 per cent to centralized wastewater, leaving an estimated 1.6 million children without safe water and 2.3 million without centralized wastewater services. Infrastructure depreciation reaches 70-90 per cent and more than 30 per cent of distributed water fails to meet EU standards for drinking water. The sector has sustained USD 4 billion in physical damage and USD 11.6 billion in financial losses since February 2022 (RDNA4), with recovery needs estimated at USD 11.1 billion. Rising energy prices drove a 34 per cent cost increase for utilities already facing 40 per cent revenue losses. 

Children, including adolescents, across Ukraine continue to face severe protection risks as a result of the widespread use of explosive weapons in populated areas and pervasive insecurity. As of January 2026, the United Nations hahs verified 763 children killed and 2,486 children injured since the start of the full-scale war (UN HRMMU). Prior to 2022, eastern Ukraine was already among the most mine-contaminated areas globally, and the Government continues to estimate that up to 30 per cent of the country may be contaminated with mines or unexploded ordnance. 

Women and girls have been disproportionately affected by the conflict, facing heightened risks of gender-based violence and exploitation. There was an increase in sexual and domestic violence affecting children since 2022, with child survivors of sexual violence increasing by 66 per cent between 2022 and 2025, and children accounting for 82 per cent of reported rape victims in 2025 (Prosecutor General). 

The war has significantly deepened child poverty and material deprivation; the share of households with children living below the actual subsistence minimum rose sharply with child poverty increasing from 20.6 per cent in 2021 to 35.5 per cent in 2023, while extreme child poverty increased nearly sevenfold, reaching 8.8 per cent. Poverty levels are highest among large families, single-parent households, families with young children, and households affected by disability or unemployment. 

Pre-existing structural gaps, skills mismatches, weak school-to-work transitions, limited apprenticeships and career guidance, and persistent gender barriers have deepened, particularly for young women facing unpaid care burdens and discriminatory labor practices. Vulnerabilities have intensified among displaced youth, young people with disabilities, Roma youth, care leavers, and youth in rural and frontline areas, compounded by rising mental health needs, social isolation and exclusion from decision-making. At the same time, 2025 has confirmed young people’s resilience: sustained civic engagement, volunteering and local action demonstrate that meaningful participation strengthens well-being and recovery outcomes. 

In 2025, the EU accession process opened opportunities to advance child and youth rights in Ukraine. In November 2025, the Government, with technical support of UNICEF, adopted the National Plan for the implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG) until 2030, together with arrangements for national coordination and reporting.  The National Action Plan covers several measures for implementation across the EU Acquis as part of EU accession process.

Humanitarian Action
In 2025, 7 million people including 2.5 million children, were reached with humanitarian support by UNICEF and its partners, with an increasing focus on delivering aid with and through local authorities. In line with the interagency Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan and informed by the global humanitarian reset, UNICEF supported children in frontline areas and under evacuation, communities affected by air strikes and the most vulnerable displaced children.
In frontline areas, UNICEF differentiated its response based on proximity to the conflict. Within 20km of the frontline, mobile teams were required to deliver child protection, health and education services. UNICEF delivered 8 million litres of safe drinking water through water trucking to Kharkiv, Donetsk and Kherson where insecurity prevented network repairs, and provided WASH supplies to 1,094,162 people. In Kharkiv, UNICEF drilled a deep borehole providing emergency water for 30,000 vulnerable people, with network connection underway to serve 350,000 residents, installed 29 portable water kiosks, and completed overhaul of Lopansky and Panasivsky collectors. 

Beyond the 20km zone, UNICEF focused on scaling up services including catch-up education, MHPSS and case management, while also repairing water and sanitation networks and rehabilitating shelters in 26 schools and 10 health facilities. UNICEF supported the development of national EORE standards and capacity strengthening of frontline workers.  In addition, 121,134 children were reached via Mobile Safety Classes, and digital behavior communication outreach covered 7 million people, including 1.3 million adolescents. 

When mandatory evacuation orders were announced by government, UNICEF initiated multipurpose cash assistance ($260 per person) payments for 4,004 households supporting 13,929 people including 6,082 children. These payments were made to families in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia. In transit centres, UNICEF partners provided mental health and psychosocial support, registration for case management and hygiene supplies for families on the move. 

As strikes on urban areas increased in mid-2025, UNICEF scaled up its partnership with the State Emergency Services of Ukraine (SESU), specifically the unit which deploys therapists in the immediate aftermath of strikes. UNICEF trained 70 SESU therapists on child-friendly techniques and support with basic supplies such as toys and hygiene items. These therapists responded across the country, alongside UNICEF implementing partners who provided MHPSS, case management, hygiene supplies and cash assistance; with the latter reaching 3,818 households  affected by missile strikes (8,782 people including 1,433 children) in 11 regions across the country. Emergency repairs in 17 education facilities damaged during air strikes facilitated 8,350 children (including 4,092 girls) to return to in-person learning after disruptions from the strike.

Over the 2025-26 winter season, humanitarian needs worsened as targeted strikes against energy infrastructure increased since October 2025, disrupting electricity, heating and water for long periods compounded by increasing cold temperatures. By the of 2025, UNICEF had provided winter cash assistance to 51,811 vulnerable households living close to the frontline, covering 168,741 people including 77,585 children. UNICEF supported 50 heating restoration projects in 2025 to ensure sustained heating availability for 1,404,087 people. Energy resilience investments extended to critical water infrastructure: solar installations in 21 health facilities ensured uninterrupted water and heating services for 125,000 people during blackouts, demonstrating that emergency response can advance climate objectives while reducing operational costs.  
 
Child and Youth-Centered Recovery and Development 

Better Start to Life   
In 2025, UNICEF played a significant role driving key institutional and systemic changes for integrated Early Childhood Care and Development. 
A major breakthrough was the institutionalization of ECD within primary health care, with the Ministry of Health operationalizing the Preventive Child Health Examinations (PCHE) model nationwide, strengthening developmental screening, referral pathways and coordination with education and social services at local level. Over 1,300 health workers were trained on PCHE and 671 on the Guide for Monitoring Child Development, enabling more than 51,000 children and caregivers to access quality, integrated ECD services in 2025.

In parallel, UNICEF supported the roll-out of the new Law on Preschool Education, advancing diversified and more cost-effective early childhood education models. With UNICEF technical support, national standards for Preschool Education were developed in line with international best practices and more than 10,000 preschool teachers were trained on social and emotional learning and referral pathways. UNICEF strengthened the evidence base for financing early childhood services, including a budget analysis on Early Childhood Education Financing in Ukraine for 2021–2025. This analytical brief provides targeted, evidence-based recommendations to improve resource allocation for children aged 0–6 and aims at supporting strategic budget planning in the education sector and complements system-level ECD reforms by helping to ensure that early learning and care services are underpinned by adequate, well-targeted and sustainable public investments.[1] Furthermore,  UNICEF in partnership with the Ministries of Health and Finance and hromada authorities, strengthened ECD financing and cross-sector integration into local planning, programmes and budgets. 

This systems work was reinforced through evidence-based social and behaviour change interventions, which reached 9.6 million people and engaged 131,000 schoolchildren, increasing positive attitudes towards vaccination to 82 per cent of caregivers (up from 67 per cent in 2023), with 85 per cent now considering vaccination safe and effective. Breastfeeding promotion and stigma-reduction initiatives reached over 3 million people, while the government-led Path of Parenting programme—facilitated by UNICEF—reached more than 600,000 people in its first months, consolidating a unified national narrative on nurturing care and positive parenting led by the state.

Furthermore, UNICEF generated evidence and advocated Family Friendly Policies with government institutions, business associations and international partners; this included the UNICEF - ILO joint study on Access to ECEC and Women’s Economic Empowerment which was completed in 2025 and presented to the MoSPFU, MoES, business associations and CSOs. UNICEF advocated for a more ambitious reform package to support working parents, especially mothers, to return to work while expanding social protection support, early childhood education and care[2] 

Better Learning and Skills

In 2025, UNICEF Ukraine advanced overall learning recovery and transform the education system amidst ongoing challenges, improving equitable access to quality learning and skills development for over 730,160 children and young people across the country, including frontline regions. Emergency education interventions reached 433,585 children (221,128 girls), representing 52 per cent of the national humanitarian target for the sector. Continuity of learning was ensured through the delivery of mobile early childhood education services and the operationalization of 374 remedial education learning spaces in frontline areas, as well as the provision of supplies and infrastructure for schools facing energy shortages. UNICEF’s technical support to the All Ukrainian School Online platform further enabled 811,792 students and 225,215 teachers to draw on quality-controlled curriculum materials. In partnership with the Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Ministry of Education and Science, UNICEF launched the establishment of a Centre of Excellence which is testing and scaling digital solutions in support of children’s learning recovery.

The development of sustainable adolescent and youth service ecosystems linking learning, employability, and mental health support were supported by UNICEF investments in evidence generation, system strengthening, as well as strategic and technical engagement with municipalities, youth councils, service providers, and employers. In parallel, UNICEF provided targeted technical assistance to Government counterparts to advance readiness for the EU Youth Guarantee, including NEET profiling, delivery model design, and cross-sectoral coordination. During 2025, a 12 innovation spaces for youth located across seven oblasts enabled 19,660 adolescents to develop science, technology, and entrepreneurship skills through hands-on, project-based learning as well as core employability skills such as teamwork, leadership, and problem-solving. Collectively, these initiatives contribute to a pipeline of empowered, resilient adolescents and young people actively shaping their communities while enhancing local service delivery. UNICEF’s support continued to demonstrate how municipal youth centers function as incubators for innovation, social responsibility, and inclusive, youth-led solutions—reinforcing individual development, social cohesion, and long-term recovery. Furthermore, a network of 52 youth centers and community spaces engaged 236,393 young people in structured volunteering and civic engagement, strengthening.

Better Care: A Family for Every Child  
The Better Care Reform expanded significantly in 2025 with UNICEF's support, contributing to the adoption of strategies and action plans in 15 oblasts, establishing sustainable foundations for community-based services and safeguards for conflict-affected children. UNICEF supporting 36 communities across western Ukraine (20 in Volyn, 6 in Lviv, 5 in Khmelnytskyi, and 5 in Zakarpattia), 15 hromadas in Odesa and Mykolaiv regions, priority communities in Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia, and advancing system strengthening in Kharkiv with the adoption of an Oblast Action Plan and establishment of an oblast-level task force. Sumy became the 14th reform pilot oblast through a three-party MoU between UNICEF, the Coordination Centre and Sumy Oblast Administration. 

With the technical and financial support of UNICEF and UK FCDO,  the government was able to support small-scale grants to community providers through its national procurement and contracting mechanisms (Cabinet Resolution No. 40), creating a functional social services marketplace enabling 120 providers, including 80 civil society organizations, to deliver services reaching more than 13,000 children and caregivers across 10 regions. 

The patronage care initiative, an emergency foster care model designed to provide immediate support to children separated from their families, expanded to 623 families across 356 hromadas, offering a safe and nurturing environment to 1,208 children. Since its inception, 3,252 children have been protected from institutionalization, including 892 infants and young children who avoided placement in baby homes, with 453 children reunified with biological families or placed in adoptive or guardianship care.

In addition, UNICEF supported the Judicial System Reform through the development of a national diversion model for children in conflict with the law and advancement of child-friendly civil justice, reaching 10 regions and 11 specialized courts with 52 judges assigned and over 130 justice and social sector professionals trained. With technical assistance from UNICEF, comprehensive regulatory and institutional reforms were advanced, including violence and bullying prevention standards, children's rights in justice regulations, and a revised Code of Ethics. Special protection for child victims and witnesses was expanded through the Barnahus model, benefiting 1,409 children in 15 regions, and the strengthening of the Free Legal Aid Register of Psychologists, which now includes 587 trained psychologists who supported 6,472 child victims and witnesses and 1,157 children in conflict with the law. 

UNICEF supported 326 Resilience Centres operating across 305 communities, which provide mental health and psychosocial support interventions, with a coverage capacity of 2.5 million people. The network of centers employs more than 1,500 trained specialists and collaborates with local partners. UNICEF strengthened capacity building across the social sector, with 3,782 professionals from 200 communities trained on information and service provision, 1,344 people (representing 858 families) from 18 regions trained on adoption and family-based care forms, 178 people trained as patronage carers, and 1,905 parents and caregivers receiving psychological consultations.

UNICEF provided critical support for children returning to Ukraine.  During 2025, 630 children returned to Ukraine, with UNICEF providing immediate reintegration support to 528 children (84%) through case management, legal aid, accommodation, cash and in-kind assistance, education, health and mental health and psychosocial support. Medium- and longer-term reintegration support reached 246 children from 141 families, while individual assessments were conducted for 1,653 children abroad. Notably, 225 children returning from institutions were supported, resulting in 97% placement in family-based care following a major return from Türkiye.

The transformation of baby homes continued at decentralized level in Lviv, Zakarpattia, Volyn and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Through strategic planning and reorientation from institutional care to family- and community-based services, the number of children in 24/7 residential care decreased by 51% in Lviv, 37% in Zakarpattia, and 100% in Dnipro. These transformations included updated institutional statutes, referrals with the National Health Service, new rehabilitation and palliative care services, and rollout of case management models.

European Child Guarantee (ECG)  
During 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Ukraine in advancing the development and initial implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG). As an EU policy framework, the ECG seeks to reduce child poverty and social exclusion by ensuring that the most vulnerable children and families have effective access to essential services, such as early childhood education and care, education, health care, housing and social protection. UNICEF provided technical and advisory support to national counterparts across line ministries participating in this process, drawing on international and European standards and best practices. 

Key results of UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support to Government partners in relation to the ECG include the appointment of a National ECG Contact Point, the adoption of a National Action Plan by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution in November 2025, and the establishment of a National Council under the Cabinet of Ministers tasked with coordinating child related reforms across sectoral line ministries. Throughout the process, UNICEF supported a participatory approach including facilitating consultations across government entities at all administrative levels (national and sub-national),  civil society organizations,  as well as EU institutions and EU Member States. 
  
The implementation of the ECG is closely linked to, and dependent on, coordinated efforts to strengthen Ukraine’s capacity to monitor the situation of children and track progress made in reducing poverty and social exclusion. In 2025, UNICEF supported the development of a monitoring and reporting framework for the ECG strengthening national capacities for measuring progress towards the elimination of all forms of child poverty and social exclusion.

Climate Responsive Water and Sanitation Systems 
UNICEF advanced Ukraine's water sector beyond emergency response toward sustainable, EU-aligned recovery. The Ministry for Development formally designated UNICEF as lead technical agency for WASH sector recovery with UNICEF co-chairing the WSS Sector Sub-Working Group under the Ukraine Donor Platform with France, enabling development of bankable project pipelines bridging humanitarian aid with recovery and reconstruction financing.

UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support assurance enabled operationalization of the EIB 100 million EUR loan for Ukraine Water Recovery, complemented by EUR 25 million in EU grant co-financing. The Kharkiv Recovery Roadmap serves as the national model for locally owned investment planning. The utility has established a Department of International Relations and Project Management Unit for sustainable governance. 

UNICEF restored water and sanitation services for 8.3 million people by supporting 133 utilities nationwide, providing 73 per cent of all donor assistance received by 81 monitored utilities. UNICEF reached over 1.4 million people across 17 oblasts with critical emergency supplies, with hygiene kit satisfaction scores of 9.9 out of 10. A hygiene voucher pilot for 43,105 people in Kherson and Mykolaiv achieved 98.8 per cent satisfaction and a 22 per cent cost reduction versus in-kind delivery, stimulating local women-led enterprises.
The solarization of Vodokanals initiative demonstrates how emergency investments can reduce both operational costs and carbon emissions. In Novovolynsk, integration of 900 kW across three operational solar stations secured water services for 60,000 residents. The State Agency for Reconstruction is now utilizing UNICEF feasibility studies covering 75 utilities to negotiate financing for nationwide energy efficiency improvements, showing how humanitarian funding designed with sustainability criteria can catalyze transformative sector financing.  

UNICEF supported climate- and energy-resilient infrastructure enabling access to safe water and sanitation for 8.3 million people. In Kharkiv, a large-scale waste management project for 1.4 million people reduced methane emissions.  Over 60 heating restoration projects reached 2 million people, and 546 institutions including schools, hospitals and IDP centres were equipped with inclusive, gender-sensitive WASH equipment, material and facilities.

UNICEF institutionalized capacity development, training 1,867 professionals (including 802 women) on EU technical standards with Ministry-endorsed curricula achieving participant ratings of 4.7 out of 5. Through the Global Water Operators Partnerships Alliance, Ukrainian utilities in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were linked with Portuguese and Dutch utilities for their capacity development. UNICEF pioneered water safety planning aligned with EU Directive 2020/2184, training 59 representatives from 30 vodokanals. UNICEF developed a comprehensive policy brief on tariff reform and supports pilot incentive-based systems in Lviv and Zaporizhzhia, with NEURC now exploring transition to performance-based regulatory frameworks.

Cross-cutting drivers for results  

In 2025, UNICEF applied cross-sectoral drivers to accelerate results for children and young people in a volatile context to amplify results beyond individual sectors.

UNICEF began scaling up its social sector financing and recovery investment, deepening its strategic partnership with the Ministry of Finance to embed child and gender responsive public finance, medium-term budgeting and public investment management at national and local levels. 

Gender equality was embedded across policies, services and recovery investments through coordinated support to government counterparts at national and subnational level, civil society organizations, and service providers. More than 17,900 frontline workers—91 per cent women—received competency training, contributing to improved quality and inclusiveness of services for children, young people, and caregivers. Targeted interventions expanded access to skills development, employment pathways and inclusive services for 7,503 adolescent girls and 6,486 young women, particularly those affected by displacement and conflict.

Social and behavioural change communication supported results across sectors by strengthening service uptake and reinforcing positive practices related to child health, parenting, social inclusion and protection. Evidence-informed interventions reached over 9.6 million people, contributing to measurable improvements in knowledge, attitudes and behaviours, particularly in early childhood development, mental health and psychosocial support, and inclusion.

These interventions remained closely linked to service delivery, improving relevance and effectiveness. AAP mechanisms strengthened programme responsiveness and trust. The Say It As It Is hotline handled 18,360 consultations, including 759 feedback cases, with a response rate above 90 per cent, enabling timely adjustments and more responsive programming. Across sectors, human-centred design approaches supported the co-creation of solutions with children, young people, caregivers and frontline workers, ensuring services reflected user needs and local realities.

Climate responsiveness was integrated across sectors, with WASH serving as a principal platform for scalable models. UNICEF provided technical guidance integrating child and youth-sensitive data into Ukraine's Nationally Determined Contributions submission to UNFCCC, advancing the country from Category C to Category B in child-climate integration assessment. UNICEF supported Ukraine’s second Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), led by young people ensuring young people’s voices shaped national climate commitments and international advocacy at COP 30. 

UNICEF launched the Multi Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) process in 2025 with the National Statistic Service with capacity development of enumerators and field team supervisors, operational field testing undertaken during the first half of the year and with data collection in second half of 2025, which is continuing into Q1 2026.  The survey, once completed, is expected to cover a sample size of nearly 24,000 households and will be a significant piece of evidence generation analytical work supporting child  and youth centered advocacy and policy dialogue, programme planning and monitoring, and evidence-based decision-making.
 
Communication and advocacy leveraged data and programming to influence public discourse on the child rights agenda, inspiring publics, partners and decision makers to champion the rights of  children and young people across Ukraine. UNICEF generated seven million engagements across digital channels and secured more than 28,300 UNICEF media mentions that strengthened the organizations' voice in delivering for children, young people, and families, alongside government and local partners, and recognizing the support from its many partners.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges  
In 2025, UNICEF continued to operate in a highly complex and volatile context shaped by protracted war, global decline in international aid financing, while balancing demand for support to Ukraine’s ambitious national reform and recovery agenda. While decentralization has created important opportunities for local ownership, uneven institutional capacity marked by human resource capacity gaps across local partners (government and csos), local budgetary and financial constraints, has limited the pace and consistency of implementation across municipalities (hromadas). At the national level, overlapping reform processes, particularly those linked to EU accession, have placed additional pressures on institutions already operating under severe resource and regulatory constraints to address the needs and rights of children and young people.
 
Balancing immediate humanitarian response with longer-term system strengthening has remained a challenge. UNICEF has needed to avoid substituting government responsibilities while retaining the agility to respond rapidly when systems are disrupted. In this context, ensuring that investments in infrastructure and emergency response are effectively leveraged to support sustainable, government-led service provision has required constant adaptation, close coordination with authorities, and a careful calibration between short-term response and longer-term reform and recovery objectives especially to address the needs  of  children, and young people and ensuring their rights.  

Lessons Learned 
UNICEF’s experience in 2025 confirmed that system-oriented approaches, particularly at decentralized level, are essential to achieving sustainable results for children. Investments in hromada-level planning, budgeting, and service delivery have demonstrated greater resilience and continuity than reliance on national-level structures alone, especially amid national leadership turnover and political volatility. Localized, upstream engagement when aligned with national reform frameworks can meaningfully influence policies, financing decisions, and service quality, while also informing national scale-up.
Another key lesson has been the importance of positioning UNICEF as a partner accompanying government-led reform and recovery processes. Working within existing national architectures, rather than through parallel delivery models, has proven more effective in shaping standards, strengthening accountability, and unlocking broader financing for children, including through engagement with IFIs and EU mechanisms. Shifting from funding to financing will be critical to sustaining recovery gains, even as it introduces new risks that require strong coordination, advocacy and risk management.

UNICEF’s agility and adaptability has remained a core strength. Preparedness measures, contingency planning, and diversified delivery modalities, including increased use of national and subnational systems, have enabled timely and at scale humanitarian response. Experience in 2025 demonstrated that humanitarian response and system strengthening are not mutually exclusive; when designed strategically, emergency interventions can serve as entry points to build or reinforce institutional capacity, strengthen coordination, and improve long-term service delivery. In the WASH sector, this was demonstrated through energy resilience investments such a solarization and backup power systems that addressed immediate service continuity needs while reducing operational costs and carbon emissions.

The year underscored the critical role of robust data and evidence in adaptive management. Surveys, service mapping, and expenditure analysis strengthened UNICEF’s ability to target vulnerabilities, prioritize investments, and inform government decision-making across its programming. This data-driven approach also enabled more differentiated responses for adolescents and young people as a distinct group. The use of age- and gender-disaggregated data informed timely adaptations to youth-focused services, improving relevance and uptake among vulnerable adolescents. These experiences highlighted the value of youth-responsive data use and decentralized systems in delivering more equitable recovery outcomes.

Similar lessons emerged in the health sector. While integrating Preventive Child Health Examinations (PCHE) into national policies and financing frameworks is essential for sustainability, effective implementation depends on the strength of subnational health systems. Empowering hromadas to plan, budget, and manage PCHE improved identification of local service gaps and supported more responsive service delivery. At the same time, the lack of integration of PCHE into the national eHealth system remains a key bottleneck for scale-up, reinforcing the need for government-led digital integration to enable routine data use, accountability, and performance monitoring.

Also in 2025, UNICEF demonstrated how working through nationally led platforms can accelerate system-level change. Initiatives such as the Better Care Award, the Hub of Inclusive TikTok, and Barrier-Free interventions showed that when national partners lead reform agendas and have catalytic reach, UNICEF’s technical assistance can leverage additional resources, including from private sector actors,  and advance cross-sectoral priorities. These examples point to opportunities to further scale impact in areas such as parenting and inclusion while accelerating reform implementation.

Finally, across all sectors in UNICEF’s programme, 2025 highlighted the importance of moving beyond activity-heavy approaches toward demonstrating measurable outcomes and system-level change. Many demonstrative models supporting the localization of national policies serve to sharpened UNICEF’s focus on scaling what works, discontinuing what does not, and ensuring that child rights monitoring, civil society engagement, adolescent and young people’s participation are integral to sustaining reform momentum. 
 
Future Outlook  
Recognizing that the Ukraine context will remain complex, volatile and unpredictable as the war continues underscores both the fragility and fluidity of the political landscape with ongoing cabinet reshuffles, governance reforms, and heightened scrutiny of corruption and public sector performance. Damage and destruction to energy infrastructure accelerated in late 2025 will drive significant new medium-to-long term investment in 2026. Fiscal space for social services will further contract under the combined pressure of reduced revenues, sustained security expenditures, and mounting recovery demands. 

UNICEF will need to maintain its adaptability and agility with its ongoing humanitarian-recovery programming, responding to Ukraine’s highly differentiated realities across regions. A stronger emphasis on conflict sensitivity and social cohesion will need to be reinforced across programming to ensure relevance and do-no-harm approaches in a rapidly evolving external environment.

Looking to 2026, UNICEF will further shift towards protecting and prioritizing social service financing, supporting decentralization reforms, and safeguarding policy space for child and youth-related reforms critical to EU accession. 

UNICEF remains committed to sustaining humanitarian readiness and advancing recovery efforts and reform continuity—remaining flexible, agile and adaptive with our programme firmly anchored in the promoting and protecting the rights and well-being of children and young people across Ukraine.

In 2025, Angola commemorated the 50th anniversary of independence amid a complex national context marked by modest economic growth, constrained fiscal space, heightened social pressures and renewed regional and global engagement. 

Angola assumed a prominent diplomatic role as Chair of the African Union and engaged in high-level fora including the African Union–European Union Summit and the African Union–United States Business Summit. In addition, the country leveraged its own peace-building experience to broker agreements between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda.

Economic performance in 2025 reflected a slow and uneven recovery: the real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in 2025 was projected at around 2 per cent, lower than the population growth of over 3 per cent. Growth was driven mainly by non-oil sectors such as agriculture, construction, and fishing. Oil production, despite stagnation, accounts for nearly 30 per cent of GDP and 95 per cent of exports. Angola remains highly vulnerable to external shocks, limiting gains in per-capita income and youth employment.

Inflation eased but stayed high, dropping from 28 per cent in 2024 to about 22 per cent in 2025, driven by exchange-rate depreciation, import dependence, supply constraints and high food prices impacting poorer households hardest. The currency stability remained fragile while persistent inflation eroded real incomes, reducing households’ ability to meet basic needs, while increasing the cost of delivering essential social services.

Despite gains in debt sustainability, fiscal space remained constrained. Public debt declined to about 60 per cent of GDP, down from over 100 per cent in 2020, yet external debt servicing absorbed approximately US$10.5 billion (30 percent of state budget) in 2025. The state budget allocations to social sectors remained below international benchmarks, with 5.7 per cent allocated for health sector—falling short of the Abuja target of 15 per cent—and education at 6.5 per cent significantly below the Education 2030 Framework for Action. Analyses show that education, social protection and sanitation continued to face budget execution challenges, directly affecting progress towards SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 and towards UNICEF Strategic Plan impact areas. 

Fiscal consolidation measures, including fuel subsidy reforms, shaped the broader socioeconomic context in 2025. Despite postponement of the full phaseout of fuel subsidies to 2028, a 33 per cent increase in diesel prices contributed to rising transport and food costs, affecting household purchasing power. In July, nationwide strikes and demonstrations reflected these economic pressures.
