The ensuing security response reportedly resulted in at least 22 casualties and more than 1,000 detentions, including minors, drawing attention to concerns related to civic space, child protection, and the broader enabling environment for children’s rights.
The release of new data from the 2024 Population and Housing Census and the Multiple Indicator and Health Survey (IIMS 2023–2024), provide a more comprehensive picture of children's living conditions, access to basic services and patterns of deprivations and disparities. Under–five mortality remains high at 52 per 1,000 live births, neonatal mortality at 16 per 1,000 live births, both off-track to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Chronic malnutrition affects 40 per cent of children under five years, and zero-dose children remain a critical issue, with 26.1 percent of those children aged 12-23 months having received no vaccines. 

Public health risks intensified in 2025 following a nationwide cholera outbreak, alongside reported cases of measles (over 39,000 and 405 deaths) and polio, placing significant strain on the health system. Declared on 7 January 2025, the cholera outbreak affected 18 of 21 provinces, with 36,341 cases (16,777 women and 19,564 men) and 895 reported deaths (337 women and 558 men), disproportionately impacting children, particular those under five (4,852 cases and 132 deaths). Persistently low access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services—only 56 per cent of households with basic drinking water and 34.6 per cent with basic sanitation facilities—contributed to heightened vulnerability and facilitated disease transmission.
Kwenda Programme (Kwenda 2.0) launch marked a critical milestone in scaling up Angola’s social protection system. Building on Phase 1, which delivered cash transfers to over one million vulnerable households, Kwenda 2.0 expands coverage to an estimated 2.2 million households, with particular emphasis on urban poverty. Kwenda 2.0 reflects a shift towards a more inclusive, child-sensitive social protection model with the integration of a human capital component that links cash transfers to health, nutrition, and early childhood development services for children under five. 

Education outcomes remained constrained by high learning poverty and an estimated 3.8 million out-of-school children. The national assessment results published in 2024 show only 37 per cent of Grade 4 students can identify clear information in a text, and 22 per cent can solve basic mathematical problems. Completion rates remain low in primary school at 58.1 per cent. The low enrolment and transition rates in Grades 3 to 5 are closely linked to the limited availability of schools, and high repetition and dropout rates. 

Data on child protection highlights areas of concern and emerging priorities. The 2023-2024 IIMS revealed that 67 per cent of children aged 0–14 years have experienced severe discipline. The national child helpline, SOS Criança, received 26,204 calls (12,537 girls and 13,487 boys) regarding violence against children in 2025. Birth registration has progressed with 38 per cent of children under five registered, however substantial investments in strengthening the Civil Registration and Vital Statistics system are still required to achieve universal birth registration. Additionally, 28 per cent of women aged 20–49 year were married or living in a union before the age of 18, underscoring persistent risks of early marriage and its long-term consequences. High teenage pregnancy rate was observed, with 27 per cent of girls aged 15–19 years having been pregnant at least once.

In 2025, Angola submitted its second Voluntary National Review (VNR), reaffirming its commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The VNR underscores advancements in governance reforms, macroeconomic stabilisation and social sector investments, including the adoption of the National Human Capital Development Plan, while recognising persistent inequalities affecting children in rural, peri-urban and drought-prone areas.

UNICEF Angola strived to advance key child rights priorities in Angola in 2025, supporting national systems to respond to a major cholera outbreak, strengthening national systems for immunization, supporting the prevention of violence against children, improving foundational learning, enhancing coordination in WASH and Education sectors and promoting public financing for children. These efforts, aligned with the Angola - UNICEF country programme of cooperation 2024-2028, the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the UNICEF Strategic Plan, resulted in enhanced national leadership, improved service delivery and expanded protection for vulnerable children.  

Following the declaration of a cholera outbreak in January 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Angola with coordinated technical and operational assistance at national level and across the 12 affected provinces. Support focused on WASH through the Case Area Targeted Intervention (CATI) approach, case management at Cholera Treatment Centres (in close collaboration with the World Health Organization), Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), Oral Cholera Vaccination (OCV) support, Safe Back to School Campaign in seven provinces (supporting 378 schools with WASH/Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) supplies, including 113 reached with adequate message for safe school management) and child protection support through the Ministry of Social Action, Family and Women’s Promotion at provincial level. UNICEF’s response aligned with the national cholera response plan and prioritised provinces with the highest disease burden. 

Three oral cholera vaccination campaigns supported by UNICEF in hotspot areas achieved a high level of coverage and operational success, with more than 3.6 million people vaccinated. UNICEF supported microplanning and technical preparation for the first vaccination round targeting high-risk neighborhoods in Luanda and Bengo. The campaign reached 926,643 people, achieving a 97.7 per cent coverage rate. A second vaccination round was conducted in May, expanding its geographic scope to five newly affected provinces and again achieving near-universal coverage, reaching 706,091 people—99.5 per cent of those targeted. UNICEF also supported the third round which targeted seven provinces and reached 1,984,232 people representing 99.2 per cent of the target population. UNICEF played a critical role throughout, offering technical support, mobilising operational funding from partners such as Gavi the Vaccine Alliance, and managing data systems and logistics that ensured vaccines were delivered safely and efficiently to some of the hardest hit communities.

Complementing vaccination, UNICEF scaled up WASH interventions using the CATI strategy to break transmission at the household and community level in hotspots including Luanda, Namibe, Benguela, Cuanza Sul and Lunda Norte Provinces. This included support to the Government’s Rapid Response Teams with technical assistance, on-the-job training, delivery of essential cholera kits, disinfection guidance for affected households, and sensitisation for the neighboring ones. Bucket chlorination, advocated by UNICEF and endorsed nationally, expanded to 1,449 water points serving an estimated 362,250 people and monitored through a digital application which improved traceability and water quality control. Of the 1,678 free residual chlorine tests, 57 per cent fell within the range of WHO-recommended drinking water standard. To protect and reach households that were not immediately accessible to response teams, UNICEF distributed 11,567 simplified cholera kits containing bleach, soap, and information material for safe household disinfection. 

Community engagement further reinforced both vaccination uptake and CATI effectiveness. Over 300,000 people were reached through door-to-door sensitisation, and thousands of communities and religious leaders were mobilised to promote prevention practices and encourage early care-seeking behaviours. These efforts contributed to improved knowledge on hygiene practices, increased acceptance of chlorinated water for drinking, and strengthened community trust in the public health response.

In collaboration with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF launched a Safe Back to School campaign and strengthened preparedness for cholera in 398 schools across 10 provinces. This initiative strengthened the capacity of 108 teachers (35 females, 73 males) and 104 school managers (23 females, 81 males) on handwashing and water treatment practices, thereby promoting a safer and healthier learning environment. UNICEF, through this initiative has reached approximately 455,483 students (including 214,142 girls) with WASH supplies and key messages focused on hygiene promotion and school safety.

Moreover, UNICEF provided supplies for cholera response to 31 residential care centres in Luanda, which provide accommodation for 2,421 children, including 1,205 girls. To strengthen local response capacity, 25 social workers from 11 municipalities received training on child protection principles, protection from sexual exploitation and abuse, and case management procedures. A study was initiated in collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MINSA) to examine gender- and child-related factors and impact in the context of disproportionately high male and child infection rates. This evidence once available in early 2026, will inform gender- responsive and child protection programming in public health emergencies.

Malnutrition remained a concern during the cholera outbreak. UNICEF supported the revision and the update of the national cholera case management protocol, adding a dedicated chapter on the treatment of children with Severe Acute Malnutrition affected by cholera. The updates align with the global best practices and emphasize the management of co-morbidities, which contributed to the initially high-case fatality rate. To facilitate the enforcement of the protocol, eight refresher training sessions have been conducted at the national and provincial levels, reaching a total of 86 healthcare professionals.

To respond to the cholera outbreak, Angola was declared L1 Emergency at the beginning of April and funds from the Emergency Programme Fund (EPF) were made available to initiate the response. In addition, the results achieved were possible thanks to the agile and quick attention given to the cholera emergency by key partners, like European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) through the Consolidated Emergency Relief Fund (CERF), Republic of Korea and the US Fund for UNICEF, among others.

In 2025, UNICEF played a strategic role in supporting the Government of Angola to develop and secure the approval of a comprehensive five-year, costed National Immunisation Strategy. This strategy was developed to address persistent immunization challenges, including recurrent measles outbreaks, ongoing poliovirus detection and a high burden of zero-dose and under-immunized children. These challenges highlighted critical gaps in vaccine coverage and underscored the urgent need for a coordinated, evidence-based approach to strengthen Angola’s immunization programme. Officially endorsed in October 2025, the Strategy provides a nationally owned roadmap to strengthen routine immunization systems, reach zero-dose children, introduce new and life-saving vaccines and improve preparedness for disease outbreaks. It also prioritises the integration of immunization services with broader primary healthcare initiatives to maximise outreach and impact, particularly in hard-to-reach and underserved communities. 

UNICEF collaborated closely with the Ministry of Health, WHO and other UN and immunization partners to develop the strategy. This multi-stakeholder collaboration ensured that the Strategy benefitted from diverse expertise and facilitated shared ownership, enhancing the likelihood of successful implementation and sustained impact. Throughout the process, UNICEF provided extensive technical assistance, including support for strategy design, costing and data-driven prioritisation to ensure resources are directed to the highest-impact areas including cold chain and vaccine management. The Strategy integrates gender-responsive approaches and social and behaviour change interventions to address demand-side barriers and promote vaccine acceptance at community level, while strengthening accountability, transparency and operational efficiency across the immunization ecosystem. By addressing both supply- and demand-side challenges, the Strategy aims to build trust in vaccines and health services, thereby increasing coverage and reducing inequities across population groups. 

Angola’s accession to the Pathfinding Alliance on Violence Against Children marked an important milestone in elevating child protection within national policy and political agendas. In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government to operationalise these commitments, with a focus on strengthening child justice systems, increasing investment in child protection services and improving governance and coordination. 

High-level political momentum was reinforced in June 2025 through the visit of the United Nations Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children (SRSG-VAC), at the invitation of the Ministry of Social Action, Family and Women’s Promotion. The visit engaged senior leaders across multiple ministries, as well as the First Lady, elevating violence against children to the highest political level and reinforcing Angola’s leadership as a Pathfinding country and strengthened national ownership of the violence-prevention agenda.

During the mission, the SRSG-VAC also engaged with civil society organizations and participated in the Ninth National Forum for Children, a national mechanism for monitoring the implementation of Angola’s 11 child-focused commitments adapted from the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The SRSG-VAC acknowledged the country’s strong political commitment, robust legislative framework, and the presence of key institutional mechanisms, including Standard Operating Procedures, the municipalization of child-related commitments, and the meaningful participation of children in decision-making through the Children’s Parliament. She also highlighted the need to deepen multi-sectoral coordination and civil society engagement.

UNICEF supported concrete follow-up actions, including a National Juvenile Justice Conference that convened 60 magistrates and prosecutors to promote child-friendly justice practices. The conference produced recommendations submitted to the Supreme Court, including improved data reporting and targeted responses for cases involving child survivors of sexual violence. To strengthen evidence-based advocacy, UNICEF supported the National Institute for Children to initiate a study on the economic cost of violence against children and teenage pregnancy, aimed at informing budget allocations and investment decisions. UNICEF also facilitated an inter-country exchange with Finland and Iceland, enabling Angolan authorities to examine the Barnahus model—a child-centred, multidisciplinary approach to addressing sexual abuse and identify practical recommendations to inform a national action plan under the Pathfinding Alliance.

Another important achievement of 2025 has been the strengthening of national leadership on foundational literacy and numeracy. Updated national learning outcomes published by the Ministry of Education confirmed the depth of the learning crisis and provided a shared evidence base for reform. UNICEF supported policy dialogue and regional engagement through platforms including the African Foundational Learning follow-up meetings, and Southern African Development Community exchanges. Evidence generated through a joint study (Teacher for All) with UNICEF Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti informed reflection on teacher deployment, costs, career pathways and capacity development, and prompted government interest in the potential use of evidence for future teacher recruitment and management planning. 

The completion of the Aprendizagem na Idade Certa (AIC, Learning at Right Time) pilot and its external formative evaluation marked a major milestone. The evaluation confirmed AIC—Angola’s adaptation of Teaching at the Right Level, as a scalable and cost-effective remedial education model. Significant gains in foundational literacy and numeracy skills were recorded among the 21,713 learners reached, including 11,205 girls. The use of a digital platform to track individual learning outcomes strengthened accountability and enabled timely, data-informed decisions. The evaluation confirmed the shifts in classroom practice, with teachers increasingly using assessment data to group learners, tailor instruction and monitor progress. School leaders also became more engaged in supporting instructional practices. Further operational and strategic shifts are needed to consolidate the model by strengthening mentoring structures, enhancing inclusivity, improving data-driven decision-making, and accelerated integration into education system. These results were largely enabled by UNICEF’s technical leadership in programme design, implementation support, monitoring and quality assurance.

UNICEF also advocated for the institutionalisation of remedial education. Through sustained policy dialogue and systems strengthening, the office facilitated discussions on a Remedial Education Decree, integration of the remedial education methodology into pre-service teacher training and the development of costed scale-up scenarios. These efforts positioned remedial education within broader teacher professionalisation reforms under the Education Partnership Compact, for strengthening coherence, fiscal realism and evidence-based decision-making.

UNICEF continued to play a critical role in sector coordination, especially in Education and WASH for coherent sector priorities and ensuring alignment of development partners around shared goals, resource optimisation and evidence-based actions.

As the Coordinating Agency of the Local Education Group, UNICEF strengthened education sector coordination and government leadership. UNICEF supported regular high-level advocacy and evidence-based policy dialogue, contributing to improved governance, financing alignment and collective action to advance more equitable learning outcomes. A key achievement was the operationalisation of the Education Partnership Compact document, developed with the support of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), which provided a central framework for reform, partner alignment and mutual accountability, with a focus on teacher capacity, workforce management and foundational learning. 

UNICEF played a pivotal role in strengthening national WASH sector coordination through support to the National Water and Sanitation Forum (FONAS), co-led with the National Directorate of Water. In 2025, FONAS convened high-level dialogues on key regulatory frameworks (including the General Regulation on Water Resources Use, Water Quality Regulation, and Regulation on Water Supply and Wastewater Sanitation), advancing analysis of systemic bottlenecks which can guide the improvement of WASH services across the country. 

The year culminated in the flagship FONAS annual event that brought together 288 participants from 120 institutions including government, partners, academia, the private sector and civil society, achieving consensus on strategic priorities for the sector, ensuring financial sustainability, and strengthening integrated information systems. It also validated the Sanitation and Water for All Mutual Accountability Mechanism and Angola’s Country Overview as key references for policy and technical dialogue. The rapid progress of FONAS in less than two years—particularly in 2025—was publicly recognised by the Sanitation and Water for All, underscoring Angola’s commitment to achieving universal access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene.

In addition, UNICEF supported the advancement of a more transparent and child-focused budgeting framework in Angola through a combination of targeted technical assistance, strengthened evidence generation and dissemination, and the promotion of participatory public finance processes. A central element of these efforts was UNICEF’s partnership with the Ministry of Finance (MINFIN), through which UNICEF served as a trusted technical partner in initiatives to enhance budget literacy, transparency and citizen engagement. This support helped ensure that public finance discussions and tools increasingly reflected children’s rights and needs, contributing to more accessible, participatory and accountable budgeting practices.

UNICEF contributed to the development and dissemination of MINFIN’s Citizens Budget 2025, a simplified and user-friendly version of the State Budget, reaching over 1,000 students across five universities. This initiative demystified complex budget information, enhancing understanding of resource allocation for social sectors critical to children’s well-being. Building on this, UNICEF supported Angola’s first Citizens Account (Conta Cidadã) for the 2023 State Accounts, enabling citizens to track government spending and assess fiscal performance. These tools strengthened citizens’ capacity to engage meaningfully in budget discussions and advocate for child-focused allocations.

UNICEF supported participatory processes in budget preparation. During the 2025 consultation cycle for the 2026 State Budget, MINFIN required for the first time that provinces and sectors conduct consultations with partners before submitting their budget proposals. UNICEF participated in several sectoral consultations to ensure children’s priorities were considered early in the process, contributing to significant increases in allocations for the hotline for child protection and disability, to name a few. UNICEF also supported MINFIN’s Consultation Forum, which gathered inputs from social and economic partners for the 2026 Budget Proposal. For the first time, the forum’s recommendations were published as an annex to the Proposal submitted to the Parliament, enhancing transparency and providing a formal record of stakeholder contributions. Evidence generation was another cornerstone of UNICEF’s approach. Through high-quality Budget Briefs and an analysis of social sector budget execution, UNICEF provided reliable, accessible information on the levels, trends, and efficiency of investments in children. This evidence equips civil society, parliamentarians, and other stakeholders to better understand fiscal allocations and advocate for children’s rights, fostering a cycle of greater literacy, transparency, and informed participation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF applied adaptive and agile management approaches across sectors in 2025 generating important lessons: these insights highlighted critical challenges and gaps that require renewed strategies, innovative solutions, and strengthened partnerships. 

The cholera outbreak placed significant strain on an already fragile health system. The re-deployment of health personnel to emergency response disrupted routine services, including immunization and nutrition, while the chronic and limited access to safe water and sanitation hindered prevention. Heavy reliance on water trucking and privately owned storage systems made it difficult to maintain adequate free chlorine residuals, highlighting systemic weaknesses in public and community water services. Social and economic barriers further limited the adoption of preventive behaviours, with families often lacking knowledge or practice on handwashing and correct use of chlorine-based products. 

Operational gaps in surveillance and case detection further challenged the response. As an example, in Luanda, 15.7 per cent of households of cholera cases could not be identified, impeding the implementation of the CATI approach to stop transmission. Additionally, cases managed at the Oral Rehydration Points were not always registered at the Cholera Treatment Centre, leading to potentially significant underreporting. These gaps highlighted the need to strengthen epidemiological surveillance, data integration and active case finding, particularly after the first wave of transmission. The experience also underscored the importance of surge capacity planning that safeguards continuity of essential child survival services during public health emergencies.

Despite these challenges, the response demonstrated the effectiveness of integrated, localised interventions. Rapid WASH actions, including bucket chlorination combined with community engagement, contributed to reduced household-level transmission. High oral cholera vaccine coverage showed that data-driven microplanning and multisectoral coordination can achieve near-universal reach, even in complex operating environments. The mobilisation of youth, traditional leaders and community actors reinforced the value of trusted local networks in promoting preventive behaviours and sustaining outbreak control. 

In the area of social protection, the design of Kwenda 2.0 reflects a key lesson from earlier social protection interventions: income support alone is insufficient to break intergenerational cycles of poverty. Building on evidence generated through the Valor Criança impact study, Kwenda 2.0 integrates a child-sensitive, human capital–focused approach that links cash transfers with access to essential services for children. The programme’s cash-plus model prioritises households with pregnant women, lactating mothers and children under five, promoting improved nutrition, immunization, early stimulation, maternal health, and birth registration. The integration of child-related service utilisation indicators into the Kwenda Management Information System marks a shift towards accountability for child outcomes rather than coverage alone.

The transition to Kwenda 2.0 underscores the importance of intersectoral coordination and system readiness. UNICEF is well positioned to support the institutionalization of the child-centered cash-plus model, ensuring that behaviour change interventions, early childhood development, nutrition, and adolescent programming are integrated into routine delivery. Looking ahead, UNICEF can play a catalytic role in shaping shock-responsive social protection that prioritises children during climate and economic crises.

UNICEF’s support to the revision of Angola’s third Nationally Determined Contribution and the development of its first National Adaptation Plan highlighted the value of systematically integrating child rights and youth participation into national climate frameworks. Through consultations conducted with the United Nations Development Programme, government institutions and civil society, children and young people from five provinces contributed with experience on local climate vulnerabilities and proposed context-specific solutions, strengthening the relevance, inclusiveness and policy coherence of Angola’s commitments under the Paris Agreement.

These processes underscored that meaningful participation must go beyond policy formulation to implementation, financing and monitoring to deliver child-responsive climate outcomes at scale. Moving forward, sustaining and institutionalising youth engagement, while translating policy commitments into tangible adaptation and resilience actions, will be critical to ensuring that children and youth are not only protected from climate impacts but also empowered as agents of change in shaping a more resilient future.

On the legislative side, UNICEF supported the National Assembly to assess gaps in national and inter-country adoption frameworks. A Hague Convention expert was brought to Angola to support the implementation of the 1993 Convention on Protection of Children and Co-operation in Respect of Intercountry Adoption, in line with international standards. Leveraging the expert’s presence, UNICEF provided technical support for a national multi-stakeholder workshop that strengthened shared understanding of legal, procedural, and institutional gaps. The workshop led to several recommendations, including establishing a national working group to review adoption legislation—particularly provisions in the Family Code requiring alignment with the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption.

Future efforts will focus on improving coordination across courts, justice and social services; establishing a national registry of eligible adoptive families; strengthening psychosocial support for children and reinforcing regulatory oversight and procedural guidance. UNICEF will also support the establishment of a multidisciplinary team to strengthen pre-adoption processes and the functioning of the Central Authority for Adoption, while continuing to prioritise children without parental care through improved protection and birth registration in residential care and prevention of child abandonment through teenage pregnancy support programming.

Despite progress in strengthening the planning and implementation of both supplementary immunization activities and routine immunization, the persistently high number of zero-dose children in Angola underscores the need for intensified outreach and tailored strategies to reach the most underserved. The endorsement of the National Immunization Strategy and Angola’s expected return to Gavi support from 2026 under the Gavi 6.0 framework present a critical opportunity to accelerate immunization recovery and strengthen health systems. Over the four-year period, Angola is expected to access approximately US$47 million to support health system strengthening, primarily on Expanded Programme on Immunization. 

Effective implementation of the National Immunization Strategy, with UNICEF’s technical assistance and Gavi’s financing, will be essential to reducing the number of zero-dose children, expanding outreach to underserved populations and strengthening resilience to future public health shocks. The successful application of Angola to the Child Nutrition Fund also opens a great opportunity for additional external and domestic financing of the sector, which still faces high levels of stunting among children under five. These investments position Angola to achieve more equitable and sustainable improvements in immunization coverage and child survival outcomes.

In 2025, Botswana’s political environment remained stable, marked by decisive government action to develop and adopted the Botswana Economic Transformation Plan (BETP) and finalize the 12th National Development Plan (NDP)12. These frameworks placed human capital, youth empowerment, and social sector reforms at the forefront of the country’s transformation agenda.
The year 2025 represented a pivotal moment for Botswana, as the nation confronted a challenging macroeconomic environment marked by recessionary pressures, volatile diamond revenues, and tightening fiscal conditions. The February flood emergency amplified the climatic risks that the country faces. These shocks reverberated across households, markets, and public systems, threatening to erode hard-won human development gains, particularly for children.
Economically, the year was characterized by persistent challenges. Botswana’s Gross Domestic Product remained in recession in the first quarter of 2025, contracting by 0.3 per cent, projected to contract by 1 per cent for 2025, an improvement from the 3 per cent contraction in 2024. However, a sharp 42 per cent decline in diamond output severely impacted jobs, exports, and fiscal revenues. Inflation surged to 3.9 per cent in October 2025 from a nine months average of 2.3 per cent (January – September) and is projected to average 3.4 per cent for 2025 well within the Bank of Botswana’s objective range (3 per cent - 6 per cent), driven by exchange rate adjustments as they pass through to consumer prices and rising import costs, while government cashflow constraints delayed payments to suppliers, slowed procurement, and placed additional pressure on service delivery. Unemployment has remained high, especially for the youth. The latest data (2024Q1) reported overall youth unemployment of 27.6 per cent and 38.2 per cent, respectively.
These macroeconomic pressures had direct implications for children and households. Escalating food and fuel prices. Eroded household purchasing power, increasing the risks of malnutrition, and school absenteeism. Vulnerability intensified among urban poor and rural households, while interruptions in service delivery threatened to widen existing inequalities in education, health, and child protection outcomes. Due to the budget constraints and health supply chain challenges the Government of Botswana declared a Public Health Emergency in August 2025, reflecting challenges that social sectors face during situations of macroeconomic and fiscal challenges.
With regards to socioeconomic development indicators, progress on child rights remains uneven. Neonatal mortality is estimated at 20 per 1,000 live births, while under-five mortality stands at 39.6 per 1,000 (UNICEF, 2024). In 2025, 4,120 new HIV infections were recorded, with adolescent girls and young women accounting for 27 per cent (UNAIDS, 2025). The adolescent birth rate remains high at 50 births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19, contributing to maternal health risks, with the maternal mortality ratio estimated at 155 per 100,000 live births (WHO, 2024). Nutrition outcomes show stunting prevalence at 21 per cent among children under five (Statistics Botswana, 2023). While Botswana maintains a strong civil registration system, gaps persist in birth registration coverage, currently at 92.3 per cent (Statistics Botswana, 2023). Education indicators highlight learning poverty at 53 per cent, with many children unable to read proficiently by age 10 (World Bank, 2024). Poverty remains a structural challenge, with children disproportionately affected by multidimensional poverty, estimated at 38 per cent nationally (UNDP, 2025).
These trends underscore the urgency of accelerating investments in health, nutrition, education, and social protection to deliver results at scale and ensure no child is left behind. While Botswana’s commitment to the Sustainable Development Goals and the principle of “leaving no child behind” remained strong, further amplified by a renewed focus on human rights, a core mantra of the new administration, the path to inclusive and sustainable development now demands renewed investment, innovation, and strategic focus. In this environment, UNICEF’s role grew significantly, providing technical leadership, robust evidence, and strategic partnerships to safeguard child-focused priorities and ensure that children’s needs remain central to Botswana’s transformation agenda.
Amidst these challenges, Botswana embarked on a new era of long-term transformation, guided by NDP 12 and the BETP. Both frameworks place human capital, social protection, skills, data systems, and governance reforms at the core of the country’s development agenda.
Within this dynamic context, UNICEF’s mandate, to ensure that every child survives, learns, and thrives, remained both urgent and profoundly relevant. Despite decades of progress, 2025 exposed widening inequalities: rising inflation and liquidity constraints pushed more households into vulnerability; stagnating learning outcomes, especially in rural areas, highlighted persistent gaps in education quality; escalating food prices increased the risk of malnutrition; and economic stress heightened the risks of violence, exploitation, and harmful coping mechanisms among children and adolescents. Children with disabilities continued to face significant barriers to essential services.

In 2025, UNICEF Botswana delivered transformative results, advancing national priorities and protecting human capital through strategic engagement. Working in close partnership with the Government, UNICEF played a pivotal role in driving reforms aligned with the National Development Plan (NDP) 12, the Botswana Economic Transformation Plan (BETP), and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).
First Decade: 0 – 9 years

Every child survives and thrives
In 2025, UNICEF advanced child survival and thriving through a dual approach: strengthening national systems and delivering catalytic actions on the ground, leveraging partnerships and resources to drive sustainable impact.
Immunization and Child Health Systems strengthening was at the core of UNICEF Botswana in 2025. To improve immunization coverage, UNICEF supported the Government to finalised and adopt the National Immunization Strategy and provided technical support for the design and planning of the Measles-Rubella (MR) campaign, now scheduled for rollout in 2026 due to fiscal constraints on the Government. UNICEF mobilized financial and technical resources through the UN Foundation to support the campaign, which aims to achieve over 90 per cent MR coverage and boost uptake of other antigens and Vitamin A supplementation.
As part of the February 2025 Flood Emergency Response which resulted in a malaria outbreak, UNICEF leveraged its supply chain system to procure malaria reagents and supplies and strengthened risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), reaching 4,500 caregivers and children in person and more than 15,000 through public address systems, reducing health risks and increasing service uptake.
Nutrition and Food Systems. To support Government to address child malnutrition, UNICEF supported the government to implement Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) and Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) social and behavior change interventions in five high-burden districts. To address national shortages, UNICEF provided 1,500 cartons of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF). To strengthen food systems, UNICEF supported a landscape analysis for reformulation of Tsabana and Malutu, Botswana’s cereal-based supplementary feeding products, focusing on micronutrient content, supply chain, and user experience. Additionally, UNICEF initiated a legal landscape analysis for front-of-pack labeling, paving the way for legislation to combat child obesity and regulation of marketing of unhealthy products.
Climate Resilience. UNICEF, in partnership with the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, updated the Climate Change Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). This evidence-based tool will inform the development of Botswana’s third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) and the review of the National Adaptation Plan, embedding child-sensitive approaches into climate-resilient systems.
HIV and Health Systems. With HIV programs under pressure from declining official development aid funding, UNICEF worked with the UN Joint Team to develop the Fourth National Strategic Framework (NSF IV) on HIV and AIDS, including an M\&E framework and costed implementation plan. The strategy prioritizes high-impact interventions for adolescents, Triple Elimination of HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B, and Early Infant Diagnosis. UNICEF successfully advocated for the inclusion of Operation Triple Zero, a proven intervention to close treatment gaps among adolescents.
Botswana achieved a historic milestone as the first high HIV-burden country globally to attain WHO’s Gold Tier status for the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, reducing transmission rates to 1.7 per cent, below the 5 per cent benchmark and ensuring 98 per cent of pregnant women living with HIV receive lifesaving treatment. UNICEF supported the development of strategic guidelines, strengthened data systems, and promoted evidence-based planning to sustain this achievement. Together with WHO, UNICEF developed a strategic roadmap to 2027 to maintain Botswana’s Gold Tier status for HIV EMTCT and achieve similar recognition for syphilis and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), integrating programmatic actions, data management, laboratory services, and critical non-clinical dimensions such as human rights, community engagement, and gender equality.
Through systems strengthening, resource mobilisation, and catalytic interventions, UNICEF reinforced Botswana’s capacity to deliver equitable, resilient, and child-centered health and nutrition services. These efforts not only address immediate needs but also lay the foundation for sustainable progress toward national and global commitments.
Every child learns
In 2025, UNICEF Botswana advanced national priorities for Early Childhood Education (ECE) by ensuring the revised curriculum under the Government’s Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEAM) programme reflects children’s developmental needs and emerging priorities, set to benefit 250,000 children aged 3–6 years. Quality learning outcomes were strengthened through South-South exchanges with Lesotho, enabling the Ministry of Child Welfare and Education to adopt regional best practices, while technical assistance supported remediation and enrichment interventions that improved foundational skills among young learners. At the policy level, UNICEF’s advisory support positioned Botswana as a continental leader, influencing regional education strategies through contributions at the African Union Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) Meeting and the Association for the Development of Education in Africa (ADEA) Triennale. During flood emergencies, UNICEF safeguarded continuity of learning and psychosocial wellbeing by distributing 1,500 education, ECD, and recreation kits, reaching 18,000 children.
Second Decade: 10 – 24 years
Every adolescent and young person survives and thrives
In 2025, with support from Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and in partnership with the Ministry of Health, the National AIDS and Health Promotion Agency (NAHPA), Botswana-Baylor and Sentebale, Operation Triple Zero Plus (OTZ+) expanded its reach to 30 sites across Botswana. Reaching 2,100 adolescents and young people living with HIV (AYPLHIV) with a comprehensive package of services such as comprehensive sexuality education, mental health and psychosocial support, disclosure and economic empowerment. The program achieved exceptional outcomes with 97 per cent AYPLHIV attending their routine monitoring appointments, 98 per cent adhering to their prescribed treatment, and over 96 per cent achieving viral suppression. The program introduced comprehensive, tailored support for 174 pregnant and breastfeeding adolescent and young mothers, addressing their unique vulnerabilities through an integrated package of services. This included psychosocial care to promote mental well-being and resilience and Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) education to ensure adherence to HIV treatment and safe infant feeding practices. By combining these interventions, the program created a supportive environment that safeguards the health of mothers and their babies as well as strengthen their capacity to thrive socially, ultimately contributing to improved maternal and child health outcomes. UNICEF, in partnership with NAHPA and Sentebale supported the establishment of Botswana's first-ever Network of Young People Living with HIV with over 300 members nationwide, alongside a Youth Advisory Panel, enabling meaningful youth participation in HIV policy and programming.
Empowering Youth for Climate Action. In 2025, UNICEF partnered with the Botswana Climate Change Network to engage adolescents in sustainability through innovative, interactive learning. A climate awareness board game was co-created with 30 young people to reflect real-life experiences and motivations. Technical validation by curriculum developers ensured alignment with national education priorities. Prototype sessions with players aged 16–24 refined the gaming experience. To scale impact, 20 District Climate Champions were trained to lead game-based sessions, reaching over 1,100 young people in schools and communities. This shift from passive learning to dynamic engagement positions youth as active problem-solvers and lays the foundation for national adoption of the game as a recognized climate education tool.
Every child learns
In 2025, UNICEF Botswana advanced digital learning to ensure no child is left behind in a connected world. Through the Giga Initiative, school connectivity expanded to 110 schools in remote regions, enabling thousands of learners to access online resources and interactive platforms that are critical for reducing learning disparities. Building on this, UNICEF supported the rollout of the Learning Passport, providing curriculum-aligned content online to sustain learning during disruptions and strengthen digital literacy among students and teachers.
To safeguard children online, UNICEF partnered with the Government on nationwide campaigns promoting digital safety and responsible technology use. Gender equity was prioritized through Girls in ICT Day, inspiring girls to pursue STEM careers and narrowing the ICT gender gap. For sustainability, UNICEF trained government IT officers to manage and optimize education technology, reinforcing institutional capacity for digital transformation and ensuring investments deliver improved learning outcomes.

Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
In 2025, UNICEF sustained its commitment to building a child-friendly justice system in Botswana through a systems-strengthening approach and strategic partnerships with the Government and the British High Commission. A landmark achievement was the development and launch of the National Multi-Sectoral Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for a child-friendly justice system. These SOPs provide a unified framework to ensure consistent, rights-based services for children in contact with the justice system, marking a significant step toward institutionalised child-sensitive practices.
Capacity development was central to this transformation. Forty-five social workers from all 31 districts were trained as master trainers in forensic report writing, cascading training to 12 districts. Additionally, 24 prosecutors and 30 magistrates received specialized training on child-friendly justice principles, while 40 High Court Judges participated in a UNICEF-led colloquium to strengthen judicial capacity. To reinforce accountability, UNICEF facilitated a South-South learning exchange with Namibia, enabling Botswana’s Ombudsman to establish its first-ever Children’s Desk, a groundbreaking mechanism for child rights oversight.
Expanding Protection Across Sectors. UNICEF advanced child protection beyond justice systems by embedding standards in media and education. Forty-five media practitioners from leading outlets were trained in child-sensitive reporting, improving ethical coverage and safeguarding children’s dignity. A documentary on child-friendly policing was produced to promote awareness of specialized services, contributing to increased reporting at child-friendly police centers, where 3,361 children accessed services in 2025.
To institutionalise prevention, UNICEF supported the Government in developing a five-year costed National Plan of Action for the Prevention and Response to Violence Against Children, providing a strategic framework for cross-sectoral alignment. In education, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Child Welfare and Basic Education to develop training manuals for responding to school-based violence. Thirty teachers piloted the toolkit, with national scale-up planned for 2026. Work also progressed on an alternative discipline manual to end corporal punishment and promote positive practices.
In response to Botswana’s high youth unemployment (38.2 per cent) and NEET rate of 41 per cent, double the global average (20.4 per cent), UNICEF supported the Government in recalibrating National Youth Programming to deliver high-impact, systemic interventions. A key milestone was UNICEF’s contribution to conceptualising and consolidating the Presidential Youth Empowerment Programme, leveraging the Generation Unlimited ecosystem and introducing the Youth Agency Marketplace (YOMA) to expand pathways for employability and entrepreneurship. UNICEF facilitated a South-South learning exchange between Botswana and South Africa’s Office of the Presidency, strengthening coordination of multi-pronged youth employment strategies.
To institutionalise accountability and sectoral coherence, UNICEF worked with the Ministry of State President, Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, and Ministry of Labour and Home Affairs to enhance coordination mechanisms. This strategy also included the nomination and endorsement of President Duma Boko as a Generation Unlimited Global leader and that of Hon Minister Chombo as a champion. Other efforts included remodeling the Youth Development Fund and reviewing the National Youth Service Programme to improve access to financing, mentorship, and internships for young entrepreneurs.
Through targeted employability training in rural communities, 5,414 youth enhanced their skills, with 240 registering on the National Labour Market system and over 30 securing employment. These efforts, coupled with revitalised youth grants and expanded apprenticeship opportunities, are building sustainable systems that empower young people with skills, resources, and networks for decent work and economic independence.

Every child has an equitable chance in life
In 2025, UNICEF supported Botswana to strengthen national systems that deliver equitable and sustainable results for children, with a strong focus on social protection reforms, public finance for children and strategic partnerships. Through evidence-based technical assistance, policy dialogue and convening power, UNICEF helped translate national commitments into scalable solutions that reach children at scale.
UNICEF played a catalytic role in strengthening Botswana’s social protection system by supporting the design and costing of social assistance reforms that enhance efficiency, integration and resilience. A major milestone was UNICEF’s technical support to the development and implementation of Infant Grant Guidelines, which enabled the rollout of a new BWP 300 grant for eligible families. This reform represents a strategic investment in early childhood development and reflects the Government of Botswana’s commitment to child-sensitive social protection grounded in evidence and fiscal sustainability.
Through sustained advocacy and national dialogue, UNICEF reinforced social protection and child poverty reduction as core development priorities. By convening high-level platforms, including the Ministerial Public Lecture on Social Protection, UNICEF influenced policy reform and ensured child-focused priorities were embedded in strategic policies.
Botswana’s social protection system remains one of the most comprehensive in the region, with strong government ownership and financing. Nearly 56 per cent of the population and 79 per cent of the poor benefit from at least one programme. UNICEF’s technical support and advocacy contributed to expanded coverage. In 2025, approximately 91 per cent of children, about 822,099, were reached through social assistance programmes, including school feeding and orphan care, demonstrating the system’s ability to deliver results at scale while prioritising the most vulnerable.
Amid fiscal pressures, UNICEF played a central role in safeguarding investments in children by strengthening public finance systems. UNICEF delivered critical costing and fiscal analysis for the Ending Violence Against Children Plan as well as completing a Child Protection Budget Brief. UNICEF advanced institutional capacity for public financial management by supporting budget transparency reforms, promoting participation of children in fiscal processes and providing technical assistance to the Ministry of Finance on developing of a a proposal for the next-generation public financial management reforms. These efforts strengthened government capacity to plan, allocate, and track resources for children more effectively.
UNICEF transformed private sector engagement by leveraging more than USD 1 million and shifting partnerships toward long-term, systems-oriented impact. Through strengthened collaboration with the CEO Council for Child Rights and a Joint Workplan, UNICEF enhanced joint accountability for private sector investments in children and young people. Results included Smart Early Childhood Education classrooms funded by Mascom, a child-friendly police centre funded by De Beers, a one-million-pula trust fund addressing children and gender-based violence funded by Lucara Diamond Corporation and expanded youth mentorship and empowerment programmes through ABSA Bank. UNICEF increasingly positioned itself as a technical partner, shaping private sector ESG strategies that prioritise children. and communication have amplified these results. The UNICEF Social Policy Dialogue Series strengthened policy coherence and knowledge exchange, while digital campaigns on immunisation and early childhood development reached over 25 per cent of the population, driving demand. At the regional level, Botswana’s hosting of the Head of State and Government Sub-Regional Commemoration of World Children’s Day reinforced political commitment and collective accountability for child rights across the Southern Africa Development Community (SADC).

In 2025, Botswana’s development landscape was shaped by a series of complex operational challenges that tested the resilience of national systems and the effectiveness of ongoing reforms. Persistent fiscal deficits constrained the government’s ability to fully implement critical initiatives, while procurement delays disrupted the timely delivery of essential supplies and services. Escalating food prices intensified the risk of child malnutrition, disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable populations. UNICEF and other actors had also to support response to the two emergenicies expereinced in the year: floods and the medical supply shortage in the country. At the district level, limited capacity hindered the rollout and sustainability of key reforms, underscoring the need for targeted investments in local systems. Furthermore, the rapid pace of digital transformation outstripped the readiness of many sectors, highlighting the importance of adaptive strategies and resource mobilization to ensure successful implementation. These challenges reinforced the imperative for agile programme design, robust partnerships and data-driven decision-making to safeguard progress and advance equitable outcomes for children across Botswana. In response, UNICEF adapted its programming and partnerships throughout the year, prioritising high-impact reforms, sequencing interventions pragmatically and leveraging evidence to inform real-time adjustments.
Several factors enabled UNICEF and partners to deliver results for children despite a challenging operating environment. Foremost were the strong leadership of the new Government and its commitment to a transformative development agenda. The articulation of clear national priorities through National Development Plan 12, the 2025 State of the Nation Address and the Botswana Economic Transformation Plan created a coherent policy framework within which UNICEF was able to align its technical assistance and advocacy. This alignment strengthened relevance, accelerated policy uptake and reinforced national ownership of reforms.
Embedding UNICEF-supported interventions within government systems proved highly effective. Social protection, health, education, child protection, adolescent and young people initiatives were designed and implemented through national institutions, enhancing sustainability and scalability. Strong government ownership enabled reforms such as the expansion of social assistance and the rollout of the Infant Grant to progress despite fiscal pressures, demonstrating the value of systems-based approaches over parallel delivery mechanisms.
UNICEF’s strategic advocacy and communications also delivered tangible results. Evidence-based policy dialogue, high-level convening, and targeted digital campaigns elevated child rights and child-sensitive investments within national decision-making processes. These efforts strengthened UNICEF’s influence beyond programme implementation, ensuring that children’s issues remained visible in policy, national budget and public discourse.
Private sector engagement evolved significantly during the year. UNICEF successfully recalibrated partnerships from predominantly philanthropic contributions towards deeper technical collaboration and alignment with corporate ESG agendas. This shift unlocked new forms of value, combining financing, innovation and expertise and strengthened joint accountability for results for children and young people.
Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF will further strengthen this agile approach. As Botswana gravitates to the implementation phase of the transformative agenda, UNICEF is poised to maximize its impact for children and young people. In 2026, UNICEF will prioritize strengthening integrated social protection systems with a focus on shock-responsiveness, advancing education transformation through foundational learning and digital innovation and reinforcing primary health care alongside integrated nutrition systems. The office will also scale up child protection and disability inclusion reforms, while intensifying advocacy for public finance for children to safeguard essential social spending as well as scale systems development and coordination for youth development and empowerment. A holistic approach to access justice by children remains a priority for UNICEF to support in ensuring that children have access to child friendly justice in a timely manner. Strategic partnerships, with the private sector, international financial institutions and development agencies, will be leveraged to expand resources and drive results at scale. Central to these efforts is the commitment to position human capital development at the heart of Botswana’s economic transformation, ensuring that every child can thrive in an inclusive and resilient society.

The gross domestic product (GDP) per capita of Burundi declined from US$250 to US$219 in 2023–2024.[1] The economy is largely informal and subsistence based. Poverty is widespread; 74.2 per cent of the population is living on less than US$3 a day, and 75.1 per cent experience acute multidimensional poverty.[2] High population density, demographic growth and macroeconomic shocks, including inflation, currency pressures and fuel and commodity shortages, are eroding household purchasing power and restricting children’s service access.

According to the 2024 census, there were 12.3 million inhabitants.[3] Nearly half (49 per cent) were under age 15. Around one in five children were under the age of 6. Most Burundians (75 per cent) live in rural areas, where poverty, limited infrastructure and long distances to services heighten barriers to care and learning.[4] The Government undertook an administrative reorganization in 2025, establishing five provinces and 42 communes. This was designed to bring public services closer to communities. It represents an opportunity to strengthen local governance and ensure effective interventions to promote child well-being.

Public social sector financing does not reflect the scale or multidimensional nature of child deprivations. Education represents the largest child-focused outlay, 15.3 per cent of the national budget in 2025–2026.[5] Health care allocations were declining, averaging 4.3 per cent of the budget.[6] Nutrition, early childhood development and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) grew from a low base, from 1.1 per cent to 1.6 per cent between 2024–2025 and 2025–2026.[7] Child protection (0.7 per cent) is chronically underfunded.[8] Social protection (5.0 per cent) supports cash transfers (funded by donors grants), school feeding and other safety nets, but many vulnerable children are not covered.[9]

Burundi faced displacements, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks in 2025. Nearly 90,800 refugees from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo arrived in December 2025; more than 36,000 refugees had arrived earlier in the year. The mpox outbreak began in 2024 and spread in 2025. There were almost 300 new cases of cholera every week at the peak of the outbreak, which caused 11 deaths in 2025.[10] More than 10,700 Burundian returnees were registered at major reception sites.[11]

Under-five mortality declined by close to 20% in 2017–2023 from 61.1 to 49.2 per 1,000 live births. Progress on neonatal and infant mortality is, however, slower.[12] Maternal mortality has declined, but is still at 299 per 100,000 live births, well above the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of 140.[13] Chronic malnutrition is a major issue. More than half (52.8 per cent) of children under age 5 are stunted. Global acute malnutrition has increased to about 8 per cent. Severe acute malnutrition is above the emergency level (= 2 per cent), at 2.2 per cent. Fewer than one in five children ages 6–23 months meets the minimum acceptable diet. These outcomes are driven by food insecurity, inadequate infant and child feeding practices, limited access to primary health care and recurrent diseases, including diarrhœa and respiratory infections.[14] In 2023, around 41 per cent of households were food insecure, almost double the share in 2014. Low agricultural productivity, limited access to inputs and irrigation, soil degradation, and climate variability undermine the resilience of livelihoods and threaten the nutritional status of children.[15]

Basic drinking water coverage reaches about 66 per cent.[16] Access to safely managed drinking water and sanitation services is low. Girls and women, who are often responsible for water collection, are thereby exposed to protection risks. About 45 per cent of households have improved, non-shared latrines.[17] Handwashing facilities are available to 24.4 per cent of households.[18]

The pre-primary gross enrolment ratio has almost doubled since 2019–2020, but remains low, at around 23 per cent. Access among rural and poor communities is limited. In basic education, net enrolment has stagnated below targets. Completion rates at the end of the third cycle are around 53 per cent. High repetition (around 27 per cent) and dropout (about 11 per cent) signal low internal effectiveness.[19]

Overcrowded classrooms, shortages of desks and learning materials, limited WASH infrastructure in schools, and an overburdened teaching workforce undermine learning. Many children do not acquire foundational literacy and numeracy from Grade 3 onward, when instruction is transitions to French. Assessments of grades 4 and 6 show low learning outcomes, particularly in language and mathematics. Fees, the cost of materials, and other expenses contribute to late entry, absenteeism and dropout, especially among the poorest.[20]

Most children (90 per cent) experience some form of violence. More than 1 in 10 girls ages 15–19 report they have experienced sexual violence.[21] Children living or working on the streets, children in conflict with the law and children without adequate family care are insufficiently reached by formal protection services. Social workforce numbers and capacities are limited. Underfunding constrains the expansion and quality of case management, psychosocial support, and community-based prevention. Burundi has one of the highest rates of birth registration on the continent (83 per cent of children under age 5 are registered).[22] Yet, more needs to be done.
Adolescents and young people have limited access to adolescent-friendly health services, including sexual and reproductive health, mental health, and psychosocial support. Low use of modern contraception, harmful social norms, and violence contribute to early and unintended pregnancies, early unions, and school drop-out among girls. HIV affects adolescents, particularly girls and young women. Pædiatric treatment coverage is low. Opportunities for post-basic education, skills development, and decent work are few. Vocational training is scarce and poorly aligned with labour market needs, leading to marginal participation of young people in the formal economy.

Gender inequalities are visible in time use, mobility, safety, access to information and decision-making. They intensify during adolescence. Children with disabilities encounter persistent stigma, discrimination, and structural barriers. Many schools, health facilities, and WASH infrastructures are not physically accessible. Assistive devices are scarce and costly. Professionals often lack the skills to provide inclusive services. Climate change is a major risk multiplier. Recurrent floods, landslides and droughts disrupt schooling, damage health and WASH infrastructure, displace families around the Lake Tanganyika basin and elsewhere, and exacerbate food and nutrition insecurity.
