UNICEF-Burundi helped reduce system bottlenecks and improve access to essential health services among children, adolescents and women in 2025 by strengthening community-based delivery and emergency preparedness. It contributed to the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework key result on social services strengthening. A total of 2,235 community health workers (89 per cent of the annual target) were trained, equipped, and supervised on integrated community case management. This assisted in establishing a 32 per cent increase in the treatment of childhood malaria, diarrhœa and pneumonia across communities. The piloting of the National Community Health Strategy (2025–2027) in Mutaho health district represented a key learning investment, allowing the Government to test integrated service delivery, supervision, and monitoring models before expansion. Simplified monitoring tools enabled the tracking of 15 tracer interventions across health, nutrition, child protection, WASH and disability inclusion, strengthening the evidence base for adaptive programming. Emergency obstetric and neonatal care capacity expanded, with 24/7 facilities increasing from 56 to 88 nationwide. In the UNICEF-supported health districts, the number of newborns receiving postnatal care within 48 hours in communities rose from 431,811 in 2024 to 433,894 in 2025 (99 per cent of the annual target). Two integrated neonatology centres were established in Kayanza and Mukenge, contributing to the improved management of complications and the continuity of newborn care. UNICEF’s multisectoral response to the mpox outbreak contributed to a significant 95 per cent reduction in confirmed cases and a contraction of affected districts from 34 to 5 by the end of 2025. UNICEF efforts during the mpox response illustrated the added value of integrated service delivery, combining clinical care, infection prevention and control, mental health and psychosocial support and community engagement.

UNICEF achieved large-scale nutrition results in 2025, while reinforcing multisectoral systems and national ownership. More than 812,000 mothers of children ages 6–23 months across 1,518 collinesin 11 of the 18 former provinces were reached through community-based platforms that integrated nutrition, early stimulation and livelihoods and helped enable the delivery of maternal, infant and young child feeding counselling.[1] Community nutrition activities were tailored, strengthened and sustained. More than 11,000 community actors and front-line workers were trained to implement the minimum package of community nutrition activities. Preventive nutrition interventions reached scale. More than 1.3 million children ages 6–59 months received one dose of vitamin A; more than 1.4 million children received deworming tablets, and approximately 250,000 children ages 6–23 months were reached with multiple micronutrients powder. Iron and folic acid supplementation reached 390,000 pregnant women (90 per cent of the annual target). The management of acute malnutrition was strengthened through improved supervision and supply chain oversight. Nearly 1.4 million children were screened. Close to 55,000 cases of severe acute malnutrition were treated, with an 88 per cent cure rate in line with the Sphere Standards.[2] UNICEF supported 20,000 kitchen gardens and 2,321 village savings and loan associations (VSLAs). Of these, 162 produced nutritious local recipes benefiting more than 9,700 children ages 6–23 months, and 103 received about 2,200 laying hens to improve animal protein intake among children under age 2. UNICEF supported the development and approval of the nutrition strategic plan in the health sector (2025–2030) and a costed plan for adolescent, school-age children and maternal nutrition, enabling an environment that promotes child nutrition improvement. Innovative financing, multisectoral coordination and private sector engagement to produce first foods were at the heart of a high-level dialogue. A forum of women leaders positioned nutrition as a key driver of human capital development.

To strengthen early childhood stimulation and positive parenting, 879 stimulation spaces (92.5 per cent of the annual target) were established and equipped with early childhood development (ECD) kits, including 675 community platforms linked to VSLAs and 204 in health facilities (Cankuzo, Kayanza, Makamba, Muramvya, Mwaro and Rutana), reaching 407,470 children under age 5. In Kayanza, UNICEF continued implementing the ECD model project, reaching over 53,000 children through a multisectoral package of services.

UNICEF combined service delivery with sectoral reform in 2025 to improve access to inclusive climate-resilient WASH services. Through strengthened community-led total sanitation integrated with Baby WASH and ECD, 184 communities were declared open defecation free, benefiting more than 222,000 people. Overall, 554,780 people gained access to at least basic sanitation services, exceeding the annual target by 85 per cent. Access to safe water was improved among 147,659 people through climate-resilient water systems in development and emergency contexts, reducing reliance on unsafe sources and easing the burden on women and girls. UNICEF supported the construction or rehabilitation of WASH infrastructure in 74 schools and 34 health centres, including gender-segregated, disability-inclusive latrines and menstrual hygiene management spaces. To promote women’s leadership at the local level, UNICEF partnered with the Association of Women Engineers. Through this collaboration, 130 women in eight cooperatives received capacity strengthening in WASH and climate-related issues, fostering their empowerment and ensuring sustainable access to water within their communities. UNICEF played a central role in enabling sectoral reform. Through its partnership with UNICEF, the World Bank, Sanitation and Water for All and the European Union, the Government committed to the WASH Compact, which is currently being finalized, passed water and sanitation legislation in November 2025, and secured additional domestic resources. Strategic advocacy and technical assistance contributed to a 52 per cent increase in national WASH budget allocations. UNICEF supported the development of the safely managed sanitation road map and the adoption of new legislation organizing public drinking water and sanitation services and strengthening accountability and sustainability. The multisectoral partnership with the World Bank, Sanitation and Water for All, and the European Union catalysed high-level government commitment to the WASH sector and enabled essential policy reviews and reforms.
 
UNICEF-supported education interventions in 2025 focused on access, inclusion, and learning quality across key stages of the education cycle, particularly among vulnerable groups. At the early learning level, the progress in the pre-primary gross enrolment ratio reflects combined investments in classroom construction, learning materials, community mobilization and educator recruitment, alongside UNICEF-led policy advocacy to expand pre-primary provision within public schools. At the primary level, UNICEF investments improved learning environments and inclusion. While the target was 120, a total of 242 classrooms were constructed or rehabilitated, benefiting more than 32,000 students and helping reduce overcrowding in high-pressure schools. Inclusive infrastructure enhanced the participation of girls and children with disabilities. Through the Education Cannot Wait–funded Komezawige Project, enrolment has increased by 19 per cent since 2022. The gains have been more rapid among girls (20 per cent) than boys (17 per cent). More than 4,600 out-of-school children reintegrated through community-based mechanisms. Inclusive education was strengthened through the LEGO Braille Bricks initiative, which equipped 25 schools, trained 264 teachers and increased enrolment among blind and visually impaired children from 107 to 394 within one academic year, reflecting reduced stigma and improved trust in the education system. UNICEF expanded learning-to-skills pathways for adolescents through programmes combining foundational skills, science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) exposure and social innovation, strengthening transitions from education to employability and resilience among vulnerable youth.

UNICEF-Burundi made progress toward a more structured, community-based child protection system in 2025 by addressing gaps in case management, workforce capacity and prevention. Standardized case management tools and strengthened social service workforce capacities enabled multisectoral support to be provided to 2,221 child survivors of violence, exceeding annual targets. UNICEF addressed critical capacity gaps in a system historically reliant on under resourced community actors by training and coaching 386 social workers and paraprofessionals. It invested in improving identification, referral and follow-up among vulnerable children, including children with disabilities and those affected by humanitarian crises. Community-based child protection committees (CPCs) were strengthened following the national mapping conducted in 2023 and the adoption of a national strategy in 2024. UNICEF supported the development of a national training guide and the establishment of a pool of 29 trainers, who began cascading training to CPC members in 2025. Direct protection services reached 48,555 children affected by displacement, mpox and other shocks through psychosocial support, case management, temporary care and family tracing. To prevent violence against children, UNICEF designed and implemented community dialogues reaching 12,946 people. Contents and messaging were based on the findings of research on social norms and sexual violence against children, which was concluded in 2025. Progress in birth registration was significant: 138,120 births were registered, and 34,453 children were registered within the legal deadline through expanded interoperability between health centres and civil registration services, reaching 132 health centres by the end of 2025.

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened its strategic engagement on public finance and social protection in a constrained macroeconomic environment. UNICEF support was provided for the strengthening of the national system through improved referral and coordination capacities. Evidence generated through budget analyses and briefs informed sustained dialogue with government counterparts, contributing to a 10.9 per cent nominal increase in social sector allocations for the 2025/2026 fiscal year, including substantial gains in WASH (+51 per cent) and social assistance. Despite the gains, UNICEF was able to highlight persistent structural constraints, including declining real-term allocations because of inflation and limited fiscal space. Technical assistance supported programme-based budgeting, procurement planning and results-based monitoring, thereby strengthening spending efficiency and accountability. In social protection, UNICEF provided technical support for the national safety net programme, which covers 661,024 children in 165,256 households.

UNICEF significantly strengthened social and behaviour change systems and community engagement in 2025. More than 2,600 community actors were trained as change agents, directly reaching more than 700,000 people through community dialogue, mass media and participatory platforms. UNICEF supported the development and validation of the National Community Engagement Strategy and revitalized the U-Report, enrolling 3,150 new users and establishing 32 commune-level clubs. Community-led engagement and mobilization initiatives, including the promotion of primary health care and vaccination, healthy feeding practices, and the prevention of violence against children, contributed to measurable positive shifts in attitudes and practices. During health emergencies, UNICEF and the Government co-led risk communication and community engagement, providing technical support to the system and partners and contributing to sustained adoption of protective behaviours, as confirmed in multi-round surveys.

Cross-cutting priorities: Gender equality, disability inclusion and climate action
Gender integration progressed through systematic analysis, targeted pilot initiatives and institutional capacity-building. Sector-specific gender analyses, including in WASH and education, informed programme adjustments to address barriers faced by girls and women. Gender-transformative approaches generated measurable change among communities. A fathers’ engagement pilot initiative implemented through woman-led and faith-based organizations reached 280 couples and resulted in a 43 per cent–55 per cent increase in fathers’ involvement in childcare, alongside shifts in attitudes towards gender roles. UNICEF engaged 75 national religious and health leaders, resulting in eight formal commitments to address gender barriers in primary health care and the establishment of a national pool of 29 trainers on gender integration in health, who cascaded training to 75 front-line providers. Multisectoral platforms, including the Oky application, reached 3,180 adolescent girls with integrated sexual and reproductive health, menstrual hygiene and life skills content, contributing to improved agency and access to information.

Disability inclusion advanced from ad hoc actions towards a more structured, programmatic approach. UNICEF provided technical support to partners to apply universal accessibility standards in education infrastructure, resulting in the construction or renovation of 336 classrooms with ramps and accessible latrines. UNICEF supported the revision of the National Policy on Persons with Disabilities and contributed to a draft ministerial text on inclusive education. Evidence generation remained central. Three studies in 2025 addressed stigma and discrimination, disability inclusion during the mpox response, and the early detection of disability, informing practical guidance and training modules. UNICEF contributed to an increase in disability integration in project design through capacity-building that reached 304 implementing partner staff, from 11 per cent of projects in 2024 to 66.6 per cent in 2025. Partnerships with an organization of persons with disabilities strengthened inclusive humanitarian response, accessibility audits and communication, including during humanitarian crises. In one of the Congolese refugee sites (Musenyi), UNICEF identified 554 refugee children with disabilities and provided individual assistance to 20 children, while strengthening the capacity of more than 60 humanitarian actors and volunteers and establishing a formally recognized committee of persons with disabilities to improve inclusive governance. In Muyinga Commune, integrated interventions were provided among 41 children with disabilities that enabled 20 children to return to school.

UNICEF positioned children at the centre of national climate action through evidence, advocacy and youth engagement. Children’s rights were explicitly integrated into the Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 and the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, marking a shift from previous frameworks. The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, developed with the Ministry of Environment, established a multisectoral evidence base on climate impacts on children and informed a national dialogue. UNICEF supported the creation of a multisectoral climate committee, enabling inclusive consultations for Burundi’s Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 and participation in the 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30). Youth engagement moved beyond consultation to co-creation whereby young people contributed directly to climate policy processes and global advocacy platforms. UNICEF supported off-grid renewable energy solutions, solar-powered water systems and climate-resilient infrastructure in schools and health facilities, strengthening service continuity and resilience in climate-vulnerable areas.

Partnerships
Of a planned amount of 36,521,249, UNICEF-Burundi mobilized US$54,762,752 in 2025 despite a constrained global funding environment. This reflected strong donor confidence and the effective stewardship of partnerships. Multilateral donors remained the main contributors (Gavi, the Global Partnership for Education, and the World Bank), followed by bilateral partners (Germany, the Republic of Korea, and the Netherlands) and National Committees (Germany, Spain, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom). New contributions were secured from the African Development Bank and the National Reparations Fund (a Democratic of the Congo fund) through the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (for emergency response), the Chinese Embassy (through in-kind education support), the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (United Kingdom) and the World Bank (for the mpox response), and the Republic of Korea (for health and WASH). Three National Committee field visits (Australia, Canada, and Germany), a virtual fund-raising visit with the BASF Foundation, and bilateral visits (the Netherlands and the US Embassy) strengthened accountability and reinforced partner confidence. The results for children have been amplified by producing over 68 human interest stories and more than 30 videos documenting the impact of multisectoral interventions in the mpox response, malnutrition, ECD, adolescent health, education, child protection, inclusion, and WASH. Meanwhile, the Neza Prize that was organized to celebrate World Children’s Day promoted creative expression and youth-led dialogue on child rights.

UNICEF concluded six new partnerships with local and international non-governmental organizations in 2025 (the Province of the Anglican Church of Burundi, RET International, SaCoDé, Save the Children, World Vision and the Youth Initiative for Climate and Development). In addition, 37 programme documents and simplified programme documents were signed with civil society partners, 16 of which supported humanitarian responses, including mpox, cholera and flood emergencies. UNICEF-Burundi continued to strengthen the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse in 2025. Among implementing partners, 95 per cent (40 of 42) demonstrated medium or full capacity; reinforced interagency coordination was established through improved tools, digital mapping and victim-centred protocols, and 86,579 people accessed safe reporting mechanisms.

United Nations Joint Initiatives
Joint programmes continued to serve as key platforms for coordination and collective action among United Nations agencies, contributing to strengthened health, nutrition, WASH and child protection outcomes.

The programme on health systems strengthening, technological innovations for immunization, and the identification of zero-dose children, implemented with the World Health Organization (WHO) under Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, consolidate the gains in immunization. For the first time since 2019, the number of zero-dose children declined in two consecutive years, from 46,983 to 44,499 in 2024–2025.

The joint Unified Budget and Results Accountability Framework Programme on HIV with the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and WHO, along with the Together for Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) initiative, provided sustained platforms for interagency dialogue. Under the One Health approach, thanks to the Pandemic Fund, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), WHO and UNICEF continued to support the national response to epidemic-related emergencies while strengthening the resilience of national systems to shocks. In parallel, through the Together for SRHR initiative, UNICEF and UNFPA jointly conducted a gender-based violence (GBV) safety and disability accessibility audit at Musenyi refugee site, generating actionable recommendations to reduce GBV risks and improve access to services for persons with disabilities.  Joint multisectoral programmes implemented with the World Food Programme and FAO of the United Nations, with the support of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation through the United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MPTF) and from KfW, contributed to improved outcomes in nutrition and resilience. Approximately 470,000 caregivers received counselling on infant and young child feeding practices, and around 200,000 children ages 6–23 months were supplemented with micronutrient powders.

Funding from the Central Emergency Response Fund enabled UNICEF and partners to provide safe drinking water to 19,370 refugees at Musenyi and to construct 134 latrines and 68 gender-segregated disability-friendly showers. In addition, 20,000 refugees received hygiene promotion and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse and GBV awareness, while 2,000 vulnerable households benefited from WASH kits, thereby improving their living conditions, reducing their diarrhœal risks and enhancing their dignity and safety.

The Joint MPTF Programme on Human Rights, funded by the Netherlands and Switzerland, supported the first phase of the roll-out of Burundi’s national child protection case management system, birth registration and issuance of birth certificates among 1,572 refugee children from the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the provision of legal aid to 747 children in contact with the law.

Finally, in 2025, UNICEF reactivated the inter-agency group on a harmonized approach to cash transfers to strengthen assurance and accountability across United Nations partnerships.

[1] In Burundi, a colline is the lowest administrative unit, equivalent to a local community within a zone.
[2] Sphere Association, The Sphere Handbook: Humanitarian Charter and Minimum Standards in Humanitarian Response, 4th ed. Geneva, 2018.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The UNICEF-Burundi programme was implemented in 2025 in an increasingly complex external environment shaped by persistent structural constraints and recurrent shocks. Macroeconomic fragility, high inflation and a continued contraction in external financing restricted public expenditure and reduced household purchasing power, directly affecting UNICEF interventions and, ultimately, the access of children to essential services. Although the national budget increased in nominal terms, real-term social sector allocations stagnated or declined, limiting the Government’s capacity to scale up and sustain interventions. These constraints disproportionately affected children living in poverty, children with disabilities, displaced children and children in remote rural areas, where service gaps are most pronounced.
An operational constraint in 2025 was the persistent and worsening shortage of fuel, which disrupted transportation, field monitoring and supply delivery, particularly in remote areas. This affected both development and emergency activities and reduced the operational capacity of implementing partners. To mitigate these disruptions and ensure the continuity in critical services, UNICEF provided fuel support to selected partners, enabling them to continue essential field activities.

The government administrative reorganization in 2025 created transitional challenges, including risks to the continuity of basic social services because of losses in expertise or movements among personnel. The reform nonetheless also represented an opportunity to strengthen decentralized governance by repositioning territorial authorities as key actors in delivering the SDGs, improving coherence under the 2023–2027 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, and enhancing the effectiveness and sustainability of basic social services through stronger local institutions and financing mechanisms.

The year was marked by overlapping crises, including climate-related hazards, outbreaks of disease, such as mpox and cholera, and a large influx of refugees from eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. These shocks exerted pressure on fragile systems and repeatedly involved the diversion of resources towards emergency response. The response of UNICEF and its partners demonstrated strong operational agility although the frequency of the crises reduced the opportunities to consolidate gains and invest in prevention and resilience.

The year reinforced lessons related to system strengthening and sustainability. Progress in interoperable birth registration, inclusive infrastructure standards, programme-based budgeting, national policy development and other areas demonstrated that upstream engagement is essential to achieving results at scale. A strong shift was realized from fragmented, project-based delivery towards more durable institutional arrangements. However, implementation exposed bottlenecks, including limited national human resource capacity, high staff turnover and weak subnational financing. These constraints underscored that systems change requires long-term investment, realistic timelines and continuous capacity development, particularly at the decentralized level where services are delivered.

Another key lesson: strategic focus matters as much as relevance. While the UNICEF programme remains aligned with national priorities and UNICEF’s global commitments, the results have been uneven across sectors and locations. Experience during the year shows that dispersing limited financial and human resources across too many activities reduces the ability to achieve measurable results. Progress was also more visible whenever implementation was closely monitored. Regular field monitoring, timely data review, and follow-up with partners helped identify bottlenecks early, facilitated adjustments in approaches and improved delivery. This confirms that effective monitoring is not only an accountability tool, but a driver of results.

Gender-focused initiatives led to important lessons. Activities that involved men and boys, alongside women and girls were more effective in changing harmful norms than activities targeting women and girls alone. However, differences in sectoral capacity, limited sex-disaggregated data and funding constraints made expanding these approaches difficult, pointing to the need for clearer responsibility and stronger evidence to inform future choices.

Not all strategies yielded the intended results. Data gaps constrained the ability to provide a comprehensive picture of the deprivations faced by girls and boys. Routine systems, such as education management information systems and District Health Information Software 2, generate valuable administrative data, and recent nutrition surveys, food security analyses and the 2024 census have been accompanied by key updated indicators. However, the absence of recent multitopic household surveys focused on children have reduced the ability of the Government and partners to monitor equity gaps and track progress against SDGs and the Strategic Plan.

UNICEF-Burundi will use these insights to adapt its programme strategy for 2026–2027. It will sharpen its focus on fewer high-impact interventions that address multiple deprivations simultaneously, particularly in high-burden convergence areas. Greater emphasis will be placed on institutionalizing multisectoral convergence through aligned planning, monitoring and budgeting, in close collaboration with decentralized authorities. Shock-responsive social protection and ECD integration will be expanded to protect children more effectively during crises and mitigate long-term developmental risks. UNICEF will also prioritize strengthening data systems, including support for a multitopic household survey. It will intensify partnerships and explore innovative financing mechanisms to offset declining external assistance and support more resilient, nationally owned systems.

The Union of the Comoros, a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) and a Least Developed Country (LDC), is a cluster of four islands in the Indian Ocean: Grande Comore, Moheli, Anjouan and Mayotte, but this last island has remained under French administration since the country’s independence. Forty-five per cent of the estimated 909,529 population in 2025 is poor, and 64 per cent live in rural areas. Children (under the age of 18) account for 43 per cent of the population. As a fragile State, the Comoros is highly vulnerable to shocks, including climate change. The country scored 21 out of 100 (158 out of 180 countries) on the Transparency International 2024 Corruption Perception Index.

In 2025, the Comorian economy grew by an estimated 3.8 per cent, according to the International Monetary Fund. While inflation decreased slightly, consumer prices remained high, undermining living conditions particularly for the most vulnerable, who were also most affected by the continued severe disruptions in electricity and water supply, and by the national waste management crisis resulting in an unsafe land and ocean environment. 

The political situation remained tense throughout the year. The ruling Convention pour le Renouveau des Comores (CRC) secured a strong majority in parliamentary and municipal elections, despite opposition boycotts and concerns over transparency. A Supreme Court-ordered re-run in several constituencies highlighted persistent disputes around electoral integrity. The President’s son, who serves as Secretary General of the Government and oversees the work of the ministries, continued to gain influence in 2025. Civic space remained restricted, with limitations placed on freedom of expression, assembly, and association.

In 2025, Comoros moved into a post epidemic stabilization phase following the major cholera outbreak of 2024, with the Government officially declaring the end of the epidemic on 31 August 2025 after months of strengthened surveillance and no new detected cases. The country also faced the lingering impact of Cyclone Chido, which struck Anjouan and Moheli islands in December 2024. The storm affected over 64,000 people, the majority in Anjouan. Several hundred people were temporarily displaced due to lost or damaged houses. Twenty-two schools sustained damage, disrupting education services in affected localities. Around 45% of crops were affected in impacted areas.

Humanitarian needs were compounded by an increase in the arrivals of migrants, including women and children, primarily linked to onward movement toward Mayotte. While there are no official figures, national media quoting government sources reported 400 migrants arriving on Comorian shores in 2025, including a significant share of women and children under 18, mainly from the Great Lakes region. Migrants reaching Comoros often arrived in highly vulnerable conditions. In the absence of an adequate national protection framework, new arrivals were frequently exposed to arrest, detention, and very limited access to basic services, with children and women facing heightened protection risks. Although communities in villages where migrants arrived generally responded with compassion, the ongoing arrival of migrants also prompted some adverse responses, with concerns primarily focused on potential public health risks.

Within UNICEF, 2025 brought significant internal restructuring as the organization adapted to a rapidly tightening global funding landscape for development, pushing the organization to consolidate resources and shift toward more cost efficient operating models. This included the rollout of the Future Focus Initiative 2025, which encouraged structural streamlining and financial optimization, and led to the decision to merge several country offices into Multi Country Offices, including the transition toward a joint Madagascar–Comoros Multi-Country Office, intended to minimize costs, enhance operational efficiency, and safeguard programme delivery in an increasingly resource constrained environment.

In 2025, UNICEF Comoros contributed to progress across health, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education, child protection, and social protection. The year saw strengthened national systems, empowered communities, expanded digital infrastructure, and growing integration of climate resilience programming across sectors — all essential elements for delivering equitable and sustainable results for children. UNICEF’s work supported the national development agenda and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), particularly its focus on equitable access to quality services, resilience building, and the advancement of child rights. 
  
Results were enabled by  robust partnerships with government institutions, civil society  organizations, communities, children, adolescents and youth, and  international partners. UNICEF Comoros would like to thank the Korean Agency  for International Cooperation (KOICA), France, ECHO, and Gavi for their  financial support, and to express its appreciation to all donors who provide  flexible funds to UNICEF, enabling response to the most pressing situations.
  
1. Child-Centered Planning, Policy and Advocacy
  
In 2025, UNICEF made  significant headway in raising awareness on the impact of climate change on  children. It supported national authorities in advancing child-sensitive  climate policies and embedding adolescent participation into national  planning processes.
  
Integrating Children’s Needs into National Climate Policies 
Throughout the year, UNICEF  raised awareness on the impact of climate change on children in the Comoros, building  national consensus on the need for child-centered adaptation. In early 2025,  the national validation of the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC)  in Comoros – a key evidence piece developed in collaboration with the  Ministry of Environment – was a turning point, bringing a newfound awareness  among decision-makers in all sectors of the disproportionate impact of  climate change on children. The national momentum to develop and test  adaptation solutions was then sustained with multisectoral climate action  programmes, one funded by KOICA and focused on development, and another  relying on UNICEF internal resources focused on disaster risk reduction. 
  
In a major policy  achievement, the Updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0)  explicitly integrated children’s needs in health and education as national  climate adaptation priorities. This integration of children's needs into  national adaptation priorities demonstrates a clear recognition that the  impacts of climate change affect children disproportionately and require more  tailored and specific measures. The revision process, led by the Ministry of  Environment and supported by UNDP, UNICEF, and other partners, included  consultations with adolescents. 
  
UNICEF also facilitated the  participation of officials from the Ministries of Environment, Education, and  Health to attend the COP in 2025, marking the first time these ministries  were jointly represented at the global climate summit. This support aimed to  strengthen national engagement in climate diplomacy and ensure that  children’s rights and climate priorities were integrated into Comoros’  official positions and high-level discussions.
  
The year closed with another significant advocacy  event to promote the integration of children’s needs and rights into climate  policies and programmes: a scientific conference organized with the Ministry  of Environment, the University of Comoros, and a youth-led organization,  Réseau Climat Océan India (RCOI). This initiative engaged 4 ministries and  nominated 15 climate champions from the government, civil society, and youth  organizations as active advocates. The event was also paired with the Local  Conference of Youth, which mobilized 324 youth from the 3 islands. These  combined events further strengthened the multisectoral momentum needed to  protect children from the growing impacts of climate change.
  
Amplifying Adolescents’ Voices in National Planning
In preparation for key planning processes, including the Government’s Emerging Comoros Acceleration Plan, the 2027–2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and the 2027-2030 UNICEF Country Programme, UNICEF partnered with the Comorian Red Crescent to conduct a large-scale consultation with 800 adolescents aged 10–19 across the 3 islands, combining an individual Kobo questionnaire with group discussions. These insights shaped the strategic directions of the new UNICEF country programme, ensuring alignment with the priorities of young people – including access and quality of education and health services, protection needs and a desire for greater participation of children and adolescents in decision-making processes that affect their lives.
  
2. Health, Nutrition and WASH
  
In 2025, UNICEF Comoros  supported national and local authorities to advance children’s access to  essential health and WASH services, strengthen epidemic preparedness, and  consolidate the country’s resilience to climate-sensitive diseases. 
  
Strengthening Immunization and Primary Health Services
UNICEF provided sustained  technical and financial support to the Ministry of Health to boost routine  immunization coverage, contributing to an increase in the uptake of the  pentavalent vaccine (first dose), which rose from 51% in January to 65% in  December 2025. Among vaccinated children, 51% were boys and 49% girls,  illustrating equitable access. UNICEF provided comprehensive expert support  in cold chain logistics, social and behavior change, and strengthening the  national immunization system. Coordinated advocacy between UNICEF, WHO and  Gavi resulted in greater prioritization of immunization within the Ministry  of Health, and in timely payment of the Government’s vaccine procurement bill,  ensuring timely availability of vaccines in the country.
  
No vaccine stockouts  occurred throughout the year, and with combined support from Mastercard  Foundation / Africa CDC, the World Bank and UNICEF, coverage of functional  cold chain equipment increased from 65% in January to 75% by December 2025,  with 80% of equipment under 5 years old. Challenges however remain in the  absence of a national maintenance system—an area where UNICEF is working with  the Ministry of Health to advocate for systemic and financial solutions.
  
A strong emphasis was  placed on evidence-based strategies, including a behavioral insights research  that assessed the effectiveness of phone-based reminders on immunization for  parents through a randomized controlled trial. Another research was conducted  to explore gender-related barriers in immunization uptake. These will equip  the Ministry of Health with actionable insights to further increase routine immunization  coverage, which is still below the 80% target.
  
UNICEF also contributed to a  successful vaccination campaign that achieved 98% coverage nationally and vaccinated  98,144 children aged 9–59 months against measles and rubella. The campaign  also integrated Big Catch Up activities, resulting in 494 zero-dose children  receiving the pentavalent vaccine. This success was largely driven by  community mobilization efforts, including local leaders, religious authorities,  teachers, and community health workers. Frontline workers were paid with  mobile money, an important innovation improving transparency. 
  
However, a second national  campaign, introducing the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine to protect girls  against cervical cancer, achieved unequal results across islands, with 47% in  Anjouan, 38% in Moheli and 5% in Grande Comore. The causes are linked to operational  constraints within the Ministry of Health, which allowed only for a short period  of communication activities prior to the campaign, and to massive disinformation,  fueled by the diaspora. These are lessons learnt for future introduction of  vaccines.
  
Reinforcing Disease Surveillance and Community Health Systems
In support of the  implementation of the national community health strategy, UNICEF helped the  Ministry of Health to develop a community-based surveillance system covering  climate-sensitive and epidemic-prone diseases. A total of 219 community  health workers were trained and equipped with tools to detect diarrheal  diseases, malaria and malnutrition, contributing to national epidemiological  surveillance and feeding data into the national health information management  system (DHIS2). Climate-related factors are also recorded, helping grow the  evidence base for climate-sensitive surveillance. This community-level  intelligence has increased the country’s capacity to anticipate and respond  to potential outbreaks, and the system can be adjusted to include additional  diseases as needed, depending on the country’s epidemiological situation. 
  
These efforts were also complemented  by a focus on reinforcing the quality of care at primary health level, with  the development of a new Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood  Illness (IMNCI) guide.
  
Consolidating Cholera Elimination
Further to an intense  cholera epidemic in 2024, UNICEF continued to collaborate with the Ministry  of Health and the Comorian Red Crescent in early 2025 to sustain community engagement  and surveillance, maintain rapid response capacity in case of new cases, and build capacity at community level on proper chlorine  dilution and water tank decontamination. UNICEF also supported the Regional Water  Directorates in Anjouan and Moheli to chlorinate 78 water networks (70 in  Anjouan and 8 in Moheli), reaching 86,117 beneficiaries. 
  
Following the official  declaration of the end of the cholera epidemic on 31 August 2025, UNICEF  worked closely with national authorities to transition into a consolidation  phase. UNICEF pre-positioned infection prevention and control (IPC) supplies and  Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD) kits in hospitals on the 3 islands, enabling  rapid treatment of up to 2,100 people in the event of a cholera resurgence. UNICEF also continued to  support the Government to strengthen risk communication and community  engagement, through provision of equipment and capacity building for 10  community radio stations, and capacity building of personnel of the national  health hotline to collect and address community feedback.
  
Improving Access to Climate-Resilient Safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene
UNICEF expanded access to  climate-resilient water systems and improved sanitation practices. In Kowe,  Anjouan island — an area acutely affected by climate-driven water shortages— UNICEF  partnered with the Regional Water Directorate to rehabilitate and extend the  water supply system, ensuring that 2,103 residents (1,072 women and 1,031  men) now have reliable access to water. Community engagement played a vital  role, with community members, particularly women, contributing labour for the  rehabilitation work. In addition to infrastructure improvements, the  intervention included hands-on training sessions for residents on source  protection techniques, such as maintaining water collection points,  monitoring water quality, and implementing measures to prevent contamination.  Additionally, 9,000 community members (4,590 women and 4,410 men) from Kowe, Mremani,  and Mrijou in Anjouan were sensitized on hygienic latrine use and sanitation  practices.
  
While progress is  encouraging, long-term sustainability challenges persist, including the cost  recovery model for water system management and the need to maintain community  engagement on source protection. UNICEF will continue to work with local  authorities to strengthen these systems.

3. Education
  
In 2025, UNICEF’s work in  education focused on modernizing governance systems, integrating climate  resilience in learning environments, and advancing inclusive and emergency-ready  education. These results were achieved in close collaboration with the  Ministry of National Education, the National Agency for Digital Development  (ANADEN), school personnel, and parent-teacher associations across the three  islands.
  
Digital Transformation of the Education System
A major milestone was the digital modernization of the education sector, achieving national-scale transformation. A tripartite partnership between UNICEF, the Ministry of Education and ANADEN resulted in the following achievements:

Digitalization of school textbooks through e-Shiyo, enabling open access to pedagogical       resources for students, parents and teachers. This is crucial since school textbooks stay at school.   
Deployment of e-Msomo, an integrated digital education management system, enhancing       administrative efficiency, transparency and data-driven planning, and applying to all public and private schools across the country. There is strong ownership from the Ministry of Education, which considers this an important education governance tool.   
Training of 2,465 users (administrative staff and teachers) on e-Msomo, ensuring gradual uptake.    
While these platforms are still evolving, and further efforts are needed to familiarize both school personnel and parents with these digital tools, this modernization has laid the groundwork for long-term systemic strengthening. It has also built a new appetite for exploring how digital solutions can further serve the education system.
  
Integrating Climate Change  into Education
UNICEF contributed to building capacity of the Ministry of Education on analyzing the impact of climate change on the education system and developing climate adaptation solutions.  To expand climate education and strengthen eco-responsible learning environments, a total of 21,309 students (10,471 girls and 10,838 boys) from 115 schools were sensitized with UNICEF support on climate change and environmental protection. The next steps will be for students to carry out  green actions to improve their school environment. To improve the resilience and connectivity of educational infrastructure, UNICEF initiated solar energy installations and provision of ICT equipment in 11 schools on the 3 islands. Thus equipped, these schools will be better able to apply the climate curriculum to be developed in 2026.
  
Advancing Inclusive  Education
UNICEF continued supporting the Ministry of Education to advance inclusive education through strengthened early identification of children with disabilities and special learning needs:
     

A disability detection campaign reached 799 children out of 1,141 children with disabilities identified in schools nationally. The initiative aimed to detect physical, sensory, and cognitive disabilities early, provide specialized consultations to children, and guide families toward appropriate services.    
Pre-primary and primary teachers from public schools across the country were trained to identify and support children with disabilities, and were provided with a printed screening guide as a reference document.    
This marks an important shift toward early intervention and the integration of inclusive practices at school level.
  
Preparedness and Response  to Emergencies
Following the impact of cyclone Chido, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education with a situation assessment, distributed school kits to 8,818 children, including 4,332 girls, on the islands of Anjouan and Moheli, and initiated the rehabilitation of 2 schools with 325  students, including 156 girls, in Anjouan. 
  
UNICEF also partnered with the Ministry of Interior’s General Directorate for Civil  Security (DGSC) for climate-resilient disaster risk reduction. This included  reviewing early warning messages and adapting them to children’s needs,  building capacity of community leaders, and conducting awareness sessions in schools across the 3 islands, reaching over 10,000 students with information  on cyclones, behaviour in case of emergency, and first aid. 
  
4. Child Protection and Social  Protection
  
In 2025, UNICEF continued  its support to modernize the civil registration system, to ensure that every  child in Comoros is visible, protected, and able to access essential services,  and improve the reliability of population data and strengthen national  planning. Considerable efforts were also directed toward enhancing State services to address violence against children and women, as well as reinforcing community protection mechanisms to more effectively respond to  climate-related protection risks. 
  
Modernizing Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS)
In partnership with the Ministry of Interior and the French Embassy, UNICEF continued its support to the modernization of civil registration. This reform stems from the government’s recognition that the existing system suffers from fragmentation, inconsistency, and insecurity of records, and requires a profound institutional overhaul. Major advancements include:
     

Drafting of the decree establishing the National Civil Registration Agency (ANEC), a public administrative agency established by the civil registration law of 2023 to modernize and oversee the entire civil registration system in the Union of the Comoros.   
Development of new civil registration forms aligned with the 2023 law and with international standards.   
Completion of the national mapping of civil registration centres, a critical step toward digitalization.    
The first national celebration of the African Civil Registration Day also helped raise awareness among institutions and communities of the 2023 law and the important changes  underway to modernize civil registration and vital statistics. 
  
Strengthening the Response to Violence Against Children and Women
In close collaboration with UNFPA and the French Red Cross, UNICEF continued to support the Ministry of Gender Promotion, Solidarity and Information’s care services for victims of  violence. Coordination among the three partners helped maintain continuity of services and strengthen quality, with particular attention to the pilot care centres that have opened in recent years and remain fragile. UNICEF also rehabilitated the Fomboni care centre in Moheli, after damage from cyclone Chido. The country’s 10 care centres assisted 779 victims including 470 children (the majority adolescent girls) with holistic care, including medical, psychosocial and legal support, in 2025.
  
Acknowledging the significant financial burden that medical care imposes on victims and their families, as care centres only cover a subset of medical acts, UNICEF supported the Regional Directorates in charge of child protection to partner with two public hospitals:
     

In Moheli, the cost of medical consultations for victims was reduced from KMF 7,500 (USD 18) to KMF 2,000 (USD 5).   
The Hombo hospital in Anjouan adopted a dedicated package for survivors of       violence.    
Another important achievement was the training of 90 temporary foster families, who were prepared to host children in need of immediate protection. This is the first time Comoros has established such a structured mechanism, reducing the return of victims to unsafe environment and improving the quality of emergency care services. 
  
UNICEF also continued to support the Ministry of Justice’s General Delegation for Human Rights to produce a national bulletin with reliable, disaggregated data on reported cases of violence, helping national authorities monitor trends and supporting informed policy decisions.
  
Mobilizing Communities for Climate Resilient Child Protection
Recognizing that climate resilience and child protection are deeply interconnected, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Gender Promotion, Solidarity and Information to build local capacity on protection risks linked with climate shocks. 
  
With support from UNICEF headquarters, UNICEF Comoros developed a training module that was contextualized to Comoros with involvement from several ministries, including the Ministry of Gender Promotion, Solidarity and Information and the Ministry of Environment. The training was offered to 960 members from 48 adolescent clubs. These clubs, established in recent years as part of a KOICA-funded child protection programme, had previously been trained on children’s rights and prevention and response to violence. Further to the trainings offered in 2025 on the links between climate change and child protection, adolescent clubs developed their climate action plan. 
  
The training was also offered to adult child  protection actors (mayors, village chiefs, police, CSOs...) in Anjouan and Moheli, to ensure that a network of community actors is in place, and is able to respond to child protection risks in the context of climate change,  providing improved protection to 13,844 children in 16 localities in Anjouan and Moheli.
  
Strengthening Shock-Responsive Social Protection
UNICEF Comoros, in collaboration with Ministry of Gender Promotion, Solidarity and Information, developed in 2025 a climate-focused cash transfer programme. Designed to strengthen the  resilience of households exposed to climate shocks, the programme provides  direct monetary support to 1,643 vulnerable families in seven  localities across Moheli and Anjouan. After extensive assessments to identify  the most vulnerable households, the Solidarity Directorate trained village committees on climate change, and households organized into groups to invest  in climate-smart income-generating activities. The intervention, designed to  help households reduce negative coping mechanisms, also supports climate adaptation  efforts in other sectors, for instance nutrition and WASH.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF's climate action efforts in 2025 offered valuable insights. A major takeaway was the value of a multisectoral approach, which helped build national momentum for child-focused climate adaptation. Every programme section within UNICEF Comoros took part in climate-resilient development and disaster risk reduction initiatives, and subsequently engaged their respective government ministries in collaborative planning. Some activities brought together several sectors, while others involved in-depth collaboration with a single ministry to co-design solutions. Although this approach was slow, it fostered strong government ownership. This strategy also encouraged greater cooperation among ministries at both national and island levels; for example, multiple ministries and regional directorates collaborated to create climate training modules and train adolescent clubs, and participation in COP strengthened connections between the Ministries of Environment, Health, and Education.

Within UNICEF, efforts focused on integrating climate initiatives across sectors and focusing interventions geographically to maximize impact and reduce fragmentation. Although eliminating silos and agreeing on shared locations took time and effort, it resulted in greater impact and efficiency. One example is the integrated community-surveillance carried out by community health workers, which covers both health and nutrition. The social protection programme provides another illustration, as it connects closely with nutrition and WASH. The income-generating activities that households have chosen include planting fruit trees for both income and protection of water sources, as well as agreements to sell fruits and vegetables directly to their community, rather than to intermediaries who then sell at the market, to facilitate access to cheaper food and ensure better nutrition. 

This successful experience with programmatic and geographic integration can serve as a model for UNICEF Comoros to further integrate its programmes, both within and across sectors—an approach that is becoming increasingly essential in today’s global financial landscape, where development funding is under significant pressure. For example, the health sector in Comoros is expected to receive drastically reduced funding in the coming years, making it even more important for UNICEF and partners to advocate for and implement integrated approaches. By doing so, it will be possible to maximize impact and achieve greater results with fewer resources, ensuring that critical services for children and communities remain effective and sustainable despite financial constraints.

Another lesson is linked to a key challenge that affects all sectors, namely the country’s limited governance and weak budget processes. The nutrition budget line that was added to the 2025 State budget after sustained UNICEF’s advocacy provides an illustration of the challenge: despite being planned, these funds went unspent, with negative consequences for children as nutrition supplies were not available. While this challenge is deep-seated and complex to tackle, digitalization can provide a politically-attractive way forward to strengthen governance. The e-Msomo platform, in the education sector, is a case in point. The Ministry of Education has shown strong ownership, and is actively using this tool for sector steering and accountability. The work underway to progress toward digitalization of civil registration and vital statistics, while a much larger and costlier undertaking that requires a long-term approach, also holds a transformational potential.

Additionally, a key lesson from the past year is that the resilience and strength of communities in Comoros are fundamental to the success and sustainability of UNICEF programmes in all social sectors. With limited fiscal space, recurrent delays in payment of civil servants, and reliance of many public services on unpaid volunteers hoping to integrate civil service, the Government is unlikely, in the short term, to increase its support to children. To fill the gap, it is necessary to increase community awareness and engagement, for community actors to direct more attention and funds toward improving the well-being of children. This grassroots strength underscores the importance for UNICEF of continuing to invest in SBC strategies to nurture local leadership, encourage collective action, and achieve lasting positive change for children and families.

Finally, insights can be derived from the 2025 experience of bringing together UNICEF Comoros and UNICEF Madagascar into a single UNICEF office. A participatory reflection process including the two offices helped identify critical vision elements: each country will retain a country programme document (CPD) tailored to its unique contexts; each location will retain strong presential UNICEF leadership; the Representative, based in Madagascar with regular travel to Comoros, will provide unified leadership and direction; and strong collaboration is expected between programme and operations teams in the two locations to ensure greater efficiency and cross-learning. In 2026, there will be opportunities to start and test ways for both offices to plan together and work collaboratively, making use of each other's strengths and experiences. This approach will help ensure that the new office can deliver greater impact, drive efficiency, and strengthen resilience for children and communities in Comoros and Madagascar.

Eritrea has an estimated population of 3.6 million [1], characterised by a predominantly rural and youthful demographic profile. Approximately 70 per cent of the population resides in rural areas and around 45 per cent are under the age of 18 [2], while nearly half of all households are headed by women [3]. The country’s development trajectory emphasises self-reliance, national ownership, and social cohesion, underpinned by strong social capital and community engagement [4]. Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth is projected to stabilise at 2.9 per cent in 2024 and increase to 3.1 per cent in 2025, while inflation declined from 4.1 per cent to 3.9 per cent over the same period [5]. Continued reliance on mining and rain-fed agriculture exposes the economy to global market volatility and climate variability [6].

Eritrea has sustained progress in child survival, with the under-five mortality rate declining from 36.6 per 1,000 live births in 2022 to 35.4 in 2023 [7]. Gains are associated with universal access to primary health care, strong immunisation coverage, and community-based health services [8]. Malnutrition, however, remains a persistent concern, particularly in drought-affected areas where stunting and acute malnutrition continue to affect children [9]. Sustained investment in maternal and child health, nutrition, and equitable service delivery remains critical to consolidating progress and reducing disparities.

Eritrea’s strategic location along the Red Sea and its policy orientation toward self-reliance continue to shape the external operating environment. Regional dynamics across the Horn of Africa—including conflict-related displacement and cross-border health risks—have implications for national systems. Cross-border movements linked to the Sudan crisis continued during 2025, placing additional demands on basic services in vulnerable host communities. Eritrea continues to engage in regional and international cooperation platforms, including the Africa–EU Ministerial Conference, and has advanced investments in renewable energy and infrastructure, including a solar energy partnership with the African Development Bank [18]. These dynamics shape the operating context for advancing child rights and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) progress, with continued emphasis on equity, resilience, and leaving no child behind.

The country’s geographic and climatic context presents significant risks for children. Eritrea ranks 31st out of 163 countries on UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index [10], reflecting high exposure to climate-related hazards. With more than 70 per cent of the population dependent on agriculture [11], climate variability continues to affect livelihoods, food security, and nutrition outcomes. Recurrent droughts and land degradation have heightened vulnerability among children and women, particularly in the Northern and Southern Red Sea and Anseba regions [12]. Water scarcity remains a concern, with 95.6 per cent of children exposed to high or extremely high water risk vulnerability in 2023 [13], and as of 2016 (latest available JMP year for Eritrea), 52 per cent of the total population use at least basic drinking-water services [14]. Government investments in solar-powered water systems and sanitation infrastructure have supported progress in access, though gaps remain in safely managed sanitation and climate-resilient service provision [15].

In education, Eritrea continued to record incremental progress toward equitable access and retention in 2025. Administrative data indicate improvements in pre-primary participation, reductions in out-of-school children at primary and lower-secondary levels, and a Grade 5 survival rate of 86.6 per cent [16]. Foundational learning outcomes remain a priority challenge. Results from the Monitoring Learning Achievement assessment indicate that 59.9 per cent of Grade 5 learners achieved minimum mastery in mother tongue, English, and mathematics [17], underscoring persistent quality gaps requiring sustained system-level responses.

Progress was also recorded in child protection. In 2025, three additional sub-zobas (administrative sub-regions) issued public declarations of abandonment of female genital mutilation (FGM), in accordance with Government protocol, bringing the total number of declaring sub-zobas to 17 of 67 nationwide. These developments reflect ongoing community engagement and prevention efforts, while underscoring the need for continued measures to strengthen protection for girls.

At the 98th session of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in January 2025, CRC experts acknowledged ongoing efforts to establish a Child and Social Protection Information Management System (CSPIMS). In its March 2025 concluding observations, the Committee encouraged accelerated operationalisation of CSPIMS and the Education Management Information System, reinforcing the importance of evidence-based planning and integrated service delivery for children.

In 2025, Eritrea sustained progress across several child-related outcomes, including continued gains in child survival, administrative improvements in education participation and retention, and additional sub-zobas issuing public declarations of abandonment of female genital mutilation. At the same time, climate risks and water scarcity remained significant structural challenges affecting children and communities.

These dynamics underscore the importance of sustained focus on equity-oriented, climate-resilient service delivery, alongside continued strengthening of national systems to sustain essential services for children and communities, particularly in hard-to-reach areas and in contexts facing environmental and mobility-related pressures.
