In 2025, under Government leadership, essential services and protective systems for children and caregivers were strengthened through reinforced delivery platforms and national systems. Across health and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education, child protection and social protection, the focus remained on equity for hard-to-reach communities while advancing policies, data systems and coordination mechanisms that sustain gains and enable scale. UNICEF contributed targeted technical assistance, supplies, delivery support and systems strengthening to reinforce birth-dose results and support more reliable and equitable service delivery over time.

Health and Nutrition
The national strategy and UNICEF priorities converged around Primary Health Care (PHC) as the backbone of equitable services. The Health Sector Strategic Development Plan anchored delivery within a three-tier system, clarifying entitlements through the Essential Health Care Package (EHCP) and strengthening referral pathways toward universal coverage. Within this approach, community-based health services remained a priority for reaching remote and hard-to-reach communities, including through barefoot doctors—community-selected and trained frontline health workers deployed to extend essential primary health services in underserved areas. UNICEF supported this Government-led platform by strengthening frontline capacity (training new and in-service providers), backing mobile clinics and outreach to extend last-mile access, and supporting readiness for maternal and newborn care, including installation of a solar-powered oxygen plant at Mendefera Referral Hospital. 

Eritrea sustained strong routine immunization performance, with 95 per cent of surviving infants receiving three doses of a DTP-containing vaccine (DTP3) before their first birthday [19]. UNICEF supported delivery and equity-focused outreach—through fixed, outreach and mobile strategies—to identify and vaccinate zero-dose and under-immunised children in hard-to-reach and border areas. UNICEF-supported 1.4 million vaccine doses enabled immunisation of more than 160,000 infants and 44,500 adolescent girls. The Hepatitis B birth dose was introduced, following UNICEF advocacy, strengthening protection for newborns during the critical first days of life. 

System strengthening helped sustain these service results. Cold-chain resilience improved through nationwide inventory, deployment of solar-powered refrigeration in priority facilities and strengthened temperature monitoring, contributing to uninterrupted vaccine availability and improved service reliability. UNICEF supported these improvements and provided strategic technical assistance to support planning for the transition to the hexavalent vaccine, which is expected to improve efficiency, reduce drop-outs and further expand coverage. The Effective Vaccine Management assessment recorded an overall score of 80 per cent, up from 77 per cent in 2021, reaching the WHO benchmark for well-functioning systems and reflecting year-on-year improvement in supply chain performance. 

Under Ministry of Health leadership, 180,143 children under five received quality case management using the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) protocol (60 per cent of an annual target of 300,000). During the year, 302,459 children received vitamin A supplementation, 275,269 were screened for malnutrition, and 41,299 children with acute malnutrition were treated. Government decisions advanced the transition from iron–folic acid to multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant women and prepared for introduction of the Hepatitis B birth dose. UNICEF supported these shifts through technical inputs and supplies, including procurement of 80,000 doses and a training-of-trainers package. With Government leadership and Gavi financing, the Digital Health Policy and the Health ICT Strategic Plan (2026–2030) were developed, with UNICEF contributing technical inputs and coordination through the Digital Health Technical Working Group. An EriTel partnership supported SMS RapidPro pilots designed for interoperability with the Health Management Information System (HMIS) and District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2). 

Within Government priorities to strengthen sustainable nutrition, UNICEF shifted from short-term supplementation to a systems-strengthening model that delivers sustainable nutrition results by investing in local food systems. Using UNICEF Regular Resources as catalytic financing, UNICEF initiated local production of 483 poultry units for the One Child, One Egg a Day programme (launching in 2026), targeting female-headed households with children under five in four prioritised zobas (Anseba, Gash-Barka, Northern Red Sea and Southern Red Sea), and finalised the equipment list for small-scale fish powder production to enrich complementary foods. The rollout of 483 small-scale poultry units is expected to directly benefit 483 households (2,415 people), while establishing scalable, locally owned solutions that can attract additional partner financing beyond Regular Resources. Implementation is designed with relevant line ministries, local authorities and community structures, with support from UN partners working on food systems and nutrition. 

WASH and Climate Resilience
In 2025, Government-led efforts strengthened climate-resilient WASH services in drought-prone communities through a combination of service delivery improvements and community engagement. With Government entities and communities implementing services and partners supporting infrastructure and behaviour change activities, 62,160 people gained access to basic drinking water and 47,360 people gained access to basic sanitation. Seventeen villages in Adi Quala, Areza, Mendefera and Segeneiti were declared open-defecation-free (ODF), with post-ODF follow-up activities—including latrine rebuilding—implemented to prevent slippage. Community dialogues in more than 761 villages reached more than 300,000 people, reinforcing sustained latrine use and handwashing practices. 

These results were enabled by strengthened systems, safeguards and climate finance that support sustainability and scale. UNICEF supported integration of environmental health indicators into the District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2) and supported Environmental and Social Impact Assessments (ESIAs) across all six regions, with findings publicly available at zoba level and online, strengthening transparency and risk-informed planning. Under the African Development Bank (AfDB) Climate Action Window, with contributions from AfDB, UNICEF and the Government, a multi-year programme of approximately USD 15 million was secured, designed to benefit around 300,000 people by strengthening climate resilience in water security—an essential foundation for children’s survival and well-being. UNICEF also supported cross-country learning with Malawi and provided technical inputs to mainstream ESIA within WASH programming, while stakeholders initiated formal WASH sector coordination and drafted terms of reference as an initial step toward more coordinated delivery. 

Education and Learning
With the Government of Eritrea leading implementation of the Education Sector Plan and partners supporting sector reforms, Eritrea recorded incremental gains in education access and learning conditions. Pre-primary enrolment increased from 22.8 to 24.6 per cent, out-of-school rates declined at both primary and lower-secondary levels, and the Grade 5 survival rate rose to 86.6 per cent, exceeding the annual target and signalling stronger progression in the early grades. Together, these gains strengthened early learning readiness and supported more consistent progression through the primary cycle, with a focus on underserved areas. UNICEF supported this Government-led progress through technical assistance, targeted support to reduce exclusion and partnerships that strengthened planning and implementation in underserved areas. 

The Government committed to expand early learning by establishing pre-primary classrooms in 2,600 rural communities and training and deploying 4,624 pre-primary teachers, a scale of ambition designed to accelerate enrolment and reduce disparities. Through combined efforts, 24,210 children accessed Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) services, supported by expanded learning spaces and inputs, including construction of 61 ECCE classrooms and furnishing of 100 classrooms with play-based materials. UNICEF enabled this Government-led expansion through technical and logistical support, including development of training materials used in the national teacher-training programme, helping ensure the planned scale-up is supported by standardised, quality-assured preparation for teachers. 

To strengthen foundational learning and reduce exclusion, UNICEF supported targeted interventions for children most at risk of being left behind. UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Education and the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to support enrolment of out-of-school children through Complementary Elementary Education, provide cash incentives to support girls’ education, distribute teaching and learning materials across nine instructional languages, and train 450 teachers in remedial instruction using Teaching at the Right Level—reaching more than 63,000 children, with an emphasis on underserved and nomadic communities. In parallel, UNICEF supported systems strengthening and digital transformation, including construction of 194 classrooms with WASH facilities in 57 schools and the development of a new Education Management Information System (EMIS), enabling faster release of gender- and location-disaggregated 2023/24 education statistics—strengthening the evidence base for planning and equity monitoring. UNICEF also helped leverage financing for girls’ education through the Global Partnership for Education Girls’ Education Accelerator, which secured USD 5.91 million to address persistently low completion rates among girls in marginalised regions. This complements USD 14 million approved in 2024 from the same partner under the System Transformation Grant and System Capacity Grant.

Child Protection
With Government leadership and community partners driving prevention efforts, Eritrea strengthened action to end female genital mutilation (FGM) and child marriage in 2025. Across 328 villages, communities reached girls and families with prevention messaging, contributing to safer environments for girls and stronger public momentum to abandon harmful practices. In parallel, three sub-zones publicly declared abandonment of FGM, signalling growing community ownership and accountability for protecting girls from violence, exploitation and abuse. UNICEF supported these efforts through technical assistance and partnership support that helped expand community-based prevention approaches and sustain engagement with local leadership and structures. 

Evidence strengthened the targeting and accountability of prevention efforts. A community mapping exercise conducted across 11 sub-zobas and 328 villages provided more localised insight into harmful practices and helped sharpen prevention strategies. Within mapped communities, reported prevalence among girls under 15 was around 3.72 per cent, while prevalence among girls under five was around 1.38 per cent. Importantly, 63.4 per cent of surveyed villages reported zero cases among girls under 15, and 85.3 per cent of villages with girls under five reported no cases. These findings reflect conditions within mapped areas rather than national prevalence, but they supported more risk-informed prioritisation and follow-up through community systems. Building on this, prevention outreach expanded markedly in 2025: approximately 146,852 children were reached through community-based prevention efforts, up from 38,900 in 2024, with girls under 15 comprising the large majority of those reached. UNICEF supported this shift through data-informed planning and structured community engagement and behaviour change approaches, including facilitation support, mentoring and ongoing advocacy to keep prevention messages consistent, locally relevant and sustained over time. 

Prevention gains were reinforced by stronger protection pathways through schools, campaigns and case management. With education actors and communities increasingly recognising schooling as a practical layer of protection, 9,886 children were supported to enrol in school in 2025. Government and partners amplified prevention messages at scale: national and community-level campaigns to end FGM and child marriage reached 260,645 girls under 15 in 2025, exceeding the annual target. To strengthen response when a child is at risk, 160 professionals were trained in child protection case management tools and supported to apply them in the field, contributing to stronger referral pathways and more consistent follow-up. UNICEF also supported initial assessments of information and communication technology capacity and workforce readiness, informing a roadmap for strengthening national child protection information management systems so that cases can be better tracked, services coordinated and data more reliably used for decision-making over time. Together, these measures strengthened prevention while improving the consistency and accountability of response when a child is at risk. 

Social Protection
With Government leadership and partners supporting delivery, Eritrea strengthened social policy and social protection in 2025 by combining policy progress with expanded services for vulnerable children and families. The Government delivered monthly cash transfers to approximately 250,000 people, including nearly 100,000 children, helping households meet basic needs and maintain access to essential services such as health, nutrition and education. UNICEF-supported community programmes provided direct assistance to 39,200 vulnerable children—98 per cent of the annual target—through a practical package of support that included income-generation assistance, school materials, psychosocial care and strengthened referral pathways. 

Disability inclusion advanced through the Community-Based Inclusive Development (CBID) approach: the number of trained community-level rehabilitation volunteers rose to 7,245—almost double the previous year’s figure—and 8,900 children with disabilities accessed assistive devices, rehabilitation services or referral pathways; in remote areas, 196 children received mobility aids, including donkeys, to improve access to school and essential services. Social and behaviour change initiatives reached more than 40,000 community members to reduce stigma and improve the safety and acceptability of services for children with disabilities. 

These service results were underpinned by strengthened policy and system foundations. Ratification of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities reinforced national commitment to disability inclusion and strengthened protections against violence, exploitation and neglect. In parallel, Eritrea advanced the foundations for more coherent and better targeted support by developing integrated information systems and beginning work towards a unified social registry—key building blocks for more coordinated planning and service delivery over time. UNICEF supported scale and quality through systems strengthening and workforce development, including training of 288 social workers and more than 3,000 allied professionals, alongside technical support to strengthen coordination and targeting. While 2025 showed clear gains, constraints continued to shape results, including limited disaggregated data affecting the precision of targeting and monitoring, geographic barriers for children with disabilities and heavy caseloads that affect follow-up; continued investment in institutional capacity—especially at community and frontline levels—alongside strengthened information systems will be important to sustain improvements in equitable access, resilience and protection for vulnerable children and families. 

Cross-sectoral Systems, Data, Climate, SBC and Coordination
System improvements strengthened linkages between policy, data and service delivery. Fieldwork for the Eritrea Population and Health Survey (EPHS) 2025 was completed with UN partner support, including UNICEF, and report drafting is underway. Environmental health indicators were integrated into DHIS2; CSPIMS advanced following Government endorsement and training; ESIA findings were publicly disclosed; and EMIS releases became more timely and disaggregated. UNICEF’s contribution focused on diagnostics, policy advice, supply and infrastructure solutions, and integration of monitoring within Government systems. Building on these gains, UNICEF supported structured consultations with core ministries to generate evidence on children’s exposure to climate-related hazards and identify practical entry points to integrate climate, environmental and disaster-risk considerations into sector policies and programmes—helping strengthen evidence-based planning and more coordinated delivery of essential services for children.

Shock-Responsive Scale-up
Under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, United Nations agencies aligned evidence and support behind national priorities to strengthen shock-responsive delivery for communities experiencing additional service pressures. Through the inter-agency Basic Services Response Priorities, UNICEF supported the scale-up of basic services for communities receiving new arrivals from Sudan, with a focus on maintaining service continuity and addressing urgent needs in vulnerable host communities. UNICEF contributed operational support across sectors, including risk communication and community engagement, alongside OCHA and other agencies including UNFPA, WHO and UNESCO. Together, this approach strengthened coordination and reduced fragmentation in multi-sectoral service delivery during periods of heightened demand, helping national and local systems respond more predictably in shock-affected contexts.

Partnerships that Enabled Scale and Reliability 
Government stewardship continued to define priorities and accountability for results, enabling service delivery to be strengthened through routine systems and more reliable operations. The Ministry of Health advanced strategic investments in oxygen plants and solar-powered cold-chain assets, paired with standard operating procedures, preventive maintenance arrangements and workforce training, while routine use of DHIS2 increasingly strengthened the application of facility data for management action. The Ministry of Education strengthened pedagogical coaching and advanced domestic expansion of early childhood classrooms. WASH authorities completed Environmental and Social Impact Assessments and integrated environmental health indicators into DHIS2, while stakeholders initiated formal WASH sector coordination. The National Statistics Office advanced EPHS 2025 implementation with UN support. UNICEF’s contribution centred on technical advice, systems design, coordination support, supplies and monitoring integration to strengthen reliability and equity in service delivery over time.  

Partnerships also strengthened alignment and coherence across the wider system. United Nations coordination platforms supported joint priorities and collective accountability, including collaboration under the UNFPA–UNICEF Joint Programme on Harmful Practices. A high-level in-country mission convened 26 donors and partners, strengthening dialogue, information sharing and alignment around national child protection priorities. UNICEF and UNESCO partnered on water-sector capacity assessments, while collaboration with OCHA supported scale-up of services for communities receiving arrivals from Sudan. Communities remained central to delivery and accountability: women’s groups, teachers, religious leaders and community facilitators supported prevention campaigns, maintained WASH facilities and reinforced classroom-level learning support. UNICEF supported these community platforms through social and behaviour change design, partner training and harmonisation. Development financing and technical partners supported service continuity and system upgrades, including oxygen infrastructure, solar cold-chain and digital health investments. With Government leadership and Gavi financing, digital health systems advanced, while EriTel supported connectivity for RapidPro pilots. UNICEF convened public and private actors to explore desalination options in water-scarce coastal areas. Together, these partnerships strengthened the reliability, sustainability and equity of service delivery by linking systems strengthening with community-level platforms and coordinated support across sectors. 

Preparations for the new Government–UNICEF Country Programme began in 2025. Implementation lessons—particularly the value of strong routine systems for service delivery, data and coordination—will inform priorities, scaling pathways and equity targeting in the next cycle. UNICEF will continue to focus its added value on systems strengthening, supplies, last-mile delivery and data for adaptive management to sustain results at scale.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF’s long-standing partnership with the Government of Eritrea continued to translate collaboration into measurable gains for children and communities. Working through national systems, UNICEF supported continuity of essential services while adapting approaches to address operational constraints and emerging risks. Experience across sectors reinforced a central lesson aligned with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan Change Strategies: progress at scale depends not only on service delivery, but on the strength, coherence and adaptability of the systems that sustain results—particularly in resource-constrained settings and hard-to-reach areas.

Several lessons emerged from implementation in 2025. First, trust-based engagement and sustained collaboration with national counterparts remained essential to addressing bottlenecks related to procurement, access and coordination, and to maintaining predictability in delivery. Second, simplifying planning and aligning closely with national priorities strengthened ownership and supported more timely decision-making, particularly where capacity constraints require tight sequencing and prioritisation. Third, integrated approaches that link system strengthening with frontline delivery—such as community-led efforts towards abandonment of harmful practices alongside school engagement and referral pathways—proved more likely to support resilient and scalable results than isolated interventions. Efficiency measures, including common services and joint monitoring, further demonstrated that strengthened coordination, clearer roles and shared accountability can enhance performance and expand reach.

What worked
Partnership between the Government and UNICEF strengthened, supporting timely financial reporting and reconciliation of programme funds, which helped keep implementation on track and supported the completion of activities under the GPE II/ Education Sector Plan Implementation Grant (ESPIG) grant.

This also enabled the use of UNICEF procurement arrangements for selected education and health supply items, helping to reduce procurement delays. Furthermore, the strengthened partnership facilitated in-country travel clearances for the UNFPA–UNICEF Joint Programme on Harmful Practices, enabling a high-level mission involving 26 technical and financial partners and strengthening engagement that mobilised additional resources.

Targeted investments in national systems demonstrated how coordinated action can strengthen results in constrained operating environments. The medical oxygen initiative exemplifies this approach. Moving from concept to operation required alignment of technical standards, financing, procurement and operational readiness with national authorities and service providers. The resulting oxygen plant at Mendefera Referral Hospital serves a catchment population of approximately 1.04 million people and supports life-saving care for an estimated 20–30 per cent of obstetric and paediatric admissions. Beyond immediate clinical benefits, the initiative strengthened resilience in the medical oxygen supply chain by addressing maintenance, spare parts availability and uptime. The partnership model—combining Government leadership, UNICEF technical support and private-sector maintenance—demonstrated an operational approach to strengthening the reliability and cost-efficiency of oxygen systems in low-resource settings.

Community-led approaches also proved critical to sustained progress, particularly in child protection. In priority regions, structured dialogue with community leaders, educators and families strengthened prevention efforts addressing harmful practices. Schools emerged as trusted platforms for prevention and early identification, with trained educators better able to recognise risks and link children to support services. This experience reinforced an important lesson: durable social change is built through local leadership, trusted institutions and continuous engagement, rather than one-off campaigns. Efficiency gains further supported service coverage and operational coherence. Common United Nations services coordinated procurement and joint field missions reduced duplication and transaction costs without compromising service quality. Joint monitoring expanded field-level oversight and improved coordination across sectors, allowing limited resources to be directed more effectively toward frontline delivery in underserved areas.

What did not work as planned
Despite overall progress, several constraints affected the pace and predictability of implementation. Procurement delays—linked to limited supplier markets, extended approval processes and global supply pressures—slowed delivery of some critical inputs. A changing funding environment required continued prioritisation and sequencing of interventions, reinforcing the importance of flexible planning and close coordination with partners. Operational access constraints, including limitations on field movements during parts of the year, reduced opportunities for routine supervision and timely follow-up in some locations.

While these challenges did not derail results, they highlighted vulnerabilities in delivery pathways, particularly for remote and hard-to-reach communities. Experience also underscored the importance of timely, interoperable data systems; where routine information flows were constrained, decision-making was less agile and course-correction was slower. Strengthening the reliability and usability of routine information remains essential to sustaining equitable delivery and enabling adaptive management during periods of constraint.

Looking ahead
Building on insights from 2025, UNICEF will continue to strengthen programme strategies that emphasise resilience, equity and sustainability. Priorities include deepening multi-level partnerships, expanding private-sector engagement where it can enhance reliability and maintenance of critical services, and further institutionalising data-informed planning within national systems. Strengthening interoperability and timeliness of routine information will remain central to adaptive management and more responsive programming. UNICEF will also continue to emphasise community-based platforms as key mechanisms for prevention, protection and behaviour change. By combining system-level investments with trusted local delivery mechanisms, UNICEF aims to accelerate progress for children most at risk of being left behind. Through continued collaboration with the Government of Eritrea, United Nations partners, communities and development actors, UNICEF will apply the lessons of 2025 to support more predictable delivery, adaptive responses to shocks and sustained improvements in the lives of children and mothers across the country.

Eswatini’s population was projected at 1,187,956 in 2023, with females comprising 51.3 per cent and males 48.7 per cent. Approximately 42 per cent of the population is under 18 years[i]. A significant proportion of the population resides in rural areas, which often shapes development challenges, particularly for children.
Eswatini is classified as a lower-middle-income country with high levels of poverty and inequality. About 65.3 per cent of children live below the poverty line of $3.65 per day and 46.6 per cent experience multidimensional poverty, facing deprivations in three or more critical dimensions. Rural children (52 per cent) are twice as likely to be multidimensionally poor compared to urban children (23 per cent) with notable regional disparities. Reducing poverty and inequality is essential for achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) such as ending hunger and ensuring food security (SDG 2), improving health and well-being (SDG 3) and providing quality education (SDG 4).
Eswatini has consistently prioritized social sector investments. In the 2025/2026 budget, education accounted for 16.2 per cent and health for 9.5 per cent of total allocations. Social Transfers saw a notable increase, representing 3.28 per cent of the national budget. These allocations underscore the government’s commitment to child-focused sectors. However, persistent weaknesses in public financial management remain a challenge. Government has introduced a Programme-based budgeting approach in 2025 aimed at enhancing transparency and improving operational efficiency, the impacts of which are to be seen in coming years.
Eswatini has made notable progress, reducing the neonatal mortality rate from 26 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2010 to 22 per 1,000 in 2022[ii] However, the country is still far from achieving the SDG3 target of reducing neonatal mortality to at least 12 deaths per 1,000 live births, underscoring the significant effort required to meet this goal by 2030.
The National Health Sector Strategic Plan 2024–2028 supports SDG 3 by aiming to improve access to equitable, high-quality, people-centered health services, promote universal health coverage, strengthen disease prevention, and build health system resilience. Among its six strategic priorities is expanding access to comprehensive, evidence-based health services that are inclusive and affordable. The plan emphasizes primary health care integration, maternal and child health, and care for vulnerable groups—key interventions that will accelerate progress toward health-related SDG targets.
In Eswatini, exclusive breastfeeding rates for infants under six months have declined from 64 percent in 2014 to 54 percent in 2022[ii], increasing the risk of disease among infants. To promote exclusive breastfeeding and improve child nutrition, the Government of Eswatini has implemented the National Food and Nutrition Strategic Plan, which strengthens coordination and delivery of nutrition interventions, including those targeting children.
Eswatini faces persistent challenges in primary education quality, with many children starting school without essential pre-literacy and pre-numeracy skills. Enrollment in early childhood education is 9 per cent of children aged 3–4 years attending early childhood education programs [ii]. While the primary school completion rate stands at 80 per cent, foundational learning outcomes remain poor—only 16 per cent of Grade 2 and 3 learners demonstrate basic reading skills, and just 8 per cent have foundational numeracy skills, with significant gender and regional disparities. These gaps hinder progress toward global education targets, including ensuring all children are school-ready, acquire foundational skills, learn in safe and supportive environments, and transition successfully to secondary education.
In response to the UN Secretary-General’s call during the Transforming Education Summit (2022), the Government of Eswatini revised the Education Sector Strategic Plan 2022–2034 to address these challenges. The plan outlines strategies to improve educational quality and learning outcomes at all levels, retain students through graduation, strengthen entry and exit points in the education system, and enhance teacher development and management, among other priorities.
According to MICS 2021/22, 79 percent of children aged 1–14 years were subjected to violent discipline. Among those, only 50 percent of boys and 67 percent of girls disclosed their experience of physical violence, and even fewer sought or received help[ii] Additionally, the 2022 Violence Against Children and Youth Survey (VACS) found that 15.8 per cent of females and 21 per cent of males experienced some form of physical, sexual or emotional violence in childhood, and 5.5 per cent and 2.1 per cent of young women and men ages 18-24 years experienced sexual violence, before the age of 18. Lifetime experience of sexual violence was 8.1 per cent among females and 3.3 per cent among males ages 18-24 years[iii]. As part of Government of Eswatini Vision 2022, the Government adopted a National Strategy to End Violence in Eswatini 2017-2027 contributing to achieving SDG Target 16.2, and supporting Eswatini’s national goal of reducing the prevalence of violence against children from 59 per cent to 20 per cent by 2030[iv]. 
In Eswatini, adolescent girls and young women bear a disproportionate share of the HIV epidemic, accounting for 67 per cent of all new infections among youth aged 15–24 and 24 percent[v] of new infections across all age groups. This underscores the urgent need to tackle the underlying factors that increase their vulnerability to HIV and early, unintended pregnancies—such as gender-based violence, age-disparate relationships, and school dropout. 
SDG Target 3.3 seeks to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030, and the UN General Assembly Special Session on HIV/AIDS urged governments to strengthen young people’s knowledge and skills to protect themselves from HIV, as youth represent a growing share of those living with the virus globally. This vision aligns closely with Eswatini’s national development priorities outlined in the National Development Plan 2023/24–2027/28.

In 2025, UNICEF Eswatini’s collaboration with the Government, particularly the Ministry of Health (MOH), Ministry of Education and Training (MOET), Deputy Prime Minister’s Office (DPMO), and the Ministry of Economic Planning and Development (MOEPD), contributed to improvements across service delivery and systems functions. The collaboration was anchored in strategies that link supply-side capacity (quality, standards, infrastructure, financing), demand generation (community engagement, social and behavior change), and governance (data, policy, accountability) to sustain outcomes for children and adolescents. Engaging these strategies contributed to maintaining continuity of essential services despite fiscal constraints that were unprecedented in 2025. 
In 2025, progress was made toward reducing child morbidity and mortality through integrated health interventions supported by UNICEF. A major achievement was the elimination of vaccine stock-outs, ensuring uninterrupted immunization services nationwide. This was accomplished through strengthened cold-chain management and improved vaccine supply chain systems within MOH. As a result, immunization coverage remained high, with MCV1 reaching 89.6 per cent and DPT3 at 86.2 per cent (HMIS, 2025), reflecting equitable access across all communities.
UNICEF’s collaboration with key MOH departments including the Expanded Programme for Immunization, Health Promotion Unit, Non-Communicable Diseases, Community-Based Health Programme, and Nutrition Council and Regional Health Management Teams, enabled the delivery of integrated basic health services, nutrition, and WASH interventions to over 20,000 vulnerable children and their families. 
To tackle inequities in health service delivery, UNICEF supported the revival and institutionalization of integrated outreach services in approximately 40 (11 percent) underserved. These outreach platforms provided primary health care, nutrition, and WASH services closer to households, reducing geographic and financial barriers to access. Furthermore, UNICEF strengthened community health systems by supporting Rural Health Motivators (RHMs) and Community-Based Health Services (CBHS). This included building leadership and governance structures, enhancing workforce capacity, and promoting sustainable financing mechanisms for community health.
In 2025, UNICEF in partnership with the European Union and UNFPA strengthened systems for early identification of disability and special needs among children and young people across healthcare facilities, schools, and communities. The initiative included strengthening monitoring and reporting systems for children with disabilities within health and education sectors; capacity building of health workers, education personnel and community health workers. The comprehensive approach resulted in increased patient referrals to Mbabane Government Hospital for specialized assessments, highlighting both the success of early identification and capacity building efforts among service providers. 
In Eswatini, effort required to meet the 2030 SDG target for stunting and overweight among under-fives is very high as 1 in 5 and almost 1 in 10 children) are stunted and obese, respectively[1]. UNICEF's continued strategic advocacy engagement with the MOH for a Nutrition Program led to government committing to reposition the Nutrition Council into an autonomous high-level statutory body to coordinate and direct nutrition programme in the country. UNICEF, in collaboration with WHO is supporting implementation of the costed STOP-Obesity Acceleration Road Map that provides strategic framework for addressing childhood obesity through multi-sectoral interventions. This comprehensive document outlines evidence-based strategies, implementation timelines, and resource requirements for obesity prevention and management initiatives. As part of this, UNICEF is supporting a Nutritional Legal Landscape Analysis which is aimed at mapping the policies and legislative frameworks regulating the Code of Marketing of Breast Milk Substitutes in Eswatini.
UNICEF-supported programmes, implemented through Baylor College of Medicine Children’s Foundation (BCMCF) and community-based partners, sustained viral suppression above 95 per cent among adolescents on ART for at least six months, with lost-to-follow-up maintained below 1 per cent. These results reflect UNICEF’s direct contribution to systems strengthening, including the introduction and scale-up of point-of-care viral load testing, which reduced turnaround times, enabled timely clinical decision-making, and improved adherence outcomes. While clinical outcomes are jointly attributable to MoH and partners, UNICEF’s contribution was decisive in financing diagnostics, strengthening clinical standards, and supporting differentiated service delivery models.
In Eswatini water, sanitation and hygiene remains a challenge with only 31 percent of household have basic drinking water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) servicesii. In this regard, UNICEF supported interventions targeting systemic weaknesses in regulation and service quality within health facilities. Applying a WASH Regulatory (WASH Reg) approach, UNICEF supported a multi-stakeholder diagnosis of gaps across affordability, consumer protection, service quality, public health, and environmental protection, strengthening regulatory capacity and alignment with human rights and SDG commitments.
Capacity of health officers and technical staff to develop a costed WASH-FIT workplan was strengthened with UNICEF support. This resulted in an actionable pathway for the introduction of a dedicated WASH in health facilities budget line within the Ministry of Health budget. 
UNICEF supported the first national Children’s Environmental Health assessment and complementary capacity building and awareness actions on environmental health, including a focus on lead poisoning. This aligns with UNICEF’s global children’s environmental health agenda on protecting children from environmental hazards.
To address the quality of education, UNICEF supported revision and validation of the National School Inspection Handbook and Standards for Primary and Secondary Schools, embedding inclusion, gender responsiveness, and ethical practice marking a transition from punitive inspections to developmental support. In 2025, UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to securing a government budget allocation exceeding E30 million for programmes previously reliant on external support—an important marker of domestic ownership and sustainability. 
In line with the global commitment to Leave No One Behind, UNICEF in partnership with World Vision, SWAGAA, and Young Heroes implemented the “Back to School for Children with Disabilities” initiative benefiting over 36,000 children, (including 5,655 with disabilities), and reintegrated 158 into mainstream education. Retention among learners with disabilities in targeted schools increased by 28 per cent supported by enhanced cross-sectoral coordination with MOH and the DPMO.
In 2025, UNICEF Eswatini strengthened child protection systems by supporting capacity to prevent and respond to violence against children (VAC) and ensuring the sustainability of essential protection services. Grounded in the theory of change that a coordinated, well-financed, and community-owned system is fundamental to every child’s right to safety and dignity, UNICEF focused on structural bottlenecks in governance, financing, coordination, and harmful social norms, while reinforcing government ownership and resilience.
One key milestone was the piloting of the Chiefdom Child Justice Committees, locally known as Umphakatsi Child Justice Committees, a breakthrough in the operationalization of the Children’s Protection and Welfare Act 2012. For the first time, this community-based restorative child justice mechanism is being operationalized as mandated by the Act. Standard Operational Procedures are in place, and 20 expert child justice pioneers have been trained to lead the pilot in 10 communities and support future scale-up. When severe funding cuts in early 2025 threatened to disrupt frontline protection services, UNICEF mobilized an emergency coordination mechanism with the DPMO, the Department of Social Welfare (DSW), and the Coordinating Assembly of NGOs (CANGO) to sustain life-saving care for survivors of violence. Within two weeks, 617 active cases of violence, including 103 cases of sexual abuse, were successfully transitioned from 24 departing NGO case workers to government social workers, ensuring uninterrupted case follow-up and protection. Among these, 20 cases resulted in arrests and 14 in ongoing prosecutions. This response not only prevented a service breakdown but also reinforced institutional ownership and resilience within government structures.
In 2025, UNICEF in collaboration with DPMO, faith-based actors, and civil society organizations utilized social behavioral change strategies to challenge harmful norms and strengthen community-led prevention of violence against children (VAC). This initiative benefited more than 15,000 including over 10,600 learners and 1,500 community leaders and caregivers and securing public commitments from some, to eliminate all forms of VAC amplifying community ownership and fostering sustainable, norm-shifting change. 
In 2025, UNICEF Eswatini accelerated transformative progress in adolescent HIV prevention and SRHR by addressing bottlenecks in service quality, youth participation, and social norms. Guided by the theory of change that adolescents thrive when health systems are responsive, communities are supportive, and young people can demand accountability, UNICEF in partnership with SAFAID, a regional NGO, established electronic feedback mechanisms in health facilities to help improve service quality for adolescent girls and boys, especially AGYW.
To strengthen demand generation and shift restrictive gender norms, UNICEF invested in community and digital behavior-change strategies. Through a partnership with SAfAIDS, adolescent girls and young women influencers produced and disseminated youth-led content under the “I Choose Safety” campaign, reaching 1,220 adolescents across six communities. Complementary radio programs on three national stations reached approximately 260,000 listeners, while Internet of God Things (IoGT) activations reached 1,000 young people. UNICEF also strengthened engagement with faith-based organizations by partnering with the Eswatini Conference of Churches to train 30 church and community leaders on HIV prevention, pregnancy prevention, and GBV response—opening new pathways for adolescent mobilization in traditionally gatekept spaces. Digital engagement exceeded expectations, with social media boosting reaching 23,675 adolescents and youth, and 36 evidence-based posts achieving a total content reach of 8,074, demonstrating the power of blended offline–online SBC strategies.
UNICEF advanced gender-transformative, community-based care through its partnership with Siphilile Maternal Child Health, a local NGO. The Program supported about 750 pregnant and lactating adolescents with consistent psychosocial and adherence support. UNICEF provided capacity to young mentor mothers and fathers resulting to over 1500 young women and men reached with life-skills, financial literacy, and empowerment programs. By the end of the year, the proportion of adolescent mothers’ confidence in accessing ante-natal care, HIV testing, and GBV services had increased by 40 per cent compared to pre-intervention situation, reflecting reduced fear, stigma, and isolation.
In 2025, Public Finance for Children initiatives targeted fragmentation and insufficiency in social sector expenditure, particularly for child protection services, early childhood education, essential health interventions, and nutrition financing. UNICEF’s focus on practical budget reform advocacy with DPMO, MOET, and MOH resulted in shifting several child-related budget lines from UNICEF funding to sustained government financing for 2026, including PRIMERO CPMIS+, the national Child Helpline 116, and capacity-building for social workers. This marks concrete progress in domestic resource mobilization and national ownership. Technical assistance contributed to finalizing the National Health Financing Strategy to diversify revenue and strengthen resilience. A costing study on children with disabilities, delivered with DPMO, quantified household financial burdens and informed options for disability-inclusive social assistance beyond the current Disability Grant. 
Social protection reforms advanced through policy design, system improvements, and evidence generation. With Social Protection Technical Assistance, Advice and Resources (STAAR), UNICEF finalized the Gender-Responsive and Age-Sensitive Social Protection Assessment, offering actionable recommendations and a sequenced reform roadmap. In partnership with DPMO, UNICEF completed the disability grant redesign study to guide adjustments beginning in 2026, reducing financial barriers for households caring for children with disabilities. The National Social Assistance Policy was finalized and submitted for parliamentary approval, emphasizing support to orphans and vulnerable children, child-headed households, and chronically poor households, with clearer objectives, eligibility, and coordination—positioning the system for greater coherence and predictability. 
On delivery systems, UNICEF, Government, and the World Bank supported a first-ever National Social Registry pilot in one of the regions (Shiselweni) that reduced inclusion/exclusion errors and improved equitable targeting, prompting scale-up to Lubombo and a government plan for nationwide coverage by 2027.
Evidence generation included comparative analysis of school support transfers in five Southern African countries (with the Universities of Oxford and Cape Town), showing that predictable child-focused benefits improve attendance, reduce dropout, and support adolescent well-being, particularly for girls and children in poverty. A comprehensive social protection system assessment and fiscal space analysis, led with DPMO, will inform feasible pathways for expanding child-sensitive programmes and improving performance. Collectively, these initiatives laid the foundation for a more inclusive, coherent system that reflects child-specific vulnerabilities and strengthens outcomes.
Across the portfolio, several change strategies and enablers from the UNICEF Strategic Plan were central to results. Systems strengthening and integration featured prominently embedding outreach within primary health care; institutionalizing inspection standards in education; integrating disability indicators across health and education data systems; Care and support for Teaching and Learning indicators (Safe Schools) and establishing WASH-FIT planning and budget pathways in health facilities. Evidence, data, and digital transformation were decisive—EMIS interoperability with DHIS2, open-access dashboards, U-Report engagement analytics, national social registry pilots, QGIS-based WASH mapping, and rapid validation for EMTCT indicators improved targeting, transparency, and real-time decision-making. Community engagement and social and behavior change underpinned HPV acceptance strategies, mentor mother and male engagement for HIV/PMTCT, breastfeeding counseling, and disability identification at community level. Partnerships and coordination—with EU, WHO, Gavi, UNESCO, universities, HISP, ECESWA, BCMCF, NDMA, and line ministries—amplified capacity, policy coherence, and innovation. Risk-informed programming and humanitarian–development nexus approaches sustained services during funding freezes and preparedness exercises, ensuring continuity under shocks. These enablers collectively improved equity-focused reach, service quality, and institutional resilience.
UNICEF core funding, the Regular Resources (RR) played an important catalytic role in several dimensions. First, RR allowed UNICEF to maintain continuity of critical adolescent HIV psychosocial and adherence support during funding disruptions—preventing service collapse and preserving high viral suppression rates. Second, RR enabled flexible systems investments (e.g., data integration, policy dialogue, coordination platforms, and cross-sector engagements) that are hard to finance through earmarked project funds but crucial for scale and sustainability. Third, RR supported multisector integration—bridging health, nutrition, WASH, education, and social protection—to address structural bottlenecks and deliver cohesive results aligned with UNSDCF outcomes and SDG targets. In effect, RR operated as a strategic lever to de-risk reforms, accelerate implementation during fiscal constraints, and position government-led financing to take over recurrent costs.
Notwithstanding progress, several challenges and risks remain. Demand-side barriers in HPV acceptance demonstrate the need for sustained, dialogic engagement and the importance of trusted messengers to move beyond compliance to informed consent. Geographic inequities persist, necessitating ongoing outreach and community systems investments to reach the last mile. Nutrition’s double burden requires a whole-of-society approach, with stronger regulatory enforcement (e.g., BMS Code), food system shifts, and multi-sector action on prevention. WASH in health facilities must be fully institutionalized, translating workplans into budget lines, standards, and routine monitoring, and expanding solarization for continuity and climate resilience. Data quality and interoperability need continuous improvement to inform targeting and accountability, especially for disability inclusion and social protection registries. Fiscal constraints underline the importance of PF4C reforms, domestic resource mobilization, and sequencing costed plans to ensure sustainability. Finally, shock readiness for outbreaks, climate events, and displacement requires ongoing preparedness, cross-sector coordination, and resilient service delivery models.
In summary, the year’s key results demonstrate how a coherent, integrated approach grounded in systems strengthening, evidence, and community engagement can deliver measurable improvements for children and adolescents, even in constrained fiscal environments. By aligning with national priorities and leveraging partnerships, digital tools using regular resources, UNICEF and government counterparts advanced equitable coverage, institutionalized inclusive practices, and created policy and financing pathways for sustainability.

In 2025, UNICEF encountered challenges presented by the global financial crisis. However, program implementation continued with success in several areas. UNICEF Eswatini continued to play its role as a convenor across government, civil society, and development partners which strengthened national policy alignment and enhanced synergy between sectors. 
Advocacy for public finance for children with government yielded positive results. In 2025 UNICEF engaged government during the budgeting process to invest for key child focused programs. As a result, several child-related budget lines previously funded by UNICEF were taken up by government financing in education, child protection and health. 
Engaging integrated Immunization Approach to advance health outcomes proved to be a driver for success. UNICEF supported a national rollout combining routine immunization with outreach services integrating cold-chain enhancements, forecasting tools, and community mobilization. This contributed to improved vaccine access in underserved areas and attainment of vaccines zero stock-out.   

Effective evidence-based engagement with government institutions propelled the social assistance discussion forward paving the way for policy formulation and laying groundwork for future scale-up.

Funding Gaps in some program areas hindered progress to attainment of planned outcomes.  For instance, sexual and reproductive health and violence prevention initiatives were hindered due to insufficient funding, limiting their integration into the broader country programme. 
While some youth and disability focused interventions performed well, gender-transformative strategies were not fully mainstreamed or consistently applied across programmes. 

UNICEF will continue to collaborate with key line ministries and partners to expand and sustain the integrated delivery of essential services, with a particular focus on priority groups.
For instance, the newly developed Community Health Strategy has strengthened the relevance of community-based interventions and formally recognized community health volunteers as an integral part of the health system workforce.
 
Key lesson is that sustainable health system strengthening requires combining infrastructure, training, clear governance structures, and ongoing operational support rather than focusing on any single element.

Ethiopia ended 2025 with promising signs of progress for children, most notably in multidimensional poverty and health outcomes, demonstrating the country’s resilience and capacity to advance child-well-being amid challenges. The country continued to face overlapping crises, including conflict, climate shocks, and disease outbreaks, all compounded by high inflation. These pressures strained household resilience and slowed gains in poverty reduction. According to 2025 World Bank Poverty and Equity Brief, monetary poverty rose from 33 per cent in 2016 to 39 per cent in 2021, with projections pointing to further deterioration. Yet multidimensional child poverty, while still extremely high, declined from its 2016 level of 89 per cent. More than eight in ten children (47.8 million), experience five or more deprivations, including shelter, sanitation, and nutrition. Children in rural areas, those living in Somali and Afar regions, girls, and children with disabilities continue to face the greatest disadvantages, reflecting persistent geographic and social inequalities.
The 2025 annual performance report of the Ministry of Health indicates meaningful progress in key health indicators. Maternal Mortality Ratio declined to 195 per 100,000 live births, while Under-Five Mortality and Neonatal Mortality fell to 46 and 27 per 1,000 live births, respectively. However, Ethiopia remains off track to achieve the 2030 SDG targets. Malnutrition persists at high level with 39 per cent of children under five stunted, while anemia affects more than half of young children and one quarter of pregnant women. The 2025 Ethiopia Nutrition Coordination Unit reports that malnutrition is rising due to the cumulative effects of conflict and climate shocks.
In education, progress at the primary level offers some optimism. The 2023/24 primary Net Enrollment Rate (NER) rose to 88.4 per cent, an increase of 5.1 percentage points from 2022/23. Yet deep disruptions continue, with millions of children out of school for up to three years due to conflict, flooding, and windstorms. Secondary enrollment declined from 32.9 per cent to 27.3 per cent, and dropout rates remained high at 35.7 per cent in Grade 8 and 20.9 per cent in Grade 1. In addition, learning outcomes remain an area needing sustained attention.
Child protection concerns are intensifying due to constrained access to services in some areas and persisting gender inequalities. Gender-based violence remains widespread, particularly in conflict-affected and displacement settings. Birth registration remains low at 27 per cent for children under five, and harmful practices—child marriage (34 per cent among women aged 20–24) and FGM (48.5 per cent among women of reproductive age)—persist. Access to basic water (56 per cent) and sanitation (10 per cent) remains limited and poses serious health risks, particularly in climate-vulnerable regions.
Economically, Ethiopia registered an estimated 8.4 per cent growth in 2024/25, driven by industry (10 per cent), services (8.8 per cent), and agriculture (6 per cent). However, fiscal pressures and debt repayments reduced social-sector spending, with education and health budgets declining from 25 per cent of total expenditure to 19.3 per cent. Major economic reforms advanced under the IMF’s USD 3.4 billion Extended Credit Facility, focusing on foreign-exchange liberalization, fiscal and monetary policy, and debt management. Under the G20 Common Framework, Ethiopia reached a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with official creditors in July 2025, with bilateral agreements to follow. A staff-level agreement on the fourth review of the programme in November 2025 unlocked USD 261 million.
Humanitarian needs deepened throughout 2025. Continued conflicts in Amhara, Oromia, and other regions severely restricted humanitarian access, displaced communities and damaged essential infrastructure, including schools, health facilities, and water systems. As of October 2025, 289 woredas were only partially accessible, and 41 were entirely inaccessible. Conflict in Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia caused extensive damage to WASH infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of internally displaced persons in overcrowded sites with limited access to essential services. According to UNHCR, Ethiopia hosts over 1.9 million IDPs, 2.8 million returnees, and 1.1 million refugees, mostly from South Sudan, Somalia, Eritrea, and Sudan.
Prolonged and recurrent droughts intensified by La Niña continued to affect Afar, Somali, Oromia, Amhara, and South Ethiopia. Severe water shortages and declining agricultural productivity have eroded livelihoods, particularly in pastoralist lowland regions where years of drought have decimated livestock herds. The Ethiopia Public Health Emergency Operations Centre warned of increasing health risks from disease outbreaks. Between January and May 2025, over 4,300 cholera cases and 2.4 million malaria cases were recorded. A Marburg virus outbreak in Jinka resulted in 14 confirmed cases and nine deaths by early December.
Children and persons with disabilities face heightened vulnerability due to stigma, discrimination, and limited access to services. The 2025 National Disability Survey found that one in five households includes a person with a disability, with prevalence reaching 30 per cent in Tigray. Gender inequality remains a significant barrier to development: Ethiopia ranked 75th out of 148 countries in the 2025 Global Gender Gap Index. Conflict and other emergencies have contributed to rising rates of gender-based violence and child marriage while restricting access to essential education and health services.

Every child survives and thrives
Child survival indicators showed significant progress in 2025 according to administrative data. Ante-natal Care visits of four or more increased from 78% to 86%; skilled birth attendance coverage improved from 74% to 80%, and early postnatal care for newborns rose from 69% to 78%. Administrative reports indicate that pentavalent third dose and full immunization coverage for children under one year reached more than 100%, despite some data quality concerns. The dropout rate from pentavalent to measles vaccination decreased from 10% to 9% in 2025. In the conflict affected areas of Tigray, Afar and Amhara 118 health facilities have been renovated/rehabilitated with different donors’ support. 
As of end of 2025, 2.25 million Zero-Dose (ZD) children, who had never received any vaccine were reached out of a total ZD estimated at 2.9 million for 2019 - 2024. The proportion of newborns treated for very severe diseases increased sharply from 32% in the previous year to 77% in the reporting year according to UNICEF program reports. Early diagnosis and treatment of pneumonia improved from 85% to 92%, while treatment of diarrheal diseases with Zinc and ORS and neonatal resuscitation for asphyxia showed modest gains, reaching 26% and 88% respectively. Ethiopia was prioritized for polio campaigns, targeting 22 zones. On average, 86% of participating woredas in targeted zones achieved a coverage of at least 95%.
In addition, 15.6 million children received Vitamin A, 11.5 million were dewormed, 18.5 million were screened for malnutrition, and 553,789 children with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment. Between January and October 2025, over 2.9 million children and pregnant/breastfeeding women received treatment for acute malnutrition and 3.9 million pregnant women, including 556,652 adolescent girls 15 to 19 years old, received iron-folic acid. Salt iodization coverage remained high at 80%, and compliance with fortification standards expanded among wheat flour and edible oil industries, improving access to essential micronutrients for women and children.
These progresses were achieved through systemic changes that strengthened the quality of Antenatal care, labor and delivery post-natal care, newborn and child health services especially at primary health care units. Childhood immunization coverage improved through a combination of strategies, including advocacy and communication, child centered design, routine immunization, Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization, Big Catch-Up initiatives, and integration with other health campaigns, including polio campaigns, outreach services, and mobile health and nutrition teams. UNICEF’s core resources contribution to the government health sector, channeled through annual work plans at national and subnational levels, supported integrated interventions across health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, and social policy. This ensured equitable access to services for vulnerable children through zero-dose identification, vaccination, essential newborn care services, nutritional screening, birth registration, and linkage to basic social services.
The Enhanced Community-Based Nutrition platform which integrated health, WASH, and food systems interventions at the community level, improved nutrition outcomes and the overall welfare of children through the possibility of children going to school thanks to access to additional income by their caregivers. Maternal nutrition policy advanced through the Government’s endorsement of a policy brief and a costed national roadmap for Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS), aiming for full coverage from 74 to 1067 woredas by 2030. UNICEF supported a market assessment to inform local production and social marketing of MMS. Research on Small-Quantity Lipid-based Nutrient Supplements for 25,000 children guided national scale-up plans. Significant site preparations for the UNICEF supported egg powder production facility, including steps toward Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points compliance was completed. Egg powder equipment is expected to arrive in March, and production is to be commissioned by June 2026. Procurement of Bühler extruders to process chickpeas and soya, enabling more than 60% of RUTF raw materials to be sourced locally by the end of 2026 is ongoing. 
In addition, UNICEF promoted climate-smart production of nutrient-rich foods in five regions, supporting 38,470 households. Institutional gardening, local recipe development, and cooking demonstrations improved dietary diversity for 2.9 million children. MMS demonstrations in 74 woredas reached 450,000 pregnant women. Adolescent programs delivered weekly iron-folate supplements to 519,828 adolescents, provided nutrition education to 5.42 million, and piloted integrated service models in Addis Ababa, reaching 175,000 adolescents. Initiatives linked food systems, life skills, and job creation, including poultry hubs in Tigray and Afar, benefiting 1,127 youth. School meal programs are planned to be tested with centralized kitchens serving 10,000 students, reducing costs by 12% per meal.  Building on the Food Urbanism pilot in Addis Ababa, the project expansion targets six sports training centers across five regions (Oromia, Amhara, Tigray, SER, and Sidama).
 
Every child learns
UNICEF Ethiopia advanced national priorities under the UNSDCF and SDG Agenda through transformative education initiatives that strengthened equity, inclusion, and systemic resilience. By December 2025, Ethiopia met three key Global Partnership for Education (GPE) triggers: reinstating block grants to conflict-affected regions, mobilizing over US$25 million in domestic financing, and digitizing Education Management Information System unlocking 40% of the grant by mid-2026. Central to this was the US$132.59 million GPE-funded System Transformation of Education Programme (STEP) (2024–2028), led by UNICEF and the Ministry of Education (MoE). UNICEF also piloted climate-smart school feeding models that reduced costs by 12 per cent, supported evidence-based planning, developed a costed disability inclusion strategy, and introduced an early childhood development parenting package. These systemic, innovative actions accelerate progress toward SDG 4 and national priorities.
With UNICEF’s support, a total of 568,782 vulnerable learners were reached. This included 361,980 out-of-school children at the primary level, out of 4.5 million primary-school-aged children who are out of school nationwide. The assistance also covered 206,802 emergency-affected students, drawn from 3.2 million primary-school-aged children impacted by emergencies across the country.
UNICEF ensured continuity of learning for children affected by emergencies and refugees through construction of 38 semi-permanent classrooms and formal and non-formal education, accelerated learning programmes, and child protection services. Investments in gender-responsive WASH facilities and classroom rehabilitation improved learning environments for 55,000 children, while psychosocial support and learning materials benefited more than 216,000 students affected by emergencies. From 2020 to 2025, UNICEF supported the construction of 84 new schools, rehabilitated 140 schools by providing various facilities, including toilets and WASH services Capacity-building initiatives strengthened inclusive pedagogy and emergency response for 13,751 educators. Under STEP, 2,800 Accelerated Learning Programme facilitators were trained, enabling 24,735 marginalized learners to catch up on foundational skills. Community engagement campaigns reached 5.5 million people and supported the re-enrolment of 51,565 children, demonstrating strong partnerships and local ownership.
Early Childhood Education (ECE) also advanced significantly. Over 202,994 children accessed improved pre-primary education through play-based pedagogy, learning materials, and enhanced classroom environments. 3,579 pre-primary teachers were trained, complemented by locally produced play materials and new ECE centers serving refugee children. Under STEP, 24.6 million curriculum-aligned textbooks were printed for pre-primary and primary students. Additionally, 50 Inclusive Education Resource Centers were established, supporting 1,702 children with disabilities, and house-to-house identification reached 794 learners. Digital learning expanded through the Ethiopia Learning Passport, bridging gaps in remote areas.
Gender-responsive education and adolescent empowerment were also prioritized. Over 213,598 adolescents, including 134,146 girls and 1,384 children with disabilities, gained life skills, resilience, and protection against gender-based violence. Menstrual health initiatives trained 24,000 girls to produce reusable products and established 380 dedicated rooms, improving attendance and dignity. Vocational training equipped 222 youth with market-relevant skills through PROSPECTS programme targeting forcedly displaced people and host communities, complemented by digital empowerment for 60 young women and leadership initiatives for nearly 200 youth. These integrated efforts reflect transformative change through innovation, strong partnerships, and local ownership, fostering equitable access and smoother transitions from learning to earning. From 2020-2025.
 
Every child protected from violence and exploitation
Ethiopia adopted the Civil and Family Registration Proclamation in 2025, replacing previous Civil Registration and Vital Statistics laws. Key reforms included removing the requirement for both parents to be present at birth registration, waiving certificate fees for timely registration, enabling registration at health facilities, and promoting digital systems. UNICEF played a pivotal role by advocating for the removal of procedural barriers and the introduction of simplified, efficient processes to boost birth registration rates.
Between July 2024 and June 2025, 48% (1,334,407) of newborns were registered and issued birth certificates an 8% increase from last year (Immigration and Citizenship Service (ICS) annual report). UNICEF contributed by supporting demand-creation campaigns, media outreach, and health system interoperability. In partnership with Refugees and Returnees Services (RRS) and ICS, UNICEF led a refugee backlog clearance, identifying 144,927 unregistered children (5,126 with disabilities) and clearing 76% of cases in Afar and Somali regions. 
To support the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) commitment to increasing national Child Protection Information Management System (CPIMS+) coverage from 2 per cent in 2024 to 20 per cent by 2030 UNICEF provided technical and financial support for expansion, accompanied by continuous advocacy to include Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) in the national CPIMS+. As a result, the Ministry of Women and Social Affairs (MoWSA) signed a MoU with six CSOs, which have begun implementing the national CPIMS+, thereby increasing CPIMS+ coverage from 2 per cent to 6 per cent within the year.
UNICEF signed a MoU with MoWSA, Addis Ababa University, and two professional associations to finalize Ethiopia’s first Social Work Act which will institutionalize workforce training, and introduce certification and supervision mechanisms, making a significant progress towards systems strengthening. This partnership now positions Ethiopia to deliver skilled, gender-responsive services, benefiting boys and girls disproportionately affected by neglect and violence. Between January and October 2025, 68,184 children (34,336 girls and 33,848 boys including 402 children with disability) who were victims of violence, abuse, or exploitation received protection services including health, legal aid, social welfare, and psychosocial support in both development and humanitarian settings.  
UNICEF continues working with partners to protect girls from harmful practices, particularly child marriage and FGM. Of the total of 3,773 child marriage cases reported, 2,051were cancelled, while 1,023 FGM cases were reported, and 829 of them were prevented. The affected girls were supported through comprehensive survivor-sensitive legal, psychosocial, and health services. In addition, 301 child marriage cases and 121 FGM cases were prosecuted, resulting in 224 and 104 convictions, respectively.
In partnership with 11 women-led organizations and 2 INGOs, UNICEF ensured quality support to Gender Based Violence (GBV) survivors in line with global standards across eight emergency-affected regions in Ethiopia. UNICEF supported One-Stop Centers, Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS) and shelters in Gambela, Amhara, and Somali through construction, furnishing, and service provision, creating safe spaces for survivors, while adapting and rolling out the global Caring for Child Survivors guideline to 442 (215 Female) front line service providers in eight regions. These efforts collectively advance GBV prevention, risk mitigation, and response while empowering locally rooted organizations through a survivor-centered approach. Through these interventions, 329,219 people were reached with GBV prevention and risk mitigation, while 1,208 survivors (449 girls, 7 boys and 752 women) received comprehensive response service.
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
In 2025, UNICEF delivered major national WASH results, strengthening children’s rights, health, and resilience by expanding access to safe water and basic sanitation. A total of 1,281,091 people gained basic water supply services. 
Electromechanical systems were installed and retrofitted to transition from diesel to solar power, reducing carbon emissions, mitigating energy shortages, and ensuring uninterrupted services for climate-vulnerable communities. In 2025, 29 solar-powered water systems were constructed, and 30 water points were solarized, bringing the total number of water system solarized from 2023 to 2025 at 210. Groundwater mapping was completed in 13 woredas to inform climate-adaptive planning which plays a critical role in helping communities and governments prepare for and respond to climate-related challenges such as droughts, water scarcity, and changing rainfall patter. 
UNICEF also continued its contribution to the consolidated water account pool fund, providing US$750,000 from Regular Resources in 2025. In addition, it provided technical and financial support for the review of One WASH National Plan Phase II and the development of Phase III, building on past successes and addressing identified bottlenecks to overcome these challenges.
UNICEF enhanced the capacity of 24 WASH utilities by improving operational efficiency through reduced Non-Revenue Water (NRW) and better users’ fees collection systems. These measures cut losses from leaks, theft, and metering errors, lowering average NRW from 36.75% to 20.6%, while improving water access and expanding service coverage.
UNICEF’s sanitation efforts delivered a significant impact: 196 communities achieved Open Defecation Free status, benefiting 584,829 people, while 492,112 gained access to basic sanitation. Hygiene promotion reached 1,183,604 people across development (635,844) and humanitarian (547,760) contexts. Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHH) initiatives advanced gender equity, supporting 114 schools and reaching 52,671 girls. Through national advocacy for the elimination of taxation on sanitary pads, UNICEF addressed a key barrier to girls’ dignity and education. Building on the 2019 tax reduction from 30% to 10%, UNICEF generated price-trend evidence, engaged decision-makers, and secured full tax exemption endorsed at the National MHH Advocacy Event, marking measurable progress toward menstrual equity for adolescent girls.
UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with the Inter-Religious Council of Ethiopia, resulting in the development and nationwide rollout of WASH guidance, which has now been cascaded to the regional and community levels. This partnership expanded hygiene promotion and cholera prevention in highly influential community settings, contributing to improved social norms and protective behaviors.
UNICEF leveraged advanced digital innovations to promote inclusion and strengthen evidence-based decision-making. Pilot initiatives, such as the TSEDU national mobile application and Virtual Reality tools, enhanced disability-inclusive hygiene education in urban programme woredas, with growing adoption by students, health extension workers, religious leaders, and communities. In parallel, UNICEF developed a real-time, multisectoral data system integrating WASH, Health, Nutrition, and Education programmes. This system enabled real-time monitoring, secure data storage, and actionable dashboards, reinforcing accountability and adaptive management across sectors for multi-sectoral programming.  UNICEF and sector-wide advocacy for repayable and private financing in WASH has led key financial institutions to introduce dedicated WASH lending products.
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life
In 2025, Ethiopia made progress in strengthening its evidence base on child poverty and institutional capacity, advancing efforts to reduce multidimensional poverty and promote equity for children. National and urban Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA) results were disseminated to more than 120 stakeholders, thereby reinforcing SDG 1.2 monitoring and policy dialogue. A key milestone was the embedding of child poverty analysis within the Policy Studies Institute (PSI), supported by recommendations to strengthen evidence-based policymaking, multisectoral coordination, and institutional capacity. According to the latest MODA conducted by UNICEF, multidimensional child poverty remains high, with 80 per cent of children deprived in five or more dimensions.
The 2024/25 Ethiopian Demographic and Health Survey achieved nationwide coverage despite insecurity, logistical barriers, financial constraints and language challenges, mitigated through regional coordination and translation support. Results will be released early 2026. The National Disability Survey data findings show that 5.78 per cent of Ethiopia’s population has a disability, including 2.46 per cent of children aged 2 to 4 and 4.1 per cent aged 5 to17. ESS, PSI, and UNICEF jointly developed a national disability data guideline to guide future data collection.
