UNICEF supported adaptive social protection systems through technical assistance and interventions ranging from shock response to resilience-building. Nearly 23 million children (estimated at 30% of the total) were covered by social protection programmes, including the Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP) and Community-Based Health Insurance (CBHI). In collaboration with MoWSA and regional bureau, UNICEF reached 60,332 displaced households (about 265,388 individuals) in conflict- and drought-affected areas with Shock-Responsive Cash Transfers (SRCTs). Improved disability identification enabled 14 per cent of SRCT beneficiary households to receive cash top-ups. Nearly 39,000 households benefited from Cash Plus interventions. In Oromia, 25,000 individuals participated in community conversations on adaptation of climate change, while 2,293 were linked to financial inclusion through revolving funds in Self-Help Groups, supporting income-generating activities for 736 households. The Child Grant pilot in five regions covered 11,471 households, linking over 90 per cent of beneficiaries to essential health, nutrition, and birth registration services. The programme also had a positive impact on women’s economic empowerment, including on their financial management skills. In Sidama, of the 1,470 beneficiaries, more than 1,439 mothers engaged in diverse income-generating activities including chicken and goat rearing, backyard gardening (rice, coffee, and avocado planting), and retail trade. To cover forcibly displaced populations, financial inclusion products for youth-led sanitation enterprises benefitted 3,570 refugees and host communities. 
UNICEF contributed to PSNP 6 design through evidence generation and active engagement in the technical committees for the shock response, linkage to available social services, and livelihoods. UNICEF facilitated a platform for women-led organizations to contribute to PSNP 6 design and strategize on structured and effective engagement in the planning, implementation, and monitoring of social protection policies and programs. A study on conflict-responsive safety nets informed the shock-response component of PSNP6 to address conflict-related shocks, based on the evidence, while a gender equality and social inclusion assessment will guide provisions for gender equality, disability inclusion, nutrition SBC, and feedback mechanisms. Technical guidelines for refugee inclusion in CBHI were developed in collaboration with ILO and UNHCR. 
UNICEF also supported macroeconomic forecasting for the Ministry of Finance, enabling revenue and expenditure projections that incorporate macroeconomic shocks and improved disaster risk finance planning. UNICEF continued support for budget transparency and accountability. Additionally, UNICEF helped pilot nutrition budget tagging across key ministries, enabling Ethiopia’s first estimation of public spending on nutrition using the Integrated Financial Management Information System.
UNICEF successfully supported the GoE to ensure that national and regional climate policies were child-centric and addressed the unique needs of children in climate crises. UNICEF supported the Government to ensure the National Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 (2025 – 2030) were child centric and included key social sectors including health and education, a milestone for ensuring climate resilient social services for children. Furthermore, UNICEF was a key player at the GoE-African Union second African Climate Summit held in Addis Ababa, amplifying youth participation, where children and youth were at the center of policy outcomes and strategic engagements, and highlighted the importance of child-focused climate responses in UN negotiations.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Despite progress achieved, the health system continues to face challenges, particularly in maternal, newborn, and child health, such as recurrent conflict, drought, floods, and disease outbreaks. Service delivery has been further hampered by interruptions of two thirds of Mobile Health and Nutrition Teams (MHNT) in Afar caused by funding cuts. As a result, over 650,000 zero-dose children remain unvaccinated at the end of 2025. Despite challenges, mentorship programs strengthened health worker skills such as providing climate resilient health services, improved immunization efficiency, and boosted community demand showing the value of capacity building and local engagement. Lessons learned highlight the need for stronger coordination with the different sectors and resource alignment. Moving forward, priorities should include optimizing PHC in selected districts, leveraging MoH initiatives to facilitate scaling MNCH interventions, sustaining MHNT, enhancing emergency preparedness, detection and responses and advocacy with partners for convergence.
Malnutrition in Ethiopia remains severe, driven by poor diets, low service coverage, and infections. Conflicts, climate shocks and funding cuts have disrupted access and supply chains, further limiting the availability of nutrition services. UNICEF’s nationwide presence, strong government partnerships, and technical expertise enabled large-scale implementation and the coordination of programs. Integration of nutrition delivery with immunization, WASH, food systems, and social protection has proven to be effective in reducing child vulnerability. Moving forward, lessons highlight the need to prioritize food systems transformation to combat child food poverty, promote climate-sensitive and gender responsive approaches and scale locally produced nutrient-rich foods.  Sustainable financing, including private sector engagement and local production of multiple nutrient supplements, will be critical for long-term impact.  
Ethiopia continues to face education challenges such as limited teachers’ capacity for the new curriculum, inadequate ECE infrastructure, and barriers for children with disabilities. These highlight the need for innovative, localized strategies, flexible delivery models, and strengthened data systems for real-time decision making. Despite these issues, strong partnerships with the MoE and regional bureaus enabled scaling of inclusive education, digital learning, and foundational skills for marginalized children. Integrated approaches combining WASH, psychosocial support, and gender-responsive pedagogy improved learning environments and boosted enrolment. In humanitarian contexts, cluster approaches and consultative meetings have enhanced resource sharing and coordination. Moving forward, UNICEF will build on these lessons to refine strategies, accelerate digital and inclusive learning, accelerate girls’ education, expand climate-smart school feeding and support the Government to roll out the education part of the NDC 3.0 for more climate responsive education services. 
Lengthy partnership processes with the Refugee and Returnee Services (RRS) and regional bureaus of MoWSA slowed implementation and constrained the effective roll-out of Proclamation 1110/2019 on refugee inclusion to ensure protection of refugee children. Divergent views among some religious leaders on provisions of the 2024 Proclamation related to medicalized FGM present challenges to eliminate FGM. GBV faced persistent bottlenecks, including shortages of trained case workers in hard-to-reach conflict-affected areas, inconsistent application of national GBV referral pathways, and delays in approving data-sharing agreements necessary for GBV case management and CPIMS+ interoperability. High turnover of frontline social workers and limited availability of safe shelters further weakened timely and confidential support for survivors. The lack of integration between the digital ID and birth registration systems has led to inefficiencies in increasing birth registration uptake.
UNICEF continues to advocate strongly with RRS to streamline bureaucratic processes and accelerate intergovernmental collaboration on integrated child protection and GBV services. UNICEF is also continued engaging the Inter-Religious Council of Ethiopia and the Ethiopian Muslim Gynecologists and Obstetricians Association to facilitate evidence-informed dialogue with Islamic leaders on the harms of FGM. UNICEF and UNHCR are working to harmonize parallel systems and co-develop a digital platform to support integrated measurement of system maturity and refugee inclusion in 2026. UNICEF and the World Bank successfully advocated for a national civil registration system compatible with digital ID. The system was launched in Addis Ababa, and UNICEF will support its expansion in other regions.
WASH programme implementation faced challenges, including funding gaps, donor reductions, rising costs, security restrictions, customs delays, and market disruptions. UNICEF mitigated these challenges by strengthening partnerships and adapting delivery methods to sustain WASH services for vulnerable populations. Infrastructure delays were tackled through stricter contractor selection and revised contracts with penalty clauses. Assessing NRW in 10 towns and implementing corrective actions improved utility performance, expanded access to safe water, increased revenues, and enhanced service coverage. This boosted financial sustainability and service reliability. 
UNICEF’s integrated approach, combining advocacy, innovation, partnerships, and risk-informed planning, advanced child rights, strengthened local systems, and promoted sustainable, climate-resilient WASH services. Capacity-building for financial institutions is also improving their ability to design and deliver WASH financing products for households and communities.  Moving forward, UNICEF will expand climate-resilient, equity-focused WASH programmes through risk-informed planning, prioritizing vulnerable and displacement-prone areas with gender-responsive approaches. Efforts will strengthen WASH systems, ensure service continuity in fragile settings, and deepen partnerships to drive innovation, financing, and coordinated action delivering sustainable WASH services that leave no one behind.
Persistent bottlenecks in social policy, such as data gaps, limited technical skills, and operational constraints, call for early planning, adaptive approaches, and robust engagement with regional actors to maintain momentum. The successful institutionalization of child poverty analysis has been essential to amplify policy relevance. Timely dissemination of evidence has proven to be a powerful tool for enhancing policy dialogue and driving concrete action toward child-focused outcomes. Multisectoral collaboration has significantly improved the uptake of evidence, while localized capacity building has enhanced analytical quality and fostered ownership at regional levels. Innovative approaches to livelihoods and income-generating activities through private sector engagement contribute to resilience-building. Multisectoral interventions to the most vulnerable populations to essential services require a dedicated, capacitated frontline workforce and contextualized service delivery.  Integrating humanitarian and development programming and layering cash transfers with care and support has become pivotal in sustaining improvements in wellbeing amid shrinking fiscal space and increasing vulnerabilities.  Looking ahead, prioritizing resilience through climate-sensitive, inclusive and gender responsive interventions, digital innovations, and strategic partnerships, including with the private sector and communities, will be essential for achieving sustainable, equitable outcomes across social sectors.

Kenya's population stands at 53,330,978 (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics [KNBS], 2025). Children aged 0-17 years make up 41.3 per cent of the population, with 11.1 million girls (50.5 per cent) and 10.9 million boys (49.5 per cent). Adolescents - ages 10-19 years - account for 11.7 million (22 per cent) of the total population, while youth 19-34 years are at 16.8 million (31.5 per cent). Kenya’s child population will peak in 2047, reaching over 28 million, offering a chance for a demographic dividend. ¿People with disabilities account for 2.2 per cent of the population (almost 1.2 million people, an estimated 484,000 children, KNBS 2019 Census).  Additionally, Kenya hosts approximately 870,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, of which 441,776 are in Dadaab, 309,944 are in Kakuma and 117,781 are in urban areas (UNHCR, 2025). 

Politically, Kenya faced heightened tensions, including renewed protests led by Generation Z over economic challenges and lack of job opportunities for young people, a leadership vacuum in the opposition following the passing of Raila Odinga, and the early signals of the 2027 general elections as well as lack of absorption capacity of development assistance. 

Kenya's gross domestic product (GDP) has been stable, with GoK’s projection for the full year at 5.3 per cent (similar to 2024). In 2025, Kenya’s inflation averaged between 3.3% and 4.6% (within target range), with food and transport costs as the main drivers. The Kenyan Shilling generally strengthened against the US dollar compared to its sharp depreciation in early 2024 and throughout the year the exchange rate remained relatively stable at 1 USD to 129 KES.  The government marginally increased national spending in social sectors from 43.7 per cent in 2024 to 44.5 per cent in 2025 of the annual budget. County budget allocation increased from 41.7 per cent to 44.6 per cent. The health sector saw a 1.48 per cent increase to 9.8 per cent, the education sector recorded a 2 per cent decline to 9.8 per cent, the water sector increased by 0.4 per cent to 4.5 per cent and the social protection sector increased marginally by 0.1 per cent to 3.3 per cent.

Two out of every five Kenyans live in monetary poverty; 42.4 per cent (9.3 million) of children live in monetary poverty while 55.3 per cent (12.2 million) are multidimensionally poor. While Kenya’s GDP grew by 43.5 per cent between 2014 and 2022, child multi-dimensional poverty increased from 45 to 55.3 per cent during the same period (KNBS, 2025).¿ This highlights a disconnect between economic growth and improvements in child well-being¿. Arid counties such as Mandera, Turkana, and Tana River consistently recorded the highest multi-dimensional poverty levels, but Lake Basin Region counties have larger absolute numbers of children affected. Higher education for women reduces child poverty risk by 18.1 per cent; rural residence increases risk by 20.4 per cent; and having children under 5 increases risk by 5.8 per cent.  Current social assistance programming cushions impacts, but coverage is currently too low to significantly reduce child poverty.

Kenya’s health sector in 2025 faces significant bottlenecks. Year on year service coverage levels for certain interventions has decreased in 2025, including for antenatal care, oral rehydration salts and zinc treatment, outpatient visits and pentavalent vaccination (KHIS 2025). There is limited health infrastructure (2.2 facilities per 10,000 people) and a shortage of health  workers (30 per 10,000, target of 45). Health financing is strained, with high out-of-pocket payments (24 per cent) and low health insurance coverage (26 per cent). Basic equipment is available in just 24 per cent of primary-level facilities and local procurement of 15 per cent remains below  targets. 

For nutrition, 63 per cent of children face food poverty, 16 per cent severe food poverty. The Arid and Semi-Arid Land (ASAL) counties remain extremely vulnerable to climate related shocks and hazards:  nationally, 741,883 children (6–59 months) are acutely malnourished, with 60  per cent living in the ASALs. Out of these, 42.3 per cent were admitted for management.  ¿At the same time, there is increasing prevalence of overweight and obesity. Among adolescent girls aged  15–19 years, the prevalence rose from 6 percent to 13 percent from 1993 to  2022, driven by unhealthy diets and high consumption of ultra-processed  foods and sugary drinks. ¿Bottlenecks in 2025 included reductions in  development partner support, limited dietary  diversity/availability of nutritious foods, frequent and recurrent shocks¿,  inadequate financing, and sub-optimal coverage of multi-sectoral services. 

The  WASH sector has made steady progress over the years: from 58 per cent access  to basic water in 2015 to 66 per cent in 2024; from 30 per cent to 36 per  cent in safely managed sanitation, and from 10 – 6 per cent in open  defecation.¿ However,  there is persistent inequality: rural households face stark disadvantages to  urban areas, with much higher reliance on surface water (25 vs 5 per cent)  and open defecation (8 vs 1 per cent), alongside wide gaps across wealth  quintiles (JMP 2024)¿. Issues include: a high WASH sector financing gap, with national estimates showing a KES 100 billion annual shortfall to meet 2030 SDG targets, exacerbated by ODA decline in 2025; low coverage of regulated water services in ASAL counties; lack of operations and  maintenance sustainability; inadequate  monitoring systems; increased urbanization; and recurring climate shocks.

In Education, the latest data from 2023 shows access to education improved, with the primary net enrolment (NER) rate at 89.1 per cent and secondary at 61.6 per cent, both exceeding targets and up from 2024 (78.1 and  54.1 per cent respectively). Learning outcomes were mixed: Grade 3 reading targets were met (50 per cent), but numeracy fell short at 52.4 against 76  per cent. The transition rate from primary to secondary was 86.7 per cent (target 88 per cent). Kenya continued its progress in analysing foundational learning assessment data to  inform both education policy and classroom practices. However, programmes such as Free Primary Education, Junior Secondary Capitation, school feeding, and support for Out-of-School Children are  under-funded. Refugee education is still reliant on humanitarian actors and  funding. Learners with disabilities and vulnerable groups lag behind, and  rising exam fees, lack of pre-primary capitation, energy insecurity, and  limited digital infrastructure continue to hinder equitable access and  learning. 
  
Child protection staffing (case workers) capacity in refugee areas has dropped sharply (e.g.,  Kakuma/Kalobeyei down 64 per cent, Dadaab ratio worsened from 1:90 to 1:266).  Safeguarding concerns for adolescents persist. The birth registration rate  has declined—from 80 per cent in 2022 to 70 per cent in 2024 (Kenya Vital  Statistic report, KNBS, 2022, 2024). Nevertheless, there is positively still significant level  of attention for Kenya, particularly harmful practices and online safety  (e.g. UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of  FGM, and on prevention of child marriage).

The UNICEF Kenya Country Programme (CP) 2022-2026 has been extended to mid-2027, aligned to the Government of Kenya’s Medium-Term Plan IV 2023-2027, and the extended United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF 2022-2027) and UNICEF Global Strategic Plan (2022–2025). In 2025, UNICEF provided catalytic support to the Government to sustain achievement of large service delivery results, leveraging Government financing despite funding cuts, while also strengthening social service systems to enable sustainability of delivery moving forward. 
 
Social Policy   
In 2025, with support of UNICEF and other partners, the Government of Kenya expanded Inua Jamii coverage to 1.703 million households, registering 696,447 new beneficiaries. UNICEF supported a major milestone—revising eligibility for the Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children (CT-OVC) to integrate broader child protection vulnerabilities, expanding coverage from 259,000 to 443,000 households. Across all UNICEF-supported social protection programs, 1.17 million children and 1.85 million households received cash transfers (exceeding the target of 829,000 and 1.1 million respectively). In partnership with UK-FCDO, UNICEF piloted anticipatory action social protection for climate shocks and other emergencies in Garissa and Turkana, using early warning data to trigger early cash assistance and enhanced maternal and child nutrition support. The pilot reached 4,416 beneficiaries, and the Government has developed a target to scale the approach to eight counties by 2030, demonstrating national uptake of evidence-driven innovation. UNICEF continued to partner with the World Bank under Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project Phase 2 to develop a US$200 million national social protection project. This project will scale up the nutrition improvement through cash and health education programme (NICHE) to 25 counties and introduce a new Adolescent Cash Plus program targeting nine counties. At national level, UNICEF supported passage of the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, strengthening the legal framework for disability rights. 
 
UNICEF played a central role in strengthening public finance management and child-focused investments. UNICEF’s advocacy efforts on domestic resource mobilization contributed to social sector allocations securing KES 5.527 billion (US$2.8 million), representing 20.6 per cent of the KES 26.86 billion (US$223.7 million).  UNICEF influenced four national PFM reform systems, including sustained child- and gender-responsive budgeting guidelines for 2026/27 and rollout of a new Programme-Based Budgeting manual that enhances reporting on child-related expenditure. UNICEF also supported 16 counties and five national sectors to integrate children’s priorities in FY 2026/27 budgets. Targeted budget engagements in Isiolo, Wajir, and Garissa led to reallocations of US$3.8 million to social sectors, while technical support in Samburu, Turkana, and West Pokot mobilized US$13.9 million in additional child-focused funding. To enhance budget transparency, UNICEF partnered with Bajeti Hub to publish 33 county citizen budgets, improving the national transparency score from 56 per cent to 64 per cent. 
 
UNICEF strengthened evidence systems through the Brighter Futures: Breaking Cycles of Poverty for Children in Kenya (with UN Women and KNBS) and the Kenya Fiscal Incidence Analysis Report: Poverty and Distributional Impacts of Fiscal Policy in Kenya – A Commitment to Equity Assessment with Extensions to Gender and Children (with KIPPRA, KNBS, and the World Bank). UNICEF also supported County Statistical Abstracts and trained county assembly committees to use child poverty evidence in legislative and budget decisions, promoting sustained, evidence-driven governance for children nationwide. 
    
Health  
In 2025, UNICEF continued to support Kenya’s Universal Health Care vision, focusing on reducing inequalities and improving essential service quality despite financial and operational challenges. Through partnership with the Ministry of Health (MOH) , UNICEF helped maintain resilient routine immunization: 1.03 million children (80% coverage, slightly down from 82% in 2024) received Pentavalent vaccines, and 1.02 million (81%, down from 82% in 2024) received Measles Rubella vaccines. Single-dose HPV vaccination reached 409,978 10 year-old girls. UNICEF’s support included ensuring cold chain capacity met the 90 per cent target, delivering 2,400 specialized vaccine fridges, and capacity building for 17,789 health workers. UNICEF also played a pivotal role in a nationwide integrated Measles Rubella and Typhoid Conjugate vaccination campaign and polio campaigns, including advocacy, communication, and community engagement; ¿procurement and distribution of vaccines;¿ microplanning; ¿and capacity building of health care workers. In total, 5.3 million children 9–59 months were vaccinated for Measles Rubella, and 16.6 million children 9 months–14 years were vaccinated for Typhoid¿. Key efforts to bridge the equity gap in immunization included the Big Catch-Up for unvaccinated children; 78,575 zero dose children were vaccinated during the campaign, while 979,700 children were reached with polio vaccines.
 
To strengthen the health system, UNICEF supported quality newborn care, with 85.5% of preterm and low-birth weight infants receiving Kangaroo Mother Care (target 85%). Two maternal and newborn health learning hubs were established in Kisumu and Lodwar, and over 200 health workers were trained in Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EmONC), Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMNCI), and newborn care. UNICEF’s system improvements included provision of MNH and ICT equipment to 20 facilities, establishing maternal and perinatal deaths surveillance and response structures in four counties, establishing 6 and supporting a further 27 Primary Care Networks (PCNs) to operationalize, expanding access to integrated health services for over 811,000 people. Early Childhood Development (ECD) mentorship, led by UNICEF, reached 14 centers and trained 452 healthcare providers, 95 Community Health Assistants (CHAs), and 675 Community Health Promoters (CHPs), reaching 97,362 children. 
 
Integration of HIV services into reproductive and maternal health programs was enhanced through UNICEF’s efforts: 20 counties developed Elimination of Mother-To-Child Transmission (EMTCT) and pediatric HIV frameworks (target 14), and 2,176 healthcare workers and community HIV champions completed skills enhancement. School-based health initiatives in 500 schools expanded adolescent access to health information and services, reaching 47,000 students.
 
On the legislative front, UNICEF contributed to developing regulations for the Primary Health Care Act and Facility Improvement Fund Acts in three counties, finalizing the Mother and Child Health Handbook and Integrated Management of Childhood Illness guidelines, and partnering with the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) on lead poisoning prevention – with the potential to improve lives for some of the estimated 15 per cent of children who are affected by this issue in Kenya. 

Nutrition  
Globally, and in Kenya, UNICEF is shifting to focus on prevention of all forms of malnutrition including wasting, overweight, and diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs). In 2025, UNICEF supported the MOH  to address malnutrition and promote adoption of positive nutrition practices by enhancing governance and systems capacity. A total of 1,625,412 primary caregivers received IYCF counselling, reaching 90.3% of the target; and supported the training of 2,828 health and nutrition workers and community health promoters to provide infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling, surpassing the target of 1,000. UNICEF supported the MOH to reach 5.16 million children aged 6–59 months with vitamin A supplementation, achieving 76.6 per cent coverage against an 84 per cent target. Fifteen counties implemented programs to improve dietary diversity in children aged 6–23 months, exceeding the target of 13. UNICEF-supported national breastfeeding campaigns reached over six million people. These efforts have helped address barriers to breastfeeding, dietary diversity, and harmful social norms, particularly in underserved counties. 
 
UNICEF supported the MOH to strengthen Kenya’s nutrition governance and data systems, enabling more evidence-driven planning and improved accountability. This support led to the development and rollout of national nutrition data standards, guidelines, and strategies, including the Joint Action to Stop Wasting (JASW) Theory of Change, the M&E framework, standardized KHIS tools. The evidence base for maternal and child nutrition strategies was strengthened by integrating nutrition indicators into the nationally representative Kenya Integrated Household Budget Survey (KIHBS) and the mini–Demographic and Health Surveys (Mini DHS). However, only one SMART survey of the 10 targeted was completed due to external funding cuts.  
 
In nutrition financing, sixteen counties implemented nutrition financial tracking (target: 14), and all 15 targeted counties developed costed county nutrition action plans, with UNICEF’s technical and financial support.A Public Financing for Nutrition (PF4N) curriculum was developed in collaboration with the MOH and the Kenya School of Government and trainings conducted for trainers of trainers. Advocacy and policy engagement were amplified through participation in national and global dialogues, including the UN Food Systems Summit (UNSFSS) and the NIPN Global Gathering. 
 
UNICEF supported life-saving interventions and strengthened health systems to deliver quality nutrition services in arid, semi-arid, and urban counties. Across 23 arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) and urban counties and Dadaab and Kakuma refugee camps, a total of 111,629 children with severe acute malnutrition were treated, achieving an 80.2% cure rate (toward an 85% target) – enabled by UNICEF’s procurement and distribution of 121,447 cartons of Ready to Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF). UNICEF supported the family MUAC approach for early detection and treatment of child wasting to be adopted in 15 counties (target: 12), and 83 per cent of health facilities in 10 arid counties implemented the IMAM surge approach (target: 75 per cent). This led to emergency outreaches screening 86,000 children for malnutrition. Additionally, UNICEF reached 122,835 households with nutrition education through NICHE. 

WASH  
Contributing to hygiene and sanitation, UNICEF supported the approval of the Sessional Paper No. 7 of the National Sanitation Management Policy, a major milestone establishing a comprehensive framework for sanitation across the service chain. UNICEF supported 423 villages achieve open defecation free status (ODF), benefiting 86,341 people, including through certification of 22 national master trainers on the RuSH (rural sanitation and hygiene) and digital monitoring systems and equipping over 100 county officers to implement and track sanitation results. UNICEF strengthened sanitation coordination through 47 county hubs and 2 national hubs, improving data quality and planning. Since 2021, UNICEF has supported certification of 6,651 ODF villages, raising ODF coverage from 17 to 44 per cent in target counties. A further 197,922 people gained access to basic sanitation through UNICEF-supported market-based and community sanitation interventions, including 56,624 people in Nairobi’s informal settlements who benefited from container-based toilets and regular waste collection. Market-based sanitation models expanded reach, with 6,318 household toilets upgraded for 38,203 people. UNICEF also strengthened basic hand hygiene by supplying handwashing facilities, soap, and hygiene kits and supporting community demonstrations and behavior-change sessions, enabling 262,921 people to access basic hand hygiene services and 573,960 people to be reached with targeted hygiene promotion (target of 550,000) during floods and disease outbreaks.
 
Strengthening WASH in institutions, UNICEF enabled 81,742 learners in 114 schools across ten counties to access improved WASH facilities, enhancing attendance and retention. A further 194 schools received WASH supplies, teacher training, and hygiene promotion support. Towards menstrual hygiene management ensuring girls attend school, UNICEF undertook procuring and distributing dignity kits and supporting education awareness that reached 54,876 adolescent girls. In health care facilities, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to county governments to rollout Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) methodology, helping facilities assess and strengthen WASH, waste management, and infection-prevention standards. Training across 39 counties enabled assessments in 291 facilities and certified 30 trainers of trainers to institutionalize the approach. 
 
In the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs), UNICEF pioneered exploratory mapping of deep aquifer potential and deep borehole drilling an innovation with the potential to provide reliable water for 4.1 million people in chronically drought-affected counties of Turkana, Samburu, Marsabit, Mandera, Wajir and Garissa and reduce displacement during dry seasons. Rehabilitation and upgrading of boreholes, pipeline extensions, and solarization further ensured climate-resilient water services for 83,691 people, below the target of 126,278, due to funding shortfalls. UNICEF also contributed to national climate finance analysis and continued to strengthen coordination by chairing or participating in multiple climate-related technical working groups, supporting long-term resilience of water services in underserved communities.
 
Education 
In 2025, UNICEF supported national and county governments to strengthen Kenya’s education system to deliver more inclusive, resilient, and quality learning for children, particularly the most vulnerable. UNICEF’s advocacy and expenditure tracking contributed to a 4 per cent increase in public investment for pre-primary education across 12 ASAL counties in FY 2024/25, promoting more sustainable early learning provision. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MOE) to advance foundational learning reforms through development of the foundational learning guidelines, addressing school readiness and learning poverty. These system-level actions reduced structural bottlenecks affecting young children, particularly in devolved contexts.
Access to education expanded for vulnerable learners through integrated partnerships with government, civil society, and communities. In 2025, UNICEF enabled enrolment of 4,170 additional out-of-school children, bringing cumulative reach since 2022 to 321,814 learners and exceeding UNICEF’s 4-year country programme target of 320,000 children. Inclusion gains were reinforced through approval of Unified English Braille, establishing a national standard for accessible learning materials and improving learning continuity for children with visual impairments. UNICEF also strengthened disability inclusion through teacher training, functional assessments, and linkages to national support systems, addressing barriers to participation, retention, and learning. At the county level, UNICEF supported Garissa County in developing a comprehensive ECDE Bill and supported the county to host the National ECD Stakeholders’ Conference, providing a critical platform for advancing national dialogue and commitment to ECDE reforms.

UNICEF advanced learning quality and innovation at scale by leveraging digital solutions and skills development. Sustained internet connectivity in 659 schools enabled 423,811 learners, including girls and children with disabilities, to access digital learning, exceeding UNICEF’s target of 272,000 due to targeting more populous schools. UNICEF supported teacher capacity through training on ICT integration and digital pedagogy, while expanding access to climate education, online safety content, and e-learning platforms through the Kenya Education Cloud. Complementary investments in skills development reached 65,946 children and young people, including refugees and adolescents, strengthening pathways for learning, empowerment, and employability. In humanitarian and climate-affected contexts, working with the MOE and UNHCR, UNICEF advanced refugee inclusion by aligning the costed education plan for refugees and host communities with the Shirika Plan and supporting registration of over 80 per cent of refugee learners in national systems. Despite severe funding constraints, UNICEF-supported interventions enabled 130,458 children to access formal and non-formal education, achieving 73.2 per cent of the annual target, with most reached in refugee-hosting and climate-affected counties. Moreover, UNICEF advanced 3 out of the 17 counties previously supported to strengthen child-sensitive risk management from planning to implementation of Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans (EPRPs). 

Child protection  
In 2025, the GoK established the State Department for Children Services placed under the Ministry of Gender. UNICEF was instrumental in this process, assisting in shaping the department’s programme structure, objectives, and budget planning, in partnership with the Joining Forces Alliance. The newly established department has the potential to significantly enhance child protection services in the country with improved budget transparency for child protection related allocation, which was much less visible when it was under the State Department of Social Protection. UNICEF supported the establishment of the Department to design sub-programmes, budget, and staffing structure. UNICEF successfully influenced the budget of the Directorate of Children Services to be increased by 400 per cent for child protection services in emergencies including for refugees and by 6 per cent up for field operation costs in the 2025/26 budget. These gains were achieved despite fiscal constraints and reflect strengthened systems, evidence-based planning, and high-level policy engagement under the Bogota pledge (the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence held in 2024).
 
¿UNICEF contributed over 168,000 children experiencing violence receiving protection services in social welfare, justice and health. Further, 23,000 children and caregivers received mental health and psychosocial support services via UNICEF’s support; 2,791 unaccompanied mostly refugee children were reached by UNICEF with support; and a further 4,370 child protection cases were supported with key care and rescue services. UNICEF contributed to the National Positive Parenting programme within the NICHE programme in the second phase of World Bank and FCDO-funded Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project, reaching over 4000 parents and caregivers with key messaging; according to the draft UNICEF Country Programme 2022-2027 Evaluation, this is having a tangible impact on attitudes and behaviors at community level in target counties.  ¿
 
Through the Global UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), in 8 high-prevalence counties, UNICEF-supported programs delivered holistic services to 10,637 girls and women at risk or affected by FGM, alongside community dialogues engaging over 83,000 participants. Capacity building extended to training 40 healthcare professionals and 150 community health promoters on person-centered communication, and equipping partners through a Humanitarian-Development Nexus Toolbox training. These achievements underscore UNICEF’s integrated approach—combining policy reform, grassroots mobilization, and digital innovation—to accelerate abandonment of harmful practices.

Cross-cutting areas & Programme Effectiveness  
UNICEF supported multi-sectoral coordination for preparedness and response to floods, disease outbreaks, and the refugee crisis, reaching over 1.2 million people. Efforts included strengthening Disaster Risk Management (DRM) structures, integrating DRM and resilience into sector plans, and supporting the enactment of national and county DRM bills and policies in 5 counties (Kisumu, Busia, Garissa, Mombasa and Wajir). UNICEF’s coordination role was pivotal in mobilizing resources, supporting government and partners, and implementing the national DRM strategy to mitigate the impacts of droughts and floods.
 
In 2025, disability inclusion advanced significantly in Kenya. The enactment of the Persons with Disability Act and the launch of the first Baseline Assessment on Disability Inclusion in County Governments strengthened policy frameworks and supported commitments from the Global Disability Summit. The NIKO (No-one is kept out) Humanitarian Innovation model reached 1,395 children with disabilities in Kisumu (two sub-counties), while inclusive education initiatives assessed 921 children and trained 95 teachers. 
 
UNICEF’s social and behavioural change interventions in 2025 focused on health promotion, disease prevention, and community engagement, particularly among high-risk and vulnerable populations. Emergency efforts addressed outbreaks of mpox, cholera, and measles, reaching over 26.5 million people with health messages and mobilized a private sector partnership with Safaricom to send out 13.4 million Mpox messages as an in-kind donation. More than 12,000 people participated in community dialogues, and nearly 1,900 used feedback mechanisms to address barriers to care and child protection. Climate-related sensitization campaigns reached over 3 million people in five counties. 
 
UNICEF intensified efforts for adolescent development as a national priority by advancing the National Adolescent Programming Framework, shaping the Adolescent Cash Plus Programme, strengthening the Children Participation guidelines and securing support for adolescent girls through the Power4Girls initiative. Through integrated programming, over 30,000 adolescents gained skilling opportunities, 54,876 adolescent girls were provided with MHM kits and education, 409,978 adolescent girls received with HPV vaccines, 47,500  reached with health awareness through health clubs, while 19,700 adolescents and young people were meaningfully engaged to amplify youth voices in UNICEF programming and advocacy.
 
In 2025, UNICEF supported the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) published, ¿and developed the office’s first Climate strategy (2025-30)¿. UNICEF supported the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) in its proposal for a climate adaptation project (AWARE) in Ewaso Nyiro River Basin, approved to the value of US$20 million by the Adaptation Fund. UNICEF Chairs the Climate Finance working group headed by the Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation, and supported the National Contribution to be 4/4 in child sensitivity¿.
 
Innovation and youth-centered approaches were central to UNICEF’s programming. A UNICEF-implemented behavioral intervention project increased immunization coverage among underserved communities using e-vouchers, digital immunization records (“Afya tracker”), and SMS reminders reaching 4,548 children with vaccines. Digital engagement continued to expand, with more than 439,000 young people actively using Yunitok, including over 128,000 new users in 2025, while an additional 60,000 engaged on YOMA. These platforms offered safe spaces for self-expression, digital learning, and skills acquisition, strengthening young people’s ability to participate in social and economic life. Through Youth for Change, 13,452 young people engaged in climate action, community mobilisation, and peer-led advocacy. Through the BeGreen and EKYAN programmes, UNICEF deepened its work on youth-led climate resilient livelihoods and green entrepreneurship, supporting 152 youth-led enterprises, generating over 846 jobs and improving livelihoods of 4,000 young people (majority female). The development of the BeGreen Africa Kenya Learning Report, produced with the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS), presented comprehensive evidence of the impact of youth-led enterprises, documenting management of 29.9 million kilograms of waste, and strong enterprise-level revenue growth. These findings are now informing policy discussions and shaping national approaches to meaningful youth inclusion in the circular economy.      
 
The office’s digital footprint continues to grow, with nearly 47 million content views and impactful campaigns conducted addressing critical health and social issues (Polio, M-pox, Measles, Typhoid and Access to education) The production of multimedia assets—including videos, human interest stories, and sector-specific articles—has amplified advocacy efforts and informed public discourse.
 
In 2025, UNICEF’s expenditure was US$59 million. Assurance activities were at 100 per cent for programmatic visits and spot checks. The office supported procurement worth nearly US$19 million and managed $8 million in supplies. The approval of the Nairobi Common Service Center signaled a strategic shift, enabling the operations team to align resources with actual needs, to efficiently serve more than 500 colleagues in Nairobi. In terms of cost savings, staff travel costs reduced by US$1.2 million and partner travel reduced by nearly half compared to 2024 –enabling more resources to be utilized for other programme interventions. Finally, UNICEF engaged members of the UNICEF Executive Board and development partners in a roundtable discussion, to review the situation for children, the impacts of ODA decline and the funding landscape, UNICEF’s response and action, and an outline of some priorities for the next Country Programme, garnering support for this work moving forward.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
Declining Donor Funding: There was a notable drop in donor funding in 2025 particularly from public sector donors, which led to significant constraints. Reduced donor support affected all sectors, particularly in health, with a stockout of critical vaccines (BCG, OPV, measles) occurring at the national level. The abrupt stop order of USAID-funded Kenya Sanitation Enabling Environment Project and Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) programmes affected the delivery of sanitation and hygiene services in high-burden open defecation counties, urban informal settlements and WASH in health care facilities in 4 counties. Similarly, paused funding disrupted services for vulnerable children affected by acute malnutrition. In response, UNICEF’s work and catalytic funding support still resulted in some key achievements – for instance the nation-wide measles and typhoid vaccination campaign, where UNICEF’s financial and technical inputs combined with Government resources enabled 16 million children to be reached. UNICEF was able to successfully advocate with the US Government later in the year to re-mobilize funding for nutrition and RMNCAH programming, preventing critical gaps.  UNICEF also worked with the Kenya Sanitation Alliance, which played a stabilizing role, helping counties sustain key sanitation activities using domestic funds. However, despite these achievements, it is likely that reduced development partner funding will continue and will have an adverse effect on services for children in Kenya. 

Government financing for nutrition, child protection and social protection remains limited. Despite education receiving the largest share of the total budget (about 16.6 per cent), allocations for critical programmes like Free Primary Education, Junior Secondary Capitation, and school feeding were cut significantly in fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025/26. ¿There is consequently still much more to do in terms of evidence based advocacy for enhanced Government financing of social sectors. However, UNICEF has had some notable successes in advocating for strengthened financing of social sectors: UNICEF’s engagement with Parliament amid Government funding cuts and Gen-Z tax protests in 2024 restored US$60 million for social services.¿ UNICEF also successfully advocated in 2025 for small budget increases at all levels (from 43.7 per cent in 2024 to 44.5 per cent in 2025 nationally, and from 41.7 per cent to 44.6 per cent at county level); these proportions and actual amounts need to be further strengthened as well as their targeting and execution, to reap the benefits for children, especially as child poverty has risen in the last decade (from 45 to 55 per cent, 2014 to 2022) while GDP has grown by 50 per cent.  

Systemic Bottlenecks 
- Frontline Worker Issues: Frontline workers across sectors face significant capacity gaps due to funding, high turnover, and limited training. The health workers strike and layoffs of health staff due to reduced donor funding constrained immunization service delivery (DTP 3 immunization rates fell from 82 in 2024 to 80 per cent in 2025). The ratio of child protection workers to the child population remains critically low despite some small advances in recent years. Community Health Promoters are overburdened as increasing demands are put on for service delivery and particularly data collection. 
- Government Coordination Issues: Coordination across government entities remained complex and resource intensive. Overlapping mandates, fragmented systems, and the need for alignment across ministries, counties, and development partners. For instance, the adolescent health landscape remains complex and faces fragmented coordination and weak multisectoral collaboration across the health, education, and social sectors.  Sub-optimal coordination platforms for county and national governments affected WASH sector progress which needs deliberate engagement with county and national governments to support water sector reform, starting with activation of the Intergovernmental Water Sector Coordination Framework. There continues to be no clear governance or coordination for climate change in education.¿ And mandates between national county levels over the child protection function causes challenges. Finally, the Ministry of Youth is now recently responsible for supporting secondary education, with limited resources. 
- Government budget release and absorption: there remains an issue of the speed of Government release of funding from national to county level which can affect implementation; further, county capacity for absorption and utilization of funding for programming is also an ongoing challenge. 
In response to these challenges, UNICEF continues to put a focus on systems strengthening support, particularly strengthening frontline workers through capacity development initiatives and advocacy for financing. UNICEF, as a multi-sectoral agency, will continue to support cross-sectoral coordination and integration of programming through its technical and upstream engagements. UNICEF continues to strengthen capacity at county level to execute and utilize funding from social service programming in support of results for children and this will be an area of focus also moving forward into the next Country Programme. 
 
Lesson
A key lesson from 2025 is that UNICEF’s ability to sustain and even expand critical services for children in Kenya, despite significant declines in ODA and donor funding, highlights the value of adaptability, strong government partnerships, and innovative approaches. By leveraging domestic resources, piloting new solutions, and maintaining evidence-based advocacy, UNICEF was able to mitigate the effects of some of the funding gaps and continue delivering impactful results for the most vulnerable populations. This experience underscores the importance of resilience, systems strengthening, and strategic collaboration to ensure continuity of essential services in challenging financial environments.
 
Way forward
Moving forward into next year and into the next Country Programme period, UNICEF will work to meet the above challenges and issues. UNICEF will continue to anchor its work in national priorities, particularly the new Government of Kenya Medium-Term Plan V (MTP V), and the new UNSDCF 2027-2032, as well as the new UNICEF Global Strategic Plan (SP) 2026-2029. The organization is committed to leveraging UN joint programmes (JPs) which are now being implemented, where it leads in Water and Nutrition JPs, and supporting the devolution agenda and social protection to ensure that interventions reach the most vulnerable populations where they live. Aligning to the global SP, UNICEF Kenya will prioritize key, catalytic areas of work, aiming for greater scale and intentionality in reaching vulnerable populations of children, while also maintaining a sharp equity approach ensuring that no child is left behind. Thematically, a central focus will be on systems strengthening and supporting the Government to scale up social sector and protection interventions to address multidimensional child poverty, at policy and financing levels, as well as supporting some service delivery on the ground, especially in humanitarian contexts. Public finance for children remains a core evidence and advocacy area, and UNICEF Kenya will continue to support budget advocacy for up-scaling of social services – even amidst possible donor funding decline. UNICEF will integrate a strong climate resilience component into its programming to support sustainable and resilient services, both within the WASH sector and across other sectoral areas. Recognizing the growing youth bulge, UNICEF will prioritize skills development and employability for adolescents and youth. All of these results will be achieved in part through prioritizing and leveraging partnerships, both with government and with public and private donors, to diversify financing and funding sources and enhance programme sustainability.

Lesotho is a landlocked country with a population of about 2 million people, of whom around 58 percent live in rural areas. Over time, the country has made gradual progress in human development, moving into the medium human development category for the first time in 2023. Despite this progress, living conditions for many families remain fragile, particularly for children. Lesotho is classified as a lower middle-income country, with an average income of about USD 1,250 per person, yet child deprivations remain widespread. 




The overall child rights situation in Lesotho reflects uneven progress across key outcome areas aligned with the UNICEF Strategic Plan and the 2030 Agenda. Poverty remains a central driver of child vulnerability, particularly in rural and mountainous areas where livelihoods are limited and access to services is constrained. Recent multidimensional child poverty analysis estimates that 46% of children are living in poverty, yet less than 20% of the poorest children are receiving child grants. Children in poor households are more likely to experience food insecurity, interrupted schooling, limited access to health care, and heightened exposure to protection risks. Geographic isolation, climate shocks, and structural inequality further compound these vulnerabilities, reinforcing intergenerational cycles of deprivation. Public spending on social sectors has flatlined in recent years, making it difficult for the government to adequately finance the expansion of essential services such as health, social protection, education, water and sanitation. 




Child nutrition outcomes remain a critical concern. An estimated 36% of children under five are stunted. This situation undermines physical growth, cognitive development, and future earnings. Persistent food insecurity, especially in rural areas, continues to weaken children’s diets and household coping capacity, with direct implications for child survival, development, and school readiness. In the area of child survival and health, Lesotho has recorded notable improvements over the past decade. Under-five mortality declined from 76 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2018 to 54 per 1,000 in 2023, while neonatal mortality declined from 36 to 26 per 1,000 live births over the same period. However, these improvements mask persistent inequities in access and quality of care. Just over half of the population has access to essential health services, and a significant share of households continues to face catastrophic health expenditures.




Lesotho continues to face one of the highest HIV burdens globally, with HIV remaining a major determinant of child and adolescent vulnerability. While access to prevention and treatment services has improved, gaps persist for children and adolescents living with HIV, particularly during adolescence, where treatment continuity and adherence remain challenges. The high prevalence places sustained pressure on health, social protection, and education systems, with implications for child survival, wellbeing, and long-term human capital development.




Access to basic education is high, with near-universal enrolment at the primary level. However, learning outcomes, progression, and early learning participation remain key challenges. Transition rates from primary to secondary education remain constrained, at around 82 percent, while participation in early learning remains low, with only about 28 percent of children aged 2–4 engaged in early learning activities. Poverty, food insecurity, long travel distances to schools, and household stress continue to disrupt attendance and learning, particularly for children in rural and low-income communities. Children and adolescents in Lesotho also face persistent protection and gender-related risks. Early marriage and adolescent pregnancy remain prevalent, particularly among girls from poor and rural households, limiting educational attainment and increasing health and protection risks. Evidence shows that many children experience physical (25.14%), emotional (16.5%), or sexual violence (20.8%) before the age of 18, with long-lasting consequences for well-being, learning, and social inclusion. While policy and legal frameworks exist, access to prevention, response, and enforcement services remains uneven, especially outside urban centres.




During the 2025 reporting period, several contextual developments had direct implications for children and for UNICEF’s ability to deliver results at scale. Climate variability and elevated food prices persisted, intensifying food insecurity in rural areas. An estimated 335,000 people (around 22 percent of the rural population) faced crisis levels of food insecurity. Slower economic growth, uncertainty in export markets, and limited fiscal space constrained investments in social sectors. Declining external development financing further reduced resources, affecting service expansion and the sustainability of some interventions especially in the health sector and placing additional pressure on frontline service delivery systems. High youth unemployment, continues to affect household resilience, with many families relying on informal livelihoods. This increased economic stress in the context of limited investments in children’s nutrition, health, education, and protection. For adolescents, limited opportunities heightened risks of school dropout, negative coping strategies, and exploitation. While national policy frameworks on gender equality and child protection are in place, gaps in implementation and service reach persisted, particularly in rural and hard-to-reach areas. 




Overall, the 2025 context underscored the need to balance shock-responsive and life-saving interventions with longer-term systems strengthening interventions. Delivering results at scale required sharper targeting, an explicit equity focus, and sustained support to national systems to maintain functionality during periods of stress. Viewed through the lens of the 2030 Agenda, the situation in 2025 highlights how persistent poverty, food insecurity, and gender inequality continue to constrain the reach and quality of services, with children from poor and rural households, children with disabilities, and socially excluded adolescents most affected. Addressing these disparities requires adaptive, equity-focused approaches that keep children’s rights at the centre of development efforts.

In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Lesotho to improve the well-being of children by strengthening national systems, expanding equitable access to essential services, and responding to emerging shocks. Despite a challenging context marked by climate stress, fiscal constraints, and service delivery pressures, progress was achieved across health, nutrition, education, WASH, social protection, and child protection. While service delivery remained essential in some areas, particularly in response to shocks, priority was placed on reinforcing national systems so that gains could be sustained beyond the reporting period.


 


a) Children in their First Decade (Decade 1)


Through ‘Decade 1’ programming, which focuses on children aged 0–9 years, UNICEF contributed to improved access and quality of health, nutrition, immunization, early childhood education, social protection, safe water and sanitation and birth registration services. 


 


Specifically, UNICEF advanced a strengthened Primary Health Care (PHC) approach through national policy reforms, including the Community Health Workers’ Policy and Strategy, an Investment Case for Community Health, and a concept note for a high-level PHC dialogue. Service quality and frontline capacity for child and maternal health were strengthened across all ten districts through provision of mobile ultrasound machines, improving community-level diagnostic capacity. UNICEF also engaged community champions, including wives of Principal Chiefs, to strengthen local partnerships for PHC delivery. At community level, digital innovations such as the Community Health Information System improved real-time data capture and coordination, enabling village health workers to identify risks earlier, support referrals, and strengthen continuity of care between communities and facilities. These efforts reinforced government ownership and contributed to more responsive and equitable PHC services. To strengthen the continuum of care, UNICEF supported newborn care guidelines, continuous professional development, simulation-based training, and standardized patient approaches. These measures established consistent benchmarks for care delivery nationwide. Their application translated into tangible improvements in clinical practice, most notably at Ntsekhe Hospital, which reported zero maternal and neonatal deaths between January and September 2025. Targeted training in emergency obstetric and newborn care, emergency triage and assessment, and integrated management of childhood illness further strengthened health workers’ capacity to manage complications and common childhood conditions. 


  


Nutrition outcomes improved through a combination of food systems engagement, policy reform, financing advocacy, and service delivery. UNICEF advanced the food systems agenda through high-level advocacy on multisectoral platforms, including SUN and REACH. With support from the Regional Office, a scoping mission on Taylor First Foods was conducted and disseminated, highlighting the need to better understand children’s diets and informing preliminary engagement toward a market survey and landscape analysis on overweight and obesity. UNICEF also supported governance and financing reforms to position nutrition as a national development priority. Through engagement in the Nutrition for Growth process and sustained policy dialogue, progress was made toward establishing a dedicated national nutrition budget line. High-level advocacy, including engagement of traditional leaders and national champions, strengthened accountability and mobilized political commitment. Alongside these system-level efforts, acute malnutrition treatment achieved a 90 percent recovery rate, reflecting strengthened case management and community screening. Integrated nutrition services reached more than 31,000 caregivers and children nationwide, while iron and folic acid supplementation reached over 31,000 pregnant women, contributing to improved maternal nutrition and birth outcomes amid high food insecurity. Together, these results contributed to national efforts to reduce stunting and advance SDG 2, particularly in food-insecure and rural communities. 


  


UNICEF advanced equitable access to immunization services through people-centered, equity-focused approaches. Working with government and civil society partners, more than 1,000 zero-dose children and over 8,000 under-immunized children were identified and referred for vaccination. Community-based approaches, including interpersonal communication, local outreach, and targeted mobilization, addressed barriers related to access, trust, and information. Significant gains were achieved during the Measles-Rubella campaign, which reached 68 percent national coverage—an improvement of 22 percentage points compared to 2022. UNICEF’s contribution included strengthening coordination structures, supporting campaign preparedness, integrating sex-disaggregated and equity-focused data tools, and expanding community engagement. These efforts demonstrated how people-centered approaches, combined with strong coordination and data use, can reverse declining trends even in constrained environments. 


  


With the aim of improving early childhood development outcomes, UNICEF contributed to progress in foundational learning by strengthening teacher quality, assessment systems, and early childhood education expansion. In a context where access to basic education is high but learning outcomes and early learning participation remain uneven, UNICEF focused on system-level reforms to improve quality and equity. Accredited pre-service and in-service teacher training programmes strengthened pedagogy and addressed the long-standing challenge of unqualified early childhood educators. In 2025, 221 teachers graduated from accredited programmes, increasing the proportion of qualified early childhood educators beyond national targets and strengthening the professional pipeline for early learning. UNICEF also supported the scale-up of digital formative assessment tools and district-level capacity to monitor learning outcomes, strengthening evidence-based planning and feedback loops between classrooms, districts, and national decision-makers. Advocacy informed by costing simulations contributed to the expansion of reception classes, advancing the national commitment to one year of free pre-primary education. Together, these efforts improved access to quality early learning for more than 47,000 learners and strengthened the foundations for improved learning outcomes.


 


Access to safe water and sanitation for young children and communities was strengthened through rehabilitation of rural water systems and community WASH facilities. More than 28,000 people gained improved access to safe and reliable water, strengthening resilience in drought-affected areas and reducing the burden of water collection for women and children. Community water and health committees were trained in operation and maintenance, reinforcing local ownership and sustainability while contributing to improved health and nutrition outcomes.


 


b) Children and Adolescents in their Second Decade (Decade 2)


Several milestones were achieved in decade 2, which targets children and adolescents aged 10–19 years, with a focus on improving learning transitions, protection from violence, adolescent health including HIV and sexual and reproductive health, climate resilience, and inclusivity of services in schools. 


 


Most notably, UNICEF strengthened governance, teacher development, inclusive curriculum and assessment, and evidence-based planning by the Ministry of Education and Training. A Teacher Continuous Professional Development Framework was developed, alongside district-level capacity building that reached 220 District Education Officers across all ten districts on Results-Based Management, planning, budgeting, and reporting, supporting development of three-year district education sector plans and a medium-term expenditure framework. Evidence generation advanced through completion of a Teaching at the Right Level feasibility study and implementation of the 2025 National Learning Assessments for Grades 3 and 7 in 209 sample schools, with analysis ongoing. System accountability was reinforced through completion of the Joint Education Sector Review and initiation of the education sector analysis and new Education Sector Plan. An Alternative Learning Pathway programme for out-of-school children was designed with primary and lower secondary streams, alongside preparations for a household survey to identify 4,500 out-of-school children. Through the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) KIX 19 Africa Hub, the Ministry of Education and Training received technical support from the Kenya Institute of Special Education to strengthen inclusive education curriculum and assessment. Digital transformation support included a Digital Maturity Assessment under GPE Tech4Edu, development of a tech-enabled classroom observation tool, procurement of 2,445 tablets, and progress on EMIS strengthening, including migration of 2020–2024 datasets. Lesotho Learning Passport users increased to 10,482, with 17,135 course registrations and 1,526 completions in 2025. Education financing was strengthened through mobilization of LSL 1 million via the inaugural Prime Minister’s Golf Day.


 


UNICEF supported progress in strengthening child protection systems by improving legal identity, standardizing services, and reinforcing prevention and response mechanisms at community and institutional levels. A major achievement was the expansion of digital birth registration, which provided more than 50,000 children with legal identity, including those from social assistance households. This represents a substantial increase from 16,600 registrations in 2024, driven by digitalization of the birth registration system and intensified outreach. This reduced barriers to accessing services and strengthened linkages between child protection, social protection, and civil registration systems. UNICEF supported the design and rollout of the digital system and coordination with relevant ministries to promote sustainability. Standardized manuals and guidelines were disseminated to improve the quality and consistency of child protection services. Capacity building for frontline workers and community structures strengthened identification, referral, and response to cases of violence, abuse, and neglect. Positive parenting initiatives supported caregivers to adopt non-violent practices and foster safer family environments, addressing household-level risk factors. 

 

UNICEF strengthened HIV programme performance by improving data accuracy, service quality, and integration with adolescent health systems, including publication of the HIV Estimates 2025, completion of data quality audits in all 10 districts, and establishment of district-level data clinics to improve reliability for planning and resource allocation. Progress toward the 95-95-95 targets was sustained, with viral load suppression reaching 99 percent nationally. Despite resource disruptions, service delivery and continuity of care were maintained: 7,601 children aged 0–9 years and 17,919 adolescents aged 10–19 years (88 percent female) received HIV testing, and 70 percent of adolescents living with HIV (72 percent female; 68 percent male) were sustained on antiretroviral treatment. UNICEF supported a nationwide HIV service assessment, and a mid-year programme review to identify gaps and corrective actions, while strengthening system capacity through on-the-job training of more than 400 health workers in HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and PMTCT. These efforts contributed to approximately 5,400 individuals being initiated on PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis) in 2025, including adolescent girls and young women, and enabled UNICEF, through partnerships with civil society organizations, to reach over 20,600 adolescents and young people with HIV and SRHR information and services, while strengthening youth leadership through support to the National AIDS Commission Youth Consortium.


 


In 2025, UNICEF improved safe, climate-resilient, and inclusive WASH services in schools by upgrading facilities in 10 rural schools, benefiting 1,434 learners (752 boys and 682 girls) and 45 teachers. The upgraded infrastructure provided gender-sensitive and inclusive sanitation, including facilities supporting menstrual hygiene management, contributing to healthier school environments and improved conditions for girls’ attendance and participation. Hygiene and water conservation practices were strengthened through school and community-based initiatives in Maseru, Mohale’s Hoek, and Thaba-Tseka districts, reinforcing behaviour change beyond the classroom. To sustain results, WASH clubs were established in participating schools in line with national WASH in Schools guidelines, strengthening learner leadership, routine maintenance of facilities, and continued access to safe water and sanitation. These results contributed to safer learning environments and increased resilience of school WASH services in climate-affected rural areas.


 


c) Social Policy


In 2025, UNICEF contributed to reducing child poverty by strengthening Lesotho’s social protection, child rights and public finance systems. Support focused on digitizing social assistance delivery, upgrading national information systems, expanding access to complementary services for Child Grant Programme beneficiaries through a Cash Plus approach, and improving budget transparency, child participation, and evidence-based decision-making for social sector financing. 


 


Significant progress was made in strengthening social protection systems and expanding coverage. Digital payment coverage under the Child Grant Programme increased from 13,000 households in 2024 to over 21,000 households in 2025, reducing travel distances and costs for caregivers, improving efficiency, and promoting financial inclusion for vulnerable families. This expansion was enabled through UNICEF’s technical support to the government’s scale-up plan, training of social workers to support the transition to mobile payments, and partnerships with private sector providers, including Vodacom and Econet. Core delivery systems were strengthened through major upgrades to the National Information System for Social Assistance (NISSA) and the Management Information System for Social Assistance (MISSA), including development of system design documentation, operational manuals, and quality assurance frameworks. On-the-job training and study tours supported national capacity, system ownership, and sustainability.


 


Integrated service delivery under the Cash Plus approach expanded access to essential services. Over 3,000 people accessed nutrition, WASH, and birth registration services through 31 community-based nutrition clubs and rehabilitated water systems benefiting approximately 9,200 people, including 704 children under five. In addition, beneficiary selection and delivery models for renewable energy solutions were finalized, targeting 1,000 Child Grant Programme households. Social assistance coverage expanded substantially during the reporting period. UNICEF provided strategic leadership to align partners around a unified Cash Plus agenda, including development of a Cash Plus Integration Framework and a Theory of Change for nutrition-sensitive social protection, supporting more coherent planning and implementation across sectors.


 


Budget transparency and public participation improved through engagement of more than 100 children and young people in 10 district-level pre-budget consultations, with inputs reflected in Ministry of Finance reports. Public access to fiscal information improved through publication of the Citizens’ Budget online and implementation of Open Budget Survey recommendations. Youth engagement was further strengthened through the Youth Power Hub (YPH), enabling young people to influence budget decisions through online platforms and policy dialogues. The YPH provided capacity building support on adaptive programming, corporate governance and public policy advocacy through district workshops, mentorship and coaching of individual organizations. 


 


Evidence-based advocacy led to increased investments in children. In this regard, UNICEF produced three budget briefs, three policy notes, and a comprehensive nutrition budget analysis, contributing to higher allocations for health, education, nutrition, and social protection, including a 10 percent increase in social assistance transfer values in the FY 2025/2026 budget. The capacity of the government to monitor budget execution was also strengthened through training Ministry of Finance officials in expenditure tracking and in problem-driven public financial management reforms. 


 


National capacities for quality data and evidence were strengthened to support child-focused policymaking and accountability. UNICEF supported final review of the revised Statistics Amendment Bill, which will replace the 2011 Statistics Act and enable more timely generation and use of official statistics. Preparations for the 2026 Population Census advanced through provision of IT equipment and technical assistance to improve data processing and secure storage systems. UNICEF also supported timely delivery of the 2025 Voluntary National Review through technical and financial assistance, enabling Lesotho to meet international reporting obligations and demonstrate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. Together, these investments strengthened the availability, credibility, and use of child-related data to inform policy, planning, and financing decisions.


 


 


d) Programme and Operational Effectiveness


In 2025, UNICEF strengthened programme effectiveness by improving how evidence, coordination, communication, and accountability were used to support results for children. These enablers were particularly important in the context of fiscal constraints and overlapping shocks, allowing UNICEF and partners to prioritize actions, respond more quickly to emerging risks, and sustain delivery of results at scale. Faced with reduced and uncertain financing, UNICEF adopted more agile, results-oriented planning and monitoring approaches to focus limited resources on the most critical results for children and maintain effective support to government systems. Innovative digital financial oversight and partnership management tools strengthened timely decision-making on programme implementation, enabling earlier identification of gaps and efficiency risks. Lessons from this approach informed broader use of similar practices within the region, contributing to more consistent results-focused management beyond the country programme.


 


Programme monitoring systems were strengthened through practical digital innovations that enhanced government ownership, accountability, and use of data. For example, UNICEF supported the Government of Lesotho to operationalize a web-based community feedback mechanism under the Accountability to Affected Populations framework, enabling systematic capture, tracking, and response to caregiver and community concerns. The platform was handed over for full government ownership, strengthening institutional capacity to use community feedback as part of routine service monitoring and decision-making. In parallel, UNICEF piloted a digital case management system to track health worker training coverage and follow-up, demonstrating a scalable approach for workforce monitoring and informing the design of a government-owned system planned for expansion. Digital data collection was also strengthened in the education sector through support to the Joint Education Sector Review, where mobile data tools replaced paper-based reporting and improved timeliness and completeness of school-level data. Improved use of routine monitoring data supported earlier identification of implementation bottlenecks and informed corrective action across sectors, contributing to more adaptive programme delivery.
