Social and Behavior Change (SBC) systems further enhanced programme effectiveness by systematically linking community insights with service delivery and policy decisions. SBC capacity was strengthened across all ten districts, enabling rapid socio-behavioral assessments that informed national strategies, including the draft Ministry of Health/Expanded Programme on Immunization 2025–2029 SBC Change Strategy. Evidence generated through these processes showed that 95 percent of caregivers expressed willingness to vaccinate their children, informing more targeted immunization responses. Inclusive approaches, including gender and disability-focused analyses, improved understanding of barriers affecting women, caregivers, and persons with disabilities and supported more people-centered interventions. 


 


Communication and advocacy functioned as strategic enablers of results by amplifying evidence, mobilizing stakeholders, and strengthening accountability. Evidence-based messaging reached more than one million people, including people with disabilities, through inclusive and accessible formats. Digital platforms and media engagement expanded reach and visibility, with social media campaigns reaching over 81,000 people, while strengthened media relations increased coverage across print, radio, and television. High-level advocacy and community engagement reinforced accountability and ownership, including mobilization of traditional leaders and youth platforms, ensuring that community priorities and youth perspectives informed policy dialogue, service delivery, and financing decisions at national and local levels. Despite resource constraints that led to the closure of the U-Report platform, UNICEF engaged a total of 17,521 volunteers through partner-supported initiatives in 2025, with 10,315 volunteers remaining active, including through youth-led climate action, social accountability, and policy consultation processes. These approaches strengthened the quality and relevance of volunteer engagement while maintaining meaningful youth participation in priority programme areas. 




Across these enabling areas, programme and operational effectiveness were further strengthened through sustained attention to gender equality and inclusion, fit-for-purpose use of technology, and strong internal governance. Systematic use of sex-disaggregated data, gender and disability analyses, and inclusive design approaches improved understanding of barriers affecting women, girls, caregivers, and persons with disabilities, enabling more equitable planning and delivery of services. At the same time, investments in use of technology emphasized practical digital solutions aligned with government capacity, improving access to timely information, reducing manual processes, and supporting adaptive programme management. These efforts were underpinned by strengthened governance, risk management, and internal coordination mechanisms, which enabled earlier identification of implementation risks and more efficient use of limited resources in support of programme results.




Together, these investments strengthened the systems, capacities, and partnerships needed to deliver coherent, accountable, and results-oriented support to national efforts for children. By improving evidence, feedback, and communication informed action, UNICEF enhanced its ability to support sustainable progress for children despite significant external constraints.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges


Despite notable progress in 2025, several factors constrained the pace and scale of results for children in Lesotho. Persistent systemic bottlenecks slowed delivery in key sectors. In immunization, human resource shortages, data quality challenges, and unreliable population denominators constrained routine coverage, even where demand-generation efforts were strong. In child protection, funding shortfalls delayed the full rollout of digitized case management systems, limiting interoperability, and timely follow-up of cases. Fiscal constraints and funding volatility further affected sustainability and scale. Tight public finances and declining external financing slowed service expansion and delayed some planned system upgrades, including social protection and complementary service delivery. 


 


These pressures required difficult prioritization and sequencing of interventions rather than comprehensive scale-up. Sustaining service quality under fiscal pressure remains a major risk, underscoring the need for more cost-effective delivery models, stronger domestic financing, and clearer prioritization of child-focused services. Strengthening sub-national implementation capacity also emerged as a critical challenge. While national policies and frameworks are in place, uneven capacity at district and community levels limited consistent translation of policy into results, particularly in child protection, early learning, and WASH system maintenance. In parallel, improving data integration and use remains an unfinished agenda, with greater emphasis needed on analysis, interoperability, and routine use of data for decision-making, not only data collection. Preventing and responding to violence against children similarly requires stronger implementation and financing of existing policy frameworks, alongside sustained community-level prevention and accountability mechanisms.


 


Lessons learned


Several approaches proved effective in advancing results for children in 2025 despite a challenging operating environment. A key lesson is that system-focused investments delivered the most sustainable gains. Progress was strongest where UNICEF supported national frameworks, standards, and institutional capacity rather than stand-alone activities. This included strengthened clinical standards and training systems in health, accredited teacher training in early childhood education, upgraded social protection information systems, and standardized child protection guidelines. These investments enabled more consistent service delivery across districts and reinforced government ownership. 


 


People-centered and equity-focused approaches also improved reach and responsiveness, particularly for marginalized populations. In immunization and social and behavior, change programming, community engagement, social listening, and real-time feedback mechanisms helped identify barriers to service uptake and adapt strategies accordingly. During the Measles-Rubella campaign, these approaches contributed to improved coverage despite broader system constraints. Similarly, integrated Cash Plus interventions helped address multiple, intersecting deprivations faced by poor households.


 


The experience further reinforced that integration increases complexity but improves impact. Linking cash transfers with nutrition and WASH services strengthened the effectiveness of social assistance, while alignment between teacher training, classroom assessment, and policy advocacy supported coherent progress in foundational learning. School-based WASH interventions similarly demonstrated the value of integrated approaches in addressing health, education, and gender-related outcomes. These experiences confirmed that integrated approaches are essential to addressing complex child vulnerabilities, but depend on strong coordination mechanisms, shared data, and realistic assessments of institutional capacity. 


 


Another important lesson is that institutional acceptance is as critical as technical quality, particularly for digital solutions. Experience with establishing a government-hosted web-based community feedback mechanism under the Accountability to Affected Populations framework demonstrated that close collaboration with government counterparts, alignment with existing business processes, and use of standard technologies are essential for adoption and sustainability. Technically sound solutions that are insufficiently aligned with institutional realities face significant uptake risks. Finally, the year reinforced that internal efficiency and coordination directly influence external results. Improvements in programme review platforms, partnership oversight, and funds monitoring enabled earlier identification of bottlenecks and faster corrective action. While largely invisible to communities, these internal adaptations were critical to maintaining delivery of momentum in a constrained environment.


 


Future outlook


Building on the lessons from 2025, UNICEF will adjust its approach to enhance the focus on impact and sustainability in alignment with the global strategy. Priority will be given to deepening systems strengthening work, with a sharper focus on sub-national capacity, institutional functionality, and domestic financing. Integrated approaches, particularly Cash Plus, SBC-informed service delivery, and school-based platforms, will be further refined to reduce fragmentation and improve efficiency. Digital and data initiatives will increasingly emphasize government ownership, interoperability, and usability, drawing on lessons from community feedback mechanisms and sectoral information platforms. UNICEF will prioritize solutions that align with national systems and decision-making processes to enable scale and sustainability. 


 


In parallel, UNICEF will continue to manage the transition to the Multi-Country Office (MCO) model in a way that safeguards programme continuity and country-level responsiveness. The transition will focus on clarifying roles and accountabilities, strengthening coordination across countries, and ensuring that technical support, quality assurance, and decision-making remain timely and closely linked to national priorities. Lessons from 2025 on systems strengthening, digital oversight, and results-focused management will inform how the MCO model is operationalized, with particular attention to maintaining strong government engagement and effective support to sub-national implementation.


 


Equity will remain central to future actions. UNICEF will continue to strengthen real-time feedback, community engagement, and disaggregated monitoring to ensure programmes remain responsive to the needs of the most marginalized children, especially in the context of climate and economic shocks. Overall, the experience of 2025 demonstrates that progress for children in Lesotho depends on adaptive programming, strong partnerships, and continuous learning. Applying these lessons will help UNICEF enhance its contribution to national priorities and accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals, ensuring that no child is left behind.

Ranked 183rd of 193 countries on the Human Development Index (HDI) in 2023, Madagascar faces deep-seated challenges limiting progress and restricting children's access to essential social services. Systemic gaps in service quality, geographic equity, and institutional capacity continue affecting children’s well-being, particularly in rural and remote regions. Rapid demographic growth further complicates this situation: the population reached an estimated 32 million in 2024. 
 
This also explains why national GDP growth of approximately 4 per cent in 2024 did not translate into significant growth in GDP per capita. Indeed, Madagascar’s GDP per capita hovered around US$453 in 2024, below its 2019 (pre-COVID) value of $467.[1]  Persistent inflation of 7–8 per cent continued eroding the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families. While an estimated 75.2 per cent of the population live under the national poverty line, in regions such as the Great South and the South-East, poverty often exceeds 91 per cent, due to insufficient market integration and the cumulative impact of seasonal climate shocks. Sustained demographic pressure and a predominantly informal economy strain already fragile infrastructures and basic services, which struggle to keep pace with the needs of a population composed predominantly of children and youth.
 
Madagascar increased its regional influence in 2025, hosting the 5th Indian Ocean Commission (IOC) Summit in April, focussing on maritime security and food resilience, and later in August the 45th Southern African Development Community (SADC) Summit, which focused on industrialization. After the SADC Summit, Madagascar was due to assume SADC’s rotating presidency, with the Government positioning the country as a leader in regional institutions. 
 
Madagascar’s major political event of 2025 was the emergence of the ‘Youth Gen Z’ protest movement. Beginning in September as youth demonstrations against chronic water shortages and electricity outages, mainly in the capital city, the movement rapidly evolved into a broader uprising against systemic governance failures, and ultimately led to the regime’s fall as the military aligned with the protesters. Colonel Michael Randrianirina was sworn in as President of Madagascar on 17 October, and a civil government was formed to oversee a ‘National Refoundation’ agenda. The President announced that the transition was due to last 24 months, during which national consultations would take place, as well as a constitutional reform and new presidential elections. The President also pledged to restore essential public services. While the African Union suspended Madagascar over the military’s seizure of power, most development partners did not interrupt their aid and chose to support the transition government, seeing the power shift as an opportunity for necessary reforms. However, Madagascar had to step down from the SADC Presidency.
 
On the social front, the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey 7 (MICS 7) – conducted in 2025 by the National Institute of Statistics – revealed that Madagascar still has much to do to realize children’s rights. Most indicators do not show significant progress compared to the previous survey in 2018. 
 
Under-five mortality remains high at about 73 per 1,000 live births; only 21 per cent of children aged 24 months are fully vaccinated, while 17 per cent of this age group have never received any vaccine doses. 
 
Access to basic water services decreased from 41 to 39 per cent between 2018 and 2025, while access to basic sanitation and basic hygiene both lost 10 percentage points over the same period (from 17 per cent to 7 per cent and from 23 per cent to 13 per cent respectively). Concerningly, 90 per cent of drinking water samples nationwide show high levels of E. coli contamination, directly contributing to high prevalence of diarrhoeal diseases and chronic malnutrition among children under five.
 
The education sector saw modest improvements in primary enrolment, from 76 per cent in 2018 to 78 per cent in 2025. Enrollment in lower and upper secondary education remains particularly limited – at 30 per cent and 15 per cent respectively – with pronounced disparities by region and wealth quintile. Structural challenges, particularly the shortage of trained teachers, continue to hinder both access to and quality of learning. Primary school completion rates are low, falling to 47 per cent in 2025 from 56 per cent in 2018, while only 18 per cent of children aged 7–14 demonstrate minimum competencies in reading and 13 per cent in mathematics. Violence against children remains prevalent, with 85 per cent of children aged 1–14 exposed to violent discipline (physical or psychological) at home.  
 
However, some positive results are also noted. In particular, chronic malnutrition (stunting) decreased from 42 per cent in 2018 to 37 per cent in 2025; while maternal mortality fell sharply from 426 to 298 deaths per 100,000 live births in the same period. Also, postnatal care is now offered to 84 per cent of mothers and 84 per cent of children in the two days after birth, compared to 72 per cent and 78 per cent respectively in 2018. Remarkably, pre-school access doubled from 15 to 29 per cent of children aged 3-5. Regarding social protection, 9 per cent of children now live in households that have received at least one cash transfer, compared to 2 per cent in 2018.
 
Girls and adolescent girls continue facing overlapping deprivations across sectors and life stages. Harmful gender norms, extreme poverty and service gaps converge to drive school exclusion, early and unintended pregnancy, child marriage, and heightened exposure to violence. In rural areas, 31 per cent of girls aged 15–19 experience early pregnancy. Violence is pervasive: 20 per cent girls aged 15–19 report physical or sexual violence. Child marriage remains widespread, with 42 per cent of girls married before 18, an increase from 39 per cent in 2018. These intersecting risks are mutually reinforcing, curtailing girls’ learning, health, safety, and future opportunities, particularly in climate-affected and rural areas. 
 
Climate change increasingly drives humanitarian needs in Madagascar. Five cyclones and tropical storms affected the country, causing widespread flooding and population displacement, destroying critical health and education facilities. These climate-related shocks disrupted education by damaging classrooms and forcing schools to serve as temporary shelters, affecting over 197,000 students. By the end of 2025, approximately 711,400 people had been affected by these repeated hazards. In the Great South, the severe drought at the end of 2024 and serious floods in the first quarter of 2025 severely affected crops, significantly compromising infant and young child feeding and child wasting, resulting in a severe nutrition crisis.

In 2025, UNICEF Madagascar operated in an environment of deep structural vulnerabilities, repeated climate shocks and a rapidly evolving political landscape. Despite these challenges, UNICEF worked with the Government to sustain essential services and protect the most vulnerable children. The organization supported national systems to maintain access to education; water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH); child protection; nutrition; and health services, while strengthening service quality. UNICEF also collected critical data and evidence on children to inform advocacy efforts and reinforced alliances with United Nations agencies and donors to advance children’s rights, align strategies, leverage comparative advantages and mobilize resources.
 
In the health sector, a landmark achievement was the World Health Organization (WHO) announcement of the end of the polio outbreak in Madagascar. This result was obtained with UNICEF support, in close collaboration with WHO and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, after seven nationwide vaccination campaigns in 2023 and 2024, which reached more than 19 million people across the country. UNICEF also continued working with the Ministry of Health to catch up children under five who had not been vaccinated during the COVID epidemic. A total of 384,137 zero dose children were vaccinated in 2025, bringing the cumulative total to 824,941 children reached over the past two years, 78.4 per cent of the target. UNICEF also supported an HPV vaccine introduction campaign, reaching 1.75 million girls aged 9–14. Routine immunization improved in priority regions supported by UNICEF, resulting into 83 per cent coverage for DTP/Penta3 according to administrative data.  
 
Child health services improved in coverage and quality in UNICEF-supported areas, with 132,490 children with diarrhoea, 135,965 with fever, and 28,729 with pneumonia receiving appropriate case management. Maternal and newborn health outcomes advanced with 849 health facilities (30 per cent of the national total) receiving direct support. These facilities – which were equipped with delivery and examination tables, and privacy screens – recorded 121,051 live births. 
 
A major gamechanger has been UNICEF’s effort to strengthen community health, both at community level and as part of the health system coordination mechanism at central level, with the Mastercard Foundation as a new key partner. The number of community health workers directly supported by UNICEF increased from 7,870 to 8,174 with 304 new community workers trained. With European Union financial assistance, UNICEF started implementing an important project to rehabilitate 42 health facilities in four regions, including one national reference hospital. UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Health to establish coordination platforms, ensure policy coherence and partner alignment, train frontline workers, provide equipment and essential medicines, and digitalize primary health care.
 
Despite these gains, several challenges persisted, including data reliability, scarcity and inequitable distribution of health workforce, limited access and utilization of health services and a weak accountability mechanism. 
 
UNICEF safeguarded and expanded essential nutrition and child development services, amid cyclones, drought-related emergencies, reduced humanitarian funding and a continuous complex programmatic environment.
 
Through active high-level advocacy and facilitation of the visit of the Scaling-up Nutrition movement coordinator, UNICEF help prepare Madagascar’s participation in the Nutrition for Growth Summit, during which the country made six major national commitments, strengthening the visibility of nutrition in financing strategies, climate action, and agricultural planning. These commitments positioned Madagascar to access new funding from UNICEF’s Child Nutrition Fund and the World Bank. 
 
Working with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF, together with WHO and the World Food Programme (WFP)_ rolled out the revised national treatment protocol for child wasting. UNICEF procured therapeutic products and supported training and quality improvement initiatives to treat 86,000 children for severe wasting, a 15 per cent increase over 2024. UNICEF also supported maternal nutrition through an expanded micronutrient supplementation programme across 7 out of 23 regions, benefitting 113,966 pregnant women – a contribution aligned with UNICEF’s global Maternal Nutrition Acceleration Plan. Through the programme for school-age children and adolescents, UNICEF reached 40,751 students in 817 schools while community activities conducted with youth organizations reached 136,500 adolescents.  
 
UNICEF launched a local version of the First Foods Africa initiative in Madagascar to reduce child food poverty. Currently, 74 per cent of young children in Madagascar do not to access and consume a nutritious and diverse diet, which is considered as child food poverty. The initiative focuses on improving access to appropriate first foods for children aged 6–23 months and is being implemented alongside the Ministry of Agriculture and other food systems stakeholders.
 
UNICEF expanded access to equitable, climate-resilient WASH services across Madagascar. UNICEF conducted a comprehensive inventory of all water points, mapping 19,977 communities and 16,041 water points in four drought-affected regions, as well as 11,751 schools and 2,575 health centres nationwide. All water sources were georeferenced and tested, and the datasets are accessible to all sector actors for smarter, more equitable investment. The inventory revealed stark inequities in WASH services, enabling more equitable targeting in the future.
 
Based on this evidence, UNICEF pump-tested and rehabilitated 250 boreholes, drilled 345 new ones, and constructed 55 solar-powered water systems, enabling 159,105 people to access safe and sustainable water. Integrated approaches also supported livelihoods, for example through small-scale irrigation for vegetable gardens.
 
Sanitation gains were accelerated through market shaping, strengthening local private sector production of affordable sanitation products (self-closing pans, container-based prototypes and female urinals). A sanitation microfinance model expanded household access, while Madagascar’s accession to the Regional Sanitation Facility Fund unlocked opportunities to scale up market-based sanitation.
 
Investments in resilience included 30 dataloggers to measure groundwater levels, improved early warning systems, and pilot climate-resilient technologies such as sand dams and rainwater harvesting. UNICEF supported sector strengthening and governance reforms by contributing to the National WASH Policy and the new Water Code, which were both adopted at the end of the year. As lead of the partners’ coordination group, UNICEF also supported national mapping of WASH actors, investments and financing gaps. Only about 5 per cent of the financing needed to meet the Sustainable Development Goals is available, highlighting the urgent need for alternative financing.
 
UNICEF continued working tirelessly to protect and expand children’s learning opportunities. Alongside providing rapid response in emergency situations to help children return to safe and functional classrooms, UNICEF assisted eight high-risk regions to develop education contingency plans, and pre-positioned 65,000 teaching and learning kits for rapid deployment.
 
With the World Bank and the French Development Agency, UNICEF played a catalytic role in mobilizing US$89 million from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) through the Integrated Programme to Transform Foundational Learning. UNICEF contributed to policy analysis and reform on teacher investment, co-authoring a landmark study with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank demonstrating the economic returns of teacher training. This analysis informed the 2025 National Teacher Policy, which is intended to train and integrate 48,000 non-certified teachers by 2028.
 
To address foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) bottlenecks, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education to initiate development of a national FLN strategy. In line with this strategy, in 2026, the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) model will be introduced in 10 regions, reaching more than 13,000 public primary schools.
 
UNICEF continued facilitating a more effective child protection system. Working closely with the Ministry of Population, other key line ministries, United Nations agencies, civil society and academic institutions, UNICEF strengthened national leadership, coordination and service delivery to better protect children from violence, exploitation and abuse. A major milestone was the first-ever national protection system mapping, which provided evidence to guide reforms and informed the development of Madagascar’s first National Child Protection Policy, expected to be adopted in 2026. UNICEF also supported legal and policy frameworks on child labour and gender-based violence and strengthened national data systems ahead of the first annual child protection statistics report. 
 
UNICEF expanded prevention of violence interventions, reaching over 165,000 people, including 113,864 children, with initiatives promoting safer families, schools and communities, and positive social norms to prevent violence. In a context with no professional social workers in the public system, UNICEF supported a major shift in service delivery by piloting the deployment of government-employed professional social workers in six districts for the first time.
 
Nearly 8,000 children received integrated medical, psychosocial and legal care in 2025, including in humanitarian settings. Together, these achievements demonstrate how UNICEF’s technical support, advocacy and partnerships are helping lay the foundation for a scalable, government-led child protection system that delivers real results for children.
 
UNICEF advanced social policy work by strengthening evidence systems and supporting public finance reforms that improve how resources reach children. Completion of the national household survey MICS7 – the first full round since 2018 – refreshed the national evidence base on child poverty, equity and service coverage at a pivotal moment as the Government of National Refoundation set social-sector priorities. 
 
UNICEF’s public finance work focused on improving the effectiveness of social-sector budgeting and spending. High-level advocacy on vaccine financing and primary school teacher training was combined with analyses of budget execution and the flow of funds from central level to primary health centres. These analyses informed practical measures to ease bottlenecks, strengthen transparency and enhance last-mile programming – helping to ensure that allocations translate into services children can actually access.
 
Shock-responsive social protection systems were strengthened to expand coverage and timeliness. UNICEF supported upgrades to the Unique Social Registry to improve inclusion and targeting, and enhancements to the Social Window (Guichet Social) management information system to enable more reliable payments and case management. 
 
The ZARA MIRA universal child benefit was expanded in Atsimo Atsinanana region, linking cash with social services through local social workers. By the end of 2025, 165,500 people – including 163,000 children, 1,600 pregnant women and 900 persons with disabilities – had benefitted, a 10 per cent increase from 2024. Cash-plus support deepened resilience through 600 savings groups and 4,400 income-generating activities across three regions, strengthening households’ ability to cope with shocks while maintaining links to services.
 
Through the social and behaviour change programme, efforts were sustained to strengthen community systems, youth participation and adoption of protective behaviours. UNICEF supported various communication channels and community engagement platforms in seven regions to disseminate safe practices related to health, nutrition, child protection and early child development among caregivers. Over 157,680 community members participated in local dialogues on vaccination, child feeding, climate and protective norms, with 4,733 trained community agents facilitating those discussions. UNICEF strengthened 30 Local Consultation Structures attached to municipalities, along with youth community groups to influence local decision making.  
 
In a year marked by a major political power shift, young people emerged as key leaders. Throughout 2025, UNICEF partnered with youth networks and organizations such as the Scout Movement and supported youth participation through 380 local youth groups and over 20,000 U-Report volunteers, enabling youth to influence public priorities and lead initiatives. This partnership proved critical during the political transition, amplifying youth leaders’ voices, enabling youth consultations and advancing their inclusion in national dialogues.
 
UNICEF Madagascar further advanced its decentralization of operations, enhancing the capacity of the five field offices and giving direct budgeting responsibilities to two of them. This brought day-to-day decision-making closer to communities, enabling faster problem-solving and more agile resourcing. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened emergency readiness across the country by training over 120 staff to enable quicker, more coordinated action when shocks occur. This enabled a lifesaving, multi-sector response to the five cyclones and tropical systems that affected Madagascar in 2025, and to the worsening malnutrition situation, compounded by a malaria outbreak in the south-east. UNICEF also reacted rapidly to socio-political unrest in major urban centres in September-October, strengthening readiness while safeguarding the continuity of basic services – particularly health and education.
 
In 2025, UNICEF helped thousands of families across Madagascar cope with multiple crises – from cyclones to rising malnutrition and disease outbreaks. More than 124,000 people gained access to safe drinking water, including over 65,000 children. To protect children’s lives, UNICEF supported the treatment of 68,494 young children suffering from severe wasting. Primary health-care services reached 80,640 children and 7,639 pregnant women in the most-affected areas. Education support ensured that 94,806 children continued learning despite disruptions caused by disasters or instability. Protection services were also reinforced: more than 168,000 people – including over 100,000 children and adolescents – received mental health and psychosocial support to help them cope with stress and trauma. Through shock-responsive social protection, 22,690 households received emergency cash top-ups to meet essential needs during crises. UNICEF’s risk communication work reached more than 6.4 million people – including 2 million children – sharing information on prevention, available services and how to stay safe.
 
These results were achieved thanks to UNICEF’s partners in a particularly challenging year marked by shrinking global aid and declining humanitarian funding. With alarming levels of malnutrition in the Great South and South-East, UNICEF intensified its resource mobilization to help Madagascar avoid a deterioration like the 2021–2022 Kere crisis.
 
As the impact of climate change on children remains a major concern in Madagascar, UNICEF helped lay stronger foundations for child-sensitive, climate risk-informed planning. The updated Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) gathers strong evidence on how climate hazards and environmental degradation are directly affecting children’s health, education, nutrition and protection. It also highlights which groups of children are most exposed and why. In parallel, the national and subnational INFORM index brings together data on risks, vulnerabilities and coping capacity, helping identify where climate and environmental pressures are highest and where systems remain weakest. Together, these tools allow UNICEF, government and partners to prioritize regions and populations, and to design investments that reduce, rather than deepen, climate risks.
 
UNICEF also provided critical technical assistance to the Government to develop the National Climate Finance Strategy and its implementing decree. By convening nine thematic working groups and working closely with government and climate actors, UNICEF helped ensure national ownership and stronger visibility of children and social sectors in climate-related investment decisions. The Strategy is expected to be adopted by decree in March 2026. In parallel, UNICEF co-led the national environmental coordination platform with the Ministry of Environment and the German cooperation agency (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit or GIZ), improving partners’ alignment and helping channel innovative climate financing toward child-centred outcomes.
 
At community level, the Ecovillage programme continued strengthening local climate and environmental resilience in the three regions of the Great South. Through integrated interventions, the programme improved local governance, expanded access to basic WASH and lighting services, supported safer cooking practices, promoted livelihoods and entrepreneurship, and reinforced environmental education. These efforts contributed to improved service delivery, greater awareness and stronger local capacities.
 
UNICEF also supported inclusive climate policy dialogue by helping integrate climate considerations across health, WASH, child protection and nutrition programmes, and by facilitating consultations with 120 young people from all 23 regions to inform Madagascar’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 process. 
UNICEF programme continued prioritizing results for adolescent girls. A multi-sector project was implemented in one district to serve as a model for a comprehensive gender-transformative approach, with the aim of promoting girl’s voices, reducing violence and child marriage risks and expanding girls’ choices (see lessons learned below). The project benefitted 14,775 girls aged 10 to 19.
 
Youth-friendly health services scaled up rapidly. UNICEF supported 32 new adolescent-friendly health centres – bringing the total to 217 – equipped with safe spaces. More than 90,000 girls received consultations, including sexual and reproductive health, anaemia screening and care, family planning services. Life skills education reached around 60,000 girls with information on gender-based violence prevention and response, menstrual health management (MHM), and sexual and reproductive health and rights, strengthening agency and protective practices.
 
Education outcomes complemented these gains. More than 7,000 girls in and out of school received targeted support for enrolment, re-enrolment, and retention, including catch-up learning and vocational pathways. Gender-responsive pedagogy and science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) options helped advance equitable learning and informed decision-making.
 
In addition, UNICEF reached 35,317 women and adolescent girls with menstrual health services and strengthened inclusive WASH in schools and health centres through updated WASH improvement tools.
 
Regarding protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), as interim lead of the Inter-Agency PSEA Task Force, UNICEF drove reforms to strengthen PSEA systems. Key achievements included revision of inter-agency standard operating procedures, the first training of trainers on the United Nations Victim Assistance Protocol, and the mapping of feedback and reporting mechanisms across all regions. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened strategic collaboration with Government institutions, United Nations agencies, bilateral partners, international financial institutions, private sector actors and civil society, enabling coherent multisector programming for children. Partnerships with the European Union, Germany (BMZ/KfW and GIZ), the World Bank, the International Fund for Agricultural Development, Norway, the U.S. Government’s Office of Foreign Assistance, the Japanese International Cooperation Agency, France, Ireland and Canada continued to drive essential service delivery and resilience across health, nutrition, education, WASH and child protection, particularly in climate-affected regions.
 
Cooperation with the EU was reinforced through the launch of the joint EU–United Nations climate adaptation initiative PACTE VERT, implemented with UNDP, FAO and WFP. This programme complements German and Norwegian-funded nexus interventions in the South and Southeast regions. UNICEF has also been leading a joint Peace Building Fund programme with IOM and UNESCO to strengthen social cohesion and climate security, while supporting national efforts for social protection, justice and child protection. Education programming expanded significantly through an award from the Global Partnership for Education, enabling closer collaboration with the World Bank, the French Development Agency, UNESCO and UNFPA in support of Government reforms on education.
 
Through the Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD), UNICEF Japan supported sanitation promotion and local production of hygiene materials. Partnership with UNICEF National Committees grew stronger in 2025. In particular, the German Committee supported a major First Food programme for young children.
 
These combined partnerships contributed to over US$60 million being mobilized in 2025, bringing total other resources mobilized for the five-year Country Programme to US$195 million (80.6 per cent of the planned amount), despite global funding constraints.
 
UNICEF expanded private sector engagement with the Malagasy Business Federation (GEM) representing over 70 companies to promote family-friendly workplace policies. UNICEF also reinforced partnerships with local media by training 100 journalists while expanding its digital reach to 393,000 followers and generating 13 million social media impressions.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF Madagascar Country Programme 2024-2028 prioritizes adolescent girls to address their complex vulnerabilities through multisectoral interventions. At the same time, the child protection programme is seeking to strengthen a coherent national system capable of preventing and responding to violence against children. To advance both goals, UNICEF tested innovative, small-scale pilots to gather feedback, refine approaches and determine next steps, including possible scale-up. 
 
By end 2025, two lessons emerged: 

An integrated, multisectoral, girl-centred approach demonstrated that aligning services and elevating girls’ voices accelerates re-enrolment and access to services for adolescent girls, while reinforcing systems to be more gender-transformative.
Deploying professional social workers at district level, part of UNICEF’s child protection system-strengthening efforts, demonstrated that a qualified workforce improves referral pathways and survivor-centred case management. 
 
1. Girl-Led Change: a multisector blueprint for adolescent empowerment
 
In 2025, UNICEF implemented an integrated, gender-transformative intervention in Vondrozo, a convergence district in Madagascar's Southeast region, to address the multiple barriers faced by adolescent girls. The initiative included education, health, protection, hygiene, and social and behaviour change interventions led by the ministries of education, vocational training, health, youth, population and solidarity.
 
Working with the Girl Scouts, UNICEF supported girl-led census and consultations with about 1,000 adolescents. They identified 5,154 out-of-school girls, with 51 per cent expressing intent to return to school: far above official records. The process exposed overlapping risks in education, protection and health. 
 
Based on these insights, the package offered re-entry and bridging to lower-secondary school; science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and vocational options; and life skills, including sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), menstrual health management (MHM), and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response.
 
Key lessons emerged:


Girls’ voices matter. Planning with and for     girls revealed hidden exclusions (girls without civil registration, those     who are married or parenting, and girls with disabilities), quantified     unmet needs, and identified barriers (education fees, domestic workloads,     safety and health). This improved targeting and positioned adolescents as     co-designers and accountability monitors through clubs and peer networks. 
A multisector approach with a gender-transformative     lens is necessary. The integrated package for girls’ empowerment,     combining life skills, service-delivery improvements, and system     strengthening, reduced multiple risks and began to shift restrictive     social norms. Differentiated pathways (formal, non-formal, and technical     and vocational education and training) were essential for diverse learner     profiles. As a result, 2,500 girls were reintegrated into lower secondary     school, and 1,000 accessed vocational opportunities. In parallel, comprehensive     sexuality education, parent sensitization on adolescent girls’ health,     training of health and social workers, and safe spaces in youth-friendly     health centres supported more than 8,000 health consultations for     adolescent girls. 
Embedding     gender-responsive practice through national reforms alongside     experimentation on the ground is critical. Gender-transformative education     has been enhanced, with the Ministry of Education adopting the first     national gender-responsive pedagogy to address stereotypes in schools –     the guide and tools developed were tested in Vondrozo district. In     addition, the education system’s first gender audit was launched to inform     programme and budget decisions. The Vondrozo pilot also enabled updates to     the frontline health worker training curriculum and informed revisions to     the national life skills programme.
 
2. Deployment of professional social workers as a basis of a district level child protection system 
 
In 2025, Madagascar deployed 12 professional social workers to six districts – its first attempt to build a formal child protection workforce. Previously, the ministry responsible for child protection employed no professional social workers and relied mainly on community volunteers to prevent and respond to violence against children. While volunteers play a critical role, the absence of a professional workforce limited the effectiveness, consistency and sustainability of case management. A child protection system, like health or education systems, requires a professional workforce to deliver specialized services, ensure quality standards and coordinate responses across sectors. 
 
In these six districts, cases of violence against children and women are now managed by qualified professionals rather than relying solely on volunteers. Led by the Ministry of Population and Solidarity through its Regional Directorates, this pilot demonstrates a scalable model for strengthening the system and shows how investing in a trained workforce can improve case management, making the case for institutionalization of social work. Social workers coordinate across multiple actors and services, generating valuable insights into system strengths and gaps. 
 
The first year highlighted the need for clearer role definitions among social workers, community volunteers, Ministry representatives and child protection networks. Districts with deployed social workers now report more coherent referral pathways, stronger community mobilization, and improved case follow-up, resulting in timelier and more coordinated support for survivors. In districts affected by climate-related risks, improvements were observed in identification of sexual violence, early pregnancy and child marriage cases, particularly among adolescent girls; for example, in October, 54 of 58 cases identified in Vondrozo district concerned adolescent girls. The pilot also reinforced national momentum to professionalize social work. Early results indicate a clear opportunity for scale-up to further strengthen district-level structures and expand support to children, women and families.
 
Implemented in collaboration with universities, NGOs, United Nations agencies and government ministries, the UNICEF-supported initiative provides strong evidence that investing in a professional social service workforce is essential for sustaining gains, expanding timely and survivor-centred services, and anchoring long-term, system-wide reform to protect children and women from violence.
 
Future outlook
Building on these insights, UNICEF Madagascar will prioritize adaptive management and cross-sector coordination to accelerate results for the most vulnerable children. 
 
1- Reinforce the monitoring and evaluation system and expand investment in adolescent girls by leveraging partnerships with the Government, United Nations agencies and major donors. UNICEF is supporting the establishment of a multi-donor platform on gender and adolescent girls to strengthen joint advocacy and national policy dialogue. The platform will coordinate efforts, expand the evidence base, deepen policy engagement and catalyse resource mobilization for the adolescent girls’ agenda.
2- Support the professionalization and expansion of child protection work at scale, including advocacy for the creation and financing of a national body of social workers, standardized training and supervision, and adoption of the National Child Protection Policy, with stronger use of data, clearer referral pathways and effective case management. 
Enhance partnerships with government, civil society, youth network and development partners to secure predictable financing and stronger accountability for child-centred results, and drive coordinated, systemwide progress on equity, girls’ empowerment and climate-resilient services.

Malawi entered 2025 facing persistent macroeconomic fragility and recurrent climate shocks that continued to erode household resilience and deepening poverty, undermining progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The external environment was marked by high inflation, foreign exchange shortages, widening fiscal deficits, national elections and political transition, all of which had direct and disproportionate impacts on children’s rights and wellbeing. This context shaped UNICEF’s programming priorities and underscored the urgency of protecting essential services for the most vulnerable.


 


Macroeconomic Environment


Economic growth remained subdued, with projections for 2025 revised downward to 2.7 per cent, signaling the fourth consecutive year of declining per capita income. An estimated 75.4 per cent of the population, or 15.8 million people, lived below the international poverty line of $3 per day. For households, the erosion of real incomes meant reduced spending on food, education, health care, and other essentials critical for child development. The cumulative effect was a narrowing of opportunities for children and heightened risks of intergenerational poverty.


 


Inflation remained exceptionally high, averaging 27 per cent across the year. Food inflation was even more severe, exceeding 33 per cent at times. This forced painful tradeoffs for many families where staple foods were prioritized over dietary diversity, health care, or school requirements. These dynamics directly undermined children’s rights to adequate nutrition, health, and education, while exacerbating inequality between urban and rural populations.


 


Foreign exchange shortages intensified, with official reserves reduced to just one week of import cover, far below the recommended minimum of three months. Limited export earnings, weak donor inflows, and suspended programme financing constrained forex availability through formal channels. As a result, reliance on parallel markets grew, with the gap between official and informal exchange rates widening sharply. While the official rate hovered around MWK 1,750 per US$, the informal market rate exceeded MWK 4,750 per US$, reflecting a premium of more than 150 per cent. This divergence undermined confidence in the formal system and had cascading effects: import dependent sectors such as fuel, fertilizer, medicines, and education supplies faced shortages and rising costs, while business performance deteriorated. Only 35 per cent of firms reported positive performance in 2024, down from over 40 per cent in 2023. For households, higher prices for transport, fuel, and basic goods compounded already high food inflation, further eroding purchasing power.


 


Fiscal pressures also mounted. The deficit widened to 11.9 per cent of GDP in FY2025/26, while public debt remained close to 88 per cent of GDP. Interest payments absorbed around half of domestic revenues, crowding out spending on social sectors. This left little fiscal space for expanding education, health, nutrition, and social protection spending, limiting the government’s ability to respond to rising child needs. 


 


Food Security and Nutrition


Food insecurity continued to be an issue in 2025. The number of people experiencing acute food insecurity rose from 4.4 million in 2023 to 5.7 million during the 2024/25 lean season. Although projections for 2025/26 suggested a slight reduction to around 4 million people in crisis (IPC Phase 3 or worse), this still represented one-fifth of the population, an elevated level compared to pre-shock years. Maize production remained below national requirements for the third consecutive year, constrained by drought conditions, limited access to fertilizer, and high input costs. Market dependence increased, but inflation and stagnant incomes reduced households’ ability to purchase sufficient food.


 


For children, the nutrition impacts were severe. Admissions for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) rose by 7 per cent from 2024 to 2025, while moderate acute malnutrition cases increased by over 24 per cent. In half of all districts, reported SAM caseloads exceeded projections, signaling both rising need and overstretched services. These trends marked a reversal of progress toward SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing), particularly for children under five and pregnant and lactating women.


 


Food insecurity also had indirect consequences for child rights. Families adopted negative coping strategies, including withdrawing children from school, reducing spending on education, and increasing reliance on child marriage and labour. Disruptions to school feeding programmes due to funding constraints further weakened attendance and learning outcomes, especially in food insecure districts.


 


Climate and Public Health Hazards


Climatic shocks remained a central driver of vulnerability. The lingering effects of the 2023/24 El Niño associated drought continued to affect agricultural production, water availability, and nutrition outcomes in early 2025. While forecasts for the 2025/26 rainy season suggested normal to above normal rainfall, this carried risks of flooding, waterborne disease outbreaks, and localized displacement, particularly in flood prone districts along the Shire River and lakeshore areas. For children, recurrent climate shocks disrupted schooling, increased exposure to disease, and undermined access to safe water and sanitation, highlighting Malawi’s limited climate resilience under SDG 13.


 


Public health was further strained by overlapping disease outbreaks. Mpox, first confirmed in April 2025, reached 146 cases and one death by December, with children accounting for 25 per cent of cases. Cholera remained a recurrent threat, with 309 cases and 15 deaths reported between July 2024 and June 2025, and additional cases emerging with the onset of rains. Measles outbreaks compounded the burden. These shocks disrupted continuity of essential child focused services, including immunization, nutrition screening, maternal and newborn care, and school-based health services.


 


Political Context


The political landscape was shaped by general elections in September 2025. Economic hardship, rising food prices, unemployment, and governance concerns featured prominently in public discourse, reflecting widespread frustration with declining living standards. Voter concerns mirrored the socioeconomic pressures affecting children and families, particularly food insecurity and access to basic services. The elections resulted in a peaceful transfer of power, but the transition occurred amid ongoing economic and humanitarian crises, raising risks of policy delays and uncertainty. Historically, election periods in Malawi have coincided with slower reform implementation, which in 2025 posed additional challenges for sustaining investments in health, education, nutrition, and child protection.


 


Implications for Child Rights and UNICEF Programming


Taken together, the economic stagnation, high inflation, forex unavailability, worsening food insecurity, and climate volatility observed between 2023 and 2025 significantly undermined children’s rights in Malawi. Rising malnutrition directly threatened survival and development. Economic pressures and food shortages increased risks of school dropout, child labour, and early marriage, particularly for girls. Fiscal constraints and aid shortfalls weakened service delivery at a time when needs were increasing.


 


From a child rights and SDG perspective, 2025 represented a year of heightened risk rather than recovery. Without scaled up, child focused investments in nutrition, social protection, education, health, and climate resilient systems, Malawi risks entrenching intergenerational poverty and inequality. For UNICEF, the context underscored the need to prioritize lifesaving interventions, protect core social services during fiscal adjustment and political transition, and advocate for policies that ensure the most vulnerable children are not left behind.

In 2025, UNICEF’s work in Malawi delivered significant results across health, nutrition, education, child protection, and social policy, contributing to transformative changes that advanced children’s rights and contributed to national priorities under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.


 


In the area of child survival and development, UNICEF accelerated Malawi’s primary health care agenda by supporting the Government to operationalize the Health Sector Strategic Plan III. This was achieved through equity-driven services that strengthened maternal, newborn, and child health. Maternal and newborn quality standards were implemented in 90 health facilities, 95 facilities received essential supplies, and nine Sick Newborn Care Units were upgraded, contributing to institutional delivery coverage of 97 per cent in supported districts. Child health services expanded through Integrated Management of Childhood Illness and integrated Community Case Management, in eighty facilities, reaching 875,200 children (411,344 male, 463,856 female), including provision of appropriate treatment for 186,240 (76,358 male, 109,882 female) pneumonia cases. More than one thousand health workers and 776 (489 male, 287 female) community providers were trained, improving access for hard-to-reach populations and reinforcing equity in service delivery. Health system resilience was strengthened through performance assessments, direct facility financing, digital tools, and emergency responses to cholera, measles, mpox, and Cyclone Chido. Integrated programming advanced HIV, adolescent health, and noncommunicable disease services, with antenatal testing, point of care diagnostics, and sexual and reproductive health services, reaching 32,605 (14,672 male,17,933 female) adolescents. These achievements underscored UNICEF’s commitment to equitable, quality care and robust primary health care systems.


 


Nutrition outcomes advanced significantly through integrated, multisectoral approaches that strengthened health, food, education, and social protection systems. UNICEF revitalized and scaled up community-based nutrition interventions, training over 2,354 (1,144 male, 1,210 female) district and community actors across coordination platforms and promoter networks. Through these strengthened systems, more than 605,705 (110,087 male; 495,618 female) caregivers received maternal, infant, and young child nutrition counselling, while over 91,891 households adopted food diversification practices, enhancing dietary diversity and access to nutrient rich foods. Preventive and therapeutic nutrition interventions were scaled up, with over two million children under five screened for wasting and oedema, leading to treatment of 47,644 children (24,025 boys, 23,519 girls) with severe wasting. Recovery rates exceeded Sphere standards at 92 per cent, supported by UNICEF’s procurement and last mile delivery of 75,957 cartons of ready-to-use therapeutic food. 


 


Vitamin A supplementation reached 773,049 children (389,824 boys, 383,225 girls), while maternal nutrition services expanded markedly, with 734,265 pregnant women receiving iron and folic acid or multiple micronutrient supplements, a four per cent increase from 2024. Screening of 617,899 pregnant and breastfeeding women identified and referred 22,889 who were referred for treatment, while targeted balanced energy supplements were provided to undernourished pregnant women during El Niño and La Niña emergencies. Adolescent nutrition also progressed, with 58,104 girls receiving iron and folic acid supplements, surpassing national targets. Social and behaviour change initiatives, including the innovative approach, engaged 128,966 adolescent girls in promoting positive attitudes toward supplementation. 


 


Community engagement remained central, with 18,910 volunteers (3,504 male, 15,376 female, 16 women with disabilities and 14 men with disabilities) trained to monitor nutrition practices and 3,124 men actively participating in household level nutrition and childcare activities. Mass media campaigns and community platforms reached over 5.4 million people (around 40 percent female) with messages on nutrition, health, hygiene, and positive parenting, driving sustainable behaviour change. UNICEF’s commitment to early childhood development complemented nutrition gains, with advocacy strengthening community ownership and male involvement in childcare, resulting in the establishment of fourteen new Community-Based Childcare Centres and expanded access to early learning for more than 235,486 children (109,579 male, 125,907 female) aged three to five. Service quality improved through training 450 caregivers (134 males, 316 females) and provision of learning materials, while a comprehensive assessment informed future investments to address gaps in functionality and food security. 


 


In learning and skills development, UNICEF supported the development of Malawi’s first year pre-primary class curriculum, positioning the country to move toward universal pre-primary education and significantly improving school readiness for vulnerable children. Rollout in high vulnerability districts expanded early learning opportunities for children most at risk of being left behind. Quality teaching was enhanced through expansion of the national teacher mentorship programme, which equipped 8,129 pre-service teachers, including 4,478 females, with practical classroom skills. More than 37,200 teachers were trained in improved numeracy programmes delivered with support from the United Kingdom. 


 


Disability inclusion advanced through strengthened resource centres and provision of assistive devices, enabling 215,224 children with disabilities, including 104,206 girls, to access primary education. Enrolment of children with disabilities increased by 11 per cent since 2023. Delivery of 22,831 desks supported over 45,000 learners, half of them girls, enhancing learning environments. Nationally, secondary school enrolment rose to 538,800 learners. Gender equity advanced through UNICEF scholarships financed by the KIND programme, reaching more than 9,000 girls, while digital learning initiatives reached nearly equal numbers of boys and girls. Alternative learning pathways supported more than 15,000 adolescent girls with functional literacy and skills training, leading to reintegration of over 1,100 learners, including 950 girls, into the formal education system. Collectively, these initiatives shifted national systems toward greater inclusion, resilience, and equitable learning outcomes. 


 


Adolescent girls at risk of early marriage or child labour were supported through functional literacy and vocational programmes that strengthened their protection, learning, and livelihood prospects. Policy advocacy on the prohibition of corporal punishment, alongside the introduction of the Positive Parenting Toolkit, contributed to national efforts to protect children from violence in schools and homes. UNICEF’s interventions in education in emergencies reached 107,740 learners, including 55,780 girls, across 54 disaster prone schools in five districts, helping children continue learning during droughts and emergencies. School level resilience and learner wellbeing were further enhanced through community engagement for supplementary meals benefiting 14,935 learners (6,000 boys, 8,935 girls) from thirteen schools, food support to 1,750 standard eight learners (955 boys, 795 girls) during exam preparation, and establishment of community gardens in eighteen schools to complement school feeding programmes. Mental health support expanded through the training of 7,620 adolescents, including 4,000 girls, as peer coaches, while sustainability was strengthened through capacity building for 315 Education Management Information System (EMIS) officers, including 110 females.


 


Child protection systems were significantly strengthened in 2025, resulting in improved legal frameworks, institutional coordination, and evidence to better protect children’s rights. Under the leadership of the Ministry of Health, and with UNICEF support, the Mental Health Bill of 2025 was enacted, shifting Mental Health and Psychosocial Support Services from a medical model to a human rights–based approach, improving protection, dignity, and access for children and adolescents. Progress toward professionalizing the social service workforce advanced through review of the 2019 Social Work Professionalization Bill, positioning it for submission to the Ministry of Justice and future enactment to establish a Social Workers Council. This laid the groundwork for regulating standards, accountability, and quality of child protection services.


 


Justice systems for children were strengthened through UNICEF supported reforms, with the National Child Justice Forum developing standard operating procedures for diversion of children in conflict with the law and assessing non-state institutions in twelve districts. UNICEF support to the Malawi Judiciary enabled review of 559 family and child related cases, improving decision quality and informing potential legal and policy reforms. In addition to increased monitoring of child rights during the general elections, which was shared as a regional best practice, national coordination on children’s rights improved with the official launch of the National Children’s Commission in December 2025. The Commission assumed responsibility for high-level multisectoral coordination, supported by national guidelines for the selection of two child representatives, strengthening child participation and accountability. 


 


The evidence base for child protection planning was significantly strengthened through UNICEF-supported studies. A systematic parenting study identified gaps in coverage and quality of parenting programmes, particularly for the most vulnerable. A national birth registration survey revealed that only 41 per cent of respondents had adequate knowledge of birth registration, informing targeted strategies to improve access to essential services. A national study on corporal punishment was initiated to inform policy and social norm change, including co-creation of non-violent discipline alternatives. These efforts were reinforced by the development and rollout of a national, evidence-based Parenting Toolkit, supported by UNICEF in collaboration with the Ministry of Gender, Children, Disability and Social Welfare (MoGCDSW). The toolkit provided simple, culturally appropriate guidance for families and social service workers to promote positive parenting and non-violent discipline. Collectively, these results strengthened child protection systems, improved accountability, and positioned Malawi for sustained, rights-based protection outcomes for children. They also demonstrated UNICEF’s role in advancing the implementation of human rights treaties and recommendations from mechanisms such as the CRC Committee and the Universal Periodic Review, ensuring that reforms were grounded in international standards and commitments.


 


In the area of social policy, UNICEF’s advocacy, evidence generation, and technical support strengthened public investment in essential services. Government spending rose from 31.0 per cent to 32.3 per cent, reflecting a modest but important shift toward prioritizing social sectors. Social protection coverage expanded significantly, with the Social Cash Transfer Programme reaching 381,735 households, up from 307,332 the previous year. This expansion benefitted 1.4 million people, including 42 per cent children and 7 per cent persons with disabilities. These gains underscored UNICEF’s role in driving equity focused policies and scaling inclusive social protection systems to reduce child poverty and vulnerability. The system was made more nutrition sensitive and shock-responsive through the rollout of cash plus initiatives in skills development, economic empowerment, and nutrition. These integrated approaches improved household resilience and child nutrition outcomes, with over 63,700 individuals, including 57,371 social cash transfer beneficiaries, gaining access to nutrition services and livelihood opportunities. UNICEF also advanced child-inclusive governance to drive systemic reforms that prioritize children’s multidimensional needs. Through strategic engagement, UNICEF supported the development of the Child Inclusive Programming Guideline, strengthened district planning processes, facilitated national dialogue on child poverty drivers, and enhanced information management systems. Sector-wide frameworks for monitoring and evaluation and shock-responsive social protection were reinforced, ensuring that policies and programmes were better aligned with the realities faced by children and families.


 


In 2025, UNICEF placed strong emphasis on emergency preparedness, coordination, and integrated service delivery, enabling the rapid scale--up of multisectoral responses that reached more than 2.1 million people, including 1.1 million children with health, nutrition, water and sanitation, education, child protection, and/or cash assistance. A key achievement during the year was the marked improvement in institutional readiness and community-level response capacity compared to the previous year. Investments in Emergency Preparedness and Response were aligned with the Core Commitments for Children and included simulation exercises, refresher training, and strengthened contingency planning systems, ensuring that both national institutions and frontline actors were better equipped to respond to crises. UNICEF supported the safe and voluntary repatriation of over 7,900 Mozambican refugees, coordinating site closures and water tracking to safeguard dignity and well-being. The organization also played a central role in Emergency Operations Centre coordination during Cyclone Jude in the first quarter of the year, ensuring that children’s needs were prioritized in the national response. At community level, cholera preparedness was reinforced through the development of a volunteer training module and the training of more than 750 (469 male, 281 female) volunteers strategically positioned to improve early outbreak detection and reduce transmission. These efforts strengthened community resilience and contributed to faster, more effective responses to public health emergencies. UNICEF advanced anticipatory action by providing technical leadership for the National Anticipatory Action Framework and developing a -child--centred UNICEF framework, supporting a shift from reactive response to risk-informed early action. This approach ensured that children were at the centre of preparedness planning and that interventions could be activated before shocks escalated into full-scale emerge


ncies. These achievements were reinforced through stronger UNICEF-led cluster coordination under the Department of Disaster Management Affairs, expanded cross-border collaboration with Zambia, Mozambique, and Tanzania to address cholera and mpox, and activation of standby partnerships in alignment with the Disaster Risk Management Act of 2023. Together, these measures demonstrated UNICEF’s leadership in building a more proactive, coordinated, and child-focused- emergency response system in Malawi.


 


In 2025, UNICEF Malawi advanced gender integration across programmes, strengthening the quality of child rights interventions delivered by Government and implementing partners and ensuring that results were achieved with a gender perspective. A critical mass of gender master trainers was established, with 64 (32 male, 32 female) trainers at national level and 1,728 (998 male, 740 female) at district level across ten districts. These trainers reached more than 18,300 (8,784 male, 9,516 female) frontline workers in health, nutrition, and protection services, who in turn engaged over 40,000 community members with messages aimed at transforming discriminatory gender norms and practices that undermine children’s wellbeing. Evidence from the field demonstrated that households exposed to these interventions were adopting gender transformative behaviours, including joint decision-making within families, women exercising greater agency in household decisions, and men increasingly participating in childcare, backyard gardening, and other roles traditionally associated with women. UNICEF also strengthened the capacity of its staff and implementing partners to protect women and children, including adolescent girls, from sexual exploitation and abuse in both development and humanitarian contexts, reinforcing accountability and safeguarding measures across all programmes.


 


UNICEF’s social and behaviour change programming combined human-centric evidence generation, behavioural sciences, and community engagement to increase demand for services and promote sustained adoption of positive behaviours. More than 700,000 people (475,964 male, 224,036 female) were reached with critical messages on health, nutrition, hygiene, gender-based violence, protection from sexual exploitation and abuse, and continuation of education. A national Accountability to Affected Populations Strategy was developed to harmonize communication channels, complaint mechanisms, and transparent service delivery across government systems. Caregivers actively used feedback mechanisms, with 206 raising concerns about nutrition screening and access to food assistance for children at risk of acute malnutrition, enabling responsive adjustments in community-based nutrition programming. UNICEF, together with the Health Promotion Division of the Ministry of Health, conducted risk communication and community engagement responses for cholera and mpox outbreaks. Capacity strengthening of district health officials on community engagement standards and interpersonal communication contributed to improved quality of interventions, while a standardized community engagement toolkit for frontline workers and faith leaders was finalized to support discussions on key family practices with households and communities.


 


Innovation and Technology for Development (T4D) was another area of significant progress. UNICEF Malawi accelerated the transition from pilot-driven digital innovation to government-led scaling by completing the first Innovation and Digital Technology Landscape Assessment for Child Wellbeing. This assessment identified critical gaps in coordination, financing, data interoperability, and digital infrastructure that constrained impact for children. The findings are now guiding UNICEF’s portfolio prioritization, policy engagement, and partner coordination, shifting investments toward scalable and sustainable solutions. Building on this evidence, UNICEF supported government led scale-up across thirteen innovation and digital transformation initiatives, with approximately 70 per cent advancing to scaling or sustainability. These included digital health systems, innovative financing mechanisms for school connectivity, expanded geospatial and real-time monitoring tools, and youth led climate and social innovation. Collectively, these efforts strengthened national digital capacities for more than 2,000 government officials and improved access to essential services for over 1.6 million people, with a strong focus on equity, inclusion, and long-term system strengthening.


 


UNICEF also invested strategically in national data systems to strengthen evidence-based decision-making. Access to key datasets, including the draft Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), the Nutrition Standardized Monitoring and Assessment of Relief and Transitions (SMART) survey, Monitoring Safely Managed On-Site Sanitation (M-SMOSS), and the Ulimi ndi Chilengedwe (UCHI) baseline, was expanded, improving identification of geographic and population level disparities and enabling precise targeting of interventions.  These gains directly supported equity-focused programming and aligned with national priorities under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. The Midterm Review of Malawi’s Implementation Plan translated stronger data use into clearer identification of underserved communities and more equitable allocation of services, reinforcing local ownership and cross-sectoral collaboration. Harmonization of indicators across UN agencies improved the accuracy and comparability of child outcome tracking, supporting integrated programming and joint accountability. UNICEF Malawi delivered a strategically focused evidence agenda that generated and applied high-quality evaluations, studies, and research to inform programme adjustments, adaptive management, midpoint reviews, and evidence-based advocacy. National evaluation systems were reinforced through capacity building across government, advancing a more coordinated, use-oriented evidence ecosystem. 46 monitoring and evaluation officers across 18 government ministries, departments, and agencies were trained to apply evaluative thinking to decision-making and to commission and use high quality, equity and rights-based evaluations. In parallel, UNICEF supported the finalization of Malawi’s first National Evaluation Plan, a milestone in operationalizing the National M&E Policy and reinforcing a systematic, country-led evaluation framework.


 


Communications and advocacy played a pivotal role in strengthening programme implementation and positioning UNICEF as a leading voice for children. Staff and partners were equipped with tools and training that improved the quality and timeliness of communications, while journalists received child rights sensitivity training ahead of the national elections. Collaboration with Government and partners ensured coherent visibility across programme areas, supported by long-term agreements that enabled timely production of high-quality content. UNICEF drove national conversations on child poverty, social sector investment, and child rights, reaching over 11 million people through digital, broadcast, and print platforms. More than 70 news stories and several high-profile events amplified programme impact nationwide, while engagement with adolescents and youth deepened child participation. 


 


Overall, UNICEF’s results in 2025 demonstrated the impact of integrated, equity-focused programming delivered in close partnership with Government, communities, and development partners. Despite persistent economic constraints and recurrent shocks, UNICEF helped strengthen national systems to deliver more inclusive, resilient, and rights-based services for children and adolescents. By combining service delivery with policy reform, evidence generation, social and behaviour change, digital innovation, and robust preparedness, UNICEF contributed to measurable gains across the continuum of child wellbeing while reinforcing national ownership and sustainability. These achievements not only advanced Malawi’s commitments under the Sustainable Development Goals and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework but also positioned UNICEF as a trusted partner for scaling impact, deepening systems transformation, and safeguarding children’s rights in an increasingly complex humanitarian and development landscape.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
