Against the backdrop of the “poly-crisis” detailed in Chapter 1, UNICEF delivered high-impact results in 2025, balancing life-saving humanitarian assistance with long-term systems strengthening. By operationalizing the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus, the organization responded to the immediate needs arising from climate shocks and conflict, whilst actively laying the groundwork for sustainable resilience. This chapter highlights strategic shifts toward integrated programming, digital innovation, and community-led approaches, underscoring how UNICEF addressed systemic bottlenecks to ensure no child is left behind.

Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives
In 2025, UNICEF’s interventions in health and nutrition were characterized by a decisive move towards integrated, climate-resilient systems capable of withstanding shocks while delivering equitable care. This approach was essential in a year marked by climate disasters and public health emergencies.
In the health sector, UNICEF achieved results at scale, safeguarding millions of children against preventable diseases through robust support to the Ministry of Health (MISAU). A standout achievement was the successful execution of two nationwide polio vaccination rounds, which reached 19.3 million children, achieving 100 per cent administrative coverage. Measles/rubella and oral cholera campaigns vaccinated 1.1 million and 2.4 million people, respectively, while the targeted Mpox response vaccinated 25,422 priority individuals (95 per cent coverage) in high-risk northern districts. Furthermore, the HPV Multi-Age Cohort campaign reached 2.97 million girls aged 9–18, representing 95 per cent of the target. This campaign was critical not only for immediate protection against cervical cancer but also for strengthening the platform for adolescent health services, engaging girls in their own health rights. 
Another systemic milestone in 2025 was the expansion of the malaria vaccine rollout. Moving beyond pilot phases, the vaccine was introduced into routine immunization schedules across 119 districts in eight provinces. This expansion marks a decisive shift from project-based implementation to routine service delivery, significantly improving protection for infants in high-burden settings and demonstrating the scalability of new health technologies in resource-constrained environments. In parallel, UNICEF addressed immediate epidemic threats through large-scale prevention campaigns, administering oral cholera vaccines to nearly 2.4 million people across 13 outbreak-affected districts.

These operational successes were underpinned by significant policy advancements. UNICEF provided critical technical support for the development of the Health Sector Strategic Plan (PESS 2025-2034) and the National Immunization Strategy (ENI) 2026–2030. The new strategy, subsequently approved by Gavi with a USD 61.5 million country investment, transitions the country from receiving fragmented, short-term financing to having a coherent, fully costed long-term roadmap. This strategic shift is vital for ensuring the financial sustainability of immunization programs and reducing reliance on ad-hoc emergency funding.
To address the persistent challenge of reaching zero-dose and under-immunized children, UNICEF led digital transformations within the health system. The Electronic Child Registry pilot was completed in 22 districts of Maputo Province, and the digitization of microplanning (RED/REC) was expanded to 35 districts in Nampula and Zambezia. These digital tools have improved the precision, timeliness, and equity of outreach services, enabling health workers to identify and reach children previously missed due to geographic isolation or a lack of data.
Beyond immunization, UNICEF strengthened the continuum of care to address the stagnation in neonatal mortality. By establishing three regional learning hubs and a national mentorship network across 29 referral hospitals, the quality of care was improved for 23,845 hospitalized newborns. Simultaneously, to address the 'silent crisis' of HIV amidst funding cuts, UNICEF piloted mobile Early Infant Diagnosis (EID) models and supported community dialogues that linked 54,730 pregnant and breastfeeding women to Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) services, ensuring vulnerable infants were identified and treated.

At the community level, UNICEF also strengthened the primary healthcare system by directly supporting the training of 976 community health worker (APS) trainers and pre-service training of 320 new APSs (128 per cent of UNICEF’s 2025 target) including in the use of UpSCALE, in UNICEF’s four priority provinces. This will increase access to essential first-contact health services to an estimated 319,000 people, significantly reducing geographic barriers to care. Crucially, UNICEF’s advocacy helped mobilize over USD 11 million for the Community Health Subsystem (CHSS) from the Global Fund and World Bank, supporting its long-term institutionalization and financing.  In 2022, on the path to ensuring 10,000 trained and equipped APS nationwide, the Ministry of Health aimed to train 2,500 new APSs by 2026. To date, UNICEF has supported the training of 1,230 new APSs, representing 49 per cent of MoH's 2026 target). Regarding upSCALE implementation in line with the institutionalization of community health, 668 APS received in-service training on upSCALE use. This brings Mozambique to approximately 3,000 trained APS in the use of upSCALE, with 2,933 considered active (defined by consistent community-level reporting through upSCALE and receipt of a monthly subsidy of 1,200 MT), serving 1,758 communities nationwide.   
Finally, in a major push for inclusion, UNICEF integrated early detection of disabilities into primary care by training 274 health workers on the Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool (MDAT) and equipping 67 facilities. This system strengthening ensures that developmental delays are identified early, connecting children with disabilities to essential care from the start of life.
A flagship achievement in 2025 was the empirically proven success of integrated programming in reducing chronic malnutrition. An impact evaluation of the EU-UNICEF programme in Sofala Province revealed a remarkable 35 per cent reduction in severe stunting among children under five in areas where nutrition, WASH, and social and Social Behaviour Change (SBC) were combined. This evidence validates the "convergence approach", demonstrating that multi-sectoral interventions deliver far greater improvements in child well-being than single-sector approaches. Based on these findings, UNICEF is now scaling this model to Zambezia, Nampula, and Cabo Delgado, positioning it as a national best practice.
Nationally, UNICEF strengthened the enabling environment for nutrition by supporting the dissemination of the Policy and Strategy for Food Security and Nutrition (PESAN 2024–2030). Furthermore, advocacy efforts ensured the inclusion of Early Childhood Development (ECD) in the National Development Strategy (ENDE) 2025–2044, elevating nutrition and ECD from sectoral concerns to central pillars of the national development agenda. 

In response to acute malnutrition, particularly in drought and conflict-affected areas, UNICEF’s support for supply chains and training enabled the treatment of 65,756 children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) out of 50,283 planned target, achieving a cure rate of 79 per cent. This represents an increase of 25 per cent compared to year 2024 results.  Innovations were also scaled up to improve early detection: the introduction of mother-led MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) screening empowered 1,928 caregivers to monitor their children's nutritional status. Community-based efforts were complemented by the expansion of the Nutrition Interventions Package (PIN), which reached over 378,000 children across 14 districts with essential services including growth monitoring and counselling. This community-led approach not only improves coverage but also builds family resilience and reduces the burden on the formal health system.

Goal Area 2: Every child learns
UNICEF’s education strategy focused on addressing the learning crisis through systems strengthening and resilient response.
To address the critical bottleneck of low school readiness of children when entering primary school, UNICEF continued to support the Accelerated School Readiness (ASR) programme. Reaching 13,212 children (50 per cent girls) in 2025, surpassing the annual target of 12,320 children by 7 per cent, the programme achieved a 100 per cent transition rate to Grade 1 for participants. Monitoring data consistently shows that ASR graduates outperform their peers in literacy and numeracy, validating this model as a cost-effective strategy for improving retention and learning outcomes in resource-limited settings. Plans are now in place to scale this successful model to Cabo Delgado in 2026.
 
To ensure retention of girls in primary school and stimulate their transition to secondary schools, particularly in rural/disadvantaged areas, UNICEF expanded the School-Based Mentoring Programme to include 83 targeted schools in 2025, where 1,147 secondary students (212 per cent of achievement) mentored nearly 7,000 (194 per cent achievement against annual target) younger learners to facilitate their primary completion and transition. Additionally, practically addressing distance barriers—a key driver of dropout—UNICEF distributed 255 bicycles to vulnerable students in Sofala, directly supporting transition and retention in(to) secondary education.
Improving the quality of education remained a priority. UNICEF supported the training of 506 teachers and 476 school managers in inclusive education pedagogies and school leadership. This initiative exceeded the annual targets, which were set at 350 for teachers and 450 for school managers. These trainings are essential for creating inclusive learning environments that can accommodate children with diverse needs. Additionally, to strengthen school governance, UNICEF trained 3,280 School Council members in 205 schools, empowering communities to manage school resources and monitor teacher attendance.
To combat violence in schools, UNICEF supported the expansion of school-based violence prevention and referral (VAC) mechanisms. In 2025, these mechanisms generated 11,636 case reports, with 3,494 cases referred for support. This represents a 124 per cent increase in reported cases compared to the previous year, a figure that signals growing trust in the protection systems and a breakdown of the culture of silence surrounding abuse in schools.

With 1.1 million children in northern provinces affected by conflict and climate-related crises, the education sector was heavily impacted by infrastructure damage and displacement. UNICEF provided 262,711 children (54 per cent girls) with access to education through temporary learning spaces, catch-up classes, and psychosocial support, surpassing planned target by 5 per cent. A significant policy win in this area was the acceptance by government entities of Alternative Learning Programmes (ALP) as a valid pathway for out-of-school adolescents. This recognition allows for the certification of learning acquired outside the formal system, bridging the gap between emergency response and long-term educational reintegration for conflict-affected youth. Complementing these pathways, UNICEF piloted 'MAZA', an innovative digital platform connecting youth to flexible learning and employment opportunities and re-initiated work around digital learning in school, benefitting from the GIGA partnership and earlier work done under Learning Passport. 

Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
In 2025, Child Protection efforts focused on cementing the legal and policy framework while expanding digitalized services for the most vulnerable.
A landmark achievement was the official launch of the Plano Nacional de Acção para a Criança (PNAC III) 2025–2034. This national action plan provides a comprehensive decadal strategic framework for advancing child rights in Mozambique, aligning national policies with international commitments. Additionally, UNICEF supported the development of regulations for alternatives to detention for children, facilitating the operationalization of the Penal Execution Code and promoting restorative justice.
In parallel, UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support contributed to the registration of 774,857 new births in the first three quarters of 2025 against 874,408 planned targets (representing 89 per cent of achievement of annual target). By supporting the expansion of health facility-based birth registration posts to 158 locations, UNICEF helped further integrate civil registration into routine health services, ensuring that more children leave the health facility with a legal identity—a fundamental prerequisite for accessing other rights and services.

UNICEF contributed to address a systemic data gap by supporting the expansion of the electronic National Registry for Alternative Care (NRAC) across four provinces. A total of 556 children were placed in the family-based care (against a total of 4,543 children planned target),in all forms of alternative care, which represents 12 per cent of achievement of annual target. These children were digitally registered and consistently monitored for the first time. This digitization through NRAC is a critical step towards ending the invisibility of children in institutions and ensuring they receive appropriate care and oversight.
Additionally, the Linha Fala Criança (Child Helpline) was strengthened and expanded to conflict-affected provinces like Cabo Delgado and Zambezia. The helpline managed 114,073 calls in 2025, referring 8,765 cases of violence and abuse (against 4,646 planned target-188 per cent of achievement) to specialized social, health, and justice services. This service remains a vital lifeline for children to report abuse and seek help in a safe and confidential manner.
Complementing these reporting mechanisms, UNICEF invested in prevention to address the normalization of violence at home. A structured positive parenting course reached 1,521 parents and caregivers (127 per cent of achievement of annual target), across 12 districts, equipping them with the skills to nurture children without resorting to violent discipline.
In Cabo Delgado, despite the ongoing conflict and access constraints, protection services reached 276,337 children and caregivers (82 per cent of planned targets) with community-based mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). UNICEF also supported the reintegration of 392 children associated with armed forces and groups (CAAFAG) against 810 planned (representing 48 per cent achievement of annual target), providing them with case management and reintegration support. Crucially, these interventions were underpinned by strengthened complaints and response mechanisms, ensuring that services remained safe, accessible, and accountable to the affected communities. This work underscores the critical role of child protection in peacebuilding and recovery efforts in the north.

Goal Area 4: Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
In 2025, UNICEF continued to play a leading role in strengthening equitable, resilient and sustainable WASH services in Mozambique across development, humanitarian and climate contexts. UNICEF’s approach combined systems strengthening, service delivery, emergency response and climate action, with a strong focus on leaving no one behind.

Institutional reform marked a major milestone in 2025. Following approval of the Water Supply and Sanitation Law in 2024 and the 2025 national elections, the Government initiated far-reaching reforms to restructure service delivery and investment management. UNICEF contributed through consultative support as new entities were established, including Fundo de Investimento e Património de Abastecimento de Água e Saneamento (FIPAAS), Águas de Moçambique, provincial water and sanitation companies, and the National Administration of Public Works. While these reforms represent a significant governance shift, regulatory frameworks remain pending, requiring continued UNICEF engagement in 2026 to support implementation and protect equitable access for vulnerable populations. UNICEF strengthened the enabling environment for WASH by reinforcing monitoring, accountability and sector capacity. Support to the assessment of the National Water and Sanitation Information System (SINAS) identified critical gaps as well as system functionality and data visualization issues, with follow-up system upgrades and strengthened sanitation monitoring planned for 2026. In parallel, UNICEF invested in workforce development, supporting 60 training sessions that reached more than 1,700 government and private-sector personnel across priority areas including procurement, WASH FIT, emergency response, CLTS, sustainability and borehole construction. A Rural WASH Capacity Assessment Study and costed action plan highlighted significant workforce shortages and skills gaps, providing a strategic roadmap for structured training pathways and partnerships with national training institutions.
In water supply, UNICEF facilitated access to improved services for more than 204,726 people (268 per cent achievement of annual target) through rural boreholes, solar water systems, small-town water supply schemes and innovative financing mechanisms such as revolving funds. Investments prioritised rural areas and small towns, while humanitarian interventions restored or extended water services in crisis-affected areas, including Cabo Delgado. Technical sustainability was strengthened through specialised training and quality control measures for borehole construction.
Sanitation and hygiene interventions reached large populations through area-wide approaches, CLTS and market-based sanitation. Over 532 (67 per cent achievement of annual target) were declared Open Defecation free, while two additional districts achieved Open Defecation Free status, bringing the national total to 13 districts, while 860 sanitation products were sold through private-sector partnerships. An impact evaluation in Sofala demonstrated that integrated WASH, nutrition and behaviour change programming contributed to a 35 per cent reduction in severe stunting among children under five, further guiding investments to achieve maximum impact going forward.
UNICEF advanced climate-resilient services in 37 health care facilities (157 per cent achievement of annual target) and 37 schools (82 per cent achievement of annual target), benefiting over 22,000 children and ensuring safe conditions for approximately 42,000 births annually, while investments in WASH FIT coaching and infrastructure design ensured that immediate response efforts contributed to long-term resilience.
Humanitarian WASH response scaled up significantly due to conflict, cyclones, drought and disease outbreaks in 2025. UNICEF reached over 723,000 people with emergency water services and supported sanitation, hygiene and infection prevention in displacement sites, schools, health facilities and cholera treatment centres, while strengthening preparedness through training and pre-positioning of supplies.

Goal Area 5: Every child has an equitable chance in life
Amidst a deepening fiscal crisis, UNICEF advocated for social spending and expanded safety nets, positioning social protection as a key tool for resilience.
The Child Grant (0-2) programme, a critical safety net for vulnerable families, was successfully expanded in Nampula and Niassa Province, reaching 11,000 new beneficiaries reached in 2025 (new registrations). This expansion brought the total reach to over 61,000 beneficiaries across 23 districts (representing 127 per cent achievement against annual target). A major operational leap in 2025 was the digitalization of payments, with 13,122 mobile money accounts opened for beneficiaries in Nampula and Cabo Delgado. This shift to mobile wallets not only improved the efficiency, security, and transparency of transfers but also enhanced financial inclusion for women, who are the primary recipients of the grant. Complementing the cash transfer, the programme strengthened its care component through targeted case management for the most vulnerable households (around 15 per cent of beneficiaries), improving early detection and response to child protection risks. In Cabo Delgado, 2,686 children were under case management, with over 50 per cent of cases closed and 717 children supported to access birth registration. In Nampula, case management covered 11,128 children from the most vulnerable households selected to receive the cash transfer, achieving a 57 per cent case closure rate and registering 93 per cent of children initially identified without birth registration. In Niassa, 606 highly vulnerable families with children were enrolled in case management, many affected by underage caregiving. 
The system’s agility was further tested in Magude District, where UNICEF implemented anticipatory actions ahead of predicted droughts. By delivering cash transfers via mobile money to 4,850 beneficiaries before the crisis peaked, the programme demonstrated that social protection can act as a proactive shield against climate shocks, rather than just a reactive safety net.
UNICEF produced critical evidence to influence fiscal policy and planning. A notable achievement was the Multidimensional Child Poverty Assessment, developed with UNICEF support and endorsed by the government. This report provides the first official non-monetary poverty estimates for Mozambique, enabling more targeted and equitable policy planning that goes beyond income measures.
Furthermore, UNICEF’s robust budget analysis and advocacy regarding the impact of debt on social sectors positioned the organization as a key partner in high-level discussions on fiscal space. This included leveraging the Child Nutrition Fund to initiate discussions on swapping sovereign debt for nutrition investments, an innovative financing mechanism that could unlock critical resources for children.

Programme Effectiveness and Cross-Cutting Priorities
UNICEF’s emergency response to the conflict in the north and to the severe climactic shocks Mozambique faced in 2025 was robust and wide-reaching, delivering immediate assistance to 1.1 million people. In humanitarian contexts like Cabo Delgado, UNICEF navigated complex security constraints to deliver water to 731,247 people and support 262,711 children with education in emergencies.
Investments in preparedness yielded tangible results. The rehabilitation of the National Institute for Disaster Management (INGD) warehouse in Nampula and the training of District Technical Councils in Disaster Risk Management strengthened local capacity to store prepositioned supplies and coordinate responses to future shocks. These efforts reflect a commitment to localization and building national capacity for disaster management.
UNICEF implemented SBC interventions to address barriers in community hygiene and feeding practices. This approach, led to the certification of 41,313 “Model Family’’ households (out of 29.000 planned target, representing 70 per cent of achievement) who successfully adopted critical health and nutrition behaviours. Communication campaigns reached 4.5 million people (out of 6.1 million initially planned, representing 74 per cent of annual achievement), driving demand for services and promoting life-saving behaviours during cholera and Mpox outbreaks. Behavioural science pilots in Sofala demonstrated that low-cost, scientifically informed interventions could significantly increase hygiene practices, providing a proven model for scale-up.
Youth engagement moved beyond consultation to active leadership and advocacy. Over 800 adolescents were engaged as active agents of change, and youth-led climate advocacy resulted in a Youth Declaration presented at national and global climate forums, including COP30. The U-Report/SMS Biz platform expanded to 921,928 users (out of 1 million planned target), serving as a critical two-way communication channel for emergency alerts, youth consultation, and health information. This massive digital reach empowers young people to participate in national dialogue and access vital information.

This declaration was informed by a massive digital consultation process: a national U-Report poll on Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) engaged 30,459 young people, ensuring that the government’s climate commitments at COP30 were directly shaped by the voices of the generation most affected.
In 2025, thanks to UNICEF’s donor partners across the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus, UNICEF Mozambique mobilised USD $43.2M in Other Resources (Regular) and USD 10M in Other Resources (Emergency). The total expenditure for 2025, including commitments, amounted to USD 153 million (of which USD 34 million are commitments), while the actual expenditure was USD 119 million. Despite this support, the resources mobilised for the 2025 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal amounted to about USD 29 million (including USD 10 million in new funding), representing only 46 per cent of the appeal target of USD 63 million.
Despite these significant financial constraints, UNICEF maintained operational agility and accountability. The Supply & Logistics team managed over USD 81 million in supplies, achieving a 97 per cent reduction in expired contracts through strengthened oversight mechanisms. Financial stewardship was evidenced by a 92 per cent implementation rate of Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) assurance activities, ensuring rigorous accountability for resources entrusted to implementing partners. Furthermore, UNICEF strengthened financial and administrative management by maintaining a strong bank optimization ratio and consistently meeting key performance benchmarks for cash disbursements, ensuring that funds reached partners and beneficiaries on time.

The results achieved in 2025 underscore UNICEF’s ability to deliver at scale while driving systemic reforms, even in the most challenging of circumstances. By leveraging high-level advocacy to secure policy shifts like the National Immunization Strategy, unlocking strategic financing through mechanisms like the GPE grant, and proving the concept of integrated programming in Sofala, UNICEF has laid a strong foundation for the next country programme cycle. The progress made—from the digitalization of social protection payments to the institutionalization of community health systems—demonstrates that transformative change for children is possible, provided that interventions are strategic, integrated, and resilient. As Mozambique navigates continued climate and fiscal challenges, UNICEF remains a steadfast partner, committed to ensuring that every child survives, learns, is protected, and thrives.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
This chapter analyses the operational strategies UNICEF employed to navigate 2025, reflecting on adaptive management amidst fiscal and security constraints and outlining strategic shifts for the future.

Adaptive Management: Navigating Constraints
To overcome access constraints in the north, UNICEF operationalized a decentralized logistics strategy. The establishment of new UN hubs in Mocímboa da Praia and Mueda, combined with 1,261 integrated mobile brigades, allowed the office to bypass logistical bottlenecks. This pivot from a centralized response to a closer-to-need model was critical for restoring essential services to conflict-affected populations that were otherwise unreachable. Furthermore, the Supply & Logistics team established new Long-Term Arrangements (LTAs) with local transport providers in Central and Northern regions, significantly reducing lead times for emergency supplies. Delays in obtaining Ministry of Health clearances and in customs processing for offshore procurement by partners—particularly for medical supplies—are directly constraining programme implementation and undermining Key Performance Indicators especially related to timeliness of delivery of sales orders. The office will proactively pursue formal arrangements with the relevant authorities to ensure these bottlenecks are addressed and processes expedited.
Fiscal contraction and security risks necessitated a shift in the delivery of resources. Accelerating the digitalization of humanitarian and social protection cash transfers—specifically the expansion of mobile money payments for the Child Grant—served a dual purpose. It improved fiduciary efficiency in a resource-constrained environment and enhanced the safety of beneficiaries and staff in volatile districts, ensuring support reached the most vulnerable without exposing them to physical risks of cash distribution.
Facing initial mistrust and fear during cholera outbreaks, the office successfully altered its strategy by incorporating behavioural science. A pilot intervention in Nampula redesigned the patient experience at Cholera Treatment Centres (CTCs)—introducing dignity-focused "cholera beds" and safe family visits. This human-centric adaptation, combined with youth-led rumour management, significantly rebuilt trust and improved service uptake.

Despite strong financial stewardship (92 per cent implementation of HACT assurance activities), acute liquidity challenges delayed cash disbursements to partners in December, highlighting the need for more robust cash forecasting to mitigate local banking volatility. Additionally, persistent delays in VAT reimbursement strained the office’s financial flows, while limited government fiscal space led to delays in customs clearance for essential supplies. 
In the education sector, a trade-off emerged between immediate restoration and long-term durability; the high volume of emergency repairs required for classrooms damaged by cyclones consumed resources that could have been invested in resilient construction. This signals an urgent need to shift infrastructure financing models toward climate-smart standards that reduce recurrent repair costs.

Lessons Learned: Accelerating Results for the Most Marginalized
The most significant lesson of 2025 is that multisectoral convergence is the most effective pathway to reduce malnutrition. An impact evaluation in Sofala demonstrated that integrating WASH, nutrition, and SBC interventions led to a 35 per cent reduction in severe stunting among children under five. This confirms that scaling the convergence model—combining nutrition counselling with sanitation and hygiene promotion—delivers far greater improvements in child well-being than isolated sectoral interventions.
The emergency context in Northern Mozambique drove critical policy shifts that will have long-term developmental benefits. A key lesson learned was that humanitarian pressure can accelerate policy reform. The government’s acceptance of ALP as a valid pathway for out-of-school adolescents—initially a response to displacement in Cabo Delgado—has now opened the door for these programmes to be certified and scaled nationally. This demonstrates that emergency interventions, when strategically positioned, can unlock systemic barriers to education for marginalized youth.
Transitioning from paper-based to digital systems proved essential for reaching "zero-dose" children. The digitalization of immunization microplanning in 35 districts enabled health workers to identify and reach underserved communities previously invisible to the system. Similarly, the roll-out of the Last Mile Supply Monitoring system enhanced the visibility of nutritional supplies, ensuring critical commodities reached remote facilities.
Experience in 2025 reinforced the need for safeguarding mechanisms to be accessible to children, not just adults. The development of PSEA (Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse) comic books and child-friendly communication materials tested in four provinces allowed children to understand their rights and reporting pathways for the first time.  To ensure these tools were effective, partners were trained on their child-sensitive application, while operators of the Linha Verde 1458 and Linha Fala Criança helplines received targeted PSEA training to strengthen the quality of response services. This transition from compliance-based adult messaging to child-friendly engagement led to a more robust, victim-centred protective environment. 
This operational focus was reinforced by structural partnership strengthening UNICEF co-chaired the National PSEA Network to drive inter-agency coordination and supported the Office of the General Prosecutor to develop national PSEA guidance. Furthermore, accountability was strengthened by assessing all implementing partners using the UN Common Tool and implementing targeted support plans where gaps remained. Beyond the humanitarian sector, prevention efforts engaged security actors, with more than 100 personnel from the Forças Armadas de Moçambique (FADM) trained on the prevention and response to grave violations against children.
Adolescents proved to be critical strategic partners rather than passive beneficiaries. Young people played a central role in shaping the NDCs ahead of COP30, with digital polling engaging 30,459 youth on climate priorities. Youth engagement extended to disaster risk reduction (DRR), where youth participation in local committees strengthened community preparedness and early warning systems.

Future Outlook: Strategic Shifts for 2026
To counter the drastic contraction in ODA, UNICEF will pivot toward innovative financing models in 2026. Building on 2025’s advocacy, the office will operationalize the Child Nutrition Fund and pursue debt swaps for social sector investment. Furthermore, UNICEF will expand the "Revolving Fund" model for water supply in small towns—which successfully connected thousands to water in 2025—as a scalable solution for financial sustainability in the WASH sector. Technical support for budget tagging in nutrition and climate will also be prioritized to help the Government unlock global climate funds.
With the relentless cycle of climate shocks acting as a threat multiplier, UNICEF will shift its infrastructure strategy from "building back" to "building forward resiliently." Investments will prioritize durable, climate-adaptive infrastructure—such as solar-powered water systems and climate-smart health facilities—which proved their resilience in 2025. The office will leverage the momentum of COP30 to advocate for child-sensitive climate policies that institutionalize these standards.
To maximize the impact of limited resources, UNICEF will fully operationalize the Field Monitoring Module and implement the Data and Capacity Action Plan (DCAP). The recently published Multidimensional Child Poverty Assessment will serve as one of the primary advocacy tools to influence the Government’s National Development Strategy 2025–2044, ensuring that resource allocation is driven by deprivation intensity rather than just population density.
These lessons and strategic shifts underscore a critical reality: the current volatile environment demands operational agility. By adapting implementation modalities to navigate these complexities, UNICEF successfully protected service continuity and sustained progress toward its core objectives. Ultimately, its ability to pivot in the face of adversity has ensured that, despite the challenging external landscape, the organization delivered on its unwavering commitment to the rights and well-being of every child.

In 2025, Rwanda continues to stand out as one of Africa’s most business-friendly and rapidly transforming economies, maintaining strong growth despite a challenging global and regional environment. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 7.8 per cent in the first half of the year. This performance reflects sustained structural transformation and Rwanda’s ability to preserve macroeconomic stability.

Economic growth has been driven primarily by strong performance in the services and industry sectors. Services remained the backbone of the economy, contributing 43 per cent of GDP, supported by continued expansion in trade, transport, tourism, and financial services. Industry, particularly construction and manufacturing, contributed 22 per cent of GDP and continued to expand, reflecting sustained public and private investment in infrastructure and productive capacity. Agriculture employs around 43 per cent of the population while contributing 27 per cent of GDP, slightly lower than in previous years. This trend highlights ongoing structural challenges and underscores the need to boost productivity, climate resilience, and value addition to sustain rural livelihoods and inclusive growth.

Rwanda’s economic outlook in 2025 reflects both resilience and ambition. Although inflationary pressures, rising debt, and external shocks present risks, the government’s strong commitment to inclusive growth, macroeconomic stability, and long-term transformation continues. The central policy objective remains ensuring that economic progress translates into improved wellbeing for all, particularly the most vulnerable.

Macroeconomic stability is supported by prudent fiscal management and adaptive policy responses. The 2025/26 national budget increased by 21 per cent—from RWF 5.816 billion to RWF 7.033 billion—signaling an expansionary stance aimed at accelerating infrastructure development and inclusive economic transformation. This approach aligns with Rwanda’s Second National Strategy for Transformation (NST2) and Vision 2050, which aim to achieve middle income status by 2035. However, despite the overall budget increase, the share allocated to social sectors—including education, health, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and social protection—declined from 26.8 per cent in 2024/25 to 22.8 per cent in 2025/26, the lowest level in five years. This raises concerns about investments in human capital and social protection amid rising living costs.
 
Economic pressure remains significant. Inflation reached 6.2 per cent year-on-year by September 2025, with sharp price increases in health services, food, education, and other essentials. Rising public debt has increased fiscal pressure, with 8.2 per cent of the national budget allocated to debt servicing. Health insurance reforms introduced in July 2025 may have contributed to rising medical costs, which increased by about 70 per cent year-on-year according to the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR) Consumer Price Index for December 2025. These increases have disproportionately affected lower income households. Rising food prices threaten food security, particularly in rural areas, while higher school fees risk limiting access to education.

Externally, Rwanda continues to face declining Official Development Assistance (ODA), which fell from 18 per cent to 14 per cent of the national budget in 2024/25. Regional instability—particularly the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)—and broader global uncertainties further compound these challenges. Rwanda’s governance remains a strong asset. The country ranked third in Africa on the 2024 Corruption Perceptions Index, shared with Botswana, reinforcing investor confidence through strong institutions and sound economic management.

1.5 million people were lifted out of poverty, as per the Integrated Household Living Conditions Survey (EICV7), launched in April 2025 which showed that national poverty declined from a recalculated 39.8 per cent in 2017 to 27.4 per cent in 2024. Extreme poverty fell from 11.3 per cent to 5.4 per cent. However, disparities persist, with poverty higher in rural areas (31.6 per cent) than urban areas (16.7 per cent), and several districts recording rates well above the national average.

EICV7 data also indicate major improvements in access to basic services. Between 2016/17 and 2023/24, access to improved sanitation increased from 86 per cent to 94 per cent, while access to improved drinking water rose from 87 per cent to 90 per cent. Electricity use for lighting increased from 27 per cent to 72 per cent nationally, with rural access rising from 15 per cent to 65 per cent. Despite these gains, more than 60 per cent of young children still live in inadequate housing conditions, and over 40 per cent lack reliable access to safe water. Among adolescents, education related deprivation—linked to attainment, attendance, and literacy—remains widespread, particularly in rural areas and female-headed or less educated households.

Maternal and child health outcomes continued to improve, according to preliminary findings from the 7th Demographic and Health Survey (DHS7) released in December 2025. Antenatal care coverage increased substantially, with women receiving four or more visits rising from 47 per cent to 78 per cent. Mortality declined across all indicators: neonatal mortality fell from 19 to 17 per cent, infant mortality from 33 to 27 per cent, and under five mortality from 45 to 36 per cent. Stunting declined from 33 per cent to 27 per cent nationally, though rates remain above 30 per cent in 11 districts. Vaccination coverage among children aged 12–23 months declined slightly from 96 per cent to 94 per cent. The full DHS7 report is expected in 2026.

Policy and legislative reforms strengthened Rwanda’s health, nutrition, and development agenda. NST2 elevated stunting reduction as a national priority, supported by the Fifth Health Sector Strategic Plan (2024–2029) and the Fifth Program for Strategic Transformation of Agriculture, which emphasize food system transformation for women and children. New regulations on processed foods and revised marketing guidelines aim to protect public health, reduce exposure to unhealthy foods, and prevent malnutrition and diet related noncommunicable diseases, laying the foundation for the First Food Africa initiative.

Adolescent girls continue to face heightened risks related to teenage pregnancy, which increased from 5 per cent in 2020 to 8 per cent in 2025, and higher HIV vulnerability than their male peers. In response, Rwanda enacted a landmark health law lowering the age of independent access to sexual and reproductive health services from 18 to 15 years, enabling confidential and rights-based access to contraception and HIV prevention. The law also modernizes the healthcare framework through regulations on assisted reproductive technologies, digital health, telemedicine, and mental health safeguards aligned with international best practices.

Rwanda strengthened its climate and environmental response through stricter emission standards and an environmental tax on imported plastic packaging. However, public health pressures persisted, including mpox, cholera outbreaks in districts near Lake Kivu, and climate-related increases in malaria, pneumonia, and diarrheal diseases.

These pressures on national systems heighten the relevance of the Government of Rwanda’s Refugee Sustainable Graduation Strategy (2025-2030), led by the Ministry of Emergency Management (MINEMA), which aims to transit refugee households from aid-dependence to self-reliance through livelihood support. Regional instability continues to drive a growing refugee population, and by December 2025, Rwanda hosted over 137,500 refugees and asylum seekers (a 3,000+ increase from 2024), mainly from the DRC and Burundi.

In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Rwanda to accelerate strategies as per the NST2 including the aim to strengthen health workforce and improve health care access, such as maternal, neonatal and child health. Focus was on digital health systems and strengthening equitable access to primary health care, while ensuring it is disability-inclusive. As part of the sector-wide health plan, UNICEF supported across 14 districts (out of 30), the screening, rehabilitation, and referral services for disabled children embedded within routine services: 92 facilities were strengthened and eight hospitals were equipped with advanced diagnostic technologies. Health system capacity was reinforced through training of over 1,900 frontline workers, enabling earlier identification and referral of children with disabilities. As a result, 1,785 children were screened and 512 received digital hearing aids, and helping these children to reach their full potential.

These gains were consolidated through policy and financing milestones, including the integration of disability services into Rwanda Social Security Board (RSSB) insurance and the inclusion of assistive devices in essential supply lists—marking a shift from pilot initiatives to institutionalized, sustainable systems. These reforms were underpinned by increased domestic financing, with government investment rising to 7 billion Rwandan francs (RWF), strengthening the foundation for inclusive, resilient primary health care.

Rwanda successfully achieved Africa’s first nationwide scaleup of Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS), improving maternal nutrition at scale and promising impact on stunting rates. With support from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, UNICEF partnered with Ministry of health (MoH) to achieve full national rollout of the MMS programme by mid-2025. Following a seven-district pilot demonstrating 95 per cent coverage and 75 per cent adherence, MMS replaced iron and folic acid supplementation across all 30 districts, reaching around 169,000 pregnant women (83 per cent coverage). Rwanda is the first country in Africa to achieve nationwide MMS supplementation—an evidence-based intervention expected to reduce low birth weight and improve neonatal outcomes—reflecting strong government ownership and system readiness for sustained delivery. This readiness is further reinforced by Rwanda’s growing use of innovative financing mechanisms such as catalytic capital for strengthening health posts and blended-finance models that expand primary healthcare infrastructure, helping sustain maternal nutrition interventions at scale.

The quality of maternal and newborn care improved in 62 facilities across four districts, contributing to approximately 23,000 safe deliveries. This progress was driven by the implementation of harmonized mentorship guidelines and improved management of neonatal and pediatric complications. Adherence to postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) management protocols reached 89.3 per cent, while neonatal hypothermia decreased to 0.8 per cent. Oxygen readiness was enhanced in 100 facilities nationwide, and Electronic Medical Records expansion to four districts improved data use for approximately 313,000 households. These are  important achievements, contributing to the overall target of reducing under-five mortality ratio from 45 to 20 per 1,000 live births by 2030, as per the NST2 objectives. 

Immunization systems achieved both scale and resilience. Services expanded to 200 health posts equipped with climate-resilient cold chain equipment and tablets for real-time reporting. Full digitization enabled proactive tracking of under-vaccinated children and contributed to  high vaccine coverage: DPT1 98 per cent, DPT3 95 per cent, MR1 94 per cent, and MR2 90 per cent, with zero stockouts nationally. UNICEF advocacy supported GAVI approval for 18 refrigerated vehicles, strengthening last mile distribution. Engagement with the Interfaith Council reached over 245,000 community members, improving vaccination uptake in hard-to-reach and underserved communities. 

Adolescent health interventions on mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and sexual and Reproductive Health rights (SRHR) delivered  results at scale. Investments in mental health and psychosocial support strengthened services in 24 districts, reaching over 36,000 schoolchildren through improved reporting systems and mentorship, —including 771 teen mothers—benefited from integrated, peer-led programming, contributing to a sharp increase in utilization of SRHR services, rising from below 20 per cent to over 70 per cent among this target group. Additionally, community engagement reached 700,000 people through mentoring circles, interactions through games and play, home visits, community dialogues, school health clubs, youth forums at youth peer network meetings, contributing to shifts in social norms, more equitable access to services, and healthier behaviors for adolescents and young people. These results show that when demand-supply and normative barriers and stigma are properly addressed, the demand for SRHR services increases.

UNICEF Social and Behavioural approach also strengthened health programming. Implemented with MoH and the Rwanda inter-faith Council on Health (RICH), SBC campaigns contributed to a five per cent increase in routine immunization uptake. After mpox and Marburg outbreaks of 2024, UNICEF engaged 5.8 million community members with support of Mastercard foundation and Pandemic Fund, in RCCE activities to reduce stigma by 45 per cent and increasing reported handwashing practices to 76 per cent within three months within the pre-and post surveys of the targeted groups as per the Community Rapid Assessment (GeoPoll, Dec 2024/25).

While the levels of stunting are reducing, as mentioned above, further progress is required to meet Rwanda’s ambitious NST2 targets. UNICEF is a key partner for the government of Rwanda by supporting the efforts across the continuum, starting with the roll out of MMS, Africa First Foods and Food fortification efforts.

Integrated nutrition, livelihoods, and social support strengthened equity for vulnerable mothers and children. Through the UN joint programme, UNICEF strengthened Maternal Infant and Young Child Nutrition (MIYCN) services in two districts by training approximately 3,400peer supporters to improve infant feeding practices at community level. Complementary livelihood interventions enhanced resilience: Over 9,200 chickens were distributed to around 2,900 vulnerable women, increasing access to animal-source protein for young children. In addition, roughly 100 Village Savings and Loan Associations were established; 75 per cent of participating mothers accessed small loans, strengthening household capacity to meet children’s nutritional needs, reinforcing the nutrition–social protection nexus. With increased access to protein, better knowledge of nutritional best practices and improved income, the aim of those activities is to tackle and reduce stunting rates.

Rwanda’s nutrition services transitioned from campaigns to resilient routine systems while maintaining high coverage. UNICEF supported the MoH to develop and pilot a transition strategy. The pilot in Nyabihu district achieved 71 per cent coverage for vitamin A supplementation, deworming, and nutrition screening through routine services. Nationwide, 94 per cent of targeted children (1.65 million) received vitamin A supplementation and deworming during the first semester of 2025, while treatment of Severe Acute Malnutrition reached 100 per cent of identified cases across all health facilities, demonstrating strong continuity of care and system maturity. 

Increased momentum for national food-systems transformation to address malnutrition sustainably. UNICEF and the Ministry of Agriculture convened a High-level Roundtable to galvanize commitment and align multisectoral action to reduce all forms of malnutrition. In 2025, multiple UN agencies were jointly advancing food transformation initiatives, including promotion of locally sourced nutrient-dense foods (poultry, livestock, horticulture), reflecting a shift toward sustainable, locally driven solutions addressing root causes of malnutrition and laying the base for next steps.

Early Childhood Development (ECD) systems were strengthened through governance, innovation, and private sector engagement. UNICEF supported the National Child Development Agency (NCDA) to strengthen governance and service delivery nationwide. The 2024 harmonized ECD standards across sectors were disseminated in 2025 to 577 district officials (100 per cent district coverage) and frontline workers, to increase quality of ECD services nationwide. A South-South exchange with China provided learning about global best practices to be later adapted to the Rwandan context. Additionally, eight market-based and cross-border ECD illustrations centers delivered integrated early learning, nutrition, and responsive care services to 701 children. These models show positive learning outcomes. 

In addition to the above  ECD-system strengthening improvements and community-based ECD, private sector partnerships expanded ECD access and sustainability. Private companies invested in 102 ECD centers and breastfeeding rooms nationwide; in 2025 alone, ten additional companies joined, extending services to 1,200 more children. These efforts provide strong advocacy for other companies to follow and for society at large to understand the importance of ECD. Parenting programmes reached around 6,000 caregivers with skills in responsive caregiving, and financial literacy, contributing to improved early stimulation, maternal nutrition, and timely antenatal care attendance. These results demonstrate how private investments anchored in government systems, equity-focused delivery, and multisectoral partnerships can contribute to increased access to quality ECD services. 

Gender-transformative Social and Behavior Change (SBC) approaches supported shifts in harmful norms, promotion of positive masculinity, and greater agency for girls and persons with disabilities. The OneEggPerChildPerDay campaign reached 9 million people, promoting weekly egg consumption for children aged 6–23 months (and showing an increase of 19 percentage points among participants). Parenting education reached over 8 million caregivers nationwide through ECD centers, community dialogues, and digital platforms (Itetero radio soap and Itetero App), including 1,100 fathers actively championing positive gender roles.  UNICEF parenting programs delivered in-home guidance and mental health support to 31,710 families, directly impacting over 58,000 children and family members, through more than 400,000 home visits completed by IZU, the child protection community workers, in 2025 - a 33 per cent increase in home visits compared to 2024. This confirms the growing coverage of the child protection system in Rwanda. 
 
Early learning expanded at national scale. Preprimary net enrolment rose from 39 per cent (2024) to 45 per cent (2025) through awareness campaigns and community-based ECD centers. Quality improvements included training 807 teachers and ECD caregivers in play-based learning (with the LEGO Foundation) and distributing learning materials to 6,240 ECD centers and pre-primary schools. More than 250,000 children aged 3–5 (approximately 25 per cent of this age group) benefited from improved learning environments.

In 2025, Rwanda reformed the basic education curriculum to strengthen foundational learning, focusing on early grade reading and remedial education to reduce persistently high repetition rates. Building on the successful 2024 pilot, summer remedial education scaled to over 840,000 primary school learners who did not meet promotion benchmarks, leveraging Global Partnership for Education (GPE) support. Following the intervention, 68 per cent of assessed learners demonstrated competencies required for promotion, reducing repetition, building confidence and saving approximately RWF 7 billion (US$ 4.8 million) for the Ministry of Education. 

Education systems became more inclusive. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MoE) to adapt and roll out globally recognized child functioning tools nationwide. With GPE and Foreign Commonwealth Development Overseas (FCDO) funding, 4,200 teachers were trained to identify and assess children with disabilities, enabling approximately 1,200 children to access assistive devices (wheelchairs, hearing aids, white canes).  UNICEF also advanced inclusion of children with disabilities, youth, and women through Family Evening Forums – village-level dialogues that bring together community members together to discuss social, economic and family issues. For example, 8,000 parents (5,600 female; 2,400 male) from 52 villages discussed barriers to girls’ education. As a result, 92 per cent of participants agreed girls should remain in school and pledged to promote this message in their households and communities. The newly launched Resilience in Secondary Education (RISE) programme, with support from Mastercard foundation, aims to ensure 70 per cent of targeted beneficiaries are girls. These interventions improve equitable participation and reduce exclusion.

Youth skilling and employability was scaled-up through private sector partnerships and Ingazi (Passport to Earning)—Rwanda’s digital platform for skills and career opportunities. UNICEF supported the launch of Ingazi as a national one-stop gateway building synergies between 4 key ministries. Partnerships with MTN and Airtel enabled zero-rated access in four and sixteen learning sites respectively, allowing 43,310 youth (36 per cent female) to complete over 90,000 skills courses at no cost. Integration of an AI-powered Career Hub strengthened job matching and data-driven guidance, improving work readiness and positioning the platform for long-term national scale.

Child protection systems expanded reach and quality. Around 333,000 children received critical child protection interventions, driven by strengthened child justice, improved service quality, and policy reforms aimed at universal prevention of violence against children, via school-based, family-based and overall system-strengthening interventions listed below.

School-based child protection systems strengthened prevention and reporting. 60,000 children across 155 schools in five districts gained  skills to identify violence, use reporting channels, and adopt self-protection strategies. Child protection and safeguarding committees improved governance and provided around 125,000 children with effective reporting mechanisms. Implemented with partners including FCDO, NCDA, the Rwanda Education Board, and Save the Children, this approach expanded safe reporting channels and embedded child-centered safeguarding within the education system for sustainability and equity.

At sector-wide level, UNICEF supported rollout of the Child Protection Case Management (CPCM) Framework in eight pilot districts, with plans to expand in 2026, including guides and training manuals for community volunteers and social workers. An additional 1,697 children (734 boys, 963 girls) experiencing violence benefited from case management and service referrals. UNICEF also strengthened MHPSS in humanitarian settings by developing training guides and training approximately 300 health professionals and 60 child protection workers; a further 2,200 service providers were trained in child protection. UNICEF supported integration of Prevention of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment across all programming.

In order to reinforce evidence-based decision-making, UNICEF also supported evidence-generation in child protection. UNICEF formed a partnership with NCDA, the Ministry of ICT and Innovation, and MTN Rwanda to conduct research on child online protection to inform national policies and strategies embedded in wider regional and global developments. 

For the first time, Rwanda is establishing a diversion mechanism for children in conflict with the law, promoting alternatives to detention. In 2025, 58.5 per cent of minors in conflict with the law benefited from diversion orders or noncustodial measures. UNICEF strengthened capacity of the Ministry of Justice and the social workers workforce by supporting deployment of 33 newly trained graduates to reduce backlogs in child justice proceedings. A partnership with the Judiciary resulted in adoption of Chief Justice Instructions on Justice for Children, laying foundations for child-friendly justice systems nationwide.

UNICEF leveraged funds for the Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) sector by supporting innovative financing: four local banks were engaged to design loan products. Bank of Kigali launched its WASH loan product, while three additional banks were finalizing similar products for private WASH operators, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and households. This aligns with the NST-2 objective to mobilizing climate finance and resources to support sustainable development. 

UNICEF supported WASH data generation by upgrading the WASH Management Information System, preparing updated household WASH estimates for the WHO-UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, integrating water quality testing in the Labor Force Survey, and conducting groundwater exploration in five districts using Geographic information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing. UNICEF strengthened the Rwanda Water Resources Board by providing 48 groundwater data loggers (being installed), geophysical equipment, and staff training, and supported formulation of a research, innovation, and development strategy for the Rwanda Water and Sanitation Corporation. 

As part of responses to floods, landslides, and the mpox outbreak, over 10,000 people and 15 healthcare facilities gained access to basic water supply, along with an estimated 22,000 children in 22 schools, thanks to the support from the Government of Japan, Korea and Mastercard foundation. Additionally, 52 healthcare facilities, 3,900 ECD centers (enrolment over 58,000 children), and eight border entry points (over 49,000 people crossing daily) were equipped with handwashing facilities. Infection prevention and control supplies (including hand sanitizers and alcohol) were distributed; capacity of over 600 healthcare facility staff was strengthened through WASH and infection prevention training. After the March 2025 cholera outbreak in limited districts, UNICEF provided emergency water supply to over 2,700 people at risk. 

In support of the climate agenda, Green Rising Rwanda (led by youth organizations) engaged over one million Rwandans (54 per cent female); 709 community members (41 per cent female, 59 per cent male) to adopt sustainable practices such as clean cooking energy and green businesses. “Friends of Nature” engages 12,000 youth (including 80 per cent girls) in climate-focused school debates referencing COP29 resolutions and Rwanda’s NDC 3.0 priorities. UNICEF and the Ministry of Youth and Culture convened a Community of Practice for 85 youth-led organizations (31 per cent girl-led), reaching over 400,000 citizens. UNICEF also supported government-led gender equality reporting and implementation contributing to Rwanda’s ranking as 4th in gender equality in Sub-Saharan Africa (Global Gender Gap Report). 

UNICEF supported Rwanda’s social protection delivery system by working with MINALOC and Local Administrative Entities Development Agency (LODA) to train over 15,000 frontline service delivery volunteers (parasocial workers) using a comprehensive curriculum developed with UNICEF technical assistance. Building on rapid support during the Marburg outbreak through the Emergency Cash Transfer Programme, UNICEF reinforced resilience by reviewing and updating operational guidelines. UNICEF also supported a pilot disability child grant reaching more than 800 households across two districts, keeping disability inclusion at the forefront of the national agenda. 

UNICEF continued to lead evidence-generation and advocacy for child-focused investments. The Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA) publication (based on the latest EICV) showed significant progress since 2016/17: multidimensional child poverty nearly halved among children aged 5–14 and reduced by one third among adolescents aged 15–17, while overlapping deprivation persists. Among younger children, housing and water remain critical challenges (over 60 per cent living in inadequate housing; more than 40 per cent lacking reliable access to safe water). Among adolescents, education is the greatest concern, with over half deprived in attainment, attendance, or literacy. In a fiscally constrained environment, UNICEF advocated for sustained social sector investments and efficiency gains, focusing on strengthening the Ministry of Finance’s research directorate and commissioning evidence on scalable, cost-effective solutions, including ECD models suitable for national scaleup. 

UNICEF advanced inclusion of children with disabilities, youth, and women through Family Evening Forums – village-level dialogues that bring together community members together to discuss social, economic and family issues - 8,000 parents (5,600 female; 2,400 male) from 52 villages discussed barriers to girls’ education. As a result, 92 per cent of participants agreed girls should remain in school and pledged to promote this message in their households and communities. 

In 2025 as always, UNICEF advanced children’s rights through partnerships, communication, and public engagement, However, there was much emphasis on keeping UNICEF and its mandate visible to the wider public and the government considering the challenging eco-context of 2025. The World Children’s Day featured  road and online safety education together with Rwanda National Police and NCDA, and the launch of the Ingazi ambassadors’ program, brought over 300 children and youth together. UNICEF advocated national priorities including youth-led climate action and continued the campaign to combat child malnutrition and stunting. Advocacy with the Private Sector Federation led to updating the Business Code of Ethics to integrate Children’s Rights and Business Principles for over 200,000 businesses, with a formal launch planned 2026. UNICEF’s social media presence recorded average growth of 10 per cent, and children’s rights were promoted through four international and continental events, including three high-level visits and two fundraising campaigns (“I AM” campaign and launch of a donation feature). 

UNICEF provided technical and financial support to NISR to produce nationally representative data (such as EICV7, enquete sur les conditions de vie des menages and the Demographic Health Survey (DHS7), critical for monitoring children and women and progress toward SDGs. The DHS7 will inform decision-making beyond health outcomes.
