NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges 

Funding cuts in overseas development aid are placing social sector gains at risk. Global reductions in development financing—following the sunset of USAID and reductions from other partners—significantly affected the eco development system globally as in Rwanda. This has impacted ongoing programs and have required recalibration within the social sectors, including health, education, gender equality, and social protection. As Rwanda’s population reached 14.1 million in 2025 and continues to grow, there are expanding needs in health, nutrition, and basic social services. Rising service uptake among a young population, persistent rural poverty, and high dependency ratios underscore growing pressure on systems. Without targeted mitigation, including through efficiency gains, decrease in social sector investments risk widening inequalities, reversing gains in women’s empowerment, and further marginalizing vulnerable groups—particularly children with disabilities, and those in hard-to-reach communities. UNICEF’s experience in 2025 confirmed that fiscal shocks disproportionately affect children already facing multiple deprivations.

Inflation and rising food prices are eroding household resilience. Inflation and food price increases directly undermined household wellbeing. Meat and cereal prices rose by 21.9 per cent and 13 per cent respectively, reducing access to diverse diets and essential services. These pressures weakened nutrition outcomes, especially in rural and low-income households, and constrained the effectiveness of interventions such as weekly egg feeding. The experience highlighted the fragility of household resilience in the absence of shock-responsive, system-linked nutrition and social protection mechanisms. 

Workforce shortages undermined service quality. Persistent workforce gaps constrained service delivery across sectors. In Early Childhood Development (ECD) centers, child-to-caregiver ratios reached up to 38:1, reducing individualized attention and structured learning. Similar shortages affected maternal, neonatal and child health (MNCH), disability-inclusive services, and child protection, delaying early identification and follow-up for high-risk children. Workforce assessments confirmed that without sustained investment in human resources, service quality and equity gains remain fragile.

Pressure on learning infrastructure compromised access and quality. Overcrowded classrooms—averaging 64 learners in preprimary and 68 in lower primary, compared to national standards of 30 and 46—undermined foundational learning. While double-shift schooling helped manage enrolment, learning quality remained compromised.

Child protection systems remain insufficiently mainstreamed. Child protection has often been treated as secondary within national systems, limiting political prioritization, domestic financing, and workforce development. In response, UNICEF leveraged established sectors—particularly the justice system—as entry points for reform. Early progress integrating child protection into justice strategies and government-led workforce planning demonstrates a viable pathway to institutionalizing child protection as a core national system.

Digital parenting platforms reached over 8 million people, but households without smartphones remain excluded, reinforcing inequities among the most marginalized caregivers. In the health sector, weak interoperability and connectivity continue to limit real-time data exchange, undermining zero-dose tracking, referrals, and continuity of care. These gaps highlight the need for inclusive, interoperable, and resilient digital public infrastructure.

Complex procurement procedures slowed implementation of WASH infrastructure efforts, particularly those funded through short-term emergency grants, reducing the immediate impact of critical interventions. Streamlining procurement remains essential to accelerate delivery and improve outcomes.

Lessons Learned
 
Rwanda is ready for innovation across the social sectors and in the private sector. Therefore, it provides fertile ground for many cutting-edge initiatives such as local manufacturing, AI  in social sectors, solarization, and health insurance schemes. The Rwanda Country Office has learned in 2025 how to position UNICEF as a knowledge broker and a convenor of partners as the above text has shown with concrete illustrations. 

Integrated, multisector delivery improves efficiency and reach. Linking efforts in health, nutrition, education, and social sector reduced fragmentation and strengthened referrals. Connecting youth corners, community health workers, schools, and community leaders improved early identification, maternal nutrition, and disability-inclusive primary health care. Sector-wide initiatives such as OneEggPerChildPerDay and the IMENA mobile training model – a multi-sectoral behaviour change programme that builds the capacity of village-level frontline workers demonstrated that systemwide approaches deliver more sustainable impact than standalone interventions, especially when layered with poverty alleviation platforms.

Community-based caregiver models improve quality in resource-limited settings. Training auxiliary caregivers improved caregiver–child ratios and service quality in ECD settings, demonstrating a scalable approach to maintaining quality despite workforce constraints. This will influence the wider initiative to achieve national wide ECD scale up. 

Investments in emergency preparedness pay off. Lessons from mpox and Marburg outbreaks showed that rapid community health workers (CHW) mobilization, contingency planning, and multistakeholder coordination enable effective response. After-action reviews identified weaknesses in surveillance and real-time data entry, reinforcing the need to strengthen digitalized surveillance systems for faster detection and response.

Strategic Direction: High-Impact Investments for 2026 and Beyond

As UNICEF marks 40 years of partnership with Rwanda in 2026, the focus will be on consolidating gains, strengthening national systems, and building durable foundations for children. Aligned with the United Nations Sustainable development framework (UNSDCF) and Second National Strategy for Transformation (NST2), UNICEF will need to be more agile to be fit for future purpose, and is already reviewing its priorities, which will include:
    
Health systems: Advancing primary health care policy, digital health interoperability, and financing reforms; supporting health workforce scholarships under the National health 4×4 strategy (which aims at quadrupling the number of health workers within 4 years); strengthening frontline capacity and evidenced-riven planning; and scaling peer-led adolescent health interventions for rural and out-of-school youth.

Nutrition and ECD: Institutionalizing integrated data use and decentralized planning; consolidating nationwide multiple micronutrient supplementation; increase food fortification and standards, mobilizing blended private sector financing to  improve food systems; strengthening recruitment and professional development of auxiliary caregivers; and scaling gender-transformative parenting education through community and digital platforms.

Education and skills: Scaling weekly remedial learning sessions nationwide; launching the 10-year RISE alternative education pathway targeting 1.1 million youth in collaboration with Mastercard Foundation; and expanding Ingazi as a national platform for skills development, career guidance, and school-to-work transition.

Child protection: Mainstreaming child protection as a core system and supporting integration of social workers in all districts by 2029; scaling high-quality case management and referral systems; and strengthening justice-based entry points.

WASH and climate: Influencing NDC 3.0 and leveraging climate financing to expand access to resilient water, sanitation, and hygiene services, in alignment with NST2 goals on increasing basic and improved sanitations access. Work on clean cooking as a way to address air pollution. 

Social policy: Advocating for increased and more efficient social sector spending and supporting innovative financing to ensure equity and inclusion.

Emergency preparedness: Scaling RCCE onboarding packages, mobilizing innovative financing for WASH and climate responses, and strengthening frontline capacity aligned with the national volunteerism policy.

Children in Somalia experienced both significant progress and persistent challenges. The year was marked by increased political commitment to child rights, as seen in major legislative milestones: Somalia ratified the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child with reservation, adopted the Juvenile Justice Bill, delisting of national forces from child recruitment violations and enacted anti-Female Genital Mutilation laws in two regions. However, Somalia’s complex governance and varying capacities across federal and state levels mean that translating these advances into tangible improvements remains challenging and requires tailored, collaborative approaches.
Humanitarian needs remained acute in 2025. Approximately 5.98 million Somalis—including 3.7 million children—required humanitarian assistance due to ongoing conflict, climate shocks like drought, disease outbreaks, and economic vulnerability. Multidimensional poverty affected 67% of the population; more than half struggled to meet basic food needs. These factors combined to create one of the world’s toughest environments for child survival, learning, and protection.
Financing constraints significantly affected the scale and continuity of services. An estimated 85 per cent funding gap in the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal (US$146 million unmet) forced difficult prioritization decisions, including the closure of nutrition centres, disproportionately affecting children in high-burden and hard-to-reach areas and threatening gains in nutrition and child survival.
Climate variability, particularly La Niña–related drought, led to water shortages, food insecurity, and negative coping strategies such as children dropping out of school—especially in rural, nomadic, and displaced communities. Disease outbreaks strained already weak services and disproportionately affected children under five.
Under the leadership of the Government, UNICEF and its partners made substantial improvements in health and nutrition services. Malaria treatment coverage increased from 75% in 2021 to 92% in 2025, and antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage for HIV reached 32%. Health initiatives resulted in 1.2 million outpatient consultations, nearly 90,000 births assisted, and the distribution of 3.08 million insecticide-treated nets, protecting 5.3 million people. Immunization campaigns vaccinated 2.6 million children against pneumonia and diarrhea, while the Big Catch-Up campaign reached 737,598 zero-dose children, helping close equity gaps in immunization.
Nutrition remains a major concern. The prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rose to 14.3%, with projections indicating that 1.85 million children under five would suffer acute malnutrition between August 2025 and July 2026. Preventive nutrition services reached 1.72 million caregivers, and 2.2 million children received Vitamin A supplementation.
Access to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services improved notably. Basic water service access jumped from 45% in 2004 to 75% in 2025. Open defecation rates dropped from 51% to 14%. Over a million people gained access to safe water, and 64 rural water points were upgraded with solar-powered pumps. Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) enabled 45,000 people to achieve open defecation-free status, and improvements benefited 44 schools and 55 health facilities.
Education improved in Somalia, with primary school enrollment rising to 35.3% and reforms enhancing data management and inclusivity. Infrastructure upgrades, teacher incentives, and community engagement brought more children, especially girls and those with disabilities, into classrooms. Still, 67% of school-age children are out of school, mainly in rural and displaced areas, and gender gaps persist in secondary education. Additional investment is needed to address data quality, teacher training, and emergency preparedness.
Government supported by UNICEF and partners advanced child protection by launching the CRVS system in 19 districts, registering 9,100 children, and supporting anti-FGM efforts. Survivor-centered GBV services reached 87,000 people, with nearly 150,000 receiving protection support. UNICEF reunited 2,274 children with families, aided 722 former child soldiers, and expanded the social workforce with 2,450 accredited social workers, 60% of whom are women.
Social protection expanded through Government/UNICEF’s Child-Sensitive Social Protection Programme, which provided cash transfers to 41,200 pregnant and lactating women, indirectly benefiting over 206,000 people. The adoption of Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA) into national statistics improved child poverty monitoring and targeting. Public spending on health, education, and social protection rose to 24% of the national budget, up from 19% in 2024, showing greater government prioritization of children’s needs. The launch of MISC 7 will provide updated data to better inform decisions in 2026 and beyond.
Reduced funding for the AU Support and Stabilization Mission (AUSSOM) has weakened operational capacity, limiting UNICEF’s ability to maintain access and deliver services in hard-to-reach areas. 

Despite these achievements, significant challenges remain. Access to essential services is highly unequal, especially in conflict-affected, rural, and displaced communities. The nutrition crisis is deepening, with 1.85 million children projected to experience wasting. Chronic funding shortfalls, an 85% gap in humanitarian appeals, forced the closure of essential services and reduced assistance for the most vulnerable.
Legal reform implementation remains slow, and entrenched social norms and weak law enforcement undermine child protection. Service delivery is inconsistent in hard-to-reach areas, and more investment is needed in data, community workforces training, and emergency preparedness to build a resilient system.
UNICEF and partners are focused on integrated, resilient, and innovative approaches, emphasizing digital transformation, girl empowerment, community engagement, sustainable financing, and risk management. The main goal is to reach the most marginalized children, especially those in remote, shock-affected areas. Strengthened government leadership and sustainable financing, including community, private partnerships, are essential to stabilize services and improve children’s survival, learning, protection, and well-being.

In 2025, UNICEF’s contributions to advancing results for children and supporting progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the 2030 Agenda were guided by the Somalia Country Programme (2021–2025) and Annual Management Plans. These efforts were fully aligned with the Somalia United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF 2021–2025), national priorities outlined in the Somalia National Development Plan 9 (2020–2024), and the initial phase of the National Transformation Plan (2025–2029).

Goal Area 1: Survive and Thrive

UNICEF and partners sustained efforts to expand coverage of the Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS), strengthen health system performance, and address priority health challenges. These interventions contributed to progress toward universal health coverage and improved health outcomes for women, children, and adolescents. At the outcome level, malaria treatment coverage increased from 75 per cent in 2021 to 92 per cent in 2025, significantly reducing malaria-related morbidity and mortality. Similarly, antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage reached 32 per cent, marking a critical step toward epidemic control and improved survival for children and adults living with HIV.
UNICEF’s leadership and technical expertise were pivotal in achieving these results. In partnership with the Federal Government of Somalia, State health authorities, and a broad coalition of actors including WHO, FCDO, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, the Global Fund, and civil society UNICEF advanced health sector reforms and positioned health and human capital development as central pillars of the National Transformation Plan. Policy-level contributions included revisions of the Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health Strategy, the Maternal and Newborn Health Acceleration Plan, and the Community Health Strategy, ensuring stronger integration of primary health care, immunization, and digital health solutions.

Operationally, UNICEF supported 1.2 million outpatient consultations, 89,452 skilled deliveries, and the distribution of 3.08 million insecticide-treated nets, protecting 5.3 million people and accelerating malaria elimination efforts in 20 districts. Immunization initiatives introduced Pneumococcal and Rotavirus vaccines, contributing to the vaccination of 2.6 million children against pneumonia and diarrhea. Through the Big Catch-Up initiative, 737,598 zero-dose children were vaccinated, representing a critical step toward reducing under-five mortality and closing equity gaps.

To drive innovation and resilience, UNICEF deployed solar-powered cold chain systems to 93 per cent of health facilities, safeguarding vaccine integrity in off-grid and climate-vulnerable areas. The Better Lives initiative introduced electronic health records in 20 per cent of facilities, with scale-up to 60 per cent planned. Community engagement strategies including the Influential Leaders Initiative and integrated digital campaigns mobilized local leaders, women, and youth, contributing to sustained demand for immunization and HIV services. Collectively, these results demonstrate UNICEF’s catalytic role in strengthening Somalia’s health system, expanding equitable access to life-saving services, and advancing progress toward SDG 3 and universal health coverage.

In 2025, Somalia faced a worsening nutrition crisis, with Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) prevalence rising to 14.3 per cent, up from 11.7 per cent in 2024. Projections indicate that 1.85 million children under five will experience wasting between August 2025 and July 2026, including 421,000 with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). Despite these challenges, UNICEF sustained and scaled life-saving nutrition services, positioning Somalia’s child wasting treatment programme as a trusted platform for integrated health, nutrition, and WASH interventions.

Through a network of 600 Outpatient Therapeutic Programme sites across 70 districts, UNICEF and partners treated 384,000 children with SAM between January and October 2025, achieving 83 per cent of the annual target. Programme performance remained strong, with a 97.6 per cent cure rate, 1.6 per cent defaulter rate, and mortality below 1 per cent, reflecting strengthened capacity and adherence to global standards. A robust supply chain underpinned these results, delivering 40.8 million sachets of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food, 59,928 tins of therapeutic milk, and 247,750 MUAC tapes for screening and case management.

Preventive interventions reached 1.72 million caregivers with counselling on optimal infant and young child feeding practices, while 2.2 million children received Vitamin A supplementation, alongside large-scale deworming interventions. UNICEF advanced sustainability by strengthening the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) mechanism at federal and state levels, promoting multisystem approaches to reduce wasting. A strategic shift in 2025 reframed prevention beyond counselling, prioritizing access to locally appropriate nutritious foods—addressing underlying drivers of malnutrition and reducing dependency on imported therapeutic products.

These achievements lay the foundation for long-term improvements in child survival, growth, and cognitive development, while reducing maternal morbidity and mortality linked to poor nutrition. By integrating nutrition with health, WASH, education, and social protection, UNICEF contributed to resilience-building and human capital development, aligned with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3.

Goal Area 2: Learn

In 2025, UNICEF Somalia achieved notable results in education, reversing negative trends and catalyzing systemic change for crisis-affected children. Through a multi-pronged strategy focused on system strengthening, access, and quality, UNICEF enabled 155,811 children, including 69,906 girls, to access learning opportunities, raising primary enrolment to 35.3 per cent and improving retention.

UNICEF’s leadership in education system strengthening delivered measurable institutional reforms. Decentralization of the Education Management Information System (EMIS) empowered ministries to manage data independently, with school-level reporting improving real-time accuracy. Policy and coordination reforms, including teacher policy development and sector planning, strengthened evidence-based decision-making and institutionalized coordination platforms, reducing duplication and enabling timely responses to climate shocks and conflict.

Access to safe and inclusive learning environments expanded through initiatives such as the Joint Resilience Programme, Education Cannot Wait Multi-Year Resilience Programme, and Eco-Village projects, reaching 155,811 learners, including 1,572 children with disabilities. Investments in infrastructure, teacher incentives, community mobilization, and double-shift systems enabled thousands of children to return to school.

UNICEF further enhanced access to resilient education by rehabilitating classrooms, constructing Early Childhood Education facilities, and integrating climate-resilient designs to ensure continuity for displaced and conflict-affected children. Gender equality and disability inclusion advanced through menstrual hygiene management kits and targeted cash assistance. At policy level, UNICEF through its regular resources supported the Ministry of Education to establish the Climate Education Task Force, with climate education materials to be piloted by 2026 in partnership with IGAD and UNESCO.

These reforms lay the foundation for sustainable improvements in learning outcomes, gender equity, and resilience, aligned with SDG 4 and national education priorities. By institutionalizing EMIS and risk-informed planning, ministries now possess enhanced capacity to allocate resources strategically and respond to shocks, ensuring continuity of education during crises. Expanded ECE access strengthens foundational learning, improving future literacy and numeracy outcomes. Gender-responsive measures and disability inclusion reduce persistent barriers, promoting equity and social cohesion. From a long-term perspective, these reforms will contribute to human capital development, enabling girls and boys to acquire skills for economic participation and leadership, while reducing intergenerational cycles of poverty and vulnerability. UNICEF’s integrated approach aligns with SDG 4 (Quality Education) and Somalia’s National Education Sector priorities, positioning education as a driver of peacebuilding, resilience, and inclusive growth.

Goal Area 3: Protection
In 2025, Somalia made measurable progress in strengthening child protection systems, laws, and social norms, with UNICEF playing a catalytic role. At federal level, Parliament endorsed the Juvenile Justice Act and the Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) Act, advancing child-friendly justice and the right to legal identity. The CRVS system became operational in 19 districts, registering 9,100 children, with growing interoperability across sectors.

Progress toward eliminating harmful practices accelerated, with anti-FGM legislation enacted in multiple Federal Member States and 43 community declarations abandoning FGM. Survivor-centred GBV services reached 87,000 individuals, while nearly 150,000 people accessed child protection and GBV services despite access and funding constraints.

UNICEF-supported interventions enabled children in conflict with the law to benefit from diversion and alternative care. The launch of Somalia’s first national child helpline, alongside policy work on alternative care and kafalah, strengthened protective mechanisms. In Puntland, revisions to the anti-terrorism law marked a critical shift in recognizing children associated with armed groups as victims entitled to rehabilitation.

Through the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism, over 1,600 grave violations affecting 1,200 children were verified, contributing to the partial delisting of Somali security forces from UN reports. UNICEF reunited 2,274 children with families, supported 722 children formerly associated with armed groups, and strengthened the national social service workforce by integrating 2,450 accredited social workers into a national platform. These achievements advance SDG 16 and Somalia’s child protection commitments.

Additionally, UNICEF provided technical assistance, advocacy, and capacity-building to advance legal reforms and institutional accountability. Through the Joint Program on Human Rights, UNICEF supported operationalization of the National Human Rights Commission and the Child Rights Council, enhancing oversight and remedies for rights violations. At the system level, UNICEF mapped and integrated 2,450 accredited social workers (60 per cent women) into a national platform, improving coordination and supervision. Strategic partnerships with government ministries, CSOs, and international actors such as UN agencies enabled alignment with global child rights standards and sustained progress toward Somalia’s commitments under international treaties. 

These achievements are already transforming the child protection landscape. By embedding legal frameworks, strengthening workforce capacity, and expanding access to identity and justice services, Somalia is building a protective environment that reduces violence, exploitation, and harmful practices. For children, this means greater safety, dignity, and access to rights, while for girls, anti-FGM legislation and community declarations signal a cultural shift toward gender equality. Over time, these reforms will contribute to breaking cycles of abuse and vulnerability, improving psychosocial well-being, and enabling children to thrive in safe, supportive environments aligned with SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) and Somalia’s national child protection priorities.

Goal Area 4: Safe and Clean Environment
In terms of Safe and Clean Environment (WASH) outcomes, Somalia has achieved remarkable progress in expanding access to basic water services, increasing coverage from 45 per cent in 2004 (JMP) to 75 per cent in 2025 (UNICEF WASH Needs Assessment). This transformation represents a major step toward universal access and signals the country’s growing capacity to deliver on foundational SDG 6 targets. The remaining challenge lies in reaching the final 17 per cent of the population, predominantly in rural and hard-to-reach areas. As basic water coverage approaches saturation, Somalia is increasingly positioned to transition toward safely managed water services—the final step on the SDG water ladder—ensuring improved service quality, reliability, and long-term sustainability.

Sanitation outcomes also reflect significant behavioral and social change. Open defecation rates declined sharply from 51 per cent in 2004 to 14 per cent in 2025, marking a critical public health milestone. However, progress in basic sanitation coverage has been more modest, increasing from 49 per cent to 54 per cent over the same period. This divergence indicates that while communities are abandoning harmful practices, many have yet to progress up the sanitation ladder to achieve safe and dignified sanitation. The next phase of programming therefore requires scaling proven and affordable sanitation models, particularly in rural settings, while embedding climate-resilient solutions to sustain gains.

UNICEF played a catalytic role in driving these long-term results by combining policy reform, service delivery expansion, and humanitarian response. At the policy level, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to federal and state Ministries of Energy and Water Resources to strengthen governance, accountability, and sector coordination. A landmark achievement was the establishment of the Water Sector Development Facility (WSDF), a national platform for coordination and investment. UNICEF was nominated to co-lead the WSDF’s technical arm, alongside the World Bank leading the investment arm. Through this mechanism, UNICEF supported the development of the National Water Resources Development Plan (2026–2030), aligned with Somalia’s National Transformation Plan and SDG 6, providing a coherent roadmap for universal access and climate resilience.

At the service delivery level, UNICEF enabled over one million people to access basic water services through the construction and rehabilitation of water systems nationwide. To enhance sustainability and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, 64 rural water points were upgraded with solar-powered pumping systems, lowering operational costs and improving service reliability. In sanitation, UNICEF scaled the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach, enabling 45,000 people to achieve Open Defecation Free status and adopt safe hygiene behaviors. Institutional WASH improvements reached 44 schools and 55 health facilities, ensuring access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene for children and frontline health workers.

UNICEF also sustained life-saving humanitarian WASH interventions throughout 2025, reaching 677,000 people with emergency water services, 13,000 with improved sanitation facilities, and 485,000 with hygiene promotion and hygiene kits. These interventions were critical in mitigating disease outbreaks and protecting vulnerable populations during climate shocks and displacement crises.

An evaluation of the Joint Resilience Programme confirmed its significant contribution to community resilience through the integration of WASH with education, nutrition, and health interventions. This multisectoral approach improved school attendance and retention while strengthening community capacity to withstand and recover from shocks.

Goal Area 5: Equitable Chance in Life and Programme Effectiveness
In 2025, Somalia made foundational progress in institutionalizing child-focused data systems and strengthening social sector governance, positioning the country for long-term and inclusive transformation. A major milestone was the Somalia National Bureau of Statistics embedding the Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA) into the national statistical architecture, enabling more precise tracking of multidimensional child poverty and targeted responses to overlapping deprivations. The planned 2026 MODA update using MICS data will generate internationally comparable child poverty profiles, strengthening SDG monitoring and evidence-based policymaking under the National Transformation Plan.
UNICEF facilitated high-level, evidence-driven dialogue on equity and efficiency through dissemination of public expenditure analyses highlighting trends affecting children. Allocations to health, education, and social protection increased to 24 per cent of the national budget in 2025, up from 19 per cent in 2024, signaling improved prioritization. Health execution rose to 83.3 per cent from 61.4 per cent, reflecting stronger absorptive capacity, while education execution declined to 47.6 per cent, exposing persistent bottlenecks now informing corrective action. These shifts expanded fiscal space for child-focused services and catalyzed policy discussions on procurement reform, capacity strengthening, and accountability. Partnerships with the Sadar Institute and the International Budget Partnership (IBP) advanced Somalia’s Open Budget Survey performance and laid the groundwork for more transparent, participatory budgeting that safeguards social investments for children.
UNICEF expanded the Child-Sensitive Social Protection Programme (CSSP), delivering cash transfers to 41,200 pregnant and lactating women with infants under one year, indirectly benefiting over 206,000 people. Beyond income support, the programme strengthened links to essential services, including birth registration for more than 15,000 children, improving legal identity and access to health and nutrition. These efforts contributed to 13.8 per cent of children in poor households accessing social protection, a critical step toward breaking intergenerational poverty and building resilience, aligned with SDG 1 and SDG 10.
With technical support from the Regional Office and Headquarters, UNICEF deployed the Government Social Protection Delivery System (SPDS), formerly Baxnaano MIS, for enrolment, verification, payments, and grievance management. SPDS was complemented by UNICEF’s Humanitarian Cash Operation and Programme Ecosystem (HOPE), providing second-level assurance for audit and donor reporting. This mixed modality enabled delivery of regular cash transfers to over 13,000 households, in collaboration with the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MOLSA), while leveraging the Unified Social Registry (USR) to strengthen system integrity, accountability, and scalability.
At the local governance level, UNICEF supported 12 districts across Somaliland, Puntland, and central-south Federal Member States to institutionalize inclusive planning through District Development Frameworks and Annual Work Plans reflecting community, women’s, and children’s priorities. These mechanisms improved alignment among service providers and responsiveness to local needs, marking a structural shift toward decentralized, community-centered governance that converts public investments into tangible gains for children.
Programme effectiveness remained a critical enabler of UNICEF Somalia’s ability to deliver results at scale in an increasingly complex and volatile operating environment. Throughout 2025, UNICEF strengthened adaptive management, risk-informed programming, and accountability mechanisms to ensure continuity of life-saving services while advancing longer-term systems strengthening and resilience in line with the UNICEF Strategic Plan.

UNICEF sustained a high level of emergency preparedness and response capacity, enabling rapid and coordinated action in response to climate shocks, disease outbreaks, and localized conflict. Strategic access negotiations strengthened partnerships with local actors, and flexible implementation modalities expanded humanitarian reach into hard-to-access districts, ensuring timely assistance for children affected by multiple, overlapping crises. These efforts reinforced UNICEF’s leadership role in emergency coordination and its credibility as a trusted partner to government, UN agencies, and humanitarian actors.

Community engagement and accountability were strengthened through the delivery of integrated, life-saving information to over 2 million people, supporting informed decision-making, behavior change, and service uptake. A major milestone was the launch of Somalia’s National Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) Strategy, which established a unified framework for crisis communication, feedback, and accountability. Partnerships with community and religious leaders, civil society organizations, and local media amplified key messages, strengthened trust, and contributed to improved utilization of health, nutrition, education, and protection services.

Programme effectiveness was further enhanced through investments in digital systems, data use, and evidence generation. Innovative tools such as Last Mile Supply Monitoring (LMSM) strengthened supply chain transparency, mitigated diversion risks, and improved value for money, while integrated management information systems across sectors enabled real-time monitoring and adaptive course correction. UNICEF also advanced national evaluation capacity by supporting the development of the Somalia National Evaluation Guidelines, institutionalizing standards for evaluative quality, learning, and results-based management across government and partners.

UNICEF’s leadership in evaluation and learning was reinforced through the successful management of the Somalia 2021–2025 UN Sustainable Cooperation Framework (UNSCF) evaluation, which directly informed the 2025 Common Country Analysis and shaped the UNSCF 2026–2030. Findings from the End of Country Programme Evaluation confirmed UNICEF Somalia’s strong alignment with national development priorities and highlighted its effectiveness in mitigating operational risks while delivering results for the most vulnerable populations.

Collectively, these programme effectiveness measures strengthened UNICEF Somalia’s capacity to operate with agility, safeguard accountability, and translate resources into measurable results. By embedding risk management, community engagement, digital innovation, and evaluative learning into programme delivery, UNICEF enhanced both humanitarian performance and development impact positioning the organization to deliver high-impact, equitable, and sustainable results under the 2026–2030 Country Programme.

Nonetheless, persistent gaps in gender equity, teacher capacity, data quality, infrastructure, and emergency preparedness constrained scale and learning quality. These challenges underscore that progress toward learning outcomes requires sustained investment in governance, workforce development, and climate- and risk-informed systems. UNICEF will deepen efforts in risk-informed planning, gender-responsive strategies, and digital tools to ensure continuity and quality learning for children affected by conflict and climate shocks.

Somalia advanced legal and policy reforms, including anti-FGM legislation and juvenile justice frameworks, contributing to stronger alignment with child rights standards. However, slow implementation, entrenched social norms, and weak enforcement continue to undermine protection outcomes. Low birth registration rates restrict access to essential services, and children associated with armed groups remain at risk of detention and prosecution. These lessons reaffirm that legal reform must be accompanied by system strengthening, social norm change, and service scale-up. UNICEF will accelerate birth registration, expand community-led prevention, and strengthen diversion and rehabilitation pathways to ensure children are protected from violence, exploitation, and harmful practices.

Progress in water access (75 per cent) and reductions in open defecation (14 per cent) demonstrate systemic gains, yet financing gaps threaten sustainability. UNICEF’s partnership with UNCDF to design blended finance instruments and explore carbon credit opportunities for solarized water systems represents a breakthrough in innovative financing. Given the scale of needs, traditional funding alone is insufficient. Future priorities include piloting blended finance models in urban settings, leveraging carbon markets, and embedding resilience in service systems to secure long-term investment for vulnerable communities.

UNICEF’s cash transfer programme demonstrated that government-led delivery systems can function under strong accountability mechanisms, benefiting 41,200 women and supporting 15,000 children to access birth registration. While donor compliance requirements slowed implementation, the experience confirmed that risk-managed integration of government systems is feasible and essential for sustainability. Going forward, UNICEF will refine its Service Delivery Model, including selective engagement with the private sector and Community Public-Private Partnerships (CPPPs) in mature districts to expand access to basic services, offset funding constraints, and strengthen household resilience.
Despite system-level investments, consistent service delivery remained uneven in conflict-affected and hard-to-reach areas. UNICEF’s leadership in localized access strategies and area-based coordination (ABC) demonstrated that community acceptance, flexible delivery modalities, and sustained field presence are critical to achieving results for the most marginalized children. In 2026–2027, access to hard-to-reach locations will be elevated as a core operational priority, with a focus on life-saving services and resilient delivery platforms to advance equity.

The 2025 End of Programme Evaluation reinforced the need for an integrated and resilient programming approach anchored in the humanitarian–development–peace nexus, with stronger emphasis on systems strengthening, cross-sectoral integration, and equity. Mainstreaming gender equality, disability inclusion, climate resilience, and child and youth participation emerged as essential for relevance, accountability, and impact. In a constrained financing environment, diversified resource mobilization and prioritization of high-impact interventions are critical.

Looking ahead, UNICEF Somalia will adopt an integrated and scalable approach to deliver high impact transformative results aligned with Strategic Plan outcomes, strengthening resilience, reducing preventable under-five mortality, advancing learning, and safeguarding child rights. Strategic partnerships with government, the private sector, including CPPPs, and communities, combined with digital transformation and innovative financing, will support cost-efficient delivery and sustainable impact. 

Evidence generation will remain central to adaptive management and accountability. UNICEF will continue investing in innovative data and monitoring systems to demonstrate results at community, district, regional, and national levels, ensuring continuous learning and measurable improvements for women and children in Somalia.

The year 2025 marked a pivotal moment for child rights in South Africa, following the formation of a restructured Government of National Unity (GNU) after the landmark 2024 national elections. This new era of coalition politics introduced broader political inclusivity, creating opportunities for consensus-driven governance. This political transition unfolded against a backdrop of severe socio-economic constraints, characterized by sluggish economic growth, mounting fiscal pressures, and persistent inequality. These structural challenges not only limited the government’s ability to expand social investments but also deepened vulnerabilities for households and children, underscoring the urgency of innovative approaches to protect and advance child rights.


As the first African country to chair the G20 presidency, South Africa brought the voice of the continent to one of the most powerful economic forums, shaping decisions that impact global trade, development, and multilateral diplomacy. UNICEF reaffirmed its commitment to ensuring children’s voices are heard in global policymaking by supporting the Children20 and participating in other related working groups. In collaboration with Children20, UNICEF facilitated meaningful engagement through the Pre-Summit. UNICEF was also actively engaged in the Development Working Group, Women’s Empowerment Working Group, Education Working Group, Finance and Health Task Force, and Digital Economy Working Group. These working groups enabled the raising of the profile of children and issues.  In a powerful moment at the G20 Social Summit, South Africa’s child delegates handed the Declaration directly to President Cyril Ramaphosa on World Children’s Day, 20 November 2025, ensuring that children’s priorities are emphasized and highlighting the global significance of children’s participation in policy dialogue. UNICEF also participated in official G20 side events to launch its flagship report, State of the World’s Children 2025, reinforcing its commitment to advancing child rights and promoting meaningful engagement in governance processes. The report, Ending Child Poverty: Our Shared Imperative, warned that progress has stalled due to climate shocks, conflict, and declining international aid. Its launch at the Social Summit created a timely political moment, reinforcing that eliminating child poverty cannot simply be a social aspiration but must be a core economic imperative for G20 nations.


South Africa has made incremental progress on several SDGs, notably in access to water and sanitation and social protection coverage, with over 90% of the population accessing basic drinking water and 63% covered by cash benefits. However, the country faces critical challenges that threaten overall achievement, including persistent inequality (Gini: 0.63), sluggish economic growth, and rising hunger and malnutrition. With 62% of children living in multidimensional poverty, and 37.1% of youth (15–24) not in employment, education, or training, these structural barriers undermine progress toward inclusive development. Despite modest declines in income poverty in the post-apartheid era, recent estimates suggest that some 63 per cent of adults live below the upper-middle-income poverty line and 62 per cent of children aged 0–17 years are multidimensionally poor. Accelerating SDGs achievement will require innovative financing, private sector engagement, and targeted interventions to address poverty, inequality, and youth unemployment.


Although historical spending on the social sectors was commendable, recent national budget allocations fall short of addressing the scale of challenges facing children. Natural disasters are increasing in frequency and severity with climate change, while weakly regulated urban expansion contributes to significant biodiversity loss and pollution. South Africa has emerged as a new migration hub, hosting an estimated 2.4 million international migrants in 2022 from across the continent and beyond.  


The Education sector was marked by a stark contrast between high access and critically low quality of learning. South Africa has achieved over 97% school attendance and gender equity among children aged 7–17. However, learning outcomes are poor, with 81% of Grade 4 learners unable to read for meaning. Furthermore, 45% and 33% of Grade 8 learners are below international mathematics and science benchmarks, respectively. School completion is challenged beyond the lower secondary level, with about 15% of learners leaving in Grade 10 and 24% in Grade 11, primarily due to poor education quality (24%) and lack of finances (22%). Socio-economic inequality, regional disparities, and social issues like teenage pregnancy, violence, and poverty exacerbate these educational deficits. The transition from school to work remains exceedingly difficult, with youth unemployment (15-34 years) at 50.2%. Systemic barriers to future-ready learning persist, as 31% of public schools still lack an internet connection. Additionally, the national rollout of the Coding & Robotics curriculum, approved in 2024, continues to be hampered by a critical lack of teacher preparedness and essential resources.


In the Health and Nutrition sector, persistent systemic challenges continue to undermine child survival and development. The under-five mortality rate, while declining marginally to an estimated 35 per 1,000 live births in 2023, remains above pre-pandemic levels, signifying a concerning reversal of nearly a decade of progress. Immunization coverage gaps pose a significant threat, as evidenced by a sharp rise in zero-dose children and outbreaks of measles and diphtheria, highlighting the vulnerability of infants to vaccine-preventable diseases. The malnutrition burden presents a triple challenge: over 1.7 million children are stunted (3 out of 10), a rate that has slightly increased from 27% in 2016 to 29% in 2024. The prevalence of wasting has doubled from 2.5% in 2016 to 5% in 2024, affecting 219,200 children and placing South Africa among the top ten countries globally for severe wasting in children under five. Concurrently, overweight and obesity in children under five have nearly doubled from 13% in 2016 to 23% in 2024, while exclusive breastfeeding rates have declined from 32% to 22% over the same period.


Children faced escalating environmental risks that compound existing vulnerabilities in the WASH and Climate Change space. South Africa is warming twice as fast as the global average, confronting more intense heatwaves, droughts, floods, and food and water insecurity, which directly threaten children's health, safety, and well-being. The country’s response includes adopting the Climate Change Act (2024) to set emission targets and manage a just transition from coal. However, significant challenges remain in adapting to extreme weather, managing water scarcity, and financing climate resilience, all exacerbated by high poverty and inequality. South Africa remains a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, and associated air pollution negatively affects children's health and development. Despite access improvements, many communities and schools struggle with climate-related water scarcity and poorly maintained WASH infrastructure, leaving children, especially in rural areas, in unsafe conditions. Poor sanitation contributes to high school absenteeism, particularly among girls, indicating an urgent need for improved WASH services.


Violence against children remains pervasive and systemic. Crime statistics show that children accounted for approximately 40% of all reported sexual offences, with rape constituting the vast majority of these crimes against children. While younger children are most affected by neglect and physical abuse, adolescents are disproportionately victims of sexual violence, homicide, assault, and kidnapping, reflecting clear age-specific risk patterns. New national data from the First South African National Gender-Based Violence Study indicates that 35.5% of women have experienced physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence in their lifetime, with childhood exposure to violence being a strong predictor of both later victimization and perpetration. The South African Child Gauge 2025 highlights the inter-generational cycle of violence, demonstrating how early exposure to abuse increases lifelong vulnerability and reinforcing the urgency of prevention-focused, systems-strengthening responses. Although adolescent birth rates are modestly declining, there is growing policy attention on statutory rape, evidenced by the 2025 Joint Parliamentary Report on the issue. 


The policy environment has been strengthened for child-centered governance. Key advancements included securing government commitment to the routine measurement of multidimensional child poverty, strengthening the national data architecture to be more child-centric, and deepening evidence-based advocacy for public finance for children. While direct reductions in child poverty rates remain a complex, long-term challenge, the foundational systems for targeting resources, reducing exclusion errors, and amplifying children's voices in budgetary processes have been notably strengthened. UNICEF's ongoing parliamentary advocacy on budgets for children contributed to better fiscal planning, with government efforts focused on containing accruals in social sector departments to enable more effective and efficient budgeting for children. The National Strategy to Accelerate Action for Children (NSAAC) and the National Plan of Action for Children (NPAC) were approved by the Cabinet.


South Africa’s upper-middle-income economy and local capacities support a thriving space, addressing the dual crises of youth unemployment and unmet child needs, which emerged as a strategic priority which is driven by skills mismatches, geographic inequality, and lack of experience. Research commissioned by UNICEF demonstrated how this twin challenge can be transformed into an opportunity through an innovative, scalable, triple-impact solution. The findings showed that empowering youth through skills development and paid work experience can simultaneously deliver measurable results for children in Education, Health, Protection, and Climate sectors. A ‘youth-force’ strategy also strengthens local systems, builds community capacity, and increases the cost-effectiveness of interventions. Powered by techno-social innovation and digital platforms, this approach aims to create a virtuous cycle, directly tackling youth unemployment while closing the child well-being gap and accelerating progress toward the SDGs.

The year 2025 marks the last year of the current country programme 2020-2025. UNICEF South Africa advanced the child rights agenda through strategic partnerships with the new Government of National Unity (GNU), civil society, academia, the private sector, and children and  young people themselves. Operating within a context of fiscal constraint and  political transition, UNICEF’s programmes were sharply focused on achieving  scalable results and strengthening systems in alignment with the final year  of the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2022-2025) and national priorities within the  United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Core funding  proved essential for agile programme design, high-level advocacy, and implementing  high-impact innovative interventions, which were subsequently scaled through  significant partnerships and other resources. The following analysis highlights key, strategically relevant achievements across programmatic  areas.


Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future


UNICEF, in a pivotal partnership with the Department of Basic Education (DBE), achieved transformative results for over 5.4 million children nationwide, directly reaching 4,087,202 and approximately 1.3 million indirectly. This was accomplished by strengthening foundational learning systems, leveraging technology, and promoting safe and inclusive school environments. To enhance the quality of Early Childhood Development (ECD), UNICEF supported the systemic roll-out of the National Curriculum Framework for children from birth to four years. Critical support materials reached a quarter of all registered ECD programmes – approximately 42,000 nationwide and are being translated into 10 languages to ensure inclusiveness.  Furthermore, 40 original storybooks were developed to promote emergent literacy and are being translated into all 12 official languages. Capacity building was central, with UNICEF training 2,000 ECD practitioners in play-based pedagogies and reaching 500 parents through the Parental/Primary Caregiver  Programme. The innovative P.L.A.Y. initiative registered 44,000 participants,  indirectly benefiting over a million children.   


To directly tackle the crisis of learning poverty, Mother Tongue-based Foundational Learning Trainings in the Northern Cape reached 43,284 learners across 129 schools, supported by the distribution of over 181,000 learning and teaching materials. Digital learning was scaled  through partnerships with Siyavula (an online mathematics and science platform) and Junior Tukkies, which collectively supported over 3.5 million  learners in 2025, helping to bridge the digital divide. Recognizing that well-being  is key to learning, UNICEF updated the national Care and Support for Teachers  and Learners Framework and Handbook, distributing them to over 24,000 schools  and 451,000 teachers to foster safer and more supportive school environments.  Concurrently, Menstrual Hygiene Management was integrated into national WASH  in Schools guidelines. To prepare youth for the future economy, UNICEF was  instrumental in the rollout of the National Coding & Robotics Curriculum,  establishing seven new hubs in underserved rural provinces. In 2025, a total of  37 Subject Specialists and 370 educators were trained, directly benefiting  7,400 learners. Cumulatively, 707 educators delivered the curriculum weekly  to 33,379 learners.  Additionally, a  STEM Mentorship Programme provided workplace exposure for 100 learners (63%  girls) through private-sector partnerships. The GIGA School Connectivity  Initiative finalized comprehensive school mapping and piloted real-time  monitoring in the Eastern Cape. To modernize the school assessment, UNICEF  supported the development of an AI-based competency measurement tool aligned  with the National 21st Century Core Competency Framework. The tool was  piloted with 600 Grade 8-10 students and is now being adapted for national  rollout under the General Education Certificate. Lastly, UNICEF contributed  to strengthening the Education Management Information System in coordination  with Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), delivering key knowledge pro

ducts  for evidence-based sector planning. 

Every child, including adolescents, survives and  thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care,  nurturing practices and essential supplies


UNICEF contributed significantly to strengthening health and nutrition  systems amid challenges of declining immunization coverage and the persistent  triple burden of malnutrition. In close partnership with the National  Department of Health (NDOH), UNICEF strengthened national guidance by leading  the revision of the Vaccinators' Manual, Cold Chain Manual, and Reach Every  District Strategy Guidelines, ensuring standardized quality service delivery  for frontline health workers nationwide. Targeted support in districts, financially  supported by ELMA Philanthropies, helped slow the increase of zero-dose  children and contributed to bringing vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks  under control in the UNICEF targeted districts showing a 42% decrease in  comparison to non-targeted districts.  To address malnutrition, UNICEF provided  technical support for the development of the Multisectoral National Food and  Nutrition Security Plan (2024-2029), the National Obesity Prevention and  Control Strategy, and draft regulations for Front-of-Package Labelling and Marketing  restrictions on unhealthy foods to children. UNICEF also advocated for the prioritization  of creating sustainable support systems for breastfeeding mothers across the government  and the private sector. Evidence generation was central to transforming  school food environments. UNICEF supported the development of an investment  case for nutritious school breakfasts, a policy brief, and a Step-by-Step  Practical Guide. The modelling of a 'Blueprint for Improving the South  African School Food Environment' identified seven evidence-based priority interventions,  forming the basis for a scale-up plan for all 28,000 public schools in the  country. UNICEF supported the government  through quality improvement initiatives to increase the number of  children 6-59 months olds admitted for treatment of severe acute  malnutrition (SAM) to 19,000, which resulted in a 58% increase  against the set target. To accele


rate progress towards an AIDS-free  generation, UNICEF’s leadership within the Global Alliance to End AIDS in  Children was pivotal. Key achievements included the successful integration of  a child-specific monitoring dashboard into the Department of Health's  reporting systems, using real-time data to identify and address gaps. A major  advocacy win was the inclusion of children in the National 'Finding the  Missing' Campaign for the first time, targeting 1.1 million people living  with HIV who are not on treatment. The adolescent girls and young women (AGYW)  Peer Mentor programme, a model of peer support, was scaled significantly,  cumulatively reaching 45,487 adolescent girls and young women with integrated  antenatal, postnatal, HIV, and GBV screening services across three provinces.  Its success has resulted in government-led scale-up in the City of Tshwane. Over  100 health professionals were also trained to expand access to pre-exposure  prophylaxis (PrEP) and holistic care.


Every child, including adolescents, has access to  safe and equitable water, sanitation, and hygiene services, and lives in a  safe and sustainable climate and environment


UNICEF advanced climate resilience and sustainable WASH services through  policy innovation, institutional capacity building, and youth empowerment. An  achievement in 2025 was the finalization and subsequent adoption by the  Eastern Cape Department of Basic Education of the National Climate-Resilient  WASH Framework. This provides a nationally standardized method for assessing  climate risks to water and sanitation systems and identifying appropriate  resilience interventions for schools, clinics, and other public facilities.  Empowering youth as agents of change,  UNICEF’s Youth-Led Water Quality Businesses initiative provided technical and  business development support to eight youth entrepreneurs across five  provinces, underlining the importance of embedding youth-led service models  within systems-strengthening efforts. Practical tools developed, including  sampling protocols and SPINABC market analysis templates (Situation, Problem,  Implication, Need-payoff, Approach, Benefits, Challenge), provide a  foundation for scaling youth-driven water monitoring. Large-scale community mobilization  saw 12,339 children and young people (56% female) engaged in hands-on climate  action. This effort led to the rehabilitation of 260 hectares of degraded  land through invasive alien plant clearing and the collection of 700 tons of  waste, directly improving water catchment health and reducing climate risks  like wildfires. At the household and community level, UNICEF fostered  resilience by supporting the establishment of 15 sustainable food gardens in  schools and communities.


Every child, including adolescents, is protected  from violence and exploitation.


UNICEF leveraged to elevate advocacy on the intersection of violence against  children (VAC) and violence against women (VAW), child online safety, and  meaningful child participation on the global stage during the meetings of various  of the G20 working groups and engagements. This visibility was reinforced by  the high-level visit of the UN Special Representative of the  Secretary-General (SRSG) on Violence against Children. A foundational  milestone was the finalization of South Africa's Model of National  Response for Children's Online Safety, providing the first strategic national  framework for coordination, investment, and accountability in this domain. Frontline  capacity was strengthened: 945 educators and stakeholders across six  provinces were trained on the Safe Online Life Orientation  curriculum for Grades 8–12, enabling an indirect reach of up to 4.85 million  learners. Alongside this, 416 social workers were trained across four  provinces. Direct engagements reached 38,507 children with digital literacy  and online safety skills, complemented by social media campaigns reaching  over 161,000 individuals. UNICEF’s convening power with the technology sector  led to the establishment of the Africa Taskforce on Child Online Protection  in 2025, scaling South Africa’s private-sector engagement model to the  regional level. Parenting support systems were reinforced through the October  2025 launch of the Parenting Support Policy Benchmarking Assessment Report,  which was developed and launched with UNICEF technical support. Direct  programme reach extended to 48,850 parents and caregivers, including 13,216  receiving digital booster messages and 1,305 completing the Parenting  Programme for Teens. In the Western Cape, UNICEF supported a Community of  Practice among 15 CSOs to align family-strengthening interventions with the  provincial violence prevention strategy. Community-based services were  expanded through the Risiha (Resilience) programme, with 13


5 social service  professionals trained across three KwaZulu-Natal districts, contributing to a  national reach of 229,704 children accessing essential psychosocial,  nutrition, learning, and protection services. A multi-year corporate  partnership with Momentum Insure concluded, supporting a Safe Park that  reached over 400 children monthly. For children on the move, UNICEF, together  with UNHCR and IOM, supported the training of 150 Border Management  Authority, South African Police Services, and South African National Defense  Force officers on protection-sensitive border management, strengthening  referral pathways. Child participation was a prominent theme: UNICEF  supported the Nelson Mandela Children's Parliament, bringing together over 60  children at the National Parliament, and facilitated children’s engagement in  G20 processes through the Children 20 (C20) Engagement Group, with their  recommendations formally presented to national leadership at the Social  Summit.


Every child has an equitable chance in life


2025 witnessed systematic progress in institutionalizing child-sensitive  governance and public finance. The percentage of children living in monetary  poverty saw a slight decrease from 51% to 49.8%, while coverage of the Child  Support Grant remained stable at approximately 13 million children,  reflecting a strategic government shift from rapid expansion to improving  targeting accuracy, informed by UNICEF's work on exclusion errors. An  innovative U-Report poll established a first-ever baseline on children’s  participation in budgets, engaging over 600 youths and building partnerships  with legislatures.  


Through persistent advocacy and technical  partnership, UNICEF secured a landmark government commitment to measure  multidimensional child poverty – Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA)  routinely every five years, with the second iteration of MODA 2 finalized at  the technical level in 2025. In a major step for national data systems,  UNICEF cemented its partnership with Statistics South Africa successfully  advocating for the integration of child-centric indicators into the revised  national data framework (Government-led Continuous Population Survey). In  public finance, while macroeconomic pressures impacted pro-poor spending  shares, UNICEF’s evidence influenced systemic accountability. A 2020  recommendation on tracking expenditure arrears resulted in the National  Treasury institutionalizing an annual report on this issue, enhancing fiscal  oversight for social service delivery. 


Cross-Cutting  Result Areas and Change Strategies


Effective Programme Coordination for Results for  Children


In 2025, UNICEF South Africa achieved significant  strides in strengthening programme effectiveness by fostering greater  internal coherence and generating relevant evidence for action. The structured  programme coordination and revitalization of cross-sectoral working groups on  Child Rights Governance, Early Childhood Development, and Adolescent  Development, with the fostering of more cross-sectoral linkage, and breaking  silos, enabling more integrated planning, implementation, and knowledge  sharing. This approach promoted co-creation, knowledge sharing, and joint  planning, enabling more holistic interventions that address the complex  realities children face.Strengthening child rights governance and education was a strategic priority.The set-aside Girls’ Education Fund was efficiently coordinated to create greater synergies and complementarity across programmes, contributing to improved education outcomes.


UNICEF championed child engagement at the highest  level by embedding children’s perspectives within the G20 Social Summit  agenda, culminating in a Children’s Declaration handed to President Cyril  Ramaphosa during the G20 Social Summit. The development of the new Country  Programme Document (CPD) process was coordinated effectively through various  coordination meetings, conversations, and deliberations, both internally and  externally, as well as with the UN Country team. The CPD has been finalized  with agreed priorities, evidence synthesis, and Theory of Change. The CPD  provides a strategic roadmap for UNICEF’s work in South Africa, aligning with  national priorities and ensuring coherent, results-driven programming.


UNICEF advanced systems for child participation and  developed transformative tools to guide policy and resource allocation. These  include the Child Climate Risk Index (CCRI) and the Data for Children  Dashboard, now operational on a government platform, empowering planners to  target resources to the most vulnerable children. UNICEF’s coordination efforts were instrumental in supporting the development and implementation of key national policies, including the National Strategy to Accelerate Action for Children (NSAAC) and the National Plan of Action for Children (NPAC).  These frameworks provide a foundation for sustained progress on child rights  and well-being. Social and Behavior Change interventions were  institutionalized within government health and education systems,  contributing to a 42% slower increase in zero-dose children in supported  districts and directly reaching millions with life-changing messages.


Adolescent Development


UNICEF achieved strategic progress in institutionalizing adolescent participation and scaling integrated health and skills interventions. A  significant systems-level achievement was the official integration of the  Girls and Boys Education Movement (GBEM) into the government's Representative Council of Learners structure, ensuring a sustainable, nationally owned  platform for adolescent voice and leadership. This foundation enabled  programmatic scale: GBEM youth leadership sessions engaged an estimated 20,000 learners in life-skills education, and a revitalized School Sport  partnership provided structured Sport-for-Development (S4D) participation for  9,600 young people. In health, a national social and behavior change campaign  reached over 1.28 million adolescents with messages on nutrition, physical  activity, and mental health. The Nutrition School Ambassadors (NUSA)  initiative was institutionalized in four provinces, empowering learners to  advocate for healthier school food environments, with plans for national  scale-up.  Digital engagement was a key  change strategy: U-Report, chatbots, and alerts reached 3.74 million young  people, and a dedicated MOOC trained over 3,000 youth in advocacy for  nutrition and mental health. UNICEF provided technical leadership to finalize  the Global Action for Measurement of Adolescent Health (GAMA) assessment,  informing a future national Adolescent Health Data Dashboard. Through  partnerships, UNICEF supported "Fix My Food" youth advocates in  generating a landmark report on campus food environments and campaigning for  stronger regulations. Health system capacity was bolstered by training 116  clinicians and deploying 112 Young Mentor Mothers across 70 facilities to  strengthen service delivery for adolescent girls and young women. 


Mobilizing Resources and Influencing Change through  Strategic Partnerships and Advocacy


The office achieved significant results in resource mobilization, raising US$ 8.3 million in 2025 from all funding source types. This success was driven by  a strategic shift in partnerships and engagement. Beyond securing funds,  UNICEF cultivated deeper relationships with the private sector, leveraging  corporate networks for advocacy and community engagement, as seen with  partners like BMW, Chery, and Woolworths. A significant innovation was the  revitalization of individual giving through modernized digital  transformation; the launch of new payment platforms like Stripe and PayPoint  led to a 27% increase in digital donations and the acquisition of over 1,300  new pledge donors. In advocacy, UNICEF’s technical and convening power was  instrumental during South Africa’s G20 presidency. By advocating across working groups and facilitating the historic first-ever ‘Children’s 20’ (C20) engagement group, UNICEF amplified children’s voices at the highest levels of global governance, directly influencing the G20 declaration and setting a new standard for child participation.


Innovation 


Innovation and T4D programming in 2025 delivered significant results centered on creating a 'Youth Force' for development and forging green skilling pathways. Overall, 43,303 young people were upskilled, 5 knowledge products developed, 5 innovative solutions deployed, and USD 7.3 million raised for scale. Aligned with the regional Youth4Change strategy, the office launched  the Green Learn to Earn (GL2E) programme, developing accredited skilling pathways in river quality monitoring, agroecology, renewable energy, waste management, and land rehabilitation. The initiative engaged 102 ecosystem partners; to date, 466 youth completed training, 358 transitioned to income  generation, and 207 trainers were capacitated. The programme has reached  3,500 young people with a three-year target of 100,000. The Recycling  Champions (ReCha) project was scaled, training 25 young people and  establishing 10 micro-businesses in waste management, which now employ 84  youth and support 339 community members. Green Rising delivered strong,  measurable results in 2025, positioning it as one of UNICEF South Africa’s  youth-led climate and green-skills initiatives: over 12,000 young people had  been reached nationally, with Phase 2 (Sept–Nov 2025) engaging an additional  7,081 youth across four provinces; young people restored 35.21 hectares of  degraded land, cleared 15 hectares of invasive alien species, removed 161 tons  of waste, planted 128 indigenous trees, and established school food gardens  while strengthening environmental clubs; this impact is reinforced by the Clean  December Campaign, which mobilizes youth through an integrated digital  ecosystem using GVI for verified volunteer management and impact tracking, U-Report  for community reporting and advocacy, Golden Volunteer for recognition and  certification, and YOMA for learning, digital credentials and livelihood  linkages creating powerful cross-platform benefits for young people while  delivering real, locally visib


le environmental outcomes; together, these  efforts place the programme on track to mobilize 20,000 youth, restore 100  hectares of land and collect 500 tons of waste by June 2026, while  systematically building sustainable green pathways for adolescents and youth.  The office also launched the Game Changers Coalition in partnership with the  National Treasury's Afri-Games Consortium, training 60 youth in gaming  development, with plans to indirectly reach 100,000 through masterclasses.  The YOMA Impact Marketplace, a digital platform linking youth to gig economy  opportunities, was endorsed by the Presidential Youth Employment Intervention  (PYEI). Strategic fundraising was highly successful, secured from donors including the Government of Qatar (Education Above All),  PwC, Accenture, and the Government of Canada to scale these innovations.  Gender equity (minimum 50% female participation) and climate action were mainstreamed across all initiatives.

Data and Evidence

South Africa’s evidence systems for children were strengthened, enabling more informed, data-driven government planning. The Data for Children Dashboard became fully operational and is now hosted on COGTA’s National Strategic Hub, with provincial child-focused profiles. It is being used by provinces to guide resource allocation. UNICEF contributed through technical development and by strengthening sub-national data use. The Child Climate Risk Index (CCRI) was completed and co-created with DFFE and COGTA, providing district-level climate vulnerability insights to support risk-sensitive planning for children. UNICEF convened partners, offered technical guidance, and funded initial development. 

Emergency Prepared and Response

UNICEF South Africa's emergency response and systems strengthening efforts delivered key results across several result areas. In Health and Nutrition, this included strengthening immunization systems via the national Reach Every District Strategy and targeted Africa Vaccination Week activities in 12 high-risk districts to reach zero-dose children, alongside urgent responses to diphtheria and Mpox outbreaks. For Child Protection, system strengthening supported the care, protection, and family reunification of 31 trafficked children. The WASH sector saw significant advancements, with the development of a draft national framework for Climate Resilient WASH and the large-scale capacity building of 15,261 children, 2,755 youth, and 1,072 community members in water quality monitoring, alongside the mentorship of 8 youth-led WASH businesses. Climate reslience action yielded tangible results through the restoration of 295 hectares of land by 19,339 youths and the development of a Child Climate Risk Index for district-level planning. Under Risk Communication and Community Engagement, systems were strengthened by training 81 health promoters, developing a Community Feedback Tool, and co-developing a community media framework for health emergencies.


Enhancing Operational Effectiveness as a Foundation for Results


UNICEF South Africa’s commitment to operational excellence in 2025 provided the critical foundation for all programme delivery. The development and  rigorous monitoring of the Annual Management Plan ensured strategic alignment  and accountability from the onset. A comprehensive peer review of operations  led to strengthened governance and more efficient workflows, directly  enabling programme teams to focus on results. Strategic financial management  recovered over ZAR 16 million in VAT refunds, freeing up significant  resources for children. Furthermore, by embracing digital transformation  and systems strengthening, the office made strides in ICT resilience and  process innovation. The appointment of a senior ICT staff member to a  regional digital advisory role and the proactive simulation of Business  Continuity Plans for the G20 summit demonstrated forward-looking operational  leadership. These efforts in risk-informed management and  efficiency gains ensured that internal systems were robust, compliant, and  agile, directly contributing to a more effective and resilient office capable  of delivering its ambitious mandate.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2025 was a year of significant political transition and persistent fiscal constraint, testing UNICEF South Africa’s agility and the resilience of its partnerships. While the formation of the Government of National Unity (GNU) fostered broader political inclusivity, the accompanying negotiations initially slowed decisions on social sector reforms. A constrained fiscal environment, with significant debt-servicing costs consuming 21% of revenue, directly compressed public investment space and challenged the scale and sustainability of programmes for children. Despite headwinds, the office adapted its strategies, deepened evidence-based advocacy, and strengthened systems for the long term.
