The following analysis distills key challenges, critical lessons, and outlines a forward-looking agenda to accelerate results for every child across the different sectors.


Education


UNICEF faced multiple operational challenges in 2025, including a persistent digital divide, limited teacher motivation, rising costs of educational technology, and overarching fiscal constraints that affected programme delivery. A key structural challenge was South Africa’s highly decentralized system, where provincial authority over implementation can lead to siloed efforts.  To mitigate risks, it is imperative that programme delivery incorporates an integrated approach that addresses institutional capacity deficits, ensures clear assignment of responsibilities and funding, and embeds strong accountability mechanisms at all levels. The lesson learned was that sustainability and scalability depend on careful alignment and coordination with provincial and district administrations, including teacher unions, from the outset. While this approach requires additional time to design inclusive sustainability plans, it is essential for continued impact beyond the project period. Tackling these challenges, UNICEF leveraged strategic partnerships like the GIGA initiative with the Department of Basic Education (DBE) and the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT). Piloting real-time connectivity monitoring in the Eastern Cape has set the stage for national expansion. Looking ahead, UNICEF will focus on institutionalizing these partnerships, integrating sustainability planning into all interventions, and using evidence from pilots like GIGA to advocate for national resource allocation to bridge the digital and quality learning divides.


Health and Nutrition


2025 reinforced key lessons on achieving systemic change amid complex challenges. The continued decline in immunization coverage, exacerbated by concurrent outbreaks diverting limited resources, underscored that sustaining gains requires moving beyond episodic support to institutionalized district-level mentorship and integrated service delivery within primary health care. The effectiveness of the Reaching Every District (RED) strategy and micro-outreach models in identifying zero-dose children proved that consistent, data-driven community engagement is irreplaceable. In nutrition, a critical lesson was the vulnerability of child-focused priorities in multisectoral policy processes, where fragmented advocacy allowed commercial interests to overshadow child health. Successful demonstrations, like economic modelling for healthier school food environments, provided the evidence needed to align government action. Moving forward, the team will prioritize institutionalizing RED mentoring across all priority districts, strengthening community-based outreach as a core service, and leveraging unified, evidence-based coalitions to advocate for policies that protect children's nutrition and health, ensuring sustainable results for the most marginalized. This challenge was compounded by major U.S. funding cuts, including the abrupt halt of PEPFAR and USAID support, which created a huge gap in health financing. The cuts led to the closure of mobile clinics and community programs, reducing access to HIV testing, treatment, and prevention, especially for children and adolescents in the country.


Social Policy


The development and implementation of nutrition and health programmes reaffirmed that shifting policy is a protracted process requiring sustained advocacy and partnership. The Cabinet’s return of the draft "cash-plus" policy necessitated a restart under a new framework by the Department of Social Development (DSD), illustrating the challenge of shifting government policy priorities. A key lesson is that while high-quality evidence (such as UNICEF’s exclusion error study) is necessary, its timing and integration into government planning cycles are equally critical for uptake. This experience underscored the indispensable value of being a consistent, reliable technical partner, as evidenced by Statistics South Africa’s direct request for continued UNICEF support on the Multidimensional Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA). The future outlook involves maintaining this trusted partnership role, using evidence to influence the revitalized social assistance policy process, and ensuring child-sensitive indicators are cemented within national data systems to guide equitable resource allocation.


WASH and Climate


The development of the Climate-Resilient WASH Framework revealed systemic vulnerabilities, including inconsistent climate-risk assessment practices, infrastructure maintenance gaps, vandalism, and external hazards like extreme wind damaging school infrastructure. Water-quality testing identified E. coli contamination linked to vermin, demonstrating the need for stronger risk-based water safety management at the facility level. Insights from supporting eight youth-led water quality businesses highlighted further systemic barriers: limited local demand for paid services, insufficient seed finance, and a lack of structured pathways to link youth enterprises with public authorities. The lesson is that technical solutions alone are insufficient without addressing market and systemic barriers to scale. Going forward, UNICEF will focus on supporting the government to institutionalize and scale the Climate-Resilient WASH Framework, strengthen provincial capacity to apply climate-risk tools, and foster an enabling ecosystem, including finance and market linkages for youth-led climate and WASH enterprises to thrive.


Child Protection


The sector faced a significant shock with the withdrawal of a major donor, which left approximately 75 per cent of planned activities for children on the move unfunded, highlighting acute vulnerability to external funding shifts. Conversely, digital parenting platforms demonstrated strong scalability but raised questions regarding sustainable handover to government and the need for dedicated technical expertise. A powerful lesson emerged from public-private engagement: South Africa demonstrated regional leadership by evolving a national roundtable with tech companies into the Africa Task Force on Child Online Protection, in collaboration with the African Union and Groupe Spéciale Mobile Association (GSMA). This illustrates the potential to pioneer scalable partnership models that align business practices with child rights. The future outlook prioritizes high-impact system strengthening, aligning digital solutions with government systems for sustainability, expanding joint resource mobilization to mitigate funding shocks, and deepening One-UN collaboration to address complex protection gaps.


Innovation


A central lesson from Innovation and Technology for Development (T4D) programming was the indispensable power of creating and maintaining shared value with partners. In a constrained financial environment, success hinges on moving beyond alignment to a state where all parties feel their core mission is advanced through joint work. This requires a dual approach: a willingness to compromise on non-essentials and the creativity to push boundaries on essentials. This persistent effort to find and reinforce mutual benefit transforms transactional partnerships into enduring coalitions for impact. Applying this lesson, the office secured $7.3 million from diverse partners by aligning youth skilling and green economy projects with donor and corporate strategies. Looking ahead, UNICEF will continue to leverage this principle through digital transformation strategy, using innovative financing and digital platforms like the YOMA Impact Marketplace to create tangible value for youth, children, and partners alike, thereby ensuring the sustainability and scale of innovation portfolios.


Adolescent Development


Significant progress in institutionalizing platforms like the Girls and Boys Education Movement (GBEM) into the Representative Council of Learners (RCL) structure was tempered by structural fragmentation between national and provincial governance, which hindered coordinated implementation and created administrative delays. A key lesson is that systemic gains require reinforced operational alignment and cross-sectoral collaboration to ensure consistent delivery to the most marginalized adolescents. Moving forward, UNICEF will leverage these insights to strengthen partnership frameworks with the government, focusing on improved integration mechanisms to overcome silos. Adaptation will include exploring alternative, less politically sensitive engagement avenues, such as channeling youth participation towards climate action to build momentum and trust, consolidating institutional achievements into sustained, scalable results for all adolescents.


Cross-Cutting Lessons and Future Outlook 


The Future Focus Initiative globally mandated budget reductions necessitated challenging programme prioritization, impacting administrative capacity and office improvement plans. Several key positions were not filled due to limited resources and efforts to reduce costs. Key lessons emerged from navigating these constraints. First, strategic convening power is a force multiplier; the structured, leadership-driven cross-sectoral working groups proved far more effective than siloed efforts. Second, proactive operational and financial resilience planning, such as pursuing VAT refunds and alternative office space, is essential to buffer against external shocks. Third, investing in foundational digital and payment infrastructure is non-negotiable for scaling public engagement and fundraising. Looking ahead, UNICEF South Africa will leverage these insights to adapt its strategies through multisectoral approaches, intersectionality, geographic focus, and enhancing alignment with the UNSDCF. It will strengthen public finance management to boost and safeguard investments in social services and ensure that they are more efficiently and equitably allocated for greater impact.  Operationally, the focus will shift to redesigning finance and administrative processes for greater efficiency and completing the office relocation. In partnerships, the office will deepen its engagement with national foundations and the private sector to build a more diverse pipeline for the new Country Programme.

In 2025, South Sudan continued to face a persistent  polycrisis marked by cascading and mutually reinforcing impacts at the community, subnational, and national levels. This polycrisis was driven by escalating climate shocks, intensifying violence, ongoing political and economic collapse, and multiple disease outbreaks—including cholera, hepatitis E, polio, mpox and anthrax.  
  
Political and Security Landscape: In 2025, South Sudan experienced a sharp rise in instability, marked by deepening political polarization, renewed armed clashes, and mounting humanitarian pressures. Tensions among political  factions intensified and the according to the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring  and Evaluation Commission, the Revitalized Peace Agreement is severely  undermined. Key  transitional benchmarks—including security sector reform, census, constitution  making-, and election planning—saw no advancement. Escalating armed conflict  resulted in the displacement of an estimated 479,000 people, including an  estimated 225,000 children.  
  
Economic Climate: South Sudan’s economy is estimated to have contracted by 23.8 per cent in 2025, largely due to the year-long shutdown of the Dar Blend oil pipeline, which transports around 63 per cent of the  country’s oil exports through conflict affected- Sudan. With limited oil revenue a substantial portion of government spending was financed through monetary expansion, leading to a sharp depreciation of the South Sudanese pound and rapidly rising inflation. As  a result, extreme poverty has risen dramatically, with nearly 9 in 10 people  affected in 2025 compared to 7.6 in 10 five years ago. The  continued weakening of the South Sudanese Pound on the informal market  underscores the economy’s fragility and persistent instability. 
  
South Sudan also ranked last out of 193 countries  on the global Human Development Index in 2025, with a score of 0.388, reflecting long-standing gaps in investments in  health, education, and essential living standards. GDP per capita is estimated at only US$313 in 2025 down from US$394 in 2020.
  
Humanitarian Context: South Sudan continues to face an acute humanitarian and socio-economic crisis driven by prolonged conflict, climatic shocks,  disease outbreaks, and large-scale population movements. By the end of 2025, 9.3 people were in need of humanitarian assistance including 5 million children.  Ongoing instability in the region, particularly in neighbouring Sudan, has significantly intensified pressures on the country’s already fragile systems.  In 2025 alone, over 1.3 million refugees and returnees, including 404,165  children, entered South Sudan, with an additional 380,000 arrivals projected  by the end of 2026. The  scale of these movements has pushed host communities and basic services to  the brink. In Renk, Maban, and surrounding areas, water systems, health  facilities, and schools are operating at 300–400 per cent of their intended  capacity.
  
At the same time, South Sudan is grappling with multiple, concurrent disease outbreaks, further burdening a  fragile health system. The country experienced its largest cholera outbreak  on record, with over 96,000 cases and 1,600 deaths reported as of November  2025. Recurrent flooding continues to fuel the spread of endemic diseases,  particularly malaria, with approximately 3.2 million suspected cases and 2,666  suspected deaths, including 1365 children, recorded between January and  October 2025. 
  
Food insecurity and malnutrition remain alarmingly high. According to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC)  September 2025–July 2026 projection, over half of the country’s population is  projected to experience crisis or worse levels of hunger (IPC Phase 3 and  above) between April and July 2026.  The burden of malnutrition has steadily  worsened, with severe and moderate acute malnutrition rising to 2.11 million  in 2025 (from 1.65 million children under five in 2023). Approximately  670,000 children are projected to suffer from severe acute malnutrition in  2026, up from 480,000 projected in mid-2024.  
  
UNICEF’s humanitarian response faced a funding gap of  49.8 per cent in 2023, which widened to 66 per cent in 2024 and reached 65  per cent unfunded in 2025. 
  
As a result of these cascading and reinforcing crises,  South Sudan remains severely off track in achieving its Sustainable  Development Goals (SDGs), including the five priority SDGs linked to UNICEF  programming, underscoring the urgent need for sustained investment,  stability, and coordinated humanitarian and development action.
  
SDG target 2(2) End all forms of malnutrition: An estimated 2.11 million children under the age of  five are projected to suffer from wasting.  While exclusive breastfeeding among infants under six months stands at 72.7  per cent, complementary feeding practices remain critically poor, with only  6.8 per cent of children aged 6–23 months receiving the minimum required  dietary diversity.
  
SDG 3 Healthy lives and  well-being for all:  In 2025, South  Sudan’s infant mortality rate is projected at 56.75 deaths per 1,000 live  births,  representing a 1.59 per cent decline compared to 2024. Despite this modest  improvement, malaria, diarrhoea, and pneumonia continue to account for more  than 75 per cent of infant deaths. South Sudan’s maternal mortality ratio  remains critically high at 1,223 deaths per 100,000 live births, making it  the country with the highest maternal mortality ratio in the world.  Persistent weaknesses in the health system, combined with low coverage of community-based  health services, continue to limit access to essential preventive and  curative care. As a result, large populations living in hard--to--reach areas  and internally displaced settings remain- significantly underserved.
  
SDG target 4(1) Ensure free, equitable and quality education:  An estimated 2.8 million children in South Sudan are  out of school, with the net enrolment rate at 38 per cent and the primary  completion rate remaining critically low at 15 per cent. Learning conditions  continued to deteriorate as 1,281 schools became non-operational due to  conflict, teacher shortages, and climate related damage. A further 112  schools were disrupted by floods, violence, cholera, or population  displacement, affecting 45,735 learners and 1,437 teachers.  Early childhood education (ECE) remains-  severely underdeveloped.  Only 11 per cent of children have access to ECE services, and gross pre-primary  enrolment stands at 11 per cent, well below the 20 per cent national target.  Structural challenges within the teaching workforce further undermine  education delivery: only 30 per cent of teachers are on the government  payroll, while 40 per cent serve as volunteers. Persistent salary delays have  driven high levels of absenteeism, contributing to very low- learner  attendance nationwide (30 per cent) and the widespread use of multigrade  classrooms. Climate related shocks, including prolonged heatwaves and  recurrent flooding, continue to force thousands of children out of school and  damage already fragile learning environments, where 45 per cent of classrooms  operate outside, under trees. These compounded pressures have deepened gender  and disability-related inequities and further weakened the education system’s  capacity to support learning continuity for the most marginalized children.
  
SDG 5  Achieve gender equality and empower women and girls: Women  and girls in South Sudan face extraordinary challenges and bear the brunt of  the legacy of the civil war, ongoing conflict, and inter-communal violence  coupled with climatic shocks that contribute to growing levels of poverty.  Limited access to education, healthcare, economic opportunities, and  political participation, coupled with harmful social norms and cultural  practices, further exacerbate gender disparities. Gender-based violence (GBV), including sexual violence,  intimate partner violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, and harmful  practices like child marriage, remains widespread. An estimated 65 per cent  of women and girls have experienced physical and/or sexual violence in their  lifetime. South Sudan also has the world’s fifth-highest rate of child  marriage, with over 52 per cent of girls married before 18. Nearly one-third  of girls become pregnant before age 15, exposing them and their babies to  dangerous health risks, including premature birth and low birth weight. Deep-rooted  inequalities in education, economic opportunity, and decision-making,  reinforced by patriarchal norms and weak social systems, heighten  vulnerability and marginalization. Access to essential services remains  uneven, and insecurity and restrictive social norms often prevent women and  girls from reaching health, education, and protection services even when  available.
  
SDG 6 Water and sanitation for all: South Sudan continued to face significant challenges  with access to clean water and sanitation in 2025. Approximately 59 per cent  of the population lacks access to safe drinking water, and only 42 per cent  have access to basic sanitation facilities that safely dispose of human  waste. The 2024 Intersectoral Needs Assessment suggests that rural sanitation  is significantly underserved, with over 60 per cent of the population  practicing open defecation. Watery diarrhoea is chronic, particularly in  areas with high rates of open defecation and lack of access to rural water,  sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services. The 2024 Food Security and Nutrition  Monitoring System reported that 25 per cent of women and girls felt unsafe  when accessing WASH facilities. 
  
SDG target 16(2) End all forms of violence against  children: Violence against children remains widespread in  South Sudan, driven by protracted conflict, recurring climatic and economic  shocks, entrenched poverty, and harmful social norms. Although comprehensive  prevalence data are limited, available evidence indicates a persistent  pattern of grave violations. According to the United Nations Mission in South  Sudan (UNMISS) Security Council Resolution Report 2779, issued in August  2025, a total of 127 grave violations against 95 children (66 boys, 24 girls,  and 5 of unknown sex) were verified in 2025.   Of these violations, 77 children were subjected to killing and  maiming, including 32 boys, 15 girls, and 3 children of unknown sex who were  killed, and 19 boys, 6 girls, and 2 children of unknown sex who were maimed.  In addition, 15 boys were recruited and used by armed actors. Among the 95  affected children, eight children (five boys and three girls) suffered  multiple violations.

In 2025, recognizing that traditional approaches were no longer sufficient particularly against the backdrop of a markedly changed funding landscape, the Country Office initiated a fundamental restructuring of its operational and programmatic model to better navigate a complex operating environment and eroding donor support. The “Strategic Reset” was anchored on five pillars:  Strengthening national systems to enhance sustainability and local ownership;  Driving operational efficiency to maximize the impact of every dollar spent;  Diversifying partnerships with government, civil society, and the private  sector; Aligning humanitarian and development efforts to promote continuity  and long term impact; and Embedding longitudinal storytelling to better  capture, communicate, and learn from evidence of change over time. Together, these shifts were designed to sharpen UNICEF’s focus and programming for impact at scale. 
  
In 2025, UNICEF improved the lives of children across South Sudan by combining high level policy engagement with direct community-based programming. Working closely with 88 non-governmental organizations – including 35 international partners and 53 national partners, among them 7 women-led organizations – and government partners at both national and local levels, UNICEF focused on strengthening essential systems for health, education, protection, nutrition and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). This collaborative effort led to major gains for children.  Polio remained under control, with 94 percent vaccination coverage protecting 3.6 million children (53 per cent girls) from the disease. Access to education expanded significantly, enabling 325,660 children (47 per cent girls) to benefit from quality learning opportunities. UNICEF also played a crucial role in containing an unprecedented cholera outbreak by improving access to safe water along with WASH and health services in affected communities. In the area of nutrition, timely treatment and care saved the lives of 292,163 severely malnourished children, contributing to reduced child mortality and improved wellbeing. At the same time, 232,844 children, adolescents, and caregivers received services aimed at preventing violence, responding to abuse, and supporting recovery and psychosocial healing. 
  
Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives:
  
In 2025, UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health continued the implementation of the Health Sector Transformation Project hence sustaining essential health services for women and children. By supporting 816 health facilities delivering over 85 per cent of the country’s maternal and child health services, UNICEF helped stabilize and expand access to essential care s for 2,037,928 women and children. 
  
Child s survival outcomes improved markedly through expanded access to Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI). More than 2.37 million children under five received timely assessment and treatment for common killer diseases, nearly doubling coverage from 2024. Strengthened malaria case management, driven by the training of 4,730 frontline health workers, enabled the treatment of 94 per cent of the 3.32 million confirmed malaria cases. This progress translated into fewer severe cases and deaths among young children, although periodic medicine stockouts and inconsistent testing practices at facility level continued to limit optimal care.
  
UNICEF’s investments across the pregnancy–childbirth–newborn continuum helped protect children from preventable complications at birth. Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care services were available around the clock in all state and teaching hospitals, while more than 70 per cent of women received uterotonics immediately after delivery, reducing the risk of maternal bleeding and improving newborn survival. Prevention of HIV transmission from mothers to children was strengthened, with 695 pregnant women initiating lifelong antiretroviral therapy across 229 facilities. Plans are in place to expand these lifesaving services to all supported facilities by 2026, supporting more children to be born HIV-free.  Despite these achievements, many children remained at risk due to low antenatal care coverage and limited skilled birth attendance, highlighting the continued impact of insecurity, distance, and supply chain disruptions on service utilization.
  
Expanded immunization services strengthened protection for children against vaccine-preventable diseases. The introduction of rotavirus and pneumococcal vaccines—supported by a nationwide PCV campaign reaching over 2 million children—boosted immunity against diarrheal disease and pneumonia, two major causes of under-five mortality. To reduce zero-dose rates of children, UNICEF supported outreach and mobile teams in 30 high-burden counties, enabling 513,484 children to access essential vaccines. The malaria vaccine reached more than 240,000 children in 52 counties, while nationwide measles and polio campaigns vaccinated over 6 million children combined. Investments in cold-chain expansion improved safe storage and delivery of vaccines across more health facilities. However, insecurity —particularly in Upper Nile — continued to restrict access to vulnerable communities. At the same time, severe financing gaps for traditional vaccines led to stockouts of key antigens such as polio and BCG, increasing children’s risk of preventable infections.
  
In comparison to 2024 where 80 per cent of children 0–11 months received the third dose of the pentavalent vaccine and 65 per cent of children under 1 year received the measles-containing vaccine, in 2025, 91 per cent of children 0-11 months received third dose of pentavalent vaccine and 74 per cent per cent of children under 1 year measles vaccine. Importantly Cold chain capacity of health facilities improved from 62 per cent in 2024 to 92 per cent in 2025. 
  
During the ongoing cholera outbreak, UNICEF’s rapid response actions directly protected children and families from a deadly epidemic. The distribution of 8.88 million oral cholera vaccine doses for children, combined with widespread risk communication, reached millions of families and contributed to reduced transmission in high-risk communities. 
  
UNICEF  enabled the Government to institutionalize nutrition through the launch of  the National Nutrition Policy and the Pre-Service Nutrition Curriculum,  embedding the nutrition workforce within national systems and driving  transformative policy reforms—including Universal Salt Iodization, the social  and behaviour change (SBC) strategy, food landscape analysis, and continued  work on the development of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk  Substitutes (BMS)—to strengthen regulation, prevention, and long-term  nutrition outcomes. At the same time, preventive nutrition services reached millions: more than 2.23 million children received vitamin A supplementation, and nearly 1.89 million were dewormed, interventions proven to reduce illness, boost immunity, and support healthy growth. Community-based counselling reached over one million pregnant and breastfeeding women and caregivers, improving infant and young child feeding during the critical first 1,000 days.
  
For children already suffering from severe wasting, UNICEF supplied lifesaving treatment in over 1,045 nutrition sites.  More than 292,163 children (55 per cent of the 530,000 targeted) received treatment for severe acute malnutrition preventing avoidable deaths. Strengthened monitoring systems and anti-diversion measures helped maintain sustained supplies of therapeutic food. 
  
Integrated programming further reduced risks to child survival and development. Access to safe water at 90 per cent of nutrition sites helped reduce disease exposure, while expanded gender-based violence risk mitigation supported safer access to services for women and girls, benefiting children’s care and wellbeing. UNICEF also began to scale up a signature cash-plus model, which provides cash assistance to 12,700 pregnant and breastfeeding women and caregivers of children under two to support their uptake of nutrition, health, and immunization services. Through this approach, more than 12,000 women were able to access integrated nutrition, health, immunization, and protection services. 
  
Collectively, these interventions helped safeguard children’s survival in fragile contexts while laying foundations for healthier growth, development, and resilience. By combining lifesaving service delivery with system strengthening and multisectoral integration, UNICEF’s support in 2025 enabled more children not only to survive preventable risks but also gain greater opportunities to thrive.
  
Goal 2: Every child learns from early childhood to adolescence 
  
In 2025, UNICEF, working closely with the Ministry of General Education and Instruction (MoGEI), enabled 325,660 children across South Sudan access and continue learning. This included 236,651 crisis-affected children (47 per cent girls) who accessed education in emergency settings, and 37,527 out-of-school children and adolescents (49 per cent girls) who re-entered education through UNICEF-supported programmes. 
  
UNICEF supported 51,482 children aged 36–59 months (47 per cent girls) to participate in school readiness and early stimulation activities, including through 23 integrated ECD centres providing play-based learning linked to basic psychosocial support, hygiene practices, and nutrition referrals.  UNICEF also trained 464 early childhood education facilitators and teachers (60 per cent female) to improve the quality of early learning environments, including strengthened inclusive early learning approaches. However, chronic underfunding continued to limit the scale of early childhood education nationwide. 
  
At community level, UNICEF strengthened school leadership and local oversight by training 740 School Management Committees, supporting improved monitoring of teaching and learning quality and stronger community engagement to keep children—especially girls—in school. UNICEF also supported adolescent girls’ retention through mentorship initiatives reaching 1,004 girls, helping reduce risks linked to dropout, early marriage, and gender-based violence. 
  
Despite these gains, the scale of need remains severe. An estimated 2.8 million children remain out of school, and only 15 per cent complete primary education. School system fragility is compounded by insecurity, overcrowded classrooms, limited learning materials, and shortages of qualified teachers, including prolonged delays in teacher salary payments. In 2025, UNICEF helped improve teaching quality by training 1,016 primary school teachers (30 per cent female) in foundational literacy and numeracy, and by assessing 20 County Education Centres to strengthen local teacher training and mentorship systems. Progress was also made toward stronger national learning measurement systems, with preparations advanced for a first national early-grade reading and mathematics assessment planned for early 2026. 
  
Beyond classroom-level support, UNICEF strengthened education system accountability and evidence for decision-making. This included improving school inspections and supporting progress on the Education Management Information System (EMIS), alongside work with the Education Transfers Monitoring Committee (ETMC) to improve transparency and predictability in education financing, including tracking teacher payments and resource flows. Together, these efforts helped sustain learning for hundreds of thousands of children while laying foundations for a stronger, more equitable and accountable education system—so that every child in South Sudan can learn, develop foundational skills, and build a better future.
  
Goal 3: Every child is protected from  violence and exploitation 
  
By working closely with the Government, civil society, and community-based organizations, UNICEF reached 232,844 children, adolescents, and caregivers (surpassing the target of 219,950) through case management, family tracing, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), explosive ordnance risk education, and gender-based violence (GBV) services. These efforts strengthened national child protection systems and supported South Sudan’s long term development goals.
  
One of  the major achievements of the year was strengthening the country’s social  service workforce, which plays a vital role in protecting children. In  partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Child and Social Welfare and the  University of Juba, UNICEF supported 269 students—154 women and 115 men—to  advance toward graduation from South Sudan’s first Social Service Certificate  Course. The University’s decision to open the programme to students beyond  UNICEF partners will enable sustainability and builds long-term national  leadership in child protection. 
  
UNICEF also supported important policy and legal reforms that help safeguard children’s rights. Progress was made toward establishing a professional body for social workers through the finalization of the Social Work Association Constitution, which will be submitted to the Ministry of Justice in 2026. UNICEF also helped advance national guidelines and frameworks on diversion, gang violence, and alternative care, helping reduce children’s exposure to detention and institutionalization. In addition, the finalization of civil registration and vital statistics regulations strengthened access to legal identity, enabling more children to officially record their births and access essential services.
  
UNICEF’s humanitarian response reached children affected by conflict, displacement, and emergency situations across 34 counties, working with 27 partner organizations. A total of 111,759 individuals (53,965 boys; 44,601 girls; 7,175 men; 6,018 women) received child protection services, including mental health and psychosocial support, helping children cope with trauma and stress. 
  
Despite funding shortages, UNICEF continued to expand support for GBV programming in 2025, 124,444 people (33,908 girls, 9,651 boys, 71,716 women, 9,169 men) were reached with GBV response, prevention and response services. Five women-led organizations and three international NGOs were supported to deliver survivor-centred care in conflict affected areas, and more than 200 frontline workers were trained to integrate GBV support with nutrition services, improving care for vulnerable women and children.
  
Goal 4: Every child lives in a safe and  clean environment 
  
In 2025, working closely with the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation, UNICEF supported important reforms that strengthened national systems and laid the groundwork for long-term improvements. Progress was made toward finalizing the national Water Policy and Water Bill, alongside continued efforts towards the operationalization of the WASH Compact and tracking of the progress from the Joint Sector Review Declaration. These advances improved coordination, accountability, and planning across the WASH sector, enabling investments better respond to the needs of communities, including women, girls, and children. Sector coordination improved significantly, with seven WASH Technical Committees operating at national and state levels, up from just one in 2022. In urban areas, reforms within the South Sudan Urban Water Corporation, the establishment of the Bor Urban Water Utility, and improvements in billing, asset management, and customer service strengthened service delivery and sustainability. However, significant challenges remain regarding the sustainable management of the facilities, as evidenced by insufficient revenue generation resulting in frequent stoppages. 
  
WASH improvements in public institutions also delivered important benefits for women and children. Seventy-three schools received improved WASH facilities, supporting safer and more dignified learning environments for girls particularly during menstruation—and helping reduce absenteeism. At the same time, 29 health facilities were equipped with reliable WASH services, strengthening  infection prevention and control and improving the quality of maternal,  newborn, and child health care. 
  
UNICEF  also expanded climate-resilient water and sanitation infrastructure, directly  improving everyday life for families. In Bor Town, a new solar powered water  treatment system, including a 750 cubic metre elevated reservoir, extended  pipelines, and 28 community water kiosks, now provides 96,000 residents with  access to affordable, safe water. For women and girls, this has reduced long  and unsafe journeys to collect water, lowered household costs, and decreased  the risk of waterborne diseases. In rural areas, more than 118,106 people  against a target of 200,000 benefited from upgraded boreholes, solarized  water yards, and strengthened community-led sanitation initiatives that  promote safer, cleaner environments. The solar-powered installation has  reduced annual operational costs by approximately USD 318,000, lowered the  carbon footprint by an estimated 64 tons of carbon dioxide per year, and  significantly decreased reliance on diesel fuel, providing uninterrupted and  environmentally sustainable water supply services for the community.
  
Humanitarian  needs remained high throughout the year due to flooding, conflict,  displacement, and disease outbreaks. UNICEF responded swiftly to protect  children and women most at risk. Some 358,430 people received essential  hygiene supplies, 476,436 people accessed safe water through solarized  systems and surface water treatment units, and 109,532 people benefited from  emergency sanitation services. These interventions played a critical role in  preventing disease outbreaks and protecting women and girls from heightened  risks associated with poor sanitation in emergency settings. As the WASH  Cluster Lead, UNICEF coordinated more than 30 partners, supporting faster,  better aligned responses in the hardest hit communities.
  
By  combining system reforms, climate resilient infrastructure, community  engagement, and emergency response, UNICEF has helped to build a stronger  foundation for sustainable WASH services in South Sudan. Core funding enabled  essential policy and system strengthening work, while donor contributions  made it possible to expand infrastructure and deliver lifesaving services on  the ground. 
  
Goal 5: Equitable chance in life 
  
In 2025,  UNICEF strengthened its support to children and families in South Sudan by addressing  hunger and malnutrition, improving access to essential services, and helping  government systems work better for children. Despite a difficult environment  marked by ongoing instability and funding constraints, UNICEF focused on  practical actions that delivered real results for vulnerable communities.
  
Cash  support played a central role in enabling families meet basic needs and  protect young children from malnutrition. In 2025, UNICEF rolled out three  major cash transfer initiatives, including its largest— the Shock Responsive  Cash Transfer (SRCT) programme—targeting pregnant and breastfeeding women and  caregivers of children under two during this crucial period for child  survival and development. Through the SRCT, 10,134 caregivers were reached out  of a target of 12,110 across seven state capitals and one Administrative Area.  Early monitoring has shown encouraging results, with families reporting  improved food consumption and reduced reliance on harmful coping strategies  such as skipping meals.
  
Building  on these gains, UNICEF expanded the Young Child Support Grant (YCSG) in Aweil  East County and piloted it in Ruweng Administrative Area, demonstrating that  cash assistance can work even in remote settings. This “Cash Plus” approach  combined cash support with nearby health services, allowing families to  access nutrition screening, cooking demonstrations, immunizations, antenatal  and postnatal care, and support to prevent GBV. Together, these services enabled  parents better care for both the immediate and longer-term health and  nutrition needs of their children.
  
In  response to the Sudan crisis, UNICEF also launched a multipurpose cash  assistance programme in Rubkona, Unity State, reaching 1,100 vulnerable  households affected by displacement and economic hardship. The first round of  transfers was completed in December 2025, with two additional rounds planned  for early 2026 to provide sustained support.
  
To promote  the use of reliable evidence to inform decisions affecting children, UNICEF  worked closely with the National Bureau of Statistics to implement the  seventh round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7). This  partnership strengthened national systems by providing hands on technical  support for survey design, fieldwork planning, and digital data collection.  The survey produced nationally representative data on 170 indicators,  including 38 Sustainable Development Goal indicators and 25 indicators  focused specifically on children. Preliminary results, expected in January  2026, will help the Government better understand child poverty and  vulnerability and improve planning and budgeting for services that matter  most to children.
  
UNICEF  also supported efforts to make education financing more transparent,  accountable, and reliable. Through the Global Partnership for Education –  Transforming Education in South Sudan (GPETESS) initiative, UNICEF worked  with the Ministry of Finance and Planning and the Ministry of General  Education and Instruction to strengthen public financial management systems.  A major achievement was the development of a Public Financial Management  Policy Framework for the education sector, which will help promote better  management of education funds so that they reach schools and classrooms more  consistently, supporting teachers and learners alike.
  
Humanitarian Action
  
As of November 2025, UNICEF reached  nearly 2.3 million children with lifesaving services against a target of 3.6  million. This impact was made possible through a combination of emergency  response modalities, including deep field static programming which are fixed,  permanent service points such as health or nutrition centres that remain  operational inside hard-to-reach areas and provide continuous, reliable  support. These static sites were complemented by mobile outreach activities  and the strategic use of international NGO rapid response mechanisms, enabling  essential humanitarian services to reach vulnerable communities through both  permanent and mobile delivery systems. Through integrated health, water,  sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and risk communication and community  engagement (RCCE) cholera response, UNICEF contributed to a significant  reduction in the cholera case fatality rate—from a peak of 1.6 percent to 0.5  percent in real time. This marked improvement reflected faster detection,  strengthened treatment pathways, and more effective community awareness  during the outbreak. In the face of a severe food insecurity and malnutrition  crisis, UNICEF also joined forces with partners across the humanitarian  system to support a multi-agency hunger and nutrition crisis prevention and  response effort. By coordinating interventions across sectors, UNICEF helped support  children and families to receive urgent support at a time of escalating  needs.
  
Programme  Effectiveness
  
In 2025,  despite major funding cuts and significant operational constraints, UNICEF  South Sudan safeguarded essential services for children with a strong focus  on financial management and oversight, enhancing partnerships, and improving  operational efficiency. Through strategic prioritization, staff funded  through Regular Resources was maintained at 54 per cent and the office generated  US$4 million in operational savings—resources that directly enabled  programmes to continue reaching children nationwide. 
  
Implementing  Partnerships remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s ability to deliver at scale.  The office collaborated with 88 nongovernmental organizations, including 35  international and 53 national partners—among them 7 women-led  organizations—to enable lifesaving services reached families in even the most  hard-to-access areas. Programme efficiency advanced substantially as the  Country Office accelerated its transition to multisectoral Programme  Documents (PDs), reducing reliance on multiple parallel, single-sector PDs  from 82 to 57. Over the year, 25 Programme Review Committee sessions resulted  in new, streamlined PDs that strengthened coherence in planning and delivery.  Financial assurance systems also remained robust, achieving a 99.5 percent  compliance rate across all monitoring activities. Internal capacity building  was prioritized, with 116 staff members receiving targeted training to  reinforce programme delivery and operational performance—supporting UNICEF in  remaining agile and effective in a challenging environment.
  
Recognizing  the powerful influence of social norms and community practices, UNICEF  strengthened evidence-based, culturally sensitive social and behaviour change  (SBC) systems to drive healthier, safer behaviours for children. Using  locally generated insights, UNICEF and partners reached over 5.2 million  people with lifesaving messages and helped achieve 94 per cent polio  vaccination coverage. SBC engagement expanded significantly: 75,000 youth (45  per cent girls) accessed the Internet of Good Things; 900 SBC actors and 800  community mobilizers were trained; and improved feedback systems engaged  420,000 community members, enabling their voices to shape programmes in real  time.
  
By the end of December 2025, the UNICEF South Sudan  Country Office reached more than 6 million people across its social media  platforms—X/Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube—meeting a significant  portion of the year’s reach targets. Average engagement per post increased  steadily over the year, rising from approximately 7,000 interactions in  January to around 10,000 by November. This growth was driven by consistent,  diversified content production; strong collaboration with regional and global  UNICEF teams; and a deliberate focus on short, high-quality videos. A modest  marketing budget helped amplify priority advocacy messages. The most popular  content included posts linked to Independence Day, human-interest stories on  health and parenting, and education features on Facebook, as well as youth-driven  messages and emergency-focused social media cards on Instagram.
  
In addition to digital engagement, UNICEF organized  field visits and hosted two donor roundtables for partners present in the  country. The Country Office also leveraged high-level visits—including those  of the UNICEF Executive Director and UNICEF Global Goodwill Ambassador Liam  Neeson—to strengthen senior-level donor engagement. Donor-focused content and  events remained a priority throughout the year, with support provided for  nine donor and high-profile visits.
  
Operational Effectiveness
  
UNICEF SSCO continued to focus on strong management  and operations systems in 2025 through adjustments to cost-control  mechanisms, refinements in planning, and several targeted efficiency  measures. These actions helped support the continuity of programmes for  children and families, with a particular emphasis on close monitoring to  effectively manage organizational risks and meet operational benchmarks. A  strategic review of the Country Office’s supply and logistics function helped  to identify areas for further strengthening and efficiency gains, and a  learning review on cash-based programme underscored the value of a ‘whole of  office approach.’ Important operational improvements—such as upgrading the  transportation fleet and moving to a leasing arrangement, establishing more  stable IT connectivity through Starlink, and continuing efforts to reinforce  security and risk-management practices—contributed to even more cost-conscious  and risk-aware programming, while recognizing that significant challenges  persisted in several high-risk locations.
  
In parallel, UNICEF South Sudan continued to focus  on enhanced enterprise risk management (ERM) practices by advancing work  toward an integrated ERM–Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfer (HACT) model.  During the year, the Country Office had an active Risk Management Committee  and agreed on a number of measures to reinforce risk assurance, particularly  through continuous monitoring, enhanced staff capacity, and targeted partner  capacity support. While these efforts contributed to safeguarding resources  and supporting service quality in high-risk and hard-to-reach areas, ongoing security  and operational constraints and challenges continued to characterize the overall  environment for programme delivery.
  
Despite  operating in a challenging environment and facing unexpected funding cuts,  UNICEF South Sudan continued to deliver programmes for children with minimal disruption  and introduced innovations and more integrated approaches in its programmes.  Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF South Sudan will focus on further strengthening  its ability to track and demonstrate results, including a renewed emphasis on  qualitative programme monitoring and risk management.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges: 
    
In 2025, UNICEF faced a convergence of systemic and operational challenges that cut across all programme areas. Severe funding reductions (12 per cent) required the office to make difficult prioritization decisions, including limiting the ability to sustain the full core staffing structure. Even with strong partnerships, logistical barriers in remote and hard-to-access locations continued to limit efficiency and continues to be impacted by incidents of aid diversion. 

Institutional and operational transitions added another layer of complexity. The shift from multiple single sector Programme Documents to multisectoral PDs demanded significant internal adaptation, increasing coordination requirements across teams. At the same time, the office worked to maintain rigorous accountability standards despite reduced staffing capacity. Sustaining a 99.5 percent financial assurance compliance rate required intensified oversight, placing additional pressure on already stretched teams.

Climate risks further shaped programme performance across sectors. Although climate-resilient infrastructure was incorporated in some cases, climate risk assessment and adaptation could be more systematically integrated across programme components. Recurrent flooding, drought, and other climate shocks continued to interrupt service delivery, underscoring the need for more comprehensive contingency planning, continuity strategies, flexible financing, and a workforce prepared to operate under climate-affected conditions.

Despite UNICEF’s strong commitment to systems strengthening, coordination across multiple government ministries remained complex and resource-intensive. Governance challenges and frequent turnover in senior leadership at national and sub-national levels created persistent coordination delays, resulting in slow decision-making and stalled programme implementation. This “coordination hysteresis” continued to absorb significant staff and management time, limiting the pace of progress.

Although the South Sudan Framework for Monitoring was developed and adopted in 2024, gaps remain in the scale, scope, and quality of field monitoring. Variability in programme quality across locations indicates that more consistent and systematic monitoring could have yielded stronger outcomes. It is not yet clear whether these gaps stem from weaknesses in the framework itself or from challenges in implementation. 

Programming effectiveness was further constrained by the use of standard UNICEF implementation modalities in a context where major programmes—such as the Global Partnership for Education, the Global Fund, and the Health System’s Strengthening Programme (HSTP)—are delivered through third-party arrangements (under the leadership of government but with UNICEF management of financial resources). Divergence in approaches has sometimes led to challenges. 

The shift in the HSTP modality toward a reimbursement system—unanticipated in the programme design—has required UNICEF to pre-finance operations at an unsustainable scale. Delays in securing necessary framework approvals have led to health workers going without incentives for up to six months and critical supplies being delayed for four months. These disruptions have exposed UNICEF to reputational risks and increased security risks for staff working in affected areas. While reductions in staffing levels and partner presence due to funding cuts have not yet significantly affected programme quality, the current scale and ambition of programming remain unchanged. This mismatch risks overextending teams and compromising future delivery. Continued efforts are needed to align programme scope with staffing capacity to maintain both quality and accountability. Finally, building internal capacity at scale remains a challenge. The pace of change—combined with system fragility and resource constraints—highlights the need for sustained investment in workforce readiness, adaptive management, and organizational resilience.
 
Lessons Learned:
    
Despite these pressures, 2025 demonstrated UNICEF’s ability to adapt and deliver results in a highly complex environment. The year reaffirmed the importance of strategic resource prioritization, which enabled the office to preserve 54 percent of core staffing and generate US$4 million in operational savings—allowing essential services to continue despite funding cuts.

Partnerships remained a critical enabler of resilience. Working with diverse and locally rooted organizations—including women-led groups—was essential for maintaining service continuity in hard-to-reach areas and strengthening community level systems. These partnerships helped sustain delivery in contexts where access barriers and operational volatility were most severe. At the same time, significant funding shifts in 2025 underscored the need to further diversify the UNICEF funding base and to pursue greater efficiencies through strengthened joint planning and programming.

The transition to multisectoral Programme Documents has delivered clear value. Streamlined, joint planning significantly improved coherence, reduced duplication, and strengthened both the efficiency and quality of programming. The shift also underscored the importance of shared implementation structures and aligned workplans in achieving integrated results. However, as programming needs vary widely in pace, scale, typology, and geographic focus, it is evident that no single model will suit all contexts. A comprehensive review in 2026 will therefore be essential to assess the cost–benefit of the multisectoral approach and outline a range of adaptable options to guide future programme design.

A key lesson from the HSTP experience is that the current financing modality—where UNICEF carries significant financial and operational risk—is proving difficult to maintain over the long term. Moving forward, the approach will likely need to evolve, including the possibility of front-loading funds to help provide more predictable financing and reduce UNICEF’s overall exposure. A structured review will also be necessary to determine which planned “transformations” can realistically be achieved under the programme’s reduced scale, and which ambitions will need to be adjusted. This will help align expectations with resources and support future programme design that is both feasible and results-focused.

Targeted capacity building emerged as a key driver of programme quality and adaptability. Training provided to 116 staff strengthened programme delivery and operational performance, enabling teams to navigate the rapidly evolving context and manage increasing multisectoral demands.

Equally important, the experience of 2025 highlighted the need to enhance qualitative and disaggregated monitoring. Integrating equity, gender, disability inclusion, and social and behaviour change objectives into theories of change and monitoring frameworks will strengthen UNICEF’s ability to demonstrate outcome level change. Routine learning mechanisms and flexible management structures improved responsiveness during uncertainty and will be essential for adaptive programming in 2026.

Finally, the year reinforced that climate resilience must become a core programming principle. Sustainable progress requires systematic climate risk assessment, strengthened contingency planning, service continuity strategies, flexible financing, and a workforce equipped to operate effectively amid increasing climate shocks.

Future outlook:
    
The significant decline in overseas development aid (ODA) over the past two years—combined with increasing fiscal and political pressures in donor countries—signals a long-term shift that will profoundly shape UNICEF’s operating environment in South Sudan. Advancing sustained results for children will require a strategic reorientation by national authorities moving away from aid dependency towards domestic resource mobilization and investment, and the financing of essential social services. In this constrained context, UNICEF’s leadership will be critical in driving greater efficiency, expanding engagement with non-traditional donors, and deepening the focus on resilience, livelihoods, and inclusive economic growth that directly benefits the most vulnerable children and families.

Delivering meaningful and lasting outcomes for children will depend on bridging the persistent gap between strong national-level policy commitments and the limited implementation capacity at state, county, and community levels. UNICEF’s future strategies must continue to align with national priorities and global frameworks while making deliberate, sequenced investments in strengthening subnational systems. This includes reinforcing the workforce, supply chains, data systems, accountability mechanisms, and domestic financing that underpin quality delivery of services across health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection, social protection, and climate resilience. Without these foundational investments, policy commitments on ECD, disability inclusion, gender equality, and climate adaptation will not translate into improved results for children.

While adaptive, delivery-focused programming will remain essential in a volatile and humanitarian-driven context, long-term sustainability for children will require greater institutionalization. Mobile outreach, emergency delivery platforms, and flexible modalities must evolve into structured entry points for strengthening local systems. This means anchoring emergency delivery in multi-year flexible financing, strong contingency planning, and clear transition pathways that gradually shift leadership to government institutions and communities. Without such pathways, lifesaving interventions risk perpetuating dependency instead of building resilience for children and families.

Equity, gender equality, and inclusion must remain at the core of UNICEF’s work. Future programming will prioritize strengthening disaggregated data systems and analytical capacity to identify which children are being left behind—especially girls, children with disabilities, and marginalized groups—and use this evidence to drive adaptive decision-making. Gender and inclusion must be systematically integrated into situation analyses, theories of change, sector strategies, and budgeting processes to support all children in having meaningful access, voice, and opportunities to thrive.

Finally, sustainability and efficiency in delivering for children will increasingly depend on integrated, preventive, and climate-responsive approaches that reduce long-term risks while continuing to meet urgent humanitarian needs. Of course, sustained peace will be a pre-requisite to progress. Multi-year pooled financing, stronger partnerships with academia and the private sector, and agile, lower-cost learning and innovation mechanisms will be key enablers of this shift. Together, these strategic directions point toward a UNICEF model that places resilience, equity, and system strengthening at the centre—protecting lifesaving services while supporting every child to gain the opportunity to survive, learn, and develop to their full potential in a resource-constrained and fragile context.

In 2025, UNICEF Uganda continued to deliver strong results for children, despite significant disruptions in external funding, public health emergencies and a slowdown in implementation due to preparation for the general elections in 2026. UNICEF Uganda, with the generous support from development partners, delivered direct services to close to six million children and leveraged government support to meet the need of an estimated another eleven million children.      
 
In 2025 Uganda’s fiscal space continued to be constrained with high level of debt servicing consuming 49 per cent of the domestic revenues in 2025/2026 financial year (FY), thus compromising investments in social sectors. Education spending marginally increased from 6.6 per cent in FY2024/25 to 7 per cent in FY2025/26, and projected health spending for FY2025/26 were still low, at 6.3 per cent. Investment in social protection remained below one per cent of the national budget.
                                
In 2024, Uganda met the least developed countries graduation criteria, however, the country continues to be highly vulnerable to economic and environmental shocks. Domestic revenue generation, averaging 13.7 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) since FY2021/22, is still inadequate to finance the ambitious development plans. Budget credibility is undermined by frequent supplementary requests (9.7 per cent in FY2021/22, way above the required threshold of 3 per cent). The private sector, expected to drive growth and employment, is largely informal (National Development Program/NDP-IV, 2025). In 2025, eight public health emergencies impacted the country, including the continuing Mpox and measles outbreaks affecting 83 per cent of the districts in the country, along with cholera, yellow fever and anthrax and the eight Ebola outbreak in January 2025. Some 162,146 individuals (38 per cent children) were affected by hydrometeorological hazards.  
 
Political decisions of the new US Administration, along with the announced foreign aid cuts by 16 donors (incl. the United Kingdom (UK), France, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany), severely impacted the United Nations’ (UN) efforts in Uganda. The cumulative impact of the funding cuts on the UN was estimated at US$ 162.5 million, undermining core humanitarian lifelines, such as refugee food and cash assistance and child protection services. The total UN workforce in Uganda reduced by an estimated 20 per cent; some 11,000 community health workers across 15 refugee hosting districts were no longer able to provide health care services for over 900,000 young children; a significant break in the Ready- to-use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) supply pipeline put at risk 300,000 children;  and 12,000 children and 2,400 women could not receive critical protection services.    
 
Increased instability in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Sudan and South Sudan saw a total of 153,933 new asylum-seekers registered in 2025, bringing the total refugee population in Uganda to 1.9 million people, of which 77 per cent are women and children (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees/UNHCR, 2025).
 
Monetary child poverty reduced from 20.3 per cent in 2019/20 to 18.5 per cent in 2024 (Uganda National Housing Survey/UNHS, 2024), and national monetary poverty rate declined from 20.3 to 16.1 per cent. However, multidimensional child poverty continues to be at 44 per cent, and sub-regional data show pockets of significant deprivations, such as Karamoja and Acholi regions with multidimensional poverty rates of 84.9 and 63.6 per cent, respectively. 
 
Uganda Demographic and Household Survey (UDHS) 2022 indicates that since 2019, the under-5 mortality decreased by 19 per cent, and the maternal mortality ratio nearly halved. However, mother-to-child Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission continues, and adolescent girls (15–24 years) account for one third of all new HIV infections. Approximately 28 per cent of maternal deaths are attributed to teenage pregnancies, and 24 per cent of girls continue to give birth before the age of 18 years (Census 2024). Although the full vaccination coverage increased from 55 to 63 per cent between 2016 and 2022, suboptimal quality and coverage of routine immunization leave 134,222 zero dose and over 83,586 under immunized children. Stunting declined but still affects 26 per cent of children (0–5 years), a rate that is stagnating for the past several years (UDHS, 2022), and some 86 per cent of children under 5 years are living in child food poverty (United Nations’ Children Fuds/UNICEF, 2024). 
 
The 2024 Census data indicate that only 40 per cent of children aged 3–5 years are attending early childhood education. Despite progress in universal primary education, one in every four children aged 6 to 17 years is out of school, and only three out of 10 pupils complete the seven-year primary education cycle, with teenage pregnancy and child marriage contributing to school dropout for girls. The Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES) data indicate that secondary school enrolment has stagnated below 30 per cent for the past decade, and an estimated 41 per cent of the 18 to 30 years old are not in education, employment or training (NEET) (Uganda Bureau of Statistics/UBOS, 2021). 
 
In 2022, more than 59 per cent of households had access to basic water and 21 per cent had access to basic sanitation, up from 43 and 19 per cent, respectively in 2012, however, over 30 per cent of the population lack access to handwashing facilities, as do around one half of the schools and healthcare facilities (World Health Organization/WHO and UNICEF, 2024). 
 
Some 76 per cent of children have experienced some form of violence in childhood (Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development/MoGLSD, 2018) and 22 per cent experience mental health challenges (53 per cent among refugee children), including depression, neurological or substance use disorders (UNHCR, 2024). Half of the girls aged 15–19 years reported that they have experienced sexual violence before the age of 15 years (UBOS, 2020), one third of young women in Uganda (UDHS, 2022) were married before the age of 18 years, and 42 per cent (6.2 million) of children under the age of 18 years are engaged in child labour. Nearly 60 per cent of children under the age of 5 years lack legal identity (Census 2014).

In 2025 UNICEF Uganda continued to prioritize high impact programs and life-saving interventions and stepped up partnerships to leverage support for children. Close to six million children received direct support though programming delivered by the Country Office (CO) in both humanitarian and development contexts, and more than 11 million were reached by leveraging partners’ health, education, nutrition, child protection, social protection and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services with key results listed below.
 
High impact results achieved during the year contributed towards the goal of the National Development Plan (NDP) III seeking to improve the quality of life of Ugandans, to enhance the social wellbeing of the population, strengthen the role of the state in development and ensure greater engagement of the private sector. The CO results also contributed to all four strategic Outcomes of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and to all five Goal areas of UNICEF’s Strategic Plan 2022-2025.     
 
The CO continued to strategically invest core resources to support policy reform in supporting the development of the National Food and Nutrition Policy and its Strategic Plan; the development of the National Adaptation Plan for WASH, bringing child focused lens to climate vulnerability reduction strategies; the development of the National Sanitation Policy and the finalizing the Environmental Health Strategy, both focusing at sub-national level and aiming to reduce communicable diseases, malnutrition, stunting and child mortality. UNICEF Uganda ensured the inclusion of child-focused measures in Uganda’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0. The approval of the Early Childhood Education and Care policy and the development of the Basic Requirements and Minimum Standards for early childhood development (ECD), was a critical milestone contributing to expanded access of over 207,952 children to pre-primary education. The CO contributed to the revision of the National Inclusive Education Policy, the Digital Strategy for Education (2026–2030) and the National Digital Skills/Competency Framework. The National Frameworks for NEET Youth and Internships were also revised with CO support and are expected to contribute to improved enrolment of Out of School (OOS) and NEET children and adolescents in education. UNICEF Uganda supported the development of the Quality Assurance System for Social Work, laying the foundations for the establishment of a Social Work Council to boost the protection of children’s rights nationwide though adequate, well-regulated and professional social services workforce. Shifting from parallel interventions to institutionalized, government-led, coordinated services, child protection was integrated within district-level multisectoral Child Well-Being Committees (CWCs), that allowed 371,139 children to access integrated health, education, justice, and social welfare services.
 
UNICEF Uganda’s advocacy continued to place the rights of children at the heart of national priorities and strategic dialogue. At the start of 2025, the CO supported the preparation of and ensured robust UNICEF participation in the African Regional Forum on Sustainable Development (ARFSD-11). Take aways from the forum were translated in a focused CO action in mobilizing financing for children, bolstering education and training systems to strengthen entrepreneurship and skilling programmes, expanding social protection measures, strengthen the quality of statistics and prevent public health emergencies, as described under the results below.   
 
Public financing for children advocacy contributed to  increases in combined budget allocations to education, health and social protection from 12.8 per cent to 13.9 per cent of the total national budget in FY 2024/2025 and ensured that monetary child poverty is incorporated in the 2023/24 UNHS report. UNICEF Ugadna supported the development of a National Action plan to End child poverty to consolidate advocacy efforts and resource mobilization for children in 2026 and beyond. Budget analytics provided critical information for advocacy towards safeguarding social sector financing within a constrained fiscal space and ensured that child rights remain at the centre of the planning and budgeting cycle at all stages.  
 
In 2025 the CO supported the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) to develop the multi-sectoral Nutrition Action Plan, catalysing coordinated action across food, health, WASH, education and social protection sectors. The CO advocacy maintained the government commitment to continue contributing US$ 1 million for RUTF procurement, as in the past three years.
 
Support to national WASH and Climate change advocacy platforms elevated visibility on child rights and sector prioritization with a child focused lens. The CO co-hosted important WASH and climate dialogues with Parliament, government ministries, civil society, and child-focused coalitions, including holding the Children’s Climate dialogue, WASH Symposium, and a National WASH-in-Schools Symposium, thus strengthening collaboration, collective advocacy, and shared commitments to child focused and climate-resilient equitable WASH services.
 
In 2025, UNICEF Uganda continued to act as the Coordinating Agency for the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and mobilized development partners (Ireland, Iceland, the European Union/EU Delegation) towards joint advocacy with the World Bank Board to unblock the significant GPE financing package of US$324.8 million for Uganda’s Learning Acceleration Programme (U-LEARN). The CO office advocacy ensured that the National Assessment on Progress of Education (NAPE), measuring the minimum literacy and numeracy proficiency for Primary 3 and Primary 6 levels, will be conducted by the Uganda National Examinations Board in 2026 and 2028. 
 
Catalytic advocacy and technical support to the National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA), supported the implementation of the Registration of Persons Regulations (2024), shifting birth registration from a project-based intervention to an institutionalized government service. As a result, over 217,813 births were notified (64 percent through health facilities), with 38.6 per cent of children under one year of age being registered in 2025, and 17,960 children under one received free birth certificates.
 
Technical support extended by UNICEF Uganda contributed to an improved quality of social service delivery for children. The CO supported the integration of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health into DHIS2/HMIS and continued to scale up the electronic Community Health Information System (eCHIS), achieving full interoperability with DHIS2. The CO supported the development of the national HIV Sustainability Roadmap 2026–2030 and worked with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and MoES to implement the School-Based Surveillance pilot in 115 schools in 18 districts to strengthen real-time infectious disease response and management. 
 
With EU financing, UNICEF Uganda supported OPM and UBOS to develop a multi-sectoral Nutrition dashboard and worked with MoH to integrate refugee nutrition data into the health HMIS system. The CO supported MoH to review and align the current national nutrition guidance to the newly released global WHO guidelines on care and management of child wasting, putting the prevention of acute malnutrition at the forefront of national policies, and worked with MoH to integrate the Multiple Micronutrients Powder into routine antenatal care to address anaemia and reduce prevalence of maternal mortality and child malnutrition, including low birthweight. 
 
The CO supported the finalization of the WASH Management Information System and trained a national cadre of trainers to strengthen harmonized reporting across three-line ministries – Ministry of Water and Environment (MoWE), MoH and MoES. UNICEF Uganda supported MoES to publish, for the first time since 2017, the Statistical Abstract of the Education Sector, based on the analysis from EMIS, with the Child Functioning Module, a data collection tool for disability inclusion, to be fully integrated into EMIS in 2026. 
 
With support from UNICEF Uganda, the MoGLSD launched the National Standards on Parenting, along with a training manual and an online Parenting Hub, offering essential tools to strengthen caregivers’ support. The CO further strengthened the SAUTI 116 helpline (recognized as a model in East and South Africa region) by including complementary chatbot application and introducing mental health and psychosocial support services. The development of the national Child Wellbeing Management Information System was initiated in 2025, seeking to harmonize routine administrative data across sectors and address long-standing data gaps on child rights violations, including for refugees. 
 
A major milestone was the finalization with MoGLSD of the Child Disability Benefit programme, with a commitment of the government to invest US$ 137,000 towards its implementation in 2026. Strategic investment of core resources supported the engagement with UBOS to conduct the first ever Uganda Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS), that will provide vital child related data and cover critical child related data gaps in the implementation of NDP-IV and the SDGs. The CO further supported UBOS to produce key thematic reports, including a Child Census Report and the Orphans and Vulnerable Children Report. The CO supported six rural Local Governments to enhance local revenue mobilization, with Kyegegwa and Mubende districts collecting some additional US$ 7,140 which were re-invested for procurement of primary school furniture to reduce the pupil–desk ratio in Kyegegwa and for provision of tuition support for children with disabilities in Mubende.
 
Important service delivery models were piloted to provide practical evidence supporting national scale up. Building on lessons learned from the COVID-19 response and bridging humanitarian and development action, in 2025 UNICEF Uganda facilitated the installation of 50 innovative "Oxygen as a Service" systems in 35 health facilities and provided medical oxygen piping systems to six health facilities, thus providing immediate support to 3,490 children in respiratory distress, with estimated extended support to a catchment population of more than 1.7 million children. The CO supported the implementation of the three-tier Interventions of the Disability in Early Childhood (IDEC) model in five districts where over 620 children with disability were identified and linked to specialized services. Flexible resources allowed continuous support to MoH to sustain the Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) of HIV service coverage above 95 per cent,  and directly supported 18,882 adolescents and women living with HIV to receive antiretroviral (ART) treatment. Implementation of the joint UN programmes: the Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) HIV Prevention Project, the Spotlight Initiative, and 2gether4SRHR, sustained peer-led, adolescent-friendly services in over 130 high-volume facilities across 17 districts.
