The CO supported the Expanded Program on Immunization across all 146 districts in the country, contributing to achieving 97 per cent DPT1 and 95 per cent DPT3 coverage. Support to two mass Yellow Fever campaigns, reached 9.2 million people with a coverage of 93 per cent, and 105 districts introduced the malaria vaccine targeting 1.1 million infants, a major milestone for malaria prevention. The Hepatitis B birth dose vaccine was launched with 949,790 (50 per cent) of the birth cohort of 2,292,458 surviving infants vaccinated. Polio prevention and eradication continued to be prioritized in border areas, entry points, and refugee-hosting communities, with 1,431,021 (94 per cent) children under one year immunized with OPV3 and 1,190,558 (78 per cent) of children immunized with IPV2 in 2025. In 2025, UNICEF Uganda supported the MoH for measles vaccination in all 146 districts of the country ensuring vaccination of 1,558,203 (92 per cent) and 1,012,823 (60 per cent) of children with first and second dose of measles vaccination.
 
The CO procured and supported the distribution of 9,171,947 Vitamin A capsules, enabling the government to reach 5,213,392 children 6-59 months in the first round and 3,958,555 children in the second round, while providing 3,876,726 caregivers with infant and young child feeding counselling (IYCF) during antenatal care visits.  Some 68,218 children with severe acute malnutrition were reached through timely RUTF procurement. The CO supported the integration of nutrition education into school curricula, and 360 schools implement nutrition activities reaching 342,727 students (10-18 years of age) with weekly iron supplementation to reduce anaemia.
 
Investments in climate-resilient water infrastructure benefited 24,800 people, and district and community capacity for Operation and Maintenance of water systems was strengthened. Korea government support through KOICA funded WASH interventions in Karamoja resulting in 44 per cent increase in overall school enrolment and a 38 per cent increase in girls’ enrolment. A total of 214,500 people and children were supported with WASH interventions in development and humanitarian setting, along with improvement of WASH facilities in 30 schools and 410 health centres.   
 
In 2025, mobile and community-based ECD models allowed 55,577 children to access early learning services, and 2,190 parents, including 4,769 fathers, were involved in parenting programs. Some 760 child mothers were re-enrolled into primary school through strengthened implementation of the revised school management guidelines implemented by 2,044 School Management Committee and Parent Teacher Associations.  Investments from the governments of Ireland, Netherlands, the EU, and UNICEF France allowed some 578,764 learners, including 8,449 learners with disabilities, to benefit from improved foundational learning and inclusive pedagogy nationwide. In Karamoja, the government of Ireland support built capacities of 30 teachers in foundational pedagogy and improved the learning environment for 720 learners by reducing the teacher pupil ratio from 1:80 to 1:50 trough classroom construction. The gross enrolment increased from 84 to 92 per cent across the region. UNICEF Uganda supported the review and approval of the U-CatchUp scale-up plan allowing 43,782 learners, including 1,109 learners with disabilities, to benefit from remedial and catch-up lessons. 
 
In 2025, some 2,346 para-social workers, child protection committees and community volunteers in refugee settlements were trained in child protection, psychosocial support, risk identification, and referrals, supporting the delivery of community-based psychosocial support to 199,470 children, adolescents, and caregivers across 33 districts, while 806 unaccompanied and separated children benefited from safe alternative care and family reunification. Efforts to prevent Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) reached 1,321,348 individuals raising awareness on SEA reporting channels, while 2,001,091 women, girls, and boys accessed GBV risk mitigation, prevention, and response services.  Strengthened collaboration between MoGLSD, MoJ, Police, and JLOS enabled 22,654 child cases to be managed, of which 8,185 were resolved, 1,450 children were diverted from formal justice processes, 1,959 were safely resettled with their families, and 1,138 received non-custodial sentences bringing child-sensitive approaches in the justice process. 
 
Cash programs funded by the governments of the Netherlands, Iceland, EU and Belgium supported the reintegration in education of 12,217 out of school children and adolescents, especially girls. Impact analysis of the Belgium supported Girls Empowering Girls (GEG) Programme demonstrated substantial gains in learning outcomes, and Kampala Capital City Authority has now integrated the GEG model in their five-year strategy. The EU funded Gender for Development Uganda (G4DU) cash-plus interventions significantly improved school retention and life skills development in seven districts. A total of 5,068 vulnerable adolescent girls received cash transfers to cover school fees, complemented by WASH upgrades, teacher training, and disability-inclusive top-ups boosting the lower secondary enrolment of girls in the 64 supported schools with over 50 per cent, compared to previous years. In addition, 35,520 vulnerable children and adolescents received grants, complementing the Universal Primary Education grants, improving access to education in 140 primary schools. 
 
In 2025, Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) interventions reached over 8.2 million people through mass media campaigns, U-Report engaged 151,376 users, and youth-led Communities of Action mobilised communities reaching people with relevant information. Over 100 young people  were trained in creative production resulting in the development of five youth and children’s media plans and the introduction of interactive radio formats, such as vox pops and dramas. A total of 87 young people were trained in storytelling and produced 80 creative outputs, culminating in more than 125 youth-centred radio shows, with achievements showcased to policymakers. Implementation of Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) allowed more than 18,682 queries and concerns to be addressed through U-Report live chats and UPartners. GBV prevention and response services reached 2,001,091 women, girls, and boys. Behaviour changes initiatives, implemented in partnership with cultural institutions (Busoga, Buganda, and Lango kingdoms), CSO and private sector partners (MTN, Girls Not Brides) addressed harmful social norms that contribute to teenage pregnancy, child marriage and FGM. The CO continued to co-chair, together with MoH, the Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) ensuring coordinated national-level SBC/RCCE leadership.
 
In 2025, more than US$ 11 million were invested in humanitarian action, including US$ 2 million from UNICEF flexible and core resources. The CO supported MoH in responding to eight public health emergencies (Ebola, Mpox, cholera, anthrax, yellow fever, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), measles, and Rift Valley fever) and to the nutrition emergencies in Karamoja and refugee hosting districts. 
 
UNICEF Uganda supported MoH to respond to the Ebola outbreak by training 1,014 VHTs for household outreach and conducting a RCCE campaign reaching over 7.8 million people, while 707,259 individuals received prevention messages, and 299,000 community members were empowered to share concerns through feedback channels (U-Report, SMS platforms, MoH hotlines, and community dialogues). Responding to the Mpox outbreak, immunization, vaccination and awareness raising were conducted in 15 districts. Some 2,310 community health workers were trained in community-based surveillance, and 706 health workers plus 302 VHTs were trained in IPC. Mpox-related information reached 2.78 million people, including 160,895 learners across 1,685 schools, while 756,000 individuals received critical WASH supplies, with WASH services extended to an estimated 1,563,780 catchment population. UNICEF Uganda supported the MoH in vaccinating 215,680 people with at least one dose of the Mpox vaccine. Technical support to MoES ensured the development and dissemination of Mpox SOPs and IEC materials to schools in all 146 districts of the country. Cash assistance programmes provided 1,321 Mpox affected households with timely cash transfers to address income loss due to prolonged isolation.
 
UNICEF Uganda’s rapid intervention in Lamwo and Kiryandongo, following the influx of refugees from Sudan, reached 21,400 people with emergency latrines, handwashing stations, water treatment materials, and disinfection supplies, and equipped the Panyandoli Health Centre IV in Kiryandongo with furniture and medical equipment to support maternal and child health services. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF Uganda continued to provide emergency nutrition to affected by the protracted drought in Karamoja children and those coming though the refugees influx from DRC and Sudan. Some 68,218 SAM children were treated in Karamoja, in all 13 refugees’ settlements and 6 transit centres, including children from host districts.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, the international development financing landscape experienced unprecedented volatility with sharp reduction in Overseas Development Assistance (ODA), especially from the United States. As a result, Uganda faced significant funding cuts, disproportionately affecting vertical programs such as HIV, TB and Family Planning. An accelerated action to reprioritize domestic resources was taken, with additional domestic resource allocation for health of US$ 146 million. The decline in ODA financing, compounded the already continuing challenges in child health and HIV linked with insufficient domestic financing, leading to critical health human resource shortages, especially at community level, combined with gaps in competencies, leadership, inadequate infrastructure, and fragmented implementation approaches that continue to hinder service quality. 
 
In nutrition, persistent global supply chain challenges coupled with funding cuts led to intermittent stock-outs of RUTF and therapeutic milks, placing children with severe acute malnutrition at heightened risk. The new WHO guidelines on malnutrition recommending RUTF use for moderate malnutrition can drive stock out up. UNICEF Uganda explored opportunities for  local therapeutic food receipt, modelled egg powder consumption and advocated for sustained government contribution towards RUTF procurement of US$ 1 million annually. Workforce shortages during refugee influx and Karamoja lean season food insecurity were addressed through surge deployments, with UNICEF Uganda supporting the institutionalization of such approach. 
 
Declining government and donor funding constrained access to quality education and reversed gains achieved in refugee settings. High teacher turnover undermines capacity-building efforts. Low and inconsistent salaries and overcrowded lower-primary classes with high teacher -pupil ratio of 117:1 and the one-teacher-per-class policy contribute to demotivation and undermine the quality of teaching. The sharp decrease of funding in refugee settings increasingly challenges the continuity of 400,000 refugee children currently enrolled in education. Infrastructure and connectivity gaps have slowed digital transformation and constrain access to online and digital learning. 
 
Entrenched social and cultural norms, religious beliefs, caregiving responsibilities, and seasonal labour demands continue to limit the participation of girls in education and influence decisions about school attendance, early marriage, and household roles. High teenage pregnancy rates remain a major challenge, and many adolescent mothers face significant barriers to returning to school, including stigma, lack of childcare options, restrictive school policies, and limited community support, perpetuating gender disparities. The inclusion of children with disabilities in education remains low. 

Against this backdrop, UNICEF Uganda managed its programme with agility and adaptation. UNICEF Uganda implemented a robust Resource Mobilization and Partnership strategy that allowed the CO to maintain stable funding levels in 2025. The CO secured US$ 29.3 million in development funding and US$ 7.8 million in emergency funding, and engaged with new public and private sector partners, including the governments of Austria, Denmark, Turkiye, the Korea International Development Agency (KOICA) and the UAE, and private partners, such as Eli Lilly, First Food Africa, Ferrin, KOFIH, Qatar Foundation and the Roger Family Foundation. Key new and continuing partnerships established in 2025 secured funds through UNICEF Korea, the Mastercard Foundation, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, and the governments of Netherlands, Sweden, Japan, and the UK. Additional support was received from EU/ECHO, Gavi, and the governments of Iceland, Ireland, Sweden and the United States, and the partnership with the World Bank strengthened. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF Uganda finalized its new Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026-2030. While the program design was conceptualised in 2024, influenced by the volatile financing situation, the CO rapidly adapted the finalised CPD design and oriented it to focus on upstream work and nationwide coverage with focus on pocket of vulnerability. The CO completed a careful affordability analysis and adjusted it organizational structure in preserving core functions within a lean structure that can support agility in rapid allocation of human resources where they are needed. Additional cost saving and efficiency measures were sought from a review and adjustment of administrative expenditures.    
 
Lessons learned underlined the effectiveness in advocating with the government for the adoption, institutionalisation and scaling up of service delivery models to bring sustainability in action. Multisectoral coordination in child protection and nutrition proved pivotal in bringing together multiple stakeholders from health, education, community services, justice, local government, and the private sector, and enabled districts to pool resources, reduce duplication, and deliver more efficient and accountable services for children. Innovations, including interactive and digital e-learning and skilling, establishment of e-courts, digital dashboards, eCHIS, HIS and EMIS have enhanced access to education and justice services, and supported enhanced community health and nutrition delivery with precisions, reduced delays, and improved child-sensitive outcomes.
 
In-country engagement with public and private partners, including strategic field visits and joint missions, proved invaluable to mobilize resources for children where they are needed, including the provision of humanitarian and flexible, non- earmarked funding allowing agility of programming. Such were the flexible funds contributions by the governments of Sweden for the entire CPD and in 2025 for the Ebola response. A high-level visit of Swedish Members of Parliament supported Sweden’s decision to sustain flexible global contributions to UNICEF. The effective diversification of the resource-partner base and sustained, proactive donor engagement ensured consistency in funding of programming for children. 
 
In looking forward, UNICEF Uganda will strive to maintain the agility of its programming for children, maintain the engagement with stakeholders and advocate for inclusion of children need in bilateral cooperation agreements. The CO will continue to generate high quality child focused data to support advocacy and investment in child rights. The CO will continue to leverage multi-stakeholder platforms and establish national coalitions to address child poverty and deprivations. The CO will continue its strong social sector budget analytics and will engage, in stronger way, in finding innovative financing solutions. UNICEF Uganda will continue to advocate for sustainable and increasing financing of social sectors, for stronger integrated service delivery, improved district-level planning and efficiencies in budget allocation and execution, to address service delivery bottlenecks. While identifying sustainable financing solutions for quality social services is critical, Uganda, in a short to medium term, will require continuous external investments to preserve the gains and expand quality service delivery in remote and underserved areas. Engagement with traditional and cultural institutions will remain critical to bring transformative change in social norms. Strengthened collaboration with the other UN agencies will help addressing the complex and interconnected needs of children and adolescents.

Tanzania’s economic performance maintained strong growth in 2025, with real GDP projected at 6.0 per cent and expected to average 6.3 per cent in 2026, rising to 6.5 per cent through 2030 (EIU Database, November 2025 Tanzania Update). Despite this performance, poverty reduction remains modest, with the national rate declining slightly from 26.5 to 26.2 per cent, and the international US$2.15 poverty line projected to fall from 43 per cent in 2025 to 41 per cent by 2027 (WB Macro Poverty Outlook[1]).  Inflation is forecast to remain stable at around 3.4 per cent, though global price volatility, geopolitical tensions, and climate-related shocks pose risks. Labour market indicators show gradual improvement, with unemployment dropping from 8.7 per cent in 2020/21 to 6.2 per cent in 2024, and youth unemployment declining from 9.9 to 8.5 per cent (ILFS 2024).
 
Aid inflows declined in 2025 as major donors, including the United States Government, reduced funding. These reductions are expected to widen financing gaps, particularly in critical sectors such as healthcare (Economic Intelligence Unit (EIU) Database, November Tanzania update), posing challenges for sustaining essential services and progress toward national development goals
 
Domestically, Tanzania strengthened tax policies and improved revenue mobilization in 2025. Key social sectors retained their share of the national budget, with nominal increases. Education rose by 20 per cent and health by 19 per cent (Ministry of Finance, Budget Insights 2025/2026). Despite these gains, inefficiencies and inequities in resource allocation and utilization continue to limit the impact of public spending. 
 
Tanzania has made notable progress across social sectors, though significant challenges persist. Under-five mortality declined sharply from 67 per 1,000 live births in 2015/16 to 43 in 2022, alongside improvements in maternal and child health indicators. Birth registration coverage rose to 68 per cent, up from 26 per cent in 2015/16, and 47 per cent of children aged 24–59 months are developmentally on track. Access to basic drinking water increased from 49 per cent to 64 per cent between 2015/16 and 2022, yet open defecation remains a concern at 10 per cent. (2022 Tanzania Demographic Health Survey-Management Information System (TDHS-MIS))
Despite these advances, children continue to face significant barriers. Neonatal mortality remains unchanged at 24 per 1,000 live births, and stunting has declined only marginally from 31.8 per cent to 30 per cent. Emerging nutritional challenges include rising consumption of sugary beverages and unhealthy foods, particularly in urban areas (2022 TDHS-MIS). HIV remains a major concern: new infections dropped by 39 per cent between 2010 and 2023 but fall short of the 75 per cent global target, with 47 per cent of new cases among 0–24-year-olds and adolescent girls and young women accounting for 80 per cent[YB1] . Education challenges persist; one in five primary-school-aged children and two in five lower-secondary-school-aged children remain out of school. (Basic Education Statistics in Tanzania (BEST 2024).
Progress has been recorded in reducing harmful practices and adolescent risks, though challenges persist. Female genital mutilation (FGM) declined modestly from 10 per cent to 8 per cent among women and from 5 per cent to 4 per cent among adolescent girls, while adolescent pregnancy fell from 26.7 per cent to 22 per cent (2022 TDHS-MIS). Violence against children remains widespread: TDHS data indicate declines in reported violence among adolescent girls, yet the Violence Against Children (VACS) 2024 findings reveal high lifetime prevalence of sexual, physical, and emotional violence among both girls and boys.
 
Tanzania is experiencing major demographic and environmental shifts that will shape the future of child well-being. Of the current 62 million people, 30 million are children, and the population is projected to reach 118 million, including 44 million children, by 2050. Urbanization has accelerated to 37 per cent (up from 18.4 per cent in 1988), increasing pressure on basic services in rapidly growing cities. 
 
Around one in five Tanzanians faces drought annually, underscoring the country’s high vulnerability to climate shocks (2022 Population and Housing Census). According to UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index, Tanzania ranks 40th out of 163 countries, placing children in the ‘high-risk’ climate category. Climate change is already eroding livelihoods, disrupting access to education and essential services, and deepening poverty and vulnerability. Seasonal floods affected several regions, including Morogoro, Iringa, Mara, Kagera, Kigoma, Mwanza, Rukwa and Mtwara, displacing an estimated 40,000 people. 
 
Public health risks intensified in 2025 with outbreaks of cholera, Mpox, Marburg Virus Disease, measles, and polio. Eight regions reported 4,405 cumulative cholera cases and 60 deaths (case fatality rate (CFR) 1.4 per cent). The Mpox outbreak affected 261 cases—209 across 17 regions in Mainland Tanzania and 52 in seven districts of Zanzibar, with no deaths recorded. In January 2025, a Marburg Virus Disease outbreak was declared in Kagera region and genetically linked to the outbreak in Rwanda.   An undeclared outbreak of measles in Kigoma Region affected 5 children under five years. Additionally,  
 
At the same time, the country hosted more than 200,000 refugees from Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), 58 per cent of whom are children, primarily residing in the Nduta and Nyarugusu camps in Kigoma region.
 
On 29 October 2025, Tanzania held its presidential election. However, the election was marked by significant unrest, including reports of violence and civilian casualties. (EIU Database, 26 November 2025). The UN Secretary General (UN Secretary General’s Press Release:31 October 2025)[2] and development partners called for conducting thorough and impartial investigations into all allegations of human rights violations. The post-election violence and concerns over human rights abuses have prompted major international partners to review or suspend aid (Joint Statement by Development Partners)[3]. The President, Samia Suluhu Hassan, (re-elected) established an independent Commission of Inquiry in November 2025 to investigate the civil unrest, violence, and deaths that occurred during and after the general election.

In support of the United Nations  Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 2030 Agenda progress, UNICEF  contributions to results for children in 2025 were guided by the UNICEF  Tanzania Country Programme (2022–2027) and fully aligned with the Tanzania  UNSDCF (2022–2027) and national priorities, including Tanzania’s Third  National Five Years Development Plan (2021–2026).   

Early Childhood Development
To enhance access to integrated services for young  children, UNICEF Tanzania advanced national Early Childhood Development (ECD)  priorities by strengthening the enabling environment, expanding integrated  service delivery, and empowering parents and caregivers to provide nurturing  care. In partnership with the Government of Tanzania, UNICEF finalized a  comprehensive ECD situation analysis in Zanzibar, informing the ongoing  development of an evidence- based Zanzibar Multisectoral Early Childhood Care  and Development Programme (2025/26–2029/30). Through sustained advocacy and  capacity building, UNICEF strengthened political commitment and improved  national and subnational ECD planning and budgeting guided by ECDI2030 data  and a shared focus on equitable investment in young children.
  
UNICEF enhanced service delivery through integrated ECD  modelling and institutionalizing early stimulation and responsive caregiving  within Village Health and Nutrition Days, embedding nurturing care within  routine community services. To improve quality and coherence of ECD services,  UNICEF strengthened the ECD workforce, supported the development of a  National Integrated ECD Training Package, and advanced standardized design  and operational guidance for ECD centres. At community level, UNICEF scaled  parenting and social and behaviour change initiatives promoting nutrition,  health, positive parenting, and WASH, reaching parents, caregivers and  communities with practical support for nurturing care. Collectively, these  achievements support sustained scale-up of initiatives to advance ECD.
  
Adolescents Development
UNICEF continued to prioritize  adolescence across sectors and facilitated cross-sectoral programming for  adolescents. UNICEF provided technical support to the Government of Tanzania,  for the evaluation of the National Accelerated Action and Investment  Agenda for Adolescent Health and Wellbeing (NAIA-AHW) 2021/22–2024/25,  generating lessons learned and recommendations to inform the next phase. In  2025, UNICEF continued to collaborate with UNFPA on the five-year joint  initiative supported by Global Affairs Canada, Kijana Imara, which  aims to improve equitable access to quality sexual and reproductive health  and rights for adolescent girls in mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. Tanzania  is a spearhead country for UNICEF’s global adolescent girls’ agenda and  successfully mobilized resources under the POWER4Girls initiative to scale up  the adolescent girls’ empowerment model from 2026 in Tabora Region, with a  projected reach of approximately 600,000 girls, boys, and stakeholders,  directly and indirectly.
  
Social norms analysis informed  gender-transformative programming on adolescent development, reaching 4.8  million parents (57 per cent male) across nine regions and establishing peer  support groups to sustain community dialogue. These efforts extended to 7.7  million young people through evidence-based modules on sexual and  reproductive health, nutrition, and mental health, improving service uptake.  In Zanzibar, engagement with 53 religious leaders challenged harmful norms  such as child marriage, fostering community-driven solutions. Out-of-school  campaigns enrolled 111,984 children—110 per cent of the target—and mapped  1,233 children with disabilities for referrals in Kigoma, Songwe, and Tabora.  Digital platforms like Internet of Good Things and U-Report engaged 61,000  youth, creating real-time feedback loops for adaptive programming. 
  
Through the  UNICEF-supported ONGEA radio program, up to 7.7 million adolescents and young  people accessed vital information on sexual and reproductive health and HIV  prevention. An independent assessment confirmed high levels of acceptability  and satisfaction among Adolescent and Young People (AYP) listeners,  positioning ONGEA as an effective platform to improve comprehensive HIV  knowledge—currently estimated at only 38 per cent for females and 42 per cent  for males. Adolescents benefited from targeted nutrition education and  supplementation interventions, including weekly iron and folic acid doses  delivered to more than 33,000 adolescent girls in Zanzibar. 

Adolescents further  engaged in programmes promoting physical activity and healthy dietary  behaviours. Community-based platforms, including Lishe ya Mwanao and Stawisha  Maisha, reached hundreds of thousands of caregivers, strengthening local  delivery systems and reinforcing positive nutritional behaviours essential  for reducing stunting and other forms of malnutrition.

To prepare Tanzania’s children  and adolescents for a digital future, UNICEF reached 1.5 million learners  with digital learning opportunities aligned with the national Digital  Learning Strategy. The Integrated Programme for Out-of-School Adolescents  (IPOSA) and in Zanzibar (ZIPOSA) engaged over 46,684 adolescents (61 per cent  girls), providing life skills, vocational training, and adolescent-friendly  services. Climate education was strengthened through 77 model schools  implementing the climate change guide, serving as a national benchmark for  replication. In Zanzibar, 9,865 adolescents (55 per cent girls) participated  in climate action initiatives, building leadership skills, developing  practical solutions, and becoming champions of sustainable development.
  
Goal 1: Every Child Survives and  Thrives
In 2025, with UNICEF support, Tanzania  developed a new National Immunisation Strategy (NIS) outlining seven  objectives to overcome key barriers to coverage. UNICEF successfully  advocated for institutionalizing outreach to missed children and Zero Dose  communities within routine primary health care (PHC), enhancing digital  infrastructure for unified and accurate immunization data, and strengthening  domestic financing for sustainability. Routine immunization coverage exceeded  targets for only two antigens, Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) at 103 per cent  and Human Papillomavirus vaccine (cHPV) at 115 per cent. Coverage for other  antigens declined: Pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib) at 84 per cent, Pneumococcal  vaccine (PCV13-3) at 83 per cent, MCV2 at 82 per cent, Inactivated Polio  Vaccine (IPV2) at 49 per cent, bivalent oral Polio vaccine (bOPV3) at 83 per  cent, and Rotavirus vaccine (dose 3) at 77 per cent. Estimates of measles  containing vaccine (MCV2) coverage declined from 91 per cent in 2024 to 84  per cent in 2025 due to exclusion of poor-quality administrative data in the  WHO, UNICEF Estimates of National Immunisation Coverage (WUENIC).  Facility deliveries continued on-track at 81  per cent. However, the coverage of newborn postnatal care (nPNC) continues to  lag at 54 per cent. 
  
UNICEF continued to strengthen  Tanzania’s primary health care (PHC) system by leading Development Partner  Coordination for the Health Basket Fund (HBF). Through this support, all  7,588 public PHC facilities delivered essential services, including outreach,  community health activities, and procurement of life-saving medicines. UNICEF  championed joint priorities such as expanding electronic medical records,  simplifying birth and death registration, and improving integrated child  health services. UNICEF’s financial contribution leveraged resources from  eight development partners mobilizing USD 55.8 million, with 90 per cent  directed to PHC services. UNICEF also led the HBF Midterm Review, with  recommendations encompassing funding flows and equity, improved facility  level planning and budget integration, and community accountability.
  
UNICEF and partners continued to  advance Tanzania’s efforts to control the HIV epidemic, achieving high  treatment coverage of 87 per cent. However, progress has not been equitable  as coverage for children and adolescents lags in most areas of progress.  Evidently, whilst ART coverage among children (0-14 years) living with HIV  has increased from 63 per cent in the preceding year to 70 per cent, it is still  below that of adults (88 per cent) and reflects a critical treatment gap  given Tanzania’s policy context of universal treatment eligibility. UNICEF  continued advocacy efforts for equitable programming. Advocacy and technical  assistance by UNICEF and WHO towards end of 2024 led to the country adopting  a new HIV treatment regimen for children using a fixed dose combination of  paediatric Abacavir, Lamivudine, Dolutegravir (pALD) which is a more  effective and efficient treatment regimen than the one currently in use. In  2025, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to develop a national  transition plan for the recently adopted treatment regimen which also  entailed including pALD in the 2026-2027 national quantification of ARVs. The  transition plan will guide the nationwide scale up scheduled for January to  June 2026.
  
To strengthen  data-driven programming, UNICEF supported the development of national  guidelines enabling teams to conduct in-depth reviews of PMTCT and pediatric  HIV data. Three deep-dive sessions were held across 12 regions, identifying programs  and data bottlenecks, and producing actionable plans to address them. These  efforts form part of Tanzania’s Path to Elimination of mother-to-child  transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B (i.e a global initiative led  by WHO and UNICEF to recognize a country’s progress in eliminating triple  elimination of vertical transmission). Progress is evident, with HIV vertical  transmission declining from 8.1 per cent in 2024 to 7.6 per cent in 2025,  though still above the target of less than 5per cent, underscoring the need  for continued action.

UNICEF, together with UNAIDS and  PEPFAR, supported the development of HIV sustainability roadmaps for both  Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. These roadmaps will guide future programming  to maintain progress in HIV prevention and treatment amid fiscal constraints,  ensuring long-term impact and resilience of national HIV responses.
  
Tanzania made  significant progress toward ensuring that more children, adolescents, and  women can access equitable, high-quality nutrition services and adopt  healthier diets and practices that support optimal child nutrition and development.  Throughout the year, the Government, supported by UNICEF, strengthened  policies, systems, and community-level programmes to address persistent maternal,  child, and adolescent undernutrition; address the emerging burden of  overweight and obesity; and promote nurturing care and child development  across the life course.

Tanzania achieved major  progress in improving nutrition through policy and programmatic action. The  revised food fortification regulations represented a significant policy  advancement, increasing population-level access to essential micronutrients  through fortified staple foods and reaching an estimated 90 per cent of  households. Coverage of essential nutrition interventions was further  expanded nationwide. In 2025, more than 9 million children (97per cent of the  target population) received Vitamin A supplementation. Additionally,  integrated Village Health and Nutrition Days were implemented in over 16,800  villages, delivering preventive nutrition and health services to more than  405,000 beneficiaries. Maternal nutrition gained renewed momentum as the  country embarked on developing a roadmap to introduce Multiple Micronutrient  Supplements into antenatal and postnatal care, aiming to improve pregnancy  outcomes and support healthier births.

Community engagement  and social and behaviour change interventions remained central to achieving  sustainable nutrition outcomes. More than 3.6 million caregivers received  counselling on infant and young child feeding practices, while more than  800,000 pregnant women received guidance on healthy, diverse diets

UNICEF strengthened  national and subnational systems by investing in evidence generation on food  systems in the frame of the First Foods Africa. Key studies, including the  Child Food Poverty Assessment, underscored the urgent need to improve food  systems for better child nutrition. Additional analyses examined the food  environment, covering packaged food surveys, labeling practices, market  trends for unhealthy products, and digital marketing targeting children.  These findings provided critical evidence that spurred government and partner  action to create healthier food environments and prevent overweight and  obesity among children in Tanzania.
  
Goal 2: Every Child Learns
In 2025, Tanzania advanced  education reforms under the revised Education Sector Development Plan (ESDP)  2029/30, supported by UNICEF. The plan strengthened system capacity, aligned  with Sustainable Development Goals, and enhanced the Education Management  Information System (EMIS) for data-driven planning. Efforts to expand  enrollment and digital learning reached 1.5 million children with digital  resources, while a Public-Private Partnership strategy improved access,  quality, and system resilience. Rising education costs highlighted the need  for sustainable and innovative financing to ensure continuity, inclusion, and  equity in learning opportunities.
  
UNICEF supported the Government to strengthen access, continuity,  and resilience in education. Through community mobilization, back-to-school  campaigns, radio outreach, and local engagement, more than 111,984  out-of-school children (54 per cent girls) were enrolled, while nearly 9.85  million community members were reached to promote the importance of  education, especially for girls. To improve learning quality and equity, over  158,000 children received learning materials, and more than 17,000 teachers  enhanced classroom instruction through targeted training. Complementary Basic  Education in Tanzania (COBET) benefited 51,640 children (48 per cent girls)  with improved learning environments. Parenting programs engaged 3,540  caregivers, and behavior change communication on positive parenting and early  stimulation reached 99,619 community members.
  
Goal 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence,  Abuse and Exploitation
In 2025, UNICEF  supported Tanzania in protecting children from violence and ensuring their  rights and reached over 1.8 million children, caregivers, and community  members with violence prevention interventions and provided quality child  protection services to more than 25,000 children.  With UNICEF support, the number of birth registration centres  increased from 11,476 in 2024 to 11,902 in 2025. As a result, over  600,000 children under five received birth certificates in 2025, through the  simplified registration system, advancing legal identity for all. UNICEF  also strengthened public financing and routine data systems for child  protection. However, key amendments to laws regarding child  marriage and corporal punishment remain significant challenges to  implementation of recommendations from human rights mechanisms.
  
UNICEF contributed to the  finalization of the 2nd national violence against children survey (VACS)  and supported the process of embedding new data into the national action  plans (NPA) to end violence against women and children in both Mainland and  Zanzibar. A situation analysis of the violence policy and programming  landscape was completed to understand the new data and the major shifts since  2009, when the 1st VACS was undertaken. In addition, an evaluation  of the child justice strategy and an assessment of alternative care were  completed to further guide the process of reform. 
  
UNICEF advanced the  implementation of National Plans of Action (NPAs), supporting coordination  work at national level on parenting, social norms, response and enforcement  of laws to ensure that programming is evidence-based and at regional level,  to ensure that front-line services have access to funds to try out new  approaches to prevention and response. Progress has also been made in  ensuring that regional and district social welfare officers plan and budget  for their work within the Comprehensive Council Social Welfare Operational Planning  tool. This will mean that social welfare officers can plan for and request  budget to deliver their protection work for women and children.
  
In 2025, Tanzania responded to  five public health emergencies including cholera, measles, circulating  Vaccine Derived Polio Type 2 (cVPD2) Marburg Virus Disease (MVD), and MPOX. UNICEF  supported the Government to deliver Mental Health and Psychosocial Support  (MHPSS) during the Marburg Virus Disease outbreak, reaching over 1,000  affected individuals and frontline workers. In refugee camps, UNICEF provided  MHPSS supplies and case management for more than 3,800 children, including  unaccompanied and separated children. 
  
UNICEF  prepared a confidential report on the implementation of the UN Convention on  the Rights of the Child, to complement the State and CSO alternative  reports.  UNICEF also supported the  preparations and facilitated engagement of CSOs and children in a pre-session  with the UN Committee on the Rights of the child, ensuring their voices  informed the review process.
  
Goal 4: Every Child has access to a Safe and Clean  Environment
UNICEF accelerated Tanzania’s  WASH agenda by strengthening climate-resilient systems, improving sector  governance, and expanding inclusive services. These efforts protect  children’s rights to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene while promoting  equity, gender responsiveness, and sustainability for healthier communities  and a more resilient environment.
  
UNICEF strengthened  Tanzania’s climate-resilient WASH systems through key policy and guideline  milestones. National water and sanitation policies for Mainland and Zanzibar  were finalized, creating a unified framework to accelerate universal access  and integrate climate adaptation. Updated Climate-Resilient Water Safety Plan  and Drinking Water Quality Monitoring Guidelines enhanced capacity to manage  climate-related risks, while new Menstrual Health and Hygiene Guidelines  advanced gender-responsive standards. UNICEF co-chaired major coordination  platforms and supported government engagement at COP30 and the Sanitation and  Water for All Ministers’ Meeting, contributing to Tanzania’s endorsement of  the High-Level Leaders Compact on Water Security and Resilience, bolstering  governance, accountability, and climate readiness across the sector.
  
UNICEF expanded equitable WASH  services to improve health, learning, and well-being for children and  families. In 2025, more than 457,114 people, including 223,985 children, gained  access to safe water, while 535,688 people, including 62,487 children,  accessed basic sanitation, bringing the cumulative reach since 2022, to 2.23  million. Makete District in Njombe Region, achieved Open Defecation Free  status, and inclusive WASH facilities in 21 schools benefited over 18,650  children. Climate-resilient WASH and infection prevention systems in  healthcare facilities improved care for over 86,479 people, enhancing  dignity, safety, and service quality.
  
UNICEF strengthened WASH data  systems to improve planning and accountability. National guidelines for  producing WASH statistics were endorsed, standardizing methodologies for  surveys and administrative data. Integration of WASH indicators into the  Education Management Information System (EMIS) advanced data quality and  informed planning. Additionally, a climate readiness report was finalized to  guide adaptation strategies and future investments.
  
UNICEF strengthened  behavior change and community engagement to overcome social norms and promote  safer, climate-resilient WASH and menstrual health practices. By empowering  1,572 frontline workers, including 389 influencers and engaging youth  networks and local structures, UNICEF reached 302,366 people, including  148,159 children. These efforts enhanced cholera prevention, menstrual  hygiene, and community ownership for sustainable WASH services.
  
Goal 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life 
UNICEF contributed to strategic  reforms that strengthened how Tanzania generates, uses, and applies evidence,  financing, and social protection systems to improve outcomes for vulnerable  children. A major milestone was the launch of the Tanzania Integrated  Statistical Portal (TISP), the country’s first platform to harmonize data  from National Bureau of statistics (NBS) and multiple sectoral systems into  one interoperable environment. By integrating 11 national data systems and  embedding child-sensitive indicators, TISP enables more consistent analysis  of social indicators, supports triangulation across administrative levels,  and links investments to development and social outcomes. This represents a  shift from fragmented datasets to a coordinated system that enhances the  Government’s ability to plan, and budget based on timely and comparable data.
  
UNICEF strengthened national  child poverty measurements. NBS completed data collection for the 2025  Integrated Household Budget Survey, which for the first time includes a  module to measure child multidimensional poverty. Developed with UNICEF’s  support, this will enable the Government to produce robust, child-specific  poverty estimates for national reporting.
  
UNICEF supported a significant  advancement in public finance reform through the revision of the Zanzibar  Public Financial Management Act, which now incorporates gender and equity  provisions directly into fiscal legislation. This strengthens the foundations  for child-sensitive public finance management by ensuring that equity  considerations are reflected in budget processes, monitoring, and reporting.  Improvements in fiscal transparency and citizen-focused budget communication  further help align public allocations and spending with the needs of  disadvantaged children and communities. In the area of social protection,  UNICEF advanced adaptive programming and strengthened systems to  improve effectiveness and expand the reach of social assistance. The second  Zanzibar Social Protection Policy Implementation Plan (2025-2030) anchors key  innovations, including a national Social Registry and e-payment systems, to  improve targeting, delivery of benefits, and multisectoral coordination. In  Mainland, UNICEF supported the establishment of thematic working groups under  the national social protection policy and contributed to the design of PSSN  III, advocating for the inclusion of cash-plus and social behavioral change  approaches to better address children’s vulnerabilities. These actions have  strengthened the system’s capacity to respond to emerging needs and shocks.
  
Reforms were reinforced by the finalization  of the first Tanzania Child Outlook, which provides a comprehensive,  data-driven analysis of inequities affecting children and highlights priority  actions for improving child well-being. In parallel, the National  Child-Focused Policy Research Agenda for Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar (2025–2030)  was revised and finalized, outlining priority evidence needs and research  gaps to guide future policy dialogue and investment decisions.
  
Collectively, these achievements  have improved how Tanzania plans, budgets, and delivers essential services,  ensuring systems are more responsive, equitable, and grounded in evidence for  the benefit of the most vulnerable children.
  
Change Strategies: Cross Sectoral
  
UNICEF strategically balanced  risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) for public health  emergencies with long-term efforts to advance children’s rights to health,  education, and protection. Evidence-based RCCE approaches reduced  stigma-related barriers by up to 30 per cent and improved adoption of  protective behaviors. Over 60 million people were reached through integrated  channels, digital platforms, mass media, and community networks supported by  real-time social listening tools to optimize targeting and impact. During the  Marburg Virus Disease outbreak in Kagera, UNICEF co-led RCCE with government  partners, using ethnographic polling and gender analysis to counter  misinformation and stigma. Gender-responsive strategies included training  1,115 stakeholders and outreach to 20 million people via community radio,  resulting in a 15 per cent increase in health-seeking behaviors. Mpox  response campaigns reached 11 million people through AI-driven digital  initiatives, while cholera interventions strengthened systems-thinking  capacity for 113 practitioners and students. In Zanzibar, media campaigns for  Acute Watery Diarrhea and Mpox reached 1.6 million people. 
  
UNICEF strengthened capacity for  Social and Behavior Change (SBC) monitoring, evaluation, and learning and advanced  human capital development by empowering 150 community representatives,  technical leaders, and ministry officials with competencies to design robust  M&E frameworks for effective SBC programming. This capacity enhancement  strengthens evidence-based planning and accountability, ensuring more  impactful and sustainable behavior change interventions for children and  families. Additionally, UNICEF facilitated an academic consortium with four  leading Tanzanian universities to advance multidisciplinary child rights  research, hosting SBC symposia and contributing peer-reviewed publications to  global journals. These efforts generated robust evidence on behavior change  dynamics, reinforcing SBC’s role in knowledge generation and policy  influence.
  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened  strategic partnerships with media, civil society, parliamentarians, and youth  to advance advocacy priorities for children, including abolishing corporal  punishment, ending child marriage, and accelerating climate action. On  climate action, UNICEF supported youth-led advocacy by convening the  Pre-COP30 National Youth Forum and the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY),  engaging 450 children and young people from across Mainland Tanzania and  Zanzibar. These forums equipped participants with negotiation skills, green  technology knowledge, and understanding of the United Nations Framework  Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) processes, culminating in the National  Youth Climate Declaration, a roadmap calling for investment in green skills,  youth-led innovation, and child-sensitive climate adaptation strategies.
  
UNICEF partnered with the  National Coalition on Ending Corporal Punishment and the Tanzania Ending  Child Marriage Network (TECMN), comprising 102 member organizations, to  develop a joint advocacy strategy aimed at raising awareness, influencing  decision-makers, and mobilizing public support to end harmful practices.  While legislative reforms are still underway, these efforts strengthened  collective advocacy and elevated child protection issues within national  discourse.
  
Throughout 2025, UNICEF engaged  over 100 editors and senior journalists on integrating children’s aspirations  into Tanzania’s Development Vision 2050. This advocacy led to a resolution  urging the Government to incorporate children’s priorities in the final  Vision 2050 draft and secured media commitments to amplify these issues  nationwide.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Despite notable progress in advancing child rights and systems strengthening in 2025, UNICEF Tanzania faced significant challenges that tested resilience and adaptability, particularly due to the sudden shifts in Official Development Assistance (ODA), which disrupted services, and reduced coverage for most services for children. 

In 2025, The abrupt termination of U.S. funding for adolescent HIV prevention disrupted programming and halted critical governance and coordination processes. Global Fund reprioritization further constrained efforts, making it difficult to sustain interventions for children and adolescents. A key lesson learned is the power of evidence-based advocacy and strategic partnerships in scaling essential interventions. UNICEF’s Family-Centered Care Approach, a peer-based model linking community and health facility services delivered strong results, including higher HIV positivity rates and improved linkage to child survival services. Building on this momentum, UNICEF will continue championing integrated, family-centered models and leveraging partnerships to expand coverage and strengthen systems for adolescent HIV prevention and child survival.

Nutrition programming was similarly affected by sudden shifts in Official Development Assistance (ODA), which disrupted services, reduced coverage, and halted key processes such as micronutrient survey and universal salt iodization study. UNICEF mitigated these impacts by mobilizing core resources to sustain critical support. A key lesson from 2025 is the growing momentum around Food Systems for Children, driven by new evidence and strong government engagement. Looking ahead, UNICEF will intensify advocacy and provide technical assistance to advance innovative financing solutions, including the Child Nutrition Fund, ensuring sustainable investments for improved nutrition outcomes.

Declining financing constrained WASH interventions and emergency responses, leaving service coverage slow and uneven, with a persistent rural–urban gap. Election-related disruptions, limited community-based capacity, and climate impacts, including floods, water shortages, and disease outbreaks—further threatened sustainability. Lessons learned underscore the importance of integrating recovery measures into emergency response and leveraging government systems and peer learning on Market-Based Sanitation to drive innovation. In 2026, UNICEF will prioritize reinforcing sector governance through resource mobilization and financing strategies, advancing commitments under the Heads of State WASH Presidential Compact, and accelerating climate-resilient WASH programming to safeguard access for every child.

In the education sector, lessons highlight the need to strengthen digital learning through adequate infrastructure, teacher capacity, and inclusive solutions such as offline platforms and solar connectivity to ensure equity in hard-to-reach communities. Engaging men, boys, and community champions proved effective in shifting norms and enhancing gender-targeted strategies, while structured public–private partnerships emerged as a powerful mechanism for mobilizing resources and fostering innovation. UNICEF will deepen these partnerships and scale digital learning solutions to close equity gaps and enhance resilience.

Social policy implementation was slowed by funding limitations, fiscal constraints, competing priorities, and frequent government staff turnover. The transition from PSSN II to PSSN III exposed gaps in adaptive capacity, particularly in maintaining child-sensitive components. UNICEF will focus on system strengthening, deepen integration of the Tanzania Integrated Statistical Portal, advance equity-focused public financial management reforms, and promote shock-responsive and digital social protection systems, while expanding evidence generation to drive inclusive reforms.

Shrinking ODA budgets and the exit of major SBC players such as USAID, coupled with recurrent public health emergencies, misinformation, and climate impacts, posed significant challenges for Social and Behavior Change programming. Lessons emphasize localization, leveraging influencers and religious leaders to shift harmful norms, and applying behavioral science for cost-effective outreach. UNICEF will support people-centered agendas, strengthen partnerships for community-driven solutions, and scale evidence-based approaches to drive measurable outcomes for children.

UNICEF strengthened partnerships and expanded collaboration with philanthropic and corporate actors to diversify funding sources amid a rapidly changing development assistance landscape. High-level visits and the first-ever family philanthropy mission unlocked transformative contributions, while renewed engagement with banks, mobile operators, and global platforms opened new funding streams. Strategic reflection identified private sector engagement pillars and entry points, including leveraging platforms such as the CEO Round Table to connect with Tanzania’s business leaders. In 2026, UNICEF will deepen private sector engagement, further expand innovative financing models, and strengthen partnerships to sustain impact for children.
The violence following the October 2025 Presidential elections, which involved grave violations of children’s rights, revealed that the child protection system designed to prevent and respond to violence and abuse is not functioning effectively. UNICEF worked with partners to strengthen the child helpline and to deliver mental health and psychological support and case management for children impacted. Weak monitoring systems, constrained data collection, and service disruptions for Burundian refugees compounded vulnerabilities, while budget cuts strained critical services for unaccompanied children and Gender Based Violence survivors. Furthermore, the continued use of incentives for routine government functions remains a barrier to sustainability. Moving forward, UNICEF will reinforce child protection systems, and advocate for cost-effective, sustainable approaches to service delivery.

Strengthening interfaith collaboration proved essential for promoting social cohesion. With UNICEF support, the Tanzania Interfaith Partnership facilitated meaningful engagement among faith leaders from the Christian Council of Tanzania (CCT), the Tanzania Episcopal Conference (TEC), and the National Muslim Council of Tanzania. Bringing these groups together to co-develop unified messages on healing, peace and justice demonstrated that interfaith dialogue remains a powerful platform for building trust and addressing community tensions. Youth inclusion emerged as a critical factor for sustainable peacebuilding. By ensuring that interfaith messages emphasize children’s rights and meaningful youth participation, UNICEF and its partners highlighted the importance of positioning young people as active contributors and not passive recipients in efforts to rebuild social cohesion.

Coordinated dissemination strengthens reach and legitimacy. The validation of interfaith messages by General Secretaries and their delivery through orientations and sermons across more than 580 faith institutions showed that high-level endorsement is crucial for consistent and widespread community uptake. A key lesson was that combining traditional platforms (such as sermons and community dialogues) with modern tools and media outreach, digital feedback mechanisms, youth-led campaigns and real-time monitoring dashboards, creates stronger, more adaptive avenues for dialogue and inclusion. UNICEF’s support for digital tools and monitoring systems demonstrated that timely, community-generated insights are essential to identify emerging risks, empower vulnerable groups and shape evidence-based strategies for reconciliation. Overall, UNICEF’s role as a convener, technical adviser and systems-strengthening partner was central to advancing social cohesion, illustrating that inclusive processes, youth engagement and multi-channel communication are key drivers for national resilience.

Looking ahead, UNICEF Tanzania remains committed to equity, resilience, and innovation across all sectors, working with government, communities, and partners to deliver sustainable results for every child in Tanzania.

During the year, Zambia’s operating environment continued to be shaped by overlapping climatic, public health, and socio-economic pressures, with direct implications for children’s rights and wellbeing. Climate variability remained a defining feature of the year, following the El Niño-induced drought that had severely disrupted livelihoods, food security, and energy generation. Although rainfall patterns improved in some areas, the lingering effects of drought continued to affect household resilience, access to basic services, particularly in rural and peri-urban communities where children are most vulnerable. Public health risks persisted, with recurrent outbreaks of cholera and the emergence of Mpox reinforcing structural weaknesses in water, sanitation, hygiene, and primary health care systems. These shocks disproportionately affected children under five, adolescents, pregnant and lactating women, and persons with disabilities. Despite these pressures, continuity of essential health and nutrition services was largely maintained, reflecting strengthened preparedness, improved surveillance, and adaptive service delivery models supported by UNICEF and partners. 
 
Economically, Zambia continued a gradual recovery trajectory, though growth remained insufficient to offset rising household vulnerability. Inflationary pressures and high food prices constrained purchasing power, deepening poverty and limiting families’ ability to meet children’s nutritional, educational, and protection needs. Poverty and inequality remained key barriers to achieving the targets set out in the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025 and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to ending preventable child deaths, malnutrition, learning poverty, and violence against children. 
 
At the same time, 2025 was marked by important policy and institutional developments. Government commitment to social sector reform was demonstrated through the launch and revision of key national policies, increased attention to child-focused planning and budgeting, and continued progress in decentralisation. Social sector investments remained significant, with education, health, social protection, and WASH continuing to account for on average a third (35%) share of public expenditure, albeit with persistent gaps between policy commitments and service quality at subnational level. 
 
Zambia also made progress in strengthening its evidence base for decision-making, with the use of administrative data, sector assessments, and analytical studies increasingly informing policy dialogue and programme prioritisation. These developments provided opportunities for UNICEF to position itself as a trusted partner and thought leader on child rights, equity, and systems strengthening, while reinforcing the call to “leave no child behind” under the 2030 Agenda. 
 
Within this context, UNICEF Zambia balanced humanitarian response with longer-term development and resilience-building, aligning its interventions to national priorities under the Eighth National Development Plan and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, while advancing equity-focused results for the most disadvantaged children and adolescents.

During the year, UNICEF Zambia delivered results across health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection, social policy, and cross-sectoral enablers, with a strong emphasis on systems strengthening, policy influence, and emergency preparedness and response. Rather than isolated interventions, UNICEF’s contribution focused on reinforcing national systems to deliver sustainable, equitable results at scale. 
 
Zambia has made notable progress in addressing malnutrition, achieving the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target for wasting, with prevalence reduced from 6% in 2013/141  to 3% in 20242. However, significant challenges persist, including a high stunting rate of 32% [2] and a concerning increase in anemia among women of reproductive age, which worsened from 31% in 20183 to 41% in 20244. These figures underscore the critical need for comprehensive and integrated nutrition interventions. UNICEF's contribution has been instrumental in expanding vital nutrition services and strengthening systemic frameworks. The Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) services were significantly scaled up, reaching 2,832 facilities, 22% above target, and benefiting over 3.18 million caregivers. Dietary diversity interventions were expanded to 21 districts, an increase from 17 in 2024.  
 
Furthermore, iron and folic acid supplementation for pregnant women saw a substantial rise, reaching 226,409 individuals, close to the target of 231,618, up from 197,162 in 2024. In addressing severe and moderate acute malnutrition, treatment reached 26,376 children with SAM (69% of target) and 64,965 with MAM. While sufficient supplies were procured for all children with SAM, coverage was limited to 49% of the estimated caseload due to challenges in case finding and last-mile distribution. A key systemic achievement was the incorporation of nutrition commodities into the national electronic Logistics Management Information System, ensuring more sustainable commodity management.  
 
UNICEF also played a pivotal role in advancing systemic reforms and advocacy to embed nutrition within Zambia’s governance and financing structures. Four high-level engagements with the Office of the Vice President, Parliament, and key partners secured commitments to accelerate stunting reduction. For the first time, the national budget call circular explicitly directed ministries and local authorities to include nutrition lines in their 2026 annual and mid-term budgets. Multi-sectoral coordination was enhanced, with the number of coordination officers increasing from 17 to 86 across the 116 districts. Critical policy documents, including the National Food and Nutrition Policy, the stunting reduction roadmap, and an investment framework, were successfully developed. As Convenor of the Cooperating Partners for Nutrition and Co-Lead of the Nutrition Cluster, UNICEF significantly improved coordination for technical assistance, service delivery, and advocacy. These achievements were made possible through robust partnerships with the EU, German Cooperation (KfW and GIZ), Irish Aid, Sida, the UK FCDO, and OCHA. 
 
UNICEF supported the Government to strengthen primary health care and community health systems, with a particular focus on last-mile service delivery and ensuring continuity of care during emergencies. A key achievement was enabling the deployment of Polyvalent Community-Based Volunteers through capacity building, provision of start-up packs, and leveraging Global Fund resources to support stipends. This enhanced outreach for maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health services in underserved areas, including targeted interventions for adolescent sexual and reproductive health. Progress under the Health Facility Solar Electrification initiative significantly improved service continuity and quality of care, especially crucial during public health emergencies. By the end of 2025, 35 health facilities were fully solarized and 41 were under installation, laying the groundwork for scaling up to 250 facilities by mid-2026. Solarization strengthened cold-chain systems, emergency obstetric care, and service delivery during power disruptions, contributing to resilient health systems. Another landmark milestone was Zambia’s introduction of the malaria vaccine into the national immunisation programme, with 139,024 children aged six to eight months in the 83 targeted district reached (target 125,993), representing 110% coverage. UNICEF provided technical and operational support across supply chain readiness, health worker training, and community engagement, contributing to national efforts to reduce malaria-related morbidity and mortality among children. 
Furthermore, UNICEF provided technical and operational support to 87 districts to develop comprehensive emergency preparedness and response plans aimed at mitigating health and environmental risks. These plans strengthened local capacities to anticipate and respond to public health emergencies. In the wake of Cholera and Mpox outbreaks, 33 districts implemented targeted lifesaving interventions, reaching approximately 1.46 million people with essential services, including case management, water, WASH support, and risk communication. These efforts contributed significantly to maintaining mortality rates below 1.5 percent for both diseases, demonstrating the effectiveness of timely and coordinated responses.  
 
UNICEF continued to strengthen WASH systems and climate resilience. A major contribution was support to the 2025 National WASH in Health Care Facilities Baseline Assessment, covering 3,134 facilities and significantly improving the national evidence base for planning and investment. Infrastructure and service improvements were delivered to 246 institutions, including health facilities and schools. Overall, more than 100,000 people gained access to basic water services, 218,000 to basic sanitation, and 246,000 to hygiene services. These results were complemented by the installation of 80 new boreholes, 250 rehabilitations of existing water points, and implementation of 22 solar-powered piped water schemes, many of which supported drought and emergency response efforts. Capacity development remained central, with government staff and health care facilities trained on WASHFIT and Infection Prevention and Control, alongside strengthened water quality and safety planning with commercial utilities. 
 
Within the education sector, Zambia has expanded access to quality early childhood education, with over half of Grade 1 entrants having prior experience but right age enrolment remains a challenge. Foundational literacy and numeracy benchmarks are now clearly defined in the early-grade curriculum and 68.6% of learners are now transitioning to senior secondary school. UNICEF supported transformative reforms in early learning and foundational education. The Early Childhood Development for Human Development programme was successfully launched and operationalized, alongside the expansion of community-based ECD to additional districts, increasing access to early learning services. The establishment of the Foundational Learning Technical Committee and implementation of the Catch-Up Programme improved foundational literacy and numeracy outcomes, particularly for learners affected by learning losses. Digital inclusion was advanced through connecting 300 schools to the internet, benefiting over 200,000 learners with access to online learning resources. Despite progress in defining benchmarks for foundational learning, persistent challenges such as high pupil-to-textbook (5 pupils share a text book) ratios highlighted the need for sustained investment in education inputs and quality. 
 
Zambia made significant progress in system-wide child protection reforms, with UNICEF providing strategic technical and advocacy support. The restructuring of the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services paved the way for recruitment of social workers and rollout of a minimum package of child protection services across 50 districts. Harmonised case management systems, improved information systems, and implementation of statutory instruments and guidelines enabled over 200,000 vulnerable children to access protection services. Professional training reached social welfare officers, para-social workers, law enforcement, and judicial officers, strengthening service quality and accountability. To ensure sustainability, a Children’s Code Act curriculum was integrated into higher learning institutions, and an investment case and cost of inaction analysis informed a draft national, costed social service workforce strengthening strategy to be finalised in 2026. 
 
UNICEF strengthened public finance and social protection systems to improve child-focused planning, budgeting, and shock responsiveness. Local government planning was enhanced through Output-Based Budgeting, integrated development plans, and improved fiscal reporting, resulting in better alignment of resources with child welfare priorities. The revised National Social Protection Policy was launched, advancing a life-cycle approach to social protection. The Social Cash Transfer programme reached over 2.2 million households with regular and emergency assistance, including nutrition top-ups during the drought. Safeguarding measures were strengthened through nationwide rollout of Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse training. Disability inclusion was advanced through capacity building of Organisations of Persons with Disabilities and national situation analyses on persons with disabilities and persons with albinism, catalyzing policy dialogue and action planning. 
 
Across programmes, UNICEF strengthened planning, monitoring, and evaluation, achieving the 1 per cent evaluation expenditure target and 100 per cent on-time donor reporting. Digital dashboards enhanced management oversight, while government staff were capacitated on HACT and results-based management. Social and behaviour change initiatives, advocacy, youth engagement, partnerships, and operational reforms further reinforced UNICEF’s ability to deliver results at scale.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Climate-induced emergencies continued to pose a major challenge in 2025, disrupting service delivery and diverting resources from long-term development. The frequency and complexity of shocks underscored the need to strengthen the humanitarian–development nexus. UNICEF’s experience in 2025 demonstrated that resilience, sustainability, and continuity of essential services must be embedded across all programmes, with greater agility and speed in emergency response. 
 
Constrained resources amid rising needs highlighted the importance of strategic prioritisation. UNICEF’s comparative advantage lies in thought leadership, evidence generation, policy influence, and systems strengthening. Clarifying what UNICEF should lead directly, what should be enabled through partners, and what should be advocated for externally will be critical to maximizing impact. 
 
Persistent poverty and inequality continued to undermine children’s outcomes, exacerbated by inflationary pressures and constrained economic growth. Experience from the year reaffirmed the centrality of social protection as a buffer against economic shocks, particularly for households with young children, adolescents, and persons with disabilities. Strengthening shock-responsive and nutrition-sensitive social protection remains essential. 
 
Quality and equitable access to social services remain significant challenges, driven by both supply and demand-side constraints, including infrastructure gaps, human resource shortages, and uneven service quality at subnational level. System strengthening, sustained capacity development, and community engagement are critical to improving service delivery, accountability, and outcomes. 
 
Coordination gaps between national and subnational levels affected the timeliness and effectiveness of service delivery, particularly during emergencies. Decentralisation presents opportunities to bring decision-making closer to communities, enhance social accountability, and improve efficiency. Strengthening the role, sustainability, and institutionalization of frontline workers will be essential to achieving results at scale. 
 
Looking ahead, UNICEF Zambia will build on lessons from 2025 to deepen systems strengthening, scale up climate-resilient and shock-responsive services, and accelerate equity-focused programming. By leveraging evidence, partnerships, and innovation, UNICEF will continue to support the Government to deliver sustainable results for children and adolescents, ensuring that no child is left behind.

In 2025, Zimbabwe’s operating context for children was shaped by significant cuts in development assistance, affecting particularly health, HIV prevention and treatment services, education and food security. Children continued to suffer the brunt of the cumulative effects of climate shocks, public health emergencies, such as cholera and malaria. Economic pressures deepened vulnerabilities and limited progress towards achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals and the realisation of rights and outcomes for children and other vulnerable populations.

Macroeconomy, Debt and External Financing
Economic conditions in 2025 in the aftermath of the El Nino-induced drought presented a mixed picture. Despite an estimated 6.6 per cent economic growth, driven by improved exchange rate stability and lower inflation (14 per cent), new tax measures kept the cost of living high for low-income households. Public debt rose from US$21.5B (2024) to US$23.4B (2025), limiting fiscal space for social services. 
Engagement in the Structured Dialogue on debt resolution and arrears clearance between the government and partners in 2025 paved the way for discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Advances were made towards macroeconomic stability, strengthening public finance management, and building confidence with international creditors, which are expected to culminate in a Staff-Monitored Programme (SMP) in 2026. A potential SMP is widely regarded as critical in resolving Zimbabwe’s debt challenge and restoring access to concessional financing from international financial institutions.
Social sector allocations reached 35.5 per cent of the national budget, up from 30.4 per cent in 2024, with 16.9 per cent allocated to education, 10.4 per cent to health, 7.4 per cent to social protection, and 1.2 per cent to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH). Continuing weaknesses in budget execution meant that less than half of social sector budgets were either disbursed or utilized, limiting tangible improvements in services for children.
Consistent with global trends, Official Development Assistance (ODA) to Zimbabwe fell from approximately US$500 million in 2024 to US$386 million in 2024, down 23 per cent. In addition to directly affecting the delivery of essential social services, reductions in ODA further resulted in a contracted footprint for United Nations entities in Zimbabwe, most notably with the withdrawal of OCHA and UNHCR, as well as a contraction in NGO operations. With the humanitarian reset, humanitarian coordination is progressively embedded in national systems led by the Department of Civil Protection (DCP).
Policy changes by donors created an abrupt, sector-significant shock impacting active and pipeline projects. In Zimbabwe, these disruptions primarily affected pregnant women during prenatal care, early infant diagnosis, paediatric HIV treatment services, diagnostics, and facility capacity. This shock coincided with the planned wind-down of the Health Resilience Fund (HRF) by June 2026, a US$ 90 million multi-donor pooled mechanism administered by UNICEF that has underpinned primary health-care delivery and systems strengthening since 2022.
 
Governance, Policy Environment and Civic Space
While important policy provisions and national strategies were concluded with regards to youth employment, sanitation and health, the passing of the Private Voluntary Organisations (PVO) Amendment Act, signed into law in April 2025, governing the registration, operations, and funding of NGOs resulted in shrinking civic space for CSOs, affecting service delivery to populations, particularly in rural areas. This was in addition to reduced operations emanating from funding losses from the exit of USAID and other donors.
The National Development Strategy 2 (NDS 2) 2026-2030 was approved reaffirming government’s commitment to human capital development, social protection, devolution, and climate resilience. NDS 2 aligns firmly with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and with explicit focus on children. Zimbabwe advanced regional priorities as SADC Chair, including climate resilience, food security, education, and migration.
