Zimbabwe's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 (2025–2035) was completed with the active engagement of children and youth.
 
Health and HIV: Mortality, Coverage and Equity
Newly published data from the 2023/24 Zimbabwe Demographic Health Survey (ZDHS) showed continuing negative trends for neonatal and infant mortality. Neonatal mortality rose from 29 to 37 deaths per 1,000 live births, while infant mortality increased from 50 to 56 deaths per 1,000 live births. These reversals placed renewed emphasis on quality of care at birth and early postnatal care. The rate of under-five mortality stagnated at 69 deaths per 1,000 live births. New maternal mortality estimates show a significant decline at 212 deaths per 100,000 live births from 651 per 100,000 in 2015. Despite this progress, maternal deaths remain high in rural areas and among adolescent mothers, reflecting persistent gaps in access to skilled care, emergency obstetric services, and health system coverage. 
National immunization performance remained relatively strong in 2025 with diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis DTP3 vaccine coverage estimated at around 95 per cent (DHIS2, 2025). However, inequities persisted, particularly among children in remote rural areas, high-density peri-urban settlements, and mobile populations, highlighting the need for more targeted activities to reach these vulnerable groups.  The number of zero-dose children declined from 10 to 8 per cent between 2015 and 2024 (ZDHS, 2024).
 
Despite achieving the 95-95-95 HIV targets nationally before recent funding cuts, Zimbabwe continues to face significant inequities among children and adolescents. ART coverage remains low at 54 per cent for children aged 10–14 years and 69 per cent for adolescents aged 10–19 years (National HIV Estimates, 2025). Although mother-to-child transmission has declined to 6 per cent and ART coverage among pregnant women has reached 96 per cent, persistent gaps reflect systemic barriers, including stigma, delayed disclosure, limited adolescent-friendly services, and weak transition from paediatric to adult care, particularly in rural areas. External funding shocks are disproportionately affecting prevention and outreach services, notably for adolescents. The intersection of HIV and HPV is an emerging concern, especially for adolescent girls and young women living with HIV who face higher risk of persistent HPV infection and early cervical cancer. Zimbabwe’s shift to a one-dose HPV vaccination schedule for girls aged 10–14 years has simplified delivery and improved efficiency, but coverage remains uneven and vulnerable to funding constraints. 
 
Nutrition: Diets, Stunting and Overweight
While efforts to address malnutrition enabled some improvements to children's diets, limited access to diverse and nutritious foods driven by inadequate food systems, food insecurity and ongoing economic stress experienced by households challenged further progress. The proportion of children aged 6–23 months receiving a minimum number of food groups per day increased to 27.3 per cent, surpassing the 20 per cent target. However, this leaves almost three-quarters of Zimbabwe’s children experiencing food poverty, including 25 per cent living in severe food poverty – consuming foods from just 2 or fewer groups daily, which is insufficient to meet their nutrient needs. Zimbabwe has the third highest prevalence of severe child food poverty in the Eastern and Southern Africa region. Exclusive breastfeeding rates have stagnated over the last 10 years, currently standing at 42 per cent. While undernutrition remains the major issue for children (with 27 per cent of Zimbabwe’s children stunted). Overweight is increasing rapidly, now surpassing the SDG target of <3 per cent for under-5’s (at 4.3 per cent). Adolescent nutrition outcomes show rising overweight with 16 per cent of overweight amongst adolescent girls and 3 per cent among adolescent boys, rising further with age.
 
Safe Access to Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene
Zimbabwe continues to face challenges in meeting the targets of SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), requiring sustained efforts to deliver climate-resilient, equitable, and child-sensitive WASH services. According to the ZDHS 2023/24, 72 per cent of the population had access to basic drinking water, 46 per cent to basic sanitation, and 29 per cent to basic hygiene services. Open defecation practices dropped from 21.7 to 17 per cent of the population between 2019 and 2024. Despite these gains, gaps such as weak financial sustainability, governance deficits, poorly maintained infrastructure, and lack of standards compromise access to WASH services, particularly in rural and informal urban areas. The Ministry of Health and Child Care (MoHCC) spearheaded the rollout of the Sanitation and Hygiene Policy alongside climate-responsive WASH planning. However, financial constraints and institutional challenges continued to limit sectoral progress. Recurrent floods, and drought exacerbate vulnerabilities, and left children exposed to various diseases, including cholera outbreaks. 
 
Education, Skills and Youth
In 2025, Zimbabwe officially launched the End Learning Poverty for All in Africa (ELPAf) Campaign. The event marked a significant milestone in the country’s commitment to foundational education. Net enrolment reached 85 per cent in primary and 49 per cent for secondary education, while 15 per cent of children aged 4 to 16 remained out of school, with rural areas, poor households and girls facing the most barriers to education. Climate shocks, food insecurity, and household poverty, further disrupted learning, particularly in drought-affected and flood-prone districts. The education system also faced considerable barriers to ensuring quality and equitable learning opportunities. The pass rates for basic education remained low. The pass rate for Grade 7 examinations was 48 per cent (43 per cent for boys and 54 per cent for girls) and 35 per cent for O-levels. According to preliminary results from the 2025 Zimbabwe Early Learning Assessment only respectively 72.5 per cent and 75 per cent of pupils achieved grade-appropriate level in Mathematics and English after completing Grade 2. 
 
Fewer than 50 per cent of secondary schools had access to internet connectivity, limiting the ability of students to acquire essential digital and 21st-century skills. Youth unemployment remained high, with 47.6 per cent of young people aged 15 to 24 classified as not in education, employment, or training (NEET), a figure that rose to 53.2 per cent among young women (QLFS Quarter 3, ZIMSTAT 2025). This disconnect from productive opportunities correlates with increasing risks of substance abuse, psychosocial distress, and other protection concerns. Despite their demographic significance, only 14.5 per cent of youth participated in decision-making processes affecting their lives, limiting their ability to influence governance and social accountability. 
 
Child Protection, Legal Identity, and Children on the Move
Zimbabwe advanced child protection, supported by key legislative and policy reforms such as the enactment of the Persons with Disabilities Act which strengthened the framework for the provision of inclusive services, improving protections for children with disabilities. Birth registration coverage improved to approximately 57 per cent of children under five. Zimbabwe’s hosting of the Migration Dialogue for Southern Africa (MIDSA) in Victoria Falls and the adoption of the Victoria Falls Declaration on Children on the Move highlighted the country’s growing regional commitment to addressing child-sensitive migration issues. This was particularly significant given the ongoing cross-border movement of children, including boys migrating from Mozambique and those transiting through border districts like Beitbridge. 
Economic stress, climate shocks, and health emergencies exacerbated vulnerabilities at the community level, heightening protection risks, whereas access to protection services remained inadequate. These challenges contributed to negative coping strategies, such as child labour, early marriage, and school dropouts, amongst others.

2.1 Overview: Sustaining progress despite significant shifts in the development 
landscape
In 2025, Zimbabwe’s delivery environment for children was shaped by sharp reductions in external financing, persistent fiscal pressures, and intensifying climate shocks. These dynamics increased risks to service continuity, particularly in health, nutrition, education and social protection, whilst accelerating the transition toward greater national responsibility and systems. Within this context, UNICEF focused on protecting core child outcomes while strengthening the systems to sustain results at scale.
 
UNICEF’s strategy centred on supporting national and sub-national systems to function reliably under constraint. This was operationalised through sustained engagement on policy reform, child-responsive public finance and regulatory standards, alongside targeted technical assistance to improve execution at service-delivery level. UNICEF supported Government efforts to safeguard social sector prioritisation within the national budget, whils recognising that weaknesses in budget execution continued to limit the translation of allocations into services.
 
At delivery level, UNICEF combined government-led district implementation with risk-informed humanitarian support, focusing on preserving critical services for children: quality of care at birth, routine immunisation, nutrition services, safe water and sanitation, and school-level functionality. This approach was vital in the response to the El Niño-related drought and disease outbreaks, where UNICEF supported integrated, multi-sectoral interventions sustaining essential services while reinforcing preparedness and resilience to reach 1.86 million children.
 
Across sectors, UNICEF prioritised execution quality and system strengthening for supply chains, frontline workforce capacity, information systems, and community engagement to reduce fragmentation and improve responsiveness. Digital tools, social and behaviour change platforms, and partnerships with civil society and the private sector were used to extend reach and sustain demand, especially for adolescents and other underserved groups.

Despite a significant contraction in programmable resources between 2024 and 2025, UNICEF  investments to delivery reached US$ 35 million. Resources were concentrated on governance and coordination, policy and legal reform, public financial management for children, decentralisation, and institutional and community-level capacity. This reflected a deliberate shift from short-term gap-filling toward reinforcing linkages between national policy, financing and frontline delivery, and across sectors at district level.
 
Through upstream engagement, UNICEF supported advancement of the National Youth Policy, social protection reforms, child protection legislation, and sanitation and hygiene standards, while contributing to education financing through the School Financing Policy currently under Cabinet consideration and strengthened advocacy for nutrition. These efforts were anchored by a Memorandum of Understanding with the Parliament of Zimbabwe, reinforcing legislative oversight and budget accountability for children. The Government’s US$480,000 contribution (in local currency) to MICS further demonstrated growing domestic ownership of child-focused data systems and marked a concrete advocacy gain for UNICEF.
 
At the same time, fragmented systems and slow approval and coordination processes continued to constrain the pace at which reforms could be implemented and scaled. The progressive transition of humanitarian coordination to nationally led structures heightened the importance of integrated humanitarian–development programming and strong sector leadership.
 
The Zimbabwe country office reduced its operational footprint and staffing structure by 24 per cent, to redirect focus to technical assistance, policy influence, and execution support. Efficiency measures helped protect delivery capacity while reinforcing fiduciary discipline. These adjustments enabled UNICEF to remain a credible, catalytic partner to Government in a year of significant external and internal transition.
 
2025 marked the penultimate year of the 2022–2026 country programme cycle, and the Country Programme Evaluation (underway) will support the office to identify and interrogate key drivers and enablers of success, sharpening strategic focus and improving impact at scale in an increasingly resource-constrained environment. It will also inform UNICEF’s on-going contributions to the United Nations Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF, 2022-2026) and the advancement of UNICEF’s Contribution to Africa’s Development Agendas in support of national development priorities and regional commitments under Agenda 2063 and Africa’s Agenda for Children 2040.

Major achievements and UNICEF contributions in 2025 can be identified in five intersectoral domains — reducing infant, child and maternal mortality; improving access to learning and learning outcomes; reducing child poverty; empowering adolescent girls; and strengthening climate resilience across sectors. 
 
2.2 Reducing infant, child and maternal mortality
Responding to rising neonatal mortality and funding disruptions affecting prevention and outreach services, UNICEF focused its 2025 support on strengthening quality of care at birth, safeguarding routine immunisation, and protecting last-mile child survival functions within the primary health-care system.
 
The planned wind-down of the Health Resilience Fund (HRF) by mid-2026 marks another transition in Zimbabwe’s health-financing landscape. With UNICEF acting as grant manager, the HRF (2022-2025), being funded by the European Union, the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) and Irish Aid, provided predictable pooled financing for primary health care, quality-of-care improvement, health security and systems strengthening, including critical equipment, digital investments, mentorship, maintenance and surveillance. Its conclusion heightens risks related to the financing of recurrent functions at primary healthcare (PHC) facility level, affecting newborn and maternal care particularly in rural and peri-urban settings. In response, UNICEF prioritised system consolidation, advocacy on domestic financing  and institutionalisation of HRF-supported gains by the Ministry of Health and Child Care (MoHCC). This included included a focus on Results-Based Financing (RBF) and Health Management Information System (HMIS), workforce and community engagement. 
 
Achievements in 2025. Under MoHCC leadership, PHC service readiness and quality improved at scale.

Quality at birth and emergency readiness improved at district and PHC levels. Thirty district hospitals were equipped for essential newborn care, and 512 health workers were mentored. By year-end, 97 per cent of facilities conducting deliveries had functional newborn resuscitation equipment, 85 per cent of PHC facilities provided all five BEmONC functions, and 83 per cent of designated EmONC facilities operated 24/7. These figures indicate a strengthening of emergency capability at the point of birth. 
Last-mile child survival capacity expanded. With funding from the Mastercard Foundation, a total of 22,601 Village Health Workers (VHWs) were trained in integrated community case management (iCCM), supporting more than 3.9 million child contacts. Ninety-five per cent of children aged 0–59 months with diarrhoea received ORS and zinc, signaling adherence to standard case management at community level. 
Immunisation remained resilient and shock-responsive. Funded by GAVI, the Vaccine Alliance, ninety-nine per cent of facilities maintained functional cold chain. National rounds reached 4.9 million children with polio vaccine (approximately 120 per cent coverage) and 1.7     million with measles–rubella (97.9 per cent). The single-dose HPV schedule was introduced using the Grade 5 platform, and 167,832 girls were vaccinated. 
Commodity financing and supply continuity were protected. UNICEF’s procurement of essential medicines (US$6.375 million) averted gaps while evidence-based advocacy supported Government procurement of US$35.1 million in essential health and nutrition commodities. This change represents a shift from donor substitution to national accountability. Support to RBF to 1,498 facilities, and budget execution at MoHCC improved to 92 per cent (from 88 per cent in 2024). 
Workforce and information systems were strengthened. UNICEF supported the creation of 14,069 health posts, pre-service training of 1,838 VHWs, upskilling of 4,697 VHWs, and enhancements to Community and District Health Information systems (CHIS)/ DHIS) underpinning 96 per cent HMIS. Reporting compliance improved supervision, micro-planning and course-correction. 
Community engagement and adolescent-responsive Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) expanded. Three national SBC strategies, co-created with MoHCC and youth networks, addressed HIV and SRHR, adolescent health and well-being, and non-communicable disease (NCD) prevention, with support from the Eli Lily and Company Foundation. Delivery through 20,000 community health workers across 63 districts reached more than three million people, supporting timely care-seeking and adherence.
UNICEF support targeted most-deprived locations, where the need for better quality and continuity of care were most acute, notably in district obstetric–newborn units, PHC sites in rural and peri-urban wards. Given constrained ODA, the focus on quality execution, domestic commodity financing and frontline capacity was a practical guard against external volatility.  

2.3 Access to learning and learning achievement
As UNICEF supported the implementation of the new heritage-based curriculum (HBC), execution reliability at school level, climate-related disruptions, and unequal access to digital learning, especially in rural and high-density peri-urban areas, constituted the key bottlenecks to learning achievement. With funding tightening, small operational interruptions — for example, power or water failures — risked cascading into losses of learning time, particularly for girls.
 
Achievements in 2025. UNICEF’s support to the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE) centred on policy, equity and foundational learning.

Policy and standards advanced. With UNICEF support, the School Financing Policy was finalised for Cabinet submission. The Teacher Professional Council Bill progressed to the Attorney-General’s office. The Zimbabwe Early Learning Development Standards (ZELDs) were     validated, and 1,066 teachers and inspectors were oriented, which clarified expectations and pedagogical benchmarks for early learning. 
Equity in disadvantaged schools was protected. Funded by the Global Programme for Education (GPE) and FCDO, School Improvement Grants (SIG) sustained 1,986 disadvantaged schools serving 624,753 learners (312,268 girls). WASH investments supplied safe water to 30 schools and mechanised systems to 3,403 learners in drought-affected areas. These measures preserved learning time and supported adolescent girls’ retention. 
Foundational learning and blended delivery strengthened the early grades. A total of 4,000 Teaching Handwriting, Reading and Spelling Skills (THRASS) kits reached 204,297 infant learners and 23,674 infant teachers. In addition, 510,000 storybooks were procured for early grades. ICT devices for 113 already solarised schools were readied for 2026 distribution for school-opening in January 2026 with first-use and maintenance manuals and a blended-learning handbook.  
Inclusion and girls’ participation in STEM improved. Statutory Instrument 13 (SI 13) on inclusive education was gazetted. The Cantoo Scribe assistive ed-tech pilot engaged more than 500 learners with 250 tablets. Gender-responsive STEM pedagogy training for 68 teachers supported 1,156 club learners (844 girls), and private-sector mobile laboratories added practical science capacity to targeted schools.
 Financing reforms were linked to execution and monitoring. Technical work on school financing and joint sector reviews promoted the importance of predictable cash disbursements (particularly of the Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM)) to disadvantaged schools,     where disbursement lags are having adverse effects on learning and retention. 

Decentralisation and stewardship reduced lifecycle costs. Community engagement and social accountability for solar investments reached 6,662 stakeholders, with 3,605 pre-engaged for Phase II districts. This engagement builds local ownership for asset care and minimises downtime for digital learning.
 
The pairing of SIG and WASH protected learning in drought affected schools with the least resources. The foundational learning package supports early-grade literacy for children most at risk of falling behind. Inclusive policy and pedagogy reduced structural barriers for learners with disabilities and for adolescent girls across the STEM pipeline.
 
2.4 Addressing Child Poverty through Social Protection and Child Protection Systems Strengthening
Achievements in 2025. UNICEF addressed child poverty by strengthening child-responsive public finance and social protection systems, focusing on scale, targeting, and system coherence. UNICEF’s upstream public finance engagement for children contributed to maintaining social sector allocations at 35.2 per cent of the national budget, while supporting all 92 local authorities to implement child-responsive plans and budgets that reflect the needs of the most vulnerable children. Through a multi-donor Social Protection Systems Strengthening Programme implemented with the World Bank and FCDO, and funded by Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG-ECHO) and Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA),  UNICEF supported completion of a national social protection system assessment, development of a simulation tool to guide evidence-based programme expansion, and preparation of an initial draft Social Protection Policy Framework. 

At programme level, UNICEF supported revisions to the Social Cash Transfer and BEAM manuals and initiated development of a national grievance redress mechanism, improving equity and accountability. Despite constraints linked to a ban on rural cash transfers, UNICEF supported a government-led urban cash transfer pilot in Chinhoyi, reaching 3,732 households (approximately 7,464 children), including children with disabilities, while generating operational lessons for future scale-up. These reforms were underpinned by UNICEF’s technical leadership on child poverty measurement, including support to ZDHS, MICS and the Household Budget Survey, ensuring both monetary and multidimensional child poverty data informs policy dialogue and budget decisions.
 
Complementing these reforms, with support from donors such as Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA) and Chinese International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA), UNICEF strengthened child protection systems, recognising violence, disability, lack of legal identity, and weak access to justice as key poverty multipliers. In 2025, UNICEF’s technical and advocacy support influenced five major child protection laws and policies, including enactment of the Persons with Disabilities Act, development of a Costed National Disability Policy Workplan, consultations on the Child Online Protection Policy, and renewed progress on the Child Justice Bill and Social Workers Act, strengthening the legal framework for protecting the poorest and most excluded children. 

At system level, UNICEF strengthened the National Case Management System and Victim-Friendly System in 14 districts, enabling 51,747 children who experienced violence to access coordinated health, social welfare, and justice services, while 99 per cent of children in conflict with the law were supported through diversion or non-custodial measures. UNICEF also expanded access to legal identity, supporting mobile and facility-based birth registration that reached 55,185 children, contributing to an increase in national under-five birth registration to 57 per cent. Together, these legal, institutional, and service-delivery results aimed to reduce key deprivations linked to child poverty and strengthened protection, inclusion, and resilience for the most vulnerable children. 
 
2.5 Empowering and enhancing services for adolescent girls
The ODA shock had its sharpest service-delivery effects where external funds historically financed prevention and community platforms. For adolescent girls, this meant disrupted SRH and HIV outreach, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) access, stigma-reduction and psychosocial support — even where diagnostic and treatment commodities stayed available. Without a pivot to sustainable, integrated models, incidence, drop-out and unmet need risk backsliding.
 
Achievements in 2025. UNICEF and partners worked at three levels.

Financing sustainability and policy coherence were strengthened. UNICEF supported the National HIV Sustainability Roadmap (2025–2030) and a rapid financing assessment with funding from the USAID Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA). Findings informed the Zimbabwe     National HIV & AIDS Strategic Plan (2026–2030) and Global Fund Cycle 8 application. With SIDA funding, technical assistance to the National Multisectoral Framework for the Prevention and Management of Adolescent Pregnancy (2025–2030) helped align actions across health, education, social protection and gender. 
Integrated, peer-led services were scaled. Utilising Regular Resources (7 per cent Set-Aside) for the reduction of HIV among Adolescent Girls, the Young Mentor Mothers (YMM) model placed 89 trained peers across 92 facilities in peri-urban and rural districts. A total of 2,463 adolescents were screened for HIV risk, mental health, intimate-partner violence and STIs, and 1,078 referrals were completed (an 88 per cent completion rate). HPV-Plus paired vaccination with SRH and GBV information and referral, which created a pragmatic entry point for adolescent girls who might otherwise not interact with services. 
Agency and pathways to opportunity expanded. A total of 26,747 adolescents engaged in civic and digital platforms under a Child & Youth Safeguarding Framework. In addition, 16,487 adolescents — including girls and refugees — gained digital, green and entrepreneurial     skills through public–private–youth partnerships (for example, the Ruwa Social Innovation Hub and the FairChance programme), with funding from KOICA, EU and GenU. The On My Mind series, co-created with adolescents, reached 81,207 young people, which improved mental-health literacy and referral.
By focusing adolescent programming around sustainability, integration, and peer leadership—spanning policy and financing upstream to service delivery at facility and community levels—UNICEF supported the continuity of services for adolescent girls most at risk of being left behind. The launch of the UNICEF adolescent girls programme further strengthened coherence and integration across sectors, leveraging private-sector partnerships to advance intersectoral strategies that accelerate equitable outcomes for adolescent girls in Zimbabwe.
 
2.6 Climate resilience across sectors
Climate variability placed stresses on access to and the provision of services, and fueled public health emergencies. Droughts and localised flooding affected water security, infection risk, malnutrition and learning time. With humanitarian leadership transitioning to national systems, risk-informed planning and service-continuity models became central to protecting child outcomes.
 
Achievements in 2025. UNICEF supported policy–delivery coherence across multiple levels.

Policy and standards were refined and implemented and refined. Dissemination of the National Sanitation and Hygiene Policy and development of a costed Sanitation and Hygiene Strategy     progressed. Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH-FIT) roadmaps and health care facility operations and maintenance tools strengthened accountability for facility WASH. Child-sensitive inputs were incorporated into NDC 3.0 and related climate planning instruments. 
Risk-informed district delivery was embedded. Under the KOICA Climate Action for the Last Mile (CALM) project (Chipinge, Mangwe, Beitbridge and Harare), district teams integrated climate risk into WASH plans. Drinking-Water Safety and Security Plans (DWSSP) were     cascaded to 23 Water Point User Committees. A total of 15 boreholes were rehabilitated,     and 7 solar-powered systems were installed, providing 22,478 people with reliable water. Twenty-three schools improved WASH and 8 health facilities were rehabilitated using WASH-FIT. A total of 106 technical staff were trained on mWater and WASH-FIT for data-driven operations and maintenance. 
Outbreak control and anticipatory action were advanced. During the 2025 cholera resurgence, with support of the Government of Japan, the Republic of Korea and pre-funding by the UNICEF Emergency Programme Fund, integrated WASH, RCCE and supply support reached more than 1.4 million people with hygiene promotion, delivered safe water to 134,284 people and essential WASH items to 85,426. Transmission was interrupted by June (cumulative 778 cases and a 2.9 per cent case-fatality rate). Subsequently, district teams pivoted to anticipatory ward-level risk management to reduce the probability of renewed surges. 
Children and youth contributed to climate literacy and policy inputs. Funded by the TUI Care Foundation, A total of 1,500 young people engaged in climate advocacy and experiential learning, including Pre-COP/ COP simulations and practical environmental clubs. These activities reinforced local stewardship and provided inputs to NDC 3.0.
 
By approaching climate risk as a factor directly impacting quality, consistency and efficient service-delivery, UNICEF ensured linkages between policy commitments, district practice, facility accountability, and community engagement, with SBC and youth engagement. In doing so, services in schools and health facilities were better able to withstand shocks.
 
2.7 Change strategies, accelerators and enablers
In 2025, the following change strategies, accelerators and enablers underpinned scale and sustainability across UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Areas.

Public finance for children (PF4C) was strengthened. UNICEF technical assistance and  engagement on PF4C with Parliament, the Ministry of Finance and sector ministries, influenced and enhanced the prioritization of children and adolescents in national budget dialogues, supporting an increase in the share of the national budget allocated to child-related sectors. The country office also advanced climate-responsive budgeting with the Ministry of Finance and Parliament (including advocacy through key parliamentary committees). The wind-down of the Health Resilience Fund reinforced the urgency for UNICEF’s engagement on PF4C to support absorption of priority health-system expenditure related to newborn and maternal care into domestic budgets. UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to Government procurement of essential medicines (US$35.1 million) and improved execution (92 per cent), and the provision of stipends for over 22,500 VHWs. These developments, which also include national investment of US$ 480,000 in MICS, supported continuity where external financing was retrenched. 
Workforce strengthening remained a core lever. Workforce strengthening remained a central change strategy for sustaining results at scale. By prioritising frontline capacity, UNICEF supported mentorship, equipment, and supervision for 512 clinicians, the creation of     14,069 health posts, pre-service training of 1,838 Village Health Workers, and the upskilling of 4,697 frontline personnel, helping to stabilise primary health care functionality and preserve the community–facility continuum amid significant fiscal pressures. Complementary investments strengthened the social service workforce, including the deployment of 20 community-based social workers, training of over 800 social workers and Community Child     Care Workers, and capacity building of nearly 600 justice sector actors, reinforcing case management, referral, diversion and follow-up for vulnerable children. In education, ZELDs orientation and gender-responsive pedagogy enhanced teacher capacity, supporting inclusive, quality foundational learning and improved participation of adolescent girls. 
Focus on decentralizing services and local governance secured delivery gains. UNICEF supported all 92 local governments to adopt child-responsive plans with equity and climate lenses. In child protection, decentralised social workers in 11 districts improved early identification and referral. The digitalization, computerization, and solarization of 20 decentralised registration offices addressed structural bottlenecks and improved service continuity. Mobile registration campaigns benefited 55,185 children, including 1,281 in hard-to-reach districts, while over 58,000 individuals, including caregivers and     children, participated in GBV prevention programmes. In WASH, DWSSP and water-point committees embedded routine operations and maintenance and cost-recovery practices.  
Community engagement and SBC were systematised. The office moved from episodic messaging to systems-based SBC. Three co-created strategies (HIV/SRHR, adolescent health and well-being, and NCDs), delivered via 20,000 CHWs across 63 districts, reached more than three million people. The adolescent-co-created On My Mind series reached 81,207 adolescents with MHPSS content and referral. 
Data, digital and innovation improved decision-making and inclusion. Strengthened CHIS/DHIS delivered 96 per cent HMIS reporting compliance. Evidence from ZDHS and ZIMLAC informed policy and targeting. The conclusion of MICS in 2026 will also strengthen policy     decision-making. The mWater and WASH-FIT tools improved facility and district performance management. Learning Passport and Giga coordination expanded inclusive digital options. The Innovation Portfolio matured youth-led, locally relevant solutions. 
Reduction and realignment of Programme Structure: After a marked contraction in flexible resources raised across the CPD period (from US$ 88 million in 2022 to US$ 23.5 million in 2025), adolescent health and HIV were integrated into the Health programme, and adolescent participation and skills were consolidated within the Education section. Other staffing reductions were commensurate with a refocus on technical assistance delivery and a realignment of the scope of programme support. The measures helped to protect delivery capacity while preserving a strong focus on national systems strengthening as the primary pathway to scale and sustainability. 
Supply and operations efficiency protected programme delivery. Operational efficiency was enhanced with the establishment of sixty-five long-term agreements, 86 per cent supply-plan implementation, US$1.06 million in VAT recovery, and office relocation. Establishing a     shared warehouse arrangement with WFP generated US$ 220,000 in savings. All staff were trained on internal controls and procedures, and assurance activities achieved 100 per cent completion, including peer reviews on travel and finance operations. 
Humanitarian action and resilience were integrated into national systems. Under the humanitarian reset, UNICEF supported nationally led coordination, anticipatory action, and integrated WASH–health–nutrition–education response, while maintaining AAP and PSEA     standards. 
El Nino Response: In 2025, UNICEF’s integrated El Niño response in Zimbabwe delivered measurable, multi-sectoral results. 1,893,403 children (6–59 months) were screened for wasting and 11,034 received treatment for severe acute malnutrition, while 626,513 caregivers received infant and young child feeding counselling. To reduce disease risk, UNICEF provided safe water to 134,284 people, distributed critical hygiene supplies to 85,426, and     reached 795,000 adults with cholera, hygiene, and nutrition messaging, contributing to elimination of cholera transmission (zero cases for 30 consecutive days). Preparedness and resilience were strengthened through a multi-hazard response plan, 96 per cent emergency preparedness score, 100 per cent compliance, pre-positioning of 1.26 million measles-rubella vaccine doses, and training of 1,176 health workers and 877 community volunteers for anticipatory action. 
Gender equality and disability inclusion were operationalised. The office completed a Gender Programmatic Review and met UN-System-wide Action Plan benchmarks. Inclusive education (SI 13) and disability-inclusive parenting and assistive referrals expanded practical     inclusion beyond policy statements.
 
2.8 Partnership and Resource Mobilisation in a constrained funding environment
In 2025, UNICEF played a leadership role as co-chair of the UNSDCF People Pillar, together with the Ministry of Public Service Labour and Social Welfare, providing technical coordination and guidance to enhance alignment of collective UN results on health, nutrition, education, social protection, and child protection with Zimbabwe’s National Development Strategy. 
 
UNICEF collaborated closely with UN agencies programmatically to strengthen national systems for children, including through the Joint UN Programme “2gether 4 SRHR” to expand adolescent-focused SRHR and HIV services, and joint work with WHO on immunisation policy review and the International Health Regulations Joint External Evaluation. UNICEF also partnered with WHO, WFP, FAO and UNHCR to finalise the National Action Plan on Child Wasting, and with UNDP, UN Women and UNFPA on MICS and ZDHS, strengthening evidence for child-focused policymaking. 
 
Since November 2025, UNICEF has partnered with UNDP, UN Women and UNFPA to implement the EU- and Switzerland-funded joint UN programme “Sustaining the Gains” to strengthen accountability for gender equality and women’s rights in Zimbabwe. UNICEF facilitated the development of an SDG Funded grant to support social protection which will be implemented alongside UNFPA. Regionally, UNICEF worked with IOM through MIDSA, contributing to the Victoria Falls Declaration on Children on the Move, and supported Government engagement with UN human rights treaty-body reporting processes. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF partnered with 32 NGOs and civil society organisations to extend reach and deliver specialised services for vulnerable children, particularly where government capacity was constrained. CSOs played a central role in child protection and GBV prevention, including disability-inclusive programming with ZPHCA, specialised protection support through Terre des Hommes, and community-based work on parenting, child-marriage prevention and social norm change. In WASH and climate-resilient programming, UNICEF worked with NGOs such as WHH, GOAL, Mercy Corps, International Medical Corps and Oxfam under the KOICA-funded CALM programme, as well as Action 24 and the Zimbabwe Sunshine Group to engage children and young people in climate action, reinforcing community engagement and accountability in hard-to-reach settings.
 
In 2025, UNICEF Zimbabwe’s country programme was supported by a mix of traditional, non-traditional and catalytic partners—including the European Union, FCDO, Ireland, GAVI -the Vaccine Alliance, SIDA, KOICA, DG-ECHO, Japan, BHA/USAID, the World Bank, SDC, KfW, CIDCA, Africa CDC, and private sector partners—sustaining life-saving health, nutrition, WASH, education and child protection results, including primary health care, polio and cholera response and through pooled mechanisms such as the HRF. 

In response to the sharp cuts in ODA, UNICEF, Zimbabwe adopted a diversified, partnership-driven resource mobilisation strategy in 2025 to broaden its financing base and reduce reliance on a narrow group of donors. This included expanded engagement with non-traditional public partners, notably a new partnership with the CIDCA, which provided US$2.3 million for Nutrition, WASH, and Child Protection.
 
The office also scaled engagement with the private sector and UNICEF National Committees, establishing five new private partnerships across tourism, and international philanthropy. These partnerships combined financial and non-financial contributions and were complemented by the launch of UNICEF, Zimbabwe’s first national digital fundraising page. Innovative local partnerships, such as with Wild Horizons, integrated programme delivery, child-sensitive standards in corporate community engagement, advocacy and joint fundraising to support climate-resilient schools while generating more flexible funding.
 
In parallel, UNICEF strengthened donor intelligence, proactive engagement, and tailored investment cases, supported by enhanced communications, including 360° virtual reality and targeted video content. Despite a challenging funding outlook, these adaptations enabled UNICEF to secure US$23.4 million in new contribution agreements in 2025, sustaining programme delivery in a constrained funding environment.
 
Catalytic resources, notably UNICEF Regular Resources and thematic funding, were used to de-risk reforms, pilot government-led cash transfers, strengthen social protection systems, and scale digital public goods, protecting core results for children while advancing resilience and systems transformation.
 
2.9 Adaptations to UNICEF support in 2026

Protect the RMNCAH service delivery. Addressing elevated neo-natal mortality, UNICEF will support consolidation of BEmONC and EmONC quality and domestic financing for essential commodities and the expansion of equity-focused outreach in peri-urban and hard-to-reach areas through integrated packages (immunisation, nutrition screening, IMCI and RCCE). 
Convert policy gains into learning outcomes. The country office will continue to support Cabinet passage and operationalisation of the school financing policy with a focus on     execution and monitoring, reinforce teacher support and local assessment for foundational skills, and extend community stewardship for solar and digital assets to protect uptime. 
Reinforcing positive outcomes for adolescent girls. Advocacy to fund and scale peer-led, integrated models (YMM and HPV-Plus) through domestic and potentially Global Fund resources, expand skills-to-earning pathways in high-risk districts (e.g., scaling the Ruwa Innovation Hub model with GenU support), and maintaining adolescent MHPSS literacy and referral as part of service packages. Further consolidation of the adolescence portfolio across Health and Education is anticipated to strengthen the connection between policy, financing and service-delivery outcomes, especially for girls. 
Scale climate-resilient delivery. UNICEF will support local authorities to replicate CALM approaches (risk-based district plans, DWSSP and mWater) in additional districts, expand WASH-FIT in schools and health-care facilities in outbreak and drought hotspots, and link to anticipatory action financing where feasible. 
Sustain PF4C and execution gains. Engagement with the Ministry of Finance and Parliament should continue to improve predictable disbursement and subnational execution. Shock-responsive social protection (for example, the social registry and grievance mechanisms) should be accelerated as fiscal space allows.
 
2.10 Strategic focus, risks and UNICEF added value in 2025
Focus on impact in a resource-constrained environment. The 2025 experience showed that population-level results depend on whether delivery systems function reliably. These systems include quality at birth, commodity execution, predictable school operations, routine data for decisions, and community engagement. 
Strategic risks. ODA volatility, macro-fiscal pressures on domestic budgets, and climate shocks remain the dominant risks. For child survival, the most sensitive risks are commodity financing and execution, community referral, and PHC workforce retention and supervision. For learning, the key risks are school-level financing reliability, water and energy, and teacher support. For adolescents, the critical risks are prevention platform continuity and the quality of peer-led models.
UNICEF’s distinctive value. In a difficult year, UNICEF’s added value lay in national systems strengthening. The organisation supported Government leadership with a disciplined mix of domestic financing support, frontline workforce development, decentralised planning and community engagement, data and digital public goods, and operational efficiency and assurance. The emphasis on execution and equity ensured that limited resources translated into measurable improvements in service delivery, continuity and effective coverage for children and adolescents.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In the fourth year of the 2022–2026 Country Programme, UNICEF continued to operate in a shifting policy, economic, and climate environment that tested systems, partnerships, and programme agility. Despite constraints, the year produced actionable insights on how to accelerate results at scale and strengthen equity outcomes, particularly for the most marginalized children.
 
Key Challenges
UNICEF’s analysis identifies four major challenges that had cross-cutting impact on service delivery, systems strengthening, and equity.
 
1. Systemic Capacity Gaps Limiting Speed and Scale
Across health, nutrition, education, child protection, and WASH, frontline systems struggled with workforce shortages, weak referral networks, limited infrastructure, periodic stockouts of essential commodities, and underdeveloped case management tools. These structural weaknesses constrained coverage, responsiveness, and scalability of interventions.
 
Fragmented systems and bureaucratic delays slowed policy adoption, weakened coordination, and reduced the ability of ministries to implement reforms at pace. These constraints limited the system’s ability to reach children at scale and respond to emerging needs.
 
2. Resource Constraints and Rising Household Vulnerability
Chronic underfunding, declining external support, and delayed budget disbursements restricted the expansion of essential services and innovations. Economic volatility, inflation, and rising household costs further reduced access, especially for marginalized families facing high transport expenses and indirect service fees.

Increasing household vulnerability contributed to negative coping mechanisms—school dropout, early pregnancy, and child labour—deepening existing inequalities.
 
3. Persistent Inequities and Hard-to-Reach Populations
Children in remote rural areas, informal settlements, and mobile/migrant communities, as well as adolescents and children with disabilities, remained disproportionately excluded from essential services. These inequities were amplified by residual COVID-19 impacts and recurrent climate shocks, which continued to disrupt immunization, nutrition, education, and protection outcomes.

Standard service delivery models were often insufficient to reach high-risk populations, requiring more precise targeting and context-specific approaches.
 
4. Weak Data Systems and Emerging Risks Outpacing System Readiness
Despite progress, monitoring systems remained fragmented. Paper-based tools, partial rollout of digital platforms, incomplete social registries, and weak feedback mechanisms constrained real-time decision-making, cross-sector coordination, and accountability.

At the same time, new risks—rapid urbanization, climate change, digital harms, adolescent substance abuse, and increasing social vulnerabilities—stretched the capacity of social systems not fully equipped for anticipatory, multi-sectoral responses.
 
Lessons Learned
 
Five key lessons cut across sectoral boundaries and shape future programming considerations.
 
1. Integrated and Adaptive Programming Accelerates Impact
District-level integrated packages—combining Health, Nutrition, WASH, Child Protection, Social Behaviour Change, and Social Policy—delivered better outcomes than siloed interventions. When programmes adapted intentionally to context changes (e.g., switching to outreach or decentralized procurement during disruptions), results improved significantly.
 
Youth-co-created solutions, such as peer-led SRHR initiatives and innovation hubs, demonstrated higher relevance and uptake, especially among adolescents. Engagement of traditional leaders enhanced local ownership and strengthened social accountability. UNICEF will seek to institutionalize adaptive planning and scale integrated district models as a core delivery approach, building flexibility into programme design, financing, and monitoring.
 
2. Precision Targeting Drives Better Equity Outcomes
Zero-dose immunization mapping, targeted outreach to high-burden districts, and adolescent-responsive service models showed that precision approaches—rather than broad, uniform expansion—yielded quicker and more substantial gains for the most underserved populations. UNICEF will deepen precision public health and equity targeting using disaggregated data, vulnerability profiling, and real-time monitoring tools to direct resources to where they are most needed.
 
3. Data Systems and Evidence-Based Advocacy Are Catalysts for Policy and Financing
Where digital systems such as eLMIS, HOPE MIS, and mWater were fully used, monitoring improved, bottlenecks were resolved faster, and policy discussions became more evidence-driven. Authoritative data (e.g., from ZDHS, MICS) and district vulnerability profiling analysis helped to elevate child rights issues with Parliament and ministries, contributing to policy progress in nutrition, social protection, and child protection. UNICEF will expand digital data platforms, strengthen interoperability across systems, and intensify evidence-based advocacy for timely public financing and systemic reforms.
 
4. Partnerships—Traditional and Non-Traditional—Are Critical for Scale
Cross-sector partnerships expanded reach and sustainability. Public–private and youth partnerships delivered stronger engagement of adolescents, improved digital access, and supported innovation. Experiences with private sector partners like Wild Horizons and Prospect Lithium Zimbabwe highlighted the value of non-financial contributions and the potential of modest catalytic funding to unlock larger investments.

UNICEF will seek to broaden its partnership ecosystem, refine value propositions, and pursue innovative financing models—including blended and pooled funding—to off-set declining public sector investment in children’s programmes.
 
5. Preparedness, Resilience, and Climate-Responsive Approaches Must Be Embedded in Systems
Responses to cholera outbreaks, drought, and acute malnutrition demonstrated that anticipatory action—pre-positioned supplies, rapid response teams, localized RCCE strategies—significantly reduced response times and improved effectiveness. Integrating climate-resilient WASH and education systems proved essential as shocks intensified. UNICEF will embed preparedness, climate resilience, and risk-informed programming across all sectors as core components of system strengthening.
 
Future Outlook
Drawing on 2025 insights, UNICEF 2026 priorities in Zimbabwe focus on consolidating gains, addressing persistent gaps, and preparing for the next Country Programme.
 
1. Strengthening Systems for Sustainability and Resilience
UNICEF will continue to invest in workforce capacity, supply chain stability, referral systems, shock-responsive models, and digital information systems, with a strong focus on maternal and neonatal health, immunization, adolescent health, and integrated outreach.
 
2. Scaling Integrated, Multi-Sectoral District Models
District-level integrated packages across Health, Nutrition, WASH, Education, Child Protection, and Social Policy will be expanded to increase efficiency and impact. Evidence and advocacy will support resource alignment and coherent provincial and district planning.
 
3. Expanding Partnerships and Innovative Financing
UNICEF will deepen engagement with Parliament, ministries, civil society, private sector entities, and international financing institutions. With donor resources becoming more constrained, UNICEF will pursue non-traditional partnerships and innovative financing to sustain essential services.
 
4. Advancing Digitalization, Data, and Accountability
Scaling real-time digital monitoring systems, community feedback mechanisms, and interoperable data systems will enable more precise targeting, faster decision-making, and stronger accountability across sectors.
 
5. Prioritizing Equity, Youth, and Gender
Targeted interventions will focus on marginalized children, including adolescents, the urban poor, remote rural communities, and children with disabilities. Youth engagement and gender-responsive approaches will be strengthened across all programmes.
 
6. Policy Influence for Sustainable Domestic Investments
UNICEF will leverage evidence to advocate timely budget releases, increased domestic financing, climate-smart social protection, and cross-sector reforms that reduce inequities and strengthen child rights systems.
 
Preparations are underway by UNICEF and the Government of Zimbabwe to develop a new Country Programme of Cooperation for 2027–2030 through a consultative, evidence-based process grounded in NDS2, national priorities, the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2026-2029), and a revised Situation Analysis. The next programme will support focused, scalable, sustainable, and equitable results for children, aligned with the UNSDCF and SDGs. Insights from 2025 will guide sharper targeting, stronger systems, and more resilient, innovative approaches to ensure no child is left behind.

Argentina is an upper-middle-income country, with gross national income per capita of USD13.440 (2024), ranked 47th out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index. Based on macroeconomic projections, Argentina could reach high-income country status between 2026 and 2028, depending on GDP growth, exchange rate dynamics, and Atlas method income thresholds.

Argentina transitioned into a period focused on structural reforms and fiscal adjustments. While the 2025 mid-term elections reinforced the government’s legislative position, decision-making continues to rely on dialogue and agreements with opposition parties and provincial authorities, consistent with the country’s federal structure.

Argentina’s economy was stagnant for more than a decade, with inflation emerging as a structural challenge. Between 2012 and 2023, the primary fiscal deficit averaged 2.7 per cent of GDP and the overall deficit 4.6 per cent. These imbalances contributed to sharp currency devaluations, leading to rising inflation and declining real household incomes. Since late 2023, the government implemented a fiscal consolidation programme of 5.5 GDP points over 2024–2025, resulting in a primary fiscal balance shift from a deficit of -2.8 per cent of GDP in 2023 to a projected surplus of 1.6 per cent in 2025 (IMF, 2025). This consolidation contributed to the deceleration of interannual inflation, expected to fall to about 30 per cent in 2025, and to a projected expansion of the economy, with GDP expected to grow by 4.6 per cent in 2025 (INDEC, BCRA and World Bank, 2025).

The first semester of 2025, 46.1 per cent of children lived in monetary poverty, showing an interannual decrease of 21 percentage points. Extreme poverty also fell from 27% in 2024 to 10% in 2025. The proportion of indebted households, conversely, grew by eight percentage points in the last year, rising to 31%. Food security remained a challenge: 29 per cent of households with children reported stopping purchases of certain food items due to income constraints and around 24 per cent stated they incurred debt to purchase food. 

In 2025, Argentina’s social protection system maintained broad coverage, reaching 95 per cent of children, although approximately 500,000 remained outside its scope. The purchasing power of non-contributory benefits increased to cover 98 per cent of the basic food basket, driven by slower inflation and the indexation formula applied to the Universal Child Allowance (AUH). This adjustment played a critical role in containing extreme poverty, which would have increased by 10 percentage points without cash transfers. In 2025, the design of the AUH for children aged 0 to 4 was strengthened by automating the verification of conditionalities, allowing the payment of the full child benefit. This reform is consistent with UNICEF’s long-standing recommendations emphasizing the reduction of administrative barriers, protection of the real value of benefits, and the effectiveness of income support for children.

Early childhood development (ECD) is a strategic priority, given its central role in reducing inequalities. The launch of the Federal Early Childhood Strategy (EFPI) in November 2025 represents a policy commitment to expand service access and improve quality. However, territorial and socioeconomic disparities persist, reflecting uneven availability across provinces and age groups. Addressing these gaps remains essential to ensure equitable early childhood outcomes nationwide.

Learning outcomes constitute one of Argentina’s most pressing challenges. While the National Plan for the Transformation of Secondary Education launched in 2025 aims to improve learning, life skills and school completion, last available data highlights the depth of the problem. In 2024, 42 per cent of final-year secondary students failed to achieve satisfactory language skills, and 86 per cent did not reach minimum proficiency in mathematics, underscoring the need for systemic improvements in educational quality.

Argentina continues to show progress in key child health indicators. Within this context, immunization remains a major challenge. Although average vaccination coverage recovered between 2023 and 2024, the recommended 90 per cent level was not achieved for any vaccine. Coverage averaged 82 per cent during the first year of life and declined to 62 per cent among children aged 1 to 5, exposing persistent gaps in preventive care. Health agenda increasingly addressed emerging issues, including adolescent mental health, as recent evidence shows that, in 2025, 11 per cent of adolescents displayed signs of depression and nearly one third experienced anxiety. 

Nutrition outcomes illustrate a complex and evolving challenge. Despite a robust regulatory framework—including legislation on healthy eating, breastfeeding promotion and the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes—implementation gaps persist. Latest data show that overweight and obesity have surpassed undernutrition as the predominant concern: in 2020, 9.4 per cent of children under five were overweight and 4.9 per cent obese, increasing to over 21 per cent and 20 per cent among children and adolescents aged 5 to 17. Poor dietary patterns continue to exacerbate nutritional risks, particularly among vulnerable populations.

Regarding children deprived of parental care, the most recent data indicate that approximately 6,400 children were placed with extended families, while 9,154 lived in residential care facilities. However, the absence of comprehensive, up-to-date and harmonized information at the federal level remains a significant challenge, limiting a full assessment of the magnitude and characteristics of children in alternative care across provinces. In this context, in 2025 the Ministry of Human Capital launched the Federal Programme for the Protection of Children and Adolescents, to strengthen the national child protection system and improve monitoring and evaluation of institutionalized children, a critical step toward safeguarding children’s rights.

In Argentina, the age of criminal responsibility is 16, and public debates continue around juvenile justice, including proposals to lower this threshold and increase penalties, alongside ongoing reflections on standards, safeguards, and potential reforms. In 2024, 4,119 children and adolescents were in conflict with the criminal law, of whom 865 were held in penal facilities—including 44 under the age of 16. 

 Argentina presents a complex yet dynamic context where macroeconomic stabilization and policy reforms coexist with structural challenges for children. Sustaining progress requires consolidating social protection, reducing territorial disparities, and strengthening evidence-based policies to ensure equitable outcomes for all children.

In 2025, UNICEF advanced an equity-focused strategy to safeguard children’s rights amid economic volatility and fiscal constraints, focusing on strengthening the social protection system, child-sensitive public finance, and subnational governance. This positioning helped keep children’s rights on the policy agenda despite fiscal consolidation. Building on this foundation, UNICEF anchored policy dialogue in robust evidence, reinforcing the importance of child poverty reduction and income protection in public decision-making. This approach supported more informed choices, encouraged coordinated action across levels of government, and consolidated national priorities for children.

In social protection, UNICEF helped sustain the prioritization of income transfers for households with children by providing decision-makers with rigorous evidence on child poverty trends and programme performance. This included strengthening the measurement and monitoring frameworks that inform policy decisions—such as provincial multidimensional analyses and Child-Care Baskets that estimate the real cost of raising children. This evidence-based advocacy reinforced the relevance of key income-protection programmes, supporting benefit adjustments and expanded coverage for adolescents in vulnerable households, especially those headed by women, to make social protection more responsive and equitable.

At the subnational level, the Municipalities United for Children and Adolescents (MUNA) initiative expanded to 160 municipalities, with potential to reach 5.4 million children and adolescents. Beyond scale, as the 2025 external evaluation of MUNA concluded, the initiative strengthened local governance for children institutionalizing intersectoral planning, monitoring, and accountability mechanisms with disability-inclusive training rolled out in about 25% of municipalities to embed inclusion in local systems. Evaluation findings and consolidated lessons enabled efficiency gains and informed a more cost-effective model, strengthening foundations for accelerated national scale-up.

Across the 2021–2025 cycle, consolidated in 2025, UNICEF played a key role in institutionalizing Public Finance for Children (PF4C). Efforts focused on improving the continuity and quality of official data on child-related spending at national and consolidated public sector levels, while progressively extending budget analysis and transparency models to provincial and local governments. In Argentina’s federal system, provinces finance two-thirds of child investment and execute 70% of spending, while the national government contributes the remaining third and coordinates policies to promote territorial equity. Compared to the start of the cycle, these actions significantly expanded PF4C beyond the national level, strengthening fiscal dialogue, transparency, and accountability for children’s rights—even amid fiscal consolidation. Notable advances included integrating budget tagging into the budget cycle in Entre Ríos province and partial progress in Santa Fe, Chaco, and Chubut, with further expansion anticipated in 2026.

At the same time, UNICEF invested in community-level responses to address immediate needs—linking systemic improvements with practical solutions for children in marginalized contexts. At the territorial level, UNICEF’s engagement strengthened community-based responses and improved access to social protection and related services for children in highly vulnerable contexts, including informal settlements, rural and indigenous communities and children with disabilities. Through partnerships with grassroots organizations, initiatives expanded health, nutrition, and livelihood support in highly isolated communities lacking basic services, reaching 25 rural areas facing deep structural inequities.  

Finally, building on consolidated results in local governance, social policy, and collaboration with the Ministry of Finance—particularly on PF4C and budget tagging—UNICEF leveraged its technical expertise to demonstrate scalability beyond Argentina. In 2025, support to UNICEF Panama produced strategic tools on social policy, costing, and public finance, strengthening that office’s capacity for high-level policy dialogue and advancing regional efforts to embed children’s rights in fiscal planning.

Early childhood development (ECD) remained a strategic priority for reducing inequalities and shaping lifelong outcomes in health, learning, and protection. In 2025, UNICEF worked with national and provincial governments, municipalities, and communities to institutionalize policy frameworks and scale programs that expand access to quality services, addressing social and territorial disparities. These efforts sustained progress despite fiscal constraints and persistent gaps in services for young children.

At the national level, UNICEF contributed to the design of the Federal Early Childhood Strategy, launched in November 2025—a major policy commitment informed by lessons from subnational work. Evidence and models developed through support to provincial and municipal governments in planning, coordination, and service delivery shaped the strategy’s design. These experiences will also guide its implementation in 2026, contributing to national commitments that build on proven approaches.

In priority provinces, UNICEF supported five governments in advancing comprehensive ECD plans through intersectoral platforms that foster coordination among ministries for better planning, resource allocation, and monitoring of results. At the municipal level, more than 70 local governments strengthened service delivery, and oversight capacity through MUNA’s structured cycle, embedding early childhood priorities within broader social policies.

Building on these governance advances, subnational authorities strengthened ECD services through innovative delivery models and large-scale capacity-building initiatives supported by UNICEF. In 2025, over 36,000 educators, health workers, community promoters, and caregivers across 10 provinces—including rural and indigenous areas—completed professional certification training to enhance ECD service quality for young children and their families. 

UNICEF also supported the Province of Salta in designing and implementing a positive parenting pilot programee positioned to inform provincial and national decision-making. Through targeted technical assistance, advocacy and impact measurement, the pilot established a scalable model that can be integrated into the EFPI and adapted across diverse contexts. Implemented with nine municipalities and backed by a university-certified training program co-developed with the Salta Early Childhood Secretariat and UPATECO, the initiative created a coordinated platform for strengthening families and generated evidence that will guide the expansion of positive parenting policies in other provinces. 

On child nutrition, UNICEF addressed persistent implementation gaps in Argentina’s regulatory framework—and urgent need given rising overweight and obesity among children—by supporting practical, locally driven measures to create healthier food environments. Fifty-four municipalities adopted standards for healthier food provision in ECD centers and schools, helping improve diets and reduce risk factors. Breastfeeding protection advanced through a digital system to monitor Code violations, breastfeeding-friendly health facility certifications in Jujuy, and updated complementary-feeding guidelines in Santa Fe. 

Adolescence is a critical stage for realizing rights and shaping future opportunities, yet many young people in Argentina face barriers such as limited learning and skills development, mental health challenges, insufficient access to reliable information, and exposure to violence. To contribute to national and subnational efforts to address these gaps, UNICEF implemented a comprehensive strategy to expand opportunities and improve adolescents’ wellbeing. The approach strengthened education systems to boost learning and skills, enhanced health services to address mental health needs, and reinforced protection mechanisms to ensure safety and access to accurate information. Evidence-based advocacy supported the scale-up of local innovations into national policies, while platforms for adolescent participation amplified young people’s voices in decision-making. These actions were underpinned by data-driven analysis and strategic partnerships—with the National Secretariat of Education, provincial education ministries, national and provincial health authorities, universities, civil society, and UN agencies such as UNESCO and ILO—which informed policy improvements, strengthened programmes, and advanced equitable opportunities for adolescents’ active citizenship and future employability.

Education transformation remained central to UNICEF’s adolescent strategy, with a strong focus on adolescent girls. In 2025, UNICEF supported seven provinces in scaling proven secondary education innovations—such as Technology-based Rural Schools and PLANEA program which strengthens teachers’ and principals’ capacities in project-based learning and computer sciences, to improve learning outcomes and skills development -benefiting over 33,000 students and informing the new federal policy on the Transformation of Secondary School. In parallel, policy dialogue through the Education Ministers’ Forum helped 9 provinces advance secondary education reforms. UNICEF also contributed to the design of the National Plan to improve Math learning outcomes and supported adolescent literacy strategies through the joint UNICEF-UNESCO Uruguay-Argentina Experts and Authorities Network initiative. 

To tackle exclusion and improve school-to-work transitions, UNICEF strengthened Generacion Unica —a multisectoral public–private partnership—implemented with key multilateral partners, including UNESCO, ILO, IDB and the World Bank. The initiative combines advocacy, evidence generation, and adolescent engagement, with a strong focus on adolescents’ girls. Its Unique Opportunities digital platform -an innovation model designed to expand learning and employability options- offered through various governmental platforms provides  free certified courses, digital and life-skills training, supporting 14,600 young people aged 15-24 in 2025.  

Through the MUNA initiative, UNICEF supported 55 municipalities to institutionalize inclusion strategies that reconnect out-of-school adolescents. The work combined diagnostics to identify exclusion patterns, tailored action plans to re-engage youth, and local data systems that inform provincial education policies. By applying MUNA’s structured cycle of technical assistance, training, and peer learning, UNICEF helped municipalities scale effective approaches to bring vulnerable adolescents back into education pathways.

In parallel, UNICEF worked with national and subnational authorities to elevate adolescent health and mental wellbeing on the public agenda, while supporting interventions to address persistent service gaps. A key innovation was the Listening Centers model —safe, community-based spaces, in schools and youth centres, where trained peer listeners provide emotional support and early detection of psychosocial distress, supervised by mental health professionals and linked to referral pathways. In 2025, the model expanded to 14 active centres, with four more under development across four priority provinces, reaching 238,663 adolescents (118,471 girls and 120,192 boys).  

UNICEF worked with the health ministries of Chaco, Salta and Misiones to position perinatal mental health as a priority and to advance the implementation of a Perinatal Mental Health programme in nine maternity clinics. This collaboration strengthened early identification, prevention and follow-up of perinatal mental health conditions among pregnant and postpartum women—particularly adolescents—in provinces with extensive rural areas, hard-to-reach communities and significant Indigenous populations. Through technical guidance, capacity development and evidence-based tools, UNICEF supported provincial teams in adapting the model to local realities and improving access to quality care for women facing the greatest barriers.

Alongside these system-level advances, UNICEF broadened its adolescent agenda to ensure young people’s voices and leadership inform decisions that affect their lives. In 2025, UNICEF’s work focused on strengthening adolescent autonomy and leadership through partnerships with local governments and youth-led organizations. Across MUNA municipalities, locally driven youth spaces enabled more than 407,000 adolescents to participate in decision-making and propose solutions on issues such as online gambling, learning, and access to employment. To further promote agency—particularly among girls—UNICEF collaborated with youth organizations to amplify advocacy and civic engagement. At the national level, the Adolescent Council (CAU) contributed insights that helped shape UNICEF’s new Country Programme, ensuring approaches remain participatory and aligned with priorities defined by adolescents themselves.

Protecting children’s rights and preventing violence remained urgent priorities in 2025, as fragmented capacities across provinces underscored systemic challenges. UNICEF responded by helping strengthen Argentina’s child protection system through justice reforms, local capacity building, and national policy development—advancing coordinated, rights-based approaches nationwide. 

At the national level, UNICEF contributed to the design of the Federal Program for the Protection of Children and Adolescents with the Undersecretariat for Family Strengthening (SENAF)—a landmark initiative approved by the Federal Council on November 5. The program establishes a unified framework to guide provincial systems and harmonize standards, laying the foundation for coordinated, rights-based child protection across Argentina’s federal structure.

In parallel, and building on long-standing engagement, UNICEF supported systemic reforms in the justice sector with national and provincial authorities to reinforce capacities and strengthen accountability. Throughout 2025, UNICEF continued working with the Network of Judges Committed to the Rights of Children, to promote new agreements that improved judicial responses through more consistent application of child-rights standards, and contributed to the VIII Meeting of the Network of Judges and Judges committed to children’s rights (Buenos Aires, 15–16 October 2025)—a federal gathering that advanced shared practices and commitments across jurisdictions

Buenos Aires Province, with Argentina’s largest population of children and adolescents, is essential for advancing juvenile justice reforms with potential for nationwide replication. UNICEF supported the province’s efforts by providing technical assistance for an integrated approach that combines prevention and restorative practices; the Entramados program mobilized 28 municipalities that offered alternatives to deprivation of liberty and restorative justice for adolescents in conflict with the law. These actions were complemented by systematizing local experiences, publishing official statistics, and strengthening REUNA—a unified case registry now active in 135 municipalities—providing reliable data for policy evaluation and public debate on Juvenile Justice.

At the policy level, UNICEF provided up-to-date evidence, expert review, and comparative international experience to inform debates on juvenile justice in the National Congress, and jointly produced a data report with the Supreme Court of Buenos Aires Province to enrich the discussion. These resources—including the report—draw on the latest global estimates of children deprived of liberty and UN guidance that prioritizes diversion and non-custodial measures with detention strictly as a last resort, and are intended to support alignment with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and related international human rights standards and recommendations.

At the local level, UNICEF strengthened child protection across Argentina by supporting provinces and municipalities to translate national standards into practical, coordinated action. Through the MUNA initiative, UNICEF helped local governments improve early detection and response to violence, expand access to protection services, and reinforce intersectoral coordination among social, health, education and justice actors. This work enabled municipalities—including rural and underserved areas—to establish or enhance local protection structures, implement comprehensive plans, and adopt rights-based approaches that reduce territorial disparities. Together, these efforts have positioned MUNA as a driver of innovation and municipal leadership, contributing to a more integrated and effective child protection system within Argentina’s federal framework.

While driving systemic reforms, UNICEF also supported government-led responses to emergencies that threatened children’s rights, ensuring continuity of essential services and protection during floods and water shortages. In 2025, UNICEF worked with local authorities in high-poverty areas of Salta and Chaco—where early childhood strategies are also underway—to address severe water scarcity and poor water quality. UNICEF provided WASH supplies -reaching 11,790 children and 9,432 adults- and promoted hygiene practices to safeguard young children’s health while longer-term solutions were developed. Later in the year, floods in Salta, Chaco, and Bahía Blanca disrupted services for children. UNICEF partnered with municipal and provincial governments to restore access to safe water, maintain education continuity, and deliver mental health support—reaching more than 21,000 children. These actions reaffirm UNICEF’s commitment to strengthening systems and supporting government-led emergency responses.

Mobilizing society is essential to making children’s rights a shared national priority. Policies alone cannot drive lasting change; it requires broad engagement from citizens, the private sector, media, and influencers to sustain collective action to protect every child. In 2025, UNICEF leveraged its convening power to turn commitment into action.
