Marking its 40th anniversary in Argentina—and in the context of an electoral year—UNICEF placed children’s rights at the center of national debate. High-level events, including at the Buenos Aires Legislature convened government leaders, civil society organizations, private sector representatives, and cultural figures. A public photo exhibition at Palacio Libertad, further elevated visibility around persistent child-rights challenges and UNICEF’s contribution to addressing them.

Strategic alliances with 180 media outlets, combined with a digital community of 1.85 million followers and 97% positive media coverage, strengthened UNICEF’s ability to shape public agendas. Argentina’s shift toward a more federal governance model—marked by decentralization and the transfer of responsibilities to provinces and municipalities—has reshaped how policies are designed, financed, and implemented. Under this context, delivering results in the current Country Programme while planning the next cycle, required balancing continuity with innovation amid uneven institutional capacities, greater coordination demands, and persistent fiscal constraints. Gaps in the quality and comparability of administrative data further underscored the need to strengthen evidence systems. These dynamics highlighted the value of early and continuous subnational engagement, effective coordination platforms, scalable capacity-building models, and agile operational arrangements to sustain impact in a rapidly evolving environment. These lessons were reinforced by two major evaluations in 2025—the Country Programme review and the assessment of the MUNA initiative—which provided clear direction for more effective implementation. Both evaluations emphasized that achieving impact at scale in a federal context requires earlier and more systematic engagement with provinces and municipalities; policy dialogue grounded in accessible evidence; and practical collaboration with subnational actors throughout design, implementation, and monitoring. They also reaffirmed UNICEF’s value as a trusted partner, rooted in its ability to provide reliable data, actionable analysis, and consistent technical support that help government counterparts address operational challenges while advancing policy commitments for children and adolescents. 

Building on these findings, UNICEF also prioritized closing information gaps to sustain evidence-based dialogue. Official data on children’s rights were regularly updated, and where gaps persisted, UNICEF produced high-quality data through targeted studies, including Kids Online and the Rapid Survey on Households with Children. These efforts ensured that decision-making at national and subnational levels remained grounded in robust and timely evidence.
UNICEF further adapted its approach to significant changes in the division of responsibilities between national and provincial authorities, including the introduction of a new federal strategy for Early Childhood Development (ECD) and the transfer of key functions to provinces.

To maintain continuity and strengthen collaboration under this new framework, the office applied flexible planning, provided targeted technical assistance where it added the most value, and used evidence from previous interventions to inform policy decisions. UNICEF was invited to working tables and provided input that helped shape the strategy’s content and implementation focus. This experience showed that national policy changes work best when engagement begins early, evidence is clear, and collaboration with provinces is structured to translate plans into consistent, quality services for children.

In child protection, decentralization created new demands for stronger local systems, clearer roles, and more effective coordination. UNICEF supported the design of the Federal Programme for the Protection of Children and Adolescents—endorsed by the Federal Council—as a unified framework to harmonize standards and strengthen provincial systems. Building on this foundation, the office advanced strategies such as evidence-based monitoring, intersectoral coordination, and scalable capacity-building models adaptable to diverse contexts. These approaches are essential to improving efficiency and impact across jurisdictions while safeguarding provincial leadership and ownership.

Consistent with the emphasis on subnational engagement and evidence-informed collaboration, UNICEF also advanced youth participation toward active leadership in policy dialogue and programme design. Through platforms such as Generación Única and provincial youth councils, adolescents helped shape strategies in education and mental health, ensuring interventions reflected their living realities. UNICEF further moved toward more institutionalized mechanisms for participation, integrating youth inputs into planning cycles and monitoring frameworks in areas including secondary education, adolescent mental health, and safer digital environments. The country programme evaluation encouraged continued innovation to deepen adolescent participation and embed their contribution more systematically across the programme.
 
Strategic communication and public engagement remained central to advancing children’s rights in 2025. Building on the visibility generated throughout the anniversary year, UNICEF strengthened its role as a convener of multisector dialogue—bringing government, the private sector, civil society, academia and young people into evidence-based conversations on the issues that most affect children. Partnerships with leading media actors expanded the reach of child-rights messaging and promoted more inclusive public debate, particularly through formats that positioned adolescents as credible voices in policy discussions. These experiences highlighted the importance of accessible, timely information and demonstrated how strategic communication can help keep children’s perspectives at the forefront of national decision-making processes.

Despite economic challenges, resource mobilization remained resilient, driven by diversified channels and strengthened long-term relationships with individual supporters and corporate partners. The approach emphasized trust, measurable results and transparent reporting. This experience highlighted the importance of aligning fundraising narratives with demonstrated outcomes and maintaining agility to redirect support as needs and policy contexts evolve. Looking ahead, efficiency, innovation and predictability will remain priorities to safeguard and scale results for children.

Experience in 2025 confirmed several enablers of success in a federal context: early and continuous subnational engagement; coordination platforms that harmonize standards while allowing local innovation; and scalable capacity-building models to address uneven institutional capacity. Equally critical was to strengthen accountability and agile operations that optimize resources amid economic constraints. Evidence generation and strategic partnerships enabled innovation, supporting both the piloting of new approaches and scaling of proven solutions. Together, these elements form a solid foundation for sustained impact for children.

Building on these insights, UNICEF will deepen collaboration with national and provincial authorities, strengthen systems, and expand partnerships to deliver solutions that work across Argentina’s diverse federal landscape. In 2026, guided by the Country Program Evaluation findings, the office will place greater emphasis on prioritization to maximize impact and improve data comparability and timeliness. The next cooperation cycle will focus on four strategic areas: health and nutrition, with emphasis  ECD, maternal and child health, and mental health; education, ensuring equitable learning and skills for life and work; protection from violence, through stronger child protection systems and prevention; and social inclusion and poverty reduction, through improved governance, budgeting, and planning for child-focused policies and services. 

By leveraging evidence-driven collaboration, innovation, and strategic partnerships, UNICEF will deliver differentiated solutions that scale across Argentina’s federal context—ensuring relevance and delivering efficient and measurable improvements in children’s wellbeing.

Economic and Social Situation of the Eastern Caribbean
In 2025, the socio-economic and political context across the Eastern Caribbean Area (ECA) was shaped by the structural vulnerabilities characteristic of Small Island Developing States (SIDS) such as heightened exposure to external shocks, intensifying climate risk, elevated public debt, and high youth unemployment. In addition, persistent child poverty and food insecurity have widened equity gaps, with ageing populations leading to shrinking labour forces and heightened pension and health-care burdens.
Trinidad and Tobago experienced the continued arrival of Venezuelan migrants - estimated at around 26,000 including some 6,100 children (UNHCR, July 2025), many of whom cannot attend school nor receive support from the social protection system. 
Regional entities like the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) and the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States (OECS) remain crucial for policy harmonization, resilience, and disaster response. However, varying levels of implementation capacity and repeated hazards, such as Hurricane Beryl in 2024 and Hurricane Melissa, drought and flooding in 2025 - have slowed progress and diverted public resources towards the emergency response, further delaying structural reforms. 
Exposure to violence, both within families and communities, remains an alarming trend. Violent discipline rates affect between 60 and 88 per cent of children across the subregion. Rising firearm incidents have created additional risks, particularly for adolescents, signaling broader systemic challenges to social cohesion. 
In 2025, peaceful and competitive general elections were held in Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Trinidad and Tobago and the Turks and Caicos Islands. Newly elected administrations signaled continuity in social policies, while emphasizing digital governance and public-sector reform, presenting an opportunity for UNICEF ECA to deepen systems-strengthening support.
Situation of Children in the Eastern Caribbean Area
Children across the Eastern Caribbean continue to face overlapping challenges in education, protection, mental health, and resilience to climate and economic shocks. Education disparities remain significant, and in some cases have widened. The OECS Education Statistical Digest (2022-2023)[1] reported that only 39 per cent of early childhood teachers are formally trained - far lower than at the primary and secondary levels with 71 per cent and 57 per cent, respectively. Pre-primary, primary and secondary enrollment remained steady across the ECA (OECS Education Digest, Barbados Education Annual Report). Learning disparities persisted, including a gender gap at secondary level, where higher repetition and dropout rates among boys were evident in Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Continued learning losses emerging from the pandemic, uneven access to digital learning, and gaps in foundational skills point to the need for sustained educational transformation. UNICEF has continued efforts in learning-loss interventions, particularly when compounded by hurricane impact. Post-Hurricane Beryl projects have sought to retrain teachers, reopen schools, and supply educational resources. UNICEF’s technical and evidence-based assistance remains focused on system-wide reform, including gender-responsive learning support, improved teacher training, and stronger retention strategies: core areas where it provides technical guidance.
Youth mental health issues continue to be of concern. The 2025 UNICEF/CARICOM Caribbean Child and Youth Mental Health Research Study[2] found that nearly one-third of adolescents reported frequent thoughts of self-harm. High levels of anxiety, depression and social isolation underscored the urgent need for multi-sectoral mental health and psychosocial support systems, early identification and referral mechanisms, and youth-centred support services. UNICEF continued to assist governments in expanding mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, promoting counselling in schools, and building youth support networks. 
Protection risks remain. A 2024 regional survey showed stagnant or declining support for banning corporal punishment, particularly in the home, and revealed limited public understanding of non-traditional forms of child sexual abuse[3]. One in four respondents reported knowing at least one actual case of such abuse. Public awareness of grooming, cyberbullying, and online exploitation was low, underscoring the need for comprehensive child protection approaches and stronger reporting and response mechanisms. Underreporting - driven by stigma, fear of retaliation, and limited institutional trust - continued to hinder the effectiveness of child protection systems. UNICEF ECA intensified efforts on prevention, legislative reform, institutional strengthening, child-friendly justice, and community-level prevention and outreach, also supporting an assessment of child protection institutions in Dominica and community violence prevention activities in Trinidad and Tobago. 
Climate-related vulnerabilities have continued to threaten children’s rights and services. In 2025, governments advanced key adaptation commitments, including Antigua and Barbuda’s updated National Adaptation Plan (NAP), and Barbados’s Second Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). Recovery is still ongoing following Hurricane Beryl in 2024, particularly in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Recurrent shocks strained education, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, and social protection systems, reinforcing the urgency of child-sensitive disaster preparedness, resilient infrastructure, and integrated shock-responsive social protection.
Social protection systems remained critical but under-resourced. In 2025, several countries made progress with key reforms. Saint Kitts and Nevis updated its National Social Protection Policy and Action Plan for 2025-2030; Grenada initiated a comprehensive review of its legislation and delivery systems; and Barbados enacted the Social Empowerment Agency Bill, which established a new institutional framework for social services. Despite this progress, data systems remain weak and beneficiary registries incomplete; financing is insufficient for scalable, shock-responsive systems. UNICEF continued to support governments integrating administrative data, strengthening case management, and advancing social protection as a climate-resilience instrument.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Regional Trends
Across the Eastern Caribbean, countries and territories faced a shared landscape of climate vulnerability, economic fragility, and institutional constraints that slowed the achievement of the SDGs. 
Progress on SDG 1 (No Poverty) has been hindered by recurrent climate-driven disasters, economic shocks, and limited fiscal space, which deepen deprivation among rural communities, women, youth, migrants, and people with disabilities. Trinidad and Tobago reflects these patterns, with persistent child poverty (with 41.6 per cent multidimensional child poverty), but has expanded social spending, including nearly US$930 million for poverty eradication and strengthened social protection systems. Challenges relating to SDG 4 (Quality Education) are widespread, including weak foundational learning, teacher shortages, digital gaps, and gender disparities. Trinidad and Tobago shows similar learning deficits, with 44 per cent of students scoring below 50 per cent in the 2025 Secondary Entrance Assessment. Education reforms aim to address inequity, remedial needs, and curriculum weaknesses. 
SDG 13 (Climate Action) remains constrained regionally by limited adaptation, finance, fragmented institutions, and dependence on climate-sensitive sectors. Trinidad and Tobago faces intensifying hazards - flooding, sea level rise, extreme heat, and Sargassum seaweed, for example - but demonstrates progress through an enhanced NDC, its first Biennial Transparency Report, a 100 MW solar farm, expanded early warning systems, and coastal resilience initiatives. Finally, SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions) is challenged regionally by gun violence, youth crime, governance gaps, and weak data systems. Trinidad and Tobago faces one of the hemisphere’s most severe security crises, with homicide rates above 45 per 100,000, but is pursuing governance reform, justice sector improvements, and gender responsive violence prevention strategies.
Overall, while each country demonstrates pockets of advancement, the region collectively faces shared structural vulnerabilities, chronic data gaps, fiscal constraints, and deepening climate impacts, resulting in uneven and fragile SDG progress.

Goal Area 2: Education
Education remained a central pillar of UNICEF ECA’s work in 2025 which supported governments to strengthen education systems, advancing resilience, inclusion, and equitable learning opportunities from early childhood into adolescence. UNICEF also supported regional learning and policy dialogue through engagement in the 2025 CSSI Ministerial Conference. To promote safer and more supportive school environments, UNICEF expanded the I Support My Friends peer-support Psychological First Aid programme, training 93 facilitators across Barbados, Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Trinidad and Tobago. Joint Programmes continued to deliver integrated resilience and education outcomes. In Barbados, the Infrastructure for Resilient Island States (IRiS) Joint Programme strengthened eight pilot schools through hazard and vulnerability assessments, provision of essential safety equipment, and EiE training, complemented by youth engagement in national climate and resilience consultations. More than 100 young people contributed to these consultations, while six communication products strengthened national awareness and informed policy dialogue. Through the SDG Joint Programme on Green and Renewable Energy Transition, UNICEF and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) advanced youth green skills and supported renewable energy readiness in schools in Barbados.
Through its engagement with the OECS Commission, UNICEF supported regional ministerial dialogue and sector planning. This included technical contributions to the development of the new OECS Education Sector Strategy, an impact assessment of the previous strategy, the 2025 Education Digest, and new mental health and psychosocial support guidelines for school counsellors.
Goal Area 3: Child Protection 
In 2025, UNICEF supported governments and regional institutions to strengthen child protection systems, advance policy reform, and expand access to MHPSS. National and regional commitments were strengthened under the OECS Development Strategy and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, contributing directly to the SDGs (particularly SDG 16.2 on ending violence against children).
Key achievements included the draft OECS Child Policy, sustaining family and juvenile courts, and advancements in legal and policy frameworks to improve child justice and protection systems. Across several CARICOM countries, over 80,000 children and adolescents were reached with MHPSS. Notably, Trinidad and Tobago built on dedicated services and Grenada advanced the Primero case management system to better coordinate responses to child protection concerns.  In addition, the Digital Public Good Alliance approved the UNICEF ECA app, the MyChild Help Line, which offers tailored digital support to children and caregivers, as a Digital Public Good. Despite access challenges, there is strong potential to scale this tool to better reach the most vulnerable children.
A major milestone was the launch of the UNICEF/CARICOM Caribbean Child and Youth Mental Health Research Study across 17 countries, the most comprehensive study of its type to date, which is now informing national MHPSS responses. UNICEF also supported Trinidad and Tobago in developing its National Mental Health Policy and National Adolescent MHPSS Strategy. A suicide decriminalization brief to guide legislation reform in Grenada, Saint Lucia and Trinidad and Tobago was completed jointly with government partners. In collaboration with the Pan American Health Organization, the OECS, CDEMA, the United Nations Resident Coordinator’s Office, Australian AID, the University of the West Indies (the UWI), and CARICOM, UNICEF developed a Regional MHPSS and Climate Change Guidance Counsellors’ Toolkit and workbook for schools[1], which provided direct support to over 80,000 children in 12 CARICOM countries. Through UNICEF’s financial and technical assistance, draft child protection and MHPSS referral protocols were developed for Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago, supporting responses at school and community levels. In Trinidad and Tobago, a mental health text line was launched with UNICEF support, while the OECS initiated work to expand the service to nine countries. The Caribbean Youth Mental Health Focal Point Network, recognized by the UNICEF Latin America and Caribbean Regional Office (LACRO) as a best practice, was expanded to 23 Caribbean countries, strengthening youth leadership in shaping policies, programmes and advocacy. Following a request from the Government of Dominica, UNICEF supported an assessment of their child protection institutions, including residential facilities.
The rights of children on the move were also supported. In Trinidad and Tobago, UNICEF assisted national agencies in ensuring birth registration for 219 children of migrant parents, strengthening their legal identity. Rising community violence involving and affecting children highlighted the urgent need to address the social drivers of such violence.  Evidence from the 2024 social survey on violence against children informed targeted, community-level interventions in 2025 across five Eastern Caribbean countries (Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Trinidad and Tobago), ensuring that programming remained data-driven and responsive to the needs of children and families. UNICEF and partners used SBC strategies such as Human-Centred Design, behavioural insights, communication campaigns and an edutainment approach to promote non-violent parenting practices, reaching more than 100,000 parents and caregivers across the subregion. These efforts, coupled with increasing donor interest, created renewed momentum for multi-sectoral collaboration and sustained investment in child protection.
Progress was enabled by strong government collaboration, regional leadership by the OECS Commission, and UNICEF’s strategic focus on evidence generation, cross-sectoral integration, and system strengthening. 
Goal Area 4: Climate Change and Resilience 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened climate resilience and disaster preparedness by helping governments integrate child- and youth-sensitive priorities into national policies, enhance risk and vulnerability data systems, and expand youth engagement in climate governance. It promoted shock-responsive systems - prioritizing climate-resilient WASH, child and social protection, and education. In Grenada, UNICEF supported inclusion of youth priorities in NDC 3.0 and the NAP processes and backed the June 2025 Climate Change National Youth Forum, which brought together youth leaders, government officials, and stakeholders to co-create policy recommendations and strengthen intergenerational dialogue. In Saint Kitts and Nevis, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Environment, Climate Action and Constituency Empowerment to integrate child- and youth-sensitive approaches into NDC and NAP processes. UNICEF and CDEMA strengthened the Caribbean Community Risk Information Tool (CCRIT) through integrating child-sensitive indicators and improved access to risk and vulnerability information. UNICEF also finalized a Climate Finance Mapping Tool and Dashboard to track climate-related financial flows and advanced an advocacy publication: Unlocking Climate Finance for Young People in the Eastern Caribbean.[4] A complementary regional study on climate trends and a socioeconomic impact study is underway, further strengthening evidence for child-sensitive climate and resilience programming.
UNICEF continued to support humanitarian recovery and resilience building in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines following Hurricane Beryl. Two reverse-osmosis systems were installed on Union and Mayreau Islands, helping to secure most of their potable and domestic water supply.  
Emergency WASH responses were supported through the distribution of hygiene kits, promotion of safe and sustainable hygiene practices, and strengthened coordination at all levels. UNICEF maintained its role as co-lead of the national and regional WASH coordination mechanism, supporting both humanitarian response and longer-term resilience building, including the deployment of ECA WASH technical surge support for sector coordination following Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica.
In partnership with the Caribbean Chamber of Commerce and CDEMA, UNICEF supported the finalization of the Humanitarian Guidelines and Supplementary Family Friendly Check List for the private sector, providing practical guidance to strengthen business preparedness, response, and recovery.  
Goal Area 5: Child Poverty (Shock-Responsive Social Protection) 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened child-sensitive, shock-responsive social protection systems across the Eastern Caribbean, linking emergency preparedness, poverty reduction and climate resilience to protect vulnerable children and families during times of crisis. UNICEF scaled its innovative emergency preparedness simulations - first piloted in Anguilla in 2024 - to Saint Kitts and Nevis and Montserrat, supporting governments to model crisis scenarios, test standard operating procedures, and establish response protocols to improve delivery of cash and social assistance to families after economic or climate shocks.
In Saint Kitts and Nevis, UNICEF provided technical support to the Livelihood Improvement for Family Transformation (LIFT) programme, contributing to the review of the national social protection policy and strengthening the management information system to improve efficiency and interoperability. UNICEF deepened its engagement on climate-sensitive social protection, providing technical and financial assistance in linking policy and social assistance systems with national adaptation goals. In a significant regional milestone, Barbados officially included social protection in its NDC. Across the region, UNICEF collaborated with the World Food Programme (WFP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization to promote dialogue on aligning social protection with climate financing instruments to ensure that future climate investments benefit children and vulnerable families.
Across the UK Overseas Territories (UKOTs), UNICEF supported the institutionalization of emergency cash assistance systems. In Anguilla, UNICEF continued to provide technical assistance to strengthen the management information system, enhancing the digital infrastructure necessary for integrated delivery of social services and more responsive, adaptive support during emergencies. This inclusive, multi-stakeholder exercise produced a comprehensive report to guide policy reform and drive evidence-based planning, resource prioritization and programme strengthening. 
Social and Behaviour Change Programming
In 2025, UNICEF employed SBC approaches such as evidence generation, edutainment, human-centred design, community engagement, and communication campaigns to promote safer, healthier, and more nurturing environments for children.  
Social data generated in 2024 and 2025 were used to ensure evidence-informed SBC strategies on violence prevention and to gain uptake for immunizations. Community engagement with local leaders and influencers continued to be used in violence-prevention programming, as well as the edutainment approach which allowed discussions on sensitive topics such as corporal punishment and child sexual abuse.
Building on UNICEF's 2024 advocacy, partner institutions increasingly adopted human-centred design approaches in 2025. More partners engaged children, adolescents, and caregivers directly in the co-creation of SBC interventions, ensuring that messaging and activities were relevant, context-specific, and community-owned. Government and NGO partners from the health, disaster management, and social protection sectors in Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines benefited from UNICEF's technical and financial support. Effective PME for Results
During the reporting period, UNICEF ECA advanced national and regional capacities for evidence-based policymaking, reinforcing commitments to the SDGs. Through targeted technical and financial support, UNICEF enabled the successful launch of the seventh round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 7) in Saint Lucia, led by the Central Statistical Office within the Ministry of Equity, Social Justice and Empowerment. Covering 3,040 households, MICS 7 delivers high-quality, disaggregated well-being data. The inclusion of innovative modules - such as early learning outcomes, adolescent mental health, attitudes toward domestic violence, and parental involvement - significantly expands the national evidence base to inform inclusive social policies, monitor SDG progress, and strengthen child-focused programming. The MICS 7 report will be available in 2026.
UNICEF also enhanced data accessibility and integration by supporting the extension of the MICS dissemination platform in Trinidad and Tobago to include poverty data through the Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis, alongside other survey and administrative datasets. 
In parallel, UNICEF generated critical insights through a Country Programme Evaluation and three strategic evaluations: Formative Evaluation of Support to the Education Sector during COVID-19[7]; Real-Time Evaluation of Children on the Move in LAC LIFT[8]; Evaluability Assessment of Care for Child Development in LAC - Trinidad and Tobago Case Study[9].
These evaluations provide actionable evidence to guide the development of the new Country Programme and the transition to a Caribbean Multi-Country Office and to support programmatic decisions, improve service quality and reach, and align interventions with the evolving needs of children. 
UNICEF strengthened national evaluation systems through flagship capacity-building initiatives: the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders (ExCEL) follow-up training and the Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems Strengthening (IMPrESS). These programmes equipped 19 participants from nine Eastern Caribbean countries and territories with advanced competencies in evaluation leadership, system strengthening, and results-based management.
Collectively, these efforts have fortified national and regional capacities to collect, analyze, and apply data for decision-making. 
Humanitarian Action 
In 2025, UNICEF ECA utilized a resilience-based nexus approach to strengthen emergency preparedness and response capacity, reinforcing regional coordination, institutional readiness, rapid response mechanisms and child-sensitive shock-responsive systems that link emergency response to longer-term resilience building. Through its initial leadership role in the UN Emergency Technical Team for Barbados and the Eastern Caribbean and the contribution agreement with CDEMA, UNICEF facilitated strategic collaboration, contributing to more coherent, multi-sectoral preparedness and contingency planning aligned with national resilience agendas. 
Working with governments and regional partners, CDEMA and UNICEF contributed to stronger child-centred shock-responsive systems through integrated WASH, education, child protection and social protection priorities. This enabled countries to move toward more anticipatory, coordinated responses that safeguard children’s safety, health and learning even when infrastructure and services are disrupted by hazards.  UNICEF maintained it co-leadership of the WASH and Education Thematic Working Groups as part of the Regional Response Mechanism. 
Emergency preparedness continued to be embedded as a core programme priority across sectors. UNICEF strengthened the region’s capacity to deliver under the Core Commitments for Children (CCCs) by expanding partnerships for climate-resilient WASH systems, including with Water Mission International. To reinforce regional emergency response preparedness under the CCCs, UNICEF pre-positioned emergency supplies such as WASH, education and shelter materials, and updated contingency supply plans and vendor mapping. Preparedness risk analysis was expanded to incorporate hydrometeorological, seismic, volcanic, migration and nutrition hazards, ensuring a comprehensive and risk-informed approach to emergency preparedness.  Regular preparedness reviews and coordination mechanisms supported contingency planning across priority response sectors, and staff capacity was strengthened through emergency procedures orientation with LACRO.
As part of South-South Cooperation and Caribbean emergency support, within days of Hurricane Melissa striking Jamaica, UNICEF ECA had coordinated two emergency shipments from its pre-positioned warehouse at the WFP-CDEMA logistics hub in Barbados, delivering tents, hygiene and education kits, schools-in-a-box, water containers, purification tablets, tarpaulins, and water tanks. Implemented jointly with UNICEF Jamaica, WFP and CDEMA, these actions enabled an immediate, well-coordinated, and life-saving response for affected communities.  An ECA WASH specialist was deployed to support assessments and coordination. UNICEF ECA also contributed technical guidance through a CARICOM-led, development partner coordination meeting on the education response and recovery, supporting guidance on best practices and approaches.  
Through this nexus approach, UNICEF helped strengthen the Eastern Caribbean’s ability not only to respond rapidly to emergencies, but to reduce vulnerability, protect children’s rights, and sustain essential services across disaster cycles.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
In 2025, UNICEF and partners delivered results amid an increasingly complex operating environment shaped by overlapping global, regional, and national pressures. Across the Eastern Caribbean, rising community crime - particularly in urban centres - created growing risks for children’s safety and well-being. Young people in high-risk areas faced heightened vulnerability to recruitment by criminal groups; exploitation, and psychological trauma and social norms that tolerate violence continued to undermine prevention efforts. These dynamics highlight the urgent need for strengthened prevention, early intervention, and rehabilitation programmes that address the root causes of youth involvement in violence and reinforce community-based child protection mechanisms.
MHPSS systems remained fragmented across education, child protection, and health sectors. A regional assessment of referral protocols, conducted by UNICEF ECA in 2023, revealed gaps in coordination, inconsistent standards of care, limited data sharing between ministries, insufficient frontline workforce capacity, and challenges in ensuring culturally and linguistically appropriate services - particularly for Spanish-speaking migrant populations in Trinidad and Tobago. 
The broader geopolitical and financing environment also posed significant challenges. Shrinking development financing and global humanitarian budgets reduced the availability of flexible funding for SIDS that fall between traditional development and emergency funding criteria. This affected both national programmes and the capacity of regional institutions to fully implement sector strategies and technical cooperation mechanisms. At the country level, changing political priorities and a decline in dedicated funding for the Venezuelan migrant response in Trinidad and Tobago limited momentum toward durable policy solutions for migrant children’s access to education and social services. Additionally, in Turks and Caicos, progress on the needs of migrants has been limited due to rising xenophobia and stigma negatively influencing political will to effect change.   
Resource mobilization efforts faced structural barriers. Several international funding windows remain inaccessible to small island states and territories given eligibility constraints tied to sovereignty status or income classification. Compressed proposal timelines, shifting donor priorities, and evolving technical requirements also demanded rapid adaptation and intensive coordination with government partners. In several cases, gaps in national data systems and limited cross-ministry coordination further slowed proposal development and underscored the capacity gaps in evidence generation, public finance analysis and programme design.
Lessons Learned
Several key lessons emerged. First: the escalation in community violence demonstrated that systems strengthening must be paired with stronger community-based and preventive approaches to child protection, complemented by addressing harmful social norms, strengthening good parenting practices and local protective networks, as well as expanding youth engagement. Integrating education, child protection, justice and social services at the community level proved critical for reaching the most marginalized adolescents who are at greatest risk of recruitment into violence. 
Second: partnerships remain essential to programmatic agility. In Trinidad and Tobago, collaboration with national and community-based organizations enabled UNICEF to maintain access to migrant children and respond quickly to emerging protection and education needs, even as funding streams fluctuated and policy environments evolved. Civil society partners not only provided service delivery capacity but also played a vital role in identifying vulnerable children who otherwise remain invisible to institutions.
Third: adaptive management depends on timely, multi-source evidence, not only formal evaluations. UNICEF’s Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning (MERL) strategy increasingly relied on real-time qualitative feedback through partner consultations, youth dialogues, community surveys and rapid assessments which provided evidence to identify impactful interventions and support scale-up. These more agile evidence streams enabled programmatic adjustments, informed advocacy messaging, and strengthened proposals. 
Fourth: early and proactive donor engagement proved critical in 2025. Proposals that clearly articulated development impact, aligned with global and regional priorities such as climate resilience, safe schools, disability and gender inclusion, green skills and embedded youth and community participation were more competitive. 
Collaborative proposal development - with partners such as UN Women, UNDP, the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), the UWI and CARICOM - demonstrated that co-creation increases both coherence and national ownership. Importantly, maintaining a repository of templates, data and theory-of-change models streamlined proposal development and reduced response time to funding opportunities.
Future Outlook
UNICEF will further sharpen its role as a strategic convener and technical partner supporting governments and regional institutions across the Eastern Caribbean to mobilize new investments for children and scale high-impact systems change. With tightening humanitarian and development budgets globally, the focus will increasingly shift toward combining traditional donor partnerships with innovative financing mechanisms that involve public and private capital to advance child-centred development. 
UNICEF will expand engagement with international financial institutions, regional development banks, and climate finance mechanisms to ensure children’s priorities are embedded in large-scale investments for climate resilience, education transformation, and child-centred, shock-responsive social protection systems. Partnerships with the CDB, Inter-American Development Bank, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF), and climate funds such as the Green Climate Fund and Global Environment Facility will secure results that integrate education safety, child-sensitive climate adaptation, adolescent skills development, and social protection into national investment programmes.   Building on Green Rising, UNICEF will support youth-led climate action, entrepreneurship, and skills development and pursue blended financing - linking youth innovation to climate finance, corporate social responsibility, and impact funds - to attract private sector co-investment in sustainable energy, digital learning, and climate resilient school and community infrastructure. led climate action, entrepreneurship, and skills development and pursue blended financing investment in sustainable energy, digital learning, and climate resilient school and community -led climate action, entrepreneurship, and skills development and pursue blended financing-investment in sustainable energy, digital learning, and climate-resilient school and community 
Education transformation will remain a central investment priority, with UNICEF continuing to work with governments to advance safe schools, inclusive education systems and digital learning platforms that enable access for children with disabilities and migrant children. Through collaboration with global education initiatives and multi-partner platforms, UNICEF will seek to mobilize new financing for large-scale teacher development, school safety retrofitting, connectivity and digital learning innovations that can be implemented regionally rather than country by country - maximizing economies of scale across the small island contexts.
UNICEF will lead institutionalization of the Caribbean coordinated service delivery model for MHPSS as a regional public good, seeking multilateral co-financing to support workforce development, digital referral systems, and integration of MHPSS into primary health care and school systems. UNICEF will also elevate adolescent mental health as a child’s rights and economic priority, linking expanded MHPSS services to productivity, social cohesion, and violence prevention agendas, rights and economic priority.
UNICEF will further advance the integration of social protection and climate financing, building on the regional policy gains that recognize social safety nets as a climate adaptation instrument. Working with development banks and climate funds, UNICEF will support governments to design shock-responsive safety net programmes that can be financed through adaptation funding, insurance schemes and contingency financing instruments. This work will strengthen governments’ fiscal preparedness for future disasters while ensuring that investments reach the most vulnerable families and children.
Recognizing the unique financing constraints, UNICEF will intensify efforts to innovate around multi-country investment frameworks that allow pooled funding, joint proposals, and shared implementation platforms. These mechanisms aim to overcome traditional single-country eligibility barriers and expand access to financing streams otherwise unavailable to SIDS contexts.
The migrant response in Trinidad and Tobago remains sensitive to evolving geopolitical dynamics and funding trends. UNICEF will continue advocacy for inclusive national education and protection policies while strengthening partnerships with local civil society actors and faith-based organizations delivering frontline services. The focus will shift toward capacity building, localization of service delivery, and durable integration solutions that are less dependent on volatile humanitarian funding cycles.
UNICEF will continue to advance child-centred humanitarian action by strengthening shock-responsive systems, ensuring that the rights and well-being of children are protected before, during, and after emergencies. This includes reinforcing national and regional social protection, education, child protection, and WASH systems to respond rapidly and equitably to shocks, especially for most vulnerable children. UNICEF will sustain close collaboration with key partners and actively engage in regional and national coordinating mechanisms to enhance preparedness, coordination, and collective accountability. 
Finally, UNICEF will deepen support for regional evidence platforms and digital public goods, including MICS dissemination tools, climate risk analytics, digital learning platforms and youth engagement mechanisms - to improve accountability, transparency and performance monitoring at scale. Strengthening regional data interoperability will underpin evidence-based advocacy, improve investment targeting, and enhance partner confidence in scaling programmes across borders.
In an evolving global development landscape, UNICEF in the Eastern Caribbean is positioning itself as a connector between governments, development banks, the private sector, academia and youth movements to unlock new investment flows for children. The outlook for the coming period is one of strategic expansion - scaling proven models, mobilizing innovative financing, and strengthening climate-smart, child-centred systems that safeguard children’s rights and well-being across the region.

Belize, a small Central American nation with a population of approximately 397,000, has a youthful demographic—over 150,000 children and adolescents under 20—underscoring the urgency of advancing rights to survival, development, protection, and participation. Despite progress under the 2022–2026 Country Programme, persistent and overlapping deprivations continue to hinder Belize’s trajectory toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the principle of leaving no child behind.
Belize’s economy demonstrated resilience in 2025, recording GDP growth of 3.5% in 2024 and of 6.1% in Q3 of 2025 driven primarily by goods-producing sectors such as agriculture and manufacturing. Inflation remained moderate at 0.8%, yet rising costs in housing, utilities, and food continue to strain household budgets, particularly in rural districts such as Punta Gorda, where inflation peaked at 2.7%. These cost pressures disproportionately affect low-income families, exacerbating child poverty and food insecurity.
Public debt reduction is a notable achievement: from 103.3% of GDP in 2020 to 64.7% by the end of 2025, signaling improved fiscal discipline and debt restructuring efforts. This creates fiscal space for social investments, but allocations remain skewed. Education commands 60.7% of social sector spending and health 35.4%, while the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs (MHDFSGA)—responsible for social protection, child protection, disability, and early childhood development—receives only 3.8%. This imbalance limits the expansion of integrated social services critical for addressing multidimensional child poverty.
Unemployment reached a historic low of 2.1% in April 2025, reflecting post-pandemic recovery and growth in tourism and agriculture. However, gender disparities persist: female unemployment stands at 3.3% compared to 1.3% for males, and women’s labor force participation (46.9%) lags significantly behind men (72.3%). These gaps perpetuate income inequality and constrain household resilience, with implications for children’s well-being.
Belize enjoys relative political stability, with the next general election scheduled for 2030. However, civic engagement is weakening: voter turnout fell to 65% in 2025, the lowest since independence, and the country scored only 1.5/10 on the Caribbean SCORE Index for civic participation. Declining trust in elected officials contrasts with higher confidence in civil society and religious leaders, signaling a governance challenge that could affect policy legitimacy and social cohesion.
Low engagement is linked to structural factors such as economic exclusion, mental health challenges, and limited youth participation in decision-making. These trends risk undermining democratic accountability and the realization of SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions). Strengthening participatory governance and creating platforms for adolescent voices are essential for advancing child rights and inclusive development.
Multidimensional child poverty remains critical: 30.5% of children aged 0–14 experience overlapping deprivations, with rural Toledo facing widespread poverty—nearly 70% of households with children are poor. Social protection coverage is only 32%, far below the regional average of 62%, leaving families vulnerable to economic shocks and climate disasters. Expanding cash transfers and adaptive social protection systems is vital for resilience.
COVID-19 disruptions persist, with over 50% of children aged 3–4 lacking access to early childhood education. Learning poverty is severe: 76% of late-primary-age children cannot read proficiently. While primary attendance is near universal, secondary enrollment and completion rates remain low (upper secondary completion at 50.2%), with stark regional disparities. Foundational skills are weak—only 42.6% of children aged 7–14 demonstrate reading proficiency, and 50.4% show numeracy skills—threatening progress toward SDG 4 (Quality Education). These challenges are compounded by Belize’s migration context, where an estimated 40,000–60,000 migrants live in the country, including many children who face barriers to accessing education and other services, placing additional pressure on the education system to be inclusive and responsive to diverse learning needs.
Under-five mortality declined to 14 per 1,000 live births, and institutional deliveries are high (95.3%). However, exclusive breastfeeding remains suboptimal (42.7%), stunting affects 13.2% of under-fives, and overweight prevalence is rising, reflecting a double burden of malnutrition. Vaccination coverage is alarmingly low (25.3%), with 9.4% of children unvaccinated, and boys twice as likely as girls to miss immunization. These gaps jeopardize SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being).
Access to drinking water is high (98.6%), but hygiene coverage lags (73.5%), and water contamination (E. coli in 33.7% of household water) poses health risks, exacerbated by climate change. Strengthening water safety and climate-resilient WASH systems is critical for child survival.
Violent discipline affects 62.3% of children aged 1–14. About 67,000 children experience violent discipline at home. Among them, 52% face psychological aggression, 45% suffer physical punishment, and nearly 4% endure severe physical punishment. Older children are at greater risk as those aged 10–14 is almost twice as likely to experience severe punishment compared to toddlers. Harmful social norms remain a major barrier, with one in five caregivers believing physical punishment is necessary.  Adolescent birth rates remain high (58 per 1,000 nationally; 118 in Toledo), and child labor affects 11.7% of children, with rural boys disproportionately engaged. Children with disabilities (7%) face systemic exclusion due to weak data systems and fragmented services. Mental health concerns are rising, with 4.1% of adolescents reporting suicide attempts, while 9.7% of 108 adolescents with symptoms of depression or anxiety talked to someone. These trends underscore the need for integrated child protection and mental health services.
Climate change amplifies vulnerabilities through rising sea levels, coastal erosion, and hurricanes, disrupting education and livelihoods. The 2024 Disability Act signals progress toward inclusion, but implementation gaps persist due to limited institutional capacity and financing. Strengthening intersectoral coordination, embedding climate resilience, gender equality, and disability inclusion across all sectors, and enhancing child and adolescent participation are critical for accelerating results at scale.
Belize’s progress for children depends on sustained political will, robust governance reforms, and strategic investments in social protection, education, and health. The final year of the 2022–2026 Country Programme offers an opportunity to consolidate gains and address persistent gaps through integrated approaches aligned with the SDGs and the call to leave no child behind.

In 2025, UNICEF Belize contributed to the strategic, system-level results that advanced national priorities, the United Nations Multicounty Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (MSDCF) and contributed meaningfully to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) and other global child-rights obligations. 
UNICEF’s focus in 2025 was to advance national systems to prevent and respond to violence, expand inclusive and resilient learning, improve survival and healthy development, and build an equitable, child centered shock-responsive systems—all underpinned by strong evidence systems and strategic  advocacy and communications that keep children’s rights at the center of policy advocacy and decision making.
The results were enabled by UNICEF’s sustained policy engagement; strategic convening across ministries and sectors; application of high-quality evidence; and targeted innovation in digital, geospatial and learning solutions. 
A CCD evaluability assessment was conducted, identifying short-, medium-, and long-term results to support effective implementation of the Care for Child Development approach, and a policy brief was developed to advocate for increased investment in early childhood.
A major breakthrough in 2025 was Belize’s launch of a national, multisector effort to end violence against children and the development of its first comprehensive EVAC Action Plan, following the Government’s pledge at the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. UNICEF played a key advocacy and technical role by bringing ministries together, aligning priorities, and supporting the use of the INSPIRE strategies to ensure the action plan focused on prevention, was grounded in evidence, and could be implemented effectively.
To address these norms, UNICEF supported the Government in pairing policy with practical tools. UNICEF supported development of a national parenting policy and update of the parenting manual so caregivers and service providers have consistent, high-quality guidance for positive parenting and non-violent discipline. These actions reflect the INSPIRE strategies, which emphasize safe environments and strong caregiver support as key to preventing violence where it most often occurs—within the home.
Justice reform progressed alongside EVAC efforts. UNICEF contributed to these results by participating in the Policy and Legal Reform Committee supporting the advancement of the Families Bill, 2025, and by investing in a nationwide diversion tour that engaged justice actors across the country. In this context, the Government streamlined child-justice governance bodies to clarify roles and strengthen accountability, expanded diversion programmes for children in conflict with the law, and advanced the Families Bill, 2025. This modern legislation establishes a Family Court, introduces care and supervision orders for vulnerable children, formally recognizes a child’s right to counselling, updates adoption rules, strengthens protections for children with disabilities, and allows recognition of parent–child relationships in succession matters. These changes are especially important for adolescents—around 70,000 young people aged 10–19, who face higher risks of violent discipline and harmful contact with the justice system.
 Equity was a guiding principle throughout. UNICEF invested in the upgrading of an existing government-owned facility to function as Belize’s first migrant family shelter, addressing a critical gap that had often resulted in the detention of migrant children or the separation of families. The retrofitting focused on making the space safe, child- and family-friendly, and suitable for temporary, dignified accommodation. In parallel, UNICEF supported development of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the Departments of Immigration and Human Development to guide the management of the shelter. The SOP was developed through consultations with Government counterparts, with IOM and UNHCR invited to contribute. With approximately 12% of Belize’s children—around 12,600—being migrants, this combined infrastructure and systems-strengthening intervention protects the right to family life and ensures safe, dignified care for a highly vulnerable group. Education results in 2025 focused on inclusion, resilience, and digital transformation. Inclusive education made strong progress. Building on lessons from the first phase of the Therapeutic Programme, work on the Special Education Policy advanced, and Phase 2 introduced 13 Therapeutic Classrooms in Cayo and Toledo. These classrooms created structured, supportive environments for 204 children with developmental delays and disabilities. This approach connected practice and policy—what worked in classrooms informed national policy, and policy provided a platform for scaling up.
UNICEF also responded to the needs of high-migrant communities. One hundred classrooms received Teacher Resource Packages with materials for English as a Second Language and tools for supporting children with special educational needs. These resources benefited about 2,000 children, helping foreign-born students and children of migrant parents integrate socially and academically, ensuring language is never a barrier to learning.
At the foundation of the system, UNICEF worked to increase demand for early learning. An Early Childhood Education campaign was launched in villages with high numbers of out-of-school preschoolers. Parents gathered in preschools, community centers, and health facilities to learn about the importance of early learning, brain development, and the benefits of play-based curricula. Initial sessions reached over 30 parents in two of Belize’s six districts and set the stage for broader efforts to boost preschool enrolment by 20%.
Belize received a US$1 million System Capacity Grant from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to strengthen the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the Belize Education Sector Plan through BEMIS. Using this support, UNICEF and the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology (MECST) co-designed the Strengthening Educational System Resilience Programme. The work began with a full evaluation of the sector plan and nationwide consultations to gather insights from stakeholders. A major milestone was the country’s first Joint Sector Review - a government-led process that brought partners together to assess progress, identify challenges, and agree on practical solutions. 
Improving instructional quality was another priority. In partnership with the University of Texas at Tyler, the ministry piloted “Building Capacity for Instructional Coaching & Teacher Appraisal” with 200 administrators and teachers. This initiative is expected to enable effective roll out of the Competency-Based Curriculum.
Resilience was a priority in both policy and practice. A Comprehensive Disaster Management audit revealed that only 41% of preparedness standards were met, exposing serious gaps in the disaster management system. To address this, UNICEF is supporting NEMO and the various line ministries to adopt and implement a shock responsive systems approach to strengthen and embed child rights and protection in governance, frameworks, service delivery and finance. This approach led to the digitization of the national Shelter and Shelter Management training curriculum, integrating child protection and gender considerations to enable delivery at scale before, during, and after emergencies. It also resulted in the development of 43 capstone projects that embed child rights into national and community planning as part of the Galen University and UNICEF postgraduate programme, as well as the capacity building of 50 emergency responders in complementary psychosocial support within a child-centred, shock-responsive service delivery model.
At the school level, improvements focused on safety and infrastructure. WASH upgrades at Kux-Lin Ha and Buena Vista Primary Schools in Cayo improved conditions for 408 boys and 381 girls. These schools also serve as national emergency shelters, so the upgrades benefited 38 teachers and about 3,500 community members. In Toledo, the shock responsive systems approach supported the education system in being better prepared to protect children during shocks and maintain continuity of learning through capacity building of 45 school principals and simulation exercises and development of school safety plans to support 383 teachers and over 3000 children.
Progresses have been made in digital transformation in education in the reporting year. The first National EdTech Summit brought together 275 educators from pre-primary, primary, and secondary schools to share experiences on using technology in teaching, access new digital resources, and join a growing peer network. UNICEF supported the launch of innovative tools such as Avatar Buddy, 501Historian, Kriol 501Historian, and 501TeacherAssistant—AI solutions designed to preserve Belizean history and language while helping teachers in the classroom. Across all districts, child-friendly USpaces provided safe hubs for digital learning and youth engagement, linking national initiatives like 501 Academy, Girls in ICT, and Code.org. Belize also strengthened its commitment to digital inclusion by sending a national delegation to the Global Connectivity Forum, reinforcing policies that promote equal access to technology.
Belize made concrete advances in primary health care, maternal and newborn health, immunization and environmental health, with UNICEF providing technical leadership and catalytic investments that reached both facilities and communities. The country developed its first National Community Health Strategy, aligned with the Health Sector Strategic Plan 2025–2034, to enhance the quality and efficiency of the Community Health Worker programme. UNICEF convened the first national stakeholder forum, established a technical working group and introduced Talking Book devices to support social and behaviour change communication in hard-to-reach communities.
On maternal and newborn health, UNICEF helped to train the first national cohort of six internationally certified lactation counselors, scaled Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative guidelines, and expanded Kangaroo Mother Care to 50 health facilities in the 6 districts. Perinatal mental health services were introduced into primary care, with over 600 health workers trained and more than 2,000 mothers screened, demonstrating how upstream policy shifts translate into improved, person-centred care.
Immunization improved with the introduction of Rotavirus and Hexavalent vaccines into the national schedule. Since October 2025, 844 and 251 children received Rotavirus first and second doses, while 775 and 750 children under one received Hexavalent doses one and two, respectively. Protocols for the Elimination of Mother-to-Child Transmission were updated, 200 health workers received refresher training, and laboratory capacity was strengthened through procurement of HBV viral load testing kits and HBIG—an end-to-end approach from policy to supply to practice.
Quality of care improved as the WASH FIT framework for infection prevention and control was implemented across seven regional/community hospitals, one national hospital, and six polyclinics. UNICEF also introduced point-of-care breast ultrasound to accelerate early detection and treatment pathways for breast cancer. The cumulative effect of these quality improvements was significant; an estimated 5,500 newborns delivered in health facilities benefited from stronger IPC and better-organized care.
Because climate risk is a health risk for children, UNICEF supported a comprehensive country situation analysis on children’s environmental health, mapping threats from air pollution, heavy metals, hazardous chemicals, waste and e-waste alongside the accelerating impacts of climate change. A practical job aid on climate and environmental hazards and their effects on pregnant women and children was disseminated to health workers and caregivers. To increase service continuity and community resilience, UNICEF worked with government and village water boards to expand access to safe water in 20 hard-to-reach communities, reaching over 50,000 people, including an estimated 7,500 children, through solar-powered water systems, rainwater harvesting and water treatment. In parallel, four health facilities and four schools were solarized to ensure reliable, sustainable energy for essential services during power disruptions.
The adolescent health agenda advanced. UNICEF supported a situational analysis on adolescent substance use, trained 75 service providers to reduce stigma and strengthen adolescent-friendly services, and advanced youth leadership in climate adaptation by training 16 youth leaders from all six districts to participate in policy reviews of Belize’s Nationally Determined Contributions to develop one of the more child sensitive NDC 3.0 in the region. To address mental health, the Helping Adolescents Thrive (HAT) initiative was digitized and embedded within the National Teachers Learning Institute, with over 200 teachers completing online training to prevent self-harm and risky behaviours.
One of UNICEF’s biggest social policy achievements in 2025 was helping restart progress on the National Social Protection Strategy. Work had slowed after the final draft was submitted in 2024, but through steady advocacy and technical discussions with the MHDFSGA, momentum picked up again in April 2025. This led to the preparation of a Cabinet Paper—a key step towards the endorsement of the NSPS as the national framework for equitable and shock-responsive social protection.
In parallel, under an ECHO-funded initiative, UNICEF helped the Government designed a Grievance Redress Mechanism policy and manual for national rollout and submitted recommendations of shock- responsive provisions to incorporate in the updating of their conditional cash transfer programme- Building Opportunities for Social Transformation (BOOST) manual. These tools aim to address existing gaps in procedures, define protocols for shock situations and create structured channels for citizen feedback and accountability. The Social Protection Technical Working Group was reactivated with representation from disaster risk management actors, strengthening operational linkages between social protection and emergency response.
In the reporting year, UNICEF used key studies to strengthen advocacy with national partners, including the Out-of-Pocket Expenditure Analysis, which showed how much families spend on health and education. Findings were used to strengthen budget advocacy, shape dialogue with the Ministry of Finance (MOF), and inform UNICEF’s fundraising initiatives from GPE.
Strategic advocacy and communications and partnerships were central to UNICEF’s positioning and accountability in 2025. The office supported 16 advocacy initiatives—including launches, conferences, awareness days, national immunization drives and regional media engagement—using multimedia content, social media campaigns, influencer partnerships, press and web stories and interviews to maximize reach. These efforts underpinned national campaigns to promote uptake for measles, HPV and rotavirus vaccines, addressing hesitancy and reinforcing the public’s confidence in immunization as a life-saving public good.
UNICEF deepened relationships with national and regional influencers to amplify children’s rights. Miss Universe Belize 2025, Isabella Zabaneh, was appointed Champion for Children, elevating advocacy for the International Day of the Girl and spotlighting gender equality. At the regional level, collaboration with UNICEF ECA and the Caribbean Broadcasting Union introduced three Child Rights reporting awards at the 36th CBU Media Awards, positioning media as a critical partner for accountability and an informed public discourse. UNICEF also engaged national journalists, commissioning opinion content to sustain dialogue on the protection of children with disabilities during emergencies. Children and adolescents were not mere beneficiaries but active participants, contributing blogs and testimonials that brought authenticity to public narratives.
The National Children’s Parliament (fifth cohort) strengthened partnerships with the NCFC, National Assembly, and Senate, creating platforms for youth to influence policy and public dialogue. Notably, the cohort tabled a bill advocating adolescents’ right to access preventive health services without parental consent, earning commendation from the House of Representatives for Cabinet consideration. Two national youth advocates, Asher Torres and Favor-Joy Hammond, were appointed to lead youth-centered advocacy and content creation across UNICEF platforms.
UNICEF’s flagship investment in 2025 was the implementation of MICS 7, a nearly a million US$ national survey co-financed with government and international partners. UNICEF funded 80%, with the remainder provided by partners that included the Ministry of Economic Transformation, the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change, the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, the Ministry of Health & Wellness, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, the Statistical Institute of Belize, and international partners such as IOM, KOICA and the Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science.
MICS 7 produced 126 indicators for national planning, 40 of which align directly with the SDGs. UNICEF introduced MICS GIS to strengthen geospatial analysis and MICSLink to connect MICS data with the Belize Education Management Information System, enabling integrated analysis of education outcomes and equity gaps. Dissemination prioritized accessibility and engagement through MICS Report Snapshots, an interactive dashboard and a youth competition that brought adolescents into data storytelling. High-level briefings reached the CEO Caucus for policy consideration and were extended to Alcalde associations and Garifuna organizations, ensuring that data were not only nationally visible but also locally meaningful.
Beyond the survey, UNICEF updated the Situation Analysis of Children with Disabilities for the first time since 2013 and supported studies on adolescent substance use and child environmental hazards. The office continued to strengthen national evaluation capacity through training in ExCEL and Impress, mentorship and on-demand technical support. A Country Programme Evaluation, guided by a national Reference Group, provided accountability and learning for the next country programme cycle (2027–2031). 
In 2025, UNICEF played a key role in driving change across sectors in five main ways. First, strong advocacy kept major reforms—such as ending violence against children, passing the Families Bill, adopting the National Social Protection Strategy, and advancing inclusive and digital education—high on the national agenda and moved them from discussion to action. Second, technical support turned policies into practical tools, including updating the BOOST manual, creating a national grievance system, piloting instructional coaching, and introducing WASH FIT and point-of-care diagnostics in health facilities. Third, UNICEF brought partners together, reactivating the Social Protection Technical Working Group with disaster risk agencies, sustaining collaboration on EVAC, and aligning education and utilities ministries to start mapping school connectivity under Giga. Fourth, evidence informed decisions: data from MICS 7, the Out-of-Pocket Expenditure Analysis, and other studies shaped budget talks and sector plans, while lessons from the Therapeutic Preschool programme helped drive the Special Education Policy. Finally, UNICEF strengthened partnerships and mobilized resources, building ties with the MOF, coordinating with UN agencies and engaging the private sector. The office finalized its new resource mobilization strategy and in partnership with UNICEF USA, facilitated a donor visit to the country resulting in twelve funding proposals now under review.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The year 2025 was a period of significant progress for UNICEF Belize, but it also revealed important lessons and gaps that must shape future strategies. While achievements in child protection, education, health, social protection, and data systems were notable, the experience underscored the need for renewed strategies and innovative approaches to reach the most marginalized children.
One clear lesson is the lack of costed strategies and action plans. Plans such as the EVAC Action Plan and the CMEU Road Map were developed without full costing, which risks slowing implementation. High-level engagement must be paired with realistic financing strategies and capacity-building to ensure that the policies, strategies and action plans are implemented.
Another lesson is that integrated approaches deliver better results. Education reforms worked well where governance, teacher development, inclusion, and resilience were addressed together. Digital transformation also proved most effective when combined with teacher training and community engagement, rather than as a standalone initiative.
Community involvement is critical for changing social norms and increasing demand for services. Efforts to promote positive parenting and early childhood education showed that sustained engagement with parents and caregivers is essential to shift attitudes and behaviors. A CCD evaluability assessment was conducted to inform effective and sustainable implementation of the Care for Child Development approach by identifying achievable short-, medium-, and long-term results based on a review of programme strategies, frameworks, and systems.
Institutionalization emerged as a key success factor. Embedding programmes like Helping Adolescents Thrive into national teacher training systems ensure sustainability beyond project cycles. Similarly, integrating disaster risk management into higher education curricula builds long-term resilience.
Finally, data ownership and use require continuous investment. MICS 7 strengthened the evidence base and improved visibility of equity gaps, but technical capacity to analyze and apply data in planning and budgeting remains limited. Building these skills will be essential for translating evidence into action.
Several challenges persist. Financing gaps remain a major barrier, especially for implementing costed plans on a scale. Human resource shortages in key ministries slow progress on reforms. Social norms that support physical punishment and restrict adolescent access to health services continue to undermine child protection and adolescent well-being. Climate risks pose an ongoing threat, with only 41% of disaster preparedness standards met and limited funding for anticipatory action. Finally, technical capacity for advanced data analysis and integration into policy cycles is still weak.
Building on these insights, UNICEF will adjust its strategies in 2026 to accelerate results for the most marginalized children:
Child Protection: Develop fully costed EVAC and CMEU implementation plans, expand positive parenting programmes, and strengthen child-friendly justice pathways. Advocacy will focus on securing financing and building institutional capacity for implementation.
Education: Finalize and roll out the Special Education Policy, scale instructional coaching and appraisal, and embed Safe Schools standards in teacher training. Digital inclusion will be expanded through USpaces and locally relevant tools, ensuring teachers and students have the skills to use technology effectively.
Health and Nutrition: Scale the Community Health Strategy, sustain vaccine uptake for new antigens, extend WASH FIT to all facilities, and consolidate perinatal mental health screening. UNICEF will also advocate policy changes to remove barriers that prevent adolescents from accessing preventive health services.
Social Protection: Secure Cabinet approval for the National Social Protection Strategy, roll out the Grievance Redress Mechanism nationally, and integrate shock-responsive provisions into BOOST operations. Stronger links between social protection and disaster preparedness will be prioritized linked to disaster risk financing/innovative financing solutions.
Evidence and Data Systems: Institutionalize MICSLink across education, health, and social protection systems, expand technical training for data analysis, and strengthen partner relationship with academic institutions for advanced visualization.  In addition, the Reference Group validated the recommendations emerging from the Country Programme Evaluation. These recommendations will guide UNICEF in taking strategic actions to enhance systemic impact, efficiency, and sustainability throughout the next Country Programme (2027–2031). This will enable UNICEF to prioritize evidence-based decision-making, ensuring that data directly informs budget allocations and sector reviews.
Climate Resilience: Scale solarization of schools and health facilities, strengthen anticipatory financing for disaster preparedness, and integrate DRM into sector plans to protect services during emergencies.
Partnerships and Resource Mobilization: Use costed plans to attract investment, engage in innovative and climate financing for children, deepen collaboration with UN agencies and private sector partners, and leverage youth voices and influencers to maintain public support and accountability.

In 2025, the Bicentennial year of the Plurinational State of Bolivia, the country entered a new political cycle that opened opportunities for renewed dialogue, institutional strengthening, and inclusive development. The results of the national election set the stage for broader consensus-building and collaboration—both domestically and internationally—even as Bolivia continued to face significant economic, social, and environmental challenges. 

Twelve-month inflation reached 20% in December 2025, the highest rate since 2008, eroding household purchasing power and driving increases in poverty. While the World Bank projected GDP growth of –0.5% for 2025, data from the National Institute of Statistics reflected a –2.8% contraction during the first half of the year, deepening the recession that began in 2024, when GDP had already declined by –1.12%.
