Net International Reserves stood at USD 3.713 billion in December 2025—comparable to 2007 levels and far below the 2015 peak of USD 15 billion. The fixed exchange rate regime in place since 2011 contributed to a nearly 50% gap between the official and parallel markets, constraining access to foreign currency for essential imports. The fiscal deficit remained high at 13% of GDP in 2025. According to J.P. Morgan’s Emerging Markets Bond Index, Bolivia registered the second-highest country risk in the region.

Environmental shocks further affected children’s rights and living conditions. Large-scale floods and wildfires had profound humanitarian impacts. UNICEF estimates that in 2025, nearly 2.1 million people were affected by floods (accounting for around 18% of the country’s total population) including over 716,000 children and adolescents, while over 913,000 people—among them nearly 311,700 children—experienced severe loss of shelter, services, or livelihoods. Wildfires in 2025 affected more than 13,000 families, leaving nearly 1,400 displaced or suffering major losses, for a total of 41,300 affected individuals, including more than 14,000 children and adolescents. These emergencies increased risks of violence, family separation, school interruptions, and physical and mental health consequences, disproportionately impacting already vulnerable children.

Human mobility also increased significantly in 2025. More than 82,000 people transited through Bolivia, including 16,800 children, while an estimated 21,300 individuals settled permanently in the country. Children on the move faced severe humanitarian needs due to limited access to health care, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and child protection services—underscoring the urgency of rights-based and child-sensitive responses.

Despite this complex context, the 2025 national elections marked a turning point after two decades of dominance by a single party. The newly elected President Rodrigo Paz initiated a new political cycle requiring broad consensus to ensure governance and stability. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly became more diverse, primarily composed of three parties previously in opposition, with minimal representation from the former ruling party. Within this setting, Bolivia is preparing its General Development Plan 2026–2035 and Economic and Social Development Plan (PDES) 2026–2030, offering opportunities to integrate UNICEF’s Strategic Plan priorities and advance the child-rights agenda. Importantly, the new Government has opened its doors to the international community—including UN agencies and International Financial Institutions (IFI)—creating a more conducive environment for cooperation and joint policy dialogue.

The 2024 Population and Housing Census recorded 11.4 million inhabitants, of whom 32% are children and adolescents. While Bolivia remains within a demographic window, the population is aging: children accounted for 38% of the population in 2012 and 45% in 2001. Both the Census and the 2023 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) provide essential evidence for policy planning. Progress was noted in maternal and child health—skilled birth attendance, postnatal care, immunization coverage, and reduced child mortality. The integration in the DHS of the UNICEF-supported first-ever module on early childhood development showed that 64% of children under five achieve age-appropriate developmental milestones. However, significant inequalities persist between Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations and among mothers with no formal education.

Malnutrition in all its forms—undernutrition, overweight, obesity, and anaemia—continues to heighten children’s vulnerability to economic shocks. Although DPT3 coverage remains high at 92%, sustained efforts are needed to prevent outbreaks, particularly in urban areas. Child mortality continues to be driven by neonatal causes, highlighting the need to expand prenatal services and improve quality of care. Adolescent pregnancy remains a concern, with 48 births per 1,000 girls aged 15–19. Eleven percent of girls in this age group are pregnant or mothers, and 8% enter early unions, limiting education and economic opportunities and perpetuating intergenerational cycles of poverty.

UNICEF continues to support the National Institute of Statistics (INE) in evidence generation on early childhood and violence against children. The situation remains critical: as of December 2025, 29 cases of infanticide and 78 femicides were recorded. According to the 2023 DHS, 69% of households use violent discipline against children under six, underscoring the need to strengthen prevention, response, and social norm change strategies, including positive parenting.

Socioeconomically, 85% of the labour force works in the informal sector, heightening vulnerability to economic shocks. Nearly 60% of the population belongs to vulnerable middle-income groups at high risk of falling back into poverty. In 2024, 38% of the population lived in poverty, and poverty among children under five reached 49%. Rising prices risk further deterioration, disproportionately affecting children and adolescents.

Beyond macroeconomic pressures, the new government faces the urgent challenge of protecting social spending and strengthening social protection systems. Sustaining investments in health, education, and child protection is essential to prevent setbacks in child well-being and to ensure that no child is left behind during this pivotal transition. UNICEF will continue working closely with the Government of Bolivia to support the design, implementation, and monitoring of policies and programmes that safeguard and advance the rights of all children and adolescents.

In 2025—the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC)—UNICEF Bolivia consolidated and scaled strategic initiatives to advance children’s rights nationwide. Programmes prioritized the most vulnerable groups—girls and young women, Indigenous children and adolescents, and children and youth with disabilities—while strengthening systems and local capacities to protect, promote, and fulfil rights amid economic, social, and environmental headwinds.

The 2025 presidential elections created a pivotal opportunity to spotlight the impact of the economic and political crisis on children—evident in rising child poverty and interruptions to services due to fiscal constraints. UNICEF’s electoral advocacy centred on a position paper presented to technical teams of all major candidates. The paper informed several flagship proposals across party platforms and was widely covered by the media, amplifying the child rights agenda. A strategic partnership with the National Electoral Body enabled UNICEF to promote the inclusion of child focused actions in candidates’ programmes.

Responding to growing needs in Indigenous and rural communities facing climate pressures, UNICEF—with the Ministry of Education—expanded Resilient Schools to 52 school communities in the Amazon and Chaco regions. Since 2021, the model has reached nearly 26,500 students (13,454 girls), nearly 2,000 teachers (982 women) and more than 2,000 community members (1,564 mothers). Beyond climate smart infrastructure, Disaster Risk Management (DRM) in curricula, and environmental education, the 2025 expansion strengthened child protection and social protection measures to safeguard learning continuity and safety during shocks.

To consolidate these efforts, the Ministry of Education approved the National Strategy to Address Violence in Schools, developed the SDG4 Atlas (under the GPE framework), and created a Child Environmental Vulnerability Index. These tools now inform planning, monitoring, and evaluation across education, health, and social sectors—aligning policies and budgets with child centred, evidence-based priorities.

In 2025, UNICEF Bolivia’s integrated approach advanced children’s rights and wellbeing across sectors. Education programmes reached rural, urban, Indigenous, and migrant communities, promoting equity and inclusion while leveraging data, digital tools, and strategic partnerships to maximize impact. Climate resilience actions strengthened school communities’ capacity to respond to environmental shocks through school-based forest nurseries in wildfire affected areas, watershed focused reforestation, and green school perimeters that reduce fire risk, soil erosion, and heat stress. These efforts were complemented by rainwater harvesting, efficient water use practices to ensure availability during prolonged droughts, clean energy installations and literacy initiatives that promote sustainable resource management and local resilience.

Under the UNSDCF and thanks to the support from the Government of Canada, UNICEF continued leading the programme on sexual and reproductive health and rights and violence prevention, jointly with UNFPA and UN Women. Baselines were completed and activities launched in 3 departments (Pando, Beni and El Alto), with implementation planned through 2029. 

Intersectoral initiatives with the Ministries of Health and Education focused on overweight and obesity prevention in schools, including more than 11,800 students, teachers, parents, and school food vendors taking part in healthy eating promotion; professionals received technical training; nutritional assessments were conducted; and communication and social mobilization promoted sustainable dietary practices.A pilot intervention for healthy school kiosks was implemented in six urban and rural municipalities, identifying routines, food offerings, barriers, and opportunities in 12 schools. Findings informed the Ministries of Health and Education, leading to improvements in school nutrition policies.

In response to the measles outbreak, UNICEF—with the Ministry of Health—expanded vaccination campaigns, communication, and social mobilization to reach families with limited access. With support from UNICEF’s Latin America and Caribbean Regional Office (LACRO) and UNDP Chile, 100,000 doses of measles and rubella vaccines were procured and rapidly distributed. Primary Health Care was strengthened across 85 municipalities and 51 health networks, increasing vaccination coverage by nearly 12%. With support from UNICEF in close coordination with the Ministry of Health, 915 health centres facilitated access to immunization, reaching 85% coverage for the third pentavalent in children under one, 87% for measles in one-year olds, and 87% for HPV in 10-year-old girls. Over 550,000 families in urban, rural, and Indigenous areas received key vaccination information—countering misinformation, building trust, and increasing uptake.

Thanks to UNICEF’s support, health care access expanded for infants and mothers along the continuum of care—from prenatal services and childbirth to breastfeeding promotion, HIV prevention, early intervention, and care through age five. Facility and community level support improved quality, equity, and continuity of services.

With the Ministry of Health, UNICEF supported Baby-Friendly Hospital accreditation was supported in 97 health centres, bringing the national total to 860 and contributing to increased breastfeeding prevalence—from 58% in 2016 to 84% in 2023, according to the DHS. Additionally, 58 lactation rooms were established in workplaces and educational institutions, guaranteeing the right to breastfeed and supporting working and studying mothers.

Early Childhood Development (ECD) services reached 93,000 children (45,318 girls) providing developmental monitoring, disability interventions, and parenting programmes. Technical assistance was provided to subnational governments to strengthen ECD budgeting—supporting more sustainable financing and accountability. For the first time, comprehensive ECD and childcare data informed three thematic reports and updates to the Child and Adolescent Information System, enhancing evidence-based policy and advocacy. 

In 2025, evaluations generated actionable insights: the “Evaluability Assessment of Care for Child Development” (CCD) recognized advances in monitoring but noted gaps in harmonization between monitoring frameworks and called for further strengthening of ECD evidence and data quality. Parents reported improved access to counselling and early intervention, while local governments began aligning budgets with service delivery standards. 

With support from UNICEF LACRO and HQ, new ECD evidence was generated through the 2023 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), officially launched in 2025. Combined with 2024 Census results, these provide a comprehensive, updated information base on children in Bolivia, including their use by the health and education sectors for the programming of their strategic sectoral plans. The “Safe Family” evaluation recommended a new approach to mental health programming, aligned with UNICEF’s new Strategic Plan. 

A key advance was the “Community Promotors” initiative, training Indigenous and local leaders to prevent violence and connect families to services. In 2025 it expanded into urban areas and incorporated leaders from intercultural and migrant Indigenous groups. Promotors now play a direct role in preventing violence, promoting healthy family practices, and reinforcing local social protection mechanisms—linking households to municipal services and improving referral pathways.

Aligned with government commitments to end violence against children—including scaling and strengthening parenting programmes—UNICEF expanded access to prevention and family support services, reaching nearly 234,000 children (112,168 girls) across multiple regions. In parallel, more than 2,300 child protection officers were trained in procedures for responding to sexual violence and safeguarding children in emergencies. These interventions improved quality, consistency, and coverage—enhancing case identification, referral pathways, and coordination between community actors and municipal protection offices—thus strengthening the system’s capacity to prevent and respond to abuse and neglect.

To safeguard the rights of Bolivian children abroad, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to develop a care protocol and build institutional capacity. This enabled the provision of birth certificates for 375 children in vulnerable situations and supported the repatriation of children, in coordination with authorities and social services in 10 other countries.
The Country Office also contributed to the Mid-Term Evaluation of UNICEF’s global WASH Strategy 2016–2030, developing a Bolivian case study to advance rights-based recommendations for advocacy with the incoming government. This learning agenda is shaping policies and programmes to respond to evolving needs in the country. In Puerto Acosta for instance, 414 families self-constructed bathroom facilities to end open defecation—demonstrating community ownership and sustained behaviour change. The UNICEF’s supported Decentralised Sustainable Sanitation (DSS) Model was scaled nationally and this included additional 37 families gaining household sanitation and 13,000 students in Montero public schools benefitting from refurbished school bathrooms. 

The ninth Community Development Guide on menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) was published, along with guidelines for sustainable decentralized urban sanitation. 112 WASH professionals received training on sanitation strategies, behaviour change approaches, and MHH—strengthening national capacity for durable impact.

In 2025, floods affected an estimated 686,000 families across 234 municipalities. In collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and Water and the Civil Defense Authorities (VIDECI), and with support from the first CERF allocation to Bolivia in 12 years (delivered jointly between UNICEF, WFP and FAO), UNICEF assisted 21,608 people (4,940 girls) with hygiene kits, water storage tanks, and filters. Additionally, 250 families affected by forest fires received WASH and education assistance. Coordination with national and local authorities strengthened preparedness and response, while lessons learned informed school level DRM plans and municipal contingency plans.

Support for migrant families continued throughout 2025, with UNICEF providing strong inter-agency leadership and playing a key role in coordinating joint responses to migration related needs and other emerging crises. Families crossing at Pisiga (Chile border) and Desaguadero (Peru border) received hygiene kits, safe water, access to showers and bathrooms, food assistance, and psychosocial support. More than 5,500 children and 13,500 adults—23% of migrants with humanitarian needs at these points—benefited from UNICEF support. Feedback from migrant families was systematically collected to inform design and improve response quality. Additionally, 4,600 people, including adolescent girls and boys, participated in GBV prevention activities at border crossings.

Girls’ leadership and advocacy were central in 2025. Twenty four adolescent girls from national and regional organizations contributed to policy dialogue at high level events—including the Plurinational Child and Adolescent Committee, the Young Afro Descendants’ Council, the Bolivian Secondary Students’ Confederation, the Departmental Federation of Secondary Students, the Pregnancy Prevention Platform of Sucre, the Mother Earth Youth Council, the Vice Presidency Youth Council, AGETIC robotics, student governments, the Association of the Blind of Riberalta, and a Special Olympics student athlete. At the Ibero American Summit, they joined the Adolescents Accelerating Results for Themselves panel. The Extreme Women and Girls event—co organized with UN Women—showcased Bolivian women and girls breaking barriers in athletics, engineering, robotics, and firefighting, challenging entrenched gender norms.

With AGETIC, UNICEF supported the Institutional Policy to Support Young Women in STEM, equipping girls with social and emotional skills for access and persistence in university and tech fields. To inform decision making, UNICEF disseminated Causes of the Gender Gap in Education: A Study with Adolescents. The STEM awareness miniseries “Naira and the Star Machine”, created with participants from UNICEF’s STEM for Girls programme, reached thousands of viewers and inspired interest in STEM among youth nationwide. These efforts combined advocacy, skills building, and visibility—shifting social norms and building pipelines for girls in high demand sectors.

Digital engagement expanded through U-Report, UNICEF’s youth feedback platform. In Bolivia, U-Report generated 15 surveys used by UN agencies and government partners to inform decisions and design. Five chatbots were launched with accessible information on health, protection, climate, and education. More than 30,000 adolescents and youth engaged across six digital communities, strengthening youth-led advocacy and creating pathways for young people to influence policies and programmes affecting their lives. Furthermore, UNICEF Bolivia provided technical support to Peru and Urugay with U-Report, expanding regional peer learning and youth voice.

UNICEF also led the national update of the Children’s Climate Risk Index in 2025, providing child sensitive evidence to quantify climate impacts. The index supports integration of child responsive approaches into national climate and environmental policies, informs advocacy across levels, and can serve as a prospective indicator within Bolivia’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) to track child wellbeing and resilience. Over time, institutional uptake is expected to strengthen public investment, risk informed planning, and accountability to children.

Youth climate advocacy was also strengthened through training platforms such as LCOY (Local Conference of Youth) on climate negotiation and policy engagement. These platforms supported adolescents to draft a Declaration articulating youth priorities on adaptation, mitigation and resilience, aligned with the UN Convention on Climate Change Five adolescents were accredited as “Party Overflow” within Bolivia’s COP30 delegation, giving youth direct access to national and international negotiation processes. UNICEF also organized the first “miniCOP30” in Bolivia, involving 40 adolescents (coming from all over the Country) who negotiated key climate issues and drafted a Joint Declaration presented to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The miniCOP30 and LCOY Declaration were aligned, ensuring youth perspectives accompanied the national delegation at COP30. These initiatives strengthened youth capacity in climate negotiation, leadership, and policy advocacy—amplifying their voice in national and global decision making and laying the groundwork for sustained youth participation in climate governance.

In 2025, UNICEF implemented comprehensive social behavioral change (SBC) strategies across health, nutrition, adolescent engagement, climate, emergencies, hygiene, migration, and disability—reaching over 137,600 people (children, adolescents, families, community leaders). 97% of participants reported actively supporting vaccination campaigns and encouraging uptake in their communities. Core approaches included community dialogues, interactive workshops, radio and digital campaigns, and locally tailored materials. In several municipalities, SBC feedback informed micro-planning for outreach, improving session timing and locations and refining messaging to address specific concerns.

Despite the global challenging financial environment, UNICEF Bolivia strengthened its Partnerships for Children unit with a diversified, resilient resource mobilization strategy, securing USD 8.12 million in Other Resources—121% of the annual target. 

The funding mix showed balanced growth from Public Partnerships (40%), driven by a landmark multi-million US dollars, multi-year and multi-sectorial cooperation agreement with KOICA. UNICEF National Committees contributed 28%, with five NatComs as strategic partners supported by strong relationship management, high quality reporting, and targeted field missions; and Private Sector generated 27% of the income through Individual Giving and corporate engagement. The remaining 5% came from other sources, further diversifying UNICEF Bolivia’s resource mobilization base.

Corporate engagement was consolidated through UNICEF’s 2025 launch of Bolivia’s Business Council for Children and Adolescents, convening influential business leaders committed to co-investing, advocating, and innovating for children’s rights in the country. This platform established a structured space for strategic dialogue and collective action, positioning UNICEF Bolivia to deliver results at greater scale in 2026 and beyond. 

While, through “Empresas que Protegen” (Businesses that Protect)—implemented with leading business associations—UNICEF catalysed a measurable shift in private sector practice through joint advocacy and peer learning. Associations reported around 300 companies enrolled in the national course on breastfeeding and family friendly workplaces, signaling growing corporate commitment to child responsible standards; one example is the previously mentioned 58 newly installed or upgraded lactation rooms  to meet national regulatory requirements. Complementing this, 45 companies engaged through the UNICEF led Global Compact working group in hands on workshops to operationalize the Children’s Rights and Business Principles (CRBP)—strengthening institutional capacity to embed child centred practices in policies, operations, and culture.
Public visibility and mobilization were boosted by the 2025 Telethon at Expocruz in Santa Cruz, Bolivia’s financial and private sector hub, which drew 4,500 attendees and hundreds of thousands of viewers nationwide—setting new records for outreach and engagement. These efforts sustained support for programmes in education, health, nutrition, ECD, child protection, WASH, climate action, and inclusion.

Operational efficiency improved through innovation and strategic partnerships. A joint market study with UNDP and UN Women laid the groundwork for a national supplier search system to streamline procurement. Automation of recruitment, service contracts, donor proposals, and reporting increased internal efficiency and reduced bottlenecks. Sustainability practices were promoted among staff and families, and pre-audit requirements for EDGE eco-certification were completed. These efforts improved delivery resilience while reducing the organization’s environmental footprint.

In 2025, UNICEF Bolivia’s integrated approach advanced children’s rights and wellbeing across sectors. WASH interventions expanded safe access to water and hygiene services. Health programmes—including vaccination, maternal and newborn care, childcare, and ECD—improved coverage, quality, and equity, particularly for marginalized populations. Efforts in violence prevention, child protection, and social protection strengthened community mechanisms and accountability structures, reducing risks for children and adolescents across the country. Gender equality advanced meaningfully, with girls and young women increasingly participating in leadership, STEM, and climate action. By building skills, creating advocacy platforms, and challenging social norms, UNICEF helped ensure that adolescents and children are not only beneficiaries but also agents of change.

The gains of 2025 position UNICEF Bolivia to contribute meaningfully to Bolivia’s new General Development Plan 2026–2035 and the Economic and Social Development Plan 2026–2030, aligned with UNICEF’s new Global Strategic Plan 2026-2029. UNICEF Bolivia will continue prioritizing the most vulnerable, promoting equity and inclusion, and leveraging evidence, technology, and partnerships. This will help ensure no child is left behind as the country enters a new policy cycle. Sustained investment, multisectoral collaboration, and innovation remain essential to protect the wellbeing and futures of Bolivia’s youngest citizens.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The economic challenges Bolivia faced in 2025 required significant adjustments to public budgets, including reductions in social and development programmes. Despite these constraints, UNICEF Bolivia ensured continuity—and in several areas, expansion—of its initiatives. This was made possible through sustained engagement with national authorities before and after the November 2025 presidential elections, allowing critical programmes in health, nutrition, ECD, education, child protection, WASH, climate action, social protection and inclusion to maintain momentum and continue supporting vulnerable children and communities.

The inauguration of President Rodrigo Paz on 8 November brought opportunities to place children’s rights at the centre of the new government’s agenda, emphasising the importance of protecting investments in essential services. UNICEF reaffirmed its commitment to support a system-wide transformation of Bolivia’s education sector, including through digital innovation. This vision aims to improve infrastructure, expand connectivity and device access, and use AI-driven personalisation to benefit learners—including those with disabilities—strengthen foundational skills, promote critical thinking, leadership, digital and green skills, as well as girls’ participation in STEM. It also seeks to equip educators with data for better, faster decision-making and move beyond content delivery towards engaging learning environments adapted to a tech-driven future.

At the same time, institutional restructuring poses risks. The division of the former Ministry of Environment and Water into two bodies—one responsible for WASH and rural development, and another for development planning and the environment—raises concerns about coordination and continuity in climate action. These shifts may affect programmes vital for child health, resilience, and access to safe water.

A major institutional change occurred with the dissolution of the Ministry of Justice, previously responsible for coordinating the Comprehensive Child Protection System (SPINNA). Although the Vice-Ministry of Equal Opportunities was elevated to the Ministry of the Presidency, the General Directorate for Children—responsible for national child protection oversight—was absorbed within a broader ministerial Directorate, creating a critical leadership gap amid rising protection needs. UNICEF has been working closely with the Ministry of the Presidency to provide technical inputs for the new Executive Branch Organization Law, seeking to ensure clarity and continuity in child-protection mandates.

Bolivia also continued to face severe emergencies in 2025, including wildfires, droughts, and floods, which disproportionately affected rural and Indigenous children and communities with limited early warning systems and response capacity. Strengthening preparedness, risk-informed planning, and inter-institutional coordination remain essential to protect children and families from intensifying climate shocks.

Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) strategies proved highly effective in increasing vaccination uptake, particularly when faith leaders, Indigenous authorities, and other trusted figures were engaged. Their involvement helped counter misinformation and build confidence in public health services. 

Community-based programming continued to deliver strong results. Local and Indigenous leadership initiatives strengthened violence prevention, improved reporting and referral pathways, and enhanced accountability. Community protection spaces offered safe environments for children to learn, play, and develop skills that reduce risks of violence, child labour, early unions, and early pregnancy. Community Promoters played a vital role in linking children and families to services, fostering trust, and ensuring continuity of care in both rural and urban settings.

The evaluability assessment of the Care for Child Development (CCD) approach, conducted with support from UNICEF’s Regional Office, recognised strong practices in adapting interventions to highly vulnerable contexts, including Indigenous populations and other at-risk families. However, it also highlighted the need for more detailed data disaggregation—particularly by disability, ethnicity, and poverty status. In response, UNICEF will strengthen information systems to support more precise, equity-focused planning and decision-making.

Despite progress, structural challenges persist. Legislative approval does not guarantee implementation; without enforcement mechanisms, sufficient financial and human resources, and institutional follow-up, policies often fail to translate into actual improvements for children. Continued advocacy, monitoring, and capacity-building will be essential to ensure that reforms deliver tangible results.

Looking ahead, UNICEF Bolivia will provide the new government with strategic evidence and programmatic proven solutions to sustain and scale high-impact interventions. The Country Office has also initiated an advocacy process with the Ministry of Planning to strengthen evaluation of national programmes and policies for children. The post-election context creates opportunities to expand alliances, increase international cooperation, and mobilise development financing—including through engagement with international financial institutions—to protect social spending for children.

A central priority will be supporting the reform of Bolivia’s social protection system to eradicate child poverty. This includes strengthening governance, advancing innovative financing for children, and improving delivery mechanisms for integrated, equitable, and shock-responsive services. The reform aims to align policies, enhance coordination, and use data to build a sustainable safety net that addresses multidimensional poverty and promotes resilience. A shift is expected from universal benefits toward targeted support for the most vulnerable households, in line with fiscal realities and government priorities. Social protection is poised to become a cornerstone of inclusive development, reducing disparities and safeguarding children’s rights.

UNICEF will also launch integrated programming in several of the most vulnerable municipalities, addressing overlapping risks through coordinated interventions in health, nutrition, education and digital learning, WASH, child protection, climate resilience, and social policy. This area-based approach will ensure that digital education transformation and shock-responsive social protection reforms translate into meaningful improvements at community level.

To maximise impact, UNICEF will work with national and subnational authorities to strengthen fiscal space for children, particularly through improved municipal planning, budgeting, and resource management. UNICEF will also support the structuring and functioning of reconfigured ministries, ensuring continuity of programmes affecting children’s lives. Ongoing efforts will reinforce teacher training, health-worker capacity, gender-transformative strategies, and community-led protection systems.

As Bolivia navigates economic uncertainty, institutional reorganisation, and escalating climate risks, UNICEF’s sustained advocacy, technical expertise, and evidence-driven support will remain essential. By keeping a strong focus on equity, resilience, digital innovation, and children’s rights, UNICEF Bolivia will continue working with government and communities to protect and advance the wellbeing of every child during this pivotal period.

This year marks an important milestone for Brazil, as the country has been removed from the FAO World Hunger Map[i]. The prevalence of undernourishment (PoU) fell to 2.4% for the 2022–2024 period, below the 2.5% threshold set by the United Nations. Severe food insecurity also dropped from 6.6% to 3.4% for the 2021–2023 period. Brazil’s progress reflects the impact of poverty-reduction policies, support to small-scale family farming, strengthened social programmes, and improvements in the labour market. Despite these achievements, nearly 9 million people (out of a population of 212.8 million in 2025) still experience moderate or severe food insecurity[ii], one of the key deprivations of the multidimensional poverty affecting 36,9 % of children and adolescents[iii].


At the same time, obesity continued to rise. Among adolescents aged 10–19, one in three is overweight[iv]. For children aged 0–5, 5.9% are obese, 8.6% overweight and 19.4% at risk of overweight[v]—together representing two million children. Among adolescents, 3.1% are severely obese, 11% obese, and 19.4% overweight. This is especially worrisome considering the potential negative impact of ultra processed food (UPF) on the development of young people, whose brains are more susceptible to addiction[vi]. 


From a socioeconomic perspective, in 2025 Brazil maintained stable inflation, while GDP growth slowed slightly compared with 2024 due to weaker demand and declining household consumption[vii]. However, GDP per capita increased, supported by a stronger labour market, minimum wage adjustments above inflation and the expansion of social programmes benefiting low-income groups[viii]. Income inequality reached a historic low[ix]: the Gini coefficient for household income dropped to 0.504[x]. Yet, children remain disproportionately affected by poverty. Among those aged 0–14, 39.7% live on less than USD 6.85 PPP per day—almost 17 million children—and 2.3 million live on less than USD 2.15 PPP per day. Among adolescents aged 15–17, 35.7% live on less than USD 6.85 PPP per day and 5.1% on less than USD 2.15 PPP per day[xi]. The UNICEF Brazil Multidimensional Child Poverty Index shows that 55.9% of children experience at least one deprivation among dimensions such as income, information, education, child labor, food security and WASH. Nearly 95 million people are registered in the CadÚnico, including almost 50 million in the Bolsa Família cash-transfer programme; 32 million of them are aged 0–17[xii].


Poverty is concentrated among Afro-descendant populations, women, and residents of the North and Northeast, highlighting persistent racial, gender and regional inequalities[xiii]. In the labour market, the average monthly income of Black workers is almost 50% lower than that of White workers. Black people form the majority of the labour force yet continue to earn less, reflecting structural barriers to equal opportunities[xiv].


Brazil ranks as the fourth country in the world with the highest proportion of youth aged 18–24 who are neither in education nor in employment, according to the OECD[xv]. In 2024, 8.7 million young people aged 14–29 had not attended or completed upper secondary education. Age-grade distortion and school dropout remain major challenges: the national age-grade distortion rate is 17.9%, rising to 34.1% in Rio Grande do Norte, 33.2% in Pará, 32.5% in Bahia and 30.6% in Sergipe[xvi]. Dropout rates reach 16.5% at age 16, 19.9% at 17 and 20.7% at 18[xvii]. Regional disparities are stark: early dropout (before age 13) is 7.8% in the Northeast and 6.1% in the North.


Violence against children increased sharply. Intentional violent deaths among those aged 0–17 rose by 3.7%, contrary to the overall national decline of 5.4%. Cases of violence also grew across categories, including child abandonment (9.4%); mistreatment (8.1%) and domestic violence-related assault (7.8%) (related to corporal punishment); and child sexual abuse (14.1%). Brazil recorded 87,545 cases of sexual violence—41.2 per 100,000 inhabitants—of which 78.3% involved children and adolescents, mostly aged 10–13. Adolescents in detention increased by 3.6% (12,506 in 2024), and nearly 70,000 adolescents were apprehended by police[xviii].


The exploitation and recruitment of children by criminal groups remain a long-standing issue. The problem gained national attention after a major police operation in Rio de Janeiro in October 2025, which resulted in 122 deaths in a single day, including two children[xix]. The operation raised serious concerns about excessive use of force and insufficient safeguards for children’s safety.


Key risk factors for adolescents’ involvement in criminal activity include lack of socioeconomic opportunities, limited family support, unstable family dynamics, and lack of childcare services, especially in female-headed single-parent households. Mothers living in poverty often work long hours with limited access to public childcare and have limited ability to supervise adolescents. School dropouts are another major risk factor[xx].


School infrastructure deficits continue to undermine children’s rights. School Census microdata shows 7,631 schools in 870 municipalities (mainly in the North and Northeast) with inadequate access to water, affecting 494,000 students—57.4% Black and 14.2% Indigenous. These proportions are significantly higher than their shares in the overall student population, demonstrating a clear overrepresentation of Black and Indigenous children among those exposed to school infrastructure deprivations. Regarding sanitation, 36,000 schools serving five million children lack adequate sewage systems; 57.6% of affected students are Black. The states with the weakest sanitation access are Acre (40.4%), Amazonas (29.4%) and Roraima (23.3%). This data reaffirms the extent of racial, ethnic and regional inequalities. Brazil has 9.1 million people above 15 years old that are illiterate, including children and adolescents that are illiterate even after having attended school, which indicates the urgent and immediate need to improve the quality of education and school retention.


Migration dynamics also influence Brazil’s landscape. Brazil has experienced growing positive migration flows in recent years, particularly from neighboring Venezuela, where economic and political crises have driven large numbers of people to seek residence and refuge. Venezuelans now constitute the largest group of foreign-born residents in Brazil, with around 271,500 Venezuelans living in the country as of 2022, up from around 2,900 in 2010. This increase reflects continued migration rather than return flows and underscores how regional inequalities and crises shape demographic trends.

In the final months of 2025, Brazil hosted the 30th UN Climate Conference of Parties (COP30). Choosing Belém, on the edge of the Amazon, highlighted both the region’s vulnerability and its resilience. Despite limited progress on fossil-fuel decisions, important advances were achieved in social participation and intersectionality. The racial dimension strongly shaped negotiations of the COP`s Gender Action Plan, and for the first time an explicit reference to Afro-descendant women and girls was included in an official document, a historic step for integrating racial, ethnic and gender perspectives.

In conclusion, while Brazil achieved meaningful progress across several indicators in 2025, deep-rooted inequities persist. Structural disparities based on race, ethnicity, gender and geography continue to restrict equal access to rights and opportunities for millions of children and adolescents.

UNICEF strengthened its national influence by positioning children at the center of Brazil’s socioeconomic, equity and environmental/climate agendas. Through the production and strategic use of evidence, UNICEF engaged in policy dialogue and influence across all priority areas—including multidimensional child poverty and public expenditures, violence prevention, health and nutrition, WASH, education, early childhood, and youth participation—while amplifying evidence-based reforms through strategic communication. Partnerships with government, justice institutions, civil society organizations, and key networks ensured that equity metrics and child rights considerations were embedded in national plans and sectoral strategies. UNICEF’s advocacy enhanced the child-responsiveness of the National Climate Plan and guided the revision of the National Protocol for protecting children in emergencies, improving standards, equity, and intersectoral governance. Through its engagement in COP30, UNICEF secured Brazil’s endorsement of the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action. Together, these efforts reinforced UNICEF’s role as a trusted advisor and catalyzed systemic shifts toward more inclusive, accountable, and child-centered public policies in Brazil.
Advocacy for Change and Policy Influence
Positioning Children at the Heart of Climate Action
UNICEF coordinated the revision of the National Protocol for the Comprehensive Protection of Children and Adolescents in Situations of Risk and Disasters[i], incorporating new regulatory standards and lessons from recent emergencies. The updated protocol includes equity and accessibility guidelines, expands its scope to justice and human rights mechanisms, and mandates active child participation throughout all phases of disaster management. The process engaged nine government institutions, civil society partners, and adolescents, strengthening intersectoral governance for emergency preparedness and response.[1]
UNICEF played an important role at the 30th Conference of the Parties (COP30)[ii] to the UNFCCC, positioning climate change as a child rights crisis and ensuring that children and young people were placed at the centre of climate action. UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to Brazil’s endorsement of the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action[iii] and strengthened the child-responsiveness of the national Climate Plan and related sectoral strategies in health, food security, Indigenous Peoples, and education.
Driving Broader Policy Influence
In 2025, UNICEF Brazil significantly strengthened its public influence, positioning children’s rights at the centre of national debate. Six federal Ministers publicly addressed child-related priorities, reflecting growing political traction for UNICEF-supported agendas. Building on this expanded reach, UNICEF translated visibility into measurable policy influence and institutional change. Advocacy efforts were deliberately aligned with evidence generation, systems strengthening, and partnerships across government, civil society, and the private sector. As a result, UNICEF advanced national reforms, shaped global agendas, and embedded equity-focused approaches within public policies—laying the foundation for the key thematic achievements outlined below.
With regards to Violence Prevention, UNICEF elevated national debate on lethal violence against children based on the evidence piece Panorama da Violência Letal e Sexual contra Crianças e Adolescentes no Brasil (2021–2023)[iv], developed with leading public security networks.
With regards to Nutrition and Global Leadership, to promote healthy diets and tackle malnutrition, UNICEF advanced Healthy School Laws to protect children from ultra-processed foods. UNICEF also partnered with the Federal Government to integrate behavioral science into strategies reducing ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption and expanding HPV vaccination. Brazil also demonstrated global leadership contributing to the World Health Assembly (WHA) resolution on regulating digital marketing of breast-milk substitutes[v].
With regards to Equity in Early Childhood, the Government embraced UNICEF’s methodology on Anti-Racist Early Childhood Methodology through its inclusion in the Strategic Action Plan of the National Integrated Policy for Early Childhood.
With regards to Institutionalizing Equity Metrics, UNICEF positioned multidimensional child poverty as a core metric in the Pluriannual Plan and the Transversal Agenda for Children and Adolescents[vi]. UNICEF also initiated an agreement with the Federal Court of Accounts Auditors to integrate this indicator into audits and evaluations, advancing systemic accountability.
With regards to expanding reach of public policies, within the framework of UNICEF One Million opportunities  initiative (1MiO), UNICEF partnered with government, the private sector, and civil society to launch a national communication campaign, mobilizing stakeholders and linking advocacy to concrete pathways for adolescent skills development and employment.
Generating Evidence for Action
UNICEF positioned evidence as a catalyst for systemic reform, embedding multidimensional child poverty at the center of Brazil’s social protection agenda. The flagship report “The Multiple Dimensions of Poverty in Childhood and Adolescence in Brazil”[vii] revealed that 28.8 million children and adolescents—55.9 per cent of those under 17—live in multidimensional poverty, creating nationwide urgency for policy action. In partnership with the Ministry of Social Development, UNICEF advanced a national metric aligned with official datasets, institutionalizing accountability and ensuring that multidimensional poverty indicators guide decision-making at scale.
To strengthen Brazil’s adaptive social protection system, UNICEF supported the development of five technical guides for social assistance workers, including protocols for family support and shelter management during emergencies. These tools have been incorporated into municipal contingency plans, improving the shock-responsiveness of social protection services nationwide.
UNICEF generated and applied evidence to strengthen education policies and protective school environments. Through the Data Must Speak initiative[viii],UNICEF partnered with Innocenti and the Maranhão State Department of Education to identify school-level practices that improve learning outcomes, offering practical insights for state and municipal policy reforms.
UNICEF led a study “Panorama da Violência Letal e Sexual contra Crianças e Adolescentes no Brasil (2021–2023)”[ix], which highlighted systemic inequities, informed ongoing policy reforms and supported the national debate on lethal violence against children.
UNICEF advanced evidence-based strategies to improve health and adolescent wellbeing. In partnership with the Question of Science Institute and the Brazilian Society of Immunizations, UNICEF launched the Vacina Br Yearbook[x],a comprehensive analysis of national immunization programme. UNICEF also led Brazil’s participation in the global GAMA initiative (first country globally that piloted the indicator’s methodology), producing the country’s first intersectoral analysis of adolescent health indicators with the participation of Governmental officers and the Brazilian National Statistics Office (IBGE).
A major step in strengthening public finance for children was the development of a unified methodology to monitor Social Spending on Children and Adolescents[xi] and produce the 2025 budget execution report for the Cross-Cutting Agenda for Children and Adolescents. Endorsement by the Ministry of Planning and Budget positions this methodology for future institutionalisation in national budget legislation.
Strengthening Systems and Policies Upstream
In 2025, system strengthening shifted decisively toward institutionalization and scale, embedding equity and resilience across public policies and services. Efforts prioritized structural reforms and digital integration, while sharpening focus on the most excluded—particularly Indigenous and Quilombola children.
Driving Equity at local level Through Implementation Platforms
In 2025, the UNICEF Seal[xii] reached a record  enrollment of 2,270 municipalities—around 40 per cent of all municipalities in Brazil—marking its evolution from a certification tool to a governance instrument driving equity-focused implementation. The new cycle (2025–2028) introduced an equity-centred, ethnic-racial methodology[xiii] co-created with federal, state and municipal partners, embedding six intersectoral systemic results (corresponding to the five Goal Areas of the Country Programme and a specific result on equity) that align incentives, set performance standards and strengthen policies across all levels of government. In its first year, UNICEF trained 2,506 Guardianship Councilors, confirmed connectivity in 37,120 schools across 1,911 municipalities, and mobilized almost 50,000 adolescents through Adolescent Citizenship Centers (NUCA). Compared with 2024, when efforts focused on certifying municipalities, 2025 shifted to institutionalization—linking results to municipal planning, budgeting, and routine monitoring, prioritizing Indigenous and Quilombola communities historically excluded from public policies.
Agenda Cidade UNICEF[xiv] evolved from initial pilots into a structured, multi-sectoral framework designed to accelerate urban equity for children and adolescents. In 2025, three of Brazil’s eight largest capitals—Rio de Janeiro, Recife, and São Luís—formally enrolled, committing to an integrated approach that combines health, education, child protection, WASH, climate resilience, and social protection.
Scaling Systems Across CPD Priorities
UNICEF scaled systems across Country Programme priorities to strengthen equity and sustainability.
UNICEF’s methodology on the Anti-Racist Early Childhood agenda (Primeira Infância Antirracista – PIA) has been adopted and appropriated by the government, securing scale and impact for Black, Quilombola, Indigenous.
Building on proven results, UNICEF and the Ministry of Health agreed on a national rollout of the Unified Early Childhood Care Protocol (UAPI)[xv] across all capitals, pairing technical guidance with capacity building and performance monitoring, an important step beyond the pilots of 2024. Immunization and healthy schools’ systems were strengthened through the integration of “Immunization at Schools”, a joint initiative of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Education, into the enrolled municipalities of the UNICEF Seal, linking vaccination to the National Health Data Network and reinforcing data-driven accountability. In parallel, healthy schools’ legislation was mainstreamed, and anthropometric data collection in primary care improved, tightening feedback loops between nutrition outcomes and policy decisions. These system-strengthening efforts contributed to expanding vaccination coverage and improving nutrition monitoring at scale, contrasting with 2024 when integration was limited to pilot areas. Mental health programming strengthened the Pode Falar! platform[xvi] through upgrades, with UNICEF reaching 21,732 adolescents and young people in 2025.
Education systems consolidated School Active Search (SAS)[xvii] as a systemic mechanism, achieving 310,340 cumulative (re) enrollments. Post-elections, mayoral adherence was prioritised, expanding SAS to 2,599 municipalities and twenty-one states, with 10,309 (re) enrollments in 2025. Digital inclusion for learning progressed as UNICEF supported the strengthening of government capacity to geolocate schools, monitor internet quality in real time, and use maps and tools for decision-making, covering 166,000 schools in all 5,570 municipalities. With the Ministry of Education and the Brazilian Network Information Center (Nic.br)[xviii], the GIGA map was localised and UNICEF supported the training of more than 2,266 municipalities to install connectivity meters. By November, 1,911 municipalities had meters in over 70% of schools, and 962 had full coverage. Under “Education that Protects” initiative, Law 13.431/2017[xix] on Violence Against Children (VAC) was embedded in “School that Protects” materials, with UNICEF training approximately 13,000 professionals.
In collaboration with the Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, UNICEF contributed to the definition of minimum standardized curricula to the Social Service Workforce, focusing on Guardianship Councils, a contribution to Brazil's child protection system. Through the Seal, UNICEF mobilized 2,462 social workers across the Amazon and Semi-arid regions, receiving training on Law 13,431/2017 and the Child Protection Information Management System. These efforts indirectly benefited 236,490 children and adolescents, while 1,455 municipalities committed to SIPIA (Sistema de Informação para Infância e Adolescência) and 19,708 Conselhos Tutelares (CT, Guardianship Councils) registered to use the system, shifting from capacity building to adoption of standards and tools. Complementing workforce development, UNICEF generated evidence to inform national debates on financing and improving the Social Assistance System, supported municipalities with practical tools to strengthen local systems, and helped reform PAIF, the Protection and Integral Support Service to the Family, to better respond to child poverty and food insecurity. Also, more than 2,500 social assistance workers enrolled in emergency response training, technical guidelines reached 10,000 views. A major step in nation-wide public policy of scale was the development and endorsement by the government of a unified methodology to monitor Social Spending on Children and Adolescents[xx]. Furthermore, the Adapta SUAS tool provided tailored recommendations for adaptive social protection.
Equity In 2025
UNICEF implementation platforms Seal and Agenda Cidade have anchored equity at their core in their new respective editions. Within Seal, a new systemic result on Gender, Race and Ethnicity was created; while in Agenda Cidade, every thematic area will have cross-sectoral equity focus. Within Selo, UNICEF has elaborated a draft ethnic and racial equity guide, a milestone which embeds intentionality into municipal planning, guiding local administrations to diagnose racial disparities, prioritize investments, and track progress.
UNICEF Country Office embedded equity into Annual Work Plans, on the one hand, by providing instructions to all programmatic areas with regards to intentionality and budget allocations necessary for the equity, and on the other hand, by providing quality assurance of all Annual Workplans that specifically looked at mainstreaming Gender, Race and Ethnicity both when it comes to intentional planning of equity but also when it comes to budget allocation.
Furthermore, UNICEF launched several partnerships for disaggregated data and equity in public policies, more specifically, an evolving partnership with the National Statistics Office (IBGE), and the ENAP (Escola Nacional de Administração Pública).
Furthermore, UNICEF Brazil advanced gender equality by placing girls and adolescent girls at the center of public policies across health, education, protection, WASH, climate action, and social protection. Through the expansion of the Menina Cidadã methodology[xxi], 10,129 girls in eight cities were empowered to lead advocacy efforts on gender-based violence, menstrual health, and girls’ rights, participating in high-level spaces such as COP30 and the National Conference on Women.
The Disrupting Harm study provided critical evidence on online sexual exploitation, reinforcing national advocacy for digital safety and contributing to the approval of Law 15.211/2025.
In health, UNICEF supported the development of gender- and race-responsive Adolescent-Friendly Health Units, based on adolescents’ consultation. In education, over 22,000 girls benefited from STEAM and digital skills training through the 1MiO initiative[xxii].
In WASH, menstrual dignity actions expanded access and coverage for over 4,000 girls, including migrants and Indigenous adolescents, enabling girls to co-created safe sanitation solutions in rural schools. These efforts promoted dignity, safety, participation, and opportunity for girls, especially in Indigenous, Quilombola, rural, and marginalized communities across Brazil. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Schools shifted to systematised, co-financed initiatives. In Barcarena (Pará), standards were applied in 61 rural schools, with 25 selected for upgrades including rainwater harvesting, chlorination, handwashing facilities, bathrooms, and wastewater systems; 2,600 students participated, including 208 girls in menstrual hygiene sessions, and 105 professionals were trained. In Manaus (Amazonas), expansion reached 43 riverside schools, training 47 managers, delivering menstrual dignity sessions to 1,216 adolescents, and engaging 2,435 students; 20 schools were selected for 2026 upgrades following a structured contest. In the Munduruku Territory (Pará), eight schools were rehabilitated, two solar pump systems and two pilot filters were installed, and 36 Indigenous WASH agents and 11 education agents trained.
Complementing these actions, UNICEF strengthened productive inclusion for youth through the 1MiO initiative, engaging 241 partner companies and governments to generate over 135,825 decent work opportunities via apprenticeships, internships, and jobs only in 2025. To ensure inclusive practices, UNICEF trained employers and launched 16 learning pathways addressing the realities of young mothers, Indigenous and Black youth, LGBTQIAPN+, and adolescents in socio-educational programs. Four Opportunity Fairs in Belo Horizonte, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador, and São Paulo connected youth with companies, resulting in almost 45,000 new registrations on the 1MiO digital platform.
In Caucaia (Ceará), the Three Star Approach reached 55 rural, Indigenous, and Quilombola schools, combining education for 1,410 children and adolescents, training for 208 professionals, and municipal co-financing for 18 additional rural schools.
UNICEF advanced resilience and protection systems, prioritizing Indigenous territories and social protection. In partnership with federal authorities, disaster risk reduction was strengthened through the Committee for Responding to Extreme Events in Indigenous Health and the Interinstitutional Working Group on Surveillance for Indigenous Territorial Protection. Together with its partners, UNICEF launched phase II of the Early Warning Systems.
Participation and Youth Engagement
UNICEF strengthened adolescent participation as a key driver of governance and climate action, ensuring that young people could exercise their right to participation in decisions that affect their lives. Through its flagship implementation platforms, the Seal (Semiarid and Amazon regions), and Agenda Cidade, UNICEF created spaces for adolescents to influence public policies and promote inclusive approaches at municipal level. UNICEF ensured the functioning of more than 1,900 Adolescent Citizenship Centres (NUCAs), fostering leadership and participation in municipal planning. Participation in climate governance advanced significantly. The relaunch of #EntreNoClima mobilized 30,500 adolescents for climate education and territorial activism, while Youth Plenaries across six biomes engaged 3,000 adolescents in partnership with the COP30 Presidency Youth Climate Champion. The 6th National Children’s Conference on the Environment[xxiii] reached nearly 1 million children in 9,000 schools, convening 800 adolescents to define priorities for climate action. At COP30, UNICEF facilitated the participation of 18 adolescents from the Amazon and Semi-arid regions as official delegates, who spoke at high-level events—including a dialogue with the UN Secretary-General—and contributed to panels on green jobs and climate inequalities.
Partnerships Driving Scale and Sustainability
UNICEF mobilized government, private sector, and civil society to scale solutions that advance education, inclusion, health, and resilience—delivering tangible progress vulnerable children and adolescents from Semiarid, Amazon regions and large urban centers.
Through the One Million Opportunities (1MiO) initiative, UNICEF connected schools, companies, and governments to expand training and decent work opportunities. In 2025, 179,750 youth completed micro-certifications, while the platform reached 207,000 registered youth, including 34,000 new users. Innovation programs such as InovaSTEAM and the Game Changers Coalition trained 475 teachers and benefited over 22,400 students in 172 public schools, prioritizing girls and gender equity. Entrepreneurship efforts engaged 20,105 youths, strengthened 18 community organizations, and trained 40 local leaders, fostering inclusive income-generation strategies. These actions help break cycles of poverty and exclusion by ensuring that adolescents not only stay in school but also gain the skills and opportunities to transition successfully into the labor market. In education, UNICEF worked with systems to advance learning and equity. The School Active Search (SAS) initiative supported 21 states and 26 UNDIME sections, linking strategies to income transfer programs and addressing barriers for 440,000 out-of-school adolescents. The Successful School Pathways (SSP) initiative[xxiv] trained 3,100 educators and reached 40,000 students in 217 municipalities, while the Petronilha Beatriz Seal, launched with the Ministry of Education, promoted anti-racist practices nationwide. These efforts reinforce the right to education and reduce dropout risks, ensuring that the most vulnerable children are not left behind. These measures strengthened Brazil’s leadership in school feeding and promoted healthier diets, reducing risks of obesity and malnutrition among millions of children. UNICEF also strengthened social protection systems through its partnership with the Ministry of Social Development. A joint study on Bolsa Família conditionalities informed financing and intersectoral coordination, securing health and education rights for vulnerable children. 
Finally, UNICEF advanced South-South Cooperation, sharing expertise on early childhood education and mental health with countries in Latin America and Africa, and contributing to a regional framework on child-focused SSC. Despite organizational restructuring affecting aspects of public partnerships and South–South Cooperation, progress remained steady. UNICEF advanced structured public cooperation, completed key phases of the IBSA-funded WASH initiative in Angola and designed a new WASH project in Eswatini, demonstrating the value of South–South technical cooperation.
Delivering Services Where Most Needed
UNICEF prioritized service delivery (Health, Nutrition, Education, Child Protection and WASH), in the Amazon, the Semiarid, and border areas in Roraima. In 2025, efforts combined emergency response and preparedness for the Amazon drought, the Yanomami humanitarian crisis and the alert system with indigenous organizations, and the Venezuelan migration in Boa Vista and Pacaraima. 
UNICEF expanded Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) across Indigenous territories, training 769 health professionals and delivering essential nutrition supplies, including 69,520 micronutrient sachets. Compared to 2024, when emergency actions dominated, 2025 focused on institutionalizing preparedness, strengthening local systems, and reducing risks of child mortality and malnutrition in remote communities.
WASH interventions improved water and sanitation in nine health facilities and provided safe water to 20,100 people during the drought. UNICEF ensured continuity of education and protection for children affected by displacement by integrating migrant students into 10 schools and providing learning and psychosocial support to 16,625 children in shelters through the Super Panas initiative. Child protection services assisted 2,573 unaccompanied children with referrals and mental health care, while new intercultural protocols safeguarded Yanomami and Yekuana children. In addition, 9,542 migrant families, including 4,634 children, were linked to Brazil’s CadÚnico[xxv], enabling access to Bolsa Família and other social programmes, strengthening the integration agenda initiated in 2024. Humanitarian communication through Radio Super Panas reached 51,533 people, promoting inclusion and voice.
Private Sector Partnerships and Fundraising (PFP)
UNICEF Brazil raised over BRL 129.7 million (approximately USD 23.4 million) from a diversified base of companies, foundations, philanthropists, and 250,000 individual monthly pledge donors. This represents a 20% growth in local currency compared to 2024. Individual Giving continued to be the cornerstone of sustainable funding. In 2025, UNICEF raised over BRL88.5 million (approximately USD 15.9 million) in flexible funds, driven by the acquisition of 53,000 new pledge donors, bringing the total to 250,000 active donors. Cash donations grew by 34%, and the successful monetization of a BRL 11.8 million (approximately USD 2.2 million) legacy gift significantly boosted unrestricted resources, underscoring the trust and commitment of individual supporters, ensuring predictable funding for UNICEF’s mandate. In addition, digital and DRTV channels accounted for 70% of new donor acquisitions, complemented by offline channels such as  face -to- face. Innovative campaigns, including a Smurfs subscription pilot, attracted over seven hundred pledge donors in four months, demonstrating UNICEF’s ability to engage new audiences through creative approaches. High-value partnerships remained a strategic priority. The Philanthropy team raised BRL 5.5 million (approximately USD 987K), while the corporate team secured BRL 30.7 million (approximately USD5.6 million), marking steady growth and laying the foundation for future expansion. Guided by a “fewer, bigger, better” strategy, the office streamlined corporate portfolio to focus on multi-year, multi-million partnerships with maximum flexibility. Key achievements included the first multi-million thematic partnership for health and nutrition in LAC, renewal of several multi-year agreements at BRL 1M per year, and two new partnerships exceeding BRL 5M each.
Operational Excellence and Enablers
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened operational systems to ensure efficiency, compliance, and readiness, creating the conditions for impactful programs under the Country Programme and aligning with the global Future Focus Initiative for agility and cost-effectiveness. The Country Office prioritized risk management, with top risks monitored, financial authorities updated, and more than fifty partnership agreements reviewed for compliance and mitigation, reinforcing accountability and safeguarding resources. Financial stewardship supported scale and impact, with US$29.1 million implemented—up from US$21 million in 2024—while maintaining rigorous controls over cash management and grant monitoring. Through HACT oversight, forty-nine implementing partners managed US$6.21 million in cash transfers under strengthened assurance measures, supported by targeted training to reduce risk exposure and ensure funds translated into tangible results for children. Procurement and supply operations ensured delivery of essential goods and services, processing 130 service contracts and purchase orders  totaling US$7.2 million, managing thirty public bidding processes, and establishing twenty-one long-term agreements to sustain efficiency. Workforce planning addressed priority recruitment, while flexible work arrangements and professional development advanced a supportive workplace, enabling teams to deliver results efficiently and adapt to evolving program needs. The Country Office reinforced security and preparedness through evacuation drills, first aid training, and monitoring of twenty-nine field missions, with responses to fifteen security incidents. Furthermore, UNICEF supported 150 partners in receiving security training.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
While 2025 marked important progress in shaping child-centred policies and strengthening institutional capacities, persistent structural challenges continued to constrain impact at scale. National policies did not always translate into tangible improvements at municipal level, particularly for children and adolescents in situations of greatest vulnerability. This gap reflects the complexity of Brazil’s federal system and uneven local implementation, where essential services remain inaccessible or lack quality. Intersectorality in public policy also remains more of a guiding principle than an operational reality. Limited coordination between sectors—exacerbated by high staff turnover and weak accountability—restricts the effectiveness of integrated responses. Systemic discrimination related to gender, race, ethnicity, culture, geography and socio-economic status, compounded by insufficient disaggregated data, continues to hinder equitable reach. In this context, UNICEF maintained a strong focus on integrated strategies, strengthened local governance and equity-driven approaches, operationalized through platforms such as the UNICEF Seal and flagship initiatives across programme areas, including UAPI.
A central lesson reinforced in 2025 was the importance of strategic agility—grounded in evidence, equity and systems thinking—to deliver results at scale in a polarized and fast-moving environment. Building on adaptive approaches refined in recent years, UNICEF strengthened how bottlenecks are diagnosed, alliances built and reforms sequenced, ensuring that national commitments translate into improved outcomes for the most vulnerable children and adolescents, particularly in the Amazon, the Semiarid and underserved urban peripheries of major capitals.
Policy advocacy required persistence and coordinated engagement to consolidate gains and protect child-centred measures from political or sectoral pushback. Following the approval of sugar-sweetened beverage taxation in 2024, efforts to dilute the measure continued throughout 2025. UNICEF sustained engagement with Parliament and key stakeholders to safeguard alignment with scientific evidence and international standards. This experience reaffirmed that policy victories require rapid consolidation—through standards, monitoring mechanisms and sustainable financing—before minimal compliance becomes normalized.
Maintaining a strategic focus on a limited number of advocacy priorities proved effective, enabling targeted and evidence-based influence. This contributed to advances in social policy (notably multidimensional child poverty), adolescent participation and engagement in global platforms, including COP30. UNICEF’s convening role helped keep equity and intersectorality at the centre of public debate, reinforcing its credibility across sectors.
Throughout 2025, progress continued toward policy-anchored systems that embed equity, accountability and intersectoral coordination into municipal routines. Implementation platforms, particularly the UNICEF Seal and Agenda Cidade, supported municipalities in coordinating across sectors, tailoring responses to local realities and adopting standardized monitoring tools that promote consistent, equity-oriented decision-making.
WASH in Schools illustrates this shift. Work moved from isolated infrastructure upgrades toward integrated processes aligned with public budgeting cycles, municipal sanitation plans and oversight mechanisms. Similarly, the scaling of Integrated Early Childhood Support Units (UAPI) strengthened early childhood development and protection systems, supporting caregivers, social workers and service managers through an integrated model. UNICEF also deepened efforts to reintegrate out-of-school adolescents, while advancing the next frontier: supporting successful transitions from education to decent work—especially for girls, Black and Indigenous youth, youth with disabilities, and those in vulnerable territories—through the Education and Skills agenda and the 1MiO) initiative.
Delays in configuring the integrated digital management tool for income-generation programmes temporarily disrupted sequencing and stakeholder engagement. Corrective measures—including technical adjustments, municipal onboarding and revised rollout timelines—helped restore momentum and enabled the first wave of municipal deployments. Building on these adjustments, UNICEF integrated STEAM skill-building and labour-market pathways into municipal youth platforms and strengthened alliances with employers to ensure training translates into economic opportunities. These steps position the initiative to move beyond pilots toward systemic adoption.
Evidence played an increasingly central role in planning, oversight and public debate. UNICEF’s work on multidimensional child poverty gained traction within national systems, drawing interest from ministries, audit bodies and statistical authorities. The remaining challenge is institutionalization through formal adoption to ensure equity guides budgeting, planning and monitoring. Persistent gaps in disaggregated data—particularly for Quilombola, riverine and Indigenous populations—remain a barrier. UNICEF addressed this by strengthening statistical and monitoring capacities and forging strategic partnerships to enhance equity-based evaluation and data use, with further consolidation planned for 2026.
Internally, UNICEF advanced equity integration through the development of terms of reference and recruitment of technical support for equity-oriented planning. The Gender, Race and Ethnicity Working Group contributed to Annual Work Plan reviews, improving quality and intentionality across programmes.
UNICEF supported strategic studies and dissemination at national and local levels, including sharing multidimensional child poverty findings in Recife to inform planning and advocacy. In evaluation, UNICEF completed two evaluations (CMAPS and BAE), generating actionable recommendations. CMAPS highlighted the need to institutionalize participatory approaches and accountability mechanisms, while BAE reinforced the importance of scaling School Active Search and embedding intersectoral strategies in municipal education systems. These lessons are shaping the consolidation of evaluation and research within planning cycles.  
UNICEF’s multi-country response to children on the move in LAC addressed urgent humanitarian needs while strengthening national systems for integration and tackling the root causes of displacement. The real-time evaluation concluded in 2025[i] confirmed UNICEF’s added value as a technical and systems partner with government, which ensured institutional sustainability. Co-produced models—such as Brazil’s community-based psychosocial services—demonstrated strong sustainability and scalability when anchored in government leadership and supported by UNICEF’s standards, evidence, and intersectoral coordination. Partnerships with ENAP, IBGE, MPO and IPEA advanced. UNICEF and ENAP launched the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders (ExCEL)—the first national adaptation of UNICEF’s global programme and the first delivered in Portuguese—training 42 participants. The experience demonstrated that evaluation capacity is a powerful lever for equity when leadership owns it, as well as a drive for strong policy design and implementation for impact at scale for children, and that national adaptation accelerates uptake across government tiers. Expansion to state and municipal levels is planned.
Despite progress in advancing gender equality and adolescent girls’ leadership, scaling remains a challenge. The Menina Cidadã project empowered over 10,000 girls, but coverage remained concentrated. Building on lessons learned, UNICEF will integrate the methodology into NUCA structures, which already mobilize nearly 50,000 adolescents across 2,270 municipalities, creating a systemic platform for civic participation and democratic engagement. Reestablishing the partnership with the Superior Electoral Court will be key to promoting conscious adolescent voting and female political leadership.
Global shifts in cooperation dynamics introduced funding uncertainties across the UN system, reducing predictability of resources. Budget cuts required reprioritisation, delayed recruitment and constrained delivery at scale, including in emergencies. In Brazil, UNICEF adapted by focusing resources on core priorities and aligning with the new Global Strategic Plan (2026–2029). While progress continued, funding reductions affected the scale and reach of key initiatives.
Local resource mobilization—particularly flexible and multi-year funding—and partnerships with civil society were critical to mitigating financial constraints. Community-based and Indigenous-led organizations played a vital role in reaching vulnerable populations and strengthening equity-focused planning. Expanding partnerships with public sector actors and financial institutions will be essential to enhance scale, sustainability and impact.
