The Republic of Chile is a member of the  Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a World  Bank ranked High-Income Country (HIC) and a regional leader in the Human  Development Index (HDI) with a score of 0.878. Over the past decade, it has  strengthened the rights-based framework and institutions for children and  adolescents by enacting a comprehensive law in 2022 guaranteeing the rights  of children, reforming adoption law, updating the National Policy and Plan on  Children and Adolescents (2024–2032), creating the Ombudsperson for Children  and the Undersecretariat for Children, and expanding local public education  and health services.
  
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) show good  progress in child survival, immunization, nutrition and drinking water with  numerous objectives reached. Chile, however, continues to stand out among its  high-income peers owing to persistent and substantial internal socioeconomic  disparities (as shown by HDI/IHDI comparison) (3) which pose ongoing  challenges in ensuring children’s rights and well-being. The richest 10 per  cent earn 20 times more than the poorest 10 per cent, significantly above the  OECD mean. In certain locations, 35 per cent of children live in  multidimensional poverty, while nationally 10 per cent live in monetary  poverty (1). According to an International Labour Organization (ILO)/UNICEF  study (2024) (2), almost 16 per cent of children are involved in child  labour.
  
The Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents (SITAN) in Chile 2025 (1) recognizes the national accomplishments and  institutional improvements 35 years after the Convention on the Rights of the  Child was ratified by the government. However, implementation obstacles  include coordination, technical capacity, inconsistent data systems and  fiscal space which limit the equal progression of rights for all children.  Thus, the most vulnerable children – such as those living in poverty, those  residing in peri-urban and rural areas, children with disabilities and  children with indigenous or migrant backgrounds – continue to be left  behind. 
  
Historically, low fertility and a dwindling child  and adolescent population are transforming Chile's demographics. The overall  fertility rate dropped from 2.51 children per woman in 1992 to 1.03 in 2024,  the lowest ever. This steady trend has reduced the percentage of children and  adolescents (0–19) from 34.1 per cent in 2002 to 24.3 per cent in 2024.  Demographic changes will affect social policy, public investment, and child  and adolescent services for years to come. Concurrently, Chile is  inherently vulnerable to recurrent natural hazards, such as earthquakes and  the escalating severity of wildfires that are associated with climate change.  These hazards disproportionately impact children in low-income, rural, and peri-urban  regions. These dynamics exacerbate child protection risks, emphasizing the  necessity of social systems that are prepared, prevention-focused, and  risk-informed. (4).
  
Child and adolescent well-being indicators also  suggest concerns. Chile ranked bottom in OECD adolescent well-being. Between  2018 and 2022, children's life satisfaction dropped from 72 per cent to 62  per cent, overweight and obesity rose from 53.8 per cent to 57.9 per cent and  academic performance worsened. Mental health treatment among adolescents  shows stark inequalities by gender, socioeconomic status, territory and  region. Girls, urban residents and higher-income adolescents are far more  likely to report receiving treatment, suggesting structural barriers rather  than differences in need. Other national assessments (5) show that 50 per  cent of grade 10 children perform below minimum proficiency levels in reading  and mathematics with pronounced disparities among migrant, indigenous and  rural students; about one-third of grade 4 pupils scored below expectation.  Gender differences follow worldwide trends with girls surpassing boys in  reading and boys surpassing girls in arithmetic. 
  
Although relatively low compared to other Latin  American countries, violence against children is rising and security concerns  are increasing. In addition to migration, security dominated national  presidential election campaigning in 2025. From 54 recorded cases in 2022 to  76 in 2024, juvenile homicide rates jumped from 1.0 to 1.7 per 100,000. In  2024, 6.3 per cent of murder victims were children, the highest percentage  since disaggregated data gathering began in 2018. According to preliminary  figures, 22 children and adolescents died in the first semester of  2025. 
  
The 2023 National Polyvictimization Survey (6) also  indicates significant rates of multiple victimization among adolescents aged  12 to 17, encompassing interpersonal violence from caregivers (39 per cent –  up from 35 per cent in 2017) and peers (36 per cent – up from 28 per cent in  2017). The demand for specialist child protection services is rising.  Although the new child rights protection system has improved and the national  birthrate is decreasing, the number of children needing specialized protection  services has increased from 171,404 in 2021 to 229,005 in 2024 putting strain  on service coverage, quality and response capacity. These patterns underscore  the critical need for national coordinated and proactive interventions across  protection, health, education and community (public and private) systems  involving parents and children.
  
Among the SDG indicators concerning children,  one-fifth are not reported by Chile, and most of those reported do not meet  international standards and criteria making it difficult to track progress  and develop timely policy changes. Enhancing monitoring capacity requires  quality, uniformity and disaggregation (e.g., by region, age, disability,  identity). The Ministry of Social Development and Family is receiving  technical assistance from UNICEF to create and implement a new National Child  and Adolescent Survey which incorporates modules from the Multiple Indicator  Cluster Survey (MICS).
  
The 2025 presidential election, which began in July, focused on security and violence, migration and social protection. Public discourse has shaped debates on migrant children’s access to basic services and on ensuring a juvenile justice system centred on growth, prevention and age-appropriate interventions. At the same time, global political and economic changes imposed funding constraints and new donor requirements. Following a comprehensive participatory review, the country office reduced costs by 24 per cent while preserving its core mandate to advocate for children’s rights and ensure no child is left behind.

Efforts undertaken by UNICEF are vital to  guaranteeing that children and adolescents completely realize their rights.  Building upon the challenges and structural obstacles identified, outcomes  were mainly achieved in four domains: 1) enhancing the recognition of  children's rights; 2) facilitating the implementation of the Integrated  System to Guarantee the Rights of Children; 3) promoting the prevention and elimination of violence against children; and 4) ensuring equity in  educational opportunities and funding. 
  
The results below are categorized according to the  primary strategies through which UNICEF contributed to progress: evidence  generation, technical assistance, advocacy, partnerships and capacity  building. These strategies are synergistic and mutually supportive, with  multiple approaches implemented concurrently to optimize effectiveness.  Specific approaches assumed a more prominent role depending on the context,  institutional requirements and desired outcomes.
  
1) Strengthening the positioning of children’s  rights to secure sustained progress, prevent backsliding and ensure that all  children can fully realize their potential
  
With an emphasis on producing evidence to address  information gaps, UNICEF released SITAN 2025, leveraging administrative data  and the insights of children and adolescents, thereby revising the 2022  edition. SITAN provides analysis disaggregated at national, territorial and  group levels (including children with disabilities, differences between girls  and boys and children with an indigenous or migratory background), identifying obstacles that hinder the realization of rights. It serves as a vital instrument for the oversight of children's rights offering essential contributions to the formulation of the new Chile/UNICEF Country Programme  Document starting in 2027. 
  
UNICEF also offered technical assistance for the  National Survey on the Characterization of the Reality of Childhood and Adolescence, conducted in partnership with the Ministry of Social Development and Family through the Undersecretariat of Social Evaluation and the  Undersecretariat for Children, in collaboration with the Ministries of Education, Health, and Women and Gender Equality. A pilot – Chile’s inaugural  comprehensive child rights monitoring instrument – is anticipated in 2026. UNICEF and the National Statistics Institute commissioned independent MICS  modules, supported by experts, to address essential deficiencies in SDG-related information and data concerning mental health, well-being, early childhood development, violence and child poverty. MICS explicitly builds upon the SDG monitoring assessment previously carried out in collaboration with the National Statistics Institute, assuring alignment with statistical priorities and enhancing the integration of child-centred indicators within  the SDG monitoring framework. It also expands upon prior technical support  from UNICEF to the Ministry of Social Development and Family in conducting national surveys, thereby consolidating rigorous methodological standards and enhancing capacities for child-centred data collection.
  
To enhance the evidence base for child-centred  policymaking, UNICEF and ILO supported the Undersecretariat for Children in implementing a Social Protection Floor for Children and Adolescents, a vital  component of the National Policy on Children and Adolescents 2024–2032.  Building upon the Guarantees and Comprehensive Protection of the Rights of  Children and Adolescents Law (No. 21.430) and ILO Recommendation 202, the  proposal delineates a comprehensive package of financial distributions and  essential services in health, education, care and family support designed to  ensure a minimum standard of well-being for all households with children. The  model, validated by government, academia and civil society, was evaluated for  feasibility in 2025, estimating an additional fiscal effort of 0.4 per cent  of gross domestic product for its implementation (2026–2027), representing a  9 per cent increase in child-related expenditure. To support this effort and  inform the development of the emerging National System of Support and Care,  UNICEF also generated new evidence – including the Child-Rearing Basket and  studies on adolescents’ time use and the determinants of child labour – which  sheds light on the costs associated with raising children, disparities in  unpaid care work and gendered patterns impacting children. The analysis  explicitly integrated gender considerations, emphasizing distinct care responsibilities and the effects of income insecurity on mothers, caregivers and girls.
  
Building on this foundation, UNICEF further  assisted the Budget Directorate and the Undersecretariat for Children in  enhancing child-centred public financial management, updating the annual  assessment of investments in children and adolescents, and progressing the  development of a child budget-tagging system to improve transparency  throughout the budget cycle. In parallel, to reinforce the position of child  rights, UNICEF provided targeted assistance across multiple sectors,  combining evidence generation with improvements to programmes for children  and families. In collaboration with the Undersecretariat for Children, a  catalogue was developed to guide municipalities in designing safe and  engaging public spaces. This effort prioritized municipalities serving 70 per  cent of households with children and enabled the expansion of the Crecer en  Comunidad programme from 58 to 119 communes.
  
Complementing these initiatives, UNICEF worked with  government experts, academic institutions and civil society to enhance the  psychosocial support programmes of the Undersecretariat of Ninez and the  National Youth Institute reaching 3,500 children and adolescents to deal with  mental health, socioemotional development and healthy relationships in the  past two years. The programmes formed the basis for recommendations to the  2026 national public budget.
  
UNICEF partnered with the National Youth Institute  to improve the Hablemos de Todo programme by creating a community dialogue  toolkit focused on mental health and healthy relationships. From its pilot  among 100 adolescents, it demonstrated high acceptability, endorsing its  expansion for 2026. UNICEF and civil society organizations collaboratively  organized a national seminar to advance investment in early childhood  parenting programmes, engaging 465 stakeholders. 
  
Further strengthening service delivery, UNICEF  trained 300 health professionals in sustainable breastfeeding promotion,  assisting the Ministry of Health in enhancing adherence to the International  Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, including efforts toward  legislative revisions. UNICEF also enhanced programmes that ensure access to  justice for children whose rights have been infringed, including the  development of a specialized guide and training for 522 professionals  involved in the Mi Abogado legal representation programme and 432  professionals from the Niñez y Adolescencia se Defienden programme, with an  emphasis on the child’s best interests and procedures for safeguarding  children in situations of human mobility, particularly in relation to  regularization processes. These initiatives enhanced programme quality,  fortified intersectoral coordination and improved the provision of effective,  child-centred services.
  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened its capacity and focus  on advocacy and developed specific advocacy strategies with various duty  bearers and stakeholders. A central area of UNICEF’s advocacy focused on  protecting adolescents in the juvenile justice system as motions in  parliament seek to increase penalties for adolescents in conflict with the  law for certain crimes. With other actors, UNICEF’s advocacy focused on  preventing regressive reforms, engaging decision makers with evidence on life  trajectories of adolescents in conflict with the law, international best  practices to prevent violence and criminal recruitment, and the importance  for rights-based approaches. It also advanced high-level advocacy to  strengthen the Specialized Protection Service, supporting the integration of  trauma-informed practices and addressing growing demands for specialized  protection measures. In partnership with the government, UNICEF is supporting  an independent evaluation of the National Specialized Protection Service  aimed at informing future advocacy and technical assistance in 2026.
  
UNICEF promoted social and behaviour change to  combat abuse and family separation, and advocated for prompt and  comprehensive local family assistance. UNICEF highlighted the need to invest  in children and families by elevating child poverty and comprehensive care  systems on the national agenda, notably during the presidential election.  These efforts elevated child rights in public discourse and increased national  commitments to prevention, family assistance and gender-responsive social  protection.
  
UNICEF spoke and participated at 62 national and  territorial seminars, maintaining its leadership in child and adolescent  rights. It also participated in academic, political, media and civil society  conversations on child rights, demonstrating its technical and normative  expertise. 
  
These actions have filled important information  gaps, enhanced local and national protection systems, and promoted gender  equality with the aim to influence and enable all children and adolescents to  achieve their rights.
  
2) Implementation of the Comprehensive Law on Guaranteeing the  Rights and Protection of Children: advancing intersectoral collaboration and  strengthening Local Offices for Children
  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened both national and  local institutions responsible for implementing the System to Guarantee the  Rights of Children. Progress was achieved through a combination of strategies  – particularly technical assistance, capacity building, child participation  and advocacy – ensuring advancement in a coherent, intersectoral and  rights-based manner. UNICEF provided technical assistance for the  implementation of the National Policy on Children and Adolescents 2024–2032,  including development of its monitoring and evaluation system, and the design  of the Integrated Well-being Indicator for Children and Adolescents. This  indicator, launched in January 2026 through a national public data platform,  will guide evidence-based territorial planning and ensure that policy  implementation remains coherent, measurable and rights-based across sectors  and territories.
  
At the local level, 339 out of 345 municipalities  have now established Local Offices for Children (OLN), the territorial  cornerstone of the System to Guarantee the Rights of Children. As the  installation phase nears completion, UNICEF supported efforts to strengthen  OLN governance and operational capacity by reviewing management models,  improving referral pathways and reinforcing local competencies. UNICEF also  helped strengthen coordination between OLN and the Local Public Education  Services (SLEP) to address rights violations and improve collaboration.  UNICEF, the Undersecretariat for Children and the Ministry of Social  Development and Family are also conducting an independent evaluation of the  OLN installation and early implementation process to generate evidence for  long-term institutional strengthening.
  
Capacity building is key to system implementation:
  
• Four virtual courses were produced – child  rights, education, social protection and participation – for the Civil  Service training platform, the Undersecretariat's learning platform and Agora;  OLN workers will use these courses in 2026. UNICEF taught 798 OLN experts and  published a handbook on determining the best interests of the child; thereby  strengthening local institutions. The Center for Learning on Evaluation and  Results for Latin America and the Caribbean, the Ministry of Social  Development and Family, the Budget Directorate and UNICEF also trained public  sector child rights and policy specialists. To improve transparent and  equitable public management for children and adolescents, the project  encourages participative, sustainable practices and rights-based design,  monitoring and evaluation. 
  
• The Maletín del Consejo resource was developed to  improve coordination, deliberation and representation in Local Child Advisory  Councils, promoting child engagement. Over 4,000 child council members and  facilitators will benefit from this toolbox in 2026. To enhance participation  across public institutions, civil society and youth networks, the  Ombudsperson for Children and UNICEF launched the Participa Niñez Hub, a  digital platform with over 350 resources and a secure system for uploading  materials and engaging in learning communities.
  
• UNICEF advocated for Senate regulation reforms to  designate children and adolescents as a group of interest under the Law on  Access to Public Information, creating a more inclusive and rights-aligned  transparency framework. 
  
• The Undersecretariat for Children was supported  in formulating the national pledges at the First Ministerial Conference to  End Violence Against Children in Colombia. At the global follow-up  conference, the Focused Prevention Unit reported national violence prevention  and child protection actions. 
  
Collaboration has improved coordination across  sectors and regions, reinforcing the institutions implementing the  comprehensive system guaranteeing the rights of children. 
  
3) Prevention and eradication of violence against children:  action plan and pledge
  
In 2025, UNICEF advanced national efforts to  prevent and eradicate violence against children through coordinated actions  across child protection and education systems. The main results are presented  in two key areas: i) strengthening national and local child protection  mechanisms; and ii) promoting safe, nurturing and violence-free learning  environments.
  
i) Strengthening national and local child  protection mechanisms to prevent and respond to violence
  
Through strategic partnerships, UNICEF worked with  national actors to advance legal, institutional and community-level progress.  At the third National Congress on Violence, comprising more than 600  authorities and experts, UNICEF advocated for advancing national discussion  on the prohibition of corporal punishment, contributing technical inputs that  informed the inclusion of a proposed article in the draft “harmonization”  bill of national child protection legislation, which is currently under  legislative consideration. UNICEF also underscored the influence of cultural  norms on violence by introducing social and behaviour change approaches  through a dedicated panel, demonstrating how community engagement and  communication strategies can shift attitudes and practices. 
  
The Undersecretariat for Children and UNICEF also  co-designed a territorial promotion pilot for OLN aimed at fostering safe and  nurturing community environments. UNICEF developed technical guidance and  trained 17 OLN professionals to carry out diagnostics that will inform  community dialogues in 2026. To reinforce positive norms, UNICEF contributed  to the national “Buen Trato en Movimiento” campaign and launched its “Tratarnos  bien, nos hace bien” initiative, disseminated across public spaces and media  to promote non-violent relationships and supportive environments,  complementing broader social and behaviour change strategies. 
  
The administrative protection component of the  comprehensive system guaranteeing the rights of children was expanded by  establishing a guide on determining the child's best interests and educating  798 OLN experts who safeguard at-risk children. UNICEF also helped the  Undersecretariat for Crime Prevention discover Comunidad Crece intermediate  outcomes and prevent child criminal recruitment through an intersectoral task  group that diagnosed risk factors and institutional solutions.
  
As a follow-up to the First Ministerial Conference  to Eradicate Violence against Children in Colombia 2024, UNICEF supported the  Focused Prevention Unit for Children of the Undersecretariat to strengthen  intersectoral information-sharing, plus early warning systems allowed OLN to  identify children at risk of fatal violence and intervene to avert potential  homicides.
  
ii) Promoting safe, nurturing and violence-free  learning environments
  
National initiatives were promoted to help children  learn in safe and healthy learning environments:
  
• UNICEF educated over 650 teachers and school  staff in formative, non-punitive discipline and gave early childhood  education leadership teams rights-based advice on good, non-violent  practices. 
  
• UNICEF helped Fundación Integra build up an  innovative early childhood approach, directly helping 40,997 children in 564  centres and indirectly impacting 41,786 children in 679 centres. The project  trained 350 professionals to establish safe and resilient learning  environments, reducing educational violence.
  
• The Superintendence of Education adopted a child  rights-based approach to school violence and maltreatment supervision to  improve institutional responses. This shifted school cohabitation from  punitive to formative, system-strengthening. 
  
• UNICEF also amplified children’s voices by  documenting their perspectives during National Violence Prevention Day,  presenting inputs to the Ministry of Education to inform policy decisions.  UNICEF led intergenerational dialogues showcased at the 10th World Congress  on School Violence in Valparaíso, where youth representing more than 18,000  students presented proposals to national and international experts.
  
The Ministry of Education also joined the worldwide  Safe to Learn Call to Action to ensure safe, inclusive and violence-free  learning settings in Chile.
  
4) Advancing equity and inclusion in the education  system
  
Evidence-based policies, structural improvements  and equitable learning for disadvantaged children and adolescents were  UNICEF's education priorities in 2025. Progress was made in the areas of  early childhood education and compulsory education with a clear focus on  reducing structural inequities, improving governance and supporting inclusive  educational pathways.
  
The Undersecretariat of Early Childhood Education received technical assistance from UNICEF to analyse and recommend  alternatives to the present finance scheme which disproportionately affects  low-income children. The collective commitment to establish a new regulatory  finance model was a milestone for promoting quality and equitable early  childhood education expected to reach more than 200,000 children (30 per cent  of all children in public preschools). UNICEF created geographical  information on enrolment gaps in Tarapacá and a projected demand model to  support national and territorial planning to meet enrolment challenges in  human mobility situations. A study on juvenile justice pathways for  adolescents was also undertaken for the Ministry of Education to promote  learning continuity for over 4,000 children as part of Social Reintegration  Services.
  
Following a 2024 midterm  evaluation jointly commissioned by the Directorate of Public Education  and UNICEF, the National Public Education Strategy was revised to prioritize  governance and educational trajectories, and addresses impediments such  socioeconomic segregation, rights vulnerabilities in educational communities  and the lack of a long-term state strategy for public education. UNICEF  promoted collaboration between SLEPs and OLN by providing data and  audiovisual resources on good intersectoral practices to increase  coordination within the region.
  
With support from UNICEF, the Ministry of Education  created the digital platform consejolocal.cl to improve student involvement  in SLEPs and promote their participation in local government. To address the  worries of adolescents about centralized and constrained decision-making, 70  SLEP participation officers were trained. UNICEF also assisted the ministry  to update Decree 524 on Student Councils promoting meaningful involvement via  technical assistance, innovation and digital resources. 
  
Comprehensive school health and well-being were promoted. UNICEF's high-level advocacy helped pass the national law requiring 60 minutes of daily physical exercise, which transforms learning, health and protective settings. UNICEF, the Food and Agriculture Organization, and Junta Nacional de Auxilio Escolar y Becas financed a 100-hour nutrition and food education credential for 229 school feeding programme workers, with growth anticipated for 2026. Social and behaviour change strategies promoted healthy eating and active lifestyles to 9,000 students and communities in La Araucanía, culminating in a handbook with 22 activities for active breaks to be shared nationwide.

These initiatives improved Chile's education system's finance, governance, territorial planning, participation and well-being, making it more equal and inclusive for children and adolescents.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges

IN 2025, UNICEF worked in a complex context with institutional changes, funding constraints and revised national objectives. Consequently, the Office was compelled to balance immediate requirements and mitigate financial and operational risk with long-term objectives, which initially impeded fundraising and programming efforts in the first half of the year. Navigating these tensions required agility, strategic prioritization, consistent staff engagement and a clear focus on ensuring that short-term actions supported broader structural changes for children at scale. 
The gender disparity exacerbates inequality gaps, as evidenced by data, including SITAN 2025. UNICEF implemented substantial initiatives to improve gender equality mainstreaming. The Gender Task Force, reactivated in 2025, met quarterly to update guidelines including the Gender Equality Action Plan 2026–2029. Gender markers were revised, enhancing the systematic integration of gender considerations into programmes.

Learning

In light of the Business Model Initiative (BMI) and UNICEF's Future Focus Initiative (FFI), the office held a Strategic Moment of Reflection and comprehensive participatory assessment to create a transformational vision for a UNICEF Chile 2.0 in line with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan (2026-2030) and Programming in HIC Strategy. With the need to prioritize and the recognition of strong national prioritization and institutional capacity in the areas of health and early childhood development after years of sustained systems-based support, UNICEF proceeded to sharpen its technical assistance to two critical program focus areas: (1) enhancing educational and learning pathways and skills for adolescents and (2) reducing violence prevention in homes and communities and juvenile justice, with a strong focus on the most vulnerable. In contrast, resource mobilization (PFSR) was prioritized to continue and expand into digital fundraising as well as corporate and legacy.
Additionally, a critical reflection was the necessity for a "whole office approach" whereby the programme, communication and fundraising teams align and coordinate advocacy and (public and private) partnership efforts with responsible national actors to achieve greater influence and impact for results at scale for children based on disaggregated evidence, foresight and analysis on children. Office-wide efficiencies and new internal mechanisms, communication, and methods of collaboration among technical teams are anticipated to generate stronger synergies and institutional coherence across interventions, enhancing the COs capacity to effect positive changes for children on a larger scale and with greater impact.
The office's humanitarian interventions in response to the regional migration crisis yielded an additional significant lesson. A substantial number of children arrive in Chile as unaccompanied juveniles or through trafficking, which presents substantial obstacles to the effective coordination of intersectoral efforts and the implementation of differentiated action protocols. UNICEF was required to reaffirm its zero-tolerance policy regarding abuse by UNICEF staff and partners, with a particular emphasis on risk mitigation, prevention, and capacity building. The United Nations Country Team PSEA Action Plan was prepared and implemented by the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) Task Force, which was co-led by UNICEF and the United Nations Population Fund. The Training of Trainers approach and section-specific metrics were employed to enhance capacity-building and accountability, and the training was used to train national and local officials in the Minimum Standards for Protection in Emergencies.
 
UNICEF has also been learning and contributing to knowledge exchange and South-South cooperation:
• Technical assistance was rendered to Uruguay and Nicaragua. Uruguay was shown Chile's Educational Trajectories Protection System to restore school attendance post-COVID-19. UNICEF also highlighted the Literacy and Early Childhood approach and included Por un Chile que Lee experience on teacher training to improve literacy learning. 
• MICS strengthened evidence creation and cross-country collaboration as essential programmatic support for UNICEF.
• UNICEF offered technical assistance to the Sumar Saberes alliance, advancing early childhood concepts in public-private partnerships for selection and scale-up. An evidence-based website enabling school administrators to choose technical support was also built. 
• UNICEF assisted Argentina in conducting adolescent violence research on perceptions and prevalence mirroring Chile's Polyictimization Survey (2017 and 2023). Argentina's national capability was strengthened via virtual and in-person technical exchanges, and survey methodological definitions. UNICEF helped Peru and Uruguay strengthen their private sector fundraising strategies and implementation. 
The SITAN development, humanitarian response, and cross-sector coordination efforts have demonstrated that the ability to prevent, identify, and respond to risks early is essential for achieving an enduring impact. These key points guarantee that UNICEF can expand its impact for the most vulnerable children and influence structural reforms. UNICEF Chile is focusing on system-level actions that will yield scalable results for the most vulnerable children, such as enhancing territorial preparedness through training on Minimum Standards for Protection in Emergencies, enhancing government accountability through improved disaggregated data, and facilitating cross-sector learning pathways, in order to build on these insights.
 
Future outlook

Advocacy that is persistent, innovative, and agile is prioritized. Building om the Country Programme Evaluation, UNICEF will enhance institutional capacities to prioritize the generation of evidence and foresight on the situation of children and adolescents, advocacy and expand partnerships to inform decision-making. This enable UNICEF to remain a trusted partner in the promotion of the rights of children and adolescents, maintains its role as a catalyst for systemic change, and effectively raises funds for UNICEF programs worldwide. Engagement with the incoming government will be influenced by many years of system-strengthening efforts across government administrations and evidence to develop a new Country Programme 2027=2030.
The establishment of Generation Unlimited is a critical objective, as it is a multi-sector partnership that is designed to improve the employment prospects of youth by providing them with quality learning and skill development. In 2025, the strategy framework will be established to align with national objectives, stakeholders will be engaged, and youth requirements will be mapped. This will prepare for co-creation sessions in early 2026 and a Phase 1 launch in mid-2026. 
The objective of the office restructuring is to position UNICEF for future effectiveness by expanding its worldwide resource mobilization efforts and enhancing its impact and influence for children. It also aims to establish a future UNICEF office model in countries that are transitioning from Middle Income Country to HIC status, while simultaneously addressing child disparities and being a net-contributing private sector fundraising operation.

Colombia closed 2025 with a modest economic recovery. Official projections estimate GDP growth at 2.6 per cent, with inflation near 5 per cent and persistent fiscal pressures. Although unemployment fell to 7 per cent from 8.2 per cent the previous year, job informality remained high, affecting 55 per cent of the workforce.  
Monetary poverty declined to 31.8 per cent nationwide, its lowest level in over a decade, but remained higher in rural areas (42.5 per cent) and among Indigenous peoples (61.6 per cent). Leaving no one behind remains a challenge for the country as poverty declines, but it still significantly affects children and adolescents.  In 2024, national monetary poverty incidence for households with two children was 52.5 per cent and 76.3 per cent with three. Maintaining the commitments established in the 2030 Agenda and moving towards SDGs targets for all are particularly relevant today for Colombia.
Colombia continues to face one of the longest-running and most complex humanitarian crises in Latin America, driven by armed conflict, climate-related disasters, violence and migration flows. Violence escalated in 2025, resulting in 1.5 million people directly affected between January and October. Armed non-state actors (ANSAs) are now present in 71 per cent of municipalities, exposing children and adolescents to child recruitment and use, gender-based violence and landmines.  
Over the past two years, over 740 children and adolescents were recruited by illegal armed groups. In the first half of 2025, 52 attacks on education were reported, including armed clashes, explosives, direct attacks, and military use of schools.  In November 2025, the Ombudsman's office presented a report on military operations, noting a growing trend in the number of children killed. According to figures from the National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, ten children died in Guaviare, one in Puerto Santander, and another one in Arauca.
Between January and September 2025, accidents involving landmines, unexploded ordinance and improvised explosive devices left 102 victims, including three children. Data revealed that 46 previously unaffected municipalities and 27 areas formerly declared mine-free now report new contamination or incidents, signaling a widening of explosive risk in new territories.
In 2025, 190,000 new victims of forced displacement were registered in 2025 (the highest recorded since systematic reporting began). Forced confinement, civilian movement restrictions and humanitarian access are becoming increasingly common in conflict-affected areas. Between January and October, one million individuals faced mobility restrictions, while more than 122,800 were victims of confinement. Humanitarian access constraints, especially in the Pacific, Amazon and border regions with Venezuela, left over one million people cut off from services and assistance, representing a 93 per cent increase compared to 2024.   
Stricter migration controls in North and Central America led to a 97 per cent drop in irregular crossings through the Darién Gap and contributed to a reverse in migration, with more than 14,000 people returning to Colombia, including unaccompanied children. 
Many conflict-affected communities are also highly vulnerable to climate shocks. More than 815,500 people were affected by disasters during the first nine months of 2025, mainly floods, windstorms, landslides and flash floods. The cumulative impact of these overlapping crises is undermining the physical and emotional development of an entire generation.  
Children living in vulnerable and conflict-affected areas, as well as Indigenous and Afro-descendant populations, face higher nutritional and health risks. 
In 2025, there were 19,132 reported cases of moderate and severe acute malnutrition among children under five. The highest rates were recorded in La Guajira, Vichada, Guainía and Chocó, departments with a high concentration of Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities and low access to safe water and sanitation. While national data reports a stunting prevalence of 10.8 per cent, UNICEF-supported SMART surveys reveal more severe conditions in historically excluded municipalities. Persistent gaps in water and sanitation services in rural and remote areas also remain a concern, with 1.4 million people nationwide still practicing open defecation, predominantly in rural settings.
The infant mortality rate was estimated at 10.82 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024, with marked territorial disparities. Mental health challenges among children and adolescents remain significant, particularly in conflict-affected communities. According to official records, suicide accounted for 16 per cent of all violent deaths among children and adolescents in the past year. 
As of November 2025, 8,776,117 children and adolescents were enrolled in the education system, reflecting a 10 per cent decline in enrollment since 2022. Approximately 926,000 children remain out of school, accounting for 9.5 per cent of the school-age population. Learning poverty, defined as the share of children who cannot read and understand a simple text by age 10, stands at 51.4 per cent nationwide. However, there are immense disparities, with some municipalities performing at the level of high-income countries, while others, most affected by poverty and conflict perform poorly, with nearly all children unable to read and understand a simple text.
Domestic violence against children remains high, with a reported rate of 57 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. In 2023, children and adolescents accounted for 81 per cent of all medico-legal examinations related to sexual violence, with girls 10-14 years old disproportionately affected.
The government continued advancing ambitious reforms to the health and pension systems amid strong congressional resistance and mounting fiscal pressures. While the administration’s sustained public discourse on climate action, peacebuilding and drug policy reform, heightened political polarization and armed confrontation constrained consensus-building.  
The adoption of Law 2447 of 2025, which prohibits and prevents child marriage and early and forced unions, reinforced the country’s commitment to eliminating harmful practices that disproportionately affect girls, as committed in SDG targets. This law is a decisive step towards full realization of children’s and adolescents’ rights by addressing one form of gender-based violence. However, one year after its presidential signature, there is no concrete evidence of the development of the national programme to prevent child marriages and early unions (as ordered by the law) nor engagement of girls and adolescents to build collective actions in line with law´s commitments.
Within the framework of peace dialogues with several non-state armed actors, the Office of the High Commissioner for Peace launched the First Floor of Peace (Primer Piso de la Paz) strategy, placing children at the centre of peacebuilding efforts and including commitments to end the recruitment, use and sexual violence against children. In 2025, four-armed groups signed child protection-related commitments linked to ongoing peace processes

The humanitarian–development–peace nexus guided UNICEF Colombia’s programming throughout 2025, ensuring that urgent support for crisis-affected children and families was linked to medium- and long-term solutions. While addressing immediate needs, UNICEF and its partners strengthened local services and the capacities of state institutions, civil society, caregivers, children and adolescents to reduce vulnerability and build more peaceful and resilient communities. 
Across programmes, UNICEF placed the rights of the most vulnerable children at the centre of public policy through advocacy, the use of equity-focused evidence to inform decision-making and accountability, and sustained investments in system strengthening, community engagement and social behaviour change. UNICEF also fostered public and private sector partnerships for social innovation and sustainability, promoted gender-responsive and transformative programming, and ensured the meaningful participation of adolescents at national and local levels. Across its interventions, UNICEF included actions to strengthen stakeholders’ knowledge and self-protection skills in the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) and ensured access to accountability and feedback mechanisms that fostered transparency and local empowerment.
To reinforce its territorial approach, UNICEF prioritized local-level action through six sub-offices covering priority municipalities in 12 departments selected based on key social and child-related indicators. This expanded presence is expected to gradually enhance UNICEF’s ability to reach children and families facing the highest risks, including those in ethnic and rural communities, migrants, displaced populations, and children affected by violence.
Conflict escalation in 2025 posed significant challenges for UNICEF’s humanitarian response. In particular, the crisis in the Catatumbo region along the Venezuela border placed a severe strain on government capacities and humanitarian actors nationwide. With support from thematic and CERF funding, UNICEF delivered a coordinated, multisectoral response that provided life-saving assistance while laying the foundations for longer-term recovery, development and peacebuilding. 
Key results achieved in 2025:
1.       Government adoption of a UNICEF-supported community-based model for early detection and management of child malnutrition
In 2025, UNICEF Colombia achieved concrete results under Outcome 2.1 of the UNSDCF, contributing to the realization of the human right to food, particularly through efforts to reduce hunger and malnutrition.
UNICEF addressed persistent maternal and child health inequities, particularly in rural and ethnically diverse territories where access to health services remains severely limited. The gaps in access, driven by geographic isolation, insecurity, and cultural and linguistic barriers, continue to place women and children at higher risk of preventable illness and death. UNICEF’s interventions focused on reducing these inequities by strengthening access to care in hard-to-reach settings and promoting systemic changes to improve the equity and effectiveness of health and nutrition services.
In this context, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health to expand and institutionalize community-based care models as an effective strategy to reach the most isolated populations. Through targeted technical assistance and evidence generation, UNICEF demonstrated the effectiveness of approaches led by community health workers (CHW) in improving the early detection and management of child malnutrition. Evidence generated during 2024–2025 directly informed national decision-making and led to a significant policy outcome: the Ministry of Health adopted a simplified, adapted community-based approach to malnutrition management as part of its emergency plan to reduce malnutrition-related mortality in prioritized municipalities  of Chocó, La Guajira and Guainía, where 26,000 children under five years of age benefited from the model. This policy marked the first time the Government of Colombia formally incorporated this strategy, representing a significant step toward reducing health and nutrition inequities in rural and ethnic communities.
Besides influencing policy, implementing this model improved coverage and the quality of care in vulnerable communities in Chocó along the Pacific Coast, while strengthening community participation in health responses. By empowering communities to play an active role in identifying and addressing child nutrition and health risks, UNICEF helped build local ownership and capacities, reinforcing the sustainability of interventions and the health system’s ability to respond more effectively to maternal and child health needs in high-vulnerability contexts.
2.      Influencing the curriculum for early childhood education 
Seeking to expand access to and improve the quality of early childhood education (ECD) nationwide, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Ministry of National Education (MEN) and the Colombian Institute of Family Welfare (ICBF) to strengthen and update the ECD curriculum framework. UNICEF’s technical assistance ensured the revised curriculum framework was aligned with national early childhood development priorities, which reinforced legal and policy frameworks that define ECD as a structured, rights-based process. In Colombia, where there is no common national curriculum, the development of a common curriculum framework for ECD is a particularly important milestone.
The new technical guidelines broaden the objectives of early childhood development and provide clear guidance for planning meaningful pedagogical experiences in the classroom. The strengthened curriculum responds to long-standing challenges in ensuring quality, inclusive, and culturally and climate-relevant early education across diverse contexts, including rural and indigenous territories.
This framework will serve as the reference for national teacher training programmes, which reach approximately 5,600 teachers who serve 90,000 children nationwide. This work contributes to Colombia’s broader goal of universalizing early childhood education with a focus on equity, territorial relevance, and intersectoral coordination.
3.      Inclusive and transformative social protection
As part of the Joint Care and Inclusion Programme implemented with UN Women, UNDP and UNFPA, and with support from the Global Fund for Disability, UNICEF worked with national government counterparts, particularly the Ministry of Equality, MEN and ICBF to strengthen the alignment between child-focused policies and inclusive education, with a specific focus on addressing the unequal burden of unpaid care work.
Building on this collaboration, and with the aim of territorializing the care policy through an inclusive early childhood development lens, UNICEF partnered with the Mayor’s Office of Barranquilla to establish a Local Management Model for care and support systems for children with disabilities and their families and caregivers, in coordination with ICBF’s Inclusion Support Centers. The model strengthens intersectoral coordination between case management and family support services, and introduces payment-for-results mechanisms linked to improved access to early childhood education and the reduction of unpaid care work.
As part of the model’s implementation toolkit, 20 online courses were developed and made available through the Agora platform, enabling replication and scale-up by other country offices across the region.
4.      Promoting inclusive and accessible education for all
An innovative pilot, led by UNICEF with the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) and the Education and Culture Secretariat in Turbo, Antioquia, integrated the Let’s All Learn to Read (ATAL) strategy with Accessible Digital Books (ADB) and Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The aim was to assess the accessibility of ADBs in early literacy, analyze their integration into teaching and learning processes in both urban and rural settings, and generate evidence on their potential impact on learning for children with and without disabilities.
The pilot evidenced high levels of acceptance among teachers and students, improvements in reading comprehension, and increased classroom participation. All participating teachers incorporated ADBs into their lesson plans, and 91 per cent of students with disabilities were able to use the resource without significant barriers. A landing page and a video were prepared to document the pilot experience and highlight the link between ADBs and UDL. 
Building on the pilot’s results, UNICEF scaled up the methodology by implementing it with 6,085 teachers, tutors, community leaders, and other key stakeholders across nine municipalities, reaching 91,275 children and adolescents. The result for children is stronger early reading skills and expanded vocabulary. The methodology also supported the development of diverse communication abilities, including oral expression and initial exposure to Colombian Sign Language. By including accessibility and Universal Design for Learning principles into classroom practice, the initiative translated the right to inclusive education into concrete action, advancing the implementation of Article 24 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
Educational innovation and the digital divide
In 2025, UNICEF advanced educational innovation through its collaboration with the IDB to develop FLAPP, an AI-based learning assessment tool that modernizes measurement processes and supports timely, evidence-based pedagogical decisions for marginalized children. This experience showed that innovation depends not only on tool design but also on enabling conditions. While FLAPP showed strong potential, limited connectivity in rural and dispersed areas, and uneven technical capacity constrained large-scale deployment. In 2026, the office will address these constraints by strengthening digital infrastructure through public-private partnerships, expanding teacher training on AI-based tools and data use, and pursuing scaling through pilots in specific communities.
5.      Adolescents as agents of change: Advancing meaningful participation across policy and community spaces 
In 2025, UNICEF Colombia achieved concrete results in strengthening meaningful adolescent participation, positioning young people as active contributors to public policy and community change. Through a multi-level approach aligned with Youth2030, the CRC, and the Committee on the Rights of the Child's concluding observations, UNICEF strengthened adolescents’ capacity to participate by equipping them with skills, platforms, and confidence, while also supporting institutions to create more inclusive and effective participation spaces.
At the community level, UNICEF partnered with 20 community-based organizations to strengthen their ability to work with and for adolescents. Through these partnerships, 7,000 children and adolescents participated in community transformation initiatives. In La Guajira, the Manaure Lab collective amplified the voices and talents of indigenous adolescents in Manaure and worked with the local government to integrate child- and adolescent-focused initiatives into municipal plans, reaching approximately 1,000 people in 2025.
At national, departmental and local levels, UNICEF enabled more than 36,000 adolescents and young people from vulnerable contexts to engage in decision-making spaces with representatives from ministries, the ICBF, governors’ and mayors’ offices, embassies, United Nations agencies and international organizations. Twenty adolescents were directly involved in updating the Atlántico Department’s youth public policy, ensuring that the needs and proposals of more than 100 adolescents and young people were incorporated into the revised policy. Furthermore, adolescents influenced key policy processes, such as the National Biodiversity Plan, the National Care Systems Plan, the Atlántico Department’s Youth Public Policy and the updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), as described below.
6.      Mainstreaming children’s rights into Colombia’s climate agenda 
Furthermore, in 2025, UNICEF promoted the engagement of children and adolescents in climate mobilization and decision-making spaces, including youth-led platforms such as Colombia’s Local Conference of Youth (LCOY). UNICEF supported the meaningful participation of children and adolescents in the update of Colombia’s NDCs.
UNICEF also supported the inclusion of the Child-Sensitive Indicators Methodology to review national climate targets and translate them into systematic, concrete, measurable actions for children and adolescents. As a result, the updated NDCs 3.0 explicitly recognize children and adolescents as rights holders and key actors in climate action and include a child-sensitive approach as a cross-cutting pillar of the framework, as well as child-sensitive indicators. By aligning the NDC with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, General Comment 26 of the Committee on the Rights of the Child, and the Paris Agreement, the normative foundation of Colombia’s climate agenda is stronger, and clearly established conditions for child-centred climate implementation and financing.
7.      Child protection results in high-risk contexts
UNICEF provided sustained support to the Government to advance the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and address the 2015 concluding observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child. Through a comprehensive approach which combined advocacy, technical assistance and capacity strengthening, UNICEF delivered tangible progress at both national and local levels. This work advanced the Children Affected by Armed Conflict (CAAC) agenda, strengthening prevention and response to recruitment and use by armed groups, gender-based violence and other forms of violence that disproportionately affect children. Results were reinforced through direct engagement in humanitarian emergency settings, particularly in Catatumbo, Cauca and Chocó, effectively linking policy dialogue with concrete protection actions on the ground.
Through risk-informed humanitarian–development nexus programming, UNICEF ensured continuity between emergency response and longer-term child protection systems strengthening. In Catatumbo, UNICEF worked with government institutions and other partners and allies, including WFP and UNHCR, to deliver a coordinated multisectoral response integrating temporary alternative care, mental health and psychosocial support, protective learning environments and family and community strengthening. As part of this response, 5,400 displaced children and adolescents and their caregivers received psychosocial support, 1,533 women and children accessed gender-based violence prevention and response services, and 7,598 displaced children regained access to learning. These interventions not only addressed immediate protection risks but also helped restore protective systems to reduce future vulnerabilities. In Catatumbo, UNICEF, as co-leader of the UN task force for the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse, established an interagency PSEA mechanism involving UN agencies, their partners and service providers, which provided a set of harmonized reporting channels, materials and communication with communities. 
UNICEF also strengthened institutional preparedness and response capacity by developing child protection methodologies, emergency protocols, and contingency plans, which were transferred to ICBF and local authorities. These tools improved risk identification, activation of protection pathways and access to specialized services, enhancing the ability of local systems to protect children in contexts of conflict, displacement and territorial control by armed actors. In parallel, UNICEF supported prevention strategies with adolescents, families, community-based organizations and traditional leaders, addressing structural risk factors and strengthening local capacities to reduce children’s exposure to various forms of violence.
At the system level, UNICEF strengthened the National Family Justice System and local child protection systems during humanitarian responses by providing technical assistance to nine national and territorial entities, standardizing care models and improving interinstitutional coordination.  UNICEF delivered training and key protocols to local authorities, including the Family Commissioners in Tibú and Acandí, to activate protection routes and request ICBF protection services based on the best interest of the child. These efforts contributed to timely, relevant and culturally appropriate humanitarian responses, particularly in municipalities with limited institutional capacity or affected by protracted crises.
In 2025, UNICEF also advanced the creation, strengthening, and scaling of innovative, evidence-based programmes aimed at generating sustainable change. These include the Mutual Care strategy for adolescents affected by recruitment and use by illegal armed groups, the Child Protection Care Networks initiative focused on community protection and social behavioural change, and the Caring for Child Survivors Toolkit, designed to improve care and response to sexual violence.
8.      Results-Based Financing (RBF) strategy for the most vulnerable children
In 2025, UNICEF Colombia made significant progress in designing and operationalizing the RBF Strategy for the most vulnerable children, under the Business Model Initiative. The strategy aims to strengthen the national impact investment ecosystem and to channel public, private, and cooperation resources toward interventions that deliver measurable improvements in child well-being, particularly in the Pacific and Border regions.
The strategic framework was finalized, and co-creation processes were launched for five priority roadmaps covering education, health and nutrition, violence prevention, climate change, and social protection and inclusion. These processes engaged national ministries, local governments and social investment actors, strengthening institutional ownership and positioning RBF as a practical tool to advance children’s rights.
UNICEF further consolidated its interest within the results-based finance ecosystem by convening a national networking event with corporate foundations, donors and impact investors, fostering strategic partnerships to structure innovative financing mechanisms and projects. In parallel, progress was made in designing a results-based financing mechanism with Canada’s OFFER Fund, focused on inclusive early childhood education in Barranquilla, which will serve as a demonstration model for future RBF interventions.
9.      Linking emergency response, recovery and peacebuilding for children
In 2025, UNICEF Colombia made significant progress in a humanitarian context marked by intensified armed conflict, recurrent climate-related disasters and growing access restrictions. Despite a 22 per cent reduction in funding compared to 2024, UNICEF consolidated its role as a key actor in protecting the most vulnerable children by concentrating efforts in priority territories, strengthening intersectoral coordination and optimizing limited resources through integrated, territorially targeted interventions. 
UNICEF responded to sudden-onset and protracted emergencies, including natural disasters, mass displacement and confinement, irregular and reverse migration and armed conflict across ten departments. [i] UNICEF enabled more than 19,700 children, adolescents and women to access essential health services and conducted 11,332 nutritional screenings in hard-to-reach rural areas. While direct attribution is not possible, these actions strengthened key enabling conditions, such as access to services, territorial coordination and community awareness, that are widely recognized as essential for sustained progress in maternal and child health outcomes.
UNICEF supported the implementation of the national Education in Emergencies policy, enabling 5,545 children and adolescents to access formal and non-formal education and providing training to 1,910 teachers. These achievements marked a significant milestone in advancing global commitments and strengthening national capacities to ensure educational continuity during emergencies. In child protection, 8,255 children and caregivers accessed essential services, and 13,790 people received training on explosive ordnance risk. These results were enabled through community-based delivery models and UNICEF-led sectoral coordination under the Humanitarian Reset.
UNICEF strengthened complementarity between humanitarian action and peacebuilding. In the Catatumbo region, UNICEF worked closely with the Victims’ Unit (UARIV), a key institution in the implementation of the 2016 Peace Agreements, to align humanitarian assistance for displaced populations with collective reparation measures under the Victims’ Law (Law 1448 of 2011). Collaboration with UARIV enabled the engagement of key local actors involved in collective reparation measures, including the Mayor’s Office of Cúcuta, ICBF, community-based organizations, the church and educational institutions, cultural centersprovi and sports schools. Within this framework, UNICEF delivered a multisectoral humanitarian response, reinforcing State-led collective reparation processes and strengthening the link between emergency response, recovery and longer-term peacebuilding efforts.
Humanitarian results were supported by investment in preparedness and territorial capacities, including early warning systems, Comprehensive School Risk Management Plans, departmental working groups and pilot initiatives for anticipatory action. These efforts reduced response times and strengthened inter-institutional coordination. Finally, flexible, unmarked resources allocated by UNICEF for humanitarian action and funding from the Central Emergency Response were essential to sustain sectoral coordination, context analysis, cluster leadership and a technical presence in prioritized territories, ensuring continuity and scalability of the response in a context where only 11 per cent of the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was funded.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Strengthening decentralization through territorial capacity development
UNICEF along with UN system supported the design of the Law on Territorial Competencies, which seeks to strengthen decentralization, clarify government roles and responsibilities and address institutional capacity gaps. UNICEF led the identification of critical local weaknesses, using a differentiated approach based on municipal typologies and population characteristics. The study provided evidence of the heterogeneity of Colombian territories , and highlighted the need for tailored capacity-strengthening strategies for dispersed rural, border, ethnic and intermediate urban municipalities.
UNICEF’s support also demonstrated that institutional capacity gaps cannot be addressed in isolation from population-level inequalities. Linking institutional assessments with disparities related to gender, ethnicity, disability and rurality proved essential to advancing inclusive decentralization. Regulatory reforms must be accompanied by sustained investments in public management systems, human resources, information systems and intersectoral coordination for decentralization to be translated into improved outcomes for children.
A lesson from this process was the need for a more coordinated and strategic United Nations presence at local level. In response, UNICEF and UN partners are advancing an interagency programme to strengthen territorial management to support prioritized territories implement decentralization processes. 
Financing for children in Colombia
In 2025, UNICEF Colombia launched its results-based financing strategy to strengthen the investment ecosystem for vulnerable children. The strategy aims to ensure that public and private investments are directed towards measurable improvements in child well-being, particularly in territories with the greatest gaps, by promoting financing mechanisms that link disbursements to verified results. The strategy promotes more efficient, equitable, and transparent use of public and private resources, with a focus on reducing territorial disparities and scaling effective interventions. It also supports national and local governments in improving planning, budgeting and results-based management, while fostering coordination and innovative financing mechanisms, including performance-based payments, social impact bonds and blended finance. Looking ahead, UNICEF will prioritize mapping key financing stakeholders, instruments and decision-making processes that shape investments in children. This will inform capacity-building efforts to strengthen the results-based financing ecosystem, enabling influence at scale and supporting territorial development.
Strengthening Colombia’s child protection system
UNICEF carried-out a comprehensive analysis of Colombia’s child protection system and identified structural gaps that limit the provision of timely, high-quality, integrated services for children. Strengthening human resources emerged as a key priority, given overwhelming caseloads, limited training and uneven access to specialized tools among frontline professionals. Strengthening multisectoral coordination and modernizing child protection information systems were also identified as essential.
In response, UNICEF developed an action plan to provide targeted technical assistance, particularly to small municipalities with limited budgets, focused on strengthening human resources, improving service quality and advancing interoperable information systems. 
Sustaining momentum beyond legislative and policy reform 
UNCIEF needs to strengthen its engagement beyond the approval of legislative and policy reforms. While UNICEF supported key child rights legislation, greater emphasis is needed on implementation to ensure sustained results. In some cases, technical assistance, cross-sectoral planning and budgeted action plans were not sufficiently consolidated. For example, following the adoption of Law 2447 of 2025, which prohibits child marriage and early and forced unions, the next phase should focus on coordinated, cross-sectoral support for implementation and enforcement. This includes strengthened collaboration with UNFPA, UN Women, and civil society organizations to translate legal commitments into concrete actions.
Preparedness, anticipatory action and coordination in humanitarian action 
A key lesson learned this year was the effectiveness of a phased approach to preparedness and anticipatory action. In 2025, the office strengthened territorial analysis tools that enabled the pre-positioning of supplies, faster response activation and improved coordination with local actors, significantly reducing response times. The experience confirmed that anticipatory action must be scaled-up and sustainably financed to effectively protect children in remote areas. Looking ahead, UNICEF’s emergency response will prioritize territorial preparedness, scaled-up anticipatory action, more efficient coordination mechanisms and stronger partnerships.
Achieving results in most complex contexts of the country
In 2025, a WASH intervention demonstrated the critical importance of selecting implementing partners with proven experience in the country, in rural dispersed areas. A chosen partner lacked knowledge of the national regulatory framework and did not show the technical or operational capacity required for infrastructure activities. Their unfamiliarity with legal contracting processes, combined with a subcontractor’s failure to apply technical standards and meet agreed timelines, resulted in unfinished rehabilitation works that delayed the project’s broader outcomes. These challenges were further exacerbated by the armed context and geographic constraints, underscore that the infrastructure component may need to be developed separately from other WASH components in future interventions.
Cross-cutting programmes
In 2025, progress on cross-cutting priorities such as child marriage, early childhood development, adolescent participation, and climate change was uneven, reflecting the inherent challenges of advancing these agendas across multiple sectors. While different teams addressed these issues, actions were often planned and implemented from sector-specific perspectives, resulting in fragmented interventions. The absence of clear operational agreements and shared programmatic indicators limited coordination and collective impact. Addressing these gaps in 2026 will require stronger intersectoral coordination, the definition of common objectives and indicators, and more deliberate joint planning to ensure coherent and mutually reinforcing action across sectors. 
UNICEF Colombia launched its 11-member Corporate Advisory Council, uniting leaders from key sectors to promote responsible business practices and advance outcomes for children, with a technical focus on school-to-work transitions and national advocacy. The country office advanced its regional alliance with CAF by developing a Colombia-adapted “Crianza Respetuosa” WhatsApp course, now under design. UNICEF also ensured child-focused inputs in the private-sector workstream of Colombia’s NDC 3.0. Advocacy efforts shaped child-rights recommendations in the 2025 UN OHCHR report. Additionally, Colombia gained global visibility through the Banco de Bogotá family-friendly workplace case, showing measurable business and child-rights impacts.
 
Managing organizational transition and staff well-being
In March 2025, the office started a new country programme. Confirming the new workplans aligned with the new CPD and adjusting to budget constraints led to important operational challenges, compounded by structural changes, recruitment processes, and staff departures. 
In 2026, a key challenge will be transitioning to the new structure with the Pacific and Border Hubs to improve territorial presence, technical assistance and support in line with UNICEF’s strengthened territorial approach. This transition will require close collaboration with other UN agencies and, internally, a clear role definition to increase the efficient use of limited resources within a more diversified territorial set-up.
A further priority for 2026 will be supporting teams through the change process by strengthening team cohesion, promoting psychological safety and prioritizing physical and mental well-being.

In July 2025, Costa Rica attained the World Bank’s high income country classification, with full graduation expected in January 2027. Social spending fell from 24% of GDP in 2020 to 20% in 2024 (State of the Nation Report, 2025), amidst rising inequality and organized crime, and intensified migration pressures—disproportionately impacting the most vulnerable. Nevertheless, Costa Rica remains a regional leader in political stability, environmental stewardship, and progressive social policy, offering scalable models for improving outcomes for children and families across Latin America and the Caribbean.

Child poverty continues to limit children’s rights, well being, and developmental potential. While household income poverty fell from 23% in 2022 to 15.2% in 2025, child poverty remains disproportionately high at 33%. Despite a four percentage point reduction since 2023, 11% of children still live in extreme poverty (INEC, 2025).

Violence against children is increasingly a barrier to realizing their rights. UNICEF supports prevention efforts by helping strengthen safe environments and improving national systems that prevent and respond to all forms of violence. This work is evidence-based and carried out with national authorities and civil society, reinforcing the State’s duty to protect children and aligning with the 2030 Agenda commitment to leave no child behind.

Over the past five years, Costa Rica’s homicide rate rose from 11.2 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2020 to 16.7 in 2025, the second highest level on record. The country registered 873 homicides, reflecting a worsening trend in lethal crimes. Official data also show a sharp rise in firearm related violence against children, with 50 child homicide victims—the highest figure ever reached of whom approximately 80% classified as “settling of accounts/revenge,” strongly suggesting a link to armed violence (OIJ 2025).

Sexual violence against children has surged, exposing entrenched gender-based violence. Between 2022 and 2024, cases of children requiring health treatment by the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS) rose by 50%, reaching 11,768. Girls bear the brunt: adolescent girls (13–17) represented 91.9% of outpatient cases, with 11 girls treated for every boy. Vulnerability peaks at ages 13–14, and attentions concentrated in San José, Alajuela, Puntarenas, and Limón—underscoring the need for targeted prevention and protection.

In 2025, the National Child Protection Agency (PANI) registered 96,476 reports of threats or violations of children’s rights—a 12.9% increase from 2024. The leading causes were physical and psychological violence (25%), negligence (21%), and violence stemming from family conflicts (18%).

Latest available PANI 2024 data reports over 13,000 children without parental care, underscoring the need to strengthen child protection systems and expand family based care options.

Adolescent and youth exclusion remains a major challenge: 146,000 youth ages 15–24 (20.7%) are not in education, employment, or training (NEET)—well above the OECD average of 12–15%. Gender gaps are significant: 22% of young women in the NEET group are outside the labor force due to family and care responsibilities, compared with 18% of young men, underscoring persistent gendered patterns in labor participation and unpaid care.

Costa Rica’s universal public health system remains a regional benchmark, yet significant challenges persist. Maternal mortality has risen sharply—from 15 per 100,000 live births in 2022 to 32.7 in 2024—driven by factors encompassing gaps in prenatal education, unequal caregiving responsibilities, and spread of misinformation. Infant mortality also increased to 10.3 per 1,000 live births, largely due to perinatal conditions and gaps in prenatal care, marking the second highest level in a decade (INEC, 2024).

Nutritional challenges compound these risks: 19.8% of children aged 6–12 are overweight, 14.1% are obese, and 1.8% are undernourished (Weight and Height Census, Ministry of Health, 2017). Despite strong legal protections, exclusive breastfeeding in the first six months remains low at 27%, and only 39% of infants continue breastfeeding alongside complementary foods (MICS, 2018).

Suicide is the third leading cause of adolescent death, and in 2022, 45% of 2,896 attempts involved children aged 5–19. Youth aged 15–19 reported approximately 959 attempts, representing a 70% increase compared to 2021 (CCSS, 2025).  

Adolescent pregnancies among 15–19 year olds fell by 11% between 2023 and 2024—from 4,560 to 4,055 cases—with births to adolescent mothers declining slightly from 9% to 8.8%, yet over 4,000 cases persist annually, underscoring the ongoing need to expand access to sexual and reproductive health information and services.

Costa Rica achieved near universal educational access, with nine in ten children and adolescents aged 4–18 attending school; however, structural disparities persist. Despite high enrollment, 9% of adolescents aged 15–17 are two or more years over age for their grade, only 72% complete secondary education on schedule. Just 51.1% finish within six years, underscoring persistent barriers to progression and completion. Inequities are particularly pronounced among marginalized groups: Indigenous students average only 6.7 years of schooling—two-years below the national mean—and migrant and refugee children experience prolonged schooling disruptions, with 40% of caregivers reporting that children aged 6–18 have been out of formal education for over a year, and up to two years for those in transit.

Violence in schools undermines learning environments, driving higher dropout rates, increasing the risk of long term social exclusion and mental health challenges. Reported cases rose from 24,641 in 2022 to 25,935 in 2024—an increase of nearly 5%—and about 44% of students (approximately 528,000) report having experienced bullying. Yet only 6% of schools have guidance counsellors, significantly limiting the education system’s capacity to prevent and respond to bullying and broader school coexistence challenges (State of the Nation Report, 2025).
