Costa Rica experienced reduced migratory flows. Returnees from Mexico and families entering through the northern border continued to arrive, with many moving onward to Panama while others remained in the country seeking economic opportunities. In the absence of a regulated north–south migration system and amid porous borders, migrant families became dispersed nationwide, while growing concentrations in San José intensified xenophobia and heightened risks of trafficking, child exploitation, survival sex, and street begging. (UNICEF, WFP, UNHCR, 2025). Amid these shifting dynamics, IOM monitoring recorded 19,923 migrants and returnees, 14,269 stranded—43% children—with shelter identified as their most urgent need.

Health, Nutrition, Environment and Sanitation 
Costa Rica’s 2024 Mental Health Policy addresses alarming trends: suicide as the third leading cause of adolescent death. With UNICEF support, the Ministry of Health developed the National Standard for Comprehensive Child and Adolescent Mental Health—an interdisciplinary, child centered model integrating health, education, and social protection systems to strengthen coordination and prevention. Set for adoption by Presidential–Ministry Decree in early 2026, it will ensure age appropriate services nationwide and reinforce prevention across schools, communities, and health facilities.

To strengthen perinatal care, UNICEF and UNFPA supported the Social Security Administration in updating Perinatal Education Procedures, emphasizing the first 1,000 days, gender and rights perspectives, and tailored approaches for diverse groups, including migrants, Afro descendants, Indigenous communities, and women with disabilities. The new guidance—developed with input from 125 health workers and postnatal women and adolescents—will be implemented nationwide, standardizing perinatal education, ensuring cultural relevance, and reinforcing frontline capacity for equitable maternal and child health services at scale.

To strengthen Local Health Governance, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Health to scale child-centered planning nationwide, leveraging interventions in Buenos Aires, Guatuso, Mora, and Talamanca—rural, indigenous, and peri-urban contexts. These experiences refined evidence-based models, now institutionalized through a virtual course, ensuring sustainable, more equitable primary healthcare nationally across all 84 cantons.

UNICEF tackled persistent barriers to breastfeeding in Costa Rica. UNICEF, with the National Education and Nutrition Comprehensive Childcare Centers (CEN-CINAI), co-created 30 culturally relevant messages under the National Breastfeeding Strategy. Backed by technical and financial support, the campaign reached 1.7 million people, promoting shared caregiving, maternal well-being, and positive parenting.

Under the FAO–UNICEF Joint Sustainable Development Goals Programme, UNICEF advanced agrifood system transformation in Buenos Aires and Guatuso—rural cantons chosen for diversity and vulnerability. By embedding community voices and strengthening governance, lessons now guide national scale-up toward resilient, inclusive food systems.

In partnership with the Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers, the Climate Change Directorate, and the Swedish Environmental Research Institute, UNICEF developed a climate rationale and action plan aligned with Costa Rica’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), strengthening water security, services, and shock resilience nationally.

Early Childhood Development and Education
In 2025, UNICEF advanced systemic reforms and large-scale initiatives to strengthen early childhood development and education in Costa Rica, in alignment with national priorities and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.  

In partnership with the National Network for Childcare and Child Development (REDCUDI), a feasibility study of cost structures and legal pathways for expanding Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC), positioned Early Childhood Development and Financing Reform as a national priority. Findings presented in 2025 elevated financing reform in ministerial debates, driving consideration for equity-focused investment to expand services for 117,000 vulnerable children.

UNICEF partnered with REDCUDI to deliver evidence-based parenting support through a train-the-trainer model, reaching 1,000 children and enabling institutional replication. Building on the Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) Study, UNICEF launched a microsite on the first 1,000 days, offering accessible guidance and advocacy tools to promote positive parenting, aiming to reach 5,000 individuals by the first quarter of 2026.  

Through the Comprehensive Safety and Risk Education Plan (SEGURED), UNICEF supported the Ministry of Public Education in institutionalizing school safety nationwide. SEGURED now reaches 4,462 public schools, with diagnostics completed in 90% of schools and safety plans in place in 76%, benefiting more than one million students. Integrated into the SABER monitoring system, all plans are digitized, enabling real-time reporting on violence, socio emotional risks, and disaster preparedness. These action plans provide schools with concrete measures to prevent and address violence—major drivers of educational exclusion, thereby strengthening protective environments and supporting improved retention and completion over time. UNICEF further enhanced national capacity by training education leaders and launching a digital course through the Professional Development Institute, embedding SEGURED within Ministry systems to ensure sustainable, nationwide safeguarding by 2026.

Through the United Nations Pact for the Future Dialogues, UNICEF and partners (UNESCO, UNFPA, IOM) established a National Education Forum, consolidating a civil society dialogue to reduce fragmentation and strengthen advocacy. Ahead of the 2026 elections, the Forum produced a joint roadmap and Charter of Principles, embedding education transformation and investment in children as cross-cutting priorities in political platforms.  

To address persistent gender gaps in Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEAM) Education, UNICEF guided the national STEAM strategy, more than doubled coverage from 200 schools in 2023 to 503 in 2025, benefiting 1.2 million students. Initiatives such as Ciber Chica-STEAM promoted digital literacy and girls’ participation in technology-rich environments.  

Child Protection
In 2025, UNICEF advanced Costa Rica’s national child protection agenda amidst escalating violence, organized crime, and social fragmentation. 

To address rising sexual violence against children, UNICEF partnered with the Legislative Assembly’s Commission on Children, Youth and Adolescents to strengthen responses to child sexual abuse, ensuring investigations and prevention efforts prioritize the child’s best interests and avoid revictimization. UNICEF provided technical guidance and shared global child-rights practices. Building on a high-level visit by Luis Pedernera, former Chair of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, UNICEF convened a landmark forum uniting the Judiciary, Legislature, and Executive leadership of PANI. These institutions jointly committed to coordinated, gender-responsive measures to protect children’s rights to safety, justice, and recovery. This momentum continues in 2026 through a new UNICEF–ILO partnership to eliminate harmful child labor, including child trafficking and all forms of sexual exploitation and abuse.

In migration and refugee contexts, UNICEF strengthened Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse through community-based awareness and improved reporting pathways. A total of 4,901 people—including 123 pregnant women and 169 persons with disabilities—received essential information on risk prevention and referral mechanisms. 

UNICEF Costa Rica’s 2025 Safe Spaces Evaluation identified key gaps: limited sexual education, persistent taboos, and lack of local protocols leave communities vulnerable and leaders without adequate institutional support, undermining confidentiality and trust. In 2026, UNICEF will strengthen 35 Child Safe Spaces through a standardized Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) policy and participatory capacity-building, in close collaboration with PANI to ensure institutional ownership. Actions include awareness campaigns, family engagement, confidential reporting mechanisms, and improved interinstitutional coordination. Full adoption is planned for early 2026 to deliver timely, coordinated protection and empower communities to break silence and stigma. To ensure sustainability, UNICEF’s technical assistance enabled the PANI to adopt a planning framework and toolkit, officially integrating Child Safe Spaces into its 2026 budget, Local Management Strategy, and mandates for Child Protection Mobile Units. In 2025, sites were streamlined from 44 to 35 while maintaining reach, engaging 2,921 children monthly in education and ludic activities.

UNICEF advanced a coordinated armed violence prevention model with PANI and the Ministries of Public Education and Public Security, reaching 15 schools in 10 high risk communities. Strengthened school–police coordination units and upgraded Police Athletic Leagues—supported with equipment, training, and structured life skills curricula—created protective pathways that reduce adolescents’ exposure to violence and recruitment risks. Anchored in UNICEF’s evidence that SDG level results require catalytic interventions that shift the priorities and resources of whole ecosystems, the programme fostered stronger institutional collaboration across education, security, and child protection actors. Complementary actions included territorially focused mapping of prevention services, formalized referral pathways, and integration of armed violence prevention into Comprehensive School Safety and Educational Risk Management Plans. These measures established the conditions for phased expansion to the 30 highest risk communities in 2026 and, progressively, nationwide.

To reduce reliance on residential care, UNICEF supported PANI in designing and implementing targeted deinstitutionalization efforts for children facing complex reintegration barriers. Integrated psychosocial, medical, and mentoring interventions enabled 400 children to advance toward family based care. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened four core protection programmes—foster care, family reintegration, independent living, and life planning—aligning shelters, NGO residences, and PANI offices into a coherent continuum that prioritizes safe and permanent family environments. 

To strengthen interinstitutional, intersectoral, and family centered responses, UNICEF worked with REDCUDI to scale the Families in Action (FAMA) programme through a virtual train the trainer model. This expansion enabled 1,000 families to access structured guidance on early stimulation, positive parenting, and violence prevention. UNICEF also supported PANI in advancing its deinstitutionalization strategy, promoting family based care and reintegration—an area central to Costa Rica’s commitments under the 2024 Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children.

Social Protection and Child Poverty
To strengthen Child-Centered Social Protection, UNICEF partnered with the Social Protection Institute (Instituto Mixto de Ayuda Social, IMAS) to develop the Case Management Module for the National Information System and Unified Registry of State Beneficiaries (SINIRUBE). Scheduled for completion in early 2026, this tool will shift social services from fragmented, institution-centric approaches to an integrated, household-centered model. It enables institutions to assess household needs, provides traceability and improves transparency through data interoperability. By identifying areas of multiple deprivations, the module strengthens targeting and coordination, ensuring timely, adequate support for children and caregivers—critical for reducing inequities and expanding social protection coverage.

UNICEF partnered with PANI to modernize outdated measurement of child-focused public expenditure, last estimated at 6.9% of GDP in 2021—¢2.3 million colones (US$4,580) per child annually. The initiative introduced automation and sustainability, enabling institutions to produce annual estimates through standardized processes and integrated systems. UNICEF supported updating expenditure estimates for 2022–2024 and strengthened capacity for evidence-based fiscal planning, enabling monitoring of the National Policy for Children and Adolescents 2024–2036 and helping identify funding gaps and mobilize resources for sustained investment in children. 

UNICEF, together with the Resident Coordinator, government and Member States, advanced Costa Rica’s child-focused financing agenda to address equity gaps. Through high-level dialogue, UNICEF strengthened evidence-based return-on-investment policymaking and mobilized public and private actors to advocate for greater investments in children most affected by poverty and multiple deprivations. UNICEF co-convened the Forum on Innovative Financing with the Inter-American Development Bank and private and public sector actors, integrating children’s rights into national and international financing discussions. This effort galvanized Costa Rica’s Finance Minister to deliver a keynote at UNICEF’s side event during the Financing for Development Conference in Sevilla (IF4D), amplifying global advocacy for child-focused investment. Several ministries are now exploring innovative financing mechanisms informed by the methodologies presented at the Forum. 

These results were made possible through core Regular Resources, strategically complemented by Social Policy thematic funding, which proved critical in enabling upstream policy engagement, system strengthening, and the delivery of results at scale.

Adolescent Development and Participation
Building on Costa Rica’s co-chairmanship of the United Nations Ocean Conference (UNOC3) with France, UNICEF joined forces with the UN Resident Coordinator and UNESCO to galvanize adolescent and youth voices in ocean and climate action. During UNOC3, UNICEF and UNESCO engaged the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) to include 100 children from coastal communities in promoting ocean protection and reducing single-use plastics, improving environmental literacy and fostering sustainable practices in areas most affected by coastal degradation. UNICEF also partnered with Mission 1.5°—a youth-led NGO—to empower 50 adolescent girls to participate in climate negotiations with national and local authorities, strengthening advocacy skills and enabling them to present proposals to legislative and municipal bodies. UNICEF, with UN partners, strengthened Costa Rica’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) Strategy 3.0 presented at COP30, ensuring adolescent and youth voices and gender perspectives informed climate policy. This advocacy embedded child rights in national climate action, reinforcing resilience and intergenerational equity. 

U-Report Consultations with 1,721 adolescents revealed gaps in rights literacy, gender disparities in unpaid care, and expectations for corporate responsibility. Drawing on nationally generated insights from U-Report, UNICEF and UNFPA produced an evidence-based advocacy brief that amplified the voices and lived experiences of adolescent girls regarding unpaid domestic and care work.

Communication and public advocacy
In 2025, UNICEF focused advocacy on the ‘leave no one behind’ principle of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Agenda, responding to persistent inequality, child poverty, and rising violence against children. High-level advocacy amplified these efforts globally: In February, Her Majesty Queen Mathilde of the Belgians visited Costa Rica as Honorary President of UNICEF Belgium, spotlighting the paradox of transitioning economies in Latin America and the Caribbean. Her visit mobilized international visibility, showcased the value of partnerships with UNICEF National Committees, and generated more than 160 media stories, amplifying calls for sustainable investment in children.

Evidence based advocacy for the elimination of violence against children (EVAC) became the strategic anchor across health, education, social protection, and emergency programming, fully aligned with UNICEF Latin America and Caribbean regional priority. In response to escalating sexual violence, UNICEF partnered with the Legislative Assembly’s Commission on Children, Youth and Adolescents to provide technical guidance and global best practices aimed to strengthen investigative protocols and reinforce prevention measures.

UNICEF advanced its strategic shift from direct implementation to systemic engagement as Costa Rica moves toward high-income status and graduation in 2027. A key driver was strengthened collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, positioning child rights at the center of national priorities and enabling policy reforms and alliances critical for systemic change. UNICEF delivered 13 government communication strategies, including Mental Health Awareness, School Gardens, and the National Youth Survey, reinforcing partnerships.

UNICEF’s communications platforms achieved a 24% increase in social media followers (226,000 total), 825 media pieces in 122 outlets, and 691 social mentions. Highlights include a Positive Parenting microsite featured in 20 news pieces, a breastfeeding campaign reaching 1.7 million people, and fundraising campaigns for Hurricane Melissa relief and end-of year “Tiempo de Dar.” 

Fundraising and Private Sector Partnerships with the private sector
In 2025, UNICEF Costa Rica grew private-sector income by 12%, from US$954,596 in 2024 to US$1,071,086, despite market challenges—reflecting a more resilient, diversified model.

A critical milestone was achieved with the launch of UNICEF’s new donation website, transforming the digital fundraising experience through improved user navigation, boosted conversion rates, and opened access to Costa Rica’s growing digital market. For the first time, UNICEF Costa Rica generated one-time online donations for global emergencies and captured high-intent leads for pledges. This strategic shift created a sustainable hybrid model that strengthens emergency responsiveness while driving long-term revenue growth.

To reinforce donor commitment, UNICEF initiated the transition to a new Costumer Relationship Model (CRM) and donor care provider, enabling omnichannel communication, WhatsApp engagement, and tailored donor journeys.

Revenue from strategic partnerships more than doubled—from US$25,947 to US$58,000—through deeper collaborations. AERIS expanded support for Child Safe Spaces and hospitalized children’s education, while Liberty advanced a multi-year partnership on cyberbullying prevention and STEAM education, integrating funding with employee engagement and advocacy. Ferreterías EPA drove growth through nationwide in-store fundraising focused on children and climate action

UNICEF strengthened system approaches by implementing the Brand Barometer to guide audience strategies and designing catalytic financing with Caricaco Foundation to mobilize blended capital for social protection. These efforts position UNICEF Costa Rica to secure diversified, sustainable resources for children.

Emergency and Humanitarian Assistance
While in 2025, migrations flows experienced overall reductions, Costa Rica faced mounting migratory pressures, driven by increasing return flows of families through the northern border with Nicaragua—19% of them children. Porous border crossings and uncontrolled mobility patterns dispersed families nationwide, heightening risks of trafficking, exploitation, survival sex, and street begging. 

The increasing presence of migrant families in urban areas risked fueling xenophobia and social tensions, particularly in the lead up to the February 2026 presidential elections. The United Nations worked closely with Costa Rican authorities to uphold a human rights–centered public narrative, consistent with Costa Rica’s longstanding leadership on human rights in the region.

Concurrently, migrant flows—both those intending to settle and those in transit—placed additional strain on overstretched services, especially along the northern border with Nicaragua and in San José. In this rapidly evolving landscape, humanitarian teams from IOM, UNHCR, UNFPA, WFP, and UNICEF coordinated to reinforce state capacities and sustain essential services for children and families, adapting support as needs and mobility patterns shifted.

Efforts focused on the highest arrival frontier and capital areas—Los Chiles (Nicaragua), Corredores (Panamanian), and San Jose—through strong collaboration with national institutions, local governments, and civil society organizations. Partnerships with counterparts including PANI and the Ministry of Health enabled timely and strengthened national response. Community based and non governmental organizations served as key implementing partners, playing a critical role in ensuring services reached children and families in the most vulnerable situations. 

Shelter capacity remained a critical gap, with EMISUR functioning as the only State run facility. As demand grew—and as other UN agencies faced unforeseen financial constraints that limited their planned support—UNICEF assumed responsibility for four additional shelters: Casa Esperanza (Los Chiles), Dormitorio Solidario, Fundación Llovera, and Beth Lehem (San Jose). Together, these shelters provided safe accommodation to 2,904 people (601 girls/adolescent women, 625 boys/adolescent men, 799 women, 875 men, and 4 non binary individuals). All facilities offered psychosocial support and referrals to government and civil society services. To optimize capacity and ensure continuity of care along the north–south corridor, UNICEF established a shelter referral network linking Los Chiles, San José, and EMISUR, strengthening coherence across the humanitarian response.

Child protection remained central, with Child Safe Spaces and mobile teams providing psychosocial support and referrals to 4,689 migrants (1,961 girls, 2,206 boys, 366 women, 156 men).

Health and Nutrition: With the Ministry of Health, life saving care and referrals reached 3,077 people (1,015 women, 1,062 men, 498 girls, 502 boys). UNICEF also assisted caregivers of children under five through lactation spaces providing nutrition support, early stimulation, SRH counseling, family planning, and violence prevention guidance, serving 541 beneficiaries.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH): Continuous WASH access was ensured in shelters and transit points, supported by awareness activities. A total of 28,221 migrants accessed 24/7 WASH facilities in Los Chiles, Corredores, and San José. UNICEF delivered hygiene kits—including menstrual hygiene supplies—to 3,970 individuals; and implemented hygiene promotion and WASH in Emergencies workshops with institutional partners. UNICEF supported the establishment of the Los Chiles WASH Coordination Platform co-led by the Ministry of Health.

Education in Emergencies: For out-of-school migrant children, UNICEF promoted family engagement and alternative education. In Los Chiles, 1,027 children and adolescents (541 boys, 486 girls) received educational support, including 395 with individual learning materials. In San José, 191 individualized educational references enabled 69 children to integrate into the national education system.

Adaptive Management, Lessons, and Way Forward  
Costa Rica entered a transition period in 2025 after achieving World Bank high-income country (HIC) status, with formal graduation expected in January 2027. Despite this milestone, persistent child rights disparities, high rates of child poverty, sustained migration pressures, and rising levels of violence, including gender-based violence and violence against children, continue to constrain equitable progress and strain social protection and public service systems. These challenges coexist with Costa Rica’s strengths in democratic governance, human rights leadership, environmental sustainability, and civic freedoms, shaping a complex development outlook for 2026. 

Guided by the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2026–2029), UNICEF accelerated its shift toward an upstream HIC engagement model, prioritizing evidence-based advocacy, policy influence, systems strengthening, and strategic partnerships over traditional service delivery. Aligned with Costa Rica’s commitments under the Universal Periodic Review, the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), UNICEF strengthened partnerships with national actors to advance systemic reforms, particularly in relation to ending violence against children (EVAC). 

Recognizing the State as the primary duty bearer, UNICEF’s 2025 Situation Analysis guided programme reprioritization to maximize focus, scale and impact. Priorities were jointly validated with key counterparts, including PANI and the Ministries of Public Education, Health, IMAS, Foreign Affairs, and MIDEPLAN. This process aligned CRC and SDG commitments with feasible delivery pathways and an engagement model suited to Costa Rica’s context. EVAC was confirmed as the strategic priority for system-wide impact, and UNICEF will continue advancing this agenda with the new administration taking office in May 2026. 

Key Gaps  
Fragmented social services, limited data interoperability, and weak case traceability continue to constrain the realization of child rights, particularly for migrant families in the informal sector. In response, UNICEF supported the strengthening of SINIRUBE’s integrated information architecture, including enhanced traceability functions to improve case management, reduce fragmentation, and facilitate coordinated assignment of social protection benefits. A strengthened, family-centered SINIRUBE is essential for timely, rights-based support and for enabling regularization pathways for migrant households. 

Traditional programmatic delivery models proved less scalable and cost-effective in a high-income setting. Fragmented responses and fiscal constraints underscored the need for stronger public and private financing for children, data-driven targeting, and durable coordination mechanisms to sustain EVAC, education quality, and inclusion outcomes. 

In addition, UNICEF’s EVAC agenda requires more consistent follow-through on Costa Rica’s commitments under the 2024 Global Ministerial Conference. Sharper sequencing, clearer accountability, and strengthened inter-institutional coordination will be needed in 2026 to translate commitments into results. 

Lessons and Innovation  
Results are strongest where policy reforms were combined with budget analysis, financing solutions, and co-created partnerships with the private sector and international financial institutions around measurable outcomes. These approaches strengthened alignment between policy ambition and fiscal feasibility. 

Child and adolescent participation remain insufficiently institutionalized and require strengthening to inform programme design and accountability. 

Targeted catalytic initiatives effectively tested and de-risked innovative approaches, while upstream engagement strengthened enabling policies. To complete the transition from project-based to system-anchored approaches, UNICEF must ensure that all initiatives have credible pathways to scale, grounded in institutional commitment, sustainable financing, and time-bound evaluations. In 2025, UNICEF’s technical support enabled PANI to integrate Child Safe Spaces into the 2026 budget, Local Management Strategy, and mandates of Child Protection Mobile Units through a dedicated planning framework and toolkit, strengthening sustainability. In contrast, the violence prevention pilot in 15 high-risk schools, while promising, still requires a jointly agreed inter-institutional roadmap defining roles, financing, evaluation mechanisms, and conditions for national scale-up. 

Sustained advocacy across the Executive, Legislative, and Judicial branches strengthened policy dialogue and institutional coordination on child rights. High-level engagement, including the Minister of Finance’s keynote at UNICEF’s side event during the Global Financing for Development Conference in Sevilla, Spain, further anchored child-focused priorities within fiscal debates. 

Through innovation, UNICEF expanded collaboration with universities, technical institutes, government partners, and UN agencies to advance digital and system-strengthening solutions. AI-based tools, virtual platforms, and hybrid learning models supported by real-time monitoring improved efficiency and coverage. Examples include MEP’s SABER digitalization of school safety plans, REDCUDI’s virtual Families in Action (FAMA), and the joint development of Sofía with UNFPA and CCSS to strengthen access to timely maternal and child health information. These initiatives generated decision-grade data and enhanced adaptive management. 

UNICEF also adapted its humanitarian response to shifting migration dynamics, ensuring continued protection and basic services for migrant children at border areas and in San José, including gender-based violence risk mitigation. In parallel, national emergency preparedness was strengthened, and UNICEF continued supporting the adoption of shock-responsive social protection mechanisms. 

Forward-Looking Adjustments 
Building on these lessons, UNICEF will consolidate a stronger upstream portfolio centered on EVAC, social policy, and inclusion, supported by clear accountability frameworks and performance benchmarks. Priority will be given to children facing the greatest structural barriers, including migrant, Afro-descendant and Indigenous populations, and children with disabilities, while addressing persistent gender inequalities, particularly sexual violence against girls. Reducing territorial disparities will remain central, with a shift from isolated pilots toward coordinated, system-embedded scale-up anchored in national institutions. 

UNICEF will also expand private sector engagement and collaboration with international financial institutions to mobilize innovative financing for child-centered public policies. Building on the 2025 Innovative Financing Forum, UNICEF will support blended finance mechanisms, social impact investments, and structured public–private partnerships aligned with priorities such as digital inclusion, violence prevention, and STEAM education.

In parallel, UNICEF will strengthen public finance for children, evidence systems, and monitoring frameworks. Building on advances in expenditure measurement and SINIRUBE, UNICEF will support automated reporting, integration of child-sensitive indicators, improved data harmonization, and expanded real-time analytics and territorial dashboards to inform the equity agenda. 

Finally, UNICEF will deepen inter-agency collaboration within the UN system, building strengthened coordination under the UN Cooperation Framework to promote integrated, system-wide results under strong government leadership. 

Together, these strategic adjustments will enable UNICEF Costa Rica to operate through a more agile, evidence-based, and partnership-driven model, strengthening institutional capacity, safeguarding children’s rights, and advancing inclusive and sustainable development in Costa Rica’s high-income transition context.

In 2025, Cuba confronted persistent economic adversity and compounding shocks that significantly impacted child and adolescent well-being. Structural demographic shifts—marked by declining birth rates, an aging population, and substantial migratory flows—further strained human and professional resources critical for sustaining social services, particularly in health and education. Despite social spending traditionally exceeding 40% of the state budget, allocations for education, health, and social assistance represented less than 4% of total national investments, exposing a critical gap in infrastructure, equipment, and essential resources.


In Cuba the disaster risk has increased due to the frequency and severity of hydrometeorological hazards (due to climate change and variability) and the progressive accumulation of socioeconomic, environmental and infrastructure vulnerability. This fragile context was aggravated by Hurricane Melissa, the fifth major disaster in four years, which struck eastern Cuba in October. Severe flooding and wind damage affected 215,000 homes, 1,859 educational institutions, and 642 health facilities across 33 municipalities in Santiago de Cuba, Granma, Holguín, and Guantánamo—areas already recovering from previous hurricanes and earthquakes. In WASH, nearly 3 million people experienced service interruptions, and over 500,000 remain without safe water access, underscoring the urgent need for climate-resilient water and sanitation systems at household and institutional levels.


Epidemiological risks escalated with the co-circulation of Chikungunya, Oropouche, and Dengue, disproportionately affecting children, adolescents, and older adults. Children accounted for over two-thirds of related mortality. Post-hurricane conditions—electricity outages, WASH disruptions, and shortages of medicines—amplified vulnerabilities. The health system faced severe stress: 68% of essential medicines were in short supply, and critical drug shortages for childhood hematologic cancers reduced survival rates from 75% to 60%. Congenital defects became the leading cause of death among children under one year, linked to limited prenatal and postnatal care. The under-one mortality rate rose to 7.1 per 1,000 live births in 2024, compared to pre-pandemic levels of 4–5 per 1,000. Maternal mortality remained below 50 per 100,000 live births (40.6 in 2024), while low birthweight prevalence increased from 5.1% (2017) to 7.6% (2024).


The energy crisis compounded service delivery challenges: 84% of water systems depend on fossil fuels, leaving large segments of the population without reliable supply. Access to safely managed drinking water remains critically low (46.3% of the population), and only 52% have safe sanitation. Aging infrastructure drives inefficiencies, with 55% of water lost through leaks. In eastern provinces, prolonged drought affected three million people, further exacerbated by hurricane damage.


Education systems faced mounting pressures, particularly in early childhood care. Coverage of day-care centers and institutional modalities remained limited. The 2024/25 school year recorded declining retention rates across all levels, most notably in technical-vocational and secondary education—key pathways for adolescent skills development and employability.


Child protection indicators reveal persistent gaps. In 2025, only six new foster families were constituted, bringing the total to 22 since 2023, while 520 children and adolescents without parental care remain in 56 institutions, with over 30% institutionalized for more than five years.


Despite these challenges, 2025 marked a landmark achievement with the approval of the Code on Children, Adolescents, and Youth, reinforcing child rights and participation. The ongoing decentralization process, grounded in constitutional recognition of municipal autonomy, continues to create opportunities for localized governance and context-specific interventions. Progress was also noted in gender equality and the recognition of rights for children and adolescents with disabilities, who represent 8.1% of the population.


However, other trends in the situation of children are the early pregnancy, school dropout among girls, low participation of adolescent girls in technical-vocational education, and limited access to menstrual hygiene supplies. Children and adolescents with disabilities face continued challenges in educational continuity, workplace transition, and social inclusion.
