In 2025, UNICEF Cuba consolidated its role as a trusted systems broker and delivery partner, advancing child rights through policy reforms, service delivery at scale, and national capacity development—despite prolonged economic constraints, energy disruptions, and climate-related shocks. The office’s strategic approach combined systemic change (laws, protocols, financing instruments), multi-sector coordination, scaled delivery, data and evaluation capability, innovation, and effective emergency response. This integrated model protected essential services, accelerated equity outcomes, and strengthened resilience for the most vulnerable children and adolescents.

UNICEF mobilized six times its annual office budget (15% of mobilized funds are ORE (2,28M/14.72M)), doubled programme implementation, and expanded operational presence through new field monitors in eastern provinces—tripling field visits relative to 2024 (5x if compared to 2023). Results were achieved through policy brokerage (e.g., the new Code on Children, Adolescents and Youth, alternative care and juvenile justice protocols; inclusive education diagnostics; national WASH self-assessment and Action Plan), delivery at scale (health, nutrition, WASH, inclusive education, adolescent services, psychosocial support), and capacity development (workforce training, local evidence systems, and evaluation culture). The office also advanced innovative financing, including climate and debt-swap mechanisms focused on solarization of social services, while integrating humanitarian response and development programming to reach over 620,000 people affected by Hurricanes Oscar, Rafael, and Melissa. advances consisted in the drafting of a Local Fund for Childhood development, which is under discussion by the government, and agreements with INRH and CITMA for a joint submission to GCF for example. This combination sustained UNICEF’s position as a credible, effective, and indispensable actor for children in Cuba.

Policy gains were matched by robust implementation pipelines. In child protection, UNICEF provided technical support for drafting the newly approved Children, Adolescents and Youth Code (CNAJ) and complementary regulations on alternative care and juvenile justice, establishing an integrated child rights protection system with specialized subsystems and a national governing body. These reforms include a monitoring mechanism on the situation of children and operational tools that ensure legal provisions translate into service pathways. The Resolution on Alternative Care Modalities—developed through participatory processes with children and adolescents living in institutions and with institutional staff—operationalizes the priority of family based care over institutionalization and lays the groundwork for a systemic reorientation of alternative care nationwide. UNICEF also supported the national validation of the Office of the Ombudsman’s Protocol for Attention to Children and Adolescents, consolidating this institution as a specialized child protection actor. The protocol has enabled more consistent child rights restoration responses and set a precedent for accessible, dedicated bodies with clear mandates for child protection. A defining feature of the reform process was meaningful child and adolescent participation. Consultations on legal norms—unprecedented in Cuba’s legislative history—led to concrete adjustments in laws, advanced institutionalization of participation in public policy, and strengthened participants’ knowledge of rights and competencies for active citizenship, reinforcing social accountability around child protection.

Education reforms advanced equity and inclusion through diagnostics and local financing design. UNICEF and national counterparts laid the foundations for a Local Fund for Early Childhood Development (FLODI), linking integral protection with local economic development to enable evidence-based planning across territories. This model ties ECD services to municipal productivity and governance, strengthening sustainability and shared responsibility across sectors. To operationalize equity at scale, UNICEF and the Ministries of Education and Labor and Social Security designed and validated the Childhood Characterization Tool, piloted in Holguín with more than 40,000 children. The instrument is a survey-based tool designed to capture the living conditions and household circumstances of children aged 0–6. It identifies key vulnerabilities across six dimensions, quantifies the number of children in vulnerable situations, and generates a robust dataset to inform decision-making for targeting at multiple administrative levels. Training for 165 methodologists and 874 educators enabled communities to identify multidimensional vulnerability and link data to local decision making and resource allocation—a turning point for improving outcomes for the youngest children. Inclusive education advanced through consolidated diagnostic protocols (ADOS 2) and strengthened coordination of Diagnostic and Orientation Centers (CDOs), creating eight regional diagnostic spaces and nationwide training for early identification and support of children with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disabilities. Gender strategies and protocols in vocational schools embedded equity and safety into adolescent training, aligning school environments with rights-based standards.

Health and nutrition policy updates were embedded into programming. UNICEF supported nationwide updates to care protocols for preterm and low weight children in primary care, and the Kangaroo Mother Care method, through a multidisciplinary team at the Ministry of Health. This ensured consistent standards across the service continuum and improved quality of neonatal and maternal care, even amid energy constraints and supply fluctuations. In parallel, WASH sector strengthening progressed through a comprehensive national self-assessment and an Action Plan derived from the RI WASHBAT process, aligned with the National Water Plan 2030 and the SDGs. Cuba’s commitment to WASH was reflected in an average annual budget growth of 124% between 2020 and 2024 and the implementation of multisectoral platforms. From the WASHBAT workshop, three critical outputs emerged: the Action Plan, technical inputs for a Climate Finance Strategy, and the Climate Rationale for the water and sanitation sector. UNICEF provided technical leadership to integrate climate rationale into sector planning, supporting identification of three strategic lines for climate finance and resilience, and promoting territorial equity in investment allocation. Through advocacy and partnership engagement—including dialogue on the Countervalue Fund and the Green Climate Fund—UNICEF strengthened accountability and positioned Cuba within global WASH platforms, including participation in the Sanitation and Water for All Ministerial Dialogue in 2025. Disaster risk reduction systems were strengthened through intersectoral mechanisms and a shock responsive approach with Civil Defense, the Red Cross, and the Ministry of Science and Environment, linking education with community preparedness for climate and environmental risks and embedding resilience within school systems and local planning.

These policy and systems advances were mirrored by delivery at scale with measurable reach. UNICEF and partners reached approximately 1,420,000 children and adolescents nationwide—about 73% of children and adolescents in the country—through strengthened health and nutrition services and essential supplies. Human Milk Banks provided nutritional support to 2,207 at risk children (1,126 girls and 1,081 boys); 17,926 mothers received breastfeeding assistance, and 3,514 mothers became donors, collectively providing 849,538 liters of breast milk. Equipment upgrades across 23 referral neonatal services improved care for 30,901 newborns (approximately 44% of total births), including incubators, ultrasound, ventilators, cardiotocographs, consumables, and other essential supplies. Preventive services were safeguarded, with 100% Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) vaccine coverage achieved for 80,000 one-year olds and over 95% coverage among young children. To protect maternal and child health amid energy disruptions, UNICEF began solarizing two polyclinics in Granma, benefiting 20,978 patients and ensuring continuity of services during the energy crisis. Neonatal care capacities were strengthened in six provinces, improving care for 23,000 newborns at risk (approximately 32% of total births). Targeted nutrition support reached approximately 8,000 pregnant and lactating women in hurricane and earthquake vulnerable territories, while multiple micronutrient powders were provided to 25,000 children (approximately 81% of children in Guantánamo and Artemisa). Medicines and critical supplies bridged gaps in care: 109,800 people in Granma and Holguín gained access to essential treatments via 69 medical kits, 49 acute diarrhea kits, and 200 packages of oral rehydration salts; 204,000 people in four provinces received medicines through 125 first aid kits; and 10,100 family mosquito nets were distributed to prevent vector borne diseases.

Adolescent friendly services and community health engagement scaled reach and participation. UNICEF supported a network of 59 adolescent spaces serving 135,000 young people and mobilized 4,089 adolescent health promoters, with 783 trained in 2025. Engagement expanded among women, with 2,192 involved in community health promotion activities. In total, 364,269 adolescents (190,473 girls)—approximately 37% of adolescents nationwide—participated in community health prevention activities led by health promoters across the country, reinforcing demand side capacities and peer led behavior change aligned with public health priorities.
Following Hurricane Melissa and the preceding Hurricanes Oscar and Rafael in 2024, WASH service restoration and resilience work addressed interrupted water supply, loss of storage, and deterioration of hygiene and sanitation conditions. UNICEF and partners supported 346,075 people with access to safe drinking water, including solutions with solar pumping; 28,000 people in Guantánamo and Artemisa received 5,600 family hygiene kits; and 10,900 people received water storage units. Recognizing the centrality of mental health within integrated WASH health education responses, psychosocial support reached up to 38,300 people as part of the recovery effort.

Education outcomes were strengthened through early childhood expansion, inclusion, and resilience measures. UNICEF supported 291 childcare centers serving 6,259 children. Support consisted of both technical methodological guidance and supplies for implementing the care and education modality. Thirty four new centers benefited 624 children—including 26 in situations of vulnerability—and enabled 519 mothers to join the workforce, demonstrating the social economic co benefits of ECD investments. In inclusive education, 92% of 2,024 children with ASD/ID in Havana, Pinar del Río, and Holguín achieved developmental milestones and individualized learning objectives, illustrating the impact of integrated diagnostics and individualized support. Skills development progressed, with 2,635 students trained in digital, life, and gender sensitive competencies, while resilience actions were implemented in 89 schools in high risk zones. Six newly outfitted polytechnic workshops and 23 multimedia classrooms enhanced learning environments and preparedness capacity, bridging pedagogy, employability, and DRR.
Protection and caregiving services expanded access to rights remedies and protective environments. A total of 1,142 children and adolescents were supported by Offices of the Ombudsman, evidencing the growing role of these institutions in restoring and defending children’s rights. Resilience actions reached 6,172 children and adolescents, including 324 with disabilities, across 89 schools in Guantánamo and Holguín. Twelve of these schools benefited from multimedia classrooms, WASH facilities, school gardens, and emergency preparedness drills. Multi risk maps, curricular proposals, scientific clubs, and evacuation exercises strengthened awareness and readiness in the 89 educational centers, further tying DRR to school continuity and child protection.

Capacity development was a central pillar, building workforce competencies, institutional systems, and community participation. In health and nutrition, 4,956 professionals were trained in comprehensive adolescent health; 2,115 received training in simulation classrooms for obstetric emergencies; 426 strengthened competencies in breastfeeding, infant and maternal nutrition, prevention of overweight and obesity, and MNP supplementation; and 3,517 were trained in nutrition and malnutrition prevention, improving comprehensive responses in the most vulnerable communities. Educational messages reached 534,776 people through online platforms, extending knowledge beyond facility walls. A targeted project in Yaguajay, Sancti Spíritus educated 3,360 children (1,459 girls) and their families on nutrition, healthy eating, and physical activity to prevent overweight and obesity, covering all primary schools in the territory. The initiative trained 493 teachers (296 women) and 54 health professionals (32 women) in nutrition related skills with a gender and life course approach, and was subsequently scaled to a school in Havana, involving 568 students (340 girls). In early childhood and inclusive education, training programmes benefited over 2,200 local actors and educators; 3,497 teachers and 2,690 families participated in specialized inclusive education capacity building across Havana, Pinar del Río, and Holguín. In vocational programmes, gender strategies and prevention of school based violence were embedded, with 135 teachers and psychologists trained—covering 100% of the country’s vocational schools. Positive parenting initiatives reached more than 7,800 parents and caregivers through community based trainings, an online parenting programme, and targeted digital and media content, strengthening caregiving practices and engagement with services. Child protection capacities were reinforced across institutions, with 1,870 professionals in justice, education, social protection, 
interior civil defense, and local governments trained in violence prevention, response, and child protection through structured processes that combined technical content with practical tools and produced reusable materials to support continued capacity development. As part of the media engagement trainings and youth participation initiatives, UNICEF reached 170 professionals and provided mentorship for 20 radio producers, while 35 adolescents were engaged in content creation—embedding children’s perspectives across media and strengthening adolescent participation in public communications.
Partnerships, evidence, preparedness, and communications functioned as enabling systems that amplified impact. UNICEF expanded alliances with national institutions, multilateral cooperation mechanisms, and UN agencies—including WFP, ILO, UNEP, UNFPA, and PAHO—to deliver integrated outcomes in health, education, WASH, and nutrition. Collaboration with UNICEF National Committees in Spain, Ireland, and Canada broadened funding and technical support. The office led the Human and Social Development Group of the UNSDCF, spearheaded monitoring and evaluation, and co led operations. A Water Working Group was established across the UN with new donors, and UNICEF was positioned as the leading agency in nutrition within the interagency group on food sovereignty and nutrition, embedding a nutrition sensitive approach in national law implementation. Education and DRR partnerships were pivotal, with intersectoral mechanisms involving Civil Defense, the Red Cross, and the Ministry of Science and Environment to mainstream resilience in the education sector and emergency response. In specialized child protection, UNICEF worked closely with the Ministries of Education, Justice, Interior, and Labor and Social Security to modernize protection norms and protocols, demonstrating sustained institutional trust and coherent public sector engagement.

Evidence generation, monitoring, and evaluation underpinned adaptive management. UNICEF contributed to country level surveys and tools through implementation of MICS7 Cuba 2025 (pre test, sample preparation, training, pilot), and developed national instruments for measuring multidimensional vulnerabilities in early childhood, centralizing data for decision making and interoperability. Capacity building in statistics was supported through national methodological meetings and workshops for educational statistics across all provinces, stabilizing data systems and enhancing the reliability of administrative data. UNICEF promoted an evaluation culture through training workshops and networks, including NECD and the LACRO strategy, reinforcing the use of evaluations in public policy and strengthening technical leadership in evidence informed decision making. Following Hurricane Melissa, a monitoring dashboard was created for the country office response, enabling real time tracking for advocacy and donor accountability and closing the loop between delivery, learning, and course correction.
Humanitarian preparedness and rapid response maintained continuity of essential services during shocks and enabled swift recovery. UNICEF participated in a CERF Anticipatory Action Mechanism, prepositioning and rapidly mobilizing supplies ahead of hurricane impact. Within two weeks, the office reached approximately 56,000 people with water services and storage and approximately 29,690 children with school supplies for rehabilitation. Medicines and critical supplies were delivered promptly, and inclusive shelter management was supported through national validation of the Inclusive Shelter Management Guide, protecting children and adolescents during evacuations and displacement and clarifying standards and procedures across sites. Deployment of local professional networks delivered psychosocial care to 5,674 children and adolescents after Hurricane Melissa, helping restore routines and reduce distress. Through integrated humanitarian and development programming, UNICEF reached over 620,000 people affected by Hurricanes Oscar, Rafael, and Melissa, supporting repair of critical WASH infrastructure and promoting long term resilience strategies that align with national plans. Preparedness and response were especially supported with the cooperation of ECHO, while anticipatory actions were displayed in collaboration with OCHA. 
On innovative financing, UNICEF advanced negotiation of climate finance and debt swap mechanisms focused on the solarization of social services, both with international cooperation actors and national authorities such as INRH and CITMA. These instruments are designed to reduce energy vulnerability, protect continuity of care, and align with national planning and public financial management frameworks. This signal a strategic shift toward a pathway for scaling climate resilient social infrastructure across provinces.

Strategic communications and public engagement strengthened the social contract around child rights and accountability. UNICEF consolidated a digital community of 57,765 followers across seven platforms and secured more than 50 features in national and local press, positioning children’s rights—including the CNAJ—and MICS7 Cuba 2025 in the public narrative. Peak engagement during emergencies demonstrated UNICEF’s capacity to mobilize public attention and support; for example, a supply arrival post related to the Melissa response generated 540,758 views and 16,298 interactions. A media observatory and guidance initiative promoted children’s direct presence in journalistic pieces and offered recommendations to avoid adult centric coverage. Operational presence was reinforced through three times more field missions compared to 2024 and the recruitment of three field monitors, who provided direct oversight of response implementation and facilitated consultations and engagement with affected populations—linking communications, accountability, and adaptive management at community level.

The cross-sector integration underpinning this portfolio explains why results held through shocks and scaled equitably. By embedding shock responsiveness into routine systems—health protocols, WASH restoration, education continuity, and protection case management—the office avoided parallel structures and maintained service delivery during crises. Standardized equity instruments, such as the Childhood Characterization tool, were tied to intersectoral referral pathways connecting schools, health facilities, and protection services. Policy gains—CNAJ, the alternative care resolution, ADOS-2 diagnostics, and the RI-WASHBAT Action Plan—were coupled with clearly sequenced implementation pipelines: costed plans, defined roles, training and supervision, and monitoring dashboards. Participation was institutionalized and safeguarded: adolescents were consulted on legal norms and engaged in media content creation, ensuring inclusive, closed loop feedback. Local development was anchored to social services through FLODI, school based DRR and continuity of learning, and solarized health facilities, increasing ownership and sustainability. Innovative financing mechanisms were explored to support essential services during shocks and accelerate climate resilient investments. Taken together, this multi sector, data driven, and partnership anchored approach enabled more scale, strengthened systems, and improved outcomes for the most vulnerable children—while maintaining agility through integrated humanitarian development action.

Looking ahead, UNICEF Cuba will continue to manage adaptively and invest in systems that deliver. Implementation roadmaps for CNAJ and alternative care will bring costed plans, training and supervision packages, and citizen communication to sustain compliance and safeguarding. Equity-driven scaling of vulnerability identification tools and inclusive protocols will extend to all provinces, supported by provincial coaching teams and dashboards that track gaps by gender, disability, and locality. Continuity of essential services frameworks will integrate health, education, and protection SOPs, with joint simulation exercises, pre positioned kits, and psychosocial support protocols embedded in municipal plans. Interoperable, privacy preserving data systems will connect health, education, and protection information with offline functionality and role based access to improve early detection and referral completion. Workforce development will expand through blended learning, micro credentials, supervised practice, and peer coaching to sustain quality at low marginal cost. Participation and public communication will be institutionalized through child and adolescent advisory mechanisms, and multi-audience campaigns clarifying rights, services, and help seeking pathways. 

UNICEF Cuba’s 2025 programme demonstrates a coherent strategy that integrates policy brokerage, system strengthening, delivery at scale, and capacity development—underpinned by data, partnerships, and emergency responsiveness. By keeping services continuous, embedding reforms in practice, and using evidence and participation to target equity, the office safeguarded and expanded outcomes for children and adolescents in a challenging environment. The combination of scaled delivery, trusted access to reform spaces, innovative financing, and strong public engagement will continue to anchor UNICEF’s role as a credible, effective, and indispensable actor for children in Cuba—ready to adapt strategies, inform future actions, and explore new opportunities for collaboration to accelerate results at national scale.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF Cuba demonstrated adaptive management and strategic agility in an environment marked by economic challenges, energy shortages, and recurrent climate and non-climate shocks, in addition to outbreaks of multiple diseases (Dengue, Oropouche and Chikungunya) happening at the same time. Despite these challenges, the office sustained essential services and advanced systemic reforms by embedding emergency and shock responsiveness into core health, education, and protection systems. Rapid acquisition and pre-positioning of supplies, coupled with integrated protocols, minimized service disruptions during crises. These measures were reinforced by strong policy dialogue and alliances, particularly with health and education authorities, ensuring that short-term actions were anchored in long-term systemic change.

Equity remained at the center of UNICEF’s approach. Standardized vulnerability identification tools and expanded diagnostic spaces improved resource allocation and developmental outcomes for marginalized children. When linked to intersectoral referral pathways, these tools accelerated identification and service delivery, reducing delays and ensuring that children most at risk received timely support. Workforce development and community engagement emerged as critical enablers. Comprehensive training for health professionals, educators, and child protection actors strengthened problem-solving capacity, while innovative communication strategies and meaningful child and adolescent participation and consultation in disaster risk reduction and policy processes enhanced relevance, ownership, and resilience.

Trusted partnerships were pivotal in advancing reforms. Legal frameworks such as the Children, Adolescents and Youth Code moved forward where technical rigor and respectful engagement built confidence among national counterparts. From 2026 onwards, implementation is a priority and requires costed plans, clarified roles, and sustained collaboration to translate normative gains into tangible results for children.

Persistent challenges underscored the need for innovation and integrated solutions. System stress caused by economic crisis and disasters disrupted supply chains, school operations, and protection services. Sector-specific contingency plans lacked integration, reducing efficiency and slowing recovery. Financing gaps threatened sustainability, as childcare centers and local investment mechanisms require predictable resources and enabling legal frameworks. Without innovative and diversified financing, gains in early childhood development and inclusive education remain fragile. Institutional capacity varies widely across provinces, and intersectoral coordination is still dependent on individual leadership rather than formal mechanisms. Continuous workforce training in inclusion and gender lacks scale, and public awareness of rights and obligations remains limited, weakening prevention and help-seeking behaviors. More data systems are required to ensure early detection and evidence-based policymaking.

From these experiences, several lessons emerged for achieving results at scale. Integrated protocols outperform siloed responses during shocks, reinforcing the need to design for resilience across services. Policy gains must be paired with implementation pipelines that include costed, multi-sector plans and accountability mechanisms. Standardized equity tools linked to interoperable referral systems improve timeliness and quality of services. Child and adolescent participation must be institutionalized, safeguarded, and feedback-driven to ensure meaningful engagement. Finally, linking social services to local development strengthens sustainability and shared responsibility, creating models that endure beyond project cycles.

Innovation priorities for the coming period reflect these lessons. Building supply chain resilience through energy-efficient cold chains, pooled procurement, and predictive analytics is essential to mitigate disruptions. Integrated data systems with privacy-preserving architecture will connect health, education, and protection services, enabling real-time monitoring and adaptive management. Workforce upskilling at scale will leverage blended learning, micro-credentials, and peer coaching to sustain quality at low marginal cost. Labor market pathways for adolescents—especially girls and those with disabilities—will be co-designed with employers to translate vocational skills into real employment opportunities. Blended financing instruments, including results-based mechanisms and local development funds aligned with national systems, will protect essential services and accelerate resilience investments.
Explicit effort required for innovate disaster risk financing, linked to climate and resilient building opportunities. The CDRFI, as well as the GCF and other contributions, will be key to support the CO's future plans. 

Building on these insights, UNICEF will implement forward-looking adjustments to consolidate gains and manage adaptively. A unified Continuity of Essential Services Framework will institutionalize integrated protocols for health, education, and protection, including psychosocial support and joint simulation exercises, reducing service disruption time during shocks. Equity-driven scaling will expand vulnerability identification tools and inclusive education protocols nationwide through provincial compacts and dashboards tracking gaps by gender, disability, and locality. Implementation pipelines for reforms such as CNAJ and alternative care will include costed roadmaps, training, supervision, and citizen communication to ensure compliance and safeguarding. Integrated information systems will prototype an interoperable, offline-capable data spine connecting health, education, and protection records, enabling faster risk detection and improved referral completion. Workforce development will deploy blended learning and micro-credentials for front-line providers across sectors, increasing competency attainment and service quality. Participation and awareness will be institutionalized through child and adolescent advisory mechanisms and multi-audience campaigns clarifying rights and services, driving higher uptake and stronger citizenship. Finally, humanitarian and development planning will be aligned through shared indicators and innovative financing anchored in national systems, protecting budgets and accelerating recovery.
Monitoring and agility will be reinforced through quarterly adaptive reviews using integrated dashboards, equity tracking by province, gender, and disability, and risk-informed planning that incorporates energy and disaster scenarios. Participatory monitoring and transparent progress reporting will strengthen accountability, while rapid learning loops will refine protocols and training based on real-time feedback.

The most durable gains of 2025 came from embedding emergency responsiveness into core systems, pairing policy reforms with implementation, and steering decisions through data and participation. Persistent challenges—economic volatility, energy shortages, uneven capacity, and data gaps—demand integrated solutions. UNICEF’s forward strategy converts lessons into joint commitments: a unified continuity framework, equity-driven scaling, implementation pipelines, interoperable data systems, scaled workforce development, institutionalized participation, and financing that bridges humanitarian and development needs. These adjustments will accelerate results for the most marginalized children and strengthen national systems to sustain gains through future shocks.

The Dominican Republic, an upper middle-income country, faces persistent social and territorial inequalities that limit equitable development. These disparities remain evident across income groups, between rural and urban areas, and in border provinces where access to basic services is weakest. Although the country has experienced notable macroeconomic dynamism, -six percent growth in recent years-, gains have not translated evenly across the population. 

For 2025, the World Bank projected a slowdown of GDP growth to four percent, with stable inflation at around four percent and unemployment at five percent. Structural vulnerabilities persist, particularly due to high labor informality, over than half of total employment. Construction, commerce, manufacturing, tourism, agriculture, free trade zones, and remittances continued to sustain overall economic performance.

According to the 2022 Census, children under eighteen represented thirty percent of the  population, and seventy-two percent lived in urban areas. Among them, one-third were aged zero to five, thirty-four percent were between six and eleven, and another third were adolescents aged twelve to seventeen. This demographic structure highlights the country’s potential for a demographic dividend, contingent on guaranteeing equitable access to social services so that children and adolescents can fully develop their capacities.

In 2025, corruption investigations affected several institutions, most notably the National Health Insurance Service, where authorities uncovered a fraud scheme of over two hundred million U.S. dollars. 

The Human Development Index ranked the Dominican Republic eighty-ninth out of one hundred ninety-three countries, placing it within the high human development category. However, inequalities in access to services and wealth distribution remained significant. Child monetary poverty declined from thirty-six percent in 2023 to thirty-one percent in 2024, while extreme poverty decreased from six to four percent. Multidimensional child poverty also fell, from twenty-one percent in 2023 to eighteen percent in 2024, although rural areas continued to experience disproportionate deprivation, with twenty-six percent of children affected. Public investment in children and adolescents increased slightly between 2016 and 2021, rising from five to nearly six percent of GDP, but remained at around five percent in 2023.
 
Progress toward the 2030 Agenda advanced steadily, particularly in areas related to children. Improvements were registered in nutrition, reductions in neonatal mortality, declines in early unions and adolescent pregnancy, and improvements in immunization. Despite these efforts, persistent challenges included physical punishment, early unions, adolescent pregnancy, maternal and neonatal mortality, school dropout, and denial of rights for children on the move. Strengthened SDG-aligned policies remain essential to ensure that no child is left behind.

In 2025, the Penal Code was updated, establishing a legal age of sexual consent and criminalizing sexual violence, harassment, and online abuse. However, exceptions related to physical punishment in the home remained (noting that 63 percent of children 1-14 years old suffer corporal punishment), and protections against discrimination for vulnerable groups were not comprehensively addressed. During 2025, nearly 378,000 immigrants were deported, an 84% increase on 2024.

Maternal mortality reached one hundred twenty-five per one hundred thousand live births in 2024, thirty percent more than 2019. Migratory measures adopted in 2025 discouraged many Haitian women from attending prenatal check-ups, contributing to increased home births or deliveries in low-quality clinics. As a result, births by Haitian women in public hospitals declined from thirty-six percent in 2024 to twenty percent by November 2025. The caesarean section rate remains high -fifty-three percent, and exclusive breastfeeding remains low, at sixteen percent. Infant mortality declined to twenty-two per one thousand live births in 2024, yet more than eighty percent of child deaths occurred during the neonatal period due to preventable causes, including respiratory distress, sepsis, asphyxia, and prematurity.

The 2024 National Micronutrient Survey revealed that vitamin A deficiency had re-emerged, affecting seventeen percent of children under five. Iron deficiency anemia affected nearly one-quarter of children, rising to almost forty percent among those aged two and three. Overweight and obesity also reached concerning levels, affecting twenty-nine percent of school-aged children and thirty-nine percent in private schools. Contributing factors included high consumption of ultra-processed foods, low levels of physical activity. There is no regulation for front-of-pack nutritional labeling regulations. Vaccination coverage remained below recommended thresholds, with 2023 levels at seventy-one percent for SRP2, eighty-six percent for PCV3, eighty-nine percent for OPV3, and ninety-one percent for the third dose of PENTA. 

The 2024 Enhogar Survey reported that ninety percent of five-year-old children could read and write, although sixteen percent of rural children continued to face literacy gaps. National literacy averaged ninety-four percent, with ninety-five percent in urban areas and eighty-seven percent in rural settings. Preschool enrollment among children aged three to five reached seventy-one percent, posing challenges for early learning and school readiness. Secondary school completion stood at sixty-one percent, while absenteeism contributed to high exclusion rates. Approximately sixteen percent of adolescents of both lower and upper secondary age were out of school.

Throughout 2025, the government maintained social protection efforts to support households living in poverty. Regular food-related cash transfers reached more than 1.4 million households by September. The Support Fund for Children and Adolescents with Disabilities expanded its coverage to nine thousand households. 

As a small island developing state, the country remained highly vulnerable to climate-related events. Between 21 and 27 October 2025, Hurricane Melissa brought torrential rains that displaced more than 3,700 people, disrupted water services for over one million users, vulnerable livelihood affectation, school interruption, and significantly affected agriculture in the southwest.

Although femicides decreased by thirty-one percent compared with 2024, gender-based violence continued to represent a major concern. Adolescent pregnancy showed a downward trend nationally, yet disparities persisted. Nearly half of girls with only primary education had given birth before age eighteen, compared with two percent of those with tertiary education. One in four girls is married or in union before tyhe age of 18.  

Internet penetration reached eighty-four percent, while 4G and 5G networks covered ninety-nine percent of the territory. Despite this expansion, usage gaps persisted in marginalized, peri-urban, and rural areas. The government launched the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, aiming to improve public management, automate administrative processes, and expand access to information.

UNICEF achieved tangible progress across most CPD results and indicators, enhancing programme effectiveness, operational efficiency, sustainable fundraising and emergency preparedness. 
Progress in strengthening its child-rights framework, included advances on the Penal Code, Legal Identity Law, and new inclusive-education regulations, reflecting partial advances with CRC recommendations. However, persistent weaknesses in coordination, data systems, budgeting, and key legal reforms. Inequities particularly for the most vulnerable children, and concerns regarding sexual and physical violence, adolescent girls’ health and protection like early unions and adolescent pregnancy continue to be important challenges. These mixed results show that while the country is advancing in some areas, significant structural challenges must still be addressed to fully meet CRC recommendations. 

Child Protection System and Violence against Children (VAC)
UNICEF supported the government in assuming the pledge “Every Child Protected”, adopted in the Global Conference on Violence against Children. The  Child Protection System (CPS) advanced to the “system enhancement” stage, under the Health System Strengthening Approach. This progress reflects strong collaboration between UNICEF and the National Council for Children and Adolescents, CONANI, resulting in expanded protection services for children affected by violence and mobility. The CPS moved from 38 to 46 points on the maturity model in 2025, driven by policy advocacy, strengthening of  service delivery, digitalization of case management, and evidence generation.

UNICEF supported CONANI to adopt a case management policy, a protocol for assisting survivors of physical violence, and guidance for sexual violence cases, including in emergencies. A PRIMERO-inspired digital case management system was introduced, registering 1,192 cases of violence against children and 20,112 cases of migrant children receiving protection services. These tools improved case tracking, referral pathways, and service coordination, contributing directly to the CPS maturity increase.

Evidence generation included two VAC studies which exposed entrenched gender norms and cultural patterns that normalise corporal punishment and legitimise control through violence. The research identified psychological, social, and structural drivers of physical punishment and highlighted entry points for intervention: practical parenting alternatives, engagement of community and faith leaders, and use of schools and health services for parenting support. 

A scalable SBC parenting strategy, implemented with the National Institute for Comprehensive Early Childhood Care (INAIPI) and Ministry of Education (MINERD), reached more than 3,000 families in four municipalities. Pre- and post-measures after four structured sessions showed violent discipline declining from 34 percent to 18 percent and marked increases in positive stimulation practices. The initiative demonstrated potential for scale-up; UNICEF’s combined role—technical assistance, digital tools, training, and evidence—was instrumental in expanding access to protection services and shifting caregiving practices.

A new Penal Code was approved after two decades of debate; UNICEF’s advocacy—both independently and within the UN system—helped secure provisions on the lowered of age of sexual consent and criminalisation of sexual violence, harassment, and online abuse. Notwithstanding these gains, the Code retains exceptions that permit certain forms of violence in the home and discriminatory practices; closing these gaps remains a priority for the future.

Legal Identity
In 2025 UNICEF supported expansion of birth registration coverage to 89 percent and birth certification to 95 percent, while ensuring protection services for vulnerable migrants and unaccompanied children during humanitarian response.

Birth registration and certification improved substantially through outreach campaigns, technical assistance, and institutional strengthening. Over 5,000 people were reached through outreach activities, and more than 10,800 individuals—including 2,221 unaccompanied children—received protection services as part of the humanitarian response to the crisis in Haiti. UNICEF provided technical support to modernise registration processes, simplify late registration, and train public officials and community actors, improving access to legal identity and enabling children to claim rights to education, health, and social protection.
 
Early Childhood Development (ECD)
The Dominican System for Measuring Early Childhood Development (SIMEDID) was formally adopted as the national monitoring mechanism. UNICEF supported  the fourth round of national application of SIMEDID including new items to enhance assessment of  developmental milestones for newborns and children aged five to six. Six Caregiving Manuals and Home Visit Guidelines were revised with INAIPI, in alignment with “nurturing care” standards; digital learning resources were developed on the Learning Passport to expand workforce capacity. 

The abovementioned SBC parenting programme pilot reached more than 3,000 families increasing positive stimulation indicators across reading, storytelling, singing, play, and outdoor activities. These results reflect UNICEF’s technical leadership in ECD monitoring, workforce development, and norm-shifting interventions.

Quality Education
Thanks to CON BASE’s strong results in foundational learning and system capacity for grades 1-3, a new three-year cooperation agreement has been signed to scale foundational learning in primary, secondary and pre-primary education, , , as well as violence prevention (“culture of peace”), and student participation. This is UNICEF's largest programme in the country, aiming to increase the impact of educational results for children and adolescents at a national scale. Progress in the digitalisation of the education system was achieved through the expansion of U-Report into schools, the implementation of the School Digitalization Certification programme, and the creation of inclusive digital books and other learning resources.
 
By 2025, CON BASE had reached 454,890 students and 23,000 teachers, with 80 out of 122 districts improving their Spanish language performance and 39 districts mathematics compared to the 2023 baseline. UNICEF supported capacity development by contributing to the creation of the second edition of six teacher guides and student booklets, developing materials for multigrade rural schools and strengthening the Digital Monitoring System (GOSDR), which is now used by 3,000 schools alongside the “Acompaña” pedagogical support module. 
 
In secondary education, UNICEF supported the development of 94 teaching sequences, as well as training for 800 technical staff and teacher trainers. To date, over 40,000 teachers have received training. 
 
Efforts to prevent early marriages and school violence, focusing on girls and boys, reached 24,844 students through awareness-raising activities this year, sustaining the excellent results achieved over the years.
 
Inclusive Education 
The Inclusive Education Model-aimed at expanding learning opportunities for children with disabilities- progressed from validation of the pilot experience to a structured scaling-up process, involving teacher training certified by local universities, as well as the provision of accessible digital resources.

The Ministry approved a scaling-up plan and committed public funding including the provision of UNICEF technical assistance for institutional capacity developing. 1,300 teachers enrolled on a Universal Design for Learning course, 60 university professors participated in an intensive hybrid programme to strengthen their capacities, and 46,128 children accessed accessible digital books. A further 14,535 teachers and technicians received training and instructional guides, while 3,500 teachers engaged with interactive U-Report courses. 
 
UNICEF designed course modules, formed alliances with INAFOCAM and ten universities, and produced accessible materials that improved the participation of approximately 35,750 children, advancing in the sustainability of these results.
 
Health System
By 2025, enhanced infection prevention measures and a broader implementation of Kangaroo Mother Care had led to significant improvements in newborn survival. The Neonatal Mortality Rate decreased from 14.28 in 2023 to 13.08 in 2024. Despite the 2025 official rate has not been published, 294 fewer deaths were registered, compared to 2024.

To prevent hospital-acquired infections in NICUs, UNICEF provided technical assistance and trained 160 health workers (including cleaning staff) in infection prevention and control. UNICEF facilitated an international exchange with Miguel Servet Hospital experts to strengthen laboratory diagnostics for group B streptococcus and early antibiogram testing. 

Essential equipment for Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) units in 25 public hospitals was provided as part of the Neonatal Mortality Reduction Acceleration Plan. In 2025, 4,104 premature and low-birth-weight babies benefited from KMC, bringing the cumulative total since 2020 to 38,344. 

UNICEF also provided training for 493 primary health care workers and 517 hospital providers in prenatal and obstetric care, respectful maternity care, neonatal resuscitation, and emergency management. Clinical monitoring tools were used across 24 hospitals, with 14 achieving protocol adherence of 75 percent or higher.
 
The "Nutremuac", malnutrition monitoring application, was updated to incorporate the latest WHO protocol, extend coverage to children up to 17 years of age, and include breastfeeding mothers.

The commitment made in 2024 resulting from the Bottleneck Analysis in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (applying UNICEF WASH BAT) in the health sector, led to the integration into sectoral planning of actions aimed at improving water and sanitation services in health centres, incorporating  water quality as a mandatory requirement for the allocation of resources in budgets for the construction, maintenance, and improvement of infrastructures. These measures are expected to enhance hygiene conditions and contribute to reducing maternal and neonatal mortality. 

In addition, UNICEF has made significant progress in effectively incorporating the proposed lines of action deriving from the application of WASH BAT for Schools into the Ministry of Education's strategic planning. This initiative aims to enhance water, sanitation, basic hygiene, and menstrual hygiene conditions in educational institutions by allocating specific budget lines for WASH in the institutional budget.

Social Protection System, Climate Change and Public Financing for Children
In 2025, the Government of the Dominican Republic made significant progress in integrating a child-rights perspective into national climate policies, with consistent support from UNICEF. A key milestone was the completion of the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), which provided actionable recommendations to strengthen the resilience of essential services for children in the face of increasing climate risks. UNICEF also contributed to the integration of a child-sensitive approach in the updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), reinforcing national climate commitments through coordinated engagement with the United Nations System. 

UNICEF advanced the national policy for prevention of early unions by strengthening girls’ agency, expanding social protection and improving institutional coordination. Through the “Girls’ Clubs” programme, 4,822 adolescents were empowered and improved their live skills; the Girl’s Clubs programme is now being scaled up with leadership and funding from the Government . Technical support improved methodologies and monitoring to ensure that girls were better equipped to pursue life trajectories free from early unions and adolescent pregnancy. In addition, UNICEF supported the design of an innovative conditional cash transfer scheme under SUPERATE, to be launched in 2026, aimed at preventing early unions and reducing school dropout
 
UNICEF assisted government efforts to automate budget tagging using artificial intelligence tools, improving the accuracy and transparency of classifications related to gender, territory, climate change, and emergency preparedness and response, while UNICEF continued the strengthening of national capacities for measuring public investment in children. The last report confirmed that the country continues to invest an average of 5.0% of GDP in programs for children and adolescents.

Evidence Generation and Data for Impact
Significant progress was made in aligning evaluation, monitoring, and knowledge management plans with the Business Model Initiative (BMI) and Future Focus Initiative (FFI). A communication strategy for the Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) area was developed, alongside support for the “Data Counts” dissemination initiative. Three data dashboards were completed: (a) General Situation Analysis (SitAn), (b) provincial data from MICS, and (c) SitAn of Violence against Children.

UNICEF’s intensive support was instrumental for the most notable achievement in this area- the successful design and implementation of ENHOGAR-MICS 2025 field work phase- involving 13 weeks of fieldwork, with initial results expected in April 2026. The SitAn on Violence Against Children was published, and contributions were made to global evaluations on innovation, emergency preparedness, Accountability for Affected Populations (AAP), early childhood education, and teaching capacities.
National evaluations included the Project for Reduction of Child Marriage and Early Unions, the Early Childhood National Policy 2013–2023, and the Evaluability Analysis of the ConBase Program (recently started). Support was provided for reporting key SDG-related indicators.

Adolescent Participation
UNICEF achieved an outstanding expansion of adolescent civic engagement across various sectors,reaching 9,269 adolescents and fostering digital participation through U-Report and RapidPro.

U-Report registered 6,315 users aged 13 to 24 and served as a rapid polling and information channel. UNICEF supported youth engagement across education (19,000 MoE members registered on RapidPro; adolescent inputs to the Culture of Peace evaluation), health (polls on HPV, food labelling, mental health, menstrual hygiene), protection (polls and participation in regional conferences), social protection (inputs to the CLAC study), and emergencies (life-saving polls and infobots during hurricane season). A diagnostic study was commissioned by 

UNICEF in collaboration with the University of British Columbia. In addition, adolescent-focused content was developed and disseminated through the KLK platform, UNICEF’s flagship digital space that amplifies youth voices and strengthens their engagement nationwide. These actions had a positive effect on the strengthening of youth voice, evidence, and policy influence.
 
Emergency Preparedness and Response
UNICEF strengthened national preparedness and response by activating emergency supply systems, formalizing standby agreements with partners, building surge capacity, and deploying child-focused assistance to more than 11,000 people during floods and Tropical Storm Melissa.
In response to the situation, internally, UNICEF activated an emergency supplies warehouse, procured hygiene kits and jerrycans, negotiated contingency agreements with seven partners, created a roster of 28 emergency experts.

Externally, implementing the Shock Responsive System(SRS)approach, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education with a digital school damage reporting and risk index tool, promoted adolescent girls' participation in Civil Defense preparedness activities (including safe menstrual hygiene for approximately 400 young women), and ran risk communication campaigns that reached over four million people. During the May and September floods and Tropical Storm Melissa, UNICEF and partners distributed 1,489 hygiene kits and reached more than 11,000 people, including approximately 3,700 children and adolescents.

Strategic Communication and Brand Positioning
In 2025, UNICEF achieved exceptional media and digital reach, amplifying child rights issues and supporting advocacy, fundraising and behavior change objectives.
From January to October, 31 informational communications ( were published, generating 3,290 media hits (2,711 digital, 304 print, 218 television and 72 radio), equating to a free press value of US$5,654,393 and reaching an estimated audience of 184,783,499. 
From January to November, the social media reach exceeded the annual goal of 15 million, reaching 21,951,932 people. The number of impressions was 24,876,773, and the number of followers increased by 20 percent to 234,180. Additionally, the video format garnered 16,199,993 views, underscoring its widespread appeal. 

Key digital activations included World Children's Day (reach: 7,106,320), ENHOGAR-MICS 2025 (reach: 5,924,841), Emergency Prevention (reach: 4,056,773), the #JuntosXLaNiñez telethon activation (reach: 3,859,485) and the U-Report launch (reach: 224,143). One hundred and twenty-three influencers, including fifteen children and adolescent creators, supported the campaigns. The website received 423,877 visitors, 16.5% of whom were returning visitors.

Sustainable Fundraising
This year UNICEF demonstrated fundraising resilience: business partnerships were retained and individual giving grew rapidly, providing most of the income and a stronger base for programme financing.

A total of USD 25.8 million in Other Resources (OR) was mobilized through public-sector partnerships and from the United States National Committee for UNICEF (US Fund). In addition, USD 459,000 was provided by the European Commission’s Humanitarian Aid Office (ECHO) to support emergency response efforts.
 
The corporate fundraising channel reached USD 495,000, 85 percent of the USD 580,000 target, including high-visibility events such as the national Telethon and the annual gala dinner. The Individual Giving channel showed a 23 percent year-on-year growth, contributing 85 percent of total income and achieving a 36 percent compound annual growth rate from 2020 to 2025. The “extra-cash” campaigns were a great success, and the office closed the year with 11,000 donors nationwide.  UNICEF's fundraising strategy encompassed a combination of traditional events, donor retention strategies, and nascent digital channels. 

Governance and Programmatic Effectiveness 
The Country Office dedicated significant effort in 2025 to strengthening internal controls and the risk management framework, responding to findings from the Peer Review conducted by the Regional Office and in preparation for the Audit exercise. The CO successfully completed the Peer Review focused on risk management practices and used lessons learned from both exercises to revise and update core governance mechanisms.
 
The Accountability Framework was updated to clarify roles and responsibilities across programme and operations teams. A comprehensive review of the Risk Management Matrix was completed, adopting a more proactive approach to identifying, assessing and mitigating potential risks across the office portfolio.
 
These efforts have resulted in heightened staff awareness of risk and fraud indicators and the progressive integration of a risk management perspective into daily operational decision-making.
 
2025 also marked a milestone in strategic alignment with national priorities. For the first time, the Country Office signed a single, unified Work Plan covering all programme areas with the Ministry of the Presidency. This consolidated agreement streamlines programme coordination, signals deeper programmatic integration, and strengthens the CO’s partnership with a key national government entity.
 
UNICEF developed and implemented the Digital Transformation Strategy for ongoing programmes, aligning it with the CPD and the national digital strategy, and further strengthened through collaboration with management and programme areas to ensure relevance, sustainability and full alignment with CPD objectives.
 
UNICEF strengthened gender-transformative programming across sectors by advancing interventions that address structural drivers of inequality affecting girls and women, including in emergencies. The office has supported the institutionalization and expansion of evidence-based approaches to prevent early unions and gender-based violence through the Girls Strategy under POWER4Girls. These approaches have been implemented to reach adolescent girls and boys through education, social protection and community-based platforms.

UNICEF has also supported the application of a gender-responsive approach in the humanization of childbirth and maternal health actions, including the elimination of obstetric violence and Kangaroo Mother iniative with a active involvement of fathers.

The positive parenting strategy promoted non-violent caregiving and increased the meaningful involvement of fathers in the care of children aged 0–5, contributing to the early prevention of violence in early childhood. UNICEF's leadership in the prevention of early unions is evident in its mobilization of public resources and provision of technical assistance and advocacy. 
 
Operational Efficiency
Operations strengthened governance, financial discipline, workforce agility, and digital innovation, improving procurement, payment processing, risk management, and programme support.
The office implemented an Accountability Framework, closed six of seven Peer Review Recommendations, completed a headquarters-led Audit, and ran 13 strategic management sessions to align with the new business model. 
 
Operational and office processes have been refined to enhance efficiency. Key tasks related to historical record-keeping have been automated. These digital investments have enhanced evidence-based decision-making processes, strengthened monitoring across various sectors, and facilitated alignment of programmes with national priorities.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF demonstrated resilience and adaptability in a year marked by achievements and systemic shifts. The Office faces the challenges and opportunities of a country transiting from middle to high-income status. The country will have more robust legal and institutional frameworks and increased resource availability; however, UNICEF availability of financial resources from public and institutional sources will be more challenging. This makes UNICEF's direct involvement in the provision of services less critical, while its role of monitoring child rights, advocating for further improvement in policies, budgets and social norms and sophisticated system strengthening become increasingly central, steering UNICEF towards a genuine knowledge organization, where knowledge generation, analysis and high-level policy advice become central.  
 
The complex global financial situation faced by the whole organization in 2025, did not spare the Dominican Republic, which suffered severe funding cuts, especially for support to vulnerable migrant children and women. 
 
The main remaining challenges for the DR to advance Child Rights relate to several aspects:
 
-   Legal and policy framework: For example, the recent penal code includes exceptions to the ban on corporal punishment.
-   Prevailing social norms:  for example, beliefs about the roles of girls and women or practices of violent discipline against small children. 
-   Allocation of public resources: While efforts by the DR on increasing funding for child related services (especially education) are commendable, significant funding gaps remain in certain sectors.
-   Capacities of certain institutions: regarding internal regulations, the skillset of workforce, accountability mechanisms, adoption of technology etc. 
 
 
Despite strong political commitment, many institutions struggle with limited technical capacity due to staff turnover, inadequate training, and weak accountability mechanisms, underscoring the need for more innovative and sustainable approaches to professional development. UNICEF faces challenges in ensuring that training for frontline workers consistently improves service quality; however, the CONBASE experience stands out as a good practice, demonstrating that a structured, medium-term capacity-development plan—featuring continuous monitoring, accompaniment, and reinforcement at multiple levels—can lead to measurable improvements in teaching practices and learning outcomes. This successful model shows that sustainable impact requires integrating initial and ongoing training, academic certification, performance-based assessment, and the use of real-time tools and data. Building on CONBASE, UNICEF aims to institutionalize training through partnerships with universities to ensure continuity beyond its eventual exit
 
Where required, UNICEF has facilitated high-level international technical expertise, following an approach based on understanding challenges quickly, identifying effective solutions, and respecting institutional ownership and leadership. These good practices have built trust and positioned UNICEF as a preferred partner for institutional strengthening. Collaboration with entities such as the Ministry of Education, CONANI, Supérate, INAIPI, and key national systems has been essential to achieving these results.
 
Neonatal Mortality (NNM) has decreased significantly in recent years  -following the adoption of the Plan for Acceleration of the reduction of NNM-, but Maternal Mortality (MM) has not. UNICEF has worked with the Government and partners in establishing strengthened monitoring and quality improvement tools and mechanisms for Delivery care, however, their impact has been limited due to structural factors, which need to be addressed at a higher policy level.
 
The strengthening of migration measures by the government included large-scale returns affecting families and children. This context underscores the importance of sustained collaboration with national institutions and communities to ensure that migrant children and adolescents receive necessary safeguards while national policies are implemented, especially unaccompanied children and those without legal documentation. 
 
 
From the top formal evaluations conducted in 2025, came some important learnings and actions for 2026 and beyond: 
a) The ECD/ECE case study showed that system- and policy-level engagement delivered UNICEF’s highest value-add, with major contributions to national frameworks (e.g., Law 342-22), continuity across political transitions and strategic investments. Strategic partnerships amplified influence and learning. Collaboration with INAIPI, the Ministry of the Presidency and academic partners strengthened policy dialogue, system coordination and the development of digital innovations such as SIMEDID, expanding reach in measurement and frontline capacity-building.
b) The evaluation of the project Prevention of Child Marriage and Early Unions (MIUT) found that gender- and rights-based approaches strengthened protective factors for adolescent girls, showing strong intermediate outcomes in agency, self-esteem, life planning and risk awareness, confirming the relevance of SBC and socio-ecological approaches for marginalized adolescents.
 
  
UNICEF has become a centre of excellence for multiple digital initiatives, but continued development requires strengthening internal capacities. 
 
 
In 2026, UNICEF will implement shifts in its programmatic strategies and improvements to its operational procedures, following the Strategic Moment of Reflection, to shift towards a more agile, effective, and impactful approach looking for results on a large scale. The priorities are:
 

Strengthen strategies to address violence against children, advocating for the elimination of legal exceptions that permit violent discipline, providing technical support for the legal reform of the National Protection System and to furnish robust evidence on violence and social norms. 
Shift from modelling quality-improvement interventions in select hospitals to influencing   national quality policies and measurement systems through strategic political advocacy, the development of the National Plan to Accelerate Maternal Mortality Reduction as the primary platform for action. 
Implement the MINERD–UNICEF agreement across six strategic programmes in education: Early education, foundational learnings (CON BASE), secondary education, inclusive education, violence prevention, and student participation.  
Analyse and disseminate the results of the EnHogar-MICS, evaluations, and in-depth studies, on priority child rights deprivations. 
Implement the Financial Sustainability Strategy, diversifying income, securing multi-year funding, increasing individual donors and corporate channels, including disaster-risk financing.   
Institutionalize the reforms to late registration, strengthening decentralized civil registry capacity and maintaining outreach mechanisms for children in crisis contexts.  
Enhance national emergency preparedness and response capacities, including humanitarian support to national institutions and civil society for the protection of children and     adolescents on the move. 
Design plans to transfer results to the government in areas where goals have already been achieved. These areas include birth registration, nutrition, and early unions, among     others. 
Pilot experience to use Artificial Intelligence to analyse and leverage public resources for children.

Despite Ecuador´s classification as an upper-middle income country by the World Bank [1], and among High Human Development countries in the Human Development Index [2], the country still faces significant challenges such as child poverty, violence, inequality and climate-related shocks.  These intersecting risks are deepening structural gaps in early childhood development, education, health, protection and social protection outcomes, threatening progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and reinforcing the urgency of a child-centered development agenda that leaves no child behind.

In 2024, Ecuador’s Gross Domestic Product contracted by 2% [3], while South America grew by 2.3%. For 2025, the International Monetary Fund projects a 3.2% growth rate for Ecuador, compared with 2.7% for the region [4]. Labor indicators show a slight but not statistically significant increase in adequate employment, rising from 33.0% to 37.1% between December 2024 and December 2025[5]. In December 2025, adequate employment reached 46.0% in urban areas and 20.2% in rural areas; by gender, it stood at 29% for women and 42.9% for men [6], highlighting persistent inequalities.

In September 2025, to ease fiscal pressure, the Government removed the diesel subsidy—equivalent to USD 1.1 billion —stating that these funds would be redirected to social programs and compensation for transport operators [7]. The decision sparked protests, particularly in Imbabura, resulting in two deaths and more than 400 injured [8].

In the political area, Daniel Noboa was re-elected in the 2025 presidential elections. In November, a national referendum was held in which Ecuadorians rejected four government proposals: (1) convening a Constituent Assembly, (2) permitting foreign military bases in the country, (3) eliminating public financing for political parties, and (4) reducing the number of members of the National Assembly.

During this period, several institutional reforms involving services for children and adolescents were implemented. These include the integration of the Technical Secretariat Ecuador Grows Without Malnutrition into the Ministry of Human Development (previously known as Ministry of Social and Economic Inclusion); the consolidation of the Secretariat for Higher Education, the Ministry of Culture, and the Ministry of Sports under the Ministry of Education; and the incorporation of the National Planning Secretariat into the Secretariat of Public Management. Additionally, since November 2025, the Vice President has led the Ministry of Public Health alongside responsibilities related to intercultural bilingual education, adolescent pregnancy, early childhood, and chronic malnutrition.

Regarding security, the escalation of armed violence represents not only a security crisis but a structural development risk. Rising homicide rates, forced recruitment, internal displacement are undermining school attendance, psychosocial well-being and community cohesion. In 2025 the country recorded its highest level of intentional homicides, and, 583 children and adolescents were killed, compared with 414 in all 2024 and 376 in all 2023 [9].  The 2025 Global Report on Internal Displacement reported nearly 101,000 internal displacements in 2024 due to violence linked to armed organized groups.

Climate change is amplifying existing vulnerabilities. Floods, environmental degradation and water insecurity disproportionately affect children in rural, Indigenous and coastal communities, disrupting access to safe water, sanitation, health services and education. Floods, earthquakes and environmental emergencies also affected over 372,000 people in 2025, straining local systems, particularly in provinces with high multidimensional poverty rates.

Early childhood—when investments yield the highest returns—faces significant obstacles. Stunting reached 19.3% in children under 2 in 2023 [10]. In 2024, income poverty affected 36.5% of children under age five, compared with a national average of 24.2% [11]. That same year, 25.8% of households with children experienced income poverty, versus 8.6% of households without children [12].  This last shows an important challenge to achieve SDG 1 and 2.

Violence against young children remains a concern, as only 32.8% of children aged 1 to 4 are free from physical or psychological violent discipline [13].  As of October 2025, early childhood development services reached 277,805 children, slightly below the coverage reported in October 2024 [14]. Initial education for children ages 3 to 4 also declined: 310,689 children were enrolled in 2024–2025, compared with 323,325 in 2023–2024 [15].

In the education sector, as of December 2025, 15.7% of adolescents (about 150 thousand) aged 15 to 17 were out of school [16], undermining progress towards SDG 4. The net attendance rate for adolescents in the same age group reached 78.5% for mestizos, while 64.7% for indigenous and 68.5% for afro descendants [17].  Across all educational levels, the challenge of recovering learning after the pandemic persists. Thus, 70% of students do not reach the minimum proficiency level in Mathematics and Literature by the end of upper secondary education [18], a similar situation occurs in the other levels.

Adolescent girls are a priority. Among girls ages 12 to 17, the main cause of hospital discharge is related to pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period [19]. Likewise, in mental health, suicide remains the leading cause of death among girls in this age group and the third leading cause among boys. In 2024, the birth rate for adolescents ages 10 to 14 was 2.0 per 1,000—slightly lower than 2.1 in 2023[20]. Among adolescents ages 15 to 17, the rate decreased from 33.7 to 30.2 during the same period [21].

Finally, a persistent challenge is the invisibility of children and adolescents in public debate. According to recent surveys, 51.3% of respondents view insecurity as the country’s main problem, followed by economic crisis and unemployment (30.6%), and corruption (14.4%) [22].

UNICEF Ecuador strategically concentrated its efforts around three interconnected priorities aligned with the Future Focus Initiative (FFI): (i) Early Childhood Development and Human Capital; (ii) Prevention of Violence in all settings; and (iii) Climate, WASH and Risk Management. This strategic focus enabled the office to concentrate resources, strengthen intersectoral collaboration, leverage partnerships with international financial institutions and local governments, and pursue results at scale through systems strengthening and sustainable financing reforms.

Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices, and essential supplies (supports Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2 and 3; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 1; National Development Plan Objective 1; UNSDCF Area 1 

UNICEF supported national and local efforts through public policy development, capacity strengthening, advocacy, service enhancement, and communication initiatives to ensure that every child and adolescent survives and thrives with improved nutrition, quality primary health care, nurturing practices, and access to essential services.

At the national level, UNICEF collaborated with the government to reinforce the policy frameworks that protect maternal, neonatal, and child health. This included technical support for the development of the National Policy for the Prevention of Maternal and Neonatal Deaths and contributions to the National Environmental Health Policy, which integrates a maternal–child perspective to address environmental risks affecting pregnant women, newborns, and young children.

UNICEF sustained advocacy to prevent all forms of malnutrition, emphasizing the promotion, protection, and support of breastfeeding. The reactivation of CONALMA’s technical advisory commission strengthened multisectoral coordination to uphold breastfeeding regulations and the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes.

UNICEF partnered with the Quito Metropolitan District to implement COMEAVENTURAS, a social and behavior change strategy that reached 2,750 children and 83 teachers, fostering healthier habits and strengthening nurturing practices at home.

UNICEF supported the nationwide implementation of ESAMyN (Mother and Child Friendly Health Facilities), benefiting 36.047 mothers and newborns through improved care, reduced HIV transmission, and enhanced early breastfeeding. UNICEF also developed a new virtual ESAMyN course, expanding equitable access to standardized professional training. Additionally, UNICEF contributed technical content for capacity-building on chronic child malnutrition, breastfeeding, immunization, and HIV prevention. UNICEF supported the update of the National Immunization Manual and contributed to the Multi-Year Strategic Immunization Plan, while also supporting communication efforts during pertussis and yellow fever outbreaks.

At the territorial level, UNICEF implemented a comprehensive community management model to prevent chronic child malnutrition, combining intersectoral coordination, community surveillance, behavior change strategies, and strengthened health services in prioritized areas. The evaluation shows high local ownership: 61% of activities continued after UNICEF’s exit. Strengths include community leadership, intersectoral coordination, and flexible tools. Weaknesses include uneven sustainability due to high turnover of authorities, limited local funding, and implementation gaps, particularly in Imbabura and Pichincha. UNICEF is currently implementing a comprehensive strategy with formal institutional backing, involving national, local, and community-level stakeholders. However, institutional weakness persists and remains a latent risk; therefore, partnerships with communities have been strengthened

UNICEF’s contribution in malnutrition prevention increasingly focused on institutionalization and financing. The integration of the Results-Based Budgetary Programme for the Prevention and Reduction of Chronic Malnutrition into national budget guidelines marked a critical step toward sustainability, embedding child nutrition within public financial management systems and enabling progressive scaling beyond pilot territories.

Overall, UNICEF advanced equitable access to nutritious diets, quality health care, nurturing practices, and essential supplies—ensuring that all children, including adolescents, survive and thrive.
