Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future (supports SDG 4; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 2; National Development Plan Objective 2; UNSDCF Area 1)

UNICEF supported the national education system to address learning poverty through technical assistance and capacity development. A key contribution was the creation of training models based on a formative assessment approach for all national promoters of the Aprender a Tiempo Program. This strengthened the capacities of 31,558 teachers in 1,490 schools serving 752,780 students, particularly in areas affected by extreme vulnerability and violence. It is worth highlighting the progress made in EiE/DRR in Ecuador with the sustained support of UNICEF and its close collaboration with the Ministry of Education, which includes teacher training, technical assistance, and the strengthening of early warning systems within the sector.

UNICEF advanced the Psychosocial Support Model for teachers and Student Counselling Departments (DECEs), promoting a comprehensive approach to self-care, team care, and community care. In 2025, implementation began with 800 teachers and 100 DECE professionals in Esmeraldas, who support more than 69,000 students, promoting mental health, psychosocial support, and care practices in schools in Esmeraldas and Lago Agrio.

In coordination with the Secretariat for Intercultural Bilingual Education and Ethno-education, UNICEF advanced two pedagogical methodologies benefiting 645 A’i Cofán children in Sucumbíos and 6,785 Afro-Ecuadorian children in Esmeraldas. These included culturally relevant learning materials, language and cultural revitalization, and improved bilingual education strategies.

Parenting skills were strengthened through four efficient mechanisms: a) the Wawamor app, which is the first Spanish and LAC adaptation of UNICEF´s Bebbo which reached more than 12,000 families, b) UNICEF with the Ministry of Education developed a virtual parenting course that will reach 13,711 early childhood teachers in 2026, c) UNICEF trained, through online live webinars, nearly 250 private sector collaborators on the importance of ECD and parenting through the PrimeroLaInfancia initiative, and d) UNICEF strengthened collaboration with Grupo Industrial Graiman, Pasamanería PASA, Diners Club del Ecuador, and Zurich Ecuador to integrate Positive Parenting and Healthy Habits guidelines into their corporate practices, reaching over 700 participants, with a potential positive impact on 3,934 children under their care.

These efforts contribute directly to strengthening Ecuador’s human capital foundation. By improving foundational learning, psychosocial well-being and culturally relevant education, UNICEF supported not only school retention and learning recovery, but also long-term productivity, social cohesion and resilience among adolescents, particularly in violence-affected and historically excluded territories.

 Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment (supports SDGs 6 and 13; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 4; National Development Plan Objectives 6; UNSDCF Area 2) 
 
UNICEF addressed persistent WASH inequalities in rural and Indigenous communities, where climate change intensifies risks for children. Working with national and local partners, including the Ministry of Environment and Energy, the Ministry of Education, and local governments in Chimborazo Province, UNICEF strengthened climate resilience across the WASH sector and ensured that child rights remained central to national policies and programmes.
UNICEF supported the national domestic wastewater regulation process and promoted a Public–Community Water Management Ordinance in Chimborazo, establishing a sustainable and replicable governance model. UNICEF and Northwestern University applied the HWISE scale in Ecuador for the first time, generating evidence on water availability, accessibility, and reliability.

UNICEF advanced child-sensitive climate policy by supporting the Ministry of Environment and Energy in launching the National Strategy for Climate Empowerment (ENACE) and strengthening Ecuador’s Second NDC through an intergenerational approach. Youth engagement expanded through the Third Climate Academy on marine conservation, which reached 37,000 adolescents, and through support for youth participation at COP30.

UNICEF led the WASH Cluster and coordinated with the GTRM to ensure timely, efficient responses. Climate-resilient WASH services were strengthened through climate-adaptive models in rural, Indigenous, and Afro-descendant communities and through the expansion of the Climate Resilient Schools model, benefiting 74,000 children. Menstrual health initiatives reached 1,500 women and adolescents.

Youth leadership was promoted through the Biodiversity and Climate Change booklet, training for 17,000 adolescents and 150 teachers, the first Ecuador–Germany Climate Dialogues, and support to youth contributions to the Convention on Biological Diversity and LCOY 2025.

By embedding child-sensitive climate resilience within WASH governance, education systems and youth participation mechanisms, UNICEF contributed to shifting from reactive emergency response toward anticipatory, risk-informed systems that protect children’s health, learning continuity and environmental rights.

 Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect, and harmful practices (supports SDGs 5 and 16; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 3; National Development Plan Objective 3; UNSDCF Area 4)
 
Armed violence has expanded across the country. This has resulted in higher risks of child recruitment, greater insecurity in families, communities, and schools, and an increased demand for specialized services, surpassing state capabilities.

UNICEF’s violence prevention approach increasingly emphasized cross-sectoral integration, linking child protection, safe and inclusive education, psychosocial support, youth engagement and social protection. This systemic approach recognizes that prevention requires strengthening protective environments across family, school and community systems rather than isolated interventions.

UNICEF strengthened Ecuador’s child protection system through a comprehensive approach that addressed individual, family, community, and institutional capacities. UNICEF prioritized evidence generation on child recruitment and adolescents in conflict with the law, informing public policy and programmatic responses.

Together with the Ministry of Human Development, UNICEF contributed to a study on the technical and financial model for alternative care, providing actionable options that prioritize family- and community-based care and efficient resource allocation. UNICEF supported the development of a specialized service for children recruited or at risk of recruitment, aligned with international standards and scheduled for implementation in 2026. UNICEF also partnered with the Judicial Council to create a national guide on alternative care for children without parental care and developed a specialized tool for justice operators working with Indigenous children who are victims of sexual violence.

UNICEF helped implement the Public Policy for children requiring emergency protection by operating two services that tested new standards, benefiting more than 400 adolescents. UNICEF strengthened the national torture-prevention mechanism and evaluated conditions in detention centers.

At the community level in response to armed violence contexts, more than 13,200 children, adolescents, caregivers, and teachers benefited from strengthened protection mechanisms and safer environments. Related to children on the move, UNICEF provided technical support for policies addressing unaccompanied and separated children. Migration-related programmes reached over 12,000 individuals with legal assistance, financial support, and specialized information. 

Child-Friendly Spaces served more than 20,000 children and referred 1,200 to state services. Safe spaces for survivors of gender-based violence and mental health needs supported more than 6,000 individuals, including women, children, adolescents, and LGBTIQ+. Comprehensive Support Spaces in Manta, Esmeraldas, and Tulcán provided services to over 33,000 people, delivering 85,000 individual care sessions.

Every child, including adolescents, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free from poverty (supports SDG 1; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 5; National Development Plan Objective 1; UNSDCF Area 1) 

Ecuador strengthened its social protection system through coordinated advocacy, evidence-based policymaking, and targeted technical assistance. These efforts supported implementation of the Early Childhood Law and expanded equitable access to services at national and subnational levels.

A key milestone was the consolidation of the Early Childhood Cooperation Platform, led by UNICEF, CAF, the IDB, and the World Bank. This platform fostered sustained policy dialogue and promoted coordinated, multisectoral action and financing.

UNICEF’s support to the Municipality of Quito generated two transformative outcomes with lasting institutional and programmatic implications: the development of the Action Plan for the Metropolitan Early Childhood Policy and the approval of a comprehensive reform of the Metropolitan Subsystem of Assistance, Scholarships, and Incentives (ABI).

The Action Plan introduced a results-oriented roadmap aligned with the Nurturing Care Framework, establishing short-, medium-, and long-term priorities grounded in evidence. It defined measurable indicators for tracking progress and enhanced coordination among municipal institutions responsible for early childhood development.

The ABI reform, approved in August 2025, modernized and expanded Quito’s social protection tools, benefiting children, youth, and vulnerable families. Key results included:
    
• A new conceptual framework distinguishing merit-based and vulnerability-based benefits and integrating the subsystem into the Metropolitan System of Protection, Care, and Social Promotion.
• Creation of a new assistance program, including a digital food voucher for more than 5,000 families with young children and strengthened support for vulnerable youth pursuing higher education or vocational training.
• Expansion of scholarships, doubling the Academic Merit Scholarship beneficiaries and maintaining access to the Sports Merit Scholarship.
• New non-monetary incentives increasing access to cultural, recreational, and mobility services for vulnerable children.
• A unified allocation and monitoring framework to reinforce transparency, equity, and targeting.

UNICEF and multilateral partners supported the Ministry of Economy and Finance in adopting the 2026 Budget Guidelines, which integrated structural reforms to strengthen results-based budgeting. Achievements included the incorporation of the programmatic structure for the Results-Based Budgetary Program on the Prevention and Reduction of Chronic Malnutrition and commitments to establish an inter-institutional monitoring framework. The Ministry also agreed to enhance capacities—particularly in the health sector—and institutionalize expenditure quality monitoring.

UNICEF also advanced policy responses to gender-based violence by supporting women’s organizations through advocacy campaigns and local dialogues in high-femicide areas. Policy recommendations on the impacts of femicide on children will be available in early 2026.  Additionally, Laaha, a secure digital platform providing sexual and reproductive health information, is being piloted with the Ministry of Education in 40 schools and implemented with the Pichincha Provincial Government through adolescent and violence victim services. UNICEF Ecuador has successfully positioned Laaha as an innovative, gender-responsive digital solution that expands access to reliable information for girls and adolescents. The initiative is increasingly being integrated into public education and protection systems, strengthening institutional ownership and sustainability

Communications and PFP

Ecuador CO strengthened its Communications and Advocacy results. Total followers across Meta, X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and TikTok reached 687,847, increasing by 48,531 compared to 2024. Meta platforms reached 8,550,524 users, TikTok 9,921,225, and website visits grew from 471,000 to 539,000. In the media, 1,217 publications mentioning UNICEF were released (valued at USD 7,884,719.62 in free press), and the CO achieved a 19.3 per cent share of voice on child-related issues.

On June 2025, UNICEF launched Wawamor, the first Spanish-language version of the Bebbo parenting app, developed with the Municipality of Quito. The Communications team localized content, producing 94 videos and the promotional campaign. The launch event attracted 500 attendees, including the Mayor of Quito, while 3,570 people visited the service fair. The digital campaign reached 4,383,089 users and generated 160,195 website visits. Media coverage included 61 publications valued at USD 724,576.89. Wawamor promotion in Quito Metro reached approximately 178,000 users daily, while three bi-articulated buses reached 5,151 users daily. By December, the app recorded 16,000 downloads.

World Children’s Day commemoration combined public activities with high-level advocacy. The digital campaign reached 1,223,368 users. Through Metro activations, UNICEF reached more than 225,000 users. Media relations and press release dissemination generated 68 publications, valued at USD 229,945.34. Activities also included an op-ed, a special TV programme, a MoU with Vice Presidency, and an event with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and youth advocates.
Youth engagement expanded through GeneraciónMÁS community and U-Report, mobilizing 106 youth leaders, reaching 1,675 young people, and generating 187,274 responses via six surveys and three chatbots. Four youth advocates represented Ecuador in high-level international forums during 2025.

UNICEF Ecuador continued positioning the private sector as a strategic partner in advancing children’s rights through a shared value approach. The office worked to strengthen corporate engagement grounded in a rights-based framework, encouraging businesses to integrate child rights into their core strategies, operations and value chains. This approach aims to generate sustainable social and economic impact, aligning business competitiveness with measurable improvements in the lives of children and adolescents across the country. Within this broader vision of partnership, the office also sustained efforts to secure unrestricted and predictable private-sector resources despite mixed internal and external conditions. Individual donors remained the primary funding source, contributing 82.3 per cent of total funds raised. The corporate channel grew by 80.9 per cent, accounting for 17.5 per cent of total income, reinforcing both financial sustainability and advocacy leverage for children’s rights in Ecuador.
 
Monitoring and evaluation 

In 2025, UNICEF strengthened monitoring and evaluation systems to promote evidence-based decision-making. The Children’s Information Lab (https://infanciaecuador.org/) was updated with new content, including risk analysis maps and early childhood development data. UNICEF, UNDP, and the National Risk Secretariat developed a child-sensitive subnational risk index to be presented to the government in early 2026. Results from the 2024–2025 Educational Community Survey were shared with the Ministry of Education. The ECHO project strengthened its monitoring system through a Third-Party Monitoring Organization, which conducted three exercises and shared findings with programme sections and implementing partners.

Given rising violence, UNICEF developed a monitoring tool to identify geographic areas facing greater barriers to accessing social services (ECD, education, health), combining traditional data sources (surveys, administrative records) with non-traditional ones – using AI- (Facebook, radio, newspapers) to inform programmes.

In evaluation, UNICEF completed the assessment of its local stunting-reduction strategy. At the request of the Resident Coordinator’s Office, UNICEF co-led the evaluation of the UNSDCF alongside WFP, to be finalized in early 2026 with support from LACRO.

Amid budget constraints and the need to realign strategies for greater impact, UNICEF contributed to the Strategic Moment of Reflection, reinforcing intersectoral synergies and identifying three priorities for the next country programme: early childhood development and human capital, violence prevention, and climate/WASH/risk management.

Ongoing support was provided to programme areas on data, evidence generation, and monitoring.
 
Field Operations

In 2025, UNICEF strengthened its territorial strategy through four programmatic pillars, advancing upstream policy engagement, subnational governance, humanitarian access, and localized service delivery. A renewed management approach enhanced coherence, efficiency, and impact across priority territories.

UNICEF applied a prioritization approach that considered poverty, chronic malnutrition, service gaps, climate exposure, and institutional capacity. This approach helped target the most vulnerable territories while ensuring that field interventions contributed to system strengthening.

Support to municipalities expanded early childhood and human capital development through integrated ECD methodologies and culturally adapted practices for Amazonian and Andean populations. Local monitoring systems and frontline worker capacities were strengthened to improve developmental follow-up.

Field operations were organized around priority territories, with tailored strategies addressing violence and displacement (Esmeraldas and Manta), border and mobility dynamics (Tulcán and Lago Agrio), and climate-related shocks and disaster risk (coastal areas of Esmeraldas).

In 2025, UNICEF continued its humanitarian operations while strengthening emergency preparedness amid escalating violence and funding constraints affecting the humanitarian sector, responding to the humanitarian impacts of armed violence, mixed migration and other emergencies such as oil spills, disease outbreaks, and recurrent flooding.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The 2025 programme year unfolded in a highly complex environment marked by escalating violence and insecurity, fiscal constraints, among others. One of the most significant challenges was operating amid continuous institutional change, with frequent leadership transitions across key ministries. This affected policy continuity, slowed decision-making, and required UNICEF to repeatedly rebuild institutional memory and re-establish working arrangements with new authorities. While the office remained flexible and proactive, these conditions underscored the need for sustained capacity-building and stronger governance frameworks to secure results at scale.

Broader social and political polarization further constrained the enabling environment for children’s rights. Fragmented public discourse and competing national priorities reduced space for consensus-driven policymaking.

At the community level, children continue to face high levels of violence, insecurity, and exposure to harmful environments, undermining their ability to learn, grow, and thrive. Increased violence in and around schools has heightened risks of dropout and psychosocial distress, while adolescents in high-risk urban, coastal, and border areas face growing threats of armed violence and forced recruitment. 

Persistent structural challenges compound these risks, particularly for rural, Indigenous, Afro-descendant, migrant, and historically excluded populations. Translating national progress in early childhood development, health, education, social protection, child protection, WASH, and climate action into equitable, high-quality services at scale remain difficult due to uneven subnational capacities, high staff turnover, and financing constraints. 

Lessons Learned

These challenges generated important lessons and reinforced principles aligned with UNICEF’s Future Focus Initiative (FFI).

A key institutional lesson in 2025 was that breadth without strategic concentration risks diluting impact. Operating in a context of fiscal constraints and institutional volatility reinforced the importance of prioritizing fewer, high-impact interventions with clear pathways to scale and sustainability. The Strategic Moment of Reflection enabled the office to sharpen its focus around early childhood development, violence prevention and climate-risk management as mutually reinforcing pillars of systemic change.

An important lesson emphasizes the necessity of genuine intersectoral programming. Merely including two programmatic areas in a project does not guarantee that there will be joint programming. To address this issue, UNICEF needs to cultivate a shared understanding of the problem and develop a common vision for the required actions. This lesson is closely linked to the FFI, which aims to enhance coordination across various areas by focusing on three shared priorities: early childhood development and human capital, violence prevention, and climate change with risk reduction. 

First, early childhood development (ECD) is the most strategic entry point for advancing human capital, equity, and long-term violence prevention. Integrated ECD approaches that combine health, nutrition, education, parenting support, social protection, and protection from violence are more effective than siloed interventions, strengthening family resilience and protective environments from the earliest stages of life.  In this area, UNICEF implemented an evaluation of its strategy for the prevention and reduction of chronic child malnutrition in three provinces of Ecuador confirms its relevance and coherence. Using a difference-in-differences approach based on administrative data, the evaluation identifies heterogeneous impacts across outcomes, including birthweight. A key lesson learned from this evaluation is that the rapid scale-up beyond the pilot phase, without sufficiently detailed planning, generated operational and resource challenges, underscoring the importance of a phased, context-responsive scaling and exit strategy from the outset.  Future scaling efforts will prioritize early integration into public systems, sustainable financing arrangements and clearly defined exit strategies from the outset.

Genuine intersectoral programming requires more than co-location of activities; it demands a shared theory of change, joint planning, integrated monitoring frameworks and aligned financing. The experience in Ecuador demonstrated that integrated approaches—such as linking nutrition, WASH, parenting support, social protection and violence prevention within early childhood platforms—generate stronger and more sustainable outcomes.

Second, violence prevention requires coordinated action across family, school, community, and social systems. Interventions that link psychosocial support, safe and inclusive schools, community-based protection mechanisms, youth engagement, and social protection show greater potential to reduce dropout, mitigate exposure to violence, and prevent forced recruitment, particularly among adolescents in high-risk contexts.

Third, adaptability grounded in real-time evidence is essential. Investments in monitoring, innovative data sources, and territorial analysis enabled timely adjustments to programming in response to evolving security, mobility, and climate conditions. Community- and territory-based approaches proved critical to ensuring service continuity when national-level institutional dynamics fluctuated.

Finally, climate-sensitive, risk-informed programming enhanced relevance and sustainability. Integrating climate resilience across WASH, nutrition, education, and protection helped mitigate shocks and reinforced the need to shift from reactive emergency response toward anticipatory action.

Future Outlook — Guided by the Future Focus Initiative

Guided by the Future Focus Initiative, UNICEF Ecuador will continue to evolve toward a leaner, more focused and impact-driven model—prioritizing systemic reforms, sustainable financing and territorial targeting to ensure that every child, especially those facing violence, poverty and climate vulnerability, can survive, develop and thrive. By concentrating efforts on early childhood development, violence prevention and climate-resilient systems, UNICEF aims to safeguard Ecuador’s human capital and contribute to a more equitable and resilient future. 

To advance these priorities, the office will:
1.       Deliver results at scale by concentrating resources and technical assistance on fewer, high-impact interventions.
2.       Strengthen partnerships and advocacy with local governments, civil society, the private sector, youth networks, and academia to mobilize resources and sustain political commitment for children.
3.       Adapt programme and operational models to increase efficiency, strengthen local capacities, and support decentralized planning using real-time data and learning.
4.       Promote innovation and foresight, shifting from reactive responses to preventive and anticipatory approaches to violence, climate, and displacement risks.
5.       Prioritize sustainability and systemic change by supporting institutions to institutionalize quality services and secure sustainable financing.

Guided by the FFI, UNICEF Ecuador will focus, adapt, and innovate to help build resilient and equitable systems that ensure every child—especially those in the most vulnerable situations—can survive, develop, and thrive.

The current national context presents a combination of opportunities, achievements and challenges for guaranteeing the rights of children and adolescents in El Salvador. Demographic, legal, social, and economic conditions shape the country’s capacity to advance toward sustainable development, with investment in children and adolescents as a key driver.

Economically, the country maintains stable and modest growth, with GDP increasing by 2.6% in 2024, below the 3.5% recorded in 2023. Fiscal vulnerabilities persist, due to high external financing and rising public debt, which in 2025 represents 28.8% of the national budget (compared to 23.6% in 2024). While the General State Budget totals USD 9.663 billion (Ministry of Finance, 2025) and exceeds the 2024 budget, the share allocated to social spending decreased from 39.9% to 35.7%, including reductions in education and health, which declined by 1.4 and 1.7 percentage points, respectively.

From a demographic perspective, children and adolescents represent 26.1% of the 6.03 million inhabitants recorded in the 2024 Census, while those aged 15 to 29 constitute the largest segment at 24.9%. This scenario reflects a demographic dividend that as long as it is strategically leveraged, can contribute to economic and social development. In terms of inclusion, an analysis based on the 2021 National Health Survey estimates that 7.8% of children under 15 live with a disability.

Within this context, the 2025 Universal Periodic Review reviewed the country’s commitments to protecting the well-being of children and adolescents. Overall, 228 recommendations were issued of which 150 were accepted. According to OHCHR, the thematic areas with the highest number of accepted recommendations include child protection, trafficking in persons, education and gender-based violence. Among the recommendations explicitly classified under child rights, 13 were accepted while two recommendations related to increasing the minimum age of criminal responsibility and strengthening measures to eradicate child labour were noted. 

Beyond the institutional landscape, the country also reported important progress in the social sector. According to the latest update on Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 presented in the 2025 Voluntary National Review (VNR), the country has made significant health advances contributing to early childhood, well-being and reductions in preventable deaths. Maternal mortality decreased from 42.3 in 2015 to 26.8 per 100,000 live births in 2023, while under-five mortality reached 10.2 and neonatal mortality 5.0, reflecting improvements in early care. 

These gains are complemented by higher immunization coverage, notably an increase in the second dose of the measles, rubella, and mumps vaccine (MMR2) from 71.39% in 2023 to 90.10% in 2024 and higher HPV vaccination coverage among adolescent girls, which increased from 79.66% to 83.13% in the same period.

Despite these advances, challenges remain. Acute malnutrition and overweight among children under five increased by 0.9 and 1.9 percentage points, respectively (VNR, 2025), underscoring the need for stronger preventive interventions to avoid entrenching these trends and increasing the risk of noncommunicable diseases later in life.

Mental health continues to be a critical challenge. The 2022 National Mental Health Survey indicates that 54.8% of adolescents aged 13 to 17 present symptoms of anxiety disorders, while 29.5% show signs of major depression. Coupled with a suicide mortality rate of 2.2 per 100,000 inhabitants (above the national target 0.93), these figures highlight the urgency of expanding preventive measures and psychosocial support in schools and communities.

In education, El Salvador has made notable progress toward SDG targets on quality education, as highlighted in the 2025 VNR. Advances are particularly evident in early childhood: enrollment in initial education increased fivefold from 2.1% to 10.4% as a result of the “Crecer Juntos” Policy. However, 2024 Census data point to significant gaps in educational continuity: 47.2% of the population reaches only basic education, 24.1% complete high school, and just 9% pursue university studies. This declining coverage at higher educational levels highlights the need to strengthen transitions to secondary and tertiary education to ensure full educational trajectories for adolescents and youth.

Among these gaps, access to water and sanitation remains critical. Although significant progress has been made, inequalities persist. The 2025 VNR on SDG 6 reports that 56% of indicators show positive trends, reflecting national efforts to improve water management. El Salvador is among the most disaster and risk-prone countries in Central America, with high exposure to hazards such as droughts, floods and earthquakes. Climate-related shocks have intensified food security and deepened territorial disparities, especially in rural areas, where climate and environmental risks, affect approximately 30% of children and adolescents living in highly exposed zones.

Human mobility adds another dimension of vulnerability. In 2024, 2,469 children and adolescents returned to the country, 20.8% of whom traveled unaccompanied (IOM, 2025), underscoring the persistence of risky migration routes and the need to strengthen cross-border protection mechanisms.

In terms of reforms, the Legislative Assembly approved constitutional amendments, including the possibility of indefinite presidential re-election and adjustments to the institutional structure. Reforms to the Juvenile Criminal Law and the Penitentiary Law introduced changes applicable to adolescents in conflict with the law (organized crime). UNICEF, UNFPA, OHCHR and the CRC expressed concerns over the reform's lack of adherence to international standards and offered policy alternatives. Additional regulatory changes include the approval of the Law on Foreign Agents which establishes reporting and tax requirements for organizations receiving external funding, with potential implications for civil society engagement. 

Within this framework, since March 2022, El Salvador has maintained a state of exception, a constitutional measure allowing the suspension of certain rights to address gang-related violence and restore public security. The Legislative Assembly has renewed this measure on a monthly basis. Official data indicates that more than 90,844 arrests have been reported alongside a significant reduction in homicide rates, from 18.3 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2021 to 1.9 in 2024. 

Overall, El Salvador has made significant progress, particularly in early childhood where improvements in health, initial education, and early care demonstrate notable efforts and concrete results. These achievements represent an opportunity to consolidate progress and extend gains throughout the life cycle, in line with international standards and the commitment to leave no child behind.

In 2025, UNICEF El Salvador advanced toward fostering a more intersectoral approach to ensuring the rights of children and adolescents in the country. Recognizing that child well-being cannot be achieved through isolated efforts, UNICEF strategically focused on strengthening collaboration across multiple sectors, including health, education, protection and social welfare. This holistic perspective allowed for the creation and implementation of coordinated initiatives that could more effectively address the multi-pronged and complex challenges faced by children and adolescents. By embedding intersectoral strategies within national programs and policies, UNICEF ensured that interventions were not only complementary but also naturally reinforcing, thereby maximizing their impact on child development, protection and inclusion. 

One example of this intersectoral work is the initiative funded by the Republic of Korea, through which UNICEF implemented a comprehensive intervention in 32 communities across six municipalities, reaching more than 38,000 people. This initiative reinforced child protection for children in vulnerable situations, promoted school retention and employability among adolescents, and supported hygiene and sanitation practices, contributing to disease prevention and children’s health and well-being, through coordinated efforts with local actors. This strategy involved close collaboration with local authorities, community leaders, and service providers, ensuring that the intervention was responsive to the local context and sustainable over time. 

In the area of child protection, UNICEF contributed to strengthening El Salvador’s specialized child protection system to ensure that children and adolescents in vulnerable situations have access to specialized services. One significant undertaking in 2025 was an assessment of the country’s alternative care system which aimed to generate evidence for improving services for children without parental care or at risk of losing it. This participatory effort included consultations with children in residential care facilities, as well as with staff from the National Council for Early Childhood, Children, and Adolescents (CONAPINA), the Office of the Attorney General (PGR), and specialized courts. The purpose was to generate evidence to inform interventions that uphold children’s right to live in a family environment and to access services that support their well-being.

Based on the assessment’s recommendations, UNICEF supported the strengthening of the Government’s “Vivir en Familia” program, which prioritizes family-based care for children and adolescents without parental care or at risk of losing it. UNICEF’s support included the provision of psychological testing tools that enhance psychosocial assessments and improve decision-making in line with the best interests of the child. These efforts helped authorities prioritize family-based alternatives, creating protective environments for children.  Between June 2024 and May 2025, the program reached 1,387 children in family-based modalities, demonstrating its potential impact.

In line with national commitments to end violence against children, UNICEF worked with national institutions to support the implementation of actions under the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children. The support focused on strengthening prevention, response and care services, promoting safe school environments, and reinforcing family-strengthening programmes. These actions reached 11,038 children, 112 caregivers and 491 officials in 2025. Additionally, in coordination with the Special Representative of the UN Secretary General on Violence Against Children and UNICEF LACRO, UNICEF El Salvador promoted national ownership among key institutions, including CONAPINA, PGR, ICJ and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to accelerate progress toward ending violence against children.  

Complementing these efforts, UNICEF supported the strengthening of protection mechanisms through a comprehensive assessment of CONAPINA’s Child Helpline 119 “Habla Conmigo,” a key entry point for identifying and responding to threats and violations of children’s rights. Based on this assessment, UNICEF provided in-person training to helpline staff and Protection Boards to enhance their capacity to respond to complex cases. In 2024, the helpline served 4,765 children, and between January and May 2025 an additional 2,995 cases were registered, highlighting the service’s growing demand and the importance of reinforcing its role for the most vulnerable children.

In parallel, UNICEF strengthened judicial and justice-sector responses through specialized training initiatives on juvenile justice and online protection, delivered in coordination with key national justice institutions. These initiatives reached 1,684 justice-sector professionals in 2025, contributing to reinforcing institutional capacities to prevent and respond to violence against children, including in digital environments. 

In early childhood, UNICEF consolidated meaningful advances by supporting the Crecer Juntos Institute (ICJ) in designing and validating the National Plan to Strengthen Parenting Practices and in developing and implementing Transitional Guidelines for Family Strengthening, aligned with the Crecer Juntos Law and the Integrated Care Model. Technical support from UNICEF brought together specialists in protection, health, and education to ensure a holistic approach. UNICEF also supported training for ICJ Territorial Facilitators who assisted families in applying the guidelines. As a result, more than 2,900 families improved their parenting practices, reaching 5,068 children aged 0 to 7, and establishing the foundation for potential large-scale expansion that could reach more than 600,000 children nationwide.

In education, UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with the Ministry of Education, Science, and Technology (MINEDUCYT) and the Office of the First Lady to build a more inclusive and resilient education system, advancing the Intersectoral National Strategy for Access and Retention for out-of-school children and adolescents. UNICEF also played a key role—together with the Office of the First Lady, MINEDUCYT, and the Agency for International Cooperation (ESCO)—in securing approval for the initiative “A Second Chance: Enrolling Out of School Children to Schools in El Salvador,” financed by the Education Above All Foundation (EAA) in partnership with the Government of Qatar. Through this interinstitutional collaboration, USD 7 million in national and international resources were mobilized to complement this initiative, which between 2026 and 2028 aims to strengthen educational access, continuity, and learning for 30,000 children aged 7 to 12.

In parallel, UNICEF supported efforts to promote school coexistence and student leadership by providing technical assistance to MINEDUCYT in implementing the “Agustine Project:  Support for Violence Prevention in El Salvador,” in partnership with the European Union, UNESCO and Expertise France. Through this initiative, UNICEF aims to strengthen students’ skills for peaceful conflict resolution, participation, and leadership by promoting safe learning environments and holistic development opportunities. In 2025, more than 5,000 students participated in consultations and learning activities in arts, sports, and technology, and more than 700 student council members strengthened their leadership skills.

Using a human-centered design approach, UNICEF also developed a Social and Behavior Change Strategy for student participation and leadership, informed by evidence generated through consultations with the education community. This strategy will serve as a key input for MINEDUCYT in developing its Soft Skills Strategy for the Promotion of Coexistence, Participation, and Student Leadership, to be launched in 2026. This strategy has the potential to reach up to 460,000 adolescents enrolled in secondary education.

These efforts respond to the persisting challenges in the transition from school to work for adolescents and youth in El Salvador. National data show that people aged 16-29 account for 48.4% of total unemployment (EHPM, 2024) and are more likely to be engaged in informal and low-quality jobs, particularly those with incomplete secondary education. By strengthening life skills, leadership and school retention, UNICEF’s education interventions contribute to improving school-to-work transitions and expanding adolescents’ opportunities for future employability, especially for those in vulnerable contexts. 

Aligned with its broader support to the education sector, UNICEF strengthened key coordination spaces and explored new opportunities to advance children’s and adolescents’ development. Under the Global Partnership for Education, UNICEF continued to support MINEDUCYT in coordinating the Local Education Group (LEG), which brings together public institutions, civil society, academia, the private sector, and national and international partners. The LEG played a key role in  the technical review and endorsement of the Expression of Interest for El  Salvador to access the new GPE Multiplier Fund, enabling the mobilization of  USD 12 million to complement a USD 150 million IDB loan for the program  “Building Human Capital: Being Born, Growing, and Learning – Program for the  Consolidation of Complete Educational Trajectories and Climate Resilience.”

To complement these efforts, UNICEF initiated the generation of strategic evidence on an investment case on adolescents and education financing, including an analysis of the efficiency of public spending in education. These analyses aim to inform policy dialogue and advocacy, to support more effective and sustainable investment decisions to strengthen educational access, quality and equity for children and adolescents. 

UNICEF also strengthened actions in the health sector to improve the sustainability and quality of essential services for children and adolescents. In coordination with the Ministry of Health (MINSAL), UNICEF began a 2025 study assessing solar energy needs in 100 health units that serve nearly one million people, including about 500,000 children aged 0 to 17 who rely on essential services such as immunization and primary care. This analysis will help guide future installation of solar systems, reducing energy costs, contributing to environmental sustainability, and ensuring the security of the vaccine cold chain and enhancing disaster resilience by supporting the continuity of essential health services during emergencies. This commitment to renewable energy has strengthened UNICEF’s role as a key partner in modernizing and enhancing the sustainability of national health services.

In parallel, and in alignment with the Law “Amor Convertido en Alimento para el Fomento, Protección y Apoyo a la Lactancia Materna”, UNICEF collaborated with MINSAL in 2025 to strengthen enabling environments for breastfeeding by equipping two human milk collection centers in two municipalities. 

Beyond infrastructure and essential services, UNICEF made significant progress in positioning mental health as a national priority for children and adolescents. In 2025, UNICEF led public outreach and social mobilization efforts to raise awareness and integrate emotional well-being into community spaces. Notable achievements include the incorporation of caregiver mental health into the National Parenting Practices Plan and the strengthening of the “Caring for Those Who Care for Us” strategy for MINSAL professionals.

During Mental Health Week (6–10 October), UNICEF’s advocacy and communication efforts expanded public dialogue on the topic, reaching more than 433,000 people on social media with content on mental health and self-care. In alliance with Clowns Without Borders USA and implementing partners, UNICEF organized a community tour that culminated in a national event with MINSAL, the Office of the First Lady, and the Technological University. More than 1,500 children, adolescents, and caregivers participated, helping raise awareness about mental health and offering practical guidance to strengthen emotional well-being.

UNICEF’s commitment to inclusion and well-being was also reflected in actions directed toward children and adolescents with disabilities. UNICEF coordinated work in education, health, and protection, advancing national guidelines for community-based rehabilitation and promoting protective environments. In education, UNICEF supported strategies to reduce gaps and ensure accessible materials, promoting universal design for learning. Institutional capacities were strengthened to ensure inclusive environments and comprehensive services for children with disabilities.

UNICEF also made substantial progress in child and adolescent participation in 2025, while consolidating its position as the most trusted voice on child rights in El Salvador among organizations working for children and adolescents. Media coverage consistently cited UNICEF as an authoritative source, generating an estimated return on investment of USD 1.4 million. Participation reached historic levels, with more than 9,400 children and adolescents involved in creative activities and dialogue spaces. UNICEF also strengthened its accountability mechanisms by developing tools to amplify and integrate children’s voices into programme design and implementation. More than 1,000 children contributed insights through consultations and digital surveys, enabling UNICEF to fine-tune interventions to their needs and priorities, including in emergency contexts.

UNICEF also elevated children’s voices in other strategic processes, including the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), an interinstitutional and intersectoral assessment of children’s vulnerability and resilience to climate change. This initiative incorporated the perspectives of more than 7,400 adolescents and youth and generated evidence on climate impacts across key sectors. The analysis provided recommendations to strengthen climate financing for adaptation and resilience, specifically in health, nutrition, education, protection, and WASH. These priorities will be integrated into the next Country Programme in alignment with government priorities and the humanitarian-development-peace agenda. 

This participatory approach was also reflected in inter-agency efforts, including the initiative on sustainable and nutrition-sensitive food systems funded by the SDG Fund. UNICEF facilitated consultative dialogues with children, adolescents, caregivers, and community actors, generating strategic inputs for inter-agency planning and national nutrition programs. The interagency campaign “For Healthier Families,” developed under this framework, reached 1.5 million people and helped position the importance of healthy food environments for children and adolescents.

Aligned with national climate and water governance priorities, UNICEF supported MINSAL in ensuring that the methodology for Climate-Resilient Water Safety Plans (CR-WSPs) became a mandatory technical guideline for local environmental health personnel. Beginning in 2026, this methodology will be integrated into annual planning to strengthen risk prevention and the safe, climate-resilient provision of water across more than 2,500 systems nationwide. By improving water quality and safety, this initiative will contribute to disease prevention and improved health and nutrition outcomes, particularly for vulnerable children and adolescents, as these systems supply more than 1.5 million people, including 450,000 children. This achievement has helped establish climate resilience as a key component of national water management.

These actions are particularly relevant in El Salvador, one of the most disaster-prone countries in the region, where recurring climate shocks and underlying vulnerabilities expose nearly 90% of the national territory to natural hazards. In this context, climate-resilient water systems are critical to shock-responsive service delivery and the continuity of essential services for children and adolescents.

The progress achieved in 2025 reflects UNICEF’s sustained commitment to multisectoral interventions aligned with national priorities and its strategic focus on expanding opportunities for children’s and adolescents’ development. By combining evidence-based programming, intersectoral collaboration, and active participation of children and adolescents, UNICEF reinforced the foundations for long-term high-level systemic improvements across child protection, education, health, and social services in terms of policies and systems. These efforts demonstrate that holistic, coordinated approaches are essential for creating protective, inclusive, and sustainable environments that allow every child in El Salvador to thrive, develop their potential, and have their rights fulfilled.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF faced significant challenges related to regulatory changes and limitations in international cooperation. These challenges highlighted the need to strengthen coordination, dialogue, advocacy and rely on strategic partnerships and technical assessments to guide evidence-based interventions and improve the quality of services for children and adolescents.

Recent reforms to El Salvador’s criminal legislation have imposed stricter measures on adolescents involved in gang-related or organized crime offenses, raising concerns regarding their compatibility with national and international standards, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Crecer Juntos Law. Comparative experiences in juvenile justice offer valuable guidance for advancing toward responses aligned with international norms, incorporating pedagogical approaches, family and community engagement, early prevention, data-driven policy, restorative justice mechanisms, and comprehensive protection frameworks that include alternatives to detention. In this context, UNICEF remains available to provide support to the Salvadoran State in identifying solutions that promote respect for the rights of adolescents in conflict with the law and ensure their reintegration.

Another significant challenge was the limited availability of updated and disaggregated public data in health, education, child protection, and adolescent well-being. These gaps hindered comprehensive needs analysis and evidence-based programming, revealing the need to strengthen national data systems and interinstitutional coordination. UNICEF promoted complementary approaches, reinforcing qualitative components through participatory processes with adolescents to capture aspects that are not visible in existing quantitative sources. This approach formed part of UNICEF’s evidence-generation strategy and will inform the design of the next Country Programme (2027–2031).

In parallel, UNICEF supported national data-generation efforts by collaborating with the Office of the First Lady by providing technical assistance on nutrition and anemia for health personnel as part of the upcoming National Survey on Children and Adolescents. Additionally, UNICEF started the development of a training module on soft skills and ethical data collection for frontline workers which will be implemented in 2026 to ensure child-sensitive data collection. 

Regarding lessons learned, evaluation processes conducted in 2025 generated critical inputs for future planning and programme management. These exercises confirmed the importance of participatory mechanisms and periodic reviews to ensure internal coherence, foster results-based management, and strengthen program effectiveness. They also demonstrated that UNICEF’s most successful strategies were those that incorporated flexibility, inclusivity, and the participation of key actors—particularly children and adolescents. The findings and recommendations from these evaluations will serve as a core input for designing the next Country Programme, ensuring participatory and evidence-based planning.

Another key lesson was the effectiveness of intersectoral work in advancing integrated responses to child and adolescent priorities. A clear example is UNICEF’s mental health work in 2025, approached from multiple dimensions: technical, advocacy, communication, and social mobilization. These actions helped to position mental health as a priority for children and adolescents and supported the development of preventive and community-level interventions. This experience reaffirmed that cross-cutting issues require close coordination across sectors and stakeholders to achieve sustainable impact. These insights were reinforced by recommendations from the Evaluability Assessment of the 2022–2026 Country Programme, which emphasized the importance of intersectoral integration.

Experiences from education interventions also showed that more integrated connections are needed between the education sector and the labor market for increased student motivation and retention. UNICEF found that educational programmes produce stronger results when designed inclusively and in coordination with the private sector, as this engagement helps create opportunities for adolescents and youth. The integration of life skills and employability components into education programs has proven effective in strengthening resilience and expanding pathways to employment. Similarly, linking education with local economic opportunities has emerged as an effective strategy to promote employability and reduce school dropouts.

Building on these lessons, UNICEF will continue prioritizing the integration of life skills and stronger connections between school and work in future educational interventions. This will include promoting partnerships with the productive sector and programs aligned with local market needs. The goal is to ensure that education remains relevant, inclusive, and capable of generating real opportunities, contributing to school retention and smooth transitions to dignified employment for adolescents and youth.

Looking ahead, UNICEF highlights the importance of strengthening meaningful participation policies and strategies specifically for adolescents, ensuring that they have real opportunities to develop life skills, access quality services, and contribute their voices to decisions that affect their present and future. Their role as agents of change must be supported by safe and inclusive environments, including community and digital spaces.

Within this framework, 2025 marked an innovative milestone in incorporating children’s and adolescents’ voices into planning processes, ensuring that their perspectives extend beyond UNICEF’s programmatic priorities and inform the broader United Nations agenda at the national level. In collaboration with the Resident Coordinator’s Office and the Joining Forces Alliance, UNICEF implemented its methodology “Adolescents Designing Their Future” to conduct consultations across the country. The findings from this methodology normally used for UNICEF Country Programme planning will also inform the design of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. This represents a broader level of influence and positions the initiative as a regional reference for adolescent participation.

Looking to the coming years, UNICEF has begun establishing and strengthening alliances to advance a comprehensive approach to adolescence. These include initial dialogue with the Directorate for Social Integration, which promotes social cohesion and development through programs in education, health, sports, and culture. Although still in early stages, this collaboration presents an important opportunity to advance the holistic development of adolescents and their families.

In the same direction, UNICEF has deepened its collaboration with CONAPINA to support the development of a National Strategy for Adolescents in 2026. This strategy will bring together policies and programs under an integrated approach to respond to the needs of adolescents. It will incorporate a rights-based, gender-sensitive, and participatory perspective, guiding interventions that promote learning, employability, and development opportunities. This joint effort is expected to continue strengthening an investment cycle that supports holistic development from early childhood through adulthood and thus maintaining the gains and investment seen in recent years on early childhood development.

Even though Guatemala’s macroeconomic indicators remain favorable and progress has been made in child survival, children continue to face multifaceted challenges including poverty, malnutrition, educational gaps, violence, and migration. Addressing these issues requires sustained collaboration and commitment from national and local governments and international partners, with a focus on strengthening child protection systems, improving access to quality health and education services, and fostering inclusive socio-economic development. The current context underscores the critical importance of targeted interventions and policy reforms to ensure that no child is left behind as Guatemala works toward the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG).
Guatemala shows a projected GDP growth rate of 3.8% for 2025 and a 1.65% inflation rate. This positive trajectory is largely driven by increased credit availability for the private sector and heightened confidence in national economic activity. However, beneath these favorable indicators, the country’s economic resilience is undermined by its substantial reliance on remittance inflows, which account for approximately 20% of GDP. This dependency poses a significant risk, especially as global migration policies evolve, potentially affecting the volume and consistency of remittance transfers from abroad.
Politically, Guatemala faces ongoing governance challenges marked by persistent tensions between its Executive and Judiciary branches. President Bernardo Arévalo, as of October 2025, has been the subject of 12 requests for the removal of his immunity, most initiated by the Public Prosecutor’s Office (Ministerio Público, MP), notably through the Special Prosecutor’s Office Against Impunity (Fiscalía Especial Contra la Impunidad, FECI). Throughout the year, the MP has sustained legal actions related to alleged electoral irregularities stemming from the 2023 elections, with several court rulings casting doubt on the legitimacy of positions secured by the governing party. Although the Constitutional Court recently overturned at least one such decision, the persistence of these disputes underscores the complexity and instability of Guatemala’s current political environment. These governance issues threaten institutional effectiveness and have direct implications for policy implementation, public trust, and the country’s broader development trajectory.
The prevailing socio-economic and political context continues to disproportionally affect Guatemalan children. As per the 2023 Living Conditions Survey, an alarming 64.8% of children live in poverty, and 20.7% face extreme poverty. Those percentages climb to 81.1% and 34.7% among indigenous children. While the country has made progress in reducing child mortality, declining to 21.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, it remains above the regional average of 15.8 per 1,000. Equally concerning is the low institutional delivery coverage, standing at just 65% compared to a regional benchmark of 94%, highlighting persistent gaps in access to essential maternal and child health services.
Malnutrition remains a significant public health challenge in Guatemala. 45.8% of under five children suffer from chronic malnutrition (61.2% among indigenous children) —the highest prevalence in Latin America— and 22,138 cases of acute malnutrition and 60 associated deaths were reported in 2025, a figure slightly lower than 2024. These data indicate an urgent requirement for comprehensive, targeted strategies to enhance nutritional status and strengthen overall health outcomes for children, especially within rural and indigenous populations.
In education, Guatemala has achieved near-universal coverage at the primary level, yet substantial gaps remain at other stages of the educational ladder. Notably, 37% of children are not enrolled in pre-primary education, and a staggering 73% of adolescents are out of upper secondary school. Learning poverty is acute—only one in ten students demonstrates proficiency in mathematics, and just one in three is proficient in reading by the end of lower secondary education. These statistics highlight the need for comprehensive reforms to improve educational quality, expand access, and ensure that children and adolescents acquire the skills necessary to succeed in a rapidly changing world.
Violence against children (VAC) continues to affect children across the country. Household well-being surveys reveal that half of adolescents aged 15 to 19 have experienced some form of violence in their lifetime. In 2025, the Public Prosecutor’s Office documented 13,110 (51% less than in 2024) cases of physical violence and 5,987 cases of sexual violence involving children and adolescents (similar to 2024). Furthermore, 56,889 pregnancies among girls and adolescents aged 10 to 19 were registered in 2025, reflecting persistent challenges around protection, reproductive health, and gender-based violence. These issues not only threaten the well-being and future prospects of affected children but also highlight systemic gaps in the country’s child protection system.
Migration dynamics are also evolving, with significant consequences for children. As November 2025, more than 13,965 children traversed Guatemala as part of migration flows to and from North America, with a notable uptick in children moving southward as a result of shifting migration policies in the region. In addition, nearly 1,904 Guatemalan children were deported from Mexico and the United States during the same period, 34% of whom were unaccompanied. The plight of unaccompanied children is particularly alarming, as they face heightened risks of exploitation, abuse, trafficking, and other forms of harm. Upon return, these children often struggle with stigma, trauma, and significant barriers for accessing essential services, further compounding their vulnerability.
Guatemala is exposed to severe disaster risks, as per INFORM index, with earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, droughts, and epidemics identified as recurrent threats. Over 60% of its population lives in high-risk areas. Socioeconomic inequalities and limited services worsen vulnerability, especially for rural, indigenous areas. In 2025, seismic swarms, floods, and droughts impacted more than 1 million people.

Within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), and due to the availability of flexible funding, UNICEF’s interventions demonstrated strategic impact across health, nutrition, education, child protection, WASH, climate resilience and social protection. By partnering with government, communities, and international organizations, UNICEF advanced national priorities, enhanced service delivery, and fostered inclusive development. These achievements contribute to Guatemala’s progress toward the SDG achievement and underscore the need for continued commitment and investment to ensure no child is left behind.
Health/Nutrition
In 2025, UNICEF Guatemala prioritized strengthening the national health system to address the needs of children and adolescents, especially in indigenous and rural communities, and in humanitarian settings. Efforts centered on institutional capacity development, improving service quality, and generating evidence to ensure equitable access to essential health services. Collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MSPAS) helped implement policies, align standards, and broaden services across all levels.
UNICEF was instrumental in implementing critical legislation on vaccination and certification for persons with disabilities, through evidence-based, targeted capacity-building initiatives. 
On immunization, SBC strategies contributed to increased vaccine acceptance in 45 under-served communities; the Vaccination Week of the Americas reached 6,576 zero-dose under-five children and 16,032 children with incomplete vaccine schedules; and HPV immunization efforts reached 33% of nine-year-old and achieved 90% schedule completion among adolescents aged 15.
UNICEF strengthened maternal/newborn health capacities by training 92 professionals in 4 departments. A bottleneck analysis was conducted to assess operational and governance constraints of MSPAS’s network-based primary health care model, generating evidence and strategies to strengthen service delivery. An epidemiological surveillance study was initiated to address gaps in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV, improving early antenatal detection and follow-up pathways.
On the humanitarian-development nexus, UNICEF adapted delivery models in response to shifting migration dynamics, transitioning from transit-focused to return-focused programming. Fixed and mobile service delivery points provided primary healthcare and nutrition services to 2,125 people on the move (512 boys, 354 girls, 674 men, 585 women).
UNICEF strengthened national capacities for HIV prevention and care via an advanced diploma completed by 543 healthcare providers. Adolescent-Friendly Spaces were consolidated in three, mainly indigenous departments and 19 health services, reaching 1,269 adolescents, 514 parents, 212 health workers, 36 community leaders. Consultations with adolescents informed standardized content on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, HIV, and HPV. Community radio partnerships disseminated audio content in indigenous languages, as part of a UNICEF-Spotify alliance.
UNICEF’s nutrition strategy focused on improving children’s diets and their development by acting across the food system, strengthening supply chains, creating supportive food environments, and promoting positive caregiving practices. Together with national authorities, UNICEF supported the operationalization of the Public Policy on Comprehensive Early Childhood Development (PPDIPI), guiding national prioritization and investment aimed at reducing chronic malnutrition.
UNICEF co-created the national strategy for the provision of Small Quantity Lipid-Based Nutrient Supplements (SQ-LNS) to undernourished children, including operational guidelines validated by 40 frontline workers. It also launched a demonstration integrated service model expected to reach 14,000 children in Alta Verapaz and Totonicapán. Therapeutic treatment was ensured for over 2,000 children with severe acute malnutrition through the provision of therapeutic milk F-75 and F-100. Supply chain processes linked to growth monitoring, micronutrient supplementation, and counselling improved the availability and quality of nutrient-rich foods for vulnerable populations.
UNICEF advanced supportive food environments through policies, regulations, and the creation of spaces where caregivers and children can access healthy food. The Breastfeeding-Friendly Workspaces initiative led to the establishment of lactation rooms in 12 companies, benefiting over 30,000 women, and 12 health services were certified as part of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (ISSALM), supporting breastfeeding for 19,800 newborns.
UNICEF supported the implementation of SBC models by training over 1,700 community actors together with the Secretariat of Food and Nutritional Security (SESAN). Community networks were strengthened by training and certifying 456 midwives as breastfeeding promoters and deploying 55 breastfeeding monitors, supporting over 25,700 families through counseling and support groups.
As cluster lead, UNICEF maintained essential nutrition services in humanitarian contexts, coordinating 17 partners and contributing to the 2026 Residual Humanitarian Needs Assessment and the Guide on Mainstreaming Child Protection in Nutrition. Mobile brigades screened 1,561 people on the move, identifying malnutrition among children and supporting pregnant and lactating women. Under CERF Anticipatory Action for drought, UNICEF trained 35 personnel, deployed three brigades that served 4,085 children and 2,904 women. Additional brigades reached 7,432 children and 1,862 women in rural areas, identifying 106 cases of acute malnutrition.
Education
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MoE)'s "Acompáñame a Crecer" program by expanding access to early education through training and certification of early childhood educators and scaling up the Comprehensive Child Development Community Centers (CECODII) in rural areas. In 2025, UNICEF operated 66 CECODIIs in Alta Verapaz, reaching 2,873 children aged 0–4, 567 community educators, 100 pregnant and 413 breastfeeding women. The intervention benefited 2,591 families across 55 communities. Nationwide, Acompáñame a Crecer currently covers 1,563 CECODIIs, serving 61,178 children and 52,529 families. UNICEF’s support was crucial for training itinerant managers and staff in the Acompáñame a Crecer methodology, ensuring quality across all program components. UNICEF also supported MoE in designing the national comprehensive model for early childhood education, updating the national curriculum, and implementing an information system to register CECODII participants, which in turn facilitated their access to the national school feeding programme. 
On primary education, UNICEF backed the Prioritized Program for Educational Innovation and Transformation, financed by the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), which aimed to enhance learning environments and educational quality. The Learning Recovery Strategy (LRS) was implemented, assessing 598,000 students in all six primary grades.
UNICEF improved school environments by promoting resilience, hygiene, and menstrual health practices, benefitting 17,550 children with adequate WASH facilities and 4,758 girls and boys with menstrual health education. Awareness campaigns and SBC interventions targeted the whole education community -teachers, parents, and students-, fostering community-wide hygiene practices. UNICEF also installed solar panels in 19 schools in Alta Verapaz, enhancing access to renewable energy. 
UNICEF led the Education in Emergencies (EiE) cluster, engaging 48 organizations in emergency preparedness and response coordination. In collaboration with MoE, it was possible to advance cross-sectoral integration of comprehensive school safety policies.
UNICEF supported the MoE in establishing Centers for Non-formal Education (CEEX), which allow out-of-school adolescents and youth accessing flexible programmes and finishing their primary, lower- and upper-secondary education at their own pace, obtaining formal-education-equivalent diplomas. In 2025, UNICEF established 28 CEEX in the mainly-indigenous department of Huehuetenango, benefiting 257 students. Of these, 35 completed primary education, 112 completed lower and 78 upper-secondary level. 
UNICEF established and equipped 34 Virtual Learning Environments (EVAs), community educational spaces that, using technological tools and innovative methodologies allow both formal and non-formal education students to acquire digital foundational and transferable skills. UNICEF-supported EVAs are located in 22 departments and directly benefit 904 students. 
UNICEF implemented “Futuros Brillantes”, a digital 11-module skills-building program focused on entrepreneurship, gender-responsive learning, community engagement and social innovation for adolescent girls, reaching 1,194 online and 1,700 offline adolescents and supporting. 180 girls’ social innovation projects through targeted bootcamps. 136 girls in highrisk situations were enrolled in flexible education programs as results of UNICEF’s efforts, and 665 girls received menstrual health kits, with 8 schools strengthening their MHHf riendly infrastructure and teacher training. Community-level training on violence prevention reached 480 community promoters and over 3,286 girls.  
In partnership with the Ministry of Culture and Sport, UNICEF set up 108 football academies in poor, rural municipalities. In addition to sport training, these academies promote the development of transferable skills, such as leadership, responsibility, teamwork, and decision-making through sports. Juego Limpio currently covers 108 municipalities in 10 departments, reaching 8,123 children and adolescents (6,298 boys and 1,825 girls) . Additional efforts were placed to ensure greater participation of adolescent girls through “Juego Limpio FEM” methodology, which will be implemented in 2026. 
Child Protection
UNICEF provided technical support to relevant Government institutions in relation to the pledges made at the 2024 Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children.
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Interior (MINGOB) implementing the National Policy for the Prevention of Violence and Crime by training 470 prevention officer and updating SBC-based operational tools to be rolled out in 2026. 
UNICEF developed and implemented a virtual training module, and conducted workshops for 209 MINGOB local staff on child rights, and VAC. Also, 76 local staff of the Presidential Secretariat for Executive Communication (SCEP) were trained on child protection, violence prevention, and public finance for children. 
Municipal child protection systems were consolidated in 10 departments, working with 152 municipal governments to strengthen local capacities on violence prevention and cross-sectoral coordination. This included building local situation analyses and developing local prevention plans that enabled municipalities to prioritize key issues such as juvenile justice, sexual violence, trafficking, and migration. Partnerships with 221 traditional and digital media outlets reached over one million people through messages promoting violence prevention and positive parenting based on care and respect. 
Targeted actions addressing sexual violence in the 15 municipalities with high incidence in the departments of Alta Verapaz, Baja Verapaz, Escuintla, and Guatemala, reaching 187,200 people with prevention messages. Workshops on sexual violence prevention reached 3,594 children/adolescents, along with 2,006 parents/caregivers. Additionally, 273 child victims received specialized care.
UNICEF assisted the Secretariat against Sexual Violence, Exploitation, and Trafficking (SVET) developing a national diagnosis on the profiles of sexual violence offenders.. Support was also given to MSPAS to disseminate the protocol on  caring for sexual violence survivors reaching 201 professionals nationwide. Additionally, a targeted collaboration with MoE in Alta Verapaz facilitated the school reintegration of 154 girls’ victims of sexual violence. In addition, UNICEF collaborated with the Secretariat for Social Welfare (SBS), the governing body for services targeting child victims and adolescents in conflict with the law. 209 officials from 16 SBS departmental offices were trained on the use of eight minimum standards for specialized care, and a non-residential outpatient program for child survivors of sexual violence was developed, reaching 184 girls and adolescents in the department of Escuintla. Additional capacity-building efforts included promoting minimum standards for temporary foster care, updating tools for multidisciplinary teams and foster families, as well as developing a curriculum for SBS staff training on prevention of VAC, psychosocial care for survivors, and special attention for adolescents in conflict with the law.
UNICEF provided technical assistance to develop the operators’ guide for hotline 1510 -managed by the National Police to receive reports of VAC in schools-, ensuring specialized, child-sensitive responses as well as comprehensive handling and referral of cases to specialized protection services for psychosocial support and access to justice.
Technical capacities of the Judiciary branch were strengthened with the completion of specialized training on justice for child victims of violence and juvenile criminal justice. As a result, 310 judges nationwide are equipped with human rights and child protection standards to resolve cases related to violence against children and juvenile justice. 
UNICEF continued its advocacy efforts, providing targeted technical assistance to update national legislation and fostering collaboration to promote a national comprehensive child protection system, based on the 2024 CRC recommendations to Guatemala.
On migration, UNICEF prioritized interventions at border areas, reception centers and shelters, delivering psychosocial support to 9,094 people, including 2,374 children. Technical support provided to the Guatemalan Migration Institute (IGM) for the implementation of the National Migration Policy had improved the protection children on the move,  including children in transit  or those deported back to Guatemala. UNICEF supported the application of the national protocol for reception and care of migrant children and deployed child protection officers in reception centers and government shelters. Collaboration with SBS facilitated the reception, sheltering and family reunification of 538 returned unaccompanied children, as well as the protection of 41 children in transit. Similarly, the partnership with the Secretariat of Social Work of the First Lady’s office (SOSEP) facilitated the reception of 770 family units, comprising 1,061 children. The follow-up of cases in four departments (San Marcos, Huehuetenango, Quiche and Quetzaltenango) facilitated family and community reintegration of 663 children and adolescents.
Within the framework of the “Retorno al hogar” plan, UNICEF also assisted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the design and implementation of the protocol for consular protection of Guatemalan children abroad, and provided targeted training to consular teams deployed to the United States and Mexico.
WASH/Climate Resilience
