UNICEF supported policy updates and planning for expanding WASH services at the national and local levels and played a key role in leveraging $16 million for WASH municipal investments in the department of San Marcos, benefiting over 69,700 people in nine municipalities.
Although core interventions were based on the Sustainable Total Sanitation and Hygiene (SAHTOSO) methodology, UNICEF also promoted market-based sanitation strategies, collaborating with local financial institutions and businesses.
Targeted support to children and adults on the move included distribution of age-appropriate WASH items in reception centers and shelters. Additionally, the Anticipatory Action framework was activated with funding unlocked from the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). These anticipatory actions were carried out in two municipalities of the Chiquimula department, located in the dry corridor, enhancing resilience and mitigating the impact of drought in the most vulnerable communities.
UNICEF focused on climate resilience through four core actions: governance, local action, youth participation, and climate-resilient social services. Technical assistance to the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (MARN) led to child and adolescent participation in climate policy updates, notably the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 and the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (PANCC) 2050. Support provided to the National Council for Protected Areas (CONAP) enabled integration of child-sensitive approaches in the National Biodiversity Strategy 2050.
By co-hosting the First National Summit on Children, Environment, and Climate Change with MoE and MARN, UNICEF facilitated the participation of over 1,000 children and adolescents, resulting in the launch of the first national survey on the subject, which was subsequently used to draft the first national declaration on children,  environment, climate change and resilience -a pioneering exercise in the region.
Partnering with the Inter-American Development Bank, UNICEF co-organized the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY) 2025, involving 260 adolescents in person and 1,000 online, with significant female participation, with the aim of providing national authorities of adolescents and young people’s concerns and proposal ahead of the COP 30 in Belém, Brazil. 
The “Agentes ECO” platform for youth climate action expanded to Petén and Izabal, counting now with 260 members. Collaboration with the National Coordinator for Disaster Reduction (CONRED) supported youth participation in national and sub-national disaster risk reduction platforms, engaging over 100 adolescents in disaster-risk-reduction decision-making processes for the first time. 
At the local level, as part of the Business and Community Resilience (BCR) initiative, UNICEF advanced the resilient municipalities’ initiative in the municipalities of San José, Iztapa, Democracia and Escuintla), securing formal commitments to involve the private sector and children's representatives in local decision-making processes, and starting expansion in Flores. 
Social Protection
UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Ministry of Social Development (MIDES) on the scaling-up of the Social Household Registry (SHR), now covering 421,760 households in 115 municipalities and 20 departments. This in turn allowed for increasing the reach of the “Bono Social” cash transfer program to 180,000 households—a 117% expansion since 2023.
UNICEF contributed to designing MIDES’ Social Programs Information System (MIS), set to optimize management of all cash transfer programs, starting with “Bono Nutrición”. Technical support facilitated the development of dashboards using SHR data, including new multi-level socioeconomic indicators and support for a Data Warehouse to host this information.
Joint advocacy with the Cash Working Group led CONRED to update the National Response Plan, formally integrating cash transfers as an adaptive social protection measure for disaster response and streamlining MIDES’ operational procedures. This policy shift strengthens preparedness for the implementation of programs such as "Bono Emergencia" and opens avenues for future funding for UNICEF.
UNICEF supported the redesign of  "Programa Vida", which targets child victims of sexual violence and adolescent mothers, enhancing referral processes and institutional coordination. Technical assistance enabled a costing exercise for scaling up the intersectoral "Mano a Mano" initiative to address poverty and malnutrition, involving 11 government institutions and analyzing 20 interventions. Recommendations suggest increasing Mano a Mano’s investment from 0.11% of GDP in 2025 to 1.17% by 2030, with further SHR expansion needed for scale.
Within the framework of the PPDIPI, UNICEF conducted a situational analysis of early childhood, examining demographic, social, and economic factors with disaggregated data by municipality, sex, ethnicity, and area of residence. The analysis covered education, health, nutrition, poverty, WASH, violence, migration, disability, and disaster risk.
Through a new EU-funded cross-sectoral program, UNICEF enhanced municipal public management and finance to combat malnutrition, establishing partnerships with the Ministry of Finance (MINFIN), the Ministry of Planning (SEGEPLAN) and SCEP. 20 guides and tools were developed for municipal management, covering project formulation, planning, results-based management, financing sources, digital tools, data collection/analysis, and costing methodologies. Some of these guides have been validated by MINFIN and SEGEPLAN, ensuring relevance and applicability. Implementation at the local level is planned for early 2026 with the aim of improving resource allocation to address malnutrition more effectively.
In collaboration with MSPAS, UNICEF conducted a costing exercise related to the certification of people with disabilities, which was based on a thorough assessment to identify gaps in human resources, equipment, and infrastructure across 11 hospitals nationwide. The exercise included the estimation of costs associated with the development and maintenance of the IT platform, as well as the central administration unit responsible for managing the certification system. All activities were executed in full compliance with ISO accessibility standards. Beyond the costing exercise, UNICEF’s technical assistance to MSPAS extended to the review and refinement of key technical and normative documents. This included the Procedures Manual and the Guidelines for the Functioning of Evaluation Boards. UNICEF also contributed to the design of process flowcharts and the creation of quick certification guides to streamline the certification process. Furthermore, an estimation was made regarding the potential future demand for disability certification, ensuring that the system would be equipped to address the anticipated needs of people with disabilities.

The issuance of stop-work orders by US government agencies in January 2025 posed significant challenges to UNICEF Guatemala’s operations, fundamentally altering the financial landscape for child-focused programming. As the United States is a major donor, these orders created an environment of uncertainty, requiring UNICEF to swiftly reassess its operational priorities, resource allocation, and long-term planning. The abrupt suspension of funding jeopardized the continuity of critical initiatives, particularly those aimed at the most marginalized and vulnerable children. In response to this setback, UNICEF Guatemala demonstrated agility and resilience by intensifying efforts to diversify its funding base, and working closely with other donors to ensure continuity of the critical initiatives. The office proactively engaged non-traditional donors, including philanthropic foundations, national corporations, and international private sector actors, in a bid to mitigate the impact of the funding gap. These outreach efforts were complemented by strategic advocacy, leveraging UNICEF’s established reputation to sustain momentum in priority areas and ensure that children's needs remained at the forefront of the national agenda. 
Despite these financial constraints, UNICEF Guatemala remained unwavering in its commitment to deliver results. The organization’s adaptability was evident in its approach to bridging funding gaps—by re-prioritizing programmatic activities, optimizing existing resources, and seeking innovative solutions. For example, UNICEF focused on strengthening partnerships with local government entities and civil society organizations, which enabled the continuation of essential services even amidst budgetary uncertainty. The organization also explored new collaborative models, such as the private sector partnership initiative “Empresas que Suman”, which provided alternative avenues for resource mobilization and program implementation. UNICEF’s strategic positioning and advocacy efforts proved instrumental in sustaining progress for children.
UNICEF deepened its collaboration with the Government of Guatemala in their second year in office, advancing a child rights agenda. Highlights of the year include the support provided for the implementation of the PPDIPI. As a trusted partner and recognized champion of ECD, UNICEF played a pivotal role in supporting policy rollout, mobilizing resources, and advocating for a cross-sectoral approach. These efforts targeted the most vulnerable children, ensuring that programmatic support extended beyond health and nutrition to include education, protection, and social inclusion. UNICEF’s technical expertise and convening power facilitated multi-stakeholder dialogues, fostering alignment between national priorities and international best practices.
Another achievement was the successful implementation of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in partnership with the National Statistics Institute. The MICS initiative marked a significant step forward in strengthening data collection and evidence-based decision-making at both national and local levels. The comprehensive survey, whose results will be available in 2026, is expected to provide updated and robust data on child-related indicators, thereby informing policy formulation and program design. This emphasis on data-driven programming underscores UNICEF’s commitment to transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement. By equipping government partners and other stakeholders with reliable data, UNICEF is helping to ensure that interventions are both targeted and effective, particularly for most vulnerable populations that are often overlooked in traditional service delivery models.
Throughout 2025, UNICEF Guatemala engaged in a series of strategic reflection activities aimed at shaping the development of a new Country Programme Document (CPD) aligned with the BMI and FFI frameworks. These reflective processes were designed to ensure that the new CPD would be responsive to evolving priorities, operational realities, and the changing needs of children across Guatemala. Central to these efforts was the implementation of InnovaLab—an innovation-driven workshop series accessible to all UNICEF staff. InnovaLab sought to strengthen the Country Office’s capacity by fostering lateral thinking, encouraging frugal innovation, and promoting prototyping. By creating a collaborative environment where staff could experiment with new approaches and share insights, UNICEF cultivated a culture of creativity and adaptability. This internal capacity-building initiative not only enhanced the organization’s ability to respond to emerging challenges but also positioned UNICEF as a leader in innovation within the development sector.
The organization’s commitment to learning and adaptation was further reinforced by a comprehensive Country Programme Evaluation in 2025, alongside a nutrition-programme-related evaluation and a multi-country evaluation on the regional response to children on the move. The findings from these evaluations provided critical inputs for the visioning and design of the CPD 2027–2031, including the recommendation to establishment of integrated impact objectives; the integration of accelerators such as  innovation/digital transformation and, SBC; as well as the establishment of differentiated urban-rural strategies to achieve results at scale. 
 These evaluations were instrumental in identifying areas of strength, exposing operational gaps, and highlighting opportunities for scaling up successful interventions. By integrating lessons learned into future planning, UNICEF ensured that its work in Guatemala would remain impactful, data-driven, and closely aligned with national priorities. The evaluation also emphasized the importance of maintaining a localized territorial approach, leveraging local knowledge, and fostering inclusive participation of local communities in program design and implementation. 
Future efforts will focus on strengthening evaluation capacity of national partners, promoting a culture of evaluability of national programs that brings results at scale for children. UNICEF will identify opportunities to work closely with ministries responsible for advancing child-related results to promote a culture of evaluation of national policies and programs.

Guyana continues to experience exceptional macro-economic growth, driven by expanding oil  production alongside strong performance in non-oil construction and services.  Growth in 2026 is expected to remain robust, while fiscal deficits are  narrowing as oil revenues significantly expand public finances and  development spending. This economic boom has generated unprecedented fiscal  space, presenting clear opportunities to scale up investments in education,  health, social protection, and child-focused services. Recent increases in  public allocations, particularly major investments in the health sector, have  the potential to improve service coverage and promote more equitable  outcomes, if resources are effectively targeted to underserved populations,  including children in rural and hinterland communities. Suriname’s economic  trajectory, by contrast, has been shaped by long-term IMF-supported reforms  aimed at addressing fiscal imbalances, strengthening monetary policy, and  improving governance frameworks. The IMF confirms macroeconomic  stability and progress on structural reforms, with growth projected at modest  levels in the near term. However, constrained fiscal space continues to  severely limit public investment in social sectors critical for children
  
Despite Guyana’s fiscal  gains and Suriname’s reform efforts, social development outcomes, particularly for children, have not kept pace with economic changes.  Inequities in access to essential services continue to undermine children´s  rights, especially in rural, hinterland, Indigenous, Maroon, migrant, and  low-income communities. Child poverty remains a central concern, compounded  by demographic shifts, uneven social protection coverage, and weak  coordination across sectors. These dynamics highlight a persistent gap  between macro-economic progress and inclusive, equitable outcomes for children. In Suriname, households continue to face high living costs and  inflationary pressures, while recent reforms and subsidy reductions have  weakened families’ capacity to absorb shocks. Limited social spending has  been translated into constrained investments in services for children. 
  
Against this backdrop, children’s ability to access quality learning opportunities remain severely  constrained in both countries. Structural inequities in education access,  retention, and learning outcomes demonstrate that economic growth and reform  have yet to translate into equitable human development. Out-of-school rates  remain high, particularly at the secondary level. In Guyana, approximately  10% of primary-school-age children, 18% of lower secondary-age children, and  33% of upper secondary-age children are out of school. In Suriname, exclusion  is even more pronounced, with 14% of primary-age children, 24% of lower  secondary-age children, and 62% of upper secondary-age children not attending  school. Even among children who remain in school, learning outcomes remain  very weak. Access to inclusive Early Childhood Development (ECD) services  remains limited, particularly for children with disabilities, Indigenous and  Maroon children, and those living in marginalized or remote communities. According to MICS 2018, just 45% of the children between 3-4 in Suriname were developmentally on track.  In  both countries, climate-related shocks further disrupt children’s learning  and well-being. Prolonged droughts have affected water supply, education  continuity, and access to health services, disproportionately impacting  children in interior areas. These environmental stressors compound existing  inequalities between urban/coastal populations and hinterland Indigenous and  Maroon communities, increasing food insecurity, health risks, and school  absenteeism. 
  
Children experience high levels of violence, abuse, and neglect, with girls, children with  disabilities, and those living in rural and hinterland areas facing the  greatest risks. 87% of adults in Suriname and 72% of adults in Guyana believe  that physical punishment is necessary to raise or educate children. Girls are  particularly vulnerable to gender-based violence (GBV). Both countries report  high numbers of children placed in institutional care, reflecting weaknesses  in family-based care, prevention services, and social work systems. While  legislative and policy frameworks exist to protect children, implementation  remains weak, fragmented, and uneven across regions. Children with  disabilities face compounded risks, including barriers to accessing justice,  limited legal protection, and inadequate GBV response services.
  
Access to comprehensive reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services remains  insufficient, particularly for children in rural, hinterland, and  marginalized communities, reflecting persistent gaps in universal health  coverage. Under-five mortality remains high with no recent improvement in  both countries, with rates of 26 per 1,000 live births in Guyana and 16 per  1,000 live births in Suriname, highlighting preventable losses of life linked  to health system weaknesses and inequitable access to care. Children and adolescents are  facing a serious mental health crisis, driven by limited access to  specialized services and persistent stigma. Countries in the region rank  among those with the highest suicide rates globally, with both Guyana and  Suriname sadly positioned near the top of this ranking. A 2024 UNICEF mental  health study further underscores the urgency, finding that 36% of adolescents  in Suriname had contemplated suicide, while access to appropriate mental  health services for young people remains insufficient. Preventive health services are also uneven.  Immunization coverage shows stark contrasts, with DTP vaccination coverage at  98% in Guyana, compared to 82% in Suriname, the lowest in the region.  Zero-dose children remain a growing concern, reflecting gaps in outreach to  marginalized populations
  
Political Transitions and Institutional Capacity 
  
The 2025 general elections and the ensuing changes in administration in both Guyana and Suriname present  a pivotal moment for children’s rights and well-being. Political transitions  can open space to accelerate reforms, unlock new investments, and elevate  child-focused priorities within national agendas. At the same time, they can  disrupt ongoing programs, shift policy direction, and weaken continuity in service delivery, risks that fall disproportionately on children and families already furthest behind. 
  
In both countries, the challenge is not only what policies are adopted, but whether the state can  deliver them effectively and equitably. Weak institutional capacity,  particularly at the subnational level, remains a structural constraint that  hinders the effective translation of national plans into high-quality,  community-level services. Modernizing the state, therefore becomes central to  achieving results for children: strengthening planning, budgeting,  procurement, data systems, supervision, and accountability; improving  inter-ministerial coordination; and ensuring that decentralization (where  applicable) is matched with real capacity, resources, and clear mandates. 
  
This modernization agenda must also address the human side of government performance. Persistent  brain-drain (mostly in Suriname) and high turnover, combined with limited  incentives, training opportunities, and career pathways, undermine the sustained capacity of public institutions. Improving the conditions of public  workers is not a narrow labor issue; it is a child rights issue. Teachers,  doctors, nurses, social workers, child protection officers, WASH technicians,  and civil registrars, to name a few, are the frontline of children’s rights,  and when systems fail to retain and support them, children lose access to  quality services.

Survive and Thrive
     
Survive and Thrive
  
In 2025, due to UNICEF’s  support, Guyana and Suriname strengthened health systems with a focus on  equity, resilience, and quality service delivery, contributing to national  health priorities. Results were driven by health systems strengthening, evidence generation, and targeted investments in hard-to-reach and  high-burden populations.
  
In Suriname and Guyana, immunization and mental health outcomes improved through strengthened systems, expanded access, and evidence-informed service delivery. In Suriname, enhanced cold chain capacity and improved access in remote hinterland and indigenous communities strengthened implementation of the National Immunization Programme, including the installation of solar power systems and solar-powered vaccine refrigerators in health facilities in Palumeu, Sipaliwini, and Apetina, ensuring uninterrupted and safe vaccine storage in areas with limited electricity. HPV vaccination for boys was introduced with support from culturally adapted, multilingual, and animated promotion materials, complemented by community-based awareness activities during health fairs, contributing to improved vaccination coverage in targeted communities in 202. In parallel, mental health and psychosocial support services expanded across both countries: Suriname advanced the scale-up of MHPSS services in Nickerie with planned expansion to two other districts reaching an additional 30,000 young people, supported by the development of a formal referral system and a community of practice for frontline workers, while in Guyana adolescent mental health outcomes improved through the finalization of the Adolescent MHPSS Operational Guide, capacity-building under the UNICEF–PAHO Joint Programme, rollout of services in six primary health care facilities, and a nationwide phase of the “Hear Me Out” anti-stigma campaign that reached an estimated 200,000 people and promoted awareness and care-seeking.
  
In Guyana, strengthening of  the national immunization program, particularly in hinterland regions, advanced  through systematic cold chain improvements. A national cold chain inventory  and gap assessment informed future government and partner investments, while  procurement of 10 solar-powered refrigerators for regions 1 and 9 improved  access to potent vaccines in communities with little or no electricity,  contributing to improved immunization and health outcomes for more than 1,500  children. Capacity building of Ministry of Health staff on preventive  maintenance enhanced sustainability of these investments. Cumulatively, cold  chain investments over the past four years contributed to an increase in MMR  coverage from 83% in 2021 to 96% in 2024. In parallel, evidence generated on  integrating COVID-19 vaccination into routine services for high-risk  populations will inform future vaccine delivery and outbreak preparedness.  HPV vaccination campaigns conducted during Vaccination Week in the Americas  contributed to an increase in HPV coverage among girls aged 15 from 44% in  2023 to 60% in 2024.
  
Maternal, infant, and young  child nutrition outcomes were strengthened in both countries. In Suriname,  community-based breastfeeding sensitization increased knowledge of exclusive  breastfeeding, infant and young child feeding, and practical techniques, while  integrating awareness of postpartum depression and referral pathways.  Distribution of breastfeeding support tools further enabled practice. A  Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices study is underway to inform a national  breastfeeding policy and targeted interventions. In Guyana, finalization of  the revised National Breastfeeding Policy aligned national practice with  international standards, including humanitarian settings and workplace  breastfeeding. Institutionalization of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative  advanced through integration into annual health facility assessments, with  nine hospitals assessed in 2025 using a new national certification process.  Development of a National Nutrition Strategy addressed maternal and child  nutrition, obesity and NCD prevention, food security, and healthy food  environments.
 
Across both countries,  results were enabled by strong government leadership, partnerships with  health authorities and community-based providers, and UNICEF’s technical and  convening role. Evidence generation—including cold chain assessments,  feasibility studies, investment cases, and KAP research—directly informed  policy decisions, program design, and resource allocation.
  
Education and Skills 
  
Education remains a central  pillar of national development in both Guyana and Suriname, with governments  prioritizing human capital development as a driver of economic growth, social  cohesion, and equity. UNICEF’s support during the year focused on systems  strengthening, policy operationalization, foundational learning, early  childhood development, and inclusive and safe learning environments.
  
 Education remained a central pillar of national  development in Guyana and Suriname, with governments prioritizing human  capital development to advance economic growth, social cohesion, and equity.  In 2025, education results were achieved through systems strengthening,  policy operationalization, foundational learning, early childhood development  (ECD), and the promotion of inclusive and safe learning environments, enabled  by UNICEF’s technical, convening, and implementation role.
  
In Guyana, increased public  investment in education, reflected in higher budget allocations, expanded  infrastructure, and accelerated digitalization, improved access across all  levels. However, persistent gaps in learning outcomes, equity, and school safety  highlighted the need for system-level reforms focused on quality and  inclusion. UNICEF’s technical engagement contributed to the finalization and  launch of the National Integrated Early Childhood Development Policy and  Guidelines (2025–2030), which established a coherent, multisectoral framework  linking education, health, nutrition, and social protection and strengthened  governance, accountability, and sustainability of ECD services nationwide.
  
In Suriname, progress  shifted from policy commitment to implementation following the launch of the  National Education Policy 2024–2031. With UNICEF’s technical assistance, the  Ministry of Education translated the policy into operational plans, planning  tools, and monitoring and reporting systems, strengthening institutional  capacity and enabling more systematic tracking of sector performance. A major  milestone was the development and endorsement of the National Multisectoral  ECD Policy 2025–2035 by four ministries. UNICEF’s technical leadership  facilitated intersectoral coordination across early learning, health, family  support, and community services, reinforcing a whole-of-government approach  to early childhood development and long-term human capital formation.
  
Foundational learning  outcomes were prioritized in both countries. In Guyana, uneven literacy and  numeracy outcomes prompted early intervention efforts. Through  UNICEF-facilitated capacity building, Training of Trainers for health-care  workers enabled the cascading of ECD knowledge to frontline providers, while  national advocacy initiatives, including the ECD Conference and the  International Day of Play, supported positive social and behavior change  around nurturing care and play-based learning. In Suriname, foundational  learning outcomes improved through an emergent literacy professional  development program developed jointly with the Ministry of Education and  academic institutions. The pilot reached nearly 9 per cent of primary schools  and benefited approximately 2,500 pupils by strengthening teacher and school  leadership capacity. Embedding the program within teacher training  institutions supported sustainability and future scale-up, contributing to  reductions in learning poverty.
  
Results also addressed  persistent barriers related to safety, gender, mental health, and inclusion.  In Guyana, UNICEF’s engagement led to the development of Social and Emotional  Learning (SEL) manuals and workbooks for secondary schools, responding to concerns  around bullying, gender-based violence, and adolescent well-being. Evidence  generated through a Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHH) Needs Assessment in  hinterland dormitory schools filled critical data gaps and informed the  Ministry of Education’s forthcoming national MHH program. Pilot interventions  and development of a national MHH Awareness Strategy reflected an  evidence-informed and adaptive approach to programming.
  
In Suriname, inclusive and  safe learning environments were strengthened through curriculum review on  mental health education and development of an online mental health course for  teachers, planned for rollout in 2026. These efforts align with regional and  global priorities on adolescent mental health and school safety.
  
Equity remained a  cross-cutting driver of results. In Guyana, targeted UNICEF engagement  improved access to education for migrant children, particularly those from  Venezuela, through English as a Second Language programming, ECD training, and provision of learning materials, addressing language barriers and risks  of exclusion. 234 Venezuelan individuals and 110 children benefited from English as a Second Language (ESL) and ECD training. Additionally, 545 migrant learners in Grades 4–6 received individual learning materials in core subjects. Overall, 18,080 children, including 416 migrants, accessed early learning opportunities, and 17,143 parents, among them 348 migrants, were reached with nurturing care education Targeted investments in hinterland regions, adolescent girls,  and vulnerable communities further reduced disparities in access,  participation, and learning.
  
Across both countries,  results were enabled by strong government ownership, cross-sector  collaboration, and UNICEF’s convening role across education, health, and  social sectors. Strategic partnerships with ministries, academic  institutions, and the World Bank, including UNICEF’s role as co-implementer  of the Global Partnership for Education System Capacity Grant in Guyana,  expanded technical capacity and resource mobilization for system-wide  reforms, including development of the Education Strategic Plan 2026–2030 and  school violence prevention policies. 
  
Child Protection 
  
In 2025, child protection  outcomes in Guyana and Suriname were strengthened through enhanced legal  frameworks, institutional capacity, and service delivery systems that  safeguard children from violence, exploitation, abuse, and neglect, while  promoting access to child-centered justice. Efforts focused on prevention,  diversion, and the operationalization of child rights within justice and  social protection systems, enabled by UNICEF’s technical, financial, and  convening role.
  
In Suriname, the legal  establishment of the Child Ombudsman Institute following the unanimous  parliamentary adoption of the Children’s Ombudsperson Act (November 2024)  provided a critical foundation towards having an independent oversight and  complaints mechanism. Through ongoing UNICEF advocacy, operationalization,  resourcing, and independent functioning of the Institute are being advanced  to ensure effective protection and enforcement of children’s rights.  Legislative reforms on alternative measures for children in conflict with the  law, finalized in January 2025, shifted the justice system toward  rehabilitative, child-centered approaches, enabling authorities to apply  diversion and alternatives in practice. Advocacy efforts further supported  progress toward ratification of the HCCH Convention on the Protection of  Children, aligning national frameworks with international standards.
  
System-level child  protection coordination was reinforced through the re-establishment of the  Integrated Child Protection Network, underpinned by a high-level government  pledge from the President, Parliament, and Ministers. Strengthened  intersectoral coordination across social services, justice, education, and  health, along with a newly established data system for children in conflict  with the law and at-risk populations, improved case tracking, informed timely  responses, and guided children through judicial and resocialization  processes. The evidence generated also supports policy dialogue and program  adjustments to enhance protection outcomes for vulnerable children.
  
At the operational level,  child-friendly pre-detention facilities in Nickerie reduced travel distances  for children, allowing them to remain in familiar environments with parental  contact. Frontline capacity was strengthened through specialized training,  reaching over 300 professionals, including 26 police officers trained as  youth investigators, and extensive train-the-trainer programs for  prosecutors, educators, care coordinators, inspectors, and youth officers.  These interventions improved ethical investigation practices, prevention of  grooming and child sexual exploitation, and responses to gender-based  violence.
  
In Guyana, institutional,  policy, and legal reforms were advanced through UNICEF’s technical and  convening support. A technical review and subsequent finalization of the  Juvenile Diversion Policy redirected juveniles committing summary offences  away from formal courts toward rehabilitative alternatives, supporting  implementation of the Juvenile Justice Act, the Restorative Justice Act, and  Sustainable Development Goal 16. Complementary social and behavior change  initiatives promoted prevention of juvenile justice involvement, diversion,  and informed communication strategies. Key milestones included the launch of  Guyana’s first Mental Health Court, the third children’s court (Charity), and  passage of the International Measures for the Protection of Children (Hague  Convention) Bill to facilitate implementation of the 1996 Hague Child  Protection Convention.
  
As a result of UNICEF  engagement, more than 450 children in regions 3, 4, 5, and 6 directly  benefited from knowledge, sharing and capacity-building sessions on bullying,  mental health, digital safety, and child rights through Guyana’s first  Children’s Conference and World Children’s Day. These events fostered  consultative, child-led feedback exercises supporting children’s rights to  freedom of expression and access to information. Additionally, over 50  children, including migrant children, along with coaches representing clubs  reaching more than 120 children, gained awareness and capacity on child  protection, child rights, and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse  (PSEA). UNICEF-facilitated social and behavior change and Accountability to  Affected Populations sessions strengthened government partners’ capacity to  deliver inclusive and participatory interventions.
  
UNICEF’s engagement also  advanced gender equality and empowerment of girls. Approximately 60  schoolgirls participated in region-wide ICT sessions at UN House, gaining  exposure to gender-inclusive digital development, ICT career opportunities,  and digital citizenship. For International Day of the Girl Child, 40  schoolgirls and teachers engaged in resilience-focused discussions led by the  Women and Gender Equality Commission under the global theme, “The girl I am,  the change I lead: Girls on the frontlines of crisis.”
  
Humanitarian support and  protection for children on the move reached 1,824 children and families,  providing forensic interviews, court support, case management, psychosocial  services, and mental health therapy. Five inter-agency coordination meetings  enhanced service integration across child protection, social services,  health, and education sectors. Community members gained knowledge and capacity to prevent and respond to child protection threats, gender-based  violence, and hygiene risks, strengthening local safeguarding and resilience.
  
Climate Resilience and WASH
  
In Guyana and Suriname,  WASH interventions strengthened access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene  in rural schools and communities, while upgrading low-carbon,  climate-resilient infrastructure to reduce water-borne diseases and ensure continuity of services during emergencies.
  
In Guyana, rehabilitation  of the Hururu well and installation of a solar-powered water system provided  safe water to over 300 students across three schools, as well as to the  village office, health centre, day care, and other facilities. Water supply  improvements in #47 Village benefited approximately 400 residents and two  schools plus the health centre. WASH assessments conducted in 21 schools  serving as emergency shelters informed targeted interventions to ensure safe  and hygienic environments for students and community members during both  regular operations and crises. Menstrual hygiene assessments in rural schools  facilitated the development of the Menstrual Health and Hygiene Awareness  program. Humanitarian interventions addressed the critical needs of  Venezuelan migrants and host communities, including construction of bathrooms  and expansion of the Mobile Hygiene Corner project, which reached 1,779  people with hygiene supplies, including 334 women and girls who received  menstrual hygiene care packages, while hygiene awareness sessions reached  over 630 people.
  
In Suriname, rehabilitation  of WASH facilities in three rural Brokopondo schools improved access for  1,000 students and teachers, with rainwater harvesting and water storage  systems enhancing resilience. In D’jumu, Sipaliwini District, a solar-powered  pump, water purification system, and storage facilities provided safe water  to over 200 people, including 60 children, while residents were trained to  operate and maintain the systems, ensuring long-term sustainability. Water  system enhancements in Peleletepu and Coeroeni addressed critical shortages  caused by prolonged droughts, benefiting 644 people in Peleletepu and  additional community members in Coeroeni through optimized distribution  systems and preventative maintenance training. Humanitarian interventions  also delivered hygiene packages to 200 people, including 45 women and girls  receiving menstrual hygiene supplies.
  
Social Protection and  Inclusion 
  
UNICEF advanced social  protection and disability inclusion in Guyana and Suriname by strategically  strengthening national systems, anchoring rights-based approaches in policy  and practice, and fostering durable multi-sector partnerships. Progress was  driven by a deliberate combination of systems strengthening, policy advocacy,  capacity building, and evidence-informed programming.
  
A central driver of results  was UNICEF’s focus on governance and institutional reform. In Guyana, support  to the National Disability Commission through the development of its  Strategic Plan significantly improved national coordination, oversight, and  advocacy for children and persons with disabilities. In Suriname, THE CO  supported the finalization of the country’s first Disability Inclusive Policy  and Strategy (2025–2029). Another key achievement is the development and  endorsement of the Core/Minimum Principles for Engaging Children with  Disabilities in both countries which created a shared national baseline for  respectful, participatory, and inclusive engagement across government, civil  society, private sector, and diplomatic actors. 
  
UNICEF’s role as a convener  and broker of partnerships further accelerated progress. National disability  conferences, multi-stakeholder consultations, and cross-sector dialogues  strengthened alignment between government priorities and civil society expertise,  while also elevating the voices of persons with disabilities. Collaboration  with technical partners and with private-sector innovators in Suriname,  expanded access to high-quality expertise and innovative solutions, including  feasibility assessments for digital wallets to improve the efficiency and  safety of social assistance delivery in remote and marginalized communities.
  
Evidence generation and  capacity strengthening served as key enablers of inclusive social protection  reforms. In both countries, UNICEF supported disability situation analyses  and regional profiles, filling long-standing data gaps related to prevalence,  access to services, and barriers to inclusion. These data products enhanced  national and subnational planning, enabling more targeted, equitable, and  responsive social protection interventions. Training and technical support to  ministries and planning bodies strengthened competencies in results-based  management, monitoring and evaluation, and inclusive planning, helping  governments translate policy commitments into implementable programs. In  Guyana, the establishment of a Monitoring and Evaluation unit within the  Ministry of Human Services and Social Security strengthened accountability  and sustainability of social protection reforms, while in Suriname, RBM  training enhanced cross-sector coordination and evidence-driven  decision-making.
  
Innovation also played a  catalytic role. The exploration of digital payment solutions in Suriname  demonstrated how technology can reduce delivery costs, minimize risks, and  improve access to social assistance for children and families in  geographically isolated communities. These efforts align with UNICEF’s  Strategic Plan emphasis on innovation and adaptive programming as enablers of  equity and efficiency.
  
Communications, Advocacy,  Youth Engagement, SBC, and Private Sector Partnerships 
  
In 2025, UNICEF Suriname  and Guyana strengthened communications, advocacy, social behavior change  (SBC), youth engagement, and private sector partnerships to advance child  rights, mental health, and healthy behaviors, while mobilizing resources for  children. Through strategic partnerships, evidence-based messaging, and  youth-centered platforms, UNICEF placed children and adolescents at the  center of public dialogue, policy, and decision-making.
  
UNICEF prioritized  adolescent mental health in response to rising stress and psychosocial  challenges. In Suriname, 20 community mental health peer agents were trained  to provide awareness in schools, increasing knowledge and support at the  community level. In Guyana, a mental health digital campaign reached  approximately 200,000 persons, complemented by training of 25 school guidance  counsellors and HFLE teachers to facilitate adolescent social-emotional  skills development. School Mental Health Literacy training for 30 teachers  and a PHC training of trainer’s pilot expanded the capacity of primary  healthcare workers to identify and support youth mental health needs.
  
In Suriname, support for  the establishment of the Child Ombudsman Institute emphasized the right to a  safe childhood, protection from violence, and access to education.  Adolescents participated as speakers, peer advocates, content creators, and  dialogue participants, including a high-level World Children’s Day 2025  dialogue with the President of Suriname, where children shared perspectives  on health, education, and wellbeing. In Guyana, over 500 children and youth  engaged in national and regional observances and forums, while consultations  with 200 children contributed to a draft Children’s Manifesto, ensuring youth  perspectives informed national policy.
  
SBC work strengthened  institutional capacity and informed community-level messaging. In Guyana, 12  Juvenile Justice Department staff participated in Human-Centered Design and  SBC workshops, laying the groundwork for a national campaign supporting the  draft Diversion Policy and restorative justice. Qualitative research informed  an SBC campaign on menstrual hygiene management (MHM) in schools,  particularly in hinterland communities. A joint UNICEF-UNFPA SBC workshop  built the capacity of 30 stakeholders and produced five draft SBC strategies  addressing bullying, adolescent pregnancy, family violence, sexual violence,  and protection of girls, expected to be finalized in 2026.
  
UNICEF leveraged  partnerships in telecommunications, insurance, and banking to mobilize  resources and deliver results. In Suriname, Telesur contributed financially  to adolescent mental health awareness campaigns, while Assuria provided USD  25,000 over six months to promote healthy lifestyles in six vulnerable  communities. Republic Bank (Suriname) N.V. committed USD 50,000 over eight  months to strengthen daycare centers and support early learning. In Guyana,  UNICEF initiated dialogue with Republic Bank Limited to support mental health  programs for children and adolescents.
  
Through the integration of  communications, advocacy, youth engagement, SBC, and B4R partnerships, UNICEF  contributed to a more enabling environment for child rights, adolescent  mental health, and healthy behaviors. The interventions strengthened youth  participation, shifted public narratives, built institutional capacity, and  mobilized private sector resources, demonstrating the value of strategic  advocacy and multi-stakeholder engagement in advancing system-level changes  for children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
