Lessons Learned and Future Outlook in a Transitioning Multi-Country Context
The past year underscored that UNICEF’s effectiveness in Guyana and Suriname is less a function of the volume of outputs delivered and more a function of how engagement is structured, sequenced, and embedded within national systems, particularly in contexts marked by constrained institutional capacity, fiscal pressures, and persistent inequities. As the office transitions into the Caribbean Multi-Country Office (MCO), these lessons provide critical guidance for shaping a model that balances regional coherence with strong country-level identity and ownership.
Strategic Lessons from Implementation
One of the clearest lessons is that early, sustained, and technically credible engagement with governments remains the single most important determinant of durable results. Where UNICEF operated as a long-term technical partner, co-designing interventions, accompanying implementation, and adapting support over time, national institutions demonstrated stronger ownership and continuity. This was particularly evident in areas such as child protection systems strengthening and disability inclusion, where progress depended less on discrete activities and more on trust, institutional confidence, and iterative problem-solving.
At the same time, the year highlighted the limits of responsiveness in the absence of predictable resources. High demand for UNICEF’s technical and financial support confirmed the relevance of UNICEF’s mandate but also exposed the tension between expectations and available financing. This reinforced the need for sharper selectivity, clearer communication with partners, and a shift toward enabling partners to mobilize and allocate domestic resources more effectively, including through child-responsive budgeting and planning support. Proper budget allocations still represent a major challenge.
Another critical lesson relates to scale and coherence. Fragmentation, across sectors, partners, and within the UN system continued to dilute impact and strain already limited national capacity. Where multi-sectoral platforms were intentionally used, alignment improved, and collective advocacy gained traction. However, coordination did not occur organically and required sustained facilitation, shared evidence, and accessible communication products to maintain momentum.
Persistent data gaps, particularly on child poverty, disability, and sub-national disparities, remain a structural constraint. Limited access to timely and disaggregated administrative data weakened advocacy, investment cases, and the ability to demonstrate results on a scale. This challenge cut across sectors and countries, reinforcing that data systems strengthening must be treated as a strategic enabler, not a technical add-on.
Implications for the Caribbean MCO Model
The transition to a wider Caribbean MCO amplifies both opportunity and risk. On one hand, regional approaches offer economies of scale, shared learning, and stronger collective advocacy, particularly on issues such as migration, climate risk, disability inclusion, and violence against children. On the other hand, the past year demonstrated that multi-country effectiveness is not automatic. Without deliberately designed coordination structures, harmonized monitoring frameworks, and clear accountability lines, the MCO model risks increasing transaction costs and weakening follow-through.
A key lesson for the future MCO is that country offices must retain clear identity, technical depth, and decision-making space, even as regional coherence is strengthened. Guyana and Suriname face distinct institutional realities: differences in governance capacity, service delivery arrangements, legal frameworks, geography, and exposure to risks require differentiated strategies. 
Cross-country learning, similarly, must be intentional. Experience shows that lessons are not transferred simply by proximity or shared reporting lines. Structured platforms for joint reflection, documentation of practice, and peer-to-peer exchange will be essential to convert country-level experience into regional public goods.
Forward Outlook: Strategic Direction under the New CPD
Looking ahead, the office will draw on these lessons to sharpen its strategic posture under the new CPD and within the Caribbean MCO framework. Program selectivity will be strengthened, concentrating on a smaller number of high-impact priorities aligned with UNICEF’s comparative advantages in system strengthening, evidence generation, and advocacy. This will enable deeper engagement, clearer value propositions to governments, and more sustainable results.
Greater emphasis will be placed on institutionalization and sustainability, with interventions designed from the outset to be integrated into government systems, financed domestically over time, and implemented at scale. This includes intensified advocacy for stronger national data ecosystems, routine and transparent reporting, and systematic disaggregation to better capture intersecting vulnerabilities related to geography, migration status, disability, and gender.
Partnerships will be broadened and formalized, not only with governments, but also with regional institutions, academia, civil society, and the private sector, to expand influence, diversify resources, and strengthen accountability. 
Operationally, the office will prioritize readiness and flexibility throughout the transition period, deliberately sequencing adjustments to remain fully functional through 2026 while absorbing short-term shocks. Within the Caribbean MCO, the emphasis will be on regional coherence with contextual differentiation, using harmonized, risk-informed frameworks and shared learning platforms, while allowing tailored country strategies that reflect institutional capacity, geography, and climate and environmental risk profiles.
Taken together, these lessons point to a future UNICEF presence that is more focused, more deliberate, and more embedded, capable of leveraging the strengths of a multi-country architecture without losing the specificity, relationships, and technical credibility that drive results for the most marginalized children in each national context

Haiti’s protracted and complex crisis further deteriorated in 2025, leading to unprecedented levels of internal displacement and acute humanitarian needs. Escalating insecurity and violence, collapse of basic social services, and rising displacement eroded child rights, and stalled progress for children. According to the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, an estimated 6 million people required humanitarian assistance in 2025, and 6.4 million are projected to need aid in 2026, including 2.6 million children, underscoring both the scale and trajectory of needsAgainst the 2030 Agenda commitment to leave no child behind, these pressures deepened disparities, constrained safe access and limited the ability of national systems and partners to deliver results at scale for the most marginalised children.
Deteriorating security and grave violations of child rights. Armed groups expanded territorial control along the Ouest–Centre–Artibonite corridor and are estimated to exert influence over around 90 per cent of Port-au-Prince. This has severely constrained civilian movement, isolated communities and disrupted access to essential services, including health care, education, safe water and protection. Cumulative killings exceeded 4,300 by the end of the third quarter, based on UN quarterly tallies. Kidnapping remains a systematic tactic used for extortion, contributing to widespread fear.  
Children face grave violations on a scale placing Haiti among the top five situations globally in the UN Secretary-General’s Children and Armed Conflict report (June 2025). Verified patterns include recruitment and use of children, abductions, and sexual violence, including collective rape, used to intimidate and control communities. Up to half of armed group members are estimated to be children. UNICEF recorded a 195 per cent increase in child recruitment in one year (2024 to 2025). Children associated with armed groups face extreme barriers to exit and risk reprisals; girls face heightened risks of sexual violence. National efforts, including the Protocol for the Handover of Children Associated with Armed Groups (signed January 2024) and the PREJEUNES programme (launched July 2025), aim to prevent recruitment and strengthen safe handover and reintegration pathways, with UNICEF support.
Gender-based violence has surged. Between January and September 2025, about 7,472 cases were documented (an average of 27 per day); 56 per cent involved sexual violence, and 65 per cent of these were collective rapes perpetrated by armed groups.
Mass displacement and cross-border dynamics. Internal displacement in Haiti reached about 1.4 million people (12 per cent of the population) by September 2025, roughly double the caseload a year earlier and the highest on record. Children comprise over half of those displaced. The crisis has expanded beyond the capital, with about 64 per cent of new displacements in 2025 occurring outside Port-au-Prince. Spontaneous internally displaced people (IDP) sites rose from about 142 in December 2024 to 238 in September 2025, yet about 85 per cent of displaced people remain with host families, increasing pressure on essential services and limited resources.
Armed groups intensified attacks in Centre and Artibonite regions from mid-year, forcing an estimated 321,000 to flee their homes.  
In parallel, in 2025, the Dominican Republic returned or deported approximately 265,215 Haitians, 37 per cent increase compared to 2024 (Migrant protection working group). Among those returned were unaccompanied children, pregnant and lactating women and families separated during procedures, underscoring urgent protection and referral needs at borders and in host communities. 
Collapse of essential services. The erosion of essential services has accelerated dramatically. Only 41 per cent of health facilities with beds in Port-au-Prince remain functional. Insecurity, infrastructure destruction, medication shortages, and the exodus of an estimated 40 per cent of medical personnel have brought maternal, neonatal, and emergency care to the brink of collapse in many parts of the country.
WASH-related health risks continue to rise amid disrupted water networks, interrupted waste collection, and overcrowded IDP sites. In 2025, 2,852 suspected cholera cases were reported (186 confirmed; 48 deaths), alongside recurring clusters of acute watery diarrhoea.
Education has suffered severe regression against SDG4. During the 2024–2025 academic year, 1,606 schools had closed across Centre, Ouest, and Artibonite, affecting 243,000 students and more than 7,500 teachers. Nationwide, 1.5 million children remain out of school or are at imminent risk of dropping out—leaving them vulnerable to recruitment, exploitation, and long-term learning loss.
Food and Nutrition insecurity remains at critical levels. The September 2025 IPC analysis indicates 5.7 million people in acute food insecurity, including 1.2 million children under five. Projections suggest an increase to 5.9 million in early 2026, with 1.9 million already in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency). The most recent available estimates suggest that approximately 22.8 per cent of children under five are stunted and 5.1 per cent are wasted; updated national nutrition survey is planned for 2026. Continued insecurity has destroyed livelihoods, restricted market access and driven up prices, with displaced families facing extreme deprivation and harmful coping strategies. These conditions heighten the risk of acute malnutrition in children and require scaled, shock-responsive social protection and nutrition services.
Humanitarian access,political and economic context. Civilians remained caught between armed groups, self-defense movements, and different security forces. Armed groups continued their expansion into regions such as Centre and Artibonite, as well as around Port-au-Prince. Humanitarian access is highly constrained by insecurity, movement restrictions and compounded by the continued suspension of commercial flights to Port-au-Prince since November 2024. 
The political environment remains deeply fragile. The Transitional Presidential Council (TPC) runs to February 2026, with elections planned for August and December 2026, subject to improvements in security and financing.  Economic conditions also remained under pressure with the real gross domestic product (GDP) estimated to have contracted by 4.2 per cent in 2024.  Haiti ranks 166 out of 193 countries and territories on the Human Development Index (HDI). World Bank Nowcasts suggest that 48.7 per cent of Haitians live on less than US$3.00 per day (2021 purchasing power parity,PPP) in 2025, while 41.3 per cent are estimated to experience multidimensional poverty (2025 MPI report based on DHS 2016–2017).

UNICEF sustained essential services and strengthened systems through development programming despite constraints linked to armed violence, while humanitarian assistance reached around 1.15 million people, including 705,000 children, across health, nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, education and protection, even as 81 per cent of the US$272 million Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal remained unfunded. In line with the 2025 Humanitarian Response Plan and inter-agency coordination arrangements, UNICEF led or co-led the WASH, Nutrition and Education clusters as well as the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, contributing to collective prioritisation and a principled response.

1. Child Survival: Health and Nutrition
Immunisation: Despite access constraints linked to armed violence, routine services were sustained and expanded. From January to October 2025, UNICEF supported routine immunisation and the cold chain, with 187,324 children aged 0–11 months (97,408 girls; 89,916 boys) receiving the third dose of the pentavalent vaccine, protecting against five diseases and signalling continuity of care within the Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI). 
To reach this result, UNICEF supported the Reaching Every District approach in all ten departments and catch-up vaccination campaigns for children who missed routine doses, improving service reach, micro-planning and monitoring and narrowing coverage gaps in hard-to-access, crisis-affected zones. UNICEF contributed to the provision of 72,500 pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and 279,200 tetanus-diphtheria (Td) doses, essential consumables, remote temperature monitoring devices, and maintenance with technician training. 
Maternal, neonatal, and child health: From January to October 2025, 21,497 live births were attended by skilled health personnel in health facilities, representing 25.46 per cent of the target. UNICEF supported the finalisation and rollout of the National Strategic Plan for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent and Elderly Health (SRMNCAH E). UNICEF equipped 89 health facilities across Ouest, Artibonite, Nord and Nord Est, and strengthened the workforce through training for 284 health professionals in Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) and Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EmONC/SONU), plus 466 multi-purpose community health workers (ASCPs). Facility upgrades and skills building improved the safety of deliveries, reduced delays in emergency care, and enabled mothers and newborns to access quality services even when movement or staffing was limited by armed groups and insecurity.
Reducing child malnutrition: To reach children beyond fixed facilities, Haiti operationalised an innovative community-based approach for the management of acute malnutrition. 124 ASCPs were trained and deployed, bringing screening and uncomplicated treatment closer to households affected by displacement. By October, 33,665 children (18,560 girls; 15,105 boys) had been screened and 9,500 children (5,429 girls; 4,071 boys) recovered through community-based care. Compared with 2022 (518 children), this represents a significant expansion in equitable access and earlier detection for families living far from services. The approach helped caregivers act sooner, reduced travel and costs, and improved continuity of nutrition care in locations where formal infrastructure is weak or disrupted. Overall, this strategy directly advanced national objectives for reducing acute malnutrition and strengthening the resilience of community health systems. In late 2025, UNICEF and the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP) launched a documentation process to capture key lessons and operational insights from this approach, to support scale-up in other municipalities and inform adaptation elsewhere.

2. Inclusive and Equitable Learning - Education
During the reporting period, UNICEF and its partners made substantial progress in improving access, quality, inclusion, and resilience across Haiti’s education sector in an extremely fragile national context. Efforts focused on sustaining learning, protecting displaced children and strengthening education governance.
Support for inclusion and learning continuity: UNICEF and partners prioritised continuity of learning for the most vulnerable children in a highly disrupted environment. Teacher capacity was strengthened, with 640 teachers trained in Liv Inik and new subject instruction, and 530 teachers supporting remedial education for 34,180 students preparing for official examinations, helping mitigate learning losses and sustain progression. Access barriers were reduced through a combination of learning materials (including 32,636 school kits, 200,000 Liv Inik, and braille and mobility materials) and cash support reaching 6,300 children, enabling learners from the poorest and displacement-affected households, including children with disabilities, to remain in school despite severe economic stress. Non-formal education programmes reconnected 5,990 out-of-school children and adolescents to learning and skills training, improving their future prospects.
Early childhood education (ECE) as a foundation of the education system: Promoting early childhood education as the foundation of learning and a critical entry point for system resilience, UNICEF supported 63 early childhood development centres, reaching 3,150 children with stimulation and learning kits. This early investment helped protect developmental gains, support school readiness, and reduce longer-term learning gaps in communities affected by crisis and displacement. A national diagnostic on preschool education was completed, informing Haiti’s ECE policy with costed models for 1-3 years of preschool. 
Education system resilience protection: UNICEF strengthened education governance, preparedness and learning environments to sustain delivery in crisis. Forty Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFP) staff were trained in disaster risk management; contingency plans were updated in four departments which facilitated the revitalization of the Ministry's emergency unit. Five national sub-clusters supported emergency coordination, and 130 school councils received support to reinforce local participation and accountability. School infrastructure was expanded or restored in priority areas, with 9 permanent schools constructed, 13 rehabilitated and 19 schools relocated, alongside WASH improvements to keep learning safe and functional. 
Safer learning environments, protection and psychosocial support: Protective and psychosocial capacities linked to schools and communities were reinforced through training for 135 Brigade for the Protection of Minors (BPM) and Educational Community Police (EDUPOL) officers in child protection, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), and protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA). Psychosocial services reached 208,689 children and community members, and 74,357 children participated in peacebuilding and social cohesion activities.
Reaching displaced children affected by armed violence: UNICEF helped identify and reintegrate 11,455 displaced children and children formerly associated with armed groups into school, while 3,842 children accessed temporary learning spaces. These actions reduced time out of school and supported safer, more inclusive pathways back to education for children on the move.

3. Resilient Water, Sanitation, Hygiene - WASH
Climate-resilient WASH services: Through Community Approaches to Total Sanitation (CATS), accelerated behaviour change and local solutions, sanitation conditions improved in 140 communities for more than 80,000 people, with community engagement and verification supporting progress toward Open Defecation Free (ODF) status. These community-led approaches reduced disease risks and strengthened resilience where formal services remain limited.  
WASH infrastructure in schools and health care facilities was rehabilitated, including latrines and handwashing stations, benefiting more than 25,000 children and health personnel and strengthening infection prevention while creating more dignified learning and care environments.
Emergency water supply, sanitation, and hygiene: UNICEF supported rapid WASH responses to displacement, cholera alerts and floods, including in peri-urban neighbourhoods affected by armed groups. Over 178,114 people accessed emergency water supply, 51,871 received sanitation services, and 131,855 received hygiene kits, reducing immediate health risks for families unable to safely access basic services. The L3 evaluation found that safe water results were stronger, while sanitation lagged due to insecurity, high logistics costs and limited partner capacity.
WASH sector governance improvement: UNICEF continued to host the WASH donors’ secretariat and co-lead WASH in emergencies with the Government, helping align partners, speed decision-making and maintain strong cluster coordination with the Direction Nationale de l’Eau Potable et de l’Assainissement (DINEPA), leading to more impactful WASH support to IDP and other crisis-affected populations. 

4. Child Protection 
Child Protection System Strengthening: Through the PREJEUNES programme, UNICEF supported the Government to develop a national approach to prevent child recruitment and support safe exit of children from armed groups. UNICEF supported the Institute of Social Welfare and Research (IBESR) to recruit and train 50 volunteer social workers. Capacity building for the Brigade de Protection des Mineurs (BPM) focused on strengthening case handling, referrals and operational readiness.
At community level, UNICEF helped establish 15 child protection committees, supported 10 women’s groups, and strengthened child protection coordination mechanisms in all 10 departments of the country. These platforms improved local prevention, early identification and safe referral for children at risk. Awareness-raising activities reached 28,523 people, supporting acceptance of children returning from armed groups and reducing stigma.
UNICEF trained 650 members of the Haitian National Police (PNH) and the Multinational Security Support Mission (MSSM), and 550 NGO frontline workers on grave violations, child safeguarding and the 2024 Handover Protocol, strengthening identification and referral in displacement sites and areas affected by armed violence.
A major achievement was the operationalization of Pwojè Espwa centre, transferred to IBESR in Les Cayes. The centre is planned to be rehabilitated with UNICEF support. The centre serves as one of Haiti’s two Transit and Orientation Centres (CTOs) for children formerly associated with armed groups, providing safe accommodation, psychosocial support, non-formal education, health services, and reintegration preparation.
Findings from the L3 response underline the need to reinforce protection-led programming and improve reach and quality of services, especially beyond Port-au-Prince.
Emergency response and psychosocial support: 97,358 children benefited from psychosocial and mental health activities. Of these, 9,552 received focused MHPSS through specialised Gender-Based Violence (GBV) partners. MHPSS coverage fell well below needs, with only 16 per cent of targeted people reached. Community-based teams identified and assisted 1,909 unaccompanied and deported children at the transit centres of Ouanaminthe and Belladère, supporting alternative care and reunification.
Additionally, 194 children formerly associated with armed groups received specialised case management and psychosocial support through Child-Friendly Spaces and the CTO Ouest. UNICEF collaborated with IBESR and Save the Children to revise national case management standard operating procedures (SOPs), strengthening the quality and consistency of services, During Tropical Storm Melissa in October, rapid assessments and deployment of mobile units ensured continuity of essential protection services for vulnerable children and caregivers.
GBV Prevention and Response: UNICEF and partners reached 22,577 individuals with awareness and prevention activities on child protection, GBV, and PSEA. UNICEF supported 20 “Espas Mwen” safe spaces and shelters, providing holistic services including medical care, psychosocial support, financial assistance, and relocation to survivors of GBV and sexual exploitation and abuse. Cross-sectoral collaboration with WASH and Nutrition strengthened referrals for adolescent girls associated with armed groups, including pregnant adolescents and young mothers. Community and religious leaders helped reduce stigma and encourage safe reporting of GBV cases. 

5. Strengthened Social Protection Systems 
Expanding cash support and access to services: UNICEF expanded cash transfers to reach families facing multiple shocks. Over 15,000 households were registered, and more than 16,400 households accessed essential services, including health, nutrition, and education. Incentive payments supported frontline delivery, benefitting 570 teachers, 388 healthcare workers and 150 social workers. UNICEF helped over 5,000 families cover school fees, while advocating for free, standardised preschool education and systematic birth registration to ease school enrolment.
An operational arrangement with DIGICEL enabled more than 92% of cash transfers to be delivered digitally, ensuring timely delivery. UNICEF is preparing an e-voucher mechanism via USSD to link cash support to specific services or products where appropriate. Ahead of Tropical Storm Melissa, 7,400 households received cash assistance within four days, with over US$600,000 disbursed through anticipatory cash support, in coordination with WFP.
Policy and system strengthening: UNICEF contributed to advancing the National Social Protection Plan (PNPS) through child-centred measures and active participation in the Social Protection Sector Round Table. Advocacy supported exemptions for free preschool education and primary healthcare, reducing access barriers for the poorest households. Working with Government, UNICEF helped secure IDB funding to integrate school nurses in 75 schools in the North region.
UNICEF continued to advocate for enhancing the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour’s Information System (SIMAST), the national social registry, which currently covers about 30% of the population, and supported strengthening of the Educational Management Information System (SIGEEE).  These efforts aim to improve targeting, grievance handling, monitoring and responsiveness to local needs.

6. Emergency preparedness and response
In a year marked by historic levels of displacement, escalating violence, and collapsing public services, UNICEF’s preparedness and emergency response efforts enabled faster, more integrated and child-focused assistance, helping safeguard the lives and well-being of the most vulnerable across Haiti. 
Preparing for shocks, readiness and rapid response: UNICEF strengthened emergency readiness and delivered faster response despite access constraints and repeated shocks. UNICEF supported the Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC) and the MSPP to update risk analyses and contingency plans, while pre-positioning multi-sector emergency supplies across high-risk areas. By end-2025, UNICEF maintained contingency stocks to cover 5 per cent of the HAC target, enabling rapid mobilisation during acute shocks, including cholera alerts, large-scale displacement, and Tropical Storm Melissa, reducing response times from weeks to days. UNICEF also strengthened and expanded its Emergency Response Mechanism, playing a central role in inter-agency response to sudden-onset crises. Through this mechanism, UNICEF delivered safe water, hygiene kits, psychosocial first aid, child protection case identification, acute malnutrition screening, and emergency learning support for affected families, bringing assistance closer to communities when they needed it most.
Continuity of essential services: Preparedness investments supported continuity of care and safe learning. UNICEF supplied 44 health facilities with cholera treatment supplies, rehabilitated 17 water systems in high-risk areas, and reinforced community-based surveillance mechanisms. In education, emergency learning materials and temporary solutions helped displaced children continue learning amid armed violence and natural hazards.
Localisation and partner capacity: To strengthen proximity and speed, UNICEF expanded its contingency partner base with 12 organizations across WASH, Child Protection, Nutrition and Education, reinforcing localization and preparedness capacities in high-risk areas. 
Cluster coordination: UNICEF led the WASH, Nutrition and Education clusters and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, supporting national leadership and strengthening information management so partners could align standards and delivery under pressure.

7. Social Behaviour Change (SBC)
Bringing trusted information into communities: UNICEF supported the MSPP to roll out the national communication strategy across all ten departments, helping families overcome uncertainty and return to lifesaving routines, particularly vaccination. Community mobilisers used U-Reporters to identify and refer children and pregnant women to services, while Community Health Workers, health professionals and departmental communication focal points strengthened Interpersonal Communication (IPC) skills to build trust in vaccines and frontline health care. These actions increased demand for essential services and improved linkages between communities and service providers.
Promoting protective behaviours in displacement settings: UNICEF led awareness campaigns on cholera prevention, combining radio messaging with hands-on demonstrations in handwashing, oral rehydration solution preparation and other essential practices. This approach enabled families to reduce health risks when formal systems were disrupted, and WASH infrastructure was limited.
Supporting return to learning and protection: UNICEF supported the communication plan for the progressive back-to-school campaign. Through U-Reporters, out-of-school children were identified and referred to schools, contributing to continuity of learning. In child protection, UNICEF supported PREJEUNES communication efforts and initiatives for children formerly associated with armed groups, promoting peace, acceptance and wellbeing. Early childhood stimulation and social cohesion activities were facilitated in displacement sites.

8. Communication and advocacy
High-level missions helped elevate global attention to Haiti’s escalating crises. Visits by Deputy Executive Director Ted Chaiban, Spokesperson James Elder, and Regional Director Roberto Benes, together with the launch of the Haiti Child Alert and successive Palais briefings provided compelling, first-hand evidence of the severe risks facing displaced children, survivors of GBV, and those recruited by armed groups. These efforts were reinforced by the Executive Director’s intervention at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), urging Member States to increase humanitarian funding, strengthen child-centred protection measures, and uphold international humanitarian law in response to grave violations of children’s rights in Haiti.
Sustained visibility generated wide international media coverage with more than 15 top-tier outlets and 150 media publications, anchoring Haiti’s child-protection crisis on the global agenda. The UNICEF Representative engaged multilateral forums, including the Ad Hoc Advisory Group on Haiti’s Working Group on Institutions and the NY-based Group of Friends on Children and Armed Conflict. Advocacy in these fora focused on support to the Handover Protocol and on reintegration pathways for children exiting armed groups.

9. Partnerships
By 31 December 2025, UNICEF mobilised US$34.9 million in humanitarian contributions, complemented by US$17.1 million in carry-over from 2024. This brought total available resources to US$47 million, or 18 per cent of the US$272 million HAC appeal. Major contributions from top three donor US Government funding, Sweden and ECHO , along with flexible funding, enabled rapid, needs-based action in an extremely constrained operating environment.
As lead of the WASH, Nutrition and Child Protection Clusters, and a key actor in the Education in Emergencies Working Group, UNICEF leveraged coordination platforms including the UN Partnership Portal to align responses with national authorities and humanitarian partners. Despite access challenges, these partnerships ensured sustained delivery of life-saving interventions.
Beyond emergency financing, UNICEF advanced multi-partner development initiatives: a new partnership with Spain to strengthen early childhood education; collaboration with the IDB and World Bank to reinforce WASH and school infrastructure; and alignment with Gavi to maintain immunisation and maternal-newborn services. High-level engagement, including a donor briefing by Deputy Executive Director Ted Chaiban, helped maintain attention to children’s needs amid escalating violence. Partnerships with national ministries, UN agencies, and public-private actors further supported continuity of essential services.

10. Gender and PSEA
UNICEF Haiti strengthened PSEA through partner assessment, capacity-building and community engagement. All active partners were assessed using the United Nations Partner Portal (UNPP) and supported to embed PSEA standards in programme delivery. A total of 519 frontline workers were trained to prevent, identify and manage SEA risks and strengthen incident response. Community sensitisation reached 236, 153 people, increasing awareness of rights, safe reporting and GBV/PSEA. With the World Food Programme (WFP), UNICEF co-funded and co-managed the inter-agency hotline 8811, providing a confidential channel for complaints, feedback and SEA reporting. Inter-agency SEA risk analysis informed targeted prevention and response measures in high-risk areas.
11. Planning, Monitoring and Evaluation
UNICEF advanced national evaluation capacity development with Government partners through the Country Office Costed Evaluation Plan, linking system strengthening, training and evidence generation.
UNICEF supported the Government to coordinate the Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems’ Strengthening training, in which 37 national officials participated, strengthening evaluation practice and evidence use. The National Evaluation Diagnostic Study was not conducted in 2025, but discussions with the Ministry of Planning and External Cooperation (MPCE) and partners will continue to finalise scope and enable implementation. Over 100 staff and partners received training on PSEA, the Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) and monitoring and evaluation, reinforcing quality and accountability. 
UNICEF supported a national preschool survey with the MENFP to inform policy. With DINEPA, UNICEF initiated an evaluation of WASH systems-strengthening, with findings expected early 2026. The UNICEF Evaluation Office completed the evaluation of the 2024 Level 3 Corporate Emergency Activation, highlighting areas of improvement in child protection, consistency and coherence of responses, and simplifications/efficiencies. 
UNICEF and the MSPP advanced preparation for a National Nutrition Survey (SMART), with data collection scheduled in the first quarter 2026.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
UNICEF Haiti’s 2025 programme was delivered under severe constraints; three cross-cutting challenges stand out, evidenced by pressure on schools used as shelters, gaps in local routine data, and the need to strengthen the convergence of essential services in high-risk areas:
Limited integration of essential services: Public health components such as nutrition, vaccination, maternal and neonatal care, adolescent health and prevention of common childhood illnesses were sometimes implemented in silos. Links with WASH, SBC and Social Protection were not consistently operationalised, reducing efficiency and quality. In displacement sites in Port-au-Prince, insecurity constrained the delivery of a fully integrated package.
Restricted access and a volatile operating environment: Insecurity and repeated displacement disrupted service continuity and delayed longer-term programming, while a continuous influx of IDPs increased pressure on WASH and education services in host communities. Schools were repeatedly used as temporary shelters and then required rehabilitation before learning could resume, illustrating the strain on the education system.
Weak decentralised routine data systems and use: Routine data systems at decentralised level are not fully functional because of capacity gaps and limited supervision. As a result, national data are often incomplete and delayed, limiting planning, prioritisation and accountability for children, women and adolescents. Some systems also miss key indicators needed for coverage tracking and early warning. For example, UNICEF is advocating with MSPP to integrate missing Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) indicators into SISNU, to avoid parallel data collection that increases workload for frontline staff and partners.
Resource constraints, especially in Child Protection: The operating environment is defined by grave protection risks, including armed violence, kidnapping and gender-based violence. Yet Child Protection remained under-resourced relative to needs, constraining the scale, continuity and quality of case management, MHPSS, and GBV services, particularly outside Port-au-Prince.

Lessons learned
Combining WASH in communities and schools, public health services, child protection including mental health and psychosocial support, Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) and Social Policy cash assistance created coherent service pathways for children and families in the most affected areas. UNICEF is at its most impactful when it takes an integrated approach to meeting the needs of children holistically. 
Community platforms and adolescent engagement are catalytic. Community health workers (ASCP) improved early detection, home follow-up and local reporting for nutrition and immunisation. Youth mechanisms such as U-Report and programmes like PREJEUNES helped strengthen prevention, protection and reintegration for children affected by armed actors, while building social cohesion.
Anticipatory action proved effective when triggers and roles are clear. For the first time, anticipatory activities during Tropical Storm Melissa enabled assistance to thousands within days, supported by pre-positioning and contingency partnerships. Where cash was linked to services, notably education and protection, access improved rapidly and equitably.
Evidence and communications amplified impact. Child-centred storytelling, content in Créole and consistent visibility increased donor confidence and policy traction. Transparent monitoring strengthened credibility, yet diversifying funding beyond traditional grants is essential to mitigate donor fatigue and over-reliance on traditional donors. 
Lessons from the emergency response reinforce three priorities aligned with 2025 experience: stronger protection centrality, more integrated delivery and clearer AAP feedback loops linked to action. These will be embedded in 2026 planning and reporting.

Future outlook
Building on 2025 implementation experience and evidence-informed learning, UNICEF will consolidate gains and reach more marginalised children through four shifts in 2026, in line with the Strategic Moment of Reflection and programme course correction.
1. Integrated service delivery and coordinated planning
Adopt standardised service packages for priority communes that integrate nutrition, immunisation, maternal and neonatal care, adolescent health, WASH in schools and facilities, child protection services and Cash plus. Implement joint training and supervision for frontline personnel, with rotational support by section leads to reinforce competencies and quality. These packages will be implemented with stronger protection centrality and clearer cross-sector coherence.
2. Data, monitoring and accountability to communities
Enhance routine systems with harmonised indicators across SISNU, SIGEEE and SIMAST and connect partner reporting through simple standard operating procedures and eTools. Small-sample surveys and third-party monitoring will complement routine systems in high-priority areas while community-level monitoring via ASCPs will track local coverage, nutrition and morbidity trends. UNICEF will strengthen accountability to affected populations (AAP), ensuring feedback mechanisms are clear, accessible and linked to corrective action. 
3. Resilience, anticipatory action and operational agility
Scale anticipatory Cash+ linked to essential services with clear triggers, pre-agreed roles and tested workflows. Maintain pre-positioning and contingency partnerships and expand mobile, integrated teams for hotspots and border points. Risk-informed disaster preparedness will be strengthened through updated multi-hazard contingency planning, scenario-based simulations and enhanced pre-positioning in high-risk areas. Streamline HACT and provide simple guidance packs to partners to reduce the cycle time from prioritisation to delivery.
4. Financing, partnerships and human resources
UNICEF will advocate for flexible, multi-year financing to sustain integrated packages and localisation while safeguarding quality. Develop innovative approaches, including public-private partnerships (PPPs) and mixed financing models, to diversify funding streams and enhance resilience; Strengthen human resources for monitoring and information management and maintain continuous mentoring and targeted capacity building for field offices and local partners.
 
UNICEF Haiti’s 2025 results demonstrated resilience and innovation in a rapidly evolving poly-crisis context. In 2026, building on PREJEUNES and strengthening multisectoral convergence, accountability, anticipatory action and risk-informed preparedness, UNICEF will improve equitable access to essential services for children, women and adolescents, balancing immediate life-saving needs with systems-level solutions.

In its latest Concluding Observations (2025), the Committee on the Rights of the Child recognizes that Honduras has taken important steps to strengthen its legal and institutional framework for the protection of children’s rights. The establishment of the Comprehensive System for Guaranteeing the Rights of Children and Adolescents, the creation and reinforcement of the Ministry for Children (SENAF), the adoption of the National Policy for Early Childhood, Childhood, and Adolescence, and the establishment of Children's Councils in approximately two-thirds of the country's municipalities, reflect a commitment by the State to guarantee protection, participation, and comprehensive guarantee of  all rights for all children within the territory of Honduras. Yet, despite these advances, the Committee on the Rights of the Child also emphasizes measures needed to address violence against children in all its forms, avoiding family separation, reinforce adolescent health, enhance access to education, and the protection of migrant and displaced children, underscoring the challenges of making national policies and programmes a reality for all girls and boys across the country. 
High incidence of poverty continues to determine the vulnerability of children in Honduras. Official data from the National Institute of Statistics (INE) indicate a significant reduction of poverty in recent years, still 60.1 percent of households live in poverty and 38.3 percent in extreme poverty (2025). This deprivation limits access to essential services such as health, education, and nutrition, perpetuating generational cycles of exclusion, particularly among historically marginalized groups such as girls, children with disabilities, indigenous and Afro-descendant populations, and migrants. Poverty is also one of the main drivers for families to place their children in alternative residential care. A recent survey (National Statistics Institute, 2025) highlighted that nearly 4,000 children as placed in some 140 of such institutions. It remains a priority to continue aiming for progressive - and responsible family reunification with all (social) protection efforts facilitating such efforts.
Honduras ranks among the most violent countries in Latin America, with a homicide rate of 26.3 per 100,000 inhabitants (2024), with 240 violent deaths of women and 236 of children and adolescents recorded. Projections for 2025 suggest a slight reduction of violent deaths (23.2 rate), yet the impact of criminal violence remains severe particularly in large urban centres and increasingly also in rural areas. Forced recruitment by gangs continues to be a leading cause of internal displacement, targeting children through coercion and threats, and stripping them of safety, education, and future prospects. Girls face specific risks of sexual violence, exploitation, and coercion to act as informants for criminal groups in exchange for protection. 
Police data reveal 1,981 complaints of sexual crimes against minors in 2024 and 1,322 so far in 2025, highlighting (and these only a small portion of the real numbers as there remains a lack of trust in the justice system which contributes to limited reporting) the urgency of integrated prevention, protection, and psychosocial support systems. Sexual violence is also one of the main drivers of high adolescent pregnancy (more than 20,000 adolescent pregnancies per year). Honduras has also the highest femicide rates in the region.
Public investment in health remains around 4 percent of GDP, well below the six percent recommended by the World Health Organization. Nevertheless, the government has implemented measures to expand access, including with the construction of eight hospitals, four neonatal centers and five maternal-infant modules. Honduras has progressively expanded vaccine availability to 25 free vaccines. However, despite major efforts, vaccine coverage remains a concern with trust in vaccine safety reducing due to the spread of disinformation. 
Education enrolment and completion remain a challenge. School enrolment for children aged 3 to 17 was only 62 percent (2024), leaving more than one million students excluded, especially in secondary education and in rural areas. Encouragingly, 2025 brought some progress through initiatives such as ‘Municipalities Champions for Education’, which contributed to the enrolment of more than 90,000 children in the 145 participating municipalities. However, half of all schools still lack basic infrastructure such as electricity, water, sanitation, and adequate furniture, requiring investments exceeding one billion dollars according to Ministry of Education. A UNICEF-led study shows that fiscal inefficiencies in education contribute to losses of 200 million dollars annually, equivalent to 20 percent of the education budget. 
Migration dynamics shifted significantly in 2025. According to the National Migration Institute (INM), more than 36,653 migrants entered Honduras from the south by November, reflecting a 90 percent decrease in northbound migration compared to the previous years. However, reverse migration toward the south has increased substantially. As a result, humanitarian needs remain while funding cuts have forced humanitarian actors to withdraw from border areas, reducing service capacity and heightening vulnerability among migrant and refugee children. 
On the other hand, INM statistics show that 38,898 people, including 4,975 children, were returned to Honduras (mostly from the USA and Mexico) between January and November, a 23 percent increase from 2024. Many returning children face reintegration challenges, including lack of family ties or language barriers.  
Climate risk adds another layer of complexity. In 2025 Honduras ranked third globally on the Climate Risk Index, making resilience strategies in education, health, and child protection a priority. Climate shocks exacerbate poverty, displacement, and health risks, demanding integrated approaches to safeguard children’s rights. Under the Global Humanitarian Reset context, Clusters were deactivated implying lower visibility and funding to respond to humanitarian crises.
The general elections held in November 2025 may bring shifts in priorities, financing, and technical capacity when the new government takes office. While the proposed 2026 budget suggests certain stability for most of 23 child-focused institutions, the resources are still not sufficient to ensure adequate capacity at sub-national levels, and also for maintaining coverage of social protection systems. 
Honduras stands at a crossroads where legal and policy advances coexist with structural vulnerabilities that threaten the fulfillment of child rights. For UNICEF, the challenge is clear: to support scaling up of health and education access to services, strengthen child protection systems, advocate for expanding social protection programs, increasing climate resilience, and expanding safeguarding programs and social spending.

Advocacy and Communication
The State of Honduras engaged in its strategic dialogue with the Committee on the Rights of the Child in January 2025, building on the reports shared by the State to the Committee in previous years. UNICEF (both the country office and the human rights team in Geneva) and representatives from civil society organizations accompanied the dialogue and provided advice and support when requested. The Concluding Observations of the Committee allowed the State, under the leadership of SENAF and the Ministry of Human Rights and with support from UNICEF, to prepare a detailed action plan to address the recommendations with clear description of roles and responsibilities. Moreover, a significant number of the recommendations from the Committee were also incorporated into the observations resulting from the Universal Periodic Review and its accompanying dialogue with the State of Honduras, including on adequate budget allocation and reinforcing national and local capacities to respond to child rights violations. 
UNICEF actively used the recommendations from the Committee on the Rights of the Child and follow-up action points from the multiple child-related international conference, in discussions with political parties and presidential candidates in the lead-up to the national- and municipal elections in November, advocating with the candidates to ensure adequate attention to children as part of their political agenda. UNICEF also contributed to discussions between the UN Country Team and presidential candidates. 
Being considered a trusted partner by the international donor community, the government, civil society, UN organizations, and other key stakeholders, and delivering relevant results at scale, UNICEF maintained solid resource mobilization for its country programme and for humanitarian action, a prospect that remains for 2026. In addition, substantive financial resources were leveraged for investment in education, health and WASH and some more careful engagement was initiated with the private sector (foundations and charities from large corporations, etc.). 
Throughout the year, UNICEF worked closely with the other UN Agencies, Funds and Programmes, aimed at delivering the results of the UNSDCF, including through participation in a significant number of joint programmes (prevention of violence in vulnerable communities - with UNODC; elimination of child labour in the coffee sector – with ILO and FAO; humanitarian action through CERF – with UNHCR, IOM, WFP and WHO/PAHO; Pandemic Fund implementation – with WHO/PAHO and FAO; Increased education enrolment – with UNECLAC and UNDP, among others. Solid collaboration also continued for sharpening security protocols and by establishing a joint field office in San Pedro Sula, with UNHCR and IOM. 
UNICEF continued to increase its visibility in traditional media (including through opinion articles in some of the main newspapers of the country) and even more in social networks with thousands of new followers in some of the networks. For example, the UNICEF Honduras YouTube channel increased from around 700 followers in 2024 to 27,000 followers in 2025. 
Institutional Strengthening and Local Governance
UNICEF continued to provide technical assistance to the Ministry of Children & Family (SENAF) in reinforcing its role as lead in the coordination of the National Council for the Integral Protection of Children and Adolescents in Honduras (SIGADENAH), bringing all child-related institutions together and discuss priorities as established in the National Policy on Children’s Rights. These priorities include: 1) early childhood development; 2) addressing all forms of violence against children; 3) deinstitutionalization of children in residential care; and 4) reintegration of returning migrant children and their families. In line with several related recommendations from the Committee on the Rights of the Child, UNICEF accompanied and advised SENAF in addressing each of these four priorities. 
With technical advise from UNICEF, and in collaboration with SENAF, the Association of Honduran Municipalities (AMHON) and in coordination with civil society organizations (members of the Global Movement for Children, chapter Honduras) approximately 245 out of the 298 municipalities in the country have established Municipal Councils for Children, with participation of all key institutions present at municipal level. These councils are all convened by senior municipal leaders. In total, 131 of these municipalities also count on a specific inter-sectoral work plan to address the biggest challenges for children in their territories. While UNICEF continued with extensive efforts at national level, increased attention was given to extend systems strengthening to municipal levels, initially in 48 prioritised municipalities and with support from 5 UNV-staff strategically located across the country, supporting the Municipal Councils in situation analysis, preparation of municipal action plans for children and in implementation of those plans. These 48 selected municipalities coincide with UNICEF programmatic action in addressing violence against children, reintegration of returning migrant children, early childhood development and/or education. The strategic partnership with AMHON significantly contributed commitment to action for children by municipal authorities. 
In line with overall programmatic prioritization of municipalities, UNICEF also initiated technical assistance in the preparation of municipal disaster preparedness and response plans in 42 municipalities which will contribute to increased cooperation and coordination of disaster response efforts from national- and local authorities. 
Child Protection
UNICEF provided technical assistance and support to several ministries in the follow-up to the Conference on the Elimination of Violence against Children, supported SENAF in its role as host of the annual meeting of the Inter-American Institute of the Child (with funding support from the LAC Regional Office) and other international conferences and discussions. 
Under the leadership of the National Statistics Institute, UNICEF supported a census of children institutional care which contributed to the preparation of an action plan for progressive and responsible deinstitutionalization of the nearly 4,000 children currently living in such institutions. So far, the percentage of children in need of special protection and placed in institutions dropped from 36% (2024) to 30% in 2025 and UNICEF is working with SENAF and other government institutions in a progressive- and responsible deinstitutionalization, starting with some 370 children in 2025, gathering all actors around support to the families of these children, where possible.  Also, US$ 3.2 million was identified within the national budget for a new round of ENDESA/MICS which is scheduled for implementation in 2026, with technical support from UNICEF. The data from this ENDESA/MICS will be of valuable support to evidence-based policy formulation and adjustments. The technical design of the survey was also completed. UNICEF also supported the preparation of situational analysis on children and adolescents at municipal level, with 23 of such analyses completed in 2025. These analyses are prepared by the local authorities and are the basis for municipal action plans for children. 
Even though only around 110 children in conflict with the law are currently in a confined environment, there are around 2,000 children in conflict with law with alternative non-confined sentences. UNICEF continued working with the national institution for children in conflict with the law, the Public Prosecutors Office, SENAF and other government organizations in strengthening capacities of the 380 civil servants attending these children, with emphasis on facilitating responsible reintegration into society and psychosocial support to these children. UNICEF also supported the introduction of feedback mechanisms for children on the services and support they are receiving. 
Education
In close collaboration with AMHON and the Ministry of Education, together with the Regional Economic Commission for Latin America & the Caribbean (UNECLAC), UNDP and the Resident Coordinator Office and with funding from the SDG-Fund, UNICEF contributed to the enrolment of an additional 70,000 children into the education system in 145 municipalities by a groundbreaking ‘Municipalities Champions for Education Initiative’. Champion municipalities saw a +0.98% increase in girls’ enrollment, nearly triple the rate of non-Champion municipalities, reflecting progress in gender equity. While the funding from UNICEF provided the conditions for the initiative to excel, investments by municipalities in education increased by some 300%, in addition to important additional investments in education at the national level. A next version of this initiative, where teachers actively search for out-of-school children in their communities, combined with a more relevant educational offer, particularly for adolescents, will be launched in early 2026. In addition to major efforts in enrolling children into schools. 
UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Education in a large range of educational reforms and new initiatives. This included significant involvement in rolling out access to digital education, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Education, International Financial Institutions and also Foundations supported by the private sector, which eventually allowed increasing digital connectivity to 13% of all, and particularly larger, schools (almost double from 2024), benefiting some 650,000 students. It is expected that 60% of schools will be connected by 2030, building major investment from international development banks and from domestic resources. Online and Offline modalities of Learning Passport consolidated as an integral component of “Educatrachos” platform, reaching a cumulative total of 351,806 users over four years, including children on the move. The MicroBit Initiative, with emphasis on empowering 6,098 girls who directly participated to strengthen their STEM skills, also received a lot of attention. With funding from the Government of Corea, and in close collaboration with the Ministry of Education and AMHON, UNICEF also continued efforts to further implement a ‘school-community model’, eventually covering 500 schools in the poorest communities of Honduras. This model aims at not only improving access to education but also to use the school as a contributor to community engagement, identification of children victim of violence, monitoring nutritional status, among others. A baseline study, including data for a control group of communities to allow for assessment of the impact of this programme was completed in 45 municipalities. With initiatives such as STEM and the reduction of child labor, UNICEF and partners promoted the participation of around 21,000 children in 332 schools across 4 departments, strengthening key competencies including communication, problem-solving, argumentation, citizenship, respect, responsibility, critical thinking, and innovation. 
Health and Early Childhood
UNICEF continued with the certification of hospitals as ‘Mother and Child Friendly Hospitals’ and 23 out of the 25 public hospitals in the country have received such certification in 2025, with particular attention to the promotion of exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months. This initiative is so far benefitting 72,000 newborns (70% of all children born annually) across the country and it is expected that the expansion of this initiative to private hospitals will allow even more children to have an optimal start in life. UNICEF, together with WHO/PAHO and with leadership of the Ministry of Health, also initiated the process of regular monitoring and recertification of each of the hospitals, ensuring that they continue implementing the ’10 steps for the promotion of exclusive breastfeeding’. 
Vaccination coverage has dropped to concerning levels over the past few years. During 2025, UNICEF worked closely with the Ministry of Health in increasing access to vaccination and particularly in generating more demand for vaccination as part of efforts to rebuild public trust in the safety and effectiveness of vaccines, which has eroded due to misinformation. As part of these efforts, UNICEF has increased its capacity within the ministry at national level and also by placing five experts for social & behavioural change communication in those parts of the country with lowest vaccination coverage rates. These experts work closely with local health authorities in vaccination promotion (including the use of the ‘Maximo’ campaign) and debunking misinformation, working closely with ‘influencers’ at the community level and have so far reached more than 12,000 children under 1 year old. UNICEF also provided valuable technical assistance in the planning of vaccine distribution and a more adequate estimate of the costing of vaccination in the country, which is important for further planning and budgeting. Along with the Ministry of Health, WHO/PAHO and FAO, work was also started in activities related to the preparedness of the impact of future pandemics, building on a significant contribution of the Global Pandemic Fund and administered by UNICEF. 
Technical assistance was provided to SENAF in the expansion of a multi-sectoral early childhood development model to 89 municipalities, benefiting 120,000 children below the age of six. For this purpose, UNICEF accompanied the municipal authorities in diagnosis and implementation of actions at community level aimed at promoting breastfeeding, early stimulation and birth registration. In addition, support was also provided, along with the World Bank and GAVI, to a study on early childhood development that will inform decision making on the implementation of a US$ 75 million loan focused on improving access to maternal- and child health services. UNICEF received US$ 200,000 from the World Bank for the implementation of the study which will be concluded in 2026. UNICEF also worked with the Honduran customs office, with technical support of the global UNICEF Supply Division, in streamlining import of (mostly emergency) supplies. 
WASH
In water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), UNICEF continued, with funding from the UN-India South-South Collaboration Fund, with the roll-out of WASH services to 10,000 persons in the department of Gracias a Dios, one of the most remote parts of the country. Across the country, UNICEF also continued to provide technical advice in the implementation of climate-resilient WASH services, particularly in schools and in some of the most vulnerable communities where presence of the State is limited. Increasingly, UNICEF is also involved in leveraging investments by International Financial Institutions and also domestic resources for the water sector (US$ 54 million) and in addressing the negative impacts of climate change (US$ 18 million from the Green Climate Fund). UNICEF also worked closely with the Ministry of the Environment in further engaging young people in climate action. In 2026, this was initiated in 88 schools in 6 municipalities that are particularly vulnerable to the impact of climate change. Student councils in these schools did not only receive information on climate change, but they also undertook concrete action. This included presenting proposals to local private sector leaders (small and large) to fund their initiatives. It is expected that this approach is to be replicated in many more schools in 2026. 
Humanitarian
Due to the rapidly changing realities in humanitarian funding and with the cluster-structure already phased-out in early 2025, UNICEF provided leadership, upon request of the UN Humanitarian Coordinator, within the UN Country Team and with the Humanitarian network of government and civil society partners, in a full humanitarian review.  Three shocks were prioritized for future humanitarian action: 1) violence; 2) mixed-migration flows; and 3) impact of climate change and in total 31 of the most vulnerable municipalities were prioritized. UNICEF, as one of the largest humanitarian actors in Honduras, is involved in addressing each of these three prioritized shocks with ever increasing emphasis on implementing a ‘nexus approach’. 
During 2025, with funding from the United States of America (BPRM), UNICEF assisted migrants traveling from north to south through Honduras with particular attention to children and their families. Moreover, capacities and protocols were reinforced in the main reception centre for returning migrant children and families and with special attention to returning unaccompanied migrant children. With funding from the Swedish Development Agency (SIDA), the Government of Korea and Global Thematic Humanitarian Funding, UNICEF also expanded its support from 5 to 12 municipalities with the largest numbers of returning migrants. In these municipalities, returning children and families are being supported with reintegration into their communities, where feasible, and access to education and health services, among others. Municipal social workers fulfill an important role in such efforts. 
Despite bleak prospects for the 2025 hurricane season, no major climate events were registered during the year except for some heavy rains that triggered a local emergency declaration in the capital city. Humanitarian action and support was mostly handled by the government and UNICEF only supported with some emergency supplies. In early 2025, UNICEF also concluded it response to the protracted crisis related to migration, violence and climate vulnerability (with funding from ECHO, SIDA, CERF and UNICEF Thematic Humanitarian Funds), particularly in vulnerable communities with limited presence of the State, in education (repairs and educational kits), nutrition (monitoring, promotion of continued breastfeeding), child protection (child friendly spaces) and water, sanitation and hygiene (rehabilitation of water systems, hygiene promotion). Approximately 265,000 people (51% children) were attended. In anticipation of future climate related events, UNICEF also pre-positioned additional emergency supplies with humanitarian partners in the most vulnerable parts of the country. 
With funding from ECHO and the United States Government (BHA), UNICEF continued its work in the prevention of armed violence and recruitment of children in criminal organizations, particularly in the most violent communities in the largest cities (Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula). Through these efforts, undertaken with a local partner with credibility at local level and therefore enabling safe access to such communities, children were supported in continuing their education, recreational activities and also through some cash assistance. In 4 departments in the North of Honduras (Atlantida, Colon, Gracias a Dios and Islas de Bahia), UNICEF worked with UNODC and a consortium of local NGOs, with funding from the Peace Building Fund – PBF) in prevention of violence in mostly Afro-Honduran and Garifuna communities where high levels of violence persist. As part of this programme, solid emphasis is placed on not only the prevention of violence but also to strengthening capacities of local authorities (departments, municipalities, police, public prosecutors, judges, social workers, child protection officers, among others) in addressing cases of violence against children and restitution of the rights of the victims. This contributed to an increase of 62% in reporting on violence 
As part of a contribution to the overall development sector in Honduras, UNICEF provided leadership in the roll-out, training and implementation of Prevention of Sexual Exploitation & Abuse (PSEA) standards within the UN and with its main partners. As per end 2025, this role is further taken forward by a dedicated staff member in the Resident Coordinator Office, co-funded by all UN agencies. In addition, as chair of the AAP Working Group, UNICEF guided an inter-agency process that culminated in an AAP Common Framework, establishing shared standards, commitments, and procedures for community engagement, feedback, participation, SEA complaints and transparency across the entire Humanitarian Network. Building on this foundation, UNICEF spearheaded the design and launch of ¡Te Escuchamos! the first collective feedback and complaints mechanism in the country, developed jointly with UN agencies, NGOs and the RCO.
