With a new National Government taking office end January 2026, UNICEF is well positioned to continue advocating for placing children and adolescents as a priority for investment and action, particularly in areas of prevention of violence against girls and boys, increased access to quality and relevant education and quality health services. However, due to the absence of a civil servant career path, there may be many changes of personnel in government institutions, leading to a need to prioritize extensive engagement with the new authorities and rapid technical capacity building of new government staff, particularly of those in technical positions. 
While approximately 60% of municipal mayors are reelected or with the current political party maintaining the leadership, a lot of attention will be required to maintain the many gains for children achieved at the municipal level. The mobilization of (UNV) staff in strategic locations within Honduras demonstrated in 2025 that this substantially contributed to close accompaniment with local authorities, allowing to expedite progress for children. It is anticipated that the deployment of these staff will continue to make a significant difference in action for children coordinated among those government institutions present at the municipal level.
In addition to specific progress to obtain results at scale and impact in specific programming sectors, UNICEF continued implementing five programmatic models (‘proof of concept’). All of these were documented and most include a specific costing. Some of these models, including early childhood development, are already taken forward by governments with scaling-up and expansion of coverage funded through domestic resources. UNICEF will continue to work with national authorities and International Financial Organizations to further scale-up these models, when evaluated positively. Moreover, a substantive part of UNICEF-administered funding is obtained through UN-joint programmes and joint-UNICEF multi-country proposals. Given the similarities in challenges for children, it is suggested to even further collaborate on joint fundraising between country offices in Northern Central America. Joint programming with other UN-entities also allowed to further clarify the roles and opportunities for each of those entities while emphasizing their unique value-add. This contributed to more impactful results and greater reach towards the populations served. 
Even though UNICEF increased its income levels for its country programme and for humanitarian action in 2025, funding from the international cooperation (excluding IFIs) to Honduras is rapidly changing with traditional donors scaling-back the contributions and new donors emerging. UNICEF is closely following these shifts, investing effort to maintain the trust of traditional donors and to build trust with emerging donor countries. 
UNICEF is also increasing its partnership with international financial organizations (World Bank, IADB, CAF) with some very good results in leveraging resources for children (i.e. in health, ECD, WASH, education and climate action). Based on evolving conversations, including the UN Country Team, UNICEF is placing more emphasis on Financing for Development, including on orientation of domestic resources and fiscal space towards priorities for children. A new partnership with a well-known economics research institute, starting in early 2026, will contribute to such efforts. UNICEF will also continue looking for opportunities to increase its engagement with the private sector (foundations, charities), including leveraging resources for children at national- and local levels (for example in education and in climate action, building on lessons from 2025).
The humanitarian review, based on a new funding landscape identified to place much more emphasis on a shock-responsive system and humanitarian – development ‘nexus’ approaches, with emphasis on disaster preparedness, (climate) resilience and solid leadership by the State at national- and at municipal levels. Such reinforced emphasis also requires new ways of working, reinforcing support to the State in meeting its accountabilities while less relying on response capacity by civil society actors within the humanitarian community.
During 2026, UNICEF will work closely with national authorities, civil society organizations, the UN Country Team and other stakeholders for the design of the next Country Programme 2027 – 2031 and the overarching UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Findings and lessons learned from sector evaluations,  such as those from the evaluation of WASH & climate change programming (2025) and from the evaluability assessment on care for childhood development, will be used by UNICEF for advocacy to sustain and strengthen the WASH and CDI initiatives, particularly in light of the 2026 government transition, and to inform joint implementation of key recommendations with relevant government partners, particularly the consolidation of a child-led climate action reporting system to inform the National Determined Contributions and National Adaptation Plan. Findings and recommendations from the ongoing Country Programme Evaluation, along with other lessons learned, evidence from research and new data, and the priorities and strategies outlined in the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026 - 2029, will be critical to inform the programme design and to continue delivering results for children with focus, scale and impact.

Jamaica has made some progress in advancing children’s rights across health, education, protection and social policy. However, progress remains uneven, and outcomes for the most vulnerable children continue to be undermined by persistent inequalities, high levels of violence and increasing exposure to climate-related shocks. Income inequality has widened over time, with the Gini coefficient increasing from 0.38 in 2017 to 0.40 in 2021. Reflecting these trends, progress towards the 2030 Agenda has slowed, with only 26 per cent of SDG indicators currently on track, down from 28 per cent in 2024, while the proportion of indicators showing regression increased from 32 per cent to 38 per cent.[1]

Children in Jamaica are on the frontline of climate change. Recurrent hurricanes, flooding and drought disproportionately affect children by disrupting education, undermining nutrition and food security, limiting access to safe water, and heightening protection risks. The impact of Hurricane Melissa has further highlighted the urgent need for climate-resilient schools, scalable and shock-responsive social protection systems, strengthened disaster risk reduction (DRR) education, and timely early recovery financing.

As recovery efforts continue, there is a heightened risk of regression in child rights outcomes if recovery and reconstruction do not adequately prioritize equity, resilience and child-centered, shock-responsive system strengthening. Sustained investment will be essential to protect recent gains and ensure that recovery efforts translate into long-term improvements for all children.

Hurricane Melissa
Hurricane Melissa made landfall in Jamaica on 28 October 2025 as a Category 5 storm crossing the western end of the island, with sustained winds of 185 mph (295 kph), a 9–13 ft storm surge and 15–30 in of rainfall.

In the aftermath, Jamaica faces a complex humanitarian situation as it transitions from emergency response to early recovery, marked by extensive infrastructure damage, population displacement and public health risks. The World Bank's GRADE (Global Rapid Post-Disaster Damage Estimation) assessment estimates approximately US$8.7 billion in infrastructural and agricultural damage, with approximately 42 per cent reflected in damage to residential homes and their contents. 

Government assessments identify urgent needs for food, safe water, childcare support and building materials, with 90,000 displaced households and approximately 740,000 people directly affected. These shocks exacerbate existing vulnerabilities, with 15.7 per cent of children living in poverty, higher rates in rural areas, and persistent service gaps for children with disabilities.

As of December 8, 2025, public health concerns remain significant, with 24 confirmed cases of leptospirosis resulting in 12 deaths, and 45 suspected cases under investigation. Health services are constrained, with 40 per cent of clinics in the Western and Southern regions non-operational, though mobile clinics, field hospitals and community outreach are supporting service continuity. Water and electricity restoration is ongoing, reaching over 80 and 60 per cent of households respectively. 

Education services have largely resumed, with 850 of 1,010 schools reopened; however, 40 schools remain as shelters, and displacement continues to affect learning.  Approximately 190,000 students island-wide have been affected with 679 schools sustaining damage - 35 % severe-. Phased recovery plans are being implemented, including remote learning, student relocation and reopening of schools as of January 14, 2026. Nevertheless, attendance continues to fluctuate with an absenteeism rate of 28% in the worst affected parishes.[2]

Health and Nutrition:
Findings from the Jamaica MICS 2022 show that two in five people experienced moderate to severe food insecurity in the preceding month. Infant and young child feeding practices remain a concern: only one in four children aged 6–23 months in the poorest households received a minimum acceptable diet. These trends point to persistent vulnerabilities that compromise children’s development, resilience and learning outcomes.

A post-hurricane Rapid Nutrition Assessment by the Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW) in collaboration with UNICEF showed that nutrition and food security conditions remain fragile in affected areas. No visible cases of acute malnutrition were reported at that time; however, mixed feeding practices are common, and breastfeeding has declined due to stress, displacement and disrupted support systems. Households remain heavily reliant on food assistance, with uneven distribution, crop losses and rising food prices limiting access to adequate diets.
MICS 2022 also revealed a fall-off in immunization rates particularly for older children. Loss of both administrative and household records as well as displacement raises the risk of children becoming lost to follow-up, widening immunization gaps at a time when communities are most at risk. 

Education and Learning:
While access to education remains strong, 99% primary completion and 95% lower secondary completion, the quality of learning continues to be a critical challenge. Only 62% of children aged 7–14 are reading at foundational levels, and half demonstrate foundational numeracy skills (MICS 2022). Learning gaps remain widest among children in rural areas, boys, children with disabilities, and those from low-income households. Recent disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa further affected instructional time, exacerbating pre-existing learning losses.

Violence Against Children:
Violence remains one of the most pervasive threats to children’s well-being. Recent surveys indicate that approximately three-quarters of children aged 1–14 experience violent discipline (MICS 2022), while adolescent reports of physical, emotional and sexual violence remain high (VACS 2023). Service coverage for prevention and early intervention is improving but remains insufficient to match the scale of need. Reporting systems, case management and referral pathways require strengthened capacity and coordinated intersectoral action.

WASH:
Jamaica’s relatively high access to improved water and sanitation (91.1%, 86.5%)[3] was severely impacted by the onset of Hurricane Melissa, particularly in rural areas. Several water and sanitation systems were severely damaged. Some health and education facilities lack resilient WASH systems, leaving children exposed to waterborne disease risks and reduced access to safe learning and care environments after emergencies. On average water services have been restored to approximately 60% of the most affected areas.

Child Poverty and Inequality:
Jamaica’s national poverty rate declined to a historic low of 7.8 per cent in 2024, down from 8.2 per cent in 2023. Extreme poverty also reached a new low of 2.7%.[4]
While these gains indicate important national-level improvements, poverty continues to disproportionately affect children and rural populations (11%), underscoring the need for sustained, equity-focused investments to ensure that economic progress translates into improved outcomes for all children.

Social protection coverage continues to lag behind needs, with only just over half of the poorest households receiving any benefit. The already rising living costs, food price volatility, resulting from the impact of Hurricane Melissa have deepened household vulnerability, particularly among single-parent families, rural communities, and families caring for children with disabilities. A UNICEF supported automated tool now drives emergency grant calculations for the Ministry of Labour and Social Security for households impacted by Hurricane Melissa. The Council for Persons with Disabilities, is also utilizing their mobile app’s new grants module – supported by UNICEF to deliver fast, inclusive recovery support where it’s needed most.
