In 2025, UNICEF Jamaica demonstrated agility and leadership in a year that tested resilience and redefined opportunity. From spearheading an effective humanitarian response to Hurricane Melissa to shaping a new business model for the Caribbean, the office strengthened its relevance and capacity to deliver results for children in both crisis and developmental contexts. UNICEF advanced innovation in social protection, reinforced national systems in health, education and WASH, and deepened evidence generation to inform policy and planning. Together, these achievements underscore UNICEF Jamaica’s commitment to ensuring that every child survives, thrives, learns and is protected — even amid evolving challenges-.

Melissa Response
When Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica in October 2025, its Category 5 winds, storm surge and flooding severely tested the country’s ability to protect its children. In the hours and days after landfall, UNICEF moved from preparedness to action, using updated emergency plans, new standby arrangements, repositioned items and lessons from Hurricane Beryl to help the Government stabilize essential services in the worst-affected parishes. Guided by the Core Commitments for Children, the response focused on safe water and sanitation, life-saving health and nutrition, protection from violence and exploitation, continuity of learning, and emergency cash and in-kind support for the most vulnerable families.

Water, sanitation and hygiene were among the most urgent priorities as Melissa’s floods damaged water systems, sanitation infrastructure and health facilities. UNICEF’s WASH teams, working with the Ministry of Health and Wellness and local authorities, has reached approximately 77,000 people with 980,000 litres of treated water, establishing 20 water distribution sites and trucking water to communities, hospitals and shelters. Families received jerrycans, buckets and water purification tablets, while 62 water storage tanks, 8,500 hygiene kits, vector control chemicals and equipment, and 300 school cleaning kits helped reduce the risk of water-borne diseases and protect children’s health in damaged environments. Rapid WASH assessments were initiated in health facilities and schools, laying the foundation for early recovery investments.

At the same time, UNICEF worked with the health and nutrition system to prevent a secondary crisis among children under five and pregnant women. Approximately 100,000 people were reached with health and nutrition supplies and services, including micronutrients and iron/folic acid supplements provided to the Ministry of Health and Wellness to prevent critical deficiencies. Training on infant and young child feeding in emergencies helped nutrition staff support safe breastfeeding and appropriate feeding practices in disrupted communities. As leptospirosis cases emerged in the aftermath of the hurricane, UNICEF supported risk communication and community engagement campaigns and backed 13 mobile clinics that brought primary health care, immunization and leptospirosis prevention messages to populations whose regular services had been cut off.

For children, Melissa was not just a physical shock but an emotional one. UNICEF and partners established fixed child-friendly spaces, mobile outreach in schools and community walk-ins that offered “community-based psychosocial support” to 1,575 children and 189 caregivers, providing safe, nurturing environments where they could regain a sense of routine, learn coping skills and reconnect with peers. UNICEF also supported Govt for alternative care in shelters and strengthening referrals for cases of CP risks and GBV.  In parallel, UNICEF worked to keep education moving: emergency supplies, including 40 School-in-a-Box, 39 ECD kits and 21 recreational kits, 92 tents and over 1,000 tarpaulins have provided safe, temporary classrooms and learning spaces for some 6000 students return to learning which was further complimented by play-based psychological first aid for students through 1000 trained counsellors.  One-time grants for minor repairs in 50 schools with moderate damage signaled a shift from immediate response toward early recovery in the education sector. 

The hurricane also exposed how quickly household incomes can collapse when livelihoods are interrupted, especially for families of children with disabilities. In partnership with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security, UNICEF supported humanitarian cash transfers targeting 40,000 children, helping families cover immediate needs without resorting to negative coping strategies. With the Jamaica Council for Persons with Disabilities, UNICEF co-designed a digital voucher system through the “My JCPD” mobile app, delivering rapid, secure assistance to 1,500 children with disabilities, complemented by in-kind food baskets for their families. These innovations—building on pre-crisis investments such as the automated “Benefit Level Calculator” and the digitization of disability records—showed how preparedness work on systems can be leveraged in real time to deliver more inclusive, shock-responsive social protection.

UNICEF co-led the UN Emergency Technical Team (UNETT) in Jamaica, a platform that, in this emergency, included not only technical staff but also heads of agencies and the Resident Coordinator, enabling faster, more political alignment around government-led priorities as well as coordinated with CDEMA at sub-regional level including working with Thematic groups. At sector level, UNICEF led coordination for WASH and Nutrition along with line Ministries, mapping needs and partner activities to reduce duplication and identify gaps, co-led the Education and child protection and actively contributed to Health and Cash Working groups’ coordination. This role allowed UNICEF to connect field realities with decision-making tables, ensuring that the specific and differentiated needs of children—and the risks they faced, including gender-based violence and sexual exploitation and abuse—were visible in joint plans and funding appeals.

None of this would have been possible without strong alliances. Bilateral and multilateral partners, as well as the private sector, mobilized more than US$8 million for UNICEF’s immediate response and early recovery work, trusting the organization’s capacity to deliver quickly and at scale alongside government. 

New Business Model for the Caribbean 
One of UNICEF Jamaica’s key contributions in 2025 has been leading the development of a new business model for the Caribbean. This initiative responds to the evolving development cooperation landscape and the decline in official development assistance, requiring UNICEF to adapt its operating model to sustain its presence and continue delivering results for children at scale across the globe.

The model seeks to achieve greater focus, scale, impact, and efficiency by strengthening strategic partnerships, fostering knowledge generation, and enhancing advocacy efforts. It aligns with UNICEF’s Future Focus initiative, which promotes innovative and sustainable approaches to deliver results in increasingly complex contexts.

To drive this transformation, three interconnected workstreams have been established. The Multi-Country Office Programme Definition workstream has enabled the 12 participating Member States to jointly identify priorities for the new cycle of regional cooperation. The Country Programme Management Plan (CPMP) Definition workstream which will determine the governance arrangements, structure, coordination mechanisms, and risk management systems required to operationalize the model. Finally, the Change Management workstream—encompassing both internal and external dimensions—is supporting the organizational and behavioral shifts necessary to ensure effective implementation.

Evidence generation  
UNICEF Jamaica strengthened both national capacity to use data and the stock of evidence available to guide decisions for children in 2025. At the institutional level, national bodies such as the Statistical Institute and the Planning Institute were supported to deepen their skills in linking household surveys with administrative data through participation in MICS Link training, improving how Jamaica produces, combines and analyses information for policy and planning.

Evidence from the evaluation on Early Childhood Development will underscore the government’s roll-out of the Irie Classroom toolkit. In addition, the capacity of 6 government evaluation practitioners was strengthened by obtaining certification in Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems’ Strengthening (IMPRESS). At the community level, the country office adapted a feedback tool so that beneficiaries can provide timely input on services, ensuring that programme adjustments are informed directly by the experiences of children and families.

UNICEF’s efforts were complemented by a series of concrete studies, systems and knowledge products that advanced child-centred policies and programmes. These included: investments in EMIS and EIR systems, which made it possible to collect and use information more systematically at school and health-facility levels, enabling more timely and evidence-based decisions; MICS-Plus analyses that underpinned key reforms in education, social policy and health by turning raw data into actionable insights; Jamaica’s contribution to a multi-country programme evaluation, generating regional learning that will feed directly into the next multi-country programme for the Caribbean; and the finalization of the Kids Online Study on violence against children in digital spaces, which provided new evidence on online risks and a clearer basis for protecting children in the digital environment.
 
Goal Area 01: Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies 
In 2025, Jamaica took important steps to strengthen its health and nutrition systems, with UNICEF playing a catalytic role through policy advocacy, digital transformation and emergency response. Cabinet approval of the National School Nutrition Policy, now tabled in the Senate, brought the country closer to implementing healthy nutrition standards across all schools, advancing a whole-of-system approach to children’s diets and well-being. UNICEF’s technical support was instrumental in conducting a comprehensive nutrition assessment among hurricane-affected populations, generating evidence that informed national emergency nutrition strategies and helped tailor the response to the specific needs of children and families in the wake of Hurricane Melissa and the leptospirosis outbreak. During Youth Month, Jamaica also became the first country in Latin America and the Caribbean to digitally launch the global “Fix My Food” initiative, positioning adolescents at the centre of youth-led advocacy for front-of-package warning labels and healthier food environments.

Building a more resilient health system remained a central priority. UNICEF continued to support the construction of a second medical oxygen plant to help secure a sustainable oxygen supply during future emergencies, while also backing a post-Melissa assessment of the national cold chain system to safeguard vaccine quality and reach. In digital health, major advances were made toward a new Electronic Immunization Registry, with UNICEF facilitating the establishment of a National Data Sharing Agreement and Policy Framework that brings together five key ministries and agencies. This work lays the foundation for a more integrated, data-driven immunization system that can better protect children before, during and after crises.

Adolescent health and well-being also remained at the forefront of UNICEF’s cooperation with Jamaica. Hurricane Melissa affected children, adolescents and caregivers received community-based Psychological First Aid, which integrated nutrition, WASH and health promotion messages and reinforced a people-centred approach to emergency response. At the same time, the successful transition of the U-Matter Chatline to the Government of Jamaica secured the sustainability of a nationwide text-based mental health support service, ensuring that young people continue to have safe, confidential channels to seek help, share concerns and strengthen their resilience in times of stress.

Goal Area 02: Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future.
In 2025, Jamaica advanced a more coherent early childhood development system, with UNICEF support translating data and evidence into better services for young children. A national early screening, referral and identification pathway for children with developmental delays was completed and handed over to government, strengthening system-wide capacities for early detection and targeted support. Policy briefs on ECD financing and on foundational literacy and numeracy, developed using MICS-Plus data, informed national ECD policy and contributed to more integrated planning across education, health and social protection.

Teacher capacity remained a central pillar of UNICEF’s cooperation. A global agora course on play-based teaching was completed by 17 per cent of teachers, helping them to apply play-based methodologies in the classroom while sensitizing students, colleagues and parents on immunization, nutrition and the importance of play. National content was converted into a free online child development course, focused on nutrition, immunization and play, widening access to quality professional development and supporting sustained improvements in early teaching and learning practices.

Major progress was made in using digital tools to strengthen both learning and education management. The rollout of the Education Management Information System (EMIS) advanced, with core modules on enrolment, attendance, staff profiles and infrastructure improving data visibility and enabling more evidence-based decision-making at school and system levels. The Learning Passport was scaled nationally with content for children aged 3–12, engaging 2,630 users across 971 courses, while Accessible Digital Textbooks (ADT) use expanded to 346,362 users; 13,000 teachers were trained in person and 700 teachers online on AI literacy to make better use of these platforms in support of inclusive learning. The national rollout of the FunDoo chatbot continued and partnerships were expanded, laying the groundwork for its handover to the Ministry of Education in 2026 as a sustainable digital tool for adolescents.

UNICEF’s support to STEM and mentorship created new opportunities to strengthen learning outcomes, particularly in mathematics. The launch of the Em² STEM-based Mathematics and Mentorship Project catalyzed the first national community of practice for math teachers and trained 140 across 75 percent of high schools. It also connected female high school and university science students with female industry leaders through multi-tiered mentoring relationships focused on problem-solving, confidence and STEM pathways. UNICEF also coordinated with CARICOM on comprehensive school safety initiatives. 

Goal Area 03. Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices.
In 2025, Jamaica — building on the pledges made during the Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Colombia — advanced a more strategic and preventive approach to violence, abuse, and exploitation, with UNICEF’s support helping to bridge national policy and community level change. A costed Child Protection Plan (NPACV) was developed based on evidence generation, stakeholder consultations and a communication strategy to promote its implementation nationally, providing a clear framework for preventing and responding to all forms of violence against children. Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse was strengthened through new and contextualized SOPs, improved workflows, training for 70 partners and 10 focal points on victim assistance, child-friendly awareness materials and reinforced inter-agency coordination, aligning national practice more closely with global safeguarding standards. UNICEF also supported a dedicated social and behavior change strategy to address corporal punishment, bullying and cyberbullying, and scaled community-level interventions in St. Thomas, reaching 495 adolescents, 28 peer educators and 71 parents with positive parenting sessions, while 32 frontline actors were trained in safeguarding to promote safer homes, schools and communities.

UNICEF’s cooperation also helped make the justice and care systems more protective for children in contact or in conflict with the law. Work began to migrate the Child Diversion case management system to DHIS2, with workflows refined to improve digital case management, information sharing and follow-up for children referred to diversion programmes. A new Standard Operating Procedure for Positive Behavior Management was launched in juvenile facilities, setting clearer expectations for staff conduct and non-violent discipline; 184 staff were trained on the SOP and 250 children took part in behavior management sessions, contributing to safer, more supportive institutional environments and reducing the risk of abuse within the justice and care system. UNICEF also supported Govt to make pledges in the “Violence against Children Conference” and progress against these pledges are undergoing. 

 Goal Area 4. Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment. 
In 2025, Jamaica took important steps to strengthen the policy and systems foundations for resilient WASH in health, with UNICEF support linking analysis, assessment and concrete upgrades. A national WASH Policy Gap Analysis was finalized with the Ministry of Health and Wellness and paired with a comprehensive WASH assessment of 345 health facilities and 75 emergency shelters, digitized through the provision of tablets to improve data collection and monitoring. Building on this evidence, UNICEF supported the rehabilitation of WASH infrastructure in one hospital and six primary health care facilities to improve neonatal care environments, and installed climate-resilient rainwater harvesting systems, turning policy and data into visible improvements for children and their families.

UNICEF’s WASH response to Hurricane Melissa demonstrated UNICEF’s convening power to quickly bring all WASH partners together at all levels to scale WASH response across affected areas. UNICEF rapidly moves from immediate relief to system-strengthening at scale, while complementing government leadership. By securing safe water and hygiene support for approximately 77,000 people through 980,000 liters of treated water, 20 water distribution sites and essential supplies such as jerrycans, buckets, storage tanks, hygiene kits, school cleaning kits and shelter kits, UNICEF helped avert secondary health crises and protect children’s well-being in the worst-affected parishes. The installation of 10 communal water points in school compounds, designed primarily to serve surrounding communities during and after emergencies, showcased UNICEF’s contribution to building more resilient, climate-ready WASH services that will continue to serve children and families long after the immediate crisis has passed.

Goal Area 5: Every child, including adolescents, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free of poverty.
In 2025, UNICEF supported a step change in how children with disabilities and their families access services, through the launch of the “My JCPD” mobile application and an upgraded management information system. These tools fully digitized Jamaica Council for Persons with Disabilities records and reduced approval times for grants and services from around 90 days to approximately 30 minutes, including through remote applications, making support more timely, accessible and transparent for families who need it most.

UNICEF also helped the Government of Jamaica make its social protection system more shock-responsive and inclusive. An automated “Benefit Level Calculator” was developed for the Ministry of Labor and Social Security and used during the Hurricane Melissa response to determine the value of cash transfers, ensuring that support levels were more needs-based and consistent. On this foundation, UNICEF supported emergency cash transfers that reached 40,000 children and worked with JCPD to provide digital vouchers and in-kind food baskets to 1,500 children with disabilities, showing how data-driven tools can translate directly into more equitable, child-focused subsidies during crises.

On the other hand, a national budget analysis on child-related expenditure was commissioned to inform dialogue on how public resources are allocated to children, and how budgeting can better reflect, equitable and child-focused investments in Jamaica.

Communication and advocacy 
In 2025, UNICEF Jamaica strengthened its leadership in advocacy and communication, maintaining a strong and credible voice on child rights. Through sustained media engagement and consistent dissemination of news releases, UNICEF’s work remained visible and influential in national dialogue.

A key highlight was the production and release of a child rights video in the Jamaican language, featuring primary-school-aged children. The video enhanced accessibility, understanding, and cultural resonance of child rights messages among children and the wider public.

Digital performance indicators reflected solid growth, with a 6.3 per cent increase in followers to 122,912, more than 7.5 million post impressions, a reach of 3.7 million, and engagement rates rising to 4.92 per cent. U-Report Jamaica also expanded its user base and engagement, strengthening youth participation, voice, and feedback.

Two major advocacy strategies were developed: one focused on increasing and improving public investment in children, and another aimed at achieving a full prohibition of corporal punishment in all settings. In addition, a social and behavior-change strategy was designed to end violent discipline, bullying, and cyberbullying, promoting safe, respectful environments for every child.

Program and Operational Effectiveness
Coordinated monitoring and reporting, effective supply and logistics support, robust risk management and policy compliance, prudent financial and budget management, and a strong focus on people and culture collectively enabled stronger results across humanitarian, development, and advocacy contexts.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF Jamaica navigated a complex operational landscape marked by systemic constraints, resource limitations, and the disruptive impact of Hurricane Melissa. Despite these challenges, UNICEF remained a trusted strategic and technical partner, driving reforms, strengthening child-centered shock-responsive systems for emergency preparedness and responses in partnership with line ministries across WASH, Health and Nutrition, Child Protection, Education, and Social Policy sectors. 

Key Challenges
Across sectors, programme implementation in 2025 was constrained by a combination of systemic, operational and shock-related challenges. Constraints in human and technical capacity at times limited the ability to fully leverage available resources, occasionally slowing implementation and affecting the overall pace of programme delivery and oversight.

Hurricane Melissa significantly disrupted planned programming across all sectors, requiring rapid reallocation of staff time and resources toward emergency response. While essential and effective, this shift delayed routine policy work, capacity-building activities and community engagement originally planned for 2025. 

Centralized governance structures and bureaucratic delays within key ministries further slowed decision-making and programme implementation, policy reform, procurement and scale-up of innovations, particularly in health, nutrition, and wash.
Digital and systems transformation initiatives faced low uptake —including social protection digitization, electronic immunization, digital case management and EMIS platforms—faced change-management challenges, connectivity gaps (especially in rural areas), and partial system interoperability, limiting full realization of intended efficiencies.
 
Lessons Learned
Several cross-cutting lessons emerged in 2025. Sustained investment in system strengthening, preparedness and digital infrastructure is essential for resilience, enabling continuity of services during crises while supporting long-term development outcomes. Hurricane Melissa demonstrated the value of pre-existing preparedness measures but also highlighted gaps in nutrition-in-emergencies, shock-responsive social protection, education and emergency child protection readiness.

Effective coordination and leadership are critical in multi-actor systems. UNICEF’s robust relations with line Ministries including ODPEM helped Co-lead in UNETT and sector lead for WASH and Nutrition making faster and coordinated response while aligning around government-led priorities, mapping needs and partner activities to reduce duplication and identify gap. UNICEF’s position as a trusted technical partner and neutral convener proved central, particularly in child protection, where fragmented mandates persist. The Ministry of Education’s leadership of the Child Protection Working Group during the emergency represented a notable advance, demonstrating the benefits of clear government stewardship. 

Meaningful participation, especially of communities, faith-based organizations and young people—strengthens relevance, ownership and sustainability. Community-based child protection responses and youth engagement in nutrition for “fix my food”, in education innovations such as FunDoo, reinforced the importance of participatory approaches.
As noted in the Evaluation of UNICEF’s work in early childhood development (ECD) and early childhood education, readiness for scale-up remains constrained by the absence of a dedicated scaling budget and the underutilization of strategic communication channels to generate sustained buy-in and momentum. Addressing these gaps will be critical in supporting systematic scale-up and institutionalization during the last CPD year.
Finally, digital innovation must be accompanied by robust change management, capacity building and user-centered design. Adoption challenges across health, education, child protection and social protection underscored that technology alone is insufficient without institutional readiness, staff confidence and public awareness.

Future Outlook
Looking ahead, UNICEF will prioritize consolidating gains from 2025 while addressing identified gaps. Core priorities include strengthening internal and national systems for faster, more flexible implementation; expanding human resource capacity; and embedding climate resilience and shock responsiveness across all sectors.

In health and nutrition, UNICEF will continue supporting policy reform, nutrition-in-emergencies capacity, digital health systems and climate-resilient service delivery. In child protection, emphasis will be placed on sustaining inter-ministerial coordination, supporting Ministry of Education in addressing capacity gaps of oversight functions between policy and implementation, scaling community-based models, and strengthening emergency preparedness. In education, continued support to ministry capacity, decentralization, digital transformation, climate resilient smart schools, ECD and inclusion as well as a focus on youth leadership will underpin system-wide reforms.

In social policy, UNICEF will focus on increasing uptake of digital platforms such as My JCPD through targeted outreach and digital literacy, expanding interoperability across systems, and strengthening pre-positioned digital payment mechanisms for future shocks. Findings from ongoing National budget analysis on child-related expenditure will be used for evidence-based advocacy to increase public resources for children to reflect equitable and child-focused investments in Jamaica.

UNICEF Jamaica’s leadership will continue for the development of a new business model for the Caribbean with greater focus, scale, impact, and efficiency by strengthening strategic partnerships, fostering knowledge generation, and enhancing advocacy efforts. 
Overall, 2025 reaffirmed that systemic change is incremental and requires sustained investment in partnerships, technology, evidence and human capacity. Building on lessons from Hurricane Melissa, UNICEF is well positioned to support Jamaica’s transition toward more resilient, inclusive and child-centered systems in 2026 programme cycle.

Children in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) continue to face significant and uneven barriers to the full realization of their rights. While the region has made important social gains over the past decades, persistent inequalities, rising violence, human mobility, climate-related shocks and complex migration dynamics continue to affect children’s ability to survive and thrive, learn, be protected and grow up in safe and inclusive environments. These challenges shape progress across the impact and outcome areas of the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025 and highlight the need for sustained investment in child-focused policies and services.
 
The broader socio-economic context continues to constrain progress for children. According to projections by the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), the region remains on a low-growth trajectory, with GDP growth expected to reach approximately 2.4 per cent in 2025 and 2.3 per cent in 2026, with slower momentum in parts of the Caribbean and Central America. Combined with persistent structural inequality, this limits fiscal space for investment in essential services for children, including primary health care, education, social protection and climate-resilient infrastructure. As a result, progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals risks slowing even in contexts where poverty indicators have improved.
 
The political and policy environment between 2022 and 2025 has also influenced the operating context for child-focused policies. Electoral turnover heightened political polarization and, in some contexts, expanded reliance on states of emergency and security-focused governance have affected policy continuity and social-sector prioritization. At the same time, evolving migration governance—including policy shifts affecting the United States–Mexico border—has altered migration routes and generated new patterns of transit and return across the region. These dynamics place additional pressure on protection systems and public services in transit and destination countries, underscoring the importance of strengthened regional cooperation, upstream policy engagement and evidence-based advocacy to safeguard investments in children in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
 
Following pandemic-related setbacks, routine immunization coverage is recovering but remains 
fragile. An estimated 1.4 million children in the region remained “zero-dose” in 2024, and several countries report DTP3 coverage below 80 per cent, indicating persistent equity gaps and outbreak risks. At the same time, the region faces a double burden of malnutrition. Approximately one in eight children (12.4 per cent) experiences stunting, while child overweight has risen to 8.8 per cent—the second highest prevalence globally. These challenges disproportionately affect Indigenous, Afro-descendant and rural children.
 
Access to basic services also remains uneven. Around 21.1 per cent of the population lacks safely managed drinking water and 48.8 per cent lacks safely managed sanitation, with the largest gaps affecting rural and marginalized communities. These deficits undermine health, nutrition and learning outcomes and are increasingly stressed by climate-related disasters. Expanding climate-resilient water, sanitation and hygiene services across households, schools and health facilities remains critical to protect development gains.
Education outcomes reflect the deep and lasting impacts of the pandemic. Learning poverty—the share of children unable to read and understand a simple text by age ten—is estimated at around 80 per cent in the region, up from roughly 50 per cent before the pandemic. School closures, unequal access to digital learning and limited remediation have widened disparities, particularly for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Boys often underperform in reading, while many adolescents leave school without essential digital and transferable skills, threatening progress toward quality education.
 
Economic vulnerability continues to affect children’s opportunities. Although monetary poverty declined in parts of the region between 2023 and 2024, inequality remains high and child-sensitive social protection systems remain uneven in coverage and adequacy. Many families lack shock-responsive support to cope with income losses, price increases or climate-related shocks, underscoring the importance of strengthening public finance for children and protecting social sector spending.
 
Violence remains a major threat to children and adolescents, generating humanitarian needs in the region. LAC records some of the highest levels of lethal violence affecting young people globally, with homicide a leading cause of death among adolescents in several countries. Organized crime and firearm availability contribute to these patterns, while violent discipline remains common in homes. Addressing these risks requires stronger multisectoral prevention systems, survivor-centred services including mental health and psychosocial support, and improved access to child-friendly justice.
 
Climate change is also intensifying risks for children. Approximately nine in ten children in the region live in areas exposed to two or more climate hazards, including floods, droughts and severe storms. These shocks disrupt health services, water systems, education continuity and protection services, particularly for rural, Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities. Joint analysis by UNICEF and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean suggests that climate change could push between 5.9 and 17.9 million additional children in the region into poverty by 2030 without increased investment in resilient systems and social protection.
 
Human mobility and humanitarian needs are also reshaping the regional landscape. In 2026, an estimated 14.1 million children across LAC are expected to require humanitarian assistance and support for return and reintegration -development approach-, due to unsafe migration, displacement, armed violence and climate-related disasters. Migration routes continue to shift across Central America, the Caribbean and the Darién corridor. In Panama, one in five migrants crossing toward Colombia are children, many exposed to trafficking, exploitation and abuse. Along the Guatemala–Mexico corridor, approximately one in ten migrant children travels unaccompanied or separated. Internal displacement remains severe in Haiti, while conflict in Colombia continues to expose children to recruitment by armed groups. Most people affected by migration crises have settled in other countries in the region (approx. 7 million Venezuelan migrants), so efforts focused on supporting their integration and regularization in the medium term are key.
 
Gender inequality further compounds these challenges. The region continues to have one of the highest rates of adolescent pregnancy. These early pregnancies interrupt education and restrict long-term opportunities for girls. Health risks remain significant with maternal conditions among the leading causes of death for girls aged 15–19. Nutrition challenges persist, 21.9 per cent of pregnant adolescents experience anaemia, and 37 per cent of adolescent girls are affected by overweight.  Education disparities remain significant, particularly for Indigenous girls, while child marriage and violence against girls continue at concerning levels.
 
Together, these trends highlight the interconnected challenges affecting children across Latin America and the Caribbean and reinforce the need for sustained, coordinated action to strengthen systems, protect essential services and accelerate equitable progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals so that no child in the region is left behind.

In 2025, UNICEF’s Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Office (LACRO) advanced its mandate to ensure that every child survives, learns, is protected and lives in a safe and equitable environment, while strengthening the region’s preparedness and response to shocks. Across the year, LACRO leveraged its regional position to amplify technical expertise, build country office capacity, support evidence-based policy dialogue, and catalyze strategic partnerships, ensuring progress across health, education, child protection, nutrition, social policy, humanitarian action, gender, inclusion, and climate agendas.

The Survive and Thrive portfolio achieved notable advances in health, nutrition, and adolescent wellbeing. Efforts to reach zero-dose children were intensified through technical support for immunization delivery, cold-chain improvements, and equity-focused use of data. Large-scale planning for solarization of health facilities progressed in Bolivia, El Salvador, Colombia, and Haiti, enhancing resilience and service continuity. Regional outbreak preparedness and response were reinforced through the Bolivia measles response, Yellow Fever preparedness in the Andean region, and emergency support for Hurricane Melissa. Collaborations with partners such as PAHO, the World Bank, ECHO, and sub-regional organizations underpinned these achievements. A regional HPV vaccination roadmap was developed, while the first UNICEF regional primary health care strategy was finalized and paired with the Public Financing for Children’s Health training, reaching 17 country offices. Community health programming advanced through national policy support, strengthened community health information systems, and the launch of the first regional community health dashboard. Maternal and neonatal health received targeted attention through EMTCT validation processes in five countries, including Brazil, complemented by extensive learning initiatives. Adolescent health, mental health, and psychosocial support were strengthened through policy engagement, digital platforms, regional roadmaps, and tools for adolescent pregnancy prevention. Nutrition programming supported governments in enhancing capacities, evidence generation, and advocacy across life course and humanitarian settings.
Education outcomes were bolstered through targeted technical assistance to 24 country offices, ensuring 100% of requests were met with timely, high-quality support. LACRO contributed to emergency education responses following Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica and Cuba, preparing two recovery plans, fundraising proposals, and surge capacity strategies. Five country offices—Colombia, Mexico, Argentina, Cuba, and Guatemala—received support aligning new country programme documents with the upcoming UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029. Collaboration with HQ and Generation Unlimited advanced the Global Digital Learning Strategy, the LAC GenU Accelerator, and programmatic guidance on the transition from education to work. Partnerships with UNESCO, ECLAC, World Bank, IADB, CAF, and CLADE facilitated the completion of flagship regional frameworks, Transforming Education in LAC and Financing Education for Transformation. Regional networks and capacity-building initiatives engaged over 180 participants across 22 countries, producing 24 investment cases and strengthening foundational learning workstreams, equitable allocation of thematic funds, and recruitment for the Education Center of Excellence.
Child protection programming remained a critical focus. Violence against children continued to impact homes, schools, and communities, with homicide and sexual violence disproportionately affecting adolescents and girls. Regional engagement included a ministerial conference convening 30 countries and more than 300 participants, reaffirming commitments to resourced prevention systems, caregiver support, school-based violence prevention, and survivor-centered services. LACRO provided over 90 technical assistance responses to country offices, addressing humanitarian protection, access to justice, alternative care reforms, and identity management. Evidence generation included a regional review on the registration of children born through surrogacy and a study on programmes proven to prevent violence, while guidance on armed violence programming and support spaces for children on the move reinforced evidence-based interventions. A regional study highlighted critical gaps in the social service workforce, demonstrating coverage as low as 2.54 per 100,000 and emphasizing the need for strengthened training and professionalization.

Water, sanitation, hygiene (WASH) and climate action were strengthened through regional coordination, technical assistance, and partnerships. Country offices received 100% of requested WASH technical support, including surge deployment to emergencies in Haiti and Jamaica. The Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency WASH thematic group and the WASH-LAC Group strengthened regional leadership, while partnerships with Veolia, SIWI, IVL, the World Bank, and IDB supported national-level programming. Knowledge products on climate-resilient WASH, migration, and emergency response enhanced technical capacity. The CEED team supported the integration of child-sensitive climate commitments into 13 countries’ NDCs, conducted nine new Climate Landscape Analyses, and produced flagship reports on the impact of climate change on child and youth poverty, WASH integration in NDCs, and environmental mainstreaming in education programs. At COP30 in Brazil, the team facilitated adolescent participation, trained young negotiators, and contributed to over 20 side events, strengthening youth engagement in climate governance.

The Social Policy function drove system-level change in child poverty reduction, care and support systems, and shock-responsive social protection. Technical assistance was provided to 15 country offices, ensuring timely support for policy dialogue, programme design, and fiscal advocacy. LACRO led the design, costing, and validation of care and support baskets across six countries, expanding in 2025 to include disability-sensitive approaches through CAF partnerships. Disability-inclusive social protection advanced through guidance, technical support, and capacity-building, consolidating a regional community of practice through the third edition of the Disability-Inclusive Social Protection course with Universidad de los Andes. Anticipatory and emergency cash responses in the Caribbean and Haiti were strengthened in coordination with humanitarian partners. Analytical outputs—including studies on shock-responsive social protection, care systems, child poverty, migration, and local governance—underpinned evidence-informed decision-making and advocacy.

Humanitarian action was a key regional enabler, with the Emergency Unit providing technical and operational support to 24 country offices. Regional preparedness included EPP reviews, EPR trainings, and simulation exercises in at least 12 countries, alongside remote support where access was constrained. Anticipatory Action advanced through four frameworks triggered in the Central American Dry Corridor, Cuba, and Haiti, while the “Ahead of the Storm” initiative operationalized impact-based forecasting. LACRO contributed to the design of the Climate, Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance platform for Caribbean SIDS and supported the renewal of Haiti’s cyclone parametric insurance under the Today & Tomorrow Initiative. Hurricane Melissa highlighted regional coordination capacity, with surge support and resource mobilization generating over USD 12 million across multiple countries. Technical oversight extended to 16 country offices responding to migration, armed violence, and sudden-onset crises, with 82–88% of offices rating regional emergency support as timely and relevant.

Cross-cutting initiatives further strengthened results. Gender-transformative programming expanded by 38%, with adolescent girls’ investment cases securing targeted funding. The ADAP Regional Young People Action Board engaged 34 youth from 22 countries in co-designing cross-sector initiatives. Disability and Indigenous inclusion progressed through technical assistance, capacity-building, and strategic partnerships, including implementation of accessible digital textbooks, DIPAS roll-out, and regional advocacy events. Migration programming strengthened both internal coordination and external positioning, supporting country offices with technical guidance on family reunification, unaccompanied children, and integration of children with disabilities in mobility contexts. Early childhood development programming reached all country offices through Caring for Caregivers packages, CCD Evaluability Assessments, CFC workshops, digital parenting tools, and strategic partnerships, including Kimberly-Clark and the Storytelling Lab. Social and behavior change (SBC) initiatives reinforced government ownership, strengthened networks and academic partnerships, and delivered high-impact technical assistance across health, nutrition, child protection, and knowledge management, including the establishment of the first SBC-in-emergencies ecosystem.
Enablers across the region reinforced these results. UNICEF LACRO strengthened advocacy, communications, and digital engagement, leveraging key moments such as the XVI Regional Conference on Women, COP30, and the CAF Banco Futuro LAC launch to advance regional agendas. Humanitarian advocacy included the Haiti Child Alert, Hurricane Melissa response, and HAC launch. Through SEO, data insights, and paid marketing, UNICEF’s digital supporter base reached 22.8 million, while the LAC Parenting Hub surpassed 3.3 million users, exceeding partnership targets. Technical assistance supported 73 country offices across advocacy, planning, social media, recruitment, and risk mitigation. Four advocacy workshops built national capacities, and LAC piloted Child Rights Advocacy in Constrained Contexts training.

Partnerships and fundraising strengthened UNICEF’s impact, raising a projected $134 million and increasing income by 9% compared to 2024, supported by more than one million pledge donors. Locally raised funds accounted for approximately 65% of total country programme funding, while private sector partners contributed $2.4 million to support Hurricane Melissa responses.
Safeguarding, and accountability initiatives reinforced organizational capacity. AAP and PSEA frameworks were advanced through webinars, regional calls, and bite-sized sessions connecting safeguarding to broader programmatic agendas. Inter-agency missions in Ecuador and Jamaica facilitated dialogue, while knowledge-sharing initiatives, partnerships with humanitarian transport, and online PSEA training enhanced regional preparedness.

Planning, data and evaluation systems were strengthened to support evidence-based programming and decision-making. Nine country programme planning processes were supported, including the finalization of country programme documents in Argentina, Mexico and Cuba. The Regional Office Management Plan 2026–2029 was also finalized, and analytical work on regional business models was commissioned to generate recommendations for improving efficiency and effectiveness.
On migration, UNICEF LACRO, through a joint agreement with UNHCR and WFP, has maintained evidence and data collection processes to inform programming and strategic decision-making at regional and national level. At the same time, UNICEF continues to actively participate in intergovernmental coordination platforms on migration (R4V, RCM, Quito process, Cartagena +40 among others) promoting regional technical assistance and improving protection of children on the move with a transnational perspective, visualizing UNICEF value added.

Child-focused data availability, quality and use were further enhanced through the implementation of Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) in ten countries, strengthened integration of administrative data, and improved evidence generation on children on the move.  Evaluation systems were reinforced through flagship training programmes such as ExCEL and IMPrESS, reaching over 150 decision-makers across 18 countries, while regional evaluations on migration and early childhood development generated actionable insights for scaling effective approaches.

The People and Culture (PnC) function played a critical enabling role in supporting UNICEF country offices to navigate a period of significant organizational change and evolving operational demands. Through strategic workforce planning, targeted surge and recruitment support, and strengthened advisory services, PnC helped offices adjust staffing capacities, redeploy talent, and maintain operational continuity amid financial constraints, humanitarian pressures, and the implementation of the Future Focus Initiative. Regional guidance supported offices in managing transitions, advising leadership teams, and promoting staff wellbeing during a period of restructuring and uncertainty. By facilitating timely talent management solutions, strengthening workforce agility, and aligning human resources with evolving programmatic priorities, PnC enabled country offices to remain focused on delivering results for children while adapting to rapidly changing circumstances across the region.

Together, these achievements demonstrate the transformative role of UNICEF LACRO in advancing child rights across Latin America and the Caribbean. By combining programme sectoral expertise, regional coordination, strategic partnerships, communication and advocacy, evidence generation, and cross-cutting enablers, LACRO strengthened systems, supported country offices, and positioned the region to deliver sustainable, equitable, and high-impact outcomes for children in 2025.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF LACRO operated in a highly complex environment shaped by financial constraints, organizational restructuring, and persistent child rights challenges, all of which influenced both programmatic and operational delivery. The implementation of the Future Focus Initiative (FFI)-driven largely by financial pressures - brought significant institutional changes. These included reductions in institutional budgets, the consolidation of programme technical assistance into Centres of Excellence, the creation of a Multi-Country Office in the Caribbean through the merger of four existing Country Offices, and the reopening of UNICEF’s corporate policy on engagement in High-Income countries. Together, these developments represented defining shifts for the region.

While these reforms aim to enhance efficiency and strategic focus, they also generated considerable uncertainty during the transition period. At the same time, significant reductions in humanitarian funding required UNICEF Country Offices across Latin America and the Caribbean to reassess programme priorities, adjust geographical scope and revised planned results in the context of the UNICEF humanitarian response in the region. In several countries, interventions were concentrated in high-risk locations to preserve life-saving services for children and families. Looking ahead, sustained funding gaps risk further weakening humanitarian response capacity and may lead to service disruptions for children and families affected by human mobility, armed violence and other crises. Sustained and flexible financing is essential to strengthen preparedness systems and ensure timely responses to increasing emergencies in the region. 

Programmatically, the year underscored the importance of innovation and agility. LACRO leveraged emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence for data analytics and network mapping, and applied foresight and network analysis methodologies in Country Programme Evaluations to respond more effectively to evolving needs. Clustered and multi-country evaluation exercises proved to be cost-effective and timely mechanisms for generating learning and informing response, enabling the region to maximize the impact of limited resources. These experiences highlight the potential to more systematically embed technological and operational innovations—such as long-term partnerships with academic institutions and the deployment of fellows—into evidence generation and programmatic support across the region.
Despite these advances, the regional evidence ecosystem remains uneven. While important connections between analytical outputs and programmatic priorities exist, many remain relationship-driven rather than strategically coordinated. Mechanisms such as the LACRO Knowledge Management and Evidence Working Group have been underutilized, limiting shared visibility of evidence priorities and constraining systematic uptake in policy and programming. Strengthening governance mechanisms, improving tracking of evidence utilization, and ensuring that lessons inform decision-making will be critical to achieving the ambitions of the Strategic Plan 2026–2029. 

At the same time, progress toward child rights and the Sustainable Development Goals continue to face significant challenges. Despite notable achievements across health, education, protection, and social policy, many regional SDG targets remain off track. Persistent inequalities, high levels of armed violence, and gaps in social protection systems continue to hinder systemic progress. In several contexts, advocacy and reform efforts—including those related to children born through surrogacy or the protection of children on the move—have encountered political resistance, underscoring the importance of sustained, evidence-based engagement with governments and partners. 

Several key lessons emerged from these challenges. First, partnerships remain central to advancing child rights in a resource-constrained environment. Collaboration with multilateral organizations, international financial institutions, regional networks, and civil society actors proved critical in sustaining programmatic delivery, policy influence, and technical innovation. Second, operational flexibility—through multi-country shared functions, rapid deployment of surge capacity, and the adoption of digital tools—proved essential in responding to diverse and time-sensitive needs. Third, evidence generation and programmatic design are mutually reinforcing. The application of AI, foresight exercises, and innovative evaluation methodologies enhanced responsiveness and informed decision-making, demonstrating the need to institutionalize these approaches rather than applying them on an ad hoc basis.
Looking ahead, the regional collective vision for 2026–2029 focuses on narrowing child inequalities and unlocking greater investment for children through prioritization, scale, and impact. This vision also emphasizes strengthening shock-resilient systems and enhancing emergency preparedness and response.

Four strategic pillars underpin this regional vision:
·         Be a partnerships powerhouse for children, shifting from small-scale initiatives to strategic public and private partnerships that influence policy and public financing at scale, working closely with governments and international financial institutions such as CAF, IDB, and the World Bank. This also includes continuing to position the region as a global leader in PSFR.
·         Promote and protect the child rights agenda in the political and public domain, advocating with key decision makers and mobilizing public opinion, youth movements, and civil society to advance children’s rights—particularly for the most marginalized and those affected by humanitarian crises.
·         Strengthen UNICEF’s role as a thought leader, generating and communicating compelling evidence, shaping national debates on child rights, influencing social norms, and supporting public discourse in favor of children.
·         Advance innovative ways of working, rethinking organizational form and function and evolving UNICEF’s modalities of cooperation with countries.

In conclusion, 2025 demonstrated the resilience and adaptability of UNICEF LACRO in the face of financial, structural, and programmatic challenges. While the Future Focus Initiative and organizational restructuring created transitional disruptions, they also catalyzed opportunities for innovation and more cost-effective programmatic and operational approaches. Moving into 2026 and beyond, LACRO will need to sustain innovation, safeguard critical programmatic and operational oversight functions, and continue to demonstrate its value to Country Offices as a service-oriented regional office focused on enabling and scaling results.
By doing so, LACRO can continue to drive meaningful and equitable impact for children across Latin America and the Caribbean, even amid financial constraints and ongoing systemic transformation.

2025 marks the last year of UNICEF´s 2020-2025 Country Programme (CPD) with the Government of Mexico and the first year of President Claudia Sheinbaum´s government administration, during which the National Development Plan (NDP) for 2025-2030 was published. The NDP states that Mexico will be a Republic of and for Children and Adolescents. Several actions are planned or have been initiated with a renewed Government commitment towards this goal: a territorial approach to poverty reduction among the most vulnerable and excluded groups; improvements to education, health and nutrition; and peacemaking combined with efforts to reduce violence. Together, they represent an opportunity to strengthen the guarantee of children’s rights. While the country is undergoing a crucial phase in terms of economic growth and social development, significant challenges remain to be addressed regarding children’s well-being, including inequality, poverty, health, nutrition, education and protection against violence. 




Mexico ranks thirty-third out of 146 countries in the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index 2024, having made progress towards gender equality, especially regarding education and the recognition of unpaid domestic work.(1) Despite that progress, divides persist in terms of economic participation, care burden and violence against girls, mostly affecting poor, indigenous and Afro-Mexican women. Children on the move also face greater challenges, including risks of abuse, exploitation and discrimination, and limited access to specialized protection services and educational continuity. According to the 2025 Sustainable Development Report, Mexico ranks 72 out of 167 countries, with 36.3 per cent of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) related indicators having been achieved or being on track, 32.5 per cent seeing limited progress and 31.2 per cent worsening(2).




The Government’s recent efforts to reduce poverty have shown significant progress. Between 2020 and 2024, multidimensional poverty has been reduced from 43.9 to 29.6% in general, and from 52.6 to 38.7% for children and adolescents, reaching the lowest levels since 2008. In particular, between 2022 and 2024, the population living in multidimensional poverty fell from 46.8 million to 38.5 million: a decrease of 8.3 million people. The population living in extreme poverty fell from 9.1 million to 7.0 million. (3) However, children and adolescents continue to be disproportionately affected by poverty, limiting their effective access to their rights. The situation is especially serious for indigenous children and adolescents, as well as for young children (aged 0–5 years), with poverty levels of 82.3(4) and 41.9%(5), respectively. Children and adolescents with disabilities face higher levels of poverty, school exclusion and violence, and there are weaknesses in service quality, cross-sectoral coordination, specialized services, care and support. According to the latest Census there are 767,000 children and adolescents living with disabilities (6). These inequalities have an immediate reflection in the country' disaster risk, due to the inequal physical exposure and populations specific vulnerabilities to natural and human-made hazards.




In recent years, the Government has expanded its social protection schemes to address vulnerable populations, including children. Cash transfer programmes such as a the Benito Juárez grants, the Pension for Persons with Disabilities and the more recent Rita Cetina and My Scholarship to Get Started cash transfer programmes in Mexico City, have contributed to improving the income of households with children and reducing poverty alongside with two increases in minimum wages, the latest for 2026, which is expected to further contribute to the reduction of poverty. In terms of access to childcare to promote women’s participation in economic activities and child well-being, the coverage is low(9%) (7) and provides unequal access, mainly benefiting higher-income households. The Law of Care System is under development to address the low coverage of this service. In 2025, the regional conference of women was held in Mexico City with the central theme of care system, building momentum and setting the scene for the future approval of the law.




Despite commitments to children and adolescents made by the new administration, public investment for children and adolescents remains a challenge. Since 2021, spending on children has not exceeded 3 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Although social spending in Mexico has increased as a percentage of total public expenditure, the share allocated to children and adolescents within total social spending has decline, averaging 19.8 per cent between 2019 (22.9%) and 2024 (17.1%) (8).




Children and adolescents face a triple burden of malnutrition, i.e. the coexistence of undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies and overnutrition. Chronic malnutrition affects 13.9 per cent of children under 5 (9), with a higher prevalence among poor (20.8%) and indigenous children (27.4 %). Acute malnutrition affects 1.2% of children and doubles its prevalence in indigenous households (2.3%) (10), and 9.4% of children of preschool age are anemic (11). Concurrently, 38.1% of adolescents are overweight or obese (12). Other persistent issues that put infant health at risk include the low rate of exclusive breastfeeding (only 34.2 per cent of children under 6 months are exclusively breastfed) (13), and the low vaccination coverage (only 45.63% of children aged 12 to 23 months and 32.37% of children aged 24 to 35 months complete a full basic vaccination program) (14). At the same time, over 4.5 million people lack access to drinking water and 4.6 million lack access to sanitation services (15), many of whom are children and adolescents. Teenage pregnancy accounts for 16.7% of all births. Children’s mental health is a growing concern, with signs of increasing anxiety, depression and suicide rates (1.8 per 100,000 children) (16). The greatest challenges faced by the health sector include shortfalls in the coverage of quality services and equitable budget allocation in rural areas and to the most vulnerable populations, especially in emergency situations.




Mexico has made significant progress in education, committing to guarantee free and compulsory education for 18 school years, from initial education  through to upper secondary school, and has achieved almost universal coverage in primary education. However, challenges persist. First, educational pathways are incomplete, especially among marginalized children and adolescents, including those living in poverty, in rural areas or with disabilities, and members of indigenous populations, children on the move and individuals with low learning achievements. Also, education services are frequently interrupted by crises due to disasters or armed violence, leading to limited access, absenteeism and drop out. Only 56 out of every 100 children starting primary school complete upper secondary education without having to repeat one or more years of study or temporarily dropping out of school. Only 2 out of 10 children aged 0–3 years attend initial education programmes and 67.6 % of children aged 3–5 years attend preschool (17). Not all children who complete their schooling acquire the core knowledge and skills required for an effective transition to adulthood. Forty-seven percent of 15-year-old students attain only a minimum level of competency in reading and 66 per cent in mathematics (18). Second, persistent structural challenges limit access and learning and reproduce inequalities, especially for children and adolescents living in poverty, in rural areas, in indigenous areas, and living with disabilities or children on the move. Educational investment does not sufficiently prioritize teacher training, remedial learning or classroom support.




The child protection system continues to face challenges in providing comprehensive, coordinated and prompt responses. Over 2 million children require attention from the Child Protection Authorities who operate with a budget gap of 143 per cent, limiting their capacity to identify, evaluate and monitor rights violations. (19) Children and adolescents face multiple forms of violence, including physical, psychological and sexual, in the home, school, community, digital environment and some institutions, including shelters, and justice, health and education systems. 55% of children and adolescents have been subject to violent discipline; 53% of adolescent girls (aged 15 to 17 years) have experienced sexual violence of some kind in their lifetime and in various settings (20); and 26 per cent of adolescents have been victims of cyberbullying (21). Moreover, 40% of girls and women over 15 years of age have experienced violence from their intimate partner. Nearly 22,000 children and adolescents reside in institutions without family care.(22) Violence against children includes homicides, disappearances, sexual exploitation, internal displacement, and recruitment and exploitation by criminal groups. In some municipalities, homicide rates exceed 133 per 100,000 inhabitants, with 47 municipalities registering rates above 30 per 100,000 inhabitants(23). 7,000 children have been reported missing between 2020 and 2024 (24). In 2024, 390,000 people in Mexico were displaced for armed violence, 30% of whom were children (25). In many of these territories, the presence of armed actors and insecurity significantly constrains humanitarian access and the ability of institutions to reach children and adolescents with timely protection services.




Irregular entries into Mexico dropped by 86 per cent between January and September 2025, with only 135,223 entries recorded, compared to the same period in 2024, when 1,005,320 people entered the country irregularly. Similarly, according to Mexico's National Migration Institute (INM), in 2025, entries by children in an irregular migration situation have also decreased by 88 per cent compared to 2024, when 115,671 were recorded, compared to only 13,552 recorded up to quarter three 2025. Official information accumulated up to quarter three 2025 highlights that of all the children in an irregular situation detected by the authorities in Mexico, currently only 5% of children travel unaccompanied and 70% are children under 12 (26).




Mexico is particularly vulnerable to extreme weather and natural hazards, exacerbated by poverty, environmental degradation and geographical conditions. These events have disproportionate impacts on women and children, deepening structural inequalities and affecting the full exercise of their human rights. Events like hurricanes, droughts, floods and pollution affect people’s well-being, limit access to essential services and undermine food security. This year, UNICEF, in support of federal and state authorities, responded to the needs of flood-affected children and families in Veracruz, Puebla and Hidalgo, ensuring access to safe water, rehabilitated schools and safe child-friendly spaces. Mobile WASH services and hygiene kits restored dignity in shelters, while psychosocial support reduced distress in affected communities. School cleaning kits quickly restarted learning, helping protect children’s learning. Also, as part of our incipient work on climate change, the office supported the government of Mexico in the development the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and the National Adaptation Policy. The NDC incorporates several references to the vulnerabilities faced by children due to climate change, which opens great opportunities for collaboration for the implementation of such policy instruments.
