Being the last year of the 2020-2025 Country Programme, important results have been achieved and consolidated in 2025, after 6 years of implementation. 2025 also marked the 10-year anniversary of the creation of the National Child Protection System (SIPINNA), as mandated by the 2014 General Law for the Rights of Children and Adolescents (LGDNNA), which was a major step towards fully recognizing children and adolescents as rights holders in Mexico. Since 2015, different reforms of the LGDNNA have strengthened and amplified this catalog of rights by incorporating provisions to recognize the right to food, prohibiting corporal punishment and ill-treatment as a method of discipline, and guaranteeing broader protection for children and adolescents deprived of a family environment, especially those in situations of abandonment, exposure or institutionalization. After some years of stagnation, there has been a repositioning of SIPINNA and its Executive Secretary under the current administration, further strengthening its leadership to articulate public policies for children across sectors with greater participation of children and adolescents. Progress has also been notable at the subnational level, with all 32 states having a law on the rights of children and adolescents.  




The creation of SIPINNA in 2015 represents the most significant institutional change to articulate the Mexican State's commitment and action around the guarantee, protection and safeguarding of children and adolescents' rights, including in emergencies. Ten years after, under the coordination of its Executive Secretariat, the national SIPINNA has contributed to the development of comprehensive mechanisms, routes and policies for the protection of children and adolescents, such as the National Strategy for the Attention of Early Childhood, the Strategic Plan of Action for the Attention of Children and Adolescents in Mobility, the Comprehensive Care Route for the Rights of Migrant Children and Adolescents and the National Plan for the Global Alliance to End Violence against Children and Adolescents, including the development of mechanisms to guarantee the right to effective participation of children and adolescents, among others. UNICEF Mexico has been a key partner in all these achievements, as the 2025 office results show. 



During this year, UNICEF advocated with the new government for the so-called “A Good Six Years for Children” initiative, which puts forward six priority actions to eradicate child poverty and ensure well-being of children and adolescents, notably universal comprehensive early childhood care, improved primary and secondary education, universal social protection, healthy nutrition from pregnancy to age 18, protection against violence, and strategic public investment in children. Through the initiative “100 Priorities for Transformation” and the 2025-2030 National Development Plan, Mexico's new Government has incorporated key actions aimed at the well-being of children and adolescents, such as the commitment to create a Republic of and for Children. Among these priorities are the universalization of cash transfers for school-aged children, the expansion of early childhood education, the establishment of a National Care System, and comprehensive policies on health, nutrition, and protection to ensure the full development of more than 38 million children in Mexico.




With Mexico being one of the host countries for the 2026 Football World Cup, UNICEF Mexico has carried out a comprehensive effort to strengthen child protection, focusing on preventing sexual exploitation, violence in home or family, and promoting the participation of children and adolescents in public decision-making. Prioritizing host cities and those with high tourist influx, UNICEF supported local institutions in designing care and response protocols. The strategy combines awareness campaigns with the reinforcement of protection systems, including the 911 emergency line, Child Protection Offices through the case management model and welfare agencies, to improve prevention, detection, and response capacities. UNICEF also formalized partnerships with a wide range of stakeholders including the Centre for Sport and Human Rights (CSHR), Host City Committees, tourism authorities and hotel associations, the Citizen Council for Security and Justice of Mexico City, and other UN agencies. These actions are being implemented before, during, and after the World Cup to leave a legacy of stronger institutions and improved protection for children and adolescents.


Main programmatic results achieved in 2025 include:

Under Strategic Plan (SP) Goal Area 1 (Nutrition) and aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) direct effect 2 (wellbeing and inclusion), UNICEF contributed with the Ministry of Health (MoH) to design the new national strategy Live Healthy, Live Happy launched by President Sheinbaum in February 2025, which prohibits the sale of unhealthy foods at all schools and promotes healthy behaviors to tackle childhood obesity, benefitting 24 million children across the country. UNICEF also supported the MoH in the development of key policy documents such as the National Care Programme for the First 1,000 Days and the Mexican Dietary Guidelines. Throughout 2025, more than 627,000 children were reached by Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) actions, such as the “Eat like a Champion” campaign to promote a healthy diet, while 28,594 children and pregnant women on the move (a total of 278,648 children since 2022) were attended with nutrition and health services in 2025. In August 2025, a new App called Código LactancIA was launched with the government to detect violations of the International Code of Breast-milk Substitute using Artificial Intelligence, with more than 1,200 violations detected since its launch. UNICEF also managed to leverage public funding for the purchase of Ready-to-use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) for the treatment of acute malnutrition.



Contributing to SP Goal Areas 2 (Education) and 4 (WASH) as well as to UNSDCF direct effects 2 (see above) and 5 (decent work and employability), UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MoE) to advance equitable, quality education for vulnerable children, expanding access, digital inclusion and emergency support. In 2025, innovations in EdTech, foundational and socio-emotional learning, and STEM reached over 400,000 children. Efforts centered on institutionalizing and scaling joint initiatives and influencing the government’s Education Sector Plan 2025–2030. UNICEF also supported federal and state level MoEs to improve quality in initial and preschool education. As a result, 133,100 preschool students received UNICEF´s socio-emotional learning program in the State of Mexico; 10,170 preschool and primary students were reached with UNICEF’s methodology to improve literacy; and 353 initial education teachers improved their capacities through training workshops. Programmes promoting access and retention in formal education for children in vulnerable contexts were consolidated, improving foundational learning outcomes among indigenous children and children on the move, as well as access to WASH services, disaster risk reduction, and emergencies response. In 2025, UNICEF trained 10,458 education staff and reached 90,481 children and adolescents with formal and non-formal education activities, improved WASH services and learning recovery programmes. Adolescents' life skills were improved through socio-emotional and STEM materials and teacher training, directly benefiting over 118,555 students and 17,720 education staff. The implementation of digital solutions for learning recovery (Learning Passport) resulted in a 9 per cent improvement in user achievement in Mathematics. In terms of humanitarian assistance, over 100,000 people were supported with WASH services, including children and families on the move in the southern and central states of Mexico.  



Under SP Goal Area 3 (Child Protection) and contributing to UNSDCF direct effect 10 (access to justice, protection of migrants, refugees, and asylum-seekers), UNICEF contributed to strengthening child protection systems and violence prevention programs so that children grow up in safer environments. With UNICEF support, the National Case Management Model and the Primero Child Protection Information Management System implemented by the Child Protection Authorities were rolled out in eight states and at the federal level, improving mechanisms to identify and support children victims or at risk, aiming to reach at least 16 states in 2031. In 2025, a total of 407,302 children and adolescents accessed prevention and response services. In July 2025, the Government of Mexico, with support from UNICEF, hosted the Americas Meeting of the Alliance of Pathfinder Countries to End Violence Against Children (VAC), led by the Special Representative of the Secretary-General VAC, who also visited Mexico and held high-level meetings with executive, legislative, and judicial authorities following-up on the commitments of the Bogotá Summit. UNICEF is currently supporting the Government of Mexico in the process of defining its national pledges under the EVAC Ministerial framework, ensuring alignment with existing national priorities and ongoing efforts to prevent and respond to violence against children. The National Programme for Parenting with Positive Awareness was adopted by the Family Welfare Agency at federal level and five state authorities, representing an advance toward institutionalization, with the goal of reaching 10 states in 2031. Specialized justice services expanded across 15 states, and the National Alternative Care Model was launched. UNICEF also advanced evidence based legal reforms to address armed violence and child recruitment, including in the States of Jalisco and Michoacán. 




In 2025, UNICEF also contributed to strengthening Mexico’s protection system for migrant children including by reinforcing psycho-social support through the institutional transfer of Safe Spaces, and by providing technical support to strengthen state protection authorities´ detection of risks, cross-border case resolution, and access to specialized services. This transition reflects both the impact of significant humanitarian funding reductions in migration, which required UNICEF to gradually phase out direct implementation, and a deliberate effort to foster national ownership by leaving installed capacities within state institutions and universities to ensure continuity and sustainability of services.



With regards to SP Goal Area 5 (Every child has an equitable chance in life) and UNSDCF direct effect 2 (see above), UNICEF supported national and subnational governments in key priority initiatives aimed at addressing child poverty and vulnerability and at ensuring sufficient public investment being directed toward critical programmes for children. This included supporting the government’s Early Childhood Commission in the formulation of the National Early Childhood Development Strategy and leading an ambitious costing exercise for the MoH’s National Care Programme for the First 1,000 Days. The diagnostic highlights that from 2018 to 2025, Mexico has invested annually about 0.5% of its GDP in early childhood interventions, which is lower than other countries from the region, such as Argentina (1.6%) and the Dominican Republic (1.3%), making the case for greater efforts to allocate resources for priority programmes targeted at children under 5 years of age. In addition, together with government partners such as the Ministry of Women and the Social Welfare Agency, as well as civil society organizations including the Inter-American Social Security Conference, Oxfam, and the Global Alliance for Care, UNICEF sponsored a series of national dialogues focused on expanding childcare services, and in Mexico City, supported the expansion and strengthening of its cash transfer programme for early childhood, which benefits about 85,000 children under 3 years of age.  



Efforts to mainstream cross-sectoral strategies and themes continued in 2025. For example, SBC methodologies were mainstreamed through the development of collection tools and indicators within several initiatives such as the National Care Programme for the First 1,000 Days with the Ministry of Health, the National Positive Parenting Campaign with SIPINNA, and the Obesity Prevention Campaign with the state governments of Yucatán and Chiapas. As for the cross-sectoral area of Adolescent Development and Participation (ADAP), UNICEF strengthened its leadership in adolescent empowerment, elevating youth influence within key public policy. A major milestone was its technical support provided to the Ministry of Environment (SEMARNAT), enabling consultations to shape Mexico’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) 3.0 where 233 adolescents participated.



With regards to UNICEF’s subnational presence, migration related interventions at the northern border with the US were mostly terminated throughout the year due to the US government decision to stop financial support, yet collaboration with the state governments in Baja California, Sonora, Chihuahua, Nuevo León, Yucatán, Michoacán, Jalisco, Mexico City, Guerrero and Chiapas was further enhanced to address multiple vulnerabilities of child rights. The State Government of Chiapas and UNICEF signed a cooperation agreement to advance the eradication of child poverty, aligning Chiapas with UNICEF’s national “Good Six Years for Children” pathway. In Chihuahua, UNICEF supported forums to advance a state positive parenting policy and, in parallel, implemented the positive parenting programme with the welfare agency to strengthen caregiving practices and child protection statewide. In Jalisco, with UNICEF support, children’s rights were embedded as a cross-cutting pillar in the 2025–2031 State Development Plan and key policies were developed, including on violence prevention and deinstitutionalization for children under special protection. In Michoacan, UNICEF advocacy and evidence (including a state-specific costing based on the national protection system study) helped secure approval of an increased budget for the child protection prosecutor’s office an additional MXN 4 million (approx. USD$220,000) per year over four years. In Baja California, UNICEF supported the review of the State Development Plan, contributing to the adoption of the Conscious Parenting Policy and the organization of a state-level forum in Mexicali that generated inputs and commitments incorporated into the Plan.




With regards to emergency response  despite Mexico’s stronger institutional and infrastructural capacities compared to many regional peers, the country still presents gaps in local-level preparedness and essential services' systems resilience. Classified as a medium-to-high risk country (InfoRM Index 2025), the country faces high seismic risk and recurrent threats from hurricanes, floods, droughts, and epidemics, which combines with notable socioeconomic vulnerability, inequality and pockets of deprivation, particularly in rural and marginalized areas. In this context, UNICEF continued to support the state of Guerrero in post-emergency recovery interventions after hurricanes Otis and John.  UNICEF also provided support to the affected populations from flooding by heavy rainfall, which caused 78 deaths and 23 missing people in 5 states in the central-southern region. In close coordination with national authorities, UNICEF activated its emergency sectoral coordination mechanisms, convening Education, Child Protection, WASH and Nutrition to assess needs, align preparedness efforts and plan the response. UNICEF’s interventions prioritized the state of Veracruz, particularly Poza Rica and Alamo municipalities given the severity of the impact, supporting water provision through mobile WASH units from other states, distribution of hygiene kits, and provision of psychosocial support to affected children, thanks to the funding received by the ECHO and individual donors in Mexico. 



Throughout the year, the UNICEF Mexico team also put significant efforts into the design of the new Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026-2031, which drew on latest data and evidence from a variety of sources, including the Country Programme Evaluation 2020-2025, the Situation Analysis and the Study on Climate Change and its Impacts on Children in Mexico. The CPD further received inputs from adolescents through 5 workshops organized in Baja California, Mexico City, and Chiapas, including with migrant and indigenous adolescents, with a total of seventy adolescents participating with an average age of 15 years and 59% being female. Consultations with federal government counterparts took place on July 16th, as part of an interagency technical dialogue on the 2026-2031 CPDs jointly organized by UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, and convened by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the International Development Cooperation Agency (AMEXCID), and the UN Resident Coordinator´s Office (RCO). Together with UNDP and UNFPA, UNICEF also engaged the embassies of the current and future members of its Executive Board for a consultation on the draft CPD, counting with the broad participation of 14 embassies (Austria, Belgium, Bolivia, Bulgaria, Canada, Cuba, France, Germany, Guatemala, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Switzerland) and the European Union. UNICEF further contributed to the development of the UNSDCF 2026-2031 and actively engaged in relevant planning and coordination fora.



In terms of advocacy and external communications, UNICEF co-created and rolled out major government campaigns, including the President’s healthy-eating initiative that banned junk food from schools. New partnerships with key communication actors, such as YouTube on positive parenting, were launched. At least 14 new local celebrity friends and influencers supported child’s rights advocacy and fundraising activities. Children’s rights were centered on major cultural events, including the Day of the Dead parade and the Guadalajara International Book Fair (FIL). Also, UNICEF Mexico collaborated closely with more than 10 institutions (MUNAL, Museo de Arte Moderno, Museo Tamayo, MACG, among others) which enabled UNICEF to reach more than 9,000 children through various events throughout the year. Ahead of the 2026 Football World Cup, nationwide school-based football tournaments with the Mexican Football Federation promoted peace through sports, involving over 500 children.



With regards to private sector fundraising, in 2025, UNICEF Mexico raised USD$19 million in PSFR revenue, a +16% growth in Gross Revenue compared to 2024 (latest estimate as of 20 November, final results available in January 2026). Growth is mainly driven by strong Individual Giving performance, especially pledge (+17% - a new pledge donors record, recruiting almost 30,000 new pledge donors, +28% vs 202) and cash (+124%). Corporate and Philanthropy as the High Value channels consolidated after a very successful 2024. UNICEF Mexico Philanthropy Team cultivated relations with some of Mexico's most affluent individuals, private foundations and other philanthropic organizations. Around MXN 43.5 million (approx. USD$2.2 million) were raised from the Carlos Slim Foundation, Víctor González Herrera and Dr. Simi Foundation, Elías Sacal, Latter Day Saints Church and the Next Gen initiative. Regarding business influence, UNICEF also strengthened collaborations with key multi-stakeholder platforms and business associations, including CCE (Consejo Coordinador Empresarial), COPARMEX (Confederación Patronal de la República Mexicana), and Global Compact to promote responsible business conduct and commitment to children’s rights. These efforts were advanced through the "Empresas que Cuidan" initiative, an evidence-based business survey on care and family-friendly policies, and participation in strategic business forums to position children’s rights.



Core regular funding (RR) was particularly useful for addressing challenges that are often underfunded by traditional donors, including violence prevention and response as well as armed violence against children. In 2025, flexible funds particularly underpinned UNICEF’s ability to accompany the Government in strengthening its national and subnational systems to prevent and respond to violence; further allowing the office to advance with the generation of critical evidence, including on the impact of armed violence on children in selected states, to inform advocacy efforts targeted at public policy design and legal reforms to address armed violence.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
