The strong commitment to social issues, particularly for women and children, of the new government led by President Claudia Sheinbaum along with a legislative majority of the major party, have presented an important opportunity to advance social policies for children in 2025, including the expansion of school scholarships, early childhood education, and child nutrition, among others. Yet at the same time, US foreign policy changes posed financial and operative challenges for UNICEF both globally and locally, in Mexico, especially with regards to the office’s migration related interventions and field office presence at the country´s northern and southern borders, resulting in the need to downsize both its programmatic activities and field presence in 2025.




Against this backdrop, drawing on both the 2020-2025 Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) and the experiences made throughout the final year of CPD implementation, main lessons learned include (i) the need to diversify funding sources through a solid partnerships and resource mobilization strategy; (ii) the urgency of having a clear and coordinated public policy advocacy strategy, both at national and subnational levels, to addresses, among others, the limited public budget allocation for children; and (iii) the importance of strengthening the focus on leveraging strategic partnerships and alliances, scalability of interventions, and influence to achieve sustainable results for children at scale. The CPE puts forward several recommendations which have informed the 2026-2031 CPD process and design, including the need to strengthen the participation of key actors in the CPD design and the urgency to prioritize support for national policies and systems that integrate intersectoral approaches to childcare. It also highlights the importance of improving UNICEF's internal and external coherence, consolidating the humanitarian-development nexus (a recommendation also provided by the regional Real Time Evaluation on Children on the Move), and integrating cross-cutting approaches into all phases of the CPD; further underscoring the importance of diversifying and securing funding, reviewing administrative processes, strengthening subnational work, and improving the monitoring system in view of strengthening the sustainability and scalability of interventions. 




These lessons and learnings have been considered when designing the new Country Programme, which, as a result, will adopt two guiding approaches starting next year: 


(a) To achieve sustainable results at scale, through support for prioritized government initiatives;   
(b) To enhance the humanitarian-development nexus by building a shock-responsive system- making services more resilient against climate events and other natural disasters to minimize negative impacts on children.
(c) To ensure comprehensive programming for the most vulnerable children and adolescents, especially in territories prioritized by the State and those with high child poverty and indigenous and Afro descendent populations. For this purpose, a regional approach will be combined with coordinated and convergent actions.


In October 2025, UNICEF facilitated a south-south learning exchange between Mexico and Brazil through participation of Mexico´s National Statistics Institute (INEGI) in the first national adaptation of the Executive Course for Leaders in Evaluation (ExCEL) organized by UNICEF Brazil in collaboration with the National School of Public Administration (ENAP) and UNICEF Regional Office, allowing a valuable opportunity to share insights and lessons learned from building and consolidating effective national evaluation systems. 




Throughout 2025, UNICEF Mexico actively engaged in the organization’s Business Model Initiative (BMI) and Future Focus Initiative (FFI), defining its vision and approach to achieve focus, scale and impact for all children during 2026-2031. This vision, entitled “The road to 39 million: From some to all children in Mexico”, underpins the new CPD and brings along a shift in the way the country office operates and does business at all levels to mobilize resources, influence and results for children at scale. As such, it foresees an integrated approach bringing together Programmes, Communications, Operations, and Private Sector Fundraising and Partnerships (including those related to humanitarian action, recovery and disaster resilience building) for stronger results achievement, brand visibility and positioning of UNICEF's work for children both at national and subnational levels. It also envisions enhanced partnerships and alliances with a broad range of stakeholders, including the private sector, media and academia, to successfully position child rights and leverage funding, evidence and influence for all children in Mexico. This vision and approach are at the core of the new CPD and will inform the actions of UNICEF Mexico during the new country programme cycle 2026-2031.

In 2025, Nicaragua maintained a stable social and institutional context. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 3.6 percent in 2024 and, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), growth is expected to fluctuate between 4 percent and 5 percent in 2025. The country remains on a path of economic growth and with a positive performance of the most relevant macroeconomic variables, as indicated by the Central Bank.
Nicaragua continues to be one of the countries in the region that has increased investments in the social sector in relation to its total public budget. Social spending in 2024 accounted for 53.4 percent of total expenditure executed. Social spending was mainly allocated to the health and education sectors, which accounted for 65.2 percent of social spending and 34.8 percent of total expenditure. According to the Nicaragua Central Bank, the country spent the equivalent of US$685 million on education and US$638.3 million on the health sector, out of a total of US$4,745.9 million of total central government spending.
For the implementation of these resources, the country has important public policy instruments such as the National Plan for Poverty Reduction and Human Development 2022-2026. This plan sets out the key priorities for achieving several of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets, such as access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation, early childhood, primary and secondary education, health and well-being, gender equality, and the empowerment of girls and women.
This priority in the social sector has allowed Nicaragua to make significant progress in the fulfillment of children's rights, although challenges remain, as indicated below.
According to the Ministry of Health (MoH), the under-five mortality rate decreased from 19.7 deaths per 1000 live births (LB) in 2018 to 12 per 1000 LB in 2025, and the neonatal mortality rate decreased from 10.7 deaths per 1000 in 2018 to 5 per 1000 LB in 2025. The average infant mortality rate for the period 2020-2025 was 13.9 per thousand LB. The maternal mortality rate was 30 per 100,000 live births in 2023. This decrease is due to the significant coverage of antenatal care in the first trimester of pregnancy, which reached 93 percent, the fourth antenatal care, which reached more than 99 percent, and the coverage of institutional births, which increased from 96 percent (2023) to 99 percent in 2025.
The MOH also reported that the Service Quality Improvement Programme increased the coverage of home visits by 28.4 percent in 2025 compared to 2024, the coverage of care in developmental surveillance went from 94 percent to 100 percent and maintained immunization coverage with third doses of pentavalent vaccines at 100 percent.
According to government data,[RO1] [BR2]  drinking water coverage reaches 93 percent in urban areas and 34.87 percent in rural areas (2024). Improved sanitation coverage reaches 43.57 percent of the rural population (2024). However, of the 5,559 existing rural water supply systems, only 458 (8.2 percent) produce drinking water.
Currently, about 1.8 million children are in school. According to MINED, in 2022, the gross completion rate was 82.2 percent in primary and 65.9 percent in lower secondary. However, an estimated 7.1 percent of children of primary school age do not. This figure rises to 14.6 percent for those who should attend lower secondary school.
The Institute of Legal Medicine (IML) served 16,217 children and adolescents who were victims of violence in 2023. Of these, 11,360 were victims of sexual violence and 4,911 were victims of physical or psychological violence against children and adolescents. 100 percent of these cases were referred by institutions in the National Social Welfare System.
In Nicaragua, between 2018 and 2022, the Institute of Legal Medicine reported 994 suicide deaths, 94 of them among adolescents under 17 years old (9.46%), which has led to the government placing greater emphasis on this area.
As the World Bank points out, Nicaragua is classified in the group with the highest risk of disasters related to climate and other natural phenomena. It is also in the group at high risk of earthquakes, floods, and epidemics, and in the group of medium risk of droughts and hurricanes. Although there were no catastrophic events in 2025, vulnerability to the effects of climate change and disasters remains a high priority in the country.

UNICEF continued to support national efforts to ensure that every child survives and thrives, even during emergencies, within the framework of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2, 3, 4, and 5, Goal Area 1 of the Strategic Plan (SP) and Goal Area 1 of the UNICEF Gender Action Plan 2022–2025 (GAP). To this end, it mobilized resources from bilateral donors such as the European Union, ECHO, the Government of Canada, and USAID, as well as thematic funds. The CO strategically used Regular Resources to ensure the implementation of activities that were not financed by other funds or to leverage other resources.
UNICEF supported the MoH and the Ministry of Family (MoF) in reducing infant and neonatal mortality and consolidating the coverage and quality of health, nutrition, and child development services, including for children with disabilities. UNICEF provided technical support to the MoH in implementing evidence-based standards down to the subnational level. Thus, 100 percent of the country's municipalities and 100 percent of the 276 child development centers (CDI) monitor standards for improving the quality and coverage of services, reaching 220,000 girls and boys, allowing them, even with disabilities, not only to survive but to thrive in their family and community environment.   
Building on UNICEF-supported roll-out and subnational monitoring of evidence-based quality standards, the MoH increased the number of health units applying quality standards and processes by 29.4 percent—from 153 units in 2024 to 198 in 2025—contributing to continued reductions in infant and neonatal mortality rates.  
The MoF, with technical assistance from UNICEF, developed the School of Values for Early Childhood "Parenting with Love for Early Childhood" (EVCAPI), aimed at pregnant women and families with children under 6 years of age, promoting rights-based care, communication and self-esteem. This strategy was implemented in 50 percent of the 276 CDIs and has generated greater participation of men in the upbringing and support of their partners. 
In addition, the MoF designed the model "For the love of our children", which recognizes families as primarily responsible for upbringing, promoting safe environments and enhancing capacities. To support the implementation of models, UNICEF contributed to capacity building of technicians and personnel in psychosocial care, mental health and psychosocial support and disability, ensuring inclusive environments in 100 percent of CDIs and foster homes, including in emergencies. 
In the same way, with the support of LACRO, UNICEF and the MoF co-facilitated the first training of trainers’ course 'Caring for the Caregiver' for 45 technicians and providers from all departments of the country, which is key to supporting parenting practices, responsive care, and violence prevention, all of which are necessary for children to reach their full potential.
UNICEF provided the MoH with 60 early stimulation kits distributed to the primary health care centers nationwide, supported the training of health personnel, and the involvement of health community volunteers in the detection of risk factors and prevention of disabilities, achieving a 20 percent increase in the coverage of children with disabilities and the expansion of neonatal screening at the national level. The screening revealed that 57 percent of the disorders were related to language, followed by motor disorders at 10 percent.
Through advocacy actions and technical support from UNICEF, the MoH conducted counseling processes, engaged communities through messages promoting caregiving, positive parenting practices, and violence prevention, reaching 60,782 parents and caregivers. These actions enabled more than 19,000 men to participate in activities about loving and responsive parenting, creating protective environments for child development in their homes. 
These results were made possible by UNICEF's technical support in building capacities among 13,197 members of the community network and 19,357 frontline health workers and CDI educators in 19 departments. In this way, social and behavior change communication strategies (SBC) increased by 23 percent in 2025 compared to those implemented in 2024. In 2025, compared to 2024, there was a 23 percent increase of health personnel and community leaders participating in SBC activities. These results were made possible thanks to UNICEF’s technical support in strengthening the capacities of 13,197 community leaders and members of community networks, as well as 19,357 frontline health workers and CDI educators across the country’s 19 departments.
To ensure that every child learns and acquires skills for the future, in 2025, Nicaragua experienced significant progress in education, aimed at greater inclusion and quality. The national education system focused on improving conditions for children with disabilities and children in rural environments, through the modernization of school infrastructure, the pedagogical training of teachers and the provision of innovative teaching tools. These efforts generated more conducive school environments for learning, which translated into better academic performance of students. 
Teacher training was consolidated as a cornerstone of educational quality. UNICEF supported the continuous training of at least 20,000 teachers in their functions as well as the initial training of future educators. Virtual platforms, networks of pedagogical meetings, and postgraduate programs were used to address issues such as disability, mathematics, literacy methodologies, gender approach, and early childhood development. 
UNICEF and the Ministry of Education (MoE) promoted the development and implementation of a basic curriculum of digital skills for teachers, in addition to technologically equipping at least 15 prototype schools. The provision of accessible technologies made it possible to respond to diverse learning needs, especially of students with disabilities, promoting more inclusive and student-centered teaching.
With funds from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), 6 schools affected by Hurricane Julia in 2022 were built and rehabilitated in rural areas, prioritizing inclusive access to water, sanitation, hygiene and school snack services. Innovative methodologies were implemented for the use of rainwater and recreational activities that strengthen mental health and emotional resilience.
The UNICEF supported national Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) programme, was expanded to all schools in the country, with more than 180,000 volunteers. Technical training in gender approach and parenting with tenderness was promoted, and 10,000 new volunteers were certified during the year. 
In alliance with the Zamora Terán Foundation, UNICEF supported the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua (UNAN) and the MoE in creating accessible digital materials, with universal design for learning. This year the second-grade primary school book was completed, progress was made in the development of the first unit of the first-grade math book, and five video books were completed with topics from the primary curriculum. In addition, a master's programme in early education aimed at technical and managerial staff of the MoE was initiated. 
UNICEF facilitated the exchange of experiences of the MoE with ministries of education in Cuba, Colombia, Uruguay, Chile, and Costa Rica, to contribute to the creation of a national programme to improve reading skills in Nicaragua, expected to be introduced in 2026.
Through coordinated efforts with UNICEF's university network of volunteers, from five public and private universities, more than 1,600 volunteers supported the implementation of training activities, academic reinforcement initiatives and school actions for violence prevention.
With the support of UNICEF, the curricula of specialties in intercultural, children's, special and inclusive education, and primary education were updated. Knowledge of gender equity and attention to students with risk factors was strengthened, as well as the accompaniment of families. 
In addition, with funding from the Global Partnership for Education, UNICEF supported the MoE in making improvements at six schools affected by Hurricane Julia in 2022, and with funding from the European Union, equipment and materials were provided to 54 school emergency brigades to strengthen contingency response.
With technical support from UNICEF, the MoE developed and validated teaching guides for teachers and secondary school students at risk of dropping out of school, facilitating independent work and family accompaniment. UNICEF promoted awareness campaigns to reduce exclusion and discrimination reaching out 20,000 students, and improved conditions of inclusion for students with disabilities. 
UNICEF supported the MoF in the implementation of a three-year programme “Strengthening the Early Childhood Development Education Model (MEIDI) with gender equity” to strengthen early education, ensuring better conditions for children between the ages of 3 and 5, with adequate infrastructure, teacher training, and a gender approach. 
In conclusion, progress in 2025 reflects a comprehensive commitment to inclusive and quality education in Nicaragua, ranging from teacher training and infrastructure to technological innovation, gender equity, and school community resilience by strengthening psychosocial support. These achievements lay the foundations for a fairer, more accessible and effective education system for all students in the country.
In 2025, UNICEF helped ensure that every child is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices by technically strengthening the child protection system in Nicaragua through key interventions.
UNICEF updated and documented practices to create protective environments, promoting behavioral changes that combat violence and early unions. The prevention of early unions was positioned as a priority in the MoF and in alliances with non-governmental organizations, which resulted in the conduct of a study on the subject and the design of a specific strategy. 27,369 adolescents were trained in the prevention of early unions through the MoF Schools of Values. 
Community outreach was significant: 27,307 mothers, fathers, and caregivers participated in the School of Values Programme and in violence prevention actions, including gender-based violence, developed by allies and faith-based organizations. The MoF, through its programs and Child Development Centers, promotes positive parenting, the transformation of gender stereotypes and positive masculinities, consolidating the prevention of early unions as a core content from 2024 and strengthening it in 2025.  
In terms of care of children and adolescents victims of violence, 45,626 children and adolescents who suffered violence received health and social work services, and 2,195 accessed legal care, as result of training, updating, and implementation of regulations and technical assistance by UNICEF. UNICEF supported inter-institutional coordination through the National Inter-institutional Commission for the Implementation of the Protocol for the Comprehensive Care of Children and Adolescents Victims of Sexual Violence, using the protocol as a national guide and ensuring the standardization and effectiveness of protection actions. 
Information on the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) reached 46,944 people, including adolescents, consultants, UNICEF staff and partners, through training and community spaces. In addition, UNICEF trained 194 technicians from the Special Protection System to improve specialized emotional recovery services. These technicians cared for 1,531 children in accordance with United Nations guidelines.
UNICEF's technical and financial support to the MoF helped to improve psychological assessment and intervention processes, strengthen foster homes and standardize special protection procedures including in emergencies. Collaboration with international and faith-based organizations was promoted, implementing actions to prevent and address violence, positive masculinities and prevention of early unions, using cascade training methodologies and updated educational materials. 
Finally, diplomas in family counseling and early warning workshops were developed, strengthening the capacities of counselors and officials of the MOF for comprehensive and preventive care. UNICEF contributed to the systematization of experiences, the continuous improvement of care mechanisms and the promotion of a rights-based approach to the protection of children and adolescents.
To achieve the goal that every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment, UNICEF continued to work with national and local institutions.
Following the principle of “leaving no one behind,” UNICEF provided technical and financial support to the ANA (National Water Authority) and the MoH to facilitate access to safe water for 29,424 people (10,539 children) living in 32 vulnerable communities in the Dry Corridor. In addition, UNICEF supported engagement of 6,200 people from 20 communities for behavior change to eliminate open defecation. This initiative aligns with national efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goal on water and sanitation (targets 6.1 and 6.2).
UNICEF supported the MOH and ANA in developing a new regulatory framework for the water, sanitation, and hygiene sector (WASH) that integrates climate change, and disaster risk reduction (DRR) aiming to ensure sustainable and equitable access to resilient services, thus protecting children's health, learning, inclusion and well-being.
The Ministry of Health (MoH), with technical support from UNICEF, developed a study titled "Analysis of the Impact of Climate Events on the Nicaraguan Health System." The study's findings support health sector planning by integrating adaptation and resilience measures. These measures facilitate the anticipation of climate risks, the updating of protocols and regulations, and the assurance of timelier and evidence-based responses to protect the health of the population, particularly children. Adapting the Total Sustainable Sanitation and Hygiene methodology (SAHTOSO) manual to the indigenous context is key to facilitating its application in more communities. This adaptation will promote the elimination of open defecation, reduce health risks, and strengthen sustainable hygiene practices. Similarly, implementing water safety plans enables the identification and mitigation of risks, the protection of sources, and the assurance of service continuity. This, in turn, increases community resilience.
The cooperation with MoH and the ANA strengthened the delivery of resilient and inclusive WASH services in homes, schools and health units, as well as the adoption of positive practices. UNICEF trained 1,059 technicians from WASH institutions and service providers who have been provided with equipment to monitor water quality in 112 communities. In addition, 1,756 adolescents and women have participated in behavior change processes on menstrual health and hygiene, receiving kits and educational materials to break stigmas.
UNICEF supported, together with the ANA and the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua (UNAN), the installation of remote water monitoring systems in three rural communities, that reached 3,699 people, including 1,695 children and adolescents. The water wells now have sensors that record in real time water quality parameters such as temperature, pH, conductivity, dissolved solids and residual chlorine, as well as flow, operation and performance of pumps and electrical systems. It is used as an early warning system in routine water supply, including emergencies. The data is continuously transmitted via GSM to a web platform accessible from mobile phones, generating early warnings and remote technical assistance. In 2026, sensors will continue to be installed in hard-to-reach, climate-vulnerable communities to strengthen twenty rural water systems. These devices will support remote monitoring, enabling early risk detection, enhanced early warning capacities, rapid response, and continuous safe water services. This will improve technical management and community resilience during any contingency.
Although the CTI-8 chlorination device was initially installed in six schools, the initiative is not limited to them. UNICEF will continue to support the Ministry of Education in conceptualizing and validating the model, with the aim of determining its technical, operational, and regulatory feasibility for possible scalability to all educational facilities that use rainwater harvesting systems to ensure a safe water supply for the student population.
In terms of Programme Effectiveness, the Country Office scored high on internal Key Programme Indicators (KPI), demonstrating it's high standards and effectiveness in internal management.
Important milestones were achieved, mainly aimed at systemic changes and overcoming bottlenecks identified in the CPD's strategic planning. Key achievements include: the development of a detailed plan to strengthen national capacities in evaluation (including training in evaluation of key officials and technical staff) with the National Planning Secretariat of the Presidency, and the design of the MoF initiative on early unions. Effective negotiations for geographic refocusing and maintaining the NICALERT programme, funded by the European Union, were achieved.
UNICEF continued to support the Ministry of Finance on three strategic areas: limited generation of information on children, low visibility of public investment, and limited institutional capacities to evaluate public spending based on results. Support focused on strengthening the collection and use of data, institutionalize annual reports and revitalize inter-institutional collaboration
In 2025, UNICEF consolidated its role as an agency that innovates and communicates effectively with cultural sensitivity, promoting art, culture, technology and active participation of young people. The MoF–Cinemateca Nacional–UNICEF alliance was strengthened as a national platform for social transformation, producing 135 digital content pieces, a podcast, and campaigns on health, mental well-being, and adolescent participation, reaching more than 5 million users and a dynamic network of volunteers and university partners. The podcasts provide adolescents and caregivers with practical guidance, stories, and expert insights on positive parenting, mental health, and child protection, presented in an engaging and accessible format.
The collaboration with the media and the private sector promoted digital inclusion and adolescent participation, highlighting programs such as "Gamers in Action", a digital skills and online safety initiative that engages 800 adolescents through gaming, coding, and interactive challenges to strengthen their competencies and amplify their voices. Productions for international days such as World Children’s Day also enabled the dissemination of key messages on child rights and safe internet use through partner digital platforms. 
Finally, with support from the Global Office of Innovation, programmatic integration, emergency preparedness and interagency work consolidated UNICEF Nicaragua as a regional reference, with updating of monitoring and response platforms, and active participation in global initiatives such as "Ahead of the Storm", a pioneering "impact-based forecasting" digital platform for imminent hurricane and other natural hazards-related disaster risks, which set the base of regional and global effort to progress in this area. 
The Future Focus Initiative (FFI) developed by UNICEF globally to adapt to changes in international development cooperation, required internal restructuring and more efficient coordination. An internal Rapid Review of the CPD was conducted to document operational challenges, innovations, and adjustments and guide planning for 2026-2027. 
Financial management was efficient, with a budget execution rate of 96 percent at the end of 2025. Invoice processing, bank reconciliations and supplier database were optimized, as well as supply management, generating savings and efficiency. The technological infrastructure was strengthened with hardware acquisition, improvements in connectivity and cybersecurity training.
In 2025, UNICEF, together with other UN agencies, funds and programmes in Nicaragua, continued to work in coordination to support progress toward the achievement of the SDGs and strengthen their linkages with national priorities

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In Nicaragua, the main challenges of UNICEF's cooperation are related to the need to increasingly mobilize non-earmarked resources to ensure technical cooperation with the government for greater scaling up of the provision of quality services and safe environments for children. 
Also, the new national regulatory framework for United Nations agencies, funds, and programs has led to the adoption of innovative implementation modalities in collaboration with government institutions. 
While significant progress continues to be made in fulfilling children's rights, it is necessary to maintain social investment in children and ensure greater coverage and quality in all areas. This will help to achieve and exceed the objectives of the National Plan to Combat Poverty and Promote Human Development 2022-2026.
Operational efficiency is affected by the changing global context, especially in imports and supplies delivery. UNICEF has taken steps such as redirecting imports to Panama for pre-positioning and shifting the consignee of medical supplies to the MoH to overcome logistical hurdles. 
Lessons learned from the implementation of UNICEF programmes in Nicaragua show that institutional coordination and support to work communities are key to the sustainability and quality of WASH services. 
The role of academia has been fundamental in developing affordable and appropriate technological solutions, and the active participation of youth in the management and operation of WASH systems has driven the adoption of positive practices and preparedness for climate events.
In terms of effectiveness, the need to increase programmatic and operational flexibility is highlighted, opting for direct implementation when necessary, even if this implies greater administrative burdens. The strategy of strengthening partners through direct assistance by consultants in key entities, such as the successful cases of the MoH and MoF, as well as the search for strategic partners – especially universities – has opened new opportunities to strengthen our technical cooperation. 
Another lesson is the need to maintain alignment of UNICEF's programmatic priorities with national institutional frameworks and priorities, achieving convergence between UNICEF's operational procedures (e.g., supply management) and the planning and implementation mechanisms of institutional counterparts.
Direct work with ministries has helped greater support to social policies, allowed the government to take ownership, facilitated scale-up of interventions, ensured sustainability and provided support to make systems shock-responsive. 
Multisectoral involvement in updating health regulations, integrating nutrition diagnostics and treatments in synergy with community network participation, providing supplies (e.g., MUAC tapes), and on-site micronutrient supplementation, increasing nutritional and community resilience to potential shocks. 
The Child Care for Development (CCD) evaluability assessment showed notable progress in integrating CCD.
The training of trainers’ methodology and cascade training have expanded the scope of beneficiaries, allowing the replication of tools for the prevention of sexual violence and early unions. 
In operational efficiency, the closer coordination and collaboration of Programs and Operations teams have generated synergies that improved office management and delivery of results. The formation of joint committees and the constant review of procedures have strengthened planning and execution, increasing the capacity to respond to contingencies. 
In conclusion, to continue contributing to the realization of the rights of children in Nicaragua, UNICEF Nicaragua must remain adaptable, flexible, open to innovative approaches, and ensure sustained engagement with the government.
Looking ahead, UNICEF and its partners have key opportunities to strengthen their work in Nicaragua. In the WASH area, UNICEF will continue to support the government through the Self-Reliance Strategy (SRS) approach. This will contribute to strengthening the national and territorial capacities of WASH sector actors in community risk management and resilience (EPR) in the context of increasing climate variability. The following actions have been identified as priorities for strengthening the four pillars of the WASH system: 1. governance and inter-institutional coordination, supporting the improvement of sectoral coordination and leadership mechanisms; 2. sustainable financing, supporting the mobilization of resources to increase access to and continuity of WASH services; 3. data management and use, promoting timely and reliable information systems for evidence-based decision-making; and 4. community programs and participation, promoting local resilience practices, risk management, and community water quality surveillance. 
The use of Artificial Intelligence and innovative practices will be promoted to expand the water quality monitoring network and improve decision-making. The office will continue to develop its automated early damage estimation model for emergencies, such as hurricanes, which is now part of the global initiative Ahead of the Storm. This tool will be fully adopted by the country's emergency team (UNETE), and the CO will support other nations in the Caribbean basin to share and implement this methodology.
UNICEF will continue to support the national scaling up initiatives in health and early childhood development, aimed at universal coverage and quality of services, including the development of evidence-based materials for the training of frontline and community health network, intersectoral coordination to promote community counseling and the use of innovative tools such as artificial intelligence for monitoring. 
Strengthening the capacities of local staff and improving intersectoral coordination and referral mechanisms across Health, Protection and Education sectors will be essential for comprehensive mental health care for children and adolescents. 
Regarding effectiveness, primary response will be strengthened through community networks, mental health and psychosocial support MHPSS, and the harmonization of protection regulations, with emphasis on violence prevention and collaboration between the ministries of health, education and family. 
The CO will support the MoE in implementing reading and writing educational strategies as the basis for improving fundamental skills in all areas of knowledge.
Operational efficiency by 2026 will be marked by new implementation modalities, such as the use of technological tools to optimize resources, consolidate progress and ensure the well-being of children and adolescents in Nicaragua.

Panama has recently attained high-income status; however, deep structural inequalities and lack of investment in quality basic services continue to impact children, adolescents and disadvantaged communities. While macroeconomic indicators remain strong, recent data highlight persistent and often severe deprivation among rural, indigenous and other vulnerable groups. 
Socio-economic Landscape and Poverty 
Children represent over one-third of Panama’s population and reflect the country’s significant ethnic diversity: one quarter identify as Afro-descendant and nearly another quarter as indigenous.  Despite some improvements, inequality remains deeply entrenched, with a Gini coefficient of 0.50, making Panama the second most unequal country in Latin America and the 10th in the world. While urban poverty has declined in recent years, poverty rates in indigenous territories remain extremely high, with around three out of four households living below the poverty line.  
Child poverty remains widespread and multidimensional. Recent national assessments estimate that nearly one in three children experience multidimensional or monetary poverty, affecting close to half a million children nationwide. In several indigenous provinces, nine out of ten children are affected. While adult poverty has declined, child poverty stagnates, indicating that progress and poverty reduction measures (including cash transfers) do not reach households with children at the same level. 
Limited social spending (approximately 9 per cent of GDP compared to 18 per cent across Latin America and the Caribbean), highly centralised public investment, high labour informality (49 per cent), and uneven investment in human capital continue to constrain equitable development. Poor households, particularly in rural and indigenous areas, have limited access to health, nutrition, education and child protection services and remain excluded from social protection mechanisms. National estimates indicate that only three in ten children living in poverty benefit from cash transfer programmes, while only half of children nationwide are covered by social security, with coverage falling below 25 per cent in indigenous communities. Children with disabilities, children without parental care and children from minority ethnic groups continue to face persistent barriers to inclusion. Social norms, such as discrimination against minorities, violence against children and gender-based discrimination, affect a large part of the population, including children, with an impact on their development and participation in society.  

Child Well-being: Progress and Persistent Challenges
Health and Nutrition: Panama continued to reduce child mortality, with the infant mortality rate reaching 12 deaths per 1,000  live births. However, the rate doubles that of other high-income countries of  the region such as Chile and Uruguay, and significant disparities persist.  Infant mortality rates in indigenous territories remain around twice the national average, largely due to limited access to prenatal, childbirth and postnatal care. Chronic malnutrition affects approximately 16 per cent of children under five, with substantially higher prevalence in indigenous territories. At the same time, overweight and obesity are increasing, particularly among adolescents. Uneven availability of health and nutrition services, especially in remote areas, remains a major barrier to equitable outcomes. 
Early Childhood Development (ECD): Participation in ECD services has slightly improved, yet major gaps persist. Nationally, around 3 per cent  of children under three attend public ECD centres, which are predominantly concentrated in urban areas. Home-based stimulation and early learning are also uneven: approximately three-quarters of children aged 24–59 months receive adequate early stimulation, leaving many without the developmental support they need. Despite being compulsory, pre-primary education continues to fall short of universal coverage, with 40 per cent of children aged four not enrolled. Insufficient classrooms and early learning services—particularly in rural and indigenous areas—remain the primary barriers to access.
Education: Education remains one of Panama’s most pressing challenges. Around 120,000 children and adolescents remain out-of-school (27%  in preschool, 12% in upper secondary), while learning outcomes are weak: three out of five students do not achieve minimum proficiency in reading, and four out of five fall below basic standards in mathematics. Although public investment in education has increased, reaching allocations equivalent to 7 per cent of GDP, the impact of its execution has been very low. Key bottlenecks include insufficient and inadequate infrastructure, outdated curricula, limited teacher training and inequitable access to digital  learning.
Child Protection: Violence and harmful practices affect large numbers of children. Nearly half of them experience violent discipline at home, and the vast majority of reported sexual violence cases affect girls below the age of 18. Early unions remain prevalent, particularly among indigenous adolescents, and over 14,000 adolescent girls in Panama are mothers, many of whom face barriers to continuing education and accessing health and protection services. Reforms to strengthen the child protection system have continued, including efforts to transition children from residential care to family-based environments, resulting in a 43 per cent decline in the number of children living in institutions in recent years.
Children on the Move: The year was marked by a sharp  decline in crossings through the Darién Gap with only 3,021 people (16 per  cent of them children) crossing the border between Colombia and Panama (versus  302,203 in 2024)), while the reverse migration flow from North and Central  America reached over 21,000 people, with children and adolescents accounting  for 20 per cent of them. These dynamics expose children to heightened life-threatening and protection risks during their transit in Panama, at a  time when financial support from the international community is dwindling. 

Implications for UNICEF Programming 
The 2025 context reinforces the need for UNICEF’s  programming to remain strongly equity-driven and focused on results at scale  through technical assistance to state institutions, advocacy, alliances and  evidence generation. Key implications include:

Prioritising the most excluded communities, particularly indigenous and rural populations and children with disabilities where multiple deprivations overlap and service gaps are most acute.    
Strengthening integrated service delivery models to ensure that the State provides basic, quality health, nutrition, ECD, protection and education services       to children who remain unreached, thus contributing to the implementation of the Law 285 of 2022 that creates a Comprehensive Child Rights Protection System.     
Deepening political, policy and budget engagement, underpinned by evidence and       disaggregated data to ensure the implementation of policy reforms, influence more equitable public investment, and keep children’s rights high on the national agenda. Develop alliances to strengthen social demand for child rights and to ensure the financial sustainability of UNICEF’s engagement in Panama.

In 2025, UNICEF sharpened its programmatic focus to concentrate limited resources on interventions with the strongest potential to drive results at scale for children through national system reforms. This strategy prioritises expanding access, particularly for the most vulnerable children, to basic, integrated and high-quality social services at the local level through evidence generation (including modelling), technical assistance, advocacy and partnerships. UNICEF’s contributions continued to be guided by systematic monitoring of child-related Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators, ensuring alignment with national and global commitments. The new UNICEF Business Model Initiative provided an opportunity for the Country Office to test and expand strategies around social policy, scaling up, advocacy and partnerships with the public and private sectors (including International Financial Institutions). In parallel, a comprehensive evaluation of the Country Programme Document 2021-2025 informed strategic adjustments to programme priorities and guided UNICEF´s contributions to the formulation of the new United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).
One intersectoral, office-wide initiative central to the programme was the continuation of the Government-led pilot of an integrated model for delivering essential services for children across health, education, early childhood development (ECD), social protection and child protection. Designed to demonstrate how Panama can expand both the coverage and quality of social services in its most vulnerable communities at an affordable cost, the model has been implemented—under Government leadership and with UNICEF’s technical support—in 13 communities in Panamá Oeste and the Indigenous territory of Emberá-Wounaan. The model has successfully demonstrated that Panama could provide basic social services to all its children in a cost-effective manner, and generated evidence to inform the scale-up through state institutions and budget, including through an independent rapid assessment.  After three years of implementation, the Government has begun scaling several components with its own budget (particularly in ECD and child protection), demonstrating strong national ownership, sustainability and clear potential for impact at scale. In 2025, with support from a joint UN programme funded by the Global Disability Fund, the model was further refined to respond more effectively to the needs of children with disabilities and their caregivers, with a strong emphasis on redistributing care responsibilities through a gender-responsive lens, and with the participation of over 10 Organisations of Persons with Disabilities. 
A second intersectoral, office-wide initiative focused on positioning positive parenting as a national priority and advocacy towards the prohibition of corporal punishment in Panama. This strategy combined communication, SBC, partnerships and community-level service delivery through the State to address violence against children and promote positive parenting from multiple entry points. Together with the First Lady and private-sector allies, UNICEF launched a communication campaign featuring influential figures reaching over 540,000 people nationwide with key parenting messages. UNICEF formalised a partnership with religious leaders, enabling faith-based networks to promote positive parenting and child protection in local contexts.   Following a rapid assessment that identified gaps in the quality and reach of existing parenting programmes, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Social Development (MIDES) to introduce Parenting for Lifelong Health, an internationally validated initiative adapted locally as Crianza Responsable y Amorosa. The programme will be rolled out nationwide in early 2026 through digital , hybrid and in-person modalities, significantly expanding access to high-quality parenting support for families with children and adolescents.  Together, these actions positioned positive parenting as a unifying agenda for policymakers, service providers, civil society and communities, contributing to a safer, more nurturing environment for all children in Panama.
1. Early Childhood Development, Health and Nutrition
UNICEF provided strategic and technical assistance to strengthen Panama’s ECD, health and nutrition systems, to improve access to quality services for young children—particularly those living in vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities. More than 5,000 children have directly benefited from improved neonatal and early childhood interventions, including through the scale-up of a model of care for newborn babies. 
UNICEF supported the government in strengthening inter-sectoral services, generating key evidence through the piloting of inclusive ECD services in 13 communities as part of the integrated social services model and successfully demonstrating that the government could significantly expand access to quality services. In 2025, the service was further refined to ensure it responds effectively to the needs of children with disabilities and their caregivers. An ECD services coverage assessment conducted by UNICEF informed Government decision-making and prompted MIDES, in partnership with CAF, to develop a significant loan project profile for the expansion of this ECD service model in 2027—demonstrating UNICEF’s catalytic role in leveraging resources for scalable, nationally-owned solutions.
Building on these system-level gains, UNICEF supported significant advances in health systems strengthening. With UNICEF technical assistance, the Ministry of Health  institutionalized and expanded of the quality of neonatal care through the internationally-recognized Kangoroo Care standards. The programme reached 4,500 newborns, with notable benefits for premature and low-birth-weight infants. Capacity development efforts included training 30 health professionals in neonatal care and child-sensitive planning, reinforcing consistency and quality across service delivery. Digital innovation further enhanced the reach of parenting and health messages: the Ministry of Health adopted a UNICEF-supported pilot providing tailored digital content to caregivers, strengthening behavior-change efforts nationwide.
UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Health on the development and operationalisation of a community-based Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) model, with the state commitment to mobilising national resources for scale-up in 2027. Developed with UNICEF’s technical assistance, the model will first be piloted in 13 communities (as part of the integrated model of social services). It will be documented and evaluated for national expansion. UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Health during the Vaccination Week  to reinforce immunization outreach.
In nutrition, UNICEF played a critical role in supporting national authorities to validate the protocol for the management of acute malnutrition and prepare for its implementation across all primary care levels. With the Ministry of Health, UNICEF developed the first national study on food marketing in school environments, that informed the implementation of school feeding regulations under the Ministry of Health leadership—strengthening child nutrition and safeguarding children from harmful food marketing practices.
2. Education
In 2025, UNICEF worked with partners to strengthen institutional capacities so that the education system can deliver inclusive and adapted learning environments promoting foundational skills for all children, including those with disabilities and children in highly vulnerable contexts.
Together with the Panamanian Institute of Special Education (IPHE) and the Ministry of Education (MEDUCA), UNICEF facilitated a participatory process involving families, teachers and school leaders across five provinces to strengthen Panama’s ecosystem for inclusive education at scale. UNICEF supported the training of 100 IPHE leaders as agents of change, initiating the institutional strengthening required for system-wide adoption. UNICEF also worked with IPHE and MEDUCA, resulting in initial agreements to strengthen the role of 2,300 special education teachers nationally and promote a more inclusive practice. This represents a significant step towards aligning pedagogical, administrative and support structures for inclusive education. To reinforce this shift, UNICEF also started supporting MEDUCA in the improvement of a national data system on disability and special educational needs, based on the Washington Group criteria. Enhanced disaggregation will enable the education system to better identify, support and monitor children with disabilities across the education system.
UNICEF documented the education component of the integrated model of social services (called Aprender es mi Derecho) implemented between 2022 and 2024 in 31 pilot schools. Key products—including implementation guides, a resource catalogue and a preliminary financial cost analysis—were developed to inform potential national scale-up. 
Taking on board the conclusions and recommendations from a UNICEF study on the cost analysis of school connectivity, the Government launched a new tender to connect 3,102 schools with high-speed Internet.  The Ministry estimates that this initiative will save US$250 million per year in the provision of internet services for all schools, benefiting more than 800,000 students and significantly reducing digital inequities between rural and urban schools.
Together with UNESCO, UNICEF convened a strategic space for policy dialogue—the Think Tank for Education— with key education actors to advance national discussions on education reforms. The Think Tank brings together civil society organisations, teacher and parents unions, students, academia, the private sector and development partners. The platform enabled the articulation of a shared national education agenda and supported collective advocacy to position education as a top national priority, while reinforcing collective accountability for improved learning outcomes. 
UNICEF conducted an education budget analysis for 2019–2024, assessing allocation and execution trends. The analysis generated policy recommendations to enhance the efficiency, effectiveness and equity of public education spending, which will be shared in 2026 with the Government to improve the strategic use of resources in line with inclusive, quality learning goals.
3. Child Protection
UNICEF continued supporting the Government of Panama in advancing reform of the national child protection system, with a strong focus on strengthening family and community-based protective environments for the most vulnerable children, preventing unnecessary family separation and expanding family-based alternative care. UNICEF’s technical assistance played a key role in driving policy reform, building institutional capacity and consolidating a protection system aligned with international child rights standards.
The Case Management Manual for community-level intervention, developed and tested by UNICEF and its counterparts in the model of integrated social services, was formally adopted as a public policy. The manual improves the interface between community actors and basic health, education and protection services, ensuring timely referrals for children at risk. As a first step towards national roll-out, 38 social workers and promoters were trained, resulting in 135 children receiving referrals to essential services and an estimated 4,000 children indirectly benefiting in target communities. A training-of-trainers process is now underway to support nationwide scale-up.
The country continued to make significant progress in the deinstitutionalisation process, achieving a 43 per cent reduction in the number of children and adolescents living in residential care centres. To support this reform, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Government to develop seven tools, protocols and technical guidelines covering the prevention of unnecessary family separation, strengthening of biological families, establishment of foster families and implementation of the national deinstitutionalisation strategy. In total, over 8,000 biological families received psychosocial support and family-strengthening services nationwide, reducing risks of separation and promoting safe family environments. To underpin these system-strengthening efforts, 230 child protection professionals—including judges and psychosocial teams—were trained on family separation prevention and deinstitutionalisation, reinforcing the capacity of national and local actors to implement the reform effectively.
UNICEF also supported the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for case management of children separated from their families and placed under special protection. The UNICEF digital case management platform Primero was adapted to the national context and taken over by the Government. It is now operational nationwide. SOPs for early case management, designed to prevent separation, are under review by the National Child Protection Authority (SENNIAF) and are expected to be integrated into Primero Panamá 2.0. To ensure system-wide adoption, all the SENNIAF professionals and 30 per cent of private shelters were trained in the use of the platform. 
In 2025, the government also advanced the transition from institutional care to family-based alternative care, with UNICEF supporting the expansion of the national foster care programme. Awareness-raising activities and a selection process reached 5,442 families across three provinces (Chiriquí, Panamá and Panamá Oeste), resulting in the recruitment of 282 families and the certification of 72 foster families, with an additional 11 in process. For the first time, Panama is expected to have a functional national foster care system, fully funded by the State, by the end of 2026. 
4. Emergency Response for Children on the Move
In close coordination with the Ministry of Security, SENNIAF and other relevant authorities, UNICEF delivered life-saving humanitarian assistance to children and families on the move, reaching nearly 12,600 migrants, including 2,847 children, with integrated protection, psychosocial, health and WASH services. This response was implemented in the context of rapidly shifting migration dynamics, prompting UNICEF to adapt its strategy to prioritise child protection, continuity of essential services and strengthened coordination with national authorities and humanitarian partners. The vast majority of the children reached were part of the return flow to their countries of origin.
UNICEF supported the humanitarian response of the authorities for families on the move across communities and migration centres in the provinces of Colón and Darién, the Emberá-Wounaan indigenous province and Panama City with integrated protection and psychosocial support through child-friendly spaces, specialised referrals and direct case management. A total of 86 unaccompanied and separated children were identified and assisted, with referral pathways activated to safeguard their protection and ensure decisions were taken in their best interests. Mobile teams further strengthened protection by presence, managing 247 additional cases with specific protection needs. Child-Friendly Spaces provided structured psychosocial care to 6,860 children and adolescents and 2,634 caregivers, while safe spaces for women and girls reached 3,268 individuals with gender-based violence prevention and response services, addressing heightened risks in mobility contexts.
In the WASH sector, UNICEF ensured life-saving access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for 11,224 people by rehabilitating critical infrastructure, improving the resilience of water systems and distributing 3,568 age- and gender-sensitive hygiene kits. UNICEF also supported essential maternal and child health services, reaching 802 migrants, including 207 children under five and 14 pregnant women. Through the provision of essential medicines and supplies to the Ministry of Health, UNICEF helped guarantee continuity of primary health care services in key transit and reception points.
Finally, UNICEF provided tailored assistance to six extracontinental families (including 10 children and adolescents) who were deported from the USA to Panama, ensuring safe and dignified living conditions and facilitating access to one-year humanitarian residence permits. To reinforce national systems and preparedness, UNICEF trained 300 public officials on the Protocol for the Identification, Referral and Care of Unaccompanied and Separated Children and Adolescents in Human Mobility Contexts, strengthening institutional readiness and coordination.
5. Child Rights Monitoring and Social Policy
To support the state in its financing of core social services for children, UNICEF positioned Public Finance for Children (PF4C) as a key enabler to ensure that Panama, as a high-income country, can sustainably guarantee equitable access to quality services for all children. In 2025, UNICEF provided support to the authorities through a PF4C roadmap that included costing exercises across child protection, ECD, social protection and education, making the case for investment in children visible and comparable across sectors. UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Ministry of Economy and Finance in developing and operationalising a child budget-tagging system linked to an open data platform to generate data on where the State is investing (or not) in children. This included sharing good practices with Argentina in close collaboration with UNICEF office in that country. In parallel, UNICEF provided technical contributions to the MIDES for the development of the National Social Development Policy, ensuring the integration of child rights principles within the country’s overarching social policy framework. 
UNICEF partnered with the World Bank and the Ministry of Economy and Finance to generate disaggregated data on child monetary poverty and issue recommendations to make cash transfer programmes more child-sensitive and effective. In addition, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the National Decentralisation Authority generating fiscal simulations and proposing a new allocation formulas for the redistribution of decentralized public funds, with a focus on equity. This new tool will support allocation of more public funds to townships with higher vulnerability indexes. Looking ahead, UNICEF is supporting the institutionalisation of child-investment monitoring systems and mobilising additional resources for children through improved public budgeting and innovative financing mechanisms, including collaboration with CAF, the World Bank and the IDB.
Child rights monitoring and evidence generation remained a core function of UNICEF’s work in Panama and a central pillar for guiding evidence-based policy and investment for children. In partnership with the National Institute of Statistics and the Ministry of Social Development, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the preparation of the 2026 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey , which will be fully financed by the State. This will generate data that are currently not available in Panama. UNICEF also collaborated with the Ministry of Environment on the Child-Focused Climate Landscape Analysis, which informed the integration of child-sensitive perspectives in the updated Nationally Determined Contributions, ensuring that Panama’s climate policy reflects children’s specific vulnerabilities and rights. 
As part of efforts to strengthen national accountability, UNICEF supported the Ombudsman in producing a report on the human rights situation of Afro-descendant children. More than 80 adolescents contributed to its development and dissemination, ensuring recommendations reflected their lived experiences. A similar report on the rights of indigenous children is under development with the leadership of the Consejo Nacional de Mujeres Indígenas de Panamá, a women-led grassroots organisation. Together, these efforts reinforced national institutional capacity for monitoring child rights, informed public policy and advanced Panama’s commitments to equity and inclusion.
6. Advocacy and Partnerships
As part of its advocacy, resource mobilisation and partnerships agenda, UNICEF secured critical contributions and expanded alliances that strengthened the Country Programme and accelerated results for children. Through strategic engagement with the private sector, UNICEF mobilised US$1.5 million, reflecting growing confidence in UNICEF as a trusted partner and demonstrating the commitment of individual donors, businesses and philanthropists to advancing child rights. The Individual Giving Programme continued to grow, with more than 6,000 monthly pledge donors, reinforcing a sustainable base of public support.
The 2025 Stars for Children Gala with the National Ambassador Omar Alfanno served as a catalyst for high-level engagement, convening influential actors from the public and private sectors and deepening alliances that will contribute to system-level change for children. Innovation also played a central role in expanding outreach and mobilising resources. The launch of the Reto de Sheldry campaign, led by newly appointed National Ambassador Sheldry Sáez, was a UNICEF  integrated fundraising and advocacy initiative in Panama, raising awareness of early childhood priorities and mobilizing private resources for children. It illustrated how digital influence and strategic communication can amplify impact.
UNICEF also formalised its first ever partnership with the Tocumen International Airport, one of the region’s largest transport hubs, to host UNICEF’s face-to-face teams. This collaboration opens a continuous channel for engaging hundreds of thousands of travelers in support of children’s rights and represents a new model for high-visibility fundraising in the country.
To strengthen alignment with national priorities and attract purpose-driven investment, UNICEF developed five investment cases, focusing on inclusive education, health, ECD, social promoters and digital parenting solutions. These investment cases articulate clear pathways for private-sector and philanthropic partners to contribute to sustainable, measurable improvements in children’s lives and support systemic change across social sectors.
Together, these achievements demonstrate the potential of coordinated public–private partnerships to unlock resources, drive innovation and advance the realisation of child rights. The resources and alliances secured in 2025 position UNICEF to maintain a strong and strategic presence in Panama and to contribute meaningfully to building a future in which every child can thrive.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
