Adapting to a Rapidly Changing Context
During the year, UNICEF Panama operated in a rapidly evolving context shaped by major shifts in the first quarter: a global reduction in funding to UNICEF affecting particularly Country Offices in High-Income Countries like Panama, the sudden freeze in funding from the United States Government and significant changes in the emergency context.
In a global context of funding cuts and Panama’s transition to high-income country status, which triggered a gradual phase-out of core organizational funding in line with UNICEF’s global resource allocation policies, UNICEF informed the Government of Panama of the phasing out of core funding to the country programme. Following a request from the Government of Panama to develop a new Country Programme Document (CPD), the country office worked on developing a new, highly focused programme with only one outcome. This finalization of the CPD was postponed due to the financial situation and the current CPD was extended for one year in 2026. The Panama CO also accelerated the transition towards a new business model designed to deliver greater focus, impact and scalability of its programme through technical assistance, evidence generation (including innovation modelling), leveraging financial resources for children, advocacy and public-private partnerships for children, as well as sustainability of its engagement through local fundraising.
In a context of constrained resources, the decision to refocus the programme around a single, system-level outcome—ensuring that the State provides access to basic, quality, integrated services to every child, especially in the most deprived areas—proved critical to prioritise the UNICEF’s engagement in Panama. At the same time, the Office strengthened and re-prioritised its fundraising strategy with the private and public sectors, thus ensuring the financial sustainability of its engagement in the country. Finally, building on these two pillars – programme and funding business models- the Office proposed a restructuration and reduction of its staffing that will be implemented in 2026. 
Changes in the migration flows and the humanitarian funding required the Country Office to rapidly adjust its emergency response. Despite the downsizing of the emergency team due to funding constraints, UNICEF was able to maintain life-saving interventions on the ground, particularly in child protection, WASH, health, and gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and response. This was made possible by a lean and adaptable operational structure, strong coordination with national counterparts and partners, and clear prioritisation of the most critical risks and needs affecting children and adolescents.
Leveraging IFI Partnerships to Reach Scale
In this context, strengthened collaboration with International Financial Institutions (IFIs) emerged as a key enabler of results at scale. Partnerships with CAF, the IDB and the World Bank enabled UNICEF to influence policy design, mobilise substantial public financing and embed child-focused priorities within national reform processes. Concrete examples include the Government’s commitment to scale up community-based ECD services—developed and piloted by UNICEF in rural and indigenous areas—through a CAF loan currently under negotiation. Another example is the inclusion of a new MICS survey as a condition within an IDB budget support operation, following direct advocacy with the Bank, ensuring full Government financing of MICS implementation in 2026. In parallel, collaboration with the World Bank strengthened UNICEF’s role as a knowledge broker, supporting evidence generation and the integration of child-focused analysis into policy dialogue and reform processes.
These experiences reinforced UNICEF’s comparative advantage in Panama: not as a direct implementer, but as a provider of evidence and high-quality technical assistance that supports policy design and helps steer large-scale public investments towards improved outcomes for children.
Access to Agile, Demand-Driven Technical Assistance
Through the Business Model Initiative, UNICEF Panama tested new approaches to accessing high-level technical expertise through an innovative country-to-country service agreement with the Argentina Country Office. This collaborative model proved highly effective in strengthening both internal and government capacity in Public Finance for Children (PF4C), decentralisation, poverty measurement and evidence-informed policy dialogue—areas of growing importance in a high-income context such as Panama. Concrete results included technical support to the Ministry of Economy and Finance to develop a child budget-tagging workplan, laying the foundation for improved transparency and systematic tracking of public expenditure for children across sectors. In parallel, UNICEF further strengthened its positioning as a strategic partner on social policy reform, including support to the National Decentralisation Authority to develop equity-based allocation formulas expected to guide the transfer of an additional USD 110 million to local governments.
Resource Mobilisation from Non-Traditional Sources
Progress in advancing private-sector engagement—including the organisation of a fundraising gala, the development of five investment cases, and the design of a pooled funding mechanism for private partners—generated valuable learning and increased visibility. Together, these efforts are laying the groundwork for a more strategic and structured approach to private-sector partnerships and for the long-term sustainability of the Country Office.
Future Outlook
Building on the lessons from 2025, UNICEF Panama will continue transforming its country-level business model to remain relevant and impactful in a high-income country marked by persistent inequalities and capacity gaps across key social sectors. The office will further consolidate its programme around achieving systemic, national-level results through modelling and evidence generation, deepen partnerships with IFIs to influence large-scale public investments, and strengthen internal capacity in social policy, PF4C and advocacy as core enablers of impact.
Insights from the year will inform the design and implementation of the 2027–2030 Country Programme, with a stronger emphasis on impact, leveraging, institutionalisation and government ownership to achieve results at scale. UNICEF will also continue strengthening private-sector engagement to attract diversified funding opportunities. Together, these adjustments aim to ensure that UNICEF Panama continues to deliver results at scale for all children—especially the most vulnerable—despite funding constraints and a shifting development landscape.

Thirty-five years after ratifying the Convention on the Rights of the Child, Paraguay continues to make significant efforts to ensure its compliance for the 1.8 million children and adolescents living in the country.
Between 2021 and 2024, the economy grew at an annual average rate of 3.6 percent, and the Central Bank estimates an expansion of 5.3 percent for 2025. This growth has been accompanied by a reduction in poverty, from 27 percent in 2014 to 20.1 percent in 2024. The Gini index fell from 0.511 to 0.444 over the same period, showing a reduction in inequality.
This progress is also reflected in the child population. Between 2010 and 2022, child mortality fell from 16.3 per 1,000 live births to 12.9 per 1,000 live births, while neonatal mortality fell from 11.7 per 1,000 live births to 9.2 per 1,000 live births, and the maternal mortality ratio fell from 100.8 per 100,000 live births to 89.5 
Efforts to improve educational access have also been successful. School attendance among children aged 6 to 14 increased from 93.6 percent in 2012 to 97.6 percent in 2022. Over the same period, attendance among young people aged 15 to 17 increased from 75.5 percent to 89.4 percent.
These changes are the result of institutional capacity building and the consistent implementation of programmes such as Tekoporâ of the Ministry of Social Development (MSD)) and Abrazo (eradication of hazardous child labor) of the Ministry of Children and Adolescents (MoC), which have been maintained for the last 15 years. Over the past two years, the Paraguay 2050 National Development Plan has been added. This plan establishes strategic guidelines for economic growth and development over the next 25 years. Other additions include the National Poverty Reduction Plan, the Zero Hunger in Schools Programme, which serves over one million students, and the Seeds of the Future Programme, which provides comprehensive early childhood care. 
However, the increased availability of resources and the strengthened public policy framework have not been accompanied by a greater prioritization of children in public spending, which fell from 4.6 percent of gross domestic product to 4 percent between 2019 and 2024. This reduction contributed to the persistence of challenges to ensure that no child is left behind. Added to this is the persistence of institutional bottlenecks in the delivery of services with universal coverage.
More than 544,000 children and adolescents—29.5 percent of the total—live in poverty. Of those children, 123,021 live in extreme poverty. 73.7 percent of indigenous children live in poverty, with 40.3 percent experiencing extreme poverty. 
Only 11 percent of children and adolescents benefit from cash transfer programmes. Approximately 12 percent of children under one year of age do not have birth certificates, a figure that rises to 42.4 percent among indigenous children.
13.2 percent of children under five suffer from chronic malnutrition, a figure that rises to 23.1 percent among indigenous children. 20.9 percent of school-age children and adolescents are obese, and 13.7 percent are overweight. Only 31 percent of children under six months of age are exclusively breastfed. 24.6 percent of Paraguayan households suffer from food insecurity.
While 91.9 percent of the population has access to an improved water source, only 25 percent of Indigenous households have access to safe drinking water. Furthermore, 11 percent of public schools and 43 percent of indigenous schools lack safe water, and 88 percent lack adequate facilities for menstrual hygiene. Additionally, 15 percent of health services lack safe drinking water, and 74 percent lack basic sanitation.
6.9 percent of children between the ages of 5 and 9 do not attend a formal educational institution, and 17 percent of young people between the ages of 15 and 24 are not in employment, education or training. The quality of education is a cause for concern. In third grade, approximately 60 percent of students are unable to solve basic math problems, while 50 percent do not understand a text appropriate for their level. In sixth grade, the difficulties become more pronounced, as between 60 percent and 70 percent of students cannot solve basic math problems and 80 percent do not reach the expected reading level for their age.
Despite the progress made, 6.2 percent of children and adolescents are engaged in economic activities in conditions that are unacceptable for their age. In addition, “criadazgo,” considered a form of forced child servitude by the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC/C/PRY/CO/4-6), affects some 46,000 girls.
Child protection continues to be a challenge. 16.7 percent of students aged 13 to 18 have experienced some form of physical or psychological abuse at school. In 2024, the Public Prosecutor's Office received 3,521 reports of sexual violence. In 2022, 139 children and adolescents committed suicide. Mental health services are less accessible to children and adolescents.96.2% of children under the age of 5 are enrolled in the Birth Registry (2024).
22.6 percent of women aged 20 to 24 were married or in union under the age of 18. This data partly explains why Paraguay has the fourth-highest rate of teenage pregnancy in the region (70 births per 1,000 women aged 15 to 19). Some social practices and norms, such as those that justify violence and the aforementioned “criadazgo,” also contribute to maintaining and perpetuating vulnerabilities and exclusion in childhood.
Paraguay is exposed to natural hazards and slow-onset risks, especially in the most vulnerable rural and indigenous communities.
Paraguay submitted two Voluntary National Reviews (2018 and 2021) documenting progress, challenges, and gaps in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The country fulfilled its reporting obligations to the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which issued Concluding Observations on the Fourth to Sixth Periodic Reports in 2024.
Taking these Observations into account and in dialogue with the Government of Paraguay, UNICEF focuses its Country Programme on reducing inequalities and advancing children's rights through intersectoral approaches that include promoting integrated services in priority regions, strengthening data-based planning, and advocating for public policies.

During 2025, the first year of implementation of the 2025–2029 Country Programme (since March), as well as the transition between the UNICEF Strategic Plan (SP) 2022–2025 and 2026–2029, the Paraguay Country Office (PCO)  consolidated its role as a technical reference for guaranteeing children's rights, strengthening the Paraguayan State's capacity to move toward more inclusive, equitable, and sustainable development.
In a context of deep institutional transformations driven by the Future Focus Initiative (FFI), UNICEF focused its efforts on high-impact strategic results, prioritizing scalable and sustainable interventions for the most vulnerable children and adolescents. Programming was supported by robust technical assistance, evidence-based advocacy, inter-institutional partnerships, and greater sectoral coherence, ensuring that national priorities and those of the United Nations Development Sustainable Cooperation Framework in Paraguay 2025–2029 (UNSDCF) were translated into concrete changes in policies, services, and outcomes for children.
To ensure that children are healthy, well-nourished, and developmentally on-track, UNICEF contributed significantly to strengthening the health system and early childhood community services, with interventions aimed at reducing the exclusion already mentioned in the context and ensuring that every child has access to care, nutrition, and stimulation from the earliest years of life.
The inclusion of the Early Childhood Development (ECD) module of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in Paraguay's Permanent Continuous Household Survey provided, for the first time in almost a decade, updated data on early childhood development that are comparable with the results of the MICS 2016. As a result of this, Paraguay has a solid evidence base to guide public policies aimed at early childhood. This progress will provide a baseline for measuring the impact of the National Comprehensive Early Childhood Care Programme “Semillas del Futuro” (Seeds of the Future) launched in 2025 by the Government of Paraguay, with technical support from UNICEF.
UNICEF continued to expand the "Maestras Mochileras" (Backpack Teachers) model and the “Educadoras Itinerantes” (mobile educators), community-based care models in the education and protection sectors that bring early stimulation to homes in dispersed rural communities. With 135 new teachers trained in 2025 —for a cumulative total of 440— the programme reached 8,640 children under the age of three, supporting their families in sensitive parenting practices, social-emotional development, appropriate stimulation, and games to strengthen early skills. This progress reflects the programmatic shift in UNICEF's Strategic Plan toward integrated interventions in the most vulnerable communities, where access to services is limited.
UNICEF supported the strengthening of public policies and resilient systems in maternal and child health, nutrition, and WASH through strategic technical assistance to the Ministry of Health (MoH), promoting evidence-based decisions and more effective territorial coordination with local governments. As a result, key primary health care regulations were updated, the Primary Health Care Georeferencing Information System (SIGAPS) platform was launched to improve real-time data management, and, for the first time in 17 years, a hospital obtained “Mother and Child Friendly” certification, raising the standards of quality and humanization of the service, after the initiative was taken up again by the current MoH authorities.
To reduce child malnutrition, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of the health system by expanding the community use of the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape, providing technical support to the Food and Nutrition Surveillance System (SISVAN), and distributing micronutrient supplements to 6,600 children under five. It also conducted a national study on anemia and malnutrition that will guide cost-effective interventions. In schools, UNICEF promoted healthy lifestyles in 50 schools, benefiting more than 10,000 students and their families and raising awareness among 400 teachers. The online campaign “Cooking is Caring” reinforced these initiatives, promoting healthy eating practices and intergenerational communication, expanding its reach through food influencers with their children and athletes.
With UNICEF's support, 289 schools gained access to safe water, helping to reduce historical disparities for children and adolescents. The "Ñamopoti Ñande Aljibe" campaign, developed in coordination with the government of the Boquerón Department (Paraguayan Chaco), provided 8,500 children with access to safe water in highly vulnerable contexts.
These actions contributed directly to Effect 2 of the UNSDCF, which seeks to improve the health and socioeconomic indicators of the population —especially vulnerable children—by 2029, reducing poverty and inequalities in access to opportunities.
To enable more children and young people to learn and develop life skills, UNICEF strengthened the education system, improving basic learning, supporting the prevention of school exclusion, and promoting accessible, inclusive, and relevant education for the most vulnerable.
UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Education and Science (MoE) in consolidating the ¡Vamos a la Escuela! (Let's Go to School!) initiative, which directly benefited 37,208 students, strengthened the management of 300 schools, and reached more than 80,000 children through diagnostic learning assessments in 28 municipalities.
Learning Recovery Spaces (ERA), a learning programme piloted with technical and financial support from UNICEF, within the framework of the¡Vamos a la escuela” initiative, are key to reversing educational gaps. In 2025, 39,000 students participated in these spaces, achieving improvements of 43 percent in communication skills and up to 90 percent in mathematics compared to their initial assessments. These advances demonstrate the sustained impact of the initiative, which has trained 1,879 teachers since its inception, including 500 trained in 2025, reflecting the education system's commitment to strengthening the quality of teaching and pedagogical attention.
UNICEF provided technical support to 16 teacher training institutes to integrate approaches to child development, early childhood education, and Universal Design for Learning into their curricula. To expand educational opportunities, PCO assisted the MoE in developing the first National Guide to Multi-grade Teaching for early childhood education, a key advance that improves the quality of practices in more than 2,200 classrooms where a single teacher teaches children of different ages. UNICEF strengthened intercultural education by producing materials in 18 indigenous languages, ensuring that young children receive support and stimulation in their mother tongue.
A significant achievement in 2025 was the development of the Multisectoral Coordination Guide Against Educational Exclusion (GAE), which, for the first time, established clear protocols for collaboration between schools, Municipal Councils for Children and Adolescents (CODENI), and community services to prevent school dropouts. With technical support from UNICEF, the GAE has the potential to strengthen the intersectoral response and timely referral of at-risk cases, moving towards a more inclusive and protective education system aligned with the UNICEF’s Strategic Plan 2026–2029.
With UNICEF's technical support, the Early Warning System to Prevent School Dropouts (SAT) began to strengthen schools' capacity to identify students at risk of dropping out early on. Although still in the adjustment and consolidation phase, this data-driven management tool has already enabled MoE management teams to explore new ways to activate personalized support actions.
UNICEF contributed to strengthening timely enrollment through a communication and advocacy campaign implemented at the beginning of the school year in 28 school districts, with events that actively involved local authorities. The campaign, disseminated on social media and community radio stations, amassed over 2,000,000 impressions, reached 1,900,000 listeners via radio, and generated over 2,000 visits to the landing page. To commemorate World Children's Day, the country office published an opinion piece on child poverty. It also launched a positioning campaign Amigo Invisible, with the support of UNICEF Brazil, reaching 1,000,000 people.
Likewise, the continued development of accessible digital books for students with visual impairments or different learning styles, as well as the validation of bilingual materials for indigenous communities, strengthened educational inclusion.
These actions contributed directly to Effect 1 of strengthening the coverage, quality, and comprehensiveness of state institutions, including education, of the UNSDCF.
To reduce the number of children living in multidimensional poverty, UNICEF supported the Paraguayan government in generating evidence, improving official data, and promoting social protection and care policies that are more inclusive, equitable, and sensitive to children's needs.
A strategic result of UNICEF cooperation in 2025 was the technical support for updating the Tekoporã Programme selection algorithm and implementing the early childhood module of the Social Household Registry in the first 10,000 households. The implementation of the revised algorithm has improved the programme’s targeting, refined eligibility criteria, and strengthened the identification and prioritization of the most deprived households. This improved accuracy was reflected in the annual expansion of beneficiary children aged 0 to 5, which increased from 82,000 to 84,650.
UNICEF contributed to strengthening the analysis of deprivation in households with children by providing technical assistance for the creation of “Canasta de Cuidados” (Care Basket), a new tool from the National Institute of Statistics that measures the economic cost of raising children and adolescents per household. Likewise, by updating the curriculum and teaching materials, PCO supported the technical course for early childhood caregivers of the National System of Training and Labor Education, with the Ministry of Labor.
The PCO contributed to strengthening social protection policies through technical assistance and generating evidence on the cost of childcare and strengthening the social registry of households, drawing on experiences from other countries in the region, for initiatives such as the National Care System, Tekoporã, and Zero Hunger. Within the framework of support for the Zero Hunger Programme and the UNSDCF, UNICEF and the Resident Coordinator's Office promoted the creation of an inter-agency coordination table and successfully advocated for Paraguay's accession to the Global School Food Coalition. 
This technical assistance strengthened the State's capacity to make informed decisions on social policies, in line with the recommendations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child and UNICEF's Theory of Change for the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. It also contributed directly to Effect 1 of the UNSDCF, which seeks to expand the coverage, quality, and comprehensiveness of social protection system institutions—with an emphasis on households with children in situations of poverty and vulnerability—reducing inequalities and strengthening social policies based on data and a rights-based approach. 
To protect children and adolescents from violence, UNICEF strengthened essential child protection services, national technical capacities, territorial responses, and community interventions aimed at preventing, detecting, and addressing situations of violence, abuse, exploitation, and psychosocial risk.
UNICEF supported government commitments to end violence through system strengthening, coordination, evidence generation and specialized victim services.
To strengthen the MoH's planning, monitoring, and evaluation capacity, UNICEF developed the first national baseline for adolescent mental health, the Child and Adolescent Mental Health – Situational Analysis (CAMH). This study is a milestone for the country: for the first time, gaps, available human resources, care pathways, and the needs of the adolescent mental health system were identified. The CAMH is a strategic tool for guiding public policy and designing evidence-based mental health interventions. UNICEF contributed to the strengthening of the National Health System through the training of 120 Ministry of Health (MoH) professionals in child-friendly clinics. These clinics provide care for girls and adolescents who have been victims of sexual violence, abuse, and child pregnancy. This training enhanced the quality and sensitivity of initial responses, thereby strengthening critical protection pathways.
To strengthen the community response to psychosocial crises, UNICEF provided training in psychological first aid and suicide prevention to 263 professionals from the fields of health, child protection, and education. Concurrently, the Safe Spaces initiative, implemented in the municipalities of Lambaré, Tobatí, and Mariscal Estigarribia, with support from UNICEF, has provided a protective environment for over 300 adolescents, enhancing their emotional well-being and facilitating community integration. 
To prevent sexual abuse, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Children and Adolescents in developing the "We Are All Responsible" campaign, which reached 1,473,659 people through digital media.
UNICEF strengthened the regulatory and programmatic framework for protection by providing technical assistance for the development of the National Adolescence Strategy—which integrates mental health, violence prevention, and a territorial approach—and the design of the Caregiver Care Strategy as a structural component of future public policies. In the legislative sphere, it provided key technical evidence for the National Congress to reject the disproportionate increase in penalties for adolescents in conflict with the law. It also strengthened the design of the future "Seeds of the Future" Early Childhood Centers, incorporating criteria for protection, mental health, and safe environments into their management models. These changes will directly benefit more than 600 children through the initial implementation phase.
These actions contributed directly to Effect 1 of the UNFDCF, which aims to ensure that social protection system institutions expand the coverage, quality, and comprehensiveness of essential services for vulnerable children and adolescents, reducing gaps in protection, mental health, and well-being, and strengthening coordinated, rights-based responses. 
To better protect children against disasters and climate and environmental risks, UNICEF supported the country in institutional preparedness, emergency coordination, promotion of resilient practices, and operational strengthening of the office to ensure continuity and timely response.
Although no large-scale emergencies requiring full activation of the system were recorded in 2025, UNICEF maintained its capacity to support the Paraguayan State in responding to crises by updating the Business Continuity Plan (BCP), coordinating with other United Nations agencies, funds, and programes, and promoting green office practices.
Throughout 2025, the CO implemented the three programmatic shifts of the Unicef Strategic Plan (SP) in a concrete and verifiable manner.
The shift towards “Focus” was achieved by concentrating efforts on prioritized territories (Chaco, which is the region where the most marginalized population lives and is one of the most vulnerable to the climate crisis, and Asunción and Concepción, which have a significant number of poor children in urban areas.) and structurally excluded populations: indigenous children, adolescents, girls who are victims of violence, rural children, and persons with disabilities.
The shift toward “Scale” was evident in the national adoption of MICS indicators for Early Childhood Development, the consolidation of ¡Vamos a la Escuela! as a replicable model, and interministerial coordination to bring community and mental health interventions to new locations.
The shift towards “Differentiation” was observed in the territorial adaptation of interventions, in the cultural validation of methodologies such as EASE, and in collaboration with government institutions to adjust services and policies to local realities.
UNICEF strengthened the private sector's commitment to family-friendly policies by promoting the Caring Companies Platform (ECU in Spanish) together with the Global Compact Paraguay. Its presentation at the Sustainability Congress of the Association of Christian Entrepreneurs (ADEC) in July led to reached 75 companies, 42 registered and 22 completing the ECU self-assessment process, enabling the next phase of plans to improve family-friendly policies. In addition, key partnerships were established with the insurance company Fénix Seguros and the Punto-Farma pharmacy chain.
In 2025, a total of 4,700 individuals contributed monthly donations to UNICEF, marking a 27 percent increase compared to the previous year. This civic and corporate commitment has strengthened the financial sustainability of the Country Programme and expanded UNICEF's social legitimacy in Paraguay.
Communication and advocacy strategies strengthened key public policies by positioning ERA as a MoE strategy to recover learning loss and promote healthy lifestyles in coordination with the National Zero Hunger Programme. The participation of influencers and partnerships with the private sector amplified the reach of the messages, allowing UNICEF to maintain its public positioning and capacity for intersectoral dialogue, even in a challenging context, to continue advocating for the rights of children and adolescents. 
In operational terms, the office’s internal efficiency was strengthened in 2025. The effective use of regular resources (RR), the timely execution of thematic funds, improvements in cash transfer processes to partners (HACT), supplies, and risk management, as well as the updating of the Business Continuity Plan and the implementation of green office measures, enabled the maintenance of high management standards in an institutional context characterized by a heavy workload and ongoing functional reorganization. This process was significantly influenced by the FFI, which involved structural adjustments, redistribution of functions, and new requirements in terms of efficiency and accountability.
PCO, in collaboration with Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay, introduced the People & Culture Multicountry model for the Southern Cone region. This strategic move aimed to consolidate and strengthen the organizational capacity of the four country offices by establishing a unified sub-regional People & Culture (P&C) function.
As a result of this initiative, there was a total cost reduction of 43%. Furthermore, the consolidated model enabled the teams to benefit from a diverse range of expertise, improving the quality and breadth of support provided to each country office.
The working environment remained stable and positive thanks to the PCO team's commitment to UNICEF's mission, their ability to adapt, and the technical and strategic support provided by the Latin American and Caribbean Regional Office (LACRO) and Headquarters, which proved crucial during the transition. Despite the pressures and complexity of the reorganization, internal coordination allowed for the timely channeling of resources and maintained programme continuity and quality throughout the year.
Coordination with the United Nations System in Paraguay was consolidated as a strategic pillar of UNICEF's work. Active participation in the planning and implementation of the 2025-2029 Cooperation Framework allowed for the alignment of priorities, optimization of resources, and promotion of multisectoral interventions with greater reach. As a result, areas such as early childhood, social protection, violence, inclusive education, and mental health took on a more integrated approach, strengthening a common vision of the UN system to accelerate progress toward the SDGs.
2025 was a year of concrete achievements and strategic preparation, which articulated the transition between the 2022–2025 SP and the 2026–2029 SP. Systems were strengthened, evidence was updated, capacities were expanded, and direct support was provided to the most vulnerable communities, laying a solid foundation for sustained transformation. It was a year that anticipated a Paraguay where every child and adolescent can grow up with real opportunities, protected and fully recognized in their dignity.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF faced both internal and external challenges, requiring constant adaptation to achieve results. This process reaffirmed the value of flexible, evidence-based management and provided key lessons on how PCO should respond while maintaining its focus on the most vulnerable children.
The implementation of the SAT to prevent school dropouts made partial progress. Due to challenges in its adoption, which included difficulties in manual data collection and technological limitations, strengthening the MoE's information management capacities will be required. The lack of unified protocols to guide the response to SAT alerts is an opportunity for improvement.
Work in adolescent mental health revealed significant gaps: insufficient specialized professionals, fragmented care pathways, limited capacity for resolution at the primary care level, and significant regional inequalities, especially in the Chaco and indigenous communities. The first national baseline made clear the system's limitations in responding to crises. 
Technical assistance for updating the Tekoporã algorithm that identifies the excluded population highlighted the fragility of social information systems. Challenges remain in interoperability, updating, data quality, and technological sustainability. UNICEF will continue supporting the MSD in overcoming these challenges.
Paraguay is vulnerable to the climate crisis. UNICEF works in coordination with other United Nations agencies to prepare for emergencies and support the Paraguayan State in the event of natural disasters.
The implementation of the FFI posed significant challenges at the operational level. These challenges included the restructuring of functions, changes in the PCO team and the reassignment of tasks. These challenges were reflected in the analysis and design of the CPMP (Country Programme Management Plan). UNICEF will continue to work to strengthen the team to respond to these changes, as well as to implement actions to maintain the working environment during 2026.
2025 provided valuable lessons learned.  “Let's Go to School” and the ERA strategy demonstrated that accurate diagnoses could mobilize the system toward learning recovery: assessments in 300 schools identified more than 30,000 students who required support. The need to integrate measurements from the outset, have clear operational models for each territory, strengthen teacher coaching, and advance the automation of the SAT and the unification of its protocols was reaffirmed. 
It was also learned that innovations such as accessible digital textbooks, that enable children with disabilities to learn through the use of available technology, require systematic coordination with the MoE, along with the corresponding institutional appropriation. The potential use of Artificial Intelligence shows opportunities, but also the need for greater support to departmental education directorates to ensure sustainability and in-service training.
Although the ERA strategy showed encouraging results and was recognized as a national strategy by the MoE, it still requires operational models contextualized to schools and a more robust tracking and monitoring system to verify the frequency of sessions and ensure the quality of implementation to effectively contribute to the improvement of learning.
The implementation of Tekoporã's new algorithm highlighted the importance of having robust, interoperable, and up-to-date information systems, showing that social modernization requires not only technical adjustments but also technological investment, good data governance, and installed capacities. 
A strategic opportunity was also identified to incorporate MUAC as a nutritional monitoring tool in early childhood, which would improve the detection and monitoring of nutritional risks. 
Finally, given the political relevance, broad coverage, and interoperable capacity of the Zero Hunger programme, it is essential to guarantee resources so that UNICEF can continue to support its interministerial implementation alongside the MSD, in line with the assistance already provided to the MoE and MoH.
At the operational level, the FFI provided valuable lessons on change management. Experience showed that staff resilience depends on clear and constant communication, emotional support, external institutional support, and realistic advance planning that reduces uncertainty.
In addition, PCO learned that operational efficiency requires more strategic procurement planning, better alignment between supply and programming, and systematic communication with implementing partners.
Focused on the future, UNICEF will use the knowledge gained during 2025 to deepen the implementation of the 2026–2029 SP, with an even more integrated, territorial, and systemic approach.
Early childhood will continue to be a strategic priority for PCO. Evidence from MICS opens the opportunity to promote an integrated national model for early childhood development. PCO will focus its efforts on consolidating integrated services in priority areas, expanding sustainable community models, and strengthening interministerial governance alongside other key actors.
UNICEF will promote an intersectoral response for adolescents that addresses poverty, school exclusion, violence, early pregnancy, care burden, and mental health, strengthening their autonomy through comprehensive health, life skills, and educational transition support, focusing on the challenges faced by girls and adolescents. Protection systems will be strengthened to prevent harmful practices such as child marriage and criadazgo. 
Territorial prioritization will be one of the pillars of UNICEF's work in the coming years. Coordination with municipalities and provincial governments will be strengthened, and the capacity of local teams to coordinate health, education, protection, and social protection services will be supported. Territorialization will make it possible to adapt interventions to highly vulnerable contexts and move toward integrated results at the community level, with data collection that will allow for the measurement of the intervention throughout the programme cycle in Paraguay.
The participation of adolescents -especially adolescent girls- will be key to ensuring culturally relevant and sustainable interventions. PCO will make a particular effort to expand its individual donor base and will establish a Funding Strategy to increase its public and private institutional donors, along with an ongoing review of the affordability plan.
Operationally, PCO will use the lessons learned from the FFI to improve internal efficiency, strengthening planning, risk management, procurement processes, and resource mobilization. A healthy work environment will be promoted, with ongoing support for staff and stronger internal communication mechanisms, while identifying actions to strengthen team capacities.
PCO will continue to explore areas of joint work with other COs in the areas of operations, fundraising, and social policy. UNICEF will expand its partnerships with the private sector, civil society, universities, and young people to promote children's rights.

In 2025, UNICEF continued working to advocate for children's rights in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), promoting a dashboard to track the advance on children's indicators. Peru has surmounted in SDG 3, 6 and 7 but needs to do an effort in SDG 4, SDG 1 and reducing inequalities around the country (Peru: Information System for Children and Adolescents, INEI 2024). At the beginning of the year the CRC shared the recommendations on the periodical government report, which has been a strategic document for UNICEF support to government and counterparts over the year.
Peru still has some political instability, as in 2025, the Congress declared the vacancy of President Boluarte’s office under the constitutional succession mechanism on October 10. Although cabinet reshuffles affected only 6 of the 18 ministries during her tenure, several ministries related to child welfare experienced frequent turnover. Following the inauguration of President José Jerí, the presidential cabinet was completely renewed. The perception of insecurity is notably high (79%), and with the 2026 elections approaching, 69% of the population has yet to express a preference for a presidential candidate (Instituto de Estudios Peruanos. Opinion Report, November 2025). 
Despite the regional context marked by external shocks, and international financial volatility, the economy showed complete recovery throughout 2025. By the third quarter, GDP had grown by 3.3% year-on-year. Inflation in Peru closed 2025 at a low of 1.5%, the lowest annual rate in eight years (OECD Economic Surveys: Peru 2025). Despite the favorable macroeconomic environment and the reduction in monetary poverty, it remains high. In 2004, it affected 27.8% of the population and 36.6% of children (INEI, National Poverty Report, 2025). Peru is considered a country vulnerable to multiple natural hazards. In the first half of 2025, the Amazon faced a severe drought with water shortage that affected crops and increased the risk of forest fires. Peru hosts over 1.66 million Venezuelans, about one-third of them minors (Landing - Peru|R4V, 2024). 
Regarding the health situation of Peruvian children, only 65% of children under three years old have completed their vaccination schedule—well below the World Health Organization’s recommended coverage of 95%. Anemia continues affecting 43.7% of children aged 6 to 35 months, with a stark gap in terms of rural (51.9%) versus urban areas (40.2%). Similarly, stunting impacts 12.1% of children under five, but prevalence rises to 20.9% in rural areas, compared to 8.5% in urban settings. Overweight is emerging as a serious issue, 8.6% among children under five, 38.4% in those aged 6–13 and 29.4% among adolescent girls (Demographic Health Survey, INEI 2025). Mental health is another growing challenge. Reported cases of attempted suicide surged from 672 in 2020 to 3,255 in 2024, with 41% involving adolescent and young adult students (CDC- Mental Health Situation Room, 2025). According to the Ministry of Health, in several mining areas, over 20% of children have blood lead levels above the risk threshold (10 µg/dL). Finally, teenage pregnancy reflects deep inequalities in access to information and sexual and reproductive health services. Rates reach 28.6% in the rural jungle, compared to just 5.1% on the urban coast, underscoring the urgent need to close gaps in access to health services 
In relation to the situation of Peruvian children's education, in 2024, the rate of timely school completion remained high. In primary education, 93.6% completed on time, though the rate was lower among children living in extreme poverty (88.1%) compared to those not in poverty (95.3%). For secondary education, 87.0% of students completed on time, with a significant gap between adolescents in extreme poverty (68.9%) and those not in poverty (90.2%). Despite these relatively high completion rates, learning outcomes remain worrying. According to the national assessment, only 32.8% of fourth-grade students achieved a satisfactory level in reading comprehension, and just 29.5% did so in mathematics. The situation is even more concerning at the secondary level: among second-year students, only 18.4% reached a satisfactory level in reading comprehension, while a mere 11.3% did so in mathematics (Educational Quality Statistics MINEDU/ESCALE), 2025).  
Regarding the situation of child protection, the prevalence of physical and psychological violence at home declined from 41.5% in 2015 to 34.7% in 2024 (children aged 9 to 11), violence at school also decreased, from 50.1% to 43.7%. Despite the improvement, the numbers remain unacceptably high. In 2024, the prevalence of sexual violence against adolescent girls reached 22.4%. Additionally, 15.2% of adolescent girls reported experiencing sexual assault before the age of 12 (National Survey of Social Relations, INEI 2025). Throughout 2025, the Women’s Emergency Centers handled more than 65,000 cases of violence against children and adolescents, one in three cases involving sexual violence, predominantly affecting adolescent girls (Women's Emergency Center - Statistical Report, MIMP 2025). Given the growing insecurity, the rights of children in Peru are at risk with the promotion of inadequate initiatives such as the reduction of the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 years, materialized in Law No. 32330 in May. 
Regarding the social protection of children, in Peru, poverty and social gaps continue to affect children and adolescents. Currently, 3.6 million children live in monetary poverty, and more than 800,000 in extreme poverty. Child labor remains a critical issue, with 860,000 children and adolescents working. The disparity between rural and urban areas is stark: in rural zones child labor rate reaches 24.5%, nearly six times higher than the 4.3% observed in urban areas (INEI, National Poverty Report, 2025). Additionally, 13.7% of adolescents aged 15 to 17 are neither studying nor working. Social program coverage shows significant funding gaps. Closing the gap in the Early Childhood Development Program would require an equivalent to 0.2% of GDP. For the Juntos conditional cash transfer program, the funding gap stands at 69.3% (Monitoring and Tracking System for Sustainable Development Goal Indicators, INEI 2025). National School Feeding Program faces a 10.4% shortfall, while the CONTIGO program, which supports people with disabilities, has a gap of 54.4% (Gaps in Social Programs 2025, MIDIS).

Every child survives and thrives   
In 2025, UNICEF Peru contributed to strengthening early childhood development and adolescent health through technical assistance to the Ministry of Health (MoH), supporting the development of national regulations on Growth and Development Monitoring (CRED, by its Spanish initials), supporting the national review of the Multisectoral Plan for the Prevention and Reduction of Maternal and Child Anemia,  and school-based mental health. The change on the CRED normative will reach out to 2 million children nationwide, extending follow-up to 11 years of age. With the UNICEF contribution growth monitoring coverage for children under five increased from 21 per cent to 44 per cent, while neonatal hearing and vision screening coverage rose to 15.9 per cent in 2025. 
These results were driven by strengthened national standards, expanded professional training, and comprehensive interventions benefiting 13,350 pregnant and 42,581 children under three with support of our implementing partners. UNICEF advanced the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative through an online breastfeeding course co-developed with MoH and the National School of Public Health, reaching 1,774 participants and integrating a digital application for national monitoring.  
In Huancavelica, anaemia prevalence among children under three declined from 47.3 per cent to 32.9 per cent, and in Ucayali from 54.1 per cent to 42.8 per cent. In immunization and primary health care, UNICEF provided technical assistance to MoH to strengthen service delivery in remote and Indigenous territories. In Datem del Marañón, brigades reached more than 53 hard-to-access communities, delivering 2,000 vaccine doses and screening more than 700 children for anaemia and acute malnutrition. In nutrition, UNICEF advanced prevention strategies through the national “Yo Activo Mi Cole” initiative, promoting healthy eating and physical activity among more than 11,000 students in public schools in Northern Lima, using an integrated social and behaviour change and capacity-building, engaging duty bearers with a multisectoral approach. 
Through UNICEF’s strategic leadership and technical support, Peru advanced adolescent health between 2021 and 2025. Intersectoral coordination was strengthened through the National School Mental Health Plan, which has been supported by UNICEF, reaching 84,000 students. Coverage of health and mental health services has expanded significantly, benefiting adolescent girls and contributing to a decline in adolescent pregnancy rates. At subnational level, UNICEF supported the approval of the Multisectoral Policy and Plan for the Prevention of Adolescent Pregnancy in Huancavelica and the Protocol for the Prevention and Care of Suicide Risk in Schools in Loreto—both critical for sustainability in high-burden regions.  
In 2025, the MoH implemented the quality standards in health facilities providing adolescent care with UNICEF support. This mechanism was formalized through a Supreme Decree issued by the Government of Peru. UNICEF with its implementing partners trained more than 1,218 primary health care professionals, 82 teachers, 40 Indigenous leaders and 120 families in comprehensive adolescent health care, with focus on mental health, HIV and gender equality. In Condorcanqui, UNICEF provided through implementing partners care to 755 Indigenous adolescents through mobile teams offering psychoeducation, counseling, and emergency kits for sexual violence. It trained health and local government institutions (UGEL, CEM) on adolescent-friendly care and coordinated health, protection, and education sectors to ensure essential services amid an HIV epidemic alert. 
Every child learns   
UNICEF promoted strategies to strengthen primary and secondary education with a focus on inclusion, gender equity, and adolescent participation, reaching directly and indirectly to 575,000 students nationwide. In primary education, in partnership with the Ministry of Education (MoE), inclusive practices were advanced through Educational Support Services (SAE) in three regions, benefiting over 1,500 teachers and creating 3,700 school-based teams. UNICEF with its implementing partners developed an Inclusive Education Toolbox and AI chatbots supported classroom implementation. Gender-responsive STEM methodologies were introduced in Huancavelica, reaching nearly 2,000 students and reinforcing science clubs, with materials in Spanish and Quechua for future scale-up. UNICEF also supported an accelerated education pilot initiative led by regional education government directorate at the subnational level, in Ucayali, enabling over-age students to reintegrate into primary education. 
At the secondary level, through and advocacy strategy with subnational governments, the “Secondary School as a Life Experience” (SEV) model expanded to 270 schools, benefiting 121,180 adolescents, alongside the “Connected to Learn” program, which improved internet access in Loreto, Lima Norte, and Huancavelica for 28,515 students. UNICEF also worked with 45 civil society organizations to integrate adolescents’ perspectives into policies. Pedagogical practice was further strengthened through the Guiding Framework for Adolescent Support in Secondary Education, peer-to-peer teacher collaboration, and decentralized technical assistance was provided to teachers and specialists. 
In participation and climate action, over 34,000 children and adolescents engaged in consultations and initiatives in alliance with national and subnational counterparts. UNICEF provided technical assistance to MIMP to translate UNICEF strategies into public policy, including implementation of the “Mi Voz Importa (my voice matters)” consultation and the scale-up of the “Brillando Perú (Peru shines)” programme in 14 regions. The “+Poder Adolescente (+Teenagers Power)” survey, co-created with adolescent girls, enabled the assessment of key services and helped to make their priorities and demands more visible. 
With UNICEF contribution, Huancavelica, Ucayali and Loreto, strengthened their participation mechanisms such as the Consultative and Participatory Councils of Girls, Boys and Adolescents (CCONNA, Spanish acronym), “Municipios Escolares” and “Encuentros de Líderes Adolescentes” were strengthened, helping to institutionalize spaces for advocacy and leadership development.  In emergency contexts, UNICEF co-led the Education Cluster in the country and supported MINEDU to implement the Safe Schools strategy and develop a Technical Guide on Protocols and Procedures for Emergencies and Disasters in Education.  
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation  
In 2025, UNICEF supported Peru in strengthening child protection systems through advocacy, policy reform, capacity-building, and humanitarian response. Efforts prioritized violence prevention, family resilience, and multi-sector partnerships. 
With MIMP, UNICEF provided technical assistance to develop a regulatory framework for Family Development Centres (CEDIF) to prevent family separation and violence, benefiting 4,000 families. Collaboration with MIDIS integrated violence prevention into Cuna Más, reaching 277,856 families through home visits and group sessions. Together with the MoE, UNICEF strengthened the Comprehensive School Violence Prevention Programme (PREVI), monitoring 1,780 secondary schools. A new family engagement module benefited 371 institutions, improving collaboration among teachers, parents, and caregivers.  
Positive parenting initiatives in Ucayali, Huancavelica, and North Lima reached 8,800 parents, while 250 service providers were trained in gender-transformative and non-violent child-rearing approaches through implementing partners. Collaboration with INABIF’s Punche Familias Programme expanded emotional regulation and positive discipline services for families at risk of separation, while a WhatsApp-based parenting course increased remote access for 1,200 parents. 
Technical assistance supported MIMP’s Crecer Seguro Programme to integrate specialized services for children without parental care, including through regulatory and operational instruments and implementation guidelines. Two national training courses—on the best interests of the child and protection from violence, including modules on disability, mobility, and gender. UNICEF and MIMP also co-organized an international seminar on strengthening foster care, promoting regional best practices. 
In 2025, UNICEF led advocacy to defend adolescent rights amid proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, partnering with the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, Lima Bar Association, and Ombudsperson’s Office. After Law No. 32330 passed, UNICEF supported a constitutional challenge and co-authored an amicus curiae. With the Ministry of Justice, UNICEF developed a national strategy promoting alternatives to detention and supported PRONACEJ and PRONAPRES in creating methodologies and training for prevention and reintegration. To improve access to justice for child victims, UNICEF assisted MIMP in linking protection services with COMUDENNA and helped the Judiciary develop guidelines for sexual violence cases. 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment   
UNICEF strengthened climate-resilient and gender-responsive WASH governance and service delivery through a school WASH intervention restoring services in 38 schools including a gender-sensitive and climate-resilient approach. SBC interventions reached more than 25,000 students, educators and parents, promoting hygiene, menstrual health, climate adaptation and facility maintenance in four territories. In Loreto, the application of the WASH FIT methodology in health centers strengthened local capacities for sustainable service management and reinforced linkages with regional planning and national WASH policies.  
UNICEF also participated in national coordination platforms led by the Ministry of Housing and the Water Group, advocating for the integration of WASH components—particularly social and behavior change—into public investment proposals to scale them up. For this purpose, UNICEF is strengthening its partnership with SUNASS and other state institutions to leverage conditions for institutionalization and financing. 
In environmental health, UNICEF supported the positioning of lead and heavy metals exposure in children as a public health priority through national and regional dissemination of study findings, strengthening policy dialogue and intersectoral coordination. Strategic partnerships were consolidated with organizations such as Pure Earth, and follow-up agendas for 2026 were promoted in Loreto and Huancavelica, laying the groundwork for sustained surveillance, prevention and response.  
Mechanisms such as CCONNA were reinforced, and environmental competencies advanced through updates to the National Environmental Education Policy and the development of two national guides on Integrated Environmental Education Projects (PEAI) on climate change and biodiversity. More than 1,200 students completed the “Climate Generation” course. 
Every child has an equitable chance in life  
UNICEF supported the Government of Peru in advancing evidence-based policies to reduce child poverty and strengthen social protection programs. Technical assistance was provided to define the baseline methodology for measuring multidimensional poverty, contributing to Supreme Decree No. 014-2024-MIDIS. INEI published the Second Technical Report updating indicators and joint deprivations, with the Multidimensional Poverty Index expected in 2026. UNICEF also advised MIDIS on governance arrangements to ensure institutional sustainability. Also, we have supported several public dialogues to enrich social policy programs in partnerships with the MIDIS and another development actors, such as World Bank, European Union, and Interamerican Development Bank.
Globally, Peru was recognized among seven countries with good practices in reducing child poverty in the study ‘What Works to Reduce Child Poverty’. The JUNTOS cash transfer programme was highlighted, and stories of adolescent beneficiaries were featured in the 2025 UNICEF State of the World’s Children. UNICEF and INEI presented the 2015–2024 SDG Progress Report and strengthened national monitoring through a public platform for children and adolescents. 
UNICEF promoted an inclusive, child-sensitive social protection system through coordination with government, civil society, and international partners, including a joint event with ILO. A roadmap was developed for governance, information systems, and care. Guidelines for the National Disability Policy were approved, and UNICEF supported disability inclusion commitments and financing gap analysis. Technical assistance to the Contigo programme and the development of a Nominal Register for children under six advanced data interoperability were provided. In the case of CONTIGO programme, UNICEF developed a pilot with policy and programme recommendations to improve it. 
Innovations included a WhatsApp messaging pilot with JUNTOS, reaching 19,200 households, and the creation of a real-time public expenditure platform. UNICEF also provided technical assistance to evaluate  the Upper Secondary cash transfer, enabling additional financing for 24,500 adolescents and providing recommendations to adjust this social protection program, also, UNICEF has provided support to subnational governments to strengthen regional health offices to optimize child-focused budgets. 
Migration and Humanitarian responses   
In 2025, UNICEF supported national and subnational authorities to uphold the rights of children in humanitarian contexts, strengthening policies and programmes aligned with the Core Commitments for Children (CCCs). Regarding migration response, UNICEF supported Migrant National Institution (SNM). Through ‘Con Mis Documentos en Regla’, 4,767 migrant families received legal assistance, 1,889 applicants obtained direct support, and 1,071 vulnerable individuals had application fees covered. About 90% of assisted families are expected to obtain ID cards, with 558 already issued.  
Under its humanitarian response, UNICEF assisted 269 unaccompanied and separated children at the Tumbes border, including 99 who received remote support and 42 integrated into Lima through implementing partners. Services expanded to include legal aid, psychological therapy, and tailored assistance for pregnant adolescents. Community-based psychosocial programs reached 3,026 children and 2,037 caregivers, promoting mental health and positive parenting. A total of 196 community leaders were trained in psychological first aid, and 89 individuals referred to specialized mental health services. 
UNICEF implemented the HALDO tool to assess learning in reading and mathematics, as well as socio-emotional skills, for 3,721 children in transit in Tumbes and Tacna, to facilitate their enrolment and access to learning materials and information to more than 3,300 family members. Following up on children assessed in the learning outcomes, UNICEF worked with 55 schools located in Lima to strengthen the inclusion of migrant students in schools, benefiting more than 4,000 children. UNICEF also provided logistical and technical support in response to heavy rainfall and earthquakes in Tumbes, helping to ensure continuity of education in affected schools. 
In Tumbes, UNICEF reached 17,092 people (including 2,610 host community members) through the Humanitarian Action Plan (PAO). In nutrition, UNICEF screened 1,516 children under five for malnutrition, ensured timely referrals, and provided counseling on infant and young child feeding. Additionally, 106 pregnant women and 489 breastfeeding mothers received support, and UNICEF distributed 316 breastfeeding kits and 1,051 nutrition support kits (including water, fruit, and cereal bars) to pregnant and lactating women and young children aged 12 to 59 months. In health, UNICEF supported the continuity of primary health care services by providing essential supplies and equipment, reinforcing local capacity to meet increased demand.  
In Datem del Marañón, drought response efforts assisted 21,637 people, including 10,937 children, while early warning systems benefited 3,360 Indigenous people through our implementing partners. Preparedness was reinforced through staff training on emergency procedures, updated emergency scenarios on the EPP Emergency Preparedness Platform. 
Cross-cutting approach and communication 
From a programme coordination perspective, UNICEF strengthened coordination across sectors and with national and subnational teams including cross-cutting areas such as SBC, gender, communication and advocacy and PM&E.  Regarding partnerships UNICEF has strengthen the dialogue with CAF (Latin American and the Caribe Development Bank) in child protection and health sectors. 
In PM&E, UNICEF developed a study on Indigenous and Afro-Peruvian children; updated child-related administrative indicators to inform advocacy and the CPD process; produced targeted analyses using national surveys; and generated evidence with the Care for Child Development (CCD) evaluability assessment along with the elaboration of policy document based on this evaluability assessment. In gender, UNICEF continued to consolidate the +Chicas Tec (more girls in technology) programme intervention in Lima Norte and laid the groundwork to adapt the model in Loreto as part of the education programme interventions. UNICEF also continued working through the +Poder Adolescente (more power for teenagers) programme to strengthen the Ministry of Women and Vulnerable Population (MIMP) training initiatives aimed at empowering girls. During the year, UNICEF further reoriented its gender approach to strengthen co-creation with sectors and reinforce the cross-sectoral function of gender across the programme. 
In SBC, UNICEF developed strategies to address physical violence against children and to promote healthy feeding practices and immunization, among other priorities. AAP was critical to the emergency response, using U-Report to listen to and respond to community feedback. UNICEF followed recommendations from the Strategic Intention Memo (SIM), based on 2024 SMR, including progress towards establishing a field office in Loreto. UNICEF also strengthened its position in mass media and social networks as a trusted reference on child rights, including through the 75th anniversary campaign and the “Vota por mí (vote for me)” campaign in the electoral context. 
UNICEF led major campaigns, including “Vota por mí” a participatory electoral initiative involving 200 adolescents—and launched “Five priorities for a better Peru for children, 2026–2031” with JNE. Additional campaigns addressed health, education, and fundraising, while UNICEF amplified its public voice through five opinion columns and youth-led media content. 
In 2025, UNICEF Peru continued working with seventeen counterparts (fourteen at national level and three at subnational level) through joint WPs with government entities and through HAC to support the migration response. UNICEF maintained engagement with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Peruvian Agency for International Cooperation (APCI, Spanish initials), as well as with counterparts across government agencies. During the year, UNICEF implemented US$10 million, from which, $1.5 Regular Resources, $5.1 ORR, $2.9 ORE. The RR was focused on acceleration of community health workers, child protection and social policy interventions. 
UNICEF representative has been engaged in UNCT meetings and Deputy Representative and M&E officer in the Programme Coordination Meetings. Private sector, PFP and operation 
In 2025, UNICEF prioritized mobilizing public investment for children by integrating private sector funding and expertise, notably through the Works for Taxes (OxI) mechanism, which is a national government mechanism to channel private taxes into essential services like health, education, and water to the most deprived population in the country. The strategy focused on three areas: securing a legal framework for UNICEF’s OxI involvement, supporting public-private models to address issues such as anemia and clean water, and identifying private partners for funding and technical expertise. The OxI and LATAM airlines initiatives are the result of the CO's work with a focus on Business and Community Resilience over the past few years.
The Business Advisory Council (BAC) held four sessions and a field visit to Loreto, emphasizing anemia reduction. Highlights included LATAM Airline’s Avión Solidario and the Ministry of Health’s OxI initiative. On March 1, Yamandú Orsi assumed the presidency, leading a new Frente Amplio (FA) government, a center-left coalition that governed the country from 2005 to 2019. Without a parliamentary majority, the FA needs to negotiate with opposition parties to advance its agenda.
Child poverty was one of the main topics discussed throughout the electoral campaign. In this context, the new government made strengthening the social protection matrix one of its three budgetary priorities, alongside accelerating economic growth to create quality jobs and to improve public safety. Early signals on tackling child poverty included allocating additional resources in the budget law (about 60% of a 0.2% GDP increase) and convening a Social Dialogue to reform the social security and social protection system, in which preventing child poverty and improving the Care System are key pillars.
In 2025, the National Institute of Statistics released an updated monetary poverty line along with the country’s first official Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI). Twenty-nine percent of children and adolescents live in households affected by monetary poverty, while 28% live in households experiencing multidimensional poverty. When both measures are combined, four out of ten children and adolescents live in households affected by monetary poverty, multidimensional poverty, or both. In all cases, poverty rates among children are twice as high as those among adults, underscoring the persistent structural nature of the “infantilization” of poverty. Families with children face greater economic needs and care-related time demands, without additional income to compensate for these demands.
One in two children and adolescents live in households experiencing at least one deprivation related to housing or basic services (based on MPI data). These findings were presented for the first time in a joint report by UNICEF and the Uruguayan Chamber of Construction. These households exhibit higher levels of overcrowding, structural deficiencies, and insecure tenure and are concentrated in peripheral areas. See also UNICEF advocacy campaign. 
With the support of UNICEF and ILO and after a 15-year data gap, Uruguay re-measured the prevalence of child labor, that was estimated at 6.8% of children and adolescents aged 5 to 17. While boys are more likely to engage in economic activities, girls are more involved in hazardous unpaid work.
Uruguay’s rate of 447 children and adolescents per 100,000 in 24-hour residential care—the highest in South America— translates into more than 3,000 children and adolescents spending an average of seven years in such institutions.
Violence against women and children remains a pervasive reality in Uruguay. According to the latest National Survey on Gender-Based and Generational Violence (EVBGG, 2019), more than seven in ten women (76.7%) have experienced gender-based violence at some point in their lives. Uruguay also registers one of the highest rates in Latin America of women killed by a current or former partner: 1.1 per 100,000 women, according to the Gender Equality Observatory of ECLAC[1]. 
The impact of this violence extends to children and adolescents. Data from the Ministry of the Interior indicate that approximately 53% of women murdered by a partner or ex-partner had dependent children[2]. Also, 20% of children and adolescents are estimated to live in households where women have suffered violence from a partner or ex-partner (EVBGG, 2019). Furthermore, in seven out of ten cases of sexual violence reported to the police, the victim is under 18 years old (Ministry of the Interior, UNICEF, 2024).
According to a UNICEF survey conducted in 2025 in localities with more than 2,000 inhabitants, four out of ten children and adolescents aged 2 to 14 were subjected to at least one violent disciplinary practice in the previous month. Psychological violence is the most frequent, affecting one in three children, while 16.1% were recently victims of physical violence. Similar levels are observed in rural areas among children aged 2 to 4, according to the 2024 Nutrition, Child Development and Health in Rural areas Survey.
Analysis of the 2023 Census by UNICEF, UNFPA, and the Ministry of Social Development shows that children and adolescents with disabilities face persistent inequalities. Disability prevalence among those aged 5 to 19 is 2.9%, and nearly half of them live in households experiencing critical deprivations. These households face greater economic difficulties, heavy care burdens, and challenges to emotional well-being issues, especially among women. Students with disabilities show higher rates of repetition and dropout, and between 2021 and 2024, educational continuity declined by 13.5 percentage points, almost twice the decrease observed in the general student population.
Absenteeism in public lower secondary education has reached critical levels. In 2023, students lost an average of more than 35 school days, and three out of four experienced chronic absenteeism (missing about 17 or more school days yearly), a trend that has intensified since the pandemic. This phenomenon especially affects adolescents from vulnerable backgrounds and is associated with poorer learning outcomes, a higher risk of repetition and dropout, and lasting negative effects on educational trajectories. According to PISA 2022, Uruguay is among the countries with the highest levels of absenteeism, and in the same year, the Educational Trajectories Protection System issued absenteeism alerts for approximately 40% of enrolled students.
Towards the end of the year, the Executive Branch approved the regulations for Law 20,376 on Guarantees for Early Childhood, Childhood, and Adolescence,creating a new inter-institutional framework to strengthen the realization of children's rights and reduce policy fragmentation. Furthermore, since 2025, a legislative bill has been under discussion to create the Office of the Ombudsperson for Children’s Rights.
Based on available evidence, despite Uruguay’s classification as a high-income country, substantial challenges remain regarding the well-being of children. Based on a World Bank new key indicator, Uruguay is classified among the 52 countries with highest income inequality (defined as a Gini index above 40), together with most LAC and Sub-Saharan Africa countries. Uruguay also continues to rank among the Latin American countries with the most pronounced disparities between children and adults. 
Within this context, on December 15, 2025, the Government of Uruguay and the United Nations System signed the Cooperation Framework for Sustainable Development 2026–2030. The Framework emphasizes key areas such as social cohesion, inclusive economic growth, governance, and international cooperation. The Government has officially requested UNICEF to negotiate a new CPD for the period 2027-2031.

Strategic Advocacy and Policy Influence in a Changing Political Context
 
In a year of political transition, UNICEF leveraged its strong positioning as an influential, technical, and experienced children’s rights organization to play a decisive role in shaping the new government’s child-focused agenda. The advocacy strategy centered on presenting Childhood as a State Priority to the new technical teams, guiding strategic and urgent priorities for children in 2025.
 
The UNICEF brand, recognized for its credibility and leadership -perceived by Uruguayans as influential (72%) and experienced (71%) (UNICEF’s Brand Barometer 2025), was instrumental in amplifying evidence-based messages and ensuring that key challenges—child poverty, domestic violence, the right to live in a family, school completion, comprehensive health services, and climate change—were placed high on the new government’s agenda. Public opinion showed strong alignment with these priorities: 59% prioritized action on issues affecting children and 80% expressed willingness to act (according to the same study). 
This positioning and trust were confirmed by the 2025 Country Programme Evaluation and are also reflected in the fact that 157,000 people donated to UNICEF in 2025 —approximately one in six adults—making Uruguay the country with the highest donor rate relative to its population, according to UNICEF data. With a 90% retention rate among new pledge donors after 12 months, Uruguay is also one of UNICEF’s highest-performing countries regarding donor loyalty. This leading position in the country is underpinned by high awareness (93%) and trust (84%) levels sustained over time.
Strategic alliances were key to expanding the impact and sustainability of actions by incorporating diverse voices into evidence-based child public policies. Partnerships with the Chamber of Construction of Uruguay, the Uruguayan Football Association, the International Solid Waste Association and other private sector actors and civil society organizations strengthened outreach to new audiences. Similarly, collaboration with Fundación Cultura Universitaria, the Universidad Católica del Uruguay and other academic stakeholders added key academic perspectives– specially on issues such as the deinstitutionalization of children living in residential care.

Influencing Public Policies to Reduce Child Poverty
 
As recognized by the 2025 Country Programme Evaluation, UNICEF contributed to bringing child poverty to the forefront of public debate and positioning it as a priority for the new government, through evidence-based analysis and concrete policy proposals. To this end, the Country Office has a multi-fold strategy. First, the generation of new strategic evidence: UCO analyzed new poverty measures and collaborated with Office of Strategy and Evidence – Innocenti on the inclusion of Uruguay in the Child Poverty in High-Income Countries report and in the future editions of the Report Card series. 
 
Second, the launch of a public awareness strategy emphasizing that reducing poverty requires a whole society approach based on further investment in children, but also on improved coordination of social protection policies to maximize impact. This approach informed the inclusion of a child-focused perspective and references to UNICEF reports on social public spending in the rationale for the National Budget Law.
 
Third, the development of specific policy proposals. Indeed, UNICEF was invited by the Office of Planning and Budget to actively participate in the evidence-gathering phase of the Social Dialogue convened by the government to reform the social protection and social security system. In this context, UNICEF presented concrete, costed proposals for modifications to the social protection system, including transfers, care systems, parental leave, and school meals. Fourth, UNICEF also reached an agreement with the Ministry of Economy to provide support to improve the monitoring of investment in children within the national budget.
 
Fifth, UNICEF’s strategy also included housing policies, a previous under-addressed area in the public agenda. To address this issue, UNICEF partnered with a key private sector actor, the Chamber of Construction, one of the country’s main business associations, which had not previously incorporated a child perspective into its analyses and proposals.
