A joint strategy for evidence generation, awareness-raising, and advocacy was implemented and resulted in the inclusion of several child-prioritized programs in the government’s Five-Year Housing and Habitat Plan. A follow-up strategy with the Ministry and CAF is planned for early 2026.
Finally, UCO prioritized children and adolescents’ participation. Within the framework of the Social Dialogue, UNICEF, in partnership with the Platform for Children and Adolescents, organized a consultation with adolescents on care, the extension of pedagogical time, and disability inclusion. Its results will be incorporated in the dialogue and will continue in 2026 through U-Report. To further improve the local impact of social policies, UNICEF is providing technical assistance to the Ministry of Social Development in redesigning its structure in relation to the country’s main outreach program, serving families living in poverty.

Comprehensive Approach and Evidence for Protection Against Violence
 
In 2025, UNICEF Uruguay consolidated a comprehensive approach to addressing the interrelation between violence against women and violence against children. To advance this results UCO work was carried out in partnership with key institutions, including the Prosecutor’s Office, the Supreme Court of Justice, and organizations specialized in women and children, all of which recognized the need for robust technical inputs to inform policies, services and protocols.
 
Building on evidence generated in previous years, as well as new research, progress was made in three critical areas: At the request of the National Institute for Women (Inmujeres), UNICEF provided technical assistance to support State institutions in developing a shared understanding of what constitutes vicarious violence and how it should be addressed.  This initiative, together with the updating of the study on children orphaned by femicide and the development of a risk-assessment tool for situations of domestic violence, aimed at establishing a common conceptual framework to guide prevention, protection, and response strategies, ensuring coordinated and effective action across all institutions involved. 
 
Furthermore, UNICEF led the generation of quantitative evidence on child sexual violence—addressing a long-standing data gap in the country—and promoted the development of new instruments for early detection and comprehensive redress. Efforts related to parenting guidelines were strengthened through the measurement and publication of updated data on the prevalence of violent discipline, indicators that had not been collected nationally for 12 years. To further evidence-based policy making, UNICEF with several partners initiated an evaluation of the system for detecting and responding to violence against children in Uruguay
 
Additionally, as part of a broader SBC strategy, quality information for families was made available through the UNICEF’s Parenting Portal, which reached 1.5 million visits, with a 70% engagement rate. Among the most consulted content was Consequences of Violence in Parenting, with 121,756 views.
 
Strengthening the Justice System with a Child-Centered Approach
 
In 2025, a comprehensive set of tools and processes was consolidated to ensure that children and adolescents´ rights and needs are at the center of judicial decision-making. UNICEF, in partnership with the Supreme Court of Justice, the Prosecutor’s Office, and influential academic actors, promoted the specialized training of judicial professionals through practical guides, protocols, and innovative strategies such as Te acompaño en el camino, a pioneering tool designed to support children throughout judicial proceedings. These efforts were complemented by advances in development of a more robust system of indicators on sexual violence, enabling the monitoring of regulatory implementation and improvements in case management.
 
Similarly, in alliance with the Supreme Court of Justice, UNICEF developed the Guide for Monitoring the Special Protection System (24 hours), designed for judges and defenders working with children whose family care has been disrupted and who are placed in residential care facilities or living with national child protection authority (INAU) caregivers. This guide is a key resource to ensure that residential care is used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest possible time.
UNICEF also contributed to specialized training in childhood and adolescence for judicial professionals nationwide. In cooperation with the Judicial Studies Center of the Judiciary, judges and defenders were trained in determining the Best Interests of the Child, based on a guide developed by UNICEF in 2024, as well as in addressing sexual violence against children. This guide has the potential to use in other LACR countries.

Advocacy and Transformation of Residential Care Modalities
 
UNICEF brought the situation of children living in residential care institutions to the public agenda through a robust, evidence-based advocacy strategy. As part of this strategy, UNICEF implemented the campaign La infancia invisible, which aimed to raise awareness about the alarming situation of children living in 24-hour care facilities and to promote a cultural and political shift toward family-based care models. This innovative campaign combined audiovisual content, expert spokespersons, evidence-based storytelling, and widespread digital dissemination. On Meta, it reached 1.9 million people (Uruguay population is 3.5 million), while it generated 3.26 million views on YouTube. LinkedIn also emerged as a key channel for technical audiences with 151,110 impressions and high levels of engagement. This strategy contributed to sustaining the issue on the public agenda, improving understanding of the problem, and positioning UNICEF as a central technical leader in the debate on alternative care.
 
A key milestone in 2025 was the establishment of a strategic agreement with the national child protection authority (INAU) to redesign policies aimed at deinstitutionalization and the prevention of family separation. Within the framework of this historic agreement, key system-level information was generated in 2025 to support transformation efforts. This included analysis of the institution’s governance model, the territorial distribution of programs and services, and the financial costs associated with each modality—data that had previously been unavailable in the institution’s management systems. This evidence will serve as the foundation for a transformation plan that includes the creation of a new program to deinstitutionalize children aged 0 to 3 years living in residential care, scheduled for implementation in 2026.

Adolescent Mental Health: Partnerships and Territorial Expansion
 
UNICEF strengthened its partnership with the new authorities of the National Youth Institute (INJU) and the Ministry of Health to promote the psycho-emotional well-being of adolescents and young people through the Ni Silencio Ni Tabú national program. UNICEF advocated reinforcing the national adolescent mental health policy. This was supported by the incoming authorities who secured an increase in the five-year budget to expand the program’s coverage and reach. 
 
As a result of this alliance, a key milestone was the opening of seven Ni Silencio Ni Tabú Centers dedicated to the care and promotion of adolescent and youth mental health. Each center has technical teams that provide individual and group care, as well as prevention and awareness activities. They have become community reference points and strategic partners for local institutions in the areas of education, health, and protection. To date, more than 14,000 adolescents and young people have participated in activities promoted by the centers.
In 2025, the Espacio Joven was consolidated as a meaningful and sustained youth participation platform within the program and as part of a broader strategy aimed at strengthening adolescent participation in public policies. This space, co-led by INJU and UNICEF, succeeded in integrating youth leaders from local centers, the INAU Advisory Council, and other motivated adolescents. It enabled participants to contribute ideas and proposals for decision-making, design mental health support tools for their peers, and amplify their voices in intergenerational dialogue.

Awareness and Strengthening of Education and Learning Pathways
 
With UNICEF’s support, ANEP (National Agency of Public Education: Uruguayan main education authority) designed and implemented a comprehensive strategy to address chronic absenteeism, a key priority for the new education authorities. To support this agenda, UNICEF generated unprecedented evidence on attendance in secondary education; including a regional seminar, the development of materials for educational centers and an evidence-based communicational strategy for families. The public service campaign sought to raise awareness among adults about the importance of regular school attendance at all stages of education (early childhood, primary, and secondary) to improve educational trajectories. The campaign’s core messages were broadcast by the Office of the President on all national TV channels and radio stations, supported by significant media investment valued at USD 600,000. The digital component reached 1.25 million people, generating more than 700,000 complete views and 21,255 clicks to informational content.
 
UNICEF also supported ANEP in designing the strategy to extend pedagogical time, a priority of the five-year education policy. It also established key partnerships to strengthen reading and writing learning strategies in secondary education through a regional alliance between UNICEF Uruguay, UNICEF Argentina, UNESCO Montevideo, and the ministries of education of both countries. This collaboration enabled the a second regional seminar, training activities, and the generation of qualitative evidence on teachers’ perceptions of reading and writing, consolidating a sustained technical exchange platform between countries. Likewise, UNICEF promoted the development of a writing diagnostic tool in Uruguay, integrated into the ReVuelta Educativa an ANEP’s initiative, to reduce student disengagement in vulnerable contexts.
UNICEF and ANEP also developed the Kit de Convivencia, an innovative resource to promote positive school coexistence through playful and participatory methodologies. The kit engages the educational community in an intergenerational dialogue and reflection. Kits were distributed to 70% of secondary education schools nationwide, and workshops and awareness-raising activities were conducted with school teams, adult mentors, and adolescents.

Promoting Adolescent Voice in public policies
 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened alliances with key stakeholders in the adolescent participation agenda through collaboration in consultation processes and by positioning a set of evidence and tools for the education system and professionals working with adolescents across different fields. New coordination spaces were established with key counterparts such as the Office of Planning and Budget, the Ministry of Environment, the National Youth Institute, and ANEP to promote meaningful participation in policies at the national level. The UNICEF Uruguay Adolescent Board (Mesa Adolescente) was consolidated as a forum for consultation and participation, contributing perspectives to office initiatives, co-designing tools and the co-creating UNICEF digital content.
 
Youth Engagement in Climate Change: From LCOY to COP30
 
UNICEF established a strategic alliance with the Youth Network for Climate Justice, a youth-led movement representing adolescents engaged with the climate crisis and adaptation strategies at both national and global levels. With UNICEF’s support, the Network organized Uruguay’s first Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), with the participation of the Ministry of Environment, civil society organizations, academia, and UNDP. During this event, participants co-created the National Youth Declaration, which compiles their concrete proposals and positions regarding the climate crisis. Three young members of the Network were invited to the Uruguayan delegation at COP30 where they presented the declaration to national authorities, contributing to the National Strategy for Adolescence, Youth, and Climate Change.
 
Evidence-Based, Inclusive Public Policies on Disability
 
To strengthen national evidence base and advancing more inclusive policies, UNICEF supported the Disability Area of MIDES in designing the 2030 strategy to institutionalize a public disability policy. This included the generation in a joint effort with UNFPA of key evidence through the study Persons with disabilities in Uruguay, which analyzed barriers to the full exercise of rights.
 
Additionally, to strengthen inclusive educational policies, UNICEF and INEEd developed new studies on the educational trajectories of students with disabilities. Using longitudinal administrative data and analysis of classroom’s curricular adaptations, relevant information was generated to inform decision-making and promote more equitable education for all children and adolescents with disabilities.
 
Innovative and Scalable Solutions for Children
 
Uruguay became the first country in the world to produce a fully accessible textbook generated with the support of artificial intelligence, thanks to UNICEF’s leadership in partnership with OpenAI, ANEP, and Ceibal. The initiative developed a technological tool to generate accessible educational materials aligned with the national curriculum and textbooks—a scalable solution that can be adapted to other subject areas and replicated in other countries.
 
The solution was released as an open-source resource, accessible to developers and technical teams, at a regional AI in education event organized by Ceibal with UNICEF’s support. The design, piloting, and evaluation of the tool’s use built lasting capacities that, together with the country’s digital education ecosystem, contribute evidence to Uruguay’s regional hub for educational innovation. The initiative, presented at Digital Learning Week | UNESCO in Paris, the Global Disability Summit in Berlin, and the 1st Ibero-American Forum on Inclusive Education in Bolivia, enables the sharing of lessons with other educational systems and demonstrates that accessibility can be integrated from the very beginning of curriculum development.
 
Another major milestone in 2025 was the agreement to launch a Behavioral Science Lab for Public Policy on Childhood and Adolescence by UNICEF, in partnership with the Office of Planning and Budget (OPP) and the Uruguayan Agency for International Cooperation (AUCI). The Lab is an innovative initiative aimed to transform how Uruguay designs and evaluates policies for children through evidence-based approaches. It will generate evidence-based behavioral interventions, foster inter-institutional collaboration, and develop a sustainable operational model. In addition, it will create a Child Well-Being Monitoring System that leverages administrative data from SIIAS and other sources to track critical indicators across age groups and territories, enabling more targeted, adaptive, and equitable public policies. By bringing together government institutions, academia, and international organizations, the initiative seeks to position Uruguay as a regional leader in social innovation, ensuring that children’s rights and well-being are at the center of public action.
These advances in innovation consolidate Uruguay’s potential as a high-income country with a manageable scale, well suited for testing innovative solutions, generating transferable knowledge, and developing replicable models. To this end, the Office is working more closely with UNICEF’s Global Innovation Office to identify and connect with companies, startups, and academic institutions within the national innovation ecosystem to design solutions that expand the impact for children. For instance, TRYOLABS (female-founded/female-led) was selected as one of promising “climate solutions” by UNICEF Office of Innovation. This potential not only drives evidence-based public policies and sustainable change for children in Uruguay but also contributes to the realization of children’s rights at the regional and global levels.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
1.      From Global Strategy to National Impact in a High-Income Country
In 2025, UNICEF Uruguay’s results demonstrate how a strategic focus on critical gaps affecting the most vulnerable children can translate into sustainable, system-wide change, fully aligned with UNICEF’s new Global Strategic Plan and its vision for engagement in high-income countries. By prioritizing high-impact areas where UNICEF brings clear technical leadership, the Country Office strengthened national responses to violence, education exclusion, mental health, disability, and social policy, grounding its interventions in robust evidence and effective advocacy.
These results also reflect UNICEF Uruguay’s contribution to advancing the Global Strategic Plan’s emphasis on scalability, sustainability, and national ownership in high-income contexts. Pilot interventions evolved into national policies, strategies were embedded in public plans and budgets, and partnerships with key state institutions ensured long-term financing and institutionalization. Together, these achievements illustrate how UNICEF’s global strategic vision is translated into national impact, accelerating equitable outcomes for children and adolescents while reinforcing public systems that leave no one behind.

2.      Evidence as a Driver of Advocacy: Consolidating and Deepening Its Use
The experience of 2025 confirmed that the generation and strategic use of robust evidence is essential for influencing public policy and directing resources towards children. UNICEF successfully positioned critical issues on the national agenda through studies on poverty, violence, housing, disability, and education.
However, sustaining and expanding the capacity to produce timely, relevant evidence remains a challenge, particularly in areas where information gaps persist, such as sexual violence, educational trajectories of children with disabilities, access to justice, and the impact of social protection policies. UNICEF must strengthen partnerships with national and academic organizations to ensure that evidence is translated into effective policies and resource allocation and is used by key decision-makers. The 2025 Country Programme Evaluation also recommends strengthening UCO’s ability to produce substantiated evidence of its contributions to public policy.
The Behavioral Science Lab for Public Policy on Childhood and Adolescence, implemented in partnership with the Office of Planning and Budget (OPP) and the Uruguayan Agency for International Cooperation (AUCI), is an initiative that will contribute to this effort.

3.      Strategic Advocacy and Partnerships: Innovating in Consensus Building
UNICEF’s positioning as a technical reference and the construction of multisectoral alliances (government, private sector, academia, civil society) were decisive in expanding the impact and sustainability of interventions.
 
UNICEF played a key role in forging new partnerships with the private sector and civil society, and in strengthening the participation of adolescents and communities in solution-building. It was also crucial for ensuring the sustainability of alliances and avoiding the dispersion of efforts by prioritizing interventions where UNICEF’s added value was a differentiator.
 
4.      Innovation and Scalability: Institutionalizing and Sustaining Progress
Uruguay allows UNICEF to be future-proof: with active government leadership, the Country Office is spearheading new programming and innovative partnerships across key areas, including mental health, education with artificial intelligence, PF4C, next-generation human rights advocacy, and the Behavioral Science Lab. These initiatives demonstrate UNICEF’s capacity to pilot and promote replicable models that transform systems and practices.
The challenge is to continue learning to institutionalize these innovations, ensuring their integration into public policies and their financial and operational sustainability. UNICEF has the capacity and position as a technical reference to support national institutions in adopting these tools, monitoring their impact, and documenting lessons learned to facilitate replication in other contexts. However, this capacity needs to be strengthened to improve agility and scope. Additionally, it is essential to manage the knowledge generated and share it regionally and globally.

5.      Meaningful Participation: Strengthening the Voice (and Action) of Children and Adolescents
Promoting spaces for adolescent participation and incorporating their voices in the design of policies and tools enriched the child rights agenda and enabled more relevant and sustainable responses.
As referenced by the 2025 Country Programme Evaluation, UNICEF deepened consultation and participation mechanisms, especially for adolescents in situations of greater vulnerability (disability, poverty, rurality, institutionalization), with a new diverse generation of the Adolescent Board (Mesa Adolescente). Also, new engagement strategies such as U-Report were launched to continue innovating in methodologies and channels to ensure that participation is meaningful and has a real impact on decision-making. Furthermore and as the Country Programme Evaluation states, it is important to continue strengthen the gender perspective in its engagement and the capacities of counterparts to facilitate inclusive and sustained participatory processes over time.

6.      Evidence-Based Communication: Expanding Reach and Social Mobilization
Evidence-based communication campaigns succeeded in raising public awareness and mobilizing new actors around children’s rights.
UNICEF must continue to innovate in narratives, formats, and channels to reach diverse audiences, especially in a fragmented media environment with high competition for attention. It is crucial to strengthen the capacity to respond to crises and fake news, and to enhance social mobilization to transform cultural practices and perceptions, particularly regarding violent discipline, inclusion, and shared family responsibility. UNICEF’s brand positioning in Uruguay is a key asset in achieving this, alongside the future Supporter Engagement HUB (an initiative that is part of UNICEF BMI), which seeks to develop new forms of mobilization and engagement, aligning institutional narrative with programmatic priorities and audience needs to transform interest and empathy into concrete support for UNICEF’s mission in Uruguay.

Final Reflection 

The lessons learned in 2025 reinforce UNICEF’s role as a catalyst for systemic change for children in Uruguay. The Government supports and benefits from UNICEF’s active technical and advocacy role to reach children in the hardest-to-reach contexts and to achieve sustainable, large-scale change. This also reflects a high level of institutional trust and a clear expectation that UNICEF will continue to remain engaged and invest in Uruguay to support the advancement of children’s rights.

The challenges that children face require an agile, innovative and results-oriented organization, capable of anticipating trends, building strategic alliances, and placing children and adolescents at the center of the public agenda. Advancing child well-being in Uruguay requires not only sustaining and scaling the progress already achieved but also adapting and providing leadership to address persistent systemic bottlenecks in a dynamic and complex context. This is particularly critical in a country that, despite its high-income status, continues to experience deep and persistent inequalities that disproportionately affect children and adolescents. At the same time, Uruguay is able and willing to share with others its successes, efforts and failures to learn and improve and to accelerate advance children´s right in other countries.

Venezuela continues to face a protracted and multidimensional humanitarian situation in which longstanding economic contraction, erosion of basic services, and limited household coping capacity intersect, placing children and adolescents at the center of persistent and compounding deprivation. Since 2013, the country has lost nearly 75% of its GDP, dropping from USD 482 billion to USD 88 billion by 2023. This contraction has had severe consequences for household incomes, the private sector, and the state’s capacity to provide basic services. According to UNDP, annual inflation in 2025 is estimated at 275%, compared with 54.6% in 2024. Families continue to be negatively affected by precarious wages, which reduce their purchasing power. According to more updated figures from the Center for Documentation and Social Analysis of the Venezuelan Federation of Teachers (CENDAS-FVM), the price of the basic food basket was USD 550.4 in June 2025, meaning a family with five members requires at least 5.7 minimum gross monthly salaries to cover the food basket in a month.

Venezuela is highly exposed to multiple natural and human-made hazards, creating significant disaster risks. The country is prone to earthquakes, droughts, heavy rains, floods, landslides, and soil desertification exacerbated by climate change. In 2025, despite the number of tropical storms that affected the country having been reduced compared to 2024 (40 vs 58), the volume of rainfall had increased by 300% according to figures reported by Ministry of Science and Technology of Venezuela. According to the INFORM 2025 Index, Venezuela ranks 27th out of 191 countries globally, while the Climate Risk Index for Children (IRCI) ranks Venezuela 60th out of 200, making it the 5th highest in the region for climate risk to children.

According to the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2026, an estimated 9.6 million people are projected to require humanitarian assistance inside the country, reflecting structural vulnerabilities that have accumulated over time rather than a sudden deterioration of conditions. Within this context, children are disproportionately affected by gaps in nutrition, health, water and sanitation services, and protection systems, with immediate consequences for survival and long-term implications for human capital and social stability.

Although there is no official data on Venezuelan migration, a report by the International Organization for Migration (IOM, March 2025) estimates that 7.9 million people have left Venezuela in the last decade, including children and adolescents. Since 2021, return flows have increased with an estimated 1.4 million people returning between Q4 2021 and Q3 2025, including at least 550,000 people returned through the Government’s “Plan Vuelta a la Patria”. According to the IOM, in 2025, the number of returnees increased by 60% compared to 2024. Population mobility and returns add a further layer of complexity to this already fragile context. Growing numbers of families with children are returning to Venezuela, often to communities struggling to absorb additional pressure on services and livelihoods.

Maternal and child health indicators remain of concern. Maternal mortality is estimated at approximately 227 deaths per 100,000 live births, and infant mortality at 13.9 per 1,000 live births (PAHO/World Bank, 2024). Immunization coverage remains below target: DTP3 at around 60–62% and measles first dose (MCV1) at about 55% (WHO-UNICEF, 2024). PMTCT progress has stalled, with limited declines in mother-to-child HIV transmission (UNAIDS, 2024). Service quality is compromised, with over half of public health centers lacking regular access to safe water and facing critical shortages of medicines, supplies, and biomedical equipment (UNICEF, PAHO, ICRC, 2024). UNFPA reported that adolescent pregnancy in Venezuela has decreased by 20% in recent years. However, the country continues to rank among the highest in the LAC region.
 
FAO’s SDG Indicators Data Portal indicates that the prevalence of undernourishment in the general population decreased by nearly 10 percentage points between 2019 and 2023. The National Nutrition Institute reports that exclusive breastfeeding among children aged 0-5 months was 72.7% in 2024. However, the HNO 2026 estimated that Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) affected approximately 3% of children nationally.

The education system continues to face low teacher remuneration, attrition, reduced learning time, and infrastructure deficits, including WASH. Since 2020, an estimated 100,000 teachers have left the education system. Emerging assessments indicate significant learning gaps in reading and mathematics at the end of primary school: 85.2% and 98.6% of sixth-grade students, respectively, lack minimum proficiency in reading, writing, and mathematics. The gross enrollment rate declined from 85.9% in 2023-24 to 60.9% in 2024-25, indicating that approximately 3 million children and adolescents are out of school.

Children and adolescents in Venezuela face high risks of violence, exploitation, abuse, and trafficking, with an increased threat of gender-based violence for girls and women. Administrative data from 100 of 335 child protection councils in 15 of 24 states report over 95,000 cases of child rights violations between August 2023 and July 2025, mainly related to the right to identity (36.5%), personal integrity (28%), and family care (15.2%). Returns and deportations from multiple countries contributed to increased family separation and reunification caseloads in 2025, requiring case management, documentation, and cross-border coordination.

An estimated 3.8 million people lack access to safe and reliable water services. The National Survey of Living Conditions 2024 revealed that 64% of households experience intermittent access to water and sanitation services and practice inadequate hygiene. In addition, the lack of availability of water in health, education, and protection facilities is critical.

UNICEF Venezuela continues to operationalize the nexus approach by integrating humanitarian response, development programming, and peacebuilding strategies to address the country’s complex and protracted crisis. This approach ensures that life-saving interventions are closely linked to medium-term efforts that strengthen systems and build community resilience. In practice, UNICEF partners with CSOs, CBOS, and public institutions to implement humanitarian actions, reinforces the capacities of local institutions, and sustains a strong field presence in the most vulnerable areas. This allows the organization to respond rapidly to urgent needs in nutrition, health, WASH, and child protection, while simultaneously investing in sustainable, system-wide improvements.

In 2025, UNICEF Venezuela advanced its mandate to protect children’s rights and promote equity through evidence-based programming across five strategic areas: Health and Nutrition, Education, Child Protection, WASH and Climate, Environment, Energy and Disaster Risk Reduction (CEED), and Social Policy and Inclusion. Efforts focused on a subset of strategic results that demonstrate accountability and reinforce UNICEF’s role as a technical partner with national stakeholders and the wider public. All results aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF 2023–2026) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)—notably SDG 1 (no poverty), SDG 2 (zero hunger), SDG 3 (health and well-being), SDG 4 (quality education), SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) and SDG 16 (peace, justice and strong institutions). Despite ongoing economic and social challenges, the year was marked by progress in strengthening institutional capacities, improving data availability, and fostering inclusive policies that prioritize vulnerable groups, including children with disabilities and Indigenous children. Through evidence-based advocacy, capacity development, and inclusive programming, UNICEF helped advance national priorities while contributing to regional and global agendas.
 
Key Results and Strategic Relevance

Health and Nutrition
UNICEF consolidated gains in maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health (MNCAH) and nutrition through a systems-strengthening approach that improved access and quality for vulnerable populations. In partnership with national and local authorities, priorities included continuity of care, workforce capacity, and health care facility functionality in regions with systemic constraints.

In 2025, UNICEF’s strategic focus on increased access and quality services drove a measurable reduction in mortality rates across supported regions, highlighted by a decline in MMR between 2024 and 2025 from 151 to 113 in Zulia, 324 to 253 in Miranda, and 80 to 62 in Bolivar. This positive trend extended to child health outcomes, with Bolivar seeing a decrease in infant mortality from 14 to 7 and Zulia seeing a decline in neonatal mortality from 21 to 15. With UNICEF’s support, Venezuela significantly strengthened its cold-chain system by installing 306 solar refrigerators between 2022 and 2025, reducing the national gap by 55%, thereby expanding equitable access to vaccines for remote and vulnerable communities.

To sustain these gains, UNICEF expanded training and supervision networks, introduced real-time communication channels between primary health care providers and specialists, and supported retention of neonatology experts. Infrastructure improvements included rehabilitation and re-equipment of health facilities across prioritized states, ensuring functionality of maternal and child services. Essential commodities—including incubators, ultrasound equipment, and obstetric kits—enhanced emergency response capacity.

UNICEF and partners screened 184,000 children under five, treated 22,000 cases of severe and moderate acute malnutrition, and distributed micronutrient powders to prevent deficiencies.  This strengthened service delivery enabled the recovery of 92% of children admitted to the nutrition program, a sector where UNICEF led 89% of the total humanitarian response. A significant transition from iron and folic acid supplements to multiple micronutrient supplements for pregnant and lactating women marked a critical step toward reducing maternal mortality.

UNICEF also demonstrated agility in humanitarian response, delivering life-saving health interventions to populations affected by floods and landslides in Apure and other states. Community outreach activities, including national care days in remote regions, ensured access to antenatal care, safe deliveries, pediatric consultations, and preventive health services for hard-to-reach populations.

Through these integrated actions, UNICEF Venezuela achieved tangible results in reducing preventable maternal and neonatal deaths, improving service quality, and addressing malnutrition and HIV. Beyond immediate service delivery, these results contributed to strengthening the continuity and quality of essential health and nutrition services for children, while reinforcing national and local capacities to prevent severe malnutrition and avoidable child morbidity and mortality. These outcomes reflect UNICEF’s commitment to equity and resilience, advancing national priorities under the UNSDCF and global goals under SDG 2 (zero hunger) and SDG 3 (health and well-being). By combining evidence-based programming, institutional partnerships, and community engagement, UNICEF continues to deliver life-saving interventions and strengthen health systems for every woman and child.

Education
In 2025, UNICEF played a pivotal role in strengthening Venezuela’s education system through systemic reforms and targeted interventions that advanced equity, quality, and inclusion. Working closely with the Ministry of Education, the Universidad Experimental del Magisterio Samuel Robinson (UNEM), and local authorities, UNICEF supported policy development, program implementation, and pedagogical innovation, introducing evidence-based tools to guide decision-making. These efforts consolidated the Child-Friendly Schools (CFS) model as a national benchmark, adapted to diverse contexts, including highly vulnerable Indigenous areas. These outcomes demonstrate UNICEF’s contribution to national priorities under the UNSDCF and global commitments to SDG 4 on quality education and SDG 10 on reducing inequalities.

At the state level, UNICEF reinforced supervisory structures and municipal CDCEs, enabling leadership and teaching improvements that drove measurable gains in school performance. According to the UNICEF monitoring system, principals and supervisors in UNICEF-supported schools improved management competencies by 72%, while selected teachers enhanced pedagogical practices by 61%, covering planning, instructional strategies, and assessment. At the university level, UNEM scaled culturally relevant training for Indigenous teachers and established standards for school principals, reducing costs and ensuring national scalability through a new Learning Management System (LMS). At the community level, free, prior, and informed consultations validated socio-productive calendars in five Indigenous communities, strengthening Indigenous Education as a quality modality.

These systemic changes translated into tangible outcomes for children. Implementation of the five dimensions of the CFS model resulted in enrolment increases of 12%, reintegration of 11% of previously out-of-school children, and a 72% improvement in regular attendance. Learning outcomes rose by 17 percentage points, with language scores increasing from 60% to 78% and math from 36% to 53%. Nutrition and WASH indicators also advanced significantly, with WASH standards improving by 44 points and nutrition by 27 points. Community participation surged by 86%, reinforcing local ownership and sustainability. These efforts supported access to learning for thousands of children, as well as strengthened institutional and school-level capacities, helping sustain education services and mitigate learning losses in a context of prolonged system stress.

The CFS model demonstrated strong adaptability and ownership, achieving 80% progress across its five dimensions in 40 core schools. Strategies to reduce gender gaps were implemented in 62% of schools, and 82% integrated cultural diversity into learning resources. Specialized training supported teachers working with children with disabilities, while intercultural approaches ensured inclusive education for Indigenous populations.

UNICEF’s approach combined multimodal training, technical assistance, and intersectoral coordination, creating spaces for sharing best practices among governmental and non-governmental actors. By strengthening leadership, teaching practices, and community engagement, UNICEF positioned itself as a leading technical reference in education capacity development. These achievements not only improved access and quality for thousands of children but also laid the foundation for scaling transformative models nationwide in 2026, promoting sustainability, equity, and inclusive education for all.

Child Protection
2025 was a pivotal year for child protection, and through strategic interventions and innovative partnerships, UNICEF leveraged the humanitarian programme as a catalyst for system-level results. Strategic interventions at national, municipal and community levels, guided by benchmark analysis, paved the way for an increasingly harmonized and standardized approach to child protection service delivery. UNICEF contributed to the gradual improvement of system maturity in line with global standards, initiated the development of child protection referral flows, and supported the National Children’s Rights Institute (IDENNA) to initiate a national-level digital register of programs and services. Outcomes included strengthening youth participation in rights-based advocacy through networks for children with disabilities and Indigenous youth. Despite a complex operating environment, UNICEF achieved systems-level improvements while delivering life-saving services, contributing to UNSDCF Outcome 3.3 and SDG 16.7 on inclusive participation.
 
UNICEF, with implementing partners and in coordination with local CP authorities, reached over 70,000 children and adolescents with essential protection services, including mental health and psychosocial support, case management, and specialized assistance for victims of violence, abuse, and exploitation. At the systems level, UNICEF worked with key government institutions, such as IDENNA, the Ombudsman’s Office, the Prosecutor’s Office, and the Supreme Court, to establish basic standards for case management and referral mechanisms for children affected by physical and sexual violence. Progress was also made toward digitalizing the national child protection information system, improving registry and service coordination.

Direct service delivery included community-based prevention, case management, and specialized support for children in migration contexts, including those left behind. Coordinated mechanisms ensured temporary care, family tracing, and reunification. In addition to direct protection services, UNICEF’s interventions helped strengthen coordination mechanisms and local capacities, contributing to more consistent identification, referral and response for children at risk of violence, exploitation and abuse.

Evidence-based advocacy remained central, addressing sensitive issues such as adolescents’ detention and access to justice. Interagency collaboration with the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA) and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) was crucial in this regard.  UNICEF facilitated consultations for a national benchmark analysis of child protection systems and supported the creation of a cross-border mechanism for family reunification of children left behind in parental deportations. These efforts reinforced UNICEF’s role in advancing rights-based solutions in complex humanitarian contexts.

UNICEF leveraged strategic partnerships to expand reach with minimal investment, turning collaboration into a catalystfor systemic change. Through alliances with the National System of Children’s and Youth Orchestras (“El Sistema”) and the Venezuelan Football Federation (FVF), UNICEF introduced safeguarding protocols and embedded mental health and psychosocial support into their curricula, impacting thousands of children in safe, trusted spaces. A groundbreaking alliance between the Ombudsman’s Office and FVF launched initiatives to prevent child trafficking in sports, setting a national precedent for cross-sectoral protection strategies.
Community-based mechanisms were strengthened through training and accreditation of child protection workers, including music teachers from El Sistema. These workers, endorsed by municipal child rights councils, now identify cases of violence, provide initial counseling, and ensure referrals for comprehensive case management. This approach enhanced local capacity and sustainability while bridging humanitarian and development objectives. Additionally, through a partnership with Movistar, girls and adolescents were able to access UNICEF’s gender-based violence prevention platform, expanding digital protection resources.

Despite funding constraints and operational challenges, UNICEF’s child protection program achieved systemic improvements and life-saving interventions, advancing national priorities under the UNSDCF and global commitments to SDG 16 on peace, justice, and strong institutions. By combining advocacy, innovation, and partnerships, UNICEF strengthened protective environments and positioned itself as a key actor in safeguarding children’s rights in Venezuela’s complex landscape.

WASH and CEED
UNICEF Venezuela ensured access to safe water and improved sanitation for vulnerable populations despite severe financial constraints and operational challenges. Through a comprehensive, cross-sectoral approach, UNICEF reached at least 235,000 people with safe water and eliminated open defecation in targeted areas. These efforts strengthened resilience in communities most affected by systemic gaps and humanitarian needs.
UNICEF prioritized institutional and community settings to maximize impact. Essential WASH services were upgraded in 57 health centers, 89 schools, 49 alternative learning spaces, 21 protection centers, and 30 shelters, creating safer and more dignified environments for children and families. Approximately 10,000 students from indigenous communities benefited from tailored interventions that respected cultural contexts and ensured relevance and sustainability.

More than 20,000 children and adolescents in schools and communities enhanced their environmental awareness and capacity for climate action through education and participatory initiatives. The 89 schools supported by UNICEF incorporated sustainable environmental practices led by students, improving learning environments and reducing negative impacts on ecosystems. Communities adopted climate-resilient WASH solutions, including chlorination systems and solar-powered pumping, ensuring reliable water access while minimizing carbon footprints. In schools, environmental projects were developed to promote sustainability and environmental care, including waste reuse/recycling, school gardens, eco-walls, composting, restoring green spaces, recycled paper production, and rainwater harvesting, among others.

The WASH program demonstrated strong integration with other sectors, amplifying its contribution to health, nutrition, and education outcomes. In nutrition care areas, access to safe water and hygienic environments reduced the risk of diarrhea and other diseases that compromise nutrient absorption, supporting recovery for children under five with acute malnutrition. Hygiene promotion among caregivers further enhances treatment effectiveness. In education, improved WASH facilities in schools and learning spaces reduced absenteeism linked to waterborne illnesses, promoted retention—particularly for girls through menstrual hygiene management—and fostered safe, inclusive environments. In health facilities, the provision of safe water, cleaning supplies, and infrastructure upgrades strengthened infection control and improved conditions for maternal and child health. Protection centers also benefited from WASH improvements, ensuring safe and dignified spaces for families in crisis.

UNICEF’s success relied on a diversified set of implementation strategies. These included direct engagement with the private sector for infrastructure works, provision of WASH supplies to key institutions, and partnerships with community-focused organizations to enhance outreach and sustainability. Alliances with institutions involved from project inception ensured ownership and long-term impact.

By combining technical assistance, infrastructure investment, and behavior change initiatives, UNICEF advanced national priorities under the UNSDCF and global commitments to SDG 6 on clean water and sanitation. These achievements underscore UNICEF’s role in delivering life-saving services, reducing health risks, and promoting equity for the most marginalized populations. Looking ahead, the program’s integrated approach provides a strong foundation for scaling WASH interventions in 2026, reinforcing resilience and safeguarding the rights and well-being of every child. Beyond improving immediate access to safe water and sanitation, these interventions reinforced the functionality and resilience of services in priority settings, reducing health risks for children and supporting the continuity of education and health services.

Social Policy and Inclusion
In 2025, national institutions responsible for disability and Indigenous affairs, CONAPDIS and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples, have integrated intersectional and life-course approaches into public policy, prioritizing inclusion of persons with disabilities and Indigenous children. With UNICEF’s technical and programmatic support, these reforms strengthened equity and non-discrimination by improving strategic planning, enhancing managerial capacities, and defining national action lines aligned with international human rights standards, advancing Venezuela’s progress toward inclusive social protection and rights-based development. Advocacy efforts positioned disability inclusion on the national agenda, reinforcing commitments under UNSDCF Pillar 1 on inclusion and SDG 10 on reducing inequalities.
 
UNICEF also advanced inclusive programming by adapting its global training package for frontline workers into Spanish and contextualizing it for Venezuela—the first such adaptation in Latin America and the Caribbean. This package, validated by CONAPDIS and organizations of people with disabilities, will be implemented in 2026 for teachers, health personnel, child protection counselors, and community authorities. This initiative contributes to SDG 10 on reducing inequalities and UNSDCF Outcome 1.4, while reflecting UNICEF’s Strategic Plan strategies on capacity development, innovation, and partnership. Core resources facilitated the adaptation process and national validation. Additionally, UNICEF supported Indigenous youth advocacy networks, promoting their participation in education policy forums and advancing SDG 4.7 on inclusive and equitable education.

UNICEF secured the integration of child multidimensional poverty measurement into Venezuela’s National Survey of Living Conditions (ENCOVI), which Andrés Bello Catholic University implements with support from the World Bank and the IMF. This breakthrough filled a critical data gap by introducing 16 indicators on education, gender inequality, technology access, health equity, maternal health, immunization, nutrition, breastfeeding, WASH, consumption, and housing conditions. By embedding these variables into national surveys, UNICEF enabled policymakers to design targeted interventions for children based on robust evidence, advancing UNSDCF Outcome 1.3 on inclusive social protection, UNICEF’s Strategic Plan priorities on equity and evidence generation, and SDG 1 on ending poverty.

UNICEF also co-led the Interagency Working Group on Disability Inclusion under the Leave No One Behind platform, reinforcing systemic advocacy and inclusion mechanisms across humanitarian and development responses. These achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s change strategies for coordinated multi-stakeholder engagement and policy convergence, enabled by core resources that sustain collaboration.

Building on 2025 gains, UNICEF will roll out inclusive training programs, launch community sensitization campaigns, and strengthen emergency protocols for children with disabilities. Continued advocacy for budget transparency and expansion of Indigenous and disability rights initiatives will further advance equity and resilience in Venezuela’s social systems, consolidating progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals and reinforcing UNICEF’s strategic positioning for 2026 and beyond.

Contribution to National and Global Priorities
These strategic results illustrate how UNICEF Venezuela advanced national priorities under the UNSDCF and global commitments under the SDGs. They were achieved through a combination of evidence generation, institutional capacity-building, advocacy, innovation, and partnerships, with core funding providing the agility and continuity needed to deliver results at scale.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Complex operating context 
In 2025, UNICEF Venezuela operated in a complex environment marked by persistent structural and operational constraints that affected programme implementation. Frequent transitions among national and state authorities disrupted coordination and limited partner access, while high staff turnover in key ministries (including education and health) compounded these difficulties. Concurrently, progressive reductions in humanitarian funding by major donors created resource gaps that temporarily disrupted implementation and delayed critical interventions for vulnerable communities.

Procurement delays and logistical challenges, exacerbated by adverse weather and precarious infrastructure, increased costs and response times, compromising the comprehensiveness of programme packages. Access restrictions in sensitive geographic areas further challenged outreach and required adaptive community strategies to maintain engagement and service continuity. Data limitations persisted across sectors due to limited access to official socio-demographic and budgetary data and delays in consolidating indicators within integrated systems.

Adaptive approaches and good practices

Despite constraints, UNICEF adopted innovative and adaptive practices that strengthened programme delivery, ensured continuity, and maximized impact. A key practice was the integration of cross-sectoral approaches—linking health, nutrition, education, WASH, and child protection—to deliver holistic outcomes. For example, WASH improvements in schools and health facilities were linked to improved education and nutrition outcomes, reducing absenteeism and supporting recovery among malnourished children.
UNICEF localized and culturally adapted global models, such as Child-Friendly Schools and inclusive education training packages, tailoring them to indigenous contexts and validating them through free, prior, and informed consultations to reinforce community ownership and sustainability. UNICEF also leveraged community-based mechanisms, training and accrediting local child protection workers and educators to identify risks, provide counselling, and ensure referrals—strengthening grassroots capacity and resilience.
Capacity building was central to sustainability. UNICEF prioritized continuous training for health professionals through universities, digital platforms, and adapted methodologies, mitigating the impact of high staff turnover and ensuring equitable access to knowledge. The Learning Management System (LMS) enabled ongoing education in priority areas such as inclusive education, gender-responsive approaches, and leadership, institutionalizing processes, and laying the foundation for scale-up.
Digital innovation further enhanced responsiveness. WhatsApp networks supported maternal health emergency coordination, while digital platforms advanced gender-based violence prevention, offering low-cost solutions that expanded access to critical services.

Strategic partnerships and community engagement
Partnerships with non-traditional actors, such as the National System of Children’s and Youth Orchestras and the Venezuelan Football Federation, enabled the embedding of safeguarding protocols and psychosocial support in cultural and sports programmes, reaching large numbers of children at minimal cost. These alliances exemplify UNICEF’s humanitarian–development nexus, bridging immediate needs and sustainability. Strategic planning and coordination with authorities helped avoid duplication and accelerate implementation, while joint needs mapping and co-selection of intervention sites strengthened ownership and operational efficiency. Community engagement through door-to-door outreach, awareness campaigns, and home visits fostered trust and improved treatment adherence.

Collectively, these practices enabled UNICEF to “do better with less,” reinforced its role as a technical leader, and positioned programmes for sustainable impact in 2026. Evidence-based advocacy and data-driven planning underpinned all interventions, ensuring alignment with national priorities and global standards and enhancing efficiency, equity, and scalability.

Key insights for future impact
The 2024 Real Time Assessment of Humanitarian Response in Venezuela and the 2025 programme implementation provided valuable lessons that will strengthen our strategies moving forward. These insights highlight opportunities to enhance contextualization, coordination, and diversification for greater impact.

Strengthen shock-resilient national and subnational systems. While continuing to address the urgent needs of the most vulnerable population, programming at scale and sustainability of key interventions require support for public systems recovery. 
Deepen local engagement: Early and meaningful collaboration with local authorities and communities is essential to build trust, ensure transparency, and secure long-term sustainability. Future interventions will prioritize inclusive dialogue from the outset.
Deepen community accountability mechanisms: UNICEF will strengthen AAP and feedback systems across all sectors and standardize tools for complaints, monitoring, and follow-up, including for sensitive issues such as SEA.
Integrate and coordinate for efficiency: Fragmented programming and limited intersectoral coordination reduce effectiveness. CO is committed to streamlined planning aligned with Venezuela’s context to optimize resources and timelines.
Strengthening partnerships and capacity: Overestimating CSO capacity and underestimating delivery timelines created operational challenges. OSCs are critical for last-mile delivery, but many still lack the resources or autonomy to manage independently. Moving forward, UNICEF will diversify implementation modalities and forge new alliances to enhance adaptability and scalability.
Leverage digital platforms for sustainability: Training efforts will expand through digital learning solutions to promote replication and long-term impact. Reinforcing inter-organizational articulation is key to efficiency and effectiveness.
Secure predictable funding: Financial constraints underscored the need for resilient institutional systems and reliable financing. Technical solutions and partnerships remain vital, but sustainability depends on robust governance and predictable resources.

In summary, the most common lessons highlight the importance of flexibility, proactive coordination and risk management, contextualized planning, diversified partnerships, and integrated approaches to ensure efficiency, relevance, and sustainability in future implementations, ensuring continuity of results for children in Venezuela’s complex context. Data-driven decision-making and digital innovation must underpin all strategies to improve real-time monitoring and responsiveness. These priorities will position UNICEF to deliver more adaptive, equitable, cost-effective, and context-sensitive programmes that respond to evolving challenges and maximize impacts and sustainable results for children in Venezuela’s complex landscape.

In 2025, the Government of Algeria accelerated  reforms and transformation initiatives aimed at advancing social and economic  objectives while strengthening the country’s convener role in African and  regional agendas. This momentum was reinforced by Algeria’s election as Vice-Chair  of the African Union Commission,  by the  creation of the Algerian International Cooperation Agency (AICA) and the  nomination of a State Secretary for African Affairs. 


  


Africa WorldSkills in Algeria elevated  the value of vocational skills as a driver of economic development and youth employability. The 4th African  Startup Conference convened startups, investors and senior decision-makers to  advance dialogue on innovation and entrepreneurship and skills-to-work transitions. The event brought  together approximately 25,000 participants, including 300 international  experts, 150 investors, 200 exhibitors and 40 African ministerial delegations.  The African Ministerial Conference on Local Production of Medicines and Other  Health Technologies reaffirmed Algeria’s leadership and Africa’s ambition to  strengthen self-reliance and supply resilience through local production,  regulatory strengthening and demand predictability mechanisms. 


  


Macroeconomic projections for 2025,  estimated growth at 4.4 per cent, expected to be driven by non-hydrocarbon  sectors (Finance law 2026; World Bank, 2025). In the 2025 budget, allocation  shares (operating and investment) included 10.4 per cent to the Education,  6.3 per cent to Health, and 15.3 per cent to subsidies and transfers to  individuals (Finance law 2025). Budget execution was projected at 70% in 2025  (Finance law 2026 presentation report). 


  


Child rights and participation gained  renewed institutional visibility. In December 2025, a Child Parliament was  formally set-up within the National People’s Assembly to raise children’s  priorities with decision makers, with young parliamentarians elected from all  Wilayas through a process led by the Ministry of Education. In parallel, the  National Plan of Action for children (2025-2030) reached an advanced stage of  consultation among national institutions and stakeholders under the  leadership of the National Body for the Protection and Promotion of Child Rights  (ONPPE).


  


In health, national leadership reaffirmed the  priority to strengthening primary and proximity-based  primary health care services to improve equity in access across wilayas. This  was further reflected in the establishment of a National School Health Week  during the back-to-school period, with a specific focus on prevention and  healthy behaviours, and on activating school health clubs as local-based platforms for health promotion among  children and adolescents. Civil society organizations led the development of  these clubs and actively participated in the intersectoral school health  commission. The Ministry of Health advanced health sector  digitalization through a cooperation agreement with the High Commission for  Digitalization focused on data exchange and managment among relevant  stakeholders.  A national immunization campaign  against poliomyelitis reinforcing preparedness and civil society engagement reached  95 per cent of under five children vaccinated (Algeria Ministry of Health). 


  


Around 12 million children enrolled at  school for the 2025-2026 school year and 489 new schools opened (APS, 2025). The  Government continued modernization efforts through school digitalization. Mainstreaming  English in curricula was supported by a cooperation agreement with the United  Kingdom to develop the capacities of English teachers and inspectors (APS, 2025), aligned national ambitions linked to  higher education and labour market requirements. Reforms in Vocational  Education and Training (TVET) continued, with the establishment of thematic  and “pole” centers of excellence to strengthen linkages between training and  industrial ecosystems, and the expansion of distance learning modalities to improve responsiveness to labour  market shifts.


  


Youth economic participation also  gained policy prominence. The President announced the creation of industrial  micro-zones to promote youth participation and reduce administrative barriers  affecting youth-led initiatives (start-ups and other economic activities). By  October 2025, more than 440,000 young people were benefiting from the unemployment  allowance (APS, 2025). The Finance Law 2026 increased the allowance from  15,000 to 18,000 DZD, alongside an increase of the minimum wage from 20,000  to 24,000 DZD (Finance law 2026, Prime Minister’s communication).


  


In parallel, national youth leadership  and engagement received expanded support through initiatives to strengthen  young leaders and promote environmental and civic engagement. . The Ministry of Youth  launched a national youth leadership  training programme to build core leadership skills and civic engagement over  a full year. These efforts were complemented by widespread citizen  participation in the national “one million trees” planting campaign, which  mobilized young people and communities around environmental stewardship and  sustainable development.


  


Legal frameworks progressed in child protection  and disability. Two executive decrees published in the Official Gazette (No.  79, 27 November 2025) strengthened oversight of child protection and  integrated a cybernetics monitoring function within the ONPPE to address rising  online and digital risks. The disability law was amended to better align with  the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, reinforcing  principles of non-discrimination, universal accessibility, and social  inclusion. Algeria reaffirmed its disability inclusion commitments at the  Global Disability Summit 2025 through endorsement of the Amman–Berlin  Declaration, including the collective target to reach “15 per cent for the 15  per cent” by 2028—i.e., ensuring at least 15 per cent of ODA-funded  programmes implemented at country level pursue disability inclusion as an  objective—and strengthening measurement and reporting on disability inclusion.Child-sensitive  social protection reforms were introduced, supporting progress toward SDG 1. Maternity  leave was extended from 98 to 150 days with full salary coverage, with  additional extensions in cases of child disability or serious health  conditions. Eligibility criteria for the solidary lump sum grant were  adjusted to improve coverage for persons with disabilities.  Coherence across schemes was strengthened by  transferring management of the special school allowance from the Ministry of  Education to the Social Development Agency under the Ministry of National  Solidarity.


  


Finally, the protracted Sahrawi refugee crisis in  Tindouf remained a major humanitarian concern. Five decades of displacement  continue to drive high vulnerability, including food insecurity and  constrained access to essential services for women and children. In a sharply  constrained funding environment, the SRRP 2026–2027 was developed and  launched in November with 27 partners, against a backdrop of budget cuts  across UN agencies. Within this context, UNICEF strengthened coordination and  leadership for children, supporting a more coherent and predictable response,  while advocating on the deteriorating nutrition situation and supporting the  rollout of the multisectoral nutrition strategy. UNICEF also sustained  life-saving immunization services and, through its partnership with Africa  CDC, supported efforts to strengthen cold chain systems. Donor missions helped  sustain advocacy and resource mobilization. UNICEF leads the Education  Sector, contributes substantially to Health and Nutrition, and plays an  active role in the Tindouf Representatives Group to strengthen preparedness, support  monitoring and evaluation, and safeguard learning continuity for nearly  40,000 refugee children.  UNICEF’s leadership was reflected in a comprehensive SRRP Education chapter  and a detailed, costed rolling workplan for 2026–2027.

Across health and nutrition, education  and adolescent development, child protection, social protection, and  cross-cutting data systems, UNICEF’s engagement in 2025—in support of  Government priorities—focused pragmatically on strengthening the foundations  for results at scale through public policy support, institutional capacity  strengthening, improved coordination mechanisms, and evidence-driven,  data-informed decision-making. The results point to a gradual shift towards  more coherent, integrated and territorially responsive systems, driven by  ongoing national reforms and supported by UNICEF. At the same time, Algeria’s  engagement in regional and continental platforms contributed to positioning  the country as an active actor in advancing shared African agendas on health  systems strengthening, Learning-to-Earning pathways, and social development.


  


Every Child Survives and Thrives 


  


In 2025, Algeria advanced reforms to  strengthen health and nutrition systems, improve equity in service delivery  and reinforce preparedness. UNICEF supported the Government to deliver on  these priorities through high-leverage contributions aligned with Africa’s  health security agenda—particularly local production, regulatory  strengthening and end-to-end supply resilience— supporting Government efforts and reinforcing the visibility of  Algeria’s priorities at national and continental levels. This direction was advanced  through UNICEF support to Government-led policy dialogue and interministerial  engagement on local production of vaccines and health technologies, and further  elevated by Algeria’s hosting of the African Ministerial Conference on Local  Production of Medicines and Other Health Technologies (November 2025),  convened by WHO. The conference helped consolidate political commitment  around expanding local manufacturing, strengthening regulatory systems and  advancing technology transfer and regional value chains, aligning national  efforts with broader African priorities on sustainable access and health  system self-reliance, coordinated with UNICEF’s regional and Supply Division  support.


  


Under Government leadership governance   within the national health system was  strengthened in 2025. With UNICEF engagement alongside the World Health  Organization and other partners, multisectoral committees covering polio  response, immunization, nutrition and school health were established and  institutionalized through ministerial decrees, strengthening structured  oversight, preparedness and coordinated decision-making. UNICEF technical  assistance supported the development or advancement of key national  instruments, including the National Immunization Strategy, the National  School Health Promotion Plan, the Strategy for Triple Elimination of  Mother-to-Child Transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis, and the National  Nutrition Strategy.


  


Primary, maternal and proximity health  services benefited from more  consistent improvements at service level. In line with national priorities to  strengthen primary and local-based health care and accelerate health sector  digitalization, UNICEF supported Government counterparts with evidence-based  planning tools, improved monitoring practices and targeted capacity  strengthening across maternal and child health services, including in  emergency contexts. In 2025, competencies were strengthened for 1,690 health  personnel to deliver maternal, neonatal and child health services, including  training on the updated immunization schedule and on management of adverse  events following immunization. UNICEF also supported practical guidance for  frontline workers and midwives with a dedicated focus on maternal and newborn  nutrition, contributing to more standardized service delivery. To reinforce  equity and territorial responsiveness, UNICEF—together with the World Health  Organization—supported improved monitoring and use of Sustainable Development  Goal 3 indicators at subnational level, including capacity strengthening for  health managers and integration of health priorities into local planning and  performance monitoring.


  


Immunization systems and coordination delivered high-coverage results during  the 2025 poliomyelitis response under the Government’s leadership, supported  by UNICEF and the World Health Organization. UNICEF supported immunization  governance and system improvements, including steps toward digital  transformation of immunization monitoring, initiation of a five-year National  Immunization Strategy (covering supply chain and cold chain management, human  resources, community engagement and immunization costing), and an Effective  Vaccine Management assessment and improvement plan. UNICEF also supported  national coordination and community engagement by training local leaders—including  Imams and Mourchidates—and civil society organizations to address vaccine  hesitancy and rumours. Under Government leadership, more than 4.5 million  children were vaccinated using novel oral polio vaccine type 2 (nOPV2),  reaching 95 per cent coverage in the first round and 96 per cent in the  second, with targeted efforts to reach vulnerable and hard-to-reach areas,  particularly in the far south. UNICEF supported the response through  procurement of nOPV2 and operational readiness, including coordination and  community engagement measures. UNICEF also supported preparedness for new  vaccine introduction by facilitating the participation of the National Cancer  Control Committee in a regional exchange on human papillomavirus (HPV)  vaccination, contributing to recommendations to the Ministry of Health and  accelerating the planned introduction in 2026–2027,


  


Nutrition and early childhood nutrition remained a priority area, with UNICEF  reinforcing multisectoral ownership while keeping progress transparent and  results-focused. The steering committee for the National Nutrition Strategy  expanded to include additional ministries alongside civil society,  reinforcing shared responsibility across sectors; at the same time, the  strategy was drafted and remained under development in 2025, with continued  work needed for finalization. UNICEF supported practical improvements in  guidance and demand generation, including guidance on prevention and  management of overweight and obesity and strengthened nutrition content in  maternal guidance. Results were tangible in reach: 23,000 children and  adolescents participated in awareness activities on nutrition and healthy  practices—3,000 through school health clubs and 20,000 through civil society  activities linked to the national nutrition committee. Exclusive  breastfeeding remained a core priority for early childhood nutrition; the 2025  indicator value reports 32 per cent of infants aged 0–5 months exclusively  breastfed. UNICEF strengthened the national toolbox through development and  central-level validation of the national Infant and Young Child Feeding  counselling guide (Guide ANJE) and integration of the national breastfeeding  promotion strategy into the ANJE plan, while providing technical support for  tools to prepare a national survey planned for implementation in 2026.


  


Humanitarian health and nutrition  services were sustained  through close coordination with authorities and partners to support Sahrawi  refugees in Tindouf. Immunization coverage and epidemic preparedness were  reinforced through procurement of 33,821 doses of pneumococcal and hexavalent  vaccines and cold chain system upgrades, supported by freeze-free vaccine  carriers and electronic temperature loggers, with a new cold room scheduled  to become operational in March 2026. In response to diphtheria outbreaks, a targeted  vaccination campaign reached over 12,300 people, including 25 per cent  children, while a joint poliomyelitis campaign with the World Health  Organization supported full coverage of children across the five camps; 53  health workers and social mobilisers were trained to address vaccine  hesitancy. Preventive services were further sustained through measles  vaccination for 21,000 UNICEF-targeted children aged six to 59 months in  humanitarian settings. Maternal, neonatal and child health and nutrition services  were strengthened through targeted capacity building: 14 midwives were  trained in emergency obstetric care, ultrasound and neonatal resuscitation;  20 health and nutrition personnel received training in breastfeeding,  complementary feeding and Early Childhood Development, with kits distributed  to all 29 primary health facilities. Nutrition governance and service  delivery were reinforced through finalization of the Nutrition Strategic  Roadmap under World Food Programme sector leadership, aligned with the  2025–2030 Multisectoral Nutrition Strategy, and findings from the 2025  Nutrition Survey informed training of Community Health Workers in anemia  screening and acute malnutrition management, strengthening service delivery  for 8,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women and 21,000 children.


  


Every Child Learns 


  


In 2025, Algeria continued to  consolidate education and adolescent development reforms, with a clear  Government emphasis on learning quality, inclusion and stronger bridges from  learning to skills and opportunity. UNICEF supported the Government’s agenda  through targeted, system-strengthening contributions that helped  operationalize reforms, strengthen national capacities, and build evidence  for scale—while aligning Algeria’s efforts with African Union Agenda 2063  priorities on human capital and youth employability. 


  


Learning-to-Earning and youth  employability platforms were  strengthened by linking foundational learning, life skills and employability  pathways, and by leveraging national and continental moments to reinforce  Government priorities on youth opportunity. WorldSkills Algeria 2025 provided  a structured space for skills demonstration, peer learning and engagement  between training institutions and labour market actors. In this setting, more  than 250 young people, including vulnerable youth, benefited from life skills  training linked to employability, while UNICEF logistical support (including  the provision of around 500 outfits to finalists) contributed to visibility  and Algeria’s positioning on regional and African stages. 


  


Youth participation and foresight were strengthened in 2025 through the  UNICEF Algeria partnership with the Higher Council for Youth and the Youth  Foresight Fellowship, which helped institutionalize structured youth input  into education and digital learning discussions. This work was also reflected  in UNICEF’s engagement in a continental platform on the future of education  and digital learning, contributing to Africa-wide reflection on more  inclusive and future-ready education systems. In parallel, the Algeria  chapter of the Child Rights Youth Foresight work translated adolescents’  lived experience into practical recommendations—more hands-on learning and  exposure to workplaces, flexible learning spaces, protected time for  extracurricular activities, and mentorship/alumni linkages—reinforcing  Government priorities on Learning-to-Earning pathways and supporting UNICEF’s  ongoing work on school-to-work linkages, career guidance and youth  participation mechanisms.


  


Generation Unlimited and continental  positioning gained  further traction in December 2025 through the 4th African Startup Conference  (“Raising African Champions”), hosted by the Government of Algeria and  organized by the Ministry of Knowledge Economy, Start-ups and  Micro-enterprises in collaboration with several ministries, including the  Ministry of Vocational Training and Education. The conference convened  approximately 25,000 participants, including international experts,  investors, exhibitors and more than 40 African ministerial delegations,  positioning innovation, entrepreneurship and skills as drivers of Africa’s  transformation.
