UNICEF Generation Unlimited was invited by the Minister to  participate as a key speaker in a high-level policy dialogue hosted by the  Minister of Vocational Training and Education, focused on bridging skills  development and entrepreneurial outcomes, aligned with the African Union  Blueprint for Best Practices in Vocational Training and Agenda 2063  objectives. This engagement reinforced Government-led approaches that connect  education quality, Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET),  innovation ecosystems and labour market policies, while advancing discussions  on institutionalizing Generation Unlimited in Algeria through multi-ministry  governance and inclusive pathways, including for youth with disabilities and  young people not in education, employment or training (NEET).


  


Building on the Government’s  National Dropout Prevention Plan, a more coherent response to school  disengagement and dropout risk continued to be structured in 2025,  strengthening the education–training continuum with UNICEF technical support.  Capacities were reinforced at central and decentralized levels to improve early  identification of learners at risk of dropout and strengthen referral  pathways toward re-engagement mechanisms, TVET opportunities and social  support services. In parallel, UNICEF engagement with the Ministry of  Vocational Training and Education supported the gradual expansion of distance  and hybrid training modalities, helping create more flexible second-chance  options for adolescents and youth outside the formal school system, including  young people in a NEET situation. 


  


Capacity development and professional  practice were a central  change strategy in 2025, supporting institutional ownership and scale-up  through national training pools and regional cascading. A national core group  of 42 pedagogical inspectors was trained in differentiated pedagogy and  adaptive teaching through a structured model combining central training and  regional demultiplication. Building on the 2024 foundation, 96 inspectors and  counsellors strengthened capacities in psycho-pedagogical support for learners  at risk of dropout through a duplication mechanism led by the Ministry of  National Education. Learning assessment capacity also advanced significantly:  a specialized technical training reached 36 professionals (26 inspectors and  10 guidance counsellors) as the national nucleus for learning assessment, and  the trained inspectors subsequently supported pedagogical use of assessment  results through regional duplication reaching at least 520 teachers.  Together, these investments brought total 2025 training reach to at least 800  professionals across inspectors, managers and teachers, strengthening the  system’s ability to prevent dropout, improve classroom practices, and use  evidence to guide quality improvement. 


  


Evidence generation for learning  quality was strengthened as  a foundation for quality and equity-focused planning. In January 2025, a  national learning assessment was conducted with 5,800 students across 21  wilayas, covering ten subjects at primary and lower secondary levels.  Contextual questionnaires completed by students, teachers and school  principals enabled analysis of learning outcomes in relation to  socio-economic, pedagogical and institutional factors. Reporting is under  finalization in line with international standards and will inform future  policy dialogue and programme adjustments. 


  


Inclusive education and disability  inclusion advanced  through targeted capacity strengthening designed for national structuring and  territorial scale-up. In 2025, autism-inclusive education capacity was  strengthened through a training-of-trainers model: 30 primary-level  pedagogical inspectors were trained at central level, followed by regional  cascading benefiting 90 regional inspectors, supporting diffusion of  inclusive practices. These efforts complemented work in TVET to  institutionalize inclusive approaches through national guidance and digital  training resources, benefiting 150 TVET professionals at national level. 


  


Systems strengthening and education  data (EMIS)  continued through modernization of the Education Management Information  System, continued through modernization of the Education Management  Information System, strengthened data governance and management, and  preparation for progressive integration of advanced digital solutions,  aligned with national frameworks, Sustainable Development Goal 4 and Agenda  2063. Capacity in planning, management and results-based monitoring—linked to  programme-based budgeting reforms—was expanded among central and local cadres  of vocational training institutions and youth governance structures. 


  


Climate education and youth engagement  at local level were  operationalized through Phase II of the Sustainable Land Management and  Renewable Energy Project in El Bayadh and Béchar, implemented with the High  Youth Council. The initiative engaged more than 125 young people and  community members, including children with disabilities, and supported the  planting of over 1,000 trees using adapted irrigation systems.  An innovative youth-led monitoring mechanism  was also established to track progress and results. 


  


Humanitarian education continuity and  adolescent participation were  sustained in the Sahrawi refugee camps under severe funding constraints. In  2025, UNICEF support enabled 35,745 children aged 3–16 to access education  across pre-primary, primary and lower secondary levels; girls accounted for  19,597 learners, representing over 54 per cent of enrolment. Access and  learning conditions were strengthened through the provision of school bags to  20,000 primary schoolchildren, reducing material barriers to attendance.  System continuity was supported through targeted quarterly incentives for  1,287 community-based education volunteers (most of them teachers), 76 per  cent of whom were women, contributing to retention and continuity in a  predominantly volunteer-based school system managed by the Sahrawi refugee  community structures. Capacity development included pre-service training for  159 newly recruited teachers (90 per cent women), delivered in partnership  with the Autonomous University of Madrid, and support to 12 national trainers  to advance enquiry-based science education practices. Strategic leadership  and evidence-based planning were strengthened through initiation of an  Education in Emergencies Situational Analysis, informing the 2026–2030  Education Sector Strategy and an Education Communications and Advocacy Plan. Adolescent  participation was reinforced through the child-led photography initiative  Through Our Eyes, involving 20 adolescents and strengthening life skills  while amplifying adolescent voices and increasing visibility of the  protracted refugee context.


  


Every Child is Protected 


  


In 2025, cooperation between the  Government of Algeria and UNICEF contributed to strengthening the foundations  for a gradual consolidation of the child protection system through policy  dialogue, analytical work and preparation of future frameworks and actions. Progress  in child protection legal framework and national policy and was  anchored in close collaboration with the National Body for the Protection and  Promotion of Childhood (ONPPE), and advanced through two executive decrees  published in the Official Gazette (No. 79, 27 November 2025): Decree No.  25-308, which sets conditions for establishing and operating specialized  child protection centres, and Decree No. 25-309, which reforms ONPPE by  integrating a cyber-monitoring function to respond to rising online risks  affecting children. 


  


Ten years after the adoption of the  Child Protection Law, 2025 also marked a constructive step in reinforcing the  child rights agenda through continued dialogue on implementation of the  Convention on the Rights of the Child, sustaining institutional commitments to  international standards and helping identify practical levers for stronger  integration within public processes. National planning and multisectoral  coordination progressed as the National Plan of Action for Children  (2025–2030) reached an advanced stage of formulation, with commissions  installed and technical expertise mobilized to support drafting and thematic  consultations using a results-based management approach, subject to formal  validation. 


  


A key catalyst for momentum and  alignment was the September 2025 child rights mission with expertise from Dr  Ghassan Khalil, which supported high-level, multisectoral dialogue on CRC  implementation and helped anchor shared priorities across ONPPE, justice  institutions and other stakeholders, strengthening prospects for coordinated  follow-up.


  


In child-sensitive justice, 2025  represented a focused preparatory phase. In partnership with the Ministry of  Justice and the École Supérieure de la Magistrature, UNICEF initiated a  discussion around a national analysis on child-sensitive justice. 


  


In parallel, operational capacity  strengthening advanced through collaboration with General Directorate of  National Security (DGSN). The establishment of a specialized pool of  trainers on filmed child interviews for child victims of sexual violence  proved highly effective—harmonizing professional practices, improving the  quality of child-centred responses, and reinforcing respect for children’s  rights and best interests. These targeted trainings, grounded in ethical and  trauma-informed approaches, strengthened the competencies of practitioners  across multiple child protection sectors. In addition, an exchange visit to  Jordan further reinforced international cooperation and peer learning,  enabling the sharing of good practices, recognition of national progress, and  mutual learning to inform future system strengthening.


  


Regarding the inclusion of children  with disabilities, UNICEF’s technical support contributed to informing  and structuring national commitments presented at the Global Disability  Summit 2025, aligned with constitutional, legislative and international  frameworks. These commitments address accessibility, inclusive education,  strengthened data systems and the participation of organizations of persons  with disabilities, reflecting a gradual shift from advocacy toward more  structured, system-level responses. 


  


At the same time, evidence gaps remain,  including limited evidence products reported in 2025 on child protection in  humanitarian action in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, highlighting a  clear area for strengthened analysis and documentation in 2026. 


  


Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life


  


In 2025, Algeria advanced key steps to  strengthen the inclusiveness of its non-contributory social protection system,  with a view to accelerating progress towards SDG 1. Two important  child-sensitive measures moved forward: (i) the revision of eligibility  criteria for persons with disabilities under the solidarity lump sum grant  (AFS), and (ii) the administrative transfer of the special school allowance  management from the Ministry of Education to the Ministry of National  Solidarity. These developments were aligned with the national assessment of  child- and adolescent-sensitive social protection programmes led by the National  Economic, Social and Environmental Council (CNESE), supported by a  multisectoral committee and UNICEF support. The assessment issued two key  recommendations: expanding AFS eligibility from “without income” to  “insufficient income”, and strengthening the role of the Ministry of National  Solidarity in managing child-related benefits—including by linking the  special school allowance to effective social support for vulnerable children  and adolescents, with a focus on preventing school dropout.


  


Building on this momentum, CNESE finalized  the Atlas of Social Equity, with UNICEF providing technical support. The Atlas provides granular  territorial analysis to help prioritize action on multidimensional  vulnerabilities affecting children and young people. It is aligned with the  National Territorial Development Plan (SNAT), positioning it as a practical  tool to inform Government efforts to reduce territorial disparities.


  


In parallel, UNICEF’s strategic  partnership with the Ministry of Finance strengthened the child lens in  public finance management through the development of a roadmap covering:  the integration of a child dimension in subsidy reform reflections,  child-focused budget transparency products, and a methodology to measure  child-focused expenditures. This work also initiated South–South exchanges  with MENA countries that have leveraged subsidy reforms to strengthen budgets  and social protection for children, alongside exploration of participatory  and inclusive citizen budgets in child-sensitive sectors.


  


Finally, under a joint UN approach,  Algeria advanced a structural initiative on social protection with  ILO, UNDP, ESCWA and the Office of the Resident Coordinator, leaded by  UNICEF. In September 2025, Phase I was launched, focusing on system mapping  and diagnostics, capacity strengthening through the regional TRANSFORM ARAB  initiative, and initial analytical work on financial sustainability—including  actuarial capacity considerations. A key milestone was the delivery of the  first TRANSFORM training in Algeria in November 2025, with institutional  anchoring through collaboration with the National School of Social Security  (ENSSS), supporting sustainable capacity development and potential  longer-term integration into national training curricula. A high-level policy  dialogue and a provisional 2026–2027 roadmap further supported coordinated  planning, role clarity and the scaling-up of system-strengthening actions.


  


Evidence Generation, Data Systems and Data-Informed  Decision-Making


  


Evidence generation and national data  systems were strengthened  in 2025 through the initiation of the seventh round of the Multiple  Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7), formalized through the signature of a  Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Ministry of Health and UNICEF.  This milestone consolidated the institutional framework for the upcoming  national survey cycle and is expected to increase the availability of  high-quality, disaggregated data on children and women, complementing routine  information systems. With results expected in 2027, MICS7 is positioned to  serve as a key evidence base for national planning, reporting and  equity-focused policy dialogue.


  


Evidence-to-policy pathways continued to influence reforms and  strategic decision-making. Findings from previous MICS cycles supported major  analytical products, including the national report on the well-being of  children and youth and the Social Equity Atlas, strengthening the analytical  foundation for identifying vulnerabilities and informing public responses. In  social protection, recommendations from the analysis of child- and  adolescent-sensitive social protection programmes—conducted by the National Economic,  Social and Environmental Council (CNESE) through a multisectoral  process in partnership with UNICEF—supported concrete adjustments to  child-rights-sensitive schemes, including disability-related benefits and  school allowance mechanisms.


  


Subnational monitoring and sector  performance tracking  were strengthened to support more equitable planning and service delivery. In  health, improved use of the Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3)  results framework at subnational level supported the territorialization of  health priorities and their integration into local planning processes. In  education and adolescent development, the national learning assessment  conducted in line with international standards further strengthened the  evidence base for policy dialogue and is expected to guide systemic  adjustments and future sector reforms.


  


Education data managment also advanced. Continued upgrading of  the Education Management Information System (EMIS) contributed to  stronger data management, and helped lay foundations for the progressive  integration of advanced digital solutions. Together, these shifts  strengthened the enabling environment for more consistent, data-informed  decision-making across sectors—linking national evidence products with  planning, budgeting and monitoring processes, and reinforcing a  results-oriented approach to equity for children and adolescents.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The year 2025 was a period of transition for UNICEF Algeria, shaped by a constrained global funding environment and adjustments in the way the office planned, managed and delivered results. These changes were introduced to strengthen accountability, strategic focus and sustainability. In the short term, they required rapid adaptation by teams and partners and influenced the pace and sequencing of some activities.


This operating context coincided with several major accountability and planning processes that demanded significant time and coordination, including the Country Office audit, the mid-term review of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, and preparation of the Sahrawi Refugee Response Plan (2026–2027). Together, these exercises strengthened strategic clarity, risk management and institutional positioning. At the same time, their simultaneity increased pressure on operational capacity and intersectoral coordination.


Within this context, a key lesson from 2025 is that durable results depend on strong programme foundations. UNICEF Algeria deliberately strengthened planning quality, results-based management and assurance processes, prioritizing interventions with the highest potential for impact and scale. While this approach sometimes slowed delivery in the short term, it improved coherence, reduced fragmentation and strengthened the conditions for sustained results—particularly for children and adolescents facing the greatest vulnerabilities.


A second lesson is that evidence has the greatest value when it helps informing public policies and programmes. Across sectors, national institutions and UNICEF invested in major analytical products and diagnostics to deepen understanding the situation of children. Experience showed that impact increases when evidence work includes clear utilization pathways from the outset—early agreement on how findings will be used, structured dissemination with the right institutions, and policy dialogue timed to decision points in planning and budgeting cycles. Strengthening these “evidence-to-action” pathways remains essential, especially for equity-focused reforms.


In health and nutrition, 2025 demonstrated the value of institutionalized intersectoral coordination, particularly during the poliomyelitis response. Formal coordination mechanisms supported clearer roles, predictability and coherence, and strengthened implementation readiness. The year also highlighted the importance of broadening institutional engagement when operational demands surge, so that leadership, technical continuity and implementation momentum are not overly concentrated in a small number of units.


In education and adolescent development, experience reinforced that system strengthening is more sustainable than isolated activities. Training pools, cascading models and structured technical support strengthened professional practice and created stronger conditions for scale-up. The year also confirmed the strategic importance of intersectoral pathways for adolescents, connecting education, skills development, youth participation and social support to expand opportunities for adolescents, including those not in education, employment or training.


In social protection, continued emphasis on system strengthening and capacity development reinforced the role of social protection as a cross-cutting policy with multiplier effects across education, health, nutrition and child protection. This experience confirmed that social protection can translate into results for children when linkages with sector services are reinforced.


Across these areas, partnerships remained a decisive enabler. Collaboration with government institutions, the United Nations system, civil society, academia and regional platforms strengthened implementation, improved policy coherence and supported national and continental positioning. The year also confirmed the importance of humanitarian–development linkages in a protracted displacement context, where service continuity is sensitive to funding volatility and operational constraints.


Looking ahead, UNICEF Algeria will build on these lessons through three practical directions. First, by strengthening evidence-to-action pathways by embedding utilization planning into major analytical work, by aligning evidence with key national policy milestones. Second, by engaging a wider range of technical experts particularly in high-demand sectors.. Third, byconsolidatingintersectoral approaches with demonstrated value, particularly those advancing child and adolescent development and Learning-to-Earning pathwaysincluding for children affected by humanitarian context.


Overall, 2025 confirmed that progress for children is accelerated when strategic focus, coordination, evidence use and partnerships reinforce one another. Building on this foundation, UNICEF Algeria will prioritize scalable, equity-focused interventions and strengthen the enabling systems required to deliver sustained results, even in a constrained financing environment.

Djibouti, with a limited land area, is a strategic country in the Horn of Africa with an estimated population of around one million people, characterized by rapid urbanization and a predominantly young demographic, with over 60 percent under the age of 30[1]. This youthful population creates opportunities for growth but also significant challenges in education, employment, and social services. Economically, Djibouti relies heavily on its strategic position as a regional trade hub, leveraging its ports and logistics infrastructure to serve neighboring landlocked countries. While GDP growth remains positive (6% according to World Bank estimates), driven by transport and logistics, structural vulnerabilities persist, including high youth unemployment (78,1%[2]), poverty, and dependence on external financing. Social indicators reveal persistent inequalities, particularly affecting women, children, and rural communities. 
With regard to geopolitics, Djibouti occupies a critical position at the crossroads of major shipping routes and hosts several foreign military bases, while serving as a gateway for international trade. This positioning brings economic benefits but also exposes the country to regional instability and security risks. Djibouti is both a transit and destination country for mixed migration flows, including refugees, asylum seekers, and migrants from Somalia, Ethiopia, and Eritrea. This situation places additional pressure on social services and protection systems, requiring coordinated humanitarian and development responses. 
Despite receiving limited attention, the humanitarian situation remains fragile. Djibouti faces recurrent climate shocks, including droughts and water scarcity, which exacerbate food insecurity and malnutrition. The country also hosts about 30,000 refugees representing 3% of the population, as well as 522,000[3] migrants (including 10% of children) representing 49% of total population, which strains already limited social resources. Vulnerable populations, particularly in rural and peri-urban areas, face heightened risks of poverty and health emergencies. Humanitarian needs are compounded by limited access to basic services, high dependency on external aid, and exposure to regional conflicts. These factors underscore the urgency of integrated approaches that combine emergency response with long-term resilience building. 
In light of this context, Djibouti is advancing reforms across key social sectors. On the social sector development front, Djibouti is finalizing its Five-Year Development Plan (2026–2030) with a focus on (i) human capital development, (ii) achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and (iii) promoting economic diversification.  The Sustainable Development Goals occupy a central place in Djibouti’s national agenda, with the country having selected 155 of the 163 SDG targets, nearly 50% of which have already been achieved according to the 2022 Voluntary National Review. In addition, Djibouti’s development plan is aligned with the ambitions of the African Union’s Agenda 2063, particularly in the areas of infrastructure development, economic transformation, regional integration, and youth empowerment. 
The allocated budget for health remains low with 6% of the national budget, which is insufficient to meet the sector's needs and significantly below the 15% recommended by the WHO. Despite this situation, the health sector has made notable progress through strategic initiatives (outreach strategies, zero dose, HPV introduction, and community health). Following an independent evaluation of the 2020–2024 National Health Development Plan, a new plan aligned with the national development framework is being prepared. The sector is also piloting programme-based budgeting, supported by a comprehensive expenditure analysis. Despite these advances, structural challenges persist such as : limited geographic coverage and financial barriers to healthcare (20% of the population do not have access to the health system), Under-five (50/1000), and neonatal mortality (28/1000) rates, inadequate antenatal care, suboptimal vaccination coverage (48% of dose of measles-containing vaccine),[4] significant levels of acute and chronic malnutrition, shortages of qualified personnel, and weak coordination mechanisms. 
Education accounts for about 11% of the national budget, making it one of the most well-financed social sectors, but below the 20% threshold set by the Abuja Declaration. It is guided by a fifteen-year strategy and a five-year action plan (PAE 2021-2025) that emphasize quality, equity, inclusion, and gender equality. Governance is reinforced through an active Education Partners Group and the meaningful involvement of parent organizations in school management. UNICEF acts as a focal point for this group. UNICEF also co-leads with MENFOP the steering group from partners of local Education. At the primary level, performance is strong, with high enrollment rates (100%) and near gender parity (0.9), reflecting progress toward universal access. However, significant challenges persist. Completion rates at primary (83%) particularly for girls (78%), and secondary education remain low (79%) and 77% for girls, which undermines equitable learning outcomes. In addition, vocational and technical education is underdeveloped, limiting opportunities for skills development and employability. 
The water sector remains a national priority amid escalating drought conditions, intensifying water stress, and the impacts of climate change. Currently, 51% of the rural population does not have access to safe drinking water, highlighting significant geographic and social disparities. The government and its partners continue to invest heavily in the sector, with UNICEF supporting the Government of Djibouti to (i) strengthen the evidence base on groundwater resources through targeted technical studies, including groundwater mapping and the planned expansion of mapping to additional regions; and (ii) convene key stakeholders to review and update national strategic policies, improving sector governance and contributing to a secure and sustainable water supply for all communities. Updated National Determined Contribution (NDC) submitted this year, recognizes the need to consider children and youth as key priorities for climate action. 
In parallel, Djibouti has recently begun implementing a new national social protection strategy that integrates preparedness and response to multiple shocks (social, economic, and environmental). The system now benefits from a dedicated operational mechanism through the National Solidarity Fund, signaling strong government commitment to resilience and social safety nets. However, coverage remains limited, primarily due to insufficient financing even though 2.4% of the national budget is devoted to non-contributory social protection in addition to the funding provided by development partners, which constrains the ability to reach vulnerable populations effectively. 
Finally, to strengthen the evidence base for policy and targeting, Djibouti is conducting the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) following its third 2024 census and 2025 poverty survey. Together, these datasets will support more detailed socio-demographic analysis to inform policy choices, resource allocation, and strategies to reduce disparities and advance inclusive growth.

Health and Nutrition:  
In 2025, UNICEF provided support to 59 health facilities and three community care sites that took care of 73,614 sick children under five years old, with 4,339 severely malnourished children among them. 11,379 children from 0 to 11 months (70%) received their three doses of pentavalent. Only 7,356 children under two years old (45%), received their two doses of measles vaccine.  And 14,422 births were assisted by quality health staff.  Although accessibility seems to have increased compared to last year, coverage remains low. 
This is the result of significant progress made in strengthening health and nutrition services in Djibouti, creating a solid foundation for future improvements. Neonatal and child health services have been improved with 13 facilities out of 54 now equipped with functional resuscitation equipment and 33 facilities delivering Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses (IMCI) services, improving care for newborns and young children. Several immunization campaigns, including two poliomyelitis response campaigns and an introduction campaign for the human papilloma virus vaccine, as well as community mobilization have laid the foundation for an extension of awareness, even though only one in six districts achieved the 80% coverage target for DTC/Penta3 among infants.   UNICEF supported the response to the outbreak of acute acquired diarrhoea in the two northern regions.  349 cases of acute watery diarrhoea were treated in the UNICEF-supported treatment center. 
Nutrition systems demonstrated resilience despite supply challenges. 83% of the establishments had access to nutritional supplies, and three quarters of these have reached a cure rate higher than 75%, reflecting an improvement in the quality of care compared to last year when the average was 66%. Regional disparities highlight opportunities for targeted interventions to replicate these successes nationwide. Progress was made on strategic work on policy frameworks, with the revised Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) protocol and Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) strategy nearing completion — critical steps towards harmonized standards and preventive action. 
Community engagement delivered tangible results. A total of 194 community agents out of the 250 planned for 2025 were trained in Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) and exclusive breastfeeding for children, strengthening demand generation and proximity services. Behavioral indicators showed promising trends, with 50% of mothers and caregivers now knowing at least five essential family practices, reaching approximately 30,000 women. These gains provide a strong platform for deepening quality through coaching, formative supervision, and geographic expansion. 
In 2026, UNICEF will continue to support all these efforts to accelerate the reduction of maternal and child mortality in Djibouti by improving the coverage of seven essential interventions with high impact on children’s health and nutrition, namely vaccination, Integrated management of childhood illnesses, emergency neonatal care, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, management of severe acute malnutrition, prevention of malnutrition, promotion of breastfeeding and the promotion of infant and child nutrition.  These interventions were selected to address the main causes of death in children under five, which are neonatal infections, neonatal asphyxia, acute respiratory infections, diarrhea, and malnutrition, that they address, the list of these interventions includes vaccination, integrated management of childhood diseases, emergency neonatal care, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, management of severe acute malnutrition, prevention of malnutrition, the promotion of breastfeeding and the promotion of infant and child nutrition. 
UNICEF’s priorities focus on converting these achievements into sustained impact. Key actions include expanding service readiness by equipping all neonatal sites, scaling Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses (IMCI) coverage, and improving immunization rates through targeted outreach and cold-chain optimization. Policies such as Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) and Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) strategies will be finalized and operationalized, supported by competency-based training and certification. It is essential to strengthen supply chain resilience to eliminate stock-outs of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and micronutrients through proactive procurement and distribution monitoring. Building provider capacity for Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) counselling and aligning facility-based services with community-level efforts will ensure integrated care. Equity actions will be accelerated in underserved regions through intensified supervision and mobile outreach, while a unified results dashboard will enhance accountability by tracking service readiness, coverage, and behavioral outcomes. 
These strategic actions will transform incremental progress into system-wide improvements, ensuring that every child, especially the most vulnerable, has access to high-quality health and nutrition services. UNICEF is committed to driving innovation, fostering partnerships, and leveraging data to deliver sustainable results for children and families across Djibouti. 
Education: 
In 2025, UNICEF achieved a measurable impact on advancing education in Djibouti, driving systemic improvements in access, equity, and quality, with a strong focus on girls’ education. Through strategic partnerships and targeted interventions, UNICEF supported the enrolment of 162,362 children, including 75,265 girls, marking a significant achievement in inclusive education. Key indicators improved with the gross enrolment rate in primary education rising from 99% to 101.7%, and access rates reaching 86.9% for Grade 5 and 80.6% for Grade 9. These gains were mainly achieved through UNICEF’s partnership with the French Development Agency (AFD) under the girls’ education and empowerment support project. 
Furthermore, in terms of capacity-building initiatives, UNICEF strengthened early childhood education. Twenty teachers (19 women), eight directors (2 women), and eight assistant directors from eight preschools in Balbala and Guelleh Batal received specialized training in classroom management to improve learning environments for young children. In addition, at the policy level, UNICEF supported the development and validation of critical instruments for institutionalizing gender-responsive practices and sustaining progress, including a Gender-Sensitive Human Resources Policy, a National Girls’ Education Strategy with a five-year action plan, and a comprehensive communication plan. 
Moreover, interventions were guided by evidence-based programming. The LIFE study findings were published, informing strategies to improve learning outcomes among children with disabilities. To further reduce dropout rates among vulnerable students and ensure inclusive education for children with disabilities, UNICEF introduced a remediation mechanism to provide targeted support to at-risk learners. At the same time, collaboration with Catholic schools under the Djibouti Diocese continued, reinforcing non-formal and second-chance education programs through Reading-Writing-Numeracy (Lire-Écrire-Compter) centres to support reintegration of children and adolescents not in education. 
In parallel, prioritising infrastructure and learning materials enhanced education quality. UNICEF supported the Ministry of National Education and Vocational Training (MENFOP) in printing pre-school manuals and booklets for the Accelerated Education Programme (PEA), addressing the needs of learners who have missed out on formal schooling. Furthermore, the construction of PK13 and PK14 schools was completed, expanding the number of safe learning spaces. In addition, surveys on school-related violence have been conducted and data analysis is underway to inform protection strategies. 
Simultaneously, the Giga Initiative advanced digital transformation by mapping connected schools to bridge the digital divide and integrate technology into education. With UNICEF's technical and financial support, eight preschools in Balbala and Guelleh Batal were rehabilitated and equipped, funded by the Japanese National Committee for UNICEF. Meanwhile, school management committees and parents were mobilized to champion early childhood education. 
At the decentralised level, governance was reinforced through the signing of annual work plans with the regional councils in Obock, Dikhil, and Ali-Sabieh, thereby ensuring localized implementation. To complement these efforts, and to strengthen girls’ employability and life skills, UNICEF recruited a national consultant for partnership development in peri-urban Balbala and an international UN Volunteer to manage technical and vocational training across three regions. These actions align with the Government Girls’ Education and Empowerment policy, equipping adolescent girls with skills for economic independence. 
In addition, community engagement and advocacy amplified impact. Fifteen schools set up clubs to promote education and gender equality, empowering students to become agents of change. These platforms foster dialogue and action, embedding social norm transformation within communities. Consequently, 14,889 adolescents and youth reinforced their skills through sessions on FGM, early marriage, and health promotion. 
Overall, through these integrated interventions, UNICEF achieved tangible results: increased enrollment and retention, strengthened institutional capacity, enhanced teacher competencies, and adoption of gender-responsive policies. Looking ahead, UNICEF will scale successful models, deepen partnerships, and leverage technology to accelerate progress. Strategic priorities for 2026 include expanding early childhood education, developing factsheets linked to girls' schooling, and embedding digital learning solutions to ensure every child especially girls can learn, thrive, and realize their full potential. 
In addition, a mid-term evaluation of a major access to education for girls programme SEFA (Soutien à l’Éducation des Filles et à leurs Autonomies) was undertaken during the reporting period. The findings will be instrumental in refining strategies related to targeting, quality and equity, with a particular emphasis on expanding education and vocational training opportunities for girls in rural areas. Ultimately, this will contribute to improved and more equitable access to the right to education for all children. 
Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF will leverage a series of planned evaluations, including those of the WASH programme, and the Social Behaviour Change (SBC) evaluability exercise, to strengthen evidence-based programming and foster cross-sector learning. To promote understanding and ownership of evaluation outcomes, UNICEF will establish strategic partnerships with national organisations, actively supporting a culture of evaluation and strengthening national evaluation capacities and competencies. Furthermore, UNICEF will continue to ensure that representatives from national evaluation bodies participate in the steering committees for each evaluation, reinforcing national leadership and accountability throughout the process. 
 Child protection: 
In 2025, protection mechanisms for girls at risk delivered in areas with high prevalence (north of the country) demonstrated modest but concrete results. Community surveillance and advocacy enabled the referral of 437 girls for protection against FGM, and 36 girls were reportedly safeguarded from FGM in the northern regions of the country, compared to zero reported in 2024. UNICEF achieved measurable progress in creating a safer environment for vulnerable children and adolescents by strengthening systems, improving coordination, and laying the foundation for long-term reductions in violence. Despite persistent gaps in justice responses, legal assistance to children, and normative transformation, interventions delivered tangible results in violence prevention and response, including within emergency contexts. 
Furthermore, a major milestone was the enhancement of child protection information management and case management systems. In October 2025, UNICEF facilitated hands-on training on the CPIMS+/Primero platform for social workers, law enforcement officers in charge of juvenile brigades, NGOs, the juvenile judge, and the National Agency for Information Systems (ANSIE). This initiative strengthened institutional capacity for secure case management, improved intersectoral coordination, and advanced integrated data systems, all critical for evidence-based decision-making and accountability. Operationalization is planned for 2026, and the platform will be used by all key child protection actors, including those supporting children on the move, from registration to case closure. 
In addition, progress in birth registration remained modest, but strategic groundwork was laid. UNICEF’s proximity-based initiative with regional councils in the north, launched in 2024 and resumed in the second quarter of 2025, expanded access and outreach. This approach not only addressed systemic bottlenecks and aligned with national priorities for universal civil registration, but also contributed to a 15% increase in birth certificates issued in 2025. 
At the institutional level, coordination advanced significantly. The reactivation of the intersectoral committee for Best Interest Determination (BID) and the revitalization of the national child protection platform through high-level engagement positioned child protection as a national priority under the leadership of the Ministry of Women and Family. In 2025, two children benefited from the BID panel recommendations and were temporarily placed at CARITAS and SOS Children’s Villages in Djibouti. 
Building on this, the launch of the mid-term review of the National Child Policy and the establishment of a technical committee to finalize inputs marked a decisive step toward policy implementation and system consolidation. 
Operationally, protection services for children on the move delivered consistent impact. Approximately 125 vulnerable children per month accessed safe accommodation, psychosocial support, and tailored social assistance. Family tracing and reunification efforts reintegrated 60 children with their families or facilitated voluntary returns through IOM support. Provision of dignity kits and essential items reinforced safety and well-being standards. 
However, justice-related interventions lagged due to limited partnerships and competing priorities. Nevertheless, government counterparts expressed their commitment to collaborate on child-friendly justice in future cycles, signaling an opportunity for strategic engagement. 
With regard to harmful practices, particularly FGM, although the most severe form has been abandoned in most of the country, the practice known as sunna persisted in 2025. Social mobilization and dialogue platforms led by religious leaders raised awareness of child rights and FGM risks. Messaging delivered in Afar, Somali, and Arabic enhanced cultural relevance, while locally adapted materials and media outreach amplified reach. Strategic shifts toward evidence-based messaging—emphasizing legal frameworks, health consequences, and religious perspectives—addressed barriers to behavior change and strengthened credibility. 
Moreover, capacity-building investments yielded measurable outcomes. Building on 2024 activities, a total of 118 community relays were trained in 2025 to detect risks, conduct prevention activities, and refer cases, while 27 women leaders strengthened their advocacy and mobilization skills. Eight women’s associations and civil society organizations received support to structure prevention actions, embedding sustainability at community level. Religious leaders emerged as influential agents of change, reaching 3,389 community members with messages aligned with child rights and FGM abandonment. A total of 10,937 individuals were engaged during the second semester of 2025. 
At the community level, a protection network of 50 trained members across ten rural localities ensured risk monitoring, case reporting, and family engagement, demonstrating the effectiveness of localized prevention structures. 
Overall, 2025 marked a transition from awareness-raising to action-oriented protection, with measurable gains in system strengthening, coordination, and community engagement. Strategic priorities for 2026 focus on two major areas: 
(i) integrating children on the move into the national child protection system, including protection, access to basic services, legal assistance, and durable solutions; and 
(ii) strengthening holistic GBV approaches through prevention, response, services, and empowerment. 
Safe and Resilient Environment: 
In 2025, Djibouti has made notable progress in two critical areas: (i) engaging young people in climate action and (ii) improving water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in healthcare facilities, alongside targeted interventions to address severe water scarcity, hygiene and sanitation challenges in vulnerable communities. The progress made this year succeeded to advance youth engagement in climate action in Djibouti through amplifying their voice to be consider as key actors in climate adaptation efforts in country and reducing the prevalence of water borne diseases as well as the impact of outbreak disease among children thanks to the improvement of water access in hard-to-reach areas and improvement of WASH in HCF. Thanks to UNICEF Djibouti efforts in water supply, access rate to water increased from 48% to 49.14% in rural areas, reaching a total of 8,000 persons with basic water services. 
A major milestone was the support to the organization of a national climate conference of youths (LCOY[1]) that brought together approximately 85 young people from across the country. Facilitated by the Ministry of Environment and the Climate Action committee (CAC), the event highlighted the importance of youth participation in climate action and resulted in a declaration outlining commitments and expectations from young people. This initiative reflects growing recognition of youth as key actors in addressing climate change. However, the conference also revealed gaps, notably the lack of inclusion of children and youth with disabilities, which future children and youths climate centered programs aim to address to ensure inclusivity and equity. 
Significant progress was achieved through a tripartite meeting between the Ministry of Health, WHO, and UNICEF to accelerate the implementation of the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASHFIT) plan. This collaboration strengthened partnerships and secured commitments to improve WASH services nationwide. Planned activities include a national training workshop on infection prevention and control and preparations for the 2025 Global Handwashing Day. These efforts underscore UNICEF’s role in promoting better health outcomes by ensuring access to safe water and sanitation in healthcare settings, which is essential for reducing infections and improving public health. This UNICEF-WHO partnership to support WASH-FIT approach in Djibouti is key for the successful implementation of a key pilar of UNICEF Djibouti CPD, contribution to the achievement of the SDG 6 and reducing child mortality through the improvement of health care services, showing an effective integration between WASH and Health for more impact on live of children and their families. 
Monitoring data from 2025 reveals a worrying situation regarding water access in rural Djibouti. Failing infrastructure, extreme weather conditions, and migration pressures have led to deteriorating sanitary conditions and frequent outbreaks of acute watery diarrhea linked to contaminated water and open defecation. UNICEF’s strategic response prioritizes the most vulnerable communities in hard to-reach areas and on the migrants, corridors focusing on critical lifesaving intervention such as rehabilitation of water systems, installation of solar pumping solutions, and the provision of emergency sanitation facilities. These interventions aim to restore access to safe water, reduce waterborne diseases, and mitigate the impact of migration-related pressures. This targeted approach demonstrates UNICEF’s commitment to life-saving measures and resilience-building in emergency contexts. 
Lessons learnt from results achieved through greening initiatives with youths show the importance of strong partnership with both ministry of agriculture and ministry of environment for mobilizing highly qualified personnel, such as an international agroforestry expert and a national reforestation consultant, to support related intervention and establish the link with the Great green wall country and global initiative. Strong community engagement and participation were observed, showing high relevance and great opportunity for ensuring sustainability communities ownership of youths led greening interventions.  
Despite persistent challenges such as the limited inclusion of youth with disabilities in climate initiatives, logistical constraints, and severe water scarcity, the progress achieved in climate engagement, WASH improvements, and emergency water interventions marks a significant step forward. Indeed, these efforts not only address immediate needs but also lay the foundation for long-term resilience, equity, and sustainability in Djibouti’s development trajectory. 
Considering CPD planning, annual review, challenges, lessons learnt from 2025 and remaining gaps, in 2026, the focus will be put on (i) strengthening access to sustainable drinking water in hard-to-reach communities; (ii) scaling-up and monitoring WASH-Fit implementation; (iii) supporting evidences generation to strengthening child sensitive climate programming; (iv) supporting youths climate advocacy effort and their implication in the Great Green wall country program; (v) supporting WASH emergency response and strengthening preparedness capacities.  
Social Policy: 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened Djibouti's social protection systems and expanded services for vulnerable groups. A major achievement was accompanying the Ministry of Social Affairs and Solidarity to create an administrative and financial manual, which standardized processes, improved oversight, and increased resource efficiency. Through governance reform, digital innovation, and outreach, UNICEF has strengthened Djibouti’s system to provide timely, equitable support to vulnerable households, reaching 72,000 children representing 80% of poor children. 
UNICEF advanced digital transformation by launching a unified platform that links various databases, particularly the social registry. This system improved beneficiary data management, sped up request processing, and enhanced intervention tracking. It also reduced programme duplication and ensured timely benefit delivery, supporting data-driven governance. 
To address geographic inequities, UNICEF has supported the acquisition and deployment of mobile service units to reach remote areas, register households, and enrol beneficiaries in social protection programmes. These efforts reduced access barriers and promoted equity. In addition, UNICEF has supported the Government in upgrading social service counters to enhance confidentiality, dignity, service quality, and operational efficiency. 
These achievements mark a shift toward a more inclusive, transparent, and tech-driven social protection system. In 2026, UNICEF will focus on capacity building on social protection schemes and increasing social protection coverage for vulnerable children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Djibouti continues to face a complex set of interrelated challenges that shape children’s rights and development outcomes. Demographic pressure remains a defining factor, with over 60% of the population under the age of 30. This youthful profile creates opportunities for economic and social progress, but it also increases demand for education, employment, health care, water, and social services. Rapid urbanization further strains service delivery, particularly in peri-urban areas where infrastructure expansion and social protection coverage often lag behind population growth. 
Economic vulnerability compounds these pressures. While GDP growth remains positive, largely driven by port and logistics activity, the economy remains narrowly based and highly dependent on external financing. High youth and female unemployment contributes to persistent poverty and limited household resilience. Inflationary trends and global volatility have continued to undermine purchasing power and food security, increasing the risk that vulnerable households fall further behind. 
Humanitarian risks intensify these structural constraints. Recurrent droughts and water stress affect livelihoods and contribute to food insecurity and malnutrition. Djibouti’s role as both a transit and destination country for refugees, asylum seekers, and migrants places additional pressure on public services and protection systems, with heightened risks for women and children, including exposure to exploitation and violence. These overlapping shocks underscore the need to combine humanitarian readiness with longer-term resilience and systems strengthening. 
What worked and how UNICEF adapted during the year 
Against this backdrop, UNICEF prioritized approaches that strengthened national systems while improving last-mile reach to the most vulnerable children and families. 
·        Systems strengthening through digitalization and improved data use: Investments in digital solutions and stronger linkages between administrative datasets improved the efficiency and transparency of programme delivery, particularly in social protection and service referral pathways. Where fragmentation previously limited targeting and follow-up, a more unified approach improved timeliness, reduced duplication, and supported more evidence-informed decision-making. 
·        Bringing services closer to underserved communities: Mobile and outreach modalities helped address geographic inequities by extending registration and service access to remote and peri-urban areas, reducing barriers linked to distance, cost, and information gaps. 
·        Partnership and coordination as delivery enablers: Strengthened coordination with Government counterparts, local authorities, UN partners, and civil society supported clearer role division, more consistent referral pathways, and faster operational problem-solving. 
·        Adaptive prioritization under constrained resources: Faced with limited and unpredictable financing, UNICEF applied more deliberate prioritization of interventions with strong equity and systems returns—sequencing activities, concentrating on scalable platforms, and leveraging partnerships to sustain essential services for the most vulnerable. 
What did not work as intended and where bottlenecks persisted 
Despite progress, several constraints limited the pace and scale of results, especially for the most marginalized children. 
·        Financing constraints and volatility: Scarce funding and shifting priorities constrained the ability to expand coverage, invest in workforce development, and sustain system improvements. Short funding cycles increased the risk of fragmented interventions rather than sustained, scalable programming. 
·        Uneven last-mile capacity: Service availability and quality remain uneven across regions. In remote and peri-urban areas, human resource gaps and operational constraints can weaken continuity of care, follow-up, and protection case management. 
·        Persistent data and monitoring gaps: While progress was made, gaps in routine monitoring, interoperability across sectors, and timely feedback mechanisms continued to affect targeting precision and performance management, making it harder to track outcomes for the most vulnerable and course-correct quickly. 
·        Structural barriers affecting demand and inclusion: Social norms, stigma, affordability constraints, and limited awareness continue to reduce uptake of services among the most marginalized, particularly girls, children in mobile populations, and families facing multiple deprivations. 
Lessons learned for results at scale and equity 
The year generated practical lessons that will shape future programming and partnerships: 
1.      Systems reforms deliver equity only when paired with proactive outreach. Digital and governance improvements increase efficiency, but equitable outcomes depend on reaching households with the highest access barriers through community-based delivery and follow-up. 
2.      Last-mile delivery is a binding constraint for marginalized children. Policy frameworks and national systems must be matched by trained personnel, functional referral pathways, and operational readiness at community level—especially in remote and peri-urban settings. 
3.      Integrated approaches are essential in a multi-shock context. Climate stress, poverty, mobility, and humanitarian risks interact; single-sector solutions are insufficient. Linking health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection, and social protection improves prevention, continuity, and resilience. 
4.      Evidence and visibility are central to sustaining results. In a constrained financing environment, timely evidence on impact, equity, and cost-effectiveness is essential to sustain partnerships and mobilize resources; monitoring and communication must therefore be treated as core delivery functions. 
5.      Innovation must solve delivery bottlenecks, not simply add tools. Technology creates value when it addresses specific constraints—targeting, case tracking, referrals, and accountability—rather than operating as a parallel digital layer. 
Future outlook and how UNICEF will use these insights 
Building on these lessons, in 2026 UNICEF will adjust programme strategies to accelerate results for the most marginalized children through five priorities: 
·        Deepen equity-focused systems strengthening: UNICEF will continue supporting Government-led reforms that strengthen service delivery and accountability, ensuring that policy and digital gains translate into practical improvements at community level. 
·        Strengthen last-mile capacity and continuity:  UNICEF will prioritize workforce capability, operational readiness, and functional referral pathways—particularly in underserved districts—so vulnerable children are identified early and supported consistently. 
·        Scale integrated resilience programming in shock-prone areas:  UNICEF will increasingly connect humanitarian preparedness with longer-term resilience, focusing on water stress and nutrition vulnerability and protecting essential services during shocks. 
·        Accelerate learning and adaptive management: UNICEF will strengthen feedback loops through improved monitoring, periodic joint learning reviews with partners, and clearer use of near-real-time data for course correction. 
·        Expand collaboration and diversify financing: UNICEF will deepen collaboration with Government, UN partners, civil society, and the private sector, while strengthening evidence-based advocacy and exploring innovative partnership and financing options that complement traditional donor support. 
Taken together, these actions reflect a shift toward more inclusive, transparent, and resilient systems that can deliver at scale, while keeping the most marginalized children at the center of programme design, implementation, and partnerships.

In 2025, the situation of children in Egypt  reflects meaningful progress and commitment among all stakeholders. Across  health, education, protection, social protection, and equity, the country  continues to advance efforts to accelerate progress on child-related SDG  targets. Egypt has made historic gains in several domains. At the same time,  some challenges remain in ensuring the wellbeing of all children and their  equitable access to essential services. These patterns mirror global trends,  with widening inequalities and heightened risks for children emerging in the  context of overlapping economic and social pressures.
  
Maintaining macroeconomic stability remains  critical to sustaining progress in realizing children’s rights. Economic  growth is projected to strengthen and reach 4.7 per cent in FY2025/26[1], supported by ongoing  reforms and efforts to expand private sector participation. Reflecting this  outlook, S&P upgraded Egypt’s sovereign credit rating from B- to B in  October 2025.
  
Inflation eased significantly to 10.3 per cent in  December 2025, down from 23.4 per cent a year earlier[2], though the impact of  earlier high inflation and currency depreciation continues to affect  household purchasing power, particularly for families with children in  vulnerable situations.
  
Key macroeconomic risks, including elevated public  debt and exposure to external shocks, remain. These constraints continue to exert  pressure on fiscal space for essential social services, underscoring the  importance of continuing to prioritize efficient, focused, and  child-sensitive public financing to safeguard progress in health, education,  and social protection.
  
In this context, important Government measures to  raise wages and pensions, extend subsidies, and expand social assistance have  helped cushion households facing vulnerabilities. The scale-up of Takaful and  Karama to 5.2 million families[3], along with a 25 per  cent increase in benefits[4], helped cushion  households facing vulnerabilities. These efforts reflect continued commitment  to Egypt’s Vision 2030.
  
Building on this progress, Egypt has maintained  momentum on reforms across social protection, education, early childhood  development, labour policies, and child protection, advancing a more  inclusive, rights-based, and lifecycle-oriented approach to human  development.
  
The Government’s National Comprehensive Development  Strategy further strengthened coherence by providing a shared, evidence-based  framework to guide reforms for growth and employment through three pillars:  1) Human Development for Quality of Life, 2) Structural Transformation  Towards Tradable Sectors, and 3) Redefining State Role and Private Sector  Empowerment. 
  
Egypt’s ongoing demographic transition, where the proportion  of children in the population is projected to decline from 39 per cent in  2023 to 34 per cent in 2030 and 27 per cent by 2050[5], presents a time-bound  opportunity to harness a demographic dividend through strategic investments  in early childhood development, quality education, skills, youth  employability, and the care economy, enhancing productivity, expanding female  labour force participation as fertility rates fall, and supporting a shift in  the dependency ratio. 
  
Multidimensional poverty continues to shape  children’s outcomes. According to the 2024 national Multidimensional Poverty  Index, over one-fifth of Egyptians experience overlapping deprivations, in  areas such as education, social protection, food security, employment and  housing, with rural areas disproportionately affected. Child poverty remains  widespread with 34 per cent of children living in households that are poor.  This rises to 52 per cent in rural Upper Egypt[6] reflecting existing  geographic inequities and underscoring the importance of systems  strengthening, integrated service delivery, and evidence-driven targeting. 
  
Labour market challenges further reinforce poverty  and exclusion. According to the Labour Market Panel Survey 2023, the  unemployment rate stood at around 6 per cent (female unemployment 13 per  cent; male unemployment 5 per cent). Further, highlighted were the labour  market challenges facing young people:26.9 per cent of young people aged  15-24 are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), with young women  disproportionately affected (40.1 vs. 15.8 per cent for young men)2. Skills  mismatches, barriers to transition to employment, and limited labor market  absorptive capacity may constrain progress towards SDG 8 and highlight the  need for stronger linkages between education, skills development, and labour  market demand. 
  
Social sector outcomes reflect steady progress  alongside areas for continued strengthening. Maternal and child health  coverage has improved, and immunization performance remains strong overall.  At the same time, trends in key survival indicators highlight opportunities  to further enhance quality of care, with neonatal mortality increasing from  14 to 18 per 1,000 live births since 2014, maternal mortality remaining an  area for continued focus, and a high Caesarean section rate of 72 per cent.  While immunization coverage is high nationally, lower uptake in some urban  areas suggests the need for targeted analysis and response.
  
Nutrition outcomes demonstrate both advances and  persistent challenges. Declining rates in stunting and wasting are  encouraging; however, an estimated 1.3 million children remain affected.  Child food poverty and anemia among under-fives remain high at 43 per cent,  alongside the coexistence of stunting and being overweight. Exclusive  breastfeeding rates of 40 per cent and gaps in young child diets underscore  opportunities to further strengthen food systems, maternal counselling, and  community-level service delivery.
  
The Government’s commitment to early childhood  development is clearly demonstrated by the endorsement of the National ECD  Strategy by 15 ministries. This unprecedented multisectoral alignment  reinforces a shared commitment to early investment and recognizes that  coordinated action across sectors is essential to delivering lasting outcomes  for young children. However, while 85 per cent of children aged 3–4 is developmentally  on track, fewer than half meet basic literacy and numeracy benchmarks, and  kindergarten enrollment is not optimal (20 per cent)[7]. These trends point to  the importance of further strengthening school readiness and promoting  equitable early learning opportunities. The momentum around the multi  sectoral ECD Strategy, plan and costing offers a strong opportunity for  integrated programming across nutrition, health, stimulation, and early  learning. 
  
Universal access to improved drinking water has  nearly been achieved, yet household-level access to piped water remains  uneven, particularly in rural areas. Sanitation coverage stagnated between  2014–2021, with existing geographic inequities. Declining access to  handwashing facilities warrants continued attention, especially as climate  shocks intensify water scarcity. WASH gaps can potentially undermine progress  in health, nutrition, and education—highlighting the need for integrated  service delivery approaches. 
  
Despite continued infrastructure expansion and  groundbreaking reforms in the education sector, learning poverty remains an area  for continued focus. According to MoETE EMIS (2019/20–2022/23), pre-primary  enrolment has declined by 15 per cent since 2019/20, and 1.4 million children  remain out of school. While primary and preparatory attendance is strong,  secondary attendance shows significant wealth-based disparities (69 per cent  for poorest versus 87 per cent for richest).  
  
Classroom overcrowding and  teacher capacity constraints are key drivers affecting learning outcomes. In this context,  major reforms in 2024/5 have  prioritised reducing class sizes, strengthening teacher quality and increasing  time on task, as well as gains in PIRLS scores. Violence, harmful practices, and exploitation  remain a challenge despite notable declines. Violent discipline affects 83 per  cent of children; child labour affects 1.3 million children; According to  national household survey data, the prevalence of female genital mutilation  among girls aged 15–17 in Egypt declined from 61 per cent in 2014 (EDHS) to  37 per cent in 2021 (EHIS), reflecting a significant generational shift.  Child marriage persists at 14 per cent among women 20–24.[8]
  
Egypt has demonstrated remarkable generosity and  solidarity in hosting people from neighbouring countries who are seeking  safety and opportunity. From 2023–2025, Egypt welcomed over 1.5 million  arrivals from Sudan (40 per cent children) and over 150,000 Palestinians.  While this situation added strain on already stretched social systems,  through its longstanding policy of inclusion, Egypt has provided access to  public services, particularly health, education, and protection, on par with  nationals, reflecting a deeply rooted commitment to human dignity. The  establishment of joint coordination platforms with the United Nations and  partners, alongside the adoption of the new Asylum Law, supporting the  gradual inclusion of non-Egyptians within national systems, further  underscores the Government’s leadership in advancing a nationally owned,  rights-based approach to asylum and refugee governance. These efforts not  only strengthen protection frameworks but also promote social cohesion and  shared responsibility at a time of growing global displacement.
  
Elevating the National Council of Childhood and  Motherhood to ministerial status has strengthened coordination and authority  on child rights. This, along with legal reforms and continued efforts to  strengthen the legal protection framework (including updates to the Child  Law, draft Alternative Care legislation, and online child protection  strategies) clearly signal the Government’s commitment to placing children at  the heart of national priorities. The submission of Egypt’s report to the  Committee on the Rights of the Child further also reflects renewed engagement  and national ownership of the child rights agenda. 
  
Overall, Egypt’s ongoing reform momentum and policy  commitments continue to provide important entry points for UNICEF to support  systems strengthening, safeguard social investments, and help translate  national priorities into equitable and sustainable results for  children.
