In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Egypt in advancing progress toward national goals for children under Egypt’s Vision 2030 and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2023-2027. Through partnerships with key ministries, public institutions, governorates, civil society, the private sector, international financial institutions, and other UN agencies, UNICEF combined evidence-based policy advice, technical expertise, and convening power to support the  realization of children’s rights and improve the capacity, resilience, and accountability of national systems across the key areas of education, child protection, health, nutrition, WASH, social protection, and youth development. 
UNICEF deepened its support for Egypt’s social protection system, including financing for children at national and sub-national levels, and strengthening evidence generation, working closely with the Ministry of Social Solidarity (MoSS), Ministry of Finance (MoF), Ministry of Local Development (MoLD), Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS), Information and Decision Support Centre (IDSC), Parliament, and international partners. These efforts contribute to advancing an inclusive social protection system, expanded real-time data availability, and lay out the groundwork for more child-sensitive public financing initiatives. Under the leadership of the Ministry of Social Solidarity (MoSS), the Government initiated the development of the National Social Protection Framework (NSPF), marking a major milestone in Egypt’s social protection agenda. UNICEF supported the process in coordination with the World Bank and across UN agencies, contributing to inclusive consultations and key policy recommendations. The NSPF underscores Egypt’s commitment to economic security, poverty reduction, and financial inclusion, while promoting inclusive growth and social justice. Complementary analytical studies on universal health insurance extension, legal frameworks, and informality among non-Egyptians provided actionable insights for policy consideration. UNICEF significantly strengthened national data and evidence systems with support for major national surveys, such as the Survey of Young People in Egypt (SYPE), Egyptian Family Health Survey (EFHS 2025), and the national female genital mutilation (FGM) Perceptions Survey, helping address priority data needs. Updates to multidimensional child poverty analysis, a policy tool for informing more targeted and effective interventions to address the deprivations facing children, were also supported. Two national databases on SDGs and child indicators were finalised, contributing to enhanced knowledge dissemination, decisi
on-making, and research. In addition, socioeconomic dashboards, highlighting social sector needs, were developed with IDSC to support evidence-based policy making. Major policy research on child data ecosystems, poverty reduction, and service delivery for displaced populations was also launched. Partnerships with J-PAL MENA and Cairo University expanded evidence-sharing platforms to support evidence-informed programming and policy dialogue. In 2026, this collaboration will be deepened by aligning with Egypt Impact Lab priorities and transitioning these platforms into government-owned policy dialogue mechanisms, reinforcing national research capabilities and embedding evidence use in government decision-making. Efforts in public finance for children (PF4C) contributed to establishing the foundations for child-sensitive budgeting at national and sub-national levels. 
UNICEF’s transparency briefs simplify complex fiscal data into accessible, child-tagged visual formats. Moreover, our support to the Citizen’s Budget document directly contributed to improvements in Egypt’s Open Budget Survey scores and positioned UNICEF’s technical contribution within broader public financial management reforms. Currently utilized by parliamentarians and senior officials to guide decision-making, these briefs bridge the gap between transparency and participation, providing the essential information base for meaningful engagement and evidence-based advocacy for children's rights.
UNICEF is supporting the Ministry of Education and Technical Education (MoETE) in transitioning to Medium-Term Budgeting Frameworks (MTBF) and Programme and Performance-Based Budgeting (PPBB) by building institutional capacity in planning and finance to align with Results-Based Management (RBM) and new public finance management (PFM) principles. Under Output 2 of the System Capacity Grant, this work includes updating the Education Sector Analysis (ESA) and planning, budgeting and prioritization capacity building to ensure education resources are allocated more equitably and monitored for results. A key recent milestone included a cross-sectoral capacity-building workshop, conducted with the Ministry of Finance and UNICEF MENARO, to train social sector officials on costing methodologies within this new PFM framework.
Parallel to these systemic reforms, UNICEF is providing technical assistance to the National Council for Women (NCW) to develop the National Investment Framework for Girls in Egypt (NIFGE). This comprehensive, costed framework aims to empower 13.8 million girls (aged 10–24) by aligning multisectoral efforts across education, health, and protection, while identifying sustainable financing mechanisms to address barriers to economic participation and social inclusion.
At the sub-national level, UNICEF and the Ministry of Local Development (MoLD) established a partnership to advance child-focused planning and budgeting. Youth-led community expenditure monitoring in Fayoum moved into the implementation phase. Similar models are being adapted to Beni Suef, together with other UN Agencies, under the umbrella of the SDG fund. 
In 2025, UNICEF’s integrated support through policy and systems strengthening, service delivery and community engagement further strengthened Egypt’s systems to deliver equitable, resilient and integrated child survival and development services for children. Through partnerships with government and civil society, more than 4.5 million children, women and caregivers were reached across early childhood development (ECD), health, nutrition, water sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and social behavioural change (SBC) interventions, reinforcing progress toward national priorities and the SDGs. 
At the policy level, UNICEF supported government efforts to strengthen the enabling environment for multisectoral ECD by supporting the reactivation of the national ECD Working Group led by the National Council for Childhood and Motherhood (NCCM), with participation from MoF and IDSC. Progress was made in costing the national ECD Strategy, strengthening monitoring systems, and advancing the ECD Knowledge and Competency Framework, contributing to improved governance and professionalization of the frontline workforce. UNICEF also supported MoSS as they led the coordination of line ministries around Egypt’s pledge that 15 per cent of official development assistance benefits persons with disabilities, helping strengthen inclusive ECD and childcare systems and contributing to a high level of ECD integration in primary health care. 
Significant progress was also observed in health and nutrition policy and systems. In 2025, the Ministry of Health and Population (MoHP) updated the Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes and finalized the first National Wasting Prevention and Management Guidelines, while the Food Security and Nutrition Committee launched the National Roadmap for Anemia Reduction. UNICEF supported MoHP and the General Health Accreditation Authority in finalizing national Baby-Friendly Facility accreditation standards, strengthening supportive infant feeding environments. Mental health and psychosocial support coordination continued under the leadership of the General Secretariat for Mental Health and Addiction Treatment, including preparations for the rollout of the Helping Adolescents Thrive approach in 2026, with a core group of trainers (20) from Ministry of Education and Technical Education (MoETE), Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS) and MoHP.  Working with the MoHP and WHO, UNICEF helped shape the National Digital Health Strategy, reinforced foundational infrastructure by establishing a national data centre and positioning DHIS2 as the backbone for priority systems such as the Well Baby Initiative, cold chain monitoring, school health and medical waste management.
In WASH, UNICEF supported system level innovations including a revolving fund for extending safe water and sanitation to underserved households, a Green Health Facility model integrating WASH, energy and waste management, and the DROPs digital reporting and planning platform in the Holding Company for Water and Wastewater to strengthen accountability and climate resilient service planning.  
UNICEF leveraged its technical expertise and catalytic funding to develop innovative, scalable models that enhanced government service delivery across early childhood development, health, nutrition, and WASH in 2025. These efforts focused on modeling interventions with potential for national scale-up.
UNICEF-supported services strengthened the continuum of care for more than 1.5 million children and youth. In early childhood development, 237,000 children and caregivers benefited from Family Counselling Rooms promoting responsive caregiving, while pilots of a scalable nursery model established the groundwork for a future national childcare system. ECD support was also integrated into emergency response, with 126 facilitators reaching 66,000 children and caregivers to ensure continuity of care.
In primary health care, community health and family counselling were prioritized with mapping and capacity development planning for rollout in 2026. National immunization systems sustained 95 per cent coverage, with UNICEF providing targeted support, including US$7.2 million in cold-chain enhancements and the procurement of over 15 million measles–rubella doses, to complement the MoHP’s leadership. A targeted immunization campaign in Aswan and the Red Sea governorates reached 534,700 children aged nine months to 10 years, helping address immunity gaps in high-risk areas. Newborn survival was further prioritized through assessments in priority governorates, the development of a Centres of Excellence model in partnership with MoHP, and the rollout of Early Essential Newborn Care. More than 700 health workers were trained, and primary health care facilities and hospitals were equipped to strengthen infection prevention and quality of care. In nutrition, 22,428 caregivers received infant and young child feeding counselling; 74,760 children were screened for wasting, and 17,300 health workers strengthened their capacities through growth monitoring and breastfeeding training. Climate-smart investments enhanced service resilience and sustainability. Infrastructure upgrades at the primary health care level benefited 500,000 people, while 490,000 individuals gained improved access to solar energy, safe water, sanitation, and waste management services in 49 health facilities, implemented in support of the MoHP and the Egyptian Health Authority. UNICEF supported expanded safe drinking water and sanitation access at household, and community levels, in alignment with the Haya Karima Presidential Initiative. Through a revolving fund implemented by national and governorate-level Water Companies, 20,080 people gained access to improved water and sanitation services. In Aswan, solar-powered upgrades improved water station reliability for 409,000 residents. 2.48 million children in 2
,652 primary schools gained knowledge on WASH, nutrition and climate action through trained teachers and local Water Company staff. More than 1 million children and families on the move, and members of the host community benefited from safe water and hygiene assistance, including 109,000 hygiene kits. 
On community engagement, UNICEF expanded Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) systems by strategically combining digital platforms with interpersonal approaches. For instance, in partnership with the Ministry of Health and Population, an integrated digital ecosystem—anchored in RapidPro and IOGT/ASK Health—enabled the delivery of life-saving information at scale, while linking real-time data collection with frontline service delivery. Through this approach, UNICEF reached 17 million people on Facebook with evidence-based messages promoting healthy behaviours. Digital performance metrics demonstrated strong audience engagement and relevance. Breastfeeding content generated the highest traction, with 67 posts reaching 3.4 million users and 136,000 engagements (a 4 per cent engagement rate). Vaccination messaging followed closely, with 42 posts reaching 3.7 million users and generating 130,000 engagements (a 3.5 per cent engagement rate). Content on parenting, nutrition, and maternal health also performed strongly, while handwashing and hygiene messages reached more targeted audiences. Overall, the platforms generated 653,000 immunization-related interactions and 452,870 engagements on nutrition and child health, reflecting sustained public interest in preventive and child-centred health messaging. To convert digital reach into improved access to health services, UNICEF supported the use of RapidPro to digitally record and analyse nearly 3 million primary health care visits. Building on these interactions, the system automatically generated six million targeted SMS reminders promoting timely immunization, nutrition, and maternal and newborn health practices. This automated outreach was complemented by an MoHP–led online parenting service, where SBC-trained health educators responded to 6,483 caregiver inquiries on breastfeeding, nutrition, routine immunization, and positive parenting. An AI-powered chatbot is being piloted to further scale this support in 2026. Beyond dig
ital platforms, UNICEF-supported community outreach reached 2.47 million caregivers and 3 million parents through skill-building sessions focused on caregiving, healthy lifestyles, and violence prevention. Post-intervention assessments showed that 59.3 per cent of participants demonstrated knowledge of at least five essential family practices, contributing to improved caregiving environments for more than 2 million children.
In 2025, UNICEF and the Ministry of Education and Technical Education (MoETE) delivered transformative progress toward Egypt’s national education priorities, strengthening the foundations of an inclusive, equitable, and future-ready learning system. UNICEF-supported initiatives expanded quality learning opportunities for more than 800,000 children, strengthened foundational literacy, advanced digital inclusion, and reinforced national efforts to improve the quality and governance of the education sector. A landmark achievement was the expansion of the Comprehensive Inclusion Programme to 840 public schools across 11 governorates, reaching 420,000 students, including 40,000 children with disabilities and 20,000 non-Egyptian learners. This scale-up reflected Egypt’s commitment to inclusive education under Education 2.0 and was enabled by a robust capacity-building model. UNICEF trained 8,400 teachers, supported a network of 350 master trainers, and introduced leadership development through the EduLeads programme, strengthening schools’ abilities to deliver safe, inclusive, and high-quality learning environments and providing MoETE with a scalable model for nationwide adoption. UNICEF also played a central role in advancing Egypt’s Foundational Learning Call to Action, particularly through the launch of the National Arabic Language Programme (NALP), a 60-hour remedial literacy programme targeting students in Grades 3–6 who were at risk of falling behind. In its first year, NALP through two phases reached 420,000 children in 2,000 schools, improving literacy scores by an average of 50 percentage points. Cairo Governorate quickly adopted the programme in all primary schools. This rigorous programme was supported by UNICEF’s training of 11,130 teachers and supervisors, a pre- and post-assessment for each student, and a study showing 17 per cent increase in learning as compared to students that did not receive the remedial programme. A second phase covering 1,000 additiona
l schools began in late 2025, including support for early grades, shifting the system toward early identification and remediation of learning gaps. 
For children outside formal education, UNICEF strengthened alternative learning pathways to ensure continuity and inclusion for children affected by displacement. Through Learning Hubs, Learning Spaces, community kindergartens, and centres in North Sinai and Qalyobia, UNICEF provided 16,000 children with foundational learning, life skills, and social cohesion programmes. A new Community Learning Centre Improvement Plan further enhanced quality across 23 centres, benefiting over 5,100 children, and introduced a new Management Information System to improve data-driven planning. Education assistance also supported continuity for displaced youth. UNICEF delivered exam preparation support to 3,100 students and education cash grants to 29,000 learners facing vulnerabilities, helping families overcome financial barriers. An innovative distance learning model was also launched, designed for children unable to access school or stable connectivity. Through community-based learning points informed by household-level assessments, the model is expected to reach up to 500  children out of school.  
UNICEF also contributed to Egypt’s expansion of early childhood education. Through analytical support and policy inputs for the national Bedaya (New Beginnings) initiative and by supporting community-based kindergarten models that promote developmentally appropriate, play-based learning for young children. Innovation and digital learning remained central pillars of UNICEF’s support for system transformation. The Mostakbaly 21st Century Skills Programme reached 38,000 young people through STEAM, digital learning, life skills, and green competencies. The climate-action component mobilized youth across five governorates to improve community environments through tree planting, recycling, and public space greening. Building on early success, UNICEF and MoETE planned to expand the model through TVET pathways in 2026, with potential reach to 100,000 students. Digital learning access also expanded through the Learning Passport, which grew to 70,000 users, and innovative Learning Passport was deployed through offline boxes in single class multigrade rural community schools to provide the experience of fast internet to quality digital learning content in areas with limited or no digital access. UNICEF worked with MoETE and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) on school connectivity through GIGA and piloted satellite-based solutions for low-connectivity areas. Evidence from digital tools, including Akelius, Big Bad Boo SEL social emotional learning-focused content, and the Matific numeracy platform, helped build evidence for future scaling-up effective digital teaching and learning. Continued investments in content development, offline access, and community-based digital learning hubs ensured outreach including girls in rural areas, children and families on the move, and young people from low-connectivity communities. UNICEF also played a central role in strengthening the textbook, curriculum, and teacher development ecosystem. UNICEF supported the 
MoETE  to develop new Arabic language textbooks based on structured pedagogy and latest literacy approaches for 12 million students and integrated girls’ empowerment, disability inclusion, child on the move representation, and climate themes. UNICEF and MoETE’s hybrid training programme, Development Ambassadors, trained 100,000 primary Arabic teachers in foundational literacy methodologies alongside the launch of the Arabic language textbooks.
UNICEF also supported roll-out of the new curriculum for children with intellectual disabilities, advancing MoETE’s commitment to inclusive pathways. Evidence generation and sector coordination were substantially enhanced. Egypt’s first Out-of-School Children Study since 2014 provided essential insights for reintegration policy. As grant agent for the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), UNICEF helped MoETE secure a US$2.1 million System Capacity Grant, establish technical working groups on foundational learning and TVET, and build partnerships with Japan and Italy to introduce AI and coding for 750,000 secondary students and expand internationally recognized TVET certifications for 150,000 learners. 
In 2025, UNICEF worked in close partnership with 26 government counterparts, UN agencies, and civil society organizations to reinforce Egypt’s national child protection system, helping ensure that children in Egypt are safer, better supported, and able to thrive. UNICEF advanced national priorities on social care and protection, human rights, girls empowerement, and safe communities, while contributing to UNSDCF outcomes on human capital and inclusive social services. In efforts to mainstream and institutionalize child protection within national statutory structures across all partnerships, UNICEF trained nearly 4,400 service providers including over 1,700 on mental health and psychosocial support [MHPSS], expanding national capacity to identify and respond to risks and to improve wellbeing for children in vulnerable situations, including non-Egyptians. As a result of this strengthened capacity, more than 134,000 children and caregivers (including 78,556 females) benefited from non-specialized MHPSS and positive parenting services delivered through 87 primary health units, as well as 20 child-friendly spaces and community platforms across 14 governorates. UNICEF and NCCM also expanded MHPSS for young people, offering counselling, referrals, and wellbeing activities through Dawwie spaces and community centres. To additionally advance protection in and around schools, UNICEF expanded the Ending Violence in School (EVIS) programme, contributing to the national Comprehensive Education Programme and the Edu-Leads initiative, as a cornerstone for safe and inclusive quality education. The programme expanded to 450 schools and introduced new training modules for principals, practical tools for social workers, and a monitoring framework, with accreditation underway and in alignment with broader inclusive education reforms. Complementary digital safety efforts reached national scale, including rollout of child online protection toolkits, adapted for children with disabilities, a
nd a youth innovation challenge with 11,000 student submissions. 
Preventing harmful practices remained a priority, addressing those deeply rooted in social and gender norms that continue to affect millions of girls and women in Egypt. UNICEF placed particular emphasis on tackling the medicalization of FGM, recognizing that more than 80 per cent of cases are performed by medical providers. Through partnerships with NCCM, the medical syndicate, and civil society, UNICEF supported over 26,000 girls, women, and family members with FGM prevention counselling, through 150 private health facilities, where trained practitioners offered sensitive, evidence-based guidance. Exit (phone-based) interviews showed 94 per cent satisfaction, reporting respectful treatment, comfortable environments, and knowledgeable providers. The sessions led to attitude shifts, with 83 per cent saying their views on FGM were significantly influenced and 78 per cent stating they would not subject their daughters to the practice. Furthermore, medical and nursing students emerged as peer educators through practical community initiatives; and religious leaders were supported to address misconceptions linking FGM and religion. 
In parallel, UNICEF provided support to national child protection stakeholders to strengthen response services for child survivors of violence and those in contact with the law, including children and families on the move and host communities. By expanding service delivery points, investing in institutional and human capacities, and evidence-based progamming across sectors, over 39,000 children accessed social, legal, and health services, including specialized MHPSS. The Ministry of Social Solidarity’s Case Management Units, supported by UNICEF across 14 governorates, strengthened alternative care monitoring and family-based care. Upgraded quality assurance systems, including assessments of 23 group homes and new inspection tools for 437 facilities, further enhanced safety and standards. UNICEF also accelerated system strengthening and governance, including initiating a capacity assessment of the national Child Helpline, a structural review of the NCCM’s SOPs and governance structures, and upgrades to digital systems. The national case management information system (IMS) is being redesigned as Egypt’s child protection monitoring platform, with an interoperable IMS between NCCM and the Office of Public Prosecution (OPP) launched and a dedicated system for displaced children and families, and migrants operationalized to streamline referrals and data-sharing. A national service mapping is additionally being digitized to improve referral mechanisms, and a community feedback guideline was introduced to strengthen accountability to affected populations (AAP).  In the justice sector, UNICEF helped expand child-friendly justice pathways. The Alexandria Child-Friendly Court was completed, and dedicated child-friendly spaces were established in Cairo prosecution offices, promoting inclusion of children with disabilities through the provision of a Braille printer to OPP. Nearly 500 justice professionals received training on restorative justice, cybercri
me, violence against children and women, and FGM. UNICEF promoted non-custodial alternatives and expanded vocational training for children in conflict with the law, implemented with private sector partners.  UNICEF also played a key role in shaping national child protection priorities, contributing to follow-up actions on Universal Periodic Review (UPR) and Treaty Body recommendations on child rights, and guiding safeguarding policies in nurseries and schools. To guide policies for children on the move and migrant children, UNICEF provided input on the Asylum Law bylaws to the National Council for Human Rights through the Protection Interagency Working Group. UNICEF also contributed to the development of the first National Child Protection and MHPSS Strategy, ensuring young people’s needs are central to national protection systems. To ensure that all child protection programming is evidence-based for children’s best interest, evidence generation remained central, including a violence against children (VAC)–violence against women (VAW) study, child marriage costing, and the national FGM household survey of 20,000 families with a complementary phone survey. 
Alongside strengthening the child protection legislative framework and service delivery, UNICEF focused on generating demand and enhancing community awareness of child rights and child-friendly practices. National campaigns reached 49 million people and generated 2.5 million engagements, while local initiatives mobilized more than 787,000 community members. Through interactive approaches, including art, theatre, sports, and community outreach, UNICEF supported the creation of safe spaces to address violence against children and women, FGM, and children’s rights, empowering children as advocates for change. These efforts were reinforced through podcasts, TV drama partnerships, exhibitions, and creative storytelling, broadening public understanding and advancing child-friendly practices nationwide.
 In 2025, UNICEF and national partners placed young people at the centre of Egypt’s development agenda, expanding opportunities for learning, participation, protection, and economic inclusion. Through partnerships with Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS), MoETE, Ministry of Planning, Economic Development and International Cooperation (MoPEDIC), National Council for Women (NCW), NCCM, and Generation Unlimited (GenU), UNICEF contributed to key national priorities and the UNSDCF by enhancing young people’s skills, voice, and agency while creating more supportive community and institutional environments. A flagship achievement was the expansion of Meshwary, a national youth skills programme led by MoYS, and supported by UNICEF. Reaching over 90,000 youth across 794 youth centres, Meshwary provided structured modules on life skills, digital literacy, employability, and entrepreneurship. National trainer accreditation and decentralization contributed to sustained quality and government ownership. With strong alignment to labour market priorities, Meshwary now serves as one of Egypt’s most scalable and sustainable youth empowerment models. UNICEF also strengthened engagement through the pilot of the Children’s Civic Empowerment Programme (CCEP) in Assiut and Fayoum. Through participatory activities such as “Zoom in on Your Community” campaigns, young people identified local priorities and recommended actionable solutions, thereby building practical leadership skills and strengthening linkages between youth, local authorities, and community structures. The pilot generated insights on effective pathways for youth participation and supports scaling aligned with Egypt’s priorities for social cohesion and youth engagement. UNICEF and partners also led national-scale SBC efforts addressing harmful behaviours, children and youth wellbeing, and positive parenting. Two nationwide campaigns reached more than 600 million digital impressions and millions more through in-person caravan
s, MoYS youth centres, TV, and radio. 
The Government’s national parenting programme gained further traction, enabling families to better understand developmental needs and support the wellbeing of young people in their households.  Girls’ empowerment advanced through the national Dawwie programme, implemented with NCW. Reaching over 210,000 girls, Dawwie delivered life skills, mentorship, safe spaces, and girls empowerment activities both online and in community hubs. The programme provided girls with opportunities to build self-confidence, make informed decisions, and contribute to community development. Strong government leadership, dedicated community facilitators, and strategic coordination with education and youth networks were central to these gains. As secretariat of Shabab Balad, in close coordination with Resident Coordinator, MOPEDIC, MOYS and key partners, UNICEF as a partner contributing to youth programmes, helped strengthen Egypt’s youth employment and skills ecosystem, supporting over 350,000 youth with digital skills, green skills, entrepreneurship training, and employability support. Public–private partnerships strengthened school-to-work transitions, enhanced alignment with labour market needs, and expanded pathways to dignified employment. In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Egypt to launch Shabab Balad Academy, one of the flagship initiatives of Shabab Balad Egypt. It is a national hub of excellence and a catalyst for an integrated ecosystem that connects young people to real opportunities for learning, engagement, employment, and entrepreneurship. 
In 2025, UNICEF continued to strengthen its role as a trusted advocate for children in Egypt, delivering impactful visibility and influence in a complex communications landscape, amplifying children’s voices, informing public discourse, and supporting the broader national agenda for child protection, wellbeing, and inclusion.  UNICEF, in partnership with the government and key stakeholders, implemented eight national advocacy campaigns addressing priority issues including FGM prevention, malnutrition, positive parenting, foundational learning, online safety, menstrual health, breastfeeding, and immunization. For example, UNICEF provided technical support to the groundbreaking Lam El-Shamsiyya television campaign on child protection, which helped foster constructive dialogue and reaffirmed UNICEF’s commitment to children.  These campaigns reached 106 million people, generated 7 million digital engagements, and resulted in 375 top-tier media mentions, with support from over 30 influential partners across government, media, civil society, youth, and private sector networks. 
In 2025, UNICEF Egypt advanced national evaluation capacity and fostered a culture of evidence, learning, and accountability across the country programme. UNICEF provided technical support for Egypt’s first National Evaluation Policy (NEP), collaborating with the IDSC and UNDP to draft, validate, and prepare the policy for operationalization. This included capacity-building for IDSC staff, workshops on international country experiences, and integration of lessons learned from Morocco, Palestine, and South Africa. 
UNICEF also helped strengthen national evaluation ecosystems through systematic support to government partners, promoting child-sensitive, equity-focused, and resilience evaluation approaches. A mapping of M&E academic programmes revealed the importance of enhancing child-focused content, leading to revisions of the Monitoring and Evaluation Diploma at the Institute of National Planning, integrating child rights, equity, and humanitarian principles. Complementary digital capacity-building included the IMPrESS online course, with 34 participants from IDSC, Cairo University, the Egypt Impact Lab, and the Ministry of Local Development. In 2025, UNICEF also initiated evaluation management responses for the Dawwie initiative and the global GAP 2 and 3 evaluation and commissioned major studies including a formative evaluation of the Comprehensive Inclusion Programme and a multi-country evaluation of the Life Skills and Citizenship Education (LSCE) Framework, scheduled for completion in early 2026. Through these efforts, UNICEF strengthened Egypt’s evidence base, promoted learning-informed decision-making, and reinforced accountability, ensuring that investments for children are guided by credible data, rigorous evaluation, and systematic knowledge-sharing.

Data and Evidence to support advocacy and decision  making
  
In 2025, UNICEF Egypt strengthened evidence  generation and utilization for children through important partnerships with  CAPMAS and the Information and Decision Support Centre (IDSC). While  challenges remain, these collaborations created important opportunities to  generate new insights and improve access to policy-relevant information. The  Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR) highlighted the importance of timely,  well-coordinated data for adaptive programming and strategic engagement.  Where recent evidence was available, including health and nutrition  monitoring or learning assessments, UNICEF and partners were able to support  planning, respond to emerging needs, and contribute to policy discussions.  Looking to 2026, UNICEF will build on these efforts and continue using  official data to inform planning and budgeting. Key priorities will include  disability data, early childhood indicators, MHPSS metrics, and information  on violence affecting children. Investments will focus on evidence-informed  decision-making through results-based management, Management Information Systems,  child-centred digital monitoring tools, and strengthened knowledge  management. UNICEF will continue supporting institutional mechanisms that  systematically integrate children’s perspectives into planning and service  improvement, fostering sustainable, evidence-driven approaches to advancing  child well-being.
  
 System Strengthening within the  Humanitarian Development Nexus
  
 In 2025, UNICEF advanced a  system-strengthening approach to respond to the needs of children and families  on the move and host communities, reinforcing government leadership,  institutional capacity, and long-term resilience. As coordination mechanisms continue  to mature and sectoral reforms shape national priorities, UNICEF provided  support to people in vulnerable situations alongside national systems. This  approach aimed not only to meet immediate needs, but also to strengthen the capacity  of government institutions to plan for, absorb, and respond to future shocks.  UNICEF provided targeted technical assistance, capacity development, evidence  generation, and support for policy and operational frameworks, including  referral and coordination mechanisms, while investing in digital tools and  data systems that improved service delivery, and accountability. 
  
At the national level, digitally enabled processes  strengthened planning, monitoring, and data ecosystems, further enhancing the  availability, quality, and use of child-focused data to design targeted  interventions for people in vulnerable situations and development  programming. Improved analytical products and institutional capacities in  results-based management, data governance, and data protection further  supported evidence-informed decision-making within government systems.  Support to key institutions, including the NCCM, NCW, MoHP, and MoLD, through  digital transformation strategies, management information systems, and  nationwide services mapping for children and families on the move, non-Egyptians,  and host communities, contributed to strengthening coordination across  sectors and improving preparedness and response readiness. 
  
By embedding child-centred and need-based  interventions within existing health, nutrition, child protection, and social  protection systems, UNICEF helped ensure service continuity during shocks  while contributing to the durability and adaptability of national systems.  Partnerships with WHO, WFP, FAO, and UNFPA further demonstrated that  joint, system-based approaches can reduce fragmentation, support alignment  with national priorities, and reinforce government stewardship. Building on  these gains, UNICEF will continue in 2026 to advance convergence,  multisectoral programming, and strengthened coordination, with the objective  of enhancing national capacities to deliver equitable, resilient, and  sustainable services for children in vulnerable situations.
  
Equity and Inclusion 
  
In 2025, UNICEF’s work highlighted both Egypt’s  progress in expanding access to services and the remaining barriers experienced  by children in vulnerable situations. For instance, some non-Egyptian  children encountered challenges related to transitions between learning  pathways, children with disabilities often required specialized support, and  girls and young people may face social or environmental constraints affecting  protection, health, or learning. Awareness of child protection pathways also  varies across communities. Programmes such as Dawwie and the Joint FGM  initiative demonstrated that sustained engagement, combining community-level  dialogue with system-wide reforms, can foster positive social and behavioural  changes. 
  
The humanitarian-development nexus further showed  that strengthening national systems enhances the inclusiveness and resilience  of services, benefiting all children in Egypt, including those impacted by  displacement, and those in living in remote areas. Looking ahead to 2026,  UNICEF will adopt a holistic life-cycle approach to child well-being,  prioritizing quality services for children who stand to benefit the most.  Support will focus on advancing the implementation of critical national  reforms in child development, primary health care, education, and child  protection, including community-based support for children with disabilities  and reinforced pathways for all children in Egypt. Child protection efforts  will emphasize awareness of reporting mechanisms, support ongoing justice  reforms, and expansion of community-based prevention, ensuring services are  accessible, and responsive to the diverse needs of all children.
  
Financing for children 
  
Financing children received growing national  attention, accompanied by opportunities to reinforce child-related  expenditure analysis and programme-based budgeting. Translating this momentum  into sustained operational financing remains an area for continued  collaboration with government partners. By making allocations visible and  understandable, key stakeholders are better positioned to advocate for  adequate and effective financing for children. In 2026, UNICEF will continue  to work with national counterparts and IFI/DFIs to strengthen  financing-for-children efforts, through financial analysis to expand  financing for child-related priorities.
  
Advocacy and Communication
  
In 2025, UNICEF Egypt’s communications and advocacy  work unfolded in a rapidly evolving environment, where new technologies and  algorithm-driven digital ecosystems shaped visibility, trust, and narrative  influence. UNICEF advanced its efforts around an evidence-based, office-wide,  and intentional advocacy approach, demonstrating that clear strategic  alignment, shared priorities, and coherence across sectors can strengthen impact.  The value of early co-creation with partners, alongside smart audience  segmentation, and data-driven optimization, proved instrumental in enhancing  campaign and communications performance, while social listening remained essential  for real-time sentiment tracking, risk scanning, and crisis preparedness.  Looking ahead, UNICEF Egypt will build on these lessons to focus on  strategic influence and engagement; embedding  evidence, analytics, and social listening into content and decision-making;  strengthening crisis readiness; responsibly leveraging AI; and deepening  partnerships with government counterparts, and high-impact allies across  society, including young people –  reinforcing its credibility and leadership as a trusted advocate and voice  for children in Egypt.
  
Innovation, Digital Transformation and Youth  Engagement 
  
In 2025, innovation remained central to UNICEF’s  programming, with digital tools and platforms in MHPSS, nutrition training,  EdTech, and monitoring showing strong potential for scale and supporting  broader national digital transformation. The year underscored the value of  aligning innovative approaches with national systems and leveraging  partnerships, demonstrating that initiatives such as joint digital learning programmes  can enhance sustainability and expand access for young people across  governorates. At the same time, opportunities emerged to harmonize youth  programming and streamline internal processes to ensure timely engagement. 
  
Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF will advance the  Community Center Model to provide multisectoral services to youth based on  needs, strengthen convergence within programming, and expand digital learning  through GIGA, digital pedagogy, and foundational learning platforms. Skills  development pathways, including Mostakbaly and the Learning-to-Earning  initiative, will be broadened to reach more youth, while digital SBC and  parenting tools will be scaled to strengthen caregiver engagement. Insights  from 2024–2025 reaffirm the importance of strong partnerships, system-based  approaches, and evidence-informed programming. While some systems and  processes continue to be refined, the year highlighted significant progress  through collaboration and convergence. In 2026, UNICEF will continue working  closely with government and partners to scale innovative solutions, advance  shared priorities, and ensure children in vulnerable situations have access  to sustainable, high-quality, and impactful services.

In 2025, Iran continued to face  a challenging socio-economic and political environment with direct and profound  consequences for the well-being of children, adolescents and families. The  country’s economy was marked by a very low growth of 0.6 per cent, record  high inflation of 44.6 per cent according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and  hence a rapid currency devaluation. Further intensified by ongoing unilateral  and renewed international sanctions, these pressures have resulted in  increased poverty and heightened vulnerabilities, disproportionately  affecting female-headed households, children in marginalized regions,  refugees, and those living in informal settlements. A significant proportion  of households experience constraints not only in income but also in access to  education, health, nutrition, and protection services. Further compounding  these pressures, the 12-day conflict between Iran and Israel in June-July  2025 resulted in 1,062 fatalities with women and children among the casualties  and contributed to heightened insecurity and regional instability. While the  conflict did not trigger large-scale internal displacement, UNICEF prioritized  continuity of essential services, emergency, WASH, health, and child  protection interventions in affected border and urban areas, ensuring that  children and families received timely support.
  
Following the regularization of the  residence of migrants in Iran and according to UNHCR, nearly 1.8 million Afghans  were returned to their country in 2025 with more than 852,000 of them deported  after the 12-day war. This leaves a population of more than 2.7 million  refugees, primarily from Afghanistan still hosted by Iran, many of whom live  in urban areas or informal settlements. Refugees and migrants face some limitations  in some areas in receiving primary health care and barriers to accessing  essential services such as education, and social protection especially for  the undocumented who fear deportation, while also confronting economic  insecurity. UNICEF’s 2025 programming emphasized equitable access to services  for these populations, with focus on registered Afghans, addressing gender,  age, and disability considerations, and promoting inclusive approaches in  collaboration with government counterparts.
  
The health and well-being of  children remained closely linked to the performance of the primary health  care (PHC) system. Although the country maintains an extensive PHC network,  access gaps persist in rural, border, and underserved areas. An estimate  15–20 per cent of PHC service delivery points were not fully operational in  high-need regions, and functioning facilities frequently faced shortages of health  workers, essential equipment, and adequate infrastructure. These constraints –  compounded by population growth, recurring natural disasters, and increasing climate-related  pressures – continued to highlight the need for system-strengthening and  capacity-building measures to ensure continuity and quality of essential  health services for children and their families
  
Education remained a national  priority. Primary school enrollment remained high, exceeding 98 per cent, yet  challenges persisted in ensuring smooth transitions to lower and upper  secondary levels, particularly in rural areas and among refugee children.  Gender disparities, gaps in disability-inclusive services, and overcrowded  classrooms were further compounded by declining public expenditure on  education and a shortage of qualified teachers. In response, UNICEF’s 2025  interventions focused on addressing these inequalities through targeted  support for teachers, development of inclusive learning materials, and expansion  of pre-primary and remedial education for children at risk of dropout.
  
Access to safe water (99.8 per cent  in urban and 97.1 per cent in rural context), sanitation (100 per cent in urban  and 96.9 per cent in rural areas), and hygiene (WASH) was generally high.  However, persistent disparities continued to affect rural and marginalized  communities. Severe droughts, critically depleted water reserves, and aging  or inadequate infrastructure significantly constrained the delivery of safe  drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene services in 2025. UNICEF prioritized  sustainable and resilient solutions, including the installation of solar-powered  water systems, support to water-quality testing laboratories, and community-level  hygiene promotion initiatives.
  
Child protection also remained a  priority. Iran made progress in strengthening legislative and policy frameworks,  including work on the   draft comprehensive Child Act, the related  Education Bill, and ongoing capacity-building for child protection  professionals, social service workers, frontliners, including the social  service workforce, law enforcement forces, judges, and prosecutors.  Nonetheless, inter-sectoral and inter-organizational coordination gaps, challenges  in establishment of protective services for children on the move, and risks  for children in street situations persisted. UNICEF’s programming therefore emphasized  systems strengthening, advocacy and policy support, and inclusive approaches  to ensure children’s rights were safeguarded in both development and  emergency contexts.
  
Overall, the 2025 context in  Iran was defined by interlinked challenges of economic vulnerability, security  incidents, refugee and migration needs, climate-related risks, and systemic  disparities. These factors collectively informed UNICEF’s programming,  requiring a dual approach that combined immediate humanitarian response and  long-term system strengthening to ensure that all children, particularly  those most marginalized, had access to essential services, protection, and  opportunities to thrive.

In 2025, UNICEF Iran delivered a  range of interventions across health, education, child protection, WASH, and  social inclusion, achieving measurable improvements in the lives of children,  adolescents, and caregivers, with a particular focus on vulnerable groups,  including Afghan refugees, girls, and children with disabilities. UNICEF’s  contributions emphasized strengthening national systems, promoting equity, and  enhancing resilience to both chronic vulnerabilities and acute emergencies.
  
Goal Area 1 – Every child  survives and thrives
  
UNICEF continued to strengthen  Iran’s Primary Health Care (PHC) system in 2025, with a focus on underserved and  border areas where   gaps in access to essential health services  persisted. UNICEF significantly enhanced access to essential health services  for more than 115,000 people through the deployment of full health-care teams  across 14 Service Delivery Points (SDPs) in Zabol and Mashhad. This support  contributed to a 40 per cent increase in overall service coverage, with measurable  improvements across key health indicators, including immunization, child  health, antenatal and pregnancy care, disease screening, and laboratory  services. Focusing on strengthening the PHC system, in Chabahar,  Sistan and Baluchestan, approximately 10,000 people gained improved access to  comprehensive primary health services through six newly equipped and  operationalized PHC SDPs, addressing geographic and vulnerability-related  service gaps. These interventions contributed substantially to improved  health outcomes and expanded equitable access to quality health care for  vulnerable communities.
  
UNICEF continued to strengthen  health emergency preparedness, response, and resilience through multiple  interventions. These included the development of a PHC Rapid Response Tool  for integration into the national health system, as well as the provision of  portable PHC tents and rapid response backpacks. These resources enable  timely health responses during emergencies and ensure the continuity of  essential PHC services for populations affected by emergencies. To build  local capacity, fifty-four PHC managers from at-risk districts of Tehran  completed six days of training on sustaining PHC operations and health  systems under urban warfare simulations, enhancing leadership, operational  preparedness, and continuity planning for essential services. In addition, at  border points, UNICEF supported the operation of six fully equipped health  connex units, providing screening and diagnostic services to over 200 Afghan  refugees daily.
  
UNICEF contributed to national vaccination  and immunization systems by supporting the installation of ten vaccine walk-in  cold rooms and training seventy cold chain managers on safe vaccine storage,  handling and quality assurance. These investments enhanced national cold  chain capacity and helped safeguard immunization coverage for a population of  over two million, including an estimated number of 160,000 children under  five.
  
UNICEF’s support to nutrition  interventions strengthened both preventive and therapeutic care. A total of  1,142,754 children under five received two mega doses of vitamin A  supplementation across 20 provinces, reducing the risk of vitamin A  deficiency and associated morbidity. Moreover, standardized therapeutic care  reached 1,512 children with severe acute malnutrition in Tehran, Mashhad,  Zabol, Zahedan, and Iranshahr, improving survival and recovery outcomes. 
  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened  adolescent health and wellbeing outcomes by expanding access to integrated,  gender-responsive services addressing mental health, life skills development,  and risk prevention. Through the Adolescent Wellbeing and Empowerment Programme  implemented in Kermanshah and Khorasan Razavi provinces, 6,562 adolescent  girls and their family members were reached, including 1,223 Afghan girls and  35 girls with disabilities. Targeted outreach reduced access barriers for  marginalized adolescents, particularly refugees, girls, and those living in  underserved areas, while structured life skills education, selective drug use  prevention, HIV prevention education, and competency-based training enhanced adolescents’  knowledge, resilience, and capacity for informed decision-making.
  
UNICEF scaled up mental health  and psychosocial support services   in 2025, reaching 36,262 children,  adolescents, youth, parents, and caregivers across multiple provinces. These  gender-responsive interventions improved emotional wellbeing, coping  strategies, and psychosocial functioning, particularly among adolescents  affected by stress, displacement, and socio-economic hardship. Parental  engagement initiatives delivered in 21 cities of Sistan and Baluchistan through  PHC centres and schools strengthened caregivers’ capacity to support  adolescent mental health, while the integration across health, education, and  community platforms reinforced continuity of care and sustainability within  national systems.
  
Beginning in 2025, UNICEF  leveraged innovation to strengthen equitable access to essential health  services by integrating human-centred design into the HeLPS-NET initiative, a  community-based, digitally enabled health promotion and engagement system. By  winning the SPARK Innovation Accelerator award, UNICEF mobilized resources to  digitalize community engagement platforms, institutionalize behaviour change  monitoring and assessment, and strengthen evidence-based planning.
  
In the field, UNICEF addressed  persistent equity gaps by harnessing emerging technologies and public–private  partnerships. For children with disabilities, Cyclops, an AI-enabled virtual  reality therapy for amblyopia, delivered care that is four times faster and  more effective than traditional methods. Piloting the initiative with twenty  children from low-income households across eight provinces, 65 per cent girls  and including children with multiple disabilities, received these free  services, demonstrating UNICEF’s contribution to innovation-driven,  inclusive, and results-oriented child health interventions.
  
Goal Area 2 – Every child learns
  
UNICEF strengthened access to  education for refugee and host-community children, focusing on equitable and  inclusive learning environments. WASH upgrades in 128 schools in Razavi  Khorasan and Sistan and Baluchistan improved safe water and sanitation for  72,108 students, including 34,000 girls, while school health and hygiene  programs reached 42,744 students. Early learning opportunities expanded to  1,200 Afghan and host-community children, and remedial classes improved  learning outcomes and retention for 4,283 students, reducing dropout risk.  Classroom conditions were enhanced through the provision of teaching and  learning materials to 142 schools, benefiting 12,000 primary and pre-primary  students.
  
For children with disabilities,  UNICEF’s interventions included sustaining school attendance and  rehabilitation for 4,118 children through targeted cash support, equipping 53  comprehensive education, rehabilitation and screening centres of the Special Education  Organization in Khorasan Razavi for 686 children annually, and training 1,500  teachers in inclusive education, reaching over 33,000 children.  Capacity-building and digital accessibility initiatives improved access to  quality learning materials, including braille textbooks and prototype digital  learning platforms, contributing to equity and inclusion.
  
UNICEF accelerated adolescent  and youth skills development through formal and non-formal education pathways  in 2025. The Adolescent and Youth Empowerment Programme expanded from two to  six provinces, equipping 1,201 adolescents, including 200 girls, with  advanced technical, digital, and soft skills. This expansion resulted in 824  certifications, 390 internships or apprenticeships, and 103 job placements,  significantly boosting young people’s readiness for learning, employability,  and livelihoods. At the same time, improvements to boarding school  facilities, the rollout of ICT-enabled learning for 2,613 adolescents, and  the training of 130 instructors created more inclusive, modern, and gender-responsive  learning environments. These efforts collectively strengthened employability,  inclusion, and gender equity across adolescent and youth programmes.
  
Goal Area 3 – Every child is  protected from violence and exploitation
  
National Child Protection in  Emergencies (CPiE) capacities were strengthened through UNICEF support to the  Iranian Red Crescent Society’s (IRCS) SAHAR (Mental Health/Psychosocial  Support) teams. A total of 402 SAHAR team members were deployed and child-friendly  were established and activated in 400 IRCS facilities, equipped with inclusive  educational, recreational and emergency supplies.  As a result, 100,520 children, adolescents,  and caregivers across 23 conflict-affected provinces received community-based  MHPSS and CPiE services. Furthermore, UNICEF, in partnership with local NGOs,  supported the deployment of 80 psychologists in five conflict-affected  provinces, providing structured MHPSS interventions to 175,000 beneficiaries,  including children with disabilities.
  
National Child Protection  systems for prevention of Violence against Children were enhanced. UNICEF  supported the establishment and operationalization of Child Protection  Technical Groups in all pediatric hospitals strengthening delivery of comprehensive,  multisectoral care and protection services in medical settings. In addition, 90  health social workers and provincial focal points were trained to deliver social  work interventions in crises and disasters, complemented by continued  development of national protocol on social work in emergencies. 
  
Capacities of the justice system  to protect children in contact with the law, including child offenders and  child victims and witnesses of crime, were strengthened through focused  investments in child-friendly justice approaches. A total of 150 law  enforcement officers, social workers, prosecutors and judges in Lorestan and  Khuzestan provinces gained enhanced ability to apply restorative justice and  diversion programmes for children in conflict with the law. In parallel, 290  justice and social service professionals in Qom, Isfahan, West Azarbaijan and  Kermanshah provinces gained strengthened knowledge of child rights and standards  for protection of child victims and witnesses of crime. At provincial level, the  capacities of 78 senior officials — including Director Generals of Social  Affairs, prosecutors, judges and State Welfare Organization heads- were  enhanced for strategic planning and coordination on child protection,  reinforcing institutional leadership and sustainability of child-friendly  justice reforms.
  
Goal Area 4 – Every child has  access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services
  
In 2025, UNICEF improved access  to safe, child-friendly water, sanitation and hygiene services in education  and health settings. WASH facilities were rehabilitated and constructed in 128  schools benefiting over 72,000 students, alongside hygiene promotion training  and distribution of hygiene kits, contributing to safer learning environments  and improved hygiene practices among children.
  
In Chabahar, UNICEF fully  supported the solarization of selected health care facilities, ensuring  reliable power supply for vaccine cold storage and strengthening infection  prevention and control for services targeting women and children. In  parallel, the application of the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility  Improvement Tool (WASH-FIT) strengthened the capacity of health staff to  identify and address gaps in water, sanitation, hygiene and infection  prevention, contributing to safer service delivery for newborns, children and  mothers.
  
At community level, water  conservation behaviours were promoted through the “Water for All” campaign. The  initiative engaged 5,000 students as water ambassadors in 20 schools in South  Khorasan, including schools with 50 per cent girls’ enrolment. The campaign  strengthened awareness and adoption of positive water-use practices among  students and surrounding communities.
  
Goal Area 5 – Every child has an  equitable chance in life
  
Availability and use of  child-centred evidence remained critical in 2025 for strengthening government  decision-making and enhancing the equity of social protection systems. Until  recently, child poverty measurement in Iran relied primarily on income-based  criteria, limiting visibility into the multiple overlapping deprivations experienced  by children. To address this gap, UNICEF supported the generation of the  country’s first comprehensive nationwide evidence on multidimensional child poverty  across education, health, housing, protection, and access to basic services  through the National Multidimensional Child Poverty (MDCP) Study in 2025.  This analysis has reportedly enabled government counterparts to apply  multidimensional eligibility and targeting criteria, improving the identification  of children facing compounded vulnerabilities and enhancing the effectiveness  and equity of social protection measures beyond income-based support alone. 
  
In 2025, UNICEF as well  supported 1,100 children living in street situations through Cash Plus  assistance, combining financial support for basic needs with protection,  education, and psychosocial services. This integrated approach reduced immediately  pressures on families, improves children’s safety and well-being and facilitated  their return to learning and essential services. At the same time, UNICEF continued  strengthening more inclusive and equitable child-protection systems,  improving access for adolescents, refugees, and children with disabilities  who are most at risk of being left behind.
  
Communications, Advocacy and Partnerships
  
UNICEF implemented a nationwide  communication and advocacy strategy to emphasize child rights, gender  inclusion, and disability-responsive approaches. Digital campaigns reached  over 12 million people, including podcasts, videocasts, and social media  content highlighting positive parenting, adolescent development, and mental  health. CRC-focused communication products were made more accessible through sign  language adaptation, animated video formats, and inclusive design, ensuring wider  reach among children and caregivers, including those with disabilities.  
  
In 2025, UNICEF Iran’s results  for children were achieved through strong collaboration with government  counterparts, civil society, United Nations agencies, private sector actors,  and international donors. The organization also acknowledges the critical  support of its donors, including the Directorate-General for European Civil  Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), Directorate-General for  the Middle East, North Africa (DG MENA), GAVI Vaccine Alliance, the  Netherlands, Republic of Korea, Switzerland, France, United Kingdom and Australia,  which, together with flexible resources, enabled UNICEF to deliver essential  services, emergency response, and systems-strengthening interventions for  children across the country.
  
Public-private partnerships  further amplified UNICEF’s resource mobilization, advocacy efforts and national  visibility on child rights. UNICEF led private sector initiatives, including  cause-related marketing, fundraising campaigns, and advocacy for  family-friendly workplace policies, while engaging partners such as Panter  Entrepreneurship Group, Iran-Austria Chamber of Commerce, Book City, and  Tejarat Bank. These partnerships reinforced UNICEF’s positioning and expanded  the reach of child rights agenda. These collaborations contributed to mobilizing  additional resources and supported programme delivery in health, education,  WASH, and child protection, ensuring continued progress toward equitable  access to services and opportunities for all children and adolescents in  2025.

In 2025, UNICEF Iran operated in  a highly complex and constrained environment shaped by economic pressures,  and natural as well as anthropogenic hazards, all of which affected programme  delivery and outcomes for children. Persistent high inflation, currency  depreciation, and fiscal constraints limited government resources and  heightened vulnerability among households, particularly. These dynamics deepened  existing inequalities, particularly for children in remote areas, those with  disabilities, and refugee communities, requiring UNICEF to prioritize  targeted interventions to maintain access to essential services. The  operating environment was further complicated by climate-related events, including  severe droughts and water scarcity, which affected communities across  multiple provinces including Tehran as the capital which is the residence to  over 10 million people. These conditions underscored the necessity of  building resilient, climate-adaptive systems, particularly in health, WASH,  and education sectors.
  
A key operational challenge in  2025 was ensuring continuity and quality of services in underserved and  high-risk areas. Despite Iran’s well-established Primary Health Care (PHC)  system, service gaps persisted in border provinces and remote communities,  where infrastructure, staffing, and cold chain facilities remained limited. UNICEF-supported  interventions, including the deployment of mobile clinics, cold chain  expansions, and vitamin A supplementation campaigns, highlighted both the  potential for rapid scale-up and the ongoing challenge of sustaining  equitable coverage in geographically dispersed populations. Similar  disparities continued to affect access to inclusive equitable education. Children  with disabilities, refugee children, and girls in rural areas faced  persistent barriers due to overcrowded classrooms, shortage of trained  teachers, and inadequate WASH facilities.  Nonetheless, these efforts underscored the  need for continued system-level support to improve retention, learning  outcomes, and equitable access for all learners.
  
The 12-day war, though brief,  had a measurable psychosocial impact on children and caregivers, revealing  gaps in preparedness for acute shocks. The rapid mobilization of MHPSS  services through IRCS and local NGO networks illustrated the importance of  pre-established partnerships and surge capacity, while highlighting the  critical need for continued training, inclusive approaches, and scaling of  child-friendly spaces in emergencies. Lessons from this response reinforced  the value of integrating emergency preparedness into ongoing programming  across health, education, and protection sectors, ensuring children’s needs  are anticipated, addressed swiftly, and sustained over time.
  
Water, sanitation, and hygiene  (WASH) interventions also faced challenges related to resource limitations,  infrastructure maintenance, and climate impacts. While access to safe water  is high nationally, disparities remain in rural and marginalized communities.  UNICEF’s water system rehabilitation efforts demonstrated the efficacy of  community-level engagement, solar-powered solutions, and gender-responsive  hygiene promotion. However, lessons learned indicated the need for more  integrated planning that couples infrastructure improvements with behavioral  change initiatives and local capacity-building to sustain long-term impact.
  
In Child Protection, inter-sectoral  and inter-organizational coordination gaps, challenges in establishment of  protective services for children on the move, and risks for children in  street situations persisted. UNICEF’s support for child-friendly spaces,  positive parenting programs, and case management illustrated that  multi-sectoral approaches, combined with capacity-building of government and  civil society actors, significantly enhance protection outcomes. Yet,  experiences from 2025 emphasized that cross-sectoral coordination mechanisms  must be strengthened to ensure timely identification, referral, and  protection of at-risk children during both development programming and  emergency responses.
  
Several lessons emerged from  2025 that will inform UNICEF’s strategy moving forward. First, equity focus remains  essential: targeting underserved populations, children with disabilities, and  refugees ensures that systemic inequalities are addressed, and services reach  those most at risk. Second, capacity-building of government and frontline  actors—from PHC staff to educators, social workers, and IRCS  volunteers—remains essential to maintain quality, coverage, and  sustainability. Third, integration of services across health, education,  protection, nutrition, and WASH amplifies outcomes, as evidenced by the  positive impacts of Cash Plus initiatives, adolescent empowerment programmes,  and school-based WASH improvements. Fourth, innovative approaches and  partnerships can bridge system and service gaps, particularly for adolescents  and children with disabilities, as demonstrated by AI-enabled therapy for  amblyopia and digital learning initiatives.
  
Looking ahead, UNICEF Iran will  focus on strengthening resilience, preparedness, and adaptive programming.  Building on lessons from recent emergencies, the office will continue to  integrate climate and disaster risk considerations into programming, enhance  surge capacity for rapid response, and expand evidence-informed interventions  that reach marginalized children. Strengthening communication and advocacy  efforts remains a priority, to influence policies, mobilize resources, and  amplify the voices of children and caregivers. UNICEF will also deepen  private sector engagement to support child rights initiatives, particularly  in education, health, and social protection, ensuring sustainability amid  constrained public funding. Finally, the office will continue to prioritize  data-driven programming, monitoring, and evaluation to inform scale-up,  enhance accountability. Experiences from 2025 reaffirmed the importance of  resilient, inclusive, and evidence-based programming that addresses both  immediate humanitarian needs and longer-term development objectives. By  drawing lessons from operational challenges, emergency responses, and service  delivery gaps, UNICEF is well positioned to refine strategies, strengthen  government and community capacities, and ensure that Iran’s most vulnerable  children are reached with essential services, protection, and opportunities  to thrive.

In 2025, Iraq was elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a three-year mandate starting in January 2026. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq (UNAMI) concluded its mandate on 31 December 2025, as requested by the Government.  The withdrawal of UNAMI is expected to reshape the UN’s coordination and convening role, placing heightened emphasis on sustained national leadership and institutional capacity to safeguard policy space and accountability for child-related commitments, including those linked to the SDGs and the National Development Plan for 2024-2028.
The country held Parliamentary elections in November 2025. The new Council of Representatives convened its first session in late December, ahead of the formation of the new government.  
Economic constraints continued to affect fiscal space for child-focused investments. Iraq has had an average annual GDP growth of 0.3 per cent since 2018, with heavy dependence on oil revenues (around 90 per cent of government revenue) and high rigidity in public spending driven by the wage bill (54 per cent of public expenditure, including pensions).[1] In 2025, these structural features were associated with widening fiscal deficits and warnings of potential fiscal contraction in 2026.
The lack of reliable, recent data on children and women remains a major constraint to track progress on child rights. While the completion of the Population and Housing Census in 2024 was a major milestone, further evidence on key child-related SDG indicators will become available with the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in 2026. 
In 2025, the Universal Periodic Report (UPR) on Iraq was presented to the Human Rights Council. 68 of the 263 UPR recommendations issued concern children’s rights[2] and the UN Committee on the Convention on the Rights of the Child (UN CRC) issued its Concluding observations[3] on the combined fifth and sixth periodic reports of Iraq.
The UN CRC welcomed the various legislative, institutional and policy measures taken by Iraq to implement the Convention. It raised concerns on the fragmentation of the laws affecting children and not in line with the Convention, and called on the government to accelerate passing of the draft child rights law; increase the age of criminal responsibility aligned with international standards; and ensure that the minimum age of marriage set at 18 years for both girls and boys without exception is enforced.  The UN CRC recommended Iraq to utilize a child-rights-based approach in the elaboration of the State budget and increase the budget allocated to social protection, education, health and access to birth registration.
Violence against children is widespread, with 80 per cent of children aged 5-14 having experienced violent discipline at home according to the latest available data.[4] Girls remain vulnerable to domestic and sexual violence, while child marriage remains a critical issue that affects girls’ education, health, and well-being.
In November 2025, the Prime Minister established a high-level interministerial legal committee, including representatives from parliament, the High Judicial Council, government and UNICEF, to accelerate the passage of pending laws and policies related to children, such as the draft Child Rights Law and Juvenile Care Law. Iraq has advanced elements of its child rights policy architecture, but the social and associated workforce remains in early stages of development, constraining system protection capacity. 
National monetary poverty has continued to decline over the long term, with the poverty rate[5] reported at 17.5 per cent in 2025 (down from 22.9 per cent in 2007). Multidimensional child poverty was still high (47.8 per cent) in 2020.
In 2025, the national social protection programme, the Social Safety Net (SSN), covered 7.6 million people[6] (16 per cent of the population), while the Public Distribution System (PDS), a quasi-universal monthly food basket, benefited 96 per cent of Iraqis[7]. While this system has historically played a crucial role in maintaining food security in the face of shocks, Iraq has now reached a level of relative stability that may no longer require this near universal food scheme. Reform could create an opportunity to shift resources towards a more adequate, comprehensive and inclusive social protection system. Vulnerable groups still face difficulties in receiving adequate support, and the sector remains challenged by the absence of reliable and up-to-date information and limited trained workforce capacity.  
Despite progress made by the Government in strengthening child health and nutrition systems, through digital transformation and integrated approaches, inequities persist regarding children’s access to essential services. Child immunization against measles significantly improved between 2023 and 2024 (from 84 per cent to 94 per cent). A slight decrease to 92 per cent in 2025 was observed, partially due to health budget allocations variations. Stunting and micronutrient deficiencies continue to be challenges, mostly due to limited dietary diversity and uneven coverage of preventive services.  
Children, especially girls, continue to face challenges in accessing quality education. Access and retention are mostly constrained by inadequate infrastructure and teachers’ capacities, poverty, and social norms impacting especially adolescent girls. In 2025, Iraq focused efforts on improving the governance and management of the education system.
In Iraq, 99 per cent of children are exposed to extreme heat, 31.6 per cent to agricultural droughts, and 26.8 per cent to sand and dust storms.[8] Water scarcity degrades water quality, increases disease risks and disrupts schools and clinics where water and sanitation systems are fragile.  
Access to water and sanitation slightly improved, with 66 per cent of Iraqi population accessing safely managed drinking water and 49.5 per cent safely managed sanitation in 2025 (against 63 and 40 per cent, respectively, 2024[9]). Inequities persist, disproportionately affecting displaced and returnee populations and rural communities.
