Child survival and development
In 2025, UNICEF supported Government efforts to strengthen child survival and development by expanding an integrated minimum package of Early Childhood Development (ECD) services through the primary health care system. Service performance indicators reflected steady coverage of essential interventions, including third dose pentavalent vaccination coverage[11] at 81 per cent, measles vaccination coverage at 92 per cent, and two out of three newborns receiving postnatal care. The integrated package brought together priority maternal, newborn and child health and nutrition services—antenatal and postnatal care, routine immunization, nutrition screening, birth registration, kangaroo mother care for premature infants, and developmental delay screening with referral pathways to secondary care—supporting continuity of care from pregnancy through early childhood.
With UNICEF technical and operational support, ECD services were rolled out in 450 health facilities in 2025[12], bringing the nationwide total to 1,156 health facilities, equivalent to 83.6 per cent of all the country’s health facilities delivering the ECD package. These services benefited approximately 400,000 children (nearly half girls) and their caregivers. UNICEF also supported the training of 800 frontline workers (320 women) to improve the quality and consistency of service delivery. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened supply chain continuity by procuring Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) and oral polio vaccines for 1.2 million infants and vitamin A for 2.5 million children under five, reinforcing readiness to deliver lifesaving services at scale[13].
Aligned with broader health system strengthening, UNICEF supported the digitalization of civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS), with the rollout of a CRVS Platform by the Ministry of Health. Birth registration became more accessible in 100 per cent of the health facility-based civil registration centres (250), with same-day issuance of a digital birth certificate (against 45 days process before digitalization) that benefited more than 500,000 children in 2025, reducing documentation barriers that can exclude children from services and enhancing CRVS monitoring. To improve resilience and continuity of primary health-care services in climate-stressed areas, UNICEF collaborated with the Government of Iraq on solar electrification of five health facilities serving over 75,000 people, contributing to more reliable service delivery where energy constraints affect care quality[14].
Water, sanitation and hygiene and environmental sustainability
In 2025, UNICEF supported Government efforts to advance climate-smart and resilient water, sanitation and hygiene systems, enhancing service access, performance and sustainability through risk-informed planning, institutional strengthening and digital transformation.
UNICEF supported the development of water, wastewater and reuse of master plans in eight of fifteen targeted governorates, strengthening evidence-based prioritization and investment planning. Digitalization of water supply systems and the launch of a Sanitation Hub improved monitoring and accountability, while the integration of digital water safety planning tools supported more systematic risk management. Climate-smart approaches were further advanced through adoption of managed aquifer recharge and measures to reduce non-revenue water, improving efficiency, treatment processes and resource allocation in a context of increasing water scarcity.
At the national policy level, UNICEF supported the development of Iraq’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0, including the water, wastewater and solid waste chapters. These contributions articulated priority adaptation and mitigation actions, incorporated quantified water gaps and methane reduction targets, and established a results-based financing framework. UNICEF also supported development of the Children’s Climate Risk Index and Disaster Risk Model (CCRI-DRM), which are being integrated into the national risk assessment framework to ensure that child-sensitive indicators inform planning and prioritization.
Building on analysis of per capita water allocation, the Government adopted updated standards and integrated them into national water distribution guidelines, supporting more equitable domestic water access and stronger resource management across governorates. UNICEF also supported development of Green School Building Guidelines, a national framework designed to promote safe, inclusive, energy-efficient and climate-smart learning environments—linking climate resilience and environmental sustainability with education system strengthening.
Learning and skills for children and young people
In 2025, UNICEF continued its support to advance national education priorities under the Iraq National Education Strategy 2022–2031. UNICEF’s contribution combined evidence-generation, policy dialogue, technical assistance and institutional capacity development, with a focus on strengthening core education system functions and supporting decentralized leaderships for results at scale.
A major achievement was the expansion of the Education Management Information System (EMIS) as a foundational system for planning, resource allocation, and accountability. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education to scale the system to an additional 2,531 schools by training 3,502 teachers (47 per cent women) in school data entry and management. This brought cumulative UNICEF-supported coverage to 7,810 schools (equivalent to 21.6 per cent of all schools in the country) and 14,020 trained teachers (50 per cent women) across nine governorates. As a result of joint efforts with education authorities, 66.9 per cent of the schools across the country operate with an education management information system. 
UNICEF also strengthened subnational planning and coordination by supporting eight Directorates of Education (DoEs) across six governorates to complete education sector analyses integrating climate vulnerability considerations, enabling development of costed three-year governorate education sector plans. Governorate-led coordination platforms convened ministries, general directorates and partners and translated planning into action. These platforms generated additional domestic financing, including support for construction of 30 school-based early childhood education (ECE) classrooms in one governorate and expansion of the EMIS to 800 additional schools in another, demonstrating strengthened local ownership and coordinated delivery.
To address exclusion, UNICEF supported the institutionalization of the Back-to-Learning campaign as a government-led mechanism for identifying and responding to out-of-school children’s needs. The campaign identified 255,905 out-of-school children (32 per cent girls) nationwide, and supported 101,679 children (30 per cent girls) to return to education through formal, non-formal or examination pathways.[15] The government-owned online Back-to-Learning dashboard strengthened availability and analysis of data on both the scale and the drivers of exclusion, improving evidence-based planning, accountability, relevance and sustainability.
In early learning, UNICEF supported the Government to advance a cost-efficient school-based ECE model, enrolling 3,059 young children (50 per cent girls) and rolling out early childhood education quality standards across 15 governorates. UNICEF also supported stronger school governance and teacher capacity, with the school-based management (SBM) model rolled out in 256 schools, with 1,166 School Management Committee members trained (38 per cent women), benefiting 72,490 children (46 per cent girls) through improved planning, resource use and learning environments.[16] In addition, 1,642 teachers and school personnel (54 per cent women) were trained in ECE pedagogy, monitoring and classroom management, as well as life skills education and psychosocial support, strengthening the system’s ability to address learning gaps and respond to children’s needs across both development and humanitarian contexts. 
Complementing these efforts, UNICEF supported inclusive education services for displaced, returnee and refugee children in the Governorates of Kurdistan, Ninawa, Salah Al-Din and Anbar, reaching 67,081 children aged 5-17 (47 per cent girls), mostly in camp settings.[17]
UNICEF advanced a strategic shift in adolescent and youth programming toward government-led, scalable systems for youth skills development, participation, and engagement. This approach aligned with national priorities under the National Youth Vision 2030 while responding to persistent challenges linked to youth unemployment, skills mismatches, and limited pathways from learning to earning.
UNICEF supported the integration of Maharati (My Skills) model into the public youth centres, as a standardized framework for adolescent and youth skills development. The model covers life skills, employability, entrepreneurship, and civic engagement and benefited more than 19,000 adolescents and young people (53.3 per cent girls) across eight governorates, who accessed structured skills development opportunities focused on transferable competencies such as critical thinking, communication, teamwork, problem-solving, leadership and digital literacy, strengthening readiness for employment and supporting girls’ leadership.  
In addition, as part of Maharati model, UNICEF supported 448 young people (54.2% girls) with seed funding to launch social and business innovations, reinforcing the link between skills development and practical application. Around 20 per cent of these projects received funding by the Ministry of Youth and Sports through the National Social Innovation Challenge.[18]
Digital platforms for youth skills building have expanded. The Learning Passport reached 2,541 new users and recorded 5,985 course enrolments, reflecting growth in access to digital, green and life skills programming through strengthened partnerships and improved content. 
Child protection
In 2025, UNICEF supported the Government of Iraq to advance a more coherent, accountable and sustainable child protection system aligned with national commitments under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. UNICEF’s contribution combined policy dialogue, institutional strengthening, social service workforce development, digitalization of case management systems and support to service integration, reinforcing the shift toward nationally anchored child protection delivery. On public financing for children, UNICEF is working with the government, which, as the 46th country to join the Global Alliance to End Violence against Children, has committed to increasing public investment to prevent and respond to violence against children, in line with SDG Target 16.2 by 2030.
A major achievement was consolidation of child protection governance mechanisms. UNICEF provided sustained technical assistance to the Child Welfare Commission, strengthening its coordination role across ministries and its oversight of national child protection priorities. This support contributed to greater alignment of policies and action plans with international standards on violence prevention, child-friendly justice and social service workforce development.
At subnational level, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA) to strengthen institutional accountability through the expansion of Child Protection Units. In 2025, these units increasingly functioned as statutory service delivery structures with clear responsibilities, standard operating procedures and stronger referral linkages across justice, health, education and law enforcement actors. UNICEF also supported improved coordination between the MoLSA, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Justice and the Supreme Judicial Council by facilitating regular meetings of the Child Welfare Commission (CWC), High Commission on Child Protection (KRI), and inter-ministerial Child Legal Protection Task Force on Northeast Syria returnee children and establishing the high legal commission under the PM’s Office, helping promote more coherent responses for children in contact with the law and children lacking civil documentation.
UNICEF advanced the institutionalization of the social service workforce as a core pillar of the child protection system by supporting strengthened regulatory and operational frameworks for social workers embedded within Child Protection Units (CPU), including standardized case management, supervision and ethical practice. UNICEF supported the creation of a pool of trainers to accompany the staffing of newly created CPU. All 460 social workers (31 per cent women) deployed in new CPU benefited training and mentoring, improving service quality, continuity of care and professionalization of frontline protection services.
Information management was a critical enabler. UNICEF supported expansion and institutionalization of the Child Protection Information Management System (CPIMS+), strengthening data availability, case tracking and referral pathways across social welfare, justice and health sectors. Improved data systems supported evidence-based planning, accountability and reporting, while reinforcing government stewardship over child protection decision-making.
UNICEF also supported efforts to strengthen child-friendly justice and expand alternatives to detention for children in contact with the law, working with the Supreme Judicial Council, juvenile courts and relevant ministries to promote diversion measures, legal aid and community-based alternatives. In addition, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health to open five new additional gender-based violence one-stop centres across Baghdad, Anbar, Muthanna, Basra and Erbil governorates, expanding access to integrated health, psychosocial and referral services, and strengthening institutional protocols and referral pathways to improve service quality and sustainability.
Social inclusion
In 2025, UNICEF concentrated support on strengthening social protection reforms, implementing child benefit pilots and advancing national disability inclusion. UNICEF supported piloting of a “cash plus” child benefit in three locations, designed to demonstrate the value of providing additional cash support to families with children while linking cash to services, case management and social and behaviour change outreach. In the Kurdistan Region, pilots in Sulaymaniyah and Duhok targeted families with children at the transition from primary to secondary school, pairing monthly payments with messaging on the importance of staying in school. In Federal Iraq, the pilot in Muthanna was implemented with the Ministries of Labour and Social Affairs and Health to register pregnant women and mothers of children under two, encouraging regular health centre check-ups and routine vaccination. In total, 6,696 persons (4,417 children under two and 2,279 pregnant women) received monthly cash payments of around 30 USD per individual and benefited from outreach activities during 2025.[19]
As part of the integrated child benefit approach, UNICEF supported strengthening of the social service workforce by training 76 social workers in 2025 in the three pilot locations. Social workers assessed participating households, identified 615 for additional support and ongoing case management, and conducted post-distribution monitoring visits to support timely receipt and reduce barriers.
UNICEF supported the Social Protection Commission within MoLSA to enhance the Social Safety Net management information system by adding functions for case management, beneficiary outreach, archiving and shock responsiveness. UNICEF also supported the establishment of the Social Safety Net’s first grievance redress hub, staffed by 15 social workers and designed to enable direct communication between beneficiaries and the Government. Since its May launch, the hub received over 28,000 calls, with more than half related to social assistance schemes[20].
To support more harmonized approaches across Iraq, UNICEF worked with the Kurdistan Regional Government—alongside partners including the World Bank and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees—to adapt the proxy means test used at federal level for the Kurdistan context and to inform regional guidelines aimed at harmonizing Social Safety Net approaches. UNICEF supported development of social protection strategies, with the Kurdistan Region strategy launched in July and a national strategy expected in early 2026. Building on early results, the Government of Iraq agreed to expand the child benefit to three governorates in 2026 using domestic resources for the cash component, with UNICEF supporting analysis of expansion options, training needs, management information system requirements and evaluation design.
Finally, the Government developed and launched its first national disability inclusion strategy on the International Day of Persons with Disabilities (3 December), with UNICEF support. UNICEF facilitated engagement across nine government entities, three networks of organizations of persons with disabilities and 12 United Nations agencies and entities, supporting a process grounded in a situation analysis of children with disabilities and assessment of social protection for children with disabilities. UNICEF also supported national training of 323 frontline workers focused on identifying barriers faced by people with disabilities and practical steps social workers can take to promote inclusion across sectors.[21]
Youth engagement and participation 
UNICEF continued to empower youth, especially girls, to engage in policy dialogue, planning, programming, and community-based actions for children’s rights. 
Through UNICEF supported youth skills building programme, innovation laboratories, UPSHIFT and design-thinking methodologies, adolescents and youth applied skills to real community challenges. As a result, 26,018 young people (13,406 girls) designed and implemented community initiatives for climate action, environmental protection, digital inclusion, girls’ education and social cohesion, demonstrating youth contributions to local development and resilience.
UNICEF continued to expand youth network through U-Report platform amplifying the voice of 133,534 U-reporters (49 per cent girls and women) for children’s rights. In 2025, 4,462 new participants (2,186 girls) joined the platform[22]. Polls and campaigns amplified youth voices on issues such as employment, mental health and climate action, while generating insights that informed programme adaptation and policy dialogue. UNICEF also supported the launch of the FunDoo platform to broaden digital engagement and learning opportunities.
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Environment to organize national consultations with 160 adolescents and youth (50 per cent girls) for the development of Iraq’s NDC 3.0. For the first time, children’s and young people’s perspectives were consolidated into a dedicated Children and Youth Chapter, embedding youth voices in national climate planning and advancing child- and youth-responsive climate governance.[23]
Communication on children’s rights 
UNICEF reached 6.2 million people with core messages and strategic content on children's rights through targeted campaigns. 
UNICEF conducted advocacy workshops for 205 journalists from leading media outlets, to support dissemination of accurate information on children’s rights for larger audience across the country.

Advancing integrated water, wastewater, and water reuse master planning
The water sector in Iraq faces severe challenges including scarcity, contamination, aging infrastructure and fragmented governance. While long term strategic planning and investment are essential to address key system challenges and build resilience, Iraq’s last Water Master Plan dates back to 1980. The development of a new water master plan that would set the priorities, budget and financing for a 25 years-time period to accelerate the progress and ensure sustainable water and sanitation services in Iraq requiring major financial investment from the Government, is only possible with strong political will, inclusive and coordinated approaches, and key system bottlenecks addressed in parallel.
In 2025, following strong advocacy efforts by UNICEF, the Government allocated around US$ 30 million to the Ministry of Construction, Housing and Public Municipalities for the development of a national water master plan, including sub-master plans at Governorate-level.  
UNICEF’s experience in building Government’s commitment in investing in the development and implementation of a robust Water Master Plan nationwide, highlights the importance of a continued multi-pronged strategy and shows that, when evidence, governance, inclusion and financing converge, a long-term vision becomes achievable.  
UNICEF supported the national environmental survey and Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in 2023 that highlighted that access to safely managed drinking water remains inadequate, with only 59.7 percent of the population covered, and only 47.6 percent for the rural population, underscoring inequalities in water service provision[1].Evidence enabled UNICEF to mobilize the Government in organizing water sector coordination and the first ever national Water Conference under the Prime Minister’s leadership in 2023. The Conference marked a key turning point in political consensus on the urgency of water sector reforms. Recommendations endorsed by the Prime Minister included the update of the Water and Sanitation Master Plan of Iraq. UNICEF provided technical support to set up the steering committee led by the Minister of Construction, Housing and Public Municipalities and gathering deputy ministers of Water Resources and Environment to coordinate water master planning development, and to help the lead Ministry in the budgeting and financing of Water Master planning. As of December 2025, eight of the fifteen targeted governorates had engaged in integrated water, wastewater, and water reuse planning. The Governorates’ master plans are expected to connect the needs with budgeted technical projects, implementation and financing plans for the short (0-5 years), medium (6-15 years), and long (16-25 years) term and consolidated into one national Master Plan.
To support and complement these efforts, to ensure master plans are designed and implemented with optimized resources, UNICEF has mobilized the Government in updating the water allocation standards and reviewing water laws and is modeling cost-effective solutions to be integrated into the Master Plan. In 2026, UNICEF will continue its focused support. By reducing losses and modernizing water services, Iraq can strengthen its water sector resilience and safeguard future generations.
Unlocking civil documentation for returnees from Northeast Syria
Civil documentation remains a critical protection and inclusion issue in Iraq, particularly for children and families affected by conflict, displacement, and return from Northeast Syria. Years of insecurity, population movement, destruction of civil registries, and complex administrative and legal procedures have left thousands of children without birth certificates or legal identity. This situation disproportionately affects children born in displacement, children formerly associated with armed groups, children of female-headed households and returnees processed through the Al Amal Center. The absence of civil documentation limits access to education, health care, social protection and justice services, while increasing risks of statelessness, child labour, early marriage, and arbitrary detention. Despite progress made by the Government in restoring civil registry services and advancing digitalization, challenges remain, including inconsistent procedures across governorates, limited legal awareness among families, administrative bottlenecks and difficulties in addressing complex cases that require judicial review or security clearance. In response, UNICEF has prioritized civil documentation as a core child protection and systems-strengthening intervention, linking humanitarian response with longer-term reintegration, social cohesion and durable solutions.
 
Key lessons learned highlight the importance of sustained advocacy and multi-sectoral engagement to address systemic and complex child rights and legal identity challenges. UNICEF, as co-chair of the Technical Working Group on the Global Framework, supported the Government through the organization of two high-level national advocacy workshops to improve access to civil documentation, held in 2024 and 2025, convening representatives of civil registry, judiciary, security, social welfare institutions and humanitarian partners. These workshops provided a structured platform to jointly analyze procedural gaps, legal constraints and operational challenges, and to develop concrete recommendations for resolving complex civil documentation cases, particularly those affecting highly vulnerable and stigmatized children. As a result of workshop recommendations and government buy-in, the rate of issuance of civil documentation more than doubled between the first and second quarter of 2025. 
 
A key lesson learned is that many documentation barriers cannot be resolved through individual case management alone, but require policy dialogue, inter-ministerial coordination and consensus at the highest levels such as the PM’s Office and the High Judicial Council. Embedding civil documentation services within Child Protection Units and strengthening the social workforce on documentation pathways, case management, and CPIMS+ improved identification, referral and follow-up of cases. Community-based outreach, legal accompaniment and mobile documentation service support emerged as good practices to increase trust, reduce fear of authorities and improve access, while digital civil registration platform helped streamline and simplify birth registration procedures. Experience underscores the need to ensure that digitalization does not inadvertently exclude the most vulnerable. 
Conclusion
The examples highlighted above, on Iraq’s water system and civil documentation for the most challenging cases, hold valuable lessons for UNICEF’s work in Iraq going forward. They demonstrate that UNICEF is a trusted partner and can leverage its strong relationships with government and partners to meaningfully improve outcomes for children but doing so requires a strong focus on areas of shared priority with government partners, sustained technical and advocacy engagement, and feedback loops from evidence to programmatic adjustments.

Jordan, with a population of 11.7 million, maintains a young demographic profile, with 40 per cent of residents under 18. Non-Jordanians continue to constitute at least one third of residents, though their composition is shifting. Since December 2024, nearly 30 per cent of registered Syrian refugees have returned to Syria, while reduced international assistance and limited formal employment continue to heighten socioeconomic and protection risks for those who remain, particularly children.
In 2025, Jordan advanced its modernization agenda amid a volatile regional context. The war in Gaza, rising violence in the West Bank, and regional escalations triggered domestic protests, temporary airspace closures and heightened security measures. Despite this, Jordan maintained a stabilizing diplomatic role, opposing the forced displacement of Palestinians and supporting a two-state solution.
Relations with Syria evolved after the 2024 leadership change, with renewed coordination on trade, energy, water and border security. Persistent risks, including narcotics smuggling, remain, but increased cooperation has strengthened Jordan’s position as a regional transit and stabilization hub
Jordan’s economy remained resilient amid regional instability and global trade disruptions, with GDP growth of 2.75 per cent by Q3 of 2025, slightly above the rate during the same period in 2024. This performance is supported by strong tourism revenues, which rose 7.5 per cent in the first eight months of 2025, and increased foreign direct investment. Inflation remains low at 1.8 per cent, among the lowest in the region, driven by stable energy prices and prudent fiscal management.
However, fiscal pressures persist. The budget deficit reached 5.8 per cent of GDP by the end of 2025, up from 5 per cent during the same period in 2024, reflecting rising interest payments and continued dependence on indirect taxation. Public debt, excluding Social Security Investment Fund holdings, stood at JOD 36 billion, equivalent to 83.2 per cent of GDP. These trends underscore the need for continued fiscal and structural reforms outlined in the Economic Modernization Vision to preserve macroeconomic stability.
Macroeconomic constraints continue to generate social pressures. The national poverty rate remains at 15.7 per cent though it is expected to have risen. UNHCR and World Bank data indicate that two thirds of refugees lived below the poverty line in 2024. Despite relatively low multidimensional poverty, 14 per cent of children experience deprivation in at least two wellbeing dimensions.
Labor market conditions show modest improvement but remain structurally constrained. Overall unemployment (Jordanians and non-Jordanians) fell slightly to 16 per cent in Q3 2025, compared to 16.3 per cent a year earlier. Among Jordanians, unemployment remains high at 21.4 per cent, with a significant gender gap: 18 per cent among men and 33.9 per cent among women Labor force participation is low at 40.5 per cent overall, and only 14.4 per cent for Jordanian women, among the lowest globally. The addition of 96,000 new Social Security subscribers between January and mid-November 2025 signals progress in formalization, though structural constraints persist.
Youth indicators are especially concerning. Youth unemployment (15–24) stands at 39.1 per cent while 40 per cent are not in education, employment, or training (NEET). NEET rates are highest for young women (51 per cent) and those in their mid-twenties (60 per cent). School to work transitions remain slow, particularly for women; only 12 per cent of graduate’s secure employment within five years. Moreover, 59 per cent of unemployed Jordanians hold high school or higher qualifications, highlighting persistent skills mismatches.
In the education sector, near universal primary enrollment with gender parity remains a significant achievement, yet secondary level access and retention challenges have persisted. Adolescents face multiple risks, including socio economic pressures, early marriage, child labor, disability, and, for refugees, administrative and financial barriers. Secondary enrollment stands at 85.6 per cent for Jordanian children, compared to 62.1 per cent for Syrian children, with notable gender disparities among Syrians (51.6 per cent of males vs. 73.4 per cent of females). Learning outcomes remain a concern. PISA 2022 results indicate declines across mathematics, reading, and science compared to 2018. Approximately 62 percent of children in Jordan at late primary age today are not proficient in reading, 10 percentage points worse than the regional average.
Pre-primary enrollment, including KG1 and KG2, increased from 26.4 per cent in 2018 to 40.5 per cent in 2023. Although inclusive learning coverage improved by 23 per cent between 2020 and 2023, adolescents with disabilities continue to lag behind their peers, according to the latest GAGE longitudinal study.
Child protection concerns remain significant and closely linked to socioeconomic stressors. Threequarters of children aged 1–14 experience at least one form of violent discipline, with higher prevalence among poorer and refugee households. Psychological distress affects more than one-third of adolescents, rising to over half among those with disabilities. Child labor remains a concern, particularly among Syrian refugees, with one in five households reporting at least one working child.
Health and nutrition indicators demonstrate both resilience and emerging risks. Immunization coverage remains high at 98.2 per cent for all pediatric antigens, nevertheless, pockets of vaccine hesitancy are increasing. Stunting affects 8.3 per cent of children under five and nearly 12 per cent among the poorest households, while overweight and obesity rates among young children have doubled over the past decade. Anemia affects nearly one third of young children and adolescent girls, with disproportionately high prevalence among refugees. Noncommunicable diseases now account for 78 per cent of all deaths, highlighting long term health system burdens.
Jordan faces extreme water scarcity, with renewable water resources stand at only 61 m³ per person annually, equivalent to 12 per cent of the global water-scarcity threshold, significantly heightening household vulnerability. While nonrevenue water declined from 50 per cent in 2022 to 40.9 per cent in 2025, overall supply remains inadequate, and many households receive water less than once per week. According to UNICEF/WHO data, 99 per cent of the population has access to basic water services, yet only 89 per cent receive safely managed drinking water, and 80 per cent have safely managed sanitation. Climate change is expected to intensify these pressures, with projections indicating an additional 15 per cent reduction in water availability by 2040, alongside increased variability and frequency of extreme weather events, further straining Jordan’s water and sanitation systems.
In 2025, Jordan advanced several high-impact reforms benefiting children, women, and vulnerable groups. Key measures included launching the National Social Protection Strategy (2025–2033) and strengthening gender equality through formalizing the Jordanian National Commission for Women and amending the Labor Law to extend maternity leave and reinforce pregnancy protections. Jordan also endorsed the National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security (2025–2027) and advanced disability inclusion with a new national framework for inclusive education. In parallel, the Education Sector Analysis neared completion to inform the Education Sector Plan (2026–2030).
Together, these dynamics underscore the need to prioritize equitable access to basic services, strengthened and shock-responsive social protection and human capital systems, protection from violence, youth economic inclusion, and climate-resilient WASH solutions, with a particular focus on the most vulnerable children and communities.

1: Health and Nutrition
In 2025, UNICEF advanced Jordan’s progress toward a more equitable, resilient child health system, prioritizing evidence-based programming for refugee and vulnerable children. A major national milestone was achieved on 20 September 2025, when the Ministry of Health, supported by UNICEF and other partners, introduced the Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine (PCV) after more than a decade of stalled efforts. This marked a strategic leap forward for routine immunization and equity.
By year’s end, 35,199 Jordanian children (exceeding national targets) and 2,256 refugee children, including 1,674 Syrians, had been vaccinated. The rollout drove a 79 per cent reduction in zero dose children, from 7,000 in 2024 to 1,480 in 2025, demonstrating strengthened national capacity to reach the most underserved.
UNICEF also reinforced immunization system resilience through expanded cold chain capacity and improved service quality, ensuring reliable vaccine delivery in remote and high-density areas and supporting the long-term sustainability of both routine and newly introduced vaccines.
In refugee settings, UNICEF continued to strengthen immunization coverage and disease prevention. In Za’atari and Azraq camps, 3,665 students in grades 1 and 10 (54 per cent girls) were vaccinated, and immunization status for other grades was verified, reinforcing alignment with the national immunization programme and reducing the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases in high-density settings.
UNICEF also strengthened early identification and support for children with disabilities in refugee camps. Through school-based screening of 5,453 students, 898 children (49 per cent girls) were identified and received 967 assistive devices, improving functional abilities, school participation and access to learning, while reinforcing linkages between health and education services.
To address critical evidence gaps in adolescent nutrition, UNICEF partnered with the Ministries of Health and Education and UNRWA to roll out the Nutrition Environment Assessment in Schools (NEAT-S). The initiative aims to generate gender-disaggregated evidence on school food environments to inform nutrition policy and programming in 2026, strengthening national capacity for evidence-based decision-making. Complementing this work, UNICEF trained 30 youth advocates, who led community awareness activities promoting healthier school food environments, reinforcing youth engagement and social and behavior change approaches.
2: Education
In 2025, UNICEF advanced equitable access to education, learning recovery, and system resilience for refugee and vulnerable children in Jordan, supporting national priorities on inclusive education and human capital development. Through policy engagement and as the education sector lead, UNICEF supported to remove barriers to school access for Syrian refugee children, including the recognition of academic documentation and fee waivers, reinforcing Jordan’s commitment to inclusive education.
At the system level, UNICEF reinforced continuity and stability of education service delivery in refugee settings, ensuring that learning was not disrupted by camp consolidation and population shifts. Through the support of IncentiveBased Syrian Volunteers, whose proactive outreach and strengthened enrolment mechanisms played a key role, 36,741 children (50 per cent girls) continued to access education across camp schools and KG2 centres, including those relocated after the closure of the Emirati Jordanian Camp. These efforts reinforced more resilient and adaptable education delivery models in fragile and displacementaffected settings.
UNICEF also advanced progress on learning recovery, responding to evidence of widespread literacy and numeracy gaps. Targeted reading recovery interventions improved foundational reading skills, with 73 per cent of learners participating (non-readers) achieving proficiency benchmarks, while reading assessments for over 10,000 children enabled timely identification of children most at risk of falling behind. In parallel, the introduction of structured numeracy recovery through the Mathematics Accelerated Programme in 12 camp schools addressed critical learning deficits and strengthened the evidence base for scaling learning recovery approaches.
To sustain results, UNICEF invested in inclusive learning environments and technical capacity development. Infrastructure enhancements included installation of two new schools and more than 50 classrooms, alongside inclusive facilities, playgrounds, and sports areas. These upgrades reduced overcrowding and improved accessibility. UNICEF further contributed to strengthening the technical capacity of teachers through an accredited professional development programme to deliver inclusive, learner-centered instruction.
3: Child Protection
In 2025, UNICEF supported measurable national progress toward a coordinated and survivor-centred child protection system in Jordan. Building on commitments from the 2024 Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, UNICEF provided technical assistance that enabled the Government to finalize Jordan’s first costed National Action Plan (2026–2030) addressing child protection, gender-based violence, and family violence. This framework establishes a strategic, integrated roadmap across legislation, policy, social services, and community engagement, positioning Jordan to strengthen prevention and response mechanisms for children and women at scale.
Significant system-level outcomes were achieved in workforce professionalization and service delivery. The approval of the Social Work Professionalization Bylaw, grounded in UNICEF-supported workforce mapping, formally recognized social work as a profession and established pathways for capacity development. Complementary development of a 100-hour accredited in-service training module, lays the foundation for a national Roadmap to Enhance the Social Service Workforce and improving the quality of services for vulnerable children.
Digitalization of protection services advanced through the national rollout of the AMAN family violence case management system. With UNICEF support, AMAN expanded to four additional governorates, registering 6,831 new cases in 2025. This outcome strengthened the ability of social and justice institutions to provide timely, coordinated support, reinforcing accountability, and survivor-centred approaches.
Evidence generation under the Safe Online project strengthened national capacity to prevent and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse (OCSEA). The Disrupting Harm study produced Jordan’s first draft of the OCSEA evidence base and informed cross-sector collaboration. In parallel, more than 200 police officers, social workers, and educators strengthened their knowledge of OCSEA risks and response procedures.
Survivor-centred service quality improved across justice and social sectors. UNICEF supported the establishment of the first child- and woman-friendly facilities in the Family Protection and Juvenile Departments in North Amman, Ajlun, and the Azraq and Za’atari camps, operationalizing a one-stop-shop model for medical, psychosocial, legal, and social services. More than 66 frontline staff of the facilities were trained in child-sensitive procedures, reducing re-traumatization.
With MOSD, targeted support for children with disabilities was expanded by establishing two additional Early Detection and Early Intervention Units, reaching over 663 children nationwide.
UNICEF strengthened national and local capacity to deliver child protection, GBV, and MHPSS services. Over 1,000 service providers were trained, enabling consistent case management, while 2,211 children accessed services addressing violence, family separation, child labour, child marriage, and emotional distress. In refugee camps, 1,034 teachers were trained, and 9,261 children participated in structured MHPSS programmes strengthening resilience, inclusion, and protective behaviors.
Community-level interventions reinforced protective environments for children and families. The Parenting Programme reached 67,372 caregivers over the past year, promoting nurturing caregiving. Structured MHPSS interventions, including LEGO-based programmes, benefited 60,273 children, with half showing improvements in psychosocial skills.
4: ADAP:
In 2025, UNICEF Jordan reached 90,497 adolescents and young people, including 59 per cent young women and 18 per cent refugees, enabling access to one or more of the following: life skills, digital skills, on-the-job training, career development, entrepreneurship, business development, and volunteering opportunities. These interventions strengthened young people’s readiness for education, work, and community leadership, while reinforcing national systems to sustain long-term impact and promote inclusive youth development.
UNICEF enhanced the capacity of government institutions, municipalities, and national partners to deliver youth-responsive services, addressing structural barriers to participation and employability, including gender and disability themes. Key achievements include the initiation of Jordan’s National Youth Strategy (2019–2025), and evidence generation through the implementation of the National Youth Survey 2025, the reform and modernization of youth centres. Youth centres are being transformed into inclusive, high-quality hubs for skills development, civic engagement, and leadership, ensuring equitable access for girls, youth with disabilities, and marginalized populations.
UNICEF Jordan, in partnership with the Vocational Training Corporation (VTC), launched the Generation Ready Partnership to support systemic reform in vocational education and training. The initiative focuses on modernizing VTC systems, upgrading curricula to align with labor market needs, and strengthening private sector linkages to improve youth employment pathways. By equipping adolescents and youth with relevant, future-ready skills, the partnership aims to position VTC as a leading provider of skilled talent and support young people’s transition from learning to earning.
Market-driven skills development reached 34,343 young people, including 57 per cent females and 35 per cent refugees. Life skills training, social innovation (UPSHIFT), and digital skills programmes equipped participants for improved employability, leading 275 youth to secure income opportunities in the gig economy. Entrepreneurship and on-the-job training supported 1,568 young people and enabled the launch of 40 micro-businesses, enhancing economic participation, particularly for young women and those with mobility constraints. Adolescent mental health and psychosocial support will be strengthened through launching the Healthy Minds, Bright Future programme, with the aim to be implemented in all MoY youth centres and several health centres.
Volunteering and civic engagement were strengthened through the Nahno platform and the support to the institutionalization of the Crown Prince Award for Voluntary Service within MoY structures, with over 46,227 adolescents and youth 62 per cent female participating in community initiatives in climate, health, and education and 262 new entities engaged on Nahno providing volunteering opportunities including private sector, public sector, NGOs and youth led initiatives.
Youth-led climate action was promoted through the training of over 9,003 Climate Leaders and Champions, who implemented community-based initiatives and advocacy events focused on water conservation, tree planting and solid waste collection. Through the young climate volunteers efforts on Nahno 19,266 trees were planted, 70,781 kg of recyclable waste collected across 10,198 km², and 100,000 cubic meter of water conserved across all governorates in over 600 locations. These efforts linked with UNICEF’s broader climate-resilient WASH and environmental programming, demonstrating how institutional platforms can advance sustainability, social cohesion, and youth empowerment simultaneously.
5: WASH:
In 2025, UNICEF continued to co-lead the Humanitarian WASH Sector with the Ministry of Water and Irrigation, supporting coordinated planning amid declining humanitarian funding and evolving refugee return dynamics. Partners were supported to prioritize WASH interventions, while technical support strengthened national monitoring of safely managed water and sanitation through SDG 6 taskforce.
Evidence-based planning was further strengthened through climate risk analysis, including the initiation of Climate Rationale and climate finance mapping for the WASH sector.
The Ministry of Health, with UNICEF support, improved WASH and IPC in healthcare facilities through guidelines, assessments, and staff training.
Progress was made on institutionalizing Climate-Resilient Water and Sanitation Safety Planning through the establishment of CR-WSSP units, and development of a national roadmap, alongside targeted capacity building within the Ministries of Water and Irrigation, Water Authority of Jordan and Water Utilities.
National menstrual health coordination improved via a new MHH Roadmap, in collaboration with Gender, promoting cross-sector collaboration with Education and Health sectors, while a social and behaviour change study and an institutional capacity assessment informed future behaviour-driven WASH programming.
In 2025, UNICEF provided safe, reliable WASH services combined with strong community engagement to support refugees in Za’atari, Azraq, and Garden camps, reaching 125,554 residents, including over 62,900 children. Water needs were met amid declining water source productivity in Za’atari and ongoing lifesaving delivery to 2,500 people in Rukban until operations ended in July 2025 following residents’ return to Syria. Safely managed sanitation was ensured through wastewater networks, on- and off-site treatment in Za’atari and desludging services in Azraq. The closure of the Emirati Jordanian camp in June 2025 resulted 1,147 refugees integrated into Azraq’s WASH systems. WASH services were further reinforced through community engagement and behavior change activities, reaching 29,431 people with messaging on handwashing, menstrual health, and climate-resilient WASH practices.
UNICEF’s WASH interventions improved safe water and sanitation access for over 74,000 Palestinian refugees through household facility rehabilitation and upgraded water and sanitation networks, enhancing public health and resilience in densely populated camps
UNICEF improved WASH access for 1,560 people in Informal Tented Settlements through cash support for water tanks, communal latrines, hygiene items, and a 970-member community network promoting hygiene, safe water management, and water conservation among vulnerable households.
In southern Jordan, UNICEF and Aqaba Water Company upgraded infrastructure, reaching 1,396 people as part of a three-year effort benefiting 30,000 residents, while strengthening Community Water Committees to enhance engagement, accountability, and sustainable, equitable WASH services.
In 2025, UNICEF enhanced WASH services in key institutions, promoting healthier, safer, and climate-resilient learning and healthcare environments. In partnership with UN-Habitat, 28 schools in Irbid and Mafraq received greywater treatment and reuse systems, benefiting 30,937 students with sustainable water use, lower consumption, and increased awareness of climate-resilient WASH practices.
UNICEF improved WASH and IPC standards in two health centres, making them the first in Jordan eligible for WASH-in-healthcare recognition. Climate Action Clubs engaged 2,286 children, including 46 with disabilities, in schools and Makani centres to promote climate action and sustainable WASH behaviors.
6: Social Policy and Social Protection
In 2025, Jordan made significant progress in building a more inclusive and shock-responsive social protection system, under the leadership of the Ministry of Social Development (MOSD), with UNICEF playing a pivotal supporting role. The year’s main achievement was the update and launch of the National Social Protection Strategy (NSPS 2025–2033), officially endorsed and launched in May under the patronage of His Majesty King Abdullah II. The strategy aligns with the Economic Modernization Vision (EMV) and introduces key innovations: a dedicated shock-responsive pillar, gender and disability-sensitive provisions, and expanded programmes for children.
The NSPS was shaped through an extensive national consultation process, comprising 19 sessions, 12 at governorate level and seven sectoral dialogues, with participation from over 900 persons (47 per cent women), including civil society, academia, private sector, youth, and persons with disabilities. This inclusive approach ensured that the strategy reflects diverse perspectives and national priorities. UNICEF provided technical leadership, evidence generation, and governance support, and helped anchor the NSPS in a costed action plan and monitoring framework, linked to major financing instruments such as the World Bank’s USD 400 million Programme-for-Results.
To foster public engagement, Jordan launched its first nationwide social protection awareness campaign, reaching more than three million people across multiple media channels. UNICEF complemented this effort with capacity building for strategic communication in partnership with the Jordan Media Institute.
Reforms advanced through the institutionalization of Cash Plus within NAF systems. In 2025, a dedicated cash plus unit was established with the support of UNICEF, and integration with NAF’s MIS and Social Registry began, paving the way for linking cash assistance to health, education, and empowerment services. UNICEF also supported improvements in NAF’s Unified Cash Transfer programme and emergency response SOPs, reinforcing efficiency and child sensitivity. Civil society engagement in social protection progressed with a proposed classification and rating framework for CBOs, as part of the technical support provided by UNICEF to the Association Registry at the MOSD.
In 2025, the Makani programme led by UNICEF in cooperation with national partners, continued to provide integrated learning support, child protection, skill-building, and parenting services nationwide through 114 centres across refugee camps, informal tented settlements, and host communities, reaching a total 105,496 beneficiaries, including 87,117 children (53 per cent girls, 36 per cent Syrian refugees, and 2 per cent children with disabilities). Evidence from the endline GAGE study confirms Makani as a best-practice Cash Plus intervention, with beneficiaries-particularly out-of-school youth, refugees, and marginalized adolescents-demonstrating stronger foundational learning, improved psychosocial well-being and coping skills, and more supportive family relationships, including shifts toward more open parent–child communication and less restrictive gender norms. Beyond service reach, UNICEF worked with MOSD and development partners to develop institutionalization scenarios, positioning Makani for gradual transition under the national social protection system, as part of the implementation of the National Social Protection Strategy. Over the year, the Hajati humanitarian cash transfer supported 2,824 vulnerable school-age children, reducing dropout risks and negative coping strategies.
Cross-Cutting
In 2025, UNICEF Jordan strengthened cross-sectoral enablers for inclusive, safe, and climate-resilient programmes, ensuring children’s rights were advanced across health, education, WASH, protection, and social protection interventions. Gender equality and disability inclusion were institutionalized through a Gender Programmatic Review, a multi-governorate assessment of 20 Organizations of Persons with Disabilities and sustained consultations with CSOs. Building on past collaborative work with the Arab Renaissance for Democracy and Development (ARDD), JCO convened an interactive consultation informed by DHS adolescent girl empowerment analyses and ARDD analytical Policy Briefs. Internally, UNICEF reinforced equity and inclusion through staff capacity development, updated Gender and Disability Action Plans (2025–2027), and organization-wide learning sessions. Safeguarding and Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) were strengthened through partner training, safe reporting channels, and supervision mechanisms, creating safer environments for children and adolescents across community, school, and camp settings.
Evidence generation and monitoring continued to guide adaptive programming and informed national policy. UNICEF led 84 programmatic and field monitoring visits, facilitated structured mid-year and annual reviews, and supported key national surveys and the Jordan Population and Housing Census 2025/2026. Evaluation efforts included seven evaluations and six active Management Responses, 79 per cent of which were completed or underway, generating actionable insights for adolescent and youth programmes, including the Maharati initiative and mental health interventions. These evidence-driven approaches strengthened programme quality, accountability, and equity, ensuring services met children’s needs even amid funding constraints and regional uncertainties. For example, evidence from the self-employment evaluation informed the redesign of the Ministry of Youth’s adolescent and youth interventions and Theory of Change, embedding gender-responsive, disability-inclusive, and equity-focused approaches.
Advocacy, social and behavior change (SBC), and resource mobilization amplified programme impact and visibility. UNICEF partnered with government, civil society, donors, and the private sector to advance national priorities, including the launch of Jordan’s first national youth mental health programme, social protection strategy update, and child-focused climate action initiatives. SBC interventions reached 7,200 children through Climate Action Clubs and over 1,775 frontline workers trained in WASH, immunization, and child protection communication. Youth engagement in climate action mobilized 9,004 volunteers for 257 environmental projects, influencing policy at COP30 and LCOYs. Strategic donor engagement and innovative communications enabled UNICEF to secure 79.9 per cent of funding requirements, sustain multi-year agreements, and showcase impact to over 12 million people via campaigns, media, and high-profile events, reinforcing UNICEF’s role as a trusted convener and advocate for children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF Jordan operated with unprecedented uncertainty, and a combination of socio-economic pressures, climate risks, and regional instability affecting children, families, and service delivery systems. Funding volatility, highly earmarked humanitarian resources, and limited fiscal space constrained the ability to scale sustainable programmes. At the operational level, policy changes, complex approval processes, and fragmented coordination across ministries and partners challenged timely implementation and monitoring. These cross-cutting challenges had implications across sectors: progress in health, education, WASH, child protection, and social protection required continuous adaptation to shifting contexts, prioritization of the most vulnerable, and innovative approaches to maintain service continuity.
H&N:
In 2025, the multi-layered government approval process delayed the start of the National School Nutrition Environment Assessment (NEAT-S) which required extensive inter-ministerial clearances and led to the delay in data collection.
Nevertheless, a key lesson learned was the critical importance of early and continuous engagement with national stakeholders throughout the assessment and implementation cycle. Involving the Ministry of Health service providers directly in field implementation facilitated operational approvals, strengthened trust with schools and parents, and eased consent procedures, demonstrating that ownership at the implementation level can significantly accelerate progress even within complex governance environments.
Building on the progress achieved in 2025, UNICEF will prioritize stronger inter-ministerial collaboration to accelerate the validation and operationalization of the Nutrition Environment Assessment in Schools, with clearer coordination mechanisms between the Ministries of Health and Education to translate evidence into action. Efforts will increasingly focus on addressing childhood overweight, obesity, and micronutrient deficiencies through gender-responsive approaches, in close partnership with national institutions and technical partners, including WHO and the Royal Health Awareness Society.
Education:
Despite progress in expanding access to education and strengthening system capacity, learning outcomes remained a critical challenge in 2025. High levels of learning poverty persisted, with many children struggling to acquire foundational literacy and numeracy skills, particularly among vulnerable groups affected by poverty, displacement, and repeated disruptions to schooling. Socio-economic pressures continued to increase the risk of drop-out, especially for older children, as families faced competing priorities related to livelihoods and basic needs. Operationally, the closure of the Emirati Jordanian Camp (EJC) posed an additional challenge, requiring rapid system adjustments to prevent learning interruptions and student disengagement during relocation.
Experience in 2025 demonstrated that access alone is insufficient to ensure meaningful learning outcomes. Structured learning recovery programmes, particularly targeted reading and mathematics interventions, proved effective in helping children catch up when they are well-designed, time-bound, and aligned with national curricula. Engagement of parents and caregivers emerged as a critical enabler of learning, reinforcing gains beyond the classroom and supporting regular attendance. The EJC transition highlighted the importance of strong coordination with the Ministry of Education and partners to ensure continuity of learning during population movements. In addition, national and regional planning for returnees underscored the value of early, coordinated approaches that link formal and non-formal education pathways and prioritize inclusion for children with disabilities.
Building on these lessons, UNICEF will prioritize improving learning outcomes by scaling evidence-based learning recovery and foundational skills programmes in close partnership with the Ministry of Education. Greater emphasis will be placed on preventing drop-out through the phased rollout of the Early Warning Tool, enabling early identification of at-risk learners and targeted school-level follow-up. UNICEF will continue to strengthen parental and community engagement as a core strategy to sustain learning gains, while reinforcing national and regional coordination mechanisms to support continuity of learning for returnees and enhance system resilience to future shocks.
Child Protection
Despite progress reaching hundreds of thousands of children, caregivers, and service providers, sustaining systemic change remained a challenge. Services remained under-resourced, particularly for children with disabilities and refugees, while harmful practices and social acceptance of violence persisted, weakening protective frameworks.
Key lessons include the value of community engagement, evidence-based programming, and continuous monitoring. Adaptive approaches focused on scaling interventions while advocating for policy reform proved critical to maintain protective environments for the most marginalized children.
ADAP
Programming for adolescents and youth in Jordan continues to face systemic and operational challenges, including fragmented efforts and limited coordination across stakeholders. This fragmentation reduces efficiency and impact, while private sector engagement remains underutilized, particularly in skills development, employment pathways, and innovation. High operational costs, funding gaps, slow adoption of new solutions and standard operating procedures, and unequal access to infrastructure and services especially for vulnerable and remote populations, further constrain scale and sustainability. Low youth awareness of available services contributes to less engagement, alongside persistent job diversity and inclusion gaps, particularly affecting young women and marginalized groups.
Implementation experience highlights several key lessons learned. Strong partnerships and effective coordination mechanisms significantly improve programme quality, reduce duplication, and optimize resources. Meaningful youth participation, beyond consultation, increases relevance, ownership, and sustainability of interventions. Participatory and community-based approaches, combined with behavior change initiatives, have proven critical in addressing harmful social norms and strengthening inclusion. The establishment of safe spaces enables adolescents and youth to engage constructively with decision-makers, while the selection of capable lead partners improves delivery quality.
Looking ahead, there are clear opportunities to strengthen impact and sustainability. Balancing system-level reforms with targeted service delivery can ensure that the most vulnerable adolescents and youth are reached. Greater alignment with national priorities, particularly the Economic Modernization Vision, provides a foundation for scale and sustainability. Mobilizing both public and private sector actors, investing in actionable evidence and innovation, and strengthening inter-agency coordination across all stakeholders will be critical to maximizing collective impact for adolescents and youth in Jordan.
WASH:
The realities of the acute water scarcity in the country, intensified by climate change, limited equitable access to safe water and sanitation for vulnerable communities. Whilst funding was ascertained for lifesaving interventions in camps, its availability to support other vulnerable populations in the rest of the country was limited.
Operational challenges included unpredictable refugee return patterns, camp closures, and capacity gaps within government water utilities, MOH, and MOE staff rotations, affecting continuity and long-term planning. UNICEF and partners adopted flexible and adaptive operational approaches, ensuring continuity of essential services while preparing for medium-term sustainability.
Social Policy and Social Protection
Mobilizing resources for social protection remains a critical challenge, with donors often prioritizing short-term humanitarian needs over long-term system strengthening. The institutionalization of the Makani programme highlighted complex governance, technical, and coordination requirements. Despite finalized transition scenarios and financing plans, sustainability depends on sustained government engagement and diversified funding approaches.
Lessons learned include the importance of early financing strategies and capacity building, and the necessity of linking policy reform with service delivery. Makani and Cash Plus demonstrated that technical planning alone is insufficient; government systems strengthening, private sector engagement, and multi-stakeholder coordination are essential for sustainable social protection outcomes.
Future efforts will focus on Makani institutionalization, financing opportunities, and government capacity building; supporting NSPS implementation, particularly its shock-responsive and child-focused pillars; and advocating for social protection as a resilience investment through evidence and partnerships.
Overall, 2025 underscored the importance of adaptive, inclusive, and system-oriented programming in a highly volatile operating environment. Across sectors, UNICEF Jordan demonstrated that sustained results for the most vulnerable children depend not only on service delivery, but on strong national ownership, partnerships, evidence-informed decision-making, and flexible implementation models capable of responding to uncertainty. Lessons from health, education, WASH, child protection, social protection and cross-sectoral support, reaffirmed the need to pair immediate responses with long-term investments in institutions, coordination, and financing.
Moving forward, UNICEF will leverage these insights to strengthen partnerships, scale proven approaches, and position child-focused policies and services as essential investments in resilience, human capital, and social cohesion ensuring that gains achieved under pressure translate into durable, nationally owned outcomes for children and adolescents.

Data, Evidence and Evaluation
Evidence generation, monitoring, and evaluation remained central to adaptive programming and policy advocacy in 2025. UNICEF Jordan continued to use evaluation findings and monitoring data to inform programme adjustments, strengthen equity and inclusion, and support national dialogue. Continued emphasis will be placed on prioritizing strategic evidence generation and reinforcing an embedded evaluation culture to inform adaptive programme design, policy advocacy, and planning for the upcoming CPD particularly amid an uncertain operating environment and funding constraints.

Lebanon faces deep socioeconomic, political, and security crises, marked by one of the world’s worst economic collapses, soaring inflation, and widespread poverty affecting nearly half the population. The escalation of armed conflict in late 2023 and 2024 worsened conditions, particularly for the most marginalized children and families. Due to the compounded effects of these crises, public services, including healthcare, education, and WASH, have deteriorated. In early 2025 the election of a new President and Prime Minister and municipal elections presented a critical opportunity to restore stability, drive reform, and strengthen human rights and the rule of law.

Following the voluntary and spontaneous return of refugees from Lebanon to Syria in 2025, 1.12 million Syrian refugees are estimated to remain in Lebanon. This figure includes an estimated 120,000 Syrians who crossed into Lebanon in 2025 fleeing insecurity inside Syria. The drivers of return to Syria are the education of children, improved security inside Syria, and the problems faced inside Lebanon including challenging living conditions, and lack of employment opportunities. For Syrian refugees inside Lebanon the restrictive environment, lack of economic opportunities and conflict trauma are undermining parents’ and families’ ability to care for and protect children, leading them to resort to negative coping strategies including child marriage and child labour. 
  
Lebanon also hosts approximately 203,000 Palestinian refugees, many of whom live in 12 camps and 42 gatherings, including approximately 180,000 Palestine Refugees from Lebanon (PRL) and 23,000 Palestine Refugees from Syria (PRS). Palestinian refugees face multiple vulnerabilities including severe financial hardship due to limited access to lawful employment opportunities, and food insecurity with nearly 30 per cent facing acute food insecurity. An estimated 93 percent of Palestinian refugees are living below the poverty line. The nutrition situation among Palestinian refugees remains critical with four percent wasting rates among Palestinian children and 9.5 percent among pregnant and lactating women, more than double the rates among Lebanese children and women. Low birthweight is reported in 40 percent of Palestinian newborns, exposing infants to heightened risks of mortality and long-term health complications. Palestinian children face protection concerns including exposure to child labour, exploitation, and heightened vulnerability to violence, abuse, and unsafe environments. Palestinian camps continue to experience instability, including intermittent violence and inadequate infrastructure, placing children at risk and undermining their access to safe services. 

The 2023/24 conflict resulted in nationwide damage, particularly in southern Lebanon, and marked Lebanon's deadliest period in decades. Displacement has continued into 2025, with families from southern villages still to be demilitarized remaining displaced, and returnees facing challenges including damaged homes, water and health facilities. Despite the ceasefire, since November 2024 the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) reports 1,308 people killed or injured inside Lebanon due to conflict, including at least 13 children killed, and 146 children injured. *

The conflict severely damaged WASH infrastructure, causing US$230.2 million in damage with over one million people losing reliable access to safe water due to damage to more than 206 water stations and distribution systems. Wastewater network damage increased contamination risks, with nearly half of healthcare facilities impacted. The conflict saw over 769 schools fully or partially damaged, 14 schools completely destroyed, and 60 percent of public schools repurposed to shelters. Following the conflict, unexploded ordnance (UXO) and white phosphorus contamination increased exponentially. With the conflict continuing in Lebanon there have been few recovery initiatives in 2025 to repair war-related damage.*

In 2025 Lebanon faced its most severe drought on record, marking a critical juncture in the country’s already fragile humanitarian and stabilization landscape. Rainfall levels fell by more than 50 per cent across much of the country, with reduced snow accumulation and earlier melt further diminishing available water resources. During the dry summer months reservoirs and springs that sustain millions of people dropped to alarmingly low levels. This prolonged shortage escalated into a nationwide water emergency, with far-reaching implications. The WASH Sector estimated that over 1.85 million people were living in areas highly vulnerable to drought in 2025, while more than 44 percent of the population relies on expensive and often unsafe water trucking. This drought is a reminder that Lebanon’s capacity to address climate challenges is severely limited, exacerbated by its ongoing compound crises. The country ranks poorly in terms of climate readiness (using the ND-GAIN index), facing vulnerabilities stemming from exposure to climate risks, inadequate infrastructure, and weak institutions. 

Infant vaccination rates remain concerning, with only about 55 percent of children under one year receiving all required vaccines on time by mid-2024 a 31 percent national decline.  Although recent measles and polio campaigns temporarily increased coverage to around 84 percent in targeted areas, overall routine immunization remains low raising risks of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks.*

The crises faced by Lebanon have deepened education inequities with approximately 58 percent of Syrian children out of school. Due to a lack of valid residency permits 28,000 children, including children from Syria and Palestinian refugee children from Syria, lack access formal education and/or to obtain examination certificates. Furthermore, youth face a crisis of opportunity with 30 percent having dropped out of school, nearly half of youth unemployed, and over 90 percent of those working in informal or low-paying jobs, leading to migration and 'brain drain'.*

The sub-national Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2023 launched in 2025 found that settlements of displaced Syrians are furthest behind on many development indicators including on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In the settlements only seven percent of the population have access to safely managed drinking water through an improved source that is free of E.Coli contamination and five percent practice open defecation. Only five percent of children from settlements of displaced Syrians attend formal primary school education, and nearly zero percent attend formal secondary school. The MICS also found that child marriage (before 18 years) ranges from 15 to 25 percent in Beirut, Mount Lebanon, Akkar, Bekaa and Palestinian refugee camps and gatherings, however among Syrian refugees in informal settlements child marriages reaches 58 percent. The Early Childhood Development Index (ECDI) measures children who are developmentally on track in health, learning and psychosocial wellbeing at age 3-4 years, and only 41 percent of children in settlements were developmentally on track. 

The global aid downturn has further impacted refugees’ access to services in Lebanon, for example in 2025 UNHCR ended its support to health care for Syrian refugees as they could no longer afford to pay for this support.*

The erosion of household income and livelihood opportunities, following the economic collapse and the 2024 conflict, is making families more vulnerable, heightening the risk of child labour, child marriage, exploitation, and other negative coping mechanisms. Concerns around gender-based violence remain significant due to safety and security concerns and vulnerable groups' prioritization of basic needs over protection. In 2024, children represented 26 per cent of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) survivors reported through the GBV Information Management System (GBV-IMS), with reports of child  labour to meet households' basic needs and child marriage making up 24 percent of cases reported through the GBV-IMS. Adolescent girls faced heightened risks due to structural gender disparities leading to limited access to secondary education, increases in early marriage, exposure to GBV and limited access to employment.*

The gradual recovery in the national budget continues to offer hope, with the national budget increasing by almost US$800 million to US$5.7 billion in 2026, including an increase of 15 percent in the share of the budget allocated to the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE), MoPH and the Ministry of Social Affairs (MoSA).

Goal Area 1: Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies
 
Health
To strengthen Lebanon’s fragile health system UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to deliver critical interventions to restore access to services and strengthen system resilience. Despite this there has been a decline in diptheria, pertussis and tetanus (DPT3) vaccination from 67 percent coverage in 2021 to 59 percent as reported by MoPH.

Through the AaSalameh community-based approach, in 2025 multidisciplinary teams reached 40 percent of primary health care centres (PHCC) providing over 123,000 child health check-ups, antenatal and postnatal consultations, and routine immunization. Health awareness sessions complemented these services, while school health programmes trained 1,270 counselors and screened 256,000 children nationwide.
 
To address newborn survival challenges, UNICEF scaled up the HAYAT programme, improving policy, access, and service quality in 11 governmental hospitals. UNICEF trained 122 Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) providers, supplied non-invasive equipment, and supported 1,500 newborns in intensive care. Post-discharge care was strengthened through referral networks and 1,238 newborn kits, while hospitalization costs were covered for 1,569 critical neonatal and paediatric cases.
 
UNICEF expanded outreach to displaced populations and refugees by activating 30 Primary Healthcare Satellite Units, delivering care to 185,000 people, procuring 1.8 million units of medication, and reaching 393,590 individuals with integrated health messages. Two solarized oxygen generation plants were installed in governmental hospitals to ensure uninterrupted lifesaving care. 

To support war-injured children, UNICEF launched the Assistance and Care for War-Wounded and Affected Children (ACWA) programme, providing specialized medical care, therapy, cash assistance, case management, and education referrals reaching 608 children and 342 caregivers in 2025. 

Digital health advanced through the Digital Health Transformation Roadmap, e-learning modules for Primary Health Care Center (PHCC) staff, and efforts to institutionalize Community Health Workers via national strategies, standardized roles, and digital registries.
 
These achievements reflect UNICEF’s commitment to rebuilding Lebanon’s health system to ensure equitable access to essential services for mothers, newborns, and vulnerable communities.
 
Nutrition and Early Childhood Development (ECD)
Despite funding constraints, UNICEF drove significant progress in child nutrition and positioned ECD as a national priority.
