Working with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH), UNICEF rolled out national wasting guidelines, training over 600 PHCC frontline workers and 100 partner staff to strengthen detection and treatment of malnutrition. Integrated Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) and wasting indicators were embedded into MoPH surveillance platforms, enabling real-time decision-making and targeted interventions. To protect breastfeeding, UNICEF supported MoPH in developing a violation tracking tool to enforce Law 47/2008 on the marketing of breastmilk substitutes.
 
UNICEF expanded access to quality ECD services by training 1,200 frontline workers and 150 partners, improving service coverage for young children nationwide. Assuming the role of technical lead on ECD, UNICEF reinforced national systems and positioned Lebanon as a regional leader, with five countries adopting tools developed in Lebanon. Building on UNICEF’s sustained advocacy and evidence generation, the Government of Lebanon (GoL) committed to investing in ECD through two World Bank concessional loans and, after more than a decade of effort, shared the final draft of the National ECD Strategy - a landmark achievement for Lebanon’s youngest children.

To advance the food systems agenda, UNICEF generated evidence and led strategic advocacy, placing children at the center of policy dialogue. Key achievements included Lebanon’s first national assessment of food retail environments with the Ministry of Economy and Trade (MoET); steps toward cross-ministerial consensus on legislation to curb harmful marketing of unhealthy foods and beverages; and the development and phased roll-out of a national nutrition extracurricular programme for public schools, progressively building food and nutrition literacy from kindergarten 1 to grade 12.
 
Palestinian Programme
For Palestinian children, with the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) and partners, UNICEF support continued for access to health, nutrition, and hygiene promotion for most vulnerable children and mothers. Almost 70,000 Palestinian children and pregnant and lactating women accessed preventive health care interventions, including antenatal and postnatal care, routine immunization, breastfeeding support, growth monitoring, developmental screening and other child health services. In addition, over 3,000 children under-1 year received penta-1 vaccine, and 3,341 caregivers of children were reached with messages on breastfeeding, IYCF, healthy diets, and maternal nutrition. Lifesaving nutrition services were integrated in programmes across Palestinian Camps and Gatherings to strengthen preventive and promotion interventions, targeting 12,972 children and 1,500 caregivers including through screening, awareness sessions, and referrals to UNRWA clinics for further management and follow-up.

Goal Area 2: Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future 
 
Education
The rate of out of school children remains high particularly among Syrians, of an estimated 1.51 million school-aged children located in Lebanon, nearly 420,000 remain out of school, over 60 percent of whom are non-Lebanese.

UNICEF continued supporting the education of marginalized Lebanese and non-Lebanese children with the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE) through the Transition and Resilience Education Fund (TREF), ensuring the most marginalized children access public education. In school year 2024/25 244,232 AM shift children were enrolled in public schools supported by UNICEF through special contract teachers and school funds. UNICEF also continued support to MEHE to implement quality inclusive education for children with disabilities through 116 public schools and supported Education Sector partners to improve the quality of learning environments through capacity building.
 
UNICEF continued support to the government to strengthen systems to increase access to and quality of education, including through the TREF aid modality, improving data systems, expanding quality education services for the most marginalized, learning recovery activities, and supporting general school operations. Under TREF, UNICEF supported MEHE to drive the national education reform agenda to strengthen efficiency, governance, accountability and transparency, including support to school level improvements for financial and data management. UNICEF continued supporting MEHE in strengthening the School Information Management System (SIMS) for communication with schools, including through infrastructure upgrade. 
 
UNICEF continued work to increase demand and access for Non-Formal Education (NFE) under TREF through the Makani and Dirasa programmes ensuring Multiple Flexible Pathways (MFP) to education for Out-Of-School Children (OOSC). The Makani multiservice community center programme offers a comprehensive package of integrated services including education (including Early Childhood Education (ECE)) child protection, youth empowerment, nutrition, digital learning, and social and behavioural change. Operating through 100 centres in communities and informal settlements, as well as in Palestinian Camps, the Makani programme provided more than 46,000 unique vulnerable children, adolescents, and youth with integrated services, including 2,191 children with disabilities (45 percent girls). The Dirasa programme supported more than 42,000 children, including 14,700 OOSC, across 69 semi-private and private schools in eight governorates.
 
The POWER4Girls’ initiative in Lebanon reached 16,000 girls in Makani and Dirasa with tailored life skills and digital assets building from grassroots girls’ networks. POWER4Girls addresses harmful gender norms and aims to strengthen girls’ leadership, skills and agency, leading to their economic empowerment. *
 
Partners also reached 12,455 community members to destigmatize disability and expanded the referral process and followed up on provision of specialized services for 300 children with disabilities enrolled in NFE activities such as: psychomotor therapy, speech and language therapy, psychotherapy, and occupational therapy. Capacity building activities focussed on the harmonization of standards tools for NFE in line with the UNRWA Policy for Inclusive Education and Learning Support guidelines.
 
Palestinian Programme
The UNICEF Palestinian programme continued to support access to quality learning opportunities from pre-school education to completion of basic education with over 12,000 refugee children reached in 2025. In school year 2024/25 UNICEF supported access to pre-school education for 7,597 children including 600 children with disabilities in the Palestinian Camps. With local partners, UNICEF improved the quality of ECE services in more than 54 ECE centres, by enhancing the physical environment and infrastructure, to ensure a safe space for children and to provide accessibility for children with disabilities. 201 ECE and primary facilitators/teachers received capacity building on topics including inclusive education, active learning, online learning, and ICT. Furthermore, over 25 ECE centres were rehabilitated or equipped to enhance accessibility for children with disabilities, fostering an inclusive learning environment. In Palestinian Camps, in coordination with UNRWA, 3,992 children received community and school-based retention support, in addition to digital learning opportunities to improve their performance and work on learning difficulties and contribute to promoting schools as safe environments for learning and development.
 
Skilling of Adolescents and Youth
UNICEF adolescents and youth programming concentrated on addressing the growing vulnerabilities of young people aged 15-28 years, adapting to crises and the conflict response by adopting a holistic, integrated approach to learning, economic empowerment, skills development, active citizenship, and wellbeing. In 2025, UNICEF reached close to 50,000 vulnerable adolescents and youth with formal and non-formal education opportunities, employability services, empowerment, and engagement activities.
 
UNICEF support to MEHE on policy and system strengthening on Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) reached a major milestone with the finalization of the TVET National Strategic Framework (NSF) (2025–2029), a five-year plan to reform and strengthen the TVET sector in Lebanon. The Strategic Framework ensures a rights-based approach to enhance adolescents’ and youth access to education, employment, and social inclusion. To re-enroll 3,500 out-of-school youth into formal TVET education by 2027, with MEHE, UNICEF designed a new legal TVET pathway programme which began roll out in 2025. The model includes an accelerated NFE package that enables adolescents who dropped out at Grades 5 or 6 to re-enter formal education. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened the TVET system through targeted interventions such as establishing a digital Education Management Information System (EMIS) infrastructure in 158 public TVET schools, supporting the solarization and repair of conflict-affected institutions, and digitizing priority curricula and learning modules to expand blended learning. UNICEF also co-developed the national Learning Continuity Plan and supported the establishment of the national TVET Task Force - key steps in improving governance, coordination, and resilience of the TVET sector post-conflict.
 
For Learning to Earning UNICEF continued strengthening pathways from skills development to income generation, through an integrated approach where youth were equipped with foundational, technical, and employability skills; engaged in work-based learning; accessed job placements; and launched small income-generating initiatives across multiple phases of support. In 2025 9,267 youth were reached with competency-based training (5,067 in the recovery response and 300 in advanced training), while 7,042 youth were engaged in work-based learning (Cash for Work), of whom 4,542 within the recovery response directly contributed to community rehabilitation in the South, Bekaa, and Baalbek.  
 
The Generation of Innovation Leaders (GIL) reached 5,000 youth with innovative, entrepreneurial, digital skilling and employment support services. In 2025 the programme trained 2,033 youth on digital skilling including robotics and coding with 74 percent of participants securing employment opportunities or income-generating activities. In addition 1,000 young people were trained on entrepreneurship and business development with the incubation successfully launching 170 youth-led start-ups and 60 micro-enterprises, creating 225 new job opportunities. As part of sustainability and expansion of the programme, a further two GIL labs were added to the network bringing a total of 14 in 2025. Additionally, GIL has successfully gamified the ‘Introduction to Entrepreneurship’ modules over WhatsApp reaching 500 adolescents in rural areas and in Makani centres - and has co-led organization of the first national entrepreneurship and innovation summit, enhancing the entrepreneurial ecosystem in Lebanon.
 
To promote youth voluntarism, the National Volunteering Platform (Nahno) was relaunched with the Ministry of Social Affairs (MoSA). Engagement through Nahno surged, with 12,355 new youth volunteers joining (making the total 25,280 youth registered on the platform), 266 volunteering opportunities posted, and 6,278 service hours completed, supported by 57 new partner entities. UNICEF advanced the youth engagement pillar in South Lebanon where 240 adolescents and youth were trained on life skills and civic engagement, and 10 youth groups led community initiatives. Additionally, 8,967 youth and adolescents were trained on healthy lifestyles while 2,071 were supported with the social cohesion package within Makani.
 
Furthermore, in collaboration with the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), UNICEF supported the National Responsible Citizenship Conference organized by the Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS) engaging 160 youth.
 
Goal Area 3: Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect, and harmful practices
Lebanon continues to face high rates of child marriage and child labour among Syrians in settlements, with the MICS finding 58 percent of women aged 20-24 years living in Syrian settlements married before aged 18 years.¿

Despite Lebanon’s crises and instability, UNICEF achieved significant child protection reforms in 2025. In partnership with MoSA, UNICEF supported a new Vision for Child and Family Care that shifts services from institutional to preventive, family- and community-based care. 
 
National child protection practices were improved with a nationwide roll-out of training on Caring for Child Survivors and updated Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for case management, clarifying roles and referral pathways. UNICEF also partnered with MEHE to introduce a Child Protection Policy in schools, creating safer learning environments.

UNICEF strengthened child protection systems by training over 1,900 professionals (including forensic doctors and juvenile judges) in child-sensitive justice and case management. Coordination forums on key child protection issues were also revitalized. 
 
Community-based mental health and psychosocial support services reached approximately 35,000 children, adolescents, and caregivers. Those in acute distress were referred to specialized services through strengthened pathways. Safe spaces offered at-risk women and girls psychosocial support, case management, and protection from GBV. 

Through the QUDWA Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) initiative, more than 53,000 people were engaged in community campaigns to prevent violence and harmful practices like child marriage and child labour, with religious and community leaders promoting positive social norms. Interactive QUDWA campaigns and community theatre fostered positive social norms by engaging community members, with over 7,500 individuals receiving child protection information materials. 

UNICEF also strengthened monitoring of grave violations against children by training 115 national trainers on the Children and Armed Conflict (CAAC) *agenda and the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism, improving evidence collection and efforts to prevent child recruitment and use.
 
UNICEF continued to strengthen interventions linked to Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA), including through enhancing PSEA systems across 15 new partners and vendors in direct contact with beneficiaries. Safeguarding standards were further integrated into programmes through development of tailored safeguarding policies and training over 2,000 UNICEF, partner and vendor staff. The scale-up of UNICEF-supported reporting channels across implementing partners enabled 140,967 individuals to access reporting mechanisms, increasing the reporting of serious safeguarding violations. UNICEF also initiated work on PSEA with MEHE and supported the finalization of an inter-agency Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) risk assessment within the humanitarian context.
 
Through community-based protection services, working with local partners, UNICEF reached 25,048 Palestinian children (including children with disabilities) with case management, mental health, and psychosocial support. In addition, in Palestinian Camps 7,935 women and girls accessed safe spaces offering psychosocial support and protection from GBV. Community engagement also remained key in the Palestinian Camps with over 31,000 community members and 6,800 caregivers attending awareness and parenting sessions on child protection and GBV.  
 
Goal Area 4: Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services and supplies, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment 
UNICEF interventions removed critical bottlenecks hindering children’s access to safe water and sanitation. Key achievements included restoring essential water systems with the capacity to provide water for over four million people - of a national population of 5.76 million people*, rehabilitating over 600 installations, and expanding wastewater management to support 13 systems serving over one million people. Solar-powered water stations and a demonstration site for treated wastewater reuse at the Zahle wastewater treatment plant enhanced climate resilience and agricultural irrigation, reaching around four million people. To address financial bottlenecks, UNICEF supported labour-intensive construction, generating livelihoods and improving infrastructure.
 
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Energy and Water (MoEW) to develop a Strategic Plan for Wastewater and on a comprehensive database of ongoing water and wastewater projects until 2027. As part of these projects UNICEF strengthened the national Water Establishments (WEs) capacity to manage wastewater treatment plants to be handed over by the Council for Development and Reconstruction (CDR) from 2026. Institutional strengthening with the MoEW included establishing the inter-ministerial Reuse Regulator Committee to ensure that wastewater reuse meets minimum standards and addresses urgent issues. UNICEF also integrated GBV risk mitigation across projects by developing a comprehensive set of tools, guidance, and checklists, and by training and coaching over 60 staff from partners and vendors. Activities paused due to the 2024 conflict resumed, including the customer database task force to improve revenue management. 
 
As the humanitarian WASH sector coordinator, co-chaired with MoEW, UNICEF played a pivotal role in Lebanon’s water sector. The Sector highlighted urgent issues such as the struggling wastewater management sub-sector and the challenges facing the Water Sector Recovery Plan which aims for the financial independence of the four regional Water Establishments by 2026.
 
Despite the acute reductions in humanitarian funding, UNICEF continued to address critical WASH needs for around 110,000 Syrian refugees in Informal Tented Settlements (ITSs), while scaling up emergency support for new refugee arrivals and more than 20,000 displaced Lebanese families affected by conflicts across Lebanon. To mitigate for reduced humanitarian funding, UNICEF invested in empowering communities to take more responsibility for water services, while scaling up climate resilient long-term solar operated solutions and power-free water treatment solutions. Amid the funding constraints, UNICEF - as the sector lead - is working with sector partners for a phased transition on the reduction of support to Syrians in ITSs while *implementing risk prioritization to mitigate public health risks.
 
WASH sensitization and mobilization was conducted in nine Palestinian camps at ten Makani centres with Water, Health and Nutrition (WHN) community mobilization and awareness raising reaching over 6,300 individuals. WHN Minimum Standards were tailored to the Palestinian context with over 100 focal points trained to apply the standards at community level.
 
Goal Area 5: Every child, including adolescents, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free from poverty 
UNICEF strengthened inclusive social protection through research, policy dialogue, and system improvements to support vulnerable children and families. A major milestone towards universal social protection coverage was the expansion of the National Disability Allowance (NDA). With UNICEF support - such as adapting the management information system and operational oversight - MoSA extended eligibility beyond adolescents (15–18 years) to include all children and older persons (65+ years). As a result, over 30,000 Lebanese persons with disabilities received assistance, with USD 10 million disbursed from national resources. Importantly, 62 percent of NDA funding came from the Government, reflecting stronger domestic ownership. UNICEF also helped advance the National Social Protection Strategy (NSPS) with agreement reached on governance and coordination structures, clarifying institutional roles and strengthening MoSA leadership. 
 
Public finance engagement remained a priority. In partnership with the Institute of Finance, UNICEF updated Lebanon’s Citizen Budget and expanded the dashboard to promote transparency and citizen participation. The Social Protection Financing Review, developed with the International Labour Organization (ILO), informed bilateral discussions on sustainable financing. Advocacy efforts contributed to increased allocations in the 2026 draft budget, including USD 11.1 million for social assistance and USD 500,000 for case management services - critical for expanding coverage and improving services for vulnerable children and persons with disabilities.
 
On the local governance agenda, UNICEF finalized the first Local Governance Strategy (2025–2030); advanced municipal law reform through a policy paper advocating for empowered, child-sensitive municipalities; and designed the national Child-Sensitive Local Governance (CSLG) Guidebook for newly elected councils. UNICEF launched a national engagement process, sensitizing over 100 municipalities on child-responsive planning and budgeting. 
 
Climate Change
UNICEF advanced its Climate Action Programme with significant progress made in solarizing education facilities with 234 schools equipped with hybrid solar systems, benefiting over 111,000 students and generating 10.5 MWp of clean energy. These interventions yielded substantial cost savings, reduced carbon emissions, and enhanced energy security. Additional measures include Light-Emitting Diode (LED) lighting upgrades, thermal insulation, and digital monitoring for optimized energy use. UNICEF worked on climate-resilient water infrastructure, especially wastewater reuse for irrigation, expanding underground water monitoring and nature-based wastewater treatment. Wastewater reuse projects, such as the Zahle wastewater treatment plant, supported irrigation and environmental preservation. Rainwater harvesting and solarization of water and wastewater systems further contributed to sustainability, with multiple systems implemented across schools and communities.
 
Youth were engaged as leaders in community-based climate resilience efforts, reaching over 5,000 youth across Lebanon in designing and implementing climate initiatives. Training and capacity building equipped them to act as climate champions, while learning sessions fostered sustainable practices. Through the Climate Action Toolkit UNICEF empowered 172 youth climate champions with cascade training leading to 6,730 young people participating across Lebanon in environmental sessions. In addition, 4,091 youth participated in youth-led climate actions, collecting over 5,200 kg of waste and planting 3,160 trees. School clubs under the Dirasa programme also empowered students to lead initiatives such as recycling, eco-art, nature walks, and school gardens, with 49 clubs implementing climate education projects.

A module was developed to explain the impact of climate change on early childhood development, addressing the effects on physical, cognitive, and emotional growth, maternal health, nutrition, mental health, education, and socioeconomic stability, while offering adaptation strategies for ECD professionals.
 
Emergency Preparedness and Response
UNICEF expanded the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) for emergencies, reaching 308,058 IDPs, returnees, and post-December 2024 arrivals with essential and life-saving supplies. In addition, 51,939 children received winter clothing kits, and 16,204 children received summer clothing kits, ensuring their protection, dignity, and wellbeing across harsh seasonal conditions. To further strengthen family resilience, 19,954 blankets were distributed to vulnerable households, reducing winter-related risks among the most marginalized communities. 

Emergency preparedness was reinforced at national and sub-national levels, including through the revision of 21 child-centred community contingency plans enabling municipalities to better prepare for and respond to emergencies. UNICEF expanded Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) in public institutions, rolling out DRR in 21 public schools, and delivering DRR training to 142 Makani center staff.
 
Evidence for Advocacy
The 2023 Lebanon Sub-national MICS was launched under the patronage of the Prime Minister. The MICS was conducted by the Central Administration of Statistics, with UNICEF support, providing high quality data on over 160 indicators, of which 26 are SDG indicators across 11 goals. Evidence-based advocacy was reinforced through key publications, notably The Future of Lebanon’s Children report, which applies global megatrends to Lebanon’s context to guide long-term strategies and investments.

Evaluations have driven course correction for learning continuity and inclusion in UNICEF Education programmes, while also shaping policy and systems choices for the social protection programme and the National Social Protection Strategy. The WASH evaluation showcased emerging applications including on-site sanitation solutions, informing adoption of this innovation. 

Gender
UNICEF-supported flagship programmes such as the NDA, Makani, and Dirasa programmes are at least gender responsive, *ensuring that the needs of girls and boys are identified and addressed such as through the adaptation of a gender-responsive digital pedagogy guide and distribution of Lahaa kits for adolescent girls. To move programming from gender-sensitive to gender-transformative, targeted programming for and with girls was strengthened in 2025 with POWER4Girls implementation in non-formal education leading to the drafting of the UNICEF-supported Girls’ Strategy with girls. To improve partners’ gender capacities, five local strategic partners were capacitated on gender, with all five partners finalizing their organizations’ gender policies to improve their gender commitments and accountabilities.

UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to strengthening commitments around inclusive and equitable education, recovery, child-sensitive local governance, disability inclusion, and evidence-based policymaking and public service reform for children and youth.* UNICEF amplified children’s voices and priorities through sustained policy advocacy, high-level public engagement, child participation including through strategic moments such as World Children’s Day, the TREF third anniversary, the MICS launch, and rollout of the Inclusive Education programme. 
 
Strategic partnerships with government institutions, UN agencies, donors, and civil society were reinforced through high-visibility events, and public statements that translated data and field realities into clear calls for action.* Media engagement remained strong, with UNICEF Lebanon maintaining a leading voice in national and international media on issues affecting children, supported by a close partnership with the Ministry of Information to amplify child rights advocacy at the national level. In 2025, UNICEF Lebanon significantly expanded public engagement through social media campaigns, real-time crisis communication, and advocacy-driven content. *The total reach across UNICEF Lebanon’s social media channels in 2025 exceeded 130 million, fostering dialogue with diverse audiences, including young people.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges and Lessons Learned
Successive and protracted crises are eroding the protective environment for vulnerable boys, girls, and women - particularly in conflict affected areas - *with ongoing hostilities disrupting children’s access to services particularly in the South of Lebanon. Crises are increasingly complex, with fluid displacement creating overlapping vulnerabilities among IDPs and host communities. A lack of post-conflict recovery to damaged facilities further limits children's and families’ access to safe services such as functional healthcare, exposing healthcare workers and patients to serious risks, including due to disruption to the supply of medical equipment and essential medication. *In communities in the South of Lebanon the lack of security due to ongoing killing and maiming, and the risk of unexploded ordnance limit access to and delivery of services, *leading to families’ lower uptake of services citing fears and mobility restrictions. Insecurity in areas, such as on the Southern border, restricts humanitarian access and limits service provision.* The severely limited post-conflict reconstruction has been driven by a lack of recovery funding* with the few contributions received remaining highly earmarked¿. Furthermore, there has been insecurity in Palestinian Camps, continuing socio-economic pressures, and the 2025 drought* exposed the insufficient national focus on climate change¿.
 
With Syrian refugees returning to Syria from Lebanon there is increased cross-border movement,* and tightening border controls are creating risks to refugees’ safe and dignified stay in Lebanon, especially for vulnerable groups. This challenges abilities to protect boys, girls and women on the move and to uphold rights-based programming.¿ New arrivals *have come to Lebanon, since the change of government in Syria in December 2024, however data limitations on these new arrivals has affected response planning¿ including due to restricted access to some borderline areas due to security concerns.¿
 
The formation of a reform-minded Government in Lebanon presents a strategic entry point for policy development and long-stalled reforms. However, policy reform and institutional capacity-building are jeopardized by insecurity, political and macro-economic instability, leading to loss of qualified public servants and limited funding for systems reform.* The Government is embarking on a national process for administrative reform, but this will take time and resources to advance system-level change¿. For example, the Water Establishments (WEs) are challenged to deliver effective wastewater management due to funding and staff shortages. *In schools, child protection progress is hindered by teachers’ heavy workload*, distress from disruptions due to hostilities, and staff turnover.¿ Limited reform leads to a prioritization of life-saving interventions over durable solutions, derailing the achievement of transformational change.¿ 
 
Funding gaps* across programmes, with shrinking humanitarian funding*, is limiting space for service coverage, longer-term system-building, and sustainability. Increased earmarking, short-term funding, and shifting donor priorities limit flexibility, challenge longer-term planning and make it difficult to provide system-wide support especially for multi-year reforms and for under-funded areas such as child protection, nutrition and waste management. Continuity of funds for Syrian refugee programming, including for WASH in ITSs, is a particular challenge. While the Government of Lebanon is gradually increasing funding for social grants to the Lebanese population, the funding environment for the non-Lebanese is decreasing. UNICEF continues to prioritize multi-year and flexible funding, but funding received is increasingly earmarked for specific areas of work.
 
In the education sector* there has been a significant decrease in non-Lebanese student enrolment in public schools (PM shift), due to denied access for children lacking legal residency or United Nations High Commission for Refugees (UNHCR) certification. Advocacy with MEHE and the Government is ongoing to ensure inclusive access for all children.¿ Aligned to this, learning losses have increased due to the delayed start of the 2024/2025 school year, particularly for the PM shift, and repeated disruptions to teaching caused by conflict and security concerns. Barriers to education include documentation requirements and sectoral gaps keeping thousands of children out of formal education, especially among newcomers and returnees.¿ This applies to the TVET sector where 6,185 refugee students were impacted *by the decision of the Government. 
 
In the health sector UNICEF is supporting interministerial coordination to establish a national referral mechanism to promote access to comprehensive care at all levels of care. However, there is a lack of regulation and of standardized newborn care strategies and policies, with data on newborn care fragmented. Data and coordination between partners affect timely decision-making, for example there is a difficulty locating and following up on war injured children due to missing personal *data and continued displacement. Aligned to this, funding constraints limit coverage for advanced treatment and continuity of care for war injured children. For nutrition, unclear accountability frameworks for Government and partners across sectors result in implementation gaps and weak delivery of nutrition outcomes.* ¿
 
To enhance coherence and find efficiencies to address complex issues, UNICEF has focused on cross-sectoral collaboration both among UN agencies and partners*, and across UNICEF programmes. As examples of joint programming, UNICEF is engaged in joint child labour and economic inclusion programming with ILO and UNHCR; child marriage programming and youth strategy development with UNFPA; and child justice programming with UNODC, UNHCR, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).*¿ To sustainably address child labour and child marriage a holistic, family-centred approach is essential to address child protection needs and support family members around education, livelihoods and social protection¿. This approach includes family-based interventions to address abuse and caregiver stress, which has been found to be a driver of child protection concerns in the household. Furthermore, the integration of social and behaviour change in programme design has contributed to improve results and sustainability¿. *
 
The Humanitarian Reset* impacted the 2026 Lebanon Response Plan (LRP), which has shifted from a needs-based to priority-based response plan. In 2025 Sectors underwent rigorous prioritization based upon a severity index, resulting in a decreased LRP budget from $2.9 billion in 2025 to $1.62 billion in 2026, Sectors decreasing from 11 in 2025 to nine in 2026, and the LRP Sector strategies being simplified with activities prioritized and logframes streamlined. Moving into 2026, there is a shift towards national coordination, phasing out sub-national Sector coordination towards Operational Coordination Groups (OCG) in the southen, northern, eastern, and central areas. In line with the Grand Bargain and the Humanitarian Reset UNICEF in Lebanon is shifting towards local partners particularly through the education, youth, and Palestinian programmes. Despite funding challenges local partners have proven faster, more sustainable, and efficient in delivering integrated services, expanding reach and resilience.¿*
 
Recent experience has highlighted important lessons, including the need for a more inclusive and anticipatory emergency preparedness approach that integrates all population groups, as well as the value of regular scenario updates and the stress-testing of contingency plans. Strengthening partnership coordination and enhancing supply chain readiness at the local level remain critical for improving overall response effectiveness.
 
UNICEF sharpened its National Evaluation Capacity Development (NECD) role by conducting a diagnosis of Lebanon’s evaluation ecosystem. The analysis found that evaluation functions and culture are structurally fragmented - lacking codified mandates, institutional coordination, and civil-service pathways for evaluative skills. The analysis set a practical reform agenda for evaluation by recommending enactment of a binding legal mandate for evaluation, establishing a governance mechanism, and institutionalizing evaluation units, training, and career incentives across ministries - alongside strengthening data infrastructure, increasing public visibility, and mobilizing non-state actors.* These messages were anchored in a high-level National Evaluation Conference, that convened State, oversight, academic, and civil-society stakeholders to position evaluation as a sovereign tool for rebuilding trust and accountability in public administration.
 
Outlook
As the Lebanese national budget gradually strengthens the UN agencies are supporting a transition towards national leadership. However, the Government budget and capacity remains fragile with a shortage of civil servants across many national institutions. *

With the return of Syrian refugees from Lebanon to Syria in 2025, and a further 200,000 Syrian refugees expected to return to Syria in 2026, *UNICEF is working cross-border with UNHCR,  UNICEF Syria and other actors for durable solutions planning to facilitate refugee returns to Syria.

Given ongoing fragility in Lebanon and the wider region, emergency preparedness and planning will remain critical, including support to Disaster Risk Management with the Presidency of the Council of Ministers. Community resilience efforts will scale up child-sensitive contingency planning and DRR in schools in vulnerable areas, as well as strengthening partner capacity in supply management, warehousing, and data systems.

Evaluations serve as bridge-builders including through national evaluation capacity development initiatives. UNICEF evaluations seek to generate compelling, localized evidence that meet the demands of international stakeholders who require results-based accountability, and domestic stakeholders by documenting tangible child outcomes. By providing actionable insights on cost-effectiveness and impact pathways evaluations aims to accelerate results for children by ensuring every decision, from program design to resource allocation, is grounded in what works best in Lebanon's unique context.
 
The development of the next UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the UNICEF Country Programme are scheduled to start in 2026, with the plans scheduled to begin implementation from 2028. With the Lebanese parliamentary elections planned in 2026 the UN system will work with the Government to identify national priorities, with UNICEF focusing on embedding child rights within the national agenda. The transition to national leadership, with the development of longer-term national plans, offers a renewed opportunity for systemic reform in Lebanon towards outcomes such as ending violence against children, and strengthening critical national systems such as child protection, education, health and nutrition, social protection and WASH.

Libya, a country marked by political instability, conflict, and recurrent natural disasters, faces multidimensional humanitarian and development challenges. Vulnerable populations—children, internally displaced persons (IDPs), and conflict-affected communities—struggle with access to essential services and protection. In 2025, this context continued to constrain fulfilment of child rights, particularly where access to services depends on local governance arrangements, fiscal liquidity, and security conditions. 
The security environment remained fragile and uneven, characterised by the presence of armed actors, intermittent localised tensions, and an operational environment that could change quickly by location. While large-scale conflict was largely avoided, periodic insecurity and administrative constraints continued to affect service continuity, staff movement, partner access and supply chains, with direct implications for UNICEF's ability to deliver at scale, especially in hard-to-reach or politically sensitive areas. 
Libya's economy remains highly exposed to hydrocarbon dynamics and political shocks. After weaker performance in 2024, Libya's growth outlook for 2025 improved mainly due to oil sector recovery, while risks remained present given political uncertainty and the potential for renewed disruptions to production and exports. This volatility leads to uncertainty for public financial management and the predictability of funding for social sectors, reinforcing a pattern where recurrent spending pressures can undermine sustained investment in system strengthening. The overall result is limited fiscal space for reforms that would improve service quality and equity for children and adolescents. 
A major progress in 2025 was the availability of updated, nationally representative child- and household-focused evidence through the Libya Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2024–2025. This closes a decade-long gap in robust social data and provides a clearer picture of where children are doing well, where deprivations persist, and which groups are being left behind. 
On child survival, MICS estimates under-five mortality at 14.6 deaths per 1,000 live births, infant mortality at 13.2, and neonatal mortality at 10.5, providing an updated baseline for tracking progress and for targeting health system bottlenecks. These figures point to the need for sustained focus on maternal and newborn care quality, continuity of essential services, and equitable access to primary health care, especially in areas where system functionality varies. 
Nutrition outcomes show persistent risks. MICS estimates stunting (height-for-age <-2 SD) at 11.8 per cent and wasting (weight-for-height <-2 SD) at 4.2 per cent among children under five, alongside underweight at 4.1 per cent. This highlight the importance of preventive and community-based nutrition services, infant and young child feeding support, and early identification of acute malnutrition, particularly for vulnerable households facing poverty, shocks, and limited access to quality health and nutrition services. 
Education outcomes reflect both significant strengths and persisting challenges. Adjusted net attendance rates show high coverage at primary level (96 per cent) and strong participation at lower secondary (92 per cent) and upper secondary (83 per cent). However, early childhood education participation remains lower, with MICS estimating attendance at 9.2 per cent for children aged 36–47 months. These patterns suggest that while retention through basic and secondary education has improved substantially, early childhood education expansion and equitable access to quality ECE services remain critical priorities, particularly in underserved areas. 
In child protection, MICS reinforces the scale of harmful practices within the home environment. It estimates that 78.2 per cent of children aged 1–14 experienced violent discipline (psychological aggression and/or physical punishment) in the last month, with 63 per cent experiencing physical punishment. While child labour prevalence is lower at 3.1 per cent among children aged 5–17, the high prevalence of violent discipline underscores the need for sustained behaviour change, parenting support, child safeguarding systems, and links between social services and community structures. 
Civil registration and legal identity are critical enablers for access to rights and services. MICS estimates birth registration for children under five at 99.6 per cent, indicating near-universal coverage and reflecting strong civil registration systems. This high level of birth registration provides a solid foundation for children's access to education, health services, social protection, and legal protections. 
MICS findings indicate high coverage of access to basic drinking-water at national level. Use of basic drinking water services (improved source on premises or within a 30-minute round trip) is 95.9 per cent, while use of safely managed drinking water services (improved source on premises, available when needed, and free from E. coli contamination) is 38 per cent. Water-quality testing shows faecal contamination at 28 per cent at the source and 46.4 per cent at the point of use, indicating contamination between collection and use. These gaps have direct implications for child health risks, including diarrhoeal disease, and reinforce the need for strengthened water safety management, routine monitoring and maintenance, and climate-resilient WASH service delivery.  
Libya remains a destination and transit country for mixed movements, exposing children to heightened protection risks and increasing pressure on already stretched services. IOM's Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Round 58 identified 894,890 migrants from 45 nationalities across Libya's 100 municipalities during the reporting period of May–July 2025, reflecting the scale and persistence of these flows. UNHCR registered 106,560 affected populations and asylum-seekers in Libya as of November 2025, the majority of whom are Sudanese nationals fleeing ongoing conflict. At the same time, OCHA estimates that 787,090 people require humanitarian assistance in Libya as of May 2025, reflecting continued pockets of vulnerability driven by instability, displacement, and service deficits. 
MICS also provides a household-level signal on mobility pressures: 10.1 per cent of households reported at least one member displaced due to conflict, and 9.1 per cent reported at least one displaced household member. These dynamics underline the importance of flexible delivery modalities and partnerships that can sustain services for mobile and vulnerable populations, including migrants and internally displaced communities.  
The convergence of political fragmentation, economic volatility, protection risks, and service gaps creates a complex operating environment for UNICEF and partners in 2025. The MICS 2024–2025 provides an essential evidence base to guide programme priorities, target the most vulnerable children and adolescents, and strengthen partnerships with government, civil society, and communities to advance children's rights and well-being across Libya.

In 2025, UNICEF Libya Country Office (LCO) achieved notable progress in its humanitarian and development mandate, delivering results across health, nutrition, education, child protection, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), social policy, and operational effectiveness. Through strategic program coordination, robust partnerships, digital transformation, capacity building, and risk management, UNICEF Libya navigated complex challenges, reinforced resilience, and laid a foundation for sustainable improvements in children's well-being. This comprehensive report details sectoral achievements, innovative strategies, challenges, and future directions, providing stakeholders, policymakers, and donors with an authoritative account of UNICEF's impact in Libya.  
UNICEF’s mission in Libya is to safeguard the rights of every child, advance equitable access to quality services, and support systemic reforms that build resilience against future shocks. In 2025, the LCO intensified efforts in both emergency response and long-term development, adapting to evolving risks and leveraging multi-sectoral expertise and partnerships to deliver tangible improvements for Libya’s children and families.  
UNICEF Libya’s strategic coordination ensured alignment with Country Programme (CP), Country Programme Management Plan (CPMP) objectives and the UNICEF´s Strategic Plan Impact Results. The office, staffed by over 50 professionals and partnering extensively with national and local authorities, maintained rigorous management structures to maximize program impact.  
 
Multisectoral interventions—such as integrating immunization with birth registration and implementing nutrition packages—were facilitated through collaborative programme coordination setups such as weekly Programme Management Team meetings. Thematic clinics targeted issues like the first 1,000 days of life, zero-dose vaccination, out-of-school children, and climate change, fostering accountability and innovation across teams. Strategic targeting of 100 high zero-dose child population municipalities enabled focused investments in primary healthcare and enhanced coordination among health, nutrition, and WASH sectors.  
Operational harmonization was achieved through standardized cash transfer modalities, resulting in an office-wide strategy that streamlined partner engagement, efficiency, compliance, and delivery speed. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) were refined to ensure clear roles and responsibilities, while monthly integration of operations and field support—covering Gender equality, Social and Behavior Change (SBC), Communication Advocacy & Partnership (CAP), Innovation, Supply, and Humanitarian Support—strengthened overall program effectiveness and responsiveness.  
Here is a comprehensive narrative that organizes all achievements from the Libya Country Office around the five Impact Results of the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029: 
Impact Result 1: Child Survival and Development 
In 2025, UNICEF continued to support national efforts to ensure that every child survives and thrives, within the framework of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2, 3, 4 and 5, Goal Area 1 of the Strategic Plan (SP) and Goal Area 1 of the UNICEF Gender Action Plan 2022–2025 (GAP).    
The expansion of primary health care coverage from 7.85% in 2024 to 11.44% in 2025 extended essential services to approximately 520,000 people, reflecting a 3.6 percentage point increase. This achievement was rooted in the strategic upgrade of 26 health facilities and the installation of solar energy systems in 22 facilities spanning 20 municipalities, which bolstered service continuity in fragile and energy-insecure contexts. By reducing reliance on unstable energy sources, UNICEF enhanced healthcare accessibility for remote and underserved populations. 
UNICEF supported access of nearly 880,000 people to essential health commodities by delivering $2.5 million worth of such supplies, including critical cold chain equipment. The cold chain infrastructure was fortified in 100 primary health care facilities and 14 municipal storage sites, ensuring the integrity of temperature-sensitive vaccines and strengthening the national immunization program. Faced with measles outbreaks, rapid immunization campaigns were launched, successfully vaccinating 313,967 children between 9 months and 9 years in eastern and southern Libya, containing the spread of disease and safeguarding vulnerable communities. 
Maternal health services experienced notable progress, with 135,000 women accessing prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services in 135 equipped facilities across 18 municipalities. UNICEF trained 547 health workers in maternal and newborn care, lifting service quality and expanding the network of skilled professionals available to mothers and infants. Health and nutrition packages distributed in schools impacted more than 2,000 students and over 600 parents in 12 municipalities, while the School Health and Nutrition Programme—implemented collaboratively with the Ministries of Health and Education—provided targeted support to Sudanese school-aged children. 
UNICEF's multisectoral approach to nutrition was facilitated by platforms such as the Nutrition Sub-Working Group. Tools like the Nutrition Environment Assessment Tool for Schools (NEAT-S) were deployed in 171 schools, engaging over 6,300 children and generating actionable data to shape the National School Health and Nutrition Strategy. As part of the Sudan people crisis response, 46,385 pregnant and breastfeeding women and caregivers received counseling on maternal nutrition and infant/young child feeding. Malnutrition screening reached 33,789 children under five, with 4,966 treated for moderate or severe wasting. An additional 25,209 women of childbearing age were also screened, extending the program's reach and impact. 
UNICEF shifted its emphasis from infrastructure-heavy investments to health system strengthening, governance, and quality of care. Technical assistance supported the development of national Breastmilk Substitutes (BMS) Code legislation and the design of behavior change strategies for improved infant feeding practices. Policy reforms addressed health financing, immunization supply chains, procurement, and workforce management—laying the foundation for the National Immunization Strategy (2025) and the first Zero-Dose Immunization Strategy to reach marginalized and migrant children. 
Impact Result 2: Learning for Life 
To ensure that every child learns and acquires skills for the future, UNICEF Libya’s education initiatives in 2025 were guided by a commitment to inclusive, quality learning experiences and robust system strengthening. Over 45,000 out-of-school children benefited from non-formal education, remedial learning, and life skills programs, reflecting targeted strategies to bridge equity gaps and promote universal access. Remedial classes in 152 public schools and 11 Baity Centers focused on addressing the learning deficits of children affected by conflict, while gender-responsive approaches provided vital support for girls at risk of dropping out. Financial and administrative barriers were reduced through documentation assistance and cash-for-education schemes, expanding opportunities for the most marginalized groups. 
Central to these achievements was the consolidation of the Education Management Information System (EMIS), which institutionalised data-driven planning and monitoring throughout the Ministry of Education. This enabled reliable data generation, improved sector coordination, and reinforced evidence-based decision-making. Capacity-building through specialized training and technical support strengthened institutional effectiveness, complemented by research that informed enrollment strategies and enhanced learning quality. 
Policy reforms advanced governance and accountability, with the Ministry of Education committing to sector coordination by early 2026. The introduction of a new learning assessment framework targeting foundational skills in grades 2–3 aligned Libya’s education system with global standards, supporting improved measurement and learning outcomes. To promote disability inclusion, UNICEF provided Social and Behavior Change-informed training and co-designed awareness videos with organizations of persons with disabilities, launching these resources on World Disability Day to encourage inclusive practices. Further integration of social and behavior change into academic programs occurred through collaboration with the School of Public Health and capacity-building for university faculty. 
Physical access to education was enhanced by rehabilitating and expanding schools, including the establishment of new facilities such as Alradefa School, and implementing greening initiatives across 400 schools. Montessori rooms and teacher kits enriched learning environments, while digital solutions like the Learning Passport ensured educational continuity during emergencies, fostered digital literacy, and improved retention rates among displaced children. 
Impact Result 3: Ending Child Poverty 
To move towards the goal of fewer children in multidimensional poverty, UNICEF advanced Libya’s social policy reform by tackling systemic barriers and bolstering shock-responsive social protection systems. A dedicated government task force was formed to spearhead these reforms, with ministries of Health, Education, Social Affairs, Finance, and Planning actively participating. In partnership with the National Economic and Social Development Board, UNICEF facilitated the development and launch of three government-validated budget briefs—covering health, education, and social protection—that delivered actionable, evidence-based recommendations for more equitable and transparent resource allocation. 
To build institutional capacity, sixteen ministry officials received training in child-responsive budgeting, equipping them to analyze public spending and advocate for increased investments in children’s well-being. A major focus was placed on strengthening the universal Wife and Children Grant, Libya’s signature social protection initiative. Comprehensive guidelines and standard operating procedures were drafted in a four-day workshop in 2025 and is expected to be implemented in 2026. UNICEF also supported the creation of digital tools, including business process maps and video tutorials, to streamline beneficiary access and standardize procedures—addressing operational inconsistencies and data system weaknesses. 
On the humanitarian front, 445 internally displaced households in eastern Libya received emergency cash assistance, and a pilot voucher-based program was launched for 200 Sudanese people households. These initiatives showcased innovative, risk-informed strategies for social protection delivery that can inform future programming. 
 Impact Result 4: Protection from Violence 
In 2025, UNICEF Libya launched a transformative, government-led child protection and welfare system, advancing from fragmented activities to unified, evidence-based protocols. Notable accomplishments included the validation of the National Handover Protocol and the creation of SOPs for justice-sector staff, establishing rights-based pathways for children who are in contact with the law or armed groups within Family and Child Protection Units under the Ministry of Interior. The professionalization of the Social Service Workforce (SSW) was propelled forward through national mapping and workshops, resulting in a roadmap for standardized qualifications and a draft national social work education curriculum. In addition, policy alignment efforts saw the revision of Libya’s Child Rights Law and the restructuring of the Higher Committee for Childhood, strengthening the legal and institutional framework for child protection. 
Building on evidence from MICS data, UNICEF scaled up positive parenting programs to address harmful practices. Through 11 Baity centers and mobile teams, more than 23,200 vulnerable children and caregivers accessed integrated protection services, including mental health and psychosocial support. 
UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, developed Libya's first Positive Parenting Curriculum in response to MICS Survey findings indicating that 78% of children experience violent discipline. These positive parenting sessions reached thousands of caregivers, fostering gender-transformative programming and shifting ownership to national stakeholders. The organization maintained 11 Baity centers and mobile teams, providing integrated services such as mental health and psychosocial support, case management, and multi-sectoral referrals to over 23,200 individuals, with priority given to conflict-affected and border areas impacted by the Sudan crisis. Through partnerships with IOM and UNHCR, Best Interest Determination panels were established to assist unaccompanied and separated children. 
UNICEF’s advocacy efforts and strong partnerships led to the Ministry of Defence’s approval of Guidelines for the Protection of Children Affected by Armed Conflict, highlighting its leadership in child protection. Nearly 1,000 frontline personnel received capacity-building training, and the handover of 5 Baity centers to government ministries ensured continuity and national responsibility for child protection services. Despite these successes, persistent barriers remain, including unclear legal frameworks, harmful social norms, and resource constraints. UNICEF is committed to completing the child protection budget brief, finalizing system reforms, and scaling up training for social service workers in 2026. Strengthening data management and integrating child protection protocols into broader social welfare systems will be pivotal in enhancing outcomes for vulnerable children. 
 Impact Result 5: Climate and Disaster Resilience 
To achieve the goal that every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment, UNICEF Libya continued to work with national and local institutions. UNICEF played a pivotal role in delivering urgent WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) assistance while laying the groundwork for long-lasting improvements in public service reliability and safety. In 2025, 642,600 individuals gained access to enhanced drinking water services, with 58% benefiting from climate-resilient solutions. This included the restoration of essential water sources and the installation of 40 solar-powered pumps, upgraded infrastructure, and reverse osmosis systems. Hygiene kits were distributed to 129,500 people.  
Throughout the year, UNICEF Libya, in partnership with government bodies and NGOs, responded to floods and supported vulnerable communities by providing WASH services that both met emergency needs and strengthened public service continuity. LCO supported 229,600 affected people access to safely managed water and 72,100 benefited specifically from climate-resilient water services. Maintenance duties for these systems were transferred to capable local authorities, ensuring their longevity. 
Following the principle of “leaving no one behind,” humanitarian interventions delivered drinking water to 128,100 individuals in areas impacted by floods and displacement, while sanitation services protected the health of 127,000 people by reducing exposure to pollutants and promoting dignified conditions. Hygiene resources were extended to those in informal settlements and detention centers, with 34,000 individuals receiving limited hygiene services. Menstrual hygiene and health initiatives supported 31,000 women and adolescent girls, helping to remove obstacles to education and overall well-being. 
Institutional WASH formed a cornerstone of UNICEF’s strategy; climate-resilient facilities were introduced in educational and health institutions. In 2025, fifteen health facilities in crisis-affected regions and two in development zones were upgraded, creating safer environments for students, patients, and staff, and enhancing readiness for future emergencies. 
Operational Effectiveness and Cross-Cutting Enablers 
Regarding Operational Efficiency, strong governance, sound financial management, and robust digital transformation formed the backbone of UNICEF Libya’s achievements. By conducting thorough risk assessments, refining cash transfer processes, and implementing operational improvements, the organization realized $701,000 in savings on non-staff expenses. Procurement activities totaled $12.5 million, and new ICT initiatives transformed workflows into secure, transparent systems—bolstering national platforms like EMIS, Learning Passport, and digital health programs. Advocacy efforts resulted in over 750 media coverage instances, while partnerships with government, UN agencies, and civil society anchored long-term sustainability. Across all programs, gender equity and data-informed decisions were prioritized, reinforcing fairness and accountability. 
The Libya Country Office (LCO) heightened operational effectiveness by focusing on governance, financial administration, supply chain management, and digital transformation—all working together to protect child outcomes and maximize value. Governance tools, such as the Country Management Team, statutory forums, updated management plans, and authority tables, were routinely used to guide performance and address uncertainty. Joint annual risk and fraud assessments strengthened prevention and response controls, maintaining continuity after an OIAI audit. By year-end, 85% of Management Action Plan tasks were completed and the rest were on track. 
UNICEF sustained service delivery despite limitations and uncertainties from external factors as well as organizational transitions such as the Future Focus Initiative. Financial teams emphasized risk reduction and process enhancements: direct cash transfer aging improved, assurance activities surpassed expectations, vendor payments quickened, and quality checks minimized rework. Administrative support included managing 247 trips and 43 events, facilitating protocol and visa processes despite inconsistent embassy procedures, and completing asset verifications in Tripoli, Benghazi, and Tunis with subsequent disposal actions. 
Shifting to a leaner operating model saved $701,168 in non-staff costs by October, largely from consolidating accommodations and warehouses (including a decrease in accommodation units, downsizing back offices, and moving warehousing to Ministry of Health facilities), shared telecom arrangements with WFP, targeted ICT purchasing, and streamlined travel plans. These efficiencies, which are expected to continue into 2026, helped maintain program capacity amid resource constraints. 
Supply and logistics were vital to UNICEF’s results, with procurement in 2025 totaling around $12.5 million ($4.5 million for supplies and $8 million for services). Offshore procurement centered on health, immunization, and nutrition. Inventory management covered $1.3 million in assets, and UNICEF secured a cost-effective 300 sqm warehouse from the Ministry of Health for two years. The office finalized 22 new long-term agreements across 10 key categories, improved emergency preparedness, and supported localization efforts by expanding the supplier database to over 300 vendors (60% new), fostering competition and resilience. UNICEF’s extended its positive influence through leadership in the UN Procurement and Logistics Working Group and organizing a local vendor conference. 
The ICT team assured business continuity arrangements and advanced modernization. Updates and tests to the Office Business Continuity and ICT Disaster Recovery Plans ensured preparedness; office-wide security and asset standards were upheld. Digital solutions built on Power Apps and SharePoint replaced ad-hoc email workflows with auditable, role-based processes (e.g., event management, leave tracking), enhancing efficiency and transparency. UNICEF ICT/T4D team supported national platforms like Digital Health & Nutrition, EMIS, Learning Passport, Ambulance Emergency System, and an AI-powered early warning system (Mozn), and launched IoGT (Sehati) with NCDC—transferring capacity to national administrators and enabling local hosting. These innovations strengthened data-driven decisions, service quality, and readiness across sectors. 
The cross-cutting programs have been properly integrated throughout the entire program. UNICEF Libya’s 2025 accomplishments were powered by effective advocacy, strategic communication, inclusive partnerships, gender integration, and strong data systems. Communications amplified budget briefs and milestone events, including the launch of Libya’s first Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7), the Baladiyati Program Final Event, and the Mozn early warning system. Over 750 media articles increased visibility, especially during the Sudanese crisis response and World Children’s Day, which featured joint EU/UK Ambassador field visits and child-led advocacy events. 
SBC intervention has been a constant presence across all sectors, working to enhance the impact of interventions and generating public involvement in driving change to achieve national goals. 
Partnerships with government, UN agencies, NGOs, and local organizations ensured programs were sustainable and fostered shared ownership. Gender equality considerations were woven throughout, notably in the Wife and Children Grant and positive parenting programs, reducing vulnerability and promoting equitable results. Data management tools—like interactive dashboards and the Programme Results Portal—enabled real-time monitoring and evidence-based decisions, while training built government and partner capacity for sustainable evaluation and oversight. 
Digital transformation boosted engagement, transparency, and efficiency. Social media reach and interaction surged, strengthening UNICEF’s advocacy and public profile. Sustainability was reinforced by embedding skills in national institutions, transitioning program ownership, and establishing protocols for maintaining infrastructure and services long-term. 
In summary, UNICEF Libya in 2025 exemplified a strategic mix of policy reform, system strengthening, evidence generation, and inclusive programming across sectors. By addressing structural barriers, promoting equity, and advancing digital and operational effectiveness, UNICEF moved Libya closer to universal access to health, education, protection, and social services. The groundwork laid in 2025 positions UNICEF and its partners for sustainable, measurable progress for children and families in the coming years. Continued dedication, collaboration, and innovation will be essential to realizing the vision of leaving no child behind as Libya progresses toward recovery and development.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
