In 2025, UNICEF Libya achieved important social policy gains, yet persistent challenges limited full implementation of required changes. Chief among these was weak inter-ministerial coordination and limited government ownership, which slowed the translation of evidence into action. While entities like the National Economic and Social Development Board provided strong leadership in generating evidence, the responsibility for enacting reforms remained with individual ministries. This required deeper bilateral engagement and ongoing advocacy to ensure ministries remained accountable and committed to action. 
Uptake of actionable recommendations from budget briefs and shock-responsiveness assessments was slow, hindered by competing government priorities and limited technical capacity. Evidence-based recommendations alone proved insufficient without their integration into national agenda. Humanitarian programming faced additional hurdles, including liquidity problems and political sensitivities on emergency cash assistance to non-Libyan groups. UNICEF had to carefully navigate these interventions, ultimately assisting hundreds of families (inclusive of host communities) while underscoring the importance of flexible delivery models and clear communication strategies for humanitarian response at scale. 
On the operational side, the Libya Country Office was challenged with requirements for short-notice procurement linked to last-minute (and short-expiry) grants, placing strain on supply teams and resource allocation. Evolving clearance processes across various government bodies led to frequent delays, inconsistent procedures, and increased costs for supplies held at port. These bottlenecks highlighted the necessity of proactive coordination and adaptable planning to ensure program continuity and cost efficiency. 
Financial sustainability concerns persisted, influenced by geopolitical instability, a reduction in international assistance, and high accommodation costs for staff (due to security requirements and restrictions). This emphasized the need for rigorous cost containment and the expansion of long-term agreements to safeguard UNICEF’s operational footprint. 
Regulatory and financial challenges persisted, such as the Central Bank’s refusal to recognize diplomatic status of the UN agencies and liquidity shortages that delayed remittances. The office adapted by prioritizing e-supply planning, centralizing liaison functions, initiating exemption procedures early, and strengthening engagement with the Food and Drug Authority to minimize clearance delays. 
Efforts in digital transformation and Technology for Development (T4D) were challenged by uneven digital literacy, weak institutional hosting, and the lack of a formal T4D governance framework. These factors resulted in system disruptions and limited oversight.  
Cross-sectoral integration among health, nutrition, and WASH remained difficult, with revitalized coordination platforms needed to address urgent needs. Data management and partner reporting improved, enabling real-time monitoring and evidence-based action, but persistent funding constraints, fragmented budgets, supply chain disruptions, and weak health information systems continued to restrict program expansion and emergency preparedness. In education, political fragmentation, infrastructure gaps, and limited ministry capacity slowed interventions. Child protection efforts were hampered by security agency crackdowns and INGO closures, exposing further gaps in ministry capacity and funding. Overlapping emergencies including local challenges, strained planning and public services, highlighting the need for improved governance, digital literacy, and operational sustainability. 
Reflecting on 2025, several key lessons emerged to inform future strategies. Standardizing cash transfer modalities and streamlining partner engagement enhanced efficiency and delivery speed, emphasizing the value of unified operational strategies. Expanded digital outreach through strengthened social media presence and partnerships increased advocacy and public engagement. Comprehensive capacity building—including staff training in analytics and results-based management—boosted institutional monitoring and decision-making. Enhanced partner reporting and data management facilitated quick identification of operational bottlenecks and reinforced accountability. Sustained advocacy helped resolve supply chain issues, with early agreements on supply types, improved shipment tracking, and streamlined customs clearance. Government exemptions for lifesaving commodities and joint annual supply planning with government partners improved alignment and reduced delays. Integrated approaches—such as linking immunization with birth registration—maximized impact and collective accountability. 
The Learning Passport rollout demonstrated the potential of digital solutions to address learning gaps. Despite progress, restrictive security measures limited NGO delivery capacity even as needs grew. Caregiver stress, fueled by ongoing crises and economic instability, remained a key driver of violence against children, reinforcing the need to connect behavior change efforts with social protection.  
Looking ahead, UNICEF and its partners see key opportunities to strengthen their work in Libya. The Libya Country Office (LCO) will focus on intensifying capacity building for government and partners to sustain evidence-based programming and policy development. Expanding integrated data management systems and interactive dashboards will support real-time monitoring and adaptive programming. Continued collaboration with regional offices and government entities will strengthen evaluation functions for sustained, measurable impact. Building on digital transformation momentum, the office will pursue innovative solutions to address emerging challenges, operational harmonization, and resource allocation, while regularly reflecting on its theory of change to ensure systemic progress and credibility. 
Youth empowerment will remain central, with the Youth Advisory Group and Accelerated Learning Programme leveraging digital platforms like Akelius and the Learning Passport to close learning gaps for out-of-school children. Policy efforts will focus on developing a national learning assessment framework, strengthening data systems, and collaborating with the Ministry of Education to improve planning and sustainability. 
For 2026, priorities include scaling up mobile-based parenting and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) modules in remote areas, ensuring financial sustainability of transitioned centers, and supporting the implementation of Children Affected by Armed Conflict (CAAC) Guidelines. The office will promote national ownership, technical quality assurance, and digital access for parenting modules, linking positive parenting more closely with social policy and child grants. With an operational focus on Libya’s East and South, mobile outreach for child protection services will be enhanced together with mentoring for centers transitioned into the government/public entities management. 
UNICEF will also reinforce climate resilience by consolidating solar system operations, securing supply pipelines, and guiding site selection with climate risk analysis. Priority will be given to bilateral advocacy, accelerating completion of guidelines, and operationalizing shock-responsive recommendations. Partnerships and additional resources will be sought for technical assistance and flexible funding. Strengthened supply protocols, ICT/T4D integration, and expanded long-term agreements will enhance continuity, transparency, and cost-effectiveness, ensuring that programmatic space and value for money are protected in an evolving context.

The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region comprises 20 countries and is served by 16 UNICEF country offices (COs), with approximately 560 million residents, including 200 million children. Although the region has achieved progress across many social indicators in recent decades, inequalities persist both between and within countries. Conflict and displacement remain key drivers of child rights deprivations. MENA countries also share development challenges, including high youth unemployment, limited investment in early years, resilient national systems and stronger child rights governance. These challenges inevitably impacted the region’s progress toward child-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) – overall, just half of child-related indicators have sufficient trend data to assess progress, among these, 30 per cent of targets have been met, and half require high, very high or historic rates of progress in the last 5 years of the SDG period.
In 2025, MENA faced the world’s largest child displacement crisis (the Sudan), the deadliest conflict for children (Gaza, State of Palestine) and the Syrian Arab Republic’s transition after 14 years of civil war. Over half of the region’s children live in countries experiencing conflict or political instability, where rights violations are most acute and systems most fragile. Heightened volatility, protracted conflicts and increased polarisation have further fragmented governance structures and complicated national reforms, resulting in 95 million people, including 45 million children, facing life-threatening risks and vulnerabilities.
Since 2000, MENA has made substantial gains in child survival, access to basic services and school enrolment. However, these gains have proven fragile, with conflict, displacement, economic shocks and climate stress triggering widespread stagnation and, sometimes, reversal. Climate-related crises are intensifying humanitarian challenges, with children particularly vulnerable to health risks stemming from extreme heat and changing disease patterns.
Alarming signals include sharp increases in the number of ‘zero dose’ children from 872,000 in 2019 to 1.8 million in 2024 and rising child mortality rates in conflict-affected countries, in some cases reverting to levels seen 20–30 years ago. Adolescents are increasingly affected by mental health disorders and noncommunicable diseases, reflecting changing risk profiles and prolonged exposure to violence and instability.
Nutrition outcomes reflect the triple burden of malnutrition: persistent undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and rising overweight and obesity. Stunting affects nearly one in five children under five, while childhood overweight has reached almost 10 per cent, driven by child food poverty, unhealthy food environments, weak regulation and economic pressures.
Chronic and worsening water scarcity means countries such as the Sudan and Yemen face immense challenges in sustaining access to safe water. Nearly a third of MENA’s schools lack water and soap. Water stress undermines health, education, gender equality and child protection, particularly for girls.
While many children attend school, learning outcomes remain poor: nearly two-thirds of 10-year-olds cannot read with proficiency. In the Sudan alone, around 19 million children (90 per cent) are currently out of formal education. 
In the region, these challenges contribute to the world’s highest youth unemployment and not-in-education-employment-or-training (NEET) rates, with nearly one in three young people being NEET and over 75 per cent of youth employment in the informal sector. Although young women now outperform men educationally, their NEET rates exceed 40 per cent due to structural and gender barriers. Extremely low youth civic engagement signals widespread disillusionment and weakened social cohesion.
Child poverty remains pervasive. In middle-income countries, one in four children is multidimensionally poor, experiencing overlapping deprivations in education, health, housing and services. MENA is the only region globally where extreme child monetary poverty has increased in the last decade. 
Further, in 2025, persistent inflation, debt distress and constrained fiscal space eroded household welfare and constrained government investment in social sectors. Meanwhile, food insecurity, labour market stagnation, high youth unemployment and increased displacement intensified the need for shock-responsive, adaptive and integrated social protection, economic inclusion and care. At the same time, governments scrutinized efficiency, targeting and financing models more closely.
Escalating armed conflict, displacement, shrinking civic space and deterrence-based governance continued to expose children to acute protection risks, including violence, exploitation, trafficking, arbitrary detention and systemic exclusion from services. In 2024 and 2025, over 12 million children across MENA have been displaced, maimed or killed in conflict.
In many settings, policy reform remained sensitive, particularly around forced displacement, subsidy reform and benefit universality. Centralised decision-making within ministries of finance and planning increased the importance of upstream engagement, alignment with macroeconomic priorities and evidence-based, incremental approaches.
Children’s rights in MENA are further increasingly shaped by interconnected megatrends: uneven demographic transitions, entrenched gender inequality, climate change and emerging digital technologies. Demographic transitions vary sharply: Gulf Cooperation Council countries face rapid population ageing, middle-income countries are navigating a narrowing demographic window amid high debt, and conflict-affected countries struggle to preserve human capital among very young populations. Gender inequality is reinforced by discriminatory legal frameworks and a growing gender backlash. Climate change is an escalating child-rights crisis, with MENA warming at twice the global average and 90 per cent of children living in areas of high or extremely water stress. Digital technologies, while offering opportunities, also deepen inequalities and expose children to risks related to protection, privacy, and algorithmic bias.
In 2025, funding from public donors declined by over 15 per cent year-on-year, affecting UNICEF’s ability to deliver for children. Donor conditionalities increased, complicating fundraising for specific countries and programmes. Geopolitical polarization further constrained humanitarian operations, restricting access in insecure contexts and stretching capacity across simultaneous large-scale emergencies.
Meanwhile, the global aid sector’s financing crisis led to reduced funding and staffing across UNICEF. MENA, heavily reliant on Other Resources to sustain large-scale humanitarian responses, was disproportionately affected. Rising demand and shrinking resources required difficult prioritization decisions and strengthened oversight to safeguard critical programmes for children.
In parallel, UNICEF advanced major institutional reforms under the Future Focus Initiative (FFI), reshaping structures, accountabilities and ways of working. For MENA, these changes coincided with preparatory work for consolidation with Europe and Central Asia, to be completed by the end of 2026. At the same time, the transition of the Djibouti and Sudan Country Offices from MENARO to ESARO required close coordination to ensure continuity of programmes, partnerships and oversight. Managing large-scale humanitarian responses, financial contraction, and complex organizational transition simultaneously demanded disciplined planning and effective change management. Despite these challenges, UNICEF MENA remained steadfast in delivering for children, prioritizing life-saving interventions, safeguarding essential services and advancing systems strengthening.

Health
In 2025, MENARO strengthened primary healthcare (PHC) systems across countries in the region and safeguarded maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health services, including immunisation. Results were achieved despite severe access constraints, including in Gaza (State of Palestine), the Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, and Yemen, where facilities were damaged, supply chains disrupted, and workforces were limited.
Progress in maternal and newborn health was driven by a pioneering multi-country assessment that guided corrective action on quality, financing and equity. Countries strengthened maternal and perinatal death surveillance and response through system improvements that enabled consistent identification of preventable causes and the generation of actionable recommendations. Libya and Tunisia advanced national follow-up to the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B, including capacity-building and strategy updates. 
Four countries adopted formal zero-dose strategies in 2025, marking the steady expansion of equity-focused immunisation approaches. Five countries reached 95 per cent or higher coverage in polio outbreak campaigns in 2025, with more than 17.4 million doses of nOPV2 administered to 10.45 million children across Algeria, Djibouti, Gaza Strip, Sudan and Yemen. Countries also expanded protection against priority diseases by introducing new vaccines – HPV in Tunisia and Djibouti, and PCV in Jordan, reflecting sustained regional advocacy, technical support and resource mobilization. Nine countries now benefit from strengthened vaccine management systems in 2025, exceeding last year’s six.
Despite operational constraints, routine immunization and catch-up activities achieved major gains. Across the region, 16.5 million children received measles-containing vaccines. The Sudan vaccinated more than 10 million children against measles–rubella and continued rolling out the malaria vaccine. Catch-up campaigns in Gaza restored measles vaccination for conflict-affected children.
Community-based PHC strategies expanded in Djibouti, the Sudan and Yemen, improving care in underserved settings, while early framework development in Libya and significant investments in Algeria and Egypt supported broader reforms. Two countries met strengthened PHC system benchmarks in 2025, and four integrated mental health and psychosocial services (MHPSS) within PHC.
Supply chain resilience improved through piloting the IMMUNIFY system in Iraq to strengthen vaccine visibility and cold-chain reliability. Iraq also established a National Centre of Excellence for Supply Chain, institutionalizing training and quality management. Standardized Arabic-language cold-chain and vaccine-management training expanded across countries. Solarization of 17 PHC centres in Gaza and 80 facilities in the Syrian Arab Republic further strengthened energy resilience and service continuity. 
Eight country offices supported timely outbreak responses in 2025. Through the multisectoral Regional Outbreaks Taskforce, MENARO coordinated surge support for responses to cholera, acute watery diarrhoea, dengue, hepatitis A/E, malaria and other outbreaks. Joint work with WASH improved the quality of infection prevention and control in healthcare facilities across several countries.
MENARO provided oversight and technical support for US$58.5 million in health investments – including US$32 million in Gavi support and US$21.7 million from the Mastercard Foundation for community health workforce development. Economic analyses and costing of immunization strategies supported domestic financing and fiscal sustainability in middle-income countries. 
Nutrition
The region faced acute nutrition challenges in 2025, particularly in Gaza (State of Palestine) and the Sudan, where severe food insecurity, disruption of basic services and displacement sharply increased risks of wasting and malnutrition among young children. MENARO sustained high-quality technical support across the region, enabling countries to expand multisectoral nutrition programming, strengthen early childhood development (ECD) and reinforce supply pipelines for lifesaving commodities.
Guided by the MENA Nutrition Strategic Direction 2030, regional and national actors accelerated efforts to prevent all forms of malnutrition. MENARO supported four countries to finalize multisectoral nutrition policies centred on breastfeeding and complementary feeding. Nine countries advanced the implementation of strategies to improve diets for children aged 6–23 months. Regional policy mapping of commercially produced complementary foods informed updated guidance and strengthened regulatory environments.
Breastfeeding protection advanced through the Baby-Friendly Hospitals Initiative (BFHI) assessment and development of a model Code for MENA. Complementary feeding guidance and local food-based recommendations improved national approaches in the Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic and Yemen. Integration of ECD into PHC expanded to 10 countries – supported by a new regional roadmap, emphasizing the first 1,000 days.
Wasting identification, treatment and prevention continued across crisis-affected settings. Five countries adopted wasting guidelines aligned with the 2023 WHO recommendations, and routine services for early detection and treatment continued in nine countries. Regional work on public financing contributed to stronger national investment cases for nutrition.
School-age and adolescent nutrition progressed through overweight-prevention interventions in eight countries and anaemia-prevention initiatives in nine countries. Regional evidence generation expanded through partnerships with AUB and Harvard, and MENARO supported national action on school nutrition environments and regulation of food marketing to children.
Humanitarian needs escalated sharply in Gaza, where MENARO provided support to sustain wasting prevention and treatment under siege conditions. In the Sudan, MENARO shaped the national famine-prevention plan and secured resources to protect therapeutic supply chains. In the Syrian Arab Republic and Yemen, regional missions supported joint planning, prioritization and strengthened multisectoral action. Nutrition information systems advanced through the launch of the Real-Time Nutrition Data and Digital Platforms Initiative in the State of Palestine, the Sudan and the Syrian Arab Republic.
By the end of 2025, more than 900,000 children had received wasting treatment, and more than 13 million women and children had accessed preventive nutrition services across the region, a significant achievement amid persistent operational challenges.
 
Learning and Skilling
In 2025, programmes across MENA enabled nearly 8 million out-of-school children and adolescents to access formal and non-formal learning opportunities. Despite these gains, many crisis-affected and marginalized children remain out of school, underscoring persistent inequities and the need for continued system strengthening.
Countries advanced foundational learning by expanding pre-primary access and early-grade literacy and numeracy interventions to address learning loss and improve retention. Skills development was systematically embedded across education and training systems, with notable progress in Lebanon, Iraq, Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia. UNICEF’s Life Skills and Citizenship Education measurement tools helped countries assess adolescents’ acquisition of 12 core life skills and inform curriculum and policy reforms.
UNICEF reinforced learning continuity for crisis-affected children, ensuring safer and more predictable access to education. With MENARO’s support, governments in the State of Palestine, the Sudan, Yemen, the Syrian Arab Republic, Iran and Lebanon strengthened contingency planning, aligned emergency responses with standards and expanded community-based, flexible and digital learning models. Across the region, 4,862,557 children received individual learning materials and benefited from scaled-up flexible modalities that preserved access during conflict-related disruptions.
Amid political change in the Syrian Arab Republic, MENARO coordinated regional efforts to safeguard learning for displaced and returning children across the country and neighbouring host nations. High-level policy dialogue produced a subregional returnee education framework and six national return strategies, enabling ministries to plan for uninterrupted learning for all. In the Syrian Arab Republic, the transition of the Education Dialogue Forum into a ministry-led Local Education Group and the strengthening of working groups reinforced government leadership and joint planning. These efforts enhanced Education in Emergencies capacities, providing more predictable and equitable pathways for Syrian refugees, returnees, and host-community learners.
Digital transformation accelerated, with half of MENA countries advancing system-wide reforms under UNICEF’s Global Digital Education Strategy 2025–2029. Four became priority strategy countries, while others joined the UNICEF–UNESCO Gateway and Learning Pioneers initiatives. Regional guidance expanded accessible Arabic content for children with disabilities, and 168,877 learners accessed digital platforms, enhancing learning continuity.
UNICEF also supported one million adolescents and young people to participate in or lead civic engagement initiatives in the region. MENARO strengthened pathways from learning to earning by scaling the Learning Passport, the Nammiskills platform and gender-transformative skills initiatives. Partnerships with Generation Unlimited, EAA and the Al Ghurair Foundation mobilized resources to extend youth skills development and livelihood opportunities in Egypt, Lebanon and Jordan.
Child Protection
MENARO advanced a coherent regional child protection agenda, translating political commitments, humanitarian imperatives and emerging evidence into stronger protection outcomes for children. This progress occurred amid escalating armed conflict, mass displacement and shrinking civic space, which all exposed children to heightened risks of violence, exploitation and exclusion.
MENARO consolidated its leadership by ending violence against children. High-level engagement across 16 countries supported movement from commitment to implementation, guided by shared regional priorities aligned with global standards. The Afaq Community of Practice expanded to more than 300 participants from civil society, academia, government and grassroots organizations – strengthening cross-country learning on violence prevention and non-violent discipline.
Work on harmful practices advanced through the UNICEF–UNFPA Joint Programme. Regional action on child marriage included new research on trends in humanitarian contexts, while female genital mutilation programming expanded through social and behaviour-change approaches, human-centred design and survivor-centred tools. The regional Love Doesn’t Cut campaign reframed female genital mutilation as violence against girls – shifting discourse across the region.
System strengthening remained essential for sustained protection outcomes. MENARO supported six countries to professionalize the social service workforce, reinforced service continuity in conflict settings and strengthened public finance capacity for child protection. 
Justice for children and children on the move remained priority areas, with MENARO consolidating its regional leadership in diversion, alternatives to detention, legal aid, and child-friendly procedures. Route-based approaches strengthened continuity of care and reduced harmful practices such as child detention, while country-level innovations informed regional practice. In Tunisia, UNICEF documented an interagency model for supporting migrant children that is now used across the region. In the Islamic Republic of Iran, UNICEF supported the government during the large-scale deportation and forced return of Afghan children, contributing to government-approved SOPs for unaccompanied and separated children and reinforcing coordination with ICRC and partners.   
Humanitarian child protection responses addressed risks of gender-based violence, need for MHPSS, explosive ordnance risk education and cross-border coordination in Level 3 and Level 2 emergencies. MENARO supported safe, voluntary repatriation of foreign children from the northeast of the Syrian Arab Republic and strengthened coordination with UNHCR for identification and follow-up of unaccompanied and separated children.
Regional leadership on survivor-centred protection, safeguarding and MHPSS expanded. Caring for Child Survivors guidelines were rolled out in Jordan and the Sudan, improving care for survivors of sexual abuse. Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) systems strengthened through risk assessments, localization initiatives and regional coordination. Six country offices received RO support to expand community-based MHPSS services in 2025. The Tammeni Annak frontline worker wellbeing programme expanded with sector-specific adaptations, an emerging network of master trainers, and enhanced content on grief and coping for protracted conflict environments, reaching more than 4,000 frontline workers. Evidence on the impact of armed conflict on children, including casualties, recruitment and detention – informed programme design.
WASH
MENARO supported WASH responses to an increasingly complex mix of crises driven by conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and climate change. Technical assistance, remote guidance and surge deployments strengthened cholera and acute watery diarrhoea responses in Lebanon, the Sudan and the Syrian Arab Republic, enhancing national readiness and operational capacity.
Emergency Preparedness and Response Plans were updated across the region, and humanitarian WASH, preparedness and ‘WASH for Peace’ training reached over 10 countries. Eleven staff from 10 countries completed regional WASH for Peace training, reinforcing the integration of peacebuilding within humanitarian and development programming. Country offices also received systematic support to strengthen HACs, situation reporting and emergency preparedness.
Systems strengthening advanced through climate-informed WASHBAT assessments, sanitation and water safety planning, and climate-related financing pathways. Through its partnership with IVL, MENARO provided upstream technical support to six countries, while regional climate rationale training improved country capacity to incorporate climate risk into programme design.
Collaboration with WHO EMRO and the IFRC strengthened WASH in health care facilities. In 2025, 13 countries applied WASHFIT standards in health facilities, continuing the upward trend from previous years and signalling strong regional uptake. MENARO also delivered a regional Training of Trainers in Jordan and supported national rollouts in six countries to improve the quality of care and infection prevention.
Solarization of schools and health facilities continued to reduce operational costs and improve resilience. Guidance on water scarcity and Green Institutes strengthened evidence for child-sensitive climate action. MENARO also advanced the regional Water Scarcity Initiative with FAO and partners, with dedicated funding to improve water scarcity response and coordination across Egypt, Jordan, Tunisia, and Yemen.
Social Protection
MENARO advanced regional leadership on child-focused social protection – helping countries navigate fiscal pressures, political volatility and rising child poverty. Regional evidence expanded through updates to the Public Finance Dashboard and Social Expenditure Monitor, adding a child-focused lens to analysis of social spending.
MENARO also helped to make social protection for children more equitable. Disability-inclusive allocations rose to 6.39 per cent of regional expenditure in 2025, exceeding the year’s target of 5.98 per cent.
Strategic partnerships strengthened MENARO’s influence. Co-chairing the Issue-Based Coalition on Social Protection and Jobs with the International Labour Organization helped shape a unified regional narrative linking child wellbeing with inclusive economic growth. Through PROSPECTS MENARO reinforced analysis of displacement, employment and social protection interactions.
In the Syrian Arab Republic, UNICEF shaped a new national cash programme grounded in child-sensitive design. In the State of Palestine, MENARO supported the integration of social protection and child vulnerability into early recovery planning. Yemen advanced shock-responsive delivery in extreme fragility. Egypt, Jordan and Oman strengthened national strategies, M&E systems and Cash Plus approaches, demonstrating the region’s upstream engagement.
Humanitarian social protection remained central as conflict and economic instability deepened. MENARO supported crisis-affected countries through technical assistance, surge deployments and system guidance, helping governments maintain continuity of social protection programmes.
Cross-Cutting and Enabling Functions
In 2025, aligned with the Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action, MENARO sustained strong preparedness and humanitarian performance despite the humanitarian reset, funding constraints, and regional restructuring. MENARO provided technical support to COs on preparedness, response, Accountability to Affected People (AAP), localization and coordination, strengthening capacity in 14 emergency-affected countries, including three L3 countries and two L1s. Eighty-three per cent of COs met HAC Quality Standards, exceeding the 80 per cent target. Emergency preparedness benchmarks were exceeded, with 96 per cent of COs meeting standards. Five country offices met epidemic preparedness support standards, 14 countries met AAP benchmarks, with 12 developing dedicated strategies. Seven COs advanced Humanitarian Access Frameworks, and 66 per cent of sudden-onset crises were followed by learning exercises.
MENARO expanded its advocacy influence in 2025, producing 74 press releases and statements, contributing to 187,790 media articles, securing a 27 per cent share of voice. Coverage in leading regional and global media reinforced UNICEF’s authority on child rights and humanitarian action. Spokespeople conducted over 1,700 interviews in 2025 (4,700+ over three years). Digital platforms generated 8.7 million impressions, nearly 100,000 engagements, and 342,000 website views, consolidating UNICEF as the key regional reference on children's rights.
Strategic campaigns – on malnutrition, health, education, the Sudan Sexual Violence Campaign, the Sudan Two-Year Mark, and global advocacy moments – combined multimedia content, reports, and high-level advocacy, elevating issues such as conflict-related sexual violence to global policy fora, including the United Nations Security Council and the Human Rights Council.
MENARO institutionalized advocacy impact by operationalizing the Regional Advocacy Strategy through a monitoring framework and action plan. Targeted support to COs, including CPD reviews, advocacy briefs, key messaging, and deployment to four emergencies ensured coherent, crisis-focused advocacy, strengthening UNICEF’s leadership, influence and action for children across MENA.
In 2025, MENARO advanced people-centred, evidence-informed programming across the region by embedding Social and Behavioural Change (SBC) in humanitarian and development frameworks. Social listening strengthened vaccination and outbreak responses, while enhanced RCCE coordination and applied behavioural science improved preparedness and trust-building. Regional capacity-building, academic partnerships, and HCD approaches reinforced SBC integration within CPD, MTR, and PBR processes. Fully CO-funded technical support reflected sustained demand for regional SBC expertise.
Climate action leadership expanded through completion of Climate Landscape Analyses for Children, climate-informed WASH and health programming, solarization of facilities and gender- and child-responsive NDC integration. Youth engagement increased through Local and Regional Conferences of Youth and preparations for COP processes, ensuring children’s perspectives informed regional decision-making. MENARO also coordinated youth-led land-restoration projects in Algeria and Djibouti, engaging 200 young people in scalable models to address desertification.
Gender-responsive approaches strengthened across sectors, supported by regional analyses and core training and tools. Adolescent girls’ leadership was elevated through cross-country learning and the design of policy tools, including a gender-responsive NDC review tool – expanding girls’ voices in climate policy spaces.
People & Culture advanced workforce agility and well-being through support and resilience measures, with the regional Staff Support Programme strengthening staff resilience and preparedness in protracted emergencies and among change-affected staff. Security services ensured risk-informed decision-making and operational continuity, including supporting mission authorizations in very-high-risk environments.
Risk management improved through strengthened internal controls, early-warning analytics and PSEA systems. All COs completed risk registers and achieved 100 per cent compliance with Business Continuity Planning. Capacity-building expanded across 14 offices through ESS, HACT and risk-management refreshers, while partnership oversight improved with a 65 per cent reduction in unsupported financial findings.
Resource mobilization strategies safeguarded funding pipelines amid global aid contraction. Through donor engagement and evidence-driven advocacy, COs maintained and, in cases, increased funding from major contributors. Collaboration with international financial institutions expanded financing opportunities, while private-sector engagement generated US$4.3 million in resources. Structured information-sharing positioned offices to access IFI resources more effectively.
Evaluation oversight strengthened evidence use. UNICEF in the region completed 12 evaluations, submitted 6 for ethical review and monitored over 25 management responses, while launching more than 15 new evaluations for completion in 2026. A multi-country evaluation covering five contexts was initiated, and AI-based approaches expanded insight generation. Oversight of Costed Evaluation Plans continued, alongside monitoring of evaluation staffing, expenditure, quality and use.
Digital transformation advanced across sectors, supported by strengthened Digital Impact and ICT services that improved cybersecurity, digital performance and emergency telecommunications, including satellite connectivity for high-risk contexts. Regional assistance enhanced connectivity, planning and service resilience, while technical support enabled digital health platforms, supply-chain automation, digital education, cash-transfer systems and AI-enabled projects. AI-driven methods also improved evidence synthesis for evaluation and planning, laying the groundwork for scaled, ethical use in 2026.
Supplies and logistics advanced localization through national manufacturing and procurement forums, including hosting the Global Vaccine Procurement Forum in Egypt. System-strengthening included an assessment of the Supply Chain Maturity Model in Iraq, the development of a national roadmap, and the submission of a regional capacity-building proposal. Procurement Services enabled access to supplies, and digital tools – including the Procurement Case Management system and the electronic Vaccine Arrival Report – improved transparency, timeliness and reliability.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
The operating environment across MENA in 2025 remained among the world’s most complex, shaped by persistent conflict, constrained access, political instability and severe economic pressures. These conditions generated wide-ranging programmatic, operational and safeguarding challenges. Intensifying hostilities, including in Gaza (State of Palestine), the Sudan and the Syrian Arab Republic, restricted mobility, disrupted service delivery and heightened fiduciary and protection risks. COs faced parallel emergencies, chronic underfunding and structural limitations within national systems, straining teams to sustain essential services while adapting to rapidly changing conditions. Varied partner capacity – particularly in financial assurance, humanitarian access and safeguarding – reinforced the need for continued systems strengthening and risk-informed programming. 
Lessons learned
Rapid shifts in geopolitical, humanitarian and financing contexts reshaped UNICEF’s operating environment in 2025. Conflict escalation, access restrictions and economic stress created volatile working conditions, with multiple COs managing simultaneous crises while navigating fiscal pressure, weakened national systems and wide variation in partner capacity. These pressures highlighted the limits of fragmented approaches and the value of coordinated regional support. 
A central lesson was the importance of early, deliberate risk management. Offices that embedded risk analysis in programme design, supported by improved data visibility tools and cross-functional collaboration, were better able to sustain operations as conditions deteriorated. Proactive financial planning, including cost-optimization and affordability reviews, helped align staffing and resources with funding realities. Strong leadership also proved critical: progress on cross-cutting commitments such as disability inclusion, gender equality and child protection was deeper where senior managers championed these agendas.
MENARO continued to strengthen programme quality and evidence use, exemplified by tailored programmatic support to the Sudan. The RO increasingly delivered multi-country public goods, research, training packages, policy guidance and harmonized tools, reducing duplication and improving coherence across issues such as child protection in emergencies, migration, disability inclusion, PSEA and MHPSS. Humanitarian operations affirmed the value of scenario-based planning, costed contingency frameworks and early inter-agency coordination. Persistent challenges – including funding constraints, access limitations and the strain of multiple large-scale emergencies – underscored the importance of scalable surge support, preparedness and subregional approaches to risk management.
Targeted surge deployments and tailored security risk management helped sustain presence in highly insecure environments. Hybrid operational models, including remote mentoring and virtual capacity-building, were essential during movement restrictions. Remaining gaps include mandatory security training and safeguarding coherence during the transition to Centres of Excellence. Social Policy progress highlighted the role of credible evidence, long-standing partnerships and cross-sector narratives in advancing reforms under political and fiscal pressure. These insights will guide MENARO’s approach in 2026.
Future outlook
Looking ahead to 2026, the Middle East and North Africa region will continue to face profound uncertainty shaped by protracted and new conflicts, economic pressures and accelerating climate risks. At the same time, the RO is undergoing significant institutional transformation as part of the consolidation of the Middle East and North Africa, Europe and Central Asia regions. In this context, RO will focus on strengthening its strategic oversight and enabling role to support Country Offices in protecting critical results for children while adapting to evolving operational and financial realities.
A central priority will be preparing for the consolidation of the two regions by the end of 2026. This process will require the alignment of planning, oversight, and knowledge management systems, alongside effective governance arrangements, while safeguarding the continuity of regional public goods. Ensuring coherence across programmes and preserving institutional knowledge will be critical as MENARO prepares to assume oversight of a consolidated 39-country region by January 2027.
At the same time, the Future Focus Initiative (FFI) is reshaping ways of working across the organization, including through the establishment of Centres of Excellence. In this evolving context, MENARO will play an important role in ensuring clear roles and coordination between Regional Offices, Centres of Excellence and Country Offices, safeguarding programmatic coherence and risk-informed oversight across countries facing diverse development and humanitarian challenges.
MENARO will continue to generate and disseminate regional public goods with the Centres of Excellence - including analytical work, policy guidance, training packages and shared tools - to strengthen programme quality and coherence across countries facing similar challenges. Strengthened knowledge exchange, digital platforms and evidence systems will remain central to enabling more adaptive and risk-informed programming across the region.
The global financial landscape will also shape priorities in the coming years. Declining official development assistance, increasing donor conditionalities, and constrained fiscal space across many countries will require stronger prioritization and more strategic partnerships. MENARO will intensify engagement with international financial institutions, regional organizations, Gulf partners and the private sector to help mobilize financing for children and support governments in protecting investments in health, education, social protection and climate resilience.
MENARO will also contribute to strengthened United Nations system collaboration under the evolving United Nations development architecture, including the UN80 agenda. In a region characterized by complex humanitarian crises, large-scale displacement and cross-border challenges, MENARO will work closely with Resident Coordinators, United Nations Country Teams and regional partners to support more coherent and integrated approaches to advancing child rights, social protection, youth development and climate resilience.
At the same time, MENARO will continue supporting Country Offices operating in fragile and conflict-affected settings, where humanitarian needs remain among the highest globally. Strengthened preparedness, risk monitoring and scenario-based planning will remain essential as conflicts, economic shocks and climate-related pressures continue to affect children across the region. Regional coordination, surge support, and cross-border collaboration will help ensure timely and principled responses to large-scale emergencies while supporting the continuity of essential services and the protection of children.
Through strengthened regional oversight, strategic partnerships and the continued generation of regional public goods, MENARO will support governments and partners in protecting children’s rights and sustaining progress for children across an increasingly complex and uncertain regional landscape.

Morocco’s socio-economic outlook remained stable despite a global environment marked by geopolitical tensions, economic uncertainty, and unpredictable climate events.  Economic growth was projected to reach 5% in 2025, an increase from 3.8 % in 2024. [1] Inflation declined to 0.9% in 2024 and is expected to stabilize at around 0.8 % in 2025.[2] Despite growing public expenditure, the budget deficit of –3.9 % in 2024 is anticipated to remain at around -3.6% in 2025.[3]  This stability is facilitated by continued reforms to the taxation system (Law No. 14-25) and subsidy schemes to broaden the tax base and rationalize subsidies through the Unified Social Registry. The Government budget for 2026 included increased allocations in education (an additional 1.5 billion USD) and health (an additional 1.1 billion USD) as investments in human capital development.[4] These were announced soon after a cohort of Generation Z engaged in public protests for more equitable social services.

Morocco continues to scale its social protection through the Direct Social Aid Programme. The recently established National Agency for Social Assistance (ANSS) ensured 3.9 million households with 12.4 million inhabitants (42% of all), including 5.5 million children, were reached with social protection (an increase from 4.8 million last year). Of the 5.5 million children covered, 1.1 million were aged 0-6 years.[5]  As evidenced by the 2026 budget and latest royal orientations, greater impetus was given to Morocco’s advanced regionalization agenda to reduce social and spatial inequalities.  The government called for a new generation of Integrated Territorial Development Programmes informed by local consultations nationwide. With a budget of 2.18 billion USD in 2026, these programmes prioritize rural and mountainous areas, focus on job creation, improved infrastructure, social services, and the sustainable use of natural resources. In addition, the Ministry of Interior authorized the collection of local taxes to a new cadre of municipal tax collectors in line with the tax reform – a measure aimed to increase local accountability and governance. 

Morocco’s parliament is examining Bill 29.24, which aims to establish the National Child Protection Agency (ANPE). As a new public actor, the ANPE will coordinate efforts for children in contact with the law and those residing in social welfare institutions.  Reforms to the Penal Code and Code of Criminal Procedure came into force in August and December 2025 respectively and strengthen justice for children by promoting alternatives to detention and prohibiting the imprisonment of children under 14.  In addition, these legal updates mandate judicial oversight for juvenile custody, require medical exams during police detention when justified, and institutionalize social and psychological support throughout the criminal process. The revision of the Family Code remains ongoing with potentially significant implications for gender, child protection and inheritance. Despite progress, challenges persist for children including the prevalence of child labor (in 2025 some 101,000 children were affected, a decrease from 110,000 children in 2023), increasing legal cases involving children (in 2025 some 33,093 children, an increase from 32, 940 in 2023) and gaps in access to accredited social workers.[6]  Morocco continues to serves as a country of transit, departure, and increasingly as a destination for mixed migration with a growing number of children, including unaccompanied and separated minors facing unique vulnerabilities. The 2024 census estimates 23,000 migrant children in Morocco.

Morocco’s health sector implemented the Territorial Health Groups (created under Law No. 08.22) which decentralize health care service delivery and governance from central level.  Following a pilot in the Tangier–Tetouan–Al Hoceima region, the Government will move to implement these more broadly. Further reforms center on securing additional human resources and the establishment of regulatory bodies to standardize service provision and health products.
In the education sector, reforms through the national education roadmap (2022-2026) are ongoing. Despite these efforts, an estimated 280,000 children dropped out of the education system last year (as compared with 294,458 last year).[7] The increased budget for education in 2026, seeks to scale the “Pioneer Schools” initiative as a means for improving teaching quality, school leadership, and student performance. These schools are continuously being evaluated by the ministry, the national authority for evaluation of education, and others.  Currently 2,214 primary schools and 201 middle schools are participating. Learning outcomes and school retention remain major policy challenges requiring integrated responses across education, skills development, and social protection.

Unemployment among young people was estimated at 37.7 %.[8] Importantly, female labor participation remains constrained. A recent study by the World Bank notes that the female labor participation rate further declined from 29% in 2000 to 20% in 2022.[9] A similar downward trend affects the rate for women with tertiary education (70% in 2000s to 60% in 2018). The study notes that barriers include perceptions of gender norms, availability of work, childcare and the level of wages.  In 2025, the Government launched the national employment roadmap, which seeks to address this issue. The roadmap identifies childcare services as a necessary lever for change and Government has committed to increasing public daycare institutions by 100 per year through to 2030.

Morocco experienced more extreme climate events – with heavy rainfall and significant snow accumulation across parts of the country. A flood in Safi city resulted in at least 37 deaths.   Optimizing water resources through cycles of droughts and floods is of growing importance for Morocco given its impact on livelihoods and a heavily agricultural economy. While unusual rains have increased dam reservoirs to 43.9% of total capacity (up from 26% the previous years), the general trend of the country’s climate is one of warming and increasing temperatures. Through its National Programme for Drinking Water Supply and Irrigation Programme (2020–2027), Morocco is seeking to modernize water planning, governance, and to develop innovative climate adaptation solutions.  The country aims to source over half of its drinking water through desalination by 2030 with plants being run by renewable energy.

With Morocco a lower middle-income country, results in programming for children are cumulative and are derived from a steady accompaniment of national partners working to achieve sectoral reforms.  In 2025, unexpected funding cuts of about 5 million USD as well as an unprecedented organizational review meant the CO focused on rationalizing resources for the most vulnerable children and families. Strategic and catalytic programme activity during this period was heavily dependent on core and flexible resources.  Finally, partners such as the Korea International Cooperation Agency, European Commission, the US Government, the Arab Gulf Programme for Development, and the Catalan Agency for Development Cooperation, Monaco, and others made it possible for UNICEF to drive meaningful results for children.

Every child survives and thrives.  UNICEF supported partners as they reinforced local capacities to deliver health services, strengthen the primary health care system, and promote positive practices in health and nutrition.

The national health reform emphasizes increased autonomy and accountability in delivering quality services at decentralized levels. In line with this, UNICEF supported a review of the implementation of child health plans in two regions: Marrakesh-Safi and Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima. This process strengthened coordination across central, regional, and provincial levels, including with other relevant sectors such as education, and introduced joint analysis and decision-making on child health priorities. In both regions, UNICEF supported annual child health reports that consolidated data and implementation findings for service quality and continuity. As a result, in 2026 the regions will focus on quarterly audits of deliveries and preventable deaths, sensitization programmes to encourage pregnant women to attend antenatal care, and mechanisms to track care for women, and to train staff on common complications during delivery and beyond.

In parallel, UNICEF supported the translation of national child health policies into operational capacities for delivering primary health care. This included the development of standardized training packages based on national guidelines for managing respiratory illnesses, infection prevention and control (IPC) and patient safety training modules.  In addition, UNICEF worked with partners to digitalize the modules in collaboration with Mohammed V University.  In nutrition, there was improved implementation in Beni Mellal–Khénifra and Marrakech–Safi of the iodine deficiency disorder (IDD) prevention programme aided by workshops on iodized salt quality control and cross-regional knowledge exchange. At the national level, UNICEF contributed to technical consultations on regulations mandating iodized salt use in food products, supporting policy institutionalization and national ownership. UNICEF also addressed quality-of-care bottlenecks supporting partners to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in health care facilities. This included the development of a national WASH in health care facilities roadmap and preparation for rolling out the globally recognized Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool approach. In 2025, UNICEF provided procurement services for over 19 million doses of vaccines and nutrients for children in Morocco with a value of nearly $11.5 million USD. Meanwhile collaboration between the Ministry of Health, Institute Pasteur of Morocco, and Africa CDC is ongoing to implement a 4.6 million USD investment to improve the national cold chain and laboratory capacity for the national immunization programme.

Partners collectively strengthened efforts to ensure children, adolescents, and parents –particularly in rural areas – have the knowledge and skills to adopt positive practices in health, hygiene, nutrition, and parenting. UNICEF supported the national measles vaccine catch-up campaign through community dialogue with 180 caregivers to help increase demand and responsiveness. Sessions brought together vaccinated and unvaccinated caregivers, using peer reassurance and positive social norms to address hesitancy. At the system level, UNICEF and WHO co-developed an interpersonal communication training package in French and Arabic. Implemented as a Training of Trainers nationwide; subsequent cascade training reached 130 health professionals and community relays. In partnership with the ministry of health, information was widely disseminated during the Africa Cup (December 2025–January 2026), promoting preventive and health-seeking behaviors during a period of high population mobility. Finally, UNICEF partnered with the Initiative Nationale du Développement Humain (INDH) to implement a nationwide early breastfeeding campaign using behavioral insights and A/B testing. Campaign videos reached over 2.1 million people with a 7.65% click-through rate following these insights. Four U-Report quizzes further engaged 6,000 adolescents (53% girls) on key health topics, reinforcing knowledge and positive practices.

Every child learns. The education programme collaborated with the ministry of education, foundations, academia and others to accelerate outcomes in early childhood education, school retention, and the school environment.

In early childhood education, UNICEF accompanied the Ministry of Youth, Culture, and Communication (MJCC), mandated to oversee daycare provision to develop national standards, including provisions for children with disabilities, and a voluntary accreditation scheme for both public and private service providers to streamline services. The standards include reference guides and training materials developed in consultation with a committee that included representatives of the ministries of the interior, education, solidarity, health, finance and INDH, demonstrating the national importance accorded to the issue. In addition, UNICEF provided technical support for the review of the 2018 curriculum for preschool. The curriculum was updated to better reflect the latest in science and evidence in childhood development and is currently under final review by Ministry of National Education Preschool and Sports (MENPS). Finally, partnerships with MENPS, and Zakoura Foundation (tasked in delivering preschool services) led to the piloting and subsequent launching of the Parenting Education Programme for Learning; the programme offers structured guidance to parents on how to support learning at home. 

Retaining children in school remains a critical priority in the face of the 280,000 that dropped out of school in 2025 and who are the focus of the “pioneer schools” initiative by the Government to address the issue.[1] In partnership with the MENPS, a multi-sector model to address this issue, particularly for adolescent girls, was finalized. It combines individualized student support with an improved learning environment.  Tools developed through the model include: a school management guide for school principals, a pedagogical guide for teachers, activity guides on UPSHIFT, menstrual hygiene support, and youth-led advocacy. These components are mutually reinforced and scaled through the model. Over 5,523 young people (3,798 girls and young women) benefited directly from related workshops, school clubs, and innovation programmes, making the school environment relevant and interesting for learners.  An evaluation of the programme (as planned in the costed evaluation programme for the cycle) was disseminated with development partners, central and regional stakeholders. It notes interventions were cost effective and surpassed initial targets. In summary, it found the programme to offer good practice through peer-to-peer participation, engagement with local communities and coalition building of actors. And, it recommends these strategies be institutionalized nationally.

In 2025, more emphasis was given to the inclusion of migrant and refugee children and adolescents in the national education system. In close collaboration with MENPS, an organizational kit was developed to accompany migrant children; it includes language transition manuals in Arabic and French, guidance materials on school reception and intercultural support. These resources provide schools and the network of Second Chance Schools (SCS) with practical instruments to fulfill obligations towards vulnerable children. Some 30 trainers across three regions – Oriental, Tangier-Tétouan-Al Hoceima – and Souss-Massa, have been trained in the material and have developed implementation plans; they will continue to duplicate the trainings across additional provinces in the regions which are impacted by migration trends.

UNICEF worked with partners to improve the quality of learning environments through climate-resilient WASH services, national systems development, and meaningful youth engagement in climate education and action. UNICEF led the rehabilitation of WASH facilities in seven schools across earthquake affected areas in Marrakech and Sous-Massa. The rehabilitated facilities integrated climate-resilient designs, gender-responsive features, and inclusive access. As a result, 3,356 students (1,662 girls and 1,694 boys) now benefit from safe and functional water, sanitation, and hygiene services. Lessons learned will be used in Morocco’s first National WASH in Schools Minimum Standards, a process that the MENPS has launched, with UNICEF technical support. In terms of adolescent and youth participation, UNICEF developed child-friendly, competency-based climate education materials and an online platform for climate action clubs enabling schools to integrate participatory, age-appropriate climate learning. 
 
In addition, teachers and inspectors from regions affected by the 2023 earthquake developed an emergency preparedness toolkit developed by teachers and inspectors. It consolidates good practice and lessons learned for reference. The toolkit is now under review by national partners and includes, among others: a user guide and pedagogical toolkit; a teaching guide for emergency situations; a teacher training module on psychosocial support; activity sheets on emergency preparedness by grade level.
 
Every child is protected. In 2025, Morocco’s Integrated Territorial Child Protection System (DTIPE) advanced from a conceptual framework to an increasingly operational mechanism implemented across the country.[2] According to the Ministry of Ministry of Solidarity, Social Integration, and the Family (MSISF), there are now 50 operational DTIPE, up from 23 in 2025. This progress was enabled by the availability of key tools: a standard Risk Assessment Framework and Procedures Manual for Provincial Committees which were translated into Arabic. This facilitated a common approach amongst provinces: enabling comparable mappings, diagnostics, and results-based action planning. In addition, the recent adoption of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) translated legal frameworks into concrete, multidisciplinary care pathways as outlined in the 2024 high-level Territorial Protocol on Child Protection. These SOPs were validated with fifteen participating institutions, reinforcing a standard for clinical, social, and judicial interventions. These results were achieved in close coordination with the MSISF, the Entraide Nationale (the national mutual aid), Public Prosecutor’s Office, INDH and the ministry of health.

Integrated Child Protection Information Systems (SIIPE) are now operational in four regions – Beni-Mellal Khénifra, Tanger -Tétouan-Hoceima, Oriental, Souss-Massa – with 27 Child Support Centers (CAPE), contributing to the use of digital case management and reporting.  With UNICEF support, two regions – Oriental and Souss-Massa – adopted integrated local child protection systems under the leadership of the Governors (Walis), denoting a high level of commitment. In the earthquake affected areas of Al Haouz and Chichaoua provinces, child protection units that previously received capacity building support continue to operate on behalf of vulnerable children. Together with local authorities and a select number of NGOs, they have reinforced community relay systems, provided functional child friendly spaces, and ensured reporting mechanisms for case management. In addition, 3,653 children (2,097 girls) received psychosocial support.

2025 marked a paradigm shift in Morocco’s justice for children system, shifting from punitive responses toward a rehabilitative, protective, and restorative model. This shift was driven by three major reforms: the expansion of judicial social assistance under Law 38.15, the consolidation of partnerships across justice and social sectors, and the implementation of Law 43.22 on alternative sentencing. UNICEF’s technical support enabled greater integration of judicial processes with social protection. Over 240 prosecutors, judges, social workers, and police officers participated in high-level regional workshops that addressed systemic bottlenecks, resulting in diversionary measures for 81% of children in contact with the law. These changes reduce stigmatization, improve reintegration, and align children’s legal pathways with their developmental needs. At the same time, UNICEF and the National Human Rights Council partnered to facilitate the role of 372 children (186 girls) to directly monitor human rights by penning a parallel report to the Committee on the Rights of the Children.  

Through UNICEF facilitated services, 27,092 children had access to child protection support.  In addition, children on the move benefited from comprehensive child protection services. This included 609 children supported in Oujda and Tétouan (through NGOs APISF and Chabiba), given their proximity to borders, while 172 children received assistance by the national mutual aid, the Entraide Nationale. Services covered safe identification, psychosocial care, health and education referrals, and socio-economic integration. UNICEF to accompany a number of line ministries to include migration-sensitive measures in formal child protection systems in Tangier, Oujda, and Agadir.

Every child has access to inclusive social protection. In 2025, UNICEF Morocco played a catalytic role as the country strengthened national and territorial systems to better realize children’s rights through evidence-based policymaking, sustainable public financing, integrated social protection, and multisectoral local governance. 

In evidence generation, and under the leadership of the ministry of health, UNICEF contributed to the roll out of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7).  Data collection by the ministry began in October 2025, with UNICEF providing comprehensive technical support for survey design, sampling, tools, training, and quality assurance. The survey will inform approximately 40 per cent of SDG indicators and strengthen the government’s capacity to identify disparities affecting children by region, gender, wealth, and place of residence.

UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Economy and Finance as it sought to ensure the adequacy, efficiency, and sustainability of social budgets for children. A key milestone was the deepening of the Feasibility Study on Sustainable Financing Options for Social Protection, conducted in close collaboration with the tax administration. Through UNICEF technical assistance, the study identifies an annual financing requirement of approximately 4.4 billion USD starting in 2027 to fund the Direct Social Aid programme and health insurance scheme. It further offers four priority fiscal options to sustain these reforms which are currently under review.

Coverage of the family benefits and social protection reached 80 per cent, up from 58 per cent in 2021. The programme now delivers predictable monthly cash transfers to 5.6 million children from the most vulnerable households. To mitigate exclusion risks linked to digital registration, UNICEF used benchmarking exercises to advocate with the National Social Support Agency (ANSS), for a localized territorial governance model, repositioning it as a coordination hub for integrated programmes. This advocacy led to the deployment of specialized staff across provinces in July 2025 and its decision to launch proof-of-concept CASH+ programmes that will measure the impact of this social assistance in the uptake of social services.

At the territorial level, UNICEF is increasingly advancing a multisectoral and people-centred approach to programming. Despite the national priority accorded to decentralization, planning and budgeting remains fragmented and siloed, particularly in programmes related to child development. To address this, UNICEF collaborated with the office of the Governor and the Regional Council of Beni-Mellal region as they coordinated a multi-sector workplan governed by a high-level steering committee, that simultaneously tackles health, child protection and social inclusion. Key activities included trainings on results based management and an orientation with local authorities and officials to better understand why priorities for children were inadequately reflected in territorial investments. 

Operationally, UNICEF delivered strong operational performance in 2025, achieving 778,000 USD in savings which enabled programme support with delivery in line with UNICEF policies. Robust financial assurance measures strengthened partner capacity—particularly for high-risk and new partners—while ICT innovations included a comprehensive inventory management tool, enhanced accuracy, transparency, and efficiency in resource oversight.  Notably, UNICEF coordinated the urgent procurement of 5.5 million of the Measles–Rubella vaccine, during a measles outbreak.
