NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The Country Office, in collaboration with the Middle East and North Africa Regional Office, conducted a mid-term review of the country programme to assess progress and challenges facing children in Morocco—particularly the most vulnerable. The review also provided an opportunity to reflect on internal and external changes impacting UNICEF, to further align resources with the most impactful partnerships, strategies, and interventions as guided by UNICEF’s new Strategic Plan.

Lessons Learned and Programme Shifts
Across its sectoral programming, the Country Office (CO) identified the following key findings and shifts:

Health and Nutrition. The CO’s programme varies from system-strengthening interventions—such as support to the national immunization programme and the roll-out of WASH standards—to lower-level service delivery activities. Moving forward, UNICEF will reduce investments in lower-level service delivery and focus more on accompanying select regions to “test and scale” evidence-based interventions.  UNICEF will also work more intentionally with central-level health partners to ensure that regional lessons inform national strategies for strengthening primary health care systems. To support this intentional feedback loop, both central and regional partners participated in the annual review, where pathways for learning, knowledge management, and advocacy were discussed. This approach supports the Government’s health reform, particularly its goal of transferring autonomy for health service delivery and governance to regional territorial health groups.
Education. Given persistent challenges with school drop-out and weak learning outcomes, the CO will prioritize a “back-to-basics” approach focused on improving quality in daycares, preschool, and primary education. This includes partnering to respond to the findings of the Measuring Early Learning Quality and Outcomes (MELQO) assessment (soon to be disseminated by the Higher Council for Education, Training and Scientific Research and UNICEF), supporting the roll-out of standards and models for daycare provision, and strengthening early detection systems for children at risk of dropping out.  UNICEF and government analyses increasingly highlight the potential of information technology to identify at-risk children and provide adaptive learning solutions; these will be further explored in 2026.
Adolescents.  In preparation for the next country programme (to be finalized in 2027), the CO will continue sharpening its programme offer to areas where UNICEF has a comparative advantage. This includes careful consideration of interventions that can now be mainstreamed by the Government.  Already, the CO has worked with the Ministry of Youth to integrate UPSHIFT (social entrepreneurship) and the Game Changers Coalition (gaming and coding) into the national youth offer. The Ministry is now positioned to lead, scale, and adapt these programmes through schools and its national network of youth centres. 
Child Protection. Child protection systems continue to mature, with growing engagement across local, regional, and central stakeholders. However, responses remain fragmented and institutionalization too frequently used. Strengthening local child protection systems therefore remains a critical priority.  The CO is now focused on mainstreaming tools that enable local actors to rapidly implement standard and functional child protection systems. At the request of local authorities during the annual review, UNICEF will also facilitate exchange and learning across regions as they operationalize these systems.
Social Protection. Morocco continues to make significant progress in expanding universal social protection with a focus on the most vulnerable. Nevertheless, multidimensional child poverty—especially in rural areas—persists.  The CO successfully advocated with national partners to pilot CASH+ models, in 2026, to demonstrate the added value and challenges of combining cash transfers with complementary services. Alongside ongoing technical assistance on durable financing pathways, these efforts will contribute to a more responsive social protection system for the most vulnerable children.

Critical Strategies Moving Forward

Diversifying funding streams. The unpredictability of overseas development assistance trends in 2025 has prompted the CO to accelerate efforts to diversify its funding base—by leveraging domestic resources and strengthening engagement with public and private sector partners. The CO has reviewed its strategies to date x and has developed a practical roadmap to guide future action. Progress on this plan will be monitored through existing country management team mechanisms.
Advancing decentralized, integrated programming. The CO has made a substantial investment in a decentralized workplan in one of Morocco’s most resource-constrained regions. This integrated approach supports local authorities to identify and address priority issues affecting children, while optimizing public finances—an approach aligned with Government priorities to expand services in the hardest-to-reach communities.  The collective effort has succeeded in mobilizing additional resources for the region and has fostered greater information sharing both across sectors and between administrative levels (central and regional). UNICEF will document these efforts to identify the enabling factors and challenges of balancing upstream and downstream work. Given Morocco’s middle-income status, the findings will be critical in shaping the next country programme.
Responding to growing demand benchmarks and innovation. As Morocco modernizes public service delivery and administrative data management, there is a growing demand for UNICEF guidance on good practices, standards, and international benchmarks. This includes support on digital applications for routine vaccination, information management systems for child protection and social protection, and innovative models for delivering health care in remote areas.  The CO will leverage UNICEF’s global digital impact strategy to better streamline these efforts and ensure that this support is anchored in child rights and international standards.
Strategic Advocacy. Morocco is increasingly emerging as a prominent actor on the global stage—through its leadership on child rights in Africa, hosting of major international sporting events, growing participation in regional and global diplomacy, and the expansion of local industries. In 2025, the CO leveraged opportunities such as the National Congress on the Rights of the Child as well as designation as the Guest of Honor at the International Book Fair for Children and Youth in Casablanca to promote child rights together with national partners.  The CO will continue to work across the organization to sharpen its advocacy agenda so that UNICEF can meaningfully position children and their rights—within Morocco and beyond.

In 2025, the Sultanate of Oman sustained steady socio-economic progress under Oman Vision 2040 and the 10th Five-Year Development Plan, maintaining its trajectory toward economic diversification and inclusive development. Human capital, digitalization and sustainability remained central pillars of national growth, supported by strategic investments in education and health systems alongside reforms in social protection and disability inclusion. 
Current trends indicate that Oman is on track to achieve numerous 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) with an SDG index score of 82.2 per cent[1]. Continued monitoring of progress against the 2023 Concluding Observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child, particularly in social protection, health, education and water and sanitation, indicates that while significant progress has been achieved, accelerated efforts are needed in areas such as early childhood development (ECD), early learning, child protection, nutrition and youth skilling.
Oman’s economy continued to grow in 2024 while maintaining low inflation. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth strengthened to 1.7 per cent in 2024, driven by robust non-hydrocarbon activities, notably in manufacturing and services[2], with GDP per capita standing at USD 20.29[3]. Growth is projected to accelerate over the medium term, reaching 2.4 per cent in 2025 and 3.7 per cent in 2026[4].
Total population reached 5.3 million in 2024, of which 2.3 million were non-Omanis, with 61.2 per cent male and 38.8 per cent female. Among Omanis, there was nearly an equal ratio (101 males per 100 females), while among non-Omanis, the ratio was higher at 308 males per 100 females due to labor trends[5]. Approximately 17 per cent of the population is under the age of nine while 31 per cent falls within the 0–19 age group[6]. The fertility rate stood at 1.9, comprising 2.8 for Omanis and 0.5 for non-Omanis[7].
By the end of 2024, Oman’s workforce stood at approximately 2.7 million employees. Expatriates continued to account for more than two-thirds of the labor force and men represented 81 per cent of total employment. The unemployment rate was 3.3 percent, 1.7 per cent for men compared to 9.7 per cent for women. Unemployment was highest among individuals with higher diploma, reaching 8.3 per cent, with rates of 18 per cent for women and 2.3 per cent for men[8].
Progress under SDG 3 continued, with the infant mortality rate declining from 8.5 per 1,000 live births in 2023 to 8 in 2024, and the under-five mortality rate decreasing from 10.8 to 9.9 per 1,000 live births[9]. Additionally, the maternal mortality ratio fell from 19.9 to 15.8 per 100,000 live births during the same period[10]. Oman maintained universal birth registration and vaccination coverage; notably, in 2022, Oman achieved a major milestone by eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis, becoming the first country in the Eastern Mediterranean Region to receive certification for this achievement.
In education, universal primary school enrollment was sustained, reflecting continued access to basic education. According to recently published data on pre-school education[11], the gross enrollment ratio increased from 41.1 per cent in 2020 to 75.1 per cent in 2023, reflecting a significant expansion of access to early learning. The launch of the National School Performance Evaluation System marked a significant step toward enhancing education quality, supporting digital transformation and strengthening the competitiveness of national talent. These reforms contribute to the promotion of a knowledge-based society and underpin Oman’s transition toward a diversified and sustainable economy. Additionally, efforts focused on improving education quality, fostering research and innovation, and strengthening links between education and the labor market. Five Omani universities were included in the QS World University Rankings[12] for 2026, with Sultan Qaboos University (SQU) achieving its best ranking ever (334th globally)[13].
In 2024, Oman recorded 69,195 persons with disabilities, representing 2.3 per cent of the Omani total population and equivalent to 1.5 per cent of Omani children up to the age of 17[14]. To strengthen protection and promote inclusion, His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tariq issued a decree in November establishing a comprehensive legal framework for the rights of persons with disabilities.
In terms of child protection, the Government of Oman is actively working to strengthen its national child protection system, with a focus on case management. In the first half of 2025, Child Protection Committees, established to prevent and respond to child abuse, handled 1,792 cases, 960 involving boys and 832 involving girls. During the same period, the national child protection hotline (1100) received 1,005 calls, of which 550 concerned boys and 455 concerned girls. More than half of these reports were related to neglect, followed by cases of physical abuse, psychological abuse, and sexual abuse[15].
In conclusion, the Sultanate of Oman has made substantial progress in enhancing the well-being of children and women, creating an inclusive and supportive environment that enables every child to reach their full potential. This advancement reflects a forward-looking national vision that prioritizes children and adolescents by safeguarding their rights, ensuring their protection and expanding opportunities for development. Oman’s development path therefore underscores a strong commitment to investing in future generations as a foundation for a diversified, knowledge-based and sustainable economy.
