In 2025, UNICEF Oman concluded the CPD 2022–2025  alongside the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025 under government leadership and  broad stakeholder consultation, advancing child-centered results through a  participatory approach. Aligned with Oman Vision 2040, the Five-Year  Development Plan (2021–2025) and legal frameworks, the CPD achieved results  spanning social protection, child protection, climate change, disability  inclusion, health and nutrition, ECD and education. These accomplishments  were enabled by initiatives in the areas of social behaviour change (SBC) and  data, research, evaluation and knowledge management, which served as critical  enablers in contributing to national progress.
  
A major  area of work remained UNICEF Oman’s continued support to the Social  Protection Fund (SPF) in its further development of a comprehensive social  protection system across the life cycle. Through an SPF-chaired steering committee that  includes all key stakeholders, and in close collaboration with the ILO, the  office is documenting the development and implementation of the Social  Protection Law from a child and family lens, highlighting good practices and  a forward-looking agenda to further the impact on children and  the population. Capacity development was  furthered via TRANSFORM training (also in collaboration with the ILO) for SPF  staff and steering committee members with an emphasis on monitoring and  evaluation system enhancement. Work is advancing on a comprehensive  monitoring and evaluation system that consolidates cross-sectoral social  protection progress in one platform to assess impact and return on  investment, aligned with SDG 1.3 and GA5. 
  
In  addition, to ensure a comprehensive package for beneficiaries that combines  cash benefits with complementary services, work is underway to establish a  ‘Cash Plus’ model focusing on persons with disabilities and early childhood  interventions such as education, health and nutrition. This model will serve  as an entry point and is intended to be replicated for other benefits in the  future, contributing to SDG 10.2 and GA5. Lastly, to strengthen resilience  and ensure a proactive social protection system, work is underway to develop toolkit  and operational guidelines for shock responsiveness, addressing health,  climate, economic and social shocks crises, supporting SDG 13 and cross-cutting  resilience goals. 
  
 
  
Furthermore, UNICEF  continued to advocate for integrated, child-sensitive and family-friendly  social protection systems through regional learning platforms. As part of  this effort, UNICEF participated in the International Social Security  Association Technical Seminar on Innovative Social Security Reforms,  contributing to regional discussions on strengthening social protection  systems to better respond to the needs of children and families. UNICEF also  presented at the HIMAYA Forum, highlighting evidence-based approaches to  family-friendly policies and their role in promoting child wellbeing and  social inclusion. At the national level, UNICEF deepened policy engagement  with key decision-makers through direct engagement with the SPF Board of  Trustees, including the delivery of a technical session focused on embedding  child-sensitive and life-cycle approaches within social protection design and  implementation. 
  
Building on this progress, UNICEF Oman will  continue supporting the Government in operationalizing an integrated  monitoring and evaluation system for social protection across sectors,  enabling evidence-based decisions. The Cash Plus model will be piloted and  scaled, while shock-responsive social protection tools and guidelines will  strengthen preparedness, resilience and protection for vulnerable  populations.
  
A significant milestone was the finalization and  launch of the updated Child Protection manual as another step forward in  strengthening the child protection system for timely and effective real-time  interventions. At the  request of the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD), UNICEF Oman facilitated  two years of multi-stakeholder consultation and technical inputs to produce  an updated manualthat defines severity levels of abuse and violence and  provides clear case management and referral pathways and operational  guidance. Capacity was strengthened through training-of-trainers for  approximately 50 participants and an online session to guide adoption across  governorates. A technical mission initiated the discussion for the automation  of referral pathways between the Ministries of Social Development, Education  and Health, with further engagement of secondary stakeholders to sustain  system improvements. These actions contribute to SDG 16.2 and GA 3.
  
Looking ahead, UNICEF will build on these  achievements by supporting the full institutionalization of the Child  Protection Manual across all governorates, integrating digital case  management tools and piloting the automated referral system to ensure timely  and coordinated responses. Additional capacity-building initiatives will  target frontline workers and secondary stakeholders to strengthen  accountability and quality of services, ensuring a more resilient and  responsive national protection system.
  
In line with government priorities to mitigate  climate impacts on access to services, UNICEF Oman partnered with the  Environment Authority to finalize the ‘Climate Landscape Analysis for  Children’, providing a comprehensive overview of policy and regulatory  progress, identifying opportunities for improvement and recommending  actionable sectoral measures to protect children and adolescents to  strengthen resilience during climate crises. Development was overseen by an  administrative decree-based committee convened by the Environment Authority  with broad stakeholder engagement, comprising the voices of children and  youth, including those with disabilities, from urban and remote areas. A  cross-sectoral workshop is planned for the first quarter of 2026 to translate  recommendations into time-bound activities, supporting SDG 13 and GA 4. A  proposed regional knowledge, attitude, and practice study to complement this  analysis was discussed with the Environment Authority but deprioritized by  the government for the current period. 
  
In addition, under the leadership of UNICEF Middle East and North  Africa Regional Office (MENARO)  and in collaboration with MoE, UNICEF Oman facilitated Oman's participation  in a regional study on the impact of heat and air quality on learning and  wellbeing. The study aims to generate evidence, raise awareness and guide  interventions that enhance resilience and improve learning environments in  the face of climate challenges. The launch of the study is expected in the  first quarter of 2026.
  
 
  
Aligned with national priorities on disability  inclusion, efforts were leveraged to strengthen equitable policies and  practices. Following  His Majesty’s endorsement of the Law on Persons with Disabilities and the  establishment of a position at the level of Undersecretary at MoSD, UNICEF  Oman sustained support to advance the welfare and inclusion of children with  disabilities. UNICEF Global Lead Gopal Mitra visited Oman to provide  technical guidance on governance, cross-sectoral coordination, data and evidence,  inclusive education and early detection and intervention. He met with the  Minister of Social Development and other key stakeholders and delivered a  keynote address at the Oman Childhood Conference and Exhibition on  Rehabilitation and Empowerment organized by the Children First Association  (CFA).
  
UNICEF Oman also facilitated MoSD and SPF  participation in the Multi-Country Capacity Building Programme on early  identification and timely intervention for children with disabilities,  strengthening national capacity to design and implement inclusive,  multisectoral early childhood interventions’ systems integrated with SBC and  addressing disability stigma. A second wave is planned with expanded  participation from the Ministries of Education and Health to deepen sector  interventions, contributing to the achievement of relevant SDGs and support  progress across GAs, particularly in learning, inclusion, and equity.
  
Additionally, UNICEF Oman will continue its  collaboration with MoSD to support the development of a comprehensive  cross-sectoral strategy on disability inclusion. Expected results include the  institutionalization of early detection and intervention protocols across  health, education and social protection systems, integration of disability  indicators into national data platforms and strengthened capacity of  frontline workers to deliver inclusive services. This strategic vision is  anchored in UNICEF’s work on supporting the development of the Cash Plus  mentioned above. 
  
Anchored in Oman’s strong health system, UNICEF  contributed to documenting and promoting evidence on health and nutrition  interventions. In  coordination with MENARO, UNICEF Oman provided policy advice and targeted  technical assistance in advancing its national efforts to prevent all forms  of malnutrition, including childhood overweight and obesity. As part of this  support, UNICEF facilitated Oman’s participation in a GCC roundtable on the  prevention of childhood overweight and obesity using a food systems approach.  The meeting enabled cross-country exchange and peer learning and supported  Oman in identifying national priorities for enhanced cross-sectoral collaboration  across education, food, and health systems. These advocacy efforts  contributed to SDG 2.2 and aligned with GA 1 and will continue in the new  country programme.
  
In addition, under the leadership of the Ministry  of Health (MoH) and in collaboration with WHO, UNICEF Oman finalized  documentation of Oman’s success in eliminating mother-to-child transmission  of HIV and syphilis, detailing key achievements, impact metrics and  recommendations for replication. The documentation is being prepared for  publication and dissemination, accompanied by a documentary showcasing good  practices at GCC, regional and global levels, strengthening the evidence base  for SDG 3.3 and contributing to GA 1.
  
Through engagement with Oman’s social sector,  UNICEF supported inclusive approaches to strengthen rights-based ECD and early  learning policies and practices. A study was finalized to inform the establishment  of integrated ECD centers that consolidate essential services for children,  including those with disabilities, and counselling for parents and caregivers  in one location. The model targets children from three months of age (post-maternity  leave per the 2023 social protection law) and ensures comprehensive services  for children with disabilities up to age eight. The study was presented to  the Minister of Social Development, Minister of Education and the Undersecretary  of Health to receive political direction for implementation. Beyond technical  design, UNICEF supported intersectoral consultations to discuss institutional  arrangements, financing options, workforce requirements and referral pathways  to identify operational and financing models for scaling up. This model  contributes to SDGs 4.2 and 4.5 while advancing UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal  Areas (GA) 2 and 5. 
  
Recognizing SBC as a key enabler, UNICEF Oman  partnered with various ministries to build capacity for sustained community  engagement. SBC  initiatives through positive parenting programmes progressed throughout the  year and addressed critical ECD priorities such as inclusion, bullying  prevention, nutrition, the father’s role in parenting, child mental health  and the elimination of violence against children. These efforts directly  contribute to UNICEF’s Strategic Plan focus on nurturing care and protective  environments.
  
To strengthen capacity on a larger scale, two training-of-trainers  sessions were delivered for the Ministries of Education and Social  Development, targeting frontline workers, including health educators, social  workers and psychiatrists, who engage directly with families. This approach  recognizes their pivotal role in translating knowledge into everyday practice  with caregivers and children, thereby accelerating behavior change and  improving outcomes for child well-being. 
  
To further institutionalize these programmes and  support the roll-out of governorate-level trainings, UNICEF Oman, in  collaboration with UNICEF Egypt, organized a study tour for a delegation from  the Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs to learn from Al-Azhar  Al-Sharif’s experience in integrating positive parenting concepts into  religious discourse. The visit focused on Al-Azhar’s accredited training  model and the role of religious leaders in promoting positive child  upbringing, family cohesion and social norms that protect children. 
  
As sustainability remains at the core of this  journey, UNICEF Oman is working closely with ministries to institutionalize positive  parenting through annual or quarterly implementation plans aligned with  sectoral work plans. A notable achievement is the MoH’s integration of positive  parenting indicators into its national electronic health system (Al-Shifa),  enabling systematic monitoring. As communicated by the MoH, health educators  have reached out to 1,321 parents and caregivers of children under 6  throughout the year for counseling.
  
Wherever possible, UNICEF Oman facilitated the  production and dissemination of knowledge and evidence, as well as evaluation  recommendations, to inform the reassessment of programmes. A  capacity-building workshop was conducted, supported by UNICEF MENARO, to  strengthen data use and analysis skills among approximately 30 entities on  disability inclusion and ECD, with a focus on disaggregation and analytical  practices. Additionally, technical discussions with the NCSI explored the  implementation of the IECD MICS7 module through a phone survey to update SDG  4.2, with internal decision-making ongoing. Furthermore, UNICEF Oman  participated in the GCC Stat World Statistics Day, presenting how data and  evidence inform public policy development.
  
UNICEF Oman partnered with SQU to review selected  papers for a special journal edition on children, with a view to strengthening  research capacities and advance knowledge in priority areas related to  children that inform decision-makers. It is anticipated that the journal will  be launched in the first half of 2026. 
  
Looking forward, high-level discussions are ongoing  to implement a new survey on nutrition, reproductive health and ECD under  MoH’s leadership to update child and women’s health indicators last measured  in 2017.
  
On evaluations, the office finalized the evaluation  of Child-Friendly Education under MoE leadership, guided by a steering  committee with MoSD, MoH and Oman Vision 2040 Implementation Follow-up Unit  representation. The evaluation assessed achievements and identified time-bound,  actionable recommendations, serving as a mid-way step toward developing the programme  next edition with focus on emerging child priorities and working to ensure  sustainability. UNICEF Oman will co-develop an operational plan and clear  guidance for schools and teachers during 2026. 
  
Lastly, knowledge management was strengthened  through a series of external engagements, including roundtables and technical  sessions with UNICEF global and regional experts on disability inclusion,  child protection and social protection. Presentations were also delivered to  students at SQU, fostering academic dialogue and awareness on child rights  and development. Internally, staff undertook field visits across governorates  to deepen understanding of programmatic work and tailor interventions to  local contexts. Knowledge-sharing was further enhanced internally through  brown-bag sessions featuring insights from both UNICEF and external experts,  and training on the 7 Habits of Highly Effective People was conducted by a  certified trainer to strengthen interpersonal skills and team effectiveness.
  
In addition, collaboration and knowledge exchange  with resident UN sister agencies, including FAO, UNFPA, and WHO, were  reinforced through joint meetings to explore areas of mutual cooperation. The  year concluded with an all-staff gathering celebrating the UN’s 80th  anniversary, graced by the presence of the Secretary-General himself, reaffirming  the shared commitment to advancing the SDGs and promoting inter-agency  synergy. 
  
UNICEF Oman continued to strengthen its work in the  area of communications and partnerships by building on established  relationships and prioritizing strategic collaboration. Efforts focused on  deepening engagement with philanthropists; reinforcing advocacy and  storytelling; and increasing media presence and brand visibility to enhance  public trust, awareness and engagement around UNICEF’s mission and results.
  
During Ramadan, UNICEF Oman launched its first-ever  organic social media fundraising content. This initiative, which resulted in  a 40 per cent increase in donations compared to the same period in the  previous year, was achieved without any paid promotion, demonstrating growing  public trust and the potential for scalable digital fundraising in the  future.
  
A key milestone in 2025 was the securing of UNICEF  Oman’s first major philanthropic gift from a prominent family, contributing  to UNICEF’s humanitarian response in Sudan. This achievement reflects the  steady progress of long-term relationship-building and advocacy efforts in  recent years. Engagement and dialogue with other philanthropists and notable  families continued throughout the year, laying the groundwork for potential  major contributions in the coming period.
  
In order to enhance the representation of children  in the media and improve the quality of content, a training programme was  organized for media professionals by UNICEF in collaboration with the MoSD  and the Ministry of Information. The training focused on promoting  child-friendly media and raise awareness among media professionals about  children's rights. The programme was implemented in partnership with the SQU,  the Arab Council for Childhood and Development, the League of Arab States and  AGFUND.
  
Furthermore, Oman hosted the MENA Communications  Network annual meeting, welcoming senior UNICEF regional and global  leadership. The convening featured contributions from key UNICEF Oman  partners, including Business Leadership Circle (BLC)[1]  member and advocate Her Highness Dr. Mona bint Fahad, Chairperson of the CFA,  who highlighted successful advocacy efforts that supported reforms in child  and education laws. The event underscored UNICEF’s added value in a high-income  context and positioned Oman as a regional example.
  
 
  
The team also strategically  leveraged high level visits by senior UNICEF colleagues to Oman to amplify  media engagement, resulting in coverage across print, online news platforms  and radio. This increased visibility strengthened UNICEF Oman’s positioning  as a credible and trusted partner for charitable giving, supporting  preparations for the expansion of digital fundraising. As part of these  efforts, a private, high-level engagement was convened with prominent high  net worth individuals known for supporting regional humanitarian responses.  The intimate dialogue with UNICEF global spokesperson James Elder provided a  deeper understanding of UNICEF’s field operations, clarified misconceptions  and fostered potential long-term partnerships and philanthropic  collaboration. In total, 15 press releases were published in 2025, as well as  three additional features of UNICEF colleagues in print media, in addition to  five radio interviews and 900 posts on social media with a cumulative reach  and impressions of over 900,000 across platforms.
  
Given Oman’s high-income status and the upstream  nature of UNICEF’s work, opportunities for direct engagement with children  are limited. Therefore, World Children’s Day serves as a key platform to  foster meaningful dialogue between children and decision-makers. 16 children  participated in eight private sectors ‘takeovers’, organized in collaboration  with the BLC. Additionally, 10 children, including those with disabilities,  joined a roundtable discussion with the Governor of North Sharqiya, where  they voiced their perspectives on issues such as bullying, accessibility for  children with disabilities and academic pressures. These initiatives  underscore UNICEF Oman’s commitment to amplifying children’s voices and  ensuring their concerns inform policies and practices.
  
Throughout the year, UNICEF participated in high  footfall[2]  public activities (such as the International Book Fair in partnership with  the Oman Human Rights Commission as well as the second edition of the CFA  Conference on Childhood, where UNICEF Oman had a booth that engaged with  thousands of individuals, students and families), to increase engagement with  the public and raise awareness of child rights and UNICEF's work.
  
In closing, in 2025, UNICEF Oman ended a  transformative chapter of the CPD 2022–2025, delivering integrated,  evidence-based results across sectors through strong national ownership and  multi-stakeholder engagement. These achievements strengthened systems,  advanced equity and reinforced Oman’s regional leadership in child rights.  Building on this foundation, UNICEF will accelerate progress under the CPD  2026–2030 to ensure every child thrives sustainably.
   

[1] Network of committed CEOs and business influencers to mobilize the private sector for children
[2] commercial term to indicate how many people visit an event

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
During 2025, and throughout  the four years of the CPD, UNICEF Oman successfully advanced multisectoral  results through strong government leadership and inclusive stakeholder  engagement, aligning interventions with Oman Vision 2040, the 10th  Five-Year Development Plan (2021–2025), and sectoral national priorities. The  focus was on strengthening systems and services in education, nutrition,  child protection and social protection, among others.
  
One of the most notable accomplishments  has been the consistent use of evidence-based studies to guide  programme design, ensuring sustainability and alignment with global good  practices reflecting strong political commitment and a shared vision for  children’s rights.
  
A key lesson learned is the  importance of institutionalizing programmes by embedding interventions within  existing government systems to ensure sustainability and scalability. The  integration of the  positive parenting  indicator, mentioned above, into Oman's national health administrative  information system, Al-Shifaa, is a prime example. This experience  demonstrates that institutionalization requires strong government ownership,  alignment with sectoral priorities and the use of digital platforms to  streamline service delivery.
  
Another critical lesson is  that achieving sustainable results for children requires strong  multi-sectoral engagement and coordinated capacity development.  For example, the updated Child Protection Manual was developed through  consultations with multiple ministries and followed by training-of-trainers  sessions for health educators, social workers and education specialists,  ensuring consistent application of case management and referral pathways  across sectors. Similarly, the strengthening of the social protection system  required coordination between MoSD, the SPF and health and education.  Disability inclusion efforts also relied on collaboration across ministries  to institutionalize early detection and intervention protocols, supported by  capacity-building initiatives and regional knowledge exchange. These  experiences underscore that multi-sectoral engagement is most effective when  paired with structured coordination mechanisms, continuous capacity  development and digital solutions that enable real-time collaboration and  accountability.
  
The revitalization of coordination  mechanisms, such as the Programme Management Group (PMG)[1], which convened twice  during the year, showing increased engagement and strengthening  collaborations, along with the establishment of programme steering  committees, have enabled joint planning and accountability. These platforms  have facilitated dialogue across sectors, ensuring that diverse perspectives  inform programme design and implementation. Currently, UNICEF Oman is  coordinating with key stakeholders through the PMG committee to finalize the  rolling workplan for 2026–2027 with clearly time-bound activities.
  
Along with these lessons  learned, challenges remain. Coordinating across multiple ministries  and agencies is complex and requires continuous effort to maintain alignment.  Institutional capacity gaps persist among social workers and educators to  strengthen the direct frontline interventions with children. UNICEF has  supported capacity development and will continue to do so ensuring long-term national  ownership and the institutionalization of programmes within government  systems as a priority. Data gaps remain a concern, underscoring the need for  updated surveys and robust monitoring systems. These gaps call for adaptive  strategies and digital innovations.
  
Looking ahead, insights from the  implementation of CPD 2022–2025 programmes will inform future actions aimed at  guiding the next phase of programming, ensuring that interventions remain  evidence-based, inclusive and aligned with national priorities. In that  regard, following His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik’s endorsement of the  11th Five-Year Development Plan (2026–2030), UNICEF Oman will  commence implementation of the new CPD 2026–2030, primarily funded by the  government of Oman, a reflection of its status as a High-Income Country. The  programme is organized around early years and adolescence, two critical  windows of opportunity characterized by peak neuroplasticity and optimum  development, along with cross-cutting components on social inclusion, child  protection and disability inclusion, focusing on the most vulnerable across  age groups. Principal change strategies across all outcomes will include  policy and programme advice, community engagement and SBC, data strengthening  and evidence generation, leveraging and mobilizing resources. Additionally, building  on the successful implementation of the Child-Friendly Evaluation during the  current cycle, UNICEF Oman intends to undertake two government-led  evaluations over the course of the country programme: a formative evaluation  of social and behaviour change interventions and a summative evaluation of  the social protection system, to inform learning, accountability and future  system strengthening efforts.
  
 
  
The key focus for  partnerships and fundraising will be shaped by the global development  climate and its associated funding constraints. In 2025, UNICEF Oman  navigated heightened public scrutiny and misinformation regarding the UN  system and UNICEF’s role on the ground. A major lesson learned is that  transparency and integrity in public engagement are essential to building  trust. Public-facing events provided opportunities to humanize an  organization that can sometimes appear distant and to reaffirm that UNICEF is  present before, during, and after crises. Given the scale of regional  emergencies, it was critical to approach criticism with openness, learn from  backlash and ensure future messaging emphasizes tangible results and impact.  These experiences will guide UNICEF Oman’s efforts to strengthen partnerships,  deepen philanthropic engagement, and expand digital fundraising, while  reinforcing trust and credibility.
  
A key strategic  partnership achievement during this CPD cycle was the continued  demonstration of the government’s trust in UNICEF Oman’s work, through the development  and endorsement of the new CPD but also, for the first time, a development of  a joint workplan funded by SPF. This partnership will advance efforts to  develop a comprehensive and resilience-responsive social protection system, reinforcing  UNICEF Oman’s role as a trusted  technical and implementation partner to the Government.
  
Collectively, these  programmes, anchored in strong partnerships and aligned with national  priorities and UNICEF’s Strategic Plan (2026–2029), are designed to inform  evidence-based decision-making, advance child well-being and secure a  prosperous and inclusive future for every child in Oman.
   

[1] PMG is UNICEF Oman's primary inter-sectoral platform for planning, coordination, and monitoring of the country programme and rolling workplans. It is chaired by the Ministry of Social Development and includes key stakeholders as members.

In 2025, the conflict entered its third year, and children in the State of Palestine bore the heaviest toll. In the Gaza Strip, at least 20,000 children have been reported killed since 7 October 2023, with nearly 5,000 fatalities in 2025. At least 11,000 children have sustained serious injuries requiring long-term care and rehabilitation. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, 239 Palestinian children were killed in conflict-related violence since October 2023, including 55 boys and 2 girls in 2025. Nearly 1,900 children were injured; over 800 by live ammunition. In 2025, 60 per cent of conflict-related fatalities in the West Bank occurred in Jenin, Nablus and Tubas governorates, and 54 per cent of live ammunition injuries occurred in Nablus and Hebron.
 
In Israel, 37 children were killed on 7 October 2023, and 36 children abducted into Gaza, with 34 released in November 2023 and the remains of two children released in February 2025. Five children were killed in Israel in 2025, mainly during the Iran-Israel conflict.
Conflicts continued to devastate Palestine’s economy in 2025. National gross domestic product (GDP) is 24 per cent below its 2023 level, while Gaza’s GDP has fallen 84 per cent since 2023, including a 8.7 per cent decline in 2025. The West Bank’s GDP has also fallen by 13 per cent since 2023, despite a 4.4 per cent increase in 2025.
 
Recorded unemployment was 46 per cent nationwide in 2025; Gaza’s unemployment was 78 per cent, and the West Bank’s 28 per cent. Poverty across Palestine reached nearly 40 per cent by early 2025. Virtually all households in Gaza are living in poverty, while in the West Bank, short-term poverty surged from 12 per cent before the conflict to 28 per cent in 2024. Price levels continued rising sharply in 2025, with essential commodity shortages in Gaza a key driver of inflation due to severe and prolonged constraints on access, movement and distribution of humanitarian and commercial goods. The Consumer Price Index increased by 11 per cent nationally compared to 2024, with a 22 per cent rise in Gaza and a 0.13 per cent decline in the West Bank.
Human development loss is equally alarming. Palestine’s Human Development Index is projected to fall from 0.716 in 2022 to 0.643 in 2024, erasing 25 years of progress. Devastatingly, Gaza’s 69 years of human development is estimated lost.
 
Persons with disabilities have disproportionately suffered, with over 62 per cent of rehabilitation facilities non-functional and 83 per cent losing essential assistive devices, severely limiting mobility and communication. Damage to schools; shelters; and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems has heightened accessibility barriers and protection risks – especially for women and girls – while loss of livelihoods, documentation, and weakened organizations of persons with disabilities further restrict access to inclusive services, leaving children with disabilities at increased risk of isolation and unmet psychosocial needs.
 
Before the October ceasefire, Gaza’s humanitarian situation was catastrophic. Multiple displacement orders and evacuations continued affecting 80.5 per cent of the territory, including the destruction of the Gaza City, resulting in prolonged displacement of 1.9 million people,. Although humanitarian access to Gaza improved after the October ceasefire, essential service delivery is still hampered due to access barriers and children remain deprived of access to basic health, education, child protection and WASH services.
Protection risks remain extreme. More than 58,000 children have lost their parents, including 2,700 with both parents killed. Moreover, the economic hardship forced one in four families to send children – some as young as six – into hazardous work.
 
The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) declared famine in Gaza on 15 August 2025, reflecting the consequences of long-standing barriers to humanitarian assistance and commercial goods. These constraints continued placing all 335,000 children under five at severe risk of malnutrition; in 2025, there were 421 malnutrition-related deaths, including 113 children.
 
All 658,000 school-aged children in Gaza faced their third consecutive year without safe access to formal, in-person education. Of 399 attacks on education since October 2023, 277 were carried out in the 2024/2025 academic year. Despite the ceasefire, students and educators entered the 2025/2026 school year with significant challenges.
 
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, 2025 saw the most intense Israeli military operations in two decades, concentrated in Jenin, Tulkarm and Tubas. These raids – combined with 2,300 demolitions since 2024 – displaced over 40,000 Palestinians, including thousands of children. Widespread settler violence continued in 2025, with 1,690 documented attacks, more than the 1,500 recorded in 2024. Health services operated intermittently, and WASH infrastructure was repeatedly damaged, cutting off access and heightening public health risks. Schools face protection risks, and the Palestinian Authority's (PA) financial crisis affects teachers' salaries, leading to fewer school days for children.
 
The PA continued advancing its Build Palestine Vision’ launched in 2024 – rooted in the National Program for Development and Reform – and the Gaza Reconstruction and Recovery Development Plan (GRRDP). In 2025, to transition GRRDP into actionable recovery planning and programmes, the PA launched the Gaza Recovery and Reconstruction Implementation Program (GRRIP), guided by the February 2025 Interim Recovery and Damage Needs Assessment (IRDNA), which estimated US$53.2 billion for recovery needs. GRRIP outlines a five-year plan with 56 sub-programmes across 18 sectors, structured into three phases: Emergency Early Recovery, Reconstruction and Recovery, and Sustainable Reconstruction. UNICEF provides sectoral leadership and analysis for the ongoing RDNA and Early Recovery on WASH, education, health, and social protection, ensuring the strategies embed child-focused priorities. These contributions shaped the Arab-backed recovery plan adopted in Cairo and informed stakeholder discussions in Brussels.

UNICEF State of Palestine continued delivering lifesaving humanitarian assistance and development programmes, despite conflict, severe access restrictions and economic decline. UNICEF sustained essential services for children and families while advancing recovery, resilience and system strengthening.
 
Following the extension of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) to 2027, UNICEF aligned its Area Programme Document accordingly. UNICEF developed two ceasefire plans – in January and September – to guide multisectoral scaling up across WASH, health, nutrition, child protection, education, and cash. The second plan integrated lessons learned from the first and reflected the evolving operational space. A Famine Response Plan was also prepared to expand acute malnutrition treatment and prevention, while Winterization Plan responded to protection needs of the population. In August, UNICEF revised its Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) Appeal to reflect evolving needs and enable rapid scaleup when access improved.
 
UNICEF developed its “Rebuild, Restore, Reimagine” Recovery Strategy to strengthen essential social services and foster resilience for all children. As sector lead in the recovery process for WASH, education and social protection, UNICEF ensured child rights and gender and disability inclusion were embedded across assessments, planning and prioritization.
UNICEF actively engaged in the newly established Civil Military Coordination Centre (CMCC), participating in the Humanitarian Assistance, Civil Governance, and Infrastructure and Engineering working groups to ensure improved facilitation of humanitarian operations across Gaza.
 
At interagency level, UNICEF contributed to the UNCT and co-led UNSDCF Outcome 2 on Social Services. UNICEF maintained leadership of the Nutrition, Education and WASH Clusters, and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility (CPAoR), ensuring coordinated, child-focused humanitarian and recovery efforts. UNICEF also participated in the Health Cluster, UNCT Disability Working Group, Gender-Based Violence AoR, and co-led the Monitoring, and co-led Evaluation and Learning Working Group.
 
UNICEF mobilized US$508 million – 71 per cent of its US$716.7 million HAC Appeal and received US$53 million in-kind contributions. Zakat funding further strengthened the response. Advocacy for ceasefire and humanitarian access continued throughout the year.
 
UNICEF sustained Gaza operations through a multi-corridor logistics system via Egypt, Jordan, Israel and the West Bank mitigating border closures and bureaucratic delays. Close coordination with authorities and streamlined customs processes from Egypt enabled rapid scaling up as access improved. UNICEF mobilized over 3,400 truckloads carrying over 80,000 pallets of supplies – its largest annual inflow into Gaza. After the October ceasefire, UNICEF deliveries in two months exceeded the previous nine and enabled prompt scale up of essential WASH, health, nutrition, education and child protection services. 
 
To strengthen last-mile delivery, UNICEF expanded warehouse capacity and reinforced supply monitoring and cleared backlogs to optimize limited windows. UNICEF also managed a high volume of contracts to sustain critical services when supply movement was delayed. Robust information and communications technology systems supported continuous coordination between warehouses and operational teams.
 
UNICEF increased its workforce from 179 to 216 staff, informed by the mid-year Resource Realignment and Optimization Exercise (RROE), which ensured staffing aligned with programme priorities and the 2025 workplan.
 
Communications drove advocacy and visibility through extensive media and digital outreach. Over 1,500 interviews, 40 press releases and 20 human-interest stories kept children’s needs visible across local and global outlets. Over 1,250 social media posts – including 300 highlighting donor contributions – reached 27 million audience, positioning UNICEF as the most visible UN presence. UNICEF delivered compelling visual storytelling; over 150 curated photo and video packages documented humanitarian needs, supported by over 100 publications and 1,200 social posts that amplified children’s experiences and UNICEF’s responses. Targeted communication products reinforced advocacy, including the award-winning documentary "Gaza Silent Threat," which brought international attention to the polio campaign and UNICEF staff. An international photo exhibition featuring Palestinian photographers in Madrid, Dublin and Brussels attracted 6,000 visitors, broadening public and strengthening public support for children.
 
UNICEF continued to work closely with a diverse network of partners, strengthening their capacities through targeted trainings and ensuring accountable, high-quality programme delivery through harmonized reporting and risk-management systems. 
 
Humanitarian performance monitoring (HPM) was systemized, strengthening results tracking, data quality, and field monitoring. UNICEF expanded third party monitoring and increased staff field monitoring by 80 per cent compared to 2024. Regular information products – snapshots and monitoring reports – were disseminated to guide programme adjustments.
 
UNICEF finalized the evaluation of Access to Water in the West Bank while evaluations of the Education programme in the West Bank and the cash transfer programme are ongoing. The L3 Emergency Response Evaluation, led by headquarters, is in inception. Four assessments for child protection and education programmes were launched alongside the RDNA.
 
Accountability to Affected Populations was strengthened through community feedback mechanisms and consultations with communities involving 126,031 people and enhanced case handling through a new service line and feedback hub.
 
UNICEF implemented its Rapid Response Mechanism in multiple West Bank governorates, swiftly addressing the urgent needs of displaced people and host communities affected by military operations, demolitions, and winter flash floods through the provision of life-saving supplies. 

UNICEF supported 4,585 adolescent girls in Gaza with Care and Protection Packages and distributed 80,000 dignity kits. Cash transfers reached 9,068 households with pregnant and breastfeeding women, and 42,159 female-headed households. UNICEF’s expenditure on gender-transformative programming reached 34 per cent.
 
Under its Disability Inclusion Strategy, UNICEF reached 693 children with assistive technology, trained 350 staff and partners, and piloted a one-stop rehabilitation centre. UNICEF trained 34 UNCT members on disability-inclusive communication, and disability screening reached 6,074 children in Gaza’s temporary learning centres.
 
In Gaza, UNICEF scaled up risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) to promote lifesaving behaviour amid famine and health risks. These efforts supported polio vaccination and routine immunization, reaching 1.8 million people through RCCE, mass media, and 1,388 social mobilizers, while identifying zero-dose and under-immunized children. 
 
UNICEF expanded Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) efforts, reaching 1.7 million people with community-led prevention activities. Safe reporting channels reached 935,553 people, supported by a 24/7 helpline and survivor-centred referrals. Partner capacity was strengthened using the United Nations Harmonized PSEA Common Assessment Tool, benefiting 55 implementing partners.
 
Health and Nutrition
In 2025, more than 90 per cent of hospitals were damaged or destroyed, while 70 per cent of West Bank health facilities were only partially functional due to attacks, movement restrictions, and supply shortages. UNICEF scaled up responses in both locations.
 
UNICEF supplied 86 primary health-care (PHC) facilities, paid incentives for four key centres, and deployed 20 mobile health teams, enabling 730,389 children and women to access services – double the 2024 reach. UNICEF supported 61 PHC facilities by December 2025 (up from 32 in June). UNICEF addressed critical care needs by supporting neonatal and paediatric intensive care units; and equipping facilities with continuous positive airway pressure machines, ventilators, and incubators. Ten NICU facilities were supported (up from five), with a 20 per cent capacity increase for these vulnerable infants. These interventions saved 22,134 newborns and critically ill children in an extremely fragile health system.
 
The third polio campaign in February vaccinated 602,795 children under 10 years, while routine immunization efforts also reached 37,387 children under one year with pentavalent 3 vaccine. In November, UNICEF, UNRWA, WHO and the Ministry of Health (MoH), implemented a catch-up campaign for routine immunization, whose first round reached 14,288 children cut off from immunization due to conflict. UNICEF maintained a functioning cold chain throughout 2025 under challenging conditions – with 47 facilities solarized for immunization, up from 21 in 2024.
 
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, UNICEF delivered medical supplies to 357,088 people, installed two oxygen plants supporting 1,000 patients monthly, and distributed sterilization kits benefiting 30,000 newborns and 350 pregnant women. UNICEF refurbished five clinics, solarized 16 facilities and provided solar-powered cold chain equipment to 60 sites, ensuring uninterrupted immunization.
 
Through its Community-Based Rehabilitation programme, UNICEF identified 418 children with disabilities, conducted 449 assessments, and provided 138 assistive devices. With a local partner, UNICEF established a 3D prosthetic production unit, training staff and procuring equipment. By December, eight children had been fitted with low-cost, locally produced 3D-printed prostheses.
 
Nutrition needs escalated under famine conditions in Gaza, prompting. In 2025, all UNICEF nutrition partners in Gaza consistently reported Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rates for the first time. Across Gaza, the monthly average GAM rate was 7.44 per cent – classified as ‘Poor’ – with August peaking at 15 per cent (‘Critical’). Despite efforts to sustain services, rates rose until the October ceasefire, worsening with Gaza City incursion and only reversing once the blockade ended. 
 
Each month, UNICEF and partners screened on average 90,961 children aged 6–59 months and cumulatively treated 69,845 for moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and 16,353 for severe acute malnutrition (SAM).To counter worsening malnutrition, UNICEF maintained preventive services, including ready-to-use infant formula for 8,133 children aged 0–6 months and ready-to-use complementary food for 75,881 children aged 6–23 months. Additionally, on average 29,080 caregivers, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, received infant and young child feeding counselling each month.
 
UNICEF worked closely with MoH on its M&E Capacity Building Programme, leading to adoption of the first National M&E Policy and initiation of a digital M&E system for real-time data tracking.
 
The Nutrition Cluster, led by UNICEF, coordinated 61 partners to deliver life-saving nutrition services amid worsening food insecurity. The Cluster’s service delivery expanded through seven stabilization centres and 180 outpatient treatment sites. The Cluster also developed technical guidance on cash-for-nutrition and supported IPC to inform humanitarian planning.
 
WASH
In 2025, UNICEF worked with the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA), Coastal Municipalities Water Utility and the WASH Cluster to provide WASH services and strengthened national water and sanitation systems.
 
In Gaza, UNICEF sustained on average 1.6 million people’s access to water for drinking and domestic use each month, including reaching 1.1 million people in hard-to-reach areas through emergency water trucking. UNICEF played a critical role to secure entry of over 5 million litres of fuel, water treatment chemicals and spare parts, and to connect major desalination plants to the electricity grid.
 
UNICEF’s sanitation services – including community-level services and rehabilitated wastewater and sewage pumping stations – reached on average 1.4 million people a month. To address overcrowded facilities, UNICEF constructed 4,031 family latrines, benefiting 60,465 people. With Joint Service Councils, solid waste management services were delivered across 17 municipalities, while frontline workers were deployed to maintain hygiene in 75 shelters. Rehabilitation of sewage pumping stations in northern Gaza protected 224,690 people from flash floods during winter, and the installation of 700 accessible latrine add-ons. Prioritizing persons with disabilities, 106,500 disability kits reached 50,000 people. 
 
UNICEF also prioritized WASH in institutions: 93 temporary learning centres were reached with basic WASH services and 29 health facilities received WASH upgrades. These interventions incorporated disability-friendly facilities and water-saving measures.
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, UNICEF supported 553,000 people to access water and 15,000 people to access sanitation services through regular provision of fuel and key supplies to WASH facilities across all governorates in coordination with PWA. UNICEF introduced WASH e-vouchers, allowing 1,400 people to obtain preferred items.
 
UNICEF strengthened PWA and other institutions’ institutional capacity on water and sanitation safety planning. Key initiatives included reviewing the WASH Building Assessment Tool, establishing Hydro-Informatics and Modelling Department, setting up a regional water utility in Yatta, and delivering WASH FIT training for over 400 health-care facilities in partnership with WHO.
 
UNICEF partnered with Environmental Quality Authority (EQA), Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority, PWA, and the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE) to embed climate priorities into national agenda. Leveraging youth as key agents, UNICEF organized the Stockholm Junior Water Prize with two students representing Palestine. With EQA, UNICEF supported the Local Conference of Youth for the second year with 600 participants.
WASH Cluster, co-led by UNICEF and PWA, coordinated 73 partners across Gaza and the West Bank. The Cluster also coordinated with UNICEF to implement Water Safety Plans and conducted WASH FIT assessments to strengthen service quality.
 
Child protection
In 2025, UNICEF sustained emergency child protection services at scale in Gaza, addressing critical protection risks and psychological well-being needs amid violence and deprivation.
 
UNICEF’s multi-layered, community-based mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) reached 271,905 children (75 per cent girls) and 90,753 caregivers, including Level 3 interventions for 33,372 children.
 
Individual case management assisted 11,106 children requiring special care, including 2,537 with injuries or disabilities. Explosive ordnance risk education (EORE) reached 282,484 children and 493,690 caregivers in Gaza, complemented by mass messaging to 441,823 adults to minimize exposure. During 2025, 3,669 families of injured children received multi-purpose cash assistance, supporting 3,884 children. UNICEF also provided 149 hearing aids and 544 wheelchairs.
 
In total 917 children were reunified with families and 1,327 children accessed alternative or family-based care. Awareness sessions reached 68,516 children and 471,424 caregivers, including distribution of child ID bracelets to prevent separation.
 
For protection from winter conditions, UNICEF provided 482,702 winter clothing kits for vulnerable children of different ages, 957,731 blankets, and nearly 3,500 tents to the most vulnerable families.
 
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, 46,757 children and 35,526 caregivers accessed MHPSS services with UNICEF support. Additionally, 125 frontline staff to were trained to scale up EORE activities, reaching 48,856 children, supported by distribution of 35,763 educational materials and recreational tools.
 
UNICEF advanced child-sensitive justice reforms by finalizing Standard Operating Procedures for juvenile and family police units, national inspection guidelines for custodial facilities and the Code of Ethics for judges and prosecutors. Direct services included legal aid for 1,012 children, legal consultations for 146 children and legal empowerment sessions for 6,632 children, alongside MHPSS for 629 children. UNICEF also strengthened the capacities of 7,369 humanitarian workers on child protection and MHPSS and 630 justice and protection personnel on access to justice and supported 23 child protection professionals to graduate from a diploma programme co-designed with a local university.
 
CPAoR, led by UNICEF, coordinated over 40 partners to deliver child protection services across Palestine. Key achievements included rolling out the Child Protection Information Management System + (CPIMS+), scaling up MHPSS and strengthening case management (including for unaccompanied and separated children).
 
Education
In 2025, UNICEF sustained access to inclusive education for children despite severe conflict-related disruptions. UNICEF supported learning continuity and promoted safe, equitable environments for children in Palestine through emergency and system-strengthening measures.
In Gaza, UNICEF supported access to learning for 251,684 children by integrating gender-responsive recreational activities for 204,286 children. UNICEF addressed acute teacher shortages by supporting recruitment of 1,794 teachers and 2,836 staff, including 49 special education teachers and 104 counsellors. UNICEF also initiated an Accelerated Learning Programme for 2026 and training for kindergarten and first grade teachers under the Ready-to-Learn programme. Screening tools for learning difficulties for 6,174 students and development of one-stop inclusive service hub to expand rehabilitation and education services were supported. 
 
UNICEF also prioritized safe learning environments. By December, 87 learning centres were operational, serving 136,360 children. To strengthen safety and preparedness, UNICEF recruited 155 health and security officers and developed mandatory evacuation training for all centres. Infrastructure improvements included latrine construction and provision of drinking water points. High-energy biscuits were provided to all children every day, and 9,263 children in six centres received hot meals. As part of its early recovery intervention, UNICEF also launched its planning for Back to Learning Campaign for all 658,000 school-aged children. 
 
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, UNICEF supported education for 57,695 children. Remedial education reached 12,661 children (7,144 girls) through community-based programmes, while 4,224 children in hotspot areas received targeted learning support. To mitigate learning loss, 2,905 teachers were mobilized for remedial education, and 1,932 primary teachers trained on inclusive learning. UNICEF advanced STEM education by training 1,468 grade 7–11 teachers and piloting summer programmes for 2,519 children. Recreational activities benefited 44,268 children, and 799 children with disabilities received specialized support.
UNICEF supported MoEHE to finalize the draft Evaluation Policy and Monitoring Protocol.
Education Cluster, co-led by UNICEF, coordinated 67 partners to sustain learning. In Gaza, it established 705 Temporary Learning Spaces, reaching 259,541 students and supporting 7,488 teachers, while ensuring Tawjihi exams for 19,500 candidates.
 
Social policy
In 2025, UNICEF reinforced its leadership in social protection and child rights programming amid the deepening fiscal crisis and sustained large-scale humanitarian cash transfers while advancing system-strengthening to link emergency response with resilience.
 
In Gaza, UNICEF implemented the largest humanitarian cash transfer programme, with $54.7 million reaching 643,500 unique beneficiaries including 99,400 families, 336,000 children and 26,500 persons with disabilities. The programme comprised multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA), nutrition, disability, child protection top-ups for vulnerable groups, and incentive payments for front-line workers. MPCA alone supported 543,000 individuals including over 286,000 children and 26,000 persons with disabilities. Nutrition top-ups reached 45,000 individuals, including 23,000 children, among whom are children with SAM and MAM. In total, 15,500 frontline workers received incentive payments, including 5,000 solid waste cleaners and 4,700 education personnel.
 
In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, humanitarian cash transfers expanded to address displacement, reaching 27,000 people (8,200 families and 14,500 children). For the first time, hygiene e-vouchers were piloted in partnership with the WASH sector, integrating cash assistance with a rapid response mechanism. UNICEF also piloted the Shock-Responsive Social Protection Protocol with the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) and UNRWA, institutionalizing emergency response in national systems.
Evidence-based decision-making remained central to UNICEF’s approach. Eleven rounds of market and recipient monitoring were completed in Gaza and two in the West Bank, generating monthly reports combining beneficiary perspectives with field-level observations. Institutional partnerships diversified stakeholders and strengthened programme reach, while the first Zakat funding was channelled to support children with disabilities through digital cash in Gaza.
Beyond humanitarian assistance, UNICEF supported MoSD to revise its Social Protection Strategy for 2025–2027. Moreover, UNICEF advanced child rights and public finance agendas by supporting the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, assisting MoSD to monitor national child plans, and institutionalizing reporting obligations through dedicated staffing. UNICEF launched a cross-sectoral budget analysis study and piloted the Child-Friendly City initiative with Ramallah Municipality in collaboration with UN Habitat, scaling up local governance models that integrate child rights.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Operating conditions in 2025 were highly volatile. Large-scale destruction in Gaza and intensified militarized operations in parts of the West Bank eroded children’s access to services. The PA’s fiscal shortfall of US$1.9 billion further threatened public services and social stability. These pressures required agile management to balance life-saving delivery with system-strengthening for the most marginalized children.
 
Supply-chain fragility was a critical challenge. The Israeli blockade caused delays and denials of clearances, sudden crossing closures and prolonged congestion, while last-mile delivery was frequently disrupted by law-and-order breakdowns. Education supplies were often blocked because they were not defined as lifesaving. Regulatory limits on new e-wallets slowed scaling up of cash assistance. These constraints underscored the need for logistics redundancy and sustained advocacy for humanitarian access. Meanwhile, managing numerous reputational risks – heightened by polarized narratives and scrutiny – remained critical to safeguarding UNICEF’s integrity and advocacy.
 
The blockade emphasized the value of diversified routing. Multi-corridor logistics through Egypt, Jordan, Israel and the West Bank reduced reliance on any single crossing and allowed rapid rerouting when approvals changed. Expanded warehouse capacity and better stock visibility supported surge readiness during narrow access windows. Reliable ICT connectivity at warehouses enabled real-time coordination for movements and inventory updates, strengthening resilience against recurring closures.
 
Rapid shifts in operating zones and blockades required constant remapping of routes and convoy protocols. Transport corridor risks necessitated tighter storage security and incident response. These realities highlighted the need of closer coordination between programmes, logistics and finance teams to align contracting and dispatch.
 
Health and nutrition continuity depended on preparedness. Rehabilitation of neonatal and paediatric intensive care, deployment of mobile health teams and solarized cold-chain sustained care for large caseloads, including children with disabilities. Expanding provider-of-last-resort functions for key commodities and extending acute malnutrition treatment to older children proved critical during famine. RCCE and counselling supported safe infant and young child feeding for pregnant and breastfeeding women.
 
In WASH, integrated packages delivered reliability. Fuel and treatment chemicals for water production, rapid repairs, emergency water trucking, sanitation rehabilitation and hygiene distributions kept minimum service levels despite access constraints. Strategic advocacy for enabling conditions, stabilized production. Piloting e-vouchers provided dignified choice and efficiency for household hygiene where markets functioned.
 
The child protection programme scaled up multi-layered, community-based MHPSS for children and caregivers. Case management addressed complex needs, including for children with injuries or disabilities. Explosive ordnance risk education expanded significantly, and justice reforms advanced through new procedures and codes of ethics. However, feedback loops and monitoring were harder to sustain during spikes in insecurity, underscoring the need for integrated service points and stronger referral pathways.
 
Education delivery benefited from integration. In Gaza, learning centres combined safer learning spaces with WASH upgrades and daily nutrition support. Health–Education integrated approach embedded early childhood development across services, linking primary health care, MHPSS, and RCCE with safe, trauma-informed learning spaces. Recruitment of teachers, counsellors and special education staff underpinned continuity, while disability screening pilots prepared for targeted support.
 
In the West Bank, remedial programmes, STEM initiatives and well-being activities mitigated learning loss. Groundwork progressed to integrate the Learning Passport as the core digital platform in 2026. Integrated services around community hubs reduced exclusion risks for children with disabilities and families facing repeated displacement.
 
Social policy instruments enabled coping but required contingencies. Digital humanitarian cash reached high numbers of beneficiaries in Gaza and expanded in the West Bank to cushion newly displaced families. Routine market monitoring informed programme calibration. Despite the restrictions on opening new e-wallets narrowed speed and reach, and intermittent disconnection caused pauses, maintaining analogue fallbacks and multiple financial service options proved essential. Piloting e-vouchers for hygiene items eased distribution bottlenecks. The shock-responsive social protection protocol was piloted with national partners, signalling momentum to institutionalize emergency response within state systems.
 
Programme effectiveness supported adaptive delivery. RCCE for the polio campaign reached millions through a large network of mobilizers, strengthening social listening and enabling rapid adjustments. Safeguarding against sexual exploitation and abuse scaled through partner capacity building, community-led initiatives and confidential reporting pathways. Governance and accountability were reinforced through spot checks, audits and continuous updates to the risk register. Finance improved efficiency and control through simplify cash transfer processing and tighter budget monitoring to prevent delays.
 
Key lessons emerged:
Preparedness pays: prepositioned cold-chain, oxygen and power solutions, plus contingency staffing, ensured continuity.
Integration accelerates results: bundling services improved equity (including disability inclusion) and efficiency.
Logistics resilience depends on redundancy: multiple corridors, forward warehousing, pre-negotiated contracts and dependable ICT created flexibility.
Governance and accountability sustain confidence: simplified financial processes and consistent partner assurance tempered risk.
 
UNICEF will harden the supply chain against recurring blockade-related shocks as the outcomes for the children depend on timeliness and reliability of life-saving and essential supplies. Priorities include sustaining multi-corridor routing, increasing forward positioning of stocks, expanding last-mile partnerships and enhancing storage security. Dispatch protocols will align with crossing schedules to compress cycle times when approvals clear. Pre-negotiated service contracts will safeguard WASH and other critical infrastructure when parts are delayed.
 
Programme strategies will deepen integrated, child-centred packages at learning centres in Gaza, combining education, WASH and child protection with on-site health and nutrition points. Learning Passport integration in the West Bank will preserve continuity during disruptions. Water security and public health protection will continue through fuel facilitation, rapid repairs and institutional strengthening with national utilities. Shock-responsive social protection will sustain digital cash with contingency rails, broaden cash-plus linkages and further institutionalize protocols with national authorities and UN partners. Community engagement platforms will refine demand generation and strengthen safeguarding. Collaboration with municipalities, utilities and financial providers will diversify last-mile networks and payment options. Routine monitoring and third-party monitoring will guide programme adaptation.
Looking ahead, UNICEF will champion a child-centered recovery agenda by driving RDNA, including physical damage assessment and early recovery planning in close coordination with the PA to prioritize education, health, and social protection. Through its leadership and capacity, UNICEF will advocate for sustained investment and partnerships to rebuild systems that safeguard every child’s right and resilience.

All five GCC states are classified as countries  with “very high human development” according to the Human Development Index,  each scoring above 0.8. GCC countries have aligned their national strategies  with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) with all countries being on  track to achieve SDG targets related to “no poverty” (SDG 1), “zero hunger”  (SDG 2), “good health and well-being” (SDG 3), “quality education” (SDG 4),  and “clean water and sanitation” (SDG 6).
  
  
  
The Gulf countries’ economies remain strongly  dependent on hydrocarbon revenues, a sector highly vulnerable to global oil  price fluctuations and external shocks such as the 2008 financial crisis and  the COVID-19 pandemic. Recognizing the implications of this volatility and  the need to ensure long-term sustainability, GCC governments have launched  national strategies—Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, We the UAE 2031, Kuwait  Vision 2035, Bahrain Vision 2030 and Qatar National Vision 2030.
  
  All GCC states are characterized by relative political stability compared to  the wider Middle East and North African region. This stability serves as a  key enabler of sustainable economic growth. High national income levels and  extensive social welfare programmes have significantly reduced extreme  poverty. Nonetheless, the region continues to experience high unemployment  rates, reflecting an underutilization of human capital.
  
Situation of children’s rights in the Gulf  countries:
  
Children in GCC countries generally enjoy high  levels of well-being across basic welfare indicators, supported by national  wealth and significant public investment.[i] All  states have ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and most  major human rights treaties, although many have not yet adopted all CRC  Optional Protocols.[ii]  National legislation increasingly reflects international child rights  principles. Nonetheless, gaps remain, particularly concerning the low age of  criminal responsibility[iii]  and child marriage under certain circumstances.[iv] 
  
Health and education indicators are generally  strong.  For example, under-five  mortality rates ranged from 5 to 9 per 1,000 live births in 2023,[v]  and youth literacy rates among 15–24-year-olds are nearly universal  according to 2014–24 data.[vi]  However, rising childhood obesity and mental health concerns indicate  emerging well-being challenges.[vii]  Education outcomes also vary, with disparities linked to teacher  training, nationality status and socioeconomic background.[viii]   Interest in early childhood  development (ECD) is growing—yet ECD systems remain underdeveloped in some  GCC countries.[ix]  All GCC countries have strengthened legal protections for persons with  disabilities, although implementation challenges remain.[x] Across  all areas, the lack of disaggregated data by nationality, disability or  socioeconomic status limits effective policy design and monitoring.[xi]  
  
While climate change and its impact on children are  increasingly understood globally and in the region, GCC governments have not  yet fully integrated climate adaptation and environmental sustainability  strategies into child-focused policies.[xii]
  
Gender equality has gradually improved, including  through delayed marriage age for girls and increasing female enrolment in  education, which now surpasses that of boys in many cases. However,  entrenched societal norms regarding education and gender-based violence  continue to limit girls’ opportunities and participation.[xiii]  Non-nationals and stateless persons continue to face barriers to education  and healthcare due to restrictive residency laws.[xiv]
  
Between 2011 and 2020, KSA, the UAE, Qatar, and  Kuwait collectively committed over US$80 billion in official development  assistance (ODA), often exceeding traditional Western donors as a share of  Gross National Income (GNI). Between 2021 and 2025, UNICEF income from GCC  countries reached US$504 million.
  
As traditional aid declines, the Gulf is reshaping  global development through a preference for bilateral, fast-moving, and  strategically aligned cooperation. To remain effective in this evolving  geopolitical context, UNICEF must move beyond resource mobilization toward  deeper strategic collaboration.
  
In late 2025, UNICEF GAO commissioned a  multi-functional review covering programmatic alignment, partnerships and  resource mobilization, communications and visibility, and GAO’s functional  role. The review concluded that the current engagement model no longer  matches the region’s scale or ambition. The Gulf has emerged as a  vision-driven group of high-income countries with significant political  influence, financial capacity, and growing global leadership aspirations. The  report outlined seven key recommendations:
  
  • Adopt a ONE UNICEF approach.
  • Elevate UNICEF engagement in the Gulf as a corporate priority.
  • Make programming purposeful, strategic, and high value.
  • Adopt a coordinated, partnership-forward approach.
  • Explore innovative financing and unlock new value.
  • Strengthen representation and brand visibility.
  • Build relevant and responsive skills and capacities.
  
In 2026, shifting from analysis to action, GAO aims  to scale results by repositioning GCC partnerships as central to UNICEF’s  2026–2029 Strategic Plan:
  
·       Domestically: support child rights through policy,  advocacy, and technical assistance to deliver outcomes for every child with a  focus on the most vulnerable.
  
·       Regionally: Support results for children within the  Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, aligning UNICEF’s mandate with  the GCC’s interest in supporting regional stability.
  
·       Globally: drive results by linking Gulf national  visions to UNICEF global strategies through large-scale resource  mobilization, agenda shaping and humanitarian diplomacy.
