Early Childhood Development
  
In 2025, Gulf countries recorded measurable  progress toward strengthened early childhood development (ECD) systems, with  UNICEF’s Gulf Area Office (GAO) contributing to results across Kuwait, Saudi  Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar including key outcomes in the UN  Strategic Development Cooperation Frameworks for KSA and Kuwait. UNICEF  supported government-led efforts through policy advocacy, technical  assistance, and partnerships to advance integrated, preventive, and  child-centred ECD systems, in line with the UNICEF Strategic Plan and the  UNICEF–WHO Global Nurturing Care Framework with examples of key results  presented below. 
  
Through strategic partnerships, UNICEF contributed  to the strengthening of policy, legislative, and regulatory frameworks  to support inclusive and integrated ECD services. In Kuwait, UNICEF’s policy  advocacy on healthy diets translated into regulatory change with Kuwait  adopting binding regulations banning sugary drinks, sodas, and highly  processed foods from all preschool and primary school cafeterias. UNICEF also  contributed to the technical review of preschool education standards,  supporting the alignment of service delivery benchmarks with international  quality standards, with potential nationwide impact across early learning  settings.   In the United Arab Emirates, UNICEF provided  technical advice to the development of the country’s first integrated  National Early Childhood Development Framework (2026–2031). The framework  reflects a life-course and multisectoral approach consistent with  international conventions and will be operationalized in 2026. In Qatar,  UNICEF supported initial government efforts to develop Early Learning  Standards and an Inclusive Education Framework, laying the groundwork for  improved quality and equity in early learning provision.
  
Additionally, and ahead of Kuwait's 4th Universal  Periodic Review (UPR) session, UNICEF, in collaboration with UNHCR and IOM,  supported government counterparts through a series of technical consultations  to address gaps in birth registration, a critical determinant of access to  services.   The consultations resulted with a set of  recommendations that were officially shared with the Government and are under  consideration.  
  
As it relates to strengthened commitment and multisectoral  action for the prevention of childhood overweight and obesity, UNICEF and  WHO, in partnership with the Government of Saudi Arabia and the Gulf Center  for Disease Control (CDC) under the GCC Secretariat led collective action  across the Gulf to address childhood overweight and obesity as a priority  public health concern. A high-level regional meeting was convened bringing  together all GCC countries. The meeting facilitated shared analysis of the  situation, existing policies, and implementation gaps, and resulted in agreed  priority actions across education, food, and health systems.  As a result, the UAE pursued the development  of a national outcome policy document to address overweight and obesity and KSA  aligned its National Overweight and Obesity Prevention and Control Strategy,  both aligning with the meeting recommendations.  Additionally, gaps in institutional capacity  on applied behavioural science were identified and will be addressed through targeted  technical support by UNICEF in 2026. 
  

  Parenting support and demand for nurturing care constituted a key area of intervention with a  focus on evidence-based parenting support and caregiver engagement. In UAE, a  national stocktaking mapping was completed for parenting programmes followed  with the preparation of a draft National Vision on Parenting that provides  the principles for all parenting work in UAE. In 2026, focus will be directed  to the operationalization of the Vision through the development of national guidelines  that will guide partner’s work.  In Kuwait, UNICEF, in collaboration with WHO,  provided technical assistance to the design and delivery of structured  parenting and newborn care curricula through a national non-governmental  organization, reaching approximately 3,000 parents. This included the  certification of 60 breastfeeding counsellors using standardized UNICEF and  WHO curricula. UNICEF and WHO also supported the national Breastfeeding  Promotion Campaign, contributing to increased awareness and demand for  optimal infant and young child feeding practices and reaching an estimated  400,000 caregivers through media and health-facility-based communication. 
  
UNICEF’s advocacy to applying an integrated  approach to early childhood development continued throughout the Gulf region  by participating as a knowledge and thought leader in global conferences  that were convened by the Gulf countries. For example, UNICEF was a knowledge  partner for the second edition of the Human Capability Initiative by the  Government of Saudi Arabia contributing to a knowledge product on early  education and human capital development.   These forums provide the platform for UNICEF and the Gulf Governments  to influence the ECD agenda in the region and globally. 
  
Child Protection 
  
Following  the commitments articulated at the Bogotá Conference on Ending Violence  Against Children (EVAC), the Gulf countries continued to translate global  pledges into strengthened national policy frameworks, legislative reform, and  system-level coordination. UNICEF has played a catalytic role in supporting  governments to align national child protection systems with international  child rights standards, particularly the Convention on the Rights of the  Child (CRC).
  
Across  the region, high-level policy and strategic interventions demonstrate  sustained political commitment to EVAC. In the United Arab Emirates  (UAE), UNICEF supported the development of a draft EVAC Road Map that  contributes to advancing strengthened services for children across sectors,  in particular a safer school environment through coordinated case management  within and beyond the school system and a more protective family environment  through nationally scaled up parenting programmes.  In the State of Qatar, UNICEF supported the  launch of the Child Protection and Social Services Workforce Report,  contributing to evidence-based policy dialogue and planning. In 2026, this  report will be used to develop a National Action Plan to strengthen the  national child protection system as well as the professionalization of the  social service workforce. Together, these initiatives reflect a shared  regional ambition to institutionalize EVAC commitments within national policy  and planning processes.
  
The  Gulf governments and in partnership with UNICEF worked together to reinforce  national accountability and child rights monitoring mechanisms. In  Qatar, UNICEF supported the development of a National Child Rights Policy to  underpin implementation of the new Child Law and provided technical  assistance for the State’s periodic report to the Committee on the Rights of  the Child, presented in Geneva in June 2025. High-level strategic dialogues  with Qatar and Kuwait in New York further reinforced sustained collaboration  on advancing child rights commitments at both national and global levels.  Additionally, regional cooperation on monitoring and accountability was  advanced through UNICEF and OHCHR-led capacity strengthening for National  Human Rights Institutions (NHRIs) including a regional training at the Middle  East and North Africa level followed by a dedicated training in Kuwait. In  KSA, collaboration with the Human Rights Commission (HRC) continued,  including technical inputs to capacity building interventions on the best  international practices for child protection and determining the best  interests in cases of human trafficking led by IOM and HRC. 
  
UNICEF  made significant contributions to the Governments’ efforts to strengthen  institutional capacity across social service, and child protection systems.  In the UAE, anti-bullying programmes were expanded to reach more than 50 per  cent of schools nationwide, including full coverage of public and private  schools in Abu Dhabi. A national cadre of trainers was established to support  quality assurance and nationwide scale-up. The UAE also introduced the  WHO–UNICEF evidence-based peer-to-peer mental health programme, I Support  My Friends, within public schools, with strong potential for national  expansion.
  
Across  the Gulf, UNICEF supported the institutionalization of child rights  education within formal systems. In Dubai, child rights training reached  over 60 per cent of schools, while in Qatar, nationwide training on  children’s rights was rolled out across all public schools under the  leadership of the Ministry of Education, reaching all 420 public school  principals of Qatar. These efforts contribute to more child-sensitive  learning environments and strengthen frontline capacity to prevent and  respond to violence.
  
Workforce  strengthening was further advanced through regional learning and peer  exchange  through the Gulf  Community of Practice, established in 2023, whose model has since been  replicated at the MENA regional level. The Community of Practice offered the  space for practitioners across the Gulf to exchange experiences, learn from  each other, address taboos and collaborate to strengthen cross country  initiatives. 
  
Advocacy,  social mobilization, and community engagement remained  central to UNICEF’s strategic partnership with the Gulf Governments. In  the UAE, joint integrated social media campaigns focusing on mental health,  positive parenting, and online safety were launched. Aligned with global  moments such as Safer Internet Day, Parenting Month, and Mental Health Month,  the campaigns leveraged influencers, child experts, and Emirati child  advocates, reaching approximately 2.6 million people and generating more than  56,000 engagements. In Qatar, the Government delivered an open-source  national orientation on alternative care, with UNICEF’s technical support  increasing awareness and shared understanding among practitioners and  stakeholders.
  
Finally, forging strategic  partnerships to advance globally child protection issues was central to  UNICEF’s collaboration with Government partners.  Recognizing the high prevalence of  technology use and online risks among children globally, and to protect  children in cyberspace, UNICEF and the Global Cybersecurity Forum continued  their multi-country partnership that supports child online protection in over  30 countries by raising parental awareness and strengthening child helpline  capacities. As a result, parenting content reached over 2.5 million views  through online platforms, with 90 per cent of surveyed users reporting they  learned something new and intended to apply the guidance with their families.  In addition, child helplines in 29 countries received technical support to  enhance protection for children online.
  
Social Policy and data 
  
Strengthening child-focused  public financing and data systems has been a core priority. In the  Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), a Royal Decree mandating a public financing  analysis on children provided a strong foundation for UNICEF engagement.  Building on this mandate,  a strategic  partnership with the Family Affairs Council (FAC) and the Ministry of Finance  (MoF) has commenced to undertake the country’s first Child-focused Public  Expenditure Measurement (C-PEM). The C-PEM will enable the Government of KSA  to systematically analyze public spending on children, identify coverage gaps  and inefficiencies, reduce duplication, and establish a baseline to track  investments over time, strengthening evidence-informed budgeting and policy  decisions. Additionally, and to address persistent gaps in disaggregated  data on children, including SDG indicators, UNICEF and the General  Authority for Statistics (GASTAT) in KSA signed a Memorandum of Understanding  and a Technical Collaboration and Data Sharing Agreement to support the  implementation of the country’s first Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey  (MICS). The survey will generate critical data on child poverty, education,  child protection, and equity. To date, capacity-building for GASTAT staff on  survey design, sampling, implementation, data management, and governance was  completed. Survey instruments were prepared, and fieldwork is planned for  2026. 
  
Strengthening institutional  capacity in child responsive local governance continued to be of interest  to cities in the Gulf  countries  through the UNICEF’s Child Friendly Cities Initiative (CFCI), which promotes  the localization of child rights and improved service delivery. In UAE, Sharja  and Abu Dhabi joined the initiative with Sharja prioritizing the preparation  of guidelines for child-friendly schools and nurseries, providing operational  standards for institutions seeking to improve child-centered services and Abu  Dhabi completing its first comprehensive child rights assessment, identifying  gaps in rights fulfillment and implementing an action plan to address those  gaps. An external evaluation was completed in 2025 for the implementation of  Sharja’s Action Plan demonstrating the achieved results – such as the parks  and social centers for children were adapted to increase accessibility for  children with disabilities -  and Abu  Dhabi’s evaluation is planned for beginning of 2026. UNICEF has also  facilitated  a learning visit by a delegation  from Qatar to Sharja which laid the ground for the development of a CFCI  roadmap for Qatar.
  
Advancing youth development,  participation, and wellbeing remained a key area of UNICEF  engagement in Qatar. In partnership with the Ministry of Sports and Youth  (MSY), UNICEF supported the implementation of the Qatar National Youth Policy  and the Third National Development Strategy (NDS) through a combination of  policy support, institutional capacity strengthening, and youth-centered  programming.
  
A central focus of this  partnership was strengthening systematic and sustainable approaches to  youth participation. With UNICEF’s technical support, youth engagement  mechanisms were institutionalized and linked to global and multilateral  processes, including the ECOSOC Youth Forum, the United Nations General  Assembly, the High-Level Political Forum, and international climate  negotiations. As a result, more than 150 adolescents and young people were  meaningfully engaged in national and international policy dialogue through  structured platforms such as the Qatar UN Youth Delegates Programme, youth  climate leadership initiatives, and national advocacy processes.
  
In parallel, UNICEF  strengthened the capacity of institutions and service providers working with  young people. Approximately 200 youth leaders, youth workers, and  ministry-affiliated practitioners were trained on meaningful youth  participation, life skills, leadership, climate action, and mental health  promotion, contributing to improved quality and reach of youth services  nationwide.
  
Youth mental health and  psychosocial wellbeing were also advanced through UNICEF’s support to Qatar’s  engagement in the UN global initiative on youth mental health. This included  contributions to high-level advocacy and convening moments, such as the Education  Above All (EAA) EMPOWER Youth Conference, as well as support for the design  of national initiatives that integrate mental health promotion through sport-  and community-based approaches.
  
On climate action, UNICEF  supported MSY to strengthen youth leadership and advocacy through the design  and rollout of the Qatar Youth Climate Leaders Programme and Green  Rising. While participation in COP30 was indirect, UNICEF contributed to  national and regional preparatory processes, policy inputs, and youth  capacity-building linked to climate governance, reinforcing young people’s  engagement in climate action at multiple levels.
  
Additionally, in Qatar, UNICEF  contributed to the State of Qatar`s Fourth Voluntary National Review (VNR)  presented at the 2025 High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development  in New York in July 2025, detailing progress on the 2030 Agenda, aligning  with the Third National Development Strategy (2024–2030) 
  
Resource Mobilization 
  
Through UNICEF’s strategic partnership  with the public and private sector in the Gulf countries, voluntary contributions  of partners amounted to a total of USD 98,255,732 to support millions of  children and their families, safeguard essential services, strengthen  national systems and deliver results that last. Significant milestones  included organizing Strategic Dialogues with the Governments of Qatar and  Kuwait, KSA’s new membership on the Polio Oversight Board with a significant  contribution to the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, and UAE’s expanded  philanthropic contributions. 
  
The first-ever High-Level  Strategic Dialogue between the State of Kuwait and UNICEF positioned both  partners as key drivers of a renewed global agenda for children—bridging  humanitarian diplomacy, development financing, and systems strengthening.  Strategic discussions underscored a shared  shift toward long-term, scalable, and systems-focused cooperation. Kuwait’s  interest in aligning programmatic work with national priorities, deepening  collaboration with key ministries, and strengthening domestic institutional  capacity reflects a partnership that also enhances Kuwait’s regional and global  leadership on child rights. For UNICEF, Kuwait’s commitment to expanding  engagement through Islamic financing mechanisms, private sector partnerships,  and South–South and triangular cooperation creates a unique platform to  leverage Gulf innovation and financing for global impact. A major milestone  was the joint decision to develop a new Partnership Framework, supported by a  Joint Cooperation Task Force in Kuwait. 
  
The State of Qatar and UNICEF  jointly developed a five-year Strategic Framework of Cooperation and  successfully hosted its 3rd global High Level Strategic Dialogue,  marking a significant shift in the partnership. At the heart of this shift,  Child Rights took centre stage in the State of Qatar's development agenda,  with a commitment to work cross sectorally both nationally and globally to  ensure no child is left behind, with a focus on education, youth skills and  empowerment and climate action. Nationally, all public schools were trained  on child rights, and globally, cumulatively,  over 5 million out of  school children were able to access a multi sectoral package of learning and  other services, through the support of Qatar's public and private partnerships  with an ongoing commitment to reach over 10 million children in the coming  years. 
  
With KSA, UNICEF strengthened  its’ strategic partnership with King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief  Center with a significant commitment made by the Government of KSA to  UNICEF and WHO towards the Global Polio Eradication Initiative enabling the  vaccination of 370 million children annually for five years and securing  KSA’s membership on the Polio Oversight Board. The Riyadh Humanitarian Forum offered  the platform to make this commitment in addition to a joint Call to Action,  with IMC, on Advancing Healthcare for Conjoined Twins and Children with  Disabilities.  The Call to Action was  followed by a high-level event in New York underscoring  inclusive health programming and sustained support.
  
Within  the philanthropy space, the UAE and Qatar continued to be the most active  market, with engagements from different foundations. Growth in foundation  income in 2025 also yielded the strongest results – most notably the Mohamed  Bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity, committing USD 8 million for polio  eradication. The UAE remains a leading market for Individual Giving (IG),  demonstrating strong growth.
  
  
In 2026,  GAO aims to enhance strategic partnerships and  resource mobilization by reinforcing the seven recommendations of the  GAO Functional Review which focus on adopting a ONE UNICEF  approach; elevating UNICEF engagement in the Gulf as a corporate priority;  making programming purposeful, strategic, and high value; adopting a  coordinated, partnership-forward approach; expanding innovative financing; strengthening  representation and brand visibility; and building relevant and responsive  skills and capacities. By implementing these measures in tandem, UNICEF is  better positioned to elevate the child related issues and strengthen  strategic alignment with Gulf partners. These measures will contribute  to strategic growth of UNICEF’s share of ODA, elevating results for children in  alignment with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan and wider UN system and moving towards  more sophisticated partnership model that is both credible and sustainable  for the medium to longer term.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

During the last quarter of 2025, UNICEF has undertaken a comprehensive functional review and organizational reset of the Gulf Area Office to ensure its operating model remains fit for purpose in a changing global environment. The review takes into account evolving development financing patterns, the increasing role of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states in international cooperation, and the need for UNICEF to adapt its engagement modalities to remain effective and responsive. The review examined GAO across four key areas: programmatic alignment, partnerships and resource mobilisation, communications and visibility, and GAO’s functional role and structure. The core objective underpinning the "Reset" is to transform GAO into a globally influential hub by leveraging the resources and ambition of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states to maximize impact for children and advance their rights. This transformation depends on a strategic repositioning of UNICEF to build deep trust and technical credibility, delivering results at scale—domestically, regionally, and globally—while ensuring organizational coherence and a strong child-rights focus.
Findings of the review provide a set of lessons learned that will guide the way forward:
    

Upstream policy engagement alone is insufficient to unlock the Gulf’s full strategic potential.
While GAO’s focus on upstream, policy-level programming is well aligned with UNICEF’s mandate, experience shows that this approach must be complemented by deliberate investment in relationship-building and partnership depth. In the Gulf context, strong relational capital is essential for leveraging the region’s influence on global programming and for engaging credibly on sensitive domestic child rights issues.


Multi-sector engagement is critical to expanding influence and resource mobilisation.
Lessons from sector-bound programming indicate that engagement limited to line ministries constrains UNICEF’s reach and impact. Meaningful upstream influence and large-scale partnerships require systematic engagement with central ministries, economic planning bodies, technology actors, and major philanthropic investors, positioning UNICEF as a multi-sector, high-impact partner rather than a single-sector implementer.


 Proactive alignment with Gulf priorities strengthens relevance and partnership appeal.
Experience demonstrates that reactive, appeal-driven outreach is less effective in a region where partners are guided by long-term national visions. UNICEF’s engagement is most compelling when it anticipates and aligns with Gulf priorities such as innovation, youth development, and climate action, translating these agendas into forward-looking child-focused propositions.


   Diversification and programmatic partnerships reduce risk and unlock greater value.
Reliance on a narrow set of partners has highlighted the importance of a more diversified and resilient partnership portfolio. Multi-year, jointly designed, programmatic partnerships aligned with Gulf development goals are more effective in mitigating concentration risk and in fully leveraging the region’s financial capacity for global child outcomes.


 Tailored alignment with national visions delivers results—but must be scaled.
Where UNICEF has successfully aligned its technical expertise with Gulf national priorities—such as in Early Childhood Development and child online safety—partnerships have gained traction and generated goodwill. These experiences underscore the value of strategic alignment and adaptation; however, the limited scaling of such successes highlights the need for more systematic replication as Gulf countries pursue ambitious global leadership roles in development and humanitarian action.

The Review calls for a deliberate transition to adjust UNICEF’s engagement model in the Gulf—from primarily programmatic cooperation toward a more strategic and partnership-driven approach that strengthens UNICEF’s ability to deliver results for children at scale, including through enhanced collaboration, resource mobilization, and coordination. The UNICEF office intends to use the insights gained in the functional review to adjust programme strategies, inform future actions and explore new opportunities for collaboration.  In 2026 onwards, UNICEF will be implementing seven recommendations to evolve its partnership model in the Gulf.   


 Adopt a ONE UNICEF Approach to UNICEF’s Strategic Engagement in the Gulf sub-region. Position UNICEF’s Gulf engagement under a unified, coherent “One UNICEF” strategic approach that aligns all programme, partnership and positioning efforts across the GCC countries covered by GAO (Saudia Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait). Develop a unified One UNICEF Gulf Strategy that presents a cohesive narrative with a strong value proposition and shared vision, informed by UNICEF’s normative role, as the foundation for credible and impactful engagement in the Gulf.


 Elevate UNICEF’s engagement in the Gulf as a corporate priority, recognizing the strategic importance of Gulf partners in the global development landscape and ensuring sustained organizational commitment to repositioning UNICEF with Gulf partners, deepening influence, building trust, and strengthening engagement across GCC countries;


  Make programming purposeful, strategic, and high value: Develop a focused, upstream and high-value Gulf programming portfolio that increases impact, advances the normative child rights agenda, reinforces UNICEF’s credibility, strengthens influence, and enables strategic partnership and resource mobilisation opportunities—without compromising UNICEF’s principles. This programming approach must be driven by strategic foresight, ensuring that domestic engagement is purposeful, high-quality, tightly scoped, and justified by its ability to unlock global gains in child rights;
 

Adopt a  coordinated, coherent, partnership-forward engagement approach with Gulf     partners  that aligns engagement and outreach     across all partner segments, ensures consistency, strategic, technical and     operational coherence. This includes strengthening co-creation processes     to ensure Gulf partners are fully engaged in sharing and driving the     partnership and see UNICEF as a coordinated, strategic counterpart. 


Explore  innovative financing and unlock new value: Undertake a careful assessment of viable     and high-impact engagement pathways in Islamic and innovative finance and     use these insights to prioritise and determine which financing instruments     and strategic partnerships to pursue to unlock Gulf-relevant, large-scale     funding opportunities for children’s results.


Strengthen  UNICEF’s representation, brand visibility and brand presence in GCC     countries while improving visibility of the GCC-UNICEF partnership:     Enhance UNICEF’s representation, brand     visibility, and access in the Gulf through strategically placed     representation and strengthened institutional anchoring, while improving     the visibility of the GCC partnership and its impact for children. 


Build  relevant and responsive skills and capacities: Equip UNICEF Gulf Area Office with the     skills, capabilities, leadership structure, and expertise required to     operate effectively in a high-income and partnership-intensive environment     and given diplomatic considerations.

Throughout 2025, Sudan continued to face a protracted and highly complex humanitarian situation, with sustained conflict, displacement and economic decline severely affecting children and the systems meant to support them. With the conflict nearing its third year, governance fragmentation persisted, essential services continued to deteriorate, and humanitarian access remained constrained across all 18 states. Political instability, economic collapse, recurrent climate shocks and large-scale displacement further undermined children’s rights, placing progress against the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025 impact indicators and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) under extreme pressure.
These dynamics unfolded within an operating environment characterised by persistent insecurity, shifting frontlines and administrative constraints that limited predictable humanitarian access. In several high-need areas, particularly those affected by active conflict or hosting large, displaced populations, access remained intermittent and uneven, complicating sustained service delivery. Against this backdrop, sustained engagement and advocacy at global, regional and national levels remained essential to protect humanitarian space, promote equitable access to life-saving services and enable delivery in hard-to-reach locations.
Children’s rights to survival and health were particularly affected. Continued insecurity, multiple disease outbreaks and repeated displacement disrupted health service delivery while simultaneously increasing demand for primary health care, emergency services and immunisation, especially in conflict-affected, hard-to-reach areas and locations hosting internally displaced populations. The health system’s capacity deteriorated sharply over the course of the year, characterised by chronic shortages of qualified health workers, disrupted financing mechanisms and damage to health infrastructure. Recent health facility assessments illustrate the depth of system collapse, with only 46 per cent of facilities operational nationwide and around 80 per cent reporting critical staffing gaps. These constraints disproportionately affected newborns, children under five and pregnant women, directly impeding progress against Strategic Plan impact indicators on under-five, neonatal and maternal mortality, as well as SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being).
The epidemiological situation remained highly volatile throughout 2025. Recurrent cholera outbreaks, a marked increase in reported malaria cases, and continued transmission risks associated with diphtheria, polio and viral hepatitis—compounded by a growing number of zero-dose and under-immunised children—heightened the risk of preventable illness and death. While improvements in disease surveillance, immunisation coverage and utilisation of primary health care services were observed in prioritised localities, access remained deeply unequal. Children living in conflict-affected, newly displaced or remote areas continued to face the greatest barriers to life-saving services and supplies, reinforcing the imperative to target the most marginalised in line with the commitment to leave no child behind.
The nutrition and food security situation deteriorated further during the year. Ongoing conflict, access constraints, large-scale displacement, disease outbreaks and severe economic decline culminated in the declaration of area-level famine and the expansion of locations at risk of famine from 16 to 20. Sudan remained among the countries with the highest prevalence of acute malnutrition globally, with surveys indicating widespread emergency and catastrophic levels in several localities. Children under five, pregnant and lactating women and displaced households faced heightened risks of mortality and irreversible developmental harm. These trends constrained progress against Strategic Plan impact indicators related to child survival and nutrition, leaving SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 significantly off track, while deepening inequalities linked to poverty, displacement and geographic isolation.
Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene continued to be a critical determinant of child health and nutrition outcomes. Conflict-related damage, flooding and prolonged under-investment disrupted water systems and sanitation infrastructure across multiple states, increasing reliance on unsafe water sources and contributing to recurrent cholera outbreaks. Overcrowded displacement settings further strained already limited WASH services, compounding risks of disease transmission and acute malnutrition. While emergency interventions mitigated some immediate risks, sustained access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation remained uneven, particularly in hard-to-reach areas and areas of population return, undermining progress towards SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) and reinforcing linked vulnerabilities across sectors.
Education outcomes were also severely affected. Insecurity, displacement, economic hardship, shortages of trained teachers, non-payment of salaries and damage to infrastructure disrupted learning continuity for millions of children, pushing progress towards SDG 4 (Quality Education) further out of reach. Although humanitarian education interventions enabled large numbers of crisis-affected children to access learning opportunities, the scale of unmet need remained vast. Many children returned to learning after prolonged interruptions and exposure to violence, negatively affecting learning outcomes, retention and transition. Adolescents—particularly girls—faced heightened risks of dropout due to poverty, early and forced marriage and insecurity, perpetuating long-term development and protection risks.
Child protection risks intensified as formal protection, justice and social welfare systems weakened further. Children were increasingly exposed to violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect, including grave violations associated with armed conflict. Gender-based violence, including sexual violence, child marriage and other harmful practices, escalated in scale and severity, particularly among displaced populations. Family separation increased as displacement continued, placing unaccompanied and separated children at heightened risk. While community-based networks and civil society organisations remained essential in sustaining protection services, their expanding role underscored the fragility of national systems and persistent gaps in coverage and quality.
The erosion of livelihoods and social services deepened household vulnerability throughout 2025. Hyperinflation and limited market functionality significantly reduced purchasing power, including among families not directly displaced by conflict. Public services across health, nutrition and education sectors continued to operate at reduced capacity due to delayed payment of wages and salaries, supply interruptions and insecurity. Limited access to routine maternal, newborn and child services increased the risk of severe malnutrition, preventable illness and long-term developmental setbacks. In this context, child-sensitive social protection remained a critical mitigating factor, yet coverage remained insufficient relative to rapidly expanding needs.
Cross-cutting risks related to gender inequality, harmful social practices and behaviours, and gaps in accountability to affected populations further compounded the crisis. Women and girls, children with disabilities and other marginalised groups continued to face disproportionate barriers to accessing essential services and information, limiting timely care-seeking and uptake of life-saving interventions. With an estimated 33.7 million people in need, including 17.3 million children, and 9.3 million people displaced nationwide, reliance on humanitarian assistance remained extremely high. Flooding and attacks on critical infrastructure damaged water and energy networks, while disease outbreaks—including cholera, measles and dengue—resurged. Famine was declared in Al Fasher and Kadugli, and acute malnutrition reached catastrophic levels in some localities, underscoring the urgency of coordinated, multisectoral action.
High dependency on humanitarian assistance also heightened exposure of affected populations—particularly children, adolescents and women—to risks of sexual exploitation and abuse. Prevention, mitigation, reporting capacity strengthening and accountability mechanisms therefore remained critical to ensuring safe access to essential services and upholding zero-tolerance principles on sexual exploitation and abuse.
Overall, the operating environment in 2025 underscored the depth and interlinked nature of Sudan’s crisis and the scale of risks facing children. The convergence of conflict, displacement, economic collapse and climate shocks reinforced the necessity of integrated, equity-focused and system-aware approaches to protect children’s rights and sustain essential services, even as progress towards the SDGs remained under severe threat.

In 2025, despite one of the world’s most complex and constrained operating environments - marked by protracted conflict, mass displacement, economic collapse, disease outbreaks and climate shocks - UNICEF delivered life-saving, protective and resilience-building results for children in Sudan. Against this backdrop, UNICEF prioritised results that combined scale with equity, speed with accountability, and emergency response with systems preservation - ensuring that the most vulnerable children were reached while safeguarding the foundations for future recovery. UNICEF’s work in 2025 was defined by adaptive management amid constant disruption and UNICEF continued to deliver measurable results for children at scale, even as the crisis deepened and access, security and funding constraints intensified.
Health and Public Health Emergency Response
Health and public health emergency response remained central to UNICEF’s contribution in 2025, as children’s survival was directly threatened by the collapse of health services, large-scale displacement and recurrent disease outbreaks. Ongoing insecurity disrupted fixed-site service delivery in many high-need areas, while repeated population movements sharply increased demand for primary health care, emergency services and immunisation, particularly in conflict-affected and internally displaced person-hosting localities. In this context, maintaining population immunity—including against polio—was critical to preventing the re-establishment of vaccine-preventable diseases amid widening immunity gaps.
Despite these constraints, UNICEF enabled 6.5 million people to access emergency health services across all 18 states, in addition to 4.4 million mothers and children accessing primary health services, exceeding planned targets. This scale was achieved through a combination of support to static primary health care facilities, mobile clinics and community-based outreach, allowing services to continue in areas where infrastructure was damaged, staffing was depleted or access was intermittent. UNICEF supported over 1,000 health facilities, including those in hard-to-reach, conflict-affected and outbreak-prone locations, and provided incentives and capacity-building support to frontline health workers, helping stabilise service delivery amid disruptions to government payroll and supervision systems.
Disease outbreaks placed sustained pressure on the health system throughout the year. Cholera, malaria, measles, dengue, hepatitis E and acute watery diarrhoea outbreaks frequently coincided with conflict escalation and seasonal flooding. Through early pre-positioning and forward-stocking, UNICEF delivered emergency health and outbreak response supplies at scale, enabling timely containment efforts. More than 43,500 cholera cases were treated using UNICEF-supplied commodities, supported by over 430 oral rehydration points and 70 cholera treatment units and centres nationwide. Integrated health–WASH response packages—combining case management, water treatment, infection prevention and control, and community engagement—proved effective in reducing transmission and mortality in high-burden areas.
Social and Behaviour Change interventions were a critical enabling component of both the cholera and immunisation responses. Activities focused on promoting early care-seeking, vaccination acceptance, safe water handling, hygiene practices and timely referral to health services. Through interpersonal communication, community dialogues, engagement of religious and community leaders and mass-media outreach, SBC efforts helped counter misinformation, address vaccine hesitancy and strengthen trust in health services, particularly in conflict-affected and displacement settings.
Several critical malaria interventions were implemented during the year. These included the distribution of 12.7 million insecticide-treated nets through mass campaigns covering 33.8 million people. First- and second-line anti-malarial medicines were distributed nationwide, including in hard-to-reach states, in quantities sufficient to treat approximately 4.9 million uncomplicated malaria cases. Injectable artesunate was distributed in quantities adequate to manage 560,000 severe malaria cases, alongside 3.9 million rapid diagnostic tests distributed across the country.
Immunisation remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s health response. Following severe disruptions in 2024, UNICEF supported the recovery of routine immunisation services in 2025, enabling over 1.5 million children under one year to receive Penta 1 vaccination, while reaching zero-dose and under-immunised children through catch-up campaigns. Preventive and outbreak-response vaccination campaigns were implemented at scale, including oral cholera vaccination reaching over 11.2 million people. UNICEF also supported targeted polio vaccination campaigns in conflict-affected areas and operationalised cross-border vaccine delivery through Chad when national supply corridors were inaccessible, ensuring continuity of immunisation services in Darfur states otherwise cut off from supply routes.
Newborn and maternal health services were strengthened despite systemic fragility. UNICEF supported newborn care across 21 health facilities in 16 states, including the rehabilitation and solarisation of Special Care Newborn Units. As a result, more than 24,000 critically ill newborns received improved care, with survival rates increasing substantially in supported facilities.
Together, these health achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s role in protecting continuity of care, sustaining population immunity and preventing excess mortality under extreme conditions.
 
Nutrition: Preventing Mortality and Protecting Child Development
Nutrition outcomes in 2025 reflected both the severity of Sudan’s crisis and the scale of UNICEF’s response. Acute malnutrition remained a leading driver of child mortality, exacerbated by conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and economic decline. In this context, UNICEF sustained life-saving nutrition services at unprecedented scale, directly preventing child deaths and protecting developmental outcomes.
In 2025, 612,134 children with severe acute malnutrition were admitted for treatment, representing a significant increase compared to the previous year and reflecting both expanded coverage and worsening needs. Over 276,000 children were treated in the highest-risk localities, where famine conditions or risk of famine were present. These results were achieved through an expanded network of more than 2,500 health facilities and mobile teams, including the establishment of additional outpatient therapeutic programmes and mobile nutrition teams in underserved areas. 
Preventive nutrition interventions were also scaled up. UNICEF supported nutrition screening for more than 6.8 million children under five, enabling early detection and referral. Integrated campaigns delivered vitamin A supplementation to approximately 6 million children, alongside deworming, infant and young child feeding counselling and micronutrient interventions. These efforts strengthened immunity, reduced vulnerability to disease and complemented curative services, particularly in displacement-affected and outbreak-prone areas. 
Maintaining uninterrupted nutrition supply pipelines was a critical achievement under volatile access conditions. UNICEF procured and delivered nutrition supplies valued at over US$ 36 million, including large volumes of ready-to-use therapeutic food, with significant quantities delivered through cross-line and cross-border operations to Darfur and Kordofan. Despite access constraints, stock-out rates were reduced substantially over the course of the year, ensuring continuity of treatment for children already enrolled in care. 
UNICEF’s leadership of the nutrition cluster and its role in evidence-based prioritisation were central to these results. Geographic targeting was informed by SMART surveys and IPC analysis, enabling resources to be directed to localities facing the highest mortality risk. Integration with health, WASH and social protection platforms further amplified impact by addressing the immediate and underlying drivers of malnutrition simultaneously.
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene: Protecting Health Gains and Dignity
Protecting health gains and dignity WASH interventions were a decisive enabler of health and nutrition outcomes in 2025, particularly in the context of recurrent cholera outbreaks, damaged infrastructure and widespread power disruptions. UNICEF supported  nearly 15 million people with access to safe drinking water, exceeding annual targets. This was achieved through sustained operation of major water-treatment plants in urban centres, rehabilitation and solarisation of water systems, and emergency water supply in displacement sites and outbreak hotspots. 
Protecting water systems under conflict conditions required continuous adaptation. Attacks on power infrastructure and fuel shortages repeatedly disrupted water supply in major cities. UNICEF mitigated these risks by providing generators, fuel and water-treatment chemicals, and by accelerating the solarisation of water facilities to reduce reliance on unstable power sources. These investments were critical in preventing large-scale service collapse and reducing disease transmission among densely populated communities. 
Sanitation and hygiene interventions focused on high-risk settings, including IDP sites, flood-affected areas and cholera hotspots. UNICEF supported access to sanitation services for nearly 300,000 people, complemented by large-scale hygiene promotion reaching millions with handwashing and infection-prevention messaging. While sanitation coverage remained constrained by funding and access limitations, targeted investments reduced open defecation and mitigated outbreak risks in priority locations.
As WASH Cluster Lead, UNICEF played a central role in coordinating a coherent, nationwide response to public-health risks. Throughout the year, UNICEF strengthened national and sub-national coordination, aligning partners around common standards, priority geographies and outbreak-response strategies. Cluster leadership enabled rapid scale-up during cholera surges, supported joint WASH–health planning, and improved real-time monitoring and information sharing, particularly in Darfur and Kordofan where access constraints were most acute. 
Capacity-building, deployment of WASH extenders and strengthened water-quality surveillance further enhanced preparedness and early response, contributing to the sustained reduction in cholera transmission toward the end of the year. WASH services in institutions were significantly strengthened. 
UNICEF supported hygiene promotion, water supply and infection-prevention measures in health facilities and learning spaces, exceeding planned targets. These interventions protected frontline service delivery, enabled safer access to care and learning, and reinforced the humanitarian–development nexus as facilities transitioned back to civilian use following displacement.
Education: Sustaining Learning as a Protective Intervention
Education remained both a critical right and a protective intervention in 2025, as millions of children faced prolonged learning disruption due to conflict, displacement and economic hardship. Despite these constraints, notable progress was achieved. The number of children without access to education declined significantly over the course of the year - from an estimated 16–17 million at the start of 2025 to approximately eight million by year’s end - reflecting increased school reopenings and expanded access to alternative learning modalities. 
UNICEF and partners enabled approximately 3.2 million children and adolescents to access formal and non-formal education, surpassing annual targets through a combination of school grants, Safe Learning Spaces, accelerated learning programmes and digital platforms. Substantial progress was made in reopening and sustaining schools. By the end of 2025, 13,005 schools were operational nationwide, representing approximately 67 per cent of all schools. UNICEF supported 7,153 schools across nine states through school grants to implement improvement plans developed by Parent Teacher Associations and school management committees, benefiting over three million children.
Teaching and learning materials were distributed to 1.9 million children, exceeding targets, while incentive payments and capacity development supported more than 39,000 teachers, helping stabilise the education workforce and improve retention and learning continuity under difficult conditions. Safe Learning Spaces (SLSs) remained a critical delivery modality in areas where schools were damaged, occupied or insecure. 
In 2025, UNICEF and partners established 1,431 SLSs, enrolling 454,900 children, of whom more than half were girls. Over 340,000 children received individual learning materials within these spaces, while more than 6,000 facilitators received incentives and training to deliver structured education and psychosocial support. 
Adolescent engagement was strengthened through clubs and life-skills activities reaching over 110,000 adolescents, contributing to wellbeing and community stability. Digital learning expanded significantly, providing pathways for children who had missed extended periods of schooling to re-engage with education. UNICEF supported 393 e-learning-enabled Safe Learning Spaces and scaled up the Let Us Learn accelerated learning programme, reaching over 49,000 children in 2025 and more than 72,000 cumulatively. 
In parallel, the Learning Passport platform reached over 12,500 children during the year, enabling continued access to curriculum-aligned content despite ongoing disruptions. As Education Cluster lead, UNICEF provided strategic coordination and leadership at national and sub-national levels, ensuring education remained recognised as a life-saving intervention within the broader humanitarian response. 
The Cluster strengthened evidence-based planning, improved information management through real-time reporting systems, and invested in localisation by building the capacity of national and sub-national coordinators, particularly in Darfur and other high-need regions. Close collaboration with global and regional partners elevated Sudan’s education response within international advocacy and learning platforms. Education interventions were closely coordinated with child protection actors to maximise protective outcomes. 
Education services reduced exposure to child labour, early marriage and recruitment, while integrated psychosocial support helped mitigate the impacts of prolonged displacement and trauma. This coordination was particularly evident in UNICEF’s support to the administration of the Grade 12 national examinations in 2025, both inside Sudan and for Sudanese refugee students in Chad. Through close coordination between the Education and Child Protection clusters, UNHCR and national authorities, UNICEF enabled thousands of students—many of whom had been denied examination opportunities for two consecutive years—to safely sit for exams, restoring access to certification, protecting future opportunities and reinforcing the stabilising role of education in crisis settings.
 
Child Protection and Mental Health: Responding to Escalating Risks
Sudan’s conflict, nearing its third year of conflict, escalated further in 2025 into a nationwide protection and governance crisis marked by the collapse of formal systems, weakened infrastructure and the loss of skilled personnel. Children in conflict-affected areas -particularly in Darfur and Kordofan -faced acute protection risks, including grave violations, family separation, exposure to explosive remnants of war, arbitrary detention and heightened risks of recruitment, child labour and gender-based violence. In this context, child protection and social welfare services continued to rely heavily on informal and volunteer-driven structures to reach affected communities.
The national child protection response is anchored in three interconnected pillars: civil society organizations, community-based child protection networks, and the government’s social service workforce. All three pillars faced major challenges, including limited funding, volunteer attrition, staff shortages and weak coordination amid ongoing insecurity. To address these gaps, dedicated strategies were developed for each pillar, alongside a unified, government-endorsed Action Plan aimed at strengthening service delivery, coordination and sustainability. Despite the extremely constrained operating environment, progress was made in strengthening Sudan’s social welfare and child protection systems. 
Capacity-building and institutional support improved access to integrated, rights-based child protection services, including in hard-to-reach areas. Enhanced coordination between government actors, civil society organizations and community-based networks supported more coherent and predictable service delivery. UNICEF advocacy efforts protected key child rights by preventing harmful amendments to the Child Act 2010, while four new justice-sector training manuals were developed and rolled out nationwide, strengthening the capacity of legal professionals and social workers to apply child-sensitive procedures. Legal reform advanced through continued review of the Child Act 2010 and the Child Care Act 1971, alongside a dedicated study on child legal aid that identified critical system gaps affecting children in contact with the law. Despite funding constraints, birth registration outreach expanded, including the establishment of four new registration centres in Red Sea State, helping safeguard children’s legal identity and access to services. 
Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services were strengthened through the development of a community-based training manual, nationwide Training of Trainers initiatives, and integration of MHPSS curricula into university programmes to reinforce sustainability. 
As lead of the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, UNICEF played a central role in coordinating the national child protection response. Throughout 2025, the Area of Responsibility strengthened strategic planning, harmonised standards and tools, and improved information management to support evidence-based prioritisation across states. Coordination mechanisms were reinforced at national and sub-national levels, including in Darfur, enabling partners to respond more effectively to grave violations, displacement-related risks and emerging protection trends. Regular coordination, joint assessments and shared advocacy contributed to more consistent service coverage and strengthened referral pathways for the most vulnerable children.
Explosive Ordnance Risk Education remained a critical life-saving intervention, particularly in areas affected by active hostilities, population movements and the contamination of civilian spaces with explosive remnants of war. Children returning to or transiting through conflict-affected areas faced heightened risk of injury and death. Through community-based delivery and integration with education and child protection platforms, 663,126 people received Explosive Ordnance Risk Education, improving awareness of safe behaviours and reducing exposure to explosive hazards. 
To address escalating protection needs, UNICEF expanded specialised services through the deployment of 17 new child protection extenders across nine emergency-affected states, provision of incentives to 322 social workers, and systematic integration of child protection services within Nutrition and Education programmes. In 2025, 3.1 million children and caregivers accessed child protection services nationwide. Critical support was provided to 20,190 unaccompanied and separated children through family tracing, reunification and alternative care services. Community-based Mental Health and Psychosocial Support reached 1.96 million children and caregivers, while gender-based violence prevention and response services supported 1.12 million women and children. Collectively, these interventions demonstrate UNICEF’s role not only in service delivery, but also in coordination, advocacy and system strengthening—protecting children from the most severe consequences of conflict while reinforcing national capacity to respond to current and future protection risks. 
Social Protection and Cash Assistance: Stabilising Communities and Households
In 2025, social protection remained a critical stabilising mechanism amid economic collapse and large-scale displacement that severely weakened household resilience. UNICEF substantially expanded its flagship Mother and Child Cash Transfer Plus (MCCT+) programme, doubling its geographical coverage to 18 localities across five states in Eastern and Northern Sudan. Overall, MCCT+ reached approximately 140,000 households with pregnant and lactating women, benefiting an estimated 840,000 household members through predictable cash transfers linked to social and behaviour change, health, nutrition, child protection, and financial inclusion services. 
Emergency cash assistance for GBV prevention and response, as well as support to local mutual aid groups operating community kitchens, complemented these efforts, providing vital safety nets to more than 12,000 vulnerable households in access-constrained areas of Central, Southern and Western Sudan, where markets and basic services had collapsed. These interventions helped reduce harmful coping strategies, improved access to essential services, and strengthened community resilience amid prolonged crisis conditions. 
UNICEF continued to strengthen subnational public financial management (PFM) systems to safeguard spending for children amid fragility and conflict. Through targeted training and technical assistance, finance and planning officers in River Nile and Northern states were supported to improve child-sensitive budgeting and expenditure tracking, while civil society actors were engaged to enhance budget transparency, oversight, and accountability.
Cross-Cutting Enablers: Accountability, Partnerships and Operational Adaptation
Cross-cutting enablers were critical in amplifying UNICEF’s sectoral results in 2025, strengthening accountability, safeguarding affected populations and sustaining delivery under extreme constraints. Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) was reinforced through expanded community feedback mechanisms across all 18 states. Inter-agency Community Feedback Mechanisms received more than 165,000 individual submissions - 85 per cent from women - and over 1,000 collective cases, reflecting the needs of more than three million people. Ninety-three per cent of cases were successfully resolved, strengthening programme quality, inclusivity and trust. UNICEF’s leadership of the AAP Working Group supported harmonised approaches and expanded participation of women, persons with disabilities and community-based organisations.
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) was systematically mainstreamed across programmes. More than 3.37 million people were reached with PSEA messaging, while 475,929 humanitarian personnel and partners - 77 per cent female - received training on Codes of Conduct and reporting mechanisms. Risk assurance activities, safety audits and partner capacity-building strengthened prevention and mitigation, contributing to safer service delivery. Operationally, UNICEF sustained a decentralised nationwide presence through a network of country, area and field offices, complemented by extenders, facilitators and implementing partners. Core operational hubs were maintained and strengthened in Port Sudan, Kassala, Gedaref, Atbara, Wad Madani, Kordofan and Khartoum, alongside cross-border operational capacity in Farchana (Chad), enabling continued delivery, coordination and monitoring in access-constrained and high-risk areas
Decentralised coordination, mobile delivery modalities, cross-border and cross-line logistics and third-party monitoring enabled continued reach in access-constrained areas. Investments in preparedness, contingency planning and adaptive supply chains reduced service disruptions and enabled faster scale-up during shocks. Partnerships and localisation were further advanced through expanded collaboration with national non-governmental organisations and community-based partners. UNICEF increased the number of implementing partners and invested in capacity enhancement, reinforcing local ownership and acceptance while sustaining frontline delivery in hard-to-reach areas. Through direct implementation by the Cash Implementation Unit, UNICEF delivered USD 57,111,654 in cash-based assistance across all 18 states, supporting 147,479 households through Mother and Child Cash Transfer Plus and humanitarian cash transfers, 15,908 schools through school grants, and 84,051 frontline workers—stabilising essential services amid economic and payroll disruptions. 
Advocacy and communications played a decisive enabling role. The launch of UNICEF’s report on child rape and sexual violence in Sudan triggered targeted advocacy that contributed to the Government of Sudan signing a Framework of Cooperation to address sexual violence against children, cited by the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict as pivotal. Following the release of Integrated Food Security Phase Classification data, UNICEF and United Nations partners advocated for urgent access in high-risk areas, supporting the delivery of lifesaving nutrition services. Strategic communications reinforced these efforts through 36 stories, 75 videos, over 400 social media posts, 39 statements and press releases, and approximately 80 media interviews. 
In summary, UNICEF’s 2025 achievements demonstrate its capacity to deliver life-saving results at scale while upholding accountability, navigating risk and protecting essential systems. Through adaptive management, strong partnerships, localisation and sustained advocacy, UNICEF reinforced its role as a trusted and indispensable partner for children in Sudan.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The 2025 operating environment in Sudan tested the limits of humanitarian delivery. Protracted conflict, widespread displacement, recurrent disease outbreaks, economic collapse and climate-related shocks combined to constrain access, weaken national systems and heighten risks for children and women. Across sectors, UNICEF was required to manage continuously shifting risks, demonstrating adaptive leadership and agility while sustaining results at scale for the most marginalized populations.
Key challenges were most acute in access, systems functionality and predictability of delivery. Persistent insecurity limited physical access to several locations, particularly in Darfur, Kordofan and parts of the east, disrupting planned interventions and exposing the vulnerability of fixed-site and campaign-based delivery models. In health and nutrition, this resulted in partial or delayed implementation of activities, including the inability to conduct certain immunization campaigns in high-risk areas. In WASH, damaged infrastructure, power shortages and flooding undermined the reliability of water systems and sanitation services, increasing outbreak risk. In addition, the lack of local production of WASH treatment chemicals (chlorine and polymer) presented WASH supply chain challenges. Similarly, repeated displacement, insecurity and the use of schools as shelters disrupted learning continuity, while shortages of trained teachers, learning materials and lack of payment of salaries constrained quality. Child protection and social protection services faced similar access barriers, with weakened formal systems limiting consistent coverage for the most at-risk children and families.
Systemic weaknesses compounded these access constraints. Across sectors, disrupted supervision, delays in third-party monitoring, limited functionality of public facilities and shortages of qualified personnel undermined service quality and continuity. Data gaps - stemming from low reporting completeness, inconsistent oversight and discrepancies between partner reports and field-level findings - constrained evidence-based planning and timely course correction. In social protection and cash-based programming, market volatility, banking constraints and verification challenges affected the speed and predictability of transfers. Across operations, permit delays, limited state-level storage capacity, high transport costs and last-mile delivery challenges affected the timely movement of supplies, particularly during peak outbreak periods and the rainy season.
Climate and seasonal factors further intensified risks. Flooding damaged roads, water systems and energy infrastructure, restricting access to communities and disrupting supply chains. At the same time, the simultaneous occurrence of multiple outbreaks—cholera, malaria, measles, dengue and acute watery diarrhoea—placed extraordinary pressure on preparedness systems and exceeded pre-positioned capacities in several states. Inadequate and inflexible funding envelopes limited rapid scale-up in some high-need locations, highlighting structural financing constraints in protracted emergencies.
Despite these challenges, 2025 generated critical lessons on what works to sustain and accelerate results in fragile and conflict-affected settings. Foremost among these was the importance of adaptive and flexible delivery approaches. Cross-border and alternative supply corridors, mobile and outreach service delivery, and decentralized coordination mechanisms proved essential to maintaining continuity when in-country access was constrained. Diversifying delivery modalities beyond static facilities was critical across sectors—from health and nutrition outreach to mobile education and community-based protection services.
Preparedness emerged as a decisive determinant of effectiveness. Early pre-positioning and forward-stocking of health, nutrition and WASH supplies consistently minimized service disruptions and accelerated outbreak response, particularly in flood-prone, remote and insecure areas. Investments in forecasting, early-warning systems and anticipatory planning yielded faster and more cost-effective responses once shocks occurred. The experience reinforced that preparedness is not a parallel activity but a core driver of results in protracted crises.
Integrated, multi-sectoral approaches consistently outperformed siloed interventions. Joint health–WASH responses were more effective in controlling cholera and other outbreaks, while integration of nutrition, health, WASH and social protection strengthened outcomes for children at highest risk of mortality. Education interventions that combined learning continuity with psychosocial support and protection referrals improved retention and wellbeing, particularly for displaced children and girls. These experiences underscored the importance of designing programmes around the lived realities of children rather than sector boundaries.
Community engagement and accountability were also decisive enablers. Across sectors, community participation in surveillance, risk communication, feedback and service delivery improved acceptance, reach and sustainability of interventions. Accountability to affected populations mechanisms strengthened trust, surfaced access constraints and informed real-time adjustments, particularly in hard-to-reach areas. Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse remained central to safe programming, reinforcing the need for consistent safeguarding, partner oversight and survivor-centred approaches.
Partnerships played a critical role in navigating constraints. Strong coordination with government counterparts, donors, UN agencies, NGOs and local actors improved prioritization, resource mobilization and operational coherence. Collective action through strengthened coordination platforms enabled more effective use of limited resources and reduced duplication in high-need areas. At the same time, the year highlighted the importance of continued investment in national and subnational capacity, particularly for service delivery, supply chain management and data systems, to reduce reliance on parallel mechanisms.
The experience of 2025 also reinforced the need to strengthen system resilience alongside emergency response. Workforce support, streamlined payment mechanisms, digital systems, data verification and real-time monitoring are essential to protect frontline continuity and accountability across sectors. In social protection, predictable financing, financial inclusion and integration with services proved critical to stabilizing households and reducing negative coping strategies. In education and child protection, community-based systems emerged as essential complements to weakened formal structures.
Looking ahead, UNICEF will apply the lessons of 2025 to further adapt programme strategies in 2026. Priority actions include expanding mobile and outreach delivery models; strengthening multi-hazard preparedness and anticipatory action in outbreak- and flood-prone areas; and scaling integrated, multisectoral packages that address the interconnected drivers of child vulnerability. UNICEF will reinforce alternative and cross-border supply corridors, invest in flexible last-mile delivery solutions and expand pre-positioned stocks to mitigate access disruptions.
Further emphasis will be placed on strengthening data systems, third-party monitoring and real-time feedback mechanisms to enable faster course correction and evidence-based decision-making. Investments in workforce resilience, digital payments and operational simplification will aim to improve service reliability and staff wellbeing. In 2025, the evaluation function continued to strengthen accountability, learning, and evidence-based decisions across the country office. The evaluation of L3 emergency response in Sudan provided key findings and lessons learned on the preparedness, planning and implementation of UNICEF's emergency response in Sudan and actionable recommendations to improve UNICEF’s ongoing operations and shape the 2026–2028 Country Programme.
UNICEF will continue to deepen partnerships with government, communities, donors and local actors, while exploring innovative financing and delivery approaches to address persistent access and system challenges.
Overall, the experience of 2025 affirmed that delivering results for children in Sudan requires agility, integration and sustained investment in preparedness and systems. By applying these insights, UNICEF aims to accelerate impact, reduce preventable risks and ensure that the most marginalized children are reached first—upholding the commitment to leave no child behind even in an increasingly complex humanitarian context.

In 2025, Syria continued to remain one of the most complex humanitarian and child rights context globally. The political changes in December 2024 and consolidation of the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic ushered in a cautious optimism with a renewed institutional engagement with the line ministries. However, this momentum unfolded against a backdrop of sporadic security escalation, persistent economic fragility, climate-induced shocks, and the cumulative toll of the fourteen-year humanitarian crisis. The protracted erosion of national capacities continued to overstretch essential services—including health, nutrition, education, WASH, and child and social protection posing challenges to meet the needs of 16.5 million people, including 7.4 million children requiring humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people (IDP), refugee returnees, and host communities.1  
With GDP contraction by 53 per cent between 2010 and 2022 and only a modest one per cent project growth for 2025, the recovery remains elusive.2 Despite the changes in the sanctions environment, banking engagement remained limited, liquidity shortages persisted, and exchange rate instability and inflation continued to erode purchasing power. With extreme poverty affecting one in four Syrians and two-thirds living below the lower-middle-income poverty line,3 these effects exacerbated vulnerabilities for families and children, due to rising costs of goods, transport, healthcare, and learning materials. Unemployment rate among youth (15-24 yrs) reached 31.5 per cent in 2024, significantly higher among young women.4     
Localized escalations, together with the regional dynamics, impacted humanitarian efforts and challenged recovery efforts. Early in 2025, armed escalations in the northeast around Tishreen Dam jeopardized electricity and water supply for over 3.5 million people.5 Although there was a landmark agreement in March with local authorities in the northeast, the security situation remained fragile. The violent unrest in the coastal Lattakia and Tartous displaced 40,000 people6 to Lebanon during March and April, whereas the wildfires in June and July affected 14,000 people forcing 1,150 people7 to flee high-risk areas. In July, escalations in As-Sweida triggered displacement of over 187,000 people8 within As-Sweida and towards Dar’a and rural Damascus governorates, with over 155,000 still displaced.9 
Syria continued to experience its most severe drought conditions in 36 years,10 affecting 8.5 million people, with 1.8 million severely affected.11 Heatwaves, limited or erratic rainfalls and harsh winters have exacerbated water scarcity, compromised agricultural production, and increased the risk of waterborne diseases, including Acute Watery Diarrhea (AWD). 
In 2025, nearly two  million IDP (including 1.1 million children) returned to their areas of origin, with Aleppo, Hama, Homs, Idleb, and Rural Damascus receiving the largest numbers of returnees.12 Refugee returns from neighboring countries also continued, bringing the total to 1.3 million.13 This has resulted in overstretching essential services and beginning to strain social cohesion. Despite the returns, overall displacement remains: 4.8 million IDP live outside formal sites, and 1.4 million reside in 1,782 sites and camps.14 
Health systems continue to operate under severe strain. Amid frequent supply disruptions and funding shortfalls, only 57 per cent of hospitals and 37 per cent of primary health care centres were functional,15 particularly affecting chronic disease management, maternal and child health, and mental health care. 
Approximately 9.1 million people faced acute food insecurity, and 6.4 million required nutrition assistance, including more than 600,000 acutely malnourished children under five. Of these, 177,000 were severely wasted and urgently needed life-saving treatment.16 Malnutrition, compounded by drought and poor sanitation, increased susceptibility to health and nutrition emergencies.
Education infrastructure remains severely degraded with approximately 8,000 non-functional schools and at least 2.4 million children and adolescents are out of school. Overcrowded classrooms, use of schools to shelter displaced families, limited functional WASH facilities, and shortages of learning materials impede access and continuity of education. 
Prolonged economic hardship, limited livelihood opportunities, persistent insecurity, and weakened social support systems have significantly exacerbated vulnerabilities among children and families, contributing to the deterioration of mental health and psychosocial well-being, increased exposure to violence, and heightened risks of gender-based violence and harmful coping strategies, including child marriage, child labour, and sexual exploitation and abuse. During 2024, the UN verified 1,301 grave violations against 1,205 children (including 238 girls).18 14 years of conflict left extensive explosive ordnance contamination across governorates, placing 15.4 million people at immediate risk of death or injury. 892 incidents resulted in 1,634 casualties—one third are children—71 children’s deaths and 436 children injured.19 
A decrease of 30 to 40 per cent in WASH technical staff has been reported as they have either fled the country or retired.20 It is estimated that restoration of pre-conflict WASH services will require US$10 billion invested over 8–10 years, while an additional US$1 billion annually is needed to sustain services, with only one-third of the population having safe access to drinking water and two-thirds having connection to the sewage system.
