In 2025, UNICEF Syria delivered programme results with an annual programme budget of US$181 million [1] through strategic partnerships with key ministries and departments, 56 civil society organizations, and UN partners to scale up humanitarian action while laying grounds for recovery and development in rapidly changing conditions. Revenue reached US$207 million, 45 per cent higher than 2024, meeting 36 per cent of the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) target. 83 per cent of the generous and timely support came from 9 major donors including Germany, Korea, United States, Japan, EU/ECHO, SHF/OCHA, GPE, GAVI, and FCDO. UNICEF acknowledges and looks forward to continuously partnering with donors for more predictable contribution patterns, to protect the rights and wellbeing of all children in Syria. 
 
Country Programme and Operational management improved internally and externally to ensure principled results for children amid a transitional political context, reduced funding, and UN reforms bolstered by UN joint collaboration, and deeper partnerships with key stakeholders. The successful integration of programme management from three locations (Gaziantep, Amman and Damascus) to ‘One Syria’ Country Office with access and delivery across the country through six field offices was a pivotal milestone in 2025. In light of the transitional context, UNICEF undertook several recalibration exercises to identify programmatic shifts and focused on three areas of support: upstream systems strengthening and national institution building, service delivery and increasing community demand and engagement.
 
UNICEF health programme supported the Ministry of Health (MoH)’s strategic policy planning and sectoral visioning through the development of the Strategic National Health Plan 2026–2028 and the National Immunization Strategy 2026–2030 in collaboration with WHO. These results, include Syrian returnee response and recovery plan, will pave way to strengthening national health system including Primary Health Care (PHC) and vaccine coverage, particularly zero-dose children. UNICEF deployed nine technical experts contributing to strengthening systems and MoH leadership, supported nationwide nursing school training, and facilitated unification of Syria’s vaccination schedule and cold-chain systems. UNICEF and MoH initiated [ZA1] the development of National Multisectoral Nutrition Strategy 2026–2030 to accelerate SDG attainment on nutrition through multisectoral approaches and completed the first SMART nutrition survey under One Syria aimed at addressing the dire nutrition indicators. Early Newborn Action Plan expanded to four additional hospitals (total 14) and Early Childhood Development (ECD) services were integrated through 79 PHCs, strengthening early identification and referral pathways of development delays. In support of a collapsed health sector, UNICEF health programme scaled-up service delivery: 14.9 million vaccine doses were procured with support from GAVI, enabling major immunization campaigns reaching 2.1 million children (1,080,871 girls), detecting 93,674 zero-dose children (46,836 girls). Additional support included 196,596 adolescent girls receiving micronutrients, 24 rehabilitated health centres along with adequate vaccine management supplies, and training for 2,744 health workers to improve quality. PHC emergency response was enhanced through 20 implementing partners operating 122 health centres and 87 mobile teams, reaching 2,631,389 children (1,044,466 girls) and 589,438 women. UNICEF led nutrition prevention and treatment through partners, deliveringintegrated wasting treatment, micronutrient supplementation, breastfeeding counselling, and deworming across all 14 governorates. A package of nutrition-sensitive cash transfers and essential services reached 8,373 households to address child food poverty. Home food fortification reached 799,000 children (398,500 girls) and anemia prevention services reached 658,000 pregnant and lactating women (PLW). Through routine services 441,000 children (224,000 girls) received vitamin A, and national campaigns reached 2.3 million children. 1.36 million children (685,745 girls) and 433,000 PLW were screened and 19,679 children aged 6-59 months (10,699 girls) were treated for severe wasting. UNICEF health programme ensured caregivers’ engagement at scale through the GAVI-supported integrated child-care pilot in Homs and Hama reaching over 10,000 caregivers (73 per cent women), and delivering 2,000+ focus group sessions, informing improved Infant and Young Child Feeding and immunization practices, and reinforcing caregiver agency. UNICEF mobilized communities to respond rapidly to multiple crises. During violence in Tartous and Lattakia (March–June), 32 mobile teams provided health and nutrition services, reaching 41,045 children (20,214 girls) and 22,105 women in childbearing age, immunizing 440 children (201 girls), and supplying medicines for 50,000 children. In July to September wildfires in Lattakia prompted mobilization of 12 mobile teams reaching 4,978 beneficiaries (2,433 children including 1,250 girls, 1,088 women). Similarly, during escalation of hostilities in southern Syria, 14 medical teams provided health and nutrition services to 52,037 children (26,036 girls) and 15,768 women, vaccination check for 9,395 children (4,864 girls) and immunizing 924 (749 defaulter children and 175 zero-dose). 
 
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MoE) strengthen the education sector governance and planning in Syria across multiple strategic areas, including Syria’s Global Partnership for Education eligibility and launch of the Education Sector Coordination mechanism (Local Education Group) in 2025. The first national school-based needs assessment (on teachers, students and infrastructure) since 14 years was completed and an Education Management Information System roadmap was developed critical to inform the Education Strategy. UNICEF helped convene two subregional meetings in Qatar (June and October) with 6 MoEs (Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt, Iraq and Türkiye) underpinning the shared commitments for inclusive, quality learning for returning refugee children. Major frameworks advanced including the ECD Strategy involving 216 stakeholders, the upcoming Teacher Professional Development framework, and a roadmap for Inclusive Education. The Better Learning Programme was handed over to the Government to support national ownership. As education sector co-lead, UNICEF supported MoE to unify coordination systems, reactivate technical groups, harmonize standards, launch joint needs assessment, streamline reporting, and broaden participation to drive recovery. In support of an overstretched Education sector, UNICEF improved quality service delivery in coordination with MoE through upgrading 56 Teacher Resource Centres in 11 governorates with essential furniture and solar panels, trained 20,353 education staff on Psychosocial Support, Early Childhood Education, and the Safe School Initiative addressing emotional and social needs of children affected by prolonged crisis and trauma. UNICEF also trained 178 teachers on digital learning and upgraded the Self Learning Programme into the Empowered Learning Programme to improve quality and credibility of non-formal education (NFE) and reintegration into formal schooling. UNICEF reached 3.7 million children (1,858,368 girls), including 24,251 with disabilities, through formal and NFE services and supplies. School infrastructure improvements included rehabilitating 78 schools, installing 126 prefabs and providing school furniture for 225,859 children (113,227 girls). Nearly two million textbooks, and additional learning materials were distributed. In collaboration with the sub-national education authorities, national examinations were successfully administered including in northeast Syria, benefitting 717,669 students (391,381 girls). Digital and distance learning opportunities expanded to benefit over 14,598 children (7,848 girls, 623 with disabilities). UNICEF mobilized communities following emergencies in the coastal region and escalated hostilities in As-Sweida, to lead the UNICEF-supported temporary learning points for 41,000 children (22,366 girls) and the provision of emergency education services for additional 73,163 children (37,300 girls). 
 
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labor (MoSAL) in a national Child Protection System Mapping and Visioning exercise generating evidence for system strengthening and updated key tools including Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), parenting, Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE), and child protection case management SOPs while preparing for MIS+ to establish foundation for quality service delivery. A national social service workforce assessment was initiated to develop a costed-action plan and address shortages of trained social workers, case managers, and supervisors. Justice reforms progressed through restorative justice efforts with the Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Interior. The latter resulted in advancing child protection systems by addressing fragmented governance, outdated tools, workforce shortages, weak justice systems, and civil registration barriers. In support of the service gaps, UNICEF delivered Child Protection services at-scale to a total of 918,484 children (470,152 girls) and 233,022 caregivers (167,027 women). UNICEF strengthened the capacity of 4,276 frontline workers (2,710 women) on MHPSS, parenting, case management, GBV risk mitigation, EORE, and Social Behavior Change. Specialized training for 323 caseworkers improved standardized identification, referral, and follow-up, supporting case management services for 14,768 children (7,262 girls). 715 professionals were trained on MHPSS and parenting, 264 on GBV risk mitigation, and 399 on EORE delivery. Age-appropriate GBV prevention reached 214,899 children (117,020 girls) and 55,927 women. Lifesaving EORE was delivered to 707,199 children (359,567 girls) and 139,233 caregivers (95,519 mothers) in contaminated areas. UNICEF also supported 1,157 humanitarian workers through structured well-being programmes enhancing resilience and frontline capacity. As lead of the Child Protection Area of Responsibility (AoR), UNICEF ensured coordinated, high-quality child protection across all 14 governorates to amplify demand for safe, child-centered services. With partners, UNICEF reached 1,523,351 people (575,951 girls, 540,481 boys, 296,385 women) including returnees and IDPs, through case management, MHPSS, parenting, and prevention services. Capacity-building efforts also reached 12,478 CP AoR partner staff (7,130 women). Around 1,000 grave violations were documented and reported through the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism. UNICEF engaged communities in prevention related to social-norms practices: 381,957 children (199,852 girls) and 95,647 caregivers (74,583 mothers) were reached through behavior-change activities on violence, child labour, child marriage, and exploitation strengthening community prevention and awareness on child protection. Community-based MHPSS supported 178,965 children (96,321 girls) while 68,274 caregivers (61,069 mothers) were engaged in structured parenting programmes. 
 
The WASH programme strengthened institutional capacity amid political transition, which enabled reform and evidence-based decision-making for humanitarian response and recovery programming. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Energy and Water through training of 30 engineers, equipping 14 water authorities with IT tools, and established a centralized database for all WASH facilities. E-learning modules launched in late 2025 will support sustained technician training. The WASH programme also contributed to an integrated family care package, promoting holistic frontline support across health, nutrition, hygiene, safety, and child development. UNICEF, as WASH Sector lead, coordinated partners in developing the 2025 Humanitarian Response Plan and contingency plans, supported national WASH vulnerability mapping, strengthened partner reporting via an online system, held five capacity-building events, and prepared for the 2025 Cluster Coordination Performance Monitoring process to improve coordination at the central and subnational level. UNICEF’s support to rehabilitation of the water infrastructure contributed to further decline in WASH services ensuring continuity of service delivery through providing 4.1 million people (1,036,762 girls, 1,037,236 boys, 1,059,348 women) with safe water and 1.6 million (380,248 girls, 403,669 boys, 451,110 women) with sanitation through 60 rehabilitation projects. Efforts improved water production, restored damaged networks, and added solar systems to address energy shortages. Major projects in Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor, Idleb, and Hama restored services for two million people (420,000 girls, 500,000 boys, 600,000 women). UNICEF also supplied sodium hypochlorite, protecting 15.4 million people (3,026,772 girls, 3,483,434 boys, 4,853,069 women) from water borne diseases. During violence in Lattakia and Tartous in March, UNICEF supplied fuel to run Al-Sin water station, supporting 1,500,000 people (225,000 girls, 270,000 boys, 540,000 women). 501,624 people (143,439 girls, 128,670 boys, 125,172 women) in IDP camps - Al Hol, Areesha, Twineh, and Mahmoudly, and collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, received critical WASH interventions including water trucking, hygiene and NFI distribution, and continued operation and maintenance of WASH facilities. During As-Sweida escalation, UNICEF rapidly delivered supplies and activated backup wells ensuring minimum water availability for approximately 185,000 displaced people (42,550 girls, 48,100 boys, 49,950 women) and 200,000 residents (36,000 girls, 48,000 boys, 64,000 women). 
 
UNICEF’s Adolescent programme contributed to fostering social cohesion in a post conflict context advancing scalable, inclusive TVET and youth engagement initiatives through partnerships with MOSAL, Ministry of Economy and Industry, MoE, Ministry of Higher Education, Chambers of Industry and Commerce, private sector, and civil society. UNICEF supported institutional partnerships on Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) models, and the development of the youth policy leadership. A pilot on public-private TVET in Aleppo was pivotal for reintegrating displaced and non-displaced youth in relevant, quality vocational education. UNICEF technically supported MoSAL to strengthen employment agenda and the newly established Ministry of Sports and Youth (MoSY) and initiated co-development of the first National Youth Policy. Capacity-building support was provided to MoSY to co-develop a joint action plan for inclusive, youth engagement strategies; and to over 100 MoSAL staff on institutional leadership and management. For service delivery in a context of high unemployment, limited social services and livelihood opportunities, UNICEF ensured continuity of skills-building programmes in 14 governorates through 44 centres and 33 mobile teams, reaching 156,662 youths (89,837 females, 6,095 with disabilities). Market driven TVET, digital skills, entrepreneurship, and apprenticeships strengthened employability, with 200 youths gaining on-the-job training and 100 transitioning to full-time jobs.  UNICEF also engaged youth groups through civic initiatives and emergency response. Over 400 UNICEF-supported initiatives empowered 221,587 young people (113,279 females, 6,393 with disabilities) to meaningfully engage. A youth female climate activist was supported to represent MENA globally through the Global Girls Leaders Advisory Group showcasing Syrian adolescent girls’ leadership role for positive change. UNICEF’s Creative Pathway programme trained 140 youth (91 females) e
nabling active youth engagement in creating digital content and documenting for cultural preservation. UNICEF and partners mobilized 69,109 young people (35,236 females, 33,873 males) during emergencies. In Aleppo, 2,000 youth volunteers supported post-hostility recovery, including 240 university volunteers and 35 TVET graduates assessing damages to facilitate rehabilitation. Additional teams managed traffic, cleaned streets, and supported debris removal. Youth mobilization in the coastal area and As-Sweida emergencies supported cash registration, awareness raising, and community initiatives, reaching thousands of families with food, support, and life skills activities. 

In support to the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, UNICEF Social Protection programme focused on system strengthening through evidence generation, policy advocacy, partnerships, and digital tools to sustain momentum as required to support the transitional recovery context. The programme co-organized a national workshop on strengthening Syria’s Social Protection system with MoSAL and UN partners, producing a shared reform roadmap. UNICEF is supporting the development of the Multidimensional Poverty Strategy for which a national workshop was conducted in collaboration with MoSAL and UNDP to guide equity focused programming and SDG 1 monitoring. In 2025, UNICEF initiated engagement with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) to advance Public Finance for Children for child-focused budget planning, expenditure analysis, and fiscal transparency. An Arab Forum on Public Finance and Budgeting was co-organized with ESCWA which facilitated agreement among four Syrian institutions on awareness-raising, capacity development, and avenues for technical assistance. UNICEF is supporting  the Government's application to the Child Nutrition Fund. UNICEF bolstered disability inclusion by co-developing an online platform, improving coordination mechanisms, leading the UNCT Disability Inclusion Working Group and supported national consultations for Syria’s first Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities report. UNICEF contributed to building resilience of most vulnerable households in the transition through continued delivery of cash-transfer services. Through Integrated Social Protection Programme (ISPP), a total of 86,708 people (24,565 girls, 25,934 boys, 19,788 women) were reached across 11 governorates in Syria, including 6,367 children with disabilities (2,630 girls) across eight governorates.. Under the ISPP/cash transfer for basic needs programme, 80,341 people (21,935 girls, 22,197 boys, 19,788 women) were reached with cash transfers for basic needs, including 41,274 people (25,844 children aged 0-23 months, 7,754 women) specifically supported through nutrition-linked cash. Further, the ISPP reached 54,623 returnees, 22,409 host community members, and 3,309 internally displaced people. The programme overall delivered life-saving support while connecting families to national Social Protection systems being developed with MoSAL and MoF.

Across programmes, UNICEF focused on demand generation and community-led participation through social behavioral Change (SBC) strategies: multi-channel health messaging and community-level dialogue reached 5.2 million people (147,678 girls, 149,199 boys, 2,771,916 women) and engaged 2.7 million (241,895 girls, 228,014 boys, 1,552,357 women) in two-way activities. A KAP study covering 20,000+ households and 2,000+ health workers informed demand barriers and enablers for routine immunization resulting in more precise targeting. UNICEF strengthened demand-generation integration and frontline quality capacity through capacitating 941 frontliners on communication and community engagement, and 447 MoH’s health workers and volunteers on gender responsive immunization. SBC enabled outbreak readiness (influenza, measles, and cholera/AWD) and supported Back-to-School mass media campaign reaching 2.4 million people including 2,425,853 caregivers (1,312,930 mothers) and 9,944 children (5,984 girls), encouraging children’s return to learning, increasing school enrolment and attendance, and motivating families to prioritize education. Community-based awareness and behavior change activities on handwashing with soap and safe water handling and storage, reached 448,720 people (147,679 girls, 131,977 boys, 100,180 women) in camps and host communities. Community engagement involved 56,331 people (18,053 girls, 16,376 boys, 17,920 women,) and caregivers (17,920 mothers) and 57 community platforms across 9 governorates, supported by social listening to address concerns and rumors, improved adaptive programming.

UNICEF elevated children’s rights nationally, issuing 16 press releases and over 25 media interviews, while expanding digital storytelling with 50 stories, 90 photo albums, and 44 videos. UNICEF became the first UN agency to appoint a National Ambassador for Children, reinforcing its leading role in child rights. Syria gained the world’s highest engagement in the “I Am” campaign. Advocacy enabled 60,000 students in Al Hasakeh, Ar-Raqqa, and Deir-ez-Zor to sit for national exams. 

Evidence generation and development and recovery planning was strengthened by establishing collaboration with the new National Planning and Statistics Commission (PSC) including a major milestone reached with the endorsement to implement Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey since the last one, 20 years ago. In preparation of the new CPD, a Rights and Results Programming training for 41 staff and two Strategic Moments of Reflection organized. The latter was informed by the Situation analysis of Children and Adolescents valuable insights. 

UNICEF launched a Gender Evaluability Assessment in September 2025 to update the 2021 Gender Programmatic Review and inform the 2027–2030 Country Programme. Preliminary findings have already shaped the SMR, identifying gaps in institutionalizing gender programming, M&E systems, capacity-building, and coordination. UNICEF and UNFPA also organized a workshop in November for participants from PSC, line ministries, and academia to strengthen national evaluation capacity and utilization to further strengthen evidence-based planning.

UNICEF ensured children’s rights and safety remain priority even in challenging environments by broadening secure reporting mechanisms and guaranteeing accountability to investigate sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) allegations through community awareness and training of partners, including contractors, on SEA to promote equity, accountability, and local ownership reaching almost 1.6 million beneficiaries including 808,595 children (432,119 girls) and 671,711 women.
Accountability for Affected Population (AAP) efforts improved programme response including to ensure[ZA2]  communities, children and young people, participate in informed decision making and access safe and responsive feedback/reporting mechanisms. A total of 774 individuals from the partners, young volunteers, third-party facilitators and community committee members were trained on AAP. Customized SMS reached 8,341 families, while the service (hot) line managed 5,325 cases of complaints and feedback from 4,160 beneficiaries, achieving a 99 per cent resolution rate. 

To improve readiness among partners to operationalize the Country Programme, the Field Operations maintained strong emergency preparedness, achieving 100 per cent compliance with the Emergency Preparedness Plan while sustaining capacity across six field offices. Pre-positioned stocks, including WASH kits, Interagency Emergency Health Kits, hygiene supplies and education materials enabled timely mobilisation at the onset of emergencies. Five emergency response plans were activated, including the inter-agency drought-like response plan, in addition to facilitating safe, voluntary return of refugees and internally displaced persons, coordinating with UN agencies and local authorities, monitoring protection risks and supporting reintegration through WASH, health and education services. 

Operations support continuously played a crucial role in delivering results by maintaining value-for-money principles, addressing operational challenges, and ensuring the safety and well-being of personnel. Effective risks management was achieved through simplified and timely quality-assurance activities, alongside transparent processes that focused on strengthening the capacities of both staff and partners in resource management and accountability. Supply chain management also improved programme delivery, humanitarian response, and early recovery by ensuring efficient procurement, streamlined logistics, and strong construction plan.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
While progress was made in 2025, delays in establishment of clear national governance, systems, and weak technical capacity compounded by large-scale refugee and IDP returnees, highlighted the limitations of fragmented, short-term approaches and overstretched public services. Experience confirmed that results for children were accelerated where timely and integrated services were delivered collaboratively with the new Government at central and subnational levels through rapid trust-building, harmonized approaches, and agile advocacy, enabling more targeted and adaptive actions to lay strong foundation for long-term planning and recovery. The recalibration exercises in 2025, such as programme bottleneck analysis and prioritization exercise, operational and management review, and accountability framework update, helped inform the way forward. 
 
Funding gaps persisted across all programme areas, and flexible funding remained limited, while reduced ODA created operational challenges. UNICEF strengthened coordination through a Resource Mobilization Taskforce, partnership mapping, regular sitreps, targeted communication materials, media engagement, donor briefings, and monthly monitoring of pipelines and projections for timely decision making. 
 
Outdated multisectoral national policies, strategies, and regulatory frameworks compromised efforts to address the immediate and underlying determinants of poor health and undernutrition. A notable lesson was the early initiation of support and engagement with MoH, resulting in the initiation of policy reforms and development, strategically prioritizing access to quality, effective and sustained services. 
 
Although UNICEF expanded school rehabilitation, insecurity in some areas and strengthened risk management measures caused delays, highlighting the need for stronger contingency planning. Key lessons included positioning schools as entry points for integrated services to strengthen system resilience and ensure children access multiple services. 
 
UNICEF delivered child protection results in a complex and sensitive context. Strategic lessons underscored the importance of investing in coordination, decentralized social workforce capacity, and standardized child protection tools to sustain impact amid volatility. 
 
Upstream engagement on capacity building and sector financing in WASH was constrained due to significant changes in institutional arrangements, reducing sustainability and resilience. Strengthened sector coordination, data collection and analysis enabled evidence-based decision-making, improving targeting of critical systems and resource allocation. 
 
Structural access barriers remained a challenge, particularly for girls and rural youth seeking life skills, citizenship education, and TVET opportunities. To counter this, services were delivered through trained mobile teams, reducing mobility, safety, and cultural constraints and contributing to increased girls’ participation and more equitable access. 
 
In addition to other challenges, high inflation and liquidity shortages constrained the Social Protection programme, hindering cash assistance and delaying key reforms. Linking humanitarian cash with emerging national social registries, accelerating disability inclusive social protection, collaboration with UN agencies and key partners and strengthening child focused fiscal planning and targeting, geographic mapping, and beneficiary de-duplication, will help to maintain reform momentum. 
 
Implementation of SBC efforts remained slow. Adaptive, cross-sector programming using mixed evidence and feedback improved programme responsiveness and delivery. Lessons highlighted the importance of gender-responsive inclusion and trust-building, while social cohesion platforms enabled local problem-solving. 
 
Persistent challenges remained, including irregular compliance by partners, limited accessibility for beneficiaries with special needs, and cultural sensitivities on SEA. This required co-designing initiatives with children, women, and adolescents, utilizing a combination of digital and in-person channels, and strengthening quality assessment measures for all implementing partners. 
 
Evaluation culture remained a challenge due to limited understanding of evaluation use and weak capacity among partners. Leveraging strategic opportunities, joint partnerships, and national capacity building enhanced institutional learning and accountability while minimizing financial and management costs. 
 
Delays in approving implementation partnerships for humanitarian response and the limited number of long-term agreements for supplies slowed implementation during emergencies and in high-risk areas such as the coastal region and As-Sweida Governorate. Quick activation of available service providers and contingency partnerships, localised procurement and prepositioning of supplies proved central to timely delivery and response.
 
Sanctions imposed on Syria continued to hinder operational effectiveness, causing delays in offshore payments, timely replenishment of supplies, and limiting the availability of critical items in the local market. Prolonged interim and transitional government procedures for clearing imported supplies and approving implementation partnerships and field missions of essential programme and operational expertise also constrained programme delivery. 

Looking ahead, UNICEF Syria will maintain an agile, systems-strengthening approach across all programmes through a twin-track approach to scale up humanitarian interventions and advance recovery and development efforts to ensure every child grows in a safe and inclusive environment. Building on 2025 progress, Health and Nutrition programme will support MoH to enforce and operationalize multisectoral national policies and strategies. In Education, the programme will leverage its leadership role and partnerships to accelerate system-wide reform and expand learning opportunities. Child protection efforts will reinforce coordination with national and sub-national authorities, sharpen strategic priorities, and scale sustainable, government-led responses. A focus on large-scale WASH infrastructure, expanding efforts in WASH in schools and health facilities will remain key, while continuing investment in sector wide coordination and data systems to guide the programme. Skills development programming will further align market-driven, future-oriented training with community-led initiatives, strengthened through partnerships with chambers of commerce, universities, and the private sector to expand employability pathways and foster social cohesion. Social Protection programme will intensify collaboration with MoSAL and MoF to advance Public Finance for Children reforms and operationalize the multidimensional poverty strategy, prioritizing integrated cash-plus models, improved targeting, disability inclusion, and sustainable, shock-responsive financing. Across sectors, greater emphasis will be placed on robust data systems, SBC monitoring, partner capacity, and systems strengthening to accelerate scalable results. UNICEF will also deepen evaluation culture through targeted capacity development and a dedicated resourcing strategy to ensure high-quality, well-funded evaluations. While programmes will continue to be implemented through partners, gradually strengthening government 
institutional capacities through financial assurance activities and tailored capacity-building plans will be central to transitioning to government partnerships and ownership. To support large-scale programming, UNICEF is already enhancing technical, operational, and funding readiness through strategic workforce alignment, addressing liquidity challenges, upstream procurement and collective partnership and resource mobilization. 
 
Together, these approaches will inform the next country programme starting in 2027, reinforcing UNICEF’s commitment to equity, resilience, adaptive, and longer-term recovery programming in a rapidly evolving context—ensuring that the most marginalized children are reached with fit-for-purpose, sustainable, transformative, and impactful joint efforts with the Government of Syria Arab Republic, UN agencies and other key partners.

In 2025, Tunisia experienced a modest economic growth, amid an evolving political and climate environment. Operating within a tight fiscal space, the government balanced economic recovery efforts with investments in social protection programmes to address inequality and poverty, while pursuing policies targeted policies to reduce regional and socio-economic disparities and promote sustainable social inclusion.
National consultation processes were conducted from regional to central level on the National Development Strategy for 2026-2030 and the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement. Parliament consolidated its role in budget oversight and legislative organization, and ministerial councils advanced financial, economic, and social reforms, budget planning, socio-economic policy coordination and the digital transformation of public administration. Tunisia also saw the appointment of a new Prime Minister and a new Minister of Finance. 
The modest economic growth in 2025 was uneven across sectors and restrained by structural challenges. Driven mainly by agricultural production and the recovery in construction and tourism, GDP is projected to grow 2.6 per cent in 2025 and stabilize at 2.4 per cent in 2026-2027[1]. Inflation eased to 4.9 per cent in October 2025 from 10.4 per cent in February 2023; food inflation fell to 5.6 per cent, reducing pressure on low-income households[2]. The budget deficit declined from 9 per cent of GDP in 2020 to 6.3 per cent in 2024 due to lower global prices and improved tax collection. In September 2025, Fitch upgraded Tunisia’s credit rating to “B-,” citing improved external positions and resilient reserves[3]. However, public debt continued to grow, reaching 84.5 per cent of GDP[4], while limited access to external financing and vulnerability to commodity price shocks linked to the subsidy regime persisted[5].
Unemployment stands at 15.4 per cent, with stark disparities - 22.4 per cent among women and 40.1 per cent among youth. Tunisia’s poverty rate is 16.6 per cent, while child poverty reaches 26.[6].[7] per cent. The centre-west records the highest rates (37 per cent overall; 50.8 per cent among children) and rural areas are disproportionately affected, with rates nearly double those in urban areas[8]. In 2025, Tunisia strengthened social protection, allocating 1.8 per cent of GDP to social promotion and security programmes, and the AMEN Social programme played an important role in mitigating economic hardship for vulnerable households. AMEN Social tripled the number of households receiving cash transfers, covering about 10 per cent of the population, increased transfer amounts, and institutionalized the child benefit for children aged 6-18[9]. This marks a major step in anti-poverty policies, ensuring vulnerable children receive monthly support and a back-to-school allowance[10].
Tunisia faces a growing child nutrition challenge, ranking among the highest in the region for child overweight, while wasting (2 per cent) and stunting (8 per cent) remain low. Maternal and child health coverage is strong (98 per cent skilled birth attendance; high immunization), yet quality and equity gaps persist. Neonatal mortality (10/1,000) and under-five mortality (19/1,000) have stagnated, with rural disparities. Health system issues include unequal service distribution, medicine shortages, limited mental health care, chronic underfunding of primary care, and high out-of-pocket costs.
Early Childhood Development progress is uneven: emotional interactions are common, but only 7 per cent of parents engage in learning activities for under-3s. Regional gaps persist in fathers’ involvement (33 per cent Centre-East vs. 17 per cent North-West). Access to quality preschool is improving, with close to 95 per cent of children attending the last pre-primary class in 2025 according to Government, the overall enrolment of children 36-59 months is 47 per cent according to MICS 2023 data and significant gaps remain for rural and poor households. The Government is scaling up ECD through a multisectoral strategy, integrating nutrition and parenting education into health and social services.
Education enrolment remains high, but disparities, dropouts, system governance and weak learning outcomes persist. While nine out of ten children complete primary education, only seven out of ten finish junior high school, dropping to 46.6 per cent among the poorest households. Foundational learning is low, with just over six in ten children mastering basic reading and only three in ten basic mathematics, with significantly lower outcomes among disadvantaged children (MICS 2023).
Despite localized rainfall[11], Tunisia remains one of the most water-stressed countries in the world[12], posing an ongoing risk that threatens agricultural productivity and increases socio-economic inequalities for rural and low-income populations.  Commissioning new desalination stations and additional boreholes ensured the supply of drinking water supply, but reduced irrigation quotas undermine crop sustainability. In 2025, environmental pressures were further exacerbated by a major industrial pollution crisis in Gabès Governorate. Due to gas leaks and continuous emissions from a state-owned complex, the incident led to hospitalizations for respiratory distress, including among children, and triggered large-scale protests[13].
In 2025, Tunisia’s migration landscape continued to evolve, shaping humanitarian and child-focused programming. The number of refugees and asylum-seekers registered in the country declined significantly, from more than 17,000 before June 2024 to 7,812 by September 2025, after the Government suspended new registrations. In parallel, Government- and IOM-supported voluntary return programmes facilitated the return of approximately 10,000 migrants in 2025. National migration policies increasingly emphasized return and border governance, reshaping the operational environment for humanitarian actors and increasing the need for adaptive, protection-sensitive responses for children on the move and host communities.

At the end of 2025, the penultimate year of the extended 2021-2026 Country Programme, a joint review found 11 of 13 outputs on track for completion, with over 17 million USD in funding delivering significant results across programme components.  
Annual work plans are developed with ministries, and partners though participatory processes that strengthen national ownership and coordination. In 2025, the UNICEF Executive Board and the UN’s 80th anniversary were leveraged to underscore Tunisia’s long-standing commitment to children’s rights and UNICEF’s decades of support. UNICEF Tunisia played a coordination role, including on social protection with the EU and World Bank, youth climate consultations for the NDC, and the UN inter-agency working group on Youth. 
 
Social Policy
In 2025, a major progress has been achieved with the institutionalisation of a child benefit for children aged 6 to 18 under the AMEN Social programme, reaching over 420,000 children from vulnerable households and consolidating the progressive implementation of a universal child benefit in Tunisia initiated in 2017 in close cooperation with the World Bank. UNICEF's support for Tunisia's AMEN Social programme also included allocation of a supplement (20 TND) to the monthly child benefit for over 2,800 children with disabilities aged 6-18, in addition to the 5,400 children covered by the national budget. The support of an evaluation of the AMEN programme for children aged 6-18, alongside an overarching research agenda on child poverty and continuous household-based impact monitoring, provided evidence for the policy breakthrough.  
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Affair's information management system by updating the application used by social workers to conduct eligibility surveys, thereby reducing a significant administrative burden. Around 100 social workers benefited from UN TRANSFORM training programme on social protection system-building, and 1,500 social workers received mobile credits to ensure constant communication with beneficiaries and effective coordination for case management. Findings from regular UNICEF-supported panel phone surveys conducted with beneficiaries of child benefits and an evaluation of the child benefit programme for children 6-18 were crucial for advocacy, policy dialogue and advancing the institutionalization and sustainability of interventions. Research and advocacy on shock-responsive social protection and climate change and disability-inclusive social protection was also launched, and fuelled dialogue on a more integrated and comprehensive social protection system in Tunisia in close cooperation with the World Bank, the EU and ILO. 
Progress was also made in strengthening national capacities on child-sensitive and climate budgeting. In this context, UNICEF supported ten social ministries and the National Child Rights Steering Committee through targeted capacity-building, fostering institutional ownership of budgeting approaches integrating children’s rights and climate considerations. Further progress included reinforcing child-sensitive budgeting and advocacy for integrating child-sensitive elements into the 2026 national budget circular, aligning allocations with children’s rights.
Beyond income-based metrics, multidimensional poverty measures provide a more accurate picture of deprivation by capturing deficits in health, education, and living standards. This enables policymakers to better understand the needs of poor populations and design integrated, effective interventions to reduce poverty. In close collaboration with UNDP, significant progress has been made toward institutionalizing multidimensional poverty measurement in Tunisia. Child-specific dimensions have been incorporated into the National Household Budget, Consumption and Living Standards Survey, ensuring regular, nationally owned collection of child-related data - a major step toward a state-led multidimensional poverty measurement system.
 
Education 
In 2025, UNICEF’s education interventions in Tunisia delivered system-level impact by strengthening policy frameworks, institutional capacity, and inclusive service delivery. UNICEF supported the finalization of the first Operational Plan (2025-2028) for the Education Sector Strategy 2025-2035, providing a costed, evidence-based roadmap for equitable resource allocation and implementation. Technical assistance enhanced data-driven planning within the Ministry of Education, improving school mapping and resource distribution, while policy dialogue advanced inclusive education through a national symposium, resulting in a roadmap and a national disability glossary.
Building on the 2024 national study on violence in and around schools-showing that 63.8 per cent of students experienced at least one form of violence-UNICEF supported interministerial preparedness for a National Symposium and laid the groundwork for a multisectoral action plan to be launched in 2026.
Simultaneously, UNICEF empowered over 700 teachers and educational personnel with new competencies in language and digital skills, directly enhancing classroom engagement and learning outcomes. The modernization of pre-service teacher training (LEE), aligned with international standards, was advanced through comprehensive analyses of the LEE bachelor’s model, including gender, inclusion, and violence in schools, ensuring future teachers are better equipped for diverse student needs. UNICEF also partnered with UNESCO-IIEP to build national capacity for large-scale learning assessments and contributed to a standardized life skills measurement tool, ready for national rollout. Innovative approaches, such as an AI bootcamp for screening learning disorders, further demonstrated UNICEF’s commitment to inclusive education solutions. To address out-of-school children, UNICEF supported the expansion of the national Second Chance Education programme, opening a new centre and standardizing professional practice. National capacities were built by training 36 trainers from three ministries. In 2025, these efforts enabled 1,096 out-of-school adolescents to re-engage with education or vocational pathways, while nearly 12,000 children gained access to multidisciplinary services, including psychosocial support, remedial education, and life skills development in schools implementing the school drop-out prevention programme. 
UNICEF’s multisectoral approach fostered innovation and collaboration across ministries, supporting extracurricular programmes and life-skills-based bootcamps that strengthened 432 vulnerable adolescents’ skills and resilience. Strategies also included mechanisms for adolescent participation in policy development, amplifying youth voices for more inclusive policies. Collectively, these achievements highlight UNICEF’s catalytic role in building a more inclusive, equitable, and resilient education system in Tunisia. In addition, under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator’s Office, and collaboration of UNDP, ILO, IOM and UNICEF, developed a system-wide framework to address the needs of adolescents and youth Not in Education, Employment or Training (NEET). UNICEF contributed substantively by supporting the articulation of a coherent joint UN response with government counterparts, multi-agency approach, aligned with national priorities, and aimed at strengthening coordination and enhancing collective impact on youth inclusion outcomes.
Early Childhood Development
In 2025, UNICEF accelerated progress toward universal preschool access and improved early learning quality. A major milestone was the issuance of a joint political note by key ministries, committing to universalize at least one year of preschool education by 2028.With less than 6% enrolment to attain to full coverage, this objective is within reach by end of 2030 SDG agenda. UNICEF supported the development and nationwide rollout of pedagogical toolkits for preschool educators and trained thousands of educators on their effective use. In partnership with NGO UTSS, UNICEF launched an online training platform for early learning and ECD professionals, expanding access to continuous professional development. These efforts, combined with infrastructure upgrades and curriculum modernization, contributed to raising coverage for the preparatory class to 95 per cent nationally, while promoting standards for safe and stimulating learning environments. Parenting programmes were scaled up in 56 localities, training nearly 200 community actors and reaching over 3,000 families, complemented by social and behaviour change campaigns that reinforced positive parenting and early stimulation.
UNICEF, alongside WHO and with financial support of the Gavi Vaccine Alliance, supported the Ministry of Health in the HPV vaccine introduction process (April 2025), including on the preparation and implementation for logistics and demand generation. Integrated training packages were developed and rolled out through ToT cascades resulting in over 5,100 frontline health workers trained (˜77 per cent women) and 4,600 education staff sensitized. A nationwide risk communication and community engagement strategy reached over 7 million people through television, media, digital and community engagement, including through outreach activities organised by CSO (Scouts, Tunisian Red crescent and medical students’ associations) following trainings and webinars on HPV, cervical cancer, HPV vaccination and on inter-personal communication. 
System resilience was strengthened through procurement of cold chain equipment, (i.e. WHO prequalified refrigerators, temperature monitoring devices and cold boxes) and the upgrades of the 24 regional vaccine warehouses. The digital transformation was a game-changer in 2025. The Cold Chain platform (Information system for immunization supply chain) was deployed nationwide with 3,245 users, covering 2,606 facilities and 4,408 cold-chain assets, following cascade user training across 100 per cent of districts. This innovation complements the upgraded EVAX platform, now covering all primary health care centres, and the e-Pharmacy system (Stock-management information system), in final deployment phase. Together, these solutions position Tunisia as one among the first African countries aiming for a fully integrated digital immunization system, spanning procurement, cold-chain logistics, and last-mile delivery where digital innovation and user-centred design transform immunization management.
UNICEF anchored nutrition as a national priority by supporting the operationalization of the National Child Feeding & Nutrition Strategy (0-18 years) and advancing a coordinated social and behaviour change (SBC) approach. In 2025, the work on breastfeeding followed a clear sequence: first, UNICEF developed an interactive Breastfeeding Toolbox as a practical resource for health professionals; next, it rolled out the toolbox through a training-of-trainers approach, creating a network of 80 certified trainers who enabled the cascade training of over 3,000 health providers on breastfeeding counselling and diversified complementary feeding. This technical capacity-building served as a strong advocacy lever, culminating in broader institutional engagement during the National Breastfeeding Week, which mobilized all 24 regional health directorates, academia, and private sector through open days, media actions, and facility-based sessions. Building on this momentum, UNICEF is now leveraging the strengthened professional network to advance the revision of the legal framework on marketing of breast-milk substitutes, including monitoring and enforcement mechanisms - laying the foundation for stronger protection of breastfeeding. Furthermore, UNICEF is providing technical support to set up and conduct the Tunisian Integrated Micronutrient and Anthropometry survey, in order to leverage data for better decision making. 
Together, these achievements advanced the right of every child to survive, learn, and thrive, laying the foundation for integrated early childhood services that combine early learning, health, and nutrition for a holistic start in life.
Child Protection 
In 2025, UNICEF Tunisia advanced child-sensitive justice and protection outcomes for children in contact with the law and children on the move by addressing critical structural and operational bottlenecks within justice and migration governance systems. Interventions prioritized a holistic approach combining improvements to child-appropriate infrastructure, frontline capacity strengthening, access to legal safeguards, and the promotion of alternatives to detention, resulting in measurable improvements in protection outcomes for vulnerable children.
A key focus was improving the conditions under which children are heard by law enforcement, responding to long-standing gaps in child-appropriate infrastructure that exposed children to intimidation and re-traumatisation. During the year, 24 specialized police and National Guard units (20 per cent) were equipped to function as child-sensitive hearing spaces, significantly improving the quality and dignity of interactions between children and law enforcement and reinforcing children’s right to be heard in a protective environment. In parallel, building on a specialized training toolkit jointly developed with the Ministry of Interior in 2024, UNICEF supported the nationwide rollout of training in 2025. A total of 301 officers were trained on child-friendly interviewing techniques, legal safeguards, referral pathways, and diversion measures, strengthening rights-based practices during arrest, questioning, and referral.
To address persistent overreliance on detention, UNICEF supported access to legal assistance for 284 children. These efforts contributed to a shift towards restorative and child-centred responses: 40 per cent of supported children were oriented towards diversion or mediation mechanisms, reducing their exposure to formal judicial proceedings. Among children initially placed in detention, 70 per cent were released prior to trial, and more than two-thirds were successfully reintegrated into education or vocational pathways.
At the systemic level, UNICEF strengthened the evidence base for reform by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the child protection legal framework. This work will inform advocacy efforts to reform the Child Protection Code and better align national legislation with international standards, particularly for children in contact with the law and children on the move.
In parallel, UNICEF reinforced inter-agency coordination on migration under a joint annual workplan with IOM and UNHCR, clarifying roles and strengthening coordinated protection responses. In a restrictive operational environment for civil society organisations working with migrant populations, UNICEF recruited 16 additional field officers, enabling expanded outreach to children on the move, including unaccompanied and separated children, with mental health and psychosocial support and case management services (approx. 300 children), and facilitating enrolment in formal schooling or access to Learning Passport (96 children).
Beyond justice and migration, UNICEF worked to strengthen the quality, sustainability, and effectiveness of child protection services and violence prevention systems. A major constraint identified was the lack of robust data to inform policy dialogue and investment decisions. In response, UNICEF supported the launch of a national study on the cost of violence against children, estimating its economic impact at nearly 2 per cent of GDP (approximately USD 860 million in 2022), strengthening the case for prevention-focused investment. UNICEF also supported the development of a national violence prevention strategy grounded in social and behaviour change approaches.
In collaboration with UNFPA, UNDP, and UN Women - and under the leadership of the Ministry of Women - the country office developed a concept note for Tunisia’s inclusion in the second phase of the Spotlight Initiative, with a focus on integrated responses to violence against women and children.
Recognising the importance of a skilled and supported workforce, UNICEF invested in strengthening professional competencies and institutional systems, including training family conciliators, assessing national training and supervision systems for child protection professionals, and strengthening frontline leadership through capacity building for Child Protection Delegates. Finally, UNICEF contributed to strengthening financial sustainability by supporting the integration of the national child helpline (1809) into the regular state budget, ensuring continuity, predictability, and national ownership of a critical protection service.
WASH
In 2025, Tunisia achieved major progress in climate resilience and WASH/IPC services through integrated actions that empowered youth, strengthened systems, and provided critical support to vulnerable populations. A national strategy for youth engagement in climate action was developed with contributions from over 500 young people from diverse backgrounds, institutionalizing their role in climate governance. This strategy envisages a coordination framework comprised of national and sub-national committees to support implementation and monitoring, with a continuous representation of youth. Additionally, 50 young people contributed in regional consultations to revising the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), covering WASH, health, education, and social protection, in collaboration with UNDP and the Ministry of Environment, promoting participatory governance and intergenerational equity. 
Education systems were reinforced through the technical validation of climate-resilient WASH standards for primary schools, while health resilience advanced with the political validation of the national WASH/IPC improvement strategy for primary healthcare centres. To operationalize this initiative, an online IPC training programme launched through the Ministry of Health’s e-learning platform enrolled over 700 frontline health workers, including school nurses, equipping them with essential skills for infection prevention.
Beyond policy engagement, youth-led climate action scaled nationwide: 3,200 young people drove ecological behaviour change through 90 community initiatives across 24 regions, including awareness campaigns, cleanup activities, and tailored trainings. Regional dialogues, titled “24 governorates discuss climate”, fostered inclusive solutions, while creative initiatives like Tunisia88 used music to amplify climate messages. Ten green startups benefited from capacity-building support, promoting innovation and sustainable entrepreneurship.
Humanitarian interventions complemented these efforts, with essential WASH services provided to 3,560 children and migrants in five UNHCR-managed centres through WASH facility upgrades and distribution of hygiene kits. Individual kits tailored to the migration crisis and existing long-term procurement agreement ensured timely and sustained support for vulnerable populations.
These achievements collectively advance Tunisia’s commitments to climate adaptation, infection prevention, and sustainable development. By integrating youth leadership, climate-resilient infrastructure, and strengthened health systems, Tunisia is building a robust foundation for resilience and inclusion. Looking ahead, priorities include scaling implementation, expanding training coverage, and deepening youth engagement through innovation hubs and climate dialogues.
Programme and Operational effectiveness and management
Throughout 2025, UNCEF Tunisia, alongside the UN System in Tunisia, laid groundwork for the development of the country programme cycle 2027-2031. A UNSDCF Evaluation and a Common Country Analysis, alongside a UNICEF Evidence Synthesis on the situation of children were conducted collaboratively. UNICEF, with Headquarters and MENA Regional Office support, spearheaded a Rigths and Results Based Management workshop for senior UN Country Team leadership and planning specialists, followed by an office-wide Results and Rights programming for UNICEF staff. By end of the year, the UN developed an outline of National Development Plan priorities to be supported by the UN and UNICEF cast the results framework and strategic intent for its next country programme through an internal Visioning exercise. 
UNICEF leadership of UN Youth Group and Operations Management Team contributed to common effectiveness and efficiency agendas and notably enabled addressing of a legal change on temporary work affecting UN personnel. UNICEF implemented several initiatives to strengthen staff resilience, well-being and capacities, including development of a comprehensive resilience guide, a visit of the UN Ombudsman and a staff retreat on living UNICEF values in practice. Trainings on Environmental and Social Safeguards policy rollout and a consultative risk assessment workshop with regional office support were conducted, and missions of regional advisors in Health, WASH and Child Protection reinforced quality of programme delivery and planning. 
In terms of resource mobilisation, the office invested in its existing partnerships and the development of new ones, including through joint UN programmes, with over 19 million USD mobilized in 2025. New partnerships were signed notably with SIDA, the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), the Peacebuilding Fund, the joint SDG Fund on Just Energy Transition, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund on the Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection for Just Transitions.
Among expenditures exceeding 17 million USD, about 8.5 million were operated as transfers to partners, in full compliance with HACT benchmarks, and 4.5 million in institutional service contracts. Construction and rehabilitation remained a support to modelling approaches prior to scale-up and human resources enabled a workforce expansion in UNV and UNOPS personnel for specific programme components.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
International Environment, Multilateral Cooperation and Stakeholder Engagement
Amid a global and national decline in support for multilateralism, and a reduction in development aid - including the dissolvement of USAID and a European shift toward migration and security priorities, the country office continued to benefit from long-standing cooperation and strong access to government counterparts. The UN’s 80th anniversary celebrations and the visit of a delegation from the UNICEF Executive Board (video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P20KnFS76C4) provided strategic opportunities to reaffirm Tunisia’s sustained investments in children over the past seven decades and to highlight UNICEF’s continued partnership - further strengthening mutual trust.
 
Government institutions remain UNICEF’s primary partners. At the same time, opportunities exist to deepen collaboration with UN agencies, international financial institutions, and regional partners such as the World Bank and the European Union, particularly on disability inclusion, climate action, and fiscal sustainability. Engagement with civil society and the private sector is gradually expanding, although the operational space for civil society has become more constrained. Meanwhile, reforms in media regulatory structures highlight the need to diversify outreach and advocacy channels.
 
Youth participation - especially in the climate agenda - is growing, supported by platforms and consultation mechanisms tailored to different age groups. However, avenues for engaging younger children still require reinforcement. A key lesson from the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) process is the importance of investing in children’s mobilization and advocacy skills, alongside sustained sensitization of government partners, to ensure that young people can contribute meaningfully and be heard. 
 
National Policy Priorities and Institutional Developments
Tunisia’s emerging national agenda prioritizes human capital, ecological transition, and social and economic planning. Inclusive consultations informed the 2026-2030 national development plan, expected to be finalized in early 2026 and to guide future UNSDCF and UNICEF programming. However, progress on structural reforms remains uneven, particularly in education, where delays in governance reforms have slowed policy development and implementation. Despite economic and political constraints, UNICEF retains strong convening power and supported significant results in 2025, including the institutionalization of a child benefit for vulnerable children aged 6-18. National discourse shifted toward a stronger emphasis on family and family cohesion, a trend that may influence public framing of child rights. In a global context of declining support for child rights, the country office exercises particular care in the articulation of these issues in public reporting. As migration management becomes more nationally driven amid rising vulnerabilities for children on the move, UNICEF continues to apply an inclusive, non-discriminatory approach, with calibrated advocacy and reporting to reach all children. This shift is occurring amid heightened vulnerabilities for children on the move, who continue to face barriers in accessing shelter, protection services, health care, and education. 
Strategic financing focus and opportunities for system strengthening
Throughout the last decade Tunisia prioritised social justice and equity in budgetary decisions, maintaining social expenditures at near constant levels according to UNESCWA, while public debt more than doubled as ratio of GDP. Prosocial decisions, including on expansion of social protection, entailed a 20 per cent year-on-year in the Ministry of Social Affair’s budget alone in the last budge law. Going forward, mobilising financing for development requires going hand in hand with improved efficiency of spending, including through the review of social service infrastructure and workforces in line with demographic trends identified in the 2024 census round. 
Budgetary constraints reinforce the importance of optimizing existing infrastructures, outcome-based streamlining of social sector workforces and institutions working on overlapping or adjacent mandates in relation to children, families and communities. UNICEF joined as a key driving agency in joint UN reflections on how to support national dialogue with development partners on financing for development and public financial management and supports sector planning and reforms in sectors including education, health and social protection. 
Evidence generation remains central to supporting reforms, informing policy dialogue and facilitating the transition from external to national financing. Opportunities lie in continuing to reinforce UNICEF’s role in technical assistance and policy advisory functions, grounded in context-specific data and UNEG-standard evaluations. Applying organisational thinking on focus, scale and impact, going forward, key interventions will be carried out with pathways to scale associated with evidence, advocacy and financing roadmaps to institutionalisation and coverage of whole child populations through strengthened national systems.
Digitalization emerges as key vector to strengthening governance and systems. In example, UNICEF strengthened the Ministry of Health’s Information Centre to securely store and process large volumes of vaccination data in real time across all 24 governorates since the COVID 19 pandemic. By 2025, 147,509 children had digital immunization records, 982,814 vaccination acts were registered, and more than 7,900 public and private health professionals were using the system. In another example, UNICEF continued to support the roll-out of a digital payment card allowing beneficiaries of the national social protection programme to withdraw cash at a time that suits them best, removing rigid withdrawal deadlines, facilitating access, and strengthening financial inclusion for vulnerable households. 
Organizational change and regional opportunities
Recent organizational developments within UNICEF, including the Africa Strategy and establishment of Centres of Excellence (COE) are expanding opportunities for South-South cooperation and cross-country knowledge exchange. These shifts support collaboration across the continent, promote shared learning, and accelerate progress on Strategic Plan impact areas and priorities such as social protection, climate resilience, and digital transformation.
UNICEF Tunisia is expected to benefit from the Amman COE and strengthened knowledge sharing among middle-income countries, enabling it to both draw on and contribute to regional expertise. This will reinforce Tunisia’s role in peer learning, technical exchange, and the dissemination of good practices, while strengthening national ownership and investment.

Yemen remains in a prolonged and multifaceted crisis for more than a decade resulting in destruction of infrastructure, collapse of basic public services, coupled with economic decline, fragmentation of public institutions, and climate shocks and hazards. These overlapping shocks have pushed large segments of population to unprecedented levels of food insecurity, malnutrition, and extreme poverty levels with children bearing the heaviest burden. In addition to this, the security situation further deteriorated in 2025 particularly in de-facto authority (DFA) controlled areas with air strikes, attacks in the red rea, and detention of United Nations staff and closure of offices.  
 
Yemen’s public finance system, which is central to sustaining essential services, has been severely disrupted. Since 2015, Yemen’s socio-economic conditions deteriorated due to collapse of public revenues, declining remittances, trade disruptions, fuel shortages, high inflation, the banking sector crisis and reduced humanitarian aid, while public revenues declined by 30 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2025. Such pressures have eroded the government’s ability to finance basic services, resulting in education, health, nutrition and water systems becoming increasingly dependent on external aid at a time when official development assistance (ODA) declining. According to World Bank Fall 2025 report, total expenditure in the first half of 2025 fell by 10 per cent year-on-year in the internationally recognized government (IRG) areas. This is mainly due to significant spending cuts, with a large share of the adjustment affecting civil servants’ payments. In addition, according to the latest available data[1], the real gross domestic product (GDP) was projected to decline by 1.5 per cent in 2024 following a –2.0 per cent contraction in 2023, a contraction that threatens to further heighten food insecurity across the country. GDP per capita dropped to just US$ 469 - less than half of its pre-conflict level- leaving families with extremely limited resources to meet children’s essential needs. 
 
 Inflation during 2025 has been highly volatile, driven mainly by exchange rate fluctuations (in IRG) and persistent supply disruptions. Early in the year, food prices surged due to depreciation of the Yemeni rial and import constraints, intensifying cost-of-living pressures. Mid-year, IRG authorities intervened in the market, stabilizing the exchange rate and triggering a sharp 34 per cent month-on-month drop in food prices in August. However, this decline reflected currency appreciation rather than improvements in supply or demand fundamentals. Overall, inflation remains fragile, with risks tied to high import costs, foreign exchange shortages, and structural trade bottlenecks, leaving price stability vulnerable to renewed pressures[2]. Soaring prices have hit poor households the hardest, as they spend the majority of their income on daily survival. For millions of women, girls and boys, this translates into fewer meals, disrupted learning of schooling, untreated illnesses, and heightened protection risks. Families increasingly find themselves with no option other than to adopt negative coping strategies, such as child labour, early marriage and reduced access to healthcare and education. 
 
Poverty reflects the depth of Yemen’s crisis. According to the recently published Multidimensional Poverty report, half of all households live in multidimensional poverty, experiencing simultaneous deprivations in income, health, education, and access to basic services. Alarmingly, nearly 7 in 10 children (68.6 per cent) face at least two overlapping deprivations - such as malnutrition, lack of safe water, inadequate healthcare, or being out of school while 1 in 2 households in Yemen live in multidimensional poverty. This represents not only an immediate humanitarian emergency but also a generational crisis that threatens Yemen’s human capital and future development[3]. In addition, the country remains at the lowest tier of human development index (HDI) globally, ranking among the world’s most vulnerable nations, and reached 0.445 in 2024 [4].
 
Layered on top of the above mentioned economic and institutional fragility, Yemen is particularly one of the world’s most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. According to the Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN), Yemen ranks 173rd out of 187 countries, reflecting both high exposure to climate hazards and limited adaptive capacity.[5] Since 2015, vulnerability of people in Yemen has deepened, not only due to the escalating effects of global warming, but also because the conflict has severely constrained the ability of the country to prepare for, mitigate or respond to climate shocks. These findings are supported by UNICEF’s Climate Risk Index for Children (2021), which reinforces this by scoring Yemen a 7.4 [6] out of a scale of 10, where 10 represents the highest risk, indicating the severe environmental and child-specific vulnerabilities Yemini children face. Climate shocks such as floods, droughts, and heat are increasingly disrupting livelihoods, damaging infrastructure, exacerbating food insecurity and disease outbreaks, putting more children at high risk.
 
All these challenges have implications on UNICEF’s programmes and operations and the organization’s ability to deliver results at scale for children. Humanitarian needs are raising sharply[7][8]. In 2025, about 19.5 million people of which 10.8 million children are in need of humanitarian assistance compared to 9.5 million children in 2024, and 4.5 million children out of school compared to 4.2 million in 2024. At the same time, 7.4 million children urgently require protection services compared to 7.0 million in 2024[9].
 
SDGs 2 - Ending all Forms of Malnutrition and 3 - Ensure Healthy Lives and Well-being for All: In Yemen, child malnutrition is among the highest in the world, and the nutrition situation continues to deteriorate. Half of Yemen’s children – or 2.3 million – are malnourished, including 600,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition. Immunization rate is another serious issue for children in Yemen. Only 69 per cent of children under one year of age are fully immunized, and 20 per cent of them have received no vaccines at all – one of the worst rates globally [10]. According to the IGME 2024 estimates, neonatal mortality and maternal mortality are also persistently high at 21 per 1,000 live births and 118 per 100,000 respectively. Epidemics and disease outbreaks coupled with limited access to clean water and proper sanitation continue to threaten the physical and mental wellbeing of millions of girls, boys and women across the country.[11] At the same time, over 55 per cent of health facilities are fully functional. Child survival in Yemen has shown steady progress despite prolonged conflict. Under-five mortality declined from 53 deaths per 1,000 live births (2013 DHS) to 41 (2023 MICS), with the latest Inter Agency Mortality Estimate (IGME) 2024 estimate at 39 per 1,000. This progress reflects the cumulative impact of sustained investments in primary health care (PHC), including maternal, newborn and child health services and routine immunization.
 
SDG 4 - Ensure Inclusive and Equitable Quality Education: Education is also facing serious crisis. Over 4.5 million school-aged children - including both girls and boys - are in need of education support with 1 in 4 children out of school[12]. Schools continue to be targeted, teachers’ salaries are unpaid, and poverty adds more layer of challenge resulting in disrupting education for children. Muhamasheen children and children with disabilities face even greater barriers resulting in limited access to inclusive education. Education system has all but collapsed with very low learning outcomes. Yemen ranks lowest in MENA with an extreme learning poverty rate of 95 per cent (Yemen Education Sector Plan (ESP) 2024–2030). 
 
SDG 6: Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
The most recent 2023 MICS-6 data shows that around 15.3 million people, including eight million children, lack access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, with 81.1 per cent of household members using improved sources of drinking water, 62.2 per cent using improved sanitation facilities, and 62.2 per cent using basic handwashing facilities where water and soap or detergent are present. The limited access to WASH facilities, services and supplies is associated with elevated risk of diseases such as cholera and dengue.
 
SDG 16.2: Ending abuse, exploitation, trafficking, and all forms of violence against and torture of children.
Child rights violations are still high in Yemen, with 562 grave violations against 499 children verified between January and September 2025, bringing the cumulative figure to about 12,000 children having been killed or maimed due to the conflict between March 2015 and the end of September 2025, according to the United Nations Country Taskforce on Monitoring and Reporting Grave Violations against Children. The true toll is likely to be far higher. However, there are currently limited feedback mechanisms to report child rights abuse.
