In Yemen’s complex political environment and multifaceted humanitarian crisis, declined financial resources, and heightened security and access constraints, UNICEF delivered impactful results for women, girls and boys  both in the DFA and IRG areas of Yemen through its five field offices and country office. 
 
In addition to nationally implemented programmes of system strengthening, unconditional cash transfer (UCT) and primary health care (PHC), Yemen country office (YCO) continued to robustly target the most vulnerable groups in deprived districts and delivered programmes through the five identified gateways (primary health care centers, schools, social service centers, internally displaced person (IDP) camps and community outreach), as well as further prioritization of implementation of lifesaving interventions in de facto authority (DFA) controlled areas as a result of the challenging operating environment. 
 
In 2025, YCO received US$85.4 million in new income from donor contributions and funds carried forward from previous years, utilized US$257.5 million to implement key lifesaving and development programming. 
 
Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives: 
Child survival in Yemen has shown steady progress despite prolonged conflict. Under-five mortality declined from 53 deaths per 1,000 live births (2013 DHS) to 41 (2023 MICS), with the latest Inter Agency Mortality Estimate (IGME) 2024 estimate at 39 per 1,000. This progress reflects the cumulative impact of sustained investments in primary health care (PHC), including maternal, newborn and child health services and routine immunization. In 2025, UNICEF maintained leadership in PHC by maintaining support to 3,100 facilities and community platforms, enabling access to essential services for 4.6 million people, mainly women and children, including in hard-to-reach areas.
 
UNICEF’s PHC strengthening focused not only on access, but on quality and sustainability. A nationwide general practitioner (GP) mentorship programme, involving 200 GPs improved clinical quality and service performance, while targeted investments expanded emergency obstetric and newborn care and strengthened referral pathways in 80 facilities nationwide. In parallel, UNICEF advanced sustainable PHC financing and optimization strategies, including policy dialogue, fiscal and regulatory assessments, and subnational pilots—marking a deliberate shift from crisis-driven system preservation toward longer-term systems strengthening and recovery.
 
In immunization, UNICEF combined PHC stabilization with equity-focused outreach, achieving a major breakthrough in DFA areas where services outside PHCs had been banned for nearly three years. This enabled over 2.2 million previously unreached children to receive vaccinations and integrated services and contributed to slowing outbreaks, alongside delivery of 15 million vaccine doses nationwide. These gains were achieved despite system-wide constraints.
 
UNICEF also strengthened preparedness and response to public health emergencies. During the ongoing cholera outbreak, UNICEF expanded treatment capacity sufficient for 120,000 cases, trained 580 health workers, and integrated vaccination, WASH, and risk communication interventions - reducing mortality and reinforcing readiness for future shocks.
 
On the nutrition front, treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) was sustained through health facilities and mobile teams, reaching over 342,000 caseload (61 per cent of the annual target), demonstrating the continued functionality and resilience of core nutrition platforms despite access limitations and operational disruptions. 
 
Preventive nutrition outcomes further highlight the effectiveness of decentralized delivery models in humanitarian contexts. A network of 21,620 community health and nutrition volunteers (CHNVs) operating across community, outreach, and facility platforms played a critical role in maintaining service utilization in hard-to-reach areas. Coverage of key micronutrient deficiency prevention interventions reached 2.05 million (65 per cent) children 6-59 months for vitamin A supplementation, 1.85 million (65 per cent) children 6-24 months for Micronutrient Powders, and 1.72 million (62 per cent) children for deworming tablets, indicating sustained population-level access despite mobility constraints. High coverage of iron–folate supplementation among 2.03 million (85 per cent) pregnant and lactating women, and 2.59 million (116 per cent) pregnant and breastfeeding women on infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling reflects strong community demand and effective outreach, while also highlighting the need for continued investments in data quality assurance to address potential double counting.
In parallel, UNICEF accelerated the rollout of malnutrition prevention strategies to strengthen sustainability and quality. The Maternal, Adolescent, Infant and Young Child Nutrition guidelines were finalized and rollout initiated, including completion of master trainer and training-of-trainers programmes reaching 96 participants (national nutrition experts, pediatricians, obstetricians and gynecologists) establishing the foundation for large-scale health worker training planned for early 2026. Complementary system strengthening actions included adaptation of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) guidelines and the Yemen Food Options package to improve complementary feeding practices, alongside the introduction of practical behavior change tools such as the bowl and spoon approach, a practical guide for teaching families on food groups for child feeding.
At the strategic level, Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Yemen, with UNICEF’s leadership and technical support, advanced the national nutrition agenda through strengthened multisectoral governance. Key milestones included finalization of the Multisectoral Nutrition Action Plan (MSNAP) Common Results Framework and MEAL framework, development of a robust Investment Case, and submission of the MSNAP Decree for Cabinet approval. Together, these achievements reinforced coordination, accountability, and alignment for sustained, high-impact nutrition action in Yemen.
 
Goal Area 2: Every child learns: 
During the reporting period, UNICEF made substantial progress in strengthening Yemen’s education system through a comprehensive approach encompassing system strengthening, access, and quality improvement. In partnership with the Ministry of Education (MoE), UNICEF advanced capacity building, aiming to improve learning outcomes for all children, particularly girls. Ten standardized training manuals were developed, and 1,123 education personnel from central, governorate, and district levels trained, 26 per cent of whom were female. This initiative significantly enhanced institutional capacity and promoted more effective education service delivery across administrative levels.
 
In collaboration with UNESCO and the MoE, UNICEF finalized the Education Management Information System (EMIS) roadmap and successfully conducted a school census in Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) areas. These efforts strengthened evidence-based planning, policy formulation, and equitable resource allocation nationwide.
 
UNICEF also expanded access to safe and inclusive learning environments. A total of 1,149 (more than double the planned figure of about 500) classrooms were rehabilitated across four governorates, benefiting 104,616 children, including 45 per cent girls, with gender-sensitive features such as improved sanitation. Additionally, 145,054 children (63 per cent of target) received teaching and learning materials across formal schools, temporary learning spaces, and IDP camps. Formal and non-formal education programmes reached 12,058 children (10 per cent of target), half of them girls, and successfully reintegrated 2,718 learners into public schools.
Quality improvements were reinforced through teacher support and professional development. UNICEF provided incentives to 559 female teachers in rural areas and supported over 5,900 (9 per cent of target), temporary, volunteer, and IDP teachers to sustain learning continuity. Furthermore, 1,378 educators (50 per cent of target), were trained in literacy, numeracy, accelerated learning, and climate change education. UNICEF also supported national examinations for 89,315 children (18 per cent of target), ensuring learning progression and system stability. Overall, there has been less interest from donor partners in investing in Yemen, particularly in the education sector. Targets were originally set based on specific funding prospects and pipelines that were later reduced or dropped altogether. On top of this, recent operational challenges in DFA areas led to a complete pause in field activities and the reprogramming of several key interventions, which meant that some agreed targets could not be met.
 
Goal Area 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation: 
In 2025, UNICEF finalized and launched Yemen’s National Plan of Action for Child Protection (NPA), establishing a unified roadmap for prevention, response, and system strengthening in fragile contexts. A central focus was strengthening the social service workforce, with consultations leading to standardized training modules and capacity building for 770 personnel, a 41 per cent increase from 2024, enhancing age-appropriate, gender-responsive child protection, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and child-friendly justice services. Birth registration progress was hindered by systemic bottlenecks and the IRG’s creation of a separate system. Community-based mechanisms were expanded with 22 centres to provide localized prevention and protection services. Accountability remained strong, with nearly 99 per cent of grave child rights violations verified, informing United Nations Children and Armed Conflict (CAAC) reporting and advocacy. UNICEF also engaged with task forces, recruitment centres, and authorities to strengthen protocols for the safe release and reintegration of children from armed groups.
Under its service delivery output, UNICEF sustained vital child protection services in Yemen despite conflict, funding shortages, and operational disruptions. Integrated MHPSS reached 39,154 individuals (78 per cent of target), strengthening resilience and coping mechanisms through schools, health facilities, and community structures. Case management prioritized highly vulnerable children, directly supporting 451 and referred 4,569 (68 per cent of the planned 7,500) children to essential child protection services, though overall reach declined due to programme suspensions in DFA areas. Legal aid was provided to 1,243 children (83 per cent target), focusing on those at risk of severe penalties, underscoring lifesaving interventions. Birth registration faced systemic bottlenecks and political complications, with only 323 children (less than 1 per cent of the planned target of 250,000) registered, highlighting the urgent need for restored reporting and system reform.
UNICEF also supported programmes addressing behaviour change. UNICEF addressed acute child protection risks in contaminated areas through Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE), reaching 309,387 people via mass media and community engagement, achieving 77 per cent of its planned target of 400,000 despite access and funding constraints. Direct assistance was provided to 500 children injured by UXO/ERW, and prosthetic supplies supported 195 children at the Prosthetic Rehabilitation Center in Sana’a. A knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) study informed Yemen’s national Mine Action Strategy. Concurrently, UNICEF tackled gender-based violence (GBV), child marriage, and female genital mutilation through an intersectoral approach, benefiting 902,398 individuals, 120 per cent above target, via prevention, risk reduction, and survivor-centered services. GBV interventions were integrated into health and education systems, with post exposure prophylaxis kits supplied for rape survivors. Life skills programs empowered 24,155 adolescents (97 per cent of target) to resist harmful practices and navigate unsafe environments, strengthening resilience despite funding limitations.
 
Goal Area 4: Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment: 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened Yemen’s WASH sector to deliver climate-resilient and sustainable services, protecting children’s health and education. Through WASH Cluster leadership, UNICEF coordinated over 100 partners, reducing duplication and ensuring timely support. Key achievements included training 87 government staff on water management, environmental and social safeguards (ESS), and emergency preparedness; completing a solarization case study; and advancing evidence-based programming through climate vulnerability assessments and Mocha water resource mapping. At the community level, 389 participants received climate resilience training, and five schools developed resilience plans. These interventions reduced disease risks, safeguarded education continuity, and enhanced dignity for children. 
 
UNICEF’s WASH programme in 2025 reached 1.17 million people (117 per cent of target), with sustainable water services through 54 projects across 11 governorates, reducing reliance on costly water trucking and improving health and hygiene. To address energy bottlenecks, 29 solar-powered systems were installed, producing 9.6 million liters daily for 240,000 people, ensuring uninterrupted supply during fuel crises. Emergency water assistance supported 618,000 people in cholera-affected and flood-hit areas, preventing outbreaks and safeguarding children’s health and education. These interventions delivered lasting benefits - safe water access, reduced disease risks, and resilience during shocks. 
Furthermore, UNICEF improved sanitation for 350,022 people (47 per cent of target), including 112,007 with safely managed services through rehabilitation, expansion, and construction of sanitation networks. Hygiene promotion reached 467,621 people (above the planned number of 250,000), complemented by 66,803 hygiene kits, emergency latrines, and desludging in IDP camps. Five villages in Dhamar were declared open defecation free, benefiting 4,200 people and reducing disease risks. At the institutional level, 83 healthcare facilities received WASH upgrades, with 10 implementing WASH FIT standards, ensuring safer maternal and child care. These interventions reduced exposure to waterborne diseases, improved hygiene, safeguarded education, and enhanced dignity for children - fully aligning with UNICEF’s mandate to uphold child rights.
 
Goal Area 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life: 
In 2025, UNICEF made a significant progress in advancing Yemen’s national capacities for evidence-based, child-focused social and economic policymaking. A major milestone was the finalization and launch of the Multidimensional Poverty (MDP) analysis. The MDP which was led by the Central Statistical Organization provided the most comprehensive insight to date on the severity and overlap of child poverty in Yemen. The findings reveal that half of households in Yemen live in multidimensional poverty and 68.6 per cent of children face multiple deprivations. Building on this evidence, UNICEF developed 22 Governorate Poverty Profiles to support localized planning and prioritization.
 
UNICEF supported Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation (MoPIC) to translate the MDP results into actionable policy through the development of evidence-based papers. During the reporting period, papers on primary health care governance and financing, and nutrition policy options were developed, with a paper on economic growth and poverty reduction being developed. This was complemented by strengthened monitoring of socio-economic vulnerabilities through two editions of the Yemen Socio-Economic Update (YSEU), with a third focused on climate impacts underway.
 
Furthermore, progress in Public Finance for Children (PF4C) included the development of a national PF4C Road Map and the establishment of a multi-ministerial Leadership Development Group (LDG), reinforcing national ownership and cross-sectoral collaboration for child-responsive budgeting. In partnership with the health programme, social policy programme supported sustainable PHC financing through a pilot sustainability optimization plan and a regulatory framework assessment in Taiz, informing a forthcoming national PHC Financing Plan.
 
Towards advancing climate-responsive and disability-inclusive social protection, UNICEF conducted assessments on climate shocks, functional difficulties among people with disabilities, and continued its technical and financial support to the Handicap Care and Rehabilitation Fund and Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour (MoSAL). The launch of Yemen’s nationally owned Social Protection Strategic Framework marked a major step toward an integrated, shock-responsive system. This was a result of the support to the Social Protection Consultative Committee (SPCC). The technical support to the SPCC continues to enable it to maintain its key convening role in support of a more coordinated and evidence-based social protection policy making and dialogue. 
 
Capacity strengthening of the Social Welfare Fund remained central, with substantial progress in institutional development and Cash Plus programming. Advanced nutrition- and education-sensitive Cash Plus models are being finalized to reach 12,000 children in 2026, despite challenges related to funding, system delays, and access constraints.
 
On Social behaviour Change (SBC) programming:  
In 2025, UNICEF sustained community engagement and social mobilization across its programmes, reaching over 7.1 million people through household visits, community events, schools, and mosques, supported by 12,000 community-based cadres, including volunteers, religious leaders, and health workers. Over 1,050 health education corners and mother groups were strengthened to engage caregivers on primary health care and lifesaving practices, while radio, television, and other audio-visual content reached an estimated 12 million people.
 
UNICEF contributed to restoring immunization demand in northern governorates, supporting the vaccination of 2.27 million children, and facilitated the successful implementation of two polio campaigns and four integrated outreach activities in the south. UNICEF also advanced nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection initiatives through behavior change interventions, including promotion of IYCF practices, hygiene and climate resilience, learning outcomes for children in and out of school, and messages on child marriage, FGM, and GBV.
 
In response to cholera and acute watery diarrhoea outbreaks, UNICEF delivered rapid multi-channel communication, including innovative partnerships with the private sector. Efforts to institutionalize social and behavior change included academic partnerships to develop SBC curricula. UNICEF strengthened interagency coordination through the community engagement-accountability to affected populations (CE-AAP) and SBC working groups, generated evidence on immunization equity, climate change, and polio, and rolled out the positive parenting package as a flagship programme.
 
On Gender Equality:
UNICEF Yemen advanced gender equality despite severe constraints, reaching 1.5 million women and children through female community-based interventions delivering life-saving health, nutrition, education, protection, and WASH services. Integrated outreach provided immunization and nutrition to 2.2 million children and pregnant women, while 2.45 million mothers received IYCF counseling and 693,755 adolescent girls received iron-folate supplements. Evidence generation, including the Gender and Immunization Analysis, informed strategies such as the national Primary Health Care Strategy 2025–2028. At the institutional level, UNICEF strengthened mechanisms through the Gender Action Plan 2025–2027, reinforcing accountability and embedding gender equality as a transformative priority for programming.
 
On the humanitarian front:
The Yemen Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal required US$212 million for UNICEF’s response in 2025, of which US$47.1 million was received in 2025 and over US$30.3 million carried forward from 2024, leaving a funding gap of over US$134.4 million (63 per cent of the total amount required) to continue UNICEF’s life-saving work in Yemen. This year the Yemen Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) embarked on a series of reforms to advance a more streamlined, effective and field-driven approach to the humanitarian response, in line with the global ‘Humanitarian Reset’ endorsed by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee and the Yemen HCT position papers adopted in 2024. In addition, the HCT carried out reprioritization exercise and agreed on focusing on life-saving interventions in DFA areas. As a result, UNICEF aligned its response and focused on providing direct life-saving assistance and building systems to strengthen linkages between humanitarian action and development/resilience programming.
 
Out of the 5.8 million children targeted to be reached under UNICEF HAC, 2.35 million children were reached with critical lifesaving interventions in health, nutrition and WASH. 294,428 children (91per cent of the target) 6-59 months with severe wasting were admitted for treatment, while 98,525 children (49 per cent) 0-11 months received pentavalent 3 vaccines. In addition,  over 2.5 million primary care givers received infant and young child feeding counselling (40 per cent of the target) for children aged 0-23, 39,154 (15 per cent of the target) children, adolescents and caregivers accessed community-based mental health and psychosocial support and  902,398 (168 per cent of the target) women, girls and boys accessed gender-based violence risk mitigation, prevention and/or response interventions. Similarly, 309,384 (37 per cent of the target) children were provided with landmine or other explosive weapons prevention and/or survivor assistance interventions. Several challenges caused shortfalls in achieving planned targets, such as reprioritized focus, changes in delivery modality due to hurdles with authorities, funding and heightened security constraints in August 2025 leading to programme pause in late October 2025, and shortage of staff as a direct result. Monitoring and reporting also posed greater challenges in obtaining timely data and later in the year, remote monitoring was adopted as a mitigating measure.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The year 2025 unfolded as a vivid reminder that delivering results for women, girls and boys in Yemen is a marathon through shifting sands. Despite commendable gains, the operating environment remained fraught with systemic and contextual hurdles that demanded bold, innovative responses.
 
Fragile systems and fragmented governance: across sectors, institutional fragility continues to undermine scale and sustainability. Health systems, though strengthened through PHC, remain vulnerable to shocks, while education governance struggles with unpaid teachers and weak data systems. Child Protection faced a stark setback with the emergence of parallel birth registration systems and suspension of programming in the north symptomatic of fragmented authority and policy divergence. Social protection frameworks, though advancing, are constrained by fiscal stress and fragmented institutions, limiting the reach of inclusive, shock-responsive services.
 
Financing volatility: In 2025, UNICEF Yemen faced severe funding contractions, including the termination of USAID BHA support, a 60 per cent cut in World Bank nutrition funding, and no Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) allocations. Nutrition programming was hardest hit, forcing reliance on supply frontloading and reprogramming to sustain life-saving interventions. WASH, child protection and education interventions were similarly constrained by donor withdrawals and unpredictable pipelines, limiting service delivery and requiring prioritization of critical needs. These financial shocks occurred amid declining official development assistance and Yemen’s deepening fiscal crisis, leaving essential services increasingly dependent on shrinking external aid.
 
Operational disruptions and access barriers: Programme continuity was undermined by escalating operational shocks. Raids on UN premises, asset confiscation, and detention of national staff in DFA-controlled areas led to programme pause and adoption of remote modalities and reprogramming interventions toward IRG areas as appropriate. Red Sea security incidents further disrupted supply chains, while prolonged clearance and regulatory hurdles including YSMO requirements delayed delivery of critical supplies.  Additionally, insecurity and bureaucratic impediments including multiple layers of clearances from authorities curtailed humanitarian reach. 
 
Gendered constraints: Gender norms, notably mahram restrictions, further limited female workforce mobility and adolescent girls’ access to services eroding equity gains and slowing progress on gender-transformative programming.  
 
Climate stressors and service reliability: Yemen’s vulnerability to climate shocks deepened the crisis. High salinity of water sources, recurrent floods, and energy volatility strained WASH systems and heightened disease risks. Without climate-risk integration and resilient infrastructure, lifesaving services remain precarious.
 
Data gaps and accountability risks: Programme suspensions and remote modalities exposed weaknesses in monitoring and verification, risking double counting and blind spots. Reliable, interoperable data systems such as EMIS and digital registries are still nascent, constraining evidence-based decision-making and equitable resource allocation.
 
Lessons Learned 
Delivering impact at scale in Yemen’s complex operating environment revealed critical insights that will shape future programming. The most significant lesson is the transformative role of community-based platforms. Primary Health Care demonstrated that when services are rooted in local systems, they remain functional during shocks and extend reach to the most deprived communities.
 
Integration emerged as a game-changer. Linking health, nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection through shared gateways of schools, health facilities, and social service centers proved effective in reducing fragmentation and maximizing outcomes. The “one-stop-shop” approach in child protection illustrated how multisectoral programming can streamline access for vulnerable children.
 
Evidence-driven planning stood out as an accelerator. Tools such as EMIS, poverty profiles, and multisectoral nutrition frameworks enabled smarter resource allocation and strengthened accountability. These mechanisms are not merely technical instruments, but enablers of scale and sustainability through government ownership.
 
Geographical and programme prioritization proved to be an effective strategy in achieving impactful results for the most vulnerable women, girls and boys. The Composite Child Deprivation Index (CCDI) analysis, re-enforced by MICS 2023 and Multidimensional Poverty Index analysis enabled UNICEF to prioritize 14 governorates and 34 most deprived districts across Yemen and delivered targeted humanitarian and development interventions, ensuring that the most vulnerable women, girls and boys were reached.   
 
Finally, social and behavioral interventions reinforced the importance of community engagement. Restoring immunization demand, promoting positive parenting, and addressing harmful gender norms were pivotal in overcoming barriers that resources alone could not resolve.
 
The experience of 2025 confirms that achieving scale in Yemen requires agility, innovation, and partnerships anchored in equity ensuring that every child, regardless of circumstance, survives, learns, and thrives.
 
The way forward
As 2025 closes, UNICEF Yemen stands at a pivotal juncture armed with hard-won insights and a renewed commitment to transform adversity into opportunity. The lessons of this year underscore a simple truth: resilience is not an abstract goal; it is built through deliberate, adaptive strategies that protect children today while shaping systems for tomorrow.
 
Recalibrating programme strategies: the office will deepen its twin-track approach delivering lifesaving interventions while accelerating system strengthening. In health, the Community PHC Strategy will be scaled nationwide, embedding quality and equity at the heart of service delivery. Nutrition programming will pivot from crisis response to prevention, leveraging the Multisectoral Nutrition Action Plan and behavior-change innovations to sustain gains. Education will prioritize inclusive, climate-resilient schools and expand EMIS-driven planning to ensure no child is left behind.
 
Driving innovation and integration: insights from 2025 reaffirm the power of integrated gateways of schools, health facilities, and community platforms as accelerators of impact. Moving forward, UNICEF will institutionalize “one-stop-shop” models linking child protection, social protection, and gender-responsive services. Digital solutions will be scaled to strengthen monitoring, accountability, and interoperability across registries and data systems.
 
Expanding partnerships and financing horizons: recognizing the volatility of traditional funding streams, the office will pursue diversified financing, tapping climate funds, development banks, and private sector partnerships. Strategic advocacy will amplify Yemen’s voice in global platforms, while local partnerships will be nurtured to reinforce community ownership and sustainability.
Embedding resilience and equity: climate-smart programming will become a cornerstone of WASH and education strategies, with solarized water systems and disaster-prepared schools safeguarding continuity. Gender equality will be mainstreamed through negotiated field protocols and expanded female workforce participation, ensuring transformative change for women and girls.
 
The commitment ahead: UNICEF Yemen will harness these insights to move beyond reactive programming toward proactive, risk-informed planning. By leveraging evidence, innovation, and collaboration, the office will chart a course where humanitarian response and development converge building resilient systems that uphold every child’s right to survive, learn, and thrive.

Status of political and socio-economic landscape 
Afghanistan has an estimated population of 45 million. Children under the age of 18 constitute about 52% of the population. The economic outlook remains uncertain due to persistent poverty, widening trade deficit and reduced GDP (2.3% to 1.9% in 2025[1]). Global shifts in aid led to a decline in funding with the UN Humanitarian Response Plan of $ $2.42 Billion funded at 44%, while UNICEF's Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) received 70% of the required $1.2 billion. 
In 2025, about 23.2 million people, including 11.7 million children, needed humanitarian assistance[2] driven largely by massive returnee crisis from neighboring countries, recurrent natural disasters and climate induced emergencies that compounded existing vulnerabilities from decades of conflict, chronic poverty, and multiple disease outbreaks that negatively impact children and women. The restriction on education for adolescent girls beyond grade six and restrictions on participation of women in the workplace, including for UN female national staff, deprives almost half of the human capital contribution to the nation’s economy and development.
Improved access across the country meant that basic services could be delivered at scale in remote areas ensuring equity. Unfortunately, improved access also increased the vulnerability of children with 189 child casualties from explosive devices recorded and 257 districts (out of 401) remain contaminated by Explosive Ordnances in 2025. Compared to 2024[3], the De Facto Authorities (DfA) issued 31 directives including 3 related to female participation in humanitarian operations.
Regional trends and dynamics that have affected Afghanistan. 
The deportation of undocumented Afghans from Iran and Pakistan resulted in 2.8 million Afghan returnees in 2025, over 60% of whom are children[4]. The influx heightened protection risks and strained available social services, especially for women and children. Cross-border tension between Afghanistan and Pakistan has constrained logistic route and disrupted shipment of UNICEF’s humanitarian supplies.
UNICEF's Climate Risk Index for Children (CCRI) report (2021) ranks Afghanistan as “extremely high" risk, with a CCRI score of 7.6 and ranks 15th out of 163 CCRI countries. Droughts, floods, erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, and glacial melt impacted water security and livelihoods affecting over 400,000 people. In 2025, over 118,137 people were affected by natural disasters[5] in addition to the 2,200 causalities and 8,471 families (about 56,000 people) impacted by the earthquake in eastern Afghanistan in August 2025.
Progress towards 2030 Agenda for SDGs and the call to “leave no child behind.”
The 2025 Human Global Report[6] notes Afghanistan’s slowed Sustainable Development (SDGs) progress due to conflict, economic fragility, recurrent humanitarian crises and restrictions on access to education and employment. Analysis of 48 child-related SDGs[7] identified the need to address neonatal mortality, stunting, violence, child poverty, birth registration, and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH).
UNICEF continue to advocate for Girls Education as a top priority for “leaving no child behind” in Afghanistan, with over 2.2 million girls and 110,000 tertiary institution students affected by the decree issued by DfA in March 2022 banning girls’ post primary education. 
Status of child rights referencing impact and outcome indicators in the Strategic Plan (SP) 2022–2025.
A multidimensional poverty index (MPI), based on MICS 2022–23, indicated 66.9% of children (around 15 million) and 56.8% of adults (over 10.6 million) live in multidimensional poverty[8]. About 70.8% of the rural population experience multidimensional poverty compared to 37.4% in urban areas. Afghanistan ranks 181 out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index with a score of 0.496.[9]
Afghanistan has a high maternal mortality ratio of 620 per 100,000 live births and under-five mortality rate of 55 per 1,000 live births[10]. Prematurity, birth asphyxia, and sepsis are leading causes of newborn deaths[11]. Polio transmission persists, with 10 cases of Wild Poliovirus type 1 (WPVI) and 69 positive environmental samples reported in 2025[12].
Child food poverty in Afghanistan is widespread, with 90% of young children lacking adequate diets.  Over 11 million people are facing severe food insecurity[13]. 3.5 million children and 1.1 million pregnant and lactating women are malnourished. Poor maternal nutrition contributes to high maternal and infant mortality rates, and low birth weight[14]. 
Nearly one-third of the population, including 6.8 million children, lack access to basic drinking water, and 24% lack sanitation (46.3% in urban areas, 16.5% in rural settings)[15].
Afghanistan’s education sector faces a crisis-level learning poverty[16], low literacy and high out-of-school children. At the primary level, 53% of children are out of school (60% girls)[17]. Only 14% of children in Grades 2 and 3 possess basic reading skills, and 93% of children at late primary age are unable to read and comprehend a short, age-appropriate text.  
Children face multiple forms of violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect, and harmful practices. Nearly 58% of children under 5 lack a birth certificate, one in five children aged 5–17 is engaged in child labour.

Advancing national priorities and alignment with  results of UNSFA
  
In 2025, the Afghanistan National Development  Strategy was released by the DfA, and common areas of focus with the United Nations Strategic Framework (UNSFA) on economic and social  development were identified. UNICEF’s contributions, aligned to the UNSFA,  focused on improving access to life-saving humanitarian assistance and basic  needs services. As the WASH, nutrition, education and child protection  cluster lead, UNICEF’s supported humanitarian cluster coordination.
  
Actions on human rights treaties, CRC and universal  periodic review
  
The United Nations Country Task Force on Monitoring  and Reporting on Children and Armed Conflict in Afghanistan, as part of our  mandate on child’s rights, contributed to the Secretary-General’s Report on  grave violations against children. Between January to September 2025, the  Country Team verified 722 grave violations against 358 children (304 boys, 54  girls), a 40% decrease compared to the same period in 2024. UNICEF also  contributed to the Universal Periodic Review. 
  
Key programme  management results
  
Health: UNICEF’s support to primary  health care reached over 20 million people (60% women), including 5.6 million  children under 5 and 1.4 million newborns, through 2,409 UNICEF supported  health facilities and community platforms. Immunization services achieved 1.6  million Penta-3 doses and 16.6 million measles vaccinations. UNICEF  established 11 mini-Skills Lab across 10 provinces, upgraded 399 existing  labour rooms with newborn care corners and established 10 Special Newborn  Care Units. As a result, 50 facilities under the Basic Package of Health  Services (BPHS) and Essential Package of Hospital Services (EPHS) recorded an  overall Quality of Care (QoC) score improvement from 29% to 50% across seven  thematic areas[1]. 
  
Over 5,000 maternal and  newborn health providers (4,472 female and 685 male) benefitted from  Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health (MNCH) trainings strengthening their  skills and clinical readiness. This expanded cadre directly contributed to  improved coverage of essential services, enabling 1.5 million pregnant women access  to their first antenatal care (ANC) and ensured 905,801 births were attended  by skilled birth attendants. UNICEF led the development of national  guidelines for ANC, postnatal care, and management of non-communicable  diseases in pregnancy. 
  
A total of 13,718 (50%  female) Community Health Workers (CHW) were trained to enhance  Community-Based Health Care (CBHC) contributing to distribution of 16,042 CHW  kits to health posts. As part of efforts to strengthen and institutionalize  the CBHC system, a national-level mapping of health posts of CHWs was  completed. Findings revealed, 32,752 CHWs (52% female) currently operate at  16,547 health posts.
  
In 2025, Afghanistan  experienced a series of outbreaks, including acute watery diarrhoea (AWD)  with dehydration, acute respiratory infections (ARI), diarrheal diseases and  measles. UNICEF supported 15,980 oral rehydration points and 154 diarrhoea  treatment centres with zinc and oral rehydration solution (ORS), enabling the  treatment of more than 150,000 cases of AWD with dehydration and 2,461,942  cases of children under 5 with AWD. In addition, 7,672 health workers were  trained in basic disease surveillance and referral mechanisms strengthening  early detection and response capacities.
  
Polio: Over 12 million children under  5 were vaccinated against polio achieving a vaccination coverage rate of 98%.  This was accomplished using 71.52 million doses of oral polio vaccine through  8 campaigns [2] and a comprehensive pull  strategy, including a digital community engagement strategy. Innovative  strategies such as a cluster approach for high-risk areas, integrated service  delivery with WASH, health and nutrition contributed to monitoring and  referral of zero dose children.
  
Nutrition: UNICEF reached 10 million  children and women with essential preventive nutrition services and supplies.  Over 10 million children under 5 were screened for wasting and 611,000  children (354,380 girls) were treated in 3,260 outpatient and 140 inpatient Therapeutic  Feeding Centres (TFUs) with an 80% cure rate. UNICEF also provided multiple  micronutrient powder to 2.7 million children aged 6–59 months and distributed  vitamin A supplements to 9.9 million children under 5 during polio campaigns.  To enhance Community-Based Nutrition Programme (CBNP) services such as  screening, supplementation, referrals and behaviour change, 31,000 CHWs were  trained benefiting 2.9 million children. Nutrition counsellors (2,483 female)  delivered growth monitoring, infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counseling  and referral support to over 2.4 million primary caregivers of children under  1 year. Construction of three new TFUs in Jalalabad, Herat, and Mazar,  including procurement of over 14,000 metric tons of ready-to-use therapeutic  food (RUTF) improved access to critical care.
  
WASH: UNICEF supported the  construction and rehabilitation of 92 climate-resilient water supply systems  providing over 2 million people with access to safe water. A total of 2,227  communities, hosting nearly 1 million people, were certified Open Defecation  Free and improved access to basic sanitation benefiting 1.8 million people.  Progress on WASH-in-institutions has remained constrained as schools and  healthcare interventions are challenged by limited budgets. Emergency WASH  response reached 2.7 million people affected by earthquakes, floods, cholera  and returnee crisis. To address climate change pressure on water resources,  UNICEF constructed check dams and initiated groundwater recharge projects.  Establishment of 45 monitoring wells in Helmand River Basin and 100 data  loggers strengthened water resource monitoring and water early warning  scarcity. Ongoing impact monitoring will guide the scaling up of managed  aquifer recharge interventions to strengthen long-term water sustainability  for affected communities.
  
UNICEF also contributed  to Afghanistan’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 2.0, integrated  children’s and women’s concerns into water and climate strategies and  promoted regional cooperation through 2025 Tashkent “Water Diplomacy in  Central Asia” conference.
  
Education: UNICEF supported over 4  million children (41% girls) in public schools, Community Based Education (CBE),  and emergency settings with teaching and learning materials. A total of  442,011 marginalized children (65% girls) accessed education through 13,971  CBE classes. Additionally, 50,956 teachers (39% female) in 14,400 public  schools and 16,427 teachers (41% female) in CBEs received teaching and  learning materials while incentive payments were made to 17,779 teachers to  sustain continuity of learning. UNICEF installed 1,105 high-performance tents  for safe learning spaces, including 200 in earthquake affected areas.  Alternative learning pathways[3] targeting out-of-school  secondary grade girls, across 34 provinces, reached 3 million children[4].
  
UNICEF rehabilitated  232[5] public schools and rolled out  Teacher Development and Support (TDS) Training modules benefiting over 54,000  participants[6]. More than 224,000 coaching  sessions and 54,000 teacher Learning Circle (TLC)[7] sessions were conducted in  5,000 schools.
  
Early Childhood  Education (ECE) instructional practices were introduced in 255 classes,  reaching over 7,000 children (60% girls), laying strong educational  foundation for children aged 4–5, particularly girls. A cadre of 20 Master  Trainers were equipped with effective ECE methodologies to train and support  teachers to develop customized instructional materials. UNICEF also conducted  parenting support programme for 10,000 parents, employing early stimulation  and plays to foster early language development in 7,500 young children. 
  
UNICEF sustained its  Girls’ Access to Teacher Education (GATE) programme supporting over 1,000  qualified female teachers to increase enrollment and retention of girls in  schools. A digital learning platform was enhanced to improve access to  resources and support teacher training in safe settings. Over 500 female students (against a target  of 1,000) graduated  from the GATE programme. As part of the education in emergency response, 79  schools were rebuilt after earthquake and flood damage, benefiting 67,700 children  (64% girls), establishment of community-based learning initiatives and  temporary learning spaces reached 442,011 children (65% girls) and 30,840  returnee children respectively. 
  
Child  Protection:  UNICEF trained 7,628 (39% women) members of community-based structures to enhance  community-based child protection systems and deliver quality preventive and  responsive services. As a result, 625,671 children (50% girls) were  registered at birth and GBV prevention efforts enhanced. Risk education for  482,171 individuals contributed to a 42% reduction in child casualties. A  total of 329,000 people received structured mental health and psychosocial  services delivered through child-friendly spaces, multi-purpose centres,  schools and health facilities. UNICEF also supported community empowerment  initiatives to create safer environments for children and women through  violence prevention, risk education, psychosocial support, and positive parenting  programmes, reaching more than 2.2 million people. In addition, UNICEF’s  support to the Monitoring and Reporting of Grave Child Rights Violation achieved  89.5% success verification rate compared to 88% in 2024. 
  
Social Protection: UNICEF provided social  assistance to 524,257 people across 79,492 vulnerable households, including  333,358 children, 5,715 persons with disabilities and 21,260 displaced or  returning individuals. UNICEF delivered humanitarian cash assistance to  14,445 vulnerable households (94,600 people, including 58,895 children) in  areas affected by severe winter conditions, prolonged drought, and  earthquakes to address immediate life-saving needs. In the first half of  2025, an additional 6,536 households (37,233 people, including 22,418  children, 782 persons with disabilities and 1,058 internally displaced people  (IDP) and returnees, received support in response to severe winter  conditions. 
  
Adolescent Girls: Anaemia affect one in three adolescent  girls aged 10–19. UNICEF introduced a Community-Based Weekly Iron and Folic  Acid Supplementation (WIFS) model, delivered supplements to girls’ homes  through 1,979 CHWs (50% female), reaching over 2.5 million adolescent girls  in addition to 15,500 health posts, 30,000 CHWs and school-based WIFS in 17  provinces. UNICEF also mapped child and adolescent mental health services and  developed the National Child and Adolescent Mental Health Action Plan to  address widespread mental health needs in the Country. Over 80,000 women and  adolescent girls received integrated package of services[8] and information in 26 women and  girls’ safe spaces, while nearly 38,000 adolescent girls participated in  skills development and vocational training.
  
Integrated  programming
  
The Mother and Child  Cash Transfer (MCCT) programme improved MNCH services by providing cash  assistance to mothers and addressing demand side barriers to service uptake.  Redesigned using lessons learned, the programme supported 65,047 households  with pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and introduced community engagement  interventions to improve maternal and child health practices, infant and  maternal feeding practices, hygiene practices, antenatal care and  vaccination. 
  
UNICEF integrated Early  Childhood Development (ECD) into nutrition platforms, transitioning 50 urban  nutrition day care centres into Urban Child Nutrition and Development Centres  in Kabul. The deployment of 192 frontline and community workers and 161 ECD  personnel (officers and master trainers) resulted in the participation of 5,000  parents and 7,500 young children in parenting sessions. Over 90,000  caregivers received guidance on responsive feeding, nurturing care, and early  stimulation. An ECD measurement framework has been integrated into nutrition  information systems, and an ECD Taskforce established to enhance  multisectoral coordination.
  
UNICEF’s advocacy  and programmes for migrant children, including displaced children 
  
UNICEF corporate  advocacy strategy for the lifting of the school ban for adolescent girls in  Afghanistan was developed to sustain organizational commitment to education  access at all levels for Afghan girls. Advocacy also supported women-led  Civil Society Organisations and national non-governmental organizations  (NGOs) to promote alternative corridors for supply logistics, improved border  customs and clearance, while advancing cross-border engagement with India and  Pakistan to safeguard continuity of humanitarian supply chain.  
  
For polio eradication,  UNICEF supported advocacy to maintain collaboration with Pakistan, and  engaged religious leaders, community elders and female vaccinators to improve  immunization coverage. UNICEF further leveraged on its operational capacity,  partner networks and engagement with local authorities to respond at scale to  the unprecedented humanitarian needs of returnees from Iran and Pakistan,  expanding access to Basic Human Needs (BHN) services in the areas of return. 
  
Inclusivity and  accessibility for children with disabilities 
  
UNICEF maintained its  engagement with the Office of the Prison Administration (OPA), enabling 1,934  children in Juvenile Rehabilitation Centers and 934 children living with  their mothers in women’s prisons to access multi-sectoral services, including  psychosocial support and legal counseling. 
  
Education programmes in  Juvenile Rehabilitation Centers provided formal and literacy education and  reintegration into schooling. Over 300,000 enrolled children in Grades 4–12  and 185 learners benefited from literacy classes, while 100 children  re-enrolled in public schools after release through a multigrade, multiyear  approach. In addition, 5,175 people with disabilities received social  protection support ensuring a positive start in the first 1,000 days of life  and strengthening households’ resilience to disasters.
  
UN collaborative  mechanisms 
  
UNICEF’s First Foods  Initiative, a multi-sectoral programme launched with UN partners, focused on  improving young children’s diets through local, food-based systems. UNICEF  also advanced the national wasting agenda by rolling out WHO-aligned  guidelines and a Joint Action Plan with WFP, safeguarding access to  life-saving treatment. In addition, UNICEF partnered with UNFPA’s 133 Family  Health Houses to expand access to routine immunization services. 
  
UNICEF consolidated its  skilling and livelihoods portfolio under the Education Section by linking  skills development to sustainable livelihoods informed by local labour market  data. Through UN-to-UN partnership with UNESCO, more than 2,100 adolescents  and youth gained literacy and skills in agriculture, textiles, and  manufacturing.
  
Key contributing  factors to achievement of results 
  
Advocacy and  partnerships:  UNICEF diversified its revenue base by mobilizing traditional and  non-traditional donors. Key bilateral contributors included the UK, EU  (INTPA, ECHO), Japan, UN OCHA (AHF, CERF), Sweden, Denmark, the Gates  Foundation, ECW and GPE, while partnerships with Germany, the Republic of  Korea, and Norway were maintained.
  
South – South  Collaboration with China and India supported critical child-focused  programmes; the Government of India agreed to supply $4 million in routine  vaccines, while UNICEF China, in coordination with the Ministry of Commerce,  provided $23 million in essential life-saving supplies. 
  
Through engagement with  donors and financial institutions—the World Bank and the Asian Development  Bank, the largest supporters of health and education sectors— UNICEF  strengthened risk management, budget management, monitoring, and  Environmental and Social Safeguards (ESS) systems to address emerging  operational risks.
  
To broaden the  portfolio of national committees, which accounted for 10 % of the 2025  funding, UNICEF undertook targeted outreach to the French, German and UK  committees leading to new relationships with the Hong Kong and Switzerland  National Committees.
  
UNICEF received  $21.1Million in flexible funding from traditional donors and National  Committees (Denmark, Sweden, UK), representing approximately 6% of funds  raised in 2025. These funds have enabled rapid response to urgent needs,  including treatment of severe acute malnutrition for children under five  years, emergency WASH services and cash assistance for families impacted by  natural disasters.  Flexible  investments from donors, partners and individuals provided an immediate  lifeline during surges in humanitarian needs, allowing UNICEF to respond with  pre-positioned supplies and immediate services while mobilizing additional  resources.
  
Generate and harness  evidence: In  2025, UNICEF strengthened evidence generation through four evaluations on  social protection, health, nutrition, and WASH, contributing to 15 research  products and achieving (79%) of planned research, studies, and evaluations.
  
Strengthened sector  management information systems improved data quality and availability;  routine treatment data, triangulated with HMIS outpatient data for children  under 5, helped identify malnutrition hotspots in urban Kabul. As a result,  SAM admissions increased from around 3,000 to over 100,000 expected cases in  2025. 
  
The Community Nutrition  Sentinel Site (C-NSS) surveillance system expanded from 313 to 451 sites  across all provinces, supporting surveillance of more than 72,000 children.  Afghanistan also became the first country globally to integrate the Early  Childhood Food Insecurity Experience Scale (EC-FIES) and the Diet Quality  Questionnaire (DQQ) for children aged 6–23-months into a unified community  surveillance platform to inform humanitarian planning, early warning, and  response. 
  
Prevention of sexual  exploitation and abuse (PSEA): UNICEF strengthened protection against sexual  exploitation and abuse by training 2,517 staff and partners, certifying 75  investigators, and enabling safe reporting mechanisms for 1.1 million people.  Awareness campaigns reached 338,573 individuals, ensuring timely access to  information and support.
  
Gender-responsive  programming: UNICEF  partnered with women-led organizations, reaching over 82,000 women and  adolescents through 26 safe spaces and delivering integrated package of  services and  information. The capacity of 4,537 frontline workers was strengthened on  gender responsive care, respectful maternity care, GBV services and PSEA risk  mitigation. As a result, 16,447 women, men, boys and girls [11] participated in dialogue  sessions on preventing child marriage, promoting the rights of adolescent  girls, and advancing gender equality. 
  
Social and behaviour  change: UNICEF  prioritized community engagement to ensure inclusive access to information  and strengthen community trust. Using diverse community platforms and  structures -such as grandmother and father groups, youth networks, teachers,  religious leaders, community health workers, and community engagement  feedback centres - UNICEF reached over 12.6 million people and engaged nearly  3 million on lifesaving and behavior-change information, improving service  uptake and strengthened community resilience. 
  
Operations: UNICEF sustained its Electronic  Fund transfer replenishment system, saving over $2.6 million, and improved  bank optimization and cash forecast-management. Digital invoice processing  enhanced efficiency, while co-location with other UN agencies saved $1.5  million.  A solarization project is  expected to yield approximately 363,540 kWh in energy savings and reduce CO2  emissions by 254 tons annually. Improved connectivity and business continuity  through VSAT[12] and satellite phone deployment  enhanced operational continuity. 
  
In 2025, UNICEF  procured nearly $300 million in goods and services both local[13] and offshore. As part of its  localisation strategy, procurement of quality-assured medicines from local  and regional markets began, to support supply-chains development and  longer-term sustainability.
  
UNICEF’s Project  Management Unit (PMU) disbursed $257.5 million[14] across all 34 provinces,  ensuring continued operation of 2,409 health facilities and payment of 37,558  frontline workers and teachers. PMU also delivered $22.2 million in  humanitarian cash to nearly 79,492 vulnerable households. Operational  efficiency improved through increased use of banks and pilot digital  payments, reducing administrative fees by 35%, while the grievance-redress  mechanism resolved 73% of 4,422 cases.
  
UNICEF strengthened  risk oversight through fraud training and assessments, recovering 67% of  ineligible expenditures, while enhancing environmental and social safeguards  awareness to better manage operational and social risks across all  programmes.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges 
Afghanistan’s operating and programming environment remained complex, shaped by regional instability, restrictions on women and girls, multiple shocks such as disease outbreaks, earthquakes, climate change impacts, displacement, a returnee crisis, and strained social systems. Funding shortfalls further constrained UNICEF’s ability to deliver essential services at scale, threatening long-term development prospects of children and women. In response, UNICEF adopted innovative programming approaches to maintain access to essential services for children, caregivers, and especially women and girls. These approaches include expanded use of community-based referral structures, integrated service delivery platforms, multi-shift education, digital tools, AI and remote monitoring. Leadership in UN clusters and targeted advocacy, particularly for girls’ education, strengthened service delivery, partner collaboration, and donor confidence throughout 2025.
Lessons learned 
Integrated service delivery linked to household food security is more effective  
Evaluation of MCCT programme showed that community-based service delivery is effective, cost-efficient, and sustainable. Strengthening links between interventions, household food security and livelihoods, alongside transition from treatment-focused to prevention-oriented programming further improves nutritional outcomes. While the programme enhanced caregiver knowledge, addressing underlying factors such as chronic food insecurity remains essential, as these constraints continue to limit dietary practices.
Nutrition outcomes improve when facility-based care and community interventions are delivered as a unified, multisectoral continuum.
Summative evaluation of UNICEF’s project on enhancing sustainable food security and nutrition practices for children and women highlighted the need for a unified prevention-treatment design linking community-based nutrition interventions with facility-based severe wasting treatment, integrating health, education and social protection. Successful strategies recommended for scale up include Grand Mother Groups (GMGs), BPHS-integrated delivery, Community Health Worker networks for efficiency, community Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation programme, and strategic engagement with community structures to enhance monitoring. 
Context-sensitive monitoring and learning tools at the design stage ensures accountability to equity principles.
Evaluation of solar water supply systems in rural Afghanistan (2016-2024) highlighted, early meaningful community engagement as a critical success factor in programming. Community involvement generated high levels of trust, perceived fairness, and local ownership - essential for site selection and community acceptance. However, commitments to equity and inclusion were not matched by verifiable evidence. While satisfaction among male users was high, the absence of standardized, disaggregated documentation made it impossible to confirm the systematic inclusion of women and marginalized groups, a gap exacerbated by contextual restrictions. A key lesson is the need to embed robust, context-sensitive monitoring and learning tools at the design and implementation stages to ensure accountability to equity principles and to verify whose voices shape programme decisions. Community willingness and ownership were consistently high but insufficient to ensure sustainability. 
Community ownership and protecting capital assets is critical for sustainability of water systems 
Although most communities expressed confidence in maintaining systems and willingness to contribute financially, systems installed before 2021 experienced rapid degradation, with 41% becoming non-functional within four to five years. The main causes were technical failures of major components and the lack of external technical and financial support. The major lesson is that sustainability depends less on strengthening community ownership and more on protecting capital assets through long-term performance and maintenance arrangements that provide external technical support for major failures.  
Fully self-sufficient community operation and maintenance is unrealistic for high-cost infrastructure in Afghanistan. While communities can manage minor repairs and cost recovery, long-term sustainability requires a tiered support system that includes technical backstopping, financial security mechanisms for major replacements, and mandatory, documented training of mechanics. From a programme management perspective, there is need to prioritize rapid repair and system maintenance over expanding new installations. Frequent breakdowns and long downtime periods severely undermined reliability and user trust. Similarly, solar water system designs insufficiently accounted for predictable seasonal and energy constraints, resulting in limited water availability.
Targeted prioritization accelerates results 
Impact Evaluation of the Afghanistan Health Emergency Response (HER) and Novel Financing Arrangement (NFA) Programme 2022-2025 identified several successful programme strategies with high potential for scale-up. These include prioritization of lifesaving MCH interventions, systematic capacity building, community awareness outreach and preventative care efforts, mobile health teams, and integrated monitoring standards to produce a culture of accountability. It also indicated that the programme demonstrated strong cost-efficiency[1], translating large-scale financing into measurable gains in essential service utilization and delivering clear value for money in a highly constrained context. However, anticipated funding reductions and limited prospects for de-facto authority ownership pose sustainability risks, requiring continued prioritization of high-impact MCH services, community-level prevention, and non-formal pathways to train and retain female health workers. 
2026 Outlook 
UNICEF’s 2026-2027 programming will be guided by four strategic shifts which are deeply interconnected and mutually reinforcing. These shifts include focus on targeted interventions in programme priority districts based on needs; scaleup of nationwide interventions¿ to sustain current reach and impact; strengthening evidence-based advocacy and coordination¿ to deliver for every child and ensure sustainable impact; and differentiation to deliver integrated services in 26 priority districts.
For 2026, UNICEF Afghanistan’s strategic intents include strengthening integration in 26 prioritized districts, reducing newborn mortality, enhancing Early Childhood Development and adolescent programming, adopting climate-resilient adaptations in programming, and using high-quality data and evidence to inform planning and demonstrate programme impact.
Afghanistan, one of the countries with highest demand for Ready to Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF), accounting for over 10% of UNICEF’s global procurement, stands to gain significantly from local manufacturing. In 2026, private sector engagement and digitalization to streamline operations, boost productivity and scale proven digital interventions across all sectors will be enhanced.

2025: Bangladesh – A Country in Transition
In 2025, Bangladesh continued to navigate a period of instability and political transition. The developments following the uprising of July 2024—including the dissolution of Parliament and the establishment of an interim government—reshaped the national governance landscape. The establishment of sectoral reform commissions created valuable space for discussion on policy and institutional reforms, including those relevant to improving outcomes for children and adolescents. While some recommendations led to immediate and welcome change, many others, particularly those related to gender and women’s rights, became the subject of negative public debate, with few moving from paper to action. The backlash against women’s rights is a further indication of a shrinking civic space for women and girls, amid growing discrimination and violence against women and children across communities in Bangladesh. At the same time, fiscal constraints and sustained turnover within the public sector have slowed decision-making and required adaptive programme implementation. While essential services have largely continued, implementation timelines have been affected. National elections scheduled for February 2026 are marked by a shift in several political party platforms toward more conservative positions on women’s rights and roles in society, with the lowest number of female electoral candidates in the country’s history.
Economic conditions in 2025 reflected a period of adjustment amid ongoing reforms. Major reforms in the financial sector strengthened oversight and laid the foundation for improved stability; however, uncertainty during the transition period tempered investor confidence, contributing to a subdued investment climate. Development expenditure remained below planned levels; by December 2025, only 17.5 per cent of the Annual Development Programme allocation had been spent—the lowest mid-year execution rate in eight years, including the period following the exceptional disruptions of 2024. Private investment remained weak, and GDP growth slowed to 3.97 per cent, the lowest since the COVID-19–affected 2019–20 fiscal year and below historical averages. Persistently high inflation and constrained domestic revenue mobilisation continued to limit fiscal space.
Within this environment, the FY2025–26 national budget contracted, with social sectors particularly affected. Education spending declined from 1.7 per cent to 1.5 per cent of GDP; health expenditure remained stable at 0.7 per cent; and social protection allocations fell from 2.4 per cent to 1.9 per cent of GDP. These fiscal pressures were compounded by tightening global financing conditions and Bangladesh’s transition toward lower-middle-income country status, which resulted in reduced overseas development assistance from several key partners.
At the household level, rising living costs placed increasing pressure on family budgets. Some households adopted coping strategies such as reducing dietary diversity and limiting expenditures on health and education—decisions with negative implications for children’s well-being and protection, including increased risks of child labour, early marriage, school dropout, and unsafe migration. Urban poor households and informal workers—often with limited access to formal safety nets—were among the most affected. With more than 96 per cent of working women in Bangladesh employed in the informal sector, women remain highly vulnerable to poverty and economic shocks, as their livelihoods are predominantly low paid, insecure, and excluded from social protection, labour rights, and safety nets.
In 2025, Bangladesh reached a critical milestone in its evidence base for children and women with the release of preliminary findings from the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, led by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics in partnership with UNICEF. As the country’s most comprehensive household survey on children and women, MICS 2025 provides timely, nationally representative data to inform policy, planning, and investment decisions at a pivotal moment of demographic, urban, and climate transition.
Demographically, after decades of decline, fertility rates show an upward trend (2.3 in 2019 and 2.4 in 2025). Over 30 per cent of the population—approximately 52 million people—resides in urban areas. Rapid urbanization has intensified inequities. Informal settlements experience poor WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) conditions and heightened environmental hazards. These trends highlight the need for urban-focused, child-sensitive planning, particularly in a climate-vulnerable context where recurrent shocks increasingly undermine children’s nutrition and learning outcomes.
Child survival has improved substantially over the past decade. MICS 2025 indicates[1] that infant mortality stands at 29 per 1,000 live births, with neonatal deaths accounting for two-thirds of under-five mortality. While 77 per cent of births are now attended by skilled personnel and institutional deliveries have increased, neonatal mortality remains a serious challenge, pointing to gaps in quality of care. Additionally, caesarean delivery rates have risen to 51.8 per cent—far above medical necessity[2]. This trend, particularly in private facilities, increases health risks for mothers and newborns and imposes significant financial burdens on families. Although postnatal care has improved (72.7% in 2025, up from 66.7% in 2019), early breastfeeding has declined sharply (from 46.6% in 2019 to 30.4% in 2025) and exclusive breastfeeding has stagnated (62.6% vs. 56.6%), exposing newborns and infants to higher risks of infection and poor growth due to suboptimal breastfeeding practices.
Nutrition outcomes reveal a widening gap between gains in chronic malnutrition and growing threats arising from acute and environmental risks. While stunting has declined over the past decade, its prevalence remains unacceptably high, reflecting cumulative and intergenerational deprivation. At the same time, acute malnutrition has worsened: wasting increased sharply from 9.8 per cent in 2019 to 12.9 per cent in 2025, signalling heightened exposure to food insecurity, disease, and climate-related shocks. Maternal and newborn nutrition indicators point to persistent structural weaknesses, with 53.1 per cent of pregnant women anaemic and 16 per cent of children born with low birth weight (BDHS 2022), reinforcing cycles of poor growth and development. Early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding have declined, dietary diversity remains limited, and bottle feeding is increasing—particularly among poor and rural households. These trends are compounded by rising consumption of nutrient-poor, ultra-processed foods, contributing to the double burden of malnutrition and undermining gains in child nutrition and survival.
New MICS 2025 data reveals a critical environmental threat: widespread lead exposure. A total of 38.3 per cent of children aged 12–59 months and 7.5 per cent of pregnant women exhibit elevated blood lead levels. This widespread exposure poses severe risks to cognitive development and long-term productivity, demanding urgent cross-sectoral action.
In education and early learning, school completion rates have improved and gender parity is favourable at most levels; however, wealth-based gaps persist in secondary education. Foundational learning assessments show that poor and rural children are far less likely to achieve reading and numeracy benchmarks. Early childhood education attendance remains low. Concerningly, early stimulation and responsive caregiving—particularly father engagement—have declined, and few households possess children’s books. While digital access and mobile phone ownership have expanded, women’s low digital literacy continues to constrain digital learning and economic participation.
In child protection, progress remains fragile in the face of economic shocks. Child marriage has declined from 51.4 per cent in 2019 to 47.2 per cent (SDG 5.3.1) but remains high. Adolescent birth rates have risen from 83 to 92 per 1,000 girls aged 15–19. Most concerning is the resurgence of child labour, which now affects 9.2 per cent of children—up from 6.8 per cent in 2019—representing an increase of 1.2 million children. Violent discipline remains widespread (85.7 per cent), and incomplete birth registration (only 59.1 per cent registered) continues to limit children’s access to essential services.
WASH trends remain mixed. Bangladesh has achieved near-universal access to improved drinking water; however, water quality remains problematic. Faecal contamination at both the source and point of use is common, and safely managed drinking water coverage has declined. While sanitation coverage has improved, safe containment and treatment of waste lag significantly behind, particularly in dense urban areas.
MICS 2025 shows that Bangladesh has achieved important gains in child survival and coverage of essential services, yet deep, intersecting inequities persist. Disparities by wealth, geography, and disability continue to disadvantage the most marginalized children across nutrition, foundational learning, WASH safety, and protection. The data provides powerful evidence of the multifaceted challenges faced by adolescent girls—extending beyond vulnerability to early marriage and childbearing—and underscores the need for a far stronger, multisectoral prioritization of this age group by UNICEF. Equally concerning is the resurgence of child labour. Environmental hazards, including unsafe drinking water and lead exposure, further restrict progress. These findings confirm that national progress does not equate to equity; accelerating SDG progress will require targeted, subnational systems-strengthening approaches that prioritise the most disadvantaged children and ensure that no child is left behind.
In 2025, the Rohingya refugee crisis intensified as conflict in Myanmar pushed the refugee population in Bangladesh to 1.2 million, including 140,000 new arrivals[3]. Despite UNICEF’s efforts to sustain essential services through the Joint Response Plan, camp conditions remained dire. Education suffered from facility closures and reduced learning hours, while child protection concerns escalated sharply. The Child Rights Monitoring Mechanism documented over 2,100 incidents of violence, including the recruitment of nearly 1,000 children by armed groups, abductions, and sexual violence[4]. The situation remains a critical humanitarian priority requiring urgent, sustainable intervention and strong government cooperation to safeguard vulnerable children.
