Every Child Thrives
UNICEF supported Bangladesh in laying the foundations for sustainable, tangible results for children and women while strengthening government ownership and national systems. Through strategic advocacy and technical assistance, UNICEF catalysed USD 41 million in government co-financing under the Child Nutrition Fund, complemented by a USD 39.12 million UNICEF grant. This marked a significant policy milestone by embedding maternal nutrition priorities into the Government’s 2025–2029 costed, multi-year health and nutrition implementation plan. The resulting financing and policy shift enabled the institutionalisation of multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) within routine antenatal care, positioning Bangladesh to reach 6 million pregnant women—approximately 60 per cent national coverage—by 2029, thereby contributing to reductions in maternal anaemia, low birth weight, wasting and stunting.
At the systems level, UNICEF strengthened nutrition governance, planning, supply chains and data utilisation across all tiers of the health system. MMS was incorporated into the National Essential Medicines List and the Essential Services Package. Engagement with public and private manufacturers established readiness for domestic MMS production of up to 120 million tablets annually, reducing costs and mitigating supply risks. Nutrition supply systems were further strengthened through digital tracking, with 81 per cent of primary health-care facilities reporting complete nutrition indicators by November 2025, and more than 90 per cent of pregnant women receiving recommended nutrition services, reflecting improved system performance in the transition to the new five-year plan.
At the service-delivery level, UNICEF expanded equitable access to quality nutrition services across the life cycle. Community-based nutrition care for low-birth-weight infants was piloted and institutionalised: 5,211 LBW babies were identified, and 4,955 received Kangaroo Mother Care at home, contributing to improved survival and growth outcomes. Integration of growth monitoring and promotion into routine immunisation enabled early detection of malnutrition, with nearly 97,000 children screened and 6,658 cases of growth faltering identified and referred. These models were incorporated into the national nutrition programme and budgeted for nationwide scale-up.
UNICEF also strengthened outcomes in early childhood development and adolescent girl nutrition. Integrated ECD services reached 85,000 caregivers, while 20,000 caregiver–child dyads received play-based parenting support, resulting in significantly higher child development and caregiving scores compared to non-participants. Weekly iron–folic acid supplementation reached 5.35 million adolescent girls across more than 20,000 schools, supported by digital monitoring systems that enhanced accountability. In partnership with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Primary Education, Dhaka University and the WHO, UNICEF completed an extensive school nutrition and food environment assessment. A representative sample of 1,200 educational institutions (400 primary schools, 400 secondary schools and 400 colleges) across all eight divisions was included. The assessment serves as an advocacy tool to improve school food and nutrition environments and to promote policies and legislation protecting children from unhealthy foods and beverages. Gender-focused private-sector engagement continued through the Mothers@Work initiative, expanded to 385 factories, thereby extending maternal nutrition and family-friendly services to working women.
For children affected by acute malnutrition, UNICEF strengthened both development and emergency responses. A total of 19,607 children received inpatient treatment for severe acute malnutrition across 394 health facilities, supported by strengthened supply chains and quality assurance measures. UNICEF completed trials of locally produced ready-to-use therapeutic food, demonstrating effective, lower-cost alternatives to imports and reinforcing the case for sustainable national scale-up of community-based management of acute malnutrition. In emergencies, 230,844 children were screened, 1,305 children with SAM received treatment and 203,516 caregivers received infant and young child feeding counselling. An Integrated IPC Acute Malnutrition Analysis across 18 disaster-prone districts identified 1.6 million children at risk of acute malnutrition in 2025, enabling more targeted, anticipatory and life-saving responses.
Together, these achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s catalytic role in translating advocacy, evidence and innovation into financed national policies, strengthened systems and improved nutrition outcomes, ensuring that the most vulnerable mothers and children can survive, grow and thrive.
 
Every Child Learns
UNICEF supported the government in transforming education and skills development programmes, which are critical for children’s development and future opportunities. UNICEF’s support spans early childhood through adolescence, addressing both in-school and out-of-school learners, and includes system strengthening through enhanced data, analysis and evidence-based advocacy, learning enhancement strategies, curriculum and assessment reforms, digital innovation, teacher development and targeted interventions with innovative pilots.
As a trusted partner in national education reform, UNICEF supported the government in shaping the vision, strategy and key components of the fifth Primary Education Development Plan (PEDP5), with a strong focus on foundational learning. This work was anchored in data and evidence generated with UNICEF’s support, including enhancements to the Integrated Primary Education Management Information System (IPEMIS), enabling more timely and reliable data, as well as studies on pre-primary education, the School Level Improvement Programme (SLIP) and broader sector analyses.
Recognizing that teacher quality is central to improving learning outcomes, UNICEF supported Bangladesh’s engagement with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) through the development of a Partnership Compact prioritising teacher professionalisation as a major reform area. In 2025, GPE approved a US$48.85 million System Transformation Grant with UNICEF as Grant Agent, jointly with UNESCO.
UNICEF advanced climate resilience in the education sector by supporting a multi-sectoral consultation process to draft a national Climate Change in Education Framework, which integrates adaptation and mitigation into school systems to safeguard vulnerable learners.
UNICEF piloted several innovative initiatives in schools, including a socio-emotional learning programme in 40 schools reaching more than 1,700 students, a Learning Enhancement Strategy for secondary education in 24 schools to address grade VI learning gaps in core subjects, and digital innovations such as gamified learning, cyber safety and internet literacy research. UNICEF also supported micro-skills and green-skills programmes in 160 schools, benefiting 2,300 teachers and more than 60,000 students.
To improve system efficiency, UNICEF helped scale the Digital Monitoring System (DMS), enabling more effective school oversight, and supported the Integrated Training and Learning Management System (ITLMS), which enhances digital and blended training and performance management for 355,000 secondary teachers.
UNICEF’s non-formal primary education programme, using multi-grade, multi-level (MGML) and Teaching at the Right Level (T@RL) approaches, directly benefited approximately 55,000 children in 2025. The Bureau of Non-Formal Education subsequently adopted UNICEF’s pedagogical packages, moving from project-based initiatives to system-wide application, reaching children at scale across Bangladesh.
Skills development initiatives gained momentum, supporting 13,000 NEET youth with 60 per cent job linkage. Following the successful institutionalisation of the skills-focused literacy programme (SKILFO) pilot for adolescents, BNFE is scaling SKILFO to 16 districts to reach more than 100,000 NEET adolescents, demonstrating strong national ownership of the model. Digital skilling efforts under Generation Unlimited (GenU) resulted in 50,000 course completions, 2,500 job connections and partnerships with 331 companies.
 
Every Child is Protected
UNICEF supported Bangladesh in strengthening child protection systems by consolidating reforms in justice, social services and community-based prevention, reaching millions of children, caregivers and community members despite significant resource constraints. Progress during the year reinforced government leadership, improved access to protection and psychosocial services and advanced national commitments under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and UNICEF’s Strategic Plan.
UNICEF-supported interventions reached over 3.7 million children, caregivers and community members through government-led systems and national platforms, including social services, justice institutions and community-based prevention mechanisms, rather than through parallel service delivery. Community-based services reached more than 5 million people, while over 2 million prevention and protection services were delivered through Child Protection Community Hubs (CPCHs). These results reflect system performance rather than stand-alone projects, demonstrating that national platforms are functioning and delivering at scale due to community and government ownership.
In justice for children, UNICEF helped embed children's rights in transitional justice and legislative reform processes, produced evidence on diversion and secured renewed commitments from the Chief Justice as Bangladesh moves toward establishing a fully independent judiciary. Increased application of diversion and non-custodial measures led to reductions in the time children spent in detention, although deprivation of liberty remains common and dedicated Children’s Courts are not yet fully established nationwide. Higher release rates and wider use of alternatives indicate shifting practices. UNICEF supported legal and policy reforms, workforce training, monitoring and advocacy, and strengthened coordination and accountability across police, courts and probation services.
Social service systems remained a critical protection pillar. Building on earlier expansion of the government social service workforce, UNICEF supported the deployment of social workers and psychosocial counsellors, including in urban and humanitarian settings. More than 30,000 children accessed structured case management, and more than 35,000 referrals were made to health, education, legal aid and social protection services. Child Helpline 1098 responded to more than 425,000 calls, providing counselling, referral and rapid response, including in cases of child marriage and child labour.
UNICEF’s contribution focused on system strengthening, including training, digital case management, supervision and coordination. UNICEF funding played a critical role in sustaining frontline services and maintaining emergency response and core systems amid resource shortfalls. These efforts advanced professionalisation of the social service workforce through deployment, supervision and improved coordination under the Department of Social Services, reinforcing child protection as a core public service.
Prevention of violence and harmful practices was further institutionalised through government-led CPCHs. UNICEF advocacy contributed to increased government approval and financing, shifting the platforms from donor dependence to national ownership. A CPCH baseline/endline KAPN study showed improvements in birth registration, reductions in violent discipline and declines in child marriage in intervention areas, demonstrating CPCHs' effectiveness as an integrated, multi-sectoral prevention platform linking protection, health, nutrition and education.
Ending child marriage remained a core priority in 2025, with the UNFPA–UNICEF Global Programme to End Child Marriage serving as a key platform for system-level impact. Through integrated prevention, harmful practices programming and adolescent girl empowerment, UNICEF-supported interventions reached millions nationwide, including through CPCHs and Sports for Development initiatives that strengthened girls' agency, mobility and social acceptance. These efforts contributed to measurable shifts in social norms, increased community-level prevention of child marriage and renewed momentum for legal and policy reforms, positioning Bangladesh to accelerate progress toward ending child marriage at scale.
 
Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment
In 2025, UNICEF Bangladesh scaled up its work on climate change and disaster risk reduction, embedding child-sensitive, gender-sensitive, youth-responsive and risk-informed approaches across national systems and policies. A major milestone was UNICEF’s technical leadership in developing Bangladesh’s NDC 3.0, now recognised globally as one of the most child-sensitive NDCs, with strong integration of adaptation and mitigation priorities across health, education, WASH, social protection and child protection, as well as youth-specific indicators in the monitoring, reporting and verification framework. Children and young people were actively engaged through nationwide consultations and a U-Report survey involving more than 30,000 youth. UNICEF also advanced global advocacy at COP, supported youth participation and strengthened engagement on climate finance and institutional reform, laying the groundwork for scaling climate-resilient social services essential for children.
UNICEF continued to play a catalytic role—despite reduced funding—towards expanding access to safely managed, climate-resilient WASH services. System strengthening, policy reform, scalable innovations and targeted service delivery remained aligned with national priorities to ensure children’s access to safe WASH services.
In collaboration with the government and sector partners, key milestones were achieved with the finalisation of the WASH Regulatory Framework, WASH Policy, WASH in Health Care Strategy and Sector Development and Investment Plans. These will support sustained financing, investment and improved service delivery.
The first nationwide baseline survey on WASH in institutions was conducted with the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics across 10,000 institutions. The findings revealed alarming gaps in access to WASH services, particularly affecting women and girls, and will now inform national budgeting, planning and decision-making. Climate-focused WASH modules in MICS provided critical evidence on climate shocks, service disruptions and adaptive behaviours.
Through direct service delivery, 365,000 people gained access to at least basic, sustainable drinking water. Arsenic mitigation efforts resulted in 792 villages being declared arsenic-free. Community-driven operations and management approaches were strengthened, benefiting 276,000 people previously affected by frequent breakdowns of water systems.
UNICEF piloted WATA technology for local chlorine production and installed 12 Water ATMs in urban slums and refugee settings. These initiatives demonstrated a low-cost, effective model for chlorine production and safe water provision through community-based and private-sector-operated systems. WATA technology addresses microbial contamination, a major barrier to ensuring safely managed drinking water.
In sanitation, development of Dhaka's sanitation masterplan began, with expected contributions to improved wastewater management across the city. A rural sanitation marketing approach supported 1.35 million people, including 580,000 children, to access basic sanitation services. UNICEF continued providing on-site sanitation systems in urban slums bearing the impacts of climate-induced migration, complementing formal sewerage networks.
A total of 683,000 children gained access to basic hygiene services in communities, schools and healthcare facilities through behaviour change interventions, including menstrual health and hygiene support for girls and women. Hygiene promotion messaging reached 1.6 million people and contributed to the installation of 184,000 household handwashing facilities.
 
Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life
MICS 2025 represented the year’s most significant evidence-generation initiative, providing critical disaggregated data on Bangladesh’s most vulnerable children—from those in the Hill Tracts and Tea Gardens to Rohingya children in refugee camps. With evidence in hand identifying children left behind, UNICEF organised extensive consultations with think tanks, Union associations, youth, government ministries and, for the first time, major political parties ahead of the upcoming election. The launch of preliminary findings generated 131 media mentions, elevating national awareness on child rights, child labour, the crisis facing adolescent girls, lead exposure and the climate crisis. More than 180 MICS 2025 indicators were established as mainstream data, informing public discourse and policy reform on child rights issues.
Bangladesh’s MICS 2025 pioneered the world’s first national survey measuring heavy metal blood contamination in pregnant women and children using haemoglobin testing. The findings of elevated blood lead levels informed new regulatory standards on lead in household products and materials. UNICEF is supporting national guideline development, training modules and awareness materials on heavy metal poisoning as part of a national strategy for a lead-free Bangladesh.
Drawing on MICS 2025 evidence, UNICEF strengthened child participation and accountability of leaders by supporting children in identifying priority interventions and advocating for change. The development of Bangladesh's first Child Rights Manifesto was a landmark achievement. Created by and with children and young people, it reflected their priorities across health, education, protection, climate action and social protection. Sharing the Manifesto with political parties enabled UNICEF to brief political leaders thoroughly on indicators and evidence regarding the situation of children. Many leaders found the briefing eye-opening and integrated the data into their policy proposals. On 1 December, ahead of the 2026 national elections, 12 political parties publicly endorsed the Manifesto, marking a shift from advocacy to political commitment. Strategic media and digital engagement extended the reach of these commitments and strengthened public accountability, demonstrating how children’s participation translated into tangible policy influence.
To address the exclusion of children and young people from decision-making processes, UNICEF reinforced youth engagement mechanisms at national and international levels. Structured consultations throughout Bangladesh engaged children with disabilities and marginalised groups in key initiatives. NDC consultations and Child Rights Manifesto sessions reached youth nationwide. The newly formed Young People’s Advisory Group became an ongoing sounding board for UNICEF’s work. UNICEF strengthened youth representation in global climate governance by supporting a young Climate Advocate to attend COP30. Through pre-COP preparation and a dedicated communications plan, UNICEF amplified youth perspectives on climate action and the NDC process via strategic messaging, social media and co-created digital content.
 
Humanitarian and Other Emergencies
In 2025, UNICEF supported Bangladesh in preparing for and responding to climate-related shocks and localised emergencies. While the country did not experience major national disasters, several sub-national emergencies required sustained humanitarian action. Overall, UNICEF reached 597,394 people—more than half of them female—including 330,581 children, representing 47 per cent of the revised Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) 2025 target.
UNICEF delivered integrated services across WASH, health, nutrition, education, child protection and cash assistance, with strong emphasis on preparedness and anticipatory action. In partnership with the Department of Public Health Engineering, UNICEF strengthened climate-resilient WASH systems, enabling 510,197 people, including 4,719 persons with disabilities, to access safe water.
Child protection interventions reached 229,177 children, adolescents and caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support. UNICEF also strengthened national Child Protection in Emergencies Working Groups and their coordination with district disaster management authorities. A national handbook for simulation-based training is scheduled for launch in early 2026, alongside the rollout of a disability-inclusive humanitarian action plan.
Nutrition services reached 287,275 people, including treatment for severe acute malnutrition and infant and young child feeding counselling. A key innovation involved introducing small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements for children under one year, strengthening the humanitarian–development nutrition continuum. In host communities, UNICEF-supported health services provided special care for 5,063 newborns, and 82,801 children received Penta-3 vaccination.
 
Sector Leadership and Support to the 1.2 Million Rohingya Refugees
The protracted Rohingya refugee response in Cox’s Bazar continued to require large-scale humanitarian support. Rohingya refugees accounted for 74 per cent of all people reached by UNICEF in 2025.
The humanitarian funding crisis posed significant challenges across all sectors, especially in education and WASH. Valuable lessons were learned, prompting substantial efforts to prioritise, rationalise and integrate approaches—not only to continue service provision with reduced funding but also to improve quality and reduce fragmentation across and within sectors. Despite financial constraints, with support from EPF and multiple donors, UNICEF ensured continued access to learning for 254,329 Rohingya and host community children, including early childhood education. Attendance remained consistently high at 89 per cent across all levels and for both girls and boys.
UNICEF-supported health facilities recorded 136,172 consultations for children under five, ensured 24/7 essential health services and expanded newborn care and HPV vaccination programmes. In WASH, 336,919 Rohingya refugees accessed safe water through strengthened, climate-resilient systems. UNICEF significantly enhanced information management, budget oversight and integration of teams, informed by lessons learned throughout the response.
 
Addressing Cross-Cutting Issues
UNICEF Bangladesh advanced gender-responsive programming across sectors with a strong focus on adolescent girls and women. Efforts prioritised girls’ needs, expanded skills and life skills, enhanced protection, created leadership opportunities and addressed systemic discrimination in education and adolescent-friendly health services. Innovative approaches, including sports for development and community dialogues, helped challenge restrictive gender norms. Partnerships with key ministries expanded girls’ participation nationwide, while engagement with marginalised groups and girl- and youth-led networks deepened understanding of vulnerabilities. UNICEF also advocated, in collaboration with UN partners, for women’s rights reforms and anti-sexual harassment legislation.
UNICEF led the Inter-Agency Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) Network in completing Bangladesh’s first national SEA Risk Assessment. PSEA and child safeguarding training reached 663 partner staff and 280 UNICEF personnel, and 43 network members were trained as trainers under the UN Victim Assistance Protocol. Across Rohingya camps, Bhasan Char and host communities, 793,538 people gained access to safe reporting channels, and a digital Complaint, Feedback and Response Mechanism was introduced to strengthen accountability.
UNICEF advanced disability inclusion among both Bangladeshi and Rohingya populations. An early identification and intervention tool integrated into the government’s digital SmartHealthBD platform screened thousands of children for developmental delays and disabilities. In Rohingya camps, 164,952 individuals were screened, with more than 3,500 persons with disabilities identified and referred.
UNICEF accelerated climate programming by embedding child- and youth-sensitive priorities into Bangladesh’s NDC 3.0, including the world’s first child-focused climate targets. Youth inputs were gathered through consultations with over 400 children and a nationwide U-Report survey. Evidence generation advanced through the Child Climate Risk Index–DRM model, updated climate landscape analysis and sectoral policy briefs. UNICEF supported national climate finance readiness and amplified youth engagement in national and global platforms, including COP30.
UNICEF and the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs expanded the cash-plus Mother and Child Benefit Programme, reaching more than 30,000 beneficiaries and improving service uptake through digital interoperability. Humanitarian cash assistance supported 1,676 flood-affected households. Early childhood development progressed through policy reform, expanded pre-primary education and successful PHC-based ECD pilots, which improved caregiving practices and child development outcomes.
Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) results strengthened through the establishment of a national Community Engagement (CE) SBC Research Repository and multiple studies informing evidence-based, tailored strategies across sectors. These insights supported implementation of sectoral CE SBC interventions and campaigns, including the TCV vaccination campaign, which achieved 97 per cent coverage. CE SBC capacity building reached more than 21,000 stakeholders across government, civil society, academia, media and faith-based institutions, promoting CE Quality Standards. Nationwide community engagement intensified through more than 18,000 CE sessions and large-scale mobilisation of religious leaders, teachers, youth networks and media, contributing to demand creation and reductions in misinformation during vaccination campaigns. Mass, community, social and print media promoted 23 child and adolescent care practices, reaching millions. U-Report, social listening and strengthened Accountability to Affected People (AAP) systems informed responsive, accountable programming aligned with global standards.
In 2025, UNICEF advanced operationalisation of Environmental and Social Standards (ESS) by integrating safeguard requirements across programmes, partnerships and monitoring systems. Core ESS tools, including Environmental and Social Risk Management plans, legal clauses and standardised monitoring instruments, were developed and incorporated into new and existing programme documents organisation-wide.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Delivering Results for Children Through a Difficult Year
Bangladesh continued to feel the effects of the 2024 uprising throughout 2025. Government capacity remained strained, leadership turnover was frequent, and planning and decision-making slowed considerably. At the same time, a weak domestic economy and declining official development assistance and humanitarian funding tightened budgets across sectors. These pressures affected both the scope and pace of UNICEF’s work, resulting in staffing reductions and the closure of several field offices. Long-standing overlaps in institutional mandates—across child protection, health, education, and water and sanitation—became more pronounced, complicating coordination and the sustainability of services. Rising conservatism and persistent gender-based violence further eroded social cohesion.
 
Children’s Environmental Health
New national data in 2025 confirmed that many children face significant environmental health risks, particularly exposure to lead. While the extent of the problem has now become visible, several sources are still being identified, although cookware, paints, and even traditional cosmetics have already been confirmed as contributors. UNICEF supported the expansion of laboratory testing capacity and introduced portable testing devices for markets to identify and remove hazardous products.
Bangladesh also remains off track on safely managed drinking water and sanitation. Poor water quality, climate-related stresses, groundwater depletion, rapid urbanization, and weak operation and maintenance systems continue to limit progress. UNICEF’s message to government and partners remains consistent: infrastructure alone cannot solve these challenges without strong regulation, sustainable financing, clearly defined roles, and robust local capacity. UNICEF will continue to advocate for sector reform and for establishing a dedicated government authority for water and sanitation to reduce duplication and strengthen accountability.
 
Children’s Health and Nutrition
Delays in approving the national health, nutrition, and population plan—followed by an abrupt shift to project-based implementation—disrupted service continuity and exposed structural weaknesses in government planning, coordination, and management. The absence of adequate transition and contingency arrangements increased the risk of service gaps in primary health care, particularly for the most vulnerable populations. This experience highlighted the need for persistent advocacy for timely policy decisions and anticipatory planning to protect equity, quality, and continuity of care.
UNICEF mitigated these risks by advancing integrated, equity-focused primary health care. Through a scaled-up community-based engagement programme, strengthened support to community health workers, and integrated service delivery models tailored to rural and urban settings, UNICEF is working with partners to reduce fragmentation, reinforce accountability, and deliver measurable results for children and women.
 
Education
The transition to an interim government in 2025 brought leadership changes across the education sector. While some pragmatic priorities were introduced, the limited mandate resulted in short-term decisions and delays to reforms that require sustained commitment. Uncertainty over whether a future elected government will continue these reforms has further slowed decision-making. Curriculum framework concerns also remain, given their central role in achieving national learning goals and preparing students for future challenges.
 
Unmet Protection Needs
Child protection efforts were constrained by funding shortages, high workforce turnover, and uneven capacities at local levels—affecting social workers, counsellors, and community facilitators. Justice reforms made progress, yet far too many children still experience deprivation of liberty, and dedicated Children’s Courts are not fully established nationwide. This underscores the urgent need to accelerate implementation of the Children Act of 2013 and expand alternatives to detention.
 
Protracted Rohingya Crisis
Eight years on, 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh. International funding continues to decline, making the response increasingly fragile. Tensions between host communities and refugees intensified in 2025, including incidents of unrest. Ensuring equitable access to basic services for host communities—alongside essential support for refugees—will be critical for maintaining social cohesion.
 
Learning and Programme Preparation
Drawing on lessons from the current programme cycle, new national surveys, and comprehensive analyses of administrative and partner-generated data, UNICEF will begin preparations for the next country programme. This process will be evidence-led and consultative, aligned with government priorities, and focused on the highest-impact, most cost-effective pathways for improving outcomes for the most disadvantaged children.
 
Looking Ahead to 2026
With the government increasingly leading service delivery for the Rohingya refugee response, UNICEF will prioritise deeper systems integration; sustained skilling of Rohingya women, men, and youth for future livelihoods; and stronger alignment with the humanitarian–development nexus. Emergency preparedness and disaster risk reduction will be mainstreamed across programmes to ensure essential services remain resilient, inclusive, and responsive to shocks. Strengthening information management capacity and knowledge management will also be a key focus, with improved forecasting and information sharing on funding gaps and implementation challenges.
 
UNICEF established the Young People Advisory Group (YPAG) in Bangladesh as a flagship achievement in embedding youth leadership within national policy and programming. Formed by graduates of UNICEF’s Young Leadership Programme, developed in partnership with the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, YPAG brings together a cohort of highly skilled young leaders positioned to contribute to policy dialogue, accountability, and reform. YPAG strengthens accountability to children’s rights by ensuring young people are recognised as partners in shaping Bangladesh’s development trajectory.
 
Despite the challenges, the youth-led transition opened a window to place children at the centre of emerging governance. National commitments on climate and child rights offer platforms for action and accountability. Evidence gathered in 2025—especially new household survey data—now supports a more targeted, government-owned, climate-aware approach focused on the most vulnerable children through community and market-based solutions.
 
Momentum is growing for a national strategy to eliminate lead exposure, with measures to regulate known sources and address informal sectors handling toxic materials. UNICEF has expanded partnerships with regulators and the private sector to accelerate this work. Community-level health service reforms have helped shape a national integrated vision for primary health care and have laid the foundation for a new directorate, positioning the country for tangible improvements in 2026.
 
In child protection, UNICEF will consolidate reforms: advancing the Children Act and associated rules; transitioning the social service workforce and Child Protection Community Hubs to sustainable government financing; responding to a resurgence in child labour; and further embedding diversion and alternatives to detention. Organizationally, UNICEF has become leaner and more focused on synergy and efficiency. Lessons from 2025 show that digital transformation will only succeed if frontline partners have the skills and connectivity to use new tools. UNICEF will invest in practical digital solutions, stronger data analysis, and robust cybersecurity, while deepening integration across health, education, and youth programmes.
 
UNICEF also established a partnership with bKASH, a leading mobile financial service provider, to run in-app fundraising appeals and receive donations at lower transaction costs than existing payment service providers. bKash is a cornerstone of Bangladesh’s digital financial ecosystem, with nearly 330,000 agents, 550,000 merchants, and nearly 80 million users, including more than 30 million active customers. Its extensive offline merchant network will also be leveraged to collect contributions directly into a UNICEF wallet, significantly expanding domestic resource mobilization at scale.
 
Finally, UNICEF will strengthen environmental and social standards by orienting government and partners before implementation, requiring contractor-specific risk management plans, and replacing one-off checks with ongoing monitoring and support. The accountability to affected people system will be expanded nationwide—backed by comprehensive mapping of existing feedback channels and targeted capacity building—so that communities can influence the services they receive and see their concerns translated into action.

Bhutan’s economy grew by 7.5 per cent in 2024[1] and is projected to reach 8.5 per cent in 2025[2], reflecting a  return to its long-term growth trajectory, primarily driven by hydropower  investments, tourism recovery, and the expansion of services[3]. Construction is rebounding,  and public investment is expected to increase, supported by  hydropower-related spending[4]. These trends create  opportunities for enhanced fiscal space, which if directed toward social  sectors can accelerate progress toward the UNICEF Strategic Plan (SP) 2022-2025  outcomes for health, education, nutrition, child protection, and social  protection.
  
However,  the recovery is accompanied by persistent structural risks. Public debt remains high at 105 per cent of GDP as of June 2025[5], and inflationary  pressures (3.87 per cent in August 2025) constrain household purchasing power[6], with potential negative  effects on child nutrition and multidimensional poverty. Overall unemployment  is low at 3.8 per cent, yet youth unemployment remains critically high  at 20.6 per cent, disproportionately affecting young women (26.5 per cent)  and urban youth (27.1 per cent)[7]. Poverty also persists  at 12.4 per cent, with rural rates (17.5 per cent) more than four  times higher than urban (4.2 per cent)[8], signaling disparities  in access to services, particularly relevant to Strategic Plan (SP) impact  indicators on child poverty, learning, and health outcomes.
  
Deepening these vulnerabilities are profound demographic shifts, including a  sharp decline in the Total Fertility Rate to 1.46 (2023), one of the steepest  global declines- mainly due to rapid urbanization, and high levels of  outmigration. Between 2017 and 2024, 32,788 Bhutanese migrated to Australia,  with the majority leaving in just the past two years. These trends are  reshaping Bhutan’s demographic profile, reducing the productive workforce and  creating shortages in essential sectors such as education and health[9]. For children, this  increases risks of reduced service availability, weakened frontline capacity,  and growing disparities for those in remote areas, directly affecting outcome  indicators on learning, immunization, WASH access, and protection.
  
Rural  depopulation and declining fertility exacerbate inequitable access to essential services, posing challenges to progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) and the commitment to leave no child behind.  High government spending in social sectors yields diminishing returns when  outmigration and demographic shifts strain service delivery systems and  reduce the tax base. Unless mitigated through integrated and forward-looking  strategies, these trends may impede Bhutan’s progress toward inclusive and  sustainable development.
  
In response, the Royal Government of Bhutan (RGoB) continues to prioritize the  social sector, allocating 30 per cent of the 2025-2026 national budget (Nu.  40.9 billion) to health and education, the key drivers of child rights  outcomes[10].  This investment benefits the 34 per cent of the population who are children  and adolescents, reinforcing national commitment to equitable human  capital development[11].
  
Emerging national initiatives particularly the Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC) and the  newly launched Pelsung programme offer transformative platforms for  adolescent engagement, skills development, and civic participation. Guided by  His Majesty the King, GMC aims to build an advanced, future-ready economy  grounded in globally recognized governance and the principles of Gross  National Happiness (GNH), creating new spaces for youth-driven innovation[12]. Launched on 7 October  2025, Pelsung serves as the third pillar of nation-building alongside  De-suung and Gyalsung, positioning young Bhutanese as co-architects and  custodians of GMC’s development. Its first cohort of 500 participants from  the civil service, private sector, student groups, and jobseekers underwent  intensive training and mentorship to develop solutions across four thematic  areas: social and cultural development, business and commercial innovation,  governance and planning, and urban design[13]. Through its  multisectoral mentorship model and emphasis on leadership, problem-solving,  and mindful development rooted in national values, Pelsung aligns strongly  with Strategic Plan Outcome 4 (Adolescent Skills and Participation) and  provides new opportunities for adolescent engagement, youth-led innovation,  and systems that enable meaningful participation at scale.
  
Bhutan’s third Voluntary National Review (VNR), presented in 2025, highlights  significant progress on SDG related to maternal, newborn, and child mortality,  safe water, sanitation, and climate resilience, underscored  by Bhutan’s status as the world’s only carbon-negative country. However, the VNR  also identifies economic diversification, youth unemployment, data systems,  and sustainable financing as areas requiring renewed attention[14], all of which are vital  for sustaining and scaling child rights gains.
  
The Government’s long-term 10X National Economic Vision 2050 aims to transform  Bhutan into a developed economy, envisioning a resilient, inclusive, and  sustainable growth model underpinned by strong private-sector development[15]. Achieving this vision  will require strengthened social sector systems, evidence-based policymaking,  and investments that reach the most vulnerable children.
  
Despite strong government commitment and ongoing progress, underlying vulnerabilities  persist with high public debt, youth unemployment, rural poverty, demographic  shifts, and workforce shortages. These factors pose risks to sustaining  outcomes for children particularly in health, education, protection, and  nutrition.
  
UNICEF, working alongside the RGoB and partners, will continue to support systems  strengthening, equity-focused programming, and innovations to advance child  rights. Priority areas will include inclusive education, social  protection, child and adolescent nutrition, and protection from  violence, ensuring that progress toward the SDGs and the Strategic  Plan is sustained and that no child is left behind.

In 2025, UNICEF Bhutan Country Office (BhCO) worked closely with the RGoB and partners to advance national priorities aligned with the Country Programme and the UNSDCF. This collaboration led to policy and systems strengthening results for children and adolescents. The launch of the Nourishing Bhutan Framework for Action positioned the country to tackle the triple burden of malnutrition, while Bhutan’s leadership on ending childhood lead poisoning elevated global advocacy on environmental health. Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 integrated gender- child-and disability-inclusive climate governance, reinforcing national resilience. Reforms such as raising the legal age of marriage for girls and expanding Women and Girls’ Safe Spaces to 14 districts strengthened protection systems. The rollout of the Education Technology Framework supported digital learning and system modernization.
The following sections present Goal Area results showcasing system shifts, field-level outcomes, and strategic contributions to advancing Bhutan’s child rights agenda in 2025.
GA1: EVERY CHILD SURVIVES AND THRIVES
In 2025, Bhutan sustained progress toward child and maternal health SDG targets. With BhCO support, national strategies enabled near universal essential service coverage: immunization remained above 98 per cent, antenatal and postnatal care exceeded 97 per cent, and nutrition supplementation reached 95 per cent + of women and children.
Robust frameworks that BhCO provided support towards include the Integrated Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health Strategy, Community Health and Nutrition Strategy, Health Promotion Strategy and Lead Poisoning Prevention Strategy strengthened primary health delivery. 
Bhutan demonstrated global leadership in child health when the Hon’ble Prime Minister, at UNICEF’s high-level event during the 80th UN General Assembly, called for urgent global action to end childhood lead poisoning, following national survey findings that 76 per cent of young children had unsafe blood lead levels. 
Health systems were further strengthened through a national immunization review, resulting in zero vaccine stockouts, and through improved newborn care via Universal Newborn Screening Guidelines. Capacity building was provided through training 146 health workers on newborn care across 12 districts and advanced neonatal and pediatric intensive care training to 30 nurses. UNICEF core resources contributed to the strengthening of capacity of health workers to deliver basic and advanced support for newborns. Health supply chain reforms were initiated through a national maturity assessment, attracting support from Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Humanitarian Emergency Logistics Programme (HELP).
To address the triple burden of malnutrition, Bhutan launched the Nourishing Bhutan Framework for Action and drafted the National Nutrition Strategy and Action Plan (2025–2030). UNICEF core resources also supported the Centre of Excellence in Nutrition to initiate, in 2025, an assessment of compliance with Micronutrient Powder (MNP) and Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS) among pregnant and breastfeeding mothers.
BhCO also collaborated closely with WHO while drafting national policy documents, including National Mental Health Strategy 1.0 (2025), National Lead Poisoning Prevention Strategy (2026–2030), and National Nutrition Strategic Action Plan (2026–2030).
Digital and in person learning innovations strengthened professional competencies, including an updated lactation management module hosted online by University of Medical Sciences of Bhutan and Infant and Young Child Feeding Practices training for 200 health workers in eastern Bhutan. Cross-sector partnerships mobilized over 140 local officials and volunteers to promote integrated childcare practices and strengthen frontline systems.
Collectively, these efforts advanced Bhutan’s commitment to ensuring every child survives, thrives, and reaches their full potential.
GA2: EVERY CHILD LEARNS
Bhutan remains broadly on track toward SDG 4, with primary and secondary survival rates at 98 per cent and 96 per cent, gender parity at 1.02, youth literacy at 97.7 per cent, and a student-teacher ratio of 16:1.However, major gaps persist: Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) coverage remains low at 38.14 per cent; foundational learning levels are weak (reading 45 per cent, mathematics 39 per cent, science 45 per cent); inclusion of children with disabilities is limited (70 per cent out of school); [1]digital competencies among youth are insufficient; and monastic schools continue to face restricted learning opportunities.
Key gains were achieved with partners. System strengthening progressed through support for the National Education Policy Implementation Plan, per capita financing reforms to reduce inequities, Education Management Information System improvements, and the second National Education Assessment for Grades III and VI providing critical evidence for improving learning outcomes. BhCO and the PEMA Secretariat advanced school based Mental Health and Psychosocial Support through a national promotion action plan and training for 80+ educators. 
BhCO advanced early learning, integrating Environment and Climate Change Education into the ECCD curriculum and piloting a new foundational reading programme for Grades PP–III in three districts. A national evaluation of home-based ECCD alternatives generated recommendations for access in remote areas.
Digital transformation accelerated through the launch of Bhutan’s first Education Technology Framework with support from EU, setting national standards and accompanied by nationwide teacher capacity building and a school connectivity assessment. Inclusion improved with Accessible Digital Textbooks in 19 schools and the Akelius English programme reaching 1,263 children. Partnerships with the Central Monastic Body and Bhutan Cricket expanded holistic learning through sports for 721 monastic youth and nuns.
The UPSHIFT programme was institutionalized within the National Scouting Curriculum and Google Classroom, equipping 11,412 adolescents and youth with skills for sustainability, employability, and citizenship.
BhCO collaborated with the United Nations Resident Coordinator’s Office (UN RCO) and Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) under the SDG Mindful Futures Joint Project. Within the Joint Project, business case on climate resilient schools was developed. In expanding UPSHIFT through the schools in the country, and organization of the National Innovation Challenge, BhCO worked closely with United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). In the implementation of the digitalization in education and development of the Education Technology Framework (ETF), UNICEF collaborated with United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). 
Overall, UNICEF’s partnerships and core resources facilitated the equity agenda through the education per capita financing formula and scaling up UPSHIFT programme for adolescents.
GA3: EVERY CHILD IS PROTECTED FROM VIOLENCE AND EXPLOITATION 
In 2025, Bhutan advanced its commitments under SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) and BhCO played a catalytic role in expanding survivor-centered and child-sensitive interventions.  
In partnership with UNDP and United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), BhCO supported the National Council in reviewing the Penal Code to reinforce sexual offence provisions. A major achievement was the amendment of the Marriage Act of Bhutan 1980, raising the minimum legal age of marriage for girls to 18 years.  
In partnership with Respect, Educate, Nurture, and Empower Women (RENEW), a Civil Society Organization (CSO), established three new Women and Girls Safe Spaces, bringing coverage to 14 of 20 districts. Community-based child protection committees were strengthened in three southern districts, and the Child Helpline 24/7 responsiveness improved.  
In addressing mental health needs, BhCO and the PEMA Secretariat convened a high-level National Mental Health Symposium with over 180 participants from five Dzongkhags and central agencies. The symposium strengthened national coordination, reaffirmed commitments to SDG 3, and contributed to the launch of Bhutan’s first National Mental Health Strategy by Her Majesty and the Hon’ble Prime Minister, elevating mental health as a national priority. The Helping Adolescents Thrive programme was rolled out in 24 schools, promoting emotional resilience and wellbeing. Overall, 42,701 women and children, including 17,569 girls, accessed quality protection and mental health services in 2025. 
Building a skilled social service workforce remained central to system strengthening. BhCO supported the capacity building of 3,069 frontline workers (1,411 female) including social workers, teachers, police, and justice officials on child-sensitive approaches, case management and justice for children. As a result, 9,083 at-risk children (4,203 girls) accessed quality protection and mental health services, and 69 per cent of children in conflict with the law were diverted from judicial proceedings toward rehabilitative, community-based alternatives. A national partnership with INTERPOL on ending Child Online Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (OCSEA) was formalized to address online crimes against children. BhCO developed national guidelines for managing child abuse in health facilities and protocols for admitting children into monastic institutions, closing long-standing service gaps, documentation and case management. A comprehensive Child Protection (CP)/Gender Based Violence (GBV) emergency SOP and coordination mechanism were institutionalized. 
In addressing prevention, 44,406 community members (23,484 females) were reached with messaging on child safeguarding, positive parenting, and gender equality. Child participation platforms in 12 schools strengthened to engage decisionmakers on child rights. Legal literacy on the Convention on the Rights of the Child expanded to 30 schools through partnerships with the Bhutan National Legal Institute and JSW School of Law.
UNICEF core resource supported the strengthening of the child protection system, which included legal and policy reviews, expansion of CP and GBV services through Women and Girls Safe Spaces and enhancing children’s access to justice through capacity building of the justice professionals and supporting the rehabilitation programmes for Children in Conflict with the Law.
GA4: EVERY CHILD LIVES IN A SAFE AND CLEAN ENVIRONMENT 
BhCO’s support strengthened Bhutan’s WASH systems ensuring safer, more reliable services for every child. Nationally, sanitation coverage has reached 81.4 per cent, while safely managed drinking water services stand at 63 per cent. 
Bhutan’s leadership, rooted in GNH, earned global recognition at the UN High Level Forum as an SDG 6 Country Acceleration Case Study, showcasing innovations in governance and climate-adapted approaches. This was facilitated by UN RCO and BhCO.
A landmark achievement was the endorsement of Bhutan’s first-ever WASH Standards for Health Care Facilities, developed with UNICEF’s support. Since 2020, 185 of 189 Primary Health Centers (PHC) have been equipped with safe water systems, achieving 97.8 per cent national coverage. To further improve hygiene, 56 PHCs across eight districts now have inclusive handwashing stations and safe drinking water infrastructure, benefitting 831 people daily. In monastic schools and nunneries, water filtration systems now provide safe drinking water to 1,760 child monks and nuns.
A comprehensive WASH assessment across all 20 districts identified service gaps, prompting the construction of climate-resilient water systems in 16 schools, reaching 8,959 students, including 4,531 girls. In a remote highland monastic school, inclusive sanitation blocks with gender-responsive toilets, water supply, and handwashing stations were built for 41 monks. 
Caretaker training across 162 schools enhanced maintenance and operational reliability, directly benefiting 63,000 children. Additionally, 89 health coordinators from schools and monastic institutions were trained to monitor sustainable WASH practices, influencing hygiene behaviors and reinforcing accountability for 13,600 children. 
To respond to declining spring flows driven by climate change, core resources were invested to advance climate-resilient water initiatives. This support enabled the launch of a spring source revival pilot project in one community in Mongar District with Department of Water, aimed at restoring water availability and strengthening long-term community health, resilience, and wellbeing.
Bhutan’s strong leadership, community action, and strategic reforms are driving faster SDG gains delivering safe, clean, climate-resilient environments that advance UNICEF’s vision for every child.
GA5: EVERY CHILD HAS AN EQUITABLE CHANCE IN LIFE
In 2025, Bhutan advanced its national aspirations to reduce poverty, inequality, and vulnerability by accelerating progress toward SDG 1.3 on universal social protection and SDG 10.4 on fiscal and social protection policies for greater equality. 
UNICEF led the development of Bhutan’s National Social Protection Strategy, a landmark framework for an inclusive, gender- and disability-responsive, shock-ready system. Planned for launch in 2026, it prioritizes vulnerable groups such as children with disabilities, rural households, out-of-school youth, and high-risk communities. To ensure national ownership, BhCO convened broad consultations across government, civil society, and partners, building consensus on needs, gaps, and reform pathways.
Bhutan’s leadership and BhCO’s sustained engagement secured the country’s selection as a Pathfinder under the UN Secretary-General’s Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection. Building on this recognition, BhCO, the World Bank, UNDP facilitated by the UN Resident Coordinator mobilized USD 425,000 in catalytic financing to develop Bhutan’s first disability-inclusive social protection programme for national scale-up and embedding disability visibility in fiscal and planning systems.
At the local level, BhCO partnered with three district administrations to identify last-mile bottlenecks and design integrated action plans tackling rural poverty, migration, water scarcity, limited services, and climate shocks, and this was supported by UNICEF core resources.
Under these plans, BhCO supported youth entrepreneurship training, capacity building for village health workers, climate-resilient water management, establishment of child protection committees, and stronger multi-sectoral task forces to coordinate child rights and protection across education, health, and justice. BhCO trained 145 district task force members on social and behavior change approaches and introduced an integrated childcare advisory package. These teams facilitated community dialogues ensuring national priorities are translated into tangible improvements for families.
Sustained engagement with local governments enabled child-focused and inclusive social protection interventions to be embedded in development plans and budgets advancing the decentralization agenda of the 13th FYP.
In 2025, BhCO advanced Bhutan’s cross-sectoral commitments to children and adolescents, driving progress across gender equality, protection, humanitarian preparedness, and climate resilience.
Gender Equality and Adolescent Empowerment: A landmark reform, through the amendment of the Marriage Act (1980), raised the legal age of marriage for girls to 18 years. UNICEF complemented this normative gain by expanding survivor-centered GBV services and leading nationwide advocacy, including Global Menstrual Hygiene Day spearheaded by Her Royal Highness, Royal Patron of Red Dot Bhutan. This catalyzed installation of 1,000 sanitary pad disposal bins across 562 schools and 32 nunneries. In parallel, 5,719 adolescent girls were equipped with holistic skills development, advancing Strategic Plan Outcome 4 on adolescent skills and participation.
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA): BhCO strengthened civil society systems, with nine of ten CSOs now fully capacitated to prevent SEA. In collaboration with the UN Country Team (UNCT) PSEA task team, awareness materials were disseminated, while WGSS staff capacities were enhanced to ensure accessible reporting channels and victim assistance in communities.
Humanitarian Preparedness and Resilience: Recognizing Bhutan’s vulnerability to natural disasters, BhCO advanced child-focused emergency preparedness by training De-suup volunteers, engaging scouts as strategic DRR partners, and finalizing the Education Sector Disaster Management and Contingency Plan with MoESD. Nutrition and WASH-in-emergency capacities were strengthened, preparedness integrated into the National Nutrition Strategy (2026–2030), and consultations initiated to roll out SoPs for GBViE and MHPSS in emergencies.
Climate Action and Systemwide Resilience: BhCO supported the integration of health, education, and WASH into Bhutan’s NDC 3.0, securing a strong mandate for child-centered climate action. With national and regional partners, a social sector policy brief and Climate Landscape Analysis for Children were developed. Youth leadership was pivotal: 9,166 young people gained resilience and innovation skills through UPSHIFT, and 901 directly shaped NDC 3.0 through consultations. Climate education was mainstreamed across the curriculum, supported by a financing business case for climate-resilient schools. BhCO also invested in climate-resilient water systems in 16 schools, ensuring safe water for 8,959 students-achievements largely enabled by UNICEF core resources.
Together, these results demonstrate UNICEF’s catalytic role in advancing SDGs 5, 16, and 13, while reinforcing commitments under SDGs 3, 4, and 6 building a future where every child in Bhutan is protected, empowered, and resilient.
Throughout 2025, BhCO applied change strategies and enablers to deliver results at scale, supported by efficient governance and strategic investments in human resources.
UNICEF’s advocacy and partnerships secured high-level commitments to advance results for women and children. The Prime Minister’s launch of the national roadmap on the triple burden of child malnutrition, along with his call at the 80th UN General Assembly for urgent global action to end childhood lead poisoning, placed child well-being at the centre of Bhutan’s development agenda and showcased national leadership in children’s rights. UNICEF Bhutan’s rapidly expanding digital presence further amplified children’s issues, with 212 posts, nearly 30 million impressions, a fivefold increase from 2024 and engagement with 79,564 followers. More than 20 mentions in leading media outlets reinforced this visibility.
Evidence remained a core priority. The evaluation of home-based ECCD highlighted the need for structured, tech-enabled training for parents and facilitators. Bhutan’s first national survey on lead prevalence in 2024 identified contamination sources and informed prevention and treatment efforts in 2025. A WASH baseline in schools and monastic institutions revealed critical infrastructure gaps. BhCO also strengthened national evaluation practices by training local administrative offices across the country, enhancing evidence-based planning with key national partners.
In 2025, UNICEF Bhutan operationalized all five Annual Management Plan (AMP) priorities, achieving all 19 performance indicators and demonstrating strong results-based management and resource efficiency. To reinforce workplace culture, the office prioritized policy awareness, regular staff reflections, and structured feedback mechanisms that supported adaptive learning. A comprehensive review of programme priorities, staffing, and affordability under the Future Focus Initiative led to a revised Programme Budget Review (PBR), positioning the office for strategic midterm review in 2026, aligned with Bhutan’s 13th Five Year Plan (FYP) and UNICEF’s evolving technical demands. Weekly stand-up meetings helped maintain staff engagement throughout this transition.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Bhutan’s graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2023, followed by the rollout of the 13th FYP in 2024, continues to reshape the national development landscape. As Bhutan aspires to attain high income status by 2034 and a developed economy by 2050, UNICEF’s principal challenge and opportunity will be to strengthen its value proposition in a context characterized by shifting development financing, increasing reliance on domestic systems, and a growing emphasis on innovation, private sector engagement, climate resilience, and youth opportunities.
In 2025, BhCO demonstrated agility and adaptive management, delivering progress across multiple sectors while embedding programmes within national systems to ensure scale and sustainability. Strengthened multisectoral partnerships drove major legal reforms, expanded service coverage, and improved national coordination in child protection and mental health. Collaboration with Parliament, UN agencies, CSOs, and line ministries advanced reforms such as the review of Bhutan’s Penal Code and amendments to the Marriage Act, while the health sector broadened partnerships with agencies such as the Department of Trade, Customs, and the National Standards Bureau to draft a regulatory framework for lead. 
BhCO also responded proactively to emerging risks through its strategic partnership with INTERPOL, enhancing national capacity to address online crimes against children. Engagement with development partners on education digitalization reinforced government commitment to inclusive education and foundational learning, laying the groundwork for long-term system strengthening. Resource mobilization was another highlight, with USD 425,000 secured under the Global Accelerator in partnership with the World Bank and UNDP, aligning support for the national social protection agenda.
Lessons learned underscored that embedding interventions within existing systems is key to achieving scale and sustainability. Integrating the Helping Adolescent Thrive programme into school counselling services proved more viable than standalone initiatives, while embedding the UPSHIFT programme into the national Scout curriculum laid the foundation for expansion to all schools, with a strong focus on digital and green skills. Complementary initiatives such as Accessible Digital Textbooks and the National Education Assessment strengthened system capacity to deliver equitable learning outcomes. Local implementation provided valuable insights into delivery systems, with governments recognizing the programs’ role in advancing child outcomes and improving multi-sector coordination. The health sector’s launch of the Nourishing Framework for Action highlighted the importance of addressing the triple burden of child malnutrition, while locally adapted innovations such as the spring water revival initiative demonstrated resilience-building in climate-affected communities. Documenting and showcasing these models with government partners proved crucial for building national ownership.
At the same time, systemic challenges demanded innovative responses. Rising risks of online sexual exploitation and abuse highlighted the need for sophisticated tools, enhanced detection systems, and specialized law enforcement training. Data fragmentation across sectors hindered coordinated case management, pointing to the importance of integrated information systems. Variation in frontline worker skills revealed the need for continuous professionalization and standardized accreditation, prompting pilots of digital learning platforms for health professionals. Climate change integration into education required specialized expertise, which the office accessed through collaboration with the UNICEF Regional Office for South Asia. Limited technical capacity hindered progress on complex social protection reforms and nutrition services, while the NDC 3.0 process illustrated the value of inclusive consultations particularly with youth groups to embed sustainability into national strategies.
Looking ahead, BhCO is strategically repositioning itself to respond to the evolving national context, declining Overseas Development Assistance (ODA), and Bhutan’s post-LDC development pathway. The office is actively engaging in discussions on shifting from direct service delivery to upstream engagement and systems strengthening, with the goal of supporting sustainable national ownership and institutional resilience. These discussions will inform adjustments during the midterm review in 2026, ensuring UNICEF remains aligned with Bhutan’s priorities and global SDG commitments.
BhCO will apply lessons learned to refine programme strategies and explore new opportunities for collaboration. Priorities include expanding child protection services through strengthened district and community teams, safe spaces for women and girls, and broader integration of mental health and psychosocial support in schools. Justice for children and digital protection will be advanced by leveraging partnerships with the INTERPOL, restorative practices, and new collaborations with technology companies, academia, faith-based organizations, and the private sector. At the same time, UNICEF will deepen its role as a trusted partner in Bhutan’s national agenda by pursuing digital innovation, inclusive education, and climate-responsive programming.
The RGoB increasingly expects UNICEF to engage beyond traditional ways of working, recognizing its capacity to provide innovative technical expertise. This positions UNICEF to lead and support emerging priorities such as mental health, obesity, dietary diversity, digitalization, skilling, and climate action. While children, adolescents, and youth up to age 24 remain central to Bhutan’s vision of preparing them for the 21st century, UNICEF must adapt and retool its approaches by strengthening technical leadership, generating data and evidence, and exercising strategic influence.
Programmatically, the BhCO will continue its prioritization exercise to identify UNICEF’s comparative advantage and niche areas relative to other UN agencies. This includes assessing opportunities to scale down or scale up activities, exploring resource mobilization prospects, and aligning required roles and skill sets—from influencing international financial institution agendas and EU budget support, to evidence generation for sustainability. Key areas of focus will include operationalizing disability-inclusive social protection, strengthening local governance capacities through Child-Friendly Local Governance, enhancing data interoperability, and advancing child-sensitive reforms. The BhCO will also accelerate systems strengthening, climate-resilient WASH programming, and supply chain improvements for medical products, while developing an investment case for nutrition to ensure sustainable, scalable impact for children and communities.

India is the world’s most populous country, with an estimated population of 1.46 billion, of which approximately 460 million are children under 18 years [1], which accounts for 17.85 per cent of world’s youth population [2]. This demographic structure continues to present significant potential for India’s future underscoring the need for sustained investments in child development. 
Urbanization is steadily rising, with 37 per cent of the population living in urban areas in 2024[3] and projected to exceed 40 per cent by 2030.4 Migration trends – 18.9 per cent rural-to-urban and 15.9 per cent urban-to-urban – reflect significant internal mobility that affects continuity in education, child health service utilization, and housing access for children of migrant families [4].
India’s economy maintained strong momentum in 2025, with real GDP growth estimated at 6.4 per cent for fiscal year (FY) 2024/25 and 8.2 per cent in Q2 of FY 2025/26 [5]. India aims to become the third-largest economy by 2030, with GDP projected at US$ 7.3 trillion [6]. 
According to Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) Study and down-to-earth database India was hit by extreme weather events on 331 of the first 334 days of 2025, up from 295 in 2024. From 1990 to 2024, India sustained average annual disaster related losses equivalent to 0.4 per cent of GDP (OECD Economic Outlook 2025 on Disaster Risk Financing). The natural resource base (e.g. food-water-nutrition) that sustain services for children (human security) will continue to come under stress due to changing climate and ensuing extreme weather events.
India is ranked 26th globally on UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index reflects its high vulnerability, with 34 million children at risk from riverine flooding by the 2040s, highlighting the urgency of child-sensitive climate adaptation [7]. Climate change and environmental risks further compound vulnerabilities, with children facing heightened exposure to extreme weather events and pollution-related health impacts. 
The National Plan of Action for Children (2016) recommends allocating 5 per cent of the Union Budget to children. However, for FY 2025/26, the share remains 2.3 per cent, similar to the previous year. Between FY 2024–25 and FY 2025–26, the total allocation for children increased by 5.6 per cent rising from approximately US$ 13.2 billion to US$ 14.0 billion [8]. Key schemes saw notable increases: Samagra Shiksha, an overarching programme for the school education sector extending from pre-school to class 12 (over 11.5 per cent), and PM SHRI aims to achieve quality and excellence in school education (over 66 per cent) [9], signalling government commitment to investing parts of education responses. 
India improved its Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) ranking from 109th in 2024 to 99th in 2025, reflecting progress on several indicators [10]. Multidimensional poverty fell from 29.2 per cent in 2013–14 to 11.3 per cent in 2022-23, lifting nearly 248 million people out of poverty [11]. On child-related SDG targets, India is on track to meet goals for survival: the under-five mortality rate declined to 29 per 1,000 live births in 2023 [12] down from 30 in 2022, and the maternal mortality ratio fell to 88 per 100,000 live births (2021-23) [13], a substantial improvement from 130 per 100,000 live births in 2014–16.
Birth registration coverage improved to 90.6 per cent [14] and access to safely managed drinking water as required by SDG 6.1, moved from being unreported to reaching 76 per cent [15].
Despite these gains, accelerated efforts are needed in nutrition, education, and child protection. Anaemia among children aged 6–59 months remains high at 67.1 per cent [16]. The government has scaled up Anaemia Mukt Bharat and fortified rice distribution, and implementation quality and behaviour change remain critical. Education indicators show mixed progress: primary retention improved to 92.4 per cent, but secondary level dropout persists at 11.5 per cent, and retention declined slightly to 62.9 per cent [17]. Citizen-led surveys indicate improvements in learning levels. The proportion of Standard 3 students able to read a Standard 2 text increased from 20.5 per cent in 2022 to 27.1 per cent in 2024. In arithmetic, the proportion of Standard 3 students able to do subtraction increased from 25.9 per cent in 2022 to 33.7 per cent in 2024 [18].
According to the NCRB’s Crime in India 2023 report, crimes against children increased by 9.2 per cent, rising from 162,449 cases in 2022 to 177,335 cases in 2023. This pushed the reported crime rate to 39.9 per 100,000 child population (up from 36.6 in 2022). In 2023, kidnapping and abduction accounted for 45 per cent of all reported offences against children, while Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO)-related reported crimes comprised 38.2 per cent. Notably, more than 97 per cent of POCSO perpetrators within the reported cases were known to the victim [19].
Child marriage prevalence remains at 23 per cent among women aged 20-24, and 16.3 per cent among those aged 18-19, with girls from rural and disadvantaged backgrounds disproportionately affected [20].
Continued inequities remain across states, rural–urban locations, and socio-economic groups. Rural under-five mortality is higher (33) compared to urban (20). Children from the poorest quintile experience mortality rates more than twice those of the richest. India ranks 131st in the Global Gender Gap Index, with slight improvements in economic participation but continued gaps in political empowerment [21].
