Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
The reporting period was marked by progress despite significant operational and programmatic challenges. Balancing strong oversight with the flexibility required for adaptive programming remained a core challenge, particularly in the context of evolving priorities under the Future Focus Initiative and the upcoming transition to a Multi-country Office model. 

Partnerships continued to play an indispensable role in achieving results. UNICEF strengthened collaboration with government ministries, civil society organizations, and private sector actors while forging new alliances through platforms such as ‘Mashvaraa’ platforms for policy dialogues. These engagements enabled policy dialogue on critical issues such as adolescent health, juvenile justice, gender equality, and climate resilience. Communication and visibility remained critical for amplifying UNICEF’s work and mobilizing support. Strategic campaigns, digital engagement, and media partnerships enhanced public awareness of child rights issues and positioned UNICEF as a trusted advocate for children. Moving forward, the office will continue to leverage communication platforms to showcase impact, engage partners, and strengthen accountability to stakeholders.

A key lesson learned is the value of staff engagement as a driver of organizational resilience, innovation and performance. Initiatives such as the Human Resources Development and Wellbeing Committee (HRDTW) and ‘Kudhinnaa Gaathun’ missions provided platforms for motivation, team cohesion, and the discovery of hidden talents, reinforcing the importance of investing in people. ‘Kudhinnaa Gaathun’ also demonstrated the power of multi-sectoral engagement at the community level, integrating health, education, protection, and social policy interventions to deliver holistic results. Similarly, HRDTW activities highlighted that staff wellbeing and professional growth are essential for sustaining performance during change management processes.

Looking ahead, 2026 will serve as a pivotal transition year for UNICEF Maldives, marking the conclusion of the current Country Programme and the shift towards a more focused, consolidated portfolio under the next CPD, alongside the transition to a multi-country office structure with Sri Lanka. This transition year will be leveraged to sharpen strategic focus, streamline interventions, and lay the foundations for delivering impact at scale in line with UNICEF’s global imperatives of differentiation, focus, scale, and impact.

The forthcoming CPD will consolidate UNICEF’s engagement around a smaller number of high-leverage priorities, reflecting lessons learned and evidence generated over recent years, particularly around the adolescent challenge where vulnerabilities in health, education, protection, and participation intersect. Rather than expanding breadth, UNICEF will deepen integration across sectors, strengthen systems-level solutions, and accelerate the translation of policy commitments into implementation, especially through schools, families, and protection systems as core platforms for adolescent wellbeing. At the same time, 2026 will be used to carefully manage the operational transition to the multi-country office model, ensuring continuity of programme delivery in Maldives while unlocking opportunities for enhanced technical depth, shared expertise, and operational efficiencies across the new arrangement.

Nepal’s development landscape in 2025 reflected both resilience and persistent challenges. The country experienced a modest but fragile economic recovery and continued its push towards graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) status. Political instability, climate crisis and a tightening global aid environment slowed progress towards the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. 

In September 2025, Nepal faced its most intense political unrest in decades. What began as a peaceful, Gen-Z-led protests against the government ban on social media platforms quickly escalated into a nationwide movement demanding accountability, transparency and digital freedoms. The unrest turned deadly with at least 74 people killed and hundreds injured in clashes between protesters and security forces. The crisis led to the resignation of the Prime Minister and the formation of an interim government, with elections scheduled for March 2026. The political instability, coupled with frequent leadership changes and weak intergovernmental coordination, continued to hinder effective implementation of social sector reforms and service delivery across all three tiers of government, particularly those affecting children’s rights and wellbeing. 

Nepal’s economic performance improved slightly in 2025. The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth for FY2024/25 was estimated at around 4.61 per cent, up from 3.67 per cent in FY2023/24. Growth was driven mainly by hydropower production and remittance inflows. Inflation moderated to about 4.1 per cent, while remittances and foreign exchange reserves helped maintain external stability. However, public debt rose from 40.7 per cent of GDP in 2024 to 43.5 per cent in 2025, and tax revenues stagnated at approximately 17-18 per cent of GDP, reflecting weak domestic demand and reduced imports. These modest macroeconomic gains contributed to increased fiscal space for some social sectors, though spending execution challenges persisted. 

Social sector allocations reached an estimated US$4.2 billion in 2025, doubling over the past seven years but still insufficient to meet growing needs. The education budget increased by 3.7 per cent, a modest rise that fell short of addressing deep-rooted challenges related to quality and equity. Health sector allocations increased by approximately 11 per cent, reversing the decline seen in previous years, yet investment gaps in maternal, newborn and child health remained. Social protection budget remained stable at around US$820 million, reflecting continued government commitment to social security allowances but also indicating a plateau after years of rapid growth. Limited provincial and municipal capacities constrained effective fund utilization and slowed progress toward Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) targets on child survival, learning and protection. These challenges underscored the need for stronger public financial management and accountability mechanisms.

Nepal continued to face the classic LDC graduation dilemma. While graduation marks an important development milestone, it also brings risks, including reduced access to concessional financing, higher borrowing costs and stricter repayment terms. 

These challenges were compounded by a global funding crisis, with declining foreign aid and shrinking donor contributions placing additional strain on development financing. This context reinforced the need to prioritize cost-effective, high-impact investments for children and to strengthen domestic resource mobilization.

In 2025, no major new national data sources were published for tracking impact and outcomes for children and women. The Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), completed during the year, is expected to address critical data gaps once results are published in early 2026. Available administrative data showed progress in immunization, with nine of 13 vaccines achieving over 90 per cent coverage. However, an estimated 34,000 children remained zero-dose or under-immunized. Net enrolment rate in basic education increased to 95.1 per cent, while gross enrolment exceeded 100 per cent. Despite gains in access, learning outcomes stagnated, with fewer than 40 per cent of Grade 5 students achieving required proficiency levels. Persistent disparities underscored the need for targeted interventions to improve quality and access.

Climate change continued to pose a serious threat. Severe floods and landslides, in July and October 2025, disrupted essential services, damaged infrastructure and increased disease risks. Children in poor, rural and hazard-prone areas were most affected by the destruction of houses, schools, health and water facilities, deepening existing inequities. Nepal submitted its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 in May, signaling stronger ambition to integrate children’s needs into climate planning. The use of Children’s Climate Risk Index-Disaster Risk Model is generating evidence to inform planning and resource allocation. Nepal also elevated the global mountain agenda by hosting the Sagarmatha Sambaad (Mount Everest Dialogue) on “Climate Change, Mountains and the Future of Humanity,” which resulted in a 25-point Call for Action. For the first time, mountain issues were formally included in COP30 negotiations, and Nepal drafted a strategic framework for sustainable mountain development. 

However, implementation gaps persisted due to limited capacity, technology and financing.
Nepal prepared for its fourth-cycle Universal Periodic Review, with national consultations and stakeholder reports highlighting progress and remaining gaps in human rights implementation ahead of the January 2026 review. Incremental gain was recorded in gender equality with Nepal’s Gender Gap Index score increasing to 0.664 from 0.659 in 2024. However, female labor force participation remained low at 27.7 per cent, virtually unchanged from the previous year, and far below the male participation rate of 53.7 per cent. This highlights barriers to women’s economic participation, despite incremental progress in other dimensions of gender equality. Gender-based violence and child marriage continued to disproportionately affect adolescent girls, particularly in rural and marginalized communities, with 33 per cent of girls married before the age of 18 years. Social norms and structural barriers limited access to education, health care and protection services for girls and children with disabilities. These inequities call for targeted interventions and inclusive policies, so no child is left behind.

In summary, political instability, fiscal constraints, climate risks and global funding pressures continued to challenge Nepal’s ability to deliver results for children. However, opportunities exist to accelerate systemic reforms, strengthen governance and leverage evidence-based advocacy to secure sustainable financing and inclusive policies. As Nepal approaches LDC graduation amid complex global and domestic pressures, building resilient and equitable social systems is critical to protecting children’s rights and advancing national development goals.

Despite a rapidly evolving global, regional and national context, and a highly disruptive political landscape, UNICEF continued to support the Government of Nepal in delivering transformative changes for children in 2025. The Country Office strategically advanced three flagship priorities—scaling up holistic and integrated early childhood development (ECD), promoting the rights and well-being of adolescent girls and accelerating climate action—while achieving strong results across programmes.   

UNICEF supported significant progress in institutionalizing integrated ECD within government systems to strengthen service delivery to young children. Four provinces out of seven—Karnali, Sudurpaschim, Lumbini and Madhesh—reactivated their ECD committees, strengthening multisector coordination and enabling consistent financing and service quality. The integrated ECD planning guideline for local governments was updated, contributing to the establishment of functional ECD steering committees and integrated ECD plans in 10 per cent of municipalities nationwide. In these municipalities, domestic financing for ECD increased by 58 per cent, demonstrating stronger local commitment. At the national level. the Ministry of Health and Population (MoHP) expanded the Care for Child Development package, embedding nurturing care within routine health services – a game changer for holistic child development. 

Key interventions delivered across sectors with UNICEF’s financial, technical and logistical assistance produced transformative results for adolescent girls’ health, nutrition, education and skills development. The nationwide introduction of the HPV vaccine represented a landmark in girls’ sexual and reproductive health. Of the 1,688,768girls 10-14, 1,461,654 (94 per cent of the target cohort) were vaccinated through school- and community-based delivery, protecting them from cervical cancer. National efforts to prevent anemia led to 1.6 million adolescent girls receiving iron–folic acid supplementation and nutrition education across 411 local governments through improved school-health facilities coordination and capacity building of school nurses and health workers. Access to education and skills was expanded through 371 quality-assured Community Learning Centers, where 18,388 adolescents (57 per cent girls) participated in back-to-school and employability programmes, directly informing the government’s national scale-up strategy. Building on previous investments, 13,038 adolescents (11,362 girls) strengthened life and financial skills, enabling them to delay marriage, access essential services and exercise agency over their futures. Girls and Inclusive Education Networks (GIEN) became active in 212 municipalities, with 22 municipalities adopting costed action plans institutionalizing accountability and sustainability for girls’ rights. These results reflect a strategic shift from pilot initiatives to government-owned, system-wide solutions, positioning UNICEF as a trusted partner and accelerating Nepal’s progress toward SDG 5 and gender equality for adolescents.

UNICEF led efforts to ensure Nepal’s third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) included world’s most child-sensitive climate commitments. Of the 47 child-sensitive indicators across water, sanitation and hygiene, health, education and protection, 46 were fully incorporated. Children, adolescents and young people directly shaped these commitments through platforms such as BaYu Sambaad (Children and Youth Dialogue). Their inputs also informed Nepal’s COP30 position paper. The Children’s Climate Risk Index–Disaster Risk Model (CCRI-DRM) developed by UNICEF, was adopted by the government to map climate risks affecting children nationwide. This evidence-based approach enables subnational authorities to identify priority risks, guide investment decisions and strengthen risk-informed planning, laying the foundation for more resilient, child-focused climate responses. 

Key results from UNICEF’s transformative actions across various sectors are summarized below.

Health
UNICEF supported the Government of Nepal to strengthen health systems and expand access to equitable services for children and women. With UNICEF technical assistance, emergency obstetric and neonatal care was strengthened in 158 strategically selected health facilities across four provinces – Karnali, Sudurpaschim, Madhesh and Lumbini, serving 643,437 women and newborns - 44 per cent of annual live births. The introduction of new clinical and quality-improvement approaches contributed to a 28 per cent reduction in birth asphyxia and a 42 per cent reduction in postpartum hemorrhage. Access to functional emergency obstetric and newborn care increased from 58 to 78 per cent, improving emergency care readiness for 500,000 women and newborns nationwide. Based on these results, all four provincial governments are now replicating these life-saving approaches in additional facilities. 

Children’s access to mental health services expanded significantly with UNICEF support. In 2025, 9,414 children received mental health services, a four-time increase from last year. This progress reflects the government’s efforts to develop its first mental health plans and an allocation of US$1.3 million to scale up services, representing an eight-fold return on UNICEF’s investment. In Karnali Province, 12,500 students benefited from school-based socio-emotional learning programme planned for nationwide expansion to reach 850,000 students annually from 2026 using government funds. Nepal also established its first evidence-based model of care for childhood non-communicable diseases (NCD), treating 455 children with chronic conditions. UNICEF supported Nepal's first national childhood NCD survey, generating critical evidence for the 2026-2030 national health strategy. 

During emergencies, UNICEF delivered life-saving health services. In Madhesh Province, 9,500 flood-affected people received essential supplies and psychosocial support within 72 hours. UNICEF also provided 50,000 cholera rapid diagnostic kits to health facilities, strengthening outbreak detection amid heightened waterborne disease risks following drought conditions.

Nutrition
UNICEF supported the government to advance national priorities for maternal, child and adolescent nutrition and progress toward SDG 2: Zero Hunger. In 2025, 19,865 severely wasted children - 41 per cent of the national caseload and a 15-per cent increase from 2024 - received life-saving treatment, achieving an 80 per cent recovery rate in line with SPHERE standards. Community-based screening for child wasting reached 3.75 million children, up from 3.6 million in 2024. Access to essential micronutrients also expanded, with 448,463 children under two receiving multiple micronutrient powder, increasing programme coverage from 42 to 60 per cent. The Mother-Baby Friendly Hospital initiative expanded to 72 hospitals nationwide, where 90 per cent of newborns were breastfed within the first hour of life.  These results were enabled by UNICEF’s support to roll out the Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) guidelines, institutionalize child malnutrition screening, strengthen commodity forecasting and availability, and build the capacity of health workers and Female Community Health Volunteers on infant and young child feeding (IYCF) and breastfeeding counselling.

With UNICEF’s catalytic support, the national adolescent nutrition guideline was adopted and rolled out in 411 local governments (55 per cent of all 753 municipalities). Over 50,000 female community health volunteers were mobilized to deliver maternal nutrition counseling and roll out the revised maternal and child health booklet, increasing service demand. The Multi-Sector Nutrition Plan (MSNP) III continued to scale nationwide, with 437 local governments allocating US$22.2 million for evidence-based nutrition actions. Digital innovation advanced through the development of an integrated information system for nutrition governance and monitoring.

Climate-resilient WASH
UNICEF supported the government to strengthen climate-resilient water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) systems in line with the 16th Development Plan, the Water Act and Policy, and SDG 6: Ensure Access to Water and Sanitation for All. Through UNICEF advocacy, the government increased the weightage of WASH indicators in the Local Governance Performance Assessment System from 1.8 to 3.1 points, linking WASH performance to local performance-based grants. This reform incentivizes local governments to develop and roll-out WASH plans, financing strategies and use the national WASH information system. The Municipal WASH Financing Strategy Manual and the Water-Safe Community guidelines were endorsed and rolled out nationwide.
In 2025, 199 municipalities adopted multi-year WASH plans, with an additional 412 under development. A total of 111 municipal WASH officers were trained in climate-resilient programming. In response to drought, Nepal’s first real-time groundwater monitoring station was established in Madhesh Province, with expansion underway in three additional water-stressed areas.

About 69,000 people, including 23,000 children, gained access to safe and reliable WASH services. Water quality surveillance, routine chlorination and water safety planning enabled 12,000 people to live in water-safe communities. In addition, 67 schools and 58 healthcare facilities gained access to gender-, disability-, and climate-responsive WASH services. During emergencies, including cholera outbreak, UNICEF supported the government to provide safe drinking water, sanitation facilities and hygiene supplies to 53,000 people. 

Education  
UNICEF accelerated education recovery and system transformation. The School Education Sector Plan (SESP) Calibration Toolkit was adopted nationwide, while the Local Education Plan (LEP) Appraisal Tool was approved by 353 local governments in 2025, with all 753 municipalities on track for completion by 2026. 

In 150 municipalities modelling the SESP implementation with UNICEF support, the LEPs helped leverage US$28 million in domestic education financing—a 27 per cent increase—demonstrating strengthened local government capacities and domestic financing to deliver quality education services. Strengthening teacher professional development systems remained a cornerstone, with 2,000 educators trained in child-friendly pedagogy, multilingual instruction and digital learning approaches. This resulted in improved learning and safety for 195,020 children (56 per cent girls), including an eight-percentage-point increase in school readiness in Grade 1 nationally, and a three-percentage-point increase in the proportion of schools applying school safety measures nationally. In target local governments, notable gains in learning outcomes were made, with a 10 per cent gain in literacy and numeracy, and a 23-percentage-point improvement in Mathematics and Nepali for Grades 2 and 3 students. 2.1 million children benefited indirectly through the national scale-up or local replications of proven models such as the GIEN, Remote Education and Learning, Accelerated Learning Programme, and Early Learning Development Standards. The integration of foundational learning tools and remedial teaching strategies further supported children at risk of falling behind.

Non-formal education was strengthened through support to 2,100 Community Learning Centers nationally, where compliance with quality standards increased from 50 to 77 per cent. Through these centers, 18,388 adolescents (67 per cent girls) accessed accredited back-to-school and employability skills programmes. UNICEF’s modelling of equivalency pathways under the National Qualifications Framework was scaled by the government nationwide.

UNICEF also supported the expansion of the Comprehensive School Safety Framework, with 26 per cent of schools nationwide now implementing climate-smart safety measures, benefiting one million children. Learning continuity was ensured for 115,000 crisis-affected children (52 per cent girls) through emergency education supplies, psychosocial support and alternative learning pathways. 

Child Protection
UNICEF strengthened Nepal’s child protection system through legal reforms, institutionalized child protection standards and increased financing. With UNICEF support, the Government of Nepal passed the second amendment to the Citizenship Act in 2025, enabling children to obtain citizenship through either parent, which represents a significant change from its patriarchal past and a landmark reform advancing child rights. Proposed revisions to the 2018 Act Relating to Children will, once passed, raise the minimum age of criminal responsibility from 10 to 12 years, promoting a more child-centered justice approach. The establishment of Nepal’s first Children’s Court marked a transformative shift toward child-sensitive and rights-based juvenile justice.

Child protection reforms accelerated at the local level. In 2025, child protection standards and procedures were institutionalized in 34 additional municipalities, bringing coverage to 59 per cent of all 753 municipalities. With UNICEF support, 22 new child rights committees were established, 100 child welfare officers were deployed, and 66 child psychologists and social workers were trained. The expansion of case management standards, digital referral pathways and the rollout of Child Protection Information Management System Plus (CPIMS+) in 42 municipalities improved service coordination, enabling 500,000 children, adolescents and women to access birth registration (increase from 461,006 under-five children in 2024 to 560,594 in 2025), psychosocial support, legal aid and gender-based violence (GBV) services.

UNICEF also strengthened national child protection data systems. The Nepal Police assumed responsibility for collecting, managing and publishing national child protection and GBV data, improving evidence-based planning and policing. Targeted interventions for children and women at risk of child marriage and GBV were expanded in high-burden provinces, reaching 19,000 children with survivor-centred services and community-based prevention. UNICEF’s high-level advocacy successfully safeguarded the legal minimum age of marriage at 20 years, preventing its reduction to 18 years and avoiding the potential over criminalization of boys under the age of 20 years accused of marrying girls of the same age. Child protection priorities were integrated into local development plans and budgets in 442 municipalities—60 per cent nationwide—covering five million children. Engagement with religious leaders and community influencers further contributed to shifting social norms and strengthening protective environments for children.

Social Policy, Governance and Evidence (SPGE)
UNICEF strengthened evidence-based policymaking, inclusive governance and social protection systems. With UNICEF support, the government conducted the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), addressing critical gaps in child and gender-disaggregated data. Work is underway to update outcome-level social development indicators sector and publish the Children’s Thematic Report and Child Situation Index, strengthening data availability at federal, provincial and local levels.

UNICEF provided technical assistance to operationalize Nepal’s new national strategy on citizen engagement in public finance management. Citizen engagement policies were drafted in 32 municipalities across three provinces (Sudurpaschim, Karnali, Madhesh), with four piloting citizens budgets to enhance transparency and public participation. Similarly, 19 municipalities began implementing Gender Equality and Social Inclusion-Costed Implementation Plans, while Child Friendly Local Governance was revitalized in 29 municipalities, ensuring child participation in local planning and budgeting. 

The completion of the Social Security Allowance impact evaluation provided the first rigorous evidence on the effectiveness of government-funded schemes, informing social protection reforms and advocacy for expanded child grants. UNICEF also supported analysis of disability-related financial burden, contributing to more inclusive social protection measures for children with disabilities and their families.

Programme Effectiveness 
In 2025, Nepal faced multiple emergencies, including floods and landslides in Koshi and Madhesh Provinces, a severe drought and cholera outbreak in Madhesh Province, and fires in Sudurpaschim Province. UNICEF supported government’s rapid response, reaching 66,500 people (25,000 children) across four provinces, with integrated health, nutrition, WASH, protection, education and temporary shelter support. To strengthen the humanitarian-development nexus, UNICEF supported the expansion of early warning systems and risk-informed planning and preparedness. Notably, 20 additional municipalities formulated and integrated the child- and disability-sensitive Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plan into their annual plans and budget this year, bringing the total to 41 municipalities since 2023. These plans institutionalize multi-sectoral coordination, financing and accountability for disaster and climate risk management.

UNICEF strengthened visibility and support for children’s rights. Through 10 high-level advocacy events with government, public and private sector partners, and media, cross-sector engagement on children’s issues was strengthened. These advocacy platforms, together with the Youth Advocates Programme, directly engaged 883 children and young people and reached millions more indirectly. Fifty impact stories were produced and disseminated, strengthening the use of inclusive, child-centered storytelling to place children’s voices at the heart of advocacy. These efforts generated 200 media mentions, significantly expanding the visibility of children’s rights. Digital campaigns reached 20 million people, amplifying child-centered priorities in both public and policy discourse. Despite a challenging funding environment, existing partnerships were safeguarded and donor confidence maintained through targeted engagement, including quality assurance of 52 donor reports and organization of five donor visits. 

Social Behavior Change (SBC) initiatives continued to lead transformative positive shifts in behaviors, norms and systems, making essential health, nutrition, WASH, education and protection services more accessible and effective for children and communities. With UNICEF support, the government, for the first time, developed two provincial immunization demand strategies and piloted an SBC training package for local health workers, aimed at integrating evidence-based SBC approaches into local health systems. These will be adopted and rolled out across five provinces from 2026. The youth empowerment initiatives made impressive progress, with 15,000 youths engaged in digital communication networks and 2,000 youths sensitized to serve as agents of change for climate action. During the Gen-Z protests, droughts, cholera and dengue outbreaks, and floods, 72,000 online insights were analyzed, supporting timely design and implementation of multisectoral humanitarian response.

Operation Effectiveness
In 2025, UNICEF Nepal strengthened governance, financial and administrative management, and organizational culture. All recommendations from the 2024 peer review were closed. Completion rates reached 100 per cent for programme assurance activities and 98 per cent for financial assurance activities, while 100 per cent of available resources - including emergency funds - were utilized. Security compliance exceeded 95 per cent.

The office managed a throughput of US$870,000 in programme supplies, US$2.32 million in service contracts and US$7.4 million in procurement services for the government. Supply benchmarks were met, with 96 per cent of procurement conducted competitively and 100 per cent of emergency supplies prepositioned. 

UNICEF continued driving the UN collaboration agenda in OMT where UNICEF is a co-chair. UNICEF led two important OMT working groups-Finance and Procurement and Supply, conducted salary survey and placed common LTAs, contributing to UN-wide efficiencies.
Financial efficiency improved through timely processing of 800 direct cash transfer advances totaling US$13 million, with 95 per cent completed within 14 days; 98 per cent planned spot checks and 15 micro-assessments were completed. All civil-society organization (CSO) partners underwent Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) risk assessments, with 100 per cent rated low or moderate risk. CSO registrations in the UN Partner Portal increased from 239 to 812, expanding the partner base.

The office completed 79 per cent of the group learning and development plan. The staff diversity profile showed a modest improvement, with the recruitment of one additional employee from the under-represented group, and two United Nations Volunteers (UNVs) with disabilities. The office Ethics and Culture Champions were appointed, and staff participated in quarterly human resource outreach sessions. Recruitment achieved a 74 per cent completion rate, and individual staff learning and capacity building were supported through stretch assignments, surge missions and on-lien posts.

Two new field offices were renovated. Operational efficiencies generated cost savings - US$12,900 from office-sharing with other UN agencies and US$110,000 from economy air tickets and local terminal cost policies. In Kathmandu, 60 per cent of trips used electric vehicles and 10 per cent were rideshared, contributing to US$2,503 savings and a reduction of 10,365 kg of CO2 emissions.

NCO continued using hybrid solar systems for power, smart energy meters, indoor air-quality monitoring, sustainable waste-management practices, while eliminating single-use plastics. NCO initiated procurement of four electric vehicles and one disability-friendly vehicle. Risk-mitigation included monitoring of EV charging infrastructure, systematic fleet-tracking, oversight of environmental performance reporting using the EFAAT tool, ensuring continuity of operations and safety across office premises. 

NCO also monitored operating risks, updated the risk register, and embedded mitigation measures in SOPs to ensure risk-informed decision making.

In 2025, UNICEF Nepal’s programming was shaped by a deliberate shift toward system strengthening, driven by the new UNICEF Strategic Plan (2026–2029), Nepal’s imminent graduation from LDC status, and declining official development assistance and fiscal constraints.  This transition reflected a strategic choice to prioritize resilient, government-led systems capable of sustaining results for children in a changing financing landscape.

Moving away from routine service delivery – except in emergencies – proved necessary but complex. While progress was evident in sectors such as nutrition and health, where interventions were increasingly embedded in government plans, budgets and systems, the transition revealed gaps in subnational capacity, planning and monitoring.  In nutrition, the integration of the MSNP III into local government planning demonstrated strong ownership and domestic financing. In health, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health and mental health services showed growing institutionalization. In areas such as child protection and WASH, direct service delivery remains essential, reflecting uneven federal capacity and the continued need for targeted technical assistance.

Despite years of investment, Nepal’s progress towards the SDGs remains uneven, particularly in child survival, learning outcomes and protection, highlighting that system strengthening is not only a technical priority but also a strategic necessity. 2025 reaffirmed that innovative models are most effective when they are designed for integration and scale within government systems from the outset.  Several first-of-their-kind initiatives—the human milk bank, real-time groundwater monitoring, the Water-Safe Community model benefiting 12,00 people in Madhesh, and a disability screening application linking thousands of children to social protection benefits—demonstrated strong potential for impact once adopted by government. 

Equity remained both a guiding principle and a persistent challenge. Reaching the most marginalized children -- particularly in remote, disaster-prone or socially excluded communities -- required tailored approaches, flexible financing and adaptive management. High-impact interventions must be paired with robust monitoring and continuous feedback to close persistent gaps. Progress in gender equality, disability inclusion and social protection was evident. However, disparities remain, underscoring the need for ongoing vigilance and innovation.

Partnerships remained central to UNICEF Nepal’s strategy and evolved in response to the changing context. Strong collaboration with government at all levels enabled the institutionalization and scale up of flagship initiatives, such as the School Education Sector Plan Calibration Toolkit, now adopted nationwide. UNICEF partnered with 138 government entities and collaborated with 44 national and international non-governmental organizations and academic institutions. New partnerships with 48 local governments and 42 provincial/district governments strengthened decentralized delivery and accountability. As UNICEF reduced direct service delivery, partnerships with civil society organizations focused on capacity-building for advocacy, SBC, monitoring and accountability. CSOs remained critical for reaching marginalized populations. However, sustainability of CSO engagement following UNICEF exit remains a challenge, highlighting the need for stronger transition planning and alignment with government systems.

UNICEF also advanced key results with UN partners, supporting gender equality through the Empowered Women, Prosperous Nepal programme, which enabled 32 municipalities to implement GESI plans. Together with UNFPA, UNICEF strengthened Nepal’s efforts to end child marriage by securing endorsement of the revised national strategy, preventing attempts to lower the legal age of marriage, and expanding joint initiatives such as Rupantaran and provincial GBV and life-skills programmes. UNICEF also partnered with UNESCO and Norway to promote a climate-smart, resilient education system, and worked with FAO, UNFPA and WFP to deliver anticipatory action in Saptari, providing cash assistance, child protection, WASH support, and contributing to the national anticipatory action framework and the 4th national dialogue on risk transfer and financing.

In a constrained funding environment, UNICEF prioritized strategic donor engagement, reporting compliance and partner visibility. High-level donor visits, joint advocacy events and digital campaigns reached up to 20 million people, strengthening child rights awareness. National Committee partnerships resulted in US$1.4 million in funding commitments, while new partner engagement—including the Embassy of Australia and the Cricket Association of Nepal—advanced girls’ empowerment through sports for development. Emerging collaboration with the private sector on family-friendly policies also laid the groundwork for future advocacy to influence business practices for young children.

Thought leadership, evidence generation and innovation continued to inform policy and programming. Nepal’s first Social Security Allowance impact evaluation generated important evidence to inform social protection reforms, while the MICS filled critical data gaps on child and adolescent wellbeing, including mental health and climate risk. The assessment of the Rupantaran programme and the disability expenditure analysis strengthened the national evidence base.

Integrated, multisectoral approaches proved essential for addressing complex, intersecting deprivations faced by children. Joint planning and service delivery through schools and health centers enabled more holistic support, particularly for the most marginalized children. In Karnali Province, school-based socio-emotional learning reached 12,500 students, while integrated WASH and health investments in 67 schools and 58 health facilities ensured gender-, disability-, and climate-responsive services. Water-Safe Community model and integrated education-health-nutrition programming demonstrated scalable approaches for community-driven change. Nonetheless, operationalizing multisectoral collaboration remains challenging, with persisting sectoral silos and limited convergence.

Digital tools improved efficiency and accountability, including through child protection case management systems, e-learning platforms, and real-time community feedback tools such as I-Hear-U and U-Report. The rollout of Nepal’s first Grade 1 digital textbook, the expansion of CPIMS+ to 42 municipalities and the introduction of disability screening app showed strong potential for scale. However, uneven digital access and capacity at the local level highlighted the need for inclusive design, sustained capacity-building and investment in digital infrastructure. 

Increased social tensions and pushbacks on child rights included the Gen-Z protests and debates over lowering the legal age of marriage. UNICEF’s rapid analysis, advocacy and engagement with government helped restore emergency coordination mechanisms and successfully protected the legal age of marriage at 20 years, highlighting importance of agility, strategic advocacy and preparedness to safeguard hard-won gains for children.

Looking ahead, NCO will deepen its system-strengthening agenda, focusing on government-led delivery, institutional capacity and sustainability in a post-LDC context. The office will pivot from service delivery to catalytic technical assistance, leveraging evidence, innovation and strategic partnerships to maximize impact. Multisectoral programming, community-driven approaches, and SBC strategies will be central to accelerating progress.

Pakistan stands at a pivotal moment in its development journey. Across the country, families are striving to give their children a better future, even as economic pressures and climate challenges shape daily life. With children accounting for more than 40 per cent of Pakistan’s 240 million people,[1] the nation’s progress depends on their well-being. Yet too many still face barriers in accessing essential services such as health, nutrition, learning, protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene. As systems strengthen and reforms advance, the imperative is clear: ensure every child survives, thrives, learns and is protected.
  
After a period of acute economic stress at the start of the 2024 financial year—marked by the threat of sovereign default – the Government took difficult but decisive measures to restore stability. Inflation fell sharply  from 23.4 per cent in FY2024 to 4.5 per cent in FY2025, foreign reserves  strengthened, and real GDP growth rose modestly to 3.0 per cent, up from 2.6  per cent the previous year.[2]  Public debt, including government-guaranteed debt, remained elevated at 76 per cent of GDP, but fiscal consolidation under the IMF programme helped  prevent further instability.[3] Poverty also edged down from 25.3 per cent to 22.2 per cent as growth recovered and inflation eased.[4]
  
To sustain this momentum, the Government launched URAAN Pakistan, a five-year economic blueprint aligned with the Prime Minister’s Transformation Agenda, and advanced reforms across state-owned enterprises, power distribution companies and business regulations. Pakistan also secured significant multilateral support, including US$1 billion under the Extended Fund Facility, US$200 million under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility, and a combined US$1.2 billion in fresh IMF disbursements.[5] Yet these gains remain highly vulnerable. High interest rates, supply-chain pressures and the devastating 2025 floods have strained fiscal space and derailed growth prospects, threatening to reverse progress for the most disadvantaged households and children. However, lower inflation and a gradual recovery in growth are likely to have eased some immediate cost-of-living pressures on families with children. Improved food affordability and more predictable spending on basic health and education services may have contributed to a modest decline in child poverty.
  
Despite these stabilization efforts, human development outcomes remain among the lowest globally. Pakistan ranks 168 out of 193 countries in the 2025 Human Development Index, with a score of 0.544, which drops by 33.1 per cent to 0.364 when adjusted for inequality.[6] Multidimensional poverty also remains widespread, with an MPI value of 0.198, unchanged from previous years.[7]  
  
Despite ongoing efforts to advance gender equality, the Gender Inequality Index of 0.536 (rank 145/172) and a Gender Development Index of 0.838 demonstrate that significant disparities persist.[8] Deep-rooted harmful social norms continue to restrict girls’ mobility and household decision-making, limit service uptake among marginalized groups, and compound economic and geographic disparities.  At the same time, climate shocks, rising costs and demographic pressures are intensifying, and the vulnerabilities of Pakistan’s youngest citizens are undermining progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 
  
Pakistan’s  demographic profile holds extraordinary potential. The country has an  exceptionally young population, with about 112 million children under 18,[9]  creating both a potential demographic dividend but also placing immense  pressure on education, health, social protection and child-protection systems  to expand rapidly in coverage, quality and equity to keep pace with this  cohort’s needs and aspirations. 
  
Malnutrition remains pervasive. Over 40 per cent of children under the age of 5 are physically stunted (too short for their age), because of long-term, hidden hunger, impairing their growth and development and preventing a child from reaching their full physical and mental potential.  A furthe  17.7 per cent of children under 5 suffer from wasting, being too thin for their height, indicating that the child has experienced recent, rapid and severe weight loss or a failure to gain weight properly. Additionally, over 50 per cent are affected by micronutrient deficiencies.[10]
  
Many young children are still dying from preventable and treatable causes. For every 1,000 babies born, 35 die in their first month, accounting for most under-five deaths. Overall, 47 out of every 1,000 children do not survive their first birthday.[11] Moreover, many children are still missing critical vaccines, about 400,000 have not received even their first routine dose. Pakistan is one of only two countries in the world that has yet to eradicate polio. Adolescents, too, face heightened health risks, with an adolescent mortality rate of 9 deaths per 1,000 young people aged 10–19.[12] Despite these critical challenges, the federal allocation to health in the 2025–26 budget amounts to just 0.2 per cent of total expenditure.[13]
  
The country is also confronting one of the world’s most acute education crises, ranking second to Nigeria in the absolute number of out-of-school children (OOSC). In proportion to its population, the scale is staggering; over 36 per cent (more than one in three) of children aged 5-16 is excluded from the system. This amounts to 25.37 million children (13.41 million girls and 11.96 million boys), creating a monumental barrier to national development.[14] Nationally, 67 per cent of children who are out of school have never entered a classroom (74 per cent in rural areas compared to 59 per cent in urban  centres). Punjab has the largest number of OOSC at 7.83 million, but  Balochistan faces the most acute proportional deprivation, with nearly 69 per cent (7 in 10) of its children out of school.[15] Despite this education emergency, public financing remains critically low.  The FY2024-25 budget allocated only Rs 112.7 billion (US$ 400 million) to education—a mere 0.7 per cent of GDP. Furthermore, spending on primary education stands at US$ 397 (purchasing power per child), 66 per cent below the South Asian regional average, leaving Pakistan’s youth significantly disadvantaged compared with their neighbours.[16]
  
Protection vulnerabilities continue to undermine children’s safety, dignity and future opportunities. Six in 10 children under the age of 5 remain unregistered, denying them legal identity and restricting access to essential services.  Some 11 million children, or one in seven, are engaged in child labour,  trapping families in cycles of intergenerational poverty. The 2023 Census  reveals 641,887 adolescents aged 15–17, representing 4 per cent of all  adolescents, were married, widowed, divorced, or separated, with girls  disproportionately affected (430,388 compared to 211,499 boys).[17]  Children with disabilities number 946,000, or 0.8 per cent of all Pakistani  children.[18]  Among refugees, vulnerabilities are even more acute: 53 per cent of Afghan  refugees in Pakistan are under 18, placing immense pressure on already  strained services.[19]  Gaps in disaggregated data across these groups hinder targeted interventions  and weaken efforts to ensure equitable service delivery.
  
Digital exclusion compounds inequality. Only 57 per cent of Pakistan’s population has internet access, concentrated largely in urban areas at 69 per cent.[20] Even among those online, 93.2 per cent use the internet primarily for entertainment, while only 11.9 per cent use it for e-learning, reinforcing disparities in access to knowledge and opportunity.[21]
  
Climate shocks pose an ongoing threat to children’s wellbeing and Pakistan’s development trajectory. The 2025 floods displaced thousands, severed access to education, health care and nutrition services, and heightened vulnerabilities among already marginalized communities. Social protection financing—Rs 734 billion (US$2.6 billion) in core allocations and Rs 32  billion (US$113.6 million) in additional support—remains insufficient in the face of increasing climate and economic risks.[22]
  
Pakistan’s progress on child rights is  hindered by deep-rooted social and cultural norms that limit access to health, nutrition, protection and education. These norms restrict access to  and use of social services, including vaccination uptake, nutrition services and educational opportunities, particularly for girls and marginalised  groups. As a result, there remain high numbers of early marriages and  children dropping out of school, particularly girls, alongside high rates of malnutrition and vaccine-preventable illnesses. 
  
To shape a more resilient, equitable and prosperous future, stronger community engagement is needed, particularly to empower women in  decision-making, support them in turning knowledge into action and ensure that all children are healthy, nourished, protected and educated, and can  reach their potential.
  
Additionally, unlocking this potential requires accelerated, child-centred investments in health, education, protection, climate resilience and social protection. Without urgent and  sustained action, the inequalities children face today will shape both their futures and nation’s trajectory for decades to come.

Despite economic pressures, climate shocks and persistent inequities, 2025 marked a year of significant gains for children in Pakistan, with encouraging progress in helping more children survive and grow up healthier. Working hand-in-hand with government institutions, communities and partners, UNICEF strengthened essential public systems while expanding life-saving and life-enhancing services to millions of children and caregivers. From improving newborn care and expanding foundational learning to scaling digital tools, empowering adolescents and embedding climate resilience across sectors, these gains show what becomes possible when evidence, innovation and community voices unite to drive change for every child.

Child and Maternal Health
UNICEF’s interventions strengthened Pakistan’s health system and improved the health and well-being of women and children. By advancing health system digitalization, integrated service delivery and climate-resilient health solutions, UNICEF accelerated progress toward universal health coverage and reduced preventable maternal and child mortality.
  
Nationwide DHIS2 scale-up achieved full transition in Balochistan and near-complete coverage in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with electronic medical records integration initiated at federal and provincial levels. These efforts enabled data-driven planning and accountability. Policy advocacy secured PKR 200 million (US$ 0.72 million) for Lady Health Worker operations and the inclusion of neonatal care units in provincial development plans. National contributions included the Health and Population Strategy and the rollout of the Behaviour Change Communication framework.
  
UNICEF supported the expansion of integrated service delivery through RED/REC and SUCCESS initiatives, combining Maternal and Child Health (MNCH), immunization, nutrition, WASH and education services in underserved districts. As a result, over 162,000 newborns benefited from enhanced care in 38 facilities, while home-based newborn care reached millions of women, integrating early childhood development and birth registration. Additionally, UNICEF-supported Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) protocols managed more than 437,000 children, reducing pneumonia and diarrhoea morbidity. HIV services were strengthened through Prevention of Parent-to-Child Transmission (PPTCT) centres and antiretroviral therapy (ART) facilities, while adolescent health advanced with UNICEF support through mental health initiatives and the Helping Adolescents Thrive package.
  
Urban health equity improved through outreach in 23  mega cities, vaccinating 62,642 zero-dose children and 151,472 defaulters,  reducing zero-dose prevalence by 27 per cent. Supply chain resilience was  reinforced through expanded cold chain capacity, solarization of 493 health  facilities and deployment of 31 refrigerated trucks, ensuring uninterrupted  vaccine availability and environmental sustainability.
  
The humanitarian response addressed climate shocks  and emergencies, delivering 40 tons of contingency supplies, essential  medicines and clean delivery kits during floods and heatwaves, benefiting  570,000 people. Mobile and fixed services provided over 210,000  consultations, 34,513 antenatal visits and 10,930 safe deliveries. Support  was extended to Afghan refugees and flood-affected communities, while  national coordination strengthened preparedness, surveillance and the  rehabilitation of damaged facilities.
  
Behavioural and Social Drivers of childhood vaccination revealed  that 93 per cent of caregivers knew where to vaccinate their children, and 81  per cent intended to do so. Using these insights, adolescent girls and  caregivers co-created messages with A/B-tested  HPV information,[1]  which informed the design of an evidence-informed  SBC HPV Strategy and campaign that achieved 74 per cent uptake. In parallel,  eight community co-created  behavioural solutions, including Immunization Champion Networks, demonstrated  a positive user experience, consistently converting intention into uptake,  driving significant gains in zero-dose  coverage among children across 16 high-priority  districts. 
  
Intensive vaccination efforts led to a decline in wild poliovirus  cases from 74 in 2024 to 31 in 2025; however, virus circulation remains  persistent. To interrupt the ongoing transmission, the Pakistan  Polio Programme intensified vaccination efforts in  high-risk areas and sustained equity-focused immunization strategies. With  UNICEF support, six Supplementary Immunization Activities were conducted,  including one Sub–National Immunization Day (SNID) and five NIDs in February,  April, May, October and December, vaccinating around 45 million children  (0–5-year-olds), in each campaign. Also, UNICEF supported five case responses  and two special campaigns with a specific regional scope. Additionally,  UNICEF supported f-IPV for the expanded age group of children from 4 months  to 15 years in Lahore in November. UNICEF ensured the timely  availability of the required vaccine for all polio vaccination activities,  with no stockouts reported in 2025. UNICEF procured and delivered 293.3  million doses of bivalent oral polio vaccine (bOPV).
  
UNICEF successfully tackled vaccination barriers through tailored  outreach, reducing refusal cases from 65,876 to 53,623, improving refusal  conversion rate from 73 per cent in February to 78 per cent in October,  driven by improved community acceptance. To reach inaccessible areas,  UNICEF’s Community-Led Vaccination Initiative (COMVI) delivered over 532,000  vaccinations in high-risk regions in 2025. Furthermore, proactive community  engagement averted 84 per cent of potential boycotts and resolved 87 per cent  of active ones, ensuring vaccination access for over 339,000 children and  maintaining crucial population immunity. In the NID in December, the number  of recorded ‘missed’ children decreased by 4 per cent compared to the NID  held in February (2025). Additionally, the number of ‘still missed’ children  decreased by 28 per cent.
  
During 2025, the polio programme used systematic data collection and  evidence to plan, implement and evaluate interventions. Key efforts included  media assessment surveys to tailor communication strategies; a community  mobilizers’ perception survey in Karachi to address field barriers; an  expanded age appropriate sentiment survey in Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar and  Quetta to guide IPV vaccination SBC strategies; an IPC skills assessment in  priority districts to identify training needs; and the SBC Evaluation (2018-2024),  which assessed UNICEF-supported interventions. Findings shaped strategies for  SIAs, expanded age-appropriate vaccination and strengthened capacity-building  for frontline workers.
  
Collectively, these interventions improved service  reach, system efficiency and resilience, positioning Pakistan to accelerate  progress toward SDG health targets and to ensure equitable access to  life-saving care for women and children.
  
Child Nutrition and  Development 
In 2025, UNICEF reinforced systems, legal  frameworks, integrated programmes, parenting support and community engagement  to ensure that children across Pakistan receive the nutrition services and  care essential for their survival, growth, development and lifelong  well-being. 

In close coordination with the health  section and respective health departments, UNICEF supported the rollout of  the DHIS-2 nutrition module in over 72 districts, strengthening the nutrition  information system. This included integrating nutrition indicators and data  into the health system to strengthen information management; integrating  nutrition and early childhood development (ECD) content into medical  curricula to enhance human resources development for nutrition and child  development; and supporting the development of a national dietary diversity  strategy and a guideline for the prevention and management of wasting and  nutritional oedema, both of which the Government endorsed for roll-out.  Nutrition is included as a strategic priority in the upcoming Pakistan Health  and Population Policy 2026-2035.

UNICEF conducted various assessments and  studies to generate evidence for informed policy, planning and programming  decisions on nutrition and child development including a study on the drivers  of malnutrition among adolescents, an assessment of the implementation of the  simplified protocols, a landscape analysis of Family Friendly Policies &  Practices in Pakistan, an ECD country evaluation, and the mid-term evaluation  of the Global Action Plan for the prevention and management of wasting and  operational research on SQ-LNS.
  
UNICEF strengthened innovative financing  for nutrition, including matching funds that have mobilized over US$13.2  million in public funds for the procurement of lifesaving nutrition  commodities. UNICEF also supported the expansion of access to essential nutrition  services, reaching 3.93 million people with nutrition and parenting messages,  treating 304,138 children with severe acute malnutrition, and supplementing  37.3 million children with Vitamin A, 722,869 adolescent girls with iron and  folic acid, and 668,502 pregnant women with multiple micronutrient  supplements. UNICEF also mobilized schoolchildren and adolescents to  participate in nutrition and food system actions, while engaging  parliamentarians, the media and religious leaders to create sustainable  support systems for breastfeeding across all contexts. 
  
UNICEF partnered with BISP and UN  agencies to integrate SAM treatment across 572 BISP facilitation centres,  strengthen SBC interventions and strategically integrate ECD/nurturing care  and maternal and adolescent nutrition services into the Benazir Nashunoma  Programme (BNP) to ensure continuum of care and strengthen the gender and  nutrition-responsive nature of social protection schemes. 
  
UNICEF supported the launch of Pakistan’s  ECD policy framework, strengthened parenting support and integrated ECD into  emergency preparedness and response. UNICEF also localized ECD kits, scaled  up Project Play, an innovation also adopted in Afghanistan and advanced the  implementation of SUCCESS[2]  approaches, which bring together and scale essential social services through  community engagement and empowerment. Through the Nurturing Care Centres of  Excellence (NCCE) initiative, 90 nurturing care centres were established  nationwide to improve health and nutritional outcomes for children and their  families.
  
UNICEF also led coordination of the  Nutrition Development Partners Forum, the ECD coordination forum, the UN  nutrition sub-group under the UNSDCF and humanitarian sector coordination, to  align efforts among UN agencies and partners, advocate jointly and accelerate  progress toward nutrition SDG targets.
  
Water, Sanitation and Hygiene  (WASH)
UNICEF WASH supported the  Government in improving safely managed, climate-resilient and equitable WASH  services by strengthening governance systems, expanding service delivery and  accelerating climate adaptation across all provinces. 
  
Through strong government  partnerships, UNICEF reinforced planning and policy, including supporting the  development and launch of the WASH Sector Climate Rationale and the 10-year  Climate Resilient WASH Sector Development Plans in Punjab and Balochistan, in  close consultation with national and provincial stakeholders. These efforts  laid the foundation for climate risk-informed WASH programming and  prioritized climate-resilient actions across provinces and federal  territories. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, UNICEF supported the  Planning and Development Department (PD&D) to review the KP Water Act  2020, identifying actions to be taken forward in 2026 to improve governance  and accountability.
  
UNICEF supported the Sindh People’s  Housing Foundation (SPHF) to strengthen the development of SBC strategies and  build the capacity of SPHF’s implementing partners to improve community  behaviour on WASH and menstrual hygiene and health (MHH), leveraging the US$  150 million in IFI-funded WASH implemented through the SPHF. Following  UNICEF’s advocacy and technical support, the Government of Balochistan  provided US$ 1.7 million to address MHH as a strategy to keep girls in  schools.

In  2025, UNICEF directly reached over 1.2 million vulnerable people, including  providing 865,464 with durable basic safe water services in development and  humanitarian contexts, an additional 459,304 with emergency water services,  168,677 with basic sanitation in development contexts, and 92,712 with  emergency sanitation services. Through community engagement, climate-adaptive  assessments and designs, and capacity building, UNICEF strengthened the  climate resilience of WASH services, safeguarding health and climate  adaptation. Notably, UNICEF applied its Climate Resilient Evaluation  Framework to the post-2025 flood damage assessments, enabling two provinces  to secure climate-resilient investment to build back better.
  
Some 510 communities were  declared open defecation free (ODF), and KP Province declared its first two  districts ODF.  

Climate Change, Energy  and Environment
UNICEF advanced  child-sensitive climate change adaptation, mitigation and loss and damage  across Pakistan’s key social sectors and climate change departments through  policy engagement, capacity building and youth involvement. 
  
UNICEF played a vital  role by providing technical support and advocating at federal and provincial  levels, resulting in a child-sensitive Nationally Determined Contributions  (NDCs) 3.0 and ensuring children’s needs are prioritized in the national  dialogue on loss and damage. UNICEF provided ongoing technical support to four provincial  departments leading on climate, focusing on planning, knowledge sharing,  policy development and coordination to keep children’s issues at the  forefront. 
  
UNICEF partnered  with Prime Minister's Youth Programme (PMYP) and Ministry of Climate Change  and Environmental Coordination (MOCC&EC) for the fourth year to engage  4,000 young people in the NDCs 3.0 consultation and 560 to participate in mock  COP 30 climate negotiations, while also strengthening the Pakistan Local  Conference of Youth. 
  
UNICEF trained 25 Master School Staff  Trainers on the Punjab Green Schools Certification Programme for roll-out in  2026 and strengthened evidence and planning for climate-resilient WASH,  including quantifying methane emissions from sanitation in KP province. 
  
In partnership  with the Punjab Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), UNICEF convened  provincial EPA Director Generals to foster regular knowledge sharing and  collaboration on environmental pollution. 
  
Child Learning and  Skilling 
UNICEF Pakistan advanced system-wide education and youth  priorities under the UNSDCF and SDG 4 through a multi-level reform strategy.  At the national level, UNICEF provided high-level policy leadership by  engaging with the Prime Minister’s Task Force, shaping consensus on priority  reforms and aligning federal direction with provincial implementation. At the  provincial level, UNICEF strengthened reform coherence through leadership and  engagement in Local Education Groups (LEGs), supporting evidence-based planning,  coordination and accountability. At the local and sub-district levels, UNICEF  reinforced implementation and resilience through Parent-Teacher  Council-supported platforms that anchored reforms closer to schools and  communities.
  
The coordinated upstream engagement, which combines policy  advisory, data and systems strengthening, and enhanced emergency  preparedness, enabled provincial governments to strengthen governance, expand  equity, and reinforce climate and emergency resilience, delivering more  inclusive, evidence-driven, and sustainable learning services for 47 million  children at scale.
  
During the reporting  period, 729,445 children, adolescents and youth, of whom 51 per cent were  girls, accessed inclusive and climate-resilient learning and skilling  opportunities supported by UNICEF. These results were underpinned by  extensive capacity development for 35,948 educators, of whom 18,961  were women, and by  community engagement with 75,991 community members, of whom 38,884  were women,  strengthening local ownership and sustainability.
  
Technical assistance,  particularly through GPE-supported reforms across all four provinces,  accelerated the national rollout of Foundational Learning and improved sector  governance. Early-grade learning outcomes improved for 418,637 children, 49  per cent of whom were girls, including 104,891 previously out of learning. Of  these, 287,750 learners, including 54,022 in early childhood care and  education, directly benefited from Foundational Learning interventions.  Parallel efforts expanded opportunities for adolescent learning and skill  acquisition for 310,808 young people, 55 per cent of whom were girls. This  included access to Accelerated Learning Pathways for 70,625 out-of-school  adolescents and the strengthening of technical and digital skills for 12,730 participants.  Youth civic engagement grew significantly, with 79,397 young people  contributing to policy dialogue, climate action and community-led solutions.
  
UNICEF also  strengthened digital and data governance by enhancing provincial Education  Management Information Systems through integrated dashboards, improved data  quality protocols and smoother interoperability. These reforms reinforced  transparency, equity-focused planning and the integration of resilience and  youth development priorities into sector policies and budgets.
  
To bolster climate  resilience, UNICEF expanded renewable energy solutions, including school  solarization and strengthened education in emergencies capacities, ensuring  learning continuity for 96,230 children during major floods.
  
UNICEF has  increasingly become the sector’s convener for foundational learning, ensuring  coherence, aligning partners, and driving sustained impact across Pakistan’s  education landscape.
  
Protection of Children  Against Violence, Exploitation, and Abuse
In 2025, UNICEF  advanced Pakistan’s child protection agenda by strengthening national  systems, expanding prevention initiatives and improving access to quality  services in line with national priorities, and following up on CRC Committee  recommendations. Programming emphasized equity and inclusion of adolescents,  children at risk of and/or experiencing violence, including harmful  practices, displaced and migrant children and children with disabilities,  while reinforcing integrated, cross-sectoral approaches.
  
UNICEF reinforced the  national child protection framework through evidence generation, policy  support and system strengthening. Nationwide child labour surveys, research  on online child sexual exploitation (Disrupting Harm II), and studies on  child marriage and on the internally displaced and Afghan refugee children  informed policy and programmatic decisions. UNICEF supported the finalization  of child protection policies, with Punjab approving its policy, and assisted  Sindh, Balochistan, and ICT in developing costed child labour plans.  Additionally, UNICEF supported the  strengthening of the National Commission on the Rights of the Child (NCRC)  and the National Commission of Human Rights (NCHR) and enhanced oversight, reporting  and justice for children. By supporting the National Database and  Registration Authority (NADRA), 50 facilities used the health-interoperable  birth registration system to register 109,929 children, advancing CRVS and  SDG commitments.
  
Prevention systems  were scaled up through the national Child Protection Prevention Framework and  the Life Skills Framework (jointly developed with UNICEF Learning and Skills  Programme), both of which were finalized and awaiting formal endorsement.  Child Rights Clubs, life skills education and positive parenting programmes  reached adolescents, caregivers and communities, equipping 1.5 million people  with awareness on child protection, protective social and gender norms and  violence prevention. The establishment and training of 599 community-based  Child Protection Committees strengthened local identification, referral and  collective action. Evidence-informed advocacy contributed to the adoption of  the Child Marriage Restraint Act in ICT and Balochistan.
  
UNICEF enhanced  national response capacity by supporting 42 District Child Protection Units  and the full operationalization of Primero for inclusive case management. In  2025, 3,917 children at risk or survivors of violence accessed essential  protection services. Specialized pilots on caring for child survivors of  sexual abuse and alternative care informed national standards, while ongoing  professionalisation of the social service workforce and academic programme  reviews ensure long-term sustainability.
  
These results  underscore UNICEF’s role as the government’s lead technical partner,  leveraging evidence, child participation, digital innovation and  cross-sectoral integration to deliver sustainable, equitable protection for  Pakistan’s most vulnerable children, including migrants, refugees and those  living in fragile contexts. Moreover, UNICEF is working closely with the  Government on integrated programming, stronger case management and referrals  for children experiencing family separation and violence, and on system-wide  ownership to safeguard children’s right to protection across Pakistan in line  with the CRC Committee Observations to Pakistan.
  
Social Policy and  Social Protection
UNICEF strengthened  shock-responsive social protection, public finance for children, inclusive  community engagement and equitable economic opportunities. Strategic advocacy  contributed to a 20 per cent increase in BISP allocations (PKR 716 billion in  2025–26, up from PKR 592 billion). UNICEF expanded digital and financial  literacy, reaching 253,457 beneficiaries through 30 Digital and Financial  Literacy Coordinators, supporting the government’s scale-up of digital  wallets for 1 million women to promote financial inclusion.
  
Through evidence  generation, institutional strengthening and high-level policy engagement,  UNICEF advanced SDG alignment, child-sensitive public financing and social  protection delivery. The SDG Status Report 2023 consolidated datasets from  all provinces, informed provincial mid-term reviews to strengthen sector  planning and resource-allocation priorities and tracked progress against key  indicators for vulnerable populations. Revisions to the National SDGs  Framework with the Ministry of Planning, Development and Special Initiatives (MoPD&SI) integrated equity-focused and  climate-responsive indicators, updated 2030 targets and identified  accelerator areas, including nutrition, girls’ education, WASH and social  protection. Public Expenditure Reviews (PERs) for KP, Balochistan and Punjab  informed provincial fiscal analysis and budget dialogue, prompting  parliamentarians to request a dedicated briefing on ‘Public Financing for  Children’ in Punjab.
  
High-level advocacy  dialogues engaged federal and provincial Planning & Development, Finance  and line departments, reaching 162 participants across forums, such as the  National Dialogue on Child- and Gender-Responsive Fiscal Policy and the  Pakistan Spatial Poverty Dialogue. Institutional strengthening trained 57  officials on multidimensional poverty measurement, HIES/PSLM data  interpretation and evidence-based planning. Applied research with the  Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE) and the Sustainable  Development Policy Institute (SDPI) produced studies on learning poverty,  catastrophic health expenditure, intergenerational labour patterns,  multidimensional child vulnerability, fiscal trends, climate-oriented skills  and adolescent transitions. 
  
Provincial initiatives  included the development of a Unified Beneficiary Registry in Azad Jammu  & Kashmir and Gilgit Baltistan, the start of a gap analysis of the MAMTA  programme in Sindh, and disability screening in Balochistan and Sindh. The Research and Evaluation  Dashboard was launched, consolidating 134 research and evaluation products  across two programme cycles (2018–2022 and 2023–2027). It improves visibility  and accessibility, supports evidence-based decision-making and tracks progress  on ongoing evidence-generation activities. These included 10 major evaluations, among  them the Kafaalat and MRVs Impact Evaluation, the BNP Social and Behaviour  Change Process Evaluation, the National Socio-Economic Registry  (NSER) thematic analysis, which examines household-level  vulnerability data used for social protection targeting, and a gender review  of Benazir Nashonuma and Waseela-e-Taleem. The Community Liaison Cell Assessment received a ‘satisfactory’ rating  under the Global Evaluation Reports Oversight System (GEROS), UNICEF’s  independent mechanism for assuring the quality and rigour of evaluation  reports.
  
Emergency and Disaster  Risk Reduction
Pakistan made  significant progress in disaster risk reduction (DRR), resilience and  Accountability to Affected People (AAP) through coordinated efforts by the  National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), UNICEF and key community and  youth partners.
  
UNICEF, in close  collaboration with NDMA, advanced the national DRR and resilience agenda  through policy reforms, technology integration and inclusive preparedness. A  key milestone was the orientation on the digitized Pakistan School Safety  Framework (PSSF) E-Checklist, delivered via a two-day workshop in February to  428 participants from federal, provincial and private education institutions.  This initiative strengthened school safety assessments and laid the  foundation for resilient learning environments nationwide. Building on this  momentum, NDMA formally handed over the PSSF to education departments in  August, reaffirming it as the nationally endorsed framework for school  safety.
  
Inclusive  preparedness remained a core priority. NDMA hosted consultations and group  discussions with national stakeholders and UN partners to gather diverse  perspectives on disaster preparedness, early warning and vulnerable  populations. These discussions directly informed the review of Pakistan’s  Early Warning Systems (EWS), culminating at Expo-PEDRR 2025, where NDMA  advocated for a unified, NDMA-led EWS framework enhanced with smart  technology integration. NDMA together with UNICEF support further showcased  Pakistan’s leadership at the Global Platform for DRR 2025, delivering an  Ignite Talk titled ‘Building Resilience One School at a Time and introducing  the Pakistan Educational Institutional Safety Framework (PEISF)’. These  efforts, alongside Pakistan’s Vice Chairpersonship of the Asian Disaster  Preparedness Centre (ADPC), positioned the country as a regional leader in  climate-resilient disaster governance.
  
Inclusive approaches were further  reinforced through UNICEF-supported NDMA’s high-impact initiatives. A side  event, ‘Invisible No More, Adolescent Girls, Disability, and Disasters’, was  hosted and the NEOC’s Sex- and Age-Disaggregated Data Portal was launched  with commitments to disability-specific indicators in DRR tools. To strengthen emergency preparedness  and support vulnerable groups during disasters, NDMA piloted a voluntary RFID  wristband system that helped responders locate and assist individuals more  quickly during field simulations and real-time drills. The wristbands  contained only basic, non-sensitive information, enabling faster  identification and reducing delays in family reunification and referrals to  essential services. The pilot was implemented in line with national standards  and UNICEF’s data-protection and ethical-safeguarding principles, ensuring  the technology remained safe, respectful and people centred. Early results  showed improved coordination among responders, more accurate accounting of  individuals in evacuation settings, and smoother communication with families,  demonstrating promising potential to strengthen government systems, meet  donor expectations for responsible innovation, and reassure the public about  privacy and protection.
  
Between July and  October 2025, UNICEF conducted training on Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) kits  across Balochistan, Sindh, Punjab and Pakistan Administered Kashmir (PAK) to  promote effective use of standardized DRR education materials. These sessions  familiarize participants with the kits’ content, structure and key messages,  while strengthening storytelling and communication skills for interactive,  child-friendly facilitation. In total, 162 participants, including education  department officials, teachers, and youth facilitators were trained across  Balochistan (Quetta, – 35 participants), Sindh (Karachi – 22), Punjab (Multan  – 36; Rajanpur– 20 online; Muzaffargarh – 20) and PAK (Muzaffarabad – 29).
  
Complementing  these preparedness efforts, UNICEF advanced Accountability to Affected People  (AAP) by introducing a Community Feedback Mechanism (CFM).
