Effective cross border collaboration, legal enforcement, and community engagement will be essential to maintain progress.
Birth registration has improved with the expansion of digital civil registration systems, but reaching universal coverage by 2027 will require focused efforts targeting migrant families, remote communities, and adolescent mothers.
Cabo Verde continues to face severe climate and environmental vulnerabilities that deeply affect children. As a SIDS, the country is highly dependent on climate sensitive sectors such as tourism, agriculture, and fisheries, and relies on scarce freshwater resources. Children remain disproportionately exposed to risks associated with drought, water scarcity, saline intrusion, flash floods, and coastal erosion.
The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children confirmed that children’s physiological vulnerability and dependence on climate sensitive services—WASH, nutrition, health, and education—make them uniquely impacted by environmental change. With more than 60% of available freshwater withdrawn annually, pressure on aquifers and small island communities continues to grow.
Climate governance is strengthening, guided by:
The National Adaptation Plan (NAP 2021),
The updated NDC 3.0, which now includes child sensitive guidance, and
The COP30 Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate, signaling strong political commitment to intergenerational equity and child-centered climate action.
Yet Tropical Storm Erin demonstrated the urgency of building resilient systems. The storm delivered 192 mm of rainfall in five hours, causing fatalities (including children), infrastructure destruction, displacement, and WASH system failures. The event revealed gaps in municipal disaster management, emergency preparedness, and the continuity of essential services.
Despite economic recovery and 7.2% GDP growth, Cabo Verde continues to face structural vulnerabilities, public debt above 100% of GDP, approximately 12% unemployment, and 13% of the population living in extreme poverty. Children represent 37% of those in extreme poverty, with the majority living in female headed households.
Government efforts to expand social protection - through the National Strategy to Eradicate Extreme Poverty (2022-2026) and modernization of the Single Social Registry - signal strong national commitment.

In 2025, Cabo Verde advanced its commitment to the rights and wellbeing of children through strengthened national systems, evidence driven policies, and effective multisectoral coordination. Across all Result Areas, UNICEF played a catalytic role by leveraging its normative mandate, technical expertise, and Regular Resources to reinforce national priorities articulated in the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), the CPD 2023–2027, and the second Strategic Plan for Sustainable Development (PEDS II). The year was marked by significant progress in universal access to essential services, climate resilience, social inclusion, and child protection. These achievements demonstrate how strategic partnerships, systems strengthening, and risk informed programming enabled sustainable and scalable results for children, particularly the most vulnerable.
RA1 — Every Child Survives and Thrives
2025 represented a milestone year for Cabo Verde in child survival, with achievements that not only improved health outcomes but also reinforced the resilience and equity of the national health system. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health in attaining two historic results:
Certification of the elimination of measles and rubella — a milestone demonstrating decades of sustained investment in immunization and primary health care.
Introduction of two new vaccines—Rotavirus and PCV13—into the national Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) with UNICEF’s support in resource mobilization, procurement, and technical assistance, strengthening the country’s capacity to prevent vaccinepreventable diseases at scale.
UNICEF’s Regular Resources were instrumental in ensuring that the vaccine introduction process was accompanied by systems strengthening, including coldchain improvements, supplychain support, and provider capacity building. These achievements directly advance UNSDCF Outcome 2, CPD Outcome 1, and SDG 3 (Health and WellBeing).
Strengthening resilience and continuity of essential services: When Tropical Storm Erin severely disrupted São Vicente and affected Santo Antão and São Nicolau, UNICEF rapidly supported the continuity of essential services for children and pregnant women, safeguarding uninterrupted access to lifesaving care. This included integrated support to the health system—leveraging RR for rapid needs assessments and ensuring the functionality of maternal, neonatal, and child health services at facility and community levels. The intervention strengthened local emergency response capacities and is fully aligned with Cabo Verde’s climate adaptation commitments and UNSDCF priorities on resilience.
Improving mortality surveillance and response: A major systemic reform was achieved through the training of 46 health professionals on standardized tools and protocols for the surveillance and investigation of maternal, perinatal, and infant deaths. The creation and operationalization of the National Commission for Surveillance and Response to Maternal and Perinatal Deaths institutionalized mandatory reporting and improved data quality for decisionmaking. This step brings Cabo Verde closer to global guidance on epidemiological surveillance and strengthens accountability within the health system.
Expanding neonatal care in remote islands: UNICEF, together with WHO, strengthened neonatal care in São Nicolau by training 25 health professionals in neonatal resuscitation and newborn care. Given the island’s geographic isolation, this investment contributes to reducing preventable mortality and enhances equity between urban and remote areas. The model will be expanded to additional municipalities in 2026, reinforcing the CPD objective of reducing subnational disparities.
Enhancing diagnostic capacity for early detection of childhood diseases: In collaboration with national authorities, UNICEF supported the technical and legal groundwork for introducing advanced diagnostics for genetic, metabolic, and infectious diseases in two central and four regional hospitals. This forwardlooking investment improves the country’s preparedness for early detection and intervention, directly contributing to SDG 3.2 on reducing neonatal and underfive mortality.
National advocacy on prematurity prevention: A major achievement in prevention and early childhood care was the nationwide dialogue on prematurity involving 93 multidisciplinary professionals. The resulting recommendations will inform national guidelines and contribute to reducing neonatal mortality, aligning with both UNSDCF health priorities and global Every Newborn Action Plan targets.
Integrated child health capacity building: UNICEF supported the training of 74 multidisciplinary health professionals—covering vaccination, nutrition, and mental health—from 59% of municipalities. This integrated approach strengthened the continuum of care and supported the expansion of childcentered Primary Health Care, promoting early identification, referral, and highquality followup.
Improving mental health and adolescent wellbeing: Through strengthened engagement with civil society, 1,989 adolescents received mental health information and linkages to services. These communitybased interventions, integrated with Education and Primary Health Care, advance the CPD’s focus on adolescent development and genderresponsive services.
Scaling up nutrition services and micronutrient interventions: UNICEF supported the nationwide distribution of iron tablets to 55,000 schoolaged children (6–12 years) and trained salt producers to meet iodization standards—critical actions for reducing micronutrient deficiencies. Progress in promoting healthy diets included nearly finalized legislation to reduce salt, sugar, and fat consumption. A highlight was the certification of Dr. Ramiro Figueira Regional Hospital (Sal Island) as a BabyFriendly Hospital. The recognition followed implementation of competencybased training and strengthened facility practices supporting early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding, enhancing growth monitoring and maternal counseling.
Driving sustainability through innovative financing: In partnership with UNDP, UNFPA, and WHO, UNICEF facilitated the development of three new health equality financing instruments under the Sustainable Investment Framework (SIF), approved by the Minister of Health. This milestone expands options for domestic resource mobilization and supports longterm financial sustainability for child and maternal health.
Strengthening national capacity to prevent harmful practices (FGM): In late 2025, the validation of the Charter of Praia marked a national commitment to preventing Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). UNICEF supported training of 100 multisectoral professionals across all 22 municipalities through SouthSouth collaboration with GuineaBissau. Resource mobilization from UNICEF Luxembourg NATCOM was essential in scaling training, community engagement, and institutional coordination—demonstrating how Regular Resources and partnerships unlock systemic change.
RA2 — Every Child Learns
In 2025, significant strides were made to strengthen the policy foundations, inclusiveness, and resilience of Cabo Verde’s education system. UNICEF’s contribution focused on evidence generation, digital learning expansion, disability inclusion, and shockresponsive education planning—core elements of the UNSDCF’s education outcomes and CPD Output 1.2.
Strengthening the governance and regulatory framework for early childhood education: UNICEF supported the development of the first Preschool Education Charter, establishing both a diagnostic baseline and a strategic vision for the subsector. Mapping of legislation connected to early childhood education created a foundation for upcoming reforms and strengthened coherence between municipal and national frameworks.
Advancing disability inclusive education: A national breakthrough was the completion of Cabo Verde’s first nationwide mapping of out-of-school children with disabilities. Supported by UNICEF Regular Resources, the evidence directly informed policy adjustments and enabled multisectoral pilots focusing on inclusive education practices. UNICEF additionally facilitated structured dialogue among all 23 multidisciplinary inclusive education teams, strengthening coordination and peer learning across the country. This work aligns with SDG 4.5 on eliminating disparities in education.
Expanding foundational learning through digital innovation: Through the Learning Passport (supported by Regular Resources) and Akelius initiatives, access to digital learning tools for mathematics and language expanded to 3,100 students from grades 1–6, representing an increase of 1,100 learners compared to 2024. The expansion reduced inequities between municipalities and improved early literacy and numeracy outcomes.
Strengthening WASH in schools and healthy learning environments: UNICEF trained 250 teachers from 11 municipalities (50% of the country municipalities) in WASH education using contextspecific materials and childfriendly games. Approximately 15,000 primary school children benefited from improved hygiene practices and better learning environments. WASH improvements included rehabilitation of school bathrooms to support menstrual hygiene management (MHM), and the installation of 110 household water connections on Maio Island, prioritizing families with children and persons with disabilities.
Ensuring learning continuity after Tropical Storm Erin: Using regular resources and in partnership with the Global Partnership for Education, UNICEF conducted rapid assessments, distributed learning kits to 6,000 vulnerable children, and collaborated with UNDP on a PostDisaster Needs Assessment. These actions ensured uninterrupted access to education and supported municipal planning for resilient and inclusive schooling.
RA3 — Every Child Is Protected From Violence and Exploitation
UNICEF continued to strengthen Cabo Verde’s child protection system through enhanced intersectoral coordination, capacity building, and improved justice system performance. The emphasis remained on preventing violence—including sexual violence and SEA—expanding birth registration, supporting survivors, and addressing harmful practices.
Strengthening birth registration and civil documentation: Cabo Verde achieved a 99% birth registration rate for children aged 0–1 (5,714 new births), reflecting systemic improvements in civil registry integration and outreach. This progress supports the national target of universal birth registration by 2027 and reinforces SDG 16.9.
Improving access to justice and protection services: UNICEF’s longstanding partnership with the Attorney General’s Office continued to yield transformative results:
4,715 paternity investigation cases closed out of 5,289 pending,
576 sexual crimes against children cases finalized in Praia alone, reducing impunity and contributing to the observed decline in SEA cases nationally.
In total, 1,555 children affected by violence accessed social work and justice system services, including 341 survivors of sexual violence.
Community engagement and prevention of violence: Through the national “Proteja” campaign, UNICEF supported training for more than 100 professionals in Fogo and Brava, while 22 positive parenting programs benefited over 520 caregivers. Additionally, 250 tour operators received training under the Global Code of Conduct for the Protection of Children in Travel and Tourism.
Strengthening sexuality education as a prevention strategy: More than 280 teachers across eight municipalities enhanced their capacities in comprehensive sexuality education, in partnership with Health and Education sectors. This multisectoral approach strengthens early detection and prevention of SEA and supports healthier development for adolescents.
Preventing harmful practices, including FGM: Through support from UNICEF Luxembourg NATCOM, over 100 professionals across sectors received advanced training on preventing harmful practices, significantly improving national preparedness for early detection and coordinated response.
Childcentered climate protection tools: UNICEF advanced child participation and climate education by producing a CLAC video game, a childfriendly CLAC report, and communication materials linking climate change and child rights. Over 500 children contributed to a national dialogue on the environment during World Children’s Day, culminating in a recommendation letter to government- a milestone in youth engagement for climate justice.
Ensuring continuity of protection services during Tropical Storm Erin: In partnership with the Government and the SOS Village, UNICEF ensured 499 children received hygiene, school, and safety kits, and 210 families accessed continued child protection services during the emergency.
RA4 — Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment
UNDP, UNFPA, and UNICEF Joint Office built on the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) to deepen climateresilient systems and youth engagement.
Childcentered climate information and engagement: The CLAC was translated, redesigned, and disseminated nationwide, increasing accessibility among policymakers, civil society, teachers, and communities. To engage children and adolescents, UNICEF launched an interactive CLAC video game and produced 1,000 copies of the childfriendly CLAC report for schools.
Improving access to safe water and sanitation: Through WASH programming on Maio Island, 110 water connections were installed, eliminating access gaps for the last 3% of the population without safe water—prioritizing households with children and disability inclusion.
Mainstreaming child rights in national climate policy: JO supported the integration of childsensitive guidance into the updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), ensuring that climate commitments explicitly address children’s needs.
Global advocacy and intergenerational justice: At COP30, Cabo Verde signed the Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate Action, signaling a strong national commitment to youth leadership and childcentered climate governance.
RA5 — Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life
UNDP, UNFPA, and UNICEF Joint Office (JO) made substantial progress in strengthening Cabo Verde’s social protection and national data systems, reinforcing evidence based policymaking and inclusive development.
Strengthening the national social protection system (CSU): Joint Office (JO) supported the operationalization and modernization of the Single Social Registry (CSU) - a transformative platform enabling targeted service delivery.
Significant performance against CPD Output 2.1 included:
Integration of social protection programs increased from 6 to 18, surpassing the target of 12.
85% of vulnerable people benefited from social protection programs, exceeding the 50% target.
These results contributed to reducing extreme poverty to 2.28%, and advanced SDG 1, SDG 10, and CCPD Outcome 2.
Gender responsive inclusion and local ownership: The CSU registered 2,779 new households (7,955 individuals) and updated 31,475 records, identifying 2,135 beneficiaries for RSI and 1,474 for the Inclusive Program. With 78.14% of registered households female headed, the CSU notably strengthened gender responsive policy implementation.
Strengthening national statistical capacity: JO provided strategic and technical support to the National Institute of Statistics (INE), contributing to strong progress toward CPD Output 2.3:
INE produced 19 publications disaggregated by age, sex, and location, nearly reaching the 2027 target of 20.
Four innovative dissemination tools became operational (Data Center, INE Website, Microdata Lab, Praia Group Website), enhancing transparency and SDG monitoring.
A key highlight was the 2025 Continuous MultiObjective Survey (IMC), which produced critical SDG indicators and included a new module on Youth Aspirations, informing national youth policy and local development planning.
In 2025, JO’s work in Cabo Verde demonstrated tangible and sustainable progress across all Result Areas. Through systems strengthening, policy advocacy, capacity building, and partnerships, supported significantly by Regular Resources, JO helped the country advance national and global commitments under the SDGs, UNSDCF, and CPD 2023–2027. These achievements reflect the collective commitment of Government, civil society, communities, and the UN system to ensure that every child in Cabo Verde survives, learns, is protected, thrives in a clean and safe environment, and enjoys equitable opportunities throughout life.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF’s work in Cabo Verde in 2025 unfolded in a context marked by institutional fluidity, uneven capacities across territories, and recurrent climate-related shocks.
Challenges: Frequent leadership transitions across partner institutions created recurrent delays in decision making and policy implementation. Maintaining programmatic alignment required sustained engagement, reinforced advocacy, and tailored information sharing. These efforts were essential to safeguard momentum and ensure coherent interpretation of priorities during periods of institutional change.
Evidence-based planning remained constrained by persistent gaps in timely, validated, and disaggregated national statistics. While administrative data enabled routine monitoring, the absence of harmonized national indicators continued to limit comprehensive reporting.
In the education sector, the lack of an updated legal and regulatory framework for early childhood education (ECE) remained a major system bottleneck. Disparities in municipal capacity, combined with inconsistent quality standards across territories, hindered equitable expansion of ECE services. Resource limitations and weak intersectoral coordination also challenged inclusive education, particularly for children with disabilities and those in remote areas.
Tropical Storm Erin exposed the vulnerability of the country’s education infrastructure and underscored fragilities in mechanisms for learning continuity. The emergency response depended heavily on external support, revealing the need for stronger local preparedness, disaster-resilient school planning, and clear protocols to ensure uninterrupted learning during crises.
Child protection systems continued to face pressures related to persistent violence against children, limited human and institutional capacity at municipal level, and fragmentation among frontline protection actors. Rising online risks, unequal access to services across islands, and heightened vulnerabilities following two major climate shocks further strained existing structures.
Cross-sectoral challenges were intensified by limited human resources at both central and municipal levels, affecting the pace of follow-up and implementation. Delays in the disbursement of non-core resources slowed activity rollout, requiring continuous adaptation to maintain progress. At the policy level, low awareness of the child–climate nexus, coupled with limited technical and financial capacity to integrate child-sensitive climate approaches, constrained the mainstreaming of climate considerations across sectors.
Lessons Learned: The year reaffirmed that systems strengthening remains the most effective pathway for building resilient and equitable service delivery. Sustained advocacy, structured information briefs, and joint planning mechanisms proved critical for preserving momentum during leadership transitions. UNICEF’s support to updated protocols, targeted technical training, and multisectoral coordination contributed to continuity of services in neonatal care, mortality surveillance, and emergency response.
Community partnerships were indispensable for expanding outreach to children, adolescents, and vulnerable households. Collaboration with civil society organizations helped bridge last-mile gaps and demonstrated that combining state-led services with community-based interventions significantly improves equity and access.
Comprehensive diagnostics—such as the nationwide disability mapping and the development of the Preschool Charter—were vital for shaping policy reforms, aligning ministerial actors, and mobilizing investments for inclusive education and ECE expansion. These exercises highlighted the value of evidence and collective visioning in driving systemic change.
Digital learning initiatives, including the Learning Passport and foundational skills tools supported by Akelius, showed strong potential to reduce disparities. When paired with teacher training, structured pedagogical support, and regular follow-up, digital tools contributed to improvements in foundational learning and demonstrated that technology can serve as a powerful equalizer when embedded within broader instructional systems.
Multisectoral coordination also proved essential in responding to complex vulnerabilities. The joint response to Tropical Storm Erin illustrated how integrated approaches—spanning education, child protection, health, and social protection—can improve service continuity during emergencies and strengthen resilience for the most affected children.
Efforts to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse advanced through engagement with families, schools, and community leaders. These approaches showed promise in tackling harmful norms and reducing silence around violence. Resource mobilization, notably through UNICEF Luxembourg NatCom, strengthened coordination across justice, health, education, and child protection sectors, illustrating the value of integrated programming and joint financing.
UNICEF’s work in climate and environment gained momentum after government endorsement of the Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate Action. Interactive, child-friendly tools—such as the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) video game and WASH-related educational games—proved effective in promoting climate awareness and behavior change.
In the social protection sector, integrated policy frameworks and territorialized planning were instrumental in surpassing CPD output targets. Eighteen programs were integrated into the national social protection system, with coverage reaching 85%. The digitalization of the Single Social Registry (CSU) was transformative, enabling real-time data updates and expanding registration to 59% of households. This modernization strengthened targeting efficiency and reinforced gender equality, with women representing more than three quarters of registered beneficiaries. Strategic partnerships and communication campaigns further boosted CSU visibility and uptake. Continuous engagement with the National Institute of Statistics improved adaptive planning and strengthened implementation quality, demonstrating the importance of proximity-based technical support.
Future Outlook: In 2026, UNICEF will deepen cross-sectoral collaboration by embedding joint planning and budgeting across health, education, nutrition, child protection, and climate programs. A key priority will be securing sustainable financing for resilience, including operationalizing innovative health financing instruments to diversify resources and protect essential services during climate shocks.
Education efforts will focus on expanding digital learning, strengthening foundational skills, and supporting inclusive education. UNICEF will collaborate with government and partners to scale digital learning nationally and integrate climate-resilient measures—such as safe school infrastructure and preparedness planning—into sector-wide strategies.
In child protection, the office will reinforce national and municipal systems by improving coordination structures, finalizing the national case management and information system, and supporting regular Situation Analyses. Prevention and response to SEA, especially sexual exploitation of children in travel and tourism, will be a major focus. UNICEF will strengthen workforce capacity, expand community-based prevention efforts, and promote sustainable financing models.
UNICEF will also strengthen national child-climate data systems, expand climate education, and promote renewable energy solutions within schools.
In social protection, efforts will prioritize enhancing the technical capacity of the Ministry of Family and Social Inclusion to strengthen access for the most vulnerable. This includes integrating registration systems, improving CSU interoperability, reinforcing technical training at central and municipal levels, and upgrading equipment for service delivery. UNICEF will continue investing in national statistical capacity through improved demographic analysis, stronger data production, and enhanced monitoring to ensure national planning and SDG reporting reflect the needs of those furthest behind.

For the children of the Central African Republic (CAR), 2025 was marked by new opportunities opened by significant political and peace-making developments, while at the same time the services that fulfil their rights as children were strained by insecurity in funding and the economy.
Simultaneous presidential, legislative and local elections, which bridged 2025 to 2026, came against a backdrop of renewed political peace efforts, with the signing in July of the N’Djamena peace agreements with armed groups, notably the 3R (Return, Reclamation, and Rehabilitation) and the UPC (Union for Peace in the Central African Republic). Following these agreements and supported by MINUSCA, disarmament and demobilization operations for fighters from these two groups were launched, creating a momentum for improved governance, decentralization and accountability. A significant number of children were released from armed groups during this period. While the peace dynamic offers hope, localized insecurity persists, with humanitarian crises driven by conflict, floods, epidemics, and regional instability.
Humanitarian needs remain acute despite a gradual decline in the number of people requiring assistance: 3.4 million in 2023, 2.8 million in 2024, and 2.4 million in 2025. However, funding for humanitarian response has sharply decreased, from 65% in 2023 to 34% in 2025, severely constraining the delivery of essential services. Basic social services remain inaccessible for the majority of the population, undermining progress towards child rights and resilience.
Economic growth remains weak, with a projected growth rate of 2.8 per cent by 2027, which according to the World Bank, is insufficient to expand access to essential services. Nevertheless, CAR’s first-ever National Development Plan, backed by $9.6 billion in pledges, represents a milestone. Yet allocation to the social sector remain marginal limiting transformative impact for children.
The 2023 Voluntary National Report on CAR’s progress towards achieving the SDGs shows that the country is still very far from the targets:65.7 per cent of Central Africans live below the international monetary poverty line ($2.15/day in 2017 PPP), limiting their financial capacity to access basic social services such as health and education.
In health, continues to face alarming indicators, Under -five mortality stands at 92 deaths per 1,000 live births the highest globally, while maternal mortality is 692 deaths per 100,000 live births. The universal health coverage index of just 33 per cent is explained by the low accessibility of health services and the lack of qualified personnel (4.67/10,000 inhabitants in 2024 versus theWHO’s standard of 23.). Malnutrition remains widespread: The 2022 SMART report showed that 40 per cent of CAR’s children suffer from stunting (chronic malnutrition) and 10 per cent of pregnant and breastfeeding women face acute malnutrition.
The education sector is in crisis, undermining human capital development. PASEC results show that in CAR 73.6% of primary school students fail to meet minimum reading standards, while nearly nine out of ten (88.4 per cent) fall below the ‘sufficient’ threshold in mathematics. Teachers' quality is a major constraint, with a large proportion of teachers being ‘parent-teachers’ (volunteers with little training), lacking formal training. The school enrolment rate is low: three per cent for preschool, 61 per cent for primary school, and eight per cent for secondary. The completion rate is equally low. Nearly 40 per cent of children do not finish primary school, and 85 per cent do not complete Fundamental II. Gender disparities are stark, with girls disproportionately excluded and exposed to child marriage (61 per cent under 18 and 26 per cent under 15) and gender-based violence. These trends jeopardize progress toward SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 5 (Gender Equality).
United Nations-verified grave violations of children’s rights show a sustained upward trend, increasing from 97 cases in 2023 to 100 cases in 2024, with indications of further deterioration in 2025. Violations reported in 2025 mainly consisted of recruitment and use, abductions, and rape and other forms of sexual violence. With the signing of the N’Djamena agreement, it is estimated that nearly 2,000 children associated with armed groups will need to be reintegrated into community. This underscores the urgency of scaling child protection interventions aligned with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan outcome indicators.
CAR ranks first among the most climate-vulnerable countries globally, with children disproportionately exposed to droughts, extreme temperatures and floods that compromise principal production activities. According to the Children’s Climate Risk Index, which ranks countries by the degree of children’s exposure to environmental stress and extreme weather events, those living in CAR are among the most exposed. The climate risks exasperate the difficulties in accessing safe drinking water and adequate sanitation, which impacts the health of the whole population. Women and girls continue to bear the burden of water collection, often walking long distances and in unsafe conditions. Although some significant improvements to water access have been made–with 48 per cent of people in urban areas and 28 per cent in rural areas having access to water–it remains low overall (according to the latest official data, from the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme 2022). Just 14 per cent of people use at least basic sanitation services, (25 per cent in urban areas and six per cent in rural areas). Twenty-five per cent of the population practice open defecation. Persistent underfunding, weak governance, and coordination challenges hinder progress toward SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation).

In 2025, UNICEF’s work in the Central African Republic (CAR) unfolded against a backdrop of fragile progress in peacebuilding, persistent humanitarian needs, and systemic challenges in health, education, child protection, and WASH. Despite these constraints, UNICEF’s sustained engagement through the 2023–2027 Cooperation Programme contributed to significant achievements that advanced national priorities, reinforced resilience, and positioned children at the center of development. This section highlights the most strategic results, focusing on how UNICEF’s interventions catalyzed systemic reforms, strengthened institutions, and delivered tangible outcomes for children and families.
HEALTH AND NUTRITION
Strengthening the health and nutrition system for mothers and children remained central to UNICEF’s work in CAR. This priority was reflected in the continued implementation of the 2024-2026 ‘Investment Dossier’ to reduce maternal, neonatal and child mortality, aligned with national priorities to guarantee children’s right to health and well-being.
The launch of the Presidential Initiative for the reduction of maternal and child mortality on 6 November 2025 highlights the strong political will to accelerate results, with a focus on innovative and multisectoral interventions, as also described in UNICEF’s new CAR 2.0 strategy, with the Health and Education sectors as entry points. UNICEF also supported the completion and adoption of the 2025-2029 Multisectoral Strategic Plan for Food Security and Nutrition, a $354 millions framework for which a donor roundtable is planned for 2026.
Progress in vaccination was notable. CAR became eligible for the Vaccine Independence Initiative, and UNICEF secured vaccine availability through an MoU with the World Bank. Administrative coverage for Penta3 rose to 91 per cent in 2025 and the WHO–UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC) are at 42 per cent. In 2025, 1.3 million children aged from 9 months to 59 months were vaccinated against measles. UNICEF provided technical and financial support with Gavi funds to the MoH to design and implement the catch-up campaigns that reached 275,000 zero-dose and under-vaccinated children aged 12–59 months. The technical support included vaccine management, a key pillar of the big catch up. The response to the Mpox epidemic was carried out in 19 health districts, where 6,428 people, including 5,804 health workers, 243 contacts, and 381 vulnerable people have been vaccinated, 45 per cent of whom are women. National campaigns continued to vaccinate more than 2.5 million children, maintaining CAR’s polio-free status since 2020. Also, CAR is progressing toward maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination.
Since 2023, UNICEF has supported the purchase and deployment of 778 solar refrigerators nationwide. With 210 of them installed in 2025 a total of 484 are now fully installed, thanks to funding from Canada, GAVI, the World Bank and the US Government. This increased the coverage of equipped health facilities from 83 per cent in 2024 to 88 per cent (1,087 of 1,235 health facilities). In 2026, this rate will reach 95 per cent with the installation of the remaining 294 units. This transition to solar is a sustainable and effective strategy for climate change adaptation, ensuring continuity and reliability of vaccine storage at both regional and health centre levels.
For UNICEF, consolidating gains and improving access and quality of primary health care for mothers, newborns, children and adolescents were priorities in 2025. The focus was on the integrated package for managing deadly childhood diseases at the community level and the functionality of the perinatal network. DHIS 2 data currently available for the 11 health districts supported by UNICEF show that the proportion of pregnant women who gave birth with qualified personnel in attendance reached 76 per cent (46,325 of 62,984) in health facilities of the perinatal network, compared to a national average of 52 per cent. This marked progress in assisted deliveries by qualified personnel in perinatal network health centres underlines the need to support scaling up this initiative under the new CAR 2.0 strategy. Similarly, when it came to major deadly childhood diseases in 2025, UNICEF ensured 189,097 children aged 0 to 5 years were treated for the three mains killer diseases, including 10,313 who received antibiotics for pneumonia and 33,013 treated with ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, and145,771 for malaria with ACTs. These results were achieved thanks to a network of 620 trained community health workers, including 380 community matrons in UNICEF target districts.
UNICEF continued to consolidate prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) activities with the screening of 53,459 pregnant women, of whom 1,807 tested positive for HIV and 1,305 were treated with anti-retroviral therapy. UNICEF strengthened access to sexual and reproductive health services for youth and adolescent girls, by supporting youth associations and providing comprehensive sexuality education, raising awareness of 1,447 young people. Of 470 youth tested for HIV (233 girls and 237 boys), 13 tested positive.
In nutrition, UNICEF support for the prevention of malnutrition, initiated in 2023 through work at the community level, resulted in 2025 in 715 health facilities (FOSAs) out of 1,171 (61 per cent) and communities implemented the minimum package of stunting prevention measures [KRC 2.6], and 318,486 mothers and caregivers learned about infant and young child feeding practices. Preventive activities were integrated into manuals for community health workers and matrons to enable scaling up.
More than 1.2 million children aged 6 to 59 months, including over 643,000 girls, received two doses of vitamin A during the polio campaigns in April and November 2025. To improve malnutrition management, UNICEF strengthened the supply chain for nutritional inputs and the capacities of health centres, enabling screening of 588,717 children under 5, of whom 49,036 with severe acute malnutrition were treated. Performance indicators meet SPHERE standards: 85 per cent recovery, 2 per cent mortality, 7 per cent default, and 6 per cent non-response. In 2025, 715 FOSAs had services to manage malnutrition, compared to 781 in 2024, a decrease of about 10 per cent due to the unavailability of nutrition inputs during the second and third quarters of 2025. This situation was corrected in the last quarter of 2025, with exceptional allocations from the US Government and MANA Nutrition.
Finally, to better integrate gender into health and nutrition programmes, the gender analysis report was validated for immunization, nutrition, and maternal, neonatal and child health programmes. These results will guide programmes in 2026 to remove gender-related barriers and accelerate sustainable results.
EDUCATION
Education remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s strategy to build human capital. In 2025, UNICEF positioned schools as hubs for integrated programming, education, child protection, and WASH activities, with a strong focus on community engagement to sustain gains, making schools the entry point for programmes to realize the rights of Central African children. Consequently, schools are gradually becoming spaces that offer holistic packages conducive to acquiring fundamental skills, a prerequisite for children’s development for a better future.
Three documents in 2025 strengthened education by prioritizing strategies and actions plans. Supported by UNICEF, the mid-term review of the Decennial Education Sector Plan assessed the past six years of implementation, evaluating policies and strategies. While the sector’s underperformance was evident, this review aims to improve the next plan’s phase, prioritizing the fight against the learning crisis. Additionally, the results of a gender diagnosis in education detailed an action plan for girls’ education. A preschool policy document also provided strategic lines of intervention.
UNICEF continued to facilitate sectoral dialogue and coordination to strengthen collaboration within the Local Education Group (LEG), in its UNICEF’s role as leader of development partners active in education. The group continued to advocate for the integration of 1,500 trained teachers into the civil service each year, 2024–2027, in expectation of improved learning.
Ongoing interventions with UNICEF support since 2023 have improved access to education for 546,361 children (162,189 in 2025), including over 200,000 girls, with more than 55 per cent receiving school kits. Additionally, 444,924 of those 200,000 girls (4,314 in 2025) also received dignity kits. The construction and/or rehabilitation of 439 (84 in 2025) classrooms and community awareness campaigns using 354 (23 added in 2025) ‘Kundukwa’ community platforms contributed to increased enrolment and retention. To improve classroom practices, 1,237 teachers/parent-teachers (764 teachers in 2025) have been trained in basic pedagogy and other relevant topics from 2023 to date, most of whom received teaching kits. Through radio clubs, 19,351 (in 2025) students were also reached. The implementation of the national evaluation system action plan, integrating a proven pedagogical remediation approach called TaRL (“Teaching at The Right Level”), was launched to better guide learning quality.
WATER, HYGIENE AND SANITATION
UNICEF’s WASH interventions in 2025 focused on creating an enabling environment for inclusive, climate-resilient services. UNICEF supported the Government in submitting follow-up commitment reports to Africasan and to the Sanitation and Water for All (SWA) initiative, as well as presenting a comprehensive proposal to the Green Climate Fund, participating in COP30, and validating WASH normative documents for health and nutrition centres, CLAC (Climate Landscape Analysis for Children), and developing the National Development Plan 3.0.
At the conclusion of the 7-year EU Bêkou Fund partnership, UNICEF handed over CAR’s first high-capacity drilling rig to ANEA (the National Agency for Water and Sanitation, under the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources) and trained 20 technicians for its long-term maintenance. UNICEF also expanded coverage of Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) (KRC8) with two national NGO partners, certifying 92 communities as Open Defecation Free and reaching 34,006 people (including 11,965 girls and 10,991 boys). Additionally, 18,572 people (including 6,535 girls and 6,002 boys) benefited from basic sanitation services in emergency responses, and over 95,200 people (including 33,487 girls and 30,773 boys) were sensitized on hygiene practices. In addition, UNICEF provided water treatment kits to 2,689 SAM-affected children and their families (14,790 people), to support the children’s recovery in outpatient care. UNICEF provided access to safe drinking water to 72,244 people (including 25,413 girls and 23,352 boys), including 23,539 in humanitarian responses, by constructing 43 boreholes, rehabilitating 83 others, and installing three water networks equipped with solar pumping systems resilient to climate change. Ninety-five water point management committees were established or revitalized to ensure sustainability.
In institutions, 36,600 children (including 19,032 girls) benefited from integrated WASH services in 122 schools, including water points, hygiene clubs, and menstrual kits for 5,125 adolescent girls. Additionally, 91 health facilities were equipped with water points, latrines, and showers, with staff trained on infection prevention, while Nola and Bouar hospitals were equipped with sustainable solar water supply systems including water points reaching inside operating and maternity rooms.
Since 2023, 357,272 people (including 125,672 girls and 115,487 boys) have gained access to safe drinking water out of a target of 615,865, a 58 per cent achievement rate. In parallel, 135,773 people (including 47,761 girls and 47,761 boys) gained access to sustainable sanitation via the CLTS approach out of a target of 335,926, a 40 per cent achievement rate.
On the humanitarian front, the WASH Cluster, led by UNICEF, remained fully operational nationally and in four field offices, improving the coherence and effectiveness of interventions as well as of advocacy and fundraising.
Finally, UNICEF is developing the CAR 2.0 strategy to mobilize resources and strengthen intersectoral integration, to provide inclusive and climate-resilient WASH services, contributing to achieving SDG 6.
CHILD PROTECTION
Child protection achievements in 2025 were shaped by the N’Djamena peace agreement, which enabled the release and reintegration of children associated with armed groups. Of 650 children identified as having been associated with armed groups, 408 were guided through individualized reintegration paths, combining education, vocational training and income-generating activities, thanks to close coordination between social services, MINUSCA, local authorities and community structures, thus strengthening inclusion and community participation. UNICEF continued to strengthen the scope and quality of reintegration services in 2025, notably by reinforcing community-based reintegration mechanisms.
With UNICEF’s deepened commitment to localization, it continued to transition from a response model dependent on international organizations to one with increased leadership by national authorities and community initiatives. Local NGOs played a key role in implementing activities, improving access to services in remote areas and consolidating institutional capacities for a more sustainable, inclusive, and child-adapted response.
To expand child protection coverage, following the validation and adoption of community child protection networks (RECOPE) guidelines, 20 new networks were created and formalized according to these guidelines, and 200 members were trained to identify at-risk children, raise family awareness of child protection risks, and ensure effective and coordinated referral to specialized services. At the same time, case management was professionalized through the certification of 20 social workers as national trainers, which in turn enabled the training of 120 case managers in the three prefectures of Ouaka, Mbomou and Haute Kottto, bringing the total to 509 case managers nationwide. These efforts consolidated the national system and aligned practices with international standards and enabled 10,490 vulnerable children at risk and/or victims of abuse, violence, and exploitation to benefit from protection, health, or justice services. In response to persistent sexual violence, UNICEF strengthened survivor-centred prevention and response. In partnership with Médecins Sans Frontières and social services, UNICEF ensured 30,432 children benefited from awareness raising, medical care, and/or psychosocial support, despite the persistent obstacles the children face to justice and specialized services. This is only 61 per cent of the number of children UNICEF planned to reach, illustrating the impact the decrease in funding has on deployment capacities.
Integrated interventions in schools in eight prefectures strengthened the identification and referral of cases of gender-based violence, reaching 197,932 people, including 79,250 children. In parallel, 30,896 people were mobilized during campaigns to promote protective social norms and encourage positive behaviours within local communities.
Intersectoral progress included interoperability tests between civil registration and health in two municipalities and late regularization of birth certification for 11,109 children. UNICEF strengthened national child protection systems by supporting the strengthening and consolidation of national leadership through the finalization of the sectoral consultation framework and increased partnerships between key sectors. The acceleration of the modernization of information systems in CAR with the launch of CPIMS+ and the assignment of a dedicated official ensured enhanced institutional ownership, as did the roll out of a national mapping of protection services. International accountability progressed with the submission of the first national report to the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (1990).
Despite these advances, security constraints, limited access and insufficient resources continue to hinder access to protection for many of the most vulnerable children. Sustained efforts remain necessary to ensure a lasting and equitable impact.
EMERGENCY AND FIELD OPERATIONS
Global financial constraints this year led to the end of the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) after eleven years of support to affected populations. In response, UNICEF developed an innovative approach based on ‘dual localization’ and a profound reorganization of the operational architecture was implemented to continue assisting affected people. UNICEF engaged double localization, based on a multisectoral mobile response strategy, to support to the Ministry of Humanitarian Action as it decentralized by strengthening the capacities of new regional and prefectural representatives, and by launching a new multisectoral mobile response approach to shocks called ‘So Fini’. This initiative benefited from the technical and strategic support of UNICEF’s EMOPS team and the Regional Office, which contributed to its design.
From January to April, the RRM provided essential household items and WASH items to 40,490 people to meet their immediate needs following shocks. With the end of the RRM, the multisectoral mobile response approach, launched in September 2025, brought essential services (health, nutrition, water, hygiene and protection) closer to vulnerable populations in the three prefectures most affected by shocks. It enabled 2,000 children from households affected by shocks to be consulted and cared for: 39 per cent of the children were treated for acute respiratory infections, 12 per cent for moderate acute malnutrition and 10 per cent for diarrhoea, and 54 per cent tested positive for malaria. Additionally, 486 of the children were vaccinated, 32 boreholes were repaired, and 41 cases of gender-based violence were identified and referred for appropriate care. These results are in addition to sectoral responses within the framework of the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal.
In parallel, UNICEF continued to respond to Sudanese refugees under the ‘Regional Refugee Response Plan’ to meet urgent needs in child protection and the WASH sectors. This response enabled 23.539 refugees (59 per cent children) to access safe drinking water, 9,400 to access dignified, safe, and clean excreta disposal facilities, the distribution of intimate hygiene kits to 1,200 women and girls, and the construction of 376 latrines. It also addressed significant child protection needs through the establishment of 25 RECOPEs among refugees and three among the host community, as well as the training of 28 case managers among refugees and three among the host community. This action identified and treated 270 cases of vulnerable children, including eight self-demobilized from armed groups. Support for durable solutions for internally displaced persons was maintained under the International Displacement Solution Fund, consolidating efforts for stabilization and resilience for internally displaced persons in Bria by improving their access to health and water. In one year, 4,500 internally displaced persons and host communities increased their access to safe drinking water through the extension and empowerment of the water network, and the rehabilitation and upgrading of a health centre near their homes, which will allow more than 9,000 people to access health services.
In 2025, UNICEF in CAR coordinated two health emergencies: the response to Mpox, triggered in 2024, continued with a vaccination campaign in 19 districts where 6,428 people, including 5,804 health workers, 243 contacts, and 381 vulnerable people, were vaccinated, of whom 45 per cent (2,890/6,428) were women. Cholera preparedness was intensified, given the evolution of the epidemic affecting all of CAR’s neighbours. For this preparedness work, under the leadership of the Ministry of Health and Population, UNICEF received funding from the Regional Office to implement anticipatory measures.
Social protection and social policy
In 2025, UNICEF intensified efforts to create a favourable political and technical environment for institutionalized public financing mechanisms in social sectors for the well-being of children and for non-contributory social protection programmes responsive to shocks. In support of these efforts, UNICEF’s technical and financial contributions enabled 11 ministries to develop their medium- and long-term sectoral expenditure frameworks as part of the transition to programme budgeting. Through this support, UNICEF promoted a budgetary nomenclature, allowing the allocation, the monitoring and execution of specific budget lines favourable to children, and advocated for increased budget allocations for social sectors in general.
In the same vein, UNICEF signed an MoU with the National School of Administration and Magistracy to strengthen the capacities of social sector ministry staff in child-sensitive public finance. To facilitate the deployment of shock-responsive social protection, UNICEF supported TRANSFORM training, in collaboration with the Ministry of Labour, the World Bank and WFP, to strengthen government capacities in social protection. UNICEF also implemented a Cash Plus Education programme in the sub-prefecture of Paoua, enabling 1,980 poor and vulnerable households to cover school fees for 5,994 children, including girls, children living with disabilities, and their continued school attendance.
External communication
All these initiatives were supported by the increased visibility of UNICEF interventions among communities and donors, both digitally and through traditional means. Notable achievements include the creation of an official version of the UNICEF logo in Sango (local language), used in several products; an advocacy report amplifying youth voices and analysing the public sector budget; two newsletters on gender; and three comics promoting respectively birth registration, girls’ education, and inclusion. On social networks, the main Facebook account recorded 4.2 million content views, with a sharp increase in traffic from May thanks to more engaging posts. Subscriber growth rose from 2 per cent in 2024 to 3.9 per cent in 2025, with more than 160,000 subscribers on Facebook, X, LinkedIn, and Instagram, and at least 640,000 individual visitors.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, UNICEF CAR operated in a rapidly evolving environment shaped by Improvements in the security and humanitarian situation in CAR; the adoption of CAR’s National Development Plan; the Humanitarian Reset; the UN80 Initiative; and UNICEF’s global Future Focus Initiative. These shifts required the UNICEF CAR Office to recalibrate its programmatic priorities and field presence.
Programmatic adjustments consisted in UNICEF programming moving from a service delivery approach to systems strengthening marked a strategic pivot, enabling greater Government’s ownership and capacity to deliver inclusive, accessible quality basic social services to all Central Africans. This adjustment positioned UNICEF to provide high-level technical assistance that will help the Government increase its capacity to mobilize domestic resources and allocate them to realize children's rights. In parallel, UNICEF will support the establishment a social protection system that will shield the most vulnerable population from shocks while strengthening demand for essential services.
UNICEF learned while implementing the current Cooperation Programme that transforming social norms can be accelerated by institutionalizing community engagement through national policy and effective population participation in behavioural change. Indeed, `the 482 community platforms created, including 156 village and neighbourhood development committees, and more than 6,000 community dialogues held in 2025 considerably strengthened the demand for basic social services and essential family practices for child well-being. During the Mpox and polio outbreaks, these mechanisms rapidly disseminated targeted and credible messages by using community and digital networks. As a result, more than 2.7 million children were vaccinated against polio, and Mpox was contained. Thanks to initiatives that demonstrate population adherence to pursued objectives–such as village development committees, Kundukwa village education networks, RECOPE community child protection networks, and U-Report–demand for health, nutrition, education, WASH and child protection services has made notable progress.
The year 2025 was marked by major challenges in mobilizing the financial resources needed to implement humanitarian and development response programmes. Resource mobilization was due to both to the notable reduction in US government funding beginning in February, andto the CAR Government’s narrative on shifting from humanitarian response to development interventions. Despite UNICEF’s increased engagement with donors, including through visits to donors in CAR and field visits by major donors, only $29.6 million was mobilized in 2025, only 60% of $49.4 million raised in 2024.
To remain efficient despite the financial challenges, UNICEF CAR shifted to lighter and more adapted operational and field presence, moving from four field offices to five ‘convergence zones’ from early 2026. The establishment of ‘UN Hubs’ in the field enable the shift from statics field offices to agile field presence in convergent zones, allowing agencies and organizations to pool resources to reduce operational costs. This new approach will be accompanied by localization through institutional strengthening and partnerships with national actors. In this context, UNICEF strengthened localization by assuring the quality of transfers to implementing partners and their compliance with HACT and PSEA procedures. Thus, for the first time, more than half of the resources transferred to implementing partners, $18 million, were allocated to local NGOs and the government.
This orientation for strengthening national capacities was also reflected at the national health system level, through support for the distribution of more than 895 tons of essential medicines and nutritional inputs in the seven health regions, consolidating the national supply chain. A notable achievement was the modernization of UNICEF’s central warehouse, improving storage and handling conditions, reducing costs, and enabling savings of more than 149 million CFA francs (around $250,000) in six months. Digitization of processes and reporting will remain a priority for 2026 to ensure optimal real-time resource management.
Despite profound changes in the national context and an evolving development aid environment, UNICEF CAR demonstrated resilience and adaptability in 2025 and resolutely enters 2026 with a renewed vision UNICEF CAR 2.0 focused on strategic and high-impact results, . This roadmap for our engagement with the Government, donors and communities aims to reposition UNICEF as the partner of choice to advance the child rights agenda in CAR. Already, with CAR 2.0, UNICEF has led the development of two high-impact business cases: one to accelerate the reduction of maternal and child mortality and the other to address the learning crisis by improving the quality of education. These initiatives provide a compelling framework for resource mobilization, strategic dialogue with the Government and donors, and programmatic priorities, ensuring that UNICEF CAR’s future actions are both transformative and sustainable in the coming years.

In 2025, Chad experienced significant policy developments with direct implications for the implementation of the UNICEF Country Programme. The Government validated the National Development Plan “Tchad Connexion 2030” (2025-2030), which establishes renewed national priorities for inclusive and sustainable development. This process was complemented by a national seminar on decentralization, during which authorities reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening local governance and improving the delivery of basic social services.
A resource mobilization roundtable convened in Abu Dhabi in November 2025 further demonstrated sustained government and partner engagement in securing the resources necessary for implementation of the National Development Plan. These milestones generated new opportunities to strengthen systems across sectors relevant to UNICEF’s Goal Areas and to advance equity focused and gender responsive programming, particularly in education, health, WASH, and the promotion of social equity and gender equality.
In parallel, the UNICEF–Government Cooperation Programme for 2027–2030 progressed toward finalization. The programme aims to leverage these national reforms to accelerate the child rights agenda and operationalize the humanitarian–development–peace nexus. The year also marked the launch of the formulation process for the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2027–2030. UNICEF actively contributed to ensure alignment between the future Country Programme, UNSDCF priorities, and progress toward child related Sustainable Development Goals.
Humanitarian needs remained acute in 2025. According to the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, 7 million people—including 3.9 million children—required assistance. The year was marked by recurrent epidemics and sustained refugee inflows linked to the Sudan crisis. Since April 2023, 902,814 Sudanese refugees and 355,903 Chadian returnees had arrived in eastern provinces, the majority of whom were children. Internal displacement also increased to 225,689 individuals, primarily in the Lake Province.
Security conditions remained volatile, with intercommunal violence in southern and eastern regions and incidents affecting humanitarian personnel and national defense forces. By the end of 2025, the Sudan Refugee Response Plan faced a 42 per cent funding gap. Despite these constraints, UNICEF and partners maintained programme delivery nationwide, implementing temporary mitigation measures as needed to ensure the safety of staff.
Chad continued to face structural development challenges. The Human Development Report 2025 estimated the country’s Human Development Index at 0.416 (2023), placing Chad in the Low Human Development category and ranking 190 out of 193 countries and territories. The Gender Development Index ranked Chad at the same level, reflecting persistent gender inequalities.
Children represented 52 per cent of the population, and widespread socio-economic disparities persisted despite projected economic growth of 3.4 per cent in 2025. Monetary poverty affected an estimated 44.8 per cent of the population, contributing to multiple and overlapping deprivations for children, especially in rural areas.
Within UNICEF, the year was marked by a sharp contraction in global humanitarian and development financing. This required programmatic reprioritization and reductions in staffing expenditures. In line with UNICEF’s Future Focus Initiative, the Country Office reoriented programming around four priority areas and adjusted its organizational structure in line with the Focus, Impact, Scale and Differentiation (FISD) shifts.
Goal Area 1 – Every Child Survives and Thrives
Progress in child survival remained limited, and outcomes continued to be among the lowest globally. The under-five mortality rate was estimated at 101.13 per 1,000 live births, meaning more than one in ten children dies before age five. Recurrent outbreaks of measles, diphtheria, meningitis and cholera further strained an already fragile health system. Malnutrition remained a major driver of child mortality, with acute malnutrition affecting 10.8 per cent of children and chronic malnutrition 36.7 per cent—both well above emergency thresholds. These trends underscored the urgent need to strengthen integrated primary health care, nutrition services and epidemic preparedness.
Goal Area 2 – Every Child Learns
Despite legislation mandating compulsory education until age 16 and enrolment rates above 90 per cent, more than 3 million school-age children remained out of school. Insufficient school infrastructure, limited availability of trained teachers, rapid demographic growth and continued refugee influx overwhelmed the system’s capacity. Gender and socio-economic disparities continued to restrict equitable access to quality learning. Without large-scale and sustained investment, progress risks plateauing, leaving the most vulnerable children behind.
Goal Area 3 – Every Child is Protected from Violence and Harmful Practices
The child protection situation remained particularly concerning. According to the 2025 Child and Women Protection Statistical Yearbook,  6,285 cases of violence, abuse and exploitation were reported in Chad in 2024, with 42 per cent involving physical violence and 25 per cent female genital mutilation. Early marriage remained widespread, affecting 60 per cent of girls before age 18 and contributing to persistently high maternal and neonatal mortality. Birth registration remained critically low, with 70 per cent of children under five unregistered, limiting access to essential services and legal protection. Strengthened investment in child protection systems remains essential to safeguarding children’s rights.
Goal Area 4 – Every Child Lives in a Safe and Sustainable Climate and Environment
Despite some progress, major gaps persisted in access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services. Approximately 47.9 per cent of households lacked basic water services, and 83.9 per cent lacked improved sanitation. These deficits contributed to recurrent waterborne diseases, heightened vulnerabilities during health emergencies, and undermined child survival and resilience. Strengthened and climate-resilient WASH systems remain essential.
Goal Area 5 – Every Child Has Access to Social Protection and Lives Free from Poverty
Social protection coverage remained extremely limited in 2025. Only 0.3 per cent of children had health insurance, and just 2.4 per cent of the poorest households benefited from social transfers. Extreme poverty affected 36.5 per cent of households, exposing families to significant socioeconomic shocks. Expanding shock-responsive social protection systems remains a key lever for reducing vulnerability and improving long-term outcomes for children.
Monitoring of child rights implementation continued to be constrained by gaps in recent socio-demographic data. The most recent national survey remains MICS6 (2019). UNICEF and the World Bank committed to supporting the implementation of a new MICS in 2026, drawing on census-mapping data generated in 2025 to strengthen evidence-based planning.

UNICEF’s 2025 portfolio in Chad delivered strategically relevant and measurable results that advanced national priorities under the National Development Plan “Tchad Connexion 2030” (2025-2030), particularly those related to foundational infrastructure, basic social needs, and cross-cutting societal and environmental priorities related to climate resilience, promotion of social equity and gender equality. Across all Goal Areas, these achievements contributed directly to the acceleration of the Key Results for Children (KRC), with overall performance reaching 83 per cent, including full attainment of targets on birth registration (KRC #8) and strong progress in immunization (KRC #1) and stunting prevention (KRC #2). Close alignment with Government priorities, strengthened multisectoral synergies, increased digitalization, enhanced community and youth engagement, and a decentralized operational footprint through subnational offices enabled UNICEF to translate national policy intent into expanded service coverage, improved quality and strengthened resilience in both development and humanitarian settings. Resource mobilization through multisectoral grants, inter-agency collaboration and strategic partnerships further reinforced this progress, while preserving social cohesion and continuity of essential services during emergencies.
As lead of the UN Basic Social Services Result Group, UNICEF strengthened interagency collaboration to advance the UNSDCF agenda across both humanitarian and development contexts. It contributed actively to joint UN planning mechanisms and worked closely with UNHCR, IOM and UNDP to harmonize child protection interventions in sensitive operational environments. UNICEF continued to collaborate closely with WFP and other partners in joint resilience programmes funded by the BMZ and the WB to strengthen social cohesion and multisectoral resilience in Chad. UNICEF also co-led accountability-to-affected-populations mechanisms with OCHA, helping to reinforce a more coherent, coordinated and people-centered UN response. In addition, UNICEF deepened its strategic positioning within the UN system by contributing substantively to the update of the Common Country Analysis and supporting the evaluation and formulation of the next UNSDCF, ensuring that children’s rights, equity and gender considerations were fully embedded in the 2027–2030 framework. Collectively, these efforts strengthened UNICEF’s role as a central actor in system-wide planning, analysis and coordination, in line with the UN 80 reform.
Goal Area 1 – Every Child Survives and Thrives
UNICEF supported major advancements in routine immunization and primary health-care system resilience. Effective Vaccine Management reached 76 per cent, 86 per cent of health facilities operated with functional cold chain equipment, and 877,911 children received the third dose of pentavalent vaccine, with 94 per cent of districts attaining at least 80 per cent coverage following Big Catch-Up strategies and targeted vaccine introductions. The digitalization of supply chains through mSupply improved real-time stock visibility and corrective action, while prevention of mother-to-child transmission services was integrated into 94 per cent of health facilities. Two neonatal units established in Sarh and Moundou strengthened the continuum of maternal and newborn care, and adolescent-responsive HIV platforms reached more than 137,000 young people with testing and awareness services. A transformative milestone was the progressive formal integration of community health workers into the national health system across 27 districts, enabling 685 trained CHWs to extend promotive, preventive and selected curative services to underserved communities and improve early identification of zero-dose and under-immunized children.
Nutrition services also demonstrated high performance. A total of 427,646 children with severe acute malnutrition were treated with a cure rate of 95.9 per cent, supported by 401,072 cartons of therapeutic food covering 98.6 per cent of national needs. Strengthened digital tracking systems safeguarded supply integrity. Community detection expanded through training of 54,515 caregivers in the family MUAC approach. Preventive nutrition services scaled up significantly, with stunting-prevention interventions implemented in 111 districts, vitamin A supplementation reaching more than 5 million children, deworming reaching 4.7 million children, and home fortification programmes serving nearly 30,000 young children. Emergency nutrition services reached 81,755 severe cases with a 94.5 per cent cure rate across 936 outpatient sites. Infant and Young Child Feeding services expanded across ten provinces, supported by 2,614 CHWs and over 9,000 mother-to-mother groups, while gender-responsive initiatives—such as father-engagement efforts under the VINA project—addressed harmful norms underlying feeding practices. Partnerships with international and national NGOs further strengthened service equity and coverage across both humanitarian and development settings.
Goal Area 2 – Every Child Learns
UNICEF supported continuity and quality of learning amid climate shocks, teacher strikes and displacement. A total of 84,696 children, including 37,183 girls, benefited from improved learning conditions through support for 301 contractual teachers, 70 temporary learning spaces, 36 gender-segregated latrine blocks and 31 inclusive climate-resilient water points. Governance and accountability improved through the training of 563 school management committee members and more than 1,200 actors on the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse. Learning quality was enhanced through the distribution of individual materials for 337,174 students and 50,384 teacher guides. Remediation programmes in 48 schools supported more than 20,000 learners facing risk of long-term learning loss.
Multisectoral collaboration helped remove structural barriers to education. School meal programmes reached 36,052 children, and 134,210 children received birth certificates enabling school enrolment. Government measures supported by UNICEF enabled 4,823 Sudanese refugee students to sit national Grade 12 examinations in Chad. Digital inclusion expanded through 20 connected schools serving 10,147 students, and HOPE/Kobo tools identified 19,039 vulnerable adolescent girls for targeted support. UNICEF mobilized over USD 4 million to expand inclusive and protective learning opportunities for more than 337,000 vulnerable children, including refugee learners and children with disabilities, and supported the development of didactic kits and training modules to strengthen teacher capacity and contribute to safer, more inclusive learning environments.
Goal Area 3 – Every Child is Protected from Violence, Exploitation, Abuse, Neglect and Harmful Practices
Significant progress was made in strengthening national systems and accelerating digital transformation. A national moratorium on supplementary birth-registration fees through 2030 removed a major barrier for vulnerable families, and interoperability between health facilities and civil registration services enabled automatic registration of facility-based births. Through the TASDJIL platform, 207,151 birth registrations were digitally processed, improving accuracy and reducing delays. Mobile birth-registration services reached 104,788 school-age children, including those in nomadic and remote communities. The “Certified Village – Zero Child Without a Birth Certificate” initiative resulted in universal registration for 41,212 previously undocumented children across 67 villages, demonstrating strong community engagement and accountability.
Child-friendly justice systems were reinforced through the training of 28 judges on child protection standards and the release and reintegration of 86 children from detention. Provincial action plans to prevent and respond to violence and harmful practices were strengthened, complemented by adolescent-led peer initiatives and public declarations by local authorities against child marriage and female genital mutilation. Joint UN engagement, including with UNHCR, IOM and UNDP, ensured coherent child-protection approaches in sensitive contexts, while collaboration with the Ministry of Defense contributed to aligning DDR processes with international standards. These gains, however, remain vulnerable to declining funding for child protection.
Goal Area 4 – Every Child Lives in a Safe and Sustainable Climate and Environment
UNICEF supported Government leadership to improve equitable access to water, sanitation and hygiene services. Community-led sanitation enabled 664,808 people to live in newly certified open-defecation-free communities, and climate-resilient water systems provided basic drinking water to 180,266 people. WASH services in 321 schools and 68 health facilities were rehabilitated using inclusive, gender-responsive and climate-resilient standards. In humanitarian contexts—including the Sudan refugee influx, cholera outbreaks and floods—UNICEF provided safe drinking water to 445,484 people, emergency sanitation to 158,103 people and hygiene support to 391,291 people, including menstrual hygiene supplies for 135,320 women and adolescent girls. Humanitarian investments were intentionally linked to durable climate-resilient infrastructure, including solarized water systems, illustrating effective integration of the humanitarian–development–peace nexus and advancing progress toward KRC #8.
UNICEF’s upstream engagement helped elevate sanitation on the national political agenda. The organization played a central role in convening the country’s first national sanitation forum and supporting the establishment of a dedicated sanitation budget line. Upstream technical work informed the development of the national water and sanitation master plan and updated groundwater monitoring roadmap. Youth engagement in climate action was institutionalized through a national platform uniting 200 youth associations. Localization was strengthened through partnerships with local organizations and by prioritizing local firms for infrastructure construction. Coordination platforms co-led by UNICEF enhanced dialogue between water, sanitation, youth and environmental authorities and supported institutionalization of integrated HDP approaches. Evidence generated through WASH accounts and joint monitoring with WHO contributed to advocacy for increased public financing for sanitation, laying the foundation for stronger accountability and more reliable services.
Goal Area 5 – Every Child Has Access to Social Protection and Lives Free from Poverty
Finally, within Goal Area 5 – Every Child Has Access to Social Protection and Lives Free from Poverty, UNICEF supported systemic reforms to promote resilience, equity and child-sensitive public finance. The Unified Social Registry expanded to 100,000 households, institutionalizing equitable and data-driven beneficiary targeting. Regular cash assistance supported more than 18,000 vulnerable households, humanitarian cash assistance reached 4,195 households during the lean season and a school-linked cash-grant programme enabled approximately 19,000 girls to enroll or remain in school.
