As 2025 marks the end of the current Country Programme Document (CPD) cycle, the major programmatic results below summarize the key achievements of 2025 and highlight progress made since the start of the CPD.


Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies. KRC#1: Immunization; KRC#2: Prevention of stunting   

In 2025, Côte d’Ivoire’s health system demonstrated strong resilience in managing epidemic threats—resilience that has been progressively strengthened since the COVID-19 pandemic with support from key partners, including Gavi, the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF. Throughout the 2021–2025 cycle, UNICEF played a catalytic role in reinforcing health governance, planning and sustainability by supporting major national frameworks, including the National Immunization Strategy (2022–2025), the Immunization Financing Transition Plan (2024–2030) and the National Community Health Strategic Plan (2022–2025), along with the Community Health Investment Case (2023–2032). UNICEF also worked with the Government to ensure continuity of essential services, contributing to the vaccination of 14.4 million people (48 per cent of the population) against COVID-19 and the deployment of 3,000 solar-powered cold chain units to date. These investments bolstered routine immunization capacity and enhanced the country’s ability to respond effectively to dengue, mpox and cholera outbreaks.


In 2025, in partnership with Gavi and WHO, UNICEF efforts contributed to consolidating routine immunization coverage to 97 per cent for DTP3 (exceeding the CPD target of 95 per cent) (KRC#1), vaccinating 3.3 million girls against HPV through innovative approaches combining digital platforms and U-Reporters, and introducing the malaria vaccine nationwide. The Effective Vaccine Management score reached 81 per cent. Through capacity-building and optimized deployment of equipment and health professionals supported by UNICEF, maternal and newborn health outcomes improved.  


UNICEF’s scaled-up, results-driven strategy accelerated progress in maternal and newborn health. With expanded support to priority regions, births attended by skilled personnel increased to 109,158/116,646 from 102,370/109,052 in 2024—sustaining 94 per cent coverage. National coverage likewise reached 94 per cent, surpassing the 85 per cent CPD target. HIV prevention and treatment services were simultaneously reinforced, ensuring that 100 per cent of the 567 women diagnosed with HIV received treatment, demonstrating a strengthened continuum of care for mothers and infants.


The innovative scale-up of Kangaroo Mother Care centres—now expanded to 22 fully functional sites—further illustrates UNICEF’s catalytic role. This network saved 1,293 newborns in 2025 alone and 4,270 newborns between 2021 and 2025, clearly demonstrating the life-saving impact of sustained system strengthening and innovation at scale.


A major innovation in 2025 was UNICEF’s support to the Government to pilot the digitalization of the community health system in five districts of the northern region. Through integrated supervision, real-time data collection and strengthened engagement of community health workers, the initiative reached over 1.1 million children during the year. Together, these strategies demonstrate UNICEF’s strategic role in positioning Côte d’Ivoire on a sustainable pathway toward universal health coverage. Strategic partnerships were central to these achievements. Through collaboration with the World Bank, UNICEF supported the procurement of routine vaccines, while financing from Canada, the Government of the United States, the Muskoka Initiative and the Government of Côte d’Ivoire helped sustain immunization, maternal and child health and community-based services.


In 2025, UNICEF further strengthened nutrition governance and evidence generation, consolidating its role as a lead partner in multisectoral coordination and policy dialogue since the start of the Country Programme. As lead of the Nutrition Donor Partners Group, together with the European Union, UNICEF contributed to shaping the national nutrition policy environment. Building on earlier achievements, UNICEF supported the operationalization of the National Multisectoral Nutrition Plan 2024–2027, ensuring alignment with national priorities and global standards, supported by the National Nutrition Information Platform. The Standardized Monitoring and Assessment of Relief and Transitions (SMART) survey conducted in 2025 provided invaluable data that will play a crucial role in shaping nutrition approaches, including geographic targeting, intensified promotion of breastfeeding, improved dietary diversity and efforts to limit the marketing of unhealthy foods. UNICEF was also instrumental in the development and approval of the Child Nutrition Fund, a transformative financing mechanism for nutrition programmes. UNICEF’s contribution to the Nutrition for Growth Summit and the organization of the National Nutrition Round Table further reinforced commitments to accountability and long-term investment. 


Strategic engagement extended to food systems and community-based approaches. The First Foods Africa initiative confirmed Côte d’Ivoire’s role as a front-runner in promoting local food processing and marketing to improve children’s diets. These efforts were complemented by innovative partnerships linking sport and nutrition to promote healthy diets among adolescents, youth and communities. In addition, a pioneering study on the taxation of unhealthy foods was launched, paving the way for systemic impact in 2026 and beyond.


Operationally, over the 2021–2025 period, care for children with severe acute malnutrition reached scale, with 100 per cent of health districts providing treatment – meeting the CPD target – and resulting in the treatment of 13,863 children aged 6–59 months in 2025 (approximately 93,000 since 2021). In 2025, UNICEF supported the review of the national protocol, in collaboration with WHO, World Food Programme and Action Against Hunger, to align with international standards, with roll-out planned for 2026. As the leading supplier of vitamin A, UNICEF, with support from the Government of Canada, ensured that nearly 5 million children aged 6–59 months received a first dose in 2025, achieving 93 per cent coverage and exceeding the CPD target of 2,928,000 children per year. This result was achieved through routine services in 73 districts and door-to-door campaigns supported by U-Reporters, in close partnership with Helen Keller International and Nutrition International. Through Muskoka funding, 49 new maternities are in the process of being designated as ‘baby-friendly,’ bringing the total to 1,326 facilities, exceeding the target of 1,244 for the 2021–2025 period, while more than 17,000 children under five received multiple micronutrients in vulnerable areas. UNICEF also strengthened 73 community nutrition platforms and partnered with women’s groups under the First Foods Africa initiative.


Innovation remained central: UNICEF initiated a prototype containerised unit for local food processing and facilitated the development of social marketing strategies for complementary foods. In addition, with support from KfW Development Bank (Germany) and the Debt-for-Development Swap (Contrat de désendettement et de développement (C2D)), UNICEF introduced the family mid-upper arm circumference innovation, empowering caregivers to monitor the nutritional status of their children. These innovations will be scaled up in 2026 and beyond.



Goal Area 2: Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future. 

KRC#3: Equitable and sustainable access to education; KRC#4: Improved learning outcomes 


UNICEF contributed to expanding access to education, improving learning outcomes, strengthening system resilience, fostering innovation in digital and vocational learning and enhancing sector governance—positioning Côte d’Ivoire for sustained progress and consolidating gains achieved throughout the 2021–2025 programme cycle. Strategic partnerships between UNICEF and donors, including World Bank, UNESCO, National Committees and Meditteranean Shipping Company, as well as collaboration with Conceptos Plásticos and several local private-sector companies in the construction and digital education sectors, enabled UNICEF to significantly advance education access, quality and equity in Côte d’Ivoire. Major achievements include the construction, rehabilitation and equipping of over 590 classrooms (163 built and rehabilitated in 2025 against a target of 140) across preschool, primary and lower- secondary levels, alongside capacity-building for over 200 School Management Committee members, fostering local ownership of school infrastructure initiatives. In 2025, the turnkey model for constructing schools using recycled plastic bricks was fully finalized, paving the way for its roll-out in early 2026. This standardized solution will enable rapid scale-up to help address the country’s significant classroom gap, estimated at 15,000 additional classrooms needed by 2030.


To support vulnerable families and teachers, UNICEF distributed school kits and self-learning tools to more than one million students from 2021 to 2025, including beneficiaries in emergency contexts. Innovative solutions, such as mobile digital classrooms (Ma classe digitale mobile) and the digital schooling platform (Mon école à la maison), reached over 10,000 children in areas lacking electricity and digital connectivity. Nationwide initiatives such as Dictée du jour, strengthened foundational literacy, contributing to a rise in primary examination pass rates from 71.3 per cent in 2024 to 86.6 per cent in 2025 – a major achievement (KRC#4).


UNICEF also led the integration of digital tools across all education levels by training techno-pedagogical specialists and developing interactive learning materials, positioning Côte d’Ivoire as the only French-speaking African country selected for the Learning Pioneer programme. Foundational learning programmes such as Programme national d’amélioration des premiers apprentissages scolaires trained over 77,880 education staff, while emergency preparedness and climate-risk tools enhanced the resilience of schools and communities in vulnerable regions.


Since 2021, efforts to support out-of-school children led to the reintegration of 78,051 learners against a CPD target of 30,000 (13,457 in 2025 against an annual target of 6,000) (KRC#3), including through targeted interventions in emergency and resilience contexts. Skills development initiatives, including mobile training units (MTUs), strengthened industrial and technical capacities for 200 learners, while UNICEF-supported professional development and equipment upgrades at the Institute for Women’s Training and Education informed the Government’s plan to scale up 104 additional MTUs nationwide. Over 6,000 adolescents benefited from vocational and life-skills training, and inclusive education efforts supported the integration of children with disabilities into public schools.


UNICEF’s technical and coordination support strengthened sector governance, data systems and policy implementation. This included support to the regionalized teacher recruitment and deployment programme, sector reviews chaired by the Prime Minister, consolidation of the 2026–2030 education results framework and contributions to research and analytical tools—based on the Situational Analysis, the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey round 7 and the National Multidimensional Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (N-MODA)—to inform evidence-based planning. 



Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices; KRC#7: Birth registration 

In 2025, UNICEF continued to play a leading role within the global World Bank–UNICEF strategic partnership, advancing a collaborative model for social sector reform at the country level. Efforts to strengthen the Social Service Workforce (SSW) led to significant improvements in the core competencies of social workers and child justice professionals, particularly in child protection case management, quality of care and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). The latter benefited from the joint WHO-UNICEF initiative on MHPSS. These efforts expanded access to care, enhanced national capacities and promoted a more integrated approach across the health and social protection sectors. Digital transformation and the certification of new e-learning modules added institutional value and enabled capacity-building at scale. All SSW training will now be hosted on the national e-learning platform, while World Bank financing for social centres will support the gradual phase-out of UNICEF’s direct cash transfers to social services, as part of strengthening prevention and care interventions for child victims. 


The Child Protection Information Management System was upgraded to its latest version, positioning Côte d’Ivoire as a regional pioneer. The system now integrates both child protection and gender-based violence cases and is jointly managed by the two ministries responsible for social affairs. In 2025, UNICEF-supported services assisted 5,888 children, surpassing the annual target by 18 per cent. Since 2021, 27,086 child victims of violence have been reached, exceeding the cumulative target by 35 per cent.[xii] These results underscore Côte d’Ivoire’s renewed commitment to ending violence against children.


Institutional progress on child labour was achieved through the ratification of the International Labour Organization (ILO) Convention 189 and the adoption of the national Child Labour Action Plan 2025–2029, focused on addressing root causes. These milestones reflect effective joint advocacy by UNICEF, ILO and the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Côte d’Ivoire remains the only country globally with a rapidly declining child labour rate, currently at 22 per cent, well below the CPD target of 26 per cent. The joint ILO-IOM UNICEF initiative to address the root causes of child labour strengthened child protection outcomes by effectively combining social, educational and economic interventions. 


Digital transformation of the national justice system was adopted in 2025, harmonizing and modernizing procedures, including those related to child justice, with implementation planned for 2026 and a focus on scale and impact. For the first time, as a result of UNICEF advocacy, domestic funding was secured for all 39 child justice services[xiii], signalling growing recognition of justice for children as a long-term investment.


A total of 589,667 children under one were registered as of 2025, bringing the cumulative number of children under one registered with UNICEF support since 2021 to 2,999,677—equivalent to 91.7 per cent of the cumulative target of 3,270,792 children (KRC#7). To improve birth registration rates within the three-month legal time frame, Parliament amended the Civil Registration Law to extend the grace period up to one year, in line with United Nations Statistics Division standards, following several years of advocacy. This reform is expected to place Côte d’Ivoire among the countries with birth registration rates of 75–90 per cent. UNICEF-supported regional plans boosted registration rates in 22 of 33 regions, with gains of up to 20 percentage points—a major breakthrough. The interoperability and decentralization model resulted in the installation of four new hospital-based registration centres, including outside Abidjan. This model will be developed as a proof of concept to secure additional domestic financing and sustain the results achieved.


Climate-resilient child protection systems and services were strengthened, as children in Côte d'Ivoire face increasing risks related to climate shocks. Further analysis is required to deepen the evidence on climate-related displacement linked to the Central Sahel crisis and child labour, in line with the programmatic shifts of the new CPD (2026–2030).



Goal Area 4: Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment; KRC#8: End open defecation 

UNICEF catalysed critical WASH sector reforms in 2025 by playing a leading role in coordination and policy development, including advocating for the Presidential Decree establishing the WASH Sector Group and supporting its operationalization. Through targeted technical assistance, UNICEF strengthened the Directorate of Rural Sanitation; advanced the integration of climate action into national policy frameworks—contributing to the Environmental and Social Management Framework, the Climate Rationale for WASH and the national endorsement of the Nationally Determined Contribution (3.0)—and supported the development of institutional data systems. Work on the National Pact for Universal Access to WASH Services was also initiated, laying the foundation for a future national declaration of the “Year of Water.” Collectively, these efforts strengthened coordination, mobilized additional financing and positioned WASH as a core pillar of resilience and sustainable development in Côte d’Ivoire. 


UNICEF interventions focused on expanding climate-resilient WASH access, preventing waterborne diseases and improving sector governance. In 2025, 36,700 people gained access to safe drinking water, contributing to a total of 156,392 people reached during the 2021–2025 programme cycle—well above the target of 122,630. This acceleration was driven by a strategic shift from stand-alone boreholes to more sustainable, climate-resilient water supply systems and solar-powered community networks. Basic WASH services were also upgraded in 24 schools and 17 health centres in 2025, improving conditions for more than 86,000 schoolchildren and 85,000 patients and caregivers. Over the full 2021–2025 period, WASH improvements were delivered in 233 schools and 191 health centres, exceeding programme targets of 100 schools and 80 health centres respectively.


Progress in sanitation was equally significant. An additional 30,000 people were declared living in open-defecation-free communities in 2025, bringing the cumulative total to 246,096—double the original CPD target of 123,230 (KRC#8). These results were enabled by a shift from village-level CLTS to broader regional approaches, deepening partnerships with NGOs and strengthening the engagement of local and regional authorities. Complementary investments in sanitation marketing, community artisans and the development of a national sanitation marketing programme contributed to sustainability and equity.


Systems strengthening remained central to UNICEF’s approach. UNICEF supported the preparation of environmental and social safeguards and reinforced national WASH data systems, including through a sector-wide sustainability check conducted with the national statistics agency. Capacity-building was prioritized, with 585 government and sector actors trained in climate-resilient sanitation, public finance and the WASH Facility Improvement Tool.


UNICEF also advanced climate action and youth engagement. UNICEF supported Côte d’Ivoire’s participation in the Thirtieth Conference of the Parties (COP 30) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, enabling the signature of the National Declaration for Children, Youth and Climate Action. Complementary community and national platforms—including U-Report, WOZO Vacances and national dialogues—amplified youth voices in WASH and climate resilience initiatives.



Goal Area 5: Every child, including adolescent, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free from poverty.

In 2025, UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire consolidated its support to inclusive, shock-responsive and child-focused social protection systems, contributing to sustained poverty reduction and stronger system foundations over the 2021–2025 programme cycle. Efforts focused on expanding social protection coverage, improving evidence-based policymaking, strengthening public finance for children and promoting inclusive economic opportunities for adolescents and youth.


Significant gains were achieved in social protection coverage. Government cash transfer programmes reached 223,080 children under five in 2025—a significant scale-up from the 2019 baseline of 85,000 and nearing the target of 400,000. UNICEF provided technical assistance to improve targeting, beneficiary management and intersectoral coordination, including operationalization of the Unique Social Registry (RSU). The RSU now consolidates data on more than 1.5 million households (against over 2 million households targeted for the period 2021-2025), enhancing linkages between cash transfers, health insurance and social services.[xiv]


UNICEF reinforced the policy and evidence base for social protection through targeted analytical and institutional support. Following the validation of the national social protection policy framework in 2024, UNICEF supported its operational anchoring by conducting a financial review and preparing a resource mobilization strategy in partnership with the World Bank, which co-led the Social Protection Donor Group with UNICEF. The updated N-MODA further informed policy dialogue, targeting decisions and prioritization.


To advance public finance for children, UNICEF supported comprehensive social sector budget analyses and consolidated participatory child budgeting initiatives across nine municipalities, in partnership with NGO Forum. In addition, an innovative territorial planning and budgeting process—both child-rights focused and climate-sensitive—was launched in the Municipality of Grand-Bassam. This approach aims to ensure that children’s rights and priority social infrastructure needs are fully integrated into the development plan, in close collaboration with the national decentralization authorities.


To address the poverty–employability nexus, UNICEF strengthened national capacities to promote skills development and economic empowerment, particularly for adolescents and young women. In 2025, 526 national actors were trained across disability inclusion, girls’ economic empowerment and skills development initiatives. Innovative initiatives such as YOMA, coupled with Ma classe digitale mobile, advanced skills development and digital inclusion. UNICEF also supported five national and regional programmes, including vocational skills training through Mobile Training Units in underserved northern regions, the Girl Power programme, and interventions led by NGO partners such as CARE International and Disability-Inclusive Development Programs and Services – DIDEPAS in Côte d’Ivoire.


Government capacities were reinforced to align education and training systems with labour market demands and to integrate life skills into formal and non-formal systems. UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to two key decrees: one establishing a quality socioeducational offer to build psychosocial and 21st-century skills, and another expanding access to technical and vocational training through mobile and digital solutions. Coverage of adolescent health services increased from 20 per cent in 2023 to 80 per cent in 2025, contributing to a reduction in adolescent pregnancies from 6,681 to 4,266.


In 2025, UNICEF’s work with adolescents and youth focused on translating policy commitments into tangible results. Following the West and Central Africa Girl Summit, Côte d’Ivoire strengthened its leadership on girls’ rights by institutionalizing girls’ spaces in all secondary schools. This nationwide measure promotes inclusive, safe and empowering learning environments, enhances access to essential services, and reaffirms the country’s determination to place adolescent girls at the centre of its education and social policies.


In 2025, UNICEF and its partners expanded community listening and human-centred co-creation to more localities and themes, advancing children’s rights across Côte d’Ivoire. These efforts reached 250 new communities, 15,000 households and over 200,000 people, driving progress in vaccination, nutrition, hygiene, water management, birth registration, social cohesion, child labour prevention and adolescent health.[xv] Under the joint ILO-IOM UNICEF initiative addressing the root causes of child labour, community listening enabled an integrated approach across 101 localities, harmonizing intervention methodologies for future scale-up. 



Enablers and office management results

UNICEF deepened its support to the reporting mechanisms of the Convention on the Rights of the Child by contributing to the country’s initial reports on the Optional Protocols, facilitating joint follow-up of the Universal Periodic Review recommendations with partners, and supporting the development of the third period report to the Committee of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child. This work will continue into 2026. 


UNICEF intensified its strategic advocacy for child rights by forging several first-ever partnerships. The partnership with the Chamber of Kings and Traditional Leaders engaged 50 traditional leaders, strengthening their commitment to promoting and protecting children’s rights. The partnership signed with Félix Houphouët-Boigny University is set to deepen research, learning and data sharing on child rights. In parallel, 70 community radio stations renewed their efforts to promote key behaviours, amplifying child-focused messages nationwide.


UNICEF also signed two ground-breaking MoUs with Société d’exploitation et de développement aéroportuaire, aéronautique et météorologique - SODEXAM and the MTN Foundation, strengthening private sector collaboration in Côte d’Ivoire. 


In 2025, UNICEF reinforced UN coordination to advance systemic reforms and played a strategic role in UN system processes, actively supporting the implementation of joint workplans and joint programmes, and contributing to the development of the UNSDCF 2026–2030. UNICEF continued to lead the UN Operations Management Team, introducing operational innovations to improve efficiency and effectiveness across UN agencies in a context of declining ODA and increasingly constrained budgets.


UNICEF strengthened partnerships across public, private and UN sectors to accelerate results for children. Over US$70 million was mobilized (US$58.6 million from public sources and US$11.4 million from private partners). Key highlights included a four-year partnership with the Mastercard Foundation valued at US$9 million and significant funding secured from the Child Nutrition Fund (US$33.7 million to support programmes over the next four years). Priority areas included health, nutrition, education, birth registration, child labour reduction and youth empowerment. The organization surpassed CPD 2021–2025 resource mobilization targets by 11 per cent and expanded partnerships to combat child labour while promoting youth employability and green economy innovation.


The digital ecosystem reached 761,428 followers and a total audience of 15.8 million people, with Facebook leading at 490,904 followers and 23 million views—an unprecedented result achieved partly due to renewed partnerships with major television and radio networks, the signing of the Ethical Charter with RTI and improved in-house digital outreach strategies. The content strategy generated over 433,000 engagements, focusing on health, nutrition and youth empowerment. Beyond metrics, UNICEF fostered active citizenship by engaging 137 young bloggers, two Youth Advocates and over 1,000 participants in communication sessions, placing youth-led advocacy at the heart of its digital mission.


The office strengthened its programme and operations management through enhanced mechanisms and renewed office committees. Programme planning for the next cycle, 2026–2030, was successfully completed, with the new CPD approved by the Executive Board in September 2025 following very positive feedback from Member States, namely Canada, Germany, Oman and Switzerland. The office also successfully implemented a smooth, inclusive and consultative staff restructuring process aligned with the new CPD vision, ensuring tailored career support for each affected staff member.


Over 90 per cent of the targets outlined in the Annual Management Plan were successfully achieved. The office also successfully piloted vaccine transport by sea, which aims to reduce carbon emissions by nearly 90 per cent, costs by over 50 per cent, and to improve cold chain control.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
In 2025, UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire operated in a context marked by persistent systemic constraints—against the backdrop of strong population growth (2.9 per cent), continued internal rural-to-urban migration, an ongoing refugee influx and rising social demand—despite progress achieved through adaptive strategies. As a result, equity gaps remained significant. Zero-dose children and underserved communities—including in peri-urban areas—continued to be difficult to reach due to supply chain limitations, uneven local capacities and disparities in funding across the national territory. Integrated supervision and digital tools helped sustain coverage, but these measures also highlighted the need for stronger coordination and real-time data systems.
Institutional transitions and fragmented governance slowed decision-making, affecting reforms in education, social protection and health. The roll-out of the General States of Education and Literacy introduced complex implementation demands, while persistent COVID-19 aftershocks and cuts in ODA further strained the education system, which was already struggling to keep pace with rapidly growing demand. Similarly, the rapid increase in social protection coverage was constrained by insufficient domestic funding and weak decentralized capacity, despite overall growth in the national public budget.
Structural issues persisted across sectors: inadequate hygiene infrastructure in schools and health facilities, incomplete digitalization of civil registration systems and gaps in climate financing undermined service quality and resilience. While legal amendments and decentralization improved birth registration rates, sustaining these gains requires institutional anchoring and predictable resource flows. Finally, the transition to Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) approaches, which have successfully encouraged the adoption of positive behaviours that improve child development outcomes, underscored the need for deeper integration into planning and budgeting frameworks. 
Resource mobilization emerged as a cross-cutting challenge, with reductions in ODA and shifting donor priorities leading to unpredictability. Private sector engagement remained challenging—particularly in sensitive areas such as child labour in cocoa supply chains—owing to apprehension among private sector actors about the perceived burden of their role in system strengthening and expectations regarding their contributions to measurable results. National technical expertise gaps also limited the scale-up of innovative approaches, from nutrition partnerships to digital solutions.
Lessons learned
A strengthened knowledge management strategy and improved documentation of results and lessons learned enabled UNICEF to more effectively capture and analyze key insights. In 2025, UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire reinforced the importance of resilient systems and integrated approaches to sustain essential services and deliver equitable results. Leveraging evidence- and data-driven strategies proved critical for targeting zero-dose and underserved populations, guiding policy decisions and improving programme efficiency. Enhanced data systems, such as the national SMART survey and nutrition information platform, demonstrated that reliable, disaggregated data remains the foundation for effective planning and accountability.
Strong partnerships and UNICEF’s convening power remained decisive in aligning resources and accelerating results for the most vulnerable children. Initiatives, such as First Foods Africa and the Child Nutrition Fund, demonstrated how innovative financing, combined with policy coherence and community engagement, can strengthen food systems and mobilize national commitments. Likewise, climate-resilient WASH solutions and sanitation marketing underscored that context-specific adaptation and community-based approaches are essential for sustainability.
Bringing services closer to rights-holders through innovation—whether via itinerant classrooms, MTUs, or digital tools—proved effective in reducing exclusion and expanding access to education and skills development. These approaches offer practical solutions for reaching hard-to-reach children and addressing underlying drivers of deprivation. Experience also demonstrated that high-level political commitment, combined with coordinated action under a One UN framework, is critical for tackling complex challenges, such as child labour, and could be replicated to strengthen violence prevention and response.
Digital transformation emerged as a cost-effective strategy for scaling social service workforce capacity, provided it is accompanied by affordable infrastructure and institutionalized training modalities. Across social policy, progress in cash transfers and integrated services underscored that system strengthening, government ownership and evidence-based advocacy are indispensable for achieving results at scale.
Overall, 2025 reinforced the core lessons of the 2021–2025 cycle: sustainable and equitable results depend on interoperable data systems, predictable and diversified financing, institutional anchoring, decentralized capacity and coordinated multi-ministerial and One UN follow-up on government commitments. Bringing services closer to communities, through integrated models and strong local systems, remains the most effective pathway to accelerate measurable gains for children.
Future outlook
Building on the lessons learned and progress achieved in 2025 and across the 2021–2025 programme cycle, UNICEF Côte d’Ivoire will prioritize scaling innovations, strengthening systems and deepening partnerships to accelerate equitable results for the most vulnerable children in the next CPD cycle. High-level advocacy for child rights and cross-sectoral coordination will remain central to driving investment in social sectors, operationalizing policy instruments and institutionalizing joint sector reviews. This will include reinforcing national leadership and leveraging UNICEF’s convening power to align resources and accelerate reforms.  
Integration and digitalization will be key drivers of equity. UNICEF will expand innovative education approaches—including digital learning platforms, itinerant teaching and mobile training units—to reach children in remote areas, children at risk, children with special needs and those facing multiple, overlapping vulnerabilities. At the same time, teacher and social worker capacities will be strengthened to improve education outcomes through school-based child protection, with these approaches embedded in national policies to ensure long-term sustainability. In health and civil registration, efforts will prioritize modernizing systems through mobile and interoperable solutions. Institutionalizing digital training for social workers will improve service quality while reducing costs, and investments in affordable, resilient digital infrastructure will be critical to ensuring sustainability and narrowing disparities in access.
Starting in 2026, UNICEF will transition toward integrated Education–Protection and Health–WASH–Nutrition technical assistance at the decentralized level. This shift is expected to strengthen integrated service delivery, equity-focused planning while reducing costs and improving the targeting of interventions.
Integration of climate-resilient strategies across sectors will remain a key priority, with programming informed by lessons from decentralized delivery and by environmental and social safeguards. UNICEF will continue to scale up solar-powered systems across Health, WASH, Nutrition and Education, while reinforcing social marketing approaches in WASH and Nutrition. Sectoral interventions will also be more systematically embedded within national climate strategies to accelerate progress toward SDG 6.
Evidence and technology will drive nutritional progress. UNICEF will scale integrated services nationwide, improve women’s nutrition and leverage the Child Nutrition Fund to build institutional capacity and strengthen data systems. Expanding community nutrition centres, reinforcing SBC and social marketing approaches – including in urban areas – and rolling out the First Foods Africa initiative through public-private partnerships will support sustainable and equitable outcomes.
Social protection – a cross-cutting strategy for reducing child poverty and vulnerability – will be strengthened through the institutionalization of reforms, the expansion of child-responsive budgeting and operationalization of the Unique Social Registry. UNICEF will deepen shock-responsive mechanisms and promote human capital investments for adolescents and youth, particularly girls, through vocational certification systems and partnerships that bridge training-employment gaps.
Finally, UNICEF will pursue diversified financing and innovative partnerships, moving beyond transactional projects toward long-term collaborations with the private sector and institutional donors. By leveraging successful pilots, building technical capacity and aligning with global priorities, UNICEF aims to secure sustainable funding and position Côte d’Ivoire as a regional model for transformative results for children.
Across all areas, the imperative remains clear: to strengthen systems, secure diversified partner and domestic financing and institutionalize innovations to deliver equitable, resilient and scalable results. Achieving this will require deepening integrated approaches, accelerating digitalization, institutionalizing climate-resilient solutions and reinforcing partnerships to ensure sustainable financing and equitable outcomes for every child.

In 2025, the realisation of child rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) was profoundly disturbed by the convergence of escalating armed conflicts, and recurrent public health emergencies, with their consequences in deepening socio economic fragility. Together, these shocks significantly reversed development gains, undermined progress towards the outcomes of DRC-UNICEF Cooperation programme, and constrained national advancement towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), with increased risks of leaving the most vulnerable children further behind.

The year opened with a sharp escalation of violence, most notably the expansion of the March 23 Movement (M23) across North and South Kivu. By February 2025, major urban centres, including Goma and Bukavu, were under siege, while parallel administrative structures emerged in several territories. These developments precipitated severe humanitarian deterioration. Between January and September 2025, an estimated 2.1 million people were newly displaced, bringing the total number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) to 5.71 million, with 72 per cent located in North and South Kivu (OCHA, 2025). Insecurity also contributed to widespread human rights violations, including killings, maiming, abductions, and the recruitment and use of children, particularly during the peak of the crisis in the east.

Macroeconomic conditions weakened further during the reporting period. National growth slowed from 6.5 per cent in 2024 to 5.3 per cent in 2025, below projections (IMF, 2025). Conflict-related uncertainty intensified exchange-rate volatility and inflation, particularly in conflict-affected provinces, eroding household purchasing power and increasing child poverty. Fiscal pressures mounted following the Government’s submission of a supplementary budget mid-year due to the loss of fiscal control in territories under M23 influence. Compared with the initial budget, allocations to education declined by 14.89 per cent, and to health by 7.85 per cent. Declining budget execution rates (education from 88.86 per cent (2022) to 60.25 per cent (2024), and health from 47.62 per cent (2022) to 25.80 per cent (2024)) further constrained the ability of social sector ministries to deliver services at scale, slowing progress towards SDG targets related to education, health, and nutrition.

Food insecurity deteriorated substantially in 2025, extending beyond conflict-affected areas. An estimated 25.6 million people faced crisis or emergency levels of food insecurity, including 6.2 million in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu (IPC; OCHA, 2025). The combined effects of conflict, displacement, inflation, and market disruptions reduced dietary diversity and increased risks of wasting and stunting, undermining child survival and development outcomes.
Access to education was severely disrupted by insecurity. Between January and October 2025, conflict accounted for 99.2 per cent of school closures, destruction, or occupation, depriving nearly 1.4 million children of learning opportunities (Education Cluster DRC, 2025). These disruptions compounded already low learning outcomes and posed a major setback to progress towards SDG 4 on inclusive and equitable quality education.

Public health risks remained acute despite the official end of the 16th Ebola outbreak in Kasaï. Recurrent outbreaks of measles, cholera, and other epidemic-prone diseases persisted, exacerbated by population movements, overstretched health systems, and weak WASH infrastructure. Cholera trends were particularly alarming, with more than 51,000 cases and 1,545 deaths reported in 2025, nearly double the caseload of the previous year. Over seven million children under five remained at high risk of measles due to immunity gaps and persistently low routine immunization coverage (WHO, 2025).

Humanitarian needs remained among the highest globally, with 21.2 million people requiring assistance. Access constraints persisted in areas controlled by armed groups, limiting the reach of essential services and partner operations. Despite these challenges, UNICEF expanded humanitarian surveillance and preparedness to all 26 provinces, strengthening early action in high-risk areas. The UniRR mechanism remained one of the fastest humanitarian response tools in the region, reaching over 830,000 displaced people, including 540,000 children, within an average of five days after assessment.

The announcement of U.S. Government funding terminations, coupled with broader austerity measures adopted by key financial partners, further compounded this challenging environment – significantly impacting UNICEF’s programmes and operations.

Anticipated fiscal constraints and declining humanitarian financing are expected to further heighten child vulnerabilities in 2026, underscoring the importance of coordinated leadership and system-strengthening approaches. In response, UNICEF sustained cluster leadership, expanded partnerships with national NGOs, and prioritised continuity of essential services and equitable results for the most vulnerable children at scale.

In 2025, the first year of the 2025–2029 cooperation programme between the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and UNICEF, efforts focused on safeguarding essential services and laying the foundations for results at scale for children affected by conflict, displacement and socio-economic shocks across key sectors. Through integrated system-strengthening and humanitarian–development nexus approaches, UNICEF and its partners advanced equitable outcomes and reinforced the commitment to leave no child behind, as reflected in the key results for children (KRC) presented below.

KRC 1: IMMUNIZATION  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened national immunization systems by supporting the development of a new national strategy, operational guidelines and supply chain improvements. Through operational support to logistics hubs in Kisangani, Lubumbashi and Kinshasa, and the procurement of 102 cold chain units, UNICEF helped ensure vaccine availability for both routine services and campaigns. These investments contributed to stronger alignment with Gavi 6.0 priorities following a high-level mission by the Gavi CEO. 

From January to October, 4,085,919 infants aged 0–11 months were targeted for routine immunization, achieving high coverage rates for Penta1 (100 per cent), Penta3 (95 per cent) and IPV (94.6 per cent). Measles coverage reached 80 per cent, remaining below national targets and highlighting a critical gap requiring intensified efforts. UNICEF support enabled the identification and vaccination of 123,747 zero-dose children and 232,285 under-vaccinated children across four provinces, demonstrating impact at scale.

Seven polio campaigns, supported by strong social mobilisation and independent monitoring, were implemented, reaching over 27 million children under five and 1,742,073 children aged 5–14 years, achieving coverage above 100 per cent. Social mobilisation helped address hesitancy, and monitoring showed that only 0.5–2.9 per cent of children were missed. Independent monitoring and lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) found that 0.5–2.9 per cent of children were missed during campaigns, underscoring the need to reach every child to stop poliovirus transmission.
Yellow fever vaccination reached 17.6 million people (87 per cent), measles–rubella 16.2 million (96.7 per cent), and cholera 10.5 million (93 per cent). In response to the Mpox outbreak, 1,493,908 at-risk individuals were vaccinated in affected provinces. UNICEF also contributed to the vaccination of 10,480,868 people against cholera (93 per cent coverage). Ebola containment efforts vaccinated 47,577 contacts and health workers, helping to halt transmission. These achievements highlight UNICEF’s commitment to universal immunization and resilience against public health emergencies.

KRC 2: PREVENTION OF STUNTING  
In 2025, UNICEF’s technical and financial leadership drove measurable progress in preventing stunting and improving child nutrition in the DRC. UNICEF enabled supplementation of 21.7 million children aged 6–59 months with vitamin A, reaching 91.5 per cent of the target, a critical step in reducing micronutrient deficiencies. Exclusive breastfeeding reached 59.6 per cent nationwide, exceeding the SDG 2030 target of 50 per cent. In provinces implementing UNICEF’s integrated stunting-reduction package, breastfeeding rates surpassed 70 per cent, demonstrating the added value of multisectoral convergence.

Preventive interventions were scaled to 111 health zones, reaching 7.85 million children with essential nutrition services, micronutrient supplements and early childhood stimulation. Additionally, 2.5 million caregivers received counselling through community-based structures and facility-based services. UNICEF strengthened demand creation through infant and young child feeding (IYCF) support groups, grandmother networks, male engagement clubs and multimedia communication, including radio, social media and U-Report.

These interventions contributed to stronger household practices and paved the way for long-term behaviour change. However, significant bottlenecks persist: only 18.9 per cent of children under two meet minimum dietary diversity, reflecting structural constraints such as food insecurity and limited access to nutritious foods. UNICEF’s evidence-driven, systems-based approach positions the country office to deepen multisectoral convergence and accelerate progress towards national targets in 2026.

KRC 3 and 4: EQUITABLE AND SUSTAINABLE ACCESS TO EDUCATION AND IMPROVED LEARNING OUTCOMES  
According to the latest Demographic and Health Survey (2023), 86 per cent of children reach the end of primary education (83 per cent for girls and 89 per cent for boys), and 18 per cent of children aged 5–17 years are out of school. Given the lack of a national learning assessment system, there are no recent data on learning proficiency. Education outcomes are constrained by very limited public funding for education. In 2025, education represented only 15 per cent of the national budget in the Finance Law. Given insufficient public funding, teachers’ strikes remain a major impediment to education service delivery in the DRC, as a significant number of teachers are paid by parents, with no stability in their employment conditions.

To contribute to increased school enrolment, UNICEF built 119 temporary learning spaces and classrooms, hosting 21,658 students (10,972 girls). A total of 341,555 students (162,252 girls) received learning materials, contributing to increased demand for education.

In the area of quality, UNICEF began implementation of the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) approach in 2025, targeting 151,400 students in 310 schools. The implementation of TaRL is coupled with implementation and scalability research and aims to strengthen the national education system in key areas of formative learning assessments, differentiated pedagogy and active pedagogy.

Since July 2025, UNICEF has led the Local Education Group. In that role, UNICEF has supported public finance for children in education through the development of a medium-term expenditure framework and the implementation of the budget programme reform in education.
A highlight of the year was UNICEF support for the organisation of national end-of-year exams across North and South Kivu. UNICEF transported 415 packages of exam materials to the most difficult-to-access zones, enabling 720,678 students (50 per cent girls) to participate in these crucial assessments and reducing the risk of drop-out.

KRC 5 and 7: PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM VIOLENCE AND EXPLOITATION, INCLUDING IN HUMANITARIAN CONTEXTS AND BIRTH REGISTRATION  
In 2025, UNICEF accelerated efforts to strengthen child protection systems, prevent violence and exploitation, and expand universal birth registration. A total of 963,060 vulnerable children received direct assistance, reflecting UNICEF’s dual focus on system strengthening and humanitarian response.

Birth registration saw unprecedented progress, with 3,763,596 children registered (153 per cent of the annual target and 60 per cent higher than 2024). This achievement was driven by UNICEF’s support to integrate birth registration into DHIS2, expand maternity-based registration, digitise the civil registry, and supply 1,160 official registers. Strong collaboration with health and education services ensured access for the most vulnerable, including GBV survivors and children formerly associated with armed groups. Justice for children also improved: 75 per cent of 17,872 children in conflict with the law benefited from non-custodial alternatives, supporting a shift towards child-sensitive justice.

UNICEF and partners assisted 236,297 children affected by violence, abuse and exploitation, while nearly 900,000 children, adolescents and caregivers accessed mental health and psychosocial support. During escalated conflict in North and South Kivu, rapid deployment of more than 300 para-social and social workers ensured uninterrupted services. Support for survivors of sexual violence expanded, including cash assistance for 672 survivors. The scale-up of PRIMERO enhanced case management, and the Toyokana safe spaces enabled 126,000 adolescent girls to access protection, life skills and mentorship.

Community-based prevention also strengthened, with 257,113 caregivers, young people and leaders engaged in social norms change. GBV risk mitigation across sectors reached nearly one million women and children. These achievements underscore significant strengthening of national systems and multisectoral services, advancing children’s rights to identity and protection.

KRC 8: WASH AND ENDING OPEN DEFECATION  
In 2025, UNICEF provided strategic support to the Government of the DRC to advance climate-resilient sanitation and accelerate the national roadmap to end open defecation. A major milestone was the integration of climate resilience principles into the National Sanitation Policy (PONA), reinforcing sustainability at system level.

UNICEF strengthened national coordination mechanisms, facilitated joint supervision missions, and trained 23 provincial trainers in Tanganyika, enhancing decentralised capacity for open defecation-free (ODF) implementation.

Implementation of the ODF roadmap in Tanganyika and Sud-Kivu provinces enabled 431,697 people in 756 communities to achieve ODF status. Additionally, in emergency contexts, 88,838 people were reached with appropriate sanitation services.

Combined development and emergency actions enabled 457,083 people to gain access to improved sanitation services, reducing exposure to faecal contamination and contributing to healthier environments for children and communities. These results reflect UNICEF’s role in strengthening institutional frameworks, building local capacity, and delivering scalable, community-based sanitation solutions.

Results achieved across key result areas were reinforced by strong cross-cutting enablers. Social and behaviour change, gender mainstreaming, PSEA, communication, advocacy and partnerships played a critical role in amplifying impact, strengthening accountability, and ensuring that interventions reached those most at risk of being left behind. These enablers were integral to translating sectoral investments into sustainable and equitable outcomes for children.

CROSS-CUTTING:   
SBC
In 2025, SBC delivered transformative results through community engagement, mass and digital communication, emergency response, cross-sectoral support, and evidence generation. More than 55,000 community platforms were mobilised, 9.1 million U-Reporters engaged, and 43 million citizens reached with life-saving messages. SBC played a pivotal role in strengthening vaccination campaigns and advancing nutrition and gender strategies, launched the Adolescent Girls’ Agenda in the Congo to promote gender equality, and supported the Ebola response through robust RCCE planning and coordination. SBC empowered young people to fight misinformation and drive local action. Using BeSD surveys and human-centred design, SBC accelerated progress for child survival, development and protection.

Gender
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened gender mainstreaming across sectors and advanced internal implementation of the GGP mechanism (Gender, GBV risk mitigation and PSEA). Key achievements included gender analyses in humanitarian action, women’s and girls’ empowerment within SVA, and rapid assessments of cholera and EVD outbreaks. UNICEF trained 160 implementing partners and 240 frontline workers on gender equality and GBV risk mitigation, and supported the development of the national gender and vaccination strategy. The Girls’ and Adolescent Agenda was launched with a national roadmap co-developed with ministries (Gender, Social Affairs, Youth and Education) and youth organisations, reinforcing multisectoral commitment.

PSEA  
In 2025, despite a high-risk and volatile operational context, UNICEF DRC strengthened its leadership on PSEA, ensuring safe access to reporting mechanisms for over 1.5 million people, including 33 per cent women and 43 per cent children. More than 3.6 million individuals received essential PSEA information, of whom 34 per cent were women and 33 per cent were children. UNICEF trained over 31,000 implementing partner staff, improving compliance with core PSEA standards. As provider of last resort, UNICEF ensured immediate and continuous support for child survivors and supported the Ministry of Public Service to develop a new national PSEA strategy, strengthening State accountability.

Communication and Advocacy
In 2025, UNICEF DRC’s communication and advocacy efforts achieved exceptional visibility, reaching 17.2 million people digitally and generating 723,672 engagements across 813 publications. World Children’s Day featured a national peace song with UNICEF ambassadors, mobilising over 500,000 people in one week. A high-level Q&A session with the Prime Minister elevated national dialogue on child rights. The DRC gained significant global visibility through contributions to the State of the World’s Children report and powerful multimedia content from eastern DRC for the global “I Am” campaign, enhancing international awareness of children’s rights and humanitarian needs.

Partnership
Despite escalating conflict, global funding pressures and structural UN reforms, UNICEF DRC demonstrated resilience in 2025, increasing total funding to USD 326.3 million, up from USD 321.5 million in 2024. Rebuilding donor confidence remains essential amid projected global revenue declines. UNICEF strengthened resource mobilisation and management capacities nationwide, advanced partner diversification, and expanded government engagement. Notably, the DRC became the first country in the region to surpass the USD 10,000 individual giving milestone. These achievements reflect strong partner trust and improved systems to sustain results for children.

MANAGEMENT PRIORITY RESULTS:    
In 2025, the DRC Country Office strengthened governance, internal controls and risk management, directly contributing to more efficient and accountable programme delivery. Reinforced governance structures at national and subnational levels enabled clearer decision-making, faster escalation of operational risks, and better alignment of resources with programme priorities. As a result, the country office improved its ability to deliver humanitarian and development interventions in a volatile environment.

Operational systems were optimised to deliver measurable efficiency gains. Enhanced use of VISION, eTools, RAM, AMP and Service Gateway streamlined workflows and reduced processing delays, enabling programme teams to receive faster financial, supply and administrative support. Strengthened financial controls ensured timely liquidation of advances, accurate commitment management, and on-time monthly closures, facilitating uninterrupted implementation and compliance with IPSAS standards.

Risk-informed management guided operational decisions. Integrated risk analysis in SMT and PRC led to proactive mitigation of security, fiduciary and access constraints. Strengthened HACT assurance through spot checks, audits and partner capacity assessments reduced fiduciary risks and improved partner performance.

During the M23 crisis, activation of emergency procedures and the Business Continuity Plan enabled sustained operations in affected zones, ensuring continued delivery of life-saving supplies and services.

Financial and administrative functions contributed directly to programme results through improved cash forecasting, timely treasury operations, and expansion of financial service providers to support cash-based programming. The successful asset count and roll-out of EzOfficeInventory enhanced accountability and asset availability for programme use. Fleet renewal through UN leasing improved mobility for front-line teams, particularly in high-risk areas.

Green energy investments in solar installations in three offices reduced operating costs and enhanced continuity in low-electricity contexts. Overall, strengthened governance, streamlined systems and risk-responsive operations enabled UNICEF DRC to deliver results more efficiently, maintain compliance, and scale programmes for children despite operational and security challenges.

While these achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s capacity to deliver results in one of the world’s most complex operating environments, they were realised amid significant operational, financial and security constraints. Reflecting on these challenges and the lessons learned is essential to understanding how UNICEF managed adaptively and how future programming can be strengthened to sustain and scale impact.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
1. Challenges 
In 2025, humanitarian operations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo were confronted with unprecedented complexity. Armed conflict escalated dramatically in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri, leading to the fall of major towns, including Beni, Goma and Bukavu, and triggering massive waves of displacement. These dynamics created severe access constraints, particularly in areas under M23 control, where insecurity, bureaucratic impediments and damaged infrastructure limited UNICEF’s ability to deliver essential services, conduct monitoring and sustain partner presence. The convergence of conflict-forced displacement, recurrent epidemics (cholera, Ebola) and deepening socio-economic vulnerabilities placed extraordinary pressure on national and subnational systems.

Another major challenge emerged from internal operational disruptions. The evacuation of staff from the east exposed gaps in contingency planning, crisis communication, logistical preparedness and duty-of-care mechanisms. Rapid relocation of personnel created strain on receiving duty stations and momentarily affected programme continuity. These evacuations underscored the need for more robust business continuity planning and stronger remote-management capacities to ensure uninterrupted service delivery during escalations.
The publication of the internal audit report highlighted systemic weaknesses in partner oversight, supply chain management, documentation and risk mitigation. Although most findings were moderate, they required urgent attention given the scale and speed of emergency operations.

Resource mobilisation faced serious contextual challenges. The humanitarian deterioration in the east sharply increased funding needs, while global financial pressures, including the announcement of United States budget cuts and austerity across traditional donors, reduced predictability. Several global processes (FFI, UN80, Humanitarian Reset) demanded internal adaptation and reinforced scrutiny on accountability. Despite these pressures, UNICEF DRC operated in a tightening funding environment just as programmatic needs expanded rapidly.

2. Lessons Learned 
Across all areas of humanitarian action, internal operations and partnerships, 2025 yielded transformative lessons that are shaping the country office’s approach.
A first key insight was the critical value of preparedness and speed. The RRM/UniRR mechanism once again demonstrated that pre-positioned supplies, streamlined procedures and multisectoral rapid assessments significantly reduce negative impacts on children when deployed within days of a shock. The importance of anticipatory action became evident as the frequency of shocks increased.

Community-based approaches emerged as essential enablers of effective emergency response. CATI interventions for cholera and robust RCCE networks during Ebola responses in Kasaï proved indispensable for outbreak control, trust-building and early detection. These approaches also reinforced the importance of engaging local leaders and strengthening local knowledge systems.
Localisation continued to prove its strategic value. National NGOs facilitated access in areas where international actors could not operate safely, while maintaining operational continuity under volatile conditions. Their role in humanitarian delivery highlighted the need for long-term, capacity-strengthened partnerships.

At programme level, cash-based interventions, when integrated with nutrition and protection support, showed strong potential to mitigate household risks, support resilience and reduce negative coping mechanisms. Integrated responses demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency gains in rapidly evolving crises.

From an internal management perspective, the evacuations highlighted the central importance of strong business continuity planning. They underscored the need for better crisis communication systems, clearer decision-making chains, pre-identified fallback locations, and expanded psychosocial support for staff. The experience also showed the necessity of security training for all personnel.

The internal audit reinforced lessons on accountability and operational discipline, emphasising the importance of consistent documentation, standardised partner oversight, better supply chain governance, and more cohesive collaboration between operations and programme teams.
Finally, in resource mobilisation, UNICEF DRC learned the necessity of early donor engagement, diversified funding strategies and clear evidence of results. Despite major pressures, the country office achieved resilient performance, growing overall funding from USD 321.5 million to USD 326.3 million. This demonstrated that strong donor communication, transparency and coordinated proposal development across sections remain critical for maintaining trust. The 2025 results further showed the importance of investing in local private sector engagement and innovative financing mechanisms.

3. Future Outlook 
Based on insights from 2025 and in alignment with the new UNICEF Strategic Plan, UNICEF DRC sharpen its focus on upstream engagement and national systems strengthening. The Country Office aims to place children’s rights at the center of the political agenda and national priorities, and to position UNICEF as a key partner recognized for its programmatic and operational excellences. The partnership strategy will increasingly center on state institutions, reinforcing national leadership and long-term sustainability. UNICEF will work with national and provincial authorities to improve the policy and regulatory environment, strengthen public financial management for social sectors, enhance planning and budgeting processes, and reinforce monitoring, data and accountability systems. This streamlining reflects a deliberate effort to concentrate resources, capacities and partnerships on a strategic set of interventions and seven priority provinces. By reducing fragmentation, the programme aims to strengthen coherence, enhance operational efficiency and accelerate progress toward outcomes for children. 

Humanitarian programming will concentrate on Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Ituri and Tanganyika, where UNICEF maintains operational presence. In these provinces, UNICEF will sustain rapid intersectoral response capacity while strengthening early warning, epidemic preparedness and anticipatory systems in collaboration with provincial authorities. Integrated health, nutrition, WASH, education and protection interventions will prioritise high-risk and hard-to-reach areas to ensure continuity of essential services for displaced and conflict-affected populations.

In Kasaï Central, Haut-Katanga and Kinshasa, UNICEF will prioritise development-focused programming centred on systems strengthening and institutional sustainability, aligned with Strategic Plan 2026–2029 Impact 1 (health and nutrition), Impact 2 (learning and skills), and Impact 4 (protection from violence).

In both contexts, peace building and social cohesion will be promoted within communities, along with social behavioral changes, in collaboration with local authorities, front line community workers and children including adolescent girls.  

On internal management, UNICEF will accelerate implementation of audit recommendations, strengthen partner due-diligence processes, reinforce supply chain, financial oversight, build a culture of accountability and strengthen oversight mechanisms including the CMT and other statutory bodies. The Business Continuity Plan will be updated and operationalised across all duty stations, including the implementation of clear remote-management protocols and enhanced security preparedness training to ensure continuity of essential programme functions during security disruptions.  The CO will continue to prioritize staff well-being and psychosocial support critical in a context of protracted crisis and challenging operating environment.

In resource mobilisation, the country office will focus on regaining partner confidence following the audit, deepening relationships with core donors, and expanding into non-traditional funding streams. Given the projected 38 per cent decline in global UNICEF revenue between 2026 and 2029, securing predictable and diversified resources is a strategic imperative. UNICEF DRC will invest in local private-sector partnerships, build on recent collaborations with Meta, Orange, Equity BCDC and Finca, pursue innovative and green financing mechanisms, and expand individual giving, leveraging the 2025 breakthrough. Close coordination between Partnerships, Communications and Social Policy will guide targeted advocacy, evidence generation and donor visibility.

At programme level, communication insights—such as the importance of localised, interactive content, despite reaching 17.2 million people—will inform efforts to enhance message uptake and community engagement.

Ultimately, UNICEF DRC will continue aligning its strategies with the SDGs and the principle of “leave no child behind.” The most vulnerable children affected by conflict, epidemics, displacement and deepening poverty will remain at the heart of all interventions as the office strengthens its capacity to respond with agility, accountability and impact.

According to the World Bank (WB), Equatorial Guinea’s national economy grew by an estimated 0.9% in 2024 (compared to -5.1% in 2023); yet, this growth was insufficient to boost employment and income or improve living standards, due to soaring food prices combined with a heavy reliance on imported food products. The economy was projected to enter another recession in 2025, with a forecasted negative growth of -3.1%, driven by decreasing hydrocarbon production and oil price fall. Growth could reach 0.6% in 2026, before GDP contracts again in 2027. Monetary poverty is  expected to decline from 57.0% to 55.8% between 2024 and 2027 due to  projected growth in labor-intensive sectors such as agriculture and services.   
  
The results of 2024 II National Household Survey indicate that half of the population lives below the national monetary poverty line, despite the country being an Upper-Middle Income Country, with  a GDP per capita of US $9,400 (PPA 2021). 11.3% of the population (181,000  people) live in extreme monetary poverty, unable to access a basic food  basket to ensure a minimum caloric intake. Around two-thirds of the  population (60%) have a high likelihood (50%) of living below the poverty  line in the next two years. 
  
In this ‘new’ economic context, inequalities are high. The Gini coefficient is 38.5 (moderately high). The richest decile of the population accounts for 29% of national consumption with only 2.6% among the  poorest. Geographical inequalities are striking; daily per-capita consumption  in Malabo is 40% higher than in the rest of the country but only 30% of the  population in Malabo lives in monetary poverty versus an average between  54-60% outside of Malabo. 511,000 out of 809,000 poor and vulnerable people  live in urban areas, but remote, rural settings have less access to basic  services such as safe water (31%), basic sanitation (37%), and electricity  (18%).   
  
Acting with foresight to mitigate the effects of these economic shocks, the Government of Equatorial Guinea has an ambitious economic diversification plan, addressing both social and economic development, as well as strategies to fight against corruption, improve financial performance and ensure territorial cohesion. The impacts of these plans and strategies will contribute to an enabling environment for the fulfillment of child rights but will require time to generate results; it is therefore critical to maintain advocacy and investment to ensure resilient social services that will mitigate an increase in poverty burdens on children and  adolescents, and contribute to human capital development.  
  
Young children are most affected by poverty as their minds and bodies are still developing, the effects are lifelong. In Equatorial Guinea, 63% live in poor households, 41% experience severe food insecurity, 30% lack access to basic sanitation and safe water, and 16% live in houses without electricity. 16% of children who are 0-6 years old are stunted. In this context, the  child-related SDGs by 2030 remain out of reach. Gains made to date may be eroded if the socio-economic situation continues to deteriorate. While investment in health and education has not reduced over the years (around 2 percent of the GDP) these numbers are below international benchmarks; should the economic situation continue to deteriorate with no increases in social sector financing, it is reasonable to expect that deprivations will increase alongside inequities.  
  
The average schooling is 11.9 years, but secondary-school dropout remains high mainly due to limited public education services, socio-economic barriers and early pregnancies. Private education is largely inaccessible for the poorest and most vulnerable families. Only one in three students completes secondary school before adulthood (25% in the poorest decile versus 45% in the  richest). There are similar disparities between Malabo (50% completion) and  other rural and urban settings (23%). Curriculum updates needed to support  national economic diversification remain pending in both systems and are critical to avoid human capital gaps, underemployment and limited  opportunities for adolescents and young people in the short and medium  term.  
  
Regarding access to health services, only 52% of people in the poorest decile seek services when they are ill, compared to 80% in the wealthiest. This gap is linked to high out-of-pocket payments, representing 7% of household consumption and 77% of total health spending (2021). Access to essential supplies, such as vaccines or anti-retroviral treatment, also remains challenging and misaligns with country’s income level and its human development performance, including health indicators. 
  
About 20% of adolescents and youth (15-29 years) is neither enrolled in school nor employed (30% for adolescent girls and young women, due to early unions, marriages, or pregnancies, and unpaid domestic work), while the economy is not growing and generating the jobs needed to  ensure broader access to the labor market. Unemployment is at 13.1%, with  steep disparities between the richest (8.7%) and the poorest deciles (15.2%).  One in five jobs is formal, and three-fourths of these are in the public sector, where salaries are 20-30% higher with better access to social  security. The private sector remains small, mostly informal and faces  barriers such as limited access to funding, complexities of the tax system,  and high transactional costs as main barriers. Consequently, the Human  Capital Index for Equatorial Guinea resembles that of low-income countries,  meaning that a child born today in Equatorial Guinea is expected to reach  only 50% of their productive potential as an adult.
  
In a global context of declining oil incomes, the WB’s policy recommendations to reduce poverty are investing progressively in human capital (targeting children) and inter-generational social mobility, fostering the growth of the private sector and job creation, and reinforcing  resilience against climatic and socio-economic shocks through  shock-responsive, adaptive social protection. Without decisive action in the  next five years, the WB foresees a decrease of 3.9% in GDP per capita between 2026 and 2030 and an increase in poverty rates to 60% (compared to 51% in  2024). A concrete recommendation to the government is to establish  child-targeted cash transfer to reverse current and foresee poverty trends, by investing between 1-2% of the GDP in this scheme, while improving access and quality of health, education, and WASH systems.
