Défis de la vaccination


En 2025, le Programme Élargi de Vaccination a continué de faire face à des contraintes structurelles freinant les progrès vers une couverture équitable. Malgré les efforts d’amélioration de la chaîne d’approvisionnement et de l’offre de services, les niveaux de vaccination stagnent et des disparités persistent entre zones urbaines et rurales, alimentées par des obstacles d’accessibilité, des coûts indirects et une demande vaccinale limitée, affectée par la désinformation et des capacités de communication insuffisantes.



En réponse, l’UNICEF a soutenu le renforcement du système national d’immunisation en améliorant l’identification des enfants non vaccinés, la planification locale et la digitalisation progressive des outils de suivi et de gestion des stocks. L’appui à la communication des risques, combiné à l’amélioration de l’accueil dans les structures de santé, a contribué à renforcer la confiance communautaire. Ensemble, ces interventions ont consolidé les bases d’un redressement progressif du programme, bien que des efforts soutenus demeurent nécessaires pour étendre la couverture dans toutes les régions.



Défis de mobilisation des ressources


Au cours des trois premières années du Programme de coopération, l’UNICEF Gabon a mobilisé 2,49 millions USD de ressources régulières, soit 57 pour cent de la cible. Les autres ressources mobilisées (2,08 millions USD) ne représentent toutefois que 26 pour cent de l’objectif initial, limitant la capacité du Bureau à couvrir pleinement les priorités programmatiques. En complément, le Bureau a bénéficié de 838,338 USD d’appuis additionnels de l’UNICEF en ressources régulières (GS, GP) et de 3,91 millions USD de financements d’urgence — soit 47 pour cent des ressources prévues — permettant de renforcer les capacités nationales en vaccination, gestion des données, gestion des déchets biomédicaux et communication des risques. Au total, 5,16 millions USD ont été mobilisés depuis le début du CPD, dont 76 pour cent provenant de financements humanitaires.




Cette structure de financement confirme une dépendance accrue aux ressources d’urgence, accentuée par le statut du Gabon comme pays à revenu intermédiaire de la tranche supérieure, qui limite l’accès aux financements concessionnels. La contraction des financements de développement réduit l’espace budgétaire pour les réformes systémiques durables et complique la transition vers un modèle davantage axé sur l’assistance technique et le renforcement des systèmes.




Les prochaines années exigeront une diversification accrue des partenariats, un dialogue stratégique renforcé avec les autorités nationales et l’exploration de mécanismes innovants de financement, y compris des partenariats publicprivé, afin de sécuriser des ressources pérennes alignées sur les priorités nationales et les besoins des enfants les plus vulnérables.




Leçons tirées de la participation des jeunes


En 2025, la redynamisation d’UReport a démontré l’importance de mécanismes de gouvernance participative centrés sur les priorités exprimées par les jeunes. La mise en place d’une task force conjointe entre la Direction Générale de la Jeunesse et les UReporters a renforcé l’appropriation nationale du dispositif et stimulé une participation accrue, confirmant que la cogestion améliore l’efficacité des systèmes de mobilisation. L’extension régionale de la plateforme a également montré que la proximité constitue un levier déterminant pour atteindre les jeunes des zones éloignées.




L’implication des UReporters dans les consultations du PNCD a mis en évidence la valeur de la plateforme comme outil robuste de participation civique, facilitant l’intégration des priorités jeunesse dans les processus nationaux de planification. La création du groupe UReporter filles a souligné la nécessité d’approches sensibles au genre pour répondre aux besoins spécifiques des adolescentes, souvent sousreprésentées dans les espaces institutionnels.



L’engagement des jeunes dans les Activités Vaccinales Intensifiées a confirmé leur rôle comme relais communautaires crédibles, notamment dans la prévention du VIH, justifiant une intégration plus systématique de leur participation dans les stratégies sectorielles de santé publique.



La participation des jeunes aux processus de négociation climatique a renforcé leurs compétences en plaidoyer et démontré l’efficacité des approches d’apprentissage expérientiel. Les mécanismes de restitution mis en place ont montré l’importance d’intégrer leurs contributions dans les politiques publiques et d’assurer un retour d’information systématique.




Ces enseignements plaident pour le renforcement durable des mécanismes de participation, incluant la structuration d’espaces de consultation, l’amélioration de l’analyse des contributions et la mise en place de dispositifs de redevabilité jeunesse afin de garantir une participation plus inclusive, équitable et institutionnalisée.




Appui opérationnel au programme


En 2025, les opérations ont joué un rôle déterminant dans l’obtention des résultats programmatiques, en assurant un appui logistique, financier et administratif essentiel. Les services et équipements fournis ont renforcé la qualité, la continuité et la mise à l’échelle des interventions, notamment dans la digitalisation, la production de contenus éducatifs et l’opérationnalisation des plateformes d’engagement des jeunes. Cet appui a permis de réduire les interruptions, d’améliorer l’efficacité opérationnelle et d’accroître la capacité du Bureau à délivrer des résultats pour les enfants.




Malgré un contexte marqué par des risques fiduciaires et des faiblesses de gouvernance, la mise en œuvre de mesures correctives ciblées a stabilisé les processus, renforcé les contrôles internes et amélioré la conformité. Ces efforts ont généré un meilleur rapport qualitéprix grâce à des évitements de coûts, une gestion plus rigoureuse des achats et un suivi accru des actifs, consolidant une culture organisationnelle axée sur la transparence, la responsabilité et la performance.




Les enseignements de l’année soulignent l’importance d’un pilotage opérationnel proactif reposant sur une planification anticipée, un suivi systématique des audits et une collaboration renforcée entre opérations et programme. Le renforcement des capacités du personnel — via des formations ciblées et une clarification des rôles — a été central pour améliorer la performance interne, restaurer la confiance des équipes et consolider les systèmes du Bureau.



Ces progrès confirment le rôle stratégique des opérations dans l’assurance qualité, la gestion des risques et l’optimisation des ressources, positionnant le Bureau pour une mise en œuvre en 2026 plus agile, plus efficace et pleinement conforme aux standards organisationnels.

In 2025, The Gambia continued to advance the child rights agenda despite a challenging global and regional operating context. While the national economy maintained a steady recovery with a projected GDP growth of 5.9% in 2025, the reduction in Official Development Assistance (ODA) by traditional donor partners necessitated a realignment of child-focused programming. Given that donor support historically financed approximately 27% of the national budget, the government focused on increasing domestic revenue to mitigate risks to social spending. This provided a framework for the UNICEF 2024–2028 Country Programme Document (CPD) to address structural vulnerabilities in services for children.  
 
Despite the decline in inflation to 7% by late 2025, the precarious nature of external funding continued to influence the scale and reach of interventions designed for the 54% of the population under the age of 19. Furthermore, the 2025 Labour Force Survey and SDG Monitoring Survey provided updated data sets that allowed for more evidence-based resource allocation, though the gap left by international financing remains a significant challenge for long-term sustainability. 
 
Child protection remained a central focus of the national legal and social discourse in 2025, following the 2024 legislative rejection of a bill to repeal the ban on Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). This legal challenge occurred against a backdrop of reported infant deaths attributed to the practice, highlighting the ongoing tension between child protection and entrenched harmful social norms. The ongoing FGM proceedings are a pivotal moment for the legal framework, as the ruling will clarify how constitutional rights—especially dignity, bodily integrity, and child rights—are upheld in relation to customary practices.
 
The Gambian Government’s move to address the recommendations from the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC), issued in early 2025; which called for a coordinated action plan to advance child rights, through combatting high rates of violence against children addressing the situation of children deprived of a family environment and low birth registration, and the establishment of a Child Rights Monitoring Unit, represented a positive step toward institutionalising the country’s international obligations within the domestic framework. This unit is tasked with bridging the gap between high-level policy commitments and the localised enforcement of the Children's Act. Moreover, the dissemination of simplified versions of the CRC recommendations to the National Assembly as well as Children’s National Assembly have increased public awareness, fostering a more informed national dialogue on the accountability of state institutions in upholding the rights of children across all seven administrative regions.
 
Institutional care settings, specifically the Majalis (Quranic memorisation institutions), emerged as a critical point of concern due to recurring health, safety and protection failures. In May 2025, the Ministry of Health confirmed a scabies outbreak at one of such residential institutions, which affected over 50 children and exposed the consequences of overcrowding and insufficient sanitation. This health crisis preceded a fire incident in which two children lost their lives while confined and chained in a locked classroom, intensifying calls for a systemic overhaul of unregulated Quranic institutions. These events prompted the government and UNICEF to reinforce the advocacy for national minimum standards of care and the promotion of family-based alternatives to institutionalisation. 
 
The persistence of child labour, street begging, and corporal punishment further indicates that the protective environment for children in non-formal education remains inconsistent with national child protection laws. The government has initiated a mapping exercise of Majalis to better understand the scale of the challenge, yet the integration of these institutions into the formal social protection system remains slow. The deaths of children in such institutions necessitate a more rigorous and standardised protection and inspection framework, though implementation is likely to be hindered by inadequate regulations, human resources and cultural sensitivities surrounding religious education. Fixing these systemic issues, however, requires more than funding. It requires sustained engagement with community leaders to ensure that the rights to safety, health, and dignity are respected within all educational environments - religious or non-religious.
 
The Gambia’s public health sector has also adapted to emerging pressures over the past year. Following the 2024 global declaration of Mpox as a public health emergency, the country identified its first domestic case in July 2025, triggering a multi-sectoral response focused on surveillance and community engagement. The existing emergency preparedness mechanisms, including a strong Expanded Programme on Immunization, experience gained from the COVID-19 and polio outbreak, and multi-stakeholders coordination contributed to this successful response. With a youthful population, children and adolescents represent great potential for development and civic engagement in The Gambia. Platforms such as the Children’s National Assembly of The Gambia and opportunities like the sub-national and national adolescent girls’ consultations have facilitated direct communication between adolescents and policymakers, focusing on improved access to basic social services, climate resilience and civic participation. 
 
The increased abuse of addictive substances among adolescents and the risks associated with irregular migration as well as the increasing impacts of climate change remain additional hurdles for children and young people of The Gambia. However, the proactive steps taken in 2025, including the National Adolescent Girls’ Summit, climate education and children and young people-led innovation sprint suggest a growing emphasis on empowering the young people   to advocate for their own interests. The upcoming election cycle will likely serve as a litmus test for the country's ability to maintain social stability while addressing the diverse needs of its youngest citizens.

2025 was the second year of the implementation of UNICEF Gambia’s five-year country programme (2024-2028), which outlines five priority areas in line with the NDP, UNSDCF, UNICEF’s Strategic Plan, and UNICEF’s regional Key Results for Children.  
In 2025, UNICEF contributed to these areas as follows: 
 
Priority 1: Every child survives and thrives (KRC1, KRC2, KRC8): 
 
In 2025, health, nutrition and WASH sectors focused on addressing the systemic bottlenecks in system strengthening, service delivery and community engagement that were identified as primary constraints during the 2024 baseline year. A significant trigger for action in 2025 was the evidence of persistent regional coverage gaps and cold chain vulnerabilities reported in the previous cycle. In response, a Joint Appraisal, was led by Ministry of Health (MOH) with strong partner participation This was not just a monitoring exercise but a strategic diagnostic that identified eight core systemic issues and generated 53 time-bound actions. Whilst the 2024 interventions, were focussed on urgent local needs, the 2025 approach focused on national stewardship through the technical and steering committees, ensuring that health outcomes were linked to broader governance capacity.
 
UNICEF supported the preparedness and response to the Mpox outbreak both technically and financially for awareness activities within border communities.  As part of the Risk Communication and Community Engagement, through UNICEF support 80 community leaders from six border regions were oriented on Mpox transmission, symptoms, and prevention.  To expand national outreach and counter misinformation, UNICEF supported the engagement of three high profile social media influencers, whose coordinated messaging across social media reached approximately 255,000 women and 245,000 men with validated Mpox prevention and reporting information.  
 
UNICEF also supported the Measles-Rubella vaccination campaign, achieving 91.45% coverage with 352,557 children immunized representing an improvement compared to the 88.4% coverage recorded during the 2023 campaign. Additionally, UNICEF supported Maternal and Neonatal Death Reviews in six hospitals, totalling 300 participants. These reviews assessed adherence to national standards of maternal and newborn care, identified preventable gaps and documented good practices to improve maternal and child health outcomes.
 
One of the most tangible responses to the logistical bottlenecks reported in 2024 was the procurement and handover of 20 tricycles to delivery partners. This intervention targeted the ‘last-mile’ challenge, ensuring that vaccines and essential commodities reached underserved, hard-to-reach communities. To complement this logistical shift, the program focused on clinical quality through the Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) approach. Building on the 2023–2024 pilot at the EFSTH, 2025 saw the successful scale-up of ETAT to three major regional hospitals: Kanifing, Farafenni, and Bansang. This structural change effectively separated paediatric from adult emergency care, reduced chronic overcrowding, and empowered nursing staff with the autonomy to manage critical interventions such as oxygen therapy and fluid plans. These clinical improvements resulted in documented reductions in preventable paediatric mortality within these facilities.In the nutrition sector, the 2024 baseline indicated a high dependency on donor-procured therapeutic foods and a lack of long-term policy vision. In 2025, UNICEF and the National Nutrition Agency continued to advocate for allocation from the national budget to support the provision of Ready to Use Therapeutic food (RUTF), following successful outcomes from last year’s advocacy which resulted in the creation of a dedicated budget line in Office of the Vice President budget. UNICEF also supported the comprehensive update of the National Nutrition Policy (2026–2036) and revision of the Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition protocols to include the latest global evidence on managing at-risk infants under six months. 
To address the detection bottleneck, the ‘Family-led Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC)’ initiative was expanded. By training 1,085 women across 162 communities to monitor their own children using MUAC tapes, the program successfully shifted the burden of early diagnosis from overburdened health workers to caregivers. This grassroots empowerment led to an 81.4% cure rate for the 3,584 children treated for Severe Acute Malnutrition in 2025. UNICEF also supported the Paediatric Association of The Gambia in hosting its 3rd annual conference focused on child nutrition. The event addressed a wide range of health and nutrition issues affecting children and provided a platform for health practitioners to share service delivery challenges, exchange knowledge, and discuss best practices. 
The WASH sector similarly moved toward evidence-based sustainability. Following the 2024 identification of climate vulnerabilities, UNICEF applied the WASH Bottleneck Analysis Tool (WASHBAT) and launched the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). These studies provided the rigorous climate rationale needed to influence public policy. Among others, they supported the review of the national water policy, and WASH sector contribution to the third Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3).   UNICEF also supported the construction of climate-resilient water systems for 25,000 people (12,750 female and 12,250 male) in flood-prone riverine communities in Central and Upper River Regions. The country’s ambition to become open defecation free (ODF) remained a priority despite limited fundings. In addition to the 33 communities certified ODF in 2025, a major achievement was the mobilisation of an $8.5 million commitment by MOH from the World Bank for sanitation services, a direct result of the political will generated during the 2025 national high-level consultation to end open defecation. By integrating sanitation indicators into the national Education Management Information System (EMIS) and Health Management Information System (DHIS2), the program transitioned from ad-hoc donor tracking to a sustainable, government-owned monitoring model, ensuring that the rights of Gambian children to safe water are embedded in a more resilient national system.
 
Priority 2: Every child learns and develops (KRC3, KRC4): 
 
In 2025, the education sector transitioned from the enrolment focused strategies of 2024 to a deeper focus on system wide inclusion and learning quality. One of the primary bottlenecks identified during the previous year was the lack of inclusion of children in traditional Majalis  in to formal education ensuring rights and quality care. In 2025, a critical response was the formation of a multisectoral taskforce co-chaired by the Ministers of Education and Gender. This taskforce developed a comprehensive roadmap for the regulation of these institutions, directly addressing the protection and educational needs of over 46,000 children who were previously invisible to the state. This initiative moved the discourse from simple advocacy toward a framework of deinstitutionalisation and family reintegration, ensuring these children are linked to national standards for health and safety.
 
To address the ‘learning crisis’ identified in 2024, where enrolment did not consistently translate to literacy and numeracy, UNICEF prioritised Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN). By training 450 teachers and education managers (190 male, 260 female) (in diagnostic pedagogies and data-driven instruction, the program stabilized the quality of classroom delivery. This was supported by the digital leap of the EMIS/School EMIS. By transitioning from fragmented paper-based tracking to a digital student-level data system, the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education gained the capacity for real-time monitoring of attendance and learning progress. This infrastructure allows for more precise interventions to prevent dropout and address learning gaps before they become irreversible.
 
The 2025 period also saw the successful implementation of the Zero Out-of-School Children initiative, which cumulatively has brought 74,898 children (38,647 girls and 36, 251 boys) into quality learning pathways. This was paired with a significant focus on disability inclusion, an area that remained under-resourced in the 2024 reporting cycle. UNICEF provided 300 children with disabilities (155 boys, 145 girls), with specialized assistive learning devices and oversaw the construction of 108 inclusive, disability-friendly toilet cubicles in 38 schools. These physical and pedagogical improvements significantly improved school attendance and dignity for adolescent girls and children with mobility challenges. Girls continue to outnumber boys in enrolment, and demonstrate higher academic performance, especially in. learning outcomes in core competencies.
 
To ensure the championing of voices reached the last mile, UNICEF deployed community caravans and local champions. In regions where schooling was previously viewed as optional for girls, these caravans reached over 39,000 parents. By facilitating reflective community dialogues, UNICEF helped empower families to support their children’s right to be heard.
 
Finally, to ensure these educational gains are sustainable, they were embedded in the revised Life Skills Manual, integrating key topics such as child rights, gender, and climate change, providing tools for skilling and empowering adolescents. 
 
Priority 3: Every child is protected from violence, exploitation and harmful practices, and has a legal identity (KRC5, KRC6, KRC7): 
2025 marked a shift in child protection by building on the systems strengthening model and strengthening coordination across multiple stakeholders including CSOs and government. The primary bottleneck identified in 2024 was the lack of legal identity for many children in rural regions and the persistent threat of harmful traditional practices. In response, 2025 saw intensive advocacy for the Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Bill. UNICEF convened 13 parliamentarians to identify registration bottlenecks, resulting in a unanimous pledge to support budgetary reforms for digital infrastructure. 
At the grassroots level, the deployment of Birth Registration Ambassadors (Ask Bajen) in the Upper and Central River Regions reached 6,000 individuals and led to 3,535 referrals. By training 160 birth registration officers to operate within health facilities, the program moved the country toward a digital, interoperable system where every child is legally recognised from birth.
 
A significant trigger in 2025 was the constitutional and parliamentary challenge to the legal ban on Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). Building on the capacity development efforts of 2024, UNICEF coordinated a multifaceted defence strategy. This involved amplifying the voices of survivors and healthcare professionals through mass media, reaching an estimated 122,000 people. When two FGM-related infant deaths occurred, UNICEF led the UN’s joint advocacy efforts, which prompted positive signals from the state, including police public statements and health professionals reporting cases for the first time. This defensive action was underpinned by the training of 14 female and 16 male journalists from 30 different national medias on sensitive child rights reporting.
 
UNICEF has also provided the Government with vital technical assistance for its defence and empowered CSOs to coordinate a robust response to the FGM case pending decision at the Supreme Court. In addition to this, UNICEF carried out training of 30 journalists who were trained on child rights and the ongoing case for adequate media coverage. Another key step was engaging over 120 religious and traditional leaders and 360 men and boys to promote positive masculinity and facilitating dialogues with nearly 8,000 community members and reaching more than 122,000 people through mass media to sustain grassroots support for the ban.
 
To challenge harmful social norms, UNICEF supported the development of a FGM SBC strategy currently under finalisation. In addition to a comprehensive Gender Programmatic Review, UNICEF also supported the promotion of gender transformative approaches, and positive masculinity to address harmful practices and violence against children. 
 
To strengthen the nation’s legislative backbone, a comprehensive legal gap analysis of the Children’s Act 2005 was completed. This analysis aligns the Act with the CRC and the African Charter, specifically targeting the prohibition of child marriage and addressing emerging threats like online grooming and digital exploitation. To ensure enforcement, UNICEF enabled the National Human Rights Commission to operationalize a dedicated Child Rights Monitoring mechanism. 
 
Finally, the sustainability of the protection system was secured through investments in professional education. 2025 saw the launch of Gambia’s first Child Rights Centre at the University of The Gambia and the nation’s first Bachelor of Science in Social Work. By embedding protection protocols into the core academic curricula for public servants, lawyers, and social workers, UNICEF has guaranteed that the next generation of professionals is equipped to handle complex cases with a rights-based approach. 
 
Priority 4: Every child lives free from poverty: 
 
In 2025, UNICEF The Gambia achieved results in its fight against child poverty by leveraging its 60th anniversary year to support the National Social Protection system strengthening. This landmark year celebrated six decades of partnership, evolving from basic health delivery to a sophisticated systems-strengthening approach that addresses the root causes of economic vulnerability for the Gambia’s young people.
 
The most significant milestone of 2025 was the transition of the National Social Protection Secretariat into a formal Government Agency. This structural evolution, supported by UNICEF’s technical and legislative assistance, moved the country away from ad-hoc welfare toward a model of legal entitlement. To back this transition, UNICEF supported the development of the new National Social Protection Policy (2026–2035). This ten-year roadmap institutionalises the government's obligation to provide a social safety net, ensuring the right to an adequate standard of living is protected by law. This was further reinforced by the full implementation of the Grievance Redress Mechanism, providing vulnerable families with a formal channel to claim their rights and hold the state accountable.
 
Furthermore, to ensure that limited resources reach the most deprived children, UNICEF supported the completion of National coverage of The Gambia Social Registry. By transitioning from paper-based tracking to a digital, interoperable data system, the government can now identify and reach marginalised households. UNICEF also integrated nutrition metrics into the DHIS2. This data-driven approach allows for the identification of ‘zero-dose’ children in underserved regions, linking poverty reduction directly to health and immunization outcomes and strengthening evidence generation nationally.
 
In 2025, UNICEF successfully elevated child poverty to a matter of national budgetary priority. The high-level advocacy at the National Assembly contributed to a significant budgetary increase for social sectors, including Health and Basic and Secondary Education. Additionally, the advocacy contributed to increased government funding complementing GAVI for the availability of vaccine from 2025 GMD 40million to 2026 GMD 50million. UNICEF strengthened the Integrated Financial Management Information System to track social sector spending for reporting and advocacy. This provided lawmakers with the evidence needed for the ongoing advocacy for allocation for the provision of RUTF from the national budget.
 
Additionally, UNICEF’s engagement with the Health and Public Finance Select Committee achieved a unanimous pledge to support budgetary allocation for social sectors focusing on critical areas, including social protection, immunization, school bus services, and welfare for children through the Family Strengthening Programme. 
 
Beyond high-level policy, UNICEF empowered communities enabling them to break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. Cash transfers were combined with complementary services like training on financial management and climate-resilient livelihoods. This ensures that even during environmental shocks, the most vulnerable households can maintain nutritional and economic standards. Furthermore, UNICEF spearheaded the establishment of a child rights coordination mechanism in CRR North and a community radio as well as enhancement of the Kuntaur Area Council as a child friendly council to strengthen child rights sub nationally. 
 
Priority 5: Cross-cutting - Championing Children’s and Adolescent’s Voices  
 
In 2025, UNICEF Gambia turned the principle of children’s participation into a cornerstone of national governance. UNICEF moved beyond traditional advocacy, to facilitating high-level dialogue and engagement with policy and lawmakers to influence decision-making particularly on matters affecting them, creating permanent platforms where young people could directly influence the laws and policies that govern their lives. 
 
A landmark achievement in 2025 was following the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child Concluding Observations in February, UNICEF spearheaded the simplification of these complex legal documents for children and the National Assembly. By translating technical terms into actionable roadmaps, UNICEF empowered local administrators, community leaders, and children themselves to understand and advocate for their rights. These simplified frameworks ensured that concerns regarding child poverty, FGM, and education were no longer confined to international forums but informed national planning and regional budgeting cycles across all seven administrative regions.
 
This helped UNICEF facilitate historic direct engagements between children, adolescents and the highest levels of Government. A centrepiece of this effort was the ‘Mansa Kunda’ intergenerational dialogue in August 2025. During this event,105 young members of the Children’s National Assembly of The Gambia (CNAG), including 69 girls and 36 boys  were equipped with the information and confidence to engage directly with nine state ministers.  The CNAG members also had a constructive dialogue with the visiting Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children, elevating Gambian children’s and adolescents’ priorities to the global level. These initiatives advanced children’s right to participation by enabling direct dialogue with decision-makers and reinforcing duty-bearers’ responsibility to meaningfully consider children’s views.
 
Adolescent girls, often the most marginalised in policy discussions, became influential voices in 2025. UNICEF supported sub-national consultations with 131 adolescent girls and 28 boys across Upper, Central and West Coast Regions. These sessions generated the evidence that informed The Gambia’s roadmap for the Regional Adolescent Girls Summit in Dakar. This momentum culminated in the National Adolescent Girls Summit in December, where adolescent girls handed a National Call to Action to the First Lady and the Minister of Gender, Children and Social Welfare (MOGCSW). 
 
Furthermore, UNICEF supported Ministry of Information and MOGCSW to launch an animated character protagonist called ‘Sona’, designed to empower children—particularly girls—to express their views and strengthen their understanding of, and ability to advocate for, their rights and promote the responsibilities of the duty bearers.
 
Priority 5: Cross-cutting - Strengthening Programme Effectiveness  
 
Building on the 2024 achievements, programme effectiveness in 2025 was enhanced through coordination and the successful capitalisation of UNICEF’s 60th year of partnership with the government of The Gambia. Under the theme ‘60 Years of Shared Commitment,’ the Country Office moved beyond traditional support by launching a high-level Public-Private Partnership Dialogue in collaboration with the Government of Japan. This initiative integrated private sector by engaging corporate leaders to invest in digital literacy and protection services for and with children and adolescents. 
 
Programme effectiveness was further enforced through the leadership of the Department of Strategic Policy and Delivery, who utilised Technical and Steering Committees to systematically identify and resolve programme implementation bottlenecks; thereby deepening national ownership.  Simultaneously, the national evidence landscape also underwent expansion. The completion of the 2025 SDG Monitoring Survey and the achievement of preparatory milestones for the 2026 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey significantly bolstered the Gambia Bureau of Statistics’ analytical capacity and infrastructure. At the subnational level, 40 Multi-Disciplinary Facilitation Team members were trained on monitoring and evaluation, decentralising results tracking to the West Coast and North Bank Regions. These data-driven efforts were reinforced by regularising Joint Sector Reviews and biannual field visits, which integrated direct feedback from community stakeholders into the planning cycle.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, global financial instability posed as one of the biggest challenges faced by the Development sector worldwide. This in turn changed the aid operational landscape. As traditional ODA becomes increasingly unpredictable, UNICEF globally has restructured its offices to force a lean, strategic reprioritisation of staff and resources. This forced UNICEF to do ‘more with less,’ shifting from a broad implementation agency to a specialised interventions.    
 
In The Gambia, one of the most sensitive developments in 2025 was the renewed challenge to the 2015 legal prohibition of FGM. Although the National Assembly of The Gambia rejected a repeal bill in 2024, the debate resurfaced in 2025, with some voices invoking ‘cultural rights’ and presenting the practice as tied to religious belief and national identity. For many girls, women, survivors, and those working to end FGM, this renewed contestation created uncertainty and fear, and advocacy became more difficult in an increasingly tense environment compounded by a more cautious public stance from some political leaders. Following the 2024 parliamentary decision, proponents of repeal, including influential religious figures, filed a petition with the Supreme Court of The Gambia, shifting the issue from the legislature to the courts.
 
In 2025, advocacy for ending FGM took on renewed urgency following reports that two infants died from complications linked to FGM, prompting widespread public concern and calls for action. Encouragingly, this was accompanied by more proactive reporting by health professionals to the police, public messaging from the police encouraging reporting, and clear public signals from Government reaffirming opposition to FGM.
UNICEF has also provided the Government with vital technical assistance for its defence and empowered CSOs to coordinate a robust response to the FGM case pending decision at the Supreme Court. In addition to this, UNICEF carried out training of 30 journalists who were trained on child rights and the ongoing case for adequate media coverage. Another key step was engaging over 120 religious and traditional leaders and 360 men and boys to promote positive masculinity and facilitating dialogues with nearly 8,000 community members and reaching more than 122,000 people through mass media to sustain grassroots support for the ban. 
 
In terms of lessons apart from FGM, UNICEF’s shift toward evidence-based advocacy proved useful in Governmental budget decisions. The National Assembly reviewed social sector budgets for Health and Education from a child focused lens.  In addition to this, the ‘Mansa Kunda’ proved that when children, especially girls, articulate their aspirations to decision-makers, it can be impactful. It is important to underscore the value of a coordinated, multi-sectoral approach. Because child rights are indivisible and interconnected, integrated action across sectors is more effective and, in a significantly constrained global financing environment, more cost-efficient, than fragmented interventions.
  
Climate change continues to be a threat for children in The Gambia. In some climate-impacted regions, some of the indicators like neonatal and maternal mortality are on the rise. In addition, livelihood is impacted, which increases illegal migration.
 
As we look toward 2026 and beyond, the strategy for ensuring child rights in The Gambia is one of sustainable independence. The sunsetting of traditional donor reliance marks a strategic pivot toward private sector integration.  For this, UNICEF is positioning child rights as a business imperative for The Gambia’s growing private and business sectors. By brokering partnerships that leverage private capital for climate-resilient WASH infrastructure and digital learning, the focus shifts from one off grants to sustainable impact investments.

Ghana today faces a demographic window of opportunity: by 2035, the proportion of working-age people will exceed younger and older populations. With the right investments, those who are children today will grow to build a prosperous and equitable future.
 
Ghana’s youth bulge includes over 14 million (40 per cent of the population) girls and boys under 18 [UNICEF Data Warehouse, 2023], all of whom share certain visions of that future. They demand equitable education and digital skills that prepare them for the jobs of the future. They look forward to a world in which connectivity and digital technology fuel opportunities in a green economy, with good governance and protections against exploitation. They envisage a future of universal access to safe water and a hygienic environment; they demand equity of opportunity and access to services; they ask for respect and freedom from violence, including from their caregivers and the eradication of poverty. 
 
Ghana is taking critical steps to realise these dreams, drawing on digital innovations and creating the conditions for a future of opportunity for children. This is enshrined in Vision 2057, a national cross-party framework that envisions child welfare and human development capital, improved health and nutrition and universal access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). 
 
One year into a new presidency, Ghana continues to demonstrate its commitment to upholding the rights of children. In December 2025, the executive board of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) completed its fifth review of the US$3 billion extended credit facility (ECF), finding broadly satisfactory progress characterized by strong growth, single-digit inflation, improved fiscal position and progress on debt restructuring, and a need for steadfast reform to consolidate these gains [IMF]. While the limited fiscal space due to debt servicing constrained spending on child welfare, ECF targets helped protect and promote critical social spending designed to safeguard children and vulnerable groups. Meeting these targets was crucial to advances in certain sectors in 2025.
 
For example, in the 2025 budget, allocations to major social-sector ministries, departments and agencies increased by 11 per cent in real terms [UNICEF Ghana Budget Briefs, 2025], reversing declining trends in recent years. With increased allocations, the country met its vaccine co-financing commitment in 2025 and exceeded the benchmark allocation for the National Health Insurance Authority. The value of key social grants – Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP), School Feeding Programme and the Capitation Grant (school fee subsidies) – were increased, strengthening social protection for children. However, allocations to programmes directly supporting child protection decreased, with potential implications for protection outcomes.
 
Ghana is a regional leader in disability inclusion, with recent advances including no-fee tertiary education for youth with disabilities and the scale-up of an early grade screening programme. In 2025, the Ministry of Education announced the full scale-up of differentiated learning into the education system as a standardized, national strategy to address the country’s learning crisis.
 
Yet significant challenges must be overcome to build on and ensure the sustainability of these gains. Children in Ghana navigate a context shaped by national and global megatrends. In addition to the opportunities opened by the demographic shift, they confront national economic challenges leading to low investments in key social sectors. Despite recent increases, spending on health, education, nutrition, sanitation, and child protection services remains below international benchmarks for universal access and service quality [UNICEF Ghana Budget Briefs, 2025]. Sustaining progress for children will require broad-based and inclusive economic growth, increased job creation and structural transformation that underpins long-term economic expansion.
 
Poverty reduction has stalled in the past decade [World Bank, Transforming Ghana in a Generation, 2025] and drives deprivation, pushing children out of school and into work or early marriage: around 2 million children are currently engaged in child labour. While access to education is high, drop out increases through education levels, and learning quality is compromised by years of under-investment in primary education. This, along with mismatch between skills acquired and labour-market needs, contributes to high youth unemployment. In 2022, 27.6 per cent of youth were not in education, employment or training [World Bank DataBank]. About 16 per cent of Ghanaian girls are married or in union before the age of 18. Child marriage is more common among girls in rural areas, living in poorer households and with little or no education [Ghana DHS, 2022]. Such girls are at greater risk of dropping out of school and are vulnerable to child protection and health risks, including early childbearing.
 
Progress in birth registration has stagnated in the last two years due to insufficient investment in civil registration services and infrastructure. Reaching remote communities, such as on islands, can be difficult to arrange, while distance and indirect costs are barriers for parents seeking to register their children. Ghana’s birth registration rate is lower relative to comparable countries. However, with the right policy instruments and advocacy, significant results can be achieved in a short period.
 
The stagnation in the decline in maternal mortality (263 deaths per 100,000 live births) [World Health Organization, 2023] is inadequate to meet the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of 70 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. A major contributor is poor access to quality emergency obstetric care: only 4 per cent of health facilities qualify as functional basic emergency obstetric and newborn care centres due to structural issues in capital budget allocation [Ghana DHS, 2022]. 
 
About 17.4 per cent of children under five are stunted and 6 per cent suffer from wasting, [Ghana DHS, 2022] driven partly by climate-driven dietary shifts. The proportion of overweight children is low but rising, driven by availability of low-quality ultra-processed food. Only 26.4 per cent of children aged 6–23 months receive a minimum acceptable diet [Ghana DHS, 2022]. Anaemia affects over 40 per cent of adolescent girls and women of childbearing age and 49 per cent of children under five [Ghana DHS, 2022]. 
 
As a signatory to the Presidential Compact on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene, Ghana is committed to eradicate open defecation by 2030, but progress is challenged by a chronic lack of sustainable spending on infrastructure, including operations and maintenance, rapid urbanization and degraded water bodies. This contributes to stagnating open defecation rates that are far higher than those of countries on a comparable development trajectory. The latter hovered around 30 per cent in rural areas and 8 per cent in urban areas in both 2015 and 2024, representing a decade of limited WASH progress [JMP Data, 2024]. By contrast, in Sub-Saharan Africa as a whole, open defecation has declined from 22 per cent to 15.5 per cent over the same period [JMP Data, 2024]. This creates the conditions for WASH-related diseases such as cholera which compromise children’s ability to survive and thrive.
 
Children experience these impacts differentially. Those in rural areas, northern regions, urban poverty hubs and island communities, and those living with disabilities, face particular challenges in accessing services and opportunities. Poverty drives exclusion from education and health, increases risks to violence and exploitation and is concentrated in rural areas. Adolescent girls are at risk of teenage pregnancy and child marriage nationwide: 15.2 per cent of girls aged 15–19 years are estimated to have been pregnant at least once [Ghana DHS, 2022], putting their bodies at greater risk of maternal mortality and morbidity. The highest rates of stunting are found in the Northern region, which also faces the highest levels of food insecurity.
 
While 2025 has laid a strong foundation for the future envisioned by Ghanaian children and youth, these gains must be deepened and accelerated. The right investments in Ghana’s children at the right time will yield high social and economic returns. Advances in digital solutions across sectors expand opportunities for young people and introduce efficiencies in service delivery. Achieving this requires child-focused policy frameworks, effective protection mechanisms, equitable and responsive services, efficient and equitable spending, sustainable and predictable financing and innovative platforms to elevate children’s voices as central to policy and programme design.
 
Thirty-five years ago, Ghana led the world as the first country to ratify the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Today, it is poised to lead once more by building on the promises made to realise a future shaped for children, bringing 14 million dreams to life.

In 2025, UNICEF supported Ghana to strengthen systems and achieve scale through paradigm shifts and commitments to children amongst the country’s leadership, evidenced through genuinely transformational policy shifts and budgetary commitments.
 
This occurred within a challenging global and national economic environment in which viable paths to the future envisaged by Ghana’s children and youth had to be remapped. For UNICEF, building relationships with core policy and financial actors in Ghana was key to driving systemic change, sustainable allocations and amplifying children’s voices amidst structural reform.
 
Mainstreaming child rights

UNICEF adopted a multi-pronged, multi-stakeholder advocacy and policy approach on child rights, engaging Parliament, relevant ministries and the National Development Planning Commission, while also leveraging key moments such as World Children’s Day and the West Africa Adolescent Girls’ Summit. These engagements enhanced oversight of child-related issues, advanced child-focused financing, and strengthened Ghana’s accountability framework for children.
 
UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Protection (MoGCSP) and the National Development Planning Commission to shift child rights advocacy from a sectoral concern to a broader priority. This culminated in a solidarity statement issued from the floor of Parliament, a legislative first, and a historic commitment by the Presidency to establish an annual Presidential National Children’s Dialogue, creating a permanent platform for adolescent voice in decision-making. 
 
Following an election in which youth voices played an unprecedented role, UNICEF identified Parliament as an influential strategic ally for children’s issues. UNICEF collaborated with Parliament to advance child-rights monitoring and legislative oversight, facilitated by the African Centre for Parliamentary Affairs (ACEPA) and the Interparliamentary Union. With ACEPA, UNICEF provided training to members of parliament (MPs) and their technical staff on reviewing policies and oversight through a child-focused lens, and introduced the first-ever dedicated module on child rights in the induction programme for new MPs; this was attended by over 100 parliamentarians out of 276. This was cascaded to the relevant committees and facilitated unprecedented demand for engagement on child rights in the incoming cohort.
 
UNICEF strengthened parliamentary oversight by arranging two parliamentary visits to observe child labour and trafficking issues and solutions first-hand, preceded by orientation sessions to sensitize them on child rights. The delegations, comprising over 25 representatives from all major parties and members of five major bipartisan committees and Parliamentary Services, visited mining and agriculture districts and engaged in discussions with communities, children and youth. Participating MPs committed to advocate for a percentage of district assembly common funds (allocated by federal government) to be dedicated to addressing chronically underfunded child protection prevention and response services.
 
Building on the Vice President’s focus on women and adolescent girls, UNICEF continued to advocate for policy shifts to further the rights of adolescent girls and women. The Affirmative Action (Gender Equity) Act, 2024 mandates gender-responsive budgeting, women’s employment and representation. Since this poses a challenge to dominant norms that marginalize girls and women, high-level commitment and robust implementation mechanisms are critical for its success. With UNICEF technical support, a Gender Equity Committee has been formed with a mandate to oversee the implementation of this Act. UNICEF ensured adolescent voices from Ghana contributed to the Dakar Declaration for Girls’ Summit in West and Central Africa. The Dakar Declaration was formally received on behalf of the President by the MoGCSP.
 
UNICEF supported the strengthening of national accountability systems and transparent governance, and advanced the national efficiency agenda by convening the first-ever Ghana Evaluation Week to build understanding of how evidence should inform decision-making; a course on child-focused evaluations for the inaugural cohort of the African School of Evaluation developed in partnership with the Regional Office; and provided technical and financial support to a summative evaluation of Medium Term National Development Policy Framework (MTNDPF) 2022–2025 in collaboration with the National Development Planning Commission. 
 
Public finance management for children
 
With UNICEF technical support, the Ministry of Finance reformed its Chart of Accounts and budget monitoring systems and produce an SDG Expenditure Report, including tracked child-focused investments at national and subnational levels, linking budget lines directly to SDG indicators. This strengthened Ghana’s ability to channel targeted investments towards children, 73 per cent of whom experience multidimensional poverty. Ghana is now positioned as a leader in SDG expenditure reporting, as the first in Africa to produce a report of this scope. 
 
Sustained budget analysis and evidence-based advocacy enhanced national resource allocations for children. Child-focused social sector allocations rose from 25.8 per cent in 2024 to 26.7 per cent in 2025. Key child-related programmes, including in education, health, capitation grant, school feeding and LEAP, among others, received increased allocations. The 2026 budget also increased allocations to child-related interventions, including the Child and Human Trafficking Fund, birth registration, domestic violence services and WASH, which had experienced declining allocations in recent years. These positive trends reflect coordinated advocacy and collaboration with Parliament and the Ministry of Finance. UNICEF worked closely with the IMF and World Bank to advocate for safeguarding investments that benefit children.
 
Health
 
In 2025, health financing saw a strategic shift towards domestic resource mobilization and sustainability. The uncapping of the National Health Insurance Levy unlocked substantial additional resources and increased the NHIS share of the total health budget to 36 per cent. This offers a path towards bridging financing gaps due to declining donor support, advancing self-financed vaccine procurement and funding initiatives such as the Free Primary Health Care Policy to provide key services at the point of use. The policy will be implemented through the primary care network and financed by the uncapped levy, as an important step towards achieving Universal Health Care and addressing stagnating maternal mortality.
 
UNICEF played a central role in these developments through a budget analysis co-created with government ministries and economic evidence developed in three high-impact studies: a Fiscal Space Analysis to identify domestic resources that could be allocated to primary health care, a cost-benefit analysis of integrating immunization into primary health-care packages and a primary health-care policy review. These provided inputs to the design of the Free Primary Health Care Policy.
 
UNICEF entered into partnerships with the Ghana Health Service to enhance quality of care and thus address maternal mortality, including guidelines for systemic audit of maternal deaths, linking district and community-level clinicians with specialist mentors, and the establishment of skills laboratories to improve training.
 
Ghana introduced the HPV vaccine into the national schedule in 2025. UNICEF supported resource mobilization, demand generation and the implementation of immunization activities. HPV vaccine introduction was guided by behavioural science research with adolescents at the heart of designing and delivering social and behaviour change interventions. Adolescent girls and their caregivers were engaged as key decision-makers and engaged in meaningful dialogue while public awareness was raised through radio, TV, social media, billboards and street theatre. UNICEF also leveraged partnerships with faith leaders who championed HPV engagement among their communities using co-designed sermon guides. As a result, 1.9 million girls aged 9–14 years – a high coverage rate of 84 per cent – were protected against the primary cause of cervical cancer, potentially preventing 40,000 deaths.
 
UNICEF advanced primary health care by strengthening the community health workforce, introducing an innovative empowerment model which transformed community health volunteers into micro-entrepreneurs. These volunteers generated incomes through the sale of essential health and nutrition commodities alongside service delivery. Through a three-year partnership with the Mastercard Foundation, this initiative extended the reach of the health system by inducting and training 3,400 volunteers to generate demand, engage households, and facilitate behaviour change, while creating livelihood opportunities.
 
In taking its adolescent health programme to scale across 190 districts, UNICEF supported Community-Based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) structures to link pregnant adolescents and adolescent mothers to health services, social protection, education retention and gender-based violence response mechanisms. Cross-sectoral integration enabled the most vulnerable adolescent girls to access joined-up support.
 
UNICEF partnered with the Food and Drugs Authority to collect critical evidence on the prevalence of heavy metals in consumer products, revealing that children and pregnant women are exposed to high levels of lead, cadmium and mercury in everyday objects, exposing them to severe neurodevelopmental and chronic health risks. UNICEF is now driving systemic change through calls for public awareness and health screening, and a collaboration with the Food and Drugs Authority to strengthen regulatory and enforcement frameworks and testing protocols.
 
Nutrition

As a pioneer of the First Foods Africa Initiative, Ghana promotes local production and consumption of nutritious, safe, affordable and sustainable first foods and food supplements. UNICEF strengthened the policy landscape for this by providing technical inputs to food-environment policies, including front-of-pack labelling, marketing regulations, procurement standards and fiscal measures. UNICEF worked with national regulatory bodies to reinforce protective frameworks, including a collaboration with the Food and Drugs Authority to expand legislation regulating breastmilk substitute marketing to cover complementary foods, and a partnership with the Ghana Standards Authority which contributed to regional complementary food standards and conducted formative research on the social marketing of complementary foods. 
 
A reliance on donor-funded procurement for essential nutrition commodities such as ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) and F75 and F100 enriched milk, renders them prone to frequent stockouts. Addressing low nutrition funding (0.4 per cent of the Ministry of Health’s programme expenditure in 2024) was thus a UNICEF priority. 
 
In 2025, Ghana took a first step towards sustainably offering universal treatment for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) by revising its essential medicines list to include key commodities including RUTF. This inclusion recognizes malnutrition as a medical condition requiring essential medication, with the aim of making the latter routinely available through the public health system. 
 
UNICEF generated evidence to support sustainable domestic funding and used it to advocate for the inclusion of maternal and child nutrition commodities in NHIS and address critically low nutrition expenditure. It reviewed community-based health and nutrition policies, analysed fiscal space for primary health care and nutrition and undertook a cost-benefit analysis of integrating nutrition into the primary health-care package. These findings informed evidence-based advocacy to include nutrition services in the NHIS and the Free Primary Health-care Policy, to be rolled out in 2026.
 
UNICEF also piloted the integration of Vitamin A supplementation tracking into Ghana’s national electronic health record system, enabling health authorities to track specific doses for individual children, identify those who missed doses and facilitate real-time supply monitoring. This established a framework to eventually incorporate growth monitoring and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) management into the national system and ensuring that no child is deprived of the nourishment needed to thrive.
 
Social protection

Ghana embarked on its first-ever comprehensive reassessment of LEAP beneficiaries, aiming to expand coverage from 350,000 to 450,000 extremely poor households by end-2026. UNICEF provided technical support and rigorous analysis of targeting and enrolment statistics, shaping an evidence-based approach to quota-setting. This ensured that poverty and vulnerability data guide decisions and that households with children in greatest need access social protection. Following UNICEF advocacy, the government increased grant values by 25 per cent, keeping their 2025 real value above 2024 levels, while payment delays dropped from 117 days (2022) to 22 days (2025). UNICEF also advocated vigorously with the IMF and development partners against the exclusion of pregnant women from LEAP.
 
UNICEF collaborated with the National Health Insurance Authority to target children aged 6–14 years for national identification registration, and thus automatically link them to NHIS. By integrating these two systems, the initiative ensured that obtaining a legal identity resulted in an immediate, tangible benefit for vulnerable children who were missed during early childhood: free access to health care.
 
Education
 
In 2025, UNICEF advocacy to make foundational learning a national priority bore fruit as senior government figures specified basic education as a key priority, complementing an existing focus on free secondary education. Key speeches by President Mahama and the deputy minister of education echoed language and priorities advocated by UNICEF, including the focus on foundational learning, the need to close gaps and address learning poverty. This commitment was reflected in a reversal of the declining trend in basic education financing, with allocations increasing from 19.6 per cent in 2024 to 24.1 per cent in 2025 after consistent decline since 2019.
 
This shift in the high-level narrative on education was made tangible through the adoption by the Ministry of Education of the Differentiated Learning Plus approach, piloted by UNICEF. Three years of Gates Foundation-funded implementation in 501 schools was demonstrated to improve inclusiveness and learning proficiency in mathematics and literacy from 19 per cent and 37 per cent respectively to 50+ per cent. The approach is now being scaled up to every public primary school in Ghana with support from the Global Partnership for Education. This represents a fundamental shift in teaching as educators group students based on skill level rather than grade level alone. It incorporates a digital dashboard for school accountability and promotes universal design and play principles to provide cost-effective, targeted support that improves overall learning quality, regardless of disability. 
 
UNICEF prepared the ground to make better use of existing and emerging education resources by providing technical support for the National Education Forum and the launch of the 2025 Foundational Learning Action Tracker, in collaboration with the Ministry of Education and Hempel Foundation. Using this digital tool, the government can now monitor its progress against the global RAPID Framework on foundational learning and enable policy-making and resource allocations that support access to quality learning for all Ghanaian children.
 
The removal of the cap on the Ghana Education Trust Fund, through which the 2.5 per cent VAT levy for education is channelled, resulted in increased resources for education in 2025. Yet for financing to meet international benchmarks, and for it to be channelled effectively to serve the aspirations of Ghana’s children, continued advocacy will be needed. UNICEF laid the ground for this through strategic advocacy and high-level engagement, including with MPs, to encourage Ghana to demonstrate its education commitments on both national and global stages, including as host of the Association for the Development of Education in Africa conference and high-level dialogue between education officials and UNICEF’s global director for education.
 
UNICEF supported the operationalization of the Re-entry Policy Guidelines for Pregnant Girls and Young Mothers, enhancing schools’ ability to identify, track and reintegrate adolescent mothers, reduce discriminatory practices and improve linkages between education, social welfare and health services.
 
Meaningful work is a critical component of the future that young Ghanaians aspire to. In 2025, UNICEF strengthened systems for technical and vocational education and training (TVET), promoted gender equity and engaged in evidence-based policy advocacy to address the mismatch between youth skills and market needs. UNICEF worked with government partners to make vocational learning environments safer and more inclusive by adapting its Safe Schools toolkit for TVET. 
 
In partnership with the newly established Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment, UNICEF strengthened systems in monitoring, evaluation and data use. Over 1,260 adolescents and young people engaged in civic, policy and advocacy processes across climate, WASH, education, development planning and youth skilling, directly informing national and subnational decision-making. 
 
Child protection
 
In 2025, UNICEF intensified its shift from direct service delivery to policy advocacy and technical support to develop sustainable child protection systems. This was anchored in Ghana’s endorsement of the Framework for Action on Strengthening Child Protection Systems in early 2025. Ghana’s child protection system was recognized by the National Child Protection Committee to have successfully reached maturity level in 2025 through scaled up child protection and justice services, child participation and coordination. 
 
To advance a more effective child protection system and holistic child well-being, UNICEF continued to support the scale up of Integrated Social Services (ISS), a government-led initiative to strengthen intersectoral collaborations to deliver individualized care and referrals. Since its inception in 2020, over 200,000 children have been reached with individualized services, over 9 million people have been reached by the Ghanaians Against Child Abuse social mobilization drive and community engagement using Child Protection Toolkits, and over 3 million vulnerable people were registered in NHIS to facilitate their access to free health services. The inclusion of the ISS in the MTNDPF 2026–2029 was agreed and implemented with government counterparts, facilitating expansion to cover 80 per cent of the country. Government-led mechanisms reached about 39,000 children with protection services and referrals in 2025. UNICEF mobilized a broad coalition of partners to align efforts with the ISS. Over 20 civil society organizations and private companies adopted the ISS approach, improving referrals, prevention and response services. 
 
Ghana is increasingly a source, transit and a destination country for child trafficking, but fragmented data systems prevent full understanding of the issue and a comprehensive response. In 2025, UNICEF supported improved enhanced interoperability of data systems to improve tracking of children subject to child labour and trafficking and thus enhance prevention and response. 
 
UNICEF partnered with the United Nations Population Fund to apply a multisectoral systems-strengthening approach which provided 144,604 vulnerable adolescent girls with prevention and care interventions to address child marriage through the Global Programme to End Child Marriage (2024-2030). 
 
Water, sanitation and hygiene
 
In 2025, UNICEF leveraged strategic partnerships with high-level government bodies to strengthen national policy frameworks and sustainably shift social norms to eradicate open defecation. It also furthered the integration of WASH and climate change, building sector capacity to understand climate risks, adapt to them, and mitigate impacts on WASH services.
 
In recent years, Ghana has fallen significantly behind comparator nations in achieving sanitation for all, however with national attention, achieving open-defecation-free status is within sight. UNICEF advocacy and support for ministerial engagement on the international stage led to the endorsement by Ghana of the High-Level Leaders Compact on Water Security and Resilience. This commitment to elevate WASH as pillars of climate adaptation and sustainable development provides a lever for UNICEF to advocate for sector reforms, climate-resilient WASH standards and the development of national Open Defecation Free and Safely Managed Sanitation plans. 
 
UNICEF strengthened the evidence base for WASH financing in partnership with the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology by commissioning a study aimed at analyzing the projected investment for safe, resilient and reliable community level water supply against the economic and environmental costs of the widespread use of plastic-packaged water (estimated at over US$55 million).
 
UNICEF successfully advocated for deeper inclusion of WASH in Ghana's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), the national climate change action plan developed under the Paris Agreement. Based on a thorough review of Ghana’s current commitments, key WASH actions were identified for inclusion in the updated NDC (NDC-3), for the first time. This will ensure that WASH is incorporated in national climate change commitments, as well as in the national adaptation plan, bringing WASH to the centre of climate change mitigation and adaptation.
 
Partnerships and resource mobilization
 
In a challenging global funding environment, UNICEF built and sustained strong partnerships to advance children’s rights. In 2025, UNICEF unlocked US$32.5 million in contributions from KOICA, the European Union, the Government of Japan, the British Government, the Global Partnership for Education, the Mastercard Foundation and National Committees. A landmark partnership with Denmark secured US$14 million for urban WASH, while the Ghana–Japan Public-Private Partnership against Child Labour mobilized US$2.3 million. Key factors in this success included strong internal operating procedures and systems to involve key stakeholders and uphold quality controls; presenting multisectoral solutions and leveraging technical expertise to strengthen impact; and working with partners to align strategies and foster long-term impact.
 
Operational efficiency and risk management

Following the 2024 Global Staff Survey, UNICEF engaged staff to identify six priority Duty of Care actions and successfully implemented four actions. UNICEF embarked on a major asset renewal programme in 2025 and completed its fleet modernization plan, generating US$434,000 over three years and reinvested these funds in a greener fleet with reduced fuel and maintenance costs.
 
The office reinforced risk management and financial controls and reduced use of Fund Commitments for low-value transactions by 98 per cent while increasing Low-Value Purchase Orders by 8 per cent and P-Cards by 108 per cent, significantly lowering administrative costs and fiduciary risk. Systematic risk monitoring, documented mitigation measures and clearly assigned ownership strengthened accountability across operations and programmes.
 
Procurement increased by 38 per cent to reach US$8.2 million in 2025. UNICEF Procurement Services also supported the government to procure supplies to the value of US$63.41 million and sourced 12 per cent locally, strengthening national markets and generating savings of US$1.2 million.
