Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, a new government took office in Ghana, entailing transitions in senior leadership positions and requiring UNICEF to proactively engage with critical stakeholders to ensure continued focus on child-focused priorities. 
 
In some instances, programme implementation slowed as the new leadership took stock of current issues and realigned priorities for ministries, departments and agencies to deliver their new mandate. Through proactive engagement and relationship building, UNICEF highlighted its availability to support the delivery of results for children and to maintain momentum on the child rights agenda in Ghana. The incorporation of a child rights module delivered by UNICEF in the parliamentarian induction process introduced new legislators to child rights as a core component of their mandate from day one in office. 
 
Some ministries – such as Ministry of Youth and Sports, Ministry of Local Government, Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources – were disbanded, restructured or had their mandates revised. UNICEF actively engaged with the new or restructured ministries to support onboarding and focus on children’s issues. Operationally, donor funds to government partners were frozen during a government review, which delayed implementation of some UNICEF-supported programmes. The resources were unlocked following engagement with government partners.
 
Early engagement with parties as they shaped their political manifestos before the election in December 2024 laid the ground for rapid engagement with the new government. This put child rights in the manifestos of major parties, and the inclusion of ambitious results for children in the government's first-year priorities and the new MTNDPF 2026–2029. The budget disbursement report, released in mid-2025, demonstrated government commitment to deliver on these plans.
 
UNICEF supported the National Development Planning Commission with the first-ever evaluation of the MTNDPF 2022-2025, which found that conceptually strong policy frameworks can be constrained by systemic weaknesses, fragmented coordination, limited capacity at the district level, inadequate financing, and persistent inequities. This underscored the need to move beyond fragmented and short-term interventions toward integrated, sustainable and locally owned development strategies, supported by district-level planning and beneficiary targeting. The evaluation also highlighted the imperative to mobilize domestic resources and reduce reliance on donor financing. These lessons were reflected in UNICEF’s programming in 2025, where strong domestic ownership, improved coordination and investment, equitable and efficient execution, and sustainable financing models proved critical to delivering results at scale despite the challenging fiscal environment.
 
A revision to the model of the UNICEF StartUp Lab showed the need to move beyond the initial incubation phase to complete an effective and holistic cycle of support in order for youth-led solutions to achieve scale. In 2025, the Lab moved beyond its six-month acceleration model, complementing it with targeted financial support (US$100,000 for high-potential start-ups), technical assistance and active engagement with government agencies to address systemic gaps. This enabled start-ups to collaborate directly with government partners and UNICEF programme specialists, pilot their solutions in real-world contexts and demonstrate tangible scaling potential. For example, TECHAiDE collaborated with the education department to train teachers to use educational technology in the classroom in contexts where connectivity is limited; and Minagie Energy piloted a clean energy solution to daily 8–20-hour power outages in remote health centres. By combining acceleration with strategic funding, technical support and government partnerships, the Lab aligned innovation with government priorities, injected funding that moved promising solutions from pilot to scale and reinforced the start-up ecosystem’s ability to integrate technology-driven solutions into formal systems. 
 
A field visit to the remote Afram Plains region showed how reflections from the field can be powerfully translated into issue-based advocacy. The visit visually documented the severe logistical barriers that prevent civil registry officials from accessing remote populations and demonstrated that low registration rates were not caused by parental reluctance but the inaccessibility of services. UNICEF presented these last-mile challenges to media editors. Through appearances on a major morning show with 3 million viewers, birth registration was positioned as an urgent child rights issue and doubled the government resources available to districts to address birth registration challenges. In the longer run, the visit informed UNICEF advocacy to focus on differentiated planning approaches and a methodological review of the resource distribution formula of District Assembly Common Fund to also consider geographical realities and vulnerabilities. With a systems-level evaluation of birth registration currently ongoing with UNICEF support and in collaboration with the Births and Deaths Registry, these and emerging lessons will support reforms that rapidly advance birth registration in Ghana.
 
Way forward
 
At the mid-point of UNICEF’s country programme, there is a need for reflection on recent changes in the operational context since the development of the country programme in 2022. In 2026, UNICEF will align its planning with the government’s identified prioritised areas in the new MTNDPF. Key to this is advancing collaboration and advocacy on key areas of child deprivation where the data suggests progress has stalled: maternal and child mortality, nutrition, foundational learning, child labour and trafficking, birth registration, child poverty and youth who are not in education, employment or training. 
 
The solutions to these challenges will be grounded in life-cycle and equity-based approach, prioritizing population groups and interventions based on evidence of impact, while strengthening government systems through technical assistance, improving programme efficiency and scalability, and avoiding the creation of parallel delivery mechanisms.
 
Sustainable change in a resource-constrained environment requires influencing national policy and domestic resource allocation. Reflecting the fiscal instability and domestic debt crisis Ghana has recently experienced, as well as UNICEF’s own global shift towards a leaner, more agile way of working, UNICEF will continue its pivot toward upstream interventions and operationalize a systematic shift away from direct service delivery towards technical assistance, advocacy and leveraging collaborations for sustained impact. UNICEF will also engage with government and non-traditional partners to strengthen transparency, efficiency, effectiveness and adequacy of public funding and to fill funding gaps through private sector partnerships and business for results.

Guinea’s population is young, fast-growing, with strong regional variations. According to the latest data, Guinea’s population is estimated at 14 million, with 64 per cent living in rural areas. Women represent 52 per cent of the population, and nearly two-thirds of Guineans are under 25. This demographic profile presents both an opportunity and a challenge, generating high demand for education, employment and basic services, while underscoring the importance of sustained investments in human capital to harness the demographic dividend.
Despite steady macroeconomic growth in recent years, structural inequalities and service delivery gaps continue to limit equitable access to opportunities and basic services for many children, particularly those living in rural and vulnerable settings.
Political, Institutional and Economic Context
The adoption of a new Constitution in September 2025, followed by presidential elections in December, formally concluded the transition period initiated after the 2021 coup. The electoral process was largely peaceful and assessed as credible by international observers, although the absence of major opposition parties highlighted ongoing challenges related to inclusive governance. The end of the transition creates a more enabling environment for institutional stabilization, policy continuity and renewed engagement with development partners, with opportunities to advance social sector reforms and strengthening national systems. Economic growth accelerated in 2025, projected 7.2 per cent,[1] driven by mining, infrastructure investments and the start of Simandou iron ore exploitation. Public expenditure increased by 22.8 per cent under the 2025 Amended Finance Law, including additional allocations for education and health. The government reiterated its commitments to prioritizing public investment, including pledges to allocate 20-30 per cent of mining revenues towards human capital development by 2040. However, in the short term, fiscal space remains constrained by high recurrent expenditures, notably electricity subsidies, limiting the immediate translation of macroeconomic gains into improved child outcomes. Efforts to strengthen budget prioritization, efficiency and equity are ongoing to advance children’s rights.
Analytical Assessment of Child Rights
While findings from Guinea’s eighth Demographic and Health Survey (DHS-8, 2024-2025) are pending national validation, available administrative data, joint UN estimates and sectoral analyses provide a sufficient basis to assess trends, disparities and implications for UNICEF-supported programmes. 
Guinea’s engagement with international human rights mechanisms, including the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) and reporting under the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), reflects renewed attention to strengthening legal, institutional and accountability frameworks for children’s rights. The 2026 UPR highlights progress in constitutional reform and renewed opportunities to strengthen legal and institutional frameworks for human rights, while underscoring the need to accelerate implementation, ratify outstanding treaties, ensure judicial independence, combat impunity, and protect vulnerable groups, including women and children, linking recommendations to the Sustainable Development Goals and other human rights mechanisms. Similarly, Guinea’s reporting under the CRC (2018) and the Committee’s concluding observations (2019) acknowledge policy efforts to improve child protection, access to basic services and legal safeguards, while identifying persistent challenges related to birth registration, equitable access to education and health services, early pregnancies, harmful practices, and protection from violence and discrimination, particularly for children in rural areas and from vulnerable households.
Every Child Survives and Thrives
Progress towards SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger) and 3 (Good Health and Wellbeing) remains mixed. In 2025, stunting affected an estimated 24-30 per cent of children and wasting between 6-9 per cent, disproportionately impacting rural populations and remote regions, such as Labé and Boké. These figures indicate stagnation rather than substantive improvement compared to 2023 and 2024[2]
At the same time, routine immunization improved significantly: coverage of the third dose of the pentavalent vaccine (Penta3) increased from around 43 per cent in 2024 to 63 per cent in 2025[3] reflecting successful efforts by the Government and partners to restore essential services following COVID-19 disruptions. 
Every Child Learns and Acquires Skills for the Future
Human capital outcomes in Guinea remain among the lowest globally. The Human Capital Index suggests that a child born today will reach only 37 per cent of their productive potential due to persistent deficits in health, education and gender equality. Education spending remains low at approximately 2 per cent of GDP.
Access, retention and learning outcomes remain major challenges. Nearly one million children aged 6-14 are out of school (28 per cent), most of them girls (61 per cent), placing Guinea 11th globally for out-of-school children. Primary completion rates are modest (56% girls; 70% boys) and drop sharply at secondary level (31% and 39% respectively), and learning poverty is acute, with a large proportion of children unable to read age-appropriate text. 
Measures to reduce inequalities included the recruitment of 12,000 primary teachers based on decentralized needs assessments and the development of a partnership compact to mobilize Global Partnership for Education financing, aimed at professionalizing the teaching workforce by 2030. However, persistent disparities and critical teacher shortages continue to undermine education outcomes, particularly in rural and vulnerable communities. 
Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life
Poverty remains widespread and unevenly distributed; monetary poverty affects over 43 per cent of the population (2019 estimates), with children disproportionately affected (49 per cent). Multidimensional child poverty remains high at 72 per cent child poverty remains, reflecting persistent deprivations in health, education, WASH, nutrition and housing.[4]
While social protection policies have expanded in recent years, they remain largely focused on monetary poverty, limiting coherence with broader interventions needed to address the multiple and intersecting deprivations affecting children. Progress towards SDGs 1 and 10 (No Poverty; Reduced Inequalities) requires continued and coordinated efforts across sectors.
Every Child is Protected from Violence, Exploitation and Abuse
Guinea has made important progress in strengthening the legal and policy framework for child protection through constitutional prohibition of female genital mutilation and strengthened protections against child exploitation and abuse, reinforced by the adoption of the revised National Child Protection Policy (2026-2035), which promotes a multisectoral and coordinated approach to protecting children.
Nevertheless, violence and harmful practices affecting children remain prevalent. Child labour remains affects 38 per cent of children, particularly in agriculture and mining, with a substantial proportion engaged in hazardous work (27 per cent).[5] To address data gaps, UNICEF plans to conduct a dedicated child labour study in 2026.
Gender-based violence and harmful practices persist, although data show a gradual generational decline in female genital mutilation and child marriage. The latest figures (2018) indicate that 39 per cent of girls age 0-14 had undergone female genital mutilation, down from 45.5 per cent in 2012, while overall prevalence decreased from 94 per cent in 2012 to 91.7 per cent. Regarding child marriage, 30 per cent of girls aged 15-19 and 47 per cent of women aged 20–24 were married before age 18 in 2018[6] - an improvement in both age groups compared to previous years.
Progress has been recorded in birth registration over the past decade, increasing from 58 per cent in 2012 to 62 per cent in 2018, although urban-rural disparities persist, limiting equitable access to services and legal protection for the most vulnerable children.[7]
Every Child Lives in a Clean and Safe Environment
Access to basic water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services is gradually improving nationwide, although urban-rural disparities remain. Access to basic drinking water increased from 63 per cent in 2015 to 74 per cent in 2024. Rural areas remain underserved, but also recorded progress, with coverage rising from 52 per cent to 62 per cent over the same period.[8]
Basic sanitation coverage improved from 23 per cent in 2015 to 33 per cent in 2024, although rural coverage remained substantially lower at 23 per cent[9] . Open defecation persists at approximately 11 per cent nationally, increasing to over 18 per cent in rural areas (reaching up to 40 per cent in Labé[10]). Hygiene conditions remain inadequate, with only 20.5 per cent of households having handwashing facilities with soap and water.[11] In schools, deficient WASH infrastructure disproportionately affects girls: only 53 per cent of schools have toilets for girls, with most lacking water, soap and washbasins. Menstrual hygiene management remains a concern, with 78 per cent of girls disposing of sanitary pads in toilets and 6 per cent in rivers, posing health and environmental risks.[12]
Humanitarian Context
Guinea remains vulnerable to climate-related shocks, including flooding and landslides, which in 2025 caused loss of life (78 fatalities), displacement, disruption of services and livelihoods, damage to infrastructure and outbreaks of waterborne diseases, particularly in Greater Conakry These shocks highlighted the importance of strengthening disaster risk reduction, climate adaptation and shock-responsive systems to protect children and sustain development gains.

In 2025, UNICEF worked with the Government of Guinea to accelerate progress for children by strengthening systems for survival, learning, protection and social inclusion, while expanding equitable access to essential services. Compared to previous years, results reflected a shift from recovery-oriented interventions and coordination set-up towards systemic change, policy reform and institutional strengthening supported by improved governance, financing alignment and integrated approaches across sectors. UNICEF’s strong collaboration with government institutions, UN agencies, civil society, national and international NGOs and development partners, advanced national priorities under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and contributed to the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDGs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10.
Every Child Survives and Thrives
In 2025, UNICEF, in collaboration with partners, made significant contributions in health and nutrition by strengthening primary health care, expanding life-saving maternal and newborn services, improving immunization system resilience and scaling up high-impact nutrition interventions. Support focused on quality, equity and system integration, ensuring that national policies, financing mechanisms and service delivery platforms worked together to reach women and children most affected by geographic isolation, fragility and service disruptions. These efforts contributed to measurable improvements in survival and health outcomes.
Immunization and Disease Prevention
Routine immunization coverage improved through strengthened delivery, integrated outreach and cold chain resilience. According to WUENIC estimates, Penta3 coverage among children aged 0-11 months reached 63 per cent in 2025, up from 47 per cent in 2023, reversing previous stagnation, although coverage remains below national and global targets.
UNICEF supported national and subnational authorities to institutionalise integrated catch-up strategies, combining immunization with nutrition and civil registration services. Through national campaigns, 163,000 children aged 0-11 months received catch-up vaccination, 35 per cent more than in 2024, contributing to a 31 per cent reduction in zero dose and under-immunised children and more equitable coverage in hard-to-reach districts.
Disease prevention and outbreak response were intensified. In response to poliovirus circulation, 5.1 million children were vaccinated through synchronized campaigns, with 100 per cent of districts achieving at least 95 per cent coverage, up from 92 per cent in 2024. Measles outbreak response campaigns reached 1.03 million children across 13 districts, exceeding targets. Guinea also introduced the malaria vaccine in four districts, reaching 50,000 children (83 per cent coverage), demonstrating strong community acceptance and system readiness.
These gains were underpinned by immunization system strengthening and national ownership. In collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene, Gavi, WHO and other immunization partners, UNICEF supported Guinea’s return to the Vaccine Independence Initiative, securing sustainable and predictable nationwide vaccine procurement. Cold chain capacity increased, with functional refrigeration rising from 1,731 units in 2024 to 1,837 in 2025, covering 90 per cent of national needs (up from 84 per cent). KS Relief and private sector partners, including Rio Tinto, complemented government and Gavi investments by supporting service delivery and cold chain resilience in vulnerable and mining-affected areas.
Following a major fire that damaged more than half of national vaccine stocks and storage capacity, UNICEF provided rapid technical support, rehabilitated remaining cold rooms, procured essential materials and worked with the Government, and partners to mobilize US$1.5 million from GAVI to finance 10 new cold rooms, safeguarding service continuity. 
Maternal, Newborn and Child Health
Access to quality maternal and newborn care improved through sustained investments in infrastructure, training and emergency preparedness. The number of facilities providing Emergency Obstetric and Neonatal Care increased from 117 in 2024 to 147 in 2025, enabling an estimated 94 per cent of the population in targeted areas to reach life-saving services within two hours. Assisted deliveries rose by 12 per cent, reaching almost 442,000 in 2025 (an 81 per cent assisted delivery rate).
UNICEF supported the establishment and equipping of 10 neonatal care units, providing specialized care to more than 2,000 premature and low-birth-weight newborns. In addition, UNICEF-supported pediatric and maternity services supported 3,229 pregnant women at delivery and 2,266 sick children. In partnership with the Global Fund, UNICEF supported the construction and operationalization of four oxygen plants in Boke, Faranah, Kindia, Mamou regions, strengthening emergency and respiratory care for newborns and children. The oxygen plants meet the needs of the four regional hospitals and supply all health facilities within their respective regions, ensuring a continuous supply of medical oxygen for women with obstetric complications, newborns and patients experiencing respiratory distress in emergency and surgical units. Beyond service continuity, the installations generated significant cost savings by eliminating recurrent transport of oxygen cylinders from Conakry or Kankan, allowing hospitals to reallocate resources to quality-of-care improvements and essential medical equipment. These results were achieved through strong collaboration between UNICEF, regional hospitals, health authorities and partners. In parallel, training of 75 health providers in neonatal resuscitation and assessment tools improved the service quality in supported facilities.
HIV services expanded significantly through increased investments in early testing, treatment and care, as well as continued scale-up of integrated delivery within maternal, child health and community platforms. The number of HIV-positive pregnant women receiving antiretroviral therapy rose from around 6,000 in 2024 to over 20,600 in 2025, while over 33,700 children under 15 received HIV care, compared to 5,900 in 2024, reflecting a major scale-up supported by UNICEF in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, the Global Fund and civil society partners, including local associations of people living with HIV/AIDS.
At community level, use of child health services increased sharply. In 2025, 1.36 million childhood illness cases were identified and treated through community platforms, up from fewer than 800,000 cases in 2024, reflecting strengthened community health systems, expanded partnerships with local NGOs and community-based organizations, and increased caregiver trust in services.
Nutrition: scaling prevention and strengthening treatment
Preventive nutrition services expanded significantly. Integrated vitamin A supplementation alongside reached 3.79 million children aged 6-59 months in 2025, achieving 97 per cent coverage. Maternal nutrition services more than doubled, with 1.39 million pregnant women receiving integrated anemia prevention, folic acid supplementation and nutrition counselling, compared to 671,000 in 2024. 
Training in health facilities supported this expansion, with the proportion of facilities implementing growth monitoring and promotion increasing from 53 per cent in 2024 to 75 per cent in 2025. The number of children benefiting from growth monitoring rose from 165,816 to 515,521 over the same period.
Infant and Young Child Feeding promotion was strengthened through integrated community and facility platforms. In 2025, 653,564 mothers and caregivers received counselling on optimal IYCF practices from health workers, community volunteers and women’s groups across 40 convergence communes, trained with UNICEF support.
Treatment of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) improved. UNICEF supported nutrition service delivery in 438 health facilities, enabling the treatment of 18,002 children with SAM. Treatment coverage increased from 30 per cent in 2024 to 47 per cent in 2025, exceeding annual targets, while maintaining Sphere-compliant outcomes. UNICEF also supported sustainable procurement of nutrition supplies through the Nutrition Matching Fund, working with government and partners to strengthen predictability, efficiency and national ownership of nutrition supply chains.
Beyond service delivery, UNICEF strengthened the enabling environment for nutrition through policy dialogue, coordination and financing reforms. UNICEF supported implementation of the National Nutrition Policy while supporting elaboration of a new the Multisectoral Nutrition Strategic Plan, strengthening alignment across health, social protection, WASH and education sectors. Coordination was reinforced through the national SUN platform and sector working groups, contributing to more coherent multisectoral action.
Every Child Lives in a Clean and Safe Environment
UNICEF worked with the Government to expand equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services, with a stronger focus on sustainability and climate resilience. Over 57,500 people gained access to sustainable drinking water through solar-powered and rehabilitated systems. Four rural communes were certified open defecation free, enabling nearly 91,000 additional people to live in healthier environments. 
UNICEF continued to strengthen WASH services in health facilities and schools, improving infection prevention and dignity for women and girls. Gender-responsive interventions reached more than 7,300 women and adolescent girls through menstrual hygiene management in schools. 
In flood-affected areas, over 45,000 people accessed emergency WASH services including safe drinking water, hygiene promotion and WASH support to health facilities and schools. UNICEF also supported governance and accountability in the WASH sector through support to policy dissemination, Water Safety Planning and the integration of WASH priorities into national climate commitments, in coordination with sector ministries, decentralized authorities and climate partners, strengthening alignment with long-term resilience goals. 
Every Child Learns and Acquires Skills for the Future
In 2025, UNICEF consolidated gains in access to education while intensifying efforts to address the learning crisis, shifting from piloting innovations to system-oriented scale-up. Progress was marked by a significant expansion of foundational learning programmes, increased access to digital learning resources and strengthened sector governance, particularly in rural and underserved areas. These efforts were enabled by strong engagement by the Ministry of Education and close collaboration with education sector partners, including the Global Partnership for Education, strengthening system-level reform, sector coordination and sustainable financing for foundational learning and education recovery.
Expanding access and addressing barriers to enrolment
UNICEF intensified advocacy, social mobilization and targeted support to address persistent barriers to school enrolment and retention, particularly for girls and children from vulnerable households. Private sector engagement was strengthened through a partnership with Orange Guinea, which supported nationwide back-to-school advocacy and community mobilization efforts. The campaign mobilized a wide range of political, religious, and community leaders at national and decentralized levels, significantly enhancing community outreach and re-enrolment efforts, and leading to the identification of more than 100,000 out-of-school children through the engagement of local authorities, community leaders, and youth representatives.
 
Advocacy messages on the importance of education and school retention, especially for girls, were disseminated through voice and text messages in four local languages and amplified by UNICEF Guinea’s Champion for Children’s Rights, footballer Naby Keita. These efforts were supported by partnerships with civil society organizations, faith-based actors and local education authorities, strengthening community ownership and sustainability. Targeted support included the distribution of 4,000 school kits, helping to mitigate financial barriers to schooling for the most vulnerable.
Scaling up foundational learning and remedial education
Addressing persistent gaps in foundational skills remained a central priority in 2025. UNICEF supported a major scale-up of remedial education through the Ministry of Education’s Programme for the Improvement of Basic Skills, expanding the Teaching at the Right Level approach from 18 schools in 2024 to 90 schools in 2025, benefiting 13,000 children across six regions (an almost tenfold increase since 2022). Implementation was enhanced by the training and deployment of 300 additional facilitators, mentors and supervisors at school and community levels. Learning outcomes improved substantially in supported schools, with reading proficiency increasing from 14 per cent at baseline to 66 per cent, and basic numeracy skills showing similar gains. 
These results reinforced the evidence base for remedial education and informed national policy decisions, including the expanded use of diagnostic assessments of foundational skills at the start of the 2025 school year, with UNICEF working closely with the Ministry of Education and partners, including the Global Partnership for Education, to translate evidence into policy and scale-up decisions. UNICEF further bolstered these efforts by facilitating the training of more than 400 elementary school inspectors on the assessment tool, laying the groundwork for national scale-up of foundational learning approaches beyond pilot areas.
Advancing digital learning and system-wide connectivity
Digital learning expanded further in 2025, with an additional 54,000 primary students accessing digital learning resources through the Learning Passport, addressing persistent shortages of textbooks and teaching materials, particularly in rural schools. Thirteen pilot schools were connected to the internet with UNICEF support, reinforcing school-level readiness for digital learning. 
Sustained advocacy and technical assistance contributed to a major policy breakthrough: the launch of a government-led national school connectivity programme, in partnership with Giga, a joint programme by UNICEF and the UN’s International Telecommunication Unit (ITU) which aims to connect all the world’s schools to the internet. In Guinea, this partnership aims to connect 2,200 schools and benefit nearly one million students and teachers, marking a shift from project-based pilots towards national system strengthening, positioning digital learning as a core component of education reform.
Alternative learning pathways for adolescents
Recognizing the high number of out-of-school adolescents, UNICEF supported alternative education pathways in 2025 through targeted skills development initiatives, including providing a mobile vocational training unit focused on industrial trades, bringing practical skills training closer to street-connected children and out-of-school youth. This initiative complemented formal education interventions by offering pathways to social and economic reintegration for adolescents at most risk of exclusion.
Every Child is Protected from Violence, Exploitation and Abuse
In 2025, UNICEF supported transformative advances in child protection, combining landmark legal reforms with expanded prevention and response services. Progress was characterized by stronger constitutional safeguards, improved accountability for harmful practices and a substantial increase in the reach and quality of protection services, despite a constrained operating environment.
Strengthening the legal and policy framework for child protection
UNICEF supported the Government of Guinea to advance a more coherent, preventive and accountable child protection framework in 2025. Through sustained advocacy with government counterparts, parliamentarians, civil society and child-led platforms, including engagement with the Children’s Parliament and the Young Girls’ Leaders Club, UNICEF contributed to ensuring that the new Constitution explicitly prohibits female genital mutilation (FGM) and strengthens protections against child exploitation, neglect, abuse and trafficking. This represents a major shift from policy-level commitments to constitutional guarantees, significantly reinforcing the legal foundation for prevention and enforcement. 
The adoption of the revised National Child Protection Policy (2026-2035), with a costed implementation plan, further reinforced a preventive and multisectoral approach. It emphasises the importance of reinforced community mechanisms, workforce development and institutional capacities at national and decentralized levels. In parallel, UNICEF supported the development and validation of a national roadmap to end violence against children through 2029, aligned with Guinea’s commitments under the Pathfinding Initiative and the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children.
Preventing and responding to harmful practices
Despite persistent social norms sustaining harmful practices, 2025 saw progress in accountability and enforcement. Public declaration ceremonies of abandonment of FGM and child marriage were organised in 56 communities, while community monitoring mechanisms remained active, with 113 cases of FGM or child marriage reported or prevented. Notably, Guinea recorded its first-ever prison sentences related to FGM, with four individuals convicted, marking a historic milestone in enforcement supported by strengthened coordination between justice actors, social services and community mechanisms.
Protection services for adolescent girls expanded, with 23,690 girls aged 10-19 benefiting from child marriage prevention and intervention services, compared to 15,456 in 2024 and 8,285 in 2023. These gains reflect cumulative investments in community structures, girls’ platforms and women’s groups across all eight governorates. In addition, 15,927 girls were identified and protected from FGM, representing a substantial increase compared to previous years.
Expanding access to integrated protection services
Access to integrated child protection services improved substantially. In 2025, UNICEF strengthened referral pathways in coordination with child welfare inspectorates, forensic medicine services and the Bar Association. As a result, 3,011 children (1,965 girls), primarily survivors of sexual violence, received integrated protection services, compared to 370 children in 2024. Overall, more than 151,000 vulnerable children (83,600 girls) were protected from violence, exploitation and abuse. These efforts were implemented in partnership with four government partner (PN-RAVEC, DNE, DNESPJJ, MPFE) three national NGOs (FMK, APRODEJ, CJFLG) and two international NGO (TDH, Tostan) working towards improving access to quality and integrated services for children.  
Strengthening community-led prevention and social norms change
UNICEF continued to invest in community-led approaches to shift harmful social norms and strengthen protective behaviours. Over 711,000 people (412,000 women and girls) were reached through community-based prevention efforts and social norms change initiatives (dialogues, religious engagement, peer education, radio and social media), an increase of 26 per cent compared to 2024. Girl-led platforms and women’s groups played a central role in prevention efforts, supported by partnerships with national NGOs and decentralized government services. 
In 2025, 141 local girls’ associations were supported, building on the expansion of adolescent girls’ platforms in previous years, while a national consultation with 100 adolescent girls informed regional priorities on gender-based violence, FGM and child marriage.
Innovative approaches were introduced to strengthen advocacy and outreach, including training adolescent girls on the use of digital tools and artificial intelligence for social media communication on harmful practices, while reinforcing online safety and fact-checking. These initiatives complemented traditional community engagement and expanded the reach of prevention messaging.
Advancing birth registration and legal identity
Progress in birth registration slowed in 2025, reflecting a strategic shift toward system consolidation and reaching harder-to-reach children amid funding constraints and institutional reforms. A total of 109,083 children under one (42,034 girls) were registered in 2025, compared to 269,781 in 2024. 
UNICEF leveraged government-led digitization reforms, working closely with civil registration authorities, health services and technical partners to strengthen the foundations of the civil registration system, by supporting the rollout of a national digital civil registration application, with 74 per cent of municipalities now regularly transmitting data, laying the groundwork for improved interoperability, sustainability and coverage. 
UNICEF worked with the government to strengthen interoperability between civil registration, health and nutrition systems, fully integrating birth registration into immunization and vitamin A campaigns. During the recent nationwide campaign, 4,185 children without birth certificates were identified, leading to the issuance of 2,671 birth certificates, despite delays linked to judicial constraints during the constitutional referendum period.
Protection in fragile and political contexts
In anticipation of the elections, UNICEF supported advocacy and awareness-raising activities through the Children's Parliament, platforms for adolescent girls, and youth groups, reaching more than 19,000 people. Advocacy messages focused on peaceful civic participation, prevention of violence against children, promotion of girls’ leadership in community dialogue, and awareness of risks related to child exploitation, abuse and harmful practices during political transitions. 
These efforts were reinforced through Peacebuilding Fund-supported initiatives, which expanded safe spaces for adolescent girls and young women to engage in peacebuilding and civic processes, strengthened intergenerational dialogue and contributed to reducing risks of youth instrumentalization and gender-based violence in fragile contexts. Collectively, these interventions complemented broader peacebuilding initiatives and contributed to peaceful electoral processes in 2025, with no reported involvement of children in election-related violence.
Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life
Guinea strengthened the foundations for more equitable access to social protection and inclusive services for children and women. Social protection coverage increased from 4.6 per cent in 2024 to 5.3 per cent in 2025, supported by improved fiscal governance, child-sensitive budgeting and coordination between national and local levels. These advances were facilitated by sustained policy dialogue and system reform efforts, together with the World Bank, contributing to financing alignment, institutional strengthening and coordination across social sectors, particularly in social protection, decentralization and service delivery reforms benefiting children.
Decentralization reforms progressed, strengthening inclusive local governance and service delivery for children. Guinea launched a nationwide revision of Local Development Plans and Annual Investment Plans across all 375 municipalities. UNICEF supported systematic integration of priorities related to health, nutrition, immunization, WASH, education, child protection and social protection into these plans, improving coherence between local needs, budgets and service delivery. Children’s participation in local governance was reinforced, notably through immersion visits by members of the Children’s Parliament during the revision of local plans, enabling children to engage directly in budget dialogues and advocate social sector investments.
In parallel, Guinea made substantive progress in strengthening the policy environment, linking social equity and child protection. The adoption of the National Child Protection Policy (PNPE) and the National Roadmap to End Violence Against Children (2026–2035) reinforced the foundations for inclusive human capital development, recognizing that protection from violence, exploitation and abuse is essential for children to benefit from education, health and social protection investments. UNICEF supported policy dialogue to ensure alignment with child-sensitive social protection, decentralization and service delivery reforms, contributing to a more integrated approach to equity and inclusion.
In addition, the adoption in September 2025 of a Law on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, introducing measures to improve access to services, reduce discrimination and establish a dedicated support fund. UNICEF contributed through policy dialogue to ensure alignment with international standards and child rights principles, in coordination with government institutions, organizations of persons with disabilities and development partners.
Coverage of cash transfer programmes expanded, reaching 131,646 households by the third quarter of 2025, benefitting an estimated 350,893 children, with women receiving transfers in 87 per cent of households. UNICEF strengthened targeting quality and equity through technical support to the Unified Social Registry, working alongside government counterparts and World bank partners, ensuring that child-related vulnerability criteria informed beneficiary identification. Complementary support through the Social Development and Indigence Fund enabled social assistants to monitor the living conditions of approximately 30,000 vulnerable children and facilitate referrals to health, nutrition, education and protection services.
Cross-cutting Integration and Efficiency
Across sectors, strengthened coordination mechanisms shifted from set-up to effective functioning in 2025, enabling joint planning, monitoring and accountability across health, nutrition, WASH and civil registration systems. Integrated national campaigns demonstrated the value of interoperability: vitamin A supplementation reached 3.9 million children and was delivered alongside catch-up vaccination for 163,000 under-immunized children and birth registration for 35,937 children. Joint delivery generated efficiency gains of nearly US$200,000, which were reinvested in routine services, demonstrating value for money. 
Gender equity and adolescence were systematically integrated through implementation of UNICEF’s gender strategic commitments and the girl-intentional programming approach. UNICEF also provided technical support to the development and operationalization of the National Gender Policy 2025-2029, strengthening institutional frameworks for gender-responsive planning and coordination across sectors. These efforts included strengthening adolescent girls’ participation platforms, notably through girl-led networks such as the Club des Jeunes Filles Leaders de Guinée, expanding services addressing harmful practices, promoting gender-responsive social protection delivery and scaling gender-responsive WASH and education interventions tailored to adolescent girls’ needs. 
UNICEF played a key role in strengthening the meaningful participation and leadership of adolescent girls at the Dakar summit. Guinean adolescent girls actively participated in consultations and helped define national priorities. The Dakar Declaration and priorities were officially presented to the Minister for the of Women promotion in the presence of the Japanese Ambassador to Guinea and other sectoral ministers.
Youth engagement through U-Reporters further advanced awareness campaigns, peer-to-peer communication and community dialogue, contributing to social cohesion and strengthening trust between young people, communities and service providers. Collectively, these approaches contributed to reducing gender-related barriers across sectors and enhanced accountability for gender equality outcomes within national systems.
System-level integration and efficiency gains were further reinforced through policy dialogue with development partners, including the World Bank, supporting alignment of financing, governance reforms and cross-sector coordination in health, nutrition, WASH, education and social protection.
Emergency response and development programming were increasingly aligned. UNICEF supported shock-responsive systems in health, nutrition, WASH and social protection, strengthening preparedness and continuity of services during floods and other shocks. Partnerships with government, UN agencies, civil society and donors were central to achieving results at scale, with Regular Resources playing a catalytic role in enabling system strengthening, integration and rapid response.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
Despite significant progress in 2025, UNICEF and partners continued to face structural and contextual challenges that constrained the pace, equity and sustainability of results, particularly for children in hard-to-reach and underserved areas.
Sustaining effective multisectoral coordination at scale. While 2025 marked a shift from establishing coordination platforms to supporting their effective functioning, translating coordination into consistently joint planning, financing and implementation across sectors remains uneven. Integrated approaches, such as combined vitamin A supplementation, catch-up vaccination and birth registration, demonstrated clear efficiencies and impact, but these models are not yet systematically institutionalized across all regions or programmes. In nutrition, limited operational linkages with WASH, education and social protection continue to constrain a holistic response to malnutrition, particularly in high-burden areas.
Financing constraints and sustainability risks. Despite progress in influencing government decisions to finance vaccines and nutrition supplies, overall fiscal space for social sectors remains limited. Heavy reliance on external financing, particularly for routine immunization, nutrition commodities, WASH infrastructure and community health, exposes programmes to funding volatility and affects continuity of services. At subnational level, delays in fund disbursement and limited budget execution capacity further constrained timely implementation, especially in remote prefectures.
Human resource gaps and uneven service quality across sectors. While 2025 saw significant investments in capacity-building (such as for community health workers, nutrition service providers and social workers) shortages of trained personnel at facility and community levels continue to limit coverage and quality. High turnover, competing demands on frontline workers and limited incentives affect service continuity, particularly in geographically isolated areas. In education and child protection, insufficient staffing at decentralized levels slowed the rollout of reforms and limited supervision and monitoring.
Geographic inequities and access barriers. Children and women in remote, hard-to-reach and underserved regions continue to face barriers to accessing essential services due to distance, poor infrastructure and limited service availability. While community-based platforms helped mitigate these barriers, as evidenced by the sharp increase in childhood illness detection and treatment at community level, facility-based access remains constrained in several regions, particularly for maternal nutrition, adolescent health and WASH services.
Uneven data availability and use. While digital platforms and monitoring systems expanded in 2025, gaps persist in real-time, disaggregated data, particularly at subnational levels, limiting the ability to consistently track equity gaps, monitor service quality and rapidly adapt programming. In child protection and education, delayed or incomplete data affected evidence-based planning and accountability.
Lessons Learned
Several critical lessons for accelerating results for children emerged during the implementation of UNICEF-supported interventions in 2025:
Integrated, multisectoral delivery enhances efficiency and impact. Integrated campaign delivery, combining nutrition, immunization and civil registration, demonstrated clear cost savings of about 1 dollar per child to support routine vitamin A supplementation in Labe region, expanded reach to under-immunized children, and improved service uptake. These approaches not only increased coverage but also strengthened systems by reducing duplication and maximizing limited resources.
Community-based platforms are essential for equity. Strengthening community health and nutrition systems, through partnerships with local NGOs, women’s groups and community volunteers, proved decisive in reaching children in hard-to-reach areas. The dramatic increase in childhood illness identification and treatment at community level underscores the effectiveness of proximity-based services in improving early detection, referrals and caregiver trust.
Domestic financing advocacy delivers results when paired with technical support. Progress in vaccine financing and nutrition supply procurement shows that policy dialogue, when supported by technical assistance and evidence, can translate into concrete financing decisions. Sustained engagement is required, however, to ensure predictability and expansion of domestic funding across social sectors.
Budgeting reforms are key levers for sustainability. Progress toward programme- and performance-based budgeting, supported by UNICEF through training and policy dialogue, enabled seven ministries to strengthen medium-term expenditure frameworks aligned with results for children. Engagement with the Ministry of Budget helped identify execution bottlenecks and informed corrective measures in the 2025 Supplementary Finance Law, including increased allocations for free schooling. These experiences confirmed that sustained technical assistance and evidence-based advocacy can translate macro-fiscal gains into child-focused investments.
Culturally grounded behaviour change approaches strengthen outcomes. The development and testing of national, micronutrient-rich complementary feeding recipes demonstrated that locally adapted solutions enhance acceptance and uptake of recommended practices, supporting more sustainable behaviour change.
Localized, inclusive communication strengthens social mobilization. The 2025 back-to-school campaign showed that localized outreach (community dialogues, rural radio and messaging in national languages) was more effective than reliance on national media alone. Youth engagement through U-Report   and mobile messaging expanded peer-to-peer advocacy and enhanced credibility at community level, contributing to the identification of more than 100,000 out-of-school children.
Preparedness and rapid response are critical to service continuity in the event of shocks. The rapid recovery of immunization services following the vaccine warehouse storage fire demonstrated that investments in preparedness, contingency planning and system redundancy are as critical as investments in coverage expansion. Strengthened cold chain infrastructure and diversified storage options, combined with rapid response actions, enabled the system to absorb shocks without major service interruptions, reinforcing the importance of resilience-focused system strengthening.
Future Outlook
Building on lessons from 2025, UNICEF in Guinea will continue to adapt its programme strategies to accelerate equitable results and strengthen systems for children, guided by the 2026–2029 Strategic Plan and the commitment to leave no child behind.
Deepening integration to reach the most marginalized. Institutionalizing integrated service delivery will be a priority, with a focus on embedding joint planning, budgeting and implementation across health, nutrition, WASH, education and child protection, particularly for high-impact campaigns and community platforms. These efforts will further integrate gender-responsive and adolescent-sensitive approaches, including girl-intentional programming and meaningful adolescent participation mechanisms to address structural barriers affecting access and utilization of services.
Strengthening sustainable financing for social sectors. UNICEF will deepen engagement with government, development partners and the private sector to expand domestic resource mobilization, reduce reliance on external financing and improve budget execution at national and subnational levels.
Advancing domestic financing and budget execution for children. UNICEF will intensify policy dialogue and technical support to ensure that gains in public financial management translate into predictable, well-executed social sector budgets. This includes continued advocacy for sustainable financing of immunization, nutrition supplies and free schooling, and support to decentralized authorities to improve absorption and execution capacity.
Expanding and professionalizing the community workforce. Capacity strengthening will be critical to sustaining gains in access and equity. UNICEF will continue to support training, supervision and performance monitoring for community-based providers, with particular attention to underserved regions.
Enhancing data systems for adaptive management. UNICEF will continue to invest in digital platforms, data integration and subnational monitoring to enable timely adjustments and improved tracking of equity-focused results to support better decision-making and accountability.
Scaling evidence-based education and youth engagement approaches. Based on the success of localized social mobilization and remedial learning models, UNICEF will support national scale-up of foundational learning approaches and inclusive back-to-school strategies, while further leveraging youth-led participation platforms and digital engagement tools to sustain engagement and accountability.
Institutionalizing coordination and implementation capacity. UNICEF will focus on consolidating multisectoral coordination mechanisms and strengthening decentralized implementation capacity to ensure that policy reforms, sector strategies and flagship programmes translate into measurable improvements in children’s lives.
Through these actions, UNICEF Guinea will build on 2025 progress to strengthen systems, scale integrated solutions and ensure that the most marginalized children benefit from resilient, high-quality and sustainable services.

In 2025, UNICEF Guinea-Bissau implemented a US$15 million programme, operating in a fragile environment shaped by political instability, structural economic vulnerability and high exposure to climate-related risks, all of which continued to constrain progress for children. Institutional capacity remained weak, fiscal space limited and inequalities deep, particularly for children in rural areas, adolescents and the poorest households. By the penultimate year of the Country Programme,  cumulative expenditure had reached over US$43 million of the planned US$45 million, reflecting sustained programme absorption and implementation capacity.

  
The most significant political development of the year occurred in late November, when a military coup resulted in the removal of the elected government and suspension of the constitution. ECOWAS, the African Union and the CPLP suspended Guinea-Bissau and imposed targeted sanctions, deepening diplomatic isolation and further constraining access to external financing and development assistance. While programme implementation continued, the rupture increased uncertainty for planning, engagement with national counterparts and resource mobilization.
  
Earlier in the year, the then Government finalized the Plano Nacional de Desenvolvimento (PND) 2026–2035, providing a long-term framework aligned with the UNICEF Country Programme 2022–2026 and the UNSDCF  2022–2026 through shared priorities on child rights, human capital and inclusive social services. Although implementation remains constrained by political fragility and fiscal pressures, the PND offers a reference framework for child-relevant social sector reforms.
  
Demographic pressures remain significant. The population reached approximately 2.2 million in 2024 and is projected to exceed 2.6 million by 2040. Children under 18 account for more than half of the population, while high fertility (4.7 births per woman) and continued growth place sustained pressure on services. Urbanization remains limited, with 64 per cent of the population living in rural areas, contributing to persistent service gaps.
  
Poverty is widespread and deeply multidimensional.  More than 50 per cent of the population live below the national poverty line, and over 52 per cent of children experience at least three overlapping deprivations across health, nutrition, education, housing, water and sanitation. Deprivation is most severe among young children: 79 per cent of children aged 0–4 experience four to six deprivations, and 95 per cent of children aged 5–14 experience four to seven, particularly in rural and eastern regions.
  
Macroeconomic conditions remain volatile. GDP per capita reached approximately US$1,008 in 2024, while dependence on cashew production – accounting for over 90 per cent of export earnings – left rural households vulnerable to price fluctuations. In 2025, this contributed to reduced spending on food, health care and education and to children being withdrawn from school during the cashew harvesting season to support family  labour.
  
Fiscal constraints remain among the most binding limitations for children. Total public expenditure stands at around 20–21 per cent of GDP, with social sector allocations remaining low: education accounts for about 11 per cent of total public expenditure, public health 8 per cent, and social protection 0.9 per cent of GDP, of which only 0.2 per cent is domestically financed. IMF projections indicate a further 1.9 per cent of GDP decline in public spending by 2028, narrowing space for essential social investments.  Social protection spending remains below 1 per cent of GDP, with most non-pension programmes reliant on external financing.
  
Climate change continues to act as a systemic risk multiplier. Guinea-Bissau ranks 159th out of 163 countries on UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index, and around 40 per cent of the population lives in low-lying coastal areas exposed to flooding, erosion and salinization.  While no major disasters were recorded in 2025, recurrent localized flooding and environmental degradation continued to disrupt services and exacerbate malnutrition. The United Nations Special Rapporteur underscored the need to integrate climate adaptation into water management and strengthen contingency planning for droughts and irregular rainfall.
  
Child survival and development indicators remain among the weakest globally. Under-five mortality is estimated at around 90 deaths per 1,000 live births, with neonatal mortality accounting for approximately 43 per cent of under-five deaths. Maternal mortality remains high at 603 deaths per 100,000 live births, and only 54 per cent of births are attended by skilled health personnel. HIV prevalence stands at 2.3 per cent among adults, rising to 3.8 per cent among adolescents, among the highest in the region. Immunization coverage has recovered since the pandemic but remains fragile, with an estimated 14,000 children zero-dose or under-immunized. Nutrition outcomes remain severe, with 28 per cent of children under five stunted and anaemia affecting more than half of young children and many adolescent girls.
  
Education outcomes remain highly fragile. Over 27 per cent of children aged 6–11 are out of school, while completion rates are among the lowest globally (27 per cent primary; 17 per cent lower secondary), with poorer outcomes in rural areas and among girls and the poorest households. Foundational learning is critically weak: only 12 per cent of Grade 2 students demonstrate basic literacy and 8 per cent basic numeracy, while 95 per cent of Grade 5 teachers lack mastery in Portuguese and 98 per cent in mathematics. Chronic underinvestment persists, with education receiving around 8 per cent of the national budget in 2024, of which 90 per cent is absorbed by salaries, limiting quality improvements.
  
Child protection risks remain widespread. Birth registration among children under five stands at 46 per cent, harmful practices persist – including 26 per cent of women aged 20–24 married before 18 and 30 per cent of girls aged 0–14 subjected to female genital mutilation – and violence against children remains prevalent though under-reported.  Social protection coverage is estimated at around 2.5 per cent of the population, far below the regional average, with benefits insufficient to mitigate shocks.
  
Overall, the 2025 context for children in Guinea-Bissau was defined by rapid population growth, deep multidimensional poverty, constrained public financing, extreme climate vulnerability and fragile institutions. These factors shape both the results achieved and the limits of delivery at scale, underscoring the importance of systems strengthening, equity-focused approaches and sustained partnerships to reach the most disadvantaged children and adolescents.

In 2025, UNICEF’s programme in Guinea-Bissau advanced priority results for children in close alignment with national development priorities, the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the UNICEF Country Programme Document (CPD) 2022–2026. Interventions remained relevant and coherent, aligned withnthe National Development Plan, sector strategies and Guinea-Bissau’s commitments under the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

  
Operating in a fragile and resource-constrained context, UNICEF focused on selected contributions that strengthened national and subnational systems, expanded equitable access to essential services and reinforced enabling conditions for child rights in health and nutrition, WASH, education, child protection, social protection and social and behaviour  change. Results were strongest where preventive services, local capacity development and community engagement were aligned, while progress dependent on structural reform, financing and decentralized functionality remained constrained.
  
Results in Child survival and development, including WASH, reflected mixed progress across service delivery, prevention and system performance. Several public health milestones were sustained or exceeded, while coverage, continuity and equity gaps persisted, particularly at subnational level. UNICEF’s contribution centred on integrated approaches linking health, nutrition and WASH, strengthened planning and coordination, and targeted support to sustain essential services in priority areas, supported through technical assistance, supply chain management, decentralized planning and community-based delivery models, combined with social and behaviour change (SBC) approaches. At community level, integrated management of childhood illness supported continued access to essential services, with more than 10,000 children under five receiving treatment for malaria, malnutrition, pneumonia and diarrhoea through UNICEF-supported community platforms.
  
At outcome level, progress on core maternal and child health indicators remained below national targets. Skilled birth attendance reached 36.41 per cent against a target of 60 per cent, indicating continued barriers to facility-based delivery, especially in rural and hard-to-reach areas. Routine immunization coverage similarly fell short:  coverage of the third dose of a DTP-containing vaccine among children aged 0–11 months reached 59 per cent against a target of 90 per cent. In parallel, campaigns achieved high reach, including measles and rubella vaccination, yellow fever immunization of over 229,000 children, and near-universal coverage in the national polio campaign, demonstrating capacity to deliver time-bound preventive interventions at scale. However, no districts reached at least 80 per cent DTP3 coverage against a target of full national coverage, highlighting persistent challenges in continuity, follow-up and decentralized delivery. 
  
Several high-impact achievements were sustained.  Guinea-Bissau maintained interruption of wild poliovirus transmission and verified elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus, supported by UNICEF’s technical assistance, vaccine procurement and cold chain management, and coordination with government and partners. In prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, 85.34 per cent of pregnant women living with HIV received antiretroviral treatment, exceeding the annual target and reflecting effective targeted service delivery combined with strengthened referral and follow-up. 
  
Nutrition outcomes followed a similar trajectory of strong preventive reach alongside slower progress on behavioural and outcome indicators. Treatment quality for severe acute malnutrition remained within international standards, with an IMAM cure rate of 77.7 per cent and low mortality. Vitamin A supplementation reached 196,576 children aged 6–59 months during the second semester, exceeding the annual target and reflecting operational capacity to deliver large-scale preventive services through integrated platforms.
  
By contrast, progress on infant and young child feeding practices remained limited. Exclusive breastfeeding among infants aged 0–5 months reached 59.3 per cent against a target of 65 per cent, and minimum dietary diversity among children aged 6–23 months remained low at 12.5 per cent against a target of 18 per cent. Stunting among children under five was reported at 28 per cent, above the national target, underscoring persistent chronic malnutrition linked to food insecurity, poverty, limited service quality and social norms, and the need for sustained multisectoral action linking nutrition, food systems, social protection and behaviour change.
  
Under health systems strengthening, UNICEF prioritized improved planning, coordination and institutional capacity. The number of health regions with operational plans developed and budgeted reached 10, indicating near-national coverage. While the target value recorded in the monitoring system was zero, suggesting a configuration limitation, the reported result points to strengthened subnational planning and improved alignment between planning and resource allocation. 
  
Immunization system performance demonstrated both progress and continuing challenges. The Effective Vaccine Management composite score reached 68 per cent, reflecting improvements supported through investments in logistics, cold chain and capacity building, while remaining below global benchmarks. Vaccine availability was sustained, with no stock-outs of key antigens reported at district level. However, service continuity remained a concern: the dropout rate between the first and third doses of a DTP-containing vaccine was 24 per cent, and urban DTP3 coverage reached 59 per cent against a target of 85 per cent. 
  
In 2025, UNICEF supported progress in WASH service quality, with stronger advances in community-level behaviour change and institutional settings than in administrative-level certification. A total of 31,175 people were living in newly certified open-defecation-free (ODF) communities, reflecting the effectiveness of Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS), sustained social mobilization and engagement with local authorities and community leaders. As a result, the proportion of the population practising open defecation declined to 3 per cent, exceeding the annual target. In parallel, 57,925 people were reached through CLTS sensitization activities, reinforcing hygiene and sanitation behaviours and reducing environmental contamination and waterborne disease risks.
  
Despite strong community readiness, progress in formal administrative-level ODF certification remained limited, with only one region declared ODF against a target of three. Delays in the government-led validation process affected follow-through, underscoring the need for sustained institutional engagement to translate community-level gains into certified outcomes.
  
In institutional settings, results were more pronounced. In the education sector, 52 schools were supported with inclusive sanitation facilities, including separate latrines for girls and boys, accessibility features for children with disabilities and facilities responsive to menstrual hygiene needs. Hygiene promotion activities reached 7,234 students, including 3,814 girls, contributing to safer and more inclusive learning environments. In the health sector, 135 health centres  were assessed for WASH and energy functionality, with targeted rehabilitation of water, sanitation and energy systems in selected facilities. Hygiene materials and infection prevention and control (IPC) communication tools were provided to strengthen service quality for women and children, and 19 health care facilities received targeted improvements to basic WASH services.
  
UNICEF also advanced system strengthening and climate resilience. A sector-wide climate risk assessment was completed with government and partners, strengthening the evidence base for climate-informed WASH planning, while technical consultations supported the definition of priorities for the forthcoming national WASH policy. Climate-resilient infrastructure investments complemented behaviour change efforts, including construction of 260 climate-resilient community latrines designed to withstand flooding and environmental stress. Integration of WASH and nutrition interventions continued in high-risk communities through combined hygiene, water and caregiving approaches. Attention to gender and inclusion remained central, with menstrual health and hygiene education reaching 19,668 women and girls, including school-aged girls and persons with disabilities.
  
Overall, UNICEF’s WASH contribution in 2025 demonstrated the effectiveness of integrated, community-based and systems-oriented approaches, while highlighting constraints related to institutional capacity, certification processes and service sustainability that will require continued investment and partnership.
  
Results under Access to learning reflected mixed progress across early childhood, primary and lower secondary education, with stronger performance in system strengthening and participation indicators than in learning outcomes and inclusion of out-of-school children. UNICEF’s contribution focused on sector coordination, policy engagement, capacity development and targeted support to early learning, basic education and alternative pathways. In total, 8,364 children accessed UNICEF-supported learning opportunities, including 7,835 enrolled in pre-primary education and 500 participating in accelerated learning programmes.
  
At early childhood level, access expanded but remained below annual targets. Attendance in early childhood education  programmes among children aged 36–59 months reached 24 per cent against a target of 27 per cent, while the gross enrolment ratio in pre-primary education also stood at 24 per cent. These results reflect gradual expansion alongside constraints related to infrastructure, workforce availability and financing, particularly outside urban centres.
  
At primary and lower secondary levels, participation indicators showed partial progress. The primary education net attendance rate reached 70 per cent against a target of 76 per cent, while the proportion of out-of-school children of primary and lower-secondary school age remained high at 25 per cent. Progression through the system remained constrained: the gross intake ratio to the last grade of lower secondary education reached 43 per cent against a target of 47 per cent, highlighting challenges in retention, completion and transition for children affected by poverty, distance and household vulnerability.
  
Learning outcomes remained the most constrained area. The percentage of children in Grades 2–3 and 5–6 achieving minimum proficiency in reading was 23 per cent against a target of 52 per cent, while minimum proficiency in mathematics was 5 per cent against a target of 25 per cent. These results underscore the gap between access and learning and the need for sustained investment in teaching quality, instructional materials, curriculum implementation and learning assessment, particularly in early grades.
  
At output level, UNICEF-supported system  strengthening and capacity development showed stronger performance. Targets  related to education sector planning and coordination were fully achieved.  The annual target for teachers trained in child-centred and inclusive  pedagogy was met. To strengthen instructional quality, 4,282 teachers were  supported to apply classroom assessment practices aligned with national  regulations.
  
Support to alternative and accelerated education  programmes also met planned targets, indicating that enabling structures for second-chance learning are in place. Complementary distance-learning approaches reached 1,555 children through radio-based lessons, with 216 broadcasts delivered to support learning continuity in hard-to-reach and crisis-affected settings. However, enrolment of out-of-school children into alternative pathways remained below target, suggesting demand-side barriers and outreach limitations. Meanwhile, accelerated learning programmes provided structured second-chance pathways, though enrolment remained below the scale required to significantly reduce exclusion.
  
Overall, UNICEF’s contribution in education in 2025 reinforced foundational system improvements and institutional capacity. While planning and capacity investments are progressing, learning quality and inclusion outcomes remain constrained and will require sustained, multi-year focus and stronger decentralized implementation.
  
Results for Child protection reflected mixed progress across systems strengthening and prevention, with several milestones achieved or exceeded alongside continued constraints in institutionalization and subnational functionality. UNICEF’s contribution focused on strengthening policy frameworks, standard-setting, data systems and coordination mechanisms, while sustaining large-scale prevention and response through partnerships with government and civil society.
  
Under systems strengthening, progress was made in the availability and use of administrative data. Birth registration services were expanded, with 40,306 children receiving free birth certificates, including 20,085 children aged 0–7 registered through interoperability with the health sector. The milestone on routine collection and publication of key child protection data was reported as achieved in principle but rated partially achieved, indicating uneven consistency, coverage and use.
  
Service delivery was extended through community outreach, enabling 3,461 children in hard-to-reach areas to obtain birth certificates and supporting registration of 8,760 children before age one.  Progress on interoperable information management followed planned sequencing, with development continuing towards end-of-cycle targets. By end-2025, 60 health facilities were providing free birth registration services, progressively transitioning to the digital SIREC system.
  
At subnational level, UNICEF supported practical system building through case management, coordination and data initiatives.  While the milestone on functioning local multi-sectoral mechanisms was not met, national case management standard operating procedures for violence against children were achieved. Response services handled 962 cases of violence against children, supported by rehabilitation, equipping and staffing of five regional child protection units with newly recruited social workers. Results exceeded targets for piloting disability-inclusive data systems, with eight regions covered against a target of four.
  
Under prevention of violence and harmful social norms, results were strong in reach and engagement. Although the milestone on costed and funded national action plans or strategies to end child marriage was not achieved, 41,930 people participated actively in evidence-based interventions addressing social norms, 14,430 adolescent girls received prevention and/or response support, and 18,864 girls and women received prevention and/or response services. Prevention efforts reached 83,203 people across 168 communities, contributing to 40 communities publicly declaring the abandonment of female genital mutilation. Parenting programmes engaged 6,361 caregivers to strengthen protective family environments, while highlighting the need for institutionalization and predictable financing for scale and sustainability.
  
Results in 2025 reflected limited measurable progress in expanding coverage of social protection for children, alongside stronger performance in policy development and selected institutional mechanisms. UNICEF’s contribution focused on supporting policy frameworks, coordination structures and system readiness, within a context of constrained fiscal space and limited administrative capacity.
  
Outcome-level data on children living in poverty  were not available for 2025. At output level, coverage-related results  remained extremely limited: the proportion of children covered by government  cash transfer programmes remained at zero per cent, and data on households  benefiting from new or expanded programmes were not available. Progress on  public financing for social sectors was rated partially achieved.
  
By contrast, results related to policy frameworks and institutional arrangements were stronger. UNICEF supported the official launch of the National Social Protection Policy (NSPP), marking a transition from policy formulation to early implementation of a more coherent and inclusive framework.
