Technical support focused on strengthening interministerial coordination and embedding shock-responsive features, including capacity development for national civil protection actors and joint assessments of emergency preparedness, contributing to improved institutional readiness to respond to climate- and shock-related risks affecting vulnerable households. While milestones related to the existence of a national social protection policy and inclusion mechanisms were fully achieved, operationalization remained constrained by political instability, high turnover of senior officials and limited fiscal space; several coordination and capacity-related indicators lacked finalized 2025 data.
  
Regular Resources played an enabling role by  providing flexibility to sustain SBC interventions, strengthen partner  capacity and maintain accountability mechanisms across sectors. The principal  challenge remains translating policy readiness and institutional foundations  into funded, scalable programmes capable of delivering sustained benefits for  children living in poverty.
  
Across sectors, SBC and community engagement functioned as a cross-cutting enabler, supporting service uptake, prevention outcomes and accountability to affected populations. In 2025, all planned indicators were achieved or exceeded. SBC capacity-building initiatives reached 3,709 partners and stakeholders, and the complaints and feedback mechanism received 11,098 calls. The Linha Saúde 24h helpline strengthened service linkages, with 7,377 valid cases referred in 2025, including 4,367 youth cases, and GBV-related calls referred to protection services.
  
SBC contributed to improved uptake of priority public health services when embedded within national and community-based platforms. Technical support to social mobilization for the national yellow fever vaccination campaign contributed to 84 per cent coverage, reaching approximately 1.7 million people, while SBC support to the seasonal malaria chemoprevention campaign helped achieve 97 per cent coverage among children aged 3–59 months in Bafatá and Gabú.
  
Progress was also made in institutionalizing SBC within national systems, including development and technical validation of the National Communication Strategic Plan for Vaccination (2024–2028), providing a framework to strengthen vaccine confidence and demand. Evidence generation strengthened SBC design, including KAP studies on birth registration and female genital mutilation in priority regions, and an evaluation of UNICEF’s partnership with 38 community radio stations confirmed trust in local radio as a primary SBC channel.
  
SBC addressed gender norms within service delivery,  with 3,346 community health workers and frontline actors trained in  interpersonal communication and gender equity, supporting more inclusive  participation of women in community health structures.
  
Youth engagement reached a positive turning point with the successful launch of U-Report Guinea-Bissau, in partnership with the private sector, CSO, government and U-Leaders. Coordinated mobilization across regions led to more than 19,000 young people registering, and three U-Report polls on civic participation, climate change and HIV/AIDS strengthened digital youth engagement and provided evidence to inform programmatic decisions. Furthermore, to inform programming, 16 youth consultations, including focus group discussions with 300 adolescents and young people across seven regions and Bissau, provided valuable insights.  Findings confirmed that radio-based programming contributed to increased knowledge, awareness and engagement on priority issues among young people.  These results illustrate how strengthened digital and community-based engagement mechanisms are enhancing youth participation and contributing to more responsive, youth-informed policies and interventions. 
  
Community engagement at scale was a notable  achievement, with 1,734,294 people directly engaged through UNICEF-supported  SBC interventions across sectors, reinforcing the role of SBC in  strengthening community ownership, supporting behaviour change and enhancing  sectoral effectiveness.
  
Communication and advocacy continued to function as  a cross-cutting enabler supporting programme delivery, partnerships and  policy engagement, rather than as a standalone results area. Efforts focused  on strengthening UNICEF’s convening role, supporting dialogue with government  and partners, and reinforcing alignment around national priorities for  children, complementing SBC approaches. Advocacy was linked to UNICEF’s  engagement in sector coordination mechanisms and UN inter-agency platforms,  sustaining attention to child rights, equity and system strengthening.  Although not captured through dedicated indicators, communication and  advocacy contributed indirectly to programme effectiveness by reinforcing  coherence across interventions and enabling collective action in support of  UNSDCF and Country Programme objectives.
  
UNICEF employed strategic communication and public advocacy to raise awareness of child rights and support programme priorities, reaching an estimated 274,000 people through digital and media platforms and generating over 15 million engagements, with 375 references to UNICEF activities across national and international outlets. Communication supported events and campaigns, including an informal dialogue with the President on Child Rights, African Children’s Fortnight, World Children’s Day and UN Day, and collaboration with national institutions supported development of the National Adolescent Girls’ Agenda by supporting participation at the Girls’ Summit in Dakar and advancing the national climate agenda through COP30 engagement.
  
Taken together, achievements in 2025 demonstrate  UNICEF’s continued relevance and contribution in Guinea-Bissau through  sustained service delivery, systems strengthening and community engagement.  While prevention gains were maintained and enabling systems advanced in  several sectors, challenges in coverage, equity, financing and decentralized  functionality remain. Accelerating equitable outcomes will depend on  consolidating decentralized capacity, strengthening routine data use and  securing predictable financing to sustain and scale progress.
  
UNICEF Guinea-Bissau collaborates with 12 out of  the 23 government line ministries to implement the Guinea-Bissau-UNICEF  cooperation programme to advance the agenda for children. Partnerships  focused on sustaining essential services, strengthening national and  subnational systems, and reinforcing coordination in a context of persistent  institutional and fiscal constraints.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Implementation of UNICEF’s Country Programme in 2025 took place in a highly constrained and fluid context shaped by persistent political instability, limited fiscal space, weak institutional capacity and deep, multidimensional child deprivation. Across sectors, UNICEF balanced immediate service delivery with longer-term systems strengthening, adapting approaches to political volatility, recurrent shocks and intensifying climate risks. Experience from the programme cycle reinforces that sustainable progress for children depends on the capacity of national and subnational systems to absorb, sustain and scale effective solutions.

High turnover among senior and middle-level government officials, compounded by disruption following the military coup, affected institutional continuity and slowed inter-ministerial coordination. UNICEF adapted its coordination approaches accordingly, drawing on long-standing partnerships with government, civil society and UN entities to sustain progress across priority child rights interventions.

Results in social areas remained constrained by chronic underfinancing, recurrent strikes, weak supply chains, limited resources and pronounced geographic disparities. Programme experience highlighted that technical gains remain vulnerable in the absence of institutional and financial anchoring. Where investments were embedded within routine systems – such as service protocols, planning processes or monitoring frameworks – results proved more resilient to political and operational shocks. Reliance on externally financed inputs without parallel government co-financing or institutionalization heightened sustainability risks.

Weak routine data systems further constrained equity-focused planning, as gaps in timely, disaggregated data limited identification of underserved populations, monitoring of service quality and effective targeting, particularly in remote and high-burden regions. Strengthening core system functions – including subnational service delivery capacity, workforce planning, supply chain management and routine data use – will be essential. Greater emphasis on prevention, early nutrition interventions and climate-resilient health infrastructure remains critical to sustaining gains.

In WASH, progress in reducing open defecation and expanding access demonstrated the effectiveness of community-based and behaviour-centred approaches. Nonetheless, access to safely managed drinking water remains limited, particularly in rural and peri-urban areas, while infrastructure is increasingly exposed to flooding, erosion and saline intrusion linked to climate change. Weak institutional coordination, limited investment in maintenance and insufficient decentralization continue to undermine service sustainability.

Programme experience confirms that WASH outcomes are strongest when technical solutions are combined with community ownership, local governance engagement and sustained follow-up. Community-led sanitation approaches have proven effective in shifting practices, but durability depends on continued institutional support and financing. Further integration of WASH within health, education and climate adaptation systems, alongside strengthened local planning and management capacity, will be increasingly important as climate impacts intensify.

Severe challenges related to access, retention and learning outcomes continue in education, with some of the lowest completion rates globally and stark regional and socioeconomic disparities. Limited public investment, shortages of trained teachers, weak learning environments and frequent system disruptions constrain progress. Gains in enrolment and gender parity at primary level have not translated into sustained progression or improved learning, particularly at pre-primary and lower secondary levels.

Experience confirms that expanding access alone is insufficient without systemic improvements in quality, governance and financing. Interventions addressing multiple bottlenecks – such as teacher support, learning materials, school WASH and community engagement – produced stronger and more equitable results. However, fragile education data systems and weak EMIS functionality limited timely tracking and targeting of out-of-school children and adolescents. Future programming will need to prioritize foundational learning, early childhood development and system-level reforms alongside strengthened data systems and decentralized planning.

In child protection, the system is constrained by limited human and financial resources, weak coordination across sectors and levels, and insufficient coverage of prevention, referral and response services. Harmful practices such as child marriage, female genital mutilation and violent discipline persist, particularly in rural areas.

Programme experience indicates that child protection outcomes improve when legal reforms are complemented by community-based prevention, strengthened social services and sustained engagement with traditional and religious leaders. Standalone legal or awareness interventions have limited impact without accessible services and functional referral pathways. Data limitations further constrain system performance, hindering effective referral, follow-up and accountability. Strengthening subnational capacity, workforce development, data systems and institutionalized prevention and response mechanisms remain critical.

In social protection, coverage remains extremely limited, reflecting structural constraints in a context dominated by informal employment and constrained public resources. Existing schemes are fragmented, underfunded and heavily reliant on external support, limiting their ability to buffer households against shocks or reduce child poverty at scale.

A key lesson is that social protection must be integrated with health, education and child protection systems to address overlapping deprivations. UNICEF’s analytical and advocacy efforts have elevated child-sensitive social protection in policy dialogue, yet expansion remains constrained by limited fiscal space, institutional fragmentation and weak data foundations. The absence of interoperable social registries further limits effective targeting and shock responsiveness. 

Across sectors, communication and advocacy remained essential for navigating Guinea-Bissau’s complex operating environment. UNICEF’s convening role and evidence-based advocacy helped sustain attention to children’s rights amid competing priorities, although effectiveness was constrained by political volatility and data limitations. Experience reinforces the importance of aligning advocacy with feasible reform pathways and maintaining consistent engagement with national and subnational stakeholders.

Social and behaviour change approaches emerged as a critical cross-cutting enabler, particularly in health, nutrition, WASH and child protection. SBC interventions were most effective when context-specific, community-driven and linked to accessible services, while fragmented or short-term campaigns proved less effective. Sustained integration of SBC across sectors, with investment in local capacity, remains essential.

Overall, the programme cycle confirms that advancing child rights in Guinea-Bissau requires sustained, adaptive engagement focused on strengthening systems, reducing inequities and building resilience. Future programming will continue to prioritize decentralization, institutionalization and partnerships, while remaining flexible in the face of political, economic and climate-related shocks.

Strengthening national and subnational data ecosystems – by institutionalizing routine data use, improving interoperability across sectoral systems and reinforcing national ownership of evidence – will be central to improving targeting, accountability and impact. Grounded in evidence, community engagement and multisectoral collaboration, UNICEF remains well positioned to support improved outcomes for children and adolescents in this complex environment.

In Liberia 2025 was marked by consolidated peace and renewed vigour in building of key institutions, capitalizing on the democratic transition and installation of the new administration in 2024. The beginning of the year was marked by the launch of the 5 year National Development Plan, the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID), aligning Liberia’s recovery with the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), creating a critical window for advancing governance and social sector reforms.
However, structural challenges persist. Donor funding accounts for approximately 70% of the social sector budget, reflecting heavy reliance on external partners in a low-income context with suboptimal public financing for children. [1]. This is most evident in the health and education sectors, often leading the poorest to forgo essential health services due to high out-of-pocket expenses or school enrolment due to affordability barriers.[2]. 
While macroeconomic performance offers a potential pathway out of this fiscal constraint, with the African Development Bank forecasting gross domestic product growth of 5.2 per cent at the start of the year, driven by the mining, agriculture, and services sectors, the benefits have yet to trickle down. Around 55 per cent of the population remains trapped in multidimensional poverty [4], with children bearing the brunt of these economic hardships as families are often forced to choose between essential nutrition and basic survival needs, underscoring a significant gap between macroeconomic growth and the lived reality of children.
This gap is evident in stagnant human capital indicators, particularly child nutrition. Stunting prevalence among children under 5 was reduced from 32 per cent in 2013 to 29.8 per cent in 2019[5] and stalled at that level, considered “serious” under the Global Hunger Index [6]. More critically, 43 per cent of children are living in severe child food poverty [7], consuming fewer than three out of the eight recommended food groups, while only 9 per cent can meet the minimum dietary diversity required for healthy growth [8]. Micronutrient deficiencies continue to jeopardize long-term cognitive potential, with anaemia affecting 71 per cent of children under 5 and 55 per cent of adolescent girls [9].
At the same time, child health outcomes ranked the country 157th globally in the 2025 Sustainable Development Report [10]. The Government reported neonatal deaths at 35.6 per 1,000 live births, infant mortality at 63.7 per 1,000 live births, and under-five mortality rate of 92.6 per 1,000 live births [11]. These findings highlight a significant population health crisis that directly threatens the country’s progress toward achieving the 2030 SDGs. This is further evidenced by a maternal mortality ratio (MMR) estimate that remains high at 628 per 100,000 live births in 2023[12]. 
Reliable immunization services remain the foundation of Liberia's primary health system and one of the most effective ways to reverse these high child mortality trends. UNICEF-supported efforts led to improvement in immunization coverage, with Penta-3 rates rising from 89 per cent to 90 per cent [13]. Critically, for the first time in recent years, no stock-outs of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), Polio, or Tetanus Toxoid vaccines occurred at the county level throughout 2025. This achievement was driven by UNICEF-supported forecasting and supply planning, alongside the deployment of 300 solar direct-drive refrigerators, which strengthened the cold chain in areas with unreliable electricity. 
The lack of resilient infrastructure remains primary driver of child vulnerability. Safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) access remains low, with over 50 per cent of healthcare facilities lacking basic WASH services, contributing to 22 per cent of under-5 deaths [14]. These deficits extend to the classroom, where only 43 per cent of schools have basic sanitation, fueling menstruation-related absenteeism among adolescent girls. 
These gaps directly mirror the broader constraints within the education sector, which is characterized by high exclusion rates. Approximately 50.1 per cent of school-aged children are out of class, and only 54 per cent complete primary school [15]. Net enrolment rate for Lower Basic increased from 43% in 2019 to 46.3% in 2025, while at upper basic level it increased from 14% to 20.7 for the same period. High over-age enrolment heightens dropout risks leading to lower enrolment in upper basic and higher studies. 
Child protection risks add to the barriers to education, often forcing children out of the classroom entirely. Teenage pregnancy affects 30 per cent of adolescent girls, contributing to school dropout and long-term vulnerability. This vulnerability is worsened by widespread violence, with 81 per cent of children experiencing psychological aggression and 71 per cent subjected to violent disciplinary practices. These factors, combined with child labour affecting 30 per cent of children and a lack of a legal identity for 34 per cent of children under 5 whose births remain unregistered, create a cycle of exclusion that prevents consistent learning. 
Governance reforms in 2025, including the establishment of the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court, signal renewed national commitment to rule of law, transitional justice and accountability. UNICEF and government efforts advanced child justice reforms, shifting toward rehabilitative, community-based care that reduces the use of adult detention and ensures legal or social crises do not permanently hinder a child’s education and future potential.
The prevailing context underscores a continued and alarming  gap between the country’s renewed focus on governance and social sector reforms and the daily realities facing children. The country still relies heavily on external support, but with the donor community and key bilateral partners scaling back funding due to the shifting global sociopolitical climate, essential services in health, nutrition, and education are often out of reach for the most vulnerable.
For UNICEF Liberia, the strategic imperative is to deliver results at scale and ensure no child is left behind. This is the cornerstone of the new Country Programme (2026–2030), which is intentionally aligned with the Government’s AAID, specifically its ambitions to reduce child mortality, expand quality education, and invest in human capital. By anchoring this work within the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2026-2029) and the UN Cooperation Framework (UNCF) (2026–2030), UNICEF serves as the vital link between these national policies and the children who need them most.

2025 marked the final year of the 2020-2025 extended Country Programme cycle, representing the culmination of six years of interventions for children in Liberia driven by strategic directions encompassing stronger focus on intersectoral and community-based approaches, evidence-based programming and data transformation, prevention and resilience-building, alongside and re-enforced by public-private partnerships. These pillars have moved the programme beyond siloed sectors toward a unified framework where health, nutrition, WASH, education, and protection services are integrated into a responsive national architecture, creating a conducive environment for a focus on providing holistic services to out of school children and adolescent girls as the two flagship programmes of the new CPD. .
By anchoring these shifts in high-level policy reform and evidence-based programming, UNICEF has built a structural foundation that ensures long-term sustainability. This final year served as both a measure of these achievements and a transition point toward the new 2026–2030 cycle. The results documented across all goal areas demonstrate that the systems now in place are better equipped to deliver equitable services, however big is the deficit between capacity and resources and the targeted deprivations of Liberia’s children. . This evolution ensures that the progress made over the last six years provides a stable, state-led platform for the next phase of Liberia's commitment to every child.
 
Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives. 
Liberia achieved a strategic pivot towards resilient, integrated health and nutrition systems in 2025, leveraging digital innovation and policy reform to scale life-saving results for women and children. Strategically aligned with the UNCF (2026–2030) and the AAID, these efforts sustained the country’s polio-free status while increasing Penta3 coverage to 90.39 per cent. A critical driver of this performance was the advancement of interoperability between the Electronic Immunization Registry (EIR) and the civil registration system, enabling the real-time registration of 61,000 births and 95,000 vaccinations, ensuring that health interventions serve as a primary entry point for establishing a child's legal identity and identifying zero-dose populations. This enhanced system reach was further demonstrated through the "Every Mother Matters, Every Birth Counts" pledge, which integrated immunization with nutrition services via the innovative HPV Plus model, reaching 38,450 adolescent girls with vaccines bundled with iron and folic acid (IFA).
A major highlight of the year was the successful treatment of 18,571 children for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). Despite significant therapeutic supply stock-outs, UNICEF’s technical leadership ensured that 56 per cent of public health facilities across all 15 counties remained operational for life-saving interventions. The quality of clinical care achieved exceptional results, evidenced by a death rate of 0.8 per cent, far below the SPHERE international ceiling of 10 per cent. To institutionalize this performance, UNICEF facilitated the first revision of the Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) guidelines since 2012. This alignment with the latest WHO standards ensures that wasting protocols are evidence-based, context-specific, and integrated into the primary health care architecture.
Digital transformation served as a primary change strategy and enabler, with the nationwide Electronic Immunization Registry (EIR) enabling real-time birth registration for 61,000 infants and the identification of zero-dose populations. This system was reinforced by the deployment of 300 solar direct-drive refrigerators, which eliminated county-level vaccine stock-outs. Beyond the clinic, UNICEF and UNFPA advanced the Nurture, Empower, and Protect (NEP) project, funded by the Government of Ireland, finalizing a national adolescent sexual reproductive health rights (SRHR) and nutrition strategy. This partnership bridges the gap between health and empowerment, equipping adolescents to manage the intersecting risks of anaemia and reproductive health through standardized training packages and operational guidelines.
To reinforce long-term prevention, UNICEF reached 670,555 caregivers with optimal Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Feeding (MIYCF) counselling, exceeding the annual target. This achievement was supported by the launch of the "First 1,000 Days of Life" campaign and World Breastfeeding Week, which utilized radio talk shows, social media, and community dialogues to reach underserved communities. The year culminated in the validation of the national Social Behaviour Change (SBC) strategy and toolkit, a framework designed to shift behavioural norms and reduce the underlying burden of malnutrition.
Furthermore, UNICEF provided critical technical support for the Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey (CFSNS). Once finalized, the CFSNS data will provide the evidence base required to update national development plans and refine food security interventions and set a tone for a renewed engagement on child nutrition. Moving into 2026, the rollout of the SBC toolkit and the integration of CFSNS findings will allow UNICEF to drive evidence-based advocacy, ensuring the gains of 2025 form a sustainable foundation for universal health coverage and child survival across Liberia.
Beyond routine services, UNICEF strengthened national emergency preparedness by coordinating the mpox outbreak response. UNICEF provided the technical support necessary to update the mpox Emergency Preparedness Plan and mobilized the resources required for its immediate implementation. This response focused on reinforcing frontline service delivery, ensuring that health workers in affected communities were equipped to manage the outbreak while maintaining essential maternal and child health services. In addition, the health sector worked closely with WASH to strengthen IPC protocols and with education to ensure the roll out of  school health protocols and reinforcing of learning-continuity measures.
 
Goal Area 4: Every Child lives in a safe and clean environment. (476 words)
In a constrained funding environment, UNICEF prioritized systems strengthening and climate integration, advancing SP outcomes on safe/equitable WASH and sustainable environments.
Through strategic technical support to strengthen national WASH governance, policy coherence, and climate integration, UNICEF contributed directly to tangible results. UNICEF led the Climate-WASH Nexus by facilitating the integration of child-sensitive goals including WASH into Liberia’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) for the first time. In parallel, UNICEF commissioned the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), a landmark study exposing how climate change and environmental degradation threaten children and guiding child-sensitive priorities for the new Country Programme.
UNICEF’s technical diplomacy facilitated the Government of Liberia to sign the Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate Action at COP30. Additionally, UNICEF-led advocacy engagements with partners amplified child and youth voices through three side events at COP30. UNICEF supported the development of a comprehensive Climate Rationale for WASH, utilizing Policy Gap Analyses and Climate Risk Assessments to create a bankable framework for future climate financing.
Beyond climate advocacy, UNICEF focused on bridging institutional gaps and improving governance in the WASH sector. A significant milestone was the update of the Presidential WASH Compact, a national commitment mechanism designed to address sector fragmentation and promote sustainable sanitation. The process renewed political attention and is pending approval. UNICEF support resulted in evidence-based planning of the National Open Defecation Free (ODF) Roadmap, through dissemination of the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) evaluation and Sanitation Marketing study accompanied by private sector consultations. UNICEF also supported the WASH Accounts Initiative, in collaboration with WHO and WaterAid, to track sector-wide financing. 
Furthermore, UNICEF also provided high-level technical and convening support to the Government of Liberia for the Water Investment Summit and the WASH Sector Ministers’ Meeting, strengthening national positioning, investment readiness, and regional policy dialogue. UNICEF also partnered with key stakeholders to engage in budget advocacy with parliamentarians and senators for domestic resource mobilization and addressing the WASH financing gap, laying foundation for further follow ups.
Addressing gender-responsive WASH gaps and Adolescent Development, UNICEF championed the "Period-Friendly Schools" initiative, thereby reaching over 30,000 people and provided 399 adolescents with life-skills training in menstrual health and reusable pad production while successfully engaging boys to dismantle menstrual stigma.
Overall, UNICEF Liberia delivered high-impact results in the climate-WASH nexus, by protecting core service outcomes while driving systemic change. Through sustained policy engagement, high-level advocacy, climate integration, evidence generation, and gender-responsive programming, UNICEF served as a trusted technical partner in a fragmented sector. In 2026, the programme will focus on scaling implementation under the CPD 2026–2030 while deepening strategic dialogues with private sector, government, and IFIs while translating policy gains into sustainable and equitable WASH services for every child in Liberia.
 
Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns.
UNICEF made significant strides to reinforce the national education system, transitioning from fragmented, input-based support toward a cohesive framework of governance and foundational learning. This strategic realignment was designed to ensure that the country’s recovery is anchored in resilient institutional structures rather than isolated interventions. Directly aligned with the national AAID and the UNCF, UNICEF utilized its role as the sector’s Coordinating Agency to chair the Local Education Group (LEG) and operationalize Technical Working Groups (TWGs) focused on Teacher Development and Data Evidence. These platforms have been instrumental in ensuring that national policy decisions are grounded in empirical evidence and that professional development is prioritized within the national framework. As an illustration, joint advocacy with UNESCO supported a comprehensive review of the Early Childhood Education (ECE) policy, to improve school readiness and address overage enrollment.
UNICEF provided essential technical and financial support to enhance the Education Management Information System (EMIS), which culminated in the delivery of the 2023/2024 Annual School Census (ASC). A definitive highlight of the year was the measurable improvement in quality, with learning outcome assessments showing proficiency levels of 71 per cent in Mathematics and 65 per cent in English. These results were achieved through a decentralized Continuous Professional Development (CPD) model that moved teacher training from distant, centralized institutes directly into 200 targeted schools. By establishing 60 school clusters and training 3,002 teachers in foundational literacy, numeracy, and formative assessment, UNICEF translated the National School Quality Standards (NSQS) into tangible pedagogical shifts. This was reinforced by the provision of 30 motorcycles to supervisors and technical support to Teacher Training Institutes (TTIs), ensuring instructional coaching reached the most remote regions.  But gender disparities still persist with the under representation of female teachers limiting professional diversity and depriving female students of essential role models.
 
On the equitable access front, UNICEF successfully co-led the integrated "Back-to-My-Classroom" Enrollment Drive, a multi-sectoral mobilization strategy championed by H.E. the President of Liberia. This initiative served as a practical application of multisectoral interoperability, bringing together  education enrollment with health and protection services. Under this integrated package, children were simultaneously screened for birth registration and reached with life-saving HPV vaccinations during the enrollment process. While the drive has an ambitious target of 250,000 children by 2027 , UNICEF’s initial demonstration of this model successfully enrolled 779 children from one of the pilot counties in the first three months of roll out. To ensure that increased enrollment leads to retention, UNICEF distributed Teaching and Learning Materials (TLMs) and school kits to benefit 25,000 students, ensuring that the "Back to School" moment was matched with the necessary resources for a quality education. Simultaneously, the programme advanced equity by reintegrating 2,990 out-of-school children into non-formal learning centers, providing a vital second chance for those previously excluded from the system.
 
UNICEF strengthened teaching and learning by improving national assessment systems and advancing key digital innovations. Investments in the Learning Passport, radio education, and solar-powered learning centers helped reduce the digital divide, while initial collaboration with Giga began mapping school connectivity. Despite notable progress, limited domestic financing, slow decentralization and low sub-national capacity continue to constrain scale-up. 
 
. 
These results demonstrate that UNICEF’s strategic focus on governance, data interoperability, and community engagement is strengthening system resilience. In 2026, alongside the ‘Back to my Classroom” campaign, priority will center on closing the gap between programme gains and national reforms, by enforcing school quality standards and institutionalizing continuous professional development to ensure sustainability. 
 
Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation (710 words)
UNICEF Liberia strengthened the core components of the national protection system by deepening strategic partnerships, coordination, and collaboration with key Government ministries and institutions.
 A definitive highlight of the year was UNICEF’s technical leadership in localizing the Bogota Commitments and the Global Call to Action to End Violence Against Children (EVAC).  At the national level, a national inter- ministerial coordinating structure was established to steer the country towards the implementation of the global commitment to ending violence against children by 2030. In addition, a national technical working group to guide the development of a national EVAC (Ending Violence Against Children) strategy has been established and will both provide technical oversight for the development and operationalization of the EVAC Strategy which will serve as the country's first comprehensive blueprint to eliminate violence against children by 2030.
 To translate this high-level oversight into frontline action and to strengthen accountability and evidence-based planning, UNICEF institutionalized a robust knowledge management system by digitizing case management through the Child Protection Information Management System (CPIMS+). UNICEF supported the training of 43 social workers and supervisors on the use of this system. Now operational in Montserrado County, CPIMS+ is already supporting the management of 204 cases (88 girls and 116 boys), demonstrating its immediate value in addressing the needs of vulnerable children. 25 Social Workers were also trained and deployed to support the Mpox outbreak, where they have provided psychosocial support to 293 persons (172 children, 121 adults) including survivors and their families, proving that Liberia’s protection system is becoming increasingly resilient.
UNICEF also contributed to revitalizing the social service workforce by deploying 20 social work interns to reinforce existing capacity and enhance case management support for children. In addition, UNICEF trained 177 civil registrars to strengthen birth registration services. The impact of this strengthened workforce was evidenced across several initiatives including the launch of the Back-to-My-Classroom Enrolment Drive in Grand Bassa, where these professionals facilitated the registration and certification of 1,339 children, demonstrating that legal identity is an essential gateway to educational access.
UNICEF provided technical and financial support for the advancement of digital interoperability between civil registration, national identity, and health systems. Through a pioneering pilot with the Ministry of Health and the National Identity Registry, UNICEF facilitated a linked data environment that reached 5,082 children under age six. This integration allows for the simultaneous issuance of national IDs and birth certificates alongside verification of immunization records during outreach activities. By ensuring children are registered from birth, the initiative strengthens protection against trafficking and lays the critical foundation for securing each child's legal identity.
 
UNICEF’s gender-responsive programming focused on dismantling the structural inequalities that drive violence and has resulted in its nomination to a high-level committee tasked with developing a national roadmap for a Policy on Traditional Practices. This policy aims to bridge the gap between cultural traditions and human rights, informing future legislation to prohibit harmful practices. Within the formal justice sector, UNICEF ensured that transitional justice remains victim-centred and child-sensitive. Care reform also achieved a measurable milestone with the official endorsement of revised foster care guidelines and standards, training 50 foster parents who are now awaiting Juvenile Court certification, a significant shift toward safe, family-based alternatives to institutionalization.
UNICEF supported the Government of Liberia in operationalizing the new juvenile wing at Sanniquellie Central Prison, reinforcing a national shift toward a child-sensitive justice system. The establishment of this dedicated facility ensures the separation of children from adults and reflects a broader commitment to creating safe, developmentally appropriate environments that uphold children’s rights and support their rehabilitation. This milestone signifies meaningful progress in advancing justice reforms that prioritize protection over punishment and promote alternatives to detention, ensuring that children in conflict with the law are treated with dignity and given the opportunity to reintegrate and thrive
UNICEF’s commitment to adolescent empowerment and climate resilience was manifested through the engagement of 988 adolescents in peer-led dialogues regarding social norms and gender roles. Through the West Point and New Kru Town Resource Centers, 750 adolescents were enrolled in technical and vocational training, with 70 already placed in internships. Innovation was further driven by a partnership with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), where over 100 adolescents participated in a "Climate Challenge" to repurpose plastic waste into household furniture and school bags. This initiative addressed environmental degradation while equipping young Liberians with green skills and a sense of agency in their communities.
UNICEF Liberia facilitated the participation of a delegation of adolescent girls at the West Africa Regional Adolescent Girls’ Summit in Dakar. This followed a UNICEF-supported National Adolescent Girls Conference in Liberia, which brought girls together in a consultative process to identify key issues and inform the Regional Adolescent Girls Agenda. The Dakar Summit concluded with the adoption of the landmark Dakar Declaration, affirming a regional commitment to advancing adolescent girls’ rights.
In addition, UNICEF supported the finalization of a Buddy Club Manual designed to promote safe schools and strengthen adolescent participation. This was a collaborative process that involved the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection.
 
 At county levels, social behavioural and norms change efforts reached over 22,000 children and adults with dialogues and advocacy on communal approach to eliminate drivers of negative social norms, gender inequality against women and girls, also addressing the emerging trend of circumcision of much younger girls. In addition, Liberia has enhanced county-level coordination for better service provision by merging the Child Protection Network with GBV Taskforces, to facilitate ease of referral and information sharing.
 
Finally, UNICEF Liberia solidified its PSEA framework by integrating strict accountability measures into its core operational procedures. Through the mandatory adoption of amended General Terms and Conditions in all new Partnership Cooperation Agreements, the office has made international PSEA standards a legally binding requirement for all partners. This structural shift is supported by the transition to the UNPP Common Assessment framework, which identified and addressed risk profiles for key implementing partners through targeted Capacity Strengthening Implementation Plans. As the lead of the UNCT PSEA Network, UNICEF optimized inter-agency governance by ratifying revised Terms of Reference for both the Network and Steering Committee. This leadership extends to the field level, where PSEA indicators are now a standard component of Programme Monitoring Visits and emergency deployments, ensuring consistent risk mitigation and victim-centred reporting across all interventions.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges: 
While 2025 was marked by significant policy milestones, the transition from "policy to practice" remains hampered by Liberia’s fiscal and logistical realities.
·       Fragility of Essential Supply Chains: The supply chain for life-saving commodities remains precarious. Heavy reliance on international donor funding for Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and specialized medicines creates a high-risk environment. Without sufficient domestic funding for the Liberia Multi-Sectoral Nutrition Costed Strategic Plan (LMNCSP), children remain vulnerable to a cycle of preventable developmental delays.
·       Fiscal Space and Seasonal Vulnerabilities: Limited domestic budget allocation for N4G (Nutrition for Growth) commitments is exacerbated by seasonal shocks. During the lean season, localized food insecurity affects nearly half a million people, pushing vulnerable households toward "Crisis" levels (IPC Phase 3). This highlights the disconnect between national policy ambitions and the actual fiscal space required to protect the most marginalized.
·       Intersectoral Coordination Gaps: Although UNICEF is making concerted efforts in this direction, achieving results for children is hindered by inconsistent coordination among line ministries. This fragmentation often leads to siloed interventions, diluting the potential impact of multi-sectoral strategies like the Back-to-My-Classroom initiative, Adolescent girls programming or nutrition-sensitive programming.
·       Data and Infrastructure Deficits: The suspension of the WASH MIS platform has created a significant data void, complicating evidence-based planning. Additionally, excessive centralization continues to limit the agility of sub-national teams in education and health to respond to localized needs. The last DHS conducted in Liberia was in 2019 and with no immediate plan for the DHS, there is a huge data gap on women and child focused indicators.
Lessons Learned: 
·       Adaptive Management and System Integration: The past year reinforced that standalone interventions are less effective than integrated, multi-sectoral platforms.
·       Integration as a Force Multiplier: Initiatives like "HPV Plus" demonstrated that combining health, nutrition, and civil registration services significantly lowers the cost of reaching the most marginalized. Leveraging existing immunization touchpoints to address adolescent nutrition and birth registration has proven to be an essential strategy for closing equity gaps.
·       Digital Interoperability: The successful launch of the Electronic Immunization Registry (EIR) proved that high-quality, disaggregated data is the most effective tool for identifying "zero-dose" children. This digital shift has moved the office from reactive response to predictive, evidence-based planning.
·       Accountability through Leadership: By chairing the Local Education Group and the UNCT PSEA Network, UNICEF Liberia successfully harmonized fragmented partner efforts. Institutionalizing PSEA within partner contracts and field monitoring tools proved more effective than periodic training, creating a permanent culture of protection.
Future Outlook: 
As the 2020–2025 Country Programme concludes, UNICEF Liberia will transition into the new Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026–2030, fully aligned with the Government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID), the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029, and the United Nations Cooperation Framework (UNCF) 2026–2030. This new cycle prioritizes transformative, equity-driven results to reduce child mortality, expand access to quality education, and invest in human capital, while advancing the 2030 Agenda and the principle of leaving no child behind. The work will emphasize focus, scale and impact to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly those related to children, while addressing challenges like inequality, humanitarian crises and climate change.
Building on 2025 gains, such as improved immunization coverage, digital interoperability for birth registration and zero-dose identification, multisectoral enrollment drives, and climate-WASH integration, the office will focus on the following strategic shifts to accelerate sustainable impact: (1) promoting an integrated multisectoral programme, (2) prioritizing support to decentralized planning, (3) positioning adolescent girls at the center of the UNICEF programme, (4) leveraging collection and use of data and (5) catalyzing advocacy for increased social sector budget allocations and innovative financing mechanisms including public-private partnerships. 
 Across specific sectors, there will be a particular focus on strengthening food systems. This will involve aggressive advocacy for increased government investment in nutrition, leveraging the Child Nutrition Fund for co-financing, and fostering public-private partnerships to enhance local production and affordability of nutritious foods—ultimately addressing stunting and severe child food poverty.
Efforts will translate climate-resilient WASH policy achievements into scaled, equitable services by bridging data gaps (e.g., reinvigorating WASH monitoring systems), deepening partnerships with International Financial Institutions (IFIs), the private sector, and government to develop climate-adaptive infrastructure, and ensuring gender-responsive access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene.
Institutionalizing decentralization will empower sub-national structures—such as County Health Teams, Teacher Training Institutes, and the social service workforce and County LISGIS team; with greater operational autonomy, digital tools, and capacity-building. This shift will move from project-based support to self-sustaining, government-led delivery of integrated services.
Efforts will be focused on minimizing the data gaps by collaborating with LISGIS not only on the MICS but also leveraging the presence of LISGIS at the county level by strengthening the county structure in real time reporting on the key performance indicators for integrated programme.
These efforts will emphasize multisectoral collaboration, innovation, prevention, and resilience-building, while prioritizing the most marginalized children (poor, unregistered, adolescent girls, and zero-dose populations). By anchoring partnerships in evidence and accountability, UNICEF will serve as a catalytic partner, ensuring that national reforms translate into tangible improvements in child survival, learning, protection, and well-being for every child in Liberia.
