GA1-Survive and thrive
In 2025, UNICEF played a key role in strengthening Nigeria's primary healthcare system. Through national and state Sector-Wide Approach dialogues and development of 17 state annual operational plans, UNICEF reinforced planning, accountability, and resource alignment across states. The Primary Health Care (PHC) Leadership Challenge Initiative fostered healthy competition and cross-learning among states, catalysing investments and improved performance PHC. The initiative is Nigeria's flagship programme, led by the Nigeria Governors’ Forum and Federal Ministry of Health, rewarding state governors for exceptional improvements in PHC delivery.
Equity remained central to UNICEF’s programming. In zero-dose communities, with UNICEF support, health insurance coverage expanded to close to 150,000 individuals, including 84,012 under-five children, reducing financial barriers to care. Birth notification and registration systems reached over 100,000 children, ensuring identity and access to essential services. Cold chain infrastructure received substantial upgrades: 280 health facilities were solarized, state cold stores rehabilitated in three states, a mega warehouse commissioned at the national store, and over 2,000 active cold chain units installed. Distribution of 20,000 vaccine carriers and over 1,000 cold boxes nationwide ensured vaccine potency to the last mile.
Under the leadership of the Government of Nigeria and with UNICEF’s support, immunization coverage improved significantly during the year, reducing zero-dose children, containing polio transmission, intensifying Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, introducing the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine, and strengthening immunization systems nationwide. UNICEF provided technical, logistical, and operational support to the National Primary Health Care Development Agency and 37 state health agencies to achieve these milestones.
The introduction of the measles-rubella vaccine, for the first time in Nigeria, was a defining milestone in 2025. With UNICEF’s technical assistance, all 452 LGAs in 21 phase-1 states achieved 99 per cent coverage, vaccinating more than 59 million children. UNICEF supported vaccine distribution to the last mile, supplied cold chains, and supported demand creation through community engagement and information materials. Polio eradication efforts also intensified. UNICEF procured and distributed polio vaccine doses to 188 million under five children across all rounds, while circulating variant poliovirus cases declined from 122 in 2024 to 75 per cent in 2025. Integration of zero-dose activities with the nationwide Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) Week reached over 651,000 previously unvaccinated children aged 12–23 months. MNCH week also integrated HPV,reaching over 1 million 9-year-old girls.
Newborn survival continued to be a government priority reflected in concrete investments. Through UNICEF support, six newborn care units were operationalized w, providing specialized treatment to over 3,130 premature and sick babies. Other key interventions included 263 newborn corners established across health facilities and training of 233 healthcare workers on essential newborn care protocols, equipping them with skills to manage complications and promote safe practices. Recognizing oxygen as a life-saving commodity, infrastructure improvements included four fully solarized oxygen plants with two more in progress, guaranteeing uninterrupted supply even in areas with unreliable electricity. To sustain these systems, 137 biomedical engineers received training, strengthening local maintenance capacity.
Government commitment to adolescent health was evident in its expansive reach: in 2025, 1.1 million adolescents across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) benefited from programmes in adolescent and youth-friendly health services and HIV prevention, including HPV-related interventions. To ensure quality service delivery, more than 3,500 health workers were trained on adolescent-friendly services at both primary and secondary health care levels, promoting confidentiality, respect, and accessibility for young people.
UNICEF supported multisectoral responses to multiple public health emergencies, including mpox, measles, diphtheria, cholera, dengue fever, and rabies, reaching over 3.1 million beneficiaries. Strategic advocacy through eight budget briefs and engagement with the Nigerian Governors' Forum advanced domestic financing, while mobilizing resources for local manufacturing reduced import dependency and improved supply chain resilience.
Nigeria achieved global firsts in nutrition programming. With UNICEF’s technical guidance, operational support, and partnership with government and health actors, the country became the first to implement 38 Nutrition SMART+ surveys in two months, ensuring rapid, high-quality data for evidence-based decision-making. UNICEF also played a key role in supporting Nigeria in nationwide rollout of multiple micronutrient supplements, reaching over 6 million pregnant women through antenatal care. Approximately 36 million children aged 6–59 months also received two doses of vitamin A supplements through biannual campaigns, while 10 million children aged 12–59 months were dewormed with albendazole tablets. Stunting prevention reached more than 600,000 children aged 6–23 months with small-quantity lipid-based supplements and micronutrient powders, significantly improving dietary quality. Approximately 4.8 million primary caregivers of children aged 0–23 months received nutrition counselling, while more than 3 million pregnant women in targeted states accessed defined counselling packages focused on the first 1,000 days of life.
Policy advances included 14 states offering six months of paid maternity leave, while public financing for child nutrition expanded through the Child Nutrition Fund (CNF) to 19 states, mobilizing US$2.9 million in domestic resources. CNF, led by UNICEF, is an innovative financing mechanism that matches state government investments 1:1 to provide essential nutrition supplies and services to combat child malnutrition.
In humanitarian contexts, treatment services for severe acute malnutrition reached 901,000 children in six states (Adamawa, Borno, Katsina, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara), achieving a 90 per cent cure rate. Katsina State rolled out the UNICEF-World Food Programme Joint Action to Stop Wasting global pilot, successfully enrolling approximately 92,000 children with severe acute malnutrition and improving treatment coverage and service quality.
GA2-Learning 
In 2025, under government leadership and with UNICEF’s support, more than 1.5 million children accessed quality, inclusive education through safe schools and alternative learning pathways, while over 500,000 gained vocational, transferable, and foundational skills via initiatives such as pre-primary curriculum development, teacher professional development, sector planning, introduction of formal curriculum in alternative learning pathways to reduce the number of out of school children and improved education data management.
The Federal Ministry of Education strengthened data infrastructure by launching a harmonized digital Education Management Information System, with UNICEF serving as a leading member of the Nigerian Education Data Initiative. This enabled more than 70,000 schools across 11 states to complete the annual school census, covering 93 per cent of schools. States operationalized the Teacher Management Information System to manage data on 240,000 teachers, improving recruitment and deployment. Nigeria also administered its first international learning assessment, Programme for the Analysis of Education Systems, benchmarking student achievement against African peers.
UNICEF is strengthening basic education finance by building capacity in results-based budgeting and expenditure tracking among officials from nine northern states, while generating evidence on education budgets at state, local government, and school levels to guide reforms. Using these data, governments in 12 states developed gender-sensitive, disability-inclusive, crisis-responsive education sector plans with UNICEF support. 
Safe learning environments became a priority as the government, with UNICEF support, trained more than 7,000 teachers in managing violence, climate change education, and early warning systems. Infrastructure upgrades enhanced climate resilience in 81 schools across six states, while the Accelerated Basic Education Programme engaged nearly 43,000 out-of-school children in non-formal learning in Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states.
Additionally, digital ecosystems expanded significantly with UNICEF support. The Nigeria Learning Passport gained 317,000 new users and now serves 2.2 million learners with 16,000 curriculum-aligned resources accessible across the country.
Furthermore, UNICEF supported the launch and dissemination of Nigeria's National Policy on Skills Development, providing a comprehensive framework for building capabilities that prepare young Nigerians for productive futures, and worked with states on policy dissemination and implementation planning. As a result, nearly 600,000 children (273,496 girls) developed these skills in 2025, advancing progress toward equipping youth with competencies for employment and entrepreneurship.
GA3-Protection from violence and exploitation
Through UNICEF’s systems strengthening support, over 5.3 million children accessed protection, birth registration, mental health and psychosocial support, gender-based violence services, justice, and social welfare in 2025. Strategic investments in policy reform, digital innovations, and workforce expansion advanced legal identity and well-being for conflict-affected and vulnerable children nationwide.
The Government of Nigeria enhanced integrated service delivery through UNICEF-supported reforms in policy frameworks, workforce capacity, and multisectoral coordination. Training nearly 2,000 auxiliary social workers expanded the professional workforce using standardized curricula. Capacity development reached health personnel from Sexual Assault Referral Centres, police, prosecutors, and judicial officers, improving competencies across protection and justice sectors. At community level, more than 1,800 child protection structures were strengthened, creating robust referral mechanisms between volunteers and formal institutions.
UNICEF’s collaboration with the Ministry of Interior on the 2024 assessment of children deprived of liberty led to a national investigative panel in 2025, uncovering systemic issues in detaining children in adult facilities. Two regulatory instruments –  Legal Aid for Children in Contact with the Law Regulations and Prosecution Guidelines for Cases Involving Children – were adopted, while partnership with the Nigerian Bar Association expanded pro-bono legal aid nationwide. Consequently, 1,084 children exited detention through diversion or non-custodial measures, supported by aftercare and reintegration services.
These interventions enabled more than 119,000 children to access protection services: 85 per cent received social welfare including psychosocial support, reintegration, and counselling; 14 per cent received gender-based violence survivor support; and 1 per cent benefited from diversion and non-custodial measures.
Government programmes empowered more than 370,000 children and mobilized 1.18 million individuals to end female genital mutilation (FGM). Interventions on positive parenting and masculinity reached more than 400,000community members, challenging harmful practices. Adolescent girls received focused support addressing FGM and child marriage, with 230,450 beneficiaries equipped with life skills and agency, while community dialogues engaged 240,000 stakeholders to promote gender equity.
The Movement for Good to End FGM demonstrated unprecedented engagement, securing more than 1 million pledges through advocacy and grassroots mobilization. UNICEF helped strengthen Sexual Assault Referral Centres in six states through partnerships with First Ladies and the Governors Spouses’ Forum, enhancing survivor support and child protection systems.
With UNICEF and partner support, Nigeria achieved a decisive shift toward universal birth registration through localization, digitization, and health sector integration. Partnership with the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria scaled a community-based model across 304 LGAs and 3,372 wards in 15 states, registering nearly 600,000 children under one year in underserved communities. Integration with primary healthcare facilities in seven Gavi-supported states contributed more than 66,000 registrations. 
Interoperability between health and civil registration systems was established in 6,590 facilities, with 2,783 trained health workers acting as sub-registrars. By year’s end, over 1.5 million children received birth certificates. 
In the northeast, the government, with UNICEF support, delivered critical services for children affected by armed conflict. A total of 238,708 children and caregivers accessed community-based mental health and psychosocial support, while social and economic reintegration reached about 3,000 vulnerable children, with 1,383 enrolling in vocational training. Family reunification was successful for 797 children through improved case management. Gender-based violence prevention and response services expanded to more than 150,000 people through UNICEF-supported facilities, with efforts focused on safe spaces, referral pathways, and community outreach.
 
GA4-Safe and clean environment
Through UNICEF support for systems strengthening and climate-resilient programming, over 1.3 million people gained access to basic water supply, while nearly 8,000 communities hosting more than 3 million people were certified open defecation free in 2025. Strategic investments in governance reform, data innovation, and community-led approaches transformed water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) service delivery across Nigeria.
The Government of Nigeria established and upgraded 96 WASH units into fully functioning departments nationwide, strengthening governance structures for sustainability. UNICEF's advocacy with state partners, service commissions, and traditional institutions in seven states (Bauchi, Benue, Kaduna, Kano, Borno, Yobe, and Zamfara) propelled this institutional transformation. The National WASH Action Plan was revised, and more than 8,000 WASH committees were revitalized to enhance accountability and community engagement. 
Water access expanded significantly as government-led efforts, supported by UNICEF, delivered safe water through construction and rehabilitation of boreholes powered by renewable solar energy. Over 940,000 people gained basic water supply, exceeding targets by 67 per cent, while 322,000 accessed safely managed water. To ensure sustainability, 105 local area mechanics were trained for operations and maintenance in hard-to-reach areas. Climate resilience advanced through development of Climate Rationales in two states and deployment of revised facility designs, resulting in over 160 climate-resilient structures constructed.
Sanitation achievements surpassed expectations. Community-led approaches to total sanitation and intensive hygiene promotion campaigns reached nearly 2.5 million people with handwashing messaging – more than double the initial target. An additional 2.3 million people gained access to basic sanitation services . Katsina State was declared open defecation free, while another 22 local governments achieved verification status. Menstrual hygiene management interventions reached more than 56,000 women and girls through training and dignity kit distribution.
Innovation strengthened data systems. Government collaboration with UNICEF and youth platforms piloted citizen science for WASH data collection, mapping over 1,700 water points in Kano State. This approach demonstrated potential for improved rural water access monitoring while comparing conventional surveys with citizen science for coverage, data quality, and cost-effectiveness.
Goal Area 5: Equitable chance in life
Through strategic policy dialogue and technical support, UNICEF helped the government advance critical reforms that positioned social protection as a central pillar of the government's Renewed Hope Agenda. This engagement catalysed the revision of the National Social Protection Policy, integrating more child-sensitive measures and laying groundwork for expanded coverage. The National Social Register now includes nearly 39 million children, while an initial feasibility study on the introduction of a universal child benefit was updated.
UNICEF's support to fiscal planning mechanisms yielded tangible shifts in public resource allocation. Six states (Abia, Benue, Gombe, Kaduna, Oyo, and Sokoto) developed Medium-Term Expenditure Frameworks and Medium-Term Sector Strategies for 2026–2028 across education, health, WASH, and social protection. These strategies detail priority projects and programmes for each sector over three years, specifying costs, funding sources, implementing entities, and alignment with the State Development Plan. State-level systems for measuring child poverty were strengthened through UNICEF’s technical and capacity-building support to State Bureaus of Statistics and government stakeholders. Key child poverty measurement tools such as the Multidimensional Poverty Index in Gombe and Kano states, Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis , and the Situation Analysis continued to guide state planning processes, ensuring evidence-based, child-sensitive planning. This enhanced capacity directly informed the design, child poverty analysis, and ongoing implementation of state-led household surveys in Oyo, Gombe, and Kaduna states, aimed at identifying poor and vulnerable households.
Cross-sectoral strategies and enablers
UNICEF Nigeria advanced results for children through focused partnerships with UN agencies across key states. With UNFPA, the EU-funded SARAH programme is expanding adolescent- and gender-responsive maternal and child health services in Sokoto, Adamawa and Kwara. Through SD3R with IOM in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe, UNICEF supports reintegration and reconciliation to strengthen social cohesion. Collaboration with the ILO under the SUSI project is reinforcing social protection systems nationwide. In Borno, joint work with UNDP through the Borno Model advances reintegration and peacebuilding, while partnership with WFP delivers a resilience programme reaching over 150,000 people and scaling up to 200,000 in conflict-affected communities.
UNICEF maintained strategic leadership in advocacy and communications throughout 2025, achieving exceptional media presence with over 8,000 mentions across television, radio, and print platforms, complemented by approximately 6,000  interviews that reinforced credibility in shaping public discourse. Digital engagement generated over 15.4 million social media interactions, demonstrating strong resonance with diverse audiences. Collaboration with the Nigerian Guild of Editors strengthened ethical reporting and secured sustained editorial space for children's issues, while engagements with AREWA24 TV and Nigerian Television Authority expanded nationwide reach, ensuring child rights remained prominent in mainstream programming. 
UNICEF’s partnership portfolio was strengthened and diversified despite global downward Official Development Assistance (ODA) trends. UNICEF retained its long-standing bilateral and multilateral donors, with top public partners including Gavi (through the Government of Nigeria), United States, United Kingdom, Germany, European Commission/ECHO and Canada, . Other key contributors included Global Fund, Gates Foundation, World Bank, and Rotary Foundation. 
Through UNICEF support, national and sub-national statistical systems were strengthened to generate granular LGA-level estimates for equity-focused planning and prioritization through the Small Area Estimation methodology. Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 7 implementation embedded training for National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) staff to independently conduct global-standard surveys, with three MICS+ waves and real-time nutritional assessments providing actionable evidence for adaptive programming. The 2025 launch of the Power of Data Initiative with NBS created a coordinated platform for systematic data use in policy and accountability, while child-focused foresight analysis with the Vice President's Office advanced long-term, risk-informed planning to shape national priorities and the next Country Programme. UNICEF facilitated the Voluntary National Review (VNR) with youths and children, ensuring inclusive participation and meaningful reflection of their perspectives in the final report. 
UNICEF’s efforts in social and behaviour change strengthened evidence generation, coordination, community engagement and strategic communications, establishing community feedback mechanisms in 133 LGAs across 19 states that engaged over 4 million people, with 51,567 feedback items recorded and 62.31 per cent resolved. UNICEF also supported emergency response to floods and disease outbreaks, reaching 4,416,114 people with life-saving messages. The launch of the Behavioral Insights Research and Design Laboratory (BIRD-Lab) at the University of Lagos in collaboration with 22 leading universities of Nigeria consolidated UNICEF’s capacity for interdisciplinary behavioral research beyond communication and public health. Through BIRD-Lab partners, three major studies and rapid assessments were completed during the year. 
UNICEF strengthened emergency preparedness and humanitarian response in 2025. Updated risk mapping for Sokoto, Zamfara, and Kebbi states informed development of standard operating procedures for sudden-onset emergencies, enhancing coordination capabilities. Decentralized pre-positioning of supplies through government and UNICEF warehouses enabled nine rapid responses throughout the year. 
UNICEF also accelerated efforts to integrate gender and adolescent development and participation across its programming. Gender analyses recommendations were implemented through training on immunization in three states (Kaduna, Kebbi and Zamfara) and gender-transformative WASH in two states (Adamawa and Kaduna), establishing a gender and health champions network in Kaduna and developing WASH gender action . Men's engagement initiatives in immunization in Katsina reached 7,289 community members, identifying 2,969 child defaulters with 73.3 per cent successfully immunized within three months. The Reaching and Empowering Adolescent Girls in Northwest Nigeria programme benefitted 457,639 adolescent girls and young women and 237,576 adolescent boys and young men in Katsina and Sokoto (2022–2025). Young people also shaped national policies including Nigeria's SDG Voluntary National Review and NDC 3.0, with insights from over 6,000 adolescents informing the West and Central Africa Girls' Rights Agenda. Generation Unlimited Nigeria reached 2.3 million young people with digital learning and skills development, mobilized over 300,000 youth for environmental action through the Green Rising initiative, and the commitment of the   Vice President to lead the GenU 9JA Board boosted the partnership with government.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges and lessons learned
In 2025, under the Future Focus Initiative, UNICEF undertook significant strategic and structural shifts to respond to the rapidly changing official development assistance (ODA) landscape. Through the Business Model Innovation (BMI) process, the office redefined its programme priorities to ensure maximum impact for every dollar invested. This involved focusing on systemic and transformative strategies such as high-level policy dialogue, leading advocacy, mobilizing partnerships, and leveraging financing for children – approaches designed to deliver results at scale despite constrained resources. Building on the comprehensive programme review conducted in 2024, and through a series of consultative processes across programmes, enablers, and field offices, the Country Office articulated a clear strategic intent around five core priorities: polio eradication and zero-dose children, the first 1,000 days of life, addressing out-of-school children and driving education reform, ending open defecation, and scaling up birth registration. These priorities are being pursued through a differentiated approach across 19 focus states, supported by a leaner, fit-for-purpose structure and guided by a rigorous affordability analysis aligned with projected funding envelopes for 2026–2027
Government ownership proved critical for sustainability, with authorities leading policy direction and financing reforms that scaled delivery systems more reliably. For instance, with UNICEF support, programme-based budgeting was institutionalized in six states with medium-term expenditure frameworks and sector strategies, strengthening results-oriented budgeting and legislative oversight, while sustained advocacy in health resulted in the release of ¿540 million to insure 45,000 vulnerable individuals under a state health insurance scheme in Kogi State.
Delivering results at scale required strong government leadership and whole of system approaches, exemplified by integrating the measles–rubella vaccine into MNCH Week activities to reach nearly 60 million children, vaccinate more than 650,000 zero dose children, and provide HPV vaccination to over 1 million 9 year old girls, a convergence that strengthened demand generation, last mile logistics, and service equity across programmes.
Decentralized service delivery further reinforced these gains, as the government’s localization of birth registration with ALGON scaled community entry points across 304 LGAs and 3,372 wards in 15 states, registering nearly 600,000 children under one in underserved areas and moving the programme from pilot to nationwide delivery.
At the same time, differentiated, context-specific strategies sustained results by balancing upstream policy, coordination, data, and financing with downstream direct service delivery. UNICEF’s support to the National Council on Climate Change enabled submission of the Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0, strengthened with child-focused targets through evidence reviews, technical working groups (TWGs), youth inputs via U-Report, and national validation.  
UNICEF’s convening power also played a pivotal role in driving national policy decisions. In social protection, convening government partners through the Policy Review Core Group and TWG advanced revision of the National Social Protection Policy, with a multidimensional social register set to begin operating in January 2026 across four states to register 1 million households. 
Climate resilience, meanwhile, was mainstreamed into policies and infrastructure, with over 160 solar-powered WASH facilities and  upgrades such as solarized pumps, raised platforms, and reflective roofing enhancing service delivery in fragile contexts. These efforts improved functionality in schools and health centres, while solarization of oxygen plants ensured continuity of life-saving supplies in areas with unreliable electricity. UNICEF’s support for climate action was reinforced through strong youth engagement, with 237,000 young people mobilized across 20 states to plant over 148,000 trees and manage 121,-002 kilograms of plastic waste alongside the launch of a children responsive Climate Policy and Action Plan. 
Finally, humanitarian–development–peace (HDP) integration expanded coverage in crises, knitting emergency coordination into routine systems to deliver stronger and more sustained results. Sanitation responses supported over 700,000 people through construction, cleaning, and de-sludging, while emergency water services reached nearly 250,000 people despite funding gaps. Child protection services delivered integrated mental health and psychosocial support and gender-based violence services to nearly 150,800 people and over 238,700 children and caregivers, while reintegration and reunification efforts exceeded targets through coordinated case management across sectors. The ongoing reset of Nigeria’s emergency coordination architecture will accelerate humanitarian–development–peace (HDP) integration by deliberately shifting crisis response from parallel, time-bound mechanisms toward government-anchored, system-strengthening approaches.
Future outlook
UNICEFs’s future programming will be anchored on strategic prioritization to achieve greater focus and scale, with 2026 marking a sharper focus on two critical priorities: addressing out of school children and advancing child survival. This focus will be implemented through a multi-sectoral approach that integrates education, health, WASH, nutrition, and social protection. A comprehensive roadmap to guide this strategic shift will be developed in 2026. This sharper focus responds to persistent inequities, overlapping crises, and declining donor funding by moving away from fragmented interventions toward integrated packages that deliver greater impact. Concentrating on proven approaches and embedding interventions within government-led systems will ensure sustainability and scale. Reforms such as programme-based budgeting, universal child benefits, and digital platforms for monitoring and accountability will reinforce this effort.
UNICEF will also operationalize HDP nexus strategies with clear action triggers, integrated modalities, and deeper localization. This includes empowering local actors, embedding community-led solutions, and formalizing contingency mechanisms. Access protocols for the Northwest and Northeast will be finalized and implemented to ensure safe, predictable humanitarian delivery and continuity of essential services in fragile contexts.
At the same time, resource mobilization and financing for social services for children will be accelerated by expanding private sector partnerships and through new fundraising strategies, including individual giving, foundation engagement, enterprise partnerships, and philanthropy targeting ultra-high-net-worth individuals. Relationships with CEOs?  will be strengthened and partnerships with non-traditional donors, such as Qatar, South Korea, Japan, and China, will be explored. Investment cases and targeted donor engagement will address funding gaps.
Thought leadership and policy engagement will drive results, advancing universal child benefits advocacy and operationalization and scaling up the Power of Data Initiative. Monitoring and evaluation systems will also be strengthened through a National Council and Community of Practice. Evidence generation, including MICS and foresight analysis, will support policy dialogue and resource allocation. 
Complementary efforts will champion child poverty-focused policies, expand youth livelihood opportunities through Generation Unlimited, and accelerate digital transformation with interoperable data systems that enhance transparency and evidence-based decision-making.

More than three decades after ratifying the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), Cameroon has made measurable progress in advancing children’s rights, particularly in child survival and education. Under-five mortality has declined to around 67 deaths per 1,000 live births and neonatal mortality to about 25 per 1,000 reflecting progress toward SDG 3, although remaining above the 2030 targets of 25 and 12 respectively (SDG Country Profiles). Education outcomes have also improved, with primary completion at approximately 76% (Ministry of Basic Education) and lower secondary completion around 45% (Ministry of Secondary Education), contributing to progress toward SDG 4, while still falling short of universal completion. Persistent disparities across regions and population groups underscore the need to consolidate gains and accelerate more equitable progress for all children.
Persistent monetary poverty (37.7%) and multidimensional child poverty (47%) continue to limit children’s access to essential services and protection, with nearly six million children living in monetary-poor households (ECAM5). Conflict, climate shocks, and constrained fiscal space, where debt service crowds out social investment, compound vulnerabilities, widen inequalities, and disrupt pathways to human capital development, challenging the SDG commitment to leave no child behind. Encouragingly, Government actions such as the submission of the first State Report under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) signal policy intent to advance the protection and inclusion of PwDs across national systems.
With UNICEF’s support, child-sensitive planning and budgeting were promoted through national events such as the 26th Children’s Parliament and the Day of the African Child. Climate financing has gained momentum, with 3.11% of the national budget allocated to climate-related actions (including 12.27% within pilot ministries). However, achieving impact at scale will depend on sustained allocations, strengthened interministerial coordination, and effective subnational implementation. Ensuring that climate adaptation measures explicitly address children’s heightened vulnerabilities is critical. 
In 2025, humanitarian crises in Cameroon remain among the world’s most underfunded. An estimated 3.3 million people, including 1.7 million children and around 500,000 persons with disabilities (Humanitarian Needs Overview 2025), needed humanitarian assistance due to conflict, intercommunal violence, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks. Violence by non-state armed groups and prolonged lockdowns in the North-West and South-West Regions continued to restrict humanitarian access, livelihoods, and service delivery. As one of the eight countries engaged in the humanitarian reset, Cameroon is transitioning toward a coordination model that prioritizes localization, with national and local actors progressively assuming greater leadership in humanitarian response.
Every child survives and thrives: Cameroon sustained its focus on reaching zero-dose children through the National Immunization Strategy (2024–2028), aligned with the Global Immunization Agenda 2030. By December 2025, national routine immunization Penta3 coverage reached 88.2% almost reaching the national target of 89% and the malaria vaccine had been integrated into routine services in 42 of 205 health districts since 2024. The April–May 2025 nationwide polio campaign conducted jointly with neighbouring countries reached 7,887,300 children exceeding the planned target of 7,442,572 children under five, reflecting strong national leadership and effective cross-border coordination. 
On nutrition, UNICEF strengthened partnerships with the government, UN agencies, NGOs, and communities to improve early detection, referral, and lifesaving treatment, reaching 61,049 children with severe acute malnutrition, particularly in hard-to-reach areas across six priority regions. In 2025, UNICEF leveraged the Child Nutrition Fund (CNF) to unlock USD 473,000 in domestic resources, matched on a one-to-one basis for the procurement of RUTF, opening to optimistic financing to scale lifesaving nutrition services. Two rounds of Vitamin A supplementation reached 6,072,947 children aged 6–59 months (96% coverage), driven by integration into polio campaigns and strengthened partnerships, including with Helen Keller International. Despite these progresses, child food poverty remains a major challenge with eight out of ten children aged 6-23 months consuming fewer than three food groups out of the eight recommended. This highlights the urgent need to strengthen and protect children’s rights to a healthy and nutritious food environment.  
Every child learns: The realization of every child’s right to education continues to be constrained by protracted conflict in the North-West, South-West, and Far North Regions, displacements, and recurrent climate shocks, with disproportionate impacts on girls, children with disabilities, internally displaced children, and refugees. In humanitarian settings, integrated education responses - including psychosocial support, safe learning spaces, and community engagement - supported enrolment and learning continuity, while alternative learning pathways and catch-up programmes provided second-chance opportunities for out-of-school children. Still, achieving SDG 4 will require sustained political commitment, increased financing, and integrated, system-wide approaches. In 2025, efforts focused on mobilizing financing and establishing technical partnerships for the implementation of the Education and Training Sector Strategy 2023-2030.
Every child is protected from violence and harmful practices: UNICEF and the Government concluded the My Name campaign,, a national initiative to strengthen decentralized civil registration, increase birth certification, and raise public awareness on the importance of legal identity for children. Forty Mayors were recognized for their leadership and resource mobilization, demonstrating the potential of decentralization to accelerate birth registration. Progress was made in strengthening education–civil registry interoperability, and research on catch-up birth registration through schools addressed a backlog affecting more than 1.5 million learners without birth certificates. As of 25 November 2025, 533,504 cases had been submitted to courts, and 1,048,170 pupils were identified for support under a joint World Bank–UNICEF initiative. Harmful practices, including child marriage and adolescent pregnancy, as well as gender-based violence, remain unacceptably high (22% of women subjected to physical and/or sexual violence in Cameroon -2023 WCAR GBV AoR Response Monitoring) and call for strengthened national awareness, leadership, and ownership to ensure effective prevention and protection for those affected.
Every child lives in a safe and sustainable environment: In April 2025, Cameroon launched a National Water Policy targeting universal urban access and 85% rural water access by 2030, alongside the establishment of a dedicated rural water fund. With continued UNICEF support, complementary policy instruments advanced, including the National Sanitation Policy and medical waste management guidelines, while a WASH Climate Rationale was developed to strengthen advocacy and access to climate financing.
Every child has an equitable chance in life: Whilst social protection coverage remains low (only about 6% of the population, and 3–10% of children), in 2025, important progress has been made through the design of the National Solidarity Fund and the enrolment of 200’000 additional households in the social registry. These advances lay the groundwork for progressively expanding social protection coverage for children, helping to reduce the multidimensional deprivations that currently affect nearly half of all children (47.5%).

In 2025,  UNICEF continued to deliver tangible results for children while strengthening  its role as a trusted partner in advancing systemic changes in Cameroon. Key  achievements included expanding equitable access to life-saving interventions,  notably immunization, and scaling up nutrition programmes within the First  1,000 Days framework. Progress was made in modernizing the civil registration  system through the decentralization of civil registration services,  strengthened interoperability with the health and education sectors, and  improved data systems at the office of civil registration (BUNEC), including  the development of a dynamic national dashboard to track results. In  parallel, UNICEF accelerated WASH service delivery through climate-resilient,  solar-powered solutions and supported the institutionalization of  child-sensitive and climate-responsive planning and budgeting across national  systems. Decentralization efforts advanced through the Child Friendly  Municipalities initiative, with one-third of municipalities registered to  join the initiative. 
  
UNICEF advanced its Girl-Intentional Approach through the Girls’  Vision for the Future initiative with the Ministry of Women’s Empowerment  and the Family (MINPROFF), promoting girls’ leadership and co-creation of  solutions. More than 15,093 adolescents—68% girls—engaged in the Girls’  Movement, including 84 members of the Adolescent Girls Advisory Board (AGAB),  100 Youth Municipal Councilors in Child-Friendly Municipalities, and  adolescents active across 31 U-Report communities. Since July 2025, the MA  COTA mentorship programme—now institutionalized under MINPROFF—has supported 121  vulnerable girls through three cohorts in Yaoundé, Bertoua, and Maroua,  mobilizing 140 mentors. Its holistic model combines mentorship, safe spaces,  psychosocial support, and strengthened education pathways. A nationwide Girls’  Movement caravan reached all ten regions, with 5,600 girls contributing to  the first Girls’ Manifesto. The first National Forum on Girls’ Rights  solidified this momentum, elevating girls’ voices in national decision-making.  In 2026, UNICEF will support Government efforts to develop a multi-sectoral National  Adolescent Girls Agenda to drive sustained, system-wide change.
  
A major milestone in 2025 was the evaluation of the Country Programme,  which engaged diverse stakeholders and generated strong evidence to shape the  vision, theory of change, and design of the next programme—reinforcing  partner ownership and UNICEF’s role in driving systemic change for children.  Key lessons underscored the need for contextual adaptation, alignment with  national priorities such as decentralization, and multisectoral, capacity-driven  approaches. The evaluation also highlighted challenges in translating strong  intermediate results into lasting impact. In a context of declining external  resources and persistent child needs, achieving transformative, sustainable  results will require prioritizing high-impact, integrated interventions  delivered through national systems, along with diversified financing and  increased public investment in children. The evaluation emphasized the  importance of strategic prioritization centered on child rights, stronger targeting  of vulnerable groups, especially adolescents, and scaling proven  interventions while adapting to varied local contexts. It also reaffirmed  that addressing harmful social and gender norms, including child marriage and  sexual and reproductive health barriers, is essential for equitable progress.  Through broad engagement, including adolescents and youth, the evaluation  delivered actionable recommendations focused on systemic transformation, high-impact  targeted interventions, cross-sectoral integration of child rights, scalable  innovation, strengthened financing, and enhanced gender inclusion and youth  participation.
  
UNICEF strengthened the long-term institutionalization of child rights by  partnering with universities and positioning academia as a key driver of  child rights realization. Child Rights Centres were established as permanent  hubs for applied research, professional training, policy dialogue, and  community engagement, complemented by UNICEF–University Think Tanks that  generated evidence to inform programmes and public policy. Cameroon hosted  the first International Conference on Academia’s Role in Promoting Child  Rights, which produced the Yaoundé Declaration. This ecosystem was further  reinforced through targeted capacity building and evidence generation,  including behavioural insight studies and an evaluation of the Social and  Behaviour Change (SBC) programme. The SBC certification with the University  of Yaoundé I advanced SBC professionalization, while evaluation caravans with  the Universities of Yaoundé I and II strengthened national evaluation  capacity. Together, these achievements mark a shift toward durable system  strengthening and position Cameroon as a growing reference for the  institutionalization of child rights through academic partnership.
  
Goal Area 1:  Every child survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality  health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies.
  
Key Result  for Children #1: Immunization
  
In 2025, Cameroon made notable progress towards the regional Key Results  for Children (KRC 1) immunization targets despite subnational disparities.  National Penta3 coverage reached 88.2% (target 89%), up from 84.5% in 2024,  driven by UNICEF-supported catch-up campaigns, urban strategies, integrated  outreach, and strong community engagement. Three-quarters of districts  achieved  at least 80% coverage, though  insecurity kept some districts below 50%. Through the Reach the Unreached  initiative, Cameroon advanced digital immunization microplanning, improving  precision in identifying priority districts and zero-dose children.
  
Since 2020, Cameroon maintained wild poliovirus interruption and maternal  and neonatal tetanus elimination. Vaccine supply and cold-chain capacity  improved, reflected in an EVM score of 75% (target 80%), though 30% of  service points still lack certified cold-chain equipment—requiring renewed  investment and partner coordination.
  
Beyond immunization, UNICEF expanded access to medical oxygen by  establishing the first oxygen production plant serving the North and Adamawa  Regions, expected to benefit 10,000 premature newborns across four regions.  Cameroon also joined the Partnership for a Lead-Free Future and the Children’s  Environmental Health Collaborative, marking progress in elevating children’s  environmental health. Awareness efforts reached 2 million people, including  high-risk groups such as mechanics in Douala. To sustain  momentum and coordination, a multi-stakeholder task force comprising 20  organizations was established to lead joint environmental health actions in  2026, laying the foundation for stronger, coordinated prevention and  mitigation efforts to protect children from lead exposure.
  
Across 63 UNICEF-supported districts in six regions, 64% of children  (0–14) and 61% of adolescents (15–19) living with HIV were identified and  initiated on antiretroviral therapy,  surpassing the 55% target. Of the 185,000 adolescents targeted, 97,506 were  tested, and no stock-outs of HIV test kits were reported, ensuring continuity  of services.
  
Key Result  for Children #2: Prevention of Stunting
  
Stunting prevention remained central to the First 1,000 Days initiative,  a core Country Programme priority aligning multisectoral actions to ensure  every child’s right to survive and thrive. In 2025, UNICEF mobilized USD  473,000 in domestic resources, matched through the Child Nutrition Fund, to  procure high-impact nutrition commodities for the critical first 1,000  days—reflecting increasing national ownership. UNICEF also positioned the Africa  First Food Initiative within national frameworks, including the Food Systems  Transition Agenda and the UN Common Country Analysis. Building on the  Stronger With Breastmilk Only initiative in the West Region, a pilot  breastfeeding room was established at Foumbot District Hospital, signaling  institutional commitment and offering a scalable model for breastfeeding-friendly  workplaces. With over 80% of children aged 6–23 months facing food poverty,  UNICEF deepened partnerships with Government, the private sector, civil  society, and communities to advance improved infant and young child feeding  through stronger policies, regulations, and caregiver support for using safe,  nutritious, locally produced complementary foods.
  
In 2025, 6,072,947 children aged 6–59 months (96% of target) received two  doses of vitamin A, and 140,070 pregnant women received iron and folic acid  (IFA) to prevent maternal anemia and neural tube defects. UNICEF supported  the transition from IFA to Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS), leading  to Ministry of Health endorsement for MMS introduction in two pilot  districts.
  
To address severe wasting, UNICEF and partners strengthened early  detection, referral, and treatment across six priority regions. 61,409  children with severe acute malnutrition were treated in UNICEF-supported  facilities, achieving a 92% recovery rate, surpassing the SPHERE standard.  Efficiency gains were realized through a cost-effective RUTF supply route via  Nigeria, reducing costs by ~10%, shortening lead times, and expanding  treatment coverage.
  
Goal Area 2:  Every child learns and acquires skills for the future.
  
Key Result  for Children #3: Equitable and Sustainable Access to Education & Key  Result for Children #4: Improved Learning Outcomes
  
In 2025, UNICEF advanced children’s and adolescents’ right to education  amid protracted crises and displacement. System-strengthening efforts focused  on teacher capacity and foundational learning: 689 teachers (368 women) were  trained in ICT, multigrade management, and music pedagogy. 105 music nuclei  reached 5,000 vulnerable children, while 84,720 secondary students benefited  indirectly through trained teachers. In teacher training colleges, 38 nuclei  engaged 1,106 future teachers, and 7,090 students studied music as a  compulsory, child-rights-based subject. 188 children (73% girls) received  scholarships, and the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) pilot improved foundational learning for 4,127 students.
  
UNICEF prioritized equitable access and safe learning in crisis-affected  regions. Over 38,000 children, including 16,083 girls, continued or resumed  learning through integrated education and psychosocial support. To improve  safe learning spaces, UNICEF built 11 classrooms, rehabilitated 23, and set  up 54 Temporary Learning Spaces in the North-West and South-West. Digital  access expanded through five solar-powered E-containers - a solar-powered  digital learning hub equipped with computers, connectivity, and interactive  educational resources-, benefiting 4,911 children, including displaced  children and children with disabilities. In the Far North alone, 38,087  children returned to safer learning environments. School supplies and devices  supported continuity for 54,549 children in the East and Adamawa, while  learning and recreational materials reached 13,500 students, 150 teachers, 17,517  children, and 62 schools nationwide.
  
UNICEF also completed its first Green Skills Study, identifying  alternative learning pathways for adolescents and youth to contribute to  climate action. The findings informed the rollout of innovation bootcamps,  reaching over 60 adolescents and young people, half of them girls, who  acquired practical skills in entrepreneurship, climate solutions, and  problem-solving.
  
Goal Area 3:  Every child is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and  harmful practices.
  
Key Result  for Children #7: Birth Registration
  
Cameroon advanced its decentralization agenda through the Forum of Mayors  and a nationwide citizenship campaign focused on civil registration. Launched  at the 2024 Mayor’s Forum and concluded in March 2025, the My Name campaign  was a strategic initiative to strengthen decentralized civil registration,  improve service delivery, and raise public awareness on the importance of  birth certification. Closely aligned with the Government’s “catch-up”  initiative, the campaign aimed to ensure that previously unregistered  children could access official examinations and continue their education  without administrative barriers. Building on this momentum, municipalities  received targeted support through the Child-Friendly Municipalities initiative,  with a focus on strengthening local capacities, promoting digitalization,  providing essential equipment, and expanding access to civil registration  services. In line with the localization dynamic launched at the 2024 Forum of  Mayors, 35 civil registration offices were established within health  facilities in 2025, bringing the total to 172 nationwide. This integration  strengthens interoperability between health and civil registration systems,  reducing distance and cost barriers by linking birth notification at the  point of delivery with immediate registration.
  
UNICEF trained 151 participants, including 19 women, on birth  registration and data collection to strengthen technical and operational  practices at national, regional, and local levels. A training-of-trainers  approach further equipped 31 participants, including 9 women, to cascade  skills to local actors, embedding a sustainable model for continuous capacity  strengthening. At community level, awareness-raising activities reached  12,540 parents and caregivers in the Far North Region. To improve efficiency  and transparency, UNICEF supported the rollout of a national digital  dashboard to monitor civil registration processes and support real-time data  use. The platform, which includes five e-learning modules, is inclusive and  gender-sensitive, visualizing rural and urban data to promote equity and  facilitate knowledge sharing.
  
As of 27 November 2025, 1,150,817 births had been notified, including  553,919 girls, and 1,008,264 births had been registered, including 483,725  girls. In addition, 1,714 birth certificates were issued to flood-affected  children in the Far North, and 7,000 delayed cases were supported in the  South-West and North-West Regions. Community-based mechanisms in parts of the  Far North also contributed to 826 birth notifications, further strengthening  outreach to hard-to-reach populations.
  
Child  Protection and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Prevention
  
In 2025, UNICEF advanced a multi-level approach to strengthening child  protection systems and gender equality. Community engagement reached 119,001  parents and caregivers (including 46,518 women) and 50,091 community members (29,953  women), contributing to positive behavioural change and supporting 34,393  adolescent girls in high-risk regions. At policy level, the adoption of a costed  national action plan to end child marriage strengthened government  accountability and alignment with regional and global commitments.
  
Systems strengthening focused on standardizing case management  nationwide. As a result, 13,347 children (7,336 girls) accessed integrated  services across health, social welfare, and justice sectors. Institutional  capacity improved through training for 49 juvenile justice actors, 90  security focal points, and 55 social workers, alongside support for 1,700  children with disabilities. Gender-transformative programming empowered 3,897  girls, mobilized 140 mentors, and certified 75 actors in SEA prevention. Gender-based  violence (GBV) prevention reached 184,605 people, while complaint  and feedback mechanisms served 213,540 individuals, strengthening  accountability and resilience, especially in crisis-affected areas.
  
Children  Affected by Armed Conflict
  
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened protection for children affected by armed  conflict across the three crisis-affected regions. Monitoring of grave  violations continued, supported by training for 25 monitors and 23 teachers  on children’s rights and reporting.
  
Following sustained advocacy, Cameroon adopted the Roadmap for the Implementation  of the Safe Schools Declaration in December 2024, and in 2025 appointed  members of the National Technical Committee—including two UNICEF  staff—enhancing coordination and accountability for protecting education from  attack.
  
Reintegration support also progressed: 346 former child associates,  including 111 girls, returned to their communities in late 2024, bringing  total reintegrated children to over 600 by December 2025. Assistance for 1,300  children and families continued at the Meri Transit Centre, providing  education, basic services, and civil registration. In the North-West and  South-West, nearly 3,000 children and adults received psychosocial support  and child protection awareness. Additionally, 101 adolescents engaged in socio-economic  activities through Youth and Adolescent Clubs, supporting reintegration and  self-reliance.
  
Goal Area 4:  Every child has access to water, sanitation and hygiene and lives in a safe  and sustainable climate and environment.
  
Key Result  for Children #8: Ending open defecation.
  
In 2025, UNICEF advanced WASH outcomes through systems strengthening,  service delivery, and climate-resilient solutions. In the East Region, the  first Regional Water Stakeholders Forum - organized with UNHCR and the Ministry of Economy,  Planning and Regional Development (MINEPAT)  - brought together key actors to address water governance and access within  decentralized systems, improving coordination for sustainable services.
  
UNICEF expanded access to safe drinking water for 70,970 people, bringing  the four-year total to 216,595 (against a CPD target of 250,000). In  sanitation, 54,195 additional people gained basic services in 2025, for a  total of 232,300 people reached since 2022. Local systems were strengthened  through capacity building for four municipalities and support to the  development of a national sanitation policy led by the Ministry of Water and  Energy (MINEE). Climate-resilient infrastructure scaled significantly: UNICEF  built 34 solar water pumping systems, solarized 8 boreholes, drilled 104,  rehabilitated 131, and constructed or rehabilitated 17 gravity-fed systems,  improving reliable water access in vulnerable communities.
  
UNICEF strengthened WASH services in schools and health facilities in  2025. 84 schools received new water points, 16 had systems rehabilitated, and  32 gained inclusive, gender-segregated latrines. To support menstrual  hygiene, 851 adolescent girls, including 80 IDPs, received reusable sanitary  towels. In health facilities, 27 centres received solar-powered water  systems, and 14 installed modern medical waste treatment systems with staff  training. To ensure continuity of essential services, UNICEF installed 111.9  kWp of solar energy with 346.6 kWh storage across eight facilities, powering  maternity wards, neonatology units, operating theatres, and laboratories.  Through Community-Led Total Sanitation, 28,728 people gained access to  improved sanitation, increasing the total in certified open-defecation-free communities  to 164,575. UNICEF also initiated strategic analysis to strengthen long-term  rural sanitation financing and outcomes.
  
Climate-resilient WASH services reached 40 communities, schools, and  health facilities through solar-powered pumping, lighting, and cold-chain  systems. To scale renewable energy, UNICEF developed an investment case for  last-mile electrification using an Energy-as-a-Service model. UNICEF also  successfully advocated for child-sensitive NDC 3.0 and a revised National  Adaptation Plan.
  
Goal Area 5:  Every child has access to inclusive social protection and lives free from  poverty. 
  
Whilst child poverty in Cameroon remains widespread and persistent—reflected in high levels of both monetary poverty (45%) and multidimensional child poverty (ECAM)—UNICEF has supported the Government in strengthening national measurement systems. Together with the National Institute of Statistics (INS), UNICEF helped produce a child-poverty analysis. Public budget allocations for health and education continue to fall below agreed benchmarks, underscoring the need for sustained advocacy for increased and more child-focused investment. To encourage greater prioritization of social sectors, UNICEF has supported budget focal points within ministries to monitor allocations and flag underinvestment. To promote transparency and accountability, UNICEF launched the first citizen budget on the loi de règlement (expenditure execution audit), which will be endorsed by the Ministry of Finance. This marks an important step toward strengthening accountability and enhancing transparency across the budget cycle.
Social protection coverage remains low (6%), but expansion of the Unified Social Registry (RESUC)—now covering 320,000+ households—marks progress toward a coordinated and shock-responsive system. UNICEF supported on-demand registration, advocated for stronger engagement of the national safety net programme, and will help operationalize its newly confirmed institutionalization, including sustainable financing through the National Solidarity Fund. In humanitarian settings, 1,300 households received cash assistance and 3,000 households received anticipatory transfers.
Decentralization advanced through the Child-Friendly Municipalities approach, with new evidence expected to guide national scale-up. An analysis conducted in 2025 across six pilot municipalities (using 2022–2024 data) shows that they invested almost 40% of the budget in child-focused actions (1.376 billion FCFA)—from education subsidies and school rehabilitation to birth-registration campaigns and WASH infrastructure. Municipalities financed 84% of the total and UNICEF contributed 16%. Results are already visible: between 2022 and 2024, pilot municipalities recorded improvements in vaccination coverage (+5–7%), birth registration (+2–7%), and primary school enrollment (+2–7%).
UNICEF’s ability to deliver results increasingly relies on stronger partnerships, innovative financing, and evidence-based advocacy. In 2025, as part of the Humanitarian Reset, UNICEF supported the transition to Area-Based Coordination (ABC) in the North-West and South-West, reinforced government-led coordination in the Far North, and worked with OCHA and NGOs to advance localization. Cluster transition plans toward the ABC model were developed in WASH, Nutrition, Child Protection, and Education with local authorities and partners.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, the fourth year of implementation of the 2022–2026 Country Programme, UNICEF Cameroon delivered tangible results for children in a complex and rapidly evolving context, while continuously adapting its strategies, partnerships, and delivery models. A comprehensive Country Programme evaluation was conducted to assess effectiveness, efficiency, and strategic relevance. Its findings are directly informing the design of the 2027–2031 Country Programme and highlight both clear progress and structural constraints that must be addressed to achieve sustainable, large-scale impact. Across sectors, 2025 demonstrated what works to deliver results at scale, as well as where new approaches are required—particularly to reach the most marginalized children affected by poverty, conflict, displacement, climate shocks, and harmful social norms.
A key success factor was UNICEF’s systems-focused approach, which increasingly shifted from parallel service delivery toward strengthening national and subnational institutions. This was evident across immunization, civil registration, nutrition, education, WASH, and child protection, where results proved more sustainable when interventions were embedded within government systems, aligned with national priorities, and supported by policy reform, capacity strengthening, and digital solutions. Progress in decentralized civil registration - enabled by interoperability between health and education systems and supported by a national digital dashboard - illustrated how institutional integration can unlock results at scale. Similarly, the rollout of digital data collection by community health workers strengthened real-time monitoring, improved birth registration, and enhanced service interoperability.
Multisectoral programming proved particularly effective in fragile and shock-prone contexts. Persistent violence in the North-West, South-West, and Far North Regions, compounded by climate shocks such as floods and disease outbreaks, continued to disrupt access to essential services across health, nutrition, education, and WASH. These crises disproportionately affected already vulnerable children facing displacement, poverty, and limited access to basic services. Integrated approaches combining health, nutrition, education, WASH, protection, and cash assistance helped sustain service continuity while strengthening community resilience. Flexible and timely funding was critical to adapt interventions to rapidly changing conditions. These approaches reduced fragmentation, improved targeting, and maximized impact in contexts where single-sector interventions are insufficient. Social and Behaviour Change programming made important progress toward deeper system strengthening and generated valuable lessons on scaling impact. Experience from 2025 highlighted the importance of reinforcing behavioural data systems, deepening frontline engagement, and strengthening cross-sectoral integration, particularly in hard-to-reach and crisis-affected areas, to sustain behaviour and social norm change over time. 
Investments in municipal and community capacity, particularly through the Child-Friendly Municipalities initiative, further enhanced sustainability. Locally driven solutions, especially those incorporating participatory planning, proved effective in fostering social accountability, community engagement, and ownership. Cross-sectoral coordination with governmental institutions, UN agencies, academia, and civil society strengthened both evidence generation and programmatic impact, underscoring the central role of partnerships in reaching vulnerable children. Especially, strategic partnerships with academia emerged as a powerful catalyst. 
UNICEF’s partnership with universities has led to the launch of formal Social and Behavior Change (SBC) training programmes, the expansion of applied behavioural research, and the establishment of Child Rights Centres. These Centres now serve as permanent knowledge hubs that promote and mainstream children’s rights, leveraging universities’ unique role in shaping values, norms, and professional ethics. The introduction of a child-rights teaching module for primary-school teachers further embeds behaviourally informed, rights-based approaches within the national education system, laying the groundwork for sustainable, system-wide change.
As lead of the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy task force, UNICEF continued to champion the inclusion of persons with disabilities across both its internal workplace and programmatic priorities. The task force supported the Government in engaging NGOs in drafting Cameroon’s initial report under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, strengthening national ownership and accountability. In social protection, anticipatory cash assistance in the Far North systematically included persons with disabilities, ensuring they were not left behind in emergency response. Going forward, UNICEF is working with the Government to reinforce early detection and screening systems for children with disabilities, laying the foundation for improved access to timely support and services including education (contributing to the operationalization of the Inclusive Education Strategy).
UNICEF’s adaptive and agile management was also reflected in its use of innovation and real-time learning. Digital tools, participatory municipal planning, solar-powered infrastructure, and alternative supply routes for nutrition commodities enabled faster responses, efficiency gains, and expanded coverage. The ongoing transition toward Area-Based Coordination in humanitarian settings offers further opportunities to strengthen government leadership, advance localization, and reinforce humanitarian-development nexus approaches. Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) supported adaptive management and programme quality by enabling real-time learning and responsiveness. Community feedback and social listening informed programme adjustments, though uneven capacities at decentralized levels affected consistent closure of feedback loops, particularly in crisis-affected areas. Lessons from 2025 reinforced that AAP delivers the greatest value when embedded in routine planning and decision-making, rather than treated as a parallel function. UNICEF will prioritize further institutionalization of AAP within government and partner systems to strengthen accountability and trust. Another notable area of progress was adolescent engagement and girls intentional programming. The Girls’ Movement demonstrated that when adolescent girls are provided with structured platforms, safe spaces, and policy entry points, they can meaningfully influence social norms and national agendas. The National Girls’ Summit, the Girls’ Manifesto, and the expansion of advisory and municipal youth platforms showed strong potential to move adolescent participation toward system-level influence. The planned National Adolescent Girls Action Plan represents a key opportunity to consolidate and institutionalize these gains in 2026.
Looking ahead to 2026, UNICEF Cameroon will build on these lessons to refine programme strategies in preparation for the 2027–2031 Country Programme. Strategic focus will centre on the first 1,000 days of life and child survival, foundational learning and reduction of out-of-school children, and protection from all forms of violence. Priorities will include scaling integrated packages of high-impact interventions; strengthening decentralized service delivery through capacity building and child-sensitive budgeting; advancing innovation across humanitarian and development programming; and reinforcing digital systems for real-time monitoring and decision-making. Partnerships with universities, civil society, and the private sector will be deepened to support evidence generation, policy influence, and innovation. Climate resilience, community empowerment, social norm programming, disability inclusion, and gender transformative programming -will be systematically integrated to ensure equitable and sustainable outcomes.
Informed by the 2025 lessons learned and the Country Programme evaluation, UNICEF Cameroon will pursue three strategic shifts at the core of the new CPD 2027–2031.
First, a shift from piloting to modelling for scale. Interventions will increasingly be designed as scalable models from the outset, with clear pathways for institutional uptake, replication, and financing. Innovations and pilots will serve as proof points, supported by rigorous documentation and learning, and scaled through policy alignment, costed action plans, and capacity transfer to national and decentralized institutions, ensuring local relevance while enabling system-wide adoption.
Second, a shift toward partnerships as the primary scaling mechanism. Partnerships will be positioned as the main drivers of impact and scale. UNICEF will deepen collaboration with line ministries, decentralized authorities, academia (Child Rights Centers), civil society, UN agencies, and the private sector to leverage complementary strengths and reinforce shared ownership. This shift will be accompanied by a stronger focus on evidence-led and adaptive programming, using evaluations, routine data, dashboards, and real-time monitoring to guide programme adjustments and policy dialogue.
Third, a shift from service delivery to systems’ strengthening as the primary pathway to impact. UNICEF will further reinforce national systems by strengthening policies, financing mechanisms, coordination platforms, data systems, and service delivery structures.  Emphasis will be placed on interoperability across sectors, ensuring that children can access a holistic package of services and be effectively referred across systems.
Together, these new visions will guide UNICEF Cameroon’s transition from delivering strong results to institutionalizing impact at scale, ensuring that progress for children is durable, equitable, and resilient in an increasingly complex operating environment.

The Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe (STP) is a small island nation located in the Gulf of Guinea. With one of Africa’s most diverse forest ecosystems, STP became the first state to have its entire territory designated as a UNESCO biosphere reserve in 2025[i]. 
The country has recorded sustained social progress, marked by improvements in health care and access to education, contributing to a rising Human Development Index reaching 0.637[ii] in 2023 (from 0.608 in 2019). In December 2024, STP graduated to lower-middle income status. 
 
The nation faces structural constraints, including geographic isolation, high exposure to climate risk and remains highly vulnerable to external shocks, exacerbated by reliance on imports and official development assistance. Gross Domestic Product growth improved to 2.9 per cent in 2025 (from 1.1 per cent in 2024[iii]), yet economic conditions remain fragile. Overlapping energy crisis and demographic shock have disrupted essential social services particularly in schools and health facilities. 
The 2024 national census revised the population to 209,607[iv] reflecting slower growth driven by high migration among the working-age population, leading to labour shortages in critical sectors. Twenty per cent of the Sao Tomeans are estimated to live abroad[v]. In 2024 only, about two per cent of the population left the country[vi]. Migration has accelerated since 2019, spurred by limited employment prospects. With 61 per cent of the population under 25, STP has a young population. However, unemployment among 15–24-year-olds stands at 21 per cent, well above the national average[vii]. Gender disparities persist, reflected in a Gender Inequality Index of 0.492 (130th out of 172 countries)[viii]. Adolescent girls remain particularly vulnerable to early pregnancy, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation[ix]. 
 
Progress against UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and towards the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) has advanced (30 per cent of the SDG achieved or on track)[x]; however, limited disaggregated data constrained measurement. The 2024 census marked a major step in updating child-related data, highlighting disparities not previously captured, while informing adjustments to core impact indicators. The upcoming Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS-7) will be a key milestone to close critical data gaps on child vulnerabilities, strengthening impact measurement.
 
Every child survives and thrives.
In terms of health and well-being (SDG-3), under-five mortality declined to 13.94 per 1,000 live births in 2023 (from 14.58 in 2022), making STP one of only two sub-Saharan African countries to meet this SDG target, while neonatal mortality decreased to 6.76 (from 7.06)[xi]. In 2025, UNICEF focused on restoring pentavalent immunization coverage to its historically high levels, above 90 per cent. STP maintained zero cases of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) mother-to-child transmission. 
Progress towards zero hunger (SDG-2) remains mixed. Stunting among children under five declined from 11.7 per cent in 2019 to a stable 10 per cent since 2022[xii]. In 2024, undernourishment rose to 17.4 per cent (16.4 per cent in 2023) while half of the population (53.3 per cent) was unable to afford a healthy diet (from 52.7 per cent in 2023). 
 
Every child lives in a clean and safe environment.
Access to clean water and sanitation (SDG-6) shows limited progress. In 2024, only 49 per cent of households had access to at least basic sanitation services (45.7 in 2019) [xiii]. The launch of the WASH multisectoral coordination mechanism and the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) represented major advances to strengthen WASH effectiveness. The government is finalising the National Adaptation Plan to reduce STP’s vulnerability to climate.
 
Every child learns.
In the 2024/2025 school year, access to pre-primary education (SDG-4) reached 88 per cent of children aged 4–5, up from 79 per cent in 2023/2024[xiv], while the primary completion rate rose to 94 per cent, amid population outflows and rising school disengagement. UNICEF focused on advancing pre-school education with a national supervision model, while accelerating the adoption of digital and blended learning through innovative platforms, expanding equitable access to education.
 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation. 
Progress on SDG targets related to child protection (SDG-5, SDG-16) remains slow, as harmful social practices and gender inequality persist. Eighty-four per cent of children experience violent discipline and 70 per cent face psychological aggression[xv]. The migration crisis has strained family structures increasing risks of neglect, abuse and school dropout. In 2025, with UNICEF’s support, the integrated case management protocol was fully implemented, a key step in strengthening multisectoral responses to violence against children (VAC)
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life. 
Almost 17 per cent of the population lived on less than US$ 2.15/day in 2025[xvi], showing limited advancement towards SGD-1, as rising living costs have eroded household purchasing power. The social protection system (SDG-1, SDG-10) reached about 25 per cent of the population in extreme poverty in 2024[xvii]. Advocacy by UNICEF and partners has contributed to sustained increases in budget allocations for health, education, and social protection, highlighting progress in prioritizing social sectors. In 2025, UNICEF continued to advance child-centred evidence, preparing the MICS-7 with the government. 
 
In January 2025, STP experienced a period of political changes marked by the appointment of a new government. The transition paved the way for the electoral framework ahead of the 2026 presidential election. The National Sustainable Development Strategy 2026–2040 was approved, setting a long-term vision for inclusive sustainable growth, endorsed by the parliament. STP submitted its third nationally determined contributions under the Paris Agreement and the Universal Periodic Review to the UN Human Rights Council, both aligned with sustainable development priorities and informed by UNICEF’s contribution. UNICEF is supporting the government to update the national contingency plan, strengthening prevention and preparedness to enhance the protection of vulnerable groups, including children.
