In a challenging funding context, UNICEF strategically prioritized resources to engage communities, focusing on scalable interventions to deliver sustainable system level impacts. The agency championed youth engagement, mobilizing 23,000 young people (38 per cent of 12-24), up from 20,600 in 2024. UNICEF generated momentum through youth participation in high-level national and regional platforms, bringing violence against children and children’s rights onto the policy agenda with a strong focus on adolescent girls. 150 adolescents (77 girls) contributed to the validation of the National Youth Strategy, reflecting youth priorities in national frameworks. UNICEF launched the podcast “The Voice of the Child,” funded by Spotify, whose edition, ‘My day, my rights’ reached 25,000 views. The U-Report Digital Platform engaged 12,225 young people (20 per cent of 12-24) and supported ten national campaigns, including on climate change and sexual abuse. UNICEF reinforced the Children’s Parliament through elections and training, including on the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and disability, increasing children’s rights awareness. A child-led Council of Ministers session allowed children to advocate for their rights, a landmark achievement in youth influence on public decision. The national forum on adolescent mental health opened a unique space for dialogue and raised the issue on the policy agenda.
Recognizing the catalytic role of social and behaviour change (SBC), UNICEF established an innovative multisectoral SBC platform in Sao Tome supported by a regional hub in Principe and trained 186 professionals (108 women) across health, education, social protection, child protection, WASH and youth services to form a national pool of trainers and accelerate equitable results at scale. 
 
UNICEF contributed to the strategic Priority Areas of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF): inclusive social system (Outcome-1), climate action (Outcome-2) and transparent and accountable institutions (Outcome-4). 
 
Every child survives and thrives. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF contributed significantly to strengthening resilient community health services, advancing progress toward the Country Programme targets and improving access to quality maternal, newborn and child health services (UNSDCF Outcome-1 and SDG-2 and 3).
 
Collaborating with international partners (GAVI, World Bank, World Health Organization-WHO), UNICEF focused on reversing the sharp decline in immunization coverage registered in 2024 to sustain progress toward SDG-3. UNICEF ensured uninterrupted vaccine availability and technical assistance to the Ministry of Health, including supplementary immunization activities that reached 957 children in three underperforming districts. Large-scale SBC interventions, led by UNICEF with youth associations last year, on human papillomavirus (HPV), COVID-19 and routine vaccination drove increased demand in 2025, reinforced with community-based sessions targeting 1,027 parents (918 women) from vulnerable families. As a result, in 2025, coverage of the third dose of the Pentavalent vaccine increased from 87 per cent to 96 per cent among children aged 0–11 months, slightly below the annual target, but returning to the historical level above 90 per cent. Zero-dose children dropped to 6 (from 796 in 2024) and incomplete vaccination schedules to fewer than 100. Measles–rubella coverage rose from 90 to 94 per cent.
Financial and technical assistance to the Ministry of Health, together with Gavi and WHO, significantly strengthened the Expanded Programme on Immunization. UNICEF enabled 50 formative supervision visits across all districts reinforcing the skills of 133 district health professionals (97 women) and enhancing service quality. Alongside its regional office and global supply division, UNICEF advanced national readiness for immunization autonomy, strengthening vaccine forecasting and costing for 2030–2035, building the capacities of 35 professionals (17 women) while financially supporting maintenance of cold-chain equipment. UNICEF also pursued high-level advocacy with national authorities to advance domestic vaccine financing.
 
Provision of essential medicines ensured uninterrupted services and contributed to the survival of 20,472 children under five representing 83 per cent (18,227 in 2024), improving child health outcomes. The provision of HIV tests and antiretroviral medicines ensured adequate follow-up care for HIV-positive pregnant women, resulting in zero cases of mother-to-child transmission. In 2025, UNICEF trained 30 district health staff (15 women) in Caue and Principe in evidence-based planning, to enhance data-driven decision-making and improve primary health-care performance, increasing the pool of trained staff to 80 nationwide. UNICEF will prioritize continuous monitoring and supportive supervision to reinforce implementation and system sustainability. A total of 67,158 children and adolescents accessed primary health care in UNICEF-supported facilities, lower than 2024 due to intensive HPV vaccination last year. With adolescents aged 10–19 representing 26 per cent of the population, strengthening adolescent health remained a priority. UNICEF maintained the HPV coverage among ten-year old girls at 95 per cent, contributing to improved health outcomes for adolescent girls. The national adolescent health strategy is expected in 2026.
 
UNICEF continued to expand Vitamin A supplementation through primary health care services supporting 24,836 children achieving 87 per cent coverage among children aged 6–59 months (85 per cent in 2024). As a result, hospital mortality linked to severe acute malnutrition fell from four cases in 2024 to three in 2025, strengthening prospects for achieving zero cases by the end of 2026.
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment. 
 
UNICEF prioritized community-level behavioural change to advance sustainable sanitation and climate-resilient practices to accelerate progress toward open defecation-free status, contributing to SDG-6 and UNSDCF Outcome-1.
 
Working with the government, UNICEF substantially supported communities in adopting safer sanitation practices, maintaining gains and strengthening preparedness for climate risks. Through the SBC platform, 24 government staff (12 women) gained practical skills in climate, environment and disaster risk reduction while 22 community leaders improved their knowledge of Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach, enabling 1,468 community members (1,146 women) to strengthen community preparedness for climate change. These efforts resulted into four new communities and 110 families (441 people) triggered for CLTS and preparing to achieve open defecation free (ODF) status by 2026. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF finalized the CLAC supported by a five-year action plan to integrate climate considerations into sectoral programming, disseminated to 216 institutional representatives and youth (87 women) across all districts, embedding climate-resilient approaches in national and local planning to strengthen long-term resilience. Youth engagement remained a key driver for effective community climate action (SDG-13, UNSDCF Outcome-2). UNICEF, together with UNDP restructured the regional youth committees for climate change, training new members to sustain the active engagement of 70 climate champions (29 girls). The appointment of a national coordinator enhanced programme implementation and climate awareness initiatives. UNICEF sponsored two youth to represent STP at the One Forest Youth Forum in Gabon and coordinated youth recommendations for COP-30 advancing the national climate agenda and youth-led solutions. A youth-produced climate video gained international visibility at the UN General Assembly in September 2025.
 
UNICEF’s technical and financial contributions enabled the operationalization of the multisectoral WASH coordination mechanism by the Ministry of Environment. The first official meeting marked a key step toward improved coordination, stronger information management and monitoring to advance climate-resilient risk-informed WASH programming and services. Reflecting these achievements, UN-Water selected STP as a case study for 2026 to highlight enabling factors driving progress on SDG-6.
 
Every Child Learns 
 
In 2025, UNICEF contributed significantly to advancing an inclusive, equitable and gender-transformative education agenda. Completion rates remained above programme targets and improved compared to 2023/2024, reaching 94 per cent in primary (from 93 per cent), 75 per cent in lower secondary (from 65 per cent) and 37 per cent in upper secondary (from 32 per cent). Girls represented 48 per cent of the completers at primary level, but 56 per cent at upper secondary levels. UNICEF’s agile and scalable approaches ensured continuity of learning while driving systemic improvements aligned with UNSDCF Outcome-1, SDG-4 and SDG-5.
 
UNICEF significantly advanced the inclusive pre-school education model, expanding support from 40 per cent to 60 per cent of the kindergartens. A total of 66 establishments received 2,350 gender-responsive curriculum guidelines and 10,000 inclusive pedagogical resources. In 2024/2025, 13,500 children (54 per cent girls) aged 4-5 benefited from enriched learning environments, contributing to a gross pre-primary enrolment rate of 88 per cent. In partnership with the World Bank and Global Partnership for Education (GPE), the national pedagogical supervision model was rolled out across all 109 kindergartens and 89 per cent of the pre-primary workforce was trained to deliver child-friendly gender-inclusive learning. Engagement with the African Early Childhood Network strengthened national capacities and opened avenues for collaboration among Portuguese-speaking countries to advance integrated early childhood development and multisectoral coordination.
 
UNICEF strengthened the National Digital Learning Programme, through targeted technical assistance and capacity building, expanding equitable access to quality primary and secondary education. In 2025, 4,176 students (44 per cent girls), 10 per cent of all students to access Akelius and the Learning Passport platforms in 15 schools, up from 2,339 in 2024, demonstrating a strong uptake of innovative digital and blended-learning approaches. With UNICEF’s support, 699 teachers (28 per cent of the workforce) were trained and gained proficiency in blended methodologies, contributing to 85 per cent of students achieving satisfactory learning outcomes. Connectivity improvements initiated in 2024 with Giga and the World Bank and capacity strengthening of the Ministry of Education and the General Regulatory Authority will enable 11 of 105 schools to be connected in 2026, benefiting 6,000 students (12 per cent) in basic and lower secondary education.
 
UNICEF promoted safer, gender-responsive and inclusive learning environments (SDG-4 and 5). Technical support expanded evidence-based school improvement planning. Sixteen of 30 supported schools demonstrated measurable gains in planning and monitoring. Remedial learning, teacher development and rehabilitation benefited 14,580 students (11,500 girls). UNICEF will scale the approach to additional schools in 2026. In 30 schools, 215 school community members received violence prevention and protection messages, reinforcing gender-responsive environments supporting retention, particularly for adolescent girls (SDG-5). To reduce learning barriers, UNICEF expanded the mapping of children with disabilities, already completed in three districts to one additional high-exclusion district, reaching 36 communities and 600 families. As a result, 110 children with special educational needs received medical assessments. 
 
Out-of-school children rose from 8.3 per cent in 2023 to 12 per cent in 2024 due to the migration crisis and economic pressure. In response, UNICEF expanded skills and digital trainings for 2,350 young children and young people (from 1,557 in 2024), improving learning, employability and advancing SDG-8, with around 10,000 beneficiaries to date. UNICEF also supported the establishment of multisectoral early warning teams for early detection, with pilots planned in two schools in 2026, and will further prioritize adolescent girls in underserved regions to strengthen retention and equitable access.
 
 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF significantly enhanced national capacities to prevent and respond to violence against children (VAC), with particular attention to sexual and gender-based violence. UNICEF expanded multisectoral implementation ensuring that services reached the most vulnerable children, supporting the achievement of SDG-16, SDG-5 and UNSDCF Outcome-4. 
 
UNICEF’s financial and technical support accelerated consistent application of standard operational procedures for case management and strengthened cross sectoral collaboration and referral mechanisms. Capacity building for 78 frontline workers and professionals from SBC platform improved response quality. Integrating referral pathways into schools enabled early identification at scale: 121 education professionals (57 per cent women) were trained, enhancing coordination across 30 schools (60 per cent) and benefitting 8,345 children and adolescents. Since 2023, 577 professionals have been trained in preventing and responding to violence and exploitation, with increased focus on risks faced by adolescent girls. In 2025, 357 children at risk or victims received assistance through UNICEF supported services (340 in 2024), surpassing the Country Programme targets. Among them, 218 victims of sexual violence were identified and referred, demonstrating stronger detection and coordinated response. UNICEF’s technical and convening support enabled the institutionalization of the Child Protection Network and its Executive Secretariat, advancing system coordination and sustainability. As a result, 60 per cent of reported cases received coordinated responses with an average response time of 72 hours. 
 
Innovative large-scale SBC interventions and adolescent engagement strengthened community awareness of sexual violence, promoted positive norms and empowered adolescent girls reaching 2,235 adolescents (70 per cent girls) in universities and secondary schools, 2,102 students and community members (54 per cent girls) through the Child Protection Network and 4,459 vulnerable families (15,229 children). By training 24 professionals (12 women) through the SBC platform, the programme delivered integrated prevention and response services to 1,250 families, laying foundations for continued scale up. Furthermore, high-visibility advocacy positioned the VAC agenda within national priorities, emphasizing violence against adolescent girls. The national march against sexual violence, a dedicated session of the Council of Ministers and the participation of three adolescent girls to the regional girls’ summit in Dakar strengthened public commitment to zero tolerance for VAC and promoted safety for adolescent girls. UNICEF raised awareness on gender and sexual-based violence and reporting mechanisms, highlighting adolescent girls’ risks, empowering 14,650 adolescents (54 per cent girls, including 43 girls with disabilities) in schools and communities with the support from the Portuguese cooperation. 
 
UNICEF, collaboratively with the Ministry of Justice further advanced justice services for child victims of violence through financial, technical and advocacy support. The specialized room for children's testimony equipped by UNICEF and located at the Public Prosecutor’s office, was inaugurated, integrating an innovative model for safer testimonies. Fifty-two professionals (35 women) were trained on child-sensitive listening protocols to reduce revictimization through trilateral cooperation with Brazil. By the end of 2026, 40 per cent of the professionals in the network are expected to apply the protocols, contributing to a more child-friendly and gender-sensitive justice system (SDG-5, SDG-16). 
 
Completion of the quantitative component of the national Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) study will provide essential data to inform gender-transformative programming and sectoral reforms (SDG-4, SDG-16, SDG-5). UNICEF trained 96 technicians (51 women) from the National Institute of Statistics on child-sensitive research methodologies and ethical protocols. In 2026, efforts will focus on mobilizing resources to implement Primero digital platform to improve data management and referrals.
 
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life. 
 
UNICEF continued to support the scaling of sustainable and child-responsive social protection services and to leverage reliable child-centred disaggregated data, achieving notable progress, remaining on track to meet the expected targets for the cycle, supporting SDG-1, SDG-8 and SDG-10. 
 
In partnership with the National Institute of Statistics, UNICEF coordinated six working sessions to operationalize the administrative data collection, improve data-systems interoperability and prepare the MICS-7, including training on child-sensitive methodologies. This enabled the integration of disaggregated administrative data into national monitoring systems across 22 institutions enhancing SDG monitoring and advancing progress towards UNSDCF Outcome-4. In 2026, UNICEF will train 36 technicians on developing child-sensitive programme budgets aligned with the National Strategy for Sustainable Development and the SDG. 
 
Seventy-five per cent of the recommendations from the Committee on the Rights of the Child have been addressed. UNICEF increased national ownership of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) while advancing child-rights monitoring, engaging 77 additional actors from Principe (291 officials trained since 2024) to integrate recommendations into sectoral plans. Together with the Human Rights Office, UNICEF convened two working sessions with 32 technicians (21 female) from 13 institutions to refine monitoring indicators and clarify roles for CRC implementation.
 
The third National Social Protection Council strengthened coherence in the national response for the most vulnerable living in extreme poverty. In 2024, the country started receiving direct financing from the World Bank to reinforce the social protection system. This milestone reflects the effectiveness of UNICEF’s long-term capacity building and system strengthening. UNICEF continued to provide technical support and advocated to expand system coverage to reach the most at risk children (SDG-1 and SDG-10), remaining on track to reach the Country Programme targets. Using regular funds, UNICEF continued to technically support the Parental Education Programme (PEP) applying to beneficiaries of the cash transfer programme, reaching 15,229 children and 5,000 families (15,654 in 2024 and 4,070 families), a slight reduction due to family graduation, emigration and revised criteria. UNICEF’s advocacy contributed to a revision of the cash-programme eligibility in 2025, prioritizing families with children and persons with disabilities (3,219 persons with disabilities, among whom 637 children) and enabling the inclusion of an additional 1,000 households in 2026. UNICEF together with partners trained 4,759 beneficiaries (4,678 women) in positive, gender-transformative parenting practices. Together with the Directorate of Social Protection, UNICEF produced a video showcasing the successes of the PEP. 
 
UNICEF delivered targeted training to frontline technicians and child deputies on the rights of children with disabilities, reinforcing national capacities. Jointly with the government, the agency finalized the new disability case-management protocol and referral mechanisms, aligned with UNICEF Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy, improving access to services for children with disabilities. UNICEF supported the training of 30 multisectoral frontline workers on their application and the situational analysis of persons with disabilities, integrating the rapid assessment on children with disabilities. A pilot intervention in Principe is planned in 2026 to operationalize the protocol. 
 
Cross-sectoral support 
 
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA)
UNICEF trained 20 staff, 55 implementing partners and 150 adolescents to respond to and prevent sexual abuse and exploitation advancing SDG-5 and SDG-16 and exceeding annual target. The agency played an active role in the UN PSEA Network, improving coordination for reporting and referral, supported by the Child Protection Network. No cases were reported through UNICEF supported mechanisms.
 
Operations excellency
UNICEF in cooperation with other UN agencies introduced targeted efficiency measures to reduce operating costs generating significant savings to reinvest in sustainable energy initiatives. A comprehensive programme risk assessment was completed to address emerging challenges. Financial processes improved, with over 95 per cent of payments executed electronically. A simplified cash forecasting system strengthened financial management. UNICEF completed 100 per cent of assurance activities, in line with 2024, and delivered HACT, Fraud and PSEA trainings to all implementing partners.
UNICEF maintained its commitment to staff well-being and inclusion. The office conducted a comprehensive learning-needs assessment to inform the training plan and set up a supervisors’ forum for dialogue and peer learning. Internal ethics sessions and dialogue with the Mediation and Ombudsman Offices increased staff awareness of reporting channels. A training session on disability for staff and partners and an assessment of the premises promoted an inclusive working environment.

Despite a complex operating and funding environment, UNICEF sustained results for children and progress towards the SDG. The country witnessed increased demand for social services, while rising emigration strained family structures and weakened community support systems heightening children’s vulnerabilities. The departure of trained personnel created critical gaps, particularly in health and education, also impeding programme delivery. Youth platforms, such as the Youth Climate Committees lost active participants. These challenges, combined with funding constraints, required replacement and retraining of the workforce and participants, as well as programme adjustment. Power outages disrupted social services and UNICEF’s operations, delaying programme implementation. 
 
In response, UNICEF further pivoted toward high-impact, innovative interventions to strengthen national systems while narrowing focus to strategic child-centred priorities, supported by communities and youth engagement. High level advocacy and policy dialogue delivered measurable shifts toward more inclusive and equitable services for children, expanding coverage and revising criteria for a more responsive social protection system. UNICEF strongly advocated for increased prioritization of public finance for children and social services, including STP’s ability to secure and manage vaccines autonomously. 
Leveraging South-South cooperation with Portuguese-speaking countries, UNICEF facilitated mutual learning and technical exchange, expanding access to specialised expertise to strengthen national systems. Deeper engagement will scale these gains and reinforce capacities to advance the national agenda.
 
The annual review confirmed the relevance of the Country Programme’s strategic approach. In 2025, UNICEF surpassed funding targets leveraging multi-agency and inter-office collaborations. The capacity to deliver at scale and maximize impact with limited resources solidified UNICEF role as a trusted partner advancing children’s rights.
 
Strengthening early warning mechanisms for vulnerable youth: Increasing vulnerabilities and rising migration heightened the need for rapid response mechanisms for at-risk youth, stronger early warning and monitoring systems and efficient multisectoral coordination. In 2025, UNICEF prioritized integrated coordination for timely identification and referral of at-risk children. In education, this led to an innovative school-based early warning mechanism to detect students at risk of dropout or abandonment; scheduled for implementation next year. Standard protocols, an effective executive secretariat, clearer referral pathways, school-based training and large-scale SBC reinforced multisectoral coordination for case management and referral, improved earlier risk detection, enabling faster, more effective responses to VAC. In 2026, UNICEF will roll out the model for education and explore integrated modalities to scale the approach across sectors based on results. 
 
Innovative integrated SBC to drive social changes: In 2025, UNICEF created an innovative integrated SBC Platform in Sao Tome supported by a hub in Principe, to ensure no child is left behind. The platform is an institutionalized pool of 186 SBC trainers across sectors. UNICEF ensures coordination, training, monitoring, planning, governance and integrated interventions. The platform acts as a catalyst for coordinated community-driven action, expanding the reach of SBC interventions, accelerating results at scale to improve outcomes for children. UNICEF successfully mobilized community engagement to advance child rights, including disability inclusion, protect adolescent girls, prevent VAC and support the climate agenda. Furthermore, UNICEF leveraged an innovative private-sector partnership with UNITEL to broadcast child protection and children’s rights message nationwide. The platform demonstrated strong multiplier effects, increasing demand for essential services and community accountability. Momentum will continue in 2026 with further investment, partners training, improved integrated interventions and the finalization of the SBC multisectoral strategy. 
 
Youth engagement as a catalytic strategy: In 2025, youth and adolescents acted as powerful catalyst for systemic change, amplifying community engagement and accelerating behaviour shifts. UNICEF expanded youth participation, elevating adolescent priorities on the national agenda, provided platforms for young people’s voices, designed youth-led programmes, reinforced their role in climate action and citizen participation, advancing adolescent girls’ agency. More than 300 young people took part in advocacy events and high profile national or regional fora, with particularly strong engagement on climate issues and adolescent girls. Participation scaled across sectors, engaging 23,000 adolescents and youth, through digital platforms, youth volunteer initiatives, climate committees, youth interaction centres and community platforms. Awareness-raising SBC interventions and capacity-building of communities, services workforces and government entities on youth empowerment proved highly effective in strengthening youth leadership and increasing accountability toward the most vulnerable. 
 
Equity focused programming to address vulnerabilities: UNICEF integrated an equity lens, focused on adolescent girls and children with disabilities across sectors, using schools as a platform and engaging youth networks, partners and communities. Targeted equity-focused partnerships with local youth platforms and communities facilitated outreach to marginalized groups, including adolescent girls and adolescents with disabilities. UNICEF elevated gender equality and prevention of gender-based violence on the national agenda, increasing public visibility, supported by high level advocacy to address root causes of inequality. Next year, UNICEF will adopt more inclusive approaches, using stronger assessments to identify specific groups of children and adolescents and tailor transformative, evidence-driven and community-centred programmes, supported by efficient integrated coordinated mechanism, including through the SBC platform. 
 
UNICEF strengthened data and evidence generation using Regular Resources, completed the CLAC and the situational analysis of persons with disabilities. Despite delays due to reprioritization and funding constraints, the KAP is close to completion, and the MICS-7 is ready for implementation once funding is secured. Both will fill critical data gaps on vulnerabilities, enabling partners and the government to design targeted interventions, track progress on the SDG and improve outcomes for children. UNICEF will expand youth engagement in data collection to improve real-time monitoring and reinforce their agency. 
 
UNICEF will continue to advance high-quality inclusive social services. Strengthening community systems will remain central to ensure sustainability, reinforcing frontline and community capacities. UNICEF will further shift toward stronger technical assistance, prioritizing transformative interventions scaling up SBC and youth engagement to expand reach and impact, notably for health, education and the climate agenda. In response to rising climate risks, supporting STP’s strong commitment, UNICEF will intensify efforts to strengthen local systems to reduce children’s exposure and build community resilience. The empowerment of girls and adolescents will remain a core priority. Looking ahead, UNICEF will reinforce these strategic interventions to advance UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029 with a strong focus on equity and sustainability.

Macroeconomic conditions in 2025 are shaped by heightened fiscal pressures and elevated public debt following the identification of significant off-balance-sheet liabilities. Public debt is estimated at around 132 percent of GDP, exceeding ECOWAS convergence thresholds [1]. In this context, Standard & Poor’s revised Senegal’s sovereign credit rating in 2025, citing widening fiscal deficits, substantial financing needs and increased risks to debt sustainability [6]. Rising debt-servicing obligations are absorbing an increasing share of public revenues, limiting fiscal space for development and social spending, with only 4 years remaining until the 2030 deadline.  Several goals are currently facing stagnation, notably Quality Education (SDG  4), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), Sustainable Cities and Communities (SDG 11), and Life on Land (SDG 15) [12]. Accelerating structural transformation to achieve the SDGs by 2030 would require an estimated USD 4 billion annually, equivalent to 13.3 percent of GDP [13].
  
Despite the adoption of a new National Development Strategy (SND 2025–2029), aligned with Vision 2050 and centered on human capital, employment and social equity, implementation remains challenging due to high financing needs and shrinking fiscal margins [8]. Public financing for children remains under strain. Education accounts for approximately 15 percent of total public expenditure, health 4 percent, WASH 2.1 percent and social protection around 2.5 percent, while child protection and early childhood education each receive about 1 percent or less [7]. Between the initial and revised 2025 finance laws, allocations to several child-related sectors stagnated or declined, while indirect taxation increased, de facto constraining equity and child wellbeing.
  
Child poverty remains widespread, with 47.3 percent of children in multidimensional poverty—down from 50.7 percent in 2024—and monetary child poverty at 43.3 percent [9]. Subjective poverty has risen sharply to 58.5 percent, reflecting heightened household insecurity—nearly one in four children (23 percent) experience overlapping multidimensional, monetary and subjective poverty.  Poverty is significantly higher in rural areas and in southern and eastern regions such as Kédougou, Kolda, Sédhiou and Tambacounda [9].
  
Health,  nutrition and education deprivations remain key drivers of child  poverty.  Limited access to functional health facilities, particularly  in rural and peripheral areas, continues to affect neonatal and child  survival outcomes [9]. Chronic malnutrition affects about one in six  children under five, with poor dietary diversity linked to poverty and  food insecurity. While primary school attendance is high, dropout rates  rise sharply at the secondary level, especially among children from  poor, rural, and flood-affected households, leading to high NEET  rates [9].
  
Despite  persistent rural–urban disparities, water and sanitation deprivations are now  less prevalent than other dimensions of child well-being, reflecting sustained  progress in the WASH sector. Access to improved drinking water has reached 81  percent in rural areas and 95 percent in urban areas, while sanitation  coverage stands at 54 percent and 71 percent, respectively. Open defecation  declined from 11.2 percent in 2022 to 6 percent in 2025 [9][10].
  
Housing  and living environment deprivations remain widespread, with children often living  in overcrowded, poorly built homes with limited ventilation. Reliance on  polluting solid fuels exposes children to respiratory illnesses. Despite progress  in birth registration, regional disparities leave many children without legal  identity. Child labour and early hazardous activities are linked to  multidimensional poverty, especially among adolescents and do not manifest in  the same way at all ages. They become evident during adolescence, when girls  are more likely to be deprived of education, protection, or opportunities,  even at comparable living standards.[9].
  
Climate  change further intensified child vulnerabilities in 2025. An  exceptionally intense rainy season caused widespread flooding in regions  including Tambacounda, Sédhiou, Kolda and Kaffrine. A UNICEF assessment  covering 6,451 households found that 24 percent were affected, with  substantial housing damage, asset losses and income disruption,  negatively impacting child nutrition, education, health and protection  [11].
  
The  2025 contextual analysis amid the sharp reduction of external financing,  fiscal stress, debt pressures and climate shocks intensifying faster than  anticipated has driven an adjustment of the CPD theory of change and  refinement of approaches with an emphasis on upstream, systems-strengthening,  resilience and equity-focused interventions to safeguard and amplify results  for children at national scale.

In the second year of the Country Programme (2024–2028), UNICEF Senegal operated in a constrained global funding environment while remaining aligned with UNICEF’s strategic frameworks and Senegal’s National Development Strategy. In response to global funding constraints and in close consultation with the Government, the Country Office undertook a strategic realignment under UNICEF’s Future Focus initiative. The exercise sharpened programmatic prioritization around high-impact areas—climate change, adolescent girls, quality education and the first 1,000 days—while deliberately shifting the portfolio toward upstream, systems-strengthening interventions to maximize and sustain results for children.
Against this backdrop, UNICEF Senegal delivered on several Key Results for Children (KRCs) identified by the West and Central Africa Region, which are critical to system-level change.  Key achievements included the adoption of the long-awaited decree on breast-milk substitutes (KRC2), the signing of the decree for free enrolment of all children without birth certificates into the Ministry of Education civil registration platform (KRC3, KRC7), the operationalization of the education budget tracking committee (COSCAB), and completion of child rights training with Cheikh Anta Diop and Geneva Universities.  Regionally, it supported the first adolescent girls’ forum, shaping an adolescent agenda that influenced policy across 24 West and Central African countries.
These achievements were enabled in part by Regular Resources, which played a critical role in risk mitigation and systems strengthening throughout the year. In a context where thematic and donor-specific funding was frequently delayed, reprogrammed, or reduced, Regular Resources ensured the continuity of UNICEF’s upstream policy engagement, convening, and monitoring functions. 
Every child survives and thrives.  In 2025, Senegal approved its Strategic Community Health Plan, along with updated policies, standards, and protocols for maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health, thereby strengthening the national framework for quality and equity in service delivery. UNICEF supported system-level reform by implementing the Every Newborn, Everywhere" (EWENE) and "Action for Child Survival" (CSA) plan. Nutrition governance advanced through UNICEF-supported advocacy that contributed to the signing of the decree regulating the marketing of foods for infants and young children. Governance was further reinforced through the development of a national policy on maternal, infant and young child feeding, a monitoring and evaluation plan for the multisectoral nutrition strategy, and an assessment of the 2013 acute malnutrition programme. In parallel, UNICEF strengthened climate and risk governance by building a stronger national evidence base, integrating climate data into planning processes to support equity-driven strategies, and supporting the finalization of the national contingency plan with UN partners, strengthening preparedness, coordination and resilience to future shocks. 
At the service level, UNICEF supported the equipping and commissioning of six additional neonatal units across four regions. Quality of care and survival outcomes improved through expanded oxygen availability, including commissioning the Thiadiaye oxygen generator, routine maintenance of 6 oxygen generator units, and training 21 technicians to sustain oxygen systems. UNICEF supported the timely introduction and rollout of the hexavalent vaccine through supply coordination and demand-generation efforts. HPV vaccination was further institutionalized by integrating it into screening and awareness activities during Pink October, contributing to sustained gains in coverage, including 94 per cent first-dose coverage. 
Nutrition service delivery was reinforced through training of 445 health providers, representing 90 percent of the programme target, on severe acute malnutrition management and infant and young child feeding, and capacity building of 285 community actors on uncomplicated Severe and Acute Malnutrition. UNICEF leveraged the Match Window to facilitate procurement of therapeutic foods and vitamin A, safeguarding continuity of critical nutrition inputs. WASH service delivery expanded through a large-scale expansion of the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach, exceeding the target, reaching 105 percent of the planned coverage (635 villages), enabling the construction of 26,300 latrines and supporting the sustained cessation of open defecation for 263,657 residents. Drinking water management was strengthened through community training and mobilization, complemented by the distribution of hygiene kits to households at heightened risk of WASH-related diseases. Climate-resilient WASH infrastructure was supported in Green Schools, alongside environmental initiatives benefiting 1,750 students, while youth engagement expanded through the Green Generation platform across multiple regions. In parallel, UNICEF contributed to flood and Rift Valley Fever responses through integrated WASH, public health, and Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) interventions, reducing the risk of waterborne and zoonotic disease transmission. 
Every child learns 
In 2025, UNICEF sustained strong engagement in advancing equitable access to quality learning and skills development, aligned with Senegal’s education and training sector strategy (PAQUET-EF) and major ongoing reforms. UNICEF supported upstream policy and system reforms that strengthened governance, planning and digital transformation of the education sector. At the national level, UNICEF contributed to the implementation of the National Digital Education Strategy, supporting operational pathways for the Global Initiative on School Connectivity (GIGA) and SOLuREM (System of Learning Remediation), while continuing to support the rollout of the Modèle Harmonisé d’Enseignement Bilingue au Sénégal (MOHEBS). Progress toward GIGA accession was formalized through letters of intent from the Ministries of Education and Communications and the establishment of a national steering committee. UNICEF played a central role in education-sector governance and coordination, serving as the lead agency for partner dialogue. Key contributions included support for the validation of the Rapport d’état du Système Éducatif National (RESEN), refinement of the sector simulation model to inform evidence-based planning, and the establishment and operationalization of COSCAB, Senegal’s joint monitoring committee for education budget support. Through the Global Partnership for Education System Capacity Grant, UNICEF mobilized US$1 million to strengthen sector planning, monitoring and capacity development. Advocacy through interministerial mechanisms contributed to a landmark decision enabling children without birth certificates to enroll in the civil registry platform, removing a significant administrative barrier to schooling and national examinations. UNICEF also supported inclusive education system reform through the ATSCALE programme, including a national baseline survey on assistive technologies and the introduction of teacher training modules to improve the detection of visual impairments, 
laying the foundation for disability-inclusive education policies through 2027. 
At the service-delivery level, UNICEF supported the expansion of early childhood education and improvements in foundational learning outcomes. In Louga and Saint-Louis, 90 community preschool structures remained fully operational, benefiting 4,667 children with improved learning and play materials. UNICEF strengthened quality by training 142 family counsellors in early stimulation and empowering preschool management committees. Since 2024, a total of 30,129 children has accessed at least one year of preschool education through UNICEF-supported community centres, daara preschools and Cases des Tout-Petits, representing 120 percent of the programme target (25,000), and contributing to an increase in gross preschool enrolment from 19.5 percent in 2023 to 25.1 per cent in 2025. Senegal also launched its national preschool assessment system, strengthening quality assurance at scale. In foundational learning, UNICEF strengthened teaching quality and learner achievement by training 2,844 teachers, supervisors and trainers on multigrade management, targeted remediation (Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) combined with SOLuREM) and bilingual pedagogy under MOHEBS. The introduction of national languages in 30 schools reached 1,776 learners and generated evidence for a national scale-up. Overall, in 2025, 44,138 learners benefited from targeted learning support, exceeding the programme target of 34,000 by more than 30 per cent. Local assessments confirmed learning gains, including 86.7 percent reading comprehension among assessed learners in Kolda and significant improvements in Kaffrine. 
 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation. 
In 2025, Senegal, with UNICEF support, improved its child protection system by focusing on accountability, regulation, professional development of the social workforce, and improved information systems. A key goal was strengthening monitoring and evidence to ensure coherent, enforceable, and sustainable protection actions across sectors. UNICEF helped conduct a national assessment with the General Directorate of Judiciary and Social Protection, producing the first detailed map of children without family care, including details on their profiles, pathways, and vulnerabilities. This evidence supports developing a context-specific care model and improving the regulation of informal care. UNICEF engaged in policy dialogue and advocacy, leading to amendments to the Child Code, enforcement against Female Genital Mutilation, and alignment with international child rights commitments under various Human Rights treaties and UN reviews. System accountability improved as the Rapid Protection digital incident-reporting system transitioned to government ownership, enhancing Senegal's capacity to register, track, and respond to violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect. UNICEF developed a multisectoral, interoperable child protection info system aligned with Senegal’s Bogotá pledges and Arise Africa commitments, improving case management, coordination, and planning. Workforce development was central to strengthening the system. UNICEF, led by the General Directorate of Social Welfare, finalised a national Code of Ethics for social workers and drafted legislation for a National Professional Order. It also expanded capacity through academic partnerships, supporting training with Cheikh Anta Diop University (UCAD) and the University of Geneva, bolstering expertise in child rights, protection standards, and monitoring. Additionally, UNICEF supported the development of legal and institutional frameworks for online child protection, including a national online safety action plan, enabling Senegal to better address digital risks impacting children. 
Alongside upstream reforms, UNICEF strengthened access to quality protection services for children at risk and survivors of violence. In 2025, 4,157 child survivors received integrated services for abuse, exploitation, or neglect. Frontline capacity increased through training 42 Educational support service providers in an open/community setting, starting in Tambacounda and Ziguinchor, expanding nationwide. Nearly 100 community volunteers, including youth leaders and local authorities, were trained to identify, refer, and report cases of violence and neglect, thereby improving community monitoring. A total of 731 professionals from social action, justice, education, and security sectors were trained to prevent and respond to violence, including online harms. Psychosocial and digital safety interventions strengthened adolescent protection. UNICEF created and shared a psychosocial support manual for community social workers and supported 396 adolescent girls, 246 in digital safety, to boost resilience. Training for 20 trainers in the Gender Transformative Approach enabled 210 community actors to prevent FGM and child marriage. Engagement reached 66,184 people, with campaigns informing nearly 3 million nationwide. The National Committee on Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) was restructured with decentralized branches and a new monitoring tool. Community engagement expanded with 2,700 members participating in dialogues, and 10,000 child auto-protection manuals distributed. The Safe Online baseline study led to the development of new training modules and advocacy materials. The Ministry of Education, supported by UNICEF, improved digital safety systems, piloted online tutorials, and integrated these into the national learning platform. UNICEF also supported Agence Nationale de la Petite Enfance et de la Case des Tout-Petits in strengthening birth registration awareness campaigns, emphasizing the legal and religious importance, and improving access to services and legal protection. 
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life. 
          In 2025, UNICEF Senegal accelerated progress toward reducing child poverty by strengthening the policy, financing and governance systems that shape children’s life chances, with a focus on protecting domestic fiscal space for children under acute fiscal stress. UNICEF also finalized and shared guides on budget literacy and child-responsive planning for officials and ministries, and trained all 165 members of parliament and 58 local elected officials on child-sensitive budgeting. UNICEF helped position public debt as a child-rights issue and supported national dialogue on debt sustainability and fiscal space for social sectors during budgetary stress. It brokered the finalization of the SDG Accelerator roadmap on jobs, social protection, and skills. This roadmap now guides policy reform and joint financing. At the decentralized level, UNICEF supported a structural shift toward child-responsive local governance. Sixteen local authorities across Sédhiou, Tambacounda and Kédougou operationalized child- and community-participation mechanisms, exceeding annual targets. Twelve communal child action plans were formally adopted, and four local governments committed to integrating child priorities into their Municipal Development Plans, anchoring children’s rights within territorial investment frameworks. As a management response to KRC and OED recommendations, UNICEF strengthened national data sovereignty and equity-monitoring systems while reinforcing intersectoral coordination among planning, monitoring, and budgeting functions. For the first time, the National Statistics Office (ANSD) conducted the national Multidimensional Child Poverty Analysis independently, confirming that 47.3 percent of children remain multidimensionally poor and validating the recent trend of reduction from the 50.7per cent multidimensional poverty rate of 2024. This evidence now underpins geographic targeting and policy prioritization. Collaboration was further institutionalized through 
a strategic MoU for MICS 2026, ensuring continuity of timely, child-focused data production, including phone-based modalities. In parallel, 120 decentralized actors were trained on SDG monitoring and child-responsive planning, strengthening evidence-based decision-making and accountability. 
Alongside upstream reforms, UNICEF supported service delivery mechanisms that directly mitigated poverty-related risks for children while reinforcing national systems. Despite fiscal constraints, education-linked cash transfers reached 3,300 vulnerable households, benefiting approximately 13,200 children and supporting school attendance, household resilience and protective outcomes. UNICEF strengthened delivery efficiency and accountability by reforming payment administration systems, improving transparency, traceability and processing speed, and resolving long-standing bottlenecks in centralized cash delivery. A comprehensive evaluation of the education cash transfer programme was completed and disseminated, strengthening accountability and informing future scale-up and system integration. 
 
Cross-sectoral and operational strategies 
In 2025, UNICEF strengthened programme effectiveness through coordinated, risk-informed planning that engaged both state and non-state actors. Localization advanced through multisectoral interventions in 11 child-friendly municipalities, where communities were mobilized, trained and organized through Citizenship Engagement Committees, Children’s Municipal Councils and girls’ youth clubs. These platforms strengthened local decision-making and institutional ownership, enabling state services and community actors to jointly prioritize, plan and monitor integrated responses that expanded vulnerable children’s access to protection, education, health, nutrition, WASH services, life skills and empowerment opportunities.  
To enhance community level delivery, UNICEF restructured its Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) function, establishing a transparent investment framework centered on adolescent empowerment, wellbeing, protection, and the transformation of harmful social norms. This strengthened sector coherence and positioned SBC as a driver of both system reform and last mile delivery. Nationally, SetAside funding enabled UNICEF to adopt a systemic, multidisciplinary approach to adolescent girls’ education and empowerment, grounded in analyses that informed a girl centered, multisectoral model integrating education, social protection and SBC. Gender-responsive solutions, including STEM remediation, mentoring in marginalized communities, and integrating girls’ perspectives into diagnostics—enhanced programme relevance and gender transformative outcomes. These efforts positioned UNICEF Senegal as a credible partner for scaling sustainable, gender-responsive models within national systems. Key achievements included the establishment of 15 STEM clubs serving 1,546 girls, training 2,445 educators in gender-responsive pedagogy, expanding HPV vaccination to 3,129 people, and producing 25,000 reusable sanitary pads to improve attendance and empowerment.
Building on this foundation, UNICEF significantly advanced the adolescent girls’ agenda in 2025. A national consultation enabled girls to articulate their priorities, directly informing the regional dialogue. These insights fed into a landmark regional summit by, for and with adolescent girls, bringing together more than 100 participants from 24 West and Central African countries and reinforcing adolescents’ right to meaningfully participate in decision-making. The summit culminated in the Dakar Declaration, calling for inclusive and gender-responsive education, adolescent-friendly health services, the elimination of child marriage and FGM, and the creation of safe spaces that ensure girls’ voices shape public decisions. The Declaration now stands as a shared regional commitment and an important milestone in advancing adolescent girls’ empowerment.
Innovation and learning complemented these efforts. A national workshop on FGM in Matam tested community-based monitoring tools that generated early insights into social norms and decision-making dynamics linked to declining FGM prevalence, while strengthening data collection and evaluation capacities. 
Flagship platforms further demonstrated integrated delivery at scale. The HPV+4Girl initiative combined HPV vaccination, deworming and menstrual hygiene education to reach adolescents directly, resulting in 2,271 girls vaccinated during the Pink October campaign. Strategic partnerships amplified outreach through edutainment, engaging 8.6 million people and generating more than 6,300 digital interactions, significantly strengthening health awareness and demand for adolescent services. Regular Resources played a catalytic role by enabling pilots such as the FGM monitoring initiative and HPV+4Girl to scale outreach and support rapid mobilization during health emergencies. 
Community governance improved through the Fankanta II programme, partnering with DECLIC, Regional Development Agencies, and Committees. Nine local authorities formed citizen groups, enhancing transparency, accountability, and youth involvement. The programme established a community feedback system, making UNICEF Senegal a leader in Accountability to Affected Populations in francophone West and Central Africa. During emergencies, responses to MPOX and Rift Valley Fever outbreaks used Social and Behavioural Change techniques, training 200 professionals and supporting containment efforts. 
In 2025, UNICEF Senegal strengthened its operational foundation, improving governance, risk management, and oversight through transparent accountability, active committees, and an updated Business Continuity Plan. The office advanced the PBR-endorsed Common Services Centre reform to enhance efficiencies across Dakar, Kolda, UNHMU, and WCARO. Investments in financial management, digital tools, and streamlined workflows increased transparency, speed processes, and protected resources, supporting service delivery and transition to the new UN House. 
UNICEF Senegal advanced 12 advocacy initiatives across education, protection, health, climate, and digital transformation, achieving policy gains like the Presidential Decree on breast-milk substitutes, integrating child rights into the National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights, and including child-sensitive provisions in Senegal’s updated climate commitments. They promoted inclusive, gender-responsive education through platforms such as the Girls’ Summit, helped draft an inclusive education policy, strengthened safeguarding measures for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games, and enabled children without civil registration to take exams. Engagement with the Human Rights Commission and media raised child rights awareness, while advocacy increased HPV vaccination and support for children with disabilities. The nomination of Khaby Lame, the world’s most followed TikTok influencer, as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador significantly boosted global visibility for children’s rights in Senegal, offering UNICEF unprecedented outreach potential.
Despite a challenging global funding environment, UNICEF Senegal mobilized over US$5 million in new resources in 2025 and diversified its partner base. Contributions were secured from GPE, the Peacebuilding Fund, GAVI, the SDG Fund, the Nutrition Match Fund, Mastercard Foundation, FCDO and the Belgian National Committee. UNICEF Senegal also submitted the Organization’s first-ever proposal to the Green Climate Fund, a US$25 million climate resilience project, signaling a strategic shift toward large-scale climate financing. Additional multi-year commitments amounting to US$ 9 million have already been secured for 2026 from the Pandemic Fund, the Spanish National Committee, the Generalitat Valenciana, UNICEF Headquarters climate financing, and TIKA. With more than 40 proposals submitted in 2025, UNICEF strengthened its positioning in areas where progress for children remains a priority, including climate change, digital education, social cohesion, flood response, and girls’ empowerment, while expanding partnerships with philanthropic, multilateral, and private-sector actors to build more resilient and diversified resource mobilization channels.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2025, the Country Office operated in a context marked by interrelated financial, institutional and system-level risks that constrained the scale-up and sustainability of programme results.  Reduced funding driven by global budget cuts constrained the scale-up of high-impact, multisectoral interventions and increased reliance on national systems with uneven capacity.
In health, persistent gaps in biomedical equipment maintenance continued to pose risks to the continuity and quality of maternal, newborn, and child health services. The decline in development financing—notably reduced Gavi support—emerged as a significant risk to sustaining high immunization coverage, increasing vulnerability to outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases. Similarly, chronic funding shortfalls in the WASH sector risk slowing progress toward the national objective of eliminating open defecation by 2030.
Additional risks persisted in child protection, where capacity gaps among government and implementing partners, fragmented approaches, weak inter-sectoral coordination and sustained underfunding — combined with fiscal constraints — risk exacerbating vulnerabilities among children. Across sectors, pressures on social spending and limited absorptive capacity at the decentralized level underscored the need for greater efficiency, coordination and system coherence.
To mitigate these risks, UNICEF prioritized system-strengthening interventions focused on policy reform, institutional capacity development and improved coordination. Increased emphasis was placed on strengthening partnerships, enhancing the use of data and evidence, and reinforcing accountability mechanisms to preserve essential results under constrained resources. This approach aimed to improve efficiency, reduce fragmentation and enhance the resilience and sustainability of national systems.
Lessons from 2025 reinforced the importance of multisectoral collaboration as a key accelerator of results. Cross-sector engagement proved particularly effective for HPV vaccination, where integrated strategies combining health, education and SBC contributed to improved coverage. Strategic government partnerships facilitated access to maternal and newborn health commodities through the Accelerator Fund and Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicine. In contrast, strong national ownership of Every Woman Every Newborn – Clinical and Systems Approach (EWENE-CSA) contributed to measurable reductions in maternal and newborn mortality. In nutrition, policy windows created by government transitions enabled the adoption of the decree regulating the marketing of foods for infants and young children, demonstrating the value of sustained advocacy and readiness to act when opportunities emerge. In education, integrated WASH interventions under the Green Schools approach directly improved learning conditions, highlighting the benefits of convergence.
Child protection programming confirmed that sensitive issues such as harmful practices and violence against children require sustained high-level advocacy combined with community-based, gender-transformative approaches to ensure ownership and sustainability. Where multisectoral coordination remained limited, targeted sector-specific interventions delivered greater impact, underscoring the importance of strategic sequencing, adaptability, and context-sensitive design.
Building on these lessons, UNICEF’s strategy focuses on consolidating system gains and ensuring sustainable impact. In vaccination, the HPV+ strategy delivers interventions for adolescent girls, using HPV vaccination as an entry point while improving health services. Through EWENE-CSA, UNICEF will strengthen neonatal units and oxygen systems to enhance Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care. Nutrition efforts will expand breastfeeding initiatives, such as the 'First Foods” program, and better integrate nutritional supplies into national supply chains. Climate resilience will improve through the wider use of the CLTS approach, helping communities adapt to climate shocks such as floods.
In social policy, UNICEF will prioritize safeguarding social spending under fiscal stress, institutionalizing the Global Accelerator roadmap, scaling decentralized child-responsive planning, and strengthening climate-responsive social protection. Experience from 2025 confirms that durable results depend on institutional reform, national ownership of data and systems, and effective alignment between decentralization, child participation and financing.
UNICEF will deepen strategic partnerships with high impact stakeholders, strengthen high level advocacy, and scale gender transformative, adolescent-, youth and women-led initiatives. By integrating policy engagement, decentralized planning and evidence driven programming, UNICEF will enhance coordination across national and subnational systems and accelerate sustainable results for children amid growing economic and climate pressures.
Building on the momentum of the Regional Adolescent Girls Forum and the Dakar Declaration, UNICEF will work closely with local councils to advance the territorialization of the adolescent girls’ agenda, ensuring that local development plans, municipal budgets and community structures systematically reflect girls’ priorities. This will anchor the regional agenda in local governance mechanisms, strengthen accountability at municipal level, and enable scalable, context responsive interventions that deliver tangible improvements in girls’ safety, education, wellbeing and participation.
In 2025, advocacy efforts yielded strong policy outcomes but highlighted the need for deeper system engagement, agility, and cross-sector collaboration. Challenges included political transitions, government coordination, social norms, and resource bottlenecks. Lessons emphasized early engagement, sustained civil society partnerships, and the use of evidence and child participation to shape national policies. Looking ahead, UNICEF aims to institutionalize advocacy planning, monitor policy influence, and lead on climate adaptation, digital safety, and child protection, including a planned partnership with the Youth Olympic Games Organizing Committee in early 2026 and the contribution to the UNCT joint support to 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
The 2025 resource mobilization environment was shaped by declining official development assistance, a shift towards bilateral donor engagement, and Senegal’s macroeconomic debt constraints. Increased competition, including within the UN, demands clearer value propositions, innovative funding, and better reporting to sustain donor trust. UNICEF Senegal aims to diversify funding, boost private-sector engagement, strengthen donor relations, and leverage its expertise to build strategic partnerships. Donor interest in climate adaptation, adolescent empowerment, and community resilience in border areas and Casamance offers opportunities in 2026 to expand impactful programs for children.
Looking ahead, UNICEF’s work will unfold in the context of a deepening global crisis of multilateralism, marked by declining official development assistance, geopolitical fragmentation and increasing competition for limited public resources. These trends are expected to further constrain traditional financing for children and social sectors, particularly in fiscally stressed countries such as Senegal. Sustaining and scaling results for children will therefore require a deliberate shift toward more diversified and innovative financing approaches and strategic leveraging. 
UNICEF Senegal will intensify engagement with non-traditional partners, including climate funds, philanthropic foundations, development finance institutions, and private-sector actors aligned with child-sensitive, impact-oriented investments. As the Country Office revises its partnership and resource mobilization strategy, it will be building on emerging opportunities in climate adaptation, community resilience in border areas and adolescent girls’ empowerment, positioning child-focused outcomes as impactful investments priorities to enable scaling beyond traditional grant-based models.
At the same time, UNICEF will strengthen its role as a convener and broker, leveraging evidence, data and trusted government partnerships to crowd in additional public and private resources, safeguard social spending and align investments behind national priorities for children.

In 2025, Sierra Leone stood at a pivotal juncture—advancing governance reforms and economic stabilization while maintaining a strong commitment to human capital investment. These gains were achieved against a backdrop of persistent public health, climate, and social risks that continued to affect the most vulnerable. Despite ongoing political polarization following the contested 2023 elections, national institutions demonstrated resilience, and Sierra Leone’s international standing continued to strengthen.

For children, measurable progress was recorded in survival, health, education, and protection. However, these advances were not uniform. Structural and social inequities persisted—particularly for the most marginalized girls and for children with disabilities. These disparities underscore UNICEF’s strategic priorities and the need for sustained equity-focused programming to ensure every child realizes their rights and potential.

1.1 Social, Political, and Economic Context
In 2025, Sierra Leone’s political environment continued to be influenced by reforms to strengthen democratic institutions after the contested 2023 elections. Civil society remained active in pushing for impartial security and better social services. Internationally, the Government of Sierra Leone (GoSL) served as a non-permanent member at the UN Security Council and continued its role as Chair of ECOWAS, contributing to regional stability and governance efforts.

Economically, Sierra Leone strengthened credibility with international financial institutions. The IMF approved US$79 million in December following a successful review of the Extended Credit Facility[1]. Inflation declined from 13.7% to 4.4%, due to tighter monetary policy[2], fiscal consolidation, and stronger agricultural output. Economic growth was projected at 4.3%, though low international reserves remained low - at 1.7 months of import cover—well below IMF benchmarks—continued to limit resilience to external shocks.

Globally, multiple conflicts intensified pressure on international aid. Major reductions in donor funding in 2025, including the closure of USAID operations, created immediate financing gaps, with further declines anticipated in the years ahead. For the UN system, including UNICEF, this has led to an overall 20% reduction in available resources, constraining the scale and reach of programmes supporting children.
 
1.2 Risks and Humanitarian Situation
Sierra Leone faced overlapping risks in 2025: public health emergencies, climate-related vulnerabilities, and persistent social norms disproportionately affecting children and women. The mpox outbreak from January through November registered nearly 5,500 cases and 60 deaths[3]. UNICEF, working with national authorities and partners, led effective efforts in coordination, risk communication, vaccination (reaching 186,000 people directly and over 2 million with public information), infection prevention, and WASH interventions, with targeted engagement of high-risk groups—including weekly U-Report SMS messaging.

Consequences of Climate Change such as flooding and drought continued to affect rural, coastal, and island communities, slowing progress on access to water (65%) and sanitation (23%). Rural children were particularly affected, underscoring the need for climate-resilient WASH and disaster risk reduction.  Available evidence indicates that[4] that climate-related disruptions disproportionately affect children, heightening exposure to waterborne diseases, undermining hygiene in households and schools, and increasing risks of malnutrition and school absenteeism.  Gender-based violence and harmful practices, including female genital mutilation (FGM; prevalence above 80%)[5], persisted despite policy improvements. 

UNICEF maintained a strong leadership in humanitarian coordination within the UN and with national authorities, ensuring child-centred, inclusive emergency preparedness and response.

1.3 Implications for Children and UNICEF Programmes
The United Nations Country Team (UNCT) supported the Government through the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025–2030, contributing to health system strengthening, elimination of the mpox outbreak, improved food and nutrition security, enhanced student learning and skills, major policy gains for children’s and women’s rights, youth empowerment, and peacebuilding. Three UN Joint Programmes were launched: the Spotlight EU-UN-GoSL Initiative addressing gender-based violence (GBV) and service delivery; the UN Joint Food and Nutrition Security Programme, signed with the Government of Ireland; and the UN Joint Flagship Programme to accelerate progress toward Universal Health Coverage (UHC) in Moyamba District.

UNICEF, as part of the UN, focused on systems strengthening, policy development and implementation, community engagement, and reaching the most vulnerable. These efforts align with post-COVID-19 recovery and climate-resilience priorities and are grounded in the SDGs as well as the principle of “leaving no one behind.” All findings are supported by the latest disaggregated data consistent with national and UNICEF situation analyses.

1.4 Highlights for Child Rights and Wellbeing in 2025
A new Child Rights Act (CRA) was passed —the first update since 2007. It strengthens legislation prohibiting all forms of violence against children and establishes a stronger framework for child protection and service delivery.

Data on children improved with the launch of the new Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), led by Statistics Sierra Leone with UNICEF support. Final results are expected in Q3 2026, providing updated national data on children. UNICEF also supported the Government in establishing a national database platform within the Ministry of Planning and the Economy (MoPED), including a new digital dashboard to track progress on the Medium-Term National Development Plan (MTNDP) and the SDGs. The dashboard improves accountability by increasing transparency on the impact of public and private investments.

UNICEF and the Government launched the new Country Programme 2025–2030 in January, aligned with the MTNDP 2024–2030 and the UNSDCF, and UNICEF’s Strategic Plan 2023-2025 with a stronger evidence-based focus on systems strengthening and Public Financing for Children (P4FC). Throughout 2025, commitments were advanced through shifts in systems strengthening, social transformation, combined national and localized geographic approaches, and P4FC. Communication, advocacy, and partnerships—including a new strategic partnership with Parliament, a national children’s dialogue on World Children’s Day, and a high-level event marking UNICEF’s 40 years in Sierra Leone—helped elevate national awareness and influence policy on public finance for children, climate change, and girls’ rights. As a result, child-friendly budgeting language was included in the national Budget reading for the first time—a landmark achievement.
