Dans un contexte marqué par les répercussions de la crise sahélienne et une reconfiguration profonde du paysage de l’aide publique au développement, l’UNICEF Togo a été confronté à des contraintes accrues de financement. La contraction des ressources internationales, combinée à une compétition renforcée pour des financements limités, a particulièrement affecté le pays, déjà considéré comme relativement orphelin de bailleurs. Cette situation a posé un défi stratégique majeur, appelant une adaptation rapide de son positionnement et de ses modalités de mobilisation des ressources afin d’assurer la continuité et l’impact des interventions en faveur des enfants les plus vulnérables.
Face à ces contraintes, l’UNICEF Togo a engagé une révision stratégique de son approche de mobilisation des ressources, reconnaissant que la simple intensification des méthodes traditionnelles ne serait pas suffisante. La stratégie partenariale a été restructurée autour de deux piliers complémentaires : la fidélisation et l’expansion.
D’une part, le bureau pays a renforcé les partenariats existants en misant sur une exécution de projets d’excellence avec des donateurs traditionnels tels que les gouvernements de la Corée, et de la France, ainsi que Gavi et la Banque mondiale. La qualité de la mise en œuvre, la rigueur de la gestion et la démonstration de résultats mesurables ont constitué des leviers clés pour maintenir la confiance des partenaires.
D’autre part, l’UNICEF Togo a déployé une stratégie d’expansion vers de nouveaux acteurs, en ciblant des institutions financières internationales non traditionnelles (Banque Africaine de Développement (BAD), Banque Ouest-Africaine de Développement (BOAD), BIDC (Banque d'Investissement et de Développement de la CEDEAO)), des entreprises du secteur privé opérant au Togo (dont Rotary International et Yas Togo), ainsi que des petites et moyennes entreprises, ces acteurs disposant de ressources, d'expertise ou d'influence bénéfiques aux enfants mais n'ayant historiquement pas financé l’UNICEF. Cette approche a permis de valoriser les avantages comparatifs de l’UNICEF, c’est à dire expertise multisectorielle, ancrage territorial, relations institutionnelles solides et crédibilité communautaire, tout en intégrant des contributions non financières telles que des infrastructures numériques, un appui logistique, des biens en nature et des opportunités de renforcement de capacités.
Grâce à cette stratégie, le bureau pays a enregistré en 2025 une augmentation de 63,9% des fonds mobilisés par rapport à 2024, atteignant 50,8% du plafond du CPD, soit 6 669 551 dollars américains. En complément, 750 000 dollars américains en ressources ordinaires (ORE) ont été mobilisés, contribuant à renforcer la stabilité financière du Bureau.
Ces résultats découlent de négociations fructueuses ayant abouti à des engagements financiers significatifs de la part de plusieurs partenaires, notamment les gouvernements de la Corée, du Luxembourg, de la France, des États-Unis, du Canada, ainsi que la Commission européenne. Par ailleurs, la stratégie d’expansion s'est concrétisée dans le domaine climatique, où l'UNICEF a établi des partenariats avec la BAD, franchissant avec succès la phase de validation pour développer des propositions détaillées. En parallèle, le Bureau pays a renforcé sa visibilité institutionnelle par le lancement d'un site web dédié et la valorisation proactive de ses réalisations à travers la publication de rapports clés et d'histoires humaines illustrant l'impact concret des interventions. Ces efforts de communication stratégique contribuent à renforcer la visibilité de l'UNICEF Togo auprès des partenaires potentiels et à créer un environnement favorable à la mobilisation de ressources futures.
Cette expérience met en évidence que la diversification des partenariats nécessite un investissement stratégique dédié, et ne peut être abordée comme un simple prolongement des pratiques existantes. Elle souligne également que le renforcement des systèmes nationaux et locaux constitue un facteur clé de durabilité, rendant les investissements plus attractifs pour les partenaires. La leçon apprise est que la qualité de l’exécution, associée à un positionnement stratégique clair et à une approche multisectorielle intégrée, demeure déterminante dans un contexte de forte concurrence pour les ressources.
Pour l’avenir, l’UNICEF Togo poursuivra cette double stratégie de fidélisation et d’expansion, tout en structurant davantage son offre de valeur, afin de se positionner durablement comme un partenaire de référence pour tout acteur souhaitant investir de manière efficace et pérenne dans le développement des enfants au Togo.

The West and Central Africa region (WCAR) has shown strong resilience in the face of numerous challenges as well as steadfast commitment to improving children's lives, making notable progress in health, nutrition, education, protection, WASH and social inclusion. Despite achievements, progress remains uneven and fragile resulting in millions of children that are being left behind. 


WCAR bears a disproportionate burden of child rights deprivations: 37% of global under-five deaths, 28% of all under-fives whose births are not registered, 21% of all stunted under-fives, and 22% of the world’s out-of-school children. Gender inequality and deeply rooted social norms and harmful practices represent critical challenges, while climate shocks, economic pressures (such as crippling debt and rising inflation), rapid population growth, and declining development assistance require adaptive and innovative responses. Furthermore, 2025 has witnessed a region traversing significant political transitions, profound security challenges, and deep institutional and governance reforms that have presented both challenges and opportunities to how UNICEF delivers programmes for children. 


Under-five mortality declined from 104.5 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2016 to 85.6 in 2023, while maternal mortality fell from 768 to 629 per 100,000 live births. These trends signal progress, yet the region continues to bear one of the highest global health burdens, with neonatal deaths accounting for a growing share of child mortality. Persistent gaps in equitable coverage and quality of care, particularly in fragile and hard-to-reach settings, underscore the need for strengthened health systems and sustained investment.


Immunization coverage improved, with DTP3 rates rising from 67% in 2016 to 72% in 2024, driven by successful campaigns and community engagement. However, WCAR remains a global priority, hosting 4 million zero-dose children—almost 30% of the global burden—primarily in Nigeria and the Democratic Republic of Congo. These figures highlight both achievements and the need for continued targeted outreach and resilient supply chains.


Adolescent girls face high SRHR and HIV risks, representing 82% of new infections among adolescents, with an incidence rate up to seven times higher than the general population across the region. Early pregnancy increases risks of stillbirths, prematurity, and maternal deaths. Structural factors affecting girls include early marriage, low school completion, and gender-based violence and consequently reduce their access to care. The region has 368,000 children living with HIV, of which only 37% received ART, and mother-to-child transmission rate is 21%, underscoring the need for adolescent-inclusive services and earlier diagnosis and treatment.


Nutrition indicators show steady, and gradual, improvement: stunting prevalence declined from 33.6 to 32.5% between 2016 and 2024, and rates of wasting and severe wasting have decreased.  However, rapid population growth has led to an increase in the absolute number of stunted children, while seasonal, climate-related, and crisis-driven spikes continue to persist, particularly in the Sahel. Exclusive breastfeeding rates remain at 38%, and efforts to improve child diet diversity and reduce child food poverty are ongoing. Progress in vitamin A supplementation and the expansion of nutrition-sensitive social protection programmes are promising steps toward reducing malnutrition and supporting healthy growth.


Education access has expanded, with more children attending school compared to previous years; however, in 2023, 26.5% of primary and lower-secondary age children were still out of school, and early childhood education attendance only reached 23.3%. Foundational learning outcomes remain a key concern, as about 80% of ten-year-olds cannot read at grade level. School completion rates have improved modestly, with the Gross Intake Ratio at lower secondary education rising to 46% from 42% in 2016. However, gender disparities persist, with girls facing greater barriers to retention and transition to secondary education, especially in conflict-affected zones. Despite the closure of over 14,000 schools due to armed conflict by June 2025, UNICEF is supporting countries to ensure continuity of learning through remote platforms, catch-up programmes, and community-based education. The African Union it it’s post CEC declaration recommended countries to allocate 4 to 7 percent (%) of GDP to finance education depending on the size of the national economy, as well as a corresponding amount of 15 to 25 percent of the annual national budget to education, with increased investments in teacher training and in learning infrastructure and equipment.


Violence against children remains widespread in WCAR with nearly 88% of children who experience violent discipline at home, and 27% of young women reporting sexual violence before the age of 18. Child marriage rates have decreased but remain high, with one in three young women married before the age of 18. WCA continues to be among the most affected regions globally, with eight situations of concern and consistently high levels of verified child rights violations, including recruitment and use, abductions, and attacks on schools and hospitals. At the same time, legal reforms are steadily advancing, with more countries prohibiting corporal punishment in all settings. Regional efforts to strengthen child protection systems, promote positive parenting, and expand access to survivor support services are helping to create safer environments for children.      


Birth registration improved from 45% in 2015 to 57% in 2024 among children under five years of age. While nearly 50 million of children still lack legal proof of identity, ongoing initiatives are addressing the removal of cost barriers and strengthening the interoperability between health and civil registration systems. Digital registration platforms and integration with routine health services offer promising opportunities to accelerate progress.


Access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene remains a major challenge. Although 69% of people now use basic water services, 196 million, including 96 million children, still lack access, especially in rural areas. Only 36% have access to basic sanitation, and nearly 20% of the population still practices open defecation—the highest rate in the world. Just 30% of people have access to handwashing facilities with soap, leaving millions of children at risk of communicable diseases.


Extreme child poverty has declined globally by about 20% over the past decade, but progress in Sub-Saharan Africa remains slow. In 2024, an estimated 412 million children lived on less than $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), down from 507 million in 2014. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for three-quarters of these children, with over 312 million affected and the regional extreme child poverty rate holding steady at approximately 52% since 2014. This concentration of poverty is particularly acute in WCA. While social protection systems are being strengthened and reforms are underway to expand coverage and institutional capacities, financing and political prioritization remain challenges, and coverage has not increased sufficiently at a par with the gravity of the situation. Evidence continues to show that well-managed cash transfer programs that are part of larger social protection systems enhance resilience, human capital investment, and social inclusion.


Demographic Trends - Rapid demographic growth coupled with accelerated and unplanned urbanization poses significant risks for children, as population increases outpace the expansion of essential services. By 2063, WCAR will be home to nearly 500 million children under 18—20% of the world’s children. Without faster and more equitable investment, already-strained systems risk being overwhelmed likely contributing to increased social and economic exclusion. Nonetheless, making substantial social investments in children is essential for turning demographic growth into a meaningful dividend. 


Economic and Development Assistance Trends - WCA continues to face a tight macroeconomic and fiscal environment marked by high debt, elevated interest rates, rising inflation, and limited fiscal space. Debt service absorbs up to 55% of public budgets, while public revenues remain below 20% of GDP in most countries. Despite constraints, economic growth (primarily driven by the services and agriculture sectors) is projected at 4.4% in 2025, above the global average. This is a significant opportunity for increased domestic revenue. The largest contributor to growth in the region is the services sector, now outpacing industry and agriculture in GDP share, according to regional economic data from the African Development Bank, UNCTAD and the World Bank. Agriculture remains a key backbone of the economy providing employment and sustaining livelihoods, especially in rural areas. Industry, in particular manufacturing and extractive activities, plays a significant secondary role and is growing as economies diversify beyond primary production, creating opportunities to broaden the domestic revenue base alongside economic growth. 


Considering the high levels of inequality in Africa, it is important to have additional and predictable resources to support equity-focused social spending and human capital development. Domestic finance deserves strong priority in a context in which external (concessional) finance and especially Overseas Development Assistance are under pressure. While per capita ODA spending until recently was close to or higher than per capita government spending in several countries in the region, the former has seen drastic cuts in 2025. These are difficult for governments to absorb.


Humanitarian Trends- Humanitarian needs remain significant due to conflicts, climate-related disasters, and public health emergencies. A total of 133 crises have been reported and addressed in the region. Around 17 million people, including 9.4 million children, have been displaced, and 42 million children require humanitarian assistance. The Sahel and Lake Chad Basin remain epicenters of instability, where fragility, conflict, and climate risks converge to exacerbate displacement, food insecurity, and weakened national systems that struggle to provide basic social services. Addressing these challenges requires integrated strategies that combine risk prevention with responsive action, strengthen basic services, and support social cohesion, especially in high-risk, underserved areas. 


Environmental Trends - WCA is among the world’s most climate-vulnerable regions, with 17 of the 30 highest-risk countries (UNICEF CCRI). UNICEF estimates that 95 million children in the region are highly exposed to these growing risks, especially the most vulnerable children including girls, those living with disabilities, and those living in poor households. 


Since 2022, extreme floods have impacted 18 of 24 countries and over 20.3 million people. In 2025 alone, 2 million people were affected across 12 countries, with approximately 387,000 displaced, mainly from the DRC, Nigeria, and Republic of Congo. Floods damaged more than 138,000 homes, 182 schools, and 95 health facilities, and destroyed over 60,000 hectares of farmland and 1,600 livestock. Ongoing risks like floods and droughts emphasize the need for greater resilience. The Sahel’s temperature climbs 1.5 times faster than average, with recent droughts affecting over 20 million people since 2016. In the Congo Basin, climate-driven health costs are projected to increase from USD 92 million in 2010 to USD 260 million by 2050, underscoring the pressing need for proactive interventions.


Governance and Security Trends - Political and security dynamics across West and Central Africa continued to evolve, shaping the operating environment for children and families. Several countries experienced political transitions, with electoral processes influencing governance and social cohesion. In a few contexts, including Benin and Guinea Bissau, isolated disruptions highlighted the importance of sustained institutional strengthening. In the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and parts of the Sahel, security challenges and localized tensions persisted. Emerging regional cooperation arrangements, such as the Alliance of Sahel States, contributed to shifts in cross border coordination. Across the region, the combined impacts of insecurity, climate-related shocks, and economic pressures continued to heighten vulnerabilities.


Addressing these challenges requires adaptive strategies, stronger systems, and resource mobilization to protect children’s rights and accelerate progress toward sustainable development. Furthermore, and in order to address the deep-seated structural and historical causes driving children's vulnerabilities, it will be necessary to advocate for high level political engagement and leadership to position children's issues as national priorities.

During the final year of the Regional Office Management Plan (ROMP) 2022-2025, WCARO supported the Regional Management Team (RMT) to accelerate and consolidate Key Results for Children (KRC) as the region’s strategic contribution to the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and to the child-focused SDGs and the African Union Agenda 2063.


During this period, progress made contributed to impact-level results, though acceleration is required to meet the SDGs by 2030:  


DTP3 vaccine coverage (KRC 1) increased to 72% in 2024 up from 69% in 2021, though it remains below the global average of 85%. 
Stunting prevalence (KRC2) has stagnated at around 32.5%. However, rapid population growth has led to an increase in the absolute number of affected children—from 29.8 million in 2021 to 31.6 million in 2024. In contrast, Vitamin A supplementation coverage improved significantly, rising from 50% to 80% and reaching approximately 83 million children each year, although substantial disparities remain across countries.
Education access improved (KRC 3) - primary out-of-school rates fell from 27.9% to 23.1%, though lower secondary rates remained at 33.9%. A total of 39.2 million children of primary and lower secondary age are still out of school. Learning outcomes need attention (KRC 4), as only 45% achieved minimum proficiency in reading and math (2023).
Child marriage rates declined (KRC 6), meeting targets, while birth registration increased to 57% in 2024 (KRC 7). Sexual violence prevalence:27% of young women reporting experiences before age 18 (KRC 5).
Open defecation dropped from 21.8% to 20% (KRC 8), but high rates persist in some countries especially in the urban areas.


Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives (KRCs 1 and 2)     


Health - WCARO enhanced its support for governments as both a delivery partner and regional health systems leader, promoting progress toward SDG3 and stronger system resilience. Regional leadership was sustained through high-level coordination and partnerships with WHO AFRO, Africa CDC, Gavi, and cross-border ministerial platforms. With thanks to GAVI and other partners, DTP3 coverage increased from 69% (2021) to 72% (2024), with twelve countries reaching =80% and six exceeding 90%. The Big Catch-Up initiative reached 3.2 million zero-dose and 4 million under-vaccinated children. Polio remained a priority, with 58 outbreak responses in 12 countries and a 2.3-fold decline in paralytic cases from vaccine-derived poliovirus, maintaining wild poliovirus-free status. Malaria and HPV vaccines coverage scaled in 15 countries, with nine integrating adolescent-friendly HPV Plus services, complemented by large measles/measles-rubella campaigns reaching millions.


Social and Behavior Change (SBC) interventions were institutionalized in 12 countries, with Human-Centered Design and BeSD (Social and Behavioral drivers) approaches applied in nine and advanced gender integration in six to target zero-dose and under-vaccinated children. Immunization systems improved through electronic registries, AI-driven microplanning, and stronger partnerships for funding, outbreak response, and service integration.


WCARO supported 24 countries to strengthen Primary Health Care as the platform for MNCAH and HIV services, with major advances in community health institutionalization, gender-responsive workforce development, and sustainable financing. Countries developed PHC financing plans and investment cases, building on momentum from the Primary Health Care (PHC) Financing Forum for West and Central Africa in Abidjan and the UNICEF-Africa CDC Joint Action Plan. Technical support helped operationalize MNCAH priorities in national development strategies. An innovative regional HIV Data Mentorship Programme was implemented in four countries which has enabled improved national data analysis capacity in DRC, Tchad, Burkina Faso, and Central African Republic, although significant gaps persist with only 37% of HIV-exposed infants received early diagnosis. Partnerships, such as with Siemens Healthineers, and complemented by Set Aside funding, supported targeted system improvements and adolescent-centered HIV responses.


WCARO strengthened emergency preparedness across the region, supported 21 countries to update national plans and operationalization of 5 risk-analysis action plans for public health emergencies for Cameroon, Chad, DRC, Ghana and Nigeria. UNICEF provided technical leadership during mpox, cholera, and Ebola outbreaks, including extensive support in DRC. Regional coordination and capacity were reinforced through staff training across 24 country offices, enhanced partnerships, and strong resource mobilization, resulting in 12 Pandemic Fund proposals and 2 successful regional submissions with Africa CDC and African Union Inter-African Bureau for Animal Resources (AU-IBAR). The Greater Virunga Landscape initiative with WHO and FAO marked a major step in cross-border, One Health preparedness.


 


Nutrition: WCARO advanced a transformative regional nutrition agenda that is contributing to reshaped markets and strengthened systems, and has positioned UNICEF as a leader in innovative, multisectoral approaches. Early mobilization of catalytic financing through the Child Nutrition Fund and the emerging First Foods Africa (FFA) initiative enabled multi-country investments in Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and Benin. These investments accelerated the shift toward locally produced fortified and complementary foods, supported the harmonization of standards across ECOWAS, and stimulated private-sector engagement. A major milestone in this trajectory was the successful high-level launch of First Foods Africa in September 2025 in Benin, co-hosted with the African Union and national authorities. This event galvanized regional political commitment, attracted strong interest from IFIs, and cemented FFA as a continental platform for expanding access to safe, affordable complementary foods. Throughout this period, UNICEF deepened its technical leadership in market-shaping through systematic assessments of production capacity, piloting containerized micro-factories, and generating actionable evidence to guide future scale-up. 


Maternal and child nutrition agendas also advanced significantly. MMS pilots provided evidence to inform national and regional policy dialogue, while major reforms were supported in child wasting management, including alignment with WHO 2023 guidance, improved MUAC-based identification of mothers with infants under six months, and groundwork to integrate support for at-risk infants into routine systems. 


In 2025, UNICEF strengthened its partnership with the World Bank on Nutrition and Early Childhood Development (ECD). This collaboration led to the establishment of a Regional Advisory Group on Nutrition and Early Childhood Development in late 2025. Building on this momentum, a high-level regional conference on Nutrition and ECD is planned for mid-2026 to further advance strategic alignment, policy dialogue, and investment in the region.


Emergency nutrition capacities were strengthened through enhanced HAC/HNO quality assurance, improved regional supply chain oversight, and closer collaboration with key donors such as ECHO and more specifically USAID. At the systems level, UNICEF embedded nutrition and early childhood development, while initiatives such as Play to Grow elevated child-centered approaches and attracted interest from global financing institutions. Together, these achievements reflect growing national ownership, harmonized regional policies, and more resilient nutrition systems capable of sustaining impact at scale.


Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns (KRCs 3 and 4) 


WCARO accelerated its multi-year commitment to expanding access to quality education for every child, including the most marginalized. Over USD 183 million from the Global Partnership for Education and Education Cannot Wait initiative supported these efforts in 16 WCAR countries.  Given the persistent high number of out-of-school children in the region (estimated at 38 million, there was intensified advocacy and continuation of existing programmes to address exclusion and inequity. 


Digital learning initiatives, including the Learning Passport (now reaching 2.5 million users) and the Airtel partnership (which in year 4 achieved its five-year goal of connecting 1,400 schools to the internet, with more than 2,000 schools now online), have scaled up digital access across several countries each year, reaching learners in both primary and lower secondary education. Digital school-in-a-box pilots were launched in Gabon, Sierra Leone, and Nigeria, while the PATHWAYS digital learning competency framework further strengthened regional evidence generation and innovation development. The “zero rate” Learning Passport eliminated digital learning cost barriers in six Airtel countries, exemplifying UNICEF’s commitment to equity and inclusion. 


WCARO made progress in learning outcomes by scaling up foundational learning, teacher reform, and system strengthening, supported by a regional education data strategy and foundational learning exchanges among the African countries. Addressing teacher development gaps and improving the quality and coverage of early childhood remained priorities to increase learning outcomes. The “Teacher for All” study identified effective strategies for improved teacher allocation in 10 countries, and, in 2023, 65% of countries had operational early childhood education systems. Building on the African Union’s Year of Education and the adoption of the Nouakchott Declaration, the region saw renewed political will for compulsory, quality education, and for the eradication of learning poverty by 2035. The publication of the Continental SDG4 Report with African Union and UNESCO, and the AU Decade of Accelerated Action for Education Transformation, Youth Skills Development, and Innovation in Africa institutionalized these priorities, calling for accelerated foundational learning, teacher reform, and digital innovation, and further contributed to cementing  UNICEF’s leadership role in the education sector in Africa was through support to educate thought leaders, young researchers and advocates Leading Minds Conference held in November 2025 in Nairobi.


Goal Area 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation (KRCs 5, 6 and 7) 


WCARO strengthened government leadership, built innovative partnerships, and delivered tangible child protection results by advancing strategies developed since 2022. These actions turned high-level commitments into practical system changes.


Following the 1st Global Ministerial Meeting on Ending Violence Against Children held in Bogotá in November 2024, nineteen governments acted on pledges to end violence, supported by technical exchanges and peer learning through the Arise Africa meeting in November 2025. UNICEF advanced the social service workforce agenda continent-wide, supporting the International Federation of Social Workers Africa Conference to establish a roadmap for workforce development. Four countries in WCAR sustained child protection services during crises using digital case management (CPIMS+), remote social work, and community-based MHPSS. Cameroon integrated a child protection helpline into CPIMS+, and Côte d’Ivoire launched an integrated child protection/GBV case management system, setting new standards for coordinated response. 


WCARO advanced efforts to end child marriage and FGM by developing pushback risk profiles for eight countries and guidance to help partners sustain reforms. Multi-country research with UNFPA and UNICEF Innocenti closed evidence gaps for programming in humanitarian settings, while the FGM Nexus toolkit was implemented in Mali, Mauritania, and Nigeria to accelerate integrated responses. The Human-Centered Design toolkit was adapted for participatory monitoring in Senegal, and new research in Ghana examines climate impact on child protection. WCARO laid the foundation to strengthen financial governance through partnership with the International Budget Partnership, supporting Open Budget Surveys in 16 countries and preparing for AI-assisted budget analysis to make child-protection spending more visible. 


WCARO accelerated progress toward universal birth registration and improved legal identity systems by focusing on interoperability, decentralization, and digitalization. Together with ESARO, a regional policy brief was developed to guide scale-up efforts. UNICEF conducted a regional assessment of CRVS digitalization, produced a systems mapping report specifically for WCAR, and supported the establishment of a technical working group on interoperability under the APAI-CRVS platform. UNICEF supported CRVS integration with other sectors in Liberia, simplification of business processes in Guinea-Bissau, Mali, and The Gambia, and expansion of digital solutions in Chad. 


Goal Area 4: Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment (KRC 8): 


WCARO rolled out climate-resilient WASH in 16 countries, completing Climate Rationales in nine and progressing in seven. Through partnerships with SIWI and IVL, the region advanced NDC/NAP processes and developed strong climate rationales using UNICEF guidance. These efforts strengthened systems, built capacity, and integrated WASH into national climate and development plans, prioritizing vulnerable communities. 


To scale investment and transform services, WCARO supported the scale up of innovative financing for sanitation in cooperation with the WASH Hub at the Office of Innovation. It also supported the mobilization of climate finance for WASH in the region, including to the GCF with the first UNICEF full proposal for CAR and the multi-country concept note CR ACCESS. These initiatives aimed to strengthen enabling environments, expand low carbon, climate resilient WASH, and ensure sustainable water resource management in 5 countries. Capacity was further bolstered via the initiative launched in partnership with the IHE & 2iE to strengthen the WASH educational offer for francophone countries and build a workforce across policymakers, utilities, regulators, local authorities, and service providers.


WCARO played a pivotal role in strategic advocacy initiatives, providing support for the Heads of State Initiative. Notably, Ghana signed and the new administration officially endorsed the Compact at the SMM Madrid. Progress continued in Nigeria with the advancement of the Clean Nigeria Campaign, while Liberia moved closer to finalizing its Compact. Additionally, Chad, Côte d’Ivoire, and Senegal initiated related processes. WCARO convened high level dialogue at PANAFCON 3 and supported AMCOW in crafting the Africa Water Vision & Policy (AWV&P) 2063, approved at AMCOW’s 14th General Assembly in Dakar and to be submitted to the AU in February 2026. UNICEF at global, regional and country level actively supported the organization of the AFRICASAN 7 Conference and provided strategic inputs to the final declaration. Additionally, UNICEF contributed to the development of a monitoring framework to track the implementation of the Africa Sanitation Policy Guidelines (ASPGs).


Goal Area 5: Every child and adolescent can access inclusive social protection and live free from poverty –WCARO continued to co-lead Phase Two (2025–2028) of the UNICEF-WFP Sahel Social Protection Joint Project, funded by German cooperation, continuing systems strengthening and cash transfers that have reached over 500,000 households in five countries (Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger) since 2020. The new phase includes a gender assessment and collaboration with STAAR to co-develop and pilot a conflict-sensitivity tool for social protection.


WCARO deepened partnerships with WFP and the World Bank on Adaptive Social Protection by launching joint research on social protection and social cohesion, publishing a coordination paper, and leading a joint donor mission to Chad showcasing adaptive cash transfer programmes. WCARO also continued to lead the WCA Regional Social Protection Platform, focusing on coverage, financing, and linkages between humanitarian and social protection assistance and coordination.


WCARO supported capacity building through TRANSFORM trainings in CAR, Chad, Niger, Nigeria, and Senegal. The sessions benefitted around 120 government officials. To strengthen advocacy in Africa, WCARO developed a Social Protection Advocacy Strategy Framework (with Hewlett Foundation support) addressing continent-wide challenges in SP financing and coverage, along with evidence summaries for the Transfer Project. WCARO support to advancing child-sensitive SP includes a Practitioner Note to support COs with region-specific guidance on Nutrition-Sensitive Social Protection and HCT. WCARO continued to support governments with SRSP (including HCT), supporting preparedness, new anticipatory action cash transfers for floods (Cameroon), and nutrition-sensitive cash transfers (Chad, DRC and Nigeria).


WCARO strengthened its role as a regional steward for child-responsive public finance, advancing institutionalization, innovation, and peer learning to improve budget outcomes for children. Senegal finalized its office-wide PF4C strategy, while Mali, Cameroon, and Togo initiated strategy development, further embedding PF4C within UNICEF’s policy engagement. In DRC, UNICEF delivered tailored PF4C training and provided technical support for budget briefs and analysis in 10 countries, strengthening evidence-based dialogue with ministries of finance on efficiency and adequacy of allocations, budget execution, and equity of social sector spending. WCARO also developed a minimum viable AI-powered budget analyst to automate data extraction and accelerate budget analysis.


A flagship regional achievement was the launching of the Community of Practice for Francophone Budget Directors (COP-Budget), hosted by Benin with UNICEF support, convening officials from 10 countries for peer learning on child-sensitive budgeting and PFM reforms. WCARO partnered with the International Budget Partnership to initiate the 2025 Open Budget Survey across 27 countries, with focused support to Mauritania and Chad, and supported Day of the African Child activities on “Budgeting and Planning for Children”, including with the AfDB.


2.2 Cross-cutting area results     


Gender: The RO significantly advanced gender integration across all country programmes through targeted technical support, alignment with financing mechanisms, and direct influence on GAVI, GPEI, and ECOWAS gender mainstreaming guidance. It designed and tested scalable innovations to tackle gender barriers in health, including the Women’s Immunization Journey in 2 countries. The RO supported country offices in mobilizing USD 3.5 million for gender-transformative programming, with implementation on track and over 100 practitioners trained. The RO provided strategic leadership shaping the UGEAP 2025–2029, supported COs’ structural adaptations under the FFI, and led the Beijing+30 review, catalyzing a new Regional Girls Agenda and solutions for adolescent girls.


Adolescents and young people: WCARO strengthened adolescent and youth programming across the region, providing technical leadership to all 24 Country Offices across programme design, implementation, and new programme cycles. WCARO led national consultations in every country to strengthen adolescent girls’ influence on policies, programs, and advocacy, and delivered targeted support on youth in humanitarian settings and climate action. A flagship achievement was the WCA Girls’ Summit in Dakar in October 2025. The girl-led Summit convened all countries and launched the Regional Girls’ Agenda and Dakar Declaration, positioning adolescent girls’ rights as a regional priority and accelerating their integration into national and regional strategies. In total, 124 young people (aged 24 and under) participated in the summit, including 22 boys and 102 girls. Of these, 72, comprising 11 boys and 61 girls—were younger than 18, making up about 65% of attendees.


Child rights-based approach to programming: Child rights governance and monitoring remain a cornerstone of UNICEF’s work in West and Central Africa. Building on the work from previous years, 2025 saw the region consolidate institutional mechanisms such as the Regional Child Rights Steering Committee, ensuring strategic oversight and rapid guidance on sensitive issues. Efforts to mainstream child rights across UNCTs advanced through regional office support in terms of advocacy and capacity-building, including training nearly 400 staff and partners through the RRP and other training sessions specific on child rights. WCARO supported country offices to strengthened national systems for child rights governance, legislative reform, and child rights monitoring, while fostering academic partnerships. These efforts culminated in the Yaoundé Declaration on Academia for Child Rights, creating a strong Francophone anchor for academic engagement, and the partnership with the Francophone university network for SBC. These initiatives position WCAR as a leader in embedding child rights in governance frameworks and institutional practice, reaffirming its commitment amid global pushback.


Climate change, energy and environment: WCARO played a catalytic role in supporting governments across the region to strengthen child-responsive climate policies, including through technical assistance for the revision and submission of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0). In 2025, six countries submitted enhanced NDCs that better incorporated children’s rights and social sector priorities. At the same time, UNICEF mobilized climate finance, developing its first Green Climate Fund proposals: USD 70 million for the Central African Republic to improve climate resilience in WASH, and USD 28 million for Senegal to support climate-resilient health systems. 


Beyond the GCF, WCARO supported 14 Country Offices to access the African Development Bank's Climate Action Window, leading to approved investments in 4 countries. UNICEF’s global and regional advocacy has also advanced political commitment for child-centered climate action, with five additional countries endorsing the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action at COP30 in Belém. Together, these efforts are embedding climate adaptation and resilience within national policies, sectoral strategies, and community-level action, while prioritizing the protection of the 95 million children in WCAR most exposed to climate risks, particularly girls, children with disabilities, and indigenous, displaced, and migrant children.


Partnerships: Since 2022, Africa has faced challenges due to declining official development assistance. WCAR raised USD 3.1 billion—an 8% decrease from the previous cycle—with one-third allocated to emergencies. Germany was the largest ORR donor, while the United States led ORE contributions; other key donors included the European Commission, GAVI, World Bank, UK, CERF, GPE, ECW, Sweden, and Japan.


WCARO steered major multi-year partnerships, including the BMZ-funded Sahel Resilience Partnership (EUR 130.5 million), KfW-WFP social protection across five Sahelian countries (EUR 204 million), the Muskoka Fund (USD 7.8 million), and an ECHO nutrition grant (EUR 18.7 million). Funding diversification accelerated through pandemic funds, a USD 44 million Islamic Development Bank engagement in Chad, AfDB proposals, and new prospects with China, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia. Regional collaboration deepened, with new agreements with ECCAS and ECOWAS, and renewed ties with AfDB and BOAD (West African Development Bank).


WCARO strengthened partnerships with philanthropy, foundations, and National Committees, commissioning a private sector landscape scan across 21 countries and an assessment of extractive industries’ impact on child rights in eight. National Committee support grew, led by the US NatCom (USD 73 million) and German NatCom’s unearmarked funding for the first food initiative. Progress was made with Gates, Mastercard, and CIFF foundations. WCARO launched three NextGen champions (Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria, Gabon), an Individual Giving platform with 2,400+ donors, and deepened corporate engagement through Business for Results, Airtel, and prospects with HIS, MTN, Africa Reinsurance, EXIM Bank, Orange, and innovative WASH and Cocoa PPPs.


Disability inclusion: WCARO supported disability inclusion regionally through the implementation of the global DIPAS (Disability Inclusion Plan of Action and Strategy), coordinating with country offices and building capacity. Following the Global Disability Summit, 31 new commitments were made by 4 national governments: Ghana (1), Mauritania (3), Nigeria (26), Cabe Verde (1).    Commitments included increasing budgets and pledging inclusion for children with disabilities. Disability-inclusive programs expanded in Ghana, Senegal, and Cameroon, with greater collaboration with organizations of persons with disabilities across several countries. The Regional Girls Summit was made more accessible, and the International Day of Persons with Disabilities featured a webinar led by adolescent girls with disabilities. In WCAR, UNICEF’s spending on disability inclusion rose from 2.42% in 2023 to 3.89% in 2025. In Cameroon, 94.6% of staff (159 colleagues) completed the UNDIS online training on disability inclusion, making it the first Country Office in the region to achieve this.


PSEA: WCARO advanced PSEA by holding three regional Community of Practice meetings, embedding PSEA in strategic frameworks, and enabling Country Offices to submit reports directly to OIAI. WCARO promoted the Joint UN-Government Cooperation Framework on PSEA, leading to greater government engagement. As chair of the Inter-Agency PSEA Working Group, WCARO helped develop inter-agency SOPs in four countries, improving regional coordination and response to SEA.


2.3 KRC Accelerators 


Social and behaviour change: SBC programming in WCA underwent a dynamic transformation between 2022 and 2025, shifting from traditional communication to innovative, system-wide approaches. By developing 103 SBC tools, certifying 31 experts, and equipping 19 countries with comprehensive SBC packages, WCARO embedded SBC in national policies, curricula, and emergency responses. WCARO empowered local actors to enhance national systems and capacities for change by providing 39 technical trainings and resources, including pocket guides on topics such as rapid prototyping, positive deviance, human-centered design, and applied behavioral science, as well as the “Culture Collection for Change.” As a result, 15 countries advanced strategic SBC programming, strengthening community systems and resilience, institutionalizing SBC through strategic partnerships with academic institutions and supporting key results for children in both development and humanitarian settings.


Monitoring, data, research & knowledge management:   The Regional Office prioritized nationally-owned SITAN processes that influenced government planning, notably in Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria; conducted innovative child-centric data initiatives such as MICS7 (14 countries) and small area estimates (2 countries); undertook a joint UNICEF-WB mission on minimum data package in Burkina Faso;  enhanced upstream influence through the launch of the UNICEF-AfDB-UNECA-AU State of the African Child report; and  contributed to continental child and gender statistics fora and platforms, including with the AfDB. Knowledge management technical assistance fostered cross-country learning, while information management increasingly supported H-D-P nexus implementation. WCARO also supported alignment with UNICEF's Africa Strategy by supporting country programme planning and aligning its own monitoring, data, and research activities.


Evaluation: WCARO played a strategic role in promoting evidence-based decision-making and regional positioning resulting from several strategic evaluative undertakings. Key achievements include conducting an Evaluability Assessment of the Regional Office Management Plan (ROMP 2022–2025), which informed the new ROMP 2026–2029. Additionally, the regional and country offices carried out over 20 thematic evaluations including six Country Programme evaluations. National evaluation capacity was strengthened through child rights evaluation training with the African Evaluation Association (AfrEA), regional IMPrESS and ExCEL trainings, targeted support to national partners, and AI-focused initiatives with Côte d’Ivoire’s Parliament. Strategic partnerships expanded via gLOCAL Evaluation Week, joint events with AfDB, and the “Best Evaluation Synthesis for Children” competition, while engagement in FIFE (Le Forum International Francophone de l’Evaluation) and National Evaluation Days increased visibility.   


Humanitarian preparedness and response - Emergency efforts in WCA were enhanced through capacity-building, technical support, and operational interventions. Onsite and online training covered seven countries, whilst simulation exercises took place in DRC, Nigeria, and other countries. WCARO secured global preparedness funding via Horizon Scan, addressing risks in northwest Nigeria and threats of flooding and refugee influxes in CAR. CAR became a global pilot for the EPP 3.0 platform ahead of its 2026 rollout. Despite increased insecurity in the Central Sahel, WCARO supported Niger, Burkina Faso, and Mali to improve humanitarian access and localization, enabling continued aid to remote areas by strengthening local systems and partnerships. In response to the escalating armed conflict in eastern DRC, WCAR supported the Country Office in scaling up its emergency response through surge deployments, ten field missions and targeted technical assistance. Strategic guidance on engagement with de facto authorities and the expansion of partnerships with local actors helped maintain continuity of services in high-risk areas. These efforts enabled UNICEF to maintain a principled presence, deliver critical assistance to thousands of children and families and reinforce localization and resilience as key components of the Level 3 emergency response.


Strategic planning contributed to the 2025 Humanitarian Action for Children documents. Information management improved regionally with standardized protocols and better data visualization. WCARO aided Mali in digitalizing humanitarian access strategies and helped Mauritania strengthen needs assessments and Sphere standards application.


T4D and innovation: WCARO accelerated results for children through technology interventions for impactful results in the region. The Airtel School Connectivity initiative expanded digital education to 2,166 schools and 1.5 million learners in six countries, with over 30 learning platforms zero-rated to extend Learning Passport to over 2 million users. Data innovation enabled real-time Humanitarian Access Monitoring in Mali (358 villages and 279 community organizations) and supported pilots in Cameroon and Nigeria. Advancing the Reach the Unreached (RtU) initiative under the UNICEF-Africa CDC Joint Action Plan 2026–2029, Guinea, Mali, Chad, Cameroon and Côte d'Ivoire have benefited from this pilot programme to detect zero-dose children, in partnership with the University of Southampton and MIT, MapAction and CartONG. As a result, 73,151 zero-dose and 100,319 under-immunized children have been supported in Cameroon alone. A new phase of the project is currently being developed with AfricaCDC Over 120 staff were trained on emerging technologies and innovation, including through TeamOne Advisory and bootcamps. A multi-country survey on CRVS digitalization mapping finalized that stressed the importance of strengthening governance, interoperable identities, policy, and adaptation.


2.4 Influencing regional/global discourse and policy  


Communication and advocacy: In 2025, the campaign around adolescent girls’ rights led to the first ever West and Central Africa Girls’ Summit, a major influencing milestone that convened about 124adolescent girls and boys, governments, civil society, and partners to accelerate the adolescent girl’s agenda across the region. The campaign achieved continent-wide visibility and momentum, reaching over 20 million people. Partnership with Brut Afrique generated 7.9 million views and 49,000 engagements, amplifying messages among youth audiences. The Regional Office presented The Girl I Am, The Change I Lead, an exhibit of 24 portraits and audio stories in which girls speak in their own voices about their rights, aspirations, and leadership. Showcased at the Girls’ Summit, the RMT meeting, and high-level stakeholder events, and featured on UNICEF’s global social media, the exhibit is now available to National Committees and UNICEF and partners’ offices for display.


Through One Basin, One Goal and the ongoing #KickOutPolio AFCON campaign, UNICEF and partners are elevating polio eradication as a shared regional priority, reinforcing that virus transmission cannot be stopped without synchronized, cross-border vaccination. By mobilizing political leaders, regional institutions, media and the football community, these platforms are driving alignment of campaign calendars, coordinated planning and sustained political commitment, positioning synchronized vaccination as a cornerstone of regional health security.


UN Reform: WCARO remained fully engaged at the strategic level with the Regional Collaborative Platform (RCP), contributing to efforts to sustain Africa’s economic momentum while addressing SDG setbacks, with only 35% of targets on track. At the technical level, the RO continued to work with OIBCs, in particular, to coordinate national data system strengthening efforts. The RO also engaged with ESARO and MENARO, as well as with other UN agencies, in the coordination and development of inputs for the Africa Regional Forum on Sustainable Development that took place in Uganda. Through the Integrated Policy and Practitioners Network (IPPN), co-led by UNDP, UNICEF and FAO, the RO supported the Sahel Flagship Programs in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger addressing food systems and climate action, energy transition, education transformation, conflict prevention and governance on integrated SDG acceleration, including investment case development, innovative financing strategies, alignment with IFIs, and an integrated Theory of Change. The RO also actively contributed to the ongoing UN80 initiative discussions, to ensure coherent country- and regional-level reset and UNCT re-configuration.


2.5 Enablers


During the reporting period, enablers made significant progress across programme areas, contributing to key results for children (KRCs). Leveraged digital innovations and strengthened governance, systems, and processes, which helped mitigate risks, optimize resources, improve partnerships, and enhance supply chain and human resource management. Critical roles were filled, capacity-building programmes implemented, and fund utilization improved through strict budget monitoring. Compliance, financial controls, reporting, business continuity, and change management were also reinforced. Results included approved staffing structures, clearer roles and accountability, stronger evidence-based decision-making, increased delivery capacity, and reduced programmatic and operational risk exposure.


WCARO Supply focused on strengthening localization, innovative financing, and partnerships to enhance supply chain resilience and emergency preparedness. The Sahel Corridor Assessment and Custom Clearance process mapping (ADEPT) across five countries, have optimized logistics operations in the region, reduced delays, and decreased costs across multiple countries. A regional workshop involving 12 countries aligned priorities on integration, digitalization, and sustainable financing. Local supplier mapping scaled up local sourcing and procurement while strong data management supported the deployment of 1.38 billion vaccine doses and cold chain equipment. Additionally, emergency preparedness has advanced with the prepositioning of buffer stock near high-risk zones, effectively reducing lead times and costs for essential supplies.


Throughout 2025, WCARO strengthened risk-informed decision-making to ensure safe and efficient delivery of results. Key achievements included advancing ERM 2.0 across Country Offices, supporting seven offices in adopting the integrated risk management model, and fully rolling out core eTools modules to strengthen partnership oversight. Fraud-risk management was reinforced through regional webinars, a dedicated session on the new Fraud Risk Policy, and expanded staff awareness on ineligible expenditures. Closer Regional Office collaboration with COs improved the quality of audit preparation and responses, with support provided during 10 internal audits and peer review processes. These efforts improved accountability, internal control and operational continuity, enabling faster, safer delivery of essential services and ensuring more resources reached children in some of the region’s most complex environments.


WCARO advanced resource optimization and strengthened governance through the Regional PBR process and alignment with FFI. Affordability analysis across all offices led to a projected 20% reduction in OR funding needs, a 19% decrease in staffing, closure of seven Zone Offices and efficiencies gained through multi-country positions. Country office staffing structures were streamlined, and the Senegal Common Services arrangement was approved to cut costs. Governance was reinforced with Annual Management Plans, 100% submission of Business Continuity Plans, and tighter financial risk controls. NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Health 


Challenge: Immunization and health programs faced fragmented funding streams and disease-specific mechanisms, which slowed progress toward integrated planning and delivery. Gender integration and Social and Behavioral Change (SBC) approaches were not fully institutionalized due to limited capacity and lack of structured planning. In addition, weak coordination between programs and inadequate tools for real-time data collection and monitoring, especially for Big Catch-Up implementation, created inefficiencies and delayed achievement of immunization targets.


Lesson Learned: Effective system strengthening required harmonized funding and integrated planning across programs. Institutionalizing gender and SBC approaches, combined with investment in digital tools for real-time monitoring and improved coordination, was essential to enhance efficiency, equity, and timely delivery of immunization and health services.


Nutrition


Challenge: Impact was constrained by weak regulatory frameworks, unpredictable financing, fragmented accountability, and limited national ownership. Multisectoral plans lacked operationalization and aligned funding, while donor engagement—particularly for FFA—was undermined by insufficient evidence and unclear positioning.


Lesson Learned: Between 2022 and 2025, experience showed that scalable nutrition impact requires early documentation of innovations, strong regulatory frameworks, predictable financing, and long-term partnerships. Unified accountability systems, national ownership, and transparent supply chains proved critical. Multisectoral ambitions demanded deliberate operationalization and aligned financing, while sustained donor engagement, especially around FFA, depended on strong evidence and clear strategic positioning.


Child Protection


Challenge: Child protection systems in WCA face persistent vulnerability to conflict, climate risks, and health emergencies. Fragmented approaches, limited integration across sectors, the lack of enough personnel duly qualified, the lack of national budget allocated and the need for continuous adaptation to emerging risks—such as digitalization, migration, and evolving harmful practices—make it difficult to ensure every child is protected and recognized.


Lesson Learned: Strengthening child protection required a holistic, resilient, and adaptive systems approach. Continuous investment in amplifying the ratio of the workforce and strengthening it, digital innovation, and multisectoral collaboration—anchored by strong government leadership and regional partnerships—enabled countries to prevent and respond to violence, exploitation and abuse in all contexts (development, humanitarian and peace), ensuring sustainable and inclusive protection for all children.


Education


Challenge: One-off technical support does not lead to lasting impact, and multisectoral initiatives require complex coordination. In addition, funding reductions and limited opportunities for peer learning hinder scale-up and delivery.


Lesson Learned: Ongoing technical support and sustained capacity development were crucial for achieving lasting results. By using UNICEF’s influence to create integrated programs across different sectors, significant changes were realized. Adaptable planning, connecting humanitarian and development nexus efforts, and South–South cooperation through organized country exchanges all helped share successful strategies.


WASH 


Challenge: Achieving universal access to basic WASH services remains difficult.  The expansion of WASH services is not keeping pace with demographic growth; persistent challenges remain related to the sustainability and affordability of WASH services. The dramatic impact of climate change on water resources, and a weak enabling environment including gaps in policy, governance, and financing.


Lesson Learned: A systemic transformation was needed to sustain and accelerate progress. Strengthening the enabling environment, prioritizing climate adaptation and innovation and scalable financing approaches, and embedding equity into all interventions proved essential. Building resilient systems that deliver safe, climate-resilient, and sustainable WASH services for children in both communities and institutions was key to overcoming these challenges and ensuring lasting, equitable results.


Social Policy and Public Finance 


Challenge: High debt and limited fiscal space restrict equity-focused social spending, despite growing needs for children.


Lesson Learned: Advocacy for domestic revenue mobilization and innovative financing is essential to protect social budgets and sustain human capital investments.


Social Behavioural Change


Challenge: Achieving cohesive, impactful SBC programming remains difficult due to fragmented interventions   limited resources, weak coordination, and the complexities of operating in fragile, crisis-affected contexts.


Lesson Learned: Strategic integration of SBC into national policies and systems, combined with participatory, community-driven approaches from the outset, was crucial for sustainable behaviour change and effective results at scale. 


Gender and Adolescent Programming


Challenge: Embedding gender-transformative and adolescent-responsive approaches across all country programs remains complex, particularly during organizational transitions and in contexts with external pushback or persistent negative perceptions about gender equality and youth participation.


Lesson Learned: Sustaining momentum required integrating gender and adolescent priorities from the outset of program design, maintaining dedicated capacity, institutionalizing youth engagement mechanisms, and leveraging partnerships and political moments to ensure transformative, inclusive change for girls, women, and young people.


Planning, Monitoring, Data and Research:


Challenge: The increasing frequency and intensity of crises in the region demand a more integrated and flexible approach to planning and monitoring across the humanitarian–development–peace nexus.


Lesson Learned: Efforts to break the silos between humanitarian and development work, from planning to evaluation, is able to make UNICEF’s work more flexible and responsive to fast changing needs. Using new technologies, like real-time data platforms, mapping tools, and artificial intelligence in support to national system strengthening can help take this to a next level.  


Enablers: 


Challenge: Unexpected drop in humanitarian funding, which triggered significant budget and staffing reductions and placed considerable strain on operational continuity


Lesson Learned: Building stronger anticipatory capacities—through external risk monitoring, funding scenario planning, and agile resource management—is essential for operations to stay resilient and responsive in an increasingly unstable environment.


3.2 Future Outlook


In 2026, WCARO will build upon the achievements of 2025 to ensure smooth transition toward the new UNICEF, in alignment with the FFI objectives, UNICEF Strategic Plan 2026–2029, the Regional Office Management Plan (ROMP 2026–2029), and in support to the SDGs and the African Union Agenda 2063. With a renewed commitment to health and education as regional priorities, the RO will focus on fulfilling its new roles and responsibilities and work closely with COEs to deliver quality and timely assistance to all 24 countries, at all times. Additionally, in the context of UN80 and Humanitarian reset, RO will continue to protect and promote UNICEF mandate and ensure regional and country capacity for emergency preparedness and humanitarian response, promoting risk-informed and rights-based programming in all situations. Concurrently, WCARO will continue to strengthen the effectiveness of CO and RO governance mechanisms with the objectives of strengthened risks management, optimizing UNICEF assets and resources, supporting localization of UNIICEF interventions, etc. To transform challenges into opportunities for children, WCARO will focus on sustainable, high-impact interventions. In line with the strategies and accelerators, WCARO will continue to mobilize domestic and private sector resources, foster digital innovation, and empower adolescents as agents of change. WCARO will also reinforce national leadership on child rights, foster community solidarity, and private-public partnerships for sustaining child-focused investments. These initiatives will ensure UNICEF work remains relevant, transformative, and sustainable, delivering measurable outcome-level results for the most marginalized children across WCAR.
